- News item (June 22, 1996): Bob Woodward’s forthcoming book "The Choice" reports that First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton held imaginary conversations with figures such as Eleanor Roosevelt and Mahatma Gandhi as a therapeutic practice, encouraged by adviser Jean Houston (co-director of the Foundation for Mind Research). Woodward says Houston advised Clinton and aided with her book revisions; some White House staff were unaware of these sessions and worried about political comparisons (e.g., to Nancy Reagan). Clinton had previously written about her imaginary talks with Eleanor Roosevelt and acknowledged work with anthropologist Mary Catherine Bateson; her spokeswoman said Clinton’s interest in Houston was not secret.

Surgeons at Johns Hopkins have performed what they say is the world’s most extensive genital transplant: a 14‑hour operation transplanting a penis, scrotum (without the donor’s testicles) and part of the abdominal wall from a deceased donor onto a U.S. military veteran who lost his genitals in an IED blast in Afghanistan. The patient, who remains anonymous, is recovering well and is expected to regain urinary function before discharge and sexual sensation within months as nerves regenerate.

The team connected multiple arteries, veins and nerves and also infused the recipient with the donor’s bone marrow to reduce rejection risk; this strategy may allow him to take a single low‑dose immunosuppressant rather than the usual multi‑drug regimen. Johns Hopkins covered the cost of the procedure and is screening other veterans as potential candidates. The hospital says it will not use the procedure for gender‑affirming surgery.

The transplant is more extensive than prior penile transplants reported in South Africa and at Massachusetts General Hospital, which involved only the penis. Surgeons emphasized the procedure addresses severe physical and psychological harm caused by genital loss but warned of ongoing risks—chiefly rejection and lifelong immunosuppression—and unresolved questions about long‑term outcomes and who will pay for such complex reconstructions. Donor identity and cause of death were not released; the donor family expressed pride that their loved one could help.

A 12-year-old boy, Melquan Kwame Robinson of Augusta, Ga., died Monday evening after being electrocuted on a chain-link fence at Fleming Athletic Complex near the Bernie Ward Community Center. Richmond County deputies and witnesses say Melquan climbed the fence to retrieve a football during practice; a live wire reportedly was touching the fence, and he was electrocuted as he came back over. Deputies rendered aid at the scene and he was taken to the Children’s Hospital of Georgia, where he was pronounced dead at 9:56 p.m. His body will be autopsied at the GBI lab.

Three others were injured—two juveniles and one adult. Two boys who rushed to help Melquan were hospitalized; one (David Sette) was moved from ICU to a regular room but faces concerns about muscle breakdown. Conditions for the other injured friend were not available. Witnesses praised the injured boys’ bravery.

Melquan, a seventh-grader at Morgan Road Middle School and a member of the Trinity Elite Titans football team, was described by family friends and coaches as energetic, athletic and protective of his siblings. The family is grieving; a community vigil is scheduled for Thursday at 6 p.m. at the Bernie Ward Community Center. All football activities at Fleming Park were canceled for the week.

The coroner, sheriff’s office and city will each investigate the incident; the coroner will focus on the death while the city will probe how the fence became energized. Georgia Power said it will cooperate with authorities and that its preliminary review indicates it does not control or maintain the voltage that energized the fence. Mayor Hardie Davis and community leaders expressed condolences and called for support for the family.

Hawaii legalized same-sex marriage and immediately positioned itself as a potential wedding-tourism hotspot. The law took effect with midnight ceremonies and dozens of couples rushing to get licenses and marry—some at mass events hosted by resorts like the Sheraton Waikiki and by clergy who supported the change. Hawaii’s permit process, which allows same-day licensing and online pre-registration followed by verification at agents across the islands, makes it particularly convenient for visiting couples.

Local wedding businesses are already responding. New and existing planners (including firms specializing in same-sex weddings), hotels, photographers and caterers are marketing packages to LGBT travelers. Some hotels, such as the Sheraton Waikiki, even provide on-site license services and are launching ad campaigns in mainland LGBT media. A Honolulu chain offers LGBT-specific travel deals, and resorts held celebratory events for the first couples to marry.

Economists and advocates expect a measurable tourism boost: a University of Hawaii estimate projects about $217 million in additional tourism revenue over three years. Observers note Hawaii’s established wedding and tourism infrastructure—hotels experienced in honeymoon and wedding services, photographers, caterers and license agents across islands—gives it an advantage over other states. The state’s long role in the national same-sex marriage conversation (dating to the early 1990s) adds symbolic resonance to its newly expanded marriage equality.

On Thursday the Nasdaq Stock Market experienced a major technical failure that halted trading in all Nasdaq-listed stocks and options for about three hours. Nasdaq sent alerts citing problems with "quote submissions," and at Nasdaq’s request the New York Stock Exchange stopped trading in Nasdaq securities and canceled all related orders back to customers. The Nasdaq Composite had been up before the suspension. The outage, an unprecedented disruption for a U.S. exchange, caused widespread confusion and frustration as Nasdaq officials worked to diagnose the issue and communicated little to the public or trading firms during the halt. Trading was resumed late in the day once exchange officials determined it was safe to reopen with roughly 35 minutes remaining in the session.

This document promotes MOTUS ergonomic hand grips (D-grip and T-grip) for snow shovels, claiming they reduce arthritis, back pain and repetitive strain injuries (e.g., carpal tunnel, tendinitis), improve posture, reduce fatigue and blistering, and lower low-back injury risk.

Product and use
- MOTUS offers two grips that attach to shovel, pusher, scoop and rake handles: a D-grip mounted mid-shaft and a T- or straight-grip mounted at the top end. They fit a variety of shaft materials and diameters.
- The D-grip provides lifting leverage for the forward hand and allows a more neutral wrist/limb alignment; the T-grip gives pushing/pulling control to the rear hand and a greater range of motion.
- Grips are adjustable for different heights and handedness, and are sold at modest prices (about $20 each).

Biomechanical case-study (Dean Kriellaars, Ph.D., Univ. of Manitoba, May 1992)
- Method: pseudo-static biomechanical assessment (no EMG/dynamic analysis) comparing lifting with and without the straight (T) grip; Newtonian static equilibrium used to estimate trunk moments.
Key findings and implications:
- Wrist/forearm: The straight grip limits ulnar deviation to about 10° vs ~35° without it, keeping the wrist near neutral and reducing compression/tension on wrist tissues that can lead to injury. It places the forearm in pronation, changing which muscles are recruited during lifting (potentially allowing more use of trunk and lower-limb muscles).
- Shoulder: Using the straight grip increases shoulder abduction by ~5–10°, shifting load to larger shoulder muscles (deltoid) and possibly lowering risk of tendinitis of smaller rotator-cuff muscles (requires EMG to confirm).
- Trunk/back: Upper-limb kinematics with the hand-grip reduce trunk flexion by ~5° and let the lifted load be carried about 5 cm closer to the sagittal plane, together lowering moments on hip/lumbar axes and reducing required back/hip extensor effort by roughly 3–10% overall. The author argues this reduction is meaningful for prevention and rehabilitation of low-back injuries and cumulative trauma in repetitive tasks.
- Other benefits: Less skin shear and therefore fewer blisters; fits varied implements and conditions though temperature can affect tightness; constrains users to particular postures (which could be mitigated by changing grip position periodically).

Author’s summarized conclusions: The hand grips promote near-neutral wrist position, encourage use of larger trunk/lower-limb musculature, may lower shoulder tendinitis risk, help maintain a more upright trunk posture saving energy and reducing cumulative trauma, reduce overall load on the spine by about 10%, and reduce blister potential. These effects suggest benefits for preventing and rehabilitating low-back injuries and reducing repetitive strain.

Contextual commentary (added text)
- The brochure also contains promotional material (newsletter signup, discounts) and briefly embeds a separate, more general discussion of the hazards of snow shoveling (noting significant annual heart-failure deaths and historical shoveling research by Frederick W. Taylor) emphasizing that shoveling is risky and that ergonomic tools and proper technique matter.

Overall takeaway
MOTUS hand grips are presented with biomechanical rationale and a case-study assessment indicating measurable ergonomic benefits—improved wrist and shoulder alignment, reduced trunk bending and spinal moments, less blistering—which together can lower the risk of low-back injury and repetitive strain when shoveling or using similar implements.

Idina Menzel and Taye Diggs have mutually decided to separate after 10 years of marriage. Their representatives say the couple’s primary concern is their 4-year-old son, Walker, and they ask for privacy. The two, both 42, met while costarring in the original Broadway production of Rent in the mid‑1990s, married in 2003 and welcomed Walker in 2009. Both had publicly acknowledged working on their marriage in recent months; Diggs was promoting The Best Man Holiday and Menzel, a Tony winner now voicing a role in Frozen, had spoken about the effort it takes to maintain their relationship.

Scientists have dated mortar and other materials from the small limestone tomb (the Holy Edicule) inside Jerusalem’s Church of the Holy Sepulchre to the mid-4th century A.D., corroborating historical accounts that a Roman delegation under Emperor Constantine identified and enshrined the site around A.D. 325–335. During a nine-month restoration in 2016, conservators from the National Technical University of Athens opened the Edicule for about 60 hours and took samples for testing. Using optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating, ground-penetrating radar and laser scanning, teams found mortar beneath and around the tomb consistent with construction and repair phases dated to ca. A.D. 335, the 11th century (post-1009 destruction), and the 16th century—supporting a sequence of Roman-era enshrinement, later rebuilding after the 1009 destruction, and Ottoman-era repairs.

While the dating cannot prove the buried individual was Jesus of Nazareth, it provides the first physical evidence linking the current tomb enclosure to the period when Constantine’s agents reputedly located and commemorated the burial cave. The restoration also revealed that much of the original burial cave survives within the shrine and uncovered an older broken marble slab incised with a cross that likely dates to the mid-4th century rather than only to the Crusader period. The full scientific results will be published by the restoration team.

Steve Wynn’s plan to sell two Pablo Picasso paintings at Christie’s was disrupted after one work was damaged during pre-auction preparation and both were subsequently pulled from the upcoming sale.

Details:
- The damaged work was Picasso’s 1943 self-portrait Le Marin (about 4 x 2.5 ft), estimated at $70 million. Christie’s said it was damaged “during the final stages of preparation” and declined to specify the nature or extent of the damage. Wynn’s spokesman also declined comment.
- A second Picasso consigned by Wynn, Femme au chat assise dans un fauteuil (1964), estimated at $25–35 million, was also withdrawn from the sale by mutual agreement.
- Both withdrawn lots had been guaranteed by Christie’s and supported by third-party guarantees; Christie’s said withdrawing a lot cancels any guarantee and that its consignment contracts include insurance provisions for damage and other contingencies.
- A third lot Wynn consigned—Andy Warhol’s Double Elvis [Ferus Type] (1963), estimated at more than $30 million—will still be offered at the May 17 postwar and contemporary evening sale.
- The episode recalled a 2006 accident in which Wynn, who has a disease affecting peripheral vision, accidentally put his elbow through Picasso’s Le Rêve. That painting was later repaired and sold to Steve Cohen in 2013.
- Wynn resigned as CEO of Wynn Resorts in February amid sexual-misconduct allegations, which he denies.

Christie’s removed the Picassos from the auction schedule and cited its insurance and contractual protections; further details about the damage were not released.

On November 8, 2018 the Camp Fire devastated Butte County near Sierra Nevada Brewing’s Chico brewery, killing scores, destroying thousands of homes and severely affecting brewery employees and the local community. In response, Sierra Nevada created Resilience Butte County Proud IPA and pledged 100% of proceeds to the Sierra Nevada Camp Fire Relief Fund (seeded with a $100,000 donation from founder Ken Grossman) to support long-term rebuilding.

Sierra Nevada shared the recipe and called on the brewing industry for help. The response was unprecedented: more than 1,200–1,400 breweries across the U.S. (including regional and major craft brands) signed on to brew Resilience and donate all sales. Malt, hop and yeast suppliers contributed ingredients; wholesalers and retailers agreed to carry the beer and forward 100% of receipts. Sierra Nevada is canning and distributing Resilience while many partner breweries will offer it on draft. Together the effort is expected to produce millions of pints (Sierra Nevada estimated millions—over 4 million pints from a December announcement and later up to about 8.6 million pints overall) and aims to raise upward of $10 million (initial goals were seven figures).

Key campaign elements:
- Resilience IPA: a West Coast–style IPA (Centennial and Cascade hops) whose proceeds go entirely to Camp Fire relief via the Golden Valley Community Bank Foundation.
- Resilience Night: a coordinated event on December 20 at participating breweries to promote the beer and fundraising.
- Distribution: Sierra Nevada is packaging cans and shipping nationally; a continuously updated locator and brewer/draught maps list participating locations.
- Community support: over 1,200 breweries, numerous malt and hop suppliers, wholesalers, and retailers volunteered time, product and distribution; Untappd offered a limited-edition badge for check-ins to participating Resilience pours.

The campaign was widely praised as likely the largest charitable collaboration in U.S. brewing history, demonstrating the craft beer community’s collective support for rebuilding Butte County.

This document is a long compilation of short health and science news items followed by a longer celebrity health story.

Key points from the news roundup (selected highlights):
- A cannabis extract (CBD) may offer a new class of treatment for psychosis; CBD and THC have opposite effects.  
- Living near fracking sites is linked to higher risk of low birth weight.  
- Over 75,000 people signed a petition urging Virgin Care to return settlement money to the NHS after a contract dispute.  
- Nursing training acceptances in England fell after the NHS bursary was scrapped.  
- A landmark study links austerity to tens of thousands of excess deaths.  
- Long commutes are associated with worse physical and mental health, including higher depression risk.  
- A large study finds obesity raises cardiovascular risk even in so-called “metabolically healthy” people.  
- Chronic sleep deprivation may cause harmful brain changes.  
- Gyms have started “napercise” classes—45-minute group naps—aimed largely at fatigued parents.  
- Concerns that Brexit could weaken the “fundamental right to health,” potentially aiding tobacco and alcohol industry legal challenges.  
- Many reported statin side effects may be due to fear/placebo rather than the drugs themselves.  
- Parental age extremes (fathers under 25 or over 51) linked to higher autism risk in offspring.  
- Cycling to work strongly lowers cancer and cardiovascular risk; walking helps too but less.  
- Ketamine shows benefit for treatment-resistant depression.  
- Playing Tetris shortly after trauma may reduce intrusive memories (potential PTSD prevention).  
- Measles outbreaks in Europe are rising due to declining vaccination rates.  
- Vaping shows lower toxin exposure than continued smoking in an observational study.  
- A common rice-cooking method can leave arsenic residues; alternative methods reduce exposure.  
- A reversible injectable male contraceptive (Vasalgel) worked in monkey trials.  
- Shift/night work may reduce women's fertility.  
- Sugary children’s breakfast cereals have seen little sugar reduction since 1992.  
- Combining two drugs markedly improved long-term survival in some pancreatic cancer patients.  
- Japan is moving to curb extreme overtime after “death by overwork” concerns.  
- Acrylamide formed in overcooked potatoes and burnt toast is a potential cancer risk.  
- Cervical screening attendance has fallen to a 19-year low.  
- High blood pressure developing in people aged 80–89 was associated with lower short-term Alzheimer’s risk in one study.  
- Most antidepressants appear ineffective for children and teens and may raise suicidal thoughts; only one drug outperformed placebo in a large comparison.  
- Early-stage Alzheimer’s research pinpoints synapse destruction mechanisms.  
- A prosthetic hand has been developed that can convey touch sensations to a paralyzed user.  
- A diabetes drug shows promise to halt early Parkinson’s signs in research.  
- Moderate, regular alcohol (especially wine) was linked with lower diabetes risk in one study.  
- The NHS agreed to fund an HIV prevention drug after losing a legal dispute.  
(Other items: green tea compound may aid cognitive function in Down’s syndrome; concerns about overuse of paracetamol in children; reports on cancer-vaccine research, arsenic in rice, and more.)

Longer feature — Tarek El Moussa (Flip or Flop):
- Real-estate TV personality Tarek El Moussa revealed his thyroid cancer was discovered after a nurse viewer emailed producers about a neck lump. He was diagnosed in 2013 at age 31; the cancer had spread to lymph nodes. Following surgery and radioactive iodine therapy, he is now in remission.  
- El Moussa reports lingering fatigue and reduced energy (“jetlagged” feeling) but says he’s in good shape, taking medications and optimistic as the odds of recurrence decline with time. He and wife Christina have two children; the couple had prior fertility struggles including failed IVF and miscarriage before his diagnosis. He says he’s slowed down and is able to relax more now.

Overall tone: the document collects a wide array of recent health, medical and science headlines—many reporting new studies or public-health concerns—followed by a human-interest account of a celebrity’s cancer survival and recovery.

Former political consultant W. Samuel (Sam) Patten, 47, pleaded guilty to failing to register as a foreign agent for lobbying work he performed in the U.S. on behalf of a Ukrainian political party and a prominent Ukrainian oligarch. Patten — a onetime State Department official who ran the International Republican Institute’s Moscow office and later co-founded Begemot Ventures with a Russian national identified in filings as “Foreigner A” (widely linked to Konstantin Kilimnik) — admitted he and the company received more than $1 million for consulting and lobbying beginning in 2014 and did not disclose that work as required by the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

Patten’s plea agreement includes cooperation with U.S. prosecutors; his case was referred to the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Washington by Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s team. The exact scope of Patten’s cooperation hasn’t been revealed. Court filings say Patten helped arrange congressional meetings and drafted talking points to influence U.S. policy. He also admitted illegally helping a Ukrainian oligarch buy a ticket to Trump’s 2017 inauguration through a straw donor; that allegation is referenced in the plea though he wasn’t charged separately for it under the cooperation deal.

The facts in filings align Patten’s client and party with figures tied to Paul Manafort’s Ukraine work (prosecutors have previously named Sergei Lyovochkin in that context). Patten previously worked with Cambridge Analytica during the 2014 cycle, according to reporting, and his Russian business partner Kilimnik — indicted alongside Manafort on obstruction charges and accused of ties to Russian intelligence — remains a central figure in related Mueller prosecutions. Patten pleaded before Judge Amy Berman Jackson; prosecutors present included figures connected to the Manafort cases. No sentencing date has been set.

South Korea’s political crisis deepened after investigators found about 360 pills of Viagra and generic equivalents in the Blue House, purchased in December for use on official trips to high-altitude African capitals (Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya). The presidential office says the drugs — never used — were procured to prevent altitude sickness, as phosphodiesterase inhibitors can help pulmonary hypertension at high elevations.

The revelation fed public outrage and reinforced perceptions that President Park Geun-hye is out of touch, at a time when she faces mass street protests and an impeachment push. Park is accused of allowing a longtime confidante, Choi Soon-sil, to unduly influence state affairs and extract money from companies. Prosecutors have raided Samsung and the National Pension Service amid allegations Samsung bribed Choi to secure approval for a 2015 merger, and say Park was collusively involved with Choi and aides who pressured firms to donate to foundations Choi controlled. The scandal has sparked sustained demonstrations demanding Park’s resignation.

Search crews hunting Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 say they have been unable to relocate faint underwater signals first detected late Saturday and early Sunday that were consistent with the 37.5 kHz “ping” emitted by aircraft black box locator beacons. Angus Houston, who is coordinating the multinational search in the southern Indian Ocean, said the towed pinger locator on Australian vessel Ocean Shield recorded two distinct events (one ~2 hours 20 minutes, another ~13 minutes) but has picked up no further transmissions since. Tuesday marked about one month since the Boeing 777 disappeared with 239 people aboard, roughly the expected battery life of black box beacons, making the window to detect live pings critical.

The search covers a roughly 30,000-square-mile zone about 1,400 miles northwest of Perth, with up to 14 ships and 14 aircraft involved in surface and acoustic operations. An autonomous submersible (Bluefin-21) is aboard Ocean Shield but Houston stressed it should only be deployed once the source of the pings is better triangulated — the sub moves slowly and can only cover a narrow swath of very deep seabed (around 2.8 miles deep). If the sub detects debris, its sonar would be swapped for a camera to photograph wreckage.

Officials cautioned the signals could be from other sources (ship systems, scientific gear, marine life) and frequencies can drift with age and pressure; the recorded tones were 33.3 kHz though manufacturers say drift is possible and past crashes showed similar offsets. No surface debris linked to MH370 has been found in 133 aerial missions so far. With black box batteries likely near end of life, the search is at a critical and urgent stage; teams warned that locating wreckage on the deep ocean floor without active pings would be extremely slow and difficult.

Kate Downing, a member of Palo Alto’s Planning and Transportation Commission and co‑founder of the housing advocacy group Palo Alto Forward, publicly resigned and announced she and her husband will move to Santa Cruz because they can no longer afford to raise a family in Palo Alto. Despite both having well‑paid tech‑sector jobs (she’s a corporate attorney; he’s a software engineer), they pay $6,200 monthly rent sharing a four‑bedroom house and estimate buying that home would cost $2.7 million — about $12,177 a month in mortgage, taxes and insurance, or roughly $146,000 a year — unaffordable even for professional incomes. 

Downing framed her departure as symptomatic of broader policy failures: an ongoing jobs‑housing imbalance fueled by the city’s slow‑growth stance and preference for office development over housing. She said council inaction has left teachers, first responders and service workers struggling, encouraged long commutes, and driven young families and long‑time residents out of the city. Downing outlined modest policy fixes she’s advocated for—allowing additional floors in mixed‑use projects, enforcing minimum densities, legalizing duplexes and granny units, permitting housing above single‑use commercial areas, and rethinking parking rules—to increase housing supply while preserving neighborhood character. 

Her resignation follows widespread local concern: petitions with over 1,000 signatures, survey results showing housing as the top resident issue, and mounting evidence of people turning down jobs or leaving the area because of cost. Downing said she’ll continue housing and transportation advocacy through her organization, even as she leaves Palo Alto.

Prince William and Duchess Kate have adopted a male cocker spaniel puppy, a few months old, bred from a litter that included a dog owned by Kate’s mother, Carole Middleton. The couple took the pup in early December and have been settling him into their North Wales farmhouse and Kensington Palace; he has been seen on walks but has not been publicly presented. St James’s Palace and palace aides say the puppy is a private pet and his name will not be released. This is the pair’s first dog together, replacing William’s late black labrador Widgeon. The adoption comes as William prepares for a six-week posting to the Falklands, leaving Kate to spend more time in London with the new pet. The story notes the royal family’s long fondness for dogs and offers background on the cocker spaniel breed.

AMC Theatres has abandoned a controversial idea to allow texting in some auditoriums after strong public backlash. CEO Adam Aron had told Variety he was open to creating “texting-friendly” screens or sections to attract millennials who resist turning off phones, but social media and customer responses were overwhelmingly negative. Within days AMC announced the proposal was “sent to the cutting room floor,” promising no texting now or in the foreseeable future. Aron said the company will instead pursue other strategies to boost attendance—investing over $1 billion in upgrades, expanding food and loyalty programs, partnering with ticketing apps like Atom Tickets, and pursuing the Carmike Cinemas acquisition—while continuing to experiment cautiously with new ideas so long as they don’t harm the moviegoing experience. The episode highlights industry tensions over phone etiquette, changing audience habits, and how exhibitors should appeal to younger viewers.

A Nevada parole board has unanimously granted O.J. Simpson parole after he served nine years of a nine-to-33-year sentence for a 2007 armed robbery and kidnapping in Las Vegas. At the hearing Simpson, 70, apologized for his role in the incident, said he’d been a model prisoner, completed violence-prevention classes, and presented stable release plans and family support; board members rated him a low risk to reoffend. He is expected to be released as early as October and said he plans to move to Florida.

Simpson avoided full responsibility for the robbery, saying associates misled him; one associate, Tom Riccio, disputed that account, accusing Simpson of orchestrating the plot. Victim Bruce Fromong testified he forgave Simpson and supported release. The case arose from an attempt to retrieve sports memorabilia at gunpoint from dealers at the Palace Station hotel; Simpson has maintained he sought personal items and did not intend to harm anyone.

Thursday’s hearing drew intense media attention, briefly reviving national interest in Simpson’s story that peaked during his 1995 murder trial for the slayings of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, where he was acquitted criminally but later found liable in civil court. The coverage reflected how themes from that trial—race, policing, celebrity and domestic violence—remain resonant in American culture.

Actor Scott Baio — a vocal Donald Trump supporter — filed a police report alleging he was physically assaulted by Nancy Mack, wife of Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith, during an elementary‑school event in Thousand Oaks, California. According to Baio (reported by TMZ), Mack confronted and loudly berated him over his support for Trump, repeatedly shouting Trump’s controversial “grab ’em by the pussy” remark despite Baio asking her to stop because children were present. Baio claims Mack then grabbed him under the arms, shook and pushed him; Mack is listed as a battery suspect and the Ventura County Sheriff’s Department is investigating.

Sources close to Mack say she was merely mimicking how Trump hugs women and did not intend harm. The incident follows public political tensions: Baio is one of the few Hollywood celebrities who actively backed Trump (he spoke at the 2016 Republican National Convention), while Chad Smith has been outspokenly critical of Trump and his supporters. Neither Baio nor Mack has publicly commented beyond the report.

Multiple former Ohio State University wrestlers have contradicted Rep. Jim Jordan’s repeated claim that he had no knowledge of sexual abuse by team doctor Dr. Richard Strauss while Jordan was an assistant wrestling coach (1986–1994). Wrestlers including Shawn Dailey, Dunyasha Yetts, Mark Coleman and others say Strauss’ inappropriate conduct—showering with athletes, forcing some to undress during exams, and groping—was widely known in the locker room and, in some cases, directly reported to coaches. Dailey said Strauss groped him several times in the mid-1990s and that locker-room talk about Strauss was common; Yetts says he complained to Jordan and head coach Russ Hellickson after Strauss tried to pull down his shorts for a thumb injury. Coleman called it implausible Jordan could have no recollection. Jordan and his spokesman continue to deny any knowledge and say he never had abuse reported to him; Jordan has not yet been interviewed by the university’s independent investigators despite requests. President Trump publicly backed Jordan.

Ohio State opened an investigation in April after former wrestler Mike DiSabato’s allegations. The university retained Perkins Coie, which has interviewed more than 150 former students and witnesses; reports of misconduct span athletes from 14 sports. Investigators have obtained video in which former head coach Hellickson said he warned Strauss to be less “hands on.” Strauss, who died by suicide in 2005, served at OSU from the late 1970s through the 1990s. Victims are urging accountability and some former athletes estimate the abuse was widespread; the independent probe is ongoing and the university says it will consider further action once the investigation is complete.

A Johnston County 911 shift supervisor, Tim Medlin, is being credited with helping locate and rescue a woman who called reporting she was locked in the trunk of a moving car on Jan. 14. The distressed caller’s voice was hard to understand and the call dropped; she wouldn’t answer callbacks. Medlin used an office cell phone to text her; she replied “Help me,” gave the vehicle’s make/color (a red Mustang), a likely destination (Fayetteville), and the boyfriend’s name, Nicholas Mattevi. Dispatchers worked with Cumberland County and Verizon to triangulate the phone, Fayetteville police intercepted the car, rescued the unharmed woman and arrested Mattevi on a false imprisonment charge. He was later released on bond. Johnston County 911 director Jason Barbour noted that while centers can receive texts, they currently cannot initiate texts from their systems—a limitation highlighted by this case; the center plans to upgrade staff phones.

U.S. payment networks are shifting to EMV chip-enabled credit and debit cards (Europay, MasterCard, Visa) to reduce card fraud, which has more than doubled in the U.S. over 15 years while falling in regions that adopted chips earlier. Chip cards store payment data on a microprocessor and generate a unique code for each transaction, making counterfeiting much harder; markets that migrated quickly saw counterfeit fraud fall roughly 60–70%.

Practical effects:
- Cards look the same but have a small metallic chip; users insert (“dip”) the card into updated readers instead of swiping.
- Transactions take longer (about 5–10 seconds versus 3–5 seconds for swipes), which could slow checkout lines during busy periods.
- Consumers will still sign for chip transactions and are protected by federal rules requiring banks to reimburse victims of fraud.
- On the liability side, starting Oct. 1 (Oct. 16 for American Express), merchants who haven’t upgraded terminals to accept chip cards will become liable for fraudulent transactions instead of the card issuers. Banks may pursue noncompliant retailers for losses.
- Not all customers had chip cards by the deadline; non-chip cards continue to work until they expire or until users activate new cards, and will function at terminals that accept chips (though new machines will prompt users to dip rather than swipe).

This document examines American college fraternities through two linked lenses: fatal and injurious incidents tied to hazing, binge drinking and unsafe housing, and the political, legal and cultural power that protects the fraternity system. It begins with a Bloomberg account of California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly), where the 2008 alcohol-related death of freshman Carson Starkey prompted the university in 2010 to delay freshman fraternity recruitment. The North-American Interfraternity Conference (NIC) immediately intervened—paying for studies, advising student leaders, lobbying administrators and coordinating campus opposition—and over three years persuaded Cal Poly to lift the recruiting moratorium in exchange for increased oversight, alcohol education and registration of parties. The article outlines the debate: proponents of deferred recruitment and critics such as Princeton president Shirley Tilghman argue freshmen are especially vulnerable during early weeks on campus and that delaying recruitment can save lives. The NIC and fraternity leaders counter that deferred recruitment is only a “Band‑Aid” for a broader campus drinking problem, infringes on students’ freedom of association, deprives freshmen of leadership and networking opportunities, and threatens chapters’ survival because recruitment is their lifeblood. The piece recounts Starkey’s initiation, the frat’s failures to get him medical help, criminal pleas and a civil settlement, and notes ongoing alcohol-related incidents and disciplinary actions at Cal Poly after the policy reversal.

A longer, reflective feature follows that expands the problem nationally and historically. It opens with a vivid anecdote about dangerous, drunken behavior (a man injured after a bottle-rocket prank) and a slip‑and‑fall lawsuit that illustrates how personal-injury litigation increasingly documents fraternity harms. The author surveys a grim pattern: since the mid-2000s dozens of deaths and many severe injuries across campuses have been linked to fraternities, with freshmen disproportionately affected. Common causes include binge drinking, hazing, sexual assault, falls from roofs, porches and windows, and unsafe sleeping‑porch conditions. Many incidents—falls, overdoses, rapes—repeat across campuses and time, suggesting predictable, preventable hazards.

The piece traces fraternities’ long history and resurgence: from 19th-century secret societies to modern Greek life’s central role in campus social life, alumni networks and fundraising. Fraternities supply housing, social programming that attracts applicants, and strong alumni ties that translate into donations—factors that make universities reluctant to confront problematic chapters. The article explains how legal and insurance pressures since the 1980s forced fraternities to professionalize risk management: national organizations centralized insurance and created best-practice manuals (notably FIPG), BYOB/guest-list systems, crisis-management protocols, and other procedures meant to limit liability. These systems, the author argues, often serve dual aims—appearing to manage risk while protecting national organizations and preserving chapters—by shifting blame onto individual members who violate policies and by creating documentation that can be used against those individuals.

Two central figures embody the clash over fraternities: Douglas Fierberg, a plaintiffs’ attorney who prosecutes fraternity-related harms and calls the system “very risky,” and Peter Smithhisler, CEO of the NIC, who defends fraternities’ educative and philanthropic value and argues they are unfairly targeted. The account is skeptical of claims that internal policies meaningfully reduce harms: it documents how BYOB/guest lists, “six-beer” rules, and crisis plans may be circumvented or used to insulate nationals and chapters from liability while leaving individual students—and their families’ finances—vulnerable to lawsuits. The narrative also explains why universities struggle to curb dangerous fraternity practices: legal protections, freedom-of-association claims, alumni pressure, housing dependencies, and the financial importance of Greek life to institutional recruitment and fundraising.

Key themes and findings:
- Freshmen are overrepresented among fraternity‑related deaths; delaying recruitment is a debated prevention strategy that national organizations often oppose.
- Binge drinking, hazing, and unsafe fraternity housing (roofs, sleeping porches, balconies, open windows) repeatedly produce severe injuries and deaths nationwide.
- The NIC and national fraternities wield substantial influence on campuses and in policy debates; they lobby, fund assessments, and mount legal threats.
- Fraternities centralized risk management and insurance to survive rising liability costs; their formal policies can paradoxically protect organizations while exposing individual members.
- Civil lawsuits have brought many incidents into public view, revealing patterns of predictable harm; outcomes vary, often producing settlements or dismissed claims due to legal doctrines and institutional defenses.
- Colleges face a conflict between student safety and institutional reliance on fraternities for housing, recruitment appeal and alumni donations, making systemic reform difficult.

The document concludes that fraternities remain powerful, deeply embedded institutions that offer leadership and community benefits for many members but also generate recurring, severe harms. Efforts to reform behavior—through deferred recruitment, oversight, education, risk-management rules, and litigation—have produced mixed results, leaving a fraught balance between fraternity tradition, student safety, university interests, and legal accountability.

Hurricane Irene, a powerful and slow-moving storm, tracked northward from the Bahamas toward the U.S. East Coast, prompting widespread emergency preparations and disruptions across multiple states. As forecasts shifted westward, officials predicted landfall near North Carolina’s Outer Banks by Saturday with damaging winds, heavy rain, significant storm surge and prolonged outages expected to affect areas from North Carolina through New England. Irene reached Category 3 strength with 115 mph winds at times and had the potential to strengthen further; forecasters warned tens of millions of people were in its path and estimated possible multi-billion-dollar insured and economic losses.

Governors in Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Connecticut and North Carolina declared states of emergency; federal and state agencies (including FEMA and DHS) mobilized resources and urged evacuations. Mandatory evacuations were ordered for many barrier islands and coastal resort towns (including Ocean City, MD, and parts of the Outer Banks), and New York City officials warned that mass transit might be suspended and advised low-lying hospitals, nursing homes and residents to evacuate. Utilities pre-positioned repair crews and warned customers—especially those dependent on medical equipment—to prepare for extended outages. Amtrak and airlines adjusted or canceled service; airports, campuses and many events were disrupted.

Locally in Washington, D.C., precautionary measures included sandbagging vulnerable Metro stations and offering free sandbags to residents. The planned Aug. 28 dedication of the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial on the National Mall was postponed (to be rescheduled for fall) because safety concerns and forecast changes could hinder travel and public safety. Across affected regions, residents evacuated, scrambled for supplies, or prepared to ride out the storm, while officials emphasized the serious, potentially historic nature of the event and urged people to take warnings seriously.

Researchers have developed a way to make distilled spirits from used coffee grounds. In the study, spent grounds from a Portuguese roaster were dried, heated in water (163°C for 45 minutes), and the liquid was separated and sweetened. Yeast fermentation followed, and the product was concentrated to raise alcohol content, producing a spirit with about 40% ethanol—comparable to vodka or tequila. A panel of eight trained tasters described the drink as smelling like coffee and tasting bitter and pungent but judged it to have quality “good enough for consumption”; researchers suggested flavor could improve with aging. Most caffeine is lost during the process, so the spirit lacks the stimulant effect found in some coffee-alcohol mixes. The work points to an inventive way to create novel flavors and reuse a common waste product.

Pope Francis expressed shock and deep sorrow after gunmen attacked a home for the elderly in Aden, Yemen, killing 16 people—including four Missionaries of Charity nuns (two Rwandan, one Indian, one Kenyan). According to witnesses and officials, the attackers entered the facility, reportedly posing as visitors, moved room to room, handcuffed residents and staff, and shot the victims in the head while breakfast was being served. No group has claimed responsibility; Yemeni authorities suspect Islamic State, and both IS and AQAP have exploited Yemen’s civil war, which has killed thousands and displaced millions. In a condolence message read by Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the pope prayed for the dead, expressed solidarity with the victims’ families and the Missionaries of Charity, condemned the “senseless and diabolical violence,” and appealed for an end to the fighting and a return to dialogue. The nun in charge of the home escaped unharmed.

A Santa Rosa mother, 30-year-old Delia Garcia-Bratcher, was arrested after allegedly confronting and grabbing a 12-year-old boy by the throat at Olivet Charter Elementary School while accusing him of bullying her daughter. The incident occurred around lunchtime Friday; Garcia-Bratcher reportedly asked her son to identify the suspected bully, approached the boy in front of other students without checking in at the office, and left visible red marks and fingerprints on his neck. School staff photographed the injuries and notified deputies. Garcia-Bratcher was booked on a felony charge of child abuse/inflicting injury on a child and released on $30,000 bail; she is scheduled to appear in court. Authorities and the school district are investigating the alleged bullying but say they have not substantiated those claims and note parents should not confront students on campus. County prosecutors are awaiting the sheriff’s report before deciding on charges.

Researchers studying African elephants in Amboseli National Park, Kenya, found that wild elephants can discriminate between human languages and between male, female and child voices, and adjust their behavior based on perceived threat. In playback experiments reported in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, scientists played the same phrase—“Look, look over there, a group of elephants is coming”—recorded by Maasai and Kamba speakers and by men, women and boys to hundreds of elephants across 47 family groups.

Elephants responded defensively (bunching, investigative smelling, cautious withdrawal) to adult Maasai male voices—associated locally with occasional lethal conflict over grazing and water—while showing little concern for Kamba male voices, female Maasai voices or boys. Groups led by older matriarchs made the best threat assessments, supporting a role for learning and social knowledge. Manipulating pitch to make female voices sound male (and vice versa) did not deceive the elephants, indicating they use subtle acoustic cues beyond simple pitch.

Authors and outside experts interpret the findings as evidence of sophisticated auditory discrimination, memory and social learning in elephants. The behavior also reflects growing, problematic human–elephant conflict: elephants now regard humans as a class of predators to monitor, underscoring conservation concerns. The study complements other work showing elephants have human-specific alarm calls and adds to evidence that many animal species can distinguish between different categories of people.

Actor Russell Crowe abruptly ended a BBC Radio 4 Front Row interview with host Mark Lawson after Lawson suggested Crowe’s accent for his role as Robin Hood contained “hints” of an Irish accent. The exchange grew heated: Crowe denied the claim, called Lawson’s ears “dead,” used expletives, mocked the suggestion, and ultimately waved his cigarette and walked out of the interview at the Dorchester Hotel. Crowe said he was “dumbfounded” anyone could hear Irish in the character; he later joked he’d aimed for an Italian accent. The discussion followed reports that voice coaches wanted a Rutland/East Midlands–style accent for the film, and amid other critics’ varied comments about Crowe’s accents. The broadcast also included other arts items, including pieces on Lambeth Palace’s library, the final series of Ashes to Ashes, and a National Theatre play.

A Brooklyn grand jury has indicted rookie NYPD Officer Peter Liang on multiple charges, including second-degree manslaughter, reckless endangerment, second-degree assault and official misconduct, for the Nov. 20, 2014 shooting death of 28-year-old Akai Gurley in an unlit stairwell of the Pink Houses public-housing complex in East New York. Liang, 27 and on the force less than 18 months, fired a single round while conducting a vertical patrol; the bullet struck Gurley in the chest as he stood on a landing with his girlfriend. Liang’s weapon was reportedly in his left hand while he held a flashlight in the other; authorities say the gun “accidentally discharged.”

The indictment — which carries up to 15 years in prison on the top count — follows a short grand jury review that began Feb. 4. Liang did not testify before the panel and is expected to surrender and be arraigned in Brooklyn Supreme Court. Gurley’s family, their attorneys and supporters including Rev. Al Sharpton praised the indictment as a step toward accountability; his partner has announced plans to sue the city for $50 million. City officials and civil-rights figures called for respect of the judicial process, while police union leaders characterized the shooting as a tragic accident and emphasized due process. The case drew intense attention amid national protests over police killings of unarmed black men and was contrasted with grand juries in the Michael Brown and Eric Garner cases.

Ron and Mary Tarnowski, an elderly Duluth couple, were found dead on Aug. 5 after being missing for eight days. The couple, 82-year-old Ron and 78-year-old Mary, were located by a U.S. Border Patrol helicopter about 150 yards off Highway 2 near Brookston, Minn., on an overgrown, swampy trail about a mile from the family hunting camp. Mary was found inside their stuck Chevy Tahoe; Ron was found outside the vehicle roughly 50 feet from the road. Authorities do not suspect foul play; autopsy results are pending but investigators and the family believe both died of exposure and dehydration the day they disappeared, July 29. Ron had early-stage dementia and Mary had long-term right-side paralysis and limited speech.

The couple had last been seen on surveillance video at a Country Corner store and had stopped for lunch and at a bank earlier that day. They left home without cellphones, Mary’s wheelchair, purse and medications, prompting a large search involving family, volunteers, retired and active firefighters, and multiple agencies. A Facebook group organized updates for thousands of supporters. Family members say Ron likely drove onto the abandoned trail, got stuck, and left to seek help; he fell in the mud. The Tarnowskis had been married 59 years; Ron was a retired Duluth firefighter and Air Force veteran. Their son urged that vulnerable adults carry GPS or phones to prevent similar tragedies. The community expressed condolences and gratitude to responders.

Pakistani TV host Aamir Liaquat Hussain has sparked controversy by giving abandoned newborns away to childless couples live on his prime-time Ramadan show, Aman Ramazan. The seven-hour daily program — a mix of religious discussion, entertainment and quiz prizes — presented two infant girls rescued by the Chhipa Welfare Association and plans to hand over another baby boy. Chhipa says it recovers many abandoned infants each month and vets prospective guardians, but adoptions were not completed before the live broadcasts and Pakistan has no formal adoption law, so recipients must seek guardianship in family court.

Supporters and Hussain argue the stunt saves babies from death or abuse, raises awareness and promotes social unity during Ramadan. Critics call it a publicity-driven ratings ploy that treats children like trophies and point to ethical and legal problems. Hussain, a polarizing media figure with a history of controversy, defended the program as spreading love and preventing social ills. The giveaways have driven record ratings amid fierce competition in Pakistan’s liberalized, sensationalist TV market, prompting both praise and sharp public backlash.

Prosecutors at the court-martial of Army Sgt. Adam Holcomb say testimony shows Holcomb and other soldiers severely hazed and racially taunted Pvt. Danny Chen, a 19-year-old Chinese American, in the weeks before Chen’s Oct. 3 suicide at an Afghan outpost. On Day Two, former platoon members testified Holcomb used racial slurs, threatened soldiers (one, Pvt. Marcus Merritt, testified Holcomb told him “I’ll kill you and put you in a body bag”), and once dragged Chen across sharp, baseball‑sized rocks, leaving him injured. Merritt said Holcomb’s treatment drove him to contemplate suicide; under cross‑examination he acknowledged he didn’t believe Holcomb literally intended to kill him but feared him.

Holcomb, 30, the first of eight soldiers to be tried in the case, faces charges including negligent homicide, assault and reckless endangerment. His superior, Staff Sgt. Darren Holt, testified he confronted Holcomb over the dragging incident and reported it. Defense lawyers argue Chen was a problematic, undisciplined soldier whose family had disowned him for joining the Army, and that harsh corrective training and rough nicknames—some racially tinged—were common in the close platoon. Some witnesses conceded much discipline was justified and said Chen showed no obvious signs of suicidal intent; the platoon medic said Chen denied suicidal thoughts when asked. The case has drawn attention from Asian American activists and media because of allegations of hazing and racism.

Instagram faced major user backlash after posting updates to its privacy policy and terms of service that many interpreted as allowing the company to share user data with advertisers and to use users’ photos in ads without compensation or notification. Users reacted strongly—complaining on social media, deleting accounts, and migrating to rival apps—which prompted company co-founder Kevin Systrom to apologize and acknowledge a failure to communicate clearly.

In response to the outcry, Instagram reverted the advertising-related clause to the original terms in effect since October 2010 and said it will not seek premature permission for hypothetical ad products. Systrom emphasized that Instagram has no intention of selling users’ photos and that users retain ownership of their images. The company also made a small clarification to the terms about how content distribution is governed by its privacy policy and said it will refine its privacy wording further.

The controversy boosted competing photo apps—Pheed and Flickr among them—seeing sharp increases in downloads and uploads as some users explored alternatives. Instagram, which has over 100 million users, and Facebook (its new owner) have not detailed how they will monetize Instagram going forward, though pressure remains to generate revenue.

New Jersey lawmakers are considering a controversial distracted-driving bill that would ban any activity “unrelated to the actual operation of a motor vehicle” if it interferes with safe driving. Sponsors, including Assemblyman John Wisniewski, say the broad language is intentional — meant to cover current and future distractions without having to rewrite the law as technology changes — and is aimed at reducing deadly, preventable crashes (federal data show about 400,000 distracted-driving crashes and 3,000 deaths in 2014). Proposed penalties are $200–$400 for a first offense, $400–$600 for a second, and $600–$800 for a third plus up to a 90-day license suspension and motor-vehicle points.

The bill does not explicitly mention eating or drinking, despite media focus on coffee-drinking drivers; Wisniewski says he cannot imagine police ticketing someone simply for sipping coffee. Supporters argue the measure could change behavior the way seat-belt laws did, reducing multitasking behind the wheel. Critics call it overly broad and difficult to enforce, noting existing statutes (unsafe, careless, reckless driving) and current bans on handheld phones and texting could cover many incidents. The bill has been introduced previously but has not yet come to a committee vote.

North Korean pair skaters Ryom Tae-Ok (18) and Kim Ju-Sik (25) secured one of the final Olympic berths at the Nebelhorn Trophy in Oberstdorf, Germany, earning North Korea a presence at the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. They delivered a strong short program and an improved free skate—skating to The Beatles and "Je suis qu'une chanson"—to take one of five qualifying spots; the ISU confirmed their qualification. The pair trained in Montreal under coach Bruno Marcotte and finished 15th at last season’s World Championships.

Their qualification is politically significant amid heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula after recent exchanges between Kim Jong Un and U.S. President Donald Trump. The IOC has encouraged North Korean participation—providing support with equipment, travel and accommodation—and other North Korean athletes (speed skaters, Nordic skiers) could still qualify. Final approval for the athletes to attend rests with the North Korean Olympic Committee. South Korean President Moon Jae-in has said Pyongyang will be given until the last minute to decide whether to participate.

Adrianne Haslet-Davis, a professional ballroom dancer who lost her left leg below the knee in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, announced she is training to run the 120th Boston Marathon on April 18. She formed a team called #AdrianneStrong about five weeks ago to raise funds for Limbs for Life, an Oklahoma City charity that provides prosthetic limbs to those who cannot afford them. Haslet-Davis—who vowed after the bombing both to dance again (which she did less than a year later, performing at the marathon finish line in 2015) and to run the marathon—said she has been training and is currently up to 10 miles on her running blade. She described the race as a thank-you to supporters and expects an emotional finish. The story also recounts her return to Boylston Street for a dance performance that highlighted her recovery and inspired onlookers, including a first-aid responder who was at the finish line during the bombing.

This document explains the FTC’s rules and guidance on “Made in USA” claims, how they interact with other labeling laws, and recent watchdog findings about mislabeled products on Walmart’s website.

Key FTC standards and guidance
- Authority and standard: The FTC enforces against deceptive U.S.-origin claims. An unqualified “Made in USA” claim is allowed only if a product is “all or virtually all” made in the United States (including states, D.C., and U.S. territories). That standard was reaffirmed in the FTC’s 1997 Enforcement Policy Statement on U.S. Origin Claims.
- What “all or virtually all” means: All significant parts and processing must be domestic; foreign content must be negligible. The product’s final assembly or processing must occur in the U.S. The FTC looks at factors including where final assembly occurs, the share of total manufacturing costs attributable to U.S. parts/processing, and how close any foreign content is to the finished product.
- Substantiation: Marketers must have a reasonable basis — competent, reliable evidence — for unqualified claims when made.
- Cost accounting: Use cost of goods sold or finished-goods inventory costs (materials, direct labor, overhead) to assess U.S. content.
- Supplier information: Businesses may rely on suppliers’ certifications given in good faith, but should seek specific percentage data rather than assume inputs are 100% U.S.-made.
- How far back to look: Look back far enough to capture any significant foreign content; early, low-cost inputs that are insignificant may be less important than direct, integral parts (e.g., imported gold in a ring vs. petroleum-derived plastic in a case).

Qualified claims, specific-process claims, and assembly claims
- Qualified claims: Describe the extent or nature of U.S. content (e.g., “Made in USA of U.S. and imported parts,” “60% U.S. content”). Use only when the product has significant U.S. content or processing, and ensure claims are clear, truthful, and substantiated. Avoid implying more domestic content than exists.
- Specific-process or part claims: Statements that a particular part or process occurred in the U.S. are permissible if clear and limited to that part/process (e.g., “Packaging made in USA,” “Designed in USA — Made in Finland”). Broad wording like “created” or “produced” can be misread as an unqualified origin claim and should be avoided or qualified.
- “Assembled in USA”: Acceptable without qualification when principal assembly and the last “substantial transformation” occur in the U.S., and assembly is substantial (not merely a screwdriver operation).

Interaction with Customs and other laws
- U.S. Customs: Enforces marking of imported goods with foreign country of origin. Customs determines country of origin based on “substantial transformation” (or tariff-shift analyses). A Customs determination that a product need not be marked as foreign origin does not automatically mean an unqualified “Made in USA” claim is permissible under the FTC standard.
- FTC v. Customs: FTC applies broader consumer-perception factors; Customs focuses on legal country-of-origin marking. Marketers must satisfy both where applicable.
- Other statutes: Specific labeling rules exist for textiles, wool, fur (detailed labeling and placement requirements), automobiles (American Automobile Labeling Act — disclosure of assembly location and percentage of U.S./Canadian equipment), and government procurement (Buy American Act requires >50% U.S. parts for “Made in USA” in procurement).

Comparative claims
- Should be truthful, substantiated, based on meaningful differences, and clearly describe the basis for comparison. Minor or insignificant differences (e.g., 2% to 4% U.S. content) are deceptive if advertised as substantial improvements.

Enforcement and reporting violations
- The FTC does not pre-approve claims; it enforces after the fact. Suspected violations can be reported to the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, U.S. Customs’ fraud hotline, state attorneys general, Better Business Bureau/NAD, or pursued under the Lanham Act by those harmed.

Truth in Advertising (TINA) / Walmart case
- TINA reported over 100 items on Walmart.com labeled “Made in USA” though evidence (packaging or product details) indicated foreign origin.
- Examples included Equate makeup sponges and teeth-whitening strips labeled “Made in USA” on the site yet packaging said “Made in China,” and an Almay eyeliner whose package listed “Made in Germany.”
- Walmart’s response: Some production had moved to the U.S. but website data lagged; some labels were removed; country-of-origin info comes from suppliers. Walmart also said errors were limited to a small percentage of listings and pledged quality assurance.
- TINA criticized Walmart’s failure to ensure accuracy and flagged that Walmart’s site design made “Made in USA” and “Assembled in USA” hard to distinguish (small, low-contrast text), which could mislead consumers given FTC distinctions between those claims.
- TINA urged Walmart to clean up labeling to restore consumer trust; the episode underscores that companies can be exposed by watchdogs and that accurate, substantiated origin claims are essential.

Practical takeaways
- Use unqualified “Made in USA” only when the product is essentially all U.S.-made and you have documentation to substantiate that.
- Use clear, specific qualified claims when significant foreign content exists; avoid wording that creates misleading net impressions.
- Obtain and document supplier certifications about origin and cost contributions.
- Ensure packaging, online listings, and advertising consistently and clearly disclose country of origin, and comply with Customs and other statute-specific labeling rules.
- Consumers or competitors suspecting mislabeling can report it to the FTC, Customs, state authorities, NAD, or pursue civil action under the Lanham Act.

Nancy Motes, 37, the half-sister of actress Julia Roberts, was found dead in a Los Angeles bathtub on Feb. 9. Officials say multiple notes were recovered and both prescription and over‑the‑counter pills were at the scene; toxicology results are pending and the coroner has deferred a final cause of death pending those tests. Early reports describe the death as an apparent overdose and possible suicide.

Motes had a long, troubled relationship with her famous sister, marked by public criticism, allegations that Julia and their mother pressured her about weight and tried to get her into rehab, and a history of substance problems, according to multiple sources. In the months before her death Motes posted angry tweets about Julia and spoke publicly about family tensions. Family statements describe the family as “shocked and devastated.”

A dispute has emerged between Motes’ fiancé, John Dilbeck, and surviving family members. Dilbeck — who discovered Motes’ body — has not publicly commented beyond denying labels such as “addict” in one brief encounter. His brother Conner and other associates claim Motes left an extensive suicide letter alleging mistreatment by Julia Roberts and suggest she may have timed her death to coincide with Roberts’ awards season. Conner and another friend have accused the Roberts family of cruelty; others caution the timing and motives are unclear. Sources close to Roberts say she repeatedly tried to get Nancy into rehab and remains privately devastated.

There are also reports that Dilbeck may seek to control Motes’ personal effects and estate, raising fears among some family members about the handling or sale of intimate items. Police reportedly hold the suicide note; neither its full contents nor definitive forensic conclusions have been released.

If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts, contact local emergency services or the U.S. Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 (or 1‑800‑273‑TALK where available).

Anthony Scaramucci, newly named White House communications director, lashed out after a Politico report published his required financial disclosure, threatening on Twitter to involve the FBI and Justice Department over what he called a felony “leak.” He later deleted the tweet and said Chief of Staff Reince Priebus was among senior officials helping to stop leaks.

The disclosure shows Scaramucci reported assets up to $85 million and significant recent income: roughly $5 million in salary and $4.9 million from his roughly 44% ownership stake in investment firm SkyBridge Capital between Jan. 1, 2016 and June 30, 2017. SkyBridge is being sold to RON Transatlantic and China’s HNA Group in a deal Bloomberg valued at $200–$230 million; Scaramucci stands to receive a large payout when that sale closes. The transaction is under review by the interagency Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States.

Though Scaramucci says he stepped down as SkyBridge’s managing director and was on unpaid leave from the Export‑Import Bank (where he briefly worked), the SkyBridge website still listed him as managing director and he continued to draw salary until June. His filing also lists other holdings — including a minority stake in the New York Mets, real estate, and a majority interest in Hastings Capital Group — and several mortgages. Scaramucci said his White House start date would be in August to ensure conflicts are resolved. Critics and watchdogs noted the clear potential for continued financial benefit and conflict as the sale proceeds.

A Democrat familiar with the decision told CNN that Hillary Clinton is not considering Bernie Sanders for vice president. Sanders, who has not officially conceded the Democratic primary, was not expecting to be offered the VP slot and does not view Clinton’s decision as a slight. According to people close to him, Sanders remains focused on changing the Democratic Party rather than joining Clinton’s ticket — joining could have led supporters to view him as a sell-out. He did not raise the matter during a roughly 90-minute private meeting with Clinton.

A new analysis of U.S. cancer registry data (SEER) finds colorectal cancer is increasingly affecting adults under 50. Reviewing about 258,000 patients diagnosed from 1998–2011, researchers led by Dr. Samantha Hendren found nearly 15% (about 1 in 7) were younger than 50. That proportion is projected to rise—by 2030, an estimated ~25% of rectal cancers and >10% of colon cancers may occur in people under 50.

Younger patients were more likely to present with advanced disease: they were ~30% more likely to have regional (lymph node) spread and ~50% more likely to have distant metastases than older patients. Consequently, younger patients with metastatic disease more often received aggressive treatment (surgery: 72% vs. 63%; radiation for rectal cancer: 53% vs. 48%). Despite presenting at later stages, younger patients had slightly better recurrence-free and overall five‑year survival within each stage: for localized disease 95.1% vs. 91.9%, regional 76% vs. 70.3%, distant 21.3% vs. 14.1%.

The study raises concerns about current screening guidelines that generally start at age 50, since nearly 15% of cases occur earlier and many young patients are diagnosed only after symptoms (e.g., dark or mixed-with-stool blood, anemia, changes in bowel habits) prompt evaluation. Authors call for improved risk assessment and clinician vigilance for colorectal symptoms in younger adults. Experts note limitations: the registry lacked data on family history and other risk factors, and treatment/outcome differences may reflect selection bias. It remains uncertain whether lowering the screening age would reduce mortality, and more research is needed before changing guidelines. Meanwhile, clinicians should consider earlier diagnostic workup for symptomatic or high-risk younger people.

State officials in Wisconsin issued two notices:

- Wisconsin Air National Guard nighttime training: The 115th Fighter Wing will conduct nighttime F-16 training flights Monday–Thursday, with takeoffs and landings possibly audible or visible through about 10 p.m. Pilots will use flight paths intended to minimize noise; nighttime operations are required for readiness even though most training is daytime. Residents can delete tweet location history (header note).

- Possible "frostquake" in southern Wisconsin: Freezing temperatures Tuesday night likely caused a cryoseism (commonly called a frostquake) that produced a loud boom and brief rumble across an area from Columbus to Fox Lake and Johnson Creek to Oconomowoc. The National Weather Service said water in the ground froze, expanded, and fractured soil and rock; no damage was reported. Frostquakes are rare but have been recorded in Wisconsin.

Following the March 11 magnitude-9.0 earthquake and subsequent tsunami, Japan faced a major nuclear crisis at the Fukushima Dai-ichi plant. Multiple reactors suffered damage—fires, explosions, loss of cooling and partial meltdowns—and spent-fuel pools in several units became a central concern because they were low on water and risked overheating and releasing more radiation. Unit 3 was especially worrying because it used MOX fuel containing plutonium.

Operators and emergency crews employed desperate measures: laying external power lines to restore cooling, spraying seawater from fire trucks, using helicopters and military water-cannon vehicles to douse reactors, and rotating small teams of workers into the high-radiation zone. Tokyo Electric Power Co. (TEPCO) reported an external transmission line was connected and additional cabling was being installed to try to restart pumps for reactors 1–4; success would be a major step toward stabilizing the site. Authorities said they might consider extreme options, including entombing the plant in sand and concrete as was done at Chernobyl if cooling could not be restored.

Japan raised the accident to Level 5 on the International Nuclear Event Scale (comparable to Three Mile Island), though some experts judged it more serious. International monitoring has detected low radiation levels far from the site, but hazardous levels remained largely confined to the plant area. The U.S. advised Americans to evacuate to a 50-mile radius, a far larger zone than Japan’s evacuation orders, and sent measurement aircraft and other assistance. The IAEA and other foreign experts warned the situation remained “very serious.”

The nuclear emergency compounded an enormous humanitarian disaster: thousands confirmed dead, many thousands missing, and hundreds of thousands homeless in freezing conditions with shortages of food, water, medicine and fuel. The crisis triggered market turmoil (including coordinated G7 intervention to support the yen) and global reassessments of nuclear safety. Japanese officials and the international community continued to push for cooperation and technical help as efforts to cool reactors and spent-fuel pools continued and uncertainty about containment and radiation releases persisted.

A multi-year scheme to steal and cash U.S. Postal Service money orders led to prosecutions and prison terms for several participants. Marc Saunders, a former USPS employee at the New Lisbon/Pemberton Township office, admitted producing fraudulent money orders using a stolen imprinting machine and supplying them to others. Saunders pleaded guilty in December 2017 and received five years probation with eight months home confinement and nearly $100,000 restitution.

Middlemen recruited to cash the phony orders received prison time and restitution: Eugene Bowen (35–36), who admitted recruiting people—including residents of Knoxville homeless shelters—to cash stolen money orders and splitting proceeds with Saunders, was sentenced to 20 months in prison, three years supervised release and $18,470 restitution; Anthony Bell, 39, received 1 year and 1 day and about $22,400 restitution; Andre Sutton received nine months and about $4,700 restitution. Sentencings were by U.S. District Judge Joseph H. Rodriguez in Camden.

A USPS Office of Inspector General investigation found the scheme exploited a printing machine left unsecured after an older money-order printer was not returned or destroyed by a postmaster in 2013. Stolen money orders were cashed across the country—primarily Philadelphia-area post offices, with some in Knoxville, York, and Jersey City—totaling roughly $100,000, with about 50 orders unaccounted for and the machine still missing. Investigators linked participants through serial numbers, cellphones and social media; many defendants had prior personal connections (family or childhood ties). The government was represented by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Camden.

The author argues that “sober January” is a misguided, guilt-driven fad and can be harmful, especially for people with genuine alcohol problems. Writing from personal experience as a recovered alcoholic, they explain how month-long abstinence became a tool of denial—something addicts can use to convince themselves they don’t have a problem because they can quit for a short time. The piece criticizes charities that promote dry January for attracting the very people who shouldn’t attempt it and notes that casual drinkers are generally uninterested anyway. Instead of a one‑month ban, the author recommends a more honest test: controlled drinking attempts, as advocated by AA co‑founder Bill Wilson—try drinking in a measured way and see whether you can stop. If you’re worried about your drinking, that kind of experiment and self‑honesty are more useful than a symbolic month off.
