- University of Winnipeg Library, in partnership with the University of Manitoba Libraries, the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, and Library and Archives Canada, has curated a growing web archive documenting Manitoba’s ongoing engagement with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The collection—funded in part by Manitoba Tourism, Culture, Heritage, Sport and Consumer Protection and the Government of Canada—captures webpages, blogs, news coverage and PDFs on survivors’ stories, apologies, cultural events, responses and other reconciliation and healing initiatives in the province. The project is ongoing and will be expanded as new material emerges.

- In separate news, a rare World War II German Enigma cipher machine sold at Artmark auction house in Bucharest for €45,000 (about $51,500). A Romanian collector had purchased the machine for €100 at a flea market; he recognized it as an Enigma and consigned it to auction. The instrument, made in 1941 and reported to be in near-perfect condition, was bought by an unnamed online bidder. The Enigma was used by the Nazi military to encrypt messages until Allied cryptanalysts—most famously at Bletchley Park, including Alan Turing—broke its codes, an achievement widely credited with shortening the war. Auction houses continue to fetch significant sums for Enigma machines, with a recent Christie's sale of a four-rotor Enigma reaching $547,500.

Scientists led by Shoukhrat Mitalipov at Oregon Health & Science University have, for the first time, successfully derived embryonic stem cell (ESC) lines from cloned human embryos using somatic-cell nuclear transfer (SCNT). The work, published in Cell, produced stable ESC lines from six embryos made with donated eggs and donor skin cells — including cells from a child with a genetic disorder — after years of refinement and prior success using monkey eggs. The team combined several technical adjustments (use of inactivated Sendai virus for fusion, electrical activation, and adding caffeine to prevent premature egg activation) that together improved efficiency; in one case 5–15 eggs yielded a line.

The achievement revives the long-pursued goal of therapeutic cloning: creating patient-matched tissues that could avoid immune rejection for conditions such as Parkinson’s disease or diabetes. Mitalipov argues SCNT could have an advantage over reprogramming methods for diseases caused by defective mitochondrial DNA because the egg supplies new mitochondrial genes.

Reaction in the field was cautious. Experts called the result a landmark but noted that induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell technology — which reprograms adult cells without eggs or embryos and won a Nobel Prize — is technically simpler and lacks the ethical controversies of destroying embryos. iPS cells, however, show molecular differences from embryonic cells, so direct comparisons between SCNT-derived ESCs and iPS cells will be important to determine clinical utility. Mitalipov’s team is conducting such comparisons.

Ethical and policy concerns persist: the SCNT approach requires donated human eggs and destroys embryos, prompting opposition from bioethicists and calls for restrictions on reproductive cloning. The work was privately funded (OHSU and Leducq Foundation) and carried out with attention to regulatory constraints on embryo research. Overall, the study provides a validated method for creating patient-specific human ESCs and adds another tool for regenerative-medicine research, while reigniting debates about ethics, safety, and whether SCNT or iPS approaches will be preferable for clinical applications.

A high-value theft of rare antiquarian books was carried out at a warehouse in Feltham, West London, on the night of 29–30 January. Reports and police statements say dozens to more than 160 books were taken while they were being stored en route to the California International Antiquarian Book Fair. Owners and dealers report losses ranging from individual caches (one dealer, Alessandro Meda Riquier, said 51 books including early Dante and Galileo editions were taken) to an overall haul widely reported at more than £1–2m.

Details and method
- Thieves reportedly accessed the building via the roof, cutting through reinforced skylights and abseiling into the warehouse, targeting four containers of rare books. CCTV captured the raid.
- The gang appears to have selected books from lists, leaving other items untouched, then removed the volumes in bags to a waiting van.
- Authorities and trade bodies have published lists of believed-stolen items and urged anyone offered these titles to alert police or the Antiquarian Booksellers’ Association.

Notable works reported stolen
- 1566 Copernicus: De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium (valued in reports at c. £215,000)
- Early editions by Galileo (Opere di Galileo Galilei, 1656)
- Isaac Newton: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica
- 1506 and 1569 editions of Dante’s Divine Comedy
- Other scientific and Renaissance works; named affected dealers include firms in Padua and Berlin.

Responses and concerns
- The Metropolitan Police are investigating (crime ref. 0502127/17) and have appealed for information; the ABA and Crimestoppers have also been notified.
- Dealers express devastation: the books represent long research, provenance work and irreplaceable stock, not just monetary loss.
- Experts warn that publicity makes legitimate resale harder but also note risks that thieves will break up or clandestinely trade the items, sell through opaque channels at steep discounts, or attempt ransom/insurance schemes. Rapid reporting and dissemination of the stolen-list is seen as critical to preventing resale.

Action requested
- Anyone with information should contact the Metropolitan Police (101) or Crimestoppers. If offered any listed titles, contact the police SCD6-ArtandAntiquesUnit@met.police.uk quoting the crime reference, and notify ABA contacts provided by the trade.

Donald Trump accused Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos of using his ownership of The Washington Post to protect Amazon from taxes and antitrust action. In a Fox News interview with Sean Hannity, Trump said the Post — which Bezos bought in 2013 — is being used “like a toy” and claimed its reporters repeatedly call with “ridiculous questions” and publish inaccurate stories about him. Trump cited Post associate editor Bob Woodward’s comment that the paper has assigned about 20 reporters to investigate Trump and said Bezos is trying to influence politicians so Amazon won’t face higher taxes or antitrust scrutiny.

The report notes Bezos has donated to both parties and that Woodward said Bezos urged the Post to extensively cover all presidential candidates so voters are well informed. Neither Bezos nor Amazon immediately responded to Trump’s allegations.

Avengers: Infinity War continued to dominate the box office in its third weekend, earning an estimated $61.8 million domestically and bringing its North American total to $547.8 million. Bolstered by a near-record $200 million opening in China, the film grossed $343.1 million worldwide that weekend and pushed its global cume past $1.6 billion, making it the fifth-highest grossing film ever. It also became the second-fastest film to reach $500 million domestically.

Two Mother’s Day–timed, female-led releases opened behind it: Melissa McCarthy’s comedy Life of the Party debuted in second with $18.5 million from 3,656 theaters (Rotten Tomatoes 41%, B CinemaScore), marking one of McCarthy’s lower opening weekends. Gabrielle Union’s low-budget thriller Breaking In launched third with $16.5 million from 2,537 locations (Rotten Tomatoes 27%), a roughly $6 million production. Studios noted both films skewed toward female audiences.

Rounding out the top five, Lionsgate/Pantelion’s Overboard was fourth with $10 million in its second weekend (domestic total about $29.6M), and Paramount’s A Quiet Place held well at No. 5 with $6.3 million in its sixth weekend (domestic total about $169M). Year-to-date U.S. box office was up 4.9% versus 2017, with anticipated boosts from upcoming releases Deadpool 2 and Solo: A Star Wars Story.

France has seen a striking cluster of infanticide cases in recent decades, prompting experts to point to a psychiatric condition called pregnancy denial as a common factor. High-profile cases include Véronique Courjault (convicted of killing three newborns whose bodies were found in a freezer), Dominique Cottrez (who admitted to smothering and burying up to eight infants discovered in Villers-au-Tertre), Céline Lesage (guilty of multiple infant murders), and several other mothers convicted in the 1980s–2000s of killing multiple newborns. In many of these cases the fathers were reportedly unaware of the pregnancies.

Pregnancy denial can take two main forms: women genuinely do not recognize or accept that they are pregnant, sometimes only realizing during labor, or they desire the state of pregnancy for identity reasons without accepting parenthood. Clinicians describe denial as strong enough to suppress usual physical signs (missed periods, weight gain) and to prevent consideration of abortion or preparation for a child. When the infant appears, some women reportedly see it not as a separate human being but as an unwanted intrusion or “trash,” leading, in a minority of cases, to infanticide.

Experts differ on origins: traumatic histories (abuse, rape) can contribute, but social and psychological factors—changes in the perceived value of parenting, failure to integrate a maternal identity, or being overweight and misattributing bodily changes—also play roles. Some specialists argue pregnancy denial is a quasi-psychotic state that should be recognized medically and legally so at-risk women can be identified and treated rather than punished alone. Authorities and clinicians warn the phenomenon is likely underreported and not uniquely French, raising concern about prevention, diagnosis, and societal responses.

This collection of articles and commentary centers on public moments and media reaction to First Lady Melania Trump’s demeanor toward President Donald Trump, portraying her as unhappy or distant and sparking public curiosity and commentary.

Key incidents cited:
- At a February campaign rally, footage showed Melania appearing startled and flinching when Donald Trump touched her arm while she prepared to deliver the Lord’s Prayer; the reaction prompted speculation on social media about possible marital or abusive dynamics.
- During the Trumps’ arrival in Tel Aviv on their 2017 foreign trip, video showed President Trump reaching for Melania’s hand and her apparently rebuffing or missing it; the clip quickly went viral and was labeled by some with the hashtag #FreeMelania.
- Similar awkward moments had been noted at the inauguration and other public events—hand-holding attempts that failed, a distanced dance, limited physical contact—that have cumulatively fueled a narrative of a cold, unhappy marriage.

Media and social reaction:
- Social media users and some columnists interpreted these gestures as signs of distress, alienation, or even abuse, with Twitter users and commentators calling the moments “sad,” “red flags,” or evidence that Melania resents her role.
- Some coverage emphasized the viral, schadenfreude element—observers on the left seeing pleasure in images of Trump being rebuffed—while others cautioned against overreading isolated public gestures that could be misinterpreted amid crowd noise and stage distractions.
- Reports noted minor controversies such as Melania’s verified Twitter account briefly liking a tweet about her facial expressions at the inauguration; staff later said the account wasn’t her primary one and passwords were changed.

Context and commentary:
- Profiles and opinion pieces framed Melania as a reluctant First Lady who did not seek this life, and suggested that Ivanka Trump has taken on many traditional first-lady duties in practice.
- Legal commentator John Dean (quoted in one piece) used the broader context of the Trump administration’s turmoil to suggest a stressful environment for staff and aides, though that point is broader than the coverage of Melania’s behavior.

Overall, the assembled reporting uses a series of public, awkward interactions between Melania and the president to argue that she appears unhappy and distant, producing widespread online speculation, commentary, and viral moments that have become a recurring subplot in media coverage of the Trump presidency.

Pantone 448 C — a drab, greenish-brown shade also called opaque couché and widely labeled the “world’s ugliest color” (associated by respondents with “tar,” “dirty” and “death”) — was selected by marketing research firm GfK after multiple studies to be used on cigarette packaging to reduce smoking’s appeal. Australia adopted the color in its 2012 plain-packaging law along with large graphic health warnings; early evaluations and international reviews indicate standardized packaging can reduce smoking prevalence and increase quit attempts. Following Australia, the UK, Ireland, France and other jurisdictions have introduced similar plain-packaging measures using the same murky color.

The document also summarizes extensive Australian tobacco data and control measures: long-term declines in smoking rates across adults and youths (e.g., adult daily smoking fell from the mid-20% range in the 1990s to about 14–16% in 2011–15, with further declines reported in later surveys), large drops in youth smoking and initiation, persistent higher rates in remote areas, disadvantaged communities and among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and decreases in tobacco clearances since 2012. It outlines a comprehensive tobacco control timeline—health warnings, advertising bans, public smoking restrictions, excise increases and the 2012 plain-packaging law—and notes government targets (reduce adult daily smoking to 10% by 2018 and halve Indigenous daily smoking) and continued excise hikes and policy measures (including reduced duty-free allowances). The summary also touches on color psychology: experts explain why 448 C repels (associations with waste or illness) while noting color perception is subjective and that color plays a strong role in branding and consumer behavior.

Kyle Schwarber’s improbable return and hot Series start powered the Chicago Cubs to a 5-1 Game 2 win over the Cleveland Indians, knotting the World Series at one game apiece. Having torn two knee ligaments in April and spent months rehabbing without playing a single regular-season game, Schwarber began his season in the World Series: he doubled off Corey Kluber in Game 1 and went 2-for-4 with two RBIs and a walk in Game 2, reaching base five times in nine plate appearances (.429) and supplying key offensive spark as the designated hitter.

Teammates and Cubs officials have dubbed his comeback “The Legend of Kyle Schwarber,” praising his relentless work ethic, film study and mental preparation while on the DL. Club president Theo Epstein and GM Jed Hoyer have managed his return cautiously—initial clearance was to hit and run bases only—but Schwarber’s early performance has prompted debate over whether he could play left field once the Series returns to Wrigley Field (where National League rules eliminate the DH). Manager Joe Maddon and the medical staff will evaluate the risk; the team plans to protect him but also take advantage of his offense, using defensive replacements if needed.

Schwarber’s story also includes personal touches—his friendship with a seriously ill young fan—and has captured teammates’ and fans’ imaginations as the Cubs head to Game 3 amid talk of him earning a legendary status if the club continues its postseason run.

A woman named Cassie Young, 31, who works as a digital director for a syndicated radio show, publicly called out a personal trainer who messaged her on Twitter offering to help her “get in shape” for her wedding. Young politely declined, saying she was happy with how she looked, but the trainer continued to pressure and shame her, insisting she should hire someone so her wedding photos would look “best.” Young posted screenshots of the exchange to Facebook with a message about body acceptance, explaining that after years of diet struggles and insecurity she has learned to love her body and won’t let someone else undermine that. She refused to name the trainer, saying she wanted the episode to be a learning opportunity rather than a public shaming. Her post went viral, drawing strong support for her stance and broader affirmation that people of all sizes deserve respect and that appearance shouldn’t determine self-worth.

Summary:

This document begins with notes about a web crawl ("Survey 7") run by the Internet Archive starting Feb 24, 2018. The crawl used Heritrix with maxHops=0 and was seeded from 339,249,218 URLs — specifically all Wayback Machine URLs that returned HTTP 200 in 2017 based on a Feb 1, 2018 query. The associated WARC files are not publicly available. The crawl is part of the Archive’s "No More 404" effort to preserve pages as they are created and the pages they reference, so links in older content can point to the version that existed when referenced and reduce broken links.

The remainder of the document covers the launch of MouseMingle (also called Mouse Mingle), billed as the world’s first Disney-focused dating site, created by Dave Tavres of Culver City. Tavres, a former Disneyland Railroad engineer, conceived the idea after struggling to find fellow Disney fans through mainstream dating services. MouseMingle offers typical dating-site features (profiles, photos, ratings), but emphasizes Disney-specific questions (favorite songs, characters, parks, memories, and a “Disney nerd level”) to match users. Profiles and photos are publicly viewable, but messaging and chats require a $12.55 monthly membership (the “55” referencing Disneyland’s 1955 opening). Tavres hopes the site will connect Disney fans worldwide, including those far from major Disney parks. MouseMingle joins a trend of niche dating sites targeting specific fandoms.

Moses Malone, the three-time NBA MVP and one of the game’s fiercest rebounders, died in his sleep Sunday in Norfolk, Va., at age 60, the Philadelphia 76ers announced. The Hall of Famer and NBA career leader in offensive rebounds was a central figure in the Sixers’ only title since 1967 — the 1983 championship — after Philadelphia acquired him in the summer of 1982. Malone’s arrival provided the physical presence coach Billy Cunningham said the team lacked and helped turn a perennial finalist into a champion.

In his first season with the Sixers Malone averaged 24.5 points and 15.3 rebounds in the regular season (team record 65-17) and 26.0 and 15.8 in 13 postseason games, earning Finals MVP as the Sixers won the title in 13 games overall. Known for a scowl on the court, a booming laugh off it, and a strong bond with teammates such as Maurice Cheeks and Julius Erving, Malone connected deeply with Philly fans. Teammates and executives recalled his basketball IQ, work ethic and personality.

Malone began pro basketball straight out of high school in the ABA, enjoyed a 19-season NBA career, was a 12-time All-Star, led the league in rebounding multiple times, averaged 20+ points for 11 straight seasons, was named to the NBA’s 50th anniversary team, and was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2001. The Sixers expressed deep sorrow, calling him “a genuine icon” and a pillar of their most storied era. No cause of death was immediately released.

FBI agents joined Cass County investigators after a mushroom hunter found human remains Monday in a remote, wooded area near E. 233rd and State Route Y, south of Belton, Missouri. A second skull was located Tuesday. The remains have been sent to the Jackson County Medical Examiner; age, sex and race have not been determined and no identifications have been confirmed.

Authorities have notified families of two long‑term missing Kansas City–area women—Kara Kopetsky (last seen leaving Belton High School in May 2007) and Jessica Runions (last seen Sept. 8, 2016)—but would not say whether the recovered remains belong to them. Both families have been working together and attending the search; they expressed desperate hope for answers and closure.

Investigators closed about 6.5 miles of State Route Y while they searched the area; searching was to continue pending daylight and weather. The probe has drawn attention to Kylr Yust, who was connected to both women: he was romantically involved with Kopetsky before her disappearance and was the last person seen with Runions. Yust was previously arrested on charges related to Runions’ burned vehicle (charged with “knowingly burning”), and has past arrests for violent offenses and animal abuse, but has not been charged in either disappearance. The sheriff’s office is continuing examinations and searches as the investigation proceeds.

Kate Gosselin, whose reality show Kate Plus 8 ended in September, has taken a non-TV job as a contributing blogger for CouponCabin.com. Starting Nov. 22 with a post on Black Friday shopping, she will write weekly money-saving tips aimed at large families, holiday shopping, stretching budgets and similar couponing advice. CouponCabin touted her as a longtime coupon user; Gosselin called coupons “like free money in your pocket.” Commentators framed the move as a pragmatic shift away from relying solely on television work, noting it keeps her children out of TV for now, gives CouponCabin publicity, and could even feed future media opportunities.

The Patriots launched a sustained, detailed public rebuttal to the NFL’s Ted Wells report on “Deflategate,” posting a dedicated website with a 20,000‑word critique by team lawyer Daniel L. Goldberg. The rebuttal challenges the Wells and Exponent findings on scientific, factual and procedural grounds, denies any wrongdoing by Tom Brady, equipment attendant Jim McNally or assistant John Jastremski, and accuses the league and investigators of selectively using or misinterpreting evidence to reach a predetermined conclusion.

Key points of the Patriots’ rebuttal
- Overall claim: The Wells Report is incomplete, incorrect, and biased — relying on ambiguous texts, flawed timelines, questionable scientific assumptions and prosecutor-style inferences rather than proof.
- Science and timing: Independent scientists (and even some aspects of Exponent’s own work) show the halftime PSI readings can be explained by the Ideal Gas Law, the cold game-day temperature (48°F), and the balls being wet. The Patriots argue Exponent’s simulations were driven by timing and other assumptions supplied by NFL lawyers (e.g., that gauging took up to 9 minutes, that Colts’ balls were measured before Patriots’ balls were re-inflated, and that the balls were not sufficiently wet), which skewed results against the team.
- Gauges and measurements: The rebuttal raises doubt about which gauges were used pre-game and at halftime, notes inconsistencies and recording errors in the officials’ logs, and faults the lack of measurement protocols and precision for both pre-game and halftime readings.
- Text-message evidence: Goldberg disputes Wells’s reading of texts between McNally and Jastremski. He offers alternate, innocuous interpretations (for example, that McNally nicknamed himself “the deflator” in a joking context about losing weight and that key “Tom” references were to others). He emphasizes that across thousands of texts there is no message describing a scheme to deflate balls or indicating Brady wanted sub‑regulation pressures.
- Brady’s conduct: Goldberg insists there is no evidence Brady requested or preferred footballs under 12.5 PSI; witnesses say Brady consistently asked for balls at the low end of the legal range for feel/consistency. Post‑game calls and texts between Brady and Jastremski are explained as reasonable responses to media attention and Super Bowl planning, not cover-up behavior. Goldberg also defends Brady’s decision not to surrender his personal phone, noting league counsel previously said that was unnecessary.
- League conduct and leaks: The Patriots accuse the NFL of leaking inaccurate PSI numbers to the media, failing to account for temperature effects, rushing to judgment, withholding key interview notes and communications with Exponent, and declining transparency about random PSI checks and their results. They say these failures created and perpetuated false public impressions.
- Personnel actions: The Patriots’ site acknowledges McNally and Jastremski were placed on indefinite unpaid suspension but offers only limited explanation (alleging Jastremski gave McNally Patriots gear without permission).

Additional details and fallout
- The Patriots posted the rebuttal shortly before the NFL Players Association formally appealed Brady’s four‑game suspension (for being “at least generally aware” of the alleged conduct). The team was also fined $1 million and docked two draft picks.
- The rebuttal cites Roderick MacKinnon, a Nobel laureate in chemistry, who reportedly disputes the scientific conclusions in the Wells/Exponent work; the Patriots later disclosed a passive investment connection with MacKinnon’s company after questions about a potential conflict arose.
- Goldberg challenges numerous specific “myths” the league relied upon — including the sequence and timing of halftime gauging, the significance of certain texts, the supposed secrecy of McNally’s movements, and the relevance of Brady’s statement that he wouldn’t expect tampering without his knowledge.

Context and conclusion
The Patriots’ response frames Deflategate as a combination of scientific misunderstanding (or manipulation), procedural sloppiness, and selective interpretation of ambiguous evidence that unfairly targeted Brady and the team. It calls for greater transparency from the NFL and argues that a proper scientific and factual review would have prevented or resolved the controversy quickly. The NFL and Wells have not publicly commented on the Patriots’ website rebuttal; Brady’s formal appeal of the suspension was filed as the rebuttal went live.

Six friends in Sydney accidentally turned up to the same wedding wearing nearly identical A$160 dresses from the same retailer. Instead of trying to avoid each other, the six guests (not bridesmaids) posed for photos with the bride, Julia Mammone, laughed it off and enjoyed the reception. Debbie Speranza posted the images to Facebook and the retailer’s page, jokingly calling the group “#backupbridesmaids.” The photos went viral—tens of thousands of shares and likes and thousands of comments—prompting amusement and similar anecdotes from users. Commenters described it as a great icebreaker for some and a nightmare for others; one related story even noted someone whose dress matched the curtains. The incident drew comparisons to the play Five Women Wearing the Same Dress and highlighted how the women embraced the coincidence and danced the night away.

Mitt Romney told CBS Evening News anchor Scott Pelley that his stance on abortion is clearer and more limited than the Republican platform: he supports legal abortion in cases of rape, incest and to protect the health or life of the mother. That position differs from language recently added to the GOP platform calling for a constitutional amendment to ban abortion without mentioning exceptions. Democrats have seized on reproductive-rights issues—highlighting Romney’s running mate Paul Ryan’s views and controversial remarks by Senate candidate Todd Akin—while President Obama warned Romney would not block efforts to restrict abortion rights. Romney called the debate a distraction and said the issue ultimately belongs to the courts, noting Roe v. Wade has been a judicial matter. His position has evolved over time: he previously backed abortion rights in a Massachusetts Senate run but as a presidential candidate opposes Roe and supports overturning it. The campaign reiterated his opposition to abortion except for rape, incest and where the mother’s life is threatened.

Reuters reports that Rafe Esquith, a once-celebrated Los Angeles elementary teacher and the only K–12 educator to receive the National Medal of the Arts, has been accused of multiple instances of sexual misconduct in a 66‑page document released by Los Angeles Unified School District. Esquith, 61, who taught fifth grade at Hobart Elementary for more than 30 years and ran the renowned "Hobart Shakespeareans" program, was removed from the classroom this spring and fired in October after the district’s investigation.

Allegations detailed in media reports include inappropriate jokes about students performing naked, comments encouraging students to view pornography, spanking, fondling and tickling female students, showing sexually inappropriate movies to fifth‑graders, and numerous sexually charged emails to students—some as young as 14—using terms like “hottie,” “supermodel,” and praising a 14‑year‑old as “sexy” and “gorgeous.” The documents also allege incidents dating back to the 1970s before he became a teacher.

Esquith has not been criminally charged and his lawyer called the district’s narrative fraudulent. In October he filed a $1 billion class-action lawsuit alleging mass wrongful removal of about 2,000 LAUSD teachers, claiming the district pressured older teachers toward resignation to avoid paying full pensions and benefits. The newly released documents have shifted public perception by substantiating many of the district’s grounds for dismissal.

More than 400 people have reported getting sick after eating at the Chipotle at 9733 Sawmill Parkway in Powell, Ohio, according to self-reports compiled on iwaspoisoned.com. The site’s founder, Patrick Quade, said 228 reports were filed suggesting 418 customers fell ill since Friday; local news accounts and the health department have received dozens to hundreds of inquiries. Reports describe symptoms such as diarrhea and stomach cramps beginning the day after eating; one account detailed a couple who ate chicken entrees and developed painful cramps and diarrhea the next morning.

Chipotle voluntarily closed the Powell restaurant on Monday for deep cleaning and removal of exposed foods and single-use items; the company said it is investigating the reports and cooperating with the Delaware General Health District. The health district inspected the restaurant, delivered 33 stool-sample kits to symptomatic patrons, and said it had received 518 related inquiries (95 emails and 423 calls). Inspectors previously visited the store last Thursday and documented two corrected critical violations (inadequate holding temperature for beans and improper cooling of cut lettuce) but also praised staff hand-washing.

Chipotle has said it is not aware of any confirmed foodborne illness cases. The company briefly closed the location and planned to reopen after cleaning. The incident follows lingering food-safety concerns for the chain dating back to 2015. (Separately noted in coverage: Chipotle promoted free guacamole for National Avocado Day and is pursuing broader menu/brand changes, but those items are unrelated to the Powell illness reports.)

Gwyneth Paltrow, 38, stars in a revealing Vanity Fair jewelry shoot photographed by Mark Seliger in which she poses topless, covering her chest with crossed arms and wearing only Louis Vuitton jewelry and fishnet tights. The photos highlight her toned, youthful figure; the coverage notes her dedication to a strict wellness routine—rising at 4:30 a.m. for yoga and eating clean—that she credits for her shape and energy. The piece also mentions Paltrow’s other activities: appearing as a surprise guest on the Glee Live tour to perform “Forget You,” running lifestyle site GOOP, publishing a cookbook (Notes From My Kitchen Table), planning a gym chain with trainer Tracy Anderson, past fashion collaborations, and recent sightings fueling speculation about a potential high‑street fashion project. The article touches on criticism of GOOP as patronizing and unrealistic for ordinary budgets.

Houston Tex‑Mex chain El Tiempo Cantina deactivated its Facebook, Instagram and Twitter accounts after backlash over a social post showing Attorney General Jeff Sessions dining there. The photo, posted Friday by the restaurant’s social media manager with a caption calling it an “honor” to serve Sessions, prompted calls for boycotts and insults; owner Roland Laurenzo says the post was made without his approval. Laurenzo and co‑owner Domenic Laurenzo said Sessions arrived with Secret Service, was treated like any other guest, and the image did not signal support for his immigration policies—specifically family separations—which the restaurant says it opposes. The controversy drew criticism from both opponents and supporters of the Trump administration and included threats to the family; El Tiempo took down the post and later suspended its social accounts amid the storm. The episode came amid a broader national debate over whether restaurants should publicly serve or acknowledge Trump administration officials.

A Chicago woman riding a Divvy bike died after colliding with a flatbed truck on July 1, 2016; authorities say this is likely the first U.S. fatality involving a bike-share bicycle. The 25-year-old, identified as Virginia Murray, was critically injured after both vehicles, traveling north on Sacramento Avenue, turned east onto Belmont and struck each other. She later died at the hospital. The city’s Major Accident Investigation Unit probed the crash; Divvy and the Chicago Department of Transportation issued condolences.

Bike-share systems—where users rent bikes from automated stations—have expanded rapidly across the U.S. since Tulsa’s 2007 launch and by 2016 reached tens of thousands of bikes in roughly 100 cities. Prior to this incident, a 2016 Mineta/TSRC study led by Elliot Martin and colleagues reported that collision and injury rates for bike-share riders are lower than for personal cyclists. Researchers and advocates attribute that lower rate to factors such as bike-share bike design (heavier, more stable, limited-speed bikes that discourage risky maneuvers), and to rider behavior; however, the study found no clear evidence that bike-sharing reduces broader-area bicycle collision rates. Safety advocates cited the crash as a reminder of street-safety gaps and urged continued infrastructure improvements and Chicago’s Vision Zero efforts to eliminate traffic fatalities. Bike-share fatalities have occurred elsewhere in North America (Canada and Mexico).

A 12-year-old Mulberry Middle School student, identified by Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd as Leviticus Jones, faces seven felony charges and one misdemeanor after sharing THC-infused gummy candy with classmates Thursday morning. Jones is charged with six counts of distribution of marijuana within 1,000 feet of a school, one count of possession of cannabis resin, and one misdemeanor count of possession of paraphernalia. Detectives are investigating how he obtained a Green Hornet brand package containing 100 mg of THC (ten 10-mg pieces), an illegal product in Florida since edibles are not available under the state’s medical marijuana program.

During second-period gym class the student shared the gummies; at least six seventh-graders — two boys and four girls — ate most of the package. Five students were transported to the hospital by ambulance and one by a parent after experiencing stomach pain, nausea, dizziness and near-fainting. School and emergency staff responded quickly; Polk County Schools Superintendent Jacqueline Byrd praised staff actions, urged parental monitoring of children’s online activity, and said all students are expected to recover. Investigators recovered the empty package in a trash can and continue probing how the 12-year-old acquired the illegal edibles. Jones’s parents are cooperating with authorities.

Overview:
The document reports two connected but distinct news threads about Hillary Clinton during the 2016 campaign: her public-persona efforts and interactions at the Iowa State Fair, and the FBI’s investigation into her use of a private email server while she was Secretary of State.

Iowa State Fair visit:
- Clinton made a highly publicized, hands-on appearance at the Iowa State Fair, consciously avoiding the guarded “rope line” image that hurt her 2008 bid.
- She embraced a very interactive style: shaking hands, taking dozens of selfies (a reporter counted 42 photos), hugging people, patting babies, sampling a pork chop, and even viewing the Butter Cow and a youth’s show cow.
- Her escort was former Senator Tom Harkin, who had just endorsed her; campaign planning appears to have placed friendly contacts along her route.
- Security blended into the crowd (wearing plaid) but the candidate was frequently swarmed; press access was limited by tight crowds.
- Clinton spent about 90 minutes moving slowly through the fair, listening to voters’ stories and responding to requests (example: she listened sympathetically to a mother seeking medical marijuana access for her gravely ill child and asked aides to follow up).
- She largely avoided the traditional soapbox stage; Bernie Sanders spoke there later to a larger crowd and drew criticism from some fairgoers for Clinton’s absence.
- On the campaign optics, observers and supporters said Clinton was more approachable than in 2008; she joked with aides and liked talking about being a grandmother.
- When pressed by reporters about her private-email controversy at the fair, she reiterated that she never sent or received marked classified information and downplayed the issue as not prominent in her town-hall interactions.

FBI investigation into Clinton’s private email server:
- FBI agents are investigating how highly classified State Department information ended up on Clinton’s private email account and are trying to trace who at State may have forwarded classified material from secure systems to unclassified accounts that later reached her.
- Some State Department emails from 2009 and 2011 circulated on unclassified systems and were then forwarded to Clinton; those emails were not marked classified, and it is unclear whether senders knew the material’s origin or sensitivity.
- The investigation is also probing possible foreign access (China or Russia), though assertions of hacking remain speculative.
- Officials say Clinton is not a target of the probe; she has denied evidence of hacking and maintained there is no proof she broke the law. Her spokesman emphasized she took classified handling seriously and that some materials may have unknowingly appeared on unclassified systems.
- The intelligence community inspector general, I. Charles McCullough III, informed Congress that “top secret” material appeared in her account; he cited two emails that he said should have been classified at the highest level (e.g., “TOP SECRET//SI//TK/NOFORN”), potentially tied to the Talent Keyhole satellite-intelligence program.
- The State Department has questioned some of those classification determinations, but the findings reflect concerns by some officials that State’s handling of classified info was lax.
- The FBI is conducting the inquiry centrally from headquarters (counterintelligence section), rather than a field office, given the national-security implications.
- Clinton previously turned over more than 30,000 work-related emails to State after deleting ~31,000 she called personal. A sampling by the inspector general found some emails containing classified content (reportedly 4 of 40 reviewed).
- Clinton’s lawyer handed a thumb drive of the 30,000 emails to the Justice Department and the firm that hosted her server (Platte River Networks) provided the physical server. Digital forensics could likely recover some deleted emails.
- Cybersecurity specialists working with the FBI will try to determine whether foreign actors accessed the server or emails.
- Prominent lawmakers have weighed in: Sen. Dianne Feinstein noted none of the emails alleged to contain classified material were authored by Clinton nor bore classification markings; others have pointed to systemic issues in how classified material is routed and marked.

Bottom line:
The piece juxtaposes Clinton’s deliberate effort to appear accessible and connect in-person with Iowa voters—an attempt to correct perceptions from 2008—with an intensifying federal inquiry into her use of a private email account that has raised national-security questions about classified material appearing on unclassified systems. Clinton presented the fair visit as proof she’s engaging directly with voters while continuing to deny wrongdoing and cooperate with investigators; the FBI investigation remains active and focused on provenance of classified information and any possible foreign access.

An elderly Massachusetts man, 90-year-old Nicholas Salerno, has been charged with soliciting a prostitute after reporting that a woman stole his necklace. Salerno told police he paid 48-year-old Karen Proia $100 earlier this summer for a sex act in his home. After she left, he noticed a missing necklace; police later recovered it at a South Yarmouth pawn shop. When Salerno reported the theft to Orleans police, an officer informed him he would be charged with solicitation; Salerno responded that he did not care. Both Proia and Salerno pleaded not guilty at their arraignments.

Michael Schumacher’s medical records have reportedly been stolen from the Grenoble hospital where he was being treated and have been offered to media outlets for around €50,000, his manager Sabine Kehm said. Kehm said the documents have been offered for several days, appear to be stolen and that the theft has been reported to authorities; she warned that buying or publishing such confidential medical data is forbidden and that the family will seek criminal charges and damages against any publication. Grenoble hospital has said it will sue for “theft and breach of medical confidentiality” to prompt an investigation. A Bild spokesperson confirmed the tabloid was offered the files but declined to buy them. Schumacher, 45, suffered severe head injuries in a December 29 skiing accident in Meribel, was kept in a medically induced coma for months, and was recently transferred to a Swiss hospital for rehabilitation.

Background: Respiratory infections like influenza have been linked to short‑term increases in atherothrombotic events. Researchers conducted a systematic review and meta‑analysis to test whether influenza vaccination reduces the risk of major cardiovascular events.

Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched through August 2013 for randomized clinical trials comparing influenza vaccine with placebo or control in patients at high cardiovascular risk and reporting cardiovascular outcomes. Six trials (five published, one unpublished) enrolling 6,735 patients (mean age 67, 51% women, 36% with prior cardiac disease) with a mean follow‑up of 7.9 months were included. Data were independently extracted; random‑effects Mantel‑Haenszel risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs were calculated for composite cardiovascular events, cardiovascular and all‑cause mortality, and individual events. Analyses were stratified by recent (within 1 year) acute coronary syndrome (ACS).

Findings: In published trials, influenza vaccination was associated with a significantly lower risk of composite major adverse cardiovascular events versus control (2.9% vs 4.7%; RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.48–0.86; P = .003). The protective effect was concentrated in patients with recent ACS (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.32–0.63) versus those without recent ACS (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.55–1.61); interaction P = .02. Results remained similar when unpublished data were added. Differences in cardiovascular mortality alone were not statistically significant in the pooled data.

Conclusions: Influenza vaccination was associated with a roughly one‑third reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events in randomized trials, with the largest benefit in patients with recent/active coronary disease. While findings support vaccination—especially for high‑risk cardiac patients—a large, adequately powered multicenter trial is warranted to confirm effects on individual cardiovascular end points. Public health implication: another reason to promote influenza vaccination, particularly among people with recent heart disease.

At least nine people died and dozens more were found injured after a Walmart employee in San Antonio alerted police to people inside a parked tractor-trailer early Sunday. An occupant of the trailer had asked the employee for water; when police conducted a welfare check they discovered eight bodies in the trailer and 31 people suffering various injuries; a ninth victim later died at a hospital. Survivors told investigators more than 100 undocumented migrants may have been inside the 18-wheeler at some point, and surveillance footage shows multiple vehicles arrived and picked up others who had been in the trailer. The truck’s air conditioning was not working and temperatures that day reached about 100°F (38°C); officials said many victims showed signs consistent with heat injury or heatstroke.

San Antonio police and federal authorities, including Homeland Security Investigations and ICE, have opened a human-smuggling investigation. The tractor-trailer driver, identified as 60-year-old James Matthew Bradley Jr. of Clearwater, Florida, has been detained and is expected to face federal charges; authorities said others involved will face state and federal prosecution. Local and state officials called the episode a horrific human-trafficking incident and urged prosecution and immigration-system reform. Walmart is cooperating with investigators and reviewed but has not released store footage. Two of the hospitalized victims are 15 years old.

KFC’s bunless Double Down — two Original Recipe boneless chicken filets used as the “bun,” with bacon, Monterey Jack and pepperjack, and a Colonel’s sauce — has arrived and reviewers tried it early. Nutritionally it’s heavy (about 540 calories, 32 g fat, 1,380 mg sodium) and very salty; most of the salt appears to come from the chicken breading.

Taste and texture impressions were mixed-to-negative. Positives: the chicken was moist and crispy, bacon was real (not artificial), and when eaten with a full bite of chicken, cheese, bacon and sauce the sandwich can be satisfying — potentially a popular “hangover” choice. Negatives: the bacon and cheese are small and often overwhelmed by the two large filets; the cheese sometimes seemed more like a spread or blended with the sauce; the sauce itself was described as an unremarkable ketchup-mustard-mayo mix. One reviewer found the chicken stringy and the cheese’s flavor intrusive. Overall ratings ranged from a cautious “not bad but wouldn’t order again” to 2/5 (“blech”); it fills you up but many felt it needed carbs or better balance.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has opened a preliminary inquiry into allegations that Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte and other officials committed crimes against humanity during the government’s “war on drugs.” ICC Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda said the office will assess whether there is sufficient evidence to proceed, focusing on alleged crimes since July 1, 2016. The inquiry is intended to be independent and the prosecutor invited cooperation from Philippine authorities.

The move follows a complaint and a 77-page report alleging Duterte’s direct responsibility for extrajudicial killings and mass murder spanning decades, including deaths in his earlier tenure as Davao mayor. Official figures cite about 4,000 police killings in anti-drug operations since Duterte took office in 2016; the complaint alleged more than 8,000 deaths. Supporters of the complaint, including opposition politician Gary Alejano and rights groups such as Human Rights Watch, say domestic institutions have failed to investigate impartially and see the ICC as the only avenue for accountability.

The Philippine government, via presidential spokesman Harry Roque, called the inquiry a misuse of ICC resources, argued many allegations predate the country's ICC membership, and described the anti-drug operations as legitimate police work. Duterte has repeatedly denounced the ICC and threatened withdrawal. The ICC’s preliminary examination is the court’s first in a Southeast Asian country; it will determine whether to open a full investigation into possible large-scale attacks against civilians that could constitute crimes against humanity.

A 51-year-old man doused himself with gasoline and set himself on fire in St. Peter’s Square in Vatican City Thursday morning. A Jesuit priest first tried to smother the flames with his frock and jacket, and two Vatican police officers then used a fire extinguisher to put out the blaze. The man was taken to a nearby hospital and then transferred to a larger facility with serious burns to the upper body; his condition was described as critical/ grave. The two officers were treated for smoke inhalation and hand injuries. Motives remain unknown; police found a note at the scene with the man’s daughter’s phone number. Reporters were not allowed into the square after the incident. Observers noted the case recalled a 2008 self-immolation in the same square.

Orexigen Therapeutics’ experimental weight-loss drug Contrave (naltrexone + bupropion) won a favorable vote from an FDA advisory panel, boosting Orexigen shares ~84% in heavy trading and lifting rival stocks. Advisors concluded the modest weight-loss benefit outweighs risks of increased pulse and blood pressure and agreed a large post‑marketing cardiovascular outcome study could be done after approval. The FDA must still decide by Jan. 31; it often follows advisory advice but is not required to.

Key data and regulatory context
- Contrave combines two long‑used drugs (bupropion and naltrexone) and is intended for patients with BMI ≥30 or ≥27 with comorbidities.
- Pooled results from four one‑year Phase III trials (≈3,200 patients) showed statistically greater weight loss than placebo (mean difference ~4.2%), and >30% of treated patients lost ≥5% of body weight — meeting one FDA efficacy standard but falling short of the FDA’s alternate mean‑difference 5% threshold.
- Safety concerns included higher pulse and blood pressure (especially early in treatment), increased rates of dizziness, nausea, and potential seizure risk (about 1/1,000 estimated). Two trial participants experienced seizures.
- The panel voted that cardiovascular risk data could be collected after approval (majority), though some members dissented, urging a pre‑approval cardiovascular trial because Contrave’s cardiovascular signal could offset expected benefits of weight loss.

Market and competitive implications
- The vote contrasts with earlier 2010 advisory rejections of Arena’s lorcaserin and Vivus’s Qnexa, which faced safety concerns and had their reviews delayed. Observers say Orexigen likely benefited from those prior setbacks by shaping its risk‑mitigation and post‑market study commitments.
- Analysts expect potential eventual approvals for Contrave and Qnexa and forecast U.S. sales potential in the $1 billion+ range for each.
- Physicians and dietitians noted the need for new obesity treatments but emphasized that lifestyle change remains critical and that the drug’s modest efficacy and safety profile mean careful patient selection and monitoring will be important.

Next steps
- FDA decision due by Jan. 31; approval timing may depend on final labeling and negotiated post‑marketing study plans.
- Vivus and Arena are responding to FDA questions about heart/birth‑defect risks (Vivus) and tumor findings in animal studies (Arena).

A Phoenix family racing to reach a funeral got an extraordinary last-minute reprieve from two pilots who turned their plane back to let them board.

Jay W. Short, 56, died of lung cancer on Dec. 16; his wife Marcia and their three children booked flights to Memphis so his body and family could be buried in Bolivar, Tennessee. Jay’s body flew to Memphis on Dec. 19; Marcia’s family departed that afternoon but a Sky Harbor cargo‑door issue delayed them, leaving only seven minutes to make a tight connection in Minneapolis. By the time they reached the gate the jetway door was closing and the plane was taxiing away; gate agents said it was too late and offered a later routing through Atlanta, which would have prevented them from attending the funeral the next day.

Seeing the family’s distress, the pilots of the Minneapolis–Memphis flight pulled back to the gate so Marcia and her children could board. The family identified the crew from badges as “Pilots Adams and Anderson” (other reports named Capt. Adam Cohen of Endeavor Air, a Delta regional carrier). Marcia and relatives say the act—rare in the industry due to strict on‑time departure rules—allowed them to make the funeral and has left them deeply grateful. Delta praised the decision as reflecting the human touch it wants customers to experience, though analysts noted such actions can risk company censure because airlines prioritize on‑time departures.

Berkshire Hathaway’s audit committee concluded that former executive David Sokol intentionally misled Warren Buffett and breached company rules by buying Lubrizol stock while promoting Berkshire’s acquisition of the company. The 18-page report says Sokol’s “misleadingly incomplete” disclosures violated his duty of candor and Berkshire’s insider-trading and ethics policies; he purchased roughly $10 million of Lubrizol shares and likely realized about $3 million in profits when Buffett announced the $9 billion deal. The committee is weighing civil action to recover trading gains and may seek damages for reputational harm, and the company will cooperate with any government investigations — the SEC is reported to be probing Sokol.

Sokol’s attorney strongly disputed the findings, saying his client’s trades were permitted by his contract and that Buffett was told about Sokol’s ownership twice. The report portrays Buffett as having been duped but appears aimed at clearing him of wrongdoing; it also notes Sokol omitted Citigroup’s role in introducing Lubrizol as a target. Sokol, once seen as Buffett’s likely successor after leading MidAmerican and NetJets, resigned in March. The committee’s findings are expected to lessen pressure on Buffett ahead of Berkshire’s annual meeting.

Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov held an extravagant, Kremlin-financed celebration for his 35th birthday in Grozny on Oct. 5 that drew international entertainers and sharp criticism from human rights groups. Photographs and video show Hilary Swank, Jean‑Claude Van Damme and violinist Vanessa‑Mae onstage at the floating, police‑cordoned event, which featured fireworks, acrobats and lavish payments reportedly in the six figures plus VIP travel and accommodations for performers.

Human Rights Watch and the Human Rights Foundation condemned the celebrities’ attendance, saying it lends legitimacy to Kadyrov, who oversees security forces accused of abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings amid the Chechen insurgency. The Human Rights Foundation said Swank had been warned about Kadyrov’s record prior to the event; her manager had emailed that she had “no current plans to attend,” yet she appears at the party and is recorded wishing Kadyrov a happy birthday. Thor Halvorssen of the Human Rights Foundation called the appearance “disheartening and shameful” and urged stars to refuse payment or reimburse fees when performing for controversial leaders.

Kadyrov downplayed who funded the celebration when asked, saying vaguely “Allah gives it to us” and otherwise saying he did not know. Some invited celebrities, including Kevin Costner, Eva Mendes and Shakira, did not attend. Representatives for the attending artists did not immediately comment. Human rights groups urged performers to avoid legitimizing figures accused of serious abuses.

Rep. Michele Bachmann’s public allegations that two prominent Muslims—Huma Abedin, a top State Department aide, and Rep. Keith Ellison—have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood provoked quick bipartisan condemnation in Washington but widespread support among her conservative base back home in Elk River, Minn. Local supporters and some former staffers say Bachmann is raising legitimate national-security concerns and remains a leading voice on the right despite her failed 2012 presidential bid and tensions with House GOP leaders who worry her conspiratorial rhetoric hurts the party.

Bachmann and four other Republicans had cited a controversial video series from the Center for Security Policy as part of a June letter asking multiple inspectors general to investigate “potential Muslim Brotherhood infiltration” of the Obama administration via Abedin. The material alleged, among other things, that anti-tax activist Grover Norquist assisted the Brotherhood’s access to the U.S. government—claims that drew broad criticism and were labeled conspiratorial by lawmakers across the aisle and some Republicans.

The controversy spurred at least one threat against Abedin, prompting NYPD and State Department questioning of a suspect and extra security. Bachmann has defended her actions as legitimate national-security inquiries and urged critics to read her letters in full; Democrats are targeting her seat again, backing businessman Jim Graves as a moderate alternative.

On the night of the Las Vegas mass shooting, concertgoers were fired upon from an elevated position in the Mandalay Bay hotel. Videos show people near the stage dropping to their stomachs—a common instinct—but that posture likely increased their exposure because the shooter’s overhead position allowed bullets, including stray high or short rounds from hurried fire, to reach areas normally sheltered from ground-level gunfire.

Audio indicates at least one weapon discharged in rapid bursts, suggesting automatic fire or a semiautomatic weapon modified for rapid fire (e.g., bump- or slide-fire). Federal rules make true automatic weapons harder to obtain, and investigators had not, at the time of reporting, confirmed whether Paddock used fully automatic weapons or altered semiautomatics. Clark County Sheriff Joseph Lombardo said authorities recovered at least 16 rifles (calibers .308 to .223) and a handgun from Paddock’s room; AR-15–style rifles were reported among them. Some firearms had been bought in Arizona.

The attack left at least 59 dead and 527 injured. Graphic video and audio from the scene captured a range of human reactions—from panic and flight to a shocked bystander’s defiant taunt—underscoring the terror and disorientation experienced by victims.

Actor Lou Ferrigno, best known as the original Incredible Hulk, was briefly hospitalized after a pneumonia vaccination that reportedly went wrong and left fluid in his bicep. The 67-year-old shared a hospital photo on Instagram and Twitter warning followers to watch how shots are administered—swabbing the site and ensuring the needle is handled properly. Fans sent well-wishes; Ferrigno said he’d be okay and attended an MMA event the night after his release. The reports note two pneumococcal vaccines (PCV13 and PPSV23) recommended for older adults, with PCV13 more commonly linked to injection-site swelling. Ferrigno’s reps had no immediate comment. The piece also recalls his recent acting work, bodybuilding career, and fitness ventures, including Ferrigno Fit.

Former Reagan budget director David Stockman told the Daily Beast he wants Republicans to force a short government shutdown as a “wakeup call” to confront America’s massive debt and fiscal imbalance. He urged Tea Party conservatives to “stand rigidly firm” to extract roughly $60 billion in cuts, dismissing warnings of severe economic harm from a brief shutdown as exaggerated and saying most furloughed federal workers would likely receive back pay. Stockman argued that even if Republicans win the immediate fight, the underlying problem will remain largely unchanged—“98 percent as large”—and the country faces a prolonged period of falling incomes, stalled growth and eventual painful debt restructuring.

Stockman criticized both parties and Beltway leaders: he called House Speaker John Boehner prone to caving, Republican budget star Paul Ryan’s plan philosophically attractive but irrelevant to current crises (it delays major changes until 2021 and does little on entitlements or revenue), and Democrats for not cutting defense more substantially. He warned that rising interest rates—potentially 300 basis points higher in coming years—would dramatically increase federal interest costs and expose Washington’s inability to find the needed savings. While acknowledging political risks for Republicans if the public reacts negatively, Stockman framed a shutdown as a necessary shock to force honest fiscal reckoning.

Here is a concise, comprehensive summary of the provided document:

1. English translation release of Book Five of Iran’s Islamic Penal Code
- The Iran Human Rights Documentation Center released the first comprehensive English translation of Book Five (Ta’zir and Deterring Punishments) of the Islamic Penal Code.
- Book Five was adopted permanently on May 22, 1996 and was not revised by the 2012/2013 amendments; it remains the operative text.
- The Book contains 29 chapters covering a broad array of offenses (e.g., crimes against state security, forgery, bribery, theft, arson, sexual morality offenses, family law violations, traffic crimes, etc.). The document excerpt reproduces many of its articles (notably Articles 498–728), specifying definitions, punishments, and mitigating/exempting provisions.

2. Key themes and provisions in Book Five (high-level points)
- National security: Articles criminalize forming or joining groups deemed to threaten security, propaganda against the state, espionage, gathering or transmitting classified information, aiding enemies, and related acts; penalties typically range from months to many years’ imprisonment, with harsher penalties in wartime and limited exemptions for repentance or cooperation.
- Religious and political protections: Insulting sacred Islamic figures or the Supreme Leader can attract imprisonment and, where considered Saab ul-nabi, capital punishment; attempts on top leaders or foreign diplomats carry multi‑year sentences.
- Forgery, counterfeiting and financial crimes: Detailed definitions and graded penalties for forgery, counterfeiting currencies, forged official documents, fake academic or medical certificates, and related offences; enhancements where intent is to disrupt the economy or state, and provisions for mitigation if offenders cooperate.
- Theft and related violent property crimes: Extensive grading of theft offenses by circumstances (nighttime, weapons, number of perpetrators, location, damage to victims), with punishments ranging from months to decades in aggravated cases; provisions for restitution and confiscation.
- Offenses by state officials: Specific articles penalize unlawful detention, abuse of authority, failure to follow legal procedures, torture or forced confessions, unlawful searches or interceptions, document concealment, and corruption; penalties include imprisonment, fines, dismissal, and bans from public service.
- Corruption, bribery, fraud and usury: Bribery (including non-cash forms), facilitating bribery, and fraud are criminalized with prison, lashes, fines and confiscation; some protections for those who report extortion; usury contracts are criminalized with prison and corporal penalties.
- Crimes against persons: Provisions on murder, attempted murder, assault, manslaughter by negligence, group fights, abduction, child endangerment, abortion, and defenses (self-defense conditions and limits). Some culturally specific rules are present (e.g., Article 630—a husband witnessing zina).
- Crimes against public morality and family: Laws criminalize indecent acts between unmarried people, public impropriety, running or facilitating prostitution, public consumption/production/import of alcohol, gambling, and failures of family maintenance; penalties include lashes, imprisonment, fines, and closure or seizure of premises.
- Cultural heritage and environment: Damaging, stealing or illicit excavation of cultural/historical assets, illegal excavation, trafficking and illicit export are criminalized with imprisonment, fines, confiscation and organizational complaint rights for the Cultural Heritage Organization.
- Property damage, arson, public infrastructure: Arson, destruction of public utilities and environmental pollution are penalized; aggravated punishments apply where acts threaten public order or are intended to oppose the state.
- Prisoner escape and concealment: Penalties for prisoners who escape; for officers whose negligence permits escapes; and for persons who aid, harbor, or conceal fugitives—scaled by severity of the fugitive’s offense.
- Procedural and mitigation notes: Numerous articles allow mitigation or exemption from punishment where offenders repent or cooperate, or where private complainants forgive; certain offenses require private complaint to be prosecuted.

3. Additional documents and human-rights context appended in the material
- Amnesty International report (excerpt): “Growing Up on Death Row: The Death Penalty and Juvenile Offenders in Iran”
  - Amnesty documents continued executions and death sentences for people prosecuted for crimes committed as minors, criticizing Iran’s partial reforms to the 2013 Penal Code as insufficient.
  - The report cites dozens of executions (73 between 2005–2015) and an estimated UN figure of around 160 juveniles on death row, with many spending years awaiting execution after unfair trials and coerced confessions.
  - Amnesty criticizes Iran for allowing execution of girls as young as nine and boys as young as 15 under domestic law, violating the Convention on the Rights of the Child which Iran has ratified (with reservations). The 2013 code allows judges discretion to consider mental maturity, and retrials were permitted, but executions and failure to inform detainees of retrial rights continued.
- Background on children’s rights & international law:
  - Summaries note Iran is a party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) but entered reservations that domestic Islamic law supersedes the CRC where conflict exists. Domestic implementation legislation is limited; some child-protection and labor rules exist (e.g., minimum employment ages, industry-specific protections).
  - The CRC text is appended in the material (full preamble and articles), emphasizing the international prohibition on executing persons for crimes committed under age 18 and standards on juvenile justice.

4. Case vignette and illustrative material
- A short case note mentions “Mahsa,” age 17, who murdered her father after an argument over marriage; her brothers seek the death penalty—an example illustrating how juvenile offenders may face capital punishment under Iranian practice and law.
- There is reference to a photo project “Waiting for Capital Punishment” (Sadegh Souri) accompanying the human-rights material.

Overall picture
- The document pairs a new English translation of Book Five of Iran’s Penal Code—detailing many ta’zir offenses and sanctions under Iranian law—with human-rights reporting highlighting continuing use of the death penalty against juvenile offenders despite limited reforms. Book Five codifies numerous criminal offenses across security, public order, morality, property, administration and family spheres, with penalties ranging from fines and imprisonment to lashes and, in some specified cases, death. Human-rights organizations argue that some statutory provisions and their application contravene international obligations, particularly regarding juvenile capital punishment and fair trial safeguards.

A group of 31 leading dementia researchers and clinicians from institutions including Oxford, Cambridge, Manchester and Imperial College have published an editorial in the Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease arguing that microbes may play a central causal role in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and calling for urgent further research and clinical trials of antimicrobial therapies.

Key points:
- The authors highlight substantial and growing evidence implicating specific microbes—principally herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV1), Chlamydia pneumoniae, and various spirochaetes (and some reports of fungi)—in the brains of elderly and AD patients. They argue these agents can lie latent and later reactivate with age, stress, or immune decline.
- They propose that such infections could trigger the hallmark AD pathologies (amyloid-β plaques and tau abnormalities) either directly or via sustained neuroinflammation. Supporting lines of evidence include colocalization of pathogen material with AD lesions, associations between HSV1 seropositivity and AD risk, animal and cell studies showing infection induces Aβ/tau changes, and the antimicrobial properties of Aβ itself.
- Genetic links are noted: the APOE ε4 allele, a known AD risk factor, also modulates immune responses and susceptibility to infections, suggesting a possible interaction between infection and genetic risk.
- The authors argue that antimicrobial or antiviral treatments (e.g., antivirals like acyclovir shown in vitro to block some HSV1-induced pathology) merit prospective clinical trials, particularly given the repeated failures of amyloid- and tau-targeted drug trials.
- They also raise implications for other neurodegenerative diseases and for blood transfusion safety, citing observations of microbes in blood components.

Responses and context:
- Dementia charities and other experts welcome more research but caution that current evidence is not conclusive that microbes cause most AD cases or that AD is contagious. They emphasize the need for rigorous studies and note ongoing research into immune and inflammatory contributions to AD.
- Some leading researchers characterize the microbial-causation view as a minority or controversial hypothesis and call for maintaining an open mind while pursuing robust evidence.
- The editorial frames the microbial hypothesis as deserving renewed attention and clinical investigation, analogous to past shifts in acceptance when microbes were found to underlie other diseases (e.g., certain cancers, Helicobacter pylori and ulcers).

Bottom line: The authors compile and synthesize decades of human, animal and molecular evidence to argue that latent infections—especially HSV1 and certain bacteria—could trigger or exacerbate Alzheimer’s pathology via neuroinflammation and induction of antimicrobial peptides like Aβ. They call for targeted research and clinical trials of antimicrobial therapies to test whether treating these infections can prevent or slow AD progression, while other experts urge cautious, evidence-driven evaluation.

Chinese authorities confirmed a forced late-term abortion in Shaanxi province after graphic images of the woman and her baby’s corpse circulated online and provoked widespread public anger. Local and provincial family planning officials said a preliminary investigation found the woman, identified as Feng Jianmei, was seven months pregnant when she was made to undergo the termination. Rights activists and Feng’s relatives say she and her husband opposed the abortion and that it was carried out because they could not pay a fine for exceeding the one-child policy. The Shaanxi provincial statement called the case a serious violation of family planning rules, said perpetrators should be punished and vowed steps to prevent recurrence; it acknowledged the act contradicted regulations banning late-term abortions. The incident has triggered outrage on Chinese social media, drawn condemnation from U.S. officials and rights groups, and revived scrutiny of China’s long-standing one-child policy and past reports of coerced abortions.

Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, an immigration adviser to President-elect Donald Trump and possible candidate for a Homeland Security post, brought a written DHS plan to a Nov. 20, 2016 meeting with Trump that was photographed by the Associated Press. The visible page, part of his “Department of Homeland Security Kobach Strategic Plan for First 365 Days,” calls for reinstating the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System (NSEERS) to track “all aliens from high‑risk areas,” and for “extreme vetting questions” for such entrants about support for Sharia law, jihad, gender equality and the U.S. Constitution. The plan also proposes ending Syrian refugee intake and references measures on arrest/removal of illegal immigrants, adding 386 miles of wall, Patriot Act–era powers, and changes to voter rolls; parts of the page were obscured in the photo.

NSEERS, created after 9/11 and which Kobach helped design, was suspended in 2011 amid civil‑rights criticism that it profiled people by religion and nationality. Civil‑liberties groups and Muslim organizations condemned the proposals as discriminatory and unconstitutional. Kobach has a longstanding record of hardline immigration and election policies and has advised Trump on border security and immigration, including support for building a wall and restricting refugees. A Trump transition statement said the meeting discussed border security, terrorism and bureaucratic reform.
