French satirical weekly Charlie Hebdo published caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad—including nudity and a provocative cover—shortly after an anti-Islam film produced in the United States sparked violent protests across the Muslim world. The magazine’s decision drew immediate criticism from Muslim leaders at home and abroad, who called it an insult and warned it could worsen tensions. French authorities condemned the publication as ill-timed and provocative but reaffirmed the country’s strong protections for freedom of expression; officials urged restraint and legal recourse for those offended.

As a precaution, France ordered heightened security at diplomatic missions and temporarily closed embassies, consulates, cultural centers and French schools in about 20 countries on Friday (jummah). Riot police were deployed to protect Charlie Hebdo’s Paris offices—targeted in a 2011 firebombing after a previous Muhammad-themed issue—and prosecutors investigated recent unauthorized protests near the U.S. embassy in Paris. Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault said requests to hold a demonstration in Paris against the film would be refused to prevent importing a foreign conflict, while Muslim community leaders in France appealed for calm and legal protest rather than confrontation.

Country star Carrie Underwood created a memorable moment at her Louisville show when she invited 12-year-old fan Chase onstage after he held a sign reading “Carrie be my first kiss.” After noting her husband Mike Fisher was in the audience and asking how they should proceed, Chase responded “Lip to lip,” and Underwood kissed him on the mouth. She later posted a photo of the kiss on Twitter thanking Chase and the Louisville crowd. The piece also notes Underwood’s Blown Away Tour will stop in Oklahoma City (Oct. 25) and Tulsa (Nov. 21).

Catherine Zeta-Jones recently checked into a mental health facility for a short stay to receive treatment for Bipolar II disorder, her publicist confirmed. The decision followed a highly stressful period for the actress, who juggled career and family responsibilities while supporting her husband, Michael Douglas, through treatment for throat cancer, and coping with other family and legal pressures (including her stepson Cameron Douglas’s prison sentence and a lawsuit involving Douglas’s ex-wife). Her rep said she is feeling well and is ready to resume work on two upcoming films. The report also notes brief context about Bipolar II—characterized by less severe manic episodes than Bipolar I—and that the couple, married since 2000, have two children.

Three adults have died and four children rescued after seven people got into difficulty in the sea off Mawgan Porth beach near Newquay, Cornwall, on Sunday afternoon.

What happened
- Around 13:15–13:30 GMT multiple 999 calls reported seven people caught in what is believed to have been a rip current.  
- A search-and-rescue response included Newquay and Padstow Coastguard teams, RNLI lifeboats, a Royal Navy helicopter from RNAS Culdrose and Devon & Cornwall air ambulances.  
- The seven comprised three adults and four children (described as teenagers). The children were rescued “walking wounded” and taken to hospital; they were uninjured and later looked after by police and staff at a nearby pub.  
- The three adults — a man in his 50s from outside the Devon & Cornwall area and a Cornish man and woman in their 40s — were recovered unconscious, given treatment on the beach (two received CPR), airlifted to Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro and later pronounced dead. Families have been informed.

Responses and context
- Police called the incident “tragic” and are investigating the full circumstances while supporting families. Local businesses and emergency services praised the rapid response.  
- Local surf operators said conditions included bigger waves and stronger currents than usual; one witness said the group were in the “wrong place at the wrong time.” It is not known whether lifeguards were on duty.  
- The RNLI and others warned that rip currents are narrow, strong flows that pull people away from shore and pose serious danger if swimmers panic or try to swim directly against them.

This incident follows another drowning off Newquay earlier the same weekend.

Vanderbilt University will remove the word “Confederate” from Confederate Memorial Hall after reaching an agreement to repay an 83-year-old donation to the United Daughters of the Confederacy. Chancellor Nicholas S. Zeppos announced the move, capping a 14-year effort to rename the 1935 dormitory that sits in the freshman commons. The UDC originally gave $50,000 in 1933 for the building’s naming rights; a Tennessee appeals court ruled Vanderbilt could only remove the inscription if it returned the gift at current value. Anonymous donors recently provided the $1.2 million required, and the Board of Trust authorized the repayment this summer. Crews began covering the carved word on the facade immediately.

Zeppos said the Confederate inscription is “deeply offensive and painful” to many and does not serve as effective history instruction; he framed the name change as part of broader diversity efforts at the university. Student leaders welcomed the decision. The UDC’s attorney criticized the move as erasing history. The story comes amid nationwide debates over Confederate symbols on campuses and public spaces, and in Tennessee specifically, where recent laws make removing such markers more difficult.

The estate of late artist Dash Snow has sued McDonald’s, alleging the chain copied and used his distinctive graffiti tag “SACE” and other signature designs as fake graffiti décor in numerous restaurants without permission. Jade Berreau, Snow’s former girlfriend, mother of his child and estate administrator, says she first asked McDonald’s in June 2016 to remove the tag from redesigned locations (notably a Brixton, London restaurant) but was ignored, and on Oct. 3 filed a federal suit in Los Angeles for copyright and trademark infringement, unfair competition, falsifying copyright-management information under the DMCA, and negligence.

The complaint argues McDonald’s prominently featured the “SACE” mark, presented it as if Snow had authorized or created the surrounding artwork, and benefited from his reputation. Snow—who began as a 1990s street artist with the IRAK crew, died in 2009, and cultivated an anti‑commercial, outsider image—never licensed his work for retail, restaurants or mass reproduction, the suit says. The estate contends the unauthorized use could damage the market value and integrity of Snow’s originals, which have fetched high prices at auction. Social media outcry over the “edgy” décor helped spur attention to the dispute.

The Wall Street Journal reconstruction and accompanying political coverage detail how last‑minute negotiations to avert the 2012 “fiscal cliff” collapsed, leaving Congress and the White House scrambling for a narrower, stopgap solution. Key points:

- Talks unraveled in mid‑December when House Speaker John Boehner tried to broker a deal with President Obama that would allow tax rates to rise for high‑income earners in exchange for spending and entitlement changes. Leaks and resistance from House Republicans undercut Boehner’s ability to sell the pact to his rank‑and‑file.

- Boehner, frustrated by caucus dissent, prepared a fallback “Plan B” to preserve Bush‑era tax cuts for incomes below $1 million. His lieutenants and several members publicly backed Plan B, and he moved to advance it when the broader deal stalled. Plan B collapsed on the House floor Thursday night amid opposition from both conservatives (who said it raised taxes) and others (who said it lacked spending cuts).

- Behind the scenes, the central impasse was revenue versus cuts. The White House insisted on immediate tax rate increases for households above $250,000 (later pressing for roughly $1.2 trillion in new revenue), while House Republicans demanded greater spending cuts and structural entitlement reforms in return for new revenue. Obama repeatedly told Boehner he wouldn’t accept a deal that replicated Mitt Romney’s tax proposals and reminded Republicans of the election outcome.

- A memorable exchange captured the dynamic: Boehner said he’d put $800 billion in revenue on the table and asked what he’d get for it. Obama reportedly replied, “You get nothing. I get that for free,” reflecting the White House view that going over the cliff would itself allow Democrats to lock in roughly $700+ billion by letting high‑income tax cuts expire.

- White House and Republican staff sparred over possible revenue sources (tax shelters, municipal bond deductions, rate increases). Negotiations included a Dec. 13 Oval Office meeting in which Obama framed a choice between a “big deal” and the economic pain of inaction. Boehner later offered to allow rates to rise on income over $1 million; the White House judged that insufficient.

- With talks stalled and Plan B defeated, leaders including Obama and congressional leaders called for renewed negotiations. Both sides expected any near‑term agreement to be a modest package — likely adopting the Senate tax bill that raises rates for incomes over $250,000, temporarily averting parts of the sequester, and postponing or narrowing the broader budget showdown — while deferring larger entitlement and deficit battles into the next year.

- The reporting suggests the 2012 election did not bridge the political divide; if anything, failed negotiations deepened distrust. Boehner faced a difficult choice about whether to try to pass a bipartisan measure (risking his standing with conservatives) or continue seeking a larger deal. The likely near‑term outcome was a “small deal” that preserves some tax increases for high earners but postpones comprehensive resolution, setting up another round of contentious negotiations around the debt ceiling and long‑term deficit reduction.

A Leipzig University professor, Annette G. Beck-Sickinger, apologised after emails she sent refusing an internship to an Indian student—citing “the rape problem in India”—were posted online. The exchange surfaced when a colleague of the student published the emails on Quora; neither the student nor the colleague identified themselves. In one message shared publicly, Beck-Sickinger wrote she did not accept Indian male interns because she could not support the reported rape problem in India and cited accounts of “multi-rape crimes” and threats to female tourists. Another student later said the professor had similarly rejected his PhD application in March 2014 for the same reason.

Beck-Sickinger, a biochemistry and bio-organic chemistry professor at one of Germany’s oldest universities (founded 1409), did not deny the emails but called the situation a “misunderstanding” arising from an “unpleasant discussion.” She said her lab was full and that she has accepted Indian students previously; she also said two Indian male students currently work in her lab. On the German Embassy website she issued a public apology: “I have made a mistake. I sincerely apologise to everyone whose feelings I have hurt.”

The German ambassador to India, Michael Steiner, publicly condemned her remarks in a letter, calling her generalisation offensive to Indians and to those working on women’s empowerment in India, and urged her to learn more about the country. The incident occurred amid renewed debate in India about violence against women following the controversy over the banned documentary India’s Daughter, which examines the December 2012 gang rape that sparked nationwide protests. The case prompted broader criticism of discriminatory, sweeping characterisations and highlighted sensitivities around women's safety, national reputation, and academic conduct.

At a routine 20-week anatomy scan, Toronto parents Kristine Barry and Christopher Havill learned their unborn son, Sebastian, had severe transposition of the great arteries (TGA) — the aorta and pulmonary artery were reversed — and, unusually, the walls between his heart’s chambers were closed. That combination meant oxygenated and deoxygenated blood couldn’t mix after birth, creating a life‑threatening situation that would allow only minutes to save him once he left the placenta.

A multidisciplinary team from Mount Sinai Hospital and The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) devised and performed a rare, and likely world‑first, in‑utero balloon atrial septoplasty (BAS) on May 18. Under ultrasound guidance, clinicians sedated and immobilized the fetus, inserted a needle through the mother’s abdomen into the fetal heart, and inflated a tiny balloon to create a roughly 3.5 mm opening in the atrial septum so oxygenated blood could mix. About 30 staff from both hospitals were on hand, including teams prepared for an emergency C‑section. The procedure took about 20 minutes and succeeded in stabilizing fetal circulation until delivery.

Five days later Barry was induced and delivered Sebastian vaginally; he was pink and crying rather than the expected “blue” infant. After birth surgeons repeated the BAS to ensure adequate atrial flow, and a week later Sebastian underwent the standard open‑heart arterial switch operation to correct the TGA. He recovered well, met early developmental milestones, and was discharged home. His medical team expects he can have a largely normal life, though he will be followed in a neuro‑development program to monitor for any later issues.

The parents expressed deep gratitude to the medical teams for the innovative lifesaving approach that allowed a safer delivery and effective postnatal repair.

Baltimore Ravens cornerback Tray Walker, 23, has died from injuries sustained in a motorcycle crash in Miami. Police say Walker was riding a Honda dirt bike without lights and not wearing a helmet when it collided with a Ford Escape around 8 p.m. Thursday; officers do not suspect alcohol, drugs or racing were factors. He died Friday afternoon at Jackson Memorial Hospital.

A fourth-round pick in the 2015 NFL Draft out of Texas Southern, Walker played eight games last season, mainly on special teams. He grew up in Miami and attended Miami Northwestern High School.

Ravens players and coaches expressed shock and grief. Owner Steve Bisciotti, coach John Harbaugh and teammates including Joe Flacco, Chris Hewitt, Terrence Brooks, C.J. Mosley, Jimmy Smith, Za’Darius Smith and Steve Smith Sr. praised Walker’s character, potential and smile, offering condolences to his family. Harbaugh also shared an open letter urging players to make wise choices and support one another in the wake of the tragedy.

A 33-year-old Bronx man, Grim LeRogue (born Joe Rogan), was arrested after running onto the field during Game 3 of the ALCS at Yankee Stadium. Police and media say he carried five photos — including one of Yankees slugger Alex Rodriguez marked with an X and a written threat (“You have to go bud, you’ve ruined too many of our white queens”), a photo of Cameron Diaz annotated “We will be together soon,” and images of Osama bin Laden (inscribed “I will serve you”), Whitney Houston (“Whitney Bin Laden” with “You will soon be my master’s wife”) and Bobby Brown (“You need to be terminated”). LeRogue, who has prior arrests for assault and burglary and is a known graffiti vandal, was tackled by security, charged with assault and interfering with a sporting event, and taken to Lincoln Hospital for psychiatric evaluation. His mother said he sought publicity and is self-publishing a novel.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, speaking on CNN’s Piers Morgan Tonight, said he’s fed up with the public debate about Warren Buffett and the so‑called “Buffett Rule.” Christie bluntly suggested Buffett should “write a check and shut up” if he wants to give more money to the government, rather than repeatedly calling for higher taxes on the wealthy. When pressed, Christie said his job is to serve all New Jersey residents and rejected framing policy as “class warfare,” arguing government should respond to everyone’s needs. The remarks came amid national discussion of income inequality and Buffett’s claim that he effectively paid a lower tax rate than his secretary.

A San Francisco home featured in the 1993 film Mrs. Doubtfire was the apparent target of a suspicious fire Monday night. Authorities responded around 8 p.m. to the Pacific Heights house at Broadway and Steiner after someone reportedly tried to set fire to the garage and front doors; investigators believe an accelerant such as gasoline may have been used and a doormat was set ablaze. Police remained on scene into the late evening; no suspects have been identified and officials said the incident did not appear to be a hate crime. The Victorian residence, which became a memorial site after Robin Williams’s death last August, is owned by Dr. Douglas Ousterhout, who told police he’s had problems with a former client but said he does not know who is responsible. An investigation is ongoing.

The Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery unveiled the official portraits of former President Barack Obama and former First Lady Michelle Obama, paintings that mark a notable shift in the tradition of presidential portraiture.

Barack Obama’s portrait was painted by Kehinde Wiley, the first African-American artist to paint an official presidential portrait for the gallery. Known for marrying contemporary urban culture with Old Master poses, Wiley depicts Obama seated against dense green foliage. The background includes flowers symbolizing key places in Obama’s life (chrysanthemum for Chicago, jasmine for Hawaii, African blue lilies for his heritage). Obama joked about negotiating his appearance with Wiley and praised the way Wiley’s work challenges ideas of power and privilege. Wiley created the work using thousands of photographs rather than traditional sittings.

Michelle Obama’s portrait was painted by Baltimore-based Amy Sherald, winner of the Portrait Gallery’s 2016 Outwin Boochever competition. Sherald, also African-American, is recognized for stylized portraits that render skin tones in gray to de-emphasize race and emphasize form and color. Her painting shows Michelle Obama in a flowing patterned halter dress, thoughtful with her chin on her hand. Michelle said she was moved by the portrait and highlighted its importance for girls and girls of color to see someone who looks like them in a major American institution.

Both portraits were chosen from portfolios of more than two dozen artists. Barack Obama’s will hang in the Hall of Presidents; Michelle Obama’s will be displayed in another gallery. Both will be open to the public.

Richard Carpenter has sued Universal Music Group and A&M Records in Los Angeles Superior Court, alleging the labels short-changed him and the estate of his late sister Karen Carpenter on digital royalties for The Carpenters’ recordings. The complaint says accountants hired by Carpenter found multiple errors: digital downloads were improperly classified as record sales rather than licensing (resulting in a lower royalty rate), downloads were undercounted, and an incorrect base price was applied to CD sales. Carpenter seeks at least $2 million in compensatory damages and asserts claims including breach of contract and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

The suit cites precedent in related litigation over Eminem’s recordings, where the 9th Circuit determined that digital downloads are licensing of master recordings rather than sales—an outcome Carpenter says supports his claim. He said he tried to resolve the dispute amicably but sued after failing to reach agreement. The Carpenters recorded 11 albums, 31 singles and won three Grammys; Karen Carpenter died in 1983. UMG had no immediate comment. Attorneys for Carpenter are Larry Iser and Greg Gabriel.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, 62, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and a leading contender for France’s presidency, was arrested and charged in New York with attempted rape, a criminal sexual act and unlawful imprisonment after a 32-year-old hotel maid accused him of sexually assaulting her in his Sofitel suite. Police say the maid told detectives Strauss-Kahn emerged naked from the bathroom, assaulted her in the bedroom and bathroom, tried to lock her in the room, and that he fled the hotel before being removed from an Air France flight bound for Paris. The woman was treated for minor injuries.

Strauss-Kahn, a former French finance minister, economics professor and corporate lawyer who earned praise for steering the IMF through the 2007–09 financial crisis and for coordinating European responses to the euro-zone debt troubles, has denied wrongdoing and is represented by prominent U.S. lawyer Benjamin Brafman. He was expected to plead not guilty. The IMF named deputy John Lipsky as acting managing director.

The allegations instantly created a leadership crisis at the IMF and upended French politics: Strauss-Kahn had been widely seen as the Socialist front-runner against President Nicolas Sarkozy and was expected to run for president. French politicians urged caution and respect for the presumption of innocence, though many said the charges effectively end his presidential prospects unless he is exonerated. The case also renewed scrutiny of Strauss-Kahn’s past sexual misconduct allegations, including a 2008 affair with a subordinate for which he apologized. If convicted, the charges carry substantial prison terms under New York law.

Summary:

Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 was shot down over eastern Ukraine, killing all 298 people aboard. Among the victims were at least six delegates and many others en route to the 20th International AIDS Conference in Melbourne—including prominent HIV researchers and global health staff such as Dutch scientist Joep Lange and WHO media adviser Glenn Thomas—which has left the AIDS community grieving and cast a sombre mood over the conference.

International responses and developments:
- The International AIDS Society, UNAIDS and numerous scientists, activists and conference attendees expressed shock and condolences. Organisers confirmed attendees were among the dead and later determined six conference delegates were aboard.
- Bodies and the plane’s flight recorders were eventually handed over, transported by train to Kharkiv and scheduled to be flown to the Netherlands; Dutch authorities led the forensic identification effort with international assistance.
- Evidence and U.S. intelligence indicate the airliner was downed by a Russian-made surface-to-air missile fired from territory controlled by pro-Russian separatists. Photographs of wreckage and forensic remarks suggested missile damage; investigators warned of site tampering and insecure conditions.
- International diplomatic fallout intensified: EU foreign ministers discussed and prepared tougher sanctions on Russia (targeting individuals, companies and potentially sectors such as defence, energy and finance) and agreed to add names to a blacklist; the U.S. planned to declassify supporting intelligence. Calls for stronger action ranged from targeted sanctions to proposals for a multinational security presence at the crash site to prevent evidence tampering.
- The incident strained EU-Russia relations and prompted global mourning: national days of mourning in the Netherlands, vigils at Amsterdam’s Schiphol airport, protests (including at the Russian embassy in Kuala Lumpur), and statements from world leaders urging full, unfettered access for investigators.

Operational and investigative notes:
- Two black boxes were recovered and handed to Malaysian and Dutch authorities; British and other experts were involved in decoding the recorders. Identification of remains involved a large forensic team using DNA, dental records and other ante-mortem data; the process was expected to take days to months.
- The crash prompted broader aviation safety discussions about advisories for conflict zones and airlines rerouting flights; ICAO’s limited role in closing airspace was noted.

Human impact:
- The loss included people from many countries (notably a large number of Dutch nationals and 27 Australians), and devastated families, colleagues and the global health community. Commentators emphasized the emotional and practical blow to HIV/AIDS research and advocacy, given the number and prominence of victims traveling to the conference.

Here are concise summaries of the two articles:

1) U.S. "Quiet Skies" air marshal program
- The Boston Globe revealed a previously undisclosed TSA program nicknamed "Quiet Skies" in which undercover federal air marshals have been conducting targeted surveillance of specific U.S. travelers on domestic flights since March (the Globe’s documents say similar activity dates back to 2010 in other forms).
- Internal documents indicate teams follow roughly 35 targets a day, observing passengers in airports and inflight and recording benign behaviors (fidgeting, using electronics, sweating, sleeping). The TSA later acknowledged the program but would not disclose selection criteria or whether it produced arrests.
- TSA defended the activity as preventative policing and denied targeting based on race, religion or nationality. Civil liberties groups and some air marshals expressed concern about constitutionality, privacy, questionable effectiveness and waste of resources.

2) Alexandria granite sarcophagus opens to reveal decomposed remains and sewage
- Archaeologists in Alexandria, Egypt, opened a 30-tonne black granite sarcophagus found under a construction site. Instead of treasures or a famous burial, they found three heavily decomposed mummies/skeletons and a red-brown liquid identified as sewage that likely leaked in through a crack and accelerated decay.
- The sarcophagus, nearly 3 m by 2 m and dating to the early Ptolemaic period, had been sealed with mortar and raised hopes it might hold a prominent figure; those hopes were dashed. An alabaster head was also recovered.
- Initial forensic work suggests the three may have been soldiers (one skull shows possible arrow trauma). Experts will analyze the remains for age and cause of death. Authorities dismissed sensational “curse” claims; the site was temporarily cleared amid concerns about odors and contamination.

A PoPville reader reports being refused service at Chinatown Coffee Co. in D.C. after asking for three shots of espresso poured over ice. According to the reader’s Yelp account, the barista declined, saying espresso over ice would "ruin it" and "shock" the drink, refused to make it, walked away, and made a snide remark. The piece notes this isn’t an isolated controversy: a similar 2008 incident at Murky Coffee in Arlington—where a customer publicly defied a barista’s refusal—went viral and prompted Murky to publish firm house rules against certain custom orders (including espresso over ice). The Washington Post covered that earlier “tempest” as well. The report raises the question of whether cafés can or should refuse to make customer-specified drinks and asks readers for their views.

A fast-spreading email malware campaign surfaced Thursday afternoon under the subject line “Here you have” (and variants like “Just For you”), flooding inboxes at many organizations worldwide and in some cases disrupting email services. The messages contained links purporting to point to PDF files or other documents; clicking a link downloads malware that masquerades as a PDF, attempts to disable security software, and propagates by sending itself to the infected user’s contacts and copying to shared drives and USBs. Because it requires a user to click the link, it is not a self-propagating worm on its own, but a social‑engineering–driven Trojan/trojan-like worm that can spread rapidly once a machine is compromised.

Affected organizations reportedly included NASA, Comcast, Disney, AIG, Procter & Gamble, Wells Fargo and several Florida agencies; federal teams including US‑CERT and DHS began investigating and issuing mitigation guidance. Security firms (McAfee, Symantec, SecureWorks) analyzed the threat, noting similarities to the 2001 “Anna Kournikova” email virus, multiple variants in the wild, and possible links to a hacker group previously tied to smaller August activity. McAfee and Symantec advise deleting the messages without clicking links, alerting IT, and ensuring up‑to‑date antivirus/security suites; officials also warned about potential Adobe Reader exploit usage in the attack. The incident highlighted the continuing effectiveness of simple social engineering and the importance of user caution and endpoint protection.

A letter dated Oct. 11, 2006, from then-Archbishop Leonardo Sandri — now a senior Vatican cardinal — confirms the Holy See received a confidential complaint in November 2000 about “serious matters” involving students at Immaculate Conception Seminary, corroborating Rev. Boniface Ramsey’s claim that he alerted the apostolic nuncio about Archbishop (later Cardinal) Theodore McCarrick’s sexual behavior with seminarians. Ramsey, previously on the seminary faculty, said his 2000 letter reported seminarians’ complaints that McCarrick invited them to his beach house and into his bed.

Sandri’s 2006 note, written while he was No. 3 in the Secretariat of State and seeking a recommendation for a former seminarian, explicitly referenced Ramsey’s prior warning. That acknowledgment supports Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano’s broader allegations that Vatican officials knew of McCarrick’s misconduct as early as 2000 and that the matter was not promptly or effectively addressed — including during Pope Benedict XVI’s papacy. Vigano has further accused Pope Francis of later reinstating McCarrick from alleged sanctions.

The disclosure is significant because it indicates the Vatican had early knowledge of the accusations long before McCarrick was named a cardinal in 2001 and before later actions (reported sanctions or restrictions) were reportedly imposed around 2009–2010. McCarrick resigned his cardinalate in July after a U.S. investigation found credible an allegation he groped a teenage altar boy; multiple former seminarians have since accused him of routinely bedding or harassing them. McCarrick denies wrongdoing and his lawyer says he will seek due process.

Summary:

Wednesday night, around 8:10 p.m., gunfire outside Frederick High School in Maryland injured two Frederick County students while a junior varsity basketball game between Frederick and Gov. Thomas Johnson High was being played inside. The school went into lockdown; about 200 people at the game were escorted to the cafeteria, questioned, and later released to parents from a nearby parking lot. The two teenage victims—one shot in the leg and the other in the back—were flown to a Baltimore hospital; injuries were initially described as non–life-threatening and later reports varied (one account said critical, others said stable). Police said the shooter(s) fled on foot, no suspects have been identified, and a motive remains unclear. Investigators are pursuing multiple leads, including student reports that four to five males wearing long coats entered the gym and left shortly before shots were fired, and tips that the attack might be gang-related or tied to school rivalries. Frederick High and nearby West Frederick Middle were closed the following day while searches and evidence collection continued; the high school reopened Friday with added security and counseling resources available. Authorities urge anyone with information to contact police.

Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies is a handsome, sober Cold War drama—based on the true story of Brooklyn insurance lawyer James B. Donovan (Tom Hanks)—that mixes procedural rigor, moral drama, and polished craft. Donovan is reluctantly recruited to defend accused Soviet spy Rudolf Abel (Mark Rylance) in a 1957 trial to demonstrate the fairness of the U.S. justice system, and later is tapped by the CIA to negotiate a prisoner exchange in Berlin after the 1960 U-2 incident (the swap of Abel for pilot Francis Gary Powers).

Tonally restrained and deliberately paced, the film emphasizes character and principle over high-octane thrills. Hanks plays Donovan as an everyman of steady decency—quiet, pragmatic, and committed to due process even as he faces public scorn, danger to his family, and pressure from intelligence agencies. Spielberg, cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, production designer Adam Stockhausen, and a veteran crew lavish the film with precise period atmosphere—muted blues and grays, elegant compositions—and meticulous staging. The Berlin sequences recreate the tense early days of the Wall and field a memorable array of German and Soviet intermediaries.

Mark Rylance emerges as the movie’s emotional center: taciturn, exacting, and quietly riveting as Abel, he steals scenes with a subtly powerful, nearly wordless performance. The screenplay—credited to Matt Charman and Joel and Ethan Coen—injects a dry, subversive wit and frames the story as a meditation on honor, duty, and the virtues of civility in a paranoid era. That moral focus makes an insurance lawyer the unlikely hero, and the film’s insistence on kindness and legal principle is its defining, sometimes muddled, strength.

Pacing can sag—especially during some of the Berlin negotiations—and the film stretches to nearly two and a half hours and supplies multiple endings. Still, Bridge of Spies is a polished, thoughtful piece of filmmaking that rewards patience, elevates Hanks’s earnest lead and Rylance’s breakout turn, and lingers as a restrained reflection on American values and Cold War brinkmanship. Critical response generally praised its craft and performances (three out of four stars in some reviews).

Netflix has officially cleared a Gilmore Girls revival — billed as a farewell season — now confirmed as four 90-minute movies set in the present day and unfolding over a calendar year (one film per season). Creator and executive producer Amy Sherman‑Palladino and her husband Daniel Palladino will write and direct all four films. After lengthy negotiations, series leads Alexis Bledel (Rory) and Lauren Graham (Lorelai) have closed deals to return, and the principal quartet is reunited: Scott Patterson (Luke) and Kelly Bishop (Emily) are also signed. Sean Gunn (Kirk) and Keiko Agena (Lane) have been confirmed as well. Production is being handled by Dorothy Parker Drank Here Productions in association with Warner Bros. Television; Netflix announced the project via tweet and the cast has already done a table read for the first film. Some original regulars (notably Liza Weil and Yanic Truesdale) had not been listed among confirmations, and Melissa McCarthy’s participation remained unclear. No final title or premiere date has been announced.

U.S. and Mexican authorities uncovered two sophisticated cross-border drug-smuggling tunnels linking warehouses in Tijuana and San Diego’s Otay Mesa industrial park on April 1–3, 2014. No drugs or contraband were found. The first tunnel, discovered Tuesday under a San Diego warehouse, ran about 600 yards, 70 feet underground, and included wooden trusses, lighting, a crude rail and a pulley hoist; the warehouse contained children’s toys and TVs. The second, found Thursday after Mexican investigators followed U.S. leads, was roughly 700 yards long and more advanced, with ventilation and a multi-tiered electric rail system. Authorities say the passages cost millions to build and represent the sixth and seventh “super tunnels” found between Tijuana and San Diego since 2010 (more than 80 cross-border tunnels have been found in the Southwest since 2006). On Wednesday ICE arrested Glennys Rodriguez, a 73-year-old Chula Vista woman accused of managing logistics for the operation; she faces federal charges related to maintaining a drug-involved premises. Investigators named several other suspected associates in the complaint, including a man previously caught building cross-border tunnels. Officials emphasized that traditional detective work, not just technology, led to the discoveries.

At the G-20 summit in Toronto, leaders of major economies agreed—amid visible tensions—on a broad framework to reduce deficits and stabilize public debt while warning that the global recovery remains fragile and fiscal cuts must be calibrated so as not to choke growth.

Key outcomes
- Developed countries pledged to halve their annual budget deficits by 2013 and to stabilize overall public-debt-to-GDP ratios by 2016. The timeline is nonbinding and “tailored to national circumstances,” with Japan explicitly not expected to meet the targets.
- The communiqué emphasized balancing short-term growth support with medium-term fiscal sustainability and included caveats that deficit reduction be paced and paired with growth-enhancing reforms.
- Leaders endorsed tougher bank capital standards and a commitment that the financial sector make a “fair” contribution to crisis costs, but deferred details (including any global bank tax) to national decisions and allowed transition periods for weaker banks.
- The G-20 urged rebalancing: surplus countries (notably China) should boost domestic demand through higher spending, infrastructure investment, stronger social safety nets and greater exchange-rate flexibility, while surplus-rich advanced economies should narrow trade gaps.

Political dynamics and disagreement
- The deficit timetable was championed by host Stephen Harper and supported by Germany and Britain; the Obama administration accepted the goal reluctantly to avoid isolating the U.S. and key partners, stressing that cuts should not undermine job creation and recovery.
- European leaders pressed harder for austerity because of sovereign-debt worries; the U.S. and some economists warned rapid, synchronized fiscal tightening risks a double-dip recession. IMF and some economists cautioned against simplistic deficit targets and urged country-specific policy mixes.
- Negotiations left several hard choices unresolved: no global bank tax agreement, timing for implementing capital rules remained flexible, and much of the technical work on financial reform was left for follow-up meetings.

Other notes
- The summit produced some wins for the U.S.: European bank stress tests, progress on financial-regulatory overhaul, and China’s pledge toward gradual currency appreciation (though language on China’s commitments was toned down at China’s request).
- The overall G-20 message was dual: heavily indebted advanced economies must gradually rein in deficits, while surplus and emerging economies should help rebalance global demand—yet leaders agreed to proceed cautiously to protect recovery.

Ivanka Trump used a personal email account extensively for White House business in 2017, according to reviews by White House ethics officials and documents obtained by watchdog group American Oversight. The review found she sent hundreds of messages from a private account (on a domain she shared with Jared Kushner) to Cabinet officials, aides and personal staffers. Most messages were logistical—scheduling, travel and family-related coordination—but fewer than 100 messages involved substantive official business with other administration officials. White House lawyers discovered the practice last fall when responding to public-records requests from several agencies.

Her lawyer and ethics spokesman say she began using the private account before being briefed on White House email rules, did not transmit classified information, did not create a private server, turned over government-related emails for preservation, and did not delete messages. The White House counsel relied on Ivanka’s personal attorney, Abbe Lowell, to review her private inbox and forward official messages to her government account. Critics, including American Oversight, argue the practice risks violating the Presidential Records Act and raises questions about whether all records were preserved and if any sensitive material was mishandled.

The revelations drew attention because of Donald Trump’s 2016 criticism of Hillary Clinton’s private-email practices; commentators and watchdogs noted the apparent hypocrisy and urged congressional scrutiny. Legal context: using a personal email is not per se illegal, but officials must forward official correspondence to government accounts within 20 days and must not transmit classified or privileged material on private systems.

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan granted longtime Trump Organization CFO Allen Weisselberg immunity and he testified before a grand jury in the federal investigation into Michael Cohen, sources tell NBC News (first reported by the Wall Street Journal). Weisselberg is identified as “Executive 1” in the criminal information from the Cohen case. Prosecutors say Cohen invoiced “Executive 1” for “Payment for services rendered for the month of January and February, 2017,” a reimbursement tied to Cohen’s payment to Stormy Daniels. Weisselberg then emailed another Trump Organization executive instructing payment from the Trust and to post it as legal expenses with a retainer description.

Weisselberg, 70, a Trump Organization fixture since the 1970s and former treasurer of the Donald J. Trump Foundation, also appears in a recorded April 2016 phone call between Cohen and Donald Trump. On that tape Cohen says he spoke with Weisselberg about setting up a company to handle a payment related to a story involving Karen McDougal and referenced coordinating with David Pecker of American Media/National Enquirer. The U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment.

Thai authorities have warned traders against price gouging as demand for black and white mourning clothes surges following the death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej and the government-declared year of mourning. The Commerce Ministry has ordered provincial offices to survey prices and supplies, asked sellers to clearly label prices and refrain from hoarding or unreasonable mark-ups, and deployed inspection teams to markets. Violators face up to seven years in jail and/or fines up to 140,000 baht. Retailers report brisk sales—especially of black shirts—with some vendors saying they buy at about 90 baht and sell at 120–130 baht. Authorities also plan to coordinate with distributors to ensure adequate nationwide supplies. Shoppers say modest price rises are secondary to observing the mourning period.

A fight over a break-room light at Philadelphia International Airport led to a deadly stabbing Thursday morning. Around 11:30 a.m. in a secure Terminal E break room used by Worldwide Flight Services (an aircraft-cleaning contractor for Frontier Airlines), three cleaning employees argued after one worker turned off a light. The dispute escalated when a third man produced a sharp implement—investigators suspect a box cutter—and stabbed 28-year-old Aaron Jenkins in the abdomen/thigh area. Jenkins was taken to Penn Presbyterian Trauma Center and later died. The two other workers fled into the departures hall but surrendered when confronted by police. Police have charged 35-year-old Kevin Emanuel with murder and possession of an instrument of a crime; the weapon has not been recovered. The incident did not disrupt airport operations. Authorities corrected earlier reports that the men were Frontier employees— they work for the cleaning contractor.

Many Afghan army units are running short of vital, armored equipment because they cannot repair damaged vehicles or obtain replacements. After a brutal fighting season, battalions across Afghanistan report large shares of Humvees and armored trucks out of service—some units have lost 15–75 percent of their vehicles to roadside bombs, RPGs and wear. Afghan mechanics often have manuals but lack spare parts, oil and trained personnel; bureaucracy and a weak, corruption-prone Defense Ministry procurement system leave units waiting months or years for parts or replacements. That degrades operations (fewer patrols, overcrowded vehicles, more walking) and affects even elite special-forces teams. NATO and U.S. officials acknowledge the problem and say they are working to improve supply chains and logistics as advisers and forces draw down, but Afghan commanders worry that another fighting season could further cripple their mobility.

Separately, as U.S. forces withdraw, vast amounts of American equipment are being scrapped in Afghanistan. Shipping everything home is prohibitively expensive, so millions of pounds of gear—often deliberately destroyed to prevent dual-use items from aiding insurgent bomb-making—is sold as scrap. The policy produces huge scrapyards around bases (notably Bagram) piled with flattened vehicles, appliances and military gear. Local entrepreneurs buy and recycle material, but many Afghans resent that usable items are destroyed rather than handed over intact (unlike past withdrawals such as the Soviet exit). The flow of scrap reflects both the rapid U.S. drawdown and Afghan anxieties about the country’s future stability.

Sen. Marco Rubio is weighing whether to run for reelection to his Senate seat after the Orlando mass shooting prompted fresh reflection, but he hadn’t decided as of midweek and said he would talk with family before announcing anything. Longtime friend Florida Lt. Gov. Carlos Lopez-Cantera—who has run in the crowded GOP primary for over a year with Rubio’s prior encouragement—pressed Rubio to reconsider running while they witnessed the aftermath in Orlando. Lopez-Cantera told Politico he remains committed to his campaign and insisted there is no secret deal between the two; if Rubio runs, Lopez-Cantera will not file by the June 24 deadline and says he’ll continue only if Rubio stays out.

Rubio’s potential candidacy has frozen fundraising and dampened enthusiasm among other Republicans, and some GOP groups have signaled reluctance to spend in the race unless a clear nominee emerges. Polling shows Rubio would be the strongest Republican against Democrat Patrick Murphy in a contest that could affect control of the Senate, which is why party leaders and donors have urged him to run. Allies and rivals have circulated rumors of backroom deals—denied by both men—which have fueled skepticism.

Friends say Rubio is torn: a return to private life would bring a bigger paycheck and more family time (he’s been interviewing for lucrative post-Senate opportunities), while staying in the Senate would preserve his platform, influence on policy (especially foreign policy), and access to classified briefings. Rubio emphasized the gravity of the Orlando attack as a factor making him reconsider public service, but both he and Lopez-Cantera stressed their friendship remains intact despite the political strain. Other GOP hopefuls are assessing their options in light of Rubio’s indecision; some will keep running regardless, while others may shift plans depending on his final choice.

This piece is a lengthy, personal reaction to Rex Reed’s scathing New York Observer review of the Melissa McCarthy–Jason Bateman comedy Identity Thief. The author opens by recalling when they first noticed McCarthy (Bridesmaids) and expresses anger at Reed for attacking her weight in his review.

They then quote and recount Reed’s critique: he gives the film one star and calls it contrived, vulgar, and unfunny. Reed summarizes the plot—Bateman’s character Sandy Patterson is victimized when McCarthy’s Diana steals his identity and runs up charges; the two embark on a cross-country road trip filled with implausible set pieces (fights, arrests, car crashes, snake den, motel scenes) while being chased by criminals and a bounty hunter. Reed argues the premise is dramatic rather than comedic once the real harms of identity theft are filled in, and that the screenplay (by Craig Mazin and Jerry Eeten) is full of holes and weak plotting. He praises McCarthy’s occasional ability to coax laughs but otherwise dismisses the film as mean-spirited, sentimental inorganically at the end, and exploitative—relying on crude jokes about weight and vulgarity. Reed also criticizes director Seth Gordon and likens the film to inferior Judd Apatow/Farrelly-style comedies, saying it wastes Bateman’s talents and undermines McCarthy’s good will from Bridesmaids.

Overall tone: outraged at Reed’s fat-shaming, and using his review to depict Identity Thief as a poorly written, badly directed, and offensively crude comedy that fails to capitalize on its performers or premise.

A Jefferson County judge dismissed the capital murder charge against Gabe Watson Feb. 23, 2012, ending his Alabama prosecution for the 2003 drowning death of his wife, Tina, during their Australian honeymoon. Circuit Judge Tommy Nail granted a defense motion for acquittal after the prosecution rested, finding the state had not presented evidence that would allow a reasonable person to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Watson intentionally killed his wife for financial gain. Nail said the evidence was “sorely lacking,” that any finding of intent would be speculative, and he found the prosecution’s proof of a profit motive unconvincing.

The ruling came before the defense presented its case and before the jury deliberated, prompting cheers in the courtroom. Watson, 34, who had previously pleaded guilty to negligent manslaughter in Australia and served 18 months there, walked out with his wife. Defense attorneys stressed that the lone eyewitness who saw the couple underwater believed Watson was trying to save Tina, and they argued Watson stood to gain little financially because Tina’s father was the beneficiary of her policy. Prosecutors had alleged Watson discussed insurance before the trip and tried to collect after her death; the judge said those links were insufficient.

Tina’s father, Tommy Thomas, had testified earlier about how the family learned of her death and why they grew suspicious of Watson, but Judge Nail limited some testimony and concluded the state’s case did not meet the standard for intentional murder. Prosecutor Don Valeska said he had not previously experienced a trial ending with a judge’s acquittal in 41 years. Legal observers called the decision a significant rebuke of the prosecution’s case.

On Dec. 2, 2015, a husband-and-wife team, Syed Rizwan Farook and Tashfeen Malik, carried out a mass shooting at a holiday event at the Inland Regional Center in San Bernardino, California, killing 14 and wounding 21. In the immediate chaos, dispatch recordings show officers and dispatchers struggling with confusion about suspects, casualties and a possible bomb. An officer quickly named Farook as a possible suspect after noting he had left a work meeting “out of the blue” about 20 minutes before the shooting and matched the gunman’s description. Witnesses described masked gunmen who fired in bursts, reloaded and fled; staff who had trained for active-shooter scenarios hid under tables as shots continued.

About four hours after the attack, a vehicle chase ended in a shootout between the couple and police; the pair fired 76 rounds and were killed after officers returned heavy fire. Recordings from the aftermath include reports of multiple dead, concern about an explosive device, and gunfire during the final confrontation.

Subsequent reporting by U.S. officials and media indicated Farook and Malik had prepared for the attack over months or longer: they practiced at a local gun range, made financial preparations (including a roughly $28,500 deposit into Farook’s account that investigators are probing), and arranged care for their infant daughter and Farook’s mother. Officials also said Farook may have discussed plotting an attack as early as 2012 with another person but backed off after terrorism-related arrests. The FBI concluded the couple had become radicalized; investigators continue to examine their preparations, financing and any earlier plotting.

Summary:

The second night of the Democratic National Convention in Charlotte centers on former President Bill Clinton delivering a prime-time speech to nominate and endorse Barack Obama for re-election. Clinton’s role is viewed as high-reward but potentially risky for Obama — he can energize and persuade undecided and white middle-class voters by recalling the 1990s recovery, yet he could also invite comparisons that spotlight differences between the two presidents. The Obama campaign says it’s had discussions with Clinton and trusts he’ll endorse Obama strongly; it had not fully vetted his text publicly but downplayed concerns.

Elizabeth Warren, the Democratic Senate nominee from Massachusetts and creator of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, is another focal point. Warren is framed as a rising Democratic star and will introduce Clinton; her contest with Republican Sen. Scott Brown is one of the nation’s closest and most expensive Senate races. The campaign contrasts Warren’s consumer- and middle-class-focused message and infrastructure agenda with Brown’s bipartisan, regular-guy appeal. Polling shows a tight race; both candidates agreed to a “People’s Pledge” limiting outside spending.

The convention program also emphasizes mobilizing female voters with several prominent female speakers (including Sandra Fluke), the formal roll call to renominate Obama and Biden, and the prospect of Obama making an unannounced appearance before his Thursday night speech. Coverage notes the tense-but-functional relationship between Clinton and Obama—respectful but not intimate—and the strategic calculations behind showcasing Clinton as a surrogate to bolster Obama’s economic credibility.

Researchers from Indiana University studied how medium (email vs. voicemail) and task type (romantic vs. utilitarian) affect senders’ physiological arousal and the emotional content of messages. In a lab experiment with 72 college-age participants, psychophysiological sensors measured arousal and facial-muscle indicators of emotion while participants composed either a voicemail or an email for a romantic or utilitarian scenario.

Key findings:
- Email triggered greater physiological arousal than voicemail across both task types.
- For romantic tasks, email messages were more positive and contained stronger, more thoughtful language than voicemails. The authors suggest senders may compensate for lack of vocal tone by carefully crafting more positive text.
- For utilitarian tasks the pattern reversed: voicemails were more positive than emails.
- Participants did not rely heavily on emoticons; instead they invested more time selecting words when composing emails.
- Gender did not affect results.
- These outcomes challenge assumptions from media naturalness theory that lean, text-based media are inherently worse for emotional communication—at least for millennials who grew up with email and texting.

Practical notes: the authors caution that richer, synchronous channels (phone, face-to-face, video) remain preferable for ensuring shared understanding or handling complex issues, but the study shows that the chosen medium influences both how senders feel and what they say.

In a KARE 11 Land of 10,000 Stories piece published June 10, 2018, Denice Juneski and Linda Jourdeans — both 72 — discovered through 23andMe DNA testing that they were switched at birth in 1945 at Bethesda Hospital in St. Paul. Denice, curious about her ancestry, first noticed her DNA matches didn’t fit her family and retested. A match on Linda’s report led Linda’s family to urge her to take a test; the results confirmed the switch.

Records show Denice Mary Mayer was born at 2:17 a.m. and Linda Jean Nielsen 31 minutes later on Dec. 19, 1945. The exact cause of the switch is unknown. Family photos and life details underscored the mismatch — Linda is a redhead in a family of blonds, while Denice was the lone blonde among brunettes and redheads; Denice also felt out of place in her athletic family, while Linda was the athlete. The women have since met repeatedly, begun meeting their biological and birth families, and visit Marianne Mayer, 99, who raised Denice but is Linda’s biological mother. Both women say the discovery, though shocking, has been a gift and are forging a relationship while planning family reunions.

Summary:

The document covers several short items centered on Taylor Swift. It opens with a brief note about Twitter location settings and then shifts to fan commentary suggesting Taylor’s album Reputation uses recurring storm/natural-disaster imagery (e.g., “swaying as the room burned down,” “windows boarded up after the storm”).

Most of the piece reports on two social-media events involving Swift in late January 2015. First, while vacationing in Maui with the Haim sisters she posted bikini photos that revealed her belly button — a light, playful account noting she’d said in the past she avoids showing her midriff to avoid fully “committing” to that look. The post includes casual mentions of hiking and whale-watching.

Second, Swift’s Twitter was hijacked by members of the hacker group Lizard Squad, who posted messages and claimed to have nude photos of her while telling followers to follow their accounts. Twitter removed the tweets, suspended the implicated accounts, and locked Swift’s account briefly. Swift responded calmly and humorously after regaining access, tweeting that there were no nudes and taunting would-be leakers (“Have fun photoshopping cause you got NOTHING”), and thanking a friend for alerting her. She also used Tumblr to post a supportive message to a bullied fan. The piece notes Swift was in Hawaii at the time.

A 35-year-old man identified as Willie Corey (Cory) Godbolt was arrested after an overnight shooting spree in Bogue Chitto and Brookhaven, Mississippi, that left eight people dead, including Lincoln County Deputy William Durr. Godbolt told The Clarion-Ledger he intended “suicide by cop” after arguing with his estranged wife about their children; he said “I ain’t fit to live, not after what I done.” Authorities charged him with one count of capital murder and seven counts of first-degree murder.

The attacks began about 11:30 p.m. Saturday at a home on Lee Drive in Bogue Chitto following a domestic disturbance. When Deputy Durr responded, Godbolt allegedly pulled a gun and opened fire. Four bodies — three women and Deputy Durr, 36 — were recovered at that scene. A second scene on Coopertown Road in Brookhaven, where shootings occurred between midnight and 5 a.m., produced the bodies of two boys. Two additional victims (a man and a woman) were found at a Brookhaven residence on East Lincoln Road, where Godbolt was later captured after law enforcement radioed that the suspect had opened fire there.

Relatives and neighbors said most victims were family members; only Durr was not related. Vincent Mitchell, the suspect’s stepfather-in-law, said Godbolt’s wife and their two children had been staying at his home after leaving Godbolt; three relatives were killed there. Godbolt claimed he had also been shot inside the home and was treated at a Jackson hospital. He spoke to officers after being detained and repeatedly expressed remorse and a desire to die.

Deputy Durr, a father and two-year Lincoln County deputy (and former Brookhaven officer), was remembered by Sheriff Steve Rushing as a hero and a beloved figure in the community. Multiple state and local agencies assisted in the response. Officials said they were awaiting next-of-kin notifications before releasing full victim names. Authorities described this as one of the deadliest crime sprees in Lincoln County history.
