A fatal March 23 crash on Highway 101 in Mountain View killed 38-year-old Apple engineer Walter Huang when his Tesla Model X struck a concrete lane divider. Tesla confirmed Autopilot was engaged with adaptive cruise control set to minimum follow-distance; vehicle logs show the driver’s hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds before the 9:27 a.m. collision, despite several earlier visual warnings and one audible alert. The logs indicate the car had about five seconds and 150 meters of unobstructed view of the crushed crash attenuator but took no evasive action.

Tesla said the severity of the crash was amplified because the crash attenuator — a safety cushion meant to reduce impacts into concrete dividers — had been crushed in a prior accident and not yet replaced. CalTrans said replacement work had been scheduled and noted that maintenance guidelines call for repairing damaged attenuators within days, though weather and other delays can intervene; reporting says the attenuator was damaged 11 days earlier.

Huang’s family says he had complained multiple times to the dealership that his Autopilot steered toward that same barrier; the dealer reportedly could not reproduce the issue. The NTSB and CHP recovered vehicle modules and are continuing their investigation.

Tesla defended Autopilot’s overall safety, citing past government findings and internal data that Autopilot reduced crash rates and that Tesla vehicles with Autopilot hardware show a lower fatality rate per miles driven compared with overall U.S. averages. The company acknowledged Autopilot cannot prevent all accidents, expressed condolences to the family, and warned that discouraging Autopilot use based on isolated incidents could cost lives. The crash occurs amid heightened scrutiny of autonomous-driving systems following other recent fatalities.

Police say performers from the all-male revue Thunder From Down Under stopped a suspected thief who produced a gun and fired once inside the Excalibur Hotel and Casino on March 18, 2014. Officers were called just before 9:30 p.m. after performers discovered missing costumes and props from their dressing area. When one dancer and the show director inspected a suitcase of stolen items, a man—wearing a SWAT hat, firefighter shirt and SWAT-style shoes—approached and claimed he had bought the items. A struggle followed; the man reportedly pulled a .44 Magnum, threatened “I got a gun. I’m gonna shoot,” and fired a round that struck a wall. Performers wrestled him down until security and police took him into custody.

The suspect identified himself as Michael Maharas, but booking records list him as Joey Kadmiri, 24. He was treated at University Medical Center for injuries sustained during the altercation and was reportedly violent with hospital staff. He was booked on counts of attempted murder with a deadly weapon, attempted robbery with a deadly weapon, and burglary with a deadly weapon. No performers were shot; one entertainer was treated and released for a weapon-related injury. MGM Resorts said the show remained on schedule.

Two researchers, historian Fletcher Crowe and anthropologist Anita Spring, announced at a Florida State University conference that they have located the long-sought 1564 French fortification Fort Caroline—not near Jacksonville, Fla., where scholars have searched for 150+ years, but on Rhetts Island at the mouth of the Altamaha River near Darien, Georgia, about 70 miles north. If confirmed, this would make Fort Caroline the oldest known fortified European settlement in what is now the United States, predating St. Augustine, Roanoke, Jamestown, and Plymouth.

Their case rests on extensive archival work in Paris—matching 16th–18th century French maps and documents (some mistranslated in past centuries) to modern coastal charts, linguistic analysis identifying the indigenous Guale-speaking peoples of the Darien area as those encountered by the French, and correlation with historical latitude reports (within the margin of navigational error). They also trace Native trade routes to gold and silver deposits inland (near Dahlonega, Ga.), which help explain French accounts of indigenous metalwork.

Crowe and Spring have a Georgia special-use permit and say they expect to begin archaeological digging soon, but no excavation or physical artifacts have yet been produced to prove the site. Their claim has provoked skepticism from some archaeologists who continue to favor a St. Johns River/Jacksonville location; critics say the map interpretations are debatable and that the logistics of the 1565 Spanish overland attack from St. Augustine need to be reconciled. Crowe and Spring propose alternative Spanish movements via the St. Marys River and Native trails.

The announcement, presented to spur scholarly challenge and further research, could substantially redefine the geographic concept of “French Florida” and local historical attributions if archaeological evidence confirms the Altamaha site.

Jonathan J. Pollard, who was convicted of spying for Israel and sentenced to life in prison, has been granted parole and will be released from the federal prison in Butner, North Carolina, in late November — roughly 30 years after his arrest. Pollard’s lawyers, who worked pro bono for years, prepared a focused case showing he met legal parole criteria (good behavior in prison and low risk of reoffending). The U.S. Parole Commission determined he satisfied those standards and set his release date. The White House said it would not challenge the decision and denied any link between the parole decision and broader U.S.-Israel tensions over the Iran nuclear deal; it emphasized the Commission followed standard procedures and that the President will not alter the parole terms.

The document is a multi-part report about the opening of the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi, highlighting athlete storylines, safety concerns around new extreme-sports events, and broader logistical and political issues.

Key athlete notes
- Profiles previewed U.S. athletes to watch (e.g., 18-year-old Mikaela Shiffrin as a rising slalom star).
- Shaun White, the marquee U.S. snowboarder, abruptly withdrew from the inaugural Olympic slopestyle event to concentrate on winning a third consecutive halfpipe gold, citing injury risk after a wrist knock and concerns about the slopestyle course. His withdrawal followed crashes and injuries to other riders during initial runs.

Slopestyle and safety issues
- Slopestyle, debuting at Sochi, is an extreme downhill obstacle course of jumps, rails and boxes. Riders are judged for daring tricks.
- Rain delayed course testing, so the first training runs came late; many athletes found jump heights intimidating. Norway’s Torstein Horgmo broke his collarbone attempting a trick in training; other riders were injured.
- After athlete complaints, organizers smoothed some jump tops and bottoms; some riders felt conditions improved, while critics questioned whether Olympic course builders had pushed the “no-limits” extreme-sports ethos too far.
- Safety advocates praised White’s decision as athlete-driven pressure that can prompt safer course designs.

Event starts and schedule
- Competition began before the opening ceremony because 12 new events were added since Vancouver. Men’s and women’s snowboard slopestyle qualifying and women’s moguls were among early events; some medals were scheduled for Saturday.
- The new team figure skating event also started at the Iceberg Skating Palace.

Security and political context
- Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Kozak argued terrorism fears were exaggerated, saying Sochi’s threat level was no worse than major Western cities and that Russia could secure the Games with its heavy security presence.
- The Department of Homeland Security warned airlines about a possible threat involving explosives concealed in toothpaste tubes on flights to Russia; U.S. officials and the U.S. Olympic Committee said they were monitoring and coordinating with local authorities.
- Islamist extremist groups in the nearby Caucasus had vowed disruption; Russia deployed large security forces, though some U.S. intelligence figures worried peripheral areas might be vulnerable.
- Kozak defended Russia’s “gay propaganda” law as protecting minors and said visitors would not be arrested; his remarks echoed President Putin’s stance and responded to international criticism.

Other notes
- Sochi’s organizing committee said a record number of world leaders would attend the Games.
- Coverage and public discussion of Sochi had also focused on accommodation and organizational issues, not just sports.

Overall, the opening phase of the Sochi Games combined excitement over new events and rising stars with high-profile safety, security and political controversies—most visibly centered on the risky debut of slopestyle snowboarding and the resulting athlete injuries and withdrawals.

President Trump phoned Michael T. Reynolds, the acting director of the National Park Service, on the morning after his inauguration to complain about a Park Service retweet that compared crowd sizes at his inauguration and Barack Obama’s 2009 inauguration. Trump pressed Reynolds to provide additional aerial photos he hoped would show larger crowds and prove media coverage wrong. Reynolds obtained and sent some extra photos through Interior Department channels, but they did not support Trump’s claim of a turnout near one million.

The exchange highlighted Trump’s intense focus on inauguration crowd size and prompted internal turmoil at the Park Service: its official Twitter account had briefly retweeted two critical posts (one on crowd comparisons and another about removed White House web pages), triggering an order to shut down agency Twitter accounts temporarily and a later apology for the mistaken retweets. The episode came amid broader friction between the new administration and career federal employees over communications and media coverage; the Park Service and Interior declined to comment on internal discussions. White House officials framed Trump’s call as hands‑on management, while experts and photographs indicate turnout for the 2017 inauguration was substantially smaller than in 2009.

Archaeologists from the University of Leicester, working with Hallaton Fieldwork Group volunteers, have excavated 11 skeletons beneath the “lost” Chapel of St Morrell on a hill above Hallaton, Leicestershire. Radiocarbon dating places the burials in the 14th century. Most strikingly, a man and woman were found interred holding hands — their fingers still entwined — suggesting they were buried together and may have been of similar age. The remains have been taken to the university for further study.

The small cemetery also includes other notable burials: an older male with a fatal skull wound consistent with a sharp implement (possibly a poleaxe), and a young male interred in a pit with legs drawn up, perhaps reflecting disease. Some graves had stones placed on the bodies, a practice seen in parts of eastern Europe thought to prevent the dead rising.

Archaeologists are uncertain why these people were buried at the chapel rather than the nearby parish church. Possibilities include that the chapel served as a special burial or pilgrimage site, or that some buried there were excluded from church burial (e.g., criminals, foreigners, or the sick). Finds such as silver pennies (12th–16th centuries), chapel wall and floor remains, and medieval plaster confirm use in the medieval period. Roman archaeology beneath the chapel indicates the hilltop was a significant place for over 2,000 years, and researchers hope ongoing work will help fill gaps between the Roman and medieval periods. The chapel’s location was identified following research by local historian John Morrison and geophysical surveying.

Scott Weiland's estate is the subject of a legal dispute after his second wife, Mary Forsberg, filed to be named executor of his will. Forsberg submitted a will signed by Weiland dated April 2007, around the time their marriage was ending and during his well-documented struggles with addiction. Forsberg is the mother of Weiland's two children and has written a memoir about their life together and his substance problems.

Weiland’s estate includes roughly $2 million and a separate trust with undisclosed assets. His widow, third wife Jamie Wachtel (married to Weiland in 2013 and with him at his death), could challenge Forsberg’s filing. A hearing in the matter is scheduled for Feb. 5. Weiland died on Dec. 3 at age 48; the medical examiner attributed his death to a mix of cocaine, ethanol and MDA and noted significant health issues including cardiovascular disease and multi-substance dependence.

House Republicans pushed two abortion-related bills through the House in late September amid a tense fight over whether to attach a Planned Parenthood defunding measure to must-pass government funding — a standoff that risked triggering a government shutdown before the Sept. 30 deadline.

Key votes and measures
- The House passed the Defund Planned Parenthood Act (241–187) to bar federal payments to Planned Parenthood for one year and redirect funds to community health centers, and the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (248–177), which would impose criminal penalties on medical personnel who fail to try to save infants born alive after attempted abortions. Both votes were largely party-line with only a handful of Democratic defections.
- Neither bill was expected to become law: Senate Democrats could filibuster them and President Obama threatened to veto.

Context and stakes
- The push followed undercover videos released by opponents alleging Planned Parenthood illegally profited from fetal tissue; Planned Parenthood denies wrongdoing and says the videos were deceptively edited.
- Planned Parenthood receives roughly $450 million annually from federal sources (mainly Medicaid and Title X) for non-abortion services; federal funds are already largely barred from paying for abortions.
- Hard-line conservatives demanded the defunding language be attached to a short-term continuing resolution (CR) to avert a shutdown; GOP leaders, including Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, tried to avoid a shutdown fight they feared would harm the party politically and could cost Boehner his speakership.

Political dynamics
- GOP leaders faced pressure from conservatives who threatened to force confrontations or even a motion to vacate the speakership if leadership relented. Leadership counters included internal polling showing voters largely oppose a shutdown over Planned Parenthood and efforts to find procedural ways (e.g., reconciliation) to pursue defunding.
- Democrats and the White House urged passage of a “clean” short-term CR without policy riders to keep the government open, while promising to block or veto attempts to link funding to defunding Planned Parenthood.
- The battle highlighted intra-GOP divisions, potential electoral consequences, and how abortion could shape messaging and mobilization heading into the 2016 campaign.

Outcome outlook
- With the Senate and president opposed, the House votes mainly served to appease conservatives and frame the issue politically rather than produce enacted law. The impasse set up a likely clash over any must-pass continuing resolution and increased the odds of a fraught, last-minute endgame on government funding.

The White House released recipes for two home-brewed beers — the White House Honey Brown Ale and a Honey Porter — marking what the administration says is the first beer brewed on White House grounds. The release came while President Barack Obama campaigned in Iowa, after weeks of public interest, an online petition, and repeated reporter queries. White House chef Sam Kass, who brews the beer in the White House kitchen, and staff developed the recipes after the president bought a home-brewing kit and received tips from local home-brewers; honey used in the brews comes from the first hive on the South Lawn. The White House stressed that Obama paid for the brewing materials himself.

Both recipes use light malt extract and White House honey; the ale additionally calls for light dried malt extract, amber crystal and biscuit malts, Kent Goldings and Fuggles hops, gypsum and Windsor yeast, while the porter uses Munich, crystal, black and chocolate malts, Hallertauer aroma hops and Nottingham yeast. Step-by-step brewing and bottling instructions (including fermentation times, temperatures and priming sugar amounts) were published alongside a “behind-the-scenes” video in which Kass praises the beer. The release also noted historical context: while George Washington and Thomas Jefferson brewed or made spirits and wine at their estates, this is believed to be the first alcohol brewed or distilled on White House grounds.

President Trump tweeted that he declined Time magazine’s offer to be its Person of the Year again because the magazine told him he was “probably” going to get the title and would have to agree to an interview and major photo shoot; Trump said “probably is no good” and “took a pass.” Time responded that his account was incorrect. Trump was Time’s Person of the Year in 2016; the designation recognizes influence, not praise, and will be announced Dec. 6. The article also compiles other contemporaneous Trump items: his condolences and calls with Egypt’s and Turkey’s leaders after a deadly Sinai mosque attack (he urged defeating terrorists militarily and promoted his travel ban and border wall), reports that Turkey said Trump told Erdogan the U.S. would stop arming Syrian Kurdish fighters (not confirmed by the White House), and items about his golf outing, criticism of NFL players who kneel, and past incidents of him displaying fake Time covers at his clubs.

A 4-year-old Coopersburg, Pa., cancer patient, Jillian Massey, who spent six months at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia after a brain cancer diagnosis in April, wanted to bring gifts to the friends she left behind when she went home for the holidays. What started as a personal goal of 50 presents grew—after her family created an Amazon wish list and her mother’s colleagues helped promote it—into a drive that collected over 3,000 gifts for patients at CHOP. Jillian’s mother, Janelle, says they will deliver the toys on Monday and that Jillian is excited to spread some cheer.

New research from the environmental group NRDC analyzing EPA and state testing data finds about 10% of U.S. coastal and lakefront beach water samples fail federal safety thresholds for bacteria, putting swimmers at risk of illnesses from stomach bugs and conjunctivitis to more serious respiratory or neurological infections. Trouble spots are concentrated in New England, the Gulf Coast and the Great Lakes, and stormwater runoff is identified as the largest contributor—carrying garbage, oil and human/animal waste into waterways. Untreated sewage—hundreds of billions of gallons annually—also contributes and is linked to some 3.5 million U.S. illnesses each year. Federal law requires beach testing and action when bacteria levels are high; for example, nearly 2,000 New York and New Jersey beaches were closed in 2012 for pollution.

In California, NRDC’s 24th annual Testing the Waters report shows the state’s beaches mirror the national trend: 9% of 2013 samples exceeded the EPA’s most protective benchmark (60 enterococci cfu/100 ml). Even during an historic drought year, many beaches recorded repeated exceedances—some failing 20–40% (or more) of the time—highlighting that less rain is not a viable solution. NRDC emphasizes prevention: green infrastructure (rain gardens, curb cuts, rain barrels, porous pavement) to capture and reuse stormwater, better protection for streams and wetlands that filter pollutants, and stronger federal safeguards (the proposed “Waters of the U.S.” Clean Water Protection Rule then open for comment) to reduce pollution sources.

The report notes both problems and successes in California: several beaches regularly exceed action levels (highest exceedance sites in 2013 included Aquatic Park and Lakeshore Park in San Mateo County, Candlestick Point in San Francisco, Inner Cabrillo Beach in Los Angeles, and Newport Bay in Orange County), while some beaches—like Newport Beach at 38th Street—are labeled “Superstar” for consistently safe water. NRDC urges beachgoers to check local water quality before swimming and calls for continued investments and policies to keep pollution out of beaches and protect public health and coastal economies.

World of Beer (WOB), a Tampa-based tavern chain with 77 locations, is hiring three paid summer interns to travel domestically and internationally visiting breweries, attending beer festivals, and reporting on their experiences. The four-month internship pays $12,000 and covers travel, food, and lodging. Applicants must be 21 or older; WOB is prioritizing strong writers and candidates with substantial social media followings since the role is primarily a social-media/content internship and published work will appear in Draft Magazine. Applications are due by March 26 and can be submitted via online video or through in-tavern interviews (several regional live interview events are scheduled). The top ten applicants will be shortlisted in early April for Skype interviews with corporate, after which three interns will be selected.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December 1948 (Resolution 217 A), is a landmark, globally drafted statement of fundamental rights meant to be universally protected. Proclaimed as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and nations, it has been translated into over 500 languages.

Preamble: The UDHR affirms that recognition of the inherent dignity and equal, inalienable rights of all people is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace. It notes that violations of human rights have led to barbarous acts, and that protecting rights by rule of law and fostering friendly relations among nations are essential. States reaffirmed commitments in the UN Charter and agreed a common understanding of rights is crucial for their realization. The Assembly called on individuals and institutions to promote respect for these rights through education and progressive national and international measures.

Key Articles and Rights (selected highlights):
- Article 1: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights and should act toward one another in a spirit of brotherhood.
- Article 2: Rights apply to everyone without discrimination (race, colour, sex, language, religion, opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status) and irrespective of a territory’s political status.
- Articles 3–7: Rights to life, liberty and personal security; prohibition of slavery and torture; legal personality and equal protection before the law.
- Articles 8–11: Right to effective remedy, protection from arbitrary arrest/detention/exile, fair and public hearing, presumption of innocence and prohibition of ex post facto criminal penalties.
- Articles 12–15: Protection of privacy; freedom of movement and residence; right to seek asylum (with exceptions); right to a nationality and protection against arbitrary deprivation of nationality.
- Articles 16–18: Equal marriage rights and free consent; protection of the family; right to own property; freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
- Articles 19–21: Freedom of opinion, expression, peaceful assembly and association; right to participate in government, equal access to public service, and periodic free elections.
- Articles 22–27: Right to social security and the economic, social and cultural rights necessary for dignity and development; rights to work, just conditions, equal pay, trade-union membership, rest and leisure; right to an adequate standard of living and health care; rights to education and participation in cultural life, including protection of intellectual property.
- Articles 28–30: Entitlement to a social and international order in which rights can be fully realized; duties to the community and permissible legal limits on rights to protect others’ rights and public welfare; nothing in the Declaration may be used to destroy the rights it proclaims.

News item: Reopening of WTC Cortlandt subway station
- After being destroyed in the September 11, 2001 attacks when the World Trade Center towers collapsed, Cortlandt Street station on the No. 1 subway line in Lower Manhattan has reopened for the first time in 17 years, now renamed WTC Cortlandt. The line had bypassed the station after part of its route collapsed under debris.
- The new fully accessible station cost $181.8 million, required rebuilding the ceiling and replacing about 1,200 ft (365 m) of track, and includes modern features such as improved ventilation and fewer platform columns for better passenger flow. Its walls include a white marble mosaic featuring text from the U.S. Declaration of Independence and the 1948 UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
- The reopening is presented as a symbol of New Yorkers’ resilience and Lower Manhattan’s recovery after the attacks, and arrives amid broader challenges facing the subway system. MTA officials marked the reopening as a meaningful step in restoring and improving the World Trade Center area.

A Pew Research Center study released Thursday finds U.S. mothers are older and better educated than two decades ago, with major shifts across racial and ethnic groups. Key findings from government data and an April 2009 survey:

- Age shifts: In 2008, 14% of newborns had mothers aged 35 or older (up from 9–10% in 1990), while teenage births fell to about 10% (down from 13% in 1990). More children are now born to mothers over 35 than to teens.
- Education: 54% of mothers of newborns had at least some college in 2008 (41% in 1990); among mothers 35+, 71% had some college.
- Marital status: Although most births occur within marriage, a record 41% of births in 2008 were to unmarried women (up from 28% in 1990).
- Birth counts and trends: There were about 4.3 million U.S. births in 2008. Births rose 2003–2007 then dipped with the economic downturn.
- Reasons and attitudes: Most parents cite “the joy of having children” as the reason for parenthood, yet roughly half say parenthood “just happened.” Women are more likely than men to report that it “just happened.” Public attitudes are increasingly accepting of older motherhood, fertility treatment and childlessness, though about one-third disapprove of childbearing after 40 or using fertility treatment.
- Causes and consequences: Delayed marriage and childbearing tied to higher education and career pursuits, improved medical care and fertility treatments (which have contributed to a rise in multiple births) help explain trends. Experts note rising single motherhood and postponed family formation have complex social implications.

Overall, the profile of the typical U.S. mother has shifted toward later childbearing and higher education, with changing family structures and evolving public attitudes about timing and methods of becoming a parent.

The 2013 Israeli election saw unusually high voter participation and produced a surprising shake-up in party strength that left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu politically weakened though still positioned to lead a coalition.

Turnout and voting day
- By 8 p.m. some 3.6 million Israelis had voted; the Central Elections Committee reported a 63.7% turnout at that time, higher than comparable points in 2009 (59.7%) and 2006 (63.2%). Voting continued until 10 p.m.
- Polling stations nationwide were very busy, with 5,656,705 eligible voters able to cast ballots at 10,132 polling stations. Reports from polling places, including Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, described long lines and constant voter flow.
- One in four Israelis had voted by noon. Police reported only isolated incidents and called the day a celebration of democracy. The Central Elections Committee was pleased with the turnout and hoped national records might be broken.

Media coverage and campaign tone
- International press attention, particularly in the U.S., was muted—partly because the vote followed President Obama’s second inauguration and partly because the campaign itself was seen as lackluster and lacking substantive debate on major issues such as Iran and Syria.
- Coverage that existed emphasized what was not being discussed—few new policy specifics, no formal platform from Netanyahu, and avoidance of certain geopolitical topics—reinforcing the impression that the election’s outcome was largely foregone.

Election results and political implications
- Exit and early counts indicated a divided Knesset and a weakened Netanyahu. His Likud-Beiteinu bloc finished first but lost seats; the newly formed centrist party Yesh Atid, led by TV personality-turned-politician Yair Lapid, finished a strong second.
- With nearly all ballots counted, the traditional blocs were evenly split: about 60 seats for right-wing and religious parties and about 60 seats for center, left and Arab parties.
- Seat totals reported: Likud-Beiteinu around 31, Yesh Atid 19, Labor 15; Shas and Jewish Home each 11; Hatnua and Meretz 6 each; Arab parties combined 12. Kadima collapsed from a previous high to just 2 seats.
- Lapid’s campaign focused on domestic “kitchen-table” issues—class sizes, housing costs—and integrating the ultra-Orthodox into the army and workforce. He avoided antagonizing the right and emphasized centrist, pragmatic priorities.
- Netanyahu acknowledged the setback, posted urgent appeals before polls closed, and quickly reached out to Lapid, offering to form the broadest possible coalition. Lapid signaled openness to working with Netanyahu but emphasized creating a strong, independent center.
- The result shifted power into coalition negotiations: while Netanyahu was likely to stay prime minister, his weakened position and the emergence of Lapid as a kingmaker raised the possibility of a fragmented coalition or paralysis—but also of a cross-spectrum government if parties agree to work together.

Overall, the election combined record voter engagement and a dynamic domestic political shift—the rise of a new centrist force—while generating relatively modest international media interest because of timing and the campaign’s limited debate on major security issues.

In 1925 Philadelphia officials and a Florida coroner recorded the death of Thomas (Tommy) Curry, a teenage charge of the Arthur G. Dozier School for Boys in Marianna, Fla., as a crushed skull or being hit by a train while escaping the school. His family in Philadelphia believed his body had been returned and buried in an unmarked plot at St. Bridget’s parish among his great-grandparents.

Since Dozier’s closure and a 2009 St. Petersburg Times exposé documenting a century of abuse, disappearances and cover-ups at the institution, University of South Florida forensic anthropologists led by Erin Kimmerle have been excavating a makeshift cemetery on the school grounds. Using ground-penetrating radar they located 55 graves—far more than previously acknowledged—and have begun identifying remains by DNA to allow proper burials and answer longstanding questions about dozens of boys who died at Dozier.

Kimmerle’s team, working with Pennsylvania state police and a Philadelphia prosecutor, exhumed Curry’s casket this week seeking skeletal evidence that could clarify his cause of death. The crate contained no human remains—only layers of wood—and Curry’s great-grandparents’ coffin lay beneath it. The discovery suggests someone in 1925 shipped an empty, wood-filled coffin north and deceived the family, though investigators cannot rule out that remains were removed later or that Curry may be among bodies already exhumed in Florida. A Curry cousin has provided DNA to test against remains recovered at Dozier.

The empty casket deepens suspicions of long-term deception linked to Dozier, which has a documented history of abuse allegations and inconsistent record-keeping. Kimmerle and law enforcement stress the exhumation was necessary to advance the broader investigation into deaths and disappearances at the reform school; DNA testing of the Florida remains may yet resolve Curry’s fate and those of other missing boys.

Disney and Lucasfilm have revealed the cast for Star Wars: Episode IX and confirmed that the late Carrie Fisher will appear as Leia Organa using previously unreleased footage from Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Director J.J. Abrams, who co-wrote the script with Chris Terrio, said they would not recast or create a CGI Leia and, with the blessing of Fisher’s daughter Billie Lourd, found a way to honor Fisher’s legacy by incorporating unseen Episode VII material. Fisher died in December 2016 at age 60. Returning cast members include Daisy Ridley, Adam Driver, John Boyega, Oscar Isaac, Lupita Nyong’o, Domhnall Gleeson, Kelly Marie Tran, Joonas Suotamo, Mark Hamill, Anthony Daniels, Billy Dee Williams and Lourd. New additions announced are Naomi Ackie and Richard E. Grant; John Williams will compose the score. Production was set to begin Aug. 1, and the film was scheduled for release Dec. 20, 2019.

A young woman who posted blurred screenshots of her post-resignation sexting with Representative Anthony Weiner told TheDirty.com she wanted to stay anonymous, but was quickly identified. BuzzFeed matched the images to now-closed Facebook and Formspring accounts and reported her as Indiana native Sydney Elaine Leathers, an early-twenties former Obama field organizer who once listed Weiner among her heroes. A high-school friend said Leathers and Weiner exchanged explicit messages last summer and that Weiner had discussed moving her to Chicago or New York; Leathers reportedly wrote that “Weiner did nothing wrong” and joked he could “continue sending dick pics every single day…as long as he continues to legislate like he does.”

Huma Abedin, having nervously defended her husband at a first press conference, published a longer, more reflective defense in an excerpt for Harper’s Bazaar titled “The Good Wife,” in which she calls Anthony “a smart, caring, and dedicated” public servant who has become “a better man.” (The final line of the document—about Alexa Internet donating crawl data to the Wayback Machine—appears unrelated to the Weiner story.)

Less than a week after U.S. officials noted a pause in provocative acts by North Korea, Pyongyang fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile that flew over northern Japan and fell into the Pacific. The launch — the first of a sophisticated weapon to pass directly over Japanese territory — came amid joint U.S.-South Korea military exercises and days after shorter-range launches. It triggered emergency alerts, halted some train services, briefly disrupted daily life in Hokkaido, and prompted Japan to ready missile defenses; millions received warning texts with only minutes to seek cover.

International reaction was swift and angry. The U.S. called an emergency U.N. Security Council meeting, President Trump reiterated that “all options are on the table,” and U.S. and Japanese leaders pledged to increase pressure on North Korea. U.N. ambassador Nikki Haley demanded serious consequences. China and Russia urged restraint and blamed U.S. military drills for escalating tensions; Russia warned further sanctions alone would not solve the problem. Experts and officials warned the launch will likely increase support for tougher measures to squeeze Pyongyang and entities that do business with it.

Analysts identified likely next targets for sanctions: remaining major export sectors such as textiles and critical imports like oil, plus stronger penalties on Chinese banks and companies that facilitate trade with North Korea. Enforcement concerns persist because China accounts for roughly 90% of North Korea’s trade, and opacity in Chinese customs reporting — especially on oil — makes monitoring and sanctioning difficult. Some analysts caution China will stop short of measures that risk regime collapse, and that overpressure on Beijing could provoke economic or diplomatic backlash against U.S. interests.

Beyond sanctions, deterrence experts say the launches reflect a deliberate North Korean strategy to develop credible nuclear delivery capability — including ICBMs — to deter U.S. retaliation and thus survive a confrontation. By threatening U.S. bases and allies and demonstrating an ability to threaten the U.S. mainland, Pyongyang aims to blunt the U.S. military option. Observers note Kim calibrates provocations to maximize political and technical gain while avoiding actions likely to trigger overwhelming kinetic retaliation, complicating response choices for Washington and its partners.

Former U.S. Rep. Corrine Brown was convicted on 18 of 22 federal charges—including conspiracy, wire and mail fraud, and falsifying tax returns—for her role in a scheme that diverted roughly $833,000 raised by One Door for Education away from scholarships. Prosecutors said the sham charity, run with Brown’s former chief of staff Elias “Ronnie” Simmons and charity president Carla Wiley, distributed only about $1,200 to students while the rest funded lavish events and personal uses (including golf tournaments, luxury boxes and concerts). Evidence presented included bank records, checks, emails and testimony from Simmons and Wiley, both of whom pleaded guilty and testified against Brown. Prosecutors also accused Brown of inflating charitable deductions and failing to report tens of thousands in income. Brown maintained her innocence, blamed Simmons as the mastermind, and plans to seek a new trial; her attorney said motions will be filed to delay sentencing. There are no mandatory minimums for her offenses, and the judge has at least three months to set sentencing. DOJ and FBI officials condemned the abuse of public trust and pledged continued enforcement against public corruption.

Summary:

In June in Casselberry, Florida, police and child protective services removed a newborn from mother Sarah Anne Markham after a pediatrician determined the baby was dehydrated, losing weight (about 10% weight loss), and needed immediate hospital treatment. Markham, a committed vegan, told doctors she preferred to use vegan/“natural” treatments and had provided an organic soy formula she bought at Whole Foods instead of following medical advice. When she did not take the child to Florida Hospital South as instructed, officers responded to a tip to the Florida child-abuse hotline, forced entry after she wouldn’t answer the door, and arrested her on a charge of child neglect. The infant was treated at Florida Hospital South and placed in state custody; Markham later bonded out.

Months later a Seminole County judge returned custody of the infant, Caleb, to Markham on condition she submit a nutritionist’s report within 10 days. The judge dismissed CPS’s claim that she was unfit to care for the child. Caleb stayed with his grandparents after removal, remained on soy formula, and was reported to be healthy and gaining weight (about 17 pounds). Markham’s attorney said he expects the criminal case to be dismissed. The sheriff’s office has said the case remains active and open.

A lightning strike at the T-Bois Blues Festival in Larose on the night of Friday, March 18, killed a 28-year-old New Orleans woman and injured two others who had been sheltering in a small personal tent during a severe storm.

Victim and injuries
- The deceased was identified by Lafourche Parish Sheriff Craig Webre as Jacqui Stavis, a 28-year-old massage therapist from New Orleans; she was found unresponsive at the scene and pronounced dead Saturday at a local hospital.  
- Two other women from New Orleans, ages 30 and 24, suffered electric-shock injuries. The 24-year-old was taken to University Medical Center in New Orleans; the 30-year-old remained hospitalized in Larose.  
- A large Labrador dog inside the tent also died.

Circumstances and response
- Deputies, volunteer firefighters and EMTs responded after a call shortly after 10 p.m.; they found all three women in the tent following a lightning strike. Investigators say the group had taken refuge in the small tent during intense winds, rain, thunder and lightning.  
- No official cause of Stavis’s death was released; National Weather Service data note that a portion of lightning strikes can cause fatal cardiac arrest or brain damage.

Context and reaction
- The three-day T-Bois festival, held on an alligator and crawfish farm and sometimes nicknamed a “Cajun Burning Man,” features camping, local food and music and was headlined by guitarist Anders Osborne. Attendees described the event as low-key and volunteer-run; organizers reportedly barred new tents from being set up the following day.  
- Friends and family remembered Stavis as a joyful, engaged member of New Orleans’ music and arts community; she was reported to be the nation’s first lightning fatality of 2016 per National Weather Service records. Relatives and friends expressed shock and grief at her sudden loss.

A widely publicized New York magazine story profiled 17-year-old Stuyvesant High School student Mohammed Islam as having made $72 million trading stocks. The piece, which went viral and spawned follow-ups from other outlets, portrayed Islam as a trading prodigy who led an investment club and had “high eight-figure” net worth. After intense media attention (including invitations to appear on CNBC), Islam and a friend featured in the story, Damir Tulemaganbetov, told the New York Observer that the claims were false: the trades were simulated, not real, and there was no $72 million. Their new crisis PR team and lawyer said Islam had exaggerated when speaking to a reporter and now regrets the fallout and embarrassment to his family. New York magazine acknowledged its fact-checking failed after a purported bank document proved to be falsified, amended its headline, and apologized. Commentary around the episode criticized both the teenagers’ choices and the media’s failure to verify an extraordinary claim before amplifying it.

FARGO, N.D. — Authorities say 22-year-old Savanna Greywind, who was eight months pregnant when she disappeared Aug. 19, was violently killed; a preliminary autopsy listed her cause of death as homicidal violence. Her body was found wrapped in plastic and duct tape in the Red River Sunday night after intensive local searches. A newborn girl believed to be Greywind’s was recovered earlier in an apartment in the same building where Greywind lived; the child is in social services care and authorities are conducting DNA testing.

Neighbors Brooke Crews, 38, and her boyfriend William Hoehn, 32, have been charged with conspiracy to commit murder, conspiracy to commit kidnapping and giving false information to police. Court documents contain conflicting suspect statements: Crews reportedly admitted luring Greywind to her apartment, advising how to induce labor, and taking advantage of her to obtain the baby; Hoehn said he returned Aug. 19 to find Crews cleaning blood and was presented with the infant as “our baby.” Hoehn also admitted disposing of bloody items. Both suspects were held on $2 million bond and did not enter pleas.

Investigators searched a nearby Minnesota farmstead and found suspicious items believed to be linked to the case. Family members and community supporters have expressed anger and grief; a memorial was placed at Greywind’s apartment building. Police and prosecutors have not released full details of how Greywind died as the investigation and autopsy continue.

The remains of Brazilian football legend Manuel Francisco dos Santos, known as Garrincha, are missing, his family and local officials say. Garrincha, who died in 1983 at age 49 and helped Brazil win the 1958 and 1962 World Cups, was buried in Raiz da Serra cemetery in Magé, Rio de Janeiro. Relatives told O Globo that the body may have been moved during an exhumation about a decade ago to make room for another family burial, but no documentation was provided and cemetery records do not confirm the transfer.

There are two memorials at the cemetery bearing his name: the original 1983 grave and a 1985 obelisk on higher ground. Family members, including daughter Rosangela Santos and cousin João Rogoginsky, say they were not given papers proving any reburial and are upset at not knowing where his remains are. Cemetery administrators say they have information the body was exhumed but lack proof.

Magé’s mayor, Rafael Tubarão, has proposed, with the family's permission, re-exhuming the sites and performing DNA tests to determine whether Garrincha’s remains are present, aiming to locate him in time for commemorations on what would have been his 84th birthday. The report also recalls Garrincha’s life: born in 1933, he overcame physical deformities to become one of Brazil’s greatest dribblers, starred for Botafogo, won two World Cups, shared the 1962 golden boot, struggled with alcoholism, and died of cirrhosis.

Summary:

In early April 2014 NASA announced it was suspending most bilateral contacts and joint activities with Russian government entities in response to Russia’s actions in Ukraine, though operations related to the International Space Station (ISS) are explicitly exempted. The freeze—spelled out in an internal memo from Michael O’Brien and in a public NASA statement—bars NASA travel to Russia, visits by Russian officials to NASA sites, bilateral meetings, and routine communications unless a specific exemption is granted. Multilateral meetings held outside Russia that include Russian participation are also allowed.

NASA stressed the exception for ISS activities and said cooperation with Roscosmos will continue to maintain safe, continuous station operations. That caveat highlights a strategic vulnerability: since the retirement of the US space shuttle in 2011, Russia’s Soyuz has been the only way to ferry crew to and from the station, making the United States dependent on Russia for human access to low-Earth orbit for the immediate future. A recent Soyuz crewed arrival on March 27 and a scheduled Progress resupply launch illustrate ongoing operational ties.

The suspension is largely symbolic—NASA and Russian space programs have relatively few bilateral projects beyond the ISS—but it intensifies political pressure and could affect broader international projects. Russian officials warned the freeze could harm global space cooperation, although they said it would not be catastrophic for Russia’s industry.

The memo and statement also refocused attention on US efforts to restore domestic crew launch capability. NASA is funding commercial crew development (SpaceX, Sierra Nevada, Boeing) and pursuing other launch systems, but schedule slips and constrained congressional funding have pushed expected first commercial crew flights from 2015 to around 2017. Until then, the US remains reliant on Soyuz seats (costing tens of millions per seat), a dependence that critics now argue must be ended by fully funding US launch programs.

A masked 21-year-old man carried out a knife- or sword-wielding attack on October 22 at the Kronan school in Trollhättan, Sweden, killing a teacher and a pupil and seriously wounding another teacher and a pupil. The assailant reportedly knocked on classroom doors and stabbed those who opened them, and some students initially thought his masked, black-clad appearance was a prank and even posed for photos. Police arrived, the attacker tried to assault officers, and officers fired two shots; the suspect was hit, taken to hospital and later died. The three survivors were treated in intensive care; one later died at hospital. Authorities searched the attacker’s home and said they found “interesting” items; police are investigating possible links to far-right extremism but have given few details. The incident, which occurred in the school’s café area and involved multiple sharp weapons, shocked the local community and prompted national expressions of grief from Prime Minister Stefan Löfven and King Carl XVI Gustaf. School attacks are rare in Sweden; investigators say no other suspects are believed to have been involved.

Itzcoatl “Izzy” Ocampo, a 25-year-old former Marine who had been charged with killing six people — four homeless men and a woman and her son — died after ingesting the cleaning product Ajax while in a single-man cell at Orange County Central Jail, his attorney said. Deputies found him shaking and vomiting Wednesday evening; he was taken to a hospital and was pronounced dead Thursday afternoon. An autopsy and an independent pathologist’s review are pending, and the Orange County district attorney’s office is investigating the in-custody death.

Ocampo had been accused of a late‑2011/early‑2012 “serial thrill-kill” rampage that prosecutors say targeted homeless men because they were vulnerable. He was charged in January 2012 with multiple counts of murder and special allegations including lying in wait and use of a deadly weapon; prosecutors had sought the death penalty. Authorities allege he stabbed three victims more than 40 times each with a single-edged blade and used the same knife in the homeless victims’ slayings. He was also charged in the October 2011 deaths of a school friend’s mother and brother.

Defense attorneys and family members had described Ocampo as mentally troubled after his return from service in Iraq, reporting headaches, tremors, hallucinations and erratic behavior; he had been placed briefly on suicide watch in jail in 2012. His attorney criticized jail supervision, saying Ocampo’s mental issues were obvious and required high scrutiny. Jail officials noted deputies are generally required to check cells at least hourly but declined detailed comment.

Victims’ relatives expressed mixed responses: one victim’s mother said she was relieved by his death, while prosecutors lamented that a trial would no longer allow formal accountability and sought to proceed with the standard investigation into the custodial death.

A federal judge in Los Angeles, U.S. District Judge S. James Otero, granted a 90-day stay Friday in Stormy Daniels’ civil lawsuit seeking to void a nondisclosure agreement tied to a claimed 2006 sexual encounter with Donald Trump. The stay followed Michael Cohen’s announcement that he would invoke his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination in the case because of a related federal criminal investigation in New York into his role in arranging a $130,000 payment to Daniels. 

Otero said the civil issues overlap with the criminal probe into Cohen — whose home and Manhattan office were raided April 9 — and that an indictment “is likely,” given the investigation’s focus on the personal attorney of a sitting president and potentially privileged documents. Daniels’ lawyer Michael Avenatti said he plans to appeal the stay; Cohen’s lawyer did not comment. Trump has acknowledged Cohen represented him in the deal and denied any wrongdoing or campaign-fund involvement. The stay reflects a common practice to pause civil proceedings when concurrent criminal investigations could force a defendant to incriminate himself.

Summary:

When Google announced its corporate restructuring into a new holding company called Alphabet — with Google becoming a slimmed-down subsidiary focused on core internet products and other bets spun out under Alphabet — it immediately ran into branding and domain-name issues.

- BMW’s fleet-services business already operates under the name Alphabet and controls the valuable alphabet.com domain. BMW told The New York Times it does not plan to sell the domain and is investigating whether Google’s use of “Alphabet” infringes its trademark, though it has not initiated legal action.
- In response, Google launched abc.xyz as Alphabet’s web address and later acquired the long domain abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz.com, while alphabet.com remained unavailable (likely receiving heavy traffic). The @Alphabet Twitter handle is owned by an individual, not Google.
- Reuters and Bloomberg note many other U.S. companies use “alphabet” in their trademarks; more than 100 registrations exist, and an Ohio company named Alphabet, Inc. has operated since 1965.
- Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin explained the rationale for Alphabet: to give disparate projects independence, clearer management and financial reporting, and allow Sundar Pichai to lead the re-focused Google. Page said Alphabet won’t be a major consumer-facing brand and isn’t expected to introduce products under that name.
- Domain experts and entrepreneurs (e.g., Paul Graham) have emphasized the value of owning the .com, but Page framed Alphabet as a corporate umbrella rather than a consumer-facing brand, mitigating some concerns.

Bottom line: The rebrand to Alphabet made strategic sense internally, but exposed Google to real-world trademark and domain conflicts—most notably with BMW’s existing Alphabet brand and alphabet.com—highlighting a common challenge even for the largest companies.

The FDA tested 94 different dark chocolate bars from around the U.S. and found milk in 61% (57 bars). Only six bars declared milk as an ingredient; the remaining 51 bars contained undeclared milk. Cross-contact during production (shared equipment, airborne powdered milk) is a major cause.

Key findings:
- 75% of bars with advisory warnings (e.g., “may contain milk,” “made on equipment shared with milk”) tested positive for milk. The FDA advises treating such warnings as “likely.”
- 15% of bars labeled “dairy-free” or “lactose-free” and 25% of bars labeled “vegan” contained milk.
- 33% of bars with no mention of milk on the label contained milk.

Implications and advice:
- Dark chocolate is a high‑risk food for people with milk allergy. Labels can be misleading or inconsistent (e.g., “vegan” paired with “may contain”).
- Consumers with severe milk allergies should avoid bars with advisory statements, be cautious of products labeled dairy-free/vegan unless from a manufacturer that guarantees milk-free production, and seek trusted allergen-free sources or brands that use dedicated equipment.
- The FDA is evaluating these findings and expects to address allergen cross-contact through proposed preventive-controls rules under FSMA, which would require manufacturers to implement plans to prevent unintended allergen contamination.

President Trump spent his third consecutive weekend at his Mar-a-Lago “Winter White House,” and on Sunday played a full round of golf with professional Rory McIlroy and others. The White House first said Trump had only played a few holes but reversed that after McIlroy posted that they had played 18 holes; spokeswoman Sarah Sanders said the president had planned to play a few holes but decided to play longer while still conducting meetings and calls.

McIlroy said Trump “probably shot around 80” and noted he’s “a decent player for a guy in his 70s.” The outing followed other high-profile rounds Trump has played with leaders and pro golfers (including Shinzo Abe, Tiger Woods, Ernie Els and Lexi Thompson), and sparked controversy online. McIlroy faced a wave of criticism from some fans and commentators who viewed playing with Trump as a political choice, while others defended him.

President Donald Trump, frustrated that the recent $1.3 trillion omnibus spending bill appropriated only $1.6 billion (including $641 million for new primary fencing and largely restricted funding) instead of the roughly $25 billion he sought, has privately suggested using Department of Defense funds to build his U.S.–Mexico border wall. He raised the notion with advisers, Defense Secretary Jim Mattis and in a White House meeting with House Speaker Paul Ryan. The idea draws on Trump’s argument that the wall is a national security priority and that the Pentagon received a large share of the omnibus (about $700 billion).

Administration officials say Trump has floated multiple alternatives to secure wall funding after negotiations with Democrats to trade $25 billion for protections for young immigrants (DACA recipients) collapsed. White House spokespeople have been noncommittal publicly. But multiple officials — speaking anonymously — and reporting from The Washington Post and CNN note that diverting defense money would face major legal and political obstacles: reprogramming existing Pentagon funds would require congressional approval (including likely supermajority votes in the Senate for budget amendments), Defense Department and congressional appropriators would resist taking money from weapons, readiness and other defense priorities, and Democrats and some Republicans would oppose the move. Critics, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, called using military funds for the wall a misuse of defense dollars and predicted legal challenges. Most observers describe the proposal as unlikely to succeed, but it underscores the administration’s determination to pursue the wall despite setbacks in Congress.

Charlottesville and Galveston, Sept. 2014 — Police searching for 18-year-old University of Virginia student Hannah Graham, missing since Sept. 13, expanded their efforts from downtown Charlottesville into surrounding rural Albemarle County and farms, urging property owners and real-estate agents to check vacant buildings and report anything unusual (tire tracks, clothing, an iPhone 5S with a pink case) as the search entered its second week. Charlottesville Police Chief Timothy Longo said investigators have found little trace of Graham despite extensive searching. A $100,000 reward was offered for information leading to her safe return.

Jesse L. “LJ” Matthew Jr., 32, the last person known to have been with Graham, was arrested Wednesday on the Bolivar Peninsula near Galveston, Texas, after a woman who recognized him called authorities. Matthew was booked after initially giving a false name; he waived extradition in a Texas court and has invoked his right to counsel. He faces a charge of abduction with intent to sexually assault Graham; police say prosecutors pressed charges after lab evidence review, though they have not publicly detailed that evidence. Investigators have searched Matthew’s car and apartment and are seeking locations he frequented as possible places to look for Graham.

Eyewitness and business-owner accounts differ slightly about Graham’s movements the night she disappeared. The owner of Tempo restaurant said Graham was outside the bar and left with Matthew after he entered; police say they have at least one witness placing her inside the bar with Matthew. Surveillance showed Graham walking with Matthew on the Downtown Mall shortly after 1 a.m., and her friends received a final text from her at 1:06 a.m.

Matthew, described by acquaintances as a “gentle giant” involved in church, hospital work and youth coaching, has ties to the Charlottesville area. Authorities in Galveston say they have no indication Graham is in Texas; they inspected Matthew’s campsite and vehicle and plan to widen searches of the peninsula. The remote Bolivar beaches, where transient campers are common, provided a place where Matthew might have blended in, local residents said.

Chelsea Clinton, now 34 and vice chair of the rebranded Bill, Hillary & Chelsea Clinton Foundation, has moved from a decade of varied private-sector experiments into a more public, hands-on leadership role in the family’s philanthropy. Raised in Arkansas and brought up in the White House, she tried many careers after Stanford and Oxford—management consulting at McKinsey, hedge-fund analysis, journalism, public-health studies and academic work—before settling into the foundation full-time in 2011. Her professional arc, she says, reflected a millennial impulse to experiment and a desire to define herself beyond the Clinton name; her 2010 wedding and the public response helped convince her to use her visibility to advance issues she cares about.

At the foundation, Chelsea’s focus has been modernization, measurement and institutional sustainability. She arrived intent on turning a sprawling, celebrity-driven charity—organized as multiple initiatives and entities and long guided by Bill Clinton’s personality—into a data-driven, more accountable organization with stronger back-office systems, greater collaboration across initiatives, and clearer impact metrics. Specific changes she’s led or championed include consolidating offices, creating cross-initiative liaison roles, building a comprehensive project database, pushing for an impact audit of the Clinton Global Initiative’s (CGI) 2,800 commitments, and bringing younger members and better digital tools into CGI. She emphasizes quantitative and qualitative measurement to identify where the foundation adds the most value and to stop projects that don’t work.

Chelsea has used her academic training and governance expertise to promote specific programs—most notably accelerating efforts to reduce child mortality from diarrhea by expanding access to Zinc/ORS and negotiating country-level commitments, and advancing juvenile justice nutrition and global women-and-girls initiatives such as No Ceilings (with the Gates Foundation). Her style combines technical fluency and operational discipline with the celebrity access the Clinton name affords, enabling rapid convening of partners and fundraising.

Her role remains complicated by the family dynamic and the organization’s past controversies (internal strife and conflict-of-interest questions raised in press reports), and by the unavoidable reality that the foundation, CGI, and the Clinton political enterprise overlap in personnel and public presence. Chelsea is often the on-the-ground operator—more hands-on than her parents—but power in many settings still shifts when Bill or Hillary are present.

Looking ahead, Chelsea keeps the door open to electoral politics. She has publicly said she might consider running for office if she felt compelled to do so, and observers envision possible future runs (e.g., Congress). For now she is balancing foundation leadership, finishing academic work, public speaking and supporting her mother’s causes while navigating the constraints and scrutiny that come with being a Clinton.

A Los Angeles entertainment executive, identified only as Jane Doe, has sued Match.com alleging she was sexually assaulted by a man she met through the dating site and asking the company to screen members against sex-offender registries. Her attorney, Mark L. Webb, plans to seek a temporary injunction to stop the site from signing up new members until screening is implemented. According to the lawsuit, the woman—an Ivy League graduate working in film and television—met the man at a West Hollywood café; after a second date he allegedly followed her home and assaulted her. She later discovered online that he had prior sexual battery convictions. Charges in the Match.com-related case are pending. Match.com representatives were not reached for comment; the company previously told KABC it posts safety tips and warns users to vet people they meet, calling such incidents rare but horrifying. The plaintiff’s lawyer argues that checking names against public sex-offender registries “isn’t a guarantee” but is better than nothing.

Operation Protective Edge entered its 24th day as Israel’s security cabinet ordered the military to press on, prioritizing the destruction of Hamas’s cross-border tunnel network. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel would finish that mission “with or without a cease-fire,” while the IDF called up another 16,000 reservists (bringing total call-ups to about 86,000) to relieve troops and maintain operational flexibility.

Casualties and damage
- Palestinian health officials report well over 1,300 dead (figures in updates range up to ~1,442) and thousands wounded (reports up to ~8,295). Tens of thousands are displaced; UNRWA says roughly 225,000 people have taken refuge in its schools. Gaza infrastructure and housing damage is extensive (estimates cited at around $4 billion and over 5,200 buildings destroyed).  
- Israeli losses include 56 soldiers and three civilians killed, and multiple soldiers wounded in ongoing ground operations around Khan Yunis, Shujaiyeh and other areas. Rocket and mortar fire from Gaza has continued to strike southern Israel and, intermittently, farther north; Iron Dome intercepted some projectiles.

Fighting and incidents
- Heavy Israeli strikes and artillery continued across Gaza, including deadly strikes on populated areas and at least two incidents involving UN-run schools/shelters (one in Jabalia/Jebaliya and damage from shrapnel near a UN shelter in Beit Lahiya). An airstrike hit a crowded market in Shujaiyah, causing dozens of casualties. Both the UN and the U.S. criticized strikes on UN facilities; UN and human-rights officials accused both sides of actions that may constitute violations of international law. UNRWA and other UN officials warned Israel would be legally responsible for protecting displaced civilians if further large-scale displacements occur.
- Israel says many Hamas weapons and launch sites are embedded in civilian areas; Hamas and other Palestinian militants have fired thousands of rockets at Israel over the campaign. Israel reports most of the uncovered tunnels have been destroyed but seeks to finish the remaining ones.

Diplomacy and cease-fire efforts
- Egypt continued mediation efforts. A temporary 72-hour ceasefire beginning Friday, Aug. 1, was later reported agreed by Israel and Hamas in statements by John Kerry and Ban Ki-moon; Hamas publicly said it would abide by a three-day truce if the other side did likewise. U.S. and UN envoys described the pause as a “lull of opportunity,” while Israeli forces were to remain in place during it. Israeli officials stressed any durable agreement must allow the military to complete the tunnel-destruction mission and address Israel’s security demands, including disarmament of Hamas. Palestinian leaders and others pressed for immediate humanitarian relief and protection; Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas called Gaza a “humanitarian disaster area” and accused Israel of war crimes in a letter to the UN.

International reactions
- The U.S. reiterated support for Israel’s security while expressing concern about Palestinian civilian casualties and backing efforts for a humanitarian cease-fire. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and other UN officials condemned attacks on civilians and accused both sides of potential war crimes. Several countries and international figures voiced criticism or assigned blame variably to Hamas or Israel. Humanitarian agencies warned of a worsening crisis as large numbers remain displaced with limited safe refuge.

Overall picture
By late July 31, 2014 the conflict remained intense despite diplomatic moves: Israel pressed a ground-and-air campaign aimed at degrading Hamas’s military infrastructure—especially tunnels—while Gaza’s civilian toll and displacement mounted, international condemnation grew over strikes on shelters and schools, and cease-fire negotiations proceeded cautiously with major security preconditions on both sides.

A 250-pound female grizzly was euthanized after DNA from hair and scat found near the body of hiker John Wallace linked the sow to the scene of Wallace’s fatal mauling in Yellowstone’s Hayden Valley. Park Superintendent Dan Wenk said the decision aimed to protect visitors and staff. Investigators cannot definitively say whether the same sow also killed California hiker Brian Matayoshi a month earlier; after Matayoshi’s death the bear had been left free because it appeared to be defending two cubs rather than acting predatory.

Wallace was hiking alone in a backcountry, bear-frequented area about eight miles from Matayoshi’s site; no witnesses saw the attack. When other hikers found Wallace a day later, one or more bears had fed on his body. Initial investigators had not found cub tracks at Wallace’s scene and had thought a different bear was responsible, but later concluded tracks may have been washed away by rain. DNA and other evidence showed multiple bears — at least nine in the area, attracted by nearby bison carcasses — were present around the time of Wallace’s death. In the investigation’s wake, park officials captured and radio-collared at least seven Hayden Valley bears and relocated the sow’s two cubs to the Grizzly and Wolf Discovery Center in West Yellowstone.

Officials said they made reasonable decisions after Matayoshi’s death given available information. Grizzly-human conflicts in the greater Yellowstone ecosystem (around 600 grizzlies) have risen: a recent report recorded a record number of run-ins last year (295), mostly involving bears seeking human-associated foods, and nine human injuries in 2010 — nearly double the long-term average.

The CDC postponed a planned Public Health Grand Rounds session on preparing for a nuclear detonation and replaced it with a webinar on influenza. The nuclear-preparedness talk — months in the works and titled “Preparing for the Unthinkable” — would have included U.S. experts on radiation and public-health response and drew unusual media interest amid heightened rhetoric between President Trump and North Korea. The agency removed promotional material (including a mushroom‑cloud photo) and said the nuclear topic will be rescheduled. CDC officials said the change was prompted by a spike in flu activity nationwide—particularly influenza A H3N2—which is stressing health systems and causing antiviral shortages in some areas, making flu guidance more immediately time‑sensitive for public‑health professionals.

Summary:

Senate Finance Committee member Sen. Chuck Grassley and other Iowa Republicans backed repealing or sharply raising the federal estate tax as part of the 2017 GOP tax overhaul, arguing it unfairly burdens family farmers and small businesses and penalizes savers. Grassley drew widespread attention and criticism for a remark that eliminating the tax "recognizes the people that are investing, as opposed to those that are just spending every darn penny they have, whether it’s on booze or women or movies."

But federal data and nonpartisan research undercut the politicians’ claims about who the tax affects. The estate tax applies to only about 5,000 U.S. estates a year; in Iowa the number owing estate tax is in the dozens annually (32–61 in recent years). Nationally, only a small share of those estates include farm assets (IRS: 682 in 2016; CRS: about 65 farm estates face liability per year), and even fewer farms lack cash to pay. USDA analysis suggests perhaps 0.4 percent of farm estates owed the tax in 2016; most affected farm estates are larger or have substantial nonfarm assets. Small businesses similarly account for only a few dozen affected estates annually.

Current law taxes estates above $5.5 million (individual) and $11 million (couple) at 40 percent. The House tax bill would double exemptions and repeal the estate tax entirely in 2024; the Senate bill would double exemptions ($11M/$22M). Those changes would reduce federal revenues by tens of billions over a decade and would mainly benefit the very wealthy: the top 1 percent pay 72 percent of estate tax receipts.

Supporters argue higher exemptions or repeal would simplify planning and spare farmers costly legal/accounting work; critics note the number of affected family farms and small businesses is tiny and that repeal primarily benefits the richest Americans. Grassley defended repeal on principle (opposing what he calls a tax on savings and double taxation) despite evidence that very few Iowa farmers are actually forced to sell land to pay estate taxes.

Headline: Robert Pattinson linked to Riley Keough — Elvis’s granddaughter — after being seen together; sparks breakup drama with ex Kristen Stewart

Summary:
- Robert Pattinson was photographed driving around Los Angeles with actress Riley Keough (24), granddaughter of Elvis Presley. They’d previously crossed paths through Kristen Stewart (they all worked on The Runaways) and more recently via Dior appearances.
- Sources describe their relationship as early-stage and fun — “in love” is not claimed; some call it short-term lust. Reports say they’ve spent much of late June together, that Riley has stayed at Pattinson’s Los Feliz home, and they planned to spend the Fourth of July together before he began filming Map to the Stars.
- Insiders say Rob appreciates Riley’s perceived trustworthiness and “lady-like” demeanor after the trauma of Kristen Stewart’s widely publicized cheating with director Rupert Sanders in 2012. Some suggest Rob fears Kristen could have been tempted again and therefore prefers Riley, who “won’t cheat.”
- Kristen Stewart, who is close to Riley and introduced her to Rob, was reportedly upset and “livid” over the budding romance; she allegedly felt betrayed. Other accounts stress Riley and Kristen are friends from The Runaways and that Riley attended Kristen’s April birthday party.
- Background: Riley Keough has modeling ties (formerly Miss Dior Chérie), was previously engaged to Alex Pettyfer, and is the daughter of Lisa Marie Presley. Pattinson has said music interested him before acting and has experienced depression amid his rise to fame.

Overall: Paparazzi sightings and insider comments fueled tabloid speculation that Pattinson and Keough are romantically involved, with sources framing the pairing as a rebound/comfortable, trusting match after Pattinson’s breakup with Kristen Stewart — a development that reportedly upset Stewart.

A CCTV report has drawn international attention after a New York real-estate agent said an anonymous Chinese mother bought a $6.5 million apartment in Manhattan’s luxury One57 building for her 2‑year‑old daughter, claiming the child would one day attend Columbia, NYU, or Harvard and therefore needed a central‑city address. One57, a 90‑story tower with lavish amenities (library with pool table, 7.3‑m aquarium, private concert hall, pet washroom), was still unfinished at the time. Sotheby’s Kevin Brown noted the condo’s value rose to about $8.9 million within two years, suggesting the purchase could also be a savvy investment.
