Theresa May and Andrea Leadsom are the final two candidates in the Conservative Party leadership contest to replace David Cameron. After two rounds of voting by Tory MPs, May led with 199 votes and Leadsom had 84; Justice Secretary Michael Gove was eliminated with 46. The party’s roughly 150,000 members will now choose the new leader by postal/online ballot, with the result due on 9 September. The winner will become Britain’s second female prime minister (the first since Margaret Thatcher).

Key contrasts between the candidates
- Theresa May: Home Secretary since 2010, long government record and seen as experienced and pragmatic. Although she campaigned officially for Remain, she has emphasized she will deliver Brexit (“Brexit means Brexit”) and argued she can unite the party’s leave and remain wings and provide “proven leadership” to negotiate with the EU. She is broadly favoured in MP and member polling.
- Andrea Leadsom: Energy minister and prominent Leave campaigner with a background in the City (former Invesco executive). She has little ministerial or cabinet experience and would be one of the least experienced prime ministers in modern times if elected. Leadsom presents herself as an energetic pro-Brexit candidate promising swift action and economic optimism; she has faced scrutiny over aspects of her CV.

Political dynamics and issues
- The contest reflects deeper party divisions exposed by the EU referendum: May represents a cautious, experienced figure able to appeal across factions; Leadsom embodies the Brexit wing seeking rapid implementation.
- Timing of Article 50 and approach to EU citizens in the UK are points of divergence: Leadsom pushes for quicker action, May has suggested a more measured timetable and has refused to guarantee automatic residency rights for EU nationals until negotiations.
- Several high-profile figures have lined up on either side: Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage backed Leadsom; several Gove supporters (including Nicky Morgan and Ed Vaizey) moved to May. Amber Rudd and other senior Conservatives warned about Leadsom’s lack of experience.

Process and electorate
- MPs reduced the field from five to two through two ballots. Conservative members who joined by 9 June can vote; ballots are sent mid-August and close at noon on 9 September. The membership electorate is older, male and middle-class compared with the general population, and while Brexit will matter, members are also focused on leadership credentials and the vision for post-Brexit Britain.

Context and stakes
- The contest follows Cameron’s resignation after the Leave vote. Whoever wins will lead Britain through the immediate Brexit negotiations and the economic and political fallout, including market volatility and potential Scottish calls for another independence referendum. The leadership choice will shape the government’s Brexit strategy and the Conservative Party’s direction.

A CDC report warns that an emerging, particularly dangerous subset of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) is increasing in the United States. These CRE produce OXA-48–like carbapenemases—enzymes that degrade carbapenem antibiotics—and, critically, the genes encoding them are carried on plasmids. Because plasmids can transfer between bacteria, including different species, this trait enables rapid spread of resistance. Although OXA-48–producers often show different susceptibility patterns (they may remain susceptible to some cephalosporins and show only low-level carbapenem resistance), that makes them harder to detect with standard lab testing; CDC broadened its surveillance definition in 2015 to improve identification.

From June 2010 through August 2015, CDC confirmed 52 isolates from 43 patients in 19 states, with cases rising to about 11 patients per year in 2013–2015. Most isolates were Klebsiella pneumoniae; urine and respiratory specimens were common sources. Many patients (two‑thirds of those with travel histories) had recent international travel, and more than half had been hospitalized abroad—India was a frequent destination—suggesting importation from overseas healthcare settings, though some U.S. clusters indicate domestic transmission in hospitals.

The report places these organisms among high-priority threats because plasmid-mediated resistance has driven rapid global spread of other carbapenemases and newly described plasmid-borne resistance (e.g., colistin resistance from China). CDC and experts recommend enhanced detection of carbapenemase mechanisms (especially in patients recently hospitalized abroad), transmission-based precautions, screening on admission when appropriate, and prudent antibiotic use to limit spread.

Royalty Exchange has created a new company, Royalty Flow, and signed a letter of intent to buy a minority stake in royalties from Eminem’s recordings (albums released 1999–2013) owned by FBT Productions (the Bass brothers’ company). Royalty Flow plans a Regulation A+ crowdfunding raise of $11 million–$50 million to purchase either 15% ($9.75M) or 25% ($18.75M) of that income stream depending on how much is raised. If the offering meets its minimum, Royalty Flow intends to seek a NASDAQ listing. Minimum investment in the offering would be $2,250 for 150 shares ($15/share).

Key points:
- The deal involves royalties from Eminem’s studio albums and some side-project tracks; FBT’s royalties reportedly totaled $5.07M in the last year and $47.2M since 2011. The catalog has sold roughly 172 million albums worldwide.
- Eminem and his label are not involved and were not consulted; a rep stated Eminem has no connection to the company or the sale.
- Royalty Flow will pay dividends to investors from the acquired income stream, reinvest some proceeds to buy more music assets, and aims to build a portfolio of royalties (masters and possibly publishing). Management will likely retain control through a dual-class share structure.
- The offering leverages the JOBS Act Regulation A+ crowdfunding route (no underwriter required). Royalty Flow differs from Royalty Exchange’s auction marketplace by enabling many investors to own fractional shares of an asset.
- The move is positioned as a new model that could let fans/smaller investors “own” portions of superstar catalogs and potentially spur more securitization of music rights, especially as streaming revenues grow. Critics warn of ethical concerns about treating creative work as commodified assets.
- Background: the Bass brothers (FBT) were early collaborators and producers for Eminem; they sold only an income stream, not copyrights, preferring to stay passive owners. The FBT-Universal legal win in 2012 helped secure ongoing digital revenue shares.

Fidel Ángel Castro Díaz-Balart, the 68-year-old eldest son of late Cuban leader Fidel Castro and nicknamed “Fidelito,” died by suicide in Havana after months of treatment for severe depression, Cuban state media reported. A trained nuclear physicist who studied in the Soviet Union, he headed Cuba’s nuclear program from 1980 until it was suspended in 1992 after the Soviet collapse. In later years he served as a scientific adviser to the Council of State and vice-president of the Cuban Academy of Sciences, though colleagues said his influence was limited and his proposals for renewable energy were largely ignored. Born in 1949 to Fidel Castro’s brief first marriage to Mirta Díaz-Balart, Fidelito spent part of his childhood in the United States before returning to Cuba after the 1959 revolution; some of his maternal relatives became prominent U.S.-based critics of the Cuban government. State media said he had recently been treated as an outpatient following a hospital stay; his family will plan the funeral. His death comes just over a year after his father’s death in 2016.

The document reports major developments in the federal investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible ties between Russia and people close to President Trump.

Key points:

- A White House memo based on Oval Office notes recounts that the day after firing FBI Director James Comey, President Trump criticized Comey to Russia’s foreign minister Sergey Lavrov and ambassador Sergey Kislyak. The meeting also became controversial because Trump disclosed classified Israeli intelligence. White House press secretary Sean Spicer did not dispute the account and defended the firing as necessary because Comey had “politicized” the Russia investigation and hindered diplomacy with Russia.

- One White House official characterized Trump’s remarks to Lavrov as a negotiating tactic intended to pressure Russia into concessions on Syria, Ukraine and other issues by invoking the “pressure” Trump faced from allegations of Russian election meddling.

- The Justice Department and FBI investigation has intensified and now identifies a current senior White House adviser as a “person of interest,” indicating the probe has reached high levels of the administration. Investigators are shifting from covert work to more overt actions—interviews, grand jury subpoenas—and the investigation’s tempo is expected to increase. Robert S. Mueller III was appointed special counsel to lead the probe.

- Investigators remain focused on former Trump aides who still draw scrutiny, including Michael Flynn and Paul Manafort, as well as current officials who had contacts with Russian officials (Jared Kushner, Jeff Sessions, Rex Tillerson). Flynn is separately under scrutiny for foreign payments and undisclosed contacts with Russia’s ambassador; a grand jury recently subpoenaed records related to his Flynn Intel Group work. Flynn also retroactively registered as a foreign agent for Turkish interests.

- The probe’s aims include: whether Trump associates coordinated with Russian operatives, whether they had financial dealings with Russia, and whether they facilitated hacking and dissemination of Democratic emails. The investigation also examines potential financial crimes. Several congressional committees are running parallel inquiries.

- Specific contacts mentioned: Kushner’s meeting with Ambassador Kislyak and with a sanctioned Russian development bank (Vnesheconombank); Carter Page’s contacts with a person later convicted as an undeclared Russian agent and a past FISA warrant on Page. Flynn’s discussions of sanctions with Kislyak and subsequent resignation after misleading officials are also noted.

- Officials cautioned that heightened investigative activity does not necessarily mean charges are imminent. Some classified briefings to Congress (the Gang of Eight) have already occurred. The White House maintains that a thorough investigation will show no collusion.

Overall, the reporting portrays an intensifying, widening probe into Russian interference and links to the Trump campaign and administration, reaching senior White House figures and moving into a more active, public investigative phase under special counsel Mueller.

Jayme Closs, a 13-year-old from Barron, Wisconsin, has been missing since early Monday, Oct. 15, 2018, when deputies responding to a 911 call found her parents, James (56) and Denise Closs (46), shot to death in their home. Investigators believe Jayme was in the house during the killings and consider her endangered; she was not at the scene when officers arrived. The deaths have been ruled homicides and no suspect or clear motive has been announced.

Since the discovery, more than 800 tips have been received. Local, state and federal agencies — including the FBI — are involved; the FBI expanded the search nationwide and added Jayme to its missing persons outreach. Authorities asked for public help via a tip line (1-855-744-3879).

Community response has included a 100-person volunteer search, canine teams, and trauma support for students. Wausau sent a school resource officer and a therapy dog, and the state’s Office of School Safety is providing counselors and training for schools, funded by an emergency grant. Searches near the home and along Highway 8 have so far turned up “nothing of evidentiary value.” Jayme is described as about 5 feet tall, 100 pounds, with green eyes and blonde or strawberry-blond hair. Authorities urge anyone with information to call the tip line.

This profile of Kate McKinnon—timed to SNL’s new season—portrays her as an unusually gifted, empathetic comic whose impressions and characters have made her one of the show’s defining performers. The piece opens with a wry meditation on the transactional, performative nature of celebrity interviews, then moves into a vivid lunch scene that introduces McKinnon’s offstage persona: unpretentious, unexpectedly pretty, nervy and watchful (“catlike”), and disarmingly nice.

McKinnon is presented as a chameleon performer whose elastic face and fearless physicality allow her to disappear into wildly different roles—older and younger women, men, and exaggerated celebrities—while always infusing them with empathy. The profile singles out her Hillary Clinton impression as a career-making performance: unlike past SNL Clintons, McKinnon’s version combines toughness, pathos and vulnerability, making the character comically rich and emotionally resonant. Her work embodying politicians (Warren, Kellyanne Conway, Jeff Sessions) helped fuel SNL’s enormous cultural relevance and ratings surge during and after the 2016 election; the piece also explores the peculiar symbiosis between SNL satire and the Trump White House, especially Alec Baldwin’s viral Trump.

The article traces McKinnon’s origins—Long Island childhood, Columbia and the Varsity Show, early sketch work and Upright Citizens Brigade—to explain how she developed her comic instincts. Peers and mentors (Lorne Michaels, Molly Shannon’s influence, writers Chris Kelly and Sarah Schneider) praise her generosity and ability to make audiences love characters who might otherwise be unsympathetic. The profile notes her transition into film (Ghostbusters, Rough Night) but argues that her work on SNL remains the most essential outlet for her talent.

Throughout, the writer emphasizes McKinnon’s emotional openness: to do great impressions she must imagine her subjects’ private lives, which makes the work psychologically intense. The piece balances affectionate portraiture with astute commentary on comedy’s role in politics and culture, portraying McKinnon as a rare comic who combines technical virtuosity, warmth, and an instinct for bringing humanity to satire.

Former Penn State assistant coach Jerry Sandusky gave a nearly four-hour, two-day interview — his first extended comments since being indicted on dozens of child-sex-abuse charges — insisting he never sexually abused any child and saying his long work with disadvantaged youths has been mischaracterized by prosecutors. He acknowledged behaviors and situations cited by investigators (giving money and gifts, opening bank accounts, taking children to games, sleeping or showering with boys, wrestling and physical affection, hosting sleepovers and trips) but framed them as benevolent, parental, or the product of an “extended family” atmosphere he created through his charity, the Second Mile. He said some actions “just happened that way,” that many boys “reached out” for wrestling or hugging, and that he often used gifts and jobs at camps to help or reward children.

Sandusky described a chaotic, boundary‑lax household in State College that functioned as a second home or recreation center for dozens of Second Mile children; he admitted his wife Dottie had warned him not to neglect their own adopted children. He confirmed he was contacted about a 2002 shower incident that led Penn State officials to discuss concerns with Second Mile’s executive director, Jack Raykovitz (who later resigned), but said Joe Paterno never confronted him about any allegations. Sandusky disputed some accounts of who knew what and when, acknowledged investigators have subpoenaed Second Mile financial records, and denied knowingly misusing donated items though he said some gifts he gave had been donated to the charity.

Throughout the interview he oscillated between subdued moments and humor, expressed distress about the damage to his reputation and to Penn State and Paterno, and spoke repeatedly about what he will miss if convicted — coaching, Second Mile, relationships and family. His attorney framed the situation as one in which long‑standing, publicly praised behavior is now portrayed as evidence of predatory motives; prosecutors, however, contend Sandusky used gifts and trust to groom and repeatedly abuse boys, and have charged him with a wide array of offenses.

Study and findings
- A large US prospective analysis (Nurses’ Health Study II) followed 15,632 women and 21,693 singleton pregnancies from 1991–2001 and recorded 854 incident cases of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
- Higher pre‑pregnancy potato intake (boiled/baked/mashed potatoes and French fries) was associated with a higher risk of GDM after adjusting for age, parity, family history, overall diet, physical activity and other factors:
  - 2–4 servings/week → ~27% higher risk
  - ≥5 servings/week → ~50% higher risk
- Substituting two servings/week of potatoes with other vegetables, legumes or whole grains was associated with a modestly lower GDM risk (about 9%, 10% and 12% reductions, respectively).

How researchers explain it
- Potatoes are high‑glycaemic‑index foods that cause rapid postprandial glucose rises, which may stress insulin-producing β cells.
- French fries also add energy density, frying‑related compounds and unhealthy fats; the fries–GDM link was attenuated after adjusting for BMI, suggesting obesity partly mediates risk.

Limitations and caution
- Observational study: cannot prove causation; residual confounding is possible.
- Diet and GDM diagnoses were self‑reported (though prior validation in this cohort showed high accuracy).
- Study population was largely white, female nurses, which may limit generalisability.
- No data on gestational weight gain or GDM severity.

Context and expert view
- UK public health bodies caution that the study doesn’t prove cause and effect and note starchy foods (including potatoes) remain an important part of the diet for fibre and nutrient intake; advice is to base meals on a variety of starchy foods and choose wholegrains where possible.
- Diabetes UK and other experts say managing weight, eating a balanced diet and staying active are proven measures to lower GDM risk.
- Authors suggest moderate potato consumption (e.g., ≤1 serving/week) or occasional swaps to lower‑GI vegetables, legumes or whole grains could be beneficial pending confirmation in randomized trials.

Bottom line
Higher habitual potato consumption before pregnancy was associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes in this cohort; modest reductions in risk were estimated if some potato servings are replaced by other vegetables, legumes or whole grains, but further studies (including trials) are needed to establish causality and guide recommendations.

In 2012 Harvard Divinity School professor Karen King announced a small Coptic papyrus fragment—the so-called "Gospel of Jesus’s Wife"—containing the line "Jesus said to them, 'My wife...,'" attracting wide attention because it suggested early traditions that Jesus might have been married. The fragment’s anonymous owner, its provenance, and its dating were always contentious.

Subsequent investigations and scholarly work have increasingly concluded the fragment is almost certainly a modern forgery. Key developments:

- Live Science traced provenance claims and found contradictions. Documents say the owner bought the fragment from Hans‑Ulrich Laukamp, who allegedly acquired it in Potsdam in 1963, but associates and records indicate Laukamp did not collect antiquities and likely could not have obtained it in East Germany as described. Berlin export records show no trace of the papyrus from that office.

- Coptic specialist Christian Askeland analyzed a second papyrus reportedly from the same anonymous owner—a two‑sided fragment with text from the Gospel of John. That fragment appears to be a fake: its line breaks match exactly a 1924 published transcription, and it uses Lycopolitan Coptic (a dialect extinct by the seventh century), which is suspicious for a purportedly ancient piece. The John fragment’s handwriting and ink are very similar to those of the Jesus’s‑Wife fragment, strongly suggesting a common modern forger or source.

- Scientific tests date the fragments to roughly the 7th–9th centuries (later than King’s initial tentative 4th‑century dating), but radiocarbon age alone doesn’t prove authenticity when other red flags exist. Ink analyses show similarities between the two fragments, and paleographic parallels further support the forgery hypothesis.

- Many papyrologists and biblical scholars have voiced skepticism or called for retraction; some describe the case as a sequence of improbable claims amounting to multiple unlikely "lottery wins." Harvard has not publicly responded to the recent findings, and the anonymous owner remains undisclosed.

Taken together—the dubious provenance, the proven forgery of a companion fragment from the same cache, matching handwriting and ink, and the absence of corroborating export records—scholars increasingly regard the "Gospel of Jesus’s Wife" as a modern forgery rather than an authentic ancient text.

At a June 18, 2013 House Intelligence Committee hearing, NSA Director Keith Alexander and other senior U.S. officials defended two bulk surveillance programs disclosed in recent leaks, saying they have helped disrupt more than 50 “potential terrorist events” worldwide since 9/11. Alexander said about 10 of those incidents had a U.S. nexus, while roughly 90% of the disruptions were attributed to PRISM/Section 702 internet‑surveillance of foreign targets; a smaller number involved the phone‑metadata collection authorized under Section 215. Deputy FBI Director Sean Joyce cited PRISM/702 as important in identifying Najibullah Zazi (the 2009 NYC subway plot) and in a plot against the New York Stock Exchange, and said internet surveillance aided in disrupting plots tied to Denmark and Mumbai. The NSA also disclosed that fewer than 300 “identifiers” (phone numbers or similar) were targeted in the call‑tracking database last year.

Officials emphasized legal bases and oversight: Deputy Attorney General James Cole said Section 702 targets only non‑U.S. persons abroad and argued the Fourth Amendment does not apply to phone‑metadata collection; he noted FISA court and other oversight requirements. Alexander and other witnesses said access to databases is tightly controlled, programs are subject to “extraordinary” oversight, and public discussion must be balanced against protecting sources and methods. They warned the leaks have caused damage and could impair capabilities; lawmakers pressed for more specifics, and agency officials said additional classified case material would be provided privately to Congress. Critics and some lawmakers questioned whether some disruptions could have occurred by other means and called for transparency about the programs’ necessity and impact.

EMILY’s List and the Susan B. Anthony List have escalated competing campaigns centered on female candidates and abortion. EMILY’s List launched an online effort called “Sarah Doesn’t Speak for Me” to oppose former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin’s “Mama Grizzly” endorsements of anti‑abortion women and to promote 32 pro‑choice female candidates. EMILY’s List president Stephanie Schriock framed Palin’s slate as “backwards‑looking,” highlighted key contests (e.g., Boxer vs. Fiorina, Clark vs. Bachmann, Denish vs. Martinez) and debuted a video mocking the “Mama Grizzly” slogan. The group says it raised $43 million in 2007–08 and has helped elect dozens of pro‑choice women since 1985.

The Susan B. Anthony List, which backs anti‑abortion women, criticized EMILY’s List as “running scared,” calling 2010 a “Year of the Pro‑Life Woman” energized by Palin. That group has mounted a bus tour through swing states and says it has helped elect many pro‑life women since 1992. Palin, who has aggressively promoted Republican female candidates through Sarah PAC, has not publicly responded to EMILY’s List’s campaign.

At the dedication of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, D.C., former President George W. Bush and First Lady Michelle Obama shared a warm, widely circulated moment that grabbed public attention. Bush — who signed the 2003 legislation that created the museum — was a featured speaker at the opening, and photographers captured Michelle Obama reaching over to hug him as their spouses looked on. The image, taken by former White House photographer David Hume Kennerly, quickly went viral and sparked positive reaction on social media as a symbol of civility and unity amid a polarized political climate; it also prompted playful photo edits and commentary online.

Here’s a concise, comprehensive summary of the document:

- New CDC surveillance data (as of May 12, 2016) show 279 pregnant women in the United States and its territories have laboratory evidence of possible Zika virus infection: 157 in U.S. states and DC, and 122 in U.S. territories (including Puerto Rico). These counts now include women who tested positive even if they were asymptomatic, so they are not directly comparable to earlier reports that counted only symptomatic cases.

- In the continental U.S. most infections reported so far were travel-associated (people infected while visiting Zika-affected areas) or through sexual transmission; as of the report no locally acquired mosquito-borne infections had been confirmed on the mainland. There are 544 total reported Zika cases in the continental U.S. and 10 confirmed sexual transmissions (it was not specified how many involved pregnant women). Puerto Rico is experiencing active local mosquito-borne spread.

- Of the 157 pregnant women in U.S. states, about 49% reported Zika-like symptoms (most commonly rash, then fever and joint pain); 25% had Zika RNA detected by rRT‑PCR. In territories, 66% of pregnant women were symptomatic and 55% had Zika RNA detected.

- Fewer than a dozen adverse fetal or infant outcomes (including microcephaly and other severe brain abnormalities) had been reported among the monitored pregnancies at the time of the update; most pregnancies were still ongoing so the ultimate number of affected babies remained uncertain.

- The CDC and state/territorial health departments launched two pregnancy monitoring systems in February 2016: the U.S. Zika Pregnancy Registry (USZPR) for states and most territories, and the Zika Active Pregnancy Surveillance System (ZAPSS) for Puerto Rico. These systems monitor pregnant women with laboratory evidence of possible infection (positive rRT‑PCR or IgM with confirmatory PRNT) whether symptomatic or not, to better characterize pregnancy and congenital outcomes and inform clinical guidance and resource planning.

- President Obama urged Congress to approve emergency Zika funding quickly (the White House requested $1.9 billion) to support vaccine development, mosquito control, diagnostics, and care for affected families; the Senate had approved $1.1 billion and the House $622 million, with the administration criticizing the House amount as insufficient.

- Public health priorities emphasized: protecting pregnant women and fetuses through surveillance, counseling, improved diagnostics and monitoring, mosquito control, research (including vaccine development), and planning services for affected families.

United Parcel Service (UPS) reported weaker fourth-quarter results and said it will begin adding residential delivery surcharges as it seeks to recoup sharply higher peak-season costs. UPS earned $1.15 billion in Q4 (EPS $1.25), roughly flat year-over-year, while revenue rose 6% to $15.9 billion. However, operating expenses jumped over 20%—driven largely by moves to handle heavier holiday volumes—causing a steep drop in operating profit in the domestic ground package unit. On a GAAP basis pension charges reduced adjusted EPS to $0.49.

After a disappointing holiday period in which the company over-invested in labor and equipment to handle surges that ultimately fell short of expectations, CEO David Abney said UPS will apply residential-package surcharges as contracts with major customers are renegotiated. UPS argues residential stops cost about three times as much as business deliveries because drivers typically deliver single packages to homes. The surcharges will be phased in over several years and are intended to ensure the company is compensated for the service. The move may prompt higher consumer shipping costs, fewer free-shipping offers, higher minimums for free shipping, and greater use of centralized pickup options (e.g., locker depots).

UPS forecast full-year 2015 earnings of $5.05–$5.30 per share (analysts expected $5.15). Shares rose modestly in early trading. The company said it had spent roughly $500 million on network improvements in 2014 and averaged more than 30 million daily deliveries during the holiday peak.

A Detroit teen was arrested after allegedly robbing a Chase Bank on West 7 Mile Monday afternoon. According to police, the 15- or 16-year-old entered the branch around 2–2:30 p.m., handed a teller a note and threatened she had a bomb to demand cash. The teller complied, then activated the bank’s “man-trap” — an automated double-door security feature that locked the suspect between two sets of doors. Police arrived, detained the youth and took him to a juvenile facility. Officials say it’s unclear whether he had a weapon and whether he will be charged as a juvenile or in adult court.

Kelly Preston told TODAY host Natalie Morales that she and husband John Travolta used Scientology’s “silent birth” method when their son Benjamin was born in November. She described silent birth as keeping spoken words to a minimum during delivery—allowing normal sounds like moans or cries but avoiding chatter, shouts and laughter—so the baby is brought into the world “as peaceful and gentle a way as possible.” Preston credited the technique with contributing to her children’s calm, happy demeanors.

Preston, 48, said she didn’t focus on the medical risks of having a child later in life and was simply grateful after three years of trying to conceive. Benjamin, their third child (they also have daughter Ella), has helped the family heal after the 2009 death of their son Jett. Preston described Benjamin’s arrival as uplifting and a source of renewed spirit, and said the response from well-wishers has been very moving.

She was also on TODAY to promote her film Casino Jack, recalling that co-star Kevin Spacey’s humor helped her return to work after Jett’s death. The interview included Preston’s fuller explanation of the Scientology silent birth philosophy.

An Oklahoma dash-cam captured a high-speed chase after officers attempted to stop a car that was initially going about 5–10 mph over the limit. Instead of pulling over, 34-year-old Luz Avilla accelerated to roughly 90–100 mph and weaved across the road as officers followed, creating a dangerous situation. A few miles from the county line she finally stopped and told officers she fled because she preferred to be jailed in Caddo County rather than Grady County. Avilla refused to exit the vehicle until backup arrived and an officer drew his firearm; occupants eventually exited and several people were arrested. Avilla faces multiple charges including DUI and evading police.

Chester “Chet Haze” Hanks, son of Tom Hanks, sparked backlash after repeatedly using the n-word in Instagram captions and a video defending his right to say it. Posts included phrases like “Fuck yall hating ass niggaz” and references to friends as “my nigga,” and he posted a long statement arguing that hip‑hop culture makes the word acceptable across races and invoking free speech. Critics called his behavior tone‑deaf, appropriative and offensive, noting a pattern of cringe‑worthy attempts to adopt hip‑hop affectations and entitlement. Commentators contrasted responsible white artists who avoid the slur with Hanks’s casual use, argued public figures bear accountability, and emphasized that routine exposure to such language contributes to everyday racism; many dismissed his explanation as ignorant and insensitive.

A 62-year-old Utah State Prison inmate, Ramon C. Estrada, died Sunday night of an apparent heart attack related to kidney failure after a dialysis technician contracted through University of Utah Health Care’s South Valley Dialysis Center failed to appear for scheduled treatments on Friday and Saturday. Estrada, due to be paroled in about two weeks, was being prepared for transport to the hospital when he died; the state medical examiner will perform an autopsy.

Six other inmates also missed dialysis and were taken to University Hospital for evaluation; several were treated and returned to the prison, while one remained hospitalized. The Utah Department of Corrections placed its Clinical Services Bureau director on leave and launched an internal investigation into the delayed response and overall handling of the missed treatments. The Unified Police Department is also investigating.

University of Utah Health Care acknowledged a scheduling/miscommunication error and said it will review and revise communications and procedures. The prison has implemented immediate measures — a dialysis schedule calendar, technician contact lists, requirements for nurses to obtain post-treatment reports and improved charting, and prompt notification to charge nurses when schedules change or technicians do not show — to prevent a recurrence.

Walmart is selling a children’s/young-readers book called Chased by an Elephant, the Gospel Truth about Today’s Stampeding Sexuality by Janice Barrett Graham, wife of Stephen Graham (president of the LDS-oriented Standard of Liberty). The book, available in about 104 Walmart stores in the Intermountain West and at BYU’s bookstore, presents conservative Mormon views on sexuality, gender roles, chastity and “the God‑given sexual appetite,” warning about pornography, fornication, promiscuity and homosexuality. It endorses teaching children “correct information and attitudes” about sexuality and cites LDS leaders’ talks. The Grahams also promote their son Andrew’s memoir, Captain of My Soul, which describes his claim to have left same‑sex attraction through family support, counseling, religious repentance and “deliverance and healing.” Both titles and their endorsements align with anti‑gay and ex‑gay therapy narratives, prompting criticism over Walmart’s carrying of the books.

A 7-year-old boy who was accidentally shot in the head Monday in Crossville, Tenn., has died, police said. The child was among four siblings left unattended in a vehicle outside a Verizon store while their mother and stepfather went inside to pay a bill. One of the children found a loaded semi-automatic pistol in the mother's purse; while attempting to remove the magazine the firearm discharged and struck the boy in the head. He was flown to a Knoxville-area trauma hospital and was in serious condition before police confirmed his death Monday evening. The Cumberland County District Attorney General’s Office and the Tennessee Department of Children’s Services are investigating. The family had been visiting from White County. Authorities described the incident as a tragic accidental shooting.

Former Bolingbrook police sergeant Drew Peterson, 58, is on trial for the 2004 death of his third wife, Kathleen "Kathy" Savio, whose bathtub drowning was initially ruled accidental. The case was reopened and charged after Peterson’s fourth wife, Stacy, vanished in 2007.

At trial, friends of Savio testified about prior statements she made accusing Peterson of violent threats and assaults. Mary Parks, who took nursing classes with Savio, testified that Savio told her Peterson once grabbed her by the throat, left bruises, and asked, “Why don’t you just die?” Parks said Savio also told her Peterson had said he could “kill her and make her disappear.” Parks reported the 2004 death to the state’s attorney’s office at the time. Kristen Anderson, who had lived in Savio’s basement after Savio and Peterson separated, testified Savio kept a knife under her mattress for protection and described an incident in which Peterson allegedly broke into the home in SWAT gear, held a knife to Savio’s throat and threatened her. Anderson said she had called police three times in 2004 but received no response.

Judge James Burmila has allowed some hearsay testimony under an Illinois law (sometimes called “Drew’s Law”) that permits such statements in rare circumstances, a decision prosecutors praised because physical evidence tying Peterson to the scene is lacking. Defense attorneys have vigorously contested the admission and reliability of the hearsay, suggesting Savio was paranoid and that witnesses’ accounts have inconsistencies; they said they may appeal convictions based on the testimony up to the U.S. Supreme Court. The proceedings have been punctuated by frequent legal disputes over hearsay admissibility and emotional testimony from witnesses.

The Court of Master Sommeliers (CMS) has voided the tasting portion of the 2018 Master Sommelier Diploma Examination after finding “clear evidence” that a master sommelier breached confidentiality by disclosing detailed information about the tasting flight before the exam. The CMS board announced on Oct. 9 that, because the blind-tasting results were compromised, diplomas awarded on that basis would be revoked for 23 of the 24 newly minted masters from the September exam; Morgan Harris is the sole member of the class of 2018 whose title remains valid because he had already passed the tasting section in 2017 and this year only needed the service portion. The master found responsible has been barred from CMS events and the board has begun procedures to terminate their membership.

The tasting portion is the exam’s most notorious element: in 25 minutes candidates blind-taste six wines and must identify grape, region and vintage. The master exam has three parts (theory, practical service and tasting) and is notoriously difficult; since 1969 only a few hundred people have passed. The invalidation affects all 54 candidates who took the 2018 exam’s tasting, and CMS said it will refund tasting fees, offer travel assistance, and provide two expedited opportunities to retake the tasting (one later in 2018 and another in spring/summer 2019). Details of the re-tests were not released.

The decision has shaken the sommelier community given the years, expense and career significance tied to the credential. CMS emphasized that protecting the integrity and reputation of the Master Sommelier title required the action. Candidates and colleagues expressed disappointment and heartbreak at having achievements overturned and facing the prospect of re-taking the toughest portion of an exam many spent years preparing for.

Phylicia Simone Barnes, a 16-year-old straight-A honor student from Monroe, N.C., has been missing since Dec. 28 while visiting her 27-year-old half-sister in Baltimore. She was last heard from via Facebook saying she was at her sister’s apartment with the sister’s boyfriend. Her cell phone and social accounts went dark the day she disappeared.

Baltimore police and the FBI are investigating; more than 35 detectives and two FBI teams have been assigned. Authorities have treated several people who were at the apartment as persons of interest, repeatedly re-interviewing them, and have executed search warrants at the sister’s apartment. Some bedding and flooring have been sent to the FBI lab, and additional security footage from nearby buildings is being reviewed, but investigators report no decisive physical evidence so far. Searches including helicopter sweeps and local canvasses have turned up no clues. Police say two main scenarios are likely: foul play in Baltimore or abduction and removal from the area.

Family and community reaction: Phylicia’s parents and classmates are pleading for her safe return; the charter school she attended held a vigil and a Facebook page, “Pray for Phylicia Barnes,” has drawn thousands of supporters. Her father and Baltimore police have publicly urged national media attention, arguing coverage has been sparse compared with other missing-teen cases and raising concerns about a possible racial double standard.

Investigative outreach: Baltimore police set up a tip line (855-223-0033); Clear Channel donated billboards along I-95 to display her photo; the FBI has posted her information online. A cash reward of up to $2,000 was offered by Baltimore Metro Crime Stoppers. Authorities continue to process evidence and follow leads.

A UK study published in JAMA Internal Medicine found that older adults who feel younger than their chronological age have lower mortality than those who feel their age or older. Using 2004–2005 data from 6,489 participants in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (average age 65.8), researchers asked “How old do you feel?” and followed deaths through March 2013 (mean follow-up 8.25 years). Most participants (69.6%) felt three or more years younger than their actual age, 25.6% felt about their actual age, and 4.8% felt more than one year older.

Mortality rates were 14.3% for those who felt younger, 18.0% for those who felt their age, and 24.6% for those who felt older. After adjusting for baseline health, disability, and health behaviors, people who felt older still had a 41% higher mortality hazard than those who felt younger. The association was strongest for cardiovascular mortality but not for cancer deaths. Excluding deaths within the first year suggested the findings were not driven by terminal illness at baseline. Because relatively few people felt older than their age, the authors call for further research and investigation into mechanisms — possibilities include greater resilience, a stronger will to live, and better adherence to health behaviors among those who feel younger. They note self-perceived age can change and suggest targeting people who feel older with interventions promoting positive health behaviors and attitudes toward aging.

PNC Wealth Management’s annual “Christmas Price Index” finds that buying every gift mentioned in “The Twelve Days of Christmas” now costs 6.1% more than a year ago — $107,300 for the full 364-item total. PNC tracked retailer and service prices (jewelry stores, dance companies, pet/aviary sources, etc.) and found no items fell in price.

Highlights:
- Biggest increases driven by birds after the 2011 drought raised feed costs: six geese a-laying up 29.6% to $210, seven swans a-swimming up 11% to $7,000 (swans are the priciest item at $1,000 each).
- Five gold rings rose 16.3% to $750; three French hens increased to $165; a pear tree is $189.99 (up 11.8%).
- Several items showed no change: partridge ($15), two turtle doves ($125), four calling birds ($519.96), eight maids-a-milking ($58), nine ladies dancing ($6,294), 10 lords a-leaping ($4,767), 11 pipers piping ($2,562) and 12 drummers drumming ($2,775.50).
- Buying one set of the core items in each verse costs $24,431 in traditional stores versus $40,440 online, partly due to shipping/live-bird costs; online prices rose 1.5%.

PNC’s index is a seasonal, tongue-in-cheek inflation measure using actual vendor prices; full details are at pncchristmaspriceindex.com.

Episode 7 of the UFC Unfiltered podcast features UFC Women’s Bantamweight champion Miesha Tate and Game of Thrones showrunners David Benioff and D.B. Weiss, alongside regulars Matt Serra and Jim Norton. The episode mixes light banter (4th of July stories, a movie trip, MeUndies) with focused interviews:

- Benioff and Weiss discuss adapting George R. R. Martin’s books, what couldn’t be translated to TV, reactions from Martin, and questions fans care about: how many episodes remain, whether they know the ending, chances of a prequel, network pushback on character deaths, and what they’ll do after GoT. They reveal production timing for Season 7 will be later than usual (likely after April 2017) because “winter is here” in the story and they need grayer, colder weather on location—meaning sunnier regions like King’s Landing or Dorne will be shown in new, gloomier ways. They confirm the plan for two shortened final seasons and suggest the series may still wrap around its usual June window depending on real-world weather.

- Miesha Tate talks at length about her upcoming title defense against Amanda Nunes at UFC 200: assessing Nunes’s strengths and weaknesses, whether the five-round title format helps her, the significance of a potential trilogy with Ronda Rousey, mental preparation as an underdog, rebounding from past losses, and what she did immediately after winning the belt.

The episode also includes segments on UFC history, Matt Serra responding to a callout from Matt Hughes, and Serra reflecting on what he misses about his fighting days.

Actor Charlie Sheen publicly disclosed he is HIV-positive in a TODAY interview, saying the diagnosis—known to him for about four years—was difficult to accept and that he decided to go public to stop extortion and false tabloid claims. Sheen said he’d paid up to $10 million over the years to keep the condition secret, money he lamented was taken from his children. He described initial symptoms as severe headaches and said he doesn’t know how he contracted HIV. Sheen denied knowingly infecting others: he acknowledged having unprotected sex with two people since his diagnosis but said both were informed and are under medical care. His physician, Dr. Robert Huizenga, stressed Sheen is HIV-positive but does not have AIDS, and that Sheen is taking a four-pill daily antiretroviral regimen reliably despite concerns about relapse into substance abuse or depression.

Sheen framed the revelation as an opportunity to reduce stigma, help others, and move into a more philanthropic, reflective period. He told ex-wives Denise Richards and Brooke Mueller and his eldest daughter; he said she handled the news resiliently. He also addressed his past public meltdown and substance-problem period, calling it separate from the HIV diagnosis and expressing remorse for past behavior. Sheen said industry response has so far been supportive and that he is discussing new projects.

The coverage also placed Sheen’s announcement in the broader HIV context: global progress has greatly increased access to antiretroviral treatment—15 million people were on treatment by 2015, ahead of schedule—leading to falls in AIDS-related deaths and new infections, though nearly 37 million people still live with HIV and many regions lag behind. The UN and aid groups warn stigma, punitive laws, and uneven funding must be addressed to meet targets to end the epidemic by 2030.

Finally, legal issues were noted: under California law, knowingly exposing someone to HIV through unprotected sex can be a misdemeanor or felony depending on intent and circumstances, punishable by jail time; as of the report, no formal complaints against Sheen had been reported.

Max Spiers, a 39-year-old British conspiracy theorist and ufologist from Canterbury, was found dead on a sofa in a Warsaw apartment on 16 July after traveling to Poland to give talks and interviews. Two days before his death he texted his mother, Vanessa Bates, saying, “If anything happens to me, investigate.” Polish authorities initially attributed the death to natural causes and, Bates says, did not perform a post-mortem there. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office said it was not investigating because the death occurred abroad; responsibility lies with Polish authorities. Friends reported Spiers had vomited a black liquid and suffered migraines and fatigue in the days before he died. His mother and some within the conspiracy community suspect foul play, arguing he was healthy and had been probing “dark” areas involving politicians, business people and celebrities.

Spiers was prominent in conspiracy and UFO circles and promoted extreme claims—about Nazi/Zionist conspiracies, a secret alien base at Dulce in New Mexico, children allegedly used for “pure energy,” and information “downloads” via sexual encounters. Online commentators and fellow researchers urged further investigation and an autopsy. Spiers’ body was repatriated and buried in Canterbury; a post-mortem was later carried out in Kent and the North East Kent coroner said investigations were at an early stage. Bates has said she has only a Polish death certificate and is awaiting toxicology and coroner’s results, which she hopes will answer whether poisoning or other foul play was involved. Some UFO researchers speculated publicly that researchers might be targeted, while mainstream experts like former UK MoD investigator Nick Pope rejected claims of government-ordered killings.

President Barack Obama and Iran’s newly elected moderate president, Hassan Rouhani, exchanged short, notably cordial letters after Rouhani’s June victory, prompting Tehran to view Obama’s offer of direct talks as an encouraging shift from the slow, multilateral negotiations with world powers. Iran’s leadership—including, apparently, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei—received the outreach positively and sees a limited window (roughly six months before domestic politics tighten) to try to reach a nuclear agreement and gain relief from crippling sanctions, especially restoration of banking access such as SWIFT.

Rouhani has signaled a conciliatory, pragmatic foreign policy—publicly rejecting nuclear weapons, proposing “constructive engagement,” offering to help facilitate dialogue on regional conflicts, and making conciliatory gestures (e.g., outreach to Jewish Iranians, releasing prisoners). He published an op-ed urging world leaders to seize the opportunity and plans a high‑profile U.N. visit with speeches and media appearances to showcase Iran’s new tone.

U.S. officials are cautiously encouraged and willing to “test” Rouhani’s intentions, but they stress that promises must be matched by concrete steps. Obama is open to direct talks but did not commit to a leader‑to‑leader meeting, and Washington warns that meaningful sanctions relief would require significant Iranian concessions on the nuclear program. Analysts note the change is significant compared with the Ahmadinejad era, but they caution that charm alone won’t lift the toughest sanctions and that internal Iranian consensus could fray if negotiations make no quick progress. The moment is seen by many on both sides as an important but fragile opening for diplomacy on Iran’s nuclear dispute and broader ties with the West.

Britney Spears’ recent radio promotional tour for her Las Vegas residency, new single “Work Bitch” and album “Britney Jean” was tightly controlled by her team: stations were told five‑minute interviews should only cover the show, single and album, with “no personal questions” and no “funny business.” Reps say the briefing was simply information for hosts, but radio insiders and several taped segments suggest the restrictions produced stilted, one‑sided interviews and awkward moments—one Houston show was pulled and another found Spears sounding detached and needing questions repeated. Meanwhile, controversy continues around Spears: allegations she’ll lip‑sync in Vegas were denied, and before/after images from a VFX studio prompted claims her “Work Bitch” video digitally slimmed her, which her team did not comment on.

Other celebrity items: Martha Stewart discussed cleanliness and dating at an awards event; Beyoncé posted an Instagram beach photo with Blue Ivy; Charlie Hunnam skipped appearances amid backlash over leaving 50 Shades of Grey; Arnold Schwarzenegger, Jim Caviezel and Sylvester Stallone were spotted dining after an Escape Plan screening; Elvis Duran and Eric Trump planned a Brooklyn Bridge walk for St. Jude; and the Off‑Broadway parody “Bayside! The Musical!” extended its run.

Separately, court documents reveal Britney’s conservator father Jamie Spears, who has received $16,000 monthly plus $1,200 for office rent since the 2008 conservatorship, filed to increase his reimbursement. He asked for an additional $800/month retroactively (Nov 2012–Aug 2013) and to raise his authorized office expense to $2,000/month going forward, citing growing duties including negotiating her Las Vegas contract—a deal that will keep Britney under the conservatorship for at least two more years and secure substantial future payments to Jamie.

Un relitto databile alla prima metà del VI secolo a.C., ritrovato nel litorale di contrada Bulala nel mare di Gela (a circa 300 m dalla costa, profondità bassa), ha restituito 39 lingotti di un metallo nobile identificato come oricalco. Scoperti inizialmente dai volontari dell’associazione Mare Nostrum e recuperati da sommozzatori della Capitaneria di Porto, Guardia di Finanza e Soprintendenza del Mare, i lingotti sono risultati, dall’analisi con fluorescenza a raggi X condotta da Dario Panetta (TQ, Genova), una lega composta per circa 75–80% di rame e 15–20% di zinco con tracce di piombo, nichel e ferro — sostanzialmente una forma antica di ottone/brass (oricalco/latone).

Il carico, probabilmente proveniente dalla Grecia o dall’Asia Minore e diretto a Gela poco dopo la sua fondazione (689 a.C.), indica scambi marittimi importanti e la presenza in età arcaica di officine artigianali locali in grado di lavorare metalli preziosi per oggetti decorativi di pregio. La scoperta è considerata unica: finora l’oricalco era noto soprattutto da fonti letterarie (Platone lo cita come metallo prezioso di Atlantide) e da rari oggetti ornamentali. Alcuni studiosi discutono tuttavia l’esatta natura dell’oricalco e interpretazioni alternative sono state proposte.

La Soprintendenza del Mare, rappresentata da Sebastiano Tusa, sottolinea l’importanza del ritrovamento per lo studio delle rotte e dell’economia metallurgica nel Mediterraneo antico e annuncia la necessità di scavare il relitto per recuperare e contestualizzare l’intero carico e aggiornare la storia economica più antica della Sicilia.

The document includes two distinct topics:

1) Internet Archive crawls
- The Internet Archive is crawling and archiving web pages as they are created and the pages they reference so that when referenced pages change or disappear, the version that was live when the referring page was written is preserved.
- The aim is to replace broken links with links to archived versions (or provide companion links) so readers can see what the page’s authors originally intended.
- This effort is framed as an attempt to "fix all broken links on the web," including crawls of supported "No More 404" sites.

2) Entertainment news — Lindsay Lohan joins Sky comedy Sick Note for season 2
- Lindsay Lohan has joined the cast of Sky 1 comedy Sick Note for its second season, which is currently shooting in the U.K.
- Sick Note stars Rupert Grint as Daniel Glass, a compulsive liar misdiagnosed with a terminal illness by his incompetent doctor played by Nick Frost; Don Johnson plays his boss. Lohan will portray Johnson’s character’s daughter.
- The first season will air this fall. Season two is already in production.
- The series is part of Sky 1’s edgier 10 p.m. comedy lineup, alongside shows such as Bliss and Bounty Hunters.
- Sick Note is produced by King Bert (Jo Sargent, David Walliams, Miranda Hart), created and written by Nat Saunders and James Serafinowicz, and directed by Matt Lipsey. Executive producer Jo Sargent expressed excitement about making the second season and welcoming Lohan to the cast.

Investigators said cockpit voice and flight-data recorders show the UPS Airbus A300 that crashed near Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport received audible warnings about an excessive rate of descent in the seconds before impact. NTSB member Robert Sumwalt said the first of two warnings occurred about 16 seconds before impact; the agency has not determined a cause and is keeping all possibilities open.

The twin-engine cargo jet struck trees about one mile from the end of Runway 18, then crashed into the base of a nearby hill and damaged two homes. Both crew members, Capt. Cerea Beal, Jr., 58, and First Officer Shanda Fanning, 37, were killed. The A300 had flown about 45 minutes from Louisville and investigators found no evidence of engine failure prior to impact.

Runway 18 is the airport’s shorter runway and lacks full precision instrument landing electronics that provide vertical guidance; the longer 12,000-foot runway was closed for light maintenance at the time, forcing use of the 7,000-foot runway that requires pilots to make visual altitude judgments amid hilly terrain. Pilots and experts noted that Runway 18 can be challenging, especially for large jets, and some pilots try to avoid it when possible.

Investigators plan to analyze aircraft weight, approach procedures, pilot experience with that runway, weather and the airport’s navigation and lighting systems to determine why the aircraft was low enough to hit trees. Weather records show the flight descended through overcast to a few clouds at 1,100 feet shortly before the impact; debris and tree strikes may have produced the observed flames. The NTSB and FBI continue to examine the crash site.

The Washington Post released classified White House readouts of two January calls between President Trump and foreign leaders — Mexico’s Enrique Peña Nieto and Australia’s Malcolm Turnbull — revealing chaotic, combative exchanges and prompting concern about both Trump’s competence and internal leaks.

Key points:
- Trump pressed Peña Nieto to stop publicly denying that Mexico would pay for Trump’s proposed border wall, at times urging both leaders to say only that they would “work it out.” He spoke disparagingly about Mexico’s role in U.S. drug problems, claimed credit for election wins, and made inaccurate or exaggerated claims about voter support (e.g., Cuban Americans, New Hampshire). Peña Nieto rebuffed the wall-paying suggestion.
- The Turnbull call escalated around an Obama-era agreement for the U.S. to vet and resettle up to 1,250 refugees Australia had detained after arriving by boat. Trump repeatedly misunderstood or dismissed Turnbull’s repeated explanations that Australia’s policy bars boat arrivals to deter people-smuggling, mischaracterized the refugees as criminals or terrorists, inflated the number to “2,000”–“5,000,” and complained the deal made him look weak. The call ended abruptly with Trump comparing it unfavorably to a call with Vladimir Putin.
- The transcripts confirm earlier media reports and contradict White House denials. Reactions included alarm at the president’s factual errors, focus on image over diplomacy, and his praise for Putin.
- The leaks themselves are notable: analysts suggest they likely came from national-security or establishment officials alarmed by Trump’s conduct. The publication is seen as both narrowly non-damaging to national security (it casts foreign leaders positively) and deeply corrosive to norms — undermining confidentiality, increasing mistrust inside government, and risking a cycle of irregularity between the White House and the bureaucracy. The broader implication: damage to U.S. diplomacy and institutional function that could outlast this administration.

The piece argues that the Republican Jewish Coalition was justified in excluding Congressman Ron Paul from its presidential forum—not merely because his isolationist stance on Israel deviates from mainstream Republican views, but because of his long association with racist, conspiratorial and extremist content published for decades under his name. Reporting uncovered archives of Ron Paul–branded newsletters from the 1980s and 1990s (Ron Paul’s Freedom Report, Political Report, Survival Report, Investment Letter) that contained overtly racist passages (denigrating Black Americans, attacking Martin Luther King Jr. and Barbara Jordan), bizarre conspiracy claims (AIDS conspiracies, “needlin’” attacks), praise for local militias and practical advice for antigovernment operatives. Those revelations have repeatedly resurfaced during Paul’s campaigns.

Paul has responded inconsistently: at times saying he took moral responsibility but did not write the pieces, other times claiming he didn’t authorize or know the authors (campaign aides and longtime associates such as Lew Rockwell have been implicated). Critics note Paul profited substantially from the newsletter operation and question how he could be unaware of its content. Defenders argue the exclusion by the RJC was politically motivated because of Paul’s opposition to foreign aid to Israel. Others suggest the newsletters reflected a past strategy of courting marginal, sometimes extreme supporters in pursuit of fringe libertarian causes.

The controversy raises broader questions about Paul’s judgment and leadership: whether he would vet people writing under his name, whom he would appoint, and whether the newsletters—once tolerated within a fringe movement—would become a political ceiling if widely publicized as he gained electoral momentum. Paul’s campaign reiterates he “disavows” the statements and blames not having paid closer attention.
