Three women — 45-year-old Suzanne Taylor and her daughters Taylor Pifer, 21, and Kylie Pifer, 18 — were found dead Sunday evening in their North Royalton, Ohio, home. A family friend discovered the bodies; one victim had an apparent knife wound, while the causes of death for the other two remain under investigation. The victims’ bodies were found in the mother’s bedroom, reportedly under covers as if tucked into bed. Investigators believe the killings were targeted, not random, and forensic testing and autopsies are ongoing.

Police identified a 45-year-old man as a suspect wanted for questioning in the deaths. He was located at a Brunswick home late Monday and refused to leave, prompting an overnight standoff that began about 9 p.m. and lasted more than eight hours. The homeowner, a woman, exited the house unharmed. Officers used a loudspeaker to communicate with the suspect from about 2:30 a.m. and ultimately entered through an unlocked front door, subduing the armed suspect with a Taser and taking him into custody just before 5:30 a.m. The investigation is continuing with assistance from the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation; no motive has been announced.

Early Sunday (around 3:45 AM) in South Seattle, Officer Anthony Reynolds stopped a car running red lights on Martin Luther King Jr. Way S. The driver, Abdul Abdashiek, told Reynolds his wife, Maly Yusuf, was in labor. Before medics arrived, Yusuf gave birth to a baby girl in the car with Reynolds and three other officers (Lorissa Johnson, Nicholas Kartes and Jason Alvord) present. The newborn cried but then had trouble breathing; Officer Reynolds, with help from the mother, cleared the baby’s airway and restored breathing. An ambulance arrived shortly after and took mother and daughter to a nearby hospital in stable condition. The couple named the baby Hadaya (Arabic for “gift”) and sent a thank-you note to the officers: “You have helped deliver a precious gift. We are so grateful.”

A magnitude-7.0 earthquake devastated Port-au-Prince and surrounding areas in Haiti, leaving vast destruction, mass casualties and chaotic, improvised rescue efforts. With buildings including the presidential palace, cathedral, hospitals and parliament collapsed or badly damaged, survivors used bare hands, sledgehammers, wheelbarrows, pickup trucks and makeshift stretchers to pull the injured and dead from rubble. Bodies lay in streets, schools and public spaces; estimates of the death toll varied widely and remained uncertain, from thousands to much higher.

Immediate needs—water, food, medical care and shelter—overwhelmed local capacity. Many hospitals were damaged or full, prompting NGOs like Doctors Without Borders and Cuba’s medical teams to set up tent clinics and field hospitals. Communications were disrupted, hindering emergency calls and coordination. Looting and prison escapes were reported, and law enforcement resources were strained despite UN peacekeepers and police attempting to maintain order.

International assistance began arriving: search-and-rescue teams, medical supplies and food from countries including China, France, Britain and the U.S. President Obama pledged a major U.S. response, deploying military assets such as the USS Carl Vinson and planning Marines and assessors to determine needs. Some flights into Haiti were temporarily restricted to prioritize military arrivals, complicating relief logistics.

Amid the chaos, thousands camped in the open, scavenged for supplies, and awaited news of missing relatives; the Red Cross launched an online tracing service. Survivors expressed despair and anger at the lack of visible organized government relief. The situation remained dire, with massive humanitarian needs for an estimated millions affected across the country.

Moe’s Southwest Grill has been named Brand of the Year for fast-casual Mexican restaurants in the latest Harris Poll, unseating Chipotle after the Denver-based chain held the top spot for three years. Harris surveyed more than 97,000 U.S. consumers across thousands of brands. Moe’s — a roughly 600–650 unit chain owned by Focus Brands — rose to first place by posting the largest brand-equity gain (13%), scoring highest on familiarity, perceived quality and purchase consideration. Placed data also show a modest (about 5%) increase in Moe’s foot traffic amid Chipotle’s troubles.

Chipotle, with roughly 1,900 locations, fell out of the top four after a year of high-profile food-safety incidents (norovirus, salmonella and E. coli outbreaks) that helped drive a roughly 30% decline in comparable sales and a significant share-price drop. Competitors such as Taco Bell, Qdoba and Baja Fresh ranked ahead of Chipotle in the poll. Analysts say Chipotle’s brand perception has suffered and that rivals are capitalizing by expanding menus, marketing and store counts. Despite the reputational hit, Chipotle still has far greater visitation and revenue overall, and the company has offered promotions and adopted new safety protocols to win customers back.

Kurt Cobain’s iconic Martin D-18E guitar — the instrument he played during Nirvana’s 1993 MTV Unplugged performance and believed to be the last he played before his 1994 death — is at the center of a bitter, potentially multimillion-dollar legal fight between Frances Bean Cobain and her estranged husband, musician Isaiah Silva.

Key points:
- Silva says Frances gifted him the guitar as a wedding present after their secret 2014 marriage and refuses to hand it over following their March 2016 separation. Frances denies ever gifting it.
- The guitar was once insured for $1 million and is now thought to be worth several times that amount. Courtney Love has called it a family heirloom that “is not his to take.”
- Negotiations have stalled, and Frances Bean is prepared to sue to recover the instrument; sources say Silva is taking “extreme and unsupportable positions” and is forcing litigation.
- As part of an interim arrangement, a judge in September reportedly ordered Frances to pay Silva $15,000 per month in spousal support while mediation over the guitar continues.
- Separately, Silva has filed for spousal support seeking $25,000 per month, claiming he left steady work based on promises Frances made to cover expenses (including private school and housing for his child) and arguing he is entitled to half of income from deals made during their two-year marriage. Frances insists her inheritance from Kurt Cobain is hers alone but is open to some support.

No comment was available from Silva’s attorney.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds have quietly ended their brief marriage, surprising friends and insiders who say no one saw it coming. The couple kept their relationship extremely private, rarely photographed together and seldom speaking about their marriage; friends doubt the full reasons for the split will ever be revealed. Their joint statement said they decided to separate “after long and careful consideration” and stressed they entered and left the relationship “with love and kindness,” asking for privacy. Sources say both will remain tight-lipped—Scarlett and Ryan likely won’t do any public interviews about the breakup, and Reynolds’ upcoming Green Lantern press tour will reportedly bar personal questions about the split.

A Delaware family fell seriously ill while vacationing at the Sirenusa Condominium Resort in Cruz Bay, St. John, after a unit in the complex was fumigated with the odorless neurotoxic pesticide methyl bromide. Paramedics were called March 20; Steve Esmond, his wife Theresa Devine, and their two teenage sons were airlifted to hospitals on the U.S. mainland. Devine was treated and released; Esmond has regained consciousness and is stable; both sons remain in critical condition and comatose weeks after exposure.

The EPA confirmed preliminary tests showing methyl bromide in the apartment where the family stayed (their unit was above a fumigated first-floor apartment) and said the chemical—banned for indoor residential use in the U.S. since 1984 and restricted to certain outdoor agricultural uses—can cause seizures, coma, lung injury and other severe effects. Investigators found that a certified applicator from Terminix applied methyl bromide at the complex targeting an indoor wood-eating beetle; the EPA also learned the chemical had been used at the resort previously (including in October 2014). The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into Terminix and the circumstances of the application.

Sea Glass Vacations, which manages rentals at Sirenusa, said it has terminated its contract with Terminix, is cooperating with authorities, and that the treated unit is unoccupied. Federal agencies including the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry are interviewing guests and staff and continuing testing and monitoring the property to determine exposure details and to prevent future occurrences.

The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that most of Texas’s 2013 abortion restrictions — notably hospital-style structural requirements for clinics — may go into effect. The measures mandate things like specific room and doorway sizes, air sterilization systems, backup generators and on-site blood supplies; providers say these upgrades cost millions and won’t improve patient safety. The court previously upheld admitting-privilege and medication-abortion rules and again found opponents did not prove the requirements impose an “undue burden” on a large fraction of women.

Before the 2013 law there were about 40 clinics in Texas; today roughly 17 remain and only seven to eight meet the new building standards (four are Planned Parenthood facilities). The ruling includes a limited exception for Whole Woman’s Health in McAllen. Advocates for abortion rights say the decision will drastically curtail access — leaving some women to travel hundreds of miles or cross into New Mexico — and plan to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. State officials and supporters argue the rules protect women’s health. The decision could be enforced in roughly three weeks unless the Supreme Court stays it.

Russia's Foreign Ministry named Hollywood actor Steven Seagal a "special representative" for US-Russian humanitarian ties, according to a statement on the ministry's official Facebook page. The unpaid role, likened to a UN goodwill ambassador, will focus on promoting cultural, public and youth exchanges between the two countries. Seagal, who became a Russian citizen in 2016 and is a close friend of President Vladimir Putin (he attended Putin's May swearing-in), has publicly defended Putin and denied Russian election meddling allegations. Putin reportedly suggested Seagal as an honorary envoy to President Obama in 2013, and Rep. Dana Rohrabacher later credited Seagal with helping arrange congressional contacts with Russia. CNN has contacted Seagal’s spokesperson for comment.

The document also contains a Russian-language account of a meeting with Tunisian Prime Minister Youssef Chahed discussing ways to expand trade, economic and investment cooperation. The parties noted growing bilateral trade and agreed to work toward a more balanced trade structure. They plan an intergovernmental commission meeting on trade, economic and scientific-technical cooperation in Tunisia in the first half of the year and urged speedy approval of a proposed 2019–2021 cooperation program. They also agreed to accelerate ratification of a prior intergovernmental agreement on peaceful nuclear energy cooperation and to finalize projects and documents easing visas, road transport and environmental cooperation. Tunisia invited Russian firms to participate in infrastructure tenders for road and rail construction; both sides welcomed regional ties (notably between Tunisia and Tatarstan) and emphasized continued practical cooperation across sectors.

A 59-year-old Russell, Kansas man, James Zordel, was killed Friday night after his 1992 Suzuki motorcycle struck a black cow on a rural paved road about six to 6.5 miles south of Interstate 70 near Russell. The crash occurred on the 3500 block of 189th Street; there were no witnesses, it was dark, and investigators have not determined whether speed or the animal suddenly entering the roadway caused the collision. Zordel, who was not wearing a helmet, was pronounced dead at the scene. No one else was injured.

Bill and Kirsten (Kris) Bresnan of Toms River have built a nearly 40-year marriage around daily, deliberate expressions of love. Bill Bresnan began leaving napkin notes and postcards for Kris in 1974 when they met during his securities-class lectures; that small habit evolved into writing her one card or letter every day of their marriage. Today more than 10,000 notes are filed chronologically in 25 boxes and kept as a “love diary” they can pull up to revisit a specific day, restaurant, trip or memory.

Their routine includes candlelit dinners, morning and evening “I love you”s, no TV in the bedroom, and shared rituals (they play Boggle at breakfast). Bill sometimes stages larger romantic gestures—recreating scenes from the movie Summertime in Venice, having hieroglyphics engraved on a ring, or sending 50 cards leading up to Kris’s 50th birthday. Both have supported each other through illnesses and emphasize never going to bed angry and talking through issues.

The couple says the key to lasting love is daily work, shared fun, presence (putting phones away) and small consistent acts of affection. They are in the process of selecting which letters to save for their children and continue the practice, though Bill admits his greatest fear is someday forgetting. For Valentine’s Day they prefer simple celebrations—dinner, wine and chocolate—over lavish gifts.

Amanda Longacre, who was stripped of her Miss Delaware title two weeks into her reign after officials said she was too old for Miss America competition, has filed a lawsuit in Delaware’s Court of Chancery against state pageant officials (including executive director Debi Wilson) and the Miss America Organization. The suit seeks reinstatement as Miss Delaware, restoration of her Miss Pike Creek title and scholarships, an age waiver to allow her to compete at Miss America in September, and monetary damages — $500,000 for Longacre and $2.5 million in a class-action claim on behalf of other contestants she says were recruited and later disqualified, for a total of $3 million.

Background: Miss America rules require contestants be between 17 and 24; Longacre was born Oct. 22, 1989 and turns 25 after this year’s national pageant. Longacre says she was recruited, repeatedly certified as eligible after submitting her birth certificate and other ID while winning Miss Pike Creek and then Miss Delaware, and performed duties expected of the titleholder (appearances, fundraising, suspending graduate work and reducing employment). Two days after her disqualification, first runner-up Brittany Lewis (born July 21, 1990) was crowned Miss Delaware and advanced to Miss America.

Claims and allegations: The complaint alleges the state pageant knowingly recruited ineligible contestants to bolster participation and fundraising, then disqualified them; it also recounts an alleged offer from the official who removed her to “make it up” with a wine-and-cheese pajama party. Longacre seeks compensation for lost scholarships, expenses (more than $4,500 on coaching, clothes, hair/makeup), lost career opportunities and clearer disclosure of age rules on pageant sites.

Responses: The Miss America Organization called the lawsuit “without merit” and said it would defend vigorously. State pageant representatives declined extended comment; some scholarship funds were later promised to Longacre after her public complaints, though she says she never received an apology.

The piece describes The Wilderness Downtown, an innovative “interactive film” created for Arcade Fire’s song “We Used to Wait.” Built with HTML5 in collaboration with Google and directed by Chris Milk (produced by Radical Media), the site asks users to enter the address of the home where they grew up and then generates a personalized, multi‑window experience: video of a running kid, animated vectors, satellite/Street View imagery of the neighborhood, and prompts (like writing a postcard to your younger self), all synced to the song. Reviewers praise how effectively it blends video, interactivity and web features to create an emotionally resonant, nostalgic experience—one that points to a new direction for music videos—while noting browser compatibility is best in Chrome, with Safari workable and other browsers inconsistent.

Authorities say eight members of the Rhoden family were executed at four Pike County, Ohio, locations in a carefully planned attack; seven of the victims were shot multiple times (one as many as nine), and several showed bruising consistent with a struggle, according to autopsy reports released April 2016. The dead include Christopher Rhoden Sr., his ex-wife Dana Rhoden, three of their children (ages 16, 19 and 20), Christopher Sr.’s brother and cousin, and a 20-year-old woman; three young children at the scenes survived. Investigators found indoor marijuana grow operations at three of the properties—one reportedly containing hundreds of plants—and evidence suggesting possible cockfighting at one site. Authorities have not announced suspects or a motive, are treating the killings as targeted and “sophisticated,” and have received hundreds of tips while sending dozens of evidence items to the state crime lab. A $25,000 reward has been offered for information. Family members deny involvement in illegal activity and say the assailants appeared to know the households. Federal agencies have offered assistance to the expanding multiagency investigation.

Google has launched a wedding-focused site that lets couples build a wedding website, edit photos and plan events using wedding-specific templates in Google Sites, Google Docs and the photo tool Picnik. Announced on Google’s official blog ahead of Valentine’s Day, the offering was developed with wedding planner Michelle Rago, who contributed the designs and planning tips. To promote the service, Google is running a sweepstakes with a $25,000 prize and a chance to receive planning help from Rago. The move is part of Google’s broader strategy to become more embedded in everyday consumer life (similar to past products such as Google Health), which has raised questions in the past about the company’s handling of sensitive personal information.

MasterCard announced at Mobile World Congress 2016 that it will let customers use biometrics—selfie facial scans (with a blink test) or fingerprints—as an alternative to passwords for authenticating online card payments. Trials in the U.S. and the Netherlands showed strong user preference (92% in one test), and the company planned a rollout that summer across many countries including the UK, US, Canada and several European markets. Customers download an app to link a device; during checkout they still enter card details but, if extra verification is required, they authenticate via the phone’s camera or fingerprint sensor rather than typing password characters.

MasterCard says biometrics are more convenient and can improve security by avoiding weak, reused passwords; it also claims the biometric data will not be transmitted in a usable form and that other fraud-detection systems will monitor for suspicious behavior. Industry observers note biometric authentication could reduce card-not-present fraud and lower costs, while critics warn facial recognition and fingerprint sensors can be spoofed, so layered protections remain important. The move follows wider industry adoption of biometrics (e.g., Apple Pay, Windows Hello, Alibaba demos) and signals a broader shift toward “who you are” factors for online authentication.

At a New Hampshire town hall Thursday night, a man asked Donald Trump when the U.S. can “get rid of” Muslims and asserted President Barack Obama is Muslim. Trump chuckled, did not challenge the premise, and responded vaguely that “we’re going to be looking at a lot of different things,” then moved on. Video of the exchange prompted immediate condemnation from Democrats, Muslim leaders and some Republicans: Hillary Clinton called the remarks “just plain wrong,” Rep. Keith Ellison said Trump showed “a lack of moral courage,” and DNC Chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz labeled him a racist. Trump’s campaign manager later said Trump hadn’t heard the Obama comment and thought the audience member was referring to training camps. Reporters tried to question Trump afterward but received no answer; Trump also canceled a planned South Carolina trip the next day. The episode revived long-running falsehoods and suspicion about Obama’s background—despite Obama’s Christian faith and Hawaiian birth—and echoes past Republican controversies over comments about Obama’s religion and origins.

Ricky Gervais opened the 73rd Golden Globes with a deliberately provocative monologue that targeted many stars and Hollywood institutions, delivering a steady stream of dark, sarcastic jokes that some found hilarious and others offensive.

Highlights of his set included barbs at Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, Roman Polanski, Jennifer Lawrence, Jeffrey Tambor, Ben Affleck, Matt Damon, Mel Gibson and others. Notable lines mocked Hollywood elites for being out of touch or “marrying well,” ridiculed NBC’s impartiality (pointing out the network had no nominations), and lampooned pay inequality, award show self-importance and recent film choices (e.g., The Martian nominated as a comedy). He made repeated jabs about scandals—referencing the Catholic Church abuse exposé in Spotlight and quipping about Roman Polanski—and used crude sexual and drug-related humor about awards and his own past Globe wins. Introducing Mel Gibson, Gervais made a line that NBC bleeped on air.

Before the show he’d teased that he would offend Hollywood and confirmed he had free rein from organizers, promising to say what he wanted while claiming he wouldn’t break the law. The piece also recaps brief background about Gervais—this was his fourth time hosting (a record), he created and starred in the original The Office, he’d had a short pop career, and he’s a past Globe winner—and references ongoing coverage of Gibson’s previous racist and abusive remarks.

Summary:

A controversy erupted in Pembroke Pines, Florida after Sgt. Jennifer Martin of the Pembroke Pines Police Department says she was effectively refused service at an Arby's drive-through because she is a police officer. According to the officer’s report, a clerk took her payment but the shift manager allegedly told her, “He doesn’t want to serve you because you are a police officer,” then laughed and later gave her a refund when she decided not to eat the food.

The Pembroke Pines police chief called the Arby’s corporate office; CEO Paul Brown and a senior VP apologized to Chief Dan Giustino and said the employees’ conduct was unacceptable and not representative of the company. The company later fired the manager involved and suspended the clerk. Arby’s also offered free meals to uniformed officers in Miami‑Dade and Broward counties and the CEO met with local police union leaders.

The incident drew protests from officers’ family members, calls from local police unions for a national boycott and for the employees to be fired, and an outpouring of support from other businesses delivering food to the department. The clerk and his grandfather described the exchange as a poorly timed joke or misunderstanding caused by busyness at the drive-through; the clerk says he never intended to insult officers. Police leaders accepted the corporate apology and described the matter as closed, but union leaders and some community members pushed for stronger action.

House Speaker John Boehner reiterated a hardline GOP stance ahead of White House talks on averting a U.S. debt default: Congress must approve entitlement cuts and cannot accept tax increases as part of any debt‑ceiling deal. Boehner said he supports raising the borrowing limit but only with spending cuts larger than the increase and "real restraints on future spending," including major changes to Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security and a balanced‑budget amendment the House will consider. He denied agreeing to tax hikes in private talks with President Obama, saying instead he favors tax‑rate simplification and reform that would spur growth and revenue. Boehner criticized the White House for insisting on more revenue through tax increases while, he said, not being serious enough about entitlement reform. The negotiations aim to finalize cuts and a debt‑limit increase before the Aug. 2 deadline.

At a House Science, Space, and Technology Committee hearing, Rep. Mo Brooks (R‑Ala.) challenged Philip Duffy, president of the Woods Hole Research Center, about causes of observed sea‑level rise (about 3.3 mm/year). Brooks suggested erosion and sediment deposition—rivers dumping silt and coastal cliffs collapsing (he cited the White Cliffs of Dover and California)—as primary contributors, arguing that deposited soil and rock reduce ocean capacity and thus raise sea level. Duffy replied that local ground subsidence can matter in some places but that on human timescales erosion and cliff collapses are “minuscule” contributors; he and other scientists attribute recent sea‑level rise mainly to melting land ice and thermal expansion driven by human‑caused warming, with satellite data showing Antarctic ice mass loss and accelerating shrinkage. Brooks also disputed that Antarctic ice is shrinking, saying some studies show increases and noting a NASA facility in his district gave him contrary information; Duffy cited NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center. The exchange drew media attention and criticism for Brooks’ framing and for promoting explanations that scientists say are negligible compared with climate‑driven ice loss and ocean warming.

Senate and House leaders worked through the weekend to avert a U.S. debt default as negotiators closed in on a bipartisan debt‑limit deal, but key differences and House resistance threatened a prompt resolution.

- Late Saturday and into Sunday, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid postponed planned votes after progress in talks among Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, Vice President Biden and White House officials. Reid and others expressed cautious optimism that direct engagement had reduced the immediate risk of default.
- A Sunday cloture vote on Reid’s separate $2.2 trillion debt‑ceiling bill failed to reach the 60 votes needed, demonstrating remaining division in the Senate (50 for, 49 against).
- Leaders described two central sticking points: Republicans’ demand for “dollar‑for‑dollar” deficit reductions with no new revenue to match any borrowing-authority increase, and the design of an enforcement “trigger” to ensure a joint House‑Senate committee produces roughly $1.6 trillion in savings by year’s end.
- House Speaker John Boehner emerged as the primary holdout. Sources said negotiators were close to a framework but Boehner had not signed off; his members would likely resist any large defense cuts that might be part of a compromise. Boehner has pushed for strict triggers (including tying future debt‑limit increases to committee success), which the White House resists as too destabilizing.
- One compromise gaining traction would impose across‑the‑board cuts if the committee fails to meet its target; to win GOP support this could mean steep reductions in defense spending, alarming Democrats who fear loss of revenue measures and protections for Medicare.
- Tensions between Reid and McConnell continued publicly—each criticized the other’s seriousness at times—while McConnell and Boehner said they were confident an agreement could be reached. Pelosi urged an end to political theater and urged compromise.
- In the House, a preemptive vote (246–173) advanced a measure that would raise the debt limit by $2.4 trillion and cut spending by $2.2 trillion, setting a negotiating posture as the Treasury’s cash buffer ran low.

Overall, leaders signaled progress and reduced immediate default risk, but significant unresolved issues—trigger/enforcement mechanisms, the size and makeup of cuts (especially to defense), and Boehner’s willingness to agree—left the outcome uncertain as the deadline approached.

The story reports on a leaked New Zealand Health Ministry discussion paper proposing large cigarette price increases as part of efforts to make the country smoke‑free by 2025. One extreme scenario modeled would raise pack prices to about NZ$100 (roughly £50) by 2020 via an initial 30–60% “shock” rise followed by around 30% annual increases; officials called that option “probably unrealistic.” More likely approaches in the paper include a shock tax increase followed by 10% annual rises (bringing packs to roughly NZ$60 by 2025) or steady 10% year‑on‑year increases (about NZ$40 by 2024). The paper also considers non‑tax measures such as treating tobacco as a highly toxic substance, banning smoking in cars with children, expanding anti‑smoking media campaigns, and removing duty‑free sales.

The Prime Minister, John Key, warned that very large price hikes could fuel a black market in tobacco and questioned their sustainability. Associate Health Minister Tariana Turia expressed strong support for doing “whatever it takes” to reduce smoking. The Health Ministry emphasized the paper was an internal discussion document, not government policy. The piece also notes criticism from smokers who argue high prices alone may not stop addiction.

This document is an in-depth guidance and public-warning compilation about giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum): an invasive, very large plant whose sap causes severe phototoxic skin reactions (phytophotodermatitis) and can cause long-lasting scars or even blindness if it contacts the eyes. It covers health risks, safety precautions, and recommended control methods (manual, mechanical, and chemical), plus notes on recent detections and the need for long-term monitoring and revegetation.

Key points

- Hazard: Giant hogweed sap contains photosensitizing chemicals (furanocoumarins). When sap contacts skin and is exposed to sunlight, painful blisters can form within 48 hours, leaving dark pigmentation and scars that can persist for months to years; sensitivity to sunlight may last years. Eye exposure can cause blindness. Reactions can begin within 15 minutes, peak 30 minutes–2 hours, and are worsened by heat and moisture.

- Identification and impact: Plants can exceed 14 feet, have hollow stems 2–4 inches across with purple/red blotches and stiff hairs, and large umbrella-shaped white flower clusters. A single plant can produce thousands of seeds; seedlings can remain viable in soil for many years (possibly up to ~15), enabling rapid spread and long-term seedbanks. Dense stands shade out native vegetation and increase erosion risk where removed.

- Recent detections: The report highlights a confirmed finding of ~30 plants in Clarke County, Virginia, and warns residents statewide to watch for sightings. Other reported sightings in Virginia (Staunton area, Middlesex County) suggest potential spread.

- Safety precautions when handling or near plants:
  - Do not touch plants or sap with bare skin; wear waterproof gloves, long sleeves, long pants, boots and eye protection (synthetic, water-resistant clothing preferred).
  - Prevent sap splashes between workers (keep distance), avoid using weed-whackers/brush cutters (sap may spray), and work in shade or after dark if possible.
  - Keep water, soap, eyewash on site. Wash exposed skin immediately with cold water and soap, keep area from sunlight for 48 hours, launder clothes and clean equipment right away.
  - Seek medical advice for reactions; early topical steroids may reduce severity.

- Control strategies:
  - Prevention: Do not plant or move soil contaminated with seeds; prevent plants from setting seed. Control small/new infestations first.
  - Manual/mechanical options (often used together and repeated for years):
    - Root cutting: cut taproot 6–10 inches below ground; remove cut parts; repeat if regrowth; herbicide can be applied to cut root for added control.
    - Flower/seed head removal: cut seed heads after seed forms but before maturity; place in sealed clear or dark bags and solarize in sun for ≥2 weeks before disposal.
    - Cutting/mowing: start when plants are small, cut at least three times a season for multiple years; remove flower heads before mowing; clean equipment to avoid spreading seeds.
    - Cut-and-cover: cut to ground and cover with black plastic/landscape fabric and mulch; monitor for seedlings, remove after a few years and re-vegetate.
  - Herbicides: Systemic herbicides (glyphosate and triclopyr) are effective; triclopyr is selective for broadleaves and allows faster grass recolonization, glyphosate is non-selective. Apply per label March–early June when leaves are actively growing, with possible follow-up in July–August. Repeat treatments over several years until no seedlings emerge. Licensed applicators should follow FIFRA 2(ee) recommendations and carry labels/letters where required.

- Long-term monitoring and site restoration: Because seeds can remain viable for many years, sites must be monitored for several years (at least three, possibly up to 15 years) and revegetated (e.g., grasses) to prevent erosion and outcompete new hogweed seedlings.

- Resources: Links to NYDEC best-practice manuals, safety pages (with graphic photos), and herbarium reports for identification and reporting sightings are recommended.

Overall recommendation: Do not handle giant hogweed without proper protection and training; report sightings to local extension or environmental authorities; use an integrated, repeated control plan (mechanical/chemical), prevent seed spread, and re-vegetate treated areas while monitoring for many years to ensure eradication.

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), the firm that tallies and delivers the sealed Oscar envelopes, accepted full responsibility for the Best Picture mix-up at the 89th Academy Awards, when Moonlight was the rightful winner but La La Land was announced. PwC said partner Brian Cullinan accidentally handed presenters Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway the duplicate Best Actress envelope (Emma Stone) instead of the Best Picture envelope, and that the company failed to follow protocols quickly enough to correct the error. PwC apologized to the presenters, host Jimmy Kimmel, and the casts of La La Land and Moonlight, and called the incident a failure after 83 years of managing the awards process.

Cullinan — who had earlier described the envelope process as thoroughly checked and said such mistakes were unlikely — had posted backstage photos on Twitter minutes before the error and later deleted his Oscar-night tweets. PwC confirmed that Cullinan and his partner Martha Ruiz each carried identical briefcases with full sets of envelopes and alternated handing them out from opposite sides of the stage; only Beatty, entering from Cullinan’s side, was given the wrong envelope.

The Academy launched a full review of its relationship with PwC and of Oscars procedures. Potential fixes under consideration include stationing two auditors at each stage entrance instead of one to provide a fail-safe. Observers noted the problem was compounded by multiple failures: the wrong envelope was handed off, presenters and producers did not immediately stop the proceedings, and corrective protocols were delayed, all contributing to the prolonged onstage confusion.

A man named Craig Mandell launched a Tilt crowdfunding campaign called "Don't Let Nickel Back" aiming to raise $1,000 to discourage Nickelback from ever playing in London. Modeled on a recent successful Tilt effort that helped bring Foo Fighters to Charlottesville, VA, Mandell’s plan is to send emails to Nickelback’s management on contributors’ behalf — the number and tone of emails scale with donation size (e.g., $1 = one email, $5 = a stronger email, $50 = email with an attached Nickelback MP3). The page says proceeds will go to charity (or "perhaps therapy" for afflicted fans). Mandell set a November 3 deadline; at the time of reporting the campaign had received no funding. A correction appended notes the crowdfunding platform was Tilt. The story also mentions a separate, successful Foo Fighters Cornwall campaign that hit its £150,000 target in two days but still needs the band's agreement to play.

This document contains two long film reviews and background pieces.

1) True Grit (Coen brothers, 2010)
- Overview: Joel and Ethan Coen’s adaptation of Charles Portis’s 1968 novel is a faithful, darkly comic and visually beautiful Western about vengeance and moral reckoning. It retells the story of 14-year-old Mattie Ross (Hailee Steinfeld), who hires one‑eyed U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn (Jeff Bridges) to hunt down her father’s killer, Tom Chaney (Josh Brolin).
- Tone and themes: The film leans into an old‑time American ethos of revenge and religious moralism. Mattie is portrayed as a hard, stoic, scripture‑quoting protagonist—both childlike and fiercely determined—whose businesslike focus on settling her father’s accounts and seeking justice propels the plot. The Coens preserve much of Portis’s language and dark humor while giving the story their own cinematographic poetry (Roger Deakins) and a balance of comic and serious moments.
- Characters and performances: Hailee Steinfeld makes a striking debut as Mattie; Jeff Bridges brings a world‑weary, nuanced Rooster distinct from but comparable to John Wayne’s Oscar‑winning turn in the 1969 film. Matt Damon plays a self‑important Texas Ranger, LaBoeuf, and Barry Pepper is memorable as a brutal antagonist. The film mixes tense, violent encounters (hangings, severed fingers) with sly character work and moral complexity.
- Critical reception in excerpts: Reviewers praise the Coens’ respect for the source, the visual composition, the performances (especially Steinfeld and Bridges), and the film’s blend of humor, heroism and grim frontier realities. One piece frames the film as both faithful reboot and a Coens‑style distillation of genre conventions.

2) Detachment (Tony Kaye)
- Overview: Tony Kaye’s Detachment is an intense, sometimes flawed high‑school drama centered on a substitute teacher (Adrien Brody) and the emotional breakdowns and systemic failings around him. The film mixes live action with animated sequences, interviews, quotations and fantasies; it aims for grand moral urgency about caring in a decaying social system.
- Tone and themes: The film’s standout moral moment is Lucy Liu’s guidance counselor rant—“it’s easy not to give a shit”—which crystallizes the movie’s plea for courage to care. Detachment attempts to use the struggles of a failing school as a metaphor for broader social and artistic struggles.
- Style and reception: Visually ambitious with a Fellini‑like reach, the movie is uneven—melodramatic, overloaded, and populated by some archetypal characters—but often powerful and emotionally wrenching. Adrien Brody’s central performance is singled out as exceptional; other performances and the screenplay receive mixed notices. The film is likely divisive but showcases Kaye’s undiminished cinematic talent and passionate engagement.
- Director background: The piece includes an extended profile of Tony Kaye—his turbulent history with American History X, public feuds (notably with Edward Norton), eccentric publicity stunts, and periods of professional exile. The profile argues that Kaye remains a combustible but gifted filmmaker whose uncompromising temperament has both hurt and defined his career. The critic suggests Detachment merits a distributor’s risk because Kaye still displays originality and emotional urgency, even if the film is imperfect.

Overall, the document contrasts two films and filmmakers: the Coens’ disciplined, reverent reinvention of a Western classic that balances humor, violence and formal control, and Tony Kaye’s fevered, uneven but passionate return with a sprawling moral drama about education, care and artistic struggle.

About three weeks after Randy Thill, 47, was killed when his Harley-Davidson crashed into the U.S. 61 median near Warner Road in St. Paul on June 25, his wife Rhonda feared she had also lost his gold wedding band. The ring wasn’t returned among his personal effects and, distraught and not ready to visit the crash site herself, Rhonda asked friends for help.

Tim Allen, a high-school friend and vice president of the Los Valientes motorcycle club, mobilized fellow riders and contacted Jay Stevens of Rapid Recovery and the Sober Soldiers motorcycle club. On July 12, about a dozen bikers—some using metal detectors, others searching on hands and knees—scoured a 100-foot stretch of the median. Stevens concentrated where paramedics’ discarded rubber gloves were found and discovered the ring pushed into soil behind a weed. The group returned the ring and other recovered items to an emotional Rhonda, who said she was grateful that people she mostly didn’t know would go to such lengths to give her closure.

A benefit and poker run, “Riding with Randy,” was later planned for Sept. 5 at the St. Paul Saloon to support the family.

A California couple’s dispute with their 64-year-old live-in nanny, Diane Stretton, drew national attention after she refused to leave their Upland home following termination.

What happened
- Ralph and Marcella Bracamonte hired Stretton via Craigslist in early March to care for their three children in exchange for room and board. After several weeks they say she stopped performing duties and retreated to her room.
- The family fired her on June 6 and asked her to leave. Stretton refused, claiming she was not terminated and asserting health issues, and threatened legal action.
- Stretton remained in the home while media and police presence grew; she has been spotted driving by and once hiding in her car near a police station. She declined to speak directly to reporters.

Resolution proposal and tensions
- In an email to the family’s lawyer, Stretton said she would move out by July 4 if the media stayed away and allowed her limited continued use of the home (sleeping for a few more nights and access to the shower). She also cited a heat wave and physical disabilities as reasons to delay moving.
- The Bracamontes suspect the conditions are a ploy; they worry she may try to barricade herself when they are briefly out of town for a family wedding. They plan to have relatives stay in the house while away.

Legal issues
- Because housing was part of the employment arrangement, Stretton has certain tenant rights; the family must use formal eviction procedures to remove her, which can be lengthy. Interfering with her room or utilities could create legal liability.
- Stretton has a long history of litigation in Southern California, with multiple cases dating back to 2002 and is listed in California as a vexatious litigant. That record includes suits involving family members and others.

Status
- As of the reports, Stretton had not yet moved out but had told the family’s lawyer she would leave by July 4 under the stated conditions; both sides remained wary and preparations for legal removal were being discussed.

A federal judge on June 16 granted a temporary stay blocking the deportation of Pablo Villavicencio, a 35-year-old Ecuadorian pizza delivery worker detained June 1 at Fort Hamilton in Brooklyn after a background check revealed a 2010 removal order. The stay, obtained by The Legal Aid Society via an emergency habeas petition, bars his deportation until July 20; Villavicencio remains in ICE custody in New Jersey while he pursues immigration relief, including a pending green card application his U.S. citizen wife filed in February.

Legal Aid attorneys — who worked overnight to file the emergency request — say Villavicencio has no criminal record and was detained after showing a city ID and signing for a daily pass during a delivery he had made many times before. They called the stay a win for due process and said they will help him secure lawful status. New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo urged DHS to investigate the case, criticized ICE’s expedited removal as unnecessary and inhumane given Villavicencio’s long New York residency and family ties (his wife and two U.S.-born daughters, one with a serious medical condition), and requested his release. The case has drawn local and national attention and prompted calls for review of ICE practices.

The Big C is a Showtime comedy-drama about Cathy (Laura Linney), a Minneapolis schoolteacher diagnosed with Stage IV melanoma who decides not to tell her family and to live recklessly — flirting with her doctor, eating only dessert, digging a pool, pulling pranks and generally acting liberated. The series assembles strong talent (Linney, Oliver Platt, John Benjamin Hickey, Gabourey Sidibe, Phyllis Somerville) and has moments of effective black humor and truthful, sardonic lines that could work well given the premise.

Critics are split. Many praise Linney’s gift for conveying a formerly reserved woman pushed into truth-telling and applaud Oliver Platt for convincingly mixing comic and tragic tones as her husband, Paul. The show’s best passages are subdued, darkly funny, and authentically patient-like in their gallows humor.

But the dominant criticism is that the program mishandles tone and characterization. Rather than a nuanced reckoning with mortality, Cathy often reads as an oddly perky, caricatured “smiley” woman — smirking through scenes where grief would be more credible — as if the creators were forcing upbeat comedy onto a grim premise. Early episodes pepper the show with exaggerated side characters and frantic antics (man-child husband, insolent teen son, eccentric homeless brother, caustic neighbor, volatile overweight student), which critics say overload the half-hour format, create tonal whiplash between comedy and pathos, and prevent emotional depth from emerging. Some reviewers also note familiar cable tendencies — putting women in extreme situations for dark comedy — and worry the show leans on sitcom clichés about cancer (cute younger doctors, support-group tropes, delayed disclosure to family).

Overall, The Big C shows real promise — great actors and intermittent sharp writing — but many find its execution uneven: too manic, too saccharine in places, and insufficiently grounded in the gravity of its subject. Critics hope later episodes will slow down, settle the tone, and let the central character’s experience breathe.

President Obama, frustrated by stalled budget talks, unexpectedly addressed reporters Tuesday and demanded that House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid either reach a deal or return to the White House daily until they do. He said he, Vice President Biden and his team were prepared to meet “for as long as possible” to resolve funding before the government’s spending authority expires at midnight Friday. Obama warned against repeated short-term extensions—he would accept only a brief two- or three-day stopgap at most—and urged lawmakers to “act like grownups” to avoid a shutdown.

The appearance followed a White House meeting with Boehner and Reid and came amid conflicting accounts about whether Boehner had told Obama he didn’t want the White House at a subsequent Boehner-Reid meeting; Boehner aides later clarified that the Speaker merely wanted a private session with Reid and then said the leaders had a “productive discussion” and would keep working. Republicans, led by Boehner, insist on deeper cuts and have suggested a one-week extension plus $12 billion in additional reductions; Democrats accuse them of pushing harmful cuts and policy riders (including attacks on Obama-era health, financial and environmental policies and Planned Parenthood funding). The White House has begun contingency planning for a potential shutdown.

Separately, House Republicans released a long-term budget blueprint from Budget Chairman Paul Ryan proposing more than $5 trillion in deficit reductions over a decade, including converting Medicare for future beneficiaries to a private-plan system and turning Medicaid into block grants for states—measures that would sharply reduce federal spending and provoke major policy disputes.

After an explosion on the London Underground at Parsons Green that injured at least 29 people and is being treated as a suspected terrorist attack, President Donald Trump tweeted that the perpetrators were “sick and demented people who were in the sights of Scotland Yard” and urged authorities to “be proactive” and “deal with” “loser terrorists” more harshly. His remarks drew swift rebukes from British officials, including Prime Minister Theresa May, who called speculation about an ongoing investigation unhelpful, and a Metropolitan Police spokesperson who dismissed the claim as speculation, saying suspects had not even been identified. London Mayor Sadiq Khan said he was focused on emergency response. National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster sought to soften the comment, saying Trump was speaking generally about law enforcement vigilance. The exchange revived tensions over U.S.–U.K. intelligence sensitivities after earlier leaks and brief interruptions in intelligence sharing, and threatened to strain the “special relationship.” The White House said Trump privately conveyed sympathy to May in a call and pledged continued close cooperation; the president also used public remarks to reiterate calls for tougher measures against terrorism and touted U.S. military strength. The Islamic State later claimed responsibility for the attack.

New Federal Reserve survey of about 4,100 U.S. adults (Sept–Oct 2013) paints a stark picture of Americans’ retirement preparedness and broader financial stress five years after the Great Recession.

Key retirement findings
- Nearly 40–41% of adults aged 45+ who were not yet retired have delayed their planned retirement because of the recession; overall, about one-third plan to retire at the same age as before 2008 and 36% now expect to retire later. Only ~5% moved plans earlier.  
- Retirement savings are widely inadequate: 31% of all respondents have no retirement savings and no pension. Among 55–64 year‑olds, 19% have zero retirement savings. Income disparities are large: 54% of those earning under $25,000 report no retirement savings or pension, versus 10% of those earning $100,000+.  
- The dominant savings vehicle is defined‑contribution plans (e.g., 401(k)/403(b)) used by 44%; only 18% have employer pensions. The shift from pensions to individual accounts places heavy planning burdens on households, but only about one‑quarter of people are actively planning for retirement.  
- Many people are uncertain about how they’ll fund retirement: 25% of all respondents—and 14% of those aged 45+—answered “I don’t know” when asked how they and their spouse would pay retirement expenses. Social Security is the single most commonly cited resource (about 45%).  
- Retirement work expectations have shifted: among those 55–64 not yet retired, only 18% expect a traditional stop‑working retirement; 24% expect to work as long as possible, 18% plan for part‑time work after retiring, and 9% expect to become self‑employed.

Broader financial and labor themes
- Access and income matter: part‑time and low‑wage workers are much less likely to have access to employer retirement plans (three‑quarters of full‑time private sector workers vs. about 37% of part‑time workers). Many respondents cite limited resources, not indifference, as the reason for poor saving.  
- Overall economic perceptions remain mixed: about one‑quarter of families said they were “just getting by” and 13% were struggling. Compared with 2008, 34% said they were worse off, 34% the same, and 30% better. Over 60% described their households as “doing OK” or “living comfortably.”  
- Other strains include credit access (one‑third of recent applicants were denied or got less than requested), 10% of households have highly variable monthly income, and wage growth has been weak—compounding difficulties in building retirement savings.

Implications
- The combination of weak savings, reliance on Social Security, uncertain planning, and delayed retirements has potential consequences for Social Security solvency, retirement income adequacy, financial markets (contributions/withdrawals), and labor market dynamics (older workers staying employed longer). The findings underscore large gaps in preparedness and awareness, especially among lower‑income and part‑time workers.

This collection of articles and posts centers on 19-year-old Modern Family actress Ariel Winter and two recent public moments: a viral "baby voice" segment on Conan that some found cringeworthy, and a social-media defense after critics attacked her outfit choice at a cast event.

- Conan appearance: Clips of Winter using a high-pitched "baby voice" on Conan drew ridicule online. One outlet mocked the sound heavily, calling it disturbing and saying it creeped out her boyfriend and friends.

- Social media stance on body/image and haters: Winter has a reputation for posting revealing photos and projecting confidence. In interviews she says she focuses on self-relationship and ignores trolls: if people dislike her posts they can unfollow her.

- Event outfit backlash and response: At a Modern Family screening Winter wore a gilded, embellished gold minidress with mesh cutouts and gold pumps while many co-stars dressed more casually. Some commenters accused her of trying to look "slutty" or being insecure. Winter responded on Instagram, defending her choice—asking why she must dress like everyone else, urging people to let others feel good about themselves, and exhorting “WEAR WHATEVER YOU WANT PEOPLE!”

Overall tone: The coverage mixes criticism and mockery (about the baby voice) with support for Winter’s assertiveness and refusal to be shamed for her appearance or wardrobe choices.

Japanese novelist Haruki Murakami, a globally bestselling but publicity-shy author often tipped for the Nobel Prize, agreed to answer readers’ questions on a special page hosted by his Japanese publisher Shinchosha. For a limited period in January (questions accepted Jan. 15–31 in several languages) Murakami will respond to queries that interest him, with his answers to be posted through the end of March on the site “Murakami’s Place” (Murakami-san no tokoro). The initiative, echoing a similar 2006 project, offers a rare chance for fans to interact with the reclusive 65‑year‑old, who is known for surreal, melancholic fiction (translated into 50+ languages), a fondness for running and cats, and support for the Yakult Swallows baseball team. The publisher noted Murakami will take “questions of any kind,” though which he answers is up to him; contact details for submissions were not yet provided. The piece also briefly notes Murakami’s background (born in Kyoto to teachers), his tendency to live abroad and criticize Japan, and mentions his 2013 bestseller Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage. (Also included in the document are unrelated poems and short pieces by other writers.)

President Obama, after promising to confront Islamic State "wherever they are," ordered unexpectedly large airstrikes in Syria that struck both Islamic State targets and the Khorasan Group, an al‑Qaeda offshoot accused of plotting attacks on Americans. The strikes, conducted with a few Arab partners, and concurrent congressional approval of funds to train moderate Syrian rebels mark a significant reversal of Obama's prior reluctance to intervene in Syria's civil war, which pits the Assad regime against a fragmented mix of opponents. His shift was driven by rapid ISIS advances in Iraq, atrocities including the beheadings of two U.S. journalists, and the perceived regional threat from extremists. Obama intends a long campaign to “degrade and ultimately destroy” ISIS without deploying combat ground forces, though military leaders have suggested sending advisors could be recommended if needed. The piece welcomes taking the fight to terrorists but warns the administration has yet to make a convincing case that the threat justifies an escalating U.S. military role in Syria and Iraq or that it has a clear, achievable strategy and objectives.

Here are the key points from the document, summarized:

1) Supreme Court declines to review Mikos death‑penalty appeal
- The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Ronald Mikos’s appeal challenging his 2005 federal death sentence for the murder of Joyce Brannon, a disabled former patient and nurse.  
- Mikos, a podiatrist convicted of killing Brannon to prevent her testifying in a Medicare‑fraud case, did not testify at his trial. His lawyers argued prosecutors improperly used his silence to suggest lack of remorse and urged that this influenced the jury’s penalty decision.  
- The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had upheld his conviction and sentence; the Supreme Court left that ruling in place. Mikos remains under federal sentence in Terre Haute. Case: Mikos v. United States, 08‑1280.

2) Federal prosecutors seek death penalty in Yingying Zhang kidnapping and presumed murder
- Federal prosecutors announced they will seek the death penalty for Brendt Christensen, a former University of Illinois physics graduate student charged in the June disappearance of 26‑year‑old visiting scholar Yingying Zhang, who is presumed dead though her body has not been found. The decision required AG Jeff Sessions’s approval and will likely delay trial preparations.  
- Prosecutors allege Christensen has other victims and claimed he “desired to be known as a killer.” They also alleged he choked and sexually assaulted another victim in 2013 (identified only by initials). In a filing they argued he poses a continuing threat to public safety.  
- Investigators tied Christensen to Zhang through surveillance video, cleaned areas of his car where Zhang would have sat, phone searches showing visits to sadomasochistic kidnapping‑fantasy forums, and audio recordings from a campus rally in which he described an “ideal victim” and admitted the kidnapping (one of the rally recordings was made by an FBI‑wired attendee).  
- Christensen initially gave inconsistent accounts to investigators. A separate woman reported an earlier abduction attempt the same day and later tentatively identified Christensen from photos; his defense is seeking to exclude that testimony, arguing uncertainty due to sunglasses.  
- The move to seek the federal death penalty follows other recent decisions by the Justice Department to pursue capital charges in separate cases.

A New York Times investigation says Wal‑Mart’s Mexican unit, Wal‑Mart de Mexico (Walmex), paid more than $24 million in bribes in the early 2000s to speed store openings and obtain permits. Company executives were alerted in 2005 and an internal inquiry reportedly found evidence of bribery but was shut down and not reported to law enforcement. The revelations prompted a U.S. Justice Department criminal probe under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and a company review; Wal‑Mart has met voluntarily with DOJ and the SEC and says it is conducting an “aggressive investigation” and strengthening controls.

The story has damaged Wal‑Mart’s reputation and knocked its stock price—Walmex and parent company shares fell sharply—while raising questions about what senior managers knew and when. Congressional Democrats Elijah Cummings and Henry Waxman have requested an in‑person meeting with CEO Mike Duke and signaled possible oversight action. Labor and governance critics have called for accountability and suggested executives could face departure if they failed to act.

Background details: Wal‑Mart de Mexico is the company’s largest foreign subsidiary and accounts for about 20% of Wal‑Mart stores. Executives tied to the Chamber of Commerce’s legal‑reform arm (which has lobbied to narrow FCPA enforcement) have had roles at Wal‑Mart. Eduardo Castro‑Wright, a key executive in Mexico during the period, and other senior managers were reportedly aware of the allegations. Potential penalties under the FCPA could be substantial; past settlements have been large and investigations can take years. Wal‑Mart emphasizes the alleged incidents are years old and, if true, are not reflective of the company’s values.

- Mark and Debby Constantino, a Nevada couple who appeared on the Travel Channel’s Ghost Adventures and worked as paranormal investigators, were found dead Tuesday inside their adult daughter’s apartment in Sparks after an hours-long barricade and hostage-style standoff.

- Events began about 6:30 a.m. when Reno police responded to a report of a man found dead at a northwest Reno home where Debby had been living; Debby was then missing. Investigators later tracked her cell phone to an apartment near Sparks High School (1100 15th Street), where SWAT teams from Reno and Sparks surrounded and evacuated the Courtside Gardens complex.

- Officers knocked on the daughter’s apartment and heard gunfire and a man yelling threats. Reno police say Mark Constantino fired at officers who approached the door; officers did not return fire. Negotiations continued, with the suspect at one point demanding “give me 15 minutes to gather my thoughts or I'll kill her,” according to Reno Deputy Chief Tom Robinson. Police eventually used explosives to breach the door; a SWAT team found Mark and Debby dead. Police have not released causes of death or ruled out anything.

- One officer was injured by broken glass during the door breach and was treated at a hospital. Sparks police emphasized that no law enforcement gunfire struck or injured the subjects.

- Court records show Debby had obtained a restraining order against her estranged husband the previous week and the couple had a pending divorce with a December court date. Debby had previously been described by police as a victim in an earlier kidnapping and domestic incident involving Mark.

- The Constantinos had been featured on paranormal programs (including episodes at the Mustang Ranch, Goldfield Hotel and San Francisco’s Market Street Cinema), lectured at paranormal conferences, and maintained a website, spirit-speak.com.

- Police are not searching for other suspects; the identity of the male roommate found dead in the Reno residence has not been released. Authorities have not disclosed the weapon type or official causes of death and continue to investigate.

Sparkle is a 2012 remake of the 1976 Motown-era musical about three Detroit sisters—Sparkle (Jordin Sparks), Sister (Carmen Ejogo) and Dee/Dolores (Tika Sumpter)—who form a girl group and chase fame amid the late-1960s music scene. Directed by Salim Akil from a script by Mara Brock Akil, the film follows familiar backstage-showbiz beats: a rise to stardom, romantic entanglements, substance abuse, domestic violence, and moral reckonings. Derek Luke plays their earnest manager Stix; Mike Epps is a sleazy comedian whose relationship with Sister triggers much of the melodrama. The soundtrack mixes Motown-era numbers retained from the original with new songs; highlights include strong vocal turns by Ejogo and a big showpiece for Sparks.

Critics agreed the movie is visually faithful to its period and occasionally entertaining in performance and costume, but overall formulaic and melodramatic, often feeling like a thin, Lifetime-style morality tale or a pedestrian Supremes/Dreamgirls pastiche. Many found the writing clichéd and dialogue wooden; Sparks’s acting was seen as limited despite a powerful musical moment, while Ejogo and Luke received praise for their presence and energy. Tika Sumpter was noted as underused but effective.

Most commentary centers on Whitney Houston’s supporting role as the girls’ mother, Emma, and her final screen appearance. Reviewers called her portrayal uneven but emotionally resonant: while her voice is diminished compared with her prime, a church performance of “His Eye Is On the Sparrow” provides the film’s most affecting scene and an elegiac highlight that may alone draw viewers. Overall, Sparkle is judged a well-styled but ultimately unremarkable remake buoyed primarily by Houston’s swan song and a few strong performances.

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, 79, was found dead on Feb. 13, 2016, at the Cibolo Creek Ranch near Marfa in West Texas. He had been a guest at the resort, attended a private gathering Friday night, retired to his room early, and was discovered unresponsive the next morning. Officials said there was no sign of foul play and he appeared to have died of natural causes; local authorities and the family reportedly decided against an autopsy and a Presidio County judge later listed a heart attack on the death certificate. A priest administered last rites at the ranch, and Scalia’s body was transported to El Paso for preparation and then escorted back toward Washington by U.S. Marshals and Supreme Court Police.

Scalia, appointed by President Ronald Reagan in 1986 and the first Italian-American justice on the Court, was a leading conservative voice and the Court’s most prominent originalist and textualist. He authored influential opinions (notably the majority opinion in District of Columbia v. Heller) and forceful dissents (including in Obergefell). His death immediately reshaped the Court’s docket—threatening 4–4 splits in several high-profile cases—and triggered an immediate political battle over whether President Barack Obama should nominate a successor during an election year. Obama said he would nominate a replacement; Senate Republicans, led by Mitch McConnell, urged waiting until after the election. Condolences and reactions poured in from across the political spectrum, and Chief Justice John Roberts and other leaders praised Scalia’s intellect, influence, and service. Scalia is survived by his wife Maureen and their nine children.

A Filipino Catholic priest rode a hoverboard down the nave and sang into a microphone during Christmas Eve Mass; a viral cellphone video showed parishioners applauding at the final blessing. The Diocese of San Pablo condemned the stunt as inappropriate, saying Mass is the church’s highest form of worship and not a venue for personal attention-seeking. The unnamed priest apologized, called the episode a “wake-up call,” and has been removed from his parish to reflect on the incident. The story circulated in late December 2015 as hoverboards were a popular holiday gift.

A 14-year-old girl from Greenwood, Delaware, fell about 25 feet from a stopped two-person gondola on the Sky Ride at Six Flags in Queensbury, N.Y., shortly after 8 p.m. Saturday. The ride had been stopped after operators were alerted that a rider was in distress. The girl struck a tree and landed in a crowd of guests and employees who had gathered to catch her; she was treated at the park, taken by ambulance to Glens Falls Hospital and then airlifted to Albany Medical Center, where she is in stable condition with no serious injuries. A 47-year-old park guest who tried to catch her was treated and released for a back injury. Officials inspected the attraction and reported no apparent malfunction, but the park closed the ride pending a thorough review. No further details were immediately available.

Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney released his personal tax returns for 2010 and an estimate for 2011 after pressure from rivals, revealing that most of his income comes from investments (capital gains, dividends and interest) rather than wages. The returns show $42.5 million in income across the two years and an estimated $6.2 million paid in federal income tax, yielding effective tax rates of 13.9% in 2010 and an estimated 15.4% for 2011—well below the top wage tax rate of 35%. Much of this tax advantage stems from favorable treatment of investment income and “carried interest,” from which Romney received about $13 million over the two years and which is taxed at capital-gains rates (15%) rather than ordinary income rates.

Details in the filings: 2010 capital gains of roughly $12.6 million, dividends of about $4.9 million and taxable interest of $3.3 million; charitable giving of about $7 million over the two years (more than 15% of income), including sizable donations to the Mormon Church; holdings in blind trusts and foreign entities (including Cayman funds and a now-closed Swiss UBS account) that campaign advisers say were legally reported and taxed; and use of prior-year investment losses to offset taxable income. The returns total nearly 550 pages (2010 return alone 203 pages) and do not cover Romney’s most lucrative Bain Capital years in the 1980s–1990s, which critics say would further illuminate how his wealth was built.

Political context: Romney’s disclosure came after criticism from rival Newt Gingrich and amid broader national debate over income inequality and tax fairness—issues President Obama planned to highlight in the State of the Union (including support for a “Buffett rule” to tax the very wealthy more). Democrats and some commentators argued the returns underscore how current tax law favors investment income and called for greater transparency (some demanded additional years). Romney’s campaign defended the filings as complete and legal, stressing that investments are held in blind trusts and taxes were paid. The release aimed to blunt attacks and regain momentum before the Florida primary.

SpaceX successfully launched a classified National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) payload, NROL-76, on a Falcon 9 from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center on May 1, 2017 at 7:15 a.m. ET. The countdown was delayed one day after a sensor anomaly scrubbed a Sunday attempt, and high-altitude wind shear during Monday’s liftoff was close to the rocket’s theoretical load limit, but the flight proceeded and SpaceX confirmed the mission was successful.

Coverage of the flight was cut short per NRO secrecy protocols, but public views showed the 230-foot Falcon 9’s first stage perform a boost-back, reentry and soft vertical landing at Landing Zone 1 a few miles south of the pad. It was SpaceX’s 10th booster recovery (four landings onshore, six on a sea barge) and continued the company’s push toward routine reusability — recently demonstrated by relaunching a flight-proven booster in March — a capability CEO Elon Musk says is key to cutting launch costs and enabling ambitions like Mars colonization.

The NRO confirmed the satellite was procured from Ball Aerospace. Observers, using the rocket’s trajectory and other clues including the mission patch, speculated the payload could be an imaging satellite in a low-Earth orbit inclined about 50–60 degrees; it might replace a 2006 satellite that failed and was controversially shot down in 2008. The flight marked SpaceX’s first dedicated mission for the NRO and a milestone in competition with established government launch providers.

Multiple news outlets report that Matthew James McCarthy, a DJ and photographer/model, is suing former reality star Josh Duggar after discovering his image was used without permission on several online dating and social media profiles—including an Ashley Madison-associated account and an OkCupid profile. McCarthy says the unauthorized use of his photo has humiliated him, led to harassment (being called “Duggar’s boy toy” and “DJ Duggar”), and cost him work; he is suing for wrongful use of his likeness and damages.

The controversy grew after investigators traced Duggar’s Ashley Madison login (joesmithsonnwa@gmail.com) to an OkCupid username (joesmithsonnwa). Screenshots of that OkCupid profile—now deleted—showed a 27-year-old man near Alexandria, Va., listed as working in politics, claiming to seek “casual sex” while also calling himself “strictly monogamous,” and answering questions implying infidelity and conservative social views. The profile photo matched McCarthy’s widely available “random guy” image, suggesting the likeness was taken from a common Google image result.

There is no definitive public proof linking the OkCupid profile to Duggar beyond the matching email handle and timing (the profile last appeared online around September 2014, near when charges on Duggar’s card for Ashley Madison activity reportedly stopped). Discrepancies exist—e.g., the OkCupid user claimed a college degree Duggar did not have—so the connection remains unproven publicly. Duggar has not responded to these specific allegations; he has faced broader scandal and lost his reality-show income and later worked at a car dealership.

UC Irvine rescinded about 499 freshman admission offers this year after taking a stricter approach to processing admissions because more freshmen accepted spots than expected. The university tightened enforcement of admissions terms — particularly deadlines, final transcript submission and acceptable final grades — and was less lenient than in past years. Of the 499 withdrawals, 299 were transcript-related (185 appeals) and 209 were grade-related (110 appeals); as of the report 63 students had been reinstated.

Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Thomas Parham apologized to applicants who felt mistreated and acknowledged “missteps,” promising to correct errors and handle appeals more compassionately. Student government demanded an apology, reimbursement for students whose offers were revoked and guaranteed admission after two years of community college for affected students. Parham said the university will not withdraw acceptances due to over‑enrollment and reiterated that students who meet the offer conditions will be admitted.

UCI received a record level of applications (over 104,000) and offered admission to 31,103 freshmen, about 7,100 of whom accepted, while the planned incoming class size was roughly 6,250. Some students reported administrative or high‑school errors (missing or misclassified transcripts) caused the withdrawals, describing emotional distress. UCI has increased appeal reviewers to expedite decisions, aiming to complete pending appeals soon; some students, unwilling to wait, have enrolled elsewhere.
