An FBI probe tied to the adultery scandal that forced CIA Director David Petraeus to resign has expanded to include Marine Gen. John Allen, the U.S. commander in Afghanistan and Obama’s nominee for NATO commander. Investigators, following a complaint by Tampa socialite Jill Kelley about harassing emails, traced messages from Petraeus’s biographer Paula Broadwell to Kelley and then uncovered thousands of emails exchanged between Kelley and Gen. Allen. The Pentagon placed Allen’s NATO nomination on hold while the Defense Department inspector general reviews roughly 20,000–30,000 pages of correspondence. Officials say they have found no classified material or evidence of criminal wrongdoing by Allen so far; Allen denies an affair or sharing classified information.

The episode began as an alleged cyberstalking complaint by Kelley that led the FBI to Broadwell and ultimately exposed Broadwell’s affair with Petraeus and classified materials on her computer. Broadwell reportedly sent pseudonymous, derogatory emails about Kelley to senior officers; Allen received one such message and forwarded it to Kelley. Views of Allen’s emails range from benign flirtation to potentially inappropriate conduct; investigators are still assessing them.

Media reporting has also focused on Kelley’s background: she serves as an unpaid “honorary consul” for South Korea (a ceremonial role without diplomatic immunity), has hosted senior military figures at her Tampa home, and faces public scrutiny over personal finances and past lawsuits. The White House and Defense Secretary Leon Panetta urged due process and said President Obama remains supportive of Allen pending the investigation.

Tony Curtis’s last will, written about five months before his death at 85, disinherits all five of his children—including actress Jamie Lee Curtis—and leaves his estate to his fifth wife, Jill Vandenberg Curtis. The Nevada-filed document, obtained by Inside Edition and reported by CBS, names each child and states Curtis “acknowledge[d] the existence of my children...and have intentionally and with full knowledge chosen not to provide for them.” One of his daughters (not Jamie Lee) unsuccessfully contested the will. Jill was named representative of the estate and called the matter a private family issue; a family member expressed shock and disbelief that he had “turned his back” on his children. Curtis, who made more than 140 films such as Some Like It Hot and Spartacus, died of cardiac arrest in September.

Austin Tice, a 34-year-old former U.S. Marine and journalist who reported for outlets including McClatchy and The Washington Post, was abducted in Syria on August 12, 2012. Apart from an early video clip showing him in custody, there has been no confirmed contact or sighting since. His family has endured multiple years of holidays without him and urges renewed, urgent government action to find and bring him home.

This week the Tice family released a public plea joined by the families of four American hostages who were killed while held by the Islamic State—journalists James Foley and Steven Sotloff and aid workers Abdul-Rahman Peter Kassig and Kayla Mueller. Those families, who previously worked with the Tices on hostage-policy reforms, urged President Obama in a joint letter to “use all appropriate means” to locate Austin Tice. They stressed their request does not call for actions that would endanger others or compromise national security, but asked the administration to set aside political or election-year concerns and act boldly.

State Department spokesman John Kirby said U.S. officials, working through the Czech government (the U.S. protecting power in Syria), are pursuing information about Tice’s welfare and whereabouts and remain in contact with detainees’ families, though he cited privacy limits on details. Unlike the other Americans named in the letter, Tice is widely believed to have been seized by Syrian regime loyalists rather than ISIS; Damascus denies knowledge of his whereabouts.

The families’ letter appealed emotionally to the president—reminding him of promises made to victim families and urging that the government not repeat past missed opportunities. They closed by affirming the Tices’ “unwavering hope” and insisting the U.S. government must not give up on bringing Austin Tice home.

A controversial PC game titled Active Shooter, developed by Revived Games and to be published on Steam by ACID, drew widespread outrage for simulating school shootings and allowing players to play either the shooter or a SWAT team member. The demo footage showed a shooter running through school hallways killing civilians and police while tracking “civ killed” and “cops killed.” Survivors and relatives of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas shooting, activists (including Emma Gonzalez and Fred Guttenberg), and public figures such as Sen. Bill Nelson called the game “inexcusable,” immoral and a profit-seeking exploitation of real tragedy. The developer’s forum posts—full of misspellings and plans to expand environments (shopping centers, gas stations) and multiplayer modes—did little to quell anger; a demo disclaimer and a line urging players to seek help were deemed insufficient.

Valve/Steam investigated and removed the game and the developer/publisher from its storefront after finding they were operated by a repeat offender using the name Ata Berdiyev (previously removed last fall under other business names). Valve characterized him as a “troll” with a history of customer abuse, copyright violations and review manipulation, and said it would not do business with such parties while noting it will revisit its broader content policies. The episode echoes past controversies (e.g., 2011’s School Shooter) and reignited debate over platform responsibility, free speech, and the ethics of games that simulate real-world mass shootings.

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi said she will not trade with President Trump for funding his border wall, calling it “a manhood issue” for him and insisting Democrats won’t barter on the symbolic project. Speaking at Harvard’s Institute of Politics, Pelosi affirmed Democrats support stronger border security but prefer bolstering existing measures as part of comprehensive immigration reform, saying a wall “is probably the worst way to protect the border.”

Trump and GOP leaders have signaled they will press for the $5 billion wall request during December appropriations talks; seven of 12 appropriations bills currently run under a continuing resolution that expires Dec. 7. Pelosi acknowledged that Republicans in a lame-duck House likely could pass wall funding, and that Senate Democrats—where Sen. Chuck Schumer has not ruled out negotiating—would be the bigger obstacle. If negotiations extend into the next Congress and Democrats win the House, Pelosi said she would have greater leverage.

Pelosi also expressed confidence about reclaiming the speakership if Democrats retake the House, said she expects leadership challenges and welcomes them, and outlined priorities for a Democratic majority: lowering health-care costs, raising pay, green infrastructure, campaign finance reform (HR 1), gun control and protecting Dreamers. She reiterated opposition to pursuing impeachment as divisive but stressed the need for serious, focused congressional oversight of the Trump administration.

At the 2014 All‑Star Game in Minneapolis, Adam Wainwright drew praise for a show of respect toward Derek Jeter—placing his glove on the mound and stepping back to let Jeter soak up the moment—but later stirred controversy with candid postgame comments. After Jeter hit an opposite‑field double (part of a first‑inning flurry that helped the AL to a 5‑3 win), Wainwright said he "was going to give him a couple of pipe shots" and that he "probably should have pitched him a little bit better." His remark was widely criticized as diminishing Jeter's moment and the integrity of the All‑Star Game; Wainwright spent minutes apologizing and calling himself a "knucklehead" for speaking.

The episode underscores wider problems with the All‑Star format since MLB tied World Series home‑field advantage to the game in 2003. The article argues that fan voting, player input, managerial selections and the Internet Final Vote create conflicting incentives that make the game a muddled showcase rather than a true competitive event. That compromise produces awkward situations—like high‑profile farewells for popular veterans such as Jeter, who might not merit a starting spot on performance alone, or players making cameo appearances despite the game's supposed stakes. Wainwright’s offhand honesty, the piece concludes, may spark renewed debate about whether the “This One Counts” policy should be retired and the All‑Star Game rethought so its purpose and competitive structure are clearer.

A Chinese visitor to Yellowstone National Park was fined $1,000 plus a $30 court processing fee for leaving the boardwalk at Mammoth Hot Springs on June 14, 2016, and collecting thermal water. A witness photographed the man walking on fragile travertine terraces near Liberty Cap and breaking through the crust, then reported it to park rangers. During the investigation the man admitted he had not read the safety information provided at park entry and said he wanted the water for medicinal purposes. He was issued a federal violation notice requiring a mandatory appearance in Yellowstone Justice Center Court.

Park officials emphasized that staying on designated trails and boardwalks protects visitors and irreplaceable thermal features, noted that collecting park resources is illegal, and thanked the witness for reporting the violation. The incident follows several recent dangerous trespasses in the park, including a fatal fall into a hot spring on June 7 and other citations for off‑boardwalk travel.

Betel nut, the seed of the Areca palm chewed across South and Southeast Asia and the Pacific, is a widespread psychoactive stimulant—used by an estimated 10–20% of the global population (around 600 million people). Often consumed fresh, dried or as a “quid” wrapped in betel leaf with slaked lime and sometimes tobacco and spices, it produces a stimulant buzz (compared to several cups of coffee) and is embedded in social and cultural customs. Users range from children to working-age men who chew to stay awake during long shifts.

Despite cultural importance and claimed traditional benefits, strong and growing evidence links betel nut use to serious health harms. The World Health Organization and other agencies classify it as carcinogenic. Regular chewing is strongly associated with oral cancer, oral submucous fibrosis (an incurable stiffening of the mouth), gum disease, tooth staining and decay, increased cardiovascular and metabolic risks, addiction, and adverse reproductive outcomes. The slaked lime in many quids causes tiny mouth abrasions that may allow carcinogens to penetrate; tobacco added to quids further increases cancer risk. Symptoms can take up to 20 years to appear, and the cancers are often disfiguring and debilitating.

Taiwan illustrates both the scale of the problem and efforts to tackle it. Betel nut chewing—nicknamed “Taiwan’s chewing gum”—is common among blue-collar workers and has contributed to Taiwan’s very high oral cancer incidence and mortality. About 5,400 Taiwanese men are diagnosed annually with oral cancer or precancerous lesions; 80–90% of those affected have chewed betel nut. The government has launched mass screening (about one million free checks), cessation programs, school education, fines for public spitting, and subsidies to encourage farmers to replace betel palms with other crops. These measures helped halve male usage rates after 2013, but resistance from the industry and deep cultural roots mean change is slow and many people already face long-term risk.

Global public-health responses—including WHO action plans—recommend combining policy, public awareness, community outreach and cessation support to reduce betel nut use and prevent further cancer and other harms.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, speaking in New Zealand near the end of a nearly two-week Asia-Pacific tour, firmly ruled out running for president in 2012 or 2016. In interviews with New Zealand TV3 and TVNZ she said she is “very pleased” to be serving as secretary of state and, while the U.S. should be ready for a woman president, “it will be someone” other than her. Clinton defended President Barack Obama and downplayed Democratic losses in the recent U.S. midterms as a serious setback but part of normal political cycles, arguing some administration actions (like the stimulus) were necessary to avert worse economic outcomes. The visit included a light moment when New Zealand Prime Minister John Key mistakenly introduced her as “President Clinton” before correcting himself.

Newly released internal e-mails show sustained White House and Energy Department support for Solyndra, the California solar-panel company that received a $535 million DOE loan guarantee in 2009 and declared bankruptcy in August 2011. The records reveal tension inside the administration—between officials eager to promote the loan as a stimulus success and Treasury and OMB lawyers warning about legal, financial and oversight problems.

Key points:
- Solyndra received a $535 million Department of Energy loan guarantee in 2009; the company later failed, laid off about 1,100 workers, and became the subject of DOJ and congressional probes.
- Steven J. Spinner, a senior adviser in the DOE loan program and a 2008 Obama fundraiser, repeatedly pushed for rapid approval and public attention for the Solyndra loan. Spinner had disclosed that his wife’s law firm represented Solyndra and agreed to recuse himself, yet e-mails show him pressing OMB and White House aides, communicating with Solyndra officials, and seeking high-level involvement (including discussion of presidential or vice-presidential participation).
- Treasury and OMB officials raised serious reservations, particularly about a 2011 restructuring that would have given private investors priority repayment over the federal government. Treasury lawyers warned that subordinating the government’s claim could violate statute and DOE regulations and advised referral to the Justice Department; DOE approved the restructuring in February 2011 anyway, concluding career lawyers had authority to find it legal.
- Energy Department officials pushed through payments and a restructuring to secure a $75 million investor infusion, but Solyndra still went bankrupt, making taxpayers likely to shoulder most of the loss.
- The e-mails also show venture capital and investor access to senior White House staff (e.g., meetings involving Carol Browner and Rockport Capital’s David Prend) and internal debate about whether to spotlight Solyndra as a stimulus success.
- Administration spokesmen say Spinner’s role was limited to coordination and public-announcement planning, that his recusal was approved by ethics officials, and that DOE lawyers concluded the restructuring was lawful. Congressional Republicans characterized the documents as evidence of improper closeness between the White House, donors and investors.

Overall, the correspondence depicts high-level advocacy for Solyndra amid internal legal and oversight objections and raises questions about ethics, decision-making, and whether proper procedures were followed in modifying the loan as the company’s finances deteriorated.

This document collects reactions from several Democratic-leaning commentators to President Barack Obama’s Afghanistan speech and broader themes about Western liberalism and political style.

Main points about Obama’s Afghanistan speech
- Tone and approach: Many commenters praised the speech’s sober, realistic tone — a national-interest, “Kissingerian” realism rather than Wilsonian idealism — and noted Obama’s effort to explain how the U.S. arrived in Afghanistan and how he plans to leave. He framed the decision as painful but necessary and set a timeline to begin withdrawal in summer 2011.
- Credibility and persuasion: Several writers found the speech rhetorically disappointing. Criticisms include overreliance on the teleprompter, tired 9/11 imagery, insufficient engagement with Afghan governance failures (notably Karzai’s corruption and a dysfunctional parliament), and vague definitions (e.g., what “no blank checks” to Karzai really means). Some saw Obama as a wartime president willing to accept hard choices; others felt he failed to make a convincing case for escalation.
- Strategy doubts: Commentators questioned whether the proposed troop increase and “civilian surge” can overcome deep institutional problems in Afghanistan and whether a “Pashtun awakening” comparable to Iraq’s Sunni awakening is realistic. Concerns were raised that escalation could extend casualties without delivering victory.
- Political consequences: Several pieces emphasize that Obama is governing as a centrist/realist rather than the progressive opponent of the Iraq-era foreign policy some supporters expected. Disappointment among left-wing allies is attributed partly to misunderstandings of Obama’s candidacy; activists will need to keep pressure on other policy fronts. The Bush-Cheney legacy and partisan attacks (e.g., Cheney’s vitriol) were noted as background context.

Broader reflections
- “Third Way” politics: The text ties Obama’s posture to a long-standing centrist trope—positioning himself between extremes—and argues his speech fits that tradition.
- War rhetoric and leadership: One piece argues Obama showed the necessary conviction to lead in wartime, contrasting his reasoned argumentation with George W. Bush’s more faith-driven appeals. Whether belief and logic will translate into success in Afghanistan is uncertain.
- Demographics, immigration and the “doom loop”: Separately, an essay critiques Derek Thompson’s “doom loop” thesis linking low fertility, immigration, xenophobia and liberal decline. The writer cautions that immigrant contributions vary by country and context: U.S. assimilation and fiscal outcomes are not automatically replicable in Europe, where recent migration waves may not match economic needs and could exacerbate stratification and backlash.

Overall assessment
- The collection captures a mix of respect for Obama’s sober, realistic framing and disappointment in his ability to persuasively justify escalation. Critics doubt the strategy’s feasibility given Afghan governance problems and the absence of a credible local political solution, while some concede Obama’s personal resolve may be the best available asset. The broader commentary connects these reactions to centrist politics and to anxieties about Western liberalism’s demographic and immigration challenges.

Alvin Cross Jr., an Albany, Georgia man on probation, accidentally texted his probation officer “you have some weed?” while apparently trying to contact a dealer. The officer notified police, who searched Cross’s home and found a bag of cocaine. Cross pleaded guilty to cocaine possession and violating probation; he was sentenced to one year in prison for possession plus another year for the probation violation. News accounts note missing details (why he was on probation, exact drug quantity) and use the episode as a cautionary tale about thinking before you hit send.

A bipartisan Commission on Wartime Contracting has released a damning interim report finding that the U.S. reliance on contractors in Iraq and Afghanistan has produced tens of billions of dollars in waste, fraud, and abuse. Since 2002 the U.S. spent roughly $117–$200 billion on contracts and grants for military support, reconstruction and related operations; the commission says a substantial portion has been misspent due to pervasive problems.

Key findings
- Overdependence on contractors: The U.S. hired roughly 200,000 contractors—about as many as uniformed troops—performing roles from base security and logistics to translation and facility construction. The government too often uses contractors as the default solution without assessing whether they are the best option or whether adequate oversight resources exist.
- Weak oversight and accountability: Contract administration has lagged as award dollars surged, leaving the acquisition workforce overstretched. Required past-performance reporting is often missing or incomplete, and barriers exist to suspending or debaring poor-performing or fraudulent firms, allowing repeat offenders to keep winning work.
- Significant human cost: Between Sept. 2001 and Dec. 2010 over 2,200 contractor deaths and nearly 50,000 injuries occurred in Iraq and Afghanistan—costs that should figure into the public’s appraisal of war’s total price.
- Corruption and poor planning: Ill-conceived projects that clash with local conditions, inadequate planning and oversight, criminal behavior, and corruption have further drained resources and reduced the effectiveness of reconstruction efforts.
- Private security concerns: Heavy use of private security contractors raises use-of-force and legal accountability problems; their prominent role has expanded under both administrations.

Major recommendations
- Reduce routine reliance on contractors and establish strong interagency standards for contingency contracting.
- Create standing federal teams of full‑time government employees trained and ready to deploy to manage and monitor contingency contracts.
- Prohibit contractors from supervising the hiring of other contractors and improve the integrity and completeness of past-performance databases.
- Embed government personnel with private security contractors to provide command, control and oversight of security operations.

Reaction and next steps
Commission leaders urged Congress and the Department of Defense to act; Sen. James Webb called for hearings. The commission will issue a final report this summer. Oversight groups and inspectors general have long raised similar concerns, and witnesses at the commission hearing highlighted gaps in federal databases and implementation that hinder holding contractors accountable.

A 43-year-old mother of two, Lucinda (Lucy) Smith of Billericay, Essex, died from sepsis and organ failure after a minor gardening scratch progressed into a severe infection. A few days after scratching her hand she developed shoulder pain and saw her GP, who diagnosed a trapped nerve, prescribed antidepressant medication to relax her and advised physiotherapy. Her condition worsened over the next three days—her arm and hand became swollen and blotchy, she vomited and experienced severe pain—and a second doctor suspected a blood clot and sent her to Basildon Hospital. A blood test there quickly confirmed sepsis; she received IV antibiotics and critical care but died two days later. An inquest ruled the cause of death toxic shock caused by sepsis. Her family say earlier testing (including blood pressure and blood tests) at the initial GP visit might have saved her. The report notes sepsis often begins outside hospital, can follow skin infections among other sources, and that early recognition and prompt treatment (antibiotics and IV fluids) are vital. Signs to watch for include fever or chills, extreme pain, clammy skin, confusion, shortness of breath and rapid heart rate.

A 60-year-old man died after setting out on foot for help when his vehicle broke down on a remote track in Western Australia’s Goldfields region. The pair — the man and a woman — were travelling between Wonganoo and Windidda stations near Wiluna when the car failed on January 4. After spending the night by the vehicle with only a small container of water, the man left early the next morning to walk about 48 km (30 miles) toward Windidda. The woman stayed behind and later also began walking; she was found by station workers and taken to Windidda, where she raised the alarm. A search located the man’s body on Wednesday about 2 km from Windidda Station. Police said there were no suspicious circumstances and a report will be prepared for the coroner. Authorities urged remote-area travellers to stay with their vehicle if stranded, carry at least three days’ food and water per person, ensure vehicles and fuel are suitable for conditions, carry emergency communications (beacon, satellite phone or CB radio), check maps and road conditions, and advise others of travel plans. Temperatures in the area reached around 40–41.5°C during the incident.

An Egyptian court on Nov. 27 handed heavy prison terms to 21 women and girls — including seven teenagers aged 15–16 — who had protested in Alexandria on Oct. 31 calling for ousted president Mohamed Morsi’s reinstatement. Fourteen women received 11-year sentences; the minors were given detention until they turn 18. Six other alleged Muslim Brotherhood members got 15-year terms. The convictions, for charges including unlawful gathering, thuggery and weapons possession, drew widespread criticism as disproportionately harsh and politicized.

The ruling came amid a broader, escalating crackdown by the military-backed government that has shifted from targeting the Muslim Brotherhood to also suppressing secular youth activists. Police recently beat and humiliated female protesters near parliament, detained 14 women and reportedly abandoned them on a remote road — tactics compared to those used under the Hosni Mubarak era. A new restrictive protest law, issued this week, bans gatherings of more than 10 people without prior police permission and imposes stiff penalties; authorities say it is needed to fight terrorism and restore order.

Hundreds of secular activists protested in downtown Cairo against the clampdown. Prosecutors ordered 24 people from a separate rally held the previous day to be held for questioning under the new law; prominent activists Alaa Abdel-Fattah and Ahmed Maher were also detained or investigated for allegedly inciting violations. The Muslim Brotherhood and its allies framed the sentences as a deterrent but sought to reach out to secular youth; the overture was rebuffed by many activists who resent the Brotherhood’s role during Morsi’s rule.

Defense lawyers say the arrests extend to legal counsel: Alexandria lawyer Ahmed El-Hamrawy, head of the defense team for the 21 women, was arrested on charges of “incitement of violence,” prompting fears lawyers involved in such cases will be targeted. Human rights groups accused the judiciary and security forces of politically motivated rulings and abuses. The crackdown intensifies tensions ahead of a referendum on constitutional amendments and risks realigning Egypt’s fragmented political opposition. An appeals hearing for the jailed women was scheduled for Saturday.

A residential building under illegal construction collapsed on Thursday evening in Thane, a suburb of Mumbai, killing at least 45 people (including around 15 children), injuring about 70 and leaving many more feared trapped. The seven‑storey block had been occupied up to its fourth floor while additional floors were being added rapidly; witnesses said construction of seven floors began about six weeks earlier and the eighth floor was under way. Residents reported the structure tilted and then fell “like a pack of cards” within seconds.

Rescue teams — including the National Disaster Response Force, dogs, bulldozers and hydraulic equipment — worked through the night to clear debris and pull survivors from the rubble; dozens were rescued but several floors remained to be searched and more than 20 people were initially reported missing. Officials said the building lacked necessary clearances and suspect substandard materials and weak structure as likely causes. Police have registered a case and are searching for the builders and officials who supervised the work.

The collapse highlights a recurring problem in India: rapid, often illegal vertical expansion to meet housing demand, use of poor materials, inadequate supervision and alleged corruption that allows unauthorized floors and entire illegal blocks to be built. Similar deadly collapses have occurred repeatedly across the country in recent years.

A 12-year-old girl who ran away from a Los Angeles group home and sat on a six-inch ledge of the York Bridge, about 80 feet above asphalt, was rescued by South Pasadena Officer Chris Perez during a routine patrol. Perez, a year into the department, calmly approached, built rapport, and learned she fled the group home claiming mistreatment and wanted to live with her only relative, an aunt. After gaining her trust through gentle conversation, he leaned over the railing, wrapped his arm around her, pulled her to safety and sat with her until paramedics arrived. The girl was taken into protective custody for medical evaluation. Police credited Perez’s patient, professional actions with saving her life; he downplayed being called a hero.

Filmmaker John Waters—cult icon known for Pink Flamingos and Hairspray—is hosting an adults-only weekend "Camp John Waters" at Camp Getaway in Kent, Connecticut, Sept. 22–24, 2017. Limited to about 300 attendees, the event will mix traditional camp activities (ziplining, canoeing) with Waters-themed programming: film screenings, Blood Mary Bingo, Hairspray karaoke, burlesque lessons, a Scotch-and-cigars session, a costume contest judged by the “Prince of Puke,” and a one-man show, book readings from his new Make Trouble, plus a Q&A. Alcohol is available for an extra fee, and each camper receives a signed copy of Make Trouble; cabin availability and pricing details were provided by the organizers.

The summary also highlights strong early praise for Make Trouble—which adapts Waters’s 2015 RISD commencement speech—characterizing it as witty, inspirational, playful, provocative and personally revealing. Reviewers from outlets including the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, Tufts Daily, Johns Hopkins News-Letter and San Francisco Book Review call it a joyful, subversive, and timely manifesto aimed at outsiders and creative troublemakers.

A late-night house fire in Youngstown, Ohio, on Sunday, Dec. 9, killed five children and critically injured their mother. The blaze at 434 Parkcliffe Ave. was reported about 11:30 p.m.; neighbors heard a loud boom and saw flames coming from first-floor windows. Fire crews found heavy fire on the first floor and believe the fire started there; investigators from the city and state fire marshal’s office say there is no indication so far that the blaze was suspicious and are still testing to determine a cause.

The victims were five children — Aleysha Rosario, 9; Charles Gunn, 3; Ly'Asia Gunn, 2; and 1-year-old twins Brianna and Arianna Negron. Their 26-year-old mother, America Negron Acevedo, reportedly jumped from a second-floor window and told firefighters the children were inside. Rescuers were able to pull three children from the house; those children and the mother were taken to hospitals, where the three children later died and the mother was transferred to a burn center in Cleveland in stable but critical condition and sedated. Two firefighters were also treated for injuries and released.

The single-family, two-story wood home—about 1,300 sq ft and built in 1924—had working smoke detectors that were sounding when crews arrived. The neighborhood and city officials have begun community support and memorial efforts for the family. Authorities continue the investigation.

Microsoft formally unveiled its long-rumored motion‑control system for Xbox 360 under the new name Kinect (formerly Project Natal) at a theatrical Cirque du Soleil–style event in Los Angeles ahead of E3. The camera-and-sensor peripheral tracks full-body motion and recognizes voices, allowing users to control games and dashboard apps without a handheld controller. Microsoft demonstrated a variety of interactions—avatar mirroring, page‑turning gestures, motion steering, virtual light‑saber combat, yoga/Tai Chi mirroring, and photo and video-dashboard controls—positioning Kinect as a direct challenger to Nintendo’s Wii (and Sony’s Move).

Playable demos shown included family‑friendly experiences and several announced titles or suites expected at launch: Kinect Sports (bowling, beach volleyball, track & field, soccer, table tennis, etc.), Joyride (hand‑steering racing), Kinectimals (interacting with virtual big cats), Kinect Adventures (river rafting and party‑style minigames), Dance Central (MTV Games dance title), and various Disney and Star Wars experiences. Kinect was also shown controlling Netflix, photo browsing and video chat on the Xbox dashboard.

Microsoft did not disclose pricing or exact ship date at the event (Kinect was expected to ship in the fall), reserving full details for its E3 press conference. The demonstration emphasized Kinect’s broad living‑room ambitions and potential, though the author judged the event more spectacle than revelation since many features had already been anticipated.

Lawyers for Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev have asked for a new trial and appealed his death sentence, arguing the case should not have been tried in Boston because pervasive publicity and community outrage — including social media posts and a newly declared local holiday marking the bombing — made it impossible for jurors to be impartial. Defense filings also challenge application of the legal term "crime of violence" in light of a recent Supreme Court ruling they say casts doubt on many convictions, and raise constitutionality questions about capital punishment, citing Justice Breyer’s dissent that the death penalty may now be "cruel and unusual."

Tsarnaev was convicted on 30 federal charges for the April 15, 2013, bombings that killed three people and injured more than 260; he was sentenced to death in June and apologized at sentencing. Defense attorneys had repeatedly sought a change of venue before trial but were denied. They also contend they lacked sufficient time to present full mitigation to spare him from execution.

If the appeal fails, Tsarnaev joins federal death row as its 62nd inmate and the youngest; however, executions under the federal system are rare and typically take many years to occur — experts expect at least a decade given lengthy federal appeals. Historically, only three federal executions have taken place in the last 50 years. Federal death row inmates come from many states, with large numbers originating from Texas, Missouri and Virginia, and many were sentenced for crimes that happened to fall under federal jurisdiction.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I‑Vt.), a Democratic presidential candidate, introduced the “Justice Is Not For Sale” Act to ban for‑profit prisons and curb practices tied to mass incarceration. Co‑sponsored in the House by Reps. Raúl Grijalva, Keith Ellison and Bobby Rush, the bill would require federal, state and local governments to phase out privately run prisons within two to three years, bar federal contracts with private incarceration companies, and end the congressional mandate that Immigration and Customs Enforcement maintain 34,000 detention beds. It would also reinstate the federal parole system (abolished in 1984), expand oversight of inmate services (like phone and banking fees), and seek to reduce immigrant detention.

Sanders frames private prisons as a “perverse incentive” that profits from high incarceration rates and undermines rehabilitation. Supporters cite research showing private prison inmates often serve longer sentences and that cost‑saving claims are dubious—especially where contracts guarantee minimum populations. Private companies (notably GEO Group and Corrections Corporation of America) now house significant shares of federal and immigration detainees and form a multibillion‑dollar industry that lobbies for tougher sentencing and detention policies.

The proposal aims to push criminal‑justice reform into the national debate on law enforcement, racial bias and recidivism, and to broaden Sanders’s appeal with African‑American and Latino voters. While a full ban would face political hurdles, bipartisan momentum on other prison reform measures and growing skepticism about “tough on crime” sentencing trends suggest parts of the reform agenda may gain traction.

A Miami physician, Arturo Carvajal, has sued Hillstone Restaurant Group (owner of Houston’s) after eating a grilled artichoke special at Houston’s in North Miami Beach in May 2009. Carvajal says he had never encountered an artichoke before, the server did not explain how to eat it, and he therefore ate the entire leaves. He alleges this caused severe abdominal pain; an exploratory laparotomy reportedly found artichoke leaves lodged in his small bowel. In an October 25/27 lawsuit filed in Miami‑Dade Circuit Court he accuses the restaurant and manager of negligence for failing to train servers to instruct patrons on the “proper method of consuming an artichoke,” and seeks unspecified damages for bodily injury, pain and suffering, disability, disfigurement, medical expenses and related claims. Hillstone calls the claim “a silly notion,” saying it has no duty to warn customers about how to eat an artichoke and plans to defend the suit.

Police in Des Moines, Washington, issued an Amber Alert after 2-year-old Ronnie Tran and his 40-year-old mother were allegedly abducted from a home Tuesday. Authorities say the mother was stunned with a stun device, bound with plastic ties, and taken with her son to a house in Fife, where she was tied in a garage and the child taken inside. The mother freed herself Tuesday afternoon and went to a relative’s home but did not call police until about 9:30 p.m.

Investigators described the case as complicated with family dynamics involved. Two female suspects — the boy’s 65-year-old paternal grandmother, Vien Nguyen, and the father’s girlfriend, identified as 46-year-old Alyssa Chang — were named by the victim. A Hyundai Sonata used in the alleged abduction was located and one woman was initially taken into custody.

The child was found safe Wednesday morning in Renton after Chang’s brother, John Truong, realized the toddler he was babysitting matched the Amber Alert. Truong contacted police, who secured the boy and reunited him with his parents later that day. Chang was taken into custody; Nguyen turned herself in and was later fingerprinted and released for medical reasons. Both face three felony charges: kidnapping, felony assault and unlawful imprisonment. The boy’s father cooperated with detectives and was not charged. Police continue to investigate.

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2 remained No. 1 at the U.S. box office for a fourth straight weekend, earning $11.3 million in its fourth frame and bringing its domestic total to about $244.5 million. New wide release In the Heart of the Sea, directed by Ron Howard and starring Chris Hemsworth, opened disappointingly in second with about $11 million against a near-$100 million production budget. Poor reviews (43% on Rotten Tomatoes) and weak buzz were blamed for the soft start; audiences gave it a B+ CinemaScore and exit polls showed 68% of early viewers were over 35. 

Other holdovers fared modestly: Pixar’s The Good Dinosaur grossed $10.5 million (third weekend, $89.7M total), Creed added $10.1 million (fourth weekend, $79.3M total), and Krampus took in $8 million in its second weekend ($28.2M total). 

In limited release, The Big Short opened strongly with $720,000 from eight theaters—an exceptional $90,000 per-theater average—boosted by strong reviews (86% on Rotten Tomatoes) and awards attention. Industry analysts noted the market was poised for a major shift with the imminent wide release of Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Final weekend totals were expected to be confirmed Monday.

Scientists from the U.S. and Denmark are conducting the first large-scale airborne survey of Yellowstone’s subsurface hydrothermal “plumbing” to map where hot water flows beneath the park and better understand geysers and rare, sometimes massive hydrothermal explosions. Starting in November, a helicopter will tow a Danish-developed hoop-shaped electromagnetic sensor—an instrument that detects contrasts between water, altered (“rotten”) sulfuric rock, and solid bedrock—to image the shallow crust down to roughly 1,500 feet (≈500 meters). 

The project, led by USGS scientist Carol Finn in collaboration with Yellowstone National Park, the University of Wyoming and Aarhus University, will focus on the Mammoth–Norris corridor and take about four weeks. Results should reveal flow paths feeding features such as Old Faithful, illuminate causes and hazards of sudden hydrothermal blasts (including the ~13,800-year-old crater beneath Yellowstone Lake), and help park managers locate unstable ground and guide future development to protect visitors and thermal features. Similar electromagnetic surveys have revealed volcanic hazards elsewhere.

In the early 1980s freelance journalist Peter Brosnan pursued a long-rumored “lost city” buried in the Guadalupe-Nipomo dunes on California’s Central Coast: the massive 1922–23 Hollywood set Cecil B. DeMille built for his silent epic The Ten Commandments. The set—an enormous faux Egyptian “City of the Pharaoh” including a 120-foot temple, plaster sphinxes, giant lions and pharaoh statues—required thousands of workers and immense materials, drove production costs to record levels, and nearly bankrupted DeMille and Paramount. To prevent rivals from reusing his work and because he’d agreed to restore the land, DeMille reportedly demolished the set and buried the remains in the shifting dunes.

Brosnan, intrigued by a line in DeMille’s autobiography and accounts from a friend, hunted for the ruins in 1983 and eventually located a plaster fragment exposed on “the dune that never moves.” The find generated worldwide media interest and launched Brosnan’s plan for a documentary, The Lost City. Early support came from archaeologists, the Smithsonian, the DeMille family trust and even Charlton Heston, but persistent obstacles—permits, endangered-species protections for the western snowy plover, and chronic funding shortfalls—delayed excavation for years. Ground-penetrating radar in 1990 indicated much of the set survived, yet Brosnan couldn’t raise the roughly $175,000 then needed for a proper archaeological dig and shelved the project for a decade.

Geography and the mineral-rich sand helped preserve the plaster pieces for decades, but coastal storms and shifting dunes increasingly expose and erode the remains. Renewed interest in the 2010s produced new funding from an anonymous donor and a county grant; archaeologists excavated much of a sphinx and Brosnan filmed the recovery, assembling footage into a near-finished documentary. The Dunes Center in Guadalupe now displays a recovered sphinx fragment and other relics but warns the ruins are vanishing faster than predicted and needs about $100,000 to unearth and conserve more before they’re lost.

Current efforts use noninvasive surveying—airborne photography and flyovers by Applied Earthworks—to locate the original 24-square-mile tent city and production camp used during filming (an estimated 2,500 people lived there). Archaeologists are aligning historical photos with modern topography to pinpoint dig sites; once targets are identified, they plan ground investigations. The project continues to balance historical preservation, environmental protection, and funding needs as it seeks to recover and document what remains of one of Hollywood’s grandest early sets.

The Deepwater Horizon disaster has triggered a contentious six-month federal moratorium on deepwater drilling in the Gulf of Mexico. Transocean, owner of the rig, and other industry figures criticized the ban as arbitrary and economically devastating; plaintiffs including Hornbeck Offshore Services and Louisiana officials sued to block it, arguing the government offered no proof existing operations posed a threat. U.S. District Judge Martin Feldman issued a preliminary injunction against the moratorium, finding the plaintiffs showed likely irreparable harm; the White House announced it will appeal and the Interior Department said it will issue a new, better-documented order "in the coming days."

The moratorium was imposed after the April 20 Deepwater Horizon explosion, which killed 11 workers and caused what officials estimate could be tens of millions of gallons of oil to spill into the Gulf. Government lawyers defended the pause as necessary to study deepwater risks and improve safety; environmental groups and Interior Secretary Ken Salazar argued the halt is appropriate while investigations continue.

BP has been heavily engaged in response and compensation efforts. The company says it has spent about $2 billion so far on cleanup, containment, relief-well work and claims, has collected record daily amounts of oil from the well, and set up a $20 billion escrow fund for victims. Kenneth Feinberg, who will administer the fund, pledged to expedite and increase transparency in payments; BP has paid out more than $100 million to date and received over 65,000 claims. The government has billed BP for federal response costs as well.

Cleanup crews report localized progress along the coast, though fishermen and residents worry about long-term ecological and economic impacts. Political pressure is intense: some Gulf elected officials and industry leaders urged not to appeal the injunction, while others and the White House back continued review and precaution. International offers of assistance, protests at industry events, and scrutiny of BP executives have continued amid ongoing efforts to stop the leak permanently.

An Indonesian Trigana Air ATR 42-300 twin-turboprop with 54 people aboard (44 adults, five children/infants and five crew) lost contact on Sunday while flying from Jayapura’s Sentani Airport to Oksibil in Papua. Authorities and local residents later located wreckage in the remote, mountainous Bintang Highlands (Tangok/Tangok mountain/Camp 3, Ok Bape district). Search crews and aircraft sighted debris and reported smoke; bad weather, failing light and rugged terrain have hampered rescue and recovery efforts, and it was not immediately known whether there were any survivors.

The 27-year-old ATR was operated by Trigana Air Service, which has a history of incidents: 14 serious events since 1991 and 10 written-off aircraft. Trigana has been on the EU’s list of banned carriers since 2007. Indonesia has faced several recent aviation disasters, including last year’s AirAsia crash in the Java Sea and a military transport crash in July, prompting government reviews and new safety measures. Officials noted that the flight was also carrying four postal bags containing about 6.5 billion rupiah earmarked for remote villagers. President Joko Widodo expressed condolences and called for national prayers. Investigations and on-the-ground recovery operations were ongoing.

The dome of the Thomas Jefferson Memorial has developed an increasing black discoloration caused by biofilm — a mixed community of microscopic organisms (algae, bacteria, fungi) that adhere to and pigment stone surfaces. First noticeable around 2006, the growth has intensified in recent years and is particularly visible on the dome, its base and the pediment. Biofilm is found widely on monuments in Washington and globally; it was treated successfully at the D.C. War Memorial in 2011.

Park Service conservators, architects and molecular biologists have been studying the problem since 2014. They say biofilm growth is encouraged by nutrients and rough, pitted stone surfaces produced by natural weathering of the memorial’s Vermont marble, and possibly by local microclimate changes and reduced air pollution. Scientists are still uncertain whether the organisms actively damage the stone — some evidence links biofilms to deterioration, but they may also sometimes have protective effects.

Removing biofilm is challenging: there is no known permanent eradication, treatments must not further harm the soft, weathered marble or encourage regrowth, and must be safe and cost‑effective. The National Park Service is testing multiple approaches on small patches, including ten chemical biocides, ozonated water and laser irradiation, and will monitor results before choosing a method. No timeline has been set; selection of treatment and funding will determine when larger restoration work can proceed. The Park Service emphasizes a cautious, research‑based approach to preserve the memorial long term.

Talia Jane, a 25-year-old Eat24 (Yelp) customer service representative who moved to San Francisco after college, published a widely read Medium post titled “An Open Letter To My CEO” (addressed to Yelp CEO Jeremy Stoppelman) describing severe financial hardship on her $12.25/hour job. She said she spent roughly 80% of her income on rent, could not afford groceries (survived mainly on a ten‑pound bag of rice), and faced transit and medical copay costs that made basic living untenable. The piece detailed coworkers’ similar struggles, high turnover on the support floor, and proposed solutions such as employee food assistance, charity-matching at checkout, or redirecting small perks to raise wages.

Within about two hours of publishing, Jane’s company email stopped working and she announced on Twitter she had been fired; Yelp said it would not comment on personnel matters. Stoppelman responded on Twitter that he agreed the Bay Area cost of living is too high, that the firing was not personally his decision and not due to the Medium post, and urged people not to rush to judgment; Yelp also noted it was expanding Eat24 support to Phoenix. The post went viral (tens of thousands of views and widespread social reaction), sparking debate about whether Yelp’s dismissal was justified versus whether the company could have used the episode to address low wages and housing-affordability issues. Jane’s letter later included an update claiming subsequent changes on Yelp’s support team and asserting her critique highlighted broader problems in the gig economy.

A historic late-May storm system brought catastrophic flooding, tornadoes and record rainfall across Texas and nearby states, killing at least 37 people (including 17 in Texas, 6 in Oklahoma and 14 in northern Mexico) and leaving many more missing and injured. The Blanco River surge in central Texas ripped through homes in Wimberley and San Marcos, sweeping away houses and people; dozens of search-and-rescue operations recovered multiple bodies and continued to search for missing residents. Urban flash floods stranded hundreds of vehicles and forced rescues in Dallas, Houston and other cities; Dallas alone saw more than 200 people pulled from flooded cars and thousands lost power. Rivers including the Colorado, Brazos and Blanco were over or near flood stage, prompting voluntary evacuations for hundreds of homes in Wharton, Parker and Hays counties. Additional storms were forecast to bring more rain—potentially 2–6 inches in some areas—raising the risk of renewed flooding as runoff moves downstream. State officials noted May was the wettest on record for Texas, hampering rescue and recovery efforts. Federal assistance was pledged, and communities continue cleanup, sheltering and rebuilding amid ongoing flood watches and warnings.

Charlie Sheen publicly acknowledged this week that he is HIV-positive, saying on the Today show that he was diagnosed in 2011 and confident the disclosure won’t derail his career. In the months before his announcement he’d been meeting with producers—including people at CBS TV Studios and Sony Pictures TV—about developing a new half-hour sitcom vehicle; nothing is currently set up. Sheen claims he spent millions to keep the diagnosis private and said there has been “no resistance” from industry contacts, though potential lawsuits from former sexual partners could complicate matters.

Reports indicate Sheen was HIV-positive throughout the run of his most recent sitcom, Anger Management (2012–2014), which he says was created around the time of his 2011 diagnosis. It’s unclear whether Lionsgate/Debmar-Mercury or FX were told; many cast and crew reportedly did not know at first, though production disruptions fueled suspicions. Leaked Sony emails from 2014 (part of last year’s hack) contain a crude remark referencing Sheen’s HIV status, suggesting some industry executives were aware by early 2014—even though the information was not publicly revealed then.

The story notes Sheen’s turbulent history (his 2011 meltdown and firing from Two and a Half Men, substance abuse) but also that he completed 100 episodes of Anger Management and is seeking another sitcom, which—if produced with him openly HIV-positive—would be a first for a major American sitcom star.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet began donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive; those daily data are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.

Two months after Casey Anthony was acquitted in the death of her daughter Caylee, Casey’s parents, George and Cindy Anthony, gave their first interview to Dr. Phil McGraw. Excerpts aired on NBC’s Today show. Cindy addressed a distraught MySpace post she wrote on July 3 that began “My Caylee is missing,” saying Caylee was “missing in my heart” that day—she believed she knew where Caylee was and posted to express her pain and to urge Casey to reveal Caylee’s whereabouts. Both parents were asked about the smell reportedly found in the trunk of Casey’s car; Cindy said she still doesn’t know what caused it, and George said he prefers not to believe Caylee was in the trunk and is relying on investigators’ information. Cindy also defended George against suggestions he knew Caylee’s location, saying he would never have endured six months of not knowing if he did. The full Dr. Phil interview was scheduled to air over two episodes, and McGraw’s production company reportedly paid a fee to Caylee’s Fund related to the interview.

A passenger bus traveling from El Paso to Los Angeles overturned early Wednesday, May 21, 2014, west of Blythe on I‑10 after striking long steel pipes that had spilled onto the highway from a jackknifed flatbed truck. The crash left four passengers dead and at least seven seriously injured; several others suffered minor injuries or were evaluated at hospitals. Thirty-two to 33 people were aboard. The bus slid down an embankment and came to rest on its side about 50 feet off the freeway. Survivors described chaotic scenes; one mother clutched her 12‑day‑old infant through the rollover and both walked away with minor injuries. The truck’s load reportedly scattered across both directions of the unlit desert interstate around 2:15 a.m., and other vehicles hit the pipes moments earlier. Neither driver was injured. Authorities inspected the truck company’s records as part of the investigation; the bus company said no maintenance or driver issues have been alleged. I‑10 was closed for hours and traffic was diverted.

Al-Balad, Jeddah’s historic port center and a UNESCO Cultural Heritage Site since 2014, retains valuable examples of Hijazi architecture—cut coral stone structures and hand-carved rawashin windows—but has suffered fires and long-term neglect as residents moved out over decades. Saudi 3D surveying firm FalconViz is helping preserve and restore Al-Balad using drones, laser scanning, photogrammetry and Autodesk/BIM tools. Their aerial and terrestrial 3D scans produce dense, colorized point clouds that are imported into AutoCAD and other Autodesk software (ReCap, Revit, 3ds Max) to create accurate 3D and CAD models with measurements to about 1 cm. These models let authorities generate as-built plans, run structural and fire-safety simulations, plan emergency responses, and guide restorations—even enabling reconstruction of buildings lost to recent fires. FalconViz says the technology dramatically speeds documentation (days versus months), cuts costs and manpower, and also supports modern urban planning, making digital documentation a practical way to safeguard Al-Balad’s cultural heritage for future generations.

New Mexico authorities say two men from Albuquerque may have been plotting to kill pop star Justin Bieber and his bodyguard. Mark Staake, 41, and his nephew Tanner Ruane, 23, were arrested in late November after an investigation tied them to a murder-for-hire conspiracy uncovered when convicted killer Dana Martin, 45, told police he had recruited them from prison.

Martin — serving consecutive life sentences for murder and described in the affidavit as obsessed with a famous person identified as “J.B.” (reported by investigators to be Justin Bieber) — told police he wanted notoriety after feeling snubbed by the celebrity. He allegedly instructed Staake and Ruane to murder four people in two separate attacks. For the first two Vermont-based victims he described a gruesome method: strangulation with a paisley tie (the same method Martin had used previously) followed by castration, with Staake allegedly to be paid $2,500 per testicle. The affidavit does not say Bieber would be castrated.

Martin claimed he had recruited Staake while both were at the Southern New Mexico Correctional Facility and that Staake had continued contact after his release. Recorded phone calls and travel mishaps appear to have disrupted the plans: Staake was arrested on a Vermont probation warrant on Nov. 19 after missing an exit and encountering border authorities; Ruane later called Martin saying he would not proceed without Staake. Martin then went to police, and Ruane was arrested in New York on Nov. 26. No killings occurred.

Staake faces New Mexico charges including conspiracy to commit murder and conspiracy to commit aggravated battery; authorities are seeking his extradition from Vermont. Martin remains in segregation in New Mexico. Bieber’s management issued a brief statement saying they take every precaution to protect his and his fans’ safety.

Iran has set bail at $500,000 each for Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, two Americans arrested with Sarah Shourd near the Iran–Iraq border in July 2009 and later convicted on espionage-related charges. Their lawyer, Masoud Shafiei, said the court informed the Swiss Embassy (which represents U.S. interests in Iran) that payment of the bonds would secure their release; Shourd was released in September 2010 after posting the same amount. President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad told The Washington Post he intends to grant a “unilateral pardon” and help arrange their return to the United States, though any pardon is subject to review by Iran’s clerical authorities and the judiciary says procedures are being followed. Bauer and Fattal were sentenced last month to eight years but can still appeal, which is why the bond is being required. Washington welcomed Ahmadinejad’s comments as encouraging. The article also notes background on the hikers (all three are UC Berkeley graduates; Bauer and Shourd worked as journalists) and describes broader diplomatic context: Ahmadinejad’s outreach ahead of the U.N. General Assembly, Iran’s overtures on nuclear talks, and his remarks on Syria, Iran’s economy, and internal political tensions.

Kelsey Grammer’s early life was marked by extraordinary tragedy and loss. Before turning 20 he endured the deaths of close family members: his grandfather when Grammer was 11, his father—who was shot and set on fire—when he was 13 (the killer was found not guilty by reason of insanity and confined to a psychiatric hospital), and at 20 he was forced to identify the body of his sister after she was raped and murdered. In 1980, two of his half-brothers died in a scuba diving accident in St. Thomas.

The document then shifts to note that some actors’ real lives are stranger than fiction, segueing into the example of Woody Harrelson. It summarizes Harrelson’s father, Charles Harrelson, a convicted contract killer who left his family in 1968, was suspected in multiple murders, evaded conviction twice (once acquitted, once mistrial), later received a sentence but served only part of it, and went on to commit further violent crime. The piece uses these biographies to underscore how actors’ personal histories can be more extreme than the dramatic backstories often given to movie characters.

Lake Superior State University released its 38th annual “List of Words to be Banished from the Queen’s English” — a lighthearted, nonbinding roundup of words and phrases voters find overused, misused or pointless. The list is compiled from nominations submitted mostly via social media from the U.S., Canada and beyond.

Highlights and top nominees:
- Selfie: the most-nominated word, criticized as narcissistic and overused for ordinary photographs.
- Twerk / Twerking: reviled following pop-culture exposure and seen as crude and ubiquitous.
- Hashtag (spoken use): the pound/Twitter symbol’s name is now leaking into everyday speech, irritating many.
- Twitter-sphere: mocked as unnecessary and overhyped.
- Mister Mom: singled out as an outdated, insulting label for fathers who are primary caregivers.
- T-bone (as verb for perpendicular car crashes): objected to for its culinary imagery.
- “On steroids”: complained as a lazy intensifier.
- Suffix trends: overuse of “-ageddon” and “-pocalypse” to dramatize events (e.g., snowpocalypse).
- Politics and sports terms: “intellectually/morally bankrupt,” “Obamacare” (instead of Affordable Care Act), “adversity” (in sports), and “fan base.”
- Other banished entries: “spoiler alert,” “fiscal cliff” (one of the most-nominated phrases), “superfood,” “guru,” “job creators/creation,” “double down,” “boneless wings,” “passion/passionate,” and “YOLO.”

Context:
- The list is tongue-in-cheek and has “banished” roughly 900 words/phrases over nearly four decades but has not stopped these words’ continued use.
- LSSU solicits nominations year-round via its website and Facebook page. The university uses the campaign to poke fun at linguistic trends driven in part by social media.

A landlocked country lacks a coastline or direct access to an ocean or sea; there are 43 such countries worldwide, the largest being Kazakhstan. Being landlocked brings some protections—reduced exposure to ocean disasters like tsunamis and hurricanes, easier monitoring of cross-border movement, and security from seaborne invasions—but also significant economic and logistical drawbacks, especially for developing states: higher transport and customs costs, dependence on neighbors for port access, and the need to keep good diplomatic relations with coastal states.

The document lists the world’s ten largest landlocked countries by area:
1. Kazakhstan – 2,724,900 km²; population ~16.4 million; largest landlocked country.
2. Mongolia – 1,566,500 km²; population ~3 million.
3. Chad – 1,284,000 km²; population ~10.3 million.
4. Niger – 1,267,000 km²; population ~15.3 million.
5. Mali – 1,240,192 km²; population ~14.5 million.
6. Ethiopia – 1,104,300 km²; population ~85.2 million.
7. Bolivia – 1,098,581 km²; population ~10.9 million.
8. Zambia – 752,612 km²; population ~12.9 million.
9. Afghanistan – 647,500 km²; population ~29.1 million.
10. Central African Republic – 752,612 km²; population ~4.4 million.
(Several entries note neighboring countries.)

The piece then focuses on Astana (Nur-Sultan), Kazakhstan’s modern capital, positioning it as an emerging and increasingly popular city-break destination. Astana’s dramatic, futuristic architecture—highlighted by projects from architect Norman Foster such as the Palace of Peace and Reconciliation and the Khan Shatyr Entertainment Centre—and new high-end hotels (Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis, Marriott, Radisson) are raising its international profile. The city hosted Expo 2017 on the theme “Future Energy,” featuring the Nur Alem spherical pavilion, and the government views the Expo as a catalyst to promote Astana globally.

Astana combines futuristic skyline developments with Soviet-era remnants and local culture: a mix of past trading-post character, Soviet grid avenues, theaters, markets and a blend of European and Central Asian influences. Practical travel details note direct flights from London with Air Astana (about seven hours) and alternative routes via Kiev or Moscow. Beyond the city, Kazakhstan offers diverse natural attractions—Charyn Canyon, Shymbulak ski resort near Almaty, and Lake Kaindy—making the country an accessible and varied destination between Europe and Asia.

Henri Bendel, the 123-year-old New York-based luxury retailer, will close all operations in January 2019. Parent company L Brands, which bought Bendel in 1985, said it will shut the brand’s e-commerce site and all 23 stores—including the iconic Fifth Avenue flagship—because of declining sales and to focus on larger, higher-growth brands like Victoria’s Secret and Bath & Body Works. Bendel’s 2018 sales were about $85 million; L Brands reported $12.6 billion in revenue for the prior year and said it is estimating closure costs. L Brands CEO Leslie Wexner called the move necessary to improve profitability but acknowledged the impact on employees. Bendel, founded as a millinery by Henri Willis Bendel in 1895 and an early U.S. luxury pioneer (introducing Chanel in 1913 and employing Andy Warhol as an illustrator in the 1960s), will continue to operate its Fifth Avenue store through mid-January and will receive new holiday merchandise. The announcement comes as L Brands faces a difficult 2018, including a roughly 55% drop in its stock price.

Kayla Mueller, a 26-year-old American aid worker abducted in Aleppo in August 2013 while volunteering with refugees, has been confirmed dead following information provided privately to her family and subsequently authenticated by U.S. intelligence. Over a tense weekend her parents publicly urged the Islamic State (ISIS) for proof; the militants then sent at least three photographs, two showing Mueller in a black hijab with facial bruising and one showing her in a white burial shroud. U.S. officials say the images and other information convinced them she had died, though they have not been able to determine precisely when or how she died and do not accept ISIS’s claim that she was killed by a Jordanian-led coalition airstrike. Pentagon and State Department spokespeople noted no evidence civilians were in the targeted area and stressed ISIS is ultimately responsible for her captivity and death.

Intelligence signals had at times placed Mueller in the custody of an ISIS commander or kept apart from other hostages; some officials believe she may have been passed to fighters or compelled into a forced relationship. Her last verified proof-of-life was in May 2014; she was among hostages the U.S. tried to rescue during a July 2014 raid but commandos arrived after hostages had been moved. U.S. reconnaissance relied largely on airborne collection and sporadic visual sightings, and in recent weeks officials said they had “lost fidelity” on her status before the family received new information.

Mueller’s family released letters she wrote from captivity describing being treated with respect and urging them not to risk their safety negotiating for her. Her relatives, friends and community remembered her deep commitment to refugee aid and service; President Obama and others offered condolences. The White House has cautioned that many reports about the details of her captivity remain uncorroborated and asked that speculation be restrained out of respect for the family.

On April 15 — the 104th birthday of North Korea’s founder Kim Il Sung, a major holiday known as the "Day of the Sun" — Pyongyang attempted to launch an intermediate-range ballistic missile but the effort failed, South Korean and U.S. officials said. The missile, likely a road-mobile Musudan (BM-25) observed moved near Wonsan the day before, deviated from a normal trajectory and was assessed to have failed on or shortly after ignition. U.S. Strategic Command and South Korea’s Joint Chiefs tracked the launch; Pentagon spokesmen described it as a "fiery, catastrophic" failure and said initial indications were that the missile did not clear the launch site.

The Musudan, untested in flight before, has an estimated range of roughly 1,500–2,500 miles (potentially threatening Guam) and could carry a large warhead. Analysts note the missile uses engines similar to those in previous failed North Korean submarine-launched ballistic missile tests; failures will underscore capability limits but also provide Pyongyang with technical lessons. Experts and U.S. defense officials view the test as part of North Korea’s broader push toward longer-range missiles and nuclear delivery systems, amid claims from Pyongyang of advances (solid-fuel engines, warhead miniaturization) that remain unverified.

The failed launch occurred against a backdrop of increased North Korean activity since a January nuclear test and a February long-range rocket launch, ongoing U.S.-South Korea military drills, and preparations for key North Korean events (a Workers’ Party congress and a domestic “70-day campaign”). Seoul remains on high alert, warning of possible further provocations including a fifth nuclear test; satellite imagery groups like 38 North have reported activity at nuclear sites that could indicate preparation for another test. The international response included condemnation from the White House and critical commentary from China’s Xinhua, which warned that continued saber-rattling harms North Korea and urged restraint in accordance with U.N. Security Council resolutions.

A widely published photograph of 9-year-old Lakhan Kale tethered by the ankle to a Mumbai bus-stop pole sparked public outrage and led to his removal from the street and placement in a children’s shelter.

Background
- Lakhan is nonverbal, deaf, and has cerebral palsy and epilepsy. His father died years ago and his mother disappeared; he was cared for by his 66-year-old grandmother, Sakkubai, and his 12-year-old sister, Rekha.
- The family were pavement dwellers. Because Lakhan tends to wander and cannot communicate, his grandmother tied him to the bus-stop pole while she sold toys and flower garlands and would tie his leg to hers at night to prevent him from straying.

Intervention
- After local newspapers ran photos of Lakhan tied up, police and charities intervened. Social worker Meena Mutha, officers from Marine Drive station and shelter staff helped secure Lakhan’s admission to The Children’s Aid Society (a shelter in Dongri). Required paperwork (Sakkubai’s consent, medical reports and a letter from Manav Foundation) facilitated the placement. The shelter will help with his care and treatment; Sakkubai hopes to visit once she obtains an identity card.

Wider issues raised
- Activists and charity workers say Lakhan’s case reflects a broader problem in India: tens of millions of people with disabilities face stigma, discrimination and severe shortages of appropriate residential and support services.
- NGOs often have expertise but lack space; government homes may lack adequate infrastructure and trained staff. Social workers and lawyers argue governments need to provide more residential centres and services.
- A rights bill for disabled people was introduced to parliament but had not yet passed; advocates hope stronger legislation and implementation will improve care and social attitudes.

The case highlighted gaps in support for disabled children in India and prompted immediate action to get Lakhan off the street and into institutional care.
