A 60 Minutes/CBS News investigation collected accounts from dozens of current and former employees of The Spotted Pig and other restaurants tied to celebrity chef Mario Batali and co-owner Ken Friedman. The reporting describes a long-running culture of sexual harassment, assault, intimidation and emotional abuse in which powerful men—Batali, Friedman and, employees say, others—used their status to harass staff and discourage complaints.

Key allegations and themes:
- Multiple women who worked at The Spotted Pig say Batali regularly made sexual advances, groped wait staff and in at least one incident was seen on surveillance video touching an apparently unconscious woman on the restaurant’s monitor. Several women say they felt pressured to tolerate misconduct to keep their jobs.
- Employees describe the restaurant’s third-floor party room as lawless—drug and alcohol use, sex and scant boundaries—and say Friedman cultivated a celebrity-focused environment where abuses went unchecked.
- Several women say Ken Friedman sexually assaulted or aggressively kissed them in his car or on site and later pressured them via texts or emails asking for “sexy” pictures. Friedman denies non-consensual activity but has apologized for unspecified mistakes and says he’s reflected on his conduct.
- One anonymous former Babbo employee alleges Batali assaulted her in 2005 after a Spotted Pig party, waking up injured and with what she believed was semen on her skirt; she sought medical care but did not file charges. Batali denies that allegation. Other women told of repeated unwanted touching and behavior by Batali.
- Many employees say there was no effective HR or safe reporting channel (the ownership didn’t have full-time HR until 2017), and some say complaints to co-owner April Bloomfield were ignored; Bloomfield said she is ending her partnership with Friedman and regrets not doing more.
- Fear of retaliation, blackballing and job loss kept many from reporting at the time; several who did complain say nothing was done. One manager says Friedman rescinded or sabotaged job offers after employees tried to leave.

Developments:
- Mario Batali stepped away from his restaurant empire in late 2017 amid earlier public accusations and said he was remorseful for past inappropriate behavior. He has since been removed from media projects and is divesting from his restaurants.
- The New York Police Department confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation into Batali based on the allegations reported; additional incidents are being examined by police.

The investigation frames these incidents as part of a broader, pervasive problem in the restaurant industry—employees say harassment and intimidation are common—and highlights the barriers that kept victims silent until recent reporting prompted renewed attention and police review.

Several investigative reports, church documents and news accounts over decades show that sexual abuse and exploitation of Catholic nuns by priests and bishops is a global, systemic problem—particularly severe in parts of Africa but also documented in Europe, Asia, Latin America and the United States. Confidential studies from the 1990s (notably by Sr. Maura O’Donohue and Sr. Marie McDonald) and later reporting by outlets such as the Associated Press and National Catholic Reporter describe patterns including coercion, rape, pregnancy followed by forced abortion, sexual extortion tied to ecclesial permissions, and punishment or dismissal of the nun while the cleric is merely reassigned.

Key factors noted across the reports:
- Power imbalances and clerical authority (spiritual direction, confession, recommendation letters) that enable coercion.
- Cultural norms that devalue women and make obedience expected, leaving many sisters reluctant or unable to resist or report abuse.
- Financial dependence of many religious women and low stipends that make them vulnerable to exploitation.
- The HIV/AIDS pandemic in Africa led some priests to target nuns and younger women as perceived “safe” partners, increasing incidence and urgency.
- Inadequate institutional responses: victims often face silence, blame, dismissal, or minimal sanctions against perpetrators; reports to bishops or Vatican offices frequently produced little visible action.

Consequences for victims and communities include trauma, loss of faith and trust, social stigmatization (especially after pregnancy), and broader disillusionment with church authority. Some local and religious communities have begun creating guidelines, raising awareness, and removing accused clerics; Vatican sources and church officials say initiatives exist at multiple levels, but the Holy See has not clearly detailed centralized measures to investigate, punish or provide pastoral care—particularly for cases involving bishops.

Recent public disclosures (buoyed by #MeToo and wider scrutiny of clerical abuse) have seen survivors in Chile, India, Europe and elsewhere go public, file police complaints, and demand accountability. These contemporary revelations echo the earlier confidential reports and highlight that the problem is persistent and global. Advocates call for taking victims seriously, transparent investigations, better protection and formation, and concrete measures to end the culture of secrecy and impunity that allows clerical sexual abuse of nuns to continue.

White House officials say a forthcoming unclassified report will reveal missed warning signs that could have prevented the Dec. 25 attempted bombing of Northwest Airlines Flight 253, and that Americans will be “a certain shock” when they read it. National Security Adviser Gen. James Jones told USA Today that President Obama is rightly alarmed that available pieces of information and behavior patterns were not acted on. Jones described fixes as “tweaks” (for example, hiring more intelligence analysts) rather than an overhaul.

Suspect Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, 23, was indicted on charges including attempted murder and attempted use of a weapon of mass destruction; he faces life in prison if convicted and is to appear in federal court. Authorities say he trained in Yemen and has acknowledged ties to an al-Qaeda-affiliated group. His father had warned the U.S. Embassy in Nigeria about his son’s turn to extremism, but Abdulmutallab’s U.S. visa was not revoked and he was not placed on the no-fly list.

U.S. and Yemeni officials report the suspect met radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki in Yemen after being recruited in London, though British officials maintain recruitment likely occurred in Yemen. Al-Awlaki has been linked to other attacks, including the Fort Hood shooting by Maj. Nidal Hasan; U.S. officials say al-Awlaki is actively instigating terrorism. Senate Intelligence Chair Dianne Feinstein urged expanding and strengthening the no-fly list, suggesting inclusion on “reasonable suspicion.” Yemeni officials also said the explosives used came from Nigeria, and noted continued concerns about al-Qaeda activity inside Yemen.

Yahoo faced intense backlash after new CEO Marissa Mayer announced a ban on remote work, prompting global debate about flexible workplace policies. The company issued a statement to the New York Times stressing the decision is specific to Yahoo — “not a broad industry view on working from home” — and declined to discuss internal details. Insiders, speaking anonymously, say Mayer believes the policy is needed to reinvigorate Yahoo’s culture, boost camaraderie, creativity and intensity, and root out employees who have become disengaged or abused remote-work privileges. Supporters inside the company argue in-person presence is essential to turn Yahoo around; outside observers warned the move could harm work-life balance, disproportionately affect women, and risk losing talented staff. The memo’s tone, which discouraged even occasional home days, drew particular criticism as tone-deaf. Mayer has stood by the decision, and Yahoo appears to be trying to contain criticism by framing the policy as a company-specific step to address its particular problems.

State documents and recent reporting reveal that Louisiana correction officials sought pentobarbital from an Oklahoma compounding pharmacy, The Apothecary Shoppe, in advance of the Feb. 5 execution of Christopher Sepulvado. The pharmacy is not licensed to sell drugs in Louisiana, which would make any such sale illegal under state law. A September 2013 email from the Apothecary Shoppe included a non‑disclosure agreement requesting confidentiality; that NDA — initially heavily redacted — was later provided in full to defense lawyers engaged in a lawsuit seeking details about execution protocols.

Louisiana’s Department of Corrections acknowledged it was “in the process of procuring” at least 15 grams of pentobarbital but has provided limited and delayed disclosure to defense counsel, who say the state’s responses have been incomplete and opaque. The Apothecary Shoppe is one of several Oklahoma compounding pharmacies suspected of supplying pentobarbital used recently in other states’ executions, including Missouri and Oklahoma, and has been linked to drug batches that critics say may have produced prolonged, possibly painful deaths.

Those concerns fit a wider national crisis: pharmaceutical companies and some countries have blocked sales of drugs for executions, forcing states to use unregulated compounding pharmacies or experimental drug combinations. Reporting and studies show executions using single‑drug pentobarbital have on average taken longer than older three‑drug protocols, and high‑profile problematic executions (e.g., Dennis McGuire’s prolonged, gasping death in Ohio; Michael Lee Williams saying he felt burning in Oklahoma) have intensified scrutiny. Compounding pharmacies are lightly regulated and tests in some states have found potency and purity problems.

The shortages and secrecy have prompted legal challenges, public criticism and proposals in some states to resurrect older methods (firing squads, electrocution, gas chambers) as contingencies if lethal‑injection drugs remain unavailable. Advocates and experts warn the mix of secrecy, untested protocols and variable drug quality risks cruel and unusual punishment and undermines transparency and public confidence in the death‑penalty system.

A Manhattan judge ruled that several personal items belonging to Madonna — including a 1995 breakup letter from Tupac Shakur, a lock of hair, underwear, a hairbrush, photos, an old checkbook and another handwritten letter about Whitney Houston and Sharon Stone — can be sold by New York auction house Gotta Have Rock and Roll. The items were originally scheduled for auction last year, prompting Madonna to obtain a temporary restraining order to block the sale after she learned via press reports that the pieces were no longer in her possession.

Judge Gerald Lebovits found Madonna had sued the wrong party by targeting Darlene Lutz, an art collector who says the two settled their disputes in a 2004 agreement and who maintained she lawfully owned the material. The judge questioned why Madonna sued Lutz rather than the assistants she alleged gave the possessions away. Lutz says the items came into her possession informally when she was often in Madonna’s circle and accepted boxes of material that staff discarded.

Gotta Have Rock and Roll co-owners said they performed due diligence and welcomed the ruling; they plan to relist the items for auction in July. Madonna has not publicly commented on the decision. The Tupac letter, dated Jan. 15, 1995, was written from prison and explains why he ended their relationship, and the lot also includes an unsent Madonna draft disparaging Houston and Stone.

Ben Carson is traveling to Jordan on Friday for a surprise visit to the Azraq refugee camp to see Syrian refugees, visit a clinic and hospital, and distribute soccer balls and Beanie Babies. He said firsthand exposure helps inform his views. The trip comes as Carson faces growing criticism over his foreign-policy knowledge and as his standing in polls has slipped since the Paris attacks—particularly in Iowa, where Donald Trump and Ted Cruz have overtaken him. Carson has opposed accepting Syrian refugees to the U.S., advocated defunding refugee programs, and likened security risks from refugees to “a rabid dog,” remarks that have drawn criticism. His foreign-policy missteps on the debate stage, including a disputed comment about China’s role in Syria, have contributed to concerns about his readiness on national security.

A few weeks before his sudden death at 43, conservative blogger Andrew Breitbart told a CPAC crowd he had college-era video of Barack Obama that would expose racial- and class-based motivations behind Obama's 2008 campaign. Breitbart died in Los Angeles shortly before the tapes were to be released. His death quickly spawned a flood of conspiracy theories—especially on Twitter and on fringe websites—claiming, without evidence, that Obama or allied groups had him killed to suppress the tapes. The rumors ranged from allegations of sexual scandal and drug addiction to elaborate assassination plots involving multiple politicians; many posts relied on Breitbart’s antagonistic history with Obama and other political foes rather than facts.

The piece also recounts Breitbart’s final public exchange on Twitter, in which he called a 29-year-old law student, Lamar White Jr., a “putz.” The two later described their banter as harmless and even complimentary: White said he wore the insult as a “badge of honor,” praised Breitbart’s energy, and rejected the assassination theories that proliferated after Breitbart’s death. The article frames Breitbart as a provocative culture warrior whose style and claims—whether about ACORN, Shirley Sherrod, or Obama—both drove his influence and fueled the posthumous conspiratorial reaction.

Elon Musk announced he is considering taking Tesla private at $420 per share, a roughly 20% premium over the then-current price, and explained the background, rationale, and next steps. He told Tesla’s board on August 2 that he personally wanted to pursue a buyout using a structure that would allow shareholders who wished to remain invested to roll their holdings into a private Tesla, while the $420 cash would be paid only to those who chose to exit. After an initial outside-directors meeting, the full board asked Musk to consult with large long-term shareholders about their willingness and ability to stay invested if Tesla went private.

Musk said he publicly announced his intention to ensure all investors had the same information simultaneously, and that his “funding secured” tweet referred to repeated, recent discussions with the Saudi sovereign wealth fund. He stated the fund’s managing director expressed strong support for financing a going-private transaction and that he left their July 31 meeting confident a deal could be closed, though the fund’s commitment is contingent on due diligence and internal approvals. Musk emphasized most funding would be equity rather than debt, that he estimates roughly two-thirds of current shares might roll over, and that reports claiming a $70+ billion debt package are overstated.

He has continued investor discussions, engaged advisors to explore structures and to better estimate rollover participation, and said a special independent board committee (and counsel) will evaluate any final proposal before regulatory approvals and a shareholder vote, if required.

Press coverage and securities-watchers raised concerns: Musk’s initial tweets lacked detail about source, terms, and amount of funding, prompting SEC inquiry about the “funding secured” claim and criticism that some board members and advisers were blindsided. Reports note Musk’s impulsive use of Twitter and that he later named prospective financial and legal advisers (Silver Lake Partners, Goldman Sachs; Wachtell Lipton and Munger Tolles among firms) while continuing to pursue the potential transaction amid intense scrutiny over Tesla’s production challenges, mounting debt, recent controversies, and regulatory investigations.

A Texas state trooper was fatally shot with a rifle during a traffic stop on Interstate 45 near Fairfield (about 90 miles south of Dallas) before 4 p.m. Thursday, authorities said. The trooper died at the scene; their identity has not been released. Suspect Dabrett Black, 32, of Linsdale, was later located more than 100 miles away—his vehicle was spotted in Hempstead in neighboring Waller County. Shots were exchanged when deputies encountered the vehicle, and Black was taken into custody shortly afterward. Black has prior charges including evading arrest, reckless driving and aggravated assault on a public servant from a July incident, KYTX-TV reported. Texas officials, including Gov. Greg Abbott and U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, offered condolences and condemned the killing.

Eight people, including five juveniles, were wounded by gunfire Monday afternoon at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park in Liberty City, Miami, after the annual MLK Day parade. Miami-Dade Police say two suspects are being questioned and two firearms were recovered. Victims are aged 11 to 30; five are in stable condition, one is critical, and two juveniles who were grazed by bullets were treated and released at the scene. The investigation is ongoing and police temporarily blocked off nearby streets.

A three-year Vanderbilt University study in metropolitan Nashville found that substantial individual bonuses for teachers did not improve student test scores. Researchers examined about 300 fifth- through eighth-grade math teachers from 2007–2009; roughly half were eligible for bonuses (up to $15,000) tied to improvements on Tennessee standardized exams, and about 40 teachers received bonuses each year. By the end of the study, modest score gains occurred in both the bonus and control groups, indicating the financial incentives alone had no measurable effect.

Lead researcher Matthew Springer said the findings suggest teacher pay systems are broken but cautioned pay alone isn’t a solution. The U.S. Department of Education argued the study was narrowly focused on individual pay incentives and didn’t address broader aims—such as changing school culture, giving feedback, or rewarding teachers willing to work in high-need schools—behind federal initiatives like Race to the Top. Teacher unions and critics used the results to argue for more training, support, and better evaluation methods rather than merit pay, while supporters of bonus programs say more research is needed (for example, on team- or school-based incentives). Overall, the study challenges the view that standalone merit pay is an effective way to raise student achievement.

Public records obtained by the San Francisco Chronicle reveal three 911 calls from early January 2018 reporting Apple Park employees who walked into large glass walls or doors at Apple’s new Cupertino “spaceship” campus. The incidents occurred Jan. 2 (two calls) and Jan. 4, all at 1 Apple Park Way near the transit center (Gate 5A). In the first Jan. 2 call a man in his late 20s hit his head, was bleeding and slightly disoriented; dispatchers gave bleeding-control instructions and sent paramedics. The second Jan. 2 call described a middle‑aged male with a cut above the eyebrow that Apple first‑aid staff thought likely required stitches. The Jan. 4 call involved a 23‑year‑old who described the mishap as “very silly” and reported no serious bleeding.

Cupertino building officials had warned Apple before the campus opened that the nearly invisible glass could be a hazard—especially after cleaning—yet the building’s design prioritized minimal visual cues and uninterrupted sight lines to reduce distractions. The three calls are from only a few days’ worth of operations (the facility has housed staff since April 2017), so additional similar incidents may have occurred. Apple reportedly discouraged ad hoc markings like post‑it notes, and OSHA records showed no applicable results. Local officials and fire department representatives say they pointed out the issue during inspections; a contractor walking into glass while they were discussing it helped underscore the concern.

Thousands of European dairy farmers and hundreds of tractors converged on Brussels for a two-day protest against low milk prices and EU milk-quota rules. Coordinated by the European Milk Board (EMB), demonstrators—many from Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Belgium—blocked major streets around EU institutions, preventing officials reaching offices, and staged dramatic actions including setting hay and tyre fires, erecting a mock gallows and spraying thousands of litres of fresh milk at the European Parliament and police.

Farmers say current wholesale prices are below production costs (the EMB cites examples such as €0.26/litre wholesale versus €0.40/litre production cost in Belgium), forcing small and medium producers out of business. They demand price increases of up to about 25% and warn that phasing out subsidies and the planned end to EU milk quotas by 2015 would worsen the situation. Organizers said the second day’s actions would be more symbolic and calmer, but the protest underscores deep anger over commodity prices, competition and falling international demand for EU milk.

Venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers has filed in San Francisco Superior Court seeking about $972,815 (rounded to $973,000) in costs from former partner Ellen Pao, who lost a high-profile gender discrimination and retaliation trial in March. The requested costs largely consist of expert witness fees (about $865,000), plus deposition and court-reporter expenses. Kleiner says it will waive the costs request if Pao agrees not to appeal; Pao’s team is considering the offer.

The firm also disclosed it had offered Pao roughly $964,502 to settle before trial—an offer Kleiner says went unanswered—allowing it now to seek certain witness fees. Pao, now interim CEO of Reddit, alleged her career at Kleiner suffered after ending an affair with a partner and that she faced retaliation and a hostile environment for women; a jury rejected her claims. Observers note such offers to forgo costs in exchange for dropping appeals are common for defendants. Data cited in the filing indicate California’s First District Court of Appeal typically affirms employer trial victories. Critics called Kleiner’s move somewhat punitive, while Kleiner framed the offer as a way to avoid continued litigation and focus on broader gender‑diversity progress.

Astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope (SH0ES team, led by Adam Riess) have produced a new, very precise measurement of the universe’s current expansion rate — the Hubble constant — finding 73.2 km/s/Mpc (≈45.5 mi/s/Mpc) with a 2.4% uncertainty. This value is about 5–9% higher than the rate inferred from observations of the early universe (cosmic microwave background) by WMAP and Planck. The result comes from improved distance measurements: about 2,400 Cepheid variable stars in 19 galaxies were measured with Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3, tied to Type Ia supernovae out to hundreds of supernovae, yielding a refined distance ladder.

The tension between “local” (late‑time) and “early‑universe” determinations of the Hubble constant has persisted after careful error analysis, and if it withstands further scrutiny it may point to new physics. Possible explanations include unexpected properties or evolving strength of dark energy, previously unknown relativistic particles or “dark radiation” (e.g., extra neutrino‑like species), unusual behavior of dark matter, or a need to modify General Relativity. Some experts urge caution and note the discrepancy could still arise from unrecognized systematic errors; the SH0ES team and other projects (including Gaia, JWST, WFIRST) aim to further reduce uncertainties and test the result.

Senior Judiciary Committee staffers secretly assisted the Trump transition in drafting the administration’s executive order that temporarily halted refugee admissions and restricted entry from seven majority-Muslim countries. They worked during the transition, signed nondisclosure agreements, and provided immigration-policy expertise — but did not inform Judiciary Chairman Bob Goodlatte or broader Republican leadership. 

Most congressional leaders and key committee members — including the entire House Homeland Security panels and several Senate homeland and foreign-relations members — learned the final language only hours after the order was signed. That late, limited coordination produced confusion and operational problems (notably the inadvertent detention or denial of entry to green-card holders and visa holders), widespread protests, and a PR and legal backlash. Senior Hill Republicans and some administration officials privately criticized the White House for the secretive, rushed rollout and for bypassing the usual chain of consultation. 

Inside the West Wing, the episode deepened tensions between factions: Stephen Miller and Stephen Bannon, who drove the order’s drafting and public defense, versus more traditional operators like Chief of Staff Reince Priebus and deputies who expected broader interagency and congressional coordination. Cabinet officials including DHS Secretary John Kelly and Defense Secretary Jim Mattis were reportedly surprised by the move. 

The White House has defended the action and later dispatched aides to brief Capitol Hill, but many lawmakers and aides angrily called for better vetting and coordination in future, saying the chaotic rollout undermined policy execution, strained relationships with Congress and allies, and produced unintended consequences that might have been avoided with more inclusive review.

The document explains a new Department of Labor rule that extends a strict fiduciary standard to retirement advisers and gives savers legal recourse (suits or arbitration) against advisers who fail to disclose conflicts or put their own interests first. Historically, two adviser types existed: registered investment advisers (fiduciaries paid fees) and broker-dealers (sales-oriented, commission-paid, held only to a “suitability” standard). The shift to defined‑contribution plans like 401(k)s has made ordinary workers responsible for investment decisions, and conflicted broker advice—especially rollovers from 401(k)s to higher‑fee IRAs—has been estimated to shave about 1 percentage point a year from returns, costing savers billions over time.

Supporters argue the rule will reduce costly conflicts, legally obligate advisers to act in clients’ interests, and save retirees large sums (the Labor Department estimates over $40 billion in 10 years). Opponents—mainly industry groups—say most brokers already behave appropriately, warn the rule is uneven (targeting retirement advice only), could prompt frivolous lawsuits, require burdensome paperwork, and likely drive many brokers away from middle‑class clients or out of the business entirely. Experience in the U.K., which adopted tougher rules and commission bans, showed a decline in adviser numbers and a shift from commission to fee income; it also revealed an “advice gap” for less wealthy savers, who may be priced out of human advisers.

Commentators note brokers will have three options: comply and accept lower commissions, switch to fee‑based models, or stop advising. Some see robo‑advice and inexpensive online guidance as adequate for many savers, since basic retirement rules are simple (save, use low‑cost index funds, don’t tap funds early). Critics in Congress have sought more study of the rule—a tactic described as likely to kill it—while proponents argue the rule has been extensively vetted and further delay will cost middle‑class investors billions by preserving conflicted advice.

An 8-year-old Santa Cruz girl, Madyson “Maddy” Middleton, was found dead Monday evening in a recycling bin at the Tannery Arts Center, the arts-loft complex where she and a 15-year-old neighbor lived, police said. Authorities believe the teen lured Maddy into his apartment, killed her there and then placed her body in the concealed bin; he was arrested early Tuesday and remains in juvenile hall. Investigators said the boy knew Maddy and had even helped search for her; video and witness statements tie him to the case. Police would not disclose cause of death or whether there was a sexual assault; autopsy results were pending. The district attorney said the teen could be charged as an adult.

Maddy was last seen on surveillance video Sunday at about 5:05–5:07 p.m. riding her scooter at the complex and was reported missing roughly an hour later. A large search followed—door-to-door canvassing, volunteers, helicopters, dogs and FBI agents—before detectives conducting a more detailed recovery search found her body around 7:50 p.m. Monday. Neighbors and community members expressed shock and grief; local officials offered condolences. Maddy’s mother described her as artistic, active and trusting. Police continue investigating motivations and details of the homicide.

MSNBC hosts Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski say White House officials tried to leverage a National Enquirer exposé about their relationship to extract an apology for their criticism of President Trump. In a Washington Post op‑ed and on Morning Joe, they alleged that top aides warned them the Enquirer planned a damaging story and urged them to call Trump and apologize so he could get the tabloid to kill it. The hosts say they refused; the Enquirer later ran a June story headlined about their “sleazy cheating scandal.” Trump tweeted that Scarborough had called him to stop the story; Scarborough denied ever speaking with Trump and said he has texts and records from White House aides.

The episode comes amid escalating public attacks between the hosts and the president—Scarborough and Brzezinski had been friendly with Trump early in his campaign but have grown sharply critical since. Media commentators warned the incident fits a pattern of Trump undermining the press and of using personal allies and tabloid coverage to retaliate against critics.

Background reporting links the Enquirer’s publisher, American Media, Inc. CEO David Pecker, as a longtime friend and supporter of Trump. The Enquirer ran strongly pro‑Trump, often sensationalist coverage in the 2016 campaign and afterward, and has a history of paying for and suppressing stories favorable to Trump’s interests. Pecker and his chief content officer deny any knowledge of or participation in White House discussions about the Scarborough/Brzezinski piece. The broader reporting on Pecker portrays the Enquirer’s commercial methods, political skew, and personal relationship with Trump as giving the White House an unusual informal channel to influence or weaponize tabloid coverage.

Summary:

When President Obama began personally tweeting from the official @POTUS account, the White House promoted it as a direct way for him to engage with the public. Almost immediately, many replies contained racist, threatening and sexually explicit messages—racial slurs, images of Obama in a noose, and graphic sexual solicitations. Under White House policy and the Presidential Records Act, the administration automatically archives tweets sent to and from official accounts (including mentions), meaning those abusive replies become part of the official record preserved for the Library of Congress. The piece highlights how the open nature of social media exposes the president to direct online hostility and how that content is nonetheless retained in government archives.

Rick Santorum released four years of joint federal tax returns (2007–2010). They show a sharp rise in income after he left the Senate and increased earnings from consulting and media work.

Key figures
- Adjusted gross income: ≈ $659,000 (2007); $952,000 (2008); $1.1 million (2009); $923,000 (2010).
- Federal taxes paid: ≈ $167,000 (2007); $262,000 (2008); $310,000 (2009); $263,000 (2010).
- Effective tax rate: roughly 25% in lower-income years and about 29% in the highest years.

Major sources and financial details
- Much of the post-Senate income came through a corporation Santorum set up, Excelsior LLC, reporting more than $820,000 in fees in 2008 and over $550,000 in 2010 from media and consulting.
- Payments included fees from corporate clients and lobby-associated firms (e.g., Consol Energy, American Continental Group, Clapham Group), media appearances (≈ $230,000 from Fox News, $80,000+ from radio), and compensation/stock options from Universal Health Services (UHS), where he served on the board until his campaign.
- The returns show modest stock sales in 2010 (Brandywine and UHS) and depreciation deductions for rental properties and a condo; an Audi A6 was claimed as a depreciated business expense in 2008.
- The Santorums own multiple rental properties in State College, Pa., and a northern Virginia home assessed at about $1.4 million in 2010; mortgage and depreciation deductions are claimed against rental properties.
- Charitable giving was a small share of income; in 2007 they took a $4,000 non-cash charity deduction. They claimed standard deductions for several of their seven children.

Context
- Santorum’s reported income and wealth are well below Mitt Romney’s (Romney reported $21.7 million in 2010) and below Newt Gingrich’s 2010 AGI (~$3.1 million), but reflect a transition from senator to a paid Washington consultant/commentator.
- The returns appear to be self-prepared. They were first made public via Politico.

Police arrested a man early Monday as a "person of interest" in a recent string of more than 50 deliberately set fires in Los Angeles; he is expected to be booked on arson charges later in the day. Authorities said no new arsons have been reported since the detention, but the investigation remains active. The fires have caused about $2 million in damage.

LAPD officials, including Chief Charlie Beck, said investigators are reviewing roughly 100 leads and are confident they have the right suspect after finding materials in the suspect’s minivan that could have been used to start fires. The man — a German national who may have been engaged in a dispute with federal immigration authorities over a relative — was stopped near Fairfax Avenue and Sunset Boulevard. The van reportedly had Canadian plates. Police are coordinating with federal immigration officials, though it’s unclear whether the immigration dispute is related to the arson spree.

Witnesses described a heavy police presence at the scene and said the detained man, seen in squad-car footage similar to previously released surveillance, smiled and made a rude gesture while in custody. Multiple patrols and checkpoints had been deployed across affected neighborhoods during the hunt. Investigators continue to gather evidence.

A new round of early 2012 Republican primary polls after the 2010 midterms shows Mitt Romney, Mike Huckabee and Sarah Palin leading on name recognition rather than substantive support. A Rasmussen national survey of likely GOP primary voters put Romney at 20%, Huckabee 19% and Palin 19%; Newt Gingrich was at 13%, Tim Pawlenty 6%, Ron Paul 5% and Mitch Daniels 3%, with 7% preferring someone else and 8% undecided. A CNN snapshot of three early states showed varying leaders—Romney and Huckabee tied in Iowa (21% each), Romney strong in New Hampshire (39%), and Palin ahead in South Carolina (25%) with Huckabee close behind. Commentators cautioned these early, national numbers mainly reflect familiarity and are poor predictors more than a year out; what will matter are state polls in early nominating states and campaign resources. The author views Romney as the likely frontrunner, Palin as his principal challenger, sees Huckabee as a potential long‑running spoiler, doubts Gingrich’s viability due to baggage, and notes the possibility of other entrants (e.g., governors or rising stars like Marco Rubio) emerging later.

General Mills announced a limited Marshmallow Only edition of Lucky Charms after receiving many fan requests. Only 10 boxes will be given away via a social-media sweepstakes running Oct. 14–18, 2015. To enter, U.S. or D.C. residents (18+) must post a selfie holding an imaginary Lucky Charms box on Facebook, Twitter or Instagram using #Lucky10Sweepstakes (one entry per platform, up to three total). Winners will be notified around Oct. 20. Promotional videos featuring Biz Markie explain the rules; full terms are on the Lucky Charms Facebook page. The giveaway is intended as a fun way to reward marshmallow-loving fans.

The Senate voted 60-37 to end debate on Trade Promotion Authority (TPA or “fast-track”), moving the measure to a final Senate vote expected Wednesday and then to President Obama’s desk if approved. TPA would require Congress to give up amendments and filibusters and allow up-or-down votes on trade agreements, clearing the way for the administration to finish the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) and later press a trans-Atlantic pact.

Thirteen Democrats joined Republicans to reach the 60-vote threshold after leaders split TPA from Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA)—a worker aid program that many Democrats insisted be tied to fast-track. TAA will be considered separately (packaged with renewal of African Growth and Opportunity Act preferences) and faces opposition in the House and among conservative senators; leaders pledged to pass both TAA and TPA by week’s end.

Supporters, including Senators Ron Wyden and Orrin Hatch, said TPA is needed to keep U.S. businesses competitive and set global trade standards. Opponents—led by Sherrod Brown, Elizabeth Warren, labor unions and progressive groups—argued fast-track risks American jobs, favors multinational companies, and grants negotiating power without Congress seeing final deals (TPP text remains largely secret). The vote was narrowly secured amid last-minute lobbying, missed votes, and defections by some conservatives (Ted Cruz, Rand Paul) and wavering Democrats; Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House Speaker John Boehner pledged to advance TAA and related trade enforcement measures.

"I, Tonya" (2017) is a darkly comic biopic directed by Craig Gillespie and written by Steven Rogers that reexamines the life and scandal of American figure skater Tonya Harding. Drawing on contradictory interviews and presented partly as a faux documentary with talking-heads, flashbacks, and fourth-wall asides, the film traces Harding’s rise from a rough, working‑class childhood in Oregon to skating success (she was one of the first American women to land a triple axel) and her public fall after the 1994 attack on rival Nancy Kerrigan orchestrated by associates of Harding’s then‑husband, Jeff Gillooly.

Margot Robbie stars as Tonya, delivering a layered performance that captures her athleticism, defiant swagger, and the emotional damage wrought by lifelong abuse. Allison Janney is widely praised for a ferocious, scene‑stealing turn as Tonya’s verbally and physically abusive mother, LaVona. Sebastian Stan plays Jeff Gillooly as a volatile, manipulative presence; Paul Walter Hauser also stands out as the bungling conspirator Shawn Eckhardt. The film balances dark humor, satire of 1990s tabloid culture, and genuine sympathy for Harding, highlighting class prejudice in skating and the personal abuse that shaped her life.

Critics praised the movie’s energy, performances (especially Robbie and Janney), and its inventive storytelling—though some noted heavy‑handed soundtrack choices and an occasionally blunt satirical tone. Rated R for pervasive language, violence, and some nudity, the 119‑minute drama was released in December 2017, later streaming/on disc March 13, 2018, and grossed roughly $29 million. Many reviewers called it one of the year’s best films, often assigning high marks (e.g., A–) for its bold, empathetic retelling of a notorious, stranger‑than‑fiction episode in sports and pop culture.

A 19-year-old Cal State L.A. student and new mother, Yaasmeen Castanada, is critically ill in the UC Irvine burn unit after developing a severe drug-induced reaction—initially diagnosed as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) that progressed to Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). The reaction began after she took an antibiotic pill offered by a friend for a sore throat on Thanksgiving. Within a day she developed burning sensations in her mouth, throat and eyes, respiratory distress, and rapidly spreading blisters; large portions of her skin and mucous membranes (doctors estimate about 65%) have detached, creating extensive open wounds.

Treating physicians have wrapped her in specialized dressings to allow wound healing without removing bandages and have performed surgeries to debride affected tissue. Complications have included infection, multiple blood transfusions, difficulty breathing requiring intubation and later a tracheotomy, and eye damage raising concern for future corneal transplant and possible vision loss. Mortality for SJS/TEN can be high, but doctors say her prognosis is cautiously hopeful with early, experienced care. Recovery will be long and may require extensive rehabilitation and additional surgeries.

Her family is devastated and urging people not to share prescription medications and to be aware of drug allergies. They have set up a GoFundMe to help with her care. The account and social posts detail her ongoing surgeries and gradual progress, including airway reconstruction and stitch removal, while noting lasting risks to skin and eyes. The Mayo Clinic defines SJS/TEN as a rare, serious reaction—usually to medications—requiring urgent hospitalization and avoidance of the causative drug.

On May 22, 2010, programmer Laszlo Hanyecz completed what became the first widely publicized real-world bitcoin transaction: he paid 10,000 BTC for two Papa John’s pizzas. At the time he mined those coins himself and believed each was worth roughly 0.003 cents; the pizzas cost about $30 total. With bitcoin’s later appreciation, those same coins would be worth millions today (about $22.5 million at the price cited), and a $100 purchase at that 2010 price would now be worth roughly $75 million.

Bitcoin is created (“mined”) by computers solving complex cryptographic problems; miners are rewarded with bitcoin and maintain the blockchain ledger. Despite ongoing association with criminal use and sharp price swings, bitcoin has experienced strong rallies driven by several factors:
- New laws in Japan allowing retailers to accept bitcoin have increased yen-denominated trading to over 40% of volume.
- Global political uncertainty has boosted demand as a perceived safe-haven asset.
- Technical debates within the bitcoin community over blockchain upgrades briefly raised fears of a split into two currencies, but those concerns eased after more acceptable alternatives emerged.

Bitcoin’s price has been volatile—breaking $1,000 in late 2013, plunging in early 2014, and trading near $900 by the end of 2016—yet it reached new highs (above $2,100 per coin in the report). The surge has also lifted many alternative cryptocurrencies (e.g., Ethereum, Ripple); estimates suggest bitcoin’s share of traded crypto has fallen as rivals gain. Some commentators warn the rapid rise may be an unsustainable bubble.

A South Carolina veteran, Ben Kinsey, who for the past three years has stood on an I-20 overpass waving an American flag for 11 hours each Sept. 11 to honor 9/11 victims, was spotted earlier this week standing on the bridge two months ahead of schedule. Kinsey was honoring the four U.S. Marines killed in the Chattanooga, Tenn., attacks and told a passerby he planned to stay four hours—one hour for each Marine. A photo and the passerby’s Facebook post went viral, prompting dozens of local residents to recognize Kinsey from prior years and many online users to offer to join him next year. Supporters praised his dedication as a visible reminder of national solidarity and remembrance.

Federal authorities executed the largest-ever Medicare fraud sweep by the Justice Department’s special strike force, charging 107 medical professionals and associates nationwide for schemes that sought to bilk Medicare of about $452 million. Arrests and actions took place across seven major metropolitan areas — including Los Angeles, Miami, Tampa, Houston, Baton Rouge, Detroit and Chicago — with 87 people arrested immediately and others sought or expected to surrender.

The defendants spanned the health care chain: doctors, nurses, licensed clinical social workers, office managers, patient recruiters and equipment suppliers. Allegations included billing for home health visits and ambulance trips that never occurred, fraudulent prescriptions and feeding tubes, unnecessary mental-health group therapy, HIV infusions, physical therapy, power wheelchairs never purchased, money laundering and kickbacks. Notable cases included:
- Los Angeles: eight defendants (including two doctors) charged with about $20 million in false claims; schemes included billing for unnecessary feeding tubes and power wheelchairs.
- Baton Rouge: seven people charged in a scheme that sought roughly $225.6 million by overbilling community mental-health centers; Medicare paid about $37.9 million to the centers.
- Miami area cases involving tens of millions in allegedly fraudulent claims, including a $63 million scheme and a previously prosecuted NANY Home Health case that generated $40 million in reimbursements.

Officials said they are seeking to recover at least $59.5 million based on reviewed complaints and indictments, though the total amount of purportedly false claims reaches roughly $452 million. Separately, Health and Human Services (HHS) took administrative action against 52 providers after data analysis flagged “credible allegations of fraud,” suspending payments in some cases. HHS Secretary Kathleen Sebelius and DOJ criminal division chief Lanny Breuer framed the takedown as part of intensified Obama-administration efforts — including tools created under the Affordable Care Act — to detect, prevent and prosecute Medicare fraud. The FBI is investigating more than 2,600 health-care fraud cases with over 500 agents and analysts; since 2007 the Justice Department has charged more than 1,300 people in Medicare fraud totaling over $4 billion.

Idaho State University has been fined $8,500 by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission after it could not account for a small sample of weapons‑grade plutonium (about 1 gram, roughly the size of a U.S. quarter) that had been used for research. The school discovered the missing source during a routine inventory in October 2018 and notified the NRC. ISU says the sample was taken out of service in 2003 but paperwork from that time was only partially completed, so while the university believes the gram-sized piece was sent to a licensed disposal facility, there are no records to confirm disposal. Officials say the quantity is too small to build a nuclear weapon and poses no direct health or public‑safety threat, though the NRC noted it could be used in a “dirty bomb.” ISU plans to return its remaining plutonium to the Energy Department and has 30 days to contest the proposed fine.

A Reddit user, BlackPanther2016, is publicly accusing Warner Bros./DC of false advertising over Suicide Squad trailers that highlighted specific Joker and Katana scenes which did not appear in the theatrical release. Comparing trailers to a food menu, he says he drove 300 miles to London specifically to see advertised moments—several Jared Leto Joker bits (e.g., banging his head on a car window, “let me show you my toys,” punching a car roof, dropping a bomb and saying “BYE BYE!”) and two Katana shots (blackened eyes and a slow‑mo soul‑taking sword shot)—but none were in the film. After complaining to theater staff he says he was laughed at and ejected, and now plans to sue for a refund, travel costs (~£160), and damages for embarrassment; he invites others who feel similarly to join his cause. The post echoes wider fan frustration over studios showing cut footage in marketing and notes that Jared Leto acknowledged many Joker scenes were cut from the final film.

Taylor Swift pledged $1 million to Louisiana’s disaster relief fund after torrential rains caused historic flooding across the state. In a statement to the Associated Press, Swift said she felt warmly welcomed when she began her 1989 World Tour in Louisiana and called the mass displacement of residents “heartbreaking.” The floods have killed at least 11 people, damaged about 40,000 homes, prompted more than 60,000 FEMA disaster-aid registrations, and required the rescue of over 30,000 people. Swift encouraged others to help and send support; the donation continues her history of charitable giving, which has included contributions to fans battling cancer and past disaster and hospital donations.

A 5-year-old Florida boy, Billy Nolin, dialed 911 from an old cellphone while his family prepared Thanksgiving dinner and invited deputies over to eat cheesecake. Walton County dispatchers, amused and pleased by the sweet call, sent Deputy Dannon Byrd and Deputy Aaron Ethridge to the home. Instead of scolding Billy, they thanked him, reminded him that 911 is for emergencies, gave him a sheriff’s badge, let him sit in a patrol car and activate the lights and siren, and asked about his future — he said he wants to be a police officer. The deputies’ visit was posted on the sheriff’s office Facebook page, went viral, and drew praise for the officers’ kindness and professionalism.

Key findings
- Southern states—especially Mississippi and Alabama—are the most religious in the U.S.; New England states (New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Vermont, Maine) rank among the least religious.
- By the study’s measure, 77% of residents in Alabama and Mississippi are “highly religious”; about one-third of residents in the four New England states qualify as highly religious.
- Christianity is the dominant religion nationally (70% of adults), with 25% evangelical, 21% Catholic, 15% mainline Protestant and 6% other Protestant. States with higher shares of evangelicals tend to be more religious overall.
- The religiously unaffiliated is the fastest-growing affiliation and grew in every state except one.

How “highly religious” was defined
- A person is “highly religious” if they report at least two of these four highly observant behaviors (or three with one low): attending religious services at least weekly, praying at least daily, believing in God with absolute certainty, and saying religion is very important in their life. People reporting low observance on any measure (seldom/never attending or praying, not believing in God, or saying religion is not important) are excluded unless other criteria are met.

Measures used and data sources
- Four measures: worship attendance, prayer frequency, belief in God, and self-reported importance of religion.
- Rankings and trends are drawn from the Pew Research Center’s 2014 Religious Landscape Study (surveying more than 35,000 adults) and compared to a 2007 survey; 24/7 Wall St. reviewed and ranked states using Pew data and supplemental demographic info from the American Community Survey.
- Caution: differences between states may not always be statistically significant due to survey margins of error.

Bottom line
- There are substantial regional differences in religiosity across the U.S., with the South substantially more religious by these measures than New England.

Canadian freestyle skier Sarah Burke, 28, suffered serious head injuries while training in the Eagle Superpipe in Park City, Utah. After a routine trick near the bottom of the pipe, she landed on her feet but fell and hit her head. Treated by ski patrol, she was airlifted to the University of Utah hospital and placed in a medically induced coma on a ventilator; she remained in critical condition. Family, including husband Rory Bushfield, flew to be with her.

Burke was a leading figure in superpipe skiing—four-time Winter X Games superpipe gold medallist, world and World Cup champion—and a major advocate for the sport’s inclusion in the 2014 Olympic program. She was also active in grassroots coaching. Doctors said inducing coma and cooling are standard care for serious brain injury; details of her injuries were not disclosed.

The incident renewed concerns about the inherent dangers of superpipe training. The Park City superpipe, with walls about 22 feet high, has produced other severe injuries, notably snowboarder Kevin Pearce’s 2009 crash. Observers noted such accidents have driven greater helmet use and safety awareness, though officials maintained the sport’s level of risk is acceptable. Organizers described Burke’s maneuver as routine, not an extreme move.

This long document combines three related threads about Chernobyl and Fukushima: a photographer’s human-focused book, Ukraine’s plans to repurpose contaminated land for solar power, and a detailed 30-year retrospective of the Chernobyl disaster and its long-term consequences.

Key points:

1. Michael Forster Rothbart’s Would You Stay?
- Forster Rothbart spent years documenting life in communities affected by Chernobyl and Fukushima. His work counters sensationalist portrayals, showing how many residents adapt and live with a new normal while acknowledging real suffering: cancer, economic decline, and emotional limbo.
- Around Chernobyl, authorities set concentric zones after 1986; the Exclusion Zone is effectively off-limits though a few hundred “self-settlers” live there and various informal activities (smuggling, farming, tourism) occur. Thousands more live in outer zones.
- Fukushima evacuees live in uncertainty in temporary housing, waiting to learn whether they can return.
- The insidious, probabilistic nature of radiation—unseen and long-term—complicates people’s perceptions of risk and recovery.

2. Ukraine’s solar revival of the exclusion zone
- Ukraine proposes using parts of the contaminated exclusion zone for solar power: cheap land, existing high-voltage transmission lines, and trained power-plant personnel make it attractive.
- The government has sought international investors; expressions of interest reportedly came from U.S. and Canadian firms. An initial 4 MW pilot and plans to leverage up to 4 GW of existing transmission capacity have been proposed; developers aim for 1 GW of solar nationally (cost ~€1 billion) and 11% renewables by 2020.
- The European Bank for Reconstruction & Development has been approached but any financing depends on viable proposals and environmental safeguards.
- Belarus is also building PV near the contaminated border area (22.3 MW plant in Brahin district), showing regional interest in using marginal land for solar.

3. Thirty years since Chernobyl — personal memory and ongoing hazards
- A long retrospective recounts April 26, 1986: the failed safety test, design flaws that caused a runaway reaction in Reactor 4, the explosion and release of radioactive material across much of Europe, and chaotic early responses.
- Eyewitness accounts (e.g., Alexandr Sirota) illustrate the human side: evacuation presented as temporary, abandoned homes and childhoods, long-term hospitalizations, and contested casualty statistics (official lower counts vs. much higher estimates by some researchers).
- Post-accident reforms: Chernobyl exposed systemic safety-culture failures in Soviet nuclear operations and catalyzed global changes in nuclear safety and transparency.
- The exclusion zone today is an eerie, overgrown “modern Pompeii” where wildlife has rebounded, tourists visit, some people return or live nearby out of attachment or poverty, and local economies are constrained. Residents commonly live with Geiger counters and avoid certain local foods, though many still consume local game and mushrooms.
- The technical and financial challenge of dealing with the reactor’s remaining radioactive mass is profound. The hastily built sarcophagus will be replaced by a new shelter intended to last ~100 years, but the waste will remain hazardous for millennia; experts warn containment and stewardship over centuries or millennia is an unresolved problem. Ukraine’s economic strains, political instability, and limited resources complicate long-term solutions.
- Debates continue about shrinking exclusion boundaries for political or PR reasons versus scientific caution.

Overall synthesis:
The pieces together show a complex picture: radiation disasters produce long-lasting, multi-dimensional problems—human, environmental, technical, political and economic. Photojournalism humanizes survivors and everyday adaptation; policy initiatives seek to convert unusable contaminated land into renewable-energy assets (solar) that leverage existing infrastructure; but technical cleanup, safety, and stewardship remain unresolved and costly challenges whose solutions will span generations.

Stephen Fry sparked widespread criticism after comments in an Attitude magazine interview — later quoted in The Observer — suggested that women do not enjoy casual sex the way men do and that “the only reason women will have sex with [men] is that sex is the price they are willing to pay for a relationship.” The remarks prompted an outcry on Twitter and social media, where Fry, who has nearly two million followers, protested he had been misquoted and posted “I give up” and “Bye bye.” 

Fry’s remarks — in which he contrasted straight and gay sexual behavior and invoked cruising and cottaging to argue women generally don’t seek casual encounters — were denounced by feminists and commentators as misguided and offensive. Prominent critics including Germaine Greer and Rosie Boycott called the assertions wrong and reductive; Attitude’s editor said Fry was merely musing rather than passing moral judgment. The episode reignited debate over male commentators speaking about female sexuality and about how Fry’s comments were reported and interpreted.

Summary:

Pentagon investigators are reviewing hundreds of e-mails between Marine Gen. John R. Allen, the top NATO commander in Afghanistan, and Tampa socialite Jill Kelley after the FBI, probing anonymous threatening messages sent to Kelley, turned over the correspondence on Nov. 11. About 15 investigators working full time have identified 60–70 e-mails that warrant close scrutiny to determine whether they violate Defense Department policy, government regulations or military law (possible issues cited include misconduct, improper use of government property and security breaches). Officials say there is no current evidence of security violations. The probe has delayed — and could imperil — Allen’s nomination as NATO supreme allied commander in Europe; it is unlikely to conclude before year’s end.

The e-mails span roughly two-and-a-half years beginning in 2010, when Allen was deputy commander of U.S. Central Command in Tampa. Accounts conflict over their tone: some law enforcement sources describe a few as sexually explicit or “flirtatious” and Pentagon briefings call several embarrassing, while Allen’s associates insist they are innocuous. Allen, who is in Kabul and has denied adultery through associates, is cooperating; interviews with him or Kelley have not been reported.

Kelley, who became prominent in the media after the scandal surrounding Gen. David Petraeus and Paula Broadwell emerged (Broadwell sent the threatening messages and later confessed to an affair with Petraeus), has hired attorney Abbe Lowell. Lowell has released materials defending Kelley, demanded to know why her name and her husband’s were leaked during the FBI probe, and sent letters disputing public comments by a businessman and a Tampa lawyer who criticized Kelley’s conduct and competence. Kelley lost an honorary consul post for South Korea amid the controversy. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Tampa has not commented publicly on Lowell’s letters.

Fairfax County police are seeking a woman who allegedly posed as a Target employee and stole more than $40,000 worth of iPhones from the store at 6600 Richmond Highway in Alexandria, Virginia. On March 15 she gained access to the stockroom, placed multiple iPhones into a box, then left—getting into a Volvo station wagon—as shown on surveillance footage released by police. Investigators say she was familiar with Target procedures, employee hours and the location of the phones in the stockroom but is not an employee. Anyone with information is asked to call Fairfax County police at 703-691-2131.

Apple debuted its iPad commercial during the 2010 Academy Awards telecast, generating immediate buzz on Twitter and tech blogs. The ad follows Apple's familiar creative style and doesn’t reveal new features beyond what had already been shown, but it raises speculation that more announcements could come before the iPad’s April 3 release. Apple CEO Steve Jobs was spotted on the Oscars red carpet—likely linked to his Disney board membership and Pixar’s involvement in the night’s winning film—which helped draw attention to the spot. The article invites readers’ reactions and notes where to follow the author.

This collection of reports chronicles voting-day problems and scenes across parts of the Northeast and elsewhere on Election Day 2012, especially in areas hit by Superstorm Sandy, and also includes broader Election Day color from battleground and local contests.

Main points — New York and New Jersey (Sandy-affected areas)
- Officials in New York and New Jersey took emergency steps—shuttle buses, consolidated polling sites, and an executive order from Gov. Andrew Cuomo allowing storm victims to vote outside their districts—to try to prevent disenfranchisement after Sandy.
- Despite those measures, many polling sites experienced confusion, long lines, poor lighting and heating, missing equipment, and organizational breakdowns:
  - Rockaway Park: several precincts consolidated into a tent on a school playground; poll workers found no generators, heaters or lights, creating chaotic conditions.
  - Hoboken: combined polling location opened late, staff struggled to access voting machines, signs directing voters by district were missing, and paper ballot contingency plans worried voters.
  - Midtown Manhattan: some sites ran out of affidavit ballot envelopes; some ballots were submitted without envelopes and thus would not count.
  - Staten Island, Midland Beach and other neighborhoods: dark, unheated tents where poll workers handed out ballots by flashlight.
  - Coney Island and other neighborhoods: closed schools with signs redirecting voters to distant locations, causing many to give up.
- Some sites worked smoothly: Teterboro served displaced Moonachie residents with shuttles and no waits. But many displaced voters faced difficulties accessing information, receiving absentee or electronic ballots, or verifying their ballots would be counted—creating anxiety about being able to vote.
- Personal anecdotes show the human impact: displaced residents driving in from other counties, seniors relying on police calls about new locations, and voters resorting to Facebook or county clerks for ballot information.

Other Election Day coverage
- National context: President Obama won re-election in 2012. The piece notes his second-term challenges—stubborn unemployment, a fragile recovery and the impending “fiscal cliff”—and emphasizes the likely continued political gridlock with a Republican House and Democratic Senate. Obama’s victory speech stressed bipartisanship on jobs, deficit reduction, tax reform and immigration.
- Massachusetts: Heavy turnout in closely contested presidential and Senate races produced long lines in many precincts; state officials expected possibly record turnout. Local vignettes include voters split-ticket voting and reactions from candidates like Scott Brown and Elizabeth Warren.
- Florida (Miami-Dade): mixed conditions—some precincts with long, multi-hour lines due in part to a long ballot and space limitations, while other sites (e.g., South Beach) had short waits.
- Miscellaneous anecdotes: Vice President Joe Biden voted in Delaware and made a playful comment about possibly running again; local moods and individual motives for voting are highlighted across locales.

Overall takeaway
Emergency measures helped some displaced voters, but storm-related disruptions and logistical failures left many polling places chaotic, poorly equipped and confusing, particularly in the hardest-hit New York and New Jersey neighborhoods. Elsewhere, high turnout and long ballots produced extended waits, while the broader political scene was dominated by Obama’s re-election and the challenges his second term would face.

Sen. John McCain, appearing on CBS' The Early Show, urged caution about premature Republican victory claims in next week's elections, noting Democrats' strong get-out-the-vote efforts and saying Senate control may hinge on late returns from California and Washington. He expressed concern about the large, often opaque campaign spending enabled by the Citizens United decision, including union and corporate money, and called the current level of outside spending troubling. On expiring Bush-era tax cuts, McCain advocated temporarily extending all cuts for a couple of years rather than immediately raising taxes on the wealthy, arguing the greater problem is federal spending. He praised former running mate Sarah Palin as an "outstanding candidate" for 2012 in principle but declined to endorse her or name a favorite, saying it's too early and Palin herself would not want an endorsement before deciding to run.

The Supreme Court heard Gill v. Whitford, a high-stakes challenge to Wisconsin’s 2011 legislative map that Democrats say is an extreme partisan gerrymander. A three-judge federal panel struck the plan down last year, finding it packed and cracked Democratic voters so that Republicans secured large Assembly majorities despite roughly even statewide vote totals. If the Court affirms that decision it could force new rules for how states draw both congressional and legislative districts nationwide.

Justices were sharply divided. Liberals (Ginsburg, Kagan, Sotomayor, Breyer) expressed alarm about maps that “preordain” outcomes and signaled willingness to let courts police extreme partisan gerrymanders using social‑science tools. Breyer sketched a multi-factor, manageable test (one‑party control, persistent partisan asymmetry, extreme outlier status). Kagan and Sotomayor argued that modern data and computer methods make neutral, scientific evaluation feasible.

Conservatives (Roberts, Alito, Gorsuch, others) were skeptical that courts can craft workable, administrable standards and warned of institutional harm and partisan perceptions if the Court intervenes. Roberts repeatedly cautioned that adopting contested metrics would invite waves of litigation and could damage the Court’s legitimacy; Alito and Gorsuch questioned the readiness and reliability of the social‑science measures, like the “efficiency gap.” Several justices also probed whether the plaintiffs even have standing to challenge statewide maps rather than individual districts.

Justice Anthony Kennedy — historically the pivotal vote on gerrymandering — asked probing questions of the defense, pressed whether a state law could mandate maps that maximize one party’s advantage, and remained silent during the challengers’ lawyer’s argument, suggesting he may be receptive to intervention if a workable standard exists.

The case turns on two linked questions: whether federal courts can and should adjudicate partisan‑gerrymandering claims, and if so, what judicially manageable standard should be applied. The Court’s decision, expected by next summer, could reshape redistricting practices nationwide or leave map‑drawing largely to state political actors.

During the Rio 2016 Olympics the world paused for a moment that came to symbolize the Games’ core values of sportsmanship and humanity. In a 5,000m heat New Zealand’s Nikki Hamblin and the United States’ Abbey D’Agostino collided and fell. D’Agostino helped Hamblin to her feet, despite having injured herself—later diagnosed as a ruptured ACL—and the pair finished the race together, embracing at the line. Their act of selflessness captured global attention.

In recognition, the International Olympic Committee awarded both athletes the Pierre de Coubertin medal, given rarely for exemplary Olympic spirit. The International Fair Play Committee (with IOC support) also honored them at Rio alongside the Norwegian men’s handball team, which declined to protest a disputed, late goal that had cost them Olympic qualification, citing sportsmanship. IOC and Fair Play officials praised these gestures as reminders that the Games are about excellence, friendship and respect as much as medals and records.

Eric Hites, a 40-year-old man from Danville, Indiana who once weighed around 567–600 pounds, set out in June to pedal a bicycle across the United States to lose weight, rebuild his life and win back his estranged wife. He began in Falmouth, Massachusetts with a small bike and a trailer carrying roughly 300 pounds of gear. Within two weeks he’d ridden about 55–90 miles and reported losing around 60 pounds, but his progress was stalled when his rims warped under his weight in Tiverton, Rhode Island.

Hites’ journey began as a personal challenge—motivated by health, self-respect and a promise to his wife inspired by the song “500 Miles”—and quickly grew into a public story after he blogged and posted updates on Facebook under “Fat Guy Across America.” Struggling with inadequate equipment, limited funds and loneliness on the road, he relied on sleeping in tents, hostels or the kindness of strangers. Word of his attempt spread; local businesses and community members rallied to help. Newport Bicycle donated a sturdier bike built to withstand his weight, the Tiverton Police Department provided supplies, donations to his GoFundMe increased, and other offers followed. Personal trainers and fitness groups have shown interest in tying his ride to broader campaigns encouraging exercise.

Hites continues to take the trip day by day while receiving medical care, working with a trainer and undergoing hormone therapy at home when needed. He plans to document the trip with blog posts and videos, interview people along the way, and eventually write a book. What began as a mission to save his marriage and health has become a larger, inspirational story for others facing similar struggles.

The NFL said the Kansas City Chiefs were wrong to penalize safety Husain Abdullah for unsportsmanlike conduct after he dropped to his knees in prayer following a 39-yard interception return for a touchdown against the New England Patriots. Although the rulebook bans celebrations while on the ground, league spokesman Michael Signora clarified that players who go to the ground as part of religious expression should not be flagged. Officials had thrown a 15-yard flag late in the fourth quarter, drawing criticism and comparisons to other players’ on-field prayers. Abdullah, a devout Muslim who previously took a year off to make the Hajj, said he believed the flag was for his slide into the end zone rather than the prayer itself; Chiefs coach Andy Reid relayed the same explanation from game officials and defended Abdullah. The Council on American-Islamic Relations urged the NFL to clarify its policy to avoid any appearance of a double standard.

Amanda Knox, who rose to international notoriety after being accused, convicted, and later acquitted (then reconvicted on appeal) in the 2007 murder of her roommate Meredith Kercher in Italy, has returned to writing in Seattle. For several months she has worked as a freelance reporter for the small West Seattle Herald. The paper’s Web Editor Patrick Robinson says they recruited her to help her reclaim a normal life and because she showed strong writing and photography skills, not to exploit her celebrity. Knox initially wrote under a pen name but later used her real name; she covers local human-interest pieces, community events and theater reviews—examples include a preview of a West Seattle High School production of Tom Stoppard’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead that she wrote for the paper. Robinson acknowledged caution about publicity her hiring might attract but said the paper treats her privately and focuses on her work, noting that extradition and the ongoing legal appeals in Italy do not affect her role there. The article also mentions Knox’s 2012 book deal and that a film based on related reporting has been produced.

Oxford Dictionaries made history in 2015 by naming an emoji — the “Face With Tears of Joy” (Laughing/LOL emoji) — its Word of the Year, the first time the annual pick was not a traditional word. Oxford University Press teamed with SwiftKey to analyze emoji usage and found that the laughing-crying emoji was the most used in the U.S., U.K. and worldwide, accounting for nearly 20% of emoji use in the U.S. and U.K. Oxford said the choice reflects how pictographic, visually driven communication has become central to digital life, conveying tone and emotion across languages. The publisher did not add emoji entries to its dictionaries, though the word “emoji” has appeared in Oxford resources since 2013.

The emoji won out over a shortlist of 2015 candidates intended to reflect that year’s cultural concerns: ad blocker; Brexit; Dark Web; lumbersexual; on fleek; refugee; sharing economy; and singular they. Oxford’s selection panel—lexicographers and staff—chose the emoji as emblematic of the year’s mood and communication trends. Observers noted the emoji’s persistent popularity on platforms such as Emojipedia throughout 2015.
