Amazon’s 2014 shareholder letter from CEO Jeff Bezos highlights several employee programs at the company’s fulfillment centers. Two programs received particular attention:

- Pay to Quit: Borrowed from Zappos, this annual offer gives eligible full‑time fulfillment-center associates a cash incentive to resign if they’re unhappy—$2,000 in the first year, increasing by $1,000 each year up to $5,000 in the fourth year. The program’s stated goal is to encourage employees to consider whether they truly want to stay; Amazon says only a small percentage accept the offer.

- Career Choice: A tuition-assistance program that pre-pays 95% of tuition for hourly employees who take courses in in-demand fields (e.g., airplane maintenance, nursing), even if the training isn’t relevant to an Amazon career. Bezos frames both programs as enabling employee choice—some workers will build careers at Amazon, others will use it as a stepping stone.

The letter situates these initiatives among many other Amazon efforts described in detail—Prime, Prime Instant Video, Fire TV, Amazon Web Services, Fulfillment by Amazon, Audible, Amazon Fresh, app and game initiatives, hiring veterans, virtual contact centers, urban campus development, packaging improvements, and internal experimentation—illustrating Amazon’s broad product, service, and operational innovations. The letter emphasizes long-term, customer-focused investment, a culture of invention, and a willingness to iterate and fail as part of growth. The piece also notes that Amazon received substantial local and state incentives for Tennessee distribution facilities.

A Minnesota probate judge sharply narrowed the field of potential heirs to Prince’s estate, excluding about 29 claimants and ordering DNA testing for six people who claim close family ties. Carver County Judge Kevin Eide’s order accepts that Prince’s sister Tyka Nelson and five half-siblings or close relatives are the primary potential heirs and directs genetic testing for Tyka plus three half-siblings who claim the same father (Sharon, Norrine and John Nelson) and for two women who say they are Prince’s niece and grand-niece. Two other half-brothers who share Prince’s mother (Alfred Jackson and Omar Baker) were not required to submit tests.

The judge dismissed a wide range of more speculative claims, including five people who asserted Prince was their biological or adoptive father, several who alleged different parentage for Prince, a woman who claimed a secret “top secret” marriage to him, and distant relatives asserting descent from a great-grandfather’s sister. The court found no credible evidence of a surviving spouse and noted that, if Prince left no will or children, Minnesota law would distribute the estate equally among siblings and the descendants of any deceased siblings. Bremer Trust, the special administrator, is assessing the estate’s value, variously estimated in reports at hundreds of millions of dollars.

Egypt plunged deeper into political crisis on Dec. 5 as clashes erupted around the presidential palace in Cairo between supporters of Islamist President Mohamed Mursi and opposition protesters angry over a contested new constitution and a presidential decree that granted Mursi sweeping powers and insulated his decisions from judicial review.

The Muslim Brotherhood called for a demonstration at the palace after opponents had staged a large sit-in there. Clashes that began Wednesday continued into Thursday with stones and petrol bombs hurled, tents torn down, makeshift roadblocks set up by residents, fires in nearby streets and reports of gunshot wounds. Medical sources reported dozens wounded in the first day of violence and later reports put the toll much higher; rival groups also accused each other of brutal assaults. Riot police were unable to stop the fighting, which spread to other cities and saw Brotherhood offices attacked in Ismailia and Suez.

Vice President Mahmoud Mekky, speaking from the palace, urged calm and offered a potential compromise: negotiate amendments to disputed articles of the draft constitution with opposition representatives, record them in writing and submit the changes to the next parliament after a planned Dec. 15 referendum. The opposition coalition — including liberals, leftists, Christians and former regime figures — said it would only enter meaningful dialogue if Mursi rescinded his Nov. 22 decree and postponed the referendum; opposition coordinator Mohamed ElBaradei warned the polarization could lead to greater violence.

Mursi has shown no sign of reversing course, banking on Islamist electoral strengths and state institutions’ general backing (with the judiciary a partial exception). International actors, including U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and Britain’s foreign minister, called for restraint and urgent, inclusive dialogue. Meanwhile, economic concerns persisted: markets rallied on hopes of stability even as Egypt pursued an IMF loan to shore up dwindling foreign reserves.

Analysts warned that a durable solution would require quiet negotiation rather than street confrontation, as mass opposition lacks a robust grassroots base to overturn the Brotherhood’s electoral dominance.

Steve Silverman argues that Tiger Woods’ decline from elite dominance to poor form is now undeniable. Citing Woods’ opening 80 at the U.S. Open at Chambers Bay and his disastrous Memorial third round earlier in the month, Silverman says even hopeful supporters must concede Woods is no longer capable of returning to his peak. He compares Woods’ current play to ordinary weekend golfers and notes a 15-year-old amateur outscored him in the U.S. Open first round.

The column traces the downturn to the 2008 personal scandal and subsequent injuries, noting that although Woods had a strong 2013 season (five wins), he hasn’t won a major since and his career total remains at 14. Silverman contrasts Woods’ fall with other all-time greats who faded more gradually and contends that, at 39, Woods should still be capable of good years but hasn’t shown the consistency or form to add majors. The piece closes bluntly: after recent performances, the author — echoing a friend’s candid assessment — concludes “Tiger, you stink.”

The article also reports the facts from Chambers Bay: Woods missed the U.S. Open cut with rounds of 80-76 (16 over), a rare missed cut in majors for him, and will next play the Greenbrier Classic before the Open at St. Andrews. Masters champion Jordan Spieth led the tournament at 5-under after two rounds.

A federal judge in Mississippi on May 15, 2017 sentenced Joshua Vallum to 49 years in prison (plus a $20,000 fine) after he pleaded guilty to killing 17-year-old Mercedes Williamson in 2015. The case was the first federal prosecution under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act involving a victim targeted because of gender identity.

Prosecutors said Vallum, a member of the Almighty Latin Kings, lured Williamson into a car, drove her from Alabama to his family home in Mississippi, shocked her with a stun gun, stabbed her, and fatally bludgeoned her with a hammer after a friend told him Williamson was transgender. Prosecutors said Vallum killed her to avoid gang reprisals, citing gang rules forbidding homosexual activity. Vallum had previously pleaded guilty in state court and received life without parole.

At sentencing, Judge Louis Guirola Jr. accepted a plea agreement recommendation for a lesser federal term than the life sentence he could have imposed, citing Vallum’s abusive, neglected childhood detailed in a sealed submission from public defenders. Vallum apologized in court. The case drew national attention from LGBT advocates and comment from then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions; advocates noted the prosecution began under the Obama administration and expressed concern about the Trump administration’s stance on transgender protections.

This editorial argues that Donald Trump’s relationship to truth is unprecedented and dangerous for American democracy. While lying has long been part of politics, the piece says Trump’s deep disregard for factual reality — whether from genuine inability to distinguish truth from falsehood or as a deliberate tactic — corrodes institutions and public discourse. He amplifies conspiracies, racist memes and fringe claims, weaponizes anger and insecurity in his audience, and substitutes “alternative facts” for verifiable evidence. That approach undermines science, law, journalism and the norms that make shared truth possible.

Beyond falsehoods, the editorial warns that Trump’s unpredictability, narcissism and contempt for governing norms compound the harm. His policy moves (on health care, environmental regulation, immigration, the Pentagon budget and education) threaten vulnerable people and the planet, but his temperament and methods make even conventional conservative policies riskier. The piece singles out three particularly troubling traits: his disrespect for institutions and the rule of law, his systematic disregard for truth, and his willingness to traffic in conspiracy theories and racist, out-of-mainstream ideas.

The editors urge active civic resistance: investigators, journalists, courts, legislators, voters and protestors must defend facts, uphold institutions, and hold leaders accountable. While the republic has survived past crises, protecting democracy now requires citizens and officials to oppose reckless policies and defend verifiable truth. This editorial is the first in a series examining these dangers.

Students and teachers returned to Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Fla., for the first time since a former student’s Feb. 14 attack killed 17 people. The school emphasized emotional readiness over academics—students were asked not to bring backpacks—and heavy security was in place, with about 50 armed officers and a police-guided arrival. Memorials of flowers and photos lined the campus; students described nervousness, grief and a desire to resume routine and support one another.

In the aftermath, student activists such as David Hogg have pushed for stronger gun laws, including an assault-weapons ban. National and local fallout included Dick’s Sporting Goods announcing it would stop selling assault-style rifles and raise its minimum gun-purchase age to 21. In Tallahassee, lawmakers heard emotional testimony as they considered measures to raise the long-gun purchase age from 18 to 21 and to allow specially trained, deputized teachers to carry concealed weapons—an idea opposed by the district superintendent.

A massive 30-mile ice jam on the Yukon River caused severe flooding in Galena, Alaska, forcing most of the roughly 500 residents to evacuate. The jam began flooding Galena Sunday and by midweek had lifted homes off foundations, submerged vehicles, inundated the sewage lagoon, cut power, water and cell service, and threatened a dike protecting the airport—the only remaining dry area. No injuries or deaths were reported, but nearly every home suffered damage and spilled fuel was visible on the floodwaters.

By Wednesday aerial surveys showed chunks breaking off the front of the jam, signaling it would soon move and water would begin to recede in Galena. Officials warned that when the jam breaks the resulting surge will travel downriver and likely flood the community of Koyukuk (about 14–30 miles downstream), which was preparing by moving people, securing supplies and standing flood watch.

Evacuations were carried out by the Alaska National Guard and state troopers; one flight moved 32 people and 19 dogs to Fairbanks. Governor Sean Parnell visited Galena and state officials were considering a disaster declaration to unlock aid. Emergency teams on site requested bottled water and MREs for those remaining. Authorities cautioned conditions could change quickly as the ice dam weakens.

Stephanie Smith, owner of Bubba Likes Tortillas and a self-described large-scale cannabis real estate developer, has sued the city of San Bernardino seeking to overturn a newly adopted municipal ordinance regulating commercial cannabis. The suit, filed in San Bernardino County Superior Court, argues the ordinance unlawfully bars property owners, tenants and others with past cannabis involvement from entering the legally regulated market, creates license monopolies, and violates due process by disqualifying people without hearings or convictions.

Background: In December police raided three warehouses Smith owns after discovering a fortified, multi-level grow operation. Authorities seized tens of thousands of plants (reports vary between about 25,000 and 35,000) and detained several people; Smith was not arrested or charged. Some of the tenant operations had applied for city licenses and reportedly received approval letters after the raids, raising Smith’s concern that the new law would retroactively render them ineligible.

Key legal and policy claims in the lawsuit:
- The ordinance can permanently bar anyone alleged to have violated local or state cannabis laws—or failed to report cannabis income—from getting commercial cannabis permits, even absent convictions or administrative hearings, violating due process.
- By allowing only 17 commercial businesses while California recognizes 19 types of cannabis licenses (cultivation, transport, testing, retail, etc.), the law could concentrate rights and create de facto monopolies.
- The ordinance departs from trends in other cities that prioritize legacy medical operators or adopt social equity measures to integrate prior operators into the legal market.

Context: The dispute follows a judge’s tentative and later final rulings invalidating parts of Measure O (a 2016 voter initiative that had guided local cannabis permitting) for spot zoning, a temporary moratorium on some cannabis activities, and ongoing litigation and regulatory flux in San Bernardino. The city attorney acknowledged receiving the lawsuit but had no immediate comment.

At a Florida GOP dinner, Congressman Allen West delivered a combative speech attacking Democrats — including President Obama, Harry Reid, Nancy Pelosi and Debbie Wasserman-Schultz — and vowed to fight what he called messages of “equality of achievement” and economic dependency. He urged Floridians to reject Democratic policies, pledged to do everything he could to stop Obama from “destroying” the country, and challenged Democrats to try to unseat him in November.

Separately, West faces a serious threat from within his own party over Florida’s redistricting. Reports say preliminary legislative maps significantly weaken his district, and sources quoted suggest a deal among Republican leaders — including House Speaker Will Weatherford, Senate President Mike Haridopolos and Senator Don Gaetz — to push the maps through with minimal changes. Critics argue the map could have been drawn differently to protect West while complying with legal requirements; a SaveAllenWest site was launched but may be too late. Updates note that Weatherford denied targeting West and West has told media the submitted maps could have preserved his district, a claim echoed in a January 30 interview with Mark Levin. Democratic SuperPACs were also reported to be targeting Tea Party incumbents.

The Buffalo Bills have hired Kathryn Smith as their quality control-special teams coach, making her the first full-time female assistant coach in NFL history. Smith, who will report to special teams coordinator Danny Crossman, has worked on Rex Ryan’s staff for seven years (most recently as administrative assistant to the head coach) and spent 12 seasons with the New York Jets in roles from gameday intern to assistant to the head coach. Ryan praised her knowledge and commitment and said she has earned the promotion; he consulted Bruce Arians, who earlier employed a woman in a temporary coaching role, in making the move. The hire follows other milestone steps for women in pro football—Jen Welter’s temporary NFL coaching role in 2015 and Sarah Thomas becoming the league’s first full-time female referee—and adds to similar advances across other major U.S. sports leagues.

Richland County Senior Deputy Ben Fields, a seven-year veteran school resource officer at Spring Valley High School in Columbia, S.C., was fired after cellphone videos showed him forcefully removing a Black female student from an algebra classroom. The footage, which went viral, appears to show Fields wrap his forearm around the seated student’s neck, flip her and her desk onto the floor, toss her toward the front of the room, handcuff her, and drag her away. A second student who objected was also arrested. Both were charged with disturbing schools and released to their parents.

Sheriff Leon Lott, who had initially suspended Fields, said an internal review concluded Fields’ use of force was “unacceptable” and violated training and procedures for dealing with non‑threatening, seated subjects; as a result Fields was terminated. Lott asked the FBI to assist and the U.S. Department of Justice opened a civil‑rights probe; possible criminal charges remain under investigation. Civil rights groups praised the firing. Fields’ attorney said Fields believed his actions were justified and lawful; Fields expressed regret that the incident occurred but the sheriff said he did not show remorse.

The student’s attorney says she sustained neck, back and arm injuries. School officials said they will review policies on using police for discipline and strengthen training for school resource officers. The incident has intensified debate over police roles in schools and questions about racial bias, though local officials have not confirmed race as a factor. Fields has faced prior complaints and lawsuits alleging excessive force or bias, some of which he has prevailed against.

Following President Obama’s announcement that U.S. forces killed Osama bin Laden in Pakistan, political leaders and public figures across the U.S. expressed widespread approval, gratitude, and relief while cautioning that the broader fight against terrorism continues.

Key points:
- Former Presidents George W. Bush and Bill Clinton both congratulated President Obama, the national security team, and U.S. military and intelligence personnel for the operation, calling it a momentous achievement and justice for 9/11 victims.
- Congressional leaders from both parties—Senators Harry Reid, Charles Schumer, John McCain; House leaders John Boehner, Nancy Pelosi; and others—praised the mission, honored the service members and intelligence community, and said the strike delivered important justice and closure while emphasizing vigilance against remaining terrorist threats.
- Republican officials and candidates (Mitt Romney, Sarah Palin, Reince Priebus, Tim Pawlenty) lauded the success as a victory for freedom and justice and thanked the armed forces and intelligence personnel.
- Families of 9/11 victims’ representatives and Democratic Party leaders (Debbie Wasserman Schultz) said the killing brings comfort and a measure of closure, thanking those involved and noting the campaign against al-Qaida must continue.
- Overall tone: unified national gratitude and a sense of vindication tempered by reminders that al-Qaida and other threats persist and continued vigilance is necessary.

Hours before New Year’s Day, someone scaled the Santa Monica Mountains and draped white and black tarps over the last two O’s of the Hollywood sign to spell “Hollyweed,” echoing a famous 1976 stunt. The tarps included peace and heart symbols and possibly referenced California’s marijuana legalization, but no suspect has been identified or arrested; police say the act was trespassing. Workers removed the coverings by mid-morning with no lasting damage.

The Hollywood Sign Trust, which maintains the landmark, said the incident revealed security gaps and announced it will deploy additional surveillance technology to deter trespassing and protect public safety. The sign has been monitored by a camera system since 1994 and updated periodically; Trust chairman Chris Baumgart said officials will analyze weak points and upgrade them. Observers noted the prank’s skillful execution and compared it to prior sign alterations by Daniel Finegood, who famously changed the sign to “Hollyweed” in 1976. The perpetrator’s identity and motive remain unknown.

Kerry O'Grady, a senior Secret Service special agent who heads the agency’s Denver district, came under scrutiny after Facebook posts—first reported by the Washington Examiner—in which she endorsed Hillary Clinton during the 2016 campaign and wrote she would “take jail time over a bullet” rather than protect what she called a “disaster” for the country (clearly referring to Donald Trump). The posts, which also included Women’s March imagery and anti‑Trump commentary, acknowledged the Hatch Act’s restrictions on partisan political activity by many federal employees. O'Grady deleted several of the posts after they drew complaints and media attention; she has said she removed them after reflection and repeatedly told the Examiner that she would not shirk her protective duties despite her political views.

The Secret Service confirmed it was aware of the postings and said it was “taking quick and appropriate action,” declining to comment on personnel specifics. The Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general’s office reportedly received a complaint in October. The episode prompted criticism on social media, with calls for her dismissal, and raised questions about Secret Service policies and social‑media guidance for agents as well as the application of the Hatch Act to uniformed protectors. O'Grady released a statement defending her service and expressing belief in free expression and dissent while reiterating her devotion to the agency’s mission.

JPMorgan Chase posted strong results for 2012 despite a multibillion-dollar trading loss tied to the “London Whale” derivatives bets. The bank reported a record fourth-quarter profit of $5.7 billion (up 53% year-over-year) and full-year earnings of $21.3 billion on roughly flat revenue (~$97–100 billion). Strength came from lending and deposit growth, a surge in mortgage activity (large increases in originations and mortgage fees), investment banking fee gains, rising asset-management income, and reduced loan-loss reserves.

However, the year was marred by a $6.2 billion loss through Q3 from the troubled Chief Investment Office trades; the bank said losses in Q4 were “modest” and Dimon said the firm was “getting near the end of it.” In response, JPMorgan’s board cut CEO Jamie Dimon’s pay roughly in half — from about $23 million in 2011 to $11.5 million for 2012 — keeping salary at $1.5 million and reducing his bonus to $10 million in restricted stock, and delayed his ability to sell roughly $79 million in stock for 18 months. The board said Dimon bears ultimate responsibility but also praised his response and cited the bank’s strong performance.

Internal and board investigations faulted oversight failures. The reports criticized Dimon for over-reliance on senior managers but placed primary blame on Ina Drew, who led the investment unit and resigned, and on other senior risk and financial officers for weaknesses in execution, oversight and controls. Regulators (the Fed and OCC) issued enforcement actions requiring improvements to risk management and cited failures in assessing and communicating potential losses.

JPMorgan continues to face legal and regulatory challenges: it agreed to an $8.5 billion settlement with federal regulators related to foreclosure reviews, spent roughly $700 million related to that review in the quarter, and faces other suits including a New York AG case over Bear Stearns-era securities. The bank has reshaped some management roles, pursued clawbacks and settled internal claims with certain former employees.

Operationally, JPMorgan saw growth across commercial and corporate lines, loan growth for the tenth consecutive quarter in commercial banking, and a notable rebound in mortgage banking (Q4 profit of $418 million vs. a loss a year earlier). Rising deposits (average $404 billion, up 10%) are pressuring margins, which narrowed to about 2.44% from 2.76% year-over-year. The bank plans to slow buybacks to build capital under Basel III and will seek regulatory approval for future repurchases.

Overall: strong underlying financial performance and record profits, offset by significant risk-management failures tied to the London Whale trades, resulting in pay penalties, leadership changes, regulatory sanctions and ongoing legal exposure.

A Savannah-based film crew shooting the Gregg Allman biopic Midnight Rider was struck Thursday by a CSX freight train on a railroad trestle over the Altamaha River in Wayne County, Ga., killing 27-year-old crew member Sarah Elizabeth Jones of Atlanta and injuring seven others, one seriously. The crew, from Meddin Studios and working with Open Road Films on the Allman adaptation, had permission from Rayonier to be on its property adjacent to the tracks but did not have CSX permission to be on the trestle, investigators said. Authorities said it was not yet clear whether crew members were on the trestle or tracks at the river’s edge, whether they were waiting for a train or were caught unaware, or exactly how debris and equipment contributed to injuries; a mattress was among items found on the rails. Georgia trespass laws make unauthorized presence on tracks a misdemeanor. CSX and Rayonier are cooperating with Wayne County investigators; the sheriff’s office treated the scene as a potential homicide until the probe clarifies circumstances. The production and studio expressed devastation; Open Road says it still plans a U.S. release though no date is set. The investigation is ongoing.

Johnny Cash’s boyhood home in Dyess, Arkansas, has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Background and listing
- The five-room farmhouse, built in 1934 as part of the Dyess Resettlement Colony by the Federal Emergency Relief Administration (FERA), was nominated in December and formally added to the Register in May 2018.
- The Arkansas Historic Preservation Program announced the listing; Arkansas State University (ASU) owns the house and led restoration efforts.

Why it was relisted
- The original nomination emphasized the house’s architecture and listed the property under Cash’s parents’ names (“Farm No. 266, Ray and Carrie Cash Home (Johnny Cash Boyhood Home)”).
- A National Register historian returned the nomination in January, asking for stronger documentation of Dyess’s influence on Cash’s development as an artist. The nomination was revised and resubmitted in April under Criterion B (association with a significant person) and retitled “Farm No. 266, Johnny Cash Boyhood Home.”
- The historian noted that while National Register listings often focus on a person’s productive period, an exception can be made when a place had a profound impact on formative years or no other extant associated places remain; he concluded the Cash home met that standard.

Significance and restoration
- Johnny Cash lived in the house from age 3 through high school. Biographers, family members and Cash himself cited Dyess as formative to his music and character. The nomination links songs such as “Five Feet High and Rising” (about the 1937 flood) and “Pickin’ Time” to his Dyess experiences.
- ASU purchased, restored, furnished and landscaped the property for about $575,000; restoration was completed in 2014, a prerequisite for National Register eligibility in this case.
- Local preservation officials and ASU Heritage Sites staff said the listing recognizes the county’s and the house’s role in shaping one of America’s most influential songwriters.

Context
- The Dyess community was listed on the National Register in 1976, but the Cash house was outside the original nomination boundary and so was not included then.
- The Cash family moved to Dyess in 1935 as part of a federal resettlement program for displaced farmers; the house was one of the larger five-room standard-plan dwellings provided to colony families.

A 17-year-old daughter’s 911 call, played at a Riverside County preliminary hearing, revealed years of severe abuse and neglect allegedly inflicted by David and Louise Turpin on their 13 children, ages 2 to 29. In a high, quivering voice she begged a dispatcher to “help my sisters,” saying two younger sisters and a brother were chained to their beds. Officers who responded freed the three shackled children and arrested the parents, who have pleaded not guilty to charges including torture and child abuse and are each held on $12 million bail.

Court testimony and interviews described a home foul with human waste, signs of starvation (one adult child weighed 82 pounds), extreme isolation, and deprivation of normal childhood activities. The children were reportedly locked in rooms for routine punishment, beaten, denied toys and adequate food, allowed only one combined meal some days, and rarely allowed outside. The 17-year-old said she hadn’t bathed for about a year, spoke like a much younger child and had limited schooling. She told investigators she planned her escape for two years, climbed out a window, and — fearful and disoriented — used a piece of paper with her mother’s address to call 911. She also reported instances of sexual abuse by her father and severe physical abuse by her mother, including choking. Journal entries kept by the children may corroborate their accounts.

Lake Travis High School junior Macie Martinez is recovering with a sense of humor after being struck by lightning inside her Dripping Springs home on Memorial Day. The strike occurred as she opened the refrigerator; she screamed, was rushed to the hospital and doctors found a “fern” rash on her back — a common sign of lightning strikes. Macie’s legs were briefly paralyzed for about 45 minutes and she has sustained nerve damage to her arms and hands. She also experiences fatigue, numbness, occasional confusion and forgetfulness, and doctors are monitoring her liver and kidneys. Her family’s home suffered extensive damage to electronics, flooring and appliances, but Macie and her parents escaped serious physical loss. Despite the trauma, Macie has been posting lightheartedly on social media (joking “call me Sparky”) and her family uses humor to cope while she follows doctors’ orders to rest and finish final exams.

Barry Byron Mills, 70, the longtime leader of the white supremacist Aryan Brotherhood prison gang, was found dead July 8 in his single cell at the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado. He died a day after his 70th birthday; authorities say the death does not appear suspicious and an autopsy is pending. Mills had been serving multiple life-without-parole sentences for murders tied to his leadership of the gang.

A native of the San Francisco Bay Area, Mills joined the Aryan Brotherhood at San Quentin in the 1970s and built it from a small prison clique into a nationwide organization with especially strong roots in Northern California. He ran operations from behind bars — directing violent hits, ordering a Central Valley bank robbery and negotiating protection arrangements (including with mob figures such as John Gotti) via couriers and coded messages. His violent reputation included a brutal attempted decapitation while in custody and involvement in a string of killings and attempted murders that helped spark racial violence inside prisons.

In the early 2000s, a major federal RICO case targeted the Aryan Brotherhood; Mills was the lead defendant. He and co-defendants were convicted in 2006 on racketeering and murder charges based largely on testimony from a former member who took a plea deal. Jurors split 9–3 for the death penalty, so Mills instead received life in solitary confinement at ADX Florence, where he remained until his death. Supporters and associates remember him as widely feared and admired among inmates; his attorney has said there were aspects of Mills the jury never saw.

On Sept. 11, 2012, an attack on the U.S. diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya, killed U.S. Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. The consulate was assaulted with gunfire, rocket-propelled grenades and a grenade that set the building on fire; Stevens and others are reported to have died of smoke inhalation while attempting to reach safety. Two U.S. compounds in Benghazi were struck in separate waves, and witnesses and officials described a chaotic scene in which Libyans helped carry Stevens to the hospital and fought alongside Americans to repel the attackers.

U.S. officials, after initial reports linking the violence to protests over an anti‑Islam film posted online, increasingly described the Benghazi attack as a coordinated, planned assault by an armed group that may have used a protest—sparked elsewhere by the film Innocence of Muslims—as a diversion. A London think tank and U.S. sources suggested the attack may have been an organized jihadist operation seeking revenge for prior al‑Qaida losses. The FBI and other agencies deployed to investigate; U.S. surveillance drones were proposed to gather intelligence in eastern Libya, and about 50 U.S. Marines were sent to the region to bolster security.

The killings drew worldwide condemnation and immediate diplomatic reactions: President Obama ordered flags at half‑staff, vowed to bring the perpetrators to justice, and increased protections at U.S. posts globally. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Vice President Biden, congressional leaders and international bodies including the U.N. Security Council condemned the attacks and expressed condolences. Libya’s interim government apologized and pledged to help apprehend those responsible.

The incident intensified scrutiny of U.S. diplomatic security and became a flashpoint in U.S. politics. Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney sharply criticized the Obama administration’s handling of the Middle East unrest and an initial embassy statement that had criticized the film; Democrats rebuked Romney’s timing and tone. The episode highlighted Libya’s fragile post‑Gadhafi security environment and broader regional volatility following the film’s circulation and protests at U.S. missions in Egypt and elsewhere.

At the East Asia Summit in Phnom Penh, President Barack Obama confronted a region-wide standoff over competing claims in the South China Sea that again dominated talks intended to focus on economic cooperation. The maritime disputes pit China against five claimants (Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Taiwan) and have repeatedly frustrated ASEAN’s ability to reach consensus and pursue its broader integration goals.

Cambodia, an ally of China and summit host, sought to limit discussion of the disputes and attempted to present a post-summit statement that the issue would not be “internationalized.” The Philippines — backed by Vietnam and supported by the United States — vocally rejected that approach. Philippine President Benigno Aquino III publicly objected when Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen announced an apparent agreement to avoid the subject; diplomats said any single ASEAN objection blocks consensus, undermining Cambodia’s move. Tensions spilled into private meetings and the post-summit lobby, with Chinese and Philippine officials reiterating their opposing positions.

The U.S. maintained it takes no side on territorial claims but warned against the use of force or blocking access to the sea and urged early negotiation of a legally binding “code of conduct” to reduce the risk of clashes — a proposal supported by Japan and Australia but with uncertain prospects given China’s preference for bilateral talks. Senior Chinese officials expressed frustration that the disputes dominated the summit. Regional fear of escalation is real: past clashes have been deadly, and recent stand-offs — especially between China and the Philippines around features like Scarborough Shoal and the Spratlys — have heightened anxieties.

Beyond security, leaders also discussed trade initiatives: ministers from China, Japan and South Korea opened talks on a potential free-trade zone, negotiations for the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) advanced, and the U.S.-led Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) continued involving four ASEAN members. Obama emphasized the need to ease maritime tensions and establish “rules of the road” while stressing economic cooperation with China. The gathering underscored ASEAN’s precarious position between U.S. and Chinese influence and how the South China Sea row hampers the bloc’s unity and broader agenda.

The Dalai Lama, speaking at a conference in Malmö, Sweden, said Europe is "morally responsible" to help people who truly face life-threatening danger but argued that refugees should be received, helped and educated only temporarily and ultimately encouraged to return and rebuild their home countries. He stated "I think Europe belongs to the Europeans" and repeated a view he has expressed before that Western nations should not be transformed demographically by mass migration. His remarks came days after gains by the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats in the national election and amid local concerns in Sweden about crime linked by some to recent refugee flows. The exiled Tibetan leader—who fled China in 1959 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989—emphasized compassion for refugees while stressing that the long-term goal of aid should be reconstruction of their countries.

Zsa Zsa Gabor, the Hungarian-American socialite and actor who died at 99, was celebrated as one of Hollywood’s most chic and witty legends—an early example of a celebrity famous for being famous. Known for her sharp one-liners and flamboyant personal life (nine marriages, seven divorces and one annulment), Gabor was famed for quips about love, marriage, aging and manners. Notable quotes include: “I’m a great housekeeper. Every time I get a divorce, I keep the house,” “You can say I’m full of s—t — but don’t say I’m old,” “Husbands are like fires. They go out when unattended,” “Personally, I know nothing about sex because I have always been married,” and comments mocking a police officer after she was convicted of battery for slapping him. Over decades she repeatedly joked about love, marriage and fame, leaving behind a legacy defined by glamour, bravado and memorable wit.

Kathy and Brandon Gunn of Kalamazoo, Mich., finally opened a wedding gift nine years after their marriage that had come with a card reading “Do not open until your 1st disagreement.” The unopened plain white box, given by Kathy’s Great Aunt Alison at their wedding, sat on a closet shelf through many fights and moves because the couple feared using it would mean they’d failed. Over time, avoiding the “rescue” box pushed them to develop tolerance, compromise and patience, strengthening their marriage. When they did open it, the box contained wine glasses and personal notes: Brandon’s note included cash and instructions to buy flowers and a bottle of wine, while Kathy’s included cash and directions to get a bath ready and buy a favorite meal. Kathy says the real lesson was that the tools for a healthy marriage were within them all along.

President Trump surprised and angered allies and lawmakers by publicly urging that Russia be readmitted to the G-7 as he departed for the summit in Quebec. He argued Russia “should be in the meeting” so it can be at the negotiating table, noting the G-7 was the G-8 before Russia’s 2014 expulsion over the annexation of Crimea. The comment came amid tense talks with NATO allies over U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum and earlier public spats with French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.

The proposal drew bipartisan criticism in Washington. Senators including Chuck Schumer, John McCain, Ben Sasse and Jeff Flake condemned the idea, citing Russia’s annexation of Crimea, support for separatists in eastern Ukraine, election interference, and other malign actions. Some critics said inviting Russia back would reward aggression and undermine U.S. credibility with allies. The British government and many European diplomats also opposed reinstatement. Italy’s new prime minister Giuseppe Conte was an exception, publicly supporting the move.

Trump’s outreach to Russia deepens existing concerns about his approach to Moscow, even as his administration has taken punitive steps such as sanctions and diplomatic expulsions. The remarks were reportedly unplanned and further strained an already acrimonious G-7 meeting dominated by disputes over trade, tariffs and broader trans-Atlantic tensions.

A Los Angeles civil suit and new public allegations have added to the dozens of claims that Bill Cosby drugged and sexually assaulted women over several decades.

Judy Huth lawsuit and developments
- Judy Huth alleges Cosby sexually abused her at the Playboy Mansion in about 1974 when she was 15. Her attorney Marc Strecker filed a sworn declaration saying he has interviewed two witnesses who corroborate her account and has reviewed photographs of Huth with Cosby at the mansion. Strecker also submitted a psychologist’s declaration concluding there is a reasonable basis to believe Huth suffered childhood sexual abuse.
- Huth has gone public with the claim and appeared at a Dec. 5 news conference with attorney Gloria Allred. Los Angeles police are investigating her allegations.
- Cosby’s lawyer Martin Singer seeks dismissal, calling the suit extortion and noting Huth reportedly tried to sell her story to a tabloid a decade ago. Many of the accusations against Cosby are limited in court by statutes of limitations.

New 2008 allegation by Chloe Goins
- Chloe Goins told MailOnline she was drugged and sexually assaulted by Cosby at a Playboy Mansion party in 2008 when she was 18. She says she woke naked with Cosby pleasuring himself and licking her feet; she believes her drink had been spiked. Goins plans to give a statement to LAPD; her account is reportedly corroborated by the friend who attended the party with her.
- Because this allegation is from 2008, it is within California’s statute of limitations for criminal charges.

Context
- More than 20 women have publicly accused Cosby of drugging and/or sexually assaulting them over decades. Cosby has denied many accusations and largely remained publicly silent, aside from comments urging media neutrality; his wife has defended him.
- Hugh Hefner and Playboy have been asked to comment; Hefner issued a statement saying the allegations are saddening and he would not tolerate such behavior.

An eight-year-old Jack Russell named Knuckles became a minor YouTube celebrity after his owner posted a clip of him howling along to the Law & Order theme; the video drew thousands of views and spurred discovery of many similar clips. Dozens of videos show dogs of all sizes whining, whimpering and howling when the show’s distinctive, high-register theme plays. Animal experts say the reaction is likely involuntary: dogs (and cats) are often sensitive to high-pitched, staccato or high-decibel sounds—sirens or certain musical timbres can trigger howling—while lower, simple tones tend to calm them. Veterinary neurologist Susan Wagner and trainers note that the theme’s high notes, clarinets and quavering beat may irritate or stimulate dogs’ auditory nerves, producing the vocal response. Composer Mike Post said he was amused and surprised that dogs seem to “sing along.”

This document mixes two strands of historical and scientific reporting about death-related inventions and research.

1) Curious 19th-century death-related patents
- Inventors patented many devices addressing burial, embalming and preventing or simulating death. Examples:
  - William Hanlon’s “Beheading Block and Ax” was actually a stage illusion designed to simulate a realistic beheading without mirrors.
  - Leland M. Speers and Abraham Clark’s “Improvement in Combined Grave, Coffin and Monument” (1875) combined coffin, grave, and monument with viewable features so friends could look at the deceased and monitor someone suspected of being in a trance.
  - J.M. Spear’s 1891 “Corpse Eye Closer” was a metal device with teeth to hold corpses’ eyelids closed for a natural appearance.
  - Graham Hamrick (1888) proposed an elaborate embalming process involving many chemicals and a burning sulfur torch, claiming long-term preservation.
  - James W. Bowles (1876) designed coffin-shaped poison bottles to warn against accidental ingestion.
  - John H. Chambers proposed a sealed, upright casket system that excluded air and removed decomposition fluids, with disinfecting traps.
- Many 19th-century patents also included safety mechanisms to detect or rescue those accidentally buried alive (air shafts, means to make noise).

2) Modern forensic chemistry: the “smell of death” study
- A laboratory study analyzed volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from decomposition of 6 human and 26 animal tissue samples over six months, using thermal desorption–gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (TD-GC/MS). Researchers identified 452 distinct VOCs across many chemical classes (esters, sulphur and nitrogen compounds, ketones, alcohols, etc.).
- Key findings:
  - A set of eight VOCs (ethyl propionate, propyl propionate, propyl butyrate, ethyl pentanoate, pyridine, diethyl disulfide, methyl(methylthio)ethyl disulfide, and 3‑methylthio‑1‑propanol) distinguished human and pig remains from other species in this controlled lab setup.
  - Five esters (3‑methylbutyl pentanoate; 3‑methylbutyl 3‑methylbutyrate; 3‑methylbutyl 2‑methylbutyrate; butyl pentanoate; propyl hexanoate) separated humans from pigs in the study’s conditions.
  - Some sulphur- and nitrogen-containing compounds (e.g., 3‑methylthio‑1‑propanol, diethyl disulfide, pyridine) were frequent in human samples, though not universally present.
  - Commonly cited compounds like cadaverine and putrescine were not detected (likely due to low volatility or rapid bacterial transformations).
- Implications and limitations:
  - The ester-based “fruity” signature helps explain how cadaver dogs can discriminate human remains; the research could improve cadaver dog training or lead to electronic “noses.”
  - However, results are preliminary: experiments used tissue samples in glass jars (not whole bodies or field conditions), some samples were frozen before decomposition, and environmental variables (soil, temperature, burial, etc.) were not represented. Thus further field studies with whole bodies and dog trials are needed to confirm human-specific markers and develop practical detection aids.

Overall, the piece juxtaposes historical attempts to manage or dramatize death with current scientific efforts to characterize human-specific decomposition chemistry—showing both the long-standing human fascination with death and the modern potential to turn a “smell” into forensic tools.

The text appears to be mixed content from customer comments and holiday opening hours for a food business serving traditional English fare. Customers praise the restaurant’s down-to-earth, good English food, noting it’s been popular for years and many recommend the Sunday roast. The business shared its Christmas/New Year opening schedule: several days around Christmas and Boxing Day are closed (including Boxing Day, Dec 27–30, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day). On Jan 2 it reopens with normal hours (7:00am–2:30pm). Separate Xmas hours list Christmas Eve open 9am–1pm, and a note about Christmas Day bookings (text is cut off). A holiday greeting—“Merry Christmas Everyone & Happy New Year!”—is included.

Jessica Hayes, a 38-year-old high school theology teacher from Fort Wayne, Indiana, was consecrated as a virgin in a public ceremony at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, becoming the Fort Wayne–South Bend Diocese’s first consecrated virgin in 25 years. Hundreds attended the rite, in which Hayes symbolically “married” Jesus Christ — a rare Catholic vocation distinct from being a nun: consecrated virgins remain lay people living in the world but make a lifelong, public commitment of virginity to Christ and service to the Church.

Hayes said the decision followed years of prayer and discernment about how to live most joyfully and fully for God. She described practical preparations (including choosing an appropriately modest wedding dress) and noted she’ll continue to be addressed as Ms. Hayes at school. Hayes hopes her example will raise awareness of and inspire vocations among young women, explaining the vocation is for those who feel called to deepen their relationship with Jesus while remaining engaged in ordinary life and parish ministry. The story notes that consecrated virginity is uncommon — about 3,000 worldwide and some 200 in the United States.

LeBron James married longtime girlfriend Savannah Brinson in a private ceremony Saturday at the upscale Grand Del Mar Hotel in San Diego. About 200 guests attended the event, the centerpiece of a three-day celebration that will end with a Sunday brunch. The couple, together since high school and parents of two sons, became engaged on Jan. 1, 2012. Security was tight: guests were escorted under tents, umbrellas shielded arrivals from news helicopters, phones were reportedly not allowed, and several Heat figures — owner Micky Arison, coach Erik Spoelstra and teammates including Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh — were among those present. The wedding came less than three months after James and the Miami Heat won their second straight NBA championship; training camp opens next month. The report was based on anonymous sources and comments previously made by Brinson and James.

First Lady Melania Trump told ABC News in an interview filmed during her solo Africa trip that she has warned President Trump there are people in his administration he "can't trust," saying "you always need to watch your back" and that such internal distrust makes governing harder. Her comments follow an anonymous New York Times op-ed by a senior administration official claiming some officials work to frustrate parts of the president’s agenda; President Trump called the essay "gutless" and labeled it "TREASON?" on Twitter. Melania also said she has been personally bullied — calling herself "one of the most bullied people in the world" — and cited those experiences as a motivation for her Be Best initiative, which targets cyberbullying and online behavior to protect children including her son Barron. The full ABC News special "Being Melania — The First Lady" will air Oct. 12.

In 2002 professional criminal Octave Durham and an accomplice broke into the Van Gogh Museum and stole two small, never-before-sold van Gogh works: View of the Sea at Scheveningen (1882) and Congregation Leaving the Reformed Church in Nuenen (1882–84). Durham describes in a new documentary and press interviews how the raid took about 3 minutes 40 seconds: they broke in through a window, entered through a hole, grabbed the two smallest paintings nearest the entry point, stuffed them into a bag, and escaped by sliding down a rope. He says he picked the museum simply because he could, not out of an interest in art, and brags of having done other high‑profile crimes. In the fall he hit the ground so hard the seascape was chipped; he left a black cap behind. A security guard called police but was not allowed to use force.

Durham and his accomplice originally wanted to steal Sunflowers and The Potato Eaters but deemed them too well guarded or too large; they later sold the two stolen canvases to the Italian mafia after failed attempts to sell them in the Netherlands. Durham has long denied involvement but was convicted in 2005, sentenced to 3.5 years, and remains liable for substantial damages to the museum. The paintings were recovered from the Italian mafia last year, held as evidence in Italy, and have now been released for return to the Netherlands. The works are of inestimable value—van Gogh landscapes at auction can fetch roughly $10–70 million—because they had never been offered on the market.

CBS abruptly overhauled The Early Show, replacing long-time co-hosts Harry Smith and Maggie Rodriguez and weathercaster Dave Price with the program’s Saturday anchors and other familiar CBS faces. Beginning Jan. 3, Chris Wragge and Erica Hill (the Saturday co-anchor team) will move to the weekday show, Jeff Glor will become the regular news reader, and Marysol Castro (formerly of ABC’s Good Morning America weekend edition) will handle weather. CBS said Smith will remain with the network as a news reporter and serve as primary substitute on the CBS Evening News, Face the Nation and Sunday Morning; new roles for Rodriguez and Price are under discussion.

Executive producer David Friedman framed the change as a move to find the right energy and chemistry to boost the show’s long-struggling ratings—The Early Show has trailed NBC’s Today and ABC’s Good Morning America—though CBS News president Sean McManus said he doesn’t expect immediate ratings shifts. Critics called the sudden shake-up surprising and possibly desperate, but CBS emphasized most of the new weekday faces are already familiar to morning viewers.
