The document celebrates the Chicago Cubs’ run to the 2016 World Series title—their first since 1908—and notes the celebrity attention that accompanied the postseason at Wrigley Field (fans included Bill Murray, Pearl Jam’s Eddie Vedder, NBA players Dwyane Wade and Jimmy Butler, Blackhawks captains Duncan Keith, Brent Seabrook and Jonathan Toews, actors like Vince Vaughn and Nick Offerman, and public figures such as Hillary Clinton).

It then recounts the long‑running “Curse of the Billy Goat,” said to have been placed on the Cubs in 1945 by William Sianis after his pet goat Murphy was denied entry to Game 4 of the World Series. The alleged curse became part of Cubs lore as the team failed to win another World Series for 71 years (and did not even appear in the Fall Classic again until 2016). The article reviews notable incidents traditionally linked to the curse—such as a black cat in 1969, Leon Durham’s error in 1984, the 1989 bullpen collapses, the 1998 and 2007–08 postseason failures, and the infamous Steve Bartman incident in 2003—along with repeated, often eccentric attempts by fans and others to break the curse (bringing goats to Wrigley, electrocutions of the Bartman ball, stunts involving severed goat heads, rituals by priests, charity pilgrimages with goats, publicity campaigns, etc.).

It also mentions the “Ex‑Cubs Factor,” listing many former Cubs who later won World Series titles with other teams. Finally, the document describes the end of the supposed curse in 2016: the Cubs posted a franchise‑best 103–58 season, won the National League pennant (clinching on October 22, 2016—the 46th anniversary of Sianis’s death) by defeating the Los Angeles Dodgers, and then overcame a 3–1 series deficit to beat the Cleveland Indians in seven games, winning Game 7 in 10 innings and capturing the World Series championship 108 years after their previous title.

Syrian and Iraqi fronts of the Islamic State (IS) threat intensified in mid‑August 2014, prompting regional and international responses.

In northern Syria, activists and monitoring groups reported that IS fighters seized key towns near the Turkish border — including Akhtarin and Turkmanbareh in Aleppo province — after deadly clashes with other rebel factions. The captures, confirmed on social media by IS supporters and by the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, extended the group's territorial gains as it continued to establish a self‑styled caliphate across parts of Syria and Iraq.

Meanwhile in Iraq, France described the situation in the Kurdish region as "catastrophic" and announced it would begin supplying arms to Kurdish forces battling IS militants. The move, coordinated with Baghdad according to Paris, came as the U.S. also increased its role: U.S. intelligence reportedly began directly arming Kurdish fighters, and 130 U.S. troops were deployed temporarily to Irbil to help plan rescues of Yazidi civilians trapped on Sinjar Mountain. France also prepared a 20‑ton humanitarian shipment of medical supplies, tents and water treatment equipment to Irbil, and urged other EU members to assist persecuted minorities. The international concern followed IS’s rapid June offensive that overran large parts of northern and western Iraq — including Mosul — killing thousands and displacing over 1.5 million people.

Aimee Copeland, a 24-year-old graduate student from Georgia who developed necrotizing fasciitis after cutting her leg in a May 1 fall from a homemade zip line, has spoken for the first time since her hospitalization. Her father, Andy Copeland, announced on Facebook and on Aimee’s blog that Sunday, May 27, was "Aimee Day" because she had spoken. Aimee has already been through multiple amputations (her left leg, one foot and both hands), began breathing on her own the previous week, and was able to sit up in a chair the prior Thursday. The family says she is aware of the large number of blood donations and ongoing support but not of the national attention.

Beneath Yellowstone National Park lies a vast supervolcano capable of ejecting more than 1,000 cubic kilometers of material in a single supereruption—an event that would blanket large parts of North America with ash, disrupt infrastructure and climate, and create widespread humanitarian impacts. Yellowstone’s last supereruption was about 631,000 years ago; geologists have identified two other similar events in the past ~2 million years. Although the system has been largely quiet for tens of thousands of years and current monitoring shows no sign of imminent eruption, new research is changing assumptions about how quickly such a system can become explosive.

Key new findings
- Rapid pre-eruption timescales: Analyses of feldspar phenocrysts from the Lava Creek Tuff (the deposit of the most recent supereruption) by researchers including Hannah Shamloo and Christy Till indicate that critical changes in temperature and chemistry in the magma chamber occurred over decades rather than centuries or millennia. Outer crystal rims record a sudden heating and an influx of barium, consistent with fresh, hotter magma moving into the shallow reservoir shortly before the eruption.
- Magma injection as trigger: The trace-element and thermometry data suggest at least two injections of new magma into the chamber in the lead-up to the eruption. Barium enrichment implies material from a deeper reservoir mixed into the chamber, and modeling with MELTS supports these interpretations (though some volcanologists call for complementary experimental validation).
- Implications for warning time: If supereruptions can be primed in decades, the potential lead time for forecasting such an event may be far shorter than previously thought—heightening the importance of detailed monitoring and understanding of eruption triggers.

Hazard modeling and monitoring
- Ash dispersion modeling (USGS Ash3D) shows a supereruption would produce an “umbrella” ash cloud that expands in all directions, often overcoming prevailing winds and creating a bull’s-eye ash distribution centered on Yellowstone. Near the caldera, meters of ash are possible; midcontinent cities could receive centimeters; coastal cities millimeters. Even small ash accumulations can severely affect transportation, power systems, health, agriculture and buildings.
- Yellowstone is one of the best-monitored volcanic systems, with ground and satellite sensors tracking deformation and seismicity. Although past episodes (e.g., several inches of uplift over years) have shown the system breathes, USGS scientists say no current signals match the rapid magmatic injection scenario described by the new study.

Uncertainties and next steps
- The new work is preliminary and based on geochemical and modeling interpretations; further studies—including laboratory experiments, broader sampling, and integrated geophysical constraints—are needed to confirm timings, mechanisms, and how to translate crystal records into operational warning signs.
- Understanding whether similar rapid recharge and mixing events can trigger future supereruptions, and how they would appear in modern monitoring data, is now a high priority for volcanologists seeking usable early-warning frameworks.

Bottom line: Yellowstone’s supervolcano remains unlikely to erupt in the near term, but recent mineralogical evidence indicates that the processes that can lead to a supereruption may occur much faster than previously believed—over decades—emphasizing the need for continued monitoring and research to better detect and interpret precursory signals.

The document portrays life in Syria as the civil war, entering its second year, increasingly engulfs Damascus and fractures President Bashar al-Assad’s base. Once treated as a refuge from nationwide violence, Damascus is now feeling the realities of war: frequent checkpoints and searches, sudden road closures, kidnappings and suicide bombings, fuel and food shortages, and a curtailing of normal social life. Residents — government supporters and opponents alike — worry the capital could become another devastated city like Aleppo. Wealthier Syrians and business owners face damaged factories, supply-chain disruption, capital flight and sanctions that complicate payments and imports; many have fled abroad or are struggling to keep firms afloat, deepening economic strain and resentment toward the regime even if they fear instability if it falls.

The article also highlights growing tensions within the Alawite community, Assad’s primary pillar of support. Reports from the Alawite coastal region describe increasing unease: a shootout in the Assad clan’s hometown Qardaha, the arrest of a prominent Alawite dissident, and mounting grief as Alawite men die on the front lines. While there is no evidence of a mass defection to the opposition, activists and analysts say many Alawites resent being heavily recruited into security forces and militias (shabiha) and fear they are being used to protect the regime’s survival. That fear of sectarian reprisals and loss of status, combined with rising casualties and economic hardship, helps bind many Alawites to Assad for now but introduces worrying strains in his support base.

Separately, activists report deadly government airstrikes in the north and rebel sabotage of oil and gas pipelines; casualty estimates and damage are severe though some claims cannot be independently verified. Overall, the piece depicts a country where military conflict, economic collapse, social dislocation and sectarian anxieties are accelerating, undermining normal life and eroding the foundations that have sustained Assad’s rule.

The Medical Examiner released autopsy reports for Christina “Tina” Anderson, 44, and her 8-year-old son, Ethan, whose bodies were found last month at the Boulevard property of family friend James DiMaggio.

- Investigators say DiMaggio killed Christina and Ethan, kidnapped Christina’s 16-year-old daughter Hannah, then remotely set incendiary devices in his house and detached garage. FBI agents later rescued Hannah and fatally shot DiMaggio in Idaho on Aug. 10.
- Christina’s autopsy found blunt-force trauma to the head with at least 12 impact sites; a crowbar was found near her body. Her ankles were bound with a plastic cable tie, duct tape was wrapped around her neck and mouth, and she had abrasions, lacerations, and a fractured right arm. The report notes an incision on her neck that was likely inflicted postmortem. Her body and the family dog (which had been shot) were found in the garage; firefighters extinguished the garage fire on Aug. 4.
- Ethan’s body was recovered in the fully engulfed two-story house. He likely died from the fire, though skeletal fractures were present and trauma could not be ruled out as contributing. He was so badly burned he required DNA to confirm identity.
- Sheriff’s homicide officials declined to comment further on the autopsy reports or release additional investigative details.

Philadelphia — Two students were wounded by a handgun fired inside Delaware Valley Charter High School’s gymnasium in north Philadelphia on Friday afternoon. A girl (18) sustained a bicep wound and was treated and released; a 17-year-old boy was also hit and remained hospitalized in stable condition. Police say the gun discharged after a student pulled it out in the gym and that seven students were present; the incident was captured on surveillance video.

Investigators identified multiple youths connected to the episode. A 17-year-old surrendered Saturday and was charged with two counts of aggravated assault and related offenses. A 16-year-old was taken in for questioning but released without charges; police said another teenage boy initially detained was not involved. Authorities have been in contact with suspects’ parents and searched transit areas for the weapon without success.

The school, which serves about 600 students and is equipped with metal detectors and security, was placed on lockdown, cleared later that day, and officials said they are reviewing safety procedures. Police and school leaders called the shooting a breach of security and emphasized efforts to keep the school safe while the investigation continues.

Staff Sgt. Robert Bales, a 38-year-old career soldier from Lake Tapps, Washington, has been identified as the suspect in a March 11, 2012 nighttime attack in Kandahar’s Panjwai district that left 16 Afghan civilians dead, including nine children. He was flown to the U.S. and is being held at the military prison in Fort Leavenworth pending likely criminal charges that could include the death penalty. U.S. officials say Bales left his base, shot victims in multiple houses, attempted to burn some bodies, then returned and turned himself in; Afghan authorities and some villagers dispute details and have demanded he be tried in Afghanistan.

Background and service record
- Bales enlisted soon after 9/11 and served multiple combat tours in Iraq and Afghanistan as a member of the 3rd Stryker Brigade, 2nd Infantry Division. He was a trained sniper, highly decorated, and had been nominated for a Bronze Star. He sustained combat wounds, including loss of part of a foot, and reportedly suffered a prior mild traumatic brain injury.
- Colleagues have described him as an exemplary, mild-mannered soldier who “saved many a life,” though his attorney and others have suggested possible combat-related stress or PTSD as factors.

Personal life and problems
- Neighbors remembered Bales as a devoted husband and father who rarely discussed deployments. His wife, Karilyn, wrote on a blog about disappointment when he failed to be promoted to sergeant first class and about hopes to relocate closer to family.
- The family had financial difficulties: a foreclosed townhouse in Auburn, unpaid HOA fees, and a house recently listed for sale.

Legal troubles and health screenings
- Court records show several incidents: a 2002 misdemeanor assault charge involving a girlfriend that led to anger-management requirements; a 2005 reported DUI for which he was not charged; and a 2008 single-vehicle rollover/hit-and-run in which witnesses saw a bleeding man in military clothing running into woods; Bales said he fell asleep at the wheel, paid fines and restitution, and the case was dismissed.
- Military records indicate he passed behavioral health and sniper-related mental screenings; he received routine behavioral health clearances after 2008.

Reaction and legal process
- The killings provoked widespread outrage in Afghanistan, straining U.S.-Afghan relations, and prompted Afghan leaders and the Taliban to demand local prosecution and to suspend some talks. U.S. officials have promised a full investigation; military authorities indicated the case will be handled in U.S. military courts, though trial location had not been finalized and Afghan witnesses might be flown to testify.
- Bales is represented by civilian lawyer John Henry Browne and will also have military defense counsel. His legal team has said it will review medical and personnel records and investigate mitigating factors; family members have publicly supported him.

Context and debate
- The case has renewed debate about the causes of wartime atrocities, the potential roles of PTSD or brain injury, leadership and unit oversight, and the danger of stigmatizing veterans broadly. Veterans advocates caution against simplistic conclusions that equate combat stress with homicidal violence.

Chris Martin gave his first extended interview since announcing his and Gwyneth Paltrow’s “conscious uncoupling,” taking responsibility for problems that contributed to the end of their decade-long marriage. Speaking with BBC Radio 1’s Zane Lowe, the Coldplay frontman said he wouldn’t call the split a “breakdown” but a maturing realization: his inability to be fully vulnerable left him “a mess” and prevented him from enjoying his life and relationships. Martin said he won’t blame anyone else and is working on changing his issues, noting that if you don’t let love in you can’t give it back. 

He explained that those struggles informed Coldplay’s new album, Ghost Stories, which he described as an honest account of the challenges life brings (love, family, illness, etc.). Martin also discussed the theme of his single “Magic,” praised One Direction and Kanye West, and mentioned personal efforts to improve his physical and mental wellbeing (including boxing and training). The hour-long interview aired on Zane Lowe’s show as promotion for the band’s upcoming release and related publicity activities.

Most US recycling has relied on exporting sorted scrap—especially plastics—to China, which for years has been the country’s largest buyer. That dependence allowed U.S. municipalities and recycling companies to avoid investing in domestic sorting and processing capacity. Now China’s recent Operation Green Fence, a strict enforcement campaign rejecting contaminated or mixed waste imports, has abruptly reduced Chinese demand for many U.S. plastic bales. Inspectors are turning away shipments for small contamination (even a syringe) and refusing certain resin types (notably plastics labeled 3, 6 and 7, including items like coffee cup lids, some clamshells, PVC pipe and flexible planters).

The result: truckloads of mixed plastics are piling up at depots (for example in Oregon), orders have been canceled, and recyclers must now re-sort material by specific resin or find new buyers. Curbside staples such as milk jugs and PET bottles remain marketable, but low‑grade, mixed rigid plastics—lids, toys, pool pieces—are most affected. Building domestic sorting and recycling plants is possible but costly because mechanical and labor-intensive separation (or expensive optical sorters) will raise costs for cities and collectors. In short, China’s crackdown exposes the U.S. recycling system’s heavy reliance on foreign markets and reveals a coming headache for municipalities that assumed their waste would be recycled somewhere else.

Authorities in York County, South Carolina, have charged 52-year-old Lana Sue Clayton with murder and malicious tampering after investigators say she admitted poisoning her 64-year-old husband, Stephen Clayton, by putting tetrahydrozoline (an ingredient in common eye drops and some nasal sprays) into his water over a three-day period from July 19–21. Stephen Clayton was found dead at the couple’s Lake Wylie home on July 21; his autopsy and toxicology report detected a high level of the chemical. Arrest warrants and police statements did not provide a motive. Lana Clayton, who worked in nursing for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs in Charlotte, surrendered after confessing, and because she is charged with murder she is being held without bond. She has no prior criminal record in South Carolina, and it was not clear whether she had retained an attorney. The couple owned an expensive home and adjacent lot; legal proceedings concerning Stephen Clayton’s estate had already been opened with Lana Clayton named personal representative, and the impact of the arrest on those proceedings is uncertain. Community members expressed shock at the arrest. The case follows another recent spousal homicide arrest in York County; further details are pending.

Joshua (Josh) Vandiver and his husband Henry Velandia married Aug. 29, 2010, in Connecticut, but Velandia now faces deportation because the 1996 federal Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) bars a U.S. citizen in a same-sex marriage from sponsoring a foreign spouse for a green card. Velandia, a Venezuelan who emigrated in 2002, runs a salsa school (HotSalsaHot), teaches dance and appeared on Univision’s Mira Quien Baila; Vandiver is a Princeton political theory Ph.D. student (Harvard and Oxford alumnus). Velandia’s work-visa application was denied and his current visa has expired; he is scheduled to appear before an immigration judge in Newark, N.J., on Nov. 17, 2010.

The couple is campaigning for repeal of DOMA, asking Congress and the Department of Homeland Security to pause deportation hearings for foreign-born spouses of U.S. citizens while legal challenges proceed, and raising awareness via campus events and a “Save our Marriage – Stop the Deportation of Henry Velandia” Facebook page. Supporters note Velandia’s contributions to campus life; the couple says they would consider leaving the U.S. together if necessary but do not want to be forced to flee to remain together. Legal experts consider delaying deportation until the Supreme Court rules a long shot, though a lower court has recently struck down DOMA.

Rep. Darrell Issa intensified the congressional fight over the ATF “Fast and Furious” gun‑walking operation by directly accusing President Obama in a letter of either having aides who coordinated with Justice Department officials to manage the program’s fallout or of improperly invoking executive privilege to obstruct Congress. Issa’s charge, based on the White House’s assertion of privilege over DOJ communications, offered no new evidence but ratcheted up political pressure as the House prepares a likely party‑line vote to hold Attorney General Eric Holder in contempt for failing to produce subpoenaed documents.

The White House rejected Issa’s claims, saying its use of privilege follows long‑standing executive‑branch legal precedent. Democrats have pushed back politically, portraying the contempt effort as an attack with racial implications and an assault that could hamper Holder’s ability to defend voting rights. Civil‑rights leaders, including Al Sharpton, planned a press event warning holding Holder in contempt could undermine protections for black and Hispanic voters; House Democratic leaders tied the timing of the contempt push to the DOJ’s opposition to state voter‑ID laws.

The contempt motion passed Issa’s Oversight Committee along party lines and is expected to reach the full House, though bipartisan support appears limited despite Issa’s claim that some Democrats have concerns about the administration’s handling of Fast and Furious. If the House finds Holder in contempt it could refer the matter to DOJ, which observers expect is unlikely to prosecute, leaving the GOP‑led House to consider a court challenge. Calls for Holder’s resignation have come from some Republicans, while Democrats characterize the probe as politically motivated and potentially racialized.

Florida International University (FIU) has temporarily suspended its Pi Kappa Alpha (Pike) fraternity chapter and launched an investigation after an anonymous email circulated screenshots from a supposedly private Facebook group that became public. The screenshots—about 70 posts—allege drug sales (cocaine and Adderall), bragging about hazing prohibited by university policy, sexualized images (including one caption claiming a partner was 17), homophobic and misogynistic slurs, body-shaming, and pride in unsportsmanlike conduct. Phone numbers posted on the page matched contacts linked to the chapter. FIU instructed the chapter to halt all meetings and events, involved campus police, and said the anonymous tip prompted the probe. Pike International said it had not known of the group until recently and is cooperating with the temporary suspension.

The FIU chapter had prior disciplinary history (probation for serving alcohol to a pledge in June) and the national fraternity has a record of past offenses at other campuses, including underage drinking, vandalism, and more severe incidents—most notably a University of Tennessee case where a student was hospitalized after participating in an alcohol enema (“butt-chugging”), prompting a 30-day administrative suspension there. A psychologist specializing in hazing linked the FIU posts to broader cultural problems in Greek life and suggested universities sometimes overlook misconduct because fraternities aid recruitment, fundraising, and housing. The FIU case is part of a wider pattern of disciplinary actions against fraternities nationwide.

An experimental Phase I clinical trial in Rennes, France, has left one volunteer brain-dead and five others hospitalized after an oral investigational drug was given to about 90 volunteers. The trial, run at the Biotrial clinic for Portuguese manufacturer Bial, began dosing participants on 7 January; severe neurological symptoms appeared within days. Hospital neurologist Pierre‑Gilles Edan said one man is brain-dead, three others may have irreversible brain damage, a fifth has neurological problems, and a sixth is being monitored but is less critical.

The drug is described by French authorities as a FAAH inhibitor acting on the endocannabinoid system (linked to pain pathways); it does not contain cannabinoids or cannabis derivatives, the health ministry said. The trial has been suspended, all participants recalled, and the Paris prosecutor has opened an investigation. French Health Minister Marisol Touraine visited Rennes, stressed the state will investigate the “tragic accident,” and noted the study had regulatory approval and prior animal testing.

Phase I trials test safety in healthy volunteers and, while rare, serious adverse events can occur; regulators and the company say they are cooperating to determine the cause.

This document combines a medical definition and a human-interest news item.

- Definition: Placenta previa is a condition in which the placenta partially or completely covers the cervix (the lower uterus opening). Because the placenta supplies oxygen and nutrients to the fetus and normally attaches to the top or side of the uterus, a low-lying placenta can cause severe bleeding before or during delivery. Pregnant people with placenta previa are often limited in physical activity and commonly require delivery by cesarean section.

- News item: In Chongqing, China, a "miracle baby" girl born at just 23 weeks—after doctors performed an emergency operation to correct a cervical problem—has survived her first week. Doctors had warned the parents that the infant would be extremely premature with very low survival chances, yet she survived the surgery. Weighing about 660 grams and 28 cm long, she was immediately placed in an incubator and is receiving round-the-clock care. Medical staff note her organs and veins are underdeveloped, complicating medication and nutrition. Local media nicknamed her the "chopstick girl" because her length matches a chopstick.

Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics report evidence that a simple repair-initiating interjection—roughly “huh?”—occurs in strikingly similar form and function across unrelated languages, and argue it is effectively universal. Analyzing nearly 200 tokens from casual conversations in ten typologically diverse languages (e.g., Cha’palaa, Dutch, Icelandic, Lao, Mandarin, Murrinh‑Patha, Spanish, Russian, Siwu, Italian), the team found the interjection is consistently a monosyllable with an unrounded low-front/central vowel, optional glottal or h onset, and questioning intonation. Although each language’s variant is calibrated to its phonology and prosody (so it must be learned and behaves like a lexical item rather than an involuntary grunt), the cross-linguistic similarity is far narrower than expected by chance.

The authors reject an innate-cry account and instead propose convergent cultural evolution: conversational pressures surrounding other-initiated repair (quickly signaling that one didn’t hear or understand so the speaker will repeat or clarify) favor a minimal, easy-to-produce syllable that also carries interrogative prosody. This “conversation ecology” provides selective pressures that push independent languages toward similar forms while allowing language-specific phonological tuning. The paper argues this is a clear case where interactional infrastructure shapes linguistic form and suggests the same mechanism may explain cross-linguistic similarities in other discourse signals (e.g., continuers mm‑hm, hesitation uh/um, change-of-state oh/ah).

Olivia Munn publicly revealed she alerted 20th Century Fox that actor Steven Wilder Striegel—a friend of director Shane Black—was a registered sex offender, prompting the studio to remove his single scene from The Predator. Striegel pleaded guilty in 2010 to charges including enticing a 14-year-old and served six months in jail. Munn says she first told Fox and waited days for a response; she pressed them again, saying she wouldn’t present at the VMAs unless the scene was cut. Fox said it was unaware of Striegel’s history and cited legal limits on background checks.

At the Toronto International Film Festival, Munn described feeling isolated and unsupported by some colleagues and by Black, whose public apology she read online but says did not reach her privately. Several co-stars skipped or withdrew from press appearances with her; a few later issued supportive statements. Munn stressed she acted out of principle—particularly in the #MeToo era—and asserted she won’t give second chances to people who harm children or animals, even if others disagree. She continued promoting the film due to contractual obligations but said the episode has been lonely and disheartening and raised questions about accountability and vetting practices in Hollywood. The Predator opened mid-September 2018.

Oyster, a New York-based ebook subscription startup founded in 2012, is winding down its service and will retire the product over the coming months. The founders said in a blog post they plan to pursue new opportunities to advance their vision for ebooks, noting a belief that phones will be the primary global reading device over the next decade. Oyster will offer refunds to subscribers on request.

Google confirmed it has hired “a portion of the Oyster team” to work on Google Play Books; reports say CEO Eric Stromberg and two co-founders joined Google in an acqui‑hire deal that likely involved compensation to Oyster investors. Google declined to detail plans, and it’s unclear whether any of Oyster’s technology or business model will be folded into Google Play Books.

Oyster launched a subscription-only model in 2013 (Oyster Unlimited, $9.95/month) and later expanded in 2015 into an ebook retail store selling individual titles after raising about $17 million. The service had amassed over 1 million titles and secured deals with three of the five largest US publishers, but subscription ebooks struggled to supplant traditional sales—readers appear less inclined to “binge-read” compared with binge-watching or music streaming. Oyster’s app-based service did not support Amazon’s Kindle e-readers, limiting reach. Amazon’s competing Kindle Unlimited and the broader market dynamics likely contributed to the difficulty of scaling Oyster’s model.

Last week a tank leak at a Freedom Industries storage facility on the Elk River near Charleston, W.Va., released the coal-processing chemical 4‑methylcyclohexane methanol (MCHM) into the river, contaminating the public water supply and forcing a do-not-use order that affected roughly 300,000 people across multiple counties. Residents faced bottled-water shortages, closed schools and businesses, and long lines for emergency water. About 169 people sought medical attention for symptoms such as nausea; ten were briefly hospitalized.

State and federal teams, including the U.S. Chemical Safety Board and the U.S. attorney’s office, have opened investigations. Officials later reported encouraging test results—some readings at the treatment plant registered 0 parts per million—allowing zone-by-zone sampling and the start of phased lifting of the ban once consistent results meet the federal guidance level (≤1 ppm). West Virginia American Water plans to notify customers via an online map and autodialers.

The spill has renewed scrutiny of West Virginia’s regulatory practices. Freedom Industries’ storage site had not been inspected by state or federal agencies since 1991; state law requires inspections only for production, not storage, facilities. Critics and environmental groups say the state has a history of weak enforcement and close industry influence—especially from coal and chemical sectors—that has left workers and residents at risk. Previous regional incidents (including a fatal 2008 Bayer explosion and long‑criticized coal‑mine safety lapses) and a 2009 petition asking the EPA to assume parts of state Clean Water Act oversight were cited as part of a pattern.

State officials say they will review and possibly tighten oversight of chemical storage facilities during the legislative session. Freedom Industries was ordered by the state Department of Environmental Protection to relocate chemicals to a safer site and begin cleanup planning; the company has not faced criminal charges yet but is under investigation. Governor Earl Ray Tomblin and others emphasized the spill stemmed from a chemical storage operation rather than a coal company, though the chemical is used in coal processing.

Former IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn gave his first TV interview since his arrest in New York, describing his encounter with hotel maid Nafissatou Diallo as an “error” and a “moral failing” but insisting it involved no violence, coercion or aggression. He said he regretted losing the chance to run for France’s presidency, accepted that the liaison was inappropriate, and will not seek the Socialist nomination for 2012 while he “takes time to reflect.” Criminal charges in the Diallo case were dropped by New York prosecutors in August due to concerns about her credibility, but she still has a pending civil suit against him. Strauss-Kahn also denied violent intent in a separate 2003 allegation by writer Tristane Banon, calling her claim imaginary and suing for defamation; a French investigation is ongoing. He said he felt afraid and humiliated by the U.S. justice system and declined to negotiate over the civil case. The interview was broadly composed and apologetic in tone, leaving open whether he will attempt a political comeback.

Starbucks is partnering with Danone to introduce Greek yogurt parfaits under the co‑brand “Evolution Fresh, Inspired by Dannon.” The yogurt will appear in U.S. company‑owned Starbucks cafes next year and be rolled out to grocery retailers in 2015, with international expansion possible later. Danone will manufacture and handle distribution; financial terms were not disclosed.

This move furthers CEO Howard Schultz’s strategy to expand Starbucks beyond cafes into packaged food and grocery channels—efforts that include past rollouts like packaged coffee, Tazo tea, Via instant, Keurig K‑cups, Evolution Fresh juices (acquired in 2011 for $30 million), and Teavana. Starbucks’ grocery and retail revenue grew rapidly (up 50% to $1.29 billion in the year to September), outpacing cafe sales.

The Greek‑yogurt market is fast growing: U.S. Greek‑style yogurt sales jumped 48% to $2.65 billion in a recent 52‑week period, amid heightened competition from established brands such as Chobani, Yoplait and Fage. Industry observers note the brand diversification is a strategic opportunity but risks diluting Starbucks’ core identity as it becomes a “house of brands.”

This document is a combined overview of Albert Mehrabian’s Baby Name Report Card and a New York Times–style article about modern baby-naming dynamics and family pressure.

Mehrabian’s Baby Name Report Card
- Purpose: Presents large-scale, decade-long survey research identifying which given names create positive or negative impressions and how those impressions can advantage or handicap people socially and professionally.
- Structure: Two main parts—guidelines and theory (preliminaries) and name evaluations. Preliminaries cover why names matter, what impressions they make, lifetime effects, how to change a name, common selection issues, general naming guidelines, and explanation of scoring.
- Measurement: Names are rated along key dimensions—Ethical-Caring (trustworthy, kind, responsible), Popular-Fun (playful, outgoing, attractive), Successful (ambitious, intelligent, confident), Masculine–Feminine, and Overall Attractiveness (a statistical composite of primary dimensions). Scores run 0–100 with 50 as average; examples illustrate wide differences (e.g., John scored 98 on Success, Knut 11).
- Content: Separate chapters list girls’ and boys’ names that connote each dimension or its opposite, plus alphabetical name lists. The work offers scientifically based guidance for parents choosing names and for adults considering name changes.
- References: Cites Mehrabian’s peer-reviewed studies and monographs on name connotations, uniqueness, nicknames, spelling, and name length effects.

NYT-style article excerpt on naming and family influence
- Theme: Contemporary parents often prioritize unique, personality-reflective names, sometimes hiring consultants or testing names against perceived future outcomes. This trend conflicts with older relatives who favor family names.
- Anecdotes: Several parents received material offers from elders to name a child after them—$10,000 for choosing a grandfather’s name, offers of family businesses or expensive weddings in exchange for using a relative’s name. Financial dependence or living arrangements can make parents feel pressured to acquiesce.
- Strategies: Parents use compromises—combining parts of family names, allowing relatives to choose middle or cultural names, using one official name while calling the child something else, or honoring other deceased relatives. Some decline offers to preserve their sole naming choice.
- Conclusion: Tension exists between honoring family traditions and parents’ desire for individuality; many pursue creative solutions to satisfy both family expectations and their own naming goals.

Overall takeaway: Names carry measurable social and psychological connotations that influence life outcomes. Modern parents balance scientific and aesthetic criteria, personal meaning, and family pressures—sometimes negotiating compromises or resisting financial incentives—to choose names they hope will benefit their children.

A controversial obituary for Cornelia June Rogers Miller, who died in February 2017, ran in the Cherokee Scout of Murphy, North Carolina and has gone viral. Unlike typical notices, it attacked Miller personally—calling drugs “a major love in her life,” saying she “made no contribution to society,” and stating “her presence will not be missed by many.” The item appeared nearly four months after her death; the family says it is false and hurtful. Miller’s son Robert blamed his sisters, though at least one sister denies writing it. A viewer noted portions resemble a 2008 Vallejo Times Herald obituary, raising plagiarism concerns. The paper’s publisher said the family’s submission overrode the editor and would not identify who sent it. Robert submitted a new obituary for publication and said he wants his mother remembered as loving and generous.

Researchers have renewed an old hypothesis linking sudden ship disappearances to massive releases of methane gas from the seafloor. Newly discovered giant craters off Norway (up to ~800 m wide and 45 m–150 ft deep) suggest explosive blowouts of methane hydrates—ice-like deposits that form under high pressure on continental margins—can release large gas bubbles that rise through the water column. Laboratory and modeling work (including a 2003 American Journal of Physics study) shows that a very large bubble erupting beneath a vessel can reduce local water density and buoyancy and, under certain positions relative to the bubble, could swamp and sink a ship.

Some scientists have proposed the same mechanism might explain a few high-profile vanishings attributed to the so-called Bermuda Triangle (the loosely defined area between Miami, Puerto Rico and Bermuda). Methane hydrates are known to exist along the U.S. North Atlantic margin (e.g., Blake Ridge), and similar gas-release processes have been invoked to explain enigmatic Siberian craters formed by permafrost gas explosions.

However, experts caution the idea remains speculative. There is no direct evidence that such large-scale methane eruptions have occurred in the Bermuda Triangle during the periods of reported vanishings, and many alleged Bermuda Triangle incidents have mundane explanations (lost navigation, storms, found wrecks, or human error). The U.S. Navy and other authorities do not recognize the Bermuda Triangle as a real, anomalous hazard, and statistical analyses show no excess of losses there compared with similar busy sea lanes. In short: methane blowouts could, in principle, sink ships and offer a plausible mechanism for some disappearances, but they do not solve the Bermuda Triangle myth and lack firm historical or observational confirmation.

After Hugh Hefner's fiancée Crystal Harris left him and moved out, twins and former girlfriends Karissa and Kristina Shannon have reportedly moved back into the Playboy Mansion. The sisters returned about a year and a half after previously leaving; reports say Karissa ended a relationship with Sam Jones III so she and her twin could move back in to support Hefner as he recovers from the breakup.

During the Senate Judiciary Committee’s extraordinary hearing for Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh — when Dr. Christine Blasey Ford testified about an alleged 1982 sexual assault — several Republican senators’ Wikipedia pages were edited to display private information (home addresses, phone numbers, emails). The changes targeted Judiciary Committee Republicans Lindsey Graham, Mike Lee and Orrin Hatch; most posted phone numbers were inaccurate or disconnected. A Twitter bot that tracks congressional Wikipedia edits flagged the changes, which were quickly removed.

On Wednesday night the U.S. Capitol Police arrested Jackson A. Cosko, 27, a former junior Senate Democratic staffer who had worked for Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) and previously for Sen. Barbara Boxer. A Hassan staffer encountered Cosko inside Hassan’s Capitol Hill office Tuesday evening and called police; he was taken into custody. Cosko had been interning in Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee’s office but was fired, and he is due in federal court.

Cosko faces multiple federal charges, including making public restricted personal information (doxing), threats in interstate communications, identity theft, witness tampering, and unauthorized access of a government computer, as well as District charges of second-degree burglary and unlawful entry. Police said edits were traced to a Capitol Hill IP address on the House side and that the investigation is ongoing; additional charges may follow. Offices of Hassan and others declined to comment while authorities investigate.

This document describes a parody campaign ad released on YouTube on October 28, 2011, in which Republican presidential hopeful Jon Huntsman’s three daughters spoofed Herman Cain’s well-known “smoking man” ad. In the short video — posted by “Jon2012Girls” — the daughters wear horn-rimmed glasses and fake mustaches and deliver deadpan lines promoting their father’s experience and record on the economy, including the tongue-in-cheek line “Even if we didn’t believe that, we’d still have to be here.” They close the parody by blowing soap bubbles in unison at the moment Cain’s aide is seen taking a drag in the original ad. The piece highlights Huntsman as the first Republican candidate to produce a direct parody of Cain’s ad.

Summary:

A robbery at the Kay Jewelers inside Rolling Oaks Mall on San Antonio’s northeast side on Sunday afternoon turned deadly. Two armed men robbed the store around 3:30 p.m.; as they fled they encountered citizens who tried to intervene. One “good Samaritan” was fatally shot by a suspect. A second citizen, legally carrying a concealed handgun, then shot and wounded one of the robbers. The other robber ran through the mall, firing as he fled and wounding additional people. Authorities reported a total of one dead and several injured — including the wounded robber, two people shot by the fleeing suspect, and two others taken to hospitals with non‑gunshot complaints (a woman with chest pains and a pregnant woman in labor). The mall was locked down and swept by police; both suspects were later reported in custody and face preliminary charges including capital murder and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Police continue investigating; names and many details have not been released. Local officials praised the coordinated response and urged calm.

Audi is rolling out an industry-first feature that tells drivers how long until a traffic light changes from red to green by linking cars wirelessly to city traffic-management systems. The countdown appears in the instrument cluster but stops a few seconds before the light changes to ensure drivers look up; if the car predicts the driver won’t clear the intersection before the light ends, it will continue counting as if the light were red. The system is available on 2017 Q7 SUVs and A4 sedans built after June 1 and will be launched city-by-city (Audi expects 5–7 cities by year-end but hasn’t named them). Audi positions the feature as a comfort and safety aid, with future possibilities like using stop-time data to shut the engine briefly or reroute; it also fits into broader vehicle-to-infrastructure work important for autonomous driving. The service is part of Audi’s paid Connect Prime package (about $199 for six months, roughly $25–$33/month), which supplies traffic, safety, entertainment services and cellular data.

This document contains two brief entertainment news items.

1) Miley Cyrus: At 17, Miley Cyrus is promoting her new album Can't Be Tamed and asserting creative and personal independence as she sheds her Disney persona Hannah Montana. Addressing criticism that her image and the title video are too provocative for her age, Cyrus says she isn’t trying to be “slutty” but wants her look to match her music and current maturity. Comfortable with her body and increasingly free to dress how she chooses, she emphasizes she wants fans to buy her music for its sound rather than sex appeal. Can't Be Tamed was set for release on Monday.

2) Heather Locklear: Media reports indicate Heather Locklear, hospitalized after an apparent overdose scare, is being moved from a psychiatric ward in a Southern California hospital into a longer-term facility for ongoing mental health and substance-abuse treatment. Sources cited by TMZ say doctors recommended more intensive, extended care than the hospital could provide.

West Virginia Gov. Jim Justice, elected as a Democrat, announced at a Huntington rally with President Donald Trump that he will change his party registration to Republican. The surprise move — which Justice said followed "lots of prayers and lots of thinking" — drew mixed reactions. Sen. Joe Manchin, the state's leading Democrat, expressed disappointment but vowed to remain a "proud West Virginia Democrat" and work across party lines. Many West Virginia Democrats felt betrayed, noting the Democratic Governors Association and unions had helped Justice’s 2016 campaign.

Commentators see the flip as confirmation of West Virginia’s rightward trend: Trump won the state handily in 2016 and remains popular there, especially for promises to restore coal jobs. Supporters say Justice’s switch aligns with local political sentiment and could draw more national attention and resources to state economic priorities; critics worry about its impact on Democrats’ standing, particularly Manchin’s 2018 reelection prospects.

Justice has prior ties to Republicans, including friendships and donations to GOP figures, and his move surprised many who had no prior notice. The announcement was made against a broader backdrop of West Virginia’s economic and public-health challenges — low incomes, declining population, high overdose rates and job losses in coal — factors that helped fuel Trump’s appeal. The White House praised the development as evidence of its policies’ benefits for the state, citing recent gains in mining and logging jobs and efforts on opioids.

The piece describes a baserunning blunder by Dodgers third baseman Juan Uribe during a 5-0 Los Angeles Dodgers win over the Tampa Bay Rays. After reaching third on a sacrifice fly with one out left in the fourth inning, Uribe briefly stepped off the bag while dusting himself—at which point the Rays quickly threw the ball to Evan Longoria, who tagged him out. Dodgers teammate Yasiel Puig responded by tweeting a joking Spanish caption and a photo demonstrating that a runner should keep a foot on the base to avoid being tagged out. (Video credit: Larry Brown Sports.)

The UN and Western officials warned of escalating violence and grave risks to civilians and children in Syria amid a collapsing ceasefire. The US State Department, citing fears the Syrian government might be preparing a new massacre in the Latakia town of Haffa, urged UN observers be allowed access; UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and joint envoy Kofi Annan expressed grave concern and said civilians appeared trapped in Homs and Haffa. UN observers and activists reported sustained heavy shelling, helicopter gunships, and fighting in Homs, Rastan, Talbisa, Idlib and other areas; a car bomb in Deir al-Zour reportedly killed 10. Damascus blames “foreign-backed terrorist gangs.” The US emphasized political and economic pressure rather than military intervention, while Russia proposed involving Iran in talks—an idea the US opposed.

A newly released UN report on children and armed conflict names Syrian government forces and allied shabiha militias among perpetrators who recruit, kill, maim, sexually abuse and use children as human shields. The report documents killings and torture of children (some as young as 8–9), forced use as shields, arbitrary detention and sexual violence, and eyewitness accounts of brutal treatment in detention. Syria is among several countries highlighted; the global report lists 52 parties responsible for grave violations against children in 2011 and details similar abuses in Somalia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Ivory Coast and elsewhere. The report also notes some progress: a few parties in Nepal, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, CAR, Chad and South Sudan have completed or begun programs to end child recruitment.

The Institute for College Access and Success (Project on Student Debt) reports that the Class of 2012 graduated with an average student loan balance of $29,400 — up from $26,600 for 2011 — and that 71% of 2011–12 bachelor’s degree recipients held debt. The increase is driven by rising tuition combined with stagnant family incomes since the recession, making students more likely to borrow and harder pressed to repay after graduation.

Key details:
- Nationwide averages: 71% of 2011–12 graduates had loans; average borrower debt $29,400. Excluding for‑profit colleges: 68% had debt, average $27,850. The College Board’s alternative estimate put those figures at 60% and $26,500.
- For‑profit colleges (about 6% of bachelor’s degrees) skew the numbers upward because their graduates borrow more and at higher rates; many for‑profit schools did not participate in the voluntary college survey used for some figures.
- State and college variations: Delaware had the highest average debt ($33,649); South Dakota had the highest share of graduates with debt (78%). The institute published a searchable college‑level database; some private colleges (e.g., Anna Maria College, Wheelock College) reported over 80% of graduates with loans and average borrower debt near $49,000.
- Loan types and servicing concerns: Most students use federal loans; about 20% hold private loans. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau announced it will regulate large loan servicers (such as Sallie Mae) after finding servicer practices often trip up borrowers seeking repayment changes. Private loans can be harder to enroll in alternative plans and servicers may apply payments in ways that increase fees or disadvantage borrowers.

Overall, rising tuition, weak family incomes and a difficult job market for new graduates are combining to push up student borrowing and leave many borrowers struggling to manage repayment.

A 45-year-old Islington artist, Robin Lee, was arrested on a London Overground train on 10 July after a police community support officer (PCSO) challenged him for plugging his iPhone into a train socket. The PCSO described the act as “abstracting electricity,” an offence under section 13 of the Theft Act 1968 that can carry up to five years’ custody. Lee was handcuffed, taken to the British Transport Police (BTP) station on Caledonian Road and later “de-arrested” for abstracting electricity. He was subsequently arrested for a second offence—“unacceptable behaviour”—after allegedly becoming aggressive while protesting his initial arrest. BTP said a decision on further action would be made in due course and that he has been reported for the unacceptable behaviour offence.

Overground sockets are clearly labelled “cleaners use only and not for public use”; forum commenters note these sockets are intended for depot cleaning equipment and can risk power surges if used by consumer devices. Lee called the arrest “overzealous” and “ridiculous,” posted then deleted photos and tweets about the incident, and the small amount of electricity involved was noted as trivial (charging an iPhone costs under £1 a year). Police will review the matter before potentially referring it to the Crown Prosecution Service. The story echoes other recent incidents of people attempting to charge phones in inappropriate places.

Police continue searching for University of Virginia sophomore Hannah Graham, 18, who was reported missing after last being seen late Friday night/early Saturday morning, September 13. Investigators released surveillance footage showing Graham on Charlottesville’s downtown mall around 1:06–1:08 a.m., followed by an unidentified white male who has been interviewed and says another man intervened. Police are now seeking a person of interest described as a Black male in his late 20s–early 30s, about 5'10"–5'11", 250–285 lbs, close-shaved head, goatee, slight “beer belly,” wearing black jeans and a white T‑shirt. He was seen with Graham in the 300–500 blocks of E. Main St. around 1:00–1:15 a.m.

Search teams have canvassed downtown, collected additional video where available, and extended the search east toward the Rivanna River and wooded areas; no items belonging to Graham have been recovered and her cellphone has not been located (it reportedly pinged only in the Wertland/14th/15th street area, not downtown). Authorities released the description and asked anyone with information or relevant surveillance footage to call the tip line at (434) 295-3851. A $50,000 reward has been offered. Community search efforts are being organized for the weekend of Sept. 20–21 (volunteers must register in advance); a candlelight vigil was planned for the UVA Amphitheater. Graham is described as about 5'11", slim, with blue eyes, light brown hair and freckles, last seen wearing a black crop top with mesh cutouts.

China’s President Xi Jinping met with about two dozen leading global tech executives at Microsoft’s Redmond campus during the U.S.-China Internet Industry Forum. Attendees included Apple’s Tim Cook, Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Facebook’s Mark Zuckerberg, Alibaba’s Jack Ma, IBM’s Ginni Rometty and many other U.S. and Chinese CEOs. Xi toured Microsoft facilities (including HoloLens demos), joined executives for a group photo and spoke for roughly six minutes about U.S.-China cooperation in cyberspace, stressing mutual respect, constructive dialogue on cybersecurity, and the complementary strengths of China’s large Internet market and the U.S.’s advanced Internet technologies.

Mark Zuckerberg highlighted a brief, personal moment during the meeting when he spoke with Xi in Mandarin, calling it a milestone; his post and the encounter sparked debate because Facebook is blocked in China and because of concerns about Western tech firms courting Beijing. The gathering—widely viewed as a symbolic display of Xi’s influence and the commercial importance of the Chinese market—was tightly choreographed and underscored tensions around issues like cybersecurity, censorship, and intellectual property even as both sides talked about cooperation.

The U.S. is retaliating against Russia by ordering the closure of Russia’s Consulate General in San Francisco and two annexes — a chancery annex in Washington, D.C., and a consular annex in New York — after Moscow forced a reduction in U.S. diplomatic staff in Russia earlier this year. The cuts required Washington to cut 755 personnel; Secretary of State Rex Tillerson had warned the U.S. would respond by September. The State Department says the move restores "parity" (each country will now have three consulates in the other country), while allowing Russia to keep some annexes to try to prevent further escalation. The closures must be completed by Sept. 2, and the U.S. says it is prepared to take further action if warranted.

Russian president Vladimir Putin and U.S. president Donald Trump met for the first time in person on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Hamburg, in a private, extended encounter that Putin can portray as a diplomatic win even if little substantive agreement emerged. The meeting—held with only each nation’s foreign minister and two translators present—minimized the chance of leaks and excluded more Russia‑skeptical U.S. aides, a format Kremlin and Western observers see as favorable to Putin.

Topics raised included allegations of Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election; U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson said Trump was focused on “how do we move forward” and reported agreement to set up a working group on non‑interference—an arrangement unlikely to assuage critics in Washington. Russian FM Sergey Lavrov later claimed Trump accepted Putin’s denials of meddling. A U.S.–Russia ceasefire in southwestern Syria was announced around the same time, exemplifying the kind of high‑level, bilateral diplomacy Putin prefers.

Trump’s preparedness and stance were under scrutiny amid ongoing investigations into possible Russia ties to his 2016 campaign and domestic concern over concessions such as returning seized Russian diplomatic properties. Before the meeting Trump had given mixed comments on U.S. intelligence assessments of election interference. Key U.S. priorities mentioned included stabilizing Syria, exploring joint mechanisms (no‑fly zones, ceasefire observers, humanitarian coordination), and coordinating on North Korea. Some U.S. lawmakers urged vigilance, warning that conciliatory moves could embolden Moscow.

Belinda Stuckey, a 35-year-old primary school teacher from Sydney, says she has gone on 136 first dates since joining eHarmony in December 2013 but never received—or offered—a second date. Despite claiming about 4,700 matches and roughly ten new matches a day, she says there has never been mutual attraction. Stuckey attributes her high interest to an honest profile and admits she only accepts about 20% of match invites. Though baffled at times and wondering what she might be doing wrong, she remains resilient and optimistic, saying she knows who she is, won’t lower her standards and will keep dating until she finds the right partner.

Warren Buffett used his annual Berkshire Hathaway shareholders’ letter to report strong 2010 results, reaffirm confidence in the U.S. economy, and signal he’s again hunting for large acquisitions to deploy the company’s growing cash hoard.

Key points:
- Berkshire’s 2010 net income was $13 billion (up ~61% vs. 2009) and book value rose 13%. Shares gained about 29% in 2010.
- Buffett emphasized his belief in America’s long-term economic potential and said Berkshire spent over $5 billion on U.S. property and equipment last year, with most future investment to remain domestic.
- The $26 billion 2009 acquisition of Burlington Northern Santa Fe (BNSF) was singled out as the highlight of 2010, boosting Berkshire’s earnings power by more than 30% and underscoring railroads’ economic and environmental advantages.
- Despite that recent megadeal, Berkshire again has a large cash balance (about $38 billion) and Buffett warned he’s ready for more major purchases: “Our elephant gun has been reloaded, and my trigger finger is itchy.”
- Buffett continues shifting toward buying whole companies rather than public stocks; non-insurance operating businesses now contribute a rising and important share of Berkshire’s earnings.
- He praised several executives (Ajit Jain, Todd Combs) but offered no definitive succession plan. He also criticized hedge-fund pay practices and consultant “style boxes.”
- Buffett discussed the Goldman Sachs preferred-share investment and noted Goldman can redeem those shares; he expects regulatory constraints to ease.
- Observers expect Berkshire to pursue opportunistic acquisitions—possibly a mix of large deals and smaller, privately held businesses—rather than any predetermined target.

Overall, the letter combined patriotic optimism, fiscal conservatism, praise for recent strategic moves (especially BNSF), and a clear signal that Buffett is actively seeking meaningful ways to deploy Berkshire’s capital.

Solar Impulse 2, a solar-powered airplane, completed a record-setting non-stop flight from Nagoya, Japan, to Hawaii on July 3–4, 2015, after nearly five days aloft. Piloted solo by Swiss aviator André Borschberg on the eighth leg of the aircraft’s round-the-world attempt, the 5,079–mile (about 4,000–5,100-mile / 8,200 km) crossing set the world record for longest solo flight by time and the longest solar-only flight by time and distance. Borschberg spent roughly 4 days, 21 hours and 51 minutes in the cramped cockpit, resting only in brief 20-minute naps, enduring extreme temperatures and repeatedly climbing and descending to manage limited solar/battery energy. The aircraft—covered with 17,000 photovoltaic cells and flown alternately by Borschberg and co‑pilot Bertrand Piccard—must climb high by day to recharge and glide slowly through the night to conserve power. The flight, delayed earlier by weather and diverted from China on a prior leg, was the riskiest so far because there was no safe diversion over the Pacific. After landing at Kalaeloa Airport on Oahu, the team prepared the next leg to Phoenix, Arizona. The mission aims both to demonstrate long-range solar aviation and to promote clean-technology solutions to climate change.

A shooting occurred Thursday morning, Sept. 20, 2018, at the Rite Aid distribution center on Perryman Road in Aberdeen/Perryman (Harford County), Maryland. Harford County deputies were dispatched at 9:06 a.m. and arrived in just over five minutes. Authorities say a single handgun was used, no law enforcement fired, and officials do not believe there is any further threat to the community.

Preliminary counts indicate multiple fatalities and multiple wounded (a law enforcement official and later the AP reported three killed; officials described fewer than 10 total victims). Several victims were transported to hospitals, including four trauma patients taken to Johns Hopkins Bayview and another to Christiana Hospital in Delaware. The suspected shooter — reported by sources to be a woman — was taken to a hospital and listed in critical condition; she was in custody. Victims were all adults and families were being notified.

Local, state and federal agencies responded, including the FBI, DEA, ATF, Maryland State Police and multiple municipal departments. Harford County activated a family reunification center at the Level Volunteer Fire Company in Havre de Grace and set up an information hotline (410-838-5800). Officials urged anyone still inside the building to call 911. Schools and motorists in the area were advised to avoid the scene while the investigation continued. Authorities stressed the investigation was in its early stages and cautioned that details were preliminary.

Kristine Bunch, convicted in 1996 of arson and felony murder for the 1995 fire that killed her 3-year-old son Tony, was released from an Indiana prison in March 2012 after the Indiana Court of Appeals granted her a new trial and a judge ordered her freed on bond. Bunch had been sentenced to 60 years and spent more than 16 years behind bars, giving birth to a second son in custody and seeing her older son, Trenton, only in prison visits. Her case was taken up by the Center on Wrongful Convictions at Northwestern and pro bono attorney Ron Safer, who, using advances in fire investigation science and reexamination of lab data, showed that the state’s evidence was flawed: tests the prosecution relied on were incorrect or altered and the child likely died of carbon monoxide poisoning rather than burns from an accelerant-fueled arson. Based on that new evidence, her conviction was reversed and prosecutors later declined to retry her.

Bunch’s release is presented as part of a broader initiative: Northwestern’s Women’s Project, launched by attorneys Karen Daniel and Judy Royal, to address wrongful convictions of women—many of which involve domestic deaths, flawed forensic science, and gendered stereotypes used to infer motive. Daniel and Royal found that women are underrepresented among exonerees in part because (1) their cases rarely involve DNA evidence that can conclusively exonerate, (2) many convictions of women involve alleged crimes that were actually accidents or natural deaths, and (3) prosecutors and juries often rely on sexist narratives about mothers and caregivers. As a result, overturning such convictions often requires expensive, technical challenges to forensic evidence (arson science, shaken-baby syndrome, etc.).

While incarcerated, Bunch engaged in ministry, converted to Catholicism, and earned degrees; after release she expressed gratitude rather than bitterness and ambitions to study law and help others wrongfully convicted. She is reconnecting with family and her teenage son, who looks forward to normal mother-son experiences. The article also highlights broader work and successes of the Center on Wrongful Convictions and its Women’s Project in identifying and litigating cases where flawed forensics and gender bias contributed to wrongful convictions.

Zimbabwe’s 93-year-old President Robert Mugabe has been seen repeatedly with his eyes closed at public events, prompting questions about his fitness to lead ahead of next year’s elections. His spokesman, George Charamba, says these episodes are not sleep but a reaction to light sensitivity and age-related eye problems; Mugabe is reportedly receiving specialised eye treatment in Singapore. Charamba compared Mugabe’s condition to Nelson Mandela’s light sensitivity and dismissed claims that the president is dozing off. Critics and observers remain concerned given Mugabe’s frequent appearances with closed eyes—images spanning more than a decade—and Zimbabwe’s deepening economic crisis, which has amplified scrutiny of Mugabe’s capacity to govern despite his insistence that Zimbabwe is not a fragile state.

This document compiles reporting and commentary from multiple outlets about the Hyperloop concept and competing companies racing to build it.

Key points:
- Hyperloop concept: Proposed by Elon Musk, it envisions passenger/cargo pods traveling in low-pressure tubes at near-supersonic speeds (up to ~700–760 mph) to cut trips like LA–San Francisco to ~30–35 minutes.
- Two main commercial efforts: Hyperloop One (formerly Hyperloop Technologies/HTI) and Hyperloop Transportation Technologies (HTT). Other players include skyTran and crowd teams like MIT and rLoop.
- HTT announced it licensed a passive magnetic-levitation system (based on Lawrence Livermore work/Richard Post) that HTT says lifts pods through motion alone, removing the need for continuous power along the track, lowering construction costs and offering safety advantages in power loss scenarios. HTI/Hyperloop One demonstrated a linear induction propulsion sled in Nevada, reaching ~115 mph in a short test and plans further testing.
- Technology state: Prototypes and demos have focused on subsystems (propulsion, levitation) rather than full systems. Teams have shown progress but remain far from operational networks.
- Challenges and criticisms:
  - Safety, passenger comfort and human physiology (high accelerations, lateral/vertical G-forces during acceleration, braking and turns) may limit practical speeds and routing, requiring trade-offs.
  - Massive infrastructure, regulatory, land-rights, environmental review, and cost hurdles (estimates like $6+ billion for an LA–SF tube). Building rights-of-way, dealing with terrain, eminent domain, and permitting pose major barriers.
  - Skepticism about timelines and realism: pundits and policy experts caution against underestimating political, bureaucratic and financial obstacles even if technical pieces succeed.
- Other items: community-driven efforts include games and crowdfunding (rLoop’s Break-a-Pod) and proposals for prototype routes or demo cities (e.g., Quay Valley). SpaceX has also run design competitions and may host a test track.

Overall: The Hyperloop idea has spurred active development, promising radically faster transit and potential energy benefits, but remains experimental with significant technical, physiological, logistical, legal and financial challenges before it could become a practical transportation system.

Militants in eastern Afghanistan have reportedly kidnapped a British aid worker — a Scottish woman in her 30s working for a U.S.-funded charity, believed to be Development Alternatives International (DAI) — after an ambush on a two-vehicle convoy traveling from Kunar province toward Jalalabad. The woman, who had several years’ experience in Afghanistan, was taken on foot despite a firefight with local police; two drivers and a guard were travelling with her. A major search involving police and tribal elders is under way.

A local militant commander identifying himself as Mohammed Osman told the Afghan Islamic Press the captors plan to demand the release of Pakistani neuroscientist Aafia Siddiqui — who was sentenced in New York last week to 86 years for attempting to kill U.S. agents and soldiers — in exchange for the British hostage. The Taliban initially denied responsibility, and a Taliban spokesman later said he was unaware of the kidnapping. Kunar is a Taliban stronghold where foreigners have been seized before.

The incident follows other high-profile attacks on foreign aid workers in Afghanistan, including the murder of British doctor Karen Woo a month earlier. DAI said it is treating the case as a suspected abduction and making its resolution a top priority. The British embassy and Foreign Office confirmed a British national was missing and said they were urgently investigating. The article also includes background on Aafia Siddiqui’s trial, conviction and sentencing and notes strong reactions in Pakistan calling for her repatriation.

Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, who survived a gunshot wound to the head less than two weeks earlier, is being moved from University Medical Center in Tucson to TIRR Memorial Hermann in Houston to begin intensive, months‑long rehabilitation. Doctors describe her progress so far as impressive — she can stand with assistance, has given her husband a neck massage, has tried to speak and responded to sights such as the Catalina Mountains — but caution that recovery from severe brain injury is unpredictable and often slow.

At the Houston center she will receive medical re-evaluation and then daily intensive therapy (speech, occupational and physical therapy, often two to three hours a day) to relearn motor skills, language and other functions. Because the bullet passed through the left side of her brain, vision and language are particular concerns; clinicians warn of risks including seizures from over‑stimulation, weight loss, depression and the possibility she may never fully recover. Surgeons have temporarily removed a portion of her skull to allow swelling; that bone will be replaced later, and she will wear a helmet during rehab.

Her care in Houston will be overseen by Dr. John Holcomb at a facility noted for treating penetrating brain injuries. Husband Mark Kelly expressed optimism about her long‑term recovery and noted he can be with her daily in Houston. Medical experts say Giffords’ youth, intelligence and strong family support improve her chances, but emphasize the rehabilitation will be grueling and progress variable. An escorted ambulance and air ambulance transport delivered her from the Tucson hospital to the airfield for the flight to Houston.

This short piece reports that Puerto Rican senator Roberto Arango—who once vice-chaired George W. Bush’s 2004 Puerto Rico campaign and is a GOP supporter—was allegedly identified on the gay hook-up app Grindr after images surfaced last week. When confronted on a Puerto Rican TV show, Arango neither confirmed nor denied the profile and offered a flippant, evasive explanation about taking photos while losing weight. The article mocks his response and highlights the apparent disconnect between his public persona and the alleged Grindr profile. A link/source is cited as Guanabee.
