Timekeepers announced a leap second will be added at the end of 2016 to keep Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) aligned with astronomical time (UT1) because Earth’s rotation is irregular and slowly slowing. For UTC zones (e.g., Britain, Ireland, Iceland, some West African countries) the last minute of 2016 will be 61 seconds: 23:59:59, 23:59:60, then 00:00:00 on 1 January 2017. Leap seconds are inserted by the IERS when the difference between UTC (atomic time) and UT1 approaches 0.4–0.9 seconds; they have been used since 1972 and were last added on 30 June 2015.

Leap seconds ensure civil time remains close to mean solar time but can cause problems for computers, data logging and telecom systems that aren’t designed to handle a 61st second. Large cloud providers smooth—or “smear”—the leap second across a longer interval to avoid a discrete extra second. Google, for example, spreads the adjustment over 20 hours by slightly slowing its clocks (0.0014% for 10 hours before and 10 hours after the leap second) and is offering its smeared-time NTP servers publicly so customers can sync during the transition. Other providers (Amazon, Akamai, Microsoft) have used similar approaches, often over 24 hours. There is ongoing international discussion about the long-term future of leap seconds, including proposals to stop them or use much larger, less frequent corrections (e.g., leap hours).

A Star Is Born, Bradley Cooper’s remake of the 1976 film, follows a familiar story: a troubled, older entertainer with an alcohol problem (Cooper as Jackson Maine) discovers and falls for a shy, gifted young singer (Lady Gaga as Ally), then struggles as her fame eclipses his. The movie is Cooper’s directorial debut; he co-wrote the script, co-stars and sings live on camera. Gaga makes her feature-film debut playing a self‑doubting performer who initially refuses to sing her own material until Maine encourages her. The first trailer focuses on their meeting, falling in love, Ally’s reluctance to perform and Jackson pushing her into the spotlight. The supporting cast includes Sam Elliott as the singers’ manager, with Andrew Dice Clay and Dave Chappelle in smaller roles. The film features original music written by Gaga, Cooper and collaborators (including Lukas Nelson, Jason Isbell and Mark Ronson) and was partly shot at Coachella in 2017. A Star Is Born opens October 5.

A newly discovered bug can permanently disable recent iOS devices if the system date is manually set to January 1, 1970. Reported Feb. 2016 and circulated on forums like 4Chan, Reddit and Facebook, the issue leaves affected devices stuck on the Apple logo and unresponsive to normal recovery attempts (including iTunes restores). It appears limited to devices with 64‑bit processors (iPhone 5s and later, iPad Air, iPad mini 2, 6th‑gen iPod touch and newer). The fault is tied to Unix time — January 1, 1970 is the epoch used to count seconds — and setting that date apparently triggers a conflict that bricks the device. Some users may be tempted to try it after seeing it as a prank or “easter egg,” but resolution generally requires service from Apple (likely a replacement); Apple had not commented at the time of reporting.

Volkswagen’s US chief executive Michael Horn publicly admitted the company “was dishonest” with regulators and the public over software that rigged diesel emissions tests, saying “we have totally screwed up” and pledging to fix the cars and restore trust. The US Environmental Protection Agency found VW installed a “defeat device” that detected testing conditions and reduced nitrogen-oxide (NOx) output during lab tests but allowed emissions up to 40 times the legal limit in normal driving. The EPA ordered a recall of about 482,000 VW and Audi vehicles sold in the US since 2009.

The fallout has been severe: Volkswagen shares plunged, wiping billions from its market value, and the company faces potential US fines up to $18 billion, possible criminal charges, and extensive civil litigation from customers and shareholders. The US Congress and the Department of Justice are preparing investigations and hearings.

International reactions and probes expanded quickly. France’s finance minister called for a Europe-wide inquiry to reassure the public. South Korea launched tests on several VW and Audi models sold there (Golf, Jetta, Beetle, Audi A3) and said its probe could broaden to all German diesel imports if problems are found. Regulators and experts warned the problem could extend to other models, manufacturers and regions, since European test procedures differ and may be more vulnerable to manipulation.

Industry bodies defended European testing regimes but acknowledged test methods are outdated and in need of reform to better reflect on-road conditions. VW CEO Martin Winterkorn apologized, ordered an external investigation and halted sales of the implicated diesel models in the US. Observers warn the scandal could have wide implications for regulatory trust, industry practices and public health given the scale of excess emissions.

Rapper Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson filed for bankruptcy in Connecticut after a jury ordered him to pay $7 million to Lastonia Leviston for posting a sex tape. In recent court papers he reports about $25 million in assets and roughly $33 million in liabilities. Assets listed include an $8 million Connecticut mansion, a $572,000 Long Island home, a $464,000 Atlanta home, about $10 million in cash, and roughly $500,000 in vehicles (three Chevy Suburbans and a 2010 Rolls‑Royce). His debts include the $7 million judgment and an alleged $18 million claim from electronics company Sleek Audio; total liabilities are reported near $33 million.

Monthly income is reported at about $185,000–$3 million annually from music and related activities, plus smaller streams from his boxing promotion and other ventures. Monthly expenses are listed at roughly $108,000, highlighted by $72,000 to maintain his Connecticut mansion, a $5,745 Bentley lease, $12,000 in child support, and payments to a stylist, barber and fitness coach. The filing notes recent large credit‑card and stylist payments and says Jackson is due back in bankruptcy court.

House Budget Chairman Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) unveiled a bipartisan framework that keeps traditional Medicare while adding a private-plan option for future enrollees. The proposal, announced at a Bipartisan Policy Center event, would begin for new retirees around 2022 and preserve government-run Medicare as a permanent choice alongside competing private plans that would bid to serve beneficiaries.

Key features:
- Beneficiaries would receive a government subsidy (premium support) to buy either traditional Medicare or private plans.
- Unlike Ryan’s earlier plan, the subsidy would be indexed to grow with the economy (similar to the standard in the Affordable Care Act) and could rise or fall with policy costs, offering more protection to seniors than the original Ryan blueprint.
- The proposal would add catastrophic coverage and cap out-of-pocket costs.
- Ryan and Wyden stress the plan preserves the “Medicare guarantee” and believe competition among plans could slow cost growth; they acknowledge savings might be less than under prior proposals and that Congress would need to act if costs continue rising.
- They are presenting a framework, not drafting legislation immediately, expecting any legislative action after the next Congress is seated.

Political context:
- The move marks a significant shift for Ryan, who had previously proposed fully privatizing Medicare for future beneficiaries and faced intense Democratic criticism. Wyden’s involvement gives Democratic cover but could complicate campaign messaging about protecting Medicare from privatization. The plan avoids debating the Affordable Care Act and aims to build bipartisan consensus on long-term Medicare reform.

A joint Daily Camera/9NEWS investigation reviewed DNA lab reports and independent expert analyses underlying former Boulder DA Mary Lacy’s 2008 public exoneration of JonBenet Ramsey’s parents. The new review finds the DNA evidence Lacy cited is far less definitive than her statement implied.

Key findings
- Samples from two spots on JonBenet’s long johns and an earlier sample from her underwear, which Lacy described as matching and used to clear the Ramseys, appear to be mixed and complex. Independent experts concluded the long-johns samples likely include genetic material from at least three contributors: JonBenet, the previously reported “Unknown Male 1,” and at least one additional unidentified person. That third contributor had not been publicly disclosed before.
- The Unknown Male 1 profile (derived initially from the underwear) may itself be a composite of multiple individuals rather than a single person’s profile, which would limit its forensic value and explain why it has never matched any CODIS record.
- Bode Technology analysts warned their 2008 testing results “should not be considered a single-source profile” and that Unknown Male 1 “could not be excluded” (or on one sample, “cannot be included or excluded”) as a contributor. Those caveats were not reflected in Lacy’s exoneration letter, which stated the profiles “matched” and that there was “no innocent explanation” for their presence at three sites on JonBenet’s clothing.

Implications and expert views
- Independent scientists say the DNA is low-level, complex, and potentially transferable (touch DNA), so innocent secondary transfer or trivial contact could account for the findings. Thus the DNA evidence is indeterminate — it neither proves an intruder theory nor definitively exonerates family members.
- Some forensic scientists recommend further targeted testing (for example Y-STR analysis to isolate male DNA) using modern methods not applied since 2008, which could clarify male contributions to the mixtures.
- Critics of Lacy’s decision say she exhibited confirmation bias by embracing an intruder theory and by publicizing an exoneration without fully disclosing the laboratory’s uncertainties. Others, including Ramsey family counsel and some experts, maintain confidence in Lacy’s judgment or see the DNA as an important investigative lead.

Case status and calls for review
- Boulder Police currently control the cold-case investigation. No new DNA testing has been done since 2008. The investigation’s renewed scrutiny of the lab reports has prompted calls from former officials and experts to reexamine the evidence with current techniques and to reassess conclusions drawn from the disputed DNA. Boulder’s current DA has said Lacy’s 2008 letter is legally insignificant and that any appropriate modern testing should be performed.

Bottom line: The DNA results Lacy cited to publicly exonerate the Ramseys are more ambiguous than her letter indicated. Independent review suggests mixed, low-level, possibly multi-person DNA and potential for innocent transfer; as a result, the DNA neither conclusively identifies a perpetrator nor definitively excludes family members, and further testing with modern methods has been recommended.

The discovery in April 2003 of Laci Peterson and her unborn son Conner’s bodies in San Francisco Bay marked a turning point in the investigation that led to the arrest and 2004 conviction of Laci’s husband, Scott Peterson, who was sentenced to death and remains incarcerated while appealing.

Two new TV specials revisiting the case—A&E’s The Murder of Laci Peterson and ABC’s Truth and Lies: The Murder of Laci Peterson—highlight ongoing disputes over his guilt and differing recollections of key moments. A clip from the A&E series shows retired Modesto detective Jon Buehler recalling Scott’s subdued reaction when told the bodies had been found, which Buehler interpreted as consistent with guilt. Scott, in a death-row phone call included in the series, disputes that portrayal, saying he had a strong physical reaction but suppressed his emotions while with detectives. Scott and his family maintain his innocence; prosecutors relied largely on circumstantial evidence, including his affair with Amber Frey, alleged inconsistent behavior around the time of Laci’s disappearance, and physical evidence linking the bodies to the Bay area near where Scott claimed to have been.

ABC’s special features interviews with Laci’s mother Sharon Rocha, who describes the emotional conflict of suspecting her son-in-law, and recounts her last memory of Laci. The program promises new material—home video of Laci, Scott’s pre-arrest Diane Sawyer interview, and other archival footage. Scott’s current appeals argue trial counsel failings and juror misconduct; the California Attorney General recently defended the conviction in a 150-page response, citing what it calls overwhelming circumstantial evidence of motive and opportunity.

European Union foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton visited Cairo and on Monday night met for about two hours with deposed Egyptian president Mohamed Morsi—her first contact with an independent official since his July 3 ouster. Ashton said Morsi appeared well, had access to television and newspapers, and she had a “friendly, open and very frank” discussion; she also said she assured his family he was well. She denied offering him a “safe exit.”

Ashton’s trip was part of EU efforts to help mediate Egypt’s political crisis after clashes that left about 80 people dead. During her two-day visit she met a wide range of actors including interim Vice President Mohamed ElBaradei, military chief Gen. Abdel Fatah al‑Sissi, liberal and Islamist figures and Muslim Brotherhood representatives. ElBaradei said Morsi had “failed” in office but argued Brotherhood participation in a political road map was important; the Brotherhood’s Freedom and Justice Party insisted any solution must include Morsi’s return to power and restoration of “constitutional legitimacy.”

The visit appeared aimed at calming tensions and encouraging dialogue; Ashton stressed the EU’s supportive, non‑impositional role and urged a democratic path forward. Morsi is under investigation on charges including espionage and murder—accusations his supporters call politically motivated and which could carry the death penalty. U.S. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel also urged restraint and an inclusive reconciliation process in talks with Sissi.

A 22-year-old Salvadoran woman, identified as "Beatriz," who suffers from lupus and kidney failure and was denied a medical abortion, underwent a Caesarean section at 27 weeks to protect her life, El Salvador’s Health Ministry said. Ultrasounds had shown the fetus had severe anencephaly (only a brain stem), and doctors delivered a baby girl who was born without a brain and died about five hours later. The operation was framed as a C-section rather than an abortion to comply with El Salvador’s total ban on abortion, which carries criminal penalties. Beatriz’s request had been rejected by the country’s Supreme Court, which found her conditions manageable, and the case prompted a non-binding ruling from the Inter-American Court of Human Rights urging the state to protect her life. The Health Ministry, preparing for emergency intervention, said the C-section was performed when clinically appropriate and that Beatriz was in stable condition afterward. The case intensified national and international debate over El Salvador’s strict abortion laws, drawing praise from both critics and supporters of abortion rights.

Summary:

- Joint Russian-Chinese naval drills in the Baltic this year were deliberately small and largely symbolic. Maxim Shepovalenko, a former Russian navy captain and analyst at CAST, said Russia had no need to mount a large-scale Baltic exercise and that China was using the event to practice projecting naval reach. The week-long exercise, commanded by Russian Vice Admiral Alexander Fedotenkov and Chinese Vice-Admiral Tian Zhong, includes anti-submarine, anti-air, anti-ship, anti-piracy and search-and-rescue drills and is being conducted in Russian. Observers note the manoeuvres also serve as a show of force after recent U.S.-India-Japan drills in the Indian Ocean; they come amid China’s expanding naval reach, including a new overseas base in Djibouti.

- Separately, NATO and Eastern European concerns persist over Russia’s planned Zapad 2017 war games in Belarus. U.S. Army Lt. Gen. Ben Hodges warned allies fear the exercises could be used as a “Trojan horse” to leave military equipment in Belarus after the drills, and said greater Russian openness would reassure neighbors. Moscow denies any intent to leave equipment and criticized Western anxiety as political posturing. NATO officials recall that past large Russian exercises included special forces, long-range missiles and UAVs—capabilities later used in Crimea, eastern Ukraine and Syria—and worry Zapad could be much larger than officially stated. Russia has said it will invite observers if troop numbers exceed 13,000, per the Vienna Document; some NATO allies suspect the exercise could involve far more personnel and even nuclear training. The U.S. and NATO plan to continue routine rotations and scheduled exercises during Zapad, with only modest additional deployments (three companies of paratroopers to the Baltic states for low-level exercises) to avoid provocative actions.

A San Antonio couple, Robert and Falon Griffin, unexpectedly delivered their daughter, Gracelyn Mae Violet Griffin, in a Chick-fil-A bathroom late one Tuesday night while en route to University Hospital. Falon, 38 weeks pregnant, urgently needed the restroom; staff let the couple in even though the restaurant was closed. When labor progressed rapidly and paramedics could not arrive in time, Robert—who is not a doctor—assisted the birth in a restroom stall. He noticed the umbilical cord was wrapped twice around the baby’s neck and was able to unwrap it; the delivery took about six minutes. Robert wrapped the newborn in a T-shirt while employees called 911 and waited for EMTs. The family’s Facebook post about the incident went viral. In gratitude, the Chick-fil-A franchise owner promised Gracelyn free Chick-fil-A for life, a job at 16, and is helping plan a chicken-nugget–themed first birthday; employees and the family formed a lasting bond from the ordeal.

Anton Martynenko, 32, of Eagan, Minnesota, was sentenced to 38 years in federal prison for running a large, years-long sextortion and child-pornography operation that targeted more than 155 teenage boys—mostly 14- to 16-year-old high school athletes—across the Midwest. Martynenko pleaded guilty in January to three child-pornography charges tied to a scheme in which he created fake social media profiles (often posing as teenage girls or local athletes), solicited nude photos and videos, and then publicly posted and shared them to humiliate and extort his victims. Prosecutors described him as a “tenacious predator” who organized meticulous “target lists” and folders of boys’ images by name, school, age and other details, and who persuaded at least three boys into sexual acts with him. At least two victims later committed suicide and others reported suicidal ideation and long-lasting psychological harm.

The investigation began after a Rosemount teen alerted police; Martynenko was arrested in November 2015 after an undercover operation on Twitter. Victims testified at sentencing about the devastating impact—public tagging, loss of reputation, anxiety, consideration of suicide—and some called the sentence a measure of relief. Martynenko apologized in court, attributed his behavior to depression and addiction to pornography, and said he would seek to make amends; a forensic psychologist noted he might be amenable to intensive psychosexual treatment but cited chat logs showing he took pleasure in exposing victims.

U.S. District Judge Richard Kyle credited Martynenko with two years off for providing investigators 40 pages of notes from conversations he had as a jailmate with Danny Heinrich (the suspect in the Jacob Wetterling case). Prosecutors disputed that Martynenko’s cooperation materially solved that case and said he sought to cast himself as a hero. Martynenko’s defense had sought the 15-year mandatory minimum; prosecutors had sought 40 years. Authorities emphasized the case as the largest child-porn production prosecution in Minnesota history and urged caution about online safety.

Adam Seger, former director of restaurants at Louisville’s Seelbach Hotel, has admitted that the story claiming he "rediscovered" a pre-Prohibition Seelbach Cocktail was fabricated as a promotional stunt. Seger told the New York Times he created the bourbon-and-champagne drink himself after taking over the hotel’s food-and-beverage operations in 1995 and concocted a plausible origin tale to give the hotel a signature cocktail tied to its historic, Gatsby-era image. His story was widely repeated in local press and picked up by cocktail books (including New Classic Cocktails and Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails), helping the drink gain international recognition. Seger later confessed the fabrication to cocktail author Gaz Regan; Regan said he suspected Seger’s role but still published the recipe. The Seelbach Hilton, aware of the admission, says the cocktail has become a tradition and will remain on the menu. The article also reproduces Seger’s Seelbach Cocktail recipe.

This document promotes quick, small short-term loans (payday/fast cash/no-credit-check loans) as a solution for urgent expenses. Key points:

- Fast cash loans are intended to cover emergency needs like medical bills, utilities, car repairs, rent, weddings, home repairs and other unexpected costs.
- They are marketed as easy to apply for—often online or paperless—with quick approval and minimal paperwork, and lenders may not require a credit check.
- Typical loan sizes are small (examples cited range from under £80 up to about £1,500) with short terms (commonly one to four weeks), and some lenders offer longer installment repayment options with monthly payments.
- Eligibility notes for UK lenders include being a permanent UK resident, at least 18 years old, in regular employment earning a minimum monthly income (example given ~£1,000), and holding a bank account for at least three months.
- The document warns that emergency borrowing has costs (fees and interest), can be expensive if not repaid on time, and that taking larger loans increases total interest and penalties. It recommends using savings where possible and avoiding predatory lenders.
- Application is described as fast: complete an online form, undergo verification, and receive funds quickly if conditions are met.

Dennis Prager’s two 2013 pieces defend saying “Merry Christmas” and Jews celebrating Christmas. He argues Christmas is both a Christian holy day and an American national holiday embraced by an overwhelming majority of the country, so Americans should freely wish each other “Merry Christmas” instead of the politically cautious “Happy Holidays.” Prager—speaking as an Orthodox Jew—says non-Christians aren’t excluded by public Christmas traditions; many Jews and other non-Christians enjoy and benefit from the season’s joy. He lists numerous iconic Christmas songs and cultural contributions by Jewish creators to show Christmas’s shared, secularized place in American life.

He views efforts to remove Christmas from public spaces as products of left-wing multiculturalism and secularization that divide Americans, citing examples like altered school performances and retail avoidance of “Merry Christmas.” Prager distinguishes secular or cultural celebration (trees, songs, family, gifts) from religious worship of Christ, which he respects as a boundary for observant non-Christians.

A lighter, related piece emphasizes that many Jews celebrate Christmas culturally—partly because modern Christmas centers more on Santa and family than theology—and notes statistics showing many Jewish households have trees. He acknowledges sensitivities from Christians who see such symbols as religious, highlights Jewish alternatives like “Mensch on a Bench,” but ultimately encourages Jews who wish to join Christmas festivities to do so and wishes all Americans a Merry Christmas.

Rescue teams scoured the Java Sea after AirAsia Indonesia Flight QZ8501 (Flight 8501) vanished Sunday while en route from Surabaya to Singapore with 162 people aboard. The Airbus A320 disappeared from radar about halfway into the flight between Belitung and Borneo; the last recorded pilot contact was a request to turn left and climb to 38,000 feet to avoid clouds, after which radar contact was lost minutes later. No distress call was received.

Search-and-rescue: Indonesia is leading a multinational search including assets from Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Japan, New Zealand, China and the U.S., with more than 1,100 personnel involved. The search area has expanded to 13 zones over roughly 156,000 sq km. Teams have reported possible signs—an oil slick, objects, a faint “ping,” and smoke seen near Long Island—but officials say none have been confirmed as linked to the plane. Bad weather and rough seas have hampered operations. Authorities believe the aircraft may be on the sea floor based on its last known track.

Possible causes and context: It is too soon to determine a cause. Weather (severe thunderstorms and possible wind shear), pilot error, structural failure, catastrophic metal fatigue, or deliberate sabotage/terrorism have been suggested as possibilities; there is currently no evidence for terrorism or pilot murder. Officials reported that air traffic control denied the requested climb because another aircraft occupied that altitude; Indonesian authorities suggested the plane may have climbed regardless. The A320 family has a strong safety record overall, and AirAsia’s Indonesian unit had no previous fatal crashes.

Investigation steps: Searchers aim to find wreckage and recover the flight data and cockpit voice recorders, whose homing beacons would help pinpoint location. If recovered, recorders and debris patterns should provide critical clues.

Human impact: Of the 162 aboard, 155 were Indonesian; others included South Korean, British, French, Malaysian and Singaporean citizens. Families have been briefed, and AirAsia arranged a charter flight to show relatives the search area. Authorities have set up victim identification facilities and may collect identifying material if needed.

Broader notes: The disappearance comes in a year already marked by two major Malaysia-linked air disasters (MH370 and MH17), though investigators say there is no known connection. Increasing air travel in Southeast Asia and past safety issues in Indonesia provide broader context for concern and scrutiny as the search and investigation continue.

A series of polls and reporting from 2013 show deep public divisions and contentious policy choices as U.S. lawmakers pushed for the most significant immigration overhaul in years. A Reuters/Ipsos online poll of 1,443 adults found that a majority of Americans favor deporting most or all of the nation’s estimated 11 million undocumented immigrants: 23% said all should be deported and 30% said most should be deported (with some exceptions). Just 5% said all should be allowed to stay legally and 31% favored most staying. Views are strongly polarized by party: about 75% of Republicans favor deporting most or all undocumented immigrants versus about 40% of Democrats. Pollsters note public opinion has been stable even as political momentum for reform grew after the 2012 elections.

At the same time, a bipartisan group of eight senators was crafting an immigration bill that would combine a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants (subject to fines, taxes and backlog conditions) with stronger border-security and worker-verification measures. One controversial proposal under consideration would require all U.S. workers—citizens and noncitizens—to carry a tamper- or “non-forgeable” electronic ID, frequently described as a biometric card using fingerprints, vein scans or other markers, to prove legal employment eligibility. Supporters (including some of the senators involved and some business and farm interests) argue a robust biometric system would curb fraud and make E-Verify-style checks more reliable. Opponents, including civil liberties groups and some policy analysts, warn it could create a de facto national ID, threaten privacy, risk mission creep into travel, voting or other activities, and be costly to implement and operate. Alternatives discussed include strengthening the existing E-Verify system with additional identity questions rather than mandatory biometrics.

Political tensions were illustrated by heated town-hall exchanges with Senator John McCain in Arizona, underscoring strong constituent concern about border security and jobs. The reporting highlights the challenge for lawmakers to balance enforcement, verification, privacy, cost, and a pathway to legal status while maintaining a fragile bipartisan coalition.

Morley Safer, the veteran CBS News correspondent who became an iconic 60 Minutes presence, has died at 84. Safer, who announced his retirement the week before and watched a CBS tribute honoring his 46-year run on the program, died in Manhattan; funeral arrangements are private.

Career highlights and impact
- Longest-serving primetime network correspondent: Safer joined 60 Minutes in 1970, replacing Harry Reasoner, and remained a defining voice on the program for 46 years.
- Groundbreaking war reporting: As head of CBS’s Saigon bureau (1964–66), he produced a 1965 report from Cam Ne showing U.S. Marines burning villagers’ huts. The piece won a George Polk award, provoked White House anger, and is credited with helping shift war coverage toward less self-censorship and greater candor.
- Signature work and range: Safer combined hard-hitting investigations (e.g., an Emmy-winning 1971 Gulf of Tonkin investigation, the 1983 “Lenell Geter’s in Jail” segment that helped free a wrongfully convicted man) with elegant cultural and human-interest pieces—profiles of Katharine Hepburn, Betty Ford, artists, architects and oddities around the globe. His reporting on the “French Paradox” helped spark a U.S. red-wine boom.
- Style and craft: Celebrated for his writing, voice and storytelling—wry, precise and conversational—Safer often rewrote scripts himself and preferred pieces that played to the ear as well as the eye. Colleagues described his work as “nearly works of art.”

Awards and recognition
- Safer received major journalism honors including 12 Emmys, three Peabodys, four duPont-Columbia awards, multiple George Polk and Overseas Press Club awards, the Paul White Award and France’s Chevalier dans l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres.

Background and personal life
- Born Nov. 8, 1931, in Toronto, Safer began as a print reporter, worked for Reuters and the CBC, and joined CBS in 1964. He was the first U.S. network correspondent to film inside Communist China (1967).
- He held dual Canadian and U.S. citizenship, enjoyed painting and classic cars, and combined travel with reporting assignments.
- Safer published a Vietnam memoir, Flashbacks: On Returning to Vietnam (1990).
- Survivors include his wife of 48 years, Jane; a daughter, Sarah Bakal, and three grandchildren, plus siblings in Toronto.

Legacy
CBS executives and colleagues lauded Safer as a pillar of 60 Minutes and one of journalism’s great storytellers whose work ranged from frontline war reporting to culturally rich, offbeat features. His blend of moral seriousness, narrative craft and dry wit left a lasting mark on television journalism. A memorial service will be announced later.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved J.R. Simplot Co.’s genetically modified “Innate” potato for commercial planting. The Innate potato is engineered to produce less acrylamide (a chemical that forms when potatoes are cooked at high temperatures and is suspected to be carcinogenic) and to resist bruising. Simplot says the fresh-potato market will embrace the variety; only about 400 test acres were planted this fall, and wider production won’t ramp up until after the 2015 harvest.

Despite Simplot’s role as a major supplier of fries and other potato products, McDonald’s said it will not source GMO potatoes and has no plans to change its sourcing. The fast‑food industry previously rejected Monsanto’s NewLeaf GMO potato more than a decade ago, leading to its withdrawal. Dehydrated potato buyers and some food-industry purchasers have advised growers not to plant GMO potatoes; some growers hope to find willing buyers to capture Innate’s benefits (reduced bruising and potentially higher yields).

Food & Water Watch praised McDonald’s decision as a consumer-driven victory and urged other chains to follow suit, noting they submitted over 90,000 petitions urging McDonald’s to reject GMO potatoes. Industry concerns center on potential consumer backlash and protecting brand equity.

A rapidly expanding sinkhole in Land O’Lakes, Pasco County, Florida, swallowed a boat, destroyed two homes and led to the voluntary evacuation of residents from 10 additional houses on July 14, 2017. Video showed a home collapsing into the hole as it grew from about the size of a small swimming pool to roughly 200 feet wide and 50 feet deep. Fire crews arrived after a caller reported a depression under a backyard boat; the boat fell in minutes as the hole opened. Firefighters rescued two dogs and recovered some belongings before the first house collapsed; a neighboring home was later destroyed. No injuries were reported. County records indicate a sinkhole had previously opened and been “stabilized” at the first property in 2012. Utilities were cut to about 100 homes, and the American Red Cross is assisting displaced residents. Authorities marked 10 homes unsafe.

A 31-year-old Galveston carpenter, identified as Josue Zurita, died in mid-October of necrotizing fasciitis after treating a severely infected wound on his upper left arm. Zurita had been helping repair homes damaged by Hurricane Harvey when the infection — a rare, fast‑spreading “flesh‑eating” bacterial disease that destroys soft tissue — likely entered through a cut exposed to floodwater or debris. He went to the hospital on October 10 and died six days later.

Local health officials noted that while flood-related infections like necrotizing fasciitis are uncommon, exposure during cleanup and reconstruction raises risk if wounds aren’t properly cared for. This is at least the second Harvey‑linked necrotizing fasciitis death in the Houston area (a 77‑year‑old woman died in September), and another man who had waded or kayaked through floodwaters survived after contracting a similar infection. Physicians emphasized the infection’s rapid progression and urged prompt medical attention for wound redness, swelling or fever, along with basic precautions: keep wounds clean and covered, avoid contact with natural water when injured, wash hands, and seek care early.

Ford announced a $1 billion, five-year majority investment in a newly revealed Pittsburgh-based self-driving startup, Argo AI, founded by Google/Waymo veteran Bryan Salesky and former Uber autonomy lead Peter Rander. Ford frames the deal as an investment (Argo will be a subsidiary for accounting) but structured to give Argo operational independence and the ability to offer meaningful equity to recruit top AI, robotics and computer-vision talent. Argo will focus on developing the “virtual driver” software for Ford’s planned SAE Level 4 autonomous vehicle and is tasked with helping Ford put a self-driving car into commercial service by 2021; Ford may later license the platform to others or pursue other commercialization paths.

The move follows Ford’s broader strategy of building mobility services and bolstering AV capabilities through prior investments in lidar and software partners. It also positions Ford to compete with tech firms and other automakers in an intense talent and technology race (Waymo, GM/Cruise, Uber/Volvo, Tesla, etc.). Argo plans offices in Pittsburgh, Michigan and Silicon Valley and aims to grow to about 200 employees in the near term. Ford says the deal combines its vehicle- and systems-integration strengths with Argo’s startup speed and robotics expertise to accelerate bringing self-driving vehicles to market.

When Carol and Willie Fowler’s daughter’s wedding was called off about 40 days before the ceremony, the Atlanta couple decided not to cancel the already-paid reception. Instead they donated the Villa Christina event — food, formal place settings, entertainment and transportation — to about 200 homeless women, children and families, working with local nonprofit Hosea Feed the Hungry and other shelters.

The donated reception, held Sept. 15 and renamed the “First Annual Fowler Family Celebration of Love,” featured hors d’oeuvres, a four-course sit-down meal (adults served salmon and chicken; children had chicken fingers, fries and fruit), passed appetizers, desserts, face painting, juggling and other entertainment. Buses brought guests from area shelters; children attended a separate activity room where they were also taught table etiquette. Organizers included motivational programming and sought to convey the message “your beginning does not determine your destiny.”

Hosea’s leaders at first thought the offer was a prank, but partnered with the Fowlers to welcome grateful guests. The family — who say they were guided by faith and hoped the gesture might inspire at least one child to thrive — plans to seek sponsors and make the event annual. They encouraged others with canceled events to consider donating them to charities instead of letting them go to waste.

Former 2012 GOP nominee and current Utah Senate candidate Mitt Romney told major Republican donors at his annual E2 Summit that he expects President Donald Trump to be easily renominated by Republicans in 2020 and to win reelection. Romney cited a strengthening economy and rising wages as key advantages for Trump and suggested Democrats may nominate a candidate “out of the mainstream,” which would further help the president. The remarks mark a notable softening from Romney’s earlier, harsh criticism of Trump during the 2016 campaign. Romney, who has praised some of Trump’s actions while criticizing his style and truthfulness, is competing for Utah’s Senate seat and is favored to win; he faces a June GOP runoff against state Rep. Mike Kennedy. At the closed-door summit, which drew prominent figures including Paul Ryan and Michael Bloomberg, Romney also predicted Republicans would retain control of both the House and Senate in the 2018 midterms.

Jason Garnett, a 23-year-old hotel worker from Harrogate, England, was treated for priapism after waking with an erection that lasted about 17 hours. Initially dismissing it and trying home remedies (an ice bath and jogging), he sought help after eight hours when the problem persisted. At hospital doctors diagnosed priapism — a rare, potentially damaging medical emergency — and drained roughly two pints (about 1.1 liters) of blood from his penis and administered multiple injections (reported as 24) of medication to restrict blood flow. Garnett described the procedure as extremely painful but said his condition has returned to normal, though the area is bruised and discolored.

Schlitterbahn Waterparks said it will permanently remove and decommission Verrückt, the 168-foot waterslide at its Kansas City park, once criminal and civil investigations are complete and a court allows it. The slide has been closed since Aug. 7, 2016, when 10-year-old Caleb Schwab — son of Kansas state Rep. Scott Schwab — died of a neck injury during a ride; two women on the raft were also injured. Schlitterbahn expressed sorrow, said safety is its top priority, and pledged cooperation with investigators, the victims’ families and their attorneys. The park’s family owners and the Schwab family have been coordinating on the decommissioning, but removal cannot occur until investigations and any potential litigation conclude. Independent investigations by attorneys and experts are underway; no criminal charges or lawsuits had been filed at the time of the statements. The tragedy has renewed scrutiny of state regulation of amusement-park rides in Kansas, which relies on private inspectors for annual checks. Schlitterbahn said it will announce future plans for the site at a later date.

Marie Joseph, 36, of Fall River, was found floating in the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Pool at Lafayette Park late Tuesday night and later pronounced dead. Police say she had been at the state-run pool on Sunday supervising a neighborhood group, including a 9-year-old boy who told investigators that Joseph unexpectedly went down the water slide with him, landed on top of him, and then went under and did not resurface. Friends and family had not reported her missing, but pool staff discovered clothing, a cell phone and her Massachusetts ID when they closed Sunday, prompting investigators to search.

Authorities are working to determine when and how she died and whether her body remained in the pool from Sunday until Tuesday. An autopsy is pending. Fall River Police Chief Daniel Racine and Bristol District Attorney C. Samuel Sutter said the death so far does not appear suspicious but is under active investigation.

The Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR), which operates the pool, closed the facility and placed the pool’s entire staff on administrative leave. The DCR temporarily closed all 30 of its deep-water pools for a 24–48 hour review of operational procedures. The pool area was locked when the body was reported Tuesday; police are probing how people accessed the site. Officials noted drownings can be silent and bodies in deep or turbid water can go unnoticed for days.

Summary:

Operation Card Shop was a two-year undercover FBI sting in which agents created and ran an online “carding” forum called Carder Profit to draw in cybercriminals who buy, sell and trade stolen credit/debit data, malware and services for producing fake cards. The operation, closed in May, led to arrests of 24 men (ages 18–25) across 13 countries and multiple U.S. jurisdictions — 11 arrested in the United States and the rest overseas — and the seizure of related sites such as UGNazi.com and Carders.org.

Authorities say the investigation identified and notified more than 411,000 compromised payment cards and prevented about $205 million in potential losses. The site functioned as an invite-only marketplace where sellers offered stolen account numbers, personal identity details, remote-access Trojans, counterfeit-card services, and logistics for shipping stolen merchandise. Notable arrests included Mir Islam (aka JoshTheGod), accused of trafficking 50,000 card numbers, and others who sold spyware and card-making tools.

Officials characterized the effort as a significant, broad strike against the organized “ecosystem” of Internet fraud, involving coordinated actions and searches in countries from Britain to Japan and cooperation with many international law enforcement agencies. While impactful, commentators noted the number of cards flagged in this sting is smaller than some prior large breaches (e.g., Global Payments’ 1.5 million-card breach), underscoring the continuing scale and sophistication of credit-card crime.

Convicted killer Carey Dean Moore was executed by lethal injection Tuesday morning at the Nebraska State Penitentiary in Lincoln. The execution began with media witnesses entering the viewing area at 10:19 a.m. and the curtain revealing Moore on the gurney at 10:24 a.m.; staff shown in the room included Director Scott Frakes and acting Warden Robert Madsen. A sequence of drugs was administered via IV: diazepam (started at 10:24), a saline flush, fentanyl (10:30) after which Moore appeared to cough and breathe heavily, then cisatracurium besylate (10:32) and potassium chloride (10:33), with saline flushes interspersed. Warden Madsen performed a consciousness check at 10:29. Moore’s chest stopped moving at about 10:31; he was pronounced dead at 10:47 a.m. by the Lancaster County coroner, out of sight of witnesses. The curtain was briefly raised at 10:53 to show Moore covered except for his face; his body was later transferred to the Nebraska State Patrol for an autopsy. The notice also included subscription access and contact information for digital access.

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor (R‑Va.) announced he will step down from his leadership post effective July 31 after unexpectedly losing his Republican primary to tea-party-backed economist Dave Brat. A University of Toulouse team led by Young-Ho Eom used link-analysis methods (inspired by Google’s PageRank) to find the most “important” people on Wikipedia. They analyzed 24 language editions and measured article centrality in three ways: PageRank (incoming links), CheiRank (outgoing links), and a combined 2DRank. Results varied by method and language: in the English-language Wikipedia 2DRank placed Frank Sinatra first, Michael Jackson second and Pope Pius XII third. Across all 24 editions combined, Adolf Hitler ranked first, with Michael Jackson second and Madonna third.

The study’s main aim was to detect biases in Wikipedia’s attention to historical figures by gender, era and geography. The authors found that most highly ranked figures are male, born in Western countries and after the 17th century, though each language edition tends to emphasize local figures. The paper also highlights methodological pitfalls: a straight PageRank produced the counterintuitive top result of Carl Linnaeus because many species pages across languages link to him, inflating his centrality. To compensate, the researchers used CheiRank and the combined 2DRank.

The work illustrates both how network-based metrics can reveal prominence patterns and how Wikipedia’s structure and cultural focus shape those outcomes. Previous related studies (e.g., on scholarly influence) have produced different top names using different methodologies.

This document compiles Rolling Stone’s long feature alleging a 2012 gang rape at the University of Virginia (UVA), the magazine’s later publisher apology for reporting failures, and contemporaneous reporting and responses from UVA, students, and officials.

Key elements:

- The alleged incident and Jackie’s account:
  - Rolling Stone published an account by a student identified as “Jackie” who said she was gang-raped at a Phi Kappa Psi fraternity party in fall 2012. Her narrative described being lured upstairs by a date called “Drew,” assaulted by multiple men over hours, and left hurt and barefoot outside the house.
  - Jackie detailed extreme trauma, long-term academic and emotional fallout, interactions with peers who minimized her experience, and involvement in campus survivor support groups (One Less).
  - She reported the assault to Dean Nicole Eramo, who explained options (criminal report, formal university hearing, or informal resolution) and assured Jackie nothing would be done without her consent. Jackie feared reporting and felt retraumatized by campus culture.

- Campus culture and institutional context:
  - The article situates the alleged assault within a persistent “party” and Greek-life culture on Rugby Road, where first-year women are particularly vulnerable. It documents traditions and songs that objectify women, reports that fraternities are overrepresented in campus sexual-assault incidents, and cites research on serial campus offenders.
  - Survivors and advocates described a longstanding pattern at UVA of survivors being discouraged, institutional secrecy, and prioritizing reputation over accountability. The piece recounts earlier cases (e.g., Liz Seccuro in 1984; others in 2002–2006) and criticizes UVA’s handling of sexual-misconduct complaints, low rates of expulsions for assault, and limited transparency in statistics and adjudications.
  - It notes UVA was among schools under federal Title IX/Office for Civil Rights scrutiny, including a proactive compliance review.

- Institutional responses after publication:
  - Rolling Stone’s piece provoked campus protests, student and alumni outrage, and calls for action. In response, UVA President Teresa Sullivan suspended all Greek social activity and later suspended fraternities, sororities and related organizations until January, citing the need for a cultural and policy review and urging anyone with information to come forward to police.
  - UVA announced investigations into the Phi Kappa Psi chapter and cooperated with local police; the chapter also said it would cooperate and suspended local activity.
  - Students and faculty organized rallies and demanded stronger measures; some administrators defended steps taken while critics called them insufficient.

- Rolling Stone’s later admission and controversy:
  - After additional reporting by the Washington Post and others surfaced discrepancies in Jackie’s account (questions about whether “Drew” was a Phi Psi member or even knew Jackie, differing witness recollections, and the fraternity’s denials about events and who worked at the pool), Rolling Stone’s managing editor Will Dana issued a statement saying the magazine had erred in honoring Jackie’s request not to contact the alleged assailants. The publication apologized for failing to get the other side and said the mistake was Rolling Stone’s, not Jackie’s, and that the magazine would continue investigating.
  - The controversy sparked broader debates about reporting standards, survivor protection vs. verification, and campus sexual-assault advocacy.

- Broader consequences and concerns:
  - The reporting and fallout intensified scrutiny of UVA’s response to sexual violence, renewed calls for transparency in reporting and adjudication, and debates over university obligations under Title IX.
  - The articles frame a larger problem: entrenched campus cultures and institutional incentives that can discourage reporting, minimize victim accounts, and protect alleged offenders—particularly in elite, tradition-focused universities with powerful Greek systems.
  - The document also references contemporaneous campus safety tragedies (the disappearance and later death of student Hannah Graham and the arrest of a suspect with prior alleged offenses), underscoring urgency about campus sexual violence.

Overall, the package paints a portrait of one student’s harrowing allegations set against a campus culture and administrative record that critics say has too often failed survivors. It catalogs institutional responses, student activism, and subsequent journalistic fallout that raised questions about both UVA’s handling of sexual assault and Rolling Stone’s reporting methods.

Today identical or similar emailed threats—claiming coordinated jihadi attacks on schools using bombs and nerve gas—targeted both New York City and Los Angeles public school systems. Details suggesting the messages were fake included their origin from the Cockmail/Cock.li email host (an 8chan‑linked service with obscene domains), misspelling “Allah” with a lowercase “a,” and other odd content; the LA email also claimed the sender had been bullied. The LA threat was traced to an IP address in Frankfurt but investigators said the true source was unknown and possibly closer. Officials initially called the LA threat “specific” and “unspecified/terror threat” at different points; after a 12‑hour probe the LAPD, LAUSD, county sheriffs and the FBI concluded it was not credible.

LAUSD Superintendent Ramon Cortines, school board president Steve Zimmer, Mayor Garcetti and LAPD Chief Charlie Beck defended the closure as a precaution given limited early information and recent local attacks (e.g., San Bernardino). A NewsChannel 5 investigation and subsequent legislative debate have raised serious questions about grading practices at the Tennessee Virtual Academy (TNVA), a for-profit online public school operated by K12 Inc. and authorized by a 2011 law. Lawmakers and teachers produced an internal December email from a TNVA vice principal instructing middle-school teachers to remove September and October progress reports from the electronic gradebook so November progress would be the only visible score. The message also instructed teachers to delete grades from assignments where most students failed, and prioritized reading and math over history and science.

Critics — including Democratic Rep. Gloria Johnson (a career teacher) and other education advocates — called the directives tantamount to grade-fixing intended to mask poor student performance. K12 and TNVA officials declined an in-person interview; TNVA principal Josh Williams said the intent was to “more accurately recognize students’ current progress” by recording the most recent progress score instead of averaging across a semester, and compared the practice to make-up work or extra credit in traditional schools. Advocates for teachers’ unions and some legislators said deleting earlier grades would make the school appear better to the public and to enrollment-based funding formulas.

TNVA’s low standardized-test results have prompted legislative scrutiny. Gov. Bill Haslam pushed a bill to cap virtual school enrollment at 5,000 (TNVA enrolls about 3,200), and another bill would effectively shut the school down. The debate became contentious: supporters of TNVA defended the school’s practices and benefits for certain students, while critics faulted K12 for lack of disclosure and possible manipulation of grades.

Detectives investigating the March 4 poisoning of former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia say they now believe the pair first came into contact with a military‑grade nerve agent at the front door of Skripal’s Salisbury home. The UK government blames the Russian state for the attack, which used a Novichok‑type nerve agent, and says more than 130 people in Salisbury could have been exposed. The government is considering further measures against Russia and has pledged a £1m support package to help Salisbury’s recovery. This document compiles multiple reports and analyses about Millennials’ demographics, work patterns, lifestyles and consumer habits.

Key findings on employment and tenure
- Government Current Population Survey data show Millennials (born 1981–1998, ages 18–35 in the cited analyses) are no more likely to “job-hop” than Generation X was at the same age. In 2016, 63.4% of employed Millennials had stayed with their current employer at least 13 months, versus 59.9% of 18–35-year-olds in 2000. About 22% of Millennials had five-year tenures, similar to Gen X in 2000.
- Higher educational attainment among Millennials helps explain longer tenure: in 2016, 25–35-year-old Millennial men and women had bachelor’s-degree rates of 38% and 46%, respectively—up from 31% and 34% for Gen X in 2000. Among college-educated 25–35-year-olds, about 75% had been with their employer at least 13 months in 2016 (slightly higher than comparable Gen X shares in 2000).
- For less-educated young adults, tenure patterns are similar across generations.
- The decline in job-switching since the 1980s is documented but not fully explained; factors like dual-career households, declining middle-skill jobs, occupational licensing and health insurance retention account for little of the trend. Longer tenure doesn’t necessarily mean better wages or security—limited outside opportunities could be a factor.

Demographics and generational size
- Census Bureau estimates (2015) show Millennials (defined here as ages 18–34 in 2015, with Pew placing oldest birth year at 1981 and assuming youngest born in 1997) have become the largest living generation at 75.4 million, edging out Baby Boomers (74.9 million). Millennials are projected to peak in population in 2036 (about 81.1 million) and then decline modestly by 2050.
- Generation X remains smaller than Millennials but will outnumber Boomers by 2028. Baby Boomers have already begun a long-term decline in numbers due to aging and mortality.

Lifestyle and social trends
- Young adults are delaying traditional adulthood milestones such as marriage and childbearing. Marriage rates are down and cohabitation has risen: cohabitation among young people increased markedly since 1975, now occurring around ages that previously corresponded to marriage.
- Educational attainment and labor-force participation for women have risen substantially: the share of women aged 25–34 who do not work to manage a household fell from 43% in 1975 to 14% recently; female labor-force participation rose from 50% to 70% in that group.
- Economic outcomes are mixed: more young men now occupy lower-income brackets than in 1975, while women have seen income gains but still lag men on median wages.

Regional and industry implications
- High local costs of living (example: Bay Area) risk pushing Millennials away, raising concerns for regional industries like tech.

Consumer behavior and brands
- Millennials and younger Gen Z shoppers are reaching peak spending power, and brands with strong online and mobile presences are most favored. A Conde Nast/Goldman Sachs study ranked Victoria’s Secret, Sephora and Nike highest among 13–34-year-old U.S. consumers; Amazon is the top overall retailer/app. Retailers emphasize e-commerce growth to capture these digitally native shoppers.

Miscellany
- Notes on web archiving: Alexa donated crawl data to the Internet Archive starting in 1996; a separate crawl described used the Wayback Machine host list and captured embedded and outbound links, but its WARC files are not publicly available.

Overall takeaway
- Contrary to the stereotype of a highly mobile, job-hopping generation, many Millennials—especially the college-educated—show job tenure equal to or longer than that of Gen X at the same ages. Demographically, Millennials are now the largest U.S. generation, reshaping labor, family formation and consumer markets as they age.

A large Northwestern Medicine study tracking 10,253 males from early adolescence into their early 30s found that becoming a father is associated with modest but meaningful weight gain. After becoming a first-time dad, a typical 6-foot man who lives with his child gained about 4.4 pounds (a 2.6% rise in BMI); nonresident fathers gained about 3.3 pounds (2% BMI rise). By contrast, non-fathers in the cohort lost about 1.4 pounds over the same period. Results controlled for age, race, education, income, physical activity, screen time and marital status, so the “fatherhood effect” is additional to known marriage-related weight gain.

Researchers suggest lifestyle changes related to parenting — less time for exercise, more calorie-dense snacks in the household, and finishing children’s leftovers — help explain the increase. The study, published in the American Journal of Men’s Health, emphasizes that the transition to fatherhood is an important developmental stage for men’s health: higher BMI raises long-term risks for heart disease, diabetes and cancer. Because many young fathers do not have their own doctors but do accompany partners or children to medical visits, pediatricians are urged to counsel fathers on nutrition, exercise and mental health during these encounters. The study was led by Dr. Craig Garfield and supported by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver NICHD.

Summary — 5 key takeaways from the Treasury Inspector General report on the IRS handling of 501(c)(4) (Tea Party–related) applications

1) No finding of partisan motive, but appearance of bias
- The IG did not conclude IRS employees were intentionally partisan or politically motivated, but found the criteria used created the appearance of partiality.  
- About 15% of flagged cases actually contained words like “Tea Party,” “patriots” or “9/12”; most were flagged for other reasons.  
- The report emphasizes that using organization names or policy positions to select cases is inappropriate.

2) The IRS used inappropriate, politically framed screening criteria
- Starting in 2010, a team in the IRS’s Determinations Unit developed criteria that focused on names and ideology rather than on activities indicating prohibited campaign intervention.  
- Management told them to change course in July 2011 to activity-based, neutral criteria, but the team reverted to the narrower test in January 2012 without approval. That was discovered and corrected again in May 2012.

3) The agency overreached by requesting donor information
- The IG found that asking groups for donor lists and other intrusive details (books read, etc.) was unnecessary and burdensome; such requests “crossed the line.”  
- IRS officials recognized this and destroyed donor lists that had been submitted for cases the IRS later determined it should not have requested.

4) Widespread delays, poor management and process failures
- Ineffective management allowed inappropriate criteria to persist for over 18 months and produced substantial processing delays. Many applications experienced extraordinary waits—some open from 206 to 1,138 days—delaying group activities and decisions across election cycles.  
- The IG documented inconsistent follow-up, unreasonable short deadlines in information requests after long inactivity, and other procedural failings.

5) Unclear whether top officials misled Congress; accountability limited
- The report does not resolve Republican allegations that senior officials (Acting Commissioner Steven Miller, former Commissioner Doug Shulman, or Lois Lerner) misled Congress about what they knew and when. That issue was left for congressional hearings.  
- The IG made nine recommendations to fix procedures; the IRS agreed to seven and proposed alternatives to two (about documenting selection reasons and training). No broad, systemic politicization was proven, but poor judgment, insubordination by a unit, and managerial lapses produced real harm to applicants.

Bottom line: The IG’s report stops short of proving intentional political targeting by the IRS, but finds the agency used inappropriate, name- and ideology-based screening criteria, overstepped by requesting donor information, and suffered significant management and process breakdowns that caused long delays. The report recommends procedural fixes; some questions about senior officials’ disclosure to Congress remain unresolved.

This CDC analysis of 2001–2015 emergency department (ED) data (NEISS‑AIP) examined nonfatal self‑inflicted injuries among U.S. youth aged 10–24. Key findings:

- From 2001–2015 there were an estimated 43,138 ED visits for first-time, nonfatal self‑inflicted injury in this age group (about 29,000 females and 14,000 males).
- Overall rates were stable through ~2008, then rose sharply for females thereafter. From 2009–2015 female rates increased 8.4% per year overall.
- The largest increase was among girls aged 10–14: rates climbed an average 18.8% per year from 2009 (≈110 per 100,000) to 2015 (≈318 per 100,000). Girls 15–19 also rose (≈7.2%/year from 2008–2015); females 20–24 showed a smaller steady increase (≈2.0%/year across 2001–2015).
- Male rates remained essentially stable across age groups.
- Poisoning (overdoses) was the most common method overall for females and increased after 2007; cutting with sharp objects among females rose steadily across the study period. Male method trends were stable.
- The reported rates likely underestimate the total burden because they include only ED visits (not outpatient or unreported cases).

The authors note these trends mirror rising youth suicide and depression reports, particularly among young girls, and call for evidence‑based prevention: better access to care for suicidal youth, creating protective environments, promoting connectedness, teaching coping/problem‑solving skills, and identifying/supporting at‑risk youth. Causes for the increase (e.g., cyberbullying, substance use, economic stress) require further study.

Former Democratic congressman Anthony Weiner’s long-running sexting scandals ended with a guilty plea and a prison sentence that closed a decades-long public saga with political and personal fallout.

Key timeline and facts:
- 1999–2011: Weiner served in Congress. He resigned in June 2011 after admitting to sending lewd messages and photos from his Twitter account.
- 2013: He attempted a political comeback with a run for New York City mayor, which collapsed after additional explicit exchanges surfaced (including messages with “Carlos Danger,” aka Sydney Leathers).
- 2016: New revelations escalated the scandal. A New York Post photo showed Weiner shirtless with his toddler beside him; a 15-year-old in North Carolina told media she had exchanged sexually explicit messages and video with him. Investigators seized Weiner’s devices as part of the probe.
- The FBI’s review of material found on Weiner’s laptop led to discovery of emails involving Hillary Clinton aide Huma Abedin, which prompted FBI Director James Comey to briefly reopen the Clinton email investigation days before the 2016 presidential election — a development many Democrats say hurt Clinton’s campaign.
- May 19, 2017: Weiner pleaded guilty in federal court to one count of transmitting obscene material to a minor, admitting he exchanged explicit messages and images with a girl he understood to be 15. He acknowledged a pattern of compulsive behavior, said he was in treatment, apologized, and agreed to register as a sex offender.
- Sentencing: In September 2017 he was sentenced to 21 months in prison and ordered to forfeit his iPhone; the plea agreement allowed for a 21–27 month sentence without appeal.

Personal consequences:
- His marriage to Huma Abedin, a longtime aide to Hillary Clinton, ended in separation after the 2016 revelations.
- The episode damaged his political career permanently, been the subject of a documentary ("Weiner"), and had broader political ramifications because of the FBI’s subsequent discovery of Clinton-related emails on his devices.

Arizona State University permanently revoked recognition of its local Tau Kappa Epsilon (TKE) chapter after the fraternity held an unregistered Martin Luther King Jr. holiday weekend party that featured racially stereotypical behavior and encouraged underage drinking. Photos circulated on social media showing attendees in stereotyped “hip-hop” attire, sagging pants, gang signs, and drinking from hollowed-out watermelon cups with the hashtag #blackoutformlk. ASU found the chapter violated four parts of the student code of conduct: discriminatory activity, alcohol-policy violations, breaches of prior disciplinary terms, and off-campus conduct risking community safety.

The 65-year-old local chapter can no longer be affiliated with ASU, be listed on university sites, recruit members, or hold on-campus meetings. The university had placed TKE on interim suspension after the party; officials continue to investigate and will handle individual student discipline. The national TKE organization said it received ASU’s findings and will release its own investigation results soon.

The decision follows prior incidents: in November 2012 about 20 TKE members attacked an African-American member of another fraternity, leaving him injured; two men later pleaded guilty to aggravated assault, and ASU had put TKE on probation through May 2014 with a ban on parties. Civil-rights leaders, who had demanded chapter expulsion and further student discipline and threatened athletic and fundraising boycotts, applauded the university’s action as a zero-tolerance stance against racism. ASU President Michael Crow cited the student code of conduct and condemned the behavior as inconsistent with university values.

This document contrasts two strands of coverage and depiction of North Korea: the brutal reality of its human-rights abuses and the tendency in Western media and entertainment to reduce the regime and its leader to clownish caricature.

First, it describes the North Korean system of hereditary punishment: entire families—grandchildren and great-grandchildren of people labeled “class enemies”—were confined in secret labor camps for decades. Many former inmates who were nominally “released” had nowhere to go and remained in camp-like conditions; others likely died in large numbers from starvation. Because the regime tightly controls information, human-rights organizations rely on satellite imagery and defectors’ accounts, which are often delayed and traumatized, making documentation difficult. Despite long-standing, massive abuses, such reporting has had limited influence on policy compared with sensational stories like the Sony hack tied to The Interview.

Second, the piece examines how Hollywood and the media feed a harmful stereotype of Asian men—the “clownish, goofy, harmless” caricature—tracing examples from William Hung and classic film characters to Psy’s U.S. reception and publicity stunts like that of Chen Guangbiao. It argues this stereotype shapes public perceptions of leaders such as Kim Jong-un, encouraging coverage that highlights absurd propaganda (e.g., unicorn lairs) and trivializes the regime’s brutality. The Interview is discussed as a case study: while it avoids the worst “clown” tropes and gives Randall Park’s Kim Jong-un some agency and menace, it still leans on crude jokes and misses an opportunity to probe how a savvy dictator manipulates image and propaganda.

Finally, the article notes a modest hopeful sign in representation: Randall Park’s role and the forthcoming sitcom Fresh Off the Boat may help expand portrayals of Asian and Asian-American men beyond long-standing goofball stereotypes. Overall, the document urges taking North Korea’s cruelty seriously rather than reducing it to laughable caricature.
