Daniel Ramirez Medina, a 23-year-old Mexican national brought to the U.S. as a child and twice approved for protection and work authorization under President Obama’s Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, was arrested by ICE in Washington state after agents went to his father’s home. Ramirez’s lawyers say he has no criminal history, a three-year-old son, and disclosed his DACA paperwork to ICE twice; they say he denied any gang affiliation and was pressured to admit one. ICE says he was detained after admitting gang membership while agents were arresting a previously deported felon, and that he is being held in Tacoma pending removal proceedings.

Ramirez’s attorneys filed a federal petition in Seattle seeking immediate release and an injunction barring further action, arguing the detention violates his DACA-based protections and due process. U.S. Magistrate Judge James Donohue ordered the government to respond quickly and set a bond hearing; he also demanded that ICE state whether Ramirez is in removal proceedings and why he remains detained despite DACA status. The case has prompted calls from local officials and lawmakers for clarification and raised alarms among immigrant-rights groups that this may be the first Trump-era arrest of a DACA recipient, signaling a possible expansion of enforcement against Dreamers.

Oregon lawmakers have introduced House Bill 2875, which would add a wholesale coffee tax of $0.05 per pound on coffee beans and ground coffee to create an “Alternative Education Sustainability Fund.” Revenue would be split evenly: half to the Oregon Military Department for the Oregon National Guard Youth Challenge Program, and half for grants to school districts that run alternative high school programs and primary-school reading programs (usable for operations and capital construction). The bill would take effect July 1, 2018, but includes no revenue estimate; it would need a three-fifths legislative majority to pass amid a projected $1.8 billion state budget gap.

Republicans criticized the idea as an ill-timed tax increase on a popular item. House Democrats’ leadership and the Revenue Committee chair say the proposal is unlikely to advance—there are over 100 bills in the Revenue Committee and most won’t move forward. The story also situates this proposal within broader 2017–2019 budget debates in Salem, including Governor Kate Brown’s budget plans, discussions of rent-control repeal bills, rural economic concerns, and justice and ethics reforms.

Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz says the company will keep aggressively expanding in China despite the country’s slowest growth in 25 years. Speaking in Shanghai, he reaffirmed Starbucks’ long-term approach and announced plans to open more than one new store per day over the next five years, targeting nearly 5,000 stores in China by 2021. Schultz recalled early skepticism, when Starbucks spent years educating Chinese consumers about coffee and initially lost money, but said the customer base has shifted from mostly expats and tourists to primarily Chinese patrons. He expects China to eventually overtake the U.S. as Starbucks’ largest market and credits early investments in people and systems for recent strong results. Schultz noted Starbucks’ advantage as a non‑high‑tech, food-and-beverage business in a sensitive market and ruled out franchising or selling its China operations, saying stores should be run by Starbucks staff. The piece also contrasts Starbucks’ success with other U.S. brands facing difficulties in China, such as KFC and McDonald’s.

A recent Daily Caller story criticized 11-year-old Barron Trump for wearing a T-shirt, khaki shorts and loafers while boarding Air Force One after a family trip from New Jersey, saying he should “dress like he’s in the White House.” The piece prompted widespread backlash on social media, with users, celebrities and public figures calling the attack mean-spirited and arguing that the president’s children should be off-limits. Chelsea Clinton, who has defended Barron before, urged the media to leave him alone and called the criticism shameful; Melania Trump thanked her and framed the responses as support against childhood bullying. The White House also asked the press to give Barron privacy as a minor. Reactions ranged from ridicule of the Daily Caller’s focus on an 11-year-old’s clothes to supportive comments noting the outfit was a common, inexpensive children’s shirt. The article originally misstated the travel origin (corrected to New Jersey).

NASCAR and 30 track operators (including International Speedway Corporation and Speedway Motorsports Inc.) issued a joint request that fans refrain from displaying the Confederate flag at NASCAR events and on track property. The statement, asking for an “all‑inclusive” and “welcoming” environment, says the request targets overt displays of the flag and urges mutual respect among attendees. NASCAR chairman Brian France had earlier said he wanted the flag eliminated from events, and the sanctioning body supported South Carolina’s removal of the Confederate flag from the state capitol.

Daytona International Speedway, hosting the upcoming Coke Zero 400, announced a voluntary flag-exchange program: fans can trade Confederate flags for American flags (the track will not ban flags in the infield this weekend). NASCAR already prohibits use of the Confederate flag in official capacities and does not sell related merchandise. Enforcement of the new request will largely rely on fans’ compliance; overt, boisterous displays may result in removal from the premises.

Three children — an 8-year-old girl and two boys aged 5 and 3 — were removed from a Salinas, California home on March 14 after deputies conducting a welfare check found them starving, neglected and showing signs of physical and emotional abuse. Authorities say the girl was the most severely abused: she appeared emaciated, had bruises, was traumatized, and had been chained at times (to a wall, occasionally at the ankle or by a collar) and possibly confined in a closet to prevent her from getting food. She was hospitalized for several days; the boys did not require hospitalization but also showed neglect.

Two women who are domestic partners, Eraca Dawn Craig (31) and Christian Jessica Deanda (44), were arrested at the scene on suspicion of felony child cruelty, false imprisonment and related charges and were arraigned; each is held on $50,000 bail with a preliminary hearing scheduled. Officials said the home was cluttered and dirty with little food, and the children had been home-schooled; the 8-year-old and the 5-year-old had been adopted, while the 3-year-old is the biological child of one woman. Investigators noted the women appeared to be preparing to move. One woman is a former corrections officer; the other has worked in counseling and ran a small business, according to online profiles. The children have been placed in foster care. Donations and support were solicited by local child-care organizations.

Federal Court Justice Robin Camp has resigned after the Canadian Judicial Council (CJC) unanimously recommended his removal for misconduct in a 2014 sexual‑assault trial. Transcripts showed Camp—then a provincial court judge—asked the 19‑year‑old complainant why she didn’t “keep her knees together,” said “pain and sex sometimes go together,” repeatedly referred to the complainant as “the accused,” and relied on myths about sexual‑assault victims. The Alberta Court of Appeal later overturned his acquittal of the accused, finding Camp had applied stereotypes.

A disciplinary panel held a public hearing last fall in which the complainant said Camp’s remarks made her hate herself and contemplate suicide. Camp apologized publicly, underwent counselling and gender‑sensitivity training, engaged feminist scholars who testified to his commitment to change, and sought permission to address the broader CJC membership in person. The CJC declined and, by 19–4, concluded his conduct was “so manifestly and profoundly destructive” to judicial impartiality, integrity and independence that public confidence was irreparably undermined and dismissal was necessary. Four male judges dissented, arguing rehabilitation made removal unnecessary.

Camp announced his resignation from the Federal Court effective March 10, 2017, and apologized. Justice Minister Jody Wilson‑Raybould had moved to seek parliamentary approval for removal—an unusual and politically significant step that became moot with his resignation. The case has reignited debate over judicial handling of sexual‑assault cases, prompted calls for mandatory judicial training on gendered violence, and been described by advocates as a watershed moment condemning rape myths in the justice system.

Three new literary adaptations—Gone Girl, The Two Faces of January and The Blue Room—explore faltering marriages, dissatisfied women and the specter of violent crime. The bulk of the coverage centers on Gone Girl, David Fincher’s film adaptation of Gillian Flynn’s bestseller.

Gone Girl
- Premise: Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck) returns home to find his wife Amy (Rosamund Pike) missing amid signs of struggle; media frenzy and police suspicion quickly turn on him. The film alternates perspectives and timelines, including Amy’s diary, upending audience sympathies and interrogating storytelling, perception and the media’s appetite for scandal.
- Direction and tone: Fincher employs his characteristic meticulous, downbeat style, supported by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’s score and strong technical craft (cinematography, editing). The film is darkly comic at times and explicitly satirical about cable-news sensationalism.
- Performances: Rosamund Pike receives high praise for a complex, icy role; Affleck captures Nick’s likeable-but-uneasy surface; Tyler Perry, Carrie Coon and Kim Dickens provide notable supporting turns (Coon singled out as a revelation).
- Criticisms: Some reviewers find the central characters insufficiently lived-in—Amy can feel more engineered than organic—and argue the film loses momentum or logical coherence in its final act, turning a brilliant first two hours into a less satisfying conclusion. Others celebrate its suspense, wit and emotional acuity, calling it both brutal and darkly funny.
- Overall: A technically assured, provocative thriller that sparks debate about marriage, media and truth, even if opinions diverge about the payoff.

(The Two Faces of January and The Blue Room are noted briefly: the former, adapted from Patricia Highsmith, is described as stylishly dressed; the latter, from Georges Simenon, is the most overtly French in tone. The piece groups all three as stories where seemingly happy marriages begin to crack and violence creeps out of the fractures.)

Scientists and the NGO APOPO are expanding the use of trained African giant pouched rats to screen for tuberculosis (TB) in crowded, high-risk settings in East Africa, starting with prisons in Tanzania and Mozambique. APOPO — known for training rats to detect landmines — has developed “HeroRATs” that are conditioned to sniff sputum samples and indicate the presence of TB. The rats begin training at about four weeks old, are ready for diagnostic work by nine months, and can screen roughly 100 samples in 20 minutes. APOPO says the rats’ detection accuracy is nearly 100% for TB presence (though they cannot differentiate drug-resistant strains) and that the method is far faster and cheaper than conventional sputum smear microscopy: a rat-screening can cost about $0.20 per sample when scaled.

APOPO’s TB detection programs have screened over 340,000 samples so far, reportedly preventing tens of thousands of subsequent infections and increasing detection rates by more than 40% in partner clinics. With funding from the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), the group plans to recruit and train more rats to expand prison screenings and eventually target other congested environments (shantytowns, factories) and high-risk populations such as people living with HIV/AIDS.

Public-health officials highlight the need: TB remains a leading infectious killer after HIV, with about 9 million new cases and 2 million deaths annually (WHO figures), and incarceration substantially raises TB risk — studies cited by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show prison TB rates in parts of Africa can be about 10 times higher than the general population. Conventional sputum microscopy is slow, costly, and limited in throughput; the World Health Organization recommends a technician test no more than 20 patients daily to avoid diagnostic errors. APOPO and Tanzanian health experts argue trained rats offer a practical, low-cost mass-screening tool to find undiagnosed cases more quickly, especially where laboratory capacity is limited.

The article also describes daily life for the rats — socialization, rewards (e.g., banana bits) and welfare practices including health checks and voluntary retirement — noting their relatively long lifespan (about eight years) and the humane approach APOPO uses in training and care.

An Indonesian Trigana Air Service ATR 42-300 twin‑turboprop flying from Jayapura to Oksibil lost contact on Sunday about half an hour into the short flight. Rescue teams located smoldering wreckage on a steep, forested mountainside in Papua province two days later; bad weather and rugged terrain delayed access. All 54 people aboard (49 passengers, including children, and five crew) were killed. Rescuers recovered all bodies, many badly burned and difficult to identify, and recovered the flight data and cockpit voice recorders in good condition. Among the dead were postal workers escorting about $470,000 in government aid and several local officials. Authorities have opened an investigation but have not released a cause; heavy rain, fog and mountainous terrain are considered possible factors. The crash adds to Indonesia’s recent poor safety record and ongoing challenges in aviation oversight.

Journalists and online reaction agreed that the opening night of the Democratic National Convention (DNC) felt far more energetic and enthusiastic than many expected — and noticeably livelier than the Republican convention the previous week. Multiple outlets (CNN, Politico, BuzzFeed, The Atlantic, NBC, The Washington Post, Salon, DailyKos, TPM) described palpable enthusiasm in the hall, saying the DNC’s tone and crowd passion made even non-primetime speeches land stronger. A minority voice (Laura Ingraham) disagreed. 

Michelle Obama’s prime-time address — focused on her husband and contrasting him with the Republican nominee — dominated social media. Her speech generated a peak of 28,003 tweets per minute (about double Mitt Romney’s peak), included many quotable, tweetable lines (notably “Being president doesn't change who you are. It reveals who you are.”), and helped push the convention’s total to over 3 million tweets by night’s end, approaching the Republican convention’s overall volume. Reactions on Twitter ranged from praise and inspiration to criticism, but overall the night was viewed as a successful, high-energy start to the DNC.

The weekend box office was led by The Angry Birds Movie, which opened at No. 1 with an estimated $39 million — the third-best animated debut of 2016 behind Zootopia and Kung Fu Panda 3. The family comedy, based on the popular mobile game and budgeted at $73 million, features voices like Jason Sudeikis and Sean Penn. Critics were lukewarm (42% on Rotten Tomatoes) but audiences were more favorable (61% liked it). Analysts credited the film’s brand recognition and strong family turnout for its success, despite a roughly 25% weaker overall weekend box office versus last year.

Captain America: Civil War slipped to No. 2 in its third week with $33.1 million, bringing its domestic total to $347.4 million and pushing its worldwide haul past $1 billion. Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising opened at No. 3 with $21.8 million — a solid but much smaller debut than the original — while Shane Black’s The Nice Guys exceeded expectations with $11.3 million in fourth. Disney’s live-action The Jungle Book rounded out the top five with $11 million, lifting its cumulative domestic gross to about $327.5 million. Final weekend totals were to be confirmed Monday.

Apple’s 2012 iPad (marketed simply as “the new iPad”) is an iterative but meaningful upgrade that reinforces Apple’s lead in tablets by improving two core aspects: the display and cellular speed—while keeping battery life and pricing much the same.

Key upgrades
- Retina display: A 9.7-inch “retina” screen at 2048 x 1536 (four times the pixels of the iPad 2) yields dramatically sharper text and richer images; Apple also increased color saturation. The effect is striking side-by-side with the iPad 2, though some third‑party apps must be updated to fully benefit.
- Faster cellular (4G LTE): Optional LTE models (AT&T and Verizon variants) deliver download speeds often faster than many home broadband connections and support personal hotspot/tethering (Verizon enabled initially). 4G usage can increase data consumption and may impact battery.
- Improved camera and video: A 5‑megapixel rear iSight camera captures 1080p video, adds face detection, low‑light performance and video stabilization. No flash, and using a tablet as a camera remains awkward for many.
- Dictation: Speech‑to‑text (the dictation portion of Siri) is present via a microphone key, but full Siri functionality is not included.
- Performance and battery: A new A5X chip with quad‑core graphics powers the Retina display and keeps the interface smooth. Battery life remains close to prior models—around 9–10 hours—thanks to a larger battery and power optimizations, at the cost of a slight increase in weight/thickness (about 8% heavier, 7% thicker than iPad 2).
- Storage and pricing: Available in 16/32/64 GB, Wi‑Fi models start at $499; Wi‑Fi + cellular models cost more (up to $829). The iPad 2 stays in the lineup at a reduced $399 entry price. Note: Retina-ready apps use much more storage, which can fill non-expandable capacity faster.

Pros
- Stunning, industry-leading display
- Much faster cellular data on LTE models
- Strong app ecosystem with 200,000+ iPad-specific apps
- Improved camera, dictation, and good battery life

Cons and limitations
- No full Siri, no camera flash, no expandable storage
- Slightly heavier/thicker
- Some apps and streaming services (e.g., Netflix) may not yet exploit the Retina screen or HD playback; Retina assets increase app storage demands
- Pricier than smaller, budget tablets (e.g., Kindle Fire)

Who should buy?
- Owners of the original iPad who want better screen, cameras and speed: a clear upgrade.
- iPad 2 owners: worthwhile but less urgent—the improvements are notable but may not justify an immediate purchase.
- New tablet buyers who prioritize screen quality, app selection and overall performance and don’t mind the price: the new iPad remains the best general-purpose tablet choice.

Overall conclusion
The new iPad isn’t a radical reinvention but it significantly sharpens the device’s core strengths—display and connectivity—while preserving battery life and the strong app ecosystem, ensuring Apple retains the crown in tablets.

An assistant executive engineer in the Central Public Works Department (CPWD), A.K. Verma, who joined in 1980, was dismissed after remaining absent from duty since December 1990. Verma went on earned leave in December 1990, repeatedly sought extensions that were not sanctioned, defied orders to return and did not cooperate with a disciplinary inquiry that began in 1992. A fresh charge sheet was issued in 2005; the inquiry report finding him guilty of wilful absence was submitted in July 2007 and accepted in August 2007, but no further action was taken until Urban Development Minister M. Venkaiah Naidu ordered his dismissal in 2015 following a review of pending vigilance and disciplinary cases. The minister has also directed officials to fix responsibility for the long delay. The case has been cited alongside wider concerns about absenteeism and accountability in India’s bureaucracy and recent efforts by the government to improve attendance.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un used his New Year’s speech to both boast of his country’s growing nuclear capabilities and signal willingness to engage with South Korea. He said a “nuclear button” is “always on my desk,” claimed the entire United States is within range of North Korean weapons, and reiterated plans to mass-produce warheads and ballistic missiles for operational deployment — while asserting they would be used only if North Korea’s security is threatened. Experts note Pyongyang’s capabilities have advanced but remain uncertain in full operational effectiveness.

At the same time Kim adopted a markedly softer tone toward Seoul, calling for reduced military tensions, offering to open dialogue, and saying he would consider sending a delegation to next February’s PyeongChang Winter Olympics. South Korea welcomed the possibility; officials and analysts said such a move could help lower tensions and might be intended to drive a wedge between Seoul and Washington or alleviate economic pressure from sanctions. The U.S. response was muted: President Trump said only, “We’ll see, we’ll see.”

Observers urged diplomacy, noting sanctions and isolation alone are unlikely to reverse North Korea’s program and that the Olympics offer a potential opportunity to begin talks that reduce the risk of miscalculation.

Environmentalists criticize bottled water largely for its wasteful packaging; about 50 billion mostly plastic bottles are discarded yearly. The International Bottled Water Association (IBWA) commissioned a study — the first of its kind for the industry — finding that North American bottled-water producers use about 1.39 liters of water to produce one liter of bottled water. The IBWA cites that result to argue bottled water is comparatively efficient: by their figures a liter of soda uses ~2.02 L, beer ~4 L, wine ~4.74 L and distilled spirits ~34.55 L.

Water experts say such comparisons understate the full “water footprint.” The Water Footprint Network’s Ertug Ercin and others argue a true footprint must include all freshwater used across the supply chain, especially packaging. Producing plastic bottles (and the oil extraction and processing behind them) and paper labels consumes additional water — estimates suggest making a 0.5 L bottle’s packaging could require around 3 L of water, meaning packaging water use can exceed the bottled volume itself. Even so, packaging-related water for bottled water is likely lower than the agricultural and processing water embedded in sugary sodas.

IBWA spokesman Chris Hogan responds that tracing every upstream input can be open-ended and that companies are working to improve efficiency because water is central to their business. The debate underscores a broader trend: beverage companies are beginning to measure water footprints more systematically to identify conservation opportunities.

The document is a collection of entertainment news items focused mainly on Madonna’s controversial MDNA tour and a shorter theater piece about actress Jennifer Westfeldt.

Jennifer Westfeldt and Greg Kinnear are beginning performances of the play The Power of Duff at Vassar’s Powerhouse Theater; Westfeldt joked about past summer-camp memories and confirmed boyfriend Jon Hamm has visited the campus.

The bulk of the piece covers multiple controversies and reactions surrounding Madonna’s MDNA tour:
- In Poland, a Catholic youth group (Youth Crusade) is petitioning Warsaw officials to cancel Madonna’s 1 August concert because it coincides with the city’s World War II Warsaw Uprising remembrance day. Protesters accuse Madonna of disrespecting religious symbols, promoting homosexuality and pornography, and point to past provocative acts (cross-burning imagery, crown of thorns).
- At Hyde Park in London Madonna performed a provocative show including a striptease during “Like a Virgin,” briefly revealing a sheer bra and black thong. Celebrity attendees included Kylie Minogue and Stella McCartney. Reviews were mixed: some praised the show and large-scale production, while many fans complained about poor sound, bad weather, a 10:30 pm curfew that forced an early daytime start, high ticket prices, and a limited selection of classic hits—leading hundreds to walk out and call it one of her worst gigs.
- The tour has drawn wider controversy in Europe for nudity and using Nazi imagery (a swastika superimposed on Jean-Marie Le Pen in a Paris multimedia segment). These incidents have hurt her reputation among conservative critics.
- Madonna cancelled planned Australian MDNA dates—the first Aussie tour in 20 years—after promoters reportedly found the shows unviable amid a crowded summer lineup; ticket pricing and earlier European controversies were noted as issues.

Overall, the document portrays Madonna’s MDNA tour as commercially ambitious but mired in public-relations problems, mixed reception from fans and critics, religious and political backlash in some markets, and at least one major cancellation, while Westfeldt’s theater news provides a lighter, unrelated entertainment note.

U.S. and South Korean militaries have confirmed that the first elements of the U.S. Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system — including missile launchers — have arrived in South Korea as part of plans to deploy the battery this year. The move followed North Korea’s test-launch of four ballistic missiles that flew roughly 1,000 km and landed in waters near Japan, an act Pyongyang framed as a response to ongoing U.S.-South Korea military exercises. Seoul’s defense ministry says it aims to make the system operational as soon as possible; some media report it could be ready by April.

THAAD is designed to intercept short- and medium-range ballistic missiles in their terminal phase using hit‑to‑kill interceptors and an X‑band radar. Washington and Seoul stress the system is defensive and intended to counter North Korean threats. U.S. Pacific Command chief Adm. Harry Harris said the recent North Korean launches reinforced the decision to deploy THAAD.

The deployment has provoked strong opposition from Beijing and Moscow, which argue THAAD’s powerful radar could undermine their strategic deterrents. China warned it will take “necessary measures” to protect its security and said the U.S. and South Korea “will bear the consequences.” Chinese protests have also targeted Lotte, the South Korean company that offered land for THAAD, and Beijing has been accused of informal economic pressure — including reduced Chinese tourism to South Korea and closures of some Lotte outlets — though China denies official retaliation. Domestically in South Korea, there is also opposition and concern that THAAD sites could become targets.

North Korea’s state media framed the missile launches as a demonstration of readiness and deterrence; leader Kim Jong Un reportedly supervised the drills and ordered heightened alert. South Korean authorities assessed the missiles were likely improved Scud-type projectiles capable of reaching Japan and U.S. bases there. The launches prompted regional and international alarm, phone consultations between U.S. and Japanese leaders, and an emergency U.N. Security Council meeting requested by the U.S. and Japan.

A large prospective analysis of Nurses’ Health Study II data finds that alcohol consumption between a woman’s first menstrual period and her first full-term pregnancy is associated with an increased, dose-dependent risk of both proliferative benign breast disease (BBD) and breast cancer later in life.

Key points
- Study population: 91,005 U.S. nurses with at least one full-term pregnancy, followed from 1989 to 2009 (part of NHSII). Researchers identified 1,609 breast cancer cases and 970 BBD diagnoses.
- Exposure window: Alcohol intake between menarche and first pregnancy (reported for several age ranges).
- Risk estimates: Each 10 g/day increase in alcohol (about six drinks/week) was linked to an ~11% higher breast cancer risk compared with nondrinkers; about one drink per day (~4–6 oz wine, one beer, or one shot) raised the risk for proliferative BBD by ~16%. Risk rose with greater intake.
- Pattern: Associations held after adjusting for multiple risk factors (including family history) and were present regardless of whether women drank after their first pregnancy. Longer intervals between menarche and first pregnancy showed stronger associations.
- Interpretation: The study shows an association, not definitive causation. Authors suggest breast tissue is more vulnerable to environmental exposures before first pregnancy, and BBD may be one pathway linking early-life alcohol exposure to later breast cancer.
- Clinical context: Baseline lifetime breast cancer risk is ~12% (one in eight); an 11% relative increase raises that to roughly 13% in absolute terms. Experts emphasize dose dependence and recommend moderation, advising women in the studied age range to limit drinking to less than one drink per day—especially before first pregnancy—to reduce risk.

Source: Journal of the National Cancer Institute (reported by HealthDay).

President Trump used a North Dakota rally supporting Republican Rep. Kevin Cramer to stress how Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy’s retirement makes control of the Senate “vital” for Republicans. Trump praised Kennedy and said he was honored Kennedy chose to retire during his term, arguing the vacancy gives him a chance to name a long-serving, intellectually strong conservative replacement who could shape the court for decades.

Trump tied the vacancy directly to the upcoming midterms, urging voters to protect the GOP Senate majority so his nominee will be confirmed. He attacked Democratic incumbent Sen. Heidi Heitkamp—who is facing Cramer in a key pickup opportunity—as someone who would oppose his Supreme Court picks, even though Heitkamp was one of three Democrats who voted to confirm Neil Gorsuch last year. He framed Heitkamp as aligned with national Democratic leaders and said she would revert to party-line votes after election-year cooperation.

Heitkamp responded that she answers to North Dakotans, not the president or party, and emphasized her willingness to work with the administration when it benefits the state. The broader political stakes: Republicans hold a narrow 51–49 Senate edge, with Sen. John McCain absent, and several moderate GOP senators (Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski) and centrist Democrats (Heitkamp, Joe Manchin, Joe Donnelly) could be pivotal on confirmation votes. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell signaled he wants a confirmation vote this fall, intensifying pressure on vulnerable red-state Democrats and underscoring how Kennedy’s retirement has elevated the midterms’ importance. The report also lists potential nominees from the White House’s previously released list of 25.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) alerted the FBI after detecting what it initially believed was a sophisticated attempt to breach its voter database. Early Tuesday, a cloud provider and a security research firm notified the DNC that a fraudulent login page had been created to mimic Votebuilder — the service used by Democratic officials and campaigns to access the party’s voter-file database — apparently aiming to harvest usernames and passwords. The DNC and the detecting companies say they believe the operation was thwarted. Late Wednesday the DNC updated that the incident was actually an unauthorized “simulated phishing test.”

DNC chief security officer Bob Lord called the voter file “the party’s most sensitive information,” and warned the attempt underscores ongoing threats as the midterm elections approach. Security experts note the episode, along with continued Russian influence operations on social media and other efforts to breach institutions, illustrates how cyber tactics have shifted from stealing secrets to exerting national power and manipulating many vulnerable systems tied to elections — from state voter-registration systems to party databases. Microsoft recently reported Russian-linked hackers targeted the Senate and conservative think tanks with fake websites, and Facebook has disclosed multiple disinformation campaigns aimed at disrupting the midterms and other global audiences.

A tourist ferry carrying about 170 people capsized Sunday, June 25, 2017, on the Guatapé reservoir near Medellín, Colombia. The four‑story party boat El Almirante sank in roughly four minutes during a busy holiday weekend. Rescuers, including firefighters and air force crews, and nearby recreational boaters and jet skis pulled survivors from the water. Authorities said 99 people were rescued, about 40 reached shore on their own, nine bodies have been recovered and roughly 28 people remain missing. Survivors reported the vessel appeared overloaded and that no one on board was wearing life vests. Officials set up a shore rescue center, called for scuba divers, and have not yet determined the cause of the sinking. The reservoir around the El Peñol rock is a popular weekend destination about an hour from Medellín.

A day of largely peaceful Occupy protests in Oakland that included a multi-hour march to and shutdown of the Port of Oakland devolved after midnight into violent clashes, vandalism and mass arrests. Several thousand demonstrators had converged for a general strike and port action to highlight economic inequality; organizers called it a victory and police estimated about 7,000 people participated during the day. Smaller solidarity actions occurred in New York, Philadelphia, Boston, Los Angeles and elsewhere.

Late Wednesday a much smaller group seized a vacant two-story building near the Frank Ogawa Plaza encampment, erected barricades, spray-painted graffiti and smashed windows at downtown businesses. Masked individuals set large trash fires and witnesses reported projectiles—bottles, rocks, concrete chunks, metal pipes, fireworks and, police said, some Molotov cocktails—thrown at officers. Police, who had been criticized for earlier crowd-control tactics after an Iraq War veteran was seriously injured in an Oakland clash the prior week, moved in shortly before midnight, declared an unlawful assembly, and used tear gas and flash-bang grenades. Dozens were arrested; at least four protesters were hospitalized (one needing stitches) and several officers sustained minor injuries.

Accounts diverged over responsibility and escalation. Police described a dangerous, violent fringe that warranted intervention; many protesters said police provoked or escalated the situation and criticized the use of gas. Within the crowd there were disputes: some demonstrators condemned the vandalism and tried to stop fires and property destruction, while others defended confrontational tactics as necessary to draw attention.

The unrest raised concerns about economic impacts (port operations were halted, affecting workers and revenue) and renewed debate over the movement’s direction—both its growing reach and its lack of centralized organization. Nationwide, protests highlighted issues from corporate influence and war profiteering to student debt; veterans marched in New York in solidarity with injured activists in Oakland.

Angel Gonzalez, a 41-year-old Mexican national, was released from Illinois prison after nearly 20 years when authorities vacated his 1994 Waukegan rape and abduction conviction and a separate prison property-damage conviction. New DNA testing on evidence from the 1994 attack identified genetic profiles of two unidentified men and excluded Gonzalez, prompting Lake County State’s Attorney Mike Nerheim to seek to throw out the conviction. The Innocence Project and the Illinois Innocence Project had pursued the case; earlier testing and investigative flaws had already cast doubt on the original prosecution, which relied on a contested “show-up” identification and a confession obtained after long custody.

Gonzalez had remained incarcerated because of a later conviction for damaging a sink while in solitary; that charge was dismissed in Livingston County, clearing the way for his immediate release. Immigration and Customs Enforcement lifted a detainer, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services was reviewing his immigration status; his lawyers argued deportation would be unjust because his prior legal status unraveled only after the wrongful conviction. Family members described emotional reunions and plans to celebrate, and lawyers and advocates noted Gonzalez used his prison time to study, earn a diploma, mentor other inmates and paint. Prosecutors apologized publicly for the case; the decision to clear Gonzalez is part of a series of recent Lake County reversals after DNA evidence undermined prior convictions.

Bellingcat and investigative partner The Insider say the man Britain identified as “Ruslan Boshirov,” one of two suspects in the March 2018 Novichok poisoning of former double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter in Salisbury, is actually Colonel Anatoliy Vladimirovich Chepiga, a highly decorated officer in Russia’s military intelligence (GRU).

Key findings
- Identity: Open-source research, leaked databases and a passport file photo link Boshirov’s cover identity to Anatoliy Chepiga, born 5 April 1979, from Nikolaevka in Amur oblast.
- Service and awards: Chepiga trained at the Far-Eastern Military Command Academy, served in the GRU’s 14th Spetsnaz Brigade, was deployed to Chechnya (and likely to eastern Ukraine), and reportedly received over 20 military awards. In December 2014 he was secretly awarded Hero of the Russian Federation, a top state honor typically bestowed by the president.
- Cover and travel: Bellingcat says Chepiga was relocated to Moscow and given the alias Ruslan Boshirov around 2009, working undercover for years. UK police say “Boshirov” and a second man, using the name Alexander Petrov, flew from Moscow to Gatwick on 2 March, visited Salisbury on 3–4 March (the date of the Skripal poisoning) and returned the same day. European arrest warrants/Interpol notices have been issued.
- Significance: The identification undermines Russian claims that the two were ordinary civilians and corroborates UK assertions they were GRU operatives acting on a government mission. Bellingcat’s sources argued sending a colonel — and a Hero of the Russian Federation — into such an operation suggests it was ordered at a very high level.

Responses and context
- Russia: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov and other officials deny the allegation, calling the suspects civilians; the two men appeared on Russian TV claiming to be tourists. State TV largely ignored Bellingcat’s claims, while private media covered them.
- UK government: Officials say the attack was state-approved. The incident prompted diplomatic expulsions, sanctions and condemnation by UK leaders; one unrelated death (Dawn Sturgess) later occurred after exposure to the same nerve agent.
- Bellingcat’s methods: The group used image searches, leaked databases, yearbooks, contacts with former officers and passport records to connect Boshirov to Chepiga and to establish his military background.

Bellingcat concludes that the man presented as a civilian was in fact a senior GRU officer, which, they say, reinforces the view that the Salisbury poisoning was a clandestine state operation.

The Fourth Kind is a 98-minute “found footage” horror film written and directed by Olatunde Osunsanmi, starring Milla Jovovich, Elias Koteas and Will Patton. Presented as a dramatization of alleged real events in Nome, Alaska, it frames Jovovich as an actress playing Dr. Abigail Tyler, an Alaska psychologist and hypnotherapist who investigates a string of mysterious awakenings, sleep disturbances and alleged alien abductions. The film alternates between staged reenactments, purported archival footage of hypnotized patients thrashing and levitating, and interview clips of the “real” Dr. Tyler—an approach meant to heighten verisimilitude but that often calls its authenticity into question.

The story’s central motif is patients reporting a smiling owl as an omen before being taken and having their memories erased; Tyler herself becomes a victim, discovering strange wounds and demonic voices on tapes. The production borrows heavily from Paranormal Activity and The Blair Witch Project, using split screens and grainy footage to create scares—some genuinely effective, many cheap. Will Patton plays an exasperated sheriff; Jovovich gives a notably restrained, strong performance amid the film’s hybrid mock-doc/recreation format.

Critics note that the faux-documentary conceit and unconvincing “archival” material undercut immersion, making it feel like a formula horror picture despite periodic thrills. The title refers to the “fourth kind” (alien abduction) on the close-encounter scale. Overall reception: mixed — solid jump-scares and a good turn from Jovovich but a flawed execution and dubious true-story framing, earning a middling grade.

Heather McGill, wife of Alabama State Sen. Shadrack McGill (R-Woodville), posted an outspoken message on his official Facebook page accusing multiple women—some possibly fake—of privately soliciting her husband with explicit photos and messages while their children might view the account. She warned she would publicly name offenders before unfriending them, framed her response as protecting her family and faith, and said she hoped the message would bolster marriages and families. 

Sen. McGill later told AL.com the post reflected frustrations built up since his 2010 campaign, when two strippers allegedly came to his home late at night and other women approached him in person. He also said his Facebook has been “hijacked” several times by women sending semi-nude photos and false claims. He praised his wife’s actions in the post’s comments and said he may stop using Facebook if such behavior continues. The post drew dozens of supportive comments and hundreds of “likes.”

NCAA and Ohio State announced suspensions for six Buckeyes after a university investigation, prompted by a federal probe of a local tattoo-parlor owner, found the players sold team memorabilia and received improper benefits.

Primary sanctions
- Five players—QB Terrelle Pryor, WR DeVier Posey, RB Dan (Daniel) Herron, LT Mike Adams and DE Solomon Thomas—will be suspended for the first five games of the 2011 season.  
- LB Jordan Whiting will be suspended one game.  
- All six are eligible to play in the Sugar Bowl on Jan. 4; the NCAA allowed bowl-game participation under its suspension policy and because the school did not adequately educate players about the rules when violations occurred.

Nature of violations and restitution
- The violations involved accepting discounted tattoo services and selling OSU items (championship rings, jerseys, shoes, awards, “gold pants,” etc.) to the tattoo-parlor owner beginning in 2009.  
- Each player must repay the assessed value to charity to regain eligibility:
  - Terrelle Pryor: $2,500 (2008 Big Ten ring, 2009 Fiesta Bowl sportsmanship award, 2008 Gold Pants)  
  - DeVier Posey: $1,250 (2008 Big Ten ring sold for $1,200; $50 in discounted services)  
  - Dan Herron: $1,150 (jersey/pants/shoes sold for $1,000; $150 in discounted services)  
  - Solomon Thomas: $1,505 (2008 ring sold for $1,000; Gold Pants $350; $155 in discounted services)  
  - Mike Adams: $1,000 (2008 Big Ten ring)  
  - Jordan Whiting: $150 (discounted services)

Reactions and next steps
- Ohio State AD Gene Smith said the school will appeal the game suspensions, calling them severe but acknowledging sanctions were warranted. Smith and coach Jim Tressel expressed responsibility and noted the university could have been clearer in educating players about rules.  
- The U.S. Attorney’s office told OSU the matter is not a criminal case with respect to the players and is not related to agent/booster activity.

Ariel Castro, a former Cleveland school bus driver, was sentenced on Aug. 1, 2013 to life without parole plus 1,000 years after pleading guilty to 937 counts including kidnapping, rape, assault and aggravated murder for crimes committed against three women—Michelle Knight, Amanda Berry and Georgina "Gina" DeJesus—who were held captive in his home for roughly a decade. The women, abducted separately between 2002 and 2004 when they were 14, 16 and 20, escaped on May 6, 2013 after Berry kicked out a door panel and cried for help.

Prosecutors and witnesses described systematic, prolonged sexual, physical and emotional abuse: the victims were chained by ankles to poles, heaters or bolted fixtures; starved and beaten; forced to wear helmets; repeatedly raped (vaginally, orally and anally); and one woman was brutally forced to miscarry five times. Castro fathered a daughter with one victim and compelled another victim to deliver the child under threat of death. He then attended vigils for the missing women and otherwise masked the prison-like configuration of his house—boarding windows, removing doorknobs, installing locks and wiring alarms—to conceal them.

Court testimony and victim diaries recounted the daily horrors and long-term trauma; mental health experts described the captivity as severe, unprecedented and permanently scarring. Castro repeatedly minimized or denied the severity of his actions in court, calling himself "sick" rather than a violent predator; experts found no psychiatric illness that would diminish responsibility. As part of his plea deal—which removed the death penalty—he forfeited the house and was fined. Victim Michelle Knight delivered a powerful impact statement telling Castro he had taken 11 years of her life and that he would "die a little every day." The case drew widespread attention to the victims’ resilience and to failures that allowed the crimes to go undetected for years.

Amal Ahmad Abdul Fateh, a 30-year-old widow of Osama bin Laden who was wounded in the May 2011 U.S. raid that killed him, gave Pakistani investigators a detailed account of the family’s movements during the nine years bin Laden spent hiding in Pakistan after 2001. Her statements, recorded in a Jan. 19 police report, trace how bin Laden, his wives and children moved among five safe houses across Pakistan—often with help from Pashtun hosts—and provide new detail about where and when several of his children were born.

Key points:
- Fateh said she married bin Laden in 2000, joined him in Afghanistan, then dispersed with the family after Sept. 11. She returned to Karachi with a newborn and they subsequently changed residences multiple times, brokered by a Pakistani family and bin Laden’s son Saad.
- From late 2002 the family moved through northwestern Pakistan but not primarily in the tribal areas. They lived in Shangla (Swat) for around eight to nine months, then in Haripur for about two years, where two children (Aasia in 2003 and Ibrahim in 2004) were born in a government hospital—allegedly using false identity papers and very short hospital stays.
- In mid-2005 they moved to Abbottabad, about 20 miles east of Haripur; there Fateh gave birth to Zainab (2006) and Hussain (2008).
- Fateh identified two Pashtun brothers, Ibrahim and Abrar (the former believed to be Abu Ahmed al-Kuwaiti, the “courier” long tracked by U.S. intelligence), as hosts who organized houses in Swat, Haripur and Abbottabad. When U.S. Navy SEALs raided the Abbottabad compound in May 2011, they killed bin Laden and the courier, his wife Bushra, Abrar, and bin Laden’s son Khalid; Fateh was shot in the leg and survived.
- Bin Laden’s three widows are under house arrest in Islamabad and likely to face charges over immigration violations; two adult daughters may also be charged. Pakistani police had earlier recommended deportation of the wives but prosecutors opted to detain them, which analysts say may reflect intelligence or investigative motives and U.S. interest in interviewing the women.
- Fateh’s account suggests U.S. military forces may have come near bin Laden as early as late 2005 (noting U.S. Chinook relief flights into Pakistan after the October 2005 earthquake). Some details in the police report are paraphrased and contain gaps, and U.S. officials said the report broadly aligns with known intelligence but could not confirm every element.

Overall, the testimony provides the most detailed public chronology so far of bin Laden’s domestic concealment in Pakistan, raises questions about local assistance and the security services’ awareness, and underscores why his family members are of keen intelligence interest.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data show substantial weight gains in the U.S. since 1960. The average American woman now weighs 166.2 lb—about the same as the average American man did in the early 1960s—while the average American man has risen from 166.3 lb in 1960 to 195.5 lb today. Women’s weight increased about 18.5% and men’s about 17.6%; both sexes are roughly an inch taller than in 1960, which explains some but not all of the rise.

Current measures of central obesity are large: average waist circumferences are about 39.7 inches for men and 37.5 inches for women. CDC figures also show that 35.1% of U.S. adults 20+ are obese and 69% are overweight or obese. Child obesity is high as well: 17.7% of 6–11-year-olds and over 20% of 12–19-year-olds are obese.

A 2012 BMC Public Health study ranks Americans as the world’s third-heaviest population (after Tonga and Micronesia). The average U.S. adult is roughly 33 lb heavier than the average French adult and about 70 lb heavier than the average Bangladeshi. Globally, adults totaled 287 million tons of biomass in 2005; if every country matched U.S. weight distribution, the world would be about 58 million tons heavier. The studies suggest that population fatness has implications for food security and ecological sustainability and point to diet and activity changes as primary drivers of rising weights.

Pulaski County, Va., authorities found the body of 5-year-old Noah Thomas in a septic tank on his family’s property Thursday, five days after he was reported missing. The medical examiner has completed an autopsy, but the cause of death is pending and no timetable was given for results. No arrests, suspects or charges have been announced; investigators say the probe will focus on facts and physical evidence and are asking the public for tips. The FBI is providing forensic support, and authorities say the family is cooperating. Police had searched roughly a 10-mile radius before locating Noah on the property during a more detailed search. Relatives have expressed suspicion of foul play, and a candlelight vigil was planned in his memory.

A demonstration iPhone 4S at a Tesco in the U.K. spoke an expletive-laden insult to 12-year-old Charlie Le Quesne after she asked Siri, “How many people are there in the world?” The girl’s mother heard the same profanity repeat when they asked again. Tesco said the handset was returned to Apple for diagnosis and is investigating; store staff suggested pranksters may have entered the rude phrase as the device owner’s name during setup, which could explain why Siri used it in reply. The incident joins other examples of Siri’s unexpected or cheeky responses—some humorous, some controversial (including earlier criticisms about search-result omissions)—and highlights how user-configured data and system behavior can produce surprising outputs.

A deal by Muqtada al‑Sadr’s Shiite movement to back incumbent Prime Minister Nouri al‑Maliki has shifted Iraq’s prolonged post-election stalemate and could hand Maliki another term, but it also heightens tensions at home and with the United States.

Key points:
- After March’s inconclusive parliamentary elections, months of negotiations left no clear government. Al‑Sadr’s bloc — which gained 39 seats and has risen politically despite its militia’s violent past and the cleric’s exile in Iran — publicly endorsed al‑Maliki, boosting his parliamentary support though he still needs additional votes to reach a majority.
- The Sadrists demand influential posts (deputy parliamentary speaker and several cabinet ministries), including control of service ministries and at least one security-related agency, enabling patronage and expanded influence. Sadrist leaders signal a long-term strategy to vie for the premiership after U.S. forces withdraw.
- The pact alarms Washington and many Iraqi opponents: the U.S. has long distrusted al‑Sadr and opposes giving his movement government power because of its militia history and ties to Iran. U.S. officials warn an administration dependent on Sadrists could tilt toward Tehran.
- The agreement risks splintering the broader Shiite coalition; key Shiite parties (e.g., the Islamic Supreme Council) and Ayad Allawi’s Iraqiya bloc oppose Maliki’s continued leadership. Iraqiya, which won the most seats (91), threatens to boycott a government dominated by Maliki and Sadrists.
- Kurds (about 57 seats) remain the likely kingmakers. They have signaled conditional support for Maliki only if their demands (territorial, economic, political concessions and inclusion of Iraqiya elements) are met.
- Security concerns are acute: the political deadlock has been linked to a rise in insurgent attacks, and some U.S. commanders have blamed Shiite extremist groups, including Sadrist affiliates, for recent attacks near the Green Zone.
- The outcome remains uncertain. Maliki has increased leverage but still faces rival coalitions and must assemble a broadly inclusive government to be seen as legitimate both domestically and internationally.

Overall, the Sadrist endorsement gives Maliki a critical boost but deepens domestic political fractures and international unease, leaving Iraq’s path to a stable, inclusive government unresolved.

CNN reports that President Trump sent a $25,000 personal check to the family of Army Cpl. Dillon Baldridge, who was killed in June by an Afghan police officer. The payment came the same day The Washington Post said Trump had promised Baldridge’s father a personal donation during a condolence call but initially did not follow through. White House spokespeople confirmed the check was sent, called the gesture sincere, and said a multistep interagency process delayed its delivery; they did not identify the agencies.

The story appears amid broader controversy over how Trump handles condolence calls to families of service members killed in action. That includes a dispute over Trump’s call to Myeshia Johnson, widow of Sgt. La David Johnson (killed in Niger), after Rep. Frederica Wilson quoted the president as making an insensitive remark Trump denies saying. The White House also faced scrutiny after Trump suggested President Obama did not call all bereaved families and pointed reporters to Chief of Staff John Kelly—whose son died in Afghanistan—on the question.

This document defends the documentary The Hunting Ground and summarizes two central cases presented in the film (Kamilah Willingham at Harvard Law and Erica Kinsman at Florida State), outlines institutional responses, legal outcomes, and related controversy.

Key points

Purpose and response
- Filmmakers and producers (Kirby Dick, Amy Ziering) reject critics who challenge the film’s findings and the credibility of its survivors, saying “the truth is on our side.” They invited viewers to judge for themselves and stood by survivors’ accounts.
- The film has drawn aggressive pushback from accused parties, some university officials, and a group of Harvard Law professors who say the film misrepresents facts. Jameis Winston’s attorneys threatened libel suits and asked CNN not to air the film; CNN aired it anyway.

Kamilah Willingham (Harvard Law) — summary of allegations and procedures
- Allegation: January 15, 2011 — Willingham reported that Harvard Law student Brandon Winston sexually assaulted her and her friend; she filed a police report on Jan 18, 2011.
- Harvard process: Willingham filed a complaint with the Harvard Law Administrative Board (April 2011). An independent fact-finder found Winston not credible and concluded Willingham did not give affirmative consent; the Administrative Board found Winston initiated sexual contact with an unconscious complainant and with an incapacitated friend, and imposed dismissal (Sept. 2011).
- Appeal: Harvard Law’s appeal/review process was criticized for multiple Title IX violations — Willingham was excluded or not interviewed at various stages; faculty later voted to overturn the findings and reinstate Winston. The Department of Education later required Harvard Law to change its appeal process in a 2014 settlement; the DOE highlighted one unnamed case as a reason for change, likely Willingham’s.
- Criminal proceedings: A grand jury later indicted Winston on two felony counts related to Willingham’s friend; in March 2015 a jury convicted Winston of non-sexual assault (misdemeanor nonsexual assault in reporting).

Erica Kinsman (Florida State University) — summary of allegations and investigation
- Allegation: Early morning Dec. 7, 2012 — Kinsman reported she was raped after drinking at a local bar; a rape kit was administered and bruises documented.
- Police and university investigation timeline: The New York Times and the film report major investigative delays and failures: investigators did not promptly obtain video, interview key witnesses, or collect DNA; Kinsman later identified Jameis Winston in class; police did not interview Winston promptly and closed the case in Feb. 2013 citing alleged uncooperativeness (which Kinsman denies).
- Later developments: Nearly a year later, state investigators obtained DNA evidence and witness interviews; in Dec. 2013 prosecutors declined to charge Winston. FSU’s internal proceedings were delayed and criticized for failing to promptly investigate or meet with Kinsman; a university hearing was held in Dec. 2014 in which Kinsman answered many questions while Winston largely refused to answer.
- Legal actions: Kinsman has sued Winston for sexual battery; Winston has counterclaimed and threatened defamation actions related to the film.

Broader context and statistics
- The film frames these cases as examples of how colleges mishandle sexual assault complaints. The document cites multiple studies estimating that roughly 20–27% of female college students experience unwanted sexual contact while in college (including The Washington Post–Kaiser poll and the 2015 AAU study), plus earlier national estimates.

Outreach and reception
- Filmmakers say they contacted presidents of every college/university mentioned; two presidents agreed to be interviewed, 35 declined or did not respond.
- The film premiered at Sundance, received favorable reviews in some quarters, and was controversial in others. It was shown on CNN despite legal threats and criticism that it omits exculpatory evidence or takes an advocacy stance, charges the filmmakers and some university critics make.

Overall thrust
- The document defends the film’s accuracy and the survivors’ accounts, documents procedural failings and alleged Title IX violations by universities (Harvard Law, FSU) and law enforcement delays, and outlines the disputes, legal threats, and public debate surrounding the film and its subjects.

A veteran meteorologist, Kyle Hunter, has sued CBS and its Los Angeles stations KCBS and KCAL alleging age and sex discrimination in hiring for prime-time weather positions. Hunter — an AMS-certified meteorologist with a geosciences degree and more than 20 years’ experience — says he contacted KCBS after longtime weatherman Johnny Mountain left in 2010 and again sought a KCAL opening, but was ignored or told there was “not an opening for you.” According to the suit, both jobs went to younger female hires (Jackie Johnson at KCBS and Evelyn Taft at KCAL), and the complaint alleges the stations prefer “attractive young women” to boost male viewership, even relaxing AMS certification requirements to hire them.

High-profile attorney Gloria Allred is representing Hunter and frames the case as possibly among the first in which a man alleges employment discrimination on the basis of age and gender in broadcast news. Hunter seeks unspecified and punitive damages plus attorney fees. CBS has called the complaint “frivolous” and said it contains “misstatements of fact” and will defend itself. The lawsuit includes references to station promotion of the female hire and social-media attention to her appearance.

Japanese whisky has taken the top spot in Jim Murray’s 2015 World Whisky Bible, surprising Scottish distillers: Yamazaki Single Malt Sherry Cask 2013 was awarded 97.5/100 and called a “near incredible genius.” It’s the first time in the 12‑year history of the Whisky Bible that a Japanese whisky has topped the list and the first time no Scottish malt made the top five. Murray—who sampled over 4,500 whiskies and personally tasted nearly 1,000—described the result as a “wake up call” for Scotch producers, warning some are producing “drab or mediocre malts” and need “a little dose of humility.” He praised the Yamazaki’s “nose of exquisite boldness” and its “light, teasing spice” finish. The review also named an English whisky (Chapter 14 Not Peated) the best European whisky. Only 18,000 bottles of the winning Yamazaki were produced, selling in limited UK specialist shops for about £100.

Lois Lowry’s 1993 novel The Giver—an influential, middle-school dystopia about a community that sacrifices memory, emotion and choice for enforced “sameness”—was adapted for film in 2014 by director Phillip Noyce. The story follows Jonas (played by Brenton Thwaites), who is chosen as the Receiver of Memory and apprenticed to the Giver (Jeff Bridges). As Jonas absorbs memories of color, love, pain and historical atrocities, he awakens to the moral costs of his society and ultimately makes choices that challenge its rules.

Critics generally say the movie is faithful in broad strokes and visually striking—opening in monochrome and gradually introducing color as Jonas gains perception—and benefits from a strong cast (Bridges, Meryl Streep, Odeya Rush, Alexander Skarsgård, Katie Holmes). Bridges’ committed performance and the film’s quieter, more reflective approach set it apart from louder YA franchises.

However, many reviews find the adaptation falls short. By the time it reached cinemas it felt derivative amid a flood of YA dystopias (The Hunger Games, Divergent, Ender’s Game, The Maze Runner), and the film often flattens the book’s ambiguity into heavy-handed, predictable beats. Key criticisms include underwritten roles (Streep’s Chief Elder and several adult parts), rushed or perfunctory emotional and memory sequences, dated or clumsy visual metaphors, and a tendency to spell things out rather than trust the audience. Some changes—Jonas aged up from 12 to a teen played by a 25-year-old—also frustrated purists. Overall assessments tend to call it a respectable but lackluster adaptation: not a bad film, but one that feels late to the genre and less than the sum of its parts (typical ratings around 2 of 4 stars).

Jacksonville International Airport was evacuated and closed for nearly five hours Tuesday after police found two suspicious packages—one described by officials as having a “destructive nature” that required offsite deactivation by a bomb squad. The evacuation began shortly after 6 p.m.; incoming flights were held on the tarmac and at least one plane preparing to depart was prevented from taking off. Passengers were eventually bused to offsite hotels as transportation became available. Airport and sheriff’s office spokesmen declined to specify which package was dangerous or to confirm media reports of arrests. The airport reopened around 11 p.m.; airlines will determine how to resume operations and handle passengers’ luggage. No injuries were reported.

An unusual and frightening spider outbreak struck Sadiya in Upper Assam beginning the evening of May 8, when swarms of large, aggressive eight-legged spiders descended on Chaulkhowa Nagaon village during a Bihu festival. Many people were bitten; dozens sought treatment at Sadiya Civil Hospital. Two victims—local resident Purnakanta Buragohain and a schoolboy—later died, though doctors and visiting scientists say it is unclear whether venom, allergic reactions, or harmful traditional treatments contributed to the fatalities. Panic spread, officials warned residents to stay indoors at night and discussed fogging, and reports later emerged of a bite incident about 600 km away in Nalbari.

A life-sciences team from Dibrugarh University and researchers from Gauhati University collected specimens on May 22. Preliminary assessments describe the spider as large, tarantula‑like and unusually aggressive—reportedly leaping at and clinging to people when disturbed—but experts have not yet identified the species or tested its venom. Some specialists suggest it might be related to Selenocosmia (a theraphosid/tarantula genus) or resemble other groups such as the black wishbone or funnel‑web spiders; others note Assam historically has no record of venomous spiders, making the appearance puzzling. Possible explanations proposed include a previously undocumented native species, accidental or deliberate introduction, or a localized population surge triggered by environmental changes (flooding and habitat disturbance can provoke unusual spider movements). Specimens were sent to the Indian Society of Arachnology for identification; further investigation is ongoing. Meanwhile, gaps in local healthcare capacity and early reliance on traditional healers complicated patient care, and authorities have been criticized for a slow and inconsistent response.

Researchers at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) are describing a previously unclassified, exceptionally cute deep‑sea octopus in the genus Opisthoteuthis. Specimens have been collected off the California coast since 1990 at depths up to about 1,476 feet, but only recently have scientists recognized this animal as distinct from the similar pink flapjack octopus (Opisthoteuthis californiana). The gelatinous, roughly seven‑inch‑diameter octopus has webbed tentacles that form an umbrella or parachute, large dark “puppy‑dog” eyes relative to its small body, and a pretty pink color. It swims using mantle fins, pulsing its webbed arms, jet propulsion, or combinations of these, and hovers above the seafloor hunting small crustaceans and worms.

Stephanie Bush, a postdoctoral fellow at MBARI who is preparing the species’ formal description, has suggested the playful specific name Opisthoteuthis adorabilis to reflect its appearance. The formal naming process will take time, involving publication, specimen deposition in museums, and detailed study. MBARI has preserved specimens and eggs aiding the work; the discovery highlights the importance of documenting species to better understand and protect ocean ecosystems.

Hillary Clinton accepted the Democratic presidential nomination in Philadelphia, becoming the first woman to top a major party ticket. Her hour-long speech highlighted two main themes: the value of community and cooperation (“Stronger Together”), and a sustained critique of Donald Trump’s temperament, record, and fitness for the presidency. Clinton contrasted her vision—emphasizing families, teachers, first responders, immigrants, veterans, and collective civic effort—with Trump’s “I alone can fix it” rhetoric, accused him of offering empty promises rather than detailed policy, and called out his business failures and overseas manufacturing.

She outlined a policy agenda shaped in part by Bernie Sanders’ primary campaign, pitching debt-free college, immigration and campaign-finance reform, and a stronger social safety net, while reaching out to Sanders’ supporters. Her delivery was described as workmanlike rather than soaring. The emotional high of the night came earlier from Khizr and Ghazala Khan, parents of a Muslim U.S. soldier killed in Iraq, whose rebuke of Trump over his anti-Muslim rhetoric drew widespread attention. Other speakers—veterans, Republicans supporting Clinton, progressive leaders like the Rev. William Barber II, and ex-generals—reinforced themes of patriotism, unity, and a bid to broaden Clinton’s coalition beyond the Democratic base. The convention’s messaging aimed to appeal to moderates, independents, and anti-Trump Republicans, and by the evening the party appeared largely united heading into the general election. The piece also included a separate retrospective anecdote about Lloyd Bentsen’s famous 1988 vice-presidential debate zinger against Dan Quayle.
