Aftab M. Aslam, a 19-year-old Johns Creek man (5'10", 165 lbs., medium-length black hair), was reported missing on April 27 after his family received a text claiming he had been kidnapped. Johns Creek Police, the FBI and the Georgia Bureau of Investigation investigated. They located the phone that sent the text and found Aslam had purchased it and no one else had handled it, leading investigators to suspect he sent the message himself. Aslam returned to his Morton Crossing home unharmed on Sunday evening around 9 p.m., telling police he left voluntarily for personal reasons. Authorities are verifying his account and have not filed charges. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. James Harris at 678-274-8348 or james.harris@johnscreekga.gov.

A piece of metal found near Augusta, Western Australia, was ruled not to be linked to Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 after investigators reviewed detailed photographs. The object, recovered about 1,000 miles from the suspected crash zone and previously labeled an "object of interest," joins a long list of false leads (trash, fishing gear, jellyfish) that have complicated the search for the jet that vanished March 8 with 239 people aboard.

Search operations in the southern Indian Ocean continue under Australian coordination. The U.S. Navy’s Bluefin-21 autonomous underwater vehicle has scanned more than 80–90% of the primary 310‑sq‑km seabed search area and began another mission; overall the vessel still has a small portion of that zone to complete. Poor weather recently grounded air searches, while surface ships and underwater drones have so far found no debris. Authorities note the previously detected acoustic pings consistent with black-box beacons are no longer emitting.

Australian and Malaysian officials say the hunt will continue and may be revised or expanded if the current underwater search yields nothing. Plans under consideration include wider search corridors along the final flight path, use of deeper-ranging side-scan sonar or deep-towed systems (lower resolution but far greater range), and reanalysis of all available data. Australia’s prime minister and other officials stressed they will not stop searching while there is reasonable hope of finding evidence, and Malaysia is assembling an international investigation team (separate from criminal inquiries) to evaluate the cause if wreckage or recorders are recovered.

Researchers revising the chronology of discoveries at Liang Bua cave on Flores, Indonesia, now say the tiny hominin Homo floresiensis—nicknamed “hobbits”—disappeared much earlier than first thought. Originally dated as recently as ~12,000 years ago (raising the possibility of overlap with modern humans), new work using expanded excavations and five independent dating methods (including uranium decay and luminescence) shows the skeletal remains likely date to 100,000–60,000 years ago, while associated stone tools range from about 190,000 to 50,000 years ago. The earlier age resulted from previously unrecognized uneven sedimentation and erosion in the cave that mixed younger deposits into layers near the entrance.

The revision reduces the likelihood of prolonged coexistence with Homo sapiens but intriguingly places the final disappearance of H. floresiensis near the time modern humans first reached the region (~50,000 years ago), leaving open but unproven hypotheses about human involvement. Other possible extinction causes include climate change, volcanic events, or ecosystem collapse following the loss of key prey such as the pygmy Stegodon.

Debate continues over H. floresiensis’s origins and status: whether it was a distinct species (possibly island‑dwarfed descendants of Homo erectus or an earlier hominin) or pathological modern humans. Anatomical evidence—such as wrist morphology—supports a separate species. Further excavations on Flores are needed to clarify their evolution, behavior, and causes of extinction.

The NFL announced it will break its long-standing use of Roman numerals for one year: Super Bowl 50 (Feb. 7, 2016, at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara) will be branded with the Arabic numeral “50” instead of “L.” The change — described as a one-year, aesthetic decision — came after design work (73 logo versions) showed the letter “L” did not work visually. Two official logos were created (national and regional), both featuring a gold “50” to emphasize the game’s golden anniversary and California’s “Golden State” identity, plus the Lombardi Trophy; the regional version adds Levi’s Stadium and San Francisco landmarks. Host-committee lobbying influenced the decision. The NFL says this is temporary: Roman numerals will return for Super Bowl LI in 2017.

Former Massachusetts state Sen. Brian A. Joyce, 55, was arrested and federally indicted on more than 100 counts after a multi‑year probe that alleges he used his legislative office to secretly enrich himself. The 102‑page (reported also as 113‑count) indictment accuses Joyce of racketeering, wire fraud, extortion, money laundering, conspiracy to defraud the IRS and related offenses stemming from schemes dating to about 2010.

Key allegations
- Joyce accepted a “stream of concealed bribes and kickbacks” in exchange for official action and pressure on local officials, and concealed payments through his law practice and a shell company. Prosecutors estimate the schemes netted roughly $1 million.
- Specific schemes cited include: receiving secret kickbacks from an energy brokerage (including purchases of stock and undisclosed financial ties while promoting related legislation); accepting a Jeep from a developer after pressuring a Milton planning board; taking hundreds of pounds of free Dunkin’ Donuts coffee and more than $100,000 in purported legal fees from a franchisee while taking legislative action benefiting that franchisee; and seeking fees from firms seeking permits or legislation.
- He is also accused of disguising personal purchases and investments (including about $471,250 in company stock) with sham retirement rollovers to defraud the IRS.
- Investigators say Joyce used his law office and entities such as “Windswept LLC” to launder corrupt payments and submitted false or backdated documents to the state Ethics Commission.

Procedural and contextual details
- Joyce was arrested at his Westport home, pleaded not guilty in federal court in Worcester, and was released on a $250,000 secured bond with passport surrender and travel limits. A status hearing was set for February.
- He represented a district including Milton, Randolph, Avon, Canton, Stoughton and other communities; first elected in 1998, he stepped down from leadership posts amid an ethics probe in 2015 and did not seek reelection in 2016 after federal agents raided his law office.
- Federal and local officials characterized the conduct as a betrayal of public trust; the U.S. Attorney described his office as run like a “criminal enterprise,” and the FBI called it greed-driven.
- Joyce’s attorney denies wrongdoing and criticized federal prosecution practice; some companies named (e.g., Energi) deny wrongdoing and say they were victimized and will cooperate.

The indictment follows media reporting and prior ethics scrutiny of Joyce’s mixing of public duties and private benefits. The investigation remains ongoing, and further charges or developments could follow.

A Portland mother, Monica Thompson, has filed an $8.6 million lawsuit against Portland Adventist Medical Center, alleging the hospital’s negligence led to the death of her newborn son, Jacob. Born by C-section on Aug. 2, 2012, Jacob was healthy. The suit says that on Aug. 6 a nurse brought the 4-day-old to Thompson’s room around 3 a.m. so she could breastfeed after the hospital had given her narcotic pain medication (Vicodin) and a sleep aid (Ambien) about midnight. According to the complaint, Thompson was drowsy and later found Jacob unresponsive in her arms; staff performed emergency measures and he was placed on life support, then transferred to Randall Children’s Hospital, where he was taken off life support and died at 10 days old.

The lawsuit accuses the hospital of negligently medicating a breastfeeding mother, leaving the infant unsupervised in her bed, and failing to have or enforce clear policies about the risks of bed-sharing while mothers are sedated. It seeks damages for Jacob’s suffering and death, Thompson’s severe emotional distress, and counseling costs for depression and PTSD. The suit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court by the Conde Law Group; the hospital declined to comment pending review. The case underscores broader concerns about hospital mother–infant bed-sharing and related safety guidance from pediatric authorities.

Researchers from the University of Vienna tested a thermoregulatory theory of yawning — that yawns help cool the brain to improve alertness — by measuring contagious yawning in pedestrians in Vienna and comparing results with an earlier Arizona study. Participants viewed images of people yawning and self-reported whether they yawned. Across climates and seasons, ambient temperature was the only significant predictor of yawning: contagious yawning was most frequent within a mid-range “thermal window” around 20°C and fell off at temperature extremes. Yawning declined when ambient temperatures approached body temperature (about 37°C) and also when it was very cold (near freezing). The findings support prior evidence that yawns follow transient rises in brain temperature and are followed by cooling, suggesting yawning functions in brain thermoregulation to restore arousal and mental efficiency; contagious yawning may help enhance group vigilance.

The document reports on the inaugural Women’s Convention, organized by the Women’s March and set for Oct. 27–29, 2017 in Detroit (Cobo Center). Framed by the theme “Reclaiming Our Time,” the three-day event aims to translate the January Women’s March energy into training, strategy and political organizing around “collective liberation” for women of all backgrounds, with a focus on building power for the 2018 elections.

Sen. Bernie Sanders was announced as an evening speaker on the convention’s opening day, drawing significant praise and criticism. Supporters and organizers (including co-founder Tamika Mallory) defended his inclusion as a longtime progressive ally who can mobilize young activists; Mallory emphasized that the convention’s leadership is overwhelmingly female and that Sanders is one of only two men among 60+ confirmed speakers. Sanders released a statement praising women’s activism and pledging to support progressive efforts.

Critics—many on social media, a petition organizer, and some sponsors such as Emily’s List—argued that having a man open the first national women’s convention in decades sends poor optics and that a woman should headline the event. Organizers clarified Rep. Maxine Waters is the convention headliner and will speak as well; other confirmed speakers include a large slate of women activists, elected officials and celebrities: Maxine Waters, Amber Tamblyn, Piper Perabo, Sally Kohn, Nomiki Konst, Leah Greenberg, Nina Turner, Ai-jen Poo, Stacey Abrams, Gretchen Whitmer, Detroit leaders Stephanie Chang and Raquel Castañeda Lopez, and transgender Latina activist Liliana Reyes, among others.

The convention will include workshops, trainings and panels designed to educate new activists and strengthen local organizing. Tickets were listed (three-day and single-day options); organizers noted many invited female elected officials (e.g., Clinton, Kamala Harris, Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand) could not attend due to scheduling. The piece also references the broader debates about inclusivity, leadership optics, and tensions lingering from the 2016 election.

A Fort Dodge, Iowa couple, Rachel and Ben Kohnen, were held at gunpoint after failing to stop for a pursuing police officer early Tuesday while rushing Rachel to the hospital in labor. Driving about 85 mph in a 55 mph zone on Highway 7 around 4 a.m., they did not pull over because Rachel said the baby was coming quickly. An officer called for backup and tire spikes were deployed; all four tires were blown out and the couple were ordered to the ground until officers realized it was a medical emergency. Rachel was rushed to the hospital and delivered their fourth child, a nearly 10‑pound daughter named Hazel, about an hour later. The couple said a 911 call likely failed because Rachel was in severe pain and incoherent between contractions. Manson Police Chief Tom Ritts said the officer followed standard protocol for a high‑speed stop and no charges have been filed so far; the county attorney will decide whether to pursue any.

The Vatican publicly reiterated its opposition to gay adoption and same-sex marriage amid protests in St. Peter’s Square. L’Osservatore Romano ran an editorial responding to an Italian Court of Cassation ruling that dismissing concerns about a child’s development in a homosexual household as “mere prejudice.” The Vatican piece argued that while children sometimes grow up without a mother or father, such situations should not be purposefully created, reaffirming the view that the masculine and feminine and the monogamous family are the ideal environment for raising children and rejecting a claimed “right” to children by gay couples.

The article noted rising opposition from Catholic leaders to legalizing same-sex marriage—Pope Benedict XVI recently restated the Church’s stance—and recorded large anti–same-sex marriage demonstrations in Paris against President François Hollande’s plans to legalize gay marriage and adoption. During the pope’s Angelus address, four topless Ukrainian Femen activists in the crowd exposed slogans such as “In Gay We Trust” and “Shut Up,” shouting against homophobia; they were removed by police amid angry reactions from pilgrims, while the pope’s prayer proceeded undisturbed.

The State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs sparked backlash on March 30, 2016 after @TravelGov posted a tweet warning travelers about scams that read, “Not a ‘10’ in the US? Then not a 10 overseas,” implying people who aren’t considered highly attractive at home could be targeted abroad. Critics called the wording sexist and patronizing; the account initially replied to defend the message, saying it wasn’t gendered and was meant to warn about scams and drink-related robberies. After sustained criticism the department deleted the tweet and issued a two-part apology, saying some were offended and reiterating that the intent was to caution Americans to be careful while traveling. The incident followed another recent @TravelGov advisory about contests that offer “free luggage” actually lined with cocaine.

Bangladesh’s elite Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) arrested Farabi Shafiur Rahman on March 2 as the main suspect in the machete killing of U.S.-Bangladeshi blogger Avijit Roy in Dhaka. RAB says Farabi, previously jailed in 2013 for social media posts supporting the murder of another blogger and linked to the Islamist group Hizbut Tahrir, was detained at a bus stop and has confessed to threatening Roy. Authorities say he posted calls for Roy’s killing on Facebook and, according to RAB, even posted images from the crime scene minutes after the attack. Roy, an engineer and prominent critic of religious extremism, was hacked to death while leaving a book fair; his wife Rafida Ahmed was seriously injured. The killing comes amid rising activity by hardline Islamist groups and continued threats to secular bloggers in Bangladesh, which ranks low on global press freedom indices.

A classified 18-page presidential directive signed by Barack Obama — Presidential Policy Directive 20 (PPD-20) issued in October — tasks senior national security and intelligence officials with identifying potential overseas targets for Offensive Cyber Effects Operations (OCEO). The directive frames offensive cyber operations as tools that can advance U.S. national objectives with effects ranging from subtle to severely damaging, and it orders agencies to prepare, within six months, a plan listing systems, processes and infrastructure against which the U.S. should establish and maintain OCEO capabilities.

Key points from the directive and reporting:
- OCEO are defined as operations conducted by or on behalf of the U.S. government through cyberspace intended to create cyber effects outside U.S. government networks.
- Agencies must weigh legal, strategic and technical consequences — including impacts on intelligence collection, retaliation risk, internet stability, political costs, and possible establishment of harmful international norms — before acting.
- Actions likely to produce significant consequences (loss of life, property damage, serious diplomatic or economic harm, or responsive action against the U.S.) require specific presidential approval.
- Cyber operations that would produce effects inside the United States also require presidential approval except in narrowly defined emergency cases that allow limited departmental authority.
- The directive authorizes offensive cyber operations abroad without the host government’s consent when U.S. national interests demand, and permits “anticipatory” actions against imminent threats.
- The document emphasizes compliance with U.S. and international law and that cyber tools should complement, not replace, diplomatic and military instruments. A declassified summary earlier released stressed prioritizing defense and law enforcement and taking the least action necessary.

Context and reactions:
- The revelation came as Obama prepared to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping; U.S. concerns about Chinese cyber intrusions were a summit topic, and China responded by accusing the U.S. of conducting comparable offensive cyber activities.
- The disclosure renews debate about the militarization of cyberspace, escalation risks (including into kinetic conflict), and hypocrisy accusations from within intelligence circles that U.S. agencies conduct widespread foreign intrusions.
- The U.S. has previously been linked to major cyber operations (e.g., the Stuxnet worm targeting Iranian centrifuges).
- The Pentagon has been expanding offensive cyber capabilities, including building Cyber Command teams; James Clapper and other officials identify cyber threats as top national security concerns.
- Civil liberties and privacy advocates worry that such moves, coupled with proposals like CISPA and other surveillance revelations, will erode online privacy and expand government powers.

Official response:
- The National Security Council spokeswoman said the administration updated a 2004 directive to integrate cyber tools with national security instruments, to enable better planning while exercising restraint, and to prioritize defense and law enforcement consistent with law and values.

Also reported: The document and summit coverage appear amid wider reporting on surveillance program leaks. Separately, Obama and Xi concluded an informal two-day Sunnylands summit aimed at improving bilateral relations, with cybersecurity, military ties, trade and North Korea on the agenda; both leaders expressed interest in cooperation while acknowledging more detailed talks were needed.

President Obama, in an exclusive ABC News interview with Diane Sawyer, downplayed Arizona Gov. Jan Brewer’s description of their tarmac meeting as “somewhat thin-skinned and a little tense,” joking he’s usually accused of being “too relaxed” and calling the episode overblown. Brewer has criticized Obama in her book for being “condescending” and for cold treatment of her staff; Obama said she sought a meeting and he agreed.

Turning to the 2012 campaign, Obama signaled an assertive re-election posture, saying he will “fight with every fiber” to win because the country needs his agenda. He criticized Republican contenders—naming Mitt Romney, Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum—arguing their low-tax, light-regulation approach had been tried for a decade and contributed to the financial crash and job losses. He defended his proposals to raise taxes on the wealthy to pay for investments and reduce deficits, saying that approach is fairer than cutting benefits for seniors or students.

Obama rejected Newt Gingrich’s “food stamp president” attacks, pushed back on right‑wing rhetoric and suggested voters will judge who unites or divides the country. He said he won’t fully engage in campaigning until Republicans choose a nominee but confirmed the first family is ready for a grueling campaign ahead; Michelle Obama is enthusiastic and the couple’s daughters are largely focused on normal childhood concerns.

On foreign policy, Obama said the U.S. is closely monitoring tensions between Israel and Iran over Iran’s alleged nuclear pursuits, insists Iran cannot pursue a weapon, supports tough sanctions, prefers a diplomatic resolution, and is keeping military options open while not discussing classified matters.

Actor Mark Wahlberg has applied to the Massachusetts Board of Pardons to have his 1988 assault conviction erased. In a petition filed Nov. 26, Wahlberg (then 16) admits that on April 8, 1988 he tried to steal two cases of alcohol outside a Dorchester convenience store, struck a man (Thanh Lam) with a wooden stick — an attack that left the victim blind in one eye, according to reporting — and punched another man while fleeing police. He was tried as an adult, convicted of assault, served 45 days of a 90-day sentence, and acknowledges he was under the influence and had a small amount of marijuana on him at the time.

Wahlberg expresses remorse in the application, saying he has spent the past 25+ years trying to become a better person and citizen, speaking publicly about the incident, doing philanthropic work through the Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation, supporting local organizations (Dorchester Boys & Girls Club, Parish Gym renovation), attending church frequently, and engaging in charitable campaigns such as One Mission’s Buzz-Off for kids with cancer. He says a pardon would be formal recognition of his rehabilitation, would help with business plans (concessionaire licenses for his Wahlburgers restaurants), and would allow him to better work with at-risk youth and law enforcement.

The Board of Pardons will investigate and may hold a public hearing before making a recommendation to the governor and governor’s council; the process could be lengthy. Critics and commentators note Wahlberg’s high-profile rehabilitation and charitable record as part of his case for official forgiveness.

Nestle failed to persuade the European Court of Justice that the shape of its four-finger KitKat bar should be trademarked in the UK. The ECJ said Nestle must prove that consumers identify the product by the shape alone, not by the shape together with other branding (such as the KitKat name), and noted shapes that stem from the product’s nature or technical function cannot be protected. The ruling follows a long dispute with Cadbury (owned by Mondelez), which opposed Nestle’s 2010 UK application and contends the shape lacks distinctiveness. Both companies said they were pleased with the judgment; the case now returns to the UK High Court for final determination.

Background: Nestle argues the four-finger form has been strongly associated with KitKat since the bar’s introduction (first sold in 1935 by Rowntree), but did not seek protection for the two-finger version. The dispute is part of wider “chocolate wars” including earlier clashes over Cadbury’s bid to trademark its purple packaging. A similar Norwegian bar, Kvikk Lunsj, predates KitKat and looks similar. The ECJ decision also reiterated that shapes with essential features arising from product nature or required for technical results cannot be trademarked.

U.S. President Barack Obama convened more than 50 world leaders in Washington on April 1–2, 2016 for his fourth and final Nuclear Security Summit to press for tighter protections against nuclear terrorism and the theft or misuse of radioactive materials. Calling nuclear terrorism “one of the greatest threats to global security,” Obama warned that groups such as Islamic State (IS) and al Qaeda would use a bomb or radioactive “dirty bomb” if they obtained nuclear material, citing recent attacks in Paris and Brussels and evidence that militants had surveilled a Belgian nuclear plant employee.

Summit outcomes and actions
- Participants reaffirmed commitments to secure vulnerable nuclear and radiological materials worldwide, pledged steps to harden facilities (including against cyberattacks) and noted progress such as ratification of an amendment tightening protections against theft and smuggling.
- The U.S. and Japan announced completion of removing all highly enriched uranium and separated plutonium fuels from a Japanese research reactor.
- Obama acknowledged measurable risk reduction but stressed that roughly 2,000 tons of fissile material remain globally and not all are properly secured.
- Leaders reviewed the Iran nuclear agreement (P5+1) and held a session coordinating efforts against IS; Obama defended the Iran deal as a diplomatic success that closes pathways to a bomb.

Context and tensions
- Russia boycotted the summit amid strained U.S.-Russia relations over Ukraine and Syria; Obama said Putin’s military buildup makes further U.S.-Russia arms-reduction deals unlikely in the remainder of his term.
- North Korea’s continued nuclear and missile tests were a major concern; Obama, South Korea, and Japan vowed to increase pressure, while North Korea rejected deterrence rhetoric.
- The summit’s results were characterized as largely technical rather than breakthrough policy moves, and experts warned progress may slow after Obama leaves office.

Politics and legacy
- Obama framed the summit as part of a legacy begun with his 2009 Prague speech advocating a world without nuclear weapons. He used the platform to criticize U.S. presidential candidate Donald Trump’s suggestion that Japan and South Korea should obtain nuclear weapons, calling it evidence of ignorance in foreign policy.

Overall, the summit underscored ongoing international efforts and some concrete steps to reduce nuclear risk, while highlighting persistent vulnerabilities, geopolitical fractures (notably Russia’s absence), and uncertainty about sustaining momentum beyond the Obama administration.

On May 1, 2018 Katie Couric appeared on Bravo’s Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen to address resurfaced comments about her former Today co-anchor Matt Lauer amid his sexual misconduct scandal. A 2012 clip of Couric joking on the show that “he used to pinch you on the ass” trended when allegations about Lauer circulated; Couric told Cohen the remark was a joke she now regrets because it was misconstrued. Speaking earlier on The Wendy Williams Show, she said she was treated “respectfully and appropriately” by Lauer and that many colleagues who knew or worked with him were shocked by the revelations. Couric suggested the full scope of the allegations may be larger than publicly known, criticized some reporting as exaggerated (including descriptions of an NBC “button” to lock doors, which she called an executive privacy perk), and acknowledged apologizing for previously joking about his behavior. The piece also notes Lauer’s limited public response, in which he denied any coercive or abusive conduct while admitting to being a poor husband and behaving inappropriately at work.

Michael Bay’s Pain & Gain is a loud, violent, and deliberately stupid-feeling true-crime dark comedy driven by macho excess. Based on Pete Collins’s Miami New Times articles (adapted by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely), the film follows Mark Wahlberg as Daniel Lugo, a steroid-using personal trainer in 1995 Miami who, motivated by entitlement and get-rich-quick self-help rhetoric, plots to extort wealth from a gym client, Victor Kershaw (Tony Shalhoub). He recruits two fellow gym rats—Adrian (Anthony Mackie), a volatile man wrestling with steroid-induced sexual problems, and Paul (Dwayne Johnson), an ex-con who claims a newfound religiosity—to kidnap and coerce Victor into signing over his assets. The plot is presented amid Bay’s signature hyperkinetic visuals, voice-over riffs on Jesus, fitness and the American dream, and scenes of grotesque humor and brutality. Though exaggerated and sometimes tasteless, the film largely sticks to the factual arc of idiotic criminality and bungled policing from Collins’s account. Strong ensemble work—Mackie’s manic-but-grounded Adrian and Johnson’s blend of hulking menace and comic humanity—matches Wahlberg’s performance, giving the movie enough depth to make its relentless vulgarity and violence feel like a pointed portrait of stupidity and entitlement rather than mere spectacle.

A Japanese woman in her early 20s, staying in Kolkata to study rural India, alleges she was lured by a man posing as a tour guide and taken to multiple locations in November and December, including Digha and Gaya/Bodh Gaya in Bihar. According to police and the victim’s FIR, the guide (identified as Wasim Khan) initially befriended her on November 20, spoke Japanese, stole about Rs 76,000 from her bank account, and then handed her over to others. She says she was held captive for weeks by an organised group—including two brothers, Zahir and Shahid—who repeatedly raped her and kept her as a hostage in a Gaya village near Bodh Gaya. The victim escaped or was released on December 26, reached Varanasi, contacted friends and the Japanese consulate, and then returned to Kolkata to file a complaint.

Following her complaint and interrogation of suspects, police from Kolkata and Gaya arrested at least three to five men in connection with the case (reports vary), including Wasim in Kolkata and the two brothers in Gaya. Authorities are searching for additional alleged accomplices. Charges include rape and cheating; investigations are ongoing. The case has drawn attention amid broader public concern in India about sexual violence and recent legal reforms stiffening penalties for rape and related offences.

Sombra (“Shadow”) is a 6-year-old German shepherd working with Colombia’s National Police counter-narcotics unit who has become a high-profile asset and folk hero after detecting roughly nine–ten tonnes of cocaine and helping secure about 245 arrests over more than 300 operations. Her major seizures included multi-ton shipments hidden in banana containers and auto parts bound for Europe, earning her awards and wide media attention.

Because her success has seriously damaged revenues of the Urabeños (Gulf Clan), Colombia’s most powerful criminal organization led by Dairo Antonio Úsuga (“Otoniel”), intelligence revealed the gang placed a bounty on her — reports put the reward between about 20–200 million pesos (roughly $7,000–$70,000). In response, police moved Sombra from the Urabá/Turbo coastal area (the gang’s stronghold) to Bogotá’s El Dorado International Airport and now deploy extra officers with her in addition to her regular handler to improve her safety. Handlers say she is friendly and calm with people but relentless on scent work; authorities say the protection measures reflect the real threat posed by traffickers.

Nine-year-old Zianna Oliphant, a fourth-grader from Charlotte, drew national attention after a tearful, impromptu speech to the City Council about racism and policing following the police shooting of Keith Lamont Scott. Watching news coverage with her mother, Zianna said she was nervous but wanted to tell leaders how she felt: that Black people shouldn’t have to live in fear or be targeted by police. She and her brother spoke at the meeting where community members demanded changes and some called for resignations of the police chief and mayor. Zianna, who participates in a police youth league and aspires to be a doctor, said her own experiences—being stopped over minor things like her hair—have shaped her views. Her remarks, calling attention to parents killed and children left grieving, drew applause and chants of “No justice, no peace.”

On July 4 outside Austin, Democrat Rep. Beto O’Rourke joined Willie Nelson onstage at Nelson’s annual Fourth of July Picnic, drawing both cheers and boos as he spoke about welcoming immigrants and inclusion, then played guitar with Nelson during the encore. Nelson later announced he will headline a free Sept. 29 rally and concert for O’Rourke at Auditorium Shores (RSVP required), with performers including Joe Ely, Carrie Rodriguez, Tameca Jones and Nelson’s sons Lukas and Micah; Leon Bridges’ participation was initially unconfirmed but later affirmed. Nelson’s publicist called the event the first public concert he’s held for a political candidate, and Nelson said he and his wife support O’Rourke because they share concerns about the country’s direction and admire his integrity. The endorsement provoked backlash from some fans on social media accusing Nelson of supporting a “socialist” agenda, while others defended him. The piece notes Nelson’s long history of liberal-leaning activism—support for environmental causes, same-sex marriage, marijuana legalization and past endorsements of Obama, Sanders and Clinton—and corrects an earlier error about the concert being his first campaign performance.

Aung San Suu Kyi began a 17-day European visit — her first to Europe since 1988 — to formally accept her Nobel Peace Prize and meet officials in Switzerland, Norway, Britain, Ireland and France. On her first full day in Geneva and Bern she received standing ovations (including at the ILO) but briefly fell ill and left a press event; a Swiss official dinner was canceled though she attended a later reception.

Suu Kyi urged foreign governments to withhold permission for their companies to form joint ventures with Myanmar’s state oil and gas company, Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE), until it adopts internationally recognised transparency and accountability standards (for example IMF fiscal‑transparency guidelines). She warned that opaque contracts—citing Chinese pipeline concessions—fuel suspicion and future problems, and called for “responsible investment” to support Myanmar’s democratic transition as sanctions are eased. She praised some Western firms (noting Total’s sensitivity to rights and environment) and said she would not push responsible investors like Total or Chevron to withdraw. Overall, she welcomed job‑creating foreign direct investment but urged sound, effective energy and extractive‑sector policies tied to democratisation.

A 54-year-old Florida man, David Edward Benes, was arrested after allegedly restraining his 80-year-old live-in girlfriend and attempting to "exorcise" her. According to a Pasco County Sheriff's Office affidavit, the woman said Benes held her down during a fight at their home near Tampa and told her he was trying to "get the devil out of her." She reported bruises and scratches on her arms and said Benes removed batteries from the house phones, took her car keys and disabled the garage door to prevent her from getting help. Deputies found Benes intoxicated and passed out on a couch; he told officers he was too drunk to remember and claimed the woman had "beat up" him. Benes was arrested on charges including domestic battery on a person 65 or older, false imprisonment and tampering with a witness, and was jailed without bail. Records show prior convictions for battery and for violating a domestic violence injunction.

Arizona's new abortion restriction, House Bill 2036, takes effect this week and bans most abortions at 20 weeks' gestational age or later. Because the law defines gestational age from the first day of a woman's last menstrual period, it effectively prohibits abortions from about 18 weeks — the time many prenatal ultrasounds detect fetal abnormalities. Arizona joins nine other states with 20-week bans, but is unique in shifting the cutoff earlier in practice. The law allows exceptions only for medical emergencies.

The ban means more pregnancies diagnosed with fatal fetal defects will be carried to term even though affected newborns may survive only minutes, hours or days. The statute requires doctors to provide information about perinatal hospice services to patients considering abortion because of a fatal fetal abnormality and directs the state to maintain an online list of organizations that offer such support. No state funding was allocated.

Two local nonprofit groups, MISS Foundation and Embrace, provide the broadly framed perinatal support the law highlights: counseling, birth planning, attendance at delivery, mementos and funeral help, meal coordination and ongoing family support. Those organizations operate mainly on private donations and volunteers and are not reimbursed by insurers; leaders worry they will be overwhelmed by increased demand when the law takes effect. They already assist families facing a spectrum of outcomes, from grieving parents of babies who die at birth to families whose children survive with serious medical needs.

The law has survived a district court challenge: U.S. District Judge James Teilborg ruled the statute constitutional, saying it may shift some decisions earlier but does not prevent any woman from obtaining an abortion and citing evidence the state offered about fetal pain at 20 weeks. The decision is being appealed to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals by reproductive-rights groups, which argue the ban violates Supreme Court precedent protecting pre-viability abortion. A related Arizona measure restricting public funding to clinics that provide abortions also faces legal challenge.

Bitcoin briefly climbed above $9,000 after G-20 finance ministers and central bank governors held “productive” closed-door talks on cryptocurrencies in Buenos Aires and agreed only to collect more information before proposing harmonized global rules in July. The rise—about 4.5–4.8% to roughly $9,000 on Tuesday—came despite a separate, troubling research finding about illicit content on Bitcoin’s blockchain.

Researchers at RWTH Aachen and Goethe University found roughly 1,600 instances of non-financial data embedded in the Bitcoin ledger (about 1.4% of transactions), including several items tied to sexual content: at least one suspected child-abuse image and two files containing hundreds of links to child-abuse material (many pointing to dark‑web services). Because the blockchain is immutable and every full node stores the complete ledger, possessing a copy could, the researchers warn, expose users to legal liability in jurisdictions where possession of such material is illegal. This risk is compounded by processes like mining or running a full node, which require downloading and storing the full blockchain.

The finding revives earlier warnings (e.g., Interpol in 2015) that blockchains can host permanent, potentially illegal data and highlights broader legal tensions with data‑protection and criminal laws. Observers note that such content could threaten participation in and the commercial viability of blockchain systems if courts or governments deem possession illegal. Despite these concerns, markets were more immediately responsive to the G-20 outcome, and bitcoin’s price remained near $9,000 as of early Wednesday.

Lois Riess, 56, a Minnesota woman already wanted in her husband David Riess’s March killing, is now charged in the murder of 59-year-old Pamela Hutchinson on Fort Myers Beach, Fla. Investigators say Riess targeted Hutchinson because the two resembled each other, fatally shot her at Marina Village at Snug Harbor, and stole Hutchinson’s cash, credit cards, ID and white 2005 Acura TL (Florida plate Y37TAA) — which she is believed to be using while on the run. Riess’s own 2005 white Cadillac Escalade was found abandoned in a Florida park. Authorities say Riess “befriends women who resemble her and steals their identity,” and U.S. Marshals are conducting a national search; she is considered armed and dangerous and may be hiding in Texas. Lee County issued warrants for murder, grand theft auto and identity-related theft; Minnesota’s Dodge County has prepared second-degree murder charges in David Riess’s death. Investigators believe the same gun was used in both killings. Anyone with information is urged to contact law enforcement.

Despite recent chatter among some Democrats and a BuzzFeed report that supporters have been quietly discussing an Al Gore 2016 presidential bid, people close to the former vice president insist he is not planning to run. Gore spokeswoman Betsy McManus said he is “laser-focused on solving the climate crisis,” and longtime aides including Mike Feldman and Roy Neel told POLITICO they’ve heard no indication Gore is considering a campaign. BuzzFeed’s piece suggested conversations among supporters were prompted by concerns about Hillary Clinton’s standing amid email controversies, slipping polls, and Bernie Sanders’ surge; the story quoted sources who described early, informal exploratory talk but emphasized there have been no concrete moves or meetings with Gore. Commentators note Gore is a conceivable fallback for Democrats alongside Joe Biden if Clinton falters, but Gore—who has concentrated on climate advocacy and business interests since 2000—has largely stayed out of presidential politics and appears uninterested in reentering the race.

A 15-year, population-based cohort study by University of Dundee researchers examined medical records from the U.K. Clinical Practice Research Datalink to assess pregnancy rates after appendectomy and/or tonsillectomy. The analysis included 54,675 women with appendectomy only, 112,607 with tonsillectomy only, 10,340 with both procedures, and 355,244 age- and practice-matched comparators from 1987–2012, with a mean follow-up of about 14.7 years.

Key findings:
- Pregnancy proportions: 54.4% (appendectomy), 53.4% (tonsillectomy), 59.7% (both) versus 43.7% in comparators.
- Adjusted hazard ratios for becoming pregnant were 1.34 after appendectomy, 1.49 after tonsillectomy, and 1.43 after both procedures, indicating higher and earlier pregnancy rates in all operated groups.
- Time to first pregnancy was shortest in women who had both surgeries, then appendectomy only, then tonsillectomy only.

Interpretation and implications:
- The association could reflect biological effects (reduced systemic inflammation or immune changes after removing chronically inflamed tissues) or behavioral confounding (women more likely to have infections may also have higher sexual activity and earlier childbearing).
- The study challenges the conventional teaching that appendectomy harms female fertility and should reassure women needing these operations that fertility is unlikely to be reduced.
- Authors and external experts caution that the data show association, not causation, and do not support recommending these surgeries to improve fertility. Further research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms.

Bryson DeChambeau won the Northern Trust by four shots at Ridgewood Country Club, closing with a 2-under 69 and finishing 18-under 266. With a comfortable final round in which he never let anyone closer than two shots, DeChambeau sealed the victory with a key chip-and-save birdie at the short 12th and moves to the top of the FedEx Cup standings. The win is his second of the year and boosts his case for one of Jim Furyk’s upcoming Ryder Cup captain’s picks.

Tony Finau finished solo second after a closing 68, moving into the world top 20 for the first time and also strengthening his Ryder Cup candidacy. Billy Horschel and Cameron Smith tied for third. Ryan Palmer, starting the week 100th in the FedEx Cup, shot 65 to climb into the top 50 and advance to the next playoff event; six players moved from outside the top 100 into the qualifying positions for the Dell Technologies Championship.

Tiger Woods, coming off a runner-up at the PGA Championship, finished tied for 40th after a 70. Asked about his relationship with President Donald Trump, Woods declined to wade into politics, saying the presidency must be respected regardless of personal views. Trump later praised Woods’ remarks and play on Twitter. Dustin Johnson’s late surge helped him narrowly remain No. 1 in the world over Brooks Koepka.

President Obama said that incidents like the deaths of Michael Brown (Ferguson) and Eric Garner have increased public awareness that law enforcement is not always applied in a colorblind way. The remark highlighted growing recognition of racial disparities in policing.

Filmmaker and explorer James Cameron completed a solo descent to Challenger Deep, the deepest point in the Mariana Trench (about 35,800–36,000 feet, nearly 7 miles), in his 12-ton submersible Deepsea Challenger over the weekend. He became the first person to make a solo trip to that depth, reaching the bottom after a 156‑minute descent and surfacing earlier than planned after 70 minutes of ascent due to a hydraulic fluid leak that damaged thrusters and coated the sub’s viewport. Cameron reported a bleak, moonlike seafloor with few visible organisms (mostly small amphipods) and said he couldn’t collect the geology or biology samples he’d hoped for before deciding to abort further bottom time. He was recovered by helicopter and the support ship Mermaid Sapphire and indicated he may return for another dive.

The mission was high‑risk: the article outlines numerous catastrophic failure modes at Challenger Deep—implosion from pressure, hypothermia if stranded, onboard fire from oxygen and electrical faults, damage from unexpected hydrothermal vents, and entanglement in seabed cables—any of which could have been fatal. Cameron trained physically for the cramped, arduous dive; the sub carried 3D cameras and powerful lighting, and National Geographic will document the expedition. No one had visited Challenger Deep since the 1960 Piccard/Walsh Navy expedition.

The Pentagon’s official Twitter account briefly reposted a tweet from activist account @proudresister calling for Roy Moore, Al Franken and President Donald Trump to resign amid sexual misconduct allegations. The retweet was quickly deleted and the Department of Defense disavowed it. Pentagon spokesman Col. Rob Manning and press secretary Dana White said an “authorized operator” had “erroneously re-tweeted” content “that would not be endorsed by the Department of Defense,” and that the operator removed it immediately. The original activist account promotes anti‑Trump merchandise. The incident came as questions about sexual misconduct allegations against multiple public figures, including Trump, were receiving renewed attention.

Newsline 9 highlights the obituary and life of Mary Agnes “Pink” Mullaney, a beloved Milwaukee woman who died at 85. Known for her warmth, generosity and quirky practical wisdom, Pink raised six children and 17 grandchildren and was remembered by family, friends and strangers for treating everyone— from doctors to the homeless— with equal kindness.

Her family wrote an unconventional, colorful obituary full of practical tips and life lessons that captured her spirit: bring a chicken sandwich to Mass for a homeless friend; kiss and befriend people at nursing homes; share magazines in waiting rooms (leave the mailing label in case someone wants to contact you); reuse pantyhose for household fixes; and simple acts of neighborliness like leaving a cold drink out for the mail carrier. The obituary also recounts her habit of writing thousands of letters and stopping to chat with people in grocery lines, and stories such as coaxing a possum from a shed.

Friends and children recalled her compulsion to reach out—kissing babies, talking to strangers and inviting newcomers to Thanksgiving dinners. The family said the obituary was meant to show who she was and to encourage others to “carry her pinkness across.” Her life and obituary inspired Newsline 9 to revive a feature, “Someone You Should Know,” inviting viewers to nominate community members doing noteworthy things. A link to the full obituary was provided.

Two Windsor residents, husband and wife Clifford (45–46) and Lataya/Latoya Knight (38), were arrested after an argument over crab legs at Royal Buffet in Manchester on Saturday evening escalated into a physical fight. A 21-year-old man was punched, suffering a cut lip and a broken front tooth. His mother used pepper spray on the assailants in what police say was self-defense; she faces no charges. Clifford Knight was charged with third-degree assault and disorderly conduct and released on a $5,000 non-surety bond; Lataya/Latoya Knight was charged with disorderly conduct and threatening and released on a $2,500 non-surety bond. Both are due in court April 14. The Manchester Fire Department ventilated the restaurant after the pepper spray was used, the health department briefly closed it to assess air quality, and it reopened the next day. An earlier report that the victim was a juvenile has been corrected: he is a young adult.

This document connects the rise of image-editing apps and social-media filters with growing concerns about body image, cosmetic surgery requests, and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), including suicidality.

Key points

- Filters and editing apps: Snapchat, Instagram, Facetune and similar tools let anyone quickly alter selfies (smoother skin, bigger eyes, whiter teeth, slimmer features, etc.). These tools normalize an edited look and spread unrealistic beauty standards among peers, not just celebrities.

- “Snapchat dysmorphia”: Clinicians and researchers have observed patients requesting cosmetic procedures to match their own heavily filtered selfies rather than the faces of celebrities. Authors call this trend “Snapchat dysmorphia,” and warn filtered images present unattainable looks that blur reality and fantasy.

- Impact on plastic-surgery demand: Surveys and surgeons report increasing numbers of patients asking for changes to appear better in selfies; one survey found 55% of facial-plastic surgeons saw such requests in 2017 (up from 42% the prior year).

- Connection to BDD: Boston University researchers argue pervasive self-editing contributes to rising body dissatisfaction and may trigger or worsen BDD, a serious psychiatric disorder characterized by obsessive preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws and repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, skin picking, camouflage). BDD often begins in adolescence.

- Suicidality and severity of BDD: Research reviewed (including epidemiologic and clinical studies) shows very high rates of suicidal ideation and attempts in people with BDD—lifetime suicidal ideation in many samples around 78–81%, and suicide attempts in roughly 24–28% of patients. Prospective data suggest high annual rates of suicidal thinking and an elevated completed-suicide rate (one study’s standardized mortality ratio was very high), though further research is needed. Youth with BDD appear especially at risk.

- Clinical features and detection: BDD sufferers usually look ordinary to others but are preoccupied for hours daily with minor or imagined defects, often with poor insight and high shame—so they may hide symptoms. Common clues include compulsive grooming, mirror checking, camouflaging, social withdrawal, and repeated requests for cosmetic procedures. Direct, nonjudgmental questioning about appearance concerns is important for diagnosis.

- Treatment and outcomes: First-line treatments are serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRIs) and cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) tailored to BDD; these have evidence of efficacy and can reduce suicidality. Cosmetic interventions are generally ineffective for BDD and can be harmful. Research is limited on treatment for highly suicidal BDD patients, and more study is needed.

- Broader implications: The democratization of photo-editing has shifted beauty norms from elite media images to ubiquitous edited images of peers, intensifying social comparison and potentially fueling “beauty sickness.” Clinicians warn this cultural shift may increase BDD incidence and related harms, but changing user behavior seems unlikely in the near term.

Overall message
Easy, pervasive photo-editing and filter use have altered perceptions of beauty, encouraged people to seek cosmetic procedures to match edited versions of themselves, and may be contributing to rising body dissatisfaction and serious psychiatric risks—especially body dysmorphic disorder and suicide. Better recognition, diagnosis, treatment, and research on BDD (and on the psychological effects of social-media editing) are urgently needed.

This document covers two maritime discoveries in the Baltic Sea and the work of German hydrographer Thomas Dehling.

1) Shipwrecks in the Baltic Sea (interview with Thomas Dehling, BSH)
- The Baltic is a major graveyard of wrecks, particularly from World Wars I and II. In the German sector (about 16,000 km², under a tenth of the Baltic), roughly 1,000 known submerged objects exist.
- Wrecks range in age from 15th–16th century wooden ships (cargo including unusual finds like copper disks) to many early-20th-century military losses, and at least one Finnish wreck over 400 years old.
- The Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH) regularly surveys wrecks, especially those that could endanger shipping; frequency depends on danger and traffic importance (from yearly to once every 25 years).
- New finds continue: improved seafloor survey technology reveals about 10–15 previously unknown objects per year in the German sector. Many are small or partially submerged and not necessarily hazards.
- BSH does not remove wrecks itself; it notifies maritime authorities who decide on removal or marking. For safety and protection of historically valuable sites, detailed location data are restricted—public maps are deliberately imprecise, and detailed information is released only to legitimate claimants.
- Recreational diving on wrecks is popular but hazardous (entanglement in nets, complex conditions), another reason for limited public dissemination of precise locations.

2) 170-year-old champagne from a Baltic shipwreck (scientific study)
- In 2010 divers found a sunken 19th-century trade schooner off Finland at about 160 ft depth containing 168 bottles of French champagne. While authorities claimed the bottles, researchers obtained samples for study.
- Analysis, led by Philippe Jeandet and published in PNAS, identified vintners via cork markings (including Veuve Clicquot) and compared chemical/sensory profiles with modern champagne.
- Key findings: the recovered champagne had lower alcohol but far higher sugar (at least ~140 g/L vs. 6–8 g/L typical today), and elevated iron, copper, sodium, and chlorine.
- Explanations: 19th-century production was less controlled—colder climate and less efficient yeasts reduced natural alcohol; large sugar additions and finishing practices raised sweetness and diluted alcohol. Metal and wood vessels, plus copper sulfate vineyard treatments and salt additions for stabilization, account for the metal and sodium/chloride signatures.
- The sugar level suggests the shipment was likely destined for Germanic markets (moderately sweet preferences), rather than the much sweeter Russian market or the drier British/American preferences.
- Sensory testing: initially off-putting descriptors (“animal,” “wet hair,” “cheesy”) shifted after aeration to “grilled, spicy, smoky, leathery” with fruity and floral notes. Low acetic acid indicated minimal spoilage. Tasting left a pronounced long-lasting aroma; individual bottles have fetched high auction prices and others were preserved in museums.
- The find provides insight into 19th-century winemaking and has prompted interest in the potential effects of deep-sea aging on wine.

Overall, the pieces illustrate the Baltic Sea’s rich undersea historical heritage—from centuries-old trade wrecks and wartime losses to recoveries that illuminate past technologies and tastes—while highlighting modern survey practices, safety concerns, and conservation constraints around shipwrecks.

The Boy Scouts of America (BSA) proposed lifting its long-standing ban on gay youth members while keeping a prohibition on gay adults serving as leaders. The Executive Council said it will submit the measure to the National Council for a vote the week of May 20. The shift — prompted in part by member surveys and internal reports showing most sponsoring religious groups were primarily concerned about adult leaders — would allow gay youths to join but require them to meet existing adult standards if they later seek to become adult leaders.

Reactions were mixed: gay-rights groups welcomed the change for youths but condemned continued exclusion of gay adults as unacceptable; many faith-based and conservative supporters criticized the compromise, warning it could cause a major rift. Major stakeholders, including the Mormon Church (which sponsors large numbers of units) said they would review the proposal before deciding. Corporate backers such as AT&T’s CEO publicly supported opening membership to youth. The proposal follows years of internal debate, a 2000 Supreme Court victory for the Scouts’ right to set membership rules, and changing public attitudes toward gay rights. The outcome of the upcoming vote remained uncertain.

A growing fantasy-sports scene is creating new full-time careers. Fantasy football is now a big industry—about 36 million players in the U.S. and Canada—and some participants are taking bigger financial risks than the casual once-a-season buy-in. Drew Dinkmeyer left his job as an investment analyst to play daily fantasy contests full-time, wagering roughly $500 or more on multiple games per day. He says after several years his fantasy winnings matched his financial-sector income, letting him treat the activity like a profession. Dinkmeyer compares daily fantasy play to day trading—identifying undervalued players (like underpriced stocks) to build the highest-scoring lineups—and supplements his income with fantasy-writing and radio hosting, expecting to continue in the field long term.

Taran Killam portrayed a caricatured, indignant Limbaugh who griped about sponsors abandoning him and joked about absurd replacement advertisers; critics said the bit recycled the same joke repeatedly and outstayed its welcome.

Engadget reported (via an unnamed internal tip) that Barnes & Noble is phasing out the e‑ink Nook 3G, with remaining units to be sold until stock runs out and retailers discouraged from placing bulk reorders. The report didn’t name sources and follows earlier Engadget items that weren’t fully accurate, so take it cautiously. Observers note it would be odd for B&N to drop a 3G model entirely while competitor Amazon continues to offer both 3G/Wi‑Fi and Wi‑Fi variants; a more likely outcome would be a refreshed, lower‑cost e‑ink Nook to better compete on price. Retail trends also show buyers favoring cheaper Wi‑Fi‑only readers, which could explain reduced 3G demand. B&N declined to comment on product plans but said the Nook 3G sold well over the holidays and remains on sale in stores. Overall: possible discontinuation of the current Nook 3G hardware, but no confirmed replacement or roadmap.

Humphries is expected to file within days and ultimately hopes to obtain an annulment to clear the record of the marriage. This marks a shift from earlier reports that he planned to accept and sign divorce papers.
