A 25-year-old man, Sidney Bouvier Gilstrap-Portley, was arrested after allegedly posing as a Hurricane Harvey evacuee and enrolling as a freshman at Dallas ISD’s Hillcrest High School under the name Rashun Richardson. He claimed displacement by the August storm to avoid standard enrollment document requirements and may have provided only minimal records such as immunization and a physical. Gilstrap-Portley also briefly played on the Hillcrest basketball team and had earlier enrolled at Skyline High School before transferring back to Hillcrest; his last day of attendance was April 25. His true identity came to light after a former high school coach recognized him playing for Hillcrest. He was booked on charges of tampering with government records and released. Hillcrest’s principal said the school notified district and local authorities as soon as the false enrollment was discovered and noted the incident highlights gaps in protections when schools enroll displaced students. A woman who spoke about his conduct said he presented himself as respectful and mature, and expressed alarm that the deception could have had more harmful consequences elsewhere.

This document contains two news items.

1) Internet Archive crawls
- The Internet Archive is running crawls to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference, preserving the exact versions cited by authors.
- The aim is to prevent broken links by replacing or supplementing live links with archived versions, with the ultimate goal of fixing broken links across the web. The crawls target supported “No More 404” sites.

2) Bank of England’s new polymer £5 note
- The Bank of England will unveil its first plastic (polymer) banknote, a Winston Churchill £5, at Blenheim Palace; it enters circulation in September.
- This marks the start of a switch from paper to polymer notes after 320 years; the Jane Austen £10 and a JMW Turner £20 are due to follow.
- Polymer notes are made from a transparent plastic film with an ink layer; advantages include enhanced security (clear windows), greater durability (last up to 2.5× longer), cleaner feel, and environmental benefits. The Bank estimates durability will offset higher production costs and save about £100m.
- Tests indicate polymer notes resist shrinkage/melting up to 120°C and should survive a washing machine spin, though they can be damaged by hot irons.
- Transition costs for shops and banks (recalibrating or replacing ATMs, vending and self-service machines) could reach up to £236m because the new notes are 15% smaller.
- Over 30 countries already use polymer notes; Australia introduced them in 1988.
- The Churchill note replaces the Elizabeth Fry £5; public concern about removing female figures led to confirmation that Jane Austen will appear on the new £10. The Churchill design shows him alongside Westminster with Big Ben at about 3pm on 13 May 1940, referencing his “blood, toil, tears and sweat” speech.
- Note: an earlier version of the article incorrectly claimed Churchill would be the first statesman on British notes; the Duke of Wellington previously appeared on £5 notes (1971–1991).

This document profiles Amazon Flex, the company’s app-based “last-mile” delivery program, and raises concerns about how Amazon uses independent contractors to handle parcel delivery.

Key points

- What Flex is: Amazon Flex lets people sign up as independent contractors to pick up scheduled “blocks” of deliveries via a smartphone app. Blocks vary from short (2 hours) to longer shifts and cover services like Prime Now and Logistics. Drivers use their own vehicles, wear no uniform, and receive only a non-photo ID badge.

- Onboarding and training: Screening is minimal—app-based forms, a background check (handled via a vendor called Accurate Background), and brief, largely video-based training. Requirements are basic: 21+, a smartphone, and vehicle or bike/public transit access.

- Work process and pay: Drivers queue at fulfillment centers to collect pre-sorted carts, scan and load packages, and follow the app’s suggested routing. Pay averages around $18–$25/hour (drivers Gizmodo spoke with averaged ~$20.50/hr), and Amazon sometimes increases pay to fill unclaimed blocks. Most drivers treat Flex as supplemental income; few rely on it full time.

- Operational problems: Drivers report mismatches between block length and actual workload, inaccurate local data, under- or overestimates of time needed (leading to unpaid over-block work), frequent program changes, and inconsistent fulfillment-center rules. Drivers say hours are effectively capped at ~40/week in some locations. Support is limited and often unhelpful; terminations or “deactivations” can come with little explanation.

- Gaming and competition: Fierce competition for blocks has driven some drivers to use bots, auto-tap software (FRep, Repetitouch), or even hardware devices (Flexbot) to secure shifts. Amazon forbids such tools, but enforcement appears uneven.

- Third-party courier companies: Amazon also hires local courier firms to run larger van routes. These companies must run Amazon’s software and use Amazon’s background checks; owners report Amazon exerts strong control over which drivers are allowed to work and can effectively remove drivers or whole companies from routes. Some couriers have subcontracted labor, which has produced lawsuits alleging wage-and-hour violations.

- Legal and labor concerns: Labor advocates and attorneys (e.g., Shannon Liss-Riordan, Catherine Ruckelshaus) argue Flex raises serious misclassification issues: drivers perform work integrated into Amazon’s core services, often under tight operational control, yet are treated as independent contractors and lack benefits, workers’ comp, and other protections. Flex contracts include arbitration clauses that limit class actions and make it harder for collective legal challenges. Government regulators and agencies contacted were often unfamiliar with or noncommittal about Flex.

- Broader context: The article situates Flex within Amazon’s enormous, fast-growing, and often secretive empire—one that aggressively pursues local incentives, reshapes local labor markets and infrastructure, and increasingly controls the end-to-end delivery chain. Flex exemplifies concerns about tech companies shifting work toward precarious contractor models that avoid traditional employer responsibilities.

Takeaway
Amazon Flex provides flexible, often well-paying supplemental work for some drivers, but the program’s minimal onboarding, opaque rules, aggressive competition for blocks, spotty support, and apparent managerial control over contractors raise significant questions about worker protections, misclassification, and accountability. Because Flex operates quietly and uses arbitration and dispersed contracting arrangements, regulatory scrutiny, legal remedies, and public awareness have lagged, leaving many drivers vulnerable.

Adam Peterson, 29, the son of Milwaukee County Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Brian Peterson, died Monday of a suspected drug overdose after being found face down at a friend’s apartment on W. Clybourn Street. First responders administered Narcan but he did not respond and was pronounced dead about 7:30 p.m. Investigators noted a history of drug use and possible homelessness; items found with him included prescription medications (topiramate, citalopram), a razor blade and cotton balls.

His death is part of a sharp, ongoing spike in drug fatalities in Milwaukee County: officials reported 70–71 probable overdose deaths in the previous seven weeks and 168 confirmed drug-related deaths as of July 27, exceeding totals from prior years and prompting the medical examiner’s office to discard earlier projections for 2016. Dr. Peterson, who has publicly highlighted the scale of the crisis, requested privacy. Community resources such as IMPACT (866-211-3380) were noted for those seeking help.

An Egyptian court in Minya has sparked international outcry after sentencing 528 supporters of ousted president Mohamed Morsi to death in a single case linked to an August attack on a police station, and beginning a separate mass trial of 683 alleged Islamists the next day. The UN human rights office called the mass death sentences “unprecedented” and a breach of international law, while rights groups, Western governments and Egyptian lawyers condemned the trials for severe procedural irregularities.

Key points:
- The first trial, which led to 528 death sentences, reportedly lasted less than an hour for the main session; most defendants were tried in absentia, defence lawyers say they were prevented from presenting evidence or calling witnesses, and many defendants and their lawyers did not attend.
- Human Rights Watch and Egyptian lawyers describe the proceedings as cursory and ridden with violations of fair-trial standards. Sixteen Egyptian rights organizations warned the judges’ actions represent a dangerous shift in the judiciary and a grave violation of the right to life.
- Egypt’s interim government defended the rulings as carefully considered; the sentences must be ratified by the grand mufti (required before execution) and can be appealed. Legal experts expect higher courts may order retrials or reduce sentences.
- The second trial, of 683 defendants (many in absentia), includes senior Muslim Brotherhood figures such as general guide Mohammed Badie and FJP chairman Saad al-Katatni. Defence lawyers boycotted that session in protest; the judge still heard witnesses and adjourned to announce verdicts on 28 April.
- The cases stem from wave of violence after security forces dispersed two pro-Morsi sit-ins in Cairo in August, an operation that left hundreds dead and was followed by mob attacks on police stations. Authorities say thousands of Brotherhood members and other Islamists have been arrested since Morsi’s removal.
- Protests and clashes erupted near the Minya court and at Minya University, where students and relatives of defendants confronted security forces and were met with tear gas and rubber bullets.

International reactions included condemnation from the UN, the U.S. State Department, EU officials and Germany’s foreign minister, all urging respect for fair-trial rights and urging suspension or review of further mass trials. The Egyptian Justice Ministry emphasized appeals are available and higher courts can order retrials.

Actor Mandy Patinkin — best known as Inigo Montoya in the 1987 film The Princess Bride — discovered that images and videos circulating online have superimposed Ted Cruz’s face onto his character. Patinkin said friends emailed him the altered pictures and clips of Cruz quoting and reenacting lines from the movie on the campaign trail, including the famous “Hello, my name is Inigo Montoya…” speech. Cruz has long cited The Princess Bride as his favorite film, saying he watched it repeatedly at Princeton; he’s even performed scenes for campaign media appearances.

Patinkin objected not to the impersonation itself but to the way Cruz uses the lines, arguing Cruz’s politics—Patinkin characterized them as fueled by fear, revenge and hostility toward immigrants and Muslims—contradict the movie’s message of love, hope and redemption. Patinkin urged Cruz to also recite a later line in the film about not knowing what to do with life after revenge, and called on politicians who stoke fear to promote compassion instead. The Cruz campaign responded that he’s “a huge fan” and that “having some fun with a cult classic” should be apolitical.

The article also profiles Cruz personally: his rise in Republican politics, leadership in the 2013 Obamacare fight, and reported interest in a 2016 presidential bid; his fondness for The Princess Bride; dislikes (he claims to despise avocados); favorite foods and hobbies (beef enchiladas, Guinness, card and board games on his phone); and education and background (Princeton, Harvard Law, Cuban heritage, clerkship for Chief Justice Rehnquist). It notes media moments in which Cruz acted out full scenes from The Princess Bride for campaign videos, drawing mixed reactions.

First Lady Michelle Obama appeared on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno to promote her "Let's Move!" initiative encouraging children to be active and eat healthily. She brought healthy snacks—apples with White House honey, sweet potato fries and a whole-wheat crust vegetable pizza—and successfully persuaded Leno, who had joked about avoiding vegetables for decades, to try them. The appearance was part of a two-day California trip where she also planned to attend Democratic fundraisers.

Conversation ranged beyond food: Obama spoke warmly about President Barack Obama’s impromptu singing (citing his Al Green, Marvin Gaye and Stevie Wonder leanings) and said she often hears him sing at home. When Leno mentioned GOP hopeful Mitt Romney’s recent rendition of “America the Beautiful,” she complimented the song itself and noted it belongs to all Americans. On the upcoming, likely intense re-election campaign, she said there’s no special mental preparation—she and the president take each day as it comes and try to do their best.

Rapper Kevin Gates was convicted of misdemeanor simple battery by a six-woman jury in Polk County after a one‑day trial and was sentenced to 180 days in jail (with credit for time served), fines, court costs and probation. The charge stems from an August 29, 2015 concert at Rumors Nightclub in Lakeland, where video showed Gates kicking fan Miranda Dixon in the chest. Dixon testified she grabbed Gates’ shorts twice to get his attention; she said he kicked her after the second grab, causing her to lose consciousness and later seek medical care. Gates admitted on previous occasions that he kicked her and argued at trial — through attorney Jose Baez — that he acted in self‑defense under Florida’s Stand Your Ground law and that the kick either was necessary or did not make contact. Club security testified there were ample guards and space onstage and no special barricade was requested. The jury found Gates guilty despite defense claims questioning Dixon’s credibility and motives; prosecutors had sought a lighter sentence than the judge ultimately imposed. Thousands had signed a petition seeking to ban Gates from Florida venues after the incident.

Since 1996 Alexa Internet has been donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive. Those daily crawls are ingested into the Wayback Machine after an embargo period as part of a program to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference. By preserving the version of a referenced page that was live when an author wrote a piece, the Archive aims to replace or supplement broken links with archived snapshots, reducing link rot across the web. Users can add and delete location data from Tweets, and the Archive also performs targeted crawls of supported "No More 404" sites to help fix broken links.

Three years after the highly publicized Casey Anthony trial, Orlando defense attorney J. Cheney Mason — who joined Anthony’s team pro bono and has written a new book, Justice in America — told CNN that Anthony remains effectively confined by public hostility despite her 2011 acquittal on first‑degree murder and other major charges in the 2008 death of her 2‑year‑old daughter, Caylee. The jury did convict her on four misdemeanors for giving false information.

Mason, an experienced death‑penalty lawyer who spent significant unpaid time and money on the defense, describes meeting a small, frightened woman who still distrusts people and avoids public life because of threats and sustained hatred. He says Anthony does clerical and legal research work from an undisclosed Florida location, has no close family relationships (no relationship with her father and virtually none with her mother), and relies on members of her defense team and their families for companionship and support.

Mason recounts key trial moments: Jose Baez’s surprise assertion in opening statements that Casey had been sexually abused by her father; prosecutors’ immediate decision to call George Anthony as their first witness, who denied the claim; the largely circumstantial prosecution case; the defense’s contention that Caylee accidentally drowned in a pool; and late plea‑discussions that Anthony vehemently rejected. Mason praises the jury’s verdict and argues the public and media misjudged her.

His book, due in e‑book form imminently and in print in August, promises behind‑the‑scenes material, legal documents, and critiques of media bias and prosecutorial conduct. Mason will promote the book publicly; he says it is about broader legal issues as well as the Anthony case.

Cate Blanchett is attached to star as Lucille Ball in an authorized biopic being produced by Ball’s children, Lucie Arnaz and Desi Arnaz Jr., alongside Sony-based Escape Artists (overseen there by Jenna Block). Aaron Sorkin is the studio’s top choice to write the script, though sources say he has not yet officially started or committed. The film will focus on Ball’s life and her 20-year marriage to Desi Arnaz; Ball’s TV career included I Love Lucy, The Lucy–Desi Comedy Hour, The Lucy Show, Here’s Lucy and Life with Lucy, and she earned 13 Emmy nominations (four wins) plus the 1979 Cecil B. DeMille Award. Blanchett’s recent and upcoming projects include Cinderella, Carol, Truth and Knight of Cups. Sorkin’s credits include The Social Network, Moneyball, the forthcoming Steve Jobs film and Molly’s Game.

Politico’s investigation alleges the Obama administration significantly understated the national-security risks of a January 2016 prisoner swap that accompanied the Iran nuclear deal. Publicly, President Obama and senior officials described the seven Iranians clemencyed in the U.S. as nonviolent “sanctions violators” or “civilians” and framed the swap as a limited humanitarian gesture in exchange for five Americans held by Iran. But the reporting says the swap—and related behind‑the‑scenes actions—went much further: U.S. authorities dropped or vacated charges and Interpol red notices not only for those seven but for 14 additional Iranian fugitives overseas, some of whom Justice Department investigators had labeled high‑value proliferation and weapons procurement targets.

Key allegations and findings
- Several of the released or de‑listed Iranians were tied to procurement networks that supplied U.S.-origin components to Iran’s nuclear, missile and weapons programs. Examples include:
  - Seyed Abolfazl Shahab Jamili, accused of orchestrating procurement of thousands of parts (including hundreds of pressure transducers used in centrifuges) for Iran’s enrichment program.
  - Individuals accused of supplying U.S.-made microelectronics used in surface‑to‑air and cruise missiles.
  - Amin Ravan, linked to smuggling U.S. military antennas and components that have been used in IEDs that killed U.S. troops.
  - Others alleged to have tried to obtain aircraft for Mahan Air (linked to the IRGC/Quds Force) or to procure assault rifles and other military hardware.
- The Justice Department quietly dismissed charges and removed international arrest warrants for 14 fugitives; their names and alleged roles were not disclosed in the administration’s public statement.
- Federal prosecutors and investigators were reportedly shocked and angry—many had been building long investigations and felt kept out of negotiations. Some said the White House and State Department delayed or blocked lures, extraditions and other actions to arrest Iran targets during negotiations, and that an informal “embargo” on Iran cases began as early as late 2014.
- Officials and experts argue the actions hampered the National Counterproliferation Initiative, undermined enforcement momentum, cost operational intelligence and lost chances to prosecute mid‑ and high‑level procurement operatives who provided insight into Iran’s networks.
- The administration defended the decisions as necessary to secure the nuclear agreement and to obtain the release of U.S. detainees; some officials stressed continued ability to prosecute if illicit activity resumed. DOJ also said it continued to charge export‑control and sanctions violators during the negotiation period.
- Critics say the political imperative to seal a diplomatic deal led the Obama team to trade away long‑term law‑enforcement leverage, weakening deterrence and enabling individuals to resume or continue activities harmful to U.S. national security.

Broader implications
- The swap and related case delays allegedly damaged interagency trust and cooperation with industry and foreign partners, and prompted some experienced investigators to leave the field.
- The revelations gained attention amid the Trump administration’s review of the Iran deal; critics see the disclosures as validating concerns that the Obama team compromised enforcement to clinch a diplomatic victory.
- Independent experts and former prosecutors call the episode “a scandal,” warning that vacating cases and removing red notices may allow dangerous procurement networks to operate with less risk of arrest.

Bottom line
Politico portrays the prisoner swap and associated dismissals of charges as a significant and largely hidden concession: beyond freeing seven individuals in U.S. custody, the Obama administration removed legal tools against multiple fugitives accused of supplying Iran’s nuclear, missile and weapons programs. According to former prosecutors, agents and nonproliferation experts interviewed, those decisions undercut long-term U.S. counterproliferation efforts and national‑security interests in order to secure the diplomatic accomplishment of the nuclear agreement.

Scientists have announced the discovery of a small, crow-sized, bird-like theropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic (about 161 million years ago) in Hebei Province, northeastern China. The nearly complete, exquisitely preserved specimen was named Caihong juji — Mandarin for “rainbow with a big crest.”

Key findings
- Plumage and color: Microscopic analysis of feather microstructures (melanosomes) found in 66 feather samples indicates Caihong had iridescent, platelet-shaped melanosomes arranged in sheets on its head, neck and chest. This organization closely resembles the melanosomes that produce hummingbird- and swift-like iridescence in modern birds, implying shimmering, color-changing feathers in those regions. Most of the rest of the body is inferred as dark/black.
- Feathers and anatomy: Caihong had extensive, well-preserved feathers across its body, including long pennaceous (vaned) and down-like feathers, large rectrices (tail feathers) with asymmetrical vanes on mid-series tail feathers, and long remiges (primary/secondary-like feathers) on the forelimbs. Small feathers near the pollex resemble an alula-like structure. The presence of asymmetrical tail feathers makes Caihong the oldest-known animal with that trait, which in birds is associated with aerodynamic control.
- Lifestyle and function: Anatomically, Caihong combined bird-like features (feathers, wing-like forelimbs, certain limb proportions) with more typical theropod traits (Velociraptor-like skull, sharp teeth, two-legged predator). Its flight ability is uncertain: forelimbs are proportionally short, but some feather arrangements could have aided gliding or aerodynamic control. The iridescent feathers and prominent bony lacrimal crests likely served as visual display structures for social or sexual signaling.
- Phylogenetic context: Caihong is a basal paravian maniraptoran closely related to other feathered taxa from the Yanliao Biota (e.g., Anchiornis). Comparative analyses place its platelet-like melanosomes in morphospace overlapping iridescent modern birds; other Yanliao theropods sampled do not show the same platelet morphology or organization.
- Preservation and methods: The study combined high-resolution imaging (SEM, FIB-SEM) to characterize fossil nanostructures and compared them with melanosomes from living birds. Electron-dense, solid structures and lack of microbial signatures support a melanosome origin rather than bacterial artifacts. Statistical and taphonomic tests argue the platelet shape and arrangement reflect original biology, not burial distortion.

Significance
Caihong juji pushes back the occurrence of complex, display-oriented feather nanostructures and asymmetrical tail feathers into the Jurassic, suggesting more colorful and behaviorally complex early paravians than previously recognized. Its mix of display features and some flight-related feather morphologies offers new insight into the early evolution of feather function (display, insulation, and possibly aerodynamic roles) before the origin of modern birds.

Juan Salaz, a 37-year-old American who escaped from the Garza East prison in Beeville, Texas, on March 22, 1997, has been captured in Mexico and is awaiting extradition to the U.S. Salaz had been serving three concurrent 35-year sentences for aggravated kidnapping with a deadly weapon and two counts of attempted capital murder of police officers stemming from a 1995 incident in which he and an accomplice abducted a man for ransom and later opened fire on undercover Houston officers; one sergeant was saved by body armor and another officer was wounded. Salaz was seriously wounded in the shootout, later pleaded guilty, and escaped by climbing over three 16-foot fences topped with razor wire. He also faces a felony escape charge. Authorities from the U.S. Marshals Service, the Texas Department of Criminal Justice Office of Inspector General and Mexican law enforcement had sought him for years; investigators previously suspected he had been living near Monterrey and moving between Mexico and Texas with family assistance. His capture leaves Jose Fernando Bustos-Diaz as the lone remaining Texas prison fugitive; Bustos-Diaz fled in April 2010 and is believed to be in Mexico.

A 25-year-old German man developed seizures triggered specifically by solving Sudoku after suffering brain hypoxia when he was buried and briefly unconscious in an avalanche. Rescued and treated for injuries including a ruptured spleen and hip fracture, he exhibited myoclonic jerks (mouth when speaking, legs when walking) and tonic-clonic seizures in his left arm while hospitalized. Weeks later, attempting Sudoku at a rehab facility provoked clonic jerks in his left arm that stopped immediately when he ceased the 3D visualization strategy he used to solve puzzles.

Neurologists led by Dr. Berend Feddersen reported the case in JAMA Neurology and concluded that oxygen deprivation had damaged inhibitory fibers in the right centro-parietal region—an area engaged by three-dimensional imagination. Loss of inhibition produced overactivation when he used 3D spatial strategies, causing reflex epilepsy confined to his left arm. The seizures were specific to tasks that strongly engaged that visuospatial/ motor combination (Sudoku, some crosswords, Excel-like grids); other math problems or reading did not trigger them. With anti-epileptic medication and avoidance of triggering activities, he has been seizure-free for over five years, though some myoclonic symptoms have improved only gradually with therapy.

The Dallas Morning News—historically a very conservative paper that hadn’t endorsed a Democrat for president since 1940—broke tradition to endorse Hillary Clinton over Donald Trump. The editorial framed the choice bluntly: “There is only one serious candidate on the presidential ballot in November.” While acknowledging its usual alignment with Republican principles and criticizing Democratic over-reliance on government, the board said Clinton’s experience, record of governance, willingness to work across the aisle, and foreign-policy credentials make her the safer, more competent choice.

The paper criticized Clinton’s judgment on issues such as her private email server and urged greater transparency around the Clinton Foundation, but called these shortcomings minor compared with what it described as Trump’s dangerous temperament, improvisation, shifts on policy, and appeals to xenophobia, racism and misogyny. It said Trump’s values are “hostile to conservatism” and that his behavior and instability raise serious concerns about judgment and impulse control.

The endorsement is notable because of the paper’s long Republican streak and Texas’s GOP history; the piece notes Texas may be more competitive than usual this cycle as a diversifying electorate and polling showed a closer race. Research cited suggests that atypical newspaper endorsements (papers endorsing outside their usual partisan pattern) can influence readers, especially older ones who see the editorial, though the overall impact may be muted today given declining newspaper reach and growing polarization.

Researchers have developed a topical drug that induces production of dark melanin in human skin samples and mice without UV exposure, offering a potential way to reduce UV damage and lower skin cancer risk for fair-skinned people. Published June 13 in Cell Reports, the study builds on earlier work with forskolin and targets signaling to activate true eumelanin synthesis (not just the surface staining of cosmetic self-tanners). In lab-treated human skin the induced melanin blocked harmful UV rays; the compound also worked in mouse models including those mimicking red-haired, fair-skinned genetics that normally can’t tan.

The team, led by Dr. David Fisher at Massachusetts General Hospital, envisions using such compounds alongside sunscreen for cancer prevention and possibly to slow photoaging. Safety testing remains to be done and the approach is not yet ready for human use; so far no safety problems have emerged in preclinical work. Experts call the approach novel and promising but emphasize more research is needed before clinical application.

Stephon Alonzo Clark, a 22-year-old Black man known to family and friends as Stephon or “Zoe,” was fatally shot by two Sacramento police officers in the backyard of his grandparents’ south Sacramento home on the night of March 18, 2018. Officers responding to 911 reports of nearby car/window break-ins confronted Clark after sheriff’s deputies in a helicopter tracked a man to the property. Police say the officers ordered him to stop, then fired at him 20 times after he advanced toward them while holding an object; they initially characterized that object as a “tool bar” and later said only a cellphone was found at the scene, with two other items (a cinder block and a piece of aluminum) recovered near a broken sliding door in a neighboring yard.

Clark was pronounced dead at the scene. Both officers were placed on paid administrative leave. The Sacramento Police Department, the county district attorney, the city attorney’s office, the Office of Public Safety Accountability, and SPD internal units are investigating. City officials pledged transparency and an expedited release of body-camera and aerial video; the department planned to show the footage to Clark’s family within days and to the public within a week (formal policy requires release within 30 days).

Family members say Clark lived with his grandparents, was returning to their home when shot, and was the father of two young sons. Loved ones and community activists, including Black Lives Matter, have demanded justice and accountability; vigils and protests followed the shooting. A GoFundMe and memorial fund were established to help the family with funeral expenses.

A powerful winter storm struck the Midwest and East Coast, dumping heavy snow, driving winds and dangerously cold temperatures across a wide swath of the U.S.

- Snow totals and scope: Parts of New England reported up to ~20–21 inches (Boxford, MA ~21 in.; some Massachusetts areas ~20 in.; Boston ~14 in.). Other totals: NYC about 5–8 in., Hartford 6–10 in., Philadelphia ~5 in., Baltimore 3–6 in., western New York up to 18 in., parts of the Midwest up to a foot or more (Chicago suburbs ~17 in.). Blizzard warnings covered coastal New England and Long Island.

- Travel and closures: Major highways (e.g., Long Island Expressway, I‑84 in NY, sections of the Thruway) were closed overnight; JFK and Boston Logan were effectively shut for a period. Thousands of flights were canceled nationwide (roughly 1,600 on Friday on top of ~2,000 on Thursday; total U.S. cancellations exceeded 2,300 in some reports). Amtrak and commuter railroads ran modified schedules. Schools across the Northeast, including NYC public schools, were closed.

- Cold and hazards: Sub‑zero temperatures and extreme wind chills (as low as −30°F in places) followed the storm, with forecasters warning of record or near‑record lows. Wind chills could cause frostbite within about 30 minutes. Salt effectiveness on roads is reduced below ~10–20°F, compounding travel danger.

- Government response and public safety: Governors in New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts declared states of emergency or closed state offices; NY closed major roads and urged residents to stay home. Cities mobilized plows and salt spreaders. Shelters extended hours and prepared extra space; outreach sought to get homeless people indoors.

- Impacts and incidents: Mass cancellations and tarmac delays disrupted travelers coast to coast. A worker died in Pennsylvania when a pile of road salt collapsed. Power/ coastal‑flooding concerns were monitored in vulnerable areas.

- Outlook: A second, even colder wave was forecast to move from the Plains and Midwest into the East later in the weekend into early next week, threatening record lows and harsh wind chills across an expanded region (including Chicago, Green Bay and parts of the South).

Authorities urged people to avoid travel, dress warmly, watch for hypothermia/frostbite, and prepare for prolonged cold.

A woman employed through a temp agency gave birth in a restroom stall at a CEVA Logistics facility in Redford Township, Michigan, and the newborn was later found dead in a bag under her cubicle. Employees discovered blood and heard moaning in the women’s restroom Tuesday morning; coworkers found the 25–26‑year‑old Wyandotte woman with blood on her and initially believed she had only been lightheaded. She denied being pregnant, had worked at the site since October, and at first declined treatment before being taken to a hospital. The infant, apparently full‑term, was also transported to a hospital where resuscitation efforts failed and the child was pronounced dead. The mother is recovering at the hospital and is under investigation; authorities are determining whether the baby was born alive and whether criminal charges are warranted. The Wayne County Medical Examiner performed an autopsy, with results expected in about two weeks. CEVA and the temp agency are providing counseling to employees and are cooperating with investigators; both companies and the woman’s family have declined further comment.

An eighth-grade history worksheet at Great Hearts Monte Vista charter school in San Antonio asked students to list “positive aspects” and “negative aspects” of slavery. A parent photographed the assignment and shared it after his son refused to complete the “positive aspects” column. The image went viral, drawing outrage from parents, local lawmakers (including Rep. Joaquin Castro and State Rep. Diego Bernal) and the community.

Great Hearts Texas Superintendent Aaron Kindel called the worksheet “very inappropriate” and said there is no debate about slavery, calling it “immoral and a crime against humanity.” The school placed the teacher on leave, removed the worksheet and pulled the Prentice Hall Classics: A History of the United States textbook for audit (and from Texas academies), saying it may be permanently replaced. Administrators will meet with affected students and promised a follow-up communication and investigation results by May 9, 2018.

Pearson, which was named in tweets, denied producing the worksheet and condemned the notion of any positive aspects of slavery. The school and district say this was limited to one teacher on one campus and apologized; they are reviewing the incident and will decide whether the teacher keeps his job.

Dunkin' Donuts will shorten its name to "Dunkin'" starting in January, rolling the new brand out on packaging, signage, social media and at new and remodeled U.S. stores, with international adoption to follow. The 68-year-old, Canton, Massachusetts–based chain (more than 12,500 restaurants worldwide) says the change reflects its shift to a beverage-led business—coffee and other drinks account for about 60% of U.S. sales—while doughnuts and other to-go food remain on the menu. The updated branding keeps Dunkin's familiar rounded font and orange-and-pink colors. The rename is part of broader efforts to modernize and appeal to younger customers, including menu simplification, dedicated mobile-ordering lanes, digital kiosks and expanded Grab & Go and drive-thru capabilities. Dunkin' also plans to add about 1,000 U.S. stores by the end of 2020.

Oracle Team USA completed one of the greatest comebacks in sailing history to retain the America's Cup, winning the deciding race in the best-of-17 series 9–8 against Emirates Team New Zealand on San Francisco Bay. Skipper James (Jimmy) Spithill and his crew rallied from an 8–1 deficit a week earlier and overcame a two-point penalty assessed before racing began for illegal modifications. Oracle ran off eight straight wins to force the final race and then used superior boat speed—keeping their foiling 72-foot catamaran up more often—to overtake New Zealand after a tense start in which the U.S. boat briefly buried its bows. Tactician Ben Ainslie and the crew held the lead as Team New Zealand tried tacks to close the gap; owner Larry Ellison boarded to celebrate at the finish. Observers compared the comeback to historic reversals in other sports, and the high-speed catamarans and dramatic finish were widely credited with bringing renewed excitement to the Cup.

This mixed document contains three short, unrelated news items:

1) Telegraph magazine apology: Following a cover story titled “The mystery of Melania” (Jan 19), the paper has acknowledged that the article contained multiple false statements and said some content should not have been published. The statement specifically disputes a claim that Melania Trump’s father was a fearsome presence.

2) Mary J. Blige supports Obama in Planned Parenthood ad: Singer Mary J. Blige appears in a new Planned Parenthood video called “Yes We Plan,” which urges voters to re-elect President Obama and highlights his record on women’s rights and health care. The ad — which also features rapper Q-Tip and actress Julianne Moore and was produced by Michael Moore with MoveOn.org — includes Blige saying Planned Parenthood was crucial to her and her family when she was a teenager.

3) Controversial Michael Moore/MoveOn.org ad: A separate ad produced by Michael Moore and MoveOn.org, framed as a message from the “Greatest Generation” to Republicans and Mitt Romney, contains explicit, confrontational language threatening violence and obscene remarks about Romney. The piece is described as more characteristic of Moore’s style than the purported source generation; viewers are warned about explicit content.

Russian spy Anna Chapman, one of 10 suspected Russian sleeper agents deported from the United States in July, posed in provocative photographs for the Russian edition of Maxim, including shots of her in nylon and lace holding a handgun. Maxim praised her popularity, saying she "has done more to excite Russian patriotism than the Russian soccer team." Chapman and the other nine agents—whose ring was reported to have failed to obtain significant intelligence—were returned to Russia in a swap for four Russians imprisoned for allegedly passing secrets to the West. The Kremlin has highlighted the case to rehabilitate the prestige of its Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), and President Dmitry Medvedev recently awarded the group Russia’s highest state honors. An interview and additional photos of Chapman will appear in the next issue of Maxim.

Plaintiffs’ lawyers and tobacco companies are still locked in major litigation in Florida thanks to the state Supreme Court’s 2006 Engle decision, which pre‑established key facts for future smoking cases (including that cigarettes were “defective” and “unreasonably dangerous”). More than 7,000 Engle‑progeny suits are pending in Florida state and federal courts, and plaintiffs have so far won over $250 million in such cases.

In a recent Florida trial in Bronson, a jury awarded $80 million to the daughter of James Cayce Horner, a two‑pack‑a‑day smoker who died of lung cancer in 1996; $72 million of that award was punitive damages. The jury attributed 10% of the fault to Horner and 90% to R.J. Reynolds. Plaintiffs’ counsel emphasized the human cost of the company’s conduct; R.J. Reynolds declined to comment. The verdict interrupts a brief defense winning streak—tobacco companies had recently won eight straight Engle cases, including a Miami victory for Philip Morris USA. 

(Separately: since 1996 Alexa Internet has been donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive; those daily data are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.)

California has agreed to end its practice of unlimited isolation for imprisoned gang leaders, settling a class-action lawsuit on behalf of nearly 3,000 inmates held in long-term segregation. The state will now confine inmates in segregation mainly for new crimes committed in prison, limit time in isolation (generally up to five years for in-prison offenses, with an extra two years possible for gang leaders), and create restrictive custody units that allow greater personal contact and privileges for high-security inmates and those who refuse rehabilitation or pose safety risks.

The policy change addresses conditions that once kept hundreds of prisoners in small, soundproofed, windowless cells for a decade or more—practices that sparked large hunger strikes, drew criticism from national figures, and were challenged as cruel and unusual. The settlement follows a lawsuit started in 2009 and upheld by the Center for Constitutional Rights; it comes after state policy shifts that already reduced the number of segregated inmates from over 4,100 in January 2012 to about 2,858.

Advocates and plaintiffs hailed the agreement as a major step toward ending solitary confinement and restoring family contact for long-isolated inmates. Officials say the changes bring California more in line with other states while preserving tools to manage dangerous inmates; correctional leaders also noted the segregation system’s origins in past prison violence and promised to address staff safety concerns voiced by guards’ unions.

Fox & Friends hosts defended President Trump’s tough border policies amid debate over an immigration compromise. Co-host Ainsley Earhardt framed the measures as necessary to “vet who’s coming across the border, in case it’s MS-13 or drugs.” Brian Kilmeade argued the president is trying to deter migrants and enforce laws, saying “somebody has to deal with this issue” and asserting migrants “aren’t our kids,” urging compassion but prioritizing U.S. taxpayers’ needs. Kilmeade later clarified his remarks. The segment came after Trump signed an executive order meant to halt the family-separation policy but that also expands the government’s ability to detain children with parents indefinitely. MSNBC’s Stephanie Ruhle criticized Kilmeade’s comments on air.

At a Friends of Syria meeting in Rome, US Secretary of State John Kerry announced a shift in US policy: Washington will for the first time provide direct, non‑lethal aid to Syrian rebel forces (medical supplies and Meals Ready to Eat) and ask Congress for an additional $60 million to bolster the Syrian Opposition Coalition’s ability to deliver basic governance and services in rebel-held areas. The move doubles US support for the civilian opposition and is framed as intended to increase pressure on President Bashar al‑Assad and strengthen moderate elements versus extremists.

The aid stops short of supplying weapons, munitions or military training, a restraint that disappointed many opposition figures and frontline commanders who have repeatedly asked for anti‑tank and anti‑aircraft systems to counter Assad’s tanks, aircraft and Scud strikes. The US says assistance will be carefully vetted to try to prevent arms or supplies reaching extremist groups. The European Union amended its embargo to allow member states to provide armored vehicles, non‑lethal military equipment and technical aid intended to protect civilians, but not weapons.

Fighting continues across Syria—Aleppo remains a major battleground, with rebels claiming capture of the Umayyad Mosque and other landmarks—while the humanitarian crisis deepens: UN estimates put deaths at more than 70,000, nearly one million refugees, and two million internally displaced, with growing risks of disease and failing services.

Rebel leaders, including SNC head Moaz al‑Khatib, expressed frustration that the international response falls short of what is needed to secure victory and to enable credible leadership inside rebel areas; some opposition plans (such as selecting a provisional prime minister) were postponed amid disappointment. Western governments say the non‑lethal assistance is an initial step coordinated with other partners and could serve as a model if further measures are approved, but major divisions remain—most notably with Russia and China—over whether Assad must step down as a condition for talks or a political solution.

A federal judge in Maryland, U.S. District Judge Peter J. Messitte, ruled that the District of Columbia and Maryland may proceed with their lawsuit alleging President Donald Trump’s business dealings violate the Constitution’s emoluments clauses. This is the first time a court has found plaintiffs have standing to sue over these clauses.

Key points:
- Messitte allowed the case to continue but narrowed its scope primarily to the Trump International Hotel in Washington, D.C., where Trump retains a financial interest. Claims against other properties (e.g., Mar-a-Lago) were largely excluded.
- The plaintiffs, D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine and Maryland Attorney General Brian Frosh, argue that foreign and state governments have steered business—such as bookings and events—toward the Trump hotel, harming competing local hotels and the jurisdictions’ own convention centers, and creating economic injury to their commercial constituencies.
- Messitte cited specific examples (clients from Kuwait and Bahrain, a nearly $1 million tax reduction by D.C. officials, and a $6 million tax break in Mississippi for a Trump-affiliated project) as evidence of potential competitive and governmental harms and of state decisions affected by the president’s business interests.
- He rejected the argument that only Congress may enforce the emoluments clauses, writing that courts may review whether the President’s actions comply with the law and warning that leaving enforcement solely to Congress could permit unchecked receipt of emoluments.
- If the case proceeds, Racine and Frosh may seek internal Trump Organization documents and tax records to determine the extent of payments from foreign and state governments. The Justice Department, defending the president, said it will seek dismissal; the Trump Organization said the ruling narrows the case and expects further grounds for dismissal.
- Background: The suits invoke two rarely litigated emoluments clauses—one barring federal officers from accepting foreign gifts/payments and another prohibiting presidents from receiving payments from states. Other emoluments suits have been dismissed for lack of standing or as political questions, but Messitte’s decision is the first to find standing for state and D.C. plaintiffs.

Attorneys general say the decision allows enforcement of the Constitution’s anti-corruption provisions; the administration disputes the merits and may appeal.

On June 30, 2013—the one‑year anniversary of Mohamed Morsi’s inauguration—mass demonstrations erupted across Egypt as millions turned out to demand the Islamist president’s removal. Hundreds of thousands filled Cairo’s Tahrir Square and marched toward the presidential palace at Itihadiya, while large pro‑Morsi rallies gathered near Rabia al‑Adawiya and in Nasser City. The protests were driven by broad frustration over political polarization, economic decline, power outages, rising prices, lawlessness, and allegations that Morsi and the Muslim Brotherhood monopolized power, forced through an Islamist‑tilted constitution and sidelined opponents. Organizers of the opposition Tamarod (Rebel) campaign claimed more than 22 million signatures calling for his ouster.

Tensions were high and violence flared: at least seven people were reported killed and hundreds injured in clashes around the country, with attacks on Brotherhood offices and exchanges of gunfire in several towns. Both sides prepared for confrontation—many pro‑Morsi supporters wore helmets and carried shields, while army troops and helicopters were deployed across Cairo after Defense Minister Gen. Abdel‑Fattah el‑Sissi warned the military would act if the crisis deepened. Opposition leaders urged Morsi to step down or face pressure including possible military intervention; some protesters openly chanted for Sisi and an army role. Morsi, who refused calls for early elections in an interview with The Guardian, defended his constitutional legitimacy and called for dialogue, while his aides acknowledged mistakes and said he sought reconciliation.

The mass mobilization reflected deep societal divisions—secularists, liberals, Christians and many ordinary Egyptians joined the opposition, while the Brotherhood and allied Islamists insisted protests could not overturn an elected president. With uncertainty over whether the military would intervene and fears of wider bloodshed, the demonstrations marked a crucial and volatile turning point in Egypt’s post‑revolution transition.

Leslie (Les) Gibson, a Republican who had been the sole declared candidate for Maine’s 57th District (Sabattus and Greene), has withdrawn from the state House race after widespread backlash over a series of insulting social-media posts aimed at Parkland shooting survivors. Gibson had called Emma González a “skinhead lesbian” and labeled David Hogg “a bald-faced liar” while defending Second Amendment rights and criticizing calls for stricter gun laws. He later apologized to González.

His comments prompted swift criticism from both parties, prompted two challengers to enter the contest — Republican Thomas Martin Jr. and Democrat Eryn Gilchrist (a 28-year-old first-time candidate who said she was “horrified and embarrassed” at the thought of Gibson representing her) — and led Gibson to make his social accounts private. Gibson said he decided to quit after consulting family, friends and colleagues, calling the choice “the best thing for everybody” and insisting he left “with [his] head held high.” The controversy reflects a broader national pushback against critics of the Parkland students, who have become prominent advocates for gun-control reform.

A large crack appeared in a 36th‑floor window of San Francisco’s 58‑story Millennium Tower over the Labor Day weekend, prompting a city inspection and safety measures. Residents reported hearing creaking and a loud pop around 2:30 a.m. before the damage was discovered. The tower, which has been sinking and tilting since construction (about 17–18 inches of settlement and roughly 14–18 inches of tilt at different reports), has been the subject of lawsuits and safety concerns since 2016.

San Francisco’s Department of Building Inspection issued a correction/violation notice requiring the building’s engineers to evaluate the cracked glass, the adjacent curtain wall system and any needed repairs within 72 hours. City inspectors could not initially access the unit to view the crack. Management placed a barrier along Mission Street and said experts would assess the “large piece of glass” and that the incident might be related to the building’s ongoing settlement. Supervisor Aaron Peskin urged the city to take the risk seriously—raising the possibility of closing the sidewalk beneath the window if needed—because curtain wall failure at height could endanger pedestrians. The building engineer reportedly told inspectors the crack did not appear to pose an immediate sidewalk safety hazard; the city said it would follow up.

Ten volunteer firefighters from the Fairmont and Orrum fire departments have been arrested after a year-long investigation into a nearly two-year campaign of deliberately setting fires to woods and abandoned structures across Robeson County, authorities said. The Robeson County Sheriff’s Office, State Bureau of Investigation, ATF and NC Forestry Service conducted the probe after a tip; about 90 arson-related charges have been filed and more arrests are possible.
