Saudi media mistakenly reported a satirical column by U.S. humorist Andy Borowitz as real news. Borowitz’s piece joked that President Barack Obama would tell Congress he is Muslim as a compromise with Republicans and included mock quotes about “Allah willing,” negotiable birthplace and joking references to being born “in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.” Prominent Saudi outlets Al-Hayat and Sabq.org ran the item straight, using headlines implying Obama was ready to “come out” as Muslim and repeating the fabricated quotes, apparently missing the satire. The article notes that despite Obama’s repeated statements that he is Christian, questions about his background have persisted because of his Kenyan-born father and his middle name, Hussein. The piece originally ran on The Borowitz Report/Huffington Post.

A viral hoax claimed iOS 8 included a “Wave” feature that lets iPhones charge wirelessly in a microwave. The fake ads—traced to a 4chan thread and spread on Twitter and Reddit—encouraged users to microwave phones for about a minute, but the claim is false. Similar microwave and waterproof-iOS pranks have circulated before. Some people posted images of damaged phones and microwaves (possibly as jokes), but the takeaway is: iOS 8 does not enable microwave charging; don’t try it.

The World Health Organization has declared Cuba the first country to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of both HIV and syphilis. An international WHO/PAHO evaluation found Cuba met the required criteria: in 2013 only two children were born with HIV and five with syphilis. WHO and PAHO credited Cuba’s universal, early-access prenatal care system for providing routine testing and timely treatment—antiretroviral therapy for HIV-positive mothers and antibiotics for syphilis—which reduced transmission risk to below 1 percent. WHO Director-General Margaret Chan and UNAIDS head Michel Sidibé called the achievement a major public‑health milestone and evidence that ending pediatric AIDS is possible, urging other countries and donors to scale up similar efforts. The agencies note global progress—children born with HIV fell from 400,000 in 2009 to 240,000 in 2013—and stress that widespread testing and treatment are essential, since many pregnant women with HIV still lack access to preventative drugs.

A search-warrant affidavit and reporting revealed that Dr. Michael Todd Schulenberg, a Minnetonka family physician, saw Prince twice in April 2016—on April 7 and again on April 20, the day before the musician was found dead in an elevator at Paisley Park. Schulenberg told detectives he delivered test results to Paisley Park the morning Prince was found and had prescribed medications to be filled at a Walgreens; the warrant did not specify what medicines were prescribed or whether Prince took them.

Investigators executed the warrant at North Memorial Medical Center (where Schulenberg had worked but no longer is employed) and sought Prince’s medical records as part of the probe into his death. The warrant was mistakenly left unsealed when filed May 6 and was obtained by news outlets before being sealed. Authorities returned to Paisley Park for further work; officials say neither foul play nor suicide is suspected and the Midwest Medical Examiner’s Office is still determining cause of death.

Reporting indicates Prince had been seeking treatment for opioid addiction in the weeks before his death. Representatives contacted California addiction specialist Dr. Howard Kornfeld on April 20; Kornfeld sent his son and another federally certified physician to Minnesota to evaluate Prince on April 21. Schulenberg is not on the federal list of practitioners authorized to prescribe buprenorphine (used to treat opioid addiction). A source told the Star Tribune the Minnesota doctor had been treating Prince for opioid withdrawal but had not prescribed opioids.

The affidavit also notes that Paisley Park manager Kirk Anthony Johnson was present when detectives arrived and told investigators Prince had been treated for an unspecified illness in 2014–15. Investigators are examining how Prince obtained prescription opioids, including reviewing state prescribing-monitoring records where permitted. Schulenberg’s medical license shows no disciplinary actions; he and his attorney declined to comment.

Robert Wang, a former Nortel engineer, invented the Instant Pot after losing his software job in 2008 and struggling with preparing healthy weeknight meals for young families. Launched in 2010 by his Ottawa-based company Double Insight, the Instant Pot is a “smart” multi-cooker combining pressure cooking, slow cooking, steaming, rice cooking and other functions. Its safety sensors, microprocessor controls and a burn-detection system were developed to make pressure cooking fast, reliable and less intimidating for novice cooks.

The appliance grew largely by word of mouth and social media rather than paid advertising. A highly active official Facebook community (750,000+ members) and endorsements from food writers and TV segments helped fuel rapid sales growth: the company became profitable in 2012 and has doubled revenue year-over-year since. It sold roughly 215,000–250,000 units on a single Prime Day and Wang anticipated up to 500,000 Amazon orders for Black Friday. Instant Pot models have expanded from a “five-in-one” to “10-in-one” by adding features such as yogurt making, sautéing, sterilizing and Bluetooth control; new products are planned.

Users and cooking instructors praise the Instant Pot for making traditionally slow dishes—beans, braises, risottos, stocks, and even octopus—much faster while preserving flavor. It’s especially popular for bone broth, chicken thighs, dried beans and quick risottos. It is not ideal for everything (pasta can get mushy, fish and some white meats can overcook), but its convenience and ability to tame pressure-cooking fears have won devoted fans and spawned cookbooks and classes.

The Instant Pot’s popularity helped create a dominant position in the multi-cooker market; growth of the overall category has been dramatic, with many competitors entering the space at varying price points. Wang’s stated mission is “an Instant Pot in every kitchen,” and he believes the market is still early—only about 5% of North American households have such a device—so he expects continued expansion.

Beyond convenience and sales milestones, Wang finds it rewarding when customers use the product in emergencies (e.g., after hurricanes) and when user feedback directly shapes new features. The overall narrative positions the Instant Pot as a practical, technology-upgraded reinvention of the pressure cooker that has become a lasting culinary trend rather than a passing fad.

Authorities say Orlando Tercero, 22, has been arrested in Nicaragua in connection with the homicide of 22-year-old Haley Anderson, a nursing student at SUNY Binghamton from Westbury, Long Island. Nicaragua’s National Police confirmed Tercero was detained Tuesday and is being transferred to El Chipote prison near Managua. Binghamton police had identified Tercero—Anderson’s ex-boyfriend and a fellow nursing student—as a person of interest after Anderson’s body was found Friday during a welfare check at an off-campus home about a mile from campus; her death was ruled a homicide following an autopsy. Investigators said Tercero left the U.S. via an international flight from JFK to Nicaragua before Anderson’s body was discovered; he reportedly holds a Nicaraguan passport and may have family ties there. A warrant is being prepared and evidence will be presented to a grand jury; if indicted, local officials intend to seek expedited extradition. Anderson, a senior close to graduation who worked locally, will be remembered at services in her hometown.

Portable Texas Department of Transportation electronic construction signs in west Dallas were hacked over the Memorial Day weekend and early Tuesday, May 31, 2016. Three portable roadside signs along westbound I‑30 (near Cockrell Hill Road and Westmoreland Road) were manually accessed and reprogrammed to display messages such as “Donald Trump is a … shape shifting lizard!,” “Bernie for president,” and “Work is canceled. Go back home.” TxDOT said the signs belong to a contractor working on I‑30, must be changed at the control panel (not remotely), and appeared to have been turned off and re‑locked before the holiday. Officials stressed the tampering is dangerous because it can replace safety warnings for motorists, is a serious offense (a third‑degree felony with potential prison time), and urged people to report suspicious activity around portable signs. All signs were returned to normal messages shortly after discovery.

A massive mudslide near Oso, Washington (along State Route 530 between Darrington and Arlington) on Saturday morning left about one square mile of mud, trees and debris, burying a mile-long stretch of highway, destroying roughly 30 homes and flattening entire neighborhoods. By Sunday and into Monday search crews had recovered at least eight bodies; officials said dozens more people remained unaccounted for on a “soft list” of 108 names but cautioned the actual number missing would likely be lower because some may have been away when the slide hit. Rescuers who briefly heard voices late Saturday were unable to reach them in the dark and, after resuming at first light Sunday, reported no signs of life. Conditions—deep, soupy, shifting mud described as “like quicksand”—made the search dangerous; teams concentrated on drier, safer areas while remaining in search-and-rescue (not recovery) mode.

Several people were injured; hospitals reported critical patients including a 6-month-old and an 81-year-old, and others in serious or stable condition. The slide also dammed the North Fork of the Stillaguamish River; water began seeping through the mud wall by Sunday, easing immediate flood fears. Officials said heavy recent rainfall likely destabilized the hillside—the same slope that partially collapsed in 2006. Governor Jay Inslee flew over the scene, described the destruction as “total devastation,” and warned of difficult days ahead. Families and neighbors gathered at shelters and community centers seeking news; volunteers and regional rescue teams continued ground and helicopter searches amid emotional, grim conditions.

A partial collapse of the Big Four Ice Caves in Mount Baker–Snoqualmie National Forest on the afternoon of July 6, 2015 killed one hiker and injured five others (three adults seriously, two juveniles with minor injuries). Dozens of visitors had been sheltering in the caves from high daytime temperatures when a large shelf of ice and rock broke loose near the cave mouth, scattering people. Eyewitness Chloe Jakubowski, 18, described chaos, helping others after the collapse; one woman was found unconscious and others suffered cuts and fractures.

Rescue response was slowed because the incident occurred in an area with no cellphone reception: it took about 45 minutes before authorities were alerted, and more than 100 rescuers subsequently responded. The body of the deceased could not be recovered immediately because unstable, dangerous ice conditions made recovery unsafe. Three injured adults were airlifted to Harborview Medical Center (a 25-year-old man initially critical, a 35-year-old man seriously injured, and a 35-year-old woman treated and released); two girls with minor injuries were treated and released from Providence Regional Medical Center.

Officials had warned since May that warming conditions were weakening the caves, and the U.S. Forest Service had previously cautioned visitors to stay on the trail and avoid the caves; signage warns of hazards. Authorities closed the area indefinitely while search-and-rescue teams and volunteers assess conditions and continue recovery efforts. This is the first fatality at the site since a child’s death in 2010 and follows a separate, noninjurious collapse captured on video the previous day.

Point Loma Nazarene University (PLNU) has launched the Beauty for Ashes Fund campaign to seed a $40,000 scholarship fund that will support survivors of human trafficking in pursuing a university education. Organized by students, staff, faculty and alumni in partnership with PLNU’s Center for Justice and Reconciliation (CJR), the fund aims to cover tuition, room and board for survivors accepted to PLNU, with smaller amounts allocated for vocational discernment and administrative support. The campaign frames college education as a critical step in long-term rehabilitation—helping survivors move from victim to survivor to thriver—and plans to begin funding students as early as September 2015.

The campaign emphasizes that human trafficking affects local communities, including U.S. teens, and that PLNU’s Christian mission to serve the marginalized underpins this effort. Donations are tax-deductible; if the $40,000 goal is not met, all collected funds will still go to the Beauty for Ashes Fund. Rather than focusing on commercial perks, the campaign highlights impact-first giving, though donated perks (art, handmade soap, etc.) are available and their fair market value must be considered for tax purposes if claimed.

Supporters are encouraged to give, share the campaign on social media, and contact BeautyforAshes@pointloma.edu to get involved. The campaign has received media coverage from outlets including KPBS, Fox San Diego, Fox News, The Examiner, and USA TODAY College.

Between Thursday and Friday, U.S. forces carried out targeted airstrikes and humanitarian airdrops in northern Iraq in response to rapid gains by the Islamic State (ISIS/ISIL), which has seized large swaths of territory, key infrastructure and driven hundreds of thousands from their homes.

Military actions and humanitarian aid
- President Obama authorized limited, targeted airstrikes to protect U.S. personnel and threatened minority populations, while stressing there would be no reintroduction of U.S. ground combat troops.
- U.S. warplanes (including F/A-18s from the carrier USS George H.W. Bush) and drones struck ISIS artillery and mortar positions and an ISIS convoy near the Kurdish regional capital, Irbil. The Pentagon said 500-pound laser-guided bombs were used; drone strikes hit mortar teams when they returned to previously struck positions.
- The U.S. also conducted airdrops to relieve tens of thousands of Yazidis trapped on Mount Sinjar: cargo planes dropped 72 bundles (about 5,300 gallons of water and 8,000 meals), with U.S. officials reporting that most pallets reached the stranded people. The U.S. later made another airdrop; Britain announced plans to support with its own drops.

Situation on the ground
- ISIS captured Iraq’s Mosul Dam (a critical hydroelectric facility on the Tigris) and has taken many towns, using heavy weapons—including equipment seized from the Iraqi army such as U.S.-made weapons and reportedly tanks—threatening downstream flooding if the dam fails.
- Tens of thousands of Yazidis fled Sinjar and are trapped on nearby mountains without adequate food, water or shelter; the group faced ultimatums to convert, pay extortionate taxes, flee or be killed. There were reports of atrocities and beheadings by ISIS.
- Kurdish peshmerga and Iraqi forces are fighting ISIS; Irbil officials warned militants were as close as about 30 km (18+ miles) from the city. Iraqi airstrikes also reported heavy ISIS casualties in Sinjar.
- The humanitarian displacement surged: roughly 200,000 people newly displaced this wave, adding to already large numbers internally displaced across Iraq.

International and political response
- The FAA restricted U.S. airlines from flying Iraqi airspace. The U.S. stressed strikes would be used to protect Americans, Kurdish civilians and to help prevent potential genocide; additional strikes to relieve sieges were possible.
- The UN, Britain, and France signaled support for humanitarian efforts and called for an international response; the UN prepared humanitarian corridors.
- Iraqi and Kurdish leaders welcomed U.S. assistance. Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government coordinated more closely, supplying peshmerga with ammunition and helicopters.
- Domestically in the U.S., some lawmakers urged a more robust response, including strikes in both Iraq and Syria and broader support to regional partners.

Context and constraints
- The action marks the most direct U.S. military engagement in Iraq since the 2011 withdrawal but is explicitly limited to airstrikes and humanitarian relief; the administration emphasized no long-term combat troop deployment and that there is no purely military solution.
- Officials maintained that strikes would be conducted with available intelligence to limit civilian harm and would be consistent with international law given Iraqi government requests for assistance.

Buffalo Bills receiver Stevie Johnson drew criticism after joking about North Korea’s nuclear threats on Twitter. In one tweet he told North Korea to “chill out,” then added, if they “do bomb 1st... Bomb Foxboro, Mass. Sincerely, #BillsMafia,” referencing Gillette Stadium and the Bills’ long losing streak there. Patriots fans and others found the remark in poor taste; Johnson later apologized and softened his tone, saying some people took it too seriously and that he respects the Patriots and all NFL teams. The piece notes public outrage but also argues many Americans aren’t taking North Korea seriously and that Johnson’s comments were unlikely to influence anyone in Pyongyang.

A ForbesWoman/NEFE-Harris Interactive online poll of 2,019 U.S. adults (Dec. 17–21) found financial infidelity is common: 31% of Americans who combine finances admitted lying to a spouse about money, and a third of partnered adults said they’d been deceived. Common offenses include hiding cash (58% of offenders), minor purchases (54%), and bills (30%); sizeable minorities also hid major purchases (16%), secret bank accounts (15%), or lied about debt (11%) or earnings (11%). Money lies cut across income levels.

Consequences are serious: among couples affected, 67% reported arguments, 42% reported reduced trust, 16% said the lie led to divorce, and 11% to separation. Therapists and attorneys describe financial betrayal as as damaging as sexual infidelity because its effects persist. Case examples range from secret gambling and hidden credit-card debt to multimillion-dollar spending on mistresses and fabricated financial histories.

Experts attribute financial dishonesty to pragmatism (planning an exit), control or revenge spending, guilt over irresponsible behavior, and fear of a partner’s reaction. Childhood and cultural money habits also shape secrecy. Men and women are equally likely to commit financial infidelity, though women more often report catching a partner and are more likely to report partners lying about earnings or debt.

Advice offered includes discussing money early (before marriage), using nonthreatening times (e.g., tax season) to review finances, and, if deception is suspected, documenting the scope of lies. Many affected couples plan to improve communication and create shared budgets going forward.

Restaurants have rapidly adopted Twitter as a key way to engage customers, who now routinely post live mini-reviews, photos and criticisms. That shift recently led to an unusual incident at Down House in Houston’s Heights: patron Allison Hiromi (aka Allison Matsu) tweeted a bartender was a “twerp,” and the restaurant’s general manager, who monitors their Twitter account, called the bar, spoke with her, and asked her to leave. Hiromi posted that she left in tears after the manager cursed at her; the restaurant’s owner defended the decision, saying businesses can set the tone in their establishments. The episode highlights how social media posts made in real time can have immediate real-world consequences and raises questions about balancing the experience of on-site diners with the broader, virtual audience. Some observers say the publicity—positive or negative—can still raise a restaurant’s profile.

A social-media prank called "Put 'Em in a Coffin" — where people do a backward dive onto car hoods (mimicking a body in a coffin) — damaged a Houston man's vehicles. Security footage reportedly shows seven teens jumping onto the hood of James McHugh’s white BMW and also denting his wife’s car at Plaza del Sol Park. McHugh, 28, says repairs will cost about $4,000. The prank began after a viral video from the rap group ThotBoyz gained millions of views, and copycat videos of teens flopping onto cars, store displays and other property have proliferated online. McHugh called the stunt a senseless, costly act for a few seconds of laughter.

James Joseph “Joe” Dresnok, the last known US soldier living in North Korea after defecting, died in November at age 74, his sons said in a state-run Uriminzokkiri video. Dresnok, who crossed the demilitarized zone in 1962 amid personal and legal troubles, became a fixture in North Korean life and propaganda—appearing in films and publicly expressing loyalty to the regime. In the video, his two sons, Ted (Hong Soon-chol) and James (Hong Chol), both born in North Korea and wearing Korean People’s Army uniforms, said their father “received only the love and care of the party” and asked them to serve Kim Jong-un. They echoed official rhetoric, warning of US “war hysteria” after recent North Korean ICBM tests and threatening retaliation if war broke out, while praising their “supreme commander” Kim Jong-un. Dresnok had previously been featured in the 2006 documentary Crossing the Line and told CBS he would not leave North Korea even for a large sum of money.

Researchers report the first direct evidence of microplastics in human stool. In a small pilot study presented at UEG Week in Vienna, scientists analyzed stool from eight healthy volunteers from eight countries (Finland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia, the UK and Austria) and detected microplastic particles in every sample. Using a newly developed analytical procedure (micro FT‑IR spectroscopy), they identified up to nine different plastic types (most commonly polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate) in particles sized 50–500 µm, averaging about 20 particles per 10 g of stool.

Participants’ food diaries showed routine exposure to plastic (plastic-wrapped foods, bottled drinks) and six had eaten fish in the week before sampling, but the exact sources remain unclear. The study is preliminary, not yet peer‑reviewed, and limited by its tiny sample size; the authors call for larger studies to confirm prevalence, identify exposure routes and investigate health effects.

Concerns stem from animal studies showing microplastics can translocate from the gut to blood, lymph and possibly liver, and may impair gut function, nutrient absorption or immune responses and carry toxins or pathogens. The findings add to mounting evidence that microplastics pervade the environment and food chain (oceans, seafood, tap and bottled water, salt), underscoring calls to reduce plastic use, improve waste management and pursue further research into human health impacts.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman traveled to Pyongyang in mid-June 2017 as a private citizen, marking his return to North Korea after visits in 2013 and 2014 when he befriended leader Kim Jong-un. Speaking at Beijing airport before his flight, Rodman said his goal was to "open the door" and continue bringing sports to the country; he downplayed raising the cases of detained U.S. citizens, saying that was "not my purpose right now." He wore clothing promoting a marijuana-focused digital currency that is sponsoring the trip.

U.S. officials said they were aware of the visit but reiterated travel warnings advising Americans not to go to North Korea for safety reasons. Rodman suggested President Donald Trump would approve of his efforts and referenced his past ties to Trump from Celebrity Apprentice; Trump previously commented positively about Rodman's visits. Rodman’s earlier trips—sometimes called "basketball diplomacy"—drew heavy criticism from human rights advocates, and he has faced backlash for remarks about detained Americans in the past. North Korean hosts have given him high-profile treatment on previous visits; a North Korean official said he would stay through Saturday.

Summary:

Tensions rose in early March 2015 as U.S.-led negotiations with Iran over curbing its nuclear program approached a late-March framework deadline. The Obama administration urged Congress not to pass new Iran-related legislation and warned President Obama would veto the bipartisan Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act, which would force any final deal’s text to be submitted to Congress within five days and block suspension of congressional sanctions for 60 days. White House officials said additional legislation would undermine negotiators’ chances.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu traveled to Washington to deliver a high-profile, controversial speech to Congress — at the invitation of House Republicans and shortly before Israeli elections — warning that a possible U.S. deal with Iran would threaten Israel’s survival. His visit deepened a rare public rift between the U.S. and Israel: Obama and senior aides criticized the timing and partisan nature of the speech, while Netanyahu framed his intervention as a moral duty and insisted it was above domestic politics. The dispute prompted boycotts by some Democrats and sharp debate in both countries about whether Netanyahu’s appearance risked undermining the U.S.-Israel relationship.

Meanwhile, international concerns persisted about Iran’s cooperation with the IAEA. Director General Yukiya Amano said Tehran had been slow to respond to questions about alleged past explosives tests and that the agency’s inquiry could not continue indefinitely, though Iran had pledged swifter cooperation. Diplomats doubted all outstanding IAEA issues would be resolved before a political agreement.

Throughout, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry continued intensive diplomacy—meeting with Iran’s Mohammad Javad Zarif and traveling between negotiation rounds and regional capitals—to try to secure an agreement while reassuring Israel and Gulf Arab states. The stakes included easing sanctions on Iran in return for limits and monitoring of its nuclear program; critics feared any deal could merely delay Iran’s path to a bomb, while proponents argued a negotiated accord would be the most effective way to constrain Tehran and could be a signature foreign-policy achievement for the Obama administration.

Mexico’s president, Enrique Peña Nieto, announced a nationwide anti-crime plan in late November 2014 in response to public outrage over the disappearance and presumed massacre of 43 trainee teachers in Iguala, Guerrero. The package would weaken municipal autonomy by placing local police under state (and in effect federal) control, give Congress power to dissolve local governments infiltrated by drug cartels, and replace roughly 1,800 municipal police units with state-level forces. It also calls for simplifying jurisdictional divisions between federal, state and local authorities, deploying more federal police to four violence-plagued states (Guerrero, Michoacán, Jalisco and Tamaulipas), introducing a single national emergency number (possibly 911), and establishing a national identity number or document. 

Pena Nieto framed the measures as necessary after the “cruelty” of Iguala exposed deep corruption and collusion between local officials and criminal gangs — allegations that include prosecutors’ claims the Iguala mayor ordered municipal police to detain the students and hand them to a gang. The announcement came amid continued gruesome violence in Guerrero (including the discovery of 11 decapitated bodies) and widespread public protests demanding credible action. Critics and analysts noted similar federal initiatives in 2004 and 2008 produced limited, temporary gains and warned the public needs concrete results rather than rhetoric; some details of the new proposals remain vague and several would require constitutional change.

Former model Christina Estrada, 54, has been awarded about £75 million (reported as $68–$75 million) in a divorce settlement by the London High Court — the largest “needs” award ever granted by an English court. Estrada, a former Pirelli calendar model who has lived in the U.K. since 1988, was married to Saudi businessman Sheikh Walid Juffali for 12 years; they share a teenage daughter. Juffali divorced her under Islamic law in Saudi Arabia in 2014 without her knowledge and subsequently married a younger model.

Estrada had sought roughly £196–£238 million, claiming a need to maintain the exceptionally luxurious standard of living she enjoyed during the marriage. Her evidence detailed costly ongoing expenses—including large annual sums for couture, furs, shoes and handbags, five cars, private jet travel and multiple homes in London, Beverly Hills and Henley — and requested specific properties and cash. The court awarded about £53.5m in cash plus about £22m in assets (total c. £75m), substantially less than her original claim but including specific provisions such as a Lamborghini or its cash equivalent. The award also took into account Estrada’s existing assets (reported at around £20m).

Juffali’s legal team disputed claims about his wealth (Estrada’s lawyers estimated c. £8bn; he said his net worth was about £113.8m–$147m) and argued he had already offered substantial provision, including cash and property use. Juffali, who has been treated in Switzerland for advanced lung cancer and could not attend court, said he intended to leave the bulk of his wealth to his three eldest children. The case highlighted England’s role as a venue for high-value divorce claims and prompted commentary about the scope and certainty of spousal maintenance law.

This article reports an interview with Sava Stoisavljevic, General Secretary of the European Chess Union (ECU), about the ECU’s new dress code implemented at the 2012 European Individual Women’s Championship in Gaziantep.

Why the rule: Stoisavljevic says the change responded to observations that many players came to games inappropriately dressed and to comments from spectators and coaches. The ECU modeled rules on dress standards from other sports and organizations and aimed to protect the image of chess and avoid problems (including potential cheating concerns related to hats).

Key points of the rules (excerpts included):
- Players must follow a casual/business-casual code during games. For men this includes dress trousers or jeans, shirts or polo, appropriate shoes; for women blouses, T‑shirts, trousers, skirts, dresses and appropriate footwear. Clothing must be clean, crisp, without excessive wear or odor.
- Cleavage is partially regulated: one additional button may be opened (the second from the top) beyond the top button.
- Sunglasses and neckties are allowed; caps or hats are banned except for religious reasons (partly to prevent hiding devices).
- Prize‑giving ceremonies require a stricter business-casual or elegant-casual dress; award ceremonies for the European Individual Championship recommend full suits and ties (women: equivalent style). National costumes are permitted if not indecent.
- Enforcement: officials can issue verbal and written warnings; repeat breaches can result in being sent away to change or being denied access to the playing area, opening/closing ceremonies, or prize ceremonies. Team captains are informed if a team member is warned.

Views and nuances:
- Stoisavljevic acknowledges women often already dress appropriately; she sees the rules as particularly useful for men’s events. She also admires that chess can be made more attractive by players’ appearance but believes limits are appropriate.
- Short skirts are not yet explicitly banned, though Stoisavljevic notes many wear very short skirts and that some organizations set minimum skirt lengths; the topic remains under discussion.
- The hat ban allows religious exceptions; it also stems from arbiters’ practical concerns about possible cheating.
- Dress expectations may consider local customs where a tournament is hosted.

Context and reaction:
- The rules were introduced at the Gaziantep women’s championship and drew media commentary about balancing professionalism, image, spectator appeal and personal appearance. Penalties are relatively strict to maintain standards.

House Oversight leaders say classified documents show former national security adviser Michael Flynn failed to disclose substantial foreign payments and may have violated the law. In private briefings Wednesday, Oversight Chairman Jason Chaffetz (R‑Utah) and ranking Democrat Elijah Cummings (D‑Md.) said Flynn omitted payments from Russian-linked entities (including a $45,000 RT speaking fee in December 2015) and more than $500,000 tied to lobbying for Turkey on his SF‑86 security‑clearance form and original financial disclosures. The committee reviewed records from the Defense Intelligence Agency that, the lawmakers said, contain no evidence Flynn sought permission or reported those foreign funds; knowingly concealing material facts on the SF‑86 is a felony.

The White House declined to provide many documents the committee requested, saying it does not possess records from before President Trump’s Jan. 20 inauguration and that some post‑Jan. 20 materials are sensitive or irrelevant. White House legislative affairs director Marc Short and press secretary Sean Spicer defended the responses; Flynn’s lawyer said Flynn briefed DIA about the RT event and has cooperated with authorities.

Chaffetz and Cummings stopped short of accusing the White House of obstruction but urged further investigation; they said Flynn could face penalties, including repayment of monies and possible criminal exposure if prosecutors can prove he “knowingly and willfully” lied. Flynn resigned in February after misleading Vice President Pence about contacts with Russia’s ambassador and has offered to testify to Congress in exchange for immunity, an offer not accepted. The revelations add to ongoing House, Senate and FBI probes into Russian interference in the 2016 election and ties between Trump associates and foreign actors.

A new glass-bottom pedestrian bridge in Zhangjiajie, Hunan province, China — billed as the world’s longest and highest — is set to open this July. Designed by Israeli architect Haim Dotan, the Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon Glass Bridge spans about 430 meters (roughly 1,400+ feet), is about 6 meters (20 feet) wide, hovers roughly 300 meters (nearly 1,000 feet) above the canyon floor, and can hold up to 800 people. The transparent walkway offers panoramic views of the sandstone-and-quartz peaks, trees and waterfalls; plans call for a bungee-jump facility and even fashion-show events from the bridge.

Safety concerns have followed previous incidents on other Chinese glass skywalks, notably cracks that appeared on a Yuntai Mountain walkway after a tourist reportedly dropped a thermos. To reassure the public, operators invited BBC reporter Dan Simmons to test one of the bridge’s glass panels by striking it with a sledgehammer: the top layer cracked visibly but the panel did not break through. Officials stress the bridge meets safety standards as it prepares to open to tourists.

A very strong earthquake struck the Caribbean Sea off northern Honduras late Tuesday night, registering a preliminary magnitude of 7.6 and a shallow depth of about 10 km (6.2 miles). The epicenter was roughly 202 km (125 miles) north‑northeast of Barra Patuca, Honduras, about 44 km (25 miles) east of the largely unpopulated Swan Islands, and several hundred kilometres southwest of the Cayman Islands.

The quake was felt across much of Honduras and as far away as parts of Mexico, Belize, Cuba, Jamaica and Puerto Rico. Reports described violent, brief shaking; some homes in Honduras’s Colón, Atlántida and Olancho provinces suffered cracks, and residents evacuated in places, but there were no early reports of serious injuries or major structural damage. Several aftershocks of magnitude 4+ followed.

Tsunami centres issued advisories and warnings for many Caribbean islands and Central American and Mexican coasts—cautioning sea-level rises of roughly 0.3–1 metre (1–3 feet)—but the alerts were canceled about an hour later and no damaging tsunami materialized. Officials noted the epicenter’s offshore location and sparse coastal population likely limited damage; the event ranks among the largest Caribbean quakes in recorded history.

Roman Polanski is a celebrated but deeply controversial filmmaker whose life mixes major cinematic achievements with traumatic personal events and serious criminal allegations.

Background and career
- Born Raimund Polanski on August 18, 1933, in Paris, he was raised in Kraków, Poland. He survived World War II orphaned after his mother died in Auschwitz and later studied at the Polish National Film Academy in Łódź.
- He began as an actor and then director; his first feature, Knife in the Water (1962), earned international attention. He moved to London and made notable early films including Repulsion (1965).
- Polanski relocated to Hollywood in 1968 and achieved major success with Rosemary’s Baby (1968) and later Chinatown (1974). After relocating to Europe he directed Tess (1979), Frantic (1988), Bitter Moon (1992), Death and the Maiden (1994), and The Ninth Gate (1999).

Personal tragedy
- In 1969 his pregnant wife, actress Sharon Tate, was murdered by members of the Charles Manson cult, a trauma that influenced the darker themes in much of his work.

Criminal case and exile
- In 1977 Polanski was charged on multiple counts related to sexual relations with a minor after a March 1977 incident in which a 13-year-old girl alleged he had drugged and raped her in Jack Nicholson’s home. He pleaded guilty to unlawful sexual intercourse, underwent a psychiatric evaluation and served about six weeks in a California state facility.
- Authorities and the judge disagreed afterward about the sentence. Fearing a much longer term, Polanski fled the U.S. after his release and has lived mainly in Europe since, technically a fugitive from U.S. justice.
- He was detained in Switzerland in 2009 during a U.S. extradition attempt but was ultimately not extradited. In 2018 the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences expelled him amid #MeToo-era ethical reforms.

Recent legal efforts
- Polanski’s lawyer has sought to unseal testimony from retired Deputy District Attorney Roger Gunson that they say would confirm a plea deal—specifically that Polanski completed an agreed 42-day stint at Chino State Prison and should not face further punishment. The defense contends the original judge, Laurence Rittenband, reneged on the deal.
- The attorney has pushed Los Angeles courts to release that testimony and to resolve the longstanding case to allow Polanski to travel freely and potentially return to the United States.

Overall, Polanski remains a polarizing figure: widely recognized for major contributions to cinema but also condemned and legally pursued for his conviction and flight from prosecution in a child sexual-abuse case.

Search teams investigating Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 reported potential acoustic leads in the southern Indian Ocean on Sunday, but cautioned they are unverified and may not be from the missing Boeing 777’s black boxes.

Key points:
- A Chinese patrol ship, Haixun 01, reported picking up brief electronic signals consistent with the 37.5 kHz frequency used by cockpit voice and flight data recorder beacons on Friday and again on Saturday. The second detection reportedly lasted about 90 seconds near 25°S, 101°E.
- The Australian naval vessel Ocean Shield detected a separate “acoustic noise” elsewhere and is pursuing it with its US Navy towed pinger locator. The British Royal Navy’s HMS Echo was also en route to investigate the Chinese detections.
- Up to 10 military aircraft, two civilian planes and 13 ships were assigned to search three areas totaling about 216,000 sq km roughly 2,000 km northwest of Perth. Chinese aircraft also spotted white objects nearby, though no debris has been confirmed as from MH370.
- Officials, led by Angus Houston (Australia’s joint search coordinator), called the contacts “an important and encouraging lead” but urged caution: the signals were fleeting, not continuous, and only one signal was heard despite each recorder carrying its own pinger.
- Time is critical: the locator batteries on the black boxes are guaranteed for about 30 days underwater, and the window for detection was closing. Experts stressed the need to rapidly get additional assets (e.g., sonobuoys and towed locators) on site to verify or rule out the signals.
- International cooperation continued: new investigative teams and ministerial committees were set up, involving Australia, China, the U.S., the U.K., France and Malaysia, as the search entered its most intensive phase.

The article disputes the notion that iconic American brands are gone, but shows many famous names no longer produce primarily in the U.S. It cites consumer preference for American-made goods (surveys showing a large share of Americans prefer or will pay more for U.S.-made products) and then lists 11 well-known brands whose “American” image masks substantial foreign ownership or production:

- Budweiser: Now part of Belgian-Brazilian Anheuser‑Busch InBev since 2008. Many U.S. operations remain, but ownership and management are global.
- Coors: Merged with Canada’s Molson (MolsonCoors) and tied into Miller/SABMiller networks, leaving Coors brands with multinational ties.
- Chevrolet Silverado (and GMC Sierra): Some assembly in U.S. plants, but significant production and parts come from Mexico and other countries; domestic content has fallen below some “American-made” thresholds.
- Ford F‑150: Assembled in the U.S. but only about 60% of parts are U.S.-made after outsourcing to meet demand and cut costs.
- Rawlings baseballs: Official MLB supplier based in St. Louis, but final baseball production has long been done in Puerto Rico, Haiti and now Costa Rica.
- Levi’s: Globalized manufacturing since the late 20th century; jeans are produced in many countries (Japan, Mexico, Cambodia, etc.), with headquarters and operations worldwide.
- American Girl dolls: Owned by Mattel since 1998; production has shifted to China and earlier to Germany, so dolls are largely made abroad.
- Craftsman tools: Historically a U.S. symbol via Sears, but parts have come from Austria, Denmark, China, India and Mexico; some Craftsman items now labeled “Made in China.”
- Schwinn bicycles: U.S. manufacturing ceased decades ago; modern Schwinn bikes are produced in Taiwan and China after bankruptcies and acquisitions.
- KitchenAid mixers: Noted as a positive counterexample—mixers are still made in Greenville, Ohio (about 700 workers) and remain a durable U.S.-manufactured appliance under Whirlpool.

Overall message: Many beloved American brands retain U.S. branding and cultural identity, but ownership and manufacturing are often globalized. Some products (e.g., KitchenAid mixers) still have significant U.S. production, but shoppers should be skeptical of patriotic marketing claims and check labels if buying American-made matters.

A Baltimore man, 30-year-old Mark-Anthony Sandang Ramiro, was arrested and charged with first- and second-degree murder plus weapons violations after his friend, 28-year-old Darnell Mitchell, was fatally shot during a basement stunt to test a bulletproof vest. According to police and charging documents, a third person filmed the event on a Cannon E07 camera. The video shows Mitchell, wearing a ballistic vest, boasting he was about to take a “deuce deuce in the chest” (a .22-caliber shot); Ramiro then fired one round that struck Mitchell above the vest. Mitchell collapsed; Ramiro and the videographer helped him and drove him to the University of Maryland Shock Trauma center, where Mitchell was pronounced dead. Investigators identified Ramiro in the footage by his clothing and distinctive tattoos. Prosecutors sought second-degree murder charges; a court commissioner also added a first-degree charge. Detectives are working to identify the third man in the video. Authorities continue to investigate intent and the circumstances of the shooting.

A newly released FBI Behavioral Analysis Unit (BAU) profile and related documents on Adam Lanza conclude he did not “snap” spontaneously on Dec. 14, 2012, at Sandy Hook Elementary, but engaged in careful, methodical planning that the profiler says may have begun as early as March 2011. The material—more than 1,500 pages including redacted grand-jury subpoenas, interviews and field notes—was compiled from agent canvasses, school and health records, internet data, and an hour-long interview with an unidentified woman who communicated online with Lanza for over two years.

Key findings and evidence:
- The BAU profiler, after reviewing Lanza’s journals, internet posts and interviews with relatives and acquaintances, described him as having an “extremely rigid and inflexible worldview.” The profiler tied Lanza’s deteriorating relationship with his mother in the months before the attack to significant stress.
- The profile states Lanza was fascinated with past shootings, researched them thoroughly, and maintained a detailed spreadsheet documenting hundreds of spree killings and mass murders.
- The FBI opened a grand jury quickly after the shooting to collect information from websites Lanza frequented; agents also canvassed his Newtown neighborhood and interviewed neighbors and family friends.
- Witnesses and field notes portray Lanza as socially isolated—having no real friends, rarely leaving his room in the months before the killings, communicating with his mother largely by email, and reacting badly to power outages after storms. He was described as socially awkward and was reportedly bullied in school.
- The online correspondent characterized Lanza as extremely fixated and disturbed, writing monthly about a range of topics: a love of Harry Potter (specifically the idea of children being taken from families at age eleven), dislike of sensory experiences (light, food textures, clothing), nightmares of being in mass shootings, and occasional casual references to suicide (though not to actively planning self-harm or harming others). She said he showed deep loneliness and no apparent enjoyment of life.
- The profile notes evidence suggesting Lanza had an interest in children that could be categorized as pedophilia, while also acknowledging no evidence he ever acted on that interest.
- The unidentified woman reported Lanza sometimes described himself as possibly asexual, and she relayed that he once said adult-child sexual relationships might be “possibly beneficial to both parties”; the report does not provide corroboration beyond her account.
- Neighbors recalled that federal agents had visited the Lanza home years earlier after Adam allegedly hacked into a government computer system in ninth grade; Nancy Lanza reportedly was told her son was smart enough to work for the agency someday.

The BAU concluded there was no evidence Lanza treated the attack like a “video game.” Overall, the documents portray a solitary individual with intense preoccupation with mass murderers, worsening familial tensions, and extensive planning that preceded the massacre in which Lanza killed his mother and 26 people at the school.

Over three days of terror in and around Paris in January 2015, security forces ended twin sieges that followed the deadly attack on satirical weekly Charlie Hebdo. Brothers Chérif and Saïd Kouachi, suspected of killing 12 people at Charlie Hebdo, were cornered at a printing plant in Dammartin-en-Goële. An employee hiding inside the building — reported as 26-year-old graphic designer Lilian Lepere — sent police tactical information by text, including his location and what he overheard, which officials say helped time the assault. The brothers briefly held a manager hostage but released him; they emerged and opened fire as police moved in and were killed.

Simultaneously in Paris, Amedy Coulibaly, linked to the brothers, seized hostages in a kosher supermarket, killed four people and demanded the Kouachis be freed. Police used a phone number supplied by a relative to help locate hidden hostages in the store; after a raid the gunman was killed, 16 hostages were freed (15 from the store, one from the plant), and four hostages at the market were found dead.

Authorities say the three gunmen had ties to Islamist networks, including al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula; AQAP claimed responsibility for directing the Charlie Hebdo attack. The Kouachi brothers had prior terrorism connections—one convicted in 2008 and both on U.S. no-fly lists—and Saïd is suspected of fighting in Yemen. Investigations also revealed links between associates of the attackers; several people, including relatives, received preliminary charges, and one suspected accomplice remained at large.

French leaders called for unity and vigilance amid unprecedented violence that left at least 20 people dead (including the three attackers) and prompted heightened security and international concern about returned Western jihadis. Charlie Hebdo lost eight journalists and others in the attack and planned a special edition produced with another paper.

Jahi McMath, a California teenager who was declared brain dead after complications from a December 2013 tonsillectomy, remains on life support and is being cared for in New Jersey. Her mother, Nailah Winkfield, posted a photo and message on the "Keep Jahi McMath on life support" Facebook page (March 15) — her first public update in over three months — saying Jahi is “as healthy and beautiful as ever,” thanking supporters, and asking for prayers and for people to wear purple in her honor. 

Background: Doctors at Children’s Hospital Oakland declared Jahi brain dead and sought to remove life support in January 2014; the family obtained a restraining order, raised nearly $50,000 in private donations, and moved her to a long-term care facility in New Jersey, where state law allows religious objections to a brain-death-based termination of support. The family is suing the hospital, alleging a botched surgery and pressure to donate organs, and Winkfield has filed to have her daughter’s death certificate voided. Medical experts maintain that brain death is equivalent to death and that apparent signs of life are due to advanced medical measures. The story drew intense media attention and, per Winkfield, raised public awareness about brain death. The Associated Press contributed to reporting.

A class-action lawsuit has been filed in federal court in California against Spin Master over its hugely popular Hatchimals toy, alleging many units fail to perform the toy’s signature function—hatching from the egg. Plaintiff Jodie Hejduk says a Hatchimal she bought for her daughter did not hatch despite following the instructions; she seeks class certification, a recall, refunds/restitution, and compensatory, statutory and punitive damages for deceptive practices, false advertising, breach of warranty and related claims.

Background: Released in October 2016 and retailing around $50–$60, Hatchimals quickly became the season’s must-have item, often selling out and fetching high resale prices. The toys are marketed to “peck” out of a plastic egg after being rubbed and tapped; the mystery of which creature inside drives demand. After many consumers reported that their Hatchimals would not hatch, complaints surged to Spin Master’s customer service and social media.

Allegations and impact: The suit contends Spin Master knew hatching was the product’s primary appeal and that a significant failure rate existed, yet did not adequately address defects, issue refunds, or recall the product. Attorneys representing plaintiffs say customer service responsiveness was poor and some consumers waited on hold for hours. The complaint cites negative online reviews and claims the company profited heavily from the craze while selling an allegedly defective product.

Spin Master response: The company says the vast majority of customers had positive experiences, that it provided troubleshooting guidance, increased consumer-care staffing and hours over the holidays, and supplied replacements where needed. Spin Master’s general counsel called the lawsuit’s allegations inaccurate.

Relief sought: Plaintiffs seek class relief nationwide and in California, a recall, restitution, and various damages; attorneys predict additional suits may follow.

NOAA investigators say a measles-like virus (morbillivirus) is the likely cause of a large bottlenose dolphin die-off along the U.S. mid‑Atlantic coast. Since July 1, 2013, 333 dolphins have stranded from New York to North Carolina, with the majority (174) in Virginia. Of 33 fresh carcasses tested, 32 showed confirmed or suspected morbillivirus infection and genetic sequencing identified cetacean morbillivirus in 11 animals. The virus suppresses dolphins’ immune systems and produces lesions in skin, lymph nodes and brain; infected animals often succumb to secondary infections or emaciation.

NOAA officials say the pattern resembles a major 1987–88 outbreak and expect mortalities could continue into spring 2014 as the virus spreads south with migrating populations. Scientists believe population immunity has waned since the last outbreak, making many animals susceptible. There’s virtually no risk of morbillivirus transmission to humans (morbilliviruses are species‑specific), though NOAA advises caution—especially for swimmers with open wounds—because secondary infections in sick dolphins could pose a hazard. There is no practical way to vaccinate wild dolphins, so the event will likely end only as susceptible animals decline and survivors gain immunity. Authorities continue necropsies and lab testing and have declared an Unusual Mortality Event to mobilize resources. Public guidance is to observe stranded dolphins from a safe distance and report strandings to local hotlines.

NASA has released a conceptual design for a one-ton robotic submarine intended to explore Kraken Mare, the largest methane–ethane sea on Saturn’s moon Titan. The Titan Submarine Phase I concept is an early-stage idea from the NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts program that envisions a nuclear-powered, electrically driven vehicle using a radioisotope Stirling generator (~1 kW) and electrically powered turbines to travel under and on the hydrocarbon seas. It would carry a seafloor camera and sampling system and study Titan’s chemistry, sea-floor composition, tides, currents, shoreline changes, and search for unusual life chemistries in the extremely cold, nitrogen‑and‑methane atmosphere (surface temperature ~–179 °C).

Kraken Mare is vast (≈400,000 km²) and may be up to ~160 m deep, with currents and tides and a round‑trip light-time to Earth of roughly 160 minutes, so the craft would need to be highly autonomous. Communications would be handled by a large dorsal fin containing a planar phased‑array antenna; the sub would surface about 16 hours per day to transmit data directly to Earth rather than rely on an orbiter relay. Ballast tanks would control diving and surfacing, though designers must solve fluid‑behavior issues unique to methane/ethane (e.g., nitrogen condensation).

Getting the vehicle to Titan poses packaging challenges for traditional landers; mission planners have suggested alternative delivery options such as a spaceplane-style carrier. The concept is preliminary, with target arrival dates for a matured descendant mission around the 2040s (some estimates ~2047), and substantial engineering work remains before deployment.

A 36-year-old unidentified homicide victim known as John Doe No. 89 has finally been identified as Andre "Andy" Drath, thanks to DNA testing prompted by renewed investigations tied to serial killer John Wayne Gacy. Drath, a 16-year-old ward of Illinois' child welfare system who disappeared in late 1978 or early 1979 heading to San Francisco, was found shot to death in San Francisco in June 1979. Although authorities do not believe Gacy killed Drath, Gacy-related cold-case efforts led the Cook County Sheriff's Office to seek DNA from relatives of missing young men from that era.

Drath’s maternal half-sister, Dr. Willia Wertheimer, submitted DNA that was entered into a federal database; in May 2015 it matched tissue samples from the unidentified body. Dental records and a tattoo reading "Andy" confirmed the identification, which Wertheimer learned of in September. San Francisco police are now investigating Drath’s 1979 homicide. The breakthrough comes amid a broader Cook County initiative begun in 2011 to use modern DNA technology to identify or close cases connected to Gacy; that effort has closed 12 cases, identified one of Gacy’s victims (William George Bundy), reunited five missing people with families, and clarified other disappearances. Sheriff Thomas Dart said the result shows the importance of persisting in cold-case work.

Charlo Greene (legal name Charlene Egbe), a former Alaska TV reporter who famously quit on live TV in September 2014 with “Fuck it, I quit” to advocate for marijuana legalization, now faces a high‑stakes criminal prosecution that highlights tensions in the evolving U.S. marijuana landscape.

Background
- Greene used her position at KTVA to reveal she ran the Alaska Cannabis Club, which supplied cannabis via membership/donation arrangements after Alaska voters approved recreational legalization in 2014 but before the state finalized retail regulations.
- The club was targeted by multiple undercover purchases and two armed raids in 2015. Greene says police exceeded warrants, intimidated members, seized property and treated volunteers and patients roughly.

Charges and legal exposure
- Greene has pleaded not guilty to numerous counts of “misconduct involving a controlled substance.” Originally indicted on eight counts with a potential 24‑year sentence, prosecutors later added six more charges (for a total of 14), raising the possible penalty to 54 years; observers judge such draconian exposure unlikely to be imposed but deeply consequential for her life.
- Prosecutors emphasized that the club was operated under Greene’s name; Greene says court records show she did not personally conduct undercover transactions and contends prosecutors mischaracterized the club’s structure to a grand jury.

Context and implications
- Alaska’s legal framework is muddled: voters legalized possession, cultivation and sale, but regulators were slow to create licensing and retail rules, leaving a gray period during which grassroots operations like Greene’s emerged.
- Critics argue the state’s aggressive criminal response—rather than fines or regulatory sanctions similar to penalties for unlicensed alcohol sales—illustrates the uneven transition from prohibition to regulation and raises concerns about disproportionate enforcement, especially against people of color.
- Greene and some advocates describe the prosecution as punitive and symbolic (“a modern day lynching”), while state regulators say early operators “got ahead” of the law. Even some legalization campaigners have distanced themselves, noting most businesses waited for formal licensing.

Human toll and public reaction
- Greene became a viral figure but says the international attention to her on‑air resignation has not translated into robust support at her trials; she reports little local backing despite her role in the legalization movement.
- The case underscores broader questions as more states legalize cannabis: how to reconcile voter initiatives with slow regulatory implementation, the proper law‑enforcement response to pre‑regulation businesses, and how criminal law will be applied during transitions from prohibition to regulated markets.

Status
- Greene’s trial was pending at the time of reporting. Observers believe lengthy prison time is unlikely but acknowledge the case’s potential chilling effect and its symbolic significance amid ongoing national shifts on marijuana policy.

Police say they may have lost key evidence after arresting a suspect in a bank robbery. Twinsburg officers arrested 35-year-old John H. Ford of Cleveland shortly after a man entered the FirstMerit branch in Streetsboro, handed a teller a note demanding money and fled in a dark Ford Escort. Dash-cam video from the traffic stop on I-480 shows Ford leaning over the hood of a police cruiser while officers searched him and removing items were placed on the hood. Officers later reviewed the footage and say Ford can be seen grabbing and putting something in his mouth — which police fear was the robbery demand note. A .38-caliber pistol was found on the driver’s-side floor of Ford’s car and a wad of cash stained with red ink was recovered on the passenger side. Ford is also a suspect in separate bank robberies in Stow and Akron.

Sotheby's is holding a high-profile rock memorabilia auction titled "A Rock & Roll History: Presley to Punk" that could include up to $5 million worth of items. Headlining the sale are Bob Dylan’s original handwritten lyrics to 1965’s "Like a Rolling Stone"—drafts on hotel stationery showing revisions and doodles—which Sotheby’s values at $1–2 million and calls a "holy grail" of lyrics. Other notable lots include an Elvis Presley stage jumpsuit adorned with rhinestones and gold lame (expected to fetch $100,000–$200,000 and still showing sweat stains), John Lennon’s piano (played also by Elton John and David Bowie) estimated at $100,000–$200,000, Lennon drawings, and Jim Morrison’s "Love Her Madly" lyrics. The auction reflects a rare moment for collectors as significant pieces of rock history come to market. The article also briefly mentions web-archiving efforts to preserve pages and prevent broken links, but the main focus is the Sotheby’s sale.

A California man filmed a rare and frightening incident last week off Mexico’s Guadalupe Island in which a great white shark smashed into and breached a dive cage with a single diver inside. The diver, Ming Chan, came away shaken but uninjured. According to the videographer’s account on YouTube, the shark lunged for a chunk of tuna used as bait, was temporarily blinded by the bite and unable to swim backward, and accidentally struck and broke part of the cage before thrusting through the top. The experienced dive instructor inside the cage remained calm, was briefly outside the bottom of the cage looking down at two great whites, then swam back up and climbed out once the shark exited. The boat crew quickly raised the cage and handled the situation; operators say the shark sustained only minor injury and is fine. The videographer and diver plan to continue shark trips, and operators are reviewing cage design and bait methods to improve safety. The footage became one of 2016’s most viral shark videos.

Devastating seasonal monsoon floods across northern India, southern Nepal and northern Bangladesh have killed hundreds and disrupted tens of millions of lives. Officials report at least 950 deaths in the three countries from widespread flooding, landslides and related causes (drowning, snake bites), while U.N. agencies and media estimates put the overall death toll across the region as high as about 1,400. Nearly 40–41 million people have been affected.

Impact by area:
- India: The worst-affected states include Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Assam. Bihar reported 367 deaths and large-scale evacuations—about 770,000 people moved, with roughly 425,000 in 1,360 relief camps. Uttar Pradesh officials say some 2.3 million people in 25 districts were affected after major rivers overflowed; authorities blamed both heavy rains and water releases from dams in upstream Nepal. West Bengal reported 152 deaths and about 15 million people affected. Assam reported at least 71 deaths; Kaziranga National Park was inundated, killing roughly 300 animals including rhinos and a tiger.
- Bangladesh: The Disaster Management Ministry reported 132 deaths and about 7.5 million people affected; over 10,000 hectares of crops were destroyed and another 600,000 hectares damaged, raising acute food-security concerns. The U.N. World Food Programme warned of potentially “devastating hunger” for many survivors who lost homes, possessions and livelihoods.
- Nepal: Authorities reported 146 deaths with about 30 people missing; floodwaters have begun to recede in parts.

Humanitarian concerns and response:
- Large-scale evacuations by army and volunteers; air force helicopters dropped food, water and medicines to marooned people.
- Health risks are rising as waters recede: outbreaks of water-borne and vector-borne diseases (diarrhea, malaria, dengue) and risks from contaminated water and mosquitoes. Health teams are distributing mosquito repellent, bleaching powder and water-purification tablets.
- Massive damage to homes, infrastructure (roads, power towers), schools and hospitals, and to agriculture threatens food supplies and longer-term livelihoods.
- Relief agencies warn urgent food, shelter and medical assistance is needed for millions left homeless or food-insecure.

Overall, the seasonal monsoon—running June to September—has triggered one of the region’s most severe flood crises in years, with continuing rescue, relief and recovery needs as waters recede and damage assessments continue.

A California man, Devorise Dixon, posted a photo on Facebook claiming a KFC chicken tender he bought was actually a deep‑fried rat. The image—showing a breaded piece with a tail‑like appendage—went viral and prompted KFC to investigate. Dixon said the restaurant manager admitted the item was a rat; he later gave the piece to KFC via his attorney for independent lab testing. KFC released photos and statements arguing the item was clearly hand‑breaded white meat chicken and that the tenders vary in shape. DNA testing at an independent lab confirmed the sample was chicken, not a rat. KFC called the claim false and has asked Dixon to apologize and stop making the allegation. Dixon did not respond to media requests for comment.

A self-published children’s bedtime book called The Rabbit Who Wants to Fall Asleep, by Swedish psychologist Carl‑Johan Forssén Ehrlin, has become a surprise Amazon bestseller by promising to help children fall asleep quickly. The 26‑page picture book follows Roger the Rabbit, Sleep Snail, Uncle Yawn and other sleepy characters, and uses specially designed language patterns, subtle cues and complementary images to encourage relaxation and sleep. Parents are instructed to read slowly, yawn on cue, and can even insert the child’s name; the technique has been described as similar to gentle hypnosis or guided meditation by sleep experts.

Originally published in Swedish in 2011 and translated into English in 2014, the book is available in multiple languages and is outselling many major titles. Reviews from parents report rapid success with previously resistant children. Ehrlin says the story’s structure aims to engage the child’s unconscious with suggestions to relax and sleep; he plans to apply similar methods in future books (for example, on potty training).

Archaeologists excavating the Sobibor extermination camp in German-occupied Poland have uncovered what they believe to be an escape tunnel used by prisoners. The roughly human-width passage was found about 5 feet (1.5 m) below ground, extended roughly 32 feet (10 m) from a sonderkommando barrack and reached under the camp’s barbed-wire perimeter. The sonderkommando — prisoners forced to work in the gas chambers and with the bodies — may have dug the tunnel, but researchers have found no evidence it was used. Experts suspect the tunnel was discovered during the war, its participants executed, and the shaft filled in. 

Sobibor operated from 1942–43 and is estimated to have been the site of between approximately 167,000 and 250,000 murders, most by gassing on arrival. The camp was partly dismantled and concealed by the Nazis after a 600-prisoner uprising in October 1943, when many escapees were recaptured or killed and only a few dozen survived the war. Ongoing excavations at the disturbed site have also revealed a crematorium, human remains, and personal items (glasses, jewelry, a child’s pin), offering new physical evidence about attempts to resist and the lives of Sobibor’s victims.

Princeton University recently posted parts of John Forbes Nash Jr.’s academic file after the mathematician and his wife Alicia died in a car crash on May 23. Among the documents is a short Feb. 11, 1948 recommendation from Richard J. Duffin, Nash’s undergraduate advisor at Carnegie Tech, which closes with the endorsement: “He is a mathematical genius.” That recommendation helped secure Nash’s admission to Princeton’s graduate program, where he completed a 27‑page Ph.D. dissertation, “Non‑cooperative games,” in May 1950 at age 21. The work introduced the concept now known as the Nash equilibrium—a foundational idea in game theory—and has been hugely influential (the dissertation alone has thousands of citations, while the term “Nash equilibrium” is cited far more broadly). Nash won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences and was recently awarded the Abel Prize in mathematics; he and Alicia had been returning from Norway to receive the Abel when they died.

This document juxtaposes two sharply contrasting perspectives on Ariel (Arik) Sharon and his legacy.

First, an eyewitness op-ed condemns Sharon for his central role in the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon and its bloody aftermath. The author, who lived through the siege and bombardment of West Beirut, recounts civilian devastation—destroyed apartment buildings near the Arab University, refugee housing obliterated by air attack, and a car-bomb intended to kill rescuers. He faults Sharon, then Israel’s defense minister, for launching a catastrophic war that produced tens of thousands of casualties, intensified the Lebanese civil war, and left Israel occupying southern Lebanon until 2000. The piece accuses Sharon of masterminding settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem—personally scouting sites by helicopter and enabling land expropriation—thereby fatally undermining prospects for a viable Palestinian state. It describes Sharon’s Gaza disengagement as unilateral control that turned Gaza into an "open-air prison." The author highlights Sharon’s earlier record of operations targeting civilians (citing Qibya, 1953) and his rhetoric dehumanizing Palestinians as "terrorists," including a cited 1982 meeting with U.S. envoy Morris Draper during the Sabra and Shatila massacres in which Sharon said, “So we'll kill them.” The writer criticizes Western media and politicians for hagiographic tributes at Sharon’s death and argues that, given his actions, he should have faced international criminal charges.

Second, the document reproduces a more sympathetic appraisal—an essay (by a former U.S. secretary of state) that frames Sharon’s trajectory from hardline warrior to reluctant peacemaker. This piece emphasizes Israel’s insecure context and the resulting hawkish strategies of its leaders. It recalls Sharon’s military accomplishments and hard-nosed realism but credits him with broadening his conception of security later in life. As prime minister, Sharon is praised for the dramatic unilateral withdrawal from Gaza and the evacuation of settlements there—actions the writer views as a courageous, if imperfect, step toward separating physical and political security and testing the prospects for negotiated peace. The essay argues that, despite setbacks (rocket attacks from nonstate groups and political opposition), Sharon’s disengagement should be respected as an attempt to move toward coexistence.

Taken together, the document contrasts bitter firsthand condemnation of Sharon’s responsibility for civilian deaths, settler entrenchment, and the destruction of Palestinian hopes for statehood, with a more forgiving diplomatic tribute that portrays his late-career withdrawal from Gaza as a meaningful, if flawed, move toward peace. The two perspectives illustrate the deep polarization in assessments of Sharon’s methods and legacy.

A New Orleans federal judge on April 27, 2016 sentenced 73-year-old New York real-estate heir Robert Durst to 85 months (seven years, one month) in prison after he pleaded guilty in February to being a felon in possession of a firearm. Durst, who appeared frail and used a wheelchair, asked the judge to speed his transfer to California so he can defend himself against a separate murder charge alleging he killed longtime friend Susan Berman in 2000; prosecutors say she was killed to prevent her from speaking about the 1982 disappearance of Durst’s first wife. The plea deal resolves related state charges in New York, Texas and Louisiana and includes forfeiture of items seized in a March 2015 search of his New Orleans hotel room (a revolver, cash, a latex mask, marijuana and other items). Judge Kurt Engelhardt agreed to recommend that Durst serve his federal term in a low-security California facility (such as FCI Terminal Island) to facilitate his move there; his lawyers said he could be in Los Angeles within weeks and is expected to be arraigned on the Berman murder charge on Aug. 18. Durst has a history of prior convictions tied to fleeing prosecution and weapons offenses and has long maintained his innocence in the murder allegations. The case drew renewed attention after the HBO documentary The Jinx aired remarks in which Durst was heard saying, “What the hell did I do? Killed them all, of course.”

Will (William) Gibb, 31, of Red Deer fought off a cougar that attacked his 80-pound husky, Sasha, in the parking lot of a Tim Hortons in Whitecourt, Alberta on Dec. 26. After hearing Sasha yelp, Gibb ran to find the cougar pinning her; he punched the animal in the head and repeatedly swung at it to protect both Sasha and his other dog, Mongo. During the rescue Sasha bit Gibb’s hand amid the chaos; Gibb sustained deep claw marks to his arms. Sasha suffered neck bite wounds, claw tears to her belly and injuries into muscle that required stitches; she was treated at a nearby veterinary clinic and has since been released. Police and wildlife officers located and killed the cougar due to public safety concerns. Local authorities noted cougars occasionally enter the town’s surrounding forests and warned pet owners to be cautious in mountain-wilderness areas.

Here are concise summaries of the main items in the document:

- Darrell Issa on Iraq and ISIL: Returning from Iraq, House Oversight Chairman Darrell Issa said Iraq’s government remains “delusional” about the urgency of fighting ISIL, still emphasizing long-term training over immediate combat readiness. Issa said he would support authorizing the U.S. military campaign President Obama requested, but insisted Iraqis — not U.S. forces — should handle ground combat. He expressed confidence the Kurds will fight effectively with U.S. air support and technical help.

- Fiscal cliff reactions — Lindsey Graham and Chuck Schumer: Sen. Lindsey Graham praised President Obama for holding firm in fiscal-cliff negotiations, predicting a political win for Obama as tax rates on the wealthy are likely to rise, though Graham disagrees with that outcome. Sen. Chuck Schumer said there’s better-than-even odds of a last-minute fiscal-cliff deal, noting such big agreements typically materialize at the eleventh hour when both sides prefer a compromise to the alternative.

- Farm bill warning from Tom Vilsack: Agriculture Secretary Tom Vilsack warned that failure to pass the expiring farm bill would severely harm agriculture and have wide ripple effects — from higher grocery prices (he suggested milk could double) to impacts on biofuels, exports, conservation programs and farmers’ markets. Vilsack defended the food stamp program, saying 92% of recipients are seniors, the disabled, or children of working families and that deep cuts are misguided.

- Fiscal cliff status and criticism — John Barrasso and Donna Edwards: Sen. John Barrasso said negotiators had not reached a deal and criticized President Obama for “outsourcing” leadership on the fiscal cliff instead of producing a proposal the House, Senate and he could all accept. Rep. Donna Edwards countered that Democrats are united on extending middle-class tax protections and blamed Republican obstruction.

- Dianne Feinstein on gun control after Sandy Hook: Sen. Dianne Feinstein urged the nation to “bite the bullet” and enact gun-control reforms following the Dec. 14 Sandy Hook massacre. She plans to introduce legislation for stricter background checks and gun registration, saying stronger measures are needed to place weapons under appropriate authority after the killing of children and others in Newtown, Conn.
