Robert McCoy was convicted and sentenced to death in Louisiana for a 2008 triple homicide. At trial his defense lawyer, Larry English, told the jury in his opening and closing statements that McCoy was guilty and urged a lesser verdict (seeking to avoid the death penalty). McCoy repeatedly and explicitly objected to this strategy, tried to fire English, and insisted on his innocence—claiming a police conspiracy. The judge refused to allow McCoy to replace his lawyer or represent himself, and English continued with the guilt concession despite McCoy’s protests.

English later said he believed the evidence against McCoy was overwhelming and that conceding guilt offered the best chance to spare his life. The Louisiana courts, including the state supreme court, upheld that strategy as reasonable trial tactics, relying in part on precedent permitting concessions when a defendant is unresponsive. McCoy’s lawyers argue that the concession over his express objection violated his Sixth Amendment right to make fundamental decisions about his defense and to have effective assistance of counsel; they say the Louisiana rule is an outlier and conflicts with other states and legal ethics principles.

The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear McCoy v. Louisiana to resolve whether a defense counsel may concede a client’s guilt over the client’s express objection. The case raises core questions about a defendant’s autonomy in choosing defense strategy, the proper role of counsel in capital cases, and when strategic concessions are constitutionally permissible. The case drew amicus briefs on both sides—from several states supporting Louisiana’s approach and from major defense, ethics, and legal-academic groups supporting McCoy.

The Dutch Safety Board’s final report on Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 (shot down over eastern Ukraine on 17 July 2014, killing all 298 aboard) concludes the airliner was destroyed by the detonation of a warhead from a Russian-made Buk surface-to-air missile. Investigators reconstructed wreckage recovered from the crash zone and found bow-tie/cube-shaped fragments and paint transfers linking missile parts on the ground to damage on the left-front side of the cockpit. The board says the warhead type was a 9N314M on a 9M38M1 missile and that the blast blew off cockpit sections and likely killed the three cockpit crew instantly; it could not determine exactly when other passengers died and did not rule out some remaining conscious during the roughly 90 seconds the aircraft took to fall.

The report delineated a 320 sq km area in eastern Ukraine from which the missile was fired and said that area was under the control of pro‑Russian separatists on the day of the crash. The investigation did not assign legal blame or identify who launched the missile; a separate Dutch criminal probe is pursuing persons of interest. The board also recommended better closure of airspace over conflict zones, noting Ukraine had sufficient reason to restrict flights but did not do so (about 160 commercial flights crossed the area that day).

Russian officials and Buk manufacturer Almaz-Antey disputed parts of the findings, arguing for alternative launch locations and older missile models; Russia called the investigation biased and has resisted an international tribunal. Western governments, Ukraine and Malaysia responded by urging accountability and cooperation with the criminal investigation. The report issued 11 safety recommendations aimed at preventing civilian overflights of conflict areas.

The George Washington Bridge, long a frequent site of suicides, set records in 2012 with 18 people dying by jumping from the 212-foot span and 43 attempted suicides, the highest totals on record. Port Authority officials and police say the rise may be linked to economic hardship; after a cluster of cases in May, patrols on the bridge were intensified and calls were made to upgrade its CCTV system.

Against that backdrop, Port Authority Police Officer Jesse Turano made a dramatic rescue on a Tuesday night in Fort Lee. Responding to a report about a man who ignored a security guard and entered the closed north walkway, Turano pursued the 40-year-old Queens resident, grabbed him as he tried to climb over the outer railing, pulled him back onto the walkway and handcuffed him for safety. The man was transported to Bergen Regional Medical Center for psychiatric evaluation and later told Turano he had been unemployed for three years and wanted to die. Turano, a seven-year bridge veteran who has helped stop multiple would-be jumpers, was praised by police representatives but downplayed his actions.

Aretha Franklin is suing satirical website The News Nerd for $10 million, claiming a recent fictional story that went viral defamed her. The News Nerd published an item headlined "Patti Labelle Arrested After Fist Fight with Aretha Franklin," alleging LaBelle attacked Franklin at an Atlanta concert after a PBS taping, and describing a Mayweather-style punch and subsequent arrest. Franklin’s publicist, Gwendolyn Quinn, said the piece “was presented as a serious news story intended to depict me in a slanderous and derogatory way.” Franklin issued a statement denying the incident, saying she and Patti LaBelle are “cool” and that the fight never happened; footage from the PBS program even shows the two hugging.

TheNewsNerd labels itself a satirical site and carries a disclaimer stating its stories are for entertainment, and the article originally appeared under a byline but has since been edited and recredited. Despite the disclaimer, the parody post was widely shared on social media (thousands of shares), and many readers treated it as real, prompting Franklin to consult lawyers and pursue legal action for defamation. Observers note that a lawsuit may face challenges because the site identifies as satire, but Franklin’s complaint has amplified attention to the issue.

A three-judge High Court in Dublin has rejected a landmark challenge by Marie Fleming, a 59‑year‑old former lecturer now severely disabled by advanced multiple sclerosis, to Ireland’s absolute ban on assisted suicide. Fleming had sought a court order allowing her partner to help her end her life without facing prosecution, arguing the blanket prohibition in the Criminal Law (Suicide) Act 1993 violated her personal autonomy and equality rights under the Irish Constitution and the ECHR.

The court found the ban justified as a proportionate measure to protect vulnerable people from being pressured or feeling compelled to choose death — citing a real risk that repealing or modifying the prohibition would leave the aged, disabled, poor, lonely or emotionally vulnerable exposed to involuntary death. The judges also held that only the Oireachtas can change the law and that the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) could not lawfully effect such a change by issuing non‑binding prosecution guidelines; however, the court said the DPP would likely exercise discretion humanely in any prosecution decision where reliable evidence showed compliance with established safeguards.

Presiding Justice Nicholas Kearns described Fleming as “in many ways the most remarkable witness” and praised her courage, but said the court could not tailor a legal solution solely to her circumstances without broader societal implications. The State agreed to pay Fleming’s legal costs. Fleming said she was “very disappointed and saddened” and is expected to appeal to the Supreme Court. The judgment, running to about 120 pages, comes amid wider public debate and recent related cases in Britain and elsewhere about legalising assisted suicide.

Mack Randall “Mack” Wolford, a 44‑year‑old Pentecostal pastor from West Virginia known regionally for handling venomous snakes as an expression of faith, died after being bitten by a rattlesnake during an outdoor “homecoming” service at Panther Wildlife Management Area. Wolford, who had been profiled last November in The Washington Post Magazine for his openness with journalists and evangelism to keep serpent‑handling practices alive, believed Mark 16:17–18 required Christians to take up serpents and trust God for healing. The service, held after Wolford had promoted it on Facebook, turned tragic about 30 minutes in when a yellow timber rattlesnake he passed to congregants was laid on the ground and bit him on the thigh. Initially taken to a relative’s home, his condition worsened; he was later transported to Bluefield Regional Medical Center where he was pronounced dead late that night. Witnesses reported he was bitten around 1:30 p.m. and died about 11 p.m., mirroring the circumstances of his father’s 1983 death from a rattlesnake bite. Wolford kept several venomous snakes at home and had actively tried to revitalize the tradition in West Virginia and neighboring states where it is illegal. Park officials said they were unaware poisonous animals were present and would not have permitted them. Friends and observers described him as articulate, media‑friendly and committed to teaching others about the faith; his funeral is scheduled at House of the Lord Jesus in Matoaka.

A 4-year-old Italian girl died of cerebral malaria after being admitted to hospital in Trento and transferred to a tropical diseases center in Brescia. The case alarmed health officials because she had not traveled to any malaria-endemic country, and Italy has been considered malaria-free since the 1950s and Europe largely so. Italy’s health ministry sent an expert team to Trento to investigate how she was infected.

Authorities noted the child had recently been on holiday in Bibione (domestic), had earlier been treated at Trento hospital for another condition, and that two other children at the Trento facility had malaria contracted in Burkina Faso. Hospital managers said there were no blood transfusions and the malaria patients were isolated using single-use equipment, making patient-to-patient transmission unlikely. Investigators are considering possibilities including infection before hospital arrival (the incubation fits the timing) or a “mosquito-in-a-suitcase” — infected Anopheles mosquitoes transported from endemic areas in luggage or by travel. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control has previously documented such suitcase-linked cases in Western Europe.

Experts noted the rarity of locally acquired malaria in recent decades but pointed to isolated European cases and warned that factors like warm weather and changing vector distributions could increase vulnerability. The WHO is holding discussions on keeping Europe malaria-free.

President Trump’s legal team believes the Justice Department and FBI — rather than Special Counsel Robert Mueller alone — are driving what they view as a politically motivated “witch hunt,” and some inside the White House want a separate special counsel to investigate the investigators. Mueller’s probe has been expansive and aggressive, producing multiple indictments and securing large volumes of evidence (for example, more than 400,000 documents and dozens of devices in the Paul Manafort matter). Trump’s immediate legal defense is led by John Dowd (a retired private lawyer), Ty Cobb (a White House lawyer paid by the government) and Jay Sekulow; they act as his attorneys, strategists and PR managers. The trio have cooperated with Mueller’s office—producing documents, counseling the president, and assuring him the investigation is nearing its end—but have been widely criticized in Washington for being under-resourced, indiscreet, and sometimes making legally dubious public comments (including Dowd’s claim that a sitting president cannot obstruct justice). Cobb lacks attorney-client privilege (as a government employee), while Dowd and Sekulow do not, a distinction with investigative implications. Trump has considered but not retained a larger roster of top litigators; some high-profile candidates declined.

The report also recounts internal tensions around events such as Deutsche Bank reporting and a Trump tweet about Michael Flynn that Dowd claimed to have written. Former members of the team (like Marc Kasowitz) and outside commentators question whether the current lawyers are adequate to represent a client with Trump’s tendencies and media presence.

Separately, Fox News reported that Justice Department official Bruce Ohr — recently demoted after concealing meetings with Fusion GPS founder Glenn Simpson and dossier author Christopher Steele — had closer ties to Fusion GPS than previously disclosed: his wife, Nellie Ohr, worked for Fusion GPS during 2016. House Intelligence Committee Republicans are probing all connections between DOJ and Fusion GPS amid allegations that the dossier (funded by Democrats) was used to obtain FISA surveillance on Trump campaign adviser Carter Page. DOJ has not publicly explained Ohr’s demotion; Democrats on the committee have characterized the probe as politically motivated.

Med Express, a refurbished medical-equipment seller, was ordered to pay $19,250 in attorneys’ fees after suing two eBay buyers in 2013 over negative feedback. The company’s founder, Richard Radey, had filed near-identical libel suits claiming bad feedback and lowered seller ratings harmed the business. One plaintiff, Amy Nicholls, left a complaint after receiving an item with $1.44 postage due despite having paid $175 plus shipping; she also gave mixed detailed seller ratings (including a 1 for communication). Med Express later apologized and said it was withdrawing the suits amid public criticism.

Nicholls retained pro bono counsel with help from Paul Levy of Public Citizen; Ohio attorneys Jeffrey Nye and Thomas Haren represented her and another buyer, Dennis Rogan, who had left a neutral review. After protracted proceedings, including two sanctions trials and inconsistent testimony from Radey, a Medina County judge found parts of Nicholls’s feedback were protected opinion and the factual statements she made were true; the judge also criticized Radey’s credibility. Earlier oral deals for partial fee payment were not honored by Med Express, prompting a second trial and the sanctions award.

Public Citizen called the ruling an important consumer win and urged anti-SLAPP protections for Ohio; Nicholls’s lawyers said the decision upheld First Amendment rights against “bully” suits. Radey did not respond to requests for comment and, as of the sanctions order, was representing himself.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a surprise demonetisation on 8 November 2016, declaring the 500- and 1,000-rupee banknotes—about 85% of cash in circulation—illegal tender from midnight. The move, framed as a “surgical strike” against corruption, counterfeit currency and tax evasion, gives people 50 days to deposit or exchange old notes at banks and post offices (with limited acceptance at airports, railways and hospitals until 11 November). The government and RBI will issue new 2,000- and redesigned 500-rupee notes and limit ATM withdrawals temporarily; ATMs and many banks were closed immediately, triggering long queues and short-term disruption.

Officials say the policy aims to flush out “black money” by forcing unaccounted cash into the banking system where large or suspicious deposits will be scrutinised and subject to tax laws. Finance Minister Arun Jaitley and other leaders argued honest citizens need not worry and touted benefits such as moving toward a less-cash economy and curbing fake notes allegedly used by terrorists. Critics and commentators warned of hardship for small traders, daily wage workers and upcoming wedding expenses; practical details (withdrawal caps, exchange limits) were initially unclear, though small exchanges will be permitted and larger sums will prompt questioning. The new notes carry updated security features and imagery (including Gandhi and, on the 2,000-rupee note, the Mangalyaan satellite) and are part of a broader push against illicit cash holdings.

Michael Cohen, an executive vice president and special counsel to Donald Trump, made headlines during a CNN interview after awkwardly disputing that Trump’s campaign was trailing Hillary Clinton in the polls. When anchor Brianna Keilar said “you guys are down,” Cohen repeatedly retorted, “Says who?” and pressed which polls she meant. The exchange drew widespread attention and the social media hashtag #SaysWho.

Earlier the campaign announced a leadership change—Kellyanne Conway as campaign manager and Steve Bannon as CEO—moves portrayed by many as a shake-up to address poor polling. Cohen insisted it was not a shake-up, praised Conway as a smart hire who understands the data, and later clarified an earlier remark about “the African American problem,” saying he meant to refer to problems that exist in the African American community and that Trump is “colourblind” but aware of racial tensions. The interview did little to reassure voters concerned about Trump’s standing in key swing states; most national and state polls at the time showed Clinton ahead.

During the opening days of Mitt Romney’s 2012 trip to Britain — billed as a foreign-policy junket but heavy on optics — the presumptive Republican nominee stumbled through a string of gaffes that made headlines and provoked British ridicule. Romney questioned whether London could pull off the Olympics, called some preparations “disconcerting,” and unnecessarily disclosed that he met the head of MI6. He also used awkward phrasing about “looking out of the backside of 10 Downing Street,” and expressed disinterest in watching his wife’s expensive Olympic-bound horse, all of which fed a narrative of tone-deafness and unfamiliarity with local sensitivities.

British officials and commentators were quick to respond: Prime Minister David Cameron delivered a sharp retort comparing London’s complex, crowded Games to Romney’s experience running the much smaller Salt Lake City Olympics in 2002, and London’s press and public mocked Romney’s missteps. The campaign’s broader foreign-policy posture — scant concrete proposals and a general “I’m different” posture contrasted with President Obama — compounded perceptions that the trip was more spectacle than substantive diplomacy.

Observers also criticized Romney’s campaign for an advisor’s anonymous comment suggesting Obama didn’t value Anglo-Saxon ties, a remark that played into divisive identity politics and reinforced concerns about the campaign’s tone. Overall, what was meant to be a presidential, reassuring overseas appearance instead underscored gaffes, awkward messaging, and missed opportunities to avoid offending a key ally.

A week-long survey led by Nancy Rabalais of the Louisiana Universities Marine Consortium found this summer’s Gulf of Mexico “dead zone” covered 5,052 square miles—about the size of Connecticut and roughly 800 square miles smaller than in 2013. The measurement matches scientists’ June predictions based on Mississippi and Atchafalaya River nutrient loads. Excess nitrogen, largely from Midwest agricultural runoff, drives massive algal blooms; when the algae die and decompose the bottom waters become hypoxic (under 2 ppm O2), killing or displacing bottom-dwelling organisms. This year’s hypoxic area is part of a five-year average of 5,543 square miles—nearly three times larger than the 1,991-square-mile reduction target set by the federal/state Mississippi River Gulf of Mexico Watershed Nutrient Task Force in 2001 (reconfirmed in 2008) and never achieved.

The dead zone is split into two areas off central/southeastern and southwestern Louisiana. Scientists note that variations in river discharge, nitrate concentrations and winds/currents influence its size; heavy Midwest rains and a late spike in nitrate this summer likely limited what might otherwise have been a larger area. Researchers warn that long-term nutrient loading—amplified by 20th-century agricultural expansion—continues to increase nitrate levels, with some nitrogen stored in sediments that can fuel future blooms. They say reducing hypoxia requires changes in land use and proven agricultural practices that retain yields and profits while cutting runoff.

Environmental groups responded by urging stricter regulation of nutrient pollution and numeric water-quality standards for the Mississippi basin, criticizing EPA and state inaction and citing recent toxic algal incidents (e.g., Toledo) as evidence of broader risks. The study was conducted by LUMCON with LSU and FSU partners and funded by NOAA, EPA’s Gulf of Mexico Program and NSF. Researchers say the Gulf dead zone is the world’s second-largest human-caused coastal hypoxic area and part of a global rise in dead zones.

General Motors is facing scrutiny over why it waited more than a decade to recall 2.6 million small cars after discovering a faulty ignition switch linked to at least 13 deaths. The company has acknowledged the defect but has pointed to other factors—off‑road crashes, high speeds, failure to wear seat belts and alcohol use—as possible contributors. The New York Times and other reporting, however, found alcohol was listed in only four of the 10 accidents it examined, and in one of those the intoxicated driver was in a different vehicle.

Families of victims have pursued lawsuits; many settlements are confidential and some plaintiffs say the payments were modest and the legal process was painful. Relatives describe being blamed for the crashes and, in some cases, charging the victims or drivers with crimes. One prominent case involves Mikale Erickson, who died in 2004 when a Saturn Ion driven by his fiancée, Candice Anderson, went off a rural Texas road and hit a tree. Airbags did not deploy. Anderson survived, later pleaded guilty to criminal negligent homicide after a trace amount of anti‑anxiety medication was found, and has lived with the conviction’s consequences. In late May she and Erickson’s family learned his death was among the 13 GM linked fatalities; Erickson’s mother says GM has not contacted the family and wants at minimum an apology and for Anderson’s record to be reconsidered given the defective vehicle.

Federal safety regulators have suggested more than 13 lives may ultimately be tied to the defect. GM has not disclosed how it will compensate the victims’ families; Kenneth Feinberg, the firm hired to design a victim‑compensation program, is expected to announce a plan for addressing the thousands of claims filed against the automaker.

Comcast drew fresh criticism after a Spokane couple discovered their billing name had been changed to “Asshole Brown” following a cancellation dispute. Lisa Brown had called to cancel cable service to save money and was transferred to a retention specialist; she says she wasn’t rude but declined the offer. The offensive name appeared on monthly statements and persisted despite her attempts to resolve it in person and by phone.

Wired and consumer advocate Christopher Elliott verified the bill and Comcast confirmed the incident. Comcast apologized, said it has “zero tolerance” for such behavior, launched an investigation, corrected the account, waived the $60 cancellation fee, and initially offered a refund of two years’ service (later clarified as a refund only). Company officials said they were working to make things right and would take appropriate steps, including possibly terminating the responsible employee.

The episode highlights longstanding complaints about Comcast’s retention tactics and customer service, and raises questions about what constitutes a fair remedy — apology, fee waiver and firing, or a larger refund. The story prompted follow-up reporting and other readers’ similar complaints about disrespectful labels used by customer-service staff.

Researchers challenge the idea that relational aggression—harming peers by damaging relationships, such as spreading rumors, ostracizing, or turning others against someone—is primarily a female behavior. Pamela Orpinas and colleagues tracked 620 students from 6th through 12th grade, asking how often they engaged in such behaviors over 30-day periods. They found that high relational aggression was more common among boys in the early years of the study (two-thirds of the high-aggression group were male), and overall relational aggression declined with age. Other studies and writers (including a 2012 multinational study and Rosalind Wiseman) have similarly questioned the stereotype that girls monopolize social nastiness and have urged more attention to boys’ social and emotional lives.

Orpinas and Wiseman argue schools, parents, and prevention programs should address relational aggression among both genders: adults must model non‑aggressive behavior, speak about and reward positive peer behavior, and give boys language and support to express worries and build social competence. Emphasizing and publicizing the many instances of kids helping and supporting one another can help make caring behavior “cool” and reduce relational aggression.

This document summarizes Pulitzer Prize winners across journalism and the arts, then provides detailed coverage of the Los Angeles Times’ investigation into the Bell, California, corruption scandal and many related developments.

Pulitzers and major arts awards
- Journalism highlights: Public Service—Los Angeles Times; Investigative—Paige St. John (Sarasota Herald-Tribune); Explanatory—Mark Johnson et al. (Milwaukee Journal Sentinel); Local—Frank Main, Mark Konkol and John J. Kim (Chicago Sun-Times); National—Jesse Eisinger and Jake Bernstein (ProPublica); International—Clifford J. Levy and Ellen Barry (The New York Times); Feature writing—Amy Ellis Nutt; Commentary—David Leonhardt (NYT); Criticism—Sebastian Smee (Boston Globe); Editorial writing—Joseph Rago (Wall Street Journal); Editorial cartooning—Mike Keefe (Denver Post); Breaking news photography—Carol Guzy, Nikki Kahn and Ricky Carioti (Washington Post); Feature photography—Barbara Davidson (Los Angeles Times). No Pulitzer was awarded for Breaking News Reporting.
- Arts prizes: Fiction—A Visit from the Goon Squad (Jennifer Egan); Drama—Clybourne Park (Bruce Norris); History—The Fiery Trial (Eric Foner); Biography—Washington: A Life (Ron Chernow); Poetry—The Best of It (Kay Ryan); General Nonfiction—The Emperor of All Maladies (Siddhartha Mukherjee); Music—Madame White Snake (Zhou Long).

LA Times Bell investigation and awards
- The Los Angeles Times won the Public Service Pulitzer for a major investigative series exposing massive corruption in the small city of Bell, where top officials secretly awarded themselves exorbitant salaries and benefits and illegally raised taxes on residents. The paper also won Feature Photography for Barbara Davidson’s intimate images of violent-crime victims in South L.A., Compton and Watts.
- The Bell investigation was led by a 20-person Times team headed by reporters Jeff Gottlieb and Ruben Vives. Reporting revealed city manager Robert Rizzo received an $800,000 salary plus large perks; Rizzo and seven other officials were subsequently charged with multiple felonies. The coverage produced legal and political fallout: criminal charges, millions in rebates to residents, new state disclosure rules, and a voter overthrow of the old council.
- The series also earned numerous other honors (Selden Ring Award, ASNE distinguished writing award, IRE top honor, George Polk Award). Times editor and reporters emphasized the civic impact—returning local control to residents and prompting reforms.

Other notable Pulitzer-related items
- The New York Times won two Pulitzers: international reporting (Ellen Barry and Clifford J. Levy) and commentary (David Leonhardt). ProPublica’s national reporting award (Eisinger and Bernstein) was the first Pulitzer for reporting that appeared only online.
- The Washington Post won for breaking news photography for its Haiti earthquake coverage. Boston Globe critic Sebastian Smee won for criticism. Joseph Rago of the Wall Street Journal won for editorial writing.

Ongoing Bell scandal developments (follow-up headlines and findings)
- Legal and pension disputes: A judge rejected former Bell police chief Randy Adams’ attempt to double his pension; Adams invoked the Fifth Amendment repeatedly at a hearing. Questions persisted about why some Bell figures were not criminally charged. CalPERS reviewed top-end pension benefits in response.
- Indictments and investigations: Rizzo and an aide were accused of conspiring to conceal benefits and bypass state law; federal prosecutors probed possible civil rights violations tied to aggressive towing and fees disproportionately affecting Latino residents.
- Financial irregularities and audits: Audits and reports found multiple instances of illegal tax increases, improper fees, rubber-stamped audits, unaccounted-for escrow funds, and questionable property deals. Illegal or dubious levies and “retirement taxes” resulted in millions owed back to taxpayers; some funds used to pay inflated salaries. The city’s conversion to charter status and obscure ballot measures were used to skirt state salary limits.
- Political fallout and community response: Residents voted to recall and replace council members; citizens fielded real choices for office for the first time in years. Stories chronicled the personal toll on residents and activists, campaign deaths and stress, and local attempts at reform.
- Broader consequences: The scandal spurred scrutiny of the state pension system (CalPERS), questions about which entities will bear pension costs, and reforms in disclosure and oversight. Other municipalities and state agencies faced reputational and financial repercussions.

Overall, the document pairs the national recognition of journalistic and artistic achievement with an extensive, journalistic chronicle of how investigative reporting at the Los Angeles Times exposed deep municipal corruption in Bell, leading to prosecutions, refunds for residents, legal and policy reforms, and national conversation about municipal governance and pension oversight.

An Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) warning followed an incident on Feb. 19 in which a woman traveling from Beijing to Melbourne suffered burns after her battery-powered, noise‑cancelling headphones exploded while she slept about two hours into the flight. She woke to a loud bang, felt burning on her face, tore the headphones off and threw them to the cabin floor; they were sparking and producing small flames. Flight attendants doused them with water and placed them in a bucket, but the battery and casing had already melted and fused to the aircraft floor. Photos released by the ATSB show singed hair, eyebrows and soot; the passenger also sustained burns to her hands and clothes. The cabin smelled of melted plastic and burnt hair for the remainder of the flight, and other passengers reported coughing and choking.

The ATSB said the fire likely originated in the headphones’ batteries and stressed that all batteries carry risk. Authorities did not disclose the headphone brand. The bureau reiterated safety guidance: use approved stowage when not in use, keep spare batteries in carry‑on (not checked) baggage, protect battery terminals, and avoid moving powered seats if a device is lost in a seat gap—notify cabin crew instead. The incident echoes prior in‑flight fires from lithium‑ion batteries (e.g., Galaxy Note 7 recalls, hoverboard bans) and underscores rising in‑flight risk as battery-powered devices proliferate.

Local photographer Muhammad Malik photographed a victim of this morning's deadly shooting near the Empire State Building as he exited the subway and posted the image to Instagram with a Nas lyric and to Facebook with "MAN DOWN! SHOTS FIRED!" Reporters soon contacted him seeking permission to use the photo; Malik initially celebrated the attention online but later told Daily Intel he was offering the image for free, saying the event had become "too much" and denying any intent to be offensive.

Mickey Rooney’s widow and several of his children have filed legal challenges to a will the 93-year-old actor signed weeks before his April 2014 death that leaves his entire estate to a stepson, disinheriting his wife Janice (Jan) Rooney, eight biological children and two other stepchildren.

Key points:
- The will (signed March 11, 2014) names stepson Mark Rooney (also reported as Mark Aber) as sole heir and executor; Mark was Rooney’s primary caregiver during his final two years and died April 7, 2014.
- Jan Rooney’s attorney, Eugene Belous, says he will appear in Los Angeles County Probate Court to argue the will contains a “blatant misstatement” and that prior settlement agreements do not terminate her rights as surviving spouse. A court filing, however, asserts Jan had signed an agreement waiving claims after the couple separated in June 2012.
- Mickey Rooney’s court‑appointed conservator/executor, Michael Augustine, calls Jan’s challenge “totally without merit,” says Rooney was of sound mind when he signed the will, and contends Rooney intended to reward the step‑son and his wife for caretaking. Augustine also suggests the widow is seeking publicity, noting the estate’s reported personal property value is only about $18,000.
- Rooney’s eight biological children separately filed a will contest alleging undue influence and elder abuse: they claim the conservator and stepson exploited Rooney’s frailty, controlled his decisions, dictated the will’s contents and arranged its execution. They seek to void the will and recover fees.
- A probate hearing to begin administering the will is scheduled for Monday.

Although Rooney’s banked personal assets were reported small, his family members point out potential value in residuals and royalties, and the dispute centers on whether the will reflects Rooney’s free and informed intent or was the product of undue influence.

On Feb. 9, 2017, White House counselor Kellyanne Conway drew widespread criticism after using a television appearance from the White House to urge viewers to “go buy Ivanka’s stuff,” promoting products from Ivanka Trump’s fashion brand. Her on-air endorsement followed President Trump’s tweet criticizing Nordstrom for dropping Ivanka’s line and prompted immediate ethical concerns because executive-branch employees are barred from using public office to endorse private products or benefit relatives’ businesses.

Responses and fallout:
- The White House said Conway had been “counseled” about the remark; Conway later said the president “supports me 100%.”
- Ethics lawyers, watchdog groups (including CREW) and lawmakers called for review or discipline. Reps. Elijah Cummings (D) and Jason Chaffetz (R) jointly asked the Office of Government Ethics (OGE) to investigate and recommend any appropriate disciplinary action, noting the president’s conflict of interest as Conway’s agency head.
- Critics argued the comment likely violated OGE rules prohibiting endorsement of products by federal employees and highlighted a broader pattern of blurred lines between the Trump family’s business interests and the presidency. Some experts said a single comment might draw a warning, while repeated conduct could lead to stronger sanctions.
- The OGE’s public-facing systems were inundated with inquiries; the agency noted it provides guidance but lacks direct enforcement authority. Enforcement would rest with agency leadership (the White House).

Context:
- The exchange occurred amid organized consumer backlash (e.g., #GrabYourWallet) and Nordstrom’s stated business decision to drop Ivanka’s line, which Trump publicly attacked. Ivanka Trump had stepped back from operational roles but retained financial interests in her brand, raising concerns about mixing family business promotion with official government platforms.

Investigators probing the Oct. 2017 Las Vegas massacre are also hunting the source of graphic crime-scene photographs of suspect Stephen Paddock that circulated online. Las Vegas Metro Undersheriff Kevin McMahill confirmed the images came from inside Paddock’s Mandalay Bay suite, show Paddock’s body and an array of weapons and casings, and that an internal investigation has been opened to find who leaked them. McMahill urged patience as investigators finish processing the room.

The leaked photos — first widely published by MailOnline and shared on social media — depict dozens of high-powered firearms (police recovered 23 guns from room 32135), many shell casings, guns mounted on tripods, possible notes or writing near Paddock’s body, electrical tape and cameras placed to monitor or record. The images reinforce officials’ account that Paddock apparently killed himself with a shot to the head before SWAT entered. Authorities said they have not publicly confirmed finding a note or motive and are still seeking information, including from Paddock’s girlfriend Marilou Danley, who returned to the U.S. and was questioned by investigators.

The article notes that leaking crime-scene images is a recurring problem for police and can trigger internal discipline or employment consequences, even if criminal charges aren’t always pursued. It cites past high-profile leaks — an LAPD officer who lost her job after leaking Rihanna photos (2009) and controversy after leaked Manchester attack photos (2016) — and warns the Mandalay Bay leaker could face serious administrative and possibly legal repercussions.

Documents from Edward Snowden show New Zealand’s signals intelligence agency, the Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB), secretly planned and began implementing a mass metadata collection program in 2012–2013—despite repeated public assurances from Prime Minister John Key that no such mass surveillance existed or would be permitted.

Key revelations and timeline
- Top-secret NSA documents reveal a GCSB project code-named “Speargun,” whose Phase I involved covert “cable access” (apparently tapping the Southern Cross undersea cable that carries most NZ internet traffic) and Phase II planned the insertion of “metadata probes” to collect dates, times, senders and recipients of communications. The first probe was scheduled for mid-2013.
- NSA records show Phase I was achieved and that completion of Speargun was explicitly contingent on passage of a new GCSB law that would allow the agency to target citizens and residents—authorities previously barred under New Zealand law.
- The law was enacted in August 2013 after the GCSB was found to have illegally spied on Kim Dotcom and others. Parliament approved the legislation narrowly (61–59), amid intense public debate and protests.

Conflicting public statements
- Prime Minister John Key and other officials consistently insisted the law only clarified existing targeted powers and would not permit wholesale, warrantless metadata collection. Key said there “is not, and never has been, mass surveillance of New Zealanders.”
- Snowden and journalist Glenn Greenwald (reporting for The Intercept) contend those assurances were false. Snowden says GCSB participated in untargeted bulk interception and contributed data and analytic development to the NSA’s XKEYSCORE system, which he worked with while at the NSA. Snowden points to features like a “Five Eyes Defeat” checkbox in XKEYSCORE as evidence that New Zealand’s traffic was being collected and could be hidden in searches—evidence inconsistent with official denials.
- After the reporting, Key admitted a mass surveillance proposal had been planned but said he rejected it before implementation, calling it a “widespread cyber protection programme” that never got off the ground and released some declassified documents in response.

Political context and impact
- The disclosures came shortly before New Zealand’s 2014 election and fed broader controversies surrounding the Key government (including the Dirty Politics scandal). They revived criticism over the GCSB’s conduct, the law that expanded its powers, and whether the government misled the public.
- The story has energized surveillance critics and political movements such as the Internet Party (funded by Kim Dotcom), which mobilized public events and campaigning around these issues.

Bottom line
Classified Snowden documents and reporting by Glenn Greenwald allege the GCSB, with NSA cooperation, actively pursued a mass metadata collection program (Speargun) that relied on newly enacted domestic surveillance legislation—contradicting repeated public assurances by Prime Minister John Key that no mass surveillance was occurring or would be authorized. The revelations raise questions about government transparency, legal safeguards, and political accountability.

Three women — Sonia Ulrich, Monica Kenyon and Marla Saltzer — say they prevented a woman from being drugged during happy hour at FIG restaurant in the Fairmont Miramar, Santa Monica. Kenyon noticed a man at a nearby table fumble with the woman’s glass and drop something into it. The trio discussed what to do; Ulrich located the woman in the restroom and warned her, but the woman said the man was “one of my best friends” and returned to the table. The women alerted restaurant staff, who reviewed security footage and confirmed the men’s actions. Santa Monica police arrived, arrested the man and reportedly found multiple small vials of a clear substance on him. The incident prompted other diners to thank the women and share similar experiences of being targeted. The women and the restaurant have been praised online for speaking up and taking action. The substance has not been publicly identified and the matter appears to be under investigation.

Nancy Mace, the first woman to graduate from The Citadel and a Charleston public-relations business owner, and state Sen. Lee Bright both plan to announce Republican primary bids to challenge U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham in South Carolina’s 2014 Senate primary. They join businessman Richard Cash as anti-Graham candidates. Mace was set to formally launch at a GOP breakfast in Goose Creek; Bright said he will enter soon, awaiting word on whether Reps. Trey Gowdy or Jeff Duncan will run. Bright emphasizes his legislative record as a limited-government conservative; Mace has criticized Graham for supporting NSA data collection, foreign policy decisions and bipartisan compromises she says betray constitutional principles and conservative values.

Political analysts say multiple libertarian/Tea Party challengers could split the anti-Graham vote and thereby help the incumbent. Graham has substantial resources ($6.3 million reported on hand) and a pro-Graham super PAC has formed; an anti-Graham group also recently launched. Observers note Graham has moved rightward on some issues as his re-election approached, but challengers could still pressure him to be less conciliatory with Democrats even if he wins.

Fundraising will be critical for challengers—Bright believes he can raise about $5 million, and outside groups such as Club for Growth or other national conservative funders could play a role. Commentators say Mace’s high-profile story and media appeal may help consolidate conservative support behind a single challenger, while Bright’s hard-edged conservative style will appeal to voters frustrated with Graham. The contested primary could send a message to Graham regardless of outcome. The coverage also includes Mace’s broader criticisms of Graham on immigration, national security, and constitutional issues, and frames her candidacy as part of a Tea Party/grassroots push for more consistently conservative representation.

Clare Bronfman, a 39-year-old Seagram heiress, and three associates of the self-help organization NXIVM were arrested and charged in New York in connection with a federal investigation alleging a range of criminal activity tied to the group. Bronfman surrendered to the FBI, pleaded not guilty to racketeering charges, and was released on a $100 million bond with house arrest; prosecutors had argued she was a flight risk given an estimated $200 million net worth. Also arrested were NXIVM co-founder Nancy Salzman, her daughter Lauren Salzman, and former bookkeeper Kathy Russell; all were released on bail without entering pleas.

Federal prosecutors say Bronfman was part of an inner circle that helped NXIVM founder Keith Raniere exert control over members through identity theft, interception of communications, money laundering and other crimes to protect the group and Raniere. Earlier filings allege she donated tens of millions to support NXIVM, paid for private flights and funded lawsuits against critics. Bronfman’s lawyer calls the charges government overreach and says she will be exonerated.

NXIVM, founded as Executive Success Programs, marketed itself as empowerment training but prosecutors allege it operated a secret “masters/slaves” subgroup in which some women were branded with a symbol resembling Raniere’s initials and coerced into sexual servitude. Raniere—arrested in Mexico in March—and actress Allison Mack previously have been charged with sex trafficking and forced labor conspiracies; additional defendants face charges including identity theft, extortion, money laundering, wire fraud and obstruction. Those charges carry lengthy potential prison sentences. Raniere, Mack and others were due to appear at a pretrial hearing following the latest arrests.

A joint Nielsen–Sony survey asked 1,077 U.S. adults (a scientific sample from Nielsen’s TV panel) whether they had watched major televised events in the past 50 years and whether they remembered where they were, who they were with and if they discussed the event afterward. Using those criteria to measure impact, the survey found news coverage overwhelmingly dominated viewers’ lasting memories over entertainment programming.

Top-ranked moments:
1. Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks (by far the most memorable)
2. Hurricane Katrina coverage (2005)
3. O.J. Simpson murder trial verdict (1995)
4. Challenger shuttle explosion (1986)
5. Death of Osama bin Laden (2011)

Other top 20 items included the O.J. Simpson White Bronco chase (1994), the 2011 Japanese earthquake and tsunami, Columbine (1999), the BP oil spill (2010), Princess Diana’s funeral (1997), Whitney Houston’s death (2012), capture/execution of Saddam Hussein (2006), Barack Obama’s 2008 election night speech, the 2011 royal wedding, JFK’s assassination and funeral (1963), Oklahoma City bombing (1995), the Bush/Gore 2000 dispute, the Los Angeles riots/Rodney King beating (1992), the Casey Anthony verdict (2011) and others.

Key findings:
- Television news events left the strongest, most persistent impressions; many expected entertainment moments (e.g., M*A*S*H finale, Beatles on Ed Sullivan) ranked much lower than anticipated.
- Demographics mattered: older viewers rated historically earlier events (e.g., JFK assassination, moon landing) as more impactful, while younger viewers emphasized recent moments (e.g., bin Laden’s death, Obama’s election night). Men and women agreed on the top three but differed on others (e.g., women rated Princess Diana’s funeral and Whitney Houston’s death far higher).
- The survey suggests TV remains a central shared social medium and could serve as a baseline for tracking how televised events imprint on public memory over time.

Katie Couric has officially announced she is leaving her role as anchor of the CBS Evening News; her contract expires in June and she is expected to step down around that time. Couric told People she’s exploring formats that allow “more multi-dimensional storytelling” and has not finalized where she’ll land next. CBS reportedly offered her a syndication daytime show and a continued role on 60 Minutes, but ABC has emerged as a strong contender, pushing for a Couric-hosted talk show plus broader exposure across its news platforms (including involvement in 2012 election coverage and prime-time specials). NBC is no longer in the mix. Insiders say CBS, tired of protracted negotiations, is prepared to let her go; 60 Minutes correspondent Scott Pelley is widely expected to be named her successor. Couric had been anchoring the Evening News since September 2006 but was unable to lift it from third place in the ratings.

This document combines three distinct threads:

1) Internet Archive crawls
- The Internet Archive is running crawls of “No More 404” sites to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference. The aim is to preserve the versions of linked content that existed when a page was written, so when referenced pages change or disappear, archived links can replace broken ones. The long-term goal: reduce or eliminate broken links across the web by providing durable archived references.

2) Engagement and relationship news about Glennon Doyle Melton and Abby Wambach
- Christian writer and mom blogger Glennon Doyle Melton announced her engagement to U.S. soccer star Abby Wambach. Melton shared the news on Facebook with a photo of the couple holding hands; Wambach posted the same image on Instagram. The relationship became public after Melton’s recent divorce from Craig Melton and Wambach’s separation from Sarah Huffman amid personal struggles. The piece notes Melton’s public advocacy for same-sex marriage and her hope that her openness supports her children. The story references other public same-sex relationship revelations (e.g., Elizabeth Gilbert).

3) Long reflective personal essays by Glennon Doyle Melton
- Several extended personal essays by Melton are included: a candid announcement of her separation from Craig, a reflection on the process of healing and changing while honoring truth over “success,” and why she chose to be public about the split despite professional risks. She describes working through trauma, counseling, co-parenting arrangements, and a commitment to honesty with her audience.
- A second essay recounts her spiritual wrestling over Christianity and homosexuality. Melton explains how she came to affirm and love gay people, arguing that Jesus’ core message is love and empathy. She rejects celibacy as a default “solution” for gay people, emphasizes that love is the highest value, and calls for Christians to prioritize broader pro-life issues (poverty, healthcare, immigration). She urges compassion for all sides, invites people to her inclusive “table,” and asks her community for support through her transition.

Overall, the document mixes a technical preservation initiative (Internet Archive) with a celebrity engagement announcement and several intimate, faith-centered essays by Glennon Doyle Melton about divorce, authenticity, recovery, and inclusive Christian love.

The Labor Department reported that U.S. payrolls rose by just 74,000 in December — the smallest monthly gain in three years — while the unemployment rate fell to 6.7% from 7.0% in November. The decline in the jobless rate partly reflected people leaving the labor force rather than finding work; the civilian labor force participation rate slipped to 62.8% from a month earlier and from 63.6% a year ago.

November and October payrolls were revised up by a combined 38,000 (November to 241,000; October unchanged at 200,000). For 2013 overall, employers added an average of 182,000 jobs per month, roughly in line with 2012’s pace. Shorter-term averages cooled: three- and six-month averages were about 172,000–195,000, and December’s weak gain pulled down longer-run trends.

By industry, retail added the most jobs in December (+55,000), with professional and business services (+19,000) and wholesale trade (+15,000) also gaining. Construction lost 16,000 jobs — its largest drop in 20 months, possibly weather-related — and the federal workforce fell by 7,000. Average weekly hours for private employees edged down to 34.4, and average hourly earnings rose two cents to $24.17 (up $0.42 year-over-year).

Xavier Jajuan Davis, 31–32, a Grand Rapids man with prior convictions including a 2012 attempted home invasion and multiple window-peeping convictions, has been arraigned on three new criminal sexual conduct charges and is being held on $400,000 bond. Police say tips from a recently released composite sketch led to his arrest. He faces:
- one count of second‑degree criminal sexual conduct for an Oct. 25 incident at DeVos Place (303 Monroe Ave NW), where court records list him as an employee, and
- two counts of first‑degree criminal sexual conduct (potential life offenses) for an alleged Dec. 28 assault on Oak Park Drive SE.

Details of the alleged assaults have not been released. A probable cause hearing is set for Jan. 30 in Grand Rapids District Court.

Separately, Davis previously sued the City of Grand Rapids and three police investigators in federal court after being arrested in January 2018 on high‑profile sexual assault allegations and held 129 days before charges were dropped. He alleges police targeted him based on a sketch, ignored exculpatory evidence (cell phone, Uber records and DNA excluding him), and coerced victim identifications. While jailed he was assaulted and placed in protective custody; he says the arrest and publicity cost him jobs, housing and led to homelessness. The lawsuit alleges violations including false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, defamation and intentional infliction of emotional distress; the city had not been served at the time of reporting. Prosecutors previously said witness issues and lack of DNA match led to dismissals in those 2018 cases.

Aubrey Jayce Carroll, a Georgia teen who disappeared from Spalding High School in late May 2016 at age 15, has been found safe and returned home, the Spalding County Sheriff’s Office announced. Now 17, Aubrey contacted his family after being tracked during an investigation that revealed he had created a Facebook account under an assumed name and had at least five separate contacts with law enforcement from Alabama to Arizona. Authorities say he traveled extensively across the West Coast and Midwest and became part of a nomadic, cash-based group whose members bartered goods and lived a Woodstock-era lifestyle. 

Law enforcement (including the SCSO, FBI and Texas Rangers) and Aubrey’s parents briefed each other in April 2018, and his family initially agreed not to directly contact him to avoid scaring him away. A relative later messaged Aubrey, who agreed to call his mother and set conditions for returning. He came home Monday; Sheriff Darrell Dix and Lt. Mike Morris later met with him, and Aubrey said he left voluntarily and was not harmed, abducted, or exploited. In a video shared by the sheriff’s office he thanks supporters, says he’s “alright” and urges others to stay positive. Authorities and family are relieved he is safe and unharmed.

At the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, spectators discovered that some of the confetti scattering through the crowd wasn’t ordinary paper but strips of poorly shredded Nassau County Police Department documents containing highly sensitive personal and law‑enforcement information. Paradegoer Ethan Finkelstein and friends found confetti printed with social security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, license-plate numbers, incident reports (including a pipe-bomb report), names of Nassau County detectives — some identified as undercover — and even details from Mitt Romney’s motorcade at a recent Hofstra debate. Macy’s said it uses commercially manufactured confetti, not shredded paper; Nassau County police confirmed concern, announced an internal investigation, and said they would review how sensitive documents are disposed of.

The piece then explains how shredded documents can be reconstructed: modern techniques scan shreds, assign IDs, analyze features (size, color, font, indentations) and use matching algorithms to propose joins for human confirmation. Ease of reconstruction depends on shred type—strip shredders produce long strips that are relatively easy to reassemble, cross-cut shredders produce smaller, harder-to-reconstruct pieces, and industrial pulverizers make reconstruction essentially impossible. Cutting direction matters (vertical cuts are more secure than horizontal). Historically, shredded documents have been reassembled by hand (e.g., CIA files after the 1979 Tehran embassy takeover) and can sometimes be reconstructed quickly with modern tools. The incident at the parade prompted concern because it exposed why proper shredding and disposal procedures are critical for protecting confidential information.

Three days after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake devastated Port-au-Prince, Haiti, relief operations were racing to respond but remained woefully inadequate for the scale of need. Large numbers of dead and wounded lay in the streets and piled at hospitals and cemeteries; UN and regional health agencies gave widely varying death estimates (initially 45,000–50,000, with some estimates up to 100,000). The UN said it had buried thousands in mass graves and fed about 8,000 people, while two to three million people were reported to be in dire need of food, water, medical care and shelter.

Airport congestion and damaged infrastructure hampered deliveries. After chaotic crowds and turnaways at Toussaint Louverture International Airport, Haitian authorities ceded control of air operations to U.S. and FAA teams to organize incoming flights; fuel shortages and limited runway capacity further constrained landings. The U.S. moved to a stronger operational role: aircraft carrier Carl Vinson with helicopters, water-purification gear, surgical facilities and U.S. troops arrived or were en route, and thousands of U.S. personnel were expected to bolster security, logistics and medical evacuation. The Obama administration also announced temporary work and deportation protections for Haitians in the U.S., and high-level U.S. envoys planned visits and fundraising efforts.

Looting and rising tensions were widespread as people ran out of food and water; reports of looting at some UN food stores and increasing thefts and confrontations prompted calls for greater security. Aid workers warned that time was running out for survivors trapped under rubble and that heavy machinery, vehicles and medical supplies remained desperately needed. The UN launched a flash appeal for roughly $550 million, and international relief groups and governments mobilized resources, but delays, security concerns and the collapse of local coordination fueled growing fear of unrest amid the humanitarian crisis.

CBS revealed the cast for Celebrity Big Brother in a commercial before the 2018 Grammys, naming Omarosa Manigault, Brandi Glanville, Metta World Peace (Ron Artest), Marisa Jaret Winokur, Keisha Knight Pulliam, Chuck Liddell, Shannon Elizabeth, Ross Matthews, Mark McGrath, Adriana Gutierrez and James Maslow. Social media reacted immediately, with fans and celebs like Andy Cohen and Lance Bass weighing in. Responses were mixed but dominated by commentary about Omarosa—many criticized her move from a White House role to reality TV, while others welcomed the potential drama she and Brandi could bring. Some viewers said Omarosa’s presence would deter them from watching, while others predicted she’d create must-see conflict. Overall reactions ranged from excitement about likely drama to dismay at the casting choices.

Russian special forces stormed the Liberian-flagged oil tanker MV Moscow University after Somali pirates hijacked it Wednesday in the Gulf of Aden about 500 miles east of Somalia. The vessel, carrying roughly 86,000 tons of crude oil (valued at about $50–52 million), had been disabled and the 23-member crew had locked themselves in a fortified safe room. The Russian anti-submarine destroyer Marshal Shaposhnikov rushed to the scene; special-forces personnel boarded a helicopter, rappelled onto the tanker in a dawn raid and freed the crew. Shots were exchanged but no crew members were injured. Reports conflict on pirate casualties: Russian and other outlets cited one pirate killed and several captured (one report said 10 captured), while Russian officials said pirates were being held aboard and casualty details were being verified. The ship’s owner said the rescue was launched knowing the crew was secure and not in immediate danger; the tanker is likely to continue toward China.

The operation followed a broader recent trend of more aggressive international naval action against Somali piracy—Danish, U.S. and EU forces have undertaken similar interventions, and multinational patrols have increased disruptions of pirate operations and destruction of pirate skiffs. Despite these efforts, piracy remains active, with hundreds of hostages still held and legal and prosecution challenges persisting internationally.

Summary:

Beitar Jerusalem, the city’s largest soccer club, announced it would permanently rename itself “Beitar Trump Jerusalem” to honor President Donald Trump’s December recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and the U.S. Embassy move. The club praised Trump’s “courage” in a Facebook post; the embassy opening in Jerusalem’s Arnona neighborhood was attended by senior U.S. officials including Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump.

The embassy move coincided with large, deadly protests along the Gaza border. Thousands of Palestinians took part in the “Great March of Return” demonstrations and clashes with Israeli forces on the day of the embassy opening. Israeli fire killed dozens (reports cite between 16 and 58 killed in different accounts) and wounded thousands; hospitals in Gaza were overwhelmed. Palestinian protesters burned tires and attempted to approach or breach the fence; some combatants used knives, firearms or explosives. Hamas backed the protests, calling for continued demonstrations, while the Israeli military said it acted to prevent breaches and protect civilians. International bodies and some countries condemned the killings; the U.S. blamed Hamas. The violence marked the bloodiest day of demonstrations since 2014.

In related fallout, Palestinian leaders condemned the U.S. decision—Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas severed ties with the Trump administration—and many countries kept embassies in Tel Aviv. The embassy opening also drew criticism for having a controversial preacher give an invocation; Senator Mitt Romney criticized pastor Robert Jeffress for past anti‑Jewish, anti‑Mormon and anti‑Islam remarks, while Jeffress defended his evangelical beliefs.

Last week federal marshals raided Gibson Guitar’s facilities in Tennessee, echoing a similar 2009 seizure, and confiscated wood as part of a Justice Department probe into possible trafficking in illegally sourced timber. The raids stem from enforcement of the Lacey Act, a law amended in 2008 to cover plants and require U.S. end users to verify the legality of their wood supply chains. A June court filing alleges Gibson’s Madagascar ebony was contraband and cites emails suggesting the company maintained supply lines tied to illegal harvests.

Gibson denies wrongdoing, says it has provided documentation showing compliance with U.S. and Malagasy law, and claims the most recent seized wood came from India; the company also says it stopped importing wood from Madagascar in 2009. Environmental investigators, including the Environmental Investigation Agency, contend Gibson knew the risks of sourcing from Madagascar and continued purchases despite export bans following political turmoil there.

The raids have unsettled the guitar industry. Some makers, like C.F. Martin’s CEO, back the Lacey Act and have stopped buying questionable wood, while dealers and luthiers fear the law’s retroactive reach and the burden of proving the provenance of wood in older instruments. Concerns include impacts on vintage-instrument trade and uncertainty about what constitutes proper compliance. Enforcement advocates say the purpose of the law is to curb illegal logging and compel responsible sourcing; resolution and clearer standards likely await formal charges and a court process.

Jonah Hill delivered another strong turn as SNL host in his third appearance, showing growing ease and comic timing—though he still isn’t in the same “all‑time host” conversation as names like Justin Timberlake. The episode was notable for a surprise Leonardo DiCaprio cameo during Hill’s monologue, a well‑received parody trailer of Spike Jonze’s Her (with Michael Cera), and a recurring “Lamborghini” sketch that finally clicked thanks to Vanessa Bayer and Cecily Strong.

Strengths
- Hill’s monologue (with DiCaprio) and several sketches showed his comic strengths.
- The “Lamborghini” sketch was a standout, earning praise for tightened chemistry between Bayer and Strong.
- Weekend Update (Seth Meyers and Strong) continued to be strong; Meyers’ impending departure raises questions about how Colin Jost will fill the role.
- Performances by Bobby Moynihan, Jay Pharoah, Kenan Thompson and Beck Bennett got positive notices in various sketches.

Weaknesses
- The cast feels overcrowded at 17 members, making it hard for individual performers to stand out or build rapport with viewers.
- Several sketches underperformed or felt stale: a weak “Benihana” installment, an odd “Boss Dinner,” and a poorly received “Ranch” sketch that leaned on lazy physical humor.
- Some recurring bits (Inside SoCal shorts, certain character repeats) showed diminishing returns.

Overall impression and score
- The episode averaged a middling score (about 5.73), with highlights buoyed by Hill and strong supporting turns, but hampered by too-large cast dynamics and a handful of weak sketches.

Lebanon has banned Lady Gaga’s album Born This Way, impounding shipments after officials said its lyrics were offensive to Christianity and in “bad taste.” The country had already barred her single “Judas” from radio. Malaysia also banned the title track, saying it “promotes homosexuality.” Despite the bans, Born This Way debuted strongly in the U.S., going platinum in its first week with 1.1 million sales, and many listeners abroad can still access it digitally. The controversy echoes earlier U.S. criticism from some religious groups over Gaga’s imagery (e.g., the “Judas” video), which ultimately drew less sustained condemnation. Gaga has publicly criticized the influence of institutionalized religion on government and social issues. Lebanon has previously banned religiously sensitive media, such as The Da Vinci Code in 2004.

News Corp. announced it will close its 168-year-old U.K. Sunday tabloid News of the World, with the upcoming Sunday edition to be its last, in response to a widening phone‑hacking scandal. The paper is accused of illegally intercepting voicemails—including those of celebrities, everyday people, and relatives of victims such as a murdered 13‑year‑old—allegations the company called "inhuman" and incompatible with its values. James Murdoch said the paper had "failed when it came to itself" and its reputation was irreparably sullied.

The closure is a crisis-management move that puts James Murdoch front and center and increases scrutiny on senior executives, notably News International chief executive Rebekah Brooks, who was editor of News of the World until 2003 and has faced calls to resign. Former editor Andy Coulson has been asked to present himself for arrest on suspicion of phone‑hacking‑related offenses.

Although News of the World accounts for a relatively small share of News Corp.'s value, the scandal has triggered multiple criminal investigations, civil suits and government inquiries that could continue for years and may imperil News Corp.'s pending bid to buy the remainder of British Sky Broadcasting. About 200 staffers face possible layoffs or transfers; the company may replace the title with a Sunday edition of The Sun or launch a new paper. Critics and a journalists’ union called the shutdown insufficient without further accountability and firings.

Nine-year-old James Savage of Los Banos completed a more-than-two-mile round-trip swim from San Francisco’s Aquatic Park to Alcatraz Island and back on Tuesday, becoming the youngest person on record to make the crossing. The fourth-grader, who is 4'6" and 57 pounds, started at 7:00 a.m. and finished in a little over two hours. About 30 minutes into the swim he struggled with waves and a strong current and considered quitting, but a fleet of paddlers, his coach Josh Weinberger and encouragement (and a cash incentive from his father) helped him press on. James said the support kept him going; his coach credited his training and technique. After completing the challenge, James said his next goal is to swim the length of the Golden Gate Bridge (8,981 feet).

Former U.S. Senator John Edwards is on trial for allegedly violating campaign finance laws by using nearly $1 million from two wealthy supporters to conceal an extramarital affair with campaign videographer Rielle Hunter and to support the child born from that relationship. Andrew Young, a longtime Edwards aide and the prosecution’s chief witness, testified in detail about his role in the concealment scheme.

Key points from Young’s testimony:
- Hunter told Edwards she was pregnant in mid-2007. Edwards initially downplayed paternity, calling her a “crazy slut” and saying there was a one-in-three chance the child was his.
- Edwards directed Young to provide money and support for Hunter, suggested enlisting heiress Rachel “Bunny” Mellon as a donor, and later urged Young to publicly claim paternity to deflect media attention during the 2008 campaign.
- Mellon wrote checks totaling roughly $750,000 (and volunteered up to $1.2 million over time) made out to interior designer Bryan Huffman; Young’s wife deposited funds into a personal account. Separately, Texas lawyer Fred Baron provided hundreds of thousands in payments and cash, including paying bills and hosting Hunter at his Aspen home.
- To conceal communications, Edwards used an extra phone—nicknamed the “bat phone”—and often called via staffers’ phones. Phone records and voicemails were introduced to show frequent contact among Edwards, Young and Hunter.
- After Elizabeth Edwards discovered the affair, Hunter was removed from the campaign and lived briefly with the Young family; Young and his family later accompanied Hunter on a cross-country period in hotels and private homes while payments continued.
- Young said he agreed to claim paternity partly out of personal opportunism—hoping to gain future benefits from Edwards’ political success—and because he trusted Edwards’ assurances that the payments were legal.

Defense position presented in court:
- Edwards denies knowing about Mellon’s checks and maintains that the payments were not campaign contributions meant to influence the election but private gifts to hide a personal matter.
- The defense has argued Young misappropriated much of the money for personal projects (including his home) and that he was not a mastermind but acted independently.

Prosecutors have charged Edwards with six counts related to concealing and reporting these payments; if convicted on all counts he faces up to 30 years in prison and substantial fines. Young’s testimony continued and is pivotal to the government’s case; the defense is set to cross-examine him.

Justin Bieber sparked headlines when, during a Dec. 17 interview on Los Angeles’ Power 106 with Big Boy, he joked that he was “retiring” and “probably gonna quit music,” saying he’d “take some time.” The 19‑year‑old framed the comment as part of wanting to grow and mature as an artist. His camp and outlets like E! and Gossip Cop said the retirement claims were not serious. Bieber was promoting his new release Journals — a compilation of ten previously released Music Mondays tracks plus five unreleased songs, videos and the Believe trailer — available on iTunes Dec. 16–Jan. 2, 2014, and his Believe concert documentary opened in theaters on Christmas.

A viral Facebook video (3.8 million views) shows a man running up to a kangaroo that has a dog in a headlock; the kangaroo releases the dog after a struggle and the man delivers a single punch to the animal. The footage came from a “final” wild pig-hunting trip for a young man named Kailem, who recently died of cancer. Trip organiser Mathew Amor says friends filmed over an hour to make a DVD for Kailem’s family. The man who struck the kangaroo is nicknamed “Goo” and has kept a low profile because he has a “good government job”; the Daily Mail reports he may be a zookeeper at Taronga Western Plains Zoo. The dog was unharmed thanks to a protective breastplate used for boar hunting. Amor says the punch only stunned the kangaroo and wasn’t hard — the group found the moment more amusing than malicious. The clip has prompted debate about authenticity and whether striking an animal in self‑defense was appropriate.

Lawmakers and media are speculating that JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon could replace Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner as Geithner faces mounting criticism over the economy and his handling of the financial crisis. The New York Post and other outlets report unnamed sources saying Dimon has raised his Washington profile, written an op-ed in the Washington Post, met with officials, and would “love to serve his country,” though he reportedly plans to stay at JPMorgan for years and has downplayed interest.

But Dimon would be a controversial choice. He departs from key Obama administration positions: he opposes a new consumer-protection agency for credit cards and mortgages—arguing it will raise costs—and he argues against capping the size of “too-big-to-fail” banks, advocating instead for regulatory structures that allow large firms to fail without taxpayer losses. Those views invite criticism that he would be representing Wall Street’s interests if appointed. Observers note the political risks of naming a sitting Wall Street CEO to Treasury given public anti–Wall Street sentiment and likely opposition in Congress, making his confirmation uncertain despite his reputation for steering JPMorgan through the crisis.

U.S. speedskating officials announced they will stop using the new Mach 39 Under Armour racing suits and revert to the previously approved Under Armour World Cup suits for the remainder of the Sochi Games. The decision followed a poor start to the Olympics—no U.S. speedskater had medaled after six long-track events—and growing concern among athletes that the unfamiliar, Mach 39 suit (developed with Lockheed Martin and unveiled only in January) might be hurting performance. Skaters reported issues such as vents letting air in and some sought onsite modifications; a few athletes and staff cited the suit as the easiest factor to change, while others defended the design and urged examining training, blades, tactics and acclimation as well. U.S. Speedskating sought ISU/IOC approval because rules require uniformity across a team; the switch was permitted because the World Cup suits had prior approval and were available to all team members. Team leaders said restoring athlete confidence was the priority. Under Armour said it stood by its suits and would help with any required logo changes; the swap risks reputational damage if medals follow in the old suits, but company and federation emphasized the goal is to enable skaters to perform at their best.

Reality Leigh Winner, 25, a former U.S. Air Force linguist and contractor, was arrested and charged by the Justice Department for allegedly leaking a classified National Security Agency memo about Russian military intelligence hacking to The Intercept. She worked for Pluribus International at a government facility in Georgia (likely Fort Gordon) and held Top Secret clearance; authorities say she printed and mailed the May 5 document and confessed to an FBI agent on June 3. She faces one count of gathering, transmitting or losing defense information and remains jailed pending a detention hearing.

Her case drew attention not because of her youth—many frontline NSA and military intelligence roles are filled by young enlisted personnel and contractors—but because it exemplifies a newer pattern: lower-level insiders who, motivated by political or moral concerns, leak classified material to the press (parallels have been drawn to Chelsea Manning and Edward Snowden). Some intelligence officials see this as an emerging insider-threat dynamic tied in part to political polarization.

Winner had an active social-media presence under handles like @Reezlie and Sara Winners, where she posted political criticisms of President Trump, followed accounts associated with dissenting or “alt” government voices, and engaged with accounts like WikiLeaks and Anonymous. Her family and attorney describe her as a passionate, previously nonpublic person—a veteran and yoga instructor—who may have acted from conviction rather than for personal gain. Her attorney disputes the government’s characterization and has not seen evidence of guilt; he also questioned possible political motives for the prosecution. The government quickly linked the leaked document to The Intercept after publication and moved rapidly to press charges.

Josh Sanchez-Maldonado, a 24-year-old U.S. financial trader based in San Francisco, has been missing in London since Oct. 22. He was last seen leaving the St Giles hotel in Feltham just after noon that day after flying into the U.K. from Japan for a job interview; police and family have been unable to confirm details of the appointment. He was due to return to San Francisco via Dublin the next day but did not board the flight. 

London’s Metropolitan Police say he had no access to money while in the city and this was his first solo trip outside the U.S. His family, who have traveled to the U.K., described him as goal-oriented, organized, communicative and loving, and expressed growing concern for his welfare. He was last in contact with his father on Oct. 21. CCTV from the hotel has been released; police are focusing inquiries in Feltham and London’s financial districts including the City and Canary Wharf.

Sanchez-Maldonado is described as white, about 5ft 8in, slim, with short dark hair; he was last seen in a dark flat cap, brown/grey T-shirt, white shorts and black trainers. Anyone with information is asked to contact Hounslow CID on 020 8247 6653/6246 or call 101. The U.S. Embassy in London is aware and assisting.

Anne Hathaway and husband Adam Shulman have welcomed their first child: a baby boy named Jonathan Rosebanks Shulman, born March 24. The couple, who married in September 2012 after getting engaged in 2011, confirmed the news through her rep; E! News first reported the name. Hathaway, 33 at the time, had publicly acknowledged her pregnancy late 2015 and shared photos of her bump on Instagram in January and ahead of the 2016 Oscars. Sources say the newborn is healthy and surrounded by family and friends in Los Angeles; Hathaway and Shulman are reportedly “ecstatic.” The birth followed a relaxed baby shower in March attended by close friends. Fans noted and praised the choice of a traditional name.

Kenai leaders have proposed adding cats to the city’s animals that must be “restrained” — defined in city code as physical confinement by leash, chain, fence or building — after what officials say are growing complaints about roaming cats and a larger cat population at the Kenai Animal Shelter. The ordinance, introduced by Mayor Pat Porter and council member Tim Navarre, would allow fines up to $500 per violation. Council members unanimously postponed a decision; a hearing and vote are scheduled for Oct. 5.
