City attorney and shelter staff say they have seen more complaints about cats defecating on private property, invading gardens and otherwise disturbing residents, and the shelter has had high demand for its six loaner live traps. Shelter intake data show monthly cat intake has varied widely; in August 2016 the shelter took in 48 cats (34 owner surrenders, 13 strays), could reasonably house about 16 cats at a time, and most cats leave for rescue centers or adoption after several days to a month. Shelter staff say they lack detailed confinement-complaint records because no cat-confinement code exists now.

Opponents, including residents and former council member Ryan Marquis, warned the law assumes compliance, may not affect feral cats, and could increase costs and workload for animal control and the shelter (more intake, housing, euthanasia, vaccinations and staff time). City Manager Rick Koch said the shelter’s FY2017 budget (about $421,265) is sufficient for current operations and recommended delaying the vote so staff can compile complaint data, trap request numbers, handling procedures and examples of other Alaska cities’ rules for council review.

Supporters of former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick rallied outside the NFL’s New York headquarters demanding he be signed before the regular season. More than 1,000 people, many wearing his jerseys, attended the event of speeches, poems and prayers. Kaepernick remains unsigned after opting out of his contract in March; supporters say the league is blackballing him for kneeling during the national anthem to protest police brutality, while critics point to his recent on-field performance and say he shouldn’t have protested.

Speakers linked Kaepernick’s treatment to broader racial and player-safety concerns. Rev. Jamal Bryant and NAACP leaders called for action and requested a meeting with Commissioner Roger Goodell; NAACP interim president Derrick Johnson said it’s “no sheer coincidence” Kaepernick is unsigned and urged protection of free speech. Women’s March organizer Tamika Mallory and others urged fans to boycott the league if it won’t stand up for young black men.

Some NFL players have joined anthem protests this preseason, including white teammates who knelt or offered support. Commissioner Goodell has denied the league is blackballing Kaepernick. The demonstrations followed earlier, smaller rallies and reflect ongoing national debate over protest, race and free speech in sports.

Hawaii ranks highest in residents’ well-being in the 2015 Gallup-Healthways Well-Being Index, followed by Alaska, Montana, Colorado and Wyoming. The index—based on more than 175,000 adult telephone interviews in 2015—measures five dimensions of well-being: purpose, social, financial, community and physical. National well-being was essentially unchanged from 2014 to 2015, but several positive trends emerged: financial well-being rose, life evaluations hit an all-time high, uninsured and smoking rates fell, reported exercise increased, and food and health-care insecurity dropped to a seven-year low. Offsetting those gains, obesity reached a new high and more part-time workers sought full-time jobs.

Regionally, higher well-being clustered in the northern plains, Mountain West and parts of the West and Northeast, while the lowest scores were concentrated in the South and parts of the industrial Midwest. State highlights: Delaware led in sense of purpose; South Carolina in social fulfillment; Alaska in financial security; Montana in community satisfaction; and Hawaii in physical well-being. West Virginia and Kentucky ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, a persistent pattern. Alabama showed the biggest improvement (up 18 places), while Vermont fell the most (down 16).

This article—adapted from a chapter of Top Secret America by Dana Priest and William M. Arkin—profiles the dramatic rise and operations of the U.S. Joint Special Operations Command (JSOC), a once-obscure special-operations organization that has become a central, highly secretive instrument of American counterterrorism since 9/11.

Key points

- Growth and scope: JSOC expanded from roughly 1,800 personnel before 9/11 to as many as 25,000 (and in some functions larger) and now runs its own intelligence elements, drones and reconnaissance assets, cyber teams, and dedicated communications bandwidth. Its core units include Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, the 24th Special Tactics Squadron, the 160th Aviation Regiment and the 75th Rangers.

- Mission and reach: JSOC conducts intelligence-gathering, capture and lethal raids across Iraq and Afghanistan and in countries with which the United States is not formally at war (Yemen, Pakistan, Somalia, the Philippines, Nigeria, Syria, etc.). Presidents and defense secretaries have given JSOC authority to nominate individuals for “kill lists” and to carry out lethal operations—an authority that has raised legal and ethical concerns about targeted killings and possible assassination.

- Secrecy and autonomy: JSOC operates with extreme secrecy—no public web presence, minimal identification in the field, multiple cover names—and is run through a military-only chain of command that takes tasks directly from senior civilian leaders. Although not legally authorized to conduct “covert action” the way the CIA can, JSOC’s activities often resemble it in practice. Under both Bush and Obama, many JSOC missions were treated as traditional military activities and often were not routinely briefed to Congress, though Obama increased limited congressional briefings for sensitive operations.

- Transformation under McChrystal: Brig. Gen. (later Gen.) Stanley McChrystal, given command in 2003, decentralized decision bottlenecks, collocated JSOC’s command center in Iraq, integrated national-agency personnel (CIA, NSA, FBI), deployed liaison officers to agencies and built a common, PC-based intelligence-sharing portal. He emphasized high operational tempo, technology integration and rapid information exploitation.

- Technology and intelligence fusion: JSOC capitalized on NSA signal collection, new bandwidth and commercial satellite capacity post–dot-com bust, tools like cellphone-locating “electronic divining rods,” and document/media exploitation teams to rapidly turn captured drives, phones and data into actionable targeting intelligence. This fusion enabled sustained, high-tempo operations and contributed to major successes (e.g., the 2006 operation that led to the killing of Abu Musab al-Zarqawi).

- Lethality, effectiveness and costs: JSOC executed hundreds of raids monthly at the height of Iraq operations, with high enemy body counts and frequent strikes in Afghanistan. Officials cite high casualty rates among JSOC forces themselves (many Purple Hearts). JSOC’s strike accuracy was imperfect—senior commanders estimated roughly a 50% “success” rate in targeting the right individuals/locations—which produced civilian casualties and local grievances that sometimes undermined broader strategic aims. Notable mistakes, such as the 2002 Kakarak (wedding party) incident, produced severe backlash.

- Detention and interrogation controversies: JSOC detained and interrogated far more detainees than the CIA’s secret prisons, using segregated facilities in Iraq and Afghanistan and holding some detainees for up to 90 days before transfer. Early in the war, some JSOC personnel were implicated in abusive interrogation and detention practices (beatings, extreme confinement, sleep disruption, deprivation), prompting investigations and discipline of dozens of soldiers. McChrystal later moved to professionalize interrogation and integrate forensic/document exploitation and legal teams to produce evidence for Iraqi courts.

- Expanding roles and institutionalization: JSOC’s remit broadened into nonkinetic roles—financial tracking, information operations (psychological operations remade as military information operations), and support to U.S. embassies. Under Obama it continued to be heavily used (including secret raids in Yemen). JSOC has moved some functions closer to Washington, opening a large National Capital Region task force to influence U.S. bureaucracy, provide targeting support to domestic agencies, and pursue priorities such as assistance related to Mexico.

Overall assessment
JSOC’s evolution produced a highly effective, technology-driven, tightly networked special-operations apparatus that has killed and detained large numbers of terrorist operatives and disrupted networks. Its successes in targeting and intelligence integration altered modern counterterrorism practice. But its secrecy, extrajudicial authority to nominate lethal targets, imperfect targeting record, civilian harm, detention abuses, and limited public or congressional transparency have generated legal, ethical and strategic concerns about accountability and the long-term political consequences of its tactics.

Two Wisconsin middle-school girls charged with the May stabbing of classmate Payton Leutner — an attack they later said was intended to gain favor with the fictional Internet character “Slender Man” — were ruled competent Thursday to stand trial on attempted first-degree intentional homicide charges.

Waukesha County Circuit Judge Michael Bohren found 13-year-old Anissa E. Weier competent after a three-hour hearing in which mental-health experts disagreed. Two defense psychologists testified that Weier, while intelligent and cooperative, is emotionally immature and has trouble making reasoned strategic decisions (for example, about plea bargains), arguing her developmental immaturity impairs her competence. A court-appointed psychiatrist, however, concluded she can rationally participate in proceedings; the judge sided with that view.

Co-defendant Morgan Geyser, 12 at the time of the attack and previously found incompetent in August, was also ruled competent after her defense declined to challenge a state psychiatrist’s recent report that treatment at Winnebago Mental Health Institute had restored her ability to understand charges and assist in her defense. Geyser’s attorney disclosed she has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and asked that she remain at Winnebago rather than be returned to the juvenile detention center; the judge granted that request for now.

Preliminary hearings to determine probable cause are set for February, after which the defense will pursue efforts to have the case moved (reverse-waived) to juvenile court. If tried as adults, the girls face up to 60 years in prison; in juvenile court they could be confined to a secure facility until age 25. Leutner survived the attack and has returned to school. The Associated Press is not naming the defendants because their attorneys may seek juvenile-court proceedings, which are closed.

Shaniece Luke, whose 33-year-old brother Rasheen Rose died in 2012 while in state care at the Bernard Fineson Developmental Center in Queens, has been sent an $11.67 million claim by the state Office for People With Developmental Disabilities (OPWDD). The notarized demand seeks reimbursement of Medicaid payments made on Rose’s behalf from Aug. 6, 2002, through the day he died, and the agency says it is following federal Medicaid rules in seeking recovery. Luke and her lawyers allege the bill is retaliatory because she filed a federal wrongful-death lawsuit accusing staff of killing Rose by restraining him in a prone position—allegedly for up to 30 minutes with multiple workers present, one of whom sat on him. The city medical examiner ruled Rose’s death a homicide, though prosecutors have not filed criminal charges and the DA’s office has left the case open. OPWDD declined further comment citing pending litigation. Attorneys representing Luke and disability advocates call the reimbursement demand improper and punitive; lawyers for other families say similar notices have recently been issued to plaintiffs who sued over deaths in state care. OPWDD and the state are defending the staff named in the suit; the dispute comes amid broader scrutiny of New York’s developmental centers and plans to close several facilities.

Salma Hayek announced on Instagram that her 9-year-old dog Mozart was found fatally shot last week on her Washington ranch. Hayek, who said she personally helped deliver him, described Mozart as loving, loyal and never aggressive, and called for local authorities to seek justice, saying he "didn't deserve a slow and painful death." The post, written in English and Spanish, included a photo of her with the dog. The piece also notes Hayek’s well-known affection for animals — she frequently posts pictures with them and recently shared a photo from the Drunk Parents set — and references her past public outrage over the killing of Cecil the Lion. The article opens with a general note about archiving web pages to prevent broken links.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s first day of confirmation hearings for President Trump’s Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh was a bitter, partisan spectacle marked by heated exchanges, dozens of arrests and sharp Democratic objections over withheld records.

Democrats, including several potential 2020 presidential contenders, repeatedly moved to delay the proceedings after the White House released roughly 42,000 committee‑confidential pages late Monday while continuing to withhold about 100,000 more as privileged. They argued the truncated vetting—especially gaps from Kavanaugh’s years in the George W. Bush White House—made meaningful review impossible. Protesters in the hearing room repeatedly interrupted the session and more than 70 people were arrested, intensifying the confrontation.

Republicans defended the process and Kavanaugh’s qualifications, arguing Democrats were politicizing the hearing and re‑litigating the 2016 election. GOP leaders remained confident they can confirm Kavanaugh with a simple‑majority vote; the party’s Senate margin was bolstered that day by Arizona’s appointment of Jon Kyl to fill John McCain’s seat.

Kavanaugh, a 53‑year‑old D.C. Circuit judge, sat through lengthy statements and delivered a roughly 20‑minute opening statement near the end of the day. He emphasized judicial independence, described himself as a “neutral and impartial arbiter” and said the Supreme Court “must never, never be viewed as a partisan institution,” promising to be “a team player on the Team of Nine.” He sought to reassure senators on issues such as separation of powers, and highlighted his record, family and support for women in law and sports.

Democrats signaled they will press him on abortion (including whether Roe v. Wade is correct, not just settled), executive power, his Bush White House role (including past denials of involvement in interrogation policy), and other hot‑button issues in upcoming rounds of questioning. Committee leaders plan more days of hearings and a likely party‑line committee vote to advance the nomination to the full Senate, setting up a contentious confirmation fight ahead of the midterms.

The document describes two separate political vignettes.

1) Nick Robinson incident: BBC political editor Nick Robinson was filmed in Westminster forcibly taking and ripping up a protester’s placard reading “Cut the war not the poor” during a live report. The footage, which shows him stamping on the sign while the protester accuses him of being shameful, was posted online. Initially Robinson defended his actions, saying he was “not even remotely ashamed,” but later posted on his blog that he had lost his temper, regretted the outburst, and softened his stance.

2) Ed Balls reflection: In his first interview since a high-profile political gaffe two weeks earlier (the moment widely seen as emblematic of Labour’s election defeat), former cabinet minister Ed Balls spoke about his “sense of loss” over the party’s failure and his personal setback. He reflected on his two decades of public service, urging focus on achievements rather than missed opportunities, and listed key policy contributions he helped secure—keeping Britain out of the euro, supporting Bank of England independence, raising the education leaving age to 18, creating Sure Start, instituting the national minimum wage, and reforms to the health service.

U.S. stocks fell sharply Tuesday after weaker-than-expected corporate results and economic data raised concerns that a strong U.S. dollar and softer global demand will weigh on earnings growth.

- Major indices: Dow fell about 234 points (1.3%) to 17,445, the S&P 500 dropped 0.9% to 2,038, and the Nasdaq lost 1.3% to 4,711. The Russell 2000 was down 0.2% but has gained recently as investors shift toward domestically focused small caps.
- Drivers: Disappointing quarterly reports and guidance from blue-chip companies were pivotal. Microsoft plunged 8.5% after forecasting fiscal-year results below estimates, explicitly blaming the strong dollar. Caterpillar fell 7.5% after missing Q4 estimates and issuing a weak 2015 outlook tied to plunging commodity prices and currency headwinds. Procter & Gamble warned currency swings could cut 2015 sales 5% and profit 12%, and other multinationals have reduced profit forecasts.
- Broader context: FactSet estimates expected only 1.1% earnings growth for Q4; with many reports in, S&P 500 earnings are tracking roughly flat year-over-year. The dollar’s rally and weak overseas activity — plus tumbling oil and commodity prices — are tightening expectations.
- Economic and market backdrop: Durable goods orders unexpectedly fell 3.4% in December, adding to growth worries. European markets fell amid renewed Greece-related uncertainty. Safe-haven assets rose: gold and Treasuries gained, while oil ticked up modestly.
- Market structure: Despite a New York snowstorm, trading was active (NYSE invoked Rule 48). Some managers are reallocating toward small-cap, U.S.-focused firms that are less exposed to currency headwinds.

Investors will watch the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting this week for signals on rate timing, which could further influence the dollar and multinational profits.

Steve Simoff, 61, of Davis City (near the Missouri–Iowa border) endures a 35‑mile commute to his overnight janitorial job at Lakeside Casino in Osceola by walking much of the way and accepting rides from locals when available. He leaves his basement apartment around 3:30 p.m. to make an 11 p.m. shift, often walking along highway shoulders and Interstate 35 for hours. Though he owns an older minivan, he can rarely afford gas; instead he relies on a network of sympathetic “road friends” — neighbors, co‑workers and even the county sheriff and deputies — who routinely give him part or all of the trip. Simoff averages nearly four hours walking on commute days and usually gets a ride three of five workdays; sometimes he walks in harsh weather and lives with osteoarthritis in one knee.

He keeps at it to support his wife Renee, who has serious health problems and receives SSI, and their adopted grandson. Simoff has a long record of steady employment in security and janitorial work and prides himself on reliability; he says he won’t stop walking as long as his health allows because missing work would mean unpaid bills. His story, likened to the widely publicized Detroit walker James Robertson, highlights how low‑wage workers go to extreme lengths to maintain housing and employment and underscores broader issues of transportation insecurity in rural America.

Michael Vaudreuil, a 54-year-old longtime night custodian at Worcester Polytechnic Institute who earned a mechanical engineering degree there in May, has accepted an engineering position with Pratt & Whitney in Connecticut. Vaudreuil’s comeback story—after losing his business, home and savings during the 2008 downturn and returning to school while working second shift and doing odd jobs—went viral following WPI’s commencement and widespread media coverage. That attention led multiple Pratt & Whitney employees to contact him, and the company offered him a role on the Production Integrated Product Team in Hot Section Engineering, which aligns with his earlier associate degree in aeronautical technology. Vaudreuil will move to Connecticut with his wife and begin July 11; he hopes his story will challenge stereotypes about older job candidates and highlight the value of life experience and perseverance.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Wednesday renewed his campaign promoting widely discredited claims linking vaccines (specifically thimerosal, a mercury-containing preservative used in some flu vaccines) to autism, announcing a $100,000 “World Mercury Project Challenge” that he says will be awarded to anyone who can produce a study proving the safety of thimerosal-containing vaccines in children and pregnant women. Speaking at a National Press Club event that included actor Robert De Niro, Kennedy repeated accusations that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is corrupt and in league with pharmaceutical companies, and said he has been in contact several times with White House aides about creating a federal “vaccine safety” commission. Kennedy claimed President Trump pledged not to back down from setting up such a panel despite pushback from the drug industry; the administration has previously described discussions as tentative.

Medical experts and major health organizations sharply denounced Kennedy’s statements. The CDC and a coalition of some 350 medical groups, led by the American Academy of Pediatrics, maintain that vaccines are safe and that there is no link between vaccines and autism; scientists called Kennedy’s challenge misleading and a distraction from real public-health work. De Niro, who has a son with autism and has previously supported airing anti-vaccine material before withdrawing it, endorsed Kennedy’s remarks as focused on safety rather than politics. Critics worry that White House engagement with Kennedy could lend credibility to vaccine skepticism despite extensive scientific refutation of the autism link.

Aaron Schock, a young Republican congressman from Peoria and the first U.S. representative born in the 1980s, has made fitness and personal responsibility central to his public image and agenda. Elected at 27 and politically active since winning a school-board seat as a 19-year-old write-in, Schock blends a conservative, deficit-hawk policy outlook with a visible, lead-by-example campaign on health, obesity, and long-term planning for issues that will affect his generation.

Fitness and public health
- Schock promotes a high-profile fitness ethic: he went from a scrawny college kid (145 lbs) to a muscular 165 lbs through weight training and structured workouts. He stresses exercise for both physical health and stress relief amid Washington’s high-pressure, food-filled social scene.
- This month he launched the “Fit for Summer, Fit for Life” challenge (hosted via MensHealth.com/schock) to encourage Americans to lose weight and lower disease risk. He models practical, approachable routines — morning DVDs, P90X sessions, heavy weight days, or simple sets of pushups/situps plus running or swimming — aimed at people who feel intimidated by gyms or short on time.
- He supports nonpartisan efforts like Michelle Obama’s Let’s Move and frames obesity and rising health-care costs as generational problems that require personal initiative and policy attention.

Policy and generational focus
- Schock argues that young Americans will bear the consequences of today’s long-term policy choices, so he emphasizes strategic, long-range thinking in government on energy independence, clean water, education (particularly math and science), and fiscal responsibility.
- He favors tax incentives to spur investment in alternative energy and infrastructure and calls for smarter education spending and long-term water management strategies.

Public image and political role
- Schock combines media savvy and youth appeal — he’s been widely covered in pop culture outlets, appears comfortable with social media and broadcast attention, and has been labeled one of Congress’s most attractive and media-friendly freshmen.
- Despite the publicity, he is active and substantive in office: he sits on multiple committees, joined the Republican Study Committee, serves as a deputy whip, hosts policy briefings (e.g., on payroll tax ideas for small businesses), and has begun doing overseas travel and campaign work for other Republicans.
- His rhetorical strategy is to use his youth and visible lifestyle as a platform to engage young people in politics and policy, urging planning, discipline, and strategic thinking both personally and nationally.

Overall portrait
Schock presents himself as an optimistic, disciplined young leader who fuses personal example (fitness and lifestyle) with a policy agenda focused on long-term national competitiveness, fiscal restraint, and public-health improvement. His combination of style, media skill, and substantive involvement has quickly made him a high-profile freshman in the House.

Three Marines based in Hawaii — Sgt. Benjamin E. Johns, Lance Cpl. Jacob D. Jacoby and Lance Cpl. Carlos Orozco III — have been referred to a general court-martial on charges stemming from alleged hazing of 21‑year‑old Lance Cpl. Harry Lew, who died by suicide in Afghanistan on April 3. No trial date has been set.

An Article 32 hearing held last month in Hawaii presented testimony that Lew fell asleep on watch four times during a 10‑day deployment at Patrol Base Gowragi, a dangerous forward outpost, and that fellow Marines grew increasingly frustrated. Leaders initially tried non‑punitive steps such as removing him from patrols, but allegations say that on his final night Lew was punched and kicked, forced to do exercises in full gear, and had sand poured in his face. Jacoby and Orozco face assault charges in addition to hazing counts; Orozco also faces cruelty and maltreatment and dereliction allegations, and Johns is charged with dereliction and hazing.

Brig. Gen. Frederick Padilla referred the case for trial; Marine Corps spokesmen emphasized that hazing is not tolerated and that the accused are presumed innocent. Lew, from Santa Clara, Calif., was the nephew of Rep. Judy Chu, whose office and Washington attention have contributed to scrutiny of the case. Commanders later suggested Lew’s sleeping might have reflected depression or a medical condition. The possible punishments, if convicted, will be determined by the general court‑martial.

Comedians, entertainers, fashion icons, media figures and fans turned out on Sunday at Temple Emanu‑El on Manhattan’s Upper East Side to honor Joan Rivers, who died at 81 after complications following a throat procedure. The star-studded service reflected the showbiz funeral Rivers had long joked she wanted: Howard Stern delivered a eulogy, Hugh Jackman sang, bagpipers played “New York, New York,” and many colleagues and friends — including Kathy Griffin, Sarah Jessica Parker, Whoopi Goldberg, Barbara Walters, Donald Trump, Diane Sawyer, Kelly Osbourne, Bernadette Peters, Alan Cumming and fashion designers Carolina Herrera and Michael Kors — attended.  

Her daughter Melissa Rivers read a light‑hearted letter, thanked mourners and later greeted fans outside the home, even handing out cupcakes. The program echoed Joan’s irreverent humor and wishes from her book, with jokes during the service about her plastic surgery and life, and her famous lines printed in the booklet. Fans lined Fifth Avenue in designer attire to honor the former “Fashion Police” host.  

Authorities continue to investigate her death; the state health department is reviewing the circumstances and the medical examiner’s tests were inconclusive. In lieu of flowers, donations were suggested to charity organizations favored by Rivers.

Seth Rogen and co-writer Evan Goldberg reflected with self-deprecating humor on their past film projects, including a poorly received airplane-set movie and The Green Hornet. Rogen recalled being told to "talk loud because the engine will be roaring" for an early-flight scene, and criticized The Green Hornet as a "perfect storm of bad s--t happening." Goldberg noted they tried to make the film for both American and Chinese audiences, and Rogen quipped that they shouldn't make expensive films that prevent them from doing the kind of crude humor—"a million dick jokes"—that fits their strengths.

A 20-something New Jersey man, Kenneth “Kenny” Bachman of Sewell, recently woke up to discover he’d been driven more than 300 miles from Morgantown, West Virginia (near West Virginia University) to his home in Gloucester County by an Uber after a night of heavy drinking. He says he blacked out at a fraternity party and later fell asleep in the vehicle; he only realized he was being taken home when the driver told him they were about an hour from New Jersey.

The trip lasted about five hours and cost $1,635.93. Bachman says he unintentionally ordered an UberXL (much pricier than UberX), which he estimates would have been about $819 without surge pricing; surge doubled nearly every charge. The fare breakdown he reported included small base and booking fees, large distance and time charges, and multiple tolls (the driver allegedly didn’t have toll money). Bachman challenged the charge, claiming he never put his home address in and that the driver used his phone while he slept; Uber confirmed the ride occurred, said the driver took the requested destination, contacted Bachman, and reached a resolution in which Bachman agreed to pay the fare. Bachman gave the driver five stars, returned home safely, and plans to go back to West Virginia to retrieve his belongings. The story notes uncertainty about records for longest rides—one prior example cited was an 11-hour, 650+ mile Uber from the Dallas area to Nashville.

An 11-year-old boy, identified as Anthony Perez McClean, died after jumping onto a frozen pond in Queens’ Forest Park to rescue his 12-year-old friend who had fallen through thin ice. The boys were playing near the pond around 4 p.m. when the older child walked onto the ice and fell in. Anthony went out to help and managed to push his friend toward safety but then fell through himself. FDNY rescuers waded into chest-high, near-freezing water, breaking through ice by hand to reach Anthony; two firefighters sustained hypothermia/minor injuries during the rescue. Anthony was pulled out unconscious, given CPR, and taken to Jamaica Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Neighbors called him a caring, heroic child. FDNY Deputy Chief George Healy urged parents to warn children about the dangers of winter ice, noting that days near freezing are especially risky and that the ice in city ponds is unsafe.

Ozzy Osbourne condemned the Westboro Baptist Church after members used his 1980 song "Crazy Train" during a protest on the steps of the U.S. Supreme Court. The Kansas-based church—known for anti-gay, provocative demonstrations at military funerals—chanted a modified line, "You're going straight to hell on your crazy train," while protesting because the court is reviewing a $5 million judgment awarded to the family of Lance Cpl. Matthew Snyder for emotional distress caused by Westboro’s actions. Osbourne called the church's use of his song "sickening and disgusting," noting the original song is a plea for tolerance, not a vehicle for hate.

A powerful, wide-ranging winter storm has battered much of the U.S., bringing heavy snow, freezing rain, ice and extreme cold from the High Plains to New England and disrupting travel, power and daily life for millions.

Scope and impacts
- More than 120 million people are affected by the storm system, with conditions from heavy snow and ice in a band from the Midwest through New England to frigid temperatures (as much as 40°F below normal) across the Plains and High Plains.  
- Nearly 1 million homes and businesses lost power across multiple states; Philadelphia-area outages alone peaked at roughly 595,000 customers, and Pennsylvania utilities reported roughly 750,000 outage-related calls. New Jersey and New York also faced widespread outages.  
- At least three storm-related deaths were reported in Kansas (including a fatal traffic crash).  
- Airlines canceled thousands of flights: flight-tracking sites reported between ~2,700 and more than 3,100 cancellations on Wednesday and nearly 12,000 delays, with major disruptions at New York-area airports, Boston, Newark, Chicago, Philadelphia and Washington. Several individual aircraft incidents tied to snowy conditions were reported.  
- Major transportation disruptions included road closures (Interstate 84 in New York), suspended or delayed rail services (SEPTA, Amtrak Keystone), speed restrictions on highways, and halted regional transit lines. Authorities urged residents to stay off roads in hardest-hit areas.

Regional actions and consequences
- New York Governor Andrew Cuomo declared a statewide emergency and waived rest rules for salt-truck drivers; New York salt supplies were strained.  
- Pennsylvania saw severe icing that toppled trees and poles, prompting calls for out-of-state utility crews. Gov. Chris Christie declared a state of emergency in New Jersey; other local governments and schools closed or delayed opening. Villanova and several colleges closed due to projected extended outages.  
- Boston and other New England areas faced heavy snowfall rates (up to 2 inches per hour) and the potential for a foot or more in parts of Massachusetts; coastal areas faced risk of strong winds, blowing/drifting snow and coastal flooding if a weekend storm intensifies.

Why it’s happening and outlook
- Meteorologists attribute the pattern to a very wavy jet stream producing sharp temperature contrasts—very cold air in the central U.S. and snow/ice along the East—with some scientists suggesting Arctic sea-ice loss may be increasing such jet-stream variability.  
- Forecasts warned the stormy pattern would continue: another potentially disruptive system was being tracked for the coming weekend (Saturday–Monday), with scenarios ranging from a single intense Atlantic-coast blizzard to two weaker systems. Additional storms were expected through at least mid-February.

Human stories
- Residents ranged from treating snow as a novelty (Boston newcomers enjoying flakes) to frustration and safety concerns as freezing rain and falling limbs made travel and recovery hazardous. Emergency crews continued responding to downed lines, stalled vehicles and icy hazards; utilities warned power could be out for days in some areas.

Overall, the storm produced widespread travel chaos, large-scale power outages, infrastructure strain and significant snow and ice impacts across a broad swath of the country, with more disruptive weather likely in the coming days.

Here’s a concise summary of the December 25, 2015 document:

- George Lucas apologized for a remark in a Charlie Rose interview where he said he had sold Lucasfilm to “the white slavers” (referring to Disney). He called the analogy “very inappropriate” and said he misspoke; Rose did not follow up on the comment during the aired interview.
- Lucas reflected on selling Lucasfilm to Disney in 2012 for about $4 billion and explained why he stepped back from involvement in Star Wars: The Force Awakens. He said Disney preferred to make a film “for the fans” rather than use his story ideas, and that he decided to let them proceed without him to avoid causing friction since he no longer had creative control.
- He described letting go of the franchise (and Indiana Jones) as “a very, very, very hard thing to do,” likening the characters to his children and explaining he sold the company because continuing his preferred approach to Episodes VII–IX would have taken a decade and he didn’t expect to be able to commit that time.
- The piece notes that while Lucas has previously seemed supportive of The Force Awakens and reportedly attended its premiere, his creative instincts differ from the film’s fan-focused, nostalgic approach.
- The document also includes an unrelated interview excerpt with Leonardo DiCaprio discussing his early career, name, Oscar nomination for What’s Eating Gilbert Grape, missed roles (including meetings about Robin, Anakin Skywalker, Spider-Man), and praise for director Christopher Nolan and the film Inception.

Urban Meyer, now Ohio State’s head coach, sent a text to The Columbus Dispatch to rebut what he called inaccurate reports about how the University of Florida and its staff treated former Gators tight end Aaron Hernandez. Meyer said Hernandez “was held to the same drug testing policy as every other player,” and that accusations the program or coaches covered up failed drug tests or mistreated Hernandez are “wrong and irresponsible.” He added that he and his staff worked hard to mentor the player.

The statements come amid renewed reporting on Hernandez after his arrest in June in the June shooting death of semi-pro player Odin Lloyd. A Rolling Stone feature preview alleges Hernandez was a heavy PCP user who became paranoid and carried a gun, that he associated with gang-affiliated people and distanced himself from family and teammates, and that he had repeatedly clashed with Patriots coach Bill Belichick—once coming close to being cut for missed practices and off-field behavior. The piece also details troubled family history, including allegations about his mother’s relationships, and repeats claims that Meyer “may have helped cover up” failed drug tests and past violent incidents while Hernandez was at Florida—claims Meyer denies.

Former Alaska governor Sarah Palin and a friend, Kristan Cole, obtained 20-day protective orders on Sept. 27–28, 2010 against 18-year-old Shawn R. Christy of McAdoo, Pennsylvania after an Anchorage magistrate found probable cause that he had stalked and threatened them since 2009. Court filings and testimony say Christy sent lengthy letters and emails, contacted friends and family, claimed a sexual relationship with Palin, sent proof of a gun purchase and a one-way plane-ticket receipt, and made statements implying he would come to Alaska and harm Palin and others. Palin testified by phone that she feared for her and her family’s safety. The orders bar Christy from contacting Palin, Cole or their families, from coming within a mile of Palin’s home and a local high school, and from following or threatening them. A hearing on a requested longer-term (six-month) order is scheduled for October. Law enforcement and the Secret Service were reported to have been notified; the Wasilla police helped develop a safety plan.

Alan Thicke’s two older sons, Robin and Brennan Thicke, have filed court papers in Los Angeles County seeking to enforce their late father’s trust and prenuptial agreement after alleging his widow, Tanya Callau Thicke, is trying to take more of the estate than Alan intended.

Key points:
- Alan Thicke died in December 2016 at age 69. His most recent trust (February 2016) named his brother Todd as trustee and then his children as successor co-trustees; Robin and Brennan now serve as co-trustees.
- The trust and related documents reportedly leave each child equal shares of the Carpinteria ranch, 75% of personal effects to the children (25% to Tanya), 60% of the “remaining estate” to the children (40% to Tanya), a $500,000 life insurance payout to Tanya, death benefits, and permission for Tanya to live at the ranch if she pays expenses and maintains it. Alan and Tanya executed a prenuptial agreement when they married in 2005.
- The sons’ petition, filed with attorney Alex Weingarten, accuses Tanya of challenging the prenup and the trust now that Alan is deceased, claiming she asserts significant community property rights, reimbursement for ranch improvements, and “Marvin” type claims that she sacrificed career opportunities to support Alan and raise his youngest son, Carter. The petition also alleges she threatened to take her claims to tabloids unless the co-trustees agreed to mediation and her demands.
- The sons ask the court to declare the extent to which trust property is Alan’s separate property and to bar Tanya’s challenge to the prenup and trust.
- Tanya’s attorney, Adam Streisand, called the sons’ filing a “distasteful public smear,” denied that Tanya threatened publicity, and said she prefers to handle matters privately while grieving.

The filing frames the suit as the sons’ effort to protect their father’s legacy and honor his testamentary intentions; the widow disputes the allegations and characterization.

Author and filmmaker Amy Krouse Rosenthal publicly prepared for life after her death from ovarian cancer by publishing a touching New York Times essay, “You May Want to Marry My Husband,” ten days before she died on March 13, 2017. The piece described her husband Jason—“an easy man to fall in love with,” a great father and thoughtful partner—and encouraged him to find happiness after her passing.

In a candid TED Talk and interviews since, Jason Rosenthal has recounted the trauma of Amy’s final weeks and the haunting memory of carrying her lifeless body to a gurney. He described the deep despair that followed her death, compounded months later by his father’s passing, and asked how humans endure such losses. He credits Amy’s public admonition that he “must go on” with helping him gradually reemerge from grief.

Jason says he still grieves often but now intentionally looks for beauty and small joys—music, nature, time with his children—habits he attributes to Amy’s outlook. Her essay led many readers to reach out, including some lighthearted marriage offers; one memorable note demanded he quit drinking. The family has relaunched the Amy Krouse Rosenthal Foundation to support ovarian cancer research and children’s literacy, causes important to Amy. Jason remains uncertain about remarrying and lives largely day to day, honoring Amy by seeking moments of joy.

President Trump released a short “America First” discretionary budget blueprint that seeks a dramatic reordering of federal priorities: a $54 billion (about 10 percent) increase for defense and higher spending for Veterans Affairs and Homeland Security (including initial funds for a border wall and more immigration enforcement), offset by deep cuts across many domestic, scientific, environmental and international programs.

Major elements
- Defense, VA, Homeland Security, the FBI and some law-enforcement and nuclear-security accounts are winners. The Pentagon increase is intended for readiness, equipment (e.g., F‑35s), munitions and personnel.
- Offsets come from steep reductions at roughly a dozen cabinet agencies: EPA (around a 31% cut, ~3,200 jobs and ~50 programs eliminated), State/USAID (≈28–29% cut), Agriculture and Labor (≈20% cuts), Transportation (≈13% cut), Commerce, Energy and others.
- The plan zeros out federal funding for numerous independent and cultural programs: Corporation for Public Broadcasting, National Endowments for the Arts and Humanities, AmeriCorps, and multiple regional commissions and smaller agencies.
- Research and climate programs take big hits: NIH would lose about $5.8 billion (~20%); climate, ocean and earth science work at NASA/NOAA and clean-energy R&D (including ARPA‑E) would be sharply reduced or eliminated; payments to the Green Climate Fund and some U.N. climate efforts would end.
- Anti-poverty and community programs face elimination or severe cuts: Community Development Block Grants, Low-Income Home Energy Assistance, some job-training programs, certain rural subsidies and long-distance Amtrak service are targeted.
- Some targeted increases include charter school and private school choice funding and additional opioid response money.
- The blueprint covers only discretionary spending (≈25% of the federal budget) and omits tax changes, most mandatory entitlement reforms (Social Security, Medicare largely untouched) and a full 10-year fiscal projection; a fuller budget is to follow in May.

Political and practical implications
- The document is intentionally lean on details (a “skinny” or “anorexic” budget), leaving many program-level and personnel impacts unspecified; agency heads were told to find savings. The White House frames it as fulfilling campaign promises and says it’s open to negotiation.
- Many proposals face likely bipartisan resistance in Congress — especially big cuts to foreign aid, State/USAID, NIH, EPA programs and popular local grants — so much of it could be revised or rejected during the appropriations process. Failure to reach agreement could raise the risk of a partial government shutdown when short-term funding expires.
- The plan aims to avoid increasing the deficit by matching defense and other increases with domestic and international spending cuts, but it does not resolve budget caps or legislative hurdles that would be required to accommodate the proposed defense boost.

Bottom line
The Trump White House presented a high-level, politically charged budget blueprint that prioritizes defense, border security and select domestic priorities while proposing sweeping reductions to environmental protection, scientific research, foreign assistance, public broadcasting and many social and community programs. Its fate depends on detailed follow-up proposals and tough negotiations with Congress.

A 61-year-old sound mixer, James M. Emswiller of Pittsburgh’s Lincoln Place, died after falling from a balcony on a Mt. Lebanon apartment building the evening of Oct. 11 while on a break from filming the new Mister Rogers movie, You Are My Friend. Officials say he fell about two stories and was taken to UPMC Mercy in critical condition; he died roughly an hour later. Police believe he may have suffered a medical event before going over the brick balcony wall. The Allegheny County Medical Examiner determined the cause of death was blunt impact injuries to the head and torso and ruled the manner an accident.

Emswiller was credited on IMDb as a sound mixer for the Tom Hanks-led project and had prior sound credits on Pittsburgh-filmed films like Jack Reacher, Abduction and Concussion. He won a 2015 Emmy for sound work on the TV movie Bessie. Production was halted for the evening; Tom Hanks was on set at the time and left after the incident. TriStar/Sony said the studio is investigating and expressed condolences. The film—based on journalist Tom Junod’s Esquire profile of Fred Rogers—chronicles the unlikely friendship that developed between Junod and Rogers.

A 1-year-old Chinese boy named Hanhang went ten days with part of a chopstick lodged in his head after it was driven up his nose when he tripped while holding it. His parents removed the visible stick and took him to a hospital, but doctors initially missed that fragments had penetrated his brain. At home his condition worsened—vomiting and lethargy—so the family returned and an X-ray revealed a six-centimeter piece in his brain. Surgeons removed the fragment; his condition improved immediately but he remains hospitalized for treatment of a resulting brain infection. The report notes similar past incidents and warns that chopsticks can be dangerous when children are not properly supervised.

A Ben Carson campaign volunteer, 25-year-old Braden Joplin of Midland, Texas and a Texas Tech student, died Tuesday from injuries sustained when a campaign van flipped on a patch of ice on Interstate 80 near Atlantic in Cass County, Iowa, and was struck by another vehicle. Joplin was flown to the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha, where he died late Tuesday afternoon. Three others in the van—staffer Drew McCall and volunteers Aaron Ohnemus and Ryan Patrick Shellooe—were treated at a local hospital and released.

Carson, who was campaigning in South Carolina, immediately suspended events for at least two days, traveled to Omaha, and said Joplin was “an amazing young man.” The campaign said it would cover the family’s travel to Omaha and later chartered a private jet for them. Candidates from both parties, including Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio, Jeb Bush and others, publicly expressed condolences. Texas Tech and Carson’s campaign issued statements mourning the loss and urging reflection on the value of life; Carson asked for prayers for those affected.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet donated daily web crawl data to the Internet Archive; after an embargo they’re added to the Wayback Machine.

The piece that follows is a first-person account of a breast cancer diagnosis and its emotional aftermath. The narrator explains how friends’ recent cancer diagnoses prompted her first mammogram despite being younger than typical screening age. She describes choosing a welcoming clinic, posting about the experience online to normalize it, and the nervous wait after imaging. An ultrasound and biopsy with Dr. Kristi Funk revealed a suspicious mass and a sentinel lymph node that suggested the cancer had spread. The author recounts the shock of the diagnosis, the surreal dissociation during the biopsy and calls to loved ones, and the flood of clinical terms—treatable, curable, chemotherapy—turning into her reality when the biopsy confirmed cancer.

Reflecting on what’s ahead, she acknowledges uncertainty about treatment and outcomes but finds that other survivors share a language and perspective she’s beginning to learn: acceptance of not knowing, finding balance in a new “gravity,” and drawing strength from love. The narrative emphasizes the oscillation between fear and connection and ends on the sustaining power of love.

A British couple returned from a Caribbean cruise with identical itchy, winding rashes on their buttocks after sunbathing on a Martinique beach. Initially treated aboard the ship with antibiotics, antifungals and steroid cream, their symptoms persisted. At Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge clinicians diagnosed cutaneous larva migrans — a skin infection caused by hookworm larvae (commonly Ancylostoma braziliense) present in contaminated sand from dog or cat feces. Both later developed respiratory symptoms; chest X-rays showed lung involvement consistent with larvae reaching the bloodstream. Anti-parasitic therapy resolved their skin and lung problems.

Physicians published the case, including color photos of the affected skin, in BMJ Case Reports with patient consent. After tabloid reproduction of the images and coverage that the patients said risked identification by acquaintances, the journal voluntarily removed (but did not retract) the article at the patient’s request, citing the distress caused. Public-health guidance emphasized avoiding direct skin contact with potentially contaminated sand—wear shoes or use mats on tropical/subtropical beaches—to reduce risk.

Russian officials deny U.S. allegations that Moscow is supporting the Taliban, calling such claims fabrications meant to excuse failures in the Afghan campaign. Zamir Kabulov, the Kremlin’s Afghanistan envoy, rejected assertions of Russian aid to the insurgents, while reiterating that Russia has limited contact with the Taliban and views both the Taliban and ISIS as banned terrorist groups.

U.S. and NATO military leaders, however, told lawmakers they have seen growing Russian influence with the Taliban and raised the possibility Moscow might be supplying the group. Army Gen. Curtis Scaparrotti, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, said he has observed “increased influence in terms of association and perhaps even supply.” Gen. John Nicholson, U.S. commander in Afghanistan, has also accused Russia of encouraging the Taliban, providing them diplomatic cover, and meeting with Taliban representatives in Moscow — moves he says could legitimize the insurgents and undermine U.S. and Afghan efforts.

The debate comes as the Taliban have expanded control in parts of Afghanistan, including the contested Helmand district of Sangin, prompting U.S. commanders to warn of a stalemate and call for more international troops to strengthen Afghan forces. Russia denies material support, saying its contacts are aimed at counter‑terrorism and peace talks; U.S. officials say any supply would mark a significant escalation.

Archive-It Partner 1067: The Political TV Ad Archive (Internet Archive) is collecting political TV ads and related social media from key 2016 primary states, extracting metadata and highlighting quality reporting to give journalists, researchers, civic groups and the public reliable information about who is trying to influence voters and how.

Separately, the FCC has released a final draft of a proposal to repeal most net neutrality protections. The draft would strip nearly all 2015-era rules that barred blocking, throttling and paid prioritization, leaving only a transparency requirement that ISPs disclose such practices. The commission labels the 2015 order “misguided” and argues removing those rules will reduce regulatory uncertainty and spur broadband investment and innovation.

The proposal relies on existing antitrust and consumer-protection laws — and Federal Trade Commission oversight — to address harms instead of specific FCC rules. It claims large web firms (e.g., Google, Netflix) are powerful enough to protect their interests in deals with ISPs and that antitrust enforcement can prevent anti-competitive deals that would hurt smaller web companies. Critics note that federal antitrust enforcement is less aggressive than targeted FCC regulation, and that removing the common-carrier classification for ISPs opens the door to practices courts once said would require treating ISPs as carriers.

The draft also seeks to bar states from enacting their own net neutrality rules, saying state laws could unduly burden broadband delivery. The commission will vote on the order at its December 14 meeting, where passage is expected.

McDonald’s is replacing plastic straws with paper ones across its 1,361 restaurants in the United Kingdom and Ireland. The phased rollout begins in September and is to be completed in 2019 after successful trials at selected sites. The company uses about 1.8 million straws a day in those markets and said most customers supported the switch; plastic straws will still be available on request and kept behind the counter for those who need them.

Suppliers Transcend Packaging and Huhtamaki will provide the paper straws made from certified sustainable sources. McDonald’s is also trialing alternatives or straw-on-request policies in a number of other countries including the U.S., France, Norway, Belgium, Australia and Sweden.

The move comes amid growing efforts to curb single-use plastic—driven by public concern, government proposals and industry pledges—and follows similar steps by other chains and retailers. Supporters, including UK Environment Secretary Michael Gove, praised the decision as an example for other businesses. Critics and disability advocates caution that some people rely on plastic straws and paper alternatives are not always suitable, so exemptions and availability for those who need them remain important.

Chinese artist and government critic Ai Weiwei was allowed his first family contact more than 40 days after being detained trying to board a Hong Kong flight on 3 April. His wife, Lu Qing, met him briefly at an undisclosed location after being summoned by police; Ai appeared physically well but tense and said he was being cared for. The meeting was closely monitored, lasted about 20 minutes, and family members were warned not to discuss it with the media. Authorities have not formally charged Ai, but say he is under investigation for suspected “economic crimes.” Observers note the detention has been incommunicado and unusual — family and lawyers had been denied contact — and that he may be held under “residential surveillance,” a measure that can be used to extend incommunicado detention. Ai, a prominent avant-garde artist and outspoken critic of government corruption and censorship (notably active after the 2008 Sichuan earthquake), has prompted international concern from governments, museums and the art world, who view his treatment as part of a wider crackdown on dissent in China.

Mary Jane Lane, 50, of Balch Springs, Texas, was arrested after Dallas police say she passed out at a red light while driving west on Northwest Highway at Ferndale around 5 p.m., then awakened and ran over her husband. Police say husband Randall Lane exited the SUV to unbuckle her seat belt; when she "came to" she pressed the accelerator, dragging him until he fell and suffered head injuries and fractures to both legs. Officers later found Mary Lane a couple miles away blocking traffic with the engine off; they observed bloodshot eyes, slurred speech and unsteady balance. She was initially booked on intoxication assault and leaving the scene but the charge was later reduced to driving while intoxicated. She is jailed on $20,000 bail. The husband’s current condition was not reported.

The CIA has highlighted a selection of once-classified UFO files from its Freedom of Information Act collection—mainly reports from the late 1940s and 1950s that were declassified in 1978—publishing them on its website with a playful nod to Fox’s X-Files reboot. The agency grouped ten items into two sets: five documents it said “Mulder” (the believer) would use and five that “Scully” (the skeptic) could use. The Mulder-leaning files include 1952 reports of flying saucers over East Germany, Spain and North Africa, a report of two fiery discs over uranium mines in the then-Belgian Congo, and minutes and memos from CIA offices and scientific advisory panels discussing UFOs. Notable anecdotes: a West German sighting describing a 13–15 m “frying pan” craft with humanoid figures and a conical tower, and reports of fast, fiery discs over Congo’s Elisabethville district. The CIA also posted photos of unexplained sightings above Minneapolis (1960), Sheffield (1962) and an investigation in Socorro, N.M. The agency emphasized that many cases from the era were later found to lack sound data or to have ordinary explanations, citing a 1953 scientific panel that criticized the low quality of most case histories—underscoring that while the files are intriguing, they don’t prove extraterrestrial activity. The release coincides with renewed public interest in UFOs driven by pop culture and Cold War‑era anxieties.

Summary:

The federal government shutdown has forced widespread furloughs and curtailed services across many science, health, and public-safety agencies, producing immediate and potentially serious effects.

Health and research:
- National Institutes of Health (NIH): About 75% of NIH staff furloughed. The NIH Clinical Center — the world’s largest research hospital — stopped admitting new patients and cannot start new clinical trials. About 1,437 ongoing studies will not enroll new participants; roughly 200 patients a week are estimated to be delayed from enrolling, including about 10 children with cancer. Basic NIH research is largely halted, though animal care continues and existing inpatients receive care.
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Roughly 9,000 employees furloughed; only ~4,000 of 13,000 staff remain. Multi-state outbreak investigations and seasonal flu surveillance programs are largely suspended; PulseNet (foodborne disease tracking) continues and some high-priority investigations remain, but surveillance for H7N9 and MERS will be much weaker.
- Food and Drug Administration (FDA): About 45% of staff furloughed. The agency will be unable to support most routine food safety, nutrition, cosmetics, and related activities; critical responses (high-risk recalls, import reviews, criminal investigations) will continue.
- Other impacts: Investigations into pathogens such as Naegleria continue in a limited way. The shutdown impairs lab sample processing and public-health communications.

Environment, natural resources, and space:
- Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): Nearly 95% furloughed; many air, water, chemical and pesticide reviews and cleanup activities are delayed, though emergency responses (major spills, leaking tanks) continue.
- National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)/National Weather Service: Weather forecasting and life‑safety services continue unchanged.
- U.S. Geological Survey (USGS): Only a handful of essential staff remain (earthquake center, volcano observatories, Landsat monitoring); Landsat data will be archived but not actively processed or distributed.
- U.S. Forest Service: Contingency plan to keep ~41% of workforce to support fire suppression, law enforcement, and essential protections.
- Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC): Has funding to operate for about a week, will maintain resident inspectors at all reactors and then focus solely on core safety functions.
- NASA: Mission Control for the ISS remains staffed; most employees furloughed, website down. Curiosity rover operations continue (staffed by non-civil servants), but some missions (e.g., MAVEN) fear launch-window delays that could mean long postponements.

Public services and communities:
- National parks and monuments: Over 400 sites closed (e.g., Yosemite, Grand Canyon, Alcatraz), with local economic losses estimated in the millions per day. Park staff shortages have impeded critical activities — for example, the search for a missing hiker at Craters of the Moon was scaled back and briefly stalled because of furloughs; some staff were later authorized as “excepted” to continue the search.
- Federal workforce and beneficiaries: More than 2 million federal workers face delayed paychecks; ~800,000 “non-essential” staff are furloughed without clear guarantee of back pay. Veterans’ disability and pension payments could be at risk if the shutdown lasts multiple weeks. Social Security and appeals offices will be limited, delaying hearings and appeals.
- Programs for families and children: WIC (Women, Infants, and Children) benefits could be disrupted after about a week without additional state funds; Head Start programs and other child services face reductions.
- Small business and economic effects: Small Business Administration will not issue new loan guarantees (existing loans still backed); contracting and tourism impacts could reduce local revenues and hiring plans.
- Food safety and inspections: Routine FDA inspections, many import monitoring and lab research stop; USDA meat and poultry inspectors remain, and emergency recalls can be activated, but routine oversight is weakened.

Overall consequences:
The shutdown causes both immediate, personal harms (patients turned away from clinical trials, furloughed workers, scaled-back searches and park closures) and broader public-health and economic vulnerabilities (reduced outbreak surveillance, delayed regulatory reviews, and lost local revenue). Some critical life‑safety functions continue, but many preventive, research, and regulatory activities are paused, with potential long-term impacts if the shutdown persists.

Finland’s state-owned postal company Posti is launching a pilot lawn-mowing service this summer as it diversifies amid falling traditional mail volumes. The nationwide service runs May–August and is offered only on Tuesdays (a lighter mail day); customers buy one-month packages and choose 30-minute sessions for €65/month or 60-minute sessions for €130/month. Orders begin via Posti’s online shop; customers must supply the lawnmower and sessions are rescheduled if it rains. Posti says the idea originated from volunteer mail carriers and fits broader moves to add home services—such as meal delivery support, pilot security work with Securitas, and cooperation with the South Karelia Social and Health Care District (Eksote) to assist home-care clients with daily tasks. The Real Estate Employers group warned postal staff may lack the expertise to safely use powered equipment. Posti notes the service is tax-deductible for domestic costs and frames these offerings as a way to leverage its everyday national delivery network to provide additional, cost-effective services.

Summary:

The Carolina Panthers deactivated Pro Bowl defensive end Greg Hardy for their Sunday home opener against the Detroit Lions after a Mecklenburg County judge found him guilty in July of assaulting and threatening his ex-girlfriend, Nicole Holder. Head coach Ron Rivera said he made the decision that morning because it was "in the best interest of the Carolina Panthers," after consulting others in the organization, and stressed the team would let the legal process play out. Hardy is appealing the conviction and faces a jury trial; the team said he will return to the lineup at some point but gave no timetable.

The move followed national scrutiny of the NFL’s handling of domestic violence cases—heightened by the Ray Rice and Adrian Peterson incidents—and public pressure about allowing players with such allegations to play. Panthers teammates expressed support for Hardy and desire to have him back, while acknowledging the larger league issues. Mario Addison started in Hardy’s place. The Panthers will still pay Hardy his game-week salary; as the franchise-tag player he is slated to earn $13.1 million this season. The situation remains developing.

A 2-year-old boy, Braydon Barnes, died of hyperthermia after being left alone in his room for about 38 hours in St. Charles, Missouri. Authorities say a space heater without an automatic shutoff had been left running and the room was extremely hot when neighbors entered. The child’s parents, 22-year-old Kathleen M. Peacock and 25-year-old Lucas R. Barnes, are accused of manufacturing and using methamphetamine at the home and allegedly ignored the child’s cries during a weekend drug binge. Both face charges including child abuse and neglect; Peacock is reportedly pregnant. Relatives and neighbors described Braydon as appearing malnourished recently and said they had distanced themselves from the couple because of drug problems. Community members and local service representatives urged awareness of available child-welfare resources to prevent similar tragedies.

Researchers have been rapidly piecing together how Zika virus infection in pregnancy affects fetuses. A new CDC analysis published in the New England Journal of Medicine used data from an outbreak in Bahia, Brazil, together with prior outbreak data (French Polynesia), to estimate the risk that first-trimester Zika infection will cause microcephaly. Depending on assumptions about how widespread infection was in the population, the estimated risk for microcephaly from first-trimester infection ranges roughly from about 1% up to nearly 14%. The uncertainty and wide range reflect incomplete and imprecise data: not all reported microcephaly cases may have been correctly diagnosed, and the fraction of pregnant women infected during the outbreak is unknown. The study also found that risk after the first trimester is much lower (well under 1%), though other research has documented additional fetal problems from infections later in pregnancy.

The CDC team’s findings align with earlier smaller studies (French Polynesia estimated ~1% risk) and with larger clinical reports from Brazil showing a broader spectrum of Zika-related fetal harm. Separate clinical studies of babies with presumed congenital Zika infection have reported a variety of severe brain and developmental abnormalities (restricted growth, brain-structure malformations, calcifications, miscarriages/stillbirths) and, importantly, eye abnormalities. Case series from Brazil and Stanford describe retinal lesions, hemorrhagic retinopathy, abnormal retinal blood vessels, pigmentary maculopathy, chorioretinal atrophy and torpedo maculopathy in infants with microcephaly; these ocular findings could cause serious visual impairment. It remains unclear whether the eye problems are direct effects of the virus or secondary to Zika-induced brain impairment.

Public-health implications: even a low percentage risk can translate into large numbers of affected infants in major outbreaks, potentially overwhelming health systems in low-resource settings. The findings reinforce that infection during early pregnancy poses the greatest danger, support CDC recommendations that infants with microcephaly in Zika-affected areas receive ophthalmologic screening, and highlight ongoing needs to clarify factors (e.g., prior dengue exposure, viral changes, environmental or maternal cofactors) that might influence risk.

A 17-year-old senior at Escambia Academy in Atmore, Alabama, Chelsey Ramer, a member of the Poarch Creek Band of Indians, was denied her high school diploma after wearing an eagle feather on her graduation cap on May 23. The private school had required graduating students to sign a contract banning “extraneous items” at graduation and stating that violations would result in withheld diplomas, transcripts, and a $1,000 fine. Ramer says she never signed the contract and wore the feather to express her Native heritage despite the school’s prohibition. One other Native student wore a feather on a necklace and faced no discipline; two others avoided wearing feathers for fear of the fine.

Ramer was allowed to participate in the ceremony but was not handed her diploma afterward. When she sought to speak with Headmaster Betty Warren days later, she was told Warren was no longer with the school; an interim headmaster, girls’ basketball coach David Walker, said he would have given Ramer her diploma if he could, but the board must approve it. Community members, including former teacher and Creek tribal member Alex Alvarez, criticized the school’s handling, arguing that private schools must still respect federal protections for Native religious and cultural practices. The school did not respond to requests for comment, and as of the report Ramer still had not received her diploma. The WARC files for the source crawl are not publicly available.

This document collects two sharply different commentaries about President Obama’s 2011 American Jobs Act and the political turn he took after the Democrats’ midterm losses.

First piece (Washington Times opinion by Joseph Curl)
- Argues Obama falsely claimed the American Jobs Act was bipartisan and fully paid for. The author calls that a lie.
- Describes internal Democratic resistance: senators balked at raising taxes ahead of 2012 elections, and leadership (including Reid and Durbin) indicated the bill lacked sufficient support.
- Relays an anecdote about a rejected bipartisan debt-ceiling compromise that purportedly angered Reid and deepened distrust.
- Concludes the president’s strategy—blaming Congress while pursuing tax hikes on wealthy Americans and corporations—alienates his caucus, makes the jobs bill effectively dead, and leaves House Republicans to craft any viable legislation.

Second piece (Newsweek-style analysis)
- Traces Obama’s recent political repositioning toward populist rhetoric attacking tax breaks for the wealthy and corporate America after a summer of setback and the 2010 midterm “shellacking.”
- Reports that aides (e.g., David Plouffe) advised a tougher message; Obama adopted a $450 billion plan focusing on middle-class jobs and tax increases for high earners and corporations, and told staff he didn’t want proposals filtered by whether House Republicans would accept them.
- Recaps Obama’s earlier outreach to business—meetings with CEOs, the U.S. Chamber, Silicon Valley—and debates over proposals like a repatriation tax holiday for offshore corporate profits. Describes tension between listening to business and skepticism about stimulus value of some proposals.
- Notes personnel moves (Bill Daley as chief of staff) and criticisms that the administration lacked enough business-savvy operatives and failed to sell its accomplishments; some advisers attribute problems to overreliance on macroeconomic theory rather than day-to-day job creation.
- Defenses point out the severe economic inheritance and argue some opposition aimed to produce political damage regardless of economic costs.
- Observes risks: the renewed “class warfare” tone could alienate wealthy donors and centrists, complicating 2012 fundraising, while the central political challenge remains reducing unemployment (~14 million unemployed at the time).

Overall synthesis
- Both pieces agree Obama shifted to a more confrontational, populist posture on jobs and taxing the wealthy after political setbacks. They diverge in tone: the first is a partisan critique declaring the jobs bill politically dead and accusing Obama of dishonesty; the second is a broader account of strategy, internal deliberations, outreach to business, and the political and practical trade-offs of the new approach. Common themes are the political constraints facing Democrats ahead of 2012, tension between bipartisanship and bold messaging, and uncertainty whether the strategy will produce jobs or electoral success.

A car drove into a crowd of children outside a primary school in Huludao, Liaoning province, on Thursday, killing five and injuring 18, local authorities said. The driver was detained and officials described the incident as a "major traffic accident" under investigation. Security footage showed the vehicle change lanes and swerve into a line of children crossing the street; authorities have not determined whether the act was deliberate or an attempt to avoid obstacles. The report notes similar recent attacks in China — including vehicle and knife assaults and a kindergarten explosion — that have killed and injured multiple people, with investigators often citing motivations such as mental illness, social alienation, or settling scores.

A CDC analysis of 2012 National Violent Death Reporting System data from 17 states examined 12,312 suicides among people aged 16 and older to compare suicide rates across occupations. Overall findings

- Suicide was the 10th leading cause of death in the U.S. in 2012; national suicide rates among those ≥16 rose 21% from 2000 to 2012.
- Most suicides in the dataset were male (77%) and concentrated in middle-aged adults (highest proportion in ages 45–54).
- Rates were calculated using standard occupational groupings and Current Population Survey denominators; the study could not produce job-specific rates (e.g., for individual types of farmers) and covers only 17 states, so it is not nationally comprehensive.

Top and bottom occupational groups (suicides per 100,000)
- Highest rates: farming, fishing, and forestry (84.5); construction and extraction (53.3); installation, maintenance, and repair (47.9).
- Lowest rate: education, training, and library occupations (7.5).
- Men had higher suicide rates than women across all occupational groups.
- Among men the highest rates were farming/fishing/forestry (90.5), construction and extraction (52.5), and installation/maintenance/repair (47.5).
- Among women the highest rates were protective service occupations (police, firefighters, corrections — 14.1), legal (13.9), and healthcare practitioners/technical (13.3).

Patterns and implications
- Elevated rates were seen in manual, often-isolated work with unstable employment (e.g., farmworkers, fishermen, lumberjacks, carpenters, miners, mechanics, construction workers).
- Lower rates occurred among educators and librarians; health care professionals (doctors, dentists) showed much lower rates compared with highest-risk groups.
- The report did not analyze causes for the differences but suggests prevention efforts focused on enhancing social support, community connectedness, access to services, and reducing stigma and barriers to help-seeking for working-age populations.

Limitations
- Data represent 17 states only and about 12,300 of ~40,000 U.S. suicides in 2012.
- Occupational coding yielded broad groups, preventing precise estimation for specific jobs or subgroups.
- Military-specific occupations were excluded because of coding challenges.

The CDC highlights occupational disparities in suicide risk and recommends targeted prevention strategies for working-age adults in high-risk occupational groups.

This compilation of reviews frames Universal’s 2017 reboot The Mummy — headlined by Tom Cruise, Sofia Boutella and Russell Crowe and directed by Alex Kurtzman from a multi-writer script — as a messy, overstuffed attempt to launch the studio’s “Dark Universe” of shared monster films. Critics fault the movie for many things:

- Tone and concept: It tries to fuse action-blockbuster spectacle, horror, black comedy and franchise-building exposition, producing tonal confusion and a sense of panic rather than a coherent identity. Dr. Jekyll’s insertion feels like a forced setup for future installments and dilutes both character and plot focus.
- Derivative plotting and heavy borrowing: Reviewers note relentless, overt riffs on many earlier genre films (American Werewolf in London, Lifeforce, Star Trek II, Evil Dead, Lucio Fulci’s Zombie, etc.), plus lifted lines and homages to classic Universal properties, making the film feel like a pastiche rather than an original reboot.
- Cultural and moral missteps: The movie opens amid real-world conflict (Iraq) used as an action backdrop, which some found tone-deaf. It also draws criticism for regressive gender coding — Boutella’s Ahmanet is an eroticized incarnation of evil and Annabelle Wallis’s Jenny is largely sidelined as a rescueable, exposition-delivering love interest.
- Performances and casting impressions: Tom Cruise’s charisma and stunt-driven energy are acknowledged but judged insufficient to overcome a thin, underwritten lead role. Russell Crowe is entertaining as Jekyll/Hyde but the character’s triple duty (mad scientist, action boss, franchise linchpin) is seen as a conceptual misfire. Boutella’s presence and physicality are admired, though her role is noted as being ill-used.
- Visuals and action: The film contains high-production set pieces (notably a plane-crash sequence) and some effective special effects, but many set pieces are criticized as CGI murk or awkwardly staged (e.g., underwater zombie chases). Comic attempts (Jake Johnson’s wisecracking undead sidekick) land unevenly and are often undermined by PG‑13 restraint.
- Franchise concerns: Reviewers worry the movie’s clumsy world-building and muddled tone bode poorly for the proposed Dark Universe, questioning whether the franchise can gain traction.

Bottom line from critics: The Mummy is a bloated, frequently derivative and tonally conflicted reboot — entertaining in small moments but overall a disappointing and dubious franchise-starter that fails to justify its high ambitions.

The California Supreme Court has added a civility pledge to the attorney admission oath, effective May 23. In addition to the existing promise to support the U.S. and California Constitutions and faithfully discharge duties as an attorney, new lawyers will now also pledge: “As an officer of the court, I will strive to conduct myself at all times with dignity, courtesy, and integrity.” The change, urged by the American Board of Trial Advocates and former State Bar president Patrick Kelly, is intended to remind new attorneys to maintain professional conduct amid concerns about rising incivility in practice—shouting, personal attacks in filings, refusal to accommodate routine requests, and efforts to intimidate judges. Supporters called the revision historic and beneficial for justice; critics and some ethics specialists questioned whether an oath will deter misconduct or feared vague language could be used for discipline.
