The court and supporters say the pledge is meant as a general admonition—a reminder of professional behavior—rather than a new disciplinary standard.

Actress Sally Struthers was arrested in Ogunquit, Maine, early Wednesday after being pulled over on U.S. Route 1 and charged with operating under the influence. The 65-year-old, best known for All in the Family and charity work, was performing in the musical 9 to 5 at the Ogunquit Playhouse. She posted $160 bail and was released. This document is a collage of several political news items from the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign cycle, centered on fundraising dynamics, candidate profiles, and controversies:

Bernie Sanders’ small‑donor strategy
- Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders has built a notable grassroots fundraising operation by rejecting super PAC support and relying heavily on many small donations. About 75% of his contributions — roughly $11.4 million — came through ActBlue in small gifts; campaign officials reported an average donation of $31.30 and total reported fundraising of $15.2 million as of July filings (with more raised since). Sanders returned part of a $10,000 donation because of legal limits, and he has limited traditional high-dollar fundraisers, instead holding rally‑style events that sometimes required only modest contributions. His campaign says it spends prudently (about $3 million spent vs. $12.1 million cash on hand at end of June) and believes it can remain competitive despite being outspent by Hillary Clinton and super PACs supporting other candidates.

David Duke praises Donald Trump
- David Duke, former Ku Klux Klan leader, publicly praised Donald Trump’s campaign, saying Trump “understands the real sentiment of America” and commending his hardline stance on immigration and H‑1B visas. Duke described Trump as “the best of the lot” among Republican contenders while also engaging in antisemitic rhetoric in the comments quoted.

Donald Trump media confrontations
- Donald Trump clashed with Univision reporter Jorge Ramos at a press event, having Ramos removed temporarily; Ramos defended his role as a journalist on Twitter. Trump also continued public attacks on Fox anchor Megyn Kelly, criticizing her professionalism and amplifying derogatory comments via tweets.

Joe Biden’s deliberation over a potential run
- Vice President Joe Biden is portrayed as ambivalent about a 2016 presidential bid while grieving his son Beau’s recent death. He has been quietly sounding out donors and advisers but remains undecided, balancing political opportunity against family and personal considerations. Biden polls well despite not announcing and has drawn some informal backers, but his wife Jill and others are skeptical of a run. The White House is giving him space; President Obama privately leans toward Hillary Clinton but won’t block Biden’s choice. Clinton’s team watches Biden closely but is cautious about attacking him given his recent loss.

ActBlue and small‑donor infrastructure
- A short promotional-style note highlights ActBlue Express, noting millions of Democratic donors have saved payment info to facilitate one‑click donations to candidates and groups.

Fundraising struggles for returning GOP candidates
- Former candidates Rick Perry and Rick Santorum, who ran in 2012, have had trouble retaining their previous donor bases in 2016. Analysis of FEC data shows many 2012 donors have shifted to other candidates (notably Ted Cruz). Both campaigns face financial strain—Perry paused many payroll payments and Santorum lost staff to a super PAC effort. Their early fundraising tallies lag far behind top contenders like Jeb Bush and Ted Cruz.

Overall themes
- The pieces collectively highlight the changing finance landscape of the 2016 campaign: the tension between big‑money super PACs and grassroots small‑donor models, the media controversies and outsider populist appeals shaping candidacies, and how personal circumstances and donor loyalty influence who runs and how campaigns are funded.

Police in New Delhi have arrested Abu Jundal (also identified as Syed/Zabiuddin, Sayed Zabiuddin alias Abu Hamza/Abu Jindal, and Ansari), a key Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) operative accused of being a principal handler and trainer for the 10 gunmen who carried out the November 2008 Mumbai attacks. The 26/11 assault—lasting about 60 hours—targeted luxury hotels, the main railway station and a Jewish cultural centre, killed 165 people and left nine attackers dead; lone survivor Ajmal Kasab was convicted and executed.

Indian agencies say Jundal, traced and tracked for years and subject to an Interpol Red Corner notice, was arrested after being deported from or arriving from a Gulf country (reports mention Saudi Arabia). He is accused of directing the attackers from a Karachi control room, providing weapons training, tutoring them in Hindi, and instructing them to conceal Pakistani identities (telling them to claim to be from the Deccan Mujahideen). Intercepted voice recordings from handlers have been matched to him, and Kasab named him in court and police testimony. Jundal is further linked to earlier incidents (a 2006 Ahmedabad blast and an Aurangabad arms haul) and had been missing since 2005 before rising in LeT ranks. Authorities plan to obtain voice samples and further question him to advance the 26/11 investigation and to probe LeT’s networks and activities in the region.

BrandZ’s 2017 Global Top 100 report values the world’s most valuable brands at $3.6 trillion, up 8% year‑on‑year and 152% over the past 12 years. Technology brands are the primary growth engine: 37 tech-related companies account for 54% of total value (vs. 37% in 2006) and tech brands grew 16% year‑on‑year versus 4% for all other sectors. Retail led category growth (+14%), driven by e‑commerce winners Amazon (+41%) and Alibaba (+20%). The BrandZ Strong Brands Portfolio rose 124.9% between 2006 and 2017, outperforming major equity indices.

Geography and age trends
- The U.S. dominates: 54 of the Top 100 brands are U.S.-based and U.S. brands represent 71% of total Top 100 value; U.S. brand value rose 12% year‑on‑year and 181% over 12 years.  
- China’s presence has surged: 13 Chinese brands now appear (up from 1 twelve years ago), with Chinese brand value up 937% over 12 years and making up 11% of Top 100 value; Chinese brands grew 1% year‑on‑year.  
- Brands are getting younger: the average Top 100 brand age is now 67 years (down from 83 in 2006); newcomers average 20 years old.

Notable movers and metrics
- Adidas led in brand value growth (+58%) through trend-driven fashion and U.S. momentum.  
- Retail and logistics B2B brands also rose: the BrandZ B2B Top 20 grew 11%, led by Shell (+23%), DHL and FedEx (+20% each).  
- Brand Contribution (a measure isolating brand strength) highlighted Aguila (Colombia), Coca‑Cola, and Pampers.

Top 10 brands (approximate 2017 brand values and highlights)
1. Google — ~$245B, still No.1, expanded into diverse services and innovation.  
2. Apple — ~$235B, No.2; modest perception of slowing innovation.  
3. Microsoft — ~$143B, driven by cloud/business services.  
4. Amazon — ~$139B, entered Top 10, +41% on expansive consumer services and AWS.  
5. Facebook — ~$130B, +27% despite content controversies; strong advertiser appeal.  
6. AT&T — ~$115B, growing brand tied to media/communications moves.  
7. Visa — ~$111B, +10%, benefited from major merchant wins.  
8. Tencent — ~$108B, first Chinese firm in Top 10; WeChat’s ecosystem and global expansion ambitions.  
9. IBM — ~$102B, +18%, with Watson boosting transformation narrative.  
10. McDonald’s — ~$98B, the only non‑tech Top 10 brand, boosted by menu adaptations and localization.

New entrants (mostly tech-related) include YouTube, HPE, Salesforce, Netflix, Snapchat, Xfinity and Sprint. Overall, the report underscores technology and e‑commerce as central drivers of global brand value growth, a growing but still secondary role for Chinese brands, and the increasing youth and dynamism of the world’s leading brands.

Joan Lee, the longtime wife of Marvel Comics co‑creator Stan Lee, has died in Los Angeles at about age 93–95 (reports differ). She passed away quietly at home surrounded by family after being hospitalized earlier in the week following a stroke, the family said; they asked for privacy to grieve. Married to Stan on December 5, 1947, the couple were together for 69 years and had two children: daughter Joan Celia (J.C.) and a son, Jan, who died days after birth.

A former British hat model, Joan briefly married an American soldier during World War II before divorcing and marrying Stan soon after. She is credited by Stan as an inspiration for his return to comics that led to the creation of the Fantastic Four in 1961. The Lees moved to California in 1981 for Stan’s TV and film work; Joan later did voice roles on 1990s animated Marvel series (Fantastic Four as Miss Forbes, Spider‑Man as Madame Web) and had a cameo in 2016’s X‑Men: Apocalypse. She also authored a 1987 novel, The Pleasure Palace, and reportedly left additional completed manuscripts.

Marvel and Stan’s POW! Entertainment acknowledged her death and thanked well‑wishers; Stan’s account posted a comic drawing of the couple and expressed appreciation for condolences.

Amanda Knox, the U.S. student accused in the 2007 murder of her British flatmate Meredith Kercher in Perugia, said in an interview she will not return to Italy and would become “a fugitive” if an Italian appeals court upholds her conviction. Knox, 26, remains in Seattle and has not attended the Florence appeal, where her former boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito is present and whose defense argued prosecutors built a flawed case. The Florentine court’s expected ruling (reported for Jan. 30) would still require validation by Italy’s Supreme Court before becoming final; only then could Italy seek Knox’s extradition from the U.S., a move that would face legal and diplomatic hurdles including arguments about double jeopardy and complex precedent.

Background: Knox and Sollecito were convicted in 2009, spent time in custody, were acquitted on appeal in 2011, but that acquittal was overturned by Italy’s highest court in 2013, which ordered a retrial. Ivory Coast national Rudy Guede is already serving a reduced 16-year sentence for Kercher’s killing; the Supreme Court instructed judges to re-examine whether Guede acted alone.

Knox maintains her innocence and says she wants someday to speak to Kercher’s family directly, though the family’s lawyers have rebuked her public comments. Her legal team plans to appeal any adverse ruling back to the Supreme Court. Observers note Knox’s “fugitive” remark may have been made lightly, but it raised questions about how U.S.-Italian extradition and final appeal processes would play out if she is reconvicted.

Producers confirmed that former New Life Church pastor Ted Haggard and his wife Gayle will appear on ABC’s new Celebrity Wife Swap, trading partners with actor Gary Busey and reportedly his partner Steffanie Sampson. The episode is set to film at the GLBT Pride Center in Colorado Springs.

Haggard, who resigned in 2006 after admitting to paid sex with a male masseuse and drug use—scandals that ended his roles as New Life’s senior pastor and president of the National Association of Evangelicals—has since returned to ministry as pastor of St. James, a nondenominational church in Colorado Springs. He and Gayle remain married. Haggard has publicly condemned homosexuality but later told GQ he might identify as bisexual if he were younger. He declined to comment about the show.

The Celebrity Wife Swap format mirrors the British original and the U.S. Wife Swap: couples swap partners for a short period, with the men setting rules first and the women taking over later. The episode is expected to highlight cultural and spiritual tensions, particularly between Haggard and Sampson, who is described as spiritual but not a fan of organized religion. Busey, a born-again Christian who has done reality TV before, has appeared on Celebrity Rehab and Celebrity Apprentice; producers have not fully confirmed Sampson’s participation.

A 150-year-old chestnut tree that comforted Anne Frank while she hid in an Amsterdam attic toppled in heavy wind and rain. The tree, mentioned several times in Frank’s diary, snapped about one metre (three feet) above the ground, fell across gardens and damaged fences, walls and sheds but missed the Anne Frank House museum; no injuries were reported. The tree had been infected by fungus and moths and was slated for felling in 2007 for safety reasons, but after a public campaign officials instead encased it in a steel support frame and propagated saplings and clones planted in Amsterdam and abroad. Supporters had believed the structure could prolong the tree’s life for decades; the Netherlands’ Trees Institute said it was surprised by the collapse and does not yet know why the support failed. Parts of the fallen tree were later listed for sale online, and there are no immediate plans to preserve the original remains or plant a replacement on the neighboring private property.

Israeli soldier Gilad Schalit returned home on Oct. 18, 2011, after more than five years in Hamas captivity in a landmark prisoner exchange that freed about 1,000 Palestinian detainees (477 released immediately, roughly 550 more to follow). Schalit, thin, gaunt and showing signs of malnutrition and shrapnel injuries from his 2006 abduction, was handed to Egyptian mediators at the Rafah crossing, briefly interviewed on Egyptian TV, then transferred to Israel, medically examined and reunited with family, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Defense Minister Ehud Barak and military leaders at Tel Nof air base before returning to his hometown Mitzpe Hila amid huge crowds.

His father, Noam Schalit, said Gilad will need time to recover from physical injuries and the psychological effects of long isolation and lack of sunlight and social contact, but the family hopes he can resume a normal life. Israeli officials described his condition as weak but noted he had improved and was being treated by the IDF.

The exchange prompted massive, jubilant celebrations across Gaza and the West Bank and was hailed by Palestinian leaders as a national victory. Hamas figures celebrated and some urged further kidnappings; Israeli leaders warned that any freed militants who return to violence would be held accountable. The deal deepened political gains for Hamas, raised concerns among bereaved Israeli families and complicated regional and domestic politics, with Egypt and Turkey seen as diplomatic beneficiaries. The swap was controversial in Israel because it released prisoners convicted of lethal attacks, and petitions to block the deal had been rejected by the High Court.

Summary:

1) Gun-control remarks by Bernie Sanders
- Sanders voiced support for President Obama’s gun-control agenda, agreeing with Obama’s statement that mass shootings may never be permanently prevented but efforts should be made to minimize them.
- Sanders endorsed measures including: significantly strengthening and expanding instant background checks; closing the gun-show loophole that allows private, unlicensed sales; eliminating the “straw purchaser” loophole that lets someone legally buy a gun and then transfer it to a criminal; and substantially expanding mental-health services to address people who are suicidal or homicidal.

- The Metropolitan Transportation Authority phased out the subway token: sales ended April 12, tokens will stop working on subways as of the May 4 fare increase (from $1.50 to $2.00), and buses will accept tokens (plus 50 cents) only through December 31; Roosevelt Island Tram will continue accepting tokens for now.
- The token, introduced in 1953 after turnstile technology made mixed coin fares impractical, evolved through several designs tied to fare increases (1953, 1970, 1980, 1986, 1995). - Officials cite savings (about $6 million annually) from eliminating token handling and the advantages of MetroCards (cheaper to produce, programmable discounts/transfers). Many unused tokens (millions) are held in storage; most are expected to be scrapped, though some have become collectibles or souvenirs. Transit staffers considered what to call former token booths (now "station service booths") and noted riders may keep using the old name out of habit.

A coordinated attack struck the luxury Corinthia Hotel in Tripoli, a seaside hub for foreign visitors, diplomats and businesspeople, killing at least 10 people (including an American and several Europeans) and wounding others. Attackers—reported as a small group of masked gunmen—stormed the lobby, firing on staff and guests; a car bomb detonated in the hotel parking lot during the assault. Security forces engaged the assailants; two attackers were reported killed and at least one reportedly detonated a suicide device. Initial reports of hostages were later denied by officials.

An organization calling itself Islamic State in Tripoli Province claimed responsibility, saying the raid was retaliation for the 2013 U.S. capture of al-Qaida operative Abu Anas al-Libi, who recently died in U.S. custody. The group released names and photos of fighters it said were killed. Authorities could not immediately verify all details.

The attack highlighted Libya’s broader collapse into factional violence since Muammar Qaddafi’s ouster in 2011: rival coalitions—Tripoli’s Libya Dawn (which backs the hotel’s area) and the eastern Operation Dignity centered around Gen. Khalifa Hifter—compete for power, and multiple militant cells have pledged allegiance to ISIS. Libya Dawn officials denied IS responsibility and blamed remnants of the old regime or rival forces; the Tobruk-based government accused Libya Dawn of allying with extremists. The assault underscored the deteriorating security environment in Tripoli, which has experienced repeated bombings and shootings amid the power struggle.

Five Southern California high school students—three girls and two boys—died when an Infiniti sedan veered off Jamboree Road in Newport Beach on Memorial Day and slammed into a tree, splitting the car and igniting a fire. The driver, 17-year-old Abdulrahman M. Alyahyan, a senior at University High School, and four passengers—Robin Cabrera, 17, a senior at Irvine High; her sister Aurora (16), a sophomore; and Irvine High juniors Cecilia Zamora (17) and Nozad Al Hamawendi (17)—were all killed. Four were thrown from the vehicle and died at the scene; one was pronounced dead at a hospital. Investigators say speed was believed to be a factor; no other vehicles were involved.

Friends and classmates described the teens as close-knit and active in school life—several were dancers, and the boys were part of a group of immigrant friends who often spoke Arabic together. The crash was so violent that the coroner had to use fingerprints to identify some victims. Irvine Unified School District officials called it a devastating loss; counselors were dispatched to help students. Newport Beach authorities called the collision one of the worst solo-car crashes in recent memory in a city with a history of high-speed, high-profile wrecks. An earlier citation for improper exhaust modification and license violations was found in court records for an Abdulrahman M. Alyahyan, but police would not confirm if it involved the driver.

Sen. Jon Kyl (R-Ariz.), the Senate’s No. 2 Republican and a three-term senator, announced Feb. 10, 2011 that he will retire at the end of his current term in January 2013 and will not seek reelection. Speaking from Phoenix, Kyl, 68, said he will remain in office for the next 22 months and focus on Senate work rather than campaigning, though he plans to help Republican allies in races. He said the vice presidency would be the only other federal office he might consider, but called that unlikely and inappropriate to pursue while serving.

A four-term former House member and long-serving Arizona incumbent who has never lost an election, Kyl is viewed as stepping down “at the top of his game.” Colleagues, including Sen. Lindsey Graham, praised his leadership and expertise in finance and national security. Kyl said he hopes his successor will share his conservative values, prioritize national security, and act ethically.

Kyl’s retirement makes him the fifth senator scheduled for re-election in 2012 to announce departure ahead of the 113th Congress, and opens a potentially competitive seat. Names floated as possible successors included Rep. Jeff Flake, Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano, and, if Kyl were to resign, Rep. Gabby Giffords. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee called Arizona a “prime pick-up opportunity” for Democrats.

Google changed some offensive autocomplete suggestions after the Observer revealed that searches beginning “are Jews…”, “are women…” and “are Muslims…” returned hateful prompts and top results linking to extremist or conspiratorial sites. Reporters found autocomplete suggestions like “are Jews evil”, “are women evil” and “are Muslims bad” and search-result pages dominated by antisemitic, misogynistic and Islamophobic pages — in some cases Holocaust-denial or neo‑Nazi sites. Google says autocomplete is algorithmically generated from web content and user activity, does not reflect its views, and that it works to prevent offensive suggestions; it said it acted within hours of being notified but did not explain why it altered some suggestions and not others.

The episode renewed criticism that search algorithms can be gamed by coordinated networks of right‑wing and fake‑news sites that create vast webs of links and traffic to manipulate rankings. Academics and commentators quoted in the report called for greater accountability — audits, transparency and possibly human editorial oversight — arguing the problem goes beyond isolated errors: search ranking and suggestion systems can amplify propaganda, influence public opinion and entrench bias. Past Google controversies — racially biased photo tags, offensive Map labels, and biased image results — were cited as part of a pattern.

Researchers described how link networks, social amplification and data‑driven targeting (including tools used by political consultants) create a reinforcing “knowledge economy” that boosts extremist content. Critics warned that the opaque, powerful role of Google and similar platforms in shaping information—combined with their expanding reach into AI and everyday services—poses democratic risks unless companies accept responsibility and regulators demand transparency and oversight. The piece frames the problem as systemic: not just technical glitches but the result of coordinated manipulation, design choices and insufficient accountability.

A rare, unsigned Jackson Pollock gouache has surfaced in Sun City, Arizona, and will be auctioned by J. Levine Auction & Appraisal in Scottsdale on June 20, 2017. The 22½ x 32-inch abstract work was discovered among a trove of mid-20th-century modern pieces (including works by Kenneth Noland, Jules Olitski, Hazel Guggenheim McKinley and Cora Kelley Ward) that came from the estate of Jenifer Gordon (Cosgriff), a longtime New York friend of critic Clement Greenberg and others in Pollock’s circle. The Sun City owner, who inherited the pieces and lived in an assisted‑living facility, reportedly did not know the significance of the paintings.

Owner Josh Levine spent nearly 18 months and more than $50,000 on provenance research, private investigators and forensic testing. Forensic analyst Peter Paul Biro reported that the pigments and binding media are consistent with mid‑20th‑century materials and contain no substances introduced after Pollock’s death; Levine says provenance and investigators’ findings further support attribution to Pollock, likely dated to the 1945–1949 period. Levine expects the painting to fetch at least $10 million to $15 million. The discovery drew attention after another found work by Noland (“Replace!”) sold for $110,000 in early 2016. The Pollock attribution remains controversial in the field, but Levine stands publicly behind it. Online and live bidding are available through J. Levine.

A five-month-old boy born to Jordanian parents is the first known baby to result from a mitochondrial replacement technique that gives the child DNA from three people. The procedure, carried out in Mexico by a US-based team led by John Zhang of New Hope Fertility Center, aimed to prevent transmission of mitochondrial mutations that cause Leigh syndrome, a fatal neurological disorder. The mother carried a pathogenic mtDNA mutation affecting about a quarter of her mitochondria and had previously lost two children to the disease.

Because the couple objected on religious grounds to discarding embryos, Zhang used spindle nuclear transfer rather than the UK-approved pronuclear transfer. In spindle transfer the mother’s egg nucleus is moved into a donor egg (whose nucleus has been removed) and that reconstructed egg is then fertilized with the father’s sperm. The team produced five embryos, implanted one that developed normally, and the child—a boy—was born on 6 April 2016 and shows no signs of disease. Tests indicated under 1% of the child’s mitochondria carry the mother’s mutation, well below the commonly cited ~18% threshold for clinical effect, though experts urge long-term monitoring in case mutant mtDNA levels rise.

Context and background:
- Mitochondria house a small distinct genome (mtDNA) inherited maternally; some mtDNA mutations cause Leigh syndrome and other severe mitochondrial diseases by disrupting oxidative phosphorylation complexes, especially complex I and complex IV. The most common mtDNA mutation in Leigh syndrome affects MT-ATP6 (part of complex V).
- Two principal mitochondrial replacement approaches exist: pronuclear transfer (fertilize both eggs then swap pronuclei) and spindle transfer (swap nuclei between unfertilized eggs then fertilize). The UK legalized pronuclear transfer in 2015 under tight regulation; the US has not approved either technique.
- Past mitochondrial interventions (1990s cytoplasmic transfer) led to safety concerns after some adverse outcomes and was halted by the FDA; about 30–50 children born from those procedures are now being reassessed.

Ethical, regulatory and safety issues:
- Advocates emphasize the technique prevents devastating inherited disease, note mitochondrial DNA constitutes a tiny fraction of total DNA and does not affect traits like appearance or personality, and argue that using a male embryo prevents onward maternal transmission.
- Critics warn of germline modification risks, potential unforeseen health effects across generations, and slippery-slope concerns about genetic modification. Some animal studies have reported functional changes after mitochondrial replacement, prompting calls for caution.
- UK regulators (HFEA) conducted extensive reviews and concluded mitochondrial replacement is “not unsafe” with further study; opponents still seek more debate and data.
- The Mexican procedure highlights regulatory patchwork: neither method is allowed in the US, and Zhang said he performed the treatment abroad because of lack of domestic authorization.

Human impact:
- The technique offers hope to families affected by mitochondrial disease; many personal accounts in the coverage recount devastating losses and strong demand for preventive options.
- Experts recommend careful follow-up of this child and any future births produced by these techniques to monitor health outcomes and mtDNA levels over time.

The full clinical findings were scheduled to be presented at the American Society for Reproductive Medicine meeting in October; the case is widely seen as a potentially revolutionary step in reproductive medicine but one that intensifies ongoing ethical and safety debates.

Researchers analyzing U.S. Health and Retirement Study data report a substantial decline in age-specific dementia prevalence between 2000 and 2012. Using nationally representative samples of adults 65+, investigators compared two cohorts (≈10,500 people each) and found dementia prevalence fell from 11.6% in 2000 to 8.8% in 2012 (about a 24% relative decline). Cognitive impairment without dementia also declined.

Key findings and possible explanations
- Education: Average years of schooling rose from 11.8 to 12.7 years across cohorts. Increased education explained part of the decline and is thought to build “cognitive reserve” and influence lifetime health, jobs and access to care.
- Cardiovascular care: Prevalence of vascular risk factors (obesity, diabetes, hypertension) increased, yet treatments intensified and control improved. Improved management—especially of diabetes and heart disease—appears to have contributed modestly to the reduction in dementia risk.
- Other associations: Higher net worth and more education were linked to lower dementia odds; older age, stroke, diabetes, and being African American or Hispanic were linked to higher odds. Underweight status was associated with higher dementia odds; overweight/obesity at older ages showed lower odds (consistent with other late-life studies).

Method and limitations
- Dementia classification used validated HRS cognitive tests and proxy reports (previously shown ~78% concordance with gold-standard clinical evaluations). Analyses adjusted for age, sex, education, wealth, race/ethnicity, and cardiovascular risk factors.
- Limitations include possible misclassification from limited test batteries, changes in survey mode and proxy use between waves, reliance on self-reported health conditions, and uncertainty about all causal factors.

Implications
- The decline suggests population brain health improved between 2000 and 2012 and points to education and better vascular disease management as contributors. However, because the U.S. population is aging, total numbers of people with dementia are still expected to rise. Continued monitoring is needed to clarify causes and guide public health planning.

Researchers Michael Kasumovic and Jeffrey Kuznekoff analysed voice chat from 163 Halo 3 multiplayer matches to investigate what triggers sexist behavior in online competitive settings. They played recorded games in which an experimental player used either a male or female voice broadcasting identical, neutral phrases, then coded teammates’ spoken comments as positive, negative, or neutral and linked those to objective performance metrics (kills, deaths) and an advertised skill rating.

Key findings
- Lower-skilled and poorer-performing male players directed significantly more negative (hostile) comments at the female-voiced teammate, especially when they themselves were performing badly.
- The same low-status, poor-performing players behaved submissively (more positive, fewer negative comments) toward male-voiced teammates.
- Higher-skilled players were more positive toward the female-voiced teammate and less negative overall; they did not show the same hostile reaction.
- The pattern persisted after controlling for game outcome and relative performance versus the experimental player.

Interpretation
- The results support an evolutionary-account hypothesis: when a woman enters a male-dominated competitive arena, low-status men who stand to lose the most from a reordering of hierarchy respond with hostility to protect status and mating opportunities. High-status men, having less to fear, respond more positively (possibly to attract attention).
- Alternative social explanations (novelty of a female voice or pitch-based reactions) were considered but performance and skill mediated the effects, consistent with the status-threat account.

Broader context and implications
- The study used ecological, real-world online interactions where anonymity and ephemeral encounters make policing behavior difficult, paralleling many online platforms (e.g., Twitter, Reddit).
- It helps explain why women often receive disproportionate harassment online: sexist hostility is concentrated among lower-status, struggling men in male-dominated spaces.
- The authors suggest interventions might include normalizing mixed-sex competition (e.g., through gaming) and teaching young males that losing to women is not socially debilitating, though they note no simple solution for ending sexism.

Methodological notes
- Data came from recorded Halo 3 matches with pre-recorded male/female voice lines; transcripts were blind-coded for comment valence. Performance metrics and skill ratings were used in generalized linear models. Intercoder reliability was substantial to excellent.

Conclusion
- The study provides empirical evidence that female-directed hostility in online competitive environments is concentrated among low-status, low-performing men, lending support to an evolutionary status-threat explanation for some forms of sexism online.

For Data Privacy Day, Facebook announced two new account-security features to help users protect their personal information: full-site HTTPS and "social authentication."

- HTTPS (secure connection): Facebook will let users browse the entire site over HTTPS (the same encrypted protocol used by banking sites). The option appears under Account Settings → Account Security → Secure Browsing and is being rolled out gradually over a few weeks. Facebook notes encrypted pages may load more slowly and some features and third‑party apps may not yet work under HTTPS; they plan to make HTTPS the default in the future. Security experts urge users to enable HTTPS as soon as it appears for their account because it prevents session hijacking attacks (e.g., via tools like Firesheep) on open wireless networks, though they criticize Facebook for making it opt‑in, for slow rollout, and for not yet covering mobile apps.

- Social authentication: When Facebook detects suspicious activity (such as geographically inconsistent logins), instead of or in addition to CAPTCHAs, it may ask users to identify friends in photos as a way to verify identity. Facebook says it will test and refine this feature with user and security‑community feedback.

Facebook links to its Security Page for more tips; the company emphasizes ongoing work to strengthen protections but acknowledges remaining limitations and a gradual transition to default HTTPS.

A 26-year-old pregnant server in Newark, Delaware, Lisa Stephenson, helped reunite two missing Maine teenage girls with their families after she grew suspicious when they applied for jobs at her restaurant on Nov. 2. The girls looked young, weren’t in school, gave no contact information on their applications, and claimed their phones and money had been stolen in New York. Concerned for their safety near nearby truck stops and motels, Stephenson wrote down their names and that evening searched Facebook, finding a missing-persons post by the 16-year-old’s mother about her daughter and a 14-year-old friend who had disappeared Oct. 25.

Stephenson messaged the mother, alerted local police and her cousins (who are county deputies), and stayed in contact. The girls were later spotted panhandling in Waldorf, Maryland; deputies picked them up and a social worker placed them temporarily. The teens told authorities they had stolen a car and driven south through Boston and New York, narrowly avoiding dangerous areas and possibly trafficking hotspots. Both girls were returned to their families in Maine, grounded (and the older girl barred from social media). The girls’ mother called Stephenson a hero for trusting her instincts and coordinating with authorities across states; Stephenson says she was simply doing what anyone should do when something seems off. No charges were filed, and the paper withheld the teens’ identities.

Prince Harry and American actress Meghan Markle announced their engagement and will marry in May at St. George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle, Kensington Palace said. The queen will attend and the royal family will pay for the wedding. Markle, who will be baptized into the Church of England and intends to pursue UK citizenship (likely taking several years), will retain U.S. citizenship during the process; dual nationality was undecided.

The couple — Harry, fifth in line to the throne, and Markle, star of Suits — revealed details in interviews: they met on a blind date in July 2016, maintained a long-distance relationship, and Harry proposed at Nottingham Cottage over a roast chicken dinner. The engagement ring, designed by Harry, incorporates a central Botswana stone and two smaller diamonds from his late mother Princess Diana’s collection.

St. George’s is a historic but more intimate royal venue than Westminster Abbey; the Church of England permits remarriage of divorcees in certain circumstances, so Markle’s prior marriage won’t block a church wedding. The couple will live at Nottingham Cottage and Markle will become a patron of The Royal Foundation. The announcement drew enthusiastic reactions across Britain, with senior royals and media calling the match a modernizing, upbeat development for the monarchy. Downing Street said there are no plans for a public holiday for the wedding.

Kristina Chesterman, a 21-year-old nursing student at Chico State, was struck by an alleged drunk driver last September and declared brain dead. Having registered as an organ donor at 18, she saved multiple lives: portions of her liver went to infant Jayden Kirby (who likely would have died without it) and another San Francisco man; a kidney went to Sakariah “Zak” Pappachan (who also received her pancreas); and her heart now beats in 64-year-old retired nurse Susan Vieira from Campbell. A 63-year-old South Bay woman also received an organ; Chesterman’s family hopes to meet her.

Her family, friends and the recipients have formed a supportive community. Jayden’s family tracked down the donor and celebrated his first birthday with Kristina’s mother, Sandra. The Pappachans have grown close to the Chestermans and are memorializing Kristina in their backyard. Vieira connected with the family after seeing news of Kristina’s bucket list and says she plans to honor Kristina by completing items on it—like skydiving and visiting continents—symbolically carrying Kristina with her.

Kristina’s bucket list, found by her mother while clearing her apartment, and her wish to help people inspired many to carry on her dreams. Fellow students and supporters have launched a memorial nursing scholarship at Chico State (raising over $30,000) and are fundraising to build a medical clinic in Nigeria in her name. Friends have undertaken activities from the list—skydiving, first-class flights, and more—to celebrate her life. Meanwhile, legal proceedings continue: a man charged with DUI and hit-and-run in Kristina’s death faces a preliminary hearing, and Kristina’s brother’s attacker will be sentenced on a separate assault charge.

Through organ donation and the actions of those she touched, Kristina’s compassion and ambitions continue to affect and inspire many.

This document contains two heartwarming, related stories about family ties maintained across distance.

1) Allegro Christmas advert (Poland)
- Allegro, a major Central and Eastern European e-commerce platform, released a widely viewed emotional Christmas advert that follows a grandfather who learns English to reunite with family who moved abroad.
- A spokesperson said the ad was meant to reflect the reality of nearly one million Poles who left the country—many to the U.K.—and the weakening of family ties despite geographic closeness. The campaign’s slogan, “what are you looking for,” ties the story to universal longings and emotions.
- The advert became a viral tear‑jerker, watched by more than 2.5 million people globally.

2) Grandpa learns Instagram to connect with grandchildren (Brazil/Korea)
- Designer Ji Lee shared a viral Facebook video about his 75‑year‑old father (Korean, living in Brazil) who started drawing daily for his grandchildren on Instagram after they moved back to Korea.
- Initially unfamiliar and reluctant with technology, the grandfather began posting drawings (with stories written by Lee’s mother) after the birth of his grandson. The project re‑energized family communication: the parents exchange the stories and images across languages (Korean, English, Portuguese).
- The Instagram account rapidly gained tens of thousands of followers after the video went viral. The family received many messages from people inspired to reconnect with aging parents through technology, and the grandfather has continued the daily drawings for over a year.

Both pieces emphasize how simple acts—an advert about a grandfather learning English, and a granddad learning Instagram and drawing—resonate widely by highlighting efforts to bridge distance, preserve family bonds, and bring joy across generations.

President Obama urged Congress to pass a small, temporary package of spending cuts and tax changes to delay the across-the-board sequester that is set to begin March 1. He said a short-term fix — enacted if a larger, permanent deficit deal can’t be reached immediately — would postpone the sharp, indiscriminate $1.2 trillion in cuts over 10 years that threaten both domestic programs and defense and could harm a fragile economic recovery. The White House did not present a detailed plan but said any delay would require tens of billions in deficit reduction via targeted cuts or revenue increases (for example, closing loopholes that benefit the wealthy or certain industries). Obama reiterated his preference for a broader deal combining spending reforms and tax changes.

Republicans, led by House Speaker John Boehner, rejected new tax increases and have been more willing to let the sequester proceed or replace it with spending-only reductions, arguing Americans oppose trading real spending cuts for higher taxes. Democrats in the Senate, including Sen. Patty Murray, backed a short-term replacement if a long-term solution isn’t possible. The push comes amid other fiscal deadlines (a late-March funding expiration and a summer debt-limit showdown) and CBO projections showing the deficit falling below $1 trillion in 2013, in part because of recent tax increases and the looming sequester.

Martin Shkreli, 32, CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals, became the focal point of national outrage after his company bought the rights to Daraprim — a 62-year-old, life‑saving drug for toxoplasmosis used mainly by people with weakened immune systems — and raised its price from about $13.50 to $750 per tablet (a >5,000% increase). Shkreli’s combative public defense of the hike and abrasive social-media presence triggered widespread condemnation from patient groups, politicians and the public; he received intense online ridicule and threats. Under heavy media pressure he later said he would reduce the price to a lower level that still yields a “very small profit.”

Background: Shkreli, the son of immigrants from Brooklyn, moved from hedge funds (including failed Elea and MSMB) into biotech. He founded Retrophin in 2011 but was ousted amid accusations of improperly using company assets; a related civil suit was filed and in 2017 he was convicted on several counts of securities fraud unrelated to the Retrophin looting claims. He launched Turing in 2015, which markets Daraprim and another drug.

Broader context: The Daraprim episode spotlighted a widespread problem: dramatic price spikes for off‑patent generic drugs when a single company controls supply and market demand is too small to attract competitors. Examples include massive increases in captopril, albuterol sulfate and doxycycline. Policy debate is under way: proposals range from forcing pharma to reinvest profits in R&D (criticized by some experts) to regulatory fixes that would speed generic approvals and encourage competition — for example, reforming FDA pathways to make it easier and faster for new manufacturers to enter small‑market generics. The consensus is that lasting change will require regulatory and structural reform rather than short‑term public shaming.

Six Czech tourists were arrested and fined in Kazakhstan after posing for photos in Astana while wearing mankinis — the revealing swimsuit made famous by Sacha Baron Cohen’s Borat character. Local authorities charged the men with “minor hooliganism” and fined each 22,500 tenge (about $67). The incident drew mixed reactions from Kazakh social media, ranging from calls for harsher punishment to praise for the publicity the stunt provided. Sacha Baron Cohen responded on Facebook, asking the men to send proof and offering to pay their fines (contacting them via an email he posted). The report notes the film Borat sparked controversy in Kazakhstan, was banned there, but later was credited by officials with boosting tourism; it also mentions other places have restricted mankinis for public-decency reasons.

Sen. Ted Cruz plans to announce a 2016 presidential run Monday at Liberty University, forgoing an exploratory committee and becoming the first high-profile Republican to formally enter the contest. His campaign team aims to raise $40–50 million and build a coalition of tea party, social conservative and libertarian voters—seeking to be the strong conservative choice and the second pick of other GOP factions to overcome the party establishment’s preferred candidate.

Cruz, 44, rose quickly after his 2012 Senate win by courting tea party activists and staging high-profile confrontations in Washington, including a 2013 effort to block spending tied to repealing the Affordable Care Act. He positions himself as an unabashed conservative who rejects the “mushy middle,” promising to abolish the IRS, dismantle the Education Department and rein in federal regulators. He has traveled to early primary states and expanded his political operation through the Jobs, Growth and Freedom PAC; his wife, Heidi, will join the campaign.

Strengths: strong appeal to the Republican base and activists who vote heavily in primaries, potential competitiveness in Iowa. Challenges: limited establishment endorsements and big-dollar donor support, negative comparison risks (including to Barack Obama’s early Senate-to-presidency run), and weak early general-election poll showings against likely Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton. If unsuccessful in 2016, Cruz would keep his Senate seat through early 2019.

Greek Parliament moved toward approving a deeply unpopular austerity package after intense debate and party maneuvering, as unions launched a rare 48-hour general strike and violent protests erupted outside Parliament. The measures—wage cuts, tax increases and privatizations—are required by the EU, ECB and IMF to unlock a €12 billion ($17 billion) bailout tranche needed to avoid a likely default next month. Prime Minister George Papandreou’s Socialist Party has a slim five-seat majority; Finance Minister Evangelos Venizelos worked to secure backing, and at least one wavering Socialist MP, Thomas Robopoulos, announced he would support the bill “for the national interest.” Opposition leader Antonis Samaras of New Democracy has refused to endorse the package.

The strike shut down transport, ports and parts of the public sector; tens of thousands marched peacefully while clashes involving hooded youths and police—who used tear gas and stun grenades—left dozens detained and several officers injured. Protesters decried bearing the cost of a crisis many blame on political elites. European officials warned there was no “Plan B” to avert default, and Brussels was pressing Greek parties and making contingency plans. After the initial parliamentary vote, lawmakers must pass an implementation bill; even if approved, many analysts worry Greece’s debt remains unsustainable and a second bailout will be needed.

This document combines two distinct pieces:

1) Internet Archive collection of Russian opposition sites and figures
- Since 1996 Alexa Internet has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive; those daily crawls are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.
- The Archive contains captured websites, blogs and other online material from 17 Russian political and cultural figures who have expressed opposition to domestic or foreign policy under Vladimir Putin. Names include prominent bloggers, journalists, politicians and activists such as Rustem Adagamov, Sergei Aleksashenko, Konstantin Borovoi, Leonid Gozman, Il’ia Iashin, Oleg Kashin, Oleg Kozyrev, Andrei Makarevich, Andrei Mal’gin, Aleksei Naval’nyi, Boris Nemtsov, Valeriia Novodvorskaia (deceased), Dmitrii Oreshkin, Sergei Parkhomenko, Irina Prokhorova, Artemii Troitskii and Nikolai Uskov.
- The archive also preserves captures of eight websites documenting political and human-rights positions and events: Civil Platform; Human Rights in Russia; Nashi (pro-Kremlin youth organization); Politkom.Ru (Center for Political Technology platform); Putin.Itogi (publishing independent expert reports, including by Boris Nemtsov); Solidarnost’ (united democratic movement); Bolotnaya Square Case (documenting repression after the May 2012 protest); and Traitor.net (a site outing people who oppose Russian actions in Ukraine).

2) Viral media story about a flock of birds forming a face resembling Vladimir Putin over New York
- An 11-second video shot by tourist Sheryl Gilbert (posted to YouTube) shows a flock of birds near the Brooklyn Bridge forming a shape some viewers perceived as a human face. Russian state-owned TV channel Zvezda highlighted the clip and suggested the outline resembled President Vladimir Putin’s face, while noting it could be faked.
- The clip went viral in Russia, drawing more than a million views and a flurry of online comments. Some Russian users interpreted the formation as a symbolic warning to the U.S.; others joked or suggested alternative faces. Gregory West, who identified himself as Gilbert’s husband, maintained the footage was real.
- Zvezda and others cautioned about authenticity; viewers offered varied and humorous identifications (from Putin to other public figures).

Overall, the document juxtaposes a factual description of a Wayback Machine archive preserving the online presence and opposition voices in Russia with a lighter viral-news item about a YouTube bird-flock video that Russian viewers and a defense-linked TV channel read as resembling Putin.

Researchers publishing in Current Biology report that, three decades after the 1986 Chernobyl accident and the evacuation of tens of thousands of people, large mammal populations in the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone (CEZ) are abundant and in many cases comparable to—or greater than—those in nearby uncontaminated nature reserves. Using long-term data from helicopter surveys (1987–1997) and systematic winter snow-track censuses (2008–2010) across the Belarusian Polessye State Radioecological Reserve (PSRER, ~2,165 km2), the team compared elk (moose), roe deer, red deer, wild boar and wolves with four nearby protected areas. They mapped habitat types and radiocaesium contamination along survey routes and analyzed trends and spatial patterns.

Key findings
- Relative abundances of elk, roe deer, red deer and wild boar in the CEZ are similar to those in four uncontaminated reserves.
- Wolf abundance in and around Chernobyl is exceptionally high—over seven times greater than in the comparison reserves.
- Aerial data show increases in elk, roe deer and wild boar during the first decade after the accident; a later wild boar crash (1993–94) was linked to disease (African swine fever) and increased wolf predation, not radiation.
- There was no clear correlation between mammal density and local radiocaesium contamination in the surveyed routes.

Interpretation and caveats
- The authors conclude that, despite documented radiation effects on individuals (e.g., mutations, cancers), chronic contamination has not prevented the CEZ from supporting an abundant large-mammal community. They attribute the recovery largely to the removal of human pressures—hunting, farming and forestry—after evacuation.
- The study does not assess individual health, reproduction or longevity, nor does it address smaller taxa (insects, birds, small mammals) where other studies have found radiation-linked declines.
- Authors and independent commentators caution that these results do not imply radiation is “good” for wildlife; rather, they highlight how powerful human impacts can be and that absence of people can allow some species to flourish even in contaminated landscapes.

Implications
- The findings demonstrate wildlife resilience at the population level under long-term low-to-moderate chronic radiation exposure and offer a useful reference point for understanding ecological outcomes of other nuclear accidents (e.g., Fukushima), while underscoring the need for further research on individual-level health effects and on non-mammal taxa.

An elderly South Texas couple died and their son was injured after a swarm of bees attacked them while cleaning a remote hunting cabin on their ranch near Hebbronville, Jim Hogg County. William “W.T.” Steele (reported ages 90–95) and his wife Myrtle (92) were stung during the incident; W.T. Steele was found dead at the scene and Myrtle was airlifted to a Corpus Christi hospital where she later died. Their son Richard (67) sustained numerous stings to his head and face, was treated at Laredo Memorial Hospital and released. According to investigators and family, the family exposed a large hive when moving a wood stove/fireplace item; the son drove miles to the nearest road to call for help. Deputies who responded were themselves swarmed but not seriously hurt. Authorities believe the bees were likely Africanized honey bees, known for aggressive swarming; USDA guidance warns untrained people not to attempt removal and to flee if attacked. The hive had not been removed and the species had not been formally identified at the time of reporting.

Iris Zink, MSN, RN, a rheumatology-certified nurse practitioner in Lansing, Michigan, donated a kidney to her longtime patient and friend, Ginny Holcomb, after Holcomb was diagnosed with kidney cancer and her renal function began to fail. Zink, who had cared for Holcomb for more than 15 years, said she had no hesitation about donating because she could not bear to see her friend die. After about a year of testing the pair were found to be a perfect match and underwent a transplant in July. Zink has fully recovered and Holcomb’s condition is improving. The women remain close, wear kidney-shaped necklaces to mark their bond, and hope their story encourages others to consider organ donation. For more donor information they point to the National Kidney Foundation’s resources.

Research In Motion (RIM), maker of BlackBerry, is facing a deep and prolonged crisis. Analysts expect RIM to report a fiscal Q1 net loss (consensus: $0.03 per share loss on about $3.1 billion revenue), a sharp deterioration from last year’s $1.33 per-share profit on nearly $5 billion. Shares have plunged roughly 68–70% over the past year, market value falling below $5 billion, and device sales and subscriber adds have deteriorated.

Multiple factors underlie RIM’s decline:
- Strategic missteps and overconfidence in its physical-keyboard BlackBerrys while touch-screen, app-centric smartphones from Apple and Android makers rapidly gained share.
- Product misfires and late, ineffective catch-up devices (e.g., Storm, Torch, PlayBook) that failed to regain consumer buzz or stem defections.
- Internal management dysfunction: for years RIM operated with co-CEOs Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie running largely separate fiefdoms, which former executives say produced poor communication, conflicting strategies, and tensions—complicating responses to market shifts. Balsillie pursued licensing and partnerships while Lazaridis focused on an OS and device remake.
- A stalled transition to new software/hardware: RIM is banking on the BlackBerry 10 OS and new phones to revive fortunes, but analysts and some insiders view the pipeline as unlikely to reverse the immediate revenue falloff. Wedge Partners predicted steep near-term declines and a potential forced sale in 2013.
- Attempts to pivot (licensing intellectual property, selling the devices unit) drew skepticism from analysts who see limited value in RIM’s manufacturing capabilities despite some valuable messaging and email technology.

Current position and outlook:
- New CEO Thorsten Heins (since January) is cutting costs, halted the previous licensing push, and has engaged bankers to explore strategic options, including a possible sale, while emphasizing the BlackBerry 10 rollout. RIM remains cash-rich (over $2 billion) and debt-free, giving it some runway.
- However, investor confidence is low; guidance for upcoming quarters could be worse, and many worry the company may be forced into a sale or restructuring if new products don’t gain traction.

In short, RIM is confronting steep revenue and market-share decline driven by product, strategic and organizational failures. Its short-term survival hinges on the success of BlackBerry 10 and possible strategic alternatives, but many analysts see a bleak near-term outlook.

More than $1 million in jewelry was stolen from Diva Diamonds & Jewels on the Santa Fe Plaza the night after Thanksgiving while the plaza was crowded for the city’s annual holiday tree-lighting. Santa Fe Police say a trio — two men and a woman — entered the busy store between about 5:15 and 5:30 p.m., removed 11 items from an unlocked display case, and left without being noticed; employees discovered the loss about 6 p.m. Investigators believe the suspects had scouted the shop in the weeks before the theft, and security-camera images from the event and prior visits have been released. Police say downtown jewelry thefts are common but not usually this large; they have some leads but are asking the public for help identifying the suspects. Tips can be reported to the Santa Fe Police (general line 505-428-3710) or directly to Detectives Abe Maes (505-231-6497) or Matthew Champlin (505-469-5707). The store’s owner, Ala (Mark) Shawabkeh, also owns other local jewelry businesses; employees at the targeted shop declined to comment per police direction.
