North Carolina’s Republican-led legislature has approved a broad gun bill that tightens penalties for firearm-law violations, expands where concealed handgun permit (CHP) holders may carry, and increases the information available for background checks. The measure now goes to Gov. Pat McCrory.

Key provisions:
- CHP holders may carry in bars and restaurants that serve alcohol (provided they don’t consume alcohol), in funeral processions, on greenways, playgrounds and other public recreation areas, and may keep locked firearms in vehicles parked on public school and university campuses.
- The bill preserves the current county sheriff-issued handgun purchase permit system (a previously proposed repeal was removed) but limits sheriffs’ discretion: they can no longer cap the number of permits an individual may obtain in a year and must document and justify any permit denials.
- Concealed-permit holder information is removed from public view.
- Penalties for firearm-law violations are increased, and mental-health and other information available in the state background-check system is expanded.

Votes: House 73-41; Senate 32-14. Supporters argue CHP holders undergo extra checks and training; opponents, including some university representatives, say allowing guns on campuses and in alcohol-serving venues raises safety concerns.

A 14-year-old U.S.-born boy known as "El Ponchis" was arrested in early December at an airport near Cuernavaca, Mexico, while trying to fly to Tijuana with two sisters and tickets to cross into San Diego. Identified only as Edgar because he is a minor, he told authorities he was kidnapped at 11 and forced to work for the Cartel of the South Pacific (a splinter of the Beltrán Leyva organization). Edgar admitted—saying he was drugged and threatened—to participating in at least four beheadings and other killings; Mexican reports said he was paid roughly $2,500–$3,000 per killing. Photographs of tortured victims were reportedly found on his phones.

Officials say the teen and several others confessed to murdering people and displaying bodies in public in Cuernavaca to intimidate rivals and authorities. Two of his teenage sisters are accused of acting as decoys and helping dispose of corpses; one sister claims to have been the girlfriend of a cartel leader, Julio "El Negro" Padilla, who controls fighting in Morelos. The detained youths came from a Jiutepec safe house in a poor Cuernavaca suburb. Mexican authorities are checking Edgar’s citizenship status; U.S. officials had not yet confirmed it.

The case highlights a broader trend: cartels increasingly recruit younger suspects—partly because they face lighter penalties in Mexico—driving up the number of juveniles detained for drug-related crimes since President Felipe Calderón’s 2006 offensive. Because juveniles in Mexico are typically handled by state courts and released at 18, Morelos authorities requested federal takeover of the case given its severity.

Bethany Townsend, a 23-year-old makeup artist from Worcester, England, who has had Crohn’s disease since age three, posed in a bikini showing the two colostomy bags she received after a life‑saving 2010 operation. Devastated initially and having given up modeling, she regained confidence after encouragement from her husband Ian during a holiday in Mexico and later shared the photo via Crohn’s and Colitis UK. The image went viral—viewed by millions, earning hundreds of thousands of likes and thousands of comments—prompting overwhelmingly positive responses and raising awareness of Crohn’s disease. Townsend says the reaction helped her accept her stomas, inspired others, and convinced her to return to modeling part‑time; she has since booked work, including for a lingerie brand that designs for people with colostomies. She continues to battle active Crohn’s and is exploring further treatments, but remains hopeful and determined to use her story to challenge beauty norms and support others with similar conditions.

A Ku Klux Klan rally protesting Charlottesville’s decision to remove the Robert E. Lee statue drew heavy counterprotest and a large police presence on a hot Saturday. About 30 Loyal White Knights KKK members, some armed and wearing robes, gathered at Justice Park and were escorted by police in riot gear to separate them from roughly 1,000 counterprotesters who drowned out Klan speakers with boos and chants. Vandals had painted the Lee statue overnight in nearby Emancipation (Lee) Park; the statue remains in place pending a court order and upcoming hearings.

More than 100 officers from multiple agencies were on hand. After the rally, police declared a nearby counterprotest an unlawful assembly, used gas canisters to disperse people and arrested 22; three people were hospitalized (two for heat-related issues and one for alcohol-related problems). City officials praised law enforcement for maintaining order, while many local residents and academics attended the counterprotest to denounce the Klan and support removing Confederate tributes. Opinions among attendees varied: some argued the statue erases history if removed, others said it honors a racist past and should go.

Charlottesville, home to the University of Virginia, has been tense over the issue; city leaders organized diversionary events and urged nonconfrontation. Another larger rally by white nationalist groups was permitted for Aug. 12, and legal battles over removing the statue are expected to continue.

Hannah Upp, a 32-year-old Montessori teacher with a rare form of dissociative amnesia called dissociative fugue, disappeared from her St. Thomas apartment on September 14 and remained missing as Hurricane Maria struck the U.S. Virgin Islands. Her car was found at Sapphire Beach and her sandals, sarong and dress were discovered on the shore. Colleagues and friends filed a police report, circulated flyers, checked hospitals and shelters, and mounted local searches, but efforts have been hampered by hurricane damage, poor cell service and diverted federal search resources.

Upp has had two prior fugue episodes: in 2008 she vanished during a run in Manhattan for nearly three weeks and was later found off an island with no memory of her travels; in 2013 she disappeared for about two days in Maryland. Friends and coworkers say stress can trigger such episodes and hope she may be wandering in a confused state rather than harmed. Family released a statement expressing fear and hope for her safe return. School officials stressed that people in a fugue can appear functional yet not be themselves, urging continued vigilance and optimism.

Summary:

Democrats’ stance on big-money politics shifted after the 2012 elections. Initially reluctant to embrace super PACs and large undisclosed donations—viewing them as a consequence of rulings like Citizens United—major Democratic donors and organizations have largely overcome those qualms following electoral success. At a private Democracy Alliance conference, senior Democratic leaders and officials met with top liberal outside groups (including Priorities USA Action, American Bridge 21st Century, House Majority PAC, America Votes, and EMILY’s List) to plan expanding a permanent network of independent groups that can mobilize money and infrastructure for 2014 and beyond, including potential involvement in state politics, policy fights and primaries. New Democratic megadonors emerged in 2012 and many pledge faster, larger responses in future cycles to compete with better-funded Republican outside networks.

Meanwhile, state regulators are increasingly pushing back against opaque tax-exempt nonprofits that spent heavily in 2012 and refuse to disclose donors. While federal agencies (the FEC and IRS) are gridlocked or slow to act, several states with stricter disclosure laws have forced revelations or are investigating groups that funneled large amounts into state campaigns. Notable cases include California’s probe into an $11 million routed through multiple nonprofits to influence ballot measures (labeled “campaign money laundering”), Idaho’s court-ordered disclosure of donors to Education Voters of Idaho, and disclosure battles involving American Tradition Partnership in Montana. Advocates for transparency argue state actions prove disclosure is achievable despite federal stalemate; groups on the other side contend they are operating lawfully as 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations and say the rules remain unclear.

A 22-year-old Middletown man, Tony Moreno, jumped from the Arrigoni Bridge into the Connecticut River around 11:45 p.m. on Sunday, July 5, 2015, after calling someone and threatening suicide. The caller reported hearing Moreno’s 7-month-old son, Aaden, crying in the background and dialed 911. Responding officers witnessed Moreno jump; firefighters pulled him from the water and he was airlifted to a hospital in serious condition but was later conscious and alert. Police believe the infant entered the river with his father and, after an initial nearly 24-hour search, reclassified the operation as a recovery. Searches using boats, paddleboards and jet skis resumed Tuesday, but officials said river conditions—poor underwater visibility and variable currents—make recovery difficult and the likelihood of finding the child alive is slim. Aaden was described in the Silver Alert as about 2 feet tall and 23 pounds, last seen in black pants and a black-and-white striped Mickey Mouse shirt. Authorities continue to investigate and expect to file charges; the community held a candlelight vigil and a Facebook group supporting the search grew rapidly. Advocates noted the case echoes patterns seen in domestic violence incidents, referencing an earlier restraining-order application by the child’s mother. Middletown police asked anyone with information to call 860-638-4000.

A decomposing body was found inside a brick entrance column at the WinCo Foods on the 700 block of West Avenue K in Lancaster on Saturday afternoon. Store staff investigated a strong, foul odor and a plumber and handyman removed bricks from the column, revealing a shoe, a leg and eventually the body. The coroner later identified the deceased as 35-year-old Raymundo Rivera; an autopsy was pending.

Los Angeles County Sheriff’s homicide detectives believe the man may be the suspect who led deputies on a traffic stop chase the previous Monday, crashed, ran into the WinCo, and disappeared after getting onto the roof. Investigators say there is roof access to the store’s fascia and interior crawlspaces; they suspect the man may have entered the crawlspace or fallen into the column and become trapped. It is unclear whether he died from a fall, entrapment, exposure or other causes. The supermarket remained closed while crews recovered the body and investigators processed the scene. Anyone with information was asked to contact the LASD Homicide Bureau or Crime Stoppers.

A humpback mother and calf became stranded on a sandbar off North Stradbroke Island (Dunwich), about 80 km east of Brisbane. Reports began Thursday night; the pair had likely been stuck overnight and became stranded again. Early Wednesday morning the calf was seen swimming anxiously and apparently nudging and pushing the distressed mother as she splashed to dislodge herself. About 40 minutes after becoming stuck, the mother freed herself at roughly 8:15 a.m. Queensland Parks and Wildlife Services (QPWS) and Sea World teams were dispatched and a QPWS boat trailed the whales to guide them through shallow water to avoid restranding until they reached deeper sea. The mother was tired but both animals ultimately swam away. Whales are common off Queensland at this time of year when many give birth and rear calves before returning to Antarctic waters.

Summary:

The article traces how the term "fake news" has shifted from meaning outright fabrications (e.g., made-up stories about Donald Trump) to a broader political weapon deployed by conservatives—most notably President Trump—to label any unfavorable coverage as false. Trump has even called negative polls "fake news" and promoted a Federalist list alleging 16 fake stories since his election. The author examines several items on that list and finds most are not deliberate fabrications: a few were errors (e.g., Time pool reporter Zeke Miller misreporting the visibility of the Martin Luther King Jr. bust in the Oval Office), some were hoaxes originating from bad actors on social media (a parody Twitter account posing as Reuters), and one was an unsupported social-media claim about a photoshopped hand. Others cited were accurate but framed mockingly by left-leaning outlets (coverage of Betsy DeVos's "grizzlies" comment), which is not the same as fake news. The piece also notes CNN's Chris Cuomo likened calling journalists "fake news" to a racial slur in its sting and offensive impact; Cuomo later apologized. Overall, the article argues that conflating honest mistakes, snarky framing, or legitimate reporting with "fake news" dangerously broadens the term and unfairly implies malicious intent.

A cat ran onto the field during the Royals-Cardinals game at Busch Stadium Wednesday night, interrupting play in the bottom of the sixth with the bases loaded and two outs. The animal wandered near Cardinals center fielder Lorenzo Cain before a stadium employee chased it down; the cat scratched and bit the employee resisting capture. On the very next pitch Yadier Molina hit a grand slam, turning a 5-4 Royals lead into an 8-5 Cardinals advantage that held for the win. The victory moved St. Louis into second in the NL Central, 1.5 games behind the Cubs. Manager Mike Matheny joked about the incident, and Molina quipped he’d seen a “rally” animal before (the 2011 “Rally Squirrel”); fans have dubbed the intruder “Yadi the Rally Cat.”

Univision has located Yaneisi Fernandez, a 21-year-old Dominican woman who was named in government records as one of the women allegedly hired as a prostitute for outings involving Sen. Robert Menendez (D‑N.J.) and Florida eye doctor Dr. Salomon Melgen. Fernandez and her family deny the allegation; she says she has never engaged in prostitution, never met Menendez, and has never visited Casa de Campo. Univision reports her mother says Fernandez is a college student and the identification is a misunderstanding.

The reporting comes amid wider scrutiny of Menendez after the FBI raided Melgen’s office and records surfaced showing Menendez reimbursed Melgen for private‑jet flights to the Dominican Republic. The Daily Caller initially reported allegations that Menendez patronized prostitutes — some underage — at Melgen’s Dominican estate. Menendez has denied the allegations.

The controversy has drawn investigations by the Senate Ethics Committee and federal authorities and renewed attention to Menendez’s ties to Melgen, including Menendez’s advocacy on behalf of a Melgen company seeking a Dominican port‑security contract. Despite the scandal, Menendez retains support from top Democrats and faces no immediate political fallout in New Jersey, where he remains a prominent and politically resilient figure.

Three Cleveland women—Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus and Michelle Knight—who were held captive for about a decade have said they are "happy and safe" and continue to heal, according to a letter released by their attorneys thanking the public for support and for respecting their request for privacy. The attorneys said the women are overwhelmed and grateful for offers of help and that the media has largely left their neighborhoods, which has aided their recovery.

Donations worldwide have poured in through the Cleveland Courage Fund: reports cite more than $650,000 initially and later roughly $825,000 collected. The fund is being distributed to the three women and Amanda’s 6‑year‑old daughter; trustees say the money will be equally split among the four once trusts are formalized and that 100% of future Cleveland Courage Fund donations will go into those trusts. Offers of medical, dental and other services, and volunteer help (including housing and cars), have also been made and some funds are already being used.

The women escaped on May 6 from a house owned by Ariel Castro; Berry freed herself and her daughter after calling 911, and police found DeJesus and Knight in the home. Castro, 52, is jailed on multiple kidnapping and rape charges on an $8 million bond. The case has spurred renewed attention to missing-persons investigations in Cleveland and prompted proposals such as a state bill to provide financial and educational aid to long-term kidnapping survivors. Local officials have taken steps in the neighborhood around the house (now boarded up), and residents have discussed tearing it down and planting trees in honor of the victims.

The U.N. Security Council on Saturday unanimously approved a statement calling for de-escalation, restoration of calm, and a return to direct Israeli-Palestinian negotiations aimed at a two-state solution. It urged reinstatement of the November 2012 cease-fire brokered by Egypt but set no timeline; Palestinian UN envoy Riyad Mansour said Palestinians expect it to take effect immediately and warned the council would be pressed further if Israel did not comply.

The statement, a nonbinding reflection of international opinion, urged protection of civilians and respect for international humanitarian law but did not name Hamas rocket fire or Israel’s military response. The council’s move followed intense international pressure, including calls for a cease-fire from Britain and diplomatic meetings planned in Vienna. Arab foreign ministers were also to meet to press for an end to what Mansour called aggression that has left more than 1,000 Palestinians killed or injured, according to him; Israeli officials say there have been no Israeli fatalities from the Gaza rocket fire.

The U.S. reiterated support for Israel’s right to defend itself while expressing concern about escalation and saying it was ready to help facilitate a cease-fire. Palestinians and their supporters had drafted a resolution calling for an immediate, durable cease-fire and condemning civilian casualties; it did not mention rockets from Gaza and would likely face a U.S. veto.

On the ground, Israel conducted raids and airstrikes in Gaza. Israeli forces briefly sent troops to raid a rocket-launching site—wounding four soldiers—and ordered residents of northern Gaza to evacuate, warning of intensified strikes. Five days of Israeli strikes had produced at least 156 Palestinian casualties; Israel said its forces had struck over 60 targets overnight, totaling some 1,160 since the start of Operation Protective Edge. Strikes included a mosque suspected of housing weapons, raising fears of further escalation during Ramadan. Israeli leaders said they were preparing all options, including a ground invasion. U.S. leaders voiced concern and urged restraint.

A California appeals court ruled that the 2006 state law banning handheld cellphone use while driving does not prohibit looking at a map app, overturning a $165 ticket issued to Fresno driver Steven Spriggs. Spriggs was cited in January 2012 for viewing a map on his iPhone while stopped in traffic; lower courts had upheld the ticket. In a unanimous 18-page opinion the 5th District Court of Appeal said the statute targets hands-on talking and listening (i.e., conversations) and was not written to ban all handheld uses such as checking maps or the time. The judges noted the Legislature later enacted a separate texting-while-driving ban, indicating the original law did not already cover all handheld uses. Spriggs, who uses hands-free calling and whose son was injured by a distracted driver, sought the ruling to prompt clearer legislation; he is entitled to his fine back. The state attorney general’s office is reviewing whether to seek review by the California Supreme Court.

Here are concise summaries of the documents provided:

1) Houston — Child abuse case
- Anthony Powell, 24, pleaded guilty to beating his three-year-old son, Tristan, to death. Court records say Powell struck the child repeatedly during potty-training accidents and at one point picked him up “like a rag doll” after knocking him down. Powell was convicted and faces a 60-year prison sentence.

2) Alexa Internet and the Internet Archive
- Since 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive. These daily data contributions are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.

3) Port Arthur — Man and dog die trapped in Corvette
- James Rogers, 72, and his Shih Tzu “Baby Girl” Leia died of suspected heat exhaustion after becoming trapped inside a recently purchased 2007 Corvette in a Waffle House parking lot. Investigators believe an unsecured cable caused the car to lose power when the door shut, disabling electronic locks and the horn. Rogers had left his cell phone inside the restaurant and apparently tried to attract help and pry himself free; fingerprints were found on the window. The 2007 Corvette does have a manual door-release on the floorboard that Rogers apparently didn’t know about. First responders ultimately had to break a window. An autopsy was planned; Rogers, a Thomas Jefferson High School graduate and U.S. Army veteran, is survived by three children and five grandchildren. Funeral visitation and service details were provided.

Donald Trump will be inaugurated next month as the 45th U.S. president despite losing the national popular vote by nearly 3 million ballots. With all 50 states and D.C. certified, the Cook Political Report tallied Hillary Clinton at 65,844,610 votes (48.2%) and Trump at 62,979,636 (46.1%); other candidates received 7,804,213 votes (5.7%).

Clinton’s popular-vote margin is the largest ever for a candidate who lost the Electoral College and is about six times larger than Al Gore’s 2000 margin. Trump secured the presidency via the Electoral College, winning 306 electoral votes on Election Day; when electors cast their ballots, he received 304 (two Republican defectors) and Clinton 227 (five Democratic defectors), with seven faithless electors voting for others.

The outcome has revived calls from many Democrats and commentators to abolish the Electoral College, which allowed a candidate with fewer total votes to win the White House.

Jimmy Kimmel addressed the news that Toys”R”Us is closing all 735 stores during his March 16, 2018 show, joking about online shopping and Amazon putting other retailers out of business. The segment featured an appearance by Geoffrey the Giraffe, the store’s mascot, who tearfully lamented the chain’s bankruptcy—at one point angrily blaming customers for buying from Amazon, admitting he was drunk, and singing the old “I’m a Toys’R’Us Kid” jingle. Kimmel comforted him and had his sidekick Guillermo escort Geoffrey offstage. The bit was presented as a comedic, bittersweet take on the retailer’s shutdown.

Summary:

After a racially motivated mass shooting at an African-American church in Charleston, S.C., former GOP presidential nominee Mitt Romney publicly urged immediate removal of the Confederate battle flag from the South Carolina Statehouse grounds, calling it “a symbol of racial hatred.” His statement prompted other Republican figures and potential 2016 presidential candidates to respond, though many stopped short of explicitly calling for removal and left the decision to South Carolina officials.

Responses among Republicans varied:
- Jeb Bush noted his 2001 decision to remove the flag from Florida’s Capitol grounds and supported a similar discussion in South Carolina after a period of mourning.
- Mitt Romney and several others (including Ohio Gov. John Kasich) expressed personal opposition to the flag’s display.
- Scott Walker, Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio, Carly Fiorina and others either urged deference to South Carolina’s process, avoided a definitive stance, or stressed local decision-making; Cruz emphasized understanding both views (those who see the flag as oppression and those who see heritage).
- Lindsey Graham and others emphasized the shooter’s culpability rather than the flag.
- Democrats, including President Obama and earlier Hillary Clinton statements, supported moving the flag to a museum.

The document also contains extended transcripts and excerpts from past Republican debates and candidate appearances on a wide range of topics — immigration, taxes, spending, Social Security, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, interrogation techniques (waterboarding), gay service members, abortion, the death penalty, gun rights, crime, race and outreach to minority voters, infrastructure and space policy. Key recurring themes among GOP speakers included calls for stronger border enforcement and opposition to amnesty; a focus on cutting spending and reforming entitlements; support for the troop surge/continued engagement in Iraq from some (notably John McCain) and calls to withdraw from others (notably Ron Paul); firm opposition to torture by McCain and disagreement over interrogation practices by others; defense of the Second Amendment with room for state regulation by some; a range of positions on social issues tied to personal faith and states’ rights; and debates over fiscal conservatism, pork spending and how to prioritize infrastructure and defense.

Overall, the immediate news focus is Romney’s call to remove the Confederate battle flag and the mixed reactions from GOP figures, set against a broader backdrop of ongoing intra-party debates about policy, values and electoral strategy.

Casey Johnson, a 30-year-old heir to the Johnson & Johnson fortune and daughter of Jets owner Woody Johnson, spent her final months in severe decline, according to multiple reports. Once heir to a multibillion-dollar estate, she was living in a rundown rented Los Angeles home without utilities and reportedly surrounded by squalor and a rotating circle of problematic companions. Friends and acquaintances described increasing substance abuse—prescription medications (OxyContin, Klonopin, Adderall) and illicit drugs (marijuana, ecstasy, cocaine)—and repeated health crises tied to brittle diabetes; sources say she had several hospital visits and two recent ICU stays for diabetic emergencies. Family members dispute claims that missed insulin was to blame, saying she used an insulin pump though her diabetes had become harder to control.

Over the past year Johnson’s life included legal and personal troubles: arrests for alleged grand theft after several break-ins, a public accusation of stealing from friend Jasmine Lennard, loss of custody of her adopted daughter, a suicide attempt in November when she was hospitalized after texting that she had taken many pills, and an early exit from rehab after being urged to seek treatment. Financially she’d also fallen behind—losing a Porsche lease and losing a lawsuit to a nanny agency.

In December she drew tabloid attention after announcing an engagement to reality personality Tila Tequila in a video in which friends say she appeared impaired. On Dec. 29 she tweeted “Sweet dreams everyone”; her body was found six days later. Initial autopsy was inconclusive with no obvious trauma or signs of suicide; toxicology results were expected to take weeks and police reported only an insignificant amount of prescription pills at the scene. Her family arranged to return her body to New Jersey, will hold a private funeral, and set up a memorial fund with the Juvenile Diabetes Foundation, noting her lifelong struggle with the disease.

J.J. Abrams has assembled a blend of original stars, established actors and fresh faces for Star Wars: Episode VII, officially titled Star Wars: The Force Awakens, scheduled for release Dec. 18, 2015. Returning veterans Harrison Ford (Han Solo), Carrie Fisher (Leia) and Mark Hamill (Luke) join franchise regulars Anthony Daniels (C-3PO), Kenny Baker (R2-D2) and Peter Mayhew (Chewbacca). Abrams also cast older film royalty Max von Sydow and performance-capture specialist Andy Serkis, plus recognizable talents Oscar Isaac and Adam Driver.

The film introduces a new generation of leads — John Boyega, Domhnall Gleeson and newcomer Daisy Ridley — alongside Lupita Nyong’o and Gwendoline Christie, creating a mix of proven performers and rising stars intended to pass the saga to a younger cast while honoring the originals. Billy Dee Williams’s return as Lando was notably absent from the announced lineup.

Principal photography has wrapped amid some on-set incidents (including Harrison Ford’s broken leg) and numerous leaks and rumors. The title, The Force Awakens, suggests a focus on both legacy elements and new characters; few plot details have been released. The movie is produced by Kathleen Kennedy and Bryan Burke.

Three crew members from the International Space Station — NASA astronauts Peggy Whitson and Jack Fischer, and Russian cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin — safely landed in their Soyuz MS-04 spacecraft on the Kazakh steppe on Sept. 2 (local Sept. 3), ending their mission. The descent began when the Soyuz undocked from the Poisk module and, after atmospheric reentry and parachute deployment, touched down near Dzhezkazgan. The capsule tipped onto its side (a common occurrence); recovery teams reached the crew by helicopter and took them to on-site medical checks before transporting them onward.

Peggy Whitson set several records on this flight: she accrued a total of 665 days in space (288 on this mission), making her the U.S. record-holder for cumulative time in space and the most experienced female astronaut; her 288-day stay was the longest single spaceflight by a woman. She also became the world’s oldest spacewoman and the most experienced female spacewalker. Fyodor Yurchikhin now has 673 total days in space, placing him seventh on the all-time list; Jack Fischer completed his first flight, totaling 136 days.

Because Hurricane Harvey disrupted NASA’s Gulfstream jet, the European Space Agency provided an aircraft to ferry Whitson and Fischer to Cologne, Germany; they will then connect to NASA transport to return to Houston. Yurchikhin will return to Russia. After landing, the astronauts will undergo a busy 45-day period of medical tests, physical rehabilitation and debriefs. Back on the station, three crew members (Randy Bresnik, Paolo Nespoli and Sergey Ryazansky) remain until the next Soyuz (MS-05) brings Joe Acaba, Mark Vande Hei and Alexander Misurkin on Sept. 12.

A new political action committee, "Trump Has Tiny Hands PAC," was launched by Portland resident Henry Kraemer to mock Republican front-runner Donald Trump over repeated jabs about the size of his hands — and the insinuation about his anatomy — that have circulated on the 2016 campaign trail. The hand-size ribbing began after Marco Rubio quipped that “you can’t trust” men with small hands; Trump angrily denied the charge, defended his hands at debates and rallies, and accused Rubio of inventing the story. Kraemer said he started the PAC when Trump began denying he has “tiny baby hands” and argued voters should know whether Trump could, for example, pick up a phone at 3 a.m. before they vote. The story also notes businesses and commentators have joined the mockery — Yelp referenced the joke in an app update, and writer Graydon Carter long nicknamed Trump a “short-fingered vulgarian,” recounting Trump’s efforts to prove otherwise. The document also mentions, separately, that the collection of sources includes diverse coverage of the Hillary Clinton email controversy.

Two Vermont lawmakers, Reps. Jean O’Sullivan and Christopher Pearson, have filed a provocative bill (House Bill 502) that would effectively reinstate alcohol prohibition in the state—making alcohol possession a misdemeanor with fines up to $500 and imposing penalties for sale and distribution of up to 30 years in prison and $1 million in fines. The sponsors say they do not actually want to ban alcohol; the measure is a tactical move intended to embarrass legislative leadership and pressure lawmakers to act on separate legalization proposals for marijuana (H.277 in the House and S.95 in the Senate).

The lawmakers argue the contrast highlights a scientific and public-health point: research shows marijuana is substantially less harmful than alcohol (one cited study found marijuana had the lowest mortality risk among ten common recreational drugs), and marijuana has no confirmed overdose deaths, whereas tens of thousands of Americans die annually from excessive alcohol use. They also point to a RAND estimate that Vermonters spent $125–$225 million on marijuana in 2014 and that a regulated, taxed market could generate $20–$70 million a year—relevant as the state faces a large budget deficit. The prohibition bill has drawn attention but has not advanced in the legislature.

Supporters quickly rebuilt the Michael Brown memorial on Canfield Drive in Ferguson, Mo., after a vehicle reportedly ran over and scattered flowers, signs and mementos left for the 18‑year‑old who was shot and killed by Officer Darren Wilson in August. Photos and eyewitnesses posted on social media prompted residents to gather and restore the makeshift shrine by Friday morning.

Ferguson Police public information officer Timothy (Tim) Zoll initially told The Washington Post no crime had been reported and questioned whether the incident warranted attention, calling the memorial “a pile of trash in the middle of the street” and suggesting he had been misquoted. After city officials opened an internal inquiry and Zoll admitted he had misled superiors about his remarks, he was placed on unpaid leave while the department evaluates disciplinary action. The city said Zoll’s comments did not reflect the department’s stance and reiterated efforts to relocate the memorial to a more secure location and rebuild trust with the community.

The article describes unusual tourist “massage” attractions that many find unsettling. It first covers snake massages, where large nonvenomous snakes press and knead a person’s body while smaller ones may slither over the face—footage reportedly shows snakes across a man’s eyes. Though touted as nonvenomous and therapeutic by operators, the writer calls the practice creepy and suggests many other animals would be better choices. The piece then criticizes elephant-backed massages in Thailand’s Maesa Elephant Camp, where elephants—sometimes switched from promised babies to adults—step on tourists’ backs to “ease stress.” The author highlights the obvious safety and ethical concerns, mocking the idea that such encounters are relaxing.

President Obama delivered a forceful defense of the July 14 Iran nuclear agreement in a major speech at American University, framing the congressional fight over the deal as the most consequential foreign-policy debate since the Iraq War. He argued the pact—the result of two years of diplomacy that would lift some sanctions in exchange for curbs and unprecedented inspections of Iran’s nuclear program—is the best available way to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, and warned that rejecting it would damage U.S. credibility, isolate America diplomatically, and raise the prospect of another Middle East war.

The White House is aggressively campaigning to shore up Democratic support before Congress returns from recess and before heavy lobbying and ad campaigns by opponents (notably Aipac and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu) intensify. Administration officials will make senior leaders, including Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz, widely available for calls, interviews and domestic appearances; Obama and his team aim to persuade undecided lawmakers and to build enough Democratic backing to sustain a presidential veto of any congressional disapproval.

Obama repeatedly linked opponents of the deal to proponents of the Iraq War, contending that the same mindset favoring military solutions risks repeating past mistakes. He dismissed claims that there is a better alternative to the deal, argued inspections provisions are robust, and rejected the notion that lifting sanctions will inevitably strengthen Iran’s regional aggression—urging instead that the U.S. confront such behavior directly and bolster partners’ defenses.

The speech drew sharp partisan pushback. Republicans—Senate leaders and critics including John McCain, Lindsey Graham and Bob Corker—called his rhetoric unfair, particularly his charge that they were making “common cause” with Iranian hard-liners. Some supporters warned Obama's tone risked alienating potential allies. Nevertheless, several Senate Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents publicly announced support in the days after the address, while influential Jewish groups remained split.

With Congress able to block the administration’s plan unless a two-thirds majority overrides a veto, the White House is campaigning intensively to secure enough Democratic votes before the September vote deadline.

Wayne Flynt, Auburn University professor emeritus and longtime friend of Harper Lee, has published Mockingbird Songs: My Friendship With Harper Lee, drawing on decades of correspondence and visits—he was one of the few people Lee continued to see after she moved into a nursing home before her 2016 death. In an exclusive New York Times interview tied to the book’s release, Flynt shares new insights into the famously reclusive author:

- Lee asked only that Flynt wait to write about her until after her death; he says the book lets her “speak beyond the grave” without violating her privacy while alive.
- Fear of obsessive fans and even assassination attempts helped drive her retreat from publicity; she once had a stalker.
- Lee called Truman Capote a “compulsive liar” in a March 2006 letter to Flynt. The two were childhood friends and collaborators—Lee assisted Capote’s research on the Clutter murders and edited his draft of In Cold Blood—but their friendship soured over jealousy after Lee’s success with To Kill a Mockingbird. Lee told Flynt, “I did something Truman could not forgive: I wrote a novel that sold,” and said Capote nursed envy for decades.
- Lee suffered intense pre-interview nerves, sometimes vomiting before speaking engagements.
- Regarding the controversial publication of her earlier manuscript Go Set a Watchman, Flynt says Lee “may not have fully participated” in that decision because of age and health issues, though she welcomed its publication at the time.

Mockingbird Songs, based largely on their letters and Flynt’s recollections, promises new personal context about Lee’s life, relationships, and attitudes toward fame.

Jamie Tull, 33, a former public elementary school teacher from Modesto, Calif., was found alive on Aug. 4, 2017, nearly three weeks after crashing her vehicle into a ditch near Le Grand in Merced County. Family and friends located her about half a mile (less than a mile/1.6 km) from the crash site in desolate grazing land, lying in tall grass and close to a cattle water trough. Emaciated, badly sunburned and weak, she was able to speak; she told rescuers she wanted food and water and said she did not want to be found. Authorities said Tull had been enduring a heatwave, had stopped taking prescription medication for emotional issues, and survived by drinking from the cattle trough and eating a few insects. She was airlifted to a Fresno hospital and then returned to relatives for care. Her father said she has bipolar disorder and had not taken medication for months. Investigators believe she remained in the immediate area without shelter while missing. Searchers said efforts would have been scaled back had she not been located then.

A veteran collapsed in the cafeteria at the Raymond G. Murphy VA Medical Center in Albuquerque and died after a lengthy delay getting to the hospital’s emergency room, officials confirmed. The man — reported as about 71 in some accounts, name not released — collapsed on Monday roughly 500 yards (about a five-minute walk) from the ER. VA staff say they followed a local policy requiring them to call 911 for emergencies occurring outside the main hospital building. An ambulance was dispatched and arrived after a delay; accounts differ on exact timings but at least 14 minutes elapsed before paramedics reached him and 20–30 minutes before he arrived at the ER. Kirtland Air Force medical personnel performed CPR until the ambulance arrived, but the veteran could not be saved.

The incident has prompted the VA to review the local policy that led staff to call external emergency services rather than transport the patient across campus, and officials say that policy varies among VA centers. Questions remain about whether an AED was available and whether on-site clinicians could or did respond. The death drew criticism from visiting veterans and concern from lawmakers; it comes amid broader scrutiny of the Veterans Health Administration over chronic delays, systemic failures and a recent federal review calling for major reforms. The VA and national officials have offered limited immediate comment while local policy and the case are under review.

Attorney Fernando Benitez, representing 18-year-old Ethan Couch in Mexico, says he is challenging the Mexican immigration detention and possible summary deportation as a constitutional and international law matter and is seeking to ensure Couch is not mistreated under the Mexican constitution. Couch and his mother, Tonya, were arrested in Puerto Vallarta after allegedly fleeing the U.S. following a probation violation related to Couch’s 2013 drunk-driving crash that killed four people; Couch had been sentenced to 10 years’ juvenile probation after pleading guilty to multiple counts of intoxication manslaughter and assault. Benitez obtained a temporary injunction delaying Couch’s deportation and said an evidentiary hearing may not occur until the end of the month, with a judge having up to 90 days to rule and appeals possible, potentially stretching the process into months.

Benitez denied reports Couch had a gun when detained and argued Mexican authorities sought a rushed deportation that could deny due process; his petition claims potential violations of Couch’s constitutional and civil rights in Mexico. Couch is being held in an immigration detention center in Mexico City; Tonya Couch was deported to the U.S. and is charged in Tarrant County with hindering apprehension, held on $1 million bond. Tarrant County officials say prosecutors plan to ask that Couch’s case be moved to adult court; a probation-violation hearing is set for Jan. 19. Legal observers say staying in Mexico long-term would likely require an asylum claim, which is unlikely to succeed based on the “affluenza” defense that drew national attention during the original sentencing.

The Daily Caller began promoting a weekly gun giveaway through Election Day 2012: new email subscribers to its site could win an FMK9C1 9mm pistol “engraved with the Bill of Rights.” The gun is produced by FMK Firearms, whose founder Jim Pontillo uses his company website and op-eds to advance strongly right-wing views—attacking progressives as collectivists who favor “communism,” arguing that secessionists are “middle class” Americans in the “Founding tradition,” criticizing liberalism for weakening reliance on church and community, and saying gun ownership counters liberal policies.

The giveaway page explains entry is limited to U.S. residents in states where firearms transfers are legal; winners must be 21+, pass an ATF Form 4473 and a NICS background check at an FFL dealer, and pay any retailer transfer fees. The Daily Caller and FMK outline standard rules: winners’ identities can be used for promotion, prizes are forfeitable, the sponsor disclaims warranties and limits liability, and the contest is subject to Delaware law. The Caller’s “Guns and Gear” section, launched in December, largely republishes NRA-related content and has been active in critiquing the Obama administration and AG Eric Holder over ATF’s Operation Fast and Furious.

Clarissa Dickson Wright, the larger-than-life cook, food historian and television personality best known as one half of the BBC’s Two Fat Ladies, has died in Edinburgh at 66 after several months of treatment. Celebrated for her formidable intellect, deep knowledge of British food history and unapologetic, non–politically correct persona, she rose from a privileged but troubled childhood and an early career as one of the youngest female barristers in England to public prominence in her 40s.

Key points:
- Two Fat Ladies: Partnered with Jennifer Paterson, Dickson Wright became famous from the 1996–99 BBC series in which the pair toured Britain in a motorcycle and sidecar, cooking richly traditional dishes and courting controversy with their high‑fat recipes and outspoken views. The series ended when Paterson died of cancer in 1999.
- Career and writing: Before TV she ran the Books for Cooks shop, worked as a private cook and caterer, served as a guild butcher, and later fronted other series such as Clarissa and the Countryman. She authored books including a memoir, Spilling the Beans, and a respected A History of English Food.
- Personality and views: Known for blunt humour, a fiery temper and eccentricity, she championed traditional country pursuits (including hunting) and provoked debates — for example urging badger meat be eaten during culls and being convicted in 2009 of attending a hare coursing event. She was openly critical of vegetarians and modern political correctness.
- Personal life: Born in London in 1947 to Dr. Arthur Dickson Wright, she endured an abusive, alcoholic father. She struggled with alcoholism herself, quitting drinking on her 40th birthday and remaining an active member of AA. She never married, lived in Edinburgh, and is survived by two sisters. She described her life as “fantastic,” despite bankruptcies and controversies.
- Tributes: Food and TV figures praised her intelligence, wit and contribution to British food culture; her agents remembered her as fearless and principled.

Dickson Wright’s public persona combined rigorous knowledge of food history with irreverence and a readiness to offend, making her an enduringly memorable, if divisive, figure in British culinary life.

Health officials are investigating and tracing contacts after a woman diagnosed with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) was treated in the U.S. The patient traveled from India to the United States in April via Chicago O’Hare, then spent time in Missouri and Tennessee before seeking care about seven weeks after arrival. She was initially isolated in a suburban Chicago hospital and subsequently transferred under special transport to an isolation room at the NIH Clinical Center in Bethesda, where she is being treated under an existing NIAID TB protocol.

XDR-TB is a rare, severe form of TB resistant to isoniazid and rifampin plus fluoroquinolones and at least one injectable second-line drug, making treatment lengthy, expensive, toxic and successful in only about 30–50% of cases. Transmission occurs the same way as ordinary TB (airborne droplets from coughing, sneezing, talking), but requires prolonged close exposure; those with weakened immune systems (including people with HIV) are at highest risk. U.S. cases are uncommon—63 reported from 1993–2011—but public health agencies treat each case seriously.

CDC and state health departments are conducting contact investigations, including obtaining the airline manifest to notify passengers who sat near the patient and identifying people who had prolonged, close contact in Illinois, Missouri and Tennessee. Officials stress the overall risk to the general public is low but are urging monitoring and testing (skin or blood tests, sputum testing if symptomatic) for exposed individuals. Diagnosis of TB is fast but determining drug resistance can take 6–16 weeks. Treatment costs for multidrug-resistant and extensively resistant TB are substantially higher than for drug-susceptible TB.

Public-health guidance reiterated: avoid prolonged close contact in poorly ventilated settings with known TB patients, ensure TB patients complete their full courses of therapy to prevent resistance, and health systems should maintain infection control, rapid diagnosis, appropriate treatment, and contact tracing to limit spread.

The Los Angeles Times reports that nearly 10,000 U.S. soldiers — many in the California National Guard — are being ordered to repay re-enlistment signing bonuses and student loan incentives they received during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. The Pentagon and National Guard Bureau say law and program rules require recovery of overpayments uncovered by audits, even when errors occurred years earlier and soldiers fulfilled their service commitments.

Background:
- The incentive programs swelled during the 2000s as the military relied on an all-volunteer force for prolonged wars; spending on selective re-enlistment bonuses rose sharply.
- Audits found bonuses were often paid too liberally and without proper eligibility checks; a prior California Guard scandal (exposed in 2010) involved misspending and criminal convictions tied to bonus fraud.

Impact on servicemembers:
- Many recipients who completed their contracts now face repayment demands, garnishments, tax liens and accruing interest. Examples include a former captain who refinanced his home to repay $46,000 and a master sergeant repaying $20,500 at $650/month.
- Veterans contest the clawbacks, saying they were eligible when paid and that errors were the result of the Guard’s or Pentagon’s oversight. Some have launched petitions and appeals; others are seeking congressional relief.

Official response:
- California National Guard officials say they cannot unilaterally waive the debts but have set up assistance centers and helped preserve some original payments. They urge Congress to act if forgiveness is to occur.
- Defense Department policy says repayment generally won’t be sought when ineligibility was due to circumstances reasonably beyond the member’s control, but auditors’ findings have prompted recovery actions nonetheless.

Context:
- The SRB (Selective Reenlistment Bonus) program allowed substantial payments (policy caps existed) intended to retain personnel in critical specialties. Early reviews focused on processing speed rather than overpayments; later audits highlighted improper payments.

The situation has provoked anger from veterans and the public, with many arguing the bureaucratic failures that led to improper payments should not be imposed retroactively on servicemembers who fulfilled their obligations.

An Alaska Airlines Boeing 737 bound from New York’s JFK to Seattle made an emergency diversion to Minneapolis–St. Paul Airport on Monday after a passenger became unruly and tried to open a rear cabin door during flight. Crew members contained the man, and he was escorted off and arrested when the plane landed in Minneapolis at about 9:45 a.m. CT; passengers were told the descent was due to a medical emergency. Witnesses said the passenger, who appeared to be in his 20s, had acted oddly during boarding, took a pill, and later spoke incoherently; air marshals and flight attendants quickly intervened. Alaska noted it is impossible to open an aircraft door while the cabin is pressurized. Minneapolis police determined he was a danger to himself and he was taken to a hospital; it was unclear whether charges would be filed. The flight later continued and arrived at Seattle–Tacoma around 1 p.m. PT.

Chicago has won the competition to host filmmaker George Lucas’ new museum. Mayor Rahm Emanuel secured a 17-acre lakefront site on parking lots between Soldier Field and McCormick Place for the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, which is to open in 2018. The self-funded, $1 billion project — backed and endowed by Lucas (who plans a $400 million endowment over time) — will showcase his vast collection of art and movie memorabilia (from Norman Rockwell paintings to Industrial Light & Magic work and Star Wars costumes) under the theme of storytelling and will be billed as the world’s largest interactive museum.

Lucas, who has strong Bay Area ties but is married to Chicago civic leader Mellody Hobson and lives part-time in Chicago, said the city was the right choice though it was a difficult personal decision. The museum board cited Chicago’s larger site, transit access, proximity to the Museum Campus, strong tourist numbers, and opportunities for collaboration as advantages. Emanuel touted cultural, educational and job-creation benefits, saying the project will pair with neighborhood schools and create hundreds of jobs.

The proposed plan would lease two Park District parking lots to the museum for $1, with most parking moved underground at Lucas’s expense and roughly 12 acres left as green space. The move follows the rejection of Lucas’s preferred Crissy Field/Presidio site in San Francisco and an aggressive recruitment effort by Emanuel. The proposal faces opposition from open-space advocates and could prompt legal challenges under Chicago’s lakefront protection policies. Lucas and Hobson have already donated to Chicago education causes, and museum renderings will be presented to city officials prior to final approvals.

Nathaniel Marston, the 40-year-old actor best known for playing Michael McBain on One Life to Live, was critically injured in a single-vehicle crash on Oct. 30 on SR447 near Reno, Nevada. According to Nevada Highway Patrol and updates from his mother, Elizabeth Jackson, Marston was driving a 1985 Ford F-150 when the truck drifted off the road, overturned multiple times and he was ejected because he was not wearing a seatbelt. Police said he was sober at the time.

He suffered severe trauma: multiple fractures to his neck and back, a broken shoulder, broken ribs, a collapsed lung and other internal injuries. Early doctors warned that, if he survived, he faced a high likelihood of being quadriplegic and dependent on a ventilator. Initial family updates described him briefly communicating and undergoing surgery with cautious hope for recovery of some upper-body movement, though walking was considered unlikely and a long recovery was predicted.

On November 11, 2015, his family announced that Marston had died peacefully at 3:15 p.m. in Reno. His mother described that his injuries did not respond to treatment, his bodily functions failed, and that he passed surrounded by family and friends. She said that, had he lived, he would have faced life as a ventilator-dependent quadriplegic — a fate she believes spared him further suffering — and expressed comfort that he is now at peace with God and deceased relatives. Memorial services are planned for New York City, Kauai and Gerlach, NV; dates will be posted later. The family thanked supporters for their prayers and love during the two-week ordeal.

Saturday Night Live’s recent episode drew mixed reactions but featured several standout moments. Aidy Bryant stole the show as Sarah Huckabee Sanders in a surprise musical sketch—cutting abruptly from a formal setting into a choreographed number to Demi Lovato’s “Confident”—that amplified Sanders’ blithe obliviousness and satirized press‑briefing rhetoric in a fresh, daring way. The review notes SNL’s strongest political pieces lately are those that lean into surreal, nightmare logic rather than relying solely on caricaturing Trump’s competence.

Larry David opened the show with a monologue that divided viewers: while some defended his freedom to tackle taboo subjects, his jokes imagining flirting in a concentration camp were widely criticized on social media as cringeworthy and in poor taste.

Alec Baldwin’s Trump also returned in a sketch involving Paul Manafort (Alex Moffat), featuring an absurd naked shower scene—joined by Beck Bennett’s Mike Pence and Kate McKinnon’s Jeff Sessions—that blended crude humor with topical jabs (including a Weinstein quip) and culminated in a gag about a presidential turkey pardon to spare Manafort from legal trouble. Overall, the episode mixed sharp political satire with controversial comedy that polarized audiences.

Transformers: Age of Extinction (2014) — directed by Michael Bay, screenplay by Ehren Kruger — is a 165-minute sci-fi/action blockbuster starring Mark Wahlberg, Nicola Peltz, Jack Reynor, Kelsey Grammer and Stanley Tucci, with voices by Peter Cullen and John Goodman. Set five years after Dark of the Moon, the film follows Texas mechanic Cade Yeager (Wahlberg) who revives Optimus Prime; surviving Autobots (Bumblebee, Hound, Crosshairs, Drift) join Cade, his daughter Tessa, and her boyfriend to evade a CIA black‑ops purge led by Harold Attinger (Grammer) and a Decepticon bounty hunter, Lockdown. Billionaire inventor Joshua Joyce (Tucci) collaborates with Attinger to create Galvatron, a new Transformer threat, and major setpieces devastate Chicago and Hong Kong.

Critics characterize the movie as technically impressive but creatively bankrupt. Bay’s hallmark set-piece direction and cutting‑edge CGI produce spectacular visuals — large-scale destruction and a striking tableau of an alien ship over Chicago are often noted — but many reviewers condemn the film for its bloated length, soullessness, thin characters, repetitive action and chaotic storytelling. Wahlberg is viewed as a functional lead (an improvement over previous human leads), Tucci provides comic relief and stands out, while Peltz’s performance as Tessa drew particular ire. The film’s loud, explosion‑driven spectacle is judged entertaining by some fan audiences but overwhelmingly described by critics as exhausting, mindless blockbuster moviemaking that prioritizes special effects over coherent plot or emotional engagement. Overall critical verdict: impressive CGI and production scale undermined by tedious pacing, shallow character work, and an overlong, noisy runtime — entertaining for franchise fans but otherwise tiresome.

President Trump and U.S. lawmakers signaled tougher measures may be needed to counter North Korea’s accelerating nuclear and missile program despite a unanimous UN Security Council vote imposing new sanctions. Trump downplayed the recent 15-0 vote as “another very small step,” though State Department officials said it represented the toughest sanctions yet and left room for further action. North Korea denounced the resolution as a U.S.-fabricated provocation and threatened severe retaliation.

In congressional testimony, U.S. officials pressed China and Russia to do more to choke off Pyongyang’s revenue streams, criticizing use of Chinese banking channels, front companies, and suspicious ship transfers (including transponder-off voyages and ship-to-ship coal transfers through Russia). Treasury and State Department officials said Washington is pushing Beijing to act and is exploring all options to increase pressure, while cautioning that measures like cutting off trade with China would have major ramifications. The administration also emphasized readiness to use both economic tools and military force if necessary, while maintaining it does not seek regime change.

Separately, South Korea announced plans to form a “decapitation” special forces brigade (nicknamed Spartan 3000) to target North Korea’s leadership, accelerating a program intended to be ready by year’s end. The unit is part of broader deterrence and contingency preparations—alongside plans such as “Kill Chain,” expanded missile capabilities, THAAD deployments, and even ambitions for a nuclear submarine—driven by growing fear of Pyongyang’s capabilities after its sixth and most powerful nuclear test and a surge in missile launches this year. The move reflects Seoul’s desire to take greater initiative in its own defense amid domestic pressure and concerns the U.S. and China are not doing enough. Critics warn such steps increase tensions, but proponents argue they strengthen deterrence against an increasingly capable North Korea.

President Donald Trump replaced White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus with Homeland Security Secretary John F. Kelly on Friday, ending Priebus’s turbulent 189-day tenure — the shortest in modern history. Trump announced the move via Twitter after arriving at Joint Base Andrews; White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Kelly will start Monday and participate in the cabinet meeting.

Priebus told CNN he had privately offered his resignation on Thursday and called the change a “reset,” pledging continued support for Trump. Other White House sources, however, suggested Priebus was forced out and that his camp only framed it as a voluntary resignation after the Kelly appointment. Priebus had come under sustained criticism for failing to curb leaks, impose order in a chaotic West Wing, and for the administration’s legislative setbacks, including the failed health-care repeal effort.

Tensions escalated this week after Anthony Scaramucci’s appointment as communications director and his profane public attacks on Priebus, published in the New Yorker. Priebus had opposed Scaramucci’s hiring; the episode accelerated his downfall. Key Trump advisers and family members — including Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner — had reportedly lost confidence in Priebus. Chief strategist Steve Bannon is expected to remain for now.

Kelly, a retired Marine general and former Southern Command chief who has led DHS since the election, is viewed as a disciplinarian caretaker who will try to bring more order to the West Wing. The transition comes amid an unusual White House power structure in which several senior advisers, including Kushner and Bannon, reported directly to the president rather than through the chief of staff. The story is developing.

Trenton Lewis, a 21-year-old UPS loader in Little Rock, walked roughly 5–5.5 miles each way—often starting before midnight—to make his 4 a.m. shift for seven months so he could keep steady work and support his newborn daughter. Never late or absent, Lewis kept his commute private until coworkers Patricia and Kenneth Bryant learned of his daily trek. Moved by his dedication, they organized donations from other UPS employees and raised about $1,900–$2,000 to buy him a reliable used car. They surprised Lewis with the keys in the parking lot; he was stunned and grateful. He now leaves at 3:30 a.m. and no longer has to walk, and the gesture resulted in a lasting bond with his coworkers.

On June 25, 2016, Fresno police officers fatally shot 19-year-old Dylan Noble at a Chevron gas station after pulling him over in response to a call about a man with a rifle. The department initially showed the body‑camera footage privately to Noble’s family but had resisted public release; it was made public on July 7 amid national attention on other recent police killings.

The released footage shows officers approaching with guns drawn and repeatedly ordering Noble to show both hands. As he exits his pickup, Noble holds his left hand up while keeping his right hand behind his back and walks briefly toward officers. After officers repeatedly shout for him to get on the ground and show his hands, one officer fires two shots; Noble falls and rolls onto his back. While he is on the ground and moving only slightly, officers fire two more rounds—one from the same officer and a later shotgun blast from another—despite continued commands and warnings. The object that fell from Noble’s hand was later identified as a 4-by-4-inch piece of clear plastic containing malleable clay.

Fresno Police Chief Jerry Dyer, who released the video, called it “extremely disturbing” and said investigators would determine whether each shot was justified and whether other tactics could have been used. He declined to name the officers citing safety concerns and noted the timing sensitivity following recent deadly incidents elsewhere. Noble’s parents and attorneys say he was not suicidal or depressed, call the shooting an “inexcusable use of excessive force,” and have filed a claim against the city seeking damages and alleging systemic civil‑rights abuses by the department. Noble’s father has demanded murder charges.

The case drew additional controversy because initial local protests included “White Lives Matter” signs and Confederate flags, complicating public reactions and discussions about race. The footage sharpened criticism of police use of deadly force and prompted questions about whether nonlethal options (K-9, TASER) were attempted. The Justice Department and local investigators examined the circumstances and the item found in Noble’s hand as part of their inquiries.

A powerful, potentially historic blizzard was forecast to hit the U.S. Northeast beginning Friday, as two storm systems were expected to merge off the coast and produce heavy snow, hurricane‑force gusts and coastal flooding from New York City to Maine. Forecasters warned of up to 2–3 feet of snow in parts of New England (Boston faced as much as 3 feet), 10–20+ inches around New York City, and lesser amounts farther south, with wind gusts up to 70–75 mph in exposed coastal areas. The storm threatened whiteout conditions, widespread power outages and further coastal damage to areas still recovering from Superstorm Sandy.

Cities and states took major precautions: schools were closed across New England, many governors ordered nonessential state workers to stay home, Amtrak and numerous airlines suspended service and thousands of flights were canceled, and municipal crews prepped plows, salt and sand. Residents flocked to stores and gas stations to stock up on essentials, generators and snow equipment. Emergency agencies staged personnel and resources to respond to outages, flooding and rescues. Officials urged people to stay off the roads and warned conditions could rival historic storms such as the 1978 blizzard, while noting forecasts could change as the system evolved.

Multiple recorded incidents have stirred national outrage over white people calling police on Black people for routine activities. The main story: at a youth soccer game in St. Johns County, Florida, a field marshal—nicknamed “Golfcart Gail” by witnesses—called deputies on a Black father who was speaking to his teen son from the sidelines. Bystanders filmed the encounter and posted it to social media under headings like “Soccer While Black.” Video shows the father saying he was coaching his son and attempting to leave to defuse the situation; the marshal insisted she felt threatened and summoned police. Deputies interviewed those involved, found no crime, did not detain the father, and said they are required to respond to disturbance calls. The Ponte Vedra athletic association said the call was prompted by a series of prior disruptive incidents at the game (including ejections for abusive behavior) and defended staff actions as protecting children.

The article places the episode in the context of a wider pattern of viral “calling-the-cops-on-Black-people” cases — such as “BBQ Becky” in Oakland, where a white woman repeatedly called police on Black people barbecuing at Lake Merritt. That incident led to her identification as Jennifer Schulte, a Stanford-trained environmental scientist; police evaluated her for a psychiatric hold but made no arrest. The Oakland episode provoked large public cookouts and heated city council debate about misuse of police resources and racialized enforcement of public-space rules.

Overall, these episodes highlight community concerns about racial profiling, social-media shaming of callers, and questions over when it is appropriate to involve law enforcement for nonemergencies.

Former President George H.W. Bush’s remains were transported from Houston to Washington, where he lay in state in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda beginning Monday ahead of an invitation-only state funeral Wednesday at Washington National Cathedral and burial Thursday in Texas beside his wife Barbara and daughter Robin.

Timeline and ceremonies:
- Morning departures in Houston: Bush’s flag-draped casket left a Houston funeral home, traveled in a motorcade to Ellington Field for a send-off ceremony with more than 100 invited guests, a military band and a 21‑gun salute. Secret Service agents assigned to him served as honorary pallbearers for the initial movement.
- The casket was flown to Joint Base Andrews aboard a presidential aircraft renamed Special Air Mission 41; George W. Bush, Laura Bush and other family members accompanied the remains.
- A brief ceremony at Andrews preceded transfer to the Capitol, where the casket was brought into the Rotunda and a series of eulogies and tributes were delivered by top officials.

Remarks and attendees:
- Senators and House leaders eulogized Bush in the Rotunda: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell praised his steadiness through WWII, the end of the Cold War and the Gulf War; House Speaker Paul Ryan called him “a great man” of character; Vice President Mike Pence lauded his lifelong service and decency.
- President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump paid respects Monday evening at the Rotunda; Trump saluted the casket and will attend the National Cathedral service but is not expected to speak. Former President Jimmy Carter plans to attend; Prince Charles will represent the Queen.
- Public and local tributes included a Houston City Hall memorial encouraging attendees to wear colorful socks in homage to Bush’s sartorial habit. Family members and dignitaries throughout the day visibly mourned; Bush’s service dog, Sully, accompanied the casket at one point.

Background:
- Bush, the 41st president (1989–1993), previously served as a WWII naval aviator, CIA director and two-term vice president under Ronald Reagan. He died Friday in Houston at age 94 after health struggles in recent months.

Evan Murray, a senior and three-sport athlete at Warren Hills Regional High School, died Friday night after being injured during the school's home football game against Summit. Murray was the team’s starting quarterback for three years and also played basketball and baseball. School and community leaders did not disclose the specific circumstances of his injury.

Students, faculty, teammates and coaches gathered at the stadium to mourn, leaving flowers and cards — one with a large Superman emblem — and described Murray as a natural leader, dedicated athlete and a steady, respected presence. Coaches and classmates emphasized his character, leadership and the close bonds he forged with peers. Interim superintendent Gary Bowen announced grief counselors would be available to students.

The school community is particularly shaken after recent losses over the past year, and staff urged students to support one another as they grieve. The football game was completed, with Summit winning 14-12. Officials continued to investigate and process the events surrounding Murray’s injury.

At the end of August 2012 Iran hosted the two-day summit of the 120-member Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) in Tehran, using the high-profile meeting to push back against Western attempts to isolate it over its disputed nuclear program and to promote its foreign-policy positions.

Key developments and themes:
- Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, insisted Iran seeks peaceful nuclear energy only — “nuclear energy for all and nuclear weapons for none” — and urged continued enrichment rights while denouncing the U.N. Security Council and U.S. policy as biased. He also called attention to Israel’s unacknowledged nuclear capability as a regional danger.
- The summit was strained by sharp divisions over Syria. Egyptian President Mohamed Mursi, making the first Egyptian visit to Iran since 1979, publicly called the Syrian uprising a legitimate revolution and urged NAM solidarity with Syrians seeking to overthrow Bashar al-Assad. His remarks prompted the Syrian delegation to walk out and underscored continuing regional rifts: Iran backs Assad, Egypt signaled distance from him.
- Iran proposed a NAM-mediated initiative on Syria — a “troika” including Egypt, Iran and Venezuela plus Iraq and Lebanon and a three-month ceasefire/reconciliation mechanism — but the plan was dismissed by many Syrian rebels and opposed by the U.S.
- U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki‑moon attended, pressing Iran to cooperate on human rights and to take concrete steps to demonstrate its nuclear program is peaceful; he also urged Iran to use its influence to curb violence in Syria. Ban’s candid remarks on human-rights concerns and calls for greater nuclear transparency were notable and, according to reports, provoked discomfort among Iranian officials and selective alteration by state TV translations.
- The summit served Tehran’s diplomatic aim of showing it still has broad support among developing countries; Iran hoped delegations’ participation (and possible visits to sites like Natanz) would counter claims of isolation. Meanwhile, Western and U.N. agencies continued to press for more access and clarity about Iran’s nuclear activities amid lingering suspicions about weaponization efforts.

Overall, the NAM meeting highlighted Iran’s attempt to legitimize its nuclear program and regional posture, exposed sharp divisions over Syria among developing states, and brought public pressure from the U.N. on Iran’s human-rights record and nuclear transparency.

Robert “Joe” Halderman, a CBS producer accused of attempting to extort $2 million from Late Show host David Letterman, is scheduled for his first Manhattan court hearing. The initial session will likely focus on scheduling and pretrial legal issues, though defense attorney Gerald Shargel may use the appearance for theatrical public attacks on Letterman, NBC legal analyst Dan Abrams warned. Halderman, indicted on attempted grand larceny charges that carry up to 15 years in prison, appears unlikely to accept a quick plea. Despite prior reports of financial strain that suggested a plea deal was probable, Halderman has raised about $100,000 for his defense and plans further fundraising; friends and his lawyer indicate he intends to take the case to trial. The story reemerged into headlines as the court date approached. 

Also noted: separate, lighter item about Levi Johnston—recent Playgirl shoot and possible SNL appearance—and Fleshbot awarding him a “Crossover Star Award” for his move into sex‑centric celebrity publicity.

San Vitaliano, a town of about 6,000 north of Naples, has temporarily banned burning solid biomass (wood, woodchips, coal, charcoal) in commercial ovens and stoves after suffering one of Italy’s worst air‑pollution records. The mayor, citing 114 days in 2015 when particulate (PM10) levels exceeded safe limits, ordered wood‑fired pizza stoves and similar burners closed unless fitted with filters that remove at least 80% of PM10. The emergency ordinance took effect mid‑December and is set to run into spring (with possible reintroduction in autumn); violations carry fines of €200–€1,032. Local pizzerias and bakers, who say they are being unfairly targeted and point out that nearby Naples has many more pizzerias without similar pollution, have protested the measure as costly and misguided. Authorities say police checks will enforce the ban while investigations continue into other possible pollution sources.

South Korea’s opposition mounted an unprecedented nine-day filibuster in late February–early March 2016 to block a ruling-party anti-terrorism bill, setting a new world record for combined speaking time. Beginning Feb. 23 at 7:07 p.m. and ending Mar. 2 at 7:32 p.m., 39 opposition lawmakers spoke a total of 192 hours 25 minutes to delay a vote they said would give the National Intelligence Service overly broad powers to collect private communications, travel and financial data and thus threaten privacy and political dissent. Minjoo Party floor leader Lee Jong-kul closed the marathon with a 12-hour 31-minute speech (751 minutes), surpassing a prior individual record set during the event. The filibuster — Korea’s first since 1969 — drew more than 5,000 visitors to the National Assembly and frequent references to George Orwell’s 1984; participants used tactics such as reading long texts and limiting breaks. Facing criticism for blocking other urgent business (including bills on electoral redistricting and North Korean human rights) and with the ruling Saenuri Party holding a parliamentary majority, the opposition ended the tactic and the contested anti-terrorism bill was put to a likely successful vote hours later. Debate centered on national security versus civil liberties.
