On a BART platform in Oakland on Sunday night, 18-year-old high school senior Nia Wilson and her 26-year-old sister Lahtifa were attacked by 27-year-old John Lee Cowell; Nia was fatally stabbed and her sister critically injured. Cowell, who has a history of violence, was arrested the next evening and charged with Nia’s murder; police have described the attack as random but have not ruled out a racial motive.

The case prompted large community vigils in Oakland and widespread social-media outcry—both over the brutality of the attack and over local news coverage. KTVU drew heavy criticism after using a photo of Nia that appeared to show her holding a gun; the image was actually a gag cell-phone case, and many argued the choice criminalized a Black teen victim and fit a broader pattern in which media portrayals of murdered Black youth emphasize negative or provocative images. KTVU anchor Frank Somerville apologized, calling the use of the photo “a huge mistake,” but many viewers rejected the apology as insufficient.

Activists also reported interference at a vigil by members of the Proud Boys. Commentators highlighted the disparity between the subdued, nonviolent way police arrested Cowell and the often-violent treatment Black people receive in encounters with law enforcement, arguing this reveals systemic bias. A GoFundMe for Nia’s family raised substantial donations, and the case has reignited conversations about media bias, racialized narratives of victims, public mourning, and police treatment.

House Republicans were buzzing before President Obama's State of the Union about whether there would be any repeat theatrics after Rep. Joe Wilson's "You lie" outburst during last year's address. House Minority Whip Eric Cantor said he hopes there will be no outbursts and urged decorum, though his prior assurances of attentiveness proved optimistic. Wilson himself promised to be a "gentleman" and instead plans a live Facebook response after the speech; Democrats (DCCC) have warned he could stage another stunt. GOP members were nonetheless vocal in pre-speech criticism: Cantor suggested Obama should have "listened and learned" that his agenda lacks public support; Rep. Jeb Hensarling quipped he agrees with much of what Obama says but not with what he does and called the proposed spending freeze more headline than substance. Conservative groups mocked the address as well—Grover Norquist’s Americans for Tax Reform circulated a State of the Union “Bingo” card filled with predictable presidential phrases.

Since entering the 2012 presidential race, Michele Bachmann’s campaign has become notable not only for loud Presley music and her vow to make Barack Obama a one-term president, but also for repeated physical confrontations between her staff and reporters. In under two months, at least five incidents have involved pushing, shoving and alleged threats toward members of the traveling press. Well-publicized episodes include ABC’s Brian Ross being shoved in South Carolina and CNN’s Don Lemon being pushed into a cart by Bachmann’s husband and staffers. Other encounters captured on camera include Fox’s Steve Brown warning a bodyguard not to touch him, and a Norwegian correspondent alleging an aide threatened to break his arm — a claim the campaign denies.

The campaign defends the conduct as security-driven: a prominent, silver‑haired former Secret Service agent and an advance woman frequently physically intervene, and spokeswoman Alice Stewart says protecting Bachmann’s safety is the top priority. Critics note the frequency and intensity of the incidents are unusual—especially in Iowa, where open access to candidates is customary—and say Bachmann’s security team has been less discriminating about handling reporters than those for other high-profile candidates. The piece also includes an anecdote about comedian Kathy Griffin’s tense exchange with Bachmann staff in Washington while researching a rally.

Captain Francesco Schettino, master of the Costa Concordia, returned to the wreck off Giglio island for the first time as part of his ongoing manslaughter and abandoning-ship trial. The 2012 disaster, when the 290m cruise ship struck a reef and capsized, killed 32 people. Schettino, who denies abandoning ship and faces up to 20 years in prison, was taken by small boat to the righted but still stranded vessel after attending a safety briefing with court-appointed experts; a judge stressed he was allowed on board as a defendant, not a consultant.

Schettino has acknowledged some responsibility publicly and asked for forgiveness, but insists he steered the ship closer to shore to avoid a greater loss of life and contests accusations that he fled. He criticized media coverage of his visit as a “frenzy,” saying he wanted to show he is “a gentleman, not a coward.” Local reactions were mixed — some residents said they were tired of the story and wanted the ship removed, while others argued it was time to move on.

His lawyer argued Schettino is being unfairly singled out by Costa Crociere, which has greater resources; five others were convicted via plea bargains in 2013, while Schettino’s request for a plea deal was rejected by prosecutors. The Costa Concordia was righted in September 2013 after an 18-hour salvage operation following months of preparation, and bids have been received globally to dismantle the wreck.

Researchers at Oxford used diffusion-weighted and resting-state fMRI to map the human ventrolateral frontal cortex (vlFC), a region implicated in high-level cognition and language, and compared it with scans from 25 macaque monkeys. In humans the team reliably parcellated the vlFC into 12 distinct areas, each with its own “neural fingerprint” of connections. Eleven of those areas had clear counterparts in macaques with similar connectivity, but one did not: a ball-shaped region called the lateral frontal pole (LFP) — two small structures above and behind each eyebrow in humans — which appears absent in macaques.

Behaviorally and functionally, the LFP is linked to strategic planning, multi-tasking and counterfactual thinking (evaluating how unchosen options might have fared), and stronger activity there predicts better ability to switch strategies. The study also found that auditory cortex connections to vlFC are much stronger in humans than in macaques, a difference the authors suggest could underlie humans’ unique capacity for speech and language processing. The findings, published in Neuron, identify a potentially unique human brain area and provide a connectivity map that may help explain cognitive specializations and inform study of psychiatric and language disorders.

Jillian Rose Jacobson, a 31-year-old photography teacher at El Dorado High School in Placentia, was found dead by students in her locked classroom on the morning of Monday, March 2, 2015. Students who noticed the locked door alerted another teacher, who opened the room and discovered Jacobson hanging from the ceiling. Staff removed her and emergency responders performed CPR, but she was declared dead at the scene. Police believe she died by suicide; no note was found and there was no sign of foul play. An autopsy was expected.

Jacobson had taught at the school about a decade and was remembered by colleagues and students as upbeat, popular and engaged with her classes. Her death shocked the campus community; many students and staff were visibly upset, some left early, and grief counselors were provided. A candlelight vigil was planned that evening. District officials said most students would return to normal schedules the next day to help restore routine.

The article notes prior tragedies at El Dorado High in recent years—including the 2014 death of a student struck by a vehicle and the 2009 death of a coach—and includes statements of sympathy from community members and an assemblywoman.

Twenty years after the Ms. Foundation launched Take Our Daughters to Work Day to familiarize girls with the workplace, that original goal has largely been met. Jennifer Allyn argues the initiative should now shift from simply showing girls jobs to actively encouraging and preparing them for leadership—“Take Our Daughters to the C‑Suite.” Women remain dramatically underrepresented at the top of corporate America (e.g., 3.6% of Fortune 500 CEOs), and many girls report feeling uncomfortable or unfit to lead. Companies can help by three main changes:

- Introduce girls to senior female role models so they can see women in power and understand that leadership is attainable.
- Explain concretely what leaders do day-to-day—how they motivate teams, solve complex problems, and deliver results—to make leadership tangible and attractive.
- Move beyond a single annual event with year-round programs that identify, sponsor and actively promote female talent. Sponsorship—leaders using their influence to create opportunities—is more impactful than mentoring alone, as shown by Princeton’s proactive encouragement of female applicants to prizes, which led to a rise in women Rhodes Scholars.

Allyn contends that without these steps, companies lose talent and competitiveness and undermine fairness. Showing offices to kids is no longer enough; deliberate exposure, explanation, and sponsorship are needed to grow the next generation of women leaders.

At the G20 summit in St. Petersburg, President Obama sought to build international pressure for a strong U.S. response to the Aug. 21 chemical-weapons attack outside Damascus, but left with only limited, nonbinding backing and no coalition willing to join strikes. After intense lobbying and a private 20-minute meeting with Vladimir Putin that produced no agreement, Obama obtained a joint statement from 10 countries (Australia, Britain, Canada, France, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Spain and Turkey, plus the U.S.) saying evidence points to the Assad government, calling for accountability and a “strong international response,” but not explicitly endorsing military action or committing participants. Russia—Assad’s main ally—did not endorse the statement, vowed to keep supplying weapons to Syria, and reportedly sent ships to the eastern Mediterranean as U.S. naval forces massed nearby.

World leaders at the summit debated whether to wait for a U.N. inspectors’ report; Russia and China have blocked Security Council action, and key allies (including Britain’s Parliament and France pending a U.N. report) were reluctant to join strikes. Obama stressed any U.S. strikes would be limited in scope and duration to deter future chemical attacks and avoid a prolonged war, comparing the choice to past humanitarian interventions. He said he would address the nation Tuesday and asked Congress to authorize force to strengthen U.S. action, even though he says he could act without authorization. White House officials began intensive lobbying of lawmakers while vice president and cabinet members worked Capitol Hill in his absence.

Domestically, public and congressional opposition was strong: polls showed a majority of Americans opposed intervention, and several members of Congress signaled resistance or sought nonmilitary alternatives. Administration officials acknowledged persuading U.S. lawmakers and the public is the central challenge; Obama promised systematic outreach but conceded he might not win a majority.

Sources tell PEOPLE that President Donald Trump and former GOP vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin were not invited to Senator John McCain’s memorial services. Fundraiser Carla Eudy, who helped plan the events and has long ties to the McCain family, confirmed invitations were not extended to the two. A Capitol Hill source and others said several longtime McCain staffers were also removed from the guest list in recent days. Insiders say the requests to stay away were communicated through intermediaries rather than formal legal notices; sources speculate the family—possibly Cindy McCain—directed the decisions as she grieves and seeks to protect her husband’s legacy.

The reports note the public, bitter history between Trump and McCain, while reactions to Palin’s exclusion were more sympathetic given her past friendship with McCain; Palin earlier paid tribute following his death and said she would remember “the good times.” The article also mentions that Cindy McCain has been discussed as a possible successor to fill McCain’s Senate seat and that Arizona’s governor was en route to Washington to discuss an appointment, with an announcement expected soon.

The piece then shifts to unrelated Washington coverage about Republican concerns over perceived tech-company bias: Axios-reported polling and quotes from Trump allies—including Donald Trump Jr. and House Republican Kevin McCarthy—describe growing conservative belief that social platforms censor the right and outline plans to press tech CEOs in upcoming hearings, and even discuss building conservative alternatives to mainstream social networks.

Taylor Swift has announced her sixth studio album, Reputation, set for release on November 10, with the lead single due the following day. She revealed the album cover—a black-and-white photo of Swift in a loose shirt, wet hair, dark lipstick and a chain choker, against a backdrop of fake newspaper clippings repeating "Taylor Swift"—and posted the third of three linked videos depicting a slithering snake. The snake imagery follows her recent social media purge and plays on a long-running critic association.

The item also recalls a prior public clash between Swift and pop producer (Harris), who went on a Twitter rant after Swift’s camp claimed credit for a song following their split—a song rumored to have contributed to the breakup. He invoked Katy Perry and accused Swift of trying to "tear" him down; supporters spammed Swift’s Instagram with snake emojis. Harris later expressed regret for his tweets.

Gambian President Yahya Jammeh announced in a televised Eid-al-Fitr address that all prisoners currently on death row will be executed by mid-September, effectively breaking a roughly 27–30 year de facto moratorium on executions in the country. He framed the move as part of a crackdown on serious crimes—naming murder, treason, drug offenses, banditry, terrorism and homosexuality among offences he said would be punished to the full extent of the law—and said security forces and the judiciary would be empowered to enforce it.

Human rights groups and foreign governments condemned the announcement. Amnesty International and Reprieve called the threat deeply troubling, noting Gambia’s record of unfair trials and the use of death sentences against political opponents. Amnesty warned any executions would be a major setback for human rights; France also urged maintaining the moratorium and moving toward abolition. Reports disagree on the number on death row—human rights activists put the figure at about 44, AFP reported 47 and judicial sources suggested it could be higher.

Jammeh, who seized power in a 1994 coup and has been criticized for repressing opposition, previously threatened to resume executions in 2009 but did not follow through. Observers say the announcement is at odds with regional and global trends away from capital punishment and raises alarm over due process and political motivations for imposing death sentences.

Karl Lagerfeld turned Chanel’s traditional Paris runway into a full-scale spoof supermarket for the brand’s Fall/Winter 2014-15 ready-to-wear show at the Grand Palais, drawing celebrities and causing a post-show scramble for the staged goods.

The elaborate set reproduced supermarket aisles filled with more than 100,000 Chanel-branded items—pasta, wine, “Tweed cola,” “Chanel crémeuh” milk and other tongue-in-cheek products—complete with trolleys, price signage (“50 percent markup”), announcements over loud pop music and metallic shopping baskets. Lagerfeld called the supermarket “the pop art of today,” saying he wanted to bring fashion into everyday life; more than 500 custom labels were produced and some items will be donated to charity.

Front-row guests included Keira Knightley (with husband James Righton) and Rihanna, who watched models browse and carry products down the catwalk. The theatrical staging—models with oversized tweed jackets, jogging suits, fluorescent leggings and baskets—was praised for its showmanship, though the generosity of the props backfired: audience members stripped shelves after the show and security had to intervene; some attendees’ bags were checked, and a fashion editor reportedly stole a Chanel doormat.

The coverage also highlights other Paris ready-to-wear shows that day: Iris van Herpen’s debut RTW outing featured body-focused, shock-driven pieces (including models suspended in oxygen-sapped plastic squares) and organic, techno-fabric garments that bordered on the surreal; Alexander McQueen’s Sarah Burton showed an emotive, 18th-century–tinged collection mixing broderie anglaise, tulle and fur references; Valentino’s Maria Grazia Chiuri and Pierpaolo Piccioli offered diaphanous, 1960s- and Pop Art–inflected feminine looks, with standout embroidered and couture-infused gowns.

Overall, Lagerfeld’s supermarket was hailed as a brilliant, populist stunt that injected humor and real-life context into haute fashion—while also illustrating the risks of turning props into free-for-all souvenirs.

Iran’s judiciary has confirmed that two U.S. citizens, Shane Bauer and Joshua Fattal, convicted in Iran of illegal entry and espionage after being arrested in July 2009 while hiking near the Iraq–Iran border, were released on bail and flown to Oman on September 21, 2011. Branch 36 of Tehran’s Appeals Court agreed to commute their detention sentences, and bail totaling $1,000,000 was reportedly posted (Oman is said to have paid the bail). Their companion, Sarah Shourd, had been released on $500,000 bail in September 2010 on medical grounds and greeted them in Oman. Bauer and Fattal, who denied espionage and said any border crossing was accidental, had been sentenced to eight years in a closed trial the previous month. Their release—announced as Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad prepared to attend the U.N. General Assembly and after diplomatic efforts by Oman, Iraq’s president, the Swiss embassy (which represents U.S. interests in Iran), and other intermediaries—was welcomed by the families and U.S. officials, including President Obama. The case had been politically sensitive in Iran, with disputes over authority to free them delaying the release until required judicial signatures were secured.

A multi-month national survey of 1,200 Americans gauged impressions of all 50 states. Overall, most states are viewed favorably; only five have net-negative ratings: California (27% favorable, 44% unfavorable), Illinois (19-29), New Jersey (25-32), Mississippi (22-28) and Utah (24-27). Hawaii is the most liked (54% favorable, 10% unfavorable). Other top-rated states include Colorado, Tennessee, South Dakota, Virginia, Montana, Alaska, Oregon, North Carolina and Pennsylvania. Several more states show strong positive nets (10+ points), while seven states have only single-digit net-positives and Louisiana breaks even.

Views vary sharply by demographics and party:
- Partisan gaps are large: Democrats favor Hawaii, Washington, Massachusetts, Oregon, Vermont, Colorado and New York; they least like Texas, Alabama and Mississippi. Republicans most favor Alaska and Texas and strongly dislike California, Illinois and Massachusetts. The biggest partisan split is California (Democrats like it 91 points more than Republicans) and Texas (Republicans like it 82 points more than Democrats).
- Gender differences: Women rate New York, Massachusetts, Delaware, California, New Hampshire, Vermont, Illinois and Connecticut substantially higher than men; men rate North Dakota, South Carolina, Wyoming, Montana, Iowa and South Dakota higher.
- Black voters dislike most Southern states; their favorites include Hawaii, North Carolina, Virginia, Tennessee, Maryland and Florida, while Alabama, Mississippi and Texas rank lowest.

Texas ranks 38th overall (40% favorable, 31% unfavorable). It elicits relatively few “not sure” responses (29%), reflecting its high visibility and strong positive and negative views. California, despite being most disliked overall, also has only 28% uncertain responses. The results highlight regional reputations and pronounced partisan and demographic divides in how Americans view states.

The document is a compilation of reviews and write-ups about Thomas Balmès’s documentary Babies, which follows four infants—Ponijao (Namibia), Bayarjargal (Mongolia), Mari (Tokyo) and Hattie (San Francisco)—through roughly their first year of life. Shot from birth and assembled from some 400 hours of footage, the film is observational: no narrator, no subtitles for foreign-language speech, no overt interpretation. Its strengths are striking cinematography, an intimate, immediate feel, and moments that highlight cross-cultural contrasts in childrearing—ranging from Ponijao’s tribal, low‑tech setting to Hattie’s urban, medicalized American life—while also underlining universal developmental milestones (cooing, crawling, tantrums, discovery).

Critics praise the film’s visual composition, the charm and candor of the babies, and the way it quietly captures individuality and shared behaviors without didacticism. Some see a subtle Rousseau-like sympathy for more “natural” lifestyles and admire the director’s restraint and patience.

At the same time, reviewers note limits: the movie contains little narrative tension or hardship—colic, disease, serious parenting struggles and many “dull bits” remain absent—so the experience can feel like an extended, polished home video that becomes tiresome for some viewers. Without explanatory context or commentary, it’s more a joyful, hypnotic visual diary of infancy than a primer on parenting or a probing cultural study. Overall responses range from warm appreciation for its immediacy and beauty to criticism that its lack of shape and conflict makes it unambitious; typical ratings cited are middling (around a C or 1.5/4 in one review) despite broad appeal for audiences drawn to the film’s adorable subjects.

Two Gwinnett County, Georgia, police officers were fired after videos circulated showing them using excessive force during a traffic stop arrest of 21-year-old Demetrius Bryan Hollins.

Incident details
- The stop occurred about 4 p.m. Wednesday in Lawrenceville for traffic violations (broken taillight, no plate, signaling issues). Hollins was later charged with multiple traffic offenses, obstruction, and possession of less than an ounce of marijuana and released on bond.
- A witness video shows Sgt. Michael Bongiovanni punching Hollins in the face as Hollins stepped from his vehicle with his hands raised. A separate video shows Master Police Officer Robert McDonald running up to Hollins after he was handcuffed and lying face-down, and appearing to stomp or kick him in the head.
- Hollins sustained visible facial injuries in booking photos and told reporters he had been trying to record the encounter when officers assaulted him.

Department response and investigation
- Gwinnett Police initially placed McDonald on administrative leave; after discovery of the second video contradicting Bongiovanni’s report, both officers were terminated the next day.
- The department opened criminal investigations; findings will be forwarded to the district attorney for possible prosecution.
- Police Chief Butch Ayers condemned the actions, called the force used “uncalled for,” and said the department would hold officers to its standards. He announced plans to equip uniformed officers with body cameras by year’s end.
- The two officers are white; Hollins is black. The incident drew condemnation from local Black Lives Matter activists, who demanded criminal charges.

Background on officers
- McDonald joined the department in 2013 and graduated the academy in 2014; his personnel file, released by police, showed commendations and prior use-of-force reports.
- Bongiovanni had served since 1998; investigators said a newly found video contradicted his account.

The widely shared footage and swift firings prompted internal and criminal reviews and public outcry about police brutality and accountability.

The document describes two tech topics. First, it outlines the concept of an "open edge cloud": a software layer that leverages standard compute and storage resources distributed in service providers’ last-mile networks to create a powerful content and application delivery platform. With Open APIs for rapid resource allocation, the edge cloud is positioned to meet the high performance needs of next-generation applications while taking advantage of service providers’ unique reach and scale. The architecture promises service providers greater control, flexibility and new ways to differentiate with services.

Second, it reports that Google’s YouTube reached a preliminary all-cash deal to acquire Twitch for more than $1 billion. If completed, the purchase would be one of YouTube’s largest since Google bought it in 2006. Twitch, founded in 2011 by Justin Kan and Emmett Shear, is a live videogame-streaming service with more than 45 million monthly users, subscription offerings, and partnerships with gaming publishers and media. The acquisition is expected to face U.S. regulatory scrutiny over potential anticompetitive concerns because YouTube already dominates online video (about 6 billion hours watched per month by 1 billion users). Twitch has raised roughly $35 million from investors, employs ~130 people, and has a significant presence in e-sports and gaming streaming—representing a growing share of downstream broadband traffic.

Calcific myonecrosis is a rare, benign but potentially problematic condition in which muscle tissue undergoes necrosis and is replaced by a central liquefied cavity surrounded by peripheral calcification. It most often follows high-energy trauma or untreated compartment syndrome—frequently with associated peripheral nerve injury—and typically affects the anterior/lateral compartments of the lower leg, though forearm and foot cases have been reported. Onset is usually decades after the initiating event (reports range from ~10 to 60 years later), and patients commonly present with a gradually enlarging, painless mass that can occasionally be tender and, in advanced cases, may erode adjacent bone or break through the skin.

Typical imaging shows a fusiform mass with longitudinal, plaque-like peripheral calcification and central liquefaction on X‑ray and MRI; this appearance helps distinguish it from entities such as soft-tissue sarcoma (which tends to show more aggressive, diffuse mineralization) and myositis ossificans (which shows central trabeculation/marrow signal and a different clinical course). Biopsy is generally discouraged because of a high risk of infection (postoperative infection rates reported up to ~30%), and some cases present already infected without prior surgery.

Management depends on symptoms. Asymptomatic lesions are often observed because surgery carries a high infection risk. Symptomatic or complicated lesions are treated with complete excision, careful closure or flap coverage, drainage (suction drains or intentional open healing) to manage dead space and seroma, and prolonged antibiotic therapy—initially broad-spectrum for gram-positive and gram-negative coverage, then tailored to cultures, often continued for 6–8 weeks. Prevention focuses on early recognition and treatment of compartment syndrome.

The article also reports a case of a 66-year-old Thai woman who developed a large calcific myonecrosis mass more than 50 years after a Malayan pit viper bite at age 14. The bite likely caused untreated compartment syndrome; the painless mass became noticeable about 10 years earlier, eventually eroded and broke through the skin, and was surgically removed with complete healing by one month post-op. The report underscores the long latency and typical clinical and radiographic features of calcific myonecrosis and the association with prior severe muscle injury, including rare instances following snakebite.

Pope Francis published a long-anticipated encyclical on the environment, Laudato Si (“Praised Be”), intended not just for Catholics but for a global audience. The document links environmental degradation, climate change and social injustice, arguing that humanity’s exploitation of nature—driven by an economic system centered on profit—threatens the poor most severely and requires an ethical, cultural and economic “revolution of hearts and minds.” Francis frames climate action as a moral imperative and urges greater stewardship of creation.

The pope timed the encyclical to influence international debates ahead of the crucial U.N. climate talks in Paris and his own high-profile appearances in the U.S. this year. Vatican officials emphasized the letter’s broad reach by having it presented by a cardinal, an Orthodox theologian and an atheist climate scientist. Francis’s scientific background (he studied chemistry) and his earlier statements acknowledging human-driven climate change lent weight to the document.

Scientists and U.N. officials welcomed the encyclical as a potentially powerful moral force that could shift public values and spur political will—arguing that faith-based appeals can reach constituencies the scientific community cannot and might influence outcomes more than technical negotiations alone. Many climate scientists, frustrated by slow policy responses and ideological resistance, saw the pope’s intervention as timely and important.

The encyclical also drew predictable pushback from conservative and right-wing figures, including some Catholic voices and U.S. politicians who warned the Church should not weigh in on controversial science or economic policy. Nonetheless, it was expected to resonate especially in developing countries and among Catholics concerned with poverty, inequality and environmental stewardship.

At the Toronto International Film Festival, Madonna premiered her second feature as director, W.E., and promoted it at a press conference. Reports in the Globe and Mail claimed that, backstage, Madonna allegedly told festival volunteers to turn their backs to her as she passed, a gesture contrasted with the festival’s customary on-screen thank-you and audience applause for the orange-shirted volunteers. Madonna’s camp has since issued a press release denying the allegation, saying neither she nor her security instructed volunteers to turn away, that she publicly thanked them from the stage, enjoyed the festival, and was puzzled by who would have made such a request.

Onstage and to reporters, Madonna discussed her filmmaking ambitions and reception: she welcomed criticism directed at her film but not personal attacks, comparing the process to having to earn her reputation in music. Critics have praised W.E.’s visuals but criticized its focus and performances; reviews ranged from very negative to mixed. Madonna described her interest in the relationship between Wallis Simpson and King Edward VIII, calling the king “very punk rock,” and explained choices such as using the Sex Pistols on the soundtrack. She also spoke about the film’s score, set camaraderie (including cast sing-alongs), and hopes for awards attention when W.E. opens widely in December.

This Associated Press profile tells the story of Evie (officially Turdi), a 66-year-old Indonesian transgender woman who once cared for young Barack Obama while he lived in Jakarta. Evie recalls being hired by Ann Dunham in 1969 for household work and to babysit the future U.S. president; neighbors confirm she worked in the Menteng neighborhood. Decades of social stigma, physical abuse and a brutal 1985 raid that left a friend dead led Evie to hide her feminine identity and live publicly as a man. Now impoverished, she scrubs laundry and lives in a tiny room in a Jakarta slum, prays at the mosque and says she has little hope for the future — though she felt pride after Obama’s 2008 election.

The article places Evie’s life in the wider context of Indonesia’s complex attitudes toward transgender people (known locally as waria). Activists estimate millions of transgender people in the majority-Muslim country; some have public roles in entertainment and beauty pageants, yet widespread prejudice persists. The influential Indonesian Ulema Council has urged trans people to live as their birth sex, and conservative attacks and ridicule are common. Economic marginalization pushes many into sex work, increasing health and safety risks; Indonesia’s human rights commission receives roughly 1,000 reports of abuses against LGBT people annually, and trans murders remain a global and local threat. Some Indonesian trans people are increasingly visible and asserting rights — for example, a transvestite recently applied to lead the national human rights commission — but many still face violence, discrimination and limited opportunities. Evie hopes Obama’s prominence and his administration’s appointment of an openly transgender official signal progress, even as she continues to struggle to survive.

Texas education officials recently revised parts of the state social studies curriculum and settled disputed recommendations from a work group, prompting debate over which historical figures and themes students should learn.

Key points:
- The work group had pared down hundreds of historical figures to fit grade-level limits; teachers who participated said they aimed for objectivity and to avoid offending anyone.
- Some high-profile removals drew criticism: Helen Keller was removed from a third-grade "citizenship" lesson (the committee noted she "does not best represent the concept of citizenship" and suggested military and first responders better illustrate that idea). Bill Clinton was recommended for removal from one list (though students still must learn about his impeachment). Supporters have urged restoring both.
- Local Texas leaders (e.g., Barbara Jordan, Sam Houston, Stephen F. Austin, Henry B. González) and local legislators received top marks and remain required study topics; Texans who became president, governor or mayor remain included even if specific names like Donald Trump were not listed.
- The State Board of Education — a 15-member body (five Democrats, ten Republicans) whose standards-setting has been contentious before — rejected several work-group proposals to remove references to the nation’s "Judeo-Christian" heritage; conservative groups praised that decision.
- Other approved changes include replacing San Jacinto Day with Constitution Day in a section on community/state/national customs and celebrations (the Battle of San Jacinto remains taught in fourth grade and U.S. history).

The revisions reignited debate over curriculum content, with Democrats and advocacy groups pushing to reinstate figures like Keller and Clinton, while conservatives defended preserving Christian references and traditional historical touchstones.

Authorities found the body of 23-year-old Catherine Johannet of Scarsdale on Sunday on Bastimento Island, Panama. Johannet was last seen around 10 a.m. Thursday on Isla Colón; she had been staying in a Bocas del Toro hostel and was reportedly heading to Red Frog Beach, planning to return that afternoon. Her friends reported her missing and posted flyers; a large search involving volunteers, the National Police, the National Civil Protection Agency, and the Bocas del Toro Fire Department located her body on an island trail. Her belongings were recovered at the hostel. A cause of death has not been released, and her family is en route to Panama. Further updates were to follow.

Sen. John Kerry’s daughter, Alexandra Kerry, 36, was arrested in Los Angeles early Thursday in a DUI-related incident after being stopped for expired vehicle registration. Police say she failed a field sobriety test and was taken to a Hollywood station; a breathalyzer at the station registered below California’s legal limit of 0.08, and she was released after posting $5,000 bail at 5:25 a.m. Kerry’s spokesperson said the senator supports his daughter and had no further comment. A court date is set for December 10. Law enforcement sources told TMZ it’s unlikely prosecutors will file charges.

A competitor in the LOTOJA 206-mile bike race died Saturday after crashing and falling from a bridge into the Snake River near Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The victim, Robert (Rob) Verhaaren, 42, of Mesa, Arizona, reportedly swerved to avoid a roadway hazard—believed to be a pothole—lost control, hit the guardrail and was catapulted about 30–40 feet into the river. Other riders rendered aid; Verhaaren was later pronounced dead at St. John’s Hospital. Authorities noted possible cervical fracture; further cause-of-death details have not been released.

Verhaaren, who would have turned 43 next week, leaves his wife Bridget and three young children. He held a B.S. in accounting from BYU and a J.D. from NYU School of Law and was managing director of Universal Equity Group Funds Arizona. Accounts from neighbors and friends describe him as an avid cyclist, devoted scoutmaster and family man.

Race officials said this is the first fatality in LOTOJA’s 30-year history. The event also experienced other serious accidents that sent two riders to hospitals and widespread early flat tires. Some locals raised concerns about road conditions and the relatively low guardrail at the crash location. LOTOJA runs annually from Logan, Utah, to Jackson Hole and draws about 1,000 riders.

A series of at least three small earthquakes struck north of Phoenix near Black Canyon City on the night of Nov. 1, 2015, with epicenters along the Agua Fria River just off I‑17. The sequence began with a 3.2 foreshock around 8:59 p.m., followed by the largest event—a magnitude 4.1 at about 11:29 p.m.—and a 4.0 tremor at 11:49 p.m. The largest quake occurred shallowly, about 6.5 km (4 miles) deep, which likely made the shaking more noticeable across the Valley from Black Canyon City and Camp Verde to metro Phoenix neighborhoods as far as Queen Creek and Scottsdale.

Residents reported rattling, brief bangs or thuds and were startled awake in some cases; emergency services received many calls but there were no reports of injuries or significant damage. Arizona Geological Survey and USGS officials said the causative fault had not been identified—small, non-surface‑rupturing quakes are hard to tie to a specific fault—and aftershocks were expected, many too small to feel. While earthquakes are relatively uncommon in Arizona, the state has experienced similar events in recent years (e.g., a 4.7 in the Sedona area in 2014).

Beginning Sunday, many PlayStation 3 owners—primarily users of older "fat" PS3 models (pre‑2009 Slim)—were hit by error 8001050F. The fault prevented sign‑ins to PlayStation Network, trophy syncing, use of dynamic themes and some PlayStation Store content, and in many cases blocked launching certain single‑player games offline (including debug/development consoles). Affected systems sometimes had their system clock reset (reportedly to Jan 1, 2000), and attempts to set date/time via the Internet returned the same error.

Initial speculation blamed PSN changes or a calendar bug; developers on forums reported debug units stuck in reboot loops. Sony acknowledged the outage, advising they were investigating and warning owners of older models to avoid using affected consoles because continuing to use them could corrupt trophy data or other content. PlayStation Slim models were reportedly unaffected.

After about 24 hours Sony confirmed the root cause was a fault in the PS3 clock functionality (not Slim models) and said a fix would be provided within 24 hours. Services and consoles began returning to normal following Sony’s updates.

David Shambaugh: scholar and China expert
- David Shambaugh is an internationally recognized authority on contemporary China, Asian international relations, the EU, and transatlantic issues. 
- Academic and professional background: former Reader in Chinese Politics at SOAS, editor of The China Quarterly, and faculty at George Washington University. Early career included analyst roles at the National Security Council East Asia Bureau and State Department’s Bureau of Intelligence & Research (1976–78).
- Institutional affiliations and fellowships: nonresident Senior Fellow at Brookings (1998–2015); director of the Asia Program at the Woodrow Wilson International Center (1986–87); board member of the National Committee on U.S.–China Relations (2009–2015); elected member of several policy bodies including the International Institute for Strategic Studies and the Council on Foreign Relations. He has held fellowships and visiting posts at the Woodrow Wilson Center, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (Fulbright), and universities across Asia, Europe, Russia, Australia, and Taiwan.
- Grants, consulting, and media: recipient of major research grants (Ford, Rockefeller, Smith Richardson, German Marshall Fund, British Academy, U.S. National Academy of Sciences, etc.), frequent media contributor, editorial board member, and consultant to governments, foundations, research institutions, and corporations.
- Publications: prolific author with more than 30 books and 300 articles.

Report: Chinese propaganda chiefs curb “Xi Dada” nickname
- Chinese propaganda authorities have reportedly instructed state-controlled outlets, including Xinhua and the 21st Century Business Herald, to avoid using the popular sobriquet “Xi Dada” (Big Daddy/Uncle Xi). The nickname had been widely promoted since Xi Jinping became China’s leader in 2012 to cast him as a folksy, paternal figure.
- Background and spread: “Xi Dada” proliferated across social media, songs, poems, videos, and state-backed performances, some spontaneous and others apparently coordinated. State media circulated smiling cartoons and humanizing vignettes (e.g., Xi visiting a dumpling shop) that reinforced the image.
- Reasons for the clampdown: Officials appear to be responding to growing unease—both domestically and internationally—that the campaign risked creating a Mao-style personality cult. Critics and scholars argue the efforts went too far, made Xi appear dictatorial or ridiculous, or undermined desired authority. Some analysts say the nickname made Xi seem overly familiar when the leadership would rather project imposing authority.
- Responses and implications: Xinhua has largely avoided the term since late April; other party publications received similar guidance. Observers see the move as a tactical refinement of image-management rather than a substantive shift in Xi’s consolidation of power. Experts (including Shambaugh, Kerry Brown, Roderick MacFarquhar, and others) view the episode as evidence that Xi has reversed post-Mao norms against personalistic rule, with some acknowledging the portrayal may have backfired and embarrassed propaganda managers.
- Uncertainty remains: No public written directive has been seen; measures may be verbal or selective. The nickname is not being comprehensively censored from the internet, but state outlets have been warned to tone down the intimate, populist framing.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences moved to block Sacha Baron Cohen from attending the 84th Oscars red carpet amid reports he planned to appear in full costume as the title character from his upcoming film The Dictator. Though Cohen had tickets as a cast member of Best Picture nominee Hugo, Academy officials — concerned he would use the high-profile, live international broadcast for an in-character stunt and disruptive promotion — told his representatives the red carpet “is not for stunting” and sought assurances he would not attend in costume or promote the film there. Deadline and other outlets reported the Academy rescinded his tickets until such assurances were given; the Academy later described the matter as still pending while it awaited a response. The move echoes past tensions over Cohen’s character-based promotions (Borat, Bruno) and follows the Oscars’ general reluctance to allow unpredictable or unsanctioned antics on the red carpet, despite a few prior sanctioned comic appearances at the ceremony.

Researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology report in PLOS ONE that great apes—chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans—can distinguish between true and false beliefs in others and use that understanding to help appropriately. Using an interactive helping task adapted from tests for 18‑month‑old human infants, experimenters hid a novel object in one of two lockable boxes. In the false‑belief condition the original experimenter left before an assistant moved the object to the other box; in the true‑belief condition the original experimenter saw the switch. When the original experimenter returned and tried (helplessly) to open the box he believed contained the object, apes were more likely to unlock the correct box for him in the false‑belief condition than would be expected by chance, and were more willing to help when the human held a false belief—mirroring results with human infants.

The study tested 34 apes (23 chimpanzees, 5 bonobos, 6 orangutans) housed at Leipzig Zoo. Subjects were trained to unlock boxes and then given multiple test trials across three rounds. First responses—touches to the locking mechanism—were coded; inter-rater reliability was perfect. The findings challenge the long‑held view that great apes cannot “read” others’ beliefs, suggesting their social cognition includes an understanding of others’ false beliefs and that differences between human and ape social cognition may lie not in basic mind‑reading capacity but elsewhere. The authors call for further research, including applying similar interactive false‑belief paradigms to other species.

A gunman opened fire in Terminal 3 at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) on Nov. 1, fatally wounding 39-year‑old Transportation Security Administration (TSA) Officer Gerardo Hernandez and wounding three others. Authorities say 23‑year‑old Paul Ciancia entered with a duffel bag, produced an assault rifle and left a note saying he wanted to “kill TSA.” Airport police shot Ciancia four times; he was taken to a hospital and later upgraded from critical to fair condition. He faces charges that carry a possible death sentence.

Law enforcement sources say paramedics waited about 150 yards away and were not allowed into the terminal for roughly 33 minutes after Hernandez was shot, even though Ciancia had been in custody for all but five of those minutes. Video reviewed by investigators shows no officers rendered first aid on Hernandez at the scene; he was eventually wheeled to an ambulance and arrived at Harbor‑UCLA Medical Center with no signs of life. Doctors worked for about an hour but Hernandez died. Officials are examining the timeline and communications between police and fire commanders to determine whether lack of coordination delayed medical care and whether earlier entry by rescue crews could have changed outcomes.

The shooting prompted chaotic initial responses amid concerns about additional suspects and possible explosives. The report highlights tensions between modern active‑shooter tactics—where officers prioritize ending the threat even if it means stepping over the wounded—and the need for immediate lifesaving care. It also notes gaps in first‑aid refresher training across LAPD ranks identified in a recent audit, though airport police do receive such training. Hundreds attended a public memorial for Hernandez, the first TSA officer killed in the line of duty.

Maverick County officials confirmed on Aug. 24, 2016 that 69-year-old Lucila Robles, who lived near U.S. Highway 277 in Quemado, Texas, died after a truck and flatbed trailer carrying Takata airbag inflators and ammonium nitrate propellant crashed, caught fire and exploded in front of her home the morning of Aug. 22. Forensic testing of dental remains recovered from the smoldering debris of her destroyed house identified Robles; Justice of the Peace June Smith pronounced her dead.

The truck, en route from Del Rio to Takata’s Eagle Pass distribution center and then on to Mexico, had swerved off the road. The driver, Mario Alberto Rodriguez, 20, and a passenger escaped before the blast but were injured, along with an elderly couple in a passing SUV; all four were hospitalized and later airlifted to San Antonio. The explosion damaged about 10 homes, hurled debris nearly a mile, cratered the road and forced intermittent closure of U.S. 277 for roughly 30 hours.

Takata said the shipment complied with regulatory requirements and was carried by a subcontractor; company and local officials are cooperating with investigators. Federal transportation authorities and hazard-transport experts noted investigators will examine packaging, placarding, driver certification and hours of service to determine any regulatory violations, and pointed out ammonium nitrate alone can cause a large explosion. Takata has had prior incidents involving its propellant, including 2006 blasts at its Monclova plant.

Sony Pictures’ comedy The Interview, about a fictional plot to assassinate North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and the subject of a destructive cyberattack, was released digitally and in roughly 300 independent U.S. theaters on Christmas Day after the studio initially canceled the wide release following threats linked to the hack. Co-directors Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg made surprise appearances at early screenings, and many shows sold out as audiences framed attendance as a stand for free expression rather than only interest in the film itself.

Sony made the movie available the previous day for $5.99 rental or $14.99 purchase on platforms including YouTube, Google Play, Microsoft’s Xbox Video and on a Sony site (SeeTheInterview.com). The emergency digital rollout — arranged after major chains declined to show the film amid security concerns — represented an unusual same-day online/theatrical release and provoked debate about censorship, free speech and distribution models. The White House and public figures urged Sony to reverse its cancellation; the U.S. government blamed North Korea for the hacking.

Initial theatrical screenings were largely uneventful and lightly policed, though some independent theaters coordinated with local law enforcement and the FBI offered guidance. Online distribution saw heavy demand and some technical issues: Sony’s site struggled early under load, Xbox Live and PlayStation Network users reported outages (claims by hacker groups were unverified), and unauthorized copies circulated widely overseas, notably on Chinese video sites. Critical response to the film was mixed to negative, but the controversy gave it outsized attention and many patrons described their viewings as political acts defending freedom of choice. Sony withheld immediate box office and sales figures while continuing to seek broader distribution partners.

In September 1977 a blonde, brown-eyed toddler was found abandoned around 11 p.m. between the sliding glass doors of the Amarillo Terminal Airport. The roughly 16–18 month-old girl, drenched and clutching a soured juice bottle, was taken to Northwest Texas Hospital, showed minor bruising, and was placed in Potter-Randall County Child Welfare custody as “Jane Doe 927.” She was fostered, proved healthy and personable, drew widespread local interest and adoption inquiries, and was adopted after parental rights were terminated in January 1978.

Decades later genealogists and family researchers uncovered a possible match. In Long Beach, Calif., Rosalee Webster had disappeared for years beginning in 1977 and returned alone; she later gave conflicting stories about her daughter Bonnie Lee Webster, born May 1976, saying she’d been abandoned in a bus terminal or died. Bonnie’s aunt posted online in 1998 seeking information. Researcher Ronda Randall linked that post to the Globe-News file and photographs of Jane Doe 927; Bonnie’s father, Charles Webster, felt the images looked like a “perfect match.”

The woman who was adopted after the Amarillo abandonment now lives as Shelley Schooley. Schooley, 41, raised in a loving adoptive family, has long known she was abandoned and kept newspaper clippings and adoption records. She describes a stable upbringing but lingering questions about her origins and medical heredity. Randall discovered Schooley via an online video in which Schooley referenced her Globe-Times baby photo. Schooley and the Websters have since contacted each other, but Schooley has declined to pay for DNA testing herself—saying she would agree to one if it would provide closure to searching relatives—so the identity of Jane Doe 927 remains unconfirmed after nearly 40 years.

Iran’s test-firing of a ballistic missile this week — the first since President Trump took office — prompted sharp warnings from the new U.S. administration and raised tensions in the region. U.S. National Security Adviser Michael Flynn, speaking from the White House, said the launch was part of a pattern of “provocative” and “destabilizing” Iranian activity (including support for Houthi rebels) and declared “we are officially putting Iran on notice.” Flynn gave no specifics about responses; U.S. officials said they are weighing a range of options, from financial measures and sanctions to possible military steps, while stressing any response would be separate from the Iran nuclear deal.

Tehran insists the test was defensive and did not violate U.N. Security Council Resolution 2231, which “calls upon” Iran to refrain from ballistic-missile activity capable of delivering nuclear weapons — language critics say is nonbinding. Iranian leaders, parliamentarians and military officials defended the missile program as a conventional deterrent and rejected foreign interference. The U.N. Security Council held an emergency meeting to refer the test to its committee; U.S. envoy Nikki Haley called the launch “unacceptable.” Allies including Israel urged stronger measures.

The episode unfolded amid multinational naval exercises in the Persian Gulf and recent close encounters between U.S. and Iranian vessels. Reactions ranged from White House warnings and promises not to “sit by and not act,” to Iranian officials’ insistence the drills and tests would not be deterred. Critics of Flynn warned his rhetoric risks escalation.

A fight between defendant Markelus Carter and a witness, inmate Steven Upham, occurred in a courthouse holding cell during a break in Carter’s murder trial and was recorded on video. Carter is on trial for the 2009 shooting death of Kenneth Warrington. A guard mistakenly placed Carter and Upham—both unhandcuffed—in the same cell; the altercation lasted about two minutes before corrections officers intervened. Video shown to the jury reportedly shows Carter landing the first punch, Upham putting Carter in a headlock and punching him, and Carter biting Upham’s arm. Both sustained only minor injuries.

Upham, a former cellmate of Carter at Allen Oakwood Correctional Institution, is testifying that Carter told him details of the murder. On cross-examination the defense challenged other ways Upham could have learned details and questioned whether Upham hoped to earn an early release; Upham denied any promise of reduced time. Three guards were stationed in the courtroom during his testimony, and the defense plans to call other inmates to contest Upham’s statements.

Carter’s attorney requested a mistrial over the cell fight, but Judge Jeffrey Reed refused and allowed the video to be shown; the judge ordered counsel to meet before court the next day about the incident. Separately, the defense accused prosecutors of surprise evidence regarding a MAC-10-style firearm; the judge found no intentional violation but left open the possibility of a continuance to allow the defense to obtain a firearm expert. The prosecution continued its case with lead detective Tim Clark’s testimony, to resume Friday. Sheriff Sam Crish said the guard’s placement of the two men together was an error and will be investigated.

Chuck Pfarrer’s new book, SEAL Target Geronimo, offers a detailed, insider account of the SEAL Team Six raid that killed Osama bin Laden while disputing several widely circulated versions of the operation. Pfarrer, a former SEAL Team Six commander who interviewed multiple participants and spoke with senior officers, describes a short, precise assault in which SEALs fast‑roped from a stealth helicopter onto bin Laden’s roof, entered his bedroom within seconds, and killed him almost immediately as he reached for an AKSU pistol. Only a handful of suppressed rounds were fired, the whole operation lasted about 38 minutes, and there was no prolonged 45‑minute running gun battle.

The book also challenges official explanations of equipment and planning: Pfarrer says the White House overruled requests for F‑18 fighter cover and the newest “ghost hawk” stealth helicopters, forcing use of older craft—one of which crash‑landed and had to be destroyed on site. He argues these decisions, and President Obama’s rapid public announcement of the death, may raise political questions because captured digital materials (12 garbage bags’ worth) might have enabled follow‑on raids against senior al‑Qaeda leaders if exploited first. Pfarrer is critical of the CIA’s published role, contending the agency insisted on embedding an officer in the raid despite limited helicopter insertion training; the book downplays CIA contributions, though the summary notes the agency’s key role in tracing bin Laden’s courier and surveilling the compound.

U.S. officials have dismissed parts of Pfarrer’s narrative as incorrect. The book also suggests Ayman Zawahiri may have indirectly exposed bin Laden by repeatedly sending a courier whose identity had been compromised. SEAL Target Geronimo has attracted controversy: its U.S. release was vetted by government officials, and the British edition is being revised over libel concerns.

Kuki Gallmann, the 73-year-old Italian-born conservationist and author of I Dreamed of Africa, was ambushed and shot in the stomach while patrolling her Laikipia Nature Conservancy in central Kenya. She was with Kenya Wildlife Service rangers assessing recent arson damage to one of her tourism lodges, Mukutan Retreat, which had been burned down last month. Gallmann was airlifted to Nairobi after receiving emergency treatment and underwent surgery; she is reported in stable but seriously injured condition.

Laikipia (about 10,000 sq km), where Gallmann’s roughly 360 sq km conservancy lies, has seen a sharp rise in violence amid a severe drought that has driven large numbers of nomadic herders and their cattle onto private ranches in search of pasture. Tens of thousands of animals have been moved onto private land, more than a dozen people have been killed in clashes, and several lodges have been torched. Police and military efforts to disarm and evict the herders — which included killing cattle during operations — have escalated tensions; herders say livestock were shot by security forces, while police say animals died in crossfire. Local ranchers and the Laikipia Farmers’ Association suspect members of Pokot and other communities of carrying out invasions and attacks, and some accuse political actors of incitement tied to upcoming elections. The situation has drawn national attention after the killing of British rancher Tristan Voorspuy in March and warnings from officials about inflammatory rhetoric.

Tens of thousands of Egyptians — supporters and opponents of President Mohamed Morsi — clashed violently around the presidential palace in Cairo in early December 2012, marking the worst street battles between Islamist and secular forces since the 2011 uprising. The confrontation began when Islamist groups, led by Muslim Brotherhood supporters and allied Salafis, mobilized to evict some 200 anti‑Morsi protesters who had been camping outside the palace in protest of Morsi’s recent decree expanding his powers and the hurried drafting of a constitution. Clashes spread along nearby boulevards as stones, sticks and firebombs were thrown; both sides accused the other of firing live rounds.

Casualties were significant: reports cited at least five dead and hundreds wounded (figures varied between accounts — more than 120 to over 600 injured were reported). Police were slow to intervene; the army and Republican Guard later deployed armored vehicles and tanks around the palace to secure the area. The violence also spread beyond Cairo, with Brotherhood offices attacked and burned in Suez and Ismailia and clashes elsewhere.

The crisis deepened political splits: several presidential advisers and aides resigned in protest of the Brotherhood’s influence and Morsi’s actions. Opposition leaders — including Mohamed ElBaradei, Amr Moussa and Hamdeen Sabahi — united in demanding that Morsi rescind his extra powers and postpone the Dec. 15 constitutional referendum, refusing dialogue until that happens. The Brotherhood defended mobilizing to “defend legitimacy,” accused the opposition of undermining democracy, and threatened legal action against opposition figures. International voices called for restraint and a transparent constitutional process, but neither side showed readiness to back down, raising fears of further bloodshed and a deepening secular‑Islamist polarization in Egypt.

A life-size foam sculpture of Donald Trump, titled "The Emperor Has No Balls" and created by anonymous guerrilla art collective INDECLINE, will be auctioned by Julien’s Auctions in Los Angeles on Oct. 22 with an estimated price of $10,000–$20,000. The orange-tinted statue—depicting a nude, exaggerated Trump—was one of five placed unannounced in public spaces in New York, San Francisco, Seattle, Cleveland and Los Angeles in August; most were removed or destroyed by authorities, and Julien’s says the Los Angeles piece (rescued by gallery owner Matt Kennedy) is the only surviving example. Julien’s plans to display the statue Oct. 17–22 at its Westside gallery, and says a portion of the proceeds will benefit the National Immigration Forum. The auction will also feature other street and contemporary works by artists such as Banksy, Keith Haring, Basquiat, Warhol and Shepard Fairey. The Los Angeles display drew controversy when police reportedly asked for the nude depiction to be obscured or moved and the gallery owner refused.

University of California officials announced they will pay medical expenses for students who were pepper‑sprayed during an Occupy Davis protest and will drop charges against 10 people arrested during the campus action. UC President Mark Yudof also created an independent advisory panel, led by former police commissioner Bill Bratton, to review the incident.

The controversy stems from video showing a campus police officer spraying seated, peaceful protesters at close range during a Friday attempt to clear an encampment. The footage provoked widespread criticism, renewed protests, and calls for Chancellor Linda P.B. Katehi’s resignation. Katehi said the police were instructed to remove tents peacefully and that she did not authorize use of riot gear or pepper spray; she placed Police Chief Annette Spicuzza on administrative leave along with two officers involved. Spicuzza has suggested Lt. John Pike authorized the spray, a claim Pike has not publicly addressed.

After a large rally and Katehi’s apology, the encampment expanded to more than 75 tents. Katehi said she would pursue negotiations rather than renewed police action, ordered officers to remain on call but out of sight, and arranged basic services for campers. The incidents triggered a systemwide UC review and plans for legislative hearings. Katehi also said campus policies and police training for handling encampments need updating to reflect contemporary student expression.

A 12-year-old Pittsburgh girl, Shamera Harris, died Sunday night after a Ford Explorer rolled backward, dragging her into a tree while her mother frantically tried to stop the vehicle. Shamera’s mother, Carla Harris, had asked her then-boyfriend Richard Benton, 53, not to drink before he volunteered to drive to pick up Shamera and a friend from the Waterworks Mall. According to police and Carla Harris, Benton appeared to be drinking; he smelled of alcohol, slurred his words and was unsteady when officers arrived. Witnesses say Benton fiddled with the gearshift and got out to take a picture; the SUV then backed away, catching Shamera as she stepped out.

Shamera was pronounced dead at the scene; the Allegheny County medical examiner ruled the death an accidental blunt force trauma. Police say Benton refused field sobriety and breath tests at the scene and at the station. After consulting the district attorney’s office, he was charged with driving under the influence, treated for minor injuries at a hospital, then booked and later released on nonmonetary bond with conditions to report to court and enter substance-abuse treatment.

Family members described Shamera as a bright, well-behaved student who made honor roll and enjoyed swimming and socializing with friends. Her mother called her a “miracle baby” and said she would not have allowed Benton to drive had she known he was intoxicated. The family is mourning another recent loss: a relative, Shakkeem Harris, was killed two years earlier. The police investigation and vehicle collision inspection continue; funeral arrangements were pending.

Matthew Hay‑Chapman, 55, a formerly homeless man who spent much of his time reading news at libraries and a McDonald’s near Golden Gate Park, helped San Francisco police capture two Orange County jail escapees. Living recently in the park and couch‑surfing, Hay‑Chapman recognized a white 2008 GMC van and one of the fugitives, 37‑year‑old Hossein Nayeri, from news coverage. After watching and confirming the man’s identity, he alerted officers and guided them until they were able to apprehend Nayeri outside a police station; a second escapee, 20‑year‑old Jonathan Tieu, was found in the van and later returned to Orange County. The third escapee had already surrendered. Police praised Hay‑Chapman’s vigilance; he is expected to receive about $140,000 in combined rewards and says he will use the money to rebuild his life and help his troubled son, disabled daughter and two grandchildren in foster care. Family and friends described him as sharp and well informed despite hardships, including chronic back pain and past instability.

This document reports that the White House website has begun adding links in the official biographies of past presidents that highlight connections to actions by President Barack Obama. Clicking through many biographies (from Calvin Coolidge onward) reveals “Did you know?”-style references—with hyperlinks—to contemporary White House initiatives such as using social media and livestreaming State of the Union addresses, protecting Medicare and Social Security, expanding veterans’ and LGBT rights, and other priorities the administration wants emphasized. Conservatives and Republicans flagged and mocked the changes (the Heritage Foundation, Commentary, ABC’s Jake Tapper, and the RNC), and the RNC posted satirical images placing Obama in famous historical moments. White House officials said the original biographical texts were unchanged; the Obama-related items appear as linked addenda that point to other pages on WhiteHouse.gov. The article uses the Coolidge biography as an example, noting how the site links Coolidge’s 1924 radio address to Obama’s use of Twitter, Facebook and other online town halls. The bios themselves come from The Presidents of the United States of America by Frank Freidel and Hugh Sidey (copyright 2006, White House Historical Association). The site hosting this piece also carries satirical content and a partisan volunteer link.

A new study in Lancet Psychiatry using fMRI found that violent psychopaths show distinct brain abnormalities in regions involved in learning from punishment, empathy, moral reasoning and social emotions. Researchers scanned 50 men: 12 violent offenders with psychopathy, 20 violent offenders with antisocial personality disorder but not psychopathy, and 18 non-offenders, while they performed a feedback-based image-matching task. The psychopathic group was slower and less able to change behavior when task rules (and punishments/rewards) changed. Their scans showed reduced gray-matter volume in areas tied to guilt, embarrassment and moral judgment and altered white-matter connections to prefrontal regions involved in learning from reward and punishment—changes not seen in non-psychopathic criminals.

The findings help explain why standard rehabilitation that works for many offenders often fails for psychopaths: they may undervalue negative consequences and fail to learn from punishment. The authors suggest these neural differences emerge early and that targeted, learning-based interventions in childhood (focused more on reward and tailored approaches rather than typical punitive methods) might alter brain development and reduce later violent crime. Researchers caution the structural and functional abnormalities are subtle and that genetic and environmental causes remain poorly understood.
