1) American Airlines apology after racial incident in Dallas
- Two Black professional basketball players — Memphis Hustle guard Marquis Teague and forward Trahson Burrell — were removed from an Envoy Air flight at Dallas-Fort Worth after a Black flight attendant accused them of stealing blankets.
- The blankets had been given to the players by two first-class passengers as they walked to coach seats.
- American Airlines’ spokesman Joshua Freed said a manager apologized to the players, who later flew first class to Sioux Falls, South Dakota.
- The airline had announced plans last month to implement implicit-bias training, CEO Doug Parker told employees.

2) Baron Davis on Donald Sterling and the Clippers’ racist environment
- Former Los Angeles Clippers guard Baron Davis described playing for then-owner Donald Sterling as similar to the racial horror themes of Jordan Peele’s film Get Out.
- On ESPN’s The Hoop Collective podcast, Davis recounted early warnings from team staff about Sterling’s behavior and said he quickly realized Sterling was racist and intolerable as an owner.
- Davis accused the organization of protecting Sterling and cited examples of Sterling’s abusive and racist conduct, including public beratings of players and disrespectful, demeaning comments directed at team members.

Progressive groups and unions have pressed incoming Republican members of Congress to decline taxpayer-funded congressional health insurance if they oppose the new federal health-care law, calling otherwise hypocritical. The controversy began when Rep.-elect Andy Harris (R-Md.) complained his congressional coverage would be delayed, prompting criticism from the White House and others; Reps.-elect Mike Kelly (R-Pa.) and Bobby Schilling (R-Ill.) said they would forgo the benefit. AFSCME’s president argued Republicans who voted to repeal reform should not enroll in government plans. A Public Policy Poll found 53% of respondents (58% of Republicans) think opponents of the law should decline government coverage.

Analysts note the financial savings are modest: using LA Times estimates for Blue Cross Blue Shield premiums, the taxpayer share for insuring an estimated 289 incoming GOP members would be roughly $2.4 million a year — symbolically meaningful but small. Defenders, including a Boehner spokesman, counter that congressional health coverage is employer-provided like for other Americans and unrelated to the legislative debate. Some Republicans (e.g., Schilling) say opting out is a personal decision to save taxpayers, not a stance on the health law.

An Indonesian woman detained in Malaysia over the killing of Kim Jong-nam told Indonesian diplomats she was paid 400 Malaysian ringgit (about $90) to take part in what she believed was a prank. Siti Aisyah, 25, said she met people who “looked Japanese or Korean” and was given a liquid described to her as like “baby oil” to smear on the victim’s face; she told officials she did not know it was poisonous.

Kim Jong-nam, the estranged half-brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, collapsed in the check-in hall at Kuala Lumpur International Airport after being apparently sprayed or splashed and died en route to hospital. Malaysian police reported tests detected VX, a highly toxic nerve agent banned under the Chemical Weapons Convention, on swabs from his eyes and face. VX is an oily, odorless liquid that can kill within minutes through skin contact and can also contaminate clothing and surfaces.

Two women—an Indonesian (Siti Aisyah) and a Vietnamese national, Doan Thi Huong—have been arrested; the Vietnamese woman has similarly told officials she thought she was participating in a television prank. A North Korean man and several other suspects have also been detained or are wanted. North Korea denies involvement, but suspicion is widespread. Malaysian authorities and forensic teams have swept the airport for contaminants as investigations continue. The dead man reportedly traveled under the name Kim Chol; North Korea has not publicly confirmed his identity.

A few items are described:

- Jim Vidmar bought 1,000 fake Twitter accounts from an online vendor in Pakistan for $58. He programs those accounts to follow other Twitter users and to rebroadcast tweets.

- Rapper Dave Murrell (Fyrare) has paid Vidmar to log into his Twitter account and follow other people to boost his popularity on the platform.

- Separately, the Internet Archive is conducting crawls to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference. The purpose is to preserve the versions of linked pages that existed when an article or page was written, so that when links later break or content changes, readers can still see what was originally intended. This effort (described as “No More 404” crawls for supported sites) aims to reduce broken links across the web by replacing dead links with archived versions or providing companion links.

Archaeologists working on London’s Crossrail project have identified 25 skeletons unearthed beneath Charterhouse Square as victims of the medieval Black Death. Teeth from 12 of the skeletons contained DNA of Yersinia pestis, and radiocarbon dating and pottery place burials in at least three episodes: the main Black Death outbreak (1348–50) and later 14th–15th century recurrences. Ground‑penetrating radar indicates many more graves across the square—likely part of a long‑lost emergency plague burial ground outside the medieval city—potentially numbering in the low thousands.

Osteological and isotope analyses reveal these were mostly poor, hard‑working people: many showed signs of malnutrition (including rickets), heavy manual‑labor injuries, high rates of back damage, and a mix of local and non‑local childhood origins (about 40% grew up outside London). Later burials show more upper‑body injuries consistent with social unrest. Sex/age profile: 13 males, 3 females, 2 children, and 7 indeterminate.

Researchers plan further excavations and genomic sequencing of the ancient plague DNA to trace how the bacterium has evolved and spread; this could shed light on whether the 14th‑century strain is ancestral to modern Y. pestis. The discovery resolves a 660‑year‑old mystery about the location of one of London’s medieval plague burial grounds and offers rare, detailed insights into the lives and deaths of medieval Londoners.

Darnell Barton, a 37-year-old Metro bus driver in Buffalo, rescued a young woman from a potentially life‑threatening situation on Oct. 18. While driving the Elmwood 20 route with about 20 McKinley High students aboard, Barton saw the woman standing on a narrow ledge outside the Scajaquada Expressway railing. He stopped, called dispatch, and after a short exchange lunged forward, wrapped his arm around her and helped her over the guardrail to the sidewalk. He sat with her and spoke briefly until a state corrections officer, a crisis counselor and emergency responders arrived. The students, shaken by the scene, quietly waited and later applauded Barton; several thanked him as they left. NFTA officials praised his calm, quick actions and humility. Barton, who previously drove school buses, said he was simply doing what was needed and hopes the incident highlights the compassion of bus drivers.

An Ebola outbreak in western Uganda, centered in Kibaale district, has killed at least 16 people and put 30 suspected cases in isolation at the main hospital after 12 new admissions; three cases have been laboratory-confirmed. Authorities are monitoring 232 people who may have had contact with patients. Health teams — including Uganda’s Ministry of Health, CDC and WHO partners and Doctors Without Borders — are urgently testing and isolating suspected cases, tracing contacts and boosting protective measures for health workers, though local facilities have struggled with shortages of funds, supplies and food.

The outbreak was identified as the Sudan strain. It likely began with a 3-month-old girl whose funeral may have seeded transmission: Doctors Without Borders reports that 15 of 65 funeral attendees later became ill and at least 11 later died. Funerals and close-contact practices are a major transmission risk because Ebola spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids.

Public fear is high: markets and religious gatherings have been curtailed, people avoid travel and handshakes, and the president has urged avoidance of casual sex and do-it-yourself burials. Officials emphasize there is no specific cure for Ebola; treatment is supportive, and containment through rapid identification, isolation and contact tracing is the primary control measure. Neighboring Kenya has reported suspected cases under investigation but has not confirmed any Ebola. Authorities say they hope to avoid a repeat of Uganda’s much larger 2000 outbreak, while warning suspected case numbers may rise.

NBA star Tony Parker has filed a $20 million lawsuit against W.i.P., the Manhattan nightclub where a widely reported brawl between entourages of Chris Brown and Drake erupted. Parker alleges the club was negligent for permitting both rival parties—despite known “bad blood”—and continuing to serve alcohol, which he says fueled the confrontation. During the bottle-throwing melee Parker suffered a corneal laceration to his left eye and other injuries; he expects to be sidelined about a week and will miss the start of France’s Olympic camp while wearing a therapeutic contact lens. The suit, filed in New York State Supreme Court, blames the club’s management for allowing the combustible situation and for inadequate security. Brown and Drake are not named as defendants in the initial filing; Parker’s attorney says they may be added pending the police investigation and review of surveillance footage. The complaint notes Parker’s $50 million Spurs contract and argues the injury could affect his NBA and Olympic performance. The club declined to comment.

Rep. Adam Schiff (D-CA), likely to chair the House Intelligence Committee, said Sunday that recent court filings about alleged illegal campaign-era payments coordinated by President Trump raise a "very real prospect" the Justice Department could indict Trump when he leaves office, potentially exposing him to jail time. Schiff also flagged a related pardon question — not only whether Trump might pardon others, but whether a future president would consider pardoning Trump.

Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-NY), likely to lead the House Judiciary Committee, said CBS filings that Trump directed his former lawyer Michael Cohen to make illegal payments would be impeachable offenses because they were committed to fraudulently obtaining the presidency, though he cautioned that impeachable conduct does not automatically mean impeachment is the right course.

Separately, White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow said on Fox News Sunday that President Trump did not know in advance about the arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou — detained in Canada on a U.S. extradition request relating to alleged sanctions violations — and reportedly had "no reaction" when informed. Kudlow framed the arrest as a Department of Justice law-enforcement matter and reiterated concerns that evidence suggests Huawei violated Iranian sanctions. The arrest, which occurred the same day Trump reached a G20 trade truce with Xi Jinping, has prompted Chinese demands for Meng’s release and threatens to complicate U.S.-China trade talks.

Former Multi-State Lottery Association security director Eddie Tipton faces new felony charges in Wisconsin alleging he rigged a 2007 Megabucks drawing to pocket a $783,257.72 prize with an accomplice, Texas businessman Robert Rhodes. A Wisconsin Department of Justice prosecutor filed six counts against Tipton — including racketeering, theft by fraud and four computer-crime charges — accusing him of planting modified code in random-number-generator (RNG) software so drawings produced predictable numbers under certain conditions. The complaint says Tipton gave Rhodes the winning numbers in December 2007; Rhodes bought the ticket, set up an LLC to collect the proceeds, and split them with Tipton.

The charges add to Tipton’s long-running legal troubles. In 2015 he was convicted in Iowa on two fraud counts for allegedly tampering with RNGs to win a $14.3 million Hot Lotto prize; that conviction is being appealed to the Iowa Supreme Court after one fraud count was dismissed on timeliness grounds. Iowa prosecutors have since linked Tipton, his brother Tommy, and Rhodes to suspect jackpots in Colorado, Oklahoma, Kansas and Wisconsin and charged them with additional counts including ongoing criminal conduct and money laundering. Rhodes also faces racketeering and theft charges and is expected to plead guilty in the Iowa matter; Tommy Tipton has been charged as well.

Tipton’s attorney contends his client is innocent, arguing the states’ theory — that Tipton shared knowledge of how certified lottery software worked — does not constitute a crime under Iowa or Wisconsin law. Tipton and Rhodes are scheduled to appear in Dane County Circuit Court in February 2017.

Former Massachusetts governor and presidential candidate Mitt Romney, writing as a Detroit native, criticizes the Obama administration’s 2009 auto bailout as crony capitalism that rewarded unions and political allies at taxpayers’ expense. Romney recalls growing up around the auto industry and argues that while Chrysler and GM were vital to the national interest, the administration handled the crisis wrongly. He says a managed bankruptcy — rapid court-guided restructuring that sheds unsustainable labor, pension and real-estate costs — was the better route and would have produced competitive companies without privileging union-controlled trusts or politically connected financiers. Romney contends the bailout’s terms shortchanged secured creditors and non-union workers while protecting union pensions and giving the UAW large ownership stakes, and he faults the Obama team (and allies who defend the rescue, including George W. Bush) for creating moral hazard and politicized outcomes.

Romney supports decisive changes in management and labor relations: replace existing executives with leaders from other industries, end adversarial labor-management relations through profit-sharing or stock grants, trim executive perks, and focus on long-term investment in product development and fuel-saving technology rather than short-term stock gains. He urges protecting strong dealers, increasing federal investment in basic energy and materials research (from about $4 billion to $20 billion annually), correcting tax biases against U.S. automakers, and not shielding shareholders and bondholders from losses. Finally, he calls for the government to divest its GM holdings responsibly and for the federal role to be limited to facilitating post-bankruptcy financing and warranty assurances so auto companies can re-emerge viable through managed bankruptcy rather than a politicized bailout.

Archaeologists from the University of Southampton have produced the first detailed, non-invasive plan of the medieval city at Old Sarum (near Salisbury, Wiltshire) using a suite of geophysical techniques (magnetometry, earth resistance, ground-penetrating radar and resistivity tomography). The survey focused on the inner and outer baileys of the Iron Age fort that later hosted a Norman castle and cathedral, and revealed a dense urban layout of late 11th–13th century occupation including domestic streets, industrial features (kilns/furnaces), quarrying after the city’s decline, and large structural complexes along the southern outer bailey.

Most strikingly, the team identified the buried foundations of a very large, courtyard-arranged complex—about 170 m by 65 m—with walls up to 3 m thick, a probable 60 m great hall, a substantial tower and multi-storey buildings. Specialists say its scale, location and design strongly suggest a royal palace, possibly built in the early 12th century (a prime candidate being Henry I). If confirmed, it would be one of the largest previously unknown medieval royal palaces discovered in Britain and changes understanding of Norman urban and high-status building in the period.

Old Sarum was founded as a Norman administrative and ecclesiastical centre after the Conquest (William the Conqueror held a major assembly there), but by the early 13th century its functions were moved to New Sarum (Salisbury), with masonry reused in the new city. Because Old Sarum has remained a largely undisturbed greenfield site, the geophysical results offer a rare opportunity to study Norman town planning without excavation. The project also doubled as training for students and the team plans further survey work to expand and refine the picture of the site.

Rep. Louise M. Slaughter, a veteran Democratic congresswoman from upstate New York, has died at age 88 after suffering a fall at her Washington, D.C., residence and being treated at George Washington University Hospital. Slaughter, who was serving her 16th term and was the longest-serving member of Congress from New York, had been hospitalized following the fall; her chief of staff, Liam Fitzsimmons, said she had sustained a concussion.

A microbiologist by training and originally from Kentucky, Slaughter first won election to the House in 1986. She was the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee and was the first woman to chair that panel (2007–2010). A prominent and often bipartisan figure, she was known for securing infrastructure funding for her district, pushing safety standards for military body armor, sponsoring ethics and health-related legislation (including work on genetic nondiscrimination and the Violence Against Women Act), and authoring a ban on congressional insider trading. She remained politically active—announcing a bid for a 17th term—and was widely praised by leaders on both sides of the aisle, including Nancy Pelosi and House Speaker Paul Ryan, who ordered flags lowered to half-staff. Her staff and colleagues remembered her as a relentless advocate for Western New York and a trailblazer for women in Congress.

China’s tight controls on rare-earth exports have driven global prices sharply higher while domestic prices remain steady. China supplies about 95% of the world’s rare earths because mining and processing are environmentally hazardous, deterring production elsewhere. In 2010 Beijing set an export quota of 30,300 metric tons; with only a few thousand tons left, global demand for raw rare earths (about 50,000 tons annually) far outstrips permitted exports. Quota rights are allocated to 32 authorized exporters and have become tradable and extremely valuable — the right to export one ton reportedly fetches roughly $40,000 — adding large implicit costs for foreign buyers.

The export restrictions and a recent temporary halt to raw-rare-earth shipments (which China later resumed) produced international alarm and diplomatic friction. Japan was hit hardest because it imports raw rare earths to process domestically; the U.S. and Europe, which mainly buy processed powders not subject to quotas, felt a more limited impact. Prices reflect this: neodymium trades at about $40,000/ton in China but roughly double abroad; lanthanum is under $4,500/ton in China and as much as ten times higher overseas. The disruption prompted U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton to raise the issue with Chinese officials and spurred industrialized nations to seek alternative supplies and to expand rare-earth development outside China. The episode also highlighted China’s geopolitical leverage and coincided with broader trade tensions, including a U.S. WTO inquiry into Chinese clean-energy policies.

This Forbes profile (Dec. 12, 2017) investigates Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross’s long-standing habit of overstating his wealth and misrepresenting his finances, concluding that roughly $2 billion he recently claimed to have moved into family trusts—and used to justify billionaire status—likely never existed.

Key points:
- Forbes found a major discrepancy between Ross’s historical public claims of billionaire status and his required federal financial disclosures filed for his Cabinet nomination, which showed less than $700 million in personal assets. Ross told Forbes he’d transferred more than $2 billion to family trusts between the election and his nomination but declined to provide documentation.
- Forbes’s reporting — corroborated in part by interviews with about ten former WL Ross & Co. employees and records of regulatory actions and lawsuits — traces a long pattern of exaggerations, omissions and misleading statements by Ross dating back to the 2000s. These included treating investors’ fund assets as his own in public valuations and inflating fund-raising totals in ways that benefited his reputation and ability to raise capital.
- The profile recounts Ross’s rise: a bankruptcy specialist at Rothschild, buying out a private-equity fund to form WL Ross & Co., and the lucrative 2003 sale of International Steel Group (which produced significant carried interest for him). While he profited substantially, Forbes argues his true personal wealth was much lower than repeatedly claimed.
- Former colleagues say Ross inflated net-worth figures to enhance his standing and attract investors; several ex-employees have sued or alleged he misappropriated interests or provided inaccurate financial information. WL Ross & Co. and its parent Invesco have faced SEC scrutiny: a 2016 settlement involved a $2.3 million fine and $11.8 million refunded to investors, and Invesco disclosed additional related regulatory expenses.
- Ross’s appointment to the Trump Cabinet forced mandatory disclosures that undermined his billionaire image. After Forbes published its findings, six Senate Democrats asked the Office of Government Ethics to investigate. The Commerce Department denied a post-election $2 billion transfer took place, even though Ross himself had told Forbes it had.
- The piece situates Ross’s decision to join the administration as partly driven by a search for renewed relevance after mixed investment-track records, and notes President Trump’s defense of appointing wealthy figures like Ross to economic posts, saying he preferred rich people in those roles.

Overall, Forbes portrays Wilbur Ross as a talented dealmaker whose career includes significant achievements but also a persistent pattern of misleading claims about his personal finances, which have had legal, regulatory and reputational consequences.

PBS Nature’s three-part miniseries Super Cats (narrated by F. Murray Abraham) premieres Wednesdays Oct. 24–Nov. 7 at 8 p.m. (episodes stream next day on pbs.org/nature and PBS apps). Filmed over 600 days in 14 countries and featuring 31 cat species, the series uses new camera technology and scientific collaboration to reveal rare and previously unseen feline behaviors — social interactions, communication, parenting, courtship and hunting.

Episode highlights:
- Episode 2, “Cats in Every Corner” (available to stream Nov. 1), spotlights the tiny but highly efficient black-footed cat of southern Africa. At just 36–52 cm long and 1–3 kg, this vulnerable species hunts mostly at night and was filmed for the first time using light-sensitive cameras and radio-collar data from researcher Alexander Sliwa. The filmmakers captured three distinct hunting strategies (fast hunting, slow stalking, and “still hunting” at burrow entrances) and documented that a black-footed cat can kill 10–14 small prey per night — a kill roughly every 50 minutes with about a 60% success rate, making it extremely effective relative to larger predators.
- Other footage in Episode 2 includes a pregnant jaguar in Costa Rica, a rare swamp tiger in India, and a family of fishing cats in Asian wetlands.
- The series also delivers on-camera firsts: nocturnal hunts by the black-footed cat, remote-camera intimacy between a Pallas’ cat mother and kittens, a puma preying on Magellanic penguins, and a swamp tiger bathing in the sea, among others.

Conservation context: many featured cat species face habitat loss and human pressures. Scientists and consultants on the series emphasize that conservation efforts can protect vulnerable populations if threats are addressed.

Production: a BBC Studios production for PBS and BBC (co-produced with France Télévisions and THIRTEEN Productions LLC) with extensive international crews, scientific consultants, and funding from multiple foundations. Episode 3, “Science and Secrets,” airs Nov. 7.

Over a 72-hour period this week, Chicago's West Side experienced a sharp spike in overdoses: emergency responders reported 74 cases — more than double the number for the same period last year. City health and police officials say many incidents involved suspected heroin possibly laced with the powerful synthetic opioid fentanyl; samples recovered from two West Side locations are being tested but results are pending. No confirmed fentanyl test results yet, and authorities were investigating whether at least one recent death in East Garfield Park was linked to the batch.

Mount Sinai Hospital treated 14 people for heroin overdoses in 24 hours, with some patients collapsing immediately after injection; two were in intensive care and several required multiple doses of naloxone (Narcan) to be revived. Fire Department officials said most victims were stabilized with a single field dose of Narcan but often needed additional doses at hospitals, prompting extra Narcan supplies for crews.

Multiple law enforcement agencies, including the DEA and Chicago police, are working to trace the source of the “extremely strong” batch, believed to be concentrated in at least two West Side locations (one in North Lawndale). Public-health officials and harm-reduction groups urged caution, recommending carrying Narcan and watching peers. The outbreak echoes a 2005–2007 wave of fentanyl-related overdoses; heroin deaths statewide have risen since 2011 and Chicago-area ER visits related to heroin are among the nation’s highest. Toxicology results and further investigations are underway.

A Sacramento man has filed a federal class-action lawsuit against Hilton, alleging the hotel charged him 75 cents for a USA Today left outside his room that he never requested and assumed was complimentary. Rodney Harmon stayed at the Hilton Garden Inn Sonoma County Airport on March 28; he later discovered the small-print disclosure about the newspaper charge on the room-key sleeve and says the fee was effectively hidden. The complaint claims the practice causes millions of guests to unknowingly pay for unwanted papers, is deceptive, wasteful, and environmentally harmful due to unused copies and paper production. Harmon's lawyer says the case is about broader unfair corporate practices. Hilton declined to comment because of the pending litigation.

This document contains two wartime-era stories from World War II.

1) Margot Wölk — forced food taster for Hitler:
- Margot Wölk, a 24-year-old secretary from Berlin, was one of about 15 young women compelled by the SS to taste food prepared for Adolf Hitler at his Eastern Front headquarters, the Wolf’s Lair, near Gross-Partsch (now Parcz, Poland). The role lasted roughly two and a half years.
- She was taken from her mother-in-law’s village home after fleeing bombed Berlin in 1941. Although food at the Wolf’s Lair was reportedly good (Hitler’s menu was vegetarian), the women lived in fear because of rumors the Allies might poison Hitler’s meals; confirming the food’s safety put the tasters’ lives at risk.
- After the July 20, 1944 assassination attempt on Hitler, security tightened; the tasters were housed under strict guard. Wölk endured sexual violence by an SS officer while interned, and later, after escaping toward Berlin with help from a lieutenant, she was raped repeatedly by Soviet soldiers during their advance, injuries from which left her unable to have children.
- She survived thanks to that lieutenant and a Berlin doctor who hid her from SS searches. Reunited with her husband Karl in 1946, she cared for him and they spent decades together. For many years she kept silent about her experiences; at age 95 she finally spoke publicly to condemn Hitler and recount the trauma. Despite everything, she says she retained humor as a survival tactic.

2) Hyde Park farm added to Virginia Landmarks Register:
- Hyde Park in Nottoway County, Virginia—purchased in 1938 by Richmond department store owner William B. Thalhimer—was added to the Virginia Landmarks Register.
- Thalhimer established Hyde Farmlands as a training farm and refuge for Jews fleeing Nazi Germany. From 1938 to 1941 about 30 Jewish immigrants lived and worked there in dairy and poultry operations; many later served in the U.S. armed forces.
- The listing is among 13 recent additions to the state register, which also included historic districts, a New Deal-era elementary school, and longstanding houses and homesteads.

Both pieces highlight different civilian experiences and humanitarian responses connected to the era of Nazi Germany—one a harrowing personal testimony of coercion, violence and survival, the other a preservation of a U.S. rescue effort for Jewish refugees.

This document contains two distinct pieces.

1) On deliberate forgetting and memory:
- Recent experiments show people can intentionally forget under certain conditions. Jeremy Manning and Kenneth Norman’s study found that when people try to forget newly learned words, their brains discard the mental context present during learning; when they try to remember, that context is actively maintained. This suggests forgetting works by removing the contextual “scaffolding” that supports memories.
- Context is also central to remembering—techniques like the memory palace exploit spatial context to aid recall. Everyday examples (e.g., moving through rooms at a party) show how varied contexts help organize and retrieve experiences.
- The essay warns that modern habits, such as photographing important moments instead of fully experiencing them, can outsource memory to images and social sharing. Photos bias recollection toward visually appealing moments and can make lived experience thinner and less emotionally truthful—a tendency called “Living Palely” by Doris McIlwain.
- The piece closes by suggesting that while techniques might someday let us selectively remember or forget, doing so requires changing how we live, not just how we think about memories.

2) On the 28 classified pages about possible Saudi links to 9/11:
- Tom Kean and Lee Hamilton, leaders of the independent 9/11 Commission, urge caution as the Obama administration prepared to release at least some of 28 pages from a separate 2002 congressional investigation that alleged possible Saudi involvement. Those pages had remained secret.
- Kean and Hamilton note the congressional pages were largely raw, unvetted FBI material—comparable to preliminary law-enforcement notes—and were never followed up by investigative work. They warn against drawing firm conclusions from such preliminary material because unsubstantiated accusations about complicity in the worst US mass murders are grave and require careful vetting.
- They emphasize that the official 9/11 Commission investigated leads in those pages and found only one implicated Saudi government employee (Fahad al Thumairy, an imam employed by the Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs), who remains a person of interest but for whom no evidence was found that he assisted hijackers. The commission concluded in 2004 there was no evidence that the Saudi government or senior officials funded al Qaeda; a 2015 congressional review found no new evidence.
- The piece notes that Director of National Intelligence James Clapper expected at least partial release of the pages by June, and that any material released should be interpreted in the context of the commission’s prior, thorough investigation.

Congress has inserted a secret restriction into the $1.1 trillion omnibus spending bill that would prevent transferring control of U.S. drone strike operations and/or unmanned aircraft from the CIA to the Defense Department, U.S. officials said. The language is tucked into a classified annex covering intelligence funding and would bar use of money to shift the covert drone campaign to Pentagon control; its exact scope is unclear. Lawmakers on the appropriations and intelligence committees, including Sen. Dianne Feinstein, have expressed concern that the military might cause greater civilian harm than the CIA, citing recent strikes in Yemen that killed civilians and appeared to violate White House guidance requiring “near certainty” of no civilian casualties.

The move is an unusually direct congressional intervention in covert operations and undercuts an Obama administration plan, announced last year, to move many counterterrorism strikes outside war zones to Defense Department oversight to refocus the CIA on intelligence and increase transparency. Administration officials had been working on logistical steps for the shift, but congressional language — possibly more complex than a simple funding block and potentially requiring Pentagon certification that it matches CIA targeting practices — would impede or delay implementation.

The restriction comes amid heightened scrutiny of U.S. drone strikes in Yemen, where a December JSOC strike on a convoy in Radaa reportedly killed up to a dozen people including civilians, and later strikes have killed wedding attendees and, as recently reported, a farmer struck by drone-fired rockets. Yemeni outrage has been intense: families and parliament have condemned strikes, demanded an end to U.S. drone operations in Yemeni airspace, and called for criminalization; victims’ families have rejected quiet settlements. Critics argue drone strikes, while targeting AQAP (a persistent threat including past near-miss attacks on the U.S.), cause civilian deaths that fuel local backlash and recruitment for extremists.

The spending bill has passed the House and is expected to clear the Senate and reach the president soon. White House, CIA and Pentagon spokespeople declined comment. The dispute reflects broader tensions over the CIA’s expanding paramilitary role, the proper oversight and transparency of lethal counterterrorism operations, and how best to balance counterterrorism effectiveness against civilian protection and international legitimacy.

Pennsylvania’s State Employees’ Retirement System (SERS) announced it will revoke former Penn State assistant coach Jerry Sandusky’s $59,000-a-year pension after his conviction on child sexual abuse charges. A SERS letter informed Sandusky he will lose his $4,908 monthly annuity and that his wife, Dottie, will no longer receive survivor benefits, citing that two convictions— involuntary deviate sexual intercourse and indecent assault—fall under the state’s pension-forfeiture law. The agency also characterized Sandusky as a “de facto” Penn State employee after his 1999 retirement because of his extensive post-retirement ties to the university. Sandusky’s attorney said he will challenge the forfeiture, arguing the statute applies only to crimes involving students where the defendant worked; legal experts noted courts have broadly interpreted the law. Sandusky joined SERS in 1969, took a $148,000 lump sum at retirement, and collected about $900,000 in pension payments through September 2012. Employees whose pensions are forfeited may keep contributions without interest (less fees or restitution) and can appeal to the SERS board and through state courts.

The article also recounts the Sanduskys’ sentencing letters and public statements, which portrayed themselves as victims of a conspiracy involving Penn State, prosecutors and the media and blamed the accusers. Those letters—and Jerry Sandusky’s courtroom and media remarks denying responsibility and attacking victims—were widely criticized by legal observers and prosecutors and likely contributed to the harsh sentence: 30 to 60 years in prison. The couple’s letters singled out their adopted son, Matt, who testified he was also molested and whose decision to come forward was condemned by his parents; his lawyers said the parents’ attacks were hurtful and unfair. The piece notes Sandusky’s lawyer declined comment and prosecutors defended their characterization of Sandusky’s conduct and statements.

This document reviews a University of Illinois study and broader context about TSA PreCheck, the TSA’s expedited screening program that requires a background check and a roughly $85 fee for five years’ membership. PreCheck is intended to improve security by pre-vetting low-risk travelers, reduce screening costs, and speed throughput at checkpoints; the TSA had targeted about 25 million participants but enrollment has lagged (roughly half that goal across PreCheck and related trusted-traveler programs).

Key findings from the Illinois study (Jacobson et al., Journal of Transportation Security):
- Waiving the $85 fee for certain high-volume travelers can be economically beneficial to TSA.
- If 25 million travelers who make at least six round trips (12 screenings) per year were enrolled at no cost, the agency would forgo about $425 million in annual fees but would save roughly $459 million a year in labor and equipment costs—netting about $34 million in annual savings.
- The analysis considers only direct TSA labor and equipment savings; additional societal benefits (passenger time savings, increased travel) would add further value.
- The study argues that enrolling high-frequency fliers for free would improve security by reducing the number of “unknown” travelers and allowing resources to focus on higher-risk individuals.
- The authors note potential backlash from less-frequent travelers and existing paying members if free enrollment is offered selectively.

Context and operational issues discussed:
- PreCheck’s early rollout included measures (e.g., admitting regular passengers into PreCheck lanes) to keep lanes populated; this created mixed messaging and reduced incentives for people to apply, hindering enrollment growth.
- Security failures and Inspector General scrutiny led TSA leadership to change practices, reducing the earlier practice of funneling non-vetted travelers into PreCheck and contributing to longer lines as non-PreCheck passengers returned to general screening.
- TSA workforce reductions, shifting priorities, and reliance on enrollment projections tied to 25 million participants have exacerbated checkpoint delays.
- Enrollment has improved recently (reported growth to ~16,000/day), and the TSA also recognizes benefits of expanding enrollment and access points.
- Proposed ways to expand enrollment include waiving fees for frequent fliers, automatically adding certain cleared government workers, expanding application/enrollment locations (including using contractors), and better marketing and customer incentives; privacy, liability, and logistical issues have slowed some efforts.
- Airports and airlines that actively promote PreCheck and facilitate enrollment (e.g., on-site centers, perks) have achieved higher adoption rates and smoother operations.

Bottom line: The study concludes that offering free PreCheck to selected high-frequency travelers can pay for itself through labor and equipment savings while improving throughput and security; operational changes, clearer messaging, easier enrollment, and targeted incentives could help the TSA reach enrollment levels that meaningfully reduce delays and costs, though political, equity, and implementation concerns remain.

Chicago police say a 15-year-old Crane High School basketball player, Steven Rosenthal, died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound after officers briefly tried to stop him Friday evening near his West Side home. The Cook County medical examiner ruled the death a suicide after an autopsy. CPD spokesmen said officers saw Rosenthal with a handgun, attempted to detain him, he ran, and then shot himself; they said there is no video or ballistic evidence that any officer fired, and no officer reported discharging a weapon.

Rosenthal’s family and supporters reject that account. More than 120 people marched through North Lawndale Sunday — from Johnson School of Excellence to Mount Sinai Hospital and the 10th District — demanding release of any footage and an independent investigation. His aunt and legal guardian, Terinica Thomas, and family attorney Andrew Stroth said eyewitnesses told them officers shot Rosenthal and called for the medical examiner and police to make evidence available, including body-camera video and the alleged weapon. Protesters chanted “justice for Steve” and vowed nightly demonstrations; police said they have not yet decided whether to release body-cam recordings and that the investigation remains ongoing.

This article reviews research showing that the blue‑rich light emitted by tablets, phones and other light‑emitting e‑readers disrupts sleep by suppressing melatonin and delaying the circadian clock — effects beyond any purely cognitive stimulation from device use.

Background
- Stimulus‑control sleep therapy (Bootzin, 1972) advises reserving the bed for sleep and sex to condition the brain to sleep there and avoid arousing activities in bed. Modern devices complicate that prescription because they both stimulate cognitively and emit biologically active light.
- Prior work by Charles Czeisler found widespread pre‑bed device use in Americans and linked greater use with poorer sleep; researchers hypothesized overstimulation and/or light exposure as mechanisms.

New study (Czeisler, Anne‑Marie Chang et al., PNAS)
- Design: Intensive inpatient, crossover study with 12 participants. For five nights each, subjects read for four hours before bedtime either on an iPad (light‑emitting) or from printed books in dim light; sleep was monitored by EEG and melatonin sampled hourly.
- Key findings:
  - Reading from iPads delayed melatonin secretion by ~1.5 hours on average.
  - Participants took longer to fall asleep, had reduced REM sleep, and reported feeling less sleepy at night but less alert the next morning, even after eight hours of sleep.
  - Light‑emission profiles of other tablets, phones and laptops were similar (blue‑enriched short wavelengths), so similar effects are expected; non‑lit e‑readers (e.g., standard Kindle) behaved like printed books.
- Implications: Evening exposure to device light can meaningfully shift circadian timing and reduce sleep quality. Chronic melatonin suppression and altered sleep are associated with long‑term health risks (e.g., obesity, diabetes, and possible links to certain cancers).

Takeaway
- The study provides physiological evidence that the light from electronic devices — particularly blue‑enriched emissions — can delay sleep onset, reduce REM sleep and shift circadian rhythms, not solely because devices are cognitively stimulating. Given pervasive nighttime device use, these effects may have broad public‑health implications and suggest reconsidering evening screen habits or device design/lighting to protect sleep.

A teenage girl who had been reported missing in April 2010 when she was 15 told police this week she escaped from a Washington Park, Illinois, home where she was held captive, beaten and sexually assaulted nearly every day and was raped by her captor. She said those assaults resulted in a pregnancy and the birth of a child, whom she left inside the house when she escaped with help from a relative.

A Washington Park tactical/SWAT team raided the home, recovered the toddler and took into custody a 24-year-old man and his mother, whom police say likely aided the crimes. Authorities allege the pair forced the girl to use a false name on medical records during her pregnancy and the birth. Neither suspect had been publicly identified or charged as of the report. Neighbors said they had seen the girl at times but did not suspect she was being held.

Detroit Tigers outfielder Delmon Young was arrested early this morning in Manhattan after an alcohol-fueled confrontation outside the Hilton New York in which police say he hurled an anti‑Semitic slur at a group of four men and tackled one of them. According to police and court papers, the incident began about 2:30–2:40 a.m. after the men spoke with a panhandler wearing a yarmulke. Witnesses say Young shouted “You bunch of f---ing Jews,” shoved 32‑year‑old Jason Shank into a hotel wall and tackled him, causing minor arm scratches; Shank refused medical attention. The charge filed is aggravated harassment in the second degree, submitted as a hate crime, a misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in jail.

Young, reportedly heavily intoxicated, was taken to Roosevelt Hospital to sober up before being processed, was arraigned later that day, and released on $5,000 bail. He apologized in a statement—issued through his attorney and PR firm—saying he “sincerely regret[s] what happened” and will work to improve himself; his lawyer also disputed some allegations and said video shows others provoked the incident. The Tigers declined detailed comment pending legal proceedings; Young missed that night’s game and the club has in the past used MLB support programs for players with alcohol‑related issues. Young, 26, is a former No. 1 draft pick with prior disciplinary history (a 2006 50‑game suspension in the minors for throwing a bat) and is under a one‑year contract with Detroit.

A U.N.-backed initiative (Solving the E-Waste Problem, StEP) has produced the first global, country-level map and dataset of electronic waste (e-waste), revealing rapidly rising and widely uneven generation of discarded electrical and electronic equipment. Key findings:

- Global scale and growth: In 2012 the world generated about 54 million tons (49 million metric tons) of e-waste — roughly 20 kg (43 lb) per person. StEP forecasts a ~33% increase by 2017 to about 72 million tons (65 million metric tons), equivalent to roughly 11 Great Pyramids or 200 Empire State Buildings. Average per-person generation worldwide is about 7 kg per year, with wealthier countries producing much more.

- Country patterns: China led production of electrical/electronic equipment in 2012 (≈12.2 million tons) and, along with emerging economies (India, Brazil, South Africa, Russia and former Soviet states), is driving much of the projected growth. The U.S. was the largest single producer of e-waste in absolute terms in 2012 (~9.36 million tons, ≈29 kg per capita) and ranked seventh in per-capita generation (~30 kg); small wealthy countries like Luxembourg and Qatar are among the highest per-capita producers. Low-income countries such as Haiti and Afghanistan produce very little e-waste per person.

- U.S. specifics: A separate U.S. report (NCER/MIT) found about 258.2 million used units of computers, monitors, TVs and cellphones in 2010; 171.4 million were collected for recycling and 14.4 million exported. The U.S. exports large volumes of CRT monitors by weight and cellphones by unit. Recycling infrastructure lags EU countries: only about half the U.S. states have formal programs, though collection rates are increasing.

- Trade, tracking and hazards: Trade in used electronics and e-waste is often opaque (items listed generically), complicating tracking. Significant volumes from rich countries still reach developing countries, where informal dismantling exposes workers and the environment to toxic substances. Proper recycling can recover valuable materials (e.g., gold, silver, palladium, copper) but primitive recycling poses health and environmental risks.

- Policy and behavior implications: The map provides comparable national data to inform policymakers and industry. Experts highlight the need for better recycling systems, clearer trade descriptions, extended product lifetimes, and consumer behavior changes (use electronics longer, increase recycling) to curb the growing e-waste problem.

Key points

- Sleep not only supports recall but can substantially improve relearning — the process of re-acquiring information that has been lost or weakened.
- In a controlled study (Mazza et al., Psychological Science), 40 adults learned 16 Swahili–French word pairs, then relearned them 12 hours later either after a night of sleep or after a day awake. Retention was tested at 1 week and 6 months.
- Initial learning was equal across groups. At relearning, the sleep group recalled more items on their first attempt (≈10 vs. ≈7) and needed roughly half as many practice cycles to regain perfect recall (≈3 vs. ≈6).
- Long-term benefits favored the sleep group: after one week they recalled ~15 pairs vs. ~11 for the wake group; after six months they recalled ~9 vs. ~3 — despite both groups having practiced to perfect performance at the relearning session.
- A control group that slept but did not do a full relearning session did not show the same long-term advantage, indicating the benefit depends on the combination of sleep after initial learning plus active relearning.
- Total sleep time correlated with better relearning and recall. This fits two possible explanations: sleep-specific consolidation processes that strengthen memory traces, or sleep simply reducing interference so ongoing consolidation can occur.
- Limitations: the study used verbal materials and scheduled learning/relearning at different times of day for the two groups (morning vs. evening), which can confound effects because circadian factors influence alertness and performance. Further work should test other materials and control time-of-day effects.

Implications

- Sleeping after initial study and scheduling additional study sessions shortly before sleep can make relearning faster and boost long-term retention.
- For mastering important material (e.g., exam preparation, professional certification), interleaving study sessions with sleep and using repeated practice appears to be an especially effective strategy.
- These findings add to evidence that sleep plays an active role in memory consolidation and can “transform” memories to make re-acquisition easier, though more research is needed to separate sleep-specific mechanisms from reduced interference and to generalize beyond verbal learning.

Two Asheville, North Carolina, police officers who responded to a noise and road-blocking complaint at a Fourth of July block party ended up joining in the fun. Neighbors had built a DIY slip-and-slide down the street for kids; when officers arrived they found the noise acceptable and the slide left enough room for cars to pass. After issuing no citations, the officers asked to take turns on the makeshift water slide. Video of the officers sliding was shared by the police department and drew national attention.

Miss Honduras 2014, María José Alvarado, 19, and her sister Sofía Trinidad disappeared after attending a friend’s birthday party late Thursday near their hometown of Santa Bárbara, Honduras. The sisters were last seen getting into a vehicle leaving the party; María José had been at home with her parents preparing to travel to London to compete in the Miss World pageant. Authorities initially did not treat the case as a crime, but later detained four people for questioning — including the party venue owner and Sofía’s boyfriend, Plutarco Ruiz — as potential witnesses or suspects. No ransom demand has been reported. The disappearance has drawn national concern; María José’s mother publicly appealed for their safe return. María José, a student and aspiring diplomat who won the Miss Honduras title in April, was due to depart for Miss World, which begins this week in London.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid is threatening to use the so-called “nuclear option” to change Senate rules so executive-branch nominees could be confirmed by a simple majority (51 votes) instead of the current 60-vote cloture threshold. The move is a response to sustained Republican filibusters that Democrats say have increasingly been used to block routine executive appointments and effectively hobble administration agencies (notably nominees to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the National Labor Relations Board). Reid has told President Obama he intends to act unless Republicans end those holds; Obama indicated support.

Supporters frame the change as a narrow, targeted fix to restore an “up-or-down” vote on administration personnel and to prevent what they call an abusive new use of the filibuster that nullifies enacted laws by preventing agencies from being staffed. Opponents warn the precedent would erode the filibuster more broadly—first executive nominees, then judicial nominees, and eventually legislation—transforming the Senate into a majoritarian body more like the House. Republicans, led by Mitch McConnell, call the move destabilizing and argue it will harm them when they next hold the majority; Democrats counter that Republicans have already expanded obstruction tactics and that the change is necessary and limited.

Behind the fight are legal disputes over recess appointments and several high-profile nominees Republicans continue to block. Some senators on both sides have tried to broker compromises and convene a summit to avert rule changes, but Democrats have rejected partial concessions unless key nominees are approved. The debate centers on institutional norms: whether to curb what Democrats see as an illegitimate weaponization of the filibuster or to preserve the filibuster’s broader role as a check on majority power.

A Smith College employee called campus police on July 31, 2018 after spotting a Black student, Oumou Kanoute, quietly eating lunch in a common room; the caller said the person appeared "out of place." Kanoute, a rising sophomore and summer teaching assistant in Smith’s STEM program, recorded part of the encounter and posted about it on social media, saying the experience left her frightened and that “all I did was be black.” The caller was placed on leave pending review.

President Kathleen McCartney apologized publicly, affirmed that the student belongs at Smith, and announced steps including mandatory anti-bias training for staff and faculty and hiring an independent investigative team. Two civil-rights attorneys (Anthony Cruthird and Kate Upatham) conducted the external investigation to determine whether college policies were violated and to recommend improvements. The investigators concluded the caller had a “legitimate, non-discriminatory reason” to contact campus police and did not find sufficient evidence that the call was based on the student’s race or color or that policies were violated, though they acknowledged the student was frightened by the encounter.

Smith has offered restorative mediation between the student and the caller and continues to consider and implement reforms (including reviewing affinity housing, training enhancements, and policy changes). The ACLU has been advising the student; no lawsuit has been filed. Some social-media attempts to identify the caller were inaccurate; the college withheld the caller’s identity citing privacy rules. The college released a Q&A addressing investigation details, training for campus police, and next steps.

Greenwich High School apologized after its football team used a play nicknamed “Hitler,” in which players reportedly charged the field shouting the name and signaled it by laying an index finger across the upper lip. The incident was reported by a Trumbull mother whose son’s freshman team faced Greenwich; she said the chant and gesture deeply offended her because her family suffered in the Holocaust. Headmaster Chris Winters posted an apology, said the practice has been stopped, and the school reached out to the local Jewish community.

The team and coaches met with the Connecticut Anti-Defamation League, which characterized the episode as a teaching moment and said there appeared to be no intent to intimidate or express antisemitism, but rather a lack of understanding. Local rabbis and community leaders condemned the usage as a failure of the school’s Athletic Code of Conduct and urged adult responsibility in educating students about the Holocaust. The play reportedly had been used for years, and the district has pledged corrective steps and outreach.

A viral video captured Helmetta, N.J. Special Police Officer Richard Recine telling a resident that police “don't have to” follow the Constitution because, in his view, President Obama “has decimated” it. The footage was recorded during a confrontation at the borough municipal building while resident Steve Wronko was taking photographs; Wronko and his wife have been campaigning for reforms at the local animal shelter after receiving a sick underage puppy and seeking reimbursement for vet bills. Police Director Robert Manney, who saw the video, called Recine’s remarks “uncalled for and unprofessional,” opened an internal affairs investigation and said it should be resolved quickly because the video provides clear evidence. Recine, a retired Franklin officer collecting a $79,000 pension, works part time in Helmetta. The town’s police say they can ask people to identify themselves in municipal buildings and maintain staff had been concerned about Wronko’s prior behavior. The incident drew public attention after the video was posted online.

Steven Spielberg’s Lincoln led major awards attention this week, topping the British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA) nominations with 10 nods, including Best Film, Best Actor (Daniel Day‑Lewis), Best Supporting Actor (Tommy Lee Jones) and Best Supporting Actress (Sally Field). The Directors Guild of America announced its feature directing nominees, giving Ben Affleck his first DGA nomination for Argo and naming four past winners—Kathryn Bigelow (Zero Dark Thirty), Tom Hooper (Les Misérables), Ang Lee (Life of Pi) and Steven Spielberg (Lincoln)—as fellow nominees. Airbus intends to demonstrate a prototype single-person, self-piloted “flying car” by the end of the year through its Urban Air Mobility division, the company’s CEO Tom Enders said at a tech conference in Munich. The unit is exploring personal VTOL (vertical take-off and landing) vehicles and larger, helicopter-style air taxis that users could summon via an app. Airbus frames the effort as a way to reduce urban gridlock, cut infrastructure spending on roads and bridges, and leverage advances in autonomy, AI and battery technology. The company stresses the project is in an experimentation phase and that any operational system would need to be environmentally clean.

Media reaction was enthusiastic but skeptical. Observers note Airbus’ track record and resources give it advantages over startups, but important technical, regulatory and practical barriers remain: reliable sense-and-avoid systems, safety certification (e.g., FAA approval), noise, cost, airspace regulation, landing/parking infrastructure, maintenance demands, and the long history of helicopter-based concepts failing to become cheap, quiet, mass-market alternatives. Airbus declined to disclose investment levels.
