Tiffany Johnson, a mother of three from Concord, N.C., survived a shark attack while snorkeling with her husband James off a shallow reef in the Bahamas during the final stop of their cruise. She said she felt a bump, turned and found a shark with her arm in its mouth; after several minutes of struggling she managed to free herself but the shark severed part of her hand and arm. Her husband jumped in to help and local doctors in the Bahamas stopped the bleeding. Travel and paperwork complications initially delayed evacuation; a Medevac to Carolinas Medical Center — initially quoted at $16,000 out of pocket — was ultimately covered by the company. Back in the U.S., Tiffany has undergone multiple surgeries and is preparing for a prosthetic; she and her family report positive medical updates and describe feeling sustained by faith. Friends and community members are encouraging prayers and financial support to help with ongoing medical needs.

Human Rights Watch found that four Israeli strikes on journalists and media facilities in Gaza during the November 14–21, 2012 hostilities violated the laws of war by deliberately hitting civilians and civilian objects that did not appear to be contributing to military operations.

Key findings
- Fatalities and injuries: Two al-Aqsa TV cameramen—Mahmoud al-Kumi (29) and Hussam Salama (30)—were killed when a missile struck their clearly marked TV car on November 20. At least 10 media workers were wounded across the incidents. Shrapnel from one strike killed a two‑year‑old boy who lived across the street from a targeted building.
- Damaged media: Four media offices and the offices of four private companies were heavily damaged. Antenna towers and studios on the roofs and top floors of several high-rise buildings housing local and international media were struck.
- Sites and strikes examined: Human Rights Watch investigated attacks on (a) the car carrying the two al-Aqsa cameramen; (b) the rooftop antenna areas of the 11‑storey Shawa and Housari Building (wounding seven Quds TV staff and damaging Alwan Radio equipment); (c) the 15‑storey Shoruq Building (damaging an al-Aqsa TV studio and injuring staff; a separate strike that day on a lower floor appears to have killed one Islamic Jihad fighter); and (d) the sixth and seventh floors of the Naama Building (damaging multiple civilian offices; shrapnel killed the toddler).
- Israeli claims: The IDF asserted the strikes hit Hamas operatives, “operational communications infrastructure,” or a Hamas “intelligence and command center.” Officials repeatedly argued that some media employees and outlets were integral to Hamas and thus legitimate targets.
- Lack of evidence: Human Rights Watch found no credible evidence provided by Israel to substantiate that the targeted individuals or antenna towers were directly participating in hostilities or used for military command-and-control. Interviews with families, colleagues, and on-site inspections found the two cameramen were reporting, not fighters; media offices and antenna towers showed no signs of military use; and some media attacked were commercial or entertainment outlets not broadcasting at the time.
- Legal analysis: Under international humanitarian law, journalists and media are civilians and civilian objects unless directly participating in hostilities or used to make an effective contribution to military action with a definite military advantage from their destruction. Expressions of opinion, propaganda, or ties to a party do not remove protection. Statements by Israeli officials framing media workers as militants or command structures based on affiliation or speech, Human Rights Watch said, unlawfully blur civilian protections and can be evidence of intent to commit war crimes.
- Recommendations and obligations: States must investigate serious laws-of-war violations, compensate victims, and prosecute those responsible for deliberate or reckless attacks on civilians. Human Rights Watch called on Israel to provide specific evidence for its claims; the IDF said it was reviewing the events and would respond after its inquiry.

Context and casualty overview
- The November 2012 exchange between Israel and Hamas/armed groups resulted in civilian casualties on both sides; Human Rights Watch noted unlawful attacks by both parties. At least 103 Palestinian civilians and four Israeli civilians died during the period.

Overall conclusion
Human Rights Watch concluded the four Israeli attacks on journalists and media facilities during the November 2012 fighting were unlawful because they targeted protected civilians and civilian objects without demonstrated direct participation in hostilities or proven military use—claims the Israeli government did not substantiate. The report stresses that opposing forces cannot lawfully convert media personnel or outlets into military targets solely on the basis of affiliation, statements, or alleged links to armed groups.

On March 18, 2015 gunmen attacked the National Bardo Museum in central Tunis, opening fire on tourists outside coaches and then taking hostages inside. Security forces stormed the museum after a siege; both attackers were killed and at least two or three suspected accomplices were sought. Authorities later said 23 people died (including 18 foreign tourists and at least three Tunisians, one a police officer) and about 40–50 were wounded; some victims remained unidentified. Nationalities among the dead reported by officials included Japanese, Italian, Colombian, Spanish, British, Australian, Polish and French citizens, though some country counts varied.

One attacker, named Yassine Laabidi, had previously been flagged by security services; the other was identified as Hatem Khachnaoui. Tunisian authorities made multiple arrests in the investigation and deployed the army to bolster security in major cities. Islamic State-linked channels later claimed responsibility, praising the assault, though Tunisia has no formal IS province and links were still being examined.

The strike — the deadliest attack on civilians in Tunisia since 2002 — struck at a major tourist site inside the parliamentary compound, dealing a severe blow to Tunisia’s crucial tourism industry and raising fears about militants returning from Libya, Syria and Iraq. Tunisians responded with large demonstrations, candles and solidarity campaigns (#JeSuisBardo), while world leaders condemned the attack and offered assistance. The government pledged to pursue militants firmly while facing public concern over balancing security measures with democratic freedoms. Authorities said the museum would reopen soon and rescue and repatriation efforts for foreign victims continued.

Researchers analyzing about 3.4 million exposed all-numeric passwords (used as a proxy for 4-digit PINs) found that people pick highly predictable PINs instead of choosing uniformly random codes. Key findings:

- A very small set of PINs dominates usage. Just one guess—1234—appears in roughly 10.7% of entries; the top three (1234, 1111, 0000) make up nearly 20%. The top 20 PINs account for about 26.8% of all PINs.
- Popular patterns are obvious: repeated digits (1111, 2222, …), simple sequences (1234, 4321), repeated pairs (e.g., 1212, XYXY), keypad patterns (2580 down the middle), and memorable numbers (birth years, anniversaries).
- Years beginning with "19" are especially common: every 19xx combination ranks above the 80th percentile, reflecting people using birth years. MMDD-style choices (birthdays) are also frequent.
- People prefer even digits over odd (e.g., 2468 more common than 1357), and many favor starting with 1 (followed by 0 and 2).
- Frequency is heavily skewed: half of all PINs are among just 426 combinations; 33% of codes can be guessed by trying only 61 combinations. Conversely, the least-used PINs occur vanishingly rarely (the rarest in the dataset appeared ~0.0007%).
- All-numeric passwords of other lengths show similar predictability: 123456 is the most common six-digit code, 12345 dominates five-digit codes, etc. People also reuse patterns, phone numbers, and cultural references (e.g., 8675309, 3141592654).
- Practical implications: predictable choices greatly increase the odds an attacker can guess a PIN; developers must avoid storing passwords in clear text and should use encryption and better security practices. Users should avoid birthdays, years, simple sequences, repeated digits, and common keypad patterns when choosing PINs.

Bottom line: many people choose memorable but highly guessable PINs—using truly random or non-obvious combinations (and following good security practices) significantly improves safety.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Chris Dodd said he will introduce a revised, comprehensive bank-reform bill and move it to a committee vote the week of March 22, likely without Republican support, after months of bipartisan talks with Sen. Bob Corker broke down. Dodd cited limited time in this Congress and pressure to complete work so other priorities (notably health care) can advance. Corker said the two were “on the five-yard line” on many issues but blamed White House and health-care politics for forcing a faster timetable; he also criticized Dodd’s plan to finish committee review in a single week as rushed.

Areas of agreement reached during negotiations included creating a consumer financial protection unit, heightened liability for credit raters, oversight of payday and other lenders, allowing bank regulators to enforce consumer rules, and a proposed veto mechanism by a five-agency panel (Treasury, FDIC, Fed, CFTC, SEC) over consumer rules if a majority agreed — though Dodd would not confirm that final structure. Remaining disputes include GOP opposition to several shareholder-empowerment provisions (proxy access, nonbinding executive “say-on-pay” votes, limits on golden parachutes) that Democrats inserted and Republicans say would empower activist groups at shareholders’ expense. Work was also continuing between Sens. Jack Reed and Judd Gregg on derivatives regulation, specifically on exemptions for end users and how much clearinghouse transparency to require.

Dodd rejected splitting the bill into pieces, saying piecemeal consideration “would be impossible in the Senate,” but acknowledged his timetable could slip and emphasized getting the bill right despite time pressure. The move shifts the process toward a partisan fight that could increase the risk of a filibuster and complicate passage of a broad regulatory overhaul.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s Port of Charleston seized two shipments totaling 2,380 counterfeit hoverboards that violated trademark protections and posed safety risks, chiefly from potentially substandard lithium‑ion batteries. If genuine, the seized units would have an MSRP of about $1.66 million. CBP stressed that enforcing product safety and intellectual property rights is a priority; nationwide, more than 50,000 potentially unsafe hoverboards (including a 16,000‑unit Chicago seizure) have been confiscated, with an estimated MSRP near $20 million. CBP urged reporting of suspected trademark or copyright infringements via its e‑Allegations system or hotline and pointed to its IPR enforcement resources for more information.

The document summarizes updated American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance (2016) and a related 2017 grieving-parent case to emphasize safe infant sleep practices to reduce SIDS and other sleep-related deaths. Key points from the AAP policy and technical report:

- Place infants on their backs on a firm, flat sleep surface (crib or bassinet) with a tight-fitting sheet. Cribs should be bare — no pillows, blankets, bumpers, soft toys or other loose bedding.
- Share a bedroom with parents, but not a sleep surface (room-sharing) for at least the first six months and preferably the first year; room-sharing can reduce SIDS risk by as much as 50%.
- Avoid putting infants to sleep on sofas, armchairs or other soft surfaces, and never allow bed-sharing on such surfaces.
- Do not use home monitors, commercial devices, wedges or positioners marketed to reduce SIDS risk.
- Offer a pacifier at naps and bedtime.
- Recommend skin-to-skin care immediately after birth (at least an hour) when the mother is stable and awake.
- Encourage breastfeeding as it provides additional protection against SIDS.
- Infants should receive all recommended vaccinations.
- Supervised awake tummy time is advised daily to support development.
- Avoid exposure to smoke, alcohol and illicit drugs.
- Physicians should discuss sleep practices with families in an open, nonjudgmental way; media and advertisers should model safe sleep.

The release notes about 3,500 annual U.S. infant sleep-related deaths and stresses simple, low-cost precautions over monitoring gadgets. The report was accompanied by a 2017 account of a mother whose 7‑month‑old son died after becoming entangled in crib blankets; her story reinforced the AAP’s “bare crib” guidance and the dangers of loose bedding.

The University of Virginia has unveiled stricter fraternity and Greek-life safety rules that must be accepted by chapters before social activities are reinstated. The measures, added to the university’s Fraternal Organization Agreement after widespread scrutiny following a Rolling Stone report about an alleged 2012 gang rape (a story later found to have reporting errors), are intended to reduce risks at parties where alcohol is present.

Key provisions for Inter‑Fraternity Council chapters (31 IFC chapters; 28 have houses):
- At least three “sober and lucid” monitored members must be on duty at every party; more monitors required as needed.
- One monitor must be stationed at the staircase to bedrooms and have immediate key access to every room.
- At least one monitor must be posted where alcohol is distributed; monitors must wear standardized identification.
- Entry management: guest lists must be used; a hired security agent will verify lists at large events, and a chapter member will do so for smaller parties.
- Alcohol rules: beer allowed only in unopened cans; wine only if visibly poured by a sober member; pre-mixed drinks, punches, kegs and other common sources are banned. Hard liquor allowed only with a licensed bartender for large events or under monitored bar setups at small events.

The university also released safety addenda for sororities and other Greek councils promoting bystander‑intervention training and educational programs on alcohol and safe-party practices. President Teresa Sullivan lifted the suspension on Greek social activities conditional on chapters agreeing to the new rules by Jan. 16. University and student Greek leaders said the changes were developed quickly with student input; some provisions (like sober monitors and guest lists) already existed in practice but will now be formalized.

The initiative grew out of the national controversy and campus debate triggered by Rolling Stone’s A Rape on Campus feature, which amplified concerns about sexual assault and UVA’s handling of reports. That long Rolling Stone piece—detailing one student’s traumatic account and broader campus culture—was later criticized for reporting errors. Regardless, university officials and Greek leaders have vowed to continue improving safety, while critics note the new rules implicitly accept that underage drinking will occur and focus on harm reduction rather than strict enforcement of under-21 alcohol laws.

Former Minnesota Governor Tim Pawlenty said Wednesday he will not sign the Family Leader's "Marriage Vow," a conservative Iowa group's pledge that asks presidential candidates to denounce same-sex marriage, pornography and certain forms of Islamic law. Pawlenty told supporters he agrees with the pledge's principles but prefers to "choose my own words," emphasizing compassion for people in broken families. He becomes the second major Republican to refuse the pledge after Mitt Romney; Michele Bachmann and Rick Santorum have signed it. Pawlenty made the announcement as he released a new radio ad and web video in which he and his wife discuss their faith.

Country singer Chely Wright married her girlfriend, LGBT activist Lauren Blitzer, in Connecticut a little over a year after publicly coming out as a lesbian. Wright, who went public about her sexuality in May 2010 and has posted wedding photos on Twitter of both women in white gowns, has spoken about the difficult fallout in country music — saying the industry would rather tolerate substance abuse or scandal than an artist being gay. She has acknowledged that coming out hurt her career, with reports noting a sharp drop in sales and a move toward Americana. The couple, Wright (40) and Blitzer (30), celebrated with family and received many congratulations on Twitter. Wright has said coming out felt like being lifted up by the friends and family who support her.

U.S. naval commanders in the Mediterranean kept two destroyers armed with Tomahawk cruise missiles together near Syria by postponing a port call in Naples so both ships remained within striking range during the crisis; Pentagon officials said this reflected local command decisions, not direct orders from Washington. Russia called on Syrian president Bashar al-Assad to allow U.N. investigators access to areas east of Damascus where a chemical attack occurred, but diplomats saw no change in Moscow’s overall support for Assad or its opposition to punitive Security Council measures. Russian statements suggested the attack might have been a rebel provocation and faulted the opposition for not cooperating with U.N. investigators; one Russian spokesman cited internet posts that appeared to predate the strikes but may have been misread because of YouTube’s California-based timestamps. Russia praised Syria for welcoming U.N. commissioner Carla del Ponte, who has previously suggested rebels used chemical weapons. U.S. media reported that American intelligence detected activity at known Syrian chemical weapons sites before the attack, possibly indicating preparations.

This piece criticizes sexist media coverage around Chelsea Clinton missing her daughter Charlotte’s first day of preschool while campaigning for her mother’s presidential run. The Daily Mail’s headline and tone framed Chelsea’s absence as a “transgression,” spotlighting that Charlotte was taken by her father Marc Mezvinsky and a nanny, and incredulously suggesting Grandma Hillary should have been babysitting despite being ill. The article calls out the Daily Mail (and a Fox 32 Chicago social post) for mom-shaming, treating routine parenting choices as newsworthy in a way that would never happen to a male parent or a male candidate’s family. It argues this coverage reinforces the tired stereotype that women must always prioritize motherhood over professional duties, notes the double standard in how fathers’ absences are ignored, and rejects the notion that balancing public life and parenting is failure. The report also includes tabloid-style details about the family’s outing, Mezvinsky’s career and lunch after drop-off, and mentions Hillary’s recent illness; the writer condemns such invasive focus and celebrates the possibility of a female president as a rebuke to the patriarchy.

Two young cousins, 8-year-old Elizabeth Collins and 10-year-old Lyric Cook-Morrissey, have been missing since shortly after noon on Friday after leaving their grandmother’s home in Evansdale, Iowa, for a bike ride. Their bicycles were found a few hours later at nearby Meyers Lake, with Elizabeth’s purse and cellphone discovered about 20 feet from the bikes. Authorities and volunteers searched the area over the weekend—more than 1,000 people helped at peak—with dive teams covering roughly 40% of the lake; the lake search could take until Monday to complete. The Black Hawk County Sheriff’s Office, joined by the FBI and the Iowa Department of Criminal Investigation, say they have found no new evidence or clues and have been interviewing family, friends and registered sex offenders in the area. Officials described the case as a missing-person investigation and temporarily suspended the large volunteer effort when it became unlikely additional volunteers would help, though tip lines remain open and incoming leads are being checked. Family members voiced hope while bracing for the worst, describing the girls as outgoing and good swimmers, and pleaded for anyone who saw them on Friday to contact authorities.

A large “fatberg” — a congealed mass of fats, oils and grease (FOG) combined with non‑degradable items like wet wipes — was found in a 100‑year‑old, 24‑inch sewer main between Baltimore Penn Station and the 1700 block of Charles Street. Engineers discovered the blockage while investigating a series of dry‑weather sanitary overflows; the fatberg is linked to at least two recent overflows, including a Sept. 21 discharge of about 1.2 million gallons of sewage into the Jones Falls at North Charles and West Lanvale Streets. DPW crews found up to about 85% of the pipe clogged, and said smaller fatbergs exist elsewhere in the system.

The city has largely scraped the mass out and sent material to landfill, and is evaluating repairs or replacement of the affected pipe once FOG removal is complete. Baltimore’s Department of Public Works enforces a FOG prevention program for food‑service businesses (requiring permits and grease control devices) and urges residents to avoid pouring grease down drains, to discard grease in the trash after it solidifies, and to never flush wipes. The city plans broader sewer upgrades and repairs under a consent decree to reduce stormwater infiltration and eliminate overflow structures by projects through late 2020.

The article analyzes the April 22, 2014 U.S. Supreme Court oral argument in American Broadcasting Companies, Inc. v. Aereo, Inc., a high-stakes copyright case that probes whether Aereo’s service—renting tiny remote antennas and DVRs so users can stream and record over-the-air TV via the Internet—constitutes an unlawful “public performance.”

Key points:

- Central legal question: Are Aereo’s transmissions private acts by individual users (like home DVR recordings) or public performances by a service provider that must obtain licenses from broadcasters?
- Aereo’s position: Each user rents dedicated equipment, initiates recordings and streams, and controls the process; by the logic of the Second Circuit’s Cablevision decision, that makes the performances private and lawful. Aereo warned that ruling against it could threaten many cloud services because many cloud-based user-initiated copies would be cast as public performances.
- Broadcasters’ position: Aereo is functionally like a cable or retransmission service that provides programs to paying customers from central facilities; calling it a private, user-initiated service is an artifice to avoid copyright obligations and would undercut broadcasters’ licensing revenue and free over-the-air broadcasting.
- Justices’ concerns and reactions: Several justices (Roberts, Scalia, Breyer) expressed skepticism that Aereo’s architecture is anything but a deliberate effort to evade copyright rules; others (Kennedy, Sotomayor, Kagan, Ginsburg) worried about the broader consequences for cloud computing, storage lockers and hardware sellers. Questions focused on the relevance of where equipment is located, who controls it, and whether multiple identical copies stored for individual users should be treated as public performances.
- Analogies and precedents: Counsel and justices used analogies (phonograph stores, car dealers vs. valet services, RadioShack antenna sales) to probe distinctions. Much of Aereo’s defense relied on the Supreme Court’s Sony Betamax fair-use principle and on the Second Circuit’s Cablevision ruling that user-controlled, unique copies are private performances.
- Unresolved issues: Broadcasters argued Aereo could not simply claim a compulsory license like cable operators; Aereo warned that a ruling for broadcasters would create chilling uncertainty for cloud services. The hearing revealed the Court’s struggle to understand the technical details and to balance copyright owners’ rights against innovation in cloud-based services.

Overall takeaway: The justices were divided and uncertain, deeply concerned about both preventing circumvention of copyright protections and avoiding a ruling that could cripple cloud computing and storage services. The decision, months away at the time, promised significant implications for copyright law’s application to modern cloud and streaming technologies.

Maria von Trapp, the last surviving member of the original Trapp Family Singers who inspired The Sound of Music, has died at age 99 at her home in Stowe, Vermont, her brother Johannes confirmed. She was the third child and second-oldest daughter of Austrian naval captain Georg von Trapp and his first wife Agathe Whitehead von Trapp. The real-life family’s escape from Nazi-occupied Austria in 1938 and subsequent concert tours, settlement in Vermont in the early 1940s and opening of the Trapp Family Lodge inspired the 1949 book by Maria von Trapp (the stepmother) and the Broadway musical and 1965 film. In Stowe, Maria (the daughter) taught Austrian dance and played accordion alongside her sister Rosmarie; she also served as a lay missionary in Papua New Guinea. Johannes remembered her as “one of the few truly good people.” The family’s lodge in Stowe continues to reflect its Austrian roots.

Actor John Travolta is facing federal lawsuits from anonymous masseurs alleging sexual assault and battery. The first plaintiff, identified as "John Doe," claims Travolta hired him for a $200-an-hour massage, drove him to the Beverly Hills Hotel, stripped naked and then touched the masseur’s scrotum and penis, attempted to perform oral sex and propositioned him for further sexual activity. The suit also alleges Travolta made remarks about having advanced his career through sexual favors in his early days and made anti-Semitic comments about Hollywood. The plaintiff seeks $2 million plus punitive damages and emotional distress, and requests a jury trial.

A second masseur later filed a similar $2 million sexual-battery suit; both accusers are represented by the same lawyer and amended complaints add sexual-harassment claims. The filings include explicit descriptions of the alleged encounter and claim documentation and witnesses in support.

Travolta’s representatives deny the allegations as “complete fiction and fabrication,” asserting that he was on the East Coast on the date in question and saying they will seek to have the case dismissed and pursue malicious-prosecution claims against the plaintiff and attorney.

Two separate polls taken immediately after Osama bin Laden’s killing show a clear boost for President Obama on terrorism and national security but little or no improvement on his standing on the economy or his overall electoral standing.

Washington Post / Pew (one-night poll of 654 adults; ±4.5%):
- Overall job approval rose to 56% (up nine points since mid‑April), the highest in these polls since 2009.
- Approval on handling Afghanistan jumped to 60%; on terrorism it hit a career high of 69%.
- Independents drove much of the gain (approval among independents up 10 points to 52%).
- Most Americans (over 75%) say Obama deserves at least some credit for the bin Laden operation; Republicans give him less credit (61% at least some; only 17% a “great deal”).
- Republicans more often credit George W. Bush for the result (81% at least some credit), while Democrats largely do not.
- Strong bipartisan praise for the military and intelligence services.
- No improvement on economic approval: Obama’s economy approval remained low at 40% (the lowest in Post polls of his presidency), underscoring that success on terrorism did not translate into gains on the economy—still the top voter concern.

Newsweek / Daily Beast (1,200 adults, two days before vs. two days after; ±3%):
- No overall change in approval: 48% approve / 49% disapprove both before and after the announcement.
- No meaningful shift in re‑electability or vote preferences; most metrics of electoral support were statistically unchanged.
- Perceptions of the country’s direction improved (right‑track responses rose from 20% to 30%), but views of the economy remained poor (only ~27–31% say it’s on the right track).
- Strong personal ratings on leadership in general (55% “strong”) and on terrorism (63% “strong”).
- On credit for bin Laden’s killing: 48% say Obama deserves more credit vs. 31% for Bush; yet when asked who did a better job prosecuting the war on terror, 45% chose Bush and 31% chose Obama.
- Most respondents reported no change in how they would vote (92% said the news did not change their vote).

Bottom line:
The bin Laden operation produced a notable security-policy bounce for Obama and increased public credit for the mission and the military, but it did not produce a sustained or broad surge in overall approval or shift public views on the economy—leaving it doubtful how durable any positive effect will be.

A Los Angeles judge, Daniel S. Murphy, reversed an earlier order and revoked a directive to artificially feed and hydrate radio legend Casey Kasem, citing medical records from St. Anthony’s Hospital near Seattle that showed artificial nutrition and fluids were causing harmful complications. The judge upheld a conservatorship giving Kasem’s eldest daughter, Kerri Kasem, authority over his care and said Kerri may continue making decisions during his final days.

The decision followed conflicting accounts from family members and doctors. Jean Kasem, Casey’s wife of 34 years, angrily protested in court and claimed her husband signaled a wish to live via eye and eyebrow movements during a brief hospital visit. She accused Kerri of stopping medications and effectively attempting to “kill him.” Kerri’s attorney and Kerri herself disputed those claims, saying doctors reintroduced fluids but had to stop because Kasem’s lungs filled and he appeared to be “almost drowning.” Kerri said staff tried everything to keep him alive; he is receiving morphine to ease suffering.

Casey Kasem, 82, is in the late stages of Lewy body disease, a progressive dementia. He was admitted to intensive care June 1 with an infection related to a serious bedsore. The family dispute has included accusations of elder abuse and emotionally charged courtroom scenes; Jean left the courtroom saying, “You have blood on your hands.” Widespread disagreement about Kasem’s wishes and the appropriate course of care remains central to the feud.

Researchers at UC Berkeley have taken a significant step toward “reading” visual experiences from brain activity. In a study published in Current Biology, subjects (many of them the researchers) watched hours of YouTube movie trailers while undergoing functional MRI, which measured blood-flow changes in visual cortex. The team used the brain data from an initial viewing to train a computational model that associated patterns of neural activity with visual features—colors, shapes and motion—by comparing them against a large database of YouTube footage. When subjects watched the trailers again, the researchers ran the recorded brain activity backward through the model to reconstruct what had been seen.

The reconstructions are continuous but low-resolution and dreamlike: blurry composites produced by layering multiple clips that matched the observed brain patterns. This experiment is notable because prior work had reconstructed static images; this is among the first demonstrations of reconstructing dynamic visual experiences. The authors say the approach helps reveal how the brain processes naturalistic, movie-like input and could eventually be extended to decode imagery that lacks external stimulation—dreams, memories or imagined scenes—though doing so will require modeling many more visual-processing modules, far larger datasets, and greater computational power. Practical and ethical limitations remain: current outputs are coarse, different brain areas contribute distinct functions (e.g., face recognition), and decoded memories would reflect the inherent inaccuracy of human memory.

North Korea has detained Otto Frederick Warmbier, a 21-year-old University of Virginia student from Cincinnati, accusing him of committing a “hostile act” and seeking “to destroy the country’s unity.” Warmbier, an Echols Scholar majoring in economics, was on a five-day New Year tour organized by China-based Young Pioneer Tours and was reportedly detained at Pyongyang airport on Jan. 2 while returning to China. North Korea’s KCNA state media said the U.S. government “tolerated and manipulated” his actions and that he is under investigation, but offered no further specifics.

The U.S. State Department said it was aware of reports and is working with its protecting power, the Swedish Embassy in Pyongyang, but gave no details citing privacy. Young Pioneer Tours and Warmbier’s family have been notified; the tour operator and a U.S. congressman said they were seeking consular assistance. The detention comes amid heightened tensions after North Korea’s nuclear test and follows other recent foreign detentions there (including a Canadian pastor sentenced to life). Historically, Pyongyang has sometimes used detained foreigners to exert pressure or extract diplomatic concessions; U.S. authorities advise against travel to North Korea.

The piece argues that Pope Francis has become unusually politically influential because he presents himself as a humble, nonpolitical moral authority. President Obama quoted Francis in a December speech on economic inequality, invoking the pope’s critique of societal indifference to poverty to bolster his own policy stance—a contrast to Obama’s earlier posture toward Pope Benedict XVI, when he framed the relationship as between “countries,” not moral leaders. Francis’s popularity—far higher than Obama’s—stems from his handling of a church in crisis (declining attendance, regional challenges, clergy scandals) and from symbolic gestures of simplicity (refusing lavish apartments and vestments, driving an ordinary car) and candid humility (calling himself a sinner and downplaying papal power). Those traits have earned him broad public admiration and given his moral voice unusual sway in global political conversation.

President Trump renewed public attacks on Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell, accusing Powell of raising interest rates too aggressively and saying he "almost looks like he's happy" doing so. In a Wall Street Journal interview Trump suggested he might regret nominating Powell, argued Fed rate hikes are a bigger risk to the economy than tariffs or geopolitical tensions, and compared his situation unfavorably to the Obama era when rates were near zero.

The Fed has raised rates multiple times this year (three quarter-point hikes, with a likely fourth), a gradual normalization Powell has defended as necessary to prevent overheating or, if done too fast, needlessly shortening the expansion. Trump has repeatedly criticized the Fed in recent weeks, calling it a threat to his economic agenda while continuing to campaign on a strong economy and promising more fiscal stimulus.

Economists and former officials largely support the Fed’s cautious approach. Janet Yellen and Gary Cohn warned that presidential comments about Fed policy are unwise because they risk undermining the central bank’s long-standing independence and credibility. The Fed declined to comment on Trump’s latest remarks.

This document describes an Internet Archive effort to crawl and preserve web pages as they’re created and as they link to other pages, so that when referenced pages change or disappear a preserved version reflecting what the author saw can be linked instead of a broken URL. The Archive’s goal is to fix broken links across the web by supplying archived alternatives (part of its “No More 404” crawls).

The file also includes a news item from December 7, 2018, about Taylor Swift: her online profiles (Instagram, Twitter, Tumblr, YouTube and website) went blank, coinciding with the third anniversary of her single “Shake It Off.” That purge sparked fan speculation—using the hashtag #TS6IsComing—that she was about to announce a sixth studio album; some suggested hacking as an alternative explanation. The Recording Academy had nominated Swift’s album Reputation for Best Pop Vocal Album for the 2019 Grammys; the awards were scheduled for February 10, 2019 on CBS. Fans reacted excitedly across social media.

Late on Monday, Sen. Ted Cruz’s official Twitter account briefly “liked” a tweet containing a pornographic video from Pornhub, causing the senator to trend widely the next morning. Cruz’s communications director, Catherine Frazier, said staff removed the like and reported the tweet to Twitter. Cruz told reporters the action was inadvertent, blamed a staff member (multiple people have access to the account), and said it was a mistake being handled internally; he denied personally liking the post.

Pornhub’s vice president issued a tongue-in-cheek statement making the clip available “to the masses.” The explicit clip — featuring adult performers and originally released by Reality Kings in 2016 — circulated across Twitter and drew mockery, memes and attention to accounts that repost adult content. The incident revived past media reminders that Cruz once recounted viewing explicit material while clerking at the Supreme Court and that, as Texas solicitor general, he defended a state ban on sex toys (a law he later called “stupid” while noting his job was to defend state statutes).

Cruz downplayed the episode with self-deprecating remarks and reiterated it would not recur; he declined to identify or say whether the responsible staffer would be disciplined. The porn actress in the clip and others noted the odd publicity amid other events, such as Hurricane Irma.

A woman in central China died after falling into an escalator mechanism at the Anliang Department Store in Jingzhou, Hubei, while protecting her young son. Surveillance footage and witness posts on Weibo show a metal footplate or floor panel giving way as the 30–31-year-old and her under-three child reached the top of the escalator. The mother pushed the child forward; a nearby woman (possibly a shop assistant) pulled the boy to safety, but the mother slipped into the void and was drawn into the moving treads. Staff briefly tried to grab her, and the escalator kept running; firefighters cut open the machine and recovered her body after more than four hours. Relatives identified her by surname Xiang (given name reported as Liujuan in some outlets). Local reports cite recent maintenance during which workers allegedly failed to re-secure an access cover or tighten screws, and netizens have criticized mall staff for not stopping or switching off the escalator. The mall has not issued a formal statement. The incident prompted widespread outrage online and recalls past fatal escalator accidents in China.

Apple is launching an in-store iPhone trade-in program this month to encourage upgrades to the iPhone 5 and capture more users, Bloomberg reports. The program, run with mobile-phone distributor Brightstar, will let customers turn in older iPhones at Apple stores and receive immediate payment toward a new device. Brightstar already handles trade-ins for carriers like AT&T and T‑Mobile and resells refurbished phones in emerging markets.

Apple’s move signals a shift into the refurbished-phone market as growth has slowed and competition—especially from Samsung’s Android phones—has strengthened. Trade-ins can reduce buyers’ out-of-pocket costs (AT&T has paid up to $200 for working iPhone 4/4S units), potentially allowing some customers to get an entry-level iPhone 5 with little or no down payment. Collected used iPhones will largely be resold in emerging markets to avoid cannibalizing U.S. sales, while boosting Apple’s presence where lower-priced devices are in demand and may slow defections to Android.

Apple already offers an online recycling program with PowerOn Services; the Brightstar partnership adds an in-store, instant-payment option. Brightstar expects to buy and resell millions of devices annually and operates global distribution and refurbishment channels. Apple’s broader aim is to expand its installed base—new and used iPhone users are important for future device sales and for services Apple plans to roll out—while countering slowing unit growth and competitive pressure.

Comedian Patton Oswalt paid tribute on Twitter to his late wife, true-crime writer Michelle McNamara, who died at home in Los Angeles last week at age 46; no cause of death has been given. In one post he wrote, “She wrote lines that stung & hummed. 13 years in her presence was happily humbling. #RIPMichelleMcNamara.” He also shared a poignant remark from their 7‑year‑old daughter Alice — “When your mom dies you’re the best memory of her. Everything you do is a memory of her.” The couple married in 2005 and have one daughter, born in 2009. Oswalt retweeted a link to 826LA, an arts organization accepting donations in McNamara’s honor to support young writers and continue her creative legacy. McNamara, a Notre Dame and University of Minnesota alum, founded True Crime Diary and coined the term “Golden State Killer”; she was working on a book based on her LA Magazine piece.

A string of bull-related fatalities and injuries occurred in Spain over the weekend. In Teruel, 29-year-old professional matador Víctor Barrio was fatally gored during a bullfight when a bull first struck his thigh and then pierced his chest, penetrating a lung and his aorta; he was pronounced dead at the ring. His death — televised live — is Spain’s first professional matador fatality in the ring since 1985 and prompted widespread reaction from colleagues, politicians and suspended festivities in Teruel. At the San Fermín festival in Pamplona, two runners were seriously gored (a 33-year-old Japanese man in the chest and a 24-year-old Spaniard in the arm) and 12 others sustained minor injuries. Separately, a 28-year-old man was killed during a village bull-run in Pedreguer near Valencia after being pierced in the lung and heart while helping another runner. Spanish towns hold numerous summer bull events each year, and injuries and occasional deaths are a recurring risk.

Two GOP holdouts flip after White House talks; amendment adds $8B for preexisting conditions

Summary:
- Reps. Fred Upton (Mich.) and Billy Long (Mo.), who had threatened to derail the House GOP’s Obamacare repeal (the American Health Care Act, AHCA), reversed course after meeting with President Trump and securing a last-minute amendment. They said an $8 billion federal fund to help cover people with pre-existing conditions convinced them to vote "yes."
- Their switch eased immediate Republican concerns about mustering the narrow margin needed in the House (leaders can lose only 22 votes). Leadership and the White House pushed for a quick vote, with some officials saying they hoped to bring the bill to the floor as soon as Thursday; Speaker Paul Ryan declined to commit to a date.
- GOP leaders and some Freedom Caucus members signaled the amendment could win broader support; moderates like Reps. Mike Coffman and Carlos Curbelo said they would review the change. House leaders remained cautiously optimistic but acknowledged more votes were needed.
- Critics called the amendment insufficient. Democrats and health-care advocates argued the change is a political bailout that doesn’t fix core problems—pointing to provisions allowing states waivers that could weaken protections and to a prior CBO score showing large coverage losses under earlier AHCA versions. Polling showed many Americans oppose letting states waive preexisting-condition protections and prefer waiting for a new CBO analysis before voting.
- Administration officials and Trump repeatedly lobbied members, making numerous calls and public appeals. GOP leaders said the bill would likely be altered further in the Senate if it advanced.

South Korea has decided to withdraw the remaining roughly 175–180 South Korean personnel from the Kaesong Industrial Complex after North Korea rejected Seoul’s demand for talks to resume operations at the jointly run factory park, which has been closed for nearly a month. Pyongyang barred South Korean managers and supplies from entering Kaesong on April 3 and recalled the some 53,000 North Korean workers; about 800 South Korean managers had been stationed there before the ban. Seoul set a 24-hour deadline for Pyongyang to agree to working-level talks, citing concern that its staff were running out of food and medicine. When North Korea dismissed the offer and accused the South of insincerity—pointing to U.S.-South Korean military drills and anti-North leaflets—it warned of “final and decisive” measures if Seoul worsened the situation.

Unification Minister Ryoo Kihl-jae framed the withdrawal as necessary to protect South Korean personnel and urged Pyongyang to safeguard South Korean property and managers’ safety as they return; he did not give a timetable. South Korean business groups said they were shocked by the decision. Analysts warned the move risks long-term deadlock or possible confiscation of South Korean assets in Kaesong, which has operated since 2004 using South Korean technology and North Korean cheap labor (workers were paid about $127 monthly). The standoff comes amid heightened tensions over North Korea’s recent nuclear test, international sanctions and ongoing U.S.-ROK drills. Kaesong, the last major symbol of inter-Korean economic cooperation, faces an uncertain future.

Tom (Thomas) McDonald, a 58-year-old Queens native and lifelong Mets fan, has spent the last seven to eight years honoring his childhood friend Roy Riegel — a master plumber and fellow baseball fanatic who died in 2008 — by carrying and dispersing small amounts of Riegel’s cremated remains at baseball- and music-related sites across the U.S. (and once in Ireland). McDonald began by sprinkling ashes discretely outside ballparks, then — inspired during a night at an Irish bar after an awkward outdoor attempt in Minnesota — switched to flushing tiny portions down stadium and venue toilets, a tribute he says befits Riegel’s trade. He has deposited ashes at 16 Major League parks (and places like the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Cliffs of Moher), always during games and from a plastic bottle wrapped in old Mets tickets; he skipped rival Cubs’ Wrigley Field out of loyalty. Friends and Riegel’s family approve, calling the offbeat ritual exactly what Roy would have wanted. McDonald has one final planned stop: Durham Athletic Park, the Bull Durham filming site, where the remaining ashes will be used.

A Montana beekeeper, Lloyd Cunniff of Beeline Honey in Choteau, recovered most of 488 honeybee hives stolen from him in California in January after an agricultural crimes task force investigation. Cunniff had taken the hives to California for almond pollination when they vanished from a Yuba City property. A tip triggered Fresno County detectives to locate stolen equipment—worth about $170,000 of the $224,000 reported missing—at three sites: a rented bee nursery, a cow pasture and hidden in a freeway drainage. Investigators say the thefts are part of a larger pattern over the past few years involving organized thefts by suspects described as Ukrainian-Russian; two people have been charged with possession of stolen property and more charges or arrests are possible, with federal authorities showing interest.

Much of the recovered gear was mixed, damaged or unusable; some hives were used by the thieves during the almond pollination season, netting an estimated $100,000. Cunniff flew to California to identify his nearly new, custom-marked hives and shipped roughly two-thirds of his equipment back to Montana. He’s quarantining the recovered colonies away from his new hives over disease and mite concerns and won’t know until fall whether the bees are viable. Insurance covered replacement hives earlier, and Cunniff has since rebuilt his operation, planning to return bees to California next season but with increased caution.

Elliott Broidy, a Los Angeles investor and prominent GOP fundraiser who served as a deputy national finance chairman for the RNC and was a Trump backer, resigned from his RNC post after reports that he paid $1.6 million to a former Playboy model he had a consensual affair with. Broidy acknowledged the relationship and apologized to his wife, saying the woman became pregnant and he offered financial help; the woman chose to end the pregnancy. Broidy said he retained Michael Cohen after Cohen informed him that the woman’s attorney had contacted Cohen.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that Cohen, President Trump’s personal lawyer, negotiated the nondisclosure agreement that provided payments over two years in exchange for silence, while allowing the woman to determine paternity and seek child support if she wished. The settlement follows other Cohen-brokered agreements, including the $130,000 payment to Stormy Daniels in 2016. Cohen’s offices and residence were searched by the FBI earlier in the week, and federal prosecutors in Manhattan have been investigating Cohen’s business dealings and efforts to suppress stories about Trump; a grand jury has been empaneled. The matter has drawn added scrutiny to relationships among Cohen, celebrity lawyer Keith Davidson (who represented the Playboy model and Stormy Daniels), and other figures linked to Trump. RNC Chair Ronna McDaniel accepted Broidy’s resignation and said she would review Cohen’s role at the committee.

Ashley Judd responded publicly to intense media and online scrutiny over her recent appearance —speculation that she’d had facial fillers after looking puffier and criticism for modest weight gain—by writing an op‑ed for The Daily Beast. She explains the puffiness was from steroid treatment for a sinus infection and the weight from “a lazy six months” of not exercising, but uses the moment to critique the broader, misogynistic culture that obsessively polices women’s bodies.

In her essay Judd decries how conversations about women’s appearances reduce personhood to objectified physical traits, are often mean-spirited, ageist and gendered, and frequently involve other women as much as men. She catalogues examples of contradictory media conclusions about her looks (accusations of surgery when she looked puffy, claims of “unnatural” smooth skin, derision when her face changed over time, insults after modest weight gain, and critiques of her appearance even when portraying an exhausted character on screen). She condemns journalists who published speculation without checking facts and calls for a feminist reframing of such conversations that recognizes how the culture harms all people’s self-image and dignity.

The piece drew supportive commentary noting Judd’s refusal to give a typical equivocal celebrity response and praising her for turning a tabloid attack into a wider critique of objectification, patriarchy, and the damaging dynamics that pit women against one another.

Historians on Oct. 9, 2014 opened a 113-year-old time capsule that had been sealed inside the golden lion statue atop Boston’s Old State House since 1901. The copper box, about the size of a shoebox and weighing 5–10 pounds, was removed during statue restoration at Skylight Studios in Woburn. Conservators found paper items in remarkably good condition—no mold or water damage—and also discovered an unexpected hardcover red book whose contents were not immediately examined because everything is fragile and tightly packed.

The Bostonian Society, which manages the Old State House, will transfer the capsule to an environmentally controlled lab to unpack and study the materials before putting them on public display. A 1901 Boston Globe item and family records from Samuel D. Rogers (the craftsman believed to have placed the capsule) indicate the box likely contains photographs, autographs, newspapers, letters and a history of the Rogers and Fernald families, but the red book remains a mystery for now.

The Old State House is a major Boston landmark (site of the 1770 Boston Massacre and the 1776 public reading of the Declaration of Independence). The society plans to install a new, easier-to-open titanium time capsule in the lion’s head and is soliciting public suggestions for items to include—already proposing to add a 2013 Boston Marathon medal and modern artifacts such as photos and electronic items.

A Richmond Police Department (RPD) officer anonymously told CBS 6 in May that during President Barack Obama’s visit to VCU, a 20-year RPD veteran and others made remarks suggesting violence against the president and First Lady Michelle Obama — including a supervisor telling a sharpshooter “you can take a couple of shots,” someone suggesting planting a bomb under the stage, and lewd comments about Michelle Obama. The Secret Service reportedly investigated and found no criminal wrongdoing; RPD said the officers involved were not assigned to the presidential detail and that the matter was considered “resolved” by the Secret Service. The department opened an internal review and has not publicly identified the officers.

The whistleblower later says he was terminated by RPD after granting the CBS 6 interview; the department cited a policy violation for speaking to the media. Two officers were fired earlier amid the controversy and have appealed, with their lawyer calling the whistleblower’s allegations “false and/or greatly embellished” and accusing city officials of pressuring firings. Employment attorneys told CBS 6 the whistleblower might be protected under the First Amendment for speaking on a matter of public concern and warned that his dismissal could chill other officers from reporting misconduct. The whistleblower is considering legal action; the fired officers are seeking to be reinstated. RPD has declined to comment on individual personnel matters.

Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie appointed Lt. Gov. Brian Schatz to fill the U.S. Senate seat left vacant by the Dec. 17 death of Sen. Daniel Inouye. Abercrombie chose Schatz from a three-person list submitted by the state Democratic Party; the other nominees were U.S. Rep. Colleen Hanabusa and Esther Kiaaina. Inouye had written that he wished Hanabusa to succeed him, and his staff expressed disappointment that the governor did not honor that request, though they wished Schatz well. 

Schatz, 40, a former state representative and past state Democratic Party chair who was elected lieutenant governor in 2010, will be sworn in quickly (as soon as Thursday) so he can vote on urgent matters in the new Congress, including averting the “fiscal cliff.” His swearing-in aboard Air Force One followed an invitation from President Obama. By joining the Senate immediately, Schatz becomes Hawaii’s senior senator; Mazie Hirono, elected in November to succeed retiring Sen. Daniel Akaka, will be the junior senator. 

Schatz will serve until a special election in 2014 fills the remainder of Inouye’s term (through 2016); he plans to run in 2014 and 2016. He pledged to work with Hawaii’s delegation, Senate leadership and the White House on pressing issues and emphasized building seniority over time. Hanabusa congratulated Schatz and said she respects the selection process. Other applicants for the seat included Tulsi Gabbard, former Rep. Ed Case and several state leaders. With Schatz’s elevation, the next lieutenant governor would likely be Senate President Shan Tsutsui, who was weighing the position.

A New York Times/CBS News poll of 965 U.S. adults conducted April 24–28, shortly after the Boston Marathon bombing and the capture of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, finds broad public support for expanded public surveillance and general satisfaction with the government’s response, alongside continued concern about terrorism.

Key findings
- 78% think installing surveillance cameras in public places is a good idea, viewing privacy trade-offs as acceptable for greater security.
- 66% favor removing online information about how to make explosives even if that restricts speech.
- Only 20% believe the government has gone too far in restricting civil liberties; 49% say the balance is about right and 26% want tougher measures.
- 66% say another terrorist attack in the U.S. is at least somewhat likely in the next few months (up from 37% a year earlier); 24% say it is very likely.
- Despite concerns, 72% do not plan to avoid large public events; only 23% are very concerned about an attack in their own area.
- 84% approve of federal and local law enforcement’s handling of the Boston bombings; 68% approve of President Obama’s response to the attacks and 56% approve of his handling of terrorism generally.
- The public is divided on whether intelligence agencies had information that could have prevented the attacks (41% yes, 45% no).
- 53% believe the suspects had links to a larger terrorist group; 32% think they acted alone.
- 70% have at least a fair amount of confidence in the federal government’s ability to protect against terrorism; confidence in state and local preparedness is lower (48% say prepared; 41% not).

Voices quoted reflect a mix of readiness to accept surveillance for safety and caution about intrusive measures like warrantless wiretapping. Overall, the poll shows heightened concern about future attacks coupled with substantial trust in law enforcement and support for measures perceived to enhance security.

The document contains two main items.

1) Game of Thrones title sequence:
- The opening titles for Game of Thrones were created by Elastic, led creatively by Angus Wall.
- The sequence was inspired by the maps that precede the novels: a map placed on the inner surface of a sphere with a central astrolabe-like sun.
- The camera moves around the map while the rotating gears and cogs—evoking Leonardo da Vinci—reveal relief-sculptured bands on the astrolabe that depict prehistory scenes: dragons attacking Westeros, the houses uniting to defeat them, and the noble houses (shown as their animals) swearing fealty to the Baratheon stag.
- Angus Wall discussed these design choices and the astrolabe close-ups in an interview.

2) Discovery of the earliest known marine astrolabe:
- A bronze marine astrolabe recovered from the wreck of the Portuguese ship Esmeralda (part of Vasco da Gama’s fleet) off Oman has been identified as the oldest known mariner’s astrolabe, dated to about 1495–1500.
- The Esmeralda sank in a storm in 1503; the object was excavated in 2014 among nearly 3,000 artifacts and initially showed only emblems (the Portuguese coat of arms and King Don Manuel I’s personal emblem).
- Researchers at the University of Warwick used advanced 3D/laser scanning to reveal previously invisible etches around the edge—markings every five degrees—confirming its function for measuring the Sun’s altitude to determine latitude at sea.
- The disc is 17.5 cm across, under 2 mm thick, and is among only about 108 confirmed mariner’s astrolabes; this find pushes back the attestable use of such instruments by several decades and fills an important gap in maritime history.
- The work was led by Blue Water Recoveries’ David Mearns and scanning by Professor Mark Williams (WMG, University of Warwick).

A Florida jury acquitted George Zimmerman of all charges in the fatal shooting of Trayvon Martin, reigniting a national debate over race, self‑defense laws and justice. Reactions were immediate and divided: President Obama called Martin’s death “a tragedy” and urged calm and reflection, noting a jury had spoken; Rep. Steve King (R‑Iowa) criticized Obama for politicizing the case; the NAACP and other critics urged the Justice Department to pursue a civil‑rights probe, and the DOJ said its investigation remains open.

Nationwide vigils, rallies and protests took place—from Sanford to Washington, D.C., and major cities—where demonstrators decried what they view as racial injustice and the dangers of laws like “stand your ground.” Supporters of Zimmerman celebrated the verdict, saying evidence did not meet the criminal standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The case spotlighted sharp divisions: some see a biased system that targets black youth, while others view Zimmerman as a citizen exercising self‑defense. With no living neutral eyewitnesses and conflicting accounts, legal analysts noted the prosecution faced a high burden. Trayvon Martin’s family, grieving and calling for action, said they may pursue civil litigation and have launched a foundation in his memory.

After Bob Dylan recorded his required Nobel lecture (submitted June 4) discussing three formative books—Moby-Dick, All Quiet on the Western Front, and the Odyssey—journalist Andrea Pitzer (Slate) and other observers noticed that numerous phrasings in Dylan’s Moby‑Dick segment closely match wording found on SparkNotes, the online study-guide site. Dylan quoted an aphorism attributed to a Quaker preacher—“Some men who receive injuries are led to God, others are led to bitterness”—that does not appear in Melville’s novel but resembles SparkNotes’ character description. Pitzer found more than a dozen sentences among the roughly 78 Dylan used on Moby‑Dick that echo SparkNotes summaries (e.g., “Ahab’s lust for vengeance,” and lines about Captain Boomer and a prophet named Gabriel), and writer Scott Warmuth spotted a similar SparkNotes-phrase in Dylan’s comments on All Quiet on the Western Front.

The allegation revived longstanding debates about Dylan’s frequent borrowing and appropriation: throughout his career he has reused melodies, lines, images and even lifted passages without explicit citation, a practice he has framed as part of folk and jazz traditions. Critics and scholars differ in response: some see the SparkNotes parallels as cribbing inappropriate for a literary lecture or classroom assignment; others treat Dylan’s lecture as a postmodern collage in keeping with his art, or as a harmless shortcut from a touring artist. Slate’s writer suggested Dylan should consider sharing some of his Nobel payout with the original SparkNotes author; commentators generally do not expect the Swedish Academy to rescind the prize. The episode adds another chapter to the long-running conversation about Dylan’s methods of appropriation and originality.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R‑Tex.) spent part of Thursday on the Senate floor urging colleagues to oppose President Obama’s attorney general nominee, Loretta Lynch, arguing her answers at the confirmation hearing showed she would continue the “lawlessness” of outgoing AG Eric Holder and would support Obama’s executive action on immigration. Cruz spoke for about 10 minutes, voted against cloture (the key procedural vote to end debate) and lost that 66–34 vote. Lynch was confirmed later 56–43.

Despite his floor opposition, Cruz did not cast a vote on the final confirmation — he was the only senator absent — saying he had to return to Texas for a fundraiser (his staff emphasized his earlier cloture vote was the decisive one). His absence drew additional scrutiny given prior missed votes. Republicans including Sen. John Cornyn voted for cloture, enabling the final confirmation.

Flint officials have issued a boil-water advisory after a large transmission line break Tuesday near Dort Highway led to a water main rupture on Dupont. The leak has been isolated and water pressures restored, and crews are assessing and beginning repairs, but the advisory will remain in place at least until bacterial test results are returned Thursday afternoon. Residents using filters are instructed to boil filtered water for one minute and let it cool; those not using filters should flush taps for at least seven minutes before collecting water to boil. Officials caution air and loose sediment may be in lines and warn against flushing filters, which can damage performance. The break is a further setback for Flint, which remains dealing with lead-contaminated infrastructure stemming from the 2014 switch to Flint River water. Mayor Karen Weaver has requested $55 million from the state to replace all lead pipes; Gov. Snyder’s office says his budget proposal includes additional funding for Flint-related needs (including water infrastructure) and the administration has sought $195 million in related support. The corrosive water has also damaged city equipment—fire pumps and trucks have shown rust and premature wear, and officials are checking fire suppression systems citywide. Contact info and national tips for microbial concerns were provided by the city.

Google apologized after its new Photos app automatically tagged images of two Black men as "gorillas," an error a New York web developer, Jacky Alciné, publicly flagged on Twitter. The incident highlighted limits and sensitivities around automatic image-labeling and machine learning: algorithms can misclassify people—especially darker-skinned faces—leading to racist and offensive results. Google’s chief architect of social, Yonatan Zunger, acknowledged the problem, said engineers were working on immediate and longer-term fixes (including avoiding certain words for people and improving recognition for dark-skinned faces), and thanked Alciné for helping identify the bug. The company said it was “appalled and genuinely sorry” and promised steps to prevent recurrence.

The story noted similar failures at other tech firms—Flickr earlier auto-tagged Black people as “ape” or “animal,” and Google Maps has returned racist search results in the past—underscoring broader challenges for Silicon Valley as AI systems scale into sensitive tasks. Users can remove incorrect tags to help algorithms learn, but critics and affected users question how training data and diversity efforts will change to prevent such harmful errors.

Researchers Matteo Borrini and Luigi Garlaschelli performed the first published bloodstain-pattern analysis of the Shroud of Turin and conclude the stain patterns are inconsistent with those that would come from a single supine corpse or a crucified, hanging body. Using real and synthetic blood on a live subject and a mannequin, they ran seven tests targeting wounds represented on the shroud (left hand, forearm, spear wound in the chest, and lumbar/waist area) and compared the direction and shape of flows to the images on the linen.

Key findings:
- Rivulets on the forearm and trickles from the hand correspond to very different arm orientations: forearm flows fit an arm held roughly 90° from the body, while hand trickles matched an arm at about 45°. Some hand marks also differ from one another by up to 10°.
- The spear wound produced rivulets in tests only when the subject was upright (consistent with bleeding while hanging), but the shroud’s mark is a solid stain rather than the rivulets observed.
- The lumbar “blood belt” on the shroud could not be reproduced in any experimental scenario, whether bleeding while supine or after standing then lying down.
- Overall, the patterns from different regions are mutually inconsistent; even allowing for multiple bleeding episodes or postmortem movement, the lumbar stains appear especially unrealistic.

Context and caveats:
- The shroud has long been debated; radiocarbon dating places the linen at 1260–1390 CE, though fabric weave and some other analyses have been inconclusive or disputed.
- The investigators suggest the inconsistencies point toward the shroud being an artistic or didactic medieval creation rather than the burial cloth of a crucified individual.
- Some experts note limitations: the experiments held body parts fixed and did not simulate potential handling, cleaning, or preparation of a corpse, which could affect patterns. The study does not explain how the shroud’s image was formed; that question remains unresolved.

The study was published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences and adds forensic evidence challenging the shroud’s authenticity while leaving open scientific questions about the cloth’s image-formation process.

A Queensland couple, Jo Grant and Jill Kindt, have been revealed as Australia’s first legally married same-sex couple. They wed privately in their Sunshine Coast garden on 15 December after officials granted an exemption from the usual 30-day waiting period because Ms Grant was terminally ill with a rare cancer and receiving palliative care. Staff from Queensland Births, Deaths and Marriages expedited the paperwork—driving about 100 km to deliver documents so the ceremony, registration and approval all took place within 24 hours. The pair had been together eight years and held a commitment ceremony in 2013; their legal marriage lasted 48 days before Ms Grant died on 30 January. The story was disclosed in Queensland’s parliament by Attorney‑General Yvette D’Ath, who praised the officials’ efforts; Kindt said she was grateful the bureaucrats “moved heaven and earth” to give them legal recognition. The couple are among 159 same‑sex marriages registered in Queensland since marriage equality laws passed.

Workers replacing century-old water mains beneath Washington Square Park in Greenwich Village uncovered two 18th- or early-19th-century burial vaults this week. The brick-roofed vaults, found about 3½ feet below the street near Washington Square Park East and Waverly Place, measure roughly 15 by 18 feet and contained more than a dozen skeletal remains — one vault held skulls and bones pushed into a corner (estimated 9–12 individuals), the other showed stacked wooden coffins. 

Chrysalis archaeologists and anthropologists are on site to document and investigate, using lights and high-zoom photography (including attempts to read coffin plates) and will comb historical records and church archives to try to identify the dead. Officials believe the vaults likely belonged to a nearby Presbyterian church; the area also served as a potter’s field for yellow fever victims in the early 1800s. 

The city’s Department of Design and Construction and the Landmarks Preservation Commission are assessing the find. Because city policy prefers to leave burial grounds undisturbed where possible, engineers are planning to re-route the water-main work; excavation and restricted access in the area will continue as archaeologists gather more information.

A 14-year-old Pakistani schoolgirl, Malala Yousafzai — who had publicly campaigned for girls’ education and written for the BBC about life under the Taliban in Swat — was shot in the head on a school bus by Taliban gunmen. Treated at a military hospital in Rawalpindi, she remains unconscious on a ventilator but showed signs of improvement after sedation was reduced: doctors reported she moved her hands and feet, was briefly taken off the ventilator, and was described as stable though recovery from the serious head injury would be slow and the next 36–48 hours were critical. A bullet was removed from her neck; doctors have not ruled on long-term brain damage. Two classmates were also wounded; one, Shazia Ramzan, vowed they would return to school together.

The attack provoked widespread national and international condemnation, large rallies in support of Malala (notably in Karachi), and calls for stronger action against the Pakistani Taliban. Pakistani authorities said arrests had been made and offered a reward exceeding $100,000 for the attackers; police reported at least three suspects detained though the gunmen remain at large. The military said it was prepared to transfer Malala abroad for further care if needed; the UAE offered an air ambulance and medical teams as a contingency.

Reactions were mixed domestically: mainstream and some Islamist leaders condemned the shooting but some groups warned against using it to justify renewed offensives in tribal areas, and others deflected attention to U.S. drone strikes. International figures, including Afghanistan’s president, denounced the attack and urged joint action against extremism. Observers suggested the assault both highlighted the risks facing activists and could galvanize support for girls’ education and anti-militant efforts, though skeptics cautioned that Pakistan has repeatedly failed to sustain decisive policy shifts against radical elements.

Governor David Paterson used a high-profile appearance on Larry King Live to forcefully deny ongoing lurid rumors about his conduct and to press the New York Times to publish — or at least clarify — a reported story that has not yet appeared. Since word of an imminent Times piece surfaced last week, speculation about sex, drugs or graft has mushroomed across media and political circles. Paterson repeatedly called the allegations "flat-out lie[s]" and urged reporters to investigate why their sources were making such claims rather than continuing to amplify them.

On the show he said addressing every rumor might only give it more life, but he denied the most sensational Post allegation (an encounter with a woman in a governor's mansion utility closet) and rejected further detailed rebuttals as unnecessary because he has already denied the charges elsewhere. He suggested someone is "after" him but declined to name suspects, and blamed lingering public sensitivity after Eliot Spitzer's prostitution scandal for the readiness to believe such stories.

Paterson criticized the Times’ handling of the situation and implored Albany bureau chief Danny Hakim to either publish or disavow the report so the speculation would end. He mixed firm denials with self-aware gallows humor, insisting he won’t resign and asking the paper to "clear the air" so he can be "out of [his] misery."

William D. Swenson, a former U.S. Army captain and Medal of Honor recipient, has formally requested to return to active duty. Swenson, 34 and living in Seattle, left the Army in February 2011 but could re-enter service and potentially be promoted to major after routine clearance steps (physical, drug test, etc.). Officials said they were processing his request and expected it to be feasible.

Swenson received the Medal of Honor from President Obama for repeatedly risking his life during the Sept. 8, 2009, Battle of Ganjgal in Kunar province, Afghanistan, where coalition forces were ambushed and pinned down for nine hours. He braved intense fire to recover bodies and aid wounded comrades, notably helping Sgt. 1st Class Kenneth Westbrook onto a medevac and kissing him on the forehead before returning to the fight. The engagement left multiple U.S., Afghan, and coalition casualties; Westbrook later died of his wounds.

Swenson’s path to the award was rocky: his Medal of Honor nomination packet was reportedly “lost” for a time, prompting congressional scrutiny and an Army inspector general investigation. Swenson had publicly criticized commanders for denying repeated requests for air support during the battle; subsequent Army investigations led to reprimands for two officers. Swenson’s actions were previously recognized when Marine Sgt. Dakota Meyer—who fought alongside him—received the Medal of Honor in 2011; this ceremony marked only the second time in half a century two survivors of the same battle earned the medal.

Swenson also holds a Purple Heart and Bronze Star. He has expressed commitment to supporting his fellow soldiers and families of the fallen and said the Army as an institution did not let him down.

A tour bus plunged off a bridge in North Hwanghae province, North Korea, on Sunday night, killing 36 people — 32 Chinese tourists and four North Koreans — and seriously injuring two Chinese. State media and Chinese outlets showed wreckage in rainy darkness; North Korea did not give a cause. Kim Jong Un visited a hospital to see injured Chinese passengers, met China’s ambassador Li Jinjun at the Chinese embassy, and expressed “bitter sorrow” and condolences, an unusually public acknowledgment of a domestic tragedy. China dispatched diplomats and a medical team to assist. Chinese tourists constitute the vast majority of visitors to North Korea and are an important source of foreign currency; the incident and Kim’s prompt outreach are being viewed partly in that diplomatic and domestic context. The report also noted generally poor road conditions and limited lighting in North Korea.

An apparent international crime syndicate carried out a highly coordinated ATM heist in Japan on the morning of 15 May, stealing about ¥1.4 billion (roughly US$12.7 million) in under three hours.

Key points
- About 100 people are believed to have used forged cards to make 14,000 withdrawals of the ATM maximum (¥100,000 each) across 1,400 convenience‑store ATMs in Tokyo and 16 other prefectures. Transactions began just after 05:00 and ended just before 08:00.  
- Police say the card data came from a South African bank (reports name Standard Bank); machine logs indicate roughly 1,600 compromised card numbers were used. The bank has called the incident a “sophisticated, coordinated fraud” and says customers did not suffer losses.  
- No arrests have been made. Investigators are reviewing CCTV and have asked South African authorities via Interpol to probe how the card details were obtained. Media suggest the perpetrators may have left Japan quickly by exploiting overseas‑issued cards and timing withdrawals on a bank holiday/weekend.  
- The case echoes earlier large‑scale ATM frauds that used leaked card data to make coordinated withdrawals across multiple countries.

Police continue their investigation into the source of the card data, the identities of the suspects and their possible international links.
