The document recounts how the Porsche and Piëch families—who together control a majority of Volkswagen’s voting shares through Porsche Automobil Holding SE—have reacted to Volkswagen’s 2015 diesel-emissions scandal and how family dynamics, governance arrangements and recent personnel moves have affected the company.

Key points:

- Diesel scandal impact: In September 2015 Volkswagen admitted using defeat-device software in some diesel cars, affecting about 11 million vehicles. The fallout included the CEO’s resignation, a historic corporate loss, multibillion-euro provisions (reported between €16.2bn and €17.8bn), an expected total bill that could exceed €30bn, a sharp share-price decline and a large hit to the family’s dividend income.

- Family response and governance: The Porsche–Piëch clan has stayed largely silent and avoided direct intervention, reflecting a long-standing family culture of consensus, discretion and outsourcing operational management to outsiders. Wolfgang Porsche, the family’s senior public figure, made few public comments but publicly pledged job protection and support for management when addressing plant workers. Investors and analysts criticized the family’s limited involvement in steering the company through the crisis.

- Succession and internal fractures: The family is large (about 80 members) and multi-generational, with many heirs pursuing varied careers and some lacking interest in the car business. The family’s older leaders have been slow to prepare successors; critics say succession should have been arranged years earlier. Ferdinand Piëch—once VW’s dominant and combative figure—was forced out of the supervisory board in 2015 after longstanding feuds, leaving Wolfgang Porsche as a less forceful representative. Piëch remains estranged from much of the clan.

- Power balance at VW: With family oversight muted, VW’s strong labor unions have exercised substantial influence—holding half the supervisory board seats and pressing management over job security and cost burdens related to the scandal. Investors worried that family infighting could impede decisive action, but Hans Michel Piech and Wolfgang Porsche later pledged support for VW’s chairman and CEO and said they would not interfere in daily operations.

- Family structures and financial effects: The family uses foundations and rules to limit share sales and preserve control across many members. The scandal sharply reduced dividends from Porsche SE, prompting a substantial dividend cut and potential financial strain for family members who rely on that income.

- Historical controversies and corporate transparency: Volkswagen’s handling of company history also generated controversy. The firm parted ways with corporate historian Manfred Grieger amid reports he criticized a study for downplaying wartime ties between Auto Union (Audi) and the Nazi regime. Academics and former insiders condemned Grieger’s departure, saying it raised doubts about VW’s commitment to transparent historical inquiry. The company denied dismissing him for that reason and said it remains committed to honestly examining its past.

Overall, the piece portrays a controlling family that has ceded operational control to executives and, by default, to unions; one weakened by internal divisions and aging leadership; and a company struggling to manage both the immediate financial and reputational fallout from the emissions scandal and scrutiny of its wartime past.

Jon Stewart announced he will step down as host of Comedy Central’s The Daily Show later this year, ending a nearly 17-year run that began in January 1999 when he replaced Craig Kilborn. He revealed the decision during a taping and said the exact timing (his contract runs through September) was still being worked out; he emphasized he isn’t leaving immediately and joked about having “dinner on a school night” with his family once free.

Under Stewart’s stewardship the program became a major cultural force and influential political satire platform, winning numerous Emmys (including a decade-long run for Outstanding Variety Series) and launching the careers of several prominent comedians and hosts (Stephen Colbert, John Oliver, Samantha Bee, Larry Wilmore, etc.). Stewart turned the show into appointment viewing for younger audiences who increasingly turned away from traditional news, and he emerged as a trusted and sometimes combative public figure—famous moments include his 2004 Crossfire appearance and advocacy on issues such as Sept. 11 first responders’ benefits. He has also expanded into other projects, notably directing the film Rosewater.

Comedy Central president Michele Ganeless praised Stewart’s influence and said the show will endure beyond his departure. Stewart called hosting the show “the honor of my professional life” and said he felt it was time for someone else to take the role. His future plans remain open.

A New York Times columnist recounts being kicked out of Marc Forgione in TriBeCa after confronting the chef for loudly berating a kitchen employee in full view of diners. The writer describes the chef’s sustained, public yelling, how it made the dining room uncomfortable, and how he briefly walked into the open kitchen to ask the chef to stop. After a terse exchange at the table—during which the chef defended his behavior as necessary for quality—the chef told the writer to leave and ejected the party. The writer admits he could have handled the incident more tactfully but stands by speaking up and says the chef offered no apology; Forgione later told him the kitchen is a “sacred space” and that the guest’s conduct (including a dismissive hand gesture) justified refusing service.

A former waitress responded angrily to the columnist’s account, calling it entitled and criticizing his decision to enter the kitchen. She outlines why restaurant work is difficult, argues that customers should respect restaurant “choreography,” and offers practical etiquette rules: make eye contact, order in a timely manner, avoid making a mess, complain promptly if something is wrong, handle the check efficiently, tip at least 20% at higher-end places, and never go into the kitchen. The piece notes an update pointing to additional coverage of Forgione’s perspective.

Cambodia has refused to extradite French architect Patrick Henri Devillers — a close associate of Gu Kailai and linked to the high-profile Bo Xilai scandal in China — saying he will remain detained in Cambodia pending further investigation. Cambodian Foreign Minister Hor Namhong said Devillers would neither be sent to China nor France; he gave no details about the arrest request from China or the grounds for Devillers’s detention. Devillers, about 52, has lived in Cambodia for at least five years and previously lived in China, where he was reported to be in Bo Xilai’s inner circle and to have business ties with Gu Kailai. Chinese authorities are understood to suspect Gu of murdering British businessman Neil Heywood and of large-scale undeclared income and moving funds overseas; Japanese paper Asahi Shimbun reported Gu admitted guilt and implicated large cross-border remittances possibly totaling billions. Cambodian officials have been unusually secretive about Devillers’s custody and location; police initially cited an immigration detention allowance of up to 60 days while China compiled evidence, but various detention centers denied holding him. Eyewitnesses said Devillers was arrested about two weeks earlier; friends and the French embassy have given little comment. Cambodia’s handling of the case highlights its close political and economic ties with China and has raised questions amid a larger investigation into Gu Kailai and associates alleged to have moved money abroad.

The provided text mixes several distinct documents and news items about presidential powers, U.S. foreign aid to Palestinians, Richard Nixon’s 1974 impeachment articles, and legal defenses of President Trump.

1) Constitutional provisions on the presidency:
- The Constitution vests executive power in a President elected to a four-year term with a Vice President. States appoint electors equal to their congressional delegation; electors meet in-state and vote. Elections are determined by electoral vote majorities, with contingency procedures in the House (for President) and Senate (for Vice President) if no majority is reached.
- Congress sets the timing for choosing electors. Eligibility requires natural-born citizenship (or citizen at Constitution adoption), age 35, and 14 years’ U.S. residency.
- Succession: the Vice President assumes the presidency upon death, removal, resignation, or inability; Congress may legislate further succession.
- The President receives a fixed compensation for his term and must take an oath to “preserve, protect and defend the Constitution.”
- Presidential powers include commander-in-chief, seeking written opinions from department heads, granting reprieves and pardons (except impeachment cases), making treaties and key appointments with Senate advice and consent, filling Senate recess vacancies, reporting the State of the Union, convening Congress, receiving foreign ministers, ensuring laws are faithfully executed, and commissioning officers.
- Impeachment and conviction for treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors remove the President, Vice President, and civil officers.

2) U.S. aid to UNRWA and Palestinian diplomacy:
- The Trump administration reportedly froze $125 million in funding to the U.N. Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA)—about one-third of U.S. annual contributions—pending a review of U.S. assistance to the Palestinian Authority after the Palestinians suspended contacts over U.S. recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital.
- U.S. officials told diplomats the freeze could be extended to cuts as large as $180 million (roughly half of U.S. UNRWA funding). A State Department official said decisions were still under deliberation and not necessarily finalized.
- Donors, U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, Israeli security officials, and others warned that large cuts would be catastrophic for UNRWA’s operations and could worsen humanitarian conditions in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, and Lebanon.
- Israeli leaders are divided: some conservative ministers press for cuts, while Prime Minister Netanyahu conveyed to the White House a preference for “gradual disengagement” and opposed large, immediate cuts to UNRWA because of security and humanitarian concerns.

3) Nixon’s Articles of Impeachment (House Judiciary Committee, July 27, 1974):
- The text reproduces the first two Articles adopted by the Judiciary Committee (these were never voted on by the full House). Article I accuses President Nixon of obstructing justice by covering up the June 17, 1972 break-in at Democratic National Committee headquarters, misleading investigators, concealing evidence, interfering with investigations, and using payments to silence or influence witnesses.
- Article II charges Nixon with abusing executive power and violating citizens’ rights by misusing agencies (IRS, FBI, Secret Service, CIA), authorizing improper surveillance and a secret White House investigative unit, and failing to ensure laws were faithfully executed. The Committee found these actions contrary to his oath and warranting impeachment and trial.

4) Legal argument about presidential obstruction of justice (Trump era):
- John Dowd, a lead attorney for President Trump, argued publicly that a sitting president cannot be guilty of obstruction of justice because the Constitution makes the president the nation’s chief law enforcement officer and thus inherently empowered to direct law-enforcement matters. He defended Trump’s public comments (including tweets about Michael Flynn) as lawful expressions of presidential view, denying they constituted obstruction.
- The argument echoes past claims about broad presidential authority (notably similar to historic defenses used by Nixon). Critics argue tweets and requests made to FBI officials—such as reported requests to “let the Flynn thing go”—could be evidence of obstruction.

Overall themes:
- The constitutional framework grants broad presidential powers but pairs them with checks: Senate confirmation, impeachment, and succession rules.
- Debates and controversies arise over the scope of those powers—particularly regarding executive influence over law enforcement and foreign aid—and can have significant legal, political, and humanitarian consequences, as seen in the Nixon era and contemporary U.S.-Palestinian relations.

This document is a collection of pieces and excerpts from Rookie, the online magazine and annual book series for teenage girls founded by Tavi Gevinson. It combines personal essays, cultural criticism, profiles, and pop-culture recommendations that illustrate Rookie’s mission: to give teens a serious, creative space to talk about music, film, fashion, body image, and identity.

Key points:

- Rookie’s format and mission: A monthly editorial theme shapes writing, photography, and artwork. The site (and its Rookie Yearbooks) published thoughtful, teen-focused journalism and cultural commentary, and built a large, engaged audience before ceasing new content and preserving its archives.

- Gendered condescension in cultural criticism: An essay (by a Teenage contributor) documents repeated experiences of grown men treating teen girls’ tastes as unimportant or laughable—dismissing fandoms, misreading young women, and assigning male journalists to interpret teen-girl culture, often producing patronizing, off-base takes. The author argues men are socialized to assume their tastes and interpretations are authoritative and urges them to listen to teen girls themselves.

- Tavi Gevinson profile: A portrait of Rookie’s founder at 17 balancing high school with running a thriving online magazine and 80-person staff, book signings, speaking engagements and acting. Gevinson began blogging at 11, expanded Style Rookie into Rookie, produces annual yearbooks, and aims to make teens feel included and respected. Despite fame, she keeps a mostly normal teenage life and rejects being labeled “voice of a generation.”

- Representation of fat women and media: Another essay critiques mainstream portrayals of fat women (e.g., Shallow Hal) that reduce them to jokes or “but you’ve got a pretty face” tropes. It praises nuanced portrayals like Rae in My Mad Fat Diary, where weight is part of a complex character rather than the sole punchline. The writer is disappointed by comic roles for fat actresses (e.g., Rebel Wilson) that repeat old stereotypes instead of offering fuller representation.

- Lorde interview excerpt: A youth-to-youth interview with singer Lorde highlights how adult journalists often misread teen audiences and pigeonhole young artists into niche stereotypes. Lorde’s music and appeal are described as broader and more nuanced than such pieces allow.

- Pop-culture lists and recommendations: Several short pieces and picks from contributors celebrate films, TV shows, music and holiday movies that shaped them—ranging from The Wonder Years, Seven Minutes in Heaven, Angel and Torchwood, to The NeverEnding Story and Nirvana’s MTV Unplugged—illustrating Rookie’s mix of nostalgic, indie, mainstream and cult tastes.

Overall, the compilation showcases Rookie’s blend of earnest teen perspectives, media-savvy criticism, and cultural curation—centered on empowering young women’s voices and critiquing the adult assumptions that too often speak for them.

Former MSNBC anchor Keith Olbermann will join Current TV as host of a one-hour prime-time program beginning in spring and will serve as the network’s chief news officer, Current announced. Current TV, the low-rated cable channel co-founded by Al Gore and Joel Hyatt, said Olbermann will have editorial independence there; reports also indicated he may take an equity stake. The move follows Olbermann’s January departure from MSNBC after disputes with management and a contractual waiting period that delayed any new on-air start.

Current, which targets younger viewers and has been expanding from user-generated content into traditional programming, hopes Olbermann’s high-profile, progressive commentary and audience will raise the channel’s visibility; Current is carried in fewer homes and often on digital tiers compared with MSNBC. Olbermann praised Current’s independent model and framed the partnership as an opportunity to continue his journalism with fewer corporate constraints. He may also pursue other digital ventures alongside the TV show.

A Langley, B.C., dog walker, Emma Paulsen, has been charged in connection with the deaths of six dogs in her care last May. Paulsen faces multiple counts under the Criminal Code — including killing or injuring an animal, causing unnecessary pain or suffering, failing to provide necessities of life, and public mischief for falsely reporting an offence — as well as two counts under British Columbia’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act for causing animals to remain in distress. The B.C. SPCA and necropsies determined the dogs died of heat stroke after being left in the back of her truck on May 13, when temperatures reached about 25 C. Paulsen initially reported the dogs stolen from her vehicle, prompting a community search; their bodies were found a week later in a ditch in the Fraser Valley. The charges carry potential penalties including up to five years’ imprisonment for some offences, fines up to $75,000 for the provincial counts, and possible lifetime bans on animal ownership. It is not yet known when Paulsen will first appear in court. Family members and owners have expressed grief and a desire for justice.

On May 13 in South Carolina, 18-year-old prison inmate Ezekiel Stevenson attempted to carjack a man during a hospital visit. The victim had his proximity key fob on him; when Stevenson forced him from the vehicle and tried to drive off, the owner repeatedly used the fob to shut down and relock/unlock the car, preventing escape and allowing police to enter the vehicle. Stevenson ran into nearby woods but was captured within an hour. The reporter notes this incident as an unusual win for proximity key technology, which often frustrates drivers but here thwarted the attempted getaway.

“If I Stay,” adapted by R.J. Cutler from Gayle Forman’s YA novel, is a polished tear-jerker in the vein of “The Fault in Our Stars.” Chloe Grace Moretz stars as 17-year-old cello prodigy Mia Hall, who, after a horrific car crash that kills members of her family, hovers between life and death in a coma and watches events unfold as a quasi-ethereal observer. The film alternates between Mia’s hospital vigil—where she must decide whether to live—and flashbacks to her idyllic life in Portland, including a budding romance with guitarist Adam (Jamie Blackley) and warm, countercultural parents played by Mireille Enos and Joshua Leonard.

Director Cutler and screenwriter Shauna Cross render the story with a soft-focus, prettified aesthetic that heightens feeling but sometimes flattens dramatic tension. Moretz plays against type, toning down her edgier strengths for a more restrained, sympathetic Mia; Blackley and Stacy Keach provide some of the film’s strongest emotional moments. Musical interludes add energy, but the film’s supernatural framing and sentimental impulses can feel overly earnest or clumsy at times. Overall, “If I Stay” delivers generous emotional payoff for young-adult audiences despite occasional silliness in its otherworldly sequences. Rated PG-13; 106 minutes.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un said in his televised New Year’s address that Pyongyang’s work on “cutting‑edge” weapons is advancing and preparations for a test‑launch of an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) are in their “final stages.” He framed 2017 as a year to complete and strengthen the country’s nuclear and pre‑emptive strike capabilities, saying North Korea will continue to make nuclear weapons a cornerstone of policy while the U.S. and South Korea maintain what he called “nuclear threats” and joint exercises.

Kim also issued an unusually personal note of apology to North Korean citizens for unmet goals in 2016 and stressed economic priorities: continuing a five‑year growth plan, boosting light industry and electrical and scientific output, completing domestic construction projects delayed by floods, and pushing national campaigns aimed at higher productivity. He criticized South Korea’s political turmoil and specifically attacked ousted president Park Geun‑hye and Seoul’s anti‑North rhetoric, while calling for measures to reduce inter‑Korean military tensions.

The remarks follow an intense year of North Korean weapons activity in 2016—including two nuclear tests and numerous missile launches, plus a satellite launch widely viewed as a long‑range missile test—and tighter UN sanctions after Pyongyang’s largest nuclear test in September. South Korea’s acting president vowed to maintain strong military readiness and proceed with deployment of the U.S. THAAD missile‑defense system despite regional objections. Analysts note Kim’s statements raise concern but many experts still judge a reliable ICBM with a nuclear warhead capable of reaching the U.S. may be years away.

This piece profiles Black Friday shoppers who treat post-Thanksgiving bargain hunting like a practiced, competitive sport. It follows veterans such as Rosemary Rizzo, who leaves late on Thanksgiving, lines up early (sometimes before midnight) at outlet centers, shops alone, travels light, and studies circulars and deal sites in advance to map a timed route. Organization — knowing budgets, keeping cards accessible, and carrying only a flyer, list and wallet — and stamina (coffee, snacks, minimal sleep) are emphasized. Rizzo and others report big wins (e.g., hard-to-find electronics, steeply discounted designer bags) and describe the “rush” and sense of accomplishment that make Black Friday an annual ritual.

Another shopper, Matt Kane, treats it as competitive strategy: researching days in advance, scouting store layouts, and prioritizing items. The article also includes a tongue-in-cheek five-tip survival guide gathered from Black Friday pros: do thorough homework on ads and timelines; set clear priorities for what you want; scout familiar stores when possible; bring backup (friends) to hold places in line and split tasks; stay energized with coffee and snacks and be prepared for late-night starts; and keep a good attitude amid the chaos. The piece ends by inviting readers to share their own Black Friday plans and tips.

- Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl, who was released from Taliban captivity on May 31 after nearly five years, is en route from Europe to the United States and is scheduled to arrive at Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio, Texas, early Friday. He has been recuperating at Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany since June 1.

- Pentagon officials say Bergdahl will continue his medical care and reintegration at Brooke. He reportedly has not yet spoken with his family; military medical staff will decide when he is ready to do so.

- Bergdahl disappeared from his post in Afghanistan’s Paktika province on June 30, 2009. A U.S. Army fact-finding inquiry concluded he left his outpost deliberately, but the Army has not made a definitive determination of desertion because intent could not be established without interviewing him.

- Details about his captivity are emerging slowly. Reports say he endured harsh treatment, including periods confined in a small, dark box, and suffers psychological trauma from physical abuse.

- The prisoner swap that freed him — Bergdahl for five Taliban detainees held at Guantanamo Bay — provoked political controversy. Critics argued Congress should have been notified and questioned the cost of the exchange; Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel defended the decision as Bergdahl’s best chance for release.

- Two letters Bergdahl reportedly wrote from captivity (2012 and 2013), published by The Daily Beast and authenticated by U.S. officials, criticize Army leadership and ask that investigators consider all evidence regarding his disappearance.

- At a House Armed Services Committee hearing, Hagel defended the handling of Bergdahl’s care and the timing of interviews, stressing the impact of prolonged captivity on his physical and mental condition.

Overview:
On March 15, 2016 Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton won major primary contests—Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Illinois—delivering a significant delegate boost and blunting Bernie Sanders’s momentum after his upset in Michigan. Republican front-runner Donald Trump also scored big victories (notably Florida) while Ohio Governor John Kasich claimed a key home-state win and Marco Rubio suspended his campaign after losing Florida.

Key Democratic takeaways:
- Clinton’s wins, particularly in Ohio, expanded her delegate lead to roughly 300 pledged delegates (plus a large superdelegate advantage), making Sanders’s path to the nomination increasingly difficult under the Democrats’ proportional allocation rules.
- Clinton’s strength came from minority voters (very strong with black voters and Hispanics in Florida), older voters and those prioritizing experience and electability. Exit polls showed many voters found her policies more realistic than Sanders’s.
- Sanders continued to energize young voters, independents and progressives with critiques of trade, Wall Street, and corporate America. He performed strongly with independents and voters under 30 but failed to translate that into sufficient delegate gains on Tuesday.
- Ohio was a pivotal test after Michigan’s upset. Clinton campaigned aggressively in the Midwest—retooling her economic message, emphasizing manufacturing and labor ties—and won coalitions in both urban black communities and parts of the working class that Sanders hoped to capture.
- Both campaigns framed next steps differently: Clinton advisers expressed confidence in holding the delegate lead and shifting toward the general election; Sanders aides argued the calendar ahead (caucuses and liberal states) could favor him and urged a string of large wins.

Key Republican takeaways:
- Trump solidified his front-runner status with big wins including Florida, North Carolina and Illinois, and by effectively knocking Rubio out of the race (Rubio suspended his campaign after losing Florida).
- Kasich’s narrow Ohio victory was his first and a symbolic rebuke to Trump, keeping open the possibility of a contested convention if anti-Trump forces coalesce.
- The GOP race remained unsettled: Trump leads in delegates but may not clinch the nomination before the convention; Cruz remains a potential challenger with a strategy focused on delegates and contested-state conventions.

Themes and dynamics:
- Economy and trade were top issues in Midwestern Democratic contests. Voters who prioritized the economy generally favored Clinton in Ohio, though Sanders won the anti-trade, working-class vote in neighboring Michigan.
- Clinton pivoted repeatedly to attack Donald Trump’s rhetoric, framing the Democratic contest increasingly as a choice about who can defeat Trump and govern in November.
- Sanders pushed progressive economic messaging and criticized Clinton’s Wall Street ties and use of a super PAC, but exit polling indicated many Democratic voters prefer Clinton’s experience and deem her proposals more realistic.
- The results suggested Democrats were trending toward unifying to oppose Trump, while Republicans faced the prospect of a fractured nominating process.

Bottom line:
Clinton’s decisive victories on March 15 greatly fortified her delegate lead and momentum toward the Democratic nomination, making Sanders’s comeback increasingly unlikely though not impossible. On the GOP side, Trump strengthened his front-runner position even as Kasich’s Ohio win and Rubio’s exit left the party’s path to a clear nominee uncertain.

After a fatal July attack on military facilities in Chattanooga, armed civilians have begun standing watch outside recruiting centers nationwide. Military commands and property owners, however, have pushed back.

Key incidents and developments:
- Lancaster, Ohio: Armed volunteers had been guarding a multi-branch recruiting center since Monday. On Thursday an armed guard, 28-year-old Christopher Reed, accidentally discharged his AR-15 while attempting to clear it; the round struck pavement and no one was hurt. The shopping-center owner ordered the volunteers off the property hours later; Reed was charged with a misdemeanor for discharging a firearm within city limits and the rifle was taken pending court. Reed said he was a gun enthusiast—not a veteran—and defended the group’s motives.
- Spanaway, Washington and other locations: Landlords and local law enforcement have asked volunteers to leave over liability and insurance concerns after similar vigil postings elsewhere.
- Nationwide response by the services: The Army and Marine Corps have warned recruiters not to interact with armed civilians, to treat them as potential security threats, and to report their presence to local law enforcement and higher command. Marines were explicitly told not to allow armed civilians into recruiting offices or handle their weapons, and to notify property lessors (e.g., Army Corps of Engineers representatives) when volunteers appear.
- Organized groups and public reaction: Activist groups such as Oath Keepers and “Three Percenters” have encouraged members to guard centers under initiatives like “Operation Warrior Guardian.” Some community members and veterans praise the volunteers as protective, while military leaders cite safety, mission disruption, and the risk of negligent discharges as reasons to discourage the practice.

Overall, while many armed volunteers say they mean well and want to protect unarmed recruiters, property owners, law enforcement and military commands have moved to limit or remove them because of legal, safety and operational concerns.

BP has sued Texas lawyer Mikal C. Watts in federal court in New Orleans, accusing him of fraudulently inflating the number of seafood-industry clients he represented after the 2010 Gulf oil spill and thus driving up BP’s settlement costs. BP says it relied on Watts’s claim that he represented more than 40,000 deckhands—nearly 80% of projected claimants—when it agreed to a $2.3 billion seafood compensation fund. The company alleges that many of those supposed clients were “phantoms”: of the 43,976 claims Watts later filed under a separate program, BP says 40% used Social Security numbers belonging to other people, 13% used incomplete or dummy numbers, and 5% used numbers of deceased people. Watts ultimately filed only 648 individual crew claims in the seafood program; BP reports only eight were found eligible, with 17 pending.

BP has paid about $1 billion from the seafood fund and wants the court to halt further payments and recover unspent money it says resulted from “brazen fraud.” Watts’s lawyer calls him innocent and says he acted in good faith, forwarding documentation provided by clients and relying on referrals. Watts resigned from the plaintiffs’ steering committee earlier this year after federal agents executed search warrants at his firm; he is also under criminal investigation. Plaintiffs’ lawyers counter that BP is using the Watts controversy to halt payments to deserving claimants and that deckhands accounted for only about $130 million of the seafood allocation, calling BP’s bid to withhold the entire program unfair. The dispute sits amid broader litigation and oversight: a court-appointed review found not systemic corruption but isolated fraud and conflicts, and appeals court and trial judge actions have temporarily paused some payments while further scrutiny proceeds.

Search operations for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 resumed in a newly defined area of the southern Indian Ocean after authorities shifted the focus about 700 miles (1,100 km) northeast of the previous search zone based on a fresh analysis of radar and other data. That analysis—partly carried out by Boeing analysts—suggested the aircraft was flying faster than first estimated and therefore would have exhausted its fuel sooner, placing a likely end-of-flight area farther north.

Over the weekend multiple surveillance aircraft (including Chinese and Australian planes) and ships scoured the roughly 123,000-square-mile (319,000 km²) search zone—about the size of New Mexico or Poland—and reported floating objects on consecutive days. Crews aboard some ships recovered items, but the Australian Maritime Safety Authority said none have been confirmed as debris from MH370; officials cautioned that ocean detritus and drifting flotsam are common and make identifications uncertain. The new zone is smaller than the previous one, closer to Perth (reducing flight time for search aircraft) and has somewhat better weather and sea conditions, but deep, cold water and the vast area still pose major difficulties.

A growing naval presence is assembling: up to 10 surface vessels were expected as well as an Australian frigate and a ship due to carry sonar and equipment for detecting the aircraft’s flight data and cockpit voice recorders (“black boxes”). The Ocean Shield and U.S. Navy gear able to detect black-box pings were being readied for deployment; pingers typically emit detectable signals for about 30 days, and Flight 370 had been missing for roughly three weeks at the time of these reports.

Malaysian officials continued to face pressure and criticism from relatives—particularly of Chinese passengers, who made up about two-thirds of the 239 people on board—over the pace and clarity of information. Malaysia’s defense minister met families and pledged the search would continue. Investigators stressed that recovered debris could provide crucial forensic clues (for example, indicating fire, impact forces, or which part of the aircraft struck the water), but drifting over weeks may limit the usefulness of surface finds for pinpointing a crash site.

Experts said the plane’s black boxes, designed to survive deep-sea immersion, could remain viable for years if recovered; however, locating them is difficult because much of the seabed in the search area lies between 2,000 meters and as deep as 6,000 meters. Weather deterioration with the approaching Southern Hemisphere winter may further delay any detailed underwater recovery operation.

Tabloid reports claim Al and Tipper Gore’s surprise separation after 40 years was triggered by an affair between Al Gore and Laurie David, the environmental activist and ex-wife of comedian Larry David. Star magazine alleges the relationship lasted about two years and grew out of the pair’s longstanding friendship and environmental work, including David’s role as a co-producer on Gore’s An Inconvenient Truth. The story prompted denials: a Gore friend called the claim “complete crap,” and a Gore spokeswoman declined to comment. The article notes Laurie David divorced Larry David in 2007 amid earlier infidelity rumors. Other gossip outlets have offered competing, unverified explanations for the Gores’ split, including allegations of homosexuality and jealousy, but no substantiated proof of an affair has been presented.

A kindergarten boy in Surprise, Ariz., was given a one-day lunch detention and a school-record referral for “sexual misconduct” after pulling his pants down on the playground. The 5‑year‑old’s mother says he did it out of fear and intimidation, not sexual intent, and that her son — who was asked to sign the referral — is too young to understand the label. An attorney later negotiated a confidential agreement with the district that removed the sexual‑misconduct designation from the child’s record.

Dysart Unified officials say staff followed district policy, which classifies exposing oneself as sexual misconduct, and that the signature only acknowledged receipt of due process. The district defends using uniform terminology and forms to ensure clarity, consistent handling and compliance with state and federal reporting requirements, while saying administrators consider age and circumstances when determining consequences.

Experts and state officials question applying adult terminology to very young children. Child‑development researchers warn that kindergartners may not grasp legal or disciplinary labels, and that labeling can harm a child’s developing sense of self; they recommend focusing discussions on the behavior and age‑appropriate correction. The Arizona Department of Education is reviewing reported data after concerns that incidents involving young children may be miscoded under standards for indecent exposure, and may offer training to districts to improve consistency between local discipline policies and state/federal definitions.

The story highlights tensions between uniform, often zero‑tolerance‑style discipline matrices (used to ensure transparency and meet reporting rules) and the need for flexibility and child‑appropriate responses for very young students.

Ted Wells’ independent 144-page investigation into the Miami Dolphins’ workplace conduct, released Feb. 14, found that guards Richie Incognito, John Jerry and center Mike Pouncey “engaged in a pattern of harassment” directed at tackle Jonathan Martin, another young offensive lineman (Player A), and an assistant trainer.

Key findings
- Harassment: The assistant trainer was repeatedly targeted with racial slurs; Player A endured homophobic name-calling and improper physical touching; Martin was persistently taunted with sexually explicit and racially insulting comments about his sister and mother. Investigators concluded the conduct toward Martin had the hallmarks of classic bullying, with Incognito the main instigator and Jerry and Pouncey following his lead.
- Evidence: The probe reviewed thousands of documents (texts, emails, a “fine” notebook from the linemen’s kangaroo court) and over 100 interviews. Notebook entries and texts showed awareness of abusive conduct (e.g., entries about “breaking Jmart” and attempts to destroy the notebook).
- Martin’s condition: Martin’s texts and other materials corroborated that the harassment caused him significant emotional distress. The report documents that Martin twice contemplated suicide in 2013; investigators consulted a psychologist who said Martin’s responses matched those of a victim of abusive treatment. The report also noted Martin’s prior history of being bullied and possible heightened sensitivity to insults, but said those vulnerabilities do not excuse the harassment.
- Intent and severity: Wells concluded Incognito, Jerry and Pouncey did not intend to drive Martin from the team or cause lasting harm, but their conduct was nevertheless abusive and inappropriate. Some public allegations (e.g., a malicious physical attack at a 2012 party) were found to be exaggerated, though humiliating episodes did occur.
- Team leadership: The report did not fault coach Joe Philbin or the front office for deliberate wrongdoing; investigators found Philbin would likely have intervened had he known. However, the investigators concluded team rules on workplace behavior were not clearly understood or enforced by some players and staff. Offensive line coach Jim Turner’s and others’ denials were in part discredited.
- Recommendations and reaction: Wells urged clearer workplace conduct rules and guidelines for the NFL. The Dolphins owner, NFL and NFLPA said they would review the report. Dolphins ownership called the language and behavior “deeply disturbing” and pledged to address the issue. Incognito’s lawyer called the report “replete with errors” and promised a rebuttal; Incognito himself has denied bullying, labeled the behavior bonding/camaraderie, and at times criticized Martin on social media.

Outcome context
- Incognito was suspended for the remainder of the season; Martin left the team in October, checked into a hospital and was placed on non-football injury/illness list. Martin remains under contract to the Dolphins but appears unlikely to play for them; Incognito becomes a free agent in March. The report absolved Philbin and much of the front office of knowledge of the misconduct but called for organizational changes to prevent future incidents.

Overall, Wells concluded that abusive conduct occurred and materially contributed to Martin’s departure, even if not intended to expel him, and recommended stronger workplace standards and enforcement across the league.

Mary Kay Letourneau and Vili Fualaau, whose illicit relationship began when she was a 34‑year‑old sixth‑grade teacher and he was her 13‑year‑old student, sit down with Barbara Walters in an ABC 20/20 interview ahead of their 10th wedding anniversary. Letourneau served about seven and a half years in prison for the relationship; the couple married in 2005 after her release and have two daughters, Audrey and Georgia. In the interview they discuss the challenges of their unconventional marriage, including stigma and media intrusion, Letourneau’s plans to teach again and to seek removal from the sex‑offender registry, and Vili’s struggles with alcoholism, depression and feeling unsupported as a teenager. The daughters, now teenagers and older than Vili was when they were conceived, are also introduced on the program. The episode airs Friday, April 10, 2015, on ABC.

Summary:

The Mississippi special Senate runoff on Nov. 27, 2018 — the final U.S. Senate contest of the 116th Congress — pitted Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith (appointed in March to replace Thad Cochran) against Democrat Mike Espy (former agriculture secretary and congressman). The winner decided whether Republicans would hold 52 or 53 Senate seats in January.

Campaign dynamics
- The race was technically nonpartisan after a Nov. 6 jungle primary produced no majority: Hyde-Smith led with 41.3%, Espy 40.9%, with a second Republican (Chris McDaniel) taking 16.4%. That forced the runoff between Hyde-Smith and Espy.
- National Republicans heavily backed Hyde-Smith with big ad buys and ground operations; President Trump held two rallies for her the day before the runoff. Democrats invested as well, with national surrogates and ad spending, but at lower levels.
- Both candidates carried political baggage: Republicans attacked Espy over a 1997 indictment (of which he was acquitted) and paid lobbying work for an Ivory Coast leader; Hyde-Smith was embroiled in multiple controversies invoking Mississippi’s racist past, most notably a remark that she’d be “on the front row” for a “public hanging,” plus comments about suppressing liberal student votes and photos connected to Confederate memorabilia and segregation-era academies. Several corporations requested refunds of donations to her campaign.

Electoral context and turnout
- Mississippi is deeply partisan and racially polarized: black voters (about 36–38% of the electorate) vote overwhelmingly Democratic, while white voters are heavily Republican, making the state relatively “inelastic” and usually a 60–40 Republican state. That structural advantage makes it hard for Democrats to convert a strong black turnout into a statewide majority without peeling off significant numbers of white voters.
- Espy’s strategy relied on translating backlash to Hyde-Smith’s comments into unusually high African-American turnout and possibly lower Republican turnout (e.g., McDaniel supporters not voting for Hyde-Smith). Special, off-cycle runoffs can produce irregular turnout patterns that sometimes benefit Democrats.

Polling and outlook
- Public polling showed Hyde-Smith with a lead in the runoff, including a Nov. 19–24 survey putting her at 54% to Espy’s 44%. An earlier Marist poll showed a wider gap. Private polls reportedly showed the race tighter, but internal polls are treated cautiously.
- Observers compared the race to Alabama’s 2017 special election (Doug Jones’ upset), but most analysts warned that Mississippi is even more challenging for Democrats and that Hyde-Smith remained the favorite.

Outcome
- Despite the controversy and a competitive finish, Hyde-Smith won the runoff by nearly eight percentage points, becoming the first woman elected to Congress from Mississippi. Her victory gave Republicans a 53–47 Senate majority for the next Congress. Espy conceded, saying he had prayed for unity in the state.

Politics on the ground
- Trump’s rallies emphasized immigration, economic accomplishments, and support for Hyde-Smith; Republicans argued his appearances and large ground game carried conservative voters to the polls. Democrats hoped the controversies would spur black turnout; national groups and surrogates campaigned for Espy but were outspent.
- After the race, Hyde-Smith framed the win as an affirmation of conservative values and thanked Trump for his help; Espy called to concede and urged unity.

Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton published competing USA Today op-eds the night before Election Day outlining their final pitches to voters. Trump’s piece repeats campaign themes — promising to “drain the swamp,” fix a “rigged” Washington and accusing Clinton of having “been the subject of an FBI criminal investigation,” a claim that ignored FBI Director James Comey’s Sunday announcement that she was cleared again. The Trump campaign did not respond about updating the piece.

Clinton’s op-ed focuses on unity and a concrete “first 100 days” agenda. She frames the election as a choice between inclusive, bipartisan governance and divisiveness. Her four priorities: a large jobs and infrastructure program (including renewable energy and support for small businesses, paid for by higher taxes on the wealthy and corporations); comprehensive immigration reform with a path to citizenship and secure borders; pushing to overturn Citizens United via a constitutional amendment to curb unaccountable money in politics; and broad criminal justice reform to reduce overly harsh penalties for nonviolent offenses. Clinton emphasizes she’ll be a president for all Americans and contrasts her approach with what she calls Trump’s campaign of “divisiveness, fear and insults.”

Eight-year-old Chloe-May Kabealo, the sole survivor of a crash in northern New South Wales, said goodbye to her mother and two siblings at a funeral at Tweed Heads Elevation Church today. Hundreds attended the service for Stephanie King, 43, and her children Ella Jane (11) and Jacob (7), who drowned after their car slid off a muddy Tumbulgum road into the swollen Tweed River during heavy rains following Cyclone Debbie.

Chloe-May escaped after unbuckling her seatbelt, floating up and climbing to the riverbank, then running to a nearby farmhouse to raise the alarm. She was treated at Tweed Heads District Hospital for lacerations, abrasions and neck pain. Police and witnesses say Stephanie King died trying to free two of her children; police called her heroic. Bystanders and a former officer tried to find the submerged vehicle but could not.

In the weeks since, the close-knit community has rallied around Chloe-May and her father, Matt Kabealo. A fundraiser coordinated by local police has raised more than A$10,000 (reports say tens of thousands raised overall) to support them. Chloe-May has spoken publicly about her escape and said her lost family members “were all loved and they’ll never be forgotten.” Authorities reiterated standard safety advice for escaping sinking vehicles.

A violent, alcohol-fueled brawl involving members of the Palin family erupted on September 6 at a birthday party near Wasilla/Anchorage, Alaska. Police broke up the melee at the home of host Korey Klingenmeyer (the party celebrated twin brothers Matthew and Marc McKenna and was also Todd Palin’s birthday). No one pressed charges.

RadarOnline and TMZ obtained police audio recorded at the scene. The tapes capture chaotic, profanity-laced exchanges: Bristol Palin, distraught and sobbing, tells officers she was pushed to the ground, dragged by her feet, had her sunglasses and shoes taken, and was called obscene slurs while defending her younger sister Willow, who says an older woman shoved and hit her. Sarah Palin is heard yelling at officers that “the bad guys” were being allowed to leave and defending her children.

Other witnesses on the audio offer conflicting accounts. One partygoer and a Palin family friend (Matthew McKenna) say Bristol was heavily intoxicated, had punched a man (Korey Klingenmeyer is named in accusations) multiple times, and was restrained by guests — including assertions that several women pushed her down to control her. The police report quotes Klingenmeyer saying Bristol repeatedly struck him, he held her back and pushed her down while restraining her arm.

The incident left visible injuries in photos released by police; parties involved were interviewed on site, but ultimately no criminal charges were filed. The family has largely kept quiet publicly, though Sarah posted a Facebook message praising her children’s loyalty. The story remains developing.

A Mississippi teenager launched Change.org petitions after discovering brominated vegetable oil (BVO) — a controversial chemical patented as a flame retardant and banned in Europe and Japan — in some sports drinks. Her petition to PepsiCo prompted Gatorade to remove BVO from its formulas after more than 200,000 signatures. She then targeted Coca-Cola’s Powerade (which used BVO in fruit punch and strawberry lemonade), gathering tens of thousands of supporters and urging removal because the drinks are marketed to athletes and schoolchildren and because studies link BVO/bromine buildup to potential health effects (hormone disruption, fertility and neurological concerns).

Following public pressure and Gatorade’s change, Coca-Cola began phasing BVO out of Powerade: bottles in several U.S. markets no longer list the ingredient and the company confirmed its Powerade brands are “BVO-free,” though timing and reformulation details weren’t provided and some product labels and the Powerade website still listed BVO during the transition. The moves reflect broader consumer-driven shifts in the food industry as manufacturers respond to demands for cleaner, more natural ingredients.

A male lion named Mohawk — a 13-year-old, well-known member of Nairobi National Park’s King Fisher pride — was shot and killed by Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) rangers on March 30, 2016 after he escaped the park and injured a man in Isinya, Kajiado County. Mohawk had wandered out of the park’s unfenced southern migration area following recent territorial fights. Hundreds of local residents had surrounded, taunted and thrown stones at the stressed animal for hours; when the lion lunged at a passing motorcycle rider and inflicted deep lacerations, rangers who arrived without tranquilizer equipment shot him, saying they acted to prevent further harm. The killing — captured on video and prompting widespread public outrage and the hashtag #JusticeforMohawk — ignited criticism that KWS lacked proper tranquilizing resources and that development and damaged fencing around the park are pushing wildlife into populated areas.

Separately, in South Africa a 3-year-old male lion nicknamed Sylvester escaped Karoo National Park for the second time. He is wearing a satellite collar and previously killed livestock during a prior breakout. Authorities initially threatened to kill him if he posed a human threat but faced public outcry and are now weighing options including recapture and relocation, improved fencing, transfer to another reserve, or, as a last resort, euthanasia if he causes “massive” damage or endangers people. Both incidents highlight the tense trade-off between public safety and lion conservation as Africa’s lion populations decline from habitat loss, hunting and human-wildlife conflict, and as expanding infrastructure and urban encroachment increase escapes and confrontations.

Peru’s top organized-crime investigator, Eusebio Felix (also named as Felix Murga), was suspended after promoting a sensational but unsupported case that police had arrested a gang of “Pishtacos” — alleged serial killers who, according to Andean legend, extract and sell victims’ body fat. At a high-profile news conference police displayed bottles they said contained human fat, claimed up to 60 people had been murdered and alleged the fat was exported for high prices to Europe. Within weeks regional investigators and experts cast serious doubt on the account: authorities in Huanuco said only one confirmed murder was linked to the suspects and suggested the fat may have been bottled as an intimidation tactic in a drug-trafficking area, not sold abroad. Medical experts said harvesting human fat for cosmetics is implausible and dangerous; anthropologists criticized police for invoking the Pishtaco myth to explain a likely isolated crime. Peru’s police chief, Miguel Hidalgo, called the probe botched and embarrassing, and political leaders warned the episode harmed the police’s credibility and risked scaring tourists.

Gillian Bennett, an 83–85-year-old woman from Bowen Island, B.C., who had been diagnosed with dementia three years earlier, posted an open letter on her blog announcing she would end her life and then died around noon after ingesting a lethal drug. Fearful of losing her identity and becoming “a vegetable,” she chose to act while still lucid. Bennett described dementia’s progressive erosion of self, her unwillingness to spend years in institutional care, and concerns about becoming a financial and caregiving burden. She urged broader public conversation and institutional change around assisted dying, advocating for living wills, clearer medical protocols, and legal reforms to permit humane assistance.

Bennett prepared a website (Deadatnoon.com) to be published after her death arguing for physician-assisted options for elderly and terminal patients. Her husband of 60 years, Jonathan, was at her side as she died; he did not assist but supported her choice. Their two adult children and other family members were aware of and visited her in her final days. Family members described her final weekend as painful but also marked by lucidity, closeness and humor; her daughter said that if legal medical assistance had been available, Bennett might have waited. Following her death, the doctor and RCMP were notified. Bennett is survived by her husband, two children, six grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. Her stated aim was to spark discussion about end-of-life options and the need for legal and medical changes to better respect individuals’ choices.

A driver in Lake Mary, Florida, told police that George Zimmerman threatened to kill him during a road confrontation earlier this week. According to police spokeswoman Bianca Gillett and 911 recordings, the driver said a truck pulled up beside his car, the occupant yelled, "Why are you pointing a finger at me?" then asked, "Do you know who I am? I will kill you." The driver identified the truck's driver as Zimmerman, pulled into a gas station and called police, but the truck had left before officers arrived.

Two days later the same man reported seeing Zimmerman outside his workplace; officers located Zimmerman in his truck, stopped and questioned him, and briefly took and then returned a handgun. The complainant declined to press charges on both occasions. Lake Mary Police Chief Steve Bracknell confirmed there was no arrest because the victim did not want to pursue charges.

Zimmerman, who was acquitted in 2013 of second-degree murder in the fatal shooting of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin, has had multiple other encounters with police since the acquittal, including an arrest last year after an ex-girlfriend accused him of pointing a gun during an argument (charges dropped when she did not cooperate) and allegations from his estranged wife of threatening behavior.

Pro-Russian protesters seized government and security buildings on April 6–7 in three major eastern Ukrainian cities—Donetsk, Luhansk and Kharkiv—near the Russian border, raising fears of a repeat of Crimea’s annexation. Manifesters, many waving Russian flags, demanded Crimea-style referendums on joining Russia; in Donetsk they proclaimed a “Donetsk People’s Republic” and called on President Vladimir Putin to send peacekeepers. Footage showed occupiers inside regional administration and security service offices; Reuters and other outlets reported injuries and, in Luhansk, claims that weapons had been taken from a security-service arsenal.

Kiev’s interim authorities accused Russia and ousted president Viktor Yanukovich of orchestrating the unrest to destabilize Ukraine and create a pretext for Russian military intervention. Prime Minister Arseniy Yatseniuk warned that Russian troops were positioned close to the border and said the protests were part of a coordinated plan; Interior Minister Arsen Avakov vowed to restore order without bloodshed. Russia has proposed federalization for Ukraine and denies direct responsibility, even as Moscow’s annexation of Crimea in March and a Russian troop presence near the frontier have heightened international tensions.

Analysts and Western officials view the eastern seizures as a Kremlin-supported campaign of political theater and destabilization intended to weaken Kiev, bolster separatist sentiments in Russian-speaking regions, and gain leverage over Ukraine’s future. The unrest complicates Kiev’s efforts to stabilize the economy and implement reforms amid negotiations for international financial aid.

Researchers at Columbia University report the discovery of a new blood-transmissible virus they’ve named human hepegivirus-1 (HHpgV-1). Its genome shows similarities to hepatitis C (which can cause liver disease) and to human pegivirus (generally thought to be harmless). The team identified HHpgV-1 by deep sequencing archived blood samples from people who received transfusions in the 1970s–80s and in people with hemophilia treated with blood products. They found the virus in a small number of samples: two initial post-transfusion samples (both individuals later cleared the virus) and two more among 106 hemophilia patients (one person had a persistent infection lasting at least 5.4 years), with no evidence the virus caused disease in these people.

Investigators emphasize there is no cause for alarm: the virus has not been linked to illness, many infected people appear to clear it, and current blood-screening and inactivation methods likely reduce risk. Experts stress more work is needed—particularly development of antibody tests and broader surveillance—to determine how common HHpgV-1 is, whether it circulates now, and if it causes disease. The study also highlights that many previously unknown viruses are present in human blood and that cataloging them is important for transfusion safety. In the same journal issue, the team reported a related discovery: a hepatitis A–like virus in seals (phopivirus), suggesting greater viral diversity and evolutionary complexity than previously recognized.

After U.S. forces killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, reports said a “fairly extensive” collection of pornography—largely modern electronically recorded video—was recovered from the compound. David Covucci, a writer for the men’s website BroBible, filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request to the CIA in late May 2015 seeking details about the pornographic materials found. The CIA replied quickly, declining to release any records. Its response said any responsive records would be part of exempt “operational files” under the CIA Information Act (50 U.S.C. 431) and noted federal law (18 U.S.C. §1461) prohibits mailing obscene matter. Media coverage framed the request as a tongue-in-cheek bid to learn personal details about bin Laden, and commentators noted the agency cited legitimate legal exemptions in refusing to disclose the materials.

Yahoo disclosed in a regulatory filing that new CEO Marissa Mayer’s compensation package is extremely large and largely performance-based, reflecting the board’s bet she can revive the struggling company. Key components:

- Base salary: $1 million.
- Annual bonus: up to 200% of base ($2 million), with potential to reach 400% ($4 million) if targets are exceeded.
- 2012 equity award: $12 million total (about $6M in restricted stock and $6M in options), vesting over three years; similar grants may follow.
- One-time retention award: $30 million total ($15M in stock + $15M in options), vesting over five years.
- Make-whole payment: roughly $14 million to compensate for equity she left behind at Google.

Taken together, Yahoo estimates Mayer will receive about $5.4 million for the remainder of 2012 and roughly $20 million per year afterward, and the company says she could receive up to about $100 million over five years depending on vesting and performance. The package is far larger than what recent Yahoo CEOs received and was debated heavily by the board; reports say activist shareholder Dan Loeb strongly supported the hire and pay. Supporters argue Mayer’s product expertise and ability to attract talent justify the cost; critics noted she had been passed over for higher roles at Google. The announcement drew wide media attention to Yahoo’s high-profile hire as it faces a long-running turnaround challenge.

In 2009 FBI agent James Craig gained a major break in the investigation of the Zeus banking malware when a seized New York–based server proved to be the gang’s Jabber command-and-control hub. Forensics teams copied tens of thousands of Russian- and Ukrainian-language chat logs, giving investigators a near-complete roadmap of the operation: roles, victim lists, money-mule networks and laundering methods. Cybersecurity firm Mandiant and FBI linguists helped parse the logs, which revealed stolen credentials, hundreds of victim institutions, and recruitment of thousands of cash-out “money mules” — many students and recent immigrants in Brighton Beach and other cities instructed to open accounts and withdraw amounts just under reporting thresholds. Mules typically kept 5–10% while most funds were funneled overseas.

The investigation uncovered a multinational fraud ring operating across the U.S. and Europe, responsible for an attributable $70–80 million in thefts (with suspected higher totals). Key operators were linked to eastern Ukraine (Donetsk): “tank” (Vyacheslav Penchukov) as manager, “petr0vich” (Ivan Klepikov) overseeing IT/hosting, and “thehead” (Alexey Bron) handling money movement. The group spent proceeds on luxury cars and vacations.

In 2010 coordinated actions, including raids in Ukraine and seizures of massive data (nearly 20 terabytes), and arrests across four countries disrupted the Jabber Zeus network and produced 39 arrests. However, several leaders escaped capture, including the alleged mastermind known online as “slavik” or “lucky12345” (Evgeniy Mikhailovich Bogachev). Investigators tied Bogachev to Zeus and its later peer-to-peer variant GameOver Zeus (GOZ), blamed for over a million infections and more than $100 million in losses. Bogachev was indicted in U.S. federal courts in 2012 and 2014 on numerous charges including racketeering, bank and computer fraud, identity theft and money laundering. He was last reported living in Anapa and Krasnodar, Russia, and remains at large.

Shaun White, seeking a historic third straight Olympic halfpipe gold at Sochi, fell short and placed fourth after a run marred by several slips, ceding the title to Switzerland’s Iouri Podladtchikov. Podladtchikov landed a flawless Yolo flip (a 1,440-degree trick with two somersaults) to score 94.75 and take gold; 15-year-old Ayumu Hirano earned silver (93.50) and Taku Hiraoka bronze (92.25). It was the first Olympic halfpipe podium without an American since the event began in 1998.

The competition unfolded amid widespread criticism of the Rosa Khutor halfpipe’s condition. Riders reported bumpy transitions and a choppy, uneven flat bottom that forced many to change lines and abandon planned tricks; several competitors, including Americans Danny Davis and Gregory Bretz, fell repeatedly. Organizers worked overnight to reshape and resurface the pipe, but athletes still called it substandard—some urged postponement—though most accepted the shared challenge.

White had withdrawn earlier from the slopestyle event over course concerns to concentrate on the halfpipe; he said he took risks rather than ride conservatively. Competitors and coaches noted the pipe amplified mistakes but maintained the best riders would prevail. Podladtchikov, who emigrated from Russia to Switzerland as a child, expressed emotional satisfaction competing successfully in Sochi. The results indicated a shifting competitive landscape in Olympic halfpipe snowboarding.

The search for Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 shifted to an underwater phase as teams deployed towed pinger locators to try to locate the plane’s black box before its beacon batteries expire. Two ships—Australia’s HMAS Ocean Shield towing a US Navy locator and Britain’s HMS Echo—are sweeping a converging 240 km track in the southern Indian Ocean within an overall search area of roughly 217,000–223,000 sq km about 1,680–1,700 km northwest of Perth. The operation is coordinated from Perth by the Joint Agency Coordination Centre under retired Air Chief Marshal Angus Houston.

Investigators used satellite “handshake” data and aircraft performance analysis to select the area of highest probability for where the aircraft might have entered the water. The black box pingers have an expected battery life of about 30 days, making the search a race against time. The locator must be towed slowly (about three knots) and has limited range, so experts warned it may be ineffective unless the search area is accurate.

Surface searches continued in parallel—up to 14 aircraft and multiple ships were scanning for debris—and several objects have been sighted but none linked to MH370. Additional assets, including Britain’s HMS Tireless submarine and a Malaysian frigate, were being committed. Authorities reiterated that while mechanical failure has not been ruled out, evidence suggests the aircraft was deliberately diverted; investigations have focused on the flight crew. Malaysian and Australian leaders visited search crews, and Malaysia faced criticism over information handling as families and nations await answers. The flight vanished on 8 March en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing with 239 people on board; no confirmed debris or wreckage has been recovered.

Consumer Reports found that supermarket store brands offer substantial savings and comparable quality to name brands. A price study across five chains (283 price quotes for 30 items) showed store brands cost on average 30% less than national brands, with some items as much as 52% cheaper—potentially saving a family spending $100/week more than $1,500 annually. In 21 blind taste comparisons, national brands won seven times, store brands won three times, and the rest were ties; many ties reflected different but equal-quality flavor profiles rather than identical recipes. Nutrition was similar for most products, though a few differences were noted (e.g., Mott’s applesauce higher in sugar than Publix, Ore-Ida fries higher in sodium than Jewel, Kellogg’s Froot Loops had more fiber than Stop & Shop Fruit Swirls).

Despite savings, some consumers—especially those 18–39—remain skeptical of store-brand quality or prefer name brands; nevertheless, 84% of Americans bought store brands in the past year and store brands made up about one-quarter of supermarket sales ($55.5 billion nationally). Store-brand manufacturers sometimes are the same firms that produce national brands, and many grocers offer money-back guarantees. Consumer Reports warns the price gap may be narrowing as national brands lower prices and increase promotions. Full results appeared in the October issue (Sept. 7 online).
