Hundreds of gravestones were vandalized at Mount Carmel Jewish Cemetery in the Wissinoming section of Northeast Philadelphia, with damage discovered just after 9:30 a.m. Sunday. Authorities estimated roughly 300 markers toppled and damaged (other reports put the count around 75–100 or “more than 100”). Volunteers are working to re-erect headstones and a GoFundMe has been started to cover repairs.

Local and national Jewish leaders, victims’ relatives and city officials condemned the act. Naomi Adler of the Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia called it “incredibly disgust[ing]” and noted it evokes Holocaust-era fears whether or not the incident was motivated by antisemitism. Mayor Jim Kenney and Gov. Tom Wolf vowed that perpetrators will be found and prosecuted; state police and homeland security resources were offered to assist.

The vandalism follows a similar recent attack on a Jewish cemetery in suburban St. Louis, and another Philadelphia cemetery in Bridesburg was struck less than two weeks earlier. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

A total reward pool of $69,000 has been pledged for information leading to an arrest and conviction, including donations from the Mizel Family Foundation/Anti-Defamation League ($10,000), an anonymous donor ($10,000), Councilman Allan Domb ($12,000), Mayor Kenney’s office ($15,000) and the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge #5 ($3,000, limited to arrest information). The investigation is ongoing.

At a town hall in Decorah, Iowa, President Obama engaged in a heated exchange with Tea Party activist Ryan Rhodes, who pressed whether Vice President Joe Biden had called Tea Party members “terrorists” during the debt ceiling debates. In public, Obama did not directly confirm the claim; he pushed back at being lectured about rhetoric, noting he has been smeared with labels like “socialist” and “not born here,” and offered to continue the discussion privately. Rhodes later told Fox News Obama denied Biden had made the comment and accused the president of dismissing him.

The dispute traces to a private meeting Biden attended during the debt ceiling fight, where Rep. Mike Doyle reportedly said Tea Party-aligned Republicans had acted like “terrorists.” Some Democrats said Biden appeared to echo that sentiment to rally support for a compromise, but Biden denied using the word in that context to CBS News. At the Iowa event, observers criticized Rhodes’s confrontation as rude and overly aggressive; Rhodes defended his actions, saying he had “said [his] piece.”

Michelle Hurst, who plays Miss Claudette on Netflix’s Orange Is the New Black, has awakened from a medically induced coma after a serious car accident that left her with major injuries and required multiple spinal-area surgeries. She is currently in the ICU at UNC Chapel Hill Hospital and is responsive; her recovery is described as slow but progressing. A fundraising page was created to help cover medical bills and lost income for Hurst and her sister; cast members Natasha Lyonne and Matt McGorry shared the appeal. The campaign quickly surpassed its initial $5,000 goal, raising thousands (reports cite amounts such as $8,684 and $12,256) from hundreds of supporters.

In 2009 James Howells, a UK IT worker, mined about 7,500 bitcoins on a personal laptop. After breaking the laptop up in 2013 and selling many parts, he kept the hard drive but accidentally threw it away during a clean-out; it was buried in Newport, South Wales landfill. With bitcoin prices having since surged, those coins are now worth well over $100 million (roughly $127M at the time of reporting).

Howells knows the landfill and has the public address for the coins (so he can see if they move), but Newport City Council has refused permission to excavate. Officials cite safety, environmental and legal issues—modern landfills are complex, hazardous engineering sites with toxic gases and risks of fires; digging up hundreds of thousands of tonnes of waste would be costly, disruptive and might still not recover a usable drive (corrosion and leachate could have damaged it). The council also notes unauthorized entry would be a criminal offence. Howells says he’s sought permission and backing for a recovery but hasn’t been allowed to proceed; he believes if bitcoin becomes valuable enough the council may reconsider and take a cut.

Howells remains involved in crypto, follows prices and speculates he would have sold some coins earlier to diversify. He also points out the coins are encrypted and would require his cooperation even if the drive were found.

Crawls were performed of the Obama White House website and its subdomains in the months just before the end of the administration (November 2016–January 2017). The crawled content includes an announcement about President Obama launching the official @POTUS Twitter account from the Oval Office (May 18, 2015). That announcement highlights that:
- The @POTUS account is intended as a direct channel for President Obama to engage with the American people, with tweets coming exclusively from him.
- The administration framed this move as part of making the White House more open and participatory.
- The announcement lists other official White House Twitter accounts for the President, Vice President, First Lady, Dr. Jill Biden, live White House coverage, press secretary, senior advisor, communications director, the Spanish-language account, and the Chief Official White House Photographer.
- It notes that location data can be added to tweets and that users can delete their tweet location history.
- It clarifies that the First Lady’s account is run by her office, that her tweets are signed “–mo,” and that tweets may be archived with a link to the White House privacy page.

The material reflects the White House’s social media engagement strategy and relevant privacy/location guidance included on the site.

Michael Clarke Duncan, a towering but gentle character actor best known for his Oscar-nominated turn as death row inmate John Coffey in 1999’s The Green Mile, died at 54 after suffering a heart attack. He died at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center; his fiancée Omarosa Manigault said he had a myocardial infarction on July 13 and never fully recovered.

Duncan — a former bodyguard turned late-blooming actor — combined a formidable 6'4" muscular presence and gravelly baritone with a warm, sweet persona that made him beloved across Hollywood and beyond. His breakout role in The Green Mile, which co-starred Tom Hanks and earned Duncan an Academy Award nomination, led to a prolific film and TV career that included Armageddon, Planet of the Apes, Daredevil, Talladega Nights, The Whole Nine Yards, Sin City, and voice work in animated films such as Kung Fu Panda and Brother Bear. He also appeared on television in shows like The Apprentice, Two and a Half Men and The Finder.

Born in Chicago in 1957 and raised by a single mother, Duncan left college to support his family and later moved to Los Angeles, where he worked as a bodyguard for celebrities before pursuing acting full time. Colleagues and fans, including Tom Hanks and Steve Harvey, expressed shock and sorrow at his passing. In recent years he had embraced vegetarianism and had appeared in a PETA video discussing its health benefits. Funeral and memorial plans were to be announced.

On Nov. 9, 1861, the 288-foot sidewheel steamer Keystone State — then the Great Lakes’ second-largest ship — sank in Lake Huron during the Civil War. Thirty-three crew members died, and the loss spawned long-running rumors that the ship’s manifest (listed as carrying “iron implements” or farm machinery) hid military cargo or gold. The vessel’s disappearance wasn’t noticed immediately; wreckage and the wheelhouse washed ashore more than a week later.

In July (announced Dec. 9), veteran shipwreck hunter David Trotter and his Undersea Research Associates located the Keystone State about 50 miles north of Michigan’s “thumb,” in under 200 feet of water. Trotter — who has found more than 100 wrecks over 35 years — used side-scan sonar and has since made dozens of dives to document the site. The wreck lies farther north than where the ship was last seen off Port Austin, suggesting it fought the storm for some time before sinking. The hull shows significant settling and damage, and the team is still assessing what occurred in the storm, on impact with the lake bottom, and over the subsequent 152 years.

The cargo hold appears empty, which might reflect crew efforts to jettison cargo to save the ship; investigators have found no gold so far, though a substantial debris field remains unexplored. Depth limits divers to roughly 15–20 minutes on the wreck with lengthy decompression times. Trotter continues to document the site to try to resolve remaining questions about the ship’s final voyage.

Two 14-year-old boys, Austin Stephanos and Perry Cohen, went missing after taking a 19-foot, single-engine boat off the Florida coast late last week. The vessel was recovered Sunday about 67 miles off Daytona Beach with no sign of the teens. Families appealed for help searching beaches from Palm Beach to Georgia for debris or clues; they believe the boys may have fashioned flotation from an engine cover, life jackets and a cooler.

Oceanographer Mitch Roffer of Roffer’s Ocean Fishing Forecasting Service analyzed satellite imagery and Gulf Stream currents to help volunteers refine search areas. Roffer warned that small variations in current speed and position—especially relative to the Gulf Stream core—can dramatically change drift trajectories over hours or days, producing differences of tens to over a hundred miles in possible locations. Volunteer pilots have been using his color-coded maps to guide searches from Melbourne and New Smyrna Beach. Local boaters and rescuers emphasized how quickly and unforgivingly the ocean can turn dangerous.

This document is a compilation of tech and political predictions, reactions to 2010 forecasts, and commentary on which predictions did or did not come true. Its main themes:

Overall tech outlook (from several commentators)
- Big companies and leaders: HP’s Mark Hurd did limited media engagement; Microsoft redesigned the Zune but not the phone expected; Apple was seen as the top investment opportunity, with strong expectations for a tablet that would reshape mobile computing at an accessible price; Intel, HP, Cisco, IBM and Oracle were identified as oversold investment opportunities late 2009; AMD’s future looked uncertain despite a settlement with Intel.
- Platforms and business models: SaaS and cloud services were predicted to expand significantly, with new OSes and enterprise/government moves to the cloud. The growth of free software models (open source, freemium, ad-supported) was expected to challenge traditional license-paid software.
- Mobile and social: Smartphones, mobile money (payments via phones), location-based services, and augmented reality were forecast to grow. Social media’s influence on marketing and content consumption was expected to increase, blurring work and personal lines (social features in ERP, “social spaghetti” integration). Real-time services and collaboration (e.g., Google Wave) were highlighted as rising trends.
- Devices and formats: Netbooks, video and video-conferencing usage, and e-readers/digital books (Amazon, Sony, B&N, others) were predicted to have breakout years. 3D TV and 3D production were expected to expand. Tablet PCs were criticized as flawed, but rumors of an Apple tablet generated excitement; later coverage notes the iPad’s strong consumer response. Netbooks were alternately predicted to surge and later judged vulnerable to tablets.
- Content and media: Social networks and user-generated content would proliferate, forcing legacy media to adapt; advertisers and studios would chase mainstream hits while niche content and fragmentation expand. Movie distribution might experiment with earlier on-demand windows. Print media and local newspapers were expected to struggle.
- Predictions about specific services: Some forecasters expected Twitter to fade or be acquired due to lack of revenue, while others predicted its growth. Google Wave was anticipated to find utility; elsewhere it was later criticized for failing to catch on.

PwC Top 10 IT predictions (grounded in momentum)
1. SaaS will expand and challenge desktop apps.
2. Netbooks will sell strongly, perhaps surpassing laptops; webcams will drive personal video.
3. Cloud services will grow with major enterprise/government moves.
4. Mobile payments will begin to emerge in the U.S., with telcos possibly entering banking later.
5. Free software models (open source, freemium, ad-supported) will reach an inflection point.
6. Tools to harvest and interpret social/web data (“web-squared”) will appear.
7. Video usage and infrastructure investment will grow for work and personal use.
8. Green IT will progress unevenly; virtualization and cloud hosting could reduce data-center footprints over time.
9. Location-based services and augmented reality will surge with many startups and some consumer friction.
10. Social features will integrate into enterprise apps, blurring personal/work lines.

Reflections and critique of 2010 predictions
- The document includes examples of prominent 2010 predictions that missed badly: unemployment failing to drop below certain thresholds, forecasts of new dominant social networks, predictions that Twitter would fade, optimistic netbook growth, Google Wave becoming central, and mobile payments becoming mainstream in 2010. It notes that many prognostications proved wrong and that forecasting remains unreliable.
- Commentators from National Review offered political and cultural predictions (e.g., elections, judicial retirements, international events) with a mix of serious and satirical items.

Key takeaways
- 2010 was expected to be a pivotal year for cloud/SaaS, mobile, social integration, and new device categories (tablets, e-readers, 3D TV), with big implications for enterprise IT, media distribution, and consumer behavior.
- Several high-profile predictions (Twitter’s demise, Wave’s rise, netbook dominance) were later proven incorrect, illustrating the difficulty of forecasting fast-moving tech and cultural trends.
- Persistent themes: rapid innovation in Silicon Valley, the growing role of social and real-time services, ongoing shifts in content creation/distribution, and the tension between hype and real adoption.

This document compiles reactions and commentary about President Trump’s public attacks on NFL players who kneel during the national anthem to protest racial injustice and police brutality. Key points:

- Trump urged team owners to fire players who kneel, calling protesting athletes “sons of b-----s” and saying they “disrespect our Flag & Country.” His comments intensified an already heated national debate.
- Critics argue Trump’s approach conflates patriotism with enforced conformity, misuses the presidential bully pulpit, and distracts from substantive issues (health care, Puerto Rico, foreign policy). Many view his rhetoric as polarizing and harmful to civil discourse.
- Supporters of the protests — including players, some owners, coaches and commentators — defended the demonstrations as peaceful, constitutional speech aimed at sparking conversation and reform around racial injustice. Responses included kneeling, linking arms, staying in locker rooms during the anthem, and public statements backing players’ rights.
- Opponents see the protests as disrespectful to the flag and military, blame them for declining NFL ratings, and believe Trump’s stance resonates with many middle-American fans who want politics kept off the field.
- Historic context: The piece invokes West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943) to underscore the principle that government cannot compel ritualized displays of patriotism and that dissenting speech is protected.
- Media and opinion voices frame the clash as part of a broader “culture war,” with Trump using cultural battles to mobilize his base amid stalled legislative goals. Some conservatives praise his intervention as defending national identity; many liberals and centrist commentators condemn it as divisive and undemocratic.

Overall, the texts present the anthem protests and Trump’s reaction as a flashpoint illustrating deep national divides over free speech, patriotism, race, and the proper limits of presidential influence on civil expression.

A 23-year-old man was hospitalized after deliberately stepping into traffic in Clemson, South Carolina, imitating the arcade game "Frogger." Around 9 p.m. Monday at U.S. 76 and College Avenue he yelled "go" and darted into the four-lane highway, where he was struck by a white 2010 Lexus SUV. He was taken to AnMed Health Medical Center in Anderson in stable condition and was expected to be released the following day. Clemson Police Chief Jimmy Dixon said the man, a local resident who is not a Clemson student, had been discussing the video game with two friends before the incident. Alcohol is suspected to have played a role but had not been confirmed pending tests. No charges are expected against the SUV driver; the victim’s name has not been released.

Director David Ayer gave fans the first official look at Jared Leto as the Joker via a Twitter post marking the character’s 75th anniversary. Leto’s version appears striking and menacing, featuring neon green hair, pale skin, silver teeth, red lipstick, a single purple glove, and numerous Joker-themed tattoos—including playing cards, repeated “Ha” text, a toothy grin on his arm, a harlequin skull on his chest, and the word “Damaged” on his forehead. The image previews Leto’s turn as the Clown Prince of Crime in the 2016 film Suicide Squad, which began filming earlier that month and stars Will Smith, Viola Davis, Cara Delevingne, Jai Courtney and Joel Kinnaman. The post coincided with coverage and archiving projects related to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission referenced elsewhere in the document.

A 28-year-old former Marine, Ian David Long, posted messages to social media during his November shooting rampage at the Borderline Bar & Grill in Thousand Oaks, California, law enforcement officials told multiple outlets. Long killed 12 people inside the country-music bar and a Ventura County sheriff’s sergeant before being found dead of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Officials said Long — who served one tour in Afghanistan and had a history of emotional problems and a recent mental-health evaluation — wrote during the attack that he was “bored but sane” and predicted his mental state would be debated. TMZ and other reports said he posted from the scene, possibly holding a phone in one hand and a gun in the other; Facebook later said it removed his accounts from Facebook and Instagram and would remove praise for the crime.

Investigators are still working to determine a motive. They found signs of anger at his home, including punched holes in walls, and learned police had been called there earlier this year for a domestic disturbance. Some reports and a former classmate suggested possible revenge motivations and that Long had PTSD and had been bullied in school; authorities are also examining whether he believed a former girlfriend would be at the bar. President Trump and others pointed to mental illness as a factor, though investigators have not reached conclusions.

The document contains two news items involving White House hospitality and President Barack Obama’s activities.

1) White House stops naming wines served at state dinners
- The Obama White House has ceased the prior practice of publicly listing the specific wines (name, vintage and appellation) served at state dinners. For Obama’s first three state dinners the White House disclosed wine details, but after the Jan. 19, 2011 dinner for Chinese President Hu Jintao — which included a highly rated, expensive 2005 Quilceda Creek Cabernet Sauvignon — subsequent state dinner menus (e.g., for Chancellor Angela Merkel and South Korea’s President Lee Myung-Bak) simply stated that “an American wine will be paired with each course” without naming labels.
- Wine professionals and commentators say the change may reflect political sensitivity amid a weak U.S. economy and concern about appearing to display wealth, but critics argue withholding names undercuts promotion of U.S. vintners and the diplomatic/trade benefits of showcasing American wine in growing markets such as China.
- Wine producers who have had wines served at the White House report meaningful business boosts and prestige from the exposure (e.g., sales in China rose markedly for some producers). The White House declined to comment on the change or to say whether wine names would be released for upcoming dinners. The article notes broader White House efforts toward transparency in other areas, and provides historical context on wine service at the Executive Residence and the tradition of showcasing U.S. wines since Lyndon Johnson.

2) Obama takes UK Prime Minister David Cameron to an NCAA tournament game in Ohio
- During David Cameron’s official U.S. visit, President Obama took him to a “First Four” NCAA tournament game in Dayton, Ohio, both as a goodwill gesture and as a chance to reach sports fans in a key swing state ahead of the 2012 election. Cameron’s first college basketball game, the outing highlighted the “special relationship” and preceded discussions on NATO and the G-8, plus a White House state dinner.
- Obama, a noted basketball fan, also revealed his Final Four picks to ESPN and appeared in a halftime interview. The trip drew criticism from some Republicans as poor timing given domestic economic concerns, but was defended as a useful public-relations move and personal touch during the visit.
- The piece recounts Obama’s long-standing affinity for basketball and mentions other details of the visit, including the presence of Ohio Governor John Kasich and commentary about Cameron’s relative unfamiliarity with the sport.

Esmond Bradley Martin, a 75-year-old American conservationist and former UN special envoy for rhino conservation, was found stabbed to death at his home in Langata, Nairobi. His wife discovered his body; police say he had a neck wound and are treating the case as under investigation, with a possible botched robbery not ruled out.

Bradley Martin was widely respected as a leading investigator of the illegal ivory and rhino-horn trade. Over decades he conducted undercover fieldwork across Africa and Asia—posing as a buyer in China, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and elsewhere—to document markets, traffickers and black‑market prices. His rigorous, often dangerous investigations produced influential reports (many published with Save The Elephants) that helped spur policy changes, including China’s bans on rhino horn in the 1990s and on domestic ivory sales more recently.

Colleagues and conservation organisations paid tribute, calling him a meticulous, fearless researcher whose death is a major loss to efforts against organised wildlife crime. His last work concerned trafficking in Myanmar; he was reportedly writing up findings at the time of his death. The killing has heightened fears about threats to conservationists confronting powerful trafficking networks.

This document reviews and fact-checks many contested claims made by Barack Obama and Mitt Romney during the 2012 campaign and first debate, focusing on taxes, deficits, health care, green-energy loans and Medicare.

Key points:

- Deficit: Romney’s claim that Obama “doubled the deficit” is inaccurate. The 2009 deficit was projected at about $1.2 trillion (it became $1.4 trillion); the 2012 deficit was about $1.1 trillion. Measured as a share of GDP the deficit fell from about 10.1% in 2009 to 7.3% in 2012.

- Romney’s $5 trillion tax-cut claim: Romney proposed cutting all marginal rates by 20%, which independent analysts estimate would reduce revenue by roughly $5 trillion over ten years. He says his plan is revenue-neutral by eliminating deductions and loopholes but has not specified which ones; proposals floated include capping itemized deductions (e.g., $17,000 per household). Tax Policy Center work suggests it’s mathematically unlikely to fully offset the $5 trillion loss without raising taxes on many middle-income households or otherwise changing commitments. Romney argues growth would close any gap.

- Simpson-Bowles and Obama’s deficit plan: Obama claimed his plan echoes Simpson-Bowles, but comparisons show his $4 trillion proposal (spread over a longer period with different assumptions) saves less and lacks some of Simpson-Bowles’ entitlement detail. Independent groups say Obama’s plan achieves roughly two-thirds of Simpson-Bowles’ savings on comparable terms.

- Health-care “takeover” claim: Romney’s assertion that the Affordable Care Act represents a federal “takeover” is overstated. The law expands federal roles—Medicaid expansion and subsidies for private insurance mean more people gain government-supported coverage—but it still relies heavily on private insurers. CBO and actuary projections show government health spending rising but not entirely replacing private coverage. The individual mandate (requiring most to have “government-approved” insurance or pay a penalty) was central to the Supreme Court decision upholding the law.

- Green-energy loan guarantees: Romney said half the companies backed by Obama’s green-energy stimulus have failed. That overstates the situation: of about three dozen Department of Energy loan-guarantee recipients, only three were in bankruptcy at the time, though several faced difficulties. Campaign contributors invested in some recipients, but contributions were not limited to Obama supporters.

- Medicare $716 billion cuts: Romney repeated the claim that Obama “cut $716 billion from Medicare” to pay for Obamacare. Fact-checkers explain the reductions were cuts to payments to providers and plans—not cuts to beneficiary benefits—and included expanded benefits like preventive care and drug coverage improvements. The reductions extended the Medicare trust fund’s solvency by several years. Restoring those payments, as Romney advocated, would likely raise beneficiaries’ premiums and hasten trust-fund insolvency. Critics note Romney/Ryan plans included similar provider-payment cuts in past budgets.

- “Small business” definition and Romney’s tax plan: Obama’s line that Romney would treat millionaires and billionaires as “small businesses” reflects how pass-through income is taxed; the federal definition of a small business (for some programs) is an employer with fewer than 500 employees. Some Trump companies would qualify. Analyses show much of the benefit of extending high-income tax cuts would flow to the very wealthy; Romney’s plan aimed to lower taxes broadly for individuals and businesses rather than targeting only small firms.

Overall, the piece underscores that many campaign claims involved accurate kernels framed with misleading emphasis or omitted context. Independent analyses frequently found Romney’s tax math optimistic or incomplete and found Republican attacks on the Affordable Care Act and green-energy loans overstated.

A 55-year-old New Jersey woman, Denise Simien of Verona, was arrested by Port Authority Police after allegedly accumulating more than $16,600 in unpaid EZ Pass tolls. Authorities say she failed to pay tolls at Port Authority crossings on more than 250 occasions. When officers sought to stop her Wednesday while she was driving a 2007 Toyota SUV, she initially ignored police directions and was later pulled over by another Port Authority officer near the Holland Tunnel entrance. Simien was charged with theft of services and obstruction of justice and is due in Jersey City Court on July 19.

(The notice following the report describes an Internet Archive effort to crawl and preserve web pages—creating archived copies to prevent broken links and maintain references to the original versions.)

A mystery human killer has been terrorizing the small north Brittany coastal village of Minihy-Tréguier by repeatedly murdering pet rabbits. Since March, more than 100 rabbits across about 15 separate incidents have been found beaten or crushed to death after their hutches were opened. Attacks have come in waves (March, August, and again most recently), and the perpetrator sometimes returns to the same sites. Victims are typically elderly residents who keep rabbits in garden hutches—chickens and geese have not been touched—which has led locals to fear the killer is watching properties and knows the area well. Local police in Côtes-d’Armor are treating the cases as deliberate acts of cruelty by a human rather than animal predation, have launched a hunt, and have appealed for witnesses. The mayor says the village of 1,300 is "gripped by fear."

Summary:

In November 2018 Ohio authorities arrested four members of the Wagner family—Angela Wagner (48), her husband George “Billy” Wagner (47), and their sons George Wagner IV (27) and Edward “Jake” Wagner (26)—in connection with the April 22, 2016 massacre that killed eight members of the Rhoden family in Pike County. Prosecutors allege the killings were carefully planned over months and tied to an “obsession with custody and control of children,” centering on 4-year-old Sophia Wagner, the daughter of Jake Wagner and victim Hanna Rhoden. Most victims were shot in their homes while asleep; some showed multiple gunshot wounds and bruising. Authorities say the Wagners studied the victims’ routines, purchased items (including materials to collect casings and possibly build silencers) and forged custody documents to keep Sophia; two women—Rita Newcomb and Fredericka Wagner, mothers of Angela and Billy—were also arrested separately on charges related to forging custody papers.

The indictment includes aggravated murder (potential death-penalty exposure) plus charges of conspiracy, racketeering, evidence tampering, unlawful weapons possession, forgery, wire interception, obstruction and aggravated burglary. Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine and Pike County Sheriff Charles Reader said investigators logged tens of thousands of hours, followed more than 1,100 tips and conducted hundreds of interviews to reach the arrests. Officials dismissed theories that the killings were drug-related and said they do not believe others were involved.

The Wagners had moved to Alaska in 2017 but returned to Ohio in spring 2018; defense attorney John Kearson Clark has maintained their innocence and said they cooperated with investigators. Trials are planned for Pike County, though defense motions for a change of venue are possible and capital-case qualifications for defense counsel complicate timing.

Background and aftermath: The victims included Christopher Rhoden Sr., his ex-wife Dana, their children Clarence “Frankie,” Hanna and Christopher Jr., plus Kenneth Rhoden, cousin Gary Rhoden and Hannah Gilley. Several young children survived unharmed, including Sophia and two other toddlers. Jake Wagner, Sophia’s father, has been caring for her full-time, won custody and set up a GoFundMe to cover steep legal costs. Authorities continue to seek tips; a reward has been offered for information leading to conviction.

Researchers in Brazil have published the first clinical test suggesting ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian plant brew with psychedelic properties, may rapidly reduce depressive symptoms. In a very small pilot study, six volunteers with depression unresponsive to at least one conventional antidepressant received a single mild dose of ayahuasca and were monitored in a quiet setting. Measured reductions in depression were seen within two to three hours and remained statistically significant at follow-up up to three weeks later. Side effects were limited (three participants vomited); no serious adverse events were reported.

The study is preliminary and limited by its tiny sample size and lack of a placebo control, so results must be interpreted with caution. Commentators note that placebo effects are common in antidepressant trials and that the only firm conclusions are tolerability and absence of immediate serious harm in this small group. Biochemically, ayahuasca’s constituents—DMT and beta-carbolines (harmine, harmaline, tetrahydroharmine)—affect serotonin signaling and monoamine metabolism, providing a plausible mechanism for antidepressant effects similar to other serotonergic psychedelics.

The work fits into a broader resurgence of interest in psychedelic compounds (psilocybin, MDMA, ketamine, LSD) for psychiatric uses. Larger, better-controlled trials are already underway in Brazil (an 80-person randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was reported to be in progress), and more rigorous studies are needed to assess efficacy, safety, and which patient groups might benefit.

Background: While nut consumption has been linked to lower mortality, evidence about effects on causes of death beyond cardiovascular disease and the dose–response pattern has been limited. This report combines results from the Netherlands Cohort Study (1986–1996) with meta-analyses of prior cohort studies to examine relationships between intake of nuts (tree nuts and peanuts), peanut butter, and overall and cause-specific mortality.

Methods: The Netherlands Cohort Study enrolled 120,852 men and women aged 55–69 in 1986. Diet and lifestyle were assessed at baseline. Mortality follow-up through 1996 used linkage to national death records. Multivariable case–cohort analyses used 8,823 deaths and 3,202 subcohort members with complete data. The authors also pooled their findings with other cohort studies in meta-analyses.

Key findings:
- Total nut intake was associated with lower overall mortality and lower cause-specific mortality from cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, neurodegenerative disease, and other causes in both men and women.
- Compared with non-consumers, multivariable hazard ratios (HRs) for total mortality were 0.88 for 0.1–<5 g/day, 0.74 for 5–<10 g/day, and 0.77 for ≥10 g/day (trend P = 0.003). The largest reductions for ≥10 g/day versus none ranged from HR ≈0.56 for neurodegenerative disease to HR ≈0.83 for cardiovascular mortality.
- Dose–response analyses using restricted cubic splines indicated nonlinear relationships; substantial risk reductions were already apparent at relatively low intakes (around half a handful, ~15 g/day), with little additional benefit at higher intakes.
- Both peanuts and tree nuts were inversely associated with mortality; peanut butter showed no association with mortality.
- Meta-analyses combining this study with prior cohorts found pooled HRs for highest versus lowest nut consumption of 0.85 for cancer mortality and 0.71 for respiratory mortality.

Interpretation and possible mechanisms: Nuts and peanuts contain monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, fiber, vitamins, antioxidants, and other bioactive compounds that plausibly reduce risks of chronic diseases. The lack of benefit for peanut butter may reflect added ingredients (salt, vegetable oils) and historically present trans fats that could negate peanuts’ protective effects.

Conclusion: Regular consumption of nuts and peanuts is associated with lower overall and several cause-specific mortality risks, with evidence of a nonlinear dose–response where modest daily intakes yield most of the benefit. Peanut butter was not associated with reduced mortality.

Five teenagers in Cocoa, Florida, will face misdemeanor charges for failing to report a death after they filmed and mocked 31-year-old Jamel Dunn as he drowned in a pond on July 7, police said. Cocoa Police Chief Michael Cantaloupe announced the decision after lengthy consultation with the State Attorney’s Office; the department is using Florida Statute 406.12—which requires anyone aware of a death to notify the district medical examiner—to bring charges. Cantaloupe said the statute is typically applied to medical examiners and believes this application may be a test case.

Video recorded by the teens (ages reported between about 14 and 16) shows Dunn struggling in the water while the group stood on the bank laughing and refusing to help; Dunn subsequently went under and died. Police said surveillance footage shows Dunn voluntarily entering the pond. Investigators are sending charging documents, the case report and evidence to the State Attorney’s Office, which will decide whether to prosecute.

The decision follows initial statements that no criminal charges would apply because Florida law does not generally require bystanders to render aid. Officials and the victim’s family urged legislative change and greater moral education for youth. Local leaders condemned the teens’ behavior as inhumane; the family’s reaction expressed hope the charges hold and that new laws prevent similar tragedies.

Students and community members gathered at a candlelight vigil on the University of Iowa campus to honor 20-year-old Mollie Tibbetts, whose body was found after she disappeared July 18. Hundreds attended the short, student-organized event at Hubbard Park, where speakers— including Mollie’s brother Jake—urged people to remember her by doing small acts of kindness, making new friends, and celebrating how she lived rather than focusing on the crime. Classmates recounted her warmth, smile, advocacy for mental health and ability to make others feel welcome; student leaders reminded those struggling to use campus support resources.

The man charged in her killing, 24-year-old Cristhian Bahena Rivera, once worked at Yarrabee Farms near Brooklyn, Iowa. The Lang family, who own the multi‑generation farm, said Rivera had been employed there for about four years under a different name and with identification and a Social Security number that initially checked out through the Social Security Administration’s verification system. Rivera reportedly lived on the property and worked with the cows; his defense lawyer says Rivera may have come to the U.S. as a minor and has no prior criminal record. Rivera led investigators to a body believed to be Tibbetts and has been charged with first‑degree murder; he was held on a $5 million cash-only bond and faces potential life imprisonment if convicted. An ICE detainer was also lodged while his immigration status remains uncertain.

The farm and its owners have faced backlash and threats since Rivera’s arrest; they say they are cooperating with investigators and are consulting legal counsel about employment verification moving forward. The case has drawn national attention and sparked debate about immigration, even as local leaders and Mollie’s family ask the public to focus on community support and the positive responses that followed her disappearance.

Three people were killed and several others wounded in a shooting at the Moscow Regional Court on Tuesday when five handcuffed defendants seized sidearms from two escorting guards and attempted to flee.

According to the Investigative Committee and news agencies, the five were in an elevator being moved to a hearing in the trial of a nine‑person gang—nicknamed in Russian media the “Grand Theft Auto gang”—accused of a 2014 crime spree that terrorized Moscow motorists. Prosecutors say the group, made up of men from Central Asia, is charged with banditry, 17 murders and other grave crimes; authorities say they placed spikes on roads, forced drivers from their cars and in many cases shot them. Russian national guard officers shot dead three of the defendants when the elevator doors opened on the third floor; two other defendants were seriously wounded. Three law‑enforcement officers were also injured, one by gunfire. State TV reported one accused had previously fought for ISIS in Syria. Investigations are underway.

A strong earthquake struck near Japan’s Ryukyu/Okinawa Islands early Saturday, centered about 10 km deep and roughly 50–85 km east of Okinawa’s capital, Naha. Magnitude estimates ranged from 6.9 (Japan Meteorological Agency) to 7.0–7.3 (USGS). Shaking lasted about 10–15 seconds and was widely felt across Okinawa; residents described it as the strongest some had experienced, but there were no immediate reports of injuries or significant damage.

A tsunami advisory/warning for the Okinawa, Amami and Tokara island areas — initially warning of waves up to about 2 meters — was issued then later canceled; authorities said there was no tsunami damage, though minor sea-level changes could continue. Local officials, emergency services and an oil refinery reported no major problems. About 20,000 U.S. military personnel stationed on Okinawa were being checked for impacts; no reports of harm from bases were reported in the immediate aftermath.

A small, niche social network called Out Military (outmilitary.com) launched in the wake of President Obama signing the law repealing the U.S. military's "don't ask, don't tell" policy. Designed as a Facebook‑style site for gay and lesbian service members and supporters, it aims to provide a platform for making friends, forming networks, and offering support — including for veterans who experienced abuse. Creator and web designer John McKinnon of Bangor, Maine built the site after following the repeal debate and thinks a dedicated network is a natural fit. Launched just over a week earlier, the site had 53 members at the time of reporting; McKinnon encourages signups but advises caution about posting revealing information until the military finalizes implementation rules and sets an effective date.

A 20-year-old man, Emanuel A. Lopes of Brockton, is expected to be arraigned on murder charges after authorities say he killed Weymouth police Officer Michael Chesna and 77-year-old Vera Adams. Lopes, who remained hospitalized with a gunshot wound to his leg and was not medically available for an earlier arraignment, may be arraigned in his hospital bed or in court.

According to Norfolk District Attorney Michael Morrissey, officers were responding to a report of erratic driving when they found a crashed BMW. While Officer Chesna was trying to locate the driver, he allegedly spotted Lopes vandalizing a home. Prosecutors say Lopes struck Chesna in the head with a large rock, took the officer’s service weapon, and fatally shot him in the head and chest. Another officer wounded Lopes in the leg; Lopes then ran and, after seeing Vera Adams through her sliding glass door, allegedly shot and killed her. Police initially described Adams as a crossfire victim but later said she was intentionally shot by Lopes.

Chesna, 42, a six-year-veteran and Iraq/Afghanistan veteran, leaves a wife and two young children. He was posthumously promoted to sergeant on the sixth anniversary of his hiring; a procession and vigil were held in his and Adams’s honor. The Weymouth police set up a fund for Chesna’s family and warned of scam calls soliciting donations.

Lopes has a criminal history and documented struggles with substance abuse and mental health. He had been arrested in 2017 on charges of selling cocaine to a minor and resisting arrest, was released on pretrial probation with conditions including random drug testing, and had been free on $500 bail since November. Court records list him as homeless at times; he entered addiction treatment late last year. He previously was arrested for property damage after allegedly throwing a rock through a bedroom window. His mother obtained a restraining order against him last year, citing severe mental health issues and fear of his behavior.

Charges against Lopes include two counts of first-degree murder, illegal possession of a firearm, destruction of property, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, and leaving the scene of an accident.

Several recent headlines claimed “some beards contain more poo than a toilet,” but that sensational claim is misleading. The story originated from a TV-news segment in New Mexico where a reporter swabbed a small handful of men’s beards and sent the swabs to a microbiologist, John Golobic, who cultured bacteria and identified some enteric (gut-associated) species. Golobic commented that those types of bacteria are the kinds you’d find in feces and recommended beard washing and hand hygiene. Media outlets extrapolated this into “poo in beards.”

There was no large, peer‑reviewed study behind the headlines — just a tiny, informal sampling and an expert noting gut-associated bacteria were present. Finding such bacteria on skin or facial hair is not the same as finding feces, and human skin commonly hosts a wide variety of microbes, including occasional gut bacteria like E. coli. Proper scientific studies are limited but give mixed results: a small Anaesthesia study found bearded men shed more bacteria than clean‑shaven men (10 per group), while a Journal of Hospital Infection study found beards were associated with lower carriage of Staphylococcus aureus and antibiotic‑resistant strains but still greater shedding — underscoring that everyone should use appropriate face coverings in sterile settings.

Bottom line: the viral headlines overstate the evidence — there’s no proof beards literally contain “more poo than a toilet,” though good beard hygiene and hand‑washing are sensible.

The Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association (TSSAA) removed Riverdale and Smyrna high school girls basketball teams from the postseason, fined each program $1,500, and placed both on restrictive probation for the rest of this school year and the 2015–16 school year after a referee’s report said players from both teams intentionally tried to lose their District 7-AAA consolation game. The game, held at Riverdale Saturday, ended 55-29 for Smyrna.

The referee reported intentional missed free throws, deliberate violations (stalling past half-court, seeking three-second calls, and nearly shooting at the wrong basket), and ultimately convened the coaches, saying officials would not allow a “travesty or mockery of the game.” TSSAA executive director Bernard Childress said the players “bought into it” and the conduct undermined the educational values of high school athletics.

Both schools’ principals met with the TSSAA and apologized; they requested the teams be allowed to continue in the postseason if coaches were removed, but the association declined. Riverdale principal Tom Nolan is suspending coach Cory Barrett for the first two games of 2015–16; Smyrna’s principal Rick Powell said he and district officials are considering discipline for coach Shawn Middleton. Tullahoma and Lawrence County advanced in the region bracket without playing the affected teams. Riverdale and Smyrna were criticized for trying to manipulate bracket placement to avoid top-ranked Blackman.

Sen. Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican often criticized by conservatives for working with Democrats, publicly proposed a compromise to break the stalemate over Guantanamo Bay and the trials of alleged 9/11 conspirators. Graham offered to pressure Republicans to support closing Guantanamo if the Obama administration agreed to try Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and four co-defendants in military tribunals rather than in a civilian New York court. He also called for a new, consistent legal framework—a “national security court”—to govern detention and trial of top terrorism suspects, arguing the current patchwork approach leaves federal judges improvising rules.

Graham’s proposal drew sharp rebukes all week from figures across the right — Sen. James Inhofe, conservative websites, Glenn Beck and Rep. Pete Hoekstra — who accused him of betraying GOP principles or enabling Obama. Graham defended his stance as principled pragmatism, saying he prioritizes doing what’s right over pleasing partisan purists and lamenting that ideological purity has overtaken compromise in both parties.

The context: Obama promised to close Guantanamo but has faced strong opposition after missing deadlines and after Attorney General Eric Holder recommended civilian trials for some detainees, including KSM. Graham’s plan is presented as a potential way for the White House to regain momentum: swap military tribunals for congressional cooperation on closing Gitmo, then jointly create a coherent legal regime for handling future terrorism cases. The White House was reviewing Holder’s recommendation and had made no final decision. The debate has intensified tensions on both sides, with liberal groups warning that abandoning civilian trials would repeat Bush-era policies.

Freud long argued that many adult dreams express erotic wishes, and modern research supports a strong link between dreaming and sexual content. Kinsey Institute data show sexual dreams are common: 70% of women and nearly all men report overtly sexual dreams; 37% of women had orgasms from sex dreams by age 45, and 5% first orgasmed via a dream. A 2019 study in Dreaming (Sleep and Hypnosis) surveyed 670 students about sleep position and dream content and found those who frequently sleep on their stomach with arms raised were more likely to report sexual dreams and related themes (e.g., being tied up, immobility, locked up); the single most common theme was erotomania (believing one has a secret admirer). Researchers suggest physical pressure on the genitals and other external stimuli during prone sleep are incorporated into dream content. Note: stomach-sleeping can increase back pain by compressing the spine, so any potential increase in erotic dreams comes with sleep-health trade-offs.

A Russian researcher at the Bellingshausen Antarctic station on King George Island, Sergey Savitsky, has been charged with attempted murder for allegedly stabbing a colleague on October 9. Interfax reports Savitsky stabbed the unnamed victim at least once in the station dining room, then surrendered to the station manager without resistance. The injured man was evacuated to a hospital in Chile. Savitsky has been placed under house arrest at the base until December 8 and is reportedly cooperating with investigators. Sources suggest the attack may have followed an emotional breakdown after the two men had lived in close quarters for more than six months. The Bellingshausen station, established by the Soviet Union in 1968, is a Russian research facility on King George Island where Russian jurisdiction applies; further court dates have not been announced.

Global markets opened 2016 with a sharp selloff after weak Chinese economic data and heightened Saudi-Iran tensions rekindled fears of slowing global growth. China’s Shanghai Composite plunged nearly 7%, triggering a newly introduced circuit-breaker and halting mainland trading; the rout spread to Europe and the U.S.

U.S. indexes fell steeply: the S&P 500 dropped 1.5% (about 31 points) — its worst New Year start in over a decade — the Dow lost roughly 276 points (about 1.6%), and the Nasdaq slid about 2.1%. All 10 S&P sectors closed lower, with financials, health care and consumer discretionary among the hardest hit. Investors moved into havens, sending gold to two-week highs and Treasuries higher.

Drivers cited include the weak Chinese manufacturing reading, concerns that China’s true growth may be far below official figures, and market mechanics like the circuit-breaker that may have amplified selling. Middle East geopolitical strains after Saudi Arabia severed ties with Iran added to volatility and briefly lifted oil prices. U.S. economic releases showed weakness too: ISM manufacturing fell to 48.2 (the lowest since the end of the recession) and construction spending declined 0.4% in November.

Notable stock moves: Baxalta jumped on takeover talk; Tesla plunged after delivery figures; Netflix and Amazon fell after downgrades. European markets tumbled (Germany’s DAX off more than 4%). The DOJ also sued Volkswagen over emissions-cheating devices, adding another corporate headline to the news flow. Analysts warned that orderly but heightened volatility could persist through 2016.

Piers Morgan discussed his contentious CNN interview with Alex Jones, calling Jones “the best advertisement for gun control” because of the interview’s “vitriol, hatred, and zealotry.” Morgan said Jones — a shock-jock radio host and founder of InfoWars and PrisonPlanet — launched into a long, rancorous rant about gun control, a 1776-style rebellion, and conspiracy theories (including 9/11 being an inside job), continuing even through a commercial break. Morgan said he knew Jones’ reputation but booked him because of Jones’ wide reach on radio and online and his ability to influence and stoke fear among millions of followers, which Morgan described as dangerous.

Morgan also addressed the “Deport Piers Morgan” petition Jones created (over 100,000 signatures) and welcomed a White House response stressing free expression. He defended his continued advocacy for gun-control coverage, saying the nation too quickly returns to normal after shootings and politicians fail to act.

Separately, after the interview Jones posted a YouTube video claiming he’d been threatened by a plainclothes NYPD officer before entering CNN and alleging New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s involvement in intimidation and mafia-style activity. Jones said CNN producers canceled a planned third segment, expressed fear for his safety, and portrayed the city as corrupt and dangerous.

Publisher Michael Joseph (an imprint of Penguin) has signed Pippa Middleton, the Duchess of Cambridge’s younger sister, to a reported £400,000 deal for her first book after a competitive auction involving major houses such as HarperCollins and Cornerstone. Industry sources say timing was a sensitive negotiation point: Middleton has agreed to delay publication until after next summer’s Queen’s Diamond Jubilee to avoid any appearance of profiting from her royal connections, with a likely late-autumn release aimed at the Christmas market.

The book will be a party-hosting guide—recipes, anecdotes and practical advice—drawing on Middleton’s experience working as a professional party planner at Table Talk and contributions to her family’s Party Pieces newsletter. Her agent David Godwin (DGA) secured the substantial advance, signalling publishers’ expectations of strong sales. Michael Joseph is known for commercial bestsellers and lists authors such as Jamie Oliver and Jeremy Clarkson. A Michael Joseph spokesperson was unavailable for comment.

The document also includes a critical, opinionated piece questioning whether Middleton’s celebrity rather than expertise justifies the large advance and noting public sensitivity about lucrative deals in a weak economy.

A woman was killed Saturday evening after being struck by a Union Pacific steam locomotive while photographing it near Henderson, a northern Denver suburb. The southbound "Denver Post Special"—a 15- to 21-car excursion pulled by historic Locomotive 844 returning from Cheyenne Frontier Days—hit the pedestrian at about 7:45 p.m. at the 124th Avenue crossing. She was one of several people taking pictures; her name has not been released. About 700 passengers were aboard the annual, Denver Post–sponsored trip; no other injuries were reported and passengers were bused back to Denver. Union Pacific is assisting local authorities as it and law enforcement investigate the incident. Locomotive 844 is a well-known preserved steam engine frequently used on excursion runs.

U.S. investigators are re-examining intercepted 2015 conversations in which Russian officials discussed associates of Donald Trump, prompted by revelations that Donald Trump Jr. met in June 2016 with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya. Some intercepted discussions referred to meetings outside the U.S. involving Russian officials and Trump business associates or advisers. Trump Jr. released emails showing he agreed to the meeting after being told the lawyer had damaging information on Hillary Clinton; he says the meeting produced no useful Clinton material and instead focused on a U.S.-Russia diplomatic dispute. Around the same time, hacked Democratic emails—later tied by investigators to Russian actors—were publicly released.

President Trump said he only learned of his son’s meeting days ago and did not fault him, calling the decision understandable in a fast-moving campaign. He reiterated that there was no collusion between his campaign and Russia and described the allegations as a Democratic “hoax.” Trump also said he raised Russian election meddling directly with President Vladimir Putin and received denials, but he acknowledged something occurred that must be investigated. The disclosures add to scrutiny of the campaign’s contacts with Russians amid earlier controversies over Trump’s positions favorable to Russia and the Republican platform’s removal of a plank calling for arming Ukraine. White House spokespeople dismissed the coverage as overblown.

Chris Brown was arrested Friday on a probation-warrant and ordered Monday to remain jailed until April 23 after a judge cited his "inability to stay out of trouble." Authorities have not officially detailed the probation violation, but media reports (TMZ) say he was expelled from a Malibu rehab facility for breaching three internal rules.

Reported violations include:
- Breaking a special rule imposed on him requiring he stay at least two feet from other women (allegedly touching a woman’s elbow/hand).
- Leaving on an unauthorized outing then initially refusing a random drug test (he later took it and tested negative).
- Disruptive behavior in a group session, making harsh comments.

Background: In November Brown was ordered to 90 days in a residential facility for anger-management issues after an incident involving throwing a rock through his mother’s car window. He spent two weeks in rehab in early October after an arrest in Washington, D.C., for allegedly assaulting a 20-year-old man; a separate D.C. criminal case is pending with a court date April 17. Court filings from the Malibu facility have said Brown has PTSD and bipolar disorder. His probation had been set to end in August but still includes about 750 community service hours; additional penalties or extensions are possible if he fails to complete required rehab.

This document combines three unrelated items about web archiving and R.L. Stine’s Twitter activity.

1) Web archiving efforts
- The Internet Archive and related projects crawl and archive web pages as they are created and the pages they reference, preserving the versions live when a page was written. The aim is to prevent broken links by providing archived replacements or companion links, with an ambitious goal of fixing broken links across the web.
- The Wisconsin Historical Society collects archived websites of Wisconsin state government agencies, boards, commissions, projects, some interstate agencies related to Wisconsin, and major social media pages of the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and First Lady. “Date” in site descriptions indicates when archiving began; “Coverage” indicates the dates of material present on the site. Internal links are typically captured; external links generally are not. Further navigation and crawl-frequency details are available on the WHS “FAQs About the Wisconsin Historical Society Web Archives” page.

2) R.L. Stine on Twitter
- Horror writer R.L. Stine announced on October 28, 2014, that he would write a new scary story live on Twitter for Halloween, though he did not share specifics. Stine, creator of Goosebumps and Fear Street, continues to publish and has a large Twitter following (130,000+). He has previously posted short spooky stories in tweet-sized installments (e.g., a 13-tweet farmer/ghost tale and a 9-tweet haunted kitchen story). He was also scheduled to take over Scholastic’s Twitter feed for a Halloween Q&A following the event.

A 2-year-old Wichita boy who was found not breathing Tuesday night has been upgraded to “good” condition and shows no current signs of long‑term brain injury, police said Thursday. Emergency crews were called about 9:30 p.m. to a home in the 4900 block of East Waterman after the child’s 36‑year‑old boyfriend was performing CPR; the boy was taken to a hospital in critical condition. Doctors removed a small, dead octopus—about 2 inches across at the head—lodged in the child’s throat; police say the octopus was not a pet and was likely intended for sushi. The child also had minor facial injuries.

Inconsistencies between the boyfriend’s accounts and the medical evidence prompted police to notify child‑protection investigators. The boyfriend, identified in records as Matthew Gallagher, was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of child abuse and later bonded out. The Wichita Police Department’s Exploited and Missing Child Unit is continuing its investigation and plans a specialist to interview the young child as part of the inquiry.

WalletHub analyzed identity-theft and fraud risk across the 50 U.S. states and DC using 10 metrics in three dimensions — Identity Theft, Fraud and Policy — to identify where consumers are most vulnerable. Data sources included the FTC, IC3, FBI, DHS, Experian and the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Key context
- Data breaches have been widespread for years: the Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) reported 9,395 breaches from Jan 1, 2005 to Aug 31, 2018, exposing over 1.1 billion records. Breach methods tracked by ITRC include hacking, insider theft, physical theft, employee error, accidental web exposure and unauthorized access.
- Governments and businesses have stepped up cybersecurity efforts, but threats and criminal sophistication continue to grow.

Top findings from WalletHub ranking
- Most vulnerable overall (No. 1 = most vulnerable): Nevada, followed by Florida, New Jersey, Delaware and California. The full ranking lists all 50 states plus DC by a composite score derived from per-capita complaint rates, loss amounts, arrests, e-commerce attack rates and state policies.
- The study scores states separately on Identity-Theft metrics (complaints per capita; average loss per online identity-theft complaint), Fraud metrics (fraud complaints per capita; median loss; persons arrested for fraud per capita; e-commerce attack rates) and Policy metrics (presence of minors’ credit security-freeze laws, identity-theft passport programs, REAL ID compliance and data disposal laws).

Consumer protection tips (WalletHub)
- Secure your primary email strongly and enable two-step verification, since it’s central to account recovery.
- Use credit monitoring to detect suspicious changes (WalletHub offers free TransUnion monitoring).
- Keep financial account contact info current and enable alerts for changes or suspicious activity.
- Practice safe online habits: avoid unknown emails/attachments, don’t send sensitive data via unsecured channels, and use sites with HTTPS.

Expert panel topics
- WalletHub consulted cybersecurity and policy experts about protecting individuals, evaluating third-party identity-protection services, Social Security number protections and changes, social media’s role in identity theft, federal processes for victims to clear their names, and regular security testing and oversight of credit bureaus.

Methodology highlights
- Each metric was scored 0–100 (100 = most vulnerable); weighted totals produced state rankings. Identity Theft and Fraud dimensions each comprised 47.5 points; Policy comprised 5 points.
- Policy metrics were binary presence/absence measures for certain consumer protections and compliance standards.

Bottom line
Data breaches and identity crimes remain pervasive and evolving. WalletHub’s state-by-state ranking identifies regions where residents face the highest measured exposure and loss from identity theft and fraud, while offering practical steps and policy considerations to reduce individual and systemic vulnerability.

A Chilean mother, Sindy Melany Ortiz, says staff at Las Higueras hospital in Talcahuano are limiting her access to her newborn after she admitted smoking marijuana days before giving birth. Ortiz, who says she used cannabis on a doctor's advice to relieve arm pain and is not a regular user, reports she can see her baby only two hours a day and is not being allowed to breast‑feed. Hospital officials say they followed protocol after tests detected substances that might endanger the infant and alerted a local court. The court has ordered the baby to remain at the hospital pending a hearing. The case unfolds amid broader debate in Chile over marijuana law reform: a bill that would decriminalize limited personal possession and cultivation and ease access for medicinal users has passed a committee and is moving through Congress.

New research presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2016 examined the link between weight cycling (repeatedly losing and regaining weight, aka yo‑yo dieting) and heart‑disease mortality among postmenopausal women.

Study design and findings
- Researchers analyzed self‑reported weight histories from 158,063 postmenopausal women, classifying them as stable weight, steady gain, maintained weight loss, or weight cycling, then followed outcomes for a mean 11.4 years.
- Among women who were normal weight at baseline, those who experienced weight cycling had substantially higher cardiac mortality: about 3.5 times the risk of sudden cardiac death and a 66% higher risk of coronary heart disease death compared with women whose weight remained stable.
- No increased cardiac death risk was observed for overweight or obese women who weight‑cycled, nor for women who only gained weight or only lost weight without regaining it.

Limitations and implications
- The study is observational and cannot prove causation. It relied on self‑reported weight history and involved relatively few sudden cardiac deaths, so chance and reporting error are possible.
- Results apply only to older, postmenopausal women; findings may not generalize to men or younger women.
- Authors call for further research before changing clinical recommendations.

Public‑health context
- Obesity is common in the U.S. and a known risk factor for heart disease. Until more is known about the risks of weight cycling, clinicians and the public are advised to follow standard heart‑health guidance (manage blood pressure and cholesterol, control blood sugar, be active, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and avoid smoking).

Former Massachusetts governor Mitt Romney announced he will not participate in the December 27 debate proposed to be moderated by Donald Trump. Speaking to Fox News’ Neil Cavuto, Romney said he has already committed to two other December debates and needs the rest of the month to campaign in early primary states (Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina, Florida). He told Cavuto he relayed this to Trump by phone, who understood and wished him well. The piece notes that Ron Paul and Jon Huntsman also declined the Trump-moderated event, while Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum have confirmed they will attend.

Anonymous, the international hacktivist collective, has intensified an online campaign against ISIS following the Paris attacks. Declaring “war” on the group, Anonymous has been compiling and posting lists of suspected ISIS-linked Twitter accounts, websites and alleged personal details—including names and physical addresses—aiming to have accounts removed and sites taken down. The collective says it has already shut down thousands of accounts (claims vary across reports from hundreds to tens of thousands) and taken down numerous websites, using DDoS attacks and other hacking techniques.

Anonymous launched similar efforts after the Charlie Hebdo attacks in January under #OpISIS and has since escalated operations with a declared #OpParis, organizing teams for intelligence gathering and dissemination. Its high-profile video threatening “the biggest ever” operation has drawn millions of views.

Security analysts and some former hacktivists warn this vigilante approach has limits and risks: ISIS supporters can quickly re-establish online presences or use encrypted channels, and uncoordinated takedowns can hinder official investigations. A splinter group, Ghost Security Group, has sought to cooperate with governments and has had some success passing actionable intelligence to authorities.

ISIS has publicly mocked Anonymous and posted guidance for supporters on how to avoid being hacked or tracked, advising operational security measures such as changing locations, avoiding suspicious links and not reusing email/usernames.

Independent verification of the personal data leaked by Anonymous is limited, and the group has previously misidentified people, so observers caution against treating all published information as accurate.

An analysis of financial-disclosure records shows that in the decade after leaving the White House (2001–2010), former President Bill Clinton earned $75.6 million from paid speaking engagements. He collected $10.7 million in 2010 from 52 paid speeches—his highest single-year total—up from $7.5 million for 36 speeches in 2009 and slightly above his previous peak of $10.2 million in 2006. Over 10 years Clinton delivered 417 paid speeches, averaging about $181,000 per event.

About two-thirds of his speaking income—roughly $44.9 million—came from 215 overseas appearances in 48 countries; in 2010 almost half of his fees ($4.8 million) came from 18 speeches in 13 foreign countries. His top foreign market was Canada ($9.1 million from 54 events), followed by the U.K., Australia and Mexico. Domestically he appeared most often in New York (54 events), California (35) and Florida (22).

Two 2010 events paid $500,000 each (Moscow for Renaissance Capital and a Novo Nordisk event in the United Arab Emirates), tying for his second-largest single-event fees. His speaking income has fluctuated with personal and professional commitments (for example, only six paid speeches in 2004 while writing his memoir and recovering from surgery, and a lighter 2008 due to campaigning for Hillary Clinton).

Clinton’s speaking disclosures are unusually visible because his wife, Hillary Clinton, held high federal office (Senator and then Secretary of State), which required disclosure and allowed ethics review of his proposed engagements. The report notes that other recent ex-presidents have also earned substantial speaking fees (e.g., George W. Bush estimated at about $15 million for roughly 140 speeches in his first 2½ years out of office). The piece also reminds that Clinton earned a $15 million advance for his 2004 memoir and has earned additional large sums from book sales.

Andrew Simes shared a heartfelt story about continuing his grandfather’s long-running tradition of sending a Christmas card to Queen Elizabeth II. His grandfather mailed a card every year from 1952 and even met the Queen at a reception in Turkey in 1972, where she recognized him and remarked on the cards. She later wrote to congratulate him on his 100th birthday. After his grandfather died in 2011, Andrew began sending the card each Christmas in his stead. In January 2012 he received a condolence letter from Buckingham Palace in which the Queen’s office explained they had researched his grandfather’s whereabouts after receiving a card from a “different Simes.” Andrew says the exchange moved him to tears and underscores how small acts of kindness—like sending cards—can make a lasting impression.

A series of recent shark bites along the U.S. East Coast — including a Wednesday incident in Daytona Beach Shores in which a 10‑year‑old visiting boy suffered minor calf lacerations — has renewed concern about shark attacks. The boy was treated on the beach and did not require hospitalization; the beach remained open. He is the second 10‑year‑old attacked in Florida in a week and at least the fourth person bitten this year in Volusia County, which has been labeled the “shark bite capital” by the International Shark Attack File.

Experts say the apparent rise in attacks largely reflects better reporting and many more people in the water, not increased shark aggression. Worldwide reported attacks were slightly lower in 2014 than 2013; Florida led the U.S. in 2014 with 28 attacks. Shark researchers advise swimmers to stay in groups and avoid inlets and areas where baiting is common.

Separately, two severe attacks off Oak Island, North Carolina — where a 12‑year‑old girl lost part of an arm and a 16‑year‑old boy lost an arm within about 90 minutes of each other — have prompted local officials to consider a temporary ban on shark fishing (including chumming) near shore through busy holiday periods. Fishing piers can attract sharks because of concentrated fish, bait, and discarded fish parts; some East Coast towns (e.g., Virginia Beach and Myrtle Beach) already ban shark fishing from piers. Authorities and scientists note uncertainty about how effective bans are, but recommend swimming farther from piers and avoiding areas where people are actively fishing with bloody bait.

Derek Jeter and Minka Kelly have ended their three-plus-year relationship. Sources say the split was amicable and they remain friends and still care for each other; reps for Kelly confirmed the breakup. The timing comes while Jeter, 37, is in the middle of the Yankees season and recently celebrated the MLB milestone of 3,000 hits (featured in the HBO documentary Deter Jeter 3K). Kelly, 31, is filming the ABC Charlie’s Angels reboot in Miami, produced by Drew Barrymore and Leonard Goldberg and co-starring Rachael Taylor and Annie Ilonzeh.

Genevieve Kelley, 50, who had been sought by U.S. marshals since November 2004 for taking her daughter in violation of a custody order and fleeing to avoid prosecution, surrendered to authorities in Lancaster, New Hampshire. Kelley and her then-husband Scott Kelley left New Hampshire with their daughter Mary (then 8) after an acrimonious custody battle in which Genevieve accused ex-husband Mark Nunes of abuse; Mark was never charged and was later awarded legal custody. Investigators and child-welfare officials concluded the mother had likely coached and alienated the child, and the family vanished in late 2004; marshals pursued leads across the U.S., Canada and Central and South America.

Genevieve has been in Coös County custody and made an initial court appearance; prosecutors and marshals say her surrender followed media attention (she was featured on CNN’s The Hunt and as the U.S. Marshals’ Fugitive of the Week). Scott Kelley remains a fugitive. The current whereabouts of Mary Nunes — now 18 — are unknown; Genevieve’s attorney has said Mary is safe and indicated Genevieve wants a jury trial on the custodial-interference charges. Mary’s father, Mark Nunes, said he remains desperate to know whether his daughter is alive and safe. The case drew broader publicity alongside other recent developments involving fugitives profiled on The Hunt.

Investigators are probing the death of 17-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Gomez, a MacArthur High School senior who was found dead Saturday morning in a room at the Hyatt Hotel off North Sam Houston Parkway after the school’s prom. Her date (reported as a boyfriend and a former classmate) discovered she was not breathing and called 911. Police recovered alcohol and prescription pain pills in the room and are awaiting autopsy results; detectives say there were no obvious signs of trauma and the boyfriend has been cooperative with investigators, with no current indication he contributed to her death.

Friends and classmates described Gomez as outgoing, working in the Kroger pharmacy and planning to attend Lone Star College to train as a pharmacy technician. She had spent the prom night with friends and left around 11 p.m. to go to the hotel room. The tragedy has left classmates and family reeling and prompted other students attending a separate prom at the same hotel to say it will make them more cautious about after-prom plans. Funeral assistance information has been shared by local media.

An envelope addressed to Sen. Roger Wicker’s Washington office was intercepted Tuesday at the off-site U.S. Senate mail facility and found to contain a white granular substance that field tests indicated was ricin. Capitol Police hazardous-material teams quarantined the envelope and sent samples to an accredited laboratory (and later to the Army’s lab at Fort Detrick) for confirmatory testing; officials cautioned that preliminary field results can be inconsistent and full analysis takes 24–48 hours.

The letter, postmarked Memphis, Tenn., had no return address and reportedly came from an individual who frequently writes to lawmakers; authorities said a suspect has been identified but no arrest was reported that night. The incident prompted the temporary closure of the Senate mail facility for additional testing and redirected Capitol Hill mail through the House facility. The Capitol complex itself was not affected, and Wicker has been assigned a protective detail.

Senators were briefed by Homeland Security and FBI officials. The discovery follows past Capitol ricin scares (including 2004) and is being investigated by the U.S. Capitol Police in partnership with the FBI. Ricin is a highly toxic castor-bean derivative with no antidote; authorities reminded offices to watch for similar letters.

Norway’s prime minister Erna Solberg formally apologized for the post‑World War II mistreatment of Norwegian women who had intimate relationships with German soldiers—often called “German girls”—and their children. Up to an estimated 50,000 women were stigmatized after liberation in 1945 and suffered reprisals including job dismissals, detention, loss of citizenship, expulsions to Germany and other indignities imposed without trial. Many relationships were consensual or youthful romances; Heinrich Himmler’s policies had even encouraged unions and births (including via Lebensborn maternity homes) as part of Nazi racial aims.

The apology, delivered at an event marking the 70th anniversary of the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, drew on a report from Norway’s Centre for Holocaust and Minorities Studies concluding the state violated the fundamental principle that citizens cannot be punished outside the courts. Solberg noted that while most of the women are now dead, the apology matters to surviving family members and children—some 10,000–12,000 born of these unions—many of whom faced removal to foster homes, institutionalization or other reprisals and later sought compensation or legal redress. Observers called the apology late but historically important; previous efforts included a 2000 apology specifically to the children of these unions.

An on-duty FBI agent was shot Saturday afternoon while conducting surveillance in Canarsie, Brooklyn. Around 3:30 p.m. the agent was sitting in a car near E. 92nd Street and Avenue N when occupants of a BMW drove by and opened fire, striking the agent in the shoulder. Sources say the agent returned fire as the suspects fled; one suspect was hit and later arrived at Kingsbrook Jewish Medical Center seeking treatment and was arrested. A second suspect was taken into custody nearby on Remsen Avenue. The agent was rushed to Kings County Hospital, conscious and alert, and underwent surgery; his injuries were not believed to be life‑threatening. Authorities have not said whether the shooters knew the victim was an FBI agent or what the surveillance target was. NYPD Chief of Department Terence Monahan tweeted there are no outstanding suspects. The investigation is ongoing.
