A magnitude-6.0 earthquake struck Napa Valley early Sunday, the largest Bay Area temblor in 25+ years. The quake—now attributed to the Browns Valley branch of the West Napa Fault—caused widespread but uneven damage across Napa and nearby communities: roads and curbs buckled, chimneys and masonry fell, water mains broke, some streets and buildings were red-tagged, schools closed, and hundreds were injured (reports ranged ~200–250 treated, with several seriously injured). Initial GPS data showed ground shifts of roughly 4 inches near the epicenter; aftershocks continued and scientists continue mapping which fault strands ruptured. The U.S. Geological Survey and state geologists are collecting surface observations and satellite/GPS data to refine the picture; the quake highlighted both the promise and limitations of earthquake early-warning systems.

Despite the disruption—estimates of damage running into the hundreds of millions to possibly over $1 billion—many residents and businesses began cleanup and recovery immediately. Water outages affected hundreds of properties while crews worked to repair pipeline breaks; evacuees used shelters and community water stations. Downtown Napa and many wineries continued to operate, though some facilities (including barrel rooms and storerooms) suffered losses of barrels and bottles; in many cases apparent damage proved less severe after inspection.

A prominent theme was large-scale volunteer and neighborly assistance. Organized teams—most visibly, dozens of Home Depot employees mobilized from across Northern California—worked house-to-house clearing debris, hauling bricks, plywood, water and supplies, and helping secure furniture. Local congregations, contractors, visiting tourists, and individuals (from engineers to painters with brooms) volunteered to box possessions, document red‑tagged homes, sweep up streets and help merchants. Stories highlighted emotional relief as strangers cleared cherished remnants and helped residents cope. Officials warned recovery would be a months-long process but noted the community response and rapid inspections mitigated what could have been much worse.

The U.S. economy added 215,000 jobs in March, driven by gains in construction (about 37,000), retail and health care, keeping hiring steady despite slower overall growth. The unemployment rate rose slightly to 5.0% from 4.9% because more people reentered the labor force, not because hiring weakened. Average hourly pay was up 2.3% year-over-year to $25.43—an improvement since early recovery years but still below the roughly 3.5% typical in a strong labor market. Manufacturing and mining (including oil and gas) continued to lose jobs, with the energy sector down sharply since 2014. Broader economic signals are mixed: consumer spending has cooled (0.1% gain in February for the third month running), the personal savings rate rose to 5.4%, existing-home sales dropped sharply on tight supply, and exports and business investment remain weak. Overall, steady hiring suggests employers view the recent slowdown as temporary.

Pepsi pulled a new TV spot starring model Kendall Jenner after widespread mockery and criticism that it trivialized protests for social justice. The ad depicted Jenner leaving a photoshoot to join a diverse, smiling crowd of protesters; tensions ease when she offers a police officer a can of Pepsi, which he drinks. Viewers and activists said the scene echoed real-life images from Black Lives Matter demonstrations and accused the commercial of co-opting and sanitizing serious protest movements with vapid, corporate messaging (signs reading things like “Join the Conversation” drew particular scorn). Pepsi apologized, saying it “missed the mark,” removed the content and halted further rollout; it also apologized to Jenner for putting her “in this position.” The backlash included viral commentary from public figures, late-night comedians and social media, and commentators noted Pepsi’s repeated missteps with controversial ads in the past.

21st Century Fox has settled former Fox News anchor Gretchen Carlson’s sexual-harassment lawsuit. The company issued an apology acknowledging Carlson “was not treated with the respect and dignity” she and colleagues deserve; Carlson said she is gratified the company acted and will focus on empowering women. Media reports (including Vanity Fair and New York Magazine) say the settlement is about $20 million and includes a public apology; terms reportedly bar Carlson from pursuing further claims against other Fox executives or the company. Fox itself was not a named defendant in Carlson’s suit, which alleged harassment and retaliation by former CEO Roger Ailes; Ailes has denied the allegations.

Carlson’s suit and the ensuing internal investigation by law firm Paul, Weiss triggered dozens of other women coming forward and precipitated Ailes’s rapid ouster from Fox News. Reporting has portrayed Ailes as presiding over a culture of harassment, surveillance and intimidation at Fox that was enabled by senior staff. The Murdoch family moved quickly to investigate and remove Ailes, ultimately negotiating a reported $40 million severance while keeping him as an adviser under a noncompete. Megyn Kelly and other high-profile women who spoke to investigators were central to the inquiry; Fox has reportedly reached settlement deals with at least two other women.

The coverage also details long-standing allegations about Ailes’s behavior and Fox’s internal practices—use of nondisclosure settlements, monitoring and opposition research—that fostered a hostile workplace for women. In response to critical reporting (notably a lengthy New York Magazine piece), Ailes’s attorneys have asked the magazine to preserve documents for a possible defamation claim, a step media outlets say echoes prior high-profile legal threats. The scandal prompted leadership changes and ongoing scrutiny of Fox’s culture and governance, including shareholder interest in whether officers and directors breached fiduciary duties.

At the Conservative Political Action Conference a week after the Parkland, Florida, school massacre, NRA executive vice president Wayne LaPierre delivered a combative defense of the gun lobby and its positions, accusing Democrats, the media and gun-control advocates of exploiting the tragedy to erode liberty and the Second Amendment. LaPierre insisted critics cared more about politics than student safety, repeated the NRA line that “to stop a bad guy with a gun, it takes a good guy with a gun,” and urged immediate hardening of schools and expanded armed security. He also attacked the FBI for failing to act on tips about the shooter and broadened his criticism to include socialism, immigration and the opioid epidemic.

The NRA had earlier released a video accusing mainstream media of exploiting mass shootings for ratings, and spokeswoman Dana Loesch drew controversy at a CNN town hall by accusing legacy media of racial bias in coverage and criticizing law enforcement and background-check failures. LaPierre’s speech drew swift rebukes from Democrats including Sen. Chuck Schumer and from gun-control advocates, who said the NRA should not shape policy. Vice President Mike Pence, speaking afterward, took a more conciliatory tone, supporting some of President Trump’s proposals such as stronger background checks and bump-stock restrictions while endorsing the search for “American solutions” and praying for unity.

The remarks came amid a shifting political climate: Parkland survivors were mounting a high-profile campaign for stricter gun laws, and President Trump and some Republicans signaled openness to modest reforms — including raising the purchase age for semiautomatic rifles to 21 — positions the NRA opposes. The debate intensified as investigators confirmed the shooter had no criminal record and had legally purchased multiple firearms, while local officials acknowledged security failures at the school. Political responses in Florida and Washington suggested possible legislative action despite NRA resistance.

Spanish police have arrested at least one person after discovering the suspected bodies of missing Dutch international volleyball player Ingrid Visser (35) and her partner Lodewijk Severein (57) buried in a shallow grave in a lemon grove near Alquerías, about 12 km from Murcia. DNA confirmation is pending, but police noted the bodies’ height matched the couple. Visser and Severein disappeared on 13 May after checking into a Murcia hotel; their rental car was later found abandoned in the city. The couple had missed appointments in the Netherlands and a reported hospital visit in Spain.

Authorities raided an apartment in Molina de Segura and found evidence of a violent crime; one man was arrested there. Spanish media named a suspect as Juan Cuenca Lorente, 36, a former director of Murcia’s volleyball team (Visser played for the team from 2009–2011). Reports also say two other suspects—described as Romanian men aged about 60 and 47—were detained in Valencia. Officials have kept many probe details confidential but Murcia’s police chief indicated the killings may have been related to “business disagreements” between the couple and the suspects. Investigation and identification are ongoing.

Rupert Murdoch personally met with the family of murdered schoolgirl Milly Dowler on July 15, 2011 and offered what the family’s lawyer called a “full and sincere” apology after revelations that journalists at the now-closed News of the World (NOTW) hacked the girl’s voicemail while police and family were searching for her. The hack—allegedly deleting messages and giving the family false hope—intensified the widening phone‑hacking scandal that already implicated NOTW in targeting celebrities, politicians, victims’ relatives and possibly even 9/11 families.

Murdoch emerged from the meeting appearing contrite and later placed a printed apology in national newspapers acknowledging “serious wrongdoing,” regret for not acting sooner, and promising concrete steps to make amends. His tone contrasted with an earlier Wall Street Journal interview in which he had minimized the company’s failings.

The crisis prompted high‑level departures at News Corp. In London, Rebekah Brooks, former editor of NOTW and then chief executive of News International, resigned as mounting pressure and political outrage made her position untenable; she denies knowledge of wrongdoing. Les Hinton, longtime News Corp. executive, also stepped down as CEO of Dow Jones. Tom Mockridge was appointed to head News International. James Murdoch signaled a shift in handling the crisis; both Rupe rt and James agreed to appear before a parliamentary committee after initial resistance.

British police investigations have led to several arrests and a recovered list of some 3,700 potential victims; fewer than 200 have been contacted so far. An independent public inquiry (Leveson) has been ordered and U.S. authorities are reviewing related allegations. The scandal has already cost News Corp. financially—shares fell and the company withdrew its bid to fully acquire BSkyB—and severely damaged Rupert Murdoch’s political influence in Britain.

At Inc.’s GrowCo conference, Mavericks owner and entrepreneur Mark Cuban spoke candidly about prejudice, race and leadership, prompting widespread reaction. In a video interview he acknowledged his own biases—saying, awkwardly, that he’ll cross the street to avoid “a black kid in a hoodie” late at night or a heavily tattooed white man—and framed that admission as part of an effort to confront and manage prejudice rather than hide it. He apologized to Trayvon Martin’s family for the hoodie reference while stressing that everyone has prejudices and that leaders have a responsibility to address them within their organizations.

Cuban had previously condemned Clippers owner Donald Sterling’s racist remarks as “abhorrent” but warned that forcing an owner to sell sets a “slippery slope.” He said the NBA had to act to protect its culture but acknowledged bigotry can’t be entirely kept out of the league and stressed education and engagement as better responses than ostracism.

The comments generated a mixed national response: some praised Cuban’s honesty and encouraged open conversations about implicit bias (Washington Post, Boston.com, ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith, Osi Umenyiora, Chris Kluwe), while others criticized his analogy as tone-deaf or dangerously close to Sterling-style thinking (Bill Plaschke, LZ Granderson). Some commentators speculated about his motives or timing. Coverage also noted Cuban’s broader remarks at the conference—about his entrepreneurial beginnings, how he built the Mavericks into an experience-driven business, his views on patents and management style—and that he hadn’t yet announced how he’d vote on the NBA’s potential ouster of Sterling. Overall, the interview sparked debate about honesty, context and how best to confront prejudice in public life and institutions.

Seminal new-wave band Devo—preparing to tour Australia and New Zealand for A Day on the Green with Simple Minds—spoke with UTR via founding member Bob Casale about their return to making new material, how modern tools changed their process, and the political and cultural views behind their work.

Why make a new album now
- Devo wanted to “be Devo again”: write songs true to their established attention to lyrical content and structure rather than imitate others.
- The band consciously embraced contemporary production and marketing methods they previously avoided: collaborating with outside producers, running focus groups, using social networking, digital file-sharing and serial remote songwriting instead of the old practice of holed-up studio marathons.
- Casale says the method shapes the art: the social, iterative remote process produced different results than working together in a bunker, but they aimed to remain relevant while staying tongue-in-cheek about adopting corporate-style promotion.

Technology, the music industry and artists today
- The internet and new distribution/consumption models forced Devo to adapt; they deliberately experimented with modern promotional tools while retaining their identity.
- Casale is critical of contemporary mainstream artists, calling much of today's pop narcissistic and self-referential—focused on wealth, status and indulgence—arguing that the culture is creatively bankrupt and dominated by capitalist excess.
- He acknowledges the chicken-and-egg problem—record companies tend not to risk presenting something unfamiliar—but notes that indulgent material still sells in huge numbers, so it reflects audience desires.

Origins and artistic approach
- Devo formed in the context of intense cultural conflict (post-Kent State era), seeing music as an immediate, low-barrier form of expression compared with film or other media.
- From early on they treated music, visuals, stage design and video as an integrated, synergistic whole; Casale emphasizes their long-standing use of visuals and stagecraft to amplify the music.

Politics and recent events
- The band’s political awareness informs their work; Casale discussed contemporary U.S. politics, criticizing Mitt Romney during the 2012 campaign and expressing relief at Barack Obama’s re-election—calling Obama the lesser of two evils and warning that a Romney/Ryan administration would have worsened economic and military problems.
- He cited examples (including a Romney incident used in a Devo game concept) to illustrate perceived character faults and hypocrisy in political figures.

Additional context and obituary material
- The piece includes news that Bob Casale (known to fans as “Bob 2”), 61, died suddenly from heart-failure–related conditions; his death came as a shock to bandmates and family. Gerald Casale praised him as a steady, talented audio engineer and performer who was “there in the trenches” from Devo’s start. Mark Mothersbaugh highlighted Bob’s long collaboration at Mutato Studios on films, TV shows (including Rugrats), commercials and video games.
- The band’s origins trace back to art students Gerald Casale and Mark Mothersbaugh at Kent State amid the 1970 antiwar turmoil; Devo’s name reflects their concept of “de-evolution,” a critique of cultural regression.
- Devo remained active into recent years, touring and performing (including the 2010 Winter Olympics) though mainstream chart success beyond hits like 1980’s “Whip It!” was limited.

Overall, the interview presents Devo as a band consciously negotiating modern production, distribution and promotional realities while holding to a politically engaged, multimedia artistic vision—now framed poignantly by the sudden loss of longtime guitarist/engineer Bob Casale.

A 21-year-old former Stanford student, Scott Bertics, fatally shot 19-year-old Clare Orton at her Walnut Creek home on July 21 and then killed himself. Investigators determined Bertics built two unregistered, untraceable “ghost guns” from mail‑ordered parts—unfinished lower receivers, trigger assemblies and other components purchased online—and assembled them legally. Neither weapon had serial numbers. Police said no one else appears to have been involved or aware of his plans.

Bertics and Orton had dated previously but not since 2013; police have not disclosed a motive. Both were engineering students—Orton at San Diego State (an honors student and athlete), Bertics at Stanford (who took a leave after fall 2014). Authorities noted the relative ease with which such parts can be bought online but emphasized Bertics “knew what he was doing.” The story echoes wider debates over so‑called ghost guns and past unsuccessful California legislation to tighten regulations on homemade firearm parts.

The document is a collection of visitor reviews, practical details, and a news story about the Vancouver Maritime Museum (VMM) in Vanier Park, Vancouver.

Key facts and visitor info
- Location: Vanier Park, 1905 Ogden Avenue, Vancouver, BC. Phone (604) 257-8300.
- Admission: fee (example cited $10–$11); Thursdays 17:00–20:00 admission by donation. Recommended visit: 1–2 hours.
- Main attraction: the St. Roch, a preserved RCMP schooner and National Historic Site—famous for voyages through the Northwest Passage and circumnavigating North America via the Panama Canal.
- Collections and features: model ships, maritime art, the boiler of the Beaver (first steamship in the Pacific Northwest), a fo’c’sle recreation, a Children’s Maritime Discovery Centre, rotating exhibits, interactive displays (e.g., remote-controlled submersible), and occasional guided tours of the St. Roch.
- Family-friendly offerings: pirate-themed birthday parties, kids’ play areas, costume activities and hands-on exhibits. Some visitors recommend going during school hours for a quieter experience.
- Parking: limited paid lot in front; possible free parking a block or two away (Maple Street/Hadden Park), but signage and pay stations have caused confusion for some visitors.

Visitor impressions (mixed but generally positive)
- Many visitors praise the St. Roch exhibit as unique and worth the visit, especially for maritime-history enthusiasts and families. Hands-on access to the ship and knowledgeable staff are highlighted.
- The museum’s atmosphere is described as modest and somewhat dated (1960s feel), which some find charming and others call old-fashioned.
- Several reviewers note some exhibits feel repetitive or pedestrian compared with other maritime museums, and a few cite aging displays and a need to refresh children’s areas.
- Overall: affordable, accessible, and a worthwhile stop for locals and tourists interested in Vancouver’s maritime history.

Controversy reported
- A Vancouver mother and teacher, Ann Pimentel, publicly objected to a new temporary exhibit ("Tattoo and Scrimshaw: The Art of the Sailor") that includes scrimshaw (etchings on whale bone/teeth), saying several pieces are sexually explicit and inappropriate for children. She complained about insufficient advance warnings.
- The museum’s curator, Patricia Owen, says the nine sexual images are displayed high in a dimly lit case with a nearby sign saying “Hide Your Eyes! These pieces of scrimshaw are not intended for children,” and that more graphic items are kept in storage. The museum says the show was designed to pair scrimshaw with tattoo art and anticipated possible concerns.
- The scrimshaw controversy has generated attention and debate about display placement, labeling, and the historical context of erotic imagery produced by 19th-century sailors. The museum also acknowledges uncertainties about provenance—some scrimshaw pieces may be later fakes.

Bottom line
The Vancouver Maritime Museum offers a distinctive, historically rich maritime experience centered on the St. Roch, with many kid-friendly and interactive elements. It is modest and somewhat dated in presentation. A recent temporary scrimshaw exhibit sparked controversy over sexually explicit images and prompted discussion about exhibit warnings, placement, and authenticity.

A 14-month-old Bronx girl, Xania Samuels, fell from a fifth-floor window of her family’s apartment on Monday and is in critical condition but expected to survive. The father said Xania had insisted on wearing her heavily padded pink winter coat on an unusually hot day, and the family believes the coat may have lessened the impact. The parents were briefly occupied—her father was bathing the twin brother and her mother was at a laundromat—when the toddler fell at about 11:29 a.m.; no charges were filed. Neighbors and an EMT who found the child on the sidewalk reported severe head bleeding; she was taken to Jacobi Hospital. Residents say upper-floor windows in the six-story building lacked required window guards, and the mother told the New York Post prior complaints to the landlord had been ignored. Authorities describe the fall as accidental.

Summary:

Pittsburgh International Airport will become the first U.S. airport to let non-ticketed visitors pass through security and access airside gates, shops, restaurants and artwork year-round, beginning Sept. 5 with TSA approval. Non-flyers must check in at a special desk, present photo ID, be screened against the "no fly" list, and pass through the same security screening as travelers. The TSA supports the change but has not added additional staff and has no current plans to expand the program.

The move drew criticism from the Association of Professional Flight Attendants (American Airlines’ union), whose national president, Bob Ross, warned it could reduce safety, lengthen security lines and lead to missed flights. He characterized the policy as a poor precedent—especially coming near the anniversary of 9/11—and said it sends the wrong message about airport vigilance. The report was part of coverage that also included TSA travel tips and referenced archiving practices used by the Internet Archive.

Newark Mayor Cory Booker won the Democratic primary for the special U.S. Senate election to fill Sen. Frank Lautenberg’s seat by a large margin and will face Republican Steve Lonegan in the Oct. 16 special election. With about 98% reporting, Booker led with roughly 59% to Rep. Frank Pallone’s 20%, Rep. Rush Holt’s 17% and Assembly Speaker Sheila Oliver’s 4%. He had been the clear frontrunner throughout the short, high-profile race, outraising opponents, winning most party organization endorsements, and mobilizing absentee voting.

Booker’s campaign faced repeated attacks from his Democratic rivals over his record, policy positions and business ties—most notably his ownership stake in Waywire, a tech startup that received backing from friends while he was mayor. Booker and his team vigorously defended his finances and record, highlighting his charity donations and arguing his pragmatic, results-oriented approach helped revitalize Newark. He emphasized bipartisanship (including a working relationship with Republican Gov. Chris Christie) and cast his moderate pragmatism as an asset to win statewide office.

Booker, a nationally recognized political figure and frequent media presence with a broad speaking profile, framed himself as a bridge-builder and pledged to seek common ground in the Senate. His victory sets up a general-election contrast with Lonegan, a conservative former Bogota mayor and activist who has aggressively attacked Booker and whose style and ideology differ sharply from Booker’s. The expedited election schedule—ordered by Gov. Christie after Lautenberg’s death—compressed the campaign calendar and drew criticism from some quarters.

Fashion designer and billionaire Peter Nygård, 70, says he has been receiving stem-cell treatments for about four years and claims a University of Miami study shows biomarkers indicating he is “reversing” his aging. Nygård has been promoting stem-cell research in the Bahamas and produced a video promoting the work and its potential to cure disease and extend life. He has explored opening a stem-cell clinic and inspected sites in Freeport—including the closed Port Lucaya Resort and nearby marina—after earlier discussion of a proposed $50 million facility at his Nygard Cay/Lyford Cay property met strong local opposition and legal challenges from residents and the Coalition to Save Clifton.

Fred Smith QC, who led legal action against Nygård’s Lyford Cay development, said he would welcome a major stem-cell investment in Freeport and urged Nygård to relocate any plans there rather than pursue commercial development in a residentially zoned Lyford Cay. Local authorities and some property owners opposed locating a commercial clinic in Lyford Cay; the Bahamas attorney general has denied Nygård drafted recent legislation to permit stem-cell medical centres.

While the article recounts Nygård’s bold claims and promotional messaging, experts cited note that stem-cell research has real promise but also raises ethical and regulatory concerns—particularly around cloning and unequal access—so claims of “immortality” or dramatic anti-aging should be viewed skeptically.

During Louisville's Midwest Regional final against Duke on March 31, 2013, guard Kevin Ware suffered a gruesome open fracture of his right tibia after landing awkwardly trying to block a shot. His lower leg bent at an extreme angle with bone protruding through the skin—teammates wept on the court, CBS halted replays, and the injury quickly trended online.

Ware was stabilized on the court, taken to the hospital, and underwent a roughly two-hour surgery that night: the bone was reset, a rod was implanted, and the wound closed. Team doctors said the injury was severe and would require a lengthy recovery, with early estimates suggesting months before signs of healing and best-case return to play in 6–8 months, though complications from the open fracture (infection, slow healing, soft-tissue damage) could lengthen recovery. Louisville’s medical staff and outside orthopedic experts were cautiously optimistic that Ware could play again.

Despite the shock, Louisville rallied and beat Duke 85–63 to reach the Final Four; teammates dedicated the win to Ware and one player wore his No. 5 jersey. Ware remained hospitalized in Indianapolis and hoped to rejoin the team in Atlanta to support them.

The widely seen injury reignited debate over the NCAA’s treatment of athletes: Ware, like other college players, receives only a scholarship and lacks worker’s compensation or broader protections, raising questions about long-term financial and medical consequences for injured student-athletes—especially those whose professional prospects may be diminished by such injuries.

Boulder prosecutors and police plan new DNA testing on key evidence in the 1996 unsolved murder of 6-year-old JonBenét Ramsey after a joint 9NEWS/Daily Camera investigation raised serious doubts about earlier test interpretation.

What prompted this
- The news organizations obtained laboratory reports, notes and correspondence from 2008 testing done for then-District Attorney Mary Lacy by Bode Technology (now Bode Cellmark). Independent forensic experts who reviewed those materials concluded the DNA evidence was more ambiguous than Lacy’s 2008 public exoneration of JonBenét’s parents and brother implied.
- Reports and lab notes indicated DNA from at least two people (in addition to JonBenét) was present on her long johns and panties; some analyses suggested three or more contributors. That raises the possibility the CODIS profile entered as “Unknown Male 1” might be a composite rather than the single individual it has been treated as.

Planned retesting
- Boulder DA Stan Garnett and Police Chief Greg Testa met recently with Colorado Bureau of Investigation (CBI) officials to discuss new, more sensitive DNA testing kits the CBI will deploy (Yfiler Plus and other upgraded kits required by CODIS standards beginning in 2017).
- Officials said they will pursue “all reasonable testing” and will evaluate how new methods can help the investigation; Garnett said the CBI lab can handle the work.

Problems with the 2008 work and Lacy’s 2008 exoneration
- The Bode reports themselves cautioned that some long-johns samples “should not be considered a single-source profile” because more than two contributors were likely.
- Despite those caveats, Lacy’s July 9, 2008 letter stated the underwear and long johns “matched” and that “there is no innocent explanation” for the DNA’s presence—claims independent experts say were unjustified by the actual lab reports.
- Correspondence shows investigators in Lacy’s office were predisposed toward the intruder theory and indicated satisfaction with the apparent “match” and little interest in additional testing unless strongly recommended—raising concerns about confirmation bias and lack of blind testing protocols.

What experts recommend
- Forensic scientists consulted by the news organizations recommend Y-STR testing (which isolates male Y-chromosome DNA) on the underwear, long johns and possibly other items (e.g., the garrote) to clarify how many male contributors are present and whether a single male profile can be reliably extracted.
- They warn low-level, mixed DNA is prone to contamination and transfer and that a detected profile—even if in CODIS—might be innocent background or a composite, so DNA alone is not definitive.

Implications
- If Unknown Male 1 is a composite, past reliance on that profile to exclude suspects and support the exoneration could be invalid. Independent reviewers say the DNA evidence is indeterminate, not conclusive, and that the case is not a “DNA case pure and simple.”
- No new DNA testing has been done since 2008; officials now say they will reassess evidence under updated testing standards and technology, though Garnett emphasizes DNA is only one piece of an overall investigation.

Additional legal note
- Separately, Dr. Werner Spitz has moved to dismiss a defamation suit filed by Burke Ramsey over Spitz’s on-air suggestion (in a CBS documentary) that Burke killed JonBenét. Spitz’s lawyers argue his statements were protected opinion on a matter of public concern; Burke’s lawyer says the statements are provably false factual accusations. A hearing on that motion was scheduled for Feb. 24, 2017.

Bottom line
- New, more sensitive DNA testing is being considered and likely to be undertaken by Colorado’s crime lab; independent experts say such testing (especially Y-STR) is warranted because prior results were ambiguous and may have been overinterpreted when used to publicly clear the Ramsey family.

Top-level diplomats — US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and UN Secretary‑General Ban Ki‑moon — will meet at UN headquarters in New York for the first senior Quartet meeting in six months; EU foreign policy chief Baroness Ashton will join by videoconference. Clinton, Lavrov and Ban will then participate in a UN Security Council debate on the Arab Spring.

Their meeting comes amid a sharp escalation between Israel and Gaza. The latest round began Friday when Israel killed senior militant figures in Gaza; Palestinian militants then launched hundreds of rockets into southern and central Israel. Israel responded with repeated airstrikes on Gaza. Over several days more than 200 rockets were reported fired from Gaza, wounding several Israelis and damaging homes; Israeli airstrikes and strikes on militant targets in Gaza killed scores of Palestinians, including militants and civilians, and injured many more. Casualty totals reported vary by source (Palestinian officials reported 20–25 killed and dozens injured; Israeli reports cited militants among the dead and several Israeli wounded).

Israel said it acted to protect civilians and urged the UN Security Council to respond to rocket fire. Palestinian representatives urged urgent Council action, accusing Israel of deadly escalation. The violence prompted international concern: UN Secretary‑General Ban Ki‑moon expressed grave concern and called for restraint; China publicly urged Israel to stop air raids to avoid civilian casualties.

The fighting included rocket impacts as far north as Gedera and strikes on Ashdod and Beersheba; Israel’s Iron Dome intercepted some incoming rockets. Southern Israeli communities faced school closures and widespread shelter use. Both sides offered conflicting accounts of several incidents, including civilian deaths in Gaza. Israel warned it was prepared to expand operations; militants pledged further rocket fire.

Egyptian mediators reportedly secured a truce agreement to halt military operations early Tuesday, though Israeli officials did not immediately comment. The fighting has renewed international attention to the stalled Israeli‑Palestinian peace process: direct talks have been frozen since September 2010, Quartet revival efforts have failed, and Palestinians have sought broader international recognition amid continued settlement disputes. The Quartet’s last top‑level meeting was at the UN General Assembly in September; many observers expect no breakthrough before the U.S. presidential election.

On Wednesday morning in Philadelphia’s Center City, a permitted demolition of a four-story building at 2136 Market Street collapsed onto the adjacent Salvation Army thrift store at 22nd and Market, killing six people and injuring 13 others. The dead have been identified as Kimberly Finnegan, Borbor Davis, Juanita Harmin, Mary Simpson, Anne Bryan and Roseline Conteh; all were inside the thrift store when it was crushed. Thirteen people were pulled alive and taken to area hospitals (several later released); a 14th survivor, 61-year-old Myra Plekan, was rescued more than 13 hours after the collapse in critical condition.

The failure occurred around 10:40–10:45 a.m. as workers using heavy machinery removed structural elements from the building being demolished. Eyewitnesses described a sudden “freight-train” rumble and said the demolition method appeared risky. Bystanders and nearby workers rushed into the dust cloud and helped pull several people from the rubble before emergency crews arrived. Firefighters, police, search-and-rescue teams and dogs worked into the night; the rescue operation ended Thursday afternoon and the former thrift store was fully torn down by 4 p.m.

City officials, including Mayor Michael Nutter, pledged a broad investigation. Questions focused on inspection and permitting practices: Licenses & Inspections Commissioner Carlton Williams said permits for the demolition were valid and a May 14 inspection found the neighboring building intact, but noted the city does not require repeated inspections during demolition. OSHA and other authorities were notified and are investigating. The demolition contractor, Griffin Campbell Construction, held permits issued in February; the property owner is STB Investments. The incident disrupted traffic, closed nearby streets and prompted a Salvation Army disaster response; local institutions such as the Mutter Museum served as staging areas for rescue efforts.

Summary:

Huguette Clark, a reclusive copper heiress who died in May at age 104, left a contested estate and two wills signed six weeks apart in 2005: an earlier will that favored distant relatives and a later one that largely disinherited family members and proposed converting her Santa Barbara estate, Bellosguardo, into a museum managed by her longtime attorney Wallace Bock and accountant Irving Kamsler. The later will also made large gifts, including over $30 million to her nurse, Hadassah Peri, and modest bequests to Bock and Kamsler.

The New York public administrator, appointed as a third executor to oversee the estate, filed court papers accusing Bock and Kamsler of massive tax misconduct that could expose Clark’s estate to well over $80 million in taxes, penalties and interest. Allegations include failing to timely file gift tax returns for roughly $56 million in gifts made from 1997–2003 (creating an estimated $41.5 million gift/GST tax), filing false returns for later years, underpaying and misrepresenting tax obligations to the IRS, charging Clark for returns that were never filed, and concealing the liabilities from Clark despite her having funds to pay them. The public administrator also alleges other breaches of trust, improper solicitations of gifts, abuse of powers of attorney, and unauthorized gifts, and has said it may seek to claw back invalid gifts.

Kamsler, a certified public accountant with a 2008 guilty plea for attempting to distribute indecent material to minors (he is a registered sex offender), resigned as an executor shortly before the public administrator’s petition was filed. Bock and Kamsler deny wrongdoing; their lawyer says they acted to preserve Clark’s wishes. Kamsler’s attorney said he resigned to let Clark’s wishes be respected. The Manhattan district attorney and the public administrator’s office have been investigating the pair; no criminal charges tied to the tax allegations had been filed at the time of the reports, though the public administrator noted willful submission of fraudulent tax returns is a felony.

Surrogate’s Court Justice Kristin Booth Glen suspended Bock and Kamsler as executors pending a hearing. Clark’s relatives, who have sought to intervene and previously challenged the later will, contend the advisers engineered the will to gain access to Clark’s wealth; they may seek to intervene more fully in the estate accounting and to recover questionable gifts. Local officials in Santa Barbara had hoped the estate would become a museum, but the legal and tax disputes have clouded that prospect.

After nearly three weeks away following the Dec. 14 massacre that killed 20 first-graders, six staff members and the gunman at Sandy Hook Elementary in Newtown, Conn., more than 400 Sandy Hook students returned to class Thursday in a refurbished school building in nearby Monroe. The former Chalk Hill Middle School, about seven miles from the original site, was overhauled—with volunteers, new paint and furniture, lowered bathroom floors and familiar desks, backpacks and lunchboxes brought from the old school—to recreate a comforting, child-sized environment. Donna Page, a former Sandy Hook principal who had retired in 2010, agreed to return to lead the school after Principal Dawn Hochsprung was killed.

Buses were full, attendance was strong, and children and teachers greeted one another with relief and excitement despite visible security: police officers, counselors, therapy dogs and parents were on site, and officials said the heavy presence would be gradually reduced to restore normalcy. Authorities described the Monroe site as highly secure while Newtown’s original school remains an active crime scene.

Connecticut Governor Dannel Malloy credited a “Herculean effort” to prepare the building and announced a 15-member commission—focused on school security, mental health services and gun laws—that will recommend reforms by March. Community support was evident in welcome signs, open houses, and volunteers helping ready the school as students and families tried to resume routines amid mourning and uncertainty about the shooter’s motive.

Police report obtained by TMZ Sports says bodybuilder and social media personality Rich Piana collapsed at his Florida home and was found to have 20 bottles of testosterone in the house. Piana, 46, reportedly collapsed in his bathroom while his girlfriend, Chanel, was cutting his hair; she said she tried to catch him but couldn’t because of his size, and that he struck his head. Chanel told officers he had a past opiate addiction but believed he was clean. Paramedics found crushed white powder, a credit card and a straw on a table and administered two doses of Narcan; Piana never regained consciousness and was taken to a hospital and placed in a medically induced coma. Chanel confirmed Piana had used steroids for more than 20 years and said he had previously had a slightly enlarged heart, though she didn’t know if that was related. She asked for prayers and said he was still alive and fighting.

In 2013 the half marathon continued to be the fastest-growing standard U.S. road-race distance. Running USA estimates 1.96 million finishers nationwide, a 6% increase from 2012 and a record high—more than six times the 303,000 finishers recorded in 1990 and roughly a 307% increase since 2000. Half-marathon participation has been driven largely by women: they made up a record 61% of finishers in 2013 (up from 53% in 2006), though the absolute number of male finishers also rose (more than 760,000 men finished halfs in 2013, exceeding total finishers in 2006).

The trend is strong in the U.S. (14 of the world’s 20 largest halfs were American in 2013), but the largest individual events were overseas: Gothenburg, Sweden (45,126 finishers) and the Great North Run in Britain (40,763) led the world. Other large races that year included Paris, the Indianapolis 500 Festival, Nike Women’s San Francisco, and several Rock ’n’ Roll and Disney events. Since 2010 the half has been the second-most popular distance by finishers after the 5K; in 2013 October hosted the most U.S. halfs (288) while January had the fewest (83). Overall the data show the half marathon’s broad and growing appeal as a mainstream fitness goal.

Portland police announced they have reopened their investigation of sexual-assault allegations against former Vice President Al Gore after finding "procedural issues" in how the bureau handled the matter in 2009. Chief Michael Reese said command-level supervisors should have reviewed the case and decided whether to proceed when the complainant, massage therapist Molly Hagerty, made a second report last year. In that 2009 review, detectives concluded there was insufficient evidence and did not contact Gore or consult the Multnomah County district attorney; Reese says those decisions should have been made at a higher level. The original matter dates to an October 2006 incident in which Hagerty told detectives Gore allegedly groped and kissed her during a late-night massage at the Hotel Lucia. In 2006 Hagerty’s attorney canceled multiple meetings with police and informed them she was pursuing civil action; the case was cleared then for lack of cooperation. Reese emphasized the bureau independently chose to reopen the probe, will assign resources to conduct a thorough, fair and expedited investigation, and will not comment on specifics while it is open.

Update (May 22): Norwegian government agency Statsbygg confirmed that water entered the entry tunnel of the Svalbard Global Seed Vault last October during an unusually warm, rainy period in Svalbard. The intrusion reached about 15 meters into the 100‑meter tunnel and then froze; no seeds or the vault’s core storage were ever at risk. Statsbygg said the event was not a flood but more water than desired, and added that measures to waterproof and secure the tunnel were already planned and are being implemented. No similar leakage has occurred this year.

Background and context: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, run by the Crop Trust and located in a mountainside on the Svalbard archipelago, opened in 2008 as a “fail‑safe” backup repository for seed collections worldwide. Seed material is stored about 110 meters from the tunnel entrance, in rock at about −18 °C. The tunnel slopes inward and was never intended to be completely watertight; annual summer permafrost melt has historically allowed some water ingress near the entrance, removed by pumping stations. Construction disturbed local permafrost and a recent heatwave increased melting, producing this more significant but contained intrusion.

Separately, Reuters reported that Syria’s civil war prompted the first-ever withdrawal request from the vault. The International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA), which relocated from Aleppo to Beirut in 2012, has asked to retrieve nearly 130 of its 325 deposited boxes (about 116,000 samples) to replace and regenerate material from a partially damaged Aleppo gene bank. Many of these accessions—wheat, barley and dryland grasses—carry valuable drought‑resistant traits useful for breeding in arid regions. The Crop Trust and Norwegian authorities emphasized that facilitating such withdrawals is a key purpose of the vault. The facility currently holds more than 860,000 samples from almost all nations and is designed to remain sealed and frozen for at least centuries even without power.

This document compiles historical outbreak data, clinical information, transmission and treatment notes, and news reporting about Marburg virus disease (MVD), an Ebola-like filovirus hemorrhagic fever. Key points:

Outbreak history and epidemiology
- Marburg virus was first identified in 1967 after 31 laboratory workers in Germany and Yugoslavia became ill from African green monkeys imported from Uganda. Additional outbreaks and sporadic cases have occurred since, often linked to exposure to infected nonhuman primates or caves inhabited by fruit bats.
- Notable outbreaks and incidents listed include:
  - 1967 (Germany/Yugoslavia): 31 cases.
  - 1975 (Johannesburg, imported from Zimbabwe): 3 cases, 1 death.
  - 1980 and 1987 (Kenya; Kitum Cave): a few travel-associated fatal cases.
  - 1990 (Russia): 1 lab-acquired case.
  - 1998–2000 (DRC, Durba/Watsa): 154 cases, 128 deaths (83% CFR).
  - 2004–2005 (Angola, Uige): 252 cases, 227 deaths (90% CFR).
  - 2007 (Uganda, mine): 4 cases.
  - 2008 (travel-associated): 1 U.S. case (recovered), 1 Dutch fatality; both linked to a Ugandan cave.
  - 2012 (Uganda, Kabale and other districts): 15 cases, 4 deaths.
- Case-fatality rates across outbreaks have ranged widely (about 23%–90%), depending on outbreak, care availability, and case ascertainment.

Clinical features
- Incubation: typically 5–10 days.
- Onset: sudden fever, chills, headache, myalgia.
- Progression (around day 5): possible maculopapular rash; then nausea, vomiting, chest and abdominal pain, sore throat, diarrhea.
- Severe disease: jaundice, pancreatitis, severe weight loss, delirium, shock, liver failure, massive hemorrhage, multi-organ dysfunction.
- Diagnosis can be difficult because early signs mimic malaria, typhoid and other febrile illnesses.

Transmission and reservoirs
- Not airborne. Transmission occurs via direct contact with blood, tissues or body fluids of infected persons or animals.
- Many human index cases are associated with exposure to infected primates or bat-inhabited caves; fruit bats are considered likely natural reservoirs in several instances.
- Healthcare workers and caregivers are at high risk during person-to-person spread without proper protective measures.

Treatment and prevention
- No specific proven antiviral therapy or licensed vaccine. Care is supportive: fluid and electrolyte management, treatment of secondary infections, blood replacement as needed.
- Experimental treatments (e.g., agents related to Ebola research) have shown promise in animal studies (e.g., Tekmira’s compounds), but no established cure exists.

2014 Uganda case and response (news reporting)
- A 30-year-old male radiographer/health worker in Uganda died of confirmed Marburg virus infection (reported late September/early October 2014).
- Authorities placed numerous contacts under quarantine (reports vary: about 80–99 contacts, including >60 health workers). Eleven suspected contacts initially tested negative; symptomatic contacts were to be retested after three days.
- Extensive contact tracing included following an embalmer to Kenya, who tested negative.
- Ugandan and international public health officials (including CDC Director Thomas Frieden) emphasized that Uganda has laboratory capacity, disease detectives, and an emergency operations center that aid rapid detection and containment, making a large outbreak unlikely if response is swift.
- Media coverage contextualized Marburg as rare but severe, related to Ebola, and stressed that early identification and control measures typically prevent large-scale spread.

Additional context
- The document also contains an unrelated excerpt about Ugandan youth and women entrepreneurship programs and a speech by President Museveni; this is not related to Marburg disease content.

Overall message
- Marburg virus causes a severe hemorrhagic fever with high variable lethality and has caused sporadic outbreaks linked to animal exposure and laboratory accidents. Early detection, rigorous surveillance, contact tracing, isolation, and infection-control measures are critical and have enabled successful containment in past Ugandan and other responses, reducing the risk of large-scale outbreaks when implemented promptly.

Doctors in Amritsar, Punjab removed 40 knives from a 42-year-old man who had been swallowing them over about two months because he "felt like eating them." The man, a police head constable, was admitted with stomach pain, loss of appetite, weight loss and weakness. Initial ultrasound suggested a mass; endoscopy and CT scans revealed multiple metallic knives of various sizes—some open, some rusted and broken, some closed—inside his stomach. A five-member surgical team performed a five-hour operation to extract the knives; the patient is now stable. Treating physicians said the case appeared linked to a psychological compulsion and called the surgery one of the most unnerving they had encountered.

French prosecutors have filed preliminary charges of complicity in murder, theft and involvement in preparing a terrorist attack against Abdelkader Merah, 29, the older brother of Mohammed (Mohamed) Merah, who was killed by police after a 30–32 hour siege of his Toulouse flat. Mohammed Merah, 23, admitted during the standoff to killing three Jewish schoolchildren and a teacher, a rabbi, and three paratroopers in separate attacks; he was shot dead by a police sniper and found to have been hit by more than 20 bullets.

Authorities say inquiries produced “grave and matching pointers” suggesting Abdelkader’s plausible participation as an accomplice in a terrorist enterprise. He was arrested with a woman (later released) and denies the charges, though he acknowledges being present when his brother stole a scooter used in the attacks. Prosecutors and police have described him as a radical Islamist; traces of possible explosive material were reportedly found in a car he owned, and he was previously questioned about allegedly helping smuggle jihadists to Iraq in 2007. Abdelkader’s lawyer says he condemns his brother’s actions and fears being made a scapegoat.

Under French law, preliminary charges indicate strong suspicion but allow magistrates more time to investigate and decide whether to bring the case to trial. Their mother, Zoulika Aziri, was questioned and released without charges. The killings prompted silent unity marches in Toulouse and Paris calling for tolerance.

The United States defeated Mexico 1-0 at Estadio Azteca on Aug. 15, 2012—its first victory in Mexico in 75 years and 25th meeting there (previously 0-23-1). The lone goal came in the 80th minute: a sequence started by substitute Brek Shea, a pass to Terrence Boyd and a backheel that found defender Michael Orozco Fiscal, who scored from close range for his first international goal. Goalkeeper Tim Howard preserved the lead with crucial late saves on Javier "Chicharito" Hernández.

Mexico dominated possession (15-6 shots, 10-0 corners) but failed to convert several good chances; the U.S. defended resolutely with a makeshift central pairing of Maurice Edu and Geoff Cameron. The American roster was below full strength as several regulars were absent and European clubs had just resumed, but coach Jürgen Klinsmann hailed the result as historic and confidence-building for World Cup 2014 qualifying. The win followed a similarly notable friendly victory over Italy earlier that year and prompted celebratory scenes among U.S. players and staff—Klinsmann quipped it was time to "change the sign" in the Azteca tunnel that had recorded the U.S.'s winless history there.

California will stop enforcing a blanket rule that barred all registered sex offenders from living within 2,000 feet of schools or parks and will instead apply residency limits case-by-case, the state corrections department announced. The policy change follows a California Supreme Court decision this month that found the so-called "Jessica’s Law" restriction unconstitutional in San Diego County; state officials say the court’s reasoning likely applies statewide. Corrections officials will review thousands of parolees over about two months to determine who should remain subject to residency limits. High‑risk offenders — those with current or prior convictions for lewd acts on a child under 14 — will still be prohibited from living within a half‑mile of K–12 schools, and officials expect parole agents to retain restrictions for people with convictions indicating a propensity to abuse children. The move aims to address critics’ concerns that blanket restrictions force many parolees into homelessness and transience in urban areas, while opponents such as Jessica’s Law author George Runner say it oversteps the court’s ruling and disregards voter intent. The state has roughly 6,000 registered sex‑offender parolees who must report addresses under Megan’s Law.

China has been strengthening defenses and realigning forces along its 880-mile border with North Korea and in neighboring regions to prepare for a possible crisis, including the prospect of U.S. military action. Chinese official military and government reporting and outside experts indicate many measures were implemented in recent months after being set in motion last year.

Key steps reported:
- Formation of a new border defense brigade conducting patrols, intelligence gathering and more detailed mapping of the tri-border area (North Korea, Russia, Mongolia).
- Deployment of 24-hour surveillance across the border area using drones, patrol vehicles and high-tech cameras.
- Increased overall combat readiness and training along the Chinese–North Korean frontier, as stated by government spokesmen.

Drivers and concerns:
- Beijing’s primary worry is not a conventional invasion but a large refugee flow from North Korea into densely populated, economically important northeastern China. Analysts predict a conflict could push hundreds of thousands or millions of civilians across the border, posing major humanitarian, economic and security strains similar to regional refugee crises elsewhere.
- Rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula—driven by North Korean missile and nuclear activity, U.S. pressure and some U.S. officials’ talk of regime change—have heightened China’s contingency planning. Chinese commentary includes calls to prepare for war contingencies and proposals (in some state media and retired officers’ op-eds) such as refugee camps in North Korean territory.

Diplomacy and posture:
- Beijing publicly encourages negotiations and has criticized both North Korean weapons tests and what it deems provocative rhetoric by the U.S. and South Korea. Official spokespeople emphasize that military means should not be used to resolve the peninsula issue, even as they note sustained readiness along the border.

Overall, China appears to be operationalizing contingency measures to manage potential military escalation or humanitarian fallout on the Korean Peninsula while continuing to press for diplomatic solutions.

Vote With Your Purse is a multi‑year research project from She Should Run (SSR), done with the Center for Responsive Politics, that analyzes women’s political giving and its relationship to women’s representation in elected office. The reports (2007, 2009, and 2012) document trends, diagnose causes, and offer practical recommendations for increasing women’s financial support of candidates—especially female candidates—to better match women’s voting and economic power.

Key findings (2010 cycle)
- Women accounted for only 26–27% of recorded federal political contributions to candidates, PACs, and party committees in 2010, down from 31% in 2008 and roughly 30% in 2006.
- Women made 27% of contributions to individual candidates (a 6.3% drop from 2008), 21% of PAC contributions, 38% of contributions to the Democratic National Committee and 24% to the Republican National Committee.
- Women contributed 30% of individual donations to Democrats and 25% to Republicans.
- Female candidates, however, were strong fundraisers: in 2010 female House incumbents raised about $100,000 more than male incumbents and female challengers raised about $74,000 more than male challengers.
- Very few candidates relied primarily on women’s donations—only 4 of 2,215 candidates received more than half their contributions from women.

Interpretation and implications
- The report identifies a probable correlation between declines in women’s political giving and the 2010 backslide in women’s representation in Congress. Women make up over half the population but only about 17% of Congress.
- SSR argues the moment is ripe to grow women’s political giving so it better reflects their economic clout and voting power. Small, coordinated gifts (e.g., $5 from many women) could materially affect the financing of female candidates.

Why women give less
- Research suggests many women do not see that small donations make a difference, do not view political giving as connected to social change, and are turned off by the perceived “dirty” aspects of politics.
- Women often don’t view political contribution as a civic responsibility on par with voting or volunteering.

Recommendations to campaigns to attract more women donors
- Emphasize the concrete impact of contributions on specific issues.
- Frame political giving as a civic or social responsibility.
- Provide clear, independent information about platforms and transparent explanations of how funds will be used.
- Create opportunities for donors to interact with campaigns and candidates, and involve women more directly in the process.

Overall message
Despite being effective fundraisers themselves, women underinvest in politics compared with men. Increasing women’s political giving—by linking donations to issues, responsibility, and transparency—could help close the gender gap in both fundraising and representation.

Summary:

Recent events on Mount Everest have highlighted two interlinked problems: overcrowding from a booming commercial climbing industry and increasing instability of the mountain environment. Dramatic images of long lines of climbers—hundreds queued between camps and again on summit days—illustrate how many amateurs now attempt the peak, often on the same narrow route and fixed ropes during a single short weather window. That congestion increases risk, especially when teams must decide whether to press on after weeks of investment.

Some operators have responded more cautiously: in May 2012 Russell Brice’s Himex abruptly abandoned its expedition, citing unusually warm temperatures, unstable ice and seracs, rockfall on the Lhotse Face, and near-miss avalanches. Brice’s decision, rare because commercial climbers find it hard to turn back after heavy investment, proved prescient after a catastrophic avalanche in April 2014 when a massive serac collapse in the Khumbu Icefall killed 16 Nepali high-altitude workers supporting guided teams—the deadliest accident in Everest history.

The human cost falls disproportionately on Nepali Sherpas and other local high-altitude workers. Sherpas perform the most dangerous work—carrying heavy loads, fixing ropes, installing ladders—and therefore spend many more hours in the hazardous Icefall and other exposed terrain. While Western climbers’ mortality has fallen in recent decades (thanks to liberal oxygen use, prophylactic medicines, better forecasting, and other advances), Sherpa fatalities have surged: analyses show Sherpa death rates on Everest far exceed those of dangerous occupations like commercial fishing or military deployment, and rates rose sharply in recent years (e.g., an especially high toll from 2004–2014). Compensation and insurance for families are small relative to the risks and earnings involved.

The avalanche triggered widespread anger among Sherpas over low government compensation offers and inadequate protections. They issued demands—higher compensation, better insurance, a relief fund partly financed by permit fees, guaranteed pay if the season is canceled, and a memorial—and threatened to strike. Many expeditions, meanwhile, weigh abandoning the season against huge financial losses.

Climate change is probably exacerbating the hazards: Himalayan glaciers have shrunk significantly, temperatures are rising, and the ice and rock are becoming more unstable, increasing the likelihood of seracs and rockfall. At the same time, modern communications and media coverage (photos, live updates, GPS tracking) have amplified Everest’s allure, attracting more climbers and turning ascents into spectator events, which perpetuates the overcrowding problem.

In short, Everest faces a dangerous convergence: more climbers concentrated into narrow summit windows and routes, and a warming, more unstable mountain environment—an arrangement that disproportionately endangers the local workers who make commercial ascents possible and that increasingly tests the limits of current management, regulation, and safety practices.

Summary:

Newt Gingrich, who registered a political group called "American Solutions for Winning the Future" (a 527) on October 6, 2006, has long used the phrase “Winning the Future.” When President Obama unveiled the same slogan during his 2011 State of the Union address, and later joked about it at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, some observers (and humorists like Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert) noted the overlap. Gingrich’s campaign, which launched with the slogan “Win the Future,” continues to use the phrase and framed the overlap as an opportunity for debate rather than a grievance; spokesman Rick Tyler said Gingrich welcomes a “head on debate” over which policies will actually “win the future.”

Summary:

Bill Cosby, 79, stood trial in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania in a high-profile case arising from Andrea Constand’s allegation that he drugged and sexually assaulted her at his home in 2004. Though more than 50 women have publicly accused Cosby of similar misconduct over decades, the criminal trial focused primarily on Constand’s account and testimony from one other accuser that prosecutors were allowed to present to show a pattern. Cosby denied wrongdoing, has said he will not testify, and previously described his contact with Constand as consensual; in a 2005 civil deposition (unsealed in 2015) he admitted obtaining Quaaludes in the past to give to women.

Background and timeline:
- Constand, then a Temple University employee, says Cosby gave her blue pills and wine, after which she became disoriented and was molested while incapacitated. She reported the incident to police in 2005, but the district attorney declined prosecution then. She filed a civil suit that was settled in 2006; Cosby gave a deposition in that case.
- The matter reemerged after a 2014 viral Hannibal Buress routine prompted dozens more women to come forward. The public outcry and the unsealing of Cosby’s deposition led prosecutors to charge him in December 2015 with three counts of aggravated indecent assault related to Constand.
- Many women who accused Cosby cannot pursue criminal charges because statutes of limitations have expired; their public accusations, however, shaped public opinion and contributed to the decision to reopen the case.

Key trial issues:
- The trial largely became a “he said, she said” dispute hinging on Constand’s credibility, the passage of time (the alleged incident occurred in 2004), and scarce forensic evidence. The defense planned to attack inconsistencies, delay in reporting, and Constand’s behavior after the alleged assault; prosecutors planned to use expert testimony to explain delayed reporting and to introduce testimony from one other accuser to show a pattern.
- Cosby’s unsealed deposition—where he said he used Quaaludes to obtain sex from women—was central evidence leading to his arrest. Cosby’s decision not to testify removed a direct courtroom denial, which defense and observers noted could complicate jurors’ impressions.
- The trial’s outcome carried broader cultural stakes: observers warned an acquittal might be perceived by the public as exonerating him of all accusations and could discourage other survivors from seeking justice, while a conviction could encourage more reporting and influence debates about statutes of limitations, rape culture, race, and celebrity accountability.

Public reaction and legacy:
- Cosby’s fall from status as a beloved cultural figure (“America’s Dad”) was swift: media projects were canceled, institutions severed ties, and public perception shifted sharply as dozens of women told similar stories of being drugged and assaulted.
- The case revived national conversations about sexual assault, evidence challenges in historic allegations, victims’ reluctance to report immediately, and whether legal rules (like statutes of limitations) should change to reflect these realities.
- Andrea Constand—portrayed as private but resolute—testified amid intense scrutiny, and many other accusers viewed her role as representing those who could no longer bring criminal charges.

Overall, while the trial addressed only Constand’s allegations in court, its proceedings and outcome had significant symbolic and practical implications for how American society treats historic sexual-assault allegations against powerful, famous individuals.

A small Northern Song dynasty Ding bowl — a finely made, thin-walled, ivory-glazed ceramic with incised lotus decoration and overlapping exterior leaves — sold for $2.2 million at Sotheby’s after being discovered at a New York garage sale. The family bought the piece for $3 in 2007 and kept it on their mantle until they sought expert advice and consigned it; Sotheby’s had estimated $200,000–$300,000. London dealer Giuseppe Eskenazi won the lot over four other bidders.

The bowl exemplifies the highest-quality Ding ware: feather-light, near-white body that needed no slip, an ivory glaze that pools in darker “tears,” and spontaneous, fluid incised design. Its shape is rare among Ding bowls but is known from contemporary Song silver examples. Only one virtually identical bowl is known — in the British Museum, bequeathed by Henry J. Oppenheim in 1947.

Ding ware was produced at kilns in Quyang, Ding county (Hebei) and was prized in later centuries as one of the “five great wares.” Early Ding pieces were simple utilitarian wares; from the late 11th century they became increasingly carved and molded. Scholars note that official Ding wares often imitated more precious materials such as gold and silver found in palace treasures. The Sotheby’s sale follows other notable “garage find” art stories, including a recent Long Island discovery of Arthur Pinajian works.

Japanese police have arrested Masaaki Osaka, a 67-year-old former high-ranking member of the left-wing Japan Revolutionary Communist League (Chukaku-ha), who had been a fugitive for more than 45 years. Osaka is accused of murdering a 21-year-old police officer during violent street protests in Tokyo’s Shibuya Ward in November 1971. Authorities say he assaulted the officer with a steel pipe, doused him in petrol and set him on fire. 

Osaka was detained in May during a police raid on an apartment in Hiroshima linked to the Chukaku-ha; he was initially arrested for an unrelated minor offence (obstructing a police officer) and later identified by DNA testing, since fingerprints from the original crime were not available. He has reportedly remained silent since his capture. Osaka’s face had appeared on wanted posters in Tokyo for over four decades; Japanese media say he evaded arrest with help from sympathizers within the group. 

Japan abolished the statute of limitations for murder in 2010, and prosecutors have formally charged Osaka with five offences including murder. The case is now being handled in Tokyo.

A California woman, 30-year-old Michelle Hadley, has been exonerated after spending nearly four months in jail on charges stemming from Craigslist “rape-fantasy” ads and alleged threats. Orange County prosecutors concluded Hadley was framed by 31-year-old Angela Maria Diaz, who has now been charged with numerous felonies and misdemeanors for orchestrating an elaborate setup.

Key points:
- Hadley was arrested in June and again in July 2016 on accusations that she violated a restraining order and posted Craigslist ads soliciting “rape fantasies” using the identity of Diaz, the pregnant new wife of Hadley’s former boyfriend (an unnamed U.S. Marshals deputy). She faced severe charges, including attempted forcible rape, and was held on bonds up to $1 million before being released in October.
- Prosecutors say Diaz fabricated the threats and postings by sending emails to herself, impersonating Hadley, using VPNs and proxy servers, forging documents, and impersonating others. Diaz is accused of posting the ads herself, luring at least two men to her residence, then calling police so those incidents appeared to corroborate her claims.
- Diaz allegedly also faked a pregnancy and a cervical cancer diagnosis, altered paychecks, pretended to be an attorney, forged doctor’s notes, and submitted a false restraining order petition under penalty of perjury.
- After a reinvestigation prompted by Hadley’s defense attorney, authorities traced the threatening emails to Diaz’s devices and locations. The district attorney publicly cleared Hadley and charged Diaz with multiple counts including kidnapping, false imprisonment, forgery, grand theft, perjury, and numerous counts of falsely reporting crimes. If convicted, Diaz faces years in prison and county jail.
- Diaz was arrested in Phoenix and awaits extradition to California. Prosecutors have not established a clear motive beyond possible interpersonal conflict involving the shared former partner; investigators say there’s no evidence the husband was involved.

Hadley, an MBA student, said the experience was traumatic; prosecutors stressed the need to clear her name both legally and publicly.

Reports say Jodie Foster and photographer Alexandra Hedison’s relationship has become very serious, prompting Foster to give up alcohol and reportedly join Alcoholics Anonymous and a 12-step program. According to tabloid sources, Hedison — a recovering alcoholic with over a decade sober — encouraged Foster to stop casual drinking after it became a point of contention. Insiders claim Hedison wants Foster sober for at least a year before marriage and that the couple are “crazy in love.” 

Separately, a National Enquirer item alleges Ellen DeGeneres warned Foster against marrying Hedison, citing Ellen’s past relationship with Hedison and suggesting Ellen has marital regrets with Portia de Rossi; the piece speculates about the state of Ellen’s marriage and urges caution. Both stories are sourced to celebrity tabloids and include speculation about commitment ceremonies and matching rings.

Playboy will stop publishing fully nude photos in its print edition as part of a redesign to take effect with the March issue. The change—approved by founder and editor in chief Hugh Hefner—reflects executives’ view that the internet has made nudity ubiquitous and pornographic content freely available, so nudity is now "passé." The magazine will continue to run women in provocative poses but not fully nude images. Playboy’s website already bans nudity to comply with social platforms, a move that boosted web traffic.

Circulation has fallen from millions in the 1970s to about 800,000 today, and executives hope the non-nude shift will broaden appeal to younger readers and advertisers and protect the brand’s licensing business. The decision prompted debate: some see it as a necessary adaptation to changing media and distribution realities, while others warn it risks alienating long-time readers and eroding Playboy’s identity, even as its strong tradition of high-profile interviews and cultural relevance remains part of its legacy.

California Assembly Majority Leader Ian Calderon introduced Assembly Bill 1884, which would require sit-down restaurants to provide plastic straws only upon customer request. The proposal applies to dine-in restaurants (not bars or fast-food establishments) and is intended to reduce single-use plastic waste that ends up in landfills, waterways and oceans. Calderon said the bill is not a ban on straws and would not criminalize servers who hand them out; he also noted the bill’s current reference to misdemeanor penalties (up to six months in jail and/or a fine up to $1,000 under the existing California Retail Food Code) would be amended during the legislative process. The move is framed as a small step to raise awareness and curb the roughly 500 million straws used daily in the U.S., a product that is rarely recycled and frequently found in coastal cleanup collections.

A Dutch father whose 17-year-old daughter, Elsemiek de Borst, was killed when Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 was shot down on July 17 published an emotional open letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin. In the Facebook post, also printed in a Dutch paper and translated into English, Hans de Borst blames Putin and the Russian-backed separatists (and also references the Ukrainian government) for the missile strike that destroyed his daughter’s future—her plans to take final exams and study engineering at Delft. He condemns those he holds responsible and signs the message “Elsemiek’s father… whose life is ruined.” The report notes the post was shared via Facebook and appeared in Hart Van Nederland. The remainder of the document contains unrelated information about web-crawling and archiving efforts.

Judge W. Mitchell Nance, who sits on the 43rd Judicial Circuit’s 2nd Division (Family Court) in Barren and Metcalfe counties, issued an order saying he will no longer hear adoption cases involving gay adults, citing a “matter of conscience” and judicial-ethics rules that require recusal when a judge has personal bias or prejudice. Nance, a judge in family court since 2004, wrote that he believes allowing a “practicing homosexual” to adopt would not be in a child’s best interest and therefore disqualified himself from such cases. He said the move was intended to minimize disruption and that the other division judge will handle any adoptions affected, so he does not expect delays for same-sex couples seeking to adopt.

The decision drew support from some conservative groups and sharp criticism from lawyers, judicial-ethics experts and LGBT advocates, who called the blanket recusal discriminatory and argued it suggests Nance cannot carry out his oath to apply the law impartially. Critics noted that Kentucky law permits gay adoption and that the Supreme Court’s 2015 Obergefell decision legalized same-sex marriage nationwide. Some legal commentators said Nance’s stance could require broader recusals in other matters involving gay litigants. Nance said he has previously recused himself from adoption cases involving gay parents and would decline to perform a same-sex marriage if asked.

A community town hall, "Rejecting Islamophobia: A Community Stand Against Hate," will be held in Dearborn, Michigan on Sunday, April 29 at 1:00 PM at the Doubletree Hotel (5801 Southfield Road). Organized by the Arab American Institute (AAI) and local partners, the event responds to an anti-Islam conference by Pamela Geller and Robert Spencer—the "Jessica Mokdad Human Rights Conference"—being held in Dearborn the same day. AAI leaders Jim Zogby and Maya Berry, journalist Sarah Posner, Eli Clifton (co-author of the report Fear, Inc.), interfaith and community leaders, and Michigan public officials will attend to challenge Islamophobic rhetoric, reject the exploitation of the late Jessica Mokdad’s name, and discuss community strategies to confront anti-Arab and anti-Muslim bias. The town hall frames recent incidents—Quran burnings, mosque protests, anti-Sharia bills, and prior provocations in Dearborn—as part of a continuing problem that undermines religious freedom and American values, and calls for a unified local and national response.

Former President George W. Bush canceled a planned February 12 keynote appearance at a Keren Hayesod charity gala in Geneva after mounting pressure and threats of protests and legal action if he visited Switzerland. Human rights groups intended to submit a 2,500-page criminal complaint in Geneva accusing Bush of authorizing torture—most notably waterboarding—at Guantanamo Bay and sought his arrest and investigation under the UN Convention Against Torture, to which Switzerland is a party. Rights organizations including Human Rights Watch, FIDH and the Center for Constitutional Rights said the cancellation was linked to those legal moves, arguing Bush feared prosecution or extradition. Swiss court officials noted former heads of state retain some diplomatic immunity, and Keren Hayesod’s organizers said they cancelled Bush’s participation for security reasons, citing concerns about protests and potential unrest, not the criminal complaints. The dispute highlights tensions between claims of impunity in the U.S. and efforts abroad to hold leaders accountable for alleged war crimes.
