Nearly three years of Syria’s civil war have produced a massive, protracted refugee crisis. Refugees have surged from about 300,000 a year ago to 2.1 million, with U.N. forecasts as high as 3.5 million by year’s end. Many Syrians, including Zakaria Deeb and his family, are making dangerous, sometimes fruitless journeys to border areas such as Kilis in Turkey, sleeping outdoors or in makeshift shelters when camps are full or access is restricted. Cross-border fighting and stray fire regularly threaten civilians; a stray bullet recently wounded a 5-year-old in a Turkish camp.

Host countries—Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq—are under growing strain. Camps are overflowing and urban neighborhoods are absorbing large numbers of arrivals, raising rents, pushing down wages and fueling local tensions. Lebanon could soon host refugees equal to a quarter of its population. Aid agencies and governments are quietly planning for a long-term crisis, emphasizing support for both humanitarian operations and the host communities and governments coping with sustained displacement.

Turkey’s border regions show porous control: people cross illegally, smugglers operate openly, and security forces engage in repeated attempts to intercept migrants. Inside Syria the conflict remains fragmented and violent, with multiple armed groups (including ISIS and various rebel factions) battling each other and government forces, causing continued displacement and widespread destruction that make return unlikely for many. The report is accompanied by extensive photographic documentation of the war’s devastation and human toll across Syria.

Former four-term Louisiana governor Edwin Edwards, 86, announced he is running for the open U.S. House seat in Louisiana’s 6th District at a Baton Rouge press conference, appearing with his wife Trina and their infant son Eli. Edwards, who served three prior terms in Congress and nearly nine years in federal prison on extortion, fraud and racketeering convictions, said he’s confident he can run and win and stressed second chances and forgiveness. He denied wrongdoing in the corruption case and noted the Constitution does not bar a convicted felon from serving in Congress.

Edwards outlined priorities including expanding Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act (criticizing Republican Gov. Bobby Jindal for refusing expansion), improving healthcare accessibility, supporting the Keystone XL pipeline, pursuing infrastructure projects such as high-speed rail between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, and addressing oil, gas and water-aquifer concerns. He said he hopes to serve on public works and agriculture committees.

Pundits view his candidacy as unlikely to flip the strongly Republican-leaning district—redistricting removed much of Baton Rouge’s African-American population—and see him more as a high-profile longshot who could reach a runoff on name recognition. The seat is open because Rep. Bill Cassidy is running for Senate. Edwards has filed candidacy papers; the Republican field already includes a dozen-plus contenders. The announcement followed recent media attention on Edwards’s post-prison life, including a brief reality TV show featuring his much-younger wife.

Republican state Sen. Frank Lasee, a candidate for the GOP nomination in Wisconsin’s 8th Congressional District, is under scrutiny over where he actually resides. Lasee lists a De Pere condo as his voting address and says he lives there most of the time, but that unit had been advertised as a “luxury” Airbnb rental for $210 a night until recently. Journal Sentinel reporters were able to attempt a booking; Lasee’s wife, who owns a separate house in Racine (in Speaker Paul Ryan’s district), questioned and then denied the request, and the listing was later removed. 

Lasee acknowledged a “crazy living arrangement,” saying he occasionally stays at the Racine house. He says a 2014 complaint about his residence was dismissed after he produced a 2011 lease showing he and his wife were occupants and could not sublease without owner consent. Records also show Lasee claimed the Racine address in past court matters and that both he and his wife are on mortgages for the Racine home. He has collected legislative mileage reimbursements consistent with commuting from De Pere. Critics and local commentators have raised doubts about his explanation, suggesting the issue is politically sensitive because declaring the Racine address would place him in Paul Ryan’s district. Lasee attributes recent attention to campaign opponents.

Two related incidents involving Ganga activists unfolded in Rishikesh. Sant Gopaldas, 36, who had been fasting since June 24 at Triveni and Bag ghats to protest mining in the Ganga riverbed, was rushed to AIIMS Rishikesh early Saturday (admitted to emergency at 3:45 a.m.). Treated in the endocrinology ward, doctors said he was dehydrated with a blood sugar of 65; he has refused food and treatment and is receiving IV fluids. Hospital authorities have been authorized to take any measures, including force‑feeding, to save his life.

Separately, prominent environmentalist G.D. Agarwal (also known as Swami Gyan Swaroop Sanand), 86, died at AIIMS Rishikesh after more than 15 weeks on a hunger strike protesting government inaction on cleaning the Ganges and opposing hydroelectric projects. Agarwal, a PhD in environmental engineering, had begun fasting on June 22 demanding a law to protect the river. His death from cardiac arrest drew widespread tributes and calls for further action from political leaders and activists, and prompted demands by some for an independent investigation. The broader context noted criticisms of the government’s flagship Ganga-cleaning program as underperforming.

Federal and state officials are investigating the suspected shooting deaths of four male southern (California) sea otters found washed up near Santa Cruz in mid‑to‑late August. Three carcasses found between August 12–19 showed gunshot wounds; a fourth, recovered August 20, was too deteriorated to confirm but may also have been shot. The US Fish and Wildlife Service has offered a $10,000 reward for information leading to arrest and conviction. The otters — a federally protected, threatened species under the Endangered Species Act and protected by the Marine Mammal Protection Act and state law — number about 3,000 in California; killing one can carry fines up to $100,000 and possible jail time. The bodies were sent to the Fish and Wildlife forensic lab in Oregon for necropsies, and investigators stressed the ecological importance of sea otters and that killings of protected wildlife are crimes.

Swiss hospital University Hospital Zurich said Sergio Marchionne, the long-time Fiat Chrysler (FCA) chief who died at 66, had been receiving recurring treatment for a “serious illness” for more than a year and that all available medical options were used. The hospital issued the statement to counter rumors about his treatment but declined to disclose details of the condition.

FCA responded that, because of medical privacy, it had no knowledge of Marchionne’s health beyond being informed that he underwent shoulder surgery earlier and, on July 20, being notified by his family of a “serious deterioration” that would prevent his return to work. The company said it acted promptly when informed. The revelations have prompted questions about how long Marchionne had been ill and what the company or board knew earlier. FCA had previously noted in its annual report the centrality of Marchionne to its strategy and said succession planning was challenging.

Workers at Goodyear’s loss-making tyre factory in Amiens, northern France, have detained two managers — production director Michel Dheilly and HR chief Bernard Glesser — inside the plant as part of a long-running dispute over plans to close the site. The factory has been the subject of sale or closure attempts for about five years and has seen violent protests, drawn government attention and generated protracted layoff procedures.

Union and works-council members say the action is a “reaction of despair” intended to pressure the company for a more generous voluntary redundancy package if no buyer is found. The detained managers have been given water and kept their phones; accounts differ on their treatment, with one saying conditions were sometimes “animated” but not cruel and the other refusing to speak under duress. Union leaders say offers of mattresses and blankets were declined.

“Bossnappings” were common during the financial crisis and, while punishable by up to five years in prison and large fines, are rarely prosecuted in France; police typically avoid intervention to prevent escalation. Goodyear called the seizure counterproductive and said efforts should focus on employees’ futures amid restructuring. Labor lawyers note such tactics often reflect desperation and have limited legal effectiveness, as pressured agreements can later be voided in court.

Oscar-winning actress Jodie Foster married photographer Alexandra Hedison over the past weekend, PEOPLE confirms. The couple had been dating since last summer and were publicly seen together at events and outings before their engagement. E! Online first reported the nuptials. Foster, 51, notably gave a widely discussed Golden Globes speech in 2013 that many viewed as her coming-out moment, during which she thanked her ex-partner Cydney Bernard, mother of her two sons. A representative for Foster confirmed the marriage.

YouTube stars Liza Koshy and David Dobrik—who together reach over 20 million subscribers—posted an emotional video announcing they split six months earlier. Both creators, known for comedic vlogs that often featured their relationship, said growing apart and busy, separate lives prompted the breakup; Liza decided to end it because she felt they’d become distant, and Dobrik admitted he’d felt it too but hadn’t acted. The video, notable for its candidness (jokes, tears and affirmations that they remain best friends), quickly went viral.

The pair explained they delayed telling fans out of anger and to avoid misleading viewers who follow their personal lives closely. Commentators note that for influencers whose brands are tied to their relationships, public disclosure can help prevent fan harassment or confusion; experts also say the split is unlikely to harm either creator’s career and could even draw attention if they later reconcile. Public reaction mixed shock and support, with many praising the mature, amicable tone of the breakup.

Researchers in Australia surveyed 532 men (ages 18–72) in the U.S. and India about their facial hair and attitudes toward women, and found a clear link between having facial hair and endorsing hostile sexism. Men were grouped by facial hair (clean-shaven, stubble, mustache, goatee, beard). Around 70% of participants had some facial hair; only about one-third of men expressed no sexist attitudes. After controlling for nationality, age, education, relationship status and other demographics, men with any facial hair scored significantly higher on measures of hostile sexism (beliefs that women are inferior, manipulative, or that traditional male dominance is legitimate) but not higher on benevolent sexism (protective, chivalrous attitudes).

Hostile sexism and nationality were the strongest predictors of whether a man had facial hair. Indian participants (86% with facial hair) scored higher on sexism than American participants (65% with facial hair). Higher education was linked to more benevolent but less hostile sexism. The authors suggest two nonexclusive explanations: men who already hold hostile, patriarchal views may grow facial hair because it accentuates masculinity and dominance; or having facial hair changes how men are perceived (more masculine/dominant) and thus encourages adherence to masculine norms, including hostile sexist attitudes. The study was published in Archives of Sexual Behavior.

Actor Mark Salling, best known for playing Noah "Puck" Puckerman on Glee, was arrested December 29, 2015, after the Los Angeles Police Department’s Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force executed a search warrant at his Sunland, California home. Authorities forced entry with a battering ram after he did not respond at the door. Officers seized his computer, tablets and cellphones after he refused to provide passwords; investigators reportedly found hundreds (reports later said over a thousand) of images of child sexual exploitation on his devices. Salling was taken into custody, booked at the LAPD Metropolitan Detention Center, and released on $20,000 bail the same afternoon; his first court date was set for January 22. Police say the probe followed a tip received up to two weeks earlier; some reports indicate an ex-girlfriend alerted authorities, though officials would not confirm the tipster’s identity. Salling previously faced a 2013 sexual battery lawsuit that was settled for $2.7 million. The investigation was ongoing at the time of reporting.

Several residents of Bennington, Vt., reported being attacked by a gray squirrel over the past week, prompting concern about possible rabies exposure. On March 15, 2011, Kevin McDonald told the Bennington Banner he was shoveling snow when a squirrel jumped onto his back and shoulders, scratched him, was thrown off, then jumped back on twice before running up a tree. Neighbors on East Street reported similar encounters; a game warden has spoken with two people there. One woman was bitten on the back of the neck and is undergoing a rabies vaccination series on her doctor's advice.

Local Game Warden Travis Buttle said he can do little unless the animal is captured; testing for rabies requires the animal be caught and euthanized. He noted that an animal rabid enough to be actively aggressive would likely have died by now and that these incidents are unusual because they appear unprovoked. Vermont Public Health Veterinarian Robert Johnson said there has never been a documented case of a squirrel transmitting rabies to a human and suggested the squirrel may have been previously kept as a pet and lost its fear of people, causing it to behave aggressively when encountering unfamiliar humans. Victims are advised to consult their doctors after any animal attack.

A government booklet from India’s Ayush ministry, compiled by the Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy (CCRYN), recommends that pregnant women avoid meat and eggs, shun “desire, anger, attachment, hatred and lust,” refrain from sex after conception (disputed by officials), keep calm, seek good company, have spiritual thoughts, read uplifting biographies, and hang pleasant pictures to benefit the child. The booklet was released ahead of International Yoga Day; Ayush officials say it compiles traditional yoga and naturopathy practices and does not explicitly advise abstaining from sex.

Medical experts and rationalists strongly criticized the guidance as unscientific and potentially dangerous in a country with high maternal malnutrition, anemia and maternal mortality. Doctors note that animal-source foods provide bioavailable protein and iron crucial in pregnancy, and that sexual activity is generally safe in uncomplicated pregnancies. Critics say the advice reflects religious or ideological influences from sections of the ruling Hindu-nationalist movement and risks worsening maternal and child health in India, where many women already face food insecurity and poor access to evidence-based care.

Summary:

The document explains that many widely used consumer chemicals—especially highly fluorinated chemicals (HFCs/PFAS), phthalates, flame retardants, phenols and fragrance compounds—are pervasive in household dust and consumer products (cookware, clothing, carpeting, food packaging, cosmetics, furniture, toys, etc.). Because HFCs have extremely strong carbon–fluorine bonds they resist breakdown, persist in people and the environment for years to millennia, bioaccumulate, and have been linked in studies to serious health effects (testicular and kidney cancer, liver dysfunction, hormonal and thyroid disruption, high cholesterol, obesity, ulcerative colitis, lower birth weight). Other common classes found in dust—phthalates and certain flame retardants—are associated with endocrine disruption, developmental and reproductive harms, decreased IQ, respiratory problems and cancer in animal studies.

Key findings and concerns:
- A meta-analysis of 26 peer-reviewed studies plus one unpublished dataset (dust samples from 14 U.S. states, multiple settings) found 45 chemicals commonly in indoor dust; 10 chemicals appeared in over 90% of samples.
- The most abundant was the phthalate DEHP; flame retardant TCEP ranked highest for estimated intake by preschool children. PFAS (PFOA, PFOS) are also widespread.
- Children are at higher risk due to hand-to-mouth behaviors and close contact with floors.
- Many chemicals lack thorough safety testing, and low-level cumulative exposures over time may be harmful. Fragrance chemicals and many others remain understudied.
- Magnetite nanoparticles from air pollution (likely vehicle exhaust) have been found in human brain tissue in small studies, raising concerns about air-derived nanoparticle impacts on brain health.

What can individuals do:
- Ask whether stain-resistant, nonstick or waterproof features are necessary.
- Avoid products labeled oil-repellant/stain-resistant; buy waterproof gear only when needed.
- Replace Teflon with cast iron, glass or ceramic cookware.
- Avoid microwave popcorn/greasy foods wrapped in paper that may contain fluorinated coatings.
- Avoid cosmetics listing PTFE or terms containing “perfluor”/“polyflor.”
- Wash hands before eating, wet-dust and vacuum with HEPA filters regularly, and mop to reduce dust ingestion.
- Walk or position yourself away from busy roads when possible to reduce inhalation of exhaust particles.

Policy and research context:
- Scientists worldwide signed the Madrid Statement urging limits on production/use of highly fluorinated chemicals; debate continues with industry responses.
- The U.S. chemical regulatory framework has been criticized as weak; recent reforms (Lautenberg Act) update the Toxic Substances Control Act but advocates remain uncertain whether it will be strong enough to remove harmful substances and protect public health.
- Researchers call for more testing, prioritization of chemicals for health assessment, development and adoption of safer alternatives, and stronger regulatory actions.

Resources and outreach:
- Advocacy and consumer pressure (asking manufacturers, supporting brands phasing out HFCs) can drive change.
- Several public health and regulatory agencies (CDC, EPA, FDA, ATSDR) provide information on specific chemicals (phthalates, etc.), and organizations like Silent Spring Institute offer tools (e.g., Detox Me app).

Bottom line:
Household dust and common consumer products are reservoirs for multiple potentially harmful chemicals. While uncertainties remain about safe exposure thresholds and combined effects, evidence of persistence, bioaccumulation, and links to adverse health outcomes—especially for children—supports taking practical steps to reduce exposures and pushing for stronger testing, regulatory action, and safer product alternatives.

A former CIA operative, Donald C. Rickard, has confessed that he played a key role in Nelson Mandela’s 1962 arrest by tipping off South African apartheid police, a revelation that has provoked calls for accountability. Rickard, who later served in various diplomatic posts and died aged 88, told filmmaker John Irvin in a recorded interview that he identified Mandela because he considered him “the world’s most dangerous communist outside of the Soviet Union.” Mandela was subsequently tried and imprisoned for nearly 28 years.

The disclosure prompted criticism from Mandela’s family and supporters. Mandla Mandela, the former president’s grandson and an ANC MP, called Rickard’s admission a “betrayal of our nation,” urged US President Barack Obama to apologize and disclose full details, and suggested the US should face UN censure for supporting the apartheid state. A veteran associate of Mandela described the CIA’s role as a “shameful act of betrayal” that hindered the anti‑apartheid struggle.

The piece also includes Rickard’s obituary, summarizing his life: born in Burma in 1928, his family fled during WWII, he studied in the US, married Elaine Grove in 1952, worked for the State Department with postings including Durban and Seoul, retired in 1978, and is survived by six children. An open memorial service was announced.

Nokia announced a major restructuring under CEO Stephen Elop: it cut its earnings forecast for the second time in nine weeks, warned the devices unit will post a deeper-than-expected second-quarter loss, and said it will eliminate up to 10,000 additional jobs (about one in three employees since Elop took over), close manufacturing and R&D sites in Finland, Germany and Canada, and wind down projects to preserve priority work. Total planned job cuts since 2010 now exceed 40,000. The actions include closing the Salo plant in Finland and facilities in Ulm and Burnaby, and selling luxury-phone unit Vertu to EQT.

Nokia’s share price plunged (around 16–18%) to lows not seen since 1996, cutting market value below €7bn (about $8.6bn). Credit-default swap spreads and analyst warnings signaled rising default risk as the company burns cash; Nokia reported €4.9bn net cash at March 31 but faces significant restructuring outflows (roughly €650m in the remainder of 2012 and €600m in 2013) and rapid cash depletion unless margins improve.

Elop reaffirmed commitment to Windows Phone and the Lumia line, which shipped just over 2 million units last quarter versus Apple’s 35m iPhones, but said product progress has been slower than hoped. Nokia aims for about €1.6bn of additional savings and to reduce annual devices-unit costs to ~€3bn by end-2013 (from €5.35bn in 2010). Several senior executives will depart or be reassigned. Analysts say Nokia must stabilize quickly to avoid insolvency or become an unattractive takeover target.

Four years after entering a Chinese modeling contest to win a laptop for school, Liu Wen — born in 1988 in Yongzhou, Hunan, and originally training to be a teacher — has become the first model of Asian descent to walk the Victoria’s Secret runway. Plucked from a regular casting call, the 21‑year‑old 5'10" model moved from China to Beijing after her contest win, graced Chinese FHM, Marie Claire, Elle and Vogue, and debuted on runways in Milan, Paris and New York for designers including Anna Sui, Dolce & Gabbana, Alexander McQueen, Chloé and Lanvin. She said she watched the Victoria’s Secret show growing up and was surprised and honored by the opportunity; she keeps daily contact with her family and plans possibly to act or return to teaching eventually.

The story also profiles the massive backstage effort behind the Victoria’s Secret show filmed at the Lexington Armory and airing on CBS: Angels spend three to five hours in hair and makeup—often with five stylists per model—and heavy body makeup and glitter are applied; some costumes are elaborate and heavy (one outfit required a 15‑pound sandbag to balance sharp, 30‑pound tinsel‑like pieces). The piece highlights veteran models like Selita Ebanks and Heidi Klum, notes spectacle elements such as a $3 million diamond bra and oversized watch wings, and emphasizes the physical demands and theatrical production that create the show’s flashy runway spectacle.

Gallup’s daily tracking poll (seven-day rolling average through Oct. 24) shows Republican Mitt Romney ahead of President Obama by 50% to 47% among likely voters (margin of error ±2 points); among registered voters Obama retains a 48–47 edge. That Gallup lead has been larger earlier in the week (5–7 points), which drew attention because it was an outlier versus most other national polls. The RealClearPolitics average has Romney up by under 1 point (47.7–47.1); an AP-GfK survey shows Romney 47–45. Battleground-state polls remain tight and mixed—Ohio polls ranged from tied to Obama +5—so many states are still toss-ups.

Analysis of recent tracking data and FiveThirtyEight’s “now-cast” suggests Romney’s post-Denver bounce may have peaked and Obama has regained some ground over the last week. On Wednesday, most daily trackers showed gains for Obama rather than Romney; FiveThirtyEight’s now-cast moved from a near tie around Oct. 12 to Obama +1.4 and raised Obama’s Electoral College win probability modestly. It’s unclear how much of this shift reflects the final debate (only a day or two of post-debate polling were included), and some movement could be statistical noise. Overall, Romney’s earlier gains are reflected in averages and models, but recent polls indicate the race may have ticked back slightly toward Obama.

The author conducted a data-driven deep dive into fortune cookies by buying 1,050 Panda-brand cookies (1,035 arrived), opening and digitizing their contents, and analyzing the fortunes, lucky-number sets, and Mandarin vocabulary printed inside.

Key findings:
- Scope and variety: The sample contained 676 unique fortunes, 556 unique lucky-number combinations, and 173 distinct Mandarin words/phrases. Because the bulk purchase represented a slice of a production run (fortunes spanning initial letters A–I and W–Y), the author estimates the total fortune corpus is roughly 1,200–1,600 unique fortunes.
- Lucky numbers: Comparing the cookie “lucky numbers” against Powerball drawings from Nov. 1997 to May 2017, treating each fortune’s numbers as tickets over 2,043 drawings, would have yielded about $4.4 million on $4.2 million of ticket purchases—better than random-number expected winnings ($1.7 million). This apparent “luck” can be explained by chance, a few matching big prizes, or post-hoc insertion of numbers; it does not prove genuine predictive power.
- Mandarin vocabulary: The 173 Chinese words approximate the vocabulary of a toddler—useful for food and basic needs, with 124 nouns (74 food-related), 21 verbs, and 21 adjectives. Not nearly enough to sustain real conversation, but enough to get by in a restaurant-shaped way.
- Fortune content and tone: Only ~22% of fortunes are predictive; the majority (~53%) address “you,” focusing on personal character, strengths and advice. Other themes appear less frequently (success/happiness, work/education, creativity, journeys, relationships). Language skews toward action and positivity (words like “good,” “life,” “go,” “never,” “make,” “always”).
- Originality and recreation: Many fortunes recycle clichés, famous quotes, or trite phrasing; some outright echo religious or pop-culture lines. The author also built a Markov-based bot using the corpus to generate new fortunes; some are bad, but occasionally the bot produces memorable lines.

Overall, fortune cookies are less about literal prophecy than short, often banal affirmations aimed at the reader. They offer a modest, food-focused pocket of Mandarin vocabulary and — by chance and repetition—occasionally produce lucky number sets that have coincidentally matched major lottery wins.

A British judge has issued a death certificate for Richard John “Lord” Lucan, more than 40 years after he vanished following the brutal murder of his children's nanny, Sandra Rivett, on Nov. 7, 1974. The High Court ruling allows Lucan’s son, George Bingham, to adopt the family name and become the 8th Earl of Lucan. Bingham said the decision brings long‑awaited closure; Rivett’s son Neil Berriman, who had opposed the application, said he believes Lucan is dead and welcomed the ruling while stressing his mother remains the forgotten victim.

Background: Lucan was suspected of attacking his estranged wife Veronica (who escaped) and fatally bludgeoning Rivett. His blood‑stained car was found abandoned near Newhaven days later and an inquest jury in 1975 named him Rivett’s killer. Dozens of unverified sightings were reported over the years in places such as Australia, South Africa and New Zealand. He was declared dead for probate in 1999, but the Presumption of Death Act (2014) enabled Bingham’s fresh application to obtain a death certificate for all purposes.

New and disputed accounts: Amid the long mystery, various theories persisted. A member of Lucan’s gambling set recently told MailOnline that Lucan shot himself at a private zoo and his body was fed to a tiger—an account sourced to a now‑dead circle of friends and impossible to verify. Other associates and investigators have suggested suicide by drowning at Newhaven or escape abroad; numerous sensational and conflicting claims have appeared over the decades.

Public reaction and legacy: The case remains contentious. Bingham acknowledged the title may be seen as tainted but called it his family name; Berriman and others continue to press for justice and answers about Rivett’s killing. The court’s decision formally closes one legal chapter of a long‑running British mystery but leaves many questions about Lucan’s fate unanswered.

Summary:

The document contains two celebrity pregnancy stories. 

- Michael Jordan and his wife Yvette Prieto are expecting identical twin girls due in April, confirmed by E! News. This will be Prieto’s first child and Jordan’s fourth; he has three grown children with ex-wife Juanita Vanoy. Jordan and Prieto married April 27 in a lavish Palm Beach, Florida ceremony attended by about 500 guests at Bethesda-by-the-Sea, followed by a larger celebration at the Bears Club near Jordan’s home.

- Bruce Willis and wife Emma Heming (Heming-Willis) are expecting their second child together, confirmed by Us Weekly and People. The couple—married in 2009—already have daughter Mabel Ray, about 20 months old. Willis, 58, who also has three daughters with ex-wife Demi Moore, has spoken about enjoying fatherhood and being more present.

A 20-year-old man, Chanel Lewis of Brooklyn, has been arrested and charged with murder in the strangulation death last summer of 30-year-old Karina Vetrano, who was attacked while out for a run near her Queens home on Aug. 2 and later found badly beaten in a marsh. Queens prosecutors say Lewis was expected to be arraigned and faces a sentence of 25 years to life if convicted. Police say DNA evidence — genetic material recovered under Vetrano’s fingernails and on her phone and neck — produced a profile that led to Lewis, and that he made “incriminating statements” when arrested. It appears the encounter was random. Information about his attorney was not immediately available.

Gustavo “Taby” Falcon, long the last fugitive of Miami’s 1980s “Cocaine Cowboys” era, was arrested April 12, 2017, more than 26 years after an arrest warrant was issued on April 10, 1991. The 55-year-old was taken into custody by U.S. Marshals in Kissimmee, Florida, while on a bicycle ride with his wife near Disney World after investigators tracked him to a rental home and conducted surveillance. Marshals confirmed his identity—despite helmets and sunglasses—before stopping him; he was booked without incident and ordered held without bond to be returned to South Florida to face conspiracy-to-import-cocaine charges.

Falcon’s brother Augusto “Willie” Falcon and partner Salvador “Sal” Magluta were major figures who smuggled roughly 75 tons of cocaine into South Florida in the 1980s. Gustavo was not considered a top leader and vanished ahead of a 1991 federal indictment that named him, Augusto and Magluta. Authorities had believed he was living abroad for years; records checks eventually tied a false Florida license to a Miami address and to the identity of “Luis Reiss,” which led marshals to the Kissimmee residence. Fraudulent IDs dated to 1997 were found; his wife also used fake identification but was not arrested.

Background: Augusto and Magluta built a multimillion-dollar drug operation and lived extravagantly; legal proceedings against them were marred by corruption (including jury bribery). Magluta later received a lengthy sentence after a second conviction; Augusto accepted a 20-year plea in 2003. Many assets from their operation were seized and sold by the government.

International outrage mounted after the Houla massacre in Syria, where more than 100 civilians — including dozens of women and children — were killed. Survivors and U.N. investigators say many victims were shot execution-style and there are strong suspicions that pro‑Assad fighters (including shabiha militias) were responsible, though the Syrian government denied culpability and blamed “armed terrorists.” The U.N. Human Rights Council called a special session and U.N. observers also verified separate killings in Deir el‑Zour.

In coordinated diplomatic protests, numerous countries expelled Syrian diplomats: the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Bulgaria and the Netherlands (in retaliation by Damascus) announced expulsions earlier in the week; Turkey and Japan joined on Wednesday, with Turkey ordering all Syrian embassy staff in Ankara to leave within 72 hours (while keeping limited consular services in Istanbul). Syria condemned the expulsions as hysteria and retaliated by expelling the Dutch chargé d’affaires; Moscow warned such moves could be misread as preludes to military intervention.

Kofi Annan, the U.N.-Arab League envoy, met President Bashar al‑Assad in Damascus as his six‑point peace plan remains unimplemented — heavy weapons and troops were supposed to be withdrawn in April but fighting has continued. His deputy briefed the U.N. Security Council, which heard bleak assessments: Western envoys urged stronger measures, while Russia and China reiterated opposition to outside military intervention and to U.N. sanctions, calling expulsions counterproductive. U.S. Ambassador Susan Rice warned that if the Security Council cannot compel compliance, the conflict could escalate into a wider, more sectarian proxy war and leave the international community considering actions outside the Council’s authority.

On the ground, shelling and clashes continued in Damascus suburbs and Homs; casualty reports from activist groups and the U.N. observer mission indicated ongoing, widespread violence. The U.S. also tightened economic pressure, announcing asset freezes on a Syrian bank. Overall, the Houla killings deepened Syria’s international isolation, exposed the failure of the Annan plan thus far, and intensified debate over whether stronger collective action is possible given Russia and China’s positions.

Renegade Pictures released a trailer for Brittany Murphy’s final film, Abandoned, in which she plays an intense role as a woman under psychiatric evaluation after her husband disappears. The release of Murphy’s death renewed attention to a pattern in show business where the last films of performers who died young often have dark, eerily prescient themes — examples cited include Heath Ledger (The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus and the posthumous impact of The Dark Knight), Aaliyah (Queen of the Damned), Bruce Lee (Game of Death), Brandon Lee (The Crow), Brad Renfro (The Informers), River Phoenix (Dark Blood, unfinished), and Judy Garland (I Could Go On Singing). 

Murphy’s sudden death also forced DVD-rental company Redbox to remove box-art images for her straight-to-DVD horror thriller Deadline after the cover — showing her character lying lifeless in a bathtub — became an insensitive reminder of her collapsing and dying in a bathroom. Redbox said it would continue to carry the film but would stop featuring that artwork and began pulling the images from kiosks and its website.

A federal judge in St. Louis has ruled that Carl and Janice Duffner can be compelled to plant turf grass in their St. Peters yard under a city ordinance requiring at least 50% turf coverage. The Duffners maintain a lush, turf-free flower garden and Janice has severe grass allergies. After receiving a compliance notice in 2014 they sought and were granted a variance that still required at least 5% turf; they refused and sued. Their case moved through state courts and into federal court in 2016. U.S. District Judge John A. Ross granted summary judgment for the city, finding the Duffners’ asserted facts insufficient to win. Their attorney, David Roland of the Freedom Center of Missouri, calls the ordinance an overreach that could lead to extreme fines or prison and plans to appeal, arguing the case raises major property-rights issues and could attract broader legal interest.

An attorney for “Victim 1” in the Jerry Sandusky child-sexual-abuse case said the teen and other alleged victims plan to testify at Sandusky’s Dec. 13 preliminary hearing in Centre County, marking their first public confrontation with the former Penn State assistant coach. Michael Boni and Philadelphia lawyer Slade McLaughlin were retained last week by the victim and his mother; they are preparing criminal-court testimony now and say they will file civil suits naming Sandusky, his charity The Second Mile, Penn State and others after the criminal case concludes.

Victim 1, who first reported abuse in 2008 and is identified in the attorney general’s grand-jury report, transferred high schools after being bullied. The attorney says recent public statements by Sandusky’s lawyer, Joseph Amendola—who has suggested some accusers may recant—have caused additional emotional distress. Amendola has not commented on the possible civil case and has said some alleged victims might later deny abuse while others may testify to inappropriate touching; Sandusky denies all charges.

The Second Mile said it is cooperating with law enforcement, urged donors to give to the Pennsylvania Coalition Against Rape, and is weighing whether to continue operating, transfer programs, or close; it is also seeking dismissal of a lawsuit that would bar it from transferring assets amid concerns about future claims. The investigation and charges—40 counts involving eight boys over about 15 years—have spawned wider controversy at Penn State over officials’ responses and led to administrative firings and separate charges against some university employees.

On January 25, 2015, 13-year-old Suhayb Jamal Hassan of Eagan was fatally shot in his home. At 11:07 a.m. police responded after a 15-year-old inside the residence initially told dispatchers his brother was unresponsive from an apparent knife accident. Responding officers, firefighters and paramedics attempted life-saving measures but Suhayb was pronounced dead at the scene.

After questioning, the 15-year-old admitted he had accidentally shot his brother while the siblings — home with their 11-year-old sister — were playing “cops and robbers.” The boys had recently discovered their father’s hidden 9 mm handgun. Although the pistol was found unloaded, a loaded magazine was nearby; at some point the gun was loaded and later believed to be unloaded. The older brother pulled the trigger during play and one round struck Suhayb in the chest. The 11-year-old sister was uninjured and did not witness the shooting.

Police described the death as a tragic accident, said no arrests were expected, and indicated no one is in custody. The investigation remains open and will be turned over to the Dakota County Attorney’s Office after completion; the Hennepin County Medical Examiner’s Office is assisting. Suhayb was an eighth-grader at Blackhawk Middle School; the district provided counselors for students. No further information has been released.
