Trent Arsenault, a 36–37-year-old tech worker from the San Francisco Bay Area, gained national attention after the FDA ordered him on November 1, 2010 to stop operating a one‑man, unregulated sperm bank. Arsenault says he has donated to dozens of couples and helped at least 14–53 pregnancies (reports vary), positioning his service as an affordable alternative to commercial sperm banks. He has framed his activity as a form of activism—helping people priced out of formal donor systems—and legal counsel has argued his private sexual practices should not be regulated.

Reporting and sources reveal additional controversial details omitted from some profiles: Arsenault produces and posts explicit videos and photo galleries of his donation process on adult sites (hundreds of videos and galleries with millions of views). He acknowledges the material exists and links to it from his donor page, but says he does not actively advertise it to recipients; some couples learned of his porn work and reacted supportively, while a tipster and others say prospective parents deserve full disclosure. Coverage also highlights discrepancies in his biography (he briefly attended the U.S. Naval Academy but left under unusual circumstances) and mentions that some have suggested he was advised to seek psychological help during that time (which he disputes).

The case has attracted wide and mixed public interest—from progressive outlets praising his “locally sourced” donor approach to conservative critics decrying government overreach. Documents and links to the FDA cease‑manufacturing order, related correspondence and inspection findings are available online. The story has been featured on national programs such as Anderson Cooper, where Arsenault described himself as “donorsexual” and discussed fathering children despite never having had intercourse. The controversy raises legal, medical and ethical questions about unregulated sperm donation, donor transparency, and the public health role of the FDA.

San Diego officials have launched an emergency sanitation and shelter response to a hepatitis A outbreak that has killed 15 homeless people and hospitalized nearly 300 over the past 10 months. Beginning Monday, contractors from Clean Harbors began power-washing downtown sidewalks and streets with a bleach- and chlorine-based solution in three designated downtown zones where large homeless encampments concentrate; the cleanings will continue on a rotating, every-other-week schedule (Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays). The city also extended hours for 14 Balboa Park restrooms to 24/7 and identified additional downtown restroom access to reduce unsanitary conditions cited by county health officials.

The county has been vaccinating and providing hygiene resources separately: about 19,000 hepatitis A vaccinations administered so far (7,300 to at-risk individuals), its own contractor installed 40 hand-washing stations where homeless people gather and more stations are planned. County health officials asked the city to submit a sanitation plan after describing parts of downtown as a “fecally contaminated environment”; they are still evaluating the city’s response.

In parallel, Mayor Kevin Faulconer announced plans to open three large temporary tent shelters — each with 100+ beds, restrooms, showers, 24-hour security and onsite service providers for counseling and job help — to provide immediate shelter relief and hygiene access. Sites have been identified at Father Joe’s Villages (East Village), a vacant lot on Sports Arena Boulevard (Midway, run by Veterans Village), and 16th Street and Newton Avenue (to be run by the Alpha Project). The first one or two shelters are expected by the end of the year, funded in part by private donations (at least $1.5 million pledged) with final costs and council approval pending. Some local business owners doubt temporary tents will be sufficient without permanent housing solutions.

Alan Miller McCarty, 36, was convicted and sentenced for threatening to kill a judge he blamed for losing custody of his children. During his trial in Daytona Beach, McCarty repeatedly disrupted proceedings with loud expletives and insults toward the presiding judge, witnesses and attorneys, forcing the judge to move him to a small room with one-way glass and continue the trial with him in handcuffs and an orange jail jumpsuit. A six-member jury found him guilty of two counts of threats or extortion and two counts of corruption by threat against a public official; he also faces additional related charges for threats to healthcare staff. Prosecutors presented recorded calls in which McCarty threatened Circuit Judge Stasia Warren and emergency dispatchers; Warren testified she was frightened by the threats. Defense counsel argued McCarty was a desperate “squeaky wheel” upset about losing his children and that his comments were just words; prosecutors maintained the threats were serious and credible. McCarty was sentenced to 20 years in prison, with a potential maximum exposure of up to 40 years at sentencing.

A federal judge in New York rejected a proposed $125 million settlement between Google and groups representing authors and publishers over Google’s book-scanning project, citing copyright, antitrust and other concerns. Judge Denny Chin ruled the deal “not fair, adequate and reasonable,” saying it would have effectively granted Google broad rights to profit from millions of books—including many orphan works whose rights-holders cannot be found—and risked creating a de facto monopoly that could bolster Google’s dominance in search and book distribution.

The settlement, negotiated after a 2005 copyright suit by the Authors Guild and the Association of American Publishers, would have let Google expand availability of out-of-print and hard-to-find books and create new revenue streams for rights-holders. Opponents—including the Justice Department, competitors (Amazon, Microsoft), academics and copyright experts—argued it gave Google exclusive advantages, raised antitrust and privacy issues, and exceeded the scope of the original litigation.

Chin indicated the core problems might be addressed by converting the deal from an “opt-out” arrangement to an “opt-in” system, thereby limiting it to works whose owners explicitly agree—an approach Google previously rejected as unworkable because it would exclude many orphan works. The ruling leaves open the possibility of a revised settlement; publishers signatory to the deal said they are willing to negotiate a narrower agreement, while the Authors Guild and Google are considering next steps. The decision could also prompt calls for congressional action on orphan works.

ITER (International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor) is an unprecedented international effort to build a machine in southern France that will create and contain a miniature, controllable “star” on Earth by fusing heavy hydrogen into helium at temperatures above 200 million °C. The device will be enormous and complex—about 100 feet tall, 23,000 tons, with the world’s largest superconducting-magnet system kept near absolute zero to confine the plasma in a vacuum chamber—and could, if successful and affordable, provide essentially carbon-free, abundant energy for millennia. Thirty-five countries participate; the project required novel financing and governance structures and is enormously costly (conservative estimates are around $20 billion and rising).

The ITER site and organization are described in detail: its location near Aix‑en‑Provence amid diverse energy infrastructure, an expanding construction campus that will include cryogenics and control facilities, and recent headquarters and planning for a complex “small city” around the reactor. However, ITER is currently in crisis over management. A damning independent assessment found serious leadership, management, and governance failures. The ITER Council reviewed and accepted the report’s conclusions at a 13 February special session and, worried the findings plus anticipated delays could prompt funders to withdraw support, restricted distribution of the report to senior managers and council members. The executive summary of the assessment was later published by The New Yorker. Science magazine covered the full story.

On Oct. 6, 1966, Roger Watson and Dave (David) Brown — both from northwest Detroit — were drafted together, trained at Fort Hood, Texas, and served in Vietnam as combat engineer demolition specialists with the 9th Infantry. They became close friends during training, went home on leave, then shipped out; during the war Brown later learned Watson was wounded (shot March 8, 1968, suffering severe internal injuries) but never knew if he survived. The two lost contact for more than four decades.

About five years ago Watson, now retired and living on Franklin Road in Berkley, befriended a nearby neighbor, Peggy Brown, over bird-watching. Peggy and her husband Dave had actually lived kitty-corner to Watson for 18 years without realizing the connection. In late October this year Peggy noticed Watson’s Purple Heart plate and 9th Infantry cap and began emailing him about birds. Her messages revealed the shared service; a quick exchange of photos and details confirmed they were the long-lost army buddies. The men met at the chain-link fence between their yards and reunited, sharing memories, war stories and friendship after nearly 50 years apart.

Both are retired family men and veterans, stunned and delighted by the coincidence of living so close for 18 years without knowing it. They now plan to spend more time together.

Actress Angela Lansbury faced heavy criticism after a Radio Times interview in which she suggested women “must sometimes take blame” because they have historically made themselves attractive — comments many read as victim‑blaming in the context of sexual harassment. Lansbury, 92, said there are “two sides to this coin” but also acknowledged “there is no excuse whatsoever for men to harass women in an abusive sexual manner.” After backlash from the public and groups such as Rape Crisis England & Wales — and responses from figures like Patricia Arquette — Lansbury issued a statement saying she was “devastated” to be thought otherwise, reaffirming her support for women’s rights and complaining her words were taken out of context and used to attack her generation and mindset. The episode drew comparisons to past remarks by others (e.g., Donna Karan) that were later recanted amid the broader #MeToo conversation.

Rosemont police released surveillance video showing 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins alone and disoriented in the Crowne Plaza Hotel in the early hours of Sept. 9–10. The clips show her arriving with others shortly after midnight, later staggering off an elevator, reeling down hallways and walking through an empty kitchen before disappearing around a corner — the last time she appears on camera. A motion-activated camera near the kitchen did not capture anyone entering the walk-in freezer where her body was later found; it shows no other activity at that spot until a person appears at 12:23 a.m. and returns with police. Jenkins was pronounced dead shortly after midnight; the medical examiner has not yet determined cause or manner of death pending further tests.

The family, represented by attorneys Larry Rogers Jr. and Sam Adam Jr., criticized the hotel and police response, saying staff did not properly search or assist when she and her friends sought help. The lawyers said they will pursue an independent investigation and possibly a second autopsy. The case generated intense social-media speculation and accusations, with some alleging foul play; Rosemont police call it a death investigation (not a homicide) and so far report no credible evidence to reclassify it. Police have interviewed multiple witnesses and continue to investigate; the hotel has offered the family private access to all surveillance footage and to help with funeral expenses, an offer the family’s attorneys said was not authorized to be relayed through activists.

The United States deployed about 80 military personnel to Chad in late June 2014 to bolster efforts to locate more than 200 schoolgirls abducted by Boko Haram from Chibok, Nigeria. The unit — largely Air Force specialists — is tasked with operating and supporting intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) aircraft, including Predator drones, conducting longer surveillance flights over northern Nigeria and neighboring areas, and maintaining and analyzing collected imagery. U.S. personnel will not carry out ground searches or combat missions; some will handle drone launch/recovery and ground security in Chad.

The move supplements an earlier small U.S. team of advisers in Abuja and around two dozen law enforcement and intelligence personnel working with Nigerian authorities. Officials emphasized the difficulty of the mission: the search area is vast (roughly the size of West Virginia) and dense, the girls may have been split into small groups or moved across borders, and any recovery poses high risks. U.S. sharing of intelligence with Nigeria is limited by concerns about misuse by Nigerian forces.

The deployment follows rising international attention and domestic protests over the kidnappings, the #BringBackOurGirls campaign, and increasingly deadly Boko Haram attacks across Nigeria. Nigeria requested U.N. designation of Boko Haram as a terrorist organization to enable sanctions; Western and regional partners agreed to share intelligence and technical assistance during a recent summit. Observers note Boko Haram’s superior organization and arms relative to Nigeria’s weakened military, underscoring the challenge of safely recovering the girls and countering the insurgency.

A California woman who had been listed as missing in Humboldt County was spotted instead as a contestant on the reality TV show The Bachelor.

Rebekah (Bekah) Martinez, 22, of Fresno, was reported missing by her mother on Nov. 18, 2017 after telling her on Nov. 12 that she planned to go to Humboldt County to work on a marijuana farm and would be out of contact for about a week. Humboldt County law enforcement said they followed leads and tried to contact Martinez and associates but were unsuccessful; on Dec. 12 the mother reported hearing from her daughter, who said she was returning home, yet deputies still could not reach her and kept her on the state missing-persons list.

This week the North Coast Journal included Martinez’s photo among “The Humboldt 35,” a slideshow of people listed as missing in the county. A reader recognized Martinez from the current season of The Bachelor and alerted the paper. The sheriff’s office then contacted Martinez by phone and removed her from the missing-person list. Martinez has been active on Instagram and Twitter since the report and has posted about appearing on the show; she jokingly complained about the photo used in the missing-person listing.

The broader North Coast Journal piece explored why Humboldt County has one of California’s highest per-capita rates of missing-person reports. Contributing factors include liberal state reporting standards (no waiting period), multiple reports for the same person, many transient workers and cannabis-industry laborers who go off-grid, and a high number of foster and transitional youth who run away. Local officials say most reports are resolved quickly; in 2016 most adult missing reports were closed, with only a small number remaining suspicious. The report also describes several long-term unresolved cases, issues with inconsistent databases (state AG list vs. the national NamUs registry), and the frustration families face when investigations stall or when listed people are actually reachable but remain in public databases. The article notes efforts to reconcile listings and the complexity of investigating disappearances in the region’s remote cannabis-growing areas.

Summary:

1) NCUA sues JPMorgan/Bear Stearns over $3.6 billion in mortgage securities
- The U.S. National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) filed a federal lawsuit in Kansas against JPMorgan Securities and Bear Stearns & Co, seeking damages tied to $3.6 billion of mortgage-backed securities the regulator says Bear Stearns misrepresented when underwriting and selling them to several wholesale federal credit unions (U.S. Central, Western Corporate, Southwest Corporate and Members United Corporate).
- The purchases allegedly caused heavy losses that contributed to the collapse of those credit unions. This is the NCUA’s largest suit to date and its second suit against JPMorgan related to credit-union losses (an earlier $1.4 billion suit from June 2011 remains pending).
- The action adds to numerous cases JPMorgan faces over conduct by Bear Stearns, which JPMorgan purchased in 2008. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon has criticized government suits, saying the bank suffered billions in costs after acquiring Bear Stearns at the Fed’s request.
- The NCUA has pursued similar suits against many other banks (Barclays, Credit Suisse, Goldman, RBS, UBS, Wachovia, etc.) and has settled some claims for about $170 million. The regulator is trying to recover losses from five wholesale credit unions seized in 2009–2010, noting wholesale credit unions faced fewer investment restrictions and thus larger crisis losses.

2) Massachusetts fines Morgan Stanley $5 million over Facebook IPO conduct
- Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin fined Morgan Stanley $5 million, finding the bank violated a longstanding agreement intended to prevent investment bankers from influencing analysts.
- The settlement stems from Morgan Stanley’s role in Facebook’s 2012 IPO process: a senior Morgan Stanley banker allegedly scripted Facebook’s treasurer on calls that provided research analysts with specific, more detailed revenue estimates—information not available to retail investors—after Facebook disclosed negative mobile-ad revenue trends. The banker and treasurer rehearsed the calls; the banker took steps to avoid overhearing the conversations.
- The state’s order cites dishonest and unethical practices and failures of supervision; Morgan Stanley did not admit or deny the charges and said it has robust compliance controls. The fine is small relative to investor losses and ongoing litigation and probes (including SEC scrutiny), drawing commentary that enforcement may be limited in deterrent effect.
- The report notes related actions: Citigroup was fined $2 million by Massachusetts over improper disclosure before the IPO, and more than 40 investor lawsuits followed Facebook’s trading decline.

Contact details and reporter/editor credits were included in the original articles.

Barrett Township in the Pocono Mountains has canceled Halloween trick-or-treating, postponed its 50th anniversary parade and 5K Scarecrow Race, and replaced door-to-door activities with a “Trunk-or-Treat” at a nearby Catholic school property while a large manhunt continues for accused cop killer Eric Frein. Hundreds of law enforcement officers have been searching thick woods around the Pike–Monroe county border since the Sept. 12 ambush that killed State Police Cpl. Bryon K. Dickson II and wounded Trooper Alex Douglass. The heavy police presence, roadblocks, school disruptions and hunting restrictions have left residents uneasy, hurt local tourism and businesses, and already cost the township about $40,000 (not including lost revenue). Some game lands and areas have been reopened to hunters, but key tracts in the main search area remain closed. Officials say Halloween plans could be reconsidered if Frein is captured before the holiday.

MIT Media Lab hosted the “Make the Breast Pump Not Suck” hackathon (Sept. 20–21) to tackle longstanding shortcomings in breast-pump design and to spur innovation in maternal and neonatal health. Organizers—parents and researchers from MIT’s Media Lab—argue that breast-pump technology has lagged for decades despite the strong public-health case for breastfeeding and growing market demand. Common problems they identified: noisy motors, many hard-to-clean parts, lack of privacy and comfortable pumping positions, stigma around pumping, poor data tracking, and high cost that limits access for low-income and working mothers.

About 150 participants (engineers, designers, parents, public-health researchers, lactation consultants) self-organized into teams to prototype new ideas, with sponsors offering cash prizes and VC pitch opportunities. Projects showcased included:
- Compress Express: a quiet, wearable compression-based pump that mimics hand expression.
- Second Nature: a pump using massage and compression with low-profile flanges.
- PumpIO: an open hardware/software platform for smarter pumping, data collection, and remote lactation support.
- Helping Hands: a minimal-parts, hands-free compression bra for manual expression.
- Mighty Mom: a discreet wearable pump that logs and analyzes personal data.

The hackathon emphasized broader goals: seeding ideas and connections, collecting user-submitted concepts (open dataset), advocating for better workplace support and policy for pumping mothers, and highlighting maternal health as an underinvested design space. Sponsors and partners included Vecna Technologies, Pejman Mar Ventures, Medela, Naia Health, Lansinoh, Simple Wishes, Ameda, MIT centers, and others. Scholarships were provided to enable participation by those serving low-income breastfeeding women.

The effort responds to widespread frustration with current pumps—often described as noisy, awkward, and dehumanizing—and aims to make pumping more dignified, discreet, data-informed, and accessible, potentially improving breastfeeding rates and health outcomes while unlocking commercial opportunity.

A 24-year-old U.S. citizen named Anna Fermanova is under house arrest in Plano, Texas, after federal agents say she tried to export three advanced night-vision/rifle sights to Russia without a required Department of State license. On March 1, Customs agents at JFK searched her luggage after a tip and found a Raptor 4X night-vision weapons sight and two other advanced rifle sights concealed in a pair of UGG boots; officials confiscated the devices but allowed her to continue to Moscow. She was arrested on her return to the U.S. and had her passport seized; she is awaiting court proceedings in New York and faces up to 10 years in prison under charges for knowingly attempting to export defense articles on the U.S. Munitions List.

Fermanova’s attorney says she legally purchased the items online for her husband, who intended to give or resell them to a hunter, and denies she is a spy. Media comparisons to recent high-profile alleged Russian sleeper agents such as Anna Chapman have circulated, though there is no evidence linking Fermanova to those cases. Born in Latvia, Fermanova is a U.S. citizen who splits time between Dallas and Moscow and holds a cosmetology license in Texas.

Geraldine “Gerry” Largay, a 66-year-old through-hiker from Tennessee nicknamed “Inchworm,” became lost on the Appalachian Trail in western Maine on July 22, 2013, after leaving the trail for a bathroom break. Over the next hour and a half she attempted repeatedly to text her husband for help, but messages would not send because there was no cell coverage. She later hiked to higher ground to seek a signal, then set up a campsite and kept a daily journal and her phone for at least 18–26 days; her last journal entry is dated Aug. 18 and the last phone activity Aug. 6.

Search-and-rescue teams conducted one of the Maine Warden Service’s longest and most costly searches, investigating numerous leads over 26 months before a forester working for the U.S. Navy found Largay’s tent and skeletal remains on Oct. 11, 2015, on Navy land about two miles from the trail. The medical examiner ruled her death due to lack of food, water and environmental exposure. Wardens’ files released in November 2015 (1,579 pages) include her journal—containing a heartbreaking Aug. 6 plea asking that her husband and daughter be notified if her body was found—and undelivered text messages describing her situation.

The recovered campsite showed deliberate survival efforts: a tent on a log-and-pine-bed platform, rain gear, a Mylar blanket, an improvised flag, a fire site, and stored food wrappers. Investigators concluded she likely had poor directional sense and became flustered when lost; friends said she avoided heavy packs because of a chronic back problem. Rescuers at times came within about 100 yards of her location, but dense, remote terrain—also used for Navy survival training—made effective searching extremely difficult. Largay’s family has requested privacy while reviewing the released case file.

Greece’s parliament narrowly approved an initial austerity and reform package demanded by European and IMF creditors amid violent protests and nationwide strikes, but analysts and officials warned it is only a preliminary, fragile step toward solving the country’s debt crisis.

Key points:
- The bill passed by a 155–138 margin after intense debate and days of demonstrations outside parliament that turned violent; police used tear gas against stone-throwing protesters. A 48-hour general strike had paralyzed Athens.
- European leaders—including Germany’s Angela Merkel, EC President José Manuel Barroso and EU Council President Herman Van Rompuy—hailed the vote as vital to avoiding default and urged rapid passage of follow-up implementation votes. Approval would unlock a further tranche of bailout funds and pave the way for talks on a second assistance package and growth-support measures.
- The measures call for roughly €50 billion in privatizations (ports, telecom, real estate, energy stakes), cuts including €1 billion from defense over five years and €2+ billion from health to 2015, tax hikes (heating oil, self-employed), and reductions in permanent and temporary public-sector employment. They do not amend constitutional job protections for permanent public employees.
- Economists cautioned the package merely buys time. Joseph Stiglitz warned Europe risks needing debt restructuring unless it adopts a cohesive framework; Kenneth Rogoff said the plan postpones the problem unless Greece achieves sustained strong growth.
- Political and practical challenges remain: the government’s political capital is weak after internal party revolts and failed coalition talks, further parliamentary votes on implementation could falter, and major reforms—especially overhauling tax collection and modernizing the tax code—are still outstanding.
- Many Greeks are pessimistic, arguing prior austerity worsened conditions; protests reflected deep public anger and fear over rising unemployment and shrinking incomes.

Overall, the vote was seen as a necessary but limited step: it reduces the immediate default risk and keeps bailout funds flowing, but significant implementation, political stability and economic growth are required to make Greece’s debt situation sustainable.

Overview:
With Republicans controlling the White House and both chambers of Congress for the first time in a decade, the 115th Congress arrived ready to pursue a broad conservative agenda aimed at rolling back much of President Obama’s legacy. The House—already long a vehicle for Republican priorities—has sent numerous bills signaling that agenda; now with a slimmer but workable Senate majority and a Republican president-elect, leaders expect to move many items that had previously stalled.

Major priorities and tactics:
- Repeal/replace the Affordable Care Act: Leaders plan quick repeal legislation (using budget reconciliation to avoid a 60‑vote filibuster) while leaving replacement details to be worked out over two to four years, raising the prospect of a politically risky “repeal and delay” approach.
- Tax overhaul: Republicans aim for large individual and corporate tax cuts (including cutting the corporate rate toward ~20%) and other long-standing tax priorities such as repealing the estate tax, likely pursued through reconciliation tools.
- Deregulation and environmental rollbacks: Undoing Obama-era rules is high priority. Congress will use measures like the Congressional Review Act and bills such as the REINS and Midnight Rules Acts to block or require congressional approval of major rules (targets include methane rules, mining and resource payment disclosures, pesticide restrictions, and other climate-related regulations).
- Financial deregulation: Republicans plan to chip away at Dodd-Frank—targeting the Volcker rule and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau—though full repeal is unlikely.
- Entitlement reform: GOP leaders have long wanted to restructure Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security (block grants, privatization options, raising retirement age are discussed), but these are politically sensitive and likely lower near-term priorities.
- Confirmations and judiciary: The Senate will consider cabinet nominees and a Supreme Court nominee. Rule changes from 2013 make many confirmations movable by simple majority, limiting Democratic blocking power. High-profile nominees are expected to face contentious hearings.
- Other measures: Early congressional action may include bills to constrain agency rulemaking, punish in‑chamber protests, and symbolic votes (e.g., on the U.N. Israel settlement resolution).

Constraints and partisan dynamics:
- Senate math and politics: Republicans hold a 52–48 Senate majority, but 10 Democratic senators up in 2018 come from states Trump won—creating potential cross-aisle vote opportunities. Still, Democrats, led by new Senate leader Chuck Schumer, plan to actively resist through messaging and Senate procedures and to slow nominations.
- Filibuster and procedural limits: Though Democrats retain procedural tools, rule changes curb their ability to block many nominees. For major legislation, Republicans will rely on reconciliation where possible, but on other bills they must weigh overreach risks and potential midterm backlash.
- Intra‑party differences and Trump alignment: Republicans are not monolithic—there are disagreements with Trump on trade, Russia policy and on the scope/timing of some reforms. Relationships among Trump, Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate leaders will shape outcomes. Vice President‑elect Mike Pence is expected to serve as a key liaison to Capitol Hill.
- Russia and investigations: Allegations of Russian election interference hover in the background. Some Republicans join Democrats in calling for investigations; an intelligence community report and related hearings could affect legislative dynamics.

Political risks:
Leaders are conscious of historical midterm punishment when governing parties overreach. Members warn against hubris and emphasize the need to deliver tangible results without alienating swing voters.

Bottom line:
Republicans arrived with an ambitious, multi‑front conservative program—healthcare repeal, tax cuts, widespread deregulation, financial rollback, entitlement debate and a conservative judiciary—but face practical limits from Senate structure, intra‑party divisions, Democratic resistance and the political costs of rapid upheaval. Early action will likely target easily reversible regulations and confirmation processes, while larger structural changes (healthcare replacement, entitlement reform, comprehensive tax reform) may play out over months to years.

Background: US life expectancy lags behind most high-income countries. This study estimated how much five modifiable lifestyle behaviors affect premature mortality and life expectancy in US adults.

Methods: Researchers used long-term data from the Nurses’ Health Study (1980–2014; n=78,865) and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study (1986–2014; n=44,354) to define five low‑risk factors: never smoking, normal BMI (18.5–24.9), ≥30 minutes/day of moderate–vigorous physical activity, moderate alcohol intake, and high diet quality (top 40%). They related a total lifestyle score (0–5) to mortality, used NHANES (2013–2014) to estimate the score’s population distribution, and applied CDC death rates and life‑table methods to project life expectancy by lifestyle score.

Key findings:
- Over up to 34 years, 42,167 deaths occurred. Compared with people with zero low‑risk factors, those with all five had much lower multivariable‑adjusted mortality hazards: all-cause HR 0.26 (95% CI 0.22–0.31), cancer HR 0.35 (0.27–0.45), cardiovascular HR 0.18 (0.12–0.26).
- Population‑attributable risk attributable to nonadherence to all five factors was large: 60.7% for all‑cause mortality, 51.7% for cancer, and 71.7% for cardiovascular mortality.
- Projected life expectancy at age 50:
  - Women: 29.0 years for those with 0 low‑risk factors vs. 43.1 years with all 5 (difference ≈ +14.0 years; 95% CI 11.8–16.2).
  - Men: 25.5 years with 0 vs. 37.6 years with all 5 (difference ≈ +12.2 years; 95% CI 10.1–14.2).
- Among the life‑extension benefit, reductions in cardiovascular deaths accounted for ~31–34% and cancer ~21–23%; the remainder was due to other causes.

Limitations: Lifestyle measures were self‑reported, and analyses did not adjust for some medical conditions (e.g., diabetes, hypertension)—intentional here because the focus was on behavior-related life prolongation.

Implications: Adopting simple healthy behaviors—especially avoiding smoking, maintaining healthy weight, regular physical activity, moderate alcohol use, and a healthy diet—could substantially lower premature deaths and increase life expectancy among US adults, even when begun later in life.

San Francisco Supervisor Scott Wiener publicly disclosed that he takes Truvada as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV infection, likely becoming the first U.S. public official to do so. In an essay he explained that after consulting his physician he began daily Truvada to remain HIV-negative and to help reduce stigma and raise awareness of PrEP as a powerful prevention tool—studies suggest up to ~99% protection with daily adherence. Wiener recounted growing up during the AIDS crisis, described ongoing new infections, and urged combining prevention tools (condoms plus PrEP), noting condoms are important but imperfect.

He addressed common concerns: daily adherence is a challenge but not unique to PrEP; evidence has not shown that PrEP increases risky sexual behavior; and regular PrEP monitoring can improve STI detection and treatment. Wiener also emphasized PrEP’s benefits for women, couples trying to conceive safely when one partner is positive, and people in abusive relationships. He called out barriers including stigma, lack of awareness, clinician reluctance to prescribe, and cost—Truvada can cost up to $14,000 a year though most insurers cover it and manufacturer or assistance programs exist. San Francisco officials are pushing initiatives to expand PrEP access and normalize its use. Wiener said his disclosure was intended to elevate public dialogue, reduce shame, and help ensure equitable access so PrEP can play a central role in ending new HIV infections.

A small fenced parking lot at 53 New York Avenue NE in Washington, near the ATF and a McDonald’s, has drawn attention because Elon Musk’s Boring Company received an early, vague D.C. building permit on Nov. 29 allowing preparatory and preliminary excavation work there. The permit is only a first step and far short of the many approvals and construction needed for Musk’s pitched East Coast Hyperloop/Loop: a proposed high-speed, mostly-underground system linking New York–Philadelphia–Baltimore–Washington that Musk has said could ferry pods (and even cars on sleds) between NY and D.C. in about 29 minutes.

Local officials are engaging cautiously: Mayor Muriel Bowser visited the Boring Company’s California tunnel, and the District Department of Transportation is evaluating what permits would be required to tunnel under city roads. Maryland has issued a utility permit and indicated the Baltimore–Washington stretch would run beneath Route 295; the White House Office of American Innovation has also been reported to have backed discussions. The Boring Company says a New York Avenue site could become a station in a distributed network of modest, frequently spaced stations rather than grand terminals.

Technical context and skepticism: Hyperloop concepts date to Musk (2012) and use low-pressure tubes to cut air resistance, with magnetic-levitation or air-cushion approaches to lift pods and linear motors for propulsion. Competing firms (Hyperloop One, HTT) employ passive maglev variants (e.g., Inductrack/Halbach arrays). Tests have achieved high speeds in short runs, but full-scale systems remain unbuilt; experts say tunneling is feasible but costly and slow, and safe, reliable management of many high-speed pods poses major challenges. Critics note Musk’s history of ambitious timelines and warn that carrying cars as well as people could undermine mass-transit benefits. Local reactions range from excitement at the prospect of dramatic trip-time reductions to skepticism about how long construction would take.

Bottom line: The permit at 53 New York Avenue is a symbolic, early move toward Musk’s East Coast Hyperloop ambitions, but it does not signal imminent construction of the full system; many technical, regulatory and political hurdles remain.

A swing-type amusement ride called the "Zumur" malfunctioned Sunday at Norwalk’s Oyster Festival in Connecticut, abruptly stopping mid-spin and causing riders to collide. Nineteen people were reported injured in initial accounts; police said 13 were transported to hospitals (12 children and one adult) and an 8-year-old boy remained hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries; the others were treated and released. Five additional people declined treatment at the scene. Preliminary state police investigation indicates no riders were ejected or fell from the ride.

The festival’s operator, the Norwalk Seaport Association, ordered the ride area closed until state inspectors checked; other rides reopened later that day. Stewart Amusement, which operates the rides, said the machine had been inspected by state officials two days earlier and characterized the incident as a mechanical failure; the company plans to disassemble the ride for further inspection. Connecticut state police fire and explosion troopers are investigating.

The accident renewed concerns about amusement-ride oversight. Experts note portable/traveling rides fall under state jurisdiction with varying inspection regimes—often only annual checks in Connecticut—and lack uniform federal oversight, prompting calls for standardized inspection and reporting across states. Witnesses described chaotic, traumatic scenes as parents reached children after the crash. Festival organizers said their primary concern is the wellbeing of those affected.

Crystal Palace’s team coach was vandalised with red, white and blue graffiti reading “Crystal Palace” while parked at a hotel near Selhurst Park before the club’s 1-0 Premier League win over Middlesbrough. The damage is estimated at around £40,000. The graffitiers are believed to have mistaken the coach for Middlesbrough’s, after Palace had loaned a bus to Boro following their flight to London. Palace used a different bus for the game; the club reported the incident to police. The match was won by a Patrick van Aanholt goal, lifting Palace out of the relegation zone.

George Zimmerman, acquitted seven months earlier of second-degree murder and manslaughter in the fatal shooting of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin, told CNN he still considers himself a victim of the confrontation, saying he was “having my head bashed into the concrete” and badly injured. He acknowledges killing Martin while working as a neighborhood watchman but maintains it was self-defense and says his faith reassures him that only God is his ultimate judge. Zimmerman said the memories don’t haunt him, though he would have “stayed home” that night if he could do it over.

Since the trial he has faced several legal and public-relations problems: traffic stops, a domestic incident reported by his wife, a girlfriend’s claim he threatened her with a shotgun (the couple later reconciled), selling paintings for substantial sums, and briefly agreeing to a charity boxing match that drew criticism and was canceled. He reports continuing death threats and says public perceptions of him are shaped by media portrayals; he argues people who meet him get a different view and notes he has Black family members. Asked about another high-profile Florida shooting case, Zimmerman said he no longer follows the news closely.

Major League Baseball approved a rule change this season to grant intentional walks via a dugout signal instead of having the pitcher throw four pitches. MLB says the change will speed up games, but reaction online was mixed.

Supporters point to small clock savings—intentional walks were relatively rare (932 in 2,427 games in 2016) and shaved only about 1–35 seconds per game depending on the math. Critics and many fans lament losing a quirky part of the game: botched intentional walks occasionally produce memorable, game-changing moments (runners scoring on overthrows, batters reaching on too-close lobs), and some feel the time benefit is negligible. Social media responses ranged from nostalgia for those odd plays to humorous suggestions for how the new dugout signal should look. Overall, the rule removes the four-pitch ritual to marginally speed play at the cost of eliminating a small but entertaining baseball tradition.

Summary:

Authorities arrested 56-year-old Florida resident Cesar Altieri Sayoc Jr. in connection with a nationwide campaign that sent at least 13–14 mail bombs to prominent Democrats, Democratic donors, outspoken critics of President Trump and CNN offices in late October 2018. Investigators traced a fingerprint and DNA from one or more packages and Sayoc’s cell phone to a white van covered with pro‑Trump stickers and crosshairs imagery, which was parked outside an AutoZone in Plantation, Florida; Sayoc was taken into custody there after an arrest using flash-bang devices.

Federal officials described the devices as real, crude explosive pipe bombs (PVC with batteries, timers, powder and broken glass) that had not detonated; they were being analyzed at the FBI lab in Quantico. The mailed packages used similar features (manila envelopes, multiple U.S. flag stamps) and often bore the return address of Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz. Targets included former President Obama, Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, former CIA director John Brennan, actor Robert De Niro, financier George Soros, Rep. Maxine Waters, Sen. Cory Booker, Sen. Kamala Harris, former DNI James Clapper, and others.

Sayoc, a registered Republican with a lengthy local arrest record (including a 2002 bomb‑threat conviction), had been living in his van and posted fervent pro‑Trump and anti‑liberal content on social media. He was charged by the Justice Department with multiple federal crimes—illegal mailing of explosives, threats against former presidents and others, and assaulting federal officers—and faced up to 48 years in prison; additional charges could follow. Authorities emphasized they were treating the incidents as an active investigation and warned there could be more packages. The case heightened national tensions ahead of the 2018 midterm elections and prompted public condemnations and calls for unity from political leaders.

Hollywood roars are fiction: new research suggests many dinosaurs probably didn’t roar like movie T. rex but produced low, closed‑mouth vocalizations more like pigeons, doves, ostriches or cassowaries.

Key findings and points:
- A study published in Evolution analyzed vocal behavior across archosaurs (birds and crocodilians) and found “closed‑mouth” vocalizations — low, resonant sounds produced into an inflating throat or esophageal pouch while the beak stays closed — occur in multiple, mainly large‑bodied bird lineages.
- Of 208 bird species studied, 52 used closed‑mouth vocalization. The trait evolved independently many times (at least 16 lineages) and is rare among small passerines, suggesting a size dependence: inflation of an elastic throat pouch is easier in relatively large animals.
- Because birds are living dinosaurs and closed‑mouth calls also appear in crocodilians, the authors argue the capacity for similar low, whooshing coos or hoots likely existed in some nonavian dinosaurs, probably in mating or territorial displays, alongside any open‑beak calls.
- Direct fossil evidence of vocal organs is lacking (soft tissues don’t fossilize), so reconstructions rely on comparative anatomy, physiology, and evolutionary modeling. Some dinosaurs may also have had birdlike air‑sac systems or syrinxes rather than mammalian vocal cords.
- The article contrasts this scientific picture with cinematic sound design: Jurassic Park’s T. rex roar was a studio creation (blended elephant, tiger, alligator, dog sounds, etc.), while some raptor and other dino sounds in film drew on real bird noises.

Bottom line: Rather than the theatrical, mammal‑style roars of films, many dinosaurs—especially larger species—may have produced low, closed‑mouth coos, hoots or whooshes similar to those of large birds today.

Last night’s Super Bowl halftime featured Bruno Mars with guests the Red Hot Chili Peppers. Observers noticed Flea’s bass lacked any cable or wireless pack, and photos plus onstage antics suggested the Peppers were playing along to a prerecorded instrumental track while Anthony Kiedis sang live. That prompted discussion about miming double standards—many had previously pounced on pop stars for lip-synching but were quieter about a rock band doing the same.

Flea posted a statement acknowledging that the band played along to a pre-recorded track. He explained the decision: the halftime show is a unique, tightly controlled TV spectacle with one take; they recorded a spirited track in advance and the three instrumentalists played along without plugging in because there was no need to amplify. He said they chose not to fake plugging in (they felt that would be disingenuous), that Anthony sang live, and that they wanted to bring their spirit to the event. Flea defended the choice as reasonable for the occasion, thanked Bruno and the NFL, and said he would do it the same way again while reaffirming the band's commitment to live performance in regular concerts.

The Republican 2016 presidential field has swollen to about a dozen declared candidates after Jeb Bush’s entry, creating an unusually large and tightly clustered race not seen since 1860. That crowded field threatens Gov. Chris Christie’s bid: with only the top 10 pollers invited to early televised debates, Christie—currently around eighth in some polls—is close to the cutoff and must quickly gain attention to make debate stages and sustain momentum.

Experts say the competition will intensify media-driven attacks and force candidates to stake out clear positions early. Christie is following that playbook by offering detailed policy plans on entitlements, immigration, taxes and education, and by making pointed attacks on rivals (criticizing Rand Paul over surveillance-authority expirations and ribbing Jeb Bush for adopting a 4% growth pledge Christie says he proposed earlier). Strategists praise Christie’s blunt, “tell-it-like-it-is” approach and argue specificity can help him differentiate in the crowded field.

Summer’s lower TV audiences and the sheer number of contenders mean major media outlets will give each candidate less attention even as debates proliferate. The prolonged nominating calendar—bolstered by outside money after Citizens United—could push the contest well into next year, possibly producing an extended fight or brokered convention. That makes early retail campaigning in New Hampshire and rapid name recognition crucial.

Christie plans to launch his campaign at his New Jersey high school without a teleprompter, then spend several days in New Hampshire for town halls, diner stops and grassroots events to emphasize his personal story, governing record in a blue state, and willingness to tackle tough issues. Key aides and campaign staffing details were also outlined.

Researchers describe Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus, a small (about 1 m) plant-eating neornithischian dinosaur from ~150 million-year-old Siberian deposits that preserves both scales and a variety of featherlike integumentary structures. Fossils show small distal-leg scales, larger imbricated tail scales, simple monofilaments on the head and thorax, and more complex branched, featherlike filaments on the humerus, femur and tibia. Because similar filamentous and branched structures were previously known mainly from theropods in China, the presence of featherlike structures in an ornithischian implies these integuments were not restricted to bird ancestors and may have been widespread across Dinosauria — possibly present in their common ancestor. Authors suggest early feathers originally functioned for insulation and signaling and only later were co-opted for flight. Some researchers caution that not all dinosaurs necessarily retained feathers as adults and that the filament structures in Kulindadromeus differ in some respects from modern feathers, leaving aspects of feather evolution open to further study.

A 12-year-old Arkansas girl, Kali Hardig, is showing encouraging recovery after contracting a rare, often-fatal brain infection caused by the amoeba Naegleria fowleri. Diagnosed in July after a visit to a sandy-bottomed water park, Kali developed primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM). Early detection, aggressive care including therapeutic cooling and an experimental breast-cancer drug, and prompt treatment cleared tests of the parasite. Kali can now say a few words ("yes," "no," "hi mama," "daddy," "nanny"), participate in therapy, and take a few assisted steps; doctors caution she may still have long-term deficits and will remain hospitalized for weeks with months of therapy ahead.

The report also notes a separate, fatal case involving 12-year-old Zachary Reyna in South Florida, who contracted Naegleria fowleri after knee-boarding in ditch water. Although antibiotics cleared the infection, he suffered catastrophic brain damage and was declared brain-dead; his family planned to remove life support to allow organ donation. The CDC says PAM is extremely rare — 128 U.S. cases from 1962–2012 — with very few survivors. It recommends reducing nose exposure to warm freshwater (use nose clips, keep head above water, avoid stirring bottom sediment, and avoid warm shallow waters during high temperatures) and warns about risks from contaminated water used in nasal irrigation (Neti pots).

The author argues that elite media and many political analysts have repeatedly misjudged President Trump and the GOP, and that this bias will lead to a large Republican victory in 2018. Citing columns by Barry Casselman and Scott Adams, the piece claims media pundits have been wrong, self-reinforcing, and resistant to questioning their errors. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act is presented as a central example: the author says media outlets falsely told Americans the law would raise taxes, produced polling based on that misinformation, and predicted the cuts would hurt Republicans politically. After the law passed, real examples (a CBS segment interviewing three families) showed each would pay less under the new law, illustrating the gap between media narrative and taxpayers’ experience.

The author draws three political consequences from this disconnect: (1) voters will be pleasantly surprised that Republicans delivered tax relief and can enact major legislation; (2) personal experience will expose media bias and reduce its influence; and (3) Democrats who opposed the bill will be punished, especially vulnerable Senate Democrats in Trump-won states. The piece frames the choice for voters as between higher taxes and bigger government (Democrats) versus lower taxes, more take-home pay, and a bigger economy (Republicans), and contends that truthful Republican messaging could produce an "astonishing" GOP win.

Finally, the author includes Scott Adams’s list of 20 prominent predictions about Trump that proved incorrect (e.g., that Trump would never win the nomination or be able to govern, that he’d be impeached quickly, that markets would collapse), arguing critics should reassess their predictive abilities if many of these were believed. The author suggests those repeatedly wrong about Trump should curb public political commentary and recommends learning persuasion techniques to predict better.

New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman has opened an investigation into whether major energy-drink makers have misled consumers about ingredients and health benefits. In July he issued subpoenas to PepsiCo (maker of AMP), Monster Beverage Corp., and Living Essentials (maker of 5-hour Energy) seeking documents on marketing and advertising practices. The probe — in its early stages and potentially expandable to other companies — is examining whether companies overstate the benefits of exotic-sounding additives (B‑vitamins, taurine, ginseng, guarana) while downplaying that caffeine is likely the main active stimulant and may not be fully disclosed on labels. Labels often omit total caffeine content; independent testing has found some products contain as much or more caffeine than a cup of coffee. If violations of New York food-and-drug laws are found, companies could face civil fines and be required to change labeling and marketing. The inquiry follows other high‑profile New York regulatory actions and comes as energy drinks remain a fast‑growing segment of the beverage market. The companies declined to comment publicly; some disclosed receiving subpoenas in regulatory filings.

This document covers several Japan-focused news items and a profile of a rising local viral site, presenting snapshots of media trends, public opinion, policy, and a cultural anecdote.

1) Global digital media expansion and Curazy’s rise
- English-language online publishers (BuzzFeed, Business Insider, Quartz) are expanding internationally; BuzzFeed plans further global launches (including Japan).
- Curazy, a Japanese humor/viral site launched January 2014 by Laugh Tech, is emerging as a local competitor. It draws about 5 million unique users monthly and closed JPY 100 million (~US$964k) in funding despite having only five full-time staff.
- Founders Shinnosuke Ito (CEO), Masahiro Kawasaki (marketing) and Taisuke Takemoto (business) are entrepreneurial but lack formal media backgrounds. Laugh Tech previously experimented with manga and a Cosmo service, then pivoted to humor content after better traction with image-based viral posts.
- Curazy aims ambitiously for 300 million monthly pageviews and an exit (IPO or acquisition) within four years. The piece notes this is a stretch compared with BuzzFeed’s scale (e.g., 150 million uniques over years). Curazy has already expanded into Taiwan with localized translation and content.
- Curazy’s leadership sees cultural differences in humor that could protect local players; they even cheekily invite BuzzFeed to acquire them.

2) Public opinion on lowering Japan’s age of adulthood
- A Cabinet Office poll shows strong resistance to lowering the age of majority from 20 to 18: 69.0% oppose ending parental authority at 18 (virtually unchanged from 2008). Only 26.2% support lowering it.
- 79.4% oppose letting 18-year-olds enter expensive contracts without parental consent; 51.5% think the minimum age to adopt should remain 20.
- Public interest in the debate is waning (69.8% interested, down 5.6 points). The survey interviewed 5,000 people (age 18+) in October 2014; valid response rate was 62.4%.
- The legal context: a 2007 law allows those 18+ to vote in national referendums and calls for discussion on lowering adulthood from 20, but related bills haven’t progressed, partly due to the Liberal Democratic Party’s reluctance.

3) Cultural note — a 20th birthday “notice”
- A human-interest anecdote: a Japanese Twitter user (@zamayuma1004) shared a tongue-in-cheek “Notice of Expiration of Child-Rearing Services” his parents gave him on his 20th birthday. The mock formal notice congratulates him and lists adult responsibilities (pension payments, legal exposure for crimes, rights to buy alcohol/tobacco, marriage without parental permission) and requests a monthly household payment (¥20,000) and interest on parental loans.
- The gesture mixes tough love and humor; the son had already been paying the amount and intends to continue helping his parents. The story highlights cultural norms—many young adults remain with parents through schooling—but also family expectations about financial responsibility at adulthood.

Other brief items:
- Alexa has donated web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996, added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.
- Small mentions about Twitter’s location features and event promotion for Startup Asia Tokyo 2014.

Overall, the document juxtaposes digital media globalization and local startup ambition (Curazy) with Japanese societal attitudes toward adulthood and a slice-of-life example showing how families mark the transition to legal adulthood at 20.

Nearly a year after arguing Twitter should double its 140-character limit to 280, columnist Farhad Manjoo finds the company is quietly moving in that direction with a different approach: “expanded tweets.” Rather than changing the core 140-character constraint, Twitter is letting select publishers and partners append richer, interactive previews to tweets that link to their content. These expanded tweets can include a headline (up to ~70 characters), a snippet (up to ~200 characters), bylines, publication and author handles, photos, and video—bringing the total possible visible content to roughly 410 characters-worth of information when combined with the original tweet.

Manjoo welcomes the change as a pragmatic way to deepen Twitter’s utility for news, conversation, and context without abolishing brevity. Expanded tweets let readers preview articles and media before clicking, follow authors, and consume more content inside Twitter itself—potentially making the service a more coherent destination for news. Critics note the early rollout favors big publishers and risks shifting Twitter away from its short-update identity; Twitter says the partner list is growing and sites can apply to participate. The company frames the feature as an extension of existing media expansion (photos and video previews) and aims to roll it out broadly on the web and mobile apps.

Megyn Kelly’s future at NBC is in jeopardy after she made on-air remarks defending, in part, the historical acceptability of white people wearing blackface for Halloween. The comments sparked immediate public outrage, an on-air and written apology from Kelly, and internal condemnation—most notably from NBC News chairman Andy Lack during a staff town hall. As fallout continued, talent agency CAA dropped Kelly and UTA declined to sign her; she has retained high-profile attorney Bryan Freedman and is headed toward settlement talks with NBC. Kelly was not expected to host the 9 a.m. show for the rest of the week and multiple outlets report that conversations are underway about winding down or ending “Megyn Kelly Today,” a process that reportedly began before this incident amid longstanding dissatisfaction at the network over her hire, high salary, low ratings, and fit with the “Today” brand. The controversy also led to guests (including House of Cards cast/EPs) withdrawing appearances and generated critical on-air responses from colleagues like Al Roker and Craig Melvin. NBC has continued to cover the controversy across its programs while negotiations about Kelly’s role and exit details remain ongoing.

San Diego’s recent “Floatopia” parties—large gatherings of people drinking on rafts, inner tubes and other floatation devices just off shore—have exploited a loophole in the city’s ban on alcohol at beaches. The 2007–08 prohibition outlaws drinking on the “beach” (defined as the sand or land bordering the water) but did not address consumption in the water itself. Since mid-2008 dozens of floating drinking events, many organized via Facebook, have drawn hundreds to thousands of mostly young participants into calm bays such as Mission Bay and areas off Pacific Beach.

Authorities say the float parties create public-safety, sanitation and cost problems: excessive drinking, trash and broken glass on beaches, heavy expenses for extra police and lifeguards, and a real drowning risk from intoxicated bathers. Organizers and participants initially exploited the loophole after being told by police the law didn’t apply to those floating; one early promoter publicized the idea online. Some floaters enjoy the novelty and see it as a way to avoid onshore restrictions, though even some participants acknowledge the gatherings have grown too large.

In response the City Council moved to close the gap: the council’s committee advanced language extending the ban to “bathers” and the full council voted unanimously to prohibit alcohol consumption in Mission Bay and within one marine league of any beach (the ban excludes drinking on boats). The measure took effect immediately despite objections that tighter restrictions could hurt tourism. City officials framed the change as necessary to protect public safety and prevent further unruly, hazardous float parties.

Sir Roger Bannister, the first person to run a sub-four-minute mile, has died in Oxford aged 88. On 6 May 1954 at Iffley Road, Oxford, he ran 3:59.4 — a landmark achievement that secured his place in athletics history even though the record stood for only 46 days before Australia’s John Landy lowered it. Bannister won Commonwealth gold over the mile in 1954, retired from elite athletics at the end of that year to focus on medicine, and went on to a distinguished career as a consultant neurologist. He devised much of his own training while a medical student at Oxford and was aided in the record attempt by pacemakers Chris Brasher and Sir Christopher Chataway. Knighted in 1975, he later disclosed a diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease (revealed publicly in 2014). His family said he died peacefully on 3 March, surrounded by loved ones. Prominent figures in athletics, including IAAF president Lord Coe, paid tribute to his enduring inspiration.

A newly installed pedestrian bridge at Florida International University collapsed on March 15, 2018, crushing vehicles stopped at a traffic light and killing multiple people. The 174–175-foot, 950-ton span had been moved into place over Southwest Eighth Street (Tamiami Trail) just days earlier using accelerated construction methods; the bridge was not yet open to pedestrians and the project was not complete.

Immediate impact and response
- The collapse occurred around 1:30–2:00 p.m. Rescue crews, including more than 100 firefighters, search dogs and cranes, worked through the night searching the rubble. Early counts reported at least four dead; updates later raised the confirmed deaths to six. Multiple vehicles (about eight) were crushed beneath the span.  
- At least nine people were pulled from the wreckage and taken to Kendall Regional and other hospitals; trauma reports included cardiac arrest, coma and severe extremity, head and chest injuries. Victims’ ages were reported roughly 20–50.  
- Bystanders and motorists immediately aided victims; officials set up a family reunification center on campus.

Project background and immediate questions
- FIU had promoted the structure as an innovative, “instant” pedestrian bridge intended to create a safe crossing between campus and nearby Sweetwater after prior pedestrian fatalities. The total project cost was about $14.2 million, largely funded by a federal TIGER grant. The span had been fabricated beside the roadway and moved into place in a single morning the previous weekend.  
- The bridge was designed by FIGG Engineering, built and installed by Munilla Construction Management (MCM); Barnhart Crane & Rigging moved the span into position. Construction engineering and inspection was handled by Bolton Perez and Associates; Louis Berger performed a required secondary design check (the Florida DOT later noted Louis Berger was not DOT–prequalified for that role under FIU’s agreement). The Florida DOT said the project was not a DOT project and pushed responsibility to the university and its contractors.

Investigations and statements
- The National Transportation Safety Board dispatched a 15-member team to investigate. Federal, state and local officials, including Governor Rick Scott and Senator Marco Rubio, called for thorough investigations and accountability. Rubio later tweeted that cables had been loosened and were being tightened at the time of collapse, though details remained unconfirmed. Officials noted an engineering “stress test” had been performed earlier that day; whether it contributed to the failure was unclear.  
- FIU President Mark Rosenberg, companies involved (MCM, FIGG, Barnhart) and local leaders expressed shock, grief and pledges to cooperate with investigators. FIU emphasized the bridge was intended to improve student safety.

Uncertainties
- The precise cause of the catastrophic failure was unknown at the time; investigators cautioned it could take days or longer to determine what went wrong. The NTSB and other agencies were leading inquiries into design, construction, inspection, materials and the recent testing activities.

Context
- FIU is a large university with tens of thousands of students; the site is a busy seven-lane roadway. The bridge had been a high-profile safety and signature infrastructure project, slated for completion in 2019. The collapse prompted widespread local, state and national attention and an ongoing investigation.

At Virginia’s gubernatorial transition, outgoing Gov. Terry McAuliffe played a prank on newly inaugurated Gov. Ralph Northam. After the Jan. 2018 swearing-in, Northam and his wife found pillowcases on their bed at the Governor’s Mansion printed with McAuliffe’s smiling face and his slogan “Sleep when you’re dead.” Northam also discovered photos of McAuliffe around the residence and reported an unidentified alarm clock that went off at 3 a.m.; McAuliffe warned there was “more to come.” The story notes such practical jokes are a tradition in Virginia—examples from past transitions include a taxidermied bear placed in a bathroom, hidden phones periodically ringing, and a life-size cutout left in a shower.

Here are concise summaries of the items in the document:

- New Vineyard Gazette sale and publisher retirement: Jerome and Nancy Kohlberg — he’s retired from KKR — bought the Vineyard Gazette for $3.5 million ($2M for the newspaper business, $1.5M for real estate). Longtime publisher Richard Reston (son of James Reston) is retiring; the new owners are looking for a replacement publisher.

- Washington Post hiring note: A memo praises Peter Wallsten’s ability to find neglected stories and sources, calling that skill valuable for a competitive beat; the memo announces his hire.

- California court ruling on alt-weeklies: The California Supreme Court declined to review lower-court decisions that ordered SF Weekly to pay $21 million in damages for selling ads below cost to drive the Bay Guardian out of business.

- Andrea Mitchell honor: Judges commend Andrea Mitchell’s reporting; she requested that the $5,000 honorarium from the Sol Taishoff Award for Excellence in Broadcast Journalism be donated to the University of Pennsylvania.

- Lowell Thomas Travel Journalism Awards (2010): The Society of American Travel Writers Foundation announced winners:
  - Top publications: Afar (new magazine), Washington Post, and San Francisco Chronicle won top honors.
  - Travel Journalist of the Year: Andrew McCarthy (freelancer; work in National Geographic Traveler, Bon Appétit, Islands, Afar).
  - Other notable winners: Outside (seven individual awards), Islands, USA Today, Los Angeles Times (four each), New York Times, Afar, National Geographic Traveler (three each). BudgetTravel.com won best online travel journalism site. Rick Steves won best travel book; Ben Mutzabaugh won best travel blog.
  - The competition drew 1,161 entries judged by UNC-Chapel Hill journalism faculty; more than $20,000 in prize money was awarded.

- Feature excerpt on Ireland (by Andrew McCarthy): A travel piece about Doolin, County Clare, exploring how Ireland’s recession has affected people outside Dublin. Despite economic hardship and widespread pessimism, traditional music and community life in villages like Doolin remain vibrant and sustaining, offering cultural resilience in hard times.

Forbes analyzed 2008 IRS county-to-county migration data (shared by Alexa Internet with the Internet Archive) to identify U.S. counties attracting — or losing — relatively wealthy movers. The ranking focused on counties where incoming households had per-capita incomes of at least $35,000 (roughly $140,000 for a family of four), had at least 500 arrivals or departures, and where incoming households were richer than non-movers while departing households were poorer (and the reverse for places the rich are fleeing).

Key findings
- Collier County, FL (Naples area) topped the list of destinations: 15,150 arrivals in 2008 with an average income of $76,161 per person (about $304,644 for a family of four). More taxpayers left Collier than arrived, but those leaving had much lower average incomes ($26,128).
- Other top destinations included Greene County, GA; Nassau County, FL (near Jacksonville); Llano County, TX; and Walton County, FL.
- Florida and Texas dominate the list (eight and four of the top 20 counties, respectively). Tax experts point to the absence of state income tax in those states as a major draw for high-income movers. After property taxes are included, Texas and Florida rank among states with the lowest personal tax burdens.
- Conversely, several high-tax states (e.g., California, New York, New Jersey, Maryland, Connecticut, Oregon, Hawaii, Wisconsin) are common origins for wealthy departures; six of the top 10 counties the rich are leaving are in those states.
- Pitkin County, CO (Aspen) is cited as an example of a wealthy exodus in 2008: higher-income residents left for cheaper nearby Garfield County and major cities like New York, Chicago, and San Francisco.

Method and caveats
- Forbes’ method compares per-capita incomes of incoming and departing households to non-movers and ranks counties by the income difference favoring arrivals. To reduce noise, the analysis required minimum income and sample-size thresholds.
- The approach highlights emerging “hot spots” rather than already-wealthy counties (so very wealthy counties can be excluded if new arrivals aren’t richer than existing residents).
- IRS migration counts are approximations: they omit non-filers (underrepresenting the poor and elderly) and returns filed after late September 2009 (which may include some wealthy filers with complex returns).

During a CNN segment about the controversy over ESPN anchor Jemele Hill, Fox Sports host Clay Travis shocked anchor Brooke Baldwin by saying, “I believe in the First Amendment and boobs.” Baldwin, incredulous, pressed him to confirm he meant “boobs” (not “booze”), then cut the interview short, telling the control room to kill his mic and ending the segment. Both reacted on Twitter afterward; Baldwin condemned the remark and praised the response she and colleagues received, calling it unacceptable and noting she would not invite Travis back. CNN later said a planned HLN interview with Travis was canceled. The exchange drew widespread criticism on social media, praise for Baldwin’s handling of the situation, and commentary on sexism in sports media.

Two Salt Lake City police officers violated department rules when they forcefully arrested University of Utah nurse Alex Wubbels after she refused to allow a blood draw from an unconscious patient without consent or a warrant, an internal affairs report found. Body‑camera footage from the July 26 incident shows Detective Jeff Payne dragging and handcuffing Wubbels as she protested that the request violated hospital policy; Payne also threatened to retaliate against the hospital. Mayor Jackie Biskupski called the footage “unacceptable” and said the findings cite possible violations including “conduct unbecoming” and improper arrest procedures. Payne and his watch commander, Lt. James Tracy, have been placed on administrative leave and have 20 days to respond; the report will go to Police Chief Mike Brown for any further action. The police department has since revised its blood‑draw request policy to align with the hospital’s rule that blood may only be released without consent if a patient is under arrest or police have a warrant. Wubbels said she accepted apologies from the mayor and police chief.

At a CNN Tea Party debate, Rep. Ron Paul defended the idea that a free society shouldn’t rely on government to provide universal health coverage. When moderator Wolf Blitzer posed a hypothetical about an uninsured man in a coma, some audience members shouted that he should be left to die; Paul answered that communities, churches and other private institutions could and historically have provided care, and that personal responsibility helps control costs. 

The next day in Tampa, Gov. Rick Perry said he was "taken aback" by the crowd’s cheers for refusing care and emphasized Republicans should be "the party of life" and seek ways to save lives, while distinguishing that from his continued support for the death penalty as a matter of justice. Perry also defended his position allowing in-state tuition for children brought to the U.S. illegally—framing it as an education issue and the right approach for Texas—and dismissed claims that his mandate of the HPV vaccine Gardasil for 12-year-old girls caused severe harm, likening such fears to the debunked vaccine-autism link and arguing the vaccine was intended to save lives.

Attorneys for Nanette Kinkade—wife, trustee and executor of the Kinkade Family Trust and Thomas Kinkade’s estate—have filed a temporary restraining order against Amy Pinto-Walsh, the artist’s reported live-in girlfriend. Filed in Santa Clara County Superior Court by Los Angeles firm Zuber & Taillieu LLP, the petition alleges Pinto-Walsh breached a confidentiality agreement she signed Feb. 25, 2011, by publicly discussing Kinkade’s health and circumstances of his death in an April 7 interview with Los Gatos Patch and by threatening to release other private materials.

The injunction seeks to bar Pinto-Walsh from making statements that defame or cast the Kinkades or any Kinkade-owned company (including Windermere Holdings LLC and Pacific Metro LLC/The Thomas Kinkade Company) in a false or negative light, from publishing or assisting publication of any material about the family or businesses, and from selling or disclosing proprietary or trade-secret information she allegedly accessed while acting as Kinkade’s personal assistant and companion. Plaintiffs say Pinto-Walsh lived in Kinkade’s Monte Sereno home and attended business meetings where confidential business plans, strategies, financials and proprietary painting techniques were discussed; declarations from family friends and a company attorney were submitted in support.

Court papers also dispute some media reports about the timing of Kinkade’s death, allege Pinto-Walsh disclosed the artist’s non-public health condition the morning after he died, and warn that release of the materials would harm Nanette Kinkade and the couple’s four daughters. An autopsy had been performed with final cause pending. A hearing before Judge Patricia M. Lucas was scheduled for April 24; the petition set deadlines for service and submission of any opposition.
