Reports from CNN, Reuters and other outlets say Secretary of State Rex Tillerson has grown increasingly frustrated with the Trump White House and may be considering an early departure ("Rexit"). Friends and anonymous sources familiar with his conversations say his mood has darkened amid recent White House turmoil — including President Trump’s public rebuke of Attorney General Jeff Sessions, the tumult around White House staffing (Anthony Scaramucci’s hiring, Sean Spicer’s resignation), and other clashes over personnel and policy.

Key points:
- Tillerson has long had tensions with the administration over Iran policy, Russia, personnel decisions, and perceived White House intrusions into State Department staffing. He has publicly and privately expressed frustration about lacking the autonomy he expected as secretary.
- Recent episodes that exacerbated his discontent include Trump’s criticism of Jeff Sessions, disagreements over recertifying the Iran nuclear deal, confusion over U.S. messaging on the Gulf crisis with Qatar, and reports that the White House blocked some of Tillerson’s nominees.
- Some sources had earlier expected Tillerson to stay through year-end to complete a reorganization of the State Department; two recent sources said his outlook seemed to have shifted and a sooner exit would not be surprising, though they conceded he may simply have been venting.
- State Department spokesman R.C. Hammond denied Tillerson is planning to leave, saying the secretary remains focused on providing U.S. leadership.
- Broader reporting notes wider foreign-policy frustration inside the administration, including national security adviser H.R. McMaster’s concerns about disorganization and ignored recommendations on Russia and Afghanistan.

Overall, multiple accounts portray a senior diplomatic leader worn down by internal White House conflicts, disputed policy direction, and limits on control over his department — raising speculation about whether Tillerson will resign in the near future.

Snoop Dogg (Calvin Broadus Jr.) received his star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on November 19 outside the El Capitan Theatre — the 2,651st star — ahead of the 25th anniversary of his debut album Doggystyle. At the ceremony he thanked family, friends, mentors and fans, and famously closed by thanking himself for hard work, persistence and generosity. Attendees included wife Shante Broadus, children Cori and Julian, mentors and collaborators such as Dr. Dre, Warren G, Quincy Jones, Pharrell Williams and Jimmy Kimmel; Martha Stewart was notably absent but publicly congratulated him.

The ceremony highlighted Snoop’s multi-decade career: breakout success with Doggystyle (1993), more than 40 million albums sold worldwide, numerous hit singles and nearly 20 Grammy nominations. Recent projects mentioned include his gospel album Snoop Dogg Presents Bible of Love, the Redemption of a Dogg musical tour, TV projects (Martha & Snoop’s Potluck Dinner Party, Joker’s Wild, GGN news show), his cookbook From Crook to Cook, and philanthropic work such as the Snoop Youth Football League. Snoop shared photos from the event on social media and recently released an Amazon Original single, “Grateful.”

Researchers report a dramatic rise in earthquakes in central Oklahoma is very likely linked to large-volume wastewater injections from oil and gas operations. A study published in Science analyzed seismic records, injection volumes and pressure-flow models and found a roughly 40-fold increase in quake rates between 2008–2013, with more than 2,500 magnitude-3+ events around Jones since 2008 (about 20% of such quakes in the central and western US in that period). The team traced much of the activity to a small number of high-rate disposal wells—four New Dominion wells that pumped roughly 4 million barrels a month to depths near 3.5 km—showing that the injected fluids can raise subsurface pore pressure over large distances (up to ~35 km / ~20 miles) and potentially trigger faults already close to failure.

The paper builds on earlier evidence that wastewater injection can induce quakes by reducing fault friction, but goes further by linking distant swarms to specific wells and by showing widespread, persistent seismicity rather than isolated aftershock sequences. Researchers caution they are still uncertain how often such injection-triggered swarms could escalate into larger magnitude events, though past ruptures suggest the potential exists. The oil company named in the study disputes the conclusions. Scientists and state geologists say more study is needed to guide regulation and disposal practices so seismic risks can be managed while oil and gas production continues.

Archaeologists have found the earliest known evidence of grape wine production at two Neolithic village sites—Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveri Gora—about 30–50 km south of Tbilisi, Georgia. Pottery fragments dated to roughly 6,000–5,800 BC contained chemical residues (notably tartaric acid, plus malic, succinic and citric acids) that fingerprint grape wine. These finds are supported by grape-decorated pottery, abundant grape pollen and other archaeobotanical indicators, and radiocarbon dating.

The large, rounded jars—similar in form to modern Georgian qvevri—were likely used for fermenting, aging and storing wine. Archaeologists infer that grapes (Vitis vinifera) were grown in nearby hills, pressed and fermented in cooler locations, then transferred to smaller vessels for village use. No tree-resin preservatives were detected, suggesting these were early, “pure” wines consumed seasonally before spoiling. The discovery predates previous grape-wine evidence from Iran and Armenia and, while fermented beverages older than this (e.g., Jiahu in China) exist, the Georgian finds represent the oldest clear evidence of domesticated grape viniculture.

The results illuminate rapid Neolithic innovation: within a few millennia of plant domestication people were cultivating grapevines and developing winemaking technology. The region’s long-standing wine culture—Georgia today has hundreds of local grape varieties and still uses qvevri-like jars—aligns with these deep roots. Researchers say the find highlights the sophistication and social dimensions of early agricultural communities. The study was published in PNAS.

Facebook updated and clarified its Community Standards and published a transparency report to explain more precisely what content is allowed, what is not, and how it handles government requests.

Key points:
- The clarification gives concrete examples across categories (safety, respectful behavior, account security, intellectual property) without changing the underlying policies. Facebook aims to reduce opacity and inconsistency in enforcement.
- Prohibited content clarified: praise or support for terrorist or violent/criminal/hateful groups; threats, bullying, and harassment; encouragement of suicide or eating disorders; sexual violence and exploitation (explicitly including revenge porn); pornography and most nudity, with nuanced exceptions (e.g., breastfeeding, post-mastectomy scarring, classical art).
- Facebook will not automatically scan and remove potentially offensive content; it continues to rely primarily on user reports and global human review teams. Safety-related reports are typically reviewed within ~48 hours, and users can appeal enforcement decisions.
- Context matters: Facebook may allow graphic or violent material when posted for newsworthiness or to raise awareness (e.g., victims sharing atrocities).
- Governments request content removals and user data; Facebook published its Global Government Requests Report for H2 2014. It restricted 9,707 items for violating local laws (up 11% from H1), with India and Turkey among the most frequent takedown requests. Government account-data requests rose slightly to 35,051; the U.S. made the most requests and Facebook complied in many cases.
- Mark Zuckerberg defended complying with lawful local orders when necessary to avoid blocking access for millions of users, while saying Facebook will challenge unreasonable requests and push for better government surveillance practices.

Overall, the changes are intended to provide clearer guidance to users and reviewers, improve transparency about government interactions, and balance free expression with safety and local legal obligations.

Orlando International Airport will become the first U.S. airport to require facial scans of all passengers on arriving and departing international flights, including U.S. citizens. The scans compare gate photos to passport images in a Department of Homeland Security biometric database to verify identity. Other large airports already use facial recognition for some international departures, but Orlando’s policy expands the program to every international gate, affecting about 6 million international travelers a year.

Privacy advocates and some lawmakers warn the expansion is premature because formal rules are lacking on data handling, error resolution, and limits on use. Critics also warn many systems show higher error rates for racial minorities, women and children—likely due to training data imbalances. U.S. citizens can opt out, officials say, but advocates contend opt-out options aren’t well publicized. Senators Ed Markey and Mike Lee have urged DHS to set formal safeguards before further expansion.

The move is part of a broader push to use biometrics across the travel experience—examples include Delta’s facial-recognition bag drop and private services like Clear—promoted as speeding processes and enabling contactless travel.

Investigators probing the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 are examining the possibility that a pilot intentionally crashed the plane. Authorities searched the homes of captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah and co-pilot Fariq Ab Hamid and seized a home flight simulator from Zaharie. Evidence prompting scrutiny of the flight crew includes the aircraft’s sudden shutdown of communication systems (ACARS and transponder) shortly after takeoff, a sharp preprogrammed turn away from its planned route, subsequent maneuvers suggesting tactical evasion, and indications the plane flew for hours after losing routine contact. U.S. and Malaysian officials, along with some analysts and lawmakers, have said the actions appear deliberate and that “those in the cockpit” are a prime focus, though terrorism and other possibilities remain under investigation.

The search widened dramatically after satellite data suggested the aircraft may have continued flying for more than six hours, creating northern and southern possible arcs that span from Central Asia to the southern Indian Ocean. That expanded area involves some 24–25 countries and forced recalibration of search assets; at times nations such as India temporarily suspended operations pending new coordinates. Officials stressed uncertainty about the plane’s final location, noting satellite pings cannot precisely fix its position.

Investigators are checking pilots, cabin crew, ground staff, passengers (including background checks), and engineers who last worked on the aircraft, and have examined the cargo manifest (no hazardous materials flagged). Historical precedent and an FAA study show pilot suicide by aircraft is rare but has occurred, complicating both motive assessment and public discussion. Families of those aboard have grown increasingly frustrated with the pace and transparency of Malaysian authorities and the airline’s communications. International teams continue searching sea and land corridors while pursuing forensic and intelligence leads.

The Hollywood Reporter revealed that actor Tom Sizemore was removed from the Utah set of the 2003 crime thriller Born Killers (shot as Piggy Banks) after an 11‑year‑old actress told her mother he had inappropriately touched her during a promotional photo session. According to about a dozen cast and crew interviewed by THR, the child — who was seated on Sizemore’s lap for a holiday tableau — later told her parents the actor had either rubbed a finger against her genitals or inserted it. Production personnel say Sizemore denied the allegation when confronted; the producers reviewed the photos but found them inconclusive and encouraged the parents to involve police, but they ultimately did not press charges. Sizemore was sent home and was later dropped by his management and agency, though months later he returned for reshoots in Malibu.

The now 26‑year‑old former child actress has hired a lawyer to explore legal action; she has requested anonymity. Several crew members described a tense, angry atmosphere on set and characterized Sizemore at the time as a problematic presence — intoxicated or drug‑affected and prone to inappropriate behavior. Producers said they took the allegation seriously but felt they lacked definitive evidence and had obligations to finish the film.

Sizemore, 55, who has a long history of substance abuse and past convictions and allegations of violence against women, has not previously been publicly accused of molestation. His representatives declined to comment. The report surfaced amid wider industry scrutiny of sexual misconduct allegations following the Harvey Weinstein revelations.

An Austrian climber on El Capitan’s Nose Route severed his right thumb when a secondary rope wrapped around it during a fall about 1,000 feet below the summit. The thumb fell roughly 80 feet onto a small two-by-one-foot ledge and was retrieved by his partner. Rangers, with a contracted helicopter crew, performed a complex short-haul extraction late afternoon to get the injured climber off the wall and to El Capitan Meadow, then transferred him to an air medical helicopter. He underwent surgery that evening in San Francisco where the thumb was successfully reattached. A ranger remained with the partner overnight and was raised the next day to the summit by traditional rock-rescue techniques. Yosemite officials described the mission as technically difficult but lifesaving and illustrative of the park’s skilled Search and Rescue teams.

Actors Ewan McGregor, 46, and Mary Elizabeth Winstead, 32, were photographed kissing and leaving together on McGregor’s motorbike after spending more than an hour in a busy London cafe, The Sun reported. The pair — who play lovers Ray Stussy and Nikki Swango in the third series of FX’s Fargo, filmed in Canada and screened in the U.S. earlier this year — were seen deep in conversation and appeared relaxed together. Winstead split from her husband Riley Stearns in May; McGregor has been married to Eve Mavrakis since 1995 and they have four daughters, though outlets report the couple have been separated since May. The story has drawn attention because of the on- and off-screen romantic connection between the co-stars. The document also includes background on McGregor’s career (Trainspotting, Star Wars) and Winstead’s film roles, plus a brief synopsis of Fargo’s new season.

GLAAD engaged with Carson Daly after remarks he made on his L.A. radio show about a recent JetBlue incident, in which he suggested gay people wouldn’t have been brave enough to restrain a disruptive pilot. Daly joked that the flight might have been full of people headed to a San Francisco pride parade and impersonated a gay stereotype. Bloggers noted the comment ignored examples like Mark Bingham, an openly gay passenger who helped storm United Flight 93 on 9/11. Daly tweeted an apology saying he had "attempted to make fun of myself & offended others by mistake," and provided GLAAD a longer statement expressing sadness that his words suggested LGBT people lacked courage, calling himself an ally and pledging to "fight with them" for equality. GLAAD said it will judge the sincerity of his apology but looks forward to working with him.

A 13-year-old Australian boy, Aaron, sparked an online debate after his mother, Estella Havisham, posted a tough-love“bill” on Facebook after he lied about homework, spoke disrespectfully and boasted he earned money on YouTube. She stripped his room of comforts (clothes, mattress, toys, lightbulbs, internet) and told him to “buy back” access by paying hypothetical monthly shares (rent $430, electricity $116, internet $21, food $150) and doing regular chores, with a $30 daily fee if she had to clean for him. Estella says the note was meant as a lesson in gratitude and independence, not an actual attempt to extract large sums; Aaron apologized, completed chores, and gradually got items returned. The post went viral (tens of thousands of shares and comments), drawing both praise for firm parenting and criticism for shaming or unreasonable punishment. Estella stands by her approach, advising parents to trust their judgment and be creative with discipline.

North Korea publicly presented an American man, identified as 29-year-old Arturo Pierre Martinez of El Paso, Texas, who said he illegally entered the country and is seeking asylum in Venezuela. Martinez appeared at a Pyongyang press conference at the People’s Palace of Culture, where he read a roughly 4,000-word prepared statement admitting illegal entry but saying he had been “pardoned” and praising his reception. North Korean officials said he entered in November after crossing from China; details of his travel and legal status in North Korea remain unclear.

In his remarks Martinez sharply criticized the U.S. political, economic and justice systems, calling U.S. foreign policy and the Iraq war predatory, the electoral system corrupt and skewed toward the wealthy, and U.S. elites “sociopathic.” He also made claims about UFOs, CIA involvement in the cocaine trade, and alleged use of ultrasonic devices to induce voices and discomfort. North Korea’s presentation came amid its protests of a U.N. rights resolution, prompting questions about possible propaganda motives.

Martinez’s mother told CNN he is bipolar, had previously tried to enter North Korea (once swimming across a river and later returned to the U.S. and hospitalized in California), then left for China after being released. She said the U.S. Embassy in Beijing was looking for him and later released a statement expressing relief and appreciation to North Korean authorities; however it is unknown whether he is free to leave North Korea. The appearance follows Pyongyang’s recent release of other Americans, including Kenneth Bae.

A Southwest Airlines flight from San Francisco to Phoenix was diverted to Los Angeles on Tuesday after a pregnant passenger went into labor shortly after takeoff. A doctor, a nurse and flight crew assisted and the baby was born aboard Flight 623 before the plane landed at LAX, where paramedics took the mother and newborn to a hospital in good condition. The aircraft was removed from service for cleaning; the other 111 passengers continued to Phoenix on another plane, arriving over two hours late. Passengers described a calm response and applause after the captain announced the birth. The airline did not release the parents’ names or the baby’s gender. Southwest has experienced similar in-flight births before; babies born on flights are typically issued a birth certificate from the state where the plane lands.

A gunman identified as 43-year-old Rick Odell Smith killed five people and critically wounded a 6-year-old girl during an early-morning attack Wednesday in Manchester, a rural Illinois village of about 300. Police say Smith forced his way into a home around 4:30 a.m., armed with a shotgun, a scoped rifle and a hunting knife, and shot victims at close range. Those killed were identified as JoAnn (Joanne) Sinclair, 66–67; Brittany (Brittney) Luark, 23 (who was pregnant); her boyfriend James (Roy) Ralston, 29; and two young boys, ages 1 and 5. A 6-year-old girl, Kassidy Ralston, was gravely injured but survived after Smith carried her to a neighbor’s house and urged they get help. 

Smith fled in a white Chevy Lumina and was located by police a few hours later following a short pursuit. He shot at officers when stopped and was shot by police; he was taken to a hospital and later pronounced dead. Authorities recovered the weapons at the victims’ home. Police have not released a motive and say the investigation is ongoing. Neighbors and officials described Smith as an acquaintance of the family; some reported he had been involved in recent custody disputes and had a criminal history including a DUI-related reckless-homicide conviction and other convictions. 

The killings stunned Manchester, where residents and local leaders said such violence was unprecedented and left the community devastated.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said her views on same-sex marriage are “evolving” and that she is reviewing the issue “very closely.” Though she has previously voted for constitutional amendments defining marriage as between a man and a woman, Murkowski signaled a softening—citing generational attitudes (her young sons and their friends) and a broader sense that public views are changing. She noted larger national priorities and questioned the focus on restricting who people may marry, but said her final position will reflect the views of Alaskan constituents, who in 1998 amended the state constitution to ban same-sex marriage. Her comments follow similar reversals by other Republicans and come as the Supreme Court was considering related cases.

An official incident report by Officer Lameen Barnes described a July incident in which inmate Mr. Dixon allegedly tried to throw an “unknown liquid substance” at officers, was searched for contraband, refused orders, was restrained and handcuffed to a gurney, and then escorted to the clinic “without any further incident of force.” Three witnesses who were present — two speaking anonymously and one via a confidential clinician email — dispute that account. They say guards wheeled Dixon into an unmonitored exam area where he begged medics not to leave him and warned “They’re going to kill me,” while about six officers crowded the gurney and one repeatedly punched him in the head. Another inmate, Mr. Lane, who had also splashed guards with a liquid and has a long history of mental illness and past solitary confinement, says officers punched him repeatedly as well.

Separately, New York City’s newly appointed jail commissioner Joseph Ponte was reprimanded by the Board of Correction for violating city law by placing up to 47 mentally ill inmates into 23-hour confinement on June 13 without prior approval from mental health clinicians. Ponte defended the move as necessary to curb escalating violence at Rikers — citing hundreds of inmates who owe time in solitary but remain in general population and an uptick in slashings — but board members said the action endangered inmates, including those on psychotropic medication who were moved from air-conditioned observation units into uncooled cells (a practice a federal judge has warned against), and others who were denied medication or have seizure disorders. The dispute highlights tensions over how to manage violence at Rikers while protecting a jail population in which roughly 40% have mental health diagnoses and many are seriously ill.

A Vancouver Catholic newspaper reported that aborted and miscarried fetal remains from British Columbia have been shipped to and incinerated at the Covanta Marion waste-to-energy facility in Marion County, Oregon, to generate electricity. The story — which cited a B.C. Health Ministry confirmation that regional health authorities contract with a waste hauler that ships biomedical waste to Oregon — spurred outrage among Marion County commissioners Sam Brentano and Janet Carlson, both pro-life. They held an emergency meeting, suspended biomedical waste shipments to the plant, and approved an order to halt receipt of medical waste until procedures ensure no fetal tissue is delivered or burned. They also intend to amend county ordinances to explicitly bar fetal tissue while allowing other human tissue and medical waste to continue being accepted.

Covanta Marion, the privately operated plant that processes roughly 500–550 tons of waste daily and sells power to Portland General Electric, said it was shocked by the allegations, is cooperating with the suspension, and blamed the county for oversight of the waste program. Stericycle (the company reportedly contracted to ship B.C.’s biomedical waste) did not respond to inquiries. Marion County officials say they do not know how much fetal tissue, if any, has been incinerated and emphasize that much biomedical waste arrives sealed and is not opened. The controversy follows recent revelations in the U.K. about use of fetal remains for energy, prompting similar public and governmental backlash.

Multiple news outlets report that Yahoo is preparing to disclose a massive data breach that exposed hundreds of millions of user accounts. Initial reports revolved around a dark‑web listing by a hacker known as “Peace,” who advertised roughly 200 million Yahoo credentials (usernames, hashed/encrypted passwords, dates of birth and some backup email addresses) allegedly from 2012 for about 3 bitcoins. Sources cited by Recode and others say the breach is “widespread and serious,” and could be larger than 200 million accounts.

Yahoo had previously acknowledged investigating the claim but did not immediately confirm it or force a company‑wide password reset. Later reporting and Yahoo statements indicate the company discovered an even larger intrusion—dating to 2014—and said up to 500 million accounts were affected; Yahoo attributed that incident to a “state‑sponsored actor,” and said the stolen data included names, email addresses, telephone numbers, birth dates, hashed passwords and security questions/answers. Yahoo reported no evidence of stolen payment data or that attackers remain in its network.

The timing raises major implications for Verizon’s pending $4.8 billion acquisition of Yahoo’s core internet business. The breach could prompt regulatory scrutiny, legal action, user distrust, and potential renegotiation of the sale price or other remedies. Security commentators note the risks of reused passwords across sites and recommend unique, strong passwords or password managers; affected users have been advised to change credentials if they haven’t since the relevant breach period.

Volusia County deputies are searching for three suspects and a possibly injured woman after a carjacking early Saturday on I-4 near Daytona Beach. At about 5:40 a.m. at mile marker 128 westbound, a 34-year-old woman stopped to help at the scene of a crash. Three young men jumped out of a vehicle involved in that crash and stole her car, a dark blue 2012 Ford Mustang convertible (FL tag V83-4QC) with a black vinyl top, spoiler and no window tint. Deputies say the suspects loaded an unresponsive, bleeding female—believed to be a teen or woman in her early 20s with short dreadlocks, wearing a red hoodie, brown jeans and black shoes—into the stolen Mustang before fleeing westbound. The carjackers are described as Black males in their late teens or early 20s (one heavy-set in a striped shirt and jeans, two thin). The initial crash vehicle was also reported stolen. The Volusia County Sheriff’s Office is charging the three with carjacking; the Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the crash. Authorities ask anyone who spots the vehicle or suspects to call 911 and not to approach them.

President Obama urged Congress to revive comprehensive immigration reform after the recent government shutdown, calling passage “this year” good for the economy, security and families and warning Republicans they would have to explain opposition. The Senate had already passed a bipartisan bill in June that included a path to citizenship for roughly 11 million undocumented immigrants, but prospects in the House are dim.

Obstacles:
- Many House Republicans oppose a citizenship pathway and are fragmented over how to proceed. Leadership faces deep distrust of the president after the shutdown and debt fight, which lawmakers and aides say has poisoned negotiations and made Republicans reluctant to enter a deal with Obama.
- A sizable faction of House GOPers doubts any piecemeal bills can get the 217 Republican votes needed if Democrats withhold support; Speaker John Boehner has indicated the House will seek smaller measures rather than back the Senate bill.
- Democrats are divided over timing: some favor immediate action to deliver to Hispanic voters who heavily favored Obama in 2012, while others prefer holding the issue to preserve political leverage for 2014 midterms.
- Looming fiscal deadlines (funding the government, debt ceiling) and limited session days (19 House days left in 2013) further shrink the window for major legislation.

Political dynamics:
- Democrats plan to hold Republicans accountable if reform stalls, framing opposition as obstructionism linked to the shutdown. Republicans counter that Obama’s approach and rhetoric have undermined trust; some conservatives accuse him of trying to damage their party politically.
- Pro-reform coalitions of business, religious and agricultural groups (including tech and chamber groups) are mobilizing to pressure House Republicans. Yet some advocates are pausing heavy investment until momentum improves.

Outlook:
Given internal GOP divisions, bitterness from recent fiscal fights, tight House calendar and upcoming budget battles, House Republican leadership has no firm plan to vote on major immigration reform before year’s end, making passage in 2013 unlikely though not impossible if bipartisan consensus emerges quickly.

This document compiles multiple news items largely focused on motorcycle lane splitting and one brief item about a proposed California fee on lead-acid batteries.

Motorcycle lane splitting (riding between lanes of moving or stopped traffic)
- Definition and perspectives: Also called lane splitting, white lining, or filtering. Motorcyclists say it reduces the risk of being rear-ended in stop-and-go traffic, improves efficiency and fuel economy, and can reduce congestion. Drivers often find it alarming and dangerous when motorcycles move between lanes.
- Legal status varies:
  - New Jersey: No explicit law allowing lane splitting, but it’s not expressly banned either. The state driver’s manual warns against “lane sharing” and riding between rows of stopped vehicles. Police can cite riders for failure to keep right. No bill has been proposed to legalize it; an online petition gathered some support.
  - California: Historically treated as neither explicitly legal nor illegal, with an informal tolerance so long as riders behave reasonably. In 2016 the Assembly passed AB 51 (69-0), sending it to Gov. Jerry Brown; the bill would authorize the California Highway Patrol (CHP) to set formal guidelines (e.g., safe speeds) for lane splitting, making California the first state to create formal rules. Early versions with specific speed caps were dropped after pushback; the final bill gives CHP discretion. Riders and advocacy groups generally want clear guidelines; some opponents resisted CHP issuing guidance in the past.
- Safety evidence and positions:
  - Motorcycle advocacy groups (e.g., American Motorcyclist Association) argue lane splitting can lower rear-end collisions in heavy traffic and cite a UC Berkeley 2015 study finding riders who split in heavy traffic were less likely to be struck from behind and less likely to suffer severe or fatal injuries.
  - The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has not endorsed lane splitting but notes it can provide an escape route and calls for more study.
  - The Motorcycle Industry Council supports state laws allowing lane splitting with reasonable restrictions.
- Enforcement and concerns: Police warn of hazards when drivers change lanes and may cite riders under existing statutes (like failure to keep right). Opinions among riders and law enforcement vary; many riders want a clear legal framework to reduce uncertainty.

Other item
- California battery fee proposal: Legislation (AB 2153) would add a $1 fee to lead-acid battery purchases (rising to $2 in 2022) to fund cleanup of contaminated sites like the Exide battery plant in Los Angeles County, potentially raising about $40 million annually. Assemblywoman Cristina Garcia authored the bill to address long-standing contamination issues.

This long report traces how the rapid corporatization of veterinary care has transformed pet medicine in the U.S., focusing on the dispute between independent veterinarian John Robb and Banfield Pet Hospital (owned by Mars Inc.) as a case study of larger industry trends.

Key points

- Industry consolidation and money: Pet care has become a huge, fast‑growing business as more Americans treat pets like family and spend heavily on veterinary services. Consolidators (VCA, Banfield, BluePearl and others) and financial buyers (private equity, pension funds) have been buying independent practices aggressively. Corporations now own roughly 15–20% of U.S. animal hospitals, and Mars’s acquisition of Banfield plus deals to add VCA and BluePearl will make it a dominant owner.

- Standardization, software and wellness plans: Chains use proprietary software and standardized protocols (e.g., Banfield’s PetWare and “wellness plans”) to streamline care, boost throughput and generate recurring revenue. Wellness plans bundle exams, tests and vaccines for a monthly fee and are central to big‑chain business models because they lock in customers and normalize regular in‑clinic procedures.

- Tensions with traditional veterinary judgment: Many independent vets and some experts argue corporate protocols encourage unnecessary testing, frequent vaccinations, and elective procedures (e.g., routine dental cleanings under general anesthesia) that increase revenue but may be unnecessary or risky for some animals. Corporate targets and metrics (average patient charge, sales of packages) can pressure clinicians to recommend more services.

- Vaccine controversy: The piece highlights disagreement over vaccination frequency and dosing. AAHA guidelines recommend core vaccines at three‑year intervals for most dogs, and some immunologists assert a single puppy series can confer long immunity; nevertheless, many clinics—especially chains—still push annual boosters. Small‑animal vaccine dosing is another disputed issue (traditional fixed-volume doses vs. weight‑adjusted or reduced doses), and adverse reaction rates are debated in the literature. Banfield historically recommended more frequent boosters and used wellness plans to promote them; the company says it has aligned with guidelines since 2010.

- Regulation and legal vulnerability: Veterinary medicine is less regulated than human medicine. Pets are legally “property,” monetary damages for malpractice are low, and malpractice insurance premiums are cheap. That legal landscape makes corporate pressure and standardized revenue models easier to sustain. When owners seek redress, legal remedies are limited; corporations can also leverage management and franchise arrangements to take over practices.

- John Robb’s fight with Banfield: Robb bought a Banfield franchise in 2008 and later lost his charter after disputes over vaccine practices (he gave reduced doses to small dogs after reactions). Banfield revoked his charter, sued him and he countersued; his case and public campaign (Boycott Banfield) highlight allegations that Banfield prioritized profits, over‑vaccinated, pressured doctors, and used contractual or administrative tactics to seize franchises or buy them cheaply. Robb has both critics and supporters; his public tactics have been confrontational, and legal outcomes have been mixed. A state panel recommended probation and restrictions on his practice, while some independent reviewers have defended his concerns about vaccine reactions and corporate motives.

- Data and outcomes: In litigation Robb compelled Banfield to disclose dental anesthesia deaths: Robb reported none in many procedures; Banfield disclosed hundreds of deaths over five years, a statistic that raised eyebrows but is hard to interpret without industrywide benchmarks. Chains argue they enable advanced care and economies of scale (VCA operates specialty centers, diagnostics labs like Antech), while critics point to rushed exams, warehousing of pets, and the commercialization of routine care.

- Mars’s growing role and implications: Mars already owns Banfield and pet‑food businesses and is moving to bring VCA and BluePearl under its umbrella. Critics worry the addition of thousands more hospitals to Mars’s network will expand “one‑size‑fits‑all” protocols and wellness plan models, further entrenching corporate practices that prioritize standardized, revenue‑driven care over individualized clinical judgment.

Bottom line

The story uses Robb’s battle with Banfield to illustrate tensions created by the corporatization of veterinary medicine: improved access, scale and advanced services on one side; pressure to sell standardized, revenue‑driven care, questionable vaccination practices, and weakened clinical autonomy on the other. The shift raises questions about quality, safety, and the future of independent veterinary practice as a handful of large corporate players—now including major consumer brands like Mars—consolidate the industry.

IntercontinentalExchange (ICE), a fast-growing Atlanta-based commodities and derivatives exchange founded in 2000, is in advanced talks to acquire NYSE Euronext in a deal worth about $8–8.2 billion, according to people briefed on the matter. ICE is expected to offer roughly $33 a share (about two-thirds in ICE stock), a roughly 37% premium over NYSE Euronext’s recent close. A formal announcement could come soon, though talks might still break down.

The proposed deal would pair ICE’s strong derivatives and commodities franchises (futures and options on oil, gas, cotton, etc.) with the historic New York Stock Exchange and its equities businesses, including the Liffe derivatives market in London and the Arca electronic equities platform. The combination would create a company encompassing some 14 stock and futures exchanges and five clearinghouses, expanding ICE’s reach and scale.

Strategic rationale
- Derivatives trading has become more important and resilient than cash equities: futures and options volumes have declined less than stock trading, and ICE has high profit margins and faster growth.
- The NYSE’s traditional equities business has weakened: the NYSE now handles only about 11% of U.S. stock trading (Arca adds ~12%), and average daily stock trading volumes have fallen since 2009.
- Mergers among exchanges aim to secure scale, cost savings, and unified back-office operations.

Regulatory and competitive context
- ICE previously partnered with Nasdaq in a hostile joint bid to break up NYSE Euronext’s planned merger with Deutsche Börse; that proposal was blocked by the U.S. Justice Department on antitrust grounds, and the NYSE–Deutsche Börse merger later failed on European antitrust concerns.
- This potential ICE acquisition could face fewer direct antitrust objections because ICE’s market focus is more in commodities than in cash equities, and both bidders would be U.S.-based. Still, rivals such as CME Group or other exchanges could oppose the deal on competitive grounds, and nationalistic objections could arise from international players.
- The deal would significantly expand ICE’s size and staff footprint (ICE has ~1,000 employees vs. NYSE Euronext’s ~3,077).

Market reaction
- NYSE Euronext shares jumped in after-hours trading after news of the talks.

Broader significance
- The takeover would underscore the long-running shift from floor-based “open outcry” stock trading to electronic trading and signal the growing dominance and value of derivatives and clearing businesses in global capital markets.

This article examines how punitive child-support enforcement in South Carolina helped shape the life of Walter Scott, a father of four who was repeatedly jailed for falling behind on payments before he was killed by a North Charleston police officer. It traces Scott’s long struggle with arrears—at times jailed multiple times, losing steady work, drinking and doing odd jobs—and shows how incarceration for unpaid support often worsens parents’ ability to comply.

Key points:
- Background on Walter Scott: Over at least a decade he fell into repeated arrears (cases noted from 2003 onward), was jailed multiple times, lost jobs after incarceration, and accumulated nearly $18,104 in child-support debt. His family and advocates say that being repeatedly imprisoned destroyed opportunities to stabilize work and pay down debts.
- South Carolina’s enforcement system: The state permits quick use of bench warrants (clerks can issue warrants after just five days past due under “Rule 24”), license suspensions, wage garnishment, seizure of tax refunds and bank accounts, and incarceration. Berkeley County alone had more than 1,100 active bench warrants for unpaid support. DSS manages most cases but lacks precise statewide warrant counts.
- Criticism and legal context: Advocates call South Carolina’s approach among the nation’s harshest, arguing it criminalizes poverty and treats debtors like criminals. A U.S. Supreme Court case years earlier found that jailing noncustodial parents without means was generally inappropriate, prompting some decline in warrant activity. Critics also note enforcement practices vary widely by county and state.
- Alternative approaches: South Carolina received an $8 million federal grant for “Operation Work,” a program in several counties that helps fathers find work, get training and suspend child-support obligations while they improve employment prospects. Advocates argue programs like this are more effective than incarceration because jail increases debt and reduces employability.
- Broader national picture: There is no national count of parents jailed for support arrears, but surveys and reports show thousands are jailed in some states and that many incarcerated parents are indigent and lack legal representation. The punitive model—orders set beyond payers’ means followed by escalating sanctions—can trap poor parents in a cycle of debt, unemployment and repeated imprisonment.

Overall, the story uses Walter Scott’s case to highlight a wider problem: punitive child-support enforcement can perpetuate poverty and instability, undermining the very goal of ensuring support for children, and prompting calls for reform and investment in work-focused assistance instead of repeated incarceration.

Ahmed Wali (Ahmad Wali/A.W.K.) Karzai, the powerful and divisive half-brother of Afghan President Hamid Karzai and the dominant power broker in Kandahar, was assassinated on July 12 at his Kandahar compound by a longtime trusted security guard who was then killed. His death removed a central — and deeply contradictory — figure in southern Afghanistan and immediately created a dangerous power vacuum.

Who he was and why he mattered
- De facto ruler of much of Kandahar through family, tribal ties, patronage and personal wealth; chairman of the Kandahar provincial council.  
- Played a pivotal role in local security and politics: brokered tribal deals, identified Taliban fighters for strikes, recruited men for pro-government forces and hosted CIA operations. U.S. and NATO forces depended on him to help keep key Pashtun tribes aligned against the Taliban.  
- Simultaneously accused of extensive corruption and involvement in the opium trade, contract favoritism and connections to militias and smuggling networks. These activities alienated many Afghans, undermined government legitimacy and repeatedly put him at odds with counterinsurgency goals that emphasized winning popular support.  
- The CIA reportedly paid him for information and services while military and civilian officials criticized his corrupting influence, illustrating persistent tensions in U.S. policy between short-term security pragmatism and long-term governance priorities.

Immediate consequences and reactions
- His death heightened fears that fragile security gains in Kandahar — the Taliban’s birthplace and a focus of a recent U.S. troop surge — could unravel as rivals and insurgents vie for influence. Some officials warned the Taliban and competing warlords would benefit.  
- U.S., NATO and Afghan leaders condemned the killing; President Karzai expressed sorrow. Security was tightened in Kandahar. The Taliban claimed responsibility, though motives and any insurgent links of the killer were unclear.  
- Analysts and U.S. officials debated whether his removal might open space for a cleaner, more legitimate local leadership or instead trigger violent competition and weaken the government’s control.

Bigger picture
- The assassination underscores a central dilemma of the U.S. presence in Afghanistan: reliance on local “big men” who can get things done in the short term but whose corruption and clientelism undermine long-term stability and popular legitimacy.  
- U.S. attitudes toward Ahmed Wali shifted with strategy — criticized during population-centered counterinsurgency, tolerated or utilized more under a narrower counterterrorism focus — highlighting conflicting U.S. objectives and tools.  
- His death reinforced why U.S. leaders, including President Obama, were intent on extricating the U.S. from a conflict they had struggled to resolve: the political networks the U.S. needed to work within are themselves a major obstacle to sustainable peace.

In sum: Ahmed Wali Karzai’s assassination removed a key but contentious broker whose mix of influence, corruption and cooperation with foreign forces both helped and hindered the Afghan and international effort. His death deepens uncertainty in Kandahar and exemplifies the intractable trade-offs that have complicated the U.S. mission in Afghanistan.

Supporters of Colorado’s health insurance exchange rolled out a provocative “Got insurance?” ad series aimed at getting young adults to enroll under the Affordable Care Act. Produced by ProgressNow Colorado and the Colorado Consumer Health Initiative (CCHI), the social-media campaign features edgy spots — including “brosurance” keg‑stand scenes and sexually suggestive ads showing a young woman holding birth-control pills saying lines such as, “OMG, he’s hot! Let’s hope he’s as easy to get as this birth control. My health insurance covers the pill, which means all I have to worry about is getting him between the covers.”

The groups say the goal is to raise awareness and drive sign-ups among young, healthy adults whose participation helps stabilize premiums. The ads intentionally target millennials and were designed to be attention‑grabbing; organizers note they run only online, not on billboards or buses.

Critics — mainly conservatives and some observers in advertising academia — condemned the campaign as demeaning to women, trivializing serious health issues and an ill-timed distraction amid problems with plan cancellations and slowed exchange sign-ups. The ads drew wide social-media backlash (including the hashtag #hosurance), press attention, and even mention during congressional hearings. Campaign defenders argue controversy equals attention and that early site traffic and enrollments justify the approach, while acknowledging future spots may be less edgy.

- The fleece/down vest—often black and from Patagonia or Uniqlo—has become an unofficial uniform for Silicon Valley venture capitalists and tech figures. It's widely seen at coffee shops, conferences, VC offices on Sand Hill Road, and even on HBO’s Silicon Valley (character Jared Dunn wears a Patagonia vest), reinforcing the stereotype.

- Reasons for the trend: practical Bay Area weather (cool, layering-friendly year-round), Patagonia’s reputation for quality without pretension, and firms handing out branded vests at events (e.g., Andreessen Horowitz). Patagonia and show costume designers noted the garment’s ubiquity when researching Valley aesthetics.

- The phenomenon reached peak visibility when a Uniqlo "To Go" vending machine at San Francisco International Airport began selling lightweight down vests (~$49.90). The machine reportedly averages about $10,000/month in sales (~200 vests), drawing viral social-media attention and jokes about “visiting VCs” buying vests on arrival.

- The author discloses a relationship with an Andreessen Horowitz employee.

A cache of Twitter direct messages forwarded to the Daily Caller and other outlets revealed inflammatory, private comments by Rebecca Mansour, a top aide, speechwriter and domestic policy adviser for Sarah Palin. Sent in mid-2010 to an online acquaintance, Mansour’s messages insulted conservative figures (calling RedState founder Erick Erickson “a total douchebag”), derided Mitt Romney supporters as “wacky” or an “AstroTurf brigade,” dismissed other GOP figures, and discussed strategic calculations about Palin’s possible 2012 presidential ambitions and endorsements (including Nikki Haley).

The most sensitive material criticized Palin’s daughter Bristol—predicting Bristol would be “held at arm’s length,” comparing family scandals to Patti Davis and Billy Carter, and discussing Levi Johnston—plus suggestions about finding a different suitor. Mansour also shared a purported “scoop” about Alaska liberal radio host Shannyn Moore’s compensation and sponsors, using crude references. Several additional messages about Palin family dynamics and internal campaign tactics were withheld from publication.

When approached, Mansour first denied authorship or claimed the messages were fabricated via screencaps, then partially admitted to sending some messages and offered changing explanations—saying they were private chats with someone she thought was a friend and that she sometimes wrote in anger to defend Palin. The Daily Caller authenticated the messages through Twitter notification emails and forensic checks. The disclosures prompted embarrassment and a headache for Palin’s operation; Mansour’s current status with SarahPAC was reported as uncertain and the campaign declined further comment.

A 15-year-old Kansas City girl, Daejona M. Holmes, has been charged as an adult with two counts of second-degree murder, two counts of armed criminal action and one count of tampering with physical evidence in the April 9 killings of her parents, Kinderly Holmes, 37, and Brian Starr, 38, at their home on Belmeade Road.

Police responded after a 911 call; officers found Kinderly shot once in the stomach and Starr shot three times (twice in the torso and once in the mouth). Daejona initially told dispatchers a robbery had occurred; when contacted at a McDonald’s she at first said her father shot her mother and that she then shot her father, and later gave varying accounts to investigators. In interviews she described hearing an argument and a gunshot, finding her mother dead, picking up a handgun, then shooting her father as he approached; in subsequent statements she admitted changing clothes, returning to the house multiple times, moving her father’s body nearer the front door, and could not explain why she waited about an hour to call 911.

Searches and evidence recovered under warrant include online queries for “scary movies where kids kill parents,” rap lyrics about wanting her father dead, a February video of Daejona holding a handgun while dancing, and a backpack drawing of stick figures labeled “me” shooting “dad.” The firearm was later found in a puddle across the street from the home. Prosecutors have requested bond of $150,000.

Rudy Kurniawan, once a celebrated rare-wine collector and dealer, was convicted in Manhattan federal court of fraud for producing and selling counterfeit vintage wines. Prosecutors showed evidence seized from his California home — hundreds of bottles, labels, corks, stamps and other materials — and called top French winemakers who testified that many bottles Kurniawan had consigned bore impossible vintages or fraudulent winery markings. Notable testimony came from Laurent Ponsot (Domaine Ponsot), Laurent Roumier (Domaine Roumier) and Aubert de Villaine (Domaine de la Romanée‑Conti), who identified forged labels and vintages and helped halt auctions where suspect bottles were offered.

Kurniawan rose rapidly in the wine world by demonstrating an exceptional palate and spending millions at auctions, including consigning a 2006 sale that raised $24.7 million. Prosecutors say he used his tasting skill to blend younger or ordinary wines with some older wine character, relabeled bottles in a home “laboratory,” and passed them off as rare vintages that fetched high prices at auction. Buyers—including billionaire Bill Koch—suffered large losses; Koch testified he bought millions of dollars’ worth of Kurniawan’s wines.

The defense argued Kurniawan was being scapegoated in a market already riddled with counterfeits, claiming he merely reconditioned bottles and used labels as decoration. The jury rejected that defense and found him guilty; sentencing was set for April (he faces up to 40 years and fines). The case is the first major U.S. federal conviction for selling fake wine and has drawn attention to fraud risks in the rare-wine market.

Hurricane Irma, a powerful Category 4 storm with sustained winds near 130 mph, approached and began impacting Florida early Sunday, its northern eyewall reaching the lower Florida Keys. The storm’s center was moving north-northwest at about 6–8 mph and was forecast to cross the Keys and move up Florida’s Gulf Coast. Tornado warnings were issued across parts of South Florida, and rapid bands of rain and tornado-producing cells moved through Monroe, Miami‑Dade and Broward counties.

Key impacts and conditions:
- The Keys reported very strong gusts (Key West measurements and a reef station recorded sustained winds of 43–66 mph with higher gusts), flooding and higher water levels; residents were urged to shelter in place and keep indoors even during the eye’s calm.
- Large power outages across South Florida: Florida Power & Light reported roughly 430,000 customers without power (about 250,000 in Miami‑Dade, 130,000 in Broward, 40,000+ in Palm Beach).
- Tens of thousands were sheltering across the state; access to some barrier islands was closed.
- Emergency officials warned against unsafe behaviors (notably a widely shared Facebook “shoot at Irma” event) and urged volunteers to help at shelters.

Wider regional notes:
- French and Dutch authorities reported that Hurricane Jose skirted their Caribbean islands with limited damage, allowing relief and security operations to continue on islands already devastated by Irma (St. Maarten, St. Martin, St. Barts). The Dutch king planned visits and evacuations/medical transfers were underway for stranded tourists and patients.
- Dutch marines and other forces were assisting with security, infrastructure restoration and evacuations on hard‑hit islands.

Officials stressed that although some forecast shifts might spare certain population centers from the worst direct hit, Irma remained a dangerous, powerful hurricane capable of causing catastrophic damage.

A 73-year-old musician, Lester Chambers of The Chambers Brothers, was assaulted onstage Saturday at the Russell City Blues Festival in Hayward after dedicating Curtis Mayfield’s “People Get Ready” to Trayvon Martin. Witnesses and Chambers’ family say a 43-year-old woman, identified by police as Dinalynn Andrews Potter of Barstow, jumped onto the stage, yelled “it’s all your fault,” and shoved Chambers to the ground. People onstage quickly subdued her; Hayward police arrested her on suspicion of battery, cited and released her, and said additional charges are possible as the motive is investigated. Chambers, who was taken to a hospital and later released, is using a cane and has a large welt on his back, a bruised rib muscle, nerve damage and soreness. His family believes the attack was racially motivated because Chambers is Black and the attacker is white, and they are urging police to pursue hate crime charges. The incident occurred the same day a Florida jury acquitted George Zimmerman in the shooting death of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin. Chambers, a noted 1960s soul singer who has long disputed unpaid royalties, and his group are slated for induction into the R&B Hall of Fame later this year.

Colin Kaepernick, the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback who gained national attention for kneeling during the national anthem to protest racial injustice, filed a collusion grievance against the NFL in October 2017. Represented by attorney Mark Geragos, Kaepernick alleges team owners conspired to keep him unsigned in retaliation for his protests. The grievance was filed through the arbitration process under the league’s collective bargaining agreement (CBA); Geragos said it followed extensive efforts to contact teams and executives. The NFL Players Association has agreed to support and assist Kaepernick, and the NFL said it was reviewing the matter.

Media reports note that proving collusion could, under CBA provisions, potentially trigger early termination of the agreement if clear and convincing evidence is found. Kaepernick, who opted out of his 49ers contract after the 2016 season and remained a free agent despite solid 2016 statistics, and his supporters contend he’s being blackballed. League officials, including Commissioner Roger Goodell, have denied any concerted blackballing, while some teams cite concern about the media attention surrounding him. Kaepernick’s goal, per his attorney, is to be treated fairly and return to the NFL.

Saudi Arabia has launched an ambitious reform program, Vision 2030, to wean the kingdom off heavy dependence on oil after prices plunged from over $110/barrel in 2014 to under $45. Officials, led by Deputy Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, say low oil revenues and large budget deficits have made structural change urgent.

Key goals and measures
- Diversify the economy and boost non-oil revenue: targets include raising non-oil receipts to 600 billion riyals by 2020 and 1 trillion riyals by 2030, and increasing the private sector’s share of the economy from 40% to 60%.
- Transform the Public Investment Fund (PIF) into a global sovereign wealth fund (target size ~2 trillion riyals, with aspirational expansion up to ~$3 trillion) by transferring assets including stakes in state oil company Saudi Aramco.
- Partially privatize Aramco: plan to list less than 5% (even a 1% sale would be the largest IPO ever), both to raise capital and increase transparency.
- Fiscal consolidation: cut subsidies and raise fuel prices (already implemented in December); consider new taxes (e.g., sales taxes, levies on luxury goods).
- Economic and industrial shifts: encourage tourism, mining, local defense production and new industries; reduce reliance on foreign labor by offering a green-card style long-term residency for expatriate Arabs and Muslims to attract investment.
- Social and labor changes: increase women’s workforce participation (target rise from ~22% to 30%), reform education to better prepare youth for a modern economy, and create jobs to reduce high youth unemployment.

Rationale and challenges
- The drop in oil income and large fiscal deficits (about 15–16% of GDP in 2015; projected slightly lower in 2016) make diversification essential. OPEC forecasts suggest oil prices will recover only slowly.
- Officials frame the reforms as necessary to protect the country from commodity volatility and future demand uncertainty (e.g., climate policies).
- The plan is bold but lacks detailed implementation roadmaps for many targets (education reform, job creation, revenue sources) and faces social, bureaucratic and political hurdles. International observers (IMF) and analysts caution that execution will be challenging.

Impact and reaction
- The announcement briefly lifted market sentiment (Saudi stocks rose), and the plan sparked widespread public debate domestically (trending on social media).
- If realized, reforms could reshape Saudi economic structures, increase transparency (via Aramco listings), and open the kingdom to more foreign investment and resident rights — but success depends on concrete policy measures, societal buy-in, and careful implementation.

Somerset County authorities say a Bridgewater woman allegedly used children's drawings to smuggle the prescription opioid Suboxone to her boyfriend incarcerated at the Somerset County Jail. Jail staff noticed irregularities in mail to inmate Michael Gill on June 15 and called the sheriff’s K-9, which alerted to drugs concealed in the drawings. Additional letters with similar drawings arrived June 20 and June 28 and were also found to contain suspected Suboxone. Casey Giles, 37, of Bridgewater, was identified by investigators and charged with third-degree possession with intent to distribute; she was held on $20,000 bail. Gill, 38, of Oxford, was charged with attempting to possess a controlled dangerous substance and had $10,000 bail set. Sheriff Frank Provenzano said details of the concealment won’t be released to avoid enabling copycats and reiterated the department’s ongoing efforts to prevent narcotics from entering the jail.

Hillary Clinton launched her 2016 presidential campaign on April 12, 2015, saying everyday Americans need a champion and she wants to be that champion. Her campaign’s YouTube channel and website (hillaryclinton.com/join) host her announcement video, speeches, policy positions and campaign updates.

Background: Clinton’s public career spans roles as First Lady of Arkansas and the United States, U.S. Senator from New York, Secretary of State, lawyer, law professor and activist. Raised in suburban Illinois, she attended Wellesley and Yale Law, worked for the Children’s Defense Fund, helped investigate President Nixon, and co-founded Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families. As First Lady, she led early efforts to reform health care and delivered a landmark 1995 speech in Beijing asserting that “women’s rights are human rights.” As senator she worked across the aisle, supported rural and small-business initiatives, and after 2008 served as Secretary of State under President Obama, championing human rights, internet freedom and expanded opportunities for women, girls, LGBT people and youth.

Campaign context: Clinton’s entry set up what could be a relatively uncontested Democratic primary and a historic opportunity to become the first woman nominated by a major party. She begins the campaign with near-universal name recognition, strong support among women, and a long public record that has both inspired and polarized voters. Her campaign planned early outreach to Iowa and a formal kickoff event the following month. The announcement followed considerable public attention, including pop-cultural commentary such as an SNL sketch parodying her launch.

Sen. Orrin Hatch (R‑Utah), a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, told reporters during a lunch break while Christine Blasey Ford was testifying that Ford was “an attractive, good witness” and that he did not think she was “uncredible,” but said it was “too early to say” definitively whether he found her credible. When asked what he meant by “attractive,” Hatch clarified, “In other words, she’s pleasing.” His spokesman later tweeted that Hatch uses “attractive” to describe personalities, not appearances. The comments came as the committee continued Ford’s testimony against Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh; Kavanaugh was scheduled to testify later the same day and the committee planned to vote on his nomination Friday. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a potential swing vote, said Ford’s testimony was credible “thus far.”

Scientists are probing ever-smaller scales of reality and confronting bizarre possibilities that could force revisions to our understanding of space and time. Historically, the notion of the universe’s smallest constituents has moved from grains of sand to atoms, to protons/neutrons and then quarks; today quarks and electrons appear point-like in experiments, but it’s unknown whether they are truly fundamental.

Point-like particles create theoretical problems (infinities when forces are calculated at zero separation). Two leading ideas that avoid these problems are:
- Superstring theory: particles are tiny loops or strings rather than points, preventing arbitrarily close approaches and taming infinities. There is currently no experimental evidence for strings.
- Discrete spacetime (space-time foam): space itself may be pixelated into minimum-size “grains,” so particles can’t come closer than that grain size.

Black-hole singularities are another candidate for the smallest objects. Classical general relativity predicts infinite density at a singularity, but most physicists expect that to be an artifact of the clash between general relativity and quantum mechanics; a correct theory of quantum gravity should reveal a finite, extremely tiny structure—likely far smaller than quarks and perhaps comparable in scale to strings.

All these possibilities converge on the Planck length (≈1.6 × 10^-35 meters), a scale far beyond current measurement and thought to mark where quantum-gravitational effects dominate and conventional notions of spacetime break down. At or below that length, uncertainty and probabilistic effects prevent meaningful measurement, and new physics (quantum gravity) is expected to take over.

A 17-year-old girl, identified by family and the ADAMS mosque as Nabra Hassanen of Reston, Va., was killed after leaving midnight Ramadan prayers with friends early June 18. According to police and mosque officials, a motorist in a red car confronted a group of teens walking to a nearby IHOP; witnesses say the driver assaulted Nabra, her friends fled back to the mosque and later reported she was missing. Her remains were recovered Sunday afternoon from a pond in Sterling; police arrested 22-year-old Darwin Martinez Torres and charged him with murder. Authorities said the investigation is not being treated as a hate or bias crime at this time and described the episode as appearing to stem from a road‑rage incident, though they said they will follow leads if evidence of bias emerges. The killing shocked the local Muslim community during Ramadan; mosque leaders, Virginia officials and residents expressed grief and called for support for the family. A chief medical examiner will confirm identity and cause of death; a GoFundMe for the family raised substantial donations and a vigil was planned.

Donald Trump nominated former Texas governor Rick Perry to be Secretary of Energy — an appointment striking because Perry once vowed to abolish the Department of Energy and famously forgot its name during a 2011 debate. The choice was confirmed by transition sources and officially announced; Trump praised Perry’s Texas record on jobs and low energy prices.

Why conservatives support Perry
- Conservatives view Perry as a manager willing to challenge DOE’s status quo and cut or reform programs they consider market‑distorting, such as renewable research, efficiency programs and loan guarantees.
- The Heritage Foundation urged a dramatic downsizing of DOE, proposing elimination of many research and loan programs and even selling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; Perry’s selection is consistent with that direction.

Areas of controversy and concern
- Perry has been a climate skeptic who has questioned the scientific consensus and accused some scientists of manipulating data for funding. He and Trump have both signaled a willingness to scale back federal climate and renewable-energy priorities.
- Environmental groups and Democrats warned Perry’s nomination imperils DOE programs that support clean energy innovation and climate research. Transition requests for names of DOE staff involved in Obama-era climate work raised fears of political targeting.
- Critics note conflicts of interest: Perry sits on the board of Energy Transfer Partners (developer of the Dakota Access Pipeline) and has financial ties to the oil industry; he would likely need to divest or resign those roles if confirmed.
- Opponents also question his qualifications to oversee DOE’s major national-security responsibilities, notably stewardship of the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile and national laboratories — areas historically led by scientifically trained secretaries.

Record and relevant experience
- Perry served 14 years as Texas governor during a period of major oil-and-gas production growth and a significant expansion of wind power in Texas. Supporters point to his management experience and the state’s energy growth as relevant strengths.
- Detractors highlight his past pledge to eliminate DOE and his repeated public skepticism of climate science and federal clean‑energy initiatives.

Practical implications if confirmed
- Policy shifts could include de-emphasizing DOE renewable-energy research, slowing appliance-efficiency rules, prioritizing fossil-fuel development, and reorienting DOE priorities on nuclear waste (e.g., renewed attention to Yucca Mountain).
- Major regulatory changes would be complex and slow, requiring many rulemakings and congressional pushback; some DOE functions (nuclear stewardship, labs) will likely be managed by deputies with technical expertise.

Political context
- Perry previously disparaged Trump during the 2016 primaries but later endorsed him. His nomination drew both praise from conservatives and strong criticism from environmentalists, some members of Congress, and scientific groups worried about politicization of career staff and rollback of climate and renewable programs.

In short: Perry’s selection signals an administration intent to shift DOE toward fossil-fuel priorities, reduce federal involvement in clean‑energy programs, and question climate-focused initiatives — while raising concerns about conflicts of interest, potential politicization of career staff, and whether he has the technical background for the department’s national-security missions.

Chris Hemsworth lost his wallet while dining with his family in a rough area of Los Angeles. Seventeen-year-old Tristin Budzyn-Baker found it, realized it belonged to the actor, and returned it intact after contacting Hemsworth’s team. Hemsworth rewarded the teen with the cash from the wallet, tickets to The Ellen DeGeneres Show, and wrote him a letter of recommendation for his Eagle Scout bid. On the show, Ellen DeGeneres (and Shutterfly, per reports) gave Budzyn-Baker an additional $10,000 for his honesty.

A 25-year-old Baton Rouge man, Adonis Forbes, was arrested after a handgun he was trying to fix accidentally fired Saturday night and fatally wounded the 13-year-old babysitter, Murrain Hawkins. Forbes and his wife had returned to their Tennessee Street home around 9 p.m. to check on their children; Forbes discovered his gun was malfunctioning and, while attempting to fix it, it discharged, striking Hawkins in the abdomen. Emergency responders transported Hawkins to a hospital where he was pronounced dead. Forbes was booked on a negligent-homicide charge with bond set at $10,000 and subsequently posted bond and was released. Authorities did not immediately say whether Hawkins and Forbes were related.
