Fourteen-year-old Caitlin Sanchez, who became the voice of Dora the Explorer in 2007, has sued Nickelodeon, Viacom and MTV Networks in Manhattan Supreme Court, alleging she was unfairly paid under a complex contract and was deprived of proper residuals and merchandise income. Her 41-page complaint says she earned only $5,115 per episode, received negligible merchandising payments, worked hundreds of studio hours, and made more than 100 promotional appearances—often with only a $40 per diem—while the companies profited from the $11 billion Dora brand. Sanchez’s lawyers say the family was pressured to sign the deal with little time to review it and that appearances and travel often yielded out-of-pocket costs.

Nickelodeon disputes the claims, saying Sanchez was well compensated, that travel and first-class hotels were provided and the $40 covered incidentals. The network also contends it replaced her because her voice changed with puberty—the same reason given when the original Dora actor left. Sanchez’s lawyer says the suit is not an attempt to regain the role but to seek proper compensation for residuals, merchandising and unpaid promotional work. Nickelodeon calls the suit without merit.

Steven Beare, a Littleton Police officer, Colorado National Guardsman and experienced mountaineer, has been missing since mid-June after attempting a solo ascent of Mount Elbrus in southern Russia. He was expected to check in June 16 but never returned; his last contact with family was when he arrived in Russia. A sudden, severe storm and subsequent blizzard produced whiteout conditions and heavy snow (reported up to about 4 feet), and Russian high‑mountain teams began a search but suspended operations because of the weather. A nearby climbing party reportedly saw him earlier but lost sight of him when they turned back.

Beare, who has scaled peaks including Kilimanjaro and many Colorado 14ers and is pursuing the “Seven Summits,” is husband to Olivia (they have a toddler and she is pregnant) and an Army veteran. Olivia has been coordinating rescue efforts from Colorado: organizing private search crews, contracting helicopters (at roughly $2,500/hour), working with friends and colleagues to raise funds through the Colorado Police Officers Foundation, and seeking assistance from U.S. officials. Progress has been hampered by Russian visa/approval issues for private teams and by continued bad weather. Family, coworkers and local officials continue efforts and appeals for donations as searches resume when conditions allow.

Gilbert P. Hyatt, a Las Vegas inventor now in his mid-70s, has sued the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) seeking decisions on two extremely old patent applications—one pending about 43 years and another about 35 years—which he says the agency has stalled. Hyatt, who previously won a pivotal 1990 patent on a “single chip integrated circuit computer architecture” and licensed many patents to Philips (netting him an estimated >$150 million), contends the PTO has been giving him the “runaround” to avoid issuing rulings it might have to defend on appeal. He has litigated the PTO repeatedly, won a Supreme Court ruling in 2012 on admissible evidence, and alleges an unofficial PTO policy of delaying his matters; the agency declines to comment because the filings predate a 1995 confidentiality law.

Observers say the PTO may be reluctant to grant broadly impactful patents and instead bottles contentious cases. Hyatt’s pending claims are confidential, though he says one concerns “square wave machine control.” Historians acknowledge Hyatt’s technical contributions but note that broader commercial developments by companies such as Intel and Texas Instruments shaped the industry’s trajectory.

The article also includes a broader editorial urging Congress to protect small inventors against reforms that could favor large tech firms. It argues that recent “patent reform” efforts and proposed measures (like “loser pays” rules or databases tracking frequent patent litigants) risk undermining independent inventors. The piece recommends strengthening PTO support for small or elderly inventors—e.g., broader access to accelerated examination, fee waivers for small applicants—to preserve innovation and prevent powerful firms from squeezing out garage inventors.

Neil Edwin Prescott, 28, of Crofton, Md., was taken into custody and hospitalized for an emergency psychiatric evaluation after police said he repeatedly threatened to "blow everybody up" at his former workplace and called himself a "joker" — a remark authorities say echoed last week’s mass shooting at an Aurora, Colo., movie theater. Prosecutors and police say the threat was phoned to Prescott’s former supervisor at a Pitney Bowes subcontractor in Capitol Heights; the supervisor alerted police.

When officers searched Prescott’s apartment they found about two dozen firearms (including shotguns, a tactical rifle and handguns), accessories and several thousand rounds of ammunition; at least 13 guns were registered to him. Officers earlier encountered Prescott wearing a T-shirt that read, “Guns don’t kill people, I do.” He was initially ordered to the hospital for a psychiatric hold and is expected to remain hospitalized for about a week; no criminal charges are expected while he is undergoing treatment and the investigation continues.

Authorities say Prescott had either recently been fired or was in the process of being fired and had previously raised concerns at the company. Local officials framed the intervention as preventing a likely violent episode and noted the danger of copycat attacks after high-profile violent crimes. Prescott has no prior criminal record in Maryland beyond a 2007 traffic infraction.

A deadly fire ripped through a Harrisburg row home on Friday, killing a 3- or 4-year-old girl and leaving two other children in critical condition at the Lehigh Valley Burn Center. Neighbors described chaotic scenes, including children on the roof and frantic rescue efforts; investigators have not released the victims’ names or updated the children’s conditions. While firefighters and police responded, Harrisburg firefighter Lt. Dennis DeVoe was fatally struck when his car was T‑boned at 14th and Walnut by a 19‑year‑old driver, Khanyae Kendall, who police say was driving a stolen vehicle. Kendall faces multiple charges including aggravated assault by vehicle while DUI, receiving stolen property, driving without a proper license, and other traffic violations; she is jailed on $200,000 bail and scheduled for a preliminary hearing March 21. DeVoe leaves a wife and four children; his department mourned him as a leader and set up a GoFundMe for the family. A separate GoFundMe was created for the fire victims’ family. The article also includes information on reporting dangerous consumer products to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.

An internal News of the World/News International review in 2007 uncovered about 300 emails suggesting widespread phone-hacking and possible illegal payments from journalists to police, but that dossier was not passed to the Metropolitan Police until June 2011. The emails (and linked cash records) reportedly show four‑figure sums — totaling around £120,000 — paid to police and indicate that hacking extended beyond the “rogue reporter” Clive Goodman. A larger set of roughly 2,200–2,500 related emails remains unaccounted for.

The findings, first disclosed in leaked documents and media reports, raise allegations that News International executives knew more than they publicly admitted and may have covered up wrongdoing, including by arranging hush-money settlements with victims (notably Gordon Taylor) that later drew criticism. Harbottle & Lewis had been asked to review staff emails in 2007 and reported they found no clear evidence tying Goodman’s illegal actions to senior editors; the letter did not address other possible misconduct. When News International later reacquired the emails they believed they contained prima facie evidence of wider hacking and police payments.

Scotland Yard has come under heavy criticism for earlier handling of the matter. Assistant Commissioner John Yates apologized publicly for not pursuing a fuller investigation after 2009, saying in hindsight he should have done more; he denied inappropriate ties to News International. Several journalists and some police officers reportedly face potential criminal charges, and senior figures including former News of the World editors (Andy Coulson, Colin Myler) and News International executives (Rebekah Brooks, James Murdoch) have come under police scrutiny. Coulson was arrested and bailed; Brooks was expected to be questioned under caution.

Allegations also include attempts by reporters to access voicemail or phone records of 9/11 victims via a US-based private investigator, heightening international legal exposure. Commentators warned the revelations could trigger U.S. legal interest (including under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) because News Corp is U.S.-listed and payments to officials could be criminal.

The scandal prompted the closure of the 168-year-old News of the World, threatened Rupert Murdoch’s bid for full control of BSkyB, provoked political action (Ed Miliband sought to delay the takeover), and intensified scrutiny of the Murdochs and News International for possible systemic illegal practices and a subsequent cover-up.

The document examines whether senior News Corp./News International executives — possibly including Rebekah Brooks and even Rupert Murdoch — could face criminal prosecution over the News of the World phone‑hacking and payments-to-police scandal. It explains that earlier prosecutions of reporter Clive Goodman and private investigator Glenn Mulcaire used the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA). A key provision, Section 79, makes corporate officers personally liable if an offense was committed with their consent, connivance or “attributable to any neglect.” 

Commentator Andreas Whittam Smith argues Section 79 is broad enough to trap directors who presided over an organization that conducted illegal activities, whether by authorizing, turning a blind eye to, or negligently failing to prevent them. He singles out Rebekah Brooks — former News of the World editor and then News International CEO — as especially vulnerable because she hired the private investigator linked to the hacking of murdered teenager Milly Dowler and presided over publication of stories based on hacked voicemails. Police were reported to be preparing to arrest former editor Andy Coulson as well.

A corporate-law specialist, Jonathan P. Armstrong, cautions that applying the “neglect” clause that broadly may be a stretch: the clause’s origins in health-and-safety law suggest prosecutions require evidence of more concrete failings likely to convince a jury beyond reasonable doubt. He says prosecutions typically proceed only where direct involvement or strong evidence of condoning can be shown, so arrests of Rupert Murdoch or his son James would be unlikely absent direct evidence tying them to the hacks.

The scandal has had wide political and commercial fallout: major public outrage, condemnation in Parliament and from Prime Minister David Cameron, damage to Murdoch’s long-standing influence in British politics, threats to News Corp.’s £12 billion bid for full control of BSkyB, calls for Brooks’s dismissal, advertiser withdrawals, and questions about succession at News Corp. Whittam Smith calls for swift, decisive action, arguing existing law (notably RIPA Section 79) provides mechanisms to hold directors to account to prevent further corruption of police, prejudice to trials, and undue political influence.

Jennifer “Jen” Houle, a 22-year-old senior studying business at the University of Minnesota and a member of the Pi Beta Phi sorority, has been missing since the early morning hours of Friday, March 27. She was last seen between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m. at Blarney Pub & Grill in the Dinkytown neighborhood of Minneapolis after a night of bar hopping with a friend; the two were separated at the bar. Her purse was found about three blocks away on the 1100 block of 4th Street SE at about 3 a.m.

Houle, described as 5'5" with long blond hair and blue eyes, was last seen wearing a green blouse, black leather jacket, black leggings and black boots. Friends say she ran into an ex-boyfriend that night, which “set off some emotions”; police have interviewed the ex and other patrons from the bar. Authorities are investigating and ask anyone with information to contact Minneapolis police. The University of Minnesota is assisting with the search and offering counseling to students. Houle’s sorority sisters have distributed posters and shared her photo online, and more than 200 friends and family held a prayer vigil at her high school in Stillwater. Authorities remain hopeful she will be found and urge anyone with information to call the MPD tipline.

Several news outlets recapped the CNN-sponsored GOP debate on national security, identifying clear winners and losers and highlighting key takeaways.

Overall outcome
- The debate exposed divisions on foreign policy and immigration while offering a chance to gauge candidates’ fluency on international affairs. There were no catastrophic gaffes, but some contenders boosted their standing and others faltered.

Winners
- Newt Gingrich: Strong debater who benefited from front-runner airtime; showed command on security issues and lively exchanges. However, his moderate stance on immigration—arguing for humane legal status solutions for some undocumented immigrants—may alienate conservative primary voters and invite attacks framing it as “amnesty.”
- Jon Huntsman: Performed well on a foreign-policy stage, leveraging his diplomatic experience to appear competent and reasonable. His performance, plus heavy pro-Huntsman ad spending in New Hampshire, could help him gain traction there.
- Mitt Romney: Avoided attacks and responded solidly when engaged, though he did not have a breakout night. He used foreign-policy answers to contrast with Obama on domestic issues and aimed criticism at Gingrich on immigration.
- Ron Paul (in some accounts): Earned airtime and pressed consistent, contrarian views on foreign policy and civil liberties that energize his base, though his positions remain outside GOP orthodoxy.
- Michele Bachmann and Rick Santorum got some positive mentions for moments of strength, but neither had a decisive breakout.

Losers
- Herman Cain: Struggled on foreign policy and failed to demonstrate the requisite command of international affairs; his momentum appeared to be slipping.
- Ron Paul (in other accounts): While he energized supporters, his isolationist and noninterventionist positions—leaving Israel to fend for itself, disentangling from Afghanistan, ending the drug war—made it hard to see him as a mainstream nominee.
- Rick Perry, Michele Bachmann, Rick Santorum: Needed a breakout moment to revive their campaigns; none delivered one. Perry faced pushback for his stances (e.g., cutting aid to Pakistan, proposing a no-fly zone over Syria) and some backtracking.
- Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP) was jokingly singled out as an alarming topic Gingrich raised.

Key themes and takeaways
- Immigration emerged as a potentially decisive issue: Gingrich’s compassionate framing could help in a general election but risks damaging primary appeal.
- Debate performance vs. polling: Gingrich’s debate strength and poll rise reinforced each other; Romney remained a steady front-runner without being attacked.
- Foreign policy divisions: Candidates differed sharply on Afghanistan troop levels, aid to Pakistan, Syria responses, and broader defense spending, highlighting ideological splits (e.g., Huntsman/Paul alignment on some civil-liberties and troop-withdrawal views).
- Competence on foreign policy mattered: Several lower-tier candidates failed to meet the minimal fluency threshold needed to remain viable.

Bottom line: The debate solidified Newt Gingrich’s debate-era momentum while underscoring immigration as a flashpoint for the GOP. Jon Huntsman gained credibility on national security, Romney remained durable but unspectacular, and several candidates—Cain, Perry, Santorum, and others—missed chances to revive or advance their campaigns.

The Alabama special Senate primary will likely head to a Sept. 26 Republican runoff and offers a test of how much President Trump’s endorsement and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s money matter in a deeply Republican state.

Republican picture
- Roy Moore, the twice-suspended former Alabama chief justice with a fervent evangelical base, led most polls (roughly 31–35%) and was projected to finish first on primary night but short of the 50% needed to avoid a runoff.
- Appointed incumbent Sen. Luther Strange, backed by Trump’s surprise endorsement, a Trump robocall and millions from a McConnell-aligned super PAC, trailed Moore in polls but was projected to finish second and advance to the runoff. Strange’s connection to disgraced ex‑Gov. Robert Bentley (who appointed him) and anti‑establishment resentment have hampered him despite establishment resources.
- Rep. Mo Brooks fought for second place but finished third and was eliminated. His campaign had its own controversies (including use of Scalise shooting audio in an ad).

Key dynamics to watch
- Whether Strange’s finish vindicates the influence of Trump and McConnell: a weak result would be an embarrassment for national GOP leaders; a stronger second-place finish would keep Strange viable going into the runoff.
- Moore’s ceiling: low overall turnout and an enthusiastic base could leave him comfortably atop the primary but likely below a majority; his campaign believed Trump’s endorsement would have limited effect on Moore’s supporters.
- The runoff’s contours depend on how decisively Strange places second—narrow entry would raise questions about establishment and presidential sway in Alabama.

Democratic picture
- Democrats offered an outside path in a deeply red state. Doug Jones, a former U.S. attorney endorsed by Joe Biden, and Robert Kennedy Jr. (a different Robert Kennedy) were the main Democratic contenders. Early polls showed Kennedy leading the field but Jones was projected as the eventual nominee in some reporting; Democrats saw the chaotic GOP primary as a potential opening, though a Democratic win in Alabama remained unlikely.

Outcome (reported projections)
- With most counties reported, Moore led with about 43.8% and Strange about 31.7%, neither reaching 50%, sending them to the Sept. 26 runoff. Brooks placed third. On the Democratic side, Doug Jones was projected the winner of that primary.

Overall, the race underscored anti‑establishment sentiment in Alabama GOP politics and set up a high‑stakes runoff that will further test Trump’s and McConnell’s influence.

The review describes Snow White and the Huntsman as a darker, more serious reimagining of the Snow White tale that restores the original Grimm-like menace rather than Disney’s sanitized innocence. Directed by Rupert Sanders from a script by Evan Daugherty, John Lee Hancock and Hossein Amini, the film foregrounds mood, medieval landscapes and grim magic while leaning on strong production elements—Greig Fraser’s muted cinematography, Dominic Watkins’ production design and Colleen Atwood’s costumes—and a Wagnerian score by James Newton Howard.

Charlize Theron dominates as Ravenna, a beautiful, violent queen who murdered the king, imprisons Snow White and feeds on youth to preserve her own beauty; Theron brings a mix of coldness and sorrow that makes Ravenna at once sympathetic and monstrous. Kristen Stewart plays Snow White as a fledgling warrior-damsel torn between two protectors: the noble William (Sam Claflin) and the more compelling, gruff Huntsman (Chris Hemsworth), whose arrival enlivens the film. The dwarfs—played by Ian McShane, Bob Hoskins, Eddie Marsan and Ray Winstone and digitally shrunken—are rough, industrial, and far from Disney-cute, reinforcing the film’s grim tone.

The movie balances gritty, human elements (the Huntsman and the dwarfs) with moments of fresh enchantment—a terrifying dark-forest slog, a fairy garden, and a refugee encampment—achieving an often mesmerizing atmosphere. The review notes the film’s thematic interest in beauty, power and female rage: Ravenna can be read as a victim-turned-avenger whose resentment is directed at other women, while Snow White must forge a different kind of “fairness” beyond mere appearance. Stewart’s performance fits the current trend of warrior heroines (compared to Katniss Everdeen), and the film is praised for taking its darker source-material seriously. Rated PG-13; running time 2h6m; opens nationwide Friday.

About 350 U.S. newspapers ran editorials on Aug. 16 in a coordinated effort to defend press freedom and push back against President Donald Trump’s repeated attacks calling news organizations “the enemy of the people.” The initiative was organized by Boston Globe op-ed editor Marjorie Pritchard and included major papers such as The Boston Globe and The New York Times, plus many regional papers (Houston Chronicle, Minneapolis Star Tribune, Miami Herald, Denver Post) and journalism groups. The editorials argued that labeling the press an enemy is dangerous to democracy and urged public support for independent journalism; several pieces also encouraged subscriptions and civic engagement.

The campaign drew criticism from some media commentators and outlets. The Times-Picayune’s editorial board declined to participate, citing independence. Commentators like Politico’s Jack Shafer and opinion pages at Investor’s Business Daily and others argued the coordinated action would reinforce Trump’s narrative of a monolithic, biased “national press cabal,” risk preaching to the choir, and could backfire by confirming suspicions of media partisanship. Critics also noted many participating papers had opposed Trump in 2016, which they said undercuts claims of neutrality.

Trump responded on Twitter (and briefly to reporters) dismissively, repeating accusations of “fake news,” misstating sale details about The Globe, and framing the coordination as proof of bias. The Senate passed a resolution affirming that the press is not the enemy of the people. The coordinated editorials highlight a growing rift over the role of the press, the impact of presidential rhetoric on journalist safety and public trust, and debate over whether unified media protest is an effective defense of press freedom or a politically risky tactic.

A 68-year-old grandfather, Roger Wilday, was walking his nine-year-old German Shepherd, Jade, in Marlborough House Community Park, Stechford, Birmingham when the dog rushed into bushes and refused to come back. Roger found a newborn girl, wrapped in a towel inside a plastic carrier bag, crying. He called 999, picked up the infant and waited; emergency responders arrived within minutes and the baby was taken to Heartlands Hospital.

Hospital staff named the baby “Jade” after the dog. Medics describe the six-pound newborn as “alert, happy and contented” and say she is being monitored by paediatricians. Police warned that the infant could have been in grave danger had she remained exposed for several more hours.

West Midlands Police are conducting house-to-house inquiries, checking hospitals and care homes, and fast-tracking forensic tests on the towel and bag; DNA from the baby is also being used to help identify her parents. Officers are appealing for witnesses, particularly anyone who saw someone carrying a bag from The Entertainer toy shop, and urge the mother to contact them on 101. Roger and his wife hope to be reunited with the child.

The NRA announced that firearms and other weapons would be banned from the arena while Vice President Mike Pence speaks at its annual convention in Dallas (May 3–6), citing Secret Service security requirements that prohibit weapons where protectees are present. The prohibition — which includes guns, gun parts, ammunition, knives, drones and even certain signs or glass containers — applies prior to and during Pence’s appearance; otherwise, lawfully carried firearms are permitted at the convention and host hotel in compliance with local laws.

Survivors and family members of the Feb. 14 Parkland school shooting criticized the move as hypocritical. Parkland students and March for Our Lives organizers (including Matt Deitsch, Cameron Kasky and David Hogg) questioned why the NRA insists on more guns in public and schools but accepts a gun-free zone to protect the vice president. Fred Guttenberg, whose daughter Jaime was killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, called the ban “enlightening,” arguing it undercuts the NRA’s “everyone should have a gun” safety argument.

Some NRA members likewise objected, saying disarming attendees for the VP makes the group’s position look inconsistent; others pointed out the ban is simply Secret Service protocol. The announcement follows continued national debate over gun policy after the Parkland shooting and ahead of expected appearances by Trump administration officials at the convention.

A large retrospective analysis of 2.7 million serious adverse event reports to the FDA (2003–2012) found a strong association between dopamine receptor agonist drugs (commonly used for Parkinson’s disease, restless leg syndrome and some endocrine conditions) and severe impulse-control disorders such as pathological gambling, hypersexuality and compulsive shopping. Of 1,580 reports of these abnormal behaviors from the U.S. and 21 other countries, 710 involved dopamine agonists. Disproportionality analysis showed the reporting rate for these behaviors was far higher with dopamine agonists than with other drugs (proportional reporting ratio [PRR] = 277.6, P < .001). The signal was strongest for pramipexole (n = 410; PRR = 455.9) and ropinirole (n = 188; PRR = 152.5), both of which have high affinity for the dopamine D3 receptor; a smaller signal was seen for aripiprazole (PRR = 8.6), a D3 partial agonist.

Authors and accompanying commentators note these behaviors can be dramatic (e.g., large gambling losses, compulsive sexual activity, ruinous spending), are often unreported by patients, and typically remit after stopping the drug. The findings reinforce earlier case reports and clinical observations and suggest involvement of the D3 receptor in impulse-control problems. The study’s authors and commentators urge greater caution in prescribing these agents, routine screening of patients and caregivers for behavioral side effects, and more prominent regulatory warnings (including consideration of boxed warnings) on these medications.

The North Carolina Office of Archives and History (including the State Archives and State Library of North Carolina) has been an Archive-It partner since September 2005. Its mission is to collect, preserve, and make available the state's historic resources so current and future residents can better understand North Carolina’s history. The office safeguards documentary and material evidence of past generations to educate citizens and protect their democratic rights. The record also notes that Tweets can include location data from the web or third‑party apps, with an option to delete Tweet location history.

Photographer and biologist Paul Nicklen (co-founder of Sea Legacy) filmed an extremely emaciated polar bear on Somerset Island in the Canadian Arctic in late summer and published the footage in December 2017. The bear, which Nicklen said he and his team observed from roughly 400 feet away, appeared to be starving—its coat patchy, muscles atrophied, and scavenging a seasonal garbage can and an old snowmobile seat. The video, viewed millions of times, provoked strong reactions and debate about whether to intervene; Nicklen explained he did not and could not practically or legally rescue or feed the animal and felt documenting its condition could help people grasp what starvation looks like.

Nicklen and Sea Legacy framed the footage as illustrating broader consequences of warming Arctic conditions. Scientists note polar bears depend on sea ice to hunt seals, and shrinking, earlier-melting ice forces longer fasting periods, increasing starvation risk. Reports and satellite records show long-term declines in Arctic sea ice and forecasts of population declines for polar bears; some experts link rising numbers of thin bears to habitat loss from climate change. Others cautioned that a single animal’s condition cannot definitively prove cause without further data (age, disease, autopsy). The video served as a powerful, emotional symbol in the climate conversation while also drawing some criticism over drawing conclusions from one case.

Hilary Duff and Canadian hockey player Mike Comrie have married. The 22-year-old actress and the 29-year-old NHL player wed in an intimate Santa Barbara, California ceremony on Saturday. Duff kept the event small and wanted a quiet affair; around 100 family and friends attended. Her sister Haylie Duff served as maid of honor, escorted down the aisle by their mother, Susan Duff. Duff wore a mermaid Vera Wang gown; Comrie was the groom. Comrie proposed in February while the couple were vacationing in Hawaii after more than two years together, and the pair shared that they were excited and grateful for well-wishes.

Danish inventor Peter Madsen, charged with murdering Swedish freelance journalist Kim Wall, was ordered detained for four more weeks as Copenhagen prosecutors presented new evidence at a pre-trial hearing.

Prosecutor Jakob Buch-Jepsen told the court investigators found video files on a hard drive from Madsen’s workshop that appear to show women being strangled and decapitated. New post-mortem findings indicate Wall received about 15 stab wounds to her ribcage and genitals “at the time of death or shortly afterwards,” and traces of a saw blade consistent with post-mortem removal of her head and limbs were also found. DNA matching Wall was recovered from Madsen’s nails, face and neck. Despite these findings, the formal cause of death has not yet been established.

Madsen, 46, denies murder and a charge of mutilating a body. He attended the hearing by video from prison, reiterated that the computer in the laboratory was used by others and claimed Wall died accidentally after being struck by a heavy hatch cover; he has previously said he then tried to bury her at sea. Wall, 30, who had been interviewing Madsen aboard his 17–18 metre UC3 Nautilus submarine on Aug. 10, went missing; a headless torso identified as hers washed ashore on Aug. 23. Madsen will next appear in court on Oct. 31.

Rap Genius co‑founder Mahbod Moghadam resigned from the company and its board after posting insensitive, misogynistic annotations on Elliot Rodger’s 141‑page manifesto following the Santa Barbara killings. His comments — praised in media reports for being tasteless (including a remark guessing Rodger’s sister was “smokin hot”) — were removed from the site and publicized by Valleywag. CEO Tom Lehman said Moghadam’s annotations “didn’t attempt to enhance anyone’s understanding” and crossed a line with “gleeful insensitivity and misogyny,” and sources say Lehman and co‑founder Ilan Zechory, with pressure from investors, forced the departure. Andreessen Horowitz partner Ben Horowitz acknowledged discussing the matter with Lehman but called it a “conversation.” Moghadam apologized on Twitter, saying he got carried away and regretted his poor judgment. The episode follows a pattern of controversial behavior by Moghadam, including prior offensive tweets and actions that drew criticism and were at times blamed on a now‑removed brain tumor; his conduct, plus past issues such as Rap Genius’s SEO controversy, prompted investors and management to distance the company from him.

The federal government closed non-emergency offices in the Washington, D.C., area Wednesday and excused absences were granted as the region braced for a big winter storm. Forecasts had predicted up to 10 inches in D.C. and more in northern and western suburbs, and airlines canceled hundreds of flights—mostly at Dulles and Reagan National.

In D.C. the storm underperformed: only fractions of an inch fell in much of the city, the National Weather Service dropped its winter storm warning, and planned events (including a large snowball fight in DuPont Circle) were largely fizzled. Some attractions remained open—the Smithsonian museums stayed open though the National Zoo closed—and Metrorail ran with some bus disruptions. More than 954,000 students in major districts across D.C., Maryland, Virginia and Ohio were given the day off, and Amtrak suspended some service in parts of the Northeast and mid-Atlantic.

Conditions were far worse in parts of Virginia, where Gov. Bob McDonnell declared a state of emergency, state police extended shifts, and 100 National Guard troops were mobilized. Wet, heavy snow and ice caused widespread power outages (shelters opened for about 215,000 Virginians), hazardous roads across many counties, and thousands of utility workers were deployed.

Along the East Coast the primary hazards were high winds, storm surge and coastal flooding rather than snow. Coastal flood warnings were issued from Massachusetts to Virginia; Massachusetts and Delaware called up National Guard troops and urged some evacuations, and portions of the coast—especially areas still vulnerable after Hurricane Sandy—faced significant flooding risk. The Chesapeake Bay Bridge was briefly closed because of high winds after an overturned tractor-trailer, and parts of the Delmarva Peninsula experienced power outages and downed trees and wires.

The same storm had earlier produced heavy snow across the Upper Midwest—about a foot in parts of Illinois, Minnesota and North Dakota—disrupting travel and breaking local records (Chicago’s O’Hare saw 6 inches). Overall, the system produced a patchwork of impacts: light amounts and canceled events in the District, significant snow and outages inland in Virginia and the Midwest, and coastal flood threats and wind damage along the Atlantic seaboard.

A previously unknown early fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen has been discovered in a filing box at the National Archives of Funen in Odense. Retired historian Esben Brage found a six-page, ink-written manuscript titled "The Tallow Candle" in October. The short, roughly 700-word story—about a tallow candle that seeks to be lit and have its inner worth recognized—bears a dedication, “To Mme Bunkeflod, from her devoted HC Andersen,” and is judged by experts to be a likely copy of an original now lost.

Museum and Andersen specialists date the piece to the mid-1820s, when Andersen was a grammar-school youth (around age 18), noting its simpler style compared with his mature works. They say the Bunkeflod widow was a neighbour and patron who Andersen visited, read to and borrowed books from. The find was described as “sensational” by Andersen expert Ejnar Stig Askgaard. The Danish paper Politiken has published an English translation of the story. The associated WARC files from the crawl reporting the discovery are not publicly available.

On June 22, 2017 Senate Republican leaders released a “discussion draft” of the Better Care Reconciliation Act (BCRA), their long‑awaited plan to repeal and replace major elements of the Affordable Care Act (ACA). The bill was drafted in secret, sparking bipartisan criticism about the closed process, and quickly drew intense public protest and political opposition.

Major provisions and policy changes
- Medicaid: The bill phases down the ACA Medicaid expansion beginning in 2021 and converts the rest of Medicaid funding to per‑capita caps (and offers a block‑grant option). Federal matching rates for expansion enrollees would step down over several years. Critics warn these changes would reduce coverage and shift costs to states.
- Individual market subsidies and coverage: The BCRA replaces ACA subsidies with age‑, income‑, and geography‑based tax credits that are generally smaller and tied to a less generous “benchmark” plan (58% actuarial value vs. ACA’s 70%). Eligibility is capped at 350% of the federal poverty level (versus 400% under the ACA). The bill allows states broader waiver authority to alter essential health benefits and other market rules.
- Mandates and enrollment rules: The individual mandate penalty is set to zero (effectively repealing it) and the bill imposes a six‑month waiting period for people with certain coverage gaps.
- Medicaid and Planned Parenthood: The draft includes provisions that would cut federal Medicaid support and bar federal funding to certain Planned Parenthood entities for one year; it contains numerous other Medicaid changes and timelines.
- Taxes and other provisions: The bill repeals many ACA taxes (including on investment income, the medical device tax, and the insurer tax), changes various health‑related tax rules, and includes funding lines for state stability programs, opioid response grants, community health centers, and other items.
- New programs and options: The draft creates a State Stability and Innovation program with federal allotments and a new Medicaid Flexibility (block‑grant) option, among many detailed technical changes to Medicaid and tax law.

Political reaction and prospects
- Republican divisions: Several GOP senators—Ted Cruz, Ron Johnson, Mike Lee, Rand Paul and later Dean Heller—publicly said they were not ready to support the draft as written, citing either that it didn’t go far enough or that it failed to fulfill promises to repeal Obamacare and reduce costs. Susan Collins said she had not yet read the full text and noted specific objections (e.g., defunding Planned Parenthood). With Democrats unified in opposition, Republicans could lose at most two Senate votes.
- Democratic and medical community opposition: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and other Democrats condemned the bill as mean and harmful to vulnerable people. Major medical and public‑health organizations (American Public Health Association, American Psychiatric Association, ACOG) urged rejection, citing likely reductions in coverage, protections, and behavioral health services.
- Public protest: Protesters, including disability‑rights groups, staged demonstrations outside Senate offices; some were physically removed and arrests were reported.
- Process and timing: The bill was prepared behind closed doors, heightening controversy. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell sought a vote before the July 4 recess; the Congressional Budget Office score was expected the following week. President Trump said he wanted the bill to show more “heart” but supported the effort and signaled willingness to negotiate.

Bottom line
The Senate draft represents a major restructuring of federal health policy—reducing federal financing for Medicaid, shrinking and reshaping subsidies on the individual market, expanding state waiver authority, and repealing many ACA taxes. It provoked immediate protests and opposition from Democrats, health organizations, and a number of Republican senators, leaving its passage uncertain.

Håvard Melvaer, a 40-year-old Norwegian captain, says it was a “stroke of luck” that he spotted the small boat belonging to missing teens Austin Stephanos and Perry Cohen while commanding the multipurpose supply ship Edda Fjord on a transatlantic voyage. About a week into the ship’s March 18 voyage from Port Fourchon, La., to Haugesund, Norway, Melvaer stepped outside after his wife urged him to get fresh air and immediately saw the 19-foot SeaCraft about 30–40 feet off the vessel’s port side — something none of the other 16 crew members had noticed. The crew hoisted the boat aboard to remove it from the shipping lane, noted it was intact and the engine had a serial number, and notified the U.S. Coast Guard.

The boat belonged to Austin and Perry, who disappeared last July after leaving Jupiter Inlet, Fla. The Coast Guard had earlier found the boat near Daytona Beach and attached a marker buoy, but the vessel later went missing when the buoy failed. Melvaer researched the discovery online, confirmed the match with officials and sent photos; some personal items recovered — including Austin’s iPhone, two rods and two small tackle boxes — have been returned to the families. The boat is packed in a shipping container and expected to arrive at Port Everglades around May 16. Melvaer, a longtime boater and father, said he and his crew treated the boat carefully and hope the find may help provide answers or some peace to the families, though he declined to discuss investigation details.

A 30-year-old fugitive, Jansen Simon, who had been sought since an alleged 2013 bar fight in Cut Off, La., was arrested after flagging down a Louisiana deputy early July 16 while walking along Highway 182 in Raceland. Simon told the off-duty deputy he had been left by friends on the side of the road; the officer — in a marked patrol car — verified his identity and took him into custody. Simon faces an aggravated second-degree battery charge for allegedly striking a man in the head with a hammer in August 2013 (the victim suffered a fractured skull) and two contempt of court warrants from the same period. He was booked into the Lafourche Parish Detention Center and is being held without bond. It is unclear whether he has legal representation.

Former Florida Republican Party chairman Jim Greer, in a 630-page deposition released from late-May testimony, accused party officials of internal scheming, mismanagement and even discussing voter suppression targeting black voters. Greer said the party was in turmoil after disagreements with then-Gov. Charlie Crist and the rise of the tea party; he described infighting between legislative leaders and party officials who resisted financial transparency and insisted legislative campaign finances were off-limits. He called some colleagues “whack-a-do, right‑wing crazies.”

Much of the deposition focused on Greer’s creation of Victory Strategies LLC, which received nearly $200,000 from the party while he was chairman. Greer acknowledged initially denying ownership of the company when questioned by party counsel Jason Gonzalez and later admitting it privately. Party leaders say Greer’s secret company justified removing him.

Greer also says he signed a severance agreement in January 2010 guaranteeing $130,000 after resigning; when payment was not made he contends legislative leaders and party officials orchestrated an FDLE and grand jury probe to avoid paying him. He alleges promises from consultants and some leaders to arrange payment never materialized, and that shortly afterward he was indicted on money‑laundering and fraud charges that have ruined his life financially and personally.

Sen. John Thrasher, who succeeded Greer, called the accusations “absurd’’ and defended the party’s actions. Other named figures either disputed Greer’s recollections or declined comment. The deposition provides a detailed, hostile portrait of internal Republican Party conflicts in Florida amid both financial and political disputes, including Greer’s explosive claim that party operatives discussed suppressing black turnout.

President Trump said the controversy over Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh has made it “a very scary time for young men in America,” arguing that men can now be treated as “guilty until proven innocent” after allegations of sexual misconduct. Speaking to reporters on the White House South Lawn, he said the climate makes it hard to refute accusations and warned Democrats that blocking Kavanaugh could energize conservatives. Trump expressed support for Kavanaugh while saying he hoped for a positive Senate vote depending on the outcome of the FBI inquiry, which was expanded amid GOP concerns. The remarks came after Christine Blasey Ford and two other women accused Kavanaugh of sexual misconduct from his high‑school and college years; Kavanaugh denies the allegations. The president — who has faced multiple sexual‑misconduct accusations himself, which he denies — also called it a “great time for women” when asked about young women. His son Donald Jr. similarly said he’s most worried for his sons.

A La Porte, Indiana mail carrier, Kristopher (Kristopher) Block (age reported as 39–40), is facing criminal charges after investigators say he failed to deliver roughly 17,000 pieces of mail over several months in 2016–2017. U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General (OIG) agents and local police began investigating when deputies in Berrien County, Michigan, found tubs containing about 11,000 pieces of frozen, undelivered mail in a ravine in February 2017. Additional investigation recovered roughly 6,000 more pieces at Block’s home in La Porte.

Court records and OIG interviews allege Block took undelivered mail home, paid a friend about $50 per bundle to burn mail he could not deliver, and stashed other mail at his residence. Block initially denied involvement, then reportedly said, “Looks like I’m going to jail,” when shown recovered items. He resigned from the Postal Service on Feb. 7, 2017. La Porte prosecutors have charged him with felony official misconduct and misdemeanor theft, and a warrant for his arrest has been issued; online records indicate he had not been taken into custody at last report. The alleged accomplice has not been located or charged.

Affected residents reported missed bills and checks; some have resorted to renting P.O. boxes. The USPS OIG emphasized that such criminal behavior is rare, that it investigates and works with prosecutors to hold employees accountable, and provided hotline and complaint information for reporting postal crimes.

A German passenger who waited four years for EU-mandated compensation after her Thomas Cook Airlines flight from Vienna to the Caribbean was delayed 22 hours secured a court order in Austria that empowered airport officials to impound a Thomas Cook jet until the $680 payout was made. The woman had hired claims firm FlightRight (which takes a 25% fee) to pursue the case after the airline failed to pay. When the airport was notified, Thomas Cook’s sister airline Condor promptly paid the amount to avoid enforcement action. FlightRight’s legal head said many airlines stall or ignore claims and only about 15% of eligible EU passengers pursue compensation. EU rules entitle travelers to fixed compensation for long delays or cancellations on qualifying routes, including some transatlantic services.

Research summary — “The Sound of Status: People Know High-Power Voices When They Hear Them”
- New research in Psychological Science (Sei Jin Ko et al.) finds that being placed in a high-power role changes basic acoustic properties of speech, and listeners reliably detect those changes and infer who holds power.
- Methods: 161 college students read a passage to record baseline voice, were randomly assigned high- or low-power roles for a negotiation task (via scenarios or memory recall), then read the same passage again. This controlled for speech content while isolating acoustic changes.
- Findings: Compared with low-power roles, high-power roles produced voices that tended to have higher pitch, flatter pitch variation (more monotone), and greater loudness variability. Listeners in a separate experiment accurately categorized speakers’ power level and associated higher pitch, louder voices, and louder variability with higher power.
- Implications: Nonverbal acoustic cues influence perceptions and outcomes in interactions where power matters (e.g., parenting, sales, diplomacy). The vocal effects observed mirrored documented changes in Margaret Thatcher’s post-coaching voice.
- Transparency: The study was partly funded by Northwestern’s Dispute Resolution Research Center, and all data/materials are publicly posted on the Open Science Framework; the article holds Open Data and Open Materials badges.

Interpol elected South Korean Kim Jong-yang as its president at the agency’s 2018 General Assembly in Dubai, defeating Russian candidate Alexander Prokopchuk. Kim, 57, a former South Korean provincial police chief who had been Interpol’s acting president and senior vice‑president since the disappearance of former president Meng Hongwei, won by a large margin and will serve the remaining two years of Meng’s term. The presidency is largely ceremonial but carries influence; the day‑to‑day running of Interpol is led by Secretary‑General Jürgen Stock.

Prokopchuk, a Russian general and longtime interior ministry official who formerly ran Interpol’s Moscow bureau, was widely viewed as the Kremlin’s preferred candidate. Human rights groups, Western governments (notably the US and UK), and prominent Kremlin critics warned that his election risked politicizing Interpol by enabling abuses of its red notice and diffusion systems to pursue critics and dissidents. Lithuania and Ukraine had threatened to quit Interpol if he were elected. Russia condemned the opposition as interference and said Prokopchuk would remain a vice‑president after the vote.

The contest highlighted longstanding concerns about misuse of Interpol’s notice system: the number of red notices has risen sharply over the past decade and watchdogs accuse some countries of issuing notices for political ends. Interpol has taken steps since 2016 to strengthen legal vetting of red notices and appeals, but diffusions (direct requests between countries) remain more vulnerable to abuse. Campaigners such as Bill Browder and Mikhail Khodorkovsky, who say they were targeted, welcomed Kim’s victory and urged further reforms, including suspending Russia over alleged serial abuses. Russian state media framed the result as the work of a “Russophobic lobby.” The assembly also rejected Kosovo’s bid to join Interpol, a separate diplomatic setback for Pristina.
