Georgia’s legislature has overwhelmingly approved a resolution (Senate vote 48–2) pressing a long-running boundary dispute with Tennessee to gain access to the Tennessee River at Nickajack. The state argues the border should lie along the 35° north latitude—set when Georgia relinquished Mississippi Territory—but an 1818 survey placed the line about a mile too far south, leaving a stretch of the river outside Georgia. The resolution (House Resolution 4, amended in the Senate and returning to the House) directs the attorney general to seek a settlement based on the alleged historic survey errors and, if necessary, sue to reclaim control of the area south of the 35th parallel.

The push is driven by acute and recurring drought in Georgia (in 2012 up to 99% of the state was affected; in 2008 similar shortages occurred) and concerns that climate change will make reliable water supplies increasingly critical. Georgia hopes the Tennessee River could provide that steady source, but any interbasin transfer would require approval from the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). TVA has stated it has not recommended using the river as a primary source for North Georgia and is not currently involved. Tennessee has previously rejected Georgia’s attempts to move the boundary; Alabama—downstream and also drought-stricken—would likely oppose losing river water as well. If Tennessee agrees to redraw the line, Congress would have to approve; if not, the dispute will likely continue through legal and political channels rather than through conflict.

An AirAsia Airbus A320-200 (Flight QZ8501) carrying 162 people disappeared Sunday during a scheduled two-hour flight from Surabaya, Indonesia, to Singapore. The jet departed Surabaya at 5:31 a.m. local time. The last radio contact came at 6:13 a.m., when the pilot requested a left turn and climb to 34,000 feet to "avoid clouds"; authorities say there was no distress signal. Indonesian officials believe the aircraft went missing somewhere over the Java Sea between Tanjung Pandan (Belitung) and Pontianak (Borneo). A multinational search-and-rescue operation involving Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia was launched—Indonesian aircraft and Singaporean C-130s and naval assets were deployed. Relatives gathered at Surabaya airport as AirAsia CEO Tony Fernandes travelled to Surabaya and posted messages of thanks and support.

Doctors have warned against extreme “new year” detox regimens after treating a 47-year-old woman who became critically ill after taking multiple herbal supplements and drinking large amounts of fluids. She was admitted to intensive care with seizures caused by dangerously low blood sodium (hyponatraemia). Her remedies included milk thistle, molkosan, l-theanine, glutamine, a vitamin B compound, vervain and valerian root; her partner also reported heavy intake of water, green tea and sage tea. The clinicians linked the case to other reports of seizures after consumption of herbal mixtures containing valerian, lemon balm, passionflower, hops and chamomile. They caution that “all‑natural” products can have side effects and that excessive water intake is risky. The British Dietetic Association called detoxing nonsense, noting the body already detoxifies via organs such as the liver and kidneys and advising a sensible diet, hydration and regular exercise as the best health strategies.

Actress and former The View co-host Sherri Shepherd has lost an appeal after a Pennsylvania court found her legally responsible for a child born via surrogate before she divorced ex-husband Lamar Sally. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court declined to hear her case, leaving in place a lower-court ruling—reported by surrogacy advocates as the state's first to treat surrogacy contracts as binding. Shepherd is required to pay $4,100 a month in child support to Sally for the now‑young child; Sally’s attorney says Shepherd has not met the one‑year‑old. Shepherd spent over $100,000 arranging the surrogacy and had tried to void the contract during a New Jersey divorce. Her lawyer said he was surprised the high court would not review the matter.

Separate media coverage quotes Shepherd discussing the emotional toll but saying she’s coping and hopeful, while Sally has discussed plans for a reality show about single fatherhood and maintains he is a hands‑on parent. Some outlets note Shepherd has sought to remove her name from the child’s birth certificate and has not had contact with the child.

Nearly 100 House Republicans, led by Rep. Jeff Duncan (R-SC), sent a letter to President Obama opposing the possible nomination of U.N. Ambassador Susan Rice as secretary of state. The 97 GOP signers argued Rice’s public statements in the days and weeks after the Benghazi attack — which killed Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans — “misleadingly” described the event and thus damaged her credibility, saying she is viewed as having “willfully or incompetently misled the American public.”

Senators John McCain and Lindsey Graham have said they will try to block any Rice nomination; other Senate Republicans have not yet committed to a filibuster. The White House and Senate Intelligence Committee Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein defended Rice, saying she relied on the best available intelligence at the time. The Constitution gives the Senate the sole power to confirm such nominees. President Obama is also reportedly considering Sen. John Kerry to succeed Hillary Clinton as secretary of state.

Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn criticized attacks that label Rice “incompetent,” calling such language coded and insulting; he defended her competence and Rhodes Scholar credentials while allowing that she could have been wrong in her assessments.

A Papillon Grand Canyon tour helicopter (Eurocopter EC130) crashed Saturday evening near Quartermaster Canyon on the Hualapai Nation, killing three of seven people aboard and injuring the other four. The aircraft carried six passengers from the United Kingdom and a pilot; three passengers—Becky Dobson, 27, Jason Hill, 32, and Stuart Hill, 30—died and their bodies were recovered Sunday. The injured—pilot Scott Booth, 42, and passengers Ellie Milward, 29; Jonathan Udall, 32; and Jennifer Barham, 39—were treated at the scene as level‑1 trauma patients, then flown to medical facilities with serious injuries (Booth suffered a severe limb injury).

First responders reached the site within about 30 minutes but faced wind, darkness and rugged terrain that required a 20‑minute hike; military aircraft from Nellis AFB assisted in evacuations. Photographs and witness accounts described fire and smoke after the crash and survivors running from the wreckage.

The FAA and NTSB are investigating; the FAA said the helicopter sustained heavy damage and the circumstances are unknown. Papillon— which flies roughly 600,000 passengers a year and called safety a priority—expressed sympathy and said it was caring for those affected. The company previously experienced a deadly 2001 crash attributed by the NTSB to pilot error; a lawyer familiar with that accident said Papillon has since improved pilot qualifications and maintenance.

This document combines two related election-focused pieces.

1) Florida’s outsized importance in the 2016 Electoral College
- FiveThirtyEight’s polls-only forecast shows Florida has a 19% chance of being the “tipping-point” (decisive) state — the single highest probability — up from 16% two weeks earlier. Pennsylvania is the only other state above 10% (12%).
- Florida’s growing centrality reflects Hillary Clinton’s small lead nationally (~+3) and a narrower lead in Florida (~+1). Because Florida’s electorate is more diverse (large Latino and African‑American populations), Clinton could potentially hold Florida even if she lost several Midwestern and small New England swing states; doing so would still allow for winning combinations that secure the presidency.
- Florida’s importance stems from two factors: (1) it closely mirrors the national vote margin (only a few states are closer), and (2) it is large — 29 electoral votes — allowing a candidate to recover losses in many smaller swing states by winning Florida.
- Losing Florida would be especially damaging for Trump: the forecast says Trump would win the presidency only 5% of the time without Florida, while Clinton would still win 33% of simulations without it. While no single state guarantees victory, Florida is as close to a “must‑win” state as exists.

2) Public doubts about vote counting and claims of a “rigged” election
- Donald Trump repeatedly asserted the 2016 general election could be “rigged,” and an AP‑NORC poll (Sept. 15–18, n=1,022, ±3.7 points) finds many Republicans share doubts: only about one‑third of Republicans have a great deal or quite a bit of confidence that votes will be counted fairly; half of those favorable to Trump have little or no confidence.
- Overall confidence is limited: 40% have a lot of confidence, another 30% are moderately confident. Partisan gaps are large: 59% of Clinton supporters express high confidence versus 29% of Trump supporters.
- Misperceptions about widespread voter fraud persist: 35% of respondents say there is a great deal of voter fraud, though studies show fraud is vanishingly rare. About half of Republicans believe there is a great deal of fraud, compared with about one‑quarter of Democrats.
- Many favor voter ID laws (nearly 80% support). Democrats worry strict ID requirements could disenfranchise poor and minority voters.
- Concerns about election cybersecurity and foreign interference are significant: 41% are very or extremely concerned about hackers, and lawmakers have concluded Russian intelligence agencies sought to influence the election; Homeland Security officials reported attempts to target voter registration systems in more than 20 states.
- The article includes examples of supporters echoing candidate claims and notes Trump’s mixed public statements about accepting the election outcome.

Together, the pieces highlight both the pivotal role of Florida in the Electoral College math and widespread partisan mistrust about the integrity of the vote count in 2016, amplified by the nominee’s rhetoric and worries about hacking and foreign influence.

The FBI and Orange County Sheriff’s Bank Robbery Apprehension Team are asking for help identifying a man nicknamed the “Keep Smiling Bandit” after two recent Citibank robberies. He first told victims to “keep smiling” during an Oct. 12 holdup at a Costa Mesa Citibank and is believed to have struck again at a Tustin Citibank on Saturday (Irvine Boulevard). In both incidents he passed notes to tellers demanding cash, warned “Keep your hands away from the alarm or I’ll shoot,” and spoke to victims; no weapon was seen. He’s described as a white male in his early 30s, about 5’7″–5’9″, 140–150 lbs., wearing eyeglasses and a baseball cap and appearing nervous. Anyone with information is urged to call 911 or the FBI at (310) 477-6565.

Summary:

The first 2012 presidential debate in Denver was widely seen as a win for Mitt Romney and a weak outing for President Barack Obama. Romney, trailing in polls, used the debate to present himself as a credible, composed alternative, adopting a more moderate, polished tone than during the primaries. He repeatedly challenged Obama on taxes, deficits and energy policy, pledged no tax cuts that add to the deficit without fully detailing how, embraced parts of Simpson-Bowles-style deficit reduction, and used memorable lines (e.g., vowing to end PBS subsidies, “I like Big Bird”). Commentators noted Romney’s shift to the center, savvy presentation, and ability to appear presidential.

Obama frequently sounded professorial and lengthy, and many critics said he appeared tired, defensive and less effective at delivering concise, resonant messages. He missed chances to dramatize contrasts on taxes, to highlight Republican obstruction on health care reform, and to deliver sharper attacks that would have made Romney’s positions look extreme.

Instant-reaction and post-debate polls and surveys favored Romney strongly: CNN found 67% of debate-watchers saying Romney won, CBS polls of undecided voters also favored him, and others showed significant short-term gains for Romney. Analysts cautioned that historical effects of a single debate are usually modest—often a few points—and that Romney’s overall chances (FiveThirtyEight estimated about 15% pre-debate) would at best improve toward a closer race rather than instantly overturn the contest. Still, the combination of Romney’s debate performance and an upcoming jobs report and further debates could materially tighten the race.

A devastating coal mine fire in Soma, western Turkey, left nearly 300 miners dead and prompted national outrage, mass protests and strikes. Rescue teams recovered bodies from deep underground as smoke and toxic gases hampered operations; officials said most deaths were from carbon monoxide poisoning. Energy Minister Taner Yildiz reported the confirmed death toll rose into the high 200s while dozens remained unaccounted for; hundreds had been inside the mine when the blast and fire erupted during a shift change.

Grief was intense in Soma—funerals, wailing women at gravesites and long waits by relatives—while nationwide anger focused on perceived government negligence and poor mine safety. Engineers from a local chamber accused the disaster of being preventable (“not fate, it is murder”), citing outdated gas-detection and ventilation systems. Opposition politicians and unions criticized the government for previously rejecting inquiries and called a one-day strike and demonstrations across cities; police used water cannon and tear gas in some protests.

The crisis further escalated after a widely circulated photo and video showed a Prime Minister’s aide, identified as Yusuf Yerkel, kicking a detained protester during Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s visit to Soma. The image provoked widespread condemnation and intensified protests; Erdogan was jeered and forced to take refuge during the visit. Erdogan’s remarks to victims’ families—which some saw as dismissive—and his government’s handling of mine-safety oversight drew sharp criticism. Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoglu defended the government and Erdogan, saying the prime minister “feels the pain of the people,” while authorities opened investigations into the accident and media-reported misconduct by the aide. Public anger centered on demands for accountability, thorough investigations, and reforms to improve mining safety.

The U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General found that the Federal Aviation Administration is not doing enough to ensure airline pilots maintain manual flying and automated-system monitoring skills. Investigators concluded the FAA cannot track how often pilots fly manually, has not ensured airline training programs adequately emphasize manual flying and monitoring, and lacks the ability to verify pilots are fully trained to use and monitor automated flight systems.

Background: modern airliners are flown by automation about 90% of the time, with pilots typically flying manually only during takeoff and landing. That reduced manual time, growing automation complexity, and some airline practices have raised concerns that pilots’ manual proficiency and monitoring vigilance are declining.

Key findings:
- Only 5 of 19 airline simulator training plans reviewed explicitly addressed pilot monitoring.
- The FAA issued a 2013 safety alert urging more manual flying practice but did not follow up to see whether airlines complied.
- New FAA rules from 2013 require training updates to enhance monitoring and manual skills, but guidance on implementation is still being developed and airlines are not required to comply until 2019.
- Two of nine airlines visited actively discouraged manual flying under normal conditions.
- The FAA lacks standards to measure how much manual flying pilots receive and hasn’t evaluated whether the new requirements increased manual flying time.

Safety context: The report cites accidents linked to automation and poor manual/monitoring skills, including the 2013 Asiana Airlines Boeing 777 crash at San Francisco (NTSB found pilot skill gaps and overreliance on automation) and the 2009 Colgan Air crash near Buffalo, caused by failures in monitoring and incorrect responses to automated stall warnings; those investigations motivated calls for stronger training on monitoring and manual skills.

FAA response: Agency officials acknowledged concerns about overreliance on automation and agreed with recommendations to develop standards for manual flying opportunities and to issue guidance on monitoring. The FAA said it was developing training guidance and engaging industry stakeholders and aimed to provide monitoring guidance by Jan. 31, 2017.

Bottom line: The watchdog warns the FAA is missing opportunities to ensure pilots retain critical manual and monitoring skills needed to safely intervene when automation fails or unexpected events occur.

Key points

- Calls for a formal probe: Incoming Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Sen. John McCain and other bipartisan senators sent Majority Leader Mitch McConnell a letter requesting a special (select) committee on cyber to investigate reported Russian interference in the November election and recommend legislative and organizational fixes. McConnell’s office said he would review the request; he has previously supported a bipartisan inquiry. Rep. Peter King also called for investigation of whether CIA Director John Brennan leaked information about Russian hacking.

- Intelligence consensus and allegations: U.S. intelligence agencies (CIA, DNI, FBI) have assessed that Russia covertly intervened in the election and sought to help Donald Trump, with a "high level of confidence" that President Vladimir Putin was personally involved. The discussion dominated Sunday shows.

- John Podesta’s remarks and concerns about collusion: Former Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta said Russians “clearly intervened” and suggested Trump associates may have colluded with Russian hackers, though he stopped short of accusing Trump personally. Podesta urged Electoral College members to know the full extent of any Trump-campaign involvement before voting. He also criticized the FBI’s handling of related intelligence and Director James Comey’s October actions.

- Podesta’s hacked emails and FBI contact: Podesta said his Gmail was breached and that the FBI first contacted him on Oct. 9—two days after WikiLeaks began releasing his emails—and he has not heard further. He described the timing of WikiLeaks’ release and the Access Hollywood tape as suspiciously coincident.

- Political fallout and next steps: Podesta called for an independent, full investigation into the hacks and for Democrats to conduct a detailed postmortem on the campaign’s losses in key Midwestern states. Debate continued over whether the email disclosures affected the election outcome; incoming White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus said Trump awaits a unified intelligence report and does not believe the hacks changed the result.

Vistara, a New Delhi-based airline, has launched a complimentary Woman Flyer service to help solo female passengers feel safer while traveling. Introduced in March, the program guarantees women traveling alone a window or aisle seat (no middle seats), offers baggage and ground-transport assistance, and provides staff escorts to and from airport-authorized taxis. Passengers must request the service by emailing the airline at least 72 hours before departure. Vistara says 75–100 women use the service daily and plans to extend it to international routes as it expands.

The initiative comes amid widespread concerns about women’s safety in India—heightened since the 2012 New Delhi gang rape—which has prompted travel warnings from countries including the U.S., U.K. and Australia. Similar measures elsewhere (women-only train cars or buses) have had mixed results: they can reduce harassment but are criticized for segregating women rather than addressing underlying gender inequality. Vistara’s program follows other airline responses, such as Air India’s earlier introduction of female-only rows, and reflects growing attention to traveler safety as India’s business travel market expands.

A CNN/ORC national poll taken July 22–25 finds Donald Trump leading the 2016 GOP field with 18% support among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, up six points since late June. Jeb Bush follows at 15% and Scott Walker at 10%; no other Republican reaches double digits. The poll of 1,017 adults (898 registered voters) has a ±3.5 point margin of error.

Key points:
- 52% of Republicans want Trump to remain in the GOP race; 33% want him to drop out and 15% want him to run as an independent. Trump has said he would consider a third-party bid if treated unfairly by RNC leaders.
- Many Republicans still view the contest as wide open (51%). Among voters who’ve narrowed their choice to one or two candidates, Trump’s support rises (24%).
- Trump’s favorability is weak nationally: 59% of all registered voters view him unfavorably, though unfavorability falls to 42% among GOP voters.
- In hypothetical general-election matchups, Trump trails top Democrats (Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders) by sizable margins; Bush and Walker perform only slightly better.
- Republican voter enthusiasm (55% extremely/very enthusiastic) exceeds Democratic enthusiasm (46%), and among highly enthusiastic Republican voters Trump does better (22%).
- On the Democratic side, Hillary Clinton remains the clear frontrunner with 56% of Democratic/leaning voters; Bernie Sanders has risen to 19%.

Other polls (NBC/Marist) show Trump leading in New Hampshire (21%) and narrowly trailing Walker in Iowa (17% vs. 19%). Overall, the poll suggests Trump’s position at the top is real but fragile given high unfavorability and a largely unsettled GOP electorate.

Racist robo-calls targeting Andrew Gillum, the likely first Black major-party nominee for Florida governor, circulated in Florida and drew widespread condemnation. The minute-long recording, produced by an Idaho-based white-supremacist group called Road to Power, features a speaker adopting a minstrel-like accent, jungle drum and monkey sounds, and mocking, racially stereotyped language urging listeners not to vote for Gillum. The call echoed and amplified recent racially charged rhetoric in the race—after GOP nominee Ron DeSantis’s earlier “monkey this up” remark about Gillum—which DeSantis insists was about policy, not race. Gillum condemned the calls and urged the campaign not to become racialized; his spokesman called the robocall “reprehensible.” Republicans including Gov. Rick Scott and a DeSantis spokesman also denounced the calls. The Southern Poverty Law Center has flagged a rise in hate-driven robo-calls nationwide; Road to Power has been linked to similar racist and anti-immigrant campaigns elsewhere.

The Weather Channel’s live stream of the Georgia Dome’s implosion turned into an unexpected comedy when a MARTA bus pulled in front of the camera at the exact moment the 71,250-seat stadium collapsed. Cameraman Jason Rudge had been streaming the crowd for 40 minutes and counted down with the audience as explosives brought down the 25-year-old dome. As the roof began to fall, a bus stopped directly in front of the lens, obscuring the dramatic view; Rudge can be heard yelling in frustration. The network posted the clip (with profanity bleeped) as “Bus Photobombs The Weather Channel’s Stream of Georgia Dome Implosion,” and the moment quickly became a meme, picked up and remixed by outlets including Sports Illustrated and the Atlanta Hawks. The incident even inspired a humorous poem and widespread social-media commentary noting that the bus-blocked shot might be the most memorable image of the demolition. A correction: Jason Rudge was the cameraman (not James Crugnale).

A nationwide manhunt for 22-year-old Syrian Jaber Albakr ended overnight when he was captured in Leipzig after two days on the run. Authorities raided an apartment in Chemnitz on Saturday and found about 1.5 kilos of TATP — the highly unstable homemade explosive used in recent jihadist attacks — and materials suggesting a bomb, possibly a suicide vest, was being prepared. Albakr slipped away from that raid carrying a backpack, prompting a nationwide search.

He was tracked down after several Syrian residents in Leipzig recognized him following police appeals in Arabic. Three Syrians detained and tied him in one apartment and alerted police; officials declined to identify them for safety reasons. Chancellor Angela Merkel publicly thanked the informant and the police.

Investigators say Albakr appears to have had contact with ISIS. A Syrian flatmate in Chemnitz, identified as Khalil A., was formally detained as a suspected accomplice accused of letting Albakr use his apartment and of helping order materials online. Police also questioned another suspected contact after raids.

Albakr entered Germany in February 2015 and was granted asylum later that year; Khalil A. received refugee status in March 2016. The case comes amid heightened security concerns in Germany after several ISIS-linked attacks and foiled plots this year and has reignited debate over intelligence access to asylum files and checks on refugees.

Maddy (Madeleine) Wilford, a 17-year-old junior and basketball player at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, spoke tearfully at Broward Health North on Monday after being treated there for at least three gunshot wounds sustained in the Feb. 14 mass shooting. Wilford underwent multiple surgeries for large-caliber gunshot injuries to her chest, abdomen and right arm, spent less than a week in the hospital, and was released the prior Wednesday. She and her parents expressed deep gratitude to the first responders, hospital staff and the community for their care and support.

Coral Springs Fire Department Lt. Laz Ojeda, who helped transport Wilford from the school, described finding her pale and initially unresponsive; after he roused her and learned she was 17, he diverted from dispatch instructions and brought her to nearby Broward Health North (about 10 minutes away) rather than a pediatric-capable hospital 30 miles away. Trauma surgeons at Broward North say that quick decision and the hospital’s preparedness — including a recent active-shooter drill and an immediate “code green” mass-casualty response — were critical to her survival.

Dr. Igor Nichiporenko, medical director of trauma services, performed urgent “damage-control” surgery to stop massive chest bleeding, repair abdominal and chest injuries, and address shattered tendons in her right upper extremity. He noted Wilford’s wounds were worsened by large-caliber bullets and that fragments remain in her body, but her chest and abdomen have healed; the arm will need several weeks to heal followed by occupational therapy. He expects a full recovery and said the choice to take her to Broward North likely saved her life.

Wilford’s parents reiterated their gratitude and emphasized both their relief that she is recovering and their sympathy for classmates and families who lost loved ones in the attack, which killed 14 students and three adults. While the broader political fallout — including scrutiny of law enforcement’s response and use of a photo of President Trump visiting Wilford’s bedside in campaign material — continues, the Wilford family has focused publicly on her recovery and the community’s support.

After a high‑profile wave of rape and bomb threats against women in the U.K. — including feminist campaigner Caroline Criado‑Perez, MP Stella Creasy and several female journalists — Twitter announced policy and staffing changes to crack down on abuse.

What happened
- Several women received threatening tweets (rape and bomb threats), provoking public outrage, police investigations by Scotland Yard’s cyber unit and at least two arrests. Anonymous accounts that sent bomb threats were suspended.
- A petition calling for an in‑tweet “report abuse” button and a zero‑tolerance approach gathered more than 120,000 signatures and prompted media and political criticism of Twitter’s earlier response.

Twitter’s response
- Twitter updated its Rules to clarify that targeted abuse and harassment are prohibited, citing factors such as sending messages from multiple accounts, accounts created solely to abuse others, one‑sided attacks and threats.
- The company said it will add more staff to handle abuse reports and roll out an in‑tweet “report abuse” button across Twitter.com and apps (already available on some mobile devices).
- Twitter U.K. will work with the UK Safer Internet Centre to expand user resources on digital citizenship and use its platform to publicize those resources.
- Twitter U.K. GM Tony Wang and Del Harvey (trust and safety) apologized to victims and pledged stronger protections globally.

Reactions
- Police and commentators urged social media platforms to take greater responsibility; the Metropolitan Police centralized investigations into multiple malicious communications. Critics argued platforms must do more to prevent online abuse rather than only respond after the fact.

Bottom line: In response to threats that drew public, political and police attention, Twitter strengthened its rules on targeted abuse, committed more moderation resources, and promised simpler in‑tweet reporting and broader safety outreach, particularly in the U.K.

US Airways and federal officials are investigating a near-midair collision Tuesday afternoon near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport involving three US Airways commuter jets carrying 192 people. The Washington Post, citing federal sources, reported that controllers cleared two outbound flights while an inbound plane was still on approach after a planned reversal of traffic pattern to accommodate a storm-induced wind shift was not fully communicated within the tower. All flights landed safely.

According to officials, Potomac Tracon in Warrenton told the National tower to reverse the flow of arrivals, but the tower failed to pass the change to all controllers; as a result an inbound plane and the first outbound aircraft closed at a combined speed implying roughly 12 seconds to impact before the tower recognized the error. The tower controller then redirected the inbound flight, which expressed fuel concerns, and had the aircraft circle for a second landing attempt. The FAA said it is investigating and will address the communication lapse; US Airways said it is cooperating.

The incident adds to a history of notable errors at National and nationwide air-traffic operational problems in recent years, including a previous case of a sleeping supervisor at National and multiple operational errors recorded by the FAA. The National Transportation Safety Board has reviewed several serious near-collisions around the country in the past decade.

Jonas Bevacqua, 34, co-founder and creative director of Irvine-based streetwear brand LRG (Lifted Research Group), was found dead in his Laguna Beach home; the Orange County coroner and police say the death does not appear suspicious and an autopsy was planned. No cause has yet been released.

Bevacqua started LRG in 1999 after dropping out of college and returning to live with his adoptive parents in Laguna Beach. He met business partner Robert Wright while DJing at local clubs; early designs were sketched in Bevacqua’s bedroom and initial funding came from friends of his adoptive father and other partners. Influenced by Southern California skate, surf and hip‑hop cultures and his multicultural upbringing, Bevacqua aimed to create a brand that reflected a “melting pot” of influences. LRG grew rapidly—Entrepreneur magazine reported sales rising from $5 million in 2002 to $150 million in 2006, ranking it No. 5 on that year’s fastest‑growing companies list—and expanded beyond clothing into music, electronics and lifestyle projects, sponsoring artists and a skate team.

Colleagues and the company described Bevacqua as a visionary, mentor and friend. He is survived by his fiancée, son, parents and seven siblings. The family has asked for privacy.

Deven Davis, the 39-year-old estranged wife of Korn lead singer Jonathan Davis, has died. The cause of death has not been released. The couple married in 2004 and had two children, Pirate (b. 2005) and Zeppelin (b. 2007); Jonathan also has an older son from a previous marriage.

The announcement of her death came shortly after Jonathan filed for a domestic violence restraining order on August 17, 2018, amid their pending divorce (filed 2016). A judge issued a temporary order barring Deven from child custody or visitation and from contacting the family dog. TMZ reported court allegations from Jonathan that Deven had long struggled with substance abuse—prescription and illegal drugs for over 20 years—had relapsed recently after time in a sober home, and that her drug use had caused neglect and emotional harm to the children. At the 67th annual Alfred E. Smith Memorial Foundation Dinner in New York City, presidential candidates President Barack Obama and GOP nominee Mitt Romney set aside the bruising campaign for a white-tie, charity roast hosted by the New York Catholic Archdiocese. Speaking and joking from the Waldorf-Astoria dais, both men traded self-deprecating humor and light barbs at one another, their running mates, the press and campaign gaffes, winning big laughs from the audience.

Highlights:
- Tone and context: The dinner served as a traditional, convivial respite amid a heated race and came two nights after an especially contentious debate.
- Obama’s humor: He poked fun at his own first-debate performance (“nice long nap”), referenced his anniversary that coincided with the debate, joked about using his middle name, quipped about Romney’s shopping for stores while he shopped at stores in Midtown, and mocked Romney’s awkward foreign trip (“I’m impressed with how well Gov. Romney has avoided” being popular with allies).
- Romney’s humor: He lampooned his own stiff image (saying his white-tie was what he and Ann wear at home), joked about debate prep (“refrain from alcohol for 65 years…find the biggest straw man”), teased Obama about redistribution and “you didn’t build that” themes, and mocked media coverage expectations.
- Running mates and others: Both targeted Vice President Joe Biden for laughs; Romney joked Obama “has Bill Clinton” as his comfort; Obama joked about Paul Ryan’s marathon timing. Al Smith IV, the host’s great-grandson, also offered jabs at both candidates and Cardinal Timothy Dolan.
- Atmosphere: Despite recent tension, the event was civil and self-deprecating, with both candidates managing a polished, humorous performance that emphasized the dinner’s role as a lighthearted pause in the campaign.

Sources cited: AP, Reuters, The Washington Post, LA Times, NBC, New York magazine and others.

Actor Randy Quaid and his wife Evi were arrested Friday night at the U.S. border crossing between Philipsburg, Quebec, and Highgate Springs, Vermont, after U.S. authorities determined they were fugitives from justice and subject to extradition to California. They were detained on outstanding felony vandalism and related charges from 2010 in Santa Barbara County, arising from allegations they squatted in and damaged a guesthouse of a former property they owned and later failed to appear at court. A Vermont judge set high bail (reported variously as $50,000 each and $500,000 each in different accounts); the couple were lodged in separate Vermont jails and Evi pled not guilty to a fugitive-from-justice charge.

Background: The Quaids left the U.S. in 2010 claiming persecution and sought refuge in Canada; Evi, whose father was born in Canada, obtained Canadian citizenship in 2012, while Randy’s refugee claim was withdrawn and his application for permanent residency was denied (citing alleged fraud). Randy was ordered to leave Canada by Oct. 14 after immigration proceedings; he had been briefly detained in Canada as a potential flight risk but an Immigration and Refugee Board member later ruled he was not. Randy has publicly claimed the couple were targeted by so-called “Hollywood star-whackers” and has characterized some of their provocative public behavior as performance. Santa Barbara prosecutors have indicated they will seek extradition.

Hurricane Michael struck the U.S. Southeast as an extremely powerful storm, making landfall in the Florida Panhandle on Oct. 10 as a Category 4 hurricane with catastrophic winds and storm surge. It devastated coastal communities—Mexico Beach and parts of Panama City among the hardest hit—flattening buildings, tossing boats and cars, and ripping homes from foundations. The storm then moved inland through Georgia, the Carolinas and Virginia as a post-tropical system, producing heavy rain, flash flooding and destructive winds far from the coast.

Human toll and damage
- At least 17 deaths were reported across multiple states (including at least eight in Florida and five in Virginia); officials warned the toll was likely to rise as rescue teams reach heavily damaged areas. Deaths were caused by flooding, falling trees, debris and storm-related crashes.
- More than 1 million customers lost power across seven states; hundreds of roads were blocked by fallen trees.
- Search-and-rescue operations combed wreckage—many areas remained inaccessible for days. Mexico Beach officials said the town could be unusable for 12–18 months.

Local impacts and recovery
- Thousands of residents returned to destroyed homes and began salvage and cleanup; many were displaced and reliant on shelters and relief distribution centers.
- Utilities and supply chains were strained; long lines formed for fuel, water and food. Some retail and airports began resuming limited operations.
- Tyndall Air Force Base and other infrastructure suffered severe damage and required extensive repairs.

Economic and agricultural losses
- Significant crop damage was reported in Georgia (pecan, cotton, peanut and vegetable losses). Georgia also reported the destruction of dozens of chicken houses, killing an estimated >2 million birds, affecting the poultry industry.

Government response and warnings
- FEMA deployed resources and warned the fatality count could climb as crews access isolated zones. Individual assistance was approved for additional Florida counties.
- A public health emergency was declared in Georgia to protect access to Medicare/Medicaid services.
- The National Hurricane Center issued its final advisory as Michael moved away over the Atlantic, but warned of lingering coastal gale winds, storm-surge impacts, and inland flooding risks from heavy rain.

Context
- Scientists noted that while climate change doesn’t necessarily increase storm frequency, warming oceans and higher sea levels make storms stronger and surge/flooding worse.

Overall, Michael left widespread destruction across the Florida Panhandle and significant impacts across several states, with long recovery needs for communities, infrastructure, agriculture and military installations.

This document is largely a collection of press releases, statements, campaign actions, and reports from Mayors Against Illegal Guns (MAIG), a bipartisan coalition cofounded in 2006 by New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg and Boston Mayor Thomas Menino. MAIG brings together mayors from across the country—Republicans, Democrats, and Independents—from large cities and small towns to push federal and state reforms intended to reduce gun violence by keeping firearms out of dangerous hands.

Key themes and activities:

- National investigations and reports
  - A 2013 national investigation found thousands of people with criminal records seeking to buy guns through online listings (Armslist.com), estimating that the site could transfer more than 25,000 guns to individuals with criminal records in a year.
  - Reports such as “Access Denied” documented how the gun lobby and some congressional actions have limited research and data collection on gun violence.
  - Earlier MAIG research (2011–2012) documented failures to submit mental-health and other disqualifying records to the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS), leaving dangerous individuals able to pass background checks.

- Campaigns and advocacy
  - Persistent national campaigns to “fix” the background check system, including the National Drive to Fix Gun Checks, DemandAPlan.org, FixGunChecks.org and related ad campaigns (TV spots, full-page newspaper ads, a Super Bowl ad featuring the coalition co-chairs).
  - Calls for Congress to require background checks for all gun sales, limit military-style assault weapons and high-capacity magazines, and make gun trafficking a federal crime.
  - Targeted grassroots and public pressure actions: rallies, a multi-state bus tour, interactive maps showing state reporting to NICS, and petitions opposing national concealed-carry reciprocity.

- Legislative and policy efforts
  - Support for federal bills such as the Fix Gun Checks Act (H.R.1781) and similar Senate proposals to close gaps in the background check system.
  - Opposition to congressional measures that would override state rules on concealed carry or eliminate state-level purchase-permit systems (e.g., efforts in Michigan and H.R.822).
  - Urging executive action to better enforce existing laws and to improve federal-state reporting to NICS without waiting for Congress.

- Public communications and survivor involvement
  - Frequent use of survivors and family members of victims in ads, videos, and public events to press for action after mass shootings (Newtown, Tucson, Aurora, Sandy Hook references).
  - Release of polls showing strong public support—including among many NRA members—for background checks and other “common-sense” measures.

- Other actions
  - Campaigns urging websites to curb illegal online gun sales (recommendations included seller/buyer registration, flagging suspicious behavior, and site audits).
  - Calls to repeal restrictions (Tiahrt amendments) that MAIG argued impeded investigations like Operation Fast & Furious by limiting ATF data sharing.

The document also contains administrative notes at the top about a 2016 crawl of Wikipedia outlinks (turned off duplicate detection; included many wikis), but the bulk of the content documents MAIG’s multi-year efforts (2011–2013 and earlier) to reform background checks, restrict access for dangerous people, increase transparency and data-sharing, and mobilize public and political pressure for federal and state gun-safety legislation.

A group of Chicago streaming subscribers and the Liberty Justice Center have sued the City of Chicago in Cook County court, challenging the city’s June decision to apply its existing 9% “Amusement” tax to online streaming services (Netflix, Amazon Prime, Hulu, Spotify, Xbox Live, etc.). Plaintiffs say the comptroller’s ruling effectively created a new tax without a City Council vote, unlawfully increasing their subscription costs and exceeding the comptroller’s authority under the municipal code.

The complaint also argues the measure violates the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act’s ban on discriminatory Internet-only taxes—claiming Chicago treats streaming differently than DVD-by-mail and other non-Internet services and taxes streamed performances at higher rates than comparable in-person entertainment. The suit highlights practical problems (e.g., how Amazon Prime’s bundled services would be taxed) and contends some taxed services don’t fit the “amusement” definition.

City officials say the ruling is a valid application of the existing tax and will defend it; the city expects roughly $12 million a year in revenue from the change as part of Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s broader effort to raise fees to close budget gaps. The case could have wide significance: it may set precedent on municipal authority to tax Internet-based goods and services and on how “nexus” and discriminatory-online-tax provisions are applied as more localities pursue “cloud” taxes.

This document gathers reporting, commentary, and personal reflection about Balthus’s painting Thérèse Dreaming and the wider controversy around the artist’s work.

Key points:

- The painting: Thérèse Dreaming (1938) by Balthus depicts a prepubescent girl reclining with skirt hiked and underwear visible. Many viewers find the pose sexually suggestive.

- Public backlash: A petition (Care2) led by Mia Merrill urged the Metropolitan Museum of Art to remove or better contextualize the work, arguing the Met is normalizing voyeurism and the sexualization of children amid heightened sensitivity to sexual assault. The petition attracted thousands of signatures. The Met declined to remove the painting, saying museums should present works from across times and cultures and that such works can prompt public conversation; it previously hosted a Balthus exhibition in 2013 that carried a warning plaque.

- Critical context and history: Balthus (Balthasar Klossowski, 1908–2001) was a celebrated but polarizing modern figurative painter, noted for recurring subjects of pubescent girls and cats. Critics and curators have long debated whether his portrayals are artful studies of adolescence or eroticizing and voyeuristic depictions of children. He denied paedophilic intent; contemporaries and later commentators have documented his obsession with young girls and noted at least one later sexual relationship with a teenage model.

- Reception and curatorial choices: Reviews of Met exhibitions (especially “Balthus: Cats and Girls—Paintings and Provocations,” 2013) highlight the tension between aesthetic qualities and troubling subject matter. Curators like Sabine Rewald have elected to present Balthus’s work in full—including the problematic pieces—sometimes adding a notice that some paintings may disturb visitors. Critics describe his work as compelling yet unsettling, capable of both formal invention and what some call voyeurism.

- Personal reflection: An essay by Jen George recounts a personal, intimate response to Thérèse Dreaming. She describes frequenting the Met while transient and emotionally vulnerable; the painting resonated with and haunted her, functioning as a companion image during a difficult period. Her account emphasizes how art can form deep, ambivalent personal connections that mingle attraction, identification, and discomfort.

- Artistic biography and critical assessment: Summaries of Balthus’s career note his early talent (the Mitsou cat drawings praised by Rilke), his anti-modernist stance, his classical influences, and his long-lasting reputation. Critics acknowledge both his technical gifts and the moral unease his subjects provoke. The debate—whether to remove, relabel, or retain such works—reflects broader cultural questions about displaying problematic historical art in the present moment.

Overall takeaway: Balthus’s Thérèse Dreaming exemplifies an enduring conflict in museums and public discourse: how to balance artistic, historical, and aesthetic value against ethical concerns about depictions that may sexualize minors. Responses range from calls for removal or clearer contextualization to defenses of preservation and public discussion; many commentators and visitors experience the work as both artistically significant and morally troubling.

An 18-year-old man, identified by officials as Abdul Numan Haider, was shot dead by a counter‑terrorism officer after stabbing two Joint Counter Terrorism team members outside Endeavour Hills Police Station in Melbourne on Tuesday evening. Haider, who had his passport cancelled on national security grounds and was under investigation for about three months, had reportedly been seen recently displaying what appeared to be an Islamic State (IS) flag and had associations with the local radical group Al‑Furqan, though he was said to have moved away from it.

Police say officers asked Haider to attend the station to discuss concerns. After a brief encounter in which hands were shaken, Haider allegedly stabbed one officer in the arm and another multiple times in the body and head; one of the wounded officers then shot and killed him. Both injured officers — one from the Australian Federal Police and one from Victoria Police — required surgery and were in stable but serious condition. A second knife was found on Haider and his car was located near a neighbouring childcare centre; the scene remained locked down.

Authorities have emphasized there were no specific threats identified, though some reports tied the attack to recent IS calls for lone‑wolf attacks. Officials (including AFP Acting Commissioner Andrew Colvin and Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Ken Lay) said they had taken early steps to monitor and intervene with Haider. The incident has prompted political and community responses: Prime Minister Tony Abbott called it a reminder of the extremist threat, Victoria’s premier urged unity across communities, and Islamic leaders criticized the speed of police statements and warned against premature labeling while also condemning the violence and urging calm amid reports the family faced threats. Investigations were ongoing.

Drake L. Kramer, 21, from San Antonio, has been missing from Grand Canyon National Park since Feb. 1, when he was last seen checking out of the Bright Angel Lodge on the South Rim. Family reported him missing Feb. 2 after receiving a text from Drake saying he “needed to be back with Mother Earth” and wanted to “set his soul free.” Park rangers searched for six days across the South Rim developed area—from Hermit’s Rest to Grandview—walking the rim and forested areas, using dog teams, conducting several over-the-rim technical searches and multiple aerial reconnaissance missions, but found no new clues. Because of the lack of evidence, the operation has been scaled back to a continuous but limited mode with rangers and pilots searching the area as available. Kramer is described as 5'7", 140 lbs, brown hair, blue eyes, last seen wearing blue jeans and an olive green sweatshirt. Posters remain posted at South Rim locations; anyone with information is asked to call the National Park Service Silent Witness Line at (928) 638-7840.

Gordon Gray, a Hollywood producer known for inspirational true-story sports films, and his wife Kristen learned in March that their daughters Charlotte (4) and Gwenyth (20 months) have an extremely rare, progressive and ultimately fatal form of Batten disease (Late Infantile NCL, CLN6). The diagnosis leaves virtually no existing treatment: children typically lose sight, motor skills, speech and the ability to feed themselves, and often die between ages 6 and 12. Because the disorder is so rare — only a handful of cases worldwide — research and funding have been minimal.

Refusing to accept that prognosis, Gray and a group of industry friends formed the Charlotte and Gwenyth Gray Foundation to raise the estimated $10–12 million needed to fund urgent research and clinical trials. An initial $2 million is required to launch trials; potential approaches they hope to accelerate include gene therapy (vector virus), stem cell therapy and small-molecule treatments. Gray has mobilized a steering committee of producers and executives and secured support from major celebrities willing to use social platforms (Facebook, Twitter, Instagram) to solicit $1 donations from followers to bootstrap the effort.

The article also profiles another family, Bekah and Danny Bowman of Orange County, whose sons Titus (5) and Ely (2) were diagnosed this year with a different late-infantile form of NCL (CLN2). Titus has already experienced rapid decline — blindness, loss of speech and mobility, feeding via tube and frequent seizures — and genetic testing showed Ely will develop the same disease. The Bowmans face mounting medical and caregiving burdens; friends created a GoFundMe and social pages to help offset costs. The Bowmans say the publicity and fundraising push led by the Grays has offered them hope and visibility for a disease that rarely receives attention.

Both families emphasize the emotional toll and the imperative to act: parents striving to cherish daily moments with their children while racing to raise funds that could accelerate research and potentially save lives. Gray likens his efforts to buying “three Hail Mary passes” before time runs out — acknowledging no guarantees but pressing forward because funding could accelerate treatments toward human trials.

A Colorado inmate was mistakenly released from the Mesa County Jail but returned within two hours after his wife noticed the error. Court records show 38-year-old James Rynerson was being held on a $2,000 cash bond awaiting charges of menacing, disorderly conduct and trespass. Deputies released him after confusing him with another inmate, Marvin March. Mesa County Sheriff’s Sgt. Henry Stoffel said jail staff failed to follow procedure by not checking Rynerson’s wristband and photo; an internal investigation is under way to see if housing-list policies need revision. Officers credited Rynerson’s wife for ensuring he surrendered back to custody.

A family was found suffering carbon monoxide poisoning in a closed garage in Valley Station. Louisville Metro police responded Wednesday morning to the 9900 block of Plaudit Way after a relative discovered three unresponsive family members. Investigators believe the father warmed the car inside the closed garage, causing carbon monoxide to build up. Juvenal Garcia Mora, 39, and his 3-year-old son Cruz Isaac Garcia were pronounced dead at Medical Center Jewish Southwest; a 7-year-old girl was transported in critical condition to Norton Children’s Hospital. The mother was not home and has been notified. Police say the incident appears to be a tragic accident and remain investigating. LMPD Lt. Emily McKinley warned that carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, can incapacitate people rapidly (in under five minutes at high concentrations), and urged caution—especially when warming cars—because symptoms often resemble the flu (headache, nausea, dizziness).

Three tickets matched all six numbers to split a record $640 million Mega Millions jackpot. State lottery officials say winning tickets were sold in Illinois (Red Bud, near St. Louis), Kansas (location not yet released) and Maryland (a 7-Eleven in Baltimore County/Milford Mill). Before taxes, each ticket is worth a bit more than $213 million; the advertised $640 million equates to about a $462 million cash lump sum ($347 million after federal withholding) to be divided among the three winners.

The winning numbers were 02-04-23-38-46 and Mega Ball 23. Maryland officials confirmed their state sold one of the jackpot tickets and also reported four $250,000 winners in Maryland; the retailer that sold the Maryland jackpot ticket will receive a $100,000 bonus. National officials were still confirming details and waiting for winners to come forward. The draw generated heavy ticket-buying nationwide and extensive local media attention at the selling locations.

CNN will air a final season of Anthony Bourdain’s Parts Unknown using footage he shot before his death. The network plans to finish and release episodes filmed in Kenya (completed with Bourdain’s original narration), Texas’s Big Bend, Spain’s Asturias, Indonesia, and four Lower East Side Manhattan segments. For episodes lacking finished narration, Zero Point Zero directors will use on-location audio recorded with Bourdain and new follow-up interviews with people who appeared on camera to help tie episodes together. Amy Entelis, CNN’s EVP of talent and content, said each episode will vary depending on available material but will still show and include Bourdain’s voice even where his full narration is absent. CNN will not continue Parts Unknown with a new host; instead it is developing new unscripted projects to fill the void. No premiere date has been announced, though the season is expected this fall based on prior schedules.

Heavy metal icon Ian “Lemmy” Kilmister, the gravel‑voiced frontman and founder of Motörhead, has died at 70 after a brief battle with cancer discovered on December 26. The band announced he died at home surrounded by family, asking fans to celebrate by playing his music loud. Known for his distinctive growl, mutton‑chops, hard‑living persona and the signature stage cry “We are Motörhead! We play rock and roll!”, Lemmy left a huge mark on rock and metal over a 50‑year career.

Born in 1945, Lemmy began in 1960s beat bands, worked as a roadie for Jimi Hendrix, and gained fame singing Hawkwind’s 1972 hit “Silver Machine.” After being dismissed from Hawkwind in 1975 following a drug arrest, he formed Motörhead, named after a Hawkwind song he’d written. With early lineup stability in the late 1970s — Lemmy, “Fast” Eddie Clarke and Phil “Philthy Animal” Taylor — Motörhead released breakthrough albums including Overkill, Bomber and Ace of Spades, and the live No Sleep ’til Hammersmith reached No. 1 in 1981. Over his life he recorded 22 studio albums; the most recent, Bad Magic, was released in 2015.

Lemmy’s music married 1950s rock’n’roll roots with punk energy and extreme volume, influencing thrash and metal scenes even as he resisted the “metal” label. His lifestyle — a long public history of drinking, drug use, collecting controversial memorabilia, and embracing rock’s excesses — was as legendary as his music, though later years brought health struggles: a cardioverter‑defibrillator implant, hematoma, gastric illness, diabetes, weight loss and mobility issues. He had recently moderated some habits (switching from whiskey to vodka, cutting smoking) but remained defiantly active onstage until the end.

Friends and peers mourned him as a warrior and legend; public remembrances and tributes poured in. Lemmy never married and spent his final years living in Los Angeles. Fans and fellow musicians are left with a vast recorded legacy and the enduring image of a singular rock’n’roll character who kept performing until his death.

A Baltimore police officer was suspended Saturday and resigned the next day after a video went viral showing him repeatedly punching and pinning a man, identified by his attorney as 26-year-old Dashawn McGrier. The encounter occurred around 11:45 a.m. in East Baltimore while officers were on a crime-suppression detail. Police say one officer recognized McGrier, released him after an initial contact, then re-approached to issue a contact sheet; the situation escalated when McGrier refused to provide identification. Video shows the officer shove McGrier, then deliver a series of punches, force him down steps and pin him—while a second officer stands nearby and later was placed on administrative duty.

Interim Police Commissioner Gary Tuggle called the footage “deeply disturbing,” ordered an investigation and initially suspended the officer; the department announced it accepted the officer’s resignation the next day. McGrier was hospitalized with suspected fractures to his jaw, nose and ribs; he was not charged. His lawyer plans to pursue legal action and said the same officer had arrested McGrier in June. The Baltimore City State’s Attorney’s Office and Internal Affairs are investigating; the incident is under criminal review.

The assault renewed scrutiny of the Baltimore Police Department’s reform efforts under a federal consent decree following patterns of unconstitutional policing highlighted after Freddie Gray’s death. Critics, including the monitor team and civil-rights leaders, urged close scrutiny of the department’s response; city leaders, including Mayor Catherine Pugh, demanded accountability. Concerns were also raised about recruit training and whether recent academy graduates are adequately prepared for constitutional policing.

Ryan Seacrest hosted E!’s Oscars red carpet under a cloud of renewed sexual misconduct allegations from former stylist Suzie Hardy, which he denies and which E! said its investigation found insufficient evidence to support. There was widespread speculation that A-list stars—particularly female nominees—would snub him, and several high-profile actresses (including the five Best Actress nominees) did not stop for interviews with Seacrest.

Still, Seacrest conducted about 20 on‑carpet interviews. Notable people who spoke with him included Allison Janney, Mary J. Blige, Christopher Plummer, Richard Jenkins, Tiffany Haddish, Kelly Ripa (who praised him), Taraji P. Henson (who offered a pointed remark—“the universe has a way of taking care of the good people”—while touching his chin), Eiza González (telling him to “be good”), and other presenters and musicians such as Diane Warren, Common and Andra Day. Much of E!’s broadcast also relied on co‑host Giuliana Rancic and a nearby Roosevelt Hotel roundtable to fill airtime.

Reports that E! considered a 30‑second broadcast delay to guard against on‑air confrontations (which the network denied) highlighted the network’s caution. Overall, the night was marked by an awkward balance: Seacrest was not universally shunned and had several friendly exchanges, but many top nominees avoided his segment and #MeToo-era tensions were an undercurrent throughout the coverage.

Sen. Lindsey Graham will headline a fundraiser Monday to support Sen. Ted Cruz’s presidential campaign, a striking reversal in the GOP primary. A draft invitation obtained by CNN says the event — a meet-and-greet during next week’s AIPAC policy conference — will “honor and support a great friend of Israel and the Jewish people.” Graham, who ended his own presidential bid in December and initially backed Jeb Bush, told CNN Cruz isn’t his preferred candidate but is “the best alternative to Donald Trump” and that he will “help Ted in every way I can.” This marks a sharp change from earlier comments in which Graham compared nominating Trump or Cruz to being “shot or poisoned.”

Separately, former candidate Marco Rubio, who suspended his campaign after losing Florida’s winner-take-all contest, said in a call with Minnesota supporters he hopes another candidate stops Trump from reaching the 1,237 delegates needed for the nomination. Rubio declined to endorse anyone but called Cruz “the only conservative left in the race.” He reflected on why his upbeat message failed to break through, blaming negative media narratives and Super PAC attack ads for undermining his momentum, and left open the possibility of future public service.

This document examines the backlash to Rush Limbaugh’s week-long attacks on Sandra Fluke, a Georgetown law student who testified that health insurance should cover contraception, and the broader conservative responses they revealed. Limbaugh famously called Fluke a “slut,” joked about her sexual behavior and offered to buy “aspirin” for students, then issued an apology under advertiser pressure that apologized for his language but did not retract or address the underlying arguments. William Saletan (Slate) uses Limbaugh’s comments as a window into several conservative positions and questions worth pressing:

- Is opposition to contraceptive coverage rooted in a blanket anti‑socialism stance (government paying for private choices) or moral disapproval of sex, especially premarital or frequent sex? Limbaugh’s repeated jokes about sex suggest the latter.
- How much sexual activity is considered excessive? Limbaugh repeatedly focused on alleged frequency, implying moral judgement without evidence.
- Is contraception viewed as enabling promiscuity rather than as legitimate health care? Limbaugh framed birth control as subsidizing “sexual habits,” echoing arguments by Catholic bishops that pregnancy isn’t a disease and contraception is elective.
- What consequences should sex carry? Limbaugh’s criticisms of “sex without consequences” raise whether conservatives view pregnancy as an appropriate consequence and oppose preventing it.
- Should men share responsibility? Limbaugh briefly asked where male responsibility and condoms are, but did not propose concrete measures (e.g., paternity enforcement) to hold men accountable.

Saletan argues these substantive questions were overshadowed by outrage over the personal insults and challenges Limbaugh to answer them directly.

The piece then recounts actress Patricia Heaton’s Twitter attacks on Fluke—echoing Limbaugh’s tone by mocking Fluke’s alleged sexual behavior and urging followers to send condoms—after which Heaton’s account was deleted amid backlash. Commentators captured and circulated her deleted tweets, criticizing her for bullying a student and for spreading misinformation, and noting that her departure from Twitter appears PR-driven.

Overall, the article frames the Limbaugh/Heaton incidents as symptomatic of a conservative discourse that often conflates contraception with immorality, avoids policy specifics on shared responsibility, and resorts to personal attacks—points Saletan urges should be answered substantively rather than drowned out by outrage at crude remarks.

Glennon Doyle Melton, the popular Christian mom blogger and bestselling author of Carry On, Warrior and Love Warrior, publicly announced in November that she is dating former U.S. soccer star Abby Wambach, just three months after divorcing her husband Craig Melton. Melton made the announcement on Facebook without using sexual labels, praising Wambach as “deeply sensitive,” “unwaveringly good,” and someone her children already love (“they call her an M&M”). She said the relationship developed quickly, that she and Craig remain supportive of each other and co-parent their three children together, and described the household as a “beautiful, modern family” with shared dinners and school events.

Wambach, who had separated from her wife earlier that year, confirmed their engagement publicly in February, posting affectionate messages on Instagram. Melton — known for candid confessional writing and for speaking at Christian venues — has long affirmed same-sex marriage and framed the relationship as part of her ongoing spiritual and personal journey. The announcement drew responses from fellow authors and some Christian supporters, and highlights broader conversations about faith, sexuality and evolving views among mainline Christians.

Kenny G says he played a small role in the creation and early direction of two Starbucks staples: the Frappuccino and selling music in stores. In a Bloomberg interview the saxophonist recalled that his uncle was an early investor who introduced him to CEO Howard Schultz, and that he himself invested early in Starbucks. He told Schultz about a popular sweet blended drink at another chain and repeatedly suggested Starbucks add something similar; he believes that customer feedback like his contributed to Starbucks developing the Frappuccino. Starbucks notes the Frappuccino concept was actually being developed by partners in Southern California in 1993 and that Starbucks introduced its first national Frappuccino flavors in 1995 after acquiring The Coffee Connection in 1994. Kenny G also said his 1994 Christmas album Miracles was the first record Starbucks sold at the counter, an experiment that proved successful.

One paratrooper was killed and seven others injured Friday morning during artillery live-fire training at Fort Bragg involving an M777 light, towed howitzer, the 18th Fires Brigade said. Two soldiers were seriously injured; one was transferred to Duke University Medical Center and the other remains at Womack Army Medical Center. The other five were treated at Womack and released. The incident is under investigation by the 82nd Airborne Division, the Army Criminal Investigative Division and the Army Combat Readiness/Safety Center. Families have been notified and the brigade said names will be released Saturday. Brigade commander Col. Stephen Smith expressed condolences and said the unit is providing support to soldiers and families.

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon survived a shareholder attempt to remove him as board chairman at the bank’s May 15, 2012 annual meeting in Tampa, held five days after the firm disclosed an emerging $2 billion trading loss. Most votes were cast before the loss was revealed; Dimon’s proposal to retain his chairmanship drew only about 40% support for removal, while his 2011 pay package of roughly $23 million was approved with 91% of the vote.

Dimon, subdued at the meeting, called the loss “self-inflicted” and said “the buck always stops with me.” Protesters and upset investors confronted him; some demonstrators threw eggs at a poster of Dimon outside the meeting. The bank’s stock plunged about 12% in two trading days—erasing nearly $20 billion in market value—then recovered modestly.

The incident intensified scrutiny of big-bank trading and revived debate over regulatory measures such as the Volcker Rule. President Obama and Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner both cited the loss as evidence for tougher rules and closer regulatory review. JPMorgan’s chief investment officer Ina Drew, who oversaw the trading unit involved, left the firm the day before the meeting.

Nearly 30 cadets at the U.S. Air Force Academy needed medical attention after an unauthorized annual ritual called "First Shirt/First Snow" turned violent last Thursday, school officials said. The event, in which freshmen attempt to toss their cadet sergeant into a snowbank, escalated into a melee; six cadets were hospitalized (all since released) and 21 others treated for bruises or lacerations. Commandant Brig. Gen. Gregory Lengyel called the incident unacceptable and said the academy is investigating. An internal memo reportedly from Brig. Gen. Dana Born described the ritual as having "devolved" into increasingly violent brawls over recent years, with prior injuries including concussions, bites and stitches. Lengyel may allow the tradition to continue only if it can be shown to follow proper order, discipline and risk management. The episode adds to other recent reputation challenges at the academy, which has faced past controversies including sexual assault investigations, alleged religious favoritism, cheating and drug-use incidents.

EU leaders met in Brussels amid warnings that the Ukraine conflict is approaching a “point of no return,” and discussed preparing tougher sanctions on Russia over what many called direct military intervention in eastern Ukraine. Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko told the summit thousands of foreign troops and hundreds of tanks were on Ukrainian soil and warned that failure to stop the escalation could mean full-scale war. He said he hoped a draft peace plan would be published soon and that a Contact Group meeting in Belarus might produce a ceasefire.

EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton and several member-state leaders, including Lithuania’s Dalia Grybauskaite and the UK’s David Cameron, accused Russia of sending arms, equipment and personnel to back pro-Russian separatists. NATO and Ukrainian officials said Russian regular forces and armored columns have supported recent rebel advances, a claim Russia denies. Fighting intensified around Donetsk and Luhansk, with Ukrainian forces ordered to retreat from towns such as Novosvitlivka and Ilovaysk; rebels opened a new front toward the port city of Mariupol after capturing Novoazovsk. UN figures put the death toll in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions at around 2,600.

EU leaders tasked the European Commission and EU diplomatic service to prepare possible new measures; France, Germany and others warned sanctions could be escalated if Russia does not reverse course, though unanimity is uncertain because of economic ties to Russia. Some eastern members urged arms supplies to Ukraine and cancellation of military contracts with Russia—an idea France resisted because of existing shipbuilding deals. European Commission president José Manuel Barroso emphasized sanctions are intended to push for a political solution while keeping diplomatic avenues open.

Ezra Klein praises Speaker John Boehner’s inaugural address to the 112th Congress as a notably smart, restrained speech that emphasized humility and comity rather than grand ideological promises. Unlike past speakers who used the moment to outline sweeping agendas, Boehner repeatedly framed the House as “the people’s House,” stressed that members are caretakers serving a frustrated electorate, and pledged greater openness and respect for minority rights and debate. He proposed procedural reforms—three days to read bills, smaller committees, more amendments and open rules, limits on fast and large bills, and cuts to congressional spending—that he said would restore transparency, accountability, and constitutional fidelity.

Klein argues the speech is politically savvy partly because of what it omitted, but cautions that rhetoric may clash with actions: the rules Boehner supports could make deficit-increasing tax cuts easier, and Republicans were already breaking their own rules by pursuing an unfunded symbolic repeal of health-care reform. Many past speakers have abandoned openness pledges when faced with political pressures, and Boehner has at times been combative. Still, Klein concludes, Boehner’s instincts so far are impressive and he may prove a more capable opponent to the White House than expected.

The included text of Boehner’s remarks reiterates those themes—humility, service, restoring trust, honoring the Pledge to America, encouraging respectful debate, and procedural reforms intended to give power back to the people.

Actor Ben Affleck, 46, has entered a live-in rehab facility to seek treatment for alcohol addiction, PEOPLE and TMZ report. The decision followed a visit by his ex-wife and co‑parent Jennifer Garner to his Pacific Palisades home; sources say Garner intervened and drove with Affleck and an unidentified woman to the treatment center in Malibu, stopping briefly en route at a Jack in the Box. The move was prompted in part by photos showing Affleck accepting an alcohol delivery at his Brentwood home and concerns about his recent behavior and new public relationship with 22‑year‑old Playboy model Shauna Sexton.

Affleck has a long history of addressing alcohol dependence, first entering treatment in 2001 and completing a program in March 2017. Friends and sources say he attends meetings, meditation and yoga, but has had setbacks; the current stay is described as extended. Garner’s priority, according to insiders, is Affleck’s sobriety and reliable co‑parenting of their three children, and her concerns have contributed to delays in finalizing their divorce. If you or someone you know needs help, contact the SAMHSA helpline at 1‑800‑662‑HELP.

A 51-year-old Toronto mother gave her 23-year-old son a mock invoice totaling $39,254 to illustrate how much she’s spent supporting him while he’s lived at home. The gag bill, posted by the son (Reddit user “Chalipo”) to r/funny and later picked up by national outlets, itemized 13 months of household costs (internet, utilities, prescriptions, cleaning, “specialty meals”), five years of tuition, health premiums, a $600 “contribution” for gifts, and a $1,000 charge for being “an unappreciative asshole.” Both say the stunt followed a misunderstanding during an argument and was intended tongue-in-cheek to make him appreciate her help, not to be collected as actual debt. The son apologized, acknowledged the lesson, and said he plans to repay his mother in the future; the episode drew mixed online reactions but reportedly improved their relationship.
