A large Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) outbreak in South Korea has infected at least 95 people and killed seven (as of June 9, 2015), with roughly 2,800–2,900 people quarantined as potential contacts. The outbreak began when a 68-year-old man returned from travel in the Middle East in early May; after developing fever and cough he visited multiple clinics and hospitals before being diagnosed with MERS on May 20. Because patients in South Korea commonly seek care at major hospitals and family members frequently visit and care for the sick in person, the virus spread rapidly inside hospitals. Two large hospitals—St. Mary’s in Pyeongtaek and Samsung Medical Center in Seoul—account for the bulk of cases: the index patient infected many at St. Mary’s (about 37 cases), and a secondary “super-spreader” who had been infected there subsequently exposed dozens at Samsung (about 35 cases), leading to nearly 700 people from the emergency ward being quarantined.

Authorities and experts say the outbreak has so far been largely nosocomial (hospital-centered), and the World Health Organization does not see evidence of sustained community transmission; WHO sent experts to assist South Korea. The government has faced criticism for delays and lack of transparency in naming affected hospitals and notifying the public, contributing to public anger and a fall in President Park Geun-hye’s approval rating. Measures taken include isolating patients, quarantining contacts, closing nearly 2,000 schools and kindergartens, canceling events, and using cellphone signal tracking to locate people violating quarantine. The health ministry pledged to cover treatment and testing costs; two patients have recovered and a third was expected to be discharged. Officials hope the outbreak may have peaked and expect the coming days to be critical in determining whether containment efforts succeed.

Agnes Nixon, the pioneering creator of the daytime soaps One Life to Live and All My Children, has died at 93 in Haverford, Pennsylvania. Celebrated as the “queen of modern daytime drama,” Nixon transformed the genre by weaving socially relevant, often taboo topics into daytime storylines—early examples include a uterine cancer/Pap smear arc in 1962 that prompted thousands of viewer letters and earned a Pioneer for Health Award, and later plots addressing the Vietnam War, racism and racial integration, abortion, drug addiction, child abuse, AIDS, homosexuality, and transgender issues. Her shows introduced prominent Black characters, featured the first legal abortion storyline after Roe v. Wade, included a popular lesbian character (Bianca) and later a transgender character, and helped broaden soaps’ audiences beyond homemakers.

Nixon began as a radio and television writer (Woman in White, Guiding Light, As the World Turns) after being mentored by Irna Phillips, then created One Life to Live (1968) and All My Children (1970). Her work was sometimes controversial and met with industry resistance and occasional station cancellations, but it was also widely influential and emulated. Over a career spanning decades, programs she created or influenced aired every weekday for 43 years. She received numerous honors, including a 2010 Daytime Emmy Lifetime Achievement Award, and was widely mourned by actors, writers and producers in the soap community. Nixon is survived by four children, 10 grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.

Operation Blue Roof is a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers program that provides free fiber-reinforced tarps to homeowners in disaster areas to cover damaged roofs until permanent repairs can be made. It lets residents stay in their homes and protects property; eligible properties are primary residences or permanently occupied rentals with less than 50% structural damage (vacation rentals and some roof types are ineligible).

After Hurricane Irma, FEMA Region 4 tweeted the program phone number but mistakenly listed 1-800-ROOF-BLU, which connects to an adult phone line. The correct number on the Operation Blue Roof website is 1-888-ROOF-BLU. The erroneous tweet was removed after attention was called to it, and FEMA Region 4 reposted the correct contact information.

Owen Labrie, a 20-year-old former St. Paul’s School student convicted last year of sexual assault, child endangerment and unlawful computer use for an encounter with a 15-year-old freshman, will be released on bail again while he appeals. A Merrimack County Superior Court judge ruled Labrie can be freed once fitted with a GPS ankle monitor and must reside at his mother’s Tunbridge, Vermont, home with a 5 p.m.–8 a.m. curfew; officials expect release between Wednesday and Friday.

Labrie had originally been released on $15,000 bail after his October conviction but had that bail revoked in March after admitting he violated his curfew multiple times — an investigation was prompted by a reporter’s tweet about seeing him on a train visiting a college girlfriend. He has spent about two months in jail since the revocation. At Monday’s hearing his attorney said the jail stay was “life-changing” and that he will comply with conditions; prosecutors argued Labrie simply dislikes being incarcerated and noted he has not completed a psycho-sexual assessment, making risk unclear. Advocacy groups criticized the decision as sending the wrong message to victims.

At trial Labrie testified the contact was consensual though he denied intercourse; prosecutors presented evidence including prior boasts. Labrie, who had been bound for Harvard prior to his arrest, is appealing the conviction and also seeking a new trial on ineffective-assistance grounds.

Nearly six months after Robin Williams’s death, his widow Susan Schneider Williams and his three children — Zak, Zelda and Cody — are locked in a bitter court dispute over his property and belongings.

Key points:
- Court filings allege conflicting claims about who may access and take items from Williams’s home shortly after his death. Susan says someone removed belongings days after he died; the children counter that Susan denied them access.
- The core dispute concerns interpretation of Williams’s will and trust. The trust reportedly left "personal effects" — including his Oscar, movie memorabilia, action figures, graphic novels, theater masks and similar items — to his three children. The children say Susan is trying to redefine terms (for example, excluding his watch collection from "jewelry") to keep items intended for them.
- Susan acknowledges she has no claim to explicitly career-related items (such as costume pieces), but she seeks to retain items she says she accumulated while married to him, including some clothing and "knickknacks" like the wedding tux.
- Sources close to the family say the dispute has become acrimonious and would have saddened Williams, who likely would have preferred the matter handled privately.

The conflict mixes financial and deeply personal elements — from collectibles and toys to photographs and fossils — and centers on differing readings of the estate documents and what the late actor intended for his children versus his widow.

France will implement a “right to disconnect” law on January 1 requiring companies with more than 50 employees to negotiate rules or, failing agreement, adopt a charter specifying when staff are not expected to send or answer work emails and smartphone messages outside contracted hours. Aimed at curbing an “always-on” culture that erodes private life and contributes to unpaid overtime, stress, burnout and sleep problems, the measure was first proposed after a 2015 report on workplace “info‑obesity” and was enacted as part of broader labour reforms in May. Supporters, including trade unions, say it protects workers beyond France’s statutory 35‑hour week; critics and some workers may be reluctant because digital tools also provide autonomy and flexibility. Research cited (U.S. and UK surveys) links after‑hours email expectations and anticipation of responses to emotional exhaustion, while many British workers continue to check emails during breaks. The rule is among the first of its kind globally and follows private-sector initiatives (e.g., Daimler) to limit holiday or out‑of‑hours email access.

A federal appeals court revived a $10 million copyright lawsuit against Justin Bieber, Usher and several publishing companies, ruling on Sept. 24 that the case should go to trial. R&B singer Devin Copeland (De Rico) and co-writer Mareio Overton sued, alleging three versions of “Somebody to Love” recorded by Bieber, Usher or both unlawfully copied elements of their 2008 song of the same name. In March 2014 a district judge dismissed the suit, finding no reasonable jury could find infringement. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals (3-0) disagreed, saying the songs’ choruses are “similar enough” and noting even the delivery of the phrase “somebody to love” shows an “almost identical rhythm and a strikingly similar melody.” The appeals court also rejected the defense that differences in genre (dance-pop/electronica versus R&B) preclude infringement, and sent the case back to the lower court for further proceedings. The suit names publishers including Universal Music Publishing Group and Sony/ATV. One Bieber version of “Somebody to Love” reached No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 2010.

Gudrun Burwitz, the eldest daughter of Heinrich Himmler, died in May at age 88. Himmler was a top Nazi leader who commanded the SS and was a principal architect of the Holocaust; he killed himself in British custody in 1945. Burwitz remained an unrepentant supporter of her father and of Nazism throughout her life, was active in far-right circles, and helped former SS members through the secretive aid network Stille Hilfe.

Following her death, German tabloid Bild reported — and the federal intelligence agency (BND) later confirmed — that Burwitz had been employed at the BND’s Pullach headquarters under an assumed name as a secretary from 1961 to 1963. The BND’s historian said she left when West Germany began reassessing the roles of former Nazis in government. Her hiring occurred when the agency was led by Reinhard Gehlen, a former Nazi military intelligence officer.

Burwitz grew up in the Nazi elite, attended events with Hitler, and as a teenager visited the Dachau camp, later denying the Holocaust and defending her father’s reputation. After the war she and her mother were detained for several years; she later married, had two children, and avoided public commentary aside from supporting and attending neo‑Nazi gatherings and aiding convicted or accused war criminals such as Klaus Barbie. German institutions have long struggled with post‑war links to former Nazis; the BND ordinarily does not discuss personnel but publicly acknowledged Burwitz’s past because she has died.

Summary:

Leaked documents and reporting reveal that the NSA, under authority of the 2008 FISA Amendments Act, conducts wide-ranging warrantless surveillance of international electronic communications that sweeps up large amounts of Americans’ emails, texts and other text-based messages crossing U.S. borders. Although the law authorizes targeting non‑U.S. persons abroad, the agency explicitly searches for “communications about the target that are not to or from the target,” meaning messages that merely mention a foreign suspect (for example, an email address or phone number) can be captured. To do this the NSA clones selected communications links, reassembles packets, runs automated searches for selectors, retains matching content for human review, and deletes the rest — a process officials say is brief and not “bulk” storage, though computer scientists note reconstructing and searching packetized traffic effectively requires collecting almost all cross‑border text data.

The leaked “targeting” and “minimization” Procedures — apparently approved by the FISA court — contain multiple broad and permissive provisions:
- They allow collection, retention and dissemination of Americans’ international communications when one end of a conversation is a foreign target; such “one‑end domestic” communications can be kept for years or indefinitely if deemed to contain foreign intelligence or evidence of crimes.
- They permit presumptions that prospective targets are foreigners abroad unless specific information says otherwise, risking misidentification.
- The definition of “foreign intelligence information” is very broad (including foreign affairs), and selection criteria (e.g., past communications with foreigners or presence in a foreign contact list) bring many routine international contacts within scope.
- The Procedures enable dragnet-style collection (IP filters, country-code targeting, etc.) that can sweep in millions of communications, including purely domestic communications.
- Collected purely domestic communications and encrypted content may be retained; attorney‑client communications receive little special protection except in narrow circumstances.
- The NSA relies on and maintains extensive “knowledge databases” and content repositories (metadata, location info like Home Location Registers), but the Procedures give few clear limits or safeguards for Americans’ privacy.

Government spokespeople and intelligence officials insist the activities are lawful, tailored, and aimed at foreign powers and agents; they emphasize automated precision and brief retention of non‑matching data. Critics and former intelligence officials counter that the procedures amount to unconstitutional domestic surveillance, built on weak safeguards, broad definitions and presumptions, and create large databases of Americans’ communications. The disclosures have amplified concerns that public assurances — that Americans are not targeted — are misleading, because the surveillance targets foreign persons while routinely capturing Americans’ communications that touch those targets.

Researchers have measured the mass and density of Kepler-78b, an Earth-sized exoplanet that orbits a Sun‑like star every 8.5 hours, and find it to be very similar to Earth in composition though far too hot for life. Using radial-velocity observations with HARPS‑N and HIRES, two independent teams determined the planet’s radius to be about 1.20 ± 0.09 Earth radii and its mass to be ≈1.7–1.9 Earth masses. That yields a mean density near 5.3–5.6 g cm−3—close to Earth’s ~5.5 g cm−3—consistent with a rocky body with an iron core.

Kepler-78b lies extremely close to its star (≈1% of the Earth–Sun distance), giving surface temperatures around 2,000 °C. Its ultra-short-period orbit is puzzling because standard formation and migration scenarios have difficulty explaining a planet surviving or forming so near the star; tidal decay will likely doom the planet within a few billion years. Although inhospitable, Kepler-78b demonstrates that small, Earth‑like composition planets exist outside the Solar System and highlights the value of follow-up radial-velocity work. Future missions (e.g., TESS) targeting nearby, cooler stars may enable similar mass-and-density measurements for more potentially habitable small planets.

Researchers reinterpreting the 3,700-year-old Babylonian clay tablet Plimpton 322 argue it is the world’s oldest—and a uniquely exact—trigonometric table, predating Greek work by more than a millennium. Plimpton 322, found in southern Iraq and now at Columbia University, contains four columns and 15 rows of sexagesimal (base-60) numbers. Since the 1940s scholars noted these numbers encode Pythagorean triples (integer side-lengths of right triangles). Daniel Mansfield and Norman Wildberger (UNSW) reexamined the tablet, reconstructed missing entries, and propose the Babylonians represented triangle information not by angles and approximate sines/cosines but by exact ratios of side lengths (short side:long side and short side:hypotenuse). Because Babylonian base-60 arithmetic admits many exact fractions, their table can give exact ratio-based trigonometric values rather than approximations, making it a “clean and easy-to-use” tool potentially useful for surveying and construction.

The claim has drawn mixed reactions: some historians and mathematicians call the idea mathematically plausible and pedagogically appealing, noting it offers a different cultural perspective on trigonometry; others call the interpretation speculative, pointing out there is no direct textual evidence that Babylonians used the tablet to solve triangle problems in this manner. Critics also argue the tablet might be a parameters table for school exercises rather than a practical surveying tool. The authors suggest the tablet may originally have been larger and that further study of other Babylonian tablets could confirm whether this ratio-based trigonometry was used more broadly.

Investigators say audio from the recovered cockpit voice recorder of Germanwings Flight 9525 strongly supports the theory that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately locked captain Patrick Sondenheimer out of the cockpit and put the Airbus A320 into a fatal descent, killing all 150 aboard. German tabloid Bild published a purported summary of the recording—leaked despite strict rules against releasing cockpit audio—showing the captain leaving to use the lavatory, telling Lubitz “you can take over,” then returning minutes later as the aircraft descended. The transcript describes alarms (“sink rate,” “terrain—pull up”), pounding on the locked cockpit door, the captain’s desperate pleas (“For God’s sake, open the door!”), passengers screaming and, ultimately, the wing striking the mountain.

French and German authorities cautioned that the investigation remains open until the flight data recorder is recovered and all technical possibilities are excluded, but prosecutors have reported finding torn sick notes and evidence Lubitz concealed medical issues from his employer. Media reports—citing unnamed sources—have suggested a history of depression, anxiety, possible psychosomatic or vision problems and prescription medications, though these details have not been fully confirmed. Forensic teams recovered numerous body fragments and DNA samples; the flight data recorder had not been found at the time of reporting.

The leak of the cockpit audio prompted criticism from investigators, pilot groups and industry figures (including Airbus chairman Tom Enders) as a breach of investigation protocol and as irresponsible speculation. In Lubitz’s hometown there have been memorials for victims alongside calls for restraint and support for his grieving family; church and community leaders urged caution about drawing conclusions before the investigation is complete.

Al-Qaida’s leader Ayman al-Zawahri announced the creation of a South Asian franchise, “Al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent,” in a video released online, saying the group aims to bring Islamic law across the subcontinent and “wage jihad” against its enemies. He presented the organization as the result of a multi-year effort to unite mujahedeen in the region, pledged allegiance to Afghan Taliban leader Mullah Omar, and named Pakistani fighter Asim Umar to lead day-to-day operations. Other speakers in the 55-minute production threatened Jews and Hindus and described violent tactics.

The announcement raised concerns in India: at least three states with sizable Muslim populations were put on alert and national security officials met to assess the threat. Indian officials and analysts noted the warning comes as Al-Qaida seeks to regain relevance after being overshadowed by the Islamic State (IS), which has attracted recruits by seizing territory in Iraq and Syria. Experts say Al-Qaida’s aging leadership is trying to compete for recruits and legitimacy; Zawahri’s message also critiqued intra-jihadist “discord,” an implicit rebuke of IS methods.

India faces vulnerabilities—large Muslim minority populations, unrest in Kashmir, and past attacks such as the 2008 Mumbai assaults—though Al-Qaida historically has had limited reach in India compared with local militant groups. The announcement could complicate domestic politics and security, but analysts also view Al-Qaida as weaker than regional insurgents and the resurgent IS. Separately, Pakistan’s TTP distanced itself from an IS-aligned splinter group and reaffirmed allegiance to the Afghan Taliban.

Clint Bench, born without fully formed hands, has long led an active life — college, marriage, mountain biking and riding roller coasters at Six Flags Over Texas. In May 2012, however, a Six Flags employee barred him from the Aquaman Splashdown ride, telling him he “could not ride Aquaman because he does not have hands.” Management later cited a policy requiring riders to “have at least one fully formed arm all the way down to the fingers.” Bench says that prior rules only required the ability to grasp — which he can do — and that the new restriction was created after the incident. He has sued Six Flags under the Americans with Disabilities Act, saying he suffered embarrassment and discrimination in front of his children and seeking unspecified damages and assurances the discrimination won’t recur. Six Flags declined comment while the lawsuit is pending. The case follows other disputes and policy changes at Six Flags regarding disabled guests.

Ko Young-tae, a 40-year-old former national saber fencer and fashion entrepreneur, emerged as a key whistle-blower in the scandal that led to the impeachment of South Korea’s president Park Geun-hye by exposing the undue influence of Park’s longtime confidante Choi Soon-sil.

Key points:
- Ko voluntarily appeared for prolonged questioning by prosecutors after returning to Korea; he is suspected of managing companies (The Blue K and Widec/Wide Sports) tied to Choi and alleged to have been used to funnel money from foundations. Prosecutors have not released interrogation details.
- Ko’s background: 1998 Asian Games gold-medalist in fencing, former host-bar worker in Gangnam (where he reportedly met Choi around 2006), later launched the accessory brand Villomillo in 2008 with Choi’s help; Villomillo gained prominence after Park was seen carrying its bag in 2013.
- Ko supplied hundreds of luxury items to Choi (and items that ended up with President Park) but denied a romantic relationship with Choi, despite media rumors and a 20-year age gap. He has said they were close friends and that Choi trusted him with roles in companies she owned in Germany.
- He provided journalists with damning material: CCTV footage of Choi ordering presidential aides and comments that Choi’s “favorite thing” was editing Park’s speeches. That comment spurred JTBC to search and find a discarded tablet containing drafts of dozens of presidential speeches and selfies, a discovery central to the scandal.
- Ko says his motive to go public was personal: after a 2014 dispute with Choi over her daughter’s puppy and subsequent mistreatment, he collected and released evidence of Choi’s influence—video, documents, and other materials—which helped trigger public outrage, investigations, and ultimately Park’s impeachment.
- Public response: Ko has been hailed by some as a whistle-blower who “opened Pandora’s box,” while Choi has disputed ownership of the tablet and Park has acknowledged inappropriate access but denies criminal intent.

Overall, Ko’s testimony and the materials he disclosed played a pivotal role in revealing Choi Soon-sil’s behind-the-scenes power over the presidency and catalyzing a major political and legal crisis in South Korea.

At the Cannes Lions festival, Michael Wolff, author of the bestseller Fire & Fury, predicted that President Donald Trump will soon be removed and that Vice President Mike Pence will become president — a change Wolff said would be disastrous for media because Pence is “the most boring person on Earth.” Wolff’s remarks and his book’s commercial success (over two million hard copies sold) figure prominently in the coverage.

Much of the document is a lengthy Rolling Stone-style profile and critical retrospective of Pence’s career and persona. Key points:

- Personal quirks and marriage: Pence’s relationship with his wife Karen has drawn attention for its old-fashioned tone. Multiple sources — including Democratic legislators who dined with the Pences in 2013 — say Pence calls her “Mother,” though his office denies it and no definitive documentary proof exists. The nickname has historical precedents among past presidents’ spouses.

- Political rise and style: Pence grew up in Indiana, embraced evangelical Christianity, worked in conservative media and think tanks, and built a steady conservative résumé in Congress before becoming governor of Indiana (2013–2017) and then vice president. He is described as disciplined, devout, and a relentless repeater of talking points; these traits made him a safe, reassuring vice-presidential pick for Trump.

- Controversial policy record as governor: The profile catalogs multiple instances where Pence advanced hardline social policies or made contentious decisions:
  - He endorsed and signed social-conservative measures (anti-gay marriage stances, efforts to defund Planned Parenthood, stringent anti-abortion laws).
  - His signing of Indiana’s Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) in 2015 sparked national backlash, economic threats, and damage to his political standing; his defensive TV performance deepened the crisis.
  - He authorized and later defended restrictive measures on refugees and resisted needle-exchange programs initially, actions tied to public-health crises (notably the Scott County HIV outbreak) that critics argue worsened outcomes.
  - He declined to apply for substantial federal pre-K funding and made other choices reflecting priorities of social conservatives over certain public programs.

- Governance criticisms and controversies: Reported problems include using campaign funds for personal expenses (in earlier campaigns), clumsy crisis response (East Chicago lead contamination), strained relations with unions (Carrier plant episode), and perceived inattention to minority and economically distressed communities in Indiana. Critics portray him as ideologically rigid, sometimes incompetent in crisis management, and prone to political calculation.

- National implications: The profile warns that Pence’s ideological consistency and influence on social issues could have far-reaching consequences if he attains greater power — for judicial appointments, abortion policy, LGBTQ rights, healthcare and related areas. At the same time, some of his temperament and demeanor (measured, pious, often perceived as dull) have been politically useful.

Overall tone: The document is highly critical, blending anecdote, reporting, and analysis to depict Pence as a socially conservative politician whose personal mannerisms (including the disputed “Mother” nickname) and policy record raise concern about the direction he might take if he becomes president. It also highlights Wolff’s prediction about Trump’s imminent removal and the media implications of a Pence presidency.

Former President George H.W. Bush, 92, and his wife Barbara Bush, 91, were both admitted to Houston Methodist Hospital. George H.W. Bush is in the intensive care unit being treated for an acute respiratory problem related to pneumonia; doctors performed a procedure to protect and clear his airway that required sedation. Hospital officials said he is stable, resting comfortably and will remain in the ICU for observation. Barbara Bush was admitted Wednesday as a precaution after fatigue and coughing.

Bush chief of staff Jean Becker had earlier confirmed his weekend admission and said he was “fine” and expected to return home in a few days. The story noted the former president’s recent health history—including Parkinson’s disease, prior hospitalizations for respiratory problems and a 2015 neck fracture from a fall—and that the couple had declined to attend President Trump’s inauguration for health and age reasons. President Barack Obama, speaking at his final news conference, sent the Bushes his “prayers and love,” calling them “as fine a couple as we know.” The situation was described as developing.

A Quinnipiac University national poll released July 2, 2014, finds deep public dissatisfaction with President Barack Obama and mixed views comparing recent presidents.

Key findings
- Worst president since WWII: 33% of voters name Barack Obama, 28% name George W. Bush. (Ronald Reagan was rated the best at 35%, followed by Bill Clinton 18% and John F. Kennedy 15%.)
- Comparing Obama to Bush: 40% say Obama has been worse than George W. Bush, 39% say he has been better, 20% say about the same. Views split sharply by party: 79% of Republicans say Obama is worse; 78% of Democrats say he is better.
- Romney hypothetical: 45% say the U.S. would be better off if Mitt Romney had won in 2012, while 38% say it would be worse. Republicans (84%) and independents (47%) largely favor the Romney hypothetical; Democrats (74%) say it would be worse.
- Job approval: Obama’s job approval stands at 40% approve / 53% disapprove, essentially unchanged since April. Partisan splits are large: Republicans 10/88 disapprove/approve; Democrats 79/13 approve/disapprove.
- Competence and attention: 54% say the Obama administration is not competent running government; 48% say he does not pay enough attention to what his administration is doing (47% say he does).
- Character and leadership: Voters are evenly split on honesty/trustworthiness (48/48) and nearly split on whether he cares about their needs (51/47 yes/no); he rates negatively on leadership qualities (47% yes / 51% no).
- Issue handling: Obama receives negative ratings on most major issues:
  - Economy: 40% approve / 55% disapprove
  - Foreign policy: 37% approve / 57% disapprove
  - Health care: 40% approve / 58% disapprove
  - Terrorism: 44% approve / 51% disapprove
  - Environment is the exception: 50% approve / 40% disapprove
- Economy sentiment: 35% of voters name the economy/jobs as the most important problem; 26% think the economy is getting better, 31% say worse, 43% say about the same. 37% say Obama has been better for the economy than Bush, 34% say worse.
- ACA support: 43% support the 2010 health care law, 55% oppose.

Methodology
- Survey of 1,446 registered voters conducted June 24–30, 2014; margin of error ±2.6 percentage points. Live telephone interviews of landlines and cell phones.

Overall takeaway
The poll shows substantial public dissatisfaction with Obama’s performance in mid-2014, large partisan polarization on every measure, eroding support among some demographic groups (notably older voters), and significant nostalgia or preference among many voters for prior Republican leadership—enough that a plurality say the country might have been better off under Mitt Romney.

E! News and Us Weekly reported that 18‑year‑old singer Demi Lovato and 36‑year‑old actor Ryan Phillippe were quietly seeing each other over the past few months in mid‑2011. Sources described their relationship as casual and “hot and heavy” for a time, but said it cooled after Phillippe’s ex‑girlfriend Alexis Knapp gave birth to a daughter in early July and as Lovato focused on promoting her new single “Skyscraper.” Representatives had not commented; one source close to Phillippe denied a relationship and called him “totally single.” Phillippe is a father to three children (one newborn whose paternity was unconfirmed at the time), and Lovato’s past relationships include Wilmer Valderrama, Joe Jonas and Trace Cyrus.

The document is a compilation of reviews and commentary about the post‑apocalyptic film The Book of Eli (directed by Albert and Allen Hughes, starring Denzel Washington, Mila Kunis, Gary Oldman, Jennifer Beals). It outlines the film’s premise, tone, performances, visuals and critical reception.

Key points:
- Premise: Denzel Washington plays Eli, a stoic, skilled wanderer traveling a ravaged, gray wasteland 30 years after a catastrophic war. He carries and protects a leather‑bound King James Bible that he believes was given to him by divine revelation and is determined to take it “west.” Gary Oldman plays Carnegie, a self‑styled tyrant who wants the book to consolidate power; Mila Kunis is Solara, Carnegie’s adopted daughter who joins Eli to escape her oppressive life.
- Tone and style: The movie is heavily stylized, moody and visually bleak—often compared to recent post‑apocalyptic films like The Road and Mad Max. Its look is likened to an extended music video or a film version of a graphic novel. Action is violent and sometimes cartoonish, with choreographed melee and gun battles.
- Themes: The film mixes biblical/religious themes with violent, survivalist storytelling. Critics note a strong didactic religious message layered over brutality, which some find dissonant and heavy‑handed.
- Performances: Washington’s presence and physicality are praised, though some critics find his restrained, monosyllabic performance emotionally limited. Oldman is cited as reveling in his villainy (often over‑the‑top). Kunis is regarded by some reviewers as miscast—too glamorous and not fully convincing in the role. Supporting performances (including Jennifer Beals, Michael Gambon, Frances de la Tour) are noted but generally seen as secondary.
- Criticism: Major complaints include a familiar, overused post‑apocalyptic aesthetic, ponderous pacing, a ponderous moral message, drab performances, and lack of emotional depth. Some critics feel it’s too brutal to be inspirational and too slow to be a satisfying action film. The film’s ending includes a twist that some find impactful.
- Positive notes: When focused on Eli alone, the film is deemed engaging—Washington’s physicality and the clash with Oldman’s Carnegie provide entertainment. The film’s stylized visuals and occasional strong action sequences earn approval from some reviewers.

Overall impression: The Book of Eli is visually striking and features compelling star power, but many critics found its religious messaging, familiar post‑apocalyptic imagery, uneven performances and heavy‑handed storytelling to undermine its emotional and cinematic impact.

In Fort Worth, Texas, two neighbors were found fatally shot outside a home on Buffalo Springs Drive early Sunday morning after an initial 4 a.m. call reporting a robbery. Police arrested 35-year-old Cary Joseph Heath the next day on a capital murder charge; he was taken into custody at Permenter Middle School in Cedar Hill, where he worked as an eighth-grade science teacher and was placed on administrative leave. Heath, a first-year teacher and former 13-year U.S. Air Force member, is held on $1 million bond. Neighbors reported hearing multiple shots and described the victims as longtime residents; police have not released the victims’ names or a motive. An earlier person detained for questioning was not arrested. The school district notified parents by automated call, though some said they had not been informed and expressed concern about a suspected killer working around children.

Sen. Scott Brown (R-Mass.) joked on Boston radio that he was "thankful" Democratic challenger Elizabeth Warren didn't "take her clothes off" to pay for college, a remark prompted by Warren’s debate reply that she borrowed and worked her way through a public university rather than posing nude. Brown, who once posed for Cosmopolitan in the 1980s to help pay for school, laughed about her comment and defended his own choices, saying he “did whatever I had to do” amid a difficult upbringing. The exchange revived criticism: the Massachusetts Democratic Party called Brown’s remarks “gutter campaigning” and demeaning to accomplished women. The story highlights the ongoing contest between Brown and a crowded Democratic field led by Warren, a Harvard Law professor who helped establish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

Jacob Hall, a 6-year-old student wounded in the Sept. 28 shooting at Townville Elementary School, died after three days on life support. His mother, Renae Hall, and family held a superhero-themed visitation and funeral at Oakdale Baptist Church to honor his love of heroes—especially the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles—and his desire to “save everybody.” Jacob was dressed in a Batman costume in his small blue casket; pallbearers and many mourners, including children, teachers and community members, wore superhero costumes or shirts. The service, open to the public, included appearances such as a Batmobile driven from West Virginia, Ninja Turtle decorations and a floral spray with action-figure heroes. The community also held a balloon release and organized a district-wide Superhero Day; schools observed a moment of silence. Prosecutors upgraded charges in the case after Jacob’s death: the 14-year-old suspect, who authorities say killed his father before driving to the school and opening fire, now faces two murder charges, three counts of attempted murder and weapon charges. Jacob’s family emphasized faith and forgiveness and urged others to care for one another in his memory.

The document critiques Donald Trump’s repeated claim during the 2015 campaign that the Obama administration planned to admit 200,000 Syrian refugees and that some might be ISIS operatives. Fact-checkers show the 200,000 figure is misleading: announcements by Secretary of State John Kerry referred to raising the total U.S. refugee ceiling (to 85,000 in 2016 and 100,000 in 2017), which could total 185,000 over two years, but that would be the total number of refugees from all countries, not Syrians. The Obama administration pledged to admit at least 10,000 Syrian refugees in the coming year. The fact-check piece gives Trump “Four Pinocchios” for using the 200,000 figure to describe Syrians and calls on reporters to challenge him.

The broader commentary condemns Trump’s pattern of repeating false, inflammatory claims—about refugees, Muslims allegedly celebrating 9/11, and crime statistics about African Americans—and warns that such lies stoke fear, prejudice and intolerance. It compares Trump to historical demagogues, criticizes media practices that give him unfettered airtime, and argues that ignoring or soft-pedaling his behavior has allowed his influence to grow. The editorial urges journalists and political leaders to confront and fact-check him rather than remain silent, asserting that holding such a figure accountable is necessary to counter the dangers of demagoguery.

Burger King is replacing its 40-year-old slogan "Have It Your Way" with a new, more personal tagline: "Be Your Way." The chain will roll out the line across U.S. marketing, including a TV spot beginning Monday and earlier online video placements. The company says the motto emphasizes self-expression and lifestyle—encouraging people to live how they want—rather than the old slogan’s focus on just customizing purchases. Fernando Machado, SVP of global brand management, framed the change as part of shifting Burger King from a functional to a stronger emotional brand appeal; the new tagline was developed with ad agency DAVID (WPP). BK plans to phase out its recent "Taste Is King" line as well and eventually introduce "Be Your Way" globally. The rebranding comes amid broader management, marketing and menu changes since 3G Capital’s 2010 buyout and the company’s public relisting, and as Burger King and other legacy fast-food chains work to boost sales against consumer moves toward fresher, higher-quality foods. Some branding experts caution such efforts can seem forced and may not align with consumers’ perceptions of the chain.

Former LAPD officer Christopher (Chris) Dorner, 33, remains at large more than 24 hours after a deadly shooting spree that triggered a massive manhunt across Southern California. Authorities say they do not know his whereabouts after finding his burned pickup truck on a remote Big Bear Mountain road; footprints in the snow led into woods but the trail went cold. Law enforcement has searched cabins and surrounding terrain, deployed hundreds of officers and SWAT personnel, and temporarily grounded helicopters because of weather.

Dorner, a Navy reservist and former LAPD officer (2006–2008), is accused of killing at least three people — including Monica Quan, 28, and her fiancé Keith Lawrence, 27 — and wounding others during a campaign he framed as revenge for his 2008 firing. His lengthy online “manifesto” rails against the LAPD, names about a dozen people and their families as targets, and threatens “unconventional and asymmetrical warfare” using his insider knowledge of police tactics. Authorities are concerned he may be heavily armed with high-powered weapons (reports mentioned a .50-caliber rifle) and could use tactical knowledge to evade capture.

Timeline highlights:
- Police linked Dorner to the deaths of Quan and Lawrence found in Irvine; investigators say he targeted Quan because of a grievance against her father, retired LAPD Capt. Randy Quan, who represented Dorner at his disciplinary hearing.
- After an aborted attempt to hijack a yacht in San Diego, officers later spotted and exchanged gunfire with Dorner in Riverside; he allegedly then shot at a patrol car at a red light, killing one officer and injuring another.
- Dorner’s wallet and an LAPD badge were recovered in San Diego; a burned truck believed to be his was found in Big Bear Lake, prompting lockdowns of businesses, schools and resort areas there.

Background and motive:
- Dorner’s manifesto and personnel records describe long-standing grievances after being fired for lying about a partner’s alleged misconduct during an arrest. He appealed the termination unsuccessfully and, according to investigators, vowed revenge.
- Colleagues and acquaintances paint a mixed picture: a capable marksman and former college athlete who displayed anger and difficulty with authority, but who was not previously seen as violent by many who knew him.
- Police caution the public and say they are mindful Dorner’s training and combat experience could make him dangerous and hard to find.

Authorities continue sweeping searches, guarding named potential targets, and urging caution as the manhunt proceeds.

Marine experts near Sydney performed a first-of-its-kind rescue to save a critically endangered grey nurse shark that was being strangled by an elastic cord tightly wrapped around its gills. Spotted off Magic Point—the species’ critical habitat—divers and a SeaLife veterinarian used a large clear-plastic “shark sock” to corral the distressed animal (the sock’s transparency also drew in other sharks). The team then wrestled the injured shark into a special stretcher and brought it to the surface, where vet Rob Jones cut away the cord and administered antibiotics to prevent infection. Jones said the elastic would have continued to cut deeper and almost certainly killed the shark if not removed. The shark swam away after treatment; officials expect the wound to heal in about a month. With only roughly 1,500 grey nurse sharks remaining off Australia, the intervention is an important conservation success.

President Obama has signed a law authorizing the Congressional Gold Medal for more than 6,000 Nisei veterans — Japanese Americans born to immigrant parents — who served the United States in World War II while many of their families were held in internment camps. The award will honor members of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, the 100th Infantry Battalion, and translators and interrogators of the Military Intelligence Service.

The 442nd, formed largely of Nisei volunteers, became one of the most decorated units in U.S. military history for its combat in Italy and France, including the famous rescue of the “Lost Battalion.” Many volunteers enlisted to prove their loyalty despite being classified initially as “enemy aliens” and facing discrimination and segregated training. The regiment suffered heavy casualties; some companies were reduced from about 200 men to only a handful by war’s end.

Survivors, including veterans from the Pacific Northwest such as Art and Akira (Ike) Iwasaki and Kenji Yaguchi, describe difficult training, the pride of service, and postwar return to civilian life as farmers, chiropractors, and other professions. Supporters, including Sen. Daniel Akaka, framed the recognition as both a tribute to the veterans’ sacrifice and a step toward a more tolerant and just nation. The Congressional Gold Medal ranks among the highest civilian honors in the United States.

University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) construction and expansion plans have been complicated by discoveries of large numbers of unmarked graves on its 164‑acre campus, the site of Mississippi’s first mental institution, the State Lunatic (Insane) Asylum, established in 1855. Ground‑penetrating radar and construction work since 2012 have exposed dozens of coffins and located caches of graves; recent testing revealed roughly 1,000 coffins in one area and researchers estimate as many as 2,000–7,000 burials across about 20 acres. The remains are believed to be former asylum patients who died between the 19th and early 20th centuries, though other cemetery areas on “Asylum Hill” may hold paupers, M.B. church members, TB victims, former slaves and possibly Civil War dead.

UMMC had planned a parking garage and other facilities (including an American Cancer Society Hope Lodge and a Children’s Justice Center) on land now shown to contain burials; officials say development and future expansion may need to be relocated. Exhuming and reburying remains privately would cost roughly $3,000 per body (potentially up to $21 million). UMMC is studying alternatives including handling exhumations in‑house over years (estimated $400,000 annually) and creating a memorial/visitors center with an on‑site lab to preserve remains and allow research.

An Asylum Hill Research Consortium of anthropologists, archaeologists and historians is coordinating study of the remains. Preliminary analyses of previously recovered burials have yielded insights into health and nutrition (e.g., tooth enamel defects, pellagra, oral microbiomes). Advocates hope to collect DNA to help identify descendants; researchers plan an online registry of asylum patients. The discoveries have also prompted calls for respectful treatment and preservation of historic features on the hill, including Civil War earthworks.

Arron (Arron/Aaron spelled variably in reports) Hughes, a 28-year-old forklift driver from Ruthin, North Wales, has reportedly become the first person to survive swimming across the Hoover Dam reservoir. While on a stag party in Las Vegas on August 8, Hughes — who says he was on a 37-hour bender — jumped into the Colorado River below the 726 ft (221 m) dam to cool off and swam from Arizona to Nevada and back. The swim took about 30 minutes; he kept his trainers on and said the water was pulling him toward the dam.

Hughes and police later said he survived largely because most hydroelectric turbines were off at the time — authorities noted nine of the ten turbines were not operating — and that had they been running he likely would not have made it. When he climbed out the police were waiting, arrested him, and fined him (around $330/£250) for “jumping, diving, swimming from dam’s spillways or other structures.” Hughes says Guinness contacted him but could not recognize the feat without an adjudicator present, and he won’t attempt it again.

He described the stunt as drink-fuelled and admitted it was risky; friends praised him, his mother disapproved, and authorities cautioned it was dangerous — 275 people have died at the site in the past decade.

New England Patriots receiver Julian Edelman reported a school threat he spotted in his Instagram comments while visiting former teammate Danny Amendola in Texas. A direct message alerted him that a user had posted that they intended to "shoot up a school." Concerned—especially in the wake of the Parkland massacre and as a parent—Edelman notified authorities. Port Huron, Michigan, police investigated, located a 14‑year‑old who admitted making the comment aimed at Central Middle School, and found two rifles at the home that belonged to the boy’s grandfather. The youth was arrested and charged with making a false report of a terrorist threat (a four‑year felony) and is being held at the Macomb County Juvenile Justice Center.

Starbucks announced it will move production of its Ethos bottled water out of California to Pennsylvania over the next six months, citing the state's historic drought and a desire to help conserve local water. The company said it is seeking a new West Coast water source and that its California stores will cut water use by more than 25 percent. Starbucks framed the decision as part of its global responsibility efforts; Ethos proceeds have funded more than $12 million in water and sanitation grants since Starbucks bought the brand in 2005 (Starbucks donates five cents per bottle).

Reporting has focused on Ethos’s California supply chain: Ethos bottles for the Western U.S. are produced at a Merced facility using spring water sourced from Baxter and groundwater that regulators classify as being in “exceptional drought.” Critics and residents have raised concerns that private bottlers draw scarce groundwater for profit while local communities face steep water cuts. California’s groundwater extraction rules are often opaque—well logs can be confidential—and local permitting changes in Merced County may affect bottlers in the future. Although bottled water is a small share of statewide use, public protests over bottled-water extraction have increased as the drought continues into a fourth year and the state enforces mandatory urban water reductions.

Key facts about melanoma and skin cancer
- Melanoma is less than 2% of all skin cancers but causes the majority of skin-cancer deaths. U.S. estimates: roughly 74,000 new melanoma cases and about 10,000 deaths in 2015–2016. Lifetime melanoma risk varies by race (roughly 1 in 40 for whites, 1 in 1,000 for blacks, 1 in 200 for Hispanics) and increases with age, though it also affects younger people.
- Total body mole (naevus) count is an important melanoma risk marker: each additional mole is estimated to raise melanoma risk by about 2–4%. However, only 20–40% of melanomas arise from pre-existing moles.

Study: using an arm mole count as a quick proxy for total-body count
- Researchers at King’s College London (TwinsUK cohort) studied 3,594 female Caucasian twins (1995–2003), counting moles at 17 body sites and recording skin type, hair/eye color and freckles. They replicated findings in an independent case-control sample including men and women.
- The number of moles on the right arm was the single best predictor of total body mole count. Specific thresholds: >7 moles on the right arm made women nine times more likely to have >50 moles on the whole body; ≥11 moles on an arm predicted a higher likelihood of >100 total moles—levels associated with substantially increased melanoma risk.
- Other predictive sites: area above the right elbow and the legs; in men the back was also strongly predictive.
- Implication: counting moles on an easily accessible body site (arm) could allow GPs to rapidly estimate total mole burden and identify patients who may need closer monitoring.

Caveats and context
- Counting arm moles is a practical, time-saving screening aid but is not the sole determinant of risk. Genetic factors, mole atypia (dysplastic nevi), UV exposure, fair skin, family history, and mole appearance remain crucial for assessing melanoma risk.
- The study’s strengths include a large, unbiased healthy Caucasian sample and external replication; applicability to non-Caucasian populations was not addressed.

Nelson Mandela’s daughters Makaziwe and Zenani Mandela, backed by several grandchildren, have filed papers in the Johannesburg High Court seeking removal of advocate George Bizos, businessman Tokyo Sexwale and lawyer Bally Chuene as directors of two companies, Harmonieux Investment Holdings and Magnifique Investment Holdings. The companies were reportedly created by Mandela’s former lawyer Ismail Ayob to receive and hold proceeds from sales of Mandela’s handprints—funds the family estimates at more than R15 million (about $1.7 million).

The sisters allege Bizos, Sexwale and Chuene were never properly appointed by the shareholder (Nelson Mandela) by formal resolution, were invited to resign and refused, and in some instances acted without the support of most family beneficiaries. The court papers also accuse the three of failing to perform director duties with due care and, particularly in Chuene’s case, of unlawfully registering himself as a director on company records. Makaziwe’s affidavit recounts prior demands for resignations and alleges instances of misleading conduct and improper appointments linked to other companies and trusts.

Bizos and Sexwale deny the claims. Bizos said the appointments were made at Mandela’s wish and called the allegations baseless and motivated by a desire “to get their hands on the money.” Chuene said he would comment after seeing the documents. Mandela family members including Zindzi and several grandchildren filed supporting affidavits. The Nelson Mandela Foundation said it was not aware of the court application. The dispute forms part of a longer-running controversy over who holds rights to sell Mandela’s handprints.

Federal lawsuits tied to former Michigan State and USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar remain in mediation, and attorneys for most parties have asked a federal judge to extend the court-ordered 90-day mediation by 30 days to Dec. 6. Since public allegations began in 2016, at least 140 women and girls have sued over Nassar’s alleged sexual assaults (more than 120 have reported him to police), and dozens have said they raised concerns about him as far back as the 1990s.

Nassar worked for decades at Michigan State University and as USA Gymnastics’ national team physician. He has pleaded guilty to federal child-pornography charges and faces sentencing in December, along with numerous state sexual-assault charges; convictions there could carry life sentences. High-profile gymnasts including Aly Raisman, McKayla Maroney and Jamie Dantzscher have publicly said Nassar abused them; Raisman detailed her abuse in a 60 Minutes interview and an upcoming memoir.

The litigation has produced steep legal bills for MSU: as of Oct. 3, outside counsel had billed the university roughly $4.17 million (6,812 hours), with major invoices from firms including Skadden and Latham & Watkins. Mediation is overseen by Jon Muth, who reported “substantial progress” but said significant work remains. USA Gymnastics has not yet taken a public position on the requested extension.

The scandal prompted leadership changes and reforms at USA Gymnastics: CEO Steve Penny resigned; Kerry Perry has been named incoming CEO; an independent review by former prosecutor Deborah Daniels urged cultural change and made 70 recommendations, all adopted, and the U.S. Center for SafeSport has been created to handle misconduct allegations.

Mary Anne Forster, an assistant principal from Williamstown north of Adelaide, was seriously injured when a koala attacked while she was walking her two dogs about two weeks ago. The dogs pulled her toward a koala at the base of a tree; the animal bit and latched onto her leg so firmly that she had to pry its jaws open with her fingers to free herself. She hobbled more than 2 km home and was taken to hospital, where she required 12 stitches and a four-day stay for treatment of infection and swelling. Forster does not blame the koala. Authorities warn people to keep dogs away from wild koalas—whose sharp teeth and claws can inflict deep wounds—and note that koalas will defend themselves when threatened.

Court filings released from Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou’s bail hearing in Vancouver provide new detail on her ties to Canada and hint at her likely defence against U.S. extradition and fraud charges.

Key facts and Vancouver ties
- Meng was arrested in Vancouver on Dec. 1 at the request of U.S. authorities, who seek her extradition on allegations she committed bank fraud by misleading lenders about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, an entity accused of doing business in Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions.
- Affidavits from Meng and her husband show the family owns two Vancouver properties (4005 West 28th Ave., bought 2009; 1603 Matthews St., bought 2016), valued in 2017 at roughly $5.6M and $16.3M respectively. Meng says she would live at the 28th Avenue home if released; family members would move to Vancouver and the homes’ equity is offered as bail collateral.
- The filings emphasize a 15-year connection to Vancouver: two children attended school there (2009–2012), her husband completed a master’s degree there, and the family has spent summers in the city. Meng also cites health concerns (hypertension) while detained.

Suggested legal strategy and defence points
- The U.S. allegations, summarized in the filings, assert Huawei “effectively controlled” Skycom until about 2014 and that Meng personally misrepresented Huawei’s relationship with Skycom—citing a Sept. 3, 2013 PowerPoint presentation in which Meng used “I” when describing compliance oversight.
- Meng’s submissions and Huawei affidavits stress that the presentation was prepared by others, that the slides emphasize Huawei’s compliance efforts, and that there is no direct evidence Meng knew of any sanctions violations. They underline Huawei’s documented compliance measures (KPMG report cited in Huawei’s 2017 annual report) and prior dealings with U.S. regulators.
- Bryan Harrison, Huawei’s U.S. lawyer, details interactions with the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Office of Export Enforcement (OEE) from 2010–2016, noting an OEE finding of no violations in 2014, regular meetings with U.S. officials on compliance, and use of U.S.-based auditors. Harrison also notes no U.S. indictments against Huawei itself and no lawsuits by the banks allegedly defrauded.

Bail proceedings and positions
- Meng’s defence argues she is not a flight risk because of her long Vancouver ties, family obligations, and reputational reasons not to flee. She says she is innocent and will contest charges if extradited.
- Crown prosecutors counter that Meng has limited meaningful ties to the jurisdiction, vast resources, and is a citizen of a country (China) without an extradition treaty with the U.S., making flight a concern.
- Bail hearings are ongoing; Meng is due back in B.C. Supreme Court.

Wider context and reactions
- The arrest has prompted strong diplomatic reaction from China, which summoned the U.S. ambassador to protest and warned Canada of consequences if Meng is not released. China demanded the U.S. withdraw its arrest warrant.
- Reuters reporting and U.S. officials link the probe to allegations that Skycom moved more than $100 million of transactions through the U.S. between 2010 and 2014. HSBC has been identified as one bank involved.
- The case has heightened U.S.–China tensions and renewed calls in the U.S. for tougher measures on Chinese telecom firms.

Overall, the documents reinforce Meng’s asserted personal and family connections to Vancouver, outline Huawei’s planned factual and legal defenses (emphasizing lack of personal knowledge and robust compliance efforts), and frame the key factual dispute as whether Meng knew of or participated in any unlawful conduct related to Skycom and Iran.

Nine-year-old Carlie Marie Trent was abducted from her Rogersville, Tennessee elementary school on May 4, 2016, after her uncle by marriage, 57-year-old Gary Simpson, signed her out using a false claim that her father had been in an accident. An Amber Alert remains active in Tennessee; law enforcement says Carlie is believed to be in imminent danger.

Simpson was last seen driving a white 2002 Dodge conversion van (Tennessee plate 173GPS). Surveillance footage shows him visiting a Rogersville-area Walmart and a Save-A-Lot shortly before and after picking Carlie up. Investigators say he purchased numerous items consistent with taking the child to a remote location: girls’ underwear, a child-sized nightgown, a bikini, a pink/purple plush throw blanket, a pink folding camp chair, girls’ khaki pants, men’s clothing, lipstick and nail polish, and nonperishable food. Authorities suspect the pair may be in an isolated campground or rural property and have canvassed state parks and private campgrounds in several states.

The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) is handling the investigation, working tips from across many states and has sifted through over 1,200 leads. The TBI and local officials emphasize this was not an “innocent camping trip” and urge the public to treat the case seriously. Descriptions: Carlie — 4'8", 75 lbs., blonde hair, blue eyes; Simpson — about 5'10", 157 lbs., balding, brown hair and eyes. The U.S. Marshals and private individuals (two banking executives and Carlie’s pediatrician) have offered rewards totaling at least $25,000 for information. A Missouri Amber Alert for a reported sighting was later canceled.

Anyone with information should call the TBI at 1-800-TBI-FIND (1-800-824-3463), the Rogersville Police Department at (423) 272-7555, or dial 911 if they see the vehicle.

The Supreme Court, in a 5–4 order Tuesday night, temporarily blocked a lower court’s decision that had invalidated two Texas congressional districts and several state House districts in four counties as racially discriminatory. By freezing that ruling pending appeal, the Court allowed the current Texas electoral maps to remain in place for now — likely meaning the disputed districts will be used in the 2018 midterms.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton had urged the stay, arguing the state could not redraw maps in time before the October 1 deadline. The Court issued a one-paragraph stay without explanation; the four liberal justices (Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan) said they would have denied it. Observers noted the narrow split highlights the influence of Justice Neil Gorsuch, whose addition prevents a likely 4–4 tie.

Civil‑rights lawyers who represent the challengers called the ruling disappointing and “inexplicable.” Lower federal courts had recently found multiple Texas voting practices — including district lines, voter ID rules, and assistance restrictions for non‑English speakers — had discriminated against Black and Hispanic voters, and had even ordered a special legislative session to redraw lines. Paxton appealed to the Supreme Court, saying redrawing now would be futile if the high court ultimately upholds the maps. The stay preserves the status quo while the Supreme Court considers the case.

A Boston-area man, 27-year-old Daniel Morley of Topsfield, Massachusetts, was arrested June 9 after family members called police following an alleged domestic assault and threats to burn down the residence. A subsequent search of his room uncovered a large stainless-steel pressure cooker, bomb-making materials (black powder, igniters), shrapnel components including ball bearings, a loaded assault rifle and handgun, several hundred rounds of ammunition, dismantled cell phones, flex-cuffs, a shoebox with a decapitated bird’s head, a burned and stabbed stuffed animal, and other suspicious items. Police say the pressure cooker was ultimately found to be non-explosive.

An unsealed 25-page affidavit states Morley told his mother he had possessed the pressure cooker and related materials before the April 15 Boston Marathon bombings. He also allegedly threatened to hijack an airplane or ship and mentioned that a close friend had boasted of knowing Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the suspects in the Marathon attack. The FBI Joint Terrorism Task Force is investigating Morley to determine whether others influenced him or any links exist to the Marathon bombings; investigators have drawn no conclusions.

Morley is charged with communicating a bomb scare, threatening arson, and two counts of domestic assault and battery; additional charges may follow. He apologized after his arrest for not taking unspecified medications and is undergoing psychiatric evaluation at Bridgewater State Hospital. His next court appearance is scheduled at Ipswich District Court. Prosecutors and the FBI declined to comment.

The Nunes memo, produced by staff for House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes (R‑Calif.), alleges serious abuses by the Department of Justice (DOJ) and FBI in their use of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) during the 2016 campaign—most prominently in applications to surveil former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page. The memo, which the White House cleared for public release over DOJ and intelligence community objections, claims the FBI and DOJ omitted material facts and relied on tainted or uncorroborated information when seeking an initial FISA order (Oct. 21, 2016) and subsequent renewals.

Key claims in the memo:
- The Steele dossier, compiled by ex‑British intelligence officer Christopher Steele and funded via Fusion GPS and the DNC/Hillary Clinton campaign, was a central component of the Carter Page FISA application. The memo says the application failed to disclose the dossier’s political origins and the role of Fusion GPS/Perkins Coie in paying for Steele’s work.
- The application cited a September 2016 Yahoo News article as independent corroboration, but the memo asserts that article relied on information Steele himself had leaked; Steele had admitted meeting with Yahoo and other outlets. The memo contends the FBI misrepresented Steele’s media contacts and reliability to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC).
- Steele had been suspended and then terminated as an FBI source for unauthorized media disclosures; the memo says the FBI concealed this and other concerns about Steele’s reliability, including his admitted anti‑Trump bias recorded by DOJ official Bruce Ohr.
- Bruce Ohr’s contacts with Steele and Fusion GPS (and Ohr’s wife’s paid work for Fusion GPS) were known within DOJ but not disclosed to the FISC, the memo alleges.
- An internal FBI source‑validation later found Steele’s reporting only minimally corroborated, yet the application relied heavily on his material; Deputy Director Andrew McCabe reportedly testified that the Steele dossier was necessary to obtain the surveillance order.
- The memo raises questions about references in the Page application to other campaign figures (e.g., George Papadopoulos) and notes personnel issues—most notably FBI agent Peter Strzok and FBI attorney Lisa Page—whose anti‑Trump text messages and otherwise improper conduct the memo portrays as evidence of institutional bias and leaks, including discussions of an “insurance” plan against a Trump presidency.

The White House letter accompanying the declassification indicates the President directed a review and, balancing public interest and national security considerations, authorized public release. The FBI and DOJ had strongly opposed release, saying the memo omitted critical facts; the FBI warned it was “gravely concerned” about missing information. The memo frames its findings as raising serious questions about the legitimacy of DOJ/FBI interactions with the FISC and possible breakdowns in processes intended to protect Americans from FISA abuses.

Comedian Arsenio Hall has filed a $5 million defamation lawsuit against singer Sinead O’Connor after she posted a Facebook rant accusing him of supplying Prince with hard drugs "over the decades" and of spiking her years ago. Hall’s lawyers say the accusations are false, that he has not supplied Prince with illegal drugs, and that he hasn’t had contact with O’Connor in 25 years. The complaint labels O’Connor a “desperate attention-seeker” known for inflammatory media posts and seeks at least $5 million in damages.

Martin Tripp, a former process technician at Tesla’s Gigafactory in Nevada, has filed a federal counterclaim against Tesla and CEO Elon Musk after the company sued him in June for allegedly hacking its manufacturing operating system (MOS), stealing confidential data, and exaggerating defects to the media.

Key allegations from Tripp’s filing
- Waste and safety concerns: Tripp says he repeatedly raised concerns about large quantities of waste and scrap parts at the Gigafactory, reuse of discarded battery parts, and punctured battery cells being reworked (e.g., glued) and returned to production without proper inspection. He claims Tesla’s MOS logged $150M–$200M in scrapped battery-module parts between January and mid‑May 2018.
- Traceability failures: He alleges Tesla discontinued systems that tracked parts, leaving traceability unknown for many components.
- Internal warnings ignored: Tripp says he alerted supervisors and emailed Musk with charts before Musk’s visit; he claims colleagues asked him to hide scrap before the visit.
- Denial of hacking and coding: Tripp denies Tesla’s claims that he hacked the MOS, wrote programs, accessed multiple computers, or stole gigabytes of data. He says he doesn’t know how to code.
- Retaliation, defamation, and safety threats: Tripp contends Tesla launched a defamatory smear campaign—publicly labeling him a “saboteur”—and published false allegations that a “friend” warned Tripp might return to “shoot up” the Gigafactory. Law enforcement found no credible threat; Tripp denies violent intent. He says Tesla declined to identify the caller and that he’s received threats and been followed since the accusations.

Procedural context and requested relief
- Background: Tesla’s initial suit accused Tripp of hacking and leaking information about punctured cells and excess scrap. Musk emailed staff calling the matter “sabotage,” and later publicly questioned a reporter who received information from Tripp.
- Counterclaim: Filed in Nevada, Tripp seeks at least $1 million plus punitive damages, alleging defamation, invasion of privacy, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. He and his attorneys assert Tesla acted negligently or maliciously in publicizing the shooting allegation and other statements.
- Additional notes: Tripp has hired lawyers and reportedly prepared a whistleblower complaint for the SEC. Tesla has denied Tripp’s factual claims and said damaged batteries did not enter vehicles. Tesla did not comment on the counterclaim in these reports.

Broader context
- The dispute arrives during a critical production ramp for Tesla’s Model 3, when the company faces investor pressure and questions about cash needs and manufacturing practices. The case has drawn attention both for the safety and quality claims Tripp raises and for the aggressive public posture taken by Tesla and Musk.

Augustus “Gus” Lee, a 20-year-old redshirt freshman defensive back for the University of Richmond and a 2017 graduate of Paul VI Catholic High School, was found dead in his snow-covered car near the Richmond campus in the early hours of Dec. 11. The Virginia medical examiner ruled his death a suicide by asphyxiation. Lee’s family will donate his brain to the VA–Boston University–Concussion Legacy Foundation Brain Bank, which researchers use to study traumatic brain injury and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE); his mother said concerns about possible brain injury from contact sports influenced that decision.

Lee was a multi-sport athlete in high school (football, lacrosse, track) and had a concussion history, including being knocked unconscious in middle school lacrosse. At Richmond he walked on to the football team, switched from wide receiver to defensive back, earned special teams playing time, was spring-game defensive MVP, and appeared in all 11 games this season. Teammates and coaches recalled him as driven, team-oriented and athletic.

During the season he experienced illness and later struggled emotionally: midseason bronchitis, increasing homesickness, fatigue, reduced appetite, and after Thanksgiving he called home upset and sought help from a mental health professional who arranged a neurological screening over winter break. He returned to campus to finish finals; his parents were expecting him home after his last exams Dec. 10. When his roommate couldn’t find him the following day, police located him in his car shortly after midnight.

Lee is survived by his parents, Phyllis and Chris, and siblings Gillian and Jackson. The family plans a funeral at Church of the Holy Comforter in Vienna. University and teammates expressed deep sorrow and praised his character; the brain donation was welcomed by Concussion Legacy Foundation officials as valuable for research.
