Police in multiple U.S. cities moved in overnight at the end of November 2011 to clear long-running Occupy encampments. In Philadelphia, authorities began dismantling the Occupy Philadelphia camp at Dilworth Plaza after a city-imposed deadline passed. The eviction started around 1 a.m.; crews used heavy equipment to remove debris and wash the plaza. Mayor Michael Nutter and Police Commissioner Charles Ramsey praised the operation as well planned. Officers gave multiple warnings; many protesters left but others marched through Center City for hours in a tense, roaming procession that repeatedly crashed through barricades while police followed. Mounted units and bicycle officers were used; a woman was injured when a police horse stepped on her foot and three officers suffered minor injuries. Police ultimately arrested 52 people on charges including failure to disperse and obstruction. Outreach workers said dozens of formerly homeless people from the camp were placed into services.

In Los Angeles, a large LAPD deployment—more than 1,000 officers staged for hours—cleared the two-month encampment outside City Hall early that morning as well. Helicopters, buses of officers, bomb-sniffing dogs and tactical teams were used; police declared unlawful assembly and made hundreds of arrests (reports say more than 200). Officers dismantled tents, removed tree-sitters (including people in treehouses), used zip-tie restraints and loaded arrestees onto buses. Authorities said the operation was planned for early hours to minimize disruption and that searches turned up no weapons; police described most arrests as peaceful, while protesters documented encounters and accused officers of occasional rough tactics. City officials cited public-safety, sanitation and planned construction as reasons for ending the encampments.

Across both cities the evictions marked a major turning point in the local phases of the Occupy movement: camps that had been centers of protest and services for weeks were dismantled, protesters vowed to continue activism even if displaced, and cities sought to balance free-speech concerns with public health, safety and redevelopment plans.

Robin Thicke publicly reacted to his separation from wife Paula Patton during a string of appearances and a concert in late February. At a Fairfax, VA show he emotionally announced to the crowd that he and Patton had separated but that he’s “trying to get [his] girl back,” dedicated the song “Lost Without U” (which he said is her favorite) to her, and visibly struggled with emotion onstage. He reportedly wore his wedding ring during the performance and later told a photographer in Washington, D.C. he’s “just trying to get her back.” Media accounts say Thicke made attempts to reconcile—flying to Canada where Patton was working—but the couple issued a joint statement saying they had mutually decided to separate. Sources connected the split in part to fans’ and insiders’ reactions to Thicke’s controversial VMAs performance with Miley Cyrus, which allegedly upset Patton. Around the same time lavish floral arrangements appeared at Patton’s home—widely presumed to be from Thicke—and Patton, her mother and assistant, and the couple’s 3-year-old son Julian were involved in a minor, non-injury car accident on Sunset Boulevard.

This document collects articles and commentary about psychedelics—especially microdosing—and the legal and research barriers that limit scientific study and therapeutic use.

Key points

- Microdosing: Some people (like Martijn Schirp) regularly take very small doses of LSD or psilocybin to boost mood, creativity, focus and mindfulness without full psychedelic hallucinations. Advocates report subtle benefits such as improved flow, better relationships, healthier habits and relief from depression or anxiety, but these reports are anecdotal.

- Lack of evidence and placebo risk: Researchers (e.g., Matt Johnson at Johns Hopkins) note there are no rigorous clinical trials proving microdosing’s benefits. Reported effects are subtle—comparable to coffee—and therefore particularly vulnerable to placebo effects. Double‑blind trials would be needed to demonstrate real effects.

- Safety and dosing uncertainties: Microdoses are tiny (e.g., ~10 micrograms of LSD) and difficult to measure reliably outside a lab. Street-obtained LSD may be impure or inaccurately dosed. Individual responses vary widely; occasional microdoses can still be overwhelming for some users. Frequent use every few days may carry unknown long‑term risks because it repeatedly alters serotonin-system functioning.

- Historical and regulatory barriers to research: Drug laws from the 1960s–1980s and UN treaties have restricted research on cannabis, MDMA and psychedelics. Scientists including David Nutt argue these restrictions have impeded study of therapeutic uses and basic neuroscience (e.g., 5-HT2A receptor effects and consciousness). Legal hurdles, funding limits and the high cost or scarcity of pharmaceutical-grade compounds make research difficult.

- Renewed interest and advocacy: Despite the bans, some clinical work and state-level marijuana legalization are shifting the landscape. Advocates and some researchers call for regulatory reform to enable controlled studies into therapeutic potential (e.g., PTSD, alcoholism, depression) and safer, standard dosing.

- Popular discourse and cultural notes: Media and online creators (e.g., PsychedSubstance) emphasize LSD’s non‑toxicity, historical use by figures like Albert Hofmann and anecdotal links to creativity (Steve Jobs, Francis Crick). They argue stigma and law have delayed exploration of potential benefits.

Overall takeaway: Microdosing and other psychedelic therapies have generated anecdotal enthusiasm and plausible biological mechanisms, but rigorous, controlled research is still limited by legal, logistical and methodological barriers. Claims of benefit remain unproven, and safety—especially with repeated microdosing and illicit supply—remains uncertain.

John Heath, 68, of Bridgewater, pleaded not guilty Tuesday in Danbury Superior Court to the 1984 murder of his wife, Elizabeth Gough Heath, whose remains were found in 2010 in a well/cistern beneath a barn on their former Newtown property. He is held on $1 million bond and was ordered to surrender his passport; he appeared in court using oxygen.

Elizabeth, 30 at the time, was reported missing by John on April 6, 1984. He initially told police she had left with $600; friends said he later told them she left with nothing. Her remains were discovered in April 2010 during barn renovations wrapped in bedding and placed head‑first in the hole; the medical examiner ruled her death a homicide from multiple blows to the head, with a broken arm consistent with a defensive wound.

Investigators developed an arrest warrant after a tip about a moving truck at Heath’s home and located him on Hannibal Road. The 30‑page arrest affidavit compiles years of interviews and circumstantial evidence — including inconsistent statements by Heath, remarks by acquaintances about the barn cistern, and suspicions expressed by family and neighbors — but police say environmental degradation over decades limited recoverable forensic evidence. A special public defender will be appointed; a probable cause hearing is tentatively set for June 19.

Hope Hicks, who served as White House communications director during the early Trump administration and resigned in February amid the Russia investigations, has been named executive vice president and chief communications officer for the soon-to-be independent Fox (the “New Fox” that will remain after Disney’s $71.3 billion acquisition of many 21st Century Fox entertainment assets). Her appointment will take effect when the Disney deal closes and the company is rebranded; she will be based in Los Angeles and report to Viet Dinh, Fox’s chief legal and policy officer.

Also joining New Fox is Danny O’Brien as executive vice president and head of government relations; he previously led government relations for GE Transportation and has extensive Capitol Hill experience, including service as chief of staff to Senators Joe Biden, Robert Menendez and Robert Torricelli.

Hicks succeeds Julie Henderson, who — along with other communications executives — is not moving to the new entity. The New Fox will focus on broadcast TV, Fox News and Fox Sports; Disney is acquiring film- and entertainment-focused assets like 20th Century Fox and FX.

Hicks’s hiring drew attention because of her close ties to President Trump (she was a campaign press secretary and long-time aide) and because of ongoing perceptions of a close relationship between the Trump White House and Fox. Supporters, including White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders, praised the move; critics, including Media Matters, argued it further aligns Fox with the Trump communications apparatus.

Francesca Matus, 52, a Canadian who spends winters in Belize, and her American boyfriend Drew (Drew DeVoursney/Devoursney), 36, were found dead on May 1, 2017 in Chan Chen Village, Corozal District, Belize. The couple had been reported missing after last being seen leaving a bar in Corozal on April 25; Matus was due to fly to Canada and DeVoursney to return to the U.S. A friend, Joseph Milholen, who was to drive Matus to the airport, discovered they were gone and alerted authorities. Their white Isuzu Rodeo was located abandoned in a sugarcane field near Paraiso on April 30, and search parties—including police and volunteers—continued the area. Local reports say the bodies were found by a search party around 5 p.m.; Belize police later stated the deaths are being investigated as homicides and U.S. consular officials have been notified. Some accounts say the pair were found with duct tape on their wrists, though official details and cause of death had not been released at the time of reporting. Canadian and U.S. consular services were involved and family and friends expressed shock and grief.

JPMorgan Chase disclosed at least $2 billion in trading losses from a complex hedging strategy run by its Chief Investment Office; CEO Jamie Dimon said losses could rise by $1 billion or more and might continue to accrue through the year. The positions centered on obscure Markit CDX corporate credit-default-swap indexes—notably the CDX NA IG Series 9 maturing in 2017—where JPMorgan had sold protection to express a view that credit would improve. That large, relatively illiquid position (trader Bruno Iksil was nicknamed the “London whale”) made the bank identifiable in the market and attracted traders and hedge funds who began betting against JPMorgan, pushing index levels higher and increasing the bank’s paper losses.

Analysts and traders say precise loss estimates are difficult because JPMorgan’s notional exposure, trade entry prices, and any offsetting trades are unknown. Some models projected far larger theoretical losses (one straight-line estimate reached ~$5.9 billion), but analysts caution such figures ignore likely offsets and market dynamics. The bank had partially hedged by buying protection in a shorter-dated index, but as that hedge approached expiry it became increasingly costly to maintain; JPMorgan allowed the position to become more of a directional bet earlier this year. Credit markets improved through January—temporarily helping the positions—but reversed in April–May, accelerating losses. Public disclosure of the loss then triggered faster unwinding pressure as counterparties exploited the bank’s plight.

The Federal Reserve is reviewing the trades and whether the Chief Investment Office’s risks were appropriate for a federally insured bank. JPMorgan’s overall financial position remains solid—analysts still expect the bank to be profitable this quarter and many retain buy ratings—yet the episode has raised regulatory and governance concerns. The CIO had been profitable over prior years but the misstep led to resignations, including CIO head Ina Drew, and criticism that a commercial bank should not house what amounted to a large hedge-fund-style proprietary gamble. JPMorgan says it will not rashly sell positions; volatility and further paper losses are possible as it attempts to defuse the trade.

This document mixes three distinct items:

1. Internet Archive crawls and "No More 404" effort
- The Internet Archive is crawling sites to capture pages as they are created and to archive the pages those pages link to. The aim is to preserve the version that was live when a page was written so that when linked pages change or disappear, archived versions can replace broken links or be offered as companion links. The broader goal is to fix broken links across the web by archiving supported sites.

2. Brief Wikipedia-style bio of Aaron Hillel Swartz
- Aaron Swartz (1986–2013) was an American programmer, writer, political organizer and Internet activist. He contributed to RSS, Creative Commons, the web.py framework and was an equal partner in Reddit after its merger with his Infogami company. He worked on civic activism, co-founded Demand Progress (notably opposing SOPA), and in 2010 became a research fellow at Harvard’s Edmond J. Safra Research Lab on Institutional Corruption under Lawrence Lessig.

3. News item about Herman Cain’s alleged gospel album
- A gospel album titled Sunday Morning, attributed to former Godfather’s Pizza CEO and 2012 Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain, surfaced online (reported via the Daily Caller). The 13-track collection is mostly slow gospel; one upbeat standout, “This is the Day,” was highlighted. The Cain campaign had not commented and its authorship wasn’t fully confirmed, though the album was reportedly published about 15 years earlier by GLC Music, Selah Sound Production & Melodic Praise Records. The item was posted as a light, entertaining political-culture tidbit.

Senate leaders struck a notably conciliatory tone Thursday as Congress rushed to avert a partial government shutdown at midnight Friday and to extend a one-year payroll tax cut affecting 160 million workers. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) and Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) said bipartisan talks were ongoing and expressed optimism a deal could be reached in the next few days. President Obama urged Congress to act before the holidays to prevent taxes from rising and to preserve unemployment benefits, but did not indicate whether he approved the pending spending bill.

Key elements and disputes
- Omnibus spending bill: Republicans and some Democrats negotiated a roughly $1 trillion omnibus to fund most of the government through next September. House Republicans filed the measure and signaled they might press it forward even without full Democratic support; Reid said remaining Democratic objections were small and resolvable. Conservatives objected to the omnibus’s $1.043 trillion spending level, so its passage without some Democratic votes was uncertain.
- Payroll tax cut and unemployment benefits: Democrats pushed to extend the payroll tax cut and long-term jobless benefits; they previously sought to pay for the $120 billion payroll-tax extension with a surtax on millionaires, but abandoned that demand in talks. Republicans remain skeptical that the tax cut spurs growth. The House-passed payroll bill links the extension to GOP priorities—such as Keystone XL pipeline approvals and other policy riders—that Democrats and the White House oppose; Obama threatened to veto that bill.
- Leverage and timing: The omnibus has been used as leverage in the payroll-tax fight. Both sides warned the other against being blamed if the tax cut lapses. Senate Democrats planned procedural moves to force votes; Republicans pushed to take up the spending measure first. With no consensus on offsets that can secure 60 Senate votes, negotiators considered a short-term (e.g., two-month, $40 billion) extension as a fallback while continuing to pursue a longer-term fix.
- Contested provisions: Other disputes include GOP additions to the payroll bill—cuts to unemployment benefits, drug tests/GED requirements for some unemployed, federal pay freeze, higher Medicare premiums for wealthier seniors, and a 60-day deadline forcing a decision on Keystone XL (which the State Dept. said would likely result in denial). The omnibus also had late sticking points such as Cuba travel rules, light-bulb standards, D.C. abortion funding, coal as military fuel, and Commodity Futures Trading Commission funding.
- Shutdown impact: If no deal is reached, many agencies would furlough staff and services (national parks closed, some passport processing halted), though some departments were already covered by earlier appropriations. Cabinet officials began notifying employees about potential shutdown contingency plans.

Outlook
Despite sharp rhetoric earlier in the week and mutual accusations of bad faith, rank-and-file lawmakers largely expected a last-minute compromise to extend the payroll tax cut and pass funding. Leaders were working through procedural and policy details, with the possibility of votes Friday or into the weekend; the primary casualty, many predicted, would be Congress’s reputation.

Paul Manafort, President Trump’s former campaign chairman, filed a federal lawsuit asking a Washington judge to void Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein’s May appointment of Robert S. Mueller III as special counsel and to dismiss the charges brought by Mueller’s office. Manafort’s 17-page filing argues Rosenstein exceeded his legal authority by empowering Mueller to investigate “links and/or coordination” between the Russian government and the Trump campaign and “any matters” that arise from that probe, giving Mueller “carte blanche” to pursue matters unrelated to the 2016 campaign. Manafort’s lawyers say the indictment—charging him with fraud, conspiracy and money laundering over secret lobbying and business dealings for a pro‑Russia Ukrainian party that largely ended in 2014—concerns pre‑campaign private conduct unrelated to the special counsel’s mandate; they contend Mueller’s actions were arbitrary, capricious and unlawful.

The suit escalates efforts by Trump allies to discredit the Russia inquiry. Manafort and his deputy Rick Gates have pleaded not guilty and remain under home detention awaiting trial. The Justice Department called the lawsuit “frivolous,” and the special counsel’s office declined comment. Legal observers noted defendants often challenge special‑counsel scope but rarely succeed; independent probes frequently have broad jurisdiction, as past examples (e.g., Ken Starr) demonstrate. The filing adds to broader political attacks on the investigation, which has already produced guilty pleas from Michael Flynn and George Papadopoulos.

Hawaii state Sen. Clayton Hee, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and Honolulu police have agreed to remove a longstanding exemption in the state’s prostitution law that effectively allowed officers to engage in sexual penetration with prostitutes while acting in the line of duty. Police told Hee they support making sexual penetration by officers explicitly illegal but want to preserve the ability for undercover officers to verbally offer sex to make arrests. Honolulu Police spokeswoman Teresa Bell said department rules already prohibit officers from having sex with prostitutes and that making it illegal would not change investigative practices, which rely on verbal offers rather than actual sexual contact. The House version of the bill had removed a clause criminalizing officers’ sexual penetration after police lobbying; public outrage following AP reporting prompted the Senate review and Hee’s move to revise the exemption. Bell said officers who have sex with prostitutes can face internal investigation and possible discipline, though she was unaware of recent disciplinary cases. Anti-trafficking advocate Kathryn Xian, who helped draft language to change the exemption, said she was surprised police agreed to the change and noted prior versions always allowed verbal solicitation by officers.

Former Spokane NAACP chapter president Rachel Dolezal defended her self-identification as black in televised interviews after her parents publicly said she is white. On NBC’s Today and in an NBC News interview with Savannah Guthrie, Dolezal said she has not taken a DNA test and questioned whether her biological parents could be proven, while insisting that “nothing about being white describes who I am” and calling herself “more black than I am white.” She acknowledged experimenting with hair and occasionally using bronzer but denied altering her skin.

Her parents, Lawrence and Ruthanne Dolezal, and other relatives have disputed many of her public claims about her upbringing—such as being born in a tepee, having a stepfather, or experiencing racially based punishments—and characterized her assertions as false. Family members also highlighted longstanding estrangement and past disputes, including allegations and counterclaims involving her brother.

Dolezal’s years of activism, academic work (including a master’s from Howard University), teaching roles in Africana studies, and leadership in local civil-rights organizations earned her credibility among some, but revelations about her racial presentation and inconsistencies in her account prompted national debate. Critics say her self-presentation raises issues of cultural appropriation, blackface, and deception, while some supporters focus on her advocacy goals. Dolezal described her identification as complex and resisted calls that she deceived people for personal advantage. The controversy has intensified scrutiny of her past statements, policing complaints she filed over the years, and the ethics and meaning of racial identity.

Pop-rock singer Avril Lavigne and Nickelback frontman Chad Kroeger have announced their split after two years of marriage. Lavigne revealed the news on Instagram; their breakup adds to a string of high-profile celebrity splits that defined summer 2015.

The 2016 ISU World Figure Skating Championships were held March 28–April 3, 2016 in Boston, Massachusetts — the first time the city hosted Worlds. Organized by U.S. Figure Skating with the Skating Club of Boston as local host, competitions took place at TD Garden (main arena) with practice sessions also held at DCR Steriti Rink. The event awarded world titles in men’s singles, ladies’ singles, pairs and ice dance and determined how many entries each federation would have at the 2017 Worlds. Argentina made its debut representation at the World Championships, and several new ISU best scores were recorded.

Qualification rules required skaters to be at least 15 by July 1, 2015 and to have attained minimum technical element scores at prior ISU events; nations could enter one to three skaters per discipline based on 2015 Worlds results.

Event highlights and results:
- Ladies: After the short program Gracie Gold led, with Anna Pogorilaya narrowly ahead of Evgenia Medvedeva for second. In the free skate Medvedeva delivered a record-setting free-skate score (150.10) to win gold. Ashley Wagner moved up to claim silver — the United States’ first World ladies medal since 2006 — and Pogorilaya took bronze. Notably, defending champion Elizaveta Tuktamysheva was not sent by Russia.
- Ice dance: Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron won the short dance and then set a new world record in the free dance (118.17) to claim their second consecutive world title. U.S. teams Maia and Alex Shibutani took silver and Madison Chock/Evan Bates bronze, marking a rare occasion with two U.S. ice dance teams on the World podium.
- Men’s and pairs events were held across March 30–April 2; overall medal tables show four nations earned golds (Russia, Canada, France, Spain) and the U.S. finished with three overall medals (no golds).

Medal summary: A total of 12 overall medals were awarded across disciplines; Russia led with two overall medals (one gold, one bronze) and the U.S. collected three medals (two silver, one bronze). Small-segment medal distributions (short/free) are also recorded.

Additional coverage included a profile of U.S. skater Gracie Gold: following struggles on and off the ice after a disappointing drop from first to fourth at the 2016 Worlds, Gold announced in 2017 she would take time off to seek professional help while preparing for Grand Prix events, citing performance and personal challenges including weight pressures and emotional strain. Her form had declined over 2016–2017, she missed the 2017 Worlds, and her coach situation changed. The report also noted contemporaneous concerns about eating disorders in the sport and mentioned issues involving Gold’s father, whose medical license was suspended amid allegations of diverting controlled substances.

A Prince George’s County police officer, Jacai Colson, 28, was killed March 13 in an “unprovoked” shooting outside the District III station in Landover. Police say a man approached the station about 4:30 p.m., opened fire at the front doors and was engaged by officers who returned fire. Colson, a four-year department veteran and undercover narcotics officer, was mortally wounded and later pronounced dead at the hospital; the suspect was shot, hospitalized in stable condition, and another man believed to have been with the shooter was taken into custody. Authorities identified the two detained as Malik and Michael Ford; police have not publicly established a motive and investigators, assisted by the FBI and ATF, are leading the probe.

Chief Henry P. Stawinski III called the attack unprovoked and praised Colson’s bravery. Colson, days shy of his 29th birthday, was remembered by family, coaches and colleagues as a high‑character leader with an “infectious smile”; his father and former coaches recounted his background in Pennsylvania and his commitment to service. The shooting prompted a temporary shelter‑in‑place order for nearby residents and left local officers and the community grieving. Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan ordered flags at half‑staff; the county’s state’s attorney vowed an aggressive investigation and prosecution.

George A. Romero, the influential writer-director widely regarded as the "father of the zombie film" and a major figure in modern horror, died at 77 after a brief, aggressive battle with lung cancer. He passed peacefully in his sleep while listening to the score of The Quiet Man, surrounded by his wife Suzanne Desrocher Romero and daughter Tina, his longtime production partner Peter Grunwald and manager Chris Roe confirmed.

Born Feb. 4, 1940, in the Bronx and raised in Pittsburgh, Romero studied at Carnegie Mellon and launched a low-budget filmmaking career. His first feature, Night of the Living Dead (1968), made for roughly $114,000, became a cult classic despite mainstream snubs and helped invent the modern cinematic zombie. A distributor’s title change pushed the film into the public domain, costing Romero and his investors substantial profits, but the film’s impact endured. He followed with Dawn of the Dead (1978), filmed in the Monroeville Mall and a commercial success, and later movies in the series — Day of the Dead (1985), Land of the Dead (2005), Diary of the Dead (2007) and Survival of the Dead (2009) — as well as a 1990 rewrite of Night of the Living Dead and other genre works.

Romero’s films combined graphic horror with social commentary (critiques of consumerism, militarism and other aspects of American life), and he frequently shot in and around Pittsburgh, helping make the city a focal point of zombie culture. His other notable films include Creepshow (1982), Knightriders (1981), The Crazies (1973), Monkey Shines (1988), The Dark Half (1993) and Bruiser (2000). He also created the Marvel graphic-novel series Empire of the Dead.

Peers and fans celebrated Romero’s influence: Stephen King called him a favorite collaborator, and comedians and critics credited him with reinventing zombies and shaping much of contemporary horror and “nerd” culture. Romero leaves behind a family, many friends and a filmmaking legacy that reshaped genre cinema.

NASA announced on Jan. 18 that astronaut Dr. Jeanette Epps will no longer fly to the International Space Station (ISS) on the June mission for which she had been assigned as a flight engineer for Expeditions 56/57. Her removal is unexplained publicly; NASA has called it a personnel matter and declined to provide details. Epps will remain in the Astronaut Office at Johnson Space Center and be eligible for future flight assignments.

Epps’s reassignment drew attention because she would have been the first African-American crew member aboard the ISS. NASA has a long history of changing flight assignments for various reasons — including medical, personal or classified issues — and several past high-profile reassignments (e.g., Ken Mattingly from Apollo 13) are noted as precedent.

Family members, notably her brother Henry Epps, have protested publicly, alleging racism and misogyny at NASA and circulating a petition asking the agency to reinstate her. The petition and social-media posts have drawn signatures and calls for NASA to explain its decision. Serena Auñón-Chancellor has been reassigned to the June crew in Epps’s place.

Background: Epps joined NASA’s 2009 astronaut class after a career that included work as a NASA fellow, at Ford, and seven years at the CIA; she holds a physics degree from Le Moyne College and a PhD in aerospace engineering from the University of Maryland. She has not yet flown in space.

A 10-year-old Ventura County girl, identified by the coroner as Jasmine Martinez, died Saturday after collapsing at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia. Jasmine collapsed in the ride station after getting off the Revolution roller coaster on June 12; she was breathing but unconscious when airlifted to a hospital and later died. An autopsy will determine the cause of death and officials have not said whether she had any preexisting condition. Magic Mountain initially paused and then briefly reopened the ride after state officials found no evidence the incident was ride-related; the park later said the ride was temporarily closed again while the incident is reviewed. Revolution is a long‑running coaster featuring a 90-foot vertical loop and speeds up to 55 mph. The park expressed condolences to Jasmine’s family.

A suspected carjacker led Los Angeles police on a televised, high-speed chase during Monday evening rush hour after officers tried to stop a vehicle listed as stolen. Beginning just after 5 p.m. east of downtown, the driver sped through southeast L.A. County and neighboring cities—often in the wrong lanes—crashing into other vehicles at least six times and forcing a 22-year-old woman, Elizabeth Yarahuan, out of her car at gunpoint. News helicopter footage showed him abandoning a crashed, smoking car, attempting further carjackings, and pulling a gun while on foot as multiple LAPD units and helicopters tracked him.

The pursuit continued onto I-105, I-710 and SR-60 before the stolen vehicle became trapped in heavy traffic on an offramp in Montebello. The suspect exited, tried to seize additional vehicles, and officers chased him on foot; as he appeared to try to carjack another car and brandished a weapon, up to three officers fired, wounding him. He was handcuffed at the scene and taken to a hospital with multiple gunshot wounds; he remained alive but unidentified, estimated in his 20s. No officers were injured and there were no immediate reports of fatalities, though several motorists were struck or sideswiped. Police recovered a semiautomatic firearm and said the suspect showed “complete disregard for other people’s lives.”

PEDAL (Centre for Research on Play in Education, Development and Learning) is a research centre based in the University of Cambridge’s Faculty of Education, launched in October 2015 with funding from the LEGO Foundation. Its mission is to conduct rigorous academic research into the role of play and playfulness in young children’s education, development and learning, and to translate findings into evidence-based policy and practice. Play—physical, object-based, symbolic, pretend and rule-based—is widely enjoyed and claimed to support learning, wellbeing, creativity and social skills, but is relatively under-researched; PEDAL aims to fill that gap with interdisciplinary studies (for example, GPS-tracked studies of outdoor play) that can inform educators and policymakers worldwide.

As part of the initiative the LEGO Foundation endowed the LEGO® Professorship of Play in Education, Development and Learning (part of a £4m gift: £2.5m for the professorship, £1.5m for PEDAL). The University invited applications (deadline 20 January 2017) for a senior scholar—ideally an educational or developmental psychologist with a strong international research record—who will serve as Professor and Director of PEDAL. The role includes research, teaching, supervision, examination and administration; the appointee is expected to build a research team and define the centre’s agenda, but not to act as a partisan advocate for play. The LEGO Foundation seeks an imaginative, interdisciplinary researcher with a “childlike” curiosity who can produce high-quality evidence on how playful learning may support 21st-century skills such as problem solving, teamwork and self-control.

State Representative Daniel B. Winslow (R-Norfolk), a former district court judge and once chief legal counsel to Gov. Mitt Romney, has officially entered the special election for the U.S. Senate, becoming the first Republican to declare. Winslow, 54, said he has contributed $100,000 of his own money toward a campaign he estimates will cost $4–6 million and will leave his law firm next month to run full time. He launched an exploratory committee and plans to meet with national Republican figures, including the NRSC.

Winslow emphasized his fiscal conservatism and support for Second Amendment rights. He faces a crowded potential Republican field (including state Senate Minority Leader Bruce Tarr, Gabriel E. Gomez, Sean Bielat and others) while Democrats Stephen F. Lynch and Edward J. Markey have already declared. Candidates must gather 10,000 certified signatures by Feb. 27 to qualify for the April 30 ballot; Winslow said he will use paid staff and volunteers to meet that requirement.

In January 1961 a B-52 broke apart over Goldsboro, North Carolina, and two 4-megaton hydrogen bombs fell to earth in one of the Cold War’s most serious near-disasters. Newly released and declassified documents confirm that both weapons progressed through most of their arming sequences during the crash. One bomb deployed a parachute and completed five of six steps toward detonation; it was stopped from exploding only by a single low-voltage safety switch. The other bomb fell in free-fall and, because impact shock rotated its arm/safe indicator to “armed,” also came alarmingly close to functioning—fortunately, impact damage to the switch contacts prevented an actual detonation.

Experts and veterans quoted in the documents describe how small mechanical failures and sheer luck averted catastrophe; Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara later summarized the situation as a matter of “the slightest margin of chance.” Had either weapon detonated its multi‑megaton yield (roughly 260 times the Hiroshima bomb) it would have caused catastrophic destruction over many miles and tens of thousands of casualties. The Air Force’s discovery that an impact could change arming switches led to design and safety changes. The Goldsboro case is one of dozens of pre-1980 nuclear-weapon accidents that have since been declassified, highlighting how close the United States has come to accidental nuclear detonations.

William “Bill” Alexander Morgan was an American drifter-turned-guerrilla who became a celebrated commander in Cuba’s revolution but was later executed by the regime he helped bring to power. The story follows his rise, disillusionment, death, and his widow Olga Goodwin’s decades-long fight to recover his remains.

Background and rise
- Morgan grew up in Ohio, ran away as a teen, had brushes with crime, a dishonorable discharge and a prison term in the U.S., and drifted through odd jobs before traveling to Cuba in 1957.
- He joined guerrillas in the Escambray mountains, earned trust through combat skill and daring, and rose to the rank of comandante leading the Second National Front of the Escambray. He became known as “El Americano” or the “Yankee Comandante.”
- In the mountains he met Olga Rodríguez (later Olga Goodwin); they fell in love, married during the war, and had children. Morgan presented himself as fighting for Cuban liberty and democracy, and wrote moving letters explaining why he’d come to Cuba.

Politics, intrigue, and duplicity
- After Batista fell, tensions surfaced between Escambray commanders (many anti-Communist and pro-democracy) and Castro’s increasingly centralized leadership, which embraced socialist policies and promoted figures like Che Guevara and Raúl Castro.
- Morgan’s position became complicated. He attracted attention from multiple sides: the U.S. intelligence community, anti-Castro conspirators (including Trujillo, ex-Batista elements, the Mob and Teamsters), and Castro’s government. He sometimes cooperated with U.S. or exile contacts, was approached about leading counterrevolutionary efforts, but also at one point helped expose a Trujillo-backed plot against Castro—winning Castro’s public embrace and earning Cuban “citizenship by birth.”
- U.S. agencies debated recruiting him; a C.I.A. background check ultimately deemed him too risky. Morgan’s loyalties remained ambiguous to outsiders: he seemed driven by a personal code, ambition, and a desire for redemption rather than by clear allegiance to any intelligence service.

Disillusionment and arrest
- As Cuba moved left, Morgan grew alarmed at arrests, property seizures, and the increasing role of Communist cadres. He began clandestinely helping anti-Castro fighters in the Escambray and secretly moved weapons at least by late 1960.
- On October 19, 1960, Cuban security arrested Morgan. He was tried on charges of conspiracy and treason in March 1961. Despite his revolutionary record and international profile, he was condemned quickly. On March 11, 1961, Morgan was executed by firing squad at La Cabaña prison; accounts say he refused to kneel and was shot in the knees before being finished. His body was buried in an unmarked grave in Havana.

Olga Goodwin and the aftermath
- Olga—who spent years imprisoned after Morgan’s death, enduring harsh conditions and beatings—eventually escaped to the United States during the 1980 Mariel boatlift and settled in Toledo, Ohio. She vowed to bring Morgan home.
- For decades Morgan’s story faded into Cold War obscurity, but recent books and articles (including a New Yorker piece, a book by Michael Sallah and Mitch Weiss, and planned film and PBS treatments) revived interest.
- With thawing U.S.-Cuba relations after high-profile prisoner exchanges (Alan Gross and members of the Cuban Five), Morgan’s Toledo attorney and U.S. lawmakers renewed diplomatic efforts to repatriate his remains. Morgan’s U.S. citizenship had been restored in 2007; advocates say returning his body would honor his family’s wish and close a Cold War chapter.

Significance
- Morgan’s life is a study in contradictory loyalties: an American who became a Cuban revolutionary hero, a man courted by conspirators and spy networks, and ultimately a victim of the revolution’s internal purges. His personal story—romance, idealism, violence, and betrayal—illuminates the messy, human complexities behind Cold War politics in Cuba.
- Olga’s decades-long campaign to retrieve his remains ties that personal tragedy back into contemporary diplomatic shifts between the U.S. and Cuba.

Simone Biles, the 2016 Olympic all-around champion, publicly announced she is one of the many women sexually abused by former USA Gymnastics team doctor Larry Nassar. In a #MeToo social-media statement posted the day before a multi-day Michigan sentencing hearing, Biles said she had long struggled with guilt but now understands the abuse was not her fault and called out Nassar, USA Gymnastics (USAG) and others for enabling the predator. Her disclosure follows similar revelations from other elite gymnasts, including Aly Raisman, McKayla Maroney and Gabby Douglas.

Nassar, who worked at Michigan State University and served as a team doctor for multiple Olympic cycles, pleaded guilty in Ingham County to sexual assaults and faces additional state and federal sentences (including a prior 60-year federal sentence for child pornography). At the state sentencing hearing, nearly 100 victims were scheduled to give impact statements describing how Nassar used his medical authority and ungloved “treatments” to abuse girls — some as young as six — and how institutions failed to stop him.

Survivors and advocates have accused USA Gymnastics and Michigan State of ignoring or mishandling complaints and protecting Nassar, prompting lawsuits, calls for leadership changes, and investigations. USAG said it was “heartbroken” and pledged support for survivors while pointing to reforms and blaming investigative failings by other entities. Victims, including Rachael Denhollander and Jamie Dantzscher, said the hearing is crucial not only to hold Nassar accountable but to confront the systemic failures that allowed his abuse and to prevent future abuse.

Denver Broncos wide receiver Kenny McKinley, 23, was found dead Monday afternoon in his Centennial, Colo., home; Arapahoe County authorities say detectives believe he died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound and are investigating. McKinley, a 2009 fifth-round draft pick, had been on the Broncos’ injured reserve this season after suffering a season-ending knee injury last year. He played eight games as a rookie, primarily on special teams.

A standout at the University of South Carolina (2005–08), McKinley is the school’s career leader in receptions (207) and receiving yards (2,781) and held a 43-game streak with a reception. He had attended USC’s recent game at Georgia and was described by coaches, teammates and the school’s athletic director as upbeat and positive. McKinley is survived by a young son.

Broncos coach Josh McDaniels and owner Pat Bowlen expressed shock and sympathy; the team planned a full meeting and made grief counselors available. Friends and former teammates noted his bright personality but acknowledged he had faced challenges transitioning from college stardom to a pro career hampered by injury.

Summary:

Actress, writer and cultural icon Carrie Fisher died at 60 after suffering a heart attack on a flight from London to Los Angeles on Dec. 23 and passing away four days later. Best known as Princess Leia in the Star Wars saga, Fisher was also an acclaimed author (Postcards From the Edge, Wishful Drinking, The Princess Diarist), a sought-after uncredited “script doctor” on many Hollywood films, and a candid advocate who helped destigmatize mental illness by publicly discussing her bipolar disorder, depression and past substance abuse.

Coverage after her death emphasized:
- Tributes from colleagues, fans and Star Wars collaborators mourning her loss and celebrating her wit, bravery and influence.
- Memorable quotes from her books and interviews that showcase her sardonic humor and unflinching honesty about mental health.
- Her role in breaking down stigma around addiction and bipolar disorder; many credited her openness with inspiring them to seek help.
- Her offbeat public persona and fashion — independent, quirky and unapologetically herself — often accompanied by her beloved French bulldog Gary, who traveled with her and became a minor celebrity and comfort companion.
- Lesser-known facets of her career: prolific script doctoring (e.g., Hook, Sister Act), memorable comedic and dramatic roles beyond Star Wars, and her influence on later female sci‑fi characters.
- Personal details: she is survived by daughter Billie Lourd, brother Todd Fisher and mother Debbie Reynolds.

Overall, the reporting portrayed Fisher as a multi‑talented, brutally honest writer and performer whose humor, candor about mental health and iconic screen presence left a lasting cultural legacy.

A Morning Consult poll of 2,200 people measured favorability for Star Wars characters and found Princess Leia highest (73%), with Luke, Chewbacca, Yoda and R2-D2 close behind. Anakin Skywalker rated 55% while Darth Vader scored 49%—a small drop given Vader’s crimes, noted Mashable. Original trilogy characters all had at least 40% favorability; none appeared among the least-liked. Contrary to common belief, Jar Jar Binks wasn’t the most hated character—he had 37% approval (just behind Rey)—and even ranked ahead of characters like Mace Windu, Kylo Ren and Emperor Palpatine. The least popular character was Supreme Leader Snoke at 26%. The poll also examined whether fans see Star Wars as political: 53% said it is not political, while among the 17% who do see politics in it, 41% are bothered by that tone. Results were also broken down by demographics and political affiliation, offering material for discussion as The Last Jedi arrived.

The piece then profiles Ahmed Best, the actor behind Jar Jar Binks. Now 43 and living in Los Angeles, Best has a varied creative and technological background—early interest in computing, musical training, and a career in performance including percussion, the acid-jazz group Jazzhole, and a lead role in the theatrical hit Stomp. His dynamic stage presence and confidence caught the eye of Lucasfilm casting director Robin Gurland during a Stomp performance, leading to his casting after an audition at Skywalker Ranch where he performed in a motion-capture suit. The profile highlights Best’s enthusiasm for technology, his creative projects (including producing visuals for shows and launching The Afrofuturist Podcast), and how his talent and persona led to the breakthrough role of Jar Jar—despite the character’s subsequent controversial reception.

Researchers have used an artificial neural network to identify which facial features drive snap social judgments—trustworthiness/approachability, dominance, and youthful-attractiveness—made within a fraction of a second. They had volunteers rate first impressions of over 1,000 internet photos on multiple social traits, measured 65 facial features for each image (jaw, mouth, eyes, eyebrows, cheekbones, etc.), and trained the model to link physical attributes to perceived traits.

Key findings:
- Approachability/trustworthiness is strongly tied to mouth shape and expression: smiling increases perceived approachability.
- Youthful-attractiveness is linked to eye shape and size (larger eyes signal youth).
- Dominance correlates with masculine face shape cues (eyebrow height, cheekbone structure) and appearance factors like skin color/texture that may signal masculinity or health/tanning.

The model could also generate caricature-like faces that reliably produced the intended impressions when shown to people, demonstrating its predictive validity. The researchers note that changeable image factors—expression, pose, lighting, camera angle—affect impressions as well as fixed facial structure, meaning one can potentially manipulate a photo to influence others’ judgments. They limited this study to Caucasian faces to control for ethnic variation and are conducting cross-cultural follow-ups.

Implications: the work quantifies how small facial differences create powerful first impressions, with applications for social media profile selection, photography, animation, and potentially worrying consequences for contexts like hiring, elections, or courts where fleeting images shape decisions. Further research is planned on cultural differences and the brain mechanisms underlying these impressions.

Summary:

Groupon’s IPO priced at $20 a share and opened much higher, trading near $30 immediately and spiking further intraday, creating a market value well above the IPO level. Early institutional buyers who received allocations are already selling into the pop. That behavior, combined with the small float (less than 6% sold), makes the stock likely to be very volatile.

The author is skeptical about owning Groupon at current prices. At roughly $30 the company implies a market cap near $20 billion, which the author thinks is far too rich given Groupon’s current transition from rapid growth to profitability. Key concerns:
- Growth is decelerating sharply (partly from the law of large numbers and because management is cutting marketing to reach profitability).
- The U.S. core business is shrinking and international operations are loss-making.
- There may be “daily deal fatigue” limiting future demand.
- Momentum investors punish deceleration, which can crush stock prices during transitions (the author cites Amazon’s painful 2000–2002 pullback as a precedent).

Financial snapshot and base-case forecasts:
- Run-rate approaching $2 billion; projected 2012 revenue ~$2.5B and 2013 ~$3B.
- Assumes operating margins rising to ~10% in 2012 and ~15% in 2013, yielding net income roughly $150M (2012) and $300M (2013).
- Using 20–30x 2013 earnings gives an implied valuation of $6B–$9B (about $9–$13 per share), well below current trading levels.

Risks and upside:
- Groupon could outperform (e.g., Goldman’s bullish estimates—40% revenue growth and 30% margin by 2013—which would justify higher multiples), but downside—stagnation, margin pressure, merchant pushback—could make it worth much less.
- The author would only consider buying if growth stabilizes or the stock falls to a level offering a clear margin of safety (he cites ~$5B market cap, ~ $7/share, as his threshold).

Conclusion:
Long-term the author is optimistic that Groupon has identified a large e-commerce opportunity and benefits from scale, but the near-term transition to sustainable profitability creates substantial risk. Given the high likelihood of meaningful deceleration and attendant stock-price pain, he prefers to watch from the sidelines and would wait for either stabilized growth or a much cheaper entry price. This is not personalized investment advice; the author personally favors diversified index funds over stock picking.

Dallas Cowboys coach Jason Garrett repeatedly declined to discuss the team’s recent cut of wide receiver Lucky Whitehead, insisting the decision made “yesterday” was “in the best interest of the Dallas Cowboys” and that the team would “stand by that decision” and move on. Garrett answered many questions with the same brief refrain and refused to elaborate on timing, fairness, or whether the team knew more than the media.

Authorities later confirmed Whitehead — whose given name is Rodney — had been wrongly identified in a June 22 shoplifting case at a Wawa in Prince William County, Virginia. Police say a man at the scene gave Whitehead’s name, birth date and Social Security number; officers matched that information to DMV records and compared the DMV photo to the suspect. The suspect received a summons for misdemeanor petty larceny; when he failed to appear in court, a warrant was issued for Whitehead, who was unaware of the incident and says he was in Dallas at the time.

Prince William County police apologized for the impact of the error, said they acted in “good faith,” and pledged to work with prosecutors to officially clear Whitehead while seeking the identity of the man who provided false information. Whitehead’s agent, David Rich, criticized the police investigation, saying the mistake cost Whitehead his job. Cowboys executive VP Stephen Jones had cited multiple past chances and the team’s desire to go “in a different direction” when announcing the cut. Whitehead says he feels hurt that the team didn’t give him a chance to clear his name; his agent declined to publicly push for his reinstatement.

Google’s 2015 security rewards recap shows the company paid over $2 million to more than 300 researchers through various vulnerability programs. Highlights:

- Overall payouts: More than $2 million to 300+ people in 2015.
- Notable recipients:
  - Sanmay Ved briefly bought Google.com after it was momentarily available; Google offered him $6,006.13 (a numeric nod to “Google”), which Ved pledged to charity and Google doubled. The donation went to the Art of Living India foundation.
  - Tomasz Bojarski was the most prolific researcher, reporting 70 bugs.
- Android: The Android Vulnerability Reward Program launched in June 2015 and paid researchers over $200,000 by year-end, including a largest single Android payment of $37,500.
- Vulnerability Research Grants (VRP): New lump-sum grants fund researchers up front so they’re rewarded even if no vulnerability is found. One grant recipient, Kamil Histamullin, used his VRP funds to discover a YouTube Creator Studio flaw that could have allowed deletion of videos; he received an additional $5,000 after reporting it.
- Continued investment: Google announced $1 million dedicated to Google Drive security research and signaled further expansions to its reward programs in 2016.

Context: The report also references similar domain-renewal slip-ups at other companies (e.g., Microsoft’s past Hotmail domain incidents) to illustrate risks around domain management.

A Minnesota restaurant owner in Lonsdale posted a controversial sign reading “Muslims Get Out” with a second line “In Support Of St. Cloud” after a stabbing at a St. Cloud mall in which the attacker reportedly asked victims about their religion. Owner Dan Ruedinger defended the sign, saying he’s standing up against extremists and invoking his right to free speech; he reported increased business and no plans to remove or change the sign despite some backlash. Locals protested the sign, saying it gives the town a bad reputation for passersby on a busy road. The piece also includes unrelated local weather and a lengthy customer review of the restaurant that praises the soft-serve ice cream and a Sloppy Joe-style sandwich but criticizes the cooked food, greasy burgers, soggy fried items, poor fountain soda, slow service, and an unpleasant atmosphere—adding that the owner’s political displays may harm business.

Former U.S. District Judge Vaughn Walker, who retired in February after 21 years on the San Francisco federal bench, spoke to reporters for the first time about his landmark decision striking down California’s Proposition 8, the 2008 constitutional amendment barring same-sex marriage. Walker said he never considered recusing himself because he is gay and argued that a judge’s sexuality (like ethnicity, national origin or gender) is not relevant to judicial impartiality and would be a “very slippery slope” if used as a basis for disqualification.

Walker, 67, a former corporate lawyer appointed by President George H.W. Bush, described himself as an independent libertarian jurist who has issued decisions expanding individual rights (including a ruling against the Bush administration’s warrantless wiretapping) and limiting government power. He defended his August ruling that Prop. 8 discriminated on the basis of sexual orientation and gender and produced no legitimate benefit to heterosexual spouses or the institution of marriage, and said he hopes appellate courts will decide the constitutionality of Prop. 8 on the merits rather than on procedural grounds.

Walker reiterated concerns he raised at trial about whether the Prop. 8 sponsors have legal standing to defend the measure after state officials declined to appeal; he prefers an appeals court ruling on constitutionality rather than invalidation for lack of defense standing, which would leave unresolved questions. He said he was surprised his sexual orientation—revealed by the Chronicle during the trial—hadn’t been public earlier and noted no party in the case ever formally sought his recusal.

He also lamented the U.S. Supreme Court’s intervention blocking live TV coverage of the trial, arguing that high-profile public trials should be more visible and that televising proceedings would educate the public about legal arguments and the court system. Walker is returning to private practice to lead a San Francisco firm focused on mediation, arbitration and other alternatives to litigation, which he found most satisfying as a judge. The article also includes commentary from critics who argued his sexual orientation and long-term relationship created an appearance of bias and should have required disclosure or recusal—an argument Walker rejected.

New U.S. data show a promising first drop in new diabetes cases after decades of rising incidence, but the burden remains high and uneven. CDC figures report 1.4 million new diabetes diagnoses in 2014, down from 1.7 million in 2008 — the first significant decline in about 25 years after rates more than tripled from the early 1990s. About 21.9 million Americans now live with diabetes, roughly 10 percent of adults, and over a third have prediabetes.

The decline’s causes aren’t certain; CDC experts attribute it partly to gradual diffusion of diabetes science, education and prevention—efforts emphasizing exercise, diet and lifestyle changes—but caution that incidence is still about 60 percent higher than in the early 1990s, so much work remains.

The trend is illustrated at the state and community level. Alabama, which has the nation’s highest diabetes prevalence (12.7 percent in 2013), has seen new-case rates taper off. Local stories from Alabama’s Black Belt — a historically poor, majority-Black region with deep roots in slavery and sharecropping — show both the disease’s heavy toll and the impact of prevention: individuals like Lynette Carpenter and music teacher Robin Williams lost substantial weight, changed diets, increased activity, and avoided progressing to full diabetes after participating in prevention programs or making sustained lifestyle changes. Public health officials emphasize continued focus on prevention and education to build on the early signs of reversal.

Bolivia publicly rejected a donation of 100,000 chickens announced by Bill Gates, calling the gift "offensive" and urging an apology. César Cocaric, Bolivia’s minister of development, said the proposal implied Bolivians live in the past and do not know how to produce food, stressing national dignity and self-sufficiency. The rejection is partly political — Bolivia’s leftist, anti-imperialist government is sensitive to gestures that imply dependence — and partly factual: Bolivia’s poultry sector has grown substantially in recent years.

Data from the Bolivian Institute of Foreign Trade show strong expansion in both egg and broiler production. Between 2008 and 2013, poultry production (eggs and meat) rose by about 35%; egg production topped 1.5 billion units in 2013 (an 11% rise over 2012), with per‑capita egg consumption rising from 130 to 143 units and chicken meat consumption from 35 to 38 kg per person. Santa Cruz and Cochabamba are the largest producing regions, and cooperatives such as CAISY supply major domestic markets. Broiler production exceeded 939 million birds in the 2008–2013 period, peaking at 180 million in 2013.

The Gateses have promoted chickens as a poverty‑reduction tool—cheap, quick to reproduce, nutritionally valuable, and often controlled by women, who tend to spend income on children’s health and education. Melinda Gates and development partners argue small-scale poultry farming empowers women economically and improves nutrition. Bolivia’s response reflects both pride in its growing poultry industry and political resistance to foreign aid framed in a way that suggests local incapacity.

Rescue teams in Genoa recovered the final missing victims from the August 14 collapse of the Morandi motorway bridge, finding three members of one family in a crushed car and bringing the confirmed death toll to 43. Nine people remain hospitalized, four critically. Crews say searches will continue to ensure no one remains under the rubble while also securing the site for investigations.

A 200–250 m section of the vital A10 viaduct fell amid heavy rain, sending vehicles and debris down roughly 45–50 m. The cause is under inquiry; preliminary engineering assessments point to multiple possible factors rather than a single support failure. Longstanding concerns about the bridge’s design and corrosion have resurfaced: its designer, Riccardo Morandi, warned in a 1979 report about aggressive corrosion of reinforced concrete and recommended continual maintenance and treatments to protect exposed reinforcements. Engineers have also questioned the bridge’s unusual concrete-encased stay cables.

Public anger and grief have been pronounced. A state funeral for 18 victims was held; some families boycotted it, accusing politicians of exploiting the tragedy and preferring private farewells. Dozens of residents protested and left messages in a central piazza.

Autostrade per l’Italia, the operator (part of Atlantia), has pledged immediate funds for victims’ families, half a billion euros to rebuild the bridge, and support for displaced residents. The government has allocated €32m, will provide temporary housing (about 300 units initially), and intends a sweeping infrastructure safety plan to be launched soon. Rome has opened procedures to revoke Autostrade’s motorway concessions and said future concessionaires will be required to reinvest more profits into maintenance. Investigations and legal reviews are ongoing.

Lindsay Lohan’s time at the Century Regional Detention Facility in Lynwood, Calif., has drawn complaints from fellow inmates and press reports of tension. A relative of an inmate told PEOPLE that Lohan receives special handling — for example, the facility is reportedly put on lockdown when she is moved or receives items — and that other residents resent the attention, saying “all the inmates are sick of Lindsay.” The Los Angeles Sheriff’s Office denied special treatment and said there are no lockdowns, while Lohan’s lawyer said Lohan is “doing well” and is following visitation rules. Separately, British tabloid reports claim Lohan was taunted by other inmates (allegedly being called “fire crotch”), cried in her cell and was briefly isolated after an outburst; she is serving a 90-day sentence for a probation violation but may be released early due to jail overcrowding.

This document centers on work–family balance, using the high-profile resignation of MongoDB CEO Max Schireson as its anchor and expanding into broader cultural and policy arguments about gender, parenting, and workplace flexibility.

Key events and facts
- Max Schireson, then CEO of MongoDB, announced he would step down as CEO and become vice chairman so he could spend more time with his family and stop commuting frequently between Palo Alto and the company’s New York-centered operations. He cited heavy travel (roughly 300,000 miles projected in a year), missed family moments (including his son’s emergency surgery and an injured family pet), and the strain on his wife, a busy doctor and Stanford professor, as reasons.
- Schireson emphasized that, as a male CEO, he had never been asked about balancing fatherhood and leadership roles the way female executives routinely are. He hoped his decision would help normalize such choices for other senior leaders.
- Dev Ittycheria, an experienced software executive and investor, was named MongoDB’s new CEO. The company is well‑funded, dual‑headquartered (NY and Palo Alto), and had grown rapidly under Schireson’s leadership.

Broader themes and analysis
- The piece situates Schireson’s choice within a long-running “having it all” debate historically aimed at women: whether it’s possible to be both a top executive and an engaged parent. Schireson’s public decision signals that men are increasingly asking the same questions and may help shift the debate beyond gender.
- Evidence from management and economics research is cited to argue that family-friendly policies and workplace flexibility can benefit firms: higher perceived performance, positive stock-market responses to family‑policy announcements, and correlations with engagement, retention, and employee health.
- The legal industry is given as an example of structural change away from rigid models (billable hours) toward alternative arrangements that improve retention and reduce costs; clients and younger lawyers are driving some of that change.
- Innovation and creativity arguments: loosening rigid schedules and hierarchies can foster play, imagination, and cross‑disciplinary interaction—conditions conducive to innovation. The “California effect” (Silicon Valley culture of leisure and experimentation) is used to illustrate how work environments that permit play and flexibility can yield creative gains.
- Men’s growing interest in active parenthood (especially among younger generations) and some senior male leaders modeling flexible work (e.g., senior managers working from home) are presented as hopeful signs for cultural change. The text notes, however, that abstract interest may test differently against concrete career trade-offs.
- The author urges reframing work–family balance as a universal social and economic issue rather than a narrowly female problem. Policies and cultural shifts that support flexible, family‑friendly work would benefit both genders and the broader society.
- Role models: the essay celebrates prominent women leaders (e.g., Hillary Clinton, Angela Merkel, Christine Lagarde, Susan Rice) while arguing that such success should become commonplace, not exceptional, and that workplaces and policies must adapt so women need not conform to a “male” model of career paths.

Tone and takeaways
- Schireson’s decision is portrayed as both personally courageous and socially meaningful: it challenges gendered assumptions about leadership and caregiving and may help normalize senior leaders—male and female—prioritizing family without stigma.
- The piece advocates for systemic changes (flexible work, alternative career tracks, supportive management) grounded in self-interest for firms: retaining trained talent and improving performance.
- Ultimately, the argument calls for moving beyond whether women can “have it all” toward building workplaces and social policies that let all people pursue happiness, family, and productive careers.

Fox Business Network announced that New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee failed to meet its qualifying threshold for next week’s GOP presidential debate and will be relegated to the undercard event. The network required a 2.5% average in four designated polls (Fox News, NBC/Wall Street Journal, Quinnipiac, and Investor’s Business Daily) to make the main stage; both Christie and Huckabee averaged 2.25%, missing the cut by a narrow margin. Sen. Rand Paul just cleared the threshold with an exact 2.5% average.

Christie—whose recent debate performance and personal remarks on addiction had drawn attention—had trended low in recent polls (2% in a recent Fox News poll), making his demotion likely. Huckabee, a 2008 Iowa caucus winner and former Fox host, was widely seen as safer but also fell short. Both reacted defiantly, saying they’d continue campaigning and debating.

The main debate will include Donald Trump, Ben Carson, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, Carly Fiorina, Jeb Bush, John Kasich, and Rand Paul. The undercard will feature Christie and Huckabee alongside former Sen. Rick Santorum and Gov. Bobby Jindal. Senators Lindsey Graham and George Pataki failed to qualify even for the undercard, not reaching 1% in the polls used.

On Tuesday morning NBA Commissioner Adam Silver announced a lifetime ban and a $2.5 million fine for Los Angeles Clippers owner Donald Sterling after the release of audio in which Sterling made racist remarks about African‑Americans. Silver also said he will push the NBA Board of Governors to force Sterling to sell the team; owners, players and sponsors immediately backed the league’s stance and many corporate partners paused relationships with the Clippers. The punishment bars Sterling from all team and league activities and was framed by Silver as necessary and within the league’s authority, though he acknowledged legal fights could follow.

The decision transformed what had been organized talk of a player boycott into a unifying, highly emotional rally at Staples Center that night. The Clippers staged a visible protest in prior games (removing warmups to hide logos) and on Tuesday the organization — staff, cheerleaders and fans — covered ads in black, displayed anti‑Sterling signs, and repeatedly chanted unity messages. Commissioner Silver’s action allowed the players and staff to play without the immediate cloud of the owner’s remarks; Doc Rivers and players described relief and a desire to begin healing.

On the court the Clippers defeated the Golden State Warriors 113–103 in Game 5, taking a 3–2 lead. DeAndre Jordan scored a playoff career‑high 25 points, Chris Paul had 20 and Jamal Crawford 19. The crowd of long‑time sellouts gave a sustained ovation and the team said it “wholeheartedly support[ed]” Silver’s decision.

V. Stiviano, the woman heard on the recording, denied leaking the audio and—through her lawyer—said she never intended harm and that claims about an affair are inaccurate; Sterling’s wife has sued Stiviano seeking return of gifts. High‑profile figures mentioned in the scandal, including Magic Johnson, praised Silver’s leadership and expressed support for the league’s response. Legal experts noted Sterling could fight any forced sale in court but would likely face long odds.

A Playmobil pirate ship toy sparked controversy after a Sacramento mother, Ida Lockett, found that the instruction booklet directs builders to place a silver neck cuff around a dark-skinned figure dressed in torn clothes and no shoes. Lockett and others say the accessory is a slave collar and that the figure and the ship’s dungeon-like features evoke slavery and are racist. The set, bought at Toys “R” Us as a birthday gift for Lockett’s five-year-old, retails for about $90 (on sale for $63). The child’s aunt, Aimee Norman, posted her outrage on Playmobil USA’s Facebook page, calling the inclusion obscene and urging Playmobil to make more diverse, non–slave-associated figures. Sacramento NAACP president Stephen Webb called for the toy to be pulled from shelves. Playmobil responded to The Washington Post saying the figure was meant to depict life on a 17th‑century pirate ship and “a pirate who was a former slave in a historical context,” not to offend. The retailer had not commented in the reports. Reactions online were mixed, with some defenders noting historical accuracy of pirates taking prisoners while others condemned the imagery.

A mother in Ouachita County, Arkansas, died in a single-vehicle crash sometime last week, and her two young sons — a 3-year-old and a 1-year-old — survived and were alone for up to four days before being found.

Authorities discovered the older boy Monday after a 911 call reported a young child walking alone on a rural stretch of Highway 24 near Camden. He was traumatized, covered in cuts and scrapes and appeared to have been outdoors for an extended period. Deputies later located the crashed vehicle where the boys’ mother was found deceased and the infant still secured in his car seat, partly twisted and upside down. The 3-year-old had apparently freed himself from a car seat and left the scene, climbing up a nearby hill.

Family members say the mother, 25-year-old Lisa Holliman, frequently took the boys with her and that she had been four weeks pregnant, a fact learned at the hospital. Both children suffered dehydration; the 1-year-old is hospitalized at Arkansas Children’s Hospital and is expected to survive. The cause of the wreck is under investigation.

Security experts described a massive, unprecedented distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) campaign in which Spamhaus — a non-profit that maintains blocklists to help email providers filter spam — was targeted, causing widespread internet slowdowns worldwide. The attack, peaking around 300 Gbps, far exceeded previous large DDoS incidents (about three times the size of a 2010 100 Gbps attack and much larger than typical bank-directed attacks). It specifically targeted Spamhaus’s Domain Name System (DNS) infrastructure, clogging key internet “on and off ramps” and producing collateral disruption to other services and networks.

Background and actors
- The incident grew out of a dispute after Spamhaus added Dutch host Cyberbunker to its blocklists. Cyberbunker (through a spokesman identifying as Sven Olaf Kamphuis) denied wrongdoing and said Spamhaus was overreaching by deciding what is allowed on the internet; Spamhaus alleges Cyberbunker worked with criminal gangs in Eastern Europe and Russia to mount the attacks.
- Five national cyber-police forces were reported to be investigating.

Tactics and impact
- Attackers used DDoS techniques and a DNS flood that is difficult to mitigate because DNS servers must remain public and open; shutting them down would break normal internet operation.
- The attack produced intermittent bursts that overloaded parts of the global routing and ISP equipment, slowing internet access and raising concerns that critical services (including banking and government internet infrastructure) could be affected.
- Spamhaus said it stayed online thanks to a highly distributed global infrastructure and assistance from major companies (e.g., Google and CloudFlare) that helped absorb traffic. When Spamhaus enlisted CloudFlare’s help, attackers shifted focus to the data-connection providers serving Spamhaus and CloudFlare.
- Security firms like Arbor Networks and researchers noted the scale was the largest they had seen; experts pointed to long-known network configuration weaknesses—ISPs failing to filter spoofed outbound traffic—as enabling the scale of the attack.

Response and assessment
- Spamhaus’s CEO said engineers had kept services running despite continuous attacks lasting over a week.
- Researchers emphasized that technical mitigation is limited for DNS floods and stressed the need to identify and prosecute those responsible, as well as to fix ISP practices that allow traffic source spoofing to amplify attacks.

Archaeologists have located the long-sought 16th-century Spanish fort San Marcos on Parris Island, South Carolina, using modern remote-sensing tools. San Marcos—one of several forts in the Spanish settlement of Santa Elena, founded in 1566—had eluded excavation for decades despite documentary descriptions and a historical drawing. Traditional digging failed to reveal the fort, but recent advances in the software that interprets data from ground-penetrating radar, magnetometers and resistivity meters enabled University of South Carolina archaeologist Chester DePratter and University of Georgia’s Victor Thompson to pinpoint the fort’s footprint by imaging subsurface anomalies such as post holes, compacted floors and other traces of human activity.

The team mapped roughly 15 acres of the settlement, identifying outlines of the fort (built in 1577 by Pedro Menendez Marquez), a church, houses, possible wells, ditches and other domestic and civic features. They believe they are close to locating Menendez de Aviles’ home—distinguished by high-end Chinese ceramics—and another governor’s residence. The site lies within the Marine Corps Recruit Depot’s former golf-course area; Marines have cooperated with the work and the remote location protects the remains.

The discovery was the result of cumulative layers of geophysical data, careful exclusion of Native American and modern Marine-era disturbances, and improved data-processing programs. Detailed analysis of the survey data will continue for six to nine months, and findings are being published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. Results will inform future digs and exhibits at the new Santa Elena History Center, deepening understanding of an important early Spanish colonial presence in what is now the southeastern United States.
