Florida Republican state Representative Brad Drake introduced a bill to repeal lethal injection in favor of electrocution or firing squad, saying executions should be more painful and that inmates should be forced to contemplate their fate daily. Drake says the idea came from a conversation with a constituent at a Waffle House following legal disputes over the Sept. 28 execution of Manuel Valle; the bill would let condemned prisoners choose between the electric chair and a firing squad. Florida used the electric chair from 1924 until switching to lethal injection in 2000 after botched electrocutions spurred constitutional concerns. The proposal drew criticism from the ACLU of Florida, which called it embarrassing and ill-conceived given the state’s troubled death-penalty record. 

The proposal also prompted commentary on television: Current’s Keith Olbermann named Drake a “Worst Person In The World,” responding to Drake’s earlier remark that he would “throw them off the Sunshine Skyway Bridge” with a profane retort aired uncensored. Media commentators noted that such invective harms political discourse and contrasted it with past suspensions for on-air profanity at other networks.

Two officials in southern Guangdong Province were arrested after allegedly buying stolen corpses from grave robbers to meet government-imposed cremation quotas, Chinese media reported. In late June a resident in Beiliu City, Guangxi, discovered his grandfather's grave had been robbed. Police arrested a suspect, surnamed Zhong, who confessed to stealing more than 20 bodies from local village graveyards, bagging them and transporting them by motorcycle into neighboring Guangdong. Zhong said he sold corpses to two funeral-management officials from Gaozhou and Huazhou, surnamed He and Dong.

Authorities in Guangdong detained He and Dong; the officials said they purchased the bodies to satisfy local monthly cremation targets set by the government. Dong reportedly bought 10 corpses at 3,000 yuan each, while He paid 1,500 yuan per body (his total number of purchases was not disclosed). The purchases were said to have been “approved” by the government, and investigations continue.

The case highlights deep tensions between state campaigns to encourage cremation—motivated by limited land and development pressures—and traditional Chinese ancestor-worship practices that favor intact burials. In many rural areas, mandatory cremation quotas have prompted families to bury relatives secretly; media have also reported suicides and other tragedies linked to burial bans and reform efforts. The story notes that similar reforms took place in Hong Kong through market forces rather than bans, suggesting less confrontational models may exist.

The Obama administration announced a one-year delay of the Affordable Care Act’s employer mandate, which had required businesses with 50+ full-time-equivalent workers to offer health insurance or face penalties beginning Jan. 1, 2014. The Treasury Department said the penalty won’t take effect until 2015 to give employers more time to adapt to new reporting systems and to allow the government to simplify those requirements. The decision does not affect the individual mandate or the scheduled Oct. 1 marketplace open enrollment and related premium tax credits.

Reactions split sharply: business groups and many Republicans hailed the move as necessary or politically advantageous, arguing it confirms the law’s problems and calling for repeal; Democrats largely offered muted support, framing the delay as prudent flexibility to implement the law correctly. Supporters worried the postponement could reduce 2014 coverage gains, push more people onto the exchanges (increasing federal subsidies), or set a precedent for further delays. Critics contended it favored employers while leaving individuals subject to the individual mandate. The administration said employers are still encouraged to comply in 2014 and that guidance and proposed rules would be issued to clarify reporting and implementation.

Online dating, which began with sites like Match.com in 1995 and expanded with services such as OKCupid and Tinder, has transformed not just how people meet but the structure of social networks. Traditional social networks consist of tight-knit clusters linked by a few weak ties that bridge groups and facilitate introductions (friend of a friend, workplace, church, etc.). Online dating creates many new, effectively random connections between strangers—“absent” or weak ties—that act like new highways linking previously separate social clusters.

Researchers Josue Ortega and Philipp Hergovich modelled this effect and find that even a small number of these new cross-group links dramatically increases interracial marriages and accelerates racial integration. Their model also predicts that marriages formed via online dating tend to be stronger (lower breakup rates), a prediction supported by some empirical studies. U.S. data shows an accelerated rise in interracial marriages beginning after the mid-1990s and steepening in the 2000s and again after Tinder’s rise around 2012–2014, a pattern consistent with the model. While other factors (e.g., changing demographics) play roles, they do not fully account for the observed increases, making online dating a plausible major driver.

In short, digital matchmaking has reshaped social ties, reduced social distance across groups, and may be fostering more integrated and stable relationships.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad told North Korea’s state media on May 30 that he intends to visit North Korea and meet leader Kim Jong Un, KCNA reported. Assad made the remark while receiving credentials from North Korea’s ambassador; there was no immediate confirmation from his office and no indication a trip is planned. He praised Kim’s leadership and expressed confidence Kim would achieve Korean reunification. The report highlights longstanding Damascus–Pyongyang ties (diplomatic relations since the 1960s and past military cooperation) and notes accusations by U.N. monitors that North Korea cooperated with Syria on chemical weapons, which both countries deny. The announcement comes as Kim has recently stepped up diplomacy — including talks with China and South Korea — and just ahead of his June 12 summit with U.S. President Donald Trump.

Sen. Ted Cruz apologized after using an old joke at the expense of Vice President Joe Biden during a June 3 campaign event in Howell, Michigan, just days after Biden’s son Beau died of brain cancer. Speaking to about 650 Republicans at a Livingston County Lincoln Day Dinner, Cruz quipped that simply saying “Vice President Joe Biden” without a punch line “works” to make people laugh—a line he has used before. The remark drew immediate criticism on social media because of Biden’s recent bereavement. Cruz issued a public apology on Facebook and Twitter within an hour, calling it a mistake to use the joke “during his time of grief,” expressing sympathy and prayers for the Biden family. Reporters said Cruz walked away when asked about the joke; his Michigan campaign chair defended him, saying he meant no disrespect though “timing could have been better.” The story noted Beau Biden’s upcoming funeral and that President Obama will deliver a eulogy.

The Leonid meteor shower will peak overnight Tuesday, Nov. 17 into the morning of Wednesday, Nov. 18, with most activity centered around local midnight when the constellation Leo rises in the eastern sky. Individual meteors can appear anywhere, but they will seem to radiate from Leo. In the U.S. you can start watching any time after sunset on Nov. 17; for best viewing go to a dark site away from city lights and look east as Leo rises around midnight local time.

This year’s display is expected to be moderate—NASA predicts about one meteor every four minutes—because the shower is mid-cycle (the last major peak was 1998). A thin crescent moon will help by keeping skies darker, but widespread cloud cover could hamper viewing across much of the U.S. The Leonids occur each November when Earth crosses the debris trail left by comet Tempel-Tuttle; the comet itself is far away and there’s no danger of collision.

Dominion Diamond Mines and partner Rio Tinto have recovered the largest gem-quality diamond ever found in North America: a 552.74‑carat yellow rough from the Diavik mine in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The stone — far larger than Diavik’s previous record (the 187.7‑carat “Foxfire” found in 2015) — was discovered during the mine’s initial screening. It shows surface abrasions from recovery but is judged gem quality and likely classifiable as “fancy yellow.” Dominion acquired the stone from Rio Tinto through an internal auction and will select a specialist cutter in the coming weeks; only a few master cutters worldwide are suited to handle such a large, technical rough. Because it is still being evaluated and was abraded in processing, Dominion has not given a value estimate; final worth will depend on cutting results. The find ranks among the seven biggest diamonds unearthed this century and within the roughly 30 largest ever recorded. It comes as Dominion — owned by billionaire Dennis Washington since last year and undergoing senior management turnover — considers investment decisions for extending the nearby Ekati mine’s life. The discovery also arrives amid a global market oversupply and pressure on mid- and low-quality stones and cutting centers, especially in India. Dominion plans to Canadamark‑certify the polished stone once completed.

Rick (also called Garrick) and Cindy Krlich, long-time residents of Hubbard, Ohio, say they have been the targets of persistent horn-honking by neighbors, town employees and officials for years—more than 5,000 honks recorded over roughly a decade. The dispute dates to a 2007 real estate conflict: Krlich successfully bid on a house next door that had been in the Clemente family for generations, provoking anger from former fire chief John Clemente Jr. and his relatives. Krlich says members of the Clemente family, their friends, and some municipal employees retaliated by repeatedly honking as they drove past his home. The couple installed video and audio cameras and have documented many honking incidents, allegedly involving fire trucks, police vehicles, school buses and local officials.

The Clementes deny orchestrating a campaign, saying some acquaintances occasionally beep as a casual goodbye and that Krlich’s litigious behavior has alienated the town. Rick Krlich has sued dozens of alleged honkers and, more recently, filed a federal lawsuit accusing the city of Hubbard, the police chief and Trumbull County of ignoring or refusing to investigate his complaints and treating him differently—seeking more than $75,000 in damages and alleging an Equal Protection violation. Local media (ABC’s 20/20) invited both families and the town to a reconciliation event to try to resolve the feud.

North Korea’s state media announced that Kim Jong-il was re-elected as general secretary of the Workers’ Party at a rare party convention in Pyongyang and that his youngest son, Kim Jong-un, had been promoted to four‑star general. This is the first time Kim Jong‑un has been named in official media and is widely seen as the opening move to anoint him as Kim Jong‑il’s successor, continuing the hereditary Kim dynasty. Kim Jong‑un, believed to be about 27–28 and educated partly in Switzerland, has little political or military experience; observers note the promotion mirrors how Kim Jong‑il was publicly elevated in the 1970s.

Kim’s sister Kim Kyong‑hui, her husband Jang (Chang) Song‑thaek, and longtime family aide Choe Ryong‑hae were also given top military ranks, suggesting a family-centered power structure and possible guardianship roles to manage the young heir’s rise. The convention—North Korea’s biggest political gathering in decades—featured public displays of support and visits to the Kumsusan Memorial Palace for founder Kim Il‑sung.

Analysts link the timing to Kim Jong‑il’s reportedly poor health (including past strokes and chronic illnesses) and say the moves aim to secure succession and continuity of the military-first (songun) policy. International reactions were cautious; the U.S. said it was watching developments closely. The elevation raises concerns because of North Korea’s nuclear program, regional tensions, and the challenge of transferring leadership to an inexperienced successor.

German and French investigators say evidence from co-pilot Andreas Lubitz’s electronic devices and the recovered flight data recorder strongly indicate he intentionally crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 on March 24, killing all 150 aboard.

Key findings
- A tablet recovered from Lubitz’s Düsseldorf apartment contained un-deleted web searches from March 16–23. Prosecutors say the searches included suicide methods, medical treatment, and—on at least one day—queries about cockpit doors and their security. Authorities have not published the exact search terms.
- Lubitz is believed to have locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately put the Airbus A320 into a fatal descent. French prosecutors said he remained alive and conscious during the event; a European official called the act premeditated murder.
- Investigators recovered both “black boxes.” The flight data recorder was found buried in debris and, despite fire damage to its casing, is expected to yield useful data (speed, altitude, control inputs) to be synchronized with the cockpit voice recorder.
- At the crash site authorities recovered 470 personal items (including about 40 badly damaged cell phones) and 150 distinct DNA sets matching the number of people aboard; formal identification will require comparison with family samples and may take weeks.
- Evidence about Lubitz’s mental and medical history: he had a prior severe depressive episode (2009) and relapsed in late 2014. In recent weeks he saw multiple doctors (reported as five or six) for sleep problems and depression, obtained “not fit to work” notes he did not give to his employer, and was prescribed strong antidepressant medication. Investigators say doctors followed procedures and found no negligence. Small handwritten notes about stress and his pilot’s license were also found in his apartment.

Policy and industry response
- Germany has set up a task force to review cockpit-door locking mechanisms and medical/psychological oversight of pilots, bringing together government, airlines and medical representatives. Airlines had already moved to require two crew members in the cockpit at all times.
- The debate includes concerns over confidentiality of pilot medical records—some warn lifting doctor‑patient confidentiality could deter pilots from seeking help—and renewed calls by some experts to revisit crash-avoidance software concepts that could override pilot controls in emergencies.

Investigations by French and German authorities continue as forensic analysis, device examinations and black box data are processed to establish a complete timeline and motive.

A large caravan of roughly 1,200 mostly Honduran migrants, organized by volunteers with Pueblos Sin Fronteras (People Without Borders), has been traveling north through southern Mexico toward the U.S. border. Most say they are fleeing extreme poverty, political unrest and violence after the contested inauguration of Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández; many chant anti-government slogans and emphasize collective protection. Organizers and migrants formed self-governing structures—groups of 10–15 with designated leaders, sectors, and committees for security, food, and logistics—to reduce reliance on smugglers and protect against gangs and cartels. The caravan’s size surprised organizers and strained small towns where it rests; local churches and residents provide food and plazas for sleeping.

About two-thirds of participants hope to enter the U.S. undetected or to request asylum; others plan to settle legally in Mexico. Organizers stress they only offer assistance and not legal papers or food distribution guarantees. The journey includes walking long distances in extreme heat, hitching rides on trucks, negotiating vans, and planning to board freight trains like “the Beast,” a dangerous but faster method north. Mexican authorities at times have not intervened despite the group crossing checkpoints and military zones. The caravan poses logistical and political challenges for both Mexico and the U.S., with potential implications for U.S. immigration policy and enforcement. The document also included a contrasting social-media opinion urging stronger border enforcement and criticizing Democrats and DACA supporters.

Mel B (Melanie Brown) has filed for divorce from her husband Stephen Belafonte and obtained a restraining order that requires him to leave their Hollywood Hills home and stay away from her and her three children. She also alleges nearly a decade of physical, emotional and sexual abuse in sworn court declarations and in media interviews.

Key allegations Mel B makes:
- Repeated physical assaults over many years, including choking, being slammed to the floor (2007), being punched and having her lip split (July 2012), and other incidents that left visible facial and body injuries that colleagues tried to cover for productions.
- Emotional abuse: Belafonte allegedly demeaned her, eroded her self‑esteem, claimed he “made” her, and sabotaged her confidence when she achieved success.
- Sexual exploitation and coercion: she alleges he forced her into threesome encounters with other women, secretly recorded sexual encounters, and threatened to release sex tapes to ruin her career and to Child Protective Services to try to take her children.
- Extortion and intimidation: threats to release tapes, destroy her career, and take her children; alleged harassment of agents, producers and co‑workers; and controlling actions that prevented her from getting help when she attempted suicide in December 2014 (she says he blocked her calls and prevented ambulance assistance).
- Nanny allegations: she claims Belafonte had sex with the family nanny, got the nanny pregnant, pressured for an abortion, and paid the nanny large sums from Mel B’s money.
- Firearm concerns: she asserts he kept a .38/.357 magnum despite a prior conviction that would bar him from having a gun; ATF agents later served a search warrant but reportedly did not find the weapon.
- She says her father’s recent death and Belafonte’s callous reaction helped push her to end the marriage.

Additional context:
- Mel B reports she was vulnerable when they married (post‑pregnancy, low self‑esteem) and that Belafonte initially presented as supportive.
- Some alleged injuries occurred while she was working on shows such as X Factor (UK/Australia); producers and medical staff were reportedly told alternative explanations and authorities were not alerted.
- She obtained the restraining order Monday and says she and her children fear for their lives. Belafonte has denied the allegations and questioned her motives.

A notable public detail: despite filing for divorce and separation (she says they have been separated since December), Mel B was photographed continuing to wear an upgraded 7‑carat, roughly $300,000 wedding ring Stephen had given her in 2014.

Lawyers for Krishna “Kris” Maharaj, a 75-year-old British-born former millionaire who has spent 27 years in a Florida prison for the 1986 double murders of Derrick Moo Young and his son Duane, have disclosed 53 witnesses and 498 documents they plan to present to persuade a Miami judge to order a retrial. Judge William Thomas will set a date next Wednesday for a full evidentiary hearing; he has said he will grant a new trial if the new evidence is of “such nature that it would probably produce an acquittal on retrial.”

Maharaj was convicted in 1987, sentenced to death (later commuted to life in 2002), and has long maintained his innocence. His lawyers, including Clive Stafford Smith of Reprieve, argue the case against him is massive and that he was framed to conceal involvement of Colombian drug cartels—specifically the Medellín cartel led by Pablo Escobar. The defense says the Moo Youngs were laundering large sums for the cartel and that cartel operatives carried out the hit. The evidence to be offered includes testimony from six witnesses who place Maharaj 30 miles away at the time of the murders, witnesses alleging another named individual committed the killings and had motive, witnesses and documents alleging perjury by key prosecution witnesses, fingerprint analyses, hotel records, and documents purportedly showing the Youngs’ drug-money dealings.

Prosecutors have already argued much of the new material is hearsay, inadmissible, or speculative and maintain confidence in the original conviction; Florida’s Supreme Court previously upheld the verdict. The judge will determine admissibility at the evidentiary hearing. Maharaj’s defense credits recent cartel-linked witnesses who say the murders were ordered because the Moo Youngs lost cartel money. Maharaj’s lawyers say this is his best chance in nearly three decades to prove innocence; family and supporters remain active in pursuing his release despite his poor health and limited finances.

Anonymous street artists plastered Los Angeles this week with posters showing Meryl Streep alongside Harvey Weinstein and a red banner reading “She knew,” implying Streep knew about Weinstein’s alleged decades-long sexual abuse of women. The posters, echoing Barbara Kruger’s signature style, appeared before dawn near Streep’s Pasadena home, the SAG-AFTRA building, Hollywood & Highland and across from 20th Century Fox in Century City. No one has claimed responsibility; artist Sabo denied involvement.

The campaign follows public criticism from Rose McGowan, who accuses Streep and other actresses of hypocrisy for planning symbolic protests such as wearing black to the Golden Globes while allegedly remaining silent about Weinstein. Streep replied via a statement saying she did not know about Weinstein’s crimes in the 1990s or later, that she wasn’t deliberately silent, and does not tacitly approve of rape. The dispute drew reactions from others in Hollywood—Amber Tamblyn urged against shaming women who are trying to effect change.

The story is part of wider fallout from the Weinstein scandal, which has prompted accusers to speak out on roundtables moderated by McGowan and renewed scrutiny of non-disclosure agreements; a former Weinstein assistant has publicly urged reform of gag-law practices after signing a settlement. Weinstein has denied non-consensual conduct.

Burberry has announced it will immediately stop destroying unsaleable products (including burning them) and will phase out the use of real fur. The move forms part of its five-year Responsibility agenda to 2022 — focused on driving positive change through 100% of its products, becoming carbon neutral and revaluing waste, and positively impacting one million people — and is reinforced by the company’s new strategy to address causes of waste. Burberry says it will continue and expand existing approaches to unsaleable goods (reuse, repair, donate, recycle) and will keep seeking recycling options for regulated items such as damaged or expired beauty products where disposal may still be required by law.

The fur ban will extend longstanding restrictions (rabbit, fox, mink and Asiatic raccoon) to also exclude angora; existing real-fur items will be phased out and none will appear in Riccardo Tisci’s upcoming debut collection. The announcement highlights recent and ongoing sustainability initiatives: partnership with Elvis & Kresse to convert at least 120 tonnes of leather offcuts into new products over five years (with half the profits to renewable-energy–focused charities); the Burberry Material Futures Research Group with the Royal College of Art to develop sustainable materials; core partnership in the Ellen MacArthur Foundation’s Make Fashion Circular initiative; procurement progress (21% of cotton via the Better Cotton Initiative, with a 2022 target of 100%); steps toward carbon neutrality in its own operations; and community programs via the Burberry Foundation supporting disadvantaged youth in London and Yorkshire and promoting a more sustainable cashmere industry in Afghanistan. Burberry notes inclusion in the Dow Jones Sustainability Index for the third consecutive year. CEO Marco Gobbetti framed the changes as part of modern luxury’s social and environmental responsibilities. Contact and further details are provided via the company’s responsibility web pages.

This long piece traces the rise, disappearance and recent rediscovery of Benny Anders, a flamboyant reserve forward for the University of Houston’s Phi Slama Jama teams of the early 1980s.

Key points:
- Anders is remembered for spectacular, audacious plays—most famously a vicious dunk against Louisville in the 1983 Final Four—and for his outsized personality, memorable quotes and flamboyant style (pink bow tie, “Outlaw” nickname, Jheri curl).
- He was a cult favorite on teams led by Clyde Drexler and Akeem/Hakeem Olajuwon, contributing more to the team’s identity than to box-score stats. He also played a critical hustle role in the 1983 title game’s final sequence.
- Anders’ collegiate career unraveled after clashes with coach Guy Lewis, a benching protest, and a 1986 incident in which he brought a gun to campus during an altercation; he was charged and kicked off the team. He had brief stints playing overseas (Philippines, South America) and then vanished from public view.
- For decades his whereabouts were unknown. Teammates, journalists and fans speculated wildly—rumors placed him in prison, abroad, undergoing surgery, or going by another name. Multiple searches (public records, family and hometown inquiries, private investigators) turned up tantalizing but inconclusive leads linking him at times to Flint, Michigan, and to odd sightings and anecdotes.
- The author recounts personal attempts to find Anders, including visits to Bernice, Louisiana (his hometown) and Flint; these searches produced rumors, dead ends and unconfirmed leads.
- The mystery was finally resolved by filmmaker Chip Rives, who made Anders’ location a priority while assembling an ESPN “30 for 30”-style documentary on Phi Slama Jama. With help from former UH player Eric Davis (a former Chicago police officer), Rives traced Anders to the Detroit area, where he was located working in a restaurant and filmed for the documentary. Anders appears in the film and closes it with the line, “A brotherly love is a very powerful thing.” He was reportedly paid to appear.
- The article notes that many questions remain—why Anders chose to live privately for decades, what he’s doing exactly now, and how he remembers his time at Houston—but concludes that his reappearance is a fitting coda to his cult legend: a brief, dazzling public flame followed by long anonymity and, at last, confirmation that he’s alive and well enough to participate in the film.

Overall, the story is both a portrait of a charismatic, self-styled “Outlaw” whose athletic flair outshone his statistics and a chronicle of a long-running sports-world mystery that ended when a filmmaker tracked him down for a documentary.

President Trump signaled a potential breakthrough in stalled immigration talks by publicly saying he is open—for the first time—to a pathway to U.S. citizenship for young undocumented immigrants protected under DACA, conditional on significant border-security concessions. In an impromptu exchange with reporters he said DACA recipients (about 690,000 people who were enrolled when he ended the program) could receive provisional legal status immediately and be eligible for full citizenship after roughly 10–12 years, provided Congress grants $25 billion for a U.S.–Mexico border wall plus $5 billion for additional border upgrades. The White House also intends to press for reductions in family-based (“chain”) immigration and changes to the diversity-visa program.

A full White House “framework” is expected to be released Monday; aides characterize citizenship as a discussion point with specific conditions to be defined. Trump’s shift comes amid a Feb. 8 deadline to pass government funding and bipartisan pressure—Democrats have said they will not back long-term spending without a DACA solution. The announcement follows weeks of mixed signals from the president, who earlier this year moved to end DACA and gave lawmakers until March 5 to devise a fix.

Reactions were mixed: bipartisan senators who have been negotiating welcomed the move as helpful to finding a deal, while Democrats said they had not been consulted on the White House plan. Key unresolved issues for lawmakers include how many Dreamers would be covered (estimates range from ~700,000 DACA enrollees up to ~1.7–2 million potential beneficiaries), the exact security and immigration changes required in exchange, and other trade-offs (family immigration limits, visa lottery overhaul, enforcement powers). Failure to reach agreement by Feb. 8 risks another partial government shutdown.

The Hope Diamond, a famous 45.52-carat blue gem now on display at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, has long been the subject of myths that it brings misfortune to its owners. The Smithsonian marked 53 years of ownership on Nov. 10 and notes the museum has remained “curse-free.” Historians, however, say many curse stories were likely embellished by owners to increase the stone’s market value.

Provenance and curse stories:
- The gem’s commonly told origin begins with 17th-century French merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, who brought a large blue diamond from India to Europe. Legend that he stole it from a Hindu idol and was mauled to death is false; he returned to France, sold the stone to King Louis XIV, and died peacefully.  
- The diamond, then called the French Blue, became part of the French crown jewels under Louis XIV. Members of the royal family later suffered during the French Revolution (Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were executed), and the jewels were stolen in 1792.  
- A cut-down version resurfaced in London by 1812 and was bought by banker Henry Philip Hope in 1839, giving the gem its modern name. Several later owners experienced tragedies—most notably Lord Francis Hope (financial ruin) and socialite Evalyn Walsh McLean (family deaths and personal miseries)—fueling the curse legend. Other owners, such as jeweler Pierre Cartier, Henry Winston, and the Smithsonian, did not suffer obvious misfortune tied to the stone, though a postman who delivered it to the museum later had several misfortunes.

Scientific and historical research:
- Mineralogists François Farges and Smithsonian curator Jeffrey Post used a recently rediscovered 17th-century lead replica, 3D modeling, and archival work to show the Hope was recut from the larger French Blue. The replica provided exact dimensions proving the link.
- Their analysis suggests the French Blue was intentionally cut with low-angle facets and a flat culet so that, when set against a gold backing, the gem produced a brilliant golden “sun” at its center — a symbolic design likely intended for Louis XIV, the “Sun King.” This visual effect was removed by later re-mounting and recutting; the French Blue was stolen in the Revolution and later became the smaller Hope Diamond.
- Researchers plan to make a replica to demonstrate the original sun effect and are continuing archival searches to confirm the design’s intentionality. They’ve also studied the chemical cause of the gem’s color and its red fluorescence under ultraviolet light (due to boron), another of the diamond’s notable scientific “secrets.”

Cultural impact:
- The Hope Diamond remains a major attraction and cultural icon, inspiring books, documentaries, games and even a Smithsonian-endorsed adventure video game, “Hidden Expedition: Smithsonian Hope Diamond,” which mixes puzzle gameplay with historical trivia about the gem. The stone’s fame endures because it combines rarity, beauty and a storied past that continues to draw public fascination.

Bottom line: The Hope Diamond’s dramatic history is a mix of documented events and embellished legend. Modern scientific work has clarified aspects of its origin, original cutting and transformation from the French Blue into today’s Hope, but the myth of a curse persists as part of its cultural allure.

Right-leaning sites circulated a leaked clip purportedly showing CBS Evening News anchor Katie Couric making snide off-air comments about Sarah Palin on the day John McCain announced her as his running mate in 2008. The footage appears to be raw, unedited rehearsal/taping material in which Couric, reading Palin family details provided for a segment, reacts aloud to the unusual names of Palin’s children — “where the hell do they get these [names]?” — and makes other brief quips about moose burgers and Palin’s hometown. Conservatives framed the clip as “proof” of contempt and biased framing of Palin by CBS; supporters argued the network’s story emphasized trivialities like beauty-pageant and lifestyle details instead of Palin’s record.

The available evidence, however, is weak. The tape is an off-air moment captured while Couric prepared to go on air, likely encountering unfamiliar names and campaign-supplied biographical bullet points for the first time; such an exclamation is not uncommon and does not necessarily demonstrate sustained bias. The clip is edited and lacks full context; CBS has described the attention as a sign of slow news and has not disputed the tape’s authenticity but declined to pursue its source. Critics note that the script items probably originated with the McCain campaign and that Couric’s broader conduct and interview record complicate claims that this brief remark constitutes a “smoking gun.”

A large, classified stealthy unmanned aerial system developed by Northrop Grumman — reported as the RQ-180 — is already flying and is slated for Air Force production and possible operational use by 2015. Funded through the Air Force’s classified budget and awarded to Northrop after competition with Boeing and Lockheed, the RQ-180 is an intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) platform optimized for operations in contested or denied airspace where non‑stealthy drones like the RQ-4 Global Hawk and Predator/Reaper cannot safely operate.

Officials and reporting indicate the aircraft combines low observable (stealth) characteristics with highly efficient aerodynamics to deliver long endurance, large range and the ability to penetrate hostile air defenses. It reportedly carries RF sensors such as AESA radar and passive electronic surveillance systems and could have electronic-attack capability. The design supersedes the smaller, shorter‑range RQ-170 Sentinel and fills the gap in deep‑penetration ISR capability left by the SR-71’s retirement.

Details remain classified: the Air Force declines comment. Public clues include Northrop Grumman financial disclosures pointing to a secret UAS program and low‑rate initial production, plus satellite imagery showing new hangars sized for 130‑ft-plus wingspans at Palmdale and Area 51. If managed like past secret ISR programs, the RQ-180 would likely be overseen by the Air Force’s Rapid Capabilities Office and operated jointly by the Air Force and CIA. The program aligns with broader moves to shift ISR assets toward contested-environment missions.

Scientists have re-examined a massive solar storm that narrowly missed Earth on July 23, 2012. The event—measured directly by NASA’s STEREO‑A spacecraft—was a superstorm formed when two coronal mass ejections (CMEs), aided by an earlier CME that "cleared the path," combined into an unusually powerful blast. Researchers estimate its geomagnetic impact would have produced a Dst around −1,200 nT, comparable to or exceeding the 1859 Carrington Event and roughly twice as strong as the 1989 Quebec blackout.

If that CME had struck Earth one week earlier, officials warn, the consequences could have been catastrophic: widespread failure of power grids, damage to transformers and satellites, GPS and radio outages, and long, difficult recovery—estimated economic losses exceeding $2 trillion. While solar storms don’t directly harm people, they threaten modern technological infrastructure. Studies published in Space Weather and Nature Communications emphasize that multiple eruptions and preconditioning by prior CMEs are key factors in producing extreme events.

STEREO‑A survived because it was in interplanetary space outside Earth’s magnetosphere; many operational satellites and terrestrial systems would be far more vulnerable. Physicist Pete Riley calculated a roughly 12% chance of a Carrington‑class storm hitting Earth within the next decade, a sobering probability that underscores the need for preparedness. Some mitigations exist—flight rerouting, grid operators’ protective procedures, and continued space weather monitoring—but gaps remain as instruments and observing geometry change. Current space weather forecasts are quiet for the next few days.

A Florida couple, Chris and Dana White of Pensacola, say they found a hidden recording device in their stateroom aboard the Carnival Fantasy during a three-day Caribbean cruise last October. The device was discovered among TV wires and pointed at their bed; the Whites filmed a ship employee inspecting and dismantling it and called security. They say Carnival initially denied it was a camera; the couple insist it was wired and warm to the touch and that their privacy was violated. Carnival acknowledged a “video transmitter” was found after an onboard investigation but said it was not connected to power or capable of recording, and the device was turned over to the FBI. The Whites say Carnival’s handling was insufficient and vow never to sail with the line again. The story was featured on Inside Edition; related reporting noted other recent cruise incidents, including disturbances on a Royal Caribbean voyage where a large corporate group reportedly disrupted passengers.

Thomas Keith Henderson, a 56-year-old West Virginia Division of Highways snow plow operator from Elkhorn, was arrested late Wednesday, Jan. 29, after being stopped on Route 6 near the top of Burke Mountain by McDowell County deputies because a headlight on the plow was out. The deputy reported smelling alcohol and observing bloodshot, glassy eyes; Henderson failed field sobriety tests and a breathalyzer at the Welch Police Department registered a BAC of 0.09. He was charged with DUI for a commercial driver (CDL limit 0.04) and defective equipment, arraigned Jan. 30, held in the county unit and released on $500 bond. The West Virginia DOT confirmed his employment but declined further comment due to the ongoing legal matter.

This document combines two related items about contemporary art and controversy. 

1) Event notice: Artist Nari Ward appeared in conversation with Massimiliano Gioni, Edlis Neeson Artistic Director of the New Museum, on March 14, 2019, in connection with Ward’s New Museum exhibition “We the People.” Ward, a prominent sculptor, is noted for transforming found materials to explore personal memory and complex political and social themes.

2) News story: A controversial video by late artist David Wojnarowicz, titled "A Fire in My Belly, A Work in Progress," began screening at the New Museum after being removed from a Smithsonian exhibition following protests. The 30+ minute work contains graphic sexual content and imagery of ants crawling over a crucifix, which drew criticism from religious groups and led Catholic League President Bill Donohue to campaign for the Smithsonian’s funding to be cut. Defenders of the New Museum and other gallery professionals framed the screening as a stand for artistic freedom and warned against censorship; the video is displayed free in the museum lobby.

Vladimir Katriuk, a 93-year-old longtime Canadian resident and former beekeeper in Quebec, has died after a prolonged illness. Katriuk was long accused of collaboration with Nazi forces during World War II and was ranked among the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s most-wanted alleged Nazi war criminals. Scholarly research, including a 2012 study by Per Anders Rudling that cited newly released KGB materials, tied a man named Volodymyr/Vladimir Katriuk to the March 1943 Khatyn massacre in what is now Belarus, alleging he fired on civilians fleeing a burning barn. Katriuk consistently denied the allegations.

Canada’s Federal Court ruled in 1999 that Katriuk had lied about his wartime service to obtain citizenship, concluding he served in a Ukrainian battalion implicated in wartime atrocities, but the court said there was insufficient evidence to prove he committed specific atrocities; in 2007 the federal government decided not to revoke his citizenship. Recently the Russian Investigative Committee sought his extradition to face charges, and the Russian embassy criticized Canada after his death for not acting on appeals to hold him accountable. Jewish groups in Canada had urged Ottawa to pursue justice, while the Ukrainian Canadian Congress and Katriuk’s lawyer said he had been unfairly harassed and denied involvement in crimes. Federal officials reiterated that war criminals are not welcome in Canada. The case had been politically sensitive amid strained Canada–Russia relations over Ukraine.

Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia have filed a brief with the U.S. Supreme Court supporting Montana’s century-old Corrupt Practices Act, asking the Court to let that state law limiting corporate direct spending in state and local elections stand or to hear full argument. The filing, led by New York’s attorney general, contends Montana’s regulation is materially different from the federal restrictions at issue in the 2010 Citizens United decision and therefore need not be invalidated by that ruling. The states — many of which have similar laws or challenges pending — argue corporate spending poses particular risks to state and local offices and that tailored state rules are permissible to prevent corruption or its appearance.

The Montana law was reinstated by the state supreme court after earlier rulings and conflicts with Citizens United prompted Virginia-based American Tradition Partnership to ask the U.S. Supreme Court to reverse Montana without a hearing. The high court has temporarily blocked enforcement of Montana’s law while it decides whether to take the case. Montana Attorney General Steve Bullock says the law regulates corporate political speech by funneling spending through PACs and cites the state’s historic corruption from powerful corporate interests as justification. American Tradition Partnership argues the ban unconstitutionally restricts corporate participation in politics.

Support for Montana’s position has come from a broad bipartisan group, including Senators John McCain and Sheldon Whitehouse, and from advocacy groups urging the Court to reconsider Citizens United’s core holdings — notably the view that independent expenditures rarely cause corruption or its appearance. Some justices and commentators have signaled openness to revisiting Citizens United, but many legal observers see it unlikely the Court will fully overturn that precedent; at most, it might clarify how Citizens United applies to state laws.

Rep. Michele Bachmann requested that her Swiss citizenship be withdrawn after media reports revealed she and her children had recently sought Swiss paperwork. Bachmann said the citizenship was automatically conferred under Swiss law when she married Marcus Bachmann, a dual U.S.-Swiss citizen, in 1978, and she asked for its withdrawal to underscore her sole allegiance to the United States. She emphasized her American roots and family military ties. Her office had earlier indicated the family had pursued Swiss registration because some of their children wanted to claim eligibility. The revelation drew criticism and accusations of hypocrisy given Bachmann’s past attacks on opponents’ loyalty and her conservative positioning; it also prompted political opponents to call the matter a distraction. Comments and coverage noted questions about optics, potential security implications, and public debate over dual citizenship.

The NYPD arrested 22-year-old Isaiah Thompson this week for subway surfing after video surfaced of him riding on the outside of a northbound C train in Brooklyn. The footage, taken by commuter Matthew Beary around 8:30 a.m. between the Clinton-Washington and Lafayette Avenue stations, shows Thompson calmly hanging onto the car and disembarking at Lafayette. Police charged him with reckless endangerment and disorderly conduct.

Authorities say this was at least Thompson’s third arrest for riding outside a train over the past year (March and November 2017), and some reports indicate a fourth 2017 arrest. Transit chief Andy Byford condemned the behavior as extremely dangerous and disruptive, noting it can cause major delays and fatalities; several recent deaths and serious injuries have been linked to similar stunts. Thompson did not comment.

2) A summary of a survey on physical inactivity in the U.S.:
- A recent annual survey found that about 83 million Americans aged 6 and older—roughly 28% of the population—were “totally sedentary” over the past year, meaning they did not participate in any of 104 specific physical activities.
- That level of complete inactivity is the highest observed since 2007.

At least 717 pilgrims were killed and 863 injured in a stampede during the Hajj at Mina near Mecca, Saudi authorities said; the incident occurred around 09:00 local time as crowds converged on the Jamarat Bridge for the “stoning the devil” ritual. Witnesses described chaotic scenes of people climbing over one another, bodies piled on the ground and overwhelmed rescue efforts. The victims were of many nationalities; Iran reported at least 95 of its citizens among the dead and criticized Saudi preparedness. Saudi leaders, including Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef and King Salman, ordered investigations and an urgent review of Hajj arrangements; officials said the crush happened when large groups converged and some pilgrims did not follow scheduled movement times. The disaster is the deadliest Hajj incident in 25 years and follows a crane collapse at the Grand Mosque days earlier that killed more than 100 people. The Hajj draws over two million pilgrims each year and has a history of deadly incidents at Mina, including major stampedes in 1990, 1994 and 2006.

RadarOnline.com is reporting that porn star and escort Devon James claims Tiger Woods fathered her son. James, 29, says she gave birth in early 2001 — before Woods and Elin Nordegren married — and alleges a 2½‑year affair with Woods that included an unprotected “two‑girl party” during which she became pregnant. She reportedly told Woods in 2006, after a chance encounter, that she believed the child was his. RadarOnline says it has seen photos of the boy and that he bears a strong resemblance to Woods, but that Woods has not been asked to take, nor taken, a paternity test; RadarOnline found no evidence Woods paid James. These claims follow other reports linking roughly 15 women to secret affairs with Woods and come amid separate allegations — highlighted in a Channel 4 documentary — that Woods fathered another secret child, with claims of DNA evidence and testimony from a journalist involved in covering up affairs. Tiger, who is scheduled to play in the U.S. Open, and his family have been in the public eye since his widely publicized infidelities and split from Elin Nordegren.

Summary:

The collected documents describe multiple measles outbreaks in the United States (with focus on California) over several periods, analyze causes and impacts, and outline public-health responses and recommendations.

Key events and findings
- California, 1988–1990: A major epidemic produced about 16,400 reported cases, 3,390 hospitalizations and 75 deaths. More than half of cases were under age 5, with highest incidence in infants <12 months. The epidemic was concentrated in low-income Hispanic communities in southern and central California and driven primarily by low immunization levels among preschool children and young adults. Complication, hospitalization and death rates were high. Outbreak-control efforts had limited success due to delayed funding and weak public uptake of community immunization campaigns. Estimated direct costs for medical care and control were at least $30.9 million. The report warned that similar epidemics would recur unless preschool vaccination rates rose.
- California / Disneyland outbreak (2014–2015): A large multi-state outbreak centered on Disneyland infected dozens to scores of people (reports cite 57 to 70+ cases overall, with most in California and some spread to five U.S. states and Mexico). Most infected were unvaccinated; a substantial share required hospitalization. Public health officials urged unvaccinated people and those too young to be vaccinated to avoid Disneyland and other crowded international hubs until risk was reduced. The outbreak prompted employer and school exclusion policies and vaccination offers for exposed employees.
- U.S. nationwide, 2011: The CDC reported 222 measles cases from 31 states and 17 outbreaks—an increase relative to the prior decade’s annual medians. About 90% of cases were linked to importations from countries where measles remains endemic; 32% were direct importations. Most U.S. cases were unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status; among vaccine-eligible U.S. residents with measles, a large proportion had philosophical, religious, or personal exemptions. Hospitalization occurred in about one-third of cases; no deaths were reported in 2011. Genotyping showed multiple imported strains. The CDC emphasized that measles elimination in the U.S. depends on maintaining high two-dose MMR coverage and rapid case recognition, reporting, isolation and vaccination.

Drivers and patterns
- Importations: International travel and measles’ continued circulation abroad are primary sources of U.S. cases. A large share of importations in 2011 originated in Europe and other regions with substantial outbreaks.
- Clusters of unvaccinated people: Local pockets with vaccination coverage below the ~95% needed for herd immunity (including low-income communities and affluent enclaves with high exemption rates) enable outbreaks after importation.
- Vaccine hesitancy and exemptions: Philosophical/religious objections and misinformation have contributed to under-vaccination in some groups; advocates of vaccine choice disputed immediate causal attribution in particular outbreaks, but public-health authorities see low coverage as a major risk factor.
- Healthcare-seeking and surveillance gaps: Misdiagnosis, delayed reporting, and undetected importations can allow transmission chains to spread before control measures begin.

Consequences
- High morbidity and preventable hospitalizations (including dehydration, pneumonia and diarrhea); some epidemics produced deaths (notably in 1988–1990 California) and substantial healthcare and outbreak-control costs.
- Disruption to schools and workplaces (exclusions, paid leave for pending immunity tests), strain on public health resources, and renewed public debate about vaccination policy.

Recommendations and responses
- Maintain and improve MMR vaccination coverage—routine schedule of first dose at 12–15 months and second dose at 4–6 years; adults without evidence of immunity should receive at least one MMR dose, with two doses recommended for health-care personnel, international travelers and certain student populations.
- Vaccinate eligible international travelers (children ≥6 months before travel, and routine 2-dose schedule for those ≥12 months).
- Rapid clinical suspicion, immediate isolation of suspected cases, prompt reporting to public health authorities, collection of specimens for laboratory confirmation and genotyping to trace importation sources.
- Public education and targeted vaccination in communities with low coverage; sufficient and timely public-health funding for outbreak control.
- Initiatives to engage broader public support for global health (e.g., advocacy campaigns to sustain international aid and vaccination efforts).

Overall message
Measles continues to threaten public health in the U.S. despite elimination of endemic transmission because of ongoing importations and local clusters of under-vaccinated people. Sustained high vaccination coverage, vigilant surveillance and rapid public-health response are essential to prevent outbreaks, reduce morbidity and preserve measles elimination.

With three Republicans still vying for the 2016 nomination, party leaders acknowledge a contested convention is possible but view the idea of selecting someone outside the current field as unlikely. RNC Chairman Reince Priebus called nominating a non-candidate an “extreme hypothetical,” though he conceded it’s technically possible and reiterated his expectation that one of the three active contenders will be the nominee.

Despite that, Politico reported high-level GOP operatives are still discussing House Speaker Paul Ryan as a potential compromise choice if the convention deadlocks. One insider gave a roughly 60% chance of a deadlock and a 90% chance delegates would turn to Ryan, who would chair the convention, creating speculation he could be asked to accept the nomination. Politico’s profile suggested Ryan deploys a tactic of publicly refusing power to maintain leverage.

Ryan, traveling in Israel, repeatedly rejected the idea on Hugh Hewitt’s radio show and in comments to The Times of Israel, saying he is not running and that “you need to run for president in order to be president.” He cited family reasons and a crowded field as part of his decision. Observers note, however, that Ryan has previously accepted leadership roles after saying he would not, so speculation may persist through the convention.

Critics warn the Ryan-for-nominee scenario would be fraught: it would risk party chaos after a long primary season; Ryan’s past national ticket experience and current polling offer no guarantee of broader electability; and a late-nominated candidate would lack the campaign infrastructure, platform, staff, and funding needed for a general-election run.

The document also includes a broader POLITICO Playbook roundup highlighting an escalating government crisis: a prolonged partial shutdown over border wall funding on day 27, the administration forcing some federal workers to work without pay, intensifying Pelosi–Trump clashes (including State of the Union dispute), concerns about governance and looming economic consequences, and a range of other political and policy items from investigations to personnel moves.

A Ride the Ducks amphibious tour boat capsized and sank on Table Rock Lake near Branson, Missouri, during a severe thunderstorm on the evening of July 19, 2018. Thirty-one people were aboard. Initial reports gave varying casualty counts; by the end of Friday investigators had recovered 17 bodies (victims aged 1–76, including nine members of one Indiana family), several people remained missing earlier in the recovery, and 14 survived (seven injured, two critically). The boat’s driver, Robert “Bob” Williams, 73, was among the dead; the captain survived.

A National Weather Service severe thunderstorm watch and later a warning—forecasting damaging winds and gusts up to 75 mph—had been issued hours before the storm. Authorities and some meteorologists noted the storm was well-predicted and questioned why the vessel remained on the lake. Witness video shows the duck boat pitching in high winds and waves before capsizing as it was heading back to shore. Local responders, dive teams and an off-duty deputy aided rescue efforts; the NTSB sent a “Go Team” to investigate and recover the sunken vessel from about 80 feet of water.

Ride the Ducks Branson (owned by Ripley Entertainment, purchased in 2017) said it was assisting authorities and noted no previous accidents in its 40-year Branson operation. Duck boats have been involved in other fatal incidents nationally, prompting longstanding safety concerns and NTSB recommendations (including added built-in flotation and design changes) and criticism that multiple regulators create inconsistent standards. Local officials set up family support at Branson City Hall and brought in grief counselors as the investigation continued.

Two men were arrested after allegedly using a taxi to burglarize a Deal, New Jersey, home and then refusing to pay the fare. Police say 46-year-old Kenneth Burke (Asbury Park) and 38-year-old Timothy Foote (Ocean Township) hailed a cab to a Norwood Avenue house on the evening of Nov. 4, told the driver to wait, then returned with a television and liquor bottles. The cabbie drove them to an Asbury Park apartment, where they exited without paying and the driver reported the incident. Deal officers found the house had been burglarized and recovered the stolen items, which were returned to the homeowner. Burke and Foote were charged with burglary, conspiracy to commit burglary, criminal trespass and theft, and were held at Monmouth County jail on $20,000 bail each; court dates are pending.

A tractor-trailer went over the side of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge‑Tunnel (CBBT) around 12:30 p.m. Thursday at mile marker 15. The driver, 47-year-old Joseph Chen of Greenville, North Carolina, was rescued from the water by a Navy MH-60 crew that was training nearby and hoisted into the helicopter after standing on top of the vehicle, but he died en route to the hospital. The Medical Examiner ruled the death accidental, caused by drowning and hypothermia.

Chen was hauling seafood for Evans Transports. A relative said he was a husband, father and founder/president of the Turn‑N‑Burn Motorcycle Club. Video showed a large section of damaged guardrail at the scene. The bridge was temporarily closed in both directions but reopened before 2 p.m.

Authorities had issued wind restrictions on the CBBT: a Level 1 restriction was in effect at the time of the crash and later moved to Level 2 (for winds over 47 mph), which places extra limits on tractor‑trailers. Meteorologists reported a water temperature of about 45°F and 5–7 foot waves at the time. The Virginia Trucking Association expressed condolences. WAVY noted prior similar incidents on the CBBT, including a fatal crash in 2014 and a nonfatal one in January 2016.

Taxi drivers across Europe staged large protests on June 11, 2014, blocking streets, airports and major thoroughfares in cities including London, Paris, Madrid, Berlin, Milan and Barcelona to oppose smartphone car‑hailing services such as Uber. More than 30,000 taxi and private‑hire drivers joined strikes and demonstrations that snarled traffic in tourist and commercial centers and disrupted airport access in Paris and elsewhere. Protesters accuse Uber and similar services of undercutting fares, flouting licensing, insurance and safety rules, and operating without the costly authorizations required of traditional cab drivers—threatening livelihoods built around heavily regulated local taxi markets.

London’s protest—featuring black cabs around Trafalgar and Parliament Squares—focused on whether Uber’s fare‑calculator amounts to an illegal taximeter; Transport for London has referred the question to the High Court. In Paris, most of the city’s taxis struck and slowed major approaches, causing long jams; Spain’s Catalonia and cities in Germany have moved to restrict or ban Uber‑style services. Authorities warned of arrests where assemblies lacked permission, but clashes and major accidents were not reported.

Uber, which has rapidly expanded to 128 cities and recently raised large funding rounds valuing it in the tens of billions, defended its legality and used the day to promote signups and discounts. The company argues it brings consumer choice, lower prices and job opportunities; regulators and courts across Europe are wrestling with how to apply existing transport rules to new technology. The protests reflect a wider backlash against disruptive platforms (e.g., Airbnb) as entrenched, regulated industries press for equal enforcement and protection against competitive change. European officials urged dialogue rather than strikes, but the demonstrations highlighted the significant political and regulatory challenges Uber and similar firms face in Europe.

Researchers warn that Darwin’s medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) faces a real risk of extinction within decades due to an introduced parasitic nest fly, Philornis downsi. First recorded in Galápagos nests in the 1990s but likely brought to the islands in the 1960s, P. downsi lays eggs in bird nests; larvae feed on brooding adults and, critically, on nestlings, killing large numbers of baby finches. Field experiments on Santa Cruz Island—comparing permethrin-treated (fly-reduced) nests with controls—provided five years of data used in population models under “good,” “neutral,” and “bad” reproductive scenarios.

Results show extinction is likely in two of three scenarios: under repeated poor breeding years the species could disappear in roughly 43–57 years, and under neutral conditions in about 65–95 years; only sustained favorable conditions allow survival up to ~100 years. Because Darwin’s finches are closely related, the threat probably extends to other species (the mangrove finch is already critically rare). The study identifies reducing nest fly infestations as a clear management target: models indicate that a ~40% reduction in infestations could prevent extinction.

Proposed interventions include insecticide-treated nests, sterile-male release, biological control (parasitoid wasps), and hand-rearing vulnerable chicks. There is also a possibility of a rapid evolutionary response by the finches, but whether adaptation can outpace the fly-driven decline is uncertain. The crisis is particularly stark because the Galápagos’ intact avifauna is invaluable for studying evolution; researchers emphasize that the situation stems from a human-mediated introduction of the fly and call for action to avert the finches’ loss.

The document also discusses broader questions about egg coloration and camouflage: recent research (Current Biology) supports the long-held idea that eggshell colors and speckling—exemplified by Japanese quail and many other species—function largely as camouflage, with mothers often selecting nesting sites that minimize mismatch with their own eggs’ patterns. The evolution of egg appearance can also be exploited by brood parasites (e.g., cuckoos) that mimic host egg patterns to trick parents into raising unrelated chicks.

A video posted by Yankee Farmer’s Market in Warner, N.H., of a newborn Scottish Highland calf named Diego (also called Pitcher Diego) warming after being born in a snowstorm went viral, drawing roughly 12–13 million views and tens of thousands of shares. The short clip — which shows the fluffy calf tied with a red rope and being dried with a hair dryer before being returned to his mother — prompted a heated, polarized response: many viewers found it adorable and left supportive comments, while animal-rights critics accused the farm of preparing the calf for slaughter and attempted to hurt the farm’s reputation by driving down its Facebook reviews and offering to adopt the calf.

Farm owner Brian Farmer said the criticism is based on misconceptions: Diego was returned to his mother, Yankee Farmer’s Market doesn’t produce veal or slaughter on site (that requires USDA licensing), and the farm raises animals — including Scottish Highlands and buffalo — on pasture without antibiotics or hormones. Farmer said Diego is likely to be registered as breeding stock to help restore a long-established Highland herd rather than being sent to market. He expressed frustration at the negative reaction but also gratitude for local supporters who defended the farm. Farmer said he will keep posting about the animals to educate people about his husbandry practices and the difference between small-scale, pasture-based farming and industrial production.

The FDA issued a Sept. 22, 2009 safety alert about Philips Lifeline pendant personal help buttons worn on neck cords, warning they can pose a choking/strangulation hazard because the cords are intentionally non–breakaway to prevent the button falling off. The agency reported at least six serious injuries or deaths (including three U.S. deaths and one in Canada) from 1998–2009 tied to entanglement of the Lifeline cord. More than 750,000 people in the U.S. and Canada use the device, primarily seniors living independently to summon emergency help. Philips Lifeline began notifying customers and updated product labeling to warn of the risk. The FDA advised users to consult health care providers to choose the safest style (for example, wrist-worn units) appropriate to their mobility and living situation, noting non–breakaway cords are especially risky for people using wheelchairs, walkers, or beds with rails. The FDA encouraged reporting adverse events to MedWatch.

The alert is linked to a local case: 86-year-old Roseann J. DiFrancesco of New Cumberland, Pa., was found dead after her medical-alert lanyard became caught on her walker following a fall; the coroner ruled the death accidental and said the lanyard lacked a breakaway feature. The incident underscores the FDA’s concerns and the tradeoff manufacturers cite between breakaway lanyards (which reduce strangulation risk) and the risk that a device could be out of reach if the lanyard breaks.

Kuşköy, a remote village on Turkey’s Black Sea coast, looks typical for the region but is notable for its whistled form of Turkish—locally called kuş dili or “bird language.” Whistled languages, documented in about 42 places worldwide, arise in rugged or forested terrain because high-pitched whistles carry far. In Kuşköy, ordinary Turkish syllables are converted into piercing whistles made with tongue, teeth and fingers; a common sentence such as “Taze ekmek var mı?” becomes six distinct whistles audible over half a mile.

Biopsychologist Onur Güntürkün studied how the brain processes this musical form of language. Using dichotic-listening tests with 31 bilingual speakers of spoken and whistled Turkish, he found that spoken syllables tend to be processed primarily by the left hemisphere (the usual language-dominant side), while whistled syllables engaged both hemispheres roughly equally. Though dichotic listening is an indirect measure, the findings suggest that the brain’s lateralization for language is more flexible than assumed and raise the possibility that whistled speech could help people with left-hemisphere damage recover communicative abilities, analogous to how singing can aid some stroke patients.

Despite its cultural and scientific value, Kuşköy’s bird language is declining. Mid-20th-century accounts described widespread everyday use by children and adults; today few young women know it and some men learn it only as a teen rite. Modern practices like texting and tourism-oriented whistling contests have reduced its practical role, though whistled Turkish remains a recognized, occasionally useful link to local identity—residents will even whistle to be understood when calling Güntürkün’s German-speaking university office.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, 62, the head of the International Monetary Fund, has been held at New York’s Rikers Island jail since his arraignment on charges including attempted rape and other sexual offenses. Because of concerns raised during his intake mental-health evaluation, he has been placed on suicide watch and is being checked around the clock. For security and health reasons he occupies a nearly empty wing used for contagious-disease cases, has a single cell with sink and toilet, eats meals there, and may leave the cell under guard for limited supervised time and outdoor recreation. He was issued a CPAP machine for sleep apnea and, as a pretrial detainee, may wear his own clothes in the cell but must wear standard slip-on shoes and a pocketless gray jumpsuit for visits. He is being held without bail pending further court appearances. The maid who accused him is reportedly in hiding; Strauss-Kahn’s lawyer denies the allegations.

A large, coordinated replication effort led by the Open Science Collaboration attempted to reproduce 100 recent studies from major psychology journals. Using high-powered designs, original materials where available, and consultation with the original authors, the project found that only 39 of the 100 studies produced results the teams judged to replicate the originals. Other metrics showed similar shortfalls: while 97% of the original studies reported statistically significant results, only 36% of the replications did; mean effect sizes in replications were about half those of the originals; and only 47% of original effect sizes fell within the 95% confidence intervals of the replication effects. When original and replication data were combined (assuming no bias in the originals), 68% of effects remained statistically significant.

The authors emphasize several interpretations: some original findings may have been false positives; some replications may have failed to detect real effects; and in many cases both studies could be accurate but differ in subtle, important methodological or contextual ways (for example, participant pools or task difficulty differing across sites). Correlational analyses indicated that the strength of the original evidence (e.g., original p-values) predicted replication success better than characteristics of the teams doing the work.

The project highlights broader issues in science: incentives favor novel, striking results over direct replications, and practices such as selective reporting and incomplete specification of experimental conditions can reduce reproducibility. The authors frame their findings not as a crisis but as an opportunity for self-correction—arguing for greater emphasis on replication, clearer methodological standards, and changes in publication and research priorities to improve the reliability and credibility of psychological science.

University of Cincinnati President Santa Ono publicly revealed that he attempted suicide twice — once at 14 and again in his late 20s — and has been symptom-free for about 25 years after receiving medication and professional help. He made the disclosure while speaking at a mental-health fundraiser for teen-focused group 1N5 and then shared it with his 70,000+ Twitter followers to reduce stigma and encourage people to seek treatment. Ono’s announcement comes as UC continues to confront student suicide: after the 2014 death of student Brogan Dulle, Ono helped expand campus mental-health services so students can receive five free counseling sessions and be referred for further care. UC health leaders and Dulle’s mother praised Ono’s openness as powerful and potentially life-saving, noting that college-aged people are especially vulnerable to depression and suicide. The story also lists local and national mental-health resources (UC Counseling & Psychological Services, National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, Crisis Text Line, Hamilton County services, Lindner Center of HOPE, and student group Active Minds).

A contested Virginia House race between Democrat Shelly Simonds and Republican Del. David Yancey left control of the House of Delegates uncertain after a three-judge panel declined to certify a recount, ruling a disputed ballot should be counted for Yancey and creating an exact tie in the Newport News 94th District.

Background and recount: On Election Day Yancey led by 10 votes. A hand recount initially produced a one-vote victory for Simonds, which would have produced a 50–50 House split and ended 17 years of GOP control. Republican leaders had briefly conceded and pledged to share power. The reversal came after a ballot that had been set aside during the recount — marked for both candidates but with Simonds’s name struck through — was reviewed in court. Judges, all elected by a GOP-controlled legislature, determined the strikeout showed the voter's intent to support Yancey and ordered the ballot counted for him.

Legal and political fallout: Democrats called the court decision erroneous and said they were assessing legal options; Marc Elias, counsel for the House Democratic caucus, criticized Republicans for first accepting the recount results and then changing course. Democrats noted guidance from the Virginia Department of Elections that certain double-marked ballots can be counted if additional marks indicate voter intent. Some legal experts expressed skepticism about Democratic remedies. If the tie stands, state law resolves it by lot — a drawing scheduled for Dec. 27 — though the losing side could seek another recount.

Wider context: The razor-thin race was part of a Democratic surge in Virginia that flipped multiple House seats and kept the governor’s office. The dispute highlights how every ballot can be decisive and recalls how some jurisdictions historically break ties by chance (coin tosses, etc.). Other recounts in Virginia were ongoing and could affect the balance of power. With the overall House balance temporarily at 50–49 for Republicans, Democrats delayed formally choosing a speaker and are weighing power-sharing options if the contested outcomes are not resolved.

Dozens of concertgoers were treated or hospitalized after Avicii’s June 25, 2014 show at TD Garden in Boston. Local reports put the total needing medical attention between about 30 and 80; Boston EMS said roughly 50 were treated on site and 36 transported to hospitals, while Massachusetts General Hospital reported receiving 13 patients aged 16–19. Officials said most cases involved dehydration, heavy alcohol consumption and some illicit drug use; the majority of patients were between 16 and 25 and none were reported in serious condition.

Dozens of ambulances responded, a staging area was set up on Causeway Street, and police issued citations for intoxication and drug use. Three men were arrested on drug charges nearby, though they were not linked to the hospitalizations. TD Garden said it had provided extra security, restricted alcohol sales and cooling areas and is taking the incident seriously; city officials planned meetings with venue management. Avicii (Tim Bergling) tweeted his concern for those affected. The event followed other recent large-music–festival medical incidents nationally, drawing attention to heat, underage drinking and drug use at dance-music shows.

Burger King is testing a new menu mash-up called the "Whopperito" — essentially a Whopper wrapped in a flour tortilla. Observed at several Pennsylvania locations (first reported by Grub Grade), the item contains the usual Whopper ingredients — flame-grilled beef, American cheese, tomatoes, lettuce, mayo, ketchup, pickles and onions — substituted inside a tortilla instead of a bun. Burger King has been contacted to confirm whether the item is a corporate test or a franchise experiment. It’s unclear if the Whopperito will roll out more widely, and the announcement has generated mixed reactions on Twitter, ranging from disgust to enthusiasm. The concept isn’t entirely new to fans who previously combined Burger King and Taco Bell items themselves.

China urged the United States on Wednesday to bar a Taiwanese delegation from attending Donald Trump’s inauguration, warning that such participation or any official contacts with Taiwan would interfere with China-U.S. ties. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying said Beijing had communicated the request to both Trump’s transition team and the outgoing Obama administration and reiterated China’s firm opposition to any actions it views as undermining the “One China” principle. 

The delegation, led by former Taiwanese premier Yu Shyi-kun and including lawmakers and a national security adviser, was scheduled to attend Friday’s inauguration and to meet with U.S. politicians, academics and overseas Taiwanese. Taipei said no meetings with the incoming administration were planned during the visit. It is routine for Taiwan to send delegations to U.S. inaugurations.

The dispute follows Trump’s post-election phone call with Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen and his comments that the U.S. “One China” policy could be renegotiated—moves that angered Beijing. China views Taiwan as a breakaway province and has never renounced use of force to achieve reunification; Taiwan’s democratically elected Tsai rejects unification under Beijing and says she seeks to maintain peace. The episode highlights heightened tensions across the Taiwan Strait and concern in Beijing about possible shifts in U.S. policy.

Palau’s president Tommy Remengesau is pushing a tourism shift from mass visits to high-end, low-volume travel by proposing a law that would permit only five‑star hotel developments going forward. The plan offers tax breaks to luxury investors who also build and provide their own infrastructure (roads, water treatment, power backups), aiming to attract wealthier visitors who spend more locally while reducing environmental and social pressures from large numbers of tourists.

Tourism accounts for about 85% of Palau’s GDP, but rising visitor numbers—especially low‑spending Chinese package tourists—have caused overcrowding, reef damage and wildlife disturbance. The government previously halved charter flights from China in 2015 and says that reduced arrivals but increased total tourist spending, supporting the “quality over quantity” strategy. A few five‑star resorts currently exist around Koror; the new policy seeks more such developments across Palau’s many islands, though questions remain about whether future projects will be sustainably designed to protect the islands’ natural assets.

The Supreme Court declined to narrow a federal ban that bars people convicted of misdemeanor domestic-violence offenses from possessing firearms. In a 6–2 decision, the justices rejected challenges from two Maine men who argued their guilty pleas for hitting their partners — including incidents they said were committed in the heat of the moment or were not intentional — should not trigger the federal prohibition. The ruling leaves intact lower-court precedent and upholds that the statute reaches reckless as well as intentional domestic-abuse conduct, a position backed by advocates for victims. Gun-rights groups had argued the men should not lose Second Amendment rights based on misdemeanor convictions, but a federal appeals court and now the Supreme Court disagreed.

Nigeria's military says it has arrested the leader of a Boko Haram intelligence cell, Babuji Ya'ari, and several women alleged to be part of the unit thought linked to the April abduction of more than 200 schoolgirls from Chibok. The defence ministry accused Ya'ari—a businessman who posed as a vigilante of coordinating deadly attacks, including the killing of the emir of Gwoza in May and strikes in Maiduguri since 2011. The military’s claims have not been independently verified and Ya'ari has not commented.

The abduction of the schoolgirls on 14 April left most still missing; Boko Haram demands the release of imprisoned fighters in exchange for the girls.
