A viral YouTube clip shows a woman in behind-the-scenes footage from Charlie Chaplin’s 1928 film The Circus appearing to hold a small black object to her ear and walk while seemingly engaged in conversation. Belfast fan George Clarke posted the clip in 2010 after studying the footage for over a year; he says he repeatedly rewound and zoomed the moment and cannot explain it, suggesting — along with some viewers — that it looks like a person using a mobile phone or even a time traveler. The clip generated wide interest (over 1.3 million views) and many theories in the comments, ranging from a hearing aid or handheld personal device to more fanciful ideas like secret government operations. Clarke invited viewers to draw their own conclusions after watching the footage.

An 18-year-old college student, Connor Golden of Fairfax County, Virginia, lost part of his left leg after stepping on a homemade explosive in Central Park on July 3 while visiting New York with two friends. The blast occurred around 11 a.m. near Fifth Avenue and East 60th–68th Street as the trio were climbing rocks to scout a slacklining spot. Witnesses described a very loud explosion and severe trauma; bystanders applied a tourniquet before EMS took Golden to Bellevue Hospital, where surgeons amputated below the knee. 

The NYPD Bomb Squad investigated and determined the blast was caused by an amateur-made firework or “explosive experimentation” left in a brown bag and not deliberately designed to be pressure-sensitive or to harm people. Investigators said the device appeared to have been left for more than a day and likely detonated from friction after being stepped on; there was no evidence linking the incident to terrorism, and the victim and his friends are not suspected of making the device. Authorities searched the area, interviewed the friends, and urged anyone with information to come forward. Mayor Bill de Blasio and NYPD officials stressed the incident was isolated and cautioned the public to leave fireworks to professionals.

Former President George W. Bush’s official White House portrait was unveiled at a ceremony where he and President Obama appeared cordial. The portrait shows Bush standing in the Oval Office with his hands on a chair in a conventional, forward-gazing political pose.

A notable detail is the painting depicted behind Bush in the portrait: a Western rider that Bush long believed represented nineteenth-century Methodist circuit riders and for which he named his 1999 memoir, A Charge to Keep. Investigations and reporting (notably by Jacob Weisberg) have challenged that provenance: the image actually first appeared as an illustration for a 1918 Country Gentleman story about a son defending inherited land, not Methodist missionaries. Some aspects of Weisberg’s account—confusion between similar Howard or Frank Koerner illustrations—have been disputed, and scholars note at least one later confirmed appearance of the composition, but the missionary interpretation is likely incorrect.

The article also explains how presidential portraits are chosen and paid for: presidents select their own artists after reviewing many submissions, sometimes with help from the White House curator or the National Portrait Gallery. Portrait costs are generally covered by private donations organized through the White House Historical Association rather than by direct taxpayer funding. The piece places the Bush portrait in the long tradition of official presidential portraits housed in the White House and National Portrait Gallery, noting several historically significant examples.

A paywall notice appears at the top asking readers to subscribe after five free articles. The article reports that Jesse L. Matthew Jr., 33, the man accused in the disappearance and killing of University of Virginia sophomore Hannah Graham, has had the charge in her case upgraded from first-degree murder to capital murder, making him potentially eligible for the death penalty if convicted. Authorities say Graham, 18, went missing in September after leaving friends in Charlottesville; witnesses and surveillance last saw her with Matthew at about 1 a.m. on Sept. 13. Her body was found weeks later about 10 miles from campus. Prosecutors allege Matthew abducted Graham “with intent to defile,” indicating an intended sexual assault. Albemarle County’s commonwealth’s attorney initially chose not to seek a capital charge after consulting Graham’s family but later upgraded the charge. Matthew also faces separate charges from a 2005 attack in Fairfax City, where his DNA was reportedly found under a victim’s fingernail.

Vice President Joe Biden chose Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor to administer his oath at the private Jan. 20 ceremony, making her the fourth woman and first Hispanic to swearing in a president or vice president. President Barack Obama will follow tradition and be sworn in by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr.; both oaths will be performed twice — privately on Sunday, Jan. 20 (the Constitutionally mandated date, which fell on a Sunday) and publicly on Monday, Jan. 21 at the Capitol before an expected crowd of up to 800,000.

Biden praised Sotomayor as a friend and an exemplar of justice and opportunity. Obama’s private swearing-in will be an intimate family affair at the White House Blue Room, with a larger public inauguration and his second inaugural address reserved for Monday, where he will outline his second-term priorities—economic recovery, immigration reform, gun control and winding down the war in Afghanistan—while saving detailed policy plans for the State of the Union. The weekend also featured community service events the Obamas hope will become an inaugural tradition.

The piece notes the sometimes tense relationship between Obama and Chief Justice Roberts, recalled from their bungled 2009 oath do‑over and subsequent ideological clashes—highlighted by Obama’s criticism of the Supreme Court after Citizens United—though Roberts joined the court’s liberals in upholding the individual mandate in 2012. Legal analysts expect further high‑profile conflicts between the president and the Roberts‑led Court over issues like affirmative action, immigration and environmental policy.

A Cincinnati woman treated at the University of Cincinnati Medical Center (UCMC) has sued the hospital, a named employee (Ryan Rawls), an unnamed UC employee believed to be a nurse, and her ex‑boyfriend, alleging that staff posted her medical record — including her name and a syphilis diagnosis — to a Facebook group called "Team No Hoes" in September 2013. A screenshot of the record was reportedly posted and emailed to members of the closed group and accompanied by insulting comments. The suit claims the ex‑boyfriend convinced UCMC employees to release the records, and that the hospital negligently supervised staff and failed to prevent further distribution; it also says the plaintiff continues to receive harassing calls.

Attorney Mike Allen says the disclosure devastated the woman, causing social ostracism and emotional distress. The plaintiff seeks more than $25,000 in damages for invasion of privacy, emotional distress, malice and negligence and requests a jury trial.

UCMC has acknowledged the lawsuit, reminded employees that unauthorized access or sharing of protected health information is a serious violation subject to termination, and said it will investigate but cannot comment on pending litigation. Some defendants have disputed involvement; Rawls told reporters she did not leak or post the records.

- What happened: In early October a US special forces detachment on a joint patrol with about 30 Nigerien troops was ambushed near the village of Tongo Tongo in southwest Niger. About 50 fighters—believed linked to an IS-aligned group—attacked with small arms, RPGs and mortars. Four U.S. soldiers and five Nigerien soldiers died.

- How the fight unfolded: The patrol had been in the village late at night and had earlier destroyed an extremist camp. Sources say roughly half the patrol passed through an ambush “kill zone” before it was sprung, trapping the rear elements. After the attack began the lead group turned to fight but, according to retired and serving special-operations personnel familiar with the incident, most Nigerien soldiers quickly withdrew, leaving small U.S. groups (about six men each) to fight for hours against a numerically superior force. A U.S. drone arrived but was unarmed. Ground troops on the scene requested air support; French Mirage jets from Mali responded but reportedly declined to engage because of poor weather, terrain and difficulty distinguishing friend from foe. French helicopter-borne forces later reached the site after roughly two hours and evacuated survivors; three U.S. bodies were recovered from the scene and the fourth (Sgt. La David Johnson) was found two days later about a half-mile away; some accounts say he may have been captured then executed.

- Casualties and equipment: Four Americans (two of them Green Berets) and five Nigerien soldiers were killed. One pickup became stuck and suffered heavy losses. Many in the U.S. special-operations community say most of the American team had little combat experience and were not warned to expect contact.

- Aftermath and controversy: The attack prompted a Pentagon investigation by AFRICOM and intense political debate in Washington about the scope and oversight of U.S. “train and equip” missions that can slide into direct combat. Republicans including Senator John McCain called it an intelligence failure tied to budget cuts. The incident also triggered a separate public controversy over President Trump’s handling of condolence calls to victims’ families. Leaks and internal messages from the special-forces community reflect anger and accusations of a “blame game” over how the mission was characterized and what went wrong.

- Additional details: Reports say insurgents burned surrounding bush to create smoke, complicating the battle. A nearby second U.S.–Nigerien team was reportedly redirected and later helped recover bodies. Local sources and CBS reporting indicate attackers may have tried to kidnap Sgt. Johnson before he was killed; Nigerien authorities maintain the patrol’s mission included a capture-or-kill objective against an extremist leader.

Tiger Woods opened the PGA Championship at Atlanta Athletic Club with a shocking 77, leaving him tied for 129th after an early share of the lead. He birdied three of his first five holes to sit 3-under, but then collapsed—carding three double bogeys (15, 18, and 6) and five additional bogeys—finishing 7-over for the round. The 77 is his highest opening round in a major and one of his worst professional rounds. Woods attributed the collapse to trying to play by feel while still reworking his swing and said he was “very angry” but not down. The poor start imperils his spot in the PGA Championship (he must make the cut—top 70 and ties—to continue) and could have wider implications: he sits 129th in FedEx Cup points and needs to climb into the top 125 by next week’s Wyndham Championship to reach the playoffs. First-round leader Steve Stricker shot a 63, matching a major record.

Daniel Holtzclaw, a 29-year-old former Oklahoma City police officer, was sentenced on 21 January 2016 to 263 years in prison after a jury convicted him in December on 18 of 36 counts, including multiple counts of first‑degree rape, forced oral sodomy and sexual battery. Prosecutors say Holtzclaw preyed on African‑American women in one of the city’s poorest neighborhoods over a six‑month period beginning in June 2014, targeting women with drug‑ or prostitution‑related records whom he believed would be less likely to be believed. Thirteen women testified at trial, describing a pattern of stops while he was on duty that escalated from groping and coercion to rape; victims included a 17‑year‑old and a 57‑year‑old grandmother whose complaint helped trigger the investigation and arrest. Victims recounted threats, fear for their lives and assaults that sometimes occurred while they were handcuffed or in a hospital bed.

Holtzclaw, who is biracial (white and Japanese), waived his right to testify and cried when the verdicts were announced. His defense argued he was trying to help addicts and prostitutes and later sought a new trial alleging discovery violations; that motion and an initial appeal were denied. Civil lawsuits by victims against Holtzclaw and Oklahoma City are pending. Community activists and civil‑rights attorney Benjamin Crump called the sentence a significant vindication for the victims and for broader concerns about the historical abuse of black women. Holtzclaw was fired in January 2015 after an internal investigation.

In 1890 Thomas Edison produced about 500 of the first talking dolls: roughly two-foot-tall figures with wooden limbs, metal bodies and a tiny, spring-wound wax-cylinder phonograph in their torsos. Edison marketed them as a way to bring the new phonograph into homes, having factory workers (likely women) record simple nursery verses such as “Hickory Dickory Dock” and prayers. The resulting audio is raw and unsettling—the recordings sound thin and eerie today, and contemporaries (including Edison) found them unpleasant. The dolls were expensive (about $200 in today’s dollars), not lifelike enough (mouths didn’t move and speech was hard to understand), and sales collapsed within a month; Edison later called them “little monsters.”

Modern scanning technology has recently made some of these fragile wax-cylinder recordings audible again. Scholars place the dolls’ creepiness in the context of the “uncanny”: talking toys sit uneasily between human and nonhuman, reviving childhood projections and fears about giving power to objects that might “turn back on us.”

An Ohio coroner said she could not determine what caused the severe brain damage that led to the death of 22-year-old University of Virginia student Otto Warmbier, who had been detained in North Korea for 17 months. Dr. Lakshmi Sammarco’s Sept. 11 report listed the cause of death as complications from chronic anoxic/ischemic encephalopathy — lack of oxygen and blood to the brain from an unknown injury more than a year before his death — and the manner of death as undetermined.

Warmbier was returned to the U.S. in a coma on June 13, 2017 and died six days later. His parents have accused North Korea of torturing him; North Korea denies mistreatment, saying he suffered botulism and complications from a sleeping pill. Sammarco said medical imaging (“virtual autopsy”) and external examination — performed at the family’s request instead of a full autopsy — found no evidence of botulism, no broken bones or healing fractures, and no dental trauma, though there were multiple scars and bruises some consistent with medical care. His body appeared well-nourished and showed no signs of bedsores, suggesting he received regular care while incapacitated.

Sammarco emphasized that without definitive evidence or testimony from those present when the initial injury occurred, the precise cause and circumstances of the brain injury likely will remain unknown. The case has fueled sharp accusations between the Warmbier family, the U.S. administration and North Korea amid broader tensions over the country’s nuclear and missile programs.

A stovepipe hat long promoted as Abraham Lincoln’s centerpiece at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum is likely not provable as his, according to two independent inquiries and a previously undisclosed FBI analysis reported by WBEZ.

Key points:
- The beaver-fur hat, acquired in 2007 as part of a $25 million purchase of Lincolniana and appraised at $6.5 million, has been the focus of authentication efforts after questions about its provenance first surfaced in 2012.
- A 2013 report by senior curators from the Smithsonian National Museum of American History and the Chicago History Museum concluded the documentation is insufficient to claim the hat belonged to Lincoln and urged the museum to “soften its claim,” avoid using the hat publicly until further research, and even consider asking the seller to take it back.
- In 2015 the FBI performed DNA testing comparing material from the hat to Lincoln-linked items (blood-stained handkerchief, clothing, hair). The FBI reported mostly contemporary DNA consistent with recent handlers and found no conclusive match to Lincoln; the analysis was described as inconclusive.
- The testing and reports were handled with secrecy: the foundation that bought the collection required confidentiality, the FBI insisted on discretion, and museum staff reportedly encouraged agents to disguise themselves while on-site. Current museum director Alan Lowe says he only recently saw the full curatorial report and was surprised at the lack of transparency.
- Foundation vice chairman Nick Kalm defends the foundation’s actions, saying the tests didn’t disprove the hat’s provenance and that the organization pursued rigorous steps, including involving the FBI. He also argued there was no obligation to release full reports while fundraising.
- The revelations arrive as the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library Foundation faces financial strain—seeking state support and donations to pay nearly $9.7 million in loans tied to the Taper collection—and have prompted calls for legislative scrutiny from local lawmakers upset the reports were not fully disclosed to state officials or museum leadership earlier.
- The museum has removed the hat from display and says it will not exhibit it again until further research and an internal investigation are completed.

Bottom line: Independent curators and FBI testing failed to produce definitive evidence that the hat belonged to Abraham Lincoln. Questions remain about provenance, the foundation’s handling of the authentication process, and transparency as it seeks public and private funding.

Richard Grenell, an openly gay Republican who was hired in mid‑April as Mitt Romney’s foreign policy and national security spokesman, resigned from the campaign less than two weeks later amid intense controversy. Grenell said he stepped down because partisan focus on his personal life had “greatly diminished” his ability to speak forcefully on policy; he also thanked Romney for treating his sexual orientation as a “non‑issue.”

His brief tenure drew two main lines of attack: social conservatives denounced his appointment because he is gay, and commentators dug up—and he deleted—past provocative tweets criticizing public figures (including Hillary Clinton, Rachel Maddow and Callista Gingrich). Those revelations, plus pressure from anti‑gay groups and conservative outlets like National Review and Daily Caller, led the campaign to largely keep him off national security briefings and out of public roles. Campaign manager Matt Rhoades said the campaign was disappointed by his decision and valued his qualifications. Attempts by senior Republicans to persuade Grenell to stay were unsuccessful.

Less than a week before they were found dead, Honey and Barry Sherman were making normal plans for their annual winter trip to Florida. On Friday their bodies were discovered in their North York, Toronto, mansion by someone associated with the property; both were found hanging near the indoor basement pool. Police have ruled the cause of death for both as "ligature neck compression" and the homicide squad has taken over the investigation, though authorities initially described the deaths as "suspicious" and said they could not yet say whether foul play was involved. Media reports and unnamed police sources floated an early theory of murder‑suicide, but the Shermans’ grown children and many friends strongly rejected that suggestion.

Barry Sherman, 75, was the founder of generic‑drug company Apotex and was estimated to be worth about $4.77 billion; Honey Sherman, 70, was an active philanthropist and board member of several charities and institutions. The couple were prominent in Toronto’s Jewish and philanthropic circles and had four adult children and a new grandchild. Neighbours, colleagues and public figures expressed shock and grief; police reported no signs of forced entry and said they were not searching for outstanding suspects while the investigation continues.

On his first trip to Europe since the inauguration, US Vice‑President Mike Pence told the Munich Security Conference that the Trump administration strongly supports NATO but expects European allies to materially increase defence spending. Pence said only five NATO members — the US, UK, Estonia, Greece and Poland — currently meet the alliance’s 2% of GDP defence-spending guideline and warned that many large allies “do not have a credible path” to meet the target. He invoked NATO’s burden‑sharing obligations and echoed President Trump’s criticism that countries must “pay their share,” while also assuring audiences that the US commitment to the alliance remains “unwavering.”

Pence balanced that pressure with a call for holding Russia accountable — insisting Moscow honour the 2015 Minsk agreement on Ukraine even as the US seeks “new common ground.” His remarks came directly after German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s address, in which she rejected being bullied over defence spending, noted Germany’s planned decade‑long increases, and argued that military spending is only one element of security (highlighting development aid). Merkel urged multilateral cooperation over “parochialism” and defended press freedom in veiled critiques of Trump‑era rhetoric.

The exchange illustrated early tensions between the Trump administration and major European partners over timelines and priorities for increased defence commitments, while both sides signalled continued willingness to work together on security issues and to confront Russian actions in Ukraine.

The IUCN’s latest Red List update finds the giraffe has suffered a dramatic decline—about 36–40%—over the past 30 years, dropping from roughly 152–163,000 individuals in 1985 to about 97,500 in 2015. As a result, Giraffa camelopardalis has been reclassified from Least Concern to Vulnerable. Major drivers are habitat loss and fragmentation from human population growth, agricultural expansion, mining and infrastructure; illegal hunting and poaching; civil unrest and conflict (which make giraffes easy targets and reduce conservation capacity); and localized disease and human–wildlife conflict. The IUCN treats giraffe as one species with nine subspecies for this assessment: five subspecies are declining, one is stable and three are increasing. Declines are most severe in central and eastern Africa (some subspecies have fallen by up to 95%), while several southern African populations have increased thanks to active park management and translocations for tourism-focused conservation.

Experts warn of a “silent extinction” because giraffes’ declines went largely unnoticed compared with high-profile species like elephants and rhinos. Conservationists say solutions exist—improved protected-area management, targeted monitoring, anti-poaching efforts, national strategies (e.g., Kenya’s), and international attention following the IUCN listing could help stabilize and recover populations, but urgent, well-funded action is required to prevent further losses and possible extinctions of some subspecies.

The Red List update also highlights broader biodiversity concerns: over 85,600 species are now assessed, with 24,307 threatened. The update included reassessments of birds (adding 742 newly recognised species, 11% threatened), the first assessments of 233 crop wild relatives (many threatened, which has implications for food security), and comprehensive coverage of Lake Victoria freshwater species—underscoring habitat loss, invasive species and other human pressures across taxa.

After the FBI searched Mr. Trump’s home, he moved from a cooperative legal strategy to a more confrontational one, hiring Rudy Giuliani (and later Emmet Flood) to replace John Dowd. Giuliani has led a public-relations offensive against special counsel Robert Mueller, promoting unfounded theories (including claims that the FBI tried to frame Trump or planted a spy) and attacking key witnesses such as former FBI director James Comey. Trump’s team argues Comey undermined his own credibility and points to an inspector general report critical of the FBI as validation.

Giuliani has repeatedly shifted and raised conditions for whether Trump will submit to an interview with Mueller, demanding that Mueller first show evidence that Trump committed a crime and that an interview is strictly necessary. Those moves — plus missed self-imposed deadlines — reflect a broader strategy to delay the process, undermine the investigation’s credibility before the midterm elections, and influence public opinion so that impeachment would become politically unviable even if Mueller’s report is damaging.

The campaign to discredit Mueller has included congressional pressure on Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein and publicizing debunked claims such as “Spygate.” Polling cited shows Mueller’s public standing has weakened, particularly among Republicans, suggesting the tactics may be having some effect.

Filmmaker Michael Bay was assaulted on Oct. 17, 2013, while filming Transformers: Age of Extinction in Hong Kong but was not seriously hurt. Bay and his press representative say the incident began when several men—apparently trying to extort “disturbance fees” from the production—had been harassing crew and demanding thousands of dollars. One man returned carrying a long air-conditioning unit and swung it at Bay’s head; Bay says he ducked, wrested the unit away and security and police subdued the assailant. Local reports and Reuters indicated two men were arrested (later reports said three or four arrests), with charges including assault and suspected blackmail; some accounts said Bay suffered minor facial injuries but his team later called reports of injuries erroneous. Bay described the attacker as acting “like a zombie,” biting a guard’s shoe, and said filming resumed that same day.

Researchers led by Rachel Winograd (University of Missouri, St. Louis) tested whether people really become different personalities when intoxicated. In a lab study of 156 participants who drank either a placebo (Sprite) or a vodka–Sprite mix to a target BAC of ~0.09, individuals completed personality measures before and after drinking and were also rated on video by outside observers. Participants reported changes across all five Big Five traits after drinking (less conscientiousness, openness, and agreeableness; more extraversion and emotional stability). Observers, however, detected reliable change only in extraversion—specifically higher gregariousness, assertiveness, and activity—while other traits showed little observable difference. The authors suggest the gap reflects different vantage points: drinkers feel internal changes that observers can’t see, whereas observers reliably detect outward shifts (notably louder or more sociable behavior). They note expectations about “drunk personality” and the lab setting may influence results and call for replication in natural drinking environments and exploration of clinical implications.

A JetBlue red-eye flight from Portland to JFK descended into chaos when 18-year-old Robert “Sandy” Vietze, a member of the U.S. Ski Team’s development roster, allegedly urinated on a sleeping 11-year-old girl aboard the plane. The girl had been briefly unattended while her father and sister used the lavatory; Vietze, seated five rows back, stumbled to her and relieved himself. Witnesses say the girl’s father—reported to be a Stage 4 cancer patient—caught Vietze midstream and angrily confronted him; flight attendants separated the men, cleaned the child as best they could using lavatory soap, and comforted her.

Vietze told police he was drunk and had consumed about eight alcoholic beverages. A separate passenger later had a medical episode (chest pains and vomiting) on the same flight, prompting a request for medical volunteers. On arrival at JFK, Port Authority officers met the plane; Vietze was issued a federal summons for indecent exposure and released. Federal prosecutors ultimately declined to pursue charges; reports suggest the father’s refusal to have his daughter interviewed contributed to that decision.

Following the incident, Vietze was removed from the U.S. Ski Team’s developmental roster. He and his family declined comment; the girl’s family sought to recover from the episode privately.

Ridley Scott’s Prometheus (2012) is an ambitious, visually striking science‑fiction film that mixes philosophical questions about human origins with pulp‑horror set pieces. Intentionally linked to Scott’s earlier masterpieces Alien (1979) and Blade Runner (1982), it borrows aesthetic DNA from Alien but goes in a different direction: creepier and more idea‑driven than purely terrifying. Critics praise Scott’s world‑building, production design (H.R. Giger influences), cinematography and his economical use of 3‑D, and single out Michael Fassbender’s android David as the film’s standout performance; Charlize Theron and Idris Elba also contribute strong support, while Noomi Rapace grows into the role as the story intensifies.

The plot: archaeologists Elizabeth Shaw (Rapace) and Charlie Holloway (Logan Marshall‑Green) discover prehistoric pictograms showing humans worshiping a star‑pointing figure. Concluding that “engineers” from elsewhere helped seed life on Earth, they secure funding from industrialist Peter Weyland to mount an interstellar expedition aboard the spaceship Prometheus. The crew finds an alien site — a vast dome/pyramid on a lifeless moon — and discovers humanoid beings whose DNA matches ours, raising the central questions of creation, purpose and free will. Exploration soon yields increasingly grotesque, parasitic biology and catastrophic consequences: infection, body‑horror, and an infamous alien pregnancy sequence. The film culminates in frantic confrontations and ambiguous revelations about the creators’ intentions.

Critical consensus is mixed. Supporters applaud the film’s grandeur, the mystery it poses, and its memorable set pieces — especially the cavern explorations and Rapace’s resourceful survival scenes — while praising Fassbender’s nuanced performance. Detractors argue Prometheus is overstuffed with big questions it refuses to answer, too self‑conscious about its themes, and tonally uneven: its intellectual ambitions clash with some predictable or implausible genre plotting. Many note that, unlike Alien’s taut suspense or Blade Runner’s philosophical economy, Prometheus pushes hard for significance and leaves many mysteries unresolved, setting up potential sequels but leaving some viewers frustrated.

Overall, Prometheus is admired for its technical mastery, atmosphere and provocative ideas, yet regarded by many as a flawed, less focused entry in Ridley Scott’s sci‑fi canon — impressive and involving, but not quite the return to form some expected.

A small Ku Klux Klan contingent staged an anti-immigration/"White Lives Matter" rally in Pearson Park, Anaheim, on Feb. 27, 2016. Six Klan members arrived in an SUV wearing black garb and Confederate patches; several dozen counter-protesters had been peacefully gathered. As the Klan pulled up a chaotic confrontation erupted: protesters threw objects, some smashed a vehicle window, and a violent brawl ensued. Witnesses and police said one Klan member stabbed three counter-protesters—using a knife and the decorative eagle tip of a flag pole—one of whom was critically injured and later stabilized. Two others were assaulted; overall reports mention multiple attackers on both sides.

Anaheim police initially arrested 12 people. After reviewing video, photos and interviews, five Klan members were released Sunday because investigators said evidence corroborated self-defense claims; seven counter-protesters remained in custody on charges including assault with a deadly weapon and elder abuse for allegedly beating and stomping Klansmen. Prosecutors will review possible charges against the released suspects. Police and community figures expressed concern over the violence and the department’s handling of the scene; some witnesses and observers said officers were slow to appear across the whole area.

The incident took place against a historical backdrop: the Klan once briefly controlled Anaheim’s city council in 1924 before being ousted, and while KKK membership has dramatically declined from its 1920s peak, hate-group activity persists. Organizers of a Klan subgroup told media that Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign had energised some white-nationalist sympathizers, an assertion noted amid national debate over the candidate’s rhetoric and endorsements from white supremacists.

Many U.S. college police departments have acquired military surplus through the federal 1033 program, which transfers excess Department of Defense equipment to law-enforcement agencies at no purchase cost (agencies pay only shipping/maintenance). At least 117 colleges obtained items ranging from mundane supplies to battlefield gear—examples include grenade launchers repurposed for tear gas (University of Central Florida, Hinds Community College), dozens of M-16 rifles (Central Florida, Arizona State, Florida International, University of Maryland among others), and even armored vehicles and MRAPs (Ohio State). Colleges justify participation as a major cost-saving measure and a way to prepare for rare but extreme incidents such as active-shooter attacks; campus chiefs and advocates say equipment is intended for specific uses, kept in storage otherwise, and issued only to trained, accredited departments.

Critics argue the militarization of campus police is inappropriate given the more common problems on campuses (alcohol incidents, sexual assault), risks chilling free expression, and can shift police culture toward viewing the community as an enemy. The program drew intensified scrutiny after the Ferguson protests, prompting congressional hearings and calls from senators and the president for review and possible limits or training requirements. Supporters counter that many schools use transfers for practical supplies as well as tactical needs, and that accreditation and internal oversight can ensure proper training and controlled use. Opponents remain concerned about oversight gaps (the Defense Department does not require training to receive gear) and the broader cultural and civil-liberties implications of arming campus police with military-grade equipment.

A year ago the sexual‑abuse revelations that began with accusations against Harvey Weinstein transformed public life and Hollywood: once‑respected figures like Weinstein, Kevin Spacey and others were exposed, leading to many famous men worldwide being accused and dismissed. The disclosures began when it emerged that actress Rose McGowan was among eight women Weinstein had paid to stay silent; her revelation helped ignite a cascade of accusations. The piece notes the ongoing fallout over the past year — including the recent Bill Cosby developments — and includes McGowan’s own social‑media remarks clarifying she never called the broader #MeToo movement a lie (she said her criticisms targeted Hollywood and Time’s Up), expressing solidarity with survivors and reflecting on a painful, triggering year while affirming pride in the movement and resolve to move forward.

Researchers at the University of Siena report that short daily sessions of bright light increased testosterone and sexual satisfaction in men with low libido. In a small controlled study of 38 men diagnosed with low sexual desire, half used a standard bright light box for 30 minutes each morning for two weeks; the control group used a dimmed/light-adapted device. After treatment the bright‑light group’s average sexual satisfaction score rose from about 2/10 to roughly 6.3, a threefold increase, while the control group’s scores stayed near baseline. Testosterone in the active group rose from about 2.1 ng/ml to 3.6 ng/ml; no change occurred in controls. Lead investigator Prof. Andrea Fagiolini suggested light may suppress pineal activity and mimic seasonal increases in natural light that boost testosterone, but cautioned the trial is small and further research is needed before light therapy can be recommended clinically. The findings were to be presented at the ECNP Congress in Vienna.

A Virgin Mary statue stolen from a Lyndonville, Vt., nativity scene in January 2016 has been recovered and returned. Lyndonville Police Chief Jack Harris found the statue in a storage area of an apartment building after a tip; municipal administrator Justin Smith had identified it in photos taken during a building inspection. The statue was returned to the Lyndon Ecumenical Council. Police say the building houses mostly college students and investigators cannot determine how the statue ended up there. A baby Jesus statue taken at the same time remains missing.

Lauren Bacall, who died Aug. 12 at 89, left an estate of about $26–26.6 million and made a point of providing for her beloved Papillon, Sophie. Court papers filed in Manhattan Surrogate’s Court show Bacall’s 2013 will set aside $10,000 for Sophie’s care and names her son Sam Robards (who was Sophie’s keeper) to look after the dog.

The bulk of Bacall’s estate—including her Dakota apartment, royalties, and remaining trust funds from Humphrey Bogart—was divided among her three children (Leslie Bogart, Stephen Humphrey Bogart and Sam Robards). She left $250,000 to each of her grandchildren, and modest bequests to two longtime employees (Maria Santos: $20,000; Ilsa/Isla Hernandez: $15,000). Her children were named executors and also entrusted with preserving certain private letters, writings, diaries and memorabilia per her request.

The filings reflect Bacall’s lifelong love of dogs—Sophie frequently accompanied her in public and on promotional appearances—and follow a trend of celebrities leaving funds for pets. The family planned a rushed filing because an auction of her artwork was expected that fall.

This document stitches together several pieces arguing that cities should welcome — not block — bars and restaurants, while also acknowledging alcohol’s serious public-health costs and considering alternatives like cannabis.

Main points:
- Local fights over nightlife moratoria are common. In Washington, D.C., a proposed moratorium on new liquor licenses for 14th and U Streets met strong opposition from pro-growth neighbors, and the moratorium looks unlikely to pass. Similar efforts have occurred in New York, Chicago and California.
- Opponents of moratoria (exemplified by Matt Yglesias and local organizers) argue that clusters of bars and restaurants are a natural and valuable urban economic phenomenon. Such clustering creates complementarities (e.g., bars, late-night food, music venues) that increase value for patrons, spur small-business creation, reuse idiosyncratic historic storefronts that big-box retailers won’t fit, and generate jobs and tax revenue. Restricting new licenses can entrench mediocre incumbents, raise prices, and leave vacant storefronts.
- Policy prescription: liquor-licensing decisions should be made with citywide economic impacts in mind rather than deferring to immediate neighbors. Instead of moratoria, cities should address nuisances directly (more policing, street cleaning) and treat food-and-drink sectors as economic-development priorities because they provide accessible entrepreneurship and employment opportunities.
- Public-health and economic-cost context: Excessive alcohol use causes large harms — tens of thousands of deaths annually in the U.S., many years of life lost, and substantial social costs. Definitions: a standard U.S. drink = 0.6 oz pure alcohol; excessive drinking includes binge and heavy drinking (binge = 4+ drinks women, 5+ men per occasion; heavy = 8+/15+ drinks per week). Short-term risks include injuries, violence, poisoning and risky sex; long-term risks include chronic disease, cancers, cognitive and mental-health problems, social harms, and dependence. Economic costs are large (studies estimate hundreds of billions annually, e.g., $223–249 billion for mid-2000s), mostly from lost productivity and binge drinking.
- Harm-reduction and substitution debate: Some commentators and preliminary research suggest cannabis might substitute for alcohol for some users, potentially reducing alcohol-related harms. Reviews find some criteria for substitution are met but evidence is mixed, sometimes biased, and insufficient to endorse prescribing cannabis to reduce drinking. Legalization of recreational marijuana is expanding, and policymakers have yet to settle how public use might be regulated (e.g., “cannabis bars” remain limited).
- Tension highlighted: pro-growth advocates emphasize urban economic gains from more nightlife, while public-health evidence warns of serious individual and societal harms from increased alcohol availability. The document suggests balancing these by shaping licensing policy at a broader level, mitigating local nuisances actively, and considering complementary strategies (including careful study of cannabis substitution) rather than blanket moratoria driven by NIMBY concerns.

Thousands of residents in western North Carolina were briefly evacuated after heavy rains from Tropical Depression Alberto caused landslides and flash flooding that threatened the integrity of the Lake Tahoma dam in McDowell County. Around 1 a.m. on May 30, officials ordered mandatory evacuations downstream from the dam after engineers found a landslide had compromised the structure and water was spilling around its sides. The National Weather Service issued urgent warnings and a flash-flood emergency as 4–6 inches of rain inundated the area, causing record creek and river levels, multiple mudslides, road closures (including I-40), water rescues and sheltering. Several thousand people were affected; about 2,000 evacuees were reported from campgrounds and communities with roughly 200 in shelters. Five minor injuries were reported from water rescues, and no fatalities were linked to the floods, though two TV crew members elsewhere in the state died earlier after a falling tree. Governor Roy Cooper declared a state of emergency for western North Carolina. By midmorning an engineer had inspected Lake Tahoma Dam, deemed it safe, and officials lifted the evacuation orders. Flooding and flood watches remained in effect across parts of multiple states as the storm’s remnants moved inland. This is a developing story.

House Speaker John Boehner asked President Obama to move a requested joint session speech from Wednesday, Sept. 7 to Thursday, Sept. 8, citing logistical and security needs (including several hours for a security sweep and the House not reconvening until 6:30 p.m. that day). The White House accepted and announced Obama would speak on Sept. 8.

The scheduling touched off a political dispute. The White House originally requested Sept. 7 and a senior administration official said that date and an 8 p.m. time had been cleared with House Republicans before the public request; Boehner’s office denied that and said it had not signed off and was not consulted. The White House downplayed any intent to conflict with a Republican presidential debate set for the same Sept. 7 evening, calling the overlap coincidental. Republicans — including RNC Chairman Reince Priebus and conservative commentators such as Rush Limbaugh — accused Obama of politicizing the timing to blunt GOP debate attention.

Obama said the speech would focus on jobs and urge Congress to put aside politics. Observers noted the Thursday date would compete with the NFL season opener, a major television draw. The back-and-forth highlighted early tensions between the White House and the newly returned Congress.

Police say they have a person of interest in custody in connection with three fake explosive devices placed around Staten Island in September. Investigators believe the devices were hoax bombs left as part of a personal grudge: a 54‑year‑old man, reportedly jealous over a 32‑year‑old woman who had just married a man on their block, allegedly targeted that new husband (35) by leaving threatening notes with each device bearing the target’s name and address.

The three improvised devices were found on Sept. 2 (a suitcase on Barrett Avenue in Port Richmond), Sept. 12 (a backpack by a parked car on Brentwood Avenue in Randall Manor), and the most recent on a Saturday (a computer bag on Duncan Road in Grymes Hill). They contained propane cylinders, liquid-filled vials, wiring, nails/screws and in some cases a nine-volt battery or a clock; police say they would not have exploded as assembled but could have caused damage if properly rigged. At least one note was written in Spanish.

The discoveries prompted evacuations, a Bomb Squad response, and formation of an NYPD task force of roughly 10 investigators. The suspect, taken in for questioning at the 121st Precinct after being detained at his Manhattan workplace, faces potential charges; police say terrorism is not believed to be the motive. Authorities ask anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

The parents of Bartlomeij “Bart” Palosz have sued the town of Greenwich and its Board of Education, alleging that school officials knew for years that their son was repeatedly and severely bullied at Western Middle School and Greenwich High School but failed to follow mandated anti-bullying policies and protect him. Bart, who emigrated from Poland with his family, was 15 when he died by suicide on August 27, 2013—the first day of his sophomore year and the first day his older sister (a protective presence) was no longer at the school.

Court filings detail a long history of abuse: name-calling, teasing, theft of property, physical assaults (including being struck with a locker requiring stitches, being kicked, and having shoelaces tied together), and the smashing of his smartphone. School records and a middle-school “sharings” document described Bart as “very socially awkward,” regularly bullied, in need of social work, and unlikely to report incidents. Staff comments and a guidance counselor email acknowledging severe bullying were cited in the lawsuit. Bart’s academic performance and behavior deteriorated in 2013—grades fell, he stopped turning in homework, and he bit his hands—and he posted suicidal messages online months before his death.

The lawsuit contends that school personnel failed to comply with district anti-bullying procedures: they did not properly report or investigate incidents, notify or meet parents, discipline alleged perpetrators, or create safety and intervention plans. The family seeks damages (an amount in excess of the $15,000 filing threshold) and says the suit aims to prompt reforms so other students won’t suffer similarly. Attorneys for both sides attempted settlement talks but did not reach agreement before the two-year statute of limitations expired.

Town and school officials have acknowledged Bart was bullied but dispute the extent of their culpability; some municipal officials said the community “failed this child.” Investigations were launched after Bart’s death, with a draft town report discussed privately but not publicly released. The town must respond to the complaint by the court deadline. The family’s attorneys say they hope the lawsuit will change how the district responds to students in need.

French economist Thomas Piketty, author of the best‑selling and widely debated book Capital in the Twenty‑First Century, has refused France’s highest honour, the Legion d’honneur. Speaking to AFP, Piketty said he declined the nomination because “it is not the government’s role to decide who is honourable,” and urged the Socialist government to concentrate on reviving growth in France and Europe. Once close to the Socialist Party, he has since criticized President François Hollande’s policies. The move is unusual—few refuse the award—and follows other high‑profile refusals (e.g., Jacques Tardi, Jean‑Paul Sartre). Piketty’s book, praised by some economists such as Paul Krugman, sold hundreds of thousands of copies and sparked broad debate on income inequality.

A Boston homeless man, Glen James, found a backpack at South Bay Mall containing a passport, about $2,400 in cash and roughly $39,500 in traveler's checks (total just over $42,000) and turned it in to police. The bag’s owner was located and the property returned; Boston police later honored James with a citation for his honesty. After media coverage, a stranger, Ethan Whittington of Midlothian, Virginia, started a GoFundMe for James with an initial $50,000 goal (later raised and then increased to $250,000). The campaign drew a massive outpouring of donations—reports variously put the total near $88,000, about $98,000, and more than $110,000—intended to reward James and help him change his life (Whittington hopes it will fund a house). Whittington said the response restored his hope and was meant as a broader statement of community. James, a former courthouse employee, said he would not have kept any of the found money.

Google released more detailed images, video and info about Project Glass—its wearable “Google Glass” headset—showing how the user interface and core features will work. The device does not place a full transparent display over the eyes but uses a small screen (a mirrored glass block) positioned slightly above and to the right of the right eye, so many POV mockups that show a large central HUD can be misleading. Voice is the primary input: saying “OK, Glass” activates listening mode. Once engaged, Glass can take photos (including an automatic interval photo mode), record video, perform web searches, provide walking directions and reminders (e.g., flight alerts), translate, send messages, and share what you’re seeing via messaging or Google+ Hangouts.

Google opened a limited public trial by inviting applicants to submit a 50‑word post (with hashtag #ifihadglass) on Google+ or Twitter by Feb. 27 explaining creative uses for Glass; winners and selected developers can buy the device for $1,500 plus tax and must pick them up at events in New York, San Francisco, or Los Angeles. Google’s promotional video suggested uses like live-streaming a ballerina’s backstage, on-the-spot translation for travelers, and family video chats.

Ross Cassidy, a Salisbury neighbour and longtime friend of former Russian military intelligence officer Sergei Skripal, has said he believes Sergei and his daughter Yulia—both critically ill after being poisoned with the novichok nerve agent—are so badly damaged they should be allowed to die. Cassidy, who became close to the Skripal family after Sergei moved in next door in 2010, described his shock on learning they had been found collapsed in Salisbury city centre on 4 March and said he has been frustrated that police would not allow him or other friends to visit them in hospital. He recalled driving Sergei to Heathrow the day before the attack to pick up Yulia and said he feels guilt for not thinking sooner about their likely fate.

Viktoria Skripal, Sergei’s niece, told the BBC she has very little hope for their recovery, saying there is maybe a one percent chance they will survive and that, if they do, they will be long-term invalids. She also said the family kept the news from Sergei’s mother to protect her.

The poisonings have prompted wide international fallout: more than 23 countries expelled over 115 Russian diplomats (Ireland later became the 24th), NATO reduced the size of Russia’s mission, and the UK led a diplomatic push against Moscow while Russia denied responsibility and demanded evidence.

Community members in Richmond, Indiana, held a candlelight vigil to support the family of 14-year-old Brandon Clegg, who died Thursday after exchanging gunfire with police at Dennis Intermediate School and then fatally shooting himself. Clegg was not a student at the school but lived nearby. His mother, Mary York, called 911 around 8:11 a.m. to report that he was armed and headed to the school after allegedly taking another family member hostage and forcing them to drive him there. Because of her tip, the school immediately went into lockdown and officers confronted Clegg as he arrived; he fired into a locked entry door, entered the hallway, was contained near a stairwell and then shot himself. No students or staff were injured.

Dozens attended the vigil Sunday to pray with and support Clegg’s mother; organizers stressed her action likely prevented many deaths. Family members said Clegg had been bullied, though they did not offer it as justification. Authorities continue a lengthy investigation; the school remained closed the following Monday.

At the 2011 Values Voter Summit straw poll, Ron Paul won decisively among attendees, reflecting his well-organized, mobilized grassroots: he received 36.9% (732) of 1,983 ballots. Herman Cain finished second with 22.5% (447), and Rick Santorum third with 16.3% (323). Rick Perry — despite heavy campaigning — placed fourth with 8.4% (167), followed by Michele Bachmann (7.9%, 157), Mitt Romney (4.4%, 88), and Newt Gingrich (2.7%, 54); Jon Huntsman and undecided trailed. Organizers noted that many Paul supporters bought single-day passes or were bused in, boosting his showing. The piece argues the straw poll reflects organization more than broad electability: Perry underperformed partly because Cain’s likability and Perry’s immigration stance dampened his support, while Santorum’s modest rise benefits from the Summit’s social-conservative audience even as Cain casts a shadow. Romney historically fares poorly at this event, and his path to the nomination depends on divisions among these conservative contenders rather than winning this constituency outright.

Oliver Stone will write and direct a film adaptation of Luke Harding’s book The Snowden Files: The Inside Story of the World’s Most Wanted Man, with longtime producing partner Moritz Borman fast-tracking it as a European co-production and aiming to begin filming before year’s end. Stone, who has publicly defended Edward Snowden and called him a hero for exposing U.S. surveillance practices, said the story is “one of the greatest of our time” and a real challenge; the Guardian is cooperating on the project and its editor praised the collaboration. The film will compete with another high-profile Snowden project: Sony Pictures bought rights to Glenn Greenwald’s No Place to Hide, to be produced by James Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

A group of 9/11 conspiracy theorists, led by prominent activist Mark Dice of the 9/11 Truth Movement, are upset with Charlie Sheen and threatening to protest his upcoming live shows. Sheen previously voiced belief that the World Trade Center collapses resembled a "controlled demolition." Dice says fellow theorists feel Sheen has abandoned the movement by focusing on his personal scandals—“bragging about smoking crack and sleeping with hookers”—instead of “asking hard questions” about 9/11. Dice claims he has tried to contact Sheen without success and warns that protests will be staged if Sheen does not address their concerns. The rest of the source page was not found.

Researchers and health officials report strong evidence that Zika virus outbreaks have been followed by large increases in cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a rare autoimmune disorder that can cause temporary but sometimes severe paralysis and respiratory failure.

Key findings
- Analysis of seven sites (Bahia state in Brazil; Colombia; the Dominican Republic; El Salvador; Honduras; Suriname; and Venezuela) covering April 2015–March 2016 found GBS incidence rose between about 2-fold and nearly 10-fold during periods of Zika transmission. Reported increases included 172% (Bahia), 211% (Colombia), 150% (Dominican Republic), 100% (El Salvador), 144% (Honduras), 400% (Suriname) and 877% (Venezuela).
- Across those locations there were roughly 164,000 confirmed and suspected Zika cases and 1,474 GBS cases; collectively nearly 1,500 people experienced temporary paralysis.
- Country examples: Venezuela expected ~70 GBS cases but reported 684; Colombia recorded 320 cases in five months when ~100 were expected; El Salvador saw GBS double from 92 to 184 as Zika peaked.
- Men were more likely than women to develop GBS (reported incidence 28% higher), and incidence increased with age. More women reported Zika infections overall, possibly due to pregnancy-related awareness.
- The investigators found no similar rise in GBS linked to dengue in these data, strengthening the Zika–GBS association.

Public-health implications
- Even modest increases in GBS pose a heavy burden because about one-third of GBS patients need mechanical ventilation and intensive care. Many affected countries have limited ICU capacity and ventilators.
- Puerto Rico reported its first Zika-related GBS death (man in his 30s–40s). Puerto Rico had over 13,000 confirmed Zika cases, 34 GBS cases and more than 1,100 infected pregnant women; models project hundreds of babies could be born with Zika-related microcephaly through mid-2017.
- Zika often causes no symptoms, making surveillance difficult; some experts suggest monitoring GBS cases could help detect Zika outbreaks. The U.S. mainland lacks formal GBS surveillance, complicating attribution as Zika spreads.

Clinical and CDC context
- GBS is uncommon (roughly 1–2 cases per 100,000 annually in the U.S.) and most patients recover, though some suffer lasting disability and rare deaths occur. GBS is known to follow infections and, rarely, vaccinations.
- CDC continues to investigate the link between Zika and GBS and advises prevention of mosquito exposure, particularly for pregnant women, because Zika also causes severe fetal brain defects.

Overall, multiple lines of public-health data indicate a clear temporal association between Zika outbreaks and sharp increases in Guillain-Barré syndrome, raising concern about clinical capacity and long-term impacts in affected regions.

On New Year’s Day, 10 states raised their minimum wages by 10 to 35 cents, mostly through automatic, inflation-linked adjustments; Rhode Island’s rise (from $7.40 to $7.75) was enacted by state law and was its first increase in five years. The changes—affecting nearly a million workers—include boosts in Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Missouri, Montana, Ohio, Oregon, Vermont and Washington (to $9.19), which already had the highest state minimum. Automatic indexing, used by nine of these states, smooths annual, predictable small increases and helps narrow pay gaps with neighboring states that do not adjust wages regularly. States with automatic increases average $8.12/hour vs. about $7.40 in states without them, a roughly $1,500 annual difference for full-time workers; some localities, like San Francisco, set even higher floors.

Supporters and some economists say higher minimums reduce turnover, raise the pay floor without harming employment, and provide predictability for businesses. Opponents, including small-business advocates and groups like the National Restaurant Association, warn that higher wages can force employers to cut hiring, reduce hours, raise prices, or lay off staff—potentially eliminating entry-level opportunities. Small business owners quoted described mixed impacts: some absorbed modest increases or passed small costs to customers, while others worried about rising input costs and competitive pricing. Federal lawmakers are also debating raising the $7.25 federal minimum, with proposals ranging around $1–$2 increases.

In this first-person piece, J.K. Rowling recounts how a single newspaper photograph of a child confined in a caged bed prompted her to found Lumos, a charity dedicated to ending the institutionalisation of children. She explains that an estimated 8 million children worldwide live separated from their families—often not because they are orphans but because poverty, lack of services, disability stigma or discrimination make families feel they have no choice. Institutional care causes measurable, often irreversible harm: malnutrition, developmental delays, psychological trauma, higher risk of abuse and trafficking, poor education and lifelong exclusion. These harms occur even in well-resourced institutions; the solution is not cosmetic improvements but replacing institutions with family- and community-based care.

Rowling argues the problem is solvable within our lifetime if governments and donors invest in inclusive education and health, social and economic support for vulnerable families, and alternatives such as fostering and adoption. She cites Lumos’s successes: a 70% reduction in institutionalised children in Moldova since 2007, a 75% fall in admissions in a Czech demonstration area, and a 54% reduction in Bulgaria alongside a 440% rise in foster carers. She stresses that ending institutionalisation is both a moral imperative and economically sensible. With growing international commitments and campaigns like #Letstalklumos, Rowling urges continued awareness and funding, and pledges to serve as Lumos president for life in the hope that removing children from families and locking them away will one day be unthinkable.

News summary — Background checks and safety concerns in online dating

As online dating has grown into a billion-dollar industry with about 20 million U.S. users, companies, public officials and safety advocates are pushing for more safeguards because dating sites can be used by people who misrepresent themselves — from married individuals to sexual predators and felons. Entrepreneurs with law-enforcement backgrounds (e.g., MyMatchChecker) and several mobile apps now offer quick, consumer-paid background checks for prospective dates. Established services such as True.com also screen applicants and report rejecting a small percentage.

States are starting to regulate the sector: New York’s Internet Dating Safety Act (and a similar New Jersey law) requires dating sites to post safety tips and disclose whether they perform criminal-background checks. Advocates say screening can improve safety; critics argue the checks are imperfect because criminal and sex-offender records are inconsistent across jurisdictions, sometimes incomplete or unavailable, and could create a false sense of security. Privacy and misuse risks from apps and data-handling problems have also been raised.

Dating-site executives and policy groups caution that mandatory, comprehensive screening is technically and legally difficult. Sites currently enjoy broad liability protection under the Communications Decency Act, which shields them from being treated as publishers of user content. Observers predict legal challenges may arise if sites charge fees and have knowledge of criminal behavior. Meanwhile experts advise users to be cautious when meeting people met online.

Police in Suffolk, Virginia, responded to a report of a gunshot victim Thursday around 10:45 a.m. after an argument in the 300 block of East Washington Street escalated. According to authorities, an argument inside a local barbershop — reportedly about whether Halle Berry had played or would play Aretha Franklin — turned physical. Forty-four-year-old Michael Jermell Hatton produced a firearm and shot 47-year-old Tony Jonathan Lundy at least once outside the shop.

Both men received emergency care from Suffolk Fire & Rescue and were transported to area hospitals. Lundy is in critical condition and remains under treatment at Sentara Norfolk General Hospital, according to a relative. Hatton was treated, released from the hospital, taken to the magistrate where warrants were obtained, and then jailed at Western Tidewater Regional Jail without bond. A nearby business reported hearing several gunshots during the incident. The investigation is ongoing.

Nancy Reed, a 77-year-old Kingwood resident and community volunteer, died Sept. 15 after developing necrotizing fasciitis — a rapidly spreading, “flesh-eating” bacterial infection — that complicated blunt trauma to her arm sustained when she fell in floodwaters at her son’s home during Hurricane Harvey. The Harris County Institute of Forensic Sciences ruled her death “flood-related,” making her the county’s 36th official Harvey-linked fatality; the death was added to the county’s list on Sept. 25. Reed was treated at Memorial Hermann hospitals before she died and was remembered at a memorial service in Kingwood.

Her case is one of at least two Harvey-associated necrotizing fasciitis infections reported locally. Former firefighter/medic J.R. Atkins contracted the disease after an insect bite while rescuing neighbors in flooded Missouri City; he survived after multiple surgeries and intensive antibiotic treatment. Health officials say such infections are rare but can increase after floods, as bacteria persist on contaminated surfaces and enter wounds. The CDC notes group A strep is the most common cause on land and vibrio species in salt water; prompt diagnosis and antibiotics are critical. Public health guidance after the storm emphasized discarding items that cannot be disinfected and continued vigilance even after floodwaters recede. Researchers at Houston Methodist are studying group A strep to find targets that could reduce the severity of these infections.

Russian forces moved into Crimea in late February–early March 2014 as Ukraine’s new, pro‑Western government mobilized troops and warned of war. Unidentified armed men in military-style uniforms—widely reported as Russian and in some cases in vehicles with Russian plates—seized airports, key facilities and the Crimean parliament building after pro‑Russian leaders there installed Sergey Aksyonov as regional premier and asked Moscow for help. Russia’s parliament quickly approved President Vladimir Putin’s request to authorize the use of Russian forces “until normalization” of the situation, with Putin citing the need to protect ethnic Russians and personnel at the Black Sea Fleet base in Sevastopol. Moscow denied an official admission of deployed forces even as Ukrainian officials, diplomats at the U.N. and Western governments reported thousands of Russian troops in Crimea and called the moves an invasion and occupation.

Ukraine’s acting president Oleksandr Turchynov and prime minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk put the military on high alert, mobilized forces nationwide, and appealed to NATO and Western partners for help while pleading for de‑escalation. Street clashes and pro‑Russian demonstrations spread in eastern and southern cities, with local officials in some regions seeking referendums or rejecting the Kiev authorities. The crisis triggered urgent diplomatic activity: President Barack Obama warned of consequences for violating Ukraine’s sovereignty, Secretary of State John Kerry condemned Russia’s actions, and Western leaders and the U.N. called for restraint. The U.S. suspended preparatory G‑8 meetings in Sochi and considered economic and diplomatic measures; NATO and EU officials urged de‑escalation. The situation raised fears of the most serious Russia‑West confrontation since the Cold War, with Crimea effectively under Russian control and the risk of broader conflict and territorial fragmentation across Ukraine.

A 13-year-old Ethan A. Chase Middle School student in Menifee, identified as Austin Lacey, dressed as Elsa from Disney’s Frozen for a school Disney-themed spirit day. Many classmates reacted positively—taking selfies and praising him—but school officials said the costume caused a large, disruptive crowd before classes and ordered him to remove the gown and wig. Romoland School District Superintendent Julie Vitale said the principal’s action followed district policy and was meant to stop a general disruption; the student faced no discipline and finished the school day. Some students afterward said the incident wasn’t a problem and defended Austin as a popular, high-achieving classmate.

Security footage captured a dramatic sinkhole collapse Wednesday beneath the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, Kentucky. The hole, roughly 40 feet deep, opened beneath a museum wing and swallowed eight Corvettes. The museum has posted multiple videos showing the collapse and interior views of the pit. Engineers are assessing the site; there is currently no timetable for removing the cars or repairing that section of the museum because safety must be confirmed before work begins. The museum also promotes its exhibits and visitor amenities nearby.

Margaux Sainte-Lagüe, a Parisian entrepreneur, turned thousands of city-raised cobblestones into a niche souvenir business, Mon Pavé Parisien. After Paris began removing and selling cobblestones in 2016 as part of a circular-economy push—salvaging historic granite pulled up during infrastructure works—Sainte-Lagüe bought five tons and launched an online shop offering five-pound stones cleaned and hand-painted in several styles: a tricolor France motif, a gilded edition with 22.5-carat gold leaf, and a “May ’68” design referencing the student protests (“sous les pavés”). She also produces custom designs (she made one for Mayor Anne Hidalgo and a painted wedding stone for a Chinese couple). Prices range roughly $63–$157; she’s sold dozens so far and plans to expand to boutiques near tourist sites.

The city sells large quantities of cobbles—some estimate up to 3 million tons available over centuries—primarily to recyclers and builders for paving and construction, while retaining iconic sites’ stones. The program supports waste reduction and reuse: municipal sales could generate meaningful revenue and supply materials for other projects. Sainte-Lagüe’s venture exemplifies how reclaimed urban materials are being repurposed as both functional building supplies and collectible souvenirs that appeal to tourists, collectors, and those seeking a tangible piece of Parisian history.

A 25-year-old woman, Adacia Avery Chambers, was arrested after driving her 2014 Hyundai Elantra into a crowd near the end of Oklahoma State University’s homecoming parade on Saturday morning, killing four people and injuring dozens more, including many children. Chambers was initially arrested on suspicion of DUI and later booked on four counts of second-degree murder; she is being held without bail and faces life in prison if convicted. Authorities were still awaiting toxicology results.

Chambers’ attorney, Tony Coleman, said he spent time with her after the crash and believes she was not intoxicated but is suffering from mental illness and may be incompetent to stand trial; he plans to request a psychiatric evaluation and competency hearing. Coleman and others reported she had not slept for days, may have untreated diabetes, and had exhibited recent self-harm behavior; family members and witnesses said she did not appear intoxicated the night before or the morning of the crash.

The victims included retired OSU professor Marvin Lyle Stone, his wife Bonnie Lynn Stone, 23-year-old University of Central Oklahoma student Nikita Nakal (Prabhakar), and a 2-year-old boy, Nash Lucas. Of 47 treated, 17 remained hospitalized and four were in critical condition; 11 of the injured were 13 or younger. Witnesses described chaotic scenes, with people thrown into the air and bystanders performing rescues. The crash occurred two blocks from Boone Pickens Stadium hours before the OSU football game, which officials ultimately allowed to proceed after a somber pregame moment. Families and the university community are grieving, and counseling was made available. Investigations into the cause of the crash and Chambers’ condition continue.

This document collects opinion commentary about a recent controversy over a joke by Robert De Niro and a wider debate about apologies, outrage, and civility in public life.

- De Niro, at a fundraiser with Michelle Obama, joked listing conservative first ladies — “Callista Gingrich. Karen Santorum. Ann Romney.” — then asked, “Now do you really think our country is ready for a white first lady?” The remark drew criticism (the first lady’s press secretary called it “inappropriate”), De Niro apologized, and some, like Newt Gingrich, demanded further apology, prompting commentary that such ritualized calls for contrition are often hollow.

- The piece situates this episode in a broader pattern of repeated public outrage over remarks or imagery from celebrities, politicians and corporations (examples cited include various entertainers, sports references, ad campaigns and pundits). The authors argue society has adopted an over-ready posture of “phony umbrage” and instantaneous moral condemnation.

- Bill Maher is invoked for an op-ed urging Americans to stop demanding insincere apologies and to grant an “amnesty” for many deliberately provocative comments — to simply change the channel rather than demand contrition. Maher’s point about partisan exploitation of insults and the constitutional protection of offensive speech is acknowledged as valid, though the commentary notes his stance is self-serving given his own history of crude attacks (e.g., on Sarah Palin).

- The piece draws a distinction between merely impolitic or risqué speech and truly dehumanizing rhetoric that fosters hatred. It defends the right to free expression while affirming that many citizens legitimately seek higher standards of civil discourse and do not want every opponent treated as an enemy.

- The conclusion rejects dismissing concerns about incivility as purely partisan theater and sides with a more unifying civic ethic, echoing Barack Obama’s 2004 remark that America should not be divided into partisan tribes but seen as one nation where people are “my brother’s keeper, my sister’s keeper.”

A federal appeals court has upheld a $25 million settlement resolving long-running fraud claims against Donald Trump’s now-defunct Trump University. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco finalized the settlement after rejecting an objection from Florida bankruptcy lawyer Sherri Simpson, who had tried to opt out of the class action to pursue a separate trial over roughly $19,000 she spent on Trump University programs.

Students alleged Trump University (active 2005–2010) used false advertising and high‑pressure sales tactics at free workshops to push expensive seminars and mentorships—ranging from $1,495 apprenticeships to $35,000 “Gold Elite” programs—causing many to lose thousands. Multiple state actions and lawsuits in California and New York were folded into the class action, which Trump settled for $25 million in January 2017; the funds were held in escrow pending appeals.

The three-judge panel ruled that the notice to class members provided only one opportunity to opt out and found the settlement fair and reasonable, noting the legal and logistical hurdles of trying Trump around his inauguration. The court said plaintiffs will receive about 80–90% of what they paid. Simpson’s lawyers considered further appeals but ultimately declined to pursue them so payments could be distributed. New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman and lead plaintiffs’ counsel welcomed the decision; Trump’s camp previously announced the litigation’s complete resolution.

Summary:

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders demanded Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder resign over the Flint water crisis, arguing Snyder and his administration knew about lead contamination but failed to act, leaving hundreds of children poisoned and thousands potentially exposed to lifelong harm.

Background and timeline:
- In April 2014, to save money while awaiting a new regional system, Flint switched its water source from Detroit/Lake Huron to the more polluted Flint River. The river water proved highly corrosive and, because corrosion-control chemicals were not added—as directed by the state Department of Environmental Quality—lead leached from aging pipes into drinking water.
- Residents immediately reported bad taste, odor and health problems; city and state officials repeatedly assured the water was safe. Independent doctors and researchers, notably Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha and a Virginia Tech team, documented elevated blood-lead levels in children and extremely high tap-water lead readings (including many samples far above EPA action levels and some exceeding levels the EPA calls “toxic waste”).
- Flint reconnected to Detroit water in October 2015, but much pipe damage and lingering contamination remained. State and federal acknowledgments and actions came slowly: Snyder first publicly acknowledged a problem in late September 2015, accepted the resignation of the state DEQ director in December, declared a state of emergency Jan. 5, 2016, activated the National Guard Jan. 12, and sought a federal emergency/disaster declaration.

Health and community impact:
- Dr. Hanna-Attisha and state officials urged treating all Flint children under six as exposed; roughly 8,657 children fall into this group (not counting unborn children or visitors). Lead exposure poses severe, potentially lifelong risks to developing brains and nervous systems.
- Hospitals and community groups began widespread testing, distribution of bottled water and filters, nutrition and mitigation programs, and door-to-door aid, but efforts have often struggled to meet demand.

Federal response:
- President Obama declared a federal emergency (authorizing FEMA to coordinate relief and cover much of the cost for water, filters and supplies, initially up to $5 million) but denied a disaster declaration reserved for natural disasters. Local and federal officials continue to seek additional funds; state estimates cited tens of millions needed for immediate response and pipe repairs.

Political fallout:
- Sanders, other elected officials and residents sharply criticized Snyder for inaction and lack of transparency. Calls for full accountability, extensive remediation, long-term medical and educational support for affected children, and replacement of lead service lines have grown louder as the crisis unfolds.

This project harvests structured data on military conflicts from Wikidata and DBpedia, cleans and combines it, and visualizes battles in nodegoat as diachronic geospatial data.

Wikidata
- Initial SPARQL checks found 8,049 instances of “battle.” Focusing on entries with date and location at first yielded 410 records, but a more thorough OPTIONAL-based query (also checking start/end times and location held on related entities) produced 2,657 battles with both a location and date.
- Data cleaning (in OpenRefine, Calc, or Excel) preceded import into nodegoat. The resulting interactive visualization lets users scroll a timeline, filter by colored time periods, and open items with links back to Wikidata.

DBpedia
- SPARQL queries returned 12,674 instances of dbo:MilitaryConflict, 4,022 of which had explicit date and location properties. Looking one level deeper for place/date references raised the count to 10,116 battles.
- DBpedia dates are generally messier (harvested from infoboxes), requiring more cleanup than Wikidata. After cleaning and import, the DBpedia set can be combined with the Wikidata set for a total of ~12,703 records; provenance is tracked so dots can be highlighted by source.
