- Differences between the sources stem from messy or differing date representations, the choice to pick a single location per battle, and coordinate rounding. Many Wikidata statements lacked robust references and frequently cited Wikipedia language editions as sources.

Connecting the data
- The team explored relationships between events and people: for example, extracting persons present at identified battles (notably many American Civil War records) enabled linking battles via individuals who participated in multiple engagements.
- Birth and death data for these people were also added to produce temporal-personal visualizations (example noted: the 1957 death of William Lundy is visible).

Outputs and files
- CSV files were generated for imports and joins. The document also references a seed description and a ranking of web pages (Wide00014 / Wide00012) used for other data collection tasks, though those items are ancillary to the conflict visualizations.

Overall: the work demonstrates how linked open data from Wikidata and DBpedia can be queried, cleaned, combined, and visualized to produce interactive, time-and-space views of historical battles and their human connections, while highlighting inconsistencies and provenance issues between the datasets.

Summary:

Jupiter reaches opposition in early May 2018 (May 8 in the Americas/Pacific; May 9 elsewhere), meaning Earth sits directly between the sun and Jupiter. At opposition the planet rises in the east at sunset, is highest around midnight, and sets at sunrise, making this the best time of year to view it because it’s up all night and near its closest approach (closest this year around May 10). Jupiter at opposition appears brighter than any star and is outshone only by the sun, moon and Venus; right after sunset you can often see Venus low in the west while Jupiter rises in the east.

In 2018 Jupiter lies in front of the constellation Libra (near the 2nd‑magnitude star Zubenelgenubi) and outshines that star by over 100 times. Oppositions occur about every 13 months, so each year’s date shifts roughly a month later (2017’s was April 7; 2019’s will be June 10).

The planet is a gas giant more than 11 times Earth’s diameter and about 300 times its mass, with a possible solid core and mostly hydrogen and helium; its interior includes metallic hydrogen, and its rapid rotation produces the banded belts and zones and features such as the Great Red Spot. Jupiter is roughly 2.5 times more massive than all the other planets combined and is often called a “failed star” because it’s far too small to ignite fusion.

NASA’s Juno spacecraft is currently orbiting Jupiter, giving unprecedented views of its polar cyclones (including infrared 3‑D flyover footage). Even small telescopes or binoculars will reveal Jupiter’s four largest Galilean moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), visible as points that move noticeably over hours and that sometimes transit or cast shadows on the planet. These moons include world‑class targets: volcanically active Io, icy Europa (possible subsurface ocean), heavily cratered Callisto, and others of scientific interest.

Practical viewing notes: translate the UTC opposition time to your local time (calendar sources list May 9 at 01:00 UTC), look east at nightfall on May 8–9, and use binoculars or a small telescope to spot the Galilean moons and atmospheric detail.

Summary:

- Robert Gordon University (Aberdeen) has revoked Donald Trump’s honorary DBA, saying his statements during the US election campaign are "wholly incompatible with the ethos and values of the university."

- Separately, a high-profile UK petition initiated by Suzanne Kelly calling for Trump to be banned from entering the United Kingdom gained rapid support. The petition argues that Trump’s rhetoric toward Muslims and other groups amounts to hate speech and should meet the same "unacceptable behaviour" exclusion criteria used to bar others from the UK. It quickly attracted hundreds of thousands of signatures—surpassing the 100,000 threshold that can prompt parliamentary consideration—and was scheduled for review by the Petitions Committee.

- The campaign ties to broader local opposition to Trump: Kelly previously campaigned against his Aberdeen golf development and had earlier petitioned the university to strip the honorary degree. Her activism has included writing for Aberdeen Voice and contributing to media coverage and documentaries critical of Trump.

- The movement drew public and political reactions in the UK: senior politicians (including David Cameron, Jeremy Corbyn, Nicola Sturgeon and Boris Johnson) publicly condemned many of Trump’s comments as divisive or offensive. The Home Office noted the home secretary has the legal power to exclude individuals if their presence is "not conducive to the public good," though no exclusion decision had been announced.

- The petitions and the university’s decision reflect growing UK backlash against Trump’s statements during his campaign and demonstrate how grassroots petitions can drive institutional and parliamentary responses.

Texas will no longer allow condemned inmates to choose special last meals. The change follows the execution Wednesday of Lawrence Russell Brewer, convicted in the 1998 hate-crime murder of James Byrd Jr. Brewer requested an extensive final meal — including two chicken-fried steaks, a triple-meat bacon cheeseburger, fried okra, a pound of barbecue, three fajitas, a meat-lover’s pizza, a pint of ice cream and a slab of peanut-butter fudge with crushed peanuts — which prison officials said he did not eat. State Sen. John Whitmire, chair of the Senate Criminal Justice Committee, called the practice “extremely inappropriate” in a letter to Texas Department of Criminal Justice executive director Brad Livingston, prompting the policy change that removes the privilege for inmates scheduled for execution.

A Swedish group of file-sharers, the Missionary Church of Kopimism, has been officially recognized as a religion by Swedish authorities. Founded in 2010 by philosophy student Isak Gerson, the movement—now about 3,000 members—treats copying and sharing information as sacred (their symbol set includes CTRL+C and CTRL+V) and opposes surveillance. After several earlier rejections, authorities approved the church once it formalized its rituals of copying and sharing. Legal recognition does not legalize copyright infringement, though founders hope the status will reduce stigma around file-sharing and be taken into account in future lawmaking. The church plans to develop its religious practices and expects membership to grow.

Eric Swenson, 64, a co‑founder of Thrasher magazine and key figure in modern skateboarding, died by suicide on June 20, 2011, after shooting himself outside the Mission Police Station in San Francisco. Witnesses saw him shoot himself around 8:30 a.m. without entering or speaking to officers. Loved ones and colleagues said Swenson was a private man who may have chosen the police station so family wouldn’t find him; they believe chronic pain and reduced mobility from a severe motorcycle injury decades earlier contributed to his decision.

Swenson co‑founded High Speed Productions (publisher of Thrasher, Juxtapoz and Slap), Independent Trucks, and Ermico Enterprises, and helped launch Deluxe Distribution. Independent’s improved skateboard trucks and Thrasher’s coverage are widely credited with transforming skateboarding from a passing fad into a distinct subculture with its own styles, music and language. Colleagues remembered him as a humble, hard‑working behind‑the‑scenes builder and problem‑solver who preferred to avoid the spotlight. He is survived by his wife Linda (Linda McKay), sister Rebekah (Rebekah Engle) and another sister, Sonja Taylor, and is mourned across the skate community. Services were private.

China and the United States engaged in military-to-military contact after a Chinese navy ship seized a U.S. unmanned underwater glider on Thursday, one of the most serious recent confrontations between the two militaries. The glider—about 3 meters long, commercially built and valued at roughly $150,000—was operating under civilian contractors from the USNS Bowditch collecting unclassified oceanographic data about 57 miles northwest of Subic Bay in the South China Sea when it was taken. The U.S. lodged a formal diplomatic complaint and demanded the vehicle's return; Pentagon officials said no shots were fired during the encounter and later reported they had secured an understanding that China would return the glider.

Beijing gave few details, saying only that relevant departments were communicating and predicting a “smooth resolution.” Chinese state media quoted military commentators who defended the seizure as lawful and in China’s rights, while criticizing U.S. public statements as unhelpful. U.S. analysts noted the incident occurred in waters within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone and may violate international law.

The seizure heightened already strained U.S.-China ties amid disputes over South China Sea militarization and friction caused by President‑elect Donald Trump’s outreach to Taiwan and his broader rhetoric on China. Trump publicly condemned the seizure on Twitter, briefly suggested the U.S. could tell China to keep the drone, and his comments risked further escalating tensions. The episode drew warnings from outgoing U.S. officials about the potential consequences of upending long-standing policy understandings with China.

Summary — Global reactions to Donald Trump’s 2016 U.S. presidential victory

Donald Trump’s surprise win prompted widespread, immediate reactions worldwide across governments, political figures, markets and the public, ranging from cautious outreach and congratulations to alarm and concern.

Political and diplomatic reactions
- Many national leaders and institutions offered pragmatic congratulations and emphasized willingness to work with the incoming administration, including China’s Xi Jinping, Japan’s Shinzo Abe, Germany’s Angela Merkel, Britain’s Theresa May, Australia’s Julie Bishop, EU leaders, NATO’s Jens Stoltenberg, and others. Several stressed the importance of maintaining alliances and trans-Atlantic ties.
- Some governments signaled specific hopes or anxieties: China called for constructive, non-confrontational management of differences; Russia expressed readiness to restore relations; Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu called Trump a friend of Israel; Iran urged the U.S. to uphold the nuclear deal; Cuba feared reversal of recent détente; Mexico reacted with shock and concern over threatened trade and immigration policies.
- Leaders of a number of countries with populist or authoritarian leanings (e.g., Hungary’s Viktor Orbán, Philippines’ Rodrigo Duterte, Cambodia’s Hun Sen) welcomed the result. Turkey sought cooperation on security and even urged extradition of Fethullah Gulen. The Vatican offered prayers for peace and wise leadership.
- Nonstate actors: the Taliban urged a U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.

Public and political class reactions
- Global publics gave mixed responses: protests, fear and dismay surfaced in many places (Mexico, Ireland, parts of Asia and Europe), while right-wing and anti-establishment figures celebrated (e.g., Geert Wilders, Marine Le Pen).
- In Muslim-majority Indonesia, social media expressed anxiety about Trump’s proposals targeting Muslims. In Mexico, citizens and markets reacted with visible shock, given Trump’s rhetoric on immigration, a border wall and trade.

Policy concerns and regional implications
- Trade and immigration were central worries: Trump’s criticism of NAFTA, threats to renegotiate or withdraw from trade deals, opposition to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, and pledges to restrict immigration raised concern in Canada, Mexico and trade-dependent economies.
- Security and alliances: NATO partners were wary after Trump’s criticism of burden-sharing; leaders stressed the need to preserve U.S. leadership and alliance ties. Countries in Asia watched closely for potential shifts in U.S. policy toward the region.
- Specific policy issues flagged: potential reversal of U.S.-Cuba normalization, possible renegotiation of the Iran nuclear deal, implications for the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and calls to change U.S. troop commitments in places like Afghanistan and the Philippines.

Market and economic reaction
- Financial markets reacted with sharp volatility: an initial sell-off was followed by a rally as investors priced in possible pro-business policies (tax cuts, deregulation). U.S. stocks recovered and closed higher; long-term bond yields jumped on inflation expectations; the dollar strengthened.
- Emerging markets and commodity-sensitive economies were hurt: the Mexican peso plunged to record lows amid fears of tariffs and disruptions to remittances and trade; Asian equities and some currencies fell; oil and gold moved but stabilized after initial swings.

Overall tone
- The outcome produced a mix of cautious engagement from many governments, jubilation from populist allies, alarm among those fearing protectionism or anti-immigrant policies, and immediate market turbulence. Leaders and institutions emphasized the need to maintain dialogue and manage differences, while publics and markets braced for uncertainty about the policy direction of the next U.S. administration.

A Cook County judge set bond at $1.5 million for Chicago police Officer Jason Van Dyke, who was charged with first-degree murder for firing 16 shots that killed 17-year-old Laquan McDonald in October 2014. Van Dyke, who surrendered to authorities Nov. 24 and had been held in custody, posted the required 10% ($150,000) and was released the same day. At the hearing Judge Donald Panarese Jr. watched portions of the silent dashcam video prosecutors say shows Van Dyke emptying a 9mm magazine over roughly 15 seconds, with most shots occurring after McDonald had fallen. The judge noted the presumption of innocence in explaining his decision.

The dashcam footage — released the day Van Dyke was charged — sparked widespread demonstrations across Chicago, calls for Police Supt. Garry McCarthy’s resignation, and the mayor’s announcement of a Task Force on Police Accountability to review oversight, training and discipline and report recommendations by March 31, 2016. Protest activity included rallies that briefly blocked holiday shoppers, arrests outside City Hall, and a largely peaceful gathering of about 150 people outside police headquarters.

Details reported by prosecutors and police: officers had been following McDonald after reports of truck break-ins; McDonald was holding a small knife, had PCP in his system, and allegedly slashed a squad car tire. Prosecutors say McDonald was walking away and about 10 feet from Van Dyke when the first shot was fired and that Van Dyke was on scene about 30 seconds and outside his vehicle roughly six seconds before he began shooting. No other officers fired.

Van Dyke’s attorney acknowledged the video appears damaging but said it does not show the whole incident and promised not to try the case in the media, suggesting there is additional information not public. The Fraternal Order of Police did not post bond but encouraged donations; its president said Van Dyke “stepped into training mode” and described McDonald as having “squared his shoulders” before shooting. Separate, related events included an arrest of a student accused of threatening violence on a university campus in apparent response to the shooting. Van Dyke is next due in court Dec. 18.

An off-duty California Highway Patrol sergeant in Concord, Calif., is being praised for her honesty after finding more than $120,000 in cash in two bank deposit bags left in the middle of a roadway in September. While driving on Concord Boulevard she swerved to avoid the bags, made a U‑turn, opened them enough to see stacks of $100 bills, and immediately reported and turned the money over to authorities. Concord police were able to locate the owner and return his life savings. The 20‑year CHP veteran, who asked to remain anonymous, said she returned the money to set an example for her children; some friends expressed surprise at her decision. CHP Golden Gate Division Chief Avery Browne commended her integrity and noted that many officers simply consider such actions part of their duty.

Hurricane Harvey struck the Texas Gulf Coast late Friday, Aug. 25, 2017, making landfall between Port Aransas and Port O’Connor as a Category 4 storm with peak sustained winds near 130 mph. The storm quickly weakened as it moved inland but stalled, leaving much of southeastern Texas under torrential rain and damaging winds that persisted for days. Authorities warned of catastrophic flooding, with some areas forecast to receive up to 40 inches of rain and localized totals of 20–30 inches likely from Corpus Christi toward Houston and Victoria.

Impacts and damage
- Severe wind and structural damage in coastal communities, especially Rockport (widespread destruction, damaged schools, collapsed roofs, senior housing roof collapse) and Corpus Christi (downed poles, roof damage, marina and boat damage).
- Major flooding in Houston and surrounding counties with flash flood emergencies, submerged roadways, rescues from vehicles and buildings, and at least one confirmed drowning.
- Large-scale power outages across the coast — reports ranged from ~211,000 to nearly 338,000 customers without power at different points — and localized communications losses.
- Evacuations and sheltering: thousands used shelters; state parks hosted evacuees; hotel tax suspended for evacuees and responders.
- Emergency response: Coast Guard and local crews conducted numerous rescues (dozens saved, including from vessels), about 1,000 personnel assigned to search-and-rescue, and roughly 1,800 Texas service members mobilized for recovery.
- Infrastructure and services: boil-water advisories issued in some cities; major road and transit disruptions; three prisons in Brazoria County were evacuated; flights and cruise operations disrupted, and nearly one-fifth of U.S. Gulf oil production was shut in as platforms were evacuated.

Government and agency actions
- State and federal response activated: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott requested and received a federal disaster declaration; federal agencies, including FEMA, prepositioned supplies; President Trump and administration officials monitored operations from Camp David and Washington.
- Officials repeatedly emphasized staying put or following evacuation orders, warned of prolonged flooding risk, and urged preparedness; ICE/CBP announced enforcement pauses at shelters.

Forecast and warnings
- National Hurricane Center and National Weather Service warned of life-threatening storm surge over a wide coastal area, extreme inland flooding over multiple days, and possible tornadoes.
- The storm weakened to a Category 1 and later to a tropical storm as it moved slowly inland, but rainfall and flood threats remained the primary danger.

Economic and logistical effects
- Extensive travel disruptions with many flights canceled and cruise ships diverted or delayed; port operations closed (Galveston).
- Energy sector impacts with significant temporary shutdowns of Gulf oil and gas production and refiners affected.

Overall, Harvey was described by officials as one of the most serious storms in Texas history, bringing destructive winds at landfall and posing a sustained, severe flooding threat as it lingered over the region.

Archaeologists will this week use ground-penetrating radar to scan the grounds of Waltham Abbey Church in Essex to test whether King Harold II — traditionally said to have been killed at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066 and depicted dying with an arrow in the eye on the Bayeux Tapestry — might instead have survived and been buried at the abbey decades later.

The survey team, Stratascan, which was involved in locating Richard III’s remains, will carry out the scan on the anniversary of the battle. The project is funded and driven by local amateur historian and stonemason Peter Burke, who has researched an alternative narrative from a 12th‑century source (Vita Haroldi) suggesting Harold was wounded, nursed back to health, possibly fled to Germany, and lived on until about 1090 as a hermit. Burke hopes the scan — focused near the east wall about 15 yards from Harold’s reputed tomb — will reveal remains consistent with an elderly man scarred on the head, or other evidence (bones, ash, or a misidentified grave) that would challenge the conventional account.

English Heritage granted permission for the non‑intrusive geophysical work; any excavation would require further consents because the site is consecrated and archaeologically sensitive. The search may be filmed for a documentary. Critics note the abbey grounds have been disturbed over centuries and doubt conclusive evidence will be found. If the scan did produce promising results, DNA testing and further investigation would be needed before any revision of the established history could be considered.

Kim Kardashian West was robbed at gunpoint early Monday in a private Paris apartment while attending fashion week. Five armed, masked men wearing fake police armbands forced entry to the building after threatening and handcuffing the concierge, then two of them entered her flat. They tied and gagged Kardashian West, held a gun to her head, locked her in the bathroom, and fled on bicycles with a jewellery box and a ring reported worth about €6m and €4m respectively (more than $10m total), plus mobile phones. She was “badly shaken but physically unharmed,” gave a police statement, and flew back to New York; her family was placed under police protection. The assailants remain at large and Paris police launched an investigation. The incident prompted political reactions about security in the city and renewed attention to recent high-profile jewellery heists in France.

Investigations after the Boston Marathon bombing turned up a variety of extremist and fringe publications connected to suspect Tamerlan Tsarnaev, indicating his exposure to a mix of conspiracy theories beyond alleged Islamist radicalization. Tamerlan, who died in a police shootout April 19, and his younger brother Dzhokhar, accused of carrying out the April 15 attack that killed three and wounded more than 260, had befriended Donald Larking years earlier when their mother worked as a health aide for Larking’s wife. Larking, who was left brain-damaged after a 1974 shooting, shared conspiracy-laden newspapers and materials with the brothers—questioning events such as 9/11 and the Newtown shootings, and including anti-Semitic and Holocaust-denial literature, according to Larking’s lawyer Jason Rosenberg and other sources.

Their relationship grew as the brothers sometimes helped care for Larking and his wife; Larking later converted to Islam and attended the brothers’ mosque. Observers at the mosque described Larking as sociable but cognitively impaired and often politically incorrect. Landlady Joanna Herlihy said she salvaged extremist publications from Tamerlan’s Cambridge apartment, including a Confederate-flag–linked Alabama publication and a weekly listed by the Southern Poverty Law Center as anti-Semitic.

Prosecutors also allege Dzhokhar possessed jihadi material on his computer—writings by an influential extremist advocate, an article glorifying martyrdom, and a magazine with instructions for building pressure-cooker bombs. Rosenberg said Larking likely didn’t teach the brothers to carry out violence but may have reinforced their beliefs by showing them a sympathetic American voice.

A man identified as 36-year-old Brian Howard of Naperville has been charged with one felony count of Destruction of Aircraft or Aircraft Facilities after investigators say he deliberately set a fire Friday morning in the basement of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Air Route Traffic Control Center in Aurora, Illinois. The center monitors high-altitude traffic into and through the Chicago area. Howard — a contract employee at the facility for about eight years who worked on telecommunications and knew the systems — allegedly cut radar feeds, damaged the host computer and communications lines, and set gas-soaked rags near sensitive equipment. The damage forced an evacuation and a temporary ground stop at Chicago O’Hare and Midway, producing hundreds of cancellations and delays regionally and rippling across the country.

According to an FBI affidavit, Howard arrived around 5:06 a.m., sent a private Facebook message saying he intended to “take out ZAU” and himself, then started the blaze about 5:36–5:42 a.m. First responders found smoke, burned towels, a gasoline can, lighter, exposed cables and a knife; Howard was located with self-inflicted stab wounds and was taken to a hospital under police guard. Authorities say he acted alone and the incident is not being treated as terrorism. Naperville police had earlier been asked to do a welfare check after family concerns and found no victims at his apartment; searches of his home revealed documents arranged to be easily found.

The Aurora center’s capacity is significantly reduced while repairs and damage assessments continue; adjacent FAA centers are handling much of its workload at dramatically reduced throughput (about 25% of normal), with only limited routes available out of Chicago. The FAA is augmenting staffing at neighboring facilities, but officials warned outages and delays could continue for days. The disruption led to thousands of cancellations and delays—O’Hare reported about 1,550 cancellations and Midway about 470 on Friday—and had an economic impact. Senator Mark Kirk called for an FAA review of screening and procedures to prevent a single individual from causing such disruption. If convicted Howard faces up to 20 years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

United Airlines has rolled out a redesigned boarding process nationwide after months of testing in major hubs (Chicago, Houston and earlier at LAX). The main change reduces gate lanes from five to two while keeping five numbered boarding groups. Lane 1 (blue) serves preboard (Global Services, Premier 1K, active military, customers with disabilities, families with young children) plus Groups 1 and arriving priority passengers; Lane 2 (green) handles Groups 2–5, with Groups 3–5 asked to remain seated until paged to reduce gate crowding. Certain Chase co-branded cardholders and other priority customers are placed in Group 2. United is also launching optional mobile app push notifications to alert customers when boarding begins (triggered when the first boarding pass is scanned), helping passengers avoid lingering at the gate.

The change aims to cut congestion, idle crowds, and stress at busy gates—which passengers had been complaining about—and to speed boarding. United says the shift follows extensive tests and customer feedback; similar simplified systems are used by competitors (American uses two lanes, Delta four). A notable difference: United allows top-tier 1K elites to pre-board before others, a privilege most carriers reserve for only the highest VIP tiers. The new lanes and gateside notifications began rolling out this week.

Also included in the release: United announced a proposed joint business agreement (JBA) with Copa and Avianca, pending regulatory approval and antitrust immunity. The airlines say the revenue-sharing, metal‑neutral partnership would integrate routes across the U.S., Central and South America (currently excluding Brazil), expand nonstop and codeshare options, align schedules and loyalty benefits, increase service and competition, and drive economic benefits for gateway cities. Implementation awaits government approvals. United cautions that forward-looking statements are subject to many operational and market risks.

Ireland voted decisively to legalize same-sex marriage in a landmark referendum, becoming the first country to approve marriage equality by popular vote. With one of the highest turnouts in two decades (about 60.5%), 62% (1,201,607) voted Yes versus 38% (734,300) No, a margin of 467,307; 42 of 43 constituencies approved the amendment (only Roscommon–South Leitrim rejected it). Dublin returned especially strong Yes figures (many constituencies above 70%). The vote followed a broad coalition of political parties, employers, celebrities and a youth-driven campaign; many Irish expatriates returned to vote. Celebrations in Dublin Castle and nationwide were jubilant, with politicians including Taoiseach Enda Kenny and ministers hailing the result as a social revolution and a beacon for equality. International figures, including Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton and Ellen DeGeneres, applauded the outcome.

The Catholic Church, which opposed the change, acknowledged the social shift after years of diminished political influence following abuse scandals; Archbishop Diarmuid Martin called for a “reality check” and said the result poses a challenge. Prominent No campaigners, including Iona Institute director David Quinn, congratulated the Yes side but urged protections for religious freedom and freedom of conscience. The referendum on lowering the minimum age for presidential candidates, held simultaneously, was defeated. Supporters said the result will reduce stigma and signal to young LGBT people that they need not be afraid.

A Morro Bay fish market owner paid a fisherman a few hundred dollars to buy and release a 70-pound octopus he named Fred rather than sell it. Giovanni DeGarimore of Giovanni’s Fish Market said his decision was personal—he’s an avid diver who respects octopuses and no longer feels comfortable selling them after a close encounter while diving. The rescue story, posted on the market’s Facebook page, has been widely shared.

The document also discusses octopus intelligence and behavior. Two-spotted octopuses have been known to cause damage in aquariums by dismantling equipment, highlighting their problem-solving ability. Jennifer Mather, a comparative psychologist, explains that octopuses show many signs of intelligence: they learn and apply techniques to open prey, switch tactics when challenged, play with objects, and display consistent personality traits (activity, reactivity, avoidance). Cephalopods possess a relatively large, centralized brain with areas specialized for memory, and about one-third of their neurons are distributed in their arms, enabling fine manipulation with numerous sucker-based “pincer” grips. Mather suggests their intelligence evolved to meet the demands of complex reef environments rather than social living. Historical anecdotes illustrate octopuses’ curiosity and knack for escaping or dismantling aquarium equipment.

House Republicans, led by Oversight Committee Chairman Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R‑Utah), introduced an impeachment resolution against IRS Commissioner John Koskinen, accusing him of violating the public trust during the probe of the IRS’s targeting of conservative groups. The resolution, sponsored by Chaffetz and 18 committee Republicans and now sent to the House Judiciary Committee, alleges Koskinen failed to preserve 422 backup tapes that might have contained Lois Lerner’s missing emails, misled Congress by saying all relevant documents had been turned over or were unrecoverable, and did not notify lawmakers when evidence was missing.

Chaffetz said impeachment is needed to restore confidence in the IRS and protect Congress’s institutional interests. The move came days after the Justice Department closed its criminal inquiry into the targeting scandal without filing charges. The IRS strongly disputes the allegations and says it has fully cooperated with investigations.

House Democrats, led by Ranking Member Rep. Elijah Cummings (D‑Md.), called the impeachment effort partisan grandstanding that wastes taxpayer dollars, noting extensive agency cooperation and no evidence Koskinen committed the alleged wrongdoing. Pursuing impeachment of an agency head is highly unusual and goes beyond prior contempt efforts used in related disputes.

Florida police captured a 12-foot, 120-pound Burmese python in Port St. Lucie after neighbors reported a very large snake in a residential block and suspected it had been killing local cats. Officers responding to the call found a dead cat and located the snake concealed in waist-high brush; several officers helped remove it. Although Burmese pythons were banned in Florida in 2012, police said this particular snake belonged to a licensed owner.

On June 30, 2017, former Bronx-Lebanon Hospital physician Dr. Henry Bello carried out a shooting rampage at the hospital, killing one doctor, wounding six others, briefly setting a nurse’s station on fire, and then dying by a self-inflicted gunshot. Bello, who had been forced to resign from the hospital in 2015 amid complaints and a sexual harassment scandal, arrived wearing a lab coat and carrying an assault rifle he had purchased about 10 days earlier. He reportedly asked for a specific doctor he blamed for his dismissal but that doctor, Dr. Kamran Ahmed, was not working that day and said he did not know why Bello had singled him out. Colleagues described Bello as aggressive and threatening, and said he had previously warned he would return to harm staff. The slain physician, Dr. Tracy Sin-Yee Tam, 32, had been covering a shift in the main hospital; neighbors and coworkers mourned her as a well-liked teacher and clinician. Six victims were hospitalized, one critically; detectives recovered the rifle’s packaging from Bello’s Bronx residence and traced the weapon to a Schenectady gun shop. The account has been corrected to note Bello used an assault rifle, not an automatic weapon.

Al Qaeda has claimed responsibility for the August abduction of 70-year-old American development worker Warren Weinstein in Lahore, Pakistan, and issued demands for his release. In a videotaped message, Ayman al‑Zawahri said Weinstein would be freed only if the U.S. stopped airstrikes in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia and Yemen and released all al‑Qaeda and Taliban detainees; Zawahiri framed the kidnapping as retaliation for U.S. detentions and called Weinstein “neck‑deep in American aid to Pakistan.”

Weinstein, a long‑time Pakistan resident and Urdu speaker who lived in Rockville, Maryland, was seized from his Lahore home on Aug. 13 just days before a planned return to the U.S. Authorities initially did not identify his captors, and analysts say he may have been transferred among criminal and militant groups before al‑Qaeda asserted control. J.E. Austin Associates, the U.S. consulting firm he led in Pakistan on USAID‑funded projects, said he is in poor health and listed numerous heart medications, urging kidnappers to provide them.

Locally, Weinstein was widely regarded as a helpful development professional. Colleagues described him as friendly and influential in projects such as dairy modernization—attracting roughly $63 million in new investment, creating over 2,150 jobs and boosting producer productivity—and supporting gem‑trade scholarships that enabled tribal students to find employment or start businesses. University and industry contacts praised his hands‑on role in building facilities and arranging international partnerships.

The Boy Scouts of America has revoked the charter of Troop 98 and its affiliated Cub Scout pack at Rainier Beach United Methodist Church in Seattle because the church refuses to remove openly gay Scoutmaster Geoffrey (Geoff) McGrath. BSA policy allows gay youth but continues to bar openly gay adults from leadership; after McGrath — a married, 49-year-old Eagle Scout — was publicly identified as gay, the national organization and local leaders told the church it must follow BSA policies or lose its charter. The BSA informed parents it had identified a local community center willing to take over sponsorship of the units.

The church’s pastor, Rev. Monica Corsaro, said the move was expected, called it unilateral and said the congregation would continue to support McGrath and its youth program even if it can no longer use BSA names, logos, uniforms or structure. About 15 boys participate in the troop and pack; some families, including two gay fathers, said they do not plan to transfer to the new sponsor. McGrath said he was shocked and lamented the lack of meaningful discussion before the charter was revoked. The case appears to be the first known expulsion of an adult leader under the BSA’s post-2013 policy that permits gay youth but not gay adult leaders.

Seattle investigative reporter Chris Halsne (KIRO-TV/CBS/Cox) returned from El Salvador after interviewing a U.S. government subcontractor who says he observed Secret Service advance-team members — including snipers, K‑9 teams and explosives specialists — partying heavily at a San Salvador strip club in the days before President Obama’s March 2011 visit to meet President Mauricio Funes.

According to the eyewitness, roughly a dozen Secret Service agents and some U.S. military personnel drank heavily and used the club’s VIP area, where strippers allegedly provided sexual favors for extra pay. The witness says he warned agents against taking escorts to their hotel rooms, but at least two agents reportedly had escorts check into their rooms. It is unclear whether those escorts were the same women from the club.

Halsne also interviewed the club owner, who confirmed a large U.S. contingent visited his venue for several nights before the presidential visit. The owner said his club caters to U.S. embassy staff and other law enforcement visitors, emphasizes privacy and security, does not permit prostitution on premises, and requires his performers to be at least 18. He said employees are free to do what they want after work, though he discourages off-premises contact with customers.

The report precedes and echoes revelations about Secret Service personnel hiring prostitutes in Cartagena, Colombia, earlier this month. Halsne says he has names of some agents allegedly involved and records that bolster the subcontractor’s account; KIRO-TV planned further stories. The Secret Service said it would investigate credible information brought to its attention. Lawmakers, including Rep. Darrell Issa and Sen. Chuck Grassley, called for independent, transparent investigations to determine whether misconduct spans multiple incidents and years. DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano stated she saw no evidence of additional misconduct but expressed disappointment in those involved.

Summary:

Michael Flynn resigned as President Trump’s national security adviser after revelations that he misled Vice President Mike Pence and other White House officials about the content of his late-December phone calls with Russia’s ambassador, Sergey Kislyak. The Justice Department and acting Attorney General Sally Yates alerted White House counsel Don McGahn on January 26 that Flynn’s account did not match intelligence about those calls; Trump and a small circle were briefed then, but Pence was not told he had been misinformed until February 9 after media reports. The White House concluded Flynn had not broken the law but said the erosion of trust made his position untenable; Spicer and Kellyanne Conway gave differing accounts of whether Flynn resigned voluntarily or was asked to leave.

Reports say Flynn discussed Russia’s response to the Obama administration’s expulsion of 35 Russian diplomats and may have raised sanctions, contradicting earlier denials. FBI agents reportedly interviewed Flynn in the administration’s early days and likely possessed transcripts or records of the calls; legal experts warned that while prosecution under the Logan Act is unlikely, false-statements charges (18 U.S.C. §1001) could arise if Flynn lied to the FBI. Flynn defended himself, saying he “crossed no lines,” condemning leaks of classified material and suggesting he inadvertently gave incomplete information to Pence due to the fast pace of the transition.

The episode reignited questions about Trump’s ties to Russia and prompted bipartisan calls for investigations. Some Republicans, including Senate leaders, urged congressional review of Flynn’s contacts; Democrats pressed for wider probes into Trump associates’ interactions with Russian officials. The controversy also intensified scrutiny of intelligence leaks and whether surveillance of the Russian ambassador—used to produce the information that reached reporters—was handled appropriately. Flynn’s abrupt fall, just 24 days after taking the job, added to the perception of chaos in the early Trump administration and raised concerns among allies about U.S. policy toward Russia.

On June 27, 2017 a blue police helicopter piloted by Oscar Pérez flew over Caracas and attacked government targets, deepening an already severe political crisis in Venezuela. The helicopter fired shots at the Interior Ministry (officials said 15 rounds) and dropped four grenades on the Supreme Court; one grenade failed to detonate and there were no reported injuries. Social media showed the helicopter carrying an anti-government banner reading “350 Freedom” and images of Pérez; he later posted a video claiming responsibility and calling on a coalition of soldiers, police and civilians to rise against what he called a “criminal” and “tyrannical” Maduro government. In the video Pérez described the group as nationalists, patriots and “institutionalists,” appealed for Venezuelans and elements of the armed forces to join them, invoked Articles 305 and 333 of the constitution, and demanded President Maduro’s immediate resignation and new elections.

President Nicolás Maduro denounced the incident as a “terrorist attack,” ordered security forces to hunt the pilot and recover the stolen German-built Bolkow helicopter, and used the episode to mobilize the armed forces. Government officials showed images intended to link Pérez to foreign influence, and accused him of acting on behalf of U.S. interests; Maduro also linked the pilot to former interior minister Miguel Rodríguez Torres, an allegation Rodríguez Torres denied. Opposition figures and some observers suspected the episode could be either a genuine rogue action by a dissident policeman or a staged provocation by the government to justify a crackdown—pointing to oddities such as the helicopter’s apparent freedom to operate and the lack of casualties.

The attack occurred amid months of anti-government protests over the economy, shortages and Maduro’s push to convene a Constituent Assembly—an upcoming July 30 vote opponents say would consolidate his power. The event coincided with judicial moves seen as weakening dissident prosecutor Luisa Ortega Díaz, further inflaming tensions. The government pursued Pérez and those involved; the helicopter was later found on the Caribbean coast, but Pérez’s whereabouts remained unknown. The incident heightened polarization and uncertainty in Venezuela, with both sides using it to bolster their narratives as the country teetered toward greater confrontation.

Domnica Cemortan, a 26-year-old Moldovan dancer who was on the Costa Concordia’s bridge when it struck rocks off Giglio in January 2012, testified at Captain Francesco Schettino’s manslaughter and abandoning-ship trial that she had been romantically involved with him and was with him that night. Cemortan said she had worked briefly for the cruise line in December 2011 and reboarded the ship as a non-paying passenger hours before the disaster; she acknowledged she and Schettino were lovers only after a judge warned her she could face charges for refusing to answer. She described dining at the captain’s table, being on the bridge as the ship approached Giglio, helping passengers evacuate, being pushed into a lifeboat by a crew member, and later handing Schettino back his laptop. She told the court Schettino urged her to “save yourself” after the collision.

Schettino faces charges related to the January 2012 wreck that killed 32 people and risks up to 20 years in prison. Defense arguments have blamed mechanical failures (watertight doors) and the ship’s Indonesian helmsman, who received a reduced sentence after a plea deal; prosecution and expert testimony have downplayed those factors. Earlier testimony noted that days before the disaster Schettino had been asked to sail close to Giglio and had directed an even closer approach the following week. The 290m ship was righted in a major salvage operation months later; remains of one missing person were recovered and one remains unaccounted for. The trial will hear testimony from many survivors and is expected to last weeks.

Nick Stoeberl, a 24-year-old artist and comedian from California, has been verified by Guinness World Records 2015 as having the longest tongue on record: 10.1 cm (3.97 in) measured from tip to the middle of the closed top lip. Stoeberl, who first noticed his long tongue imitating Gene Simmons as a child, enjoys the attention and can lick his nose and elbow, though he jokes it means longer tongue brushing. His measurement surpassed Brit Stephen Taylor’s 9.8 cm record from 2002.

The story also highlights 18-year-old Adrianne (Adrienne) Lewis of Michigan, who claims a 4-inch tongue and has viral photos and videos showing she can touch her nose, chin, elbow and even her eye with help. Lewis is in talks with Guinness World Records to see if she can officially break Stoeberl’s record.

The feature appears in the 60th anniversary Guinness World Records 2015 book, which includes other record stories and new Augmented Reality content, and the organizations’ social and video channels for more record-breaking coverage.

ABC has given a straight-to-series eight-episode midseason revival order to Roseanne, bringing back the Conner family nearly 20 years after the original sitcom ended. Network president Channing Dungey announced the pickup, saying the multicamera comedy will find the Connors facing "the economic challenges of living pay check to pay check in 2018."

Original stars returning include Roseanne Barr and John Goodman, with Sara Gilbert, Laurie Metcalf, Michael Fishman and Lecy Goranson also confirmed. Sarah Chalke, who previously substituted as Becky, will appear in a different role. Gilbert helped spearhead the revival and joins Barr, Tom Werner and Bruce Helford as executive producers; Whitney Cummings and Tony Hernandez are also EPs, and Carsey-Werner will produce.

The reboot drew interest from other buyers (including Netflix) and is part of a broader trend of resurrecting popular series (Will & Grace, The X-Files, etc.). ABC positions the revival as a way to reconnect with working-class viewers in the post-2016 political landscape. Roseanne will be ABC’s only multicamera comedy on its 2017–18 slate. A premiere date was not announced.

John Oliver devoted a Last Week Tonight segment to seriously dissecting Donald Trump’s signature proposal to build a wall along the U.S.–Mexico border and have Mexico pay for it. Oliver highlighted multiple practical and factual problems:

- Cost and funding: Trump’s estimates ($4–$12 billion) are far below expert estimates (about $25–$26 billion). There’s no evidence Mexico would pay; Mexican officials have rejected the idea.
- Geography and logistics: Building along the Rio Grande and other areas is legally and physically complicated—past border fencing has sometimes been built inland, even cutting off U.S. land, and the 1970 treaty limits obstructing the river. Construction could take many years and run into private-property complications.
- Effectiveness: Much unauthorized immigration occurs via legal entry points with people overstaying visas, so a wall wouldn’t address that. People could also circumvent a wall with ladders, ropes, or tunnels.
- Safety and rhetoric: Trump frames immigrants as criminals, but long-term research shows immigrants are not more crime-prone than native-born Americans, undermining the wall’s purported safety rationale.

Oliver framed the wall as partly symbolic—appealing to voters who want to feel protected—but ultimately absurd and wasteful. He ended with a satirical counterproposal: spend far less to buy every American an electric waffle iron—cheaper, harmless, and (jokingly) just as effective at “keeping out immigrants and drugs,” while producing waffles.

A Cobb County, Ga., police lieutenant, Greg Abbott, has been fired after dashcam video from a July 2016 traffic stop captured him saying, "we only shoot black people," while addressing a frightened passenger. The footage was obtained by WSB-TV via an open-records request and prompted an internal investigation; Abbott had been placed on administrative leave. Police Chief Mike Register said the remark was inexcusable and inconsistent with department values, noting Abbott claimed he was being sarcastic and trying to de-escalate. Register, who has worked to improve community relations since becoming chief in June, called the comment unacceptable and announced the termination. Local Black leaders welcomed the swift action but warned the remark may reflect deeper, systemic problems in the department. Abbott’s attorney had previously said Abbott was cooperating with the probe; he did not immediately comment on the firing.

Cypriot authorities investigated reports that a bright object streaked over the Troodos mountains shortly before midnight, producing a blue glow, loud explosions and sensations of the ground shaking. Police and the Cyprus Geological Department said there’s no sign the object hit the ground; it likely exploded in the sky and may have been a meteor. Hundreds of witness calls came from across the southern half of the island, especially Nicosia and Limassol, but there were no injuries or damage reported and air traffic was normal. Officials are searching for possible meteorite fragments; if recovered, they could provide scientific insights into the early solar system.

Four separate overcharging incidents in central Venice have provoked outrage and a police probe after several foreign tourists received unexpectedly high restaurant bills.

- Most recently, four Japanese students who live in Bologna say they were charged about €1,100 for four steaks, a fried-fish plate (reported variously as for four people), mineral water and service at an osteria near St Mark’s Square; they filed a complaint with police on returning to Bologna. Three women dining nearby reportedly paid about €350 for three plates of seafood pasta. Venice police have opened an investigation after the local citizens’ group Gruppo 25 Aprile publicised the case.

- Italian reports say the restaurant is owned by a Chinese woman and run by an Egyptian. Gruppo 25 Aprile plans to publish tips for tourists to avoid being overcharged and warned that few eateries in that tourist quarter are locally owned.

- The incidents amplify a broader debate about tourists being ripped off in Venice. Mayor Luigi Brugnaro condemned the latest episode and vowed to punish offenders if the claims are confirmed, but has also defended some high bills as legitimate and chided visitors who don’t speak Italian. His remarks drew criticism from local activists, who say the mayor’s stance risks normalising exploitative practices and undermines residents’ interests.

- The controversies come amid ongoing tensions over mass tourism in Venice; the mayor has taken measures to curb tourist numbers, and Italy recently approved plans to ban cruise ships from the city centre.

Unesco experts have concluded that a wreck off Haiti examined after claims it was Christopher Columbus’s flagship, the Santa Maria, is not from 1492 but from a much later period. The Paris-based cultural body said artefacts recovered—particularly bronze/copper-alloy fasteners—indicate shipbuilding techniques typical of the late 17th–18th centuries, whereas the Santa Maria would have used iron or wood fixings. The site is also farther offshore than contemporary accounts suggest the Santa Maria was wrecked.

The announcement responds to US marine investigator Barry Clifford’s May claim that the wreck was the Santa Maria; Clifford and some collaborators, including Professor Charles Beeker, have argued the site remains the best candidate and pointed to older photographs showing what may have been 15th–16th century lombard cannon (now looted) and other evidence needing further study. Unesco’s team, led by former Spanish underwater archaeology chief Xavier Nieto Prieto, said a metal tube seen in earlier expeditions was no longer present and emphasized that no tests had been done on ballast or some bronze objects to determine provenance or age.

Unesco noted the actual Santa Maria could be buried under coastal sediments or lost to erosion and plans further searches in several locations—including possible former seabed now marshland near Haiti’s north coast—subject to better understanding coastal geomorphology. The decision and proposed search areas have provoked controversy: critics say Unesco ignored photographic evidence and earlier expedition records, did not fully test recovered materials, and relied heavily on an edited passage of Columbus’s diary to justify searching on land. The report also led Unesco to advise Haitian authorities against the US-led team’s proposal, citing nonconformity with underwater heritage standards—an action that has stirred tensions, given fraught US–Unesco relations.

Clifford and supporters maintain the site should not be dismissed without comprehensive excavation, argue there are plausible explanations for the bronze fasteners, and stress the lombard photos are crucial evidence. Unesco insists its multidisciplinary examination provides “indisputable proof” the examined wreck is later than Columbus’s era, while continuing efforts to locate the Santa Maria elsewhere.

Tiffany & Co. said protests and increased security around Trump Tower have reduced foot traffic at its Fifth Avenue flagship and contributed to softer sales there, though that store accounts for under 10% of global revenue. The company’s third-quarter results (period ended Oct. 31) showed a modest recovery: worldwide net sales rose about 1–1.2% to ~$949m and comparable-store sales fell 2%, while net income rose 4.5% to $95.1m (76¢ EPS), beating some expectations. Sales were stronger in Japan, China (double-digit growth) and in fashion jewelry (notably the “Tiffany T” gold bracelets), helped by a stronger yen and new lower-priced silver lines and engagement-ring marketing. U.S. sales declined at their slowest pace in five quarters. Management cautioned it cannot rule out further negative effects on flagship sales from ongoing election-related activity and remained cautious about a full recovery despite early encouraging signs. Shares jumped as much as ~8% on the results.

Conflict Armament Research (CAR) released a 200-page investigation, based on three years of fieldwork in Iraq and Syria (2014–2017), documenting more than 40,000 weapons and related items recovered from Islamic State (IS) frontline positions. Using serial numbers and other markings, CAR traced many arms back to their manufacturers and mapped how they reached IS.

Key findings
- Rapid diversion: Some weapons bought by or supplied to U.S.-backed forces reached IS extremely quickly. CAR documented an EU-manufactured anti-tank missile tube exported to the U.S. Army on Dec. 12, 2015, that was in IS hands in Iraq by Feb. 9, 2016—just 59 days later. Photographic evidence links similar weapons to Syrian rebel groups that received external support, suggesting a short chain of custody and diversion.
- Sources and scale: While many weapons were looted from Iraqi and Syrian government stockpiles during IS’s 2014 offensive, the influx of externally supplied arms to Syrian conflict parties significantly increased the quantity and quality of weapons available to IS. More than half of the documented small arms came from Russia and China; over 30 percent originated in EU countries (notably Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary and Germany).
- Diversity and longevity of arsenal: CAR found arms ranging from contemporary weapons to decades-old pieces, including a Mauser rifle made in 1941. Examples include Chinese-made light machine guns (122 found south of Mosul) issued in serial sequence and accompanied by amphetamine pouches—indicating organized stockpiling and drug-assisted issuance. CAR also documented drones modified in IS workshops and sophisticated improvised explosive components.
- Supply-chain concealment and contractual breaches: CAR reports that some transfers involved export-contract violations and deliberate concealment (removing or painting over factory markings, repackaging). Weapons sold by Eastern European manufacturers to intermediaries (including sales to Saudi Arabia and the U.S.) were sometimes re-exported to Syrian militias and subsequently diverted.
- Policy and accountability implications: CAR’s tracing has prompted criminal investigations in some cases (e.g., Belgian probes into IED component supplies). U.S. Defense spokespeople said alleged diversions would be taken seriously and could curtail support if verified; CAR said it had not received a U.S. reply to a trace request. Experts warn the findings highlight risks of arming poorly controlled or lightly vetted armed groups.

Conclusion
CAR’s granular documentation illustrates how a mix of battlefield capture, illicit purchase, and rapid diversion from international supply chains expanded IS’s arsenal—raising concerns about arms transfer oversight, export controls, and the unintended consequences of arming non-state actors in complex conflicts.

John McCone, a California industrialist and engineer who became CIA director in November 1961 after Allen Dulles was forced out following the Bay of Pigs, was charged with restoring order at the agency. After JFK’s assassination in November 1963, President Lyndon Johnson kept McCone in place and the director cooperated with the Warren Commission, testifying that the CIA had no evidence Oswald was part of a conspiracy. The Warren Commission concluded Oswald acted alone.

A once-secret 2013 internal CIA history by David Robarge—quietly declassified last fall—concludes that McCone and other senior CIA officials were “complicit” in a “benign cover-up” that withheld incendiary information from the Warren Commission. Most important, the agency concealed long-running CIA assassination plots against Fidel Castro—some involving the Mafia—which meant the commission was never prompted to investigate whether Oswald had Cuban links or if Castro or his supporters had motive for retaliation. The report also says the CIA may have had contact with Oswald before 1963 and monitored his mail under the HTLINGUAL program; either McCone was not told about that program or he withheld it from the commission.

Robarge portrays McCone as hands-on in restricting CIA assistance to the commission—providing “passive, reactive and selective” help—and possibly sharing the Johnson administration’s desire to avoid disclosures that might fuel conspiracy theories or calls for retaliation. McCone later testified in 1978 that he had been unaware of the Castro plots when he appeared before the commission; Robarge’s report finds that testimony “neither frank nor accurate,” since McCone had been informed of the plots months earlier. The report stops short of challenging the Warren Commission’s core finding that Oswald was the lone gunman, but it says the CIA’s nondisclosure seriously undermined the commission’s credibility and left crucial investigative paths unexplored.

The report also notes complicating factors: Allen Dulles—McCone’s predecessor and a Warren Commission member—had run the anti-Castro covert actions, and McCone had informal, undocumented communications with Attorney General Robert Kennedy in the days after the assassination. Although most of the 2013 report was declassified, it still contains deletions, indicating some relevant files remain secret. The CIA says it released the report to correct misconceptions tying the agency to the assassination; the declassification, however, amounts to an institutional acknowledgement decades later that senior officials misled the Warren Commission by withholding significant information.

Comedian and television personality Rosie O’Donnell revealed on her blog that she suffered a “widow maker” heart attack last week but initially kept it secret. In a poem-style post dated August 20, she recounted experiencing chest pain, sore arms, nausea, clammy skin and vomiting after helping a woman from her car. She took an aspirin after recognizing many of the symptoms online but did not call 911. The following day a cardiologist’s EKG sent her to the hospital, where doctors found her LAD artery 99% blocked and placed a stent. O’Donnell warned other women to learn heart-attack symptoms, listen to their instincts and call 911, noting that about half of women having heart attacks don’t call for help and that roughly 200,000 women die of heart attacks each year in the U.S. She said she feels fortunate to be alive.

Here are concise summaries of the two pieces in the document:

1) Neal McDonough quits Scoundrels over sex scene
- Actor Neal McDonough left the new ABC show Scoundrels three days into filming because the script required him to perform a sex scene. 
- McDonough, a married Catholic father of three, has a long-standing personal policy of refusing sex scenes and has lost roles previously for that reason. 
- The scene in question involved Virginia Madsen; walking away may have cost him as much as $1 million. ABC described the departure as a “casting change.” An insider said he’s lost work but is “sticking to his principles.”

2) Excerpt and interview about Sex at Dawn — critique of lifelong monogamy
- Christopher Ryan and Cacilda Jethá, authors of Sex at Dawn, argue Western marriage is struggling because lifelong monogamy clashes with human evolutionary history. They claim pre-agricultural humans lived in less sexually possessive, more sexually fluid groups, and that the rise of agriculture introduced property concerns that encouraged exclusive pairing and paternity certainty.
- The authors marshal anthropology, primate behavior (notably bonobo promiscuity), historical accounts, and human anatomy (testicle size, penis design, ejaculate volume) to suggest humans evolved with significant sperm competition and nonexclusive mating tendencies. They also note modern sperm-count declines likely linked to environmental factors.
- Ryan (a psychologist, gay man) contends gay men often have a more pragmatic understanding of love vs. sex and are more likely to adopt nonmonogamous arrangements. He criticizes American cultural attitudes — idealized Hollywood narratives of love and a moralistic intolerance of sexual ambiguity — as contributing to marital dissatisfaction, high divorce rates, and sexless unions.
- The book does not prescribe a single alternative to monogamy; instead it urges greater tolerance, clearer communication about sex vs. love, and recognition that marriage’s durable functions (especially child-rearing and social stability) are separate from sexual passion, which often fades.

U.S. District Judge Denise Cote ruled that Nomura Holdings and Royal Bank of Scotland misled Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac by selling mortgage-backed securities with materially defective loans, finding the offering documents “enormously” false. In a 361‑page opinion after a three‑week bench trial, Cote concluded underwriting guidelines were routinely ignored, citing sample reviews showing 45–59% of loans had underwriting defects and many appraisals were inflated. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), as conservator for Fannie and Freddie, sued over roughly $2 billion of securities; Cote said FHFA is entitled to judgment and set a damages framework that could lead to about $450–500 million (her calculations indicated entitlement to $624.4 million less roughly $178 million already recovered). She rejected the banks’ defenses that the housing crash—not loan defects—caused losses and found documentary and email evidence (including internal descriptions of loans as “crap” and warnings like “Danger Batman!!”) showed deficient due diligence and efforts to preserve relationships with originators. Nomura plans to appeal and called its conduct candid; RBS declined comment. The ruling — the first trial decision among some 18 FHFA suits and following prior large settlements totaling about $17.9 billion with other banks — may prompt more settlements to avoid adverse judgments and publicity.

A judge in Phoenix reduced bond to zero and ordered electronic monitoring for Leslie Merritt Jr., who has been charged in a series of freeway shootings last year that struck panic across the Phoenix area. Merritt, who has pleaded not guilty to drive-by shooting, aggravated assault and related charges, was jailed for seven months and celebrated as he left the courtroom. His defense argued that recent developments — including ballistic test results and phone-record evidence they say provide an alibi, as well as similar shootings after Merritt’s arrest — undermine authorities’ claim he was the shooter. A gag order prevents lawyers and officials from discussing the new evidence; prosecutors and the Arizona Department of Public Safety declined comment. Judge Warren Granville set a May 18 court date and warned Merritt to appear.

Separately, Alabama State Troopers reported that a driver suspected of shooting at motorists on U.S. 278 and later exchanging gunfire with officers during a pursuit was killed after a crash and shootout in Blount County. The incident began after 911 calls about someone firing on highway motorists; authorities located a matching vehicle, pursued it, and the driver was later pronounced dead. Names and further details, including identities of the officer involved, were not released.

This piece describes the scale and human cost of mass disappearances, abuse and killings during Libya’s uprising against Moammar Gaddafi.

- Context: Protests that began peacefully in Benghazi in February escalated into a six-month conflict. Rebel leaders estimate nearly 60,000 additional people disappeared during the fighting, adding to thousands already missing under Gaddafi’s long rule. After rebels seized Tripoli they opened prisons and freed thousands, but only about 10,000 freed detainees have been accounted for; many families fear others remain in secret detention or mass graves.

- Personal accounts:
  - Faraj, a 25-year-old rebel, disappeared on the eastern front in March; his family feared he was dead. The story highlights widespread uncertainty and the crisis of missing persons.
  - Abdul Rauf was held 48 days at the notorious Abu Salim prison, long associated with brutal treatment and the 1996 massacre of 1,200 inmates. He reports daily beatings and electric shocks, overcrowded cells (70 men sleeping on the floor), severe deprivation and humiliation. He learned of the revolution while imprisoned. He was later transferred to Tajura prison and freed when pro-Gaddafi and anti-Gaddafi guards unlocked cells as rebels entered Tripoli; his homecoming was emotional.
  - Muneer Masoud Own, 33, recounted being detained with his brother and dozens of others in a warehouse near the 32nd Brigade headquarters in early August. Detainees were beaten, deprived of food and water, and kept in filth. After guards promised release, they allegedly tossed a grenade into the packed warehouse and opened fire; many were killed. Own escaped but lost track of his brother. When rebels later examined the site they found charred remains—volunteers recovered roughly 150 bodies—and additional graves with decomposing bodies and few documents to identify victims.

- Themes and implications: The accounts illustrate systematic brutality in Gaddafi’s detention system, the terror of arbitrary arrests, and the difficulty of accounting for the missing. Families remain desperate for answers; rebel authorities call the situation a “human crisis” as searches continue for mass graves and hidden detention sites.

Libyan leader Col. Muammar Gaddafi gave an hour-long interview in Tripoli to the BBC, ABC and the Sunday Times in which he denied nationwide protests, asserted he had no official position to resign from, and claimed most Libyans loved him and would die to protect him. He dismissed calls from Western leaders to quit, accused the West of betrayal and attempting to recolonize Libya, and blamed al-Qaeda and drugged “terrorists” for inciting the unrest. He denied attacking civilians, saying only military and ammunition sites had been targeted, and challenged accusations about his foreign assets.

The interview came as anti‑Gaddafi protests and fighting continued: opposition forces controlled towns in the east (including Benghazi) and Zawiya near Tripoli, Misrata saw clashes, and about 100,000 people had fled the violence. International pressure intensified—UN officials and foreign ministers called for Gaddafi to go, the EU imposed sanctions (arms embargo, asset freezes and travel bans), and the US froze $30bn of Libyan assets. US and UN leaders condemned the crackdown; US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton accused Gaddafi of using “mercenaries and thugs” and said his leaving might help end violence if accountability were ensured. US Ambassador to the UN Susan Rice called Gaddafi “delusional” and unfit to lead after the interview. Gaddafi remained defiant, refused to go into exile, invited international fact‑finding, and portrayed himself as misunderstood and still in control despite mounting domestic and international opposition.

The Pentagon has drawn up contingency plans to deploy small special-operations teams into Syria to secure or destroy chemical weapons sites if the White House decides intervention is necessary, U.S. officials say. President Obama warned that any Syrian move to use or transfer chemical munitions would cross a “red line,” but U.S. planners are chiefly concerned about preventing the stockpiles from falling into the hands of rebels, extremist militias or foreign proxies. Options under consideration include covert raids by chemical-weapons-trained special forces and precision strikes designed to neutralize agents without dispersing them. U.S. satellites and drones are already monitoring known sites.

U.S. intelligence assesses Syria possesses hundreds of tons of chemical agents—sarin, mustard gas and possibly VX—stored at bunkers and facilities near Aleppo, Hama, Homs and Latakia. Experts note agent potency degrades over time and that delivery systems (including unguided rockets and Scud-type missiles) are inaccurate, so use might cause more panic than mass fatalities. Officials stress no large-scale U.S. intervention has been ordered and detailed operational planning would await direct presidential direction; a unilateral decision to send small teams remains possible, though major action is likely only as part of an international coalition.

On the ground, Syria’s 17-month uprising has escalated into widespread civil war with heavy government offensives in Damascus and Aleppo. Activists and monitoring groups report large numbers of civilian deaths from shelling, helicopter gunships and artillery; Amnesty International documents numerous indiscriminate attacks on residential areas. Battles are also reported for an airfield near the Iraqi border and along supply routes from Iraq and Turkey. The conflict has spilled into Lebanon, notably renewed sectarian violence in Tripoli.

The Assad government denies it will use chemical weapons except in response to foreign intervention. Russia, a Syrian ally, publicly doubts Damascus intends to employ such weapons. International diplomats and leaders continue talks about responses; U.N. mediator Lakhdar Brahimi is engaging opposition figures but stresses the limits and risks of external military intervention without Security Council backing.

Here’s a concise, comprehensive summary of the reporting:

- Incident: On Monday night, 49-year-old actress Demi Moore was rushed from her Beverly Hills home to a nearby hospital after convulsing at a small, all-female birthday gathering for friend Heather Parry. Guests included longtime friend Jennifer Meyer. Paramedics were called after one guest dialed 911 when Moore appeared to have a seizure; she was later released.

Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan Chase announced they are creating an independent, non‑profit‑incentivized company to tackle rising U.S. healthcare costs and improve services for their combined 1.1+ million U.S. employees. Details are sparse: the new entity will initially focus on technology solutions to simplify care, increase transparency and improve outcomes, and will be led in its formation by Todd Combs (Berkshire), Marvelle Sullivan Berchtold (J.P. Morgan) and Beth Galetti (Amazon). CEOs Warren Buffett, Jeff Bezos and Jamie Dimon stressed the effort is long‑term, experimental and intended to use the partners’ scale and resources to drive change.
