Analysts and experts said the U.S. system is ripe for disruption and welcomed employer‑led innovation, but cautioned meaningful cost reduction and better outcomes will be difficult and could take time. Observers noted Amazon’s technology and data capabilities—including potential use of information sharing and AI—could be especially influential if the effort expands beyond the three companies’ employees.

Frank Taaffe, a once-vocal public defender of George Zimmerman after the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, has reversed course and told a federal grand jury he now believes Zimmerman may have racially targeted the teen. Taaffe—who spent months appearing on national TV during Zimmerman’s legal saga, portraying Martin as a troublemaker and Zimmerman as a good neighbor—said he received an anonymous call after the shooting in which a man made racist remarks about Martin; he now thinks that caller may have been Zimmerman, though he admits he cannot be certain.

Reporting into Taaffe’s background notes he has a long criminal and personal history—including arrests and at least two convictions, domestic-violence and other allegations, a DUI-related plea to reckless driving, and family estrangement and tragedies—and a record of making virulently racist public statements on radio, podcasts and social media. Those statements and his on-air legal and forensic commentary drew criticism from other commentators and experts, who questioned why outlets gave him a national platform to opine on technical legal and scientific matters.

Taaffe says recent personal losses (the deaths of two sons and a brother) and a desire to “clear his conscience” motivated him to contact the FBI and testify that Zimmerman racially profiled Martin. He expressed remorse to the Martin family and urged that neighborhood suspicions should be left to law enforcement. Taaffe’s change of heart comes as the Justice Department’s civil-rights probe into Martin’s death continues; he did not testify in Zimmerman’s criminal trial, in which Zimmerman was acquitted of murder.

Yulia Skripal, one of two people poisoned with a nerve agent in Salisbury, is improving rapidly and is no longer in a critical condition, Salisbury District Hospital said; doctors report she is stable, conscious and talking, and continues to receive 24-hour specialist care. Her father, 66-year-old former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal—believed to have been the primary target—remains critically ill but stable.

Police believe the pair were poisoned with a Novichok nerve agent that was smeared on Sergei Skripal’s front door; forensic tests found the highest concentration there and lower concentrations at other town locations. About 130 people may have been exposed in the aftermath. Around 250 counter-terrorism detectives are investigating, reviewing more than 5,000 hours of CCTV, 1,350 seized exhibits and 500 witnesses. As a precaution, officers cordoned off a children’s play area near the Skripals’ home to search it.

The UK government accuses the Russian state of responsibility; Moscow denies the allegation. In response to the incident, at least 26 countries expelled Russian diplomats and Russia announced reciprocal expulsions and other measures, including closing the British Council in Russia. Det Sgt Nick Bailey, a Wiltshire police officer exposed in the response, was discharged from hospital on 22 March but has said his life will likely never be the same.

San Juan County, Utah — a county heavily dependent on tourism and composed mostly of state, federal or tribal lands — declared a state of emergency and announced plans to forcibly reopen several National Park and Monument sites closed by the federal government. Commissioners, led publicly by Phil Lyman, said they would remove barricades at sites such as Natural Bridges National Monument and mobilize at least 60 personnel (sheriff’s deputies, search-and-rescue volunteers, firefighters, EMTs), portable toilets, garbage trucks and three mobile command centers to staff entrances, provide sanitation, run search-and-rescue and law-enforcement functions, and otherwise keep parks open. They cited the economic pain to local businesses (about 70% depend on park visitors) and said they might seek state financial support.

County officials framed the move as civil disobedience and public interest action, saying they did not intend to threaten federal employees. The National Park Service had warned the county such actions are illegal; trespassing in a national park can lead to fines and jail. County leaders said they had informed the regional superintendent and were postponing immediate action to give Utah Gov. Gary Herbert time to speak with Interior Secretary Sally Jewell. Gov. Herbert said he was ready to provide funding and staff to reopen parks and had asked the president to authorize state support. The commissioners also planned to maximize media attention and stage photo opportunities to explain their actions.

A Bronxville man, 43-year-old investment banker William McCormack, is suing Lawrence Hospital Center and Dr. Michael Kerin after learning he still had his appendix roughly a year after an appendectomy at the hospital. According to the complaint filed in state Supreme Court, Kerin performed and electronically signed an operative report dated Jan. 27, 2013, stating the appendix was removed. McCormack was later told by Kerin that the procedure had been successful.

In March (the following year) McCormack developed severe abdominal pain while in the Adirondacks, went to Adirondack Medical Center in Saranac Lake, and underwent emergency surgery where doctors found his appendix intact. The lawsuit includes a Lawrence Hospital pathology report that says a specimen labeled "appendix" was received but the final diagnosis found "no evidence of appendix," and alleges the hospital never informed McCormack of that discrepancy. McCormack claims the removed tissue was a "yellowish mass," not an appendix, and is seeking unspecified damages for pain, suffering and having to undergo surgery twice. Lawrence Hospital says it is investigating and declines to comment on pending litigation; Kerin has not responded to requests for comment.

Actor George Takei defended calling Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas a “clown in blackface” on Facebook, saying “blackface” is theatrical jargon for a white actor portraying a black buffoon and insisting his comment was “theater lingo” and “not racist.” Takei argued Thomas had “abdicated” his African American heritage by suggesting slavery and Japanese American internment did not strip dignity from people; Takei, an internment survivor, said a sitting justice should know better.

Writer Alex Griswold responded harshly, saying people were offended by the remark itself, not Takei’s intent, and accused Takei of downplaying blackface’s racist history. Griswold called Takei’s claim that blackface “is not racist” nonsensical, criticized Takei for declaring Thomas a traitor to his race because of his politics, and argued Takei mischaracterized Thomas’ views by taking them out of context. Griswold noted Thomas’ own background under Jim Crow and lamented the lack of wider left- and Hollywood-based condemnation, singling out Marc Lamont Hill as a notable critic.

A pediatric dentist in Jacksonville, Florida, Dr. Howard S. Schneider, is the subject of multiple civil lawsuits, criminal Medicaid-fraud charges, state and public scrutiny, and numerous abuse allegations by former patients and their parents.

Key allegations and actions
- A class-action lawsuit filed in Duval County accuses Schneider of decades-long assault, battery, false imprisonment and intentionally inflicting severe emotional distress on largely low-income, non‑English‑speaking children, describing his practice as a “house of horrors.” Plaintiffs allege he targeted vulnerable families, used threats to silence victims, and derived sexual or sadistic pleasure from inflicting pain.
- Specific claims include choking children until unconscious instead of using adequate anesthesia, extracting healthy baby teeth or performing unnecessary procedures without anesthetic, leaving children injured and bruised, and fraudulently billing Medicaid for procedures not medically necessary.
- At least 60 identified victims are cited in the suit, with plaintiffs’ attorneys suggesting there could be many more (possibly hundreds to a thousand) who haven’t come forward.
- Dozens of parents have protested outside his office, shared viral videos and social media posts, and filed individual lawsuits; one attorney ultimately took 131 cases and 104 were later settled without admission of wrongdoing.
- The Florida Attorney General’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit charged Schneider (2015) with 11 counts of Medicaid provider fraud and one count of scheme to defraud, alleging nearly $4 million in Medicaid payments over five years for inappropriate or unperformed services. Schneider pleaded not guilty and remains free on bond.

Investigations and professional status
- The Florida Board of Dentistry’s actions, if any, are not publicly known (its investigations are confidential). Schneider voluntarily surrendered his license while under pressure, avoiding a full board hearing.
- Law enforcement (Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office) was called to his office in 2001 and 2013 over excessive-force complaints; two malpractice suits from 1995 were dismissed.
- The Attorney General’s investigation collected parent and patient statements describing screaming, injuries, children found face-down, and procedures performed without proper consent or adequate sedation.
- Medical experts consulted by investigators criticized Schneider’s consent forms, poor record-keeping, substandard work quality, and inadequate sedation. Follow-up dentists reported restorations and fillings by Schneider often failed or disappeared.

Criminal case status and competency proceedings
- Schneider’s criminal trial was delayed after a defense expert said he was not competent to stand trial; the prosecution’s expert disagreed. A judge has appointed a third psychologist to perform an evaluation to resolve the competency question. A hearing was scheduled for November; no trial date has been set.
- Schneider has denied the abuse allegations, insists he used anesthesia appropriately, and says surrendering his license was not an admission of guilt. He has also sought a ruling of mental incompetence to avoid trial.

Public reaction and fallout
- Viral videos and social media posts from parents drew widespread attention and prompted sustained protests at his clinic. Several high‑profile cases (e.g., children named Bri-el and Zion) generated national media coverage.
- Families have pursued civil damages; the class-action seeks more than $15,000 (and a jury trial for damages), while many individual suits have been settled.

Overall, the case centers on serious abuse and fraud allegations spanning decades, a growing number of victims and lawsuits, ongoing criminal charges for Medicaid fraud, and pending determinations about Schneider’s competency to stand trial.

John Tice, president of the Brevard Hall of Fame in Melbourne, Florida, is pushing to repatriate Jim Morrison’s remains from Paris to Melbourne, where Morrison was born on Dec. 8, 1943. Tice, who founded the nonprofit hall of fame in 2012 and runs a small Morrison display there, says Paris cemetery officials reportedly indicated Morrison’s grave lease is nearing expiration and expressed concern about vandalism—so they may be open to relocating the singer’s remains. He plans to contact Père Lachaise Cemetery and, if allowed, would organize fundraising and handle legal issues to bring Morrison to Melbourne for display.

The article notes Morrison’s brief early ties to Melbourne (his family lived there while his father trained) but clarifies longtime rumors that he graduated from Melbourne High are false; his family moved to Clearwater when he was an infant. On July 24, 2017, White House senior adviser Jared Kushner met privately with Senate Intelligence Committee staff and was scheduled to meet the House panel the next day. He released an 11-page statement and later told reporters he “did not collude with Russia” and had “no improper contacts,” asserting he hadn’t relied on Russian funds and had been transparent in updating his security-clearance (SF-86) form.

Key disclosures and claims from Kushner’s statement:
- He identified four contacts with Russians during the campaign and transition (out of many thousands of overall contacts) and described them as routine and not impactful to the election.
- Campaign-period contacts:
  - A brief April 2016 encounter with then-Ambassador Sergey Kislyak at a foreign-policy event, limited to pleasantries.
  - A June 9, 2016 Trump Tower meeting (the one arranged by Donald Trump Jr.) with a Russian lawyer; Kushner says he arrived late, found the meeting focused on adoptions, left after about ten minutes, and did not recall the email chain arranging it until attorneys showed it to him.
  - An October 2016 extortion-like email from a sender calling itself “Guccifer400,” which he treated as a hoax and reported to Secret Service.
- Transition-period contacts:
  - A Dec. 1, 2016 meeting with Kislyak and Michael Flynn at Trump Tower, where Kushner says Kislyak offered to convey information from Russian generals about Syria and Kushner asked if the embassy had a secure line to transmit it; Kislyak declined and Kushner denies proposing an ongoing “secret backchannel.”
  - A Dec. 13, 2016 meeting with Sergey Gorkov, head of state-connected Vnesheconombank (VEB), at Kislyak’s urging; Kushner says the meeting was brief, about Russia’s economy, and did not include discussions of sanctions, business deals, loans or his companies. He says Gorkov gave him two small gifts (a piece of art and a bag of dirt) which he registered with the transition.
- SF-86 disclosure issues: Kushner says an assistant prematurely filed a draft of his clearance form that omitted all foreign contacts; he submitted supplements afterward and ultimately disclosed more than 100 contacts with officials from 20+ countries. He says he has cooperated with investigators and provided documents and records.

Reactions and context:
- Kushner’s account disputes some media reports (e.g., Reuters’ claim of two calls with Kislyak) and contradicts details suggested by other sources, including press accounts that the Dec. 1 meeting sought a secret communications channel. Those discrepancies — plus the meetings with Kislyak and Gorkov and his attendance at the June 9 meeting — have prompted scrutiny and questions from lawmakers and observers who say many assertions can be checked by investigators.
- House Speaker Paul Ryan defended special counsel Robert Mueller as nonpartisan amid President Trump’s repeated criticism of the probes. Trump continued public attacks on Democratic investigators and urged probes into Hillary Clinton’s Russia ties.
- Senate and House intelligence committees planned further interviews; Sen. Mark Warner indicated bipartisan expectation Kushner would be called back.

Overall, Kushner seeks to deny wrongdoing and limit concern by framing his interactions as limited and innocuous, but his detailed account raises specific factual points investigators can verify and has prompted continued scrutiny.

This document is a collection of short film reviews and notes, with most space devoted to the romantic comedy Did You Hear About the Morgans? and a longer piece on Jeff Bridges’s Crazy Heart.

- Did You Hear About the Morgans?
  - Reviewers find the Marc Lawrence–directed rom-com thin and often painfully unfunny. Hugh Grant and Sarah Jessica Parker play a Manhattan couple on the verge of divorce who witness a murder and are placed in witness protection in rural Wyoming. The fish-out-of-water premise has potential (city sophisticates humbled by red‑state life), but jokes land awkwardly, with long dead silences before weak payoffs. Despite likable leads—Grant’s dry deadpan and Parker’s presence—the script’s reliance on stereotypes (privileged, Blackberry‑addicted urbanites vs. “real America”) and formulaic beats undercut the film. Sam Elliott and Mary Steenburgen appear as their country hosts. Rated PG-13; running time about 1 hour 43 minutes.

- Crazy Heart
  - Adapted and directed by Scott Cooper from Thomas Cobb’s novel, the film follows aging country singer Bad Blake (Jeff Bridges), a fallen honky‑tonk star hollowed out by booze and solitude. A relationship with a small‑town journalist (Maggie Gyllenhaal) and her son triggers a slow, believable moral and emotional recovery. Reviewers praise the film as a well-made, adult American drama that treats its subject with tenderness and restraint; Bridges’s performance anchors the film and evokes the genre’s darker roots.

- Other brief capsule reviews:
  - Fall Down Dead: A standard exploitation/horror entry featuring a masked serial killer, some gore and stunt casting (Dominique Swain, Udo Kier, David Carradine). Watchable but unexceptional, with a weak ending.
  - Home: Ursula Meier’s debut about an insular family whose attempt to block highway noise escalates into paranoia. The film is praised for its confident, strange tone, strong visuals (DP Agnès Godard), and Isabelle Huppert’s presence; it explores intimacy, isolation, and escalating claustrophobia effectively.

Overall tone: the roundup favors thoughtful, character‑driven work (Crazy Heart, Home) and is dismissive of formulaic commercial rom‑com fare (Did You Hear About the Morgans?), while noting solid performances even when material is weak.

- In early 2017, then-FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe authorized a federal criminal inquiry into whether Attorney General Jeff Sessions lied (lacked candor) in his January 2017 congressional testimony about contacts with Russian officials and knowledge of campaign contacts with Russians. The probe was prompted by a March 2017 letter from Sens. Patrick Leahy and Al Franken asking the FBI to investigate Sessions’ contacts and whether laws were broken.

- The inquiry was briefed to top lawmakers in a closed-door session with McCabe and Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein. By the time Rosenstein was overseeing the Russia-related matters (after Sessions’ recusal), the investigation became one of the matters handled by the special counsel’s office; Robert Mueller later interviewed Sessions. According to Sessions’ attorney, Chuck Cooper, the special counsel has since informed him Sessions is not under investigation for false statements or perjury related to his confirmation testimony, and the inquiry has been closed without charges.

- Sessions originally told the Senate he had no contacts with Russians connected to the campaign; subsequent reporting and testimony revealed he had met the Russian ambassador during the campaign and later acknowledged those meetings, saying they were not campaign-related. George Papadopoulos’ later guilty plea and statements about contacts with Russians raised further questions about what Sessions knew.

- McCabe was fired less than 48 hours before his planned retirement after an inspector general report found he had “lacked candor” in interviews about authorizing an interview with reporters in 2016. Officials told ABC and NBC that Sessions was not aware of the FBI’s earlier Sessions perjury probe when he fired McCabe. McCabe denies wrongdoing and says his dismissal was retaliatory due to events after James Comey’s firing.

- No charges have been brought against Sessions concerning false statements, and the perjury inquiry did not lead to prosecution. The reporting notes that perjury referrals from partisan actors are common but prosecutions are rare because they’re difficult to prove.

At a Democratic Platform Committee meeting in Orlando, supporters of Bernie Sanders failed to secure explicit language opposing the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP); the committee instead adopted wording opposing “trade agreements that do not support good American jobs.” Sanders’ team called the outcome disappointing but noted other gains, including platform language backing a $15 federal minimum wage.

Meanwhile, Hillary Clinton announced health-policy changes seen as concessions to Sanders’ progressive agenda. Her proposals include:
- Increasing mandatory funding for Federally Qualified Health Centers (community health clinics) by $40 billion over 10 years, effectively doubling support for primary care at those centers that serve low-income and uninsured populations.
- Reaffirming support for a public-option insurance plan within the Affordable Care Act exchanges.
- Allowing people aged 55 and older to buy into Medicare (a Medicare “buy-in”).

Clinton said the clinic funding would be paid for through savings, innovations, and tax changes aimed at closing loopholes and making the wealthy pay more. Sanders praised the moves as important steps that would save lives, cut costs, and expand access, and he acknowledged growing alignment between his campaign and Clinton’s. The policy shifts—together with a separate college affordability proposal Clinton expanded earlier in the week—appear aimed at courting Sanders’ progressive supporters ahead of his expected endorsement of Clinton at a joint event in New Hampshire.

Tropical Storm Isaac disrupted the start of the 2012 Republican National Convention in Tampa, forcing planners to cancel Monday’s events, shift the schedule, and shorten the four-day meeting to three days. The storm’s arrival scrapped Donald Trump’s planned Monday appearance — one of the convention’s highest-profile casualties — as well as other sessions and led organizers to open briefly on Monday then recess until Tuesday. Officials stressed safety and noted the potential political optics of staging a celebratory convention as a dangerous storm approached the Gulf Coast.

Trump, in Florida to receive a Sarasota GOP “statesman of the year” award, said he had been given a “big role” but would likely return to New York because of the conflict. He reiterated his long-running “birther” attacks on President Barack Obama and urged Republicans to abandon political correctness and “fight fire with fire.” His spokesman defended the canceled appearance as a would-have-been spectacle; some Republicans welcomed the change.

Despite losing a day, GOP leaders said they would press their plan to use the convention to define Obama’s record as a failure and to elevate Mitt Romney as the alternative. Full proceedings were set to resume Tuesday with adoption of the platform and Romney’s formal nomination; some speeches would be shortened and officials did not rule out extending the convention a day if needed. Delegates and speakers expressed concern for storm-affected communities—especially Louisiana—and discussed the logistics of the compressed schedule.

The convention’s lead-up was already complicated by other political issues: controversies around Rep. Todd Akin’s remarks on rape and abortion, disputes over Romney and Paul Ryan’s positions on social issues and Medicare reform, and ongoing attacks from the Obama campaign framing Romney’s “reinvention.” Polling cited in the report showed a close national race with voters viewing Obama as more in touch with everyday concerns while giving Romney advantages on managerial and economic issues. Overall, Republicans aimed to focus the convention on Romney’s economic case against Obama despite weather disruptions and internal controversies.

Archaeologists from the University of Reading, working with Historic England, Wiltshire Museum and other partners, have uncovered exceptionally well-preserved Neolithic and Bronze Age remains at Marden Henge and nearby Wilsford in the Vale of Pewsey, Wiltshire — a landscape midway between Stonehenge and Avebury. Excavations this summer revealed the floor plan of a rectangular Neolithic house more than 4,300 years old, with thousands of white chalk fragments used as a plaster-like surface, and a scatter of flint tools, finely worked arrowheads and blades. Organic and food remains recovered include decorated pottery with charred food residues, masses of seeds and grains, pig bones (probably the remains of at least 13 animals), scorch marks from a central firepit, and small animal bones — evidence the building was used for large communal feasting rather than permanent domestic occupation. The house stood on a terrace within a small banked circle that formed part of the enormous Marden Henge: ramparts up to three metres high once enclosed about 15 hectares, making it larger than Avebury and far bigger than Stonehenge. The team believes such monumental scale expressed status and the ability to mobilise labour.

At nearby Wilsford, archaeologists unearthed a 4,000-year-old Bronze Age skeleton, likely that of a child buried in a fetal position and wearing an amber necklace; scientific analysis will investigate age, sex, diet and provenance. Other discoveries across the project include shale and copper bracelets, a Roman brooch and the previously unrecorded remains of a Roman complex. Many earthworks at Marden have been largely erased by centuries of farming and later development, which has limited past study; the current multi-year dig aims to better understand the prehistoric communities that inhabited the fertile river valleys linked by the Avon. The site will be opened to the public for an archaeology festival open day with finds on display and tours.

A small Piper PA-31 twin-engine plane crashed off Long Island near Indian Wells Beach/Amagansett Saturday afternoon amid severe thunderstorms. Four people were aboard: veteran East Hampton builder Bernard (Ben) Krupinski, 70; his wife Bonnie Krupinski, 70; their 22-year-old grandson William (Will) Maerov; and 47-year-old pilot Jon Dollard. Two bodies were recovered from the water; two people remained missing and presumed dead. Authorities had not publicly confirmed which victims were recovered. The U.S. Coast Guard searched the scene and later suspended operations; the NTSB will investigate the cause. 

Ben Krupinski, a prominent local contractor known for building luxury homes for clients including Martha Stewart, Billy Joel and Roger Waters, was a well-known figure in East Hampton; the couple owned substantial local property and businesses. The crash occurred about 3 p.m. and officials say the aircraft appears to have entered a thunderstorm before falling off radar. This was the second small-plane fatality on Long Island that week.

Seventeen-year-old Kristian Perez of Orofino went missing after leaving the Orofino High School prom on the night of April 14–15. He signed out of the prom at 9:32 p.m., and when he did not return home his mother reported him missing. Investigators recovered his tuxedo jacket, one shoe and his broken cell phone near the relative’s vehicle he had ridden to the prom in.

A canine tracking team followed a trail west from the National Guard Armory (where the prom was held) to a nearby parking lot along U.S. Highway 12, but the track ended there and authorities believe he may have entered a vehicle. Police issued an attempt-to-locate to neighboring agencies and followed a possible sighting in Lewiston; initial tips included a reported sighting at a Zip Trip on Main Street, but surveillance video later showed the person was not Perez.

Orofino Police obtained a search warrant for Perez’s cell-phone records and are reviewing call and text data and pursuing all tips. On April 18, police located Perez at a residence on Indio Avenue in Orofino after a tip; he was found in good health and taken into custody on a runaway charge. The residence belonged to 26-year-old Tyson Imel, who may face charges for assisting Perez. The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information was asked to contact Orofino Police at 208-476-5551.

The Accountant, starring Ben Affleck, opened at No. 1 with an estimated $24.7 million, proving Affleck remains a strong box-office draw. The Gavin O’Connor-directed action-thriller (budget $44 million) received mixed critical response (51% on Rotten Tomatoes) but strong audience approval (CinemaScore A), helping its weekend performance. Kevin Hart’s concert film Kevin Hart: What Now? placed second with $11.98 million on a $10 million budget, already profitable and surpassing the opening of his 2013 concert movie; it earned 78% on Rotten Tomatoes and an A– CinemaScore. Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children finished fourth ($8.9M, $65.8M total), and Deepwater Horizon rounded out the top five with $6.4 million ($49.3M total). Accessory Outlet, an online retailer, included a hidden and coercive clause in its Terms of Sale that attempted to forbid customers from complaining or even threatening to complain for 90 days after a purchase. The clause states that customers “agree not to file any complaint, chargeback, claim, dispute, or make any public forum post, review… or to threaten to do so within the 90 day period,” and imposes a $250 penalty plus additional fees and ongoing damages for breaches. It also requires binding arbitration in New York City as the sole method of dispute resolution.

A Wisconsin customer, Cindy Cox, ordered a $39.94 iPhone case on July 6, 2014. The retailer emailed a tracking number but the package didn’t appear in USPS records. After requesting cancellation and later saying she would request a chargeback, Cox was told she would be fined $250 and that her account would be sent to collections, which would harm her credit and generate collection calls. Accessory Outlet threatened additional hourly and flat fees for dispute-related correspondence and sent aggressive, personal emails warning her to “contact your lawyer” and that she had “made a very bad mistake.” The case escalated: Cox received the case nine days after it was purportedly shipped, but it arrived defective. Her complaints were ignored.

Cox, represented by Public Citizen, sued in New York state court seeking a declaration that the $250 “debt” is invalid and that the retailer engaged in deceptive and unconscionable practices. The complaint argues the terms are unenforceable because they are hidden in fine print and customers are not required to acknowledge them during checkout, and because they unreasonably bar consumers from seeking ordinary remedies (public complaints or chargebacks). Public Citizen says the clauses are coercive and unenforceable.

Independent checks also show Accessory Outlet misrepresented third‑party endorsements: the Better Business Bureau listed the firm with an “F” rating and said it is not accredited and has been asked to stop displaying the BBB badge; buySAFE, Angie’s List, and Trusted Shops representatives confirmed the retailer is not certified by them either. After the story circulated, Accessory Outlet’s sites were taken down for “maintenance.”

This document is a running Associated Press roundup of events and developments on Election Day for Alabama's special U.S. Senate race between Republican Roy Moore and Democrat Doug Jones.

Key points:
- Doug Jones won the election, defeating Roy Moore and narrowing the Senate Republican majority to 51–49. Jones, a former prosecutor, campaigned on moving past the controversies around Moore and benefited from national Democratic support.
- The race drew intense national attention because Moore faced multiple allegations that he had sexual contact with teenage girls decades earlier; he denies the accusations. The allegations divided the GOP, though President Trump and the Republican National Committee continued to support Moore.
- Election-day scenes: polls opened at 7 a.m. and were expected to see turnout around 18–20% (possibly up to 25%). Observers noted heavier-than-expected turnout in some Republican areas and increased participation by young and black voters, which could help Jones.
- Campaign moments included Moore riding to vote on horseback, Jones greeted by cheering supporters at his polling place, and heightened security at Moore’s election-night gathering; The Washington Post (which first reported the allegations against Moore) was allegedly denied press credentials at Moore’s event.
- The Department of Homeland Security monitored the election with security and cybersecurity advisers in Montgomery as part of preparations after last year’s concerns about foreign targeting of state election systems.
- The race was widely framed as significant for both parties: Democrats sought momentum and to break a losing streak in 2017 special elections, while Republicans aimed to hold a reliably red seat despite the controversy.

Here are the key points from the document:

Ryan Adams and Mandy Moore
- Ryan Adams and Mandy Moore have announced they are divorcing after nearly six years of marriage. The split was described as mutual, respectful and amicable; both asked for privacy.
- They were married in March 2009, four weeks after announcing their engagement.
- The couple occasionally collaborated musically: Moore worked with Adams on her music and sang background on his 2011 album Ashes & Fire (including tracks "Trouble" and "Am I Safe"); in 2012 she said she was working with him on her next album.
- Adams has kept his marriage private in the past. He has also faced health struggles (Ménière’s disease) and family loss that influenced the mood of his recent work; he’s touring with Jenny Lewis this spring and has an Austin City Limits episode airing.

Patrick Dempsey and Jillian Fink
- Patrick Dempsey and his wife of 15 years, Jillian Fink, are separating. They issued a joint statement saying the decision was made with mutual respect and careful consideration, asking for privacy and emphasizing concern for their children’s wellbeing.
- TMZ reports Fink filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences; there is no prenup. Dempsey is reported to be worth about $40 million.
- The couple married in 1999 and have three children: Tallula (12) and twins Darby and Sullivan (7). Fink is reportedly seeking joint custody as well as spousal and child support.

Pete Davidson joked about his failed engagement to Ariana Grande in a new Saturday Night Live promo by mock-proposing to musical guest Maggie Rogers (“Hey Maggie, I’m Pete. You wanna get married?”), then quipping he’s “0 for 3” in relationships. Grande reacted publicly on Twitter, posting a now-deleted remark — “for somebody who claims to hate relevancy u sure love clinging to it huh” — and later tweeting “thank u, next,” signaling she wasn’t amused by the joke. The exchange follows the couple’s rapid romance and split after getting engaged this summer; both have since moved on publicly, covering matching tattoos and returning to work (Grande announced a world tour). Davidson has repeatedly referenced his breakup in his comedy appearances. Sources have described the split as mutual and attributed it to the relationship developing “too much too soon.”

Key findings
- For the first time, complications of preterm birth are the leading global cause of death in children under five. In 2013 an estimated 6.3 million under‑five deaths occurred; nearly 1.1 million (about 17%) were due to preterm birth complications (965,000 in the first 28 days; 125,000 between one month and five years).
- Other major causes in 2013: pneumonia (≈935,000 under‑five deaths) and intrapartum/childbirth complications (≈720,000).
- Preterm deaths are concentrated geographically: India (≈361,600), Nigeria (≈98,300), Pakistan (≈75,000), DRC, China, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Ethiopia, Angola and Kenya top the list. West Africa (including Ebola‑hit countries) has very high rates.
- Some high‑income countries show a high share of under‑five deaths due to prematurity (e.g., Macedonia 51.0%, Slovenia 47.5%, Denmark 43.0%); the United States: 28.1% of under‑five deaths (≈8,100), with a 2013 preterm birth rate of 11.4% and marked racial disparities (16.3% for black women vs ~10% for white and Asian/Pacific Islanders).

Trends and causes
- Global under‑five mortality fell from 76 to 46 per 1,000 live births (2000–2013), largely from progress against infectious causes. Preterm mortality declined more slowly (≈2.0% annually) while prematurity incidence has risen: ~15.1 million babies born preterm each year (>1 in 10).
- Much of the historic child‑survival progress came from investments in vaccines, bed nets, antibiotics and treatments that have less impact on prematurity. Many preterm births are spontaneous and the biological triggers of labor remain poorly understood.
- Known risk factors and prevention opportunities include family planning (optimal spacing, avoiding very young/old maternal age), reducing multiple embryo transfers in fertility treatment, avoiding elective C‑sections before 39 weeks, addressing obesity, hypertension, infections, nutrition, stress, pollution, and broader socio‑economic drivers.

Response and initiatives
- Global attention is increasing: World Prematurity Day mobilizes governments, NGOs, UN agencies, health professionals and the public; the Every Woman Every Child movement, Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP) and Ending Preventable Maternal Mortality (EPMM) provide policy frameworks and targets.
- Four major research efforts (totaling about $250 million) aim to discover causes and preventive interventions within 3–5 years:
  1) Global Coalition to Advance Preterm Birth Research (GCAPR) — NICHD, March of Dimes, Gates Foundation, GAPPS and others.
  2) March of Dimes’ $75 million Campaign to End Premature Birth — multi‑center, multidisciplinary research network.
  3) UCSF Preterm Birth Initiative (PTBi) — $100 million, 10‑year global program co‑funded by Gates Foundation and Marc & Lynne Benioff.
  4) GAPPS research program (with Gates and USAID funding) focusing on mechanisms of prematurity.
- Research is highly transdisciplinary (obstetrics, neonatology, genetics, immunology, engineering, physics, mathematics, etc.) and includes work on uterine pacemakers, electrical signaling of labor, biomarkers, the maternal microbiome, gene–environment interactions, and population differences (e.g., low prematurity among Somali women in the U.S. vs high rates for many black women).
- Scale‑up and care interventions: Kangaroo Mother Care (skin‑to‑skin contact) could save up to ~450,000 preterm newborns annually; emphasis on family planning, infection prevention, antibiotics, neonatal resuscitation, and care for small/sick newborns. USAID’s Every Preemie–SCALE ($9 million, five years) and partnerships like Survive and Thrive, the Global Collaborative Network to Prevent Preterm Birth, and many professional and civil society partners support implementation in high‑burden countries.

Implications
- Prematurity is now a leading global child‑survival challenge requiring different medical, research and policy approaches than those that reduced infectious child deaths.
- Many deaths could be prevented with known, low‑cost interventions and with rapid advances expected from current, well‑funded, collaborative research efforts. International coordination, funding, and scaling of effective prevention and newborn care strategies are being intensified to reduce preterm births and improve survival.

Ikea and the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) issued a nationwide repair program/recall covering about 27–29 million chests and dressers after reports that unsecured units can tip forward and crush children. The action covers roughly 7 million Malm dressers (sold since 2002) and about 20 million other Ikea chests and dressers. Ikea and CPSC cited at least three confirmed child fatalities tied to Malm tip-overs (including deaths in 2014 and 2015) and additional deaths involving other models since 1989; later reporting described a separate February death of a Minnesota toddler now under CPSC review.

Rather than requiring returns, the recall/repair program provides free wall-anchoring kits to consumers; Ikea has urged customers to pick up or order the kits, and to move unsecured units out of children’s reach until anchored. Ikea says it has sent hundreds of thousands of kits and is expanding outreach. The CPSC and safety advocates stress that many consumers—especially renters—may be unable or unaware to anchor furniture, and call on manufacturers to design inherently more stable products. The CPSC’s chairman commended Ikea’s step but urged broader industry leadership and stronger U.S. stability standards similar to Europe’s.

Families of victims and their attorneys have criticized the program as insufficient, arguing a full recall with buybacks and replacements of unstable units would be more effective. Lawsuits have been filed on behalf of families of children killed in tip-overs, and attorneys are seeking other affected consumers. Consumers can obtain a free anchoring kit by visiting Ikea stores, registering at IKEA-USA.com/saferhomestogether, or calling Ikea’s toll-free number.

George Talley’s 1979 Corvette, stolen from Detroit in July 1981, was found in Mississippi after more than three decades. Michigan State Police’s Southwest Commercial Auto Recovery unit (SCAR) became involved after the Michigan Secretary of State flagged two 1979 Corvettes being registered with the same VIN. SCAR, Mississippi authorities and the National Insurance Crime Bureau traced the recovered silver Corvette (located at a Columbia/Hattiesburg, Miss., residence and currently held at the Hattiesburg police station) back to Talley. Investigators determined Talley’s insurance never paid a claim, so he remains the car’s owner. The car reportedly runs and shows about 47,000 miles.

Talley, now 71, was surprised and relieved by the news but worried about transporting the car back to Michigan. After hearing Talley’s story on WJR radio, GM Executive Vice President Mark Reuss offered to have General Motors pick up and deliver the Corvette to him at the company’s expense. GM will notify Talley with timing details in the coming days. The investigation into the vehicle’s history over the past 30+ years is ongoing.

Bob Schieffer, the long‑time anchor and moderator of CBS News’ Face the Nation, announced at Texas Christian University that he will retire this summer after more than 50 years in journalism and 46 years at CBS. The 78‑year‑old, who has anchored Face the Nation for 24 years and interviewed every president since Nixon, made the announcement at the annual Schieffer Symposium, reflecting on his career from a $1‑an‑hour radio job in Fort Worth through stints at the Fort Worth Star‑Telegram, the Air Force, and CBS. He praised colleagues and mentors, singled out Executive Producer Mary Hager as a key partner, and said he’s proud of CBS News’ current strength and Face the Nation’s standing.

CBS management is actively searching for Schieffer’s successor. Internally, likely candidates include Major Garrett (chief White House correspondent), Norah O’Donnell (co‑anchor of CBS This Morning and frequent substitute host), and John Dickerson (political director). The network is also considering outside talent such as CNN’s Jake Tapper and ABC’s Jonathan Karl, though both may be contractually tied to their employers. Executives say the looming 2016 presidential campaign is a major factor shaping the selection. Schieffer’s career highlights include moderating three presidential debates, anchoring the Saturday CBS Evening News for 23 years and briefly serving as interim weekday anchor, winning numerous journalism awards, and having TCU name its journalism school and college of communication in his honor.

A queen bee became trapped in the boot of a silver Mitsubishi Outlander in Haverfordwest, prompting her colony—estimated at 10,000–20,000 bees—to cluster on the car and follow it for two days. Park ranger Tom Moses first noticed the large brown mass on the car while the owner shopped and called Pembrokeshire Beekeepers’ Association. Several beekeepers, rangers and passers-by spent hours coaxing the swarm into a cardboard box; one beekeeper reported being stung multiple times. A gust of wind blew the box off the roof and the queen slipped back into the boot. Later, the car owner returned, drove off unaware the queen remained trapped, and the swarm continued to follow the vehicle, even appearing on the boot the next day. Beekeepers described the behaviour as unusual but natural—swarms follow their queen—and expressed concern for public safety and the bees’ welfare.

Tom Hanks has once again gifted the White House press corps a new espresso machine. Continuing a tradition that began during the Bush administration, the Oscar-winning actor replaced an aging machine he originally bought for reporters and staff — and which he had previously upgraded in 2010 after finding it dirty and worn. The replacement was left in the press break room with a note reading, “To the White House Press Corps. Keep up the good fight for Truth, Justice, and the American Way. Especially for the Truth Part,” accompanied by an illustration of American troops. The gesture was reported after the machine was spotted in the press area during the first weeks of the Trump administration.

JPMorgan Chase disclosed that losses in its Chief Investment Office (CIO) have swollen to $5.8 billion and that a review of roughly 1 million emails and tens of thousands of voice tapes indicates some traders may have deliberately misstated position prices to hide the full extent of first-quarter losses. The loss originated from large, illiquid synthetic credit-derivative positions built in London under CIO management (notably by trader Bruno Iksil), and prompted the departure of all employees who worked on synthetic credit derivatives. CIO head Ina Drew retired days after the initial disclosure; the bank said it will seek clawbacks where appropriate and has overhauled CIO management and governance.

For the second quarter, JPMorgan reported net income of $4.96 billion ($1.21/share), down 9% from a year earlier, with the CIO trading loss larger than analysts had anticipated. The bank restated first-quarter earnings, trimming prior net income by $459 million, and said securities sales and an $800 million accounting benefit helped offset some damage. Management warned the CIO loss could increase by up to $800 million in an extreme scenario. Dimon held an extended in-person analyst session to address the episode.

Other Q2 results: revenue fell 16% to $22.9 billion; fixed-income and equities markets revenue dropped; adjusted EPS missed some analyst estimates. JPMorgan increased litigation reserves by $335 million and faces broader regulatory probes (including energy-market gaming and interest-rate investigations). The bank benefitted from stronger mortgage and consumer lending as refinancing activity rose and delinquencies improved, but net interest margin remained under pressure from low rates. The episode has dented investor confidence and weighed on JPMorgan’s stock and CEO Jamie Dimon’s reputation as a risk manager.

This document compiles several news-and-opinion pieces about celebrity reactions to controversial political figures and campaigns, focusing on two main threads: (1) celebrities threatening to leave the U.S. if Donald Trump or other candidates win, and (2) the long-running public feud between Donald Trump and Rosie O’Donnell.

Key points:

- Many celebrities publicly vowed to leave the United States if Donald Trump became president. Named figures include Whoopi Goldberg, Jon Stewart, Rev. Al Sharpton, Raven-Symoné, Sienna Miller, Bryan Cranston, Rosie O’Donnell, Cher, Samuel L. Jackson, Jon Stewart, Eddie Griffin, Omari Hardwick, Katie Hopkins, Barry Diller, and others. Some remarks were hyperbolic or joking (e.g., Stewart threatening to leave Earth), while others claimed concrete plans (Raven-Symoné said she’d bought a ticket to Canada).

- The phenomenon of “threatening to leave” when dissatisfied with election outcomes is presented as a recurring celebrity tactic; examples from earlier cycles include Eddie Vedder and Stephen Baldwin. Media coverage and satirical responses (e.g., offers of relocation campaigns like “Cape Breton If Donald Trump Wins”) and Trump family jabs (Donald Jr. offering to buy airfare for departing celebrities) are noted.

- Bill O’Reilly said he would move to Ireland if Bernie Sanders were elected president, illustrating that such vows cross ideological lines.

- A longer chronology details the decades-long, often vicious public feud between Donald Trump and Rosie O’Donnell. It traces incidents from 2006 onward: O’Donnell’s early criticisms of Trump, Trump’s repeated public insults and tweets calling her a “loser” and other derogatory names, moments of apparent civility (e.g., Trump tweeting get-well wishes after her heart attack), and numerous exchanges on social media and in broadcast settings. The feud resurfaced repeatedly during Trump’s 2016 campaign and presidency—Trump cited O’Donnell in debates and tweets, and O’Donnell became an outspoken critic of his presidency, protesting at the White House and denouncing his election on social media.

- The coverage frames celebrity departures as often performative—many who vowed to leave stayed—and highlights how celebrity statements become part of the broader political media spectacle. It also emphasizes the elevated consequences now that Trump became president, making the Trump–O’Donnell feud more consequential because Trump holds real power.

Overall, the pieces portray a mix of celebrity political grandstanding, ongoing cultural conflict around Trump’s candidacy and presidency, and a detailed example of personal animus between two high-profile figures that played out publicly for years.

RadarOnline reports that Ben Affleck visited Lindsay Lohan at Cliffside Malibu while she was in rehab. A fellow patient said Affleck arrived late one night with an assistant a few days before Lohan’s July 2 birthday, stayed about an hour, and spoke with her about a possible role in his film Live by Night; Lohan reportedly told others she’d play a dark‑haired character with an Irish accent. A source for the movie, while denying Lohan is being considered, did not dispute the visit. 

Separately, OWN released promos for Lohan’s upcoming interview with Oprah Winfrey, showing Winfrey asking tough questions about Lohan’s addiction and whether she can “turn it around.” Winfrey has called Lohan “honest,” “authentic,” and appearing “strong” and “healthy.” The full interview airs Aug. 18 at 9 p.m. on OWN.

Former Chicago police officer William Whitley, 61, pleaded guilty in federal court to one count of sex trafficking a minor for paying underage girls for sex while he was a CPD officer. Federal prosecutors said Whitley paid a 14-year-old runaway for sex multiple times in 2015, and also admitted to commercial sex with three other teenage girls, including a 16-year-old. The girl identified as Minor A told investigators Whitley kept his CPD uniform hanging on the bedroom door, bragged about being a cop, stored a loaded gun under his pillow, took explicit photos of her, and communicated with her by phone “hundreds of times.” Investigators found matching photos, leopard-print bedding and condom wrappers in his apartment, and phone contacts suggesting he solicited other sex workers.

A notable element of the federal case was the interstate-commerce nexus: prosecutors stressed that Whitley used Trojan Magnum and LifeStyles condoms manufactured outside Illinois, which—along with use of a cellphone and money—provided a federal jurisdictional basis under statutes addressing sex trafficking. That allowed federal charges carrying a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years (and up to life), a stiffer penalty than the likely state-level minimum. Whitley’s sentencing is set for Sept. 4; he must register as a sex offender and was ordered detained when he could not find suitable housing consistent with registry rules. Chicago police stripped him of his powers in 2015; he was arrested in November 2016.

Administration lawyers have presented President Obama with four options for restructuring the NSA’s controversial phone‑surveillance program, delivered ahead of his March 28 deadline by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Justice Department.

The four options are:
- Keep phone companies in control of call records, allowing the NSA access on request.
- Transfer custody of the data to another government entity (e.g., the FBI or oversight by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court) to separate investigators from the data.
- Place the data with a private, non‑telecommunications, non‑government third party (considered unlikely; Obama has warned this would effectively be a government function with higher cost, legal ambiguity, and little privacy gain).
- End the bulk-collection program entirely.

Obama’s recent comments favor one of the first two options (either keeping providers as custodians with NSA access or shifting custody to another government body), but no final decision date has been announced.

Congress was racing to avert a possible partial government shutdown before a Monday night funding deadline, but deep partisan divisions made a resolution uncertain.

What happened in the House and Senate
- The Republican-led House voted early Sunday for a short-term continuing resolution to fund federal agencies through Dec. 15 that also would delay major parts of the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) for one year and repeal the 2.3% medical-device tax.
- Senate Democrats and the White House oppose any changes to the health law; President Obama would veto legislation that guts or delays it. Senate leaders planned to strip the anti-Obamacare provisions from the House measure when the Senate reconvened.
- Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid led Democrats in a hard line: refuse concessions on the health law and force Republicans to either accept a “clean” funding bill or bear responsibility for a shutdown. Democrats argued that any concession would encourage larger GOP demands on future fiscal fights.

Politics and motivations
- House Speaker John Boehner backed the delay effort largely because conservative House Republicans demanded a confrontation over the health law; some conservatives might prefer a brief shutdown to show they fought.
- Republicans hoped to score at least a repeal of the medical-device tax, citing prior bipartisan Senate support, though key Democrats opposed attaching it to the spending bill.
- Democrats believed political pressure from any shutdown would ultimately force Republicans to accept funding without anti-Obamacare riders.

Possible outcomes
- A compromise between House and Senate could be reached quickly, but practical obstacles in the Senate made that uncertain.
- Short-term options included passing a very brief funding extension to buy time; otherwise a partial shutdown could begin and raise pressure to compromise afterward.
- The Senate could table or vote down the House amendments with a simple majority; delaying tactics or additional amendments (including from activists like Sen. Ted Cruz) remained possible.

Local and economic consequences
- The Washington region stood to be hit particularly hard: estimates put losses at roughly $200 million per day and more than 700,000 local jobs affected if a shutdown began. The area’s heavy dependence on federal payrolls and contracting would magnify the impact.
- Immediate service disruptions would include halted new applications for benefits (Medicare, Social Security, housing, small-business loans), suspended clinical trials at NIH, closed federal museums/parks (hurting tourism), and furloughed “nonessential” federal employees—potentially 60% of local federal workers.
- Local governments and jurisdictions were preparing contingency plans and tapping reserves to blunt revenue losses and service interruptions.

Bottom line: With both chambers and the White House dug in over whether funding must include changes to the Affordable Care Act, a shutdown was a real possibility. Democrats, led by Reid, pushed to force Republicans to choose between passing a clean continuing resolution or owning the political fallout from a shutdown; Republicans, driven by conservative pressure, pushed anti-Obamacare provisions into the stopgap, making an impasse likely unless a last-minute compromise or very short extension is agreed.

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and President Hu Jintao met visiting North Korean official Jang Song‑thaek in Beijing as part of efforts to steady and deepen ties between China and North Korea. Wen urged Pyongyang to use market mechanisms and legal, regulatory, customs and investment reforms to revive its struggling economy, signaling Beijing wants North Korea to pursue bolder economic reform and reduce reliance on Chinese aid. Both Chinese leaders praised the bilateral relationship and expressed support for closer party‑to‑party and state ties.

Jang’s six‑day visit—the highest‑profile North Korean trip to China since Kim Jong‑un took power—followed concerns in Beijing after North Korea’s recent rocket test. It included talks on developing two border special economic zones, Rason and Hwanggumphyong, with cooperation agreements signed to boost manufacturing, logistics, tourism, IT, agriculture and garments. China has already increased exports to the North and made direct investments in sectors such as food, medicine, electronics and mining, but overall trade with North Korea remains small compared with ties to South Korea.

Beijing balances support for Pyongyang as a strategic buffer with frustration over provocations (including nuclear and rocket tests) and occasional incidents like seizures of Chinese fishermen. While China has backed sanctions at times and can curtail aid, analysts say it is cautious about measures that might destabilize the North and trigger refugee flows; instead Beijing prefers encouraging economic engagement and controlled reforms.

Dove—long known for its “Real Beauty” femvertising—released a limited UK run of six body-wash bottles shaped to evoke different female body types. The bottles, produced by Ogilvy London for Unilever’s Dove, were intended as a physical expression of Dove’s message that “beauty comes in a million different shapes and sizes” and to reinforce findings from its Global Beauty and Confidence Report about social‑media pressure on women.

The stunt immediately provoked widespread mockery and criticism on social media. Critics argued the idea was silly, tone‑deaf and condescending: turning bodies into packaging trivializes the complex issues around body image, and the in‑store and functional implications of shaped bottles (awkward handling, the need to “choose” a body type, unintended hierarchy of shapes) undercut the campaign’s stated goals. Many pointed out the commercial motive behind femvertising and highlighted the hypocrisy of Unilever owning both Dove and more stereotypically sexist brands like Axe. Supporters and Dove framed the campaign as a celebration of diversity and a gift to influencers helping spread the “real beauty” message.

Overall, commentators saw the Real Beauty Bottles as a misstep—well‑intentioned but ultimately incoherent and counterproductive—raising questions about whether a brand can authentically use feminist themes while primarily selling product.

Video recorded by a passerby appears to show Bexar County sheriff’s deputies shooting and killing 41-year-old Gilbert Flores during a response to a domestic disturbance in northwest San Antonio on Aug. 28, 2015. Deputies Greg Vasquez and Robert Sanchez arrived around 11:30 a.m. and found a woman with a head cut and an infant who seemed injured. Authorities say Flores was armed, resisted arrest and a roughly 20-minute struggle ended when nonlethal tools (including a Taser and a shield, officials said) failed and the two deputies fired; Flores doubled over and died shortly afterward. 

A witness video aired by KSAT shows Flores shirtless, standing with his hands up near a sheriff’s SUV as two deputies, about 10 yards away, take aim; the recording’s final moments have prompted concern from Sheriff Susan Pamerleau and Bexar County District Attorney Nicholas LaHood, both of whom said the footage is troubling but emphasized that investigators must review all evidence, including additional videos and 911 and witness statements. Vasquez and Sanchez, each with more than 10 years with the office, have been placed on paid administrative leave while the sheriff’s office and the district attorney investigate. Flores had prior convictions dating back to the 1990s and 2003. The shooting is being examined alongside multiple witness recordings and other case materials.

Summary:

Talcum powder is made from talc, a mineral used in many personal care products to absorb moisture. Naturally occurring talc can contain asbestos, a known carcinogen when inhaled; however, U.S. consumer talc products have been asbestos-free since the 1970s. Scientific attention has focused on two concerns: lung disease risk among workers exposed to raw talc and a possible link between genital talc use and ovarian cancer.

Evidence from laboratory and human studies is mixed. Animal studies of asbestos-free talc have shown inconsistent tumor results. Human research includes many case-control studies that sometimes show a small increased ovarian cancer risk from perineal talc use, but prospective cohort studies have not found an association. For lung cancer, some studies of talc miners and millers suggest increased risk, but these are hard to interpret because occupational talc can contain asbestos and workers may have other exposures; use of cosmetic talc has not been linked to increased lung cancer. Other cancer links are weak or unproven; a few studies have explored endometrial or stomach cancer with inconclusive findings.

Major agencies’ positions: IARC classifies asbestos-containing talc as carcinogenic to humans, inhaled asbestos-free talc as “not classifiable,” and genital use of talc-based body powder as “possibly carcinogenic.” The U.S. National Toxicology Program has not completed a full review.

Given uncertainty, people concerned may choose to avoid or limit talc-containing products.

Legal developments: Several high-profile U.S. lawsuits have resulted in large jury awards against Johnson & Johnson (J&J). In St. Louis, a jury awarded more than $70 million to Deborah Giannecchini, who alleged decades-long use of J&J baby powder caused her ovarian cancer; other St. Louis verdicts this year totaled $72 million and $55 million. Plaintiffs’ lawyers argue research dating to the 1970s links genital talc use to increased ovarian cancer risk. J&J maintains its products are safe, plans to appeal, and points to scientific studies and recent New Jersey rulings that dismissed cases for lack of reliable evidence. Imerys, a talc supplier, expressed disappointment and said plaintiffs’ theories lacked scientific foundation. Thousands of similar lawsuits are pending nationwide.

Malaria is a preventable, treatable mosquito-borne disease that causes fever, chills and flu‑like illness and can be fatal if untreated. In 2013–2016 hundreds of millions of cases and hundreds of thousands of deaths occurred worldwide, with the heaviest burden in sub‑Saharan Africa—especially young children. Global malaria control expanded substantially since 2000 (wider use of insecticide‑treated nets, indoor spraying, rapid diagnostic tests and artemisinin‑based therapies), driving large declines in incidence and mortality, but funding remains insufficient and drug and insecticide resistance are growing threats.

New research from Mali documents a striking example of adaptive introgression between two African malaria mosquito species, Anopheles gambiae and Anopheles coluzzii. During a brief breakdown in reproductive isolation in 2006, an entire “island of divergence” on chromosome 2L—including multiple insecticide‑resistance alleles—moved from A. gambiae into the A. coluzzii genome and then rose rapidly in frequency. The timing coincided with a major insecticide‑treated bed net distribution campaign, suggesting increased insecticide exposure created selection that favored hybrids carrying the A. gambiae resistance region. The work provides a rare, time‑resolved example of adaptive introgression in animals and explains a mechanism for the rapid evolution of insecticide resistance in an important malaria vector.

Researchers warn this evolved resistance can undermine the effectiveness of long‑lasting insecticidal nets and other vector control tools, highlighting an urgent need for new control strategies (new insecticides, biological controls, genetic approaches) and continued surveillance. The study was led by Gregory Lanzaro (UC Davis) with collaborators from UC Davis and Mali and funded by NIH grants.

Steven Spielberg’s big-budget adaptation of Roald Dahl’s The BFG opened poorly over the July 4th weekend and is shaping up as a rare box-office disappointment for the director. The film cost about $140 million to produce but earned only roughly $18.6–24 million domestically over the holiday frame (about $22–24M across various reports and $22.3M for the four-day weekend), plus modest early international receipts (about $2M in Australia and $1.9M in Russia). With those returns it will likely need substantial overseas success to avoid a sizable loss; some analysts project a domestic run in the $55–65M range.

Why it underperformed:
- Heavy competition and timing: It opened during a crowded Independence Day weekend dominated by family hits like Finding Dory, leaving little room for another family title.
- Weak brand recognition: Dahl’s The BFG is less familiar to contemporary U.S. family audiences than franchises like Harry Potter or Pixar releases; the title acronym also confused potential viewers.
- Marketing challenges: The film lacked a major star presence or an immediately arresting visual/spectacle hook to sell in trailers and posters; Mark Rylance’s acclaimed motion-capture performance (praised by critics) wasn’t enough to draw broad audiences.
- Tonal and audience ambiguity: Critics gave generally positive but mixed reviews (around 71% on Rotten Tomatoes) and audiences liked it (A- CinemaScore), yet the film sat awkwardly between a children’s picture and a more adult-leaning drama—appealing strongly to neither demographic.
- Creative choices: Reviewers and some viewers felt the movie emphasized beautiful visuals over the darker, sharper edges of Dahl’s original book, making it feel “pretty” but emotionally muted.

Context and implications:
- The BFG isn’t universally panned—Rylance’s performance and the film’s effects received consistent praise—but its modest box office points to being unremarkable rather than disastrously flawed.
- If it fails overseas, it could become one of Spielberg’s first major commercial misfires for a mainstream tentpole-style project. Observers caution against over-reading this as proof Spielberg has “lost his touch” or that book adaptations are in decline; future projects (e.g., Ready Player One) still generate excitement.
- The film’s struggles highlight risks of high-budget family fare without a clear brand, star power, or a strong marketing hook—especially in a crowded summer slate.

A teen in Washington, D.C., says a female police officer broke up a park fight Monday and — after spotting 17-year-old Aaliya Taylor dancing to Silentó’s “Watch Me (Whip/Nae Nae)” — challenged her to a spontaneous dance-off. The officer matched Taylor step for step as bystanders cheered; the two later hugged, exchanged names and called it a tie. Taylor said the friendly interaction changed her view of police. She posted the video to Facebook, where it received hundreds of thousands of views within a day. The Metropolitan Police Department confirmed the officer is with their department, and Mayor Muriel Bowser praised the moment as an example of community-police engagement.

The Toronto Zoo is investigating after a YouTube video showed a woman apparently climbing over a protective boardwalk fence into the Sumatran tiger area to retrieve a fallen hat while a tiger, separated by a second fence, lunged toward her. She returned to the public area unharmed amid onlookers’ criticism. No zoo staff were at the tiger pen at the time; the employee assigned to that area was likely attending other nearby enclosures. Communications director Jennifer Tracey called the act “very irresponsible” and urged visitors to notify staff if items fall into enclosures, since staff have proper equipment to retrieve them.

The zoo’s Safety and Security branch opened an investigation after seeing the video. Multiple warning signs were posted at the site, and city zoo by-laws prohibit entering enclosures or tampering with barriers; violations can lead to fines up to $2,000, a ban, or other penalties at the CEO’s discretion. The woman has not been identified; the zoo is asking witnesses or the person involved to come forward.

A new headquarters for the Trayvon Martin Foundation opened at Florida Memorial University, a historically black school in Miami Gardens. The small facility, located off a narrow stairwell, displays artwork—mostly depictions of a young man in a hooded sweatshirt—and serves as a reflective, community-focused space. About 100 people attended the ribbon-cutting ceremony, including university leaders, politicians, foundation members and local residents. Remarks were given by university president Roslyn Artis and by Trayvon Martin’s parents, Sybrina and Tracy Fulton, who emphasized faith, healing, and the foundation’s mission to help families affected by violent crime and to support at-risk youth. The university provided financial support and views the site as a “learning laboratory” where students can reflect and generate ideas to reduce violence and influence policy. Foundation wristbands and family photos were shared with visitors; organizers stressed the foundation’s universal reach beyond racial lines and cited collaboration with parents of other gun-violence victims.

Separate reporting on George Zimmerman—acquitted last year in Martin’s death—details his financial affidavit filed in a divorce case. Zimmerman, 30, reported no job or income, $14,000 in assets (largely a 2008 pickup), about $2.5 million in debts (mainly attorney fees), and monthly expenses of roughly $3,304 including $200 for counseling and $100 for vacations. His legal defense fund reportedly has about $300 remaining. The affidavit does not clarify proceeds from a reported $100,000 eBay sale of a painting. Zimmerman’s family and lawyers describe him as transient and without stable housing.

A member of the family that founded Purdue Pharma, which faces more than 1,000 lawsuits over its role in the U.S. opioid epidemic, has been named as an inventor on a new patent for an opioid-use-disorder treatment. The January-issued patent lists Dr. Richard Sackler — a former Purdue president and son of one of the company’s founders — among six inventors. It covers a new buprenorphine formulation: a sublingual wafer designed to dissolve faster than existing tablets or films, with the patent arguing faster dissolution can reduce diversion. Critics fear the patent could allow a Sackler family member to profit from treatments for an addiction crisis critics say Purdue helped create; Purdue denies wrongdoing.

The patent’s description references criminal activity driven by addiction and notes the wafer could also treat pain in humans or animals. Meanwhile, Purdue is defending itself in consolidated litigation (largely in Ohio) and other suits, including a Massachusetts case that recently named the Sackler family as defendants. Congress has requested a copy of a deposition that Richard Sackler gave in a 2015 Kentucky case settled by Purdue — believed to be the only time a Sackler was questioned under oath about OxyContin marketing and addiction risks — and media outlets have sought that deposition as well.

Purdue did not comment on the patent. Separately, the company has promoted steps it says address the crisis: supporting safer prescribing initiatives, donating to the National Sheriffs’ Association for naloxone purchases and training, and contributing $3.4 million this week toward development of a low-cost naloxone nasal spray.

The document also includes an unrelated entertainment piece about Julia Roberts discussing her new film Ben Is Back, which centers on a mother dealing with her son’s opioid addiction, and notes her involvement in an Amazon TV series, Homecoming.

Manufacturers have been quietly shrinking household tissues and toilet paper—reducing sheet counts, narrowing rolls, enlarging cardboard tubes, and making sheets smaller—while sometimes marketing products as “bulkier.” Kimberly‑Clark, for example, introduced Kleenex it says is 15% “bulkier,” but the boxes contain 13% fewer sheets. This practice, called “desheeting,” has consumers concerned about value.

Consumer Reports tests toilet paper for strength, softness, disintegration, and tearing ease. Its top picks include White Cloud 3‑Ply Ultra (a Best Buy at 25¢ per 100 sheets) for excellent strength and softness and very good disintegration/tearing, and Charmin Ultra Strong, which had excellent tearing ease though weaker on other measures and costs about 41¢ per 100 sheets. Less impressive options in the tests were Scott 1000 (cheap at 8¢ per 100 sheets but neither soft nor strong), Marcal Small Steps (harsh and hard to tear), and some Cottonelle variants (costly and less soft than expected). Brand name alone isn’t a reliable guide—different products from the same brand can score very differently.

An iguana wandered onto a power line in Lauderdale Lakes, Fla., was electrocuted and ignited a fire on the pole, cutting power to The Palms Care Center. The facility switched to generator power but only half the building was being cooled effectively, so firefighters moved residents to cooler parts of the home and, as a precaution due to overcrowding of cooled areas, 20 patients were transferred to area hospitals. None were in distress. Power was restored shortly before 11 p.m., and the hospitalized residents were to be returned after evaluation. The nursing home is licensed for 120 beds.

Hillary Clinton is positioning herself for possible 2016 politics by stepping into a more public, issue-focused role while taking a formal place in the Clinton Foundation. In a major speech to the American Bar Association in San Francisco she forcefully criticized the Supreme Court’s rollback of a key Voting Rights Act provision and denounced recent state-level voting restrictions—especially strict voter ID laws and cuts to early voting—as efforts that disproportionately burden minorities and undermine democracy. She urged stronger Justice Department enforcement, Congressional fixes to the Voting Rights Act, and legal and civic action to protect voting access. Clinton framed the remarks as the first of several policy speeches (on national security and global leadership later this year), signaling she will continue weighing in on issues important to the Democratic base as debate intensifies over whether she will run.

Parallel to that public re-engagement, Clinton has officially joined the renamed Clinton Foundation alongside Bill and Chelsea Clinton. Her arrival follows an internal review and Chelsea’s expanded role; a new CEO and closer coordination among the three offices are aimed at professionalizing and institutionalizing the organization. The foundation gives Hillary a visible platform to work on chosen issue areas—women and girls, early childhood development and economic development—without re-entering government, and it can serve as a springboard for message-building if she runs. Observers note this helps her stay relevant and substantive while avoiding overexposure, though the foundation will also face increased scrutiny.

The document also covers related voting-rights news: North Carolina’s new voter ID and election-law changes—shortened early voting, elimination of same-day registration and straight-ticket voting—were signed by Gov. Pat McCrory and immediately met with multiple lawsuits alleging racial discrimination and unconstitutional burdens on voting. Civil-rights groups and Democrats argue the measures will disenfranchise many, particularly African-American voters; Republicans defend them as common-sense safeguards. Additional political items mentioned include Anthony Weiner’s interview in which he discussed his personal rehabilitation and ties to Huma Abedin, and a few campaign and political updates (state elections, candidates, and party moves).

Jamaican lawmakers have passed legislation that decriminalises small amounts of marijuana and creates a framework for a regulated medical cannabis industry. Key points:

- Possession of up to 2 ounces (56.6g) of marijuana is now a petty, non‑arrestable offence that carries a fine rather than a criminal record. Cultivation of up to five plants per premises is permitted.
- The law establishes the basis for a Cannabis Licensing Authority to regulate cultivation and distribution for medical, scientific and therapeutic purposes; details of the regulatory regime will be developed in coming months.
- Rastafarians are explicitly allowed sacramental use of ganja, and foreign tourists with medical prescriptions abroad can apply for permits to buy small amounts in Jamaica.
- Government officials emphasized the change is not a free‑for‑all: law enforcement will continue to target trafficking, illegal large‑scale cultivation and activities that violate international treaty obligations.
- Supporters hope the move will develop a legal medical‑cannabis sector, health tourism and value‑added products (Jamaica already has examples like Canasol for glaucoma), offering economic potential amid IMF loan conditions.
- The reform follows broader international trends toward liberalising cannabis laws (multiple U.S. states, Uruguay, etc.), but U.S. officials reiterated that trafficking into the U.S. remains illegal.

The measure was presented as correcting long‑standing criminalisation—particularly of poor and Rastafarian communities—while seeking to balance domestic reform with international obligations.

Tilman Fertitta, a billionaire restaurateur and Galveston native, has agreed in principle to buy the Houston Rockets from Leslie Alexander for a record NBA franchise price of $2.2 billion, pending approval by the NBA Board of Governors. Fertitta — owner of Landry’s, Inc. and Golden Nugget Casinos & Hotels and star of CNBC’s “Billion Dollar Buyer” — has been a longtime Rockets courtside attendee and called the purchase of his hometown team a “dream come true.” The transaction includes operation of the Toyota Center and Fertitta confirmed he has no partners in the deal. If approved, Golden Nugget in Las Vegas would be barred from offering bets on Rockets games.

Alexander, who bought the team in 1993 for $85 million and under whose ownership the Rockets won two championships, praised Fertitta as a capable successor. Forbes had valued the Rockets at $1.65 billion earlier in the year, but the team reportedly received multiple offers starting at $2 billion. Reports also noted Beyonce was rumored to be part of a bidding group but did not secure the team. The sale announcement came as Houston continued recovering from Hurricane Harvey, a timing both parties acknowledged with regret. ESPN’s Adrian Wojnarowski and Darren Rovell contributed reporting.

Pennsylvania State Police say 47-year-old Michele Leonard of Somerset was involved in two separate drunk-driving crashes on the same Saturday evening and was arrested twice.
