The Kansas House passed House Bill 2453 (72–49), a controversial measure allowing businesses and state employees to refuse services to same-sex couples on religious grounds. Critics say its broad language effectively legalizes wide-ranging discrimination — from stores, restaurants, hotels, gyms and movie theaters to government services like ambulances, parks and state hospitals — and grants immunity from civil suits while forcing plaintiffs to pay defendants’ legal fees. Supporters frame the bill as protecting “sincerely held” religious beliefs in light of court rulings on same-sex marriage; sponsors cited national cases involving bakers, photographers and innkeepers. Opponents, including the ACLU and LGBT groups, call it tantamount to state-sanctioned discrimination comparable in spirit to Jim Crow-era legal stigma.

The bill provoked a national outcry and swift pushback from Kansas business leaders and major employers, who warned it would harm recruitment, tourism, and employers’ ability to manage staff and customers. As a result Senate President Susan Wagle said a majority of Senate Republicans do not support the bill as written and sent it to committee for major revisions; fewer than half of Senate Republicans would back it, making passage unlikely without Democratic votes. Legislative leaders and some bill supporters signaled willingness to rewrite the measure — notably removing public employees from its scope — and to seek compromise language that protects religious liberty while preventing discrimination. The state business community and chamber groups urged substantial changes; House leaders acknowledged the bill’s wording is ambiguous and said it will be reworked.

A 68-year-old grandfather, William Hannah of Bolton, died after cleaning detergent was accidentally used to flush his lungs at Salford Royal Hospital following a September 2017 road-traffic collision. Hannah had been admitted with a traumatic brain injury, multiple fractures and a lung infection while on a ventilator. During a routine saline lung wash, lawyers for his family say a healthcare assistant handed an unlabelled bottle of detergent prepared for cleaning equipment instead of saline; the doctor unknowingly used the solution. The error was discovered when the doctor sought the cleaning fluid to clean instruments; a further washout was performed but Hannah’s condition worsened and he died the next day. 

An internal Salford Royal investigation found multiple contributing factors — an unstocked trolley, distractions from other critical tasks, poor two-way communication, lack of bottle labeling, inadequate staff training and absent risk assessment — and said the clinical impact on the patient was not yet clear. The Trust apologised, acknowledged substandard care, and said it has introduced measures to prevent recurrence. Hannah’s family, who say they have been insufficiently supported during the investigation, have instructed lawyers and are suing the Trust; hearings are due to begin in February 2019 and an inquest is scheduled for February.

A 15-month-old girl, Sania Cunningham, was killed by a stray bullet Saturday afternoon in Irvington, N.J., after a violent gunfight on Ellis Avenue. The family had moved into the second-floor apartment two days earlier. Witnesses and officials say three men in black hooded sweatshirts fired multiple rounds down the street, exchanging fire with two other men; bullets struck several homes and a vehicle. One projectile penetrated the wall of Sania’s bedroom as she bounced on a bed with her parents nearby; she was taken to Newark Beth Israel and pronounced dead about 30 minutes later.

Neighbors described the area as long-plagued by violence and expressed shock that the shooting occurred in broad daylight. Bullet holes were found in multiple houses, a Lexus trunk and an air conditioner; one round hit a second-floor wall behind a neighbor’s bed. Authorities recovered ballistic evidence and are reviewing surveillance footage and witness statements. Essex County Acting Prosecutor Carolyn Murray and other investigators urged public assistance; Essex County Sheriff’s Crime Stoppers is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction. A prosecutor’s press conference was scheduled and local clergy and anti-violence activists visited the block to comfort residents and call for accountability.

Summary:

Reporting by The Wall Street Journal and the Associated Press reveals multiple, previously undisclosed cyber intrusions by foreign hackers—particularly those traced to Iran—into U.S. water and power systems beginning around 2012–2014. Key incidents include:

- A classified 2013 breach in which Iranian-linked hackers probed the control system of a small New York-area dam. Investigators say the attackers did not seize control but were mapping vulnerabilities; the White House became involved after initial confusion about the target’s size and location.

- A broader campaign uncovered by security researcher Brian Wallace and firm Cylance that traced malware activity to Iran-based IP addresses and exposed a major intrusion into Calpine, a power producer. Attackers stole tens of thousands of files, including engineering diagrams, usernames and passwords for 71 plants, and network maps that could enable attackers to reach operations networks controlling turbines and other “mission critical” equipment.

Context and risks:
- These incidents fit a known pattern of nation-state actors (Russia, China and Iran are repeatedly cited) probing U.S. critical infrastructure to “map” networks and build footholds for potential future attacks. U.S. officials, including the NSA director, have warned some foreign states could disrupt portions of U.S. infrastructure.

- The Department of Homeland Security handled increasing numbers of industrial-control incidents (295 in FY2015 vs. 245 the prior year). Private and government studies warn a coordinated attack on key substations or plants could cause extended, economically and socially devastating blackouts.

- Vulnerabilities are widespread: many industrial control systems run on outdated software or hardware, utilities are increasingly networked (often via contractors), and smart-grid devices and third-party vendors expand attack surfaces. Attribution remains difficult and much of the government’s response and incident details are classified or unreported.

Responses and gaps:
- DHS, FERC and industry bodies have issued warnings, provided briefings, and offered assistance to some firms, but officials acknowledge defenses lag and parts of the largely private grid fall outside federal regulation. Utilities vary in preparedness; some large operators have active cyber teams that can isolate threats, but experts say motivated, well-funded adversaries can find ways in.

- Lawmakers and experts call for clearer rules of engagement and standards defining when cyber intrusions constitute espionage, crime, or acts of war and what the appropriate U.S. response should be.

Overall, the reporting underscores that foreign cyber actors have repeatedly penetrated and collected sensitive operational information from U.S. energy and water systems—sometimes remaining undetected for years—raising serious concerns about preparedness, attribution and policy for defending critical infrastructure.

"War for the Planet of the Apes," directed by Matt Reeves and co-written with Mark Bomback, is a powerful, emotionally rich conclusion to the recent Apes trilogy. The film continues the arc of Caesar (Andy Serkis), now the simian leader trying to protect his community after a devastating conflict. When a fanatical military leader known only as the Colonel (Woody Harrelson) attacks the apes and captures many of them, Caesar embarks on a personal, revenge-driven mission that tests his role as a moral leader and the limits of his compassion.

Blending classic war-film influences with the franchise’s own mythology, Reeves balances large-scale action and clear staging with quiet character moments. Motion-capture performances—especially Serkis’s Caesar, the wise orangutan Maurice (Karin Konoval), and the unexpectedly poignant Bad Ape (Steve Zahn)—succeed in making the apes deeply sympathetic and humanized in ways that eclipse the original series’ rubber masks. The movie moves from guerrilla skirmishes to an intense, prison-camp–style second half that invokes Holocaust and internment imagery and contemporary political resonances (notably a symbolic wall), sometimes with heavy-handedness.

Strengths include coherent storytelling, emotionally serious violence (never glamorized), strong pacing and editing, and scenes that foreground moral ambivalence rather than simple spectacle. Criticisms center on some blunt political symbolism, a lack of sympathetic human characters beyond a mute young girl who bonds with the apes, and occasional overstatement in the Colonel’s caricature. Overall, the film is widely praised as a thoughtful, adult blockbuster and a stirring finale that elevates the trilogy.

Apple’s iOS 7 introduced a clean visual redesign but added extensive motion — zooms, slides, full-screen transitions and a parallax home screen — that many users find disorienting. People with vestibular disorders, other balance/neurological conditions, or heightened sensitivity to visually induced motion report dizziness, nausea and vertigo when using the system; some have even reverted devices to iOS 6. Experts explain this as visual-vestibular conflict, where the eyes signal motion while the inner ear and body do not. Estimates of who’s affected vary; while visually induced motion sickness is thought to affect a minority of the general population, prevalence is much higher among those with vestibular dysfunction (millions of adults).

Apple provides a “Reduce Motion” setting in iOS 7, but it only disables parallax and does not stop zooming and sliding transitions, leaving many users without an adequate remedy. Advocates and accessibility experts say Apple appears to have overlooked balance-related accessibility even though it otherwise has strong accessibility features. They urge Apple to acknowledge the issue, work with affected users and developers, and offer a more comprehensive, system-level way to disable motion. Developers are also encouraged to provide opt-outs for animations and use motion only where it supports function rather than decoration; some apps (e.g., PCalc) have already added such options. In the short term, experts advise affected users to rest often, avoid close-up viewing that reduces peripheral cues, or limit device use, and to contact Apple’s accessibility team requesting more complete controls.

Former tennis star Jennifer Capriati was rushed to a hospital early today after a reported possible drug overdose at a hotel in Riviera Beach, Florida, sources tell TMZ. Paramedics responded and she was taken to a nearby hospital; her father told TMZ she is recovering well.

Capriati, who turned professional at 13, won 14 career titles including three Grand Slams (Australian and French Opens) and an Olympic gold medal in 1992. After early success and burnout in the mid-1990s—during which she faced legal troubles, rehab stays and loss of endorsements—she made a major comeback in 1999 and won the Australian Open in 2001 and 2002. She has not returned to competition following later injuries and has been reported to have suffered from depression.

U.S. officials say at least 16 Americans—primarily U.S. embassy staff and possibly family members—have been affected by mysterious “incidents” in Havana that began in late December 2016. The State Department calls the situation unprecedented; symptoms have varied but include hearing loss, headaches, nausea, vision problems, balance and memory issues. Medical evaluations reviewed by CBS diagnosed some affected diplomats with conditions as serious as mild traumatic brain injury and likely central nervous system damage. Some victims were evacuated to Miami for treatment, and U.S. medical teams and experts (including physicians consulted at the University of Miami) have assessed personnel in Cuba.

U.S. investigators—including the FBI and the State Department’s Diplomatic Security—are probing the incidents. Officials have not identified a perpetrator or found any device; some sources suggest exposure to a directed sonic or acoustic device, but the cause remains unconfirmed. The incidents reportedly stopped in the spring, though delayed or varying onset of symptoms means some people continue to experience effects.

Washington has pressed Cuba— which denies involvement and says it is cooperating—on its obligation to protect diplomats under the Vienna Convention; the U.S. expelled two Cuban diplomats from Washington in May (described as a response to Havana’s failure to ensure safety, not an explicit finding of guilt). Secretary of State Rex Tillerson has called them “health attacks,” while the State Department uses the term “incidents” pending investigation. There have been no reports of similar problems at other embassies.

Separately, despite the diplomatic dispute, U.S. Treasury actions removing multiple Cuba-related domain names from a sanctions list have signaled ongoing, complex policy shifts aimed at easing some business and travel restrictions—though officials say the delisting largely reflects removal of one company with many domains rather than a broad policy change.

In the early 1980s, veteran Lubbock elementary teacher Linda Hooper was warned about a disruptive sixth-grader, Cruz Riojas, whom she initially called a “holy terror.” Cruz arrived distraught and behind academically—two grades below in reading, dyslexic, and classified for special education—and acted out violently at school. At home he lived in severe poverty and abuse with his mother, five half-siblings and an abusive stepfather (“No. 5”), which fueled his need for attention and his aggression.

Over that school year Cruz began to change after Hooper gave him responsibilities in class, paid him for odd jobs at her home and treated him with consistent care. He formed a close bond with Linda and her husband Gale, a retired firefighter, and increasingly took refuge with them when conflicts at home escalated. In February 1983, after a violent fight with his stepfather that led to Cruz being kicked out at age 12, his mother brought him to the Hoopers; what was meant to be a brief stay became permanent.

The Hoopers provided clothing, steady meals, a first job, emotional support and advocacy. With the help of another teacher, Cruz improved academically and by high school had tested out of special education. Although Linda feared losing him to his family and lived with anxiety for years about having no legal rights, the family bond deepened. As an adult, Cruz decided to formalize that bond: in 1998, at age 29, he and his wife legally adopted the Hooper surname in a ceremony that symbolized his gratitude and solidified the parent–child relationship.

Today Cruz lives in San Antonio, works in payroll, has two children, and maintains pride in both his Mexican heritage and his Hooper family ties. Linda says Cruz transformed her life and her teaching—she came to view every student as a potential “Cruz”—and calls adopting him the best thing she’s done. The story is one of a troubled child rescued by patient, persistent care that led to lifelong family and personal transformation.

Actress Melissa Gilbert, best known for Little House on the Prairie, faces a federal tax lien of $360,551 filed by the IRS on Feb. 3 alleging unpaid income taxes for 2011–2013. The lien, recorded in Livingston County, breaks down to $219,989 for 2011, $99,405 for 2012 and $41,157 for 2013. California has also filed state tax liens against her totaling $112,527 since 2013. Gilbert, 51, who moved to Howell, Michigan, with husband Timothy Busfield in 2013, attributed the arrears to the recession’s impact on her stalled acting career, a prior divorce and the housing crash. She says she has negotiated an IRS installment plan and is confident she can pay the debt off.

Gilbert and Busfield have rented a Victorian home near downtown Howell and are planning to move to a log house elsewhere in Livingston County; Busfield says the move is unrelated to the tax issue. While in Michigan, Gilbert wrote My Prairie Cookbook and has remained active in charity and occasional acting/directing projects. Their landlord and local residents describe them as good tenants and welcomed community members. The article also briefly notes other celebrity tax cases, citing Dolce & Gabbana as an example.

A North Carolina woman’s 911 tip ended the manhunt for Dylann Storm Roof, the 21-year-old suspect in the mass shooting that killed nine people at Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, S.C. Early Thursday police circulated surveillance images and a car description. Debbie Dills of Kings Mountain spotted a man with a “bowl” haircut and the described white license plate while leaving church, called her husband and 911, and officers located and stopped the vehicle in Shelby, N.C. Roof was arrested at about 10:44 a.m., cooperated with police, waived extradition, and was cleared to return to South Carolina.

In the days after the attack investigators and acquaintances sketched a portrait of Roof as a young white man with racist views. A childhood friend, Joseph Meek Jr., said Roof had recently reconnected with him on Facebook and voiced extremist comments about Trayvon Martin, Freddie Gray and black people “taking over the world,” advocating segregation and saying “someone needed to do something” for the white race. Roof’s social media showed imagery linked to former white-minority regimes (Rhodesia and apartheid-era South Africa) and his license plate reportedly displayed a Confederate flag. Friends and family described him as once quiet and likable; some said they never suspected he would commit violence.

Court records show a pending adult felony drug charge from March and a misdemeanor trespass charge from April. The Southern Poverty Law Center said Roof appeared to be a “disaffected white supremacist” based on his online profile, noting the incident highlights the ongoing threat of homegrown extremism tied to racial backlash.

Summary:

Dr. Gordon Hamilton, a 50-year-old glaciologist from the University of Maine’s Climate Change Institute, died October 22, 2016, when the snowmobile he was riding fell into a crevasse in the McMurdo Shear Zone about 25 miles south of McMurdo Station, Antarctica. The Shear Zone is a heavily crevassed, three-mile-wide, 125+-mile-long region where the Ross and McMurdo ice shelves meet; ice there is up to 650 feet thick. Hamilton’s body was recovered and will be returned to his family in Maine. The U.S. Antarctic Program (USAP), managed by the National Science Foundation (NSF), has opened an accident investigation.

Hamilton was conducting research using robots equipped with ground-penetrating radar to study the stability of the Ross and McMurdo ice shelves and to map and remediate crevasses for safe traverse routes. At the time of the accident, his science team was camped about 200 yards from the USAP traverse crevasse-remediation team; both teams included experienced personnel, had received crevasse and glacier safety training, and were accompanied by mountaineers familiar with the area. Crevasses had been identified and filled earlier in the week and work on a newly identified crevasse was beginning when the accident occurred.

NSF and university officials expressed condolences and noted the inherent risks of polar fieldwork despite mitigation efforts. Hamilton, a respected researcher and mentor who had worked extensively on Greenland and Antarctic ice-sheet studies, is survived by his wife Fiona and two sons.

Summary:

A controversy erupted in Pembroke Pines after Sergeant Jennifer Martin of the Pembroke Pines Police Department says she was effectively denied service at the Arby’s on Pines Boulevard because she is a police officer. According to Martin’s report, employee Kenneth (Kenny) Davenport took her card at the drive‑through window, then manager Angel Mirabal approached and told her, “He doesn’t want to serve you because you are a police officer,” later laughing and saying the clerk could refuse service. Martin accepted a refund and contact info from the manager but declined to eat the meal. The incident prompted protests by officers’ spouses and calls from local police unions for the employees’ firing and a national Arby’s boycott.

Pembroke Pines Police Chief Dan Giustino called the Arby’s corporate office; Arby’s CEO Paul Brown and SVP Scott Boatwright apologized, told the chief the behavior was unacceptable and not representative of company values, and the chief said he accepted the apology and considered the matter closed. Arby’s issued a statement calling the incident isolated and saying it would reinforce inclusion policies with staff. Local reporters said Arby’s corporate did not respond to their direct inquiries.

Davenport and his grandfather describe the episode as a poorly timed joke, with Davenport saying he was busy and the manager made the remark; his grandfather called the situation blown out of proportion. The episode has stirred broader debate about respect for law enforcement and led union leaders to link the incident to wider anti‑police sentiment.

Jeffrey Zaslow, a 53-year-old Wall Street Journal reporter and best-selling author based in West Bloomfield, Mich., died in a car crash on a snow-covered road in northern Michigan on Friday. According to the Antrim County Sheriff’s Office, he lost control of his car on M-32 near Elmira and was struck by a semi; he had been in Petoskey earlier for a book signing. Zaslow is survived by his wife, Fox 2 Detroit anchor Sherry Margolis, three daughters (Jordan, 22; Alex, 20; Eden, 16), and his parents.

A prolific and empathetic writer known for human-interest work, Zaslow rose to prominence in part after covering Randy Pausch’s “last lecture,” which he later turned into the international best seller The Last Lecture. Other notable books include The Girls from Ames, Highest Duty (with pilot Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger), Gabby: A Story of Courage and Hope (with Rep. Gabrielle Giffords and Mark Kelly), and his most recent, The Magic Room, about a Michigan bridal shop and the women who shop there. He had previously won the job of Ann Landers’s successor at the Chicago Sun-Times as part of a Wall Street Journal feature and wrote a relationship column for the Journal.

Colleagues and collaborators praised his depth, warmth and ability to draw emotional stories from ordinary life. The Wall Street Journal and others noted his awards and influence; funeral arrangements were to be handled by Ira Kaufman Chapel in Southfield, Mich.

A Long Island woman, Kathi Fedden, has filed a federal wrongful-death lawsuit alleging Suffolk County police and others are responsible for the July 30–31, 2013 death of her 29-year-old son, Peter Fedden, who died after crashing his mother's car into a Hauppauge marketing firm. The complaint claims Peter — “severely intoxicated” and visibly injured after an earlier high-speed crash that night — was not arrested or documented by officers who responded to the first crash. Instead, the suit alleges officers, many of whom were regular customers at Peter’s deli and received discounted meals there, had his car towed and drove him home. After being dropped off, Peter allegedly left in his mother’s car and crashed minutes later while driving at very high speed.

The suit also names the local Ruby Tuesday where Peter had been drinking earlier, accusing the restaurant and a bartender of over-serving him due to inadequate training. It contends responding officers failed to take photographs or witness statements at the first crash, told other occupants to leave, and “conspired” not to charge him because of their familiarity with him and his deli’s discounts. The plaintiff seeks damages — reports vary between $30 million and $130 million.

Suffolk County officials declined to comment due to pending litigation. The owner of the damaged marketing firm called the lawsuit frivolous, noting Peter chose to drive again that night; Ruby Tuesday did not comment. Peter’s attorney and the county had not provided detailed responses in the reporting.

Ken Mehlman, who managed George W. Bush’s 2004 re-election campaign and chaired the Republican National Committee (2005–2007), has publicly acknowledged that he is gay in a long Atlantic interview with Marc Ambinder. He says he only recently came to terms with his sexuality, has told family and friends, and now plans to advocate for gay rights—particularly same‑sex marriage—while remaining a Republican. Mehlman has already been advising the American Foundation for Equal Rights, which backed the legal challenge to California’s Proposition 8.

Commentators note the significance: Mehlman is the most prominent Republican to come out, and his disclosure could influence GOP colleagues and public opinion by humanizing homosexuality and framing support for gay marriage in conservative terms (individual freedom, limited government, and marriage’s social value). RNC figures like Michael Steele and Ed Gillespie offered supportive reactions, with Gillespie noting generational shifts on gay rights within the party.

The news has provoked mixed responses elsewhere: some conservatives express indifference or call for civility in debate, while critics on the left and within the gay community fault Mehlman for his past role in GOP anti‑gay strategies and demand apologies. Mehlman acknowledges regret for not being public earlier and asks for understanding as he shifts toward advocacy.

Over one week, protests sparked by U.S. military personnel burning copies of the Koran in Afghanistan set off deadly violence and exposed a major vulnerability in Washington’s plan to shift from large NATO combat forces to small advisory teams embedded with Afghan units.

Violence included several "green-on-blue" attacks — Afghan security personnel killing NATO troops — most recently the slayings of two high-ranking NATO officers and two U.S. troops, plus an attack on a U.S. base in Kunduz that wounded seven Americans. Afghan deaths in related unrest reached about 25. In response, the top NATO commander in Kabul ordered advisers out of key Afghan ministries, and the U.S., Britain, Germany and France temporarily withdrew hundreds of military and civilian advisers, disrupting day-to-day cooperation and depriving Afghan ministries of expertise.

The incident has renewed doubts about whether Afghan forces can be trusted to protect Western advisers — a core requirement of the planned “advise and assist” endgame, which envisions far smaller Western footprints (U.S. forces falling from a 100,000 peak to about 68,000 by summer, then further reductions, with all combat troops gone by end of 2014). Military analysts warn that small advisory teams (often a dozen troops) may be more vulnerable to insider attacks than conventional units, and that rebuilding trust will be difficult and perhaps long-lasting. Some advisers argue that closer, risk-accepting relationships with Afghan partners reduce that danger, but acknowledge the persistent cultural and political risks.

Policy debates continue over how few advisers are required to sustain Afghan security forces and government functions; estimates suggest NATO might manage with as few as 25,000 advisory troops if they can call in air support, sustain logistics, and curb major corruption. For now, cooperation is largely on hold, Afghan leaders have appealed for calm, and U.S. officials say they remain committed to partnership even as questions mount over the feasibility and safety of the advisory strategy.

A draft of the Third National Climate Assessment, compiled by more than 240 scientists and released by a federal advisory committee, concludes there is “unambiguous” evidence that the Earth is warming and that human activities—primarily burning fossil fuels—are the main driver. It documents observed U.S. impacts already underway (longer, hotter summers; more frequent/intense heat waves, heavy downpours, floods and droughts; rising seas; melting glaciers and arctic sea ice; and ocean acidification) and details regional harms to water supplies, agriculture, infrastructure and coastal communities.

Key findings and projections:
- Average U.S. temperatures have risen roughly 1.5°F since 1895, with over 80% of that rise occurring since 1980.
- In coming decades most areas are projected to warm another 2°F–4°F.
- By 2100, temperatures could rise about 3°F–5°F if global emissions are sharply reduced after 2050, or as much as 5°F–10°F under continued high emissions.
- The assessment ties increased extreme weather (heavy precipitation, intense Atlantic hurricanes in some regions, western heat waves and drought) to climate change and warns of growing risks to agriculture, water resources, public health, electricity grids, and coastal infrastructure.

Reactions and process:
- Environmental groups and climate advocates urged stronger action—stricter power-plant carbon standards and investments in community resilience.
- Some political figures, including Rep. Lamar Smith, said the science should be further vetted and questioned attribution and extent of human influence.
- The draft is open for three months of review (public and scientific) and will be reviewed by the National Research Council; a final report is expected in early 2014.

The report refrains from prescribing policy but frames climate change as a present, accelerating threat that will be far more severe if global greenhouse-gas emissions are not curtailed.

Cuban researchers have developed a promising, low-cost therapeutic lung cancer vaccine called Cimavax, and U.S.–Cuba cooperation may finally bring it to American patients. Roswell Park Cancer Institute agreed during New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s recent trade mission to Havana to partner with Cuba’s Center for Molecular Immunology to obtain full documentation and pursue U.S. FDA approval and clinical trials. Roswell Park CEO Candace Johnson hopes to file for U.S. testing within months and start trials within about a year.

Background: Cuba has a strong, resourceful biotech sector despite decades of economic hardship and the U.S. embargo. The country prioritized medical research after major public-health crises, producing vaccines (e.g., meningitis B, hepatitis B), interferon, monoclonal antibodies and novel cancer immunotherapies. Cimavax, developed over 25 years and provided free in Cuba since 2011 at roughly $1 per dose, stimulates antibodies against epidermal growth factor (EGF) to slow tumor growth and metastasis. A 2008 Phase II trial showed a survival benefit of about four to six months. While Cimavax is unlikely to be a standalone game-changer in its current form, Roswell Park plans to test it as a preventive vaccine and to explore broader applications because EGF is implicated in other cancers. Another Cuban candidate, Racotumomab, targets tumor membrane lipids and has also attracted international collaboration.

Political and commercial context: The Roswell Park deal—finalized during Cuomo’s visit—was part of broader engagement between New York businesses and Cuban counterparts (including software company Infor). Such exchanges reflect Obama-era easing of travel and some restrictions on medical and research equipment; however, full expansion of collaborative research awaits congressional lifting of the embargo. Proponents argue engagement will foster mutual benefit and allow U.S. researchers to learn from Cuba’s innovative, cost-constrained approaches to medicine.

Russian president Vladimir Putin participated in a gala ice hockey match at the All-Russia Festival of the Night Hockey League in Sochi, wearing number 11 and playing with a team dubbed "NHL Stars" that included retired Soviet greats like Vyacheslav Fetisov and Pavel Bure. Footage showed Putin missing several shots—teammates appeared to nudge the puck in for him on multiple occasions—before he finally scored; state media later claimed he finished with six goals and five assists, a tally not independently verified. The opponents were reportedly amateurs. The event, attended by officials including Defense Minister Sergey Shoigu, is part of a league launched in 2011 for over-40s and has grown to include teams from other countries. Putin framed the game as a friendly boost for sport and physical culture. The outing continues a pattern of highly staged, macho publicity stunts—ranging from horseback rides and encounters with wild animals to staged scuba “finds”—used to bolster his public image.

Snap is making its Spectacles camera sunglasses available for purchase online in the U.S. at Spectacles.com for $129.99 (previously sold only via surprise Snapbot vending machines and a short-lived NYC pop-up). Customers can buy up to six pairs per household; shipping is estimated at two to four weeks. Snap will also sell $49.99 charging cases and $9.99 cords directly (removing them from Amazon). Snapbots and pop-ups will still appear sporadically.

Spectacles record circular 10–30 second videos that integrate with Snapchat and helped generate strong buzz during the limited rollout—some buyers resold pairs for huge markups—but Spectacles have not yet produced significant revenue, and Snap’s IPO filing warned of near-term production and operating losses exceeding Spectacles-related revenue. The wider online availability is intended to make the product more accessible while Snap evaluates whether hardware can contribute meaningfully to its business and attract more content creation on Snapchat.

Facebook plans to unveil a long-rumored music platform at its f8 developer conference on September 22 that will deeply integrate third-party streaming services into the Facebook experience. Rather than hosting or streaming music itself, Facebook will act as a platform connecting users with partner services so subscribers can listen, share songs and playlists, and see what friends are playing from within Facebook.com.

Reported initial launch partners include Spotify, Rdio and MOG (other reports also list Rhapsody and Slacker), though Facebook may open the platform to many third-party developers rather than favoring specific services. The initiative is positioned to increase user engagement on Facebook and could eventually expand beyond music to other media like movies. Facebook has declined to announce details publicly, saying integrations with popular music services already exist and partner discussions are ongoing.

For music services, tighter Facebook integration could drive discovery and subscription growth by making friends’ listening activity and shared playlists more visible. The move follows earlier evidence of a code-named music project and comes as competition in digital music intensifies (Apple, Google and Amazon pursuing their own strategies and Apple among those launching new streaming/locker services). Previous social-network music efforts (e.g., Myspace) show social integration can help but not guarantee success.

Summary:

U.S. officials say Russian-linked hackers last year breached the White House’s unclassified computer network after first gaining a foothold in the State Department system. Although the compromised White House network did not hold classified material, intruders accessed sensitive non-public information, including real-time details of President Obama’s schedule. Investigators believe the attack began with a phishing email sent from a hijacked State Department account that installed malware and spread to White House machines.

The FBI, Secret Service and intelligence agencies treated the intrusion as one of the most sophisticated against U.S. government systems; forensic traces and other markers led investigators to attribute the activity to actors working for Russia, though the White House declined to formally confirm attribution. Officials said classified systems were segregated and not believed compromised, and steps were taken to shut down and harden the unclassified network while remediation continued. The episode heightened concerns about Russian cyber capabilities, prompted calls for stronger defenses, and fed broader debates about government cybersecurity practices.

Raphaël Domjan’s long-held ambition to circumnavigate the globe on solar power became reality when the MS Turanor PlanetSolar, a 115-foot catamaran covered with 38,000 solar cells, returned to Monaco after a 37,294‑mile, 584‑day voyage. Conceived in 2004 and funded in part by German entrepreneur Immo Stroeher, the carbon‑built vessel uses its solar array to charge six blocks of lithium‑ion batteries and supply propulsion, demonstrating that solar energy can power sustained ocean travel.

Launched from Monaco in September 2010, PlanetSolar crossed the Atlantic and Pacific, transited the Panama and Suez canals, and made port calls including Miami, Cancún, Brisbane, Singapore and Abu Dhabi. The trip was deliberately slow and included stops to promote solar power, occasional delays to wait for sunlight and even an encounter with pirates. Domjan and his team framed the voyage as a proof of concept and a platform to raise awareness about sustainable energy rather than a ready‑made commercial solution, though the journey also aligns with industry efforts to improve fuel efficiency.

With the mission complete, the team is weighing future options for the vessel—including renting it for scientific or commercial use, selling it, or using it as a large mobile solar battery—and plans to produce a book and documentary. The arrival celebrations in Monaco featured a light show powered by the boat’s batteries and were streamed on the PlanetSolar website. Domjan said the expedition showed the technology and knowledge exist to move toward more sustainable maritime practices.

President Donald Trump’s first foreign trip as president (May 19–27, 2017) is a nine-day, five-country tour across Saudi Arabia, Israel/Palestine, the Vatican/Italy, Belgium (EU/NATO) and Sicily for the G7. The White House frames it as a pilgrimage to the birthplaces of the three Abrahamic faiths—Islam, Judaism and Christianity—with goals of projecting American power, building relationships with world leaders and promoting a message of religious unity against extremism. Senior aides call the itinerary unprecedented and heavy with religious symbolism; critics say it is also highly risky and tests Trump’s diplomatic judgment.

Key elements and tensions of the trip:
- Saudi Arabia (Riyadh, May 20–21): Trump will meet King Salman and Gulf leaders, sign defense/economic agreements, and deliver a high-profile speech to some 50 Muslim-majority countries urging them to confront “radical ideology.” Advisers hope to use the Saudi summit to unite Muslim leaders against extremism, but experts warn Trump’s past anti-Muslim rhetoric, the draft speech’s association with Stephen Miller, and Saudi Arabia’s own promotion of austere religious doctrines make the event delicate and potentially counterproductive. A proposed center to combat radicalism and a regional roundtable on religious freedom (including Christians in Muslim-majority countries) have been discussed.
- Israel and the West Bank (Jerusalem & Bethlehem, May 22–23): Trump will visit Yad Vashem, speak at the Israel Museum, pray at the Western Wall, visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and meet Israeli and Palestinian leaders (Netanyahu, President Rivlin, and Mahmoud Abbas). The administration says he will reiterate opposition to further settlement growth outside existing blocs and has not abandoned the two-state solution, but will not present a formal peace plan on this trip. The visit was marred by several diplomatic frictions: confusion over whether the Western Wall is in Israeli sovereign territory, the cancellation of a planned Masada landing, and reports Trump disclosed classified Israeli-sourced intelligence to Russia—issues that raised Israeli concern.
- Vatican (Rome, May 24): Trump will meet Pope Francis for a brief private audience to discuss religious freedom, humanitarian cooperation and human trafficking. The two men have had public disagreements (e.g., over immigration and the border wall), but both indicated they will listen and seek common ground.
- Brussels and NATO (May 25): Trump will meet EU and NATO leaders, reaffirm U.S. commitment to the alliance while pressing allies to share burdens—a recurring theme since the campaign. The visit comes amid European skepticism about Trump’s “America First” rhetoric.
- Sicily/G7 (May 26–27): Trump will attend the G7 summit to discuss trade, terrorism, refugees and possibly decide about U.S. membership in the Paris climate agreement after the trip.

Political context and risks:
- The trip takes place with significant domestic turmoil—most notably the firing of FBI Director James Comey and a growing Russia probe—which increases scrutiny and could undermine messaging abroad.
- Trump has limited history of religious engagement and has previously used inflammatory rhetoric about Muslims and made controversial comments about Jews and the Pope. While his administration has courted conservative Christians (e.g., Supreme Court nominee Neil Gorsuch), Jewish and Muslim groups have criticized other administration actions (handling of bomb threats, travel bans).
- Advisors hope the religious framing will attract attention and help reset relations with key partners (Saudi Arabia, Israel, the Vatican, NATO), but analysts warn that improvisation, blunt rhetoric, or missteps could inflame audiences and damage U.S. interests.

Other notes:
- First Lady Melania Trump will join and conduct separate outreach to military families and foreign women/children at several stops.
- The trip replaces some planned symbolic moves (e.g., Trump delayed moving the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem) and is intended to both reassure allies and press strategic agendas (anti-extremism, burden-sharing, economic issues).

Summary:

Jeb Bush’s presidential bid ran into serious trouble early on, and many close to him point to the decision to hold frequent senior staff meetings at a Dallas/Fort Worth airport Hyatt as emblematic of a campaign that became disjointed and awkward. What began as a convenient meeting spot for a geographically scattered team soon alienated donors and reinforced perceptions that the campaign wasn’t properly rooted in Florida. Internal tensions grew as new advisers rapidly hired staff, factions argued over resource allocation between Bush’s official campaign and its allied super PAC (Right to Rise), and leaders clashed over strategy and staffing.

Bush’s exploratory phase was marked by overconfidence—relying heavily on anticipated fundraising heft and a “shock-and-awe” launch to deter rivals—while underestimating voter attention and the strength of other candidates. Although his operation raised large sums and assembled an experienced advisory network, expectations that the super PAC would raise some $100 million proved optimistic. On the trail, Bush’s moderate, wonky style—especially on immigration and education—has often appeared out of step with the conservative base. A poorly handled sequence of media appearances in mid-May about whether he would have authorized the Iraq War crystallized criticisms about his reluctance to repudiate his brother’s record and damaged confidence among donors.

By late spring, polls showed Bush slipping from front-runner status into a multi-way cluster near the top. Donors and Republican operatives grew uneasy; some believed he might not secure the nomination. Internal disputes intensified over personnel and priorities. David Kochel, initially serving as a de facto campaign manager, saw his authority diminished amid complaints he focused too much on staffing rather than countering attacks. Bush’s inner circle, including Mike Murphy and longtime consultant Sally Bradshaw, pushed changes. Danny Diaz was named campaign manager, with Kochel shifted to a chief strategist role emphasizing early-state planning.

Responding to criticism, Bush defended the reorganization while asking for patience and insisting there was plenty of time to recover. He and aides plan a more aggressive push to challenge rivals—particularly Marco Rubio, Rand Paul and Scott Walker—and to use his financial resources and outreach operations to regain momentum. Allies remain hopeful the changes will steady the campaign, but the episode exposed strategic missteps, internal friction and the limits of relying chiefly on money and establishment backing.

Belgian and French counter‑terror police say they have foiled an imminent Islamist plot to attack police by dismantling an active cell that spanned both countries. In coordinated overnight raids, authorities arrested 15–17 suspects (reports vary: 13 in Belgium and 2–4 in France) and shot dead two suspects and wounded a third after a firefight in Verviers, Belgium, near the German border. The three gunmen in Verviers were Belgian nationals thought to have recently returned from fighting in Syria. Police recovered weapons (including Kalashnikovs), ammunition, explosives, police uniforms, communications equipment, false documents and cash at Verviers and found investigative material in Molenbeek and other locations.

Belgian federal prosecutors said the cell intended to kill police officers and target police stations; officials called the operation “an eleventh‑hour” prevention of a major attack. Belgian authorities put security at high alert, closed several Jewish schools and placed troops and additional police on standby. French and German police also made related arrests; Europol and intelligence sources warned Europe faces many radicalised individuals and loose “sleeper” networks — estimates cited up to 20 cells (120–180 people) potentially able to strike in France, Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands. Authorities believe some returnees were directed by ISIS to carry out reprisals for airstrikes.

The raids came amid a wider counter‑terror response after the recent Paris attacks that killed 17 people; dozens more arrests around Europe targeted people linked to those attacks or to Islamist recruitment. European agencies stressed the challenge of detecting decentralized, semi‑independent actors and urged closer cooperation among security services.

A hydroelectric saddle dam under construction in Attapeu province, southeastern Laos — part of the Xepian-Xe Nam Noy (Xe-Pian Xe-Namnoy) hydropower project — collapsed Monday, releasing a massive volume of water that swept away homes, killed at least 19 people, left dozens missing and displaced more than 6,000–6,600 people across several villages. Local authorities and national leaders, including the prime minister, mobilized rescue and relief efforts; boats and emergency teams are searching for missing residents and evacuating survivors. Provincial officials and aid groups have issued urgent appeals for food, drinking water, clothing, medicine and cash.

The project, financed largely by Thai lenders and built by a joint venture led by South Korean firms SK Engineering & Construction and Korea Western Power (with Thailand’s Ratchaburi and the Lao state holding stakes), cost over $1 billion and was to power a 410 MW plant exporting about 90% of output to Thailand. The collapsed structure was reported as an auxiliary “saddle” dam; heavy seasonal rains and possible overflow are cited as contributing factors. South Korea has dispatched company and government representatives and evacuated its nationals involved in construction.

The disaster highlights long-standing environmental and social concerns about Laos’ expanding hydropower program — including impacts on the Mekong basin, resettlement of local and ethnic-minority communities, and regional ecosystem risks — and comes amid limited domestic press freedom, which has constrained reporting from the country.

The 2019 Golden Globe nominations produced several notable surprises and many high-profile snubs across television and film.

Television highlights and surprises
- Unexpected nods: The Good Place finally earned a Best Comedy Series nomination (Kristen Bell also nominated), Sacha Baron Cohen scored a Best Actor in a Comedy nomination for Who Is America?, BBC/Netflix thriller Bodyguard landed Best Drama Series and lead actor Richard Madden, and Candice Bergen was nominated for the Murphy Brown reboot.
- Big TV snubs: The Handmaid’s Tale (season 2) missed a Best Drama Series spot despite lead acting noms for Elisabeth Moss and Yvonne Strahovski. Westworld’s second season was largely overlooked (only Thandiwe Newton got a supporting nod), and Ozark’s season 2 was excluded from drama series nominations even though Jason Bateman was nominated. Atlanta and GLOW were shut out of top comedy series slots (though Donald Glover and Alison Brie received acting nods). Jodie Comer (Killing Eve) and Robin Wright (House of Cards) were also unexpected omissions.
- Acting shakes in drama: Several expected Best Actor in a Drama nominees — Sterling K. Brown, Bob Odenkirk, John Krasinski, Liev Schreiber and Milo Ventimiglia — were left out in favor of surprise entrants like Stephan James (Homecoming), Billy Porter (Pose), Richard Madden (Bodyguard) and Jason Bateman. Ted Danson missed a comedy acting nomination despite The Good Place’s wins.
- Limited series snubs: Maniac (and star Emma Stone) and Patrick Melrose were passed over in the limited-series category; Benedict Cumberbatch did receive a nomination for Melrose, while Benicio Del Toro (Escape at Dannemora) was also overlooked.

Film highlights and surprises
- Upsets and omissions: Sam Elliott was surprisingly absent from Best Supporting Actor for A Star Is Born despite awards-season momentum. Ethan Hawke did not receive a Best Actor nomination for First Reformed, a troubling sign for that film’s campaign.
- Direction and craft choices: The Globes nominated Peter Farrelly (Green Book) and Adam McKay (Vice) for directing over more critically adventurous choices such as Yorgos Lanthimos (The Favourite) and Marielle Heller (Can You Ever Forgive Me?), a notable miss for female-director representation. Nicholas Britell’s score for If Beale Street Could Talk and other strong scores (Can You Ever Forgive Me?, Wildlife) were omitted.
- Foreign-language and music snubs: Pawel Pawlikowski’s Cold War was left out of Best Foreign Language Film. Mary Poppins Returns received several nominations (including Emily Blunt and Lin-Manuel Miranda) but none for Best Original Song.
- Other film snubs called out widely: Ryan Gosling (First Man), Ryan Coogler and Ryan Reynolds (various projects), Chadwick Boseman and Michael B. Jordan (Black Panther acting noms), Clint Eastwood (The Mule), Widows (and Viola Davis), The Grinch (animated), A Quiet Place (mostly ignored beyond score), and Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again were among those the Globe voters passed over.

Overall tone
- The HFPA both confirmed and upended awards-season expectations: some mainstream picks and late-breaking TV shows made the cut, while many critics’ favorites, veteran series and presumed frontrunners were surprisingly ignored. The nominations reflected the Globe voters’ appetite for both surprises and celebrity-driven choices, producing an unpredictable and debated field heading into the awards.

A Baltimore County police officer, 29-year-old Amy S. Caprio, was killed on Monday, May 21, 2018, after confronting occupants of a suspicious black Jeep Wrangler in the suburban Perry Hall neighborhood. Responding to a call about a suspicious vehicle (and possibly a burglary), Caprio confronted the vehicle on Linwen Way just after 2 p.m.; witnesses reported hearing a gunshot and seeing the Jeep speed off and run over the officer. She was transported to MedStar Franklin Square Medical Center and pronounced dead at 2:50 p.m. Authorities recovered the Jeep and found damage to a patio door nearby, prompting investigators to treat the incident as a homicide and to open a large manhunt.

A 16-year-old, later identified in court records as Dawnta Anthony Harris, was charged as an adult in Caprio’s death; three other teenage males were initially sought and later taken into custody. Police said suspects were believed to be armed and dangerous and reviewed the officer’s body-worn camera as part of the investigation; the exact cause of death (gunshot, vehicle impact, or both) awaited autopsy results.

The shooting triggered an extensive neighborhood search, road closures and shelter-in-place orders; nearly 2,000 students at nearby schools were kept on lockdown for hours. Governor Larry Hogan ordered flags at half-staff until the funeral. Caprio, a four-year department veteran due to mark her fourth anniversary in July, had been recognized for investigative work—most notably closing multiple package theft cases last winter—and was praised by police leadership for her promise and dedication. Funeral services and public remembrances were planned for the following days.

On Thursday President Trump held an 77–80 minute solo news conference in the White House East Room—ostensibly to announce Labor Secretary nominee Alexander Acosta—but spent much of it blasting the media, defending his administration amid recent scandals, and repeating controversial claims.

Tone and coverage
- Trump was combative, defensive, and often improvisational: he repeatedly denounced reporters and major outlets as “fake news” (later “very fake news”), accused the press of bias and “hatred,” and warned that coverage would portray him as “ranting and raving.” He alternated between joking, lecturing, and mocking questioners.
- He singled out CNN (criticizing its ratings and joking about personnel), taunted reporters by name, and at times praised friendly questions. Reactions in the media were split: some supporters called it candid and presidential in style; critics called it unhinged and evasive.

Russia, Flynn and leaks
- Trump defended his decision to fire National Security Adviser Michael Flynn, saying Flynn misled Vice President Pence and denying he had directed Flynn to discuss sanctions with the Russian ambassador. He insisted he has “nothing to do with Russia” and called stories about campaign contacts with Russians “fake news,” though he also said the leaks themselves were “real.”
- He blamed leaks—possibly from the prior administration—for the recent revelations, accused intelligence and press sources of feeding damaging stories, and refused to provide details about potential military responses to provocations.

Foreign policy and nuclear warnings
- Trump said he wants good relations with Russia and repeated that U.S. and Russian nuclear arsenals make cooperation desirable. He warned that “nuclear holocaust would be like no other.”
- Asked about a Russian spy ship spotted near Connecticut and other provocations, he declined to preview military responses, saying he won’t “telegraph” moves.

Domestic policy and administration
- He reaffirmed plans to repeal and replace Obamacare, aiming to submit a health-care plan “early to mid-March.”
- He announced Acosta as the Labor nominee and noted other administration priorities (defeating ISIS, coordinating on drugs, immigration enforcement).
- On immigration he defended the rollout of his travel ban, blamed Homeland Security Secretary Kelly for timing advice, and said a revised executive order would be issued. He expressed a sympathetic but legally constrained attitude toward DACA recipients.

Race, anti-Semitism and outreach
- Trump rejected charges of racism and anti-Semitism, calling himself “the least anti-Semitic” and “the least racist” person. He defended his record but deflected responsibility when asked about a rise in anti-Semitic incidents.
- When asked about engaging the Congressional Black Caucus, he invited a black reporter (April Ryan) to “set up the meeting.”

Fact and optics
- Trump made several inaccurate factual assertions (for example about his Electoral College margin and other statistics); when corrected he brushed off some challenges.
- He insisted his administration is “a fine‑tuned machine” despite widespread reporting of disarray, leaks, a stalled cabinet confirmation, and the Flynn resignation.
- The event was seen by supporters as an effective reclaiming of the narrative; by detractors as chaotic, evasive, and illustrative of the administration’s early struggles.

Bottom line
The marathon news conference served as a showcase of Trump’s combative media style—mixing policy announcements with personal attacks on the press, denials about Russia ties, and misleading claims—eliciting polarized reactions and doing little to resolve key questions about leaks and campaign contacts with Russia.

Researchers at the Universities of Nottingham and Bristol have identified how changing day length controls seasonal fertility and other seasonal traits in mammals. Published in PNAS, the study shows that melatonin — the night-time hormone produced by the pineal gland that signals day length — regulates which forms of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) are made in a specific region of the pituitary. In sheep, long winter nights (long melatonin secretion) induce VEGF isoforms that inhibit blood-vessel growth between melatonin-sensitive and hormone-producing pituitary regions and simultaneously stimulate production of sex hormones, triggering the winter breeding season. Shorter melatonin signals in summer favor VEGF forms that promote angiogenesis and suppress reproductive activation. This angiogenesis-mediated communication provides the previously missing link between melatonin detection and control of pituitary hormone cells. The discovery explains how animals time reproduction, coat changes and antler growth, may help farmers manipulate lambing timing in a changing climate, and could have broader implications for seasonal biology and human health.

JC Penney drew online mockery after its official Twitter account posted a string of incoherent, typo-filled tweets during Super Bowl weekend — e.g., “Who kkmew theis was ghiong tob e a baweball ghamle. #lowsscorinh 5_0” and “Toughdown Seadawks!! Is sSeattle going toa runaway wit h this??” Users speculated the posts were from a drunk or inept intern, or that the account had been hacked, and reacted with sarcastic and critical replies. The incident came days after TIME reported J.C. Penney was raising prices only to discount them again for Valentine’s Day, a tactic that drew negative attention; observers tied the social media fiasco to broader perceptions of the retailer’s struggles. J.C. Penney later apologized, blaming “typos” and saying they were “#TweetingWithMittens.”

The Bank of England announced that novelist Jane Austen will appear on the new £10 note, likely issued in 2017, replacing Charles Darwin. The decision came after public outcry earlier in the year when the Bank said Elizabeth Fry would be replaced on the £5 note by Winston Churchill—an announcement that briefly left no historical British women (other than the Queen) on circulating banknotes. Protests, an online petition (tens of thousands of signatures) and activist pressure led incoming Governor Mark Carney to say the Bank had listened and would ensure banknotes celebrate a diverse range of figures.

Carney confirmed Austen at a news event at her Hampshire home and pledged a review of the Bank’s selection criteria and a more transparent process for choosing future note subjects. Campaigner Caroline Criado‑Perez, who led the drive for female representation, welcomed both Austen’s selection and the promised procedural review.

Design details shown in a prototype include Austen’s portrait (based on a sketch by her sister), a quote from Pride and Prejudice—“I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading!”—an illustration of Elizabeth Bennet, an image of Godmersham Park, and a silhouette of her writing desk. Austen will be only the third non-royal woman to appear on a Bank of England note (after Elizabeth Fry and Florence Nightingale). The move also responds to concerns that future male monarchs could reduce the visibility of notable women on currency.

Crawl of Wikipedia outlinks
- A crawl of outlinks from wikipedia.org began in March 2016. These files are not currently publicly accessible.
- For this run several changes were made compared with earlier efforts:
  - Duplicate detection was turned off so the collection would be complete (important because sharing data that points to other collections complicates distribution).
  - The seed list was expanded to include all wikis (865 collections) rather than only the English Wikipedia as in earlier runs.

Washington Post–ABC News poll on Obama, Congress and the sequester (March 7–10)
- Obama’s approval: Barack Obama’s overall job-approval rating fell to 50 percent (down 5 points since January), erasing much of his post-reelection “honeymoon.” Independents showed the largest decline: two months earlier 54% approved, now only 44% do.
- Trust on the economy: In December Obama had an 18-point edge over congressional Republicans on who the public trusted more to handle the economy. By March that gap narrowed to a near tie (44% for Obama vs. 40% for Republicans), with “neither” rising into double digits. Even among his core supporters there were drops in confidence (notably liberals and women).
- Polarization: The electorate remains deeply divided; Obama and George W. Bush are the only recent post-WWII presidents to face similarly large partisan gaps (over 70 points) in assessments.
- Congress: Very low public standing—16% approve, 80% disapprove—with both parties viewed negatively (Democrats 34/62 favorable/unfavorable, Republicans 24/72).
- Sequester views: A slim majority disapprove of the across-the-board budget cuts, though nearly three-quarters say they personally feel no impact yet and fewer than half expect family financial harm if cuts continue. Nonetheless majorities expect the sequester will harm the economy, military, and government services; 68% want the parties to negotiate to stop the cuts. On responsibility for the sequester, 47% blame congressional Republicans, 33% blame Obama.
- Issue-by-issue trust: Obama and congressional Republicans are roughly even in whom the public trusts on gun control (Obama 42%, Republicans 41%). On immigration, Obama leads by six points (45% to 39%). On deciding which government spending to cut, the public is split (44% with Republicans, 43% with Obama).
- Policy preferences around cuts and taxes: Large majorities oppose cutting popular entitlement programs—71% oppose cutting Medicaid, 60% oppose raising Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 67. There is modest support (56%) for limiting tax deductions for high-income earners as part of resolving the sequester. There is also majority support for targeted defense cuts even as across-the-board military cuts faced opposition in another poll.
- Economy and public perception: Despite strong market and job statistics, only a little over half say the economy has begun recovering; perceptions of the economy correlate strongly with presidential approval (73% of those who sense growth approve of Obama; 73% of those who don’t see recovery disapprove).
- Methodology: The poll surveyed 1,001 adults March 7–10; margin of sampling error ±3.5 percentage points.
- Reporting: The poll and analysis were reported by The Washington Post and ABC News, with polling conducted by Capital Insight.

Josh (Joshua) Browder, a 19-year-old London-born Stanford undergrad, built DoNotPay — a free AI “robot lawyer” chatbot that helps people contest parking tickets and other low-level legal issues. Launched in London and expanded to New York, the chat-like service asks simple questions (e.g., about visible signs) to determine if an appeal is possible and then guides users through the appeals process. In about 21 months it handled roughly 250,000 cases and won about 160,000 (a ~64% success rate), overturning over $4 million in fines. Browder says the tool helps vulnerable people who are often treated as revenue sources by local governments.

Browder also described another blockchain-based project that lets people with HIV create a permanent, anonymous record proving they disclosed their status to partners — intended to prevent disputes years later when companies or records may no longer exist. He sees blockchain as a durable, transformative technology beyond finance, with legal uses emerging.

In interviews he framed government regulation as generally harmful to innovation, preferring innovation to occur outside bureaucracies; he’s open to some regulation but skeptical of heavy intervention. Browder plans to expand DoNotPay to more cities and additional legal areas (flight delay claims, refugee/legal-rights guidance), and to build a developer platform enabling non-coders with legal expertise to create similar chatbots. The project illustrates practical, scalable uses of AI and blockchain for social good and legal access.

President Obama will not attend Justice Antonin Scalia’s funeral Saturday, the White House confirmed; instead he and First Lady Michelle Obama will pay respects Friday while Scalia lies in repose in the Supreme Court’s Great Hall. Vice President Joe Biden and his wife Jill Biden, who share Scalia’s Catholic faith, will attend the funeral at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception.

Press secretary Josh Earnest said the Friday visit is an “important opportunity” for the president to honor Scalia’s service. The decision drew criticism from conservatives and some commentators as a partisan snub, while others — including a former Scalia clerk — called the choice reasonable and noted there’s little precedent for presidents attending justices’ funerals. Obama publicly praised Scalia as a “brilliant legal mind” and “one of the most consequential judges,” even as his administration prepared to confront Senate efforts, led by Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, to block any Obama Supreme Court nominee until after the 2016 election.

The White House insisted the Constitution gives the president the right to nominate a qualified successor; no nomination is expected this week while Congress is in recess. Some Republicans signaled openness to hearings, and a few — including Sen. Dean Heller and Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley — did not fully rule out consideration, but McConnell urged Republicans to hold firm. Earnest also addressed Obama’s past role in the 2006 Alito debate, saying the president regrets how Senate Democrats handled that fight but views the current situation as different.

This week’s LOOK magazine issue (promoted by Lauren O’Callaghan) is out, featuring stories including a reported emotional letter from Tom Cruise to ex-wife Katie Holmes, a royal bodyguard warning about Kate Middleton's baby, new-season fashion trends, Kristen Wiig reflecting on her past, concerns about "ratter" cyber spies, and tips from a top make-up artist, plus lots of high-street fashion picks and a digital edition available on iTunes.

Key item: After divorcing in July last year, Tom Cruise is said to have written an emotional letter to Katie Holmes as July approached, hoping to rekindle their friendship if not more. Insiders say Cruise, aware a phone call would be unwelcome, sent a measured note expressing he still cares and understands why she left. The letter reportedly touched Holmes, who has been building a new life in New York with their daughter Suri; sources suggest she appreciated the gesture but is unlikely to immediately return to him.

(The piece also briefly notes Alexa Internet has been donating web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996 for inclusion in the Wayback Machine after an embargo.)

CBS News reports new details in the case of George Zimmerman, who fatally shot 17-year-old Trayvon Martin. Zimmerman says he shot Martin in self-defense after a violent struggle; his defense hinges on that alleged fight. Funeral director Richard Kurtz, who prepared Martin’s body, said Martin had a gunshot wound to the chest but showed no other visible injuries—no signs of a scuffle, knuckle or bruise marks. Surveillance video taken about 40 minutes after the shooting shows Zimmerman in handcuffs with no obvious head or facial injuries, though police reports noted he was “bleeding from the nose and the back of the head.” Zimmerman’s father and others say Martin attacked Zimmerman, breaking his nose and beating him; the family’s attorney and critics point to the video as evidence Zimmerman was not seriously injured and argue the police didn’t promptly arrest him. A special prosecutor will decide whether Zimmerman will be charged.

Researchers report that small amounts of Neanderthal DNA present in people of Eurasian ancestry measurably influence a variety of modern human traits and disease risks. Using genomic data linked to the electronic health records of 28,000 patients in the eMERGE network, the team compared each person’s Neanderthal-derived DNA segments with their clinical histories and found statistically significant associations across immunological, dermatological, neurological, psychiatric and reproductive conditions.

Confirmed links include Neanderthal variants affecting skin biology—particularly risk for sun-induced keratoses—supporting earlier hypotheses about keratinocyte-related adaptations. Novel findings include a Neanderthal-derived variant that increases risk of nicotine addiction and multiple variants that modulate depression risk in both directions. The study also highlights a Neanderthal-associated increase in blood coagulation that may once have been protective against infection or injury but today raises risks for stroke, pulmonary embolism and pregnancy complications.

The authors interpret the pattern as evidence that some Neanderthal alleles were adaptive as modern humans moved into non-African environments (different pathogens and sun exposure), but many of those effects are now neutral or detrimental in contemporary settings. The work, led by John Capra and Corinne Simonti and published in Science, demonstrates a scalable approach for using medical biobanks to evaluate evolutionary questions and plans to extend analyses to richer clinical data (lab results, notes, images). The study was supported by NIH and NHGRI grants and involved collaborators across multiple institutions.

The Philae lander, carried by ESA’s Rosetta mission, successfully touched down on Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko and returned historic images and scientific measurements, including attempts to drill and sample beneath the comet’s surface. After a bouncy, uncontrolled triple touchdown and failure of its anchoring harpoons, Philae came to rest on its side in the shadow of a cliff or large boulder. That position left only a small solar panel illuminated and reduced sunlight from the expected 6–7 hours to about 1.5 hours daily.

Engineers raced to maximize the science return during the lander’s primary ~60‑hour battery lifetime and to secure a longer mission by recharging secondary batteries with solar power. They prioritized lower-power instruments (COSAC was selected over PTOLEMY for sampling) and managed to deploy a 1.2 m arm, extend a drill about 25 cm, and operate several experiments — yielding roughly 80–90% of the planned science if sample delivery is confirmed.

Facing rapidly depleting power, controllers uploaded commands to try two risky maneuvers to improve sunlight: firing the leg springs to “hop” or using the internal flywheel to cartwheel the probe into a sunnier orientation. Those commands succeeded in rotating Philae by about 35 degrees, and the lander reported the move and transmitted final data. However, the rotation apparently came too late to recharge the batteries, and Philae entered hibernation after sending its last burst of data.

Communication remains intermittent through Rosetta; exact touchdown coordinates are still uncertain, though teams are narrowing a search area using radio triangulation and images. The comet will approach the Sun in 2015, increasing illumination; engineers hope Philae’s solar panels may then recharge its systems and wake it from hibernation. Meanwhile, Rosetta will continue orbiting and studying the comet with its instruments. Despite the setbacks, mission leaders regard the operation as a major success for the unprecedented comet landing and the data returned so far.

Matthew McConaughey is returning to teach a filmmaking course at his alma mater, the University of Texas at Austin, this fall. The upper-level, once-a-week class in the Moody College of Communications will admit 30 juniors and seniors (no prerequisites or fees) and will take students "behind the scenes" of his film Free State of Jones through recorded videos and at least one on-campus visit. McConaughey will co-teach with director Gary Ross and university lecturer Scott Rice; the instructors will show film clips accompanied by recorded explanations of creative and technical choices. This is a repeat of a similar course offered in spring 2016, which required nondisclosure agreements while the film was unreleased. McConaughey, a 1993 UT graduate, is a frequent campus visitor and supporter of UT athletics.

An 81-year-old Sebring woman, Mary H. Musselman of 5240 Kenilworth Blvd., was arrested after repeatedly violating court orders to stop feeding black bears. Musselman had first been cited in November 2012 after Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officers found she had been feeding bears; one bear that had been fed by her was euthanized after being deemed a public-safety problem. Initially given diversion, she later violated that agreement and was placed on one year of probation with a judge’s order prohibiting her from putting out food and directing weekly FWC checks of her property.

FWC officers say they repeatedly found birdseed, corn, bowls and other food on her property, and on Jan. 29, when they moved to arrest her on a probation-violation warrant she ordered them off her land, allegedly lunged at and kicked officers, and threatened to kill an officer once released. She was charged with violation of probation, resisting an officer with violence and battery on a law-enforcement officer; a deputy relayed the alleged death threat. Musselman’s supporters — former students and neighbors — describe her as a gentle, animal-loving retired teacher who may not fully grasp the legal seriousness; they are seeking mental-health advocacy and trying to assist her, noting her husband is terminally ill and they have no caregiver.

FWC officials emphasized feeding wildlife is illegal in Florida (including bears, alligators, raccoons, pelicans and sandhill cranes) because it conditions animals to seek human food, often forcing authorities to trap and euthanize habituated animals rather than relocate them. The agency conducted outreach in the area—canvassing homes and doing radio outreach—to educate residents about living safely in bear country. Musselman is due back in court March 3.

The Happytime Murders is a 2018 R-rated adult puppet comedy directed by Brian Henson that imagines a seedy Los Angeles where puppets and humans coexist but puppets are second-class citizens. The noir-tinged plot follows Phil Phillips (voice/puppetry by Bill Barretta), a blue puppet ex-cop turned private eye, and his human ex-partner, LAPD Detective Connie Edwards (Melissa McCarthy), who reunite to investigate a string of murders targeting the former cast of a popular 1990s puppet sitcom, The Happytime Gang. The investigation pulls them into a vulgar puppet underworld of strip clubs, porn shops and drug-fueled poker games.

Critics praised the craftsmanship of the puppetry and noted Henson’s lineage and technical skill, and some supporting performances—particularly Maya Rudolph as Phil’s secretary Bubbles and Elizabeth Banks in a cameo—receive positive mentions. But nearly every review calls the film unfunny, derivative and overly reliant on gross-out, R-rated shock gags (sex, drug use, crude language), many of which wear thin or feel gratuitous. Reviewers compare it unfavorably to Who Framed Roger Rabbit, Sausage Party and Team America, saying it lacks their wit, inventiveness and sustained satire. Melissa McCarthy’s comic talents are seen as underused or mismatched to the material. Overall the film is characterized as a flawed premise with competent puppetry undermined by weak writing, stale jokes and excessive raunch, making it better suited to home viewing than the big screen.

Scarlett Johansson is the world’s highest-paid actress for June 1, 2017–June 1, 2018, earning $40.5 million pretax—about four times her 2017 haul—largely thanks to her role as Black Widow in Marvel’s Avengers films. She dethrones Emma Stone. Angelina Jolie is No. 2 with $28 million (boosted by Maleficent 2 pay), followed by Jennifer Aniston at $19.5 million, Jennifer Lawrence, Reese Witherspoon ($16.5 million) and others. The top 10 collectively earned $186 million, up 16% from 2017; figures are pretax and based on box-office and industry data.

Gal Gadot is the only newcomer at No. 10 ($10 million), propelled by Wonder Woman’s success and a Revlon deal. The ranking highlights industry trends: big franchise and endorsement deals drive top paydays, leading to higher cast costs on tentpoles; yet female roles remain limited—female characters accounted for only 28.7% of speaking roles in a 2016 study—so few women reach high earnings. Only two actresses topped $20 million this year (down from three in 2017), and several previous high earners (including Emma Stone, Amy Adams, Emma Watson, Charlize Theron) fell off the list. Sixty percent of this year’s top-paid actresses are over 40, and some, like Witherspoon, have created production companies to generate more female-led opportunities.

RadarOnline and the National Enquirer reported that the California Attorney General’s office is conducting a preliminary inquiry into allegations that former Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger used state-funded security (California Highway Patrol officers and official vehicles) to escort women into his suite at the Sacramento Hyatt Regency to conceal extramarital liaisons. The allegations come primarily from William Taylor, a former hotel security chief, who says he saw CHP dignitary protection vehicles bring young women into the governor’s private wing; he reportedly passed a polygraph and is likely to be interviewed.

The story follows Schwarzenegger’s admission that he fathered a child with a former housekeeper and calls by some lawmakers and Democratic Party officials for probes into whether public or campaign funds were used to cover up affairs. Schwarzenegger’s PR team and his attorney strongly deny the Enquirer’s claims, calling them false and sourced to an unreliable, paid informant. Several retired CHP officers and the Hyatt Regency Sacramento general manager also refute Taylor’s account, saying they never witnessed inappropriate conduct and do not recognize Taylor. The Attorney General’s office declined public comment, calling it a criminal matter.
