A GoFundMe campaign organized by Dugg Kirkpatrick seeks nearly $200,000 to help actress Dawn Wells (best known as Mary Ann from Gilligan’s Island) cover medical bills, IRS penalties, and related costs. The fundraiser says Wells, 79, lost her savings after the 2008 financial crash, endured a life‑threatening surgery and a two‑month hospitalization after an accident, and recently broke her knee while recovering from complications. Kirkpatrick — who appears to have worked with Wells as a hairstylist — says she has lost her home, has no family support, and was denied placement in a smaller industry‑focused assisted living facility because of outstanding debt. The campaign raised nearly $120,000 within about 10 days; organizers say funds became withdrawable on September 13. Requests for comment were sent to Wells, her agent, and Kirkpatrick.

Ukrainian forces withdrew from the strategic rail hub of Debaltseve early Wednesday after intense fighting and a rebel advance that Kiev and Western officials said violated a recent, European-brokered ceasefire. Columns of tanks, troop carriers and other vehicles moved toward the government-held town of Artemivsk; Russian state TV showed separatists raising a flag in Debaltseve and rebel spokesmen later claimed the town was under their control, though small government pockets reportedly remained.

President Petro Poroshenko said the pullback was planned and orderly and denied that Ukrainian troops were encircled; he called for an international response to what he labeled Russia’s violation of the Minsk ceasefire. NATO’s secretary-general and other Western leaders condemned the rebel offensive and urged Russia to use its influence to enforce the truce; Russia’s foreign minister countered that the rebels had not broken the ceasefire because Debaltseve was rebel-held when the agreement was signed.

Eyewitnesses and reporters described exhausted Ukrainian units leaving amid continued shelling, shortages of ammunition, and fears of encirclement. Casualty figures were disputed: Kiev acknowledged some prisoners and reported at least 22 soldiers killed over three days, while rebels claimed hundreds of Ukrainian deaths. Around 7,000 civilians were believed still trapped in the Debaltseve area despite most of the town’s prewar population having evacuated.

Debaltseve is strategically important because it sits on the railway linking Donetsk and Luhansk. Observers have been unable to enter the town, and although the broader ceasefire has largely held elsewhere and some heavy weapons had been withdrawn, the offensive there raised concerns that the wider Minsk agreement could be undermined. The conflict in eastern Ukraine began in April 2014 after Russia’s annexation of Crimea; Kiev accuses Russia of backing the separatists, an allegation the Kremlin denies.

Harper Lee lived much of her adult life in New York, where she wrote To Kill a Mockingbird in a small Yorkville apartment. A key but long-secret factor in the novel’s creation was the support of a New York couple, Joy and Michael (Marion Martin) Brown, who quietly gave Lee a year off from work so she could write full time. In a Christmas Eve surprise in 1956 Lee found an envelope from the Browns reading, “You have one year off from your job to write whatever you please,” which Lee later described as turning a “fantastic gamble” into “a sure thing.” That year of freedom led to the 1960 publication of Mockingbird, which won the 1961 Pulitzer Prize and has since sold some 30 million copies and been translated into over 40 languages.

The Browns’ gift—structured as a loan that Lee repaid—was revealed publicly decades later and is documented in Mary McDonagh Murphy’s documentary Hey Boo: Harper Lee & To Kill a Mockingbird, in which the Browns give a rare on-camera interview. Michael Brown, a Broadway lyricist and creator of widely seen industrial shows such as the DuPont “Wonderful World of Chemistry” at the 1964 World’s Fair, met Lee through Truman Capote, who had asked him to look after his childhood friend. The Browns’ modest financial help and belief in Lee proved decisive.

The piece also notes Lee’s later retreat from public life, the controversy over a recent unauthorized-seeming biography, and reflections from friends and commentators—such as Anna Quindlen—about Lee’s choice not to publish another book.

Dick Clark will return to co-host ABC’s "Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve" for the program’s 40th anniversary on Dec. 31, appearing alongside Ryan Seacrest. The special begins at 10 p.m. EST, pauses for local news, then continues through the Times Square midnight ball drop. Seacrest has shared duties since 2005 after Clark suffered a stroke in late 2004 that impaired his speech; Regis Philbin filled in the year of the stroke. Despite health challenges, Clark remains actively involved in production and makes on-air appearances—producers say the show is very important to him and they will continue to present it live.

The anniversary broadcast will open with a retrospective of highlights spanning four decades and feature a nearly six-hour lineup that includes about 29 musical performances. Headliners and performers include Lady Gaga (the prime Times Square slot), Justin Bieber, Pitbull, Hot Chelle Rae, Florence + The Machine, Nicki Minaj, Taio Cruz, Gym Class Heroes, and Beyoncé performing from London. Producers note booking is difficult on New Year’s Eve but the show offers unmatched exposure.

"Rockin’ Eve" remains the dominant New Year’s Eve telecast—drawing nearly 19 million viewers around midnight last year—and will face specials on NBC, Fox, MTV and others. Clark, now in his 80s, conducts interviews by email and has said he hopes this isn’t his last show; colleagues and critics alike view his continued presence as a comforting, inspirational staple of the broadcast.

Jahmel Binion, a Warren, Mich. man diagnosed with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia — a rare genetic disorder that can cause sparse hair, missing teeth, altered facial features and inability to sweat, which impairs temperature regulation and can cause heat stroke — has sued NBA star Shaquille O’Neal, former Michigan/Utah Jazz player Trey Burke and rapper Waka Flocka Flame. Binion alleges the three publicly mocked a selfie he posted last summer by reposting or parodying the image on social media, conduct he says reached some 8.4 million people and amounted to invasion of privacy, defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence.

The complaint contends the defendants’ posts publicly disclosed embarrassing private facts, placed Binion in a false light, and implied he was an appropriate object of ridicule, lowering his reputation among those who respect the defendants’ opinions. Binion says the ridicule compounded longstanding hardships from his condition — including difficulty keeping employment and vulnerability to overheating — and although O’Neal and Burke later apologized and contacted him, Binion felt the apologies were belated and insufficient. He has since launched an anti-bullying campaign, Hug Don’t Judge. The suit, filed in Macomb County Circuit Court, seeks more than $25,000 in damages.

Nearly 50 years after the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Olympics pairs event, the International Olympic Committee has clarified its records: Soviets Lyudmila Belousova and Oleg Protopopov remain gold medalists; Canada (Debbi Wilkes and Guy Revell) and West Germany (Marika Kilius and Hans-Jürgen Bäumler) are recorded as sharing silver; and Americans Vivian and Ronald Joseph are officially bronze medalists.

Background: At Innsbruck the Soviets beat the favored West Germans in a close 5-4 decision; Canada placed third and the Josephs fourth. During the Games it emerged the West Germans had signed a contract with Holiday on Ice, violating amateurism rules. After an I.O.C. inquiry, Kilius and Bäumler returned their medals in January 1966 and the Canadians and Josephs were elevated and given new medals. The Josephs learned they were medalists and accepted the bronze, though the transfer was low-key.

Confusion persisted when, in 1987, the I.O.C. quietly reinstated the West Germans’ silver medals after they were deemed “rehabilitated,” without notifying U.S. or Canadian skating officials. Different record books afterward showed inconsistent results—some listing the Germans alone as silver medalists, others showing shared silver and the Josephs as bronze. The Josephs only discovered discrepancies decades later and felt awkward citing their medal.

A 2013 New York Times report prompted U.S. Figure Skating and the I.O.C. to resolve the matter formally. The I.O.C. has now confirmed that since 1987 the intended official outcome was shared silver for Canada and West Germany with the Josephs holding bronze, and this has been reflected in its records. The siblings expressed relief and vindication, even as they noted the medal was not the highlight of their careers.

Iraq’s president, Fouad Massoum, on Monday nominated veteran Shiite politician Haider al-Abadi (also spelled Haider al-Ibadi) to form a new government, giving him 30 days to present a cabinet to parliament. The move, aimed at breaking the stalemate as Islamic State (IS) militants seized large areas in the north, drew immediate backing from the U.S. — President Obama and Vice President Biden both called Abadi and publicly endorsed his nomination — and from broad Shiite, Kurdish and some Sunni lawmakers who say an inclusive government is needed to blunt Sunni support for IS.

Incumbent Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki rejected the decision, calling it illegal, filing a challenge with the Supreme Court and warning in a televised address that he would fight to remain in office. He deployed elite security units and armored vehicles around Baghdad’s Green Zone and mobilized supporters, prompting concerns about a possible internal clash. Many in Maliki’s own State of Law coalition defected to back Abadi, and key institutions including the army signaled they answer to the state rather than to Maliki personally.

The political shift comes amid escalating military pressure from IS. The U.S. has been conducting airstrikes and airdrops and has begun supplying weapons directly to Kurdish peshmerga forces fighting IS in northern Iraq. Tens of thousands of civilians — notably persecuted Yazidis who fled Mount Sinjar and crossed into Syria and then returned to Iraqi Kurdistan with Syrian Kurdish assistance — remain displaced and in need of shelter and aid. U.S. officials say expanded assistance to Iraq depends on formation of an inclusive government that represents the country’s sectarian and ethnic groups. Abadi, a British‑educated former communications minister, pledged to prioritize rolling back IS influence but faces the difficult task of forging a cohesive, broadly acceptable cabinet while Maliki remains caretaker prime minister.

Yad Vashem recently received a striking artifact: a yellowed copy of the Nazi family magazine Sonne ins Haus whose cover showed the “perfect Aryan baby.” The child was actually Hessy Levinsons (later Hessy Taft), a Jewish infant whose photograph had been secretly submitted to and won a Nazi contest by the Berlin photographer Hans Ballin, who later told her parents he did so to mock Nazi racial ideology. The image reportedly was chosen by propaganda officials and widely distributed on postcards, but the Nazis never learned the child’s true identity.

Hessy was born in Berlin in 1934 to Jacob and Pauline Levinsons, Latvian-born classical singers who had moved to Germany in the 1920s. After anti-Jewish persecution intensified—her father lost work, was briefly arrested in 1936 on a fabricated charge, and the family feared exposure—they left Germany, spent time in Latvia, then moved to Paris. When Paris fell, the family escaped with help from the French resistance to Cuba in 1942, where they lived for seven years before emigrating to the United States in 1949. Hessy became a chemistry professor in New York.

Presenting the magazine to Yad Vashem, Hessy said she feels a measure of vindication and “a little revenge” that the Nazis had unknowingly hailed a Jewish child as their Aryan ideal. The episode—documented by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum and other sources—remains a powerful, ironic example of individual resistance and the absurdity of Nazi racial claims.

This document is a mixed news gallery and short report. The gallery (images 1–42/43) showcases a wide range of recent technology and transport-related exhibits and demonstrations from around the world, including:
- Futuristic personal aircraft (Jet Capsule’s I.F.O.), concept and fuel-cell cars (Jaguar I‑PACE, Toyota Mirai, Singulato’s Tigercar), and electric/connected-vehicle technologies and demonstrations (UK Autodrive project, Toyota’s connected strategy, Nissan VR).
- Numerous robots and robotic demonstrations: humanoid and manned giant robots (Method‑2, TRX03 dinosaur suit), musical robots (Waseda’s WAS‑5 saxophonist, J apan Robot Week performers), industrial/interactive robots (Mimus), ultra-mobile chassis robots (AnyWalker), robotic fish, and other automation displays at expos in India, Japan, Singapore, South Korea and elsewhere.
- Rail and aerospace items: a panda-shaped suspension railway test line in Chengdu, JAXA’s Kibo module models, Aurora Flight Sciences’ cockpit automation (ALIAS) work, and an Israeli unmanned aerial vehicle by Elbit Systems.
- Consumer electronics exhibits (Samsung Gear S3, Gear VR) and various auto-show displays and concept vehicles.

Separately, the text reports a criminal case from Algiers: an Algerian man was sentenced to two years in prison after posting a photo on Facebook showing him dangling his baby cousin out of a 15th‑floor window with the caption “1000 likes or I will drop him.” The image—claimed by the defendant to have been photoshopped (he also said protective balcony bars had been removed)—provoked public outrage and calls for child‑abuse charges; the court rejected his explanation. Last updated 21 June 2017.

A 14-year-old Chilean girl with cystic fibrosis, Valentina Maureira, made a video plea asking President Michelle Bachelet to authorize euthanasia so she could “be put to sleep forever.” The video, reportedly posted on Facebook, shows her speaking from a hospital bed; her father said she has endured multiple operations, constant symptoms and that her older brother died from the same disease. Valentina is a patient at Santiago’s Universidad Católica clinic and was described as stable. The government said the health ministry is providing medical and psychological support and explicitly ruled out euthanasia, noting it is illegal in Chile. The case sparked public debate about euthanasia; while President Bachelet—who has pursued other social reforms—visited Valentina after the video went viral, her administration has not pursued legal changes on assisted dying.

Pete and Alisha Arnold, a 30-year-old married couple from Apple Valley, Minnesota, created BirthOrNot.com to let the public vote on whether they should continue Alisha’s current pregnancy or have an abortion. They’ve been blogging since September with health updates and ultrasound images; the fetus is about 17 weeks and confirmed male. A PollDaddy poll atop the site asks “Should We Give Birth or Have an Abortion?” (at the time of reporting it favored abortion 54–46%). The poll closes December 7, and the couple says they’ll check for voting fraud and use the results—though not as an absolute mandate—to guide their decision before the 20-week cutoff for abortion.

The Arnolds say they’re serious, not joking or running a pro-life campaign; Alisha identifies as pro-choice. They explain the vote as an extreme civics lesson and a way to engage people in the abortion debate. Reporters and commentators reacted with shock and condemnation, pointing out flaws in the couple’s logic (e.g., many pro-choice people are not pro-abortion) and noting poll manipulation by online trolls. Observers proposed three interpretations: a publicity stunt/prank, a pro-life provocation, or a genuine intention to follow an Internet vote. Critics argued the stunt trivializes a painful, personal decision and suggested the couple should not parent, with some commentary becoming vitriolic. An update in the piece leans toward the conclusion that the project is likely a pro-life stunt.

This is a short blog post (March 28, 2011) reporting that Bill Ayers jokingly claimed to have written Barack Obama’s memoir Dreams from My Father. The author (citing American Thinker and John Hawkins) interprets Ayers’s remark as sarcastic — part of a long-running gag Ayers uses to mock people who believe conspiracy theories about Obama’s authorship. The post recounts a 2009 encounter in which Ayers, when approached by a conservative blogger, unpromptedly said he’d written the book, offered to split the royalties, and pressed the joke when the blogger suggested he’d at least edited it. The writer suggests Ayers likely repeats the line to bait or ridicule credulous listeners.

The Federalist reports that the New York Times is preparing another critical story about Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh based on a 1980s letter he allegedly wrote organizing a “Beach Week” with high-school classmates. After failing to corroborate sexual-assault allegations, the Times has reportedly contacted former classmates about the tongue-in-cheek note, which details the Maryland rental location, costs (total $398, each organizer owing $50), logistics, inside jokes, warnings to notify neighbors about “loud, obnoxious drunks,” and instructions for keeping order if too many people arrived. The letter, addressed to classmate Patrick “P.J.” Smyth and signed “Bart,” portrays typical teenage partying and awkwardness around girls; Kavanaugh’s lawyers have said it is a 1983 Beach Week planning note.

Classmates interviewed by The Federalist describe the letter as innocuous and say Kavanaugh was the most organized and among the more reserved members of the group, though he and friends did drink at large backyard parties and once celebrated finishing many kegs. Several classmates who witnessed or discussed those parties later signed a letter endorsing Kavanaugh’s nomination. The Federalist frames the new Times inquiry as another attempt to smear Kavanaugh after earlier contentious Times pieces—one about a yearbook inside joke and another alleging he might have thrown ice—while noting the Senate is awaiting completion of an FBI supplemental background check before voting on his confirmation. White House spokeswoman Kerri Kupec criticized the Times for focusing on decades-old adolescent drinking.

President Obama’s 2013 budget proposal—a $3.8 trillion plan unveiled as an election-year policy blueprint—combines new investments and tax increases on the wealthy with spending restraints but stops short of major entitlement reform.

Key goals and tone
- Framed around “fairness”: giving everyone a fair shot, asking the wealthy to pay more, and investing in growth-enhancing areas.
- Presented as a continuation of prior deficit-reduction and State of the Union themes; largely political as well as fiscal.

Deficits and debt
- Projects a FY2012 deficit of about $1.33 trillion and a FY2013 deficit of $901 billion (5.5% of GDP).
- Deficits remain large throughout the decade (above $500 billion annually), and the plan would add roughly $7 trillion to debt held by the public from 2013–2022.
- Administration says the plan would cut roughly $4 trillion from deficits over 10 years through a mix of spending limits and tax increases, and cut $2.50 in spending for every $1 in new taxes.

Spending and investments
- Proposes targeted increases for infrastructure, education and manufacturing: e.g., $30 billion to modernize schools, $30 billion to retain/hire teachers and first responders, a six-year, $476 billion surface transportation program, and an $8 billion, three-year Community College to Career Fund to train workers.
- Discretionary spending constrained by the Budget Control Act caps; overall discretionary spending is projected to fall from 8.7% of GDP (2011) to 5.0% by 2022.
- Lists 210 program cuts/eliminations yielding $24 billion in 2013 and $520 billion over a decade (examples: eliminating an unnecessary Air Force satellite program; consolidating some Treasury functions).
- Proposes $217 billion in mandatory-spending savings over a decade by trimming selected farm subsidies and federal employee retirement/health benefits.
- Defense spending trimmed—about $487 billion less over 10 years per Pentagon plans.

Taxes and revenue
- Seeks $1.5 trillion in tax increases: allows Bush-era tax cuts to expire for high earners (families making over $250,000), taxes carried interest as ordinary income, and applies the “Buffett Rule” (no household earning over $1 million pays less than 30% effective tax rate).
- Proposes a bank tax to help cover bailout costs and foreclosure assistance, and elimination of certain corporate and energy tax breaks; corporate tax reform to be detailed later.
- Calls for a one-year extension of the payroll tax cut and extended unemployment insurance.

Entitlements and long-term outlook
- Modest health-program savings: more than $360 billion cut from Medicare, Medicaid and related health programs over a decade—but the budget offers little in the way of deep structural reform to entitlements (Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security).
- Critics say without major entitlement changes the budget does not address long-term fiscal pressures from aging and rising health costs; the administration’s measures stabilize debt over the next decade but do not solve post-decade entitlement-driven challenges.

Political and process context
- Republicans criticized the plan as insufficient on entitlement reform and as a campaign document; Democrats defended the balance between deficit reduction and protecting recovery.
- The proposal adheres to Budget Control Act caps and repeats elements from a prior September deficit-reduction submission.
- The budget is a presidential request only; Congress will debate, revise, and ultimately decide funding through a lengthy appropriations process.

Additional program detail
- Community college initiative: $8 billion over three years for training, employer partnerships, internships, and online entrepreneurship courses; $1.5 billion to help workers hurt by trade over three years.
- The economic forecast underlying the budget was prudent and dated to mid-November, so it did not incorporate later economic improvements.

Bottom line
The 2013 budget emphasizes progressive tax changes, targeted investments in education, infrastructure and job training, and spending constraints under statutory caps. It aims to reduce deficits through a mix of higher taxes on the wealthy and program cuts, but it avoids major entitlement rewrites, leaving significant long-term fiscal challenges unresolved.

The Texas Rangers are investigating a viral video from a Venezuelan winter league game showing their catcher Yorvit Torrealba striking an umpire in the face. In the clip, Torrealba, playing for Leones del Caracas, strikes out, argues a called strike with home-plate umpire Dario Rivero Jr., and then pushes the umpire’s facemask with an open hand; the umpire ejects him. Rangers GM Jon Daniels confirmed the club is aware and will look into the incident, noting possible discipline “depends on circumstances.” Torrealba is entering the second year of a two-year, $6.25 million contract after hitting .273 with seven homers and 37 RBIs in 113 regular-season games last year; his postseason role was reduced when Mike Napoli became the team’s primary catcher. Media reaction called the act inexcusable and disappointing given Torrealba’s reputation.

This document combines two unrelated pieces.

1) Internet Archive crawls — The Archive is conducting crawls to capture web pages as they are created and to archive the pages those new pages reference. The aim is to preserve the versions of referenced pages that were live when a page was written, so links won’t break as sites change or disappear. The Internet Archive hopes archived links will replace broken links or serve as companion links so readers can see what the original page’s authors intended. The broader goal is to “fix all broken links on the web,” including crawls of supported “No More 404” sites.

2) Allison Williams at 92Y — Actress Allison Williams (best known as Marnie on HBO’s Girls and for NBC’s Peter Pan Live) made her 92Y debut February 18 in conversation with Seth Meyers. She discussed her career and publicly addressed her father Brian Williams’ six-month suspension from NBC after he admitted to embellishing an Iraq story. Allison defended her father, calling him honest, truthful and a man of integrity who cares deeply about journalism, and said the episode has been very hard but they are “counting our blessings.” She shared a personal anecdote about a surprise call from him when she was in ninth grade, and expressed confidence he will work to regain viewers’ trust and return to TV.

An Aeroméxico-operated Embraer 190 (flight AM2431) carrying 103 people (99 passengers including two infants, plus four crew) crashed shortly after takeoff from Durango’s General Guadalupe Victoria International Airport on Tuesday afternoon. The aircraft encountered severe weather — passengers and officials reported heavy rain, hail and strong gusts; authorities said a sudden wind gust or air current rocked the plane and forced a rapid descent. The left wing struck the ground, two engines detached, and the jet came to rest roughly 300 meters from the runway before catching fire.

All on board evacuated using emergency slides; most walked away or escaped through breaks in the fuselage. Dozens were injured — officials reported around 85 people with mostly light injuries, 37 hospitalized and two in critical condition; the pilot was among the more seriously hurt but stable after surgery. There were no fatalities.

Rescue teams extinguished the fire and recovered the aircraft’s recorders; Mexican investigators, assisted by two U.S. specialists and support from Embraer, are examining the cause, a process that could take months. Aeroméxico expressed regret; preliminary accounts and the airport operator pointed to the bad weather as the likely primary factor. The 10-year-old jet had been leased by Aeroméxico and Embraer has dispatched technicians to assist.

The CIA’s official Twitter account drew widespread criticism after it live-tweeted the 2011 raid that killed al‑Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, posting an hour-by-hour account of the mission “as if it were happening today” to mark its five-year anniversary. Tweets detailed key moments — approvals by President Obama and senior officials, helicopters departing from Afghanistan, one chopper crashing, troops assaulting the Abbottabad compound, Bin Laden being found and killed, and later confirmation of identification. The move, intended to highlight the CIA’s role and the raid’s place in Obama’s legacy, prompted many users to call it “grotesque” or embarrassing and respond with derisive memes and gifs, though some defended the posts. CIA director John Brennan used the anniversary to stress al‑Qaeda’s diminished but not eliminated threat and compared the need to dismantle remaining terrorist leadership to efforts against IS leader Abu Bakr al‑Baghdadi.

20th Century Fox has fired director Bryan Singer from the Freddie Mercury biopic Bohemian Rhapsody after a pattern of absences and escalating tensions on set. Production, shooting in London with Rami Malek as Mercury, was halted Dec. 1 because Singer was "unexpectedly unavailable." Insiders said Singer repeatedly missed shooting days—forcing cinematographer Newton Thomas Sigel to cover—and clashed with Malek and other cast members; a confrontation with Malek reportedly involved Singer throwing an object. After Thanksgiving Singer did not return to the U.K. set and is believed to have been in the U.S. for about 10 days, prompting Fox to terminate him under his pay-or-play contract with roughly two weeks of principal photography remaining. 

Singer disputes the account, saying he sought time off to care for a gravely ill parent and deal with his own health, and that Fox would not accommodate him. He denied that his departure stemmed from a dispute with Malek, saying they had resolved creative differences before Thanksgiving. The studio plans to name a new director within days; the film’s targeted release remains unchanged.

Michael Cohen, a lawyer and adviser to Donald Trump, told the Daily Beast that “by the very definition, you can’t rape your spouse” while defending Trump against a decades-old allegation from his ex-wife Ivana. The allegation — first publicized in Harry Hurt III’s 1993 book Lost Tycoon and based on divorce deposition excerpts — quotes Ivana saying she was “raped” by Trump during a violent 1989 incident; she later issued a statement saying she felt “violated” and did not intend the term in a literal or criminal sense. Cohen insisted Ivana meant an emotional violation, claimed there is “very clear case law” that spouses can’t be raped (which is incorrect — New York eliminated the marital rape exemption in 1984), and then threatened the Daily Beast with lawsuits and personal financial retaliation if it published the story.

The piece recounts Hurt’s description of the alleged assault, Trump’s longstanding denials, Ivana’s later public conciliatory statement calling the claims “without merit,” and a Trump campaign response labeling the story “old news” and an attempt to exploit the divorce. The Daily Beast and Business Insider criticized Cohen’s legal assertion and threats; the outlets defended their reporting and questioned whether Trump shares his lawyer’s views. The controversy is placed in the context of Trump’s history of provocative comments about rape and sexual assault and notes uncertainty over whether the revelation would damage his political standing.

Polish historians have published what they call the most complete online list to date of Nazi SS commanders and guards who served at Auschwitz. Compiled by historian Aleksander Lasik over more than 30 years and assembled by the state-run Institute of National Remembrance and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial, the database contains more than 8,500 Auschwitz entries and Lasik’s broader work lists over 25,000 guards from various German-run camps (research continues). Entries, available in Polish, English and German, typically include birth data, nationality, education, military and party service, and sometimes photos; where applicable, judicial documents from prosecutions in Poland are attached. Dates of service at Auschwitz are still being verified. Lasik said the effort aims to expose individuals responsible as war criminals; he estimates up to 200 former guards could still be alive. Nazi hunter Efraim Zuroff praised the publication, noting it could aid investigators, including in Germany. The release comes against the backdrop of Auschwitz’s wartime toll: roughly 1.1 million people killed there between 1940–45, including about 1 million Jews, up to 75,000 Poles, some 21,000 Roma and about 15,000 Soviet POWs.

A white North Charleston police officer, Michael T. Slager, was fired and charged with murder after a bystander's video showed him firing eight times at 50-year-old Walter L. Scott as Scott ran away following a traffic stop for a broken taillight. The footage—shot after a brief struggle—appears to show Slager drawing his handgun and shooting Scott in the back; Scott fell after the eighth shot. Slager then walked back, handcuffed the motionless man and dropped something near his body. The coroner confirmed Scott was struck from behind by five bullets. Slager, a five-year department veteran, says Scott grabbed his Taser; the video does not clearly show that, though authorities say a Taser probe was later found on Scott.

The video was provided to Scott’s family and publicized, prompting swift action: Slager was arrested within hours, his original attorney withdrew, and the city’s mayor and police chief condemned the shooting. The mayor ordered that every uniformed officer be outfitted with body cameras (the city purchased 150 cameras in addition to 101 already ordered through a state grant) and said he would open a community discussion on police policies. The FBI and the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division have opened probes, and local prosecutors plan to seek a grand jury indictment.

Scott, a Coast Guard veteran and father of four with no violent criminal record, is mourned by family and community members. The release of the video intensified already strained town–police relations and spurred protests led by Black Lives Matter and others; demonstrators demanded accountability and criticized longstanding practices they say targeted black residents. Officials and activists stressed the case’s wider significance amid national scrutiny of police use of force in incidents in Ferguson, Staten Island and elsewhere. The Scott family’s attorneys plan civil litigation, asserting the video was crucial to forcing criminal charges that might not have occurred otherwise.

A U.S. Navy MH-53 Sea Dragon from Helicopter Mine Countermeasures Squadron 14 (HM-14) crashed into the Atlantic about 20 miles east of Cape Henry during a training flight Wednesday morning. Two sailors — Lt. Wesley Van Dorn, 29, a pilot from Greensboro, N.C., and Petty Officer 3rd Class Brian Collins, 25, an aircrewman from Truckee, Calif. — died after being taken to Sentara Norfolk General Hospital. A third crew member, pilot Lt. Sean Christopher Snyder, 39, was reported missing; the Navy and his family acknowledged ongoing rescue and recovery efforts. Of five crewmembers aboard, four were pulled from the water; one was released from the hospital, another remained in serious but improving condition. The Coast Guard and Navy conducted an exhaustive search across more than 600 square miles before suspending active search operations late afternoon, while continuing to recover wreckage and remains. The crash produced a large debris field; recovery teams used side-scan sonar and divers. Investigators have launched a Navy inquiry; it’s unclear whether the aircraft made an emergency landing or crashed. Cold 40-degree water and survival-suit limits complicated rescue prospects.

The report notes broader concerns about the aging MH-53 Sea Dragon fleet: the type has had multiple major accidents since 2012, a higher crash rate than other Navy helicopters, and was slated for retirement years ago but kept in service because no replacement was ready. The Navy previously invested in upgrades, maintenance personnel and training after a 2012 fatal crash; there are currently no plans to ground the fleet.

Separately, a U.S. Air Force HH-60 Pave Hawk crashed on the east coast of England during low-altitude training, killing four airmen assigned to RAF Lakenheath. The crash scattered live ammunition over marshland, creating a hazardous debris field about the size of a football field. British police, the RAF and the U.S. Air Force are investigating; the coroner conducted an initial scene assessment before remains were removed. Commanders paid tribute and noted the investigation will continue under UK and U.S. military air safety authorities.

The document is a two-part response to Lena Dunham’s reported multi‑million‑dollar book advance from Random House, using the deal to critique corporate publishing while also defending the potential value of Dunham’s work.

Main criticisms:
- The author, a longtime industry insider, argues the $3.7M advance exemplifies what’s wrong with big corporate publishers today: profit-driven, short-term thinking, heavy overhead, risk-averse behavior and a tendency to chase one big bestseller (“get me the next Bossypants”) rather than build a diverse, lasting list.
- Such huge advances raise unrealistic expectations and invite harsher critical scrutiny; Random House’s positioning of Dunham as the next Tina Fey/Nora Ephron/David Sedaris puts excessive pressure on a young writer.
- The author contrasts this approach with the ethos of indie-minded publisher Barney Rosset, who invested modest advances across many promising writers and built a durable backlist of culturally important works. He argues that dividing $3.7M among many emerging writers (e.g., 370 at $10k or 37 at $100k) would likely produce longer‑lasting cultural returns.
- Corporate publishers, accountable to shareholders and quarterly earnings, lack the patience to nurture writers over time; that vacuum has allowed small presses (Graywolf, McSweeney’s, Soho, Bellevue, etc.) to thrive and win literary prizes.

Defenses/positive take:
- Another voice in the piece acknowledges that while the advance is huge and provocative, Dunham is a marketable figure with a unique perspective. Her TV audience is sizable but not blockbuster, so the economics are uncertain.
- The defense stresses the potential value of her ideas rather than simply her celebrity: her proposal promises candid, specific essays about gender, age, workplace sexism, body image and everyday fashion for non‑celebrity women—topics with real demand but limited authentic coverage. These personal, concrete stories could resonate in ways generic advice pieces do not.

Overall takeaway:
The deal is emblematic of a broader tension in contemporary publishing: corporate houses’ high‑risk, high‑reward bets on media personalities versus a more sustainable, culturally productive model of investing smaller amounts across many writers. While Dunham’s book might succeed on its own merits, the author contends the industry would be better served by spreading resources to cultivate long‑term literary voices.

Pope Francis used his Wednesday general audience, held on UN World Environment Day in St. Peter’s Square, to condemn a growing “culture of waste” driven by consumerism, particularly the routine disposal of good food. He said wasting food is comparable to stealing from the poor and hungry, noting that past generations avoided throwing away leftovers. The pontiff linked materialism to diminished concern for human suffering—calling it normalised while financial market losses are treated as tragedies—and urged care for creation and greater personal and institutional austerity. He reiterated calls for the Church to defend the poor and for global financial reform. The remarks echoed UN figures that about 1.3 billion tonnes (one third) of food produced for humans is lost or wasted annually, and referenced a U.N.-backed report recommending practical steps (better storage, smaller portions) to reduce waste. The audience also included a personal moment for Francis, who greeted Italian relatives, and drew praise from Italy’s farmers’ group for highlighting farmers’ role and the harms of unregulated global markets.

In February, Amanda Carpenter, former communications director for Sen. Ted Cruz, was trapped in an Amtrak elevator at Baltimore–Washington International Airport. She tweeted for help and posted a photo showing the elevator’s inspection certificate had expired. Amtrak responded at the time—within 16 minutes—saying BWI agents were aware and working to get her out. Seven months later, after someone re-tweeted her original plea, Amtrak’s corporate account mistakenly replied asking if she was “still in the elevator.” The company clarified the delay was prompted by the re-tweet, apologized, and offered Carpenter a complimentary Acela ride. The exchange drew attention and amusement online.

Dr. David Newman, a Mount Sinai emergency physician and published author, was arrested and arraigned on charges that he sexually assaulted two female patients while on duty. Authorities say a 22-year-old patient treated for a shoulder injury on Jan. 11 was allegedly given an extra morphine injection by Newman, became partially incapacitated, and was groped; she alleges he masturbated and ejaculated on her face, leaving semen on her hospital gown and blanket, which she preserved as evidence. Police are awaiting DNA results and sought a court order for Newman’s DNA; reports conflict on whether he volunteered a sample. A second 22-year-old woman has since come forward, saying she was groped during a chest exam in September after visiting the ER for a cold.

Newman, who has worked at Mount Sinai, written a book and contributed to major outlets, surrendered to police and was ordered held on $150,000 bond ($50,000 cash). He was immediately suspended by Mount Sinai, which is conducting an internal inquiry and cooperating with investigators. Newman’s lawyer has said he has no criminal record and called him a “good man,” while some colleagues have defended him. Police believe there may be additional victims and are urging anyone with information to come forward. Newman is due back in court Feb. 23.

A Missouri appeals court judge, Roy L. Richter, was appointed by the Missouri Supreme Court to take over Ferguson’s municipal court and implement reforms after a U.S. Justice Department report sharply criticized the city’s police and court practices following the Michael Brown shooting. Richter will hear all current and future Ferguson municipal cases starting March 16 and is empowered to overhaul court policies; staff from the state court administrator’s office will assist him.

The move followed a DOJ report that found racial profiling, bigotry by police, and a profit-driven municipal court system that relied heavily on fines and fees—about $3.1 million, nearly one-quarter of Ferguson’s $13.3 million 2015 budget. The report said the court routinely imposed monetary penalties, issued arrest warrants for missed payments or court dates, and in some cases jailed people for minor code violations. It also documented instances of officials having tickets “fixed” for colleagues and friends, citing this as evidence of a racially grounded double standard.

Ferguson Municipal Judge Ronald J. Brockmeyer resigned the same day, saying his departure would help restore public confidence; the city also recently fired court clerk Mary Ann Twitty. Responses to the state’s intervention were mixed locally. Missouri Gov. Jay Nixon praised the Supreme Court’s actions. In Richter’s first session after the takeover, he reviewed the state court system and announced reductions in some fines.

Ripple Foods, an Emeryville startup founded by Adam Lowry and Neil Renninger, is preparing to launch a pea‑based dairy alternative after raising $15 million in 2015. Using a proprietary process that isolates flavorless, white protein from split yellow peas, Ripple produces a high‑protein (8 g per serving) vegan milk blended with water, sunflower oil, stabilizers and flavoring in plain, sweetened, vanilla and chocolate varieties. The product is free of common allergens (soy, nuts), gluten and GMOs, supplies about 45% of daily calcium, and the sweetened version contains roughly half the sugar of cow’s milk (though the added cane sugar differs nutritionally from milk’s natural sugars).

Founders emphasize environmental advantages: Ripple estimates its product uses roughly 96% less water than almond milk and 98.5% less than cow’s milk and claims a 93% smaller carbon footprint than traditional dairy—though current importation of French peas raises emissions and makes its footprint comparable to almond milk until U.S. sourcing ramps up later in 2016. The company is pursuing patents on its pea‑protein separation technology, which could enable other plant‑based products and expand ingredient options for manufacturers. Ripple plans an organic version and will debut in Bay Area stores and a national chain soon; potential extensions include pea‑based yogurts that could challenge existing dairy and plant‑based yogurt lines.

Thomas S. Monson, the 16th president and prophet of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, died at home in Salt Lake City at 10:01 p.m. at age 90. A lifelong Mormon from Salt Lake City, Monson served more than five decades in senior church leadership after being called as an apostle in 1963 at age 36, and led the church from February 2008 until his death. A World War II Navy veteran and business graduate, he combined administrative roles in church-owned enterprises with decades of ecclesiastical service.

Monson was widely remembered for a pastoral, personal style—frequent hospital and funeral visits, attention to individuals, and storytelling in sermons—and for making humanitarian service a hallmark of his presidency. His tenure saw major institutional initiatives: expansion of temple building and missionary programs, growth of membership worldwide, enlargement of welfare and disaster-relief efforts, the Perpetual Education Fund, and modernization measures (including greater transparency about church history and modest increases in women’s visibility in church settings). His October 2012 decision to lower the minimum missionary ages produced a historic surge in missionaries and was one of his signature actions.

His presidency also coincided with intense public scrutiny and controversy: the church’s prominent support for California’s Proposition 8 in 2008, a 2015 policy regarding same-sex couples and their children that drew widespread criticism, and ongoing debates over gender roles, race, and immigration. Under Monson the church later engaged in outreach to LGBT people, backed nondiscrimination protections in Utah while safeguarding religious liberties, and issued a forceful 2017 statement condemning white supremacy. He maintained ecumenical ties and often emphasized cooperation with other faiths.

Monson’s health had declined in later years; he reduced public appearances beginning in 2015. He was married in 1948 to Frances Beverly Johnson (who died in 2013); they had three children, eight grandchildren and 11 great-grandchildren. Russell M. Nelson, the longest-tenured apostle, is expected to succeed him following church protocol. Public viewing and funeral services were scheduled in Salt Lake City in January. Colleagues and observers described Monson as warm, approachable and devoted to individual ministering—a leader remembered more for personal compassion and charitable outreach than for public controversy.

The number 13 and Friday the 13th are widely considered unlucky, influencing behaviors like skipping floors, avoiding 13 guests at dinner, and postponing weddings or travel. Scientific evidence, however, does not support an inherent bad luck tied to the number. Researchers such as Igor Radun argue no data can prove a number is unlucky, and many studies have mixed, inconclusive, or misinterpreted results.

Notable research includes a 1993 British Medical Journal Christmas-spoof analysis that found fewer cars on the road but a higher hospital admission risk on Friday the 13th—yet its authors intended the piece as lighthearted and not rigorous. Later studies have disagreed on whether accidents increase on Friday the 13th and whether any sex differences exist; a 2004 BMC Public Health study found no increase in injury accidents for either men or women on that day. Analysts caution that much work focuses on statistical correlations without linking superstition-driven beliefs to behavior, even though such beliefs clearly change choices (e.g., people avoiding to drive, marry, or book venues on the date).

Anecdotal and cultural evidence shows real effects: many couples avoid marrying on Friday the 13th, prompting vendors to offer discounts to attract bookings; nightlife and hospitality businesses sometimes see reduced activity. Superstitions also influence settings—skipping 13th floors or seats—and popular culture and history have reinforced the fear (e.g., associations with the Last Supper, the 1307 arrests of the Knights Templar, famous triskaidekaphobic figures like Roosevelt). Conversely, some groups view 13 positively (pagans link it to the number of full moons).

Psychologists explain the persistence of the superstition by human tendency to notice confirmatory events and ignore non-events. Overall: there’s no scientific proof that 13 or Friday the 13th is intrinsically unlucky, but the belief has measurable social and economic effects because it changes people’s behavior.

Two sisters, Nazila Sharaf (35) and Lida Sharaf (33), who ran Universal Preschool in Livermore, have been charged with endangering infants by tightly swaddling them. Arrested the week before and arraigned in Alameda County Superior Court, each pleaded not guilty to three felony counts of child abuse and neglect and four misdemeanor counts, and were released after posting reduced bail of $340,000 each. A plea hearing is pending.

Police allege the sisters tightly bound seven infants (ages about 7–11 months), using heavy knots and sometimes covering infants’ faces with blankets, which restricted breathing and limb movement and put the babies at risk. Investigators say three of the affected infants had upper respiratory conditions, increasing the danger. A police statement also accused Nazila of carrying multiple infants by their arms, risking serious injury. Doctors who examined the children reportedly found no signs of injury related to the alleged abuse.

The Department of Social Services closed the facility on March 15 after an unannounced March 12 inspection found multiple licensing violations, including inappropriate swaddling, overcrowding, improper sleeping arrangements (infant in car seat and high chair), and an unvetted caregiver. State officials seek permanent revocation of the preschool’s license and have banned both women from working in state-licensed child care pending appeals. Lida previously operated a childcare center that was shut down in 2010 over a similar swaddling violation; at that time she relinquished license rights but continued working at the reopened center, which Nazila later licensed.

Both sisters maintain they did not intend to harm the children and contend their swaddling was not abusive. Family members told reporters both women are pregnant and were visibly distressed in court. The case prompted strong reactions from parents and child-advocacy supporters; about 30 parents of 19 infants were interviewed during the investigation.

Assailants rammed a van into Microsoft’s Greek headquarters in the Maroussi suburb of Athens in the pre-dawn hours of June 27, 2012, then ignited an incendiary device, police said. Three people were believed to have been in the vehicle; witnesses and police said at least two gunmen—reportedly armed with pistols and a machine gun—forced two security guards outside before reversing the van through the building’s front doors. The device, described as camping gas canisters and multiple gasoline containers, burned out the van and heavily damaged the office’s ground floor. No injuries were reported. Forensic teams examined the scene; the security guards were giving statements. Microsoft closed the office while assessing damage, which the fire brigade estimated at about €60,000. There was no immediate claim of responsibility and no warning call prior to the attack. Police cautioned it was too early to identify perpetrators; Greece has a history of small-scale anarchist and left-wing extremist attacks against banks, foreign firms and state symbols that have increased during the economic crisis and austerity unrest.

A series of lawsuits allege Johnson & Johnson’s talc-based baby powder can cause ovarian cancer. In Los Angeles, a judge overturned a $417 million jury verdict for Eva Echeverria—who had claimed long-term use of the powder led to her ovarian cancer—granting J&J a new trial after finding errors, jury misconduct, and that punitive damages were excessive and malice wasn’t proven. Echeverria’s lawyers plan to appeal.

Separately in Missouri, an appeals court vacated a $72 million verdict for Jacqueline Fox, finding Missouri courts lacked proper jurisdiction under a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that narrowed where plaintiffs may sue companies (stemming from the Bristol-Myers Squibb/Plavix decision). That decision casts doubt on many large Missouri awards: over 1,000 similar suits have been filed there, and several multimillion-dollar juries have ruled for plaintiffs, but J&J is appealing and argues its products are safe.

Background: Talc is widely used in consumer products; most major studies and health organizations find little or no link between cosmetic talc and ovarian cancer, though some smaller studies suggest a small association and the International Agency for Research on Cancer labels genital talc use “possibly carcinogenic.” The legal fights continue amid ongoing appeals and new trials.

Protesters in Durham, N.C., pulled down a nearly century-old Confederate soldier statue outside the old courthouse on the evening of Aug. 14, 2017, during a rally against racism sparked by the weekend’s violence in Charlottesville. Activists used a ladder and a rope to topple the 15-foot bronze monument—dedicated in 1924 “In memory of ‘the boys who wore the gray’”—and cheered as people kicked and posed with the crumpled statue. The crowd swelled to over 100 and included local groups such as the Triangle People’s Assembly, Workers World Party, Industrial Workers of the World, Democratic Socialists of America and antifa; speakers cited Charlottesville as motivation and urged removing Confederate symbols across the South.

Sheriff’s deputies and police watched and recorded the action but did not intervene; no arrests were reported. Protesters later blocked and walked along Main Street before dispersing peacefully after authorities ordered them to leave county property. Durham County officials said they understand the unrest and stressed civility; County leaders began researching the monument’s history and relevant state law.

Removal of Confederate monuments in North Carolina is constrained by a 2015 state law that prohibits taking down such “objects of remembrance” on public property without state approval and makes damaging public property a misdemeanor. Gov. Roy Cooper condemned the Charlottesville violence and urged that there is “a better way to remove these monuments.” Supporters of the Durham action said it would inspire similar removals elsewhere.

Thousands of Tunisians poured into Tunis on Friday, gathering especially outside the Interior Ministry on Avenue Bourguiba, celebrating what many saw as an impending victory after weeks of deadly unrest. Protesters — including many first-time demonstrators from relatively affluent, educated backgrounds and large numbers of young women without veils — blamed cronyism, corruption and high unemployment for the uprising. They targeted President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and his influential second wife, Leila Trabelsi, chanting “Ben Ali, out!” and accusing the ruling clan of seizing businesses across major sectors.

Media and social networks played a central role: protesters thanked Al Jazeera for sustained coverage and used the #sidibouzid Twitter feed (named for the town where a self-immolation sparked the unrest) to organize and share solidarity across the Arab world. The immediate flashpoint followed Ben Ali’s televised pledges — including firing his interior minister, promising investigations and new freedoms, cutting prices on staples and saying he would leave office in 2014 — which failed to appease crowds. Police response included tear gas and beatings by plainclothes officers, but on Friday many police held back, allowing thousands to converge on the ministry and even climb its roof.

The unrest has left scores dead (official and opposition counts differ) and many injured, deeply shaken the tourism sector, prompted evacuations and travel warnings, and triggered at least one diplomatic resignation. State news reported Ben Ali dismissed his government and planned early legislative elections in six months; protesters continued to demand his immediate removal and justice for those killed.

Greece’s stock market rebounded modestly on Tuesday after a record plunge on Monday, but banking shares continued to drag the main Athens index lower. Nineteen of the 25 blue-chip stocks rose and non-bank sectors saw strong gains—retail jumped over 11% and names like Aegean Airlines and OPAP gained—suggesting investors were picking up historically low valuations outside finance. Still, banks plunged about 29% and hit their 30% daily loss limit for the second day as lenders face urgent recapitalization needs after months of deposit outflows. That kept the benchmark .ATG down about 1.2% on the day.

Officials expected trading to calm in the coming days. Markets remain deeply depressed overall—levels roughly equal to 1990 and about 52% below last year’s highs—and Greek banks estimate they will need €10–25 billion in fresh capital. The economy is sliding back into recession, with the European Commission forecasting a 2–4% contraction this year, manufacturing at record lows and economic sentiment near a three-year low.

Greece is in bailout talks with EU partners and aimed to conclude an accord by Aug. 18; officials signaled progress but gave few details. There was little spillover to other European markets, as many investors have already reduced exposure to Greece and are focused on core markets.

For U.S. investors: most mutual funds have only tiny Greek exposure. Emerging-market funds that hold Greek stocks typically allocate about 0.5% to Greece; across all fund types the average is about 0.3–0.4%. International and emerging-market funds are the most likely to include Greek names; even some U.S.-focused categories (e.g., MLP funds) can hold Greek shipping or other stocks. Largest Greek listed companies include Coca‑Cola HBC, Hellenic Telecom and betting operator OPAP.

A German artist has sparked a local gold rush at Folkestone’s Outer Harbour beach by burying 30 24‑carat gold bars worth about £10,000 as a participatory artwork for the Folkestone Triennial. When low tide exposed the beach, more than 150 people arrived to dig; organisers have said finders may keep any bars they uncover. Curator Lewis Biggs and project producers Situations describe Folkestone Digs (by Michael Sailstorfer) as an experiment in public art and participation: mass digging will itself create temporary land art, and the work deliberately raises questions about value—whether a found bar is worth more as gold or as an artwork. To complicate searches, many metal washers were also buried to frustrate metal‑detector users. Sailstorfer is not present in town, wanting the piece to “unfold”; organisers expect varying responses from the public and note the work’s lasting uncertainty—no one will ever truly know if all the gold has been recovered. The project is part of the Triennial (30 Aug–2 Nov), which features over 20 commissioned artists including Yoko Ono and aims to use contemporary art to reimagine Folkestone’s future.

Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei sharply criticized President Donald Trump’s decision to decertify the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and warned that Tehran would “shred” the agreement if the U.S. formally tore it up. Speaking to students and on state media, Khamenei dismissed Trump’s remarks as “rants” and “whoppers,” accused the U.S. of deceit and meddling in the region, and said Iran would not be the first to violate the pact but would retaliate if Washington withdrew.

Khamenei urged European governments and companies—many of which have invested in Iran since the deal—to do more than verbally defend the accord and to resist any U.S. practical measures that would undermine it. He emphasized Europe’s economic stake in the agreement and called for concrete support rather than mere admonitions to Trump. His comments reflect Tehran’s hope that European commercial interests and diplomatic pressure can help preserve the deal as Congress considers possible reinstatement of sanctions after Trump’s decertification.
