A 51-year-old German tourist, identified as Oliver Park, died at Machu Picchu after slipping from a ledge while trying to pose for a mid‑leap photograph. According to witnesses and Peruvian officials, Park bypassed a security cordon and entered a restricted area near a cliff edge above the Inca citadel. He asked another visitor to take the photo, lost his balance as the camera was being handed over, fell onto a narrow ledge and continued about 130 feet (roughly 100 meters) into a ravine. Rescuers reached the scene about 90 minutes later; his body was recovered the next day and taken to a morgue in Cusco. Authorities and witnesses noted that park rangers had been warning visitors to keep back from dangerous edges; the death is the latest in a series of accidents linked to risky photo-taking and selfies at scenic sites worldwide. Machu Picchu, a UNESCO World Heritage site at about 8,000 feet altitude, has seen several previous tourist fatalities.

This document criticizes Washington Post columnist Richard Cohen for a passage in a column about GOP politics that portrays discomfort with interracial and same-sex families as a “conventional” view among cultural conservatives. The piece opens by urging Jeff Bezos, as the Post’s owner, to consider whether publishing such racist-tinged op-eds is good business in a majority-Black city. It then quotes Cohen’s paragraph about the GOP being “deeply troubled” by cultural changes and that “people with conventional views must repress a gag reflex” at New York mayor Bill de Blasio’s biracial family and wife’s past lesbianism.

The remainder of the document collects and amplifies reactions condemning Cohen: critics call him racist, out-of-touch, and a repeat offender on race issues; they mock his defenses and note his repeated pattern of provocative race-related columns. They argue his language (e.g., calling disgust at interracial marriage “conventional”) reveals latent prejudice and poor editorial oversight. Several commentators urge the Post to fire or retire him, and one pleads with Bezos to act. The original column’s broader context—analyzing Republican prospects in Iowa and the rise of hard-right Christian conservatives like Ted Cruz—is noted, but the controversy centers on Cohen’s racialized wording and the backlash it produced.

A 3-year-old girl in Lorain, Ohio, is in critical condition after being shot in the head Sunday morning by her 4-year-old brother who found a loaded .40-caliber handgun in a dresser. The children were playing alone in a bedroom around 10 a.m. when the boy obtained the gun and, police say, accidentally pulled the trigger. Responding officers found the girl in her father's arms; the boy was crying and repeatedly told officers he was sorry. The girl was flown to Rainbow Babies Children's Hospital. Investigators recovered the weapon and interviewed three other people who were in the house. The Lorain County prosecutor’s office is reviewing the case to decide whether charges will be filed.

This document examines the political dynamics of Obamacare in Arkansas and nationally, and reports President Obama’s announcement that roughly 7.1 million people enrolled through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces by the end of the initial enrollment period.

Key points:

- Arkansas presents both opportunity and risk for anti-Obamacare campaigns. The state’s rightward shift makes attacking Democrats easy, but its Republican-led legislature implemented a Medicaid “private option,” splitting conservative groups (Tea Party/AFP vs. business interests) and preventing Arkansas from joining the broader GOP rebellion against the law.

- Americans for Prosperity ran high‑spending ads in Arkansas portraying canceled plans under the ACA—even though the state had extended those plans until 2017—illustrating how political messaging can diverge from local policy realities.

- On April 1, President Obama announced in the Rose Garden that over 7 million Americans (7.1 million) had selected plans via federal and state marketplaces since Oct. 1, a milestone the administration had targeted and which exceeded revised projections despite early website failures on HealthCare.gov.

- The administration argued the number shows progress and asserted many opponents’ claims have been debunked; Obama declared the law “here to stay.” Yet officials acknowledged important unknowns: how many enrollees were previously uninsured, the age/health mix of enrollees (which affects premiums), and how many had paid premiums to finalize coverage.

- Reactions were sharply partisan: Democrats highlighted individual stories of new coverage and rising public support for the law, while Republicans (House leaders and Senate Minority Leader spokesmen) renewed vows to repeal, criticizing higher premiums, plan cancellations and Medicare cuts.

- The administration credited grassroots organizing, social media, celebrity outreach, and last‑minute signups for the surge. Polling at the time showed public opinion nearly evenly divided, with some improvement in support for the ACA compared with the previous fall.

Overall, the piece situates the enrollment milestone as a political and symbolic victory for the administration while underscoring unresolved implementation questions and the continuing partisan conflict—both nationally and within states like Arkansas.

Washington voters narrowly approved Referendum 74, upholding a state law legalizing same-sex marriage and making Washington the third state (with Maine and Maryland) to approve marriage equality by popular vote. With about three-quarters of ballots counted soon after the election, R-74 led roughly 52%–48%; opponents conceded the race. King County (Seattle) provided the decisive margin, giving the measure about two-thirds of its vote.

The law, passed earlier in the year and signed by Gov. Chris Gregoire, had been on hold pending the referendum. If certified, couples can begin applying for marriage licenses Dec. 6 and—after a three‑day waiting period—be legally married Dec. 9. The statute exempts religious organizations from being required to perform same‑sex marriages.

Supporters hailed the outcome as historic and a turning point for equality; organizers and high-profile donors (including Jeff Bezos, Bill Gates and Michael Bloomberg) heavily out‑funded opponents, with roughly $12 million raised by proponents versus $2.7 million by opponents. Preserve Marriage Washington expressed disappointment and said it would continue its advocacy.

The vote is part of a broader shift: before this election most states that allowed same‑sex marriage had done so via courts or legislatures; Washington, Maine and Maryland were the first states to approve it at the ballot box. The result also energized activists in neighboring states (e.g., Oregon) considering future efforts to overturn bans.

This morning some New York City polling places opened late after ballots and poll books were misdelivered. Election officials located and retrieved materials in some sites, others used affidavit (provisional) ballots, and some voters left. NYC requires poll workers to arrive at 5 a.m. to set up within the hour before opening; unlike many jurisdictions that permit pre–Election Day setup, the city keeps materials locked until Election Day citing security concerns about sites it does not control. Election expert Tammy Patrick says many jurisdictions set up beforehand (sometimes the night before) which helps catch misdeliveries and other problems, and that security can be preserved with tamper-evident seals and logs.

Separately, many news organizations have formed unprecedented collaborative efforts to monitor and report voting problems and debunk misinformation on Election Day. The largest, Electionland, links over 400 newsrooms (led by ProPublica with partners including USA Today and the New York Times) to aggregate tips from social media and a national hotline into a shared newsroom for real-time leads on long lines, voter intimidation, equipment failures and hoaxes. Regional teams, journalism students and national desks triage tips for local follow-ups; participating outlets say the collaboration helps under-resourced local newsrooms and improves accuracy on a high-stakes day.

Other initiatives include Votecastr, which will publish near real-time turnout and precinct-level projections from selected battlegrounds to surface potential voting issues. Major networks are also dedicating staff to monitor cyber and voting irregularities, and fact-checking organizations like Snopes are deploying teams to counter internet hoaxes. Organizers acknowledge risks: some outlets have declined to join, and critics—particularly supporters of Donald Trump—may portray the cooperative coverage as partisan collusion. Still, proponents argue these joint efforts are vital to detect and report problems quickly and to preserve the integrity and clarity of Election Day coverage.

This document compiles several short items and focuses mainly on a University of Waterloo study about receptivity to pseudo-profound statements. Key points:

- Twitter and location: Users can add or delete location information on Tweets; more details are available from Twitter.
- Alexa Internet has been donating web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996; those data are added daily to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.
- Main item — study on pseudo-profound “bulls***”:
  - Researchers led by PhD candidate Gordon Pennycook published a paper titled “On the reception and detection of pseudo-profound bulls***,” which repeatedly uses that term and defines it as grand-sounding statements that imply meaning but contain little or no substantive content.
  - The researchers used a website that randomly generates noise-filled, aphorism-like sentences (examples: “Hidden meaning transforms unparalleled abstract beauty,” “This life is nothing short of an unveiling quantum leap of mythic rejuvenation”).
  - Nearly 300 participants rated sentences (pseudo-profound, genuine philosophical quotes, and mundane lines) for profundity on a 1–5 scale. While mundane sentences were recognized as such, many participants rated the fabricated pseudo-profound lines as similarly profound to actual spiritual/new-age authors’ tweets.
  - Analysis showed that people who rate these vague, buzzword-filled statements as profound tend to be less reflective, score lower on cognitive ability measures (verbal and fluid intelligence, numeracy), and are more prone to ontological confusion and conspiratorial thinking.
  - Such participants were also more likely to hold religious or paranormal beliefs and to endorse complementary and alternative medicine.
  - The authors conclude that susceptibility to pseudo-profound statements is a real psychological phenomenon related to specific cognitive and belief traits.

Summary:

President Barack Obama personally apologized to Doctors Without Borders (MSF) after a U.S. airstrike struck the organization’s trauma hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan, on October 3, killing dozens (MSF reports at least 22, including 12 staff) and wounding many more. Obama’s call to MSF president Dr. Joanne Liu expressed regret, condolences, and support for a U.S. Department of Defense investigation and joint NATO/Afghan probes; he also called Afghan President Ashraf Ghani. The U.S. military has acknowledged the hospital was mistakenly struck and said it will investigate, retrain forces on use of force, and hold anyone responsible accountable. U.S. accounts of the strike have shifted — from defending U.S. troops, to supporting Afghan forces under fire, to saying Afghan forces requested air support — prompting MSF to reject reliance on internal probes.

MSF is demanding a truly independent inquiry and has urged activation of the International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission (IHFFC), a Geneva Conventions body created in 1991 that has never been used. The commission can be convened at the request of a state party; however, neither the U.S. nor Afghanistan recognizes it, and as of the report no other signatory nation had stepped forward to request activation. MSF leaders say GPS coordinates of the hospital had been shared with authorities beforehand and call the attack an assault on the Geneva Conventions that could amount to a war crime. MSF described harrowing scenes as the hospital burned and staff treated wounded and each other; the group warns that failing to pursue an independent investigation would set a dangerous precedent for protection of medical facilities in conflict. The UN has condemned the strike but is awaiting the outcome of ongoing investigations before deciding on support for an independent probe.

An 8-year-old Dorchester boy, Martin Richard, was among the dead in the Boston Marathon finish-line bombings; his mother Denise and 7-year-old sister sustained serious injuries and remain hospitalized. Hundreds gathered for a vigil in Dorchester, and neighbors left flowers and candles outside the family’s home. Martin, a former student at Pope John Paul II Catholic Academy, had been at the race to watch his father.

Two other victims identified were 29-year-old Krystle Campbell of Medford, who had gone to the finish to photograph a friend, and a Boston University graduate student from China (name withheld at the family’s request). Families have described the shock, grief and, in one case, a traumatic hospital mix-up where Krystle Campbell’s parents were first told their daughter had survived before learning she had been killed.

City and federal officials, including Mayor Thomas Menino and the FBI, pledged increased security and an exhaustive investigation; Mayor Menino and others emphasized Boston’s resolve to heal. The city mobilized support services—mobile kitchens, aid at a downtown armory for displaced runners and volunteers—and national and international leaders, including President Obama and Pope Francis, offered condolences and praise for first responders. The sealed crime scene was reduced in size as transit and daily life began a cautious return to normal.

Republican Washington state representatives Matt Shea, David Taylor and Bob McCaslin introduced House Bill 1015, which would bar public stadium authorities, local governments and private operators leasing public facilities from prohibiting people with valid concealed pistol licenses from carrying concealed firearms in stadiums, arenas, convention centers and similar venues. The proposal would affect public-land venues such as Safeco Field (Seattle Mariners) and CenturyLink Field (home to the Seattle Seahawks and Seattle Sounders), where current facility policies can ban firearms even though state law does not currently make carrying into games a standalone crime.

The bill’s text would strip the ability of public stadium authorities, local governments and private operators of leased public facilities to enforce bans on concealed pistols by licensed carriers. Supporters frame it as expanding gun-rights protections; opponents point to safety concerns—alcohol, heated crowds and restricted entry policies (e.g., the NFL’s clear-bag rules)—that make introducing firearms into sports venues risky. The NFL told the Washington Post it opposes the measure and maintains a policy forbidding weapons in its stadiums. Observers expect strong pushback in heavily Democratic Washington state and foresee the league and other stakeholders using influence to resist the law if it advances.

Former Florida governor Jeb Bush published hundreds of thousands of emails from his time in office online as a transparency project—but failed to sufficiently protect senders’ private information. The archive, searchable by date and initially available as unredacted Outlook (.pst) files, exposed names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, medical details and, in many cases, Social Security numbers and other highly sensitive personal data from constituents, staff and third parties.

Coverage and reactions
- News outlets (The Verge, Daily Dot, Ars, AP) and independent auditors found widespread personally identifiable information (PII) across the files; an audit by Identity Finder reported over 12,000 people had their names, birthdates and SSNs exposed.
- Some emails included pleas about medical, legal or employment crises and explicitly requested privacy; others contained personnel actions and other sensitive government details.
- Critics argued Bush displayed poor judgment and a misunderstanding of reasonable privacy expectations: while Florida’s public records law is broad, certain information (notably Social Security numbers) is legally exempt from disclosure.
- Bush’s team and spokesman said the posted data replicated public records on file with the Florida Department of State and that the PAC wasn’t involved; after being alerted, Bush said the personal information would be removed.

Legal and practical issues
- Florida law broadly makes officials’ correspondence public under Sunshine laws, but SSNs are confidential and exempt; responsibility for preventing release typically rests with the legal custodian of records.
- Penalties for improper disclosure under state law are limited (a noncriminal infraction with small fines unless willful violation can be shown), complicating accountability.
- Because the raw .pst files were downloadable, once released the data spread quickly and was difficult to retract; other groups and researchers had already obtained and mirrored the files.

Outcome
- Bush’s site later removed the raw .pst files and his team reported redacting personal information they could locate, but copies and cached versions persisted, and researchers continued to find PII in the archive. The episode drew wide criticism as a tone-deaf privacy lapse that turned a transparency initiative into a substantial data-exposure incident.

Edgar Wright’s Baby Driver is a high-energy, music-driven summer heist thriller built around a knockout lead turn from Ansel Elgort and Wright’s trademark visual and rhythmic precision. Elgort plays “Baby,” a taciturn but brilliant Atlanta getaway driver who copes with chronic tinnitus by constantly listening to an eclectic soundtrack through his earbuds; the film stages many of its action beats and car chases in strict sync with the music. Baby works for the calculating crime boss Doc (Kevin Spacey) and ferries volatile crew members—Bats (Jamie Foxx), Griff (Jon Bernthal), Buddy (Jon Hamm) and Darling (Eiza González)—on heists he’d rather not be part of, all under the familiar “one last job” setup.

Baby’s desire to escape and start a new life with waitress Debora (Lily James) provides a tender counterpoint to the escalating violence in the third act. Wright’s direction emphasizes in-camera stunts, meticulous choreography, kinetic editing and playful references to genre touchstones (from Walter Hill to Reservoir Dogs and Point Break), producing chase sequences that feel immediate and original. Supporting performances (notably Hamm’s unhinged charm and Foxx’s menace) and a rousing soundtrack—from Queen and Simon & Garfunkel to Martha Reeves & the Vandellas—drive the film’s tone.

Critics praised Baby Driver as a dazzling, crowd-pleasing fusion of action, humor and music; it’s visually ambitious, rhythmically precise, and likely to be a major summer hit. Rated R, 113 minutes.

A Northern California man, Conal O’Rourke, says a year-long billing dispute with Comcast over his home TV and Internet service escalated into his being fired from his job at PricewaterhouseCoopers and has led him to threaten legal action. O’Rourke, a former corporate controllership professional, documented the dispute with invoices, a spreadsheet, photos and correspondence that he shared with Ars and his attorney.

Key points:
- O’Rourke moved to San Jose in 2013 and signed up for Comcast because AT&T U‑Verse wasn’t available in his building. Early bills were riddled with errors—his name was misspelled, promotional premium channels vanished after three months instead of nine, he was billed for three “additional HD outlets” ($26.25/month), and for cable boxes he says he never activated.
- Problems continued through late 2013 when his Internet performance degraded and, after a trip overseas, he returned to multiple unexpected boxes and a December bill for over $2,000 that included roughly $1,820 for equipment he insists he didn’t order (items listed included an “AnyRoom Hub” and a “Pace Host”).
- He returned the equipment to a Comcast store; an employee cleared those charges but failed to correct the underlying billing/accounting issues despite O’Rourke providing detailed records. Repeated calls and a sarcastic, unsent draft complaint he emailed to a store employee didn’t prompt resolution.
- Comcast reportedly referred his account to collections in early 2014. When O’Rourke escalated by contacting a Comcast controller’s office, a follow-up representative berated him on the phone. O’Rourke says his remarks about Comcast’s accounting and the regulator that oversees public-company accounting (“PCAOB”) triggered internal alarms at Comcast.
- O’Rourke claims the dispute ultimately led to his dismissal from PWC; he has hired a lawyer and demands a full retraction and apology, reinstatement, and $100,312.50 from Comcast by October 14 or he will sue.

The story is based on O’Rourke’s extensive documentation and interviews; the article republishes materials he provided.

A new analysis of nearly 275,000 calls to U.S. poison control centers from 2000–2012 (published in the Journal of Medical Toxicology) finds a large and growing number of exposures to dietary supplements—about one call every 24 minutes—with many incidents involving children and some causing serious harm.

Key findings
- Overall trend: From 2005–2012 the rate of supplement-related calls rose about 49%. In 2012 the rate was nearly 10 adverse exposures per 100,000 people.
- Volume and demographics: 274,998 exposures were reported from 2000–2012. Seventy percent involved children under age 6; 82.9% of all exposures were unintentional. Most calls involved acute exposures rather than chronic issues.
- Medical outcomes: 4.5% of exposures led to serious medical outcomes (mostly in young children). There were 34 deaths during the study period; notable contributors included ma huang (ephedra), homeopathic agents and yohimbe.
- Common symptoms: Rapid heart rate, vomiting, nausea, irritability, drowsiness and dizziness were frequently reported.

Products of greatest concern
- Homeopathic agents: Largest single cause of calls (36%); reports rose sharply between 2000–2010.
- Botanicals: Second largest category (31.9%). Two botanicals singled out as particularly dangerous:
  - Yohimbe (yohimbine) — a bark extract marketed for sexual enhancement. Of 1,818 yohimbe exposures, 512 were serious; children accounted for 78% of exposures (ages six or older were commonly affected). Reported effects include arrhythmias, seizures, kidney failure and at least one death. Even recommended doses can cause dizziness, anxiety, insomnia, hypertension and tachycardia.
  - Ma huang (ephedra) — linked to strokes and heart attacks; after the FDA ban in 2004, poisonings and deaths fell sharply.
- Energy products and hormonal supplements (e.g., androgen supplements) were also associated with a high proportion of serious outcomes.

Causes and recommendations
- Regulation gap: Because dietary supplements are not regulated like drugs, they do not require pre-market FDA approval or clinical trials. The authors and poison center directors point to inconsistent quality, mislabeling and contamination as problems that likely contribute to harm.
- Prevention advice: Most exposures are unintentional—often children finding supplements or caregivers confusing them with other medicines. Recommendations include child-resistant packaging, caregiver education, storing supplements out of children’s reach, and stronger FDA oversight (the authors call for regulation of yohimbe and certain energy products similar to the ephedra ban).

Expert perspectives
- Study authors and poison center leaders urge treating supplements like medicines—keep them out of children's reach and re-evaluate whether household storage is necessary.
- Industry group urges safe storage and consultation with clinicians; notes some categories (e.g., homeopathic products) are regulated differently.
- The FDA is reviewing the findings and continues to advise safe storage and reporting of adverse events.

Bottom line: Dietary supplements—especially certain botanicals (yohimbe, ma huang), energy products and some homeopathic agents—pose a growing poisoning risk to children and others. Lack of stringent pre-market regulation and inconsistent product quality contribute to these risks; experts recommend better packaging, public education and stronger regulatory action.

On March 22–25, 2014 a massive mudslide struck Oso, Washington, sweeping a mile‑wide swath of earth, trees and debris across homes and Highway 530. The disaster destroyed about 30 homes, left dozens more damaged, and produced extremely difficult search conditions—up to 20 feet of compacted mud, debris‑filled terrain likened to concrete or quicksand, and unstable slopes that at times forced crews to suspend work.

Rescue and recovery operations involved local fire and sheriff’s personnel, specially trained dogs, sonar and heat‑sensing equipment, hovercraft and aircraft, the Washington Army National Guard, FEMA teams and mortuary assistance. Despite intensive efforts, no survivors had been found in the debris after the first few hours. Dramatic footage released during the week shows a 4‑year‑old boy, Jacob Spillers, being evacuated by helicopter; Jacob was one of only two members of his immediate family known to have survived.

Officials confirmed at least 16 bodies recovered by Tuesday, later reporting they believed they had located eight additional bodies that could not safely be retrieved immediately. At various points authorities reported as many as 176 people unaccounted for, a number officials cautioned included duplicates and would likely be revised as names were verified. Several injured were treated at area hospitals, including a critically ill infant.

The slide’s estimated volume was roughly 175 million cubic feet. Experts warned the slope could continue to move and that more slides were possible, so monitoring equipment was planned. Investigators and residents noted prior warnings that parts of the neighborhood (Steelhead Haven) were slide‑prone because of steep gradients and soil conditions. President Obama signed an emergency declaration to provide federal assistance. The event ranks among the deadliest recent landslides in U.S. history.

PolitiFact named "death panels" its 2009 Lie of the Year after Sarah Palin’s August Facebook post claimed Democratic health-care legislation would create government boards to decide whether seniors and the disabled were "worthy" of care. Palin’s phrase — apparently original to her post — quickly spread through media, town hall meetings and political commentary, fueling fears that reforms would permit euthanasia or rationing of care.

The claim traced back to a controversial interpretation of a Medicare provision that would allow optional, reimbursed doctor visits to discuss advance directives and end-of-life wishes. Fact-checkers (including PolitiFact) rated stronger versions of the claim Pants on Fire, noting there were no mandatory counseling sessions or proposals to encourage euthanasia. Conservatives such as Betsy McCaughey and some GOP leaders amplified the charge; Democrats and policy experts called it false and inflammatory. Polling showed roughly 30% of the public believed "death panels" shortly after the claim surfaced, with belief split more by party than by age.

Commentators argued the claim succeeded politically because it tapped deep anxieties about government control and costly end-of-life care; critics said Democrats initially responded poorly, underestimating the emotional appeal. The controversy increased public discussion about advance directives and palliative care and energized opposition to reform, while also prompting Democrats to use the episode to accuse Republicans of grandstanding. Palin has repeatedly defended her wording, saying it was rhetorical and that she would not retract the criticism.

At a dress rehearsal for Donald Trump’s Jan. 20, 2017 inauguration, four U.S. Army band members served as stand-ins for the president-elect, first lady–elect, vice president-elect and his wife to rehearse the ceremony at the Capitol. Sgt. Maj. Greg Lowery portrayed Trump and Army Spc. Sara Corry portrayed Melania Trump; two other band members filled the Pence roles. Selected by command and auditioned, the stand-ins were chosen mainly for matching heights so escorts, microphone and lighting placement, camera angles and security movements could be practiced realistically. The Joint Task Force National Capital Region ran the rehearsal to find and fix any issues before the real event. Participants, all members of the Army’s “Pershing’s Own” band, said the work was serious and important for safety and the flawless broadcast of the peaceful transfer of power, though they also enjoyed dressing the part.

Boston police arrested 34-year-old homeless man Bodio Hutchinson in the unprovoked stabbing of two unarmed park rangers on Boston Common Tuesday afternoon, authorities said. A 46-year-old ranger sergeant with 20 years on the job was stabbed in the abdomen and underwent surgery at Massachusetts General Hospital with life‑threatening injuries; a 23‑year‑old rookie ranger suffered multiple, less serious wounds and was treated at Tufts Medical Center.

Police Commissioner William Evans said witnesses followed Hutchinson, provided cellphone video, and helped lead officers to him as he fled into the Public Garden. Officers recovered a knife from the nearby pond. Witnesses reported Hutchinson told officers to shoot him before they tackled and arrested him. Hutchinson has a “very violent, assaultive past history” and an open warrant for assault and battery on a police officer; he faces at least two counts of attempted murder plus outstanding assault and drug charges, Evans said.

City officials praised the public and police response, and Mayor Marty Walsh said the parks commissioner will review whether rangers need more equipment or personnel. The monument area was cordoned off as investigators processed the scene.

Gujarat, a western Indian state, has amended its Animal Preservation Act to impose the country's toughest penalties on cow slaughter and beef transport: life imprisonment for killing cows and up to 10 years' jail for transporting beef. Fines have been doubled from 50,000 to 100,000 rupees. State leaders framed the changes as reflecting cultural sentiment; the law takes effect after the governor’s approval.

The move comes against a backdrop of rising vigilante violence by hard-line Hindu groups who consider cows sacred. The report cites a recent case in which 15 men transporting dairy cows were stopped by a mob in Rajasthan; one victim, Pehlu Khan, died days later of his injuries. Video showed the men being beaten with sticks and iron rods; no arrests had been reported. Since Narendra Modi became prime minister in 2014, there has been increased pressure from Hindu nationalists to curb beef sales and a rise in attacks on people—often Muslims—accused of transporting or eating beef. Rumors about beef consumption have previously sparked deadly mob violence.

Facebook, Inc. builds social products for users, developers and advertisers: people use Facebook to connect, discover and share; developers use its platform to build apps and integrate websites; advertisers can target more than 900 million monthly active users by demographics and interests. In late 2013 Facebook completed a couple of small acquisitions (Mobile Technologies on Sept. 25 and Onavo in October) and Mail.Ru disposed of its remaining Facebook shares in September.

At a Menlo Park event Facebook unveiled Graph Search, a new search feature designed to index the company’s vast social content—photos, posts, games, places and people—and return precise answers from within a user’s social graph. Unlike traditional web search, which returns links ranked by PageRank, Graph Search prioritizes content shared by your network so you can find “games my friends play,” nearby places friends visited, people, etc. Facebook has partnered with Microsoft’s Bing to surface web results for queries that aren’t answered from Facebook’s own data. Graph Search positions Facebook to keep users inside its ecosystem and creates competitive pressure on recommendation and local services (e.g., Yelp, Foursquare) and on Google’s attempts to add social signals to web search. Bloomberg and WSJ covered the product unveiling live from Facebook’s campus.

A Good Samaritan who rescued a family from a rolled-over van in Elk Grove, California, received a $143 “first-responder” bill weeks later.

Derrick Deanda stopped at the September 2015 crash, smashed a window, and helped free a father and three children. He suffered a small cut and was checked by paramedics on scene, who gave him water. Months later the Cosumnes Community Services District mailed him a first-responder fee, prompting Deanda to complain publicly and plan an appeal.

Deputy Chief Mike McLaughlin confirmed the district billed him because anyone assessed by crews is treated as a patient, but called the case “unique” in his 28 years and said there is an appeals process and a desire to make it right. The district instituted the fee two years ago to help avoid fire station brownouts. Deanda says the charge could discourage people from helping at accidents.

Satellites and other observations show Antarctica’s ice loss is accelerating sharply, with about 200 billion tonnes now melting into the ocean each year (Imbie team), up roughly threefold since the previous assessment in 2012. Cumulatively the continent has lost ~2.7–3 trillion tonnes of ice since 1992, raising global sea level by ~7.5 mm (BBC) to 7.6 mm (AP). Current Antarctic melting contributes about 0.6 mm/yr to sea-level rise and, if trends continue, Antarctica alone could add on the order of 16 cm (~½ foot) to global sea level by 2100.

Most loss is concentrated in West Antarctica and the Antarctic Peninsula, driven mainly by warmer ocean waters undermining and thinning marine‑terminating glaciers and by the collapse of protective ice shelves that allowed faster ice flow. West Antarctica’s annual losses increased from ~53 to 159 billion tonnes (1992–2017); the Peninsula rose from ~7 to 33 billion tonnes; East Antarctica shows small net gains (~5 billion tonnes/yr) or modest loss depending on the period, but these do not offset losses elsewhere. Overall, Antarctic contribution is now comparable to or larger than Greenland’s.

The findings synthesize 24 independent satellite-based assessments plus airborne and ground data. Studies in Nature also examine related processes: bedrock uplift (isostatic rebound) can locally slow retreat by re-grounding ice fronts, but rebound is too slow and ocean warming will likely make this insufficient to halt ongoing retreat. Researchers link ocean warming and changing winds—tied to human-driven climate change—to much of the observed melting, and warn that rising seas will increase coastal flooding and storm impacts.

Arlington police are asking for public help to find a man who fatally shot 26-year-old Brittany Daniel of Fort Worth in an apparent road-rage incident on Interstate 30 near Cooper Street the evening of Jan. 27, 2016. Daniel was driving a co‑worker home between 6:45 and 7 p.m. when another vehicle pulled up alongside, its occupants exchanged words with Daniel’s car, and a passenger in the backseat rolled down a window and fired at least two shots. Daniel was struck, pulled over, and told her friend to call 911 but was pronounced dead about 7:30 p.m. at Texas Health Arlington Memorial Hospital. Authorities have no surveillance footage and only a limited description: the shooter is believed to be a light‑skinned Black or Hispanic man in his mid‑20s who was seated in the back of a small, dark four‑door sedan with tinted windows. Police ask anyone who was on I‑30 near Cooper Street between 6:45 and 7 p.m. or has other information to contact Detective Steve Griesbach at 817‑459‑5325; anonymous tips can be made to Tarrant County Crime Stoppers at 817‑469‑TIPS. Family and friends are grieving and urging anyone with information to come forward.

A France Telecom/Orange employee in Mérignac, near Bordeaux, has died by suicide after setting himself on fire in the company car park shortly after arriving at work. The 57-year-old, a 30‑year veteran and father of four, had reportedly been unhappy about multiple internal transfers. Staff and union representatives described colleagues as “overwhelmed” by the death.

The case comes amid a wider crisis: a wave of employee suicides and serious psychological distress at France Telecom that began in 2008. Reports and union counts have placed the number of suicides at more than 30–35, with labour inspectors’ April 2010 findings recording 19 deaths, 12 suicide attempts and eight severe depression or work‑cessation cases. Unions have blamed harsh restructuring, aggressive reassignment and unrealistic performance targets tied to the company’s transformation from a state agency into a private firm; management has disputed that the suicide rate is abnormal for a workforce of about 100,000.

In response to the crisis, former CEO Didier Lombard, six other executives and Orange (formerly France Telecom) face trial on charges of “moral harassment” (psychological harassment) for their alleged role in creating a hostile work environment. The accused deny wrongdoing; some have been placed under court supervision. Labour and union leaders say prosecutions should deter the use of “social violence” in management. (Help resources such as Samaritans were also noted for anyone in distress.)

Former Indiana University student John (Phillip) Enochs, 21, pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery with moderate bodily injury in June 2016 after initially being charged with two counts of rape stemming from alleged assaults at the Delta Tau Delta fraternity house in Bloomington. As part of a plea deal, the rape charges were dismissed and Enochs was sentenced to one year of probation and served one day in jail.

According to court documents, the most recent incident occurred in April 2015. The victim said she had been drinking, went into the fraternity house bathroom, and next remembered being naked in a private room with an unknown man having sex; she told police she repeatedly told him to stop and was held down, and later sustained a laceration to her genitals. Security video reportedly shows Enochs entering the room with the woman and her leaving about 24 minutes later.

During the investigation, police identified a similar alleged attack from 2013. DNA evidence, victim identification and witness statements led to Enochs’s arrest in September 2015. The reduced sentence and dismissal of felony rape charges prompted public criticism and comparisons to other high-profile lenient sexual-assault sentences; social media users raised concerns about preferential treatment. Indiana University said Enochs is no longer a student, and the university has faced scrutiny over its handling of campus sexual-assault cases, including multiple open Title IX complaints.

This illustrated article traces how NASA dealt with the basic human need to urinate and defecate during early crewed spaceflights, from Mercury through Apollo, explaining makeshift solutions, design changes and the practical realities aboard tiny capsules and lunar modules.

Key points:
- Early oversight: Mercury capsules and suits were high-tech but initially didn’t include dedicated waste systems because flights were planned to be short. Astronauts often waited many hours prelaunch, exposing the flaw.
- First improvisations: Alan Shepard, facing a long wait before his 15-minute Freedom 7 flight, relieved himself in his suit after biomed sensors were turned off. Gus Grissom flew with an improvised system—a garter belt and condom connected to a bag—prompting development of better urine collection devices.
- Mercury solutions: External urine-collection tubes leading to one-way bags became standard; on later Mercury flights multiple bags and a pump-out option were added for longer missions and sample return.
- Gemini introduced fecal challenges: Because Gemini aimed for multi-day and two-week flights, planners added a fecal containment system—adhesive-rim tube bags with moisture-absorbing crystals. Using them was awkward, unpleasant, and sometimes avoided; recovery crews noted offensive odors after long missions.
- Apollo arrangements and lunar surface: Apollo’s larger spacecraft offered very limited privacy. For moonwalks, astronauts wore urine collection bags and “maximum absorbency garments” (diapers) under their suits. Diapers were intended to be a last resort; cleaning was difficult in the LM, so astronauts generally avoided using them, though accidents (e.g., Charlie Duke’s detached collection system on Apollo 16) did occur.
- Evolution: Long-duration missions (and mixed-gender crews) later required improved, more private and practical toilets aboard stations like Mir and the International Space Station. The story underscores that many crucial spacecraft systems grew from pragmatic fixes to uncomfortable but necessary human realities.

Overall, the article highlights how an unglamorous, overlooked problem—the need to manage human waste in microgravity—was solved incrementally by improvisation, engineering adaptations, and hard-earned operational lessons as missions grew longer and more complex.

Pope Francis arrived in Seoul on Aug. 14, 2014, beginning a five-day visit to South Korea — his first trip to Asia as pope and the first papal visit to the country in 25 years. The visit aims to highlight the growing Korean Church, promote evangelization in Asia and press for reconciliation on the divided Korean Peninsula.

Key events and messages
- In his opening speech to President Park Geun-hye and officials the pope urged diplomacy, dialogue, forgiveness and mutual respect instead of “fruitless criticisms” and “displays of force,” calling Korea’s quest for peace important for regional and global stability. He delivered several speeches in English to accommodate Asian audiences.
- He will beatify 124 Korean martyrs (18th–19th century) and celebrate a reconciliation Mass at Myeong-dong Cathedral. He also planned to participate in Asian Youth Day and meet families of Sewol ferry victims.
- Francis met bishops, greeted relatives of ferry victims and descendants of martyrs on arrival, and sent a rare airborne telegram to Chinese President Xi Jinping as his plane passed through Chinese airspace — a small sign of warming Vatican–China ties despite no formal diplomatic relations.

Security and North Korea
- North Korea conducted multiple short-range rocket/artillery firings off its east coast around the pope’s arrival (three before and two after he landed). Neither the pope nor President Park publicly referenced the launches, but Francis’ appeal for dialogue and avoidance of shows of force was framed against the backdrop of these tensions.
- Organizers had invited a delegation of North Korean Catholics to attend the pope’s Mass for peace, but North Korea declined to participate. There are no Vatican-sanctioned institutions or resident priests in North Korea, and the regime severely restricts religious freedom.

Context and reception
- South Korea’s Catholic Church is growing and seen as a model for evangelization in Asia; Catholics make up over 10% of South Korea’s population (about 5.4 million). The visit generated broad public interest and expectations that it might help heal national traumas (Sewol ferry, recent deaths of young soldiers) and inspire young people.
- President Park welcomed the pope’s visit as a source of healing for the nation’s “long wounds of division.” The beatification ceremony at Gwanghwamun Square could draw up to a million attendees.

Broader follow-up
- The trip is part of the Vatican’s outreach in Asia; Francis planned further visits to Sri Lanka and the Philippines in January. His use of Chinese airspace and the telegram to Beijing were noted as modest steps toward improved Vatican–China relations.

General Mills has voluntarily recalled about 10 million pounds of flour — including select lots of Gold Medal, Gold Medal Wondra and Signature Kitchens (private-label) products — after a multi-state outbreak of E. coli O121 sickened 38 people across 20 states between Dec. 21, 2015 and May 3, 2016. The CDC found about half of those ill reported making something homemade with flour before becoming sick, and some reported using a General Mills brand; roughly 10 people were hospitalized and no deaths have been reported. Three Minnesota cases (two adults and a child) recovered without hospitalization.

Although E. coli O121 has not been detected in General Mills’ flour products or its manufacturing facility and the company has received no direct consumer illness reports, the company said it recalled the affected UPCs and lot codes out of an “abundance of caution.” The recall covers six Gold Medal SKUs, two Signature Kitchens SKUs and one Gold Medal Wondra SKU; the notice lists UPCs and “better if used by” dates to identify recalled packages. Affected retailers include Safeway, Albertsons, Jewel, Shaws, Vons, United, Randalls and Acme. General Mills produced much of the flour in its Kansas City plant.

General Mills urges consumers not to eat raw dough or batter, to thoroughly wash hands, surfaces and utensils after contact with raw flour or dough, and to contact a physician and local health authorities if they suspect illness. Consumers can check product details at generalmills.com/flour or call 1-800-230-8103.

Context: E. coli O121 can cause bloody diarrhea and dehydration and is especially dangerous for the elderly, young children, pregnant women and immunocompromised people. Flour is not routinely heat-treated because that can affect baking performance; heat-treated flour is used in some ready-to-bake products. The recall follows General Mills’ October recall of gluten-free Cheerios products and coincides with unrelated recalls announced the same day by other companies for different contaminants.

A class-action lawsuit claimed Taco Bell’s seasoned beef is only 36% meat and largely made of non‑meat “extenders.” Taco Bell President and Chief Concept Officer Greg Creed strongly denied the suit, calling it bogus and inaccurate, and said the company will pursue legal action for false statements. Taco Bell’s published ingredient breakdown says the seasoned beef is 88% USDA‑inspected quality beef and 12% seasonings, water and other ingredients: about 3–5% water, 3–5% spices (salt, chili pepper, onion powder, tomato powder, sugar, garlic powder, cocoa powder, a proprietary Mexican spice blend and natural flavors) and 3–5% oats, starch, sugar, yeast, citric acid and similar components that contribute taste, texture and moisture. Creed emphasized there are no “extenders” used to add volume and compared the seasoning process to how home cooks add spices to chili or meatloaf.

The piece also places this controversy in a wider context of “fake” or misleading food ingredients uncovered across the food industry—examples include blueberry flavorings that aren’t real fruit, McDonald’s oatmeal using a maple‑related extract instead of real maple syrup (with Vermont stores offering real syrup on request), processed chicken products that include many parts beyond muscle, and some chocolate bars containing low percentages of actual chocolate. The article notes that while such revelations can be disconcerting, ingredient information is increasingly easy to find online, leaving consumers to decide what they’re comfortable eating.

Summary:

The Tamiment Library Economic and Social Justice Web Collection, started in 2010, archives webpages from left‑leaning and progressive organizations focused on economic and social justice issues—such as corporate accountability, immigrant rights, unemployment, homelessness, urban justice, healthcare reform and wealth redistribution. It places special emphasis on the Occupy Wall Street movement (begun September 2011), capturing sites for its working groups and related projects. The archived sites contain diverse media (YouTube, PDFs, blogs, petitions, news feeds, audio, etc.) that document activities, events and advocacy. Most sites are crawled quarterly, with more frequent snapshots during rapid updates; password‑protected or robot‑blocked content is not archived, and linked pages are sometimes missed.

Also included is a posting (Aug 27, 2016) promoting Micah White’s book The End of Protest. White—co‑creator of Occupy Wall Street and director of an activist consultancy—argues that traditional protest tactics have become ineffective and calls for tactical innovation. Drawing on Occupy and other uprisings, he outlines a theory of revolution, eight principles for tactical innovation, and three revolutionary scenarios for future movements. He frames Occupy as a “constructive failure” that points a way forward toward long‑term spiritual, political and social revolutions, and contends movements must think in centuries rather than days. The piece highlights White’s activist credentials and public profile.

The Road, adapted from Cormac McCarthy’s Pulitzer-winning novel, is a visually powerful but emotionally uneven film about a father (Viggo Mortensen) and his young son (Kodi Smit-McPhee) traveling through a bleak, post-apocalyptic America. Director John Hillcoat and screenwriter Joe Penhall faithfully render the story’s ruined landscapes, the constant threat of cannibalistic survivors, and small acts of kindness that stand in for hope — aided by strong production design, costumes, and Mortensen/Smit-McPhee’s convincing performances. Flashbacks with Charlize Theron and a haunting turn from Robert Duvall add texture.

Critics praise the film’s disturbing realism and its respect for McCarthy’s minimalism, but argue it fails to capture the novel’s transcendent emotional core. Without McCarthy’s spare, poetic prose, the movie often feels like an endurance test: effective at horrification and atmosphere but short on the spiritual or metaphoric resonance that made the book so powerful. Some reviewers also fault Hillcoat for playing too safely—suggesting that a bolder, more stylized approach might have better conveyed the novel’s deeper forces—while acknowledging the film as a serious, admirable adaptation rather than a wholly successful one. Running time 119 minutes; Rated R.

The Senate Judiciary Committee moved forward with a scheduled Friday morning vote on Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court nomination after a highly charged, day‑long hearing that featured emotional testimony from both Kavanaugh and his accuser, Dr. Christine Blasey Ford. Key Republican senators remained undecided late Thursday, leaving the outcome uncertain: Republicans hold a narrow 51–49 Senate majority and can afford to lose only one vote to advance the nomination. Sen. Jeff Flake said there was “more doubt than certainty,” while GOP leaders including Mitch McConnell and Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley said the committee vote would proceed as planned. Tennessee Sen. Bob Corker announced his support Thursday night.

Ford testified that Kavanaugh sexually assaulted her in high school and said she was “100%” certain; Kavanaugh likewise insisted he was “100%” innocent, forcefully rejecting the allegations as a political smear. The hearing focused intense attention on a small group of pivotal senators — notably Flake, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski — who sought more information or an FBI inquiry before deciding how to vote. Collins and Murkowski have voiced particular concern; Murkowski said she would take time to consider the testimony.

The White House and Trump reacted strongly in Kavanaugh’s favor. President Trump praised Kavanaugh’s combative defense on Twitter and aides said they were heartened by his aggressive, unapologetic approach, though some officials worried that Republican questioning and the GOP-hired prosecutor Rachel Mitchell’s performance had failed to blunt Ford’s credibility. Administration figures also noted that Ford’s testimony had appeared sincere and troubling to many viewers, but emphasized that the critical audience was the handful of undecided Republican senators. By evening, the White House mood had improved, though the nomination’s path to confirmation remained uncertain.

Summary:

Recent coverage has focused on efforts to identify Bitcoin’s pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto and strong evidence pointing to Australian computer scientist and entrepreneur Craig Steven Wright. A UCLA professor’s public nomination of Nakamoto for the Nobel Prize in Economics highlighted a separate issue: Nobel rules bar public disclosure of nominations for 50 years and the prize cannot be awarded anonymously or posthumously, so Nakamoto would be ineligible unless he reveals a verified identity.

WIRED and other outlets obtained leaked documents, blog posts, emails and corporate records that together suggest Wright could be Nakamoto or is running an elaborate, long‑planned hoax. Key links include: pre‑2009 blog posts by Wright referencing an upcoming “cryptocurrency paper” and “triple entry accounting”; a PGP key tied to an address similar to Satoshi’s; a January 2009 blog entry about Bitcoin’s beta; leaked emails describing plans for a P2P distributed ledger and investments in computing hardware; and a purported “Tulip Trust” PDF (signed by the late Dave Kleiman) assigning 1.1 million bitcoins — the same massive early‑mined stash historically attributed to Satoshi. Public records also show Wright invested large bitcoin sums in startups and built major supercomputing clusters used for mining and research.

Counterarguments remain: some incriminating blog content appears to have been edited or added after 2013, leaked documents could be forged, and certain academic and supercomputing claims have shown inconsistencies. After WIRED contacted him, Wright replied from anonymized accounts with cryptic messages but declined to confirm identity; he has publicly signaled ambivalence about recognition and defended his privacy. Authorities later raided Wright’s home in Australia in a tax investigation unrelated, officials say, to the Bitcoin reports.

In short, reporting has produced the strongest circumstantial case yet that Craig Wright is—or is trying to present himself as—Satoshi Nakamoto, but definitive proof is lacking and the possibility of an elaborate hoax remains. The stakes are high: a confirmed Satoshi identity (and control of the large coin holdings) could have major market and historical implications for Bitcoin.

U.S. District Judge Bernard Friedman struck down Michigan’s constitutional ban on same-sex marriage and its prohibition on same-sex adoption, ruling the 2004 Marriage Amendment violates equal protection. Friedman’s 31‑page opinion concluded voter disapproval and appeals to “traditional” marriage cannot override constitutional rights; he also found the state’s expert testimony weak and the plaintiffs’ evidence credible. He did not issue an immediate stay.

The ruling prompted some Michigan counties (Washtenaw, Oakland, Muskegon and others) to open clerks’ offices to issue marriage licenses—Washtenaw even opened for a limited Saturday session with reduced fees and residency restrictions—while Attorney General Bill Schuette immediately sought an emergency stay from the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to halt marriages pending appeal. Schuette vowed to defend the voter-approved amendment; opponents called the decision illegitimate.

The case was brought by Hazel Park nurses April DeBoer and Jayne Rowse, who sought the ability to marry and for each to adopt the couple’s special-needs children. They and supporters celebrated the decision as a major victory for families and equality, while religious and conservative groups criticized it. The ruling adds Michigan to the growing number of states where federal courts have invalidated same-sex marriage bans, contributing to a nationwide legal patchwork many expect the U.S. Supreme Court to resolve.

At least six to seven people were killed and dozens wounded after heavy fighting erupted near Tripoli’s international airport on July 13, as rival militias battled for control of the facility. Gunfire, explosions and anti-aircraft volleys were reported; thick black smoke and rocket strikes were visible from the city. Civil aviation authorities ordered the airport closed for three days and several international carriers—including EgyptAir, British Airways and Turkish Airlines—canceled flights; hundreds of passengers were stranded. The UN temporarily relocated some international staff because of the violence.

Fighting pitted Zintan forces, which have guarded the airport since Gadhafi’s fall, against militias from Misrata and allied units claiming to free the airport for government control. The central government condemned the attackers as acting without legal authority. Reports gave differing casualty totals (six to seven dead, 25–36 wounded).

The clashes underscore persistent instability in post‑Gadhafi Libya, where powerful militias often fill security roles while competing for resources and influence. The violence came amid political uncertainty following disputed parliamentary elections and follows broader security and economic strains—kidnappings and factional fighting in other regions, and sharply reduced oil production that has deepened a national budget crisis.

The document is a pair of strongly contrasting opinion pieces about LeBron James’ prime-time ESPN special announcing his free-agent decision.

One piece is a blistering personal attack: the writer calls James a self-aggrandizing “villain” for turning his team choice into an hour-long spectacle, accusing him and ESPN of exploiting viewers and using charity as cover for self-promotion. The author compares James unfavorably to Kevin Durant’s low-key extension, condemns the prolonged drama of his free agency as manipulative and disrespectful to Cleveland fans, and portrays James as a salesman who values adulation more than basketball. The column uses profanity and hyperbole to emphasize disgust with James and ESPN’s complicity.

The second piece is more measured and media-focused. It acknowledges some criticism that an ESPN special may be disproportionate given James’ lack of an NBA championship, but argues the event reflects enormous public interest and is therefore defensible as news programming. The writer criticizes James’ team for not better leveraging new-media marketing to build the drama (e.g., using his website, video diaries, Twitter, fan voting) and suggests the production could have been even bigger with smarter promotion. The column frames the show as a natural outcome of intense public appetite for a star who aspires to Michael Jordan–level status and defends media coverage as responding to audience demand.

Together, the pieces capture two dominant reactions to “The Decision”: visceral backlash against the perceived self-promotion and media enablement, and a pragmatic view that, whether one approves or not, the spectacle is a market-driven event media outlets are justified in covering.

Oprah Winfrey said she’s “sorry” a media frenzy erupted after she described an incident in Zurich in which a sales clerk at an upscale boutique allegedly refused to show her a luxury handbag because she assumed Winfrey couldn’t afford it. On the red carpet at the Los Angeles premiere of Lee Daniels’ The Butler, Winfrey reiterated that the episode was “just an incident in Switzerland,” that she had not named the store deliberately, and that she was using it as an example of being judged by appearance. Swiss tourism officials and the boutique owner issued apologies, which Winfrey said were unnecessary because the incident involved one person, not the whole country.

The boutique’s sales assistant has strongly denied Winfrey’s account. Speaking anonymously to Swiss media, she said she offered to show similar bags, explained price differences, and even asked if Winfrey wanted to see the expensive crocodile-leather piece. The assistant called the racism claim “absurd,” said she treats all customers politely, and described feeling “powerless” after the accusations. The dispute has drawn widespread attention and sparking debate over what happened during Winfrey’s short visit to the store.

This document compares and promotes several pelvic‑floor training products and explains why pelvic‑floor health matters.

Key points about pelvic floor importance
- Pelvic floor muscles support bladder and bowel control, pregnancy and postpartum recovery, pelvic stability and lower‑back health, and sexual function. Weakness can cause incontinence, pain, reduced sexual sensation, and other problems. Strengthening these muscles with Kegel exercises can prevent or improve many issues without surgery.

kGoal (by Minna Life)
- Product: kGoal is a smart Kegel trainer consisting of a squeezable vaginal insert with sensors and vibration motors plus a smartphone app. The device measures squeeze force, duration, and endurance and provides real‑time multimodal biofeedback (touch, visual, audio).
- Features: tailored exercise plans developed with physical therapists and doctors, performance tracking over time, adjustable fit via a vented squishy pillow, splash resistance, USB charging, and medical‑grade silicone construction. Many functions work without the app; app requires Bluetooth Low Energy (iPhone 4S+/iPad3+; Android planned). Color will be decided by backers.
- Benefits: helps users learn correct pelvic contractions (important because ~30% of women contract wrong muscles), improves adherence by making training engaging (games planned), and enables tracking for users and clinicians.
- Commercial details: launched via Kickstarter to get user feedback and cover manufacturing costs; manufacturing ramp in August, first shipments targeted for December; US delivery included in pledges, $25 international shipping plus local duties. Pre‑sales reportedly sold out; expected retail price $125 at December launch.
- Team/testimonials: developed by Minna Life (San Francisco startup). Positive early user quotes and endorsement from pelvic‑floor PT Liz Miracle emphasize real‑time tactile feedback and fit for varied anatomies.

Private Gym (The Private Gym, LLC)
- Product/Program: An FDA‑registered exercise program for men consisting of an eight‑week interactive DVD training (four weeks basic Kegels, then four weeks resistance training) plus patented resistance equipment with silicone‑covered magnetic weights that fit around the erect penis to provide measurable resistance.
- Claims/Benefits: strengthens pelvic muscles to improve erection rigidity, reduce premature ejaculation, heighten orgasms, support prostate health, and improve urinary control; may help prevent erectile dysfunction. Cites studies (e.g., Dorey 2005) reporting significant improvements from pelvic floor training in men.
- Background: Developed with urologists and pelvic‑floor experts including Dr. Andrew Siegel and Professor Grace Dorey. Product sold through privategym.com.

Context and expert perspective
- Pelvic‑floor training for women is widely recommended (Mayo Clinic) though evidence varies on precise protocols and outcomes; experts find apps and biofeedback promising but call for long‑term studies to confirm benefits.
- The broader trend: wearable and connected devices (like Fitbit) are expanding into pelvic health, offering objective tracking and guided programs to improve adherence and outcomes.

Overall takeaway
- The document positions kGoal as a modern, app‑driven, biofeedback device addressing gaps in pelvic‑floor training for women, complementing other programs like Private Gym for men. Both approaches emphasize that targeted pelvic muscle training can improve urinary and sexual health, and new technology aims to increase accuracy, motivation, and measurable results.

Search teams hunting AirAsia Flight QZ8501, which crashed into the Java Sea on Dec. 28 with 162 people aboard, have detected large wreckage on the seabed and recovered debris and bodies, Indonesian officials said. Using sonar, ships located four large objects — the biggest about 18 m long and 5.4 m wide — plus smaller scattered pieces and an oil slick; visibility and strong currents have so far prevented clear ROV imagery or immediate diver inspection. About 30 bodies have been recovered; authorities say more are unlikely to be found floating after nearly a week, though some remains and debris have washed up on beaches.

Weather is believed to have been a major factor. Indonesia’s meteorological agency reported that the aircraft likely encountered severe conditions and possible engine icing; radar suggests the jet made an unusually steep climb before contact was lost. Investigators are probing whether appropriate weather procedures were followed.

Separately, Indonesia’s Transport Ministry suspended AirAsia Indonesia’s Surabaya–Singapore flights and opened a review after finding the carrier was not authorized to operate that route on Sundays — the day of the accident. AirAsia Indonesia said it will cooperate with authorities. The black boxes have not yet been recovered; locating intact wreckage and recorders remains the priority for determining the cause. International search assets, including ships with sonar, ROVs and divers from multiple countries, are assisting the recovery and investigation.

The Coast Guard has ordered Taylor Energy to implement a new containment plan and hire a contractor to stop chronic oil sheens from a damaged platform off southeast Louisiana, threatening fines up to $40,000 per day for noncompliance. New federal estimates put the leak from the Taylor Energy MC-20 “Saratoga” site at roughly 10,500–29,000 gallons per day—5 to 13 times higher than last year’s estimates—potentially making it one of North America’s largest, longest-running spills. Taylor disputes the figures and the source of the sheens; company scientists contend the visible oil comes from oil-saturated seafloor sediment and drilling fluids disturbed at the site, not from pressurized, leaking wells. Taylor says full containment could cost upward of $1 billion and calls the new estimates “ridiculous” and based on flawed science; it has also litigated over $432 million remaining in a trust set up for response costs.

Background: Taylor’s 550-foot platform was destroyed by Hurricane Ivan in 2004, triggering a mudslide that buried a cluster of 28 wells. Taylor plugged some wells and installed containment domes, but environmental groups and remote-sensing analyses have for years documented persistent sheens—Skytruth once mapped a sheen more than 20 miles long. Federal scrutiny increased in 2016; prior government estimates (2017) ranged from 42 to 2,300 gallons per day, but this year’s government assessment cited the much larger daily rates and warned of “hundreds of barrels per day” at worst.

Dispute and implications: Taylor and its hired scientists point to sediment contamination and presence of drilling fluid in surface sheen samples as evidence the oil is seafloor-sourced and that disturbing the bottom (e.g., for cleanup) can itself trigger sheens. Independent advocates and regulators say the prolonged leak has likely caused environmental harm that has been understudied; at the high end, the cumulative release over 14 years could approach the scale of some major spills. The Coast Guard has not publicly detailed how it calculated the new estimate pending review. The case has broader resonance with ongoing Gulf spill response and enforcement efforts, including past large incidents like Deepwater Horizon.

Kathleen Dawn “Kat” West, 42, a Calera, Alabama mother and wife, was found partially nude and dead near her home early Saturday, Jan. 13. Calera police have classified the case as a homicide but have not released the cause of death or identified suspects; no arrests have been made. Neighbors reported the body was discovered in the roadway across from the Wests’ house; a witness said she was wearing only a sports bra and bleeding from the head, with a cell phone and a green liquor bottle nearby, though police have not confirmed those details.

West lived with her husband and their 12-year-old daughter in a house they built in 2015. Family members have largely remained private; her mother, Nancy Martin, issued a public plea asking for prayers and donations to help pay for funeral services. Neighbors described the family as private and Calera as a quiet community that rarely sees violent crime.

Outside of her family life, West maintained an active online presence under the name “Kitty Kat West,” including Twitter and Instagram accounts and a subscription adult site charging $15.99/month. Her online activities and images have become a focus of local and national coverage and intense scrutiny on social media.

Private Facebook groups and other online amateur “investigators” have formed to speculate about the killing, circulating theories that range from a deranged subscriber or stalker to involvement by her husband. Media coverage and widespread social-media conjecture have amplified lurid details of her online persona; police say much of the circulated information and speculation has hindered the investigation. Observers and some reporters caution that there is currently no public evidence linking West’s online activity to her death, and that conjecture risks victim-blaming and interfering with official inquiries.

Local outlets and wire services have reported the story, noting West’s dual public identities—presenting as a stay-at-home mom on Facebook while marketing adult content elsewhere—and community reaction to the shock of a homicide in a usually tranquil town. Her family is seeking funds for funeral expenses while the investigation remains ongoing.

The U.S. handed over Ali Mussa Daqduq, the last detainee in Iraq, to Iraqi authorities as American forces withdraw, the White House said. Daqduq, accused of organizing a 2007 Karbala raid that killed five U.S. soldiers and linked to Hezbollah, had been the subject of months-long U.S. efforts to keep him in U.S. custody or transfer him to a military commission or Guantánamo. Under the 2008 U.S.–Iraq security agreement, remaining detainees must be returned to Iraqi custody, and Baghdad refused U.S. requests to extradite him. National Security Council spokesman Tommy Vietor said the administration sought alternatives and received Iraqi assurances that Daqduq will be tried. Republican senators — including John McCain, Lindsey Graham, Joe Lieberman and Mitch McConnell — sharply criticized the transfer, calling it “disgraceful” and warning that Iraq might release Daqduq for political reasons, potentially allowing him to rejoin anti-U.S. forces.

Police in parts of England are warning the public about a growing craze of people dressing as clowns to frighten others, with multiple recent sightings and disturbing incidents across Greater Manchester, Cheshire and elsewhere.

Greater Manchester Police said they received a call after children were frightened by people in clown masks in Stretford, including reports of a white car whose occupants chased girls on Park Road. The Manchester Evening News and social media posts describe frightened and upset children and parents, with commenters urging people to stop the prank because it is not funny and harms vulnerable youngsters.

Cheshire police said they have had a small number of reports tied to the trend—widely publicized in the U.S.—and warned that deliberately scaring people, especially children and vulnerable people, is unacceptable and could be an offence. They urged anyone witnessing suspicious activity or who has been intimidated to contact them on 101.

Separately, national reports say incidents have occurred elsewhere in England: Gloucestershire police logged six reports of clowns acting suspiciously or threateningly (no arrests because suspects left before police arrived), and officers reported a masked man with a knife threatening children in Durham and clown-related chasing in Suffolk. Authorities are treating the behaviour seriously and advising the public to report threats.

Chelsea Handler closed out her seven-year run on E! with a star-studded, irreverent finale of Chelsea Lately that both celebrated and epitomized the show’s tone: self-aware, shameless, and gleefully silly. Handler repeatedly called the series “seven years of ridiculous stupidity,” a description that captured its mix of celebrity gossip, bawdy skits, and panel comedy. That blend—often crude and uneven—worked because Handler embraced the triviality of tabloid culture and openly mocked herself for profiting from it, creating a candid, unpretentious space that many guests preferred to the more scripted network press stops.

The finale featured a parade of A-listers (Jennifer Aniston, Sandra Bullock, Mary McCormack, Gwen Stefani, Fergie, Gerard Butler, Melissa McCarthy, Selena Gomez, Tim Allen, Ellen DeGeneres and many more), spoof bits (a fake intervention staged by Aniston, Bullock and McCormack), and musical numbers, including a large farewell ensemble. Highlights were Handler’s spontaneous, off-script moments—her banter with ex 50 Cent and unfiltered quips—which often outshone the show’s more scripted panel segments. While the roundtable bits launched some comics’ careers, they could also feel stale and contrived.

More than being simply a female late-night host, Handler brought a distinct point of view: provocative, polarizing, and unapologetic. That edge won her devoted fans and vocal detractors alike, making her one of the most controversial figures in late night. She ended the show by teasing her move to Netflix—a stand-up special and a forthcoming talk show—signing off with the trademark irreverence that defined Chelsea Lately.

Seven advertisers had suspended ads on Rush Limbaugh’s radio show as of Sunday after Limbaugh called Georgetown law student Sandra Fluke a “slut” and “prostitute” while criticizing her advocacy for broader contraceptive coverage. ProFlowers announced on Facebook it would halt advertising, saying his comments were a personal attack and contrary to company values; the decision followed pressure from activist group UltraViolet, which said 91,000 people had signed a petition urging the move. Other companies that pulled ads included Quicken Loans, Sleep Train, Sleep Number, Citrix, Carbonite and LegalZoom. Carbonite’s CEO David Friend said Limbaugh’s remarks crossed reasonable bounds of decency, noted the company’s broader use of talk radio, and described plans to meet Limbaugh; he added that the outcry was unprecedented. Republican presidential contenders Newt Gingrich, Rick Santorum and Ron Paul criticized Limbaugh’s remarks, while a Mitt Romney adviser called Limbaugh’s apology “appropriate” and urged a tone-down of extreme rhetoric across the spectrum.
