On July 6 Asiana Airlines Flight 214 crashed at San Francisco International Airport. On July 12 the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) issued an apology after an on-air report falsely identified the flight crew with offensive, fabricated names. The NTSB said a summer intern, acting outside his authority, erroneously confirmed the names to a media outlet; the agency emphasized it does not release or confirm crewmember identities and regretted the incident, promising corrective action.

The local station KTVU broadcast the bogus names, later apologized and blamed the NTSB confirmation; the station said it corrected the mistake within minutes and is reviewing procedures. KTVU’s handling drew widespread criticism as screenshots and clips circulated online. Asiana Airlines said the false report harmed the pilots’ reputations and indicated it may pursue legal action. The Asian American Journalists Association and others condemned the offensive nature of the names and the newsroom failures that allowed them on air. The NTSB confirmed it did not officially release crew names to any news organization.

Google announced a holiday promotion offering free Wi‑Fi at 47 U.S. airports from mid‑December through January 15, 2010 (and extended access on Virgin America flights within the continental U.S.). The program covers many mid‑sized and regional airports — e.g., Boston Logan, Houston Bush Intercontinental, Las Vegas McCarran, Seattle‑Tacoma — but notable hubs such as Chicago O’Hare/Midway, LAX, Minneapolis‑St. Paul, Dallas‑Fort Worth and the New York area airports are not included because Google’s partners don’t operate in every terminal.

Google partnered with airports and providers including Time Warner Cable, Boingo Wireless, Advanced Wireless Group and others; where partners aren’t present, Microsoft’s Bing/JiWire deal provides an alternate one‑search‑for‑access option at many hotels and some airports (including JFK, Midway, O’Hare and Dulles). Yahoo has also run its own temporary Wi‑Fi promotions this season.

Google’s offer requires no payment or credit‑card entry to connect; users will be asked (but not required) to donate to one of three charities via Google Checkout, with Google matching donations up to $250,000 and awarding $15,000 to the airport that generates the most donations. Google may collect aggregate, non‑personally identifiable data from the sessions; it’s unclear whether the free access will include ads. Google is also running a photo contest tied to in‑airport or in‑flight Wi‑Fi usage.

Stephen Lancaster Dennis, 49, a former money-processing manager at Brink’s Birmingham facility, has been charged with one count of bank theft for stealing $196,000 in quarters from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta while handling the Fed’s coin inventory. An FBI probe found that between Jan. 1 and Feb. 20, 2014, Dennis removed four ballistic bags and skids, filled the bags with beads, and replaced them in the coin room so only a small visible amount of quarters showed through each bag’s neck window. An April 2014 audit discovered the tampering: the four bags contained beads and only $1,000 in quarters. In total Dennis swapped about 784,000 quarters (roughly $196,000). He has agreed to plead guilty, will repay the funds (Brink’s already reimbursed the Fed), and faces federal penalties—up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The case is prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office with assistance from the FBI.

President Barack Obama and Republican vice presidential nominee Paul Ryan clashed Friday over Medicare and the 2010 health-care law at the AARP Life@50+ event, each accusing the other of misleading seniors. Speaking by satellite, Obama said the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) “strengthened Medicare,” cutting waste and fraud, expanding preventive care and lowering drug costs, and called Republican claims that the law cuts $716 billion from Medicare “simply not true.” Ryan, speaking in person to the same AARP audience, repeated GOP charges that the law weakens Medicare and “turns Medicare into a piggy bank,” insisting repeal is the first step to strengthening the program; his remarks were met with repeated boos from the crowd.

The dispute highlights Medicare as a central November campaign issue, especially in swing states with large senior populations. Obama argued his reforms use Medicare’s purchasing power to reduce unnecessary tests and costs, and warned Ryan’s proposal would shift costs to seniors by creating a voucher-like subsidy system—an assertion Ryan denied, saying his plan guarantees seniors can afford coverage.

Separately, Mitt Romney released his 2011 tax return showing $13.7 million in income and a 14.1% effective federal tax rate, and his campaign summarized returns from 1990–2009 showing an average federal effective rate of 20.2%. Democrats, including Obama’s campaign and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, called the disclosure insufficient and pressed Romney to release more years and fuller details.

Both campaigns continued to spar over leadership and policy. Obama framed leadership as rejecting “bad ideas” and noted elements of the ACA trace to Romney’s Massachusetts plan, while Republicans criticized Obama’s inability to change Washington. The exchange at the AARP event, combined with other campaign controversies and fundraising figures showing Obama leading in August, underscored growing tensions and strategic adjustments on both sides with weeks to go before the election.

A Toyota Corolla driven by Nabila Altahan ended up suspended from a telephone pole guy wire Wednesday evening in Mendon after she reacted too quickly to sudden GPS instructions to “turn around.” The car left the westbound lane of Route 4 near Sugar & Spice Restaurant at about 8 p.m., went off the road and became stuck on the support wire. Altahan and her passenger were uninjured; a nearby witness said the driver jumped out while the car was hanging. State police and Rutland City Fire Department responded to the scene.

Solar Impulse 2, the solar-powered experimental aircraft, resumed its attempt to cross the Pacific on Monday, taking off from Nagoya (Komaki) Airport after a frustrating four-week grounding that began June 1. Flight engineers launched the plane in a narrow pre-dawn weather window; the team kept the departure decision late to ensure safe conditions after a prior last-minute cancellation. Project spokeswoman Elke Neumann said the support crew and the inflatable hangar will be flown to Kalaeloa Airport near Honolulu, the expected landing site after an estimated nonstop flight of about five days and nights (roughly 120 hours, ~8,000 km).

The single-seater plane, piloted by Swiss co‑founder Andre Borschberg for this leg, is powered by 17,000 solar cells charging batteries that drive four electric propellers. This Pacific crossing (leg 8 of the round‑the‑world mission that began in Abu Dhabi) is the most challenging stage so far and has been delayed by poor forecasts and a cold front that forced an unscheduled landing in Japan after a May 31 departure from Nanjing. With takeoff from Nagoya, the aircraft has passed its “point of no return”; Borschberg must continue to Hawaii regardless of later weather changes. If batteries don’t recharge adequately, he is prepared to bail out and await rescue, though the team hopes that won’t be necessary.

If successful, this would become the longest-duration solo flight and the greatest distance flown by a purely solar-powered craft. The mission will continue from Hawaii across the U.S. to the Atlantic, with Bertrand Piccard slated to pilot the next Pacific segment. The multi-month delays have tightened the schedule and raised concerns about completing the Atlantic crossing before the peak of hurricane season. The team thanked Japanese hosts, regional officials and sponsors for support during the challenging stopover.

Senate Republican leaders Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn sent June 27 letters to six major sports leagues (NFL, MLB, NBA, NHL, PGA and NASCAR) warning them not to assist the Obama administration in promoting the Affordable Care Act. The senators said partnering with the administration would risk damaging the leagues’ apolitical brands given the law’s divisiveness and cited its unpopularity in polls. The letters also urged the leagues to report any perceived “policy retaliation” or pressure by the administration to secure support, saying Republicans would investigate.

The letters followed Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius’ remarks that she had discussed possible outreach with the NFL; HHS said there was no deal. House Republican Study Committee chair Steve Scalise separately asked the NFL and NBA for details about any HHS requests and cautioned against being “coerced” into promoting the law.

An NFL spokesman later said the league has no plans to engage on the law, had no substantive contacts with the administration about implementation, and denied being pressured. McConnell’s office clarified the senator was not alleging the administration had already threatened the leagues, only warning against potential coercion. HHS and the White House did not comment. Democrats noted prior public-private partnerships on health reforms (e.g., Massachusetts’ 2007 outreach), a comparison Republicans argued was inapt because the federal law was passed without bipartisan support.

Federal health officials and politicians sparred over mandatory 21-day quarantines imposed by New York, New Jersey and Illinois on health workers returning from Ebola-affected West Africa after a Doctors Without Borders physician in New York tested positive.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, argued the quarantines are unnecessary and potentially counterproductive. He said science shows asymptomatic people do not transmit Ebola and that active, direct monitoring can achieve the same protection without discouraging volunteers needed to stop the epidemic at its source. Fauci called quarantines “draconian,” urged treating returning caregivers as heroes rather than stigmatizing them, and stressed that the best protection is halting the outbreak in Africa.

Gov. Chris Christie defended New Jersey’s mandatory quarantine as necessary for public safety in a densely populated region and predicted wider adoption, criticizing reliance on voluntary compliance. Rep. Darrell Issa voiced broader concerns about the Obama administration’s handling of the crisis and questioned leadership choices for coordinating the response.

The debate highlighted tension between science-based disease control measures and political pressure to appear tough on public health risks, with officials disagreeing over the balance between strict quarantines and monitored, evidence-based approaches.

Commissioner Rob Manfred denied Pete Rose’s 2015 application for reinstatement from baseball’s permanently ineligible list in a three-page decision, ruling “I, therefore, must reject Mr. Rose’s application for reinstatement.” Rose, 74 and MLB’s all-time hits leader, was placed on that list on Aug. 23, 1989, for betting on baseball; the Hall of Fame’s board then declared anyone on that list ineligible for election. Manfred made clear he has no authority over Hall of Fame eligibility and that such debate must occur in a different forum; the Hall later reiterated that its bylaws keep Rose ineligible while he remains on baseball’s ineligible list.

Manfred emphasized the central importance of Rule 21 (which bars anyone with a duty to perform in baseball from wagering on the game) and said reinstatement requires objective evidence that an applicant has “fundamentally changed his life” and no longer poses a risk of violating the rule. He found Rose’s submissions and his Sept. 24 interview insufficient. Manfred said Rose did not appear to fully grasp the scope of his violations, disputed Rose’s memory of misconduct documented in the Dowd Report and Michael Bertolini’s betting notebook, and noted Rose admitted to currently betting legally and recreationally on horses and sports, including baseball—initially denying that and later “clarifying” his answer. Manfred also questioned whether Rose has accepted full responsibility, understands the damage caused, or avoided associations that contributed to his past misconduct. Nonetheless, Manfred acknowledged Rose’s exceptional playing career and will allow limited, preapproved ceremonial appearances that pose no integrity risk. MLB rules bar Rose from associating with Major or Minor League clubs without review.

Newly surfaced documents obtained and reported by ESPN’s Outside the Lines—copies of pages from a betting notebook seized from associate Michael Bertolini in an October 1989 postal raid—provide written records that Rose bet extensively on baseball, including on the Cincinnati Reds and on games in which he played in 1986. The notebook, authenticated by former postal inspectors and stored under seal in the National Archives, covers March–July 1986 and shows Rose (identified repeatedly as “PETE”) on MLB betting slips on at least 30 days, with 21 entries clearly on the Reds. Typical bets were about $2,000 and some larger; Rose did not appear to bet against the Reds in those entries. The notebook bolsters the Dowd investigation’s allegations—Dowd had testimony and recordings implicating bettors who placed wagers for Rose and witnesses saying Rose bet on the Reds from 1984–86—but the notebook is the first written documentation tying Rose to bets while still an active player. Dowd and others say it also strengthens the case that Rose used mob-connected New York bookmakers via Bertolini and was heavily indebted, raising serious integrity concerns.

Rose has long maintained he never bet on baseball as a player; he admitted betting on baseball only as a manager in 2004. After the notebook’s reporting, Rose’s lawyer declined to comment on reinstatement specifics pending further meetings with Manfred. MLB officials and investigators reviewed the notebook as part of the reinstatement review; Manfred’s decision cites the notebook and other evidence as reasons Rose has not shown the necessary rehabilitation and understanding to merit reinstatement. Reds CEO Bob Castellini said the team respected Manfred’s decision, appreciated the separation of reinstatement and Hall of Fame issues, and expects to coordinate any future celebrations of Rose’s career with the Commissioner’s Office.

Silk Road was a hidden online black market (2011–2013) where thousands of vendors sold hundreds of kilograms of illegal drugs and other illicit goods to over 100,000 buyers, using Bitcoin for anonymous payments. U.S. prosecutors say the site generated more than $213 million in revenue and that Ross Ulbricht, accused of operating under the alias “Dread Pirate Roberts,” took millions in commissions. Ulbricht was arrested when the site was shut down in October 2013, convicted in February 2015 on multiple counts (including narcotics distribution and running a continuing criminal enterprise) and faces sentencing in May; prosecutors also alleged he commissioned murders-for-hire, though no killings were proven.

The Silk Road case and related prosecutions have damaged Bitcoin’s public image by associating it with crime, but some in the Bitcoin community argue prosecutions show law enforcement can still catch offenders. Charlie Shrem, an early Bitcoin entrepreneur and founder of BitInstant, pleaded guilty in 2014 to aiding and abetting an unlicensed money-transmitting business and was sentenced to two years; he remains a prominent, unapologetic figure who plans to return to the industry after serving his sentence.

The investigation was further marred by alleged corruption among law-enforcement agents. Former DEA agent Carl Force and former U.S. Secret Service agent Shaun Bridges—both involved in Silk Road probes—were accused of stealing bitcoins and laundering proceeds, using undercover roles to extort or divert funds into personal accounts and offshore holdings. Force is charged with money laundering, wire fraud, theft and conflict of interest; prosecutors allege he extorted Ulbricht and misappropriated bitcoins from a digital exchange. Bridges is charged with wire fraud and money laundering and is accused of transferring more than $800,000 in stolen bitcoins through Mt. Gox. Both agents resigned from their agencies; Force was jailed pending hearings, and Bridges was released under pretrial supervision and denies wrongdoing.

Overall, the Silk Road saga highlights the intersection of illicit online markets, cryptocurrency’s anonymity, criminal prosecutions, regulatory follow-up, and even misconduct within the law enforcement teams that pursued the case.

Syrian government forces massed around Aleppo in late July 2012 and stepped up shelling and air strikes on rebel-held neighborhoods as both sides prepared for a major battle for the country’s biggest city. Activists and residents reported heavy overnight bombardment, helicopter and fixed‑wing strikes, tank columns and reinforcements arrayed on Aleppo’s southern outskirts, while rebels — including foreign fighters and Free Syrian Army units — dug in across eastern and southern districts, set up checkpoints and snipers, and claimed control of substantial parts of the city. Civilians faced mounting fear, displacement, shortages of bread, fuel and medical supplies, and rising casualties; opposition tallies and local activists reported dozens killed in Aleppo and surrounding areas.

The United States warned the buildup risked a massacre but reiterated opposition to military intervention, distinguishing Aleppo from the NATO action in Libya. International responses were mixed: Turkey voiced concern about Kurdish advances near its border and threatened measures against perceived terrorism while tightening cross‑border trade; Russia and Iran continued to back the Assad government; Arab states considered taking the Syrian question to the UN General Assembly after repeated Security Council vetoes. The UN monitoring mission in Syria was reduced and its mandate only briefly extended.

Fighting was also intense elsewhere — heavy clashes and shelling around Damascus, including attacks on the Yarmouk Palestinian camp and southern suburbs, produced further civilian deaths and displacement. High‑profile defections (including Brig. Gen. Manaf Tlass and two diplomats) fed debates about post‑Assad leadership, with some external actors exploring transitional figures. Meanwhile, Kurdish groups consolidated control of towns in northeastern Syria as regime forces focused on major urban battlegrounds. Overall, the country’s conflict intensified, with Aleppo poised for a potentially large and bloody government counteroffensive.

Ava DuVernay’s film Selma—starring David Oyelowo as Martin Luther King Jr.—is the first major feature to center on King himself and the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery campaign. DuVernay and screenwriter Paul Webb chose to avoid using King’s actual, copyrighted speeches, instead paraphrasing his cadence and meaning so Oyelowo’s lines evoke King without literal quotation. That creative choice, along with Oyelowo’s portrayal of a strategic, conflicted leader rather than an untouchable icon, produces an intimate yet epic drama that won praise from many real-life participants, including Andrew Young and King’s family.

The film’s avoidance of King’s speeches reflects broader legal and historical constraints: the King estate (King, Inc.), controlled by his descendants, has aggressively asserted copyrights over his speeches for decades, licensing them to studios (notably to DreamWorks/Steven Spielberg) and suing media outlets and producers who used unlicensed excerpts. Past litigation—against USA Today, CBS, and the producers of Eyes on the Prize—plus high licensing fees have curtailed public and artistic uses of central texts like “I Have a Dream.” Copyright law and successive extensions (now life of the author plus 70 years, putting King’s works in copyright until at least 2039) enable the estate to both monetize and control King’s image and words. Critics argue this conflicts with King’s ethos and obstructs historical storytelling; defenders say the estate is legally protecting a legacy and brand. The result has been artistic compromises (as in Selma) and heated debate about whether extant copyright terms properly balance creators’ rights with public access to pivotal historical material.

This long piece profiles Bernardo Bertolucci—his life, recent work and the controversy around the infamous “butter” scene in his 1972 film Last Tango in Paris—blending a new interview about his later life with resurfaced archival material and reactions.

Key points:

- Current life and career: Bertolucci, now in his seventies and wheelchair-bound after complications from multiple back surgeries, lives in Rome and rarely leaves home. Directing again gave him purpose: he adapted Niccolò Ammaniti’s novel Me and You into a confined, mostly basement-set film that suited his limited mobility and helped pull him out of depression. He remains an astute cinephile, praises modern TV (e.g., Breaking Bad) and credits long-term psychoanalysis with deepening his work.

- Filmmaking approach and history: Bertolucci is described as charismatic but single-minded and sometimes ruthless on set. He favors improvisation and leaving room for unexpected reactions—an approach he attributes to Jean Renoir. His major works include The Conformist, Last Tango in Paris, 1900, The Sheltering Sky, The Last Emperor (nine Oscars) and Little Buddha. Last Tango made him internationally famous despite legal trouble in Italy and persistent scandal.

- The Last Tango controversy: The article revisits the notorious butter-assisted rape scene in Last Tango in Paris, in which Marlon Brando’s character performs a simulated anal assault on Maria Schneider’s character. A 2013 interview with Bertolucci—recently resurfaced—confirms that Bertolucci and Brando devised the butter detail on the morning of shooting and did not inform Schneider in advance because Bertolucci “wanted her reaction as a girl, not as an actress.” He called not telling her “horrible” yet said he did not regret the scene, though he expressed some guilt and lamented being unable to apologize after Schneider’s death in 2011.

- Maria Schneider’s account and fallout: Schneider long maintained the sequence was not in the script, that she learned of it only immediately before the take, and that she felt humiliated and “a little raped.” She linked the film’s notoriety to a downward spiral in her life—drug problems and mental-health crises. Brando later said he, too, felt manipulated by the filming. The scene and Bertolucci’s admission have reignited debate over on-set consent and exploitation.

- Public reaction: When footage of Bertolucci’s 2013 remarks spread, prominent actors and filmmakers voiced outrage on social media, calling the conduct reprehensible and arguing that surprise, non-consensual humiliation of an actor is unacceptable. Some demanded consequences; others emphasized the ethical line between creating “real” reactions and abusing performers.

Overall tone and implications:
The piece situates Bertolucci as a complex, brilliant filmmaker whose ambition and improvisatory methods produced landmark cinema but also caused serious ethical breaches—most notably in Last Tango in Paris. The resurfaced admissions have reopened debates about consent, the treatment of young actors, and how to judge historic films and artists whose methods are now seen as abusive.

The Florida U.S. Senate race between Democratic Sen. Bill Nelson and Republican Gov. Rick Scott is headed to a recount after Scott took a slim lead in early returns. With more than 8 million votes cast, Scott’s margin over Nelson is under 0.5% (roughly 30–39,000 votes depending on updates), which triggers an automatic recount under Florida law. Nelson’s campaign said the result was disappointing but did not concede and confirmed it would proceed with a recount, deploying monitors to all 67 counties and working with Democratic attorney Marc Elias of Perkins Coie. County supervisors must recheck tallies (initially due by noon on Nov. 10), and campaigns will follow up on ballots not counted for technical reasons. Scott’s team criticized Nelson’s move as inappropriate and premature; Scott had already declared victory and framed his campaign remarks around uniting after divisive contests. The recount recalls Florida’s pivotal 2000 recount, which ultimately decided that year’s presidential contest.

WGN‑TV Chicago apologized after a staffer mistakenly used a Nazi-era symbol in a Yom Kippur news segment. During anchor Tom Negovan’s brief explanation of the Jewish Day of Atonement, a graphic behind him showed a yellow Star of David patch marked “Jude” on striped material resembling concentration camp uniforms. Viewer Marc Karlinsky posted a screenshot to Twitter, which quickly drew widespread criticism. News Director Jennifer Lyons and General Manager Greg Easterly said the image had come from the station’s image bank and that staff “failed to recognize” the offensive symbol. The station issued on‑air and online apologies, called the error “extremely embarrassing,” and said it is reviewing and changing in‑house policies to prevent a repeat.

The article explores how real biological phenomena—especially polycephaly (multiple heads)—may have inspired ancient myths like the Hydra Heracles fought. It recounts the myth briefly, then surveys scientific and historical evidence that two- and multi-headed animals occasionally occur across many groups (fish, sharks, dolphins, turtles, snakes, kittens, salamanders) and even in the fossil record. Causes include incomplete splitting of embryos (conjoined twins), experimental manipulations (Spemann’s salamander hair-loop experiments), misplaced “organiser” cell groups that trigger head formation, and genetic pathways such as Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) that control facial width. Environmental factors like high temperature can increase developmental abnormalities. Most polycephalic animals have poor survival—many die as embryos or shortly after metamorphosis—so such forms remain extremely rare.

The piece also notes alternative natural sources for multi-headed imagery (for example, mating aggregations of snakes can appear as many heads on one body), and that cultural reactions of fear and disgust likely amplified such sightings into terrifying monsters. Myth and science have influenced each other (Linnaeus named hydra-like animals after the mythic creature), but while real polycephaly plausibly fed ancient storytelling, its biological rarity explains why multi-headed beasts remained legendary rather than commonplace.

Two regional commuter trains collided head-on Monday evening in Granges-près-Marnand in western Switzerland, about 8 km south of Payerne on the Payerne–Lausanne route. The crash occurred around 6:45 p.m.; rescue teams including paramedics, firefighters, police and an air-rescue helicopter responded. Authorities reported around 40–44 people injured (reports vary), with four to five seriously hurt. One locomotive driver was unaccounted for and crews were trying to access a crushed cab; police said one person had yet to be recovered from the wreckage. The two trains remained locked together on the tracks. Investigators have not determined the cause. Service between Payerne and Moudon was suspended at least until midnight.

Commercial satellite imagery and an analysis by the Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) indicate the Nov. 12, 2011 explosion at an Iranian military base near Bid Kaneh was far more destructive than Iranian officials portrayed. A DigitalGlobe image taken Nov. 22 shows most buildings across the sprawling, secured complex extensively damaged or demolished, with only a few structures left standing and much debris remaining. ISIS judged the damage likely resulted from the blast itself rather than post‑event demolition or cleanup, noting there is little heavy equipment on site and the number of trucks visible after the incident is similar to images from two months earlier.

Iran has acknowledged the blast killed 17 military personnel, including Gen. Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, a founder of its missile program, and officials called it an accident that would set research back only days. ISIS’s analyst, Paul Brannan, said institute sources indicated the explosion occurred during a volatile missile‑engine procedure tied to a major milestone in developing a new missile. The satellite photos cannot determine whether the blast was accidental or sabotage, but they show damage inconsistent with the limited setback described by Iranian authorities.

NBC’s The Tonight Show is cutting costs: host Jay Leno has taken a substantial pay reduction and roughly 20–25 staffers have been let go, with additional senior staff accepting pay cuts, as part of a budget restructuring. Although the program remains the top-rated late-night show, it has been only breaking even—partly because its production budget stayed at prime-time levels after Leno’s brief move to prime time in 2009–10. Leno’s previous salary was reported between $25M and $30M; he volunteered to take a cut (some reports put his new pay near $20M–$27M) to help preserve jobs. The show’s weekly production budget is being trimmed from about $2.3 million to roughly $1.7 million, closer to levels during Leno’s earlier late-night tenure. NBC declined detailed comment; Leno’s spokesman later said Jay’s primary concern was protecting his staff. The cuts follow broader cost-trimming at NBC since Comcast’s takeover. The initial report was published by Deadline Hollywood.

Summary:

Stormy Daniels’ lawyer Michael Avenatti released a memo alleging that President Trump’s personal attorney Michael Cohen funneled hundreds of thousands of dollars into his company Essential Consultants — the same entity Cohen used to pay Daniels — from several corporate and foreign-linked sources after the 2016 election. Key claims Avenatti and subsequent reporting highlight:

- Alleged payments: Avenatti says $4.4 million flowed through an Essential Consultants First Republic account (Oct 2016–Jan 2018). Of particular note are eight payments totaling about $500,000 from Columbus Nova (Jan–Aug 2017), an American firm tied in public filings to Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg and his Renova Group. Avenatti suggested those funds may have “replenished” the account after Cohen’s $130,000 hush payment to Daniels.

- Other corporate payors: Avenatti asserted Novartis made four payments of roughly $99,980 each (~$400,000 total); AT&T made four payments of $50,000 each ($200,000 total); and Korea Aerospace Industries paid $150,000. Novartis and AT&T confirmed they paid Essential Consultants and provided brief explanations (Novartis: a one-year agreement on U.S. healthcare policy; AT&T: “insights” on the new administration, no lobbying). Novartis said Mueller’s team contacted it in November and it cooperated.

- Responses and denials: Columbus Nova and its counsel denied that Vekselberg or Renova controlled or funded Columbus Nova’s payments and said Columbus Nova is American-owned; Columbus Nova said it retained Cohen as a business consultant after the inauguration. Cohen disputed Avenatti’s accounting as “inaccurate” but gave no details. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan and First Republic declined comment.

- Mueller and other probes: Reporting (NYT, CNN, AP) says Mueller’s team and FBI agents have questioned Viktor Vekselberg and others about payments by Columbus Nova to Cohen and about large political donations by Andrew Intrater (Columbus Nova CEO and Vekselberg’s cousin), including $250,000 to Trump’s inauguration. Vekselberg was later sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury; he has not been accused of wrongdoing in these matters. Cohen is under criminal investigation in Manhattan (including seizures from raids); prosecutors have not charged him concerning these payments yet.

- Significance: The payments — especially from firms with government interests and a company linked to a Russian oligarch — raise questions about Cohen’s business relationships, potential access or influence- related motives, and whether foreign-linked money touched Trump-related finances (including inauguration funding). Legal analysts note hiring the president’s personal lawyer for “insight” is unusual and could look improper, though such arrangements aren’t necessarily illegal if no lobbying or prohibited activity occurred.

Overall, the disclosures allege a network of post-election payments into Cohen’s consulting vehicle from both U.S. corporations and a firm affiliated with a Russian oligarch, prompting scrutiny from media and investigators and prompting denials from implicated parties.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg will officiate a same‑sex wedding Saturday at the Kennedy Center in Washington — believed to be the first time a sitting U.S. Supreme Court justice has done so. Ginsburg will marry Kennedy Center president Michael M. Kaiser and government economist John Roberts in a private ceremony attended by about 220 guests from the arts and civic worlds. A longtime friend of Kaiser and a frequent Kennedy Center attendee and opera lover, Ginsburg said she agreed to officiate because she admires him and views the ceremony as a statement that couples who love each other should enjoy marriage’s “blessings and the strife.”

The wedding follows the Supreme Court’s landmark rulings in June that expanded federal recognition of same‑sex marriages and struck down part of an anti‑gay marriage law; Ginsburg was in the majority in those decisions and has argued for equal treatment of marriages. She noted justices generally avoid political stands, suggesting previous reluctance to officiate same‑sex ceremonies may have reflected concerns about impartiality before cases were decided. Ginsburg, who turned 80 this year and is a prominent liberal voice on the court, said she has no immediate plans to retire.

Kuwaiti telecom Zain released a three-minute Ramadan TV ad that went viral across the Middle East, garnering millions of views and sparking intense debate. The music-driven spot depicts a man assembling a suicide vest and walking through the aftermath of a bus bombing, only to be confronted by survivors and victims of past attacks—children, a wedding survivor, a mosque bombing survivor and others—who correct his religious invocations and urge mercy. Emirati singer Hussain (Hussein) al‑Jassmi leads a chorus that frames the response to extremism as “love” and “mercy,” with lines such as “let’s bomb extremism with mercy.”

The ad was timed for Ramadan, when TV audiences in the Arab world are at their largest, and follows previous high‑profile Zain campaigns that promoted peace. Reactions were sharply divided. Many praised the emotional, anti‑violence message and the attempt to reclaim faith from extremists. Critics objected to the commercial use of victims’ images, the simplified portrayal of terrorism, and the decision to include an actor resembling Omran Daqneesh (the Aleppo boy widely photographed after an airstrike), which drew particular condemnation since his injuries were caused by regime bombing rather than jihadi attacks. Commentators also argued the ad sidesteps deeper political causes of extremism and questioned whom the message is aimed at—the perpetrators or society at large.

Overall, the ad succeeded in re‑igniting public discussion about countering violence and extremism, while exposing tensions over representation, context, and the limits of media-based moral appeals.

Recent reports depict a worsening heroin epidemic across multiple U.S. communities, marked by rapid spikes in overdoses, increased deaths, and expanding geographic reach.

Key local outbreaks and responses
- Orange County, Florida: Deputies reported at least 11 heroin overdoses in 24 hours near Blossom Park/Orange Blossom Trail; several victims hospitalized and some died. Law enforcement increased visible patrols to deter sales and use.
- Cedar Rapids and Eastern Iowa: Overdoses have surged—Cedar Rapids saw 52 overdose calls through early June, 44 heroin-related (85% of overdose calls). Iowa’s crime lab shows suspected heroin submissions from 37 counties, concentrated in Scott, Linn and Johnson counties, linked to distribution via Chicago-based networks. Authorities warn the situation will worsen without stronger intervention.
- Washington County, Pennsylvania: A single weekend produced 16 overdoses in 24 hours and 25 over two days, with three fatalities. Officials suspect fentanyl-laced heroin; widespread naloxone (Narcan) use saved many lives but highlighted the crisis’s scale.
- New Jersey: Heroin-related deaths rose dramatically—781 deaths in 2014 (more than double 2010). Tens of thousands entered treatment programs for heroin/opiate use. Narcan was deployed over 1,000 times in 2014; treatment admissions and overdose death rates outpace many other causes of death in parts of the state.
- Marion, Ohio and other small towns: Longstanding community impacts—families shattered, increased property crime tied to addiction, and repeated overdoses addressed by police and harm-reduction tools like Narcan and Vivitrol.

Why heroin is surging and becoming deadlier
- Transition from prescription opioids: Many users begin with prescription painkillers (oxycodone, hydrocodone) and switch to heroin when prescriptions end—heroin is cheaper and often more potent.
- Distribution networks: Heroin flows from Mexican cartels and metropolitan hubs (e.g., Chicago), with local gangs and cellphone-based deals replacing open-air markets, complicating enforcement.
- Purity variability and fentanyl contamination: Heroin purity can vary widely, making dosing unpredictable; dealers increasingly lace heroin with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid up to 80 times more potent, greatly increasing overdose risk.
- Demographics: Use is rising across demographics, notably among women and 18–25-year-olds; many victims are young adults in their 20s–40s, including people with little prior exposure to heroin.
- Economic and regional concentration: The epidemic disproportionately affects Rust Belt, Great Lakes, and Northeast regions, though suburban and rural areas are also hit.

Consequences and challenges
- Overdose deaths have risen sharply nationwide (e.g., CDC: heroin deaths nearly tripled 2010–2013), surpassing many other causes of mortality in hard-hit areas.
- Law enforcement and prosecutors face hurdles: a 2014 Supreme Court decision raised standards for proving distribution-caused deaths, making some prosecutions harder; proving causation is complicated by polysubstance use.
- Treatment capacity is limited: There are far fewer inpatient rehab beds than needed; harm-reduction tools like naloxone reverse overdoses but don’t address addiction’s root causes.
- Social fallout: Families and communities experience deep trauma—lost loved ones, increased crime, and long recovery journeys for survivors. Some areas are investing in prevention, treatment (Vivitrol, expanded rehab access), and targeted law enforcement to disrupt supply chains.

Responses underway
- Increased law enforcement visibility and targeted investigations to trace supply.
- Wider distribution of naloxone to first responders and the public, saving lives but highlighting recurring overdoses.
- Prevention, treatment and prosecution initiatives, including federal and local funding for prevention officers and support for medications like Vivitrol to reduce relapse.
- Community efforts to expand treatment access and public awareness campaigns, though capacity limits and shifting drug markets (e.g., substitution to crack when blocked from opioids) complicate solutions.

Bottom line: Heroin use and overdose deaths are rising sharply across diverse U.S. communities. The crisis is driven by prescription opioid addiction, cartel-distributed heroin, unpredictable purity, and fentanyl contamination. Responses mix law enforcement, harm reduction, and treatment, but limited treatment capacity, legal hurdles in prosecuting dealers, and the spread of fentanyl make the epidemic increasingly lethal and difficult to control.

Danish, family-owned Lego Group reported strong first-half 2014 results driven largely by tie-ins to The Lego Movie. Revenue rose 11% year-over-year to 11.5 billion kroner and net profit increased 14% to 2.7 billion kroner (about $480 million). Sales climbed by double digits across Europe, the Americas and Asia; the company now tops rivals Mattel and Hasbro in revenue and profit. Popular new sets — including a sold-out female-scientist set — and the movie’s box-office success helped fuel demand. Lego executives hope the momentum continues into the crucial holiday period and with the movie’s DVD release. The company employs roughly 12,000 people and remains privately owned by the founding Kristiansen family. Incidents of organized Lego thefts totaling over $300,000 were also reported this summer.

A new study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition by UNC researchers led by Barry Popkin finds that fast food is more a marker of unhealthy overall eating patterns than the sole cause of childhood obesity. Using NHANES data on 4,466 children (ages 2–18) from 2007–2010, the team categorized children by (a) how much of their daily calories came from fast-food restaurants (none, low ≤30%, high >30%) and (b) their eating pattern when not eating fast food: a “Western” pattern (high in saturated fat and added sugars) versus a “prudent” pattern (more fruits, vegetables, lean protein, less sugar and saturated fat).

Key findings:
- Children who followed a Western dietary pattern when not eating fast food had the highest rates of overweight and obesity—even if they didn’t consume fast food.
- Children following a prudent diet had substantially lower obesity risk, even if they were high fast-food consumers.
- Low fast-food consumers were 1.5 times more likely, and high consumers 2.2 times more likely, to follow the Western pattern than nonconsumers.
- The authors conclude that where food is obtained matters less than its nutritional quality; targeting fast-food outlets alone is likely necessary but insufficient to reduce child obesity unless broader dietary habits are addressed.

The study underscores that unhealthy home and overall food environments—excess processed foods, sugary beverages, too few fruits and vegetables, and constrained parental resources or time—drive many of the dietary behaviors linked to obesity. The researchers urge public health efforts to focus beyond fast-food access to improving the entire diet and household food environment. A related Illinois study also highlighted modifiable early-life risk factors for preschool obesity: insufficient sleep, parental high BMI, and restrictive feeding practices.

Researchers have discovered how Southeast Asian "flying" snakes (notably Chrysopelea paradisi) generate lift while gliding: by flattening and S-curving their bodies to form a UFO‑like cross section. Using 3-D printed models of that cross section tested in a water tunnel (to replicate airflow), the team found the flattened, saucer-shaped body produces substantially more lift than a normal cylindrical shape and is aerodynamically comparable, at that scale, to familiar lifting surfaces. The snakes launch from high branches, splay their ribs to flatten their bodies, and undulate while airborne; the flattened cross section explains much of their glide performance, though the purpose of their periodic undulation (about once or twice per second) remains under study. The researchers note this body shape is an unusual aerodynamic solution not used by other animals or engineered flyers and wouldn’t scale well to large, fast aircraft. Possible ecological reasons for gliding include predator avoidance, moving between trees, and hunting.

The House GOP tax overhaul unveiled in early November proposes eliminating the federal adoption tax credit, a move that has alarmed adoption advocates, some conservatives, and religious groups who see the credit as a key “pro-family” and “pro-life” policy. The credit helps subsidize steep adoption costs (agency and legal fees, travel, post-adoption services) and in 2017 provided a maximum of about $13,570 (adjusted annually). It was first created in 1996 after bipartisan support and traces to Republican “pro-family” proposals.

Why it matters
- Adoption can be costly—private and international adoptions often run tens of thousands of dollars—so the credit materially affects many families’ ability to adopt. Survey and IRS data show middle and upper-middle income households capture most of the current benefit because the credit is nonrefundable and phases out at higher incomes.
- Experts argue the credit is cost-effective: research indicates each dollar spent facilitating foster-care adoptions returns multiple dollars in government savings (reduced criminal-justice, special-education, and other social costs). Eliminating the credit could make adoption harder, especially for lower- and middle-income families and for adoptions from foster care, where adoptees often need ongoing services.
- Advocates have been pushing instead to make the credit refundable so lower-income families and those adopting multiple children could benefit more. Bipartisan bills to do so were introduced this year.

Political context and reactions
- House Ways and Means Chair Kevin Brady, an architect of the bill and an adoptive parent, has defended dropping the credit as part of a broader choice to simplify the tax code and shift benefits into larger standard deductions and a bigger child tax credit “every year,” arguing some provisions are one-time and less efficient.
- The elimination has triggered criticism from adoption advocates, some GOP lawmakers (e.g., Sen. Ben Sasse, Rep. Mark Walker), and conservative commentators who call it inconsistent with pro-family and pro-life commitments. Advocates warn the change could have a chilling effect on adoptions and asked lawmakers to preserve or make refundable the credit.
- The projected federal savings from abolishing the credit are relatively small (the tax expenditure was about $300 million in 2015), raising questions about the net fiscal wisdom given longer-term costs associated with children remaining in foster care.

Status
- The House proposal remains a draft subject to change as negotiations continue. Supporters of the credit are mobilizing to preserve it or secure a refundable version before final tax legislation is enacted.

A 40-person team at VCU Medical Center in Richmond delivered healthy sextuplets on May 11 via cesarean section to Ajibola and Adeboye Taiwo. Ajibola Taiwo, a native of western Nigeria who had tried to conceive for 17 years, was 30 weeks and two days pregnant when she gave birth to three boys and three girls weighing between 1 lb. 10 oz. and 2 lbs. 15 oz. All six infants are doing well in the Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU’s Level 4 NICU and receiving specialized care, including kangaroo (skin‑to‑skin) contact and comforting measures such as crocheted octopus toys to mimic the womb.

The delivery—believed to be the hospital’s first sextuplet birth—followed months of coordinated planning, drills and multidisciplinary preparation involving maternal‑fetal medicine, labor and delivery, anesthesia, neonatal medicine, respiratory therapy, nursing, social work, nutrition, cardiology and chaplain services. Hospital leaders praised the teamwork that made the complex, simultaneous delivery possible; the parents have been actively involved in NICU care and Ajibola Taiwo was discharged May 18. The hospital and family are not currently doing media interviews. Sextuplet and other higher‑order births are very rare in the U.S.; in 2015 only 24 births were quintuplets or higher.

Actress and Harvey Weinstein accuser Rose McGowan is facing arrest after Washington Dulles International Airport police say narcotics tested positive on personal items she left behind following a Jan. 20 flight from Los Angeles. Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Police spokesman Rob Yingling said a felony charge was issued, a bench warrant entered into a national database, and officers have tried to contact McGowan to appear in Loudoun County, Virginia court.

McGowan, who has accused Weinstein of raping her in 1997 and has alleged a close associate offered her $1 million to stay silent, pushed back on the warrant on Twitter, suggesting it could be an effort to silence her and calling the accusation “a load of horseshit.” She also posted other tweets criticizing Hollywood and referencing recent allegations against Kevin Spacey, adding, “We are an army of thorns.”

Hillary Clinton made a rare public appearance after conceding the 2016 election to surprise Katy Perry at UNICEF’s annual Snowflake Ball, where she presented the singer with the Audrey Hepburn Humanitarian Award. Clinton praised Perry’s humanitarian work—noting her field visits, fundraising and commitment to complex global problems—and compared Perry’s compassion and energy to Audrey Hepburn’s. The surprise appearance drew sustained standing ovations.

Perry, a UNICEF ambassador since 2013 who has raised over $1 million for the organization and visited Madagascar and Vietnam, was moved to tears. In her acceptance speech she credited Clinton with helping her use her voice for more than music and vowed to continue her international advocacy. Both women made light political jabs—Clinton joked about Perry’s many Twitter followers “getting some competition,” and Perry referenced climate change as real—while calling for unity and continued humanitarian work.

The gala at Cipriani Wall Street, hosted by Octavia Spencer, also honored others and featured performances by Sara Bareilles and the cast of The Color Purple. The Snowflake Ball celebrates UNICEF’s work for children and has raised $27 million over the past 11 years.

A federal advisory panel, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, recommended that routine mammograms not be performed for women in their 40s, sparking intense debate about the recommendation’s meaning and motives. The task force based its guidance on cost-benefit and effectiveness data: breast cancer incidence in women 40–49 is low (about 1.4%), screening yields many false positives (nearly 10%), and the number of women needing screening to prevent one death is higher in their 40s than in their 50s. It recommended routine mammography every two years for women 50–74 and said evidence is insufficient for those 75 and older.

Coverage and political fallout followed immediately. HHS Secretary Kathleen Sebelius clarified the recommendations are not government policy, urged women to consult their doctors, and noted that government programs like Medicaid will continue to cover routine mammograms and that insurers have signaled they will too. Critics — including the American Cancer Society, some members of Congress, and breast cancer survivors — called the task force’s framing patronizing, argued it may put a bureaucratic cost calculus ahead of individual patients, and announced plans for hearings. Supporters acknowledge the guidance reflects efficiency and resource-allocation decisions that could inform broader health-care coverage debates, while opponents fear it signals the start of rationing preventive care.

NBC News has reached a tentative deal to keep Brian Williams at the network after his six-month suspension ends in August, a decision driven by new NBC News chairman Andrew (Andy) Lack, who has long been an ally of Williams. Williams will not return as anchor of NBC Nightly News; Lester Holt, who filled in during the suspension, will be named the permanent Nightly News anchor, making him the first African-American solo weekday network nightly news anchor.

Williams will return in a reduced role focused on breaking news: anchoring breaking news and special reports for MSNBC and serving as a breaking-news anchor for NBC News special reports when Holt is unavailable. His salary will be substantially reduced from the lucrative contract he signed last year. NBC conducted an internal investigation that found Williams made a number of inaccurate statements about his field reporting—mostly in off-air appearances and late-night programs—and declined to publish detailed findings. Williams issued an apology and has been conducting meetings with staff; NBC executives framed the move as offering him a second chance while protecting the network’s interests and avoiding the risk of him appearing elsewhere. The arrangement prompted internal discontent among some staff who wanted Williams dismissed.

At the Code Conference in Rancho Palos Verdes, Hillary Clinton broadly assigned blame for her 2016 loss beyond her own campaign choices, which she says she accepts. She reiterated that James Comey’s late-October letter about her private email server cost her critical ground and criticized the media for sensationalizing the issue “like Pearl Harbor” while failing to report substantive policy coverage.

Clinton faulted multiple external factors:
- Russian interference: She called the DNC and campaign hacks, the rapid release of John Podesta’s emails via WikiLeaks, and widespread “fake news” on platforms like Facebook part of an unprecedented, “weaponized” misinformation campaign. While not explicitly accusing Trump’s campaign of collusion, she said Russians likely had guidance from Americans on how to exploit and time releases and urged investigation into who “told them” and coordinated with them.
- Democratic National Committee weaknesses: She said the DNC handed her an inferior data operation after the nominating contest, contrasting that with Republican investment in data infrastructure, and described the party as organizationally “bankrupt” and in need of rebuilding.
- Sexism and media treatment: Clinton argued gender played a role in how controversies (such as her paid speeches) were portrayed and again dismissed the email story as overblown. She blamed the media’s framing and lack of context for damaging coverage.
- A complacent assumption of victory: She said a broad belief she would win created an attitude that hurt her campaign and made it harder to overcome the challenge of succeeding a two-term president from her own party.

On politics going forward, Clinton said she is not running again but will remain active publicly. She urged Democrats to focus on coming gubernatorial races and the 2018 midterms—calling flipping the House “certainly realistic”—and emphasized the need to strengthen party institutions and data capabilities. She also criticized President Trump’s temperament and policy moves, including plans to withdraw from the Paris climate agreement.

At a TED Talk interview with Gayle King in Vancouver, pregnant tennis star Serena Williams said her pregnancy announcement on Snapchat was accidental. Williams explained she had been photographing her baby bump weekly while on vacation and had intended to save the image, but accidentally shared it; she realized when missed calls started coming in. Her rep later confirmed she and fiancé Alexis Ohanian are expecting their first child this fall. Williams also talked about post-baby plans, expressing confidence about returning to top form—citing Roger Federer as an example—and joking that she hopes her child will be in the stands cheering her on.

Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes’ divorce was finalized quickly and quietly. Holmes filed for divorce on June 28, seeking sole custody of their daughter Suri, and the couple reached a settlement within days. Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Matthew Cooper signed the judgment and the court papers were sealed. Reports say Holmes was awarded primary physical custody of six‑year‑old Suri and the agreement includes restrictions limiting Suri’s exposure to the Church of Scientology. A source close to Cruise told E! News he is “very happy and relieved” to be moving on and that his priority remains being a good father. The pair had married in November 2006 after dating and a highly publicized romance.

Researchers in South America have discovered that larvae (tadpoles) of the Argentine horned frog (Ceratophrys ornata) produce a brief, clear metallic “scream” when threatened—marking the first recorded case of sound production by anuran larvae and, apparently, the first sound-producing vertebrate larvae. Dr. Guillermo Natale and colleagues heard the noise while netting tadpoles and then reared wild-caught adults in captivity to study it. The distress call is a short series of higher-frequency pulses lasting ~0.05 seconds, produced by expelling air from lungs that develop unusually early (even three-day-old tadpoles can call). Calls occur when tadpoles are touched, prodded, removed from water (more often out of water), or contacted by objects, and may function to deter attacks and reduce cannibalism—C. ornata tadpoles are carnivorous and often eat other species’ larvae but rarely each other. The finding suggests underwater larval acoustic communication may be more widespread than realized and prompts further study of how the calls develop, what information they convey, and how other tadpoles perceive them.

This document is a collection of reactions, recap and critique of the 2017 Comic Relief short Red Nose Day Actually — a 10–12 minute reunion of Richard Curtis’s 2003 ensemble rom‑com Love Actually that revisits several original storylines and characters to raise money for charity.

What the special did
- Brought back many original cast members (Hugh Grant, Liam Neeson, Colin Firth, Keira Knightley, Bill Nighy, Andrew Lincoln, Rowan Atkinson, Martine McCutcheon, Lucia Moniz, etc.) in brief vignettes showing “where they are now.”
- Included new cameos (Kate Moss) and callbacks to iconic moments: Mark’s cue cards, the Prime Minister’s dance, Rufus’s obsessive wrapping, Jamie and Aurelia’s language gag, Sam and Joanna’s reunion, Billy Mack’s publicity stunts.
- Avoided including Emma Thompson’s storyline out of respect for Alan Rickman’s death; one subplot implied another character’s death (Billy Mack’s manager).
- Aired as part of Comic Relief/Red Nose Day with the explicit aim of driving donations rather than being a full cinematic sequel.

Critical responses (mixed)
- Positive: Many viewers enjoyed the nostalgia, the star appearances, and the charitable purpose; fans posted affectionate reactions to specific moments (Hugh Grant dancing, Kate Moss cameo).
- Negative: Several critics found it thin, cobbled-together, overly sentimental, and underwhelming humor-wise — a “squib” that felt too long for its length and reliant on fan goodwill. Specific complaints included weak jokes (e.g., Colin Firth’s pregnancy gag), awkward or contrived beats (some deaths or poignancy), and a sense that some characters’ continuations (Andrew Lincoln’s creepily persistent Mark, Jamie’s poor Portuguese) made relationships look unhealthy or bizarre.
- Broader criticism of the Red Nose Day broadcast noted uneven quality across the night’s programming, technical issues, and segments that didn’t always match the charity’s serious appeals.

Interpretations and themes
- The reunion prompted debate about what constitutes a “healthy” relationship in the original film’s melodramatic vignettes; some updates were read as dark or troubling rather than purely sweet.
- Commentators observed that the sketch worked more as nostalgia and fundraising device than as a meaningful creative sequel; the short’s purpose was ultimately to support Comic Relief.

Bottom line
Red Nose Day Actually was a star-studded, nostalgia-driven charity sketch that delighted many fans but divided critics: praised for goodwill, cameos and callbacks, yet criticized for weak writing, strained jokes and an overall sense that it existed chiefly to raise money rather than to offer a satisfying artistic sequel.

At the 90th Academy Awards, three of Harvey Weinstein’s most prominent accusers — Ashley Judd, Salma Hayek and Annabella Sciorra — appeared together in a video montage about equality, representation and the momentum of the #MeToo/Time’s Up movements. Speaking to the live audience, Sciorra noted that many had “spoken their truth” and that a new path is emerging; Judd credited “the powerful sound of new voices” for driving change and declaring “time’s up”; Hayek saluted those who “kicked ass and broke through” biased perceptions about gender, race and ethnicity. The segment included other industry figures such as Mira Sorvino, Kumail Nanjiani and Greta Gerwig discussing the importance of representation. The piece came amid the broader fallout over decades of sexual-harassment and assault allegations against Weinstein — accusations he has denied as to nonconsensual sex while reportedly admitting “boorish behavior” — and highlighted the Time’s Up Legal Defense Fund as a resource for survivors. The event was part of the Oscars broadcast from the Dolby Theatre on March 4, 2018.

This document combines two topics: the Internet Archive's "No More 404s" crawls and Wolfram Alpha’s new ImageIdentify tool.

- Internet Archive "No More 404s": The Archive is crawling and saving web pages as they’re created and the pages those pages reference, so when referenced pages change or disappear, a preserved version from the time of citation is available. The aim is to replace or supplement broken links with links to these archived versions to reduce web link rot.

- Wolfram Alpha’s ImageIdentify: Stephen Wolfram launched ImageIdentify (imageidentify.com), a photo-recognition feature that analyzes uploaded pictures and returns computer-generated guesses of what they show. Trained on “tens of millions” of images—including whimsical or tricky examples like cats in spacesuits and Chewbacca—the system can recognize roughly 10,000 common objects but has trouble with specific people, art, non-everyday items and some tech products. Its results are often impressively accurate (e.g., identifying dog breeds, flowers, food) but frequently vague, incorrect, or unavailable under load; mistakes often appear human-like. Wolfram stores thumbnail uploads to improve training and for sharing, and users can give feedback to correct or choose alternate guesses. Beyond novelty, the tool is intended as a building block for developers and could power large-scale photo categorization, content analysis, or apps that translate images into useful data.

A young Syrian boy, Omran Daqneesh—whose image of him dazed, dusty and bloodied in the back of an ambulance after an August airstrike became an international symbol of Aleppo’s civilian suffering—has reappeared in photos and a short video posted by pro-government media. The footage, shared by pro-Assad TV presenter Kinana Allouche and other regime-aligned outlets (including Kremlin-funded Ruptly), shows Omran apparently healthy and living in government-controlled Aleppo. In a brief interview his father, Mohammed Daqneesh, accused opposition forces and international media of “trading in his blood,” said Omran’s injuries were minor, and claimed he had changed his son’s name and cut his hair to protect him from kidnappers and intimidation. The father also said he refused offers to leave Syria, arguing they were aimed at discrediting the Syrian army.

Observers and independent analysts warned the family was unlikely to be speaking freely under government control and raised concerns the appearance may have been coerced or used for propaganda. The original ambulance photo and video were filmed and disseminated by pro-opposition groups after an attack that also fatally wounded Omran’s older brother. The broader context is Aleppo’s bitter years-long siege and retreat of rebel forces late last year and the Syrian civil war that began in 2011 and has killed hundreds of thousands. Media commentators noted this episode fits a wider pattern of both sides exploiting high-profile children and images for political messaging during the conflict.

The article explains Ron Paul’s oft-quoted line “We are all Austrians now” by distinguishing between two meanings of “Austrian” economics and then critiques the more radical Mises–Rothbard strand Paul embraces. It notes that Friedrich Hayek—an important, Nobel-winning figure from the Austrian tradition—has been influential in mainstream economics and public policy, but Paul’s reference points instead to a narrower, extreme libertarian school associated with Ludwig von Mises and Murray Rothbard. That version rejects most government intervention, including fiscal stimulus, conventional monetary stabilization, and even modest central-bank interest-rate management, arguing that low rates cause “malinvestment” and that stimulative policies trigger recessions.

The piece challenges the Austrian claim on theoretical and empirical grounds: if cheap money necessarily misleads investors, why wouldn’t private actors anticipate it; reclassifying past investment as “malinvestment” does not explain why overall spending collapses in a recession; and historical experience (e.g., responses to the Great Depression) undermines the idea that markets always self-correct without policy. The author then turns to an alternative framework, invoking Knut Wicksell’s “natural rate of interest”: recessions reflect a gap between the natural rate and the policy rate, and central-bank rate cuts can close that gap and restore equilibrium. Although the financial crisis pushed the natural rate very low (possibly below zero), and the Fed cannot cut nominal rates below zero, the article argues that gradual recovery is likely because each month of growth narrows the gap between the actual and natural rates.

Concretely, the author predicts accelerating growth and improving employment from a low base: rising bank credit, stronger durable-goods and auto purchases, increased housing starts (especially multifamily), more renters forming households, and a reduction in state and local budget pain as tax revenues recover. The recovery won’t recreate the tight labor market of the late 1990s, but relative to the previous four years it would feel like a robust boom.

The U.S. Department of Labor has filed lawsuits and an administrative action against the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS), some of its leaders, and affiliated businesses after a multi‑year probe found alleged child labor and wage violations during the 2012–2013 pecan harvest. The complaints, filed in federal court and administratively, accuse FLDS leaders of pulling children out of school in Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Ariz., to work unpaid on the Southern Utah Pecan Ranch in Hurricane. Investigators found as many as 175 children under 13 among roughly 1,400 children and adults who harvested pecans and performed tasks such as pruning, mowing, shaking trees, bagging pecans and operating equipment. 

The DOL seeks back wages for the estimated 1,400 unpaid workers and is pursuing $1.9 million in penalties for child labor violations. Named defendants include FLDS Bishop Lyle Jeffs, ranch supervisor Dale Barlow, the Corporation of the President and the Corporation of the Presiding Bishop (the church’s operating entities), Paragon Contractors Corp., and owner Dan Jessop. Paragon and Jessop are also accused of violating a 2007 injunction related to earlier child labor findings. Court filings include testimony from a woman who said she began working at 15 and later handled sign‑in sheets for child workers, confirming they were unpaid. DOL Wage and Hour Division head David Weil said the actions underscore the department’s commitment to protecting vulnerable workers and enforcing child labor laws.

Following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in March 2014, Western governments imposed targeted sanctions on senior Russian officials, businessmen and banks close to President Vladimir Putin, triggering measurable economic fallout and growing isolation for Moscow.

Economic effects and market reaction
- Russian markets and the ruble weakened sharply: the MICEX/RTS index fell double digits year-to-date, the ruble was one of the worst-performing emerging-market currencies, and large capital outflows accelerated. Investors pulled billions from Russian equities and bonds.
- Rating agencies cut outlooks to negative, and analysts warned of an increased risk of a sovereign downgrade. Banks and state-linked companies faced higher borrowing costs; Russia’s central bank raised rates to defend the currency.
- Firms and households felt immediate disruption after payment processors temporarily halted services to some sanctioned banks (e.g., Bank Rossiya, SMP), prompting withdrawals and worries about access to foreign payment networks. Proposals in the Duma to ban foreign-based transaction services and to build a national payments system raised fears of greater economic isolation.

Sanctions content and reach
- The U.S. and EU enacted travel bans and asset freezes targeting about 20 officials, oligarchs and at least one bank; the U.S. signaled it could expand sanctions to sectors including finance, energy, metals/mining and defense.
- Western leaders cancelled or suspended high-level venues—most visibly declining to hold the G8 summit in Sochi—declaring Russia’s annexation illegal and warning of further, coordinated sectoral sanctions if Moscow escalated.

Political and social responses
- Putin’s domestic popularity rose sharply after the annexation; Kremlin-aligned commentators and some experts argued targeted sanctions would have limited effect on elites and mainly hurt ordinary Russians by increasing economic uncertainty and costs.
- Russian authorities and sanctioned figures described the measures as ineffective or counterproductive, and Moscow retaliated with its own travel bans. Some Russian lawmakers and businesses framed the sanctions as an argument for de-offshorization and developing domestic alternatives to Western services.

Broader strategic implications
- Analysts warned the crisis marked a new, economically focused standoff between Russia and the West that could take years to stabilize. Western officials pursued measures intended to pressure Russia by constraining access to Western finance, freezing assets, and potentially exposing corrupt dealings by Kremlin-linked figures.
- High-profile corruption and bribery investigations — for example, the arrest of Ukrainian businessman Dmitry Firtash in Austria on U.S. charges — raised the prospect of intelligence and legal avenues being used to deepen sanctions or target individuals tied to Gazprom, state energy interests, and the Kremlin’s financial networks.

Overall, the initial round of targeted Western sanctions and the threats of broader sectoral measures have already weakened market confidence, disrupted some banking services, and contributed to Russia’s diplomatic isolation—while hardening domestic political support for Putin and prompting debate inside Russia about economic decoupling from the West.

A University of Calgary student, first-year Carlos Zetina, tried to find a woman named Nicole he met at a campus bar after the number she gave him turned out to be wrong. Using the university directory, he mass-emailed 246 account holders with “Nicole” (and variants) in their names asking for a Nicole from the Netherlands who thinks Nietzsche is depressing. The message sparked conversation among recipients, and one student, Nicole DuGraye, created a Facebook group called “Nicole From Last Night.” The like-named women organized a meetup dubbed the “Congress of Nicoles” and began socializing regularly. The intended Nicole hadn’t received the original email (she learned about it via social media) and said she had accidentally given Zetina a new Canadian number; she later contacted him through the Facebook group. Zetina and the original Nicole have since reconnected and plan to meet; the group of Nicoles plans to keep meeting monthly. The story went viral on social media under #nicolefromlastnight.

A Reddit post praises a quick-thinking bystander who doused a boat fire without a fire extinguisher. Despite doubts from onlookers, the person successfully put out the blaze and earned admiration for handling the situation swiftly and heroically.

Police in Ludhiana, Punjab, arrested several people after a newborn was allegedly sold through a deal arranged on Facebook. Authorities say 47-year-old Feroz Khan kidnapped his grandson shortly after the baby’s birth and, with help from two temporary hospital staff, sold the infant for 45,000 rupees to a nurse. The nurse then reportedly sold the baby for 300,000 rupees to a lab assistant, who posted photographs and offered the child for sale on Facebook; a Delhi businessman allegedly bid 800,000 rupees. Police raided the buyer’s home, recovered the baby and returned him to his mother, Noori Khan, who had filed the complaint; five people have been arrested and charged with kidnapping. Officials called the case indicative of a wider child‑trafficking problem in India, where large networks traffic children for adoption, labour, begging and sexual exploitation. If convicted, the accused face up to seven years’ imprisonment.

This piece explains how Fueled, a New York City mobile app development firm led by Ryan Matzner, rigorously vets app ideas and rejects many popular but impractical concepts. While apps are ubiquitous across categories (weather, travel, dating, etc.), the crowded market makes truly novel, viable ideas rare. Fueled hand-picks projects and polishes them through a strict selection process before any design or development begins.

The article lists common types of bad or misguided app ideas the company regularly encounters and why they fail:

- Fundamentally terrible concepts
  - "Airbnb for public parking": impractical effort for tiny returns.
  - Tinder-style apps for dogs: trivial replications of existing models.
  - GPS-based local chat/geo-networking: people generally won’t chat just because others are nearby; many past attempts failed.
  - Novelty apps like “pee break” alerts or shock bracelets that punish inactivity: implausible or ethically questionable.

- Ideas that are poor to people who understand technology
  - Apps promising to aggregate happy-hour deals: oversaturated and low-value.
  - Custom emoji apps: Apple’s emoji set is built into iOS, so “new” emoji apps simply reuse existing characters—founders often misunderstand technical limits.
  - Building full POS systems: massive, resource-intensive undertakings that require big sales forces and have limited upside.
  - Apps that depend on a huge user base from day one or can’t function with a small initial group.
  - “Pay when you walk out” store payment systems: smart in concept but often ignorant of practical, technical, or business realities.
  - Daily scavenger hunts: low engagement and weak value propositions.

- Other recurring bad behaviors and misconceptions
  - People trying to sell raw “million-dollar ideas” without execution ability—companies like Fueled ignore these pitches.
  - Unrealistic budgets: clients expect complex social networks or large apps to be built for tiny sums, reflecting a misunderstanding of development costs and complexity.

Overall message: despite abundant app ideas, many are impractical, technically naive, or poorly scoped for real-world constraints. Fueled emphasizes careful selection and a rigorous vetting process—only well-conceived, technically sound, and realistically resourced projects move forward into design and development.

President Obama, speaking from vacation in Martha’s Vineyard on Aug. 14, 2014, urged calm and unity after the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri. He called Brown’s death “heartbreaking and tragic,” urged peaceful protest and respect for public order, and demanded police be “open and transparent” in the investigation. Obama condemned both looting and the excessive use of force against peaceful demonstrators, criticized arrests and harassment of journalists, and said the Justice Department was assisting local authorities. He praised Governor Jay Nixon and said Attorney General Eric Holder was involved; the Department of Justice, FBI and St. Louis County prosecutor were investigating.

On Iraq, Obama reported progress in the limited U.S. mission: air operations helped break the ISIL siege of Mount Sinjar, enabling many Yazidis to reach safety, and further airstrikes and humanitarian aid would continue.

Locally, Missouri Gov. Jay Nixon handed command of Ferguson security to Capt. Ronald S. Johnson of the Missouri State Highway Patrol and promised a softer, less militarized approach. That shift accompanied largely peaceful daytime marches, clergy-led actions, and community vigils, although some nights had seen looting, arson (a QuikTrip), clashes, tear gas, sonic devices and arrests. Critics—residents, activists, elected officials and media groups—condemned heavy-handed police tactics, the detention of journalists, and lack of transparency; Sen. Claire McCaskill and others urged demilitarizing the response. St. Louis County Prosecuting Attorney Robert McCulloch defended the county police and criticized Nixon’s change in command. The ACLU sued for police reports; civil-rights groups pushed for DOJ action; Anonymous claimed (and later misidentified) the officer’s name and reportedly disrupted county websites. The unrest impacted local businesses and prompted delays in school openings and national attention, including planned rallies and a UN conference discussion of U.S. racial justice concerns.
