Police arrested 56-year-old Anthony Joseph Palma in connection with the 1997 disappearance and presumed killing of 8-year-old Kirsten Hatfield of Midwest City, Oklahoma. Kirsten was taken from her bedroom window on May 14, 1997; torn, bloodstained underwear and blood on the window sill were recovered at the time, but several key items were never DNA-tested or produced inconclusive results with the technology then available.

The case was reassigned in June 2015 to Detective Darrell Miller, who had untested evidence re-examined by the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation. In July 2015 the OSBI crime lab produced a DNA match tying Palma to the blood evidence; investigators say the statistical odds of a coincidental match were astronomically small (reported as on the order of 10^23–10^26 to 1). Palma, who has lived near the victim’s former home since 1991 and has an earlier assault/battery conviction from the 1980s, was interviewed in 1997 and again in 2015; police describe inconsistencies in his statements. He was arrested at his Midwest City residence and booked into the Oklahoma County Jail on charges of kidnapping and first-degree murder.

Authorities believe Kirsten was likely killed shortly after abduction and say Palma may have targeted her for sexual assault; her body has not been found. Investigators continue to work the case, have interviewed and collected DNA from multiple men linked to the original investigation, and say there could be additional suspects. Family members expressed exhaustion from the long ordeal but gratitude and hope after the arrest.

Ben Affleck and Ted Kennedy Jr. both announced they will not run for the Massachusetts Senate seat expected to open when John Kerry is confirmed as U.S. secretary of state. Affleck posted on Facebook that he loves Massachusetts but will focus on his work with the Eastern Congo Initiative, veterans’ issues, hunger advocacy and filmmaking; he said he expects strong Democratic candidates to emerge. Ted Kennedy Jr., who lives primarily in Connecticut, issued a statement declining to run now while leaving open the possibility of future public service. Their decisions leave the likely Democratic field largely unchanged — most often cited are Reps. Michael Capuano, Stephen Lynch and Ed Markey — while former Sen. Scott Brown remains the leading Republican contender. President Obama has pledged to support and fundraise for the eventual Democratic nominee.

Economists call it an “efficiency wage” — paying employees more than the market rate to get greater loyalty, effort and productivity. In 2015 Walmart quietly tested that idea after new leadership concluded years of aggressive cost-cutting had degraded in‑store service, driven away customers and left its workforce disengaged. The company announced a package of “investments”: higher base pay (a $10 floor for trained hourly associates, department managers to $15), more predictable scheduling in pilot stores, and 200 training academies to create clearer career paths from hourly work to management.

Early results have been mixed but instructive. Customer-service scores and same-store sales recovered after the changes, and managers report attracting applicants more interested in careers than stopgap jobs. Training and promotion opportunities appear to matter as much as headline pay increases. However, higher labor costs have weighed on U.S. operating income and Walmart’s stock has lagged peers, leaving investors skeptical about near-term returns. Critics note the measures are incomplete — many hires don’t reach the $10 threshold quickly, schedule reforms are limited in scope, and Walmart still falls short of “good jobs” models used by some rivals.

The Walmart experiment matters beyond the company. If efficiency-wage theory is right, broader employer investment in pay and training could boost productivity and consumer demand — addressing long-term U.S. problems like weak wage growth, slow productivity and a shrinking labor share of income. So far Walmart shows that paying and training workers can improve service and sales at the store level, but not yet profitability. Whether this becomes a lasting strategic shift or a temporary response remains uncertain — and the answer could have important implications for the wider economy.

Here are the key points from the document:

- Rick Santorum downplayed Mitt Romney’s 38–31 percent win over him in the CPAC straw poll, suggesting Romney’s campaign may have boosted turnout by buying tickets for supporters (similar to past tactics attributed to Ron Paul). Santorum said his own campaign did not engage in that practice. Romney’s campaign denied Santorum’s implication, with spokeswoman Andrea Saul calling Santorum’s claim untrue and noting Romney also won a CPAC nationwide conservative survey and the Maine caucuses.

- Ron Paul questioned Romney’s self-description as a “severe” (or “serious”) conservative, saying he wasn’t sure what Romney meant and asking Romney to clarify.

- White House Chief of Staff Jack Lew defended President Obama’s position on contraception and Catholic institutions as consistent. He said the administration’s recent “accommodation” for churches and church-run hospitals and schools is its policy, and asserted insurers would likely pay less for plans that include birth control because such coverage can reduce pregnancies.

Irish lawmakers passed the Protection of Life During Pregnancy Bill after a marathon multi-day debate, legalizing abortion in the Republic of Ireland only when a woman’s life is at risk — including where pregnancy would likely lead to suicide. The Dáil voted 127–31 in favor; the bill was pushed by Taoiseach Enda Kenny’s coalition and provoked strong divisions within his Fine Gael party (five TDs were expelled from the parliamentary party, and one minister, Lucinda Creighton, was removed for opposing the measure).

The law responds to a 1992 Supreme Court ruling and a high-profile case last year of a woman who died after being denied a termination, but it is narrowly framed: abortion remains criminalized in most other circumstances (penalties of up to 14 years’ imprisonment remain), and it does not cover rape or fatal fetal anomalies. Pro-choice groups, campaigners for terminations in cases of fatal fetal abnormality, and civil libertarians warned the law will leave many women forced to travel to Britain (about 4,000 Irish women did so last year) or to seek clandestine options; they and some politicians expect legal challenges, including potential cases in domestic courts or the European Court of Human Rights.

The parliamentary sessions were emotionally charged and chaotic, with large and vocal pro- and anti-abortion demonstrations outside Leinster House. The bill’s passage was hailed by supporters as a necessary, if limited, step toward protecting women’s lives; opponents said it broke election promises and fell far short of broader reproductive rights.

The Muslim Brotherhood, Egypt’s long-banned Islamist opposition movement, emerged from the 2011 uprising with renewed political opportunity but deep internal divisions that make its future role uncertain.

Key fault lines
- Generational split: Young activists (e.g., 29-year-old Moaz Abdel Karim) who helped organize the protests favor political pluralism, human rights, cooperation with secular groups and pragmatic engagement in democratic politics. They used new media to build cross-ideological ties and pushed the Brotherhood into street activism.
- Conservative old guard: Senior leaders (e.g., 66-year-old Supreme Guide Mohamed Badi) represent a hard-line, anti‑Western, Islamist strand that has used inflammatory rhetoric about Jews, supported armed Palestinian groups, and favors a stronger religious role in the state.
- Reformers vs. hard-liners: A pragmatic, electoral wing that has worked in parliament and on social issues clashes with conservative elements that prefer proselytizing, secrecy and strict doctrinal stances. Leadership contests and repression under Mubarak left conservatives dominant in the guidance council.

Recent dynamics
- During the 2011 uprising the Brotherhood’s youth cooperated closely with secular movements; the senior leadership was initially reluctant but later allowed members to participate individually and publicly called for free elections while pledging not to run a presidential candidate.
- The group announced plans to apply for legal party status and issued statements envisioning a “democratic, civil state” informed by Islamic values, but outside observers remain skeptical about how authoritative and lasting such moderation would be.
- Historically the Brotherhood renounced domestic violence in 1972 and has significant social-welfare networks and parliamentary experience (winning 88 seats in 2005), but parts of its movement have spawned violent offshoots and its conservative leadership has at times rolled back moderate positions.

International reactions
- Israel and some U.S. critics fear a takeover by more extreme elements and the potential for a theocratic turn; others, including President Obama and some U.S. analysts, urge engagement and a wait‑and‑see approach, noting the Brotherhood’s heterogeneity and its noninclusion on U.S. terrorist lists.
- Debate in Washington ranges from viewing the Brotherhood as a pragmatic political force to warnings that outside Islamist groups could radicalize it.

Outlook
The Brotherhood’s influence after Mubarak depends on whether the newly empowered youth and pragmatic factions can retain leverage against a conservative leadership that remains strong institutionally and culturally within the movement. That internal contest will shape whether the Brotherhood becomes a moderate political actor integrated into Egypt’s transition or drifts toward a more doctrinal, exclusionary Islamist stance.

Newly filed legal documents obtained by TMZ allege that radio legend Casey Kasem is in severe decline from advanced Parkinson’s disease and dementia. An examining physician reportedly found major impairments in short-, long- and immediate-term memory; verbal communication; basic calculations, planning and reasoning; severe disorganized thinking; and moderate hallucinations. The papers say Kasem is largely bedridden, can only “shuffle short distances,” and has been deteriorating over the past 3–4 years.

The filings were submitted by Julie Kasem, one of Casey’s three children from his first marriage, who is seeking a conservatorship to give her and her husband authority over his health-care decisions. Julie alleges Casey’s wife of 33 years, Jean, has isolated him from his children and prevented phone contact for months. Jean is opposing the move.

Researchers analyzing a 40,000‑year‑old human jawbone (Oase 1) from Peștera cu Oase in southwestern Romania report that this early modern European carried the highest fraction of Neanderthal DNA seen in any Homo sapiens to date. Published in Nature, the study finds 6–9.4% of Oase 1’s nuclear genome derives from Neanderthals, with long Neanderthal-derived segments indicating an ancestor as close as four to six generations back (possibly the equivalent of a great‑great‑grandparent) — perhaps only 100–150 years prior to the individual’s life. 

This shows that interbreeding between modern humans and Neanderthals occurred more recently and in Europe itself, not only earlier in the Near East as previously assumed. Despite living in Europe between about 42,000 and 37,000 years ago, Oase 1’s lineage appears to have been a pioneer population that left little genetic legacy in later Europeans; his genome shares more variants with present‑day East Asians and Native Americans than with Europeans. The finding refines understanding of when and where Homo sapiens and Neanderthals mated and underscores that early admixture events were complex and regionally variable.

This piece recounts the 1984 disappearance of 8-year-old Marjorie “Christy” Luna from Greenacres, Fla., and describes a controversial Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office social‑media campaign on the 33rd anniversary of her vanishing. Christy left home on Memorial Day weekend to buy cat food and never returned; despite extensive investigations over decades—including publicity on billboards, milk cartons and America’s Most Wanted—no arrest was ever made and she was never found. Her mother Jennie Johnson and the community were haunted by the unresolved case; investigators pursued at least four suspects over the years but lacked sufficient evidence.

To spur new leads, the sheriff’s office ran a three‑day campaign (May 26–28) in which Christy’s “voice” was used in real time on Facebook and Twitter to narrate her last hours and plead for help. The posts recreated details of the day, described fear during an apparent abduction, and appealed directly to the public and Christy’s mother. Reactions were mixed: many found the campaign moving and expressed gratitude, while others called it eerie or inappropriate. The effort was modeled on an earlier Royal Canadian Mounted Police campaign that produced tips though no arrest.

The article reviews past investigative threads, including a suspect named Victor Wonyetye—linked by some inmates’ claims and circumstantial timing to other missing‑child cases—who was never charged in Christy’s disappearance and later died in 2013 after a separate prison sentence and release. Two neighborhood brothers were also investigated but not tied to the crime. The sheriff’s office closed the social campaign with a plea to share Christy’s story and provide any information that could finally bring answers and justice for the Luna family.

A Memphis woman, Faith Pugh, says she was betrayed after a date, Kelton Griffin, stole her black Volvo during an outing and used it to take her god-sister on a date. Pugh, who knew Griffin from high school, said he arrived without a car and they ended up at a gas station where he asked her to buy cigars; while she was inside he drove off. Her mother picked her up, and later her god-sister texted that Griffin had asked her out. Using the god-sister’s GPS, Pugh and police tracked Griffin to the Summer Drive-In on Summer Avenue, where officers found him in Pugh’s car; he was arrested and charged with theft of property. WMC notes Griffin has a prior arrest from 2016 related to a restaurant robbery. Pugh said she never wants to see him again.

Samsung’s updated Smart TV privacy policy says voice recognition data — including any spoken words that contain personal or sensitive information — may be captured and transmitted to third-party providers (currently Nuance) for processing. Samsung explains voice commands are sent off-device so speech can be converted to text and the feature can be improved; users must explicitly activate voice search via a remote or on-screen button. The policy notes users can disable voice recognition in settings, though that disables the feature entirely and Samsung may still collect other usage and device data (IP, device identifiers, cookies, viewing and click history) for recommendations and feature evaluation. The TVs also include a camera for gesture control and optional facial-recognition sign-in; facial images are stored locally but Samsung may log when the feature is used. Third-party apps and content providers may collect additional data and have separate privacy practices. Samsung says data is encrypted, that a microphone icon appears when voice features are active, and owners can disconnect Wi‑Fi to stop networked data flows.

The policy provoked public backlash and comparisons to Orwell’s 1984 and to other always-listening consumer devices. Critics pointed to the combination of always-available mics/cameras in internet-enabled home devices and the forwarding of voice data to third parties as a troubling privacy trend. The document similarly echoes earlier concerns raised about Microsoft’s Xbox One Kinect, which runs in a low-power “listening” state to respond to spoken wake commands and raised questions about constant ambient listening and potential misuse. Microsoft and Samsung both assert they implement privacy safeguards and give users ways to disable or limit features.

After the Senate's failed attempt to pass a "skinny" Obamacare repeal, President Trump urged changing Senate rules to require a simple 51-vote majority for legislation instead of the traditional 60-vote threshold (the filibuster). He tweeted that Republicans must move to a 51-vote standard to pass future legislation, though he later acknowledged some measures still need 60 votes. The repeal effort collapsed early Friday when three Republican senators — John McCain, Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins — joined Democrats to sink the bill in a 49-51 vote; the reconciliation process being used would have required only 51 votes, but the GOP did not reach that. Trump criticized the defecting senators and suggested letting Obamacare "implode" if repeal failed, prompting rebukes from Democrats who said such threats would harm innocent people. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has said he does not support abolishing the 60-vote threshold, and many major bills (like spending measures) would still need 60 votes unless rules are changed.

Defense Secretary James Mattis delivered a spirited pep talk to U.S. service members while on a visit to Jordan, Turkey and Ukraine last week; a smartphone video of the remarks has circulated on social media. In the clip—likely filmed in Jordan—Mattis praised the troops, thanked them for service, joked that he “flunked” retirement and said he returned to serve alongside “selfless” and “rambunctious” young service members.

Mattis told the forces to “hold the line” amid partisan divisions and turmoil in the U.S., urging them to maintain professionalism “until our country gets back to understanding and respecting each other.” He framed America’s military power in two forms—“inspiration” and “intimidation”—calling the troops the deterrent against threats to U.S. families, the country and allies, and saying the nation will “get the power of inspiration back.”

The remarks came during a week of national controversy following deadly violence at a white supremacist rally in Charlottesville and immediately before President Trump issued a memo to bar most transgender recruits and limit transition-related care. Mattis’s comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled rebuke of the political climate in Washington and of the administration’s handling of those events; the transgender policy change, which had reportedly surprised some Pentagon leaders, drew criticism from service members, veterans and lawmakers.

Activists and city officials are clashing over an aggressive Detroit Water and Sewerage Department (DWSD) campaign to cut service to customers at least 60 days delinquent. DWSD says the shutoffs — which have ramped up since March and resulted in thousands of residential disconnections in recent months — are aimed at recouping roughly $175 million in unpaid bills and reducing costs that drive up rates for paying customers. DWSD also says payment plans and assistance programs exist and recently designated $1 million for low-income residents.

Protesters, aided by local and international supporters and backed by a U.N. human-rights finding that some disconnections constitute rights violations, have staged regular demonstrations and civil disobedience. On Thursday about 50 people blocked the lot of Homrich, the contractor that executes residential shutoffs; at least nine protesters — including religious leaders and a school board member running for state office — were arrested and charged with disorderly conduct. Activists say shutoffs have targeted vulnerable households, including families with young children, the elderly and disabled, while some large commercial and governmental accounts with substantial debts (examples cited include golf courses owing hundreds of thousands and the State of Michigan owing about $70,000) have not been pursued as aggressively.

DWSD officials acknowledge commercial customers are delinquent as well but say their contractor is equipped mainly for residential shutoffs and the department is mobilizing its own crews for larger commercial accounts. The department posted a list of major commercial delinquents and says tougher collections are necessary; critics counter that enforcement has been inequitable and disproportionately harms the poorest residents in a city with roughly a 44% poverty rate and household water bills that average about $75 — nearly double the national average.

The dispute has drawn national and international attention, prompted appeals for federal assistance from Detroit’s congressional delegation, and produced emergency aid efforts such as cross-border deliveries of bottled water. Activists vow further direct action if DWSD continues shutoffs, while the utility insists it must collect payments to sustain operations.

A 27-year-old French-Canadian, Alexandre Bissonnette, was charged with six counts of first-degree murder and five counts of attempted murder after a mass shooting during evening prayers at the Centre Culturel Islamique de Québec that left six men dead and at least 19 wounded. The attack occurred shortly before 8 p.m. with more than 50 people present; victims included a butcher, a university professor, a pharmacist, an accountant and a mosque concierge, and ranged in age from about 21 to 60. Five people remained hospitalized (two critical), and others treated for minor injuries.

Bissonnette, a Laval University student who also worked at Héma-Québec, made a brief, mostly silent court appearance in shackles and was remanded until a Feb. 21 hearing. Police arrested him after he parked about five kilometres from the mosque and called 911 to cooperate. Authorities initially detained a second man outside the mosque but later released him as a witness. Provincial police are treating the incident as a terrorist act and said terrorism charges could be considered later; prosecutors charged Bissonnette with murder and weapons offences based on available evidence.

Observers and activists noted Bissonnette’s social-media activity and local reputation for far-right, nationalist views, including support for France’s Marine Le Pen and anti-multicultural positions. The shooting has intensified concerns about Islamophobia in Quebec, where debates over religious accommodation and bans on religious symbols have been prominent.

National leaders condemned the attack: Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called it a terrorist act, pledged solidarity with Canada’s Muslim community and attended a vigil; Quebec Premier Philippe Couillard and municipal leaders likewise expressed shock and vowed solidarity. The incident prompted increased security at mosques in some cities and vigils across Canada and abroad. Investigations, including searches of residences, continued as authorities sought motive and evaluated whether further charges (including terrorism-related) were warranted.

La FDA aprobó AquAdvantage, el primer animal modificado genéticamente destinado al consumo humano: un salmón Atlántico de AquaBounty que crece aproximadamente el doble de rápido gracias a un gen de hormona de crecimiento del salmón Chinook y un promotor del pez ocean pout. Tras una extensa revisión científica, la agencia concluyó que el salmón GE es tan seguro y nutritivo como el salmón no modificado; los genes insertados son estables, la carne es segura para personas y animales, la modificación no daña a los peces y cumple la función de crecimiento más rápido. La FDA también evaluó impactos ambientales y determinó que la aprobación no tendría un efecto significativo en EE. UU., dado que la producción estará confinada a instalaciones en tierra en Canadá y Panamá con múltiples medidas de contención; además, la compañía asegura que los peces son hembras y estériles.

La aprobación impone condiciones: cría sólo en tanques terrestres en dos instalaciones específicas y auditorías regulares; no permite por ahora cría en EE. UU., aunque podrían solicitarse futuras autorizaciones. La decisión generó fuertes críticas de grupos ambientalistas, pescadores y algunos legisladores que temen riesgos ecológicos y precedentes para otros animales GE; varios minoristas ya se han comprometido a no vender el producto. La FDA no exigirá etiquetado especial porque no encontró diferencias materiales en el perfil nutricional, aunque publicó orientaciones sobre etiquetado voluntario y permitirá comentarios públicos. Dado el volumen limitado de producción inicial, expertos prevén que el salmón GE no será ampliamente encontrado pronto en el mercado.

During a March 21, 2013 speech to university students in Jerusalem, President Barack Obama was briefly interrupted by a heckler reportedly demanding the release of Jonathan Pollard, a former U.S. Navy intelligence analyst serving life for spying for Israel. Obama deflected the interruption with humor, telling the audience the heckle had been “arranged” to make him “feel at home” and that he wouldn’t be comfortable without at least one heckler. The article notes efforts in Israel and the U.S. to press the Obama administration for Pollard’s release, but recalls Obama’s March 14 statement that Pollard committed “a serious crime” and there were “no plans” to release him. It also mentions prior public hecklings of Obama, including Rep. Joe Wilson in 2010 and a reporter in 2012.

Sean Penn has been charged with misdemeanor battery and vandalism over an October altercation with a photographer outside a Brentwood store. Los Angeles city prosecutors allege Penn kicked the photographer and broke his camera; TMZ video shows Penn chasing the photographer, striking him and shouting “get out,” though the footage does not show the camera leaving the photographer’s hands. If convicted, Penn faces up to 18 months in jail. He is due to be arraigned March 22 in Los Angeles County Superior Court. Penn’s representatives have not commented. The new charges follow earlier incidents: he received a suspended sentence 25 years ago after assaulting journalists pursuing then-wife Madonna, and he has prior on-set and paparazzi-related run-ins.

The document also profiles Penn’s extensive Haiti relief work since the Jan. 12, 2010 earthquake. Penn moved to Port-au-Prince soon after the quake, helped fly in supplies and staffed relief flights, and became camp manager of a large J/P Haitian Relief Organization site that shelters some 55,000 people. The camp—built on a former golf course—includes medical care, cholera treatment, a market and other services; it costs about $450,000 a month to run. Penn has used personal funds, arranged aid with nonprofits (Oxfam, Save the Children) and at times negotiated with local gang leaders to maintain security. He is portrayed as driven, exhausted and deeply committed, alternating between Haiti and home in Malibu while also working on a film.

The piece situates Penn among other Hollywood relief efforts (Paul Haggis, Maria Bello, Ben Stiller, Patricia Arquette, etc.), highlights challenges in Haiti—cholera outbreaks, hurricane threats, gang violence, slow international response—and includes several human-interest vignettes (a school visit, a women’s clinic in Cité Soleil, a film school in Jacmel). It also touches on Penn’s personal life: his 2010 availability for Haiti work followed a costly divorce from Robin Wright (he says he “got taken for one-half of everything”), and he describes the emotional toll of not raising his son in an intact family. Overall, the article contrasts recent legal trouble with Penn’s high-profile humanitarian commitment and personal sacrifices.

The news content centers on leaked nude photographs of Prince Harry taken during a Las Vegas hotel party. Tabloid and gossip outlets published grainy images showing the 27-year-old royal nude; TMZ reported several women took photos and videos on their cellphones. Playgirl’s publisher, Vincent Stevens, publicly suggested Harry would be a lucrative candidate for a nude centerfold—estimating offers would start in the low six figures and possibly reach around a million dollars—though no formal approach had been made. Australia’s Thunder From Down Under producer also quipped Harry would be a draw for their revue.

Rupert Murdoch’s The Sun ran the photos on its front page arguing public interest, a move privacy lawyer Chris Hutchings said might be defensible because Harry represents Britain abroad, though the images are inherently private. Oklahoma Gov. Mary Fallin signed Senate Bill 1023, banning cities and counties from setting local minimum wages, paid-sick-day or vacation requirements. The measure was framed by supporters as protecting businesses and jobs: Fallin said local minimum-wage mandates would drive businesses away, raise consumer prices and risk job losses (citing a CBO report on potential national job impacts). Proponents in the Legislature argued the ban keeps Oklahoma economically competitive.

Critics say the law was aimed at stopping an Oklahoma City grassroots effort to place a $10.10 minimum-wage initiative on the local ballot (above the $7.25 federal rate). Organizers, led by attorney David Slain/Slane, said they are disappointed, will continue signature-gathering and are considering legal challenges or pursuing a statewide initiative. Opponents also fault supporters’ characterization of typical minimum-wage workers as mostly teenagers, noting Economic Policy Institute data showing most affected workers are older than 20 (average age 35), many work full time and many have children. Some lawmakers called the bill “immoral,” arguing the current wage can leave full-time workers in poverty.

Rudy Giuliani has withdrawn from consideration for a Cabinet post in President-elect Donald Trump’s administration, ending his public bid for secretary of state. The transition team said he pulled out on Nov. 29; Trump praised Giuliani’s campaign service and called him a close friend, saying he may be called on for advice or a future role. Giuliani explained his decision as wanting to avoid being a distraction to the transition and preferring to advise from the outside while returning to his private-sector work; the transition described his stated reason as wanting to remain in the private sector.

Giuliani had campaigned vigorously for the secretary of state job and remained in internal discussions into the week before withdrawing. His high-profile self-promotion, questions about his stamina for the demands of the role, concerns about contentious confirmation hearings, and scrutiny of paid foreign consulting work were cited by aides as factors that hurt his chances. Other contenders for secretary of state include Rex Tillerson (reported as the leading candidate), Mitt Romney, Sen. Bob Corker, retired Adm. James Stavridis, John Bolton and former Ford CEO Alan Mulally. Allies say Giuliani is disappointed but will remain a close adviser to Trump; the transition reiterated he may serve in other capacities later.

- A WHO and U.S. National Cancer Institute study finds tobacco use costs the global economy more than $1 trillion annually in healthcare and lost productivity, far exceeding annual tobacco tax revenues (~$269 billion in 2013–14). The peer‑reviewed report projects tobacco‑related deaths to rise from about 6 million per year today to about 8 million by 2030, with over 80% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Although prevalence is falling in some populations, the total number of smokers is increasing because about 80% of smokers live in LMICs.

- The 688‑page study stresses that governments have effective, low‑cost tobacco control tools—higher tobacco taxes and prices, comprehensive smoke‑free laws, bans on tobacco marketing, prominent pictorial warnings—and that revenues from tobacco taxes can fund mass‑media campaigns and cessation services. However, governments currently spend under $1 billion on tobacco control (2013–14 estimate) and are generally not using available measures effectively. The report rejects claims that tobacco control harms economies and calls for urgent action.

- The article also covers legal and policy developments around plain packaging. Australia’s landmark plain‑packaging law (introduced in 2011) was defended successfully in an investor‑state arbitration: Philip Morris Asia’s 2011 challenge under a Hong Kong–Australia investment treaty was dismissed for lack of tribunal jurisdiction. Australian officials and public‑health groups hailed the ruling as reinforcing plain packaging and encouraging other countries to adopt similar measures. Philip Morris said it was reviewing options and criticized the procedural outcome.

- Plain packaging is under additional international scrutiny: a World Trade Organization complaint by Cuba, Indonesia, Honduras and the Dominican Republic is pending, and other countries (including Norway, Canada, Singapore, Belgium, South Africa, France, Britain and Ireland) are considering or moving to similar laws. The article notes broader trade‑policy concerns about investor‑state dispute mechanisms that can allow corporations to challenge public‑interest regulations.

This document combines two unrelated pieces: a brief note about web-crawling by the Internet Archive and a longer item about cat behavior based on British biologist John Bradshaw’s work.

- Internet Archive effort: The Archive performs crawls to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference, so that when referenced pages change or disappear, links can point to the version that was live when the citing page was written. The aim is to reduce broken links across the web by archiving supported "No More 404" sites and encouraging use of those archived links.

- Cat behavior (John Bradshaw): Bradshaw, author of Cat Sense and director of the Anthrozoology Institute at the University of Bristol, explains common feline behaviors and what they mean for human–cat relationships:
  - Tail-up and rubbing against legs is a friendly greeting cats use with each other (often by smaller toward larger cats) and was adapted to communicate affection to humans as cats domesticated.
  - Owners should let cats initiate contact—cats prefer to start interactions, and waiting for the tail-up gesture helps interactions last longer.
  - Purring can signal contentment but also serve as an attention-seeking or help-seeking signal rooted in kitten behavior.
  - Key signs a cat is fond of you are: the tail-up/rub ritual, resting in contact, and mutual grooming. A cat needn’t show all three to be affectionate; consistent tail-up/rubbing is a strong positive sign.
  - For more detail, Bradshaw’s book Cat Sense and its publisher’s site are recommended.

Researchers investigated whether regional populations of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae contribute to wine “terroir” by influencing Sauvignon Blanc aroma and chemistry. Building on earlier work that sampled 3,900 S. cerevisiae isolates from native forests, vineyards and spontaneous ferments across six New Zealand wine regions (Hawke’s Bay, Martinborough, Nelson, Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley and Central Otago), the team selected representative genotypes from each region based on Bayesian ancestry profiles and regional allele frequencies. Six genotypes per region (plus regional co-inoculations combining the six) were fermented in triplicate in sterilized, homogenized Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc juice, producing 126 experimental ferments; after removing failed or suspect ferment replicates, 112 successful ferments were analyzed.

Analyses:
- Measured 39 volatile compounds and standard wine quality parameters by targeted GC-MS and FTIR.
- Used PERMANOVA, constrained correspondence analysis (CCA) and ANOVAs to test effects of yeast origin, genetic relatedness, and co-fermentation versus blending on chemical profiles.

Key findings:
- Region of yeast isolation had a small but statistically significant effect on volatile chemical profiles of wines made by single genotypes. Region explained about 10–13% of overall variation (R2 ≈ 0.10–0.13; P ≤ 0.002). Using inferred genetic clusters instead of geography raised explained variance to ~15%, and restricting to genotypes with clear regional ancestry increased the regional R2 to ~20%.
- Pairwise comparisons showed varying degrees of regional differentiation: Nelson yeasts produced the most distinct chemical signature (notably higher levels of esters linked to apple/sweet-fruit aromas), while Awatere and Wairau Valleys showed the least distinct profiles. Central Otago, Martinborough and Hawke’s Bay were intermediate.
- Many individual compounds varied by region: 29 of 39 measured compounds showed region-associated variation. Key drivers included esters such as ethyl isobutyrate, ethyl-2-methyl butanoate and ethyl butanoate, and β-damascenone, which mapped to plausible sensory descriptors (apple, sweet fruit, peach, honey/floral) and differed predictably among regions.
- Genetic distance (microsatellite profiles) among yeast strains correlated significantly with chemical profile distance (Mantel R2 = 0.189, P < 0.0001), supporting a genetic basis for the chemical differences.
- Co-fermentation (inoculating all six regional genotypes together) vs blending (mixing finished single-genotype wines) produced different chemical outcomes; co-ferments were more variable and differed in specific ethyl esters. Co-fermentation tended to weaken—but did not fully eliminate—the regional signal, while blending appeared to erode regional differences more.

Conclusions:
- Natural, regionally structured populations of S. cerevisiae impart a measurable, genetically correlated influence on wine volatile chemistry, providing experimental evidence that microbes are a component of terroir. The microbial contribution is modest compared with other terroir factors but is statistically robust and chemically meaningful—especially for fruity ester compounds. Co-fermentation interactions among strains modify, and can partially obscure, the regional chemical signatures. The study suggests potential for using or manipulating regional yeast communities to influence wine character and calls for further work to assess sensory impacts and contributions of other microbial taxa.

Steve Jobs resigned as Apple’s CEO but remains chairman of the board, a move that may change little operationally. Jobs had already handed day-to-day duties to Tim Cook in January while on medical leave; Cook has now been named CEO and added to Apple’s board, increasing it from seven to eight directors. Other board members include co-lead directors Andrea Jung and Arthur Levinson, plus William Campbell, Millard Drexler, Al Gore and Ronald Sugar.

Although Jobs is no longer the company’s operational leader, he has stayed involved in major decisions this year (for example, unveiling the iPad 2). Many products in Apple’s near-term pipeline — including the then-upcoming iPhone 5 and likely iPad 3 — were developed under Jobs’ influence, so Apple will continue to reflect his imprint for some time. Observers argue the timing of the resignation was strategic: Apple was at peak strength, reporting record earnings and poised to release key products, making it a good moment for a leadership transition that gives Cook room to establish himself.

Commentary highlights a broader debate about Apple’s future without Jobs: one perspective credits Cook for operational and supply-chain mastery that helped make Apple hugely profitable; another worries that without Jobs’ visionary role the company could shift toward control-, marketing- and litigation-driven strategies rather than breakthrough innovation. Ultimately, while Jobs’ formal role has changed, his influence remains, and Apple’s long-term direction will depend on how internal factions and new leadership balance operational excellence with product-driven innovation.

Twitter removed verification badges from several prominent far-right figures after announcing plans to change its verification process. Some users, like Tim “Baked Alaska” Gionet, were permanently banned and reacted publicly and wildly; others, including neo‑Nazi organizers Richard Spencer and Jason Kessler, lost verification but remain active on the platform. The moves have been portrayed as largely symbolic — aimed at distancing Twitter from extremist figures without fully removing them.

Laura Loomer, a controversial right‑wing activist and former Project Veritas employee, reacted particularly strongly to losing her blue check. Around the same time, she launched an anti‑Muslim rant on Twitter after the New York terror attack that referenced the suspect’s former job as an Uber driver. Her posts included calls to avoid Muslim drivers and a photo-targeting people in hijabs. Uber and Lyft confirmed her accounts were deactivated; Loomer said she would sue both companies. Her remarks drew widespread criticism and reports of hate speech, with celebrities and others condemning her.

McDonald’s pulled and apologized for a U.K. TV advert that many viewers and charities said inappropriately used childhood bereavement to promote its food. The 90‑second spot, created by Leo Burnett and first aired May 12, shows a young boy asking his mother about his deceased father; after she lists qualities the boy doesn’t share, they visit McDonald’s and she reveals they both liked the Filet‑o‑Fish. Social media users and bereavement groups called the ad “insensitive,” “cynical” and “exploitative,” and Grief Encounter said it fielded numerous calls from upset parents. Around 100 complaints were lodged with the Advertising Standards Authority. McDonald’s said upsetting people was never its intention, pledged to review its creative process, began withdrawing the ad (with the last airing scheduled for May 17) and is reviewing customer feedback. Grief charities and affected families criticized the ad’s timing (near Father’s Day), its suggestion a meal can “cure” grief, and the lack of support information for bereaved viewers.

Joseph P. Kennedy III has formally entered the race for the U.S. House seat being vacated by Barney Frank, marking the most visible step yet toward restoring Kennedy representation in Congress for the first time since 2010. At 31, Kennedy — a Stanford and Harvard Law graduate, former Peace Corps volunteer and current assistant district attorney in Middlesex County — plans to resign his DA post when the new term begins to run for the Massachusetts seat. His move ends months of speculation and is being framed as both a family comeback and a potential boost to Democratic hopes in Massachusetts after recent setbacks, notably Scott Brown’s 2010 upset of Ted Kennedy’s Senate seat. Some longtime Kennedy loyalists wished he had built a longer prosecutorial or district attorney record before seeking elected office, but supporters point to his oratory, pedigree and the switch to Middlesex County (a more Democratic base than Cape Cod) as strategic advantages. The campaign is portrayed as part of a broader Democratic effort to reclaim Massachusetts for the party and re-energize the electorate alongside rising figures like Elizabeth Warren.

Acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) is a rare, sudden-onset, polio‑like neurologic syndrome that chiefly affects children and has shown a worrying rise in the United States in recent years. It produces rapid limb weakness (often asymmetric), facial droop, difficulty swallowing or breathing, and spinal cord gray‑matter lesions on MRI; some patients require ventilator support. Most affected children report a preceding fever or respiratory illness.

Epidemiology and trends
- CDC surveillance began in 2014 after a cluster in Colorado; that year 120 confirmed cases occurred (Aug–Dec), mostly in children. Follow‑up showed partial recovery for many but very few full recoveries.
- Cases fell in subsequent years but climbed again in 2016: by Aug 31 there were 50 confirmed cases across 24 states (up from 21 cases for all of 2015). Through July of an earlier report there were 32 confirmed cases in 17 states; overall AFM remains rare but the trend has alarmed clinicians who note similarities to the 2014 pattern and expect more cases in late summer and fall when enteroviruses circulate.

Cause and investigations
- The cause remains unproven. AFM has been linked epidemiologically to enteroviruses (notably enterovirus D68, EV‑D68) and other viruses including adenoviruses and West Nile, but direct causation has not been definitively established: many AFM spinal fluid samples have been negative for enteroviruses even when respiratory samples sometimes test positive.
- The 2014 AFM surge coincided with a large EV‑D68 respiratory outbreak; some investigators found EV‑D68 in respiratory samples from AFM patients, but CDC stresses causality is unconfirmed.
- Ongoing laboratory and animal work (including a mouse model reportedly reproducing paralysis after EV‑D68 infection) aims to clarify mechanisms and test therapies.

Clinical care and outcomes
- No proven specific antiviral or immunologic therapy exists. Treatments tried include intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), steroids, and other agents; evidence of benefit is limited. Rehabilitation (physical, occupational, speech therapy) is central to care.
- Many patients improve somewhat over months, but significant residual weakness often persists; in many cases recovery plateaus after about a year.

Public health response and advice
- CDC and state health departments are actively tracking cases and issuing alerts to clinicians to report suspected cases and submit specimens.
- Because a viral trigger is suspected, public health guidance emphasizes routine hygiene and infection‑prevention measures (handwashing, avoiding close contact with sick people, cleaning surfaces), staying current on vaccinations (including polio), and mosquito protection where relevant.

Human impact
- The reports include multiple heartbreaking family stories of rapid, inexplicable paralysis in previously healthy children—illustrating medical uncertainty, long rehabilitation needs, and the emotional toll on families.

Bottom line: AFM is a rare but disabling neurologic syndrome that has resurged in recent years. Its cause is still under investigation, treatments are unproven, and public health officials urge vigilance, reporting of cases, and basic infection‑prevention practices while research continues.
