Separately, many medical startups aim to diagnose many diseases from a single drop of blood—appealing because fingerpricks are less invasive and easier to use in low-resource settings. However, researchers at Rice 360° Institute for Global Health found large variability between multiple fingerprick drops from the same person: in tests of seven drops from 10 people, measures like hemoglobin and platelet counts varied enough that the authors advised caution about relying on a single drop. To match the accuracy of standard venous draws in their work, they had to average six to nine drops per person. 

Theranos, which once claimed broad testing from a few drops, has faced regulatory scrutiny. Other companies such as Genalyte are pursuing single-drop diagnostics too; unlike Theranos, Genalyte has published peer‑reviewed studies and is initially targeting autoimmune diseases like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.

Summary:

Capnocytophaga is a group of bacteria commonly found in the mouths of dogs and cats (present in a large proportion of pets) and in some humans. Transmission to people can occur through bites, scratches, or close contact (including licking). Most exposures do not cause illness, but in rare cases—especially in people with weakened immune systems—the bacteria can invade the bloodstream and cause severe infections including sepsis, septicemia, endocarditis, gangrene, abscesses, and inflammation of eyes, lymph nodes or brain membranes. Typical symptoms appear within 1–14 days and may include fever, localized redness, swelling, pus, blisters, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and muscle or joint pain. Preventive advice includes avoiding risky contact with animals and seeking prompt care after bites; people with higher-risk conditions should consult their doctors about safely interacting with pets.

Case example: In late June 2018 a 48-year-old Wisconsin man, Greg Manteufel, developed fulminant Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis after likely exposure from a dog. He initially thought he had the flu; within hours he progressed to septic shock and within days required multiple amputations (both legs through the knees and hands down to mid-palms) and extensive reconstructive procedures. His family says he remains grateful to be alive but faces a prolonged recovery, many surgeries and the need for prosthetics; a GoFundMe was created to help cover costs. Medical experts stress this outcome is extremely rare and that most dog owners will never experience it.

Kevin Curran, a veteran TV comedy writer and producer, died at his Los Angeles home after a long illness. He was 59. A Harvard College graduate and former Harvard Lampoon editor, Curran met longtime colleague Al Jean at Harvard. He spent about 15 years on The Simpsons (on staff since 2001), most recently as co‑executive producer, wrote notable episodes including “I’m Spelling as Fast as I Can,” “Don’t Fear the Roofer,” and co‑wrote/conceived the 2002 Treehouse of Horror segment “The Island of Dr. Hibbert.” He shared three Emmys for The Simpsons (among many nominations).

Earlier he won three consecutive Emmys (1985–87) as part of the writing team on Late Night with David Letterman. His other TV credits include Married... with Children (where he also voiced the family dog Buck), Unhappily Ever After (executive producer), and The Good Life. Curran is survived by a son and a daughter with former partner author Helen Fielding. Colleagues, including Al Jean and former Letterman writers, paid tribute on social media, remembering him as brilliant, funny and kind.

A senior White House official’s refusal to address questions about national security adviser Michael Flynn added to growing uncertainty about Flynn’s standing in the Trump administration. Stephen Miller, the White House senior policy adviser, repeatedly declined on Sunday to say whether President Trump still has confidence in Flynn, saying that question should be answered by Trump, Vice President Mike Pence or Chief of Staff Reince Priebus. The choice to send Miller — whose responsibilities do not include foreign policy — to multiple Sunday shows appeared calculated to avoid a definitive response.

Flynn’s future is in doubt after reports that he may have misled colleagues, including Pence, about conversations with Russia’s ambassador in the weeks before the inauguration. The FBI has reportedly investigated whether Flynn discussed U.S. sanctions with Ambassador Sergey Kislyak and whether his contacts violated rules barring private citizens from conducting diplomacy. Flynn had denied discussing sanctions but his representative later said Flynn couldn’t be certain the topic never came up. Since The Washington Post’s report, the White House has largely avoided publicly defending Flynn; Trump said he was unaware of the report and later tweeted support for Miller’s statements without mentioning Flynn.

Separately, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer urged Trump to abandon his travel-ban executive order, calling it ineffective, unconstitutional and economically harmful. Schumer argued the order doesn’t improve security in meaningful ways and noted vulnerabilities in the visa-waiver program, warning that threats could come through friendly countries more easily than from the seven nations targeted. He also said the ban’s “genesis” made it especially toxic.

Other items from Sunday’s coverage: Miller defended intensified ICE enforcement as fulfilling campaign promises to remove criminal immigrants, and said the administration was exploring all options — including new executive actions or appeals — after a federal appeals court blocked Trump’s travel ban, criticizing judges for overstepping.

Miami Gardens Police Chief Stephen E. Johnson, 53, was arrested Feb. 27, 2015, in a Broward Sheriff’s Office undercover sting in Dania Beach for soliciting prostitution and was fired the same day. Detectives had placed an escort ad on Backpage.com and posed as escorts in a hotel room. According to the sheriff’s affidavit, Johnson called the ad, agreed to pay $100 for a “two-girl” 30‑minute encounter, arrived at the hotel with two condoms in his pocket, handed over cash and was immediately arrested; the encounter was recorded. He posted a $300 bond and apologized to the community, attributing his actions to job-related stress.

City Manager Cameron Benson terminated Johnson within hours and named Assistant Chief Antonio Brooklen interim chief. Mayor Oliver Gilbert and city officials emphasized that the department would move forward and said Johnson’s conduct would not reflect on the rank-and-file. Johnson had been hired in spring 2014 to help repair the department’s reputation after prior controversies, including allegations of racial profiling and a recent officer-involved fatal shooting that had prompted protests. Johnson previously served long tenure in North Miami, including as police chief and as city manager, and is also listed as a pastor.

This document is a two-part critical review of Catherine Hardwicke’s 2011 film Red Riding Hood, starring Amanda Seyfried. Both critics find the movie visually striking in places and anchored by Seyfried’s screen presence, but ultimately uneven, tonally confused and disappointing.

Key points:
- Rating and content: The film is PG-13 for “violence and creature terror, and some sensuality.” It contains mild bloodshed, some eroticized moments (notably Seyfried’s sensuality), and a tame, unconvincing CGI wolf.
- Performances and direction: Amanda Seyfried’s charisma and beauty are highlighted as the film’s main asset; she commands the screen. Catherine Hardwicke, who previously directed Thirteen and Twilight, shows an eye for young actors and striking aerial shots, but her handling of the material is inconsistent and occasionally careless.
- Story and tone: The film modernizes the fairy tale and emphasizes adolescent sexuality and moral ambiguity—Valerie (Seyfried) is torn between two suitors, Peter (Shiloh Fernandez) and Henry (Max Irons), while also navigating family and village pressures. Hardwicke attempts to explore themes of sex, death, and female agency, but the screenplay (by David Leslie Johnson) treats these themes weakly, aiming at young-adult audiences with contemporary touches that sometimes feel like pandering or sloppy costume/production decisions.
- Supporting elements: Gary Oldman plays an over-the-top Father Solomon whose showy arrival and contraptions (including a large elephant-shaped torture device) add busywork rather than genuine menace. Julie Christie as the grandmother and Virginia Madsen and Billy Burke in parental roles are noted. The wolf effects are widely criticized as laughable and unthreatening.
- Context and influences: The review notes the film’s flirtation with the Twilight-style formula (romantic danger, brooding suitors) and references literary retellings—particularly Angela Carter’s darker, feminist take—suggesting Hardwicke’s version lacks the bite of those precedents.
- Overall judgment: Visually interesting at times and buoyed by Seyfried’s presence, Red Riding Hood is nevertheless an implausible, overly serious, and tonally muddled adolescent fantasy that fails to convincingly marry its fairy-tale roots with the adult themes it tries to address.

Practicals: Directed by Catherine Hardwicke; screenplay by David Leslie Johnson; runtime ~100 minutes; released by Warner Bros.; principal cast includes Amanda Seyfried, Shiloh Fernandez, Max Irons, Gary Oldman, Julie Christie, Virginia Madsen, and Billy Burke.

Pope Francis capped a packed first full day in New York City with an evening Mass at Madison Square Garden that transformed the arena into a bustling place of worship for about 24,000 people. Preceded by a star-studded program (“A Journey in Faith”) featuring Martin Sheen, Jennifer Hudson, Harry Connick Jr. and others, the Mass drew thunderous applause, loud spontaneous greetings and emotional moments — Cardinal Timothy Dolan embraced the pope and presented him a golden chalice, the crowd cheered his processional ride-through, and Francis blessed a baby and asked attendees to pray for him in English at the close.

The Garden appearance followed a day of high-profile stops across Manhattan: a major address at the United Nations urging action on climate change, a solemn visit and interfaith prayer service at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum where he laid a white rose and comforted victims’ families, and a warm meet-and-greet with schoolchildren in East Harlem. In Central Park he rode the popemobile to cheers from some 80,000 people before continuing to MSG.

Throughout his remarks and appearances Francis emphasized themes central to his U.S. visit: the dignity and inclusion of the poor, migrants and the marginalized in big cities; care for the environment and opposition to its destruction; the need to combat extreme poverty by empowering people with housing, work and land; and support for diplomatic efforts such as the Iran nuclear agreement. He also reaffirmed traditional Catholic positions on abortion, contraception and gay marriage. His messages won broad popular acclaim and drew praise from some political leaders while provoking controversy among certain critics.

The pope’s New York program mixed solemn pastoral ministry — consoling 9/11 families, praying for victims, participating in an interfaith service — with warm, populist encounters and media-savvy moments that reinforced his reputation for humility and accessibility. He spent the night at the Vatican UN representative’s residence and was scheduled to fly to Philadelphia the next morning.

Former Florida governor and Republican presidential candidate Jeb Bush sparked immediate controversy after telling an evangelical audience in Nashville that he wasn’t “sure we need half a billion dollars in funding for women’s health programs” while arguing Planned Parenthood should be defunded. He framed the remark as a preference to redirect federal funds to community health centers and reiterated opposition to government funding for abortion. Democrats, led by Hillary Clinton, seized on the comment, portraying it as evidence Republicans devalue women’s health; Clinton cited examples such as early cancer detection and contraception access. The Democratic National Committee condemned Bush and his remark was quickly amplified on social media and in campaign events.

Bush and his campaign moved quickly to walk back and clarify the comment, with Bush posting that he “misspoke,” praising community health centers and reiterating that he was specifically referring to roughly $500 million in federal funding to Planned Parenthood amid allegations about fetal tissue practices. The episode intensified scrutiny of Bush’s unscripted style after several recent gaffes (on work hours, Medicare, and Iraq) and raised concerns that the clip could be used in future Democratic ads. The report also reviews Bush’s mixed record on women’s health in Florida—highlighting programs he signed and funded (Mary Brogan breast and cervical cancer program, a “Fight Breast Cancer” license plate, and an Office of Women’s Health strategy) alongside statistics showing rising uninsured rates and growing Medicaid costs during his governorship.

A deadly fire tore through the cells at a state police station and detention center in Valencia, Carabobo state, Venezuela, on March 28, 2018, killing 68 people, Attorney General Tarek William Saab said. Saab said 66 of the dead were men and two were women, and four prosecutors were assigned to investigate. Officials and rights groups said the blaze erupted amid a disturbance or attempted breakout; local monitors reported an armed detainee shot an officer in the leg, inmates set mattresses alight and flames spread quickly through overcrowded cells. Rescuers had to break through a wall to free some prisoners.

Angry, distraught relatives gathered outside the station seeking information and clashed with police; officers used tear gas and riot police were deployed. Witnesses and advocacy groups highlighted squalid, overcrowded conditions in police-station jails, where detainees are often held long-term and contraband, weapons and corruption are common. Human-rights monitors and opposition politicians demanded accountability and clearer information about the victims. The fire is one of Venezuela’s deadliest jail disasters in decades and underscores chronic problems in the country’s prison system.

President Barack Obama honored veterans at a Veterans Day ceremony Nov. 11 at Arlington National Cemetery, laying a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknowns and speaking at the Memorial Amphitheater. He paid tribute to "the heroes over the generations" and emphasized that ceremonies and thanks are not enough — the nation must "serve you as well as you've served us" every day. Obama highlighted the Sept. 11 generation’s service in Iraq and Afghanistan, noting this was the first Veterans Day in a decade without U.S. combat troops in Iraq and that a decade-long Afghanistan campaign is winding down. He warned that more than 1 million service members will transition to civilian life in coming years and urged sustained public support for veterans and their families. He also pressed for faster, improved care and benefits — particularly addressing the claims backlog and treatment for veterans with PTSD. After the ceremony, he and First Lady Michelle Obama, Vice President Joe Biden and Jill Biden greeted families in Section 60, where many graves of those killed in Iraq and Afghanistan lie.

On October 24, 2014, a shooting at Marysville-Pilchuck High School in Washington occurred during an early lunch period. Freshman Jaylen Fryberg, who had recently been named freshman homecoming prince, walked up to a table of classmates in the school cafeteria and fired multiple shots into the backs of students. He killed one female student and then died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Four other students—two girls and two boys, all under 18—were wounded and hospitalized in intensive care; three were reported very critically ill and one in serious condition. Several of the wounded were cousins of Fryberg.

Eyewitness accounts described chaos: students ducking under tables, screaming, and fleeing the cafeteria; some initially thought the noise was a drill. Authorities received a 911 call around 10:39 a.m., secured the campus, and later said there was only one shooter. Investigators traced the gun, believed to be a Beretta .40-caliber handgun, to Fryberg’s father and searched the family home. Authorities and the FBI conducted an overnight investigation at the school, which was closed through the following week.

Students and community members expressed shock—many described Fryberg as popular and involved in sports; his social media showed both hunting imagery and anguished posts. The Tulalip Tribes, of which Fryberg was a member, provided counseling and crisis support. School officials and regional education leaders highlighted mental-health needs for students; a federal grant to improve local student mental-health services was noted. Authorities continued interviewing witnesses to determine motive.

A 20-month-old Allentown boy, Zymeir Perry, died May 9 at Lehigh Valley Hospital‑Cedar Crest, six days after his mother allegedly pushed him from the 52‑foot Hamilton Street Bridge into the Lehigh River. Witnesses say 19‑year‑old Johnesha Perry took the child from a stroller, kissed him, placed him on the railing and pushed him into the water, then jumped in herself. Officers found the child about 700 yards downstream; two officers pulled him from the river and performed CPR. Zymeir was hospitalized in critical condition, later declared brain dead and taken off life support; an autopsy found blunt‑force trauma and drowning. The mother was treated for minor injuries, admitted to investigators she intended to kill her son, and was initially charged with attempted homicide, aggravated assault and reckless endangerment. After the child’s death, prosecutors upgraded charges to criminal homicide and endangering the welfare of a child; she remains jailed awaiting arraignment. An autopsy and further details were pending.

At the White House "Made in America Product Showcase," Rep. Claudia Tenney discovered that the silverware in use was Oneida-branded and made in China, despite President Trump’s creation of the event to promote U.S.-made goods. Tenney and others have lobbied the administration for months to purchase flatware from Sherrill Manufacturing, an Upstate New York company that is the last U.S. flatware maker and sells the Liberty Tabletop brand. In November, Trump told Tenney he would buy the American-made flatware, but Sherrill executives say follow-up from the White House was limited.

Sherrill’s founders, former Oneida executives who bought and reopened the local plant in 2005, said the company has grown since being invited to the White House in July 2017: production up 33 percent, employment up from 42 to 54, and projected net income above $5 million. They also report larger federal sales, including orders for the Navy and State Department. At the showcase, White House staff and several senior advisers viewed the company’s products; a military aide recognized the flatware from use aboard the USS Ronald Reagan. Sherrill hopes Trump’s reported interest after a private State Dining Room tour will lead to actual purchases.

Researchers analyzing data from NASA's Cassini spacecraft have found compelling evidence that Saturn's moon Enceladus hosts a warm, possibly hydrothermally active ocean beneath its icy crust. Cassini detected tiny silica-rich particles in Saturn’s E-ring and magnetosphere; modeling of their size and chemistry indicates they formed in hot (at least ~190–200°F / ~90–95°C) water reacting with rock on Enceladus’s seafloor, then were carried up through geysers that feed the ring. The inferred ocean appears relatively low in salinity (<4%) and alkaline (pH ~8.5–10.5), and may be over 30 miles deep in places.

These conditions—heat, water, rock, and organics like methane and carbon dioxide previously detected—are similar to Earth’s hydrothermal-vent environments (e.g., Lost City) and are considered promising for supporting microbial life. Tidal heating from Saturn and orbital neighbors likely contributes to the moon’s warmth, though some researchers suggest additional heat from water–rock chemical reactions may be required. The findings, published in Nature, are based on indirect evidence from ring and plume particles; Cassini’s planned close flybys through Enceladus’s plume later this year are expected to provide more direct data. Scientists say follow-up missions with modern instruments would be needed to definitively assess habitability or detect life.

David Gregory, host of NBC’s Meet the Press, acknowledges his program is struggling: it has fallen to third place among Sunday political shows after a three-year ratings slide, finishing behind CBS’s Face the Nation and ABC’s This Week during early 2014. Once dominant under Tim Russert, Meet the Press now posts its lowest-ever viewing in the key 25–54 advertiser demo, prompting internal concern at NBC and attention from new news president Deborah Turness. NBC commissioned outside consulting last year to better understand Gregory’s performance; the network calls the work a “brand consultant” review, while reporting originally described it as a “psychological” assessment.

NBC has also installed a new executive producer, Rob Yarin, and Gregory says the program has been retooled to be faster-paced, broader in topics and shorter in interview segments — moving away from the Russert-era long grilling of a single newsmaker. Competitors are changing too: ABC’s This Week, under new EP Jonathan Greenberger, is acting more like a fast-moving magazine, while Face the Nation’s Bob Schieffer is largely keeping the show’s traditional format and currently leads in total viewers and the 25–54 demo.

Despite the shake-up and controversies — including Gregory’s on-air moments that drew criticism — all three flagship Sunday shows remain durable and influential. NBC has renewed its public commitment to Gregory, who says he respects Russert’s legacy but is building his own version of the program; some observers believe time and forthcoming turnover at rival shows could favor Gregory long-term.

An 18-year-old Arizona man arrested on terrorism-related charges, Mahin Khan of Tucson, was assaulted by other inmates while jailed on July 2, the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office and his defense team reported. Khan suffered minor, non–life-threatening injuries, was evaluated at a hospital, and has since been moved to segregated housing at Lower Buckeye Jail. Authorities say he had been offered “voluntary segregation” because of the nature of his charges but declined and was initially placed in medium-security general population at Towers Jail.

Khan has been indicted on charges alleging he conspired to bomb a Motor Vehicle Division office in Maricopa County and to target government buildings in Maricopa and Pima counties between April 2015 and July 1, 2016; he pleaded not guilty on July 12 and is being held without bond. The FBI alleges he contacted the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) and sought to obtain firearms. Sheriff Joe Arpaio ordered that Khan and future inmates with similar charges be automatically placed in segregation. Khan’s public defenders have asked that future hearings be sealed, citing risks to his family and the recent jail attack as reasons media presence could jeopardize his right to a fair trial. A bond hearing is scheduled for Tuesday.

Lady Gaga—born Stefani Germanotta in 1986—emerged as the defining millennial pop star by fusing theatricality, past-pop influences (notably the ’80s), and savvy internet-era image-making to create a devoted fanbase called “Little Monsters.” Trained in piano and musical theater, she studied at NYU’s Tisch program, worked various small screen and performance gigs, fronted SGBand, and then teamed with producer Rob Fusari (origin of her stage name). After a brief stint with Def Jam, she developed a neo-burlesque stage act with Lady Starlight and signed with Interscope/Kon Live in 2007, where collaborations with Akon and producer RedOne yielded the breakthrough hits “Just Dance,” “Poker Face,” and “LoveGame.” Her 2008 debut The Fame and the 2009 companion The Fame Monster (featuring “Bad Romance”) propelled her into global superstardom.

Gaga sustained momentum with the 2011 album Born This Way—whose title track became an empowerment anthem—and extensive touring, TV specials, and remixes. She faced interruptions from injuries (hip surgery in 2013) but continued releasing albums: Artpop (2013), which debuted strongly; the jazz standards duet project Cheek to Cheek with Tony Bennett (2014), which topped the charts and won a Grammy; and Joanne (2016), a more personal, genre-blending record that regained momentum after her acclaimed 2017 Super Bowl halftime performance. Gaga also expanded into acting and film—earning a Golden Globe for American Horror Story and later starring in A Star Is Born—and into songwriting for film (“Until It Happens to You,” Oscar-nominated).

Alongside music, Gaga’s work is notable for bold visual and technological stunts: during the ARTPOP era she unveiled Volantis, a “flying dress” developed by her TechHaus/Studio XO team, showcased at an ArtRave event as part of the multimedia launch for ARTPOP. Throughout her career she has shifted managers and collaborators, explored diverse genres, and maintained a high-profile presence across music, fashion, art, and film.

Since late February’s Russian takeover of Crimea, abductions, beatings and intimidation of Ukrainian activists, journalists and minorities have become routine across the peninsula. Multiple reported incidents describe pro-Kremlin militias, former Berkut riot police and other armed men detaining, assaulting and disappearing pro‑Ukrainian figures. Examples include two EuroMaidan activists seized at Simferopol station on March 9 and not seen since; activist Igor Kiriushchenko forced to flee after death threats in Sevastopol; ATR journalist Ibraim Umerov hospitalized with a broken knee after being beaten while filming a seizure; and dozens more reportedly missing or harassed. Many former Berkut officers and “titushkas” from Kyiv are now part of Crimean self‑defense groups and checkpoints, often acting with impunity.

Human-rights groups say these tactics echo the abuses seen during the EuroMaidan protests in Kyiv. The takeover has driven over 500 people, including activists and Crimean Tatars, to leave Crimea, and Ukrainian border guards and their families report harassment. Psychologists note a “mirror effect” in which pro‑Russian activists have adopted Maidan‑style camps and symbolism, and widespread public celebrations followed the March 16 referendum that moved Crimea toward Russia — but fear keeps many residents from opposing the new authorities.

A detailed account from three young Ukrainian women who traveled from Kyiv to Crimea to show support for Euromaidan illustrates the dangers firsthand. Stopped at a checkpoint near Armyansk, they and companions were detained, forced to their knees, beaten, humiliated (including forced hair-cutting), and subjected to mock executions. They were held for three days, moved to a Russian naval base in Sevastopol and interrogated. The women say Russian military personnel treated them more respectfully than the Berkut and eventually escorted them out; none suffered life‑threatening injuries, but all lost equipment and endured severe trauma. The detainees warn other activists against traveling to Crimea amid the continuing risks.

Danielle Fishel, best known as Topanga from Boy Meets World, married longtime boyfriend Tim Belusko on Oct. 19 at Los Angeles’ Vibiana. The 32-year-old bride wore a white lace strapless gown and carried a dark purple bouquet; bridesmaids wore midnight-blue dresses to match the fall-themed color scheme. Around 200 guests attended, including her former on-screen husband Ben Savage. Fishel praised the day as one of the most amazing of her life and shared photos with Us Weekly.

After the wedding photos ran, Fishel faced rude online comments about her weight. While on her honeymoon she responded on Twitter, defending herself—stating she’s 5'1" and weighs 107 pounds—calling the critics “the worst kind of people” and condemning body-shaming and its link to eating disorders. She closed her message by reaffirming that love and happiness win.

Princess Charlotte turned two on May 2, and the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge released a new photograph taken by Kate at the family’s Norfolk home, Anmer Hall, in April to mark the occasion. In the image Charlotte wears a navy bow and a yellow cardigan; her parents said they were “delighted to share” the photo, thanked well-wishers, and hope people enjoy it. The family will celebrate privately at home; the birthday falls just after the U.K. May Day holiday.

The story notes highlights from Charlotte’s second year: her first royal tour to Canada in September (where she charmed the public at a children’s event), her appearance at the Christmas Day church service, and an upcoming role as a bridesmaid at her aunt Pippa Middleton’s wedding on May 20 (with big brother Prince George as page boy). Candid portraits by the Duchess have become a family tradition — Kate also photographed Charlotte for her first birthday — and the outfits worn by the children often sell out soon after the photos are released.

Former and current Black employees have filed a class-action lawsuit against CNN, Turner Broadcasting and parent company Time Warner (now WarnerMedia), alleging long-standing, systemic racial discrimination in hiring, evaluations, pay and promotions.

Key points:
- Plaintiffs: The suit names two lead plaintiffs, Celeslie Henley (former executive administrative assistant at CNN) and Ernest “Ernie” Colbert Jr. (senior manager at TBS). Attorney Daniel Meachum, who represents them, says 20–30 additional current and former Turner employees provided information and more have contacted him since the filing. DeWayne Walker, a CNN integrated marketing manager who has an active separate $50 million individual suit alleging repeated promotional passes and retaliation, is a client of Meachum but not a named plaintiff in this class action.
- Scope: The 40-page complaint, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, seeks class status for all Black employees in salaried and mid-level managerial positions at Turner networks in the U.S. from April 1997 to present.
- Allegations: The suit accuses Turner/CNN of a company-wide pattern and practice of discrimination—rather than isolated incidents—claiming Black employees, especially men, receive disproportionately lower performance evaluation scores, are promoted at much lower rates, are underpaid relative to similarly situated white colleagues, and are terminated at higher rates. It alleges formal and informal policies that let supervisors handpick candidates subjectively, preventing equal opportunity and even knowledge of openings. The complaint cites data reportedly provided by Turner showing the disparities.
- Specific accusations: The filing quotes instances of racial slurs and prejudicial comments by superiors and contends Black employees are underrepresented in senior/high-pay-grade roles and in key divisions (Media Group, Legal, Strategy). Henley alleges race-, sex- and pregnancy-based mistreatment and claims she was fired in retaliation after complaining to HR. Colbert alleges long-term underpayment, lack of a proper job description for years, repeated denial of promotions while white peers advanced, and missing personnel records that nullified positive evaluations.
- Context: Meachum says he investigated for about three years before filing, and that other recent lawsuits against CNN exist (including Walker’s and separate suits by Omar Butcher and Ricky Blalock). Turner/CNN declined to comment on the new filing; company executives previously declined to comment on related suits.

The complaint seeks to address what plaintiffs characterize as entrenched discriminatory practices across Turner’s networks that have hindered Black employees’ careers for decades.

Australian search vessel Ocean Shield, towing a U.S. pinger locator, detected two additional acoustic signals in the southern Indian Ocean that officials say are consistent with the locator beacons of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370’s black boxes. The pings were recorded Tuesday at about 4:27 p.m. and 10:17 p.m. Perth time, lasting roughly 5 minutes 32 seconds and 7 minutes respectively. These follow two earlier acoustic events detected by Ocean Shield on Saturday (one lasting about 2 hours 20 minutes, another about 13 minutes). Analysis by the Australasian Joint Acoustic Analysis Centre found the Saturday signals showed a stable 33.331 kHz tone pulsing every 1.106 seconds and concluded they were unlikely to be natural, likely originating from electronic equipment and consistent with a flight data recorder.

Retired Air Chief Marshal Angus Houston, head of the Joint Agency Coordination Centre, said the detections have allowed authorities to refine the search to a single concentrated zone of about 75,423 sq km roughly 2,261 km northwest of Perth. Surface searches (air and sea) are being intensified in that area while Ocean Shield prepares to conduct sonar and refine underwater search patterns. Up to 11 military aircraft, four civilian aircraft and as many as 14 ships were scheduled to assist. An RAAF aircraft was diverted to deploy buoys to create a sonar-buoy pattern to improve detection and triangulation, and the autonomous underwater vehicle Bluefin-21 remains available to search the seabed once a sufficiently precise location is established.

Searchers cautioned the signals are weakening — either because search assets are not yet close enough or because the pinger batteries (certified for about 30 days) are starting to fail — and time is limited. The detections, while encouraging, have not yet been corroborated by visual wreckage, and investigators stress they must visually identify wreckage before confirming MH370’s final resting place. Families and observers remain wary given prior false leads and the absence so far of debris or bodies to confirm the find.

James Bacon interviews 71-year-old John Wayne shortly after the actor’s open-heart surgery, granted despite doctors’ orders to avoid interviews. Wayne, famous as “the Duke” and “the last cowboy,” has survived both lung cancer in 1964 (which led to removal of a lung) and recent heart valve replacement in Boston—surgeons used a pig valve—and says his voice and health have returned. Bacon recalls Wayne’s toughness, resilient personality, hard-drinking reputation, love of parties, fishing and yachting (his boat is The Wild Goose), and anecdotal moments like a long baptism celebration and catching a record-size mahi-mahi.

The article describes earlier attempts to conceal his illnesses with misleading press releases, Wayne’s frustration with studio image control, and the morale boost his recovery gave cancer and heart-disease patients who wrote him. Now convalescing in Newport Beach with morning walks and light activity, Wayne plans to work on a new film, Beau John, a family story that could become another acclaimed role after his Oscar-winning turn in True Grit. Despite sentimentality over fans’ support, Wayne insists he’s resilient and eager for more life and work.

Love bombing is a grooming tactic in which a person (or group, as in cults) overwhelms a target with excessive flattery, attention and affection to gain influence, obedience, or resources. It mimics genuine care—lavish compliments, gifts, constant contact, grand romantic gestures and rapid talk of the future—but is used instrumentally to hook victims so the abuser can later control, exploit or discard them.

Why it works
- It meets deep emotional needs: targets feel seen, special, and safe after deprivation or criticism, so they quickly bond to the giver.  
- It is especially effective on people raised by narcissistic parents: they were trained to seek external validation, compete for scarce approval, and accept conditional affection.  
- Paired with intermittent reinforcement—sporadic affection amid cruelty—the tactic creates instability, longing and a trauma bond. Occasional kindnesses become magnified (the “small kindness perception”), making victims cling to hope and tolerate abuse, much like gambling addiction or Stockholm Syndrome.

Common patterns
- Rapid idealization (extreme praise and attention) followed later by devaluation, control, jealousy, or punishment.  
- Triangulation: making the target feel uniquely chosen, then setting them against others or cycling in new “targets” to provoke insecurity and competition.  
- Superficial alliances mistaken for deep connection because of intense early chemistry and quick escalation.

How to protect yourself (immunity methods)
1. Build internal validation: affirm the qualities flattered by others yourself and seek healthy people who recognize you without strings attached. Be wary of excessive praise linked to requests.  
2. Recognize and value what makes you irreplaceable: resist negative comparison and cultivate self-awareness about your strengths so charm can’t easily manipulate you.  
3. Differentiate flattery from true connection: require time, consistency, reciprocity, boundaries and reliability before investing; prioritize relationships that grow gradually and sustainably.

Bottom line: generous-sounding attention isn’t always benign. Healthy relationships develop through steady actions and mutual respect; love bombing and its combination with intermittent reinforcement are manipulative patterns intended to control and exploit vulnerable people.

Yesterday’s graduation of 884 new NYPD officers at Madison Square Garden was marked by boos, heckling and turned backs for Mayor Bill de Blasio, continuing a pattern of public displays of contempt by rank-and-file officers and their union since the non‑indictment in Eric Garner’s death. Similar gestures — officers turning their backs at the funeral of Rafael Ramos and after the deaths of Ramos and Wenjian Liu — were meant to protest the mayor’s criticism of policing and his remarks about racial risk to his own son, but critics argue they instead made the department look childish, entitled and undeserving of its special status.

Tensions escalated after Ismaayil Brinsley murdered officers Liu and Ramos, an act he said was retaliation for police killings; instead of prompting reflection, union leader Patrick Lynch accused the mayor and protesters of having “blood on their hands,” and the Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association encouraged officers to slow enforcement under department rules. Reports suggest summonses and arrests have dropped sharply since late December. City officials and commentators note that while officers are understandably anxious after the killings, policing is a voluntary, protected profession and does not justify abdication of duty or victim-blaming.

The articles place these events in the broader context of longstanding complaints about NYPD abuses — Eric Garner’s chokehold death, Akai Gurley, and other killings and misconduct — and credit public protests, critical editorials, and Mayor de Blasio’s stance for helping reduce practices like stop-and-frisk. Many argue that the union’s retaliatory posture damages the department’s credibility and dishonors solemn occasions, further alienating communities most affected by police violence.

A 12-year-old boy, Charlie Bothuell V, was found alive on June 25, 2014 hiding behind a 55-gallon drum in the basement of his father’s Detroit townhouse after being missing for about 10–12 days. Investigators executing a search noticed a barricaded area in the basement near an underground tunnel that links units and leads outside. Police say Charlie told them his stepmother, 37-year-old Monique Dillard-Bothuell, was helping him hide and providing food.

Earlier searches had failed to find him. Evidence recovered from the home included a PVC pipe with blood on it and blood in the boy’s room and on clothing. Authorities are investigating possible child abuse related to a strict exercise/discipline regime the boy had been subjected to while being homeschooled; Charlie’s father, Charlie Bothuell IV, admits to disciplining his son but denies abuse. Sources indicated the father was expected to face child-abuse charges; the stepmother could also face charges.

Monique Dillard-Bothuell was taken into custody on a bench warrant for violating probation from an earlier guilty plea to purchasing a pistol without a permit. Child Protective Services removed two other children (ages 4 and 10 months) from the home. Charlie was treated at Children’s Hospital, released in good physical health, interviewed by the FBI and investigators, and placed with his biological mother. Police are also noting the proximity of the stepmother’s uncle’s unit—three doors away—since the units are connected by the basement tunnel; he is Detroit attorney and candidate Godfrey Dillard, though no connection has been confirmed.

Actor Shia LaBeouf has checked into rehab in Los Angeles after a June 26 arrest in New York City following a string of highly publicized drunken incidents. Observers in L.A. saw him carrying Alcoholics Anonymous’s “Big Book” and described him as nervous but aware he needed help. This follows a recent episode in NYC—after drinking margaritas at a midtown bar to watch the World Cup—where he was arrested and charged with harassment, disorderly conduct and criminal trespass, and earlier Times Square and Broadway disturbances.

LaBeouf’s struggles with alcohol are longstanding: he attended AA meetings as a child with his father, had arrests in 2007 (Walgreen’s) and 2008 (DUI), and publicly called himself an “alcoholic” in 2011 after a bar brawl. He has periodically shown commitment to sobriety (celebrating 60 days in AA in 2008) but also relapsed, with reported incidents such as boasting about drinking moonshine and using LSD for roles. Recent behavior in L.A. included being banned from a restaurant after publicly urinating and causing a disturbance. The rehab check-in appears to be the latest and most serious effort to get sober.

North Korea’s foreign minister Ri Yong Ho told Russia’s TASS that U.S. President Donald Trump “lit the wick (or fuse) of war” with his bellicose U.N. remarks and that the North would answer “with a hail of fire,” not words. Ri framed Pyongyang’s nuclear and ballistic programs as a “sword of justice” and a deterrent that guarantees regional security, said North Korea will not negotiate away its weapons, and claimed the country is close to achieving a balance of power with the United States.

The comments intensify an already heated exchange of rhetoric between Trump and Kim Jong Un after North Korea’s recent missile launches and its sixth nuclear test. Trump’s U.N. speech had threatened to “totally destroy” North Korea if necessary and mocked Kim as “Rocket Man.” The statements came amid stepped-up military signaling — U.S. B-1B bombers flew training missions with South Korea and Japan near the peninsula — and growing concern in Washington: some U.S. politicians, including Republican Sen. Bob Corker, warned the rhetoric risks escalation, while Defense Secretary James Mattis emphasized a preference for a peaceful resolution but ordered forces to be ready.

As longstanding sexual-assault allegations against Bill Cosby intensified, a new accusation surfaced alleging a bizarre backstage ritual: Cosby reportedly asked young female Late Show staffers, interns and assistants to gather and watch him eat curry in the green room before his appearances. The account, from an anonymous source cited by the New York Daily News, described the women as uncomfortable but compelled to comply because producers honored Cosby’s requests. Cosby’s scheduled appearance on David Letterman was canceled amid the scandal.

The report situates this anecdote within a much larger, decades-spanning series of allegations from more than a dozen women who say Cosby sexually assaulted or raped them, often after drugging them. The piece recaps many of those accusers and episodes, including:
- Andrea Constand’s 2004 allegation and 2005 civil suit, which was settled in 2006; she described being given pills and then sexually assaulted at Cosby’s home.
- Former comedy writer Joan Tarshis, who says she was rendered incoherent by a drink at Cosby’s bungalow in 1969 and was sexually assaulted.
- Linda Traitz, who says Cosby offered pills from a briefcase in 1969 and tried to assault her on a beach.
- Former Playboy-affiliated women Victoria Valentino and Meg Foster’s contemporaneous accounts of being given pills and allegedly assaulted in 1969–1970.
- Tamara Green, who alleges Cosby drugged and assaulted her in the early 1970s while she worked for him.
- Barbara Bowman, who says Cosby assaulted her beginning when she was a teenager in the 1980s; her account was part of the circle of claims connected to a Denver talent agent who referred young women to Cosby.
- Other public accusers named in recent weeks include Janice Dickinson, Joan Tarshis, Louisa Moritz and several women assembled as “Jane Does” in Constand’s civil action.

The article emphasizes recurring patterns across allegations: victims tended to be young women drawn in by Cosby’s fame and promises, drugs or pills were allegedly used to incapacitate them, and victims often felt unable to report incidents at the time. It chronicles the cultural shift that has allowed many of these women to come forward decades later, noting Hannibal Buress’s recent onstage comments that helped spark renewed scrutiny and social-media momentum.

Cosby’s response has included broad denials from his attorneys, who characterize recent accounts as unsubstantiated, and public statements by Cosby asserting he will not respond to “innuendo.” His legal team has also questioned some accusers’ credibility. The fallout for Cosby’s career was immediate: planned TV projects, specials and appearances were postponed or canceled, syndication and honors were reconsidered, and institutions associated with him faced pressure.

The piece also recounts Cosby’s public life and rise—from I Spy to The Cosby Show and his status as an emblematic family figure and philanthropist—and contrasts that image with the accounts of alleged misconduct spanning the 1960s through the 2000s. It profiles several accusers in detail, outlines the 2005 criminal inquiry that did not result in prosecution, and describes how the civil settlement with Constand largely suppressed broader public attention until the recent wave of new allegations and renewed media focus.

Overall, the article presents the curry-watching anecdote as one more troubling detail amid a pattern of alleged predatory behavior that has dramatically reshaped public perception of Cosby and disrupted his attempted comeback.

Less than three months before the Boston Marathon bombings, Tamerlan Tsarnaev visited a federal immigration office and filed a Jan. 23, 2013 petition to change his first name to "Muaz," honoring Emir Muaz, a slain Dagestan rebel fighter. Authorities say "Muaz" was also the nickname given to Tamerlan during a six-month 2012 visit to Dagestan and that he became increasingly radicalized there. On the petition he crossed out "Tamerlan" and wrote "Muaz" instead of signing the oath of allegiance portion.

Defense attorneys for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev—who faces federal capital charges for his alleged role in the April 2013 bombings that killed three and wounded more than 260—have used this and other evidence to portray Tamerlan as the dominant, more radical influence who supplied motivation, planning and ideology for the attack. They contend Tamerlan’s anger toward the U.S. was heightened by multiple FBI contacts after Russian warnings about his travel to the Caucasus, arguing those interactions (which they say included requests that he act as an informant) increased his paranoia and helped precipitate the violence. Prosecutors say they have no evidence the FBI sought to recruit him as an informant and assert the brothers were never FBI sources.

Government investigators and a House Homeland Security report concluded Tamerlan returned from Dagestan with heightened extremist views—evidenced by mosque tirades, militant online activity and an unsuccessful bid to join rebels—and likely played a leading role in the attack. Dzhokhar’s lawyers are seeking extensive records (FBI, immigration, FISA, internet searches, and other evidence) to support mitigation at sentencing, arguing Tamerlan’s deeper radicalization and possible psychological domination over his 19-year-old brother should weigh against the death penalty. The defense acknowledges such coercion claims are difficult to prove but considers them central to illustrating relative culpability.

Researchers at Melbourne’s Murdoch Children’s Research Institute report a major advance in treating peanut allergy in children using a combined probiotic–oral immunotherapy (PPOIT). In the 2013 clinical trial 48 children were randomized to 18 months of daily treatment with increasing doses of peanut flour plus a high dose of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus, or placebo. At the end of treatment 82% of children who received PPOIT were able to eat peanuts versus about 4% in the placebo group. In follow-up testing up to four years later, roughly 80% of those initially cured were still eating peanuts without following a maintenance regimen and about 70% passed formal challenge testing, indicating durable tolerance.

The probiotic is thought to modulate the immune response and support development of lasting tolerance when paired with gradual peanut exposure. Lead researcher Prof Mimi Tang called the results life-changing for children and families. The institute plans to work with venture capital to commercialize a powder formulation for daily use over 18 months; larger trials will be needed before widespread approval and availability.

Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel failed to win an outright second term in the Feb. 24 election and must face Cook County Commissioner Jesus “Chuy” Garcia in an April 7 runoff — the first mayoral runoff Chicago has held since switching to nonpartisan elections in 1995. With nearly all precincts counted, Emanuel finished first but with roughly 45% of the vote to Garcia’s about 34%; the other candidates (Willie Wilson, Bob Fioretti, William “Dock” Walls) split the remainder.

The result was a surprise given Emanuel’s huge financial advantage and high-profile backing: he raised and spent millions on TV ads (roughly $13–16 million raised, many millions spent in the final quarter) and even brought President Barack Obama to campaign for him and record an endorsement. Garcia ran a low-budget, populist campaign that energized progressives, Latino voters and the Chicago Teachers Union after teacher-union leader Karen Lewis withdrew due to illness.

Emanuel’s shortcomings on issues such as the 2013 closing of 50 public schools, clashes with teachers (including a 2012 strike), and persistent violent crime were cited as key reasons voters withheld a majority. Garcia attacked Emanuel as aligned with wealthy interests and neglectful of neighborhoods outside downtown, and pledged change and more police. Turnout was low (about mid-30s percent), and Garcia won many heavily Latino wards.

The runoff rematches a well-funded incumbent with a grassroots challenger; Emanuel remains the favorite financially, but must now face Garcia one-on-one and try to win over voters who supported other challengers.

Nancy Gordeuk, founder and principal of TNT Academy, a non-traditional private school in Stone Mountain, Georgia, was fired by the board after a video of her making a racially charged remark at a recent graduation went viral. At the ceremony she mistakenly dismissed attendees before the valedictorian spoke, then said on the microphone, "Look who's leaving, all the black people." The comment prompted protests and an exodus. The board chair, Heidi Anderson, said the board voted to dismiss Gordeuk and would focus on supporting recent graduates and continuing school services during the transition. Gordeuk apologized, calling the comment racist and blaming emotional frustration; she also said she did not intend a racial slur. Separate coverage noted controversy around her son, Travis Gordeuk, whose Twitter account posted offensive tweets (which family members say were from a hacked account), drawing additional scrutiny.
