Lauriann Bartell has been in a coma for over three years after suffering a bleeding ulcer in August 2015 that caused massive blood loss and oxygen deprivation to her brain. Her husband Mike has been her full-time caregiver and also cares for their six children; older children help when they can, but the family faces mounting medical bills and everyday expenses and fears losing their home.

A GoFundMe created to support the family has received a high-profile donation: singer Taylor Swift gave $15,500 (signed “Love, Taylor, Meredith and Olivia Swift”), which helped boost the campaign toward its $40,000 goal and inspired additional donations. The family and fundraiser organizers thank donors, ask for prayers and shares, and note any assistance is greatly appreciated. The article also places this gift in the context of Swift’s well‑documented history of philanthropic giving.

This document contains two distinct items:

1) Internet Archive effort: The Archive is crawling and saving webpages as they are created and also archiving pages those new pages reference. The aim is to preserve the exact versions that were live when content was written so that when linked pages change or disappear, archived links can replace broken links or be offered as companion links. The long-term goal is to eliminate broken links across the web by crawling supported “No More 404” sites.

2) News report: A New York woman, Jennifer Connell, is suing her 8‑year‑old Westport nephew, Sean Tarala, over an incident at his 2011 birthday party in which he leapt into her arms, causing her to fall and break her wrist. Four years after the incident she seeks $127,000 and asks a six‑member Connecticut Superior Court jury to find the child negligent. At trial the boy (now 12) appeared with his father; his mother has since died. Connell, a Manhattan HR manager who has no children, testified she didn’t scold him at the time because it was his party but said the injury has since affected her daily life (navigating a third‑floor walk‑up) and social activities. The lawsuit argues a reasonable eight‑year‑old would have known that such a forceful greeting could cause harm.

A model’s brief appearance at Mexico’s first televised presidential debate drew more attention than the candidates and sparked controversy. Julia Orayen, a former Playboy model hired as an edecan (event hostess) by an independent production firm, carried a box of cards with speaking order and stood onstage for about 24 seconds in a tight white dress with a plunging neckline. Her look provoked gasps and jeers in the press room, went viral on Twitter, and dominated morning-news discussion the next day.

Organizers and election officials apologized, calling the outfit a “production error” that distracted from the debate’s substance. The Federal Electoral Institute (IFE) said the edecan was contracted by a production company and asked that no distracting elements be used; the firm’s producer, Jesús Tapia, said Orayen was chosen because of her height relative to the candidates and that the dress was her own choice. Candidate Josefina Vázquez Mota and IFE members criticized the choice as inappropriate and an “outrageous stereotype,” noting it undermined the debate’s seriousness. A second debate is scheduled for June 10.

Protests across the Arab world spread and hardened over the weekend as governments in Libya, Yemen, Bahrain, Algeria and elsewhere responded to mass demonstrations that were inspired by uprisings in Tunisia and Egypt.

Libya
- Benghazi was the epicenter of the most violent crackdown. Security forces, including snipers and heavy weapons, fired on protesters and funeral marches; hospitals reported dozens killed (estimates varied, with dozens more wounded). Opposition activists and rights groups said special forces and foreign mercenaries were used and that much of the dead suffered gunshot wounds. The government cut Internet access. Moammar Gadhafi sent his son Saadi to try to calm the city, but his gestures were dismissed by many protesters, who chanted “The people want to topple the regime.”

Yemen
- In Sanaa, confrontations between anti-government demonstrators and pro-Saleh supporters turned violent. Government supporters opened fire, leaving at least one dead and several wounded; clashes involved bottles, rocks and machetes. President Ali Abdullah Saleh insisted protesters were part of a foreign plot but offered limited concessions such as saying he would not run in 2013.

Bahrain
- After an earlier deadly crackdown, the military briefly withdrew from Pearl Square and demonstrators reoccupied it, celebrating but wary of further attacks. The government faced international pressure (including calls from President Obama) to hold accountable those responsible and to pursue reform. Protesters prepared defenses in the square despite the withdrawal.

Algeria
- Thousands attempted antigovernment marches in Algiers but were broken up by baton-wielding police; authorities have promised to lift the long-running emergency law but keep restrictions on protests. Dissatisfaction stems from corruption and high youth unemployment despite oil and gas wealth.

Other developments
- Kurdistan region (Iraq): Student protests were met with gunfire, wounding a dozen.
- Egypt: The military government moved toward reforms—announcing plans to lift the emergency law within months, drafting constitutional amendments, and recognizing a newly formed political party—while the aftermath of Mubarak’s ouster continued to reverberate.
- Across the region, governments that had seen leaders fall in Tunisia and Egypt increasingly opted for forceful suppression to prevent unrest from growing into full-scale revolts.

Overall picture
- The wave of protests has produced divergent outcomes: in some countries (Tunisia, Egypt) entrenched rulers were driven out, while in others (Libya, Yemen, Bahrain, Algeria) regimes responded with violence and repression to try to halt the momentum. Human rights groups and Western governments condemned the killings, and activists warned that heavy-handed tactics were hardening resolve among protesters.

Ursula K. Le Guin, a towering figure in fantasy and science fiction, died at 88, prompting widespread tributes from writers, institutions and readers. Over her long career she published more than 20 novels, 100+ short stories, a dozen poetry books, seven essay collections, 13 children’s books and translations; her work—noted for feminist themes and literary ambition within genre fiction—has been translated into over 40 languages and sold millions of copies. She won multiple Hugo and Nebula awards and the National Book Awards’ Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters.

Colleagues and admirers mourned her influence on their work and on the field: Stephen King called her a “literary icon,” N. K. Jemisin credited Le Guin with helping make her a writer, and Neil Gaiman described her as one of the “deepest and smartest” writers. Authors, publishers and cultural figures highlighted her storytelling, moral seriousness, and the diversity and humanity of the worlds she imagined—reminding readers that she used speculative fiction’s metaphors to explore serious social concerns. Many urged people to read her books and reflected on the profound personal and artistic impact of her writing.

Egypt held the final phase of its first parliamentary elections since Hosni Mubarak’s ouster as prosecutors resumed the former president’s trial. Voting in nine governorates, including Sinai and Brotherhood strongholds in the Delta, completed balloting for about 150 seats with roughly 14 million eligible voters. Early returns from the first two rounds left the Muslim Brotherhood’s Freedom and Justice Party in the lead (about 40–50% of seats awarded so far), and analysts expected Islamists overall to consolidate control, though final seat-allocation formulas remained unclear. The Salafi Nour party has emerged as a surprisingly strong second force, while liberal and left-leaning parties hold most of the remaining seats. The outcome sets up likely political struggles over authority with the ruling military council—especially whether the new parliament will control the appointment of an interim prime minister—a point the military has resisted.

Meanwhile, Mubarak’s trial resumed with chief prosecutor Mustafa Suleiman denouncing him as a “tyrant” who engineered a plan to install his son Gamal as successor and allowed security forces to crush protesters. Prosecutors are presenting evidence in a multi-day session against Mubarak and other defendants, including his sons (facing corruption charges) and former Interior Minister Habib el-Adli, accused of ordering violence. Mubarak, who has pleaded not guilty to corruption and complicity in killing protesters, could face the harshest penalties if convicted. The elections and trial are occurring amid economic decline—sharp drops in foreign reserves and equities—and growing public unrest, with plans for renewed mass protests on the revolution’s anniversary.

A 51-year-old Orange County woman was air-rescued after getting stuck on a steep, 50-foot slope behind her Silverado Canyon home while trying to retrieve her adopted black kitten Monday morning. Around 8 a.m. she climbed up the hill on Kitterman Drive, slipped while descending, twisted her ankle and scraped her arms and legs, and became unable to climb up or down. Neighbors called 911 after hearing her calls for help. An urban search-and-rescue firefighter rappelled down and secured her with a harness; both were hoisted into an Orange County Fire Authority helicopter and flown to paramedics on the ground. She was evaluated, declined hospitalization, and was driven home. The kitten descended the hill on its own. Fire officials stressed that cats often come down by themselves and advised leaving food out rather than risking a rescue.

Key points

- The U.S. Federal Reserve Bank of New York was aware as early as August 2007 of problems with how Libor (the global benchmark interbank rate) was being set. After inquiries with Barclays in spring 2008, the New York Fed shared analysis and reform suggestions with UK authorities.

- The timing and extent of Fed engagement raise questions in Washington about whether regulators acted sufficiently or whether crisis-fighting priorities (e.g., after Bear Stearns, Lehman, AIG) sidelined Libor concerns. Congress has sought more information: Rep. Randy Neugebauer requested transcripts of New York Fed-Barclays communications (Aug 2007–Nov 2008), and Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Johnson has scheduled briefings and will question senior officials, including Treasury Secretary Geithner and Fed Chair Bernanke.

- Barclays admitted wrongdoing and agreed to a $453 million settlement with U.S. and U.K. authorities for manipulating Libor. The scandal has led to resignations at Barclays and public outrage in Britain, but investigations are broadening: more than a dozen banks (including Citigroup, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, HSBC, UBS, RBS) are under scrutiny.

- Manipulating Libor mattered because the rates affect about $550 trillion of loans, securities and derivatives. Banks could benefit by skewing reported rates to profit on trades or to appear healthier during the liquidity stress of the financial crisis.

- Barclays’ timeline: it first contacted the Fed on Aug. 28, 2007 about Libor issues and had multiple subsequent communications through Oct. 2008. Barclays told regulators it repeatedly raised concerns about how the credit crisis was affecting Libor setting.

- The New York Fed held internal discussions about Libor (Timothy Geithner’s calendar lists a “Fixing LIBOR” meeting on April 28, 2008). Fed staff produced research in 2008–2010 suggesting reporting distortions, but definitive evidence of misreporting was initially inconclusive. Fed staffers had means (e.g., Fedwire transaction records) that could have been used as a backstop to verify reported borrowing costs.

- Analysts and former Fed officials say the New York Fed had the authority to pressure (“jawbone”) banks and the resources to investigate, but the extraordinary focus on preventing systemic collapse in late 2008 likely diverted attention. Observers note no single regulator had clear ultimate responsibility for ensuring truthful Libor submissions, which contributed to regulatory gaps.

- Political fallout continued in the U.K.: Barclays’ CEO Robert Diamond agreed to forfeit up to £20 million in bonus as lawmakers pressed the bank’s leadership over the scandal (leading to resignations, including Diamond and chairman Marcus Agius).

Overall takeaway: Evidence shows U.S. and U.K. authorities, including the New York Fed, were aware of Libor problems by mid‑2007–2008 and discussed reforms, but questions remain about how decisively and quickly they acted amid the broader financial crisis. The scandal has prompted large penalties, executive resignations, expanding investigations into many banks, and scrutiny of regulatory responsibilities.

Summary:

Manti Te'o, Notre Dame linebacker and Heisman runner-up, has said he was the victim of an elaborate online hoax in which a purported girlfriend, “Lennay Kekua,” who Te'o said died of leukemia in September, never actually existed. Notre Dame and Te'o maintain their version: the relationship was virtual (Internet and phone), Te'o grieved Kekua’s supposed death the same day his grandmother died, and he learned on Dec. 6 via a phone call that the woman was not real. Te'o released a brief statement calling the situation a “sick joke,” and Notre Dame athletic director Jack Swarbrick said the school is investigating.

The story unraveled when Deadspin reported that no records, family members, or verifiable evidence supported Kekua’s existence; the photograph used for her identity belonged to a living woman who said she never met Te’o. Deadspin traced the hoax through social media and anonymous tips, raising questions about who created and perpetuated the ruse.

Despite Te’o’s explanations, many journalists, commentators and fans remain skeptical. Critics cite inconsistencies: Te’o’s public comments after Dec. 6 implying he’d lost a girlfriend to cancer; earlier interviews (including a Sports Illustrated transcript) in which he described meeting Kekua in person; and tweets and social-media interactions that referenced Kekua. Some writers suggest Te’o may have exaggerated the relationship; others believe he was genuinely duped. The NCAA and Notre Dame say they are still determining the facts. With Te’o nearing the NFL draft, teams and the public are awaiting further answers about whether he was simply deceived or complicit in misleading the media.

An EgyptAir domestic flight (MS181) from Alexandria to Cairo was hijacked on 29 March and forced to divert to Larnaca, Cyprus. The lone hijacker—reported by Cypriot authorities as Seif Eldin Mustafa but subject to conflicting early claims—appeared to be wearing a white explosive “suicide” belt; Cypriot officials later said the device was fake. After several passengers were released during the standoff and a crew member escaped through a cockpit window, the hijacker surrendered and all remaining hostages were freed. No one was injured.

Motives remain uncertain: some reports say he wanted to speak with an estranged Cypriot wife and deliver an envelope to a named woman in Cyprus, while other accounts suggested he sought the release of female prisoners in Egypt. Cyprus’s president said the incident was not terrorism-related. Larnaca airport was temporarily closed and flights diverted.

The event renewed scrutiny of Egyptian airport security following the October Metrojet bombing over Sinai. Video showed the suspect passing through security in Alexandria; commentators raised concerns about how someone described as mentally unstable could board with materials resembling a bomb and about the risk posed by bluffing would-be attackers. The plane carried about 56 passengers (26 foreigners) and seven crew.

Ari Mahler, a registered nurse at Allegheny General Hospital and the son of a retired rabbi, publicly described treating suspected Tree of Life shooter Robert Bowers after the Oct. 27 synagogue attack that killed 11 people. Mahler — who did not reveal his Jewish identity to Bowers — wrote that when he looked into Bowers’ eyes he saw confusion, lack of depth and intelligence, and no overt “evil,” and that Bowers later thanked him for saving him and treating him kindly. Mahler said Bowers had shouted anti-Semitic slogans (“death to all Jews”) as he was brought in and speculated Bowers was lonely, easily influenced by propaganda, and attention-seeking.

Allegheny General’s president, Dr. Jeff Cohen, also Jewish and a Tree of Life congregant, confirmed that two of the lead clinicians who treated Bowers were Jewish (an ER attending and a nurse), praised their professionalism for putting duty above emotion, and described Bowers as “lost” rather than demonic. Mahler detailed his own longtime experiences with anti-Semitism, recounted his path from finance into nursing, and framed his decision to treat Bowers with compassion as a moral response and an affirmation that “love in the face of evil” is the message he wants to share.

WHO:
- Karolina Kurkova, Czech supermodel and Victoria’s Secret model, whose smooth midriff drew attention because she appeared to lack a visible belly button.
- Medical professionals and commentators referenced include plastic surgeons (e.g., Dr. Matthew Schulman) and other people who shared similar experiences.
- Other cases mentioned: a Houston woman (Lori Jones) who lost her navel after a tummy tuck/hernia repair and disputes with her surgeon; several readers who recounted childhood hernia repairs, gastroschisis, lotus births, or cosmetic umbilicoplasty.

WHAT:
- Kurkova was seen on a US catwalk with a barely-there or smooth navel, prompting media speculation about whether it was natural, the result of infant surgery, cosmetic work, or photo retouching. Her agency initially declined to comment beyond denying alien theories; later reporting quoted her rep saying she “had an operation when she was an infant.”
- Medical explanation offered: the most likely cause is repair of an infant umbilical hernia or a congenital abdominal defect (e.g., gastroschisis), which can alter or eliminate the typical navel appearance. Adults can also lose or have a navel reconstructed during abdominal surgeries (hernia repair, tummy tuck) or by cosmetic umbilicoplasty. Photo retouching can also add or remove a visible navel in images.
- Additional human-interest examples: readers’ anecdotes of missing navels from childhood surgery, premature birth, midwifery technique, being a former conjoined twin, or cosmetic procedures; and the Houston case where a patient claims her surgeon failed to preserve or warn her about losing her belly button after surgery and plans legal action.

WHY:
- Why Kurkova’s navel is smooth: most plausibly due to surgery in infancy (likely to correct an umbilical hernia) that altered the umbilicus; magazine images sometimes show a navel because photographers retouch photos.
- Why this matters culturally: the story captured public curiosity because belly buttons are a common, familiar anatomical feature and Kurkova’s celebrity status made the anomaly newsworthy. It also opened discussion of medical causes (congenital conditions and surgical outcomes), cosmetic procedures (umbilicoplasty), birth practices (lotus birth), and the role of image retouching in media.
- Broader takeaway: absent or altered navels are uncommon but explainable—usually from infant surgery, congenital conditions, or adult abdominal procedures—and can be reconstructed if desired; public reaction mixes genuine medical curiosity with fascination about celebrity appearance.

Bottom line: Kurkova’s missing-looking belly button is most likely the result of infant abdominal surgery (commonly an umbilical hernia repair); media images may hide or recreate a navel by retouching. Similar cases arise from congenital defects, surgical repairs, or cosmetic procedures, and the topic sparked wide public interest and anecdotal responses.

Israeli authorities stepped up security around former prime minister Ariel Sharon’s funeral, held Monday near his family farm about 10 km from the Gaza Strip, after two rockets were reported fired from Gaza hours beforehand. The army said the rockets did not appear to land in Israel and caused no injuries or damage; Israeli media reported they fell into the sea. An Iron Dome battery was deployed near the burial site and police increased forces for the ceremonies. Israel warned Gaza’s rulers not to permit rocket fire during the funeral; there was no immediate response from Hamas or other factions.

Sharon, who died at 85 after eight years in a coma, was to be honored in a Jerusalem parliamentary memorial before burial at his Sycamore Farm ranch. U.S. Vice President Joe Biden—among delegations from 18 countries—planned to attend both the memorial and burial and to discuss stalled peace efforts and concerns about Iran’s interim nuclear deal with Israeli leaders. Israeli officials said they were prepared for potential threats, stepping up aerial patrols and readiness to respond if necessary. Since the 2012 Gaza war, Hamas has mostly restrained rocket fire though smaller groups sometimes launch attacks.

An East Liverpool, Ohio, police officer accidentally overdosed after coming into contact with suspected fentanyl during a traffic stop Friday night but has since recovered.

What happened
- Around 8:50 p.m. officers stopped a blue Monte Carlo after observing what they believed was a drug transaction. The driver, 25-year-old Justin Buckle, and passenger, 24-year-old Cortez Collins, were detained when officers saw them trying to discard evidence.
- Officers found multiple piles of white powder in the front of the car, on the floor, seats, shoes and even on an open drink can; small knotted baggies were also present. The suspects at first said it was cocaine, then said it was fentanyl. A field test returned negative for cocaine.
- Patrolman Chris Green followed station protocol by donning gloves and a mask to search the vehicle. Back at the station another officer saw powder on Green’s shirt; he brushed it off by instinct. About an hour later Green became ill and passed out from an apparent fentanyl exposure.

Medical response and outcome
- EMS administered one dose of naloxone (Narcan) at the station; at the hospital Green received three additional doses. Capt. Patrick Wright said Green was fine by Sunday.

Consequences and context
- Buckle (East Liverpool) and Collins (Cleveland) are charged with tampering with evidence; bond was set at $100,000 each. Collins also had an outstanding Euclid warrant. Police expect additional charges.
- The incident highlights risks fentanyl poses to first responders — it can be absorbed through the skin or inhaled — and has led departments to change procedures (e.g., no longer field-testing drugs) to reduce accidental exposures.

Swedish researchers have transferred embryos into four women who previously received transplanted wombs in an experimental attempt to enable them to carry their own biological children. The program, led by Dr. Mats Brannstrom at the University of Gothenburg, has performed nine uterine transplants since 2012 using living donors (mostly mothers or close relatives); two transplanted wombs were later removed due to complications. The recipients had IVF beforehand using their own eggs. Brannstrom said further transfers will be attempted as patients are ready and predicted three or four of the seven remaining recipients might ultimately give birth, while one or two may miscarry and others may not conceive.

Earlier uterine transplant attempts in Turkey and Saudi Arabia did not result in live births (one pregnancy ended in miscarriage), and teams in Britain and Hungary are planning transplants using deceased donors. The Swedish recipients will be maintained on low doses of immunosuppressant drugs and treated as high-risk pregnancies; the transplanted wombs are intended to be removed after a maximum of two pregnancies. Medical experts praised the step as promising but urged caution, noting uncertainties about blood flow, physiological adaptation of a transplanted uterus during pregnancy, donor surgical risks when living donors are used, and the ethical issues of a non–life-saving but risky donor operation.

St. Joseph Abbey, a Benedictine monastery in Louisiana, began making handcrafted caskets after Hurricane Katrina damaged its timber income. The monks invested $200,000 in a woodshop and sell simple, blessed cypress coffins priced $1,500–$2,000, made by monks as part of supporting the monastery’s work. Soon after they publicized the venture, the Louisiana State Board of Embalmers and Funeral Directors issued a cease-and-desist, citing a state law that limits sale of “funeral merchandise” to licensed funeral establishments. Licensing would require a funeral parlor, display area, licensed director and embalming facilities—requirements the abbey says are unnecessary for selling “just a big box.”

After failed legislative efforts to change the law, the abbey sued with help from the libertarian Institute for Justice, which aims to challenge protectionist economic regulations. In July a federal judge ruled the restriction unconstitutional, finding it driven by economic protectionism; the state board has appealed and the case will be heard in the New Orleans circuit court. The state defends the law as consumer protection and argues courts should defer to legislatures under the rational-basis standard; courts in other circuits have split on similar statutes. The Institute for Justice hopes an appeals decision will draw Supreme Court review. Abbot Justin Brown says the dispute has not disrupted monastery life and is willing to see the case advance if necessary.

Jason Alexander apologized after recounting on The Howard Stern Show why Seinfeld’s writers killed off his character George Costanza’s fiancée, Susan Ross (played by Heidi Swedberg). On the show he said he struggled to find the right comedic chemistry with Swedberg—her instincts and his often “misfired”—and that cast members, including Julia Louis-Dreyfus, eventually joked about “killing” the character. Larry David then used that idea as an inventive way to end the engagement arc in Season 7, culminating in Susan’s death from licking cheaply made envelopes.

Alexander said his intention was never to criticize Swedberg personally and later posted an apology on Twitter, calling her “a kind, lovely person” who worked hard on the role. He acknowledged he should have handled his own insecurities better and regretted any way his retelling might have diminished her. Swedberg continued acting after Seinfeld and now focuses on music and teaching ukulele.

On February 14, 2013, model and TV personality Reeva Steenkamp was shot dead at about 3 a.m. in the Pretoria home she shared with Olympian Oscar Pistorius. Detective Hilton Botha, a veteran homicide investigator, was among the first officers on the scene. He found Steenkamp’s body at the foot of the stairs and the primary crime scene in a bathroom cubicle riddled with bullet holes; a bloodied cricket bat, two phones and a 9mm pistol were on the floor. Botha concluded from wound trajectories, casing locations and other scene details that Pistorius fired at close range with his prosthetic legs on, and that the killing was not the result of a panicked defense against a burglar, as Pistorius later claimed. Botha believed the evidence showed Steenkamp had been cowering in the small toilet cubicle and had no realistic chance of survival. He arrested Pistorius, who said he had mistaken someone in the bathroom for an intruder and fired through the locked door.

The article profiles both principal figures. Pistorius — celebrated worldwide as the “Blade Runner” for competing with prosthetic legs, and a once-adored national icon after Paralympic and Olympic appearances — is portrayed as increasingly aggressive, entitled, gun‑toting, and prone to volatile behavior. Friends and acquaintances recount incidents of threatening conduct, heavy drinking, gun use, and controlling behavior toward women; prior allegations of assault from 2009 were dropped. Pistorius’s family and spokesmen framed his actions as a product of living in crime‑rife South Africa and insisted on his innocence.

Reeva Steenkamp is depicted as ambitious, outspoken, and committed to campaigning against violence toward women. She had a rising modeling and TV career, a law degree, and had recently been engaged in advocacy and media projects. Her family and friends mourn her as driven and generous; they angrily rejected perceived slights from the Pistorius camp after her death.

Botha aggressively pursued a murder theory and opposed bail, arguing Pistorius faced life imprisonment and could be a flight risk. During bail proceedings, however, Botha’s testimony was vigorously challenged by the defense; issues about witness identification, forensic interpretations, and inconsistencies in his statements surfaced. Botha was subsequently removed from the case and later resigned amid a reopened investigation into unrelated attempted‑murder charges against him, which damaged his credibility.

The prosecution initially charged Pistorius with premeditated murder (Schedule 6), placing the burden on the defense to show exceptional circumstances for bail. Public reaction was polarised: women’s groups and many in South Africa condemned Pistorius and demanded accountability, while supporters emphasized crime fears, his disability, and his celebrity status as mitigating context. The case drew intense local and international media attention, raising broader debates about intimate partner violence in South Africa (where “intimate femicide” is a leading cause of violent death among women), celebrity culture, the influence of sponsors and the press, and national pride amid scandal.

The article stops short of resolving guilt or innocence. It presents damning details and testimony that nudge toward the conclusion Pistorius intentionally shot Steenkamp, but it also notes remaining reasonable doubts, witness conflicts, and questions about the principal investigator’s reliability. Ultimately, the story frames the tragedy as both a personal loss for Steenkamp’s family and a public crisis exposing violence against women, flaws in policing and celebrity insulation, and a courtroom spectacle that will re-open painful national conversations.

Heirs of German Jewish art dealer Alfred Flechtheim have sued the State of Bavaria and the Bavarian State Paintings Collections in U.S. federal court seeking the return of eight modernist paintings they say were taken from Flechtheim after he fled Nazi Germany in 1933. Plaintiffs Michael Hulton (Flechtheim’s grand‑nephew) and Penny Hulton (widow of Flechtheim’s nephew and heir) allege Flechtheim left the works behind when he escaped Berlin for Paris and that Bavaria now holds several of them, some on display at Munich’s Pinakothek der Moderne.

The lawsuit contends the titles claimed by Bavaria are tainted by Nazi‑era dispossession and points to connections with Nazi dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt—whose son Cornelius’s cache of roughly 1,280–1,400 works was discovered in 2012—as evidence of how confiscated or coerced sales were channeled into German collections. Bavaria disputes the claims and has indicated the suit lacks merit and jurisdictional basis; its counsel declined to comment further.

The eight works named are six by Max Beckmann (Duchess of Malvedi; Still Life with Cigar Box; Quappi in Blue; Dream—Chinese Fireworks; Champagne Still Life; Still Life with Studio Window), Juan Gris’s Cruche et Verre sur un Table, and Paul Klee’s Grenzen des Verstandes. The complaint recounts Flechtheim’s prominence as an avant‑garde dealer, his impoverished exile and 1937 death in London, and the wider history of disputes over artworks seized, sold or hidden during the Nazi era. The case is Hulton et al. v. Bayerische Staatsgemaldesammlungen et al., S.D.N.Y. No. 16‑09360.

The Supreme Court ruled 6–2 in EPA v. EME Homer City Generation upholding the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2011 “good neighbor” interstate air pollution rule, a major victory for the EPA, downwind states, and public health. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote the majority opinion, joined by Roberts, Breyer, Kagan, Kennedy and Sotomayor, explaining that EPA’s cost‑based, state‑budget approach to reducing cross‑state emissions was “permissible, workable and equitable” and that regulators must account for the vagaries of wind and chemical transformations of pollutants as they travel. The rule requires about 28 eastern states and roughly 1,000 power plants to limit nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide emissions that contribute to smog, soot and associated health harms.

The D.C. Circuit’s contrary decision—requiring a precise state‑by‑state apportionment of responsibility and more deference to state plan‑making—was overturned; the Court also held EPA need not wait for states to act before imposing federal controls. EPA Administrator Gina McCarthy and public‑health and environmental groups hailed the decision as lifesaving, while industry groups and petitioning states (and dissenters Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas) criticized it as an expansion of unelected bureaucratic power and a departure from the Clean Air Act’s cooperative federalism. Justice Alito recused himself.

The Officer Down Memorial Page has launched ODMP K9 to honor police canines killed in the line of duty. The article highlights a recurring, preventable tragedy: dozens of police K-9s have died from heat-related causes after being left inside vehicles.

Cases and causes
- Primo, a New Orleans Police Belgian Malinois, died of heat shock in May 2009 after being left in a police SUV with the air conditioning off or failing; his body temperature neared 110°F. Officer Jason Lewis was initially charged and later pleaded to a misdemeanor; he was reinstated to the department but no longer works K-9. Primo’s death helped prompt changes in NOPD policy under a 2012 federal consent decree.
- Other examples: Ike (Arizona DOC) died after seven hours in a vehicle; Vegas and Hades (Bexar County, TX) died after nearly 30 hours; Sasha (Warwick, GA) was found dead after days in a vehicle; Beny (Montville Township, OH) died after more than four hours. Many handlers say they “forgot” the dog or mistakenly relied on vehicle AC.
- Between April and September, BuzzFeed confirmed 29 heat-related K-9 deaths from 2007 onward across 14 states; PETA identified 20. No federal tracking exists; Connecticut’s Police Work Dog Association logs K-9 service deaths generally (2,000+ since 1940) but not comprehensively by cause.

Why dogs are vulnerable
- Dogs cool mainly by panting and lack widespread sweat glands; thick-coated breeds commonly used in police work (German shepherds, Belgian Malinois, Dutch shepherds) are especially susceptible. Temperatures inside closed cars can rise extremely fast—studies show interior temps can reach well over 110–128°F within an hour even when outside is much cooler—causing seizures, organ failure, and death.

Prevention and response
- Simple technologies exist (marketed as “Hot Dog,” “Hot-N-Pop,” or heat-alert systems) that detect rising interior temperatures and automatically ventilate the vehicle, activate fans, or trigger alarms/sirens. These systems typically cost $500–$1,000 per vehicle and can be effective; some agencies have installed them (NOPD since 2010; Arizona DOC installed motion-sensing alarms after a death).
- Despite availability, adoption has been inconsistent. In one case Bexar County purchased systems but did not install them prior to the deaths of two K-9s. Departments that experienced deaths often report adopting new measures afterward.
- Advocacy groups like PETA urge nationwide installation of heat-alert systems; experts call the deaths “needless” and emphasize training, procedures, and equipment changes.

Context and impact
- Police K-9s are valuable operationally and emotionally—there are an estimated 20,000 working police dogs in North America, and procurement plus training and outfitting costs can exceed tens of thousands of dollars per dog. Their deaths are treated by handlers and communities as the loss of a partner or family member, and some incidents have produced legal charges, suspensions, public outcry, and calls for better policies.

Bottom line
Many K-9 heat deaths are preventable through existing, relatively inexpensive technology, clear procedures, and better training and oversight. Greater, consistent adoption of heat-alert systems and stronger policies could significantly reduce these tragic losses.

CVS Caremark announced it will stop selling cigarettes and other tobacco products in all CVS/pharmacy stores by October 1, citing a conflict between selling tobacco and the company’s purpose of helping people on a path to better health. CEO Larry Merlo and CMO Troyen Brennan framed the move as consistent with the company’s expanding role in health care—through 7,600 stores, 800+ MinuteClinics, 26,000 pharmacists and nurse practitioners, and a major pharmacy-benefit-management business—and as aligned with medical organizations that oppose tobacco sales in pharmacies.

The company will launch a national smoking-cessation program this spring, offering counseling, treatments and online resources at CVS/pharmacy and MinuteClinic locations and through plan-member programs. CVS said roughly 70% of smokers want to quit and about half try each year.

CVS expects to lose about $2 billion in annual tobacco-related sales—approximately 1.6% of revenue—reducing earnings by about 17 cents per share annually and by 6–9 cents per share for 2014 given the timing. The company says this will not change its 2014 financial guidance or five-year projections and expects to offset the profit impact through other opportunities.

The decision has drawn praise from public health groups and political leaders, including the AMA, American Cancer Society, Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and President Obama, who noted its potential to reduce tobacco-related disease and health care costs. CVS positions the move as reinforcing its credibility with clinicians and payers as it shifts from a retailer toward being an integrated health-care partner.

Summary:

Yo is an ultra-minimal messaging app created by Or Arbel that lets users send a single notification containing the word “Yo” (or “YoYo” with a double tap) to contacts. Built in about eight hours after a suggestion from investor Moshe Hogeg, the app launched in April and quickly attracted attention after raising about $1 million from angel investors linked to Hogeg. Arbel moved from Tel Aviv to San Francisco to work on Yo full time and plans to hire staff, open an office, and develop an API for brand and service integrations.

Arbel positions Yo as “context-based,” lightweight, non‑intrusive notification technology rather than a gag: use cases include quick social signals (“thinking of you,” “good morning”), live alerts (e.g., World Cup goals), publisher notifications for new stories, or transactional prompts (Starbucks order ready). The app’s simplicity is deliberate — Arbel resists adding features and highlights that Yo collects little personal data and is less prone to misuse than richer messaging platforms.

Reaction in tech circles has been mixed: the app went briefly viral on Twitter and attracted both amused endorsements and scorn, with critics questioning the product’s utility and whether large investments in such minimalist apps signal a tech bubble. Supporters argue Yo’s speed and focused utility could make it valuable or an attractive acquisition target; skeptics see the funding as emblematic of froth in the startup market. The long‑term viability of Yo — as a communications model or a business — remains to be seen.

In early November 2014, Democratic state Rep. Roger Freeman of Washington’s 30th Legislative District appeared to win re-election despite having died of colon cancer the previous week. Because Washington votes by mail and many ballots had already been returned before Freeman’s late-October death, many voters were unaware and still cast ballots for him. Early results showed Freeman leading Republican challenger Jack Dovey by roughly six points (about 53–47).

Under state law, if Freeman won, local Democratic precinct leaders would nominate three replacement candidates and the King and Pierce County councils would appoint one to fill the seat temporarily; a special election would be held the following year to fill the remainder of the term. If the Republican won, he would simply take the seat. The episode was noted as an unusual but not unprecedented occurrence — the article cites other examples of deceased candidates being elected — and highlighted procedural rules and practical complexities that apply when a candidate dies after ballots are mailed.

The Olsen twins’ luxury brand The Row has a $39,000 crocodile-skin backpack that is selling out at Barneys New York. Ashley Olsen told Women's Wear Daily it was the first item to sell out. Barneys began stocking the expensive bags in July to attract younger, high-spending customers who want durable, classic pieces that may be unique. Barneys’ fashion director noted the strategy was to offer an alternative to ultra-luxury labels and that exclusivity is a selling point.

Freestyle Releasing is positioning a new faith-based romance, Old Fashioned, as a deliberate counterprogramming choice to the mainstream erotic drama Fifty Shades of Grey by opening both films on Valentine’s Day 2015. Written, directed by and starring Rik Swartzwelder, Old Fashioned follows a former frat boy (Swartzwelder) and a free-spirited woman (Elizabeth Ann Roberts) attempting an “old-fashioned” courtship built on a Christian, “higher standard” for relationships. Its tagline is “Chivalry makes a comeback,” and the filmmakers emphasize chastity and Godly romance rather than sex or objectification. Freestyle—fresh off the surprise hit God’s Not Dead—calls Old Fashioned the first faith-based theatrical title aimed specifically at “underserved” Christian singles. Producers include Swartzwelder’s Skoche Films, Nathan Nazario, Dave DeBorde and Nini Hadjis; the cast also features Dorothy Silver, Tyler Hollinger, Lejon Woods, Maryann Nagel and Joseph Bonamico. The announcement arrived shortly after Universal released the first Fifty Shades trailer; Fox is also releasing a Poltergeist reboot that same weekend. Responses in some coverage have been cheeky or skeptical about the film’s premise and marketing as an explicit alternative to Fifty Shades.

This document combines a Meetup group description and a news report of a violent incident at a 2010 Kentucky campaign event.

- Meetup group: The group presents itself as a discussion and action forum to “restore the Constitution and Liberty” in Kentucky and the U.S., emphasizing common-sense moderation. It was created to discuss liberty, freedom and the Constitution and will also provide information and discussion about the Second Amendment and Open Carry events in Kentucky. The group links to opencarry.org and notes its picture is the Second Amendment dollar (with a link to Buds Gun Shop). It explicitly disclaims any encouragement of violence, saying it supports peaceful discussion and demonstration. The page notes topical similarity to a Lexington Rand/Ron Paul Campaign for Liberty Group.

- News report: A separate item recounts a violent episode in Lexington, Kentucky, during the 2010 Senate campaign: Lauren Valle of MoveOn.org was pushed to the ground while trying to take a photo with Republican nominee Rand Paul and was then stomped by a man. Video shows one man stepping on her head; that man was later identified as Tim Profitt, Bourbon County coordinator for Paul. Profitt admitted to the AP that he stepped on Valle’s head. Lexington police identified Profitt and said he was being served with a criminal summons to appear in Fayette County District Court. The Rand Paul campaign disavowed the volunteer and condemned violence; campaign manager Jesse Benton said any aggression or violence was deplorable and would not be tolerated.

Damien Hirst’s major retrospective at Tate Modern includes a gift shop selling high-priced limited-edition merchandise modeled on his work. The most eye-catching item is Hallucinatory Head, a plastic skull painted like his spin paintings, limited to 50 and priced at £36,800. Other items include a £10,500 set of china plates, £700 a roll of butterfly-print wallpaper, a £480 spotted skateboard, a £310 deckchair and a £195 butterfly umbrella. The shop is run by Other Criteria, which Hirst co-founded.

The show displays many of Hirst’s best-known—and controversial—pieces: the formaldehyde shark (The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living), A Thousand Years (a rotting cow’s head with maggots and flies), Horror at Home (a giant ashtray of cigarette butts), And Out Of Love (a live butterfly installation) and For the Love Of God (a platinum human skull encrusted with 8,601 diamonds, valued at about £50 million), housed in a darkened Turbine Hall room.

The merchandise launch came amid criticism from art critic Julian Spalding, who called Hirst a “con artist” and urged collectors to sell before values fall. Hirst defended the prices, arguing art’s value depends on demand and likening it to how designer jeans acquire worth beyond materials. The exhibition runs from April 4 to September 9.

The Pentagon has quietly released detailed records of its Excess Property (1033) Program — which transfers surplus military gear to federal, state and local law enforcement — after years of resisting full disclosure and amid criticism following the Ferguson unrest. The newly posted Defense Logistics Agency spreadsheets show the program has supplied more than $4.3 billion in equipment since 1997 (including $449 million in 2013), with the bulk of transfers occurring since 2006.

The inventory runs from mundane items (battery chargers, televisions marked “for personal/home use,” snowshoes, fence posts) to specialty and combat-grade hardware (armored mine-resistant vehicles, helicopters, robots for bomb squads, rifles in 5.56mm and 7.62mm calibers, grenade launchers). Many small and rural agencies — including town and college police departments and sheriff’s offices serving populations of only a few thousand or tens of thousands — are among recipients of heavy equipment such as MRAPs and rifles. Examples cited include Del Rio, Texas; Washington, Iowa; Rehoboth, Massachusetts; and Saddleback College Police in California. Some unusual items listed include French horns sent to small departments and 500 pairs of snowshoes to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department.

The data reveal substantial state-level distributions (more than $160 million to agencies in California) and underscore concerns about the militarization of local police forces and whether small departments need or are trained to use such military-grade equipment.

Investigators intensified a multi-day manhunt after convicted killers Richard Matt and David Sweat escaped Clinton Correctional Facility. Authorities reviewed gas-station surveillance footage and K-9 scent trails that led from the prison to a nearby station with a Subway, where dogs tracked scents east toward Cadyville. Officials found a possible shoe/boot imprint and a food wrapper and are trying to determine if the area was used as a resting spot. Roads in the search area were closed, residents were told to shelter in place, a local school was closed, and infrared technology was employed as part of the effort. State police closed Route 374 east of Dannemora for a lead; hundreds of officers have searched woods, farms and campsites around the region and on Lake Champlain, and authorities have not ruled out flight to Vermont, Canada or farther afield. Fifty digital billboards with the fugitives’ photos were posted across several states.

The report places the breakout in historical context: Clinton Correctional Facility, open since 1845, has a long history of escapes—tunneling through sewers, disguises and scaling walls—with many escape attempts ultimately ending in recapture. Past inmates’ accounts describe escape as a persistent preoccupation. The piece includes a profile of Timothy Vail, who escaped Elmira in 2003 and was caught two days later; he expressed admiration for Matt and Sweat and suggested patience and avoiding further crimes might help fugitives remain free, while also noting the psychological and practical hazards fugitives face. Overall, authorities emphasized widespread searching beyond the immediate area and urged public vigilance.

The document contains four short film reviews that mix criticism with plot summaries and colorful asides.

1) Bitch Slap (Michael Ordoña)
- A hyper-stylized, green-screen, exploitation tribute to “hot-women-in-peril” movies that feels like Zack Snyder meets Roger Corman (with a nod to Christopher Nolan’s Memento structure).
- Plot involves buried treasure, the CIA and a fractured timeline, but the film exists mainly to showcase its actresses’ bodies, frequent girl-on-girl fighting, and scant humor.
- Occasional enjoyable bits (a gratuitous water fight, an unhinged villain, a sudden make-out scene) are outweighed by endless fistfights, a predictable shock ending, and underused stunt talent (notably Zoë Bell).
- Verdict: slickly sexualized but surprisingly prudish—teasing without payoff; appeals only to a narrow niche that revels in women fighting.
- MPAA: R; runtime: 1h44; playing at Landmark Nuart Theatre, West L.A.

2) Daybreakers (Michael Ordoña)
- A vampire thriller set a decade after a plague leaves humans nearly extinct and vampires reliant on bottled or substitute blood.
- Ethan Hawke stars as a hematologist searching for a blood substitute; Willem Dafoe plays a lapsed vampire who may hold a key to a cure; Sam Neill plays corporate antagonists who prefer preserving privilege.
- The film mixes chase and moral dilemmas with graphic gore and effects (including implausible vampire weaknesses), and features conspicuous Chrysler product placement.
- Themes hint at resource exhaustion and elites clinging to profit, but the movie is undone by predictable plotting, wooden characters, clichéd scares, and gloomy cinematography.
- Verdict: not enough originality to relieve vampire fatigue, though visually intense moments persist.
- MPAA: R; runtime: 1h38; in general release.

3–4) Wonderful World (Mark Olsen and an additional short paragraph)
- Matthew Broderick plays Ben Singer, a burned-out former children’s musician turned misanthropic proofreader whose life is pared down to pot-smoking and chess with his Senegalese roommate, Ibou (Michael K. Williams).
- When Ibou falls into a diabetic coma, his sister Khadi (Sanaa Lathan) moves in and becomes the catalyst for Ben’s gradual emotional renewal—echoing the immigrant-as-salvation trope seen in films like The Visitor.
- Writer-director Josh Goldin’s debut is uneven: it aims for a redemptive arc but doesn’t fully explore why Ben was a kids’ performer or deeply probe his psyche. The film finds genuine warmth in brief musical moments but largely fails to sustain them.
- Broderick’s portrayal leans into a melancholy, beaten-down persona (accentuated by a beard), and Lathan is miscast in an implausible role. The script and production feel limited in ambition and budget.
- Verdict: Promising but flawed; touching moments exist but the story is thin and underdeveloped.
- MPAA: R; runtime: 1h29; playing at the Laemmle Music Hall in Beverly Hills.

Overall tone: all four pieces are critical, noting stylistic ambitions and occasional strengths but highlighting predictable plotting, shallow character work, and limited payoffs.

The Khizanat al-Qarawiyyin library in Fez, Morocco—widely regarded as the world’s oldest library, founded in 859 by Fatima al‑Fihri—is reopening after a multimillion‑pound restoration that began in 2012. Canadian‑Moroccan architect Aziza Chaouni led the project, which sought to preserve historic fabric while making the complex usable again for students, researchers and residents rather than only tourists.

Key restoration work and features
- Structural repairs and conservation of woodwork, tiles, courtyards and original decorative elements, informed by earlier French repairs from the 1940s.
- New mechanical and conservation facilities: a lab to treat, preserve and digitize manuscripts, high-resolution scanners to detect tiny defects, and machines to condition fragile papers.
- Climate‑controlled, highly secured rooms for the most precious items, plus an underground canal/sewerage system to remove damaging moisture.
- Modern sustainability measures (solar panels, water collection) and careful integration of technology so the building remains a living institution.

Collections and significance
- The library holds roughly 4,000 manuscripts, including a ninth‑century Qur’an in Kufic script on camel skin and an original copy of Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah. Texts span subjects from theology and law to astronomy and grammar.
- Khizanat al‑Qarawiyyin is part of a complex that includes the Qarawiyyin Mosque and university—the latter historically a major center of learning and cross‑cultural exchange with alumni such as Maimonides and Ibn Khaldun.

Context and goals
- The reopening is framed both as cultural preservation and as a component of restoring Fez’s status as a spiritual and cultural capital. Chaouni emphasizes that the library must “continue to live,” serving locals as a communal space as well as researchers and visitors.
- The project also responds to regional threats to heritage and national efforts to protect Morocco’s identity and archives; King Mohammed VI inspected the works and is expected to inaugurate the reopening, planned before 2017 (no fixed date given in the piece).
- The restoration is linked to broader urban improvements in Fez (river clean‑up, festivals, quarter renovations) aimed at sustainable revitalization while maintaining the medina’s living character.

Atmosphere and stewardship
- The restored reading room retains the musty, fragile quality of ancient books and houses stringent security: historically, some doors required multiple keyholders. Caretakers describe fierce custodianship of the collection—“You can hurt us, but you cannot hurt the books.”

Overall, the project balances careful conservation of an irreplaceable manuscript heritage with upgrades to protect and digitize the collection and to reintegrate the library into the everyday life of Fez.

Transparency International’s 2013 Global Corruption Barometer, based on responses from over 114,000 people in 107 countries, finds widespread everyday bribery and rising concern about corruption. Key findings:

- 27% of respondents reported paying a bribe in the previous 12 months; in Liberia and Sierra Leone the figure exceeded 75%. Despite this, two-thirds said they refused to pay when asked.  
- Police and the judiciary are the most corruption-prone institutions: about one-third of respondents who had contact with police paid bribes, and 24% paid bribes in dealings with the judicial system. In countries where police or courts are viewed as most corrupt, the incidence of bribe requests rises sharply (about 53% for police in the 36 worst-rated countries; 30% for judiciary in the 20 worst-rated).  
- More than half of respondents said corruption has increased over the past two years. On a 1–5 scale where 5 = “corruption is a very serious problem,” the global average was 4.1; Liberia and Mongolia scored worst at 4.8.  
- Political parties were named the most corrupt institution in over 50 countries. Public confidence in governments’ anti-corruption efforts has fallen—only 22% now consider them effective, down from 31% in 2008.  

Transparency International emphasizes both the high level of bribe-paying and the significant portion of people willing to resist and fight corruption.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, speaking hoarsely and emotionally, revealed he has a “50-50” chance of surviving liposarcoma, a rare cancer, and described the diagnosis as the hardest thing he’s faced. He said chemotherapy has left him fatigued and emotional — “some nights, I just cry myself to sleep” — and that the illness’s biggest pain has been its effect on his young children. Ford apologized for his voice and credited treatment side effects for his difficulty speaking.

After being hospitalized in mid-September, Ford withdrew from the mayoral race and is now running for his former Ward 2 (Etobicoke North) city council seat. He has 13 opponents and has been seen canvassing at least once since discharge, but skipped a Ward 2 all-candidates debate and doubts he will be well enough for more. Reactions from rivals split: Andray Domise called Ford’s candidacy “highly irresponsible” if he won’t campaign or present a platform, while candidate Luke LaRocque said it’s Ford’s personal decision and residents should decide at the ballot box. Polls suggest Ford retains a large lead.

Ford spent time at City Hall reading get-well cards and signing letters; he also helped put up campaign signs. His brother Doug Ford has taken over the mayoral campaign and unveiled a transit plan similar to Rob’s previous platform: a $9-billion, 32-km subway proposal funded through other government assistance, public-private partnerships and asset sales. Doug’s plan places the downtown (Yonge) relief line higher priority than Rob’s earlier focus on Finch and Sheppard lines.

A Guardian investigation found that sex traffickers across the U.S. are actively recruiting women from inside prisons and jails, using government websites, public records and the bail bond system to identify, contact and control them so they can be forced into prostitution after release. Traffickers gather mugshots, charges, release dates and bail information posted online and exploit commissary accounts, inmate mail and phone systems to groom inmates with promises of money, housing or love. They also use corrupt bondsmen or post bail themselves, then coerce women to “work off” debts under threat of rescinded bonds, violence or re-incarceration.

The reporting drew on testimony from more than 20 survivors in 11 states, correctional staff, prosecutors and convicted traffickers and documents cases in Florida, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and Mississippi. It details both individual predators—such as Richard Rawls, convicted of trafficking at least 18 former inmates in Florida—and systemic patterns: traffickers cultivate relationships via letters and money, pay in-house recruiters, and wait outside facilities to collect newly released women “like a line of cabs.” Many targeted women are repeatedly incarcerated, often for non-violent or drug-related offenses, and are highly vulnerable because of poverty, addiction, trauma and lack of support.

Advocates warn prisons and jails are “perfect hunting grounds” because isolation and criminal records deepen vulnerability; they say the criminal justice system’s public records and lax protections facilitate predation. Survivors and prosecutors describe widespread exploitation of bail and bond processes and routine passing of inmate information by bondsmen. Only a handful of prosecutions—Rawls’s case among them—have resulted from these practices.

Campaigners call for urgent reforms: better staff training, stronger protections for inmates’ personal data, oversight of bail bond practices, improved in-facility prevention and post-release support (housing, employment, trauma recovery) to reduce reliance on traffickers. Authorities like the Florida Department of Corrections say they have adopted anti-trafficking measures, but advocates say support remains inadequate and many women remain trapped in a cycle of exploitation and criminalisation.

NOAA has declared an "unusual mortality event" after 30 large whales washed up in the western Gulf of Alaska since May — roughly three times the historical average for the region. The strandings include 11 fin whales, 14 humpbacks, one gray whale and four unidentified cetaceans. Six additional large whale deaths have been reported off British Columbia in the same period; Canadian and U.S. agencies are coordinating investigations.

The designation unlocks additional resources and a formal, multi-agency inquiry, but progress is hampered by extremely limited sample availability: only one Alaska carcass has yielded a sample so far (described as less than ideal), and two necropsies in B.C. are pending results. A leading hypothesis is toxins from harmful algal blooms, but there is no conclusive evidence linking blooms to the deaths. Investigators cite logistical challenges — remote, inaccessible coastline, floating carcasses that rarely beach, and safety risks such as bears feeding on carcasses — that limit necropsies and definitive cause determination.

NOAA and partners will expand data collection, environmental and historical analyses, and consult seabird/other mortality patterns; such investigations can take months to years. The public is urged to report dead or distressed marine mammals (Alaska hotline: 877-925-7773; B.C. hotline: 1-800-465-4336) but not to approach or touch animals.

Students in the Pi Kappa Alpha fraternity at California State University, Chico are facing federal criminal charges after U.S. Forest Service investigators say fraternity members illegally cut down more than 32 trees and fired guns at a campground in Lassen National Forest during an April initiation event. A camper reported about 80 people at the site and identified fraternity president Evan Jossey and three others as members who said they were holding an initiation ceremony. The Forest Service released surveillance photos showing men buying tools believed used in the vandalism, and photos taken at the scene documented the damage. Each named member faces charges including vandalism, illegal firearms use, and degrading U.S. territory; the fraternity and Jossey are due in court June 26, 2017. The chapter disputes at least some allegations on its Facebook page and says members have faced community threats and condemnation from peers.

A 14-year-old Clayton County girl, Ayvani Perez, who was abducted from her Ellenwood home early Tuesday, was found and returned to her family Wednesday night. Authorities located her at a Conyers residence; she was evaluated and appeared in good health. Two men, Wildrego Jackson, 29, and Juan Alberto Rodriguez, 40, were arrested in connection with the case. Jackson faces conspiracy to commit kidnapping charges and has a long criminal history; Rodriguez is being held on immigration-related charges. Investigators say the two arrested are not the armed men shown in released sketches and that the sketch suspects remain at large. Police say two armed men broke into Ayvani’s home, demanded money and jewelry from her mother, then abducted the girl. Federal agents would not disclose how they found Ayvani. Reporting uncovered a prior connection between Rodriguez and Ayvani’s mother: both were arrested in a 2012 Henry County drug case in which about 500 pounds of marijuana were found; those charges were later dropped. Neighbors expressed relief and lingering questions about the circumstances of the kidnapping.

Sienna Miller is preparing to join legal action against the News of the World and Scotland Yard over phone hacking. Her lawyers say she will seek a judicial review of the Metropolitan Police’s handling of the investigation after discovering that private investigator Glenn Mulcaire had obtained her mobile numbers, account number and voicemail PIN—information needed to intercept messages. Miller learned only in October 2009 that police had held this material since Mulcaire’s 2006 arrest; the force delayed responding for months after her lawyers queried them. Miller, who previously settled privacy claims with the paper in 2008, noticed voicemail anomalies and changed numbers, but Mulcaire’s records suggest he found her new number.

Miller intends to join a legal challenge run by Bindmans seeking a judicial review of the police’s failure to warn potential victims; others in the action include former deputy prime minister John Prescott, ex–Scotland Yard deputy assistant commissioner Brian Paddick, Chris Bryant and journalist Brendan Montague. Police say they told the director of public prosecutions in 2006 they would contact “potential victims,” but many with clear evidence of hacking were not warned until the Guardian revived the story in 2009. Authorities refuse to disclose how many people have been warned because identifying numbers could reveal victims.

Separately, former News of the World reporter Sean Hoare—who told media outlets that hacking was widespread at the paper and implicated former editor Andy Coulson—has been interviewed under caution by police (he was not arrested). Another ex-staffer, Paul McMullan, has also been contacted about questioning under caution. MPs’ Standards and Privileges Committee will seek legal advice on whether phone hacking could amount to contempt of Parliament; it will initially consider the legal question rather than investigate individual cases. Other public figures, including Steve Coogan and Chris Tarrant, are also pursuing legal action after their details were found among Mulcaire’s records.

California Gov. Jerry Brown issued an executive order in response to a worsening multi-year drought and record-low Sierra Nevada snowpack, calling for mandatory urban water reductions and new conservation measures after voluntary targets largely failed.

Key points:
- The order targets a 25% reduction in statewide urban water use in 2013 versus recent baselines, shifting from largely voluntary cuts to mandatory action.
- Urban measures include banning watering of roadway medians, partnering with local agencies to remove 50 million square feet of turf in favor of drought-tolerant landscaping, rebates for high-efficiency appliances, required drip or microspray irrigation for new developments using drinking water, and stricter water-rate structures and fees to discourage waste. Golf courses, campuses and cemeteries must cut usage.
- Local water agencies will receive conservation targets based on past performance; early adopters are effectively rewarded while laggards face stronger requirements. The state can fine noncompliant local agencies up to $10,000 per day.
- The order requires agricultural districts in depleted groundwater basins to share groundwater use data with the state, but critics say it doesn’t go far enough in addressing agricultural water use and groundwater protection.
- Officials noted the Sierra Nevada snowpack was measured at only ~5% of the April 1 average—the lowest on record since 1950—which threatens reservoir refill and underscores the need for continued and possibly deeper restrictions later in the year.
- Reactions: Southern California agencies and some city leaders welcomed the mandate as timely; environmental and water experts said mandatory conservation was necessary and more measures (even bans on outdoor use) may be needed. Farmers face severe impacts already, with possible further fallowing of Central Valley acreage due to lack of irrigation deliveries.

Overall, the order aims to force rapid urban water-saving changes amid an acute drought and critically low snowpack while providing regulatory mechanisms and incentives to accelerate conservation; enforcement and agricultural groundwater protection remain contentious issues.

A rare "Blue Moon" drew wide attention and photos on a clear Tuesday night. Though popularly understood as a second full moon in a calendar month, the original astronomical definition is the third full moon in a season that has four—both definitions produce a Blue Moon only every few years. The modern, simpler "two full moons in one month" interpretation arose from a mistake published in Sky & Telescope in the 1940s and has become the common usage. The moon is not literally blue in most cases, though atmospheric particles from major volcanic eruptions (Krakatoa in 1883, El Chichon in 1983, Mount Pinatubo in 1991) or large fires can tint it blue; the last such event producing a blue-tinted moon occurred over Edinburgh in 1950. The next Blue Moon under the popular calendar-month definition was July 31, 2015; under the traditional seasonal definition, it would be May 21, 2016. Social media and news outlets buzzed with photos, jokes and references to the moon’s many folk names (Full Sturgeon Moon, Green Corn Moon, Grain Moon, Full Red Moon).

Here’s a concise, comprehensive summary of the document:

It notes that Arlene Castro (Ariel Castro’s daughter) told the show she was the last person to see 14-year-old Gina; she said they parted after Arlene borrowed 50 cents to call her mother. Maria Rose Belding, a 20-year-old American University sophomore, co-founded MEANS Database (Matching Excess And Need for Stability), an online platform and app that connects donors with surplus food to food banks and pantries that need it. Sparked by watching a pantry discard thousands of boxes of expired macaroni and cheese as a high school volunteer, Belding built MEANS to solve the information gap that leaves food wasted while millions face insecurity. Co-founder Grant Nelson developed the technology; Belding organized donors and partner agencies.

MEANS lets donors list available items, notifies nearby recipients, and enables claiming and pickup. In its first year the system rescued roughly 4,000 pounds (about two tons) of food, attracted more than 200 donor and recipient accounts representing over 2,000 partner agencies across 24–27 states, and grew a staff of about 11 plus interns and volunteers. The project won several awards and grants, including the GW New Venture Competition and a $10,000 L’Oréal Paris Women of Worth prize, helping fund operations.

MEANS differentiates itself by enabling small organizations and individuals to participate in food recovery at a micro scale that large organizations can’t efficiently serve. Belding emphasizes using data science to make the network effective—discovering, for example, that roughly half of online listings for emergency food providers have incorrect contact information—and plans to create a public searchable directory of pantries.

To become more sustainable and less grant-dependent, MEANS is developing a program to track donation data to help retailers claim tax benefits and plans to take a small fee while keeping the platform free for users. Belding stresses that practical analytics and entrepreneurship, paired with empathy, can help reduce both food waste (an estimated 40% of U.S. food) and food insecurity (tens of millions affected), and hopes to expand MEANS into more states and refine its systems while finishing college.

Nicky Hilton Rothschild and husband James Rothschild are expecting their first child this summer, multiple outlets (E! News, Us Weekly, PEOPLE) report. The newlyweds, who married in July 2015 in a high-profile ceremony at Kensington Palace after an August 2014 engagement on Lake Como, have begun telling close friends and family and are said to be "over the moon" and excited. Coverage notes details of their wedding (Nicky’s white lace Valentino gown) and mentions sister Paris Hilton’s enthusiasm about nieces/nephews. Insiders say Nicky is feeling well and the couple have been spotted shopping for children’s items. (The document also includes unrelated headlines and brief items on other topics.)
