On Oct. 22, 2013, 13-year-old Andy Lopez was shot and killed by Sonoma County Deputy Erick Gelhaus as the boy walked in southwest Santa Rosa carrying an airsoft BB gun that resembled an AK-47. Gelhaus fired eight rounds, striking Andy seven times. The killing sparked widespread protests across Santa Rosa, the Bay Area and statewide, with activists calling the incident an example of police brutality and demanding justice.

On July 7, 2014, Sonoma County District Attorney Jill Ravitch announced she would not file criminal charges against Gelhaus, concluding his actions were lawful. Ravitch released a 52-page summary and a larger investigative file supporting the decision. Key findings cited by the DA’s office included that Gelhaus and his partner reasonably believed the gun was real and that Gelhaus faced a rapidly evolving “do-or-die” threat; technical analysis showed the deputy could fire eight rounds in two seconds and reconstructed shot trajectories. The report also revealed significant levels of THC in Andy’s system (consistent with smoking marijuana roughly an hour before his death), which experts said could have impaired judgment and reaction time — a point critics later questioned as deflecting blame.

The DA’s announcement prompted immediate protests and strong criticism from activists, family attorneys, and community members who called for accountability and decried police militarization. Andy’s family has filed a federal civil-rights lawsuit against Gelhaus and the county; that suit and a federal review by the Justice Department were noted as ongoing. Local officials urged peaceful demonstrations, and the sheriff proposed legislative changes to require imitation firearms be made clearly distinguishable to help prevent similar tragedies. The county’s grand jury and federal authorities received the full report; the state Attorney General declined to review it. Ravitch characterized the case as a tragic, painful chapter for the community and emphasized the need to rebuild trust.

Violence in the U.S. has declined substantially since the 1990s (from 685 violent incidents per 100,000 people in 1995 to 366 per 100,000 in 2014), but significant variation remains between states. 24/7 Wall St. created an index ranking states by peacefulness using violent crime and homicide rates, estimated household gun ownership, and incarceration levels; Maine ranked most peaceful, Louisiana least. Experts emphasize that violence exists on a continuum and is highly localized—even within cities and neighborhoods—and is driven by many interlocking factors such as poverty, the concentration of young men (ages 15–25), environmental disorder (vacant housing, broken streetlights), low educational attainment, and unemployment or disengagement from the labor force.

Key patterns in the data:
- More peaceful states generally have higher household incomes and lower poverty rates; among the 25 most peaceful states only five have poverty above the national rate (15.5%).
- Less peaceful states tend to maintain larger law enforcement forces: eight of the 10 least peaceful states exceed the national ratio of 282 law-enforcement employees per 100,000 residents, while most of the 10 most peaceful states have smaller forces.
- The relationship between policing and safety is complex—more officers don’t automatically yield less crime, and aggressive tactics can alienate communities.

Profiles of five of the 10 least peaceful states highlighted:
- Arizona (10th least peaceful): Violent crime rate ~400/100,000, median household income ~$50,068, elevated property crime and several mass-shooting incidents; 339 law-enforcement workers per 100,000 residents.
- South Carolina (9th): Violent crime ~498/100,000 (7th highest), murder rate 6.4/100,000, median income ~$45,238, high gun ownership (~44.4%), though the state has made notable five-year crime-rate improvements.
- Florida (8th): Violent crime ~541/100,000 (5th highest), murder rate 5.8/100,000, median income ~$47,463; experienced many mass shootings with high casualties (including Orlando), and ranks high on robbery, aggravated assault and property crime.
- Missouri (7th): Violent crime ~443/100,000, one of the highest murder rates (6.6/100,000), driven largely by Kansas City and St. Louis; policing controversies (e.g., Ferguson) and relatively high law-enforcement staffing (335 per 100,000).
- Arkansas (6th): Violent crime ~480/100,000, median household income ~$41,262 (one of the lowest), low labor-force participation and low college attainment correlate with higher violence.

Overall, the report underscores that crime rates reflect socioeconomic conditions, local environments, demographics, firearm prevalence, and policing strategies, and that addressing violence requires attention to these multiple, localized causes rather than simple, one-size-fits-all solutions.

The document chronicles the U.S. federal government shutdown and debt-ceiling standoff in mid-October 2013, as lawmakers raced to avoid a first-ever default. After two weeks of a partial shutdown and rising public frustration—especially among furloughed federal workers—Senate leaders intensified talks with a Thursday deadline looming when the Treasury’s extraordinary borrowing authority was expected to run out.

Key points:
- Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D) and Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R) engaged in last-minute negotiations; both expressed guarded optimism about reaching a deal to reopen the government and avert default.
- Democrats, sensing political leverage from public disapproval of Republicans, pushed to reopen the government only on terms that wouldn’t lock in deeper sequester-era spending cuts for an extended period. They sought a short funding extension so they could renegotiate cuts before they worsened in mid-January.
- Republicans, notably McConnell, backed a bipartisan proposal led by Sen. Susan Collins that would reopen the government and extend the debt limit while keeping sequestration-level cuts in place through January (with borrowing authority extended into early 2014). Some GOP senators and House conservatives opposed rolling back the sequester.
- A group of bipartisan senators, including Democrats working with Collins, said they were negotiating but did not support the proposal in its current form.
- Treasury Secretary Jack Lew warned the government could exhaust borrowing capacity by Oct. 17 and likely begin missing major payments by early November; investors were most concerned about interest payments due Oct. 31.
- Markets and business leaders urged a quick resolution; polls showed heavy public disapproval of House Republicans’ handling of the crisis.
- International reaction included warnings from IMF chief Christine Lagarde about global disruption from a U.S. default and a Chinese commentary urging a move toward a less U.S.-centric world order.
- Ultimately, Congress moved toward a compromise: legislation to fund the government into mid-January and extend the debt ceiling into early 2014 was approved and signed in an 11th-hour deal, ending the shutdown and averting immediate default.

The standoff highlighted continuing partisan divisions over long-term spending and health-care policy, the political risk for Republicans, and the broader economic and international fallout such budget crises can produce.

President Barack Obama will meet with House and Senate Democrats on Capitol Hill Wednesday at 9 a.m. in the Congressional Visitors Center auditorium to coordinate defenses of the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) against planned Republican repeal efforts early in the next Congress. The meeting, first reported by Politico, comes as Republicans pledge a rapid repeal — possibly using budget reconciliation to avoid a 60‑vote threshold — and may delay repeal’s effective date for up to three years to craft a replacement.

Democrats are strategizing a range of responses: blocking repeal and conservative replacement efforts (Sen. Chuck Schumer has vowed to do so), emphasizing the law’s benefits (House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and others), and mobilizing grassroots support with a “day of action” on Jan. 15 targeting threats not only to ACA but to Medicare and Medicaid. Obama’s session is expected to touch on health-care strategy and other priorities such as Dodd‑Frank and environmental policies as Democrats prepare to defend his domestic achievements. The article notes the ACA’s impact — more than 20 million insured, protections for young adults and people with preexisting conditions, and slower health-care cost growth — and the difficulty of preserving popular provisions without the less popular elements that fund them, a point highlighted in debates over what a Republican replacement might keep.

Jack McAtee, a 27-year-old Breckenridge resident, went missing after a bizarre incident on Sept. 18–19, 2014. On the evening of Sept. 18 his black sedan veered off a paved bike path above Dillon Reservoir, rolled across dirt and gravel for roughly 135 feet, went airborne about 110 feet, flipped end over end and crashed into the water. The car was nearly submerged; McAtee miraculously swam free with a single cut above his left eye. He told a trooper he had fallen asleep at the wheel; the trooper noted erratic mood swings but saw no signs of intoxication. Family members later said McAtee had recently stopped taking medication for bipolar disorder.

Authorities took McAtee to a hospital and then to a mental-health facility; he was released the next morning, Sept. 19, with $67, a red hoodie and a tan hat. He was last seen leaving the facility and never contacted family again. Early searches and widespread public appeals — targeting truck stops, shelters, remote “off‑the‑grid” communities, and locations tied to his interests (Moab, Alaska, Northern California, Burning Man, Slab City, etc.) — yielded no confirmed sightings. The family organized extensive ground searches in Summit County, posted flyers at trailheads, enlisted search-and-rescue teams, sought tips from hunters, and ran a website (findjackmcatee.com) to coordinate efforts and share updates. They also asked people to look for his missing blue Trek mountain bike, which remains unaccounted for and could be a key clue.

For months the family alternated between hope and fear, noting Jack had previously disappeared briefly after stopping medication but never this long. Investigators treated his disappearance as a missing-person case. In August 2015 hikers found a skull near Peak 1 on the Tenmile Range; DNA testing later confirmed the remains were Jack’s. Summit County officials say the investigation into his death is ongoing; no manner or cause of death has been released. The family has expressed gratitude for the public’s support, continues to seek answers and closure, and has created a memorial fundraising effort in his name. Authorities asked anyone with information to contact the Summit County Sheriff’s Office.

In July 2012, 26-year-old Caitlan “Caity” Coleman of Stewartstown, Pennsylvania, and her husband Joshua Boyle, a Canadian, set off on an extended backpacking trip through Central Asia. Though Caitlan’s family believed they intended to avoid Afghanistan, the couple ended up there and were last heard from in October 2012 when Joshua emailed that they were in an “unsafe” area and a final bank withdrawal was made in Kabul. In 2013 the Haqqani network, an affiliate of the Taliban, surfaced as their captors.

Since then Caitlan and Joshua have been held in captivity—believed to be in Pakistan—and have appeared in a handful of Taliban videos pleading for their release. In those videos they warn that their captors will kill them and their two young sons—born in captivity—if Afghan authorities continue executing Taliban prisoners. The most recent clip surfaced in mid‑2016 and is being examined by U.S. and Canadian officials; Taliban spokesmen say the footage may date to 2015 and that the family remains alive and “in good health.”

The story has shocked Caitlan’s hometown: she’s remembered as a devout, generous, adventurous young woman who kept her pregnancy secret before the abduction and gave birth twice while captive. Public attention has been limited, and family and friends say media coverage and political focus have waned as other crises dominate. Reporting and former military testimony have also highlighted past bureaucratic failings in U.S. hostage‑recovery efforts—criticisms that helped prompt the 2015 creation of the Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell—but resolving cases in Pakistan remains especially difficult politically and operationally. The U.S. government has made only sparse public statements, urging their immediate humanitarian release while declining to discuss operational details. The family continues to plead for mercy and for the couple and their children to be returned.

Johann Breyer, an 89-year-old former SS guard living in Philadelphia, died Tuesday night at a hospital a day before a U.S. magistrate approved his extradition to Germany to face Nazi war crimes charges, his lawyer said. Magistrate Timothy Rice found probable cause that Breyer was the same person sought for aiding and abetting murder at Auschwitz, saying no statute of limitations protects murder and that Breyer’s role as an armed SS guard at a camp run as a killing center established probable cause of complicity. German authorities had issued a 2013 warrant charging him with 158 counts of accessory to murder tied to some 216,000 victims brought to Auschwitz in 1944. Breyer, who immigrated to the U.S. in 1952 and held American citizenship, acknowledged serving as a guard but maintained he was stationed away from the death camp’s killing operations and denied personal wrongdoing. He had been hospitalized and his attorneys cited frail health, including mild dementia, heart conditions and prior strokes; he was held without bail pending extradition, which would also have required final U.S. government approval.

The European Commission is examining reports that some TVs may be programmed to reduce power use during the standardised energy-efficiency test, potentially misleading official ratings. Two independent studies prompted the follow-up. ComplianTV (an EU-funded consortium including the UK’s Energy Saving Trust) found one Samsung LCD model’s power draw fell from about 70W to 39W within a minute of the IEC test video starting. The Swedish Energy Agency reported that displays from a different, unnamed maker appeared to “recognise” the standard test film and immediately lower brightness and power.

Samsung denies wrongdoing, saying the observed effect comes from its “motion lighting” feature—an out-of-the-box backlight control introduced in 2011 that reduces brightness when motion is detected in real content as well as during lab tests. The company says this is a consumer energy-saving function, not a test-specific defeat device.

Campaigners and regulators are concerned because the behaviour echoes the Volkswagen diesel emissions scandal: software that alters device performance under test conditions could mean products pass lab compliance but use more energy in real life. The European Commission said it will verify the findings, assess scale and whether any “defeat devices” lead to falsely compliant products, and has proposed clarifying ecodesign rules to outlaw such practices. Past UK and US investigations have flagged similar anomalies, and further testing is planned to determine whether manufacturers are gaming test procedures. Televisions are a significant and growing share of household electricity use in Europe, which underlines the potential impact if ratings are being manipulated.

Perez Hilton (Mario Lavandeira Jr.), the 34-year-old openly gay blogger, announced on his blog that he became a father earlier this month to a healthy baby boy with “lots of hair.” He posted a photo of himself cradling the newborn but did not disclose the child’s name, the birth mother’s identity, or whether the baby arrived via adoption or surrogacy. In the announcement, Hilton thanked his readers for their support, expressed his joy and readiness for parenthood, and noted his family’s happiness. The piece also references that Hilton had previously said he hoped to be a father by 35 and had looked into surrogacy.

A gunman attacked Reina, a popular Istanbul nightclub, during New Year’s celebrations around 1:30 a.m. on January 1, killing 39 people—mostly foreigners—and wounding dozens. The attacker killed a police officer and a civilian at the door before entering and firing hundreds of rounds in the club for several minutes, shooting many victims who were already down. Islamic State claimed responsibility.

Multiple survivors described playing dead to survive. William (Jake) Raak, a 35-year-old small-business owner from Greenville, Delaware, told NBC he stayed motionless after being hit in the hip (the bullet traveled to his knee) and was among a group of nine in which seven were shot; the State Department said he was the only U.S. citizen injured. Other survivors recounted the gunman shouting “Allahu Akbar,” throwing explosives and deliberately targeting crowded areas. Some victims were shot at close range or point-blank.

Turkish authorities detained eight people in connection with the attack and released an image of a suspect from surveillance video; they said they had recovered fingerprints and were continuing an international manhunt. Victims included citizens of Canada, India, Lebanon, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Kuwait, and Syria. The assault drew comparisons to previous militant attacks on crowded venues and prompted international repatriation and assistance efforts for victims’ families.

President Trump pardoned former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio on Aug. 25, after privately exploring ways to halt the criminal case earlier in the year. Trump asked Attorney General Jeff Sessions if the government could drop the case but was advised that doing so would be inappropriate; he then decided to let the case go to trial and planned to grant clemency if Arpaio were convicted. Arpaio had been found guilty of contempt for defying a federal judge’s order to stop detaining people on suspicion of being undocumented immigrants and faced up to six months in jail. Trump’s longtime political friendship with Arpaio—rooted in shared “birther” activity and a mutual focus on immigration—helped drive the decision. White House aides including Stephen Miller and Stephen Bannon advocated for the pardon, the White House Counsel’s Office prepared paperwork, and Trump signed the clemency order without the normal Justice Department review; Arpaio’s lawyer received the signed document by email the evening it was issued.

The pardon triggered widespread criticism across the political spectrum. Democrats condemned it as approval of racially discriminatory conduct; several Republicans, including Sens. John McCain and Jeff Flake and House Speaker Paul Ryan, also expressed disapproval, saying it undermined respect for the rule of law and law‑enforcement responsibilities. Critics said Trump’s initial effort to intervene directly in the prosecution displayed a troubling disregard for the Justice Department’s independence and resembled other alleged attempts by Trump to influence investigations. The decision was announced amid a cluster of controversial Friday-night moves by the administration (including personnel changes and transgender military guidance), a timing some aides said was intended to minimize media scrutiny as Hurricane Harvey dominated coverage.

Astronomers have for the first time directly imaged a large section of the cosmic web—the filamentary network of matter that theory predicts links galaxies—by using a distant quasar as a “cosmic flashlight.” Using the 10‑m Keck I telescope, a team led by Sebastiano Cantalupo (UC Santa Cruz) observed a glowing nebula of hydrogen gas about 2 million light‑years across around quasar UM287, roughly 10 billion light‑years away. The quasar’s intense radiation causes the diffuse, cold gas to emit Lyman‑alpha light, revealing filamentary structure that appears to trace underlying dark‑matter filaments predicted by cosmological simulations.

This is the first direct image of such extended, cold intergalactic gas (previous work mostly detected gas indirectly through absorption or by finding smaller “dark galaxies”). The observed nebula is unusually large—at least twice the size of previously detected nebulae—and suggests there may be more ordinary gas in these filaments than current simulations predict (roughly an order of magnitude higher), possibly pointing to resolution limits or missing physics in the models. The result supports the standard cosmological picture in which dark matter shapes a web of filaments that ordinary matter follows, and offers a new method for mapping these structures at great distances. The findings are published in Nature.

Archaeologists in northeastern Greece have uncovered a large, early Hellenistic tomb at Amphipolis, dated to about 300–325 B.C. The site—about 100 km northeast of Thessaloniki and reportedly the largest ancient tomb found in Greece—is surrounded by a 497-meter marble outer wall and was topped by a five-meter lion sculpture believed to have been part of its monument. Excavations since 2012 revealed a broad marble-paved approach with 13 steps, frescoed masonry walls, and an entrance crowned by two headless, wingless sphinxes. Officials say the tomb appears to belong to a prominent Macedonian of the era, but there is no evidence linking it to Alexander the Great or his family. Archaeologists expect to enter the tomb within weeks to learn who is buried there; the site is under heavy security. Prime Minister Antonis Samaras called the find especially significant for the region.

Heavy fighting between Israel and Hamas continued, with intense air strikes and ground operations in Gaza despite international calls for a cease-fire. Palestinian health officials reported more than 1,100 dead and over 6,500 wounded since the current conflict began; the Gaza Health Ministry said at least eight children were among 10 people killed when shells struck a beach-area refugee camp during Eid al-Fitr celebrations. Israel reported significant battlefield losses as well: the IDF said 10 soldiers were killed Monday (part of a larger toll of 53 soldiers to date in one report and 43 in another), including five who died repelling a tunnel attack aimed at Israeli civilians.

Israel said its ground offensive aims to destroy Hamas tunnels used for attacks and to stop rocket fire; Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Israelis to prepare for a “protracted campaign” and Defense Minister Moshe Yaalon said Israel would not negotiate while attacks continue. Both sides blamed each other for strikes that hit civilian sites — hospitals, a UN school shelter, playgrounds and a radio station — and investigations and competing claims surrounded incidents such as an errant mortar that struck a UN school courtyard, killing and wounding dozens.

International pressure intensified: UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called for an immediate halt to violence and an unconditional humanitarian cease-fire for Eid, and world leaders including Obama, Cameron, Merkel, Hollande and Renzi discussed the crisis and backed efforts for an Egyptian-brokered truce. The UN Security Council supported a durable truce and negotiated, long-term settlement toward two states, though Palestinian representatives pressed for stronger language demanding Israeli withdrawal. Humanitarian concerns rose sharply as tens of thousands were displaced and agencies warned of devastating impacts if evacuations ordered by leaflets were carried out.

Researchers report that whale sharks—the world’s largest fish and gentle filter-feeders—have been increasingly observed around the Azores, a chain of nine volcanic islands in the central North Atlantic west of Portugal. Using 16 years (1998–2013) of tuna-fishermen observer records and spatial models relating sightings to sea surface temperature, food (chlorophyll-a), and seafloor features, the team found a sharp rise in sightings beginning in the unusually warm year of 2008 and continuing afterward.

Key findings:
- Whale sharks normally prefer warm tropical waters (about 26.5–30 °C / 79–86 °F). The Azores historically lie on the cooler edge of that range, but recent warming has made local conditions more favorable.
- Higher sea surface temperatures around southern Azores (e.g., Santa Maria) and increased chlorophyll-a concentrations correlated with more shark sightings, suggesting shifts toward areas with richer planktonic food.
- Sharks were also more frequently observed near underwater hills, slopes and seamounts, features that concentrate productivity and prey.
- Fishermen in the region have long used whale sharks (“pintados”) as indicators of tuna schools, and whale-shark–watching has become an emerging tourism activity.

Implications:
- The Azores may become an increasingly important habitat for whale sharks in years of elevated temperatures, illustrating how climate-driven ocean warming can shift distributions of large marine animals.
- Further research is needed to explain seasonal residency (e.g., summer stays), the role of seamount-associated food versus social or reproductive behaviors, and long-term distributional changes under ongoing climate change.

The study by Pedro Afonso and colleagues was published in PLOS ONE. The article also situates these findings within broader conservation concerns for sharks and rays, many of which face severe declines from overfishing and international trade.

President Trump spent the day after Thanksgiving at his Mar-a-Lago resort and returned to his West Palm Beach golf course. In an early-morning tweet from Florida he urged both parties to unite on a "major Border Security package" that would include funding for his proposed southern border wall, saying "after 40 years of talk, it is finally time for action." He has signaled he may accept a government shutdown if new funding bills do not include wall money; Congress has until Dec. 7 to finish funding after postponing several appropriations. Trump also called for Congress to pass criminal justice reform and urged Senate leaders Mitch McConnell and Chuck Schumer to act, though he mistakenly tagged a Schumer fan account. The wall demand faces strong Democratic opposition after the midterm shift that gave Democrats control of the House, and McConnell has expressed skepticism that criminal justice legislation can be passed during the lame-duck session. Over Thanksgiving Trump also phoned troops, visited a Coast Guard station, answered reporters and dined at Mar-a-Lago.

The document traces a recent wave in pastry innovation through two emblematic items—the pretzel croissant from Maury Rubin’s City Bakery and Dominique Ansel’s Cronut—and uses them to explore why hybridized pastries have become so culturally and commercially salient.

Key points:

- Hybrid pastries: The pretzel croissant (croissant dough shaped/topped like a soft pretzel) and the Cronut (a croissant-like doughnut) exemplify a broader trend of “mutated” pastries — crossovers like bagel-croissant hybrids and other mashups — that blend sweet and savory or two familiar formats into a novel bite.

- Why pastry leads innovation: Pastry has structural advantages for culinary invention. Historically and technically, pastry chefs have pushed culinary boundaries (Adrià’s claim that pastry leads innovation). Baking’s alchemy—transforming basic ingredients into something wholly different—encourages experimentation. Professional distinctions (boulanger, pâtissier, chef pâtissier) create internal competition that fuels creativity.

- Maury Rubin / City Bakery: Rubin trained in Paris in the 1990s, returned to New York and founded City Bakery. The pretzel croissant emerged organically in 1996 when pretzel-making and croissant-making happened side-by-side; adding rock salt and sesame produced a hybrid that married savory and sweet breakfast preferences. For Rubin the product is a reliable bestseller and an example of purposeful, iterative innovation—not a gimmick. He also notes the rising input costs (butter, flour, oil) that make margins tight, and views viral phenomena like the Cronut as partly driven by the blogosphere and changing public taste for pastry.

- Dominique Ansel / Cronut: Ansel, with classical French training and high-end restaurant experience, opened his SoHo bakery aiming for creative, seasonal pastries made in small batches. His D.K.A. (kouign amann variant) preceded the Cronut. The Cronut—croissant-style laminated dough fried like a doughnut—was developed after months of tweaking; it went viral after early blog coverage. Ansel limited production, resisted mass commercialization, and treated the Cronut as one creative item among many, even while the craze required security and perks for waiting customers. He attributes its success to marrying two familiar American favorites (doughnut and croissant) in a way that feels both novel and accessible.

- Commercial responses: Large chains have noticed the trend. Dunkin’ Donuts introduced a national “Croissant Donut” (explicitly avoiding the term “Cronut”), positioning it as a mass-market, lower-priced croissant–doughnut hybrid. Dunkin’ frames its version as part of normal product development and trend-watching; executives claim theirs is not copying a single bakery and say their product is preferable. The rollout is tied to strategic goals to boost sales and profitability amid stronger breakfast competition.

- Cultural reading: The piece frames these hybrids as symptomatic of a foodie era shaped by innovation, the internet/blogosphere, and commercialization. Some view items like the Cronut as fleeting crazes (the “hula-hoop” analogy), others as legitimate culinary contributions that will enter common practice. The author highlights tensions: genuine craft vs. PR-driven hype; artisanal limits vs. mass-market adaptation; and the economics of making high-butter pastries in a world of rising costs.

Overall, the story uses Rubin and Ansel as case studies to show how pastry inventiveness, professional rivalry, consumer appetite for novelty, and mass-market interest combine to produce both small-batch sensations and large-chain imitations—raising questions about what survives as lasting contribution and what fades as transient craze.

Syrian Deputy Foreign Minister Faisal Mekdad signaled a modest shift in Damascus’s stance by saying the government was open to talks with Syrian religious and community leaders “who have influence on the ground” with fighters. That acknowledgment—linking elements of the armed opposition to parts of Syrian society—softened the regime’s long-standing portrayal of the rebellion as wholly foreign-led, but left unresolved the central difficulty of identifying opposition interlocutors who can both deliver results and be acceptable to the government.

Mekdad expressed confidence that President Bashar al‑Assad’s forces had gained the upper hand militarily and touted diplomatic and military gains, including the agreement to relinquish Syria’s chemical weapons to avert a U.S. strike. He reiterated the regime’s assertion—contradicted by U.S. officials and some UN investigators—that rebel forces, not government troops, were responsible for the August chemical attack around Damascus. Speaking from his Damascus office, he also called for international pressure on Israel to give up its unacknowledged nuclear arsenal.

The account appears against the backdrop of a brutal civil war that has killed over 100,000 people and displaced millions. Accompanying imagery and reports document widespread destruction, civilian casualties, and ongoing clashes across many parts of Syria—particularly Aleppo, Damascus suburbs and other contested areas—illustrating the scale of the humanitarian and security crisis and the complex, fragmented nature of the opposition.

An Ohio woman and her 21-month-old daughter were killed when a car allegedly engaged in street racing struck them while they were crossing Bayshore Boulevard in Tampa.

Jessica Raubenolt, 24, was pushing daughter Lillia in a stroller across the northbound lanes Wednesday midday when a black 2018 Ford Mustang driven by 18-year-old Cameron Herrin hit them. Both were taken to Tampa General Hospital; Jessica was pronounced dead the same day and Lillia died the following day. Police say witnesses heard engine revving and saw the Mustang racing a gold Nissan driven by 17-year-old John Alexander Barrineau; the vehicles reportedly raced north, changing lanes to pass traffic. Tristin (Tristan) Herrin, 20, was a passenger in the Mustang.

Cameron Herrin and Barrineau were arrested at the scene and each face counts including vehicular homicide and street racing; both posted $10,000 bail and were released. Tristin Herrin was charged with a misdemeanor for racing and released after posting $500 bail. Authorities said Raubenolt was crossing legally at the intersection.

Family and community members remembered Jessica as a devoted mother, health and fitness advocate, and avid gardener who had recently married and was visiting Tampa while her husband completed flight training. Her uncle expressed forgiveness and said the family is praying for those involved. The Catholic Diocese of St. Petersburg and others offered prayers for the victims. Investigations and enhanced charges were noted after the child’s death.

An Associated Press investigation documents widespread misuse of agrochemicals across Argentina’s farm belt and links that misuse to growing health problems in rural communities.

Background and scale
- Since Argentina embraced genetically modified (GM) soy, corn and cotton in the late 1990s—largely driven by companies like Monsanto—soy acreage tripled and farmers adopted no‑till, spray-after-planting systems that enable faster, cheaper production and multiple harvests per year.
- Pesticide use initially fell but then rose sharply as weeds developed resistance. AP analysis of government and industry data found agrochemical use increased roughly ninefold since 1990 and that Argentine farmers now apply about twice the amount of agrochemical concentrate per acre as U.S. farmers.

How chemicals are used
- In practice, pesticides are often applied in ways that violate regulations or safety guidance: spraying during windy conditions, near homes and schools, without buffer zones, and with little advance warning to residents.
- Farmworkers commonly handle concentrates with no training or protective gear; some farmers load and clean equipment in or beside populated areas. Empty pesticide containers are frequently reused for water storage or other household uses.
- Provinces set very different buffer limits (from none up to 3 km), enforcement is weak or absent, and a federal environmental rule meant to halt activities that threaten public health has not been applied to farming. A federal commission set up in 2009 to study spraying impacts has not met since 2010.

Health findings and concerns
- Local doctors and epidemiologists report increases in cancers, birth defects, miscarriages, neurological disorders and respiratory illnesses in areas dominated by intensive farming.
- Epidemiological work in Santa Fe reached tens of thousands of people and found cancer rates two- to four-times the national average in some towns. In Chaco province, congenital defects reportedly quadrupled in the decade after GM crops and expanded agrochemical use.
- A government study in one neighborhood (Ituzaingo Annex) found high soil and water contamination and that 80% of children tested carried traces of pesticide in their blood.
- Case examples include former farmworker Fabian Tomasi, now gravely ill with polyneuropathy after years of unprotected pesticide exposure, and communities reporting children fainting from drifted spray.

Scientific debate and regulatory stance
- Many regulatory agencies, including the U.S. EPA and the EU, consider glyphosate safe when used properly; the EPA in 2015 raised allowable residue levels based on industry studies. Industry representatives stress proper use and stewardship.
- Argentine scientists warn that real-world practices—higher concentrations, mixtures of chemicals, repeated exposures, and application drift—are not reflected in standard safety tests. Some laboratory studies (e.g., by Dr. Andrés Carrasco) suggest developmental effects from very low-dose exposures in embryos; those studies have been contested by industry.
- Researchers and public-health advocates argue that longer-term, population-level epidemiological studies and stricter enforcement are needed rather than waiting for absolute causal proof.

Governance and response
- Provincial rules vary and many lack enforcement capacity. Complaints and court orders are often ignored; activists and teachers report intimidation, and local officials sometimes downplay health concerns for fear of threatening the export-oriented agricultural model.
- Monsanto and other agribusinesses say they do not condone misuse and promote responsible use, but critics say industry and government reliance on existing safety studies has left real-world harms uninvestigated and unaddressed.

Bottom line
- The AP’s reporting portrays a system in which agrochemicals have driven agricultural growth but are routinely misapplied, contaminating water, homes and schools and coinciding with troubling local health trends. Scientists and local doctors call for rigorous, long-term health studies and stronger enforcement of application rules to protect vulnerable rural populations.

Action on Sugar research (embargoed 17 Feb 2016) found alarmingly high sugar levels in hot flavoured drinks sold by major UK coffee chains. Of 131 drinks surveyed, 98% would score a “red” (high) sugar label per serving; 35% contained as much or more sugar than a can of Coca‑Cola (9 tsp). More than half (55%) provided the adult/teen daily recommended maximum of free sugars (30 g / ~7 tsp) in a single serving.

Worst offenders:
- Starbucks Hot Mulled Fruit (Grape with Chai, Orange & Cinnamon) Venti (568 ml): 99 g sugar (~25 tsp).  
- Costa Chai Latte (large): 79.7 g (~20 tsp).  
- Starbucks White Chocolate Mocha (Venti): 73.8 g (~18 tsp).  
Other high items included Starbucks Signature Hot Chocolate, KFC Mocha and Caffè Nero Caramelatte. Some “healthy‑seeming” drinks (e.g., Starbucks Chai Tea Latte Venti, matcha lattes) also contained double‑digit teaspoons of sugar. Starbucks’ larger Venti and Trenta sizes (454–568 ml) were highlighted as contributing to excessive intake.

Action on Sugar calls for government action in the forthcoming Childhood Obesity Strategy: mandatory reformulation targets (50% sugar, 20% fat reductions proposed), compulsory sugar labelling and colour‑coding, a 20% duty on sugar‑sweetened drinks, and bans on marketing unhealthy products to children. Experts argue coffee chains must cut added sugar, stop selling very large sizes and improve labelling; consumers are advised to choose plain drinks or minimal, sugar‑free syrup in the smallest size. Starbucks responded that it will reduce added sugar in indulgent drinks by 25% by 2020 and already provides nutritional information and sugar‑free options.

This piece reports early reactions to the second day of U.S. Supreme Court arguments over the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate. Journalists present said the government’s solicitor general, Donald Verrilli, struggled to defend the law as several conservative justices — especially Anthony Kennedy, along with Antonin Scalia, Samuel Alito and Chief Justice John Roberts — pressed skeptical, pointed questions. Commentators (Jeffrey Toobin, Adam Serwer, Mike Sacks) described the day as disastrous for the Obama administration and predicted the mandate might be struck down. The article cautions, however, that such immediate readings can be unreliable: the court’s deliberative process is opaque, and the mandate can only survive if at least one of the conservative-leaning justices joins the four more liberal justices.

A deadly gunfight broke out at a wedding in Deh Salah district, Baghlan province in northern Afghanistan late Sunday, killing at least 20–21 people and wounding 8–10 others, officials said. Accounts vary slightly: provincial police put the toll at 20 dead and 10 wounded, while district and other provincial officials reported 21 dead and eight wounded. Victims were all male guests aged roughly 14–60, including two teenagers.

Officials said two armed groups—reported as local militias or rival factions, not necessarily Taliban—exchanged insults and then open fire; one account says a local security official first fired into the air before the shooting escalated. Some reports say the clash followed a long-running feud and the assassination of a relative of a provincial police official during the party. Around 400 people had been attending the wedding. Investigators have been sent to the scene.

The attack underscores Afghanistan’s fragile security and the heavy civilian toll from both insurgent violence and local clashes. The report recalled other deadly wedding-related incidents in recent years—accidental mortar fire in Helmand that killed 17 women and children, a 2012 suicide bombing at a lawmaker’s daughter’s wedding, and a 2011 attack on a wedding—against the backdrop of ongoing peace talks between the Afghan government and the Taliban and continued insurgent offensives.

The Backstreet Boys announced 21 new dates for their Larger Than Life Las Vegas residency (July 25–28; Aug. 1, 3–4, 8, 10–11; Oct. 24, 26–27, 31; Nov. 2–3, 7, 9–10, 14, 16–17) and revealed new music. In a Twitter HQ Q&A they confirmed they've chosen a new single, teasing an upbeat snippet with the lyric “baby don’t go breaking my heart” and saying the release is “really soon.” The track, titled “Don’t Go Breaking My Heart,” was released early Thursday — the group’s first new single since 2013 — and will appear on an untitled album due later this year to coincide with the band’s 25th anniversary. Presale tickets for the Vegas shows are available to fan club members now, with general on-sale starting Friday.

A Baton Rouge mother, 30-year-old Schaquana Evita Spears, was arrested June 2016 on two counts of cruelty to juveniles after admitting she struck three of her sons (ages 10, 12 and 13) with an RCA cord after catching them breaking into a neighbor’s home and stealing electronics, a hoverboard and other items. The 13-year-old reportedly had lacerations to both arms and marks across his leg, shoulder, back and stomach; the 12-year-old had cuts on his arm and the youngest a small scratch. Spears turned the stolen items back, and the victims’ homeowner said she believed Spears should be commended for disciplining her children rather than charged.

The arrest drew national attention and polarized reactions: some community members and commentators, including state Treasurer John Kennedy and an 83-year-old caller, defended Spears as a single mother who disciplined her kids; others, and the state child welfare chief Marketa Garner Walters, stressed that discipline crosses into abuse when it leaves a child cut, burned, bloody or bruised. East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar C. Moore III said the case is under review and noted the law allows parental discipline but not excessive pain or cruelty; he also said he would consider the seriousness of the injuries and Spears’ lack of criminal convictions. Spears, a single mother of six who runs a small catering business, bonded out after bail was reduced and said she thought she was doing the right thing. Her children were placed temporarily with their grandmother while custody and criminal decisions were pending. The episode sparked widespread online commentary and at least one public offer to help pay bail or donate.

Eight-year-old Sa’fyre Terry — a burn survivor of a 2013 arson that killed her father and three younger siblings and left her with severe injuries and multiple surgeries — asked for Christmas cards as her only wish. Her request went viral, and she has since been flooded with support: more than 300,000 letters and cards (and thousands of packages) from around the world, delivered with help from local postal officials and volunteers who are helping the family open the mail.

Baking Memories 4 Kids, a charity that funds free vacations for children with life‑threatening illnesses, surprised Sa’fyre, her aunt/guardian Liz Dolder, and family with a cost‑free weeklong trip to Walt Disney World in February, with lodging provided by Give Kids The World. The gift was in part prompted by a classmate’s nomination; the classmate’s family had previously received a vacation from the same charity.

The outpouring also includes a YouCaring fundraiser that has topped $300,000. The family plans to photograph the sea of cards laid out on their lawn to thank donors. Mail can still be sent to: Sa’fyre Terry, P.O. Box 6126, Schenectady, NY 12306.

On June 29, 2016 at the National Cancer Moonshot Summit, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and IBM Watson Health announced a two‑year public‑private partnership to expand precision oncology for veterans. Using IBM’s Watson for Genomics, the VA plans to provide genomic analysis and precision treatment guidance for 10,000 veterans with cancer—roughly a 30‑fold increase over current capacity within the VA system.

Process and benefits
- Tumor DNA will be sequenced and de‑identified genetic alteration files fed into Watson, which rapidly analyzes literature and data to identify likely cancer‑driving mutations and rank potential therapies and clinical trials by level of evidence.
- Watson for Genomics aims to speed and scale what has typically required time‑consuming molecular tumor board reviews, enabling more patients (including those outside major cancer centers) to access personalized treatment options.
- Data and literature‑based findings will be shared with the research community to advance genomic research.

Context and background
- The VA is America’s largest integrated health system and treats about 3.5% of the nation’s cancer patients; veterans have disproportionately high cancer rates.
- IBM has spent years training Watson for Genomics with leading cancer centers; early results show Watson’s recommendations align with expert molecular tumor boards.
- The collaboration supports the Cancer Moonshot goal of accelerating advances in cancer care through data and collaboration.

Overall, the partnership is intended to democratize access to precision oncology across the VA, increase throughput of genomic case reviews, and contribute findings to broader research efforts.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 85, was hospitalized after a fall in her office Wednesday evening that left her with three fractured ribs on her left side. She initially went home but, feeling discomfort overnight, went to George Washington University Hospital early Thursday, where tests confirmed the fractures and she was admitted for observation and treatment. The injury kept her from attending the formal investiture for Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

Ginsburg, the court’s eldest justice and a leader of its liberal wing, has a history of serious health issues—including colon and pancreatic cancers, a 2014 heart stent, and a prior rib fracture in 2012—but has continued to work actively on the bench. Appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1993, she is renowned for her work on gender-equality law and civil rights, her long-term plan to remain on the court into her 90s, and her celebrity status as the “Notorious RBG.” The Supreme Court said it would provide updates as more information becomes available.

The Senate Standing Committee of Correspondents has tabled Breitbart News’ application for permanent Senate Press Gallery credentials and will not renew the outlet’s temporary Capitol credentials when they expire May 31. The committee cited ongoing, unresolved concerns about Breitbart’s editorial independence and inconsistent or incomplete information about its masthead, office location and ties to political actors.

Key concerns:
- Possible ties to Steve Bannon and Rebekah Mercer: The committee remained unconvinced Breitbart is independent of Bannon (former chairman) and Mercer (major funder), given past overlap with the Mercer-funded Government Accountability Institute (GAI), which Bannon co-founded.
- Staff and masthead inconsistencies: CEO Larry Solov submitted a masthead that included editors who also worked at GAI and later said at least one (Managing Editor Wynton Hall) had resigned; the committee found these discrepancies troubling.
- Office-space questions: Breitbart listed a Capitol Hill townhouse (“Breitbart Embassy”) as its Washington address, but the property is not zoned for commercial use and appears unsuitable as an office; Solov says the outlet still lacks permanent D.C. office space, partly for security reasons.
- Policy compliance: The press gallery requires editorial independence from advocacy groups, lobbyists and entities that lobby the federal government. Committee members said Breitbart has not yet demonstrated compliance with those rules.

The committee rejected Solov’s proposal to credential individual reporters rather than the organization, explaining it evaluates the news organization as a whole. Breitbart can reapply if it resolves the committee’s concerns; without credentials, its reporters will retain only public access to Hill events and will face limits on Capitol and White House access. Breitbart disputes the decision and says it remains entitled to permanent credentials.

A Manhattan Criminal Court judge ordered Twitter to turn over tweets and account data for Brooklyn writer Malcolm Harris, who was arrested with hundreds of Occupy Wall Street protesters on the Brooklyn Bridge in October and charged with disorderly conduct. Prosecutors subpoenaed Harris’s tweets from shortly before the protests through the end of 2011 because they may contradict his expected defense that police led protesters into the roadway. Judge Matthew Sciarrino Jr. ruled that publicly posted tweets are not protected like private speech and that, under Twitter’s terms, Harris had granted the company broad distribution rights, so he lacked standing to quash the subpoena. Twitter had separately tried to block the request; the company said it was disappointed and was considering options.

The case highlights broader legal and privacy questions about social media and law-enforcement access. The ACLU filed a brief arguing that prosecutors should need search warrants and that users should have a court chance to oppose requests. Twitter also released data showing that U.S. law enforcement made the bulk of its government requests in the first half of 2012: 849 requests overall, 679 from U.S. agencies (80% of total), with data handed over in 63% of cases (75% for U.S. requests). Twitter noted requests can seek location, IP addresses, searches and third-party tracking data; some data are retained only 18 months unless preserved. Twitter’s transparency policy includes notifying users of requests unless forbidden; in this case prosecutors tried to block notification but Twitter informed Harris. The episode underscores the growing power of social-media records as evidence and the evolving legal framework around public versus private online speech.

Former Arkansas governor and former 2008 Republican presidential contender Mike Huckabee is reportedly launching an online news site called the Huckabee Post. A Craigslist ad seeking reporters describes it as “a new and exciting online news publication” with offices in New York and Washington covering politics, U.S., international, media, sports and general news. Media outlets contacted Huckabee but had not received comment.

The story appears amid Huckabee’s broader media and political activity: his Fox News platform, a recently ended radio show, and renewed public conversations about a possible 2016 presidential bid. Huckabee has said he’s “keeping the door open” to running again, has met with potential donors and supporters, and has granted interviews to raise his profile. Observers note his appeal to social conservatives and evangelicals and cite fundraising ability as a key obstacle—he would have to leave Fox and forego steady income if he pursued a serious campaign. Conservative media ventures launched by personalities such as Glenn Beck (TheBlaze) and Andrew Sullivan (The Dish) are presented as precedents for turning personal brands into media outlets.

An advanced tsunami early-warning system that could have given faster, more reliable alerts for the deadly tsunami that struck central Sulawesi has been stalled in testing for years and never moved beyond a prototype. The system—developed with U.S. National Science Foundation funding and collaboration from U.S. and Indonesian scientists—uses seafloor sensors, sound-wave data transmission and fiber-optic links to provide authoritative tsunami information within 1–3 minutes, far quicker than existing gauges and defunct buoys. Only limited funding (about 1 billion rupiah, ~$69,000) and inter-agency disputes over responsibilities prevented completion of the final fiber-optic connection off Padang and left Indonesia reliant on a weaker network of 134 tidal gauges, land seismographs, some nonworking buoys and about 55 sirens.

When a magnitude-7.5 quake hit near Palu, warnings were issued and then canceled within minutes; however, large waves up to about 6 meters still struck, killing at least 832 people and highlighting gaps in detection, warning dissemination and public preparedness. Power outages disabled sirens, and many residents—shocked or unsure what to do—remained near the shore even as waves approached. Experts note current tsunami models don’t always account for multiple quakes, submarine landslides or complex rupture behavior, and that immediate self-evacuation to higher ground after coastal quakes remains critical.

Scientists say the Sulawesi tsunami may have been caused by unusual factors for a strike-slip fault—minor vertical motion, interaction with varying seafloor topography, or quake-triggered undersea landslides—and that seafloor studies will be needed to determine the exact cause. The disaster has been called both a scientific and humanitarian tragedy because a more capable detection network existed in prototype form but was not fully implemented.

Merriam-Webster has released the sixth edition of The Official Scrabble Players Dictionary, adding more than 300 new entries to its roster of over 100,000 words. The update, produced in consultation with the North American Scrabble Players Association and commissioned by Hasbro, adds a mix of short, high-utility terms, contemporary expressions, foreign borrowings, and playable jargon. Notable additions include two- and three-letter staples like OK and ew; interjections such as yowza; qapik (a q-without-u word); and high-scoring plays like bizjet. Other new entries reflect changing usage and digital culture—emoji, facepalm, botnet, twerk, sheeple, bokeh, and more—as well as culinary and foreign terms now common in English, e.g., macaron, arancini, bibimbap, cotija, sriracha, and schneid. Merriam-Webster notes the inclusion of more “transcribed speech” spellings prompted by texting and social media. The first official Scrabble dictionary appeared in 1976; updates have occurred every four to eight years. (Associated Press)

An elderly Bedford, Pennsylvania woman in her 80s discovered an unknown man had been living in an upstairs closet of her two-story home for several weeks. Limited to the first floor because of mobility issues, the homeowner and her daughter only found the intruder after hearing noises upstairs. Police identified the man as Mark Potts, the boyfriend of the woman’s caretaker; officers said they found several suitcases, a duffel bag, other personal items and a small handgun in the room. Potts faces criminal trespassing charges, and the caretaker is under investigation and may also be charged for allegedly helping him. Bedford County officials say the intrusion caused the homeowner significant fear and have pledged to hold those responsible accountable.

A powerful earthquake and tsunami disabled power and backup systems at the aging Fukushima Daiichi nuclear complex, forcing operators to shut reactors but leaving cooling systems crippled. As pressure built inside Reactor No. 1, crews carried out controlled venting to avoid an uncontrolled rupture. Shortly afterward an explosion—most likely from hydrogen accumulation (or possibly steam)—blew off the outer wall and roof of the reactor building, though authorities say the inner steel containment vessel remained intact.

Radiation above normal levels has been measured around the site (including cesium, indicating fuel damage), and as many as 160 people may have been exposed; three workers were reported with acute radiation sickness. Officials emphasized that readings so far were not high enough to pose a major health risk for brief exposures, and the government moved to prepare iodine distribution and issued sheltering guidance (close windows/doors, cover noses and mouths). Confusion over the blast’s precise location and cause persisted in early reports.

Experts warned the critical unknown is the condition of the reactor core and any spent-fuel pool; a core loss-of-cooling could lead to fuel damage or melting (a meltdown), which would increase releases. TEPCO has begun flooding the reactor with seawater—a step that likely dooms the unit but is intended to cool fuel and avert worse releases. Most international specialists said design differences make a Chernobyl-style disaster unlikely even in a severe meltdown, but they stressed the situation remained serious and evolving, with continued efforts to restore cooling and fully assess fuel damage to the reactors and spent-fuel storage.

Researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology used a new nanolithography technique to reproduce the Mona Lisa on a canvas about one-third the width of a human hair (≈30 microns wide). The “Mini Lisa” is a 240 × 320–pixel grayscale image with pixels spaced 125 nm apart and details down to ~0.125 µm, produced with an atomic force microscope (AFM) using ThermoChemical NanoLithography (TCNL).

TCNL works by heating the AFM cantilever tip and lowering it onto a polymer “molecular canvas” whose surface contains chemically protected sites. Local heating triggers confined nanoscale reactions that remove protecting groups and create new surface molecules; higher temperatures yield higher local concentrations (lighter tones when visualized with fluorescent dye), while lower temperatures yield darker tones. The Georgia Tech team formed the image pixel-by-pixel to demonstrate precise control of molecular concentration gradients at sub-micrometer scales.

Currently TCNL has been demonstrated for creating gradients of amine and carboxyl groups, but the researchers expect the method to be compatible with other chemistries and properties (e.g., patterning conductivity in graphene). Advantages include high spatial resolution and faster operation compared with some existing methods. Potential applications span nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, bioengineering, lab-on-a-chip surfaces, and integrating nanoscale patterning into large-scale or everyday materials to produce “smart” surfaces.

NASA says astronaut Scott Kelly is about 2 inches taller after spending nearly a year aboard the International Space Station — a temporary and expected effect caused by spinal elongation in microgravity. Kelly spent 342 days (340+ on ISS) with cosmonaut Mikhail Kornienko as part of a yearlong mission designed to study long-term spaceflight effects. His identical twin, retired astronaut Mark Kelly, served as an Earth-based control in the “twin study,” enabling researchers to compare physiological, genetic, cognitive and microbiome changes between brothers.

Ten official twin-study experiments are probing issues such as gene expression and epigenetics, immune function, accelerated arterial plaque, vision changes related to fluid shifts, cognitive and perceptual effects, and gut-microbe alterations. Blood samples and other measurements were taken repeatedly to capture immediate and time-course changes. While the sample size is one pair and not statistically definitive, sequential differences in Scott that don’t appear in Mark could point to spaceflight-linked effects—data NASA hopes will guide protections for future long-duration missions, including planned Mars missions.

Kelly returned to Houston where he reunited with family, including Mark and Gabrielle Giffords, and was greeted by public figures such as Jill Biden. He emphasized the mission’s collective nature and prepared to brief the public and scientists on findings as analyses continue.

Dwright Boone-Doty, 22, was charged with the November 2 fatal shooting of 9-year-old Tyshawn Lee and the October 18 killing of 19-year-old Brianna Jenkins, crimes prosecutors say were committed as part of a violent gang feud on Chicago’s South Side. Authorities allege Boone-Doty, a member of the Bang Bang Gang/Terror Dome faction of the Black P Stones, and accomplices targeted rivals in retaliation after the October 13 slaying of Tracey Morgan. Prosecutors say Boone-Doty and two others sought to terrorize rivals—originally planning to kidnap and mutilate Tyshawn’s grandmother—and ultimately lured Tyshawn from Dawes Park by offering to buy him something, led him into an alley and shot him execution-style. Tyshawn was struck multiple times, including in the head; part of his thumb was shot off as if he raised a hand to block the gunfire.

An inmate informant who agreed to wear a wire secretly recorded Boone-Doty boasting about the killings in jail; prosecutors say he laughed about shooting Tyshawn, wrote a rap referencing the slaying, and said he regretted not returning to kill more. Evidence includes recorded statements, physical evidence and GPS data; a gun recovered from Boone-Doty matched the weapon used in Jenkins’ killing. Two other suspects have been implicated: Corey Morgan (charged with murder) and a third man, Kevin Edwards/Williams, who remains at large.

Boone-Doty, who had prior drug and weapons convictions and was on parole, was ordered held without bail. The case drew condemnation from city officials—Cook County State’s Attorney Anita Alvarez and Interim Police Superintendent John Escalante called the murder among the worst they’d seen—and heightened community fear and outrage over gang violence that claimed an innocent child.

Joan Fontaine, the Oscar-winning actress known for her delicate screen presence and memorable roles in 1940s films such as Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca and Suspicion, died Dec. 15 at her home in Carmel, Calif. She was 96. Her death of natural causes was confirmed by an assistant.

Born Joan de Beauvoir de Havilland in Tokyo on Oct. 22, 1917, Fontaine rose to stardom playing fragile, elegant women; Hitchcock cast her as the nervy second Mrs. de Winter in Rebecca (1940) and opposite Cary Grant in Suspicion (1941), for which she won the 1942 Academy Award for Best Actress — the only acting Oscar ever awarded for a Hitchcock film. She earned additional acclaim and nominations for roles in The Constant Nymph, Jane Eyre, The Affairs of Susan, Letter From an Unknown Woman, and others, and later worked in television and on stage.

Fontaine’s career began in the mid-1930s and included both high points and a long run of supporting work. She also took on atypical parts — for example in Ivy (1947) and Island in the Sun (1957), the latter provoking hate mail because of its interracial themes. Beyond acting she was a licensed pilot, prize-winning balloonist, Cordon Bleu–trained cook, interior decorator and tuna fisherman. She published a memoir, No Bed of Roses, in 1978.

Her personal life was marked by four marriages (to Brian Aherne, William Dozier, Collier Young and Alfred Wright Jr.) and two daughters. Fontaine was the younger sister of actress Olivia de Havilland; the two had a bitter, lifelong feud that became public and never fully healed. Olivia de Havilland, a two-time Oscar winner, is living in Paris.

A new NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll shows Americans are increasingly anxious about national security after Islamic State’s brutal beheadings of two journalists and its growing territorial gains in Iraq and Syria. Forty-seven percent of Americans now say the U.S. is less safe than before 9/11 (up sharply from 20% in 2002 and 28% last year); only 26% feel safer. Awareness of the beheadings was nearly universal (94%), and over 60% say military action against ISIS is in the national interest.

President Obama was preparing a prime-time address to outline plans for expanded operations against ISIS — expected to emphasize intensified airstrikes, reliance on allies, and no large-scale ground troop deployments — and enjoys short-term bipartisan and public support for action. Polls show rising backing for airstrikes (71% in a Washington Post-ABC poll), though analysts warn the effort could be long and complex.

Commentators cited differing diagnoses of how the crisis emerged: some blame U.S. policies (failure to build inclusive Iraqi governance, slow intervention in Syria, tolerance of regional authoritarianism and uneven U.S. engagement), while others fault the 2011 U.S. withdrawal from Iraq and argue for sustained commitment. Experts differ on prospects: some see the fight against radical Islamist militancy as a potentially decades-long struggle akin to the Cold War; others urge a goal of making threats “manageable” rather than decisively winnable. Overall, the piece frames a nation wary of renewed, possibly open-ended military involvement as leaders and allies weigh responses to ISIS.

The writer reflects on drinking culture among modern women through the lens of a hangover and a widely read essay by Kristi Coulter, who argues that many women drink to cope with sexism. The author neither fully agrees nor dismisses Coulter, acknowledging that sexism shapes women’s lives but noting it’s often impossible to untangle how much of everyday behavior—like drinking, grooming, or fashion—is driven by patriarchy, culture, or habit.

Drawing on personal experience of getting sober, the author describes how alcohol is everywhere: rosé displays, office mini-bars, booze at yoga and cooking classes, champagne at movies, and wine at baby showers and fitness events. Drinking serves multiple roles: bonding with friends, celebration, a social lubricant, and a way to soften daily frustrations. The writer recounts being tokenized on a company panel and then commiserating over cocktails with female colleagues—a scene Coulter uses to illustrate women using booze to blunt workplace sexism. Yet the author also defends some drinking as empowering or catalytic, noting decisions and plans hatched over wine.

As sobriety progresses the tone grows sharper: the author becomes angrier at the cultural pressures that demand women be perpetually “on,” and at the normalization of alcohol as a remedy for structural problems. She criticizes the commodification of female downtime and the idea that “women must do everything,” arguing that relying on alcohol to get through life is unaffordable personally and socially. But she ends on a hopeful, pragmatic note: whether or not patriarchy drives female drinking, what matters is what women do together—plotting change, supporting one another—and invites collective action (with or without wine) to address the challenges of being a woman today.

The Trump administration announced it will terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for about 200,000 Salvadoran immigrants on Sept. 9, 2019, giving them an 18-month window to leave, seek lawful residency, or face possible deportation. TPS had been granted after devastating 2001 earthquakes in El Salvador. Officials said the decision reflects El Salvador’s recovery and a broader policy that TPS is temporary, not a path to permanent residence. The move is part of wider enforcement steps that will affect roughly 250,000 people from multiple countries over the next two years; Haitians and Nicaraguans have already been cut off and Hondurans may lose status soon.

The decision drew strong criticism from immigrant advocates who warned it would separate families, destabilize migrants’ lives, and ignore ongoing violence and economic weakness in El Salvador—one of the world’s most violent countries. Many TPS holders have long U.S. ties, businesses, and U.S.-born children; advocates note about 275,000 U.S.-born children have a TPS parent. Businesses and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce warned that ending work authorization would harm industries that rely on these workers.

El Salvador’s government said it welcomed the 18-month lead time and will seek alternatives, including U.S. congressional action to protect migrants. Congressional Democrats supported finding a permanent solution, but prospects are politically complicated amid other immigration fights, including protections for Dreamers and conservative demands for tougher border measures. Supporters of the administration’s move say past extensions undermined the program’s temporary intent.

A group led by Russian nanoscientist Dr. Igor Ashurbeyli has unveiled plans for "Asgardia," a proposed independent space nation intended to open access to space technologies, foster peace and protect Earth from cosmic and manmade threats (like asteroids and space debris). The project frames Asgardia as a legal, scientific and technological initiative rather than an immediate physical settlement: its initial territory would be a single satellite planned for launch, while citizens would remain on Earth but could also register as Asgardians via a website. The team aims to crowdsource symbols (flag, anthem, insignia) and gather at least 100,000 registered citizens before applying for UN recognition.

Proponents say Asgardia would create a legal platform free from terrestrial state restrictions and eventually act as a "launch state" responsible for its space activities, challenging aspects of the Cold War–era Outer Space Treaty, which currently assigns liability to the nation that launches objects. Supporters argue the project could democratize space access and enable new forms of governance and planetary protection.

Experts and legal scholars caution the venture faces major hurdles: existing international law requires territory, population and recognition by other states for nationhood; liability and how Asgardia would fit into current space regulations remain unresolved. Historical precedents (e.g., the unrecognized "Nation of Celestial Space") highlight the difficulty of winning legitimacy. Despite uncertainties, interest has been strong online, with thousands registering within hours of the announcement.

A $6.3 million grant from the Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust will fund efforts to improve survival after cardiac arrest across Iowa. The Iowa Department of Health will use the money to buy LUCAS 2 automated chest compression systems — each costing about $10,000 — for use in ambulances and hospitals and to provide related training. The devices deliver continuous, consistent CPR and studies indicate they can improve outcomes by roughly 5–50%. The article also notes that Leona Helmsley, a once-prominent NYC businesswoman nicknamed the “Queen of Mean,” remains involved posthumously in estate disputes in New York, where a $100 million executor fee is being challenged by the state attorney general.

The 111th Congress adjourned after a tumultuous, highly productive two-year term that combined sweeping legislation with intense political backlash. Dominated by Democrats, it passed the most significant set of laws since the 1960s Great Society: an $814 billion economic stimulus, the biggest overhaul of financial regulations since the Depression, a landmark health-care law extending coverage to about 32 million people, and major social and foreign-policy measures (including repeal of "don't ask, don't tell," ratification of the New START arms treaty with Russia, and expanded 9/11 first-responder health benefits). In the lame-duck session it also approved two-year tax extensions, extended unemployment aid, payroll-tax cuts, an overhaul of food-safety rules, and confirmation of Supreme Court justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan.

Those accomplishments came amid sharp polarization: frequent filibuster threats, explosive town-hall protests, and the rise of the Tea Party. Voter frustration over high unemployment (around 9.5–9.6%) produced a Republican landslide in the Nov. 2 midterms—Democrats lost 63 House seats and ceded control of the chamber, while their Senate majority was narrowed. The partisan divide blocked measures such as a climate bill, immigration reform, and some tax changes, and Congress failed to pass any of the 12 annual appropriations bills.

Economically, stimulus spending is credited with creating or saving roughly 3.3 million jobs and helping markets recover: the S&P 500 rose strongly during the session, major banks reported improved revenues, GM repaid much of its bailout, and AIG accessed bond markets. Critics and some businesses argued the new regulatory scope and uncertainty restrained hiring and investment.

Observers described the term as both one of the most productive and one of the most dysfunctional in modern times: Democrats aimed to “write their agenda into law” before losing electoral ground, while Republicans focused on long-term political gains. With divided government incoming, many expect a sharp slowdown in major legislation next year.

XPRIZE has launched a three-year, $7 million global competition—the Shell Ocean Discovery XPRIZE—to accelerate ocean mapping and drive innovation in underwater robotics, sensing and imaging. With only about 5–7% of the seafloor meaningfully mapped, the challenge seeks teams to build shore- or air-launched autonomous systems that can operate to 4,000 meters depth and complete tasks including: creating high-resolution seafloor maps, capturing high-definition images of specified objects, and identifying notable features in a “treasure hunt.” A $1 million bonus, funded by NOAA, rewards technology that can track a specified chemical or biological signal back to its source in the water column.

The prize purse is structured with $4 million for first place, $1 million for second, $1 million for the bonus, and additional awards for other top teams. The competition is open to anyone worldwide; registration is open now and runs through September 2016, with tests staged first at 2,000 m and later at 4,000 m. The initiative, part of XPRIZE’s Ocean Initiative (one of five multi‑million dollar ocean prizes planned by 2020), is run in partnership with NOAA and Shell to spur interdisciplinary advances—underwater robotics, computer vision, digital imagery and chemical/biological sensing—that will improve our understanding of the deep ocean. For details and registration: oceandiscovery.xprize.org.
