NORAD’s long-running Santa-tracking tradition (dating to 1955) has shifted its mapping partner from Google to Microsoft Bing after five years of using Google Maps. The change is described as mutual; NORAD will host its tracking service on Microsoft’s Bing Maps and Windows Azure and offer Windows 8, Windows Phone 8, and Android apps. NORAD continues to use a combination of sensors and tools—radar, satellites, Santa Cams and fighter jets—to “track” Santa, and its site typically draws millions of users (about 25 million reported this year). Microsoft’s Outlook.com will be used for an email update option, and the official phone line (1-877-HI-NORAD) and social channels will provide live updates.

Google is not abandoning Santa-themed features: it built a new route algorithm for its Santa Tracker, will track Santa via its own website, Chrome extension and Android app, and will keep a role by hosting NORAD dispatches on YouTube. Both services begin tracking on Dec. 24 (NORAD at 2 a.m. ET; Google at 2 a.m. PT). The split prompted media attention as a notable tech breakup; NORAD says the move was mutual and many volunteers continue to support the annual event.

A Bronx woman, 39-year-old Liana (Kristina) Barrientos, has been arrested and faces felony charges after prosecutors say she married 10 men between 1999 and 2010 in what authorities describe as an apparent marriage scam. She was arrested after a court appearance and, along with her niece, charged with subway fare evasion; Barrientos had earlier been arraigned on two counts of filing a false instrument and pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors say Barrientos used marriage licenses and applications that contained false statements — including a 2010 license claiming it was her “first and only marriage” to groom Salle Keita — and submitted varying versions of her name and her real Social Security number on documents. Investigators believe she repeatedly married men, at times remaining legally married to multiple husbands simultaneously (at one point reportedly married to eight men and currently to four). Seven of the grooms are from countries flagged by authorities (Egypt, Turkey, Georgia, Pakistan, Mali and others); seven men filed for permanent status based on marriages to her. In at least one instance a groom (Rashid Rajput) was later deported after a terrorism-task-force investigation. The Bronx DA’s office says some men received money and some later divorced and refiled for status using other marriages, while Barrientos has told Homeland Security she did not know nine of the men.

If convicted on the false-instrument charges she faces up to four years in prison. The case was referred to the Bronx DA by ICE and DHS investigators; officials have highlighted broader security concerns about fraudulent marriages enabling immigration fraud.

Peggy Sue Gerron Rackham, the Texas woman who inspired Buddy Holly's 1958 hit "Peggy Sue," has died at age 78 at University Medical Center in Lubbock. Her family permitted the hospital to confirm the death but requested no further details. Gerron, born in Olton and raised in Lubbock, met Holly in high school and later married — and divorced — Crickets drummer Jerry Allison. In 2008 she published a memoir, Whatever Happened to Peggy Sue?: A Memoir by Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue, drawing on roughly 150 diary entries from the period she knew Holly; she said she wanted to give Holly "his voice" and remembered him as one of her best friends. Her son-in-law noted the song’s name was changed to honor her after Allison persuaded Holly. The article recalls Holly’s other hits, his death in the 1959 plane crash that also killed Ritchie Valens and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson, and cultural tributes including films and the Buddy Holly Center in Lubbock. The closing lines reference web-archiving efforts to preserve pages and prevent broken links.

Cerro Gordo, a 19th-century silver and lead mining town high in California’s Inyo Mountains near Death Valley, has been sold for $1.4 million. The 300+ acre property includes about 22 remaining historic structures — a saloon, hotel, church, bunkhouse, hoist house and caretaker’s residence — and extensive patented mining claims and artifacts preserved by the long‑time owning family. Listed at $925,000 in June, the sale drew roughly a dozen serious offers after widespread interest.

Buyers Brent Underwood and Jon Bier led a group of Los Angeles‑based investors and plan to preserve the town’s historic character while making select restorations and adding visitor amenities. Immediate goals include structural repairs, installing running water and Wi‑Fi, and renovating a few buildings for extended stays. Longer‑term plans call for events and programming such as writing retreats, music and theater, stargazing, photo shoots and dining experiences. The buyers say the family favored their bid because it prioritized preservation and public access; longtime caretaker Robert Desmarais will remain on site. The new owners estimate about $1 million in initial investments to rehab the property.

Jordan Peele’s directorial debut Get Out is a sharp, terrifying horror-satire that turns familiar genre tropes into a pointed critique of contemporary racism. Mixing influences from films like Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner, Rosemary’s Baby and Invasion of the Body Snatchers, the movie stays true to horror conventions—creepy atmosphere, mounting dread, and shocking reveals—while foregrounding racial anxiety as its central theme rather than subtext.

The story follows Chris (Daniel Kaluuya), a young Black photographer who visits his white girlfriend Rose’s (Allison Williams) parents at their affluent upstate estate. Although Rose insists her family is liberal and welcoming, Chris encounters a series of disquieting microaggressions, intrusive comments about his body and “genetics,” and unsettling behavior from the family’s Black housekeeper and groundskeeper. Peele deliberately sustains ambiguity long enough for the audience to share Chris’s doubts about whether he’s being paranoid, then escalates the menace into a sinister conspiracy.

Peele’s command of tone, pacing and visual storytelling—evident in stand-out moments like a tense opening prologue and hypnotic, Kubrick-inspired sequences—makes the film both entertaining and incisive. Kaluuya gives a magnetic lead performance, LilRel Howery provides sharp comic relief as Chris’s skeptical friend Rod, and Catherine Keener and Bradley Whitford convincingly embody the Armitage parents’ smug, liberal racism. The film mines the absurdity and horror of contemporary “admiration” and fetishization of Blackness, making Get Out a memorable, timely, and righteous genre piece that transforms social critique into visceral scares.

This document outlines ways to support and participate in the It Gets Better Project, which raises awareness and funds suicide-prevention and anti-bullying programs for LGBT youth. Options include:

- Donate: Financial contributions fund programs and resources for LGBT youth.
- Record: Submit an "It Gets Better" video to share your message.
- Share your story: If you can’t record, send a written story to be shared later.
- Take the pledge: Commit to spreading the “It Gets Better” message of hope.
- Wear your support: Buy branded merchandise; proceeds support the project.
- Buy the book: Purchase the It Gets Better book (available in stores).
- Order the book for your hometown: For a $25 donation, a copy of the book will be sent to a local library or school.

Airbus’s A350 XWB is a next-generation long-haul jet designed to improve fuel efficiency, passenger comfort, and long-term technological relevance. Key features and benefits:

- Lightweight composite structure: Over 50% of the airframe uses carbon fiber–reinforced plastic, reducing weight and corrosion and supporting a claimed 25% fuel-burn improvement versus similarly sized competitor aircraft (helped by larger, bird‑wing–inspired wings, redesigned flaps that follow the flight path, and efficient Rolls‑Royce engines).
- Reduced jet lag and better cabin environment: Programmable LED lighting mimics natural daylight cycles to support passengers’ circadian rhythms, cabin air is refreshed every 2–3 minutes, and cabin pressure is maintained at the equivalent of 6,000 ft to enhance comfort.
- More comfortable, adaptable interior: A slightly wider fuselage provides marginally larger economy seats and easier aisle movement; the cabin and avionics are built with an open, upgradable architecture so airlines can reconfigure seats and update systems more easily over the aircraft’s projected ~30‑year life.
- Development and deployment: Airbus invested about $15 billion in R&D and logged ~2,600 test flight hours. Qatar Airways is among the first operators—its A350 made the type’s first U.S. landing—though early operational incidents (an aborted takeoff on one delivery flight) remind that new models still face teething issues.

Overall, the A350 XWB targets lower operating costs and improved passenger wellbeing, aiming to compete with Boeing’s 787 and long‑haul 777 models while remaining adaptable to future technology.

The UK government will ban the sale of new petrol and diesel cars and vans from 2040 as the centrepiece of a broad clean-air plan aimed at cutting harmful emissions and protecting public health. Environment Secretary Michael Gove said the move is necessary to tackle pollution that contributes to climate change and tens of thousands of premature deaths in the UK each year. The ban aligns with similar French commitments and is part of a longer ambition for nearly all vehicles to be near-zero tailpipe emission by 2040 and for every vehicle to be zero-emission by 2050.

Key details:
- The ban covers new gasoline and diesel vehicles (and is intended to include hybrids) beginning in 2040. Britain is the second-largest car market in Europe, with 2.7 million new registrations in 2016.
- Government investment commitments total roughly £1.4–3bn across various programmes: funding for ultra-low-emission vehicles, charging infrastructure, plug-in grants, local authority air-quality measures, retrofitting buses, a green bus fund, cycling/walking investment, and targeted scrappage support.
- Local authorities will be given new funding (including a £255m allocation for accelerating local plans) and will be required to set out plans for pollution hotspots by March 2018 and finalise them by year-end. Measures suggested include retrofitting public transport, road-layout changes, traffic-light reprogramming and targeted scrappage schemes. Clean air zones (CAZs) and charging measures remain options but are presented as last resorts.
- The government’s announcement follows legal pressure: courts found previous proposals inadequate and ordered stronger plans to meet EU air quality limits.
- Industry responses are mixed: experts and some academics welcome the signal to electrify, but automakers warn the transition requires major investment, infrastructure and cost reductions before consumers fully adopt electric, plug-in hybrid and hydrogen vehicles. Concerns cited include affordability, range anxiety and charging availability. The auto sector—supporting over 800,000 UK jobs—urges careful planning to avoid lost jobs and investment.
- Environmental and public-health campaigners cautiously welcomed the long-term ban but stressed the need for immediate, concrete action, stronger local measures (including fully funded scrappage schemes), and faster reductions to meet legal obligations and reduce thousands of premature deaths attributed to air pollution annually.

On Wednesday, Nov. 29, 2018, Elizabeth Midlarsky, a 77-year-old Jewish professor at Columbia University’s Teachers College who researches the Holocaust, discovered two red spray-painted swastikas and the anti-Semitic slur “Yid” in the entryway to her private office. She reported the vandalism to campus security; the NYPD Hate Crimes Task Force opened an active investigation and is treating the incident as aggravated harassment. Teachers College buildings require ID for entry. Midlarsky said she was shocked and shaken; colleagues helped escort her home. The vandalism echoes a previous 2007 incident in which a swastika was spray-painted on her door and anti‑Semitic flyers were left in her mailbox. College officials, including President Thomas Bailey, and Barnard and the Office of University Life issued statements condemning the act and expressing support for Jewish students and faculty. The incident coincided with reports that three current professors and a former professor at Teachers College received mailed hate images this week (swastikas and, in one case, a noose), and no arrests have been announced.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell said he believes the sexual misconduct allegations against Alabama GOP Senate nominee Roy Moore and that Moore should leave the race. The Washington Post report, based on interviews with more than 30 people, alleged Moore pursued relationships with teenage girls in his 30s, including one woman who said she was 14 when Moore initiated sexual contact. Moore denied the claims and said he would sue the Post; he responded to McConnell by tweeting that McConnell should step aside and has “failed conservatives.” McConnell’s statement marked a stronger stance than earlier comments from some Republicans who had conditioned calls for Moore to quit on the allegations’ veracity; others, like Sen. John McCain, already urged Moore to withdraw. The Republican Party is exploring alternatives, including a write-in campaign, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee has cut fundraising ties with Moore.

President-elect Donald Trump tweeted on Nov. 29, 2016 that burning the American flag should carry penalties — “perhaps loss of citizenship or year in jail.” His statement ignited debate because two Supreme Court rulings (Texas v. Johnson, 1989, and United States v. Eichman, 1990) have held flag desecration to be protected political expression under the First Amendment, and a 1958 decision bars stripping citizenship as criminal punishment.

Responses from politicians and legal analysts were mixed. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, Rep. Kevin McCarthy and others noted that while they oppose flag burning, the courts have found it protected speech; Rep. Justin Amash and Rep. Sean Duffy likewise defended the constitutional protection despite personal disapproval. Jason Miller, a Trump transition spokesman, repeatedly insisted on CNN that flag burning should be illegal. Senator John McCain said he personally disapproved and favored punishment but acknowledged the Supreme Court’s ruling.

The tweet came amid post-election protests in which some demonstrators burned flags (including an incident at Hampshire College), and drew commentary that Trump’s provocative social-media remarks often serve to rally supporters or distract from other activities. Legal commentators pointed out that both the Supreme Court precedent protecting flag burning and constitutional limits on expatriation make Trump’s proposed punishments legally untenable without major legal or constitutional changes. Congress has previously tried—and failed—to pass laws or a constitutional amendment to ban flag desecration.

President Donald Trump held a raucous campaign-style rally in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, his first trip to the state since taking office, defending his record amid multiple Washington troubles. Speaking for more than an hour to a boisterous crowd, he denounced the Russia probes as a “witch hunt,” attacked the news media, celebrated recent Republican special-election wins, and repeated many of his campaign themes while largely avoiding detailed discussion of the scandals surrounding his administration.

Trump touted economic signs—job gains and a rising stock market—as proof his policies are working, praised wealthy Cabinet appointees like Gary Cohn and Wilbur Ross (“I just don’t want a poor person”), and vowed he will secure funding for a Mexico border wall, floating variants such as a “solar wall.” He said he does not expect Democratic help on major legislation, including healthcare repeal, calling Democrats obstructionist. On foreign policy he lamented difficult issues like North Korea and expressed frustration at limited Chinese cooperation despite praising President Xi.

The event, which included protesters removed by police and supporters waving “Drain the Swamp” signs, highlighted Trump’s comfort in campaign settings and the White House aides’ push to get him out of Washington to rally his base. He used the appearance to celebrate GOP special-election victories and energize supporters amid low approval ratings and ongoing investigations into election meddling.

Clint Eastwood’s American Sniper dominated the Super Bowl weekend box office, earning a stellar $30.7 million in its third weekend and narrowly missing the all-time Super Bowl weekend record of $31.1 million set by the 2008 Miley Cyrus concert film. The Oscar-nominated war drama has now become the highest-grossing war film domestically (not adjusted for inflation), surpassing Saving Private Ryan, with a new domestic total of about $247.98 million. 

New releases fared modestly over the football-focused weekend, when theater attendance typically dips. Found-footage time-travel thriller Project Almanac (produced by Michael Bay’s Platinum Dunes) and family film Paddington each earned estimated weekend grosses of $8.5 million, with Paddington likely to claim the No. 2 spot once final numbers are in. Project Almanac opened to a B CinemaScore; it was delayed a year while Bay tinkered with it and stars Jonny Weston, Sofia Black-D’Elia, Sam Lerner, Allen Evangelista and Virginia Gardner.

Mike Binder’s racially charged drama Black or White, starring Kevin Costner and Octavia Spencer, debuted at No. 4 with about $6.5 million from 1,823 locations and an A- CinemaScore; 78% of its audience was over 25. Costner invested personal money in the $9 million film after studios passed; the story centers on a bitter custody battle between a maternal grandmother and a grandfather. Universal’s holdover The Boy Next Door took No. 5 with an estimated $6.1 million. 

The Loft, an English-language remake of a 2008 Dutch film starring James Marsden and Karl Urban (with Matthias Schoenaerts reprising his role), opened weakly at No. 10 with $2.9 million. The $14 million thriller changed distributors several times before being released by Open Road.

The piece also includes a separate reader-style commentary praising American Sniper’s author and soldier perspective, arguing that the memoir offers an authentic frontline portrayal of war and its moral complexities, highlights the soldier’s duty to protect comrades, and discusses the strain military service placed on family life—ultimately recommending the book as an insightful account of dedication to God, country and family.

Federal prosecutors have recommended felony charges against retired Gen. David Petraeus for mishandling classified information, though no charges have been filed and Attorney General Eric Holder must decide whether to proceed. The investigation began when Jill Kelley reported anonymous threatening emails; the FBI traced them to Paula Broadwell, searched her emails, and uncovered evidence of an affair between Broadwell and Petraeus. The relationship reportedly began in 2011 while Broadwell was interviewing Petraeus for her book. Petraeus resigned as CIA director shortly after President Obama’s 2012 re-election, acknowledging the affair and calling his judgment “extremely poor.” President Obama said he had no evidence the disclosures harmed national security and praised Petraeus’s service. Investigators concluded the exchanges constituted a significant security breach and recommended charges, noting lower-ranking officials have been prosecuted for lesser leaks. DOJ and Petraeus’s lawyer declined immediate comment; a Justice Department spokesman also would not discuss the inquiry. FBI Director James Comey declined to explain the investigation’s length.

Ford has introduced the 2018 F-Series Super Duty Limited, a luxury-focused trim of its heavy-duty pickups that blends high-end interior appointments and advanced tech with full Super Duty capability. The Limited is offered on F-250, F-350 and F-450 crew-cab models (single- or dual-rear-wheel) and is powered exclusively by Ford’s 6.7-liter Power Stroke diesel V8 (440 hp, 925 lb-ft), with a quoted towing capability of about 30,000 lb.

Interior and exterior highlights:
- Two-tone Camelback leather seats (heated/ventilated front, heated rear), Miko suede headliner, hand-finished dark ash wood trim, leather-wrapped steering wheel/armrests, and a laser-etched serial number on the center console.
- Satin-finish twin-bar grille with chrome accents, quad-beam LED headlamps and satin tailgate appliqué, plus a full panoramic moonroof.

Technology and safety:
- Class-leading features include SYNC 3 infotainment, high-definition 360° camera with Trailer Reverse Guidance, trailer-aware BLIS (blind-spot information system), adaptive cruise control, adaptive steering, lane-keeping alert and forward-collision warning with brake support.
- Practical truck-oriented touches such as a flat rear load floor with fold-up locking storage.

Pricing:
- F-250 Limited 4x4: $80,835 (incl. $1,295 destination)
- F-350 Limited 4x4: $82,010
- F-450 Limited 4x4: $87,100
- A fully optioned F-450 can reach about $94,455—into flagship luxury-sedan territory.

Ford positions the Limited toward buyers who want both maximum capability and luxury (ranchers, contractors, RV owners), noting that premium trims already make up over half of Super Duty sales. The Super Duty Limited arrives at dealerships in winter.

A Hungarian arrest warrant for “firearm or ammunition abuse” shows former Trump deputy assistant Sebastian Gorka was wanted in Hungary while he served seven months in the White House. The warrant, first reported by Hungarian outlet 444 and BuzzFeed, was issued Sept. 17, 2016, and was filed with the Budaörs police station. Details are sparse; 444 says the underlying incident could date back to as early as 2009. Hungarian police did not respond to requests for comment.

Gorka, a former Breitbart editor and Trump campaign surrogate linked to Steve Bannon, denied wrongdoing on Twitter and noted he moved to the U.S. in 2008. He has a well‑documented interest in firearms: in 2016 he had a pistol confiscated at Reagan National Airport and told Recoil magazine his “everyday carry” includes two pistols, a knife, a tourniquet and a copy of the U.S. Constitution. Critics have long questioned his counter‑terrorism credentials and ties to fringe right‑wing groups in Hungary and the U.S.

Bloomberg Businessweek reports that Target was warned it was under attack nearly two weeks before it took action. Target had hired FireEye and installed its malware-detection system months earlier; FireEye’s Bangalore monitoring team alerted Target headquarters on Nov. 30 and again on Dec. 2 after detecting intrusions. According to logs and a two-month investigation, those alerts did not prompt an effective response from Target’s Minneapolis security team, and the breach continued, eventually compromising tens of millions of customers’ payment and personal data.

The FireEye system included honeypot/sandbox technology and had an option to automatically remove detected malware, but Target’s security team had disabled that automatic remediation—leaving human operators to decide how to respond and creating a window for attackers. The article portrays the incident as a series of internal failures at Target rather than a FireEye product defect; Target’s CIO at the time, Beth Jacob, resigned and CEO Gregg Steinhafel said the company is conducting a full investigation.

The piece also mentions a possible suspect—an online card seller known as Rescator, potentially linked to a Ukrainian individual—but notes there is no definitive proof tying that person to the breach.

This article tells the story of Samantha (Sam) Anderson’s severe dysphagia (loss of the ability to swallow) and surveys recent medical and technological efforts to help people with swallowing disorders.

Case of Sam Anderson
- Sam, a healthy 40-year-old mother and jewellery-maker from Brisbane, suddenly found she could not swallow a bite of toast. Over hours and days the problem persisted and worsened: she choked repeatedly, lost weight (from 60 to 45 kg), became malnourished, and suffered social isolation and severe anxiety.
- Early doctors misattributed her symptoms to stress or psychological causes; after months she was finally diagnosed with dysphagia. Only after nine months did physicians identify preceding shingles in her left ear that had damaged four cranial nerves and triggered her swallowing failure.
- Sam underwent extensive treatment: a dietitian prescribed high-calorie liquid feeds, and when malnutrition progressed she had a feeding tube for 18 months. Video studies showed her swallow function was as weak as that of a 90-year-old.
- She adapted to carefully managed eating routines (foods that dissolve with water, careful head positioning, and supervised meals), still cannot eat alone, and remains cautious but gradually regained some oral intake. She has enrolled for stem-cell trials and finds renewed determination while grappling with lasting limitations and social fallout from earlier misdiagnosis.

Why dysphagia is hard to treat and why food form matters
- Bread is highlighted as a particularly dangerous and difficult-to-swallow food: it absorbs saliva and forms sticky masses that can block the throat. Ordinary pureed bread is easier to swallow but unappealing and low in “meal appeal.”
- Palatability and appearance matter: people on modified diets (thickened liquids or pureed foods) may eat less and risk dehydration or malnutrition. One study found stroke patients on modified diets were more likely to become dehydrated in the week after stroke, raising questions about whether unappealing textures cause reduced intake.

Innovations and research
- Japan’s EN Otsuka has developed iEat Bread—an enzyme-treated bread that looks and tastes like regular bread but absorbs little saliva, is easily mashed by the tongue, and is far less sticky.
- Moulding and 3D-printing approaches are being used to make pureed foods look like familiar dishes to increase appeal and intake. The EU-funded PERFORMANCE consortium and German firm Biozoon demonstrated 3D-printed peas, pasta and a full meal (roast pork with gnocchi), with commercial availability projected within a few years.
- Medical and surgical interventions are being explored:
  - The Swallow Expansion Device (a titanium rod and implanted plate) mechanically pulls the larynx forward to open the upper esophageal sphincter on demand; it has entered a phase I trial.
  - Drug trials include using donepezil (an Alzheimer’s drug) to aid nerve function.
  - Trials are underway for muscle stem-cell therapy to strengthen tongue muscles.
  - Other groups are working on reducing radiation damage and developing better oesophageal dilation techniques.

Broader points
- No single treatment will suit everyone; a range of interventions—rehabilitative exercises, drugs, devices, modified food textures, and new food technologies—are needed.
- Greater awareness among clinicians is essential: in Sam’s case, later recognition of shingles-induced cranial nerve damage led to appropriate treatment and rehabilitation, improving her outcome and alerting other clinicians to similar presentations.
- For patients, improvements can be incremental but life-changing: regaining safe oral intake restores not only nutrition but also dignity and quality of life.

Overall, the piece combines a human, detailed patient narrative with an overview of technological, dietary, pharmacological and surgical advances aimed at making swallowing safer and eating more appealing for people with dysphagia.

The Pentagon announced late Friday that Defense Secretary Jim Mattis has approved a service recommendation to delay implementing the policy allowing openly transgender people to enlist or be newly commissioned until Jan. 1, 2018. The six-month deferral, announced hours before the Obama-era July 1 deadline for opening accession to transgender recruits, will not affect an estimated 15,500 transgender service members already serving openly under the policy set by former Secretary Ash Carter. Services were directed to review accession plans and report on how accepting transgender applicants would affect "readiness and lethality."

The delay follows requests from some service leaders (notably the Army and Marine Corps) and a May order from Deputy Secretary Robert Work to assess readiness concerns. Supporters of open service — including LGBT advocacy groups and researchers such as Rand and the Palm Center — criticized the decision, saying studies show negligible impact on readiness and warning the postponement forces applicants to hide their identities. Some members of Congress backed the delay; Rep. Vicky Hartzler praised it and has pursued legislative measures to reverse the Carter policy. Advocacy groups signaled they expect the ban to be lifted in January 2018 and warned further delays would harm military readiness and recruitment.

New scientific analyses reported in the Harvard Theological Review strengthen Harvard professor Karen L. King’s claim that a small Coptic papyrus fragment known as the “Gospel of Jesus’s Wife” is very likely ancient rather than a modern forgery. King introduced the fragment 18 months ago; it drew global attention because it contains the first explicit reference to Jesus saying “My wife” and a line implying “She will be able to be my disciple.” King has not argued the fragment proves Jesus was married, only that it is a historically significant witness to early Christian debates about women, family, and celibacy.

Key findings and background
- Carbon dating: A new radiocarbon test by Harvard produced a mean date around 741 A.D. (eighth century Egypt), later than King’s original estimate but still ancient. An earlier, less reliable AMS test had given an earlier range.
- Ink and microscopic analysis: Columbia researchers using micro-Raman spectroscopy found the ink chemically consistent with ancient carbon-based inks, and high-magnification imaging showed no microscopic ink pooling that critics had claimed indicated modern application.
- The fragment is tiny (about business-card size) with eight partial lines in a crude hand. King hypothesizes it may have been copied from an earlier Greek text and relates to debates on whether wives and mothers could be disciples, or to discussions of celibacy.

Remaining uncertainties and controversy
- Tests do not definitively prove ancient authorship: standard ink-dating would destroy the fragment, and a hypothetical highly skilled forger could have used period materials. New non-destructive ink-dating methods under development at Columbia may offer firmer answers.
- Scholarly dispute persists: Critics, notably Brown Egyptologist Leo Depuydt, argue the text is a modern pastiche relying heavily on the Gospel of Thomas, contains grammatical errors a native Coptic speaker would not make, and even mirrors an apparent typo from an online edition—evidence some consider decisive for forgery. Depuydt and others remain unconvinced by the scientific results.
- King and supporters counter that the textual parallels with the Gospel of Thomas are not necessarily indicative of forgery, that similar grammatical forms exist in authenticated Coptic texts, and that the combination of poor Coptic and the correct ancient materials and microscopic consistency would be unlikely in a forger.

Provenance issues
- The fragment’s ownership and history are obscure. Its owner, who remains anonymous, said he bought it in 1999; an accompanying undated German note mentions a Professor Fecht who reportedly identified it as unique.

Publication and reactions
- King’s article, delayed by testing and criticism, appears in the Harvard Theological Review. Papyrus and ink specialists including NYU papyrologist Roger Bagnall find no compelling argument against its antiquity, while skeptics maintain their objections.

Bottom line
The new scientific evidence makes a modern forgery less likely and supports King’s view that the fragment is ancient. However, because definitive ink dating would be destructive and provenance remains uncertain, the debate over authenticity and interpretation continues.

Mark Zuckerberg donated about $1 billion in Facebook stock to the Silicon Valley Community Foundation, the foundation’s largest-ever gift, as part of his broader pledge to give away more than half his wealth. The foundation will help allocate the assets over time; Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have said they’re focused on education and health but have not detailed plans. This gift follows a similar donation last year that has roughly doubled in value as Facebook’s share price rose.

The announcement accompanied a planned Facebook stock offering that would raise nearly $1.5 billion by selling 27 million new shares, and disclosed that Zuckerberg is selling roughly 41.35 million of his personal shares (about $2.3 billion) to cover taxes resulting from exercising an option to buy 60 million new shares. After these transactions Zuckerberg’s voting control will drop only slightly—from about 65.2% to roughly 62.8%—and he will still own about 444.2 million shares worth more than $24 billion at the time.

The article notes Facebook’s strong financial position (more than $9 billion cash on hand) and the company’s recovery since its 2012 IPO, driven largely by rapid growth in mobile advertising. Speculation followed about possible large acquisitions (such as a reported, ultimately rebuffed $3 billion offer for Snapchat). The piece also highlights the extraordinary tax implications of Zuckerberg’s stock sales—potentially $2–3 billion in taxes over two years—illustrating how large stock sales by the ultra-wealthy contribute a significant share of state and federal income tax revenues.

A new Emerson College poll shows Sen. Ted Cruz (R) leading Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) in the Texas Senate race by 38% to 37%, a 1-point margin well within the survey’s 4.4-point margin of error. Four percent prefer another candidate and 21% are undecided. The poll of 550 likely voters (Aug. 22–25) underscores a tightening contest in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in three decades; other recent polls (e.g., NBC News–Marist) and the Cook Political Report’s move from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican” reflect similar narrowing. Emerson notes O’Rourke’s relative popularity (37% favorable) and shows him leading among voters ages 18–34 and 35–54, while Cruz leads among those 55 and older.

Candy Spelling’s 57,000-square-foot Holmby Hills mansion, known as “The Manor,” appears to be headed toward sale. The French chateau–style estate, built by late TV producer Aaron Spelling in 1991 on five acres and featuring amenities such as a bowling alley, beauty salon, flower-cutting and gift-wrapping rooms, a “Prince Charles suite,” and parking for 100 cars, had been listed at $150 million and remained on the market through the downturn. The buyer is reported to be 22-year-old heiress Petra Ecclestone, daughter of Formula One boss Bernie Ecclestone; she plans to split time between London and Los Angeles after an August wedding. The final sale price was not disclosed. Candy Spelling, who had said she wanted to downsize and recently bought a Century City condominium, declined to comment. The potential deal would highlight foreign buyers’ role in high-end U.S. real estate against the backdrop of a weak national market. Additional background: the estate was shown since 2008 and officially listed in March 2009; listing and buyer representation came through Hilton & Hyland and Coldwell Banker. The document also includes a standard explanation of how automated property “estimates” (AVMs) are calculated and their limitations.

At Howard University’s commencement, President Barack Obama delivered a forceful, unapologetically black speech that praised recent activism around policing and racial injustice while urging a pragmatic path to lasting change. He acknowledged the role of a new generation of activists—from Black Lives Matter organizers to “black Twitter”—in raising awareness of mass incarceration, the school-to-prison pipeline, the wage gap and other inequities. But he stressed that awareness and protest alone are insufficient: structural change requires legal and cultural shifts achieved through political participation, compromise and working at the table with opponents.

Obama singled out Brittany Packnett for engaging in his 21st-century policing taskforce and argued for both street pressure and policy engagement. Prominent activists quoted in the piece—DeRay Mckesson, Samuel Sinyangwe and April Reign—largely agreed, saying protest and policy must inform one another; protest can force conversations, but activists also need to help shape policy outcomes or risk half-measures (e.g., body cameras) that don’t match movement goals.

The president urged graduates to be confident in their blackness, to expand their “moral imagination” to empathize with diverse groups (refugees, immigrants, the rural poor, transgender people and even economically anxious white men), and to convert passion into votes and strategy. He emphasized democracy’s need for compromise and free expression—rebut opponents rather than silencing them. The speech was widely praised as timely, emotionally resonant and a frank articulation of black identity and civic responsibility.

New Jersey faced a critical shortage of road salt after a series of winter storms, leaving state and local salt reserves dangerously low and forcing some municipalities to curtail salting, mix salt with brine, or use sand. The state sought a waiver of the Jones Act (the 1920 Maritime Act), which requires U.S. domestic cargo movements between U.S. ports to be on U.S.-flagged vessels, so it could quickly move 40,000 tons of salt from a foreign-flagged ship in Searsport, Maine, to Port Newark. The Department of Homeland Security declined to approve the waiver, leaving the foreign vessel (reported as the Anastasia S) to sail empty and forcing New Jersey to pursue slower, multi-trip alternatives using U.S.-flag barges that would take much longer and carry less capacity. State officials said supplies might only last through one or two more storms and described efforts to conserve and redistribute dwindling salt stocks. The administration’s refusal drew attention because emergency Jones Act waivers have been granted in past crises (e.g., post–Hurricane Sandy fuel shipments), and maritime industry groups said domestic carriers were mobilizing to respond.

Investigators say residue of Tannerite, a widely available brand of binary explosive used as rifle targets, was found on the device that exploded in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood. Tannerite and similar products are sold as two inert components (typically ammonium nitrate as an oxidizer and powdered aluminum as fuel) that only become explosive once mixed. Because the parts are non‑explosive separately, the ATF does not regulate their sale as it does conventional explosives, though it has issued advisories warning they are high explosives once combined.

Tannerite is popular with shooters because a high‑velocity rifle strike reliably produces a loud bang and visible puff, making hits obvious. The manufacturer says their product can only be detonated by a successful high‑power rifle impact and vaporizes in the process; the company is investigating whether its product was used in the Chelsea blast. Law enforcement sources and some news reports have linked Tannerite residue to bombs found in New York and New Jersey tied to suspect Ahmad Khan Rahami, who faces multiple attempted murder charges, but the company and independent experts note uncertainty about how the material might have been initiated in these incidents. Experts caution that while binary explosives have inherent safety features, they can be dangerous—especially when confined in containers, which can create deadly fragmentation—and that other methods and standard detonators can be used to set off ammonium nitrate/aluminum mixtures.

The ATF advises reporting suspicious purchases or unusual activity involving these materials. Some states, like Indiana, have considered tighter retail restrictions (age limits and behind‑counter sales) in response to injuries and misuse.

This piece mixes a short social-media admonition with a TMZ Sports note about golf. The social comment urges people not to judge, bully, or make examples of others (tagging @lohanbeachclub), advising instead to live in gratitude and be happy, ending with the hashtag #DOTHELILO. Separately, TMZ Sports reports PGA legend John Daly saying Barack Obama is “pretty good” at golf but is no match for the best presidential golfer, George H.W. Bush.

On Jan. 2, 1988, a newborn boy was found dead, wrapped in a blanket near a tree in a Meriden parking lot; he had frozen to death. The infant, full-term with blond hair and blue eyes, was named "David Paul" by local clergy and was buried after the Meriden Police Department collected funds and effectively "adopted" him. Despite efforts, police never identified or charged anyone in connection with his death; investigators hoped finding the mother might reveal a trauma rather than seeking punishment.

Each year since, Meriden police and local clergy hold a small memorial at Walnut Grove Cemetery to honor the child and to symbolize their commitment to protecting vulnerable children. At the most recent service, about 20 officers, retired Chief Robert Kosienski and Rev. Alden Barnes attended; Barnes read a prayer remembering David Paul and referenced the Sandy Hook anniversary as a reminder of children's vulnerability. Attendees also discussed Connecticut’s 2000 Safe Haven law, which allows parents to surrender infants under 30 days old at hospitals anonymously so the children enter Department of Children and Families custody.

ESPN and other outlets report that BMX legend Dave Mirra, who died by suicide in February at age 41, was posthumously diagnosed with chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). University of Toronto neuropathologist Dr. Lili‑Naz Hazrati examined Mirra’s brain and, with independent confirmation from multiple U.S. and Canadian neuropathologists, found trademark tau protein deposits in the frontal and temporal lobes identical to those seen in former football and hockey players with CTE. This appears to be the first confirmed CTE diagnosis in an action sports athlete.

Mirra suffered numerous head traumas over his life and career — notably a skull fracture and blood clot after being hit by a car at 19, repeated concussions from BMX crashes, and later involvement in boxing — which experts say likely contributed to the disease. His widow, Lauren Mirra, described marked personality and mood changes in his final year and said the family hopes the diagnosis will spur better detection, prevention and research. CTE can currently only be diagnosed after death, though research is ongoing to detect it in living people.

Mirra was a pioneering and highly decorated freestyle BMX rider (formerly holding the X Games medal record), a video-game and MTV figure, and later competed in rallycross and triathlon. He will be honored at the X Games and inducted into the National BMX Hall of Fame. The family plans to create a platform for CTE awareness and research.

Marcia Clark, the lead prosecutor in the O.J. Simpson murder trial, says in an upcoming Dateline NBC special that she partially blames herself for Simpson’s acquittal. In a preview of her interview with Josh Mankiewicz, Clark describes the guilty verdict as “physically painful,” saying she thought of Ron Goldman and Nicole Brown and felt the outcome was wrong. She also reiterated that she opposed letting Simpson try on the gloves found at the scene—an act she says was not her decision and which became an iconic setback for the prosecution. Co-counsel Christopher Darden, who suggested the gloves be tried on, later apologized; Clark responded that even if that moment cost them the case, they likely had no way to persuade that jury. The Dateline special — timed amid renewed interest from FX’s The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story — includes interviews with Kris Jenner, Denise Brown, Fred Goldman, Alan Dershowitz, Kato Kaelin and others connected to the case.

A viral video filmed in the Chernobyl exclusion zone shows a tame-looking fox carefully stacking and carrying off a multi-layer sandwich given to it by journalists. The footage, shot near abandoned Pripyat, has attracted over a million views and highlights how wildlife — including foxes, wolves and bears — has increased in the area since humans fled after the 1986 nuclear disaster. Separately, Ukrainian authorities reported they contained a large forest fire near Chernobyl on April 28, 2015; firefighters, planes and a helicopter were deployed, radiation levels remained normal, and the blaze was described as the largest in Ukraine since 1992.

Library of Virginia (partnered with Archive-It since Sept 2005) is the Commonwealth’s archival agency and reference library at the seat of government in Richmond. It is a major research institution for Virginia history, politics, and culture, drawing researchers nationally and internationally to its physical collections and digital resources (http://www.lva.virginia.gov). The document also notes that mobile marketing—particularly SMS messaging campaigns—is growing as an important, increasingly integral advertising tool for small businesses to reach current and potential customers. Finally, it references that tweets can include location information (city or precise location) from the web and third‑party apps, and that users can delete their Tweet location history.

This text describes two unrelated items. 

1) An archival effort: Web crawls are being conducted to archive pages as they are created and to capture the pages they reference. The aim is to preserve the version of referenced pages as they existed when cited, so that when original pages change or disappear, archived links can replace broken links or serve as companion links showing authors’ original intent. The broader goal is to fix broken links across the web, focusing on supported "No More 404" sites.

2) A shooting incident in Modoc County: On Oct. 19, Modoc County Sheriff's Deputy Jack Hopkins was fatally shot while responding to a disturbance about eight miles south of Alturas. He was killed instantly after being confronted and shot by 47-year-old Jack Lee Breiner. As Breiner fled, he engaged another deputy in a gunbattle and was shot and wounded. Breiner has been charged with murder and other crimes related to the killing.

Lisa Murkowski appears to have pulled off the rare feat of winning re-election as a write-in in Alaska after losing the Republican primary to tea-party favorite Joe Miller, a setback that highlights Sarah Palin’s waning influence in her home state. Murkowski’s victory—still to be certified as officials finish processing ballots—doesn’t change the Senate balance, but it’s a symbolic blow to Palin, who had promoted Miller vigorously.

Nationwide, Palin’s 2010 endorsement record was mixed. She backed about 60 candidates; roughly half have prevailed so far. In the House she endorsed 34 candidates, with only 15 wins. On the Senate side five of 12 endorsements succeeded. High-profile hits included Vicky Hartzler (who defeated long-serving Democrat Ike Skelton) and Michael Grimm; notable failures included Joe Miller (pending Alaska results) and several losses or shortfalls in marquee races such as Barney Frank’s district.

Observers say Palin often chose ideologically aligned insurgents rather than the most electable contenders and focused on broad publicity and branding—“mama grizzlies”—more than developing policy-focused protégés. That strategy boosted her name recognition and grassroots standing among conservatives but limited her endorsement success and national credibility. As a result she emerges from 2010 with durable brand visibility but diminished stature as a national kingmaker, while other Republican figures (e.g., Rand Paul, Marco Rubio, Haley Barbour) move into the spotlight as potential leaders.

Researchers ran an experiment testing how people engage with privacy policies (PP) and terms of service (TOS). They created a fictitious social network, modeled long documents on real-world examples (about 8,000 words for the PP, 4,000 for the TOS), and inserted two absurd “gotcha” clauses—one allowing data sharing with the NSA and third parties that could affect employment, travel, etc., and another claiming users must “assign their first-born child” to the site. 543 undergraduates participated.

Key findings:
- 74% used a “quick join” option and skipped the privacy policy entirely; 399 participants skipped all fine print.
- Average time spent reading (for those who did not skip) was 73 seconds for the PP and 51 seconds for the TOS—far too short to meaningfully read 8,000 and 4,000 word documents (which would take roughly 29–32 and 15–17 minutes at normal reading speeds).
- Overall, 97% agreed to the PP and 93% to the TOS; only about 2% noticed the inserted “gotcha” clauses (i.e., roughly 10–11 people).
- Regression analysis showed perceived information overload made participants less likely to read TOS when signing up or when policies changed.
- Qualitative responses framed policies as nuisances to be ignored in order to use digital services.

The study corroborates prior work showing most people don’t read or understand online agreements, highlighting how lengthy, dense legal language and information overload lead users to consent to significant terms they don’t see. The authors conclude that current disclosure formats allow companies to do almost anything with user data so long as it’s in the text, and call attention to the need for more usable, comprehensible policy design.

The Economist Intelligence Unit’s Worldwide Cost of Living Index 2014 (a twice-yearly survey) compares more than 400 prices across some 160 products and services—food and drink, clothing, household and personal care items, housing, transport, utilities, private schools, domestic help and recreation—across global cities. The survey, used by HR and finance managers to set expatriate allowances and compensation, presents city-to-city comparative indices referenced to New York (index =100) and has been run for over 30 years.

Key finding: Singapore is the most expensive city in the world in the 2014 survey. The EIU attributes this primarily to a stronger Singapore dollar and relatively high costs for cars, utilities and clothing. Although Singapore’s cost-of-living position has risen steadily over the past decade (helped by about 40% currency appreciation plus inflation), its cost relative to New York actually fell over the most recent 12-month period. The full report (and detailed city rankings) is available for download/purchase from the EIU.

Mitt Romney was formally nominated as the Republican presidential candidate at the 2012 Republican National Convention in Tampa, which had been compressed into a shorter schedule and shadowed by Hurricane Isaac. New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and other GOP leaders set a confrontational tone toward President Barack Obama, with party chairman Reince Priebus mocking Obama’s private-sector experience. Romney’s victory was sealed during the roll call of states; he watched with his wife, Ann, who was slated to give a prime-time speech to humanize him.

The convention quickly adopted a conservative platform endorsing across-the-board extension of the 2001/2003 tax cuts, an additional 20 percent income tax-bracket cut supported by Romney, repeal of the Affordable Care Act, rollback of post-2008 financial regulations, and a strict anti-abortion stance declaring a fetal right to life. The platform was in places more conservative than Romney’s own positions. Delegates also registered protest votes for Ron Paul and displayed residual tensions from the primary fight.

Security was tight around the convention, and some events and speeches were rescheduled because of storm concerns. Republicans emphasized the economy — with 8.3 percent unemployment — as the dominant campaign issue and argued Romney was more trusted on economic matters, while Democrats countered on demographics and social issues, highlighting GOP stances on immigration and reproductive rights to appeal to Hispanics, women and other groups. President Obama, preparing for his own convention, toured battleground states and took federal actions related to Isaac’s impacts.

The report notes the convergence of campaign pageantry, media coverage, and competing narratives — Romney as the challenger focused on economic recovery, and Obama defending his record and mobilizing support among key voter groups.

A Morro Bay Burger King on Quintana Road was forced to close after employees, responding to a prank call claiming to be from the fire department and instructing them to "ventilate" the building, smashed the restaurant’s windows and caused other damage (the manager on duty even drove a car into the building). The incident occurred Saturday night; repairs (~$35,000) were underway Monday and the restaurant is expected to reopen Tuesday at 6:30 a.m. The owner has suspended the employee who rammed the building. Morro Bay Police ask anyone with information, photos or video to contact them at (805) 772-6225 or Det. Mark Martin at (805) 772-6233.

Former President Bill Clinton delivered a nearly 50-minute, off-script endorsement of Barack Obama at the 2012 Democratic National Convention, earning widespread praise from commentators for making a detailed, persuasive case for Obama’s re-election. Clinton framed Obama as a pragmatic problem-solver blocked by Republican obstructionism, defended the administration’s record on the economy, health care, and consumer protections, and contrasted Democratic policies as benefiting the middle class while portraying Republican plans as favoring the wealthy.

The coverage is twofold: glowing reactions from many pundits and analysis that questioned several of Clinton’s claims. Supporters said Clinton clarified complex policy issues, energized the convention, and offered a potent message for persuading independents. Critics and fact-checkers pointed out omissions and oversimplifications in his speech: gridlock is portrayed as mainly Republican-driven though both parties and Obama’s own choices (e.g., Rahm Emanuel as chief of staff) contributed; recent low health-care spending growth is likely more due to economic weakness than the Affordable Care Act, whose strongest cost-control measures hadn’t taken effect; Clinton nostalgically cited 1990s prosperity while downplaying late-term financial vulnerabilities and his support for repealing Glass-Steagall, which some link to the 2008 crisis; and his jab about campaign fact-checking drew attention to his own history of deceptive public statements during the Lewinsky scandal.

Overall, Clinton’s oration was hailed as the convention’s highlight and a model for Democrats’ messaging, even as analysts warned it contained selective facts and omitted complexities that undercut some of its stronger claims.

The document contains two unrelated items.

1) A legal challenge to Florida’s ban on gay adoption: Martin Gill and his partner have fostered two brothers (now ages 4 and 9) in North Miami for four years. After the children’s parental rights were terminated in 2006, the couple sought to adopt them, but Florida law has automatically prohibited adoption by gay people since 1977 even while allowing gay and lesbian foster parents. With ACLU support, Martin challenged the ban; a juvenile court judge granted the adoption last November, but the state attorney general immediately appealed, so the case remains unresolved. Meanwhile the boys remain in the couple’s care.

2) Description of a 2011 large-scale web crawl dataset from the Internet Archive: The crawl ran from March 9 to December 23, 2011, used Heritrix (3.1.1-SNAPSHOT) and an Alexa top-1M seed list, producing 2,713,676,341 captures across 2,273,840,159 unique URLs and 29,032,069 hosts. Robots.txt was respected and scope was generally unlimited with a few exclusions. The crawl used new distributed crawling software (HQ) and was somewhat experimental, so there were operational issues (missed embedded/linked resources due to queue growth, repeated crawls of some Argentine government sites skewing country results). The Archive made the raw dataset available “warts and all” for researchers and invites requests for access via info@archive.org, noting they will evaluate requests case by case.

President Barack Obama said the United States will not send ground troops into Yemen or Somalia, but will work with international partners to keep Americans safe. In an interview with People, he noted that al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in Yemen has grown more serious and that the U.S. has partnered with Yemen to target terrorist camps and cells. He made similar observations about al Shabaab in Somalia, where large areas remain outside government control.

Gen. David Petraeus, head of U.S. Central Command, echoed that U.S. forces do not intend to deploy on the ground in Yemen and said Yemeni leaders have expressed they do not want U.S. troops there. Petraeus said the U.S. will increase security assistance to Yemen from about $70 million to at least $150 million and provide additional economic aid, while other Gulf states have pledged substantial support as well. He emphasized continued U.S. intelligence and assistance to help Yemen combat AQAP, which U.S. officials believe was linked to the failed Dec. 25 airliner attack.

Petraeus described AQAP’s growth over recent years but said it is not “industrial strength”; he stressed that the principal theater against al Qaeda remains the Pakistan‑Afghanistan border. He warned that while al Qaeda’s capabilities have diminished overall, the group still poses a threat and requires sustained pressure.

Former Bakersfield High student Mitch Carter sued the Kern High School District (KHSD) after suffering severe injuries, including a traumatic brain injury, in a violent “dog pile” during a 2010 pep rally. Carter had been wearing a chicken costume as part of a tradition in which someone dressed as the opposing team’s mascot was mocked; during the skit members of the football team pounced on him, punching, kicking and piling on. Carter says he tried to stop performing mid-skit and told an administrator he would not continue before being knocked down.

A jury found the district negligent. With a damage phase underway and jurors reportedly inclined to award more than $45 million, KHSD and its insurers agreed to a $10.5 million settlement—mostly paid by Everest National Insurance—ending the seven-day civil trial. Carter’s attorney Nicholas Rowley said Carter will use the funds for medical care and that the settlement should prompt policy changes so the incident cannot recur.

The trial exposed alleged lapses in safety oversight, disorganization between KHSD police and school administrators, and conflicting testimony about who saw or approved the skit. Carter’s lawyers accused the district of a conspiracy and cover-up and criticized school leadership, including football coach Paul Golla, whose courtroom testimony conflicted with other witnesses. Defense counsel described the episode as “embarrassing and inexcusable” but sudden and not the result of a cover-up; KHSD said it will reevaluate policies and accepts responsibility.

Attorneys for Carter rejected earlier, much smaller settlement offers and asserted they want structural changes and accountability at the district. Carter said he hopes to use his experience to help others someday, possibly by attending law school.

Texas health officials finalized rules requiring hospitals, clinics and other medical facilities to cremate or bury fetal remains rather than dispose of them in landfills, a change announced to take effect Dec. 19. The Department of State Health Services first proposed the rule in July, drew more than 35,000 public comments and faced sustained opposition from abortion-rights groups, medical providers and some funeral- and waste-industry representatives who said the policy is costly, difficult to enforce and creates barriers for people seeking abortions or experiencing miscarriages.

Advocates led by NARAL Pro-Choice Texas rallied outside the department and delivered over 5,500 signatures opposing the rule, calling it a transparent effort to restrict abortion access. Opponents also argued the rule could force patients into emotionally harmful situations (for example, requiring burial after rape) and that it intrudes on personal beliefs. The Center for Reproductive Rights said it would likely challenge the rule in court.

State officials, including a department spokeswoman and Gov. Greg Abbott, defended the change. The department said its analysis shows overall facility costs won’t increase because the new disposition methods would offset current expenditures for transportation, storage, incineration and landfill disposal; Abbott said fetal remains should not be treated like medical waste. Health officials clarified the requirement does not apply to miscarriages or abortions occurring at home and does not mandate filing birth or death certificates.

Because the rule was adopted under agency rulemaking authority, it did not require immediate legislative approval, though some Republican lawmakers plan to codify the requirement into statute when the legislature meets. Similar fetal-remains restrictions exist or have been proposed in other states; legal challenges could raise constitutional questions about burdens on abortion access and the legal status of removed biological material.

Monday Properties has proposed demolishing two aging Rosslyn office buildings at 1401 Wilson Blvd and 1400 Key Blvd as part of a major mixed-use redevelopment that would replace the structures and the underlying parking garage — the site where Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward met his Watergate source “Deep Throat” (FBI official Mark Felt) — with a 32-story residential tower and a 29-story office tower. The project would total nearly 1 million square feet (about 500,000 sq ft office, 385,000 sq ft residential and 60,000 sq ft retail, including a full-service grocery) and set aside roughly half the land as public open space.

The redevelopment plans were only recently submitted and must pass Arlington’s site plan review, a process that typically takes one to four years; Monday does not expect work to begin until around 2016–2017 if approved. The garage, built in the early 1960s and considered near the end of its useful life, would be removed, but Monday Properties and Arlington officials say they hope to preserve and reincorporate the historical marker (installed by Arlington County in 2011) or otherwise commemorate the site’s Watergate significance during the approval and design process. Arlington’s Site Plan Review Committee is scheduled to meet about the proposal on Oct. 21.

Rep. Louie Gohmert said there’s “no personal” animosity between him and Attorney General Eric Holder after a heated House hearing, but accused Holder of failing to do his job. On Fox & Friends Gohmert called Holder “likable” but said the attorney general is making “personal choices” about prosecutions and refusing proper oversight by withholding Justice Department documents about a Texas-based Islamic charity. The previous day’s hearing included sharp exchanges over those documents and the Fast and Furious scandal; at one point Holder warned Gohmert, “You don’t want to go there.” Holder, who referenced the confrontation without naming Gohmert in a speech to Al Sharpton’s National Action Network, described the committee’s treatment of him as unprecedented and divisive. Other Republicans at the hearing, such as Blake Farenthold, also criticized Holder publicly.

Police and doctors in Uttar Pradesh, northern India, are trying to identify a girl believed to have been living in a forest with monkeys after she was found in January in the Katarniaghat forest near Bahraich.

Key facts:
- The girl is estimated to be about 8–12 years old. She was naked, emaciated, had long tangled hair and nails, and bore wounds when rescued.
- Villagers and woodcutters first saw her roaming with a group of monkeys; attempts to approach were thwarted by the animals. A police officer eventually rescued her as the monkeys attacked.
- On arrival at the government hospital in Bahraich she could not speak, initially walked and behaved like an animal (running on hands and feet, screeching, eating from the floor). After treatment she began walking upright, eating with her hands, recognizes and smiles at staff but remains nonverbal.
- Medical staff report gradual physical and behavioral improvement; wounds are healing, hair and nails have been cleaned and trimmed. She will be transferred for further medical and psychological care and housed in a juvenile facility until identified.
- Police are checking missing-children records and investigating how long she had been in the forest and whether she was abandoned or lost. Locals and officials have compared her to Rudyard Kipling’s “Mowgli”; authorities have nicknamed her “Forest Durga.”

- In Utah, six-term Republican Sen. Orrin Hatch decisively won the GOP primary, defeating tea party-backed former state Sen. Dan Liljenquist. Hatch, 78, had not faced a primary since 1976 but overcame concerns about his age and occasional departures from tea party priorities by mounting a well-funded, organized campaign (about $10 million), securing key endorsements (including Mitt Romney), and shifting rightward on some issues. He narrowly missed avoiding a convention runoff but prevailed in the primary and is a heavy favorite for the November general election against Democrat Scott Howell.

- Liljenquist emphasized the national debt and painted Hatch as part of the problem but lacked Hatch’s financial and organizational resources. Hatch stressed this would be his final term and cited the prospect of chairing the Senate Finance Committee if Republicans retake the Senate.

- In New York, longtime Democratic Rep. Charles Rangel won a hard-fought primary over state Sen. Adriano Espaillat. Despite past ethics censure, health problems and a changed district with more Latino voters, Rangel — first elected in 1970 and a co-founder of the Congressional Black Caucus — held on by about five percentage points and pledged to serve the next two-year term.

- Other notable primary results: Mitt Romney easily won Utah’s presidential primary, and in Oklahoma Rep. John Sullivan faced a close contest and ultimately lost to a tea party-backed challenger, Jim Bridenstine, reflecting continuing intra-party fights in GOP primaries.

Bob Dylan gave a long, wide-ranging interview to Bill Flanagan for bobdylan.com, discussing his new triple-album of standards Triplicate (three interconnected 32-minute discs), his approach to singing and arranging, and many memories from a lifetime in music.

Key points about Triplicate and the recording:
- Triplicate completes a thematic trilogy following Shadows in the Night and Fallen Angels; Dylan says the three records are interconnected and resolve one another.
- He chose the three-disc format because each 10-song, ~32-minute disc feels like a complete unit (he cites LP-side length, the symbolic nature of the number 32, and optimal sound quality).
- The sessions used a live horn section and full arrangements; Dylan appreciates working with charts and found that constraints can free a vocalist to inhabit melodies without overthinking.
- These are live studio performances with minimal overdubbing; vocal cracks (he cites “September of My Years”) were left because fixing them would have been difficult and might harm the live feel.
- He aims to honor the songs’ direct realism and human truth, not to be nostalgic; he sees them as relevant expressions of the human condition rather than wistful memory trips.
- Dylan credits arrangers and musicians (naming James Harper) and emphasizes trusting their expertise; he describes choices on phrasing and rhythm and the kinds of drummers he admires.
- He says singing standards lets him go places he wouldn’t in his own songwriting—vulnerability and sentiment that he might avoid writing himself.

Reflections on influences, technique, and repertoire:
- Sinatra is an acknowledged guide—Dylan knew Sinatra had recorded many of these songs and recalled a polite encounter at Sinatra’s house in which Sinatra complimented “Forever Young.” He also notes performing “Restless Farewell” at Sinatra’s request for a TV tribute.
- He deliberately imagined some standards as if unaware of Sinatra’s versions when recording, while accepting Sinatra’s influence as a directional guide.
- Dylan discusses vocal approach (not acting but a hypnotic repetition), the importance of intros/verses in older songs, and why some standards require a different, more circumspect delivery than his vernacular songs.
- He sees early pop, big band, doo-wop and early movie/pop songs as part of the same continuum that led to rock and roll; rock was an explosive, “atomic” culture shift but not wholly disconnected from earlier forms.
- He doesn’t expect the standards to directly shape his next original songs; their complexity and formal constructions are different from his songwriting instincts.

Personal memories and anecdotes:
- He recalls childhood Duluth wartime austerity and how life experience lets him better inhabit these songs now than in his youth.
- Recollections include seeing Sinatra live, an anecdote about Sinatra’s dinner party remark about “blue eyes,” and a humorous reversal about an Elvis Presley session with George Harrison—Presley did show up, Dylan says, but it was Dylan and Harrison who didn’t.
- He reflects on musicians who recently died (Muhammad Ali, Merle Haggard, Leonard Cohen, Leon Russell) as leaving “empty spaces.”
- Dylan recalls encounters with jazz figures (seeing Coltrane, knowing Ornette Coleman), his longstanding affinity for jazz, and how jazz musicians and he sometimes faced comparable critical resistance.
- He remembers early TV, the Twin Cities’ rock scene, his musical awakenings hearing Lead Belly and Josh White, and friendships or encounters with many famous figures (John Wayne, Sinatra, the Beatles in the audience, etc.).
- He comments on songcraft, influence, and tradition: reworking melodies/lyrics has always happened across genres; standards are durable and widely accessible; nostalgia is not his aim.

Miscellaneous:
- He still listens mainly to CDs and named recent favorites (Iggy Pop’s Après, Imelda May, Valerie June, Amy Winehouse).
- He discusses performance habits (now more often on piano), why he sometimes places odd songs at the start of albums, and why he doesn’t socialize much on the road beyond his band.
- On the album title: Triplicate nods to trilogy structures (Sinatra’s trilogy and Greek drama); Dylan intended each disc to tell a different story and to build thematically.

Overall, the interview mixes detailed studio insights about Triplicate and Dylan’s interpretive choices with personal history, musical opinions, and anecdotes about peers and influences—revealing how he approaches standards as a mature interpreter rather than as tribute or nostalgia.

The Justice Department has found a pattern of unconstitutional use of force by the Cleveland Division of Police and reached an agreement with the city to negotiate a consent decree requiring reforms and independent oversight.

Key findings
- Federal investigators reviewed nearly 600 force incidents from 2010–2013 and concluded there is reasonable cause to believe Cleveland police engage in a pattern and practice of excessive and unnecessary force.
- Problems include unnecessary deadly force (shootings, head strikes), excessive use of less-lethal methods (Tasers, chemical spray, fists), disproportionate force against people with mental illness, and dangerous tactics that put officers and civilians at risk.
- The department also fails to adequately investigate or review force incidents, discipline officers, or detect patterns of concerning behavior.

Illustrative incidents cited
- A 2012 high-speed chase in which 13 officers fired 137 shots, killing two unarmed occupants.
- Cases in which restrained or prone suspects were kicked or struck, a 13-year-old in handcuffs was punched, a man was shocked while strapped to a gurney, a mentally ill man was pepper-sprayed through a spit hood and not decontaminated, and a driver was accidentally shot inside his car.

Next steps and context
- Cleveland and the Justice Department agreed on principles that will lead to a formal consent decree; an independent monitor will oversee implementation of reforms, with details to be negotiated in coming months.
- Attorney General Eric Holder framed the move as part of a broader national conversation on police-community relations amid recent high-profile deaths (including Michael Brown, Eric Garner and Tamir Rice). The DOJ investigation began in March 2013 and predates the November 2014 killing of 12-year-old Tamir Rice, though that case will be considered when shaping required changes.

Fifteen-year-old Javon (Jovan) Wilson, grandson of U.S. Rep. Danny Davis, was fatally shot in his Englewood, Chicago home on the evening of Nov. 18, 2016. Police say the killing stemmed from a dispute over basketball shoes with two juveniles who were known to the family; a 15-year-old boy allegedly pulled a gun and shot Javon in the head while a 17-year-old girl was also involved. Two juvenile suspects are in custody and first-degree murder charges are expected as detectives continue interrogations.

Rep. Davis and family members described Javon as a typical, improving 15-year-old who loved basketball and music. Davis and others lamented the ubiquity of guns and routine gun violence facing Chicago youth. Officials characterized the slaying as a targeted, senseless act rather than a random home invasion. The homicide comes amid a sharp citywide rise in shootings and homicides in 2016.

Bill de Blasio, New York City’s public advocate, emerged as the surprise front-runner in the Democratic mayoral primary, polling just above the 40 percent threshold needed to avoid an automatic runoff. Running on a platform to reverse Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s policies, de Blasio focused on economic inequality, ending racial profiling and stop-and-frisk, replacing Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly, and funding universal prekindergarten with taxes on the wealthy. His message — amplified by ads featuring his biracial family and appeals to voters concerned about jobs, schools and policing — resonated broadly across boroughs, genders and racial groups.

Former comptroller Bill Thompson finished second with roughly 26 percent and signaled he would contest a runoff if de Blasio falls below 40 percent once all ballots are tallied. Christine Quinn, the early front-runner and Bloomberg ally, placed third at about 16 percent, hampered by voter backlash over her support for Bloomberg’s third term. Other notable Democrats fared poorly: John Liu and Anthony Weiner each drew single-digit shares. Exit polls showed roughly three-quarters of Democratic voters wanted a break from Bloomberg-era policies.

On the Republican side, Joseph J. Lhota, the former MTA chairman and Giuliani deputy mayor, won the nomination over billionaire John Catsimatidis. Lhota, a Bloomberg policy supporter, emphasized tough-minded approaches to crime and city finances and will face the Democratic nominee in November.

In other races, Scott M. Stringer defeated Eliot Spitzer for city comptroller, and Letitia James and State Senator Daniel L. Squadron advanced to a runoff for public advocate. With Democrats outnumbering Republicans in the city but no Democratic mayor since 1989, the fall contest will pit de Blasio’s promise of change against Lhota’s continuity-minded platform. Final results and the question of a Democratic runoff hinge on remaining absentee and provisional ballots.
