Since the late 1970s China has transformed from a closed, centrally planned economy into a far more market-oriented and globally influential one. Gradualist reforms—starting with decollectivizing agriculture and expanding to price liberalization, fiscal decentralization, greater autonomy for state firms, growth of the private sector, capital markets and banks, and opening to foreign trade and investment—helped raise GDP more than tenfold since 1978. By 2017 China averaged just over 7% real growth from 2013–2017, became the world’s largest economy on a PPP basis (surpassing the U.S. in 2014), and is the largest exporter (since 2010) and largest trading nation (since 2013). Nonetheless, per-capita income remains below the world average and development is uneven, being stronger on the coast than inland.

Exchange rate and capital controls: China moved in 2005 to an exchange-rate regime tied to a currency basket. The renminbi appreciated from 2005–2008, was effectively pegged during the global financial crisis, then resumed gradual appreciation from 2010. It depreciated in 2015–2016 amid capital outflows, then appreciated in 2017. The renminbi entered the IMF’s SDR basket in 2015 and Beijing has signaled intentions toward full convertibility, but since late 2015 authorities tightened capital controls and oversight of outbound investment to manage the exchange rate and financial stability.

Ongoing economic challenges: Beijing faces many structural problems, including very high domestic savings and low household consumption; elevated corporate debt and off-balance-sheet local-government debt; speculative real-estate investment and industrial overcapacity; the need to create higher-wage jobs for migrants and graduates while maintaining competitiveness; and raising productivity via better capital allocation and innovation support. Demographic issues—an aging population aggravated by decades of the one-child policy (relaxed to two children in 2016)—and environmental degradation (air pollution, soil erosion, falling groundwater, and loss of arable land) add long-term constraints. China is diversifying energy away from coal toward gas, nuclear, and renewables and ratified the Paris Agreement, committing to peak CO2 emissions between 2025 and 2030.

Policy stance and state role: The 13th Five-Year Plan (2016–2020) stresses innovation and boosting domestic consumption to rebalance away from investment, exports, and heavy industry. However, progress has been stronger on subsidizing innovation than on rebalancing. Although officials pledge a greater market role, policies still favor state-owned enterprises (SOEs), with renewed support for strategic sectors deemed important to “economic security,” and leaders have reaffirmed the state’s dominant economic role—actions that risk discouraging private initiative and reducing long-term efficiency. The plan targets at least 6.5% annual growth through 2020 to meet a pledge to double GDP by 2020. The 2017 growth uptick gave Beijing some room to pursue financial deleveraging and supply-side structural reforms.

Defense and security spending and regional implications: China has substantially increased military spending in recent decades (more than doubling since 2006), reflecting economic growth, expanding global interests, and regional territorial disputes. Announced defense spending rose (an example figure cited: roughly 670 billion yuan / $106 billion, reflecting an 11.2% increase in one reported year), making China the world’s second-largest military spender after the U.S. Official defense outlays are lower as a share of GDP (about 1.3% in 2011) than in the U.S., but analysts argue true totals may be materially higher due to off-budget items, though some of these have been reduced and certain items (e.g., veterans’ support) are now included. Domestic security spending has outpaced military spending in recent years, reflecting concerns about social unrest in places such as Tibet and Xinjiang.

China’s military modernization—new fighters, precision missiles, an aircraft carrier undergoing sea trials, and extensive missile deployments opposite Taiwan—has alarmed neighbors and the U.S. over its expansive maritime claims (notably in the South China Sea) and disputes with Japan, Vietnam, the Philippines and India. Beijing insists its defense buildup is “reasonable and appropriate” and aimed at safeguarding sovereignty and protecting growing global economic interests—such as large numbers of workers overseas, convoy and evacuation missions, anti-piracy deployments, and securing trade routes and energy supplies—rather than threatening other countries. The U.S. maintains a much larger defense budget but has shifted strategic focus toward the Asia-Pacific, contributing to regional tensions.

Market and investor reactions: Defense-related firms and satellite makers saw stock gains following budget announcements, reflecting investor expectations of continued defense-sector demand.

Overall, China’s economic rise has been rapid and deep, but it faces significant structural, demographic, environmental, and debt-related challenges. At the same time, continued state-led industrial and military modernization, expanding global interests, and assertive territorial claims are reshaping regional security dynamics and prompting concern among neighboring states and the United States.

Halle Berry and her ex, model Gabriel Aubry, returned to court over control of their 6-year-old daughter Nahla’s hair. Berry’s attorney accused Aubry of straightening and highlighting Nahla’s naturally curly hair—allegedly to make her appear less African American. Berry did not attend; her lawyer argued the changes were inappropriate. The judge ordered that neither parent may alter Nahla’s natural hair color or texture and directed that her hair be allowed to grow back naturally.

The dispute comes amid ongoing custody tensions between Berry and Aubry. They share joint custody and have previously fought over moves and physical altercations between family members. Separately, Berry has sought to reduce monthly child support payments to Aubry—claiming he’s unemployed and living off $16,000/month in support—and requested a reduction to around $3,000/month. The couple settled earlier on annual support and educational/health expense arrangements. Berry has publicly said she identifies as black and has discussed how Nahla, who is mixed-race, might choose her own identity.

President Barack Obama began a three-day trip to the Caribbean and Central America with a low-key arrival in Kingston, Jamaica, the first visit by a sitting U.S. president to Jamaica since Ronald Reagan in 1982. The trip — which includes meetings with Caribbean Community (CARICOM) leaders in Jamaica and attendance at the Summit of the Americas in Panama — comes as the U.S. seeks to strengthen ties amid growing Chinese investment in the region and a diminished role for oil-rich Venezuela.

Obama’s recent policy moves (immigration executive actions, efforts to slow Central American migrant flows, and outreach to Cuba) have put renewed U.S. focus on the hemisphere. Energy security is a top priority on his Caribbean agenda: the U.S. aims to help meet the region’s energy needs through American resources, infrastructure expertise, and cooperation, following a White House-convened Caribbean Energy Security Summit earlier in the year.

China’s expanding “checkbook diplomacy” financing roads, bridges and other projects across the Caribbean has heightened competition for influence, according to regional analysts. During his brief stop in Kingston, Obama paid an unscheduled visit to the Bob Marley museum, toured the late reggae star’s former home, and spoke with young regional leaders in a town-hall format as part of an effort to engage new generations in civic and political life.

The document contains several news items focused on President Donald Trump, media controversies, and an Internet Archive effort.

1) Oval Office encounter with RTE reporter Caitríona Perry
- RTE Washington correspondent Caitríona Perry attended the Oval Office as Trump made a congratulatory phone call to Irish Taoiseach Leo Varadkar. During the call Trump drew attention to the Irish press, called Perry over, asked where she was from and told Varadkar she “has a nice smile” and probably “treats you well.” Perry laughed and returned to her seat and later described the moment as “bizarre.”
- A short video Perry posted of the exchange went viral and sparked debate over workplace sexism. Critics called the comment inappropriate and demeaning, asking whether a male reporter would have been addressed similarly; defenders called it a harmless compliment and questioned why women cannot accept compliments.

2) CNN retraction and fallout
- CNN retracted a web story about Anthony Scaramucci’s alleged pre-inaugural meeting with a Russian investment fund; three journalists resigned. The episode gave the White House ammunition to renew attacks on “fake news.”
- At a White House briefing Sarah Huckabee Sanders highlighted a Project Veritas hidden-camera video in which a CNN producer criticized the network’s Russia coverage, calling the video “a disgrace” if accurate and urging the public to watch it. Conservative activist James O’Keefe released the video; Project Veritas has a history of sting operations.
- Trump and allies seized on the CNN mistakes to allege broader bias and to deflect attention from other issues (e.g., the Russia probe and a stalled health-care vote). Trump tweeted attacks on CNN, and conservative media called for management changes.
- CNN defended the producer involved and stressed that diverse personal opinions are acceptable. Network sources said the retraction underscored the need for error-free reporting. Coverage of the controversy intensified cable-news rivalry, especially between CNN and Fox News.

3) Internet Archive note
- A brief note describes an archival effort to crawl and archive web pages as they are created so that referenced pages remain available even if the originals change or are removed — an initiative aimed at reducing broken links on the web.

Overall, the pieces highlight tensions between the Trump administration and mainstream media, a viral Oval Office moment that reignited discussions about gender and professionalism in the workplace, and a separate technical effort to preserve web content.

Swiss authorities arrested two Syrian men in Geneva after traces of explosives were found in the car they were driving, prosecutors said. The men, who had Syrian passports, had only recently arrived in Switzerland, spoke Arabic but not French, and were detained the day they arrived following heightened police vigilance. Geneva prosecutor Olivier Jornot said tests detected explosive residues (not toxic gas) and prosecutors opened proceedings for manufacture, concealment and transport of explosives and for violating laws against groups like al‑Qaeda and IS. Jornot stressed the vehicle had at some point been used to transport explosives but it was not established that the two suspects themselves had done so. 

The arrests occurred amid a wider hunt for suspected IS-linked jihadists in the Geneva region after US intelligence reportedly warned of a potential cell; Geneva raised its terrorism alert to level three, deployed armed police to sensitive sites (UN offices, consulate, synagogues, transport hubs) and published photos of four other suspects. Authorities said there was no clear evidence the Geneva suspects were connected to the November 13 Paris attacks, and Swiss officials indicated there was no specific threat to the UN in Geneva.

A Philadelphia Common Pleas jury awarded $2.5 million to Austin Pledger, now 20, whose family sued Janssen Pharmaceuticals (a Johnson & Johnson subsidiary), finding the company failed to adequately warn that the antipsychotic Risperdal can cause gynecomastia (abnormal breast development in males). Pledger, who has autism, began taking Risperdal in 2002 at age eight—before the drug was FDA-approved for children—and later developed size 46DD breasts that his lawyer says can only be removed by mastectomy. His mother testified about the severe emotional impact; his prescribing doctor said he was unaware gynecomastia could result.

The case is the first Risperdal gynecomastia lawsuit to go to trial amid more than 1,200 similar suits filed in Philadelphia. It recalled broader legal trouble for J&J: two years earlier the company paid $2.2 billion to resolve claims it illegally marketed Risperdal to children and the elderly. Former FDA commissioner David Kessler testified for the plaintiffs that Janssen knew of the risk. Janssen said it was disappointed, believes the verdict should be overturned, and contends the FDA-approved label and prescriber were properly informed and that the drug benefited many patients.

Mayo Clinic overview
- Mayo Clinic offers appointments in Arizona, Florida, Minnesota and at Mayo Clinic Health System locations. Its general interest e‑newsletter covers many health topics.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — key symptoms and guidance (Mayo Clinic)
- DKA signs can develop rapidly, sometimes within 24 hours, and may be the first sign of diabetes. Common symptoms:
  - Excessive thirst, frequent urination
  - Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
  - Weakness or fatigue, shortness of breath
  - Fruity‑scented breath, confusion
- Home testing may show high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) and high urinary ketones.
- When to contact a doctor:
  - If you’re ill or stressed, check blood sugar frequently and consider an over‑the‑counter urine ketone test.
  - Call your doctor immediately if you are vomiting and can’t keep down food/liquids, your blood sugar is above target and won’t respond to home treatment, or urine ketones are moderate/high.
- When to seek emergency care:
  - Persistent blood glucose >300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L)
  - Ketones in urine and you cannot reach medical advice
  - Multiple DKA symptoms (thirst, frequent urination, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, fruity breath, confusion)
- Untreated DKA can be fatal.

Sydney case: parents charged after death of diabetic 6‑year‑old
- Two Sydney parents were arrested and charged with manslaughter and gross negligence after their six‑year‑old son, a diabetic, was found unconscious and died on April 30, 2015, after attending a nearby “self‑healing” workshop.
- Authorities allege the parents were complicit in deliberately depriving the child of insulin and food.
- The workshop’s leader, Hongchi Xiao, a self‑described healer who runs a therapy called “paidalajin” (involving fasting, stretching and skin‑slapping), left Australia after the death and remains at large. He has been linked to another death: a 71‑year‑old woman died during a retreat he ran in England, where he was later questioned and released on bail.
- Xiao has denied being a doctor and cited a small study he described as supporting paidalajin for diabetes, though that study noted patients might need medical support during fasting to prevent ketoacidosis.
- The Tasly Healthpac Centre in Hurstville said Xiao rented a room to run seminars and that the boy was not their patient.
- The parents were granted conditional bail and face up to 25 years in prison if convicted.

Some coffee drinkers prioritize flavor and origin, but many just want caffeine. South Africa–based Black Insomnia, launched in 2016, now claims the title of “world’s strongest coffee.” Independent testing cited by the company found it contains about 702 mg of caffeine per 12-ounce cup—surpassing rival Death Wish (about 660 mg) and far above a typical 12-ounce cup (~150 mg). Both specialty brands exceed the 400 mg daily limit health experts recommend for most adults. Black Insomnia says it achieves high caffeine by using robusta beans (higher in caffeine than arabica) while aiming to avoid burnt or overly acidic flavors; it describes its profile as slightly sweet and walnut-like. The product is now sold in the U.S. (16-oz bag ~$19.99 on Amazon).

The summary also flags health guidance: the Mayo Clinic advises up to 400 mg of caffeine daily is generally safe for healthy adults, but children, pregnant or breastfeeding people, those sensitive to caffeine, or those on certain medications should limit intake. Excessive caffeine can cause insomnia, nervousness, rapid heartbeat, digestive issues and other symptoms; it can worsen sleep deprivation and interact with drugs or supplements (e.g., ephedrine, theophylline, echinacea). To cut back, track intake, reduce gradually, choose decaf or herbal options, shorten tea brew times, and check labels (some pain relievers contain caffeine).

Stuart Rothenberg and accompanying election analysis outline how President Barack Obama’s party faces historically poor midterm results and how the Senate map complicates future control.

Key points on midterm losses:
- Obama is on track to be the first president in 50 years to suffer two very bad midterms in a row. Democrats lost 63 House seats in 2010 and are expected to lose an additional 5–12 (or more) in the next midterm, putting his two-midterm House losses around 68–75 seats—worse than recent two-term presidents and approaching Harry S. Truman’s postwar totals.
- In historical context: Truman lost 83 House seats across his two midterms (55 in 1946, 28 in 1950); Eisenhower lost 66. Other presidents typically had one bad midterm and one modest one (examples: Clinton, Reagan, George W. Bush).
- Senate losses for Obama are also significant: Democrats lost 6 seats in 2010 and appear likely to lose 5–10 more, producing a two-midterm Senate loss of roughly 11–16 seats. That could approach—but likely won’t exceed—Truman-era Democratic Senate losses (17).

Causes and accountability:
- The piece suggests both structural factors (partisan polarization, unfavorable Senate-class maps) and presidential responsibility (perceived lack of leadership or centrist moves) explain the losses.

Outlook for 2016 Senate map (from Politico excerpt):
- Republicans winning the Senate could be short-lived because the 2016 map tilts toward GOP vulnerability: several first-term GOP senators elected in 2010 serve in states Obama carried in 2008/2012 (e.g., Kirk, Toomey, Johnson, Portman, Ayotte, Rubio), creating pickup opportunities for Democrats.
- Democrats view a GOP majority as likely narrow and temporary; they’re optimistic about reclaiming seats in blue states. Republicans counter that competent governance could help defend those seats.
- Both parties see specific vulnerable targets on each side: Democrats eye GOP seats in Obama-won states; Republicans target Democrats such as Harry Reid (NV) and Michael Bennet (CO).
- Several potential Democratic challengers and funding positions are noted (e.g., Kirk, Toomey, Johnson fundraising figures and possible challengers like Lisa Madigan, Russ Feingold, Joe Sestak).

Overall takeaway:
- The midterm cycle marks a historic setback for Obama’s Democrats in House and Senate losses driven by both political dynamics and leadership perceptions, while the 2016 Senate map gives Democrats reason for optimism about reversing some of those gains.

Two 17-year-old students and acquaintances at Plano East Senior High School — Ritu Sachdeva and Hillary Kate Kuizon — were found dead within hours of each other over a weekend in Murphy, Texas. Relatives discovered Sachdeva at her home shortly after midnight Sunday; Kuizon’s body was found a few hours later in a wooded area near Kimbrough Stadium. Murphy police say both deaths are being investigated as likely suicides, with no signs of foul play so far; the medical examiner will determine official causes. Investigators are interviewing family members to determine whether the deaths are connected and have not identified any motives. The school and district have provided grief counselors on campus, lowered flags to half-staff, and student peers expressed shock and sadness. Authorities urged caution about unconfirmed rumors of a suicide pact and reminded anyone in crisis to contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline.

A 12-year-old boy in Maple Heights (near Cleveland), Reginald “Reggie” Fields, runs a small summer lawn business called “Mr. Reggie’s Lawn Cutting Service” with help from his siblings and cousins. While mowing a customer’s yard last weekend, he unintentionally trimmed about a foot of a neighboring property where the property line is unclear. The neighbor called the Maple Heights Police Department, who spoke with the group but took no action. The customer, Lucille Holt, posted a video of the encounter to Facebook; it went viral, drawing thousands of views, shares and supportive messages. As a result, Reggie has received hundreds of requests and calls for jobs, and his business has surged—he plans to use earnings to buy equipment and expand. Holt said the neighbor has a history of calling police over minor incidents; the neighbor declined to be on camera.

A chance discovery in the Flinders Ranges, South Australia, has revealed a rock-shelter (Warratyi) with well-preserved archaeological deposits showing Aboriginal occupation between about 49,000 and 46,000 years ago. Found by archaeologist Giles Hamm and Adnyamathanha elder Clifford Coulthard, the site yielded ~4,300 artefacts and ~200 bone fragments recovered from carefully controlled hand excavations and stratigraphic recording. Multiple dating methods were applied — single-grain OSL/TT-OSL on quartz, radiocarbon (14C) on hearth charcoal and eggshell, and Bayesian modelling integrating the dates — supporting the 49–46 ka age range.

Key findings:
- Early inland occupation: The dates place humans deep in the arid interior far earlier than previously documented there (previous arid-zone sites ~38 ka), implying rapid southward dispersal after initial coastal colonization and possibly an even earlier arrival on the continent.
- Technology and culture: The assemblage includes early bone and stone tools, hafted axes, wood-handled tools, ochre use (earliest reliably dated in Australia/SE Asia at ~49–46 ka), gypsum, and evidence of local innovation in technology (e.g., bone needles; hafting).
- Human–megafauna association: Bones of Diprotodon optatum (giant wombat-like megafauna), juvenile remains, and eggshells (emus and an extinct large bird) occur in secure stratified contexts with artefacts. Morphology and site topography indicate humans carried these remains into the shelter, providing strong evidence of interaction — likely hunting or butchery — which bears on megafauna extinction debates.
- Rigorous methodology: Excavation used fine 1-m grids, 5-cm spits, sieving, in situ plotting of finds, refitting studies to test deposit integrity, use-wear and residue analyses, and thorough luminescence and radiocarbon protocols. Results and materials will be deposited in museums and an Adnyamathanha keeping place, with data provided in supplementary information.

Significance:
Warratyi is one of Australia’s most important prehistoric sites — it pushes back reliably dated human presence in the arid interior to ~49 ka, documents early technological and symbolic behaviours, and provides clear evidence that people and megafauna coexisted and interacted in southern Australia shortly after initial colonization. The work, published in Nature and conducted in collaboration with the Adnyamathanha Traditional Lands Association, challenges prior assumptions about the timing, speed, and cultural complexity of early Indigenous occupation of the Australian interior.

An 89-year-old Moses Lake, Washington, store owner, Miyo Koba, fought off an attempted robbery at her longtime shop, Frank’s Superette, using a golf club after the suspect—described as a tall, slender male in a ski mask and dark sunglasses—pulled a roughly three-foot sword and tried to open the cash register. Koba, who has owned the store for 60 years, refused to hand over money, threatened the man with scissors, was pushed and briefly knocked down, then grabbed a golf club and struck his legs. The suspect fled on a BMX bike with the cash register but later dropped it; Koba recovered the register and the money. Witnesses and police said the suspect rode off and apparently removed his clothing; his clothing was later recovered. Police continued to search for the suspect and asked anyone with information to contact Moses Lake Police.

Former Florida governor and Republican presidential candidate Jeb Bush told Iowa audiences he would not categorically rule out resuming harsh interrogation methods in some circumstances, stopping short of endorsing torture but refusing a blanket promise to uphold President Obama’s ban on "enhanced interrogation." He said he generally considers such techniques inappropriate, was glad the CIA largely stopped them, and acknowledged the Senate report’s findings but insisted the methods had produced useful intelligence in the past. Bush implied there could be scenarios where brutal interrogations might be needed to protect the country, though he declined to define the difference between enhanced techniques and torture.

Bush also defended elements of his brother George W. Bush’s Iraq policy while acknowledging mistakes—singling out the disbanding of the Iraqi military—and blamed the Obama administration for leaving Iraq too quickly and creating conditions that allowed ISIS to grow. He praised the 2007 troop surge and argued for a more aggressive posture against ISIS that excludes large-scale U.S. ground invasions but could include special operations forces, continued use of drones, and keeping detainees at Guantánamo Bay. His remarks reflect a deliberate effort to distance himself from unpopular aspects of his brother’s legacy while emphasizing hawkish national-security credentials.

Ryan Gosling marked Eva Mendes’ 42nd birthday during a Palm Springs getaway by heroically rescuing a dog that wandered into a busy highway. While the couple was heading to pick up takeout from Rick’s Desert Grill, Gosling jumped out of their car, grabbed the light-colored dog and returned it to its owner. The trip reportedly included their 1-year-old daughter Esmeralda and a four-night stay at Frank Sinatra’s former Palm Springs estate, which rents for about $2,600 per night. The story was reported by Entertainment Tonight and picked up by other outlets, which also noted previous instances of Gosling helping people in public. The report briefly mentions Hilary Duff adopting a French bulldog named Peaches.

Jamaica’s government has announced a major legislative agenda for 2016–17 that includes a constitutional amendment to remove Queen Elizabeth II as head of state and replace the Governor‑General with a non‑executive President, effectively moving Jamaica toward republican status. The plan was outlined in the Throne Speech delivered by Governor‑General Sir Patrick Allen at the parliamentary opening.

Key legislative priorities:
- Constitution (Amendment) Bill to replace the Queen with a non‑executive President and another amendment addressing judicial review of the Director of Public Prosecutions.
- Fixed election dates (local and general) and term limits for the Prime Minister.
- Full legalization of marijuana for specified purposes via amendments to the Dangerous Drugs Act.
- Creation of a single anti‑corruption body (Integrity Commission Bill) and an Impeachment Bill to enable action against corrupt officials and parliamentarians.
- Legal and justice reforms including Arbitration Bill, Criminal Justice (Plea Negotiations and Agreements) amendments (reduced sentences for guilty pleas), INDECOM amendments, Mutual Assistance (Criminal Matters) amendments (CCTV/video evidence), Trafficking in Persons changes, and measures on judicial accountability.
- Institutional reforms: establishment of a National Human Rights Institute and enhancement of the Office of the Public Defender; tax, pension and financial system reforms; debt management and growth/job creation measures including Special Economic Zones and SME support.

These proposals must be passed by Parliament to become law. The agenda follows the February election win of the Jamaica Labour Party under Prime Minister Andrew Holness and echoes earlier calls to pursue republican status. The move would mirror similar conversations in other Caribbean nations where the Queen is head of state.

A Texas middle-school teacher, Julie Marburger, posted a lengthy Facebook rant about perceived disrespect from students and parents that went viral after she shared photos showing classroom mess and damaged books. Marburger, 45, said a confrontational phone call with a student’s mother—conducted in front of the class—left her emotionally drained and prompted her to announce she plans to leave teaching at year’s end, though she’s reconsidering after the post drew worldwide responses and broad support from colleagues, parents and administrators. In her post she criticized parents for not engaging until report cards and for coddling children, warning that it harms kids’ futures. The story comes amid broader teacher unrest nationally over pay and support, including recent strikes. Parenting editor Ericka Souter responded by urging parents to treat teachers as partners and offered practical tips: stay involved, be proactive in responding to teacher concerns, and enforce consequences for misbehavior.

Dallas Mavericks guard J.J. Barea, the NBA’s only active native Puerto Rican, has been actively raising money and organizing relief for his homeland after Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico as a Category 4 storm. He and his wife, Viviana Ortiz, set up an online fundraiser that has raised over $140,000. After not being able to reach his parents until Sunday, Barea learned they were safe though the island faces widespread devastation and prolonged outages. Mavericks owner Mark Cuban loaned the team plane so Barea could fly food, water and supplies to Puerto Rico; Barea left Monday afternoon, planning to return Tuesday night and miss the first day of training camp. Coach Rick Carlisle said Barea will transport supplies and bring his mother and grandmother back to Dallas, while his father will remain in Puerto Rico to help with recovery efforts. Barea hopes either to bring his parents to Dallas or visit again soon to assist family and friends.

A video filmed in Baltimore during unrest after Freddie Gray’s death showed a mother, later identified as Toya Graham, confronting and repeatedly striking a hooded teenage boy — her 16-year-old son — after seeing footage of him allegedly throwing rocks at police. The clip, captured by WMAR and widely shared on social media, prompted praise for the woman (some calling her “mom of the year”) and was even referenced by Baltimore Police Commissioner Anthony Batts as an example of parents taking responsibility amid the violence. Graham told CBS News she intervened because she didn’t want her son to become another Freddie Gray and opposed vandalism of police. The incident occurred amid larger protests, some violent; city leaders condemned the destruction, volunteers began cleanup efforts, and social media buzzed with reactions and related hashtags such as #PrayForBaltimore.

Molly Wei, a 19-year-old former Rutgers freshman, has admitted her role in viewing a secretly streamed webcam recording of roommate Tyler Clementi having a sexual encounter with another man and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors. In Middlesex County Superior Court she waived indictment and entered a pretrial intervention (PTI) program: three years of supervision, 300 hours of community service, counseling on cyberbullying and alternate lifestyles, and a requirement to testify against co-defendant Dharun Ravi. If she completes the program without further legal trouble, the two invasion-of-privacy charges against her will be dropped.

Wei and Ravi were accused in the September 2010 incident in which Ravi allegedly hid a camera in his dorm room, streamed a recording of Clementi and another male (identified as M.B.) from a laptop in Wei’s room, and alerted others about a planned second encounter. Clementi, 18, died by suicide days later after jumping from the George Washington Bridge; his death sparked national attention on bullying, privacy violations online and LGBT bias. Ravi faces a 15-count grand jury indictment including invasion of privacy, bias intimidation and related charges and faces up to 10 years in prison; he is free on $25,000 bail and is due to be arraigned May 23. Clementi’s parents said they were consulted about Wei’s deal and found her actions substantially different from Ravi’s, while also stating that there must be accountability for violations of basic human behavior.

The SS United States is a 990-foot-long historic American ocean liner—longer than the Titanic and nearly as tall as the Chrysler Building if stood upright—designed for speed and built with unprecedented amounts of aluminum to reduce weight. Launched in 1952 after a secret Cold War-era program, she still holds the transatlantic speed record. Her beam (101 feet) was chosen to fit Panama Canal locks with minimal clearance.

Mooring in Philadelphia and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the ship has faced years of deterioration and mounting upkeep costs. The SS United States Conservancy, which has sought to convert the vessel into a museum and mixed-use destination, recently warned it could be forced to sell the ship for scrap unless supporters stepped in. In response, the Conservancy raised more than $100,000 from global donors—enough to delay scrapping—and will meet to decide the ship’s future. The organization needs over $60,000 per month to sustain rehabilitation efforts.

The document also compiles numerous testimonials and appeals from public figures, historians, former crew and supporters—ranging from Presidents and journalists to ship designers and ordinary citizens—arguing the liner is an irreplaceable piece of American engineering, cultural history and national pride. Contributors emphasize the SS United States’ technical achievements, historic significance, symbolic value, and potential to create jobs and preserve maritime heritage, urging donations and widespread support to save and restore the vessel.

Fighting continued across Libya as rebels pressed gains in Tripoli and moved toward Muammar Gaddafi’s hometown Sirte. International and regional bodies — including the UN, Arab League, OIC, African Union and EU — warned the crisis had entered a decisive phase and urged a rapid, well-coordinated transition built on inclusiveness, reconciliation and national unity. The UN stressed urgent needs: ending fighting, restoring order, policing help (if requested), and addressing severe shortages of fuel, food, medical supplies and threatened water supplies for millions. The U.N. welcomed the Security Council’s decision to unfreeze $1.5 billion in Libyan assets but participants and rebel leaders said more funds must be released quickly to stabilize the country and run basic services.

On the ground, NATO and rebel forces continued strikes and assaults on regime positions. British jets struck a large bunker in Sirte and aircraft destroyed loyalist air-defense and command sites near Tripoli and Al Watiyah. Rebels explored tunnels beneath Gaddafi’s Bab al-Aziziya compound and found a decayed military infrastructure, rusting aircraft and a professional TV studio. Heavy fighting persisted in districts such as Abu Salim and around Tripoli’s airport, where loyalists shelled positions and rebels cautiously responded amid concern for civilians.

Reports of mass killings and abuses emerged from multiple locations. Dozens of decomposing bodies were found in an abandoned Tripoli hospital and other bodies — some bound and with apparent execution-style wounds — were discovered near Bab al-Aziziya. Amnesty International documented abuses by both pro-Gaddafi forces and rebel units, including summary killings of detainees and violence against sub-Saharan migrants suspected of being mercenaries. The International Criminal Court has already issued an arrest warrant for Gaddafi for crimes against humanity. The UN and human-rights officials urged all sides to prevent revenge attacks and promised investigations.

Politically, the opposition’s National Transitional Council (NTC), recognized by dozens of countries, began moving its base from Benghazi to Tripoli to assert governance despite ongoing insecurity. The African Union’s Peace and Security Council stopped short of full recognition but called for an inclusive transitional government, constitutional and legal frameworks, election support and national reconciliation. International actors emphasized early assistance for elections, transitional justice, policing, rule-of-law rebuilding and socioeconomic recovery to secure a stable transition.

Vermont Gov. Peter Shumlin says he believes he has won re-election, but Republican Scott Milne has not conceded and is awaiting official totals. An AP tally showed Shumlin ahead by about 2,200 votes (roughly 46.7% to Milne’s just over 45%) with only a tiny town’s results outstanding. Because no candidate reached the constitutional threshold of more than 50% of the vote, the state Legislature will decide the governor’s race in January; Democrats control both houses and historically the Legislature almost always elects the statewide vote leader. Shumlin’s failure to clear 50% could weaken momentum for his top priority, a universal health-care overhaul.

Shinichi Mochizuki of Kyoto University claims to have proved the ABC conjecture, a deep number‑theory statement about when integers a, b, c with a + b = c can have unusually small prime factors. In 2012 he posted a roughly 500‑page proof built on a massive new framework he invented, Inter‑universal Teichmüller Theory (IUTeich). Although Mochizuki is a respected mathematician and a few collaborators who have studied his work with his help report finding no flaws so far, the wider community has not reached a consensus on the proof’s validity.

The core difficulty is that IUTeich is a dense, novel theory that many experts find extremely hard to penetrate; verifying the ABC proof requires first mastering that entire apparatus. Mochizuki has criticized other mathematicians for not studying his work from the ground up and says most are “simply not qualified” to judge it without doing so. Others respond that Mochizuki needs to make the ideas more accessible — for example by simplifying exposition or lecturing more widely — because one‑on‑one tutoring is not scalable and journals will want independent reviewers.

The situation has left the claimed proof in limbo: taken seriously, but neither widely understood nor definitively accepted or refuted. Observers compare Mochizuki’s reticence to past solitary proofs in mathematics; for now the community continues to study IUTeich and seeks a clear resolution.

A Florida police officer replaced an elderly Alzheimer's patient’s stolen engagement ring after learning it had been pulled from her finger while she was sedated in a hospital. Arthur Wagner told officers his wife Betty had worn the ring—purchased for $400 in 1946—on her finger for 67 years; bruising suggested someone forcibly removed both rings and left the wedding band. Officer Laurie Graber, moved by the couple’s story, bought a replacement heart-shaped ring at J.C. Penney with her own money, left it with hospital nurses and a note: “It's not much, it's not the same. But 67 years of a promise kept should be recognized.” Plantation Police are investigating the theft using hospital surveillance; the original ring is believed to be worth about $4,500 today. Graber said she acted because it was the right thing to do, and the new ring has comforted the couple.

Authorities confirmed Wednesday that a partially decomposed body found Tuesday in a remote agricultural area of Moreno Valley is 17-year-old Norma Lopez, a Valley View High School student who disappeared July 15 after leaving a summer biology class. Dental records and an autopsy identified the remains; officials did not release a cause of death.

Lopez’s sister reported her missing after she failed to meet family and friends; some of Lopez’s belongings and signs of a struggle were found in a vacant field about 1½ blocks from the school, a commonly used shortcut. A resident found the body more than two miles away while working in a distant field. Because the remains were exposed to heat, decomposition obscured immediate identification.

Riverside County investigators and the FBI have no suspects yet. They are following leads—including reports of a newer-model green SUV seen speeding from the area at the time of her disappearance—and have interviewed friends, associates and local offenders. The department has offered a $35,000 reward and asked the public to call or email tips. Authorities have withheld many investigative details to avoid compromising the case.

The discovery prompted sorrow and a vigil in Moreno Valley; classmates and school officials described Lopez as a quiet, good student who loved dancing. Police urged parents to be vigilant while the investigation continues.

A federal judge in Manhattan ordered the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) to run a controversial bus ad paid for by the American Freedom Defense Initiative (AFDI) after the agency had refused it. The ad, produced by Pamela Geller’s AFDI, quotes a purported Hamas media source saying “Killing Jews is worship that draws us close to Allah” alongside the line “That’s his Jihad. What’s yours?” — a parody of the Council on American-Islamic Relations’ “My Jihad” campaign. The MTA declined to run the ad last year, citing concerns it could be read as a call to violence or otherwise endanger public safety.

U.S. District Judge John G. Koeltl granted a preliminary injunction, finding the ad constitutes protected speech under the First Amendment and that the MTA had not presented objective evidence the advertisement would likely incite imminent violence. He noted similar ads ran previously in Chicago and San Francisco without incident and stayed his order for 30 days to allow for potential appeals. Koeltl suggested the MTA could mitigate confusion by posting an adjacent counter-ad clarifying the AFDI ad is a parody.

Reactions split sharply: Geller hailed the ruling as a victory for free speech, saying she would expand the campaign; AFDI’s attorney criticized public officials he said caved to “Sharia” fears. City leaders, including representatives of Mayor Bill de Blasio, condemned the ads as inflammatory and divisive. The MTA said it was disappointed and would consider its options. The case echoes prior disputes in which AFDI successfully sued the authority over rejected ads.
