A police report obtained by TMZ reveals inconsistencies in a jeweler's accounts of how Lindsay Lohan allegedly stole a $2,500 necklace, inconsistencies that could aid her defense. Initially the jeweler told police Lohan had visited the store three times previously and had been looking at the necklace; the next day she said it was actually a ring Lohan had been eyeing and that Lohan had not previously looked at the necklace. The owner also gave two different descriptions of how the necklace disappeared: on January 23 she told police surveillance showed Lohan reach to her neck, remove the necklace and put it in her black Chanel bag; the following day she said Lohan had simply walked out wearing the necklace, explaining the change by saying she viewed the footage on a different monitor the second time. The owner's credibility matters because Lohan asserts the necklace had been loaned to her.

Separately, Lohan—while maintaining her innocence—is reportedly eager to plea bargain to avoid jail time and is willing to plead guilty if assured she won’t serve time. Prosecutors reportedly want jail, creating a stalemate. The report notes that with only one charge, a defendant can sometimes secure an agreement directly with the judge (bypassing the DA) to plead without incarceration; judges commonly reduce such offenses to misdemeanors if the defendant stays out of trouble for a year.

(Extra unrelated note in the document: Since 1996 Alexa Internet has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, which adds those data to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.)

Algerian forces ended a four-day hostage crisis at the In Amenas gas facility in eastern Algeria after Islamist militants seized the plant, killing and taking dozens of foreign and Algerian workers. Algerian authorities said at least 23 hostages and 32 militants died; state media reported seven hostages and 11 militants were killed in a final assault, though casualty figures and details remain unclear and unverified. About 685 Algerian workers and 107 foreigners were freed, but several nationals from many countries remain unaccounted for — including Americans, Britons, Norwegians, Japanese and others — and some countries reported confirmed dead among their citizens.

The attackers, linked to Moktar Belmokhtar’s al Qaeda–associated network, had reportedly mined the facility, threatened to blow it up and strapped explosives to some hostages. Algerian forces launched multiple assaults amid concerns the militants planned to detonate the site; authorities continued clearing explosives afterward. The Algerian government faced international criticism for the timing and conduct of its operations, as foreign governments sought fuller details and pressed for accountability.

World leaders — including U.S. President Barack Obama and U.K. Prime Minister David Cameron — condemned the attack, vowed to work with Algeria and allies to counter regional extremist groups, and warned the episode underscored growing militant threats in North Africa and the Sahel. Investigations and searches at the complex were ongoing, and the final death toll and exact circumstances remained uncertain.

The author, a longtime Times-Picayune journalist, expresses sadness and concern over Advance Publications’ decision to cut staff, dismiss top editors, and reduce the paper’s print editions to three days a week (Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays) while claiming to boost 24/7 digital coverage via NOLA.com. He mourns the loss for former colleagues and for New Orleans, which needs strong local reporting given its complex civic challenges and vulnerability to disasters.

Advance frames the move as a necessary digital-first reorganization—creating NOLA Media Group for content and Advance Central Services for print and distribution—and says it will combine the paper’s journalism with NOLA.com under editor Jim Amoss. But the author and analysts note the announcement is heavy on corporate structure and light on practical details; previous attempts to marry print and digital have had limited success.

The change follows a wider industry pattern of cutting print frequency as publishers confront steep declines in print readership, advertising and revenue. Print still supplies most industry dollars, but print revenue has plunged since 2007, while print production remains costly. Advance has been an aggressive adopter of reduced print schedules across its papers and reports some readers and advertisers migrating online. Supporters call experimentation necessary to sustain journalism; skeptics warn the shift will be jarring for print-loyal readers and could risk losing audience and ad revenue.

Practically, the Times-Picayune will still publish on the three most lucrative ad days (Sun., Wed., Fri.), but the paper will cut staff—estimates suggest roughly half the newsroom may go—leaving about 100 journalists for a metro region of 1.2 million. That raises concerns about diminished local coverage. The Times-Picayune, founded in 1837 and lauded for its Hurricane Katrina reporting (Pulitzer Prize 2006), has seen daily circulation fall sharply since Katrina, underscoring the financial pressures behind the decision.

Researchers led by Ellen Martinsen at the Smithsonian’s Conservation Biology Institute have discovered that white‑tailed deer along the U.S. East Coast commonly harbor a previously unrecognized malaria parasite, Plasmodium odocoilei. The parasite was first detected serendipitously while screening mosquitoes for bird malaria at the National Zoo; PCR and microscopic follow‑up found infections in roughly 18–25% of deer at eastern sites (no infections were found in the western samples). Screening of other hoofed species (cattle, goats, elk, etc.) turned up no infections.

This is the first confirmed native mammalian malaria in the Americas. Genetic analyses revealed two deeply divergent lineages of the parasite—probably distinct species—whose split dates to roughly 2.3–6 million years ago. That timing suggests malaria traveled with deer ancestors when they crossed from Eurasia into North America, meaning these parasites have been present in the New World for millions of years.

The infections are typically cryptic and low‑level, so obvious disease in deer has not been widely observed; whether these infections impose subtle fitness costs remains unknown and is a priority for further study. The finding highlights how much remains undiscovered about parasite diversity and natural history, and underscores connections between wildlife disease research and broader conservation and public‑health concerns. Results were published in Science Advances.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) concluded that fatigue and excessive speed were the primary causes of the June 7, 2014 crash on the New Jersey Turnpike that killed comedian James “Jimmy Mack” McNair and severely injured Tracy Morgan and three others. Truck driver Kevin Roper, a Wal‑Mart employee, had been awake for more than 28 hours — after driving roughly 800 miles overnight to his base and beginning a 14‑hour shift — and was traveling about 65 mph in a 45 mph construction work zone. Investigators determined that at the posted 45 mph speed the truck could have stopped before impact.

The customized 10‑seat limo/van lacked functioning exits for its rear passengers: a plywood panel separating the cab and passenger compartment and added customizations prevented escape, and none of the rear passengers or the limo driver were wearing seat belts or had received a safety briefing on belt use. After the truck struck the limo from behind, the limo hit three vehicles, rolled onto its side, and became jammed; it took about 37–40 minutes to extricate some victims. The crash initiated a multi‑vehicle chain reaction that ultimately affected 21 people in six vehicles.

The NTSB also criticized Wal‑Mart for not having a comprehensive fatigue‑management program (though it provided some fatigue information and has since begun improving driver education) and noted Roper’s prior safety incidents recorded by the truck’s onboard system. Roper was later charged with vehicular homicide and assault by auto; he pleaded not guilty and his attorney said they would dispute the NTSB findings. Morgan suffered multiple fractures and a traumatic brain injury, spent time in a coma, has struggled to recover, and later settled a civil suit with Wal‑Mart confidentially. The NTSB urged measures to address operator fatigue, vehicle modifications that impede escape, seat‑belt use, and emergency responder training.

A University College London study suggests alcohol consumption in England may be much higher than self-report surveys indicate. Researchers compared alcohol sales data from HM Revenue & Customs with two 2008 national self-report surveys (the General Lifestyle Survey and the Health Survey for England) and found almost half of alcohol sold was not accounted for by reported consumption. When the “missing” alcohol was distributed across drinkers (assuming under-reporting was equal), the study estimated substantially more people exceed recommended limits: 19% more men and 26% more women regularly exceed daily guidance, and weekly excess drinking rises by 15% for men and 11% for women.

Authors and public-health experts attribute the gap to under-reporting driven by factors such as not admitting or tracking intake, misjudging drink sizes, mixing drinks, drinking across venues, and not counting irregular heavy-drinking occasions (holidays, celebrations). The researchers plan to study who under-reports and why. They argue guidelines and harm assessments should reflect actual consumption rather than self-reports. The Department of Health said the finding will inform its review of alcohol guidance and pointed to existing measures (awareness campaigns, minimum unit price proposals, licensing changes, GP screening and treatment). Labour’s Diane Abbott called the results a wake-up call to strengthen alcohol-harm policy.

The FDA has recommended that all U.S. blood donations be screened for Zika virus to protect the blood supply, expanding prior guidance that applied only to areas with active transmission. Agency officials said new scientific and epidemiological information and the risk that most Zika infections are asymptomatic justify nationwide testing. The rollout calls for blood establishments in 11 states (including Alabama, Arizona, California, Georgia, Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, New Mexico, New York, South Carolina and Texas) to begin testing within four weeks and for all states to be testing within 12 weeks.

The move follows the first locally acquired Zika cases in the continental U.S. (dozens in South Florida) and thousands of cases in U.S. territories. Zika is primarily mosquito-borne (Aedes aegypti) but can also spread sexually; infection during pregnancy is linked to serious birth defects such as microcephaly. To date there have been no confirmed U.S. transfusion-transmitted Zika cases, though at least one donated unit in Florida was removed after testing. Florida officials and the governor urged more federal support and emergency funding as local transmission spreads.

Lindsey Buckingham has settled his civil lawsuit against his former Fleetwood Mac bandmates after being removed from the group's 2018–19 North American tour. Buckingham, who was replaced on the tour by Mike Campbell and Neil Finn, did not disclose settlement terms but said, “We’ve all signed off on something” and that he’s “happy enough with it.” He also said he doesn’t expect to rejoin the band.

Buckingham filed suit in October, alleging he was “cut off entirely” in January without explanation and claiming the ouster cost him roughly $27 million. The dispute reportedly arose over scheduling conflicts between Fleetwood Mac’s planned tour and Buckingham’s desire to play solo dates; band members, including Stevie Nicks, have characterized the split as a scheduling disagreement. Buckingham says he agreed to postpone his solo shows to join the tour and that he was told by manager Irving Azoff that Nicks didn’t want to perform with him after the MusiCares event.

In his first TV interview since the firing, Buckingham described the episode as painful, said he has had little contact with band members (aside from a recent email from Christine McVie), and expressed limited hope for reconciliation. He’s spent the past year curating a retrospective of his solo work and plans to tour behind it instead of anticipating a Fleetwood Mac reunion.

Mother Jones flagged that a trademark application to protect the campaign wordmark "Jeb!" has been abandoned. The filing was made in January by BHAG LLC (later revealed to be owned by Jeb Bush) to reserve rights to sell merchandise—mousepads, money clips, golf towels, key chains, stuffed toys, etc.—bearing the exuberant "Jeb!" logo. The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office requested written consent from Bush to use his name; no response was provided and the application was officially abandoned on November 9 (with a technical window to revive it by January 9). 

The article treats the lapse as emblematic of Bush’s faltering campaign: despite early financial heft via a pro-Bush super PAC, donor and retail demand for Jeb!-branded goods has been weak and his poll numbers have slipped. An update notes the campaign says the mark was tied to Bush’s time as governor and wasn’t filed specifically for the campaign, and that they may still be able to stop unauthorized uses. The piece contrasts Bush’s misstep with Donald Trump’s continued trademarking of his own name.

The Tribeca Film Festival drew heavy criticism for scheduling Vaxxed: From Cover-up to Catastrophe, a documentary by Andrew Wakefield that promotes the discredited claim that vaccines cause autism. Wakefield — whose research linking MMR vaccine to autism was widely discredited, found to involve misconduct, and led to his medical license being revoked — directed the film and appears in its trailer making sensational allegations about CDC fraud. Tribeca co-founder Robert De Niro defended screening the film, saying he and his wife have a child with autism and want the issue openly discussed; he added he does not personally endorse the film nor oppose vaccination. His statement prompted substantial backlash online and from filmmakers and public-health advocates who called the festival’s decision irresponsible, arguing that presenting Wakefield’s work under Tribeca’s prestige risks legitimizing dangerous misinformation. Filmmaker Penny Lane wrote an open letter urging Tribeca to cancel the screening, saying Vaxxed is deceptive advocacy rather than legitimate documentary journalism and could contribute to decreased vaccination and harm. The film was scheduled to screen on April 24, with a post-screening discussion planned.

The pieces defend Amy Schumer’s casting as the lead in a live-action Barbie movie and frame her as a positive, necessary counter to pervasive body-shaming. Critics have attacked Schumer’s body as unsuitable for Barbie, prompting her to push back and highlight the cultural problem of policing women’s bodies. The authors argue this criticism is symptomatic of broader “body fascism” in media and society—learned from a young age and reinforced by magazines, celebrities and peers—and that public, unapologetic resistance matters because girls absorb these messages.

Schumer is presented as well-suited to reshape Barbie: she’s successful, funny, sharp, self-made, and involved in rewriting the screenplay with her sister, so she’s likely to subvert the old saccharine, limiting Barbie archetype. Mattel has already begun diversifying Barbie body types, and casting Schumer—who celebrates her curves and insists on self-acceptance—could give children a healthier model of confidence. The pieces conclude that fighting body-shaming is exhausting but essential work, and Schumer’s casting could help change cultural expectations about women’s bodies and what girls see as possible.

The Club for Growth—an influential, fiscally conservative advocacy group—announced a $1 million TV ad buy in Iowa to attack GOP front-runner Donald Trump, marking the first major paid effort to dent his lead. Launching the day after the second GOP debate, the ads highlight Trump’s past statements and positions on health care, taxes, eminent domain and bailout support to portray him as “very liberal,” “just another politician,” and aligned with Democrats such as Hillary Clinton. Club for Growth leaders say Trump will say anything to get elected and pledge the campaign is only the beginning of their efforts.

The move follows weeks of public feuding between Trump and the Club—sparked in part by a request from the group’s president for a $1 million donation that Trump refused—and reflects a deeper clash over GOP economic orthodoxy. The Club, which has long backed candidates favoring lower taxes, spending cuts and entitlement reform, views Trump’s pledges to protect Social Security and Medicare and to tax the wealthy as threats to its agenda. Major donors to the Club’s super PAC include conservative heavyweights who’ve funded rivals such as Scott Walker, Ted Cruz and Carly Fiorina.

Observers note the ads test whether fiscal-conservative attacks will sway Trump’s anti-establishment base—supporters who have largely ignored similar critiques so far—and whether this first sizeable conservative-funded campaign will meaningfully slow his momentum in Iowa.

Scientists have described a new, highly adapted cave-dwelling centipede, Geophilus hadesi, found in deep caves of the Velebit Mountains, Croatia. Published in ZooKeys, the species was recorded as deep as 1,100 m (3,609 ft), making it the deepest-known habitat for any centipede. Named after Hades to mirror a previously discovered cave-exclusive geophilomorph, Geophilus persephones, G. hadesi is one of only two geophilomorph species known to spend their entire lives underground.

G. hadesi shows classic troglomorphic adaptations: extremely elongated antennae, fur‑like setae on its appendages for sensing in total darkness, a long flattened body for moving through crevices, and unusually long, thin claws for gripping rock. It has 33 pairs of legs and venomous jaws used to capture small invertebrate prey (larvae, springtails, worms, woodlice, spiders), but poses no known threat to humans. The species endures cold cave temperatures (around 3 °C) and likely evolved its subterranean lifestyle over long timescales in response to external environmental changes.

The discovery adds to the rich subterranean biodiversity of the Dinaric Karst region and the Velebit cave systems—an area already known for many pale, cave-adapted species—and highlights how much remains unknown about cave ecosystems.

Speaker John Boehner, weakened by a surprisingly close reelection in which 12 House Republicans defected, is moving to rebuild unity in the GOP conference and demonstrate he can lead a governing House majority. In a closed-door meeting he declined to punish dissenters, saying he holds no grudges and will keep an open door. Lawmakers expect the next two to three months — centered on fights over raising the $16.4 trillion debt limit, replacing looming automatic sequestration cuts, and averting a government shutdown — to be decisive for his leadership.

Boehner insists any debt-ceiling increase must be paired with spending cuts, reiterating a position he has held since 2011 and citing a GOP poll he said shows public support for that approach. Republicans plan to use the conference retreat in mid-January to coordinate strategy; leadership aims to craft debt- and spending-related legislation that can win 218 House votes, a tougher task given a smaller, more restive GOP majority. Members acknowledge the conference has been easier to unite around opposition than positive policy proposals, and that past failures to marshal GOP support doomed initiatives like parts of the farm and postal bills.

Some Republicans view the defections as a warning against bringing bills to the floor without majority GOP backing; others say the revolt could paradoxically strengthen Boehner by signaling to the White House that House conservatives are serious about spending reductions. President Obama, having hailed the bipartisan "fiscal cliff" deal that raised taxes on the wealthy and averted middle-class tax hikes, has said he will not negotiate over the debt ceiling — setting up another high-stakes showdown. Both sides publicly emphasize willingness to cut spending, but disagree on whether the debt limit is negotiable. Republicans signal they will act early to force a choice rather than accept last-minute compromises.

Anchorman 2: The Legend Continues reunites Will Ferrell’s egotistical newsman Ron Burgundy with his old San Diego crew — Steve Carell’s dimwitted weatherman Brick Tamland, Paul Rudd’s vain reporter Brian Fantana and David Koechner’s boorish sports anchor Champ Kind — and sends them to New York in 1980 to help launch GNN, a 24-hour cable news network. The sequel lampoons the birth and excesses of round‑the‑clock television news: relentless, jingoistic pandering to viewers, breathless car‑chase coverage, cluttered graphics, and ratings-driven spectacle. Classic bits from the original return (jazz flute, the big news‑team rumble) alongside new gags — notably puppy montages, patriotic sign‑offs, and Brick’s absurd antics — and a parade of celebrity cameos.

Critics generally find the film intermittently hilarious but uneven. Its strengths are loose, improvisational performances (especially Carell and Kristen Wiig’s maddeningly silly Brick/Chani subplot), dense sight gags, and sharp moments of satire about modern media. Its weaknesses include a bloat of recycled bits, a meandering subplot about Ron’s marriage and career nadir, and a few contrived detours that overstay their welcome. Overall, Anchorman 2 recaptures much of the predecessor’s anarchic spirit and offers plenty of laughs, even if it lacks the surprise and tighter construction of the original. Rated PG‑13, runtime ~119 minutes.

Overview:
The document is a pair of opinion pieces arguing that the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) has an authentic, serious scandal—centered on falsified wait-time records, concealed waiting lists, and veterans dying while awaiting care—and that the Obama administration’s response has been inadequate. The writers call for firmer action, management changes, and criminal investigations.

Key allegations and findings:
- VA facilities (notably Phoenix, and reportedly Albuquerque and possibly others) allegedly falsified appointment records or maintained secret waiting lists to hide long delays in care.
- Reports tie these manipulations to as many as 40 veteran deaths.
- There are claims of document destruction and systemic “gaming” of performance metrics rather than isolated incidents.

Criticism of VA leadership and White House response:
- Secretary of Veterans Affairs Eric K. Shinseki is portrayed as failing to convey understanding, urgency, or leadership; commentators argue he should be replaced.
- The administration’s response, including President Obama’s public reaction, is judged muted and insufficient given the gravity of the allegations. White House statements that the president is “madder than hell” are viewed as inadequate without concrete action.
- Republicans and some Democrats call for outside criminal probes (e.g., FBI involvement) beyond the VA Office of Inspector General review.

Context and caveats:
- The writers acknowledge the VA also provides high-volume, often high-quality care—serving over 200,000 veterans daily and scoring well on some satisfaction surveys—so the critique focuses on wait times and possible deception rather than a wholesale indictment of all VA care.
- One piece notes earlier warnings to the White House (a May 2013 letter from House Veterans Affairs Chairman Jeff Miller) that allegedly were not acted upon, reinforcing claims of administrative neglect.

Calls to action:
- Replace or remove current VA leadership, clean house, and bring in outside investigators to determine whether crimes were committed and to hold accountable those responsible.
- Treat the matter with urgency and seriousness given promises owed to veterans and the potential loss of life.

Tone and political framing:
- The pieces contrast this scandal with other contested issues (IRS, Benghazi, Fast and Furious), arguing those were overblown while the VA matter is a genuine, potentially criminal failure deserving bipartisan outrage and immediate corrective measures.

Eleven-year-old Frank Giaccio of Falls Church, Virginia, mowed the White House Rose Garden lawn on Sept. 15 after writing a letter to President Trump offering free landscaping services (he normally charges neighbors $8). Frank, who runs a small mowing business called FX Mowing, received a safety briefing and protective gear from U.S. Park Service grounds staff and spent the morning watering beds and trimming the 50-by-100-foot lawn with a power mower while supervised by a Park Service employee and his father, Greg.

Partway through, President Trump made a surprise appearance, watched Frank work, exchanged jokes and high-fives, praised him as “the future of the country,” and predicted he might become president or a Navy SEAL. After finishing, Frank and his father were invited into the Oval Office for photos; they also met Vice President Pence and later visited the press briefing room. White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders had earlier highlighted Frank’s letter and entrepreneurial spirit. Frank called the day “probably the biggest day” of his life and said he won’t raise his neighborhood rate despite the new accolade.

Researchers at the University of Florida have confirmed the first documented human infection with Keystone virus, a mosquito-borne virus first isolated in Keystone, Florida, in 1964. The case involved a 16-year-old boy from north-central Florida who sought care in August 2016 with fever and a severe rash amid the Zika outbreak; standard testing for Zika and other pathogens was negative. After about 18 months of laboratory work, investigators isolated Keystone virus from the patient and published the finding in Clinical Infectious Diseases.

Keystone virus is carried by Aedes atlanticus mosquitoes, relatives of Aedes aegypti, and has been detected in animal populations along U.S. coastal regions from Texas to the Chesapeake Bay. Human infection appears to cause mild illness—fever and rash—and the reported teen did not develop encephalitis, though laboratory data show Keystone can infect brain cells and it belongs to a virus group known to cause encephalitis in some species. Past serology from the Tampa Bay region found antibodies in roughly 19–21% of people tested, suggesting human exposure may be fairly common but largely undetected because routine clinical tests did not exist until now. The university says biotech firms are interested in developing diagnostic tests, and researchers emphasize the need for more study of vector-borne viruses and continued mosquito-bite prevention.

This document is a New York Times letter and column exchange focused on Donald Trump’s revival of the “birther” controversy about President Barack Obama, and a columnist’s critical response to Trump’s claims and persona.

Key points:
- Trump wrote a letter defending his attacks on columnist Gail Collins, accusing her of bias and poor facts and defending his questioning of Obama’s birthplace. He repeats common birther claims: an alleged tape of Obama’s Kenyan step-grandmother asserting he was born in Kenya; skepticism about Obama’s “certificate of live birth” versus a full birth certificate; assertions that there are no Hawaiian records (doctors, nurses, bills) of Obama’s birth; and a broader claim that the press protects Obama and would expose a fraud if one existed.
- Collins’s column rebuts these claims, noting:
  - The supposed tape of Sarah Obama was misinterpreted; fuller transcripts show she identified Hawaii as the birthplace.
  - A certificate of live birth is a routinely issued document in Hawaii, acceptable for passports; FactCheck.org examined the Obama document and found it legitimate, including a stamp and serial number.
  - Anecdotes about people who knew Obama as a child undermine Trump’s “came out of nowhere” claim; video interviews with Hawaiians remember him from school.
- Collins mocks Trump’s manner and motives: she portrays him as a showman and reality-TV promoter (Celebrity Apprentice), prone to bluster, self-aggrandizement and exaggeration—traits she likens to his TV program. She criticizes his business record and publicity tactics, suggests his birther activism may be attention-seeking or campaign positioning, and notes his sensitivity to criticism.
- The piece highlights Trump’s contradictory behavior (publicly questioning Obama’s legitimacy while later producing his own birth certificate) and frames his birther rhetoric as factually weak, politically motivated, and characteristic of his promotional style.

Overall, the document presents Trump’s renewed birther allegations and personal attacks on Collins, and offers a detailed rebuttal showing the birther claims to be based on misinterpretation, misinformation, and performative politics rather than substantive evidence.

In June 1962, Frank Morris and brothers John and Clarence Anglin escaped Alcatraz after chiseling a hole in their cell walls, using papier-mâché and human-hair dummy heads to fool guards and a makeshift raft of stolen raincoats to cross San Francisco Bay. Officials long held the men drowned, preserving Alcatraz’s claim that no inmate ever successfully escaped. 

More than 50 years later, the Anglin family has for the first time cooperated with investigators and presented new leads suggesting the brothers survived into at least the mid-1970s and possibly lived much longer. The family’s nephews, David and Ken Widner, are featured in a History Channel special, “Alcatraz: Search for the Truth,” which presents several pieces of supportive evidence: unsigned, postage-free Christmas cards reportedly sent to their mother in the years after the escape; a photo the nephews say proves the brothers were alive in the 1970s; and DNA testing that ruled out a set of bones found in 1963 as belonging to the Anglins (the bones could still belong to Morris, who has no living relatives for comparison). The Widners also cite a 2014 letter from mobster Whitey Bulger asserting he taught John and Clarence how to navigate bay currents and advising fugitives to sever all ties—advice Bulger claims they followed.

Retired U.S. Marshal Art Roderick, who led the Anglin investigation for two decades, calls the family’s material “the best actionable lead” he’s seen, and says it has prompted about 10 new interviews and discussions about searching in Brazil, where the brothers might have gone. If alive today, the brothers would be in their mid-80s and might be beyond extradition, but Roderick says he would still want to interview them. If they are dead and recoverable, the Widners want the brothers returned to the family plot in Ruskin, Florida.

The History Channel special is criticized for being long, heavily produced and Anglin-family–centric, offering much padding and emotional appeal but relatively little broader Alcatraz context or new hard proof. Still, the show has reinvigorated the cold case and encouraged renewed investigation into one of America’s most famous prison escapes.

A retired-detective’s tip helped police identify and locate 56-year-old Dwight Lamon Jones as the suspect in a series of shootings that left six people dead across the Phoenix area over about four days in early June 2018. Officers found Jones at an Extended Stay America in Scottsdale on Monday; he fired at police and was later found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in his room.

Authorities say Jones targeted people connected to a bitter divorce nearly a decade earlier. Victims included forensic psychiatrist Dr. Steven Pitt—who had evaluated Jones and testified about his mental state in the couple’s 2010 divorce—two paralegals, Veleria Sharp and Laura Anderson, who worked at the law firm that represented Jones’s ex-wife, and Marshall Levine, a marriage counselor who appears to have been mistaken for someone else who formerly used his office. Ballistics tied the killings at Pitt’s office, the law firm and Levine’s office to the same gun; Jones’s DNA was found on a spent casing and traffic cameras placed a car matching his near the law firm. Police also connected Jones to two additional deaths in a Fountain Hills home, bringing the total believed to be linked to him to six.

Jones had a prior 2008–2009 arrest for domestic violence and had reportedly been living in extended-stay hotels for years. His ex-wife Connie Jones described him as “very emotionally disturbed” and said her current husband, a retired detective, made the link between the divorce and the crime scenes and alerted police. The killings prompted heightened security for medical and legal communities and community shock in otherwise quiet suburbs. Authorities called the killings senseless; officials described the case as providing closure but lamented the loss of innocent lives.

Jeff Russell Hall, 32, a regional director for the neo‑Nazi National Socialist Movement and a former candidate for the Western Riverside Municipal Water District board, was shot dead inside his Riverside home early Sunday. Officers responding to reports of shots found Hall with a single gunshot wound; Riverside firefighters later pronounced him dead. Two handguns were recovered at the scene. Police said the shooting was being investigated as intentional and that they were not seeking additional suspects.

Hall’s wife and five children were in the house at the time. Authorities identified one of Hall’s sons — described only as a juvenile — as a suspect; the child was booked in connection with the killing and Child Protective Services were notified. Police declined to release further details about the child or the shooting while awaiting autopsy results.

Hall had drawn attention regionally for his leadership role with the National Socialist Movement, which advocates white separatism, and for organizing and participating in anti‑immigrant, neo‑Nazi rallies that provoked violent confrontations with counter‑protesters. Neighbors described months of intimidation by Hall and other movement members; some expressed relief after the killing. Hall ran unsuccessfully for the water board in November, receiving over 25% of the vote despite his extremist ties. The investigation into the motive and circumstances remains ongoing.

This document describes animal procedures, experimental methods, and key findings from a study investigating how fibre-derived acetate affects appetite and hypothalamic metabolism in rodents, together with discussion and media framing of the work.

Study design and animals
- Most animal work was performed at Imperial College London (approved under UK regulations); high-resolution magic-angle spinning (HR-MAS) experiments were done at Instituto de Investigaciones Biomédicas ‘Alberto Sols’ (IIB) under their ethical approvals. Male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks) were routinely used and single‑housed under controlled conditions unless otherwise stated; some intracerebroventricular (i.c.v.) experiments used male Wistar rats.

Diets and inulin intervention
- Mice were randomized to high‑fat diets (HFD) differing only by fibre: HFD with inert cellulose (HF‑C) or HFD with oligofructose‑enriched inulin (“Synergy”, HF‑I). Diets were isocaloric and fed ad libitum for 8 weeks; body weight and food intake were recorded three times weekly. HF‑I mice ate less and gained less weight than HF‑C controls.

Measurement of short‑chain fatty acids (SCFAs)
- Acetate and other SCFAs in colonic contents and serum were quantified by gas chromatography (protocols given for sample preparation, internal standards, and instrumentation). Serum SCFAs were also measured after protein filtration and internal standard addition, with GC conditions and calibration described.

Acetate biodistribution and imaging
- 11C‑acetate PET–CT was used to trace systemic versus rectal (colonic) delivery (i.v. or intrarectal) in anesthetized mice; dynamic PET acquisitions and CT-based attenuation correction and image reconstruction methods are detailed. Percentage injected dose per gram (%ID/g) calculations and analysis methods are described.

Acetate administration experiments and behavioural assays
- Effects of acetate on food intake were tested by: intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of sodium acetate (500 mg/kg) or saline (food measured 1, 2, 4 h post), intracerebroventricular (i.c.v.) injection in rats (2.5 μmol acetate or control in crossover design), and rectal / colonic administration tracked by PET. Liposome‑encapsulated acetate (LITA) nanoparticles were produced (thin‑film hydration) to assess controlled delivery; characterization included particle sizing, 1H NMR quantification of encapsulated acetate, and rhodamine labelling to study biodistribution (4 h post i.p. — liposomes found in liver/heart but not brain). Behavioural observations following acetate vs saline vs LiCl (aversive control) injections classified activity into ten categories over 1 h.

Metabolic and hormonal assays
- An acetate tolerance test (500 mg/kg i.p.) measured blood glucose changes (glucometer). Plasma gut hormones PYY and GLP‑1 were assayed by established in‑house radioimmunoassays. Hypothalamic gene expression (including AgRP and POMC) was quantified by RT‑qPCR/TaqMan assays; total hypothalamic RNA extraction and cDNA synthesis procedures are given.

Hypothalamic signaling and imaging
- Hypothalamic AMPK activity and related proteins (phospho‑AMPK, phospho‑ACC) were assayed by immunoprecipitation and western blotting using specified antibodies and fluorescent secondaries with infrared imaging. Manganese‑enhanced MRI (MEMRI) at 9.4 T was used to assess activity changes in hypothalamic nuclei (ARC, VMH, PVN, PE) and nucleus tractus solitarius; analysis methods and regions of interest are specified.

Hypothalamic metabolism tracing (13C HR‑MAS)
- Mice received [2‑13C]acetate i.p. or [U‑13C]inulin by gavage; brains were fixed within seconds by microwave fixation at defined timepoints (0, 15, 30, 180 min), hypothalamus dissected, and 13C and 1H HR‑MAS NMR performed at 11.7 T. 13C incorporation was normalized to myo‑inositol resonance and processed with appropriate software; 1H spectra were analyzed by LCModel for metabolite concentrations. Statistical approaches for outlier handling and tests are described.

Data analysis and statistics
- Normality tests (Shapiro–Wilk), transformations, and comparisons (two‑tailed unpaired/paired t‑tests, one‑way ANOVA with post hoc corrections) were used. MEMRI and PET intensity profiles were analyzed with generalized estimating equations (GEE) and nonparametric tests where appropriate. Significance thresholds and reporting conventions are provided.

Main experimental findings (as presented and interpreted in media)
- Fermentable fibre (inulin) increased colonic and systemic acetate in mice; 13C‑labelled inulin produced 13C‑acetate that was detected in the hypothalamus, where it entered metabolic pathways (notably the glutamine–glutamate cycle).
- Mice fed HFD with inulin ate less and gained less weight than controls on HFD with cellulose. Direct administration of acetate (i.p., i.c.v., or rectally) reduced short‑term food intake in rodents.
- Imaging and metabolic tracing indicate acetate reaches the brain and is metabolized in appetite‑regulating hypothalamic circuits; downstream biochemical changes and neuronal activation patterns consistent with appetite suppression were reported.
- Liposome encapsulation approaches and controlled‑release strategies are being explored to deliver acetate therapeutically because acetate’s action is short‑lived.

Context, interpretation, and caveats
- Authors propose that acetate produced by microbial fermentation of fibre signals to the hypothalamus to suppress appetite, providing a mechanistic link between dietary fibre and reduced food intake/weight gain in mice.
- Commentators urge caution: some critique the extrapolation to humans and the mechanistic simplicity (changes in neurotransmission are tightly regulated). High experimental fibre levels in mice may have effects (e.g., gastrointestinal discomfort) that could confound reduced intake. Human relevance, required acetate doses, and safe, acceptable delivery methods remain to be established.
- Media coverage highlighted the potential for acetate‑based appetite‑suppression therapies or supplements, while noting challenges in translating mouse doses to feasible human interventions.

Overall, the study combines dietary interventions, tracer studies, imaging (PET, MEMRI), neurochemical and molecular assays, and behavioral testing to argue that acetate—produced by gut microbial fermentation of fermentable fibre—can reach and be metabolized in the hypothalamus and reduce food intake in rodents. The authors and media suggest this mechanism could inform future appetite‑modulating treatments, but several translational and mechanistic uncertainties remain.

South Korean police discovered about 196 lapel pins bearing the image of late North Korean leader Kim Jong Il in a hotel flowerbed near Incheon International Airport. Authorities are reviewing security camera footage and investigating whether the pins arrived via North Korean propaganda balloons; possession of North Korean propaganda items is illegal under South Korea’s National Security Law. The pins are significant because North Koreans are required to wear portraits of the Kim leaders; pins showing both Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il are especially valued.

The find comes amid heightened tensions following North Korea’s fourth nuclear test in January. The rivals have resumed Cold War–style psychological warfare: South Korea has broadcast anti-Pyongyang messages and K-pop across the border, while the North has responded with its own broadcasts, balloon launches carrying leaflets, and repeated missile tests and threats. South Korea’s military also found bags of propaganda leaflets near the Han River recently. North Korea’s U.S. affairs official warned that U.S.-South Korea actions — including sanctions and deployment of the THAAD missile defense system — have pushed the peninsula “to the verge of war” as annual joint war games approach.

President Trump tweeted on August 5, 2018 that California’s wildfires “are being magnified & made so much worse by the bad environmental laws” that, he claimed, prevent “massive amount of readily available water” from being used and instead divert it “into the Pacific Ocean,” and urged more tree clearing. His focus on water policy puzzled and drew quick pushback from experts and state officials.

Cal Fire spokeswoman Lynette Round said she was not aware of firefighters lacking water. UC Merced wildfire/climate specialist LeRoy Westerling called the tweet “boggling,” noting California’s rivers are tightly managed and water is already allocated many times over. He said diverting more water or removing riparian habitat would not offset moisture losses driven by warming climate and drought. Other experts emphasized that the main drivers of recent catastrophic fires are fuel buildup, prolonged drought and climate change, not a shortage of firefighting water caused by environmental regulations.

At the time, California faced at least 18 active wildfires that had killed nine people, destroyed over 1,000 homes and burned roughly 470,000 acres. Major incidents included the Mendocino Complex (one of the largest in state history) and fires threatening Yosemite and communities near Redding. The Trump administration approved a federal disaster declaration for the state.

A small randomized crossover pilot trial and related reporting conclude that raw (unpasteurized) milk does not reduce lactose malabsorption or the symptoms of lactose intolerance compared with pasteurized milk.

Key points:
- Lactose intolerance results from low levels of lactase and causes gas, bloating, cramping and diarrhea 30 minutes–2 hours after consuming dairy. It is common worldwide (estimates ~75% globally; prevalence varies by ancestry).
- Stanford researchers enrolled 16 adults with confirmed lactose malabsorption/intolerance. Each participant consumed three 8-day treatment phases (organic raw whole milk, organic pasteurized whole milk, and soy milk as a lactose-free control), with one-week washouts between phases. Drinks were flavored to mask identity; symptom severity and hydrogen breath tests were used as outcomes.
- Findings: raw milk did not decrease objective lactose malabsorption (hydrogen breath) or subjective symptoms versus pasteurized milk. Soy milk produced different results as expected.
- Authors note limitations (small sample, relatively short exposure) but emphasize there was no signal of benefit. They urge caution about anecdotal claims that raw milk protects against lactose intolerance and call for properly designed trials if other benefits are asserted.
- Context: raw milk advocates claim health advantages (including improved lactose tolerance), but public-health bodies (FDA, AAP) warn of infection risks from pathogens in raw milk; sales remain legal in many U.S. states.
- Additional context from popular reporting: lactase persistence (ability to digest milk into adulthood) is a genetic adaptation concentrated in northern Europeans and some other populations; lactose intolerance has no major health consequences for most people and calcium can be obtained from non-dairy foods.

The document is a multi-source, largely negative set of reviews of the 2010 sci‑fi thriller Repo Men (dir. Miguel Sapochnik), starring Jude Law and Forest Whitaker, based on Eric Garcia’s novel The Repossession Mambo. All reviewers summarize the premise: in a near-future world a corporation called the Union leases artificial organs; when customers fall behind, violent “repo men” surgically remove those organs. Law plays Remy, a top repo man who receives an implanted heart and then falls behind on payments, becoming a target of his former partner Jake (Whitaker). Liev Schreiber plays the coldly efficient boss.

Critic consensus and main points:
- Tone and originality: Reviewers find the film derivative, tonally confused (part action, part satire) and heavy-handed rather than clever. It is compared unfavorably to Repo! The Genetic Opera and other sci‑fi touchstones (Blade Runner, A Clockwork Orange, Children of Men).
- Violence and graphic content: The movie is extremely violent and gory, with multiple graphic organ removals and blood-soaked set pieces; some critics call it revolting and misogynistic.
- Performances: Jude Law is criticized as unconvincing in the action/antihero mold; Forest Whitaker is better but miscast; Liev Schreiber provides a few moments of skillful camp. Supporting actors (Alice Braga, Carice van Houten) are underused or hampered by the material.
- Direction and script: Miguel Sapochnik’s debut feature is described as unsubtle and incoherent; the screenplay telegraphs plot points and leans on studio-explanatory lines. A late twist is judged a copout.
- Production values: Production design and visual effects get some praise for creating a believable near-future look, but aesthetics don’t salvage the story.
- Overall verdict: The film is labeled tedious, mean-spirited and bad enough to warrant scorn—one critic gives one star and others predict Razzie consideration. Some reviewers note the movie’s inadvertent satirical argument for universal health care but say that’s about its only effective statement.

Bottom line: Repo Men is seen as a violent, poorly executed, and derivative sci‑fi thriller that wastes its cast and premise.

IKEA is investigating reports that its stainless-steel "Blanda Blank" serving bowl can concentrate sunlight and start fires. A Swedish man, Richard Walter, said he smelled smoke while eating grapes from the bowl during a heatwave, spotted a focused bright point where sunlight hit the bowl, and later filmed the bowl setting a scrap of paper alight. The video has drawn attention online. IKEA told Aftonbladet it takes the claim seriously and will test the product; a spokesperson said product safety is a priority and that risk is considered very low because multiple factors would have to coincide and the bowl’s shape limits spread. The Blanda Blank bowls sell for roughly $1.99–$11.99 and IKEA’s US product page contains no fire-related warnings.

This prospective cohort study used MRI to compare brain structure in first-time mothers before and after pregnancy, with each woman’s pre-pregnancy scan serving as her personal baseline. Data were collected over ~5¼ years. Participants were recruited as nulliparous individuals planning or not planning pregnancy; group assignment was based on whether they became parents between sessions. Final longitudinal sample sizes with complete Pre and Post scans: 25 primiparous women, 20 nulliparous control women, 19 first-time fathers, and 17 control men. Average time from Pre to Post was ~1.3 years and the Post scan occurred on average ~74 days after birth. Groups did not differ significantly in time interval, education or age (trend for age in male groups was controlled for with negligible effect).

Main findings
- Pregnancy was associated with localized reductions in gray matter (GM) volume in multiple brain regions (11 locations reported) when comparing women who became mothers to control women who did not. Changes were detected using longitudinal symmetric diffeomorphic modeling of T1-weighted MRI and were confirmed with stringent whole-brain family-wise error correction.
- Multivariate classification based on whole-brain GM change maps could reliably distinguish women who had undergone pregnancy from controls (very high accuracy), indicating a consistent spatial pattern of change across subjects.
- The GM changes overlapped with brain networks implicated in social cognition and theory of mind and with regions activated when mothers viewed images of their own infants. Some pregnancy-related brain changes predicted aspects of maternal attachment as measured by the Maternal Postnatal Attachment Scale.
- No comparable GM changes were observed in first-time fathers, supporting that the effects are specific to pregnancy rather than parenthood per se.
- Follow-up data from 11 of the primiparous women scanned about 2.3 years after birth indicated that most of the observed GM changes persisted at ~2 years postpartum.

Controls and additional analyses
- The study tested potential confounds: natural versus assisted conception (including IVF/ICSI), fetal sex, pregnancy/delivery complications, type of delivery, breastfeeding, postpartum depression (one participant), timing of Post scan, head-coil changes, and inclusion of age as covariate. None of these altered the main results substantially, though sample sizes limited power to detect subtle effects.
- Blood hormone samples were collected before and after pregnancy but not during pregnancy (only two women), so changes could not be directly tied to specific endocrine measures.
- Complementary analyses included white-matter proxy maps, surface-based cortical thickness and area measures, manual pituitary delineation, and fMRI responses to own vs other baby images. Cognitive tests showed no declines across sessions.
- MRI acquisition used a Philips 3T scanner; a temporary different head coil was used for 28 scans and was included as a nuisance covariate; removing those scans did not change results.

Methods summary
- Longitudinal voxel-based morphometry (SPM12) with symmetric registration to a within-subject midpoint, DARTEL normalization, and 12-mm smoothing produced GM change maps for statistical testing.
- Strict voxel-wise FWE correction (P < 0.05) and cluster thresholds were applied.
- Multivariate pattern analyses (PRoNTo) including linear SVM classification, multiple-kernel learning, and kernel ridge regression were used to classify pregnancy status and predict maternal attachment scores with permutation testing and leave-one-out cross-validation.

Conclusions
- Pregnancy produces reproducible, regionally specific reductions in gray matter volume that are likely driven by pregnancy-related biological factors (e.g., sex-hormone surges), not by caregiving or fatherhood. The pattern and persistence of changes, their overlap with social-cognition networks, and associations with maternal attachment suggest these neural alterations may reflect adaptive brain remodeling that helps prepare women for motherhood. Limitations include modest sample sizes for subgroup analyses, lack of hormonal measures during pregnancy, and incomplete long-term follow-up.

Singer Sinead O’Connor has announced the end of her marriage to Barry Herridge after just 18 days. The couple wed in Las Vegas last month, but O’Connor said on her website that they rushed into the union for “altruistic reasons” and that Herridge had been unhappy, so she ended the marriage. When reporters visited her Ireland home to ask about the split, O’Connor briefly stepped outside wearing only a towel and her tattoos. The short-lived marriage surpasses prior brief celebrity unions in notoriety; O’Connor called Herridge “a wonderful man” and acknowledged the mistake of marrying too quickly.

International Monetary Fund managing director Christine Lagarde sparked widespread controversy after a blunt interview with The Guardian in late May 2012, in which she urged Greeks to “pay their tax” and contrasted their situation unfavorably with impoverished children in sub‑Saharan Africa. Her comments — calling out Greeks who “try to escape tax” and saying “it’s payback time” — provoked anger across Greece and criticism in France and beyond. Greek politicians from across the spectrum condemned the remarks as insulting; social media flooded Lagarde’s Facebook page and spawned rival pages. Observers accused her of tone‑deafness given her high, tax‑exempt IMF salary, and The Guardian itself noted her prior role as France’s finance minister and questioned her placing blame largely on southern European borrowers rather than northern lenders.

Lagarde’s intervention also reflected growing impatience among the IMF, EU and ECB as Greece’s revenues plunged and as Athens prepared for elections amid fears it might leave the euro. She reiterated that the IMF would not soften austerity conditions and defended imposing strict fiscal measures on richer countries as well as poor ones. The episode came amid wider eurozone turmoil — market pressure on the euro, bank rescue talks in Spain, debate over eurobonds, and German‑French disagreements on crisis responses — and reinforced perceptions of mounting international pressure on Greece to improve tax collection and implement austerity. The revelations that IMF salaries are tax‑exempt added fuel to criticism of international institutions’ pay and privileges.

Former Michigan State University dean Dr. William Strampel, 70, has been arrested and is listed as an inmate in the Ingham County jail; no formal charges were posted publicly as of the listings. MSU confirmed the arrest but provided no details; Michigan State Police referred inquiries to the state attorney general’s office, which has not confirmed it publicly. The arrest comes one day before a scheduled press conference by an investigator hired by Michigan’s Attorney General Bill Schuette to probe MSU’s handling of the Larry Nassar scandal.

Strampel headed MSU’s College of Osteopathic Medicine for many years and has been a central figure in investigations into systemic failures that allowed Nassar — a sports medicine doctor convicted of extensive sexual abuse and federal child pornography offenses and serving lengthy prison sentences — to continue treating patients. After a 2014 complaint by Amanda Thomashow, Strampel reinstated Nassar with conditions (chaperones, gloves, full explanations and minimizing skin-to-skin contact). According to police reports and survivor statements, Strampel did not ensure colleagues were informed of or enforced those restrictions, and he later acknowledged he did not follow up. Nassar continued to abuse patients during the period he remained employed and under investigation; dozens of additional victims say they were assaulted after the 2014 decision. Strampel fired Nassar in September 2016 after learning he had ignored the guidelines.

Survivors and others have criticized Strampel’s conduct and attitudes — including documented instances in performance reviews describing repeated sexually inappropriate remarks, an office culture of fear, and dismissive communications about survivors such as Rachael Denhollander. Strampel stepped down as dean in December citing medical problems; MSU has initiated a tenure revocation process to begin firing him. He is also a co-defendant in many civil suits related to Nassar’s abuse, and the attorney general’s investigation has sought his work phone, computer and calendars. Lawyers for more than 150 survivors welcomed the arrest as a sign the Attorney General is pursuing accountability for institutional failures.

A 52-year-old man, Darin Bolar, was arrested Sept. 26 and charged with first‑degree kidnapping and two counts of second‑degree rape for the abduction and repeated sexual assault of a 14‑year‑old girl in Seattle in October 2007. The victim says she was grabbed on Beacon Hill while looking for a pay phone, forced into a yard and raped; the attacker allegedly used a garden hose to try to remove evidence, threatened to kill her, drove her to his home, and held, beat and raped her repeatedly over two days before she escaped. Harborview Medical Center collected a rape kit after the assault, but that kit — one of more than 1,000 that languished untested in Seattle’s backlog — was not analyzed until Dec. 28, 2017. Testing produced a DNA match to Bolar, a Level III sex offender previously convicted in 1993 of third‑degree child rape. The testing came after a 2015 Seattle Police initiative to send previously untested kits to the state crime lab; statewide efforts to inventory and test thousands of kits are underway with federal grant funds.

After Justin Bieber’s Jan. 23 arrest in Miami Beach on charges including DUI and resisting arrest, police body- and jailhouse-camera footage and new photos have become the focus of legal and media disputes. TMZ obtained clips showing Bieber in a cell doing push-ups and other moments; law enforcement says some footage shows him appearing under the influence, though that is disputed. Two of five unreleased video clips depict Bieber’s genitalia during a urine test, prompting a Miami-Dade judge to order that the remaining footage be released only after sensitive portions are blacked out to protect his privacy. Attorneys for Bieber and news organizations agreed redactions were appropriate; prosecutors said the five clips will be released after the court-ordered obfuscation is completed. The police have also struggled technically to blur moving images in a video that allegedly shows Bieber urinating. The Miami Beach Police Department released 18 still photos from the arrest (many close-ups of tattoos). Previously released evidence showed a breath test below the .02 threshold for underage drivers and a urine test positive for marijuana’s active ingredient and the anti-anxiety drug Xanax. Bieber has pleaded not guilty; a trial date has not been set.

This document contains three distinct items:

1) End of Term web-archiving continuation
- A collaborative project extends the 2016 End of Term web-archiving effort to continue documenting the federal government’s web and social media presence. Partner organizations include the Environmental Data & Governance Initiative and the Data Refuge project.
- URLs supplied by partner institutions and public nominations will be crawled regularly; the collection is deduplicated against the 2016 End of Term archive.
- The public, especially government information specialists, are invited to nominate sites via a public nomination tool. More details are available on the End of Term Archive site.

2) HUD proposed nationwide public-housing smoking ban (news article)
- The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) proposed a rule to require more than 3,100 public housing agencies to adopt smoke-free policies across the nation’s roughly 1.2 million public housing units. The rule would ban lit tobacco in living units, indoor common areas, administrative offices and nearby outdoor areas.
- HUD Secretary Julián Castro and public-health officials framed the rule as protecting vulnerable residents—especially children and the elderly—from secondhand smoke and as producing cost savings (HUD cited an estimated $153 million annually in health, repair and fire-prevention savings).
- The move builds on prior HUD encouragement since 2009; over 600 agencies had already adopted smoke-free policies, covering more than 228,000 units.
- Health groups praised the proposal; public housing authorities and legal representatives generally supported the health goals but raised concerns about enforcement, residents’ privacy and autonomy, impacts on elderly or disabled smokers, staffing constraints, and the need for reasonable accommodations or designated smoking areas.
- HUD will solicit public comments before issuing a final rule. The article also notes broader anti-smoking trends and statistics (e.g., smoking remains the leading preventable cause of death in the U.S., about 480,000 deaths annually).

3) Miscellaneous metadata
- The document also references a crawl of open-access PDF URLs provided by Unpaywall and includes a Reuters photo credit and related links to other HUD coverage.

A sudden, powerful hailstorm struck Cheyenne Mountain Zoo in Colorado Springs on Monday, pelting the facility with golf-ball- to softball-sized ice that shattered windows, damaged vehicles and sent animals and visitors scrambling for cover. About 3,400 people were at the zoo; roughly 400 cars in the parking lot were damaged. Fourteen people were reported injured—five taken to hospital and nine treated on site—and the zoo evacuated guests, who were bused to a nearby high school. Two animals were killed (a 13-year-old turkey vulture named Motswari and a Muscovy duck called Daisy); a second vulture initially reported dead was later found severely injured. Video showed bears seeking shelter as hail pummeled enclosures. The storm also knocked out power to nearly 2,000 customers, prompted closure of part of U.S. Highway 24, and damaged nearby properties including The Broadmoor resort. The zoo closed the next day to assess and repair damage and care for injured animals, while forecasters warned of additional storms and localized flooding risks.
