After photos surfaced of former Cosby Show actor Geoffrey Owens working as a cashier at a New Jersey Trader Joe’s, he was publicly shamed by some outlets and on social media. Owens, 57, initially felt humiliated and worried about embarrassing his family, but received widespread support from colleagues, fans and friends — including Keshia Knight Pulliam, Malcolm-Jamal Warner and Sabrina Le Beauf. The incident prompted many offers and opportunities: filmmaker Tyler Perry publicly invited Owens to join an OWN drama (reports later indicated a recurring, 10-episode role on The Haves and the Have Nots), and Owens said he’d been contacted with a “handful” of TV offers. Owens stopped working at Trader Joe’s for the time being, describing the leave as necessary for his dignity and wellbeing, though the store reportedly offered to hold his spot.

Rapper Nicki Minaj announced on her Queen Radio show that she would donate $25,000 to Owens, calling him “a legend” and vowing to have her team reach out. Owens has called the experience both painful and a “blessing,” saying it underscored the dignity of working and the importance of perseverance; he expressed gratitude for the outpouring of support and the new professional opportunities that followed.

Rep. Trent Franks (R-Ariz.) said he wished “there had been one more gun” in Tucson during Saturday’s shooting, implying another armed, responsible person might have stopped Jared Lee Loughner sooner. His remark, made during a briefing where GOP lawmakers were being updated by the FBI and security staff, echoes a broader pro-gun argument that more firearms can increase public safety — a point also voiced by Rep. Steve King (R-Iowa). Critics and commentators note the line between successful intervention and further tragedy can be thin: an armed civilian with no formal training may help stop an attacker or accidentally harm bystanders. The briefing also covered security steps for lawmakers: Speaker John Boehner’s team will provide written guidance, members discussed better coordination with local law enforcement, and several representatives (including Jason Chaffetz and Steve Scalise) said they are taking steps to improve or designate local security contacts.

Congress approved a bipartisan $1.3 trillion omnibus spending bill that funds the government through September and averts a potential shutdown. The 2,232‑page measure, hurriedly released the night before votes, passed the House 256‑167 and the Senate 65‑32 after late‑night delays and procedural objections from conservatives. The bill raises spending above previous caps, increases Pentagon funding, and provides funds for domestic priorities — including roads, child care, opioid programs and $1.6 billion to start border wall work — producing broad tradeoffs that angered fiscal conservatives who had campaigned on spending restraint.

The deal marked a partisan compromise: many Republicans criticized the package for boosting deficits (along with recent tax cuts) and condemned the last‑minute process; 90 House Republicans and about two dozen senators voted against it. Democrats secured numerous domestic priorities and celebrated the outcome, with leaders saying they used their leverage to win concessions. Key omissions included renewal of Affordable Care Act insurance subsidies after disputes over abortion restrictions. The rushed release and length of the bill drew public criticism about congressional procedure and transparency.

President Obama’s repeated promise that healthcare.gov would make buying insurance “real simple” collapsed with the site’s disastrous October 1, 2013, launch. The malfunctioning portal prompted an emergency federal fix led by Jeffrey Zients and Microsoft executive Kurt DelBene. While performance has improved, lingering errors and enrollment-record problems remain, and the debacle damaged public confidence in the president and the Affordable Care Act.

Much of the blame is traced to government procurement and management failures rather than a single political conspiracy. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) kept systems-integration responsibilities in-house instead of hiring an integrator to coordinate all the disparate processes feeding the site. CMS contracting practices favor a small pool of prequalified firms able to meet burdensome federal contracting rules, which helps explain why CGI Federal—a large, low‑profile government contractor with extensive federal experience—was selected as the lead contractor.

CGI Federal is a unit of CGI Group, a Canadian roll-up consulting-and-IT company founded in 1976 that grew rapidly by acquiring dozens of firms including American Management Systems (AMS) and Stanley Inc. CGI is large and profitable, performs extensive government work, and was already on a 2007 CMS umbrella (ID/IQ) contract that limited bidders for the ACA site to preapproved firms. In 2011, under time pressure, CMS evaluated four bidders (CGI, IBM, CSC, QSSI) on technical and cost proposals and selected CGI—deemed “technically superior”—for an initial $93 million award that grew to about $293 million.

Critics point out that CGI’s American acquisitions, especially AMS, had a history of troubled government IT projects (missed deadlines, large cost overruns, and notable failures) that should have raised concerns. Federal rules require consideration of past performance, but documentation shows CMS made past performance a low-weighted evaluation factor and limited review to work performed under the 2007 umbrella contract. Some former CMS officials say the agency “dropped the ball” by not thoroughly weighing predecessor-company failures. CMS career contracting officials ran the process and have defended it as nonpolitical.

CGI itself has faced prior problems on other government projects and internal critics say it missed deadlines and understaffed healthcare.gov. The company disputes some comparisons to AMS and emphasizes the improvements it helped deliver; CMS and the White House faulted both contractor performance and administrative mismanagement, along with political and policy delays that complicated development.

Separately, CGI’s financial reporting has drawn scrutiny from investors and short sellers who question the quality of its earnings amid aggressive growth by acquisition, but healthcare.gov represents only a small portion of CGI’s multi‑billion-dollar business.

In short: the healthcare.gov failure was the product of rushed timelines, federal contracting practices that favor a narrow set of veteran government vendors, insufficient attention to historical performance, and program-management shortfalls—problems that combined to produce a flawed launch with political and operational fallout that persists even as technical repairs continue.

The State Department issued a global travel alert warning that al Qaeda—particularly al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP)—may be planning unspecified attacks across the Middle East, North Africa and beyond over the coming weeks. U.S. officials, citing growing intelligence, said AQAP appears to be in the final stages of planning and that activity increased as Ramadan neared, with concern focused on key dates such as Laylat al-Qadr. Officials emphasized Western targets broadly—not only U.S. interests—could be struck and that terrorists might use a variety of means, including attacks on public transit and tourist sites.

In response, the U.S. temporarily closed 21 diplomatic posts Sunday (17 embassies and several consulates) across the region—from Afghanistan, Yemen and Libya to Algeria, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and others—with closures possibly lasting beyond a day. Senior military and security officials described the threat as unusually specific and serious; President Obama and congressional leaders were briefed and praised Yemeni security cooperation. The alert extends through the end of August, and the precise target country and timing remain uncertain, prompting a broad, precautionary response.

A new spider genus and species, Trogloraptor marchingtoni, was described in Zookeys (17 Aug 2012) and placed in its own new family, Trogloraptoridae. The species was found in caves and old-growth forest understory in the Klamath–Siskiyou region of southwest Oregon and northwest California. About a dozen specimens (mostly from cave roofs, one juvenile from redwood debris) were collected by researchers and cavers.

Key diagnostic and biological points
- Trogloraptor is a medium-sized spider (legspan roughly that of a half-dollar) with distinctive raptorial claws on the tarsi, indicating a specialized predatory habit.
- Morphological characters, especially an oblique membranous division of the basal segment of the anterior lateral spinnerets, identify it as a haplogyne and suggest Trogloraptoridae is the sister group to the other Dysderoidea families (Dysderidae, Oonopidae, Orsolobidae, Segestriidae).
- Electron microscopy revealed unique features implying an ancient lineage; the discovery may prompt revisions in understanding spider evolution.
- Little is known of its behavior: mating biology and diet remain uncertain—captive specimens refused offered prey.

Context and significance
- The species was found in a biologically ancient, topographically complex region known for relict flora and fauna; many caves and inaccessible habitats there mean further undiscovered taxa are possible.
- Collecting organizations included the Western Cave Conservancy, California Academy of Sciences, and San Diego State University.

Overall, Trogloraptor marchingtoni represents a previously unknown, evolutionarily distinct spider lineage specialized for cave and old-growth forest microhabitats, highlighting the Klamath–Siskiyou region’s role as a refuge for ancient biodiversity.

Three people — including two young children — were killed in Delhi on India’s Independence Day after their throats were slit by glass- or metal-coated kite strings (manja), a material used to cut down rival kites. Victims included 3-year-old Saanchi Goyal, 4-year-old Harry, and 22-year-old Zafar Khan, who was riding a motorcycle when the string caused him to fall fatally. A police officer was also injured.

Manja, treated with powdered glass or metal to make it abrasive, is repeatedly linked to fatal and serious injuries to people and to large numbers of birds each year. Delhi’s bird hospital received at least 500 injured birds over three days; it treats up to 8,000 birds annually. Animal-rights group PETA had petitioned the National Green Tribunal for an immediate ban, calling manja “a menace to public safety.”

In response, the Delhi government has banned the sale, production and storage of glass- or metal-coated manja (including Chinese manjha), announced public-awareness campaigns, and set penalties for violations: fines of 100,000 rupees and up to five years’ imprisonment.

Researchers at the London School of Economics analyzed data from the Millennium Cohort Study, which follows about 18,000 British children, to examine how maternal age affects child development. Published in Biodemography and Social Biology, the study found that children born to mothers in their 30s scored highest on cognitive tests and generally outperformed those born to mothers in their 20s and slightly better than those born to mothers in their 40s.

The investigators suggest the advantage may stem from socioeconomic and behavioral differences: first-time mothers in their 30s are more likely to be better educated, have higher incomes, be in stable relationships, plan their pregnancies, seek earlier prenatal care, and have healthier lifestyles. Older mothers (in their 40s) were more likely to breastfeed, read to their children and smoke less, but their children were more prone to obesity and, according to the study, these mothers spent less time playing with their kids. The children in the analysis were assessed at age five.

The researchers cautioned the small number of mothers in their 40s in the sample (only 53) limits conclusions and more research is needed. The study’s authors and commentators also note broader questions about how intelligence is defined and the role of long-term environmental and socioeconomic factors in shaping child outcomes. The report comes as the average maternal age in the UK has risen (from 24.5 in 1980 to about 28.1 today).

An 18-year-old man who played paintball was treated for a severe liver laceration after initially being diagnosed with appendicitis, according to a BMJ Case Reports paper and media coverage. He presented with abdominal pain, loss of appetite and low-grade fever and was taken to surgery for presumed appendicitis. Surgeons discovered intra-abdominal bleeding from a lacerated liver instead of an inflamed appendix and controlled the hemorrhage by "repacking" the liver with pressure pads overnight; it was repacked again the next day before bleeding stopped.

Afterward the patient reported being hit twice in his lower right abdomen during a paintball game two days earlier. There were no overlying skin bruises. He was discharged two days after surgery but returned three weeks later when imaging showed pooled blood being reabsorbed; further testing confirmed no new damage and normal liver function. Doctors noted this is the first reported paintball-related liver injury and only the fourth reported solid-organ injury from paintball (previous reports involved kidney and genital trauma). They emphasized that paintballs, fired at muzzle velocities of roughly 100–300 ft/s, can cause serious internal injuries and that participants and clinicians should be aware of these risks. The patient was reported to be recovering and continuing his studies.

Michael (Mike) Oreskes, NPR’s senior vice president for news and editorial director, has resigned after multiple sexual harassment allegations surfaced dating to the 1990s and beyond. Oreskes issued a statement saying he was “deeply sorry,” called his behavior “wrong and inexcusable,” and accepted full responsibility. He informed NPR CEO Jarl Mohn of his decision to step down after being placed on leave; Chris Turpin was named interim news chief.

The Washington Post reported that two women who interacted with Oreskes while he was Washington bureau chief at The New York Times said he abruptly kissed them during meetings in the 1990s. Those women later filed formal complaints with NPR and spoke to the Post on condition of anonymity. Separately, an NPR employee, Rebecca Hersher, told editors she filed an internal complaint in October 2015 about an uncomfortable, boundary-crossing career meeting and dinner with Oreskes after he joined NPR in 2015. NPR’s HR reportedly rebuked Oreskes at that time and Hersher said she experienced no retribution.

NPR leadership said it takes such allegations seriously and encouraged staff to come forward; CEO Mohn noted the organization reviews concerns promptly to ensure a safe workplace. Oreskes had been a longtime news executive, including roles at The New York Times and the Associated Press, before joining NPR in 2015.

Conservative The View co-host Elisabeth Hasselbeck sparked criticism for comments suggesting some women “turn to” lesbian relationships later in life because older men pursue younger women, leaving these women “with no one.” Hasselbeck added such women might seek companionship rather than sex. Liberal co-host Joy Behar called the idea “ridiculous,” arguing sexual orientation isn’t a choice people suddenly make and noting many were constrained by social expectations to marry. The item notes Hasselbeck’s history of contentious remarks on other topics.

Myanmar has begun releasing another large group of political prisoners as part of reforms pushed by President Thein Sein. Government officials said 69–73 detainees were freed on Tuesday, reducing the number of political prisoners to below 100 for the first time in years. The releases follow Thein Sein’s recent European visit, where he pledged to free all remaining political prisoners by year’s end. A 19‑member Committee to Scrutinise Remaining Political Prisoners—made up of former prisoners, government appointees and mediators—reviews cases to distinguish political from criminal detention and meets monthly to process releases.

Rights groups welcome the releases but warn many activists remain jailed and repressive laws that enable such detentions are still in force; activists say arrests and trials of peaceful protesters continue, with dozens more facing trial recently. Exact counts vary between the government, embassies and advocacy groups, but around 200 political prisoners were believed jailed before this round of releases.

Two Chow Chow dogs painted to look like pandas were seized from a travelling circus near Brescia, Italy, after visitors—many of them children who paid to pose with the animals—were misled into believing they were pandas. The white dogs, imported from Hungary, were displayed before shows; police action followed a tip-off. Italy’s environmental police said the animals were generally healthy but had watery eyes, likely worsened by continuous camera flashes. Authorities seized the dogs on animal-cruelty grounds and investigating false paperwork: the animals were said to be younger than their documents claimed, potentially exposing the circus owner to charges including falsifying passports and fraud for deceiving customers. The circus denied mistreatment and insisted the animals “should have been obvious” as dogs; the animals have been returned but may no longer be used in performances. The story notes a related trend in China of dyeing Chow Chows to resemble pandas, where painted dogs command higher prices.

A man using the name Nolan Daniels posted a Facebook photo claiming to be the as-yet-unidentified second winner of the roughly $588 million Powerball jackpot and promised to give $1 million to a random person who shared the image. The image shows the winning numbers, and Daniels’ post and comments drew massive attention—hundreds of thousands of shares and thousands per minute at peak. He also warned doubters they would be excluded from the “drawing.”

However, the claim is almost certainly a hoax. Lottery officials have confirmed one winning ticket was sold in Missouri (holders Cindy and Mark Hill) and that a second winning ticket was sold in Arizona, but they have not publicly identified that winner. Observers and reporters noted multiple signs the Facebook photo is fake: the ticket’s numbers are not printed in the required numerical order (Powerball tickets print the first five numbers sorted), the image appears poorly photoshopped, and surveillance footage of the Arizona winner does not match Daniels. Media outlets reached out to Daniels for comment. The episode highlights how quickly dubious social posts can spread when tied to big lottery jackpots.

Construction workers in Gdansk, northern Poland, uncovered a marble bust of Adolf Hitler while working in the interior garden of the city's National Museum. The 50 cm, ~60 kg sculpture is signed "Thorak 1942," attributing it to Josef Thorak, a leading sculptor of the Third Reich who produced large official works. Museum staff say the piece was deliberately buried—likely in 1945 as Soviet forces neared the city—and remained hidden despite later gardening and landscaping. The museum will not display it immediately; it has been moved to storage for scientific study to determine its origin, original location, and how it came into the museum collection. Thorak’s oeuvre included monumental public pieces (including horse sculptures once outside Hitler’s chancellery), making the find notable both artistically and historically.

NPR fired longtime senior news analyst Juan Williams after he told Bill O’Reilly on Fox News that he feels “nervous” on airplanes when he sees people in Muslim dress. NPR said Williams’ comments violated its editorial standards and undermined his credibility; executives had previously warned him about controversial remarks on Fox and asked that he not use the NPR name there. NPR CEO Vivian Schiller said analysts should not express such personal, controversial opinions in ways that appear to represent NPR; she later apologized for a flippant remark about Williams’ psychiatrist/publicist. 

Williams defended his remarks as an honest personal reaction tied to 9/11 and said he had also told O’Reilly that Muslims should not be lumped with extremists. He said he was told by NPR news vice president Ellen Weiss that the decision to terminate his contract was final. Civil rights groups including the Council on American‑Islamic Relations criticized his comments; others, including Whoopi Goldberg, called the firing excessive. 

Republicans attacked NPR’s decision as censorship; Fox News quickly signed Williams to a multi‑year contract and published a column in which he called the firing a “chilling assault on free speech” and criticized NPR leadership. NPR emphasized regret over the decision but maintained the move was necessary because his public statements were inconsistent with its ethics and values.

Katherine Heigl has returned to Hollywood after stepping away in 2009 to focus on family and reassess her career. In an exclusive interview, she said she’d overcommitted to romantic comedies, which left her creatively burned out and feeling betrayed by the Hollywood machine. Taking time off allowed her to ask what she really wanted; she’s now back with a U.S. TV series, State of Affairs, and the animated film The Nut Job. Heigl says she’s found a better life–work balance, negotiating only 15 episodes per season so she can return to Utah and pursue other inspirations, while acknowledging she still has a “Hollywood animal” side.

The piece also notes Marie Claire’s August 2014 issue and other features, and includes a separate item about Ryan Gosling and Rachel McAdams. Director Nick Cassavetes revealed on VH1 that Gosling and McAdams had severe on-set tensions while filming The Notebook—Gosling even asked for McAdams to be replaced during a scene. After a heated confrontation and private argument, their working relationship improved somewhat. Despite the conflict, the pair later began an off-screen relationship that was tumultuous and ended in 2007.

A powerful storm system and the remnants of Hurricane Patricia brought days of heavy rain and flash flooding to large parts of Texas, triggering rescues, transportation disruptions and localized evacuations.

- Rainfall and flooding: Many areas saw extreme totals — parts of Navarro County reported 18–21 inches in 24 hours, Dallas–Fort Worth saw more than 7 inches in some storms, and other locations received nearly two feet since Friday. Flash-flood watches covered major population centers (Houston, Galveston, Waco, Austin, San Antonio, Corpus Christi, Laredo, Brownsville) with some watches extending through Monday.

- Train derailment and rescues: A 64-car Union Pacific freight train derailed near Corsicana (Navarro County) early Saturday after floodwaters washed out tracks. One locomotive and several cars were partially submerged; both crew members swam to safety and were rescued by a high-water team. Authorities reported about 72 swift-water rescues in the county.

- Missing person and other rescues: In San Antonio a man walking his dog was swept into a flooded drainage ditch and went missing; firefighters suspended the search temporarily because of weather (the dog was found). In Temple, a driver escaped a floating car and was rescued after calling 911.

- Infrastructure and travel impacts: Major highways were closed (Interstate 45 was shut overnight near Corsicana, creating long backups). Hundreds of flights were canceled or delayed at Dallas–Fort Worth International Airport (about 100 cancellations reported Saturday). Power outages and flight disruptions were widespread.

- Coastal concerns and evacuations: Galveston County issued a voluntary evacuation for Bolivar Peninsula because of forecasts of 8–12 inches of rain and 4–5 foot tides; officials warned residents could be cut off. Tornado watches were in effect for parts of southeast Texas.

- Storm status and outlook: Patricia made landfall Friday in southwestern Mexico as a Category 5 and was downgraded to a tropical depression by Saturday. Forecasters expected its remnants to add rainfall across South and East Texas through the weekend, with the heaviest rain easing by Sunday night but flooding problems lingering into early next week.

Bernie Sanders reintroduced a comprehensive "Medicare for All" single-payer bill in the Senate, putting universal, government-run health coverage back at the center of Democratic debate. The proposal would expand Medicare to cover all U.S. residents with a broad benefit package (hospital, primary care, maternity, prescription drugs, dental, vision, reproductive care, substance-abuse treatment) and eliminate premiums, deductibles and most cost-sharing. It phases in universal eligibility over four years and would bar competing employer plans; VA and Indian Health Service would remain separate.

Support and political impact
- The bill gained significant Democratic backing among the party’s progressive wing and some high-profile potential 2020 presidential contenders (Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, Kamala Harris, Cory Booker, Kirsten Gillibrand and others), turning support for single-payer into a litmus test for many activists and candidates.
- Many Democratic leaders and vulnerable, moderate or red-state Democrats (including Chuck Schumer, Nancy Pelosi, Sherrod Brown, Dianne Feinstein, Claire McCaskill, Joe Manchin, Patty Murray and others) declined to endorse the bill. Several proposed alternatives (Medicare buy-ins, Medicaid buy-ins or a public option) aim to expand government coverage without full single-payer.
- Republicans quickly attacked the plan as radical and tax-heavy; passage is effectively impossible in a GOP-controlled Congress, but backers view it as an aspirational benchmark to shift party policy and the national conversation.

Policy, costs and uncertainties
- Sanders asserts the plan would be largely financed by progressive tax increases on households, capital gains, estates, and employers, and by reallocating existing health spending; he claims large net savings over a decade. Detailed financing was not included with the initial rollout and remains a central unanswered question.
- Analysts note trade-offs: single-payer could lower administrative costs and reduce price variation by adopting Medicare rates, but Sanders’s unusually generous, zero cost-sharing benefit package and higher payment rates for former Medicaid patients could raise utilization and overall costs. Past attempts (e.g., Vermont) stalled when financing needs became clear.
- Public opinion has shifted toward greater demand for government responsibility in ensuring coverage, and support within the Democratic base is strong; national support for a government-run single-payer system is more mixed.

Broader context
- The bill arrives amid ongoing GOP efforts to repeal/replace the ACA and parallel Senate talks to stabilize insurance markets. Progressive activists see Sanders’s legislation as a long-term “North Star” to push Democrats left on economic and health policy, while more moderate Democrats favor shoring up the ACA and pursuing incremental or politically feasible expansions.

Bottom line: Sanders’s Medicare-for-All bill formalizes a potent progressive policy agenda that has already reshaped Democratic politics by elevating single-payer from the fringe to a mainstream litmus test for many candidates. However, major political resistance, unanswered financing details, and practical transition challenges mean it is unlikely to become law in the near term; its chief immediate effect is to influence party direction and debate.

David Oliver Relin, a journalist and adventurer best known as co-author of the 2006 best seller Three Cups of Tea, died by suicide on Nov. 15 in Multnomah County, Oregon. He was 49. His family said he “suffered from depression” and that the controversy over the accuracy of Three Cups of Tea had left him emotionally and financially hurt.

Relin had built a career in the 1990s reporting humanitarian stories—on child soldiers and travels in Vietnam—and was hired to help tell Greg Mortenson’s story of building schools in Pakistan and Afghanistan. The book sold more than four million copies, but questions about its central anecdotes and the operations of Mortenson’s Central Asia Institute emerged in 2011 after a CBS “60 Minutes” report and Jon Krakauer’s e-book Three Cups of Deceit. Critics said key episodes in the book were fabricated, some schools never existed or were built by others, and funds were misused to promote the book. Mortenson later acknowledged some inaccuracies and agreed to repay more than $1 million in inappropriate expenses; a federal suit accusing the authors and publisher of defrauding readers was dismissed this year. Relin largely stayed out of public debate over the allegations but hired legal counsel to defend himself.

Born Dec. 12, 1962, in Rochester, Relin graduated from Vassar in 1985 and was a fellow at the Iowa Writers’ Workshop. He is survived by his wife, Dawn; his mother Marjorie; stepfather Cary Ratcliff; and sisters Rachel Relin and Jennifer Cherelin. He had completed a new book about two doctors working to cure cataract-related blindness in the developing world, scheduled for publication by Random House in spring 2013.

Austin voters rejected an attempt by Uber and Lyft to overturn a city ordinance requiring fingerprint-based criminal background checks for ride-hailing drivers, handing the companies an embarrassing defeat. Despite spending more than $8 million (about $200+ per vote) — making it the costliest campaign in Austin history — the companies lost 56% to 44%. Mayor Steve Adler said the firms are “welcome to stay” and offered continued negotiation, but both Uber and Lyft responded angrily: Lyft said the new rules prevent “true ridesharing” and will suspend operations, and Uber expressed strong disappointment. 

The outcome is likely mixed: supporters of Proposition 1 and emergency crews favor stricter vetting and reduced mid-street pickups, while riders and many drivers face immediate disruption in a car-dependent city with weak transit and pricier taxi alternatives. The result could also encourage other cities to pursue fingerprint checks, showing they can withstand heavy opposition from ride-hailing firms.

Summary:

1) Bombardier-beetle–inspired anti-theft ATM coating
- Researchers at ETH Zurich developed a self-defending surface modeled on the bombardier beetle’s chemical defense. The design uses two layered plastic films with honeycomb cavities: one filled with hydrogen peroxide, the other with manganese dioxide, separated by a thin lacquer layer.
- If the surface is breached (for example by an ATM thief), the barrier ruptures, the chemicals mix, and a rapid exothermic reaction produces hot foam, vapor, oxygen and heat (foam temperatures measured around 80°C). The foam contains dye to stain banknotes and perpetrators and can include DNA nanoparticles to trace cash back to a source.
- The system is intended to deter vandalism and theft and could be applied to other contexts (protecting goods, keeping animals from gnawing trees). It’s still in testing with no immediate rollout planned.

2) Personal reflection from a Clinton voter on the 2016 election
- A reader, Megan, writes a candid confession blaming her own reticence and lack of visible, outspoken support for Hillary Clinton as partly responsible for Clinton’s loss. She recounts repeatedly voting for Clinton privately in past primaries, avoiding public expression of support, and tempering praise with caveats about Clinton’s imperfections.
- She describes avoiding political confrontations with friends and family who leaned toward Trump, failing to engage with her undecided relatives, and self-censoring emotional responses out of fear of being labeled “too emotional”—behaviors she sees as reinforcing double standards women face in public life.
- Her central regret is that by qualifying support and not asserting unequivocal backing (language she observed in many editorials and commentaries), she contributed to a narrative that treated Clinton as uniquely flawed compared with male candidates.

Briggs Fussy and Brittney Husbyn, now 22, first crossed paths at age 3 when Briggs served as ring bearer and Brittney as flower girl at Briggs’s godmother’s wedding in Minnesota. They reconnected in high school in 2007—Brittney recognized Briggs by his uncommon name and an old photo—and began dating two years later while attending Mankato State University. On Jan. 10 the couple married in front of 310 family and friends, recreating the childhood photos and becoming the bride and groom after once sharing the aisle as children. Their unusual story has attracted public attention and delight from relatives (especially Briggs’s godmother) and strangers alike; the newlyweds plan to save clippings to show their future children.

Mira Sorvino has published an open letter apologizing to Dylan Farrow and expressing regret for working with Woody Allen. Sorvino, who won an Oscar for Allen’s 1995 film Mighty Aphrodite, says that as a “naïve young actress” she accepted the media framing of Farrow’s longstanding abuse allegations as part of a custody dispute and failed to look more deeply into the matter. Although Sorvino says she personally never experienced inappropriate behavior from Allen, she acknowledges that her admiration for him caused her to turn a blind eye and that she is sorry for doing so.

Her decision to speak out followed conversations with Ronan Farrow after Sorvino publicly accused Harvey Weinstein of sexual harassment; Ronan directed her to publicly available information about Dylan’s claims, which convinced Sorvino that Dylan’s account is credible. In the letter Sorvino expresses remorse for contributing—by silence—to Dylan’s pain, announces she will never work with Allen again, and offers Dylan her belief, support and admiration for her courage.

Sorvino joins other former Allen collaborators—Ellen Page and Greta Gerwig—in publicly distancing themselves from the director and expressing regret for having worked with him. The letter reiterates the broader point that alleged abuses must be re-examined and that celebrated figures should not be immune from consequences.

Researchers analyzing insurance claims found firearm injuries drop sharply during National Rifle Association (NRA) annual conventions. A New England Journal of Medicine analysis of nearly 76 million privately insured claims from 2007–2015 compared injury rates during each convention to the three weeks before and after. Nationwide, firearm-related injuries fell about 20% during conventions (from 1.5 to 1.2 per 100,000); in the host state the decline was much larger (about 63%, from 1.9 to 0.7 per 100,000). The reductions were concentrated among men and were strongest in the South and West and in states with high gun ownership. Gun-related crime rates did not change.

Authors Anupam Jena (Harvard) and Andrew Olenski (Columbia) suggest the pattern is consistent with reduced firearm use while many owners and operators of shooting venues attend conventions—plus possible secondary effects such as temporary closures of ranges or hunting trips. They argue the findings counter the claim that accidents only occur among inexperienced users, noting that injuries fall when even experienced owners are absent. External experts called the result plausible, and researchers noted the study shows correlation not causation.

The story also notes wider context: about 265–300 million guns in U.S. private hands, substantial unintentional firearm injuries and deaths annually, and debate over gun safety. The NRA dismissed the study’s findings as illogical, arguing relatively few owners attend conventions and cannot explain the scale of the decline. Separately, in the wake of high-profile mass shootings such as Parkland, gun-rights groups report surging memberships and renewals even as gun-control advocacy and public support for reforms grow—highlighting the politically charged backdrop to discussions about firearm safety and regulation.

A 29-year-old man, identified as Carnell Marcus Moore of Beaumont, was killed after firing a gun inside the ticketing area of Terminal B at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport on Thursday afternoon. Witnesses reported hearing multiple shots that caused passengers and employees to scatter and hide. A Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) special agent, whose office is about 150 feet from the scene, heard the gunfire, confronted Moore, identified himself and ordered Moore to drop the weapon. The agent fired once as Moore turned toward him; at almost the same moment Moore shot himself. Moore died at the scene and no one else was injured.

Authorities found a Smith & Wesson AR-15 with a fully loaded magazine in a black suitcase beside Moore, additional .223 ammunition in his car, and a handwritten note on Hotel Derek stationery in which Moore wrote that he had “changed his mind” and wanted to spare others. Earlier the same day he had posted on Facebook references to death and to committing a mass shooting. An autopsy was scheduled for Friday.

Terminal B was closed temporarily, passengers were rerouted to other terminals, and parts of the terminal were later reopened. The FBI, HSI and Houston Police interviewed numerous witnesses and searched Moore’s home in Beaumont. Neighbors described Moore as reserved but remembered him as friendly; colleagues called him a good guy. Authorities said there was no visible damage to the facility and that the rest of the airport remained open.

Starbucks announced a new North America dress code that relaxes several longtime appearance rules to let employees express themselves more while maintaining a neat, food-safe look. Effective immediately, partners may wear shirt colors beyond solid black and white — including gray, navy, dark denim and brown, plus some patterns — and may wear dark-wash jeans, shorts, skirts, dresses, and certain hats (beanies, fedoras, and other “suitable” hats; not bucket hats, sports caps, berets, or cowboy hats). Most notably, employees are now allowed to dye their hair unconventional colors as long as the color is permanent or semi-permanent (temporary dyes, chalk, or glitter can pose food-safety issues). 

The policy still restricts brightly colored shirts, some prints, hoodies, distracting socks, UGG boots and other items; other rules tied to food safety (no nail polish, minimal jewelry) remain. Starbucks framed the update as reflecting what partners already wear, improving morale and aligning with its brand; some stores and Reserve locations had already piloted the look. The change follows years of partner complaints and petitions seeking more freedom to show personal style, and builds on prior relaxations such as lifting visible-tattoo bans.

Two men from Douglas, Georgia — 30-year-old Michael Mancil and 22-year-old James Dryden Jr. — were arrested by Coffee County Sheriff’s investigators after authorities say they plotted to attack the High Frequency Active Auroral Research Program (HAARP), a research facility now owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks that has long been the subject of conspiracy theories.

Investigators seized a large arsenal at a residence on Jim Road: four AR-15s, four Glock handguns, a Remington rifle, thousands (estimated 2,000–3,000) of rounds of ammunition, radios, two flak jackets, about $5,500, and a small amount of marijuana. Officials described the stockpile as resembling “a small army” preparing for war. The investigation began with a probe into Mancil for suspected drug sales and was aided by a local gun shop that reported unusual weapons purchases.

Authorities say Mancil and Dryden planned to infiltrate HAARP — motivated by conspiratorial beliefs that the facility manipulates weather, controls minds or “traps souls” — and discussed stealing a scientist’s car and ID to gain access. A detective reported the suspects confessed that “God told them” to destroy the facility. HAARP officials and UAF spokespeople stressed the center conducts ionospheric research and noted they have security measures in place; they thanked Georgia law enforcement for the arrests.

Charges announced include selling methamphetamine, possession of marijuana, possession of a weapon during the commission of a crime, and for Mancil, use of a telecommunication device to facilitate a felony. Additional charges are pending.

Steve Aisthorpe, a 55-year-old mountaineer and Church of Scotland mission development worker from Kincraig, Scotland, says he has finally found some closure after the remains of his two friends, Icelandic climbers Kristinn Rúnarsson and Þorsteinn Guðjónsson, were discovered more than 30 years after they vanished on Pumori (near the Nepal–Tibet border).

Rúnarsson and Guðjónsson, both 27 at the time, were last seen on 18 October 1988 at about 21,650 ft during a four-man Pumori expedition. Aisthorpe had fallen ill during the climb and sent the pair ahead. He returned to the high camp days later to find their tent empty; helicopter searches at the time turned up nothing and he left after several weeks convinced they had fallen into a crevasse. Their remains were found last month by an American climber at the snout of a glacier below the west face, suggesting they had fallen down the face and been carried down over decades by the retreating glacier.

Local climbers recovered the bodies, took them to Kathmandu, and after identification—assisted by photos and items Aisthorpe provided—held a cremation service attended by family members who returned the ashes to Iceland. Aisthorpe said the discovery has brought strong emotions but also brought people together and should help provide closure and peace; he plans to visit Reykjavík to meet families. Two rolls of camera film found in a jacket pocket have been sent to Australia for development and may offer further clues.

Aisthorpe recalled the anguish of the 1988 search, how his Christian faith and scripture sustained him, and noted the event did not end his connection to Nepal—he later lived and worked there for 12 years with his family and with relief organisations. The article also highlights the Church of Scotland’s ongoing involvement in Nepal through partnerships such as the United Mission to Nepal and post‑earthquake reconstruction efforts.

At a Spike TV tribute, One Night Only: Alec Baldwin, held at Harlem’s Apollo Theater, Alec Baldwin received a surprise appearance and praise from former president Bill Clinton, who opened with a jab at Donald Trump and recalled Baldwin’s long-running interest in politics and early acting ambitions. Robert De Niro also praised Baldwin’s now-famous SNL Trump impression and urged him to keep lampooning the president, adding his own scathing aside about Trump.

Friends, co-stars and family—including Julianne Moore, Tracy Morgan, Jane Krakowski, Jack McBrayer and Baldwin’s brothers—shared tributes and humorous roasts. Baldwin’s 21-year-old daughter Ireland recounted their reconciliation after a widely publicized 2007 voicemail incident and expressed pride in her father. Baldwin closed the evening with sharp, roast-style jabs at attendees rather than a conventional thank-you.

The special airs July 9 on Spike TV. Separately, Baldwin told CNN he plans to reprise his Donald Trump impersonation on Saturday Night Live this fall—albeit sparingly because of his busy schedule—continuing a role that has become one of his most memorable SNL contributions.

The family of Walter L. Scott, the African-American man who was shot in the back and killed by North Charleston police officer Michael T. Slager on April 4, has reached a $6.5 million settlement with the city. The North Charleston City Council unanimously approved the deal, which bars the family from pursuing further civil claims and also protects current and former city employees from suit. About $1 million is expected to come from the state Insurance Reserve Fund and the remainder from the city’s fund balance.

A bystander’s cellphone video showed Slager firing at Scott as he ran away, sparking nationwide protests and contributing to a broader debate over police use of force against black men. Slager was fired, has been jailed since April 7, and was indicted on murder charges in June; his lawyer denies his culpability. Scott’s family had planned civil suits but instead negotiated the settlement through months of talks with city officials and lawyers, who said resolving the matter without litigation or public depositions would be healthier for both sides.

City and family representatives characterized the settlement as historic and a model for handling such cases peacefully. Officials noted the payment is in line with other recent high-profile police-related settlements (e.g., Eric Garner, Freddie Gray). Family attorneys said the amount was realistic given the city’s fiscal limits; part of the settlement will be donated to flood relief, and the family intends to focus now on the criminal prosecution of Slager. The agreement brings a civil resolution to a case that has fueled national calls for police accountability and reform.

A Pittsburgh man, Robert Trostle, and his wife Krystsina have sued Kennywood Entertainment after he says he contracted microsporidia keratitis — an eye infection caused by a parasite that "eats away at the cornea" — when he was splashed in the left eye on the Raging Rapids ride on July 2. The complaint filed in Allegheny County Common Pleas Court alleges the ride’s water was "dirty, stagnant and sludge-like" and that a waterfall feature was not operating. Trostle developed redness, pain, itching and light sensitivity within days; initially treated for conjunctivitis on July 5, he was diagnosed with microsporidia keratitis on July 14. According to the suit, surgeons scraped the parasite from his eye but could not remove it entirely; he continues to suffer blurry and impaired night vision, redness, dryness, inflammation and pain, and microsporidia reportedly remain present. The Trostles claim Kennywood lacked adequate water-inspection and safety procedures and seek more than $35,000 in damages.

Kennywood declined to comment on pending litigation, calling the parasite allegation unproven and reiterating that ride and water safety are priorities. The Allegheny County Health Department says it notified state and federal agencies, assisted with an investigation and that inquiries remain ongoing; it has not released water-test results. The plaintiffs’ attorney says a Right-to-Know request for the health department’s findings was denied, prompting the lawsuit. The report notes a recent, separate high-profile case involving a fatal Naegleria fowleri infection linked to a rafting facility’s inadequate water treatment.

This document explains wind shear’s role in tropical cyclone development, illustrates how it’s measured, gives practical rules of thumb, and uses case studies and 2017 reporting on Hurricane Irma to show impacts and forecasting uncertainty.

Key points on wind shear and hurricanes
- Wind shear is any change in wind speed or direction along a line; for hurricanes the important component is vertical shear (surface up through the troposphere, roughly surface to ~40,000 ft).
- A common diagnostic is the 200–850 mb shear (top vs. lower troposphere, ~40,000 ft vs ~5,000 ft), often computed over a large radius (e.g., 700 miles). This is a crude measure: it may miss directional changes, smaller-scale jets (e.g., near the Saharan Air Layer), and other local features because upper-air observations over ocean are sparse.
- Shear harms tropical cyclones by displacing heat and moisture from the core, tilting and ventilating the vortex, and disrupting the inflow/outflow balance that powers storms. Large shear (typically 20–40 kt) inhibits development; low shear (≤10 kt) favors intensification and rapid intensification.
- Zonal (east–west) shear is more important to storms than meridional (north–south) shear.

Rules of thumb and caveats
- Shear ≤20 kt generally needed for strengthening; rapid intensification is common when shear ≤10 kt.
- Strong, large hurricanes can sometimes resist high shear (examples like Hurricane Wilma intensified despite ~40 kt shear).
- Low shear alone isn’t sufficient: dry air aloft or upper-level troughs can prevent development. Upper-level anticyclones (high pressure aloft) are favorable.

Measurements and analyses
- The University of Wisconsin CIMSS produces useful wind-shear analyses by deriving upper-level winds from satellite cloud motion, subtracting mean low-level winds, and removing the storm’s own circulation to show the environmental shear. Their plots (updated frequently) include shear magnitude and direction overlaid on water-vapor imagery to highlight dry-air intrusions.

Examples
- Tropical Storm Gabrielle (2007): strong upper-level southwesterlies at 200 mb (~20 kt) blew thunderstorms away from the low-level center; differing low-level flow around the vortex made shear vary locally from ~10 to 30 kt, inhibiting central convection.
- Hurricane Wilma (2005): intensified to a major hurricane despite ~40 kt shear in analyses, underscoring exceptions.

Context: Hurricane Irma (late Aug–early Sept 2017)
- Irma was a rapidly intensifying Cape Verde hurricane in the eastern Atlantic and forecast to strengthen to Category 4 before reaching the Lesser Antilles. Low upper-level shear and a steering ridge to the north favored westward intensification.
- Forecast track beyond several days was highly uncertain. Models diverged: the U.S. GFS leaned to a more northerly track (reducing U.S. landfall chances), while the European ECMWF showed a stronger ridge forcing a more westerly track toward the Caribbean, Bahamas, and possibly Florida or the Gulf. Large-scale, non-tropical systems (ridges, troughs) would determine whether Irma recurved or made U.S. landfall.
- Meteorologists advised Caribbean and U.S. East Coast interests to monitor forecasts and prepare, noting that even a relatively small hurricane can cause severe impacts beyond its eye.

Broader seasonal context (2017)
- The 2017 Atlantic season was expected to be active: neutral ENSO conditions (reducing El Niño suppression), warmer-than-expected sea-surface temperatures in genesis regions, and a strong West African monsoon. As of Aug 31 there had already been above-average named storms.
- Harvey’s impacts (Texas flooding, energy and transport disruptions) heightened concerns about another major hurricane affecting U.S. coasts.

Definitions
- Cape Verde hurricane: a storm forming near the Cabo Verde Islands that develops into a hurricane while crossing the eastern Atlantic—often the most intense, long-track systems (typically August–September).

Overall takeaway
Wind shear is a principal environmental control on hurricane development and intensity: low shear fosters strengthening and rapid intensification, while strong or complex shear patterns inhibit storms. Forecasting intensity and long-range tracks remains challenging because large-scale steering and smaller-scale shear features evolve and models can disagree, as illustrated by Irma’s 2017 evolution and by historical examples.

A recently spotted wild European bison near Lebus on the German-Polish border was shot on instruction of a local public order official, prompting criminal charges from WWF and condemnation from conservationists. The bison — Europe’s largest land mammal, classed as vulnerable and “strongly protected” in Germany — had probably wandered from Poland’s Ujście Warty/Border Park. Critics said there was no clear threat to the public, that non-lethal options (e.g., tranquiliser darts) and expert handling were available, and blamed poor local training and past mismanagement of wildlife in Brandenburg.

The report situates this incident in the wider context of bison recovery and conservation in Poland, centered on the primeval Białowieża Forest. Once hunted to near-extinction (the last wild European bison in Poland was shot in 1919/1921), the species was rescued by captive breeding from a tiny founder stock and reintroduced; global numbers now exceed 4,600, with Poland hosting over 1,200 free-ranging animals and Białowieża home to several hundred. Wolves and other large carnivores have also rebounded due to protections.

A filmed encounter in snow-covered Białowieża showed wolves attempting to isolate calves but being driven off by adult bison, illustrating bison social defenses. The forest — part of a UNESCO site straddling Poland and Belarus — supports rich biodiversity but faces management dilemmas: low genetic diversity from the founder effect, disease risk amplified by winter feeding practices that concentrate animals, and regular culls (up to ~50 bison a year) carried out by park authorities to control numbers, a practice criticized by some ecologists.

Conservationists and naturalists argue for less interventionist, landscape-scale solutions: enlarging protected zones, creating habitat corridors and more open grassland areas better suited to large herbivores, and allowing more natural processes (including scavenging) to occur. Practical and political obstacles remain: local economic interests and forestry priorities often favor tree protection and hunting quotas, cross-border barriers (a fence through the forest) separate bison populations and reduce genetic exchange, and poaching/legal hunting in neighboring countries complicates rewilding efforts. The piece mixes on-the-ground observations — a guided field visit, encounters with rangers and biologists, and descriptions of forest life — with broader debate about human management versus letting nature regulate itself.

Summary:

Facebook agreed to buy about 650 patents and applications from Microsoft for $550 million; Microsoft had just paid roughly $1.056 billion to acquire 925 AOL patents and is keeping roughly 275 of them while licensing some rights back to Facebook. The transaction will substantially enlarge Facebook’s patent portfolio—bringing it to well over 1,000 patents—and gives the company defensive and offensive leverage as it heads into an expected IPO and ongoing patent fights (notably with Yahoo).

Beyond the IP mechanics, the deal is widely seen as part of a broader strategic alignment between Facebook and Microsoft against a common rival, Google. Microsoft and Facebook have deepened ties in recent years (including Bing-Facebook search data sharing and Microsoft’s equity stake in Facebook), and both view Google as the primary competitive threat in search, advertising and mobile. Microsoft is likely to retain AOL patents tied to search while Facebook will get patents focused on mobile, web and messaging technologies. Yahoo says the transaction won’t affect its lawsuit against Facebook.

Observers view the purchase as an example of the growing importance of patent stockpiling among big tech firms—for protection, bargaining power, and to deter or counter litigation—and as an indirect way for Microsoft to bolster Facebook without overtly damaging other partnerships (e.g., with Yahoo).

This piece recounts the December 2011 takedown of PonyArchive.org, a popular fan site that hosted high-quality episode downloads of My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic for international fans, and the resulting fallout within the “brony” community. Bronies—mostly adult male fans who embraced the 2010 reboot for its strong writing, animation, and positive themes—grew out of online communities like 4chan and built vibrant fan sites, news outlets, meet-ups and conventions. PonyArchive, based in Sweden and serving roughly 30,000 weekly visitors, ignored Hasbro’s initial takedown notice and replied defiantly; after a second notice it removed the episodes and posted a profane farewell message that polarized the fandom.

Reactions ranged from embarrassment and condemnation (fans saying PonyArchive behaved childish and harmed the community’s image) to frustration from international supporters who relied on the site to access episodes. Torrents and other fan sites continued to circulate episodes. The article situates this incident amid broader coverage explaining who bronies are, how the subculture formed on 4chan, and why the show attracted an unexpected adult audience: creator Lauren Faust designed a kids’ program with cross‑age appeal, and Bronies value the series’ quality and positive message despite ridicule. The takedown highlights tensions between fan-sharing practices and corporate IP enforcement, and underscores the fandom’s resilience.

A former Royal Canadian Mint employee, 35-year-old Leston Lawrence of Ottawa, has been sentenced to 30 months in jail and ordered to pay $190,000 after being found guilty of stealing 22 solid gold “pucks” from the mint. Lawrence worked sampling molten gold for purity tests and exploited times when he was out of sight of the room’s lone security camera. He sold 17 pucks to a local gold buyer for about $130,000; the full estimated value of the missing gold is $190,000. He used proceeds to buy a house in Jamaica and a boat in Florida.

Lawrence was convicted of theft, possession of property obtained by crime, conveying gold out of the mint and breach of trust. Evidence against him was largely circumstantial: the pucks matched a unique mint ladle, Vaseline and latex gloves were found in his locker, several pucks were recovered from a safety-deposit box, and he triggered the metal detector more often than colleagues (though wand checks were negative). He was caught after a bank employee flagged the cheque cashing; police seized an 18th puck before its sale.

At sentencing, Crown sought three years and the $190,000 restitution; defence argued for 18 months and that Lawrence should only repay the $130,000 he actually received, citing lax mint security. Justice Peter Doody imposed the 30‑month term and the $190,000 fine, with an additional 30 months to be served if the fine isn’t repaid within three years of release. The mint says it has since upgraded security systems, screening, and camera coverage.

A group of men in their 20s in Spokane, Washington posted a Craigslist ad seeking a “generic dad” to grill at their Father’s Day weekend gathering. The ad asks for someone with at least 18 years’ experience as a dad and 10 years’ grilling experience, who can bring his own grill; burgers and hotdogs will be provided. The role also calls for talking about stereotypical “dad” topics—lawnmowers, deck building and Jimmy Buffet. Payment is food and beer. Several applicants have responded, according to KHQ-TV.

Ford said Wednesday it will largely exit the traditional car market in North America and focus on trucks, SUVs and commercial vehicles, keeping only the Mustang and a new Focus Active crossover in its car lineup. By 2020 the company expects roughly 90% of its North American portfolio to be trucks, SUVs or commercial vehicles, and it is shifting investment and product development accordingly — including hybrid powertrains for the F-150, Mustang, Explorer, Escape and Bronco and plans for high-performance and electric SUVs.

The announcement accompanied first-quarter results: $1.7 billion net income (43 cents per share), revenue up 7% to $42 billion, and pretax profit down 14% to $2.2 billion. The quarterly profit beat expectations mainly because of a lower effective tax rate; higher commodity costs (aluminum, steel, copper) depressed operating results and are expected to be a $1.5 billion headwind for the year. Regionally, North American pretax profit fell to $1.9 billion; Europe showed a $149 million pretax profit while South America, Asia/Pacific and the Middle East/Africa posted losses.

Ford also unveiled plans to cut an additional $11.5 billion in costs from 2019–2022 on top of $14 billion previously announced, and to reduce capital expenditures by $5 billion over that period. Executives said cuts will touch engineering, materials, marketing and sales, but it’s too early to say if layoffs will result.

The move responds to persistent consumer demand shifts away from sedans (Ford cited poor car sales) and follows industry trends (e.g., Fiat Chrysler’s earlier retreat from some sedans). Ford will discontinue models such as the Taurus, Fusion, Fiesta and C-Max in North America (timing not specified). Analysts called the strategy bold but unsurprising as Ford reallocates resources toward more profitable and growing segments.

Armed civilian groups and self-styled militias have mobilized in response to President Trump’s warnings about Central American migrant caravans, with some organizers urging volunteers to travel to the U.S.–Mexico border to “observe and report,” offer aid and, in many cases, carry guns. Groups such as the Texas Minutemen, the Minuteman Project and smaller patriot militias have publicly called members to converge along the southwest border; leaders say volunteers will support law enforcement by reporting crossings, while many acknowledge they will be armed where legal.

U.S. military and law-enforcement planners are concerned. Defense Department documents and Newsweek reporting warn that up to a few hundred “unregulated” militia members could self-deploy to the border, sometimes operating as “citizen patrols,” and include unverified reports of militia thefts of National Guard equipment. The Army has flagged the potential for confusion and unsafe encounters if vigilantes operate alongside thousands of deployed troops, Border Patrol agents and migrants.

Local reaction in border and near‑border communities is mixed and largely wary of outside militias. Some established local volunteer groups and ranchers — such as Michael Vickers of the Texas Border Volunteers and King Ranch heir Stephen “Tio” Kleberg — say they will not permit private militias onto their property and prefer official law-enforcement or military presence. Many landowners fear outsiders could be “trigger-happy,” damage property, interfere with Border Patrol operations, or escalate violence. In small border towns like Columbus, N.M., officials and residents likewise rebuffed militia offers of help and urged people to let federal agencies handle enforcement.

Militia members interviewed portray their role as extra “eyes and ears” and insist they will defer to authorities, but their presence has heightened tensions and prompted authorities to advise the public not to interfere with official operations. Local leaders and many residents emphasize coordination with Border Patrol and caution against fear-driven responses, noting longstanding cross-border ties and the humanitarian composition of much of the caravan.

Manuel "Meme" Uribe, a Mexican man once recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's heaviest person, has died at age 48. Uribe, who at his peak weighed about 1,230 pounds (560 kg) in 2006, had later reduced to roughly 867 pounds (394 kg). Confined to bed since about 2002 and reliant on family and friends for care, he was hospitalized on May 2 after experiencing an abnormal heartbeat and was transported with a crane because he could not leave home on his own. Doctors have not yet certified a cause of death; he had known cardiac arrhythmia and was believed to have liver problems. Uribe married Claudia Solis in 2008—one of the rare occasions he left home after his weight loss efforts that reportedly reduced him to about 701 pounds at that time.

House Speaker Paul Ryan released a slick 45-second video titled “Politics These Days” as part of a #ConfidentAmerica agenda, promoting unity and decrying “identity politics” and divisive campaigning. The clip, which repackages remarks he gave to Capitol Hill interns, has the tone of a campaign ad and has reignited speculation that Ryan could become a compromise GOP presidential nominee at a contested Republican National Convention — despite his repeated and increasingly forceful denials that he will run or accept a nomination.

Ryan has insisted he is not a candidate, comparing the situation to his 2015-16 refusal to enter the presidential race and pointing out differences between becoming House Speaker (which he accepted after initial reluctance) and running for president. His office and spokeswoman AshLee Strong have publicly disavowed “Draft Ryan” efforts and said he will not accept a nomination. Still, many Republicans and observers—concerned about the prospects of front-runners like Donald Trump or Ted Cruz—continue to float his name, and figures such as John Boehner and Rep. Tom Cole have praised him as a potential alternative. The video’s release, and Ryan’s high profile as convention chair, ensure renewed attention to whether he might be a late compromise option.

A small white dog named Soshe was rescued from a Pender County, North Carolina home flooded by Hurricane Florence and reunited with her owner thanks to the Humane Society of Missouri’s Disaster Response Team. The owner had evacuated and was stuck in Wilmington, unable to reach her pet. Rescuers made three boat attempts—during which floodwaters at times reached rooflines and their boat once broke down—before paddling half a mile to the house. They heard barking, kicked in a door, and found Soshe sitting on a floating couch after nearly a week alone. The team dried and removed the dog, turned her over to a friend of the owner, and reunited Soshe with her tearful owner. The nine-member HSMO team spent 10 days in North Carolina with partners rescuing and transporting multiple animals (dogs, cats, chickens, goats, horses) and assisting the Coast Guard; donations were solicited to support the effort.

A striking new pedestrian bridge, the Cau Vang or “Golden Bridge,” opened in June at the Bà Nà Hills resort near Da Nang, Vietnam. About 150–500 feet long depending on accounts and sited roughly 1,000–1,400 meters (3,280–4,600 ft) above sea level, the gilded walkway appears to be lifted by two giant stone‑colored hands, a design intended to evoke “the giant hands of gods pulling a strip of gold out of the land.” TA Landscape Architecture (Ho Chi Minh City/TA Corporation) is credited with the landscape concept and initial design.

The bridge is part of the Thien Thai Garden development and a larger ~$2 billion tourism investment for Bà Nà Hills, which already draws millions of visitors annually and features attractions such as a replica French village, cable cars, Fantasy Park, and French gardens. The Golden Bridge’s dramatic setting—fog, mountain vistas and planted borders (purple lobelia/chrysanthemums)—and the oversized hands have generated major local and international attention, photo-ops, a bridal fashion show and new tourist traffic.

The story has been widely circulated alongside coverage of other notable, unusual footbridges worldwide, placing the Golden Bridge in the context of architecturally expressive pedestrian structures that function as both infrastructure and landmark.

Authors Christopher A. Thorstenson and A. D. Pazda (with supervision and revision by A. J. Elliot) designed and ran two experiments testing whether emotion alters color perception; Thorstenson drafted the manuscript and all authors approved submission.

Purpose and background
- Prior work shows emotion can influence low-level visual processing and that languages commonly pair emotions with colors (e.g., “feeling blue”), suggesting a possible link between mood and color perception.
- The authors hypothesized that induced sadness would alter color perception, possibly via mechanisms involving dopamine.

Methods
- Two experiments used film clips to induce mood and tested participants’ accuracy identifying highly desaturated color patches.
- Experiment 1: participants (n = 129 college students) viewed either a sad clip (a scene from The Lion King) or an amusing clip, then completed 48 trials identifying 24 desaturated patches (each shown twice) as red, yellow, green, or blue.
- Experiment 2: similar procedure but compared a sad clip to a neutral screensaver; all clips were converted to grayscale to control for color fatigue.
- Emotional state checks followed the mood inductions.

Key findings
- In both experiments, participants in the sad condition were less accurate at identifying colors on the blue–yellow axis but showed no impairment on the red–green axis.
- Amusement did not improve red–green performance relative to neutral, and grayscale conversion in Experiment 2 rules out a simple color-fatigue explanation.
- The specificity to the blue–yellow axis argues against a global reduction in arousal causing uniform color impairment.

Interpretation and implications
- The authors speculate dopamine may mediate the effect, since blue–yellow perception has been linked to dopamine-related conditions (e.g., ADHD, Parkinson’s), but they did not measure neurotransmitter levels here.
- Results support the notion that mood can exert “top-down” influences on perception: sadness may literally make the world look less colorful along particular chromatic dimensions.
- The findings add evidence to psychophysical links between emotion and basic sensory processing and suggest avenues for further work on neurochemical mechanisms.

Citation
- Thorstenson CA, Pazda AD, Elliot AJ. Sadness Impairs Color Perception. Psychological Science. 2015.

A magnitude ~9.0 earthquake and ensuing tsunami on March 11, 2011 severely damaged Japan’s northeastern coast and crippled the Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear complex, cutting power and disabling reactor cooling systems. Operators, facing overheating fuel and rising pressure, vented radioactive steam from Unit 1 despite knowing it contained hydrogen and risked an explosion. They judged the risk preferable to a total core meltdown. Hydrogen formed when zirconium cladding reacted with water as temperatures climbed, and the vented hydrogen later exploded, destroying the Unit 1 containment building. Authorities began last-ditch measures including continuous seawater and boron injection and efforts to restore electrical power to resume normal cooling.

Experts warned that if core temperatures rose further, fuel pellets could melt through the reactor vessel and containment, releasing large amounts of radioactive material, potentially prompting drastic measures (e.g., burial in cement and sand similar to Chernobyl) and rendering surrounding land uninhabitable for long periods. Officials declared states of emergency for six reactors at two nearby complexes and ordered local evacuations.

The disaster compounded massive human and infrastructure loss from the quake and tsunami: at least thousands dead and many more missing (national estimates at the time put the toll past 10,000 in hardest-hit areas), widespread destruction of towns, fuel shortages, frozen survivors in shelters without power or water, and major rescue and relief efforts mobilized including military and international assistance. The government described the situation as Japan’s worst crisis since World War II, warned of prolonged outages and rationing, and continued emergency operations amid ongoing fears of further explosions and radiation spread.

Fitch Ratings placed the United States' long‑term 'AAA' foreign and local currency Issuer Default Ratings and all outstanding U.S. sovereign debt securities on Rating Watch Negative (RWN) on 15 October 2013, and also put the U.S. short‑term foreign currency rating at 'F1+' on RWN. The long‑term outlook had already been negative; the U.S. country ceiling remains affirmed at 'AAA'. Fitch said it expects to resolve the RWN by the end of Q1 2014, subject to developments around any debt‑ceiling agreement.

Key drivers for the action
- High risk: Political brinkmanship over raising the federal debt ceiling, with the Treasury’s “extraordinary measures” expected to be exhausted around 17 October and cash reserves near $30bn, reduces financing flexibility and increases the risk of a default. Fitch highlighted uncertainty about whether the Treasury could legally prioritise debt service and warned of possible widespread payment delays (including to suppliers, employees and social security), which would harm U.S. sovereign creditworthiness and the economy.
- Medium risk: Repeated brinkmanship undermines confidence in government effectiveness, institutions and policy credibility, with some negative economic effects.
- Longer‑term fiscal concerns: Although the U.S. retains strong fundamentals—large, diversified economy; reserve currency status; deep Treasury markets; rule of law; and improving fiscal metrics—public debt remains high. Fitch notes the federal deficit has halved since 2010 and projects debt stabilising around 72% (federal) and 104% (general government) of GDP over the medium term, below Fitch’s thresholds for losing 'AAA'. Still, elevated debt levels leave the U.S. vulnerable to shocks absent further fiscal reform.

Potential outcomes and sensitivities
- A failure to make interest or principal payments on time would prompt downgrade to 'Restricted Default' until cured, and affected securities could be downgraded (to 'B+' for issues in default).
- If a debt‑ceiling deal is reached, Fitch will reassess taking into account the deal’s terms, duration and the perceived likelihood of recurrence, plus implications for institutional effectiveness, funding costs and medium‑term fiscal consolidation prospects.

Assumptions
- Fitch assumes an agreement will ultimately be reached to end the impasse and that Treasury securities will continue to be honoured. Its fiscal projections incorporate CBO assumptions and factor in recent BEA GDP revisions (which lower debt/GDP ratios statistically) but have modestly reduced near‑term growth forecasts (2013: 1.6%; 2014: 2.6%).

Bottom line: Fitch put the U.S. 'AAA' ratings on negative watch because the ongoing debt‑ceiling standoff and risk of payment disruptions threaten confidence in U.S. creditworthiness and the dollar’s reserve role; while the U.S. retains strong economic fundamentals and some fiscal improvement, high debt levels and political risk could prompt a downgrade if a default or similar episodes occur.

Chelsea Handler has moved her late-night show Chelsea Lately from a small Santa Monica studio to the larger Stage 1 at Universal Studios, a space previously used by The Jack Benny Show and Conan O’Brien’s Tonight Show. The upgrade expands audience capacity from 75 to 200 while retaining an intimate, participatory vibe that’s central to Handler’s standup-based format. The new studio offers improved sound and lighting and personal conveniences Handler highlighted with humor—most notably a private shower so she no longer has to walk past queued audience members in a robe. Handler joked about staging bigger bits (including animal entrances for sidekick Chuy Bravo) and plans to involve the audience in onstage antics. Jennifer Aniston will be the first guest in the new studio, followed by Fergie, Miley Cyrus and Christina Aguilera; Handler says she feels committed to the show and ready to go “full throttle.” The move was marked by a comedic shower sketch featuring Sandra Bullock.

British police probing Madeleine McCann’s 2007 disappearance have contacted Australian authorities after skeletal remains of a fair‑haired child were found inside a suitcase beside a rural highway near Wynarka, South Australia, earlier this month. The remains, believed to be of a girl about 2–4 (or possibly up to 7) years old, were discovered by a passing motorist and had likely been dumped weeks to months earlier. Clothing and a distinctive handmade quilt with identifiable fabric patches were found with the body; police say some fabric was manufactured in New York around 2008. Forensic indicators suggest the child was killed elsewhere some time after 2007 and that foul play was involved.

Scotland Yard has made inquiries, but Australian investigators stress there is currently no evidence linking the remains to Madeleine McCann. South Australia’s Detective Superintendent Des Bray and Police Commissioner Grant Stevens emphasized the investigation is focused on domestic leads and on identifying the child, noting it is “highly unlikely” to be McCann. Authorities have released images of the quilt’s patches and other items to the public and received a large volume of tips. Forensic testing is under way and police urge anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

An 86-year-old Port St. Lucie man, William J. Hager, has been arrested and charged with first‑degree premeditated murder after telling deputies he shot his 78‑year‑old wife, Carolyn Hager, because she was ill and he could not afford her medications. Deputies were called to the Meadowlark Lane home on May 16 after Hager phoned them and invited them in, saying, “I have bad news. I shot my wife at 7:30 this morning. I want to apologize I didn’t call earlier. I wanted to tell my kids what happened first.” Officers found Carolyn dead of a gunshot wound to the head.

According to the arrest affidavit, William Hager said he had contemplated killing his wife for several days because she was in pain; she had reportedly told him she wanted to die in the past but never explicitly asked to be killed. Neighbors and officials described Carolyn as suffering long‑term ailments, including severe arthritis, and the couple had financial difficulties (they filed for bankruptcy in 2011). Hager reportedly drank coffee and called his daughters after the shooting before contacting authorities. He was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail without bond. Officials noted that community resources exist for people struggling to afford care and medications.

Researchers have discovered a large, year‑round “snow aquifer” beneath parts of the Greenland ice sheet: a slushy, liquid‑water layer held in firn (partly compacted snow) that covers roughly 70,000 km² (about the size of Ireland or West Virginia) in southeast and some southern/southwestern regions. Drilling in 2011 and 2013 and radar surveys showed liquid water persisting through winter — even when air temperatures reached about −15 °C — because thick late‑season snowfall insulates the buried firn and prevents freezing.

The team estimates the aquifer contains on the order of 140 billion tonnes of water, equivalent to about 0.4 mm of global sea‑level rise if released to the ocean (roughly half Greenland’s current annual contribution). However, key unknowns remain: the age of the water, whether and how quickly it drains to the ocean, and whether it is hydraulically connected to basal drainage systems that could lubricate glaciers. The presence of this large liquid reservoir adds complexity to Greenland’s hydrology, can act as a heat sink, and may help explain some discrepancies between modelled and observed mass loss. Researchers plan further work to determine the aquifer’s dynamics and its implications for future sea‑level rise.

Democratic strategist and CNN contributor Hilary Rosen sparked bipartisan backlash after saying on CNN that Ann Romney has “never worked a day in her life.” Rosen’s remark — meant to argue that Ann Romney hasn’t had to both raise children and earn a paycheck like most American women — was widely condemned as dismissive of stay‑at‑home mothers and insensitive given Ann Romney’s record as a full‑time mom who raised five sons and battled MS and breast cancer.
