Ann Romney posted her first-ever tweet in response, saying staying home and raising five boys “was hard work.” Obama campaign figures including Jim Messina and David Axelrod publicly disavowed Rosen’s comments, and others from both parties and Romney’s family defended Ann Romney. Rosen stood by her point on Twitter and in a Huffington Post piece, arguing her critique targeted Mitt Romney’s use of his wife as an authority on women’s economic concerns, not Ann personally, and stressing that most American women must both work and care for children.

The incident amplified the campaign’s gender politics: it gave Republicans material to show Democratic insensitivity to stay‑at‑home moms, while Democrats could use the episode to question whether Ann Romney’s experience aligns with the economic struggles of many women. Rosen later revised her blog post to remove a more provocative line about Mitt Romney “hiding behind his wife’s skirt.”

A 14-year-old Cuban boy, Emanuel Zayas, died after surgery in Miami to remove a massive facial tumor. Zayas and his family had traveled from Cuba for the operation at Holtz Children’s Hospital at Jackson Memorial. Surgeons said the 10-pound growth—benign but huge enough to risk suffocation or neck injury—was caused by polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, a condition where scar-like tissue replaces bone. Dr. Robert Marx, chief of oral and maxillofacial surgery for the University of Miami Health System, said the physiological stress of the procedure was too great for Emanuel’s compromised anatomy and that efforts to save him were unsuccessful. The family has decided to donate his body to science to help researchers better understand the disease.

A Minnesota couple anonymously donated a $500,000 personal check by dropping it into a Salvation Army red kettle at a Cub Foods in Rosemount over the weekend — the largest single kettle gift ever recorded for the Twin Cities and, confirmed by national headquarters, the biggest single kettle donation in the country. The check cleared the bank. Salvation Army spokespeople said the donors have given large kettle gifts before (with advance notice) but never at this scale and asked to remain anonymous. They said their motivations included honoring a father who served in World War I and remembered the Army’s coffee-and-doughnut service to soldiers, and repaying help they once received when money was tight and they survived on discarded grocery food. The gift far surpasses the previous Twin Cities record of $25,000 and boosts the Twin Cities campaign toward its $11.6 million Christmas goal; the charity had raised about $2.2 million so far. Separately, an anonymous benefactor known as “St. Grand” has been leaving roughly $1,100 in kettles at local stores in recent days. The Salvation Army continues to seek kettle volunteers and stressed that every dollar helps fund toys, meals, shelter and groceries for people in need this season.

Indiewire published its annual Oscars prediction charts for the 86th Academy Awards (winners to be announced March 2, 2014), including categories from Best Picture through technical awards, and offered an awards-season newsletter.

Ellen DeGeneres was announced as host for the March 2, 2014 broadcast — her second time emceeing (she previously hosted in 2007). She announced the news on Twitter and in a press release, joking about “the third time’s the charm.” Producers Craig Zadan and Neil Meron, rehired in April to helm the ceremony, praised DeGeneres’s comic warmth and broad appeal. Their decision was made under outgoing Academy president Hawk Koch and later endorsed by newly elected Academy president Cheryl Boone Isaacs.

Choosing DeGeneres signals a tonal shift after criticism of Seth MacFarlane’s 2013 hosting (notably a controversial song about actresses’ nudity). Zadan and Meron defended MacFarlane’s entertainment value and noted strong ratings for that show. The 86th Academy Awards will air on ABC; Indiewire will update its prediction charts in the lead-up.

On December 16, 2014, seven Taliban gunmen wearing suicide vests stormed the Army Public School and Degree College in Peshawar, northwest Pakistan, in the deadliest terrorist attack in the country’s recent history. The militants scaled an undefended rear wall after a diversionary car explosion, entered classrooms and an exam auditorium, and proceeded room to room shooting pupils and staff. Security forces and Special Services Group commandos engaged the attackers during an hours‑long siege; all seven attackers were later killed. 

Official tallies put the death toll at about 141–145 people: roughly 132 children (mostly aged 12–16), 9–10 school staff, and several soldiers; more than 100 people were wounded. Survivors described extreme brutality—students and teachers shot at close range, some burned, bodies and pools of blood in corridors—and harrowing escapes as rescuers evacuated pupils to hospitals. Parents, medical staff and volunteers scrambled to donate blood and identify the dead. The school’s principal and several teachers were among the victims.

The Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) claimed responsibility, saying the attack was revenge for military operations in tribal areas; the TTP also asserted they intended to target older boys. The massacre prompted nationwide grief, mass funerals, a three‑day mourning period and international condemnation. Pakistan’s government and military vowed a harder line against militants, including resuming strikes in militant strongholds and ending a moratorium on the death penalty for terrorism cases. The atrocity intensified debate over security at vulnerable institutions and underscored the persistent capacity of the TTP to carry out large‑scale, indiscriminate violence.

Summary:

President Barack Obama’s medical reports and public appearances have repeatedly noted his ongoing struggle to quit smoking and his frequent use of nicotine gum. White House physician Navy Capt. Jeffrey Kuhlman’s examinations described Obama as generally in “excellent” health but recommended continued “smoking cessation efforts,” including nicotine gum, and advised dietary changes to lower borderline-high cholesterol. The 90‑minute 2011 physical found slightly elevated total cholesterol and LDL, mild tendinitis and some left‑knee issues likely tied to basketball, good vital signs and fitness otherwise, and routine follow‑ups for colon cancer screening and leg-strengthening exercise.

Obama’s visible gum chewing—often Nicorette—has drawn media attention and criticism at several high‑profile events (APEC in Beijing, D-Day ceremonies, India’s Republic Day parade, Air Force One, campaign stops). Critics, including some foreign commentators and conservative pundits, called it disrespectful or undignified, especially in diplomatic settings. Others pointed out gum’s widespread popularity in China and questioned the criticism. Obama has acknowledged a lifelong struggle with smoking and supports anti‑tobacco measures aimed at keeping youth from starting.

Hackers linked to Anonymous in Mexico took down at least two websites tied to Pope Benedict XVI’s upcoming visit, claiming the trip is a political maneuver to bolster the conservative National Action Party (PAN) ahead of Mexico’s July 1 presidential election. The Mexican Episcopal Conference said its papal-visit page was blocked by a “cyber attack,” disrupting logistics and event information for the pope’s itinerary in Guanajuato, a PAN-governed, heavily Catholic state. Anonymous IberoAmerica credited operations named “Pharisee” and “freeloader,” and Anonymous Mexico posted a video arguing the visit wastes public money that could aid the poor and will be used by PAN to win Catholic votes. Calderon’s office noted the invitation to the pope dated from 2007.

Other sites with travel and event details and the Guanajuato state government site also went offline amid unclear causes. Some critics questioned the pope’s choice not to visit Mexico City, citing its legalization of abortion and gay marriage and the Vatican’s claim about high altitude. 

The pope begins a three-day visit Friday, also addressing widespread drug-related violence that has killed roughly 50,000 people in five years. Security is extensive; local clergy urged calm despite past narco-intimidation and recent banners from a La Familia offshoot promising not to attack during the visit. Officials expect the pope to speak on violence, moral guidance and social cohesion. His itinerary includes a meeting with President Felipe Calderón and a large open-air Mass in Guanajuato.

Chicago health officials have warned the public after an outbreak of severe bleeding linked to use of synthetic cannabinoids (commonly called “K2,” “spice,” or “fake weed”). Since early March, Illinois hospitals have treated dozens of patients reporting unusual, significant bleeding—nosebleeds, bleeding gums, bloody urine, coughing up blood, bleeding from eyes or ears, and heavier menstrual bleeding. The Illinois Department of Public Health first reported 17 severe-bleeding cases; that number rose to 32 cases statewide, concentrated in the Chicago area and especially in the Peoria/Tazewell region. No deaths have been reported.

Investigators shut down a Lawndale corner store after finding potentially deadly synthetic cannabis for sale, and officials say many patients reported obtaining products from convenience stores, dealers or friends. Synthetic cannabinoids are mixtures of many man-made chemicals that act on the same brain receptors as THC and can cause hallucinations, psychosis, kidney failure and violent behavior. Severe bleeding is an unusual and newly observed symptom; its cause is unknown, though a recent change in product formulation or contaminants is suspected. Because manufacturers frequently tweak compounds to evade bans, the exact chemicals involved and a single common source have not yet been identified.

Public health officials advise people not to use any synthetic cannabinoid products and to seek emergency care (call 911 or go to an ER) if they experience unexplained bleeding or bruising. Authorities continue to investigate and track cases.

A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to immediately restore CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s White House press credentials and re-activate his “hard pass,” granting him access while CNN’s lawsuit over the revocation proceeds. U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, granted a temporary restraining order after finding that the White House’s decision-making was opaque and likely violated due process under the Fifth Amendment; he noted that once the White House opens its grounds to reporters, First Amendment protections apply. The judge also found Acosta would suffer irreparable harm and rejected the government’s claim that CNN could simply rely on other reporters.

Acosta’s pass had been pulled after a heated Nov. 7 news conference with President Trump and a disputed interaction with a White House intern over a microphone. The White House’s explanations for the suspension shifted—from alleging improper physical contact to saying Acosta was unprofessional—and included a circulated edited video that exaggerated the encounter. In court, government lawyers argued the president has broad discretion to exclude reporters and that Acosta could cover the president by other means; CNN argued the ban was unprecedented, arbitrary, and constituted viewpoint discrimination and denial of due process.

Following the ruling Acosta returned to the White House. Trump said the administration would write new rules to satisfy the court’s concerns and vowed to continue the legal fight; the White House press secretary emphasized there is no absolute First Amendment right to access the White House. The case drew wide media attention and support from numerous news organizations and the White House Correspondents’ Association, which warned against granting the president unfettered authority to bar reporters. Further briefing in the litigation was ordered by the judge.

This document compiles several archaeological and historical reports about ancient symbols and large-scale ground artworks from different regions and periods.

Swastika: ancient origins and Nazi appropriation
- The swastika is a hooked-cross motif with a history of at least 5,000 years, appearing across Neolithic Eurasia and later in Europe, India, Indonesia and other cultures. The Sanskrit name svastika means “good fortune” or “well‑being,” and it remains a sacred symbol in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism.
- Nineteenth‑century archaeology (notably Heinrich Schliemann’s finds at Troy) revived interest in the motif. That revival was co‑opted by nationalist and racialist movements that sought to assert an “Aryan” heritage.
- The Nazi Party formally adopted the swastika (Hakenkreuz) in 1920. Under the Nazis it became the central emblem of propaganda and racial ideology—used on flags, armbands, posters and insignia—and thus its public meaning was irrevocably transformed into an emblem associated with hate and genocide.
- The text quotes Hitler’s description of the flag design in Mein Kampf and notes that the swastika had also been used by other post–World War I far‑right groups in Germany before the Nazis monopolized it.

Geoglyph discoveries across Eurasia and Central Asia
- A large elk/deer geoglyph was identified near Lake Zjuratkul in the Ural Mountains of Russia via historical Google Earth imagery. The stone figure measures about 275 meters (900 feet) across; fieldwork shows a complex stone construction with larger edge stones, inner fills, passageways and small walls. Lithic artifacts and tool types recovered suggest a Neolithic–Eneolithic (4th–3rd millennium B.C.) date, which—if confirmed—would make it significantly older than Peru’s Nazca Lines. Researchers link it to a regional megalithic tradition that includes hundreds of stone monuments and island megalithic complexes.
- Over 50 geoglyphs were discovered across the northern Kazakh steppe using Google Earth. These earthen‑mound geoglyphs form squares, rings, crosses and even swastikas, ranging roughly 90–400 meters (295–1,312 feet) in diameter. Excavations and surveys by Kostanay University and partners have found hearths and structural remains at some sites, suggesting ritual use; dating and interpretation remain preliminary. Such geoglyphs may mark territory or have ceremonial functions, but their exact purpose and builders are unknown.
- The Middle East contains thousands of stone “wheel” structures—circular monuments with radiating spokes—across Jordan, Syria and Saudi Arabia. Often visible only from the air, these wheels (25–70 meters across) and related stone landscapes (kites, pendants, walls) have been known since early aerial reports and are now extensively mapped with satellite imagery. They appear to be at least 2,000 years old, though dating is difficult without excavation. The wheels’ functions are debated: possibilities include ritual or funerary uses, astronomical or seasonal markers, or other social practices. Associations with cairns and spatial clustering suggest complex cultural roles; like other geoglyphs worldwide, their meaning remains enigmatic.

Broader context
- Geoglyphs are a global phenomenon: aside from Peru’s Nazca Lines, similar large ground designs have been found in Central Asia, Russia, the Middle East, Britain, Brazil and North America. High‑resolution satellite imagery and programs like Google Earth have greatly expanded their discovery and study.
- Scholars emphasize the need for more fieldwork, dating (including paleoenvironmental studies), and careful excavation to establish chronologies and cultural attributions. Many of these large-scale landscapes likely served ritual, territorial or commemorative purposes, but concrete interpretations remain tentative.

References and further reading are cited for the swastika’s history and the Antiquity article and LiveScience coverage are noted for the geoglyph discoveries.

NASA researchers using a new satellite-based method have for the first time mapped the regional extent and impact of "understory fires"—low, slow-burning fires that occur beneath the Amazon canopy and have been largely hidden by the treetops. Analysis for 1999–2010 shows these fires burned over 33,000 square miles (85,500 km²), about 2.8% of the forest, and in peak years (e.g., 2005, 2007, 2010) affected several times more forest area than cleared by agricultural deforestation.

Key findings
- Understory fires burn slowly (a few feet per minute) with short flames but can last weeks and kill 10–50% of trees in burned areas; recovery is slow.
- At regional scale, climate conditions—especially low nighttime humidity and low soil moisture—are the main controls on when and where understory fires occur, not the rate of adjacent deforestation.
- People provide ignition sources (campfires, cigarettes, land-management fires, etc.), but severe understory fire seasons are preceded by dry conditions detectable months earlier by satellites (AIRS for humidity; GRACE for soil water storage).
- There was no positive correlation between high deforestation years (2003–2004) and understory fire incidence; some of the largest understory fire events occurred in areas without recent clearing, including indigenous reserves.
- Because understory fires kill many canopy trees over large areas, they likely contribute significant carbon emissions that are not yet well quantified in climate models.

Implications
This new ability to detect and map understory fires changes understanding of Amazon fire impacts, highlights the importance of climate and soil moisture monitoring for fire risk, and suggests a need to include understory-fire emissions in carbon accounting and to target both human ignition sources and climate-driven vulnerability in mitigation efforts.

On 3 June The Guardian published an interview in which Michael Douglas said his throat cancer "is caused by HPV, which actually comes from cunnilingus." Douglas’s publicist Allen Burry later insisted the actor did not say oral sex was the cause of his own cancer, only that oral sex (via HPV) is one known cause of some oral cancers. The Guardian rejects that characterization and posted audio and a verbatim transcript of the exchange, in which Douglas links HPV to oral sex. In subsequent remarks while being honored by the American Cancer Society, Douglas framed his comments as a PSA about HPV — a sexually transmitted virus that can cause oral cancer and for which vaccines exist — and denied he was definitively attributing his personal illness to oral sex. His publicist declined to say whether Douglas tested positive for HPV. Other coverage noted reactions from family and the press.

Study overview
- A UK population-based cross-sectional survey (UCL Bereavement Study) examined whether bereavement by suicide confers specific risk for suicide-related outcomes in young adults. The sample comprised 3,432 staff and students aged 18–40 across 37 higher education institutions who reported a sudden bereavement of a close friend or relative since age 10.
- Respondents were classified by perceived mode of death: sudden natural, sudden unnatural (eg, accidents), or suicide. Analyses adjusted for nine a priori confounders including age, gender, socioeconomic status, kinship, prebereavement depression and suicidal behaviour, and used HEI as a clustering variable.

Key findings
- Compared with those bereaved by sudden natural causes, people bereaved by suicide had a higher probability of making a suicide attempt after the bereavement (adjusted OR 1.65; p=0.012) — roughly a 65% increased odds, translating to an absolute risk approaching about 1 in 10 in this sample — and were more likely to have dropped out of education or work (AOR 1.80; p=0.005).
- When suicide-bereaved people were compared with those bereaved by other sudden unnatural causes, there were no significant differences in postbereavement suicidal ideation or suicide attempt; however, suicide bereavement was associated with worse social functioning (AOR 1.46; p=0.005).
- Kinship (blood-related versus non-blood-related, including friends) did not modify associations: elevated risk applied to peers as well as relatives.
- Perceived stigma about the death was higher among those bereaved by suicide. Adding stigma to models attenuated the associations between suicide bereavement and both suicide attempt and occupational drop-out (effects became non-significant), suggesting stigma and reduced help-seeking may mediate part of the effect.
- Sensitivity analyses (including exclusion of older deceased, student-only or women-only subsamples) generally supported the main findings, though accounting for repeated exposure to multiple sudden bereavements attenuated associations.

Interpretation and implications
- The study provides evidence that bereavement by suicide is specifically associated with increased risk of suicide attempt (vs sudden natural bereavement) among young adults, independent of prebereavement psychopathology, and that this risk extends to friends and non-blood relatives.
- Stigma may be an important modifiable factor linking suicide bereavement to adverse outcomes; reducing stigma and improving post-loss community and clinical support may help mitigate risk.
- Clinicians and risk assessment protocols should consider suicide history not only in blood relatives but also among friends and non-blood contacts. Employers should be aware of potential occupational impacts and support return to work.
- The authors call for trials of interventions for people bereaved by suicide and further research on moderators of risk and the causal role of stigma.

Strengths and limitations
- Strengths: large national sampling frame, access to non–help-seeking young adults, use of two bereaved control groups (sudden natural and sudden unnatural), adjustment for prebereavement psychopathology, and validated outcome measures.
- Limitations: HEI-based sample over-represented women and more highly educated individuals (limiting generalisability to other young adults and men), potential selection and recall biases, reliance on respondents’ subjective classification of mode of death, possible residual confounding (eg, substance misuse, financial hardship), and inability to precisely estimate response rates or count multiple distinct exposures per respondent.

Bottom line
Bereavement by suicide in young adults is associated with a higher risk of subsequent suicide attempt and with worse occupational functioning compared with bereavement by sudden natural causes. Perceived stigma appears to attenuate these associations, highlighting stigma reduction and improved post-bereavement support as promising targets for prevention and intervention.

When Jane Austen died in 1817 her portable writing desk passed through family hands and in 1999 was entrusted to the British Library. Stored in a drawer were three pairs of spectacles long believed by family tradition to have belonged to Austen. The Library had the lenses tested for the first time (with conservation oversight and assistance from Birmingham Optical). All three were convex (“plus”) lenses consistent with longsightedness and use for close work; however the strengths vary markedly:

- Wire-framed: R +1.75 / L +1.75  
- Tortoiseshell A: R +3.25 / L +3.25  
- Tortoiseshell B: R +5.00/-0.25 x84 / L +4.75/-0.25 x49

London optometrist Professor Simon Barnard suggested several explanations: Austen may simply have needed progressively stronger reading glasses over time, or the strongest pair was for very close tasks like fine embroidery. More speculatively, progressive worsening of prescriptions could signal a pathological process such as cataract formation. Barnard and the Library note that arsenic poisoning—common in 19th‑century medicines, some water supplies and household items—can cause cataracts and skin pigmentation, and has previously been proposed (notably by writer Lindsay Ashford) as a possible accidental contributor to Austen’s death. Other historically proposed causes include Addison’s disease, Hodgkin’s lymphoma and cancer.

The Library cautions that several uncertainties limit firm conclusions: there is no proof the glasses were prescribed for, worn by, or even owned by Austen (they could have been purchased off‑the‑shelf), and changing prescriptions can have multiple causes (e.g., diabetes, though it was often fatal then). The Library published the test results to solicit further input from eye specialists and scholars; the spectacles are now on display in its Treasures Gallery and have already attracted interest from literary scholars exploring Austen’s references to eyewear.

Summary:

Forty coffins carrying some of the first recovered victims of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 were flown from Kharkiv, Ukraine, to Eindhoven, the Netherlands, on Dutch and Australian military aircraft. They were met at Eindhoven air base by relatives, Prime Minister Mark Rutte and members of the Dutch royal family amid nationwide mourning: bells tolled, flags flew at half-mast, a minute’s silence was observed and a silent march took place in Amsterdam. The coffins were transferred to hearses and taken to the Korporaal van Oudheusden barracks in Hilversum, where a formal identification process using DNA, dental records and fingerprints will begin; Dutch officials warned identification could take weeks or months. Two more planes were expected the following day and roughly 200 victims’ remains are anticipated to be flown out this week, though more than 80 bodies were believed still at the crash site.

International teams, including a nine-member UK disaster victim identification unit, will assist the Dutch-led effort. There is controversy and concern over recovery conditions and handling of remains: Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott warned some bodies might still be exposed at the site, and UK sources allege separatists tampered with evidence and moved bodies. Separatist leaders said they delayed moving remains awaiting experts; the OSCE denied advising them to leave bodies in place.

Investigations continued: the Dutch air safety board reported the cockpit voice recorder had been successfully downloaded, and Western intelligence officials presented evidence pointing to an SA-11 surface-to-air missile fired in eastern Ukraine, with analysts suggesting rebels may have mistaken the airliner for another aircraft. Meanwhile, fighting in eastern Ukraine persisted, complicating recovery and probe efforts.

This collection of articles and commentary covers the 2015 Met Gala — its spectacle, notable outfits, celebrity drama and context — with a focus on standout looks and reactions.

Key points:
- Solange Knowles arrived in a Giles printed mini dress with a striking 3-D, fan-like silhouette, continuing her reputation for eccentric, statement-making fashion. Her Instagram quip noted Cartier as her “date.”
- Beyoncé drew criticism for arriving two hours late and for a revealing dress some compared unfavorably to past Met missteps.
- Sarah Jessica Parker made a major impression wearing a Philip Treacy flame-like headpiece that instantly became meme fodder; online viewers likened it to everything from emojis and pop-culture villains to the Human Torch.
- Other attendees drew mixed reviews: Jennifer Connelly’s lace Louis Vuitton look and Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Roland Mouret gown were called fashion failures by some critics for ill-fitting or confusing silhouettes. Anne Hathaway’s Ralph Lauren gown was noted for evoking Star Wars/Jawa/Jedi aesthetics in a playful, nerdy-pleasing way.
- The pieces remind readers why the Met Gala is such a cultural moment: an elite, high-profile fundraiser for the Costume Institute (2015’s exhibit: “China: Through the Looking Glass”), hosted by Anna Wintour with celebrity co-chairs, where daring fashion, celebrity behavior and occasional controversy (notably last year’s widely seen elevator incident involving Solange, Jay Z and Beyoncé) dominate the conversation.
- Coverage highlighted how attendees’ looks generate immediate online reaction and memes, and noted increased scrutiny of celebrity behavior and security after past leaks, while filmmakers were documenting the event, which may temper on-camera antics.

Summary:

Gary McKinnon, a 43-year-old British man with Asperger’s syndrome, faces extradition to the United States on charges of hacking into Pentagon and NASA computers. Medical evidence submitted by consultant psychiatrist Professor Jeremy Turk described McKinnon as suffering severe major depressive disorder, anxiety and panic attacks, and a fixed belief that he would kill himself rather than be extradited; the report warned suicide was an “almost certain inevitability.” Despite this, Home Secretary Alan Johnson decided not to block extradition on medical or human-rights grounds, saying the new material was not materially different from evidence previously considered by the High Court, which upheld the extradition earlier in the year. Johnson also noted assurances from US authorities that McKinnon’s needs would be met and that he would not, if convicted, serve time in a supermax prison; the Government would pursue repatriation if required.

The decision provoked strong criticism from McKinnon’s family, MPs, campaigners and the National Autistic Society, who called it cruel and dangerous and announced plans to seek a judicial review. McKinnon’s lawyers said they would pursue emergency legal remedies but have been given only seven days to file for review; they warned his life could be at risk and compared the situation to a death-row case. Critics also renewed concerns about the Extradition Act 2003, arguing it disadvantages UK citizens by requiring less evidence from US authorities than the UK must provide when extraditing Americans. Legal sources suggested McKinnon could be extradited by Christmas if judicial challenges fail. McKinnon maintains he hacked in search of UFO information; US authorities allege he caused significant damage to military systems.

The TF-2 (also called the Transition in coverage) is a three-part road-air transport system designed to let passengers ride a single cabin that transfers between a road vehicle and an aircraft, so users can travel door-to-door without changing vehicles. It combines VTOL-like vertical/short-field capability (takes off like a helicopter and then flies like an airplane) with highway driving using electric propulsion, modern materials and manufacturing for safety and reliability.

Key facts:
- Classification: Designed as an FAA "light sport" aircraft (max 1,320 lb), but the manufacturer exceeded that by ~120 lb to include required road-vehicle safety features. The FAA granted an exemption allowing it to remain in the light-sport category.
- Configuration: Two-seat vehicle with folding wings (electrically actuated) and a rear-facing propeller for flight; front-wheel drive for road use.
- Performance: Cruise speed ~115 mph, range ~460 miles, useful load ~450 lb, fuel efficiency ~30 mpg on roads. It needs a ~1,700-foot runway to take off and can fit in a standard garage.
- Safety/utility: Company emphasizes the ability to drive home in bad weather instead of flying as a safety advantage.
- Commercial: Priced around $194,000; about 70 orders placed with $10,000 deposits held in escrow (refundable if the company fails before delivery).

Source: The Register.

Iran said it will bolster its naval presence in the Persian Gulf to reinforce control over three islands — Greater and Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa — whose sovereignty is disputed by the United Arab Emirates. IRGC Commander Mohammad Ali Jafari announced the creation of a fifth "naval defense zone" at Bandar Lengeh and said the Revolutionary Guards were expanding and improving naval defensive capabilities specifically to protect Iran’s islands. The long-running 41-year dispute, inflamed by a presidential visit to Abu Musa and repeated UAE protests calling Iran’s presence an occupation, has strained Tehran’s relations with Arab neighbors; Tehran has at times signaled it might downgrade ties over the issue. 

Separately, Iranian media report a domestically built VTOL (vertical take-off and landing) drone that can hover and reportedly operate silently will be unveiled in February. Iran has previously claimed drone-derived imagery of Israeli sites and frequent unmanned incursions from Lebanon — assertions Israel disputes — and such Iranian military-technology claims are typically difficult to independently verify.

Portland officials drained 38 million gallons from Mt. Tabor’s Reservoir 5 after surveillance showed an 18-year-old, identified as Dallas Swonger (also reported as Dallas Delynn), apparently urinating near the open-air drinking reservoir early Wednesday. Tests of the reservoir water the next day found no urine-related toxins, and public-health experts said any urine would have been extremely diluted and not likely to pose a health risk. Still, city leaders — citing an abundance of water and advice from utility professionals — decided to empty and clean the reservoir to eliminate even minimal risk. The decision drew national and international ridicule and local criticism as wasteful; proponents of a proposed independent water district called the move a public-relations choice and said a different board might act differently. Swonger and two friends received trespassing citations; Swonger was also cited for public urination and may face additional charges. In interviews he insisted he urinated on a wall next to the reservoir, not into the water, and expressed frustration at becoming a national laughingstock. The episode comes amid ongoing controversy in Portland over open-air reservoirs, which must be taken offline under federal rules.

Summary:

British police temporarily stopped sharing Manchester Arena investigation material with US authorities after a series of leaks to US media, including the bomber’s name and graphic forensic photos of bomb debris and a bloodstained backpack. The leaks—published notably by the New York Times and earlier reported in US outlets—provoked fury across Whitehall, among police chiefs and families of victims, and prompted Prime Minister Theresa May to raise the issue with President Trump at a NATO summit. US officials said they condemned the leaks and promised investigations; sharing of other intelligence continued and the information-sharing pause was lifted after “fresh assurances.”

Attack and investigation:
- The suicide bombing at an Ariana Grande concert on 22 May killed 22 people (including an 8-year-old) and injured many others (116 reported; dozens hospitalized, some in critical care).
- Salman Abedi, a 22‑year‑old Manchester-born man of Libyan descent, was identified as the bomber. CCTV and travel records show recent movements including transit through Dusseldorf and trips to Libya; he may have returned from Libya days before the attack.
- Police and security services treat the event as networked rather than a lone-wolf incident. Eight men have been arrested in the UK (including Abedi’s older brother); Abedi’s father and younger brother were detained in Libya, where officials say the younger brother confessed to knowledge of the plot.
- Raids and controlled explosions were carried out at multiple addresses; investigators say searches have recovered “very important” material and are pursuing accomplices and links abroad. Security forces raised the UK threat level to “critical” and deployed troops to protect key sites.

Bomb analysis and concerns:
- Published forensic images and official preliminary assessments indicate a carefully packed improvised explosive device that used metal nuts and screws as shrapnel, a substantial 12‑volt lead‑acid battery as a power source, and a lightweight metal container concealed in a backpack or vest. Evidence suggested high-velocity blast effects and a possible switch in the bomber’s left hand.
- Officials worry the released images may hinder the investigation and could aid future bomb-makers; police stressed that intelligence-sharing depends on strict controls and trust.

Wider reaction and context:
- The leaks strained the UK–US intelligence relationship and prompted internal reviews in the US; British police described the disclosures as an “unauthorised disclosure” that risked undermining the investigation and causing distress to victims’ families.
- The Queen visited injured victims; the city of Manchester held vigils and large symbolic gestures of unity (including a joint £1m donation by Manchester’s football clubs).
- Authorities reiterated limits on monitoring resources—Abedi was reportedly a former “subject of interest” for MI5 but not under active surveillance—and stressed the difficulty of prioritizing among thousands on counter‑terrorism lists.

Investigations into the origin of the leaks and fuller inquiries into Abedi’s network and possible bomb-makers remain ongoing.

A controversy arose over whether President Donald Trump used the word “shithole” or the similar-sounding “shithouse” during a contentious immigration meeting where he reportedly disparaged Haiti and some African countries. Some attendees, including Senators David Perdue and Tom Cotton, have defended Trump or said they don’t recall the specific word used. National Review’s Rich Lowry told ABC’s This Week that his sources say Trump said “shithouse” (pronounced like “S-house”) rather than “shithole,” though Lowry added that Trump’s broader remarks and the general tone of the discussion were accurately reported. The story sparked debate on Sunday morning shows about whether the president’s comments were misrepresented.

Chelsea Manning, the transgender former Army intelligence analyst who leaked more than 700,000 military and State Department records to WikiLeaks, gave her first major interviews since being freed from the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth after seven years. Manning said she felt a responsibility to the public and was driven by the human cost she witnessed in Iraq—“death, destruction and mayhem”—which transformed sterile reports into people and prompted her to spark public debate by leaking the documents. She maintained she did not believe the disclosures would harm national security, accepted personal responsibility for her actions and said no one directed her to leak.

Convicted by a military tribunal on multiple counts (but acquitted of the most serious charge of aiding the enemy), Manning was sentenced to 35 years; President Barack Obama commuted the sentence to time served shortly before leaving office. Manning remains in the Army but is off duty while appealing her court-martial conviction.

She described severe struggles during incarceration, including two suicide attempts and a fight to receive hormone treatment for gender dysphoria—care she and her lawyers say was crucial and ultimately helped change military policy on transgender prisoners. Since release on May 17, Manning has been documenting daily life on social media, expressed gratitude to Obama for the commutation, and said she still respects the military and the people who serve.

Swiss voters will decide on June 5 whether to adopt a nationwide unconditional basic income — a first for any country. The proposal, driven onto the ballot through Switzerland’s direct-democracy process by artists and intellectuals, would guarantee every adult citizen and legal resident a tax-free payment of about $2,600 per month and $650 per child, regardless of employment or wealth. The benefit would replace existing social payments up to that amount and would be partially funded by raising the value-added tax among other measures.

Supporters argue the stipend would let people cut hours, increase motivation, and stabilize the economy; some younger voters say it would meaningfully help them. Critics — including parliamentarians and the government — warn it would damage work incentives, threaten the current social system, and require large tax hikes or spending cuts to cover an estimated annual cost near $200 billion. Polls indicate the measure is likely to be defeated, but its national vote is seen as a significant milestone for the basic-income movement and fuels debate about similar policies elsewhere, including the United States.

Admiral Mike Mullen, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, warned that suicides and other family crises among U.S. service members are likely to rise as large numbers of troops return to home stations after years of repeated deployments. With the Iraq drawdown accelerating, installations such as Fort Lewis and Fort Hood are seeing unprecedented influxes of soldiers who will spend extended time back with families — a period when many service members face accumulated stresses like PTSD, financial and relationship problems, substance abuse and the effects of multiple deployments.

Mullen said suicide is the military’s urgent emergency, noting rising suicide rates across all service branches since 2004 and record highs in the Army. He predicted problems will grow before improving even as the military increases dwell time between deployments and shifts training priorities.

Fort Hood is experiencing an acute surge: since January it has recorded 14 confirmed and six suspected soldier suicides — on pace to exceed prior annual highs — including multiple deaths over one recent weekend and a suspected murder-suicide. Post leaders launched an exhaustive review to identify at-risk soldiers, ordered commanders to report those cases, and began checking privately owned weapons registrations and visiting off-post residences (about 70% of Fort Hood troops live off post). Officials say post-suicide reviews have shown no single common cause or link to the Nov. 5 mass shooting there, and attribute the rise to a mix of stressors. Fort Hood and the Army have expanded programs to reduce stigma and encourage help-seeking and peer intervention, but leaders acknowledge the problem remains difficult and driven largely by leadership and support challenges.

President Trump’s wide-ranging interview with CBS’ Lesley Stahl, aired Oct. 14 on 60 Minutes, covered climate change, foreign policy, the Khashoggi disappearance, North Korea, trade, Russia, the Mueller probe, the Kavanaugh confirmation and turmoil in his White House. Major points:

- Climate change: Trump softened his past “hoax” claim, saying “something’s happening” but he’s unsure it’s manmade and suggested temperatures could “change back.” He expressed reluctance to adopt costly measures that could cost jobs or put the U.S. at an economic disadvantage, and questioned scientists’ motives linking climate change to stronger storms.

- Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi: He said an investigation was underway and promised “severe punishment” if Saudi involvement is proven, but resisted curtailing major arms sales he said would cost U.S. jobs.

- North Korea: He reiterated personal trust and rapport with Kim Jong Un, calling the relationship useful for reducing hostilities and missile tests, while acknowledging uncertainty about denuclearization progress.

- China and trade: Trump defended tariffs as leverage to secure fairer trade and market access, saying he wants China to negotiate but denied seeking to crush its economy.

- Europe and NATO: He accused the EU of taking advantage of the U.S. on trade and reiterated that NATO allies must pay more, disputing claims about NATO’s role and saying he knows more about the issue than Defense Secretary James Mattis.

- Russia and Putin: He said Putin is “probably” involved in assassinations and that Russia meddled in 2016, but also claimed China and other countries meddled; he insisted he has been tough with Putin.

- Mueller investigation: He denied collusion, declined to pledge not to shut down the probe but said he had no intention of doing so.

- Brett Kavanaugh: He took credit for helping secure Kavanaugh’s confirmation and defended his mocking of Christine Blasey Ford as politically necessary.

- White House and politics: Trump dismissed reports of chaos as “fake news” while admitting he doesn’t trust everyone in the West Wing. He described Washington as deceptive and vicious, said he’s learned to feel comfortable as president, and repeatedly touted his administration’s first‑two‑year accomplishments on taxes, regulations and trade.

Throughout the interview Trump was often combative with the reporter, alternately boastful about achievements and defensive about criticisms, while emphasizing economic priorities when weighing policy choices.

Kanye West was hospitalized voluntarily for exhaustion and sleep deprivation after canceling the remaining dates of his Saint Pablo tour. Contrary to some reports, PEOPLE and other sources say he was not placed on an involuntary psychiatric 5150/51-50 hold, was not restrained, and went to the hospital at his physician’s advice; family and friends—including wife Kim Kardashian West—are supporting him and confident he will recover. Kim canceled a planned public appearance at the Angel Ball and flew back to Los Angeles to be with him.

The tour cancellation—21 remaining dates—could trigger large refund obligations (Billboard estimated more than 300,000 tickets, roughly $27.3 million). Whether those losses will be covered by insurance remains unclear. Industry-standard artist cancellation policies can cover illnesses that prevent performance, but exhaustion and sleep deprivation are harder to document than a clear injury and often face exclusions for drug-related causes, “unreasonable or capricious behavior,” or preexisting conditions. Promoter Live Nation likely has its own policy that may cover some promoter-level losses even if an artist policy is denied. Reports from other outlets suggested a psychiatric evaluation and referenced an insurance claim; insurers can deny claims for preexisting conditions or behavior excluded by the policy. Overall, details remain limited and final determinations about insurance coverage and financial liabilities are pending further information.

Researchers led by San Diego State University seismologist Tom Rockwell found the San Jacinto fault can produce larger earthquakes than previously thought and may rival the San Andreas in strength. The 130-mile strike-slip San Jacinto system, which runs from Imperial County through Anza, Borrego Springs and into Riverside and San Bernardino areas, was studied at Hog Lake near Anza. By reconstructing 21 events over the past 4,000 years, the team concluded that central and northern sections can rupture together, producing quakes in the magnitude 7.6–7.7 range (up from the commonly accepted maximum of about 7.5). If a rupture propagated onto the San Andreas, it could approach magnitude 8.0, though there is no evidence that has occurred in the past few thousand years. The San Jacinto and San Andreas together accommodate roughly 80% of plate-slip in the region; past San Jacinto-related events include a 6.5 in 1968 and a 6.7 on the Superstition Hills strand in 1987.

French serial killer Michel Fourniret, 75, has confessed to the 1990 murder of British language student Joanna Parrish, her family lawyer said. Fourniret, known as the "Ogre of the Ardennes" and serving life for the rape and murder of seven girls, admitted during recent interviews with Paris instructing magistrates that he killed Parrish and French teenager Marie-Angele Domece. Lawyer Didier Seban said Fourniret made detailed, repeated confessions and investigators will question him further; prosecutors declined to comment while inquiries continue.

Joanna Parrish, a 20–21-year-old Leeds University student working as a language assistant in Auxerre, Burgundy, disappeared in May 1990; her body, raped and beaten, was found in the River Yonne the following day. Domece, who had learning disabilities, vanished in July 1988 and her body has never been found. Fourniret had long been a prime suspect; his ex‑wife Monique Olivier previously accused him then retracted and was later convicted as an accomplice in five murders and jailed for life. Fourniret had been charged over the two cases in 2008 but a 2011 appeal court dismissal was reopened in 2012; Seban hopes the new admissions will lead to trial and bring the Parrish family some closure.

On May 22, 2017, an explosion occurred in the foyer of Manchester Arena just after an Ariana Grande concert as crowds were leaving. Authorities quickly treated the event as a terrorist incident. Initial reports of multiple fatalities and many injured were later confirmed: 22 people were killed (including children) and roughly 50–59 others were wounded, some critically. Witnesses described a loud blast, smoke, chaos and a panicked rush for exits; videos from inside the venue showed terrified teenagers and families fleeing.

Police identified the attacker as 22-year-old Salman Abedi, who died at the scene when he detonated an improvised explosive device. Investigators searched properties in Manchester and arrested at least one man in connection with the attack while working to determine whether Abedi acted alone or as part of a network. Islamic State claimed responsibility but provided no corroborating evidence; officials continued to investigate links.

The U.K. raised its threat level to "critical," deployed additional armed personnel to protect key sites and events, and urged the public to avoid the area while emergency services responded. The attack prompted a national outpouring of grief and solidarity—vigils in Manchester, condemnations from world leaders, and messages of support from celebrities. Local communities mobilized to help victims and those stranded, offering shelter and free transport. Authorities warned against reprisals and stressed investigations would continue. Ariana Grande and members of her team were reported safe; she publicly expressed sorrow for the victims.

The document combines two items: a note about web archiving and a news report on the death of Rick Calamaro.

- Web archiving: The Internet Archive is running crawls of "No More 404" sites to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference, so that when linked pages change or disappear a preserved version from when the citing page was written remains available. The aim is to reduce broken links by replacing or supplementing them with links to archived versions.

- News report: Rick Calamaro, 46, a longtime personal assistant and close friend of Charlie Sheen and a Los Angeles club promoter, was found dead in his L.A. apartment on Sunday; TMZ reports he had likely been dead for several days and that numerous pain medications and an open bottle of alcohol were present. Calamaro was reportedly with Sheen during a widely publicized 36-hour drug binge in October 2010 and has been accused by some of being a bad influence or drug supplier to the actor. Cause of death has not been determined, and Sheen has not issued a statement.

Hard-line Iranian students stormed two British diplomatic compounds in Tehran on Tuesday, scaling gates, smashing windows, setting a car alight and replacing the Union Jack with Iranian banners. The attacks followed a parliamentary move to downgrade relations with Britain after London supported new Western sanctions over Iran’s disputed nuclear program. Protesters chanted anti-British slogans, burned flags and hauled out pictures, and state-linked media said six embassy staff were briefly held (officials later said all personnel were accounted for and safe). Police intermittently clashed with demonstrators and made arrests; authorities later said they regretted the attacks and would protect diplomats.

Britain condemned the incidents as “outrageous and indefensible,” warned of “serious consequences,” and checked on staff welfare. The U.N. Security Council and the U.S. also strongly condemned the assault. Iranian officials offered mixed accounts: some blamed spontaneous student action while others suggested the protests advanced hardline parliamentarians’ push to expel the British ambassador amid internal political infighting. The events evoked memories of the 1979 U.S. embassy takeover and highlighted rising tensions between Iran and Western nations over nuclear-related sanctions.

Heather Locklear marked her daughter Ava Sambora’s 21st birthday with a heartfelt Instagram video, captioned “Happy Birthday Sweet Child of Mine,” showing framed photos and praising Ava as “the kindest, funniest, smartest, most beautiful child.” In the clip Locklear — who is currently in long-term rehab for substance abuse and mental health treatment after entering a facility in July — lights candles, jokes about Vegas and says she loves and misses her only child, whom she shares with ex Richie Sambora. Ava earlier posted a birthday message for her mother when Locklear turned 57 in September.

Locklear’s rehab stay followed a highly publicized June incident in which police say she was “extremely intoxicated,” allegedly fought with officers and EMTs, and was later hospitalized for a possible overdose. She faces criminal charges including interfering with an officer and two counts of battery. Separately, TMZ reports a paramedic plans to sue Locklear, claiming head and neck injuries and verbal abuse from the June episode. Locklear has also posted a recent note mourning a friend lost to addiction and emphasizing recovery.

This document profiles Julius Rosenwald—Sears co‑founder, major early‑20th‑century philanthropist, and a largely underappreciated figure in American business and civil‑rights history—through a book by Peter Ascoli and a new documentary by Aviva Kempner.

Key points:
- Background and business career: Born to German Jewish immigrants, Rosenwald apprenticed in New York clothing manufacture, later joined Sears, Roebuck, and transformed it into the nation’s largest retailer. He also helped found Chicago’s Museum of Science and Industry and developed large Chicago housing projects.
- Philanthropy and influence: Deeply influenced by Jewish teachings (tikkun olam) and by Rabbi Emil Hirsch, as well as by Booker T. Washington, Rosenwald became a leading philanthropist. He funded Jewish causes and provided early support to the NAACP. He created the Rosenwald Fund during WWI, which he chose to end in 1948.
- Rosenwald schools: Working with Booker T. Washington and using a matching‑funds model (one‑third each from the fund, local black communities, and white communities), Rosenwald helped build more than 5,300 schools for African‑American children across the rural South, dramatically expanding educational access during Jim Crow.
- Support for black culture: After school building, the Rosenwald Fund shifted to support promising black artists and cultural figures; historians and artists (Rita Dove, Langston Hughes, Jacob Lawrence, Marion Anderson) credit it as a pivotal 20th‑century fund for African‑American culture.
- Documentary and legacy: Kempner’s film “Rosenwald,” featuring interviews and archival footage with figures such as Maya Angelou, John Lewis, Julian Bond, and others, highlights Rosenwald’s impact on education and culture and celebrates early black–Jewish cooperation. Viewers and former Rosenwald school students recount the lasting personal and communal effects—many unaware their schools bore his name until recently. Kempner presents Rosenwald as an exemplar of Jewish philanthropy and hopes the film will inspire continued commitment to social causes.

Overall, the piece paints Rosenwald as a complex figure: a shrewd businessman who gave away vast wealth (about $62 million in his lifetime), used strategic philanthropy to create lasting institutions, and played a significant but often overlooked role in advancing African‑American education and culture.

Astronomers have for the first time found a comet whose water matches the chemical signature of Earth’s oceans, strengthening the possibility that comets helped deliver Earth’s water. Using the Herschel Space Observatory, an international team measured the deuterium-to-hydrogen (D/H) ratio in the water ice of comet 103P/Hartley 2 and found it nearly identical to seawater. Previous D/H measurements of several Oort Cloud comets showed about twice the deuterium fraction of Earth’s oceans, which led scientists to conclude comets could account for at most ~10% of Earth’s water and pointed toward asteroids (whose meteoritic material matches ocean D/H) as the main source.

Hartley 2 is a Kuiper Belt object rather than an Oort Cloud comet; its lower D/H suggests the reservoir of Earth-like water in the early solar system is larger than thought and includes some cometary material. Researchers say this widens the possible contributions of comets to Earth’s oceans and implies models of early Solar System dynamics and water delivery may need revision. They emphasize more D/H measurements of short-period (Kuiper Belt) comets are needed to determine how widespread Hartley 2’s composition is. Future observations with facilities such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) should help resolve these questions.

Storm Barney is sweeping the UK and Ireland, prompting warnings against taking “storm selfies” and causing travel and safety disruptions. The storm is moving across central Ireland, where gusts reached 78 mph in County Carlow; severe gales there are expected to ease, but winds will strengthen later across Wales and southern England, with inland gusts up to about 70 mph and higher coastal gusts. Power cuts, fallen trees and flight diversions have been reported, and airports including Gatwick and Heathrow could be affected. Natural Resources Wales warned of strong onshore winds and large waves on the west coast; moderate flood impacts are expected now because tidal levels are low, but flood alerts may be issued if needed.

Authorities including the Environment Agency and RoSPA have cautioned people not to risk their lives attempting dramatic photographs in these conditions. RoSPA highlighted the danger of being swept out to sea and the additional risk to rescue services. Barney is the second named storm following Abigail and is driven by a series of Atlantic low-pressure systems; separate warnings of heavy rain were issued for northwest England and Wales.

The article also places these warnings in the wider context of a global trend of dangerous “selfies,” recounting multiple recent deaths and injuries—from drownings and falls to animal attacks and accidental shootings—linked to people taking risky photos. Officials in several countries, including Russia and India (where “no-selfie zones” have been designated at hazardous tourist spots), have launched campaigns and measures to discourage dangerous selfie-taking.

Newly unsealed court records detail a plot and gruesome December killings in Griswold that left Kenneth (56), Janet (61) Lindquist and their 21-year-old son, Matthew, dead.

Key points:
- The records say Matthew Lindquist arranged to exchange guns kept in his parents’ safe for drugs and cash with people connected to siblings Ruth and Sergio Correa. Texts from Matthew to a Correa phone discussed meeting locations, timing (after his father went to bed) and access to the safe.
- Prosecutors arrested 23-year-old Ruth Correa and charged her with murder, murder with special circumstances, robbery, arson and home invasion. Sergio Correa (26) has not been charged; his lawyer says he denies involvement.
- According to Ruth Correa’s statements to investigators and a cooperating witness, the plan was to stage a fake robbery and blame it on two Black men. Correa said things turned violent when Matthew panicked and fled. Her brother chased him with a machete, then stabbed him. Ruth admitted stabbing Matthew about 10 times; his remains were later found in woods in May, and his death was ruled a homicide by stabbing.
- Ruth described entering the Lindquist home through an unlocked basement, confronting Kenneth inside, and a violent struggle over safe keys. She said Sergio beat Kenneth with a bat; when Janet emerged Ruth led her into a bedroom and told her the son had “set them up.”
- Ruth said Sergio retrieved the safe keys, brandished a gun at Janet, used a rope to choke her, struck her repeatedly with a bat, and the siblings collected items from the house. They doused areas with a flammable liquid and set the house on fire. Fire crews responded to a 5:12 a.m. Dec. 20 911 call; Kenneth and Janet were found dead in the burned home. Their deaths were ruled homicides—Janet’s including blunt force injuries and smoke/thermal injury, Kenneth’s including skull fractures and cerebral contusions.
- Matthew’s car was later found burned in a Glastonbury apartment parking lot.
- Investigators had earlier identified Matthew as a person of interest because of resurfacing drug problems and his text exchanges; those texts are cited in the affidavit as prompting the meeting that led to the killings.

The affidavit provides graphic, first-person detail of the sequence—text arrangements, the chase and stabbing of Matthew, the assault of Kenneth and Janet, theft of property and arson—based largely on Ruth Correa’s admissions and a witness account. Sergio Correa currently denies involvement, and he is already incarcerated on unrelated charges.

Jeffrey (56) and Jeanette (55) Navin of Easton, Connecticut, were reported missing Aug. 7 after being last seen Aug. 4 near their home and at Jeffrey’s refuse business in Westport. Their pickup was found Aug. 9 in a Merritt Parkway commuter lot off Exit 42. Relatives initially thought they might have taken a spur‑of‑the‑moment trip—something the couple did—but relatives say bank accounts appear untouched and deny financial troubles explain the disappearance.

Within days before they vanished, a judge denied Jeffrey Navin’s second attempt to appeal in a long‑running foreclosure case over a Guilford property. HSBC sued in 2007 after alleged nonpayment on a roughly $1.3 million mortgage; the debt had grown to about $2.2 million by late 2014. Other financial actions include a court order to repay about $138,000 in unpaid electric bills in weekly installments and the 2012 sale of a home tied to an earlier foreclosure. The family also sold a longtime Weston house for $900,000 in May and had recently moved to a rental in Easton.

Easton police do not suspect immediate foul play but have handed the investigation to the State Police Western District Major Crime Squad. Detectives and Bridgeport police searched the Navins’ son’s home after evidence from the abandoned truck was sent to a state forensic lab. Investigators are reviewing bank, credit card and phone records and interviewing acquaintances; as many as half a dozen detectives are working the case. Authorities say they are investigating all possibilities. The Navins ran J&J Refuse (their son is listed as operations/GM) and Jeanette worked 18 years as a paraprofessional at Weston Intermediate School. Family, school officials and their longtime attorney express shock and hope for their safe return.

Two FBI employees who previously worked with Special Counsel Robert Mueller — agent Peter Strzok and FBI lawyer Lisa Page — exchanged roughly 375 text messages during the 2015–2016 campaign that disparaged Donald Trump, expressed support for Hillary Clinton, and mocked other political figures (including Bernie Sanders, Jeff Sessions, Eric Holder, John Kasich and Martin O’Malley). The messages, turned over to Congress and released to the press, show repeated negative references to Trump (calling him an “idiot” and “loathsome”), private discussion of election concerns and a notable exchange in August 2016 in which Strzok compared taking precautions against a Trump presidency to an “insurance policy.” Some texts indicated worries about Russian interference and WikiLeaks’ role.

Mueller removed Strzok from the Russia probe immediately after DOJ officials learned of the messages in late July; Page had already left the special counsel’s office. The texts were found during an inspector general inquiry into alleged political influence on investigative decisions and were released to congressional committees and the media by DOJ ahead of the inspector general’s final report, a decision that drew bipartisan controversy. Republicans say the messages show bias that could have tainted FBI investigations of Clinton and Trump and have called for further scrutiny; Democrats argue the exchanges were private and reflect views widely held by others.

Deputy AG Rod Rosenstein said DOJ consulted the inspector general and ethics officials before providing the material to Congress; Democrats on the Judiciary Committee have asked the department to explain its decision-making and to disclose who authorized the public release. Critics warned the early disclosure risks politicizing an internal investigation and harming morale at DOJ and the FBI. Some messages were redacted to protect privacy and sensitive information; the inspector general’s review was still pending at the time of release.

Susan Olsen, best known as Cindy Brady on The Brady Bunch, was fired from her co-host role on LA Talk Radio’s “Two Chicks Talkin’ Politics” after posting a homophobic and abusive message on Facebook. The incident followed a December 7 broadcast in which Olsen interviewed openly gay actor Leon Acord-Whiting, who later criticized her on Facebook for spreading “outrageous misinformation” and called for the station to remove her. Olsen responded on Facebook and — according to Acord-Whiting, who posted a screenshot — sent him an expletive-laden private message containing homophobic slurs and threats. LA Talk Radio announced on December 9 that it had severed ties with Olsen, saying the station values its relationship with the LGBT community and will not tolerate hateful speech.

U.S. officials announced heightened security at federal buildings in Washington, D.C., and other major cities following recent violent attacks abroad and ongoing threats from terrorist groups. The Department of Homeland Security, led by Secretary Jeh Johnson, described the measure as precautionary—not prompted by intelligence of a specific, credible plot—and said it responds to public calls by terrorist organizations and recent violence, including the Ottawa Parliament shooting. The Federal Protective Service will implement increased, law-enforcement-sensitive protections at selected facilities; precise measures and locations were not disclosed and will be continually re-evaluated. Officials emphasized continued vigilance, intensified law enforcement, border protection, and intelligence sharing to protect government personnel, installations, and visitors. President Obama condemned the Canadian attack.

The Obama administration is preparing to shift responsibility for much of the U.S. role in Iraq from the military to civilians and contractors as American combat troops withdraw by the end of August 2010 and all forces leave by the end of 2011 under the U.S.-Iraq agreement.

Key elements of the plan
- Mission shift: With combat operations ending, the State Department will take on major responsibilities—most notably training the Iraqi police by October 2011—using private contractors to carry out much of that work.  
- Expanded contractor security: To protect diplomats and civilians in a still-dangerous environment, the State Department plans to more than double its private security force in Iraq to as many as 7,000 personnel. These contractors would protect five fortified compounds, run radar and counter-rocket systems, search for roadside bombs, operate reconnaissance drones and field quick-reaction forces.  
- Diplomatic footprint: Two new $100 million diplomatic outposts in northern Iraq will house U.S. diplomats expected to mediate sectarian tensions between Iraqi forces and Kurdish pesh merga in the absence of American troops.  
- Small residual military role: The military presence after 2011 would be minimal—several dozen to a few hundred officers working from the embassy to help Iraq purchase and field U.S. equipment—but military officers have warned that larger forces could be needed for tasks such as training crews on M-1 tanks, artillery and F-16s, protecting Iraqi airspace, and supporting counterterrorism operations.

Debate and risks
- Officials portray the shift as timely given reduced violence and improving Iraqi security capability, and stress it is a transition, not a withdrawal of U.S. commitment.  
- Some experienced diplomats and military officers caution the civilian-heavy approach may be insufficient for security and technical military needs; some suggested thousands of troops (estimates cited at 5,000–10,000) might be required later, but political and diplomatic constraints—both U.S. domestic politics and the Iraqis’ insistence on a 2011 deadline—complicate public discussion or negotiation of a larger post-2011 force.  

Context and timeline
- U.S. combat operations officially end in late August 2010 with troop levels reduced to about 50,000 for the remainder of the year; the mission name changes to Operation New Dawn. The administration emphasizes ongoing long-term civilian engagement and support for Iraq even as it ends combat operations.

Hollywood adjusted publicity and premiere plans for several holiday releases after the school shooting in Newtown, Connecticut. Paramount reviewed and revised marketing for Jack Reacher (starring Tom Cruise), reportedly removing a shot of Cruise firing a semi-automatic weapon from promotional spots; the Pittsburgh premiere was postponed and rescheduled, and a New York screening and discussion were canceled out of respect for victims. The Weinstein Company canceled the Los Angeles premiere for Quentin Tarantino’s violent Django Unchained (though a cast-and-crew screening will still occur) and said the decision reflected national mourning. Studios and broadcasters made other sensitivity moves: some canceled red-carpet events, pulled or delayed broadcasts, and Warner Bros. previously delayed Gangster Squad to remove a theater gunfight scene after the Colorado shootings. The responses reflect heightened industry concern about depictions and promotion of violence in the wake of the tragedy, a debate underscored by differing remarks from filmmakers and stars and by public expressions of sympathy from celebrities.

The Harvard Crimson revealed that members of the 2012 men’s soccer team compiled an explicit “scouting report” rating incoming women’s soccer recruits by physical appearance and sexual appeal. Six members of the women’s 2012 recruiting class published a statement naming themselves and condemning the report, rejecting anonymous media framing, and describing the emotional harm, disgust, and broader cultural problem of men objectifying women. They emphasized solidarity as athletes, called for men to help end this behavior, and offered forgiveness while urging campus- and culture-wide change.

Following that story, reporting uncovered similar practices on other teams: men’s cross country maintained annual spreadsheets before an inter-team dance that sometimes included sexually explicit comments about women. Team messages show alumni awareness, embarrassment, attempts to restrict access to older files, and recognition that the spreadsheets worsened in earlier years. Current cross country leadership acknowledged past misconduct, said the culture has changed, and reported cleaner recent documents.

Harvard administration responded: after discovering the soccer practice continued beyond 2012, the university canceled the remainder of the men’s soccer season and held conversations across Athletics about team cultures. University officials and athletic leadership condemned the behavior and pledged to address credible reports.

Members of the 2016 men’s soccer team published a team apology accepting responsibility, expressing shame, and outlining a commitment to confront sexism: they described meetings with university officials, proposed educational efforts, invited community input, and pledged to work toward cultural change and rebuild trust with the women’s team and broader campus.

New court filings in a long-running civil matter tied to the Casey Anthony case include explosive allegations by private investigator Dominic Casey. In a recent 15-page affidavit filed in Anthony’s bankruptcy proceedings, Dominic Casey claims he witnessed Anthony naked at attorney Jose Baez’s office and alleges Baez had a sexual relationship with her and privately told him Anthony had killed and dumped her daughter Caylee. Jose Baez strongly denies the accusations, calling them “unequivocally and categorically” false, asserting he behaved ethically, and warning that legal action is forthcoming. 

Background: Roy Kronk, who found remains in 2008, sued Anthony in 2011 alleging she and her lawyers falsely accused him of killing Caylee; that defamation suit was delayed by Anthony’s 2013 bankruptcy and later continued in bankruptcy court. Dominic Casey—whose prior depositions and two books contain disputed and unproven theories about the case—has been deposed in Kronk’s litigation.
