Tracy Fain, mother of a 7-year-old boy named Ethan, has been declared brain dead after suffering a brain aneurysm and massive stroke on August 7 while at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta’s Egleston campus for her son’s post‑op appointment. Ethan had been severely mauled by neighbor dogs on Christmas Eve, losing an ear and undergoing reconstructive surgery; Tracy was at the hospital to have his stitches removed when she collapsed in the lobby and was rushed for emergency surgery. Although she was initially stabilized and placed in a medically induced coma, her condition worsened and doctors declared her brain dead. The family, already reeling from Ethan’s attack and the recent death of Tracy’s nephew, is devastated. They are seeking prayers and support; donations can be made via the family’s GoFundMe (https://www.gofundme.com/496vn2w).

A new progressive effort called the Agenda Project has launched an outspoken anti–tea party campaign called the "F*ck Tea" project. Founded by Erica Payne, a veteran progressive fundraiser and Democracy Alliance co-founder, the initiative aims to "dismiss the tea party and promote the progressive cause" through merchandise, polling releases, and satirical videos. Payne said the group will roll out consumer items (humorous gifts referencing figures like Glenn Beck) and other products to help people express opposition to the tea party.

The campaign’s materials include polling highlights intended to portray tea party activists as alarmist or out of step with mainstream views. Some of the statistics cited: large shares of tea party supporters reportedly believe America's best years are past (64%), doubt or dismiss serious global warming (66%), view George W. Bush favorably (57%), would consider Sarah Palin a good president (40%), and approve of Glenn Beck (59%). Other cited positions include support for stricter abortion laws (45%), reduced legal immigration (42%), no legal recognition for gay couples (41%), and 32% saying violent action against the government could be justified.

The project marks a shift from earlier Democratic critiques that focused on corporate backing of the tea party; instead, the Agenda Project’s tactic is direct opposition and public mockery.

Emerson College will launch a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Comedic Arts beginning fall 2016, expanding on a successful comedy minor launched the previous year. The hands‑on program, created by Martie Cook, combines academic study of comedy history and theory with practical training — sitcom writing and production, sketch and stand‑up performance, comedy editing, late‑night writing, and portfolio development — and will use both Emerson’s Boston and Los Angeles campuses. Faculty include industry professionals, and the school plans master classes and guest lecturers from notable alumni and working comics. Emerson cites growing cultural relevance of comedy for younger generations; notable comedy alumni include Jay Leno, Denis Leary, Bill Burr and others. Supporters say the degree will equip students with scripts and production experience to enter the entertainment field, though some performers note real‑world stage experience remains essential.

This article explains the history, purpose, practice, and cessation of plural marriage (polygamy) in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Key beliefs and origins
- The Church teaches that the Lord’s usual law of marriage is one man and one woman, but that God sometimes commanded plural marriage in biblical times to “raise up seed.” By revelation, Joseph Smith was commanded in the early 1840s to restore the practice among some Church members; the instruction is recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 132.
- Plural marriage was connected doctrinally to the restoration of priesthood keys and temple sealings and to the concept of eternal marriage—binding families beyond death.

Introduction and early practice
- The principle was introduced cautiously and confidentially in the 1830s–1840s. Joseph Smith entered into plural marriages and authorized others to do so. Available documentation is fragmentary, so many details remain uncertain.
- In Nauvoo and after the Saints’ move west, plural marriage was practiced among a minority of members. Sealings included both “time-and-eternity” marriages (often implying marital relations) and “eternity-only” sealings (often interpreted as non-sexual).

Effects and lived experience in 19th-century Utah
- From roughly 1852 to 1890 plural marriage was publicly practiced, primarily in Utah. Most polygamous men had only two wives; at its peak a large portion of Utah Saints experienced plural marriage directly or indirectly, though the percentage declined over decades.
- Practitioners testified to both hardships and spiritual blessings. Observed social effects included increased birthrates in believing families, broader marriage opportunities for women, some reduction in per-capita economic inequality, more ethnic intermarriage among immigrants, and strengthened group identity.
- The arrangement posed particular challenges for many women and was sometimes mitigated by options for divorce or remarriage; some marriages involved young brides by standards then common on the frontier.

Joseph Smith, Emma, and early controversies
- Joseph Smith’s plural marriages and sealings (some to women already married) have complex, debated explanations: spiritual sealings, linking families, attempts to obey revelation while limiting earthly marital relations, or women seeking temple blessings. Ages and circumstances varied; documentation is incomplete.
- Emma Smith’s feelings were conflicted; she at times accepted and at other times opposed plural marriage. The revelation required a wife’s consent but also provided an exception if a first wife “received not this law,” which added to the complexity.

Public opposition, legal pressure, and the end of practice
- Beginning in the 1860s the U.S. government enacted laws against plural marriage; prosecutions and property seizures followed. Facing legal and practical threats to the Church’s institutions, President Wilford Woodruff issued the 1890 Manifesto, declaring intent to obey U.S. law and effectively ending new plural marriages in the United States.
- Some plural marriages continued in Mexico and Canada for a time. In 1904 President Joseph F. Smith issued a Second Manifesto making new plural marriages subject to Church discipline and excommunication, and later presidents have consistently enforced that the Church is no longer authorized to practice plural marriage.

Legacy and closing points
- The practice tested faith and brought intense controversy and persecution, but also produced many descendants who became faithful Church members and leaders. The Church honors those pioneers’ sacrifices.
- Today the Church does not authorize plural marriage. Temple sealings for the living remain between one man and one woman; the Church allows sealings on behalf of deceased persons who had multiple legal spouses, leaving questions about the eternal nature of such relationships to be resolved by God.
- Many historical details are ambiguous due to the secrecy and fragmentary records surrounding the earliest period; understanding remains “line upon line.”

Kira Kazantsev, Miss America 2015 and a triple-major honors student at Hofstra who advocates for women’s health and domestic-violence awareness, was revealed in late 2014/early 2015 to have been expelled from her Alpha Phi sorority in April 2013 after an investigation into hazing complaints. An anonymous Jezebel source alleged that, as Recruitment Committee President after returning from study abroad, Kazantsev and a friend subjected new pledges to verbal abuse, degrading comments about appearance, and physically demanding tasks. Hofstra’s code of conduct defines many such actions as hazing and threats to student safety; the university enforces sanctions for violations, though FERPA prevents public disclosure of disciplinary specifics.

After Kazantsev’s Miss America win, Alpha Phi’s national and Hofstra chapters did not publicly celebrate her, which insiders say reflected awareness of the earlier incident. The Miss America Organization stated Kazantsev had been “fully/very transparent” with them about her termination and defended her accomplishments. Kazantsev denied the hazing accusations on Good Morning America and on her website, saying her termination stemmed from a hazing-related joke in an e-mail that was taken out of context and from her missing a disciplinary hearing while finishing school; she denied name-calling, physical hazing, or degradation. The controversy was framed as a potential chance to discuss campus hazing culture, even as Miss America’s PR also faced separate scrutiny over scholarship-claims highlighted by John Oliver.

PETA condemned Kim Kardashian after she posted Instagram photos and video of herself riding captive dolphins during a Mexican vacation, calling the activity “intrusive, dangerous, and stressful” for the animals. PETA Senior VP Lisa Lange told RadarOnline that while Kardashian could leave the pool, captive dolphins face lifelong confinement and harm. The organization and the broader animal-rights community argue that “swim-with” and petting programs subject highly social, intelligent cetaceans to constant human interaction, injury, illness from foreign bacteria, stress, aggression, and severely restricted natural behaviors.

The article expands the critique to marine parks and aquariums broadly, citing examples (SeaWorld, Miami Seaquarium, Marineland) and documented harms: family separations from wild captures, abnormal behaviors and injuries in captivity (collapsed dorsal fins, teeth damage, self‑harm), shortened lifespans, and high mortality rates. It notes specific cases (Tilikum, Lolita, Kiska, Nakai) and summarizes scientific evidence of cetacean intelligence, social complexity, and culture that make captivity especially damaging.

The piece also criticizes weak regulatory enforcement in the U.S. and highlights global moves to prohibit or restrict keeping cetaceans—naming countries that have banned or limited captivity. It concludes with recommended actions for the public: avoid visiting facilities that keep cetaceans for entertainment, oppose breeding and acquisition, press for rehabilitation-and-release priorities, leaflet, lobby against subsidies, and support legislation to ban or restrict marine mammal captivity.

Nike has unveiled the HyperAdapt 1.0, a consumer-ready self-lacing shoe that brings the power-lacing concept from Back to the Future II into retail form. The system uses pressure sensors in the sole to detect foot position when you step in, triggering a battery-powered pulley-and-spool mechanism that tightens the shoe. Wearers can fine-tune fit with plus/minus buttons on the sides and can hold a button to fully loosen the shoe. Nike says the battery lasts about two weeks per charge.

The HyperAdapt 1.0 builds on the technology used in Nike’s limited Air Mag commemoratives but is designed for broader sale: it will be offered this holiday season in three colors to Nike+ members (price TBD). Nike designers describe the product as a first step toward more automated, biometric-driven shoes that auto-adjust in real time and learn personal preferences over time. The company acknowledges tradeoffs—dependence on battery power and possible malfunctions—but presents the shoe as an early move toward a more adaptive, wearable ecosystem.

David Steele, 42, a veteran sprint car driver and multiple United States Auto Club (USAC) champion, was killed Saturday night in a crash during the Southern Sprint Car Shootout Series main event at Desoto Speedway in Bradenton, Fla. Steele, a native of Indianapolis who lived in Tampa, was a two-time Little 500 winner, the 2004 USAC Silver Crown champion, the defending Southern Sprint Car Series champion and was seeking his 100th career sprint car victory in Florida.

The incident occurred just after the green flag on the 35-lap feature. Starting near the back of the 16-car field, Steele attempted an outside pass into Turn 1; his left front wheel contacted another car’s right rear, the cars hooked wheels, and Steele’s car went airborne, struck the outside retaining wall, spun perpendicular to the track and came to rest. Track emergency crews reached the car within seconds, but Steele was pronounced dead at the scene. Witnesses said his car’s damage was consistent with a left-side impact on the wall and that no other vehicle struck his car after the wall impact.

Desoto Speedway posted condolences on Facebook; the track reported good weather and track conditions and said fully trained medics and emergency personnel were on site. The fatality is the first at the speedway in many years and the first in the Southern Sprint Car Series, now in its second season. Reactions poured in on social media from fellow drivers and teams, including Tony Stewart Racing, Alex Bowman and Kasey Kahne, praising Steele’s talent and mourning the loss. Steele is survived by his wife, Lynn Bunn Steele, and three young children.

The New York Times reported that leaked NSA documents (from 2011, via Edward Snowden) show the agency intercepts “millions” of images daily from digital communications and extracts roughly 55,000 images per day deemed good enough for facial recognition. The NSA has been expanding use of facial-recognition tools—including in-house systems and commercial software such as Google‑owned PittPatt—to analyze photos from email, messaging, videoconferencing and social media. The agency views biometric images (faces, fingerprints) as intelligence-relevant as written and oral communications and says the technology has “tremendous untapped potential” for tracking targets.

The report notes it’s unclear how many people, including Americans, are affected. Under U.S. law images are treated as content, so the NSA generally needs court approval to collect imagery of Americans, but cross-border communications and other collection methods create legal and practical gray areas. An NSA spokesperson denied access to driver’s license or passport photo databases and declined to say whether it collects social-media photos by means other than communications intercepts. Privacy experts and activists have long warned about facial-recognition risks; commercial advances (e.g., Facebook’s DeepFace) and the proliferation of tagged selfies make large-scale identification easier and raise significant privacy concerns.

The Queen has become Britain’s longest-reigning monarch, surpassing her great-great-grandmother Queen Victoria after 23,226 days, 16 hours and roughly 30 minutes on the throne. Marking the milestone at age 89 in the Scottish Borders, she thanked well-wishers “for their touching messages of great kindness,” saying the record was “not one to which I have ever aspired.” She carried out a normal engagement—travelling by steam train with Prince Philip to open the new £294m Scottish Borders Railway—and spoke briefly to assembled crowds.

Public commemorations included a Thames procession of historic and leisure vessels and a four-gun salute from HMS Belfast. In Parliament, business was briefly halted for tributes: Prime Minister David Cameron praised her long service and stability; other politicians and Commonwealth leaders offered warm congratulations; and ministers will present her with a bound copy of cabinet papers from 1952. Buckingham Palace released official photographs taken in the Queen’s private audience room at Balmoral, where she is on her summer break.

Commentary stressed the Queen’s understatement and preference for routine even on a landmark day, and noted Prince Philip’s companionship through her 63+ year reign. Historical context highlighted parallels with Queen Victoria—who likewise celebrated quietly at Balmoral when she exceeded earlier records—and explained how researchers and the Royal Archives calculated the exact timing of the milestone (placing it in early September). While most responses were celebratory, republican critics used the moment to call for constitutional reform rather than celebration.

Patton Oswalt and Meredith Salenger married on November 4, 2017 at the Jim Henson Studios in Los Angeles. The couple announced the wedding via Instagram posts showing Salenger walking down the aisle with Oswalt and his daughter Alice, and both shared engagement-era photos and messages earlier in 2017.

Their relationship became public in early 2017 and they became engaged in July—about 15 months after the sudden April 2016 death of Oswalt’s first wife, Michelle McNamara. Oswalt and Salenger faced some online criticism for the timing of the engagement; both defended their relationship publicly, with Oswalt thanking a blogger who articulated support and Salenger writing about honoring Michelle’s memory while building a new family with Patton and Alice.

Reports recount Oswalt’s grief after McNamara’s death (later attributed to a combination of prescription medications and an undiagnosed heart condition), his struggles adjusting for the sake of their daughter Alice, and his eventual openness to love again. The wedding details beyond photos and social posts were not immediately released.

John W. Caltabiano Jr., 49, of Catskill, New York, was convicted in October 2015 of conspiracy to commit mail fraud, multiple counts of mail fraud, and theft of government property for pretending to be blind to collect Social Security Disability and workers’ compensation benefits. He had told agencies that a 2006 workplace accident left him almost completely blind and relied on his girlfriend to lead him into hearings. Investigators, however, recorded video and photos showing him reading, driving, shopping and working out at a gym — activities inconsistent with total blindness. Prosecutors say he stood to collect more than $500,000 (reports at times cite up to $1.3 million) had he not been caught.

In April he was sentenced to 57 months in prison, three years’ supervised release and ordered to repay $27,784 to the SSA; his girlfriend, Colleen McCarten, received probation after being convicted for her role. Authorities emphasized that disability fraud is widespread, harmful to taxpayers and aggressively pursued by the U.S. Attorney’s Office and the SSA Office of Inspector General. Judges and prosecutors noted Caltabiano’s extensive prior criminal history, including sexual‑assault convictions, as aggravating factors at sentencing.

Underwater pumping began Sunday to remove roughly 500,000 gallons (about 2,300 tonnes) of fuel from the Costa Concordia, nearly a month after the cruise ship struck a reef and capsized off Giglio, Italy. The operation, led by Dutch salvage firm Smit with an Italian partner, focuses first on six forward tanks that hold about 62–65% (about 84% across the first of 15 tanks targeted) of the fuel. Valves are being fitted to underwater tanks and hoses attached so warmed oil can be pumped out to a crane barge and transferred to a tanker while seawater is pumped in to replace the fuel. Bad weather and the initial search-and-rescue delayed the start; officials expect about 28 consecutive days (roughly four weeks) of pumping and hope to remove most fuel within days if weather allows. 

Fears of contamination of the protected waters around Giglio—home to dolphins, whales and porpoises—have driven the urgent effort; no major leaks have been reported. The Concordia ran aground Jan. 13 after the captain deviated from course. About 4,200 people escaped; 17 bodies have been recovered and 15 remain missing and presumed dead. Captain Francesco Schettino is under house arrest on charges including manslaughter, causing a shipwreck and abandoning ship; he denies wrongdoing. Memorial services and calls from Italian leaders for truth and justice have taken place as investigations continue.

In May 2015 the RATAN-600 radio telescope in Zelenchukskaya, Russia, recorded a single strong radio spike at 11 GHz (2.7 cm) from a patch of sky that aligns in right‑ascension with the sun‑like star HD 164595, ~94–95 light‑years away in Hercules. The detection (amplitude ~750 mJy) was reported by an international team including N.N. Bursov, Claudio Maccone and others and circulated via a presentation; the group called for continued, permanent monitoring of the target. If the signal were an isotropic beacon its implied power would be enormous (~10^20 W, comparable to a Kardashev Type II civilization); if it were a narrow beam aimed at Earth the required power drops to ~10^13 W (Type I scale). The team estimated a low (~2×10^-4) probability that the event was produced by signal‑like noise.

HD 164595 is a Sun‑like star (~0.99 M☉, ~6.3 Gyr) with one known warm-Neptune (HD 164595 b, ~0.05 MJ, 40‑day orbit); additional planets could exist. The discovery stirred rapid follow-up: the Allen Telescope Array (ATA) and other facilities searched for repeats but initially found nothing. Observers cautioned that terrestrial interference (including satellites or military transmissions), the wide 1‑GHz receiver bandwidth used in the Russian observation (which can dilute narrow signals), and other natural or instrumental causes remain plausible explanations. The RATAN team and others have noted the provisional nature of the claim and plan to discuss the finding at the IAA SETI committee during the 67th International Astronautical Congress. Subsequent Russian statements and ATA non‑detections suggest no confirmed extraterrestrial origin; the signal remains “interesting” but unconfirmed and under further scrutiny.

Actress Amy Adams gave her first-class seat on a Delta flight from Detroit to Los Angeles to an American serviceman and took his coach seat instead. The incident was reported on Twitter by Jemele Hill, who witnessed Adams glance at the soldier, speak with a travel companion and request the swap through a flight attendant. A fellow passenger, Ernest Owens, later took a selfie with Adams and said she told him she wanted to do it. Adams told Inside Edition she did it “for the troops,” not for attention. Hill and others noted Adams’s military ties—she was born on a U.S. base and lived on bases as a child. Adams, a five-time Oscar nominee, did not have a representative comment for TODAY.com.

A U.S.- and Russia-brokered cease-fire in Syria took effect at sundown on Monday, intended to halt fighting between the U.S.-backed opposition and the Russian- and Iranian-backed Syrian government. The weeklong truce allows continued strikes on ISIS and al-Qaida-linked militants; if it holds for seven days the U.S. and Russia will begin intelligence sharing and coordinated strikes against jihadist groups and set up a joint operations center. Russia says it will use drones to monitor compliance.

The Syrian government and its main allies publicly committed to the truce; President Bashar al-Assad made a rare public appearance in Daraya and said the state was determined to reclaim and rebuild all areas. Rebel responses were mixed: some groups voiced guarded cooperation or “harsh reservations,” others were initially skeptical. Humanitarian organizations hope the pause will permit aid deliveries to besieged areas like Aleppo and allow safer corridors.

Ahead of and as the cease-fire began, violence was still reported in several areas, with activists saying government airstrikes and rebel offensives continued in parts of Aleppo, Idlib and Quneitra. Observers warned enforcement and monitoring remain uncertain, with few clear penalties for violations, and noted past cease-fires in Syria have quickly unraveled. The truce is seen as a crucial test of U.S.-Russia cooperation and a possible opening to renewed political talks, but its success is uncertain and carries high stakes for millions of Syrians affected by the five-year war.

A judge declared a mistrial in the second murder trial of Quinton Tellis, who was accused of killing 19-year-old Jessica Chambers after she was found burned alive in her car in Courtland, Mississippi, on December 6, 2014. This is the second hung jury in the case; a 2017 trial also ended without a verdict. Chambers was alive when first responders arrived but later died; she reportedly told medical personnel “Eric did this to me.” 

The investigation drew federal help (FBI, US Marshals, ATF), widespread publicity, billboards across three states and a $54,000 reward. Prosecutors said technological data, including cellphone records obtained via subpoenas, led to Tellis’s 2016 indictment. Panola County District Attorney John Champion said prosecutors will “assess things” before deciding whether to retry Tellis, though defense counsel suggested a third trial may be unlikely because the prosecution’s strategy is now better known to the defense.

Tellis is also facing separate homicide charges in Louisiana in the 2016 stabbing death of University of Louisiana Monroe student Ming-Chen Hsiao; he is expected to be returned to Louisiana to face that case, but no trial date has been set. Prosecutors have not announced whether they will pursue a third trial in the Chambers case.

Over the weekend, Adele publicly denied tabloid reports that she’d been tapped for the 2017 Super Bowl Halftime Show. Speaking to a Los Angeles crowd, she said she declined because “that show is not about music” and she doesn’t dance. The NFL and sponsor Pepsi countered that while they’d spoken with several artists and are fans of Adele, no formal offer has been made to her or anyone else. The 2017 Super Bowl is set for Feb. 5 in Houston; Adele is currently on a sold‑out world tour supporting her album 25.

Former US President Barack Obama gave a rare post-presidency interview to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, guest-edited by Prince Harry. Recorded in September and first broadcast in late December, it was Obama’s first interview since leaving office in January. Key points:

- Social media and misinformation: Obama warned against the irresponsible use of social media, saying it can create separate “realities” that reinforce biases and distort complex issues. He urged leaders to help rebuild a common online space and stressed the importance of offline, face-to-face interaction—meeting in pubs, places of worship or neighborhoods—to counteract oversimplification and extreme views.

- Reflections on leaving office: He described feeling “serene” on his final day despite unfinished work, likening the presidency to a relay race where passing the baton successfully is the goal. He praised his family—especially Michelle Obama—for their support and called public service a sacrifice worth the rewards of making positive change.

- Achievements and outlook: Obama highlighted Obamacare, saying about 20 million Americans gained health insurance, and emphasized his commitment to training future leaders. He remained optimistic about the world’s progress (healthier, wealthier, better educated) while urging civic engagement—participation, volunteering and speaking out—to solve problems.

- Light-hearted moments: In a rapid-fire segment, Obama revealed personal preferences (Aretha Franklin over Tina Turner, Michael Jordan over LeBron James) and declined to answer a question about boxers or briefs.

- Prince Harry’s role and wider programme: Harry, who also interviewed his father Prince Charles and focused his guest-editing on armed forces, mental health, youth crime and climate change, said the conversations were important and educational. When asked about inviting Obama to his May wedding to Meghan Markle, Harry said the guest list was not yet finalized.

A U.S. Navy guided-missile destroyer, USS John S. McCain, collided with a civilian oil tanker near Singapore on August 21, causing a large gash in the destroyer’s port side, extensive flooding of crew berthing, machinery and communications spaces, significant damage to the hull, and at least five injured sailors evacuated to Singapore. Ten sailors remain missing and multinational search-and-rescue teams (Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and U.S.) are involved. The McCain was escorted to Changi Naval Base for inspection and damage assessment.

Admiral John Richardson ordered an operational pause across U.S. fleets and directed a wide, rapid investigation—led by Admiral Phil Davidson—into the 7th Fleet’s operations, maintenance, personnel, training, equipment and readiness. Richardson said the probe will consider all possibilities, including cyber intrusion or sabotage, though he stressed there are currently no indications of hacking.

Speculation about possible cyber causes (including GPS spoofing or malware) has circulated among some cyber experts, who note the coincidence of two major 7th Fleet collisions this year and point to prior regional GPS interference incidents. Others urge caution: GPS spoofing that would cause a collision would likely affect many vessels and be more readily detectable, and Navy ships use multiple navigation methods and watchstanding practices that should catch hazards.

The McCain incident is the second major 7th Fleet collision in two months: on June 17 the destroyer USS Fitzgerald struck a container ship off Japan, flooding berthings and killing seven sailors; that event led to removal of senior Fitzgerald officers and findings pointing to human error and poor seamanship. Other recent mishaps include the cruiser USS Antietam running aground in Tokyo Bay and USS Lake Champlain colliding with a South Korean fishing boat. The Navy review aims to determine root causes and address any systemic issues amid high operational tempo in the Pacific.

A militant siege at the Tigantourine natural gas complex in southeastern Algeria left dozens dead and highlighted growing Islamist threats across the Sahara and Sahel. Algerian forces stormed the facility after militants seized hostages; Algerian officials said 37 foreign hostages were killed and 29 attackers were killed, with three captured. Among the dead were citizens from multiple countries: the U.S. confirmed three Americans killed (two bodies were reported recovered after an earlier announcement), seven Americans escaped, and other confirmed foreign fatalities included Japanese, Filipino and British nationals; several foreign bodies remained unidentified and five foreigners were still missing. Nearly 700 Algerian workers and about 100 other foreigners survived.

Algeria’s prime minister Abdelmalek Sellal said the attackers—who he said came from countries across north and west Africa and included a Canadian identified only as “Chedad”—had planned the raid in Mali and transited through Libya and Niger. Veteran jihadist Mokhtar Belmokhtar claimed responsibility, framing the assault as retaliation for French operations in Mali. Algerian officials and some analysts argued a rapid military response was necessary to prevent the militants from moving hostages to Mali or blowing up the plant; critics from Britain, Japan and others questioned Algeria’s forceful, fast-paced assault and the resulting high hostage death toll.

Reports from survivors and families described executions, hostages used as human shields, and violent exchanges including helicopter strikes and explosions. Western officials noted they might have pursued prolonged negotiations and more intelligence-driven, precision options—using drones, surveillance and eavesdropping—to reduce casualties, but said they had not been consulted in advance. The attack raised wider concerns about regional security following Libya’s instability and weapons flows after Gaddafi’s fall, and prompted pledges of increased Western support to African governments confronting jihadist networks.

Congress is on track to record the least productive two-year session since World War II. As of 2012, only 61 bills had become law (out of 3,914 introduced) — under 2% of proposals — bringing the total for the 112th Congress (2011–12) far below recent norms. In 2011 Congress enacted just 90 laws; together these totals make the 112th the least legislative output in the post‑1945 record kept by the House Clerk. By comparison, recent two‑year swings include much higher outputs (for example, 245 laws in 1996 after a low in 1995).

The low productivity reflects sharp partisan division: Republicans took the House in 2011 while Democrats held the Senate, leading to repeated failures to agree on major items (a stalled bipartisan “Super Committee,” unresolved Bush tax‑cut expirations, budget disputes over $109 billion in automatic cuts, a stalled drought‑relief package, a farm bill stuck between chambers, and postal overhaul legislation). House leaders counter that the House passed more than 30 economic measures that the Democratic Senate and White House blocked.

The legislative stalemate has coincided with historically poor public approval of Congress. Gallup reported a 10% approval rating (the same low recorded in February 2012), with similarly low marks across party groups; other polls have shown approval as low as 9%. The 112th Congress will end after the post‑election lame‑duck session, having been defined by partisan gridlock and unusually sparse lawmaking.

President Trump told reporters he would beat Oprah Winfrey if she ran for president in 2020, but said he doesn't think she will run. Speaking during a meeting on immigration, he called Oprah “a lot of fun,” noted he knows her well and recalled appearing with his family on one of her final shows. The remarks follow renewed speculation about a possible Winfrey run after her Golden Globes speech; friends and Gayle King have said Winfrey is “intrigued” and taking the idea seriously. The story notes Trump has praised Oprah in the past and once mentioned her as a potential running mate when he first considered a presidential bid in 2000.

The UN Human Rights Committee has ruled that Ireland’s near-total ban on abortion violated the rights of Amanda Mellet, a Dublin woman denied a 2011 termination after doctors found her fetus had a fatal heart defect. The 29‑page decision found Ireland’s law—which allows abortion only to save the mother’s life—subjected Mellet to discrimination and “cruel, inhuman or degrading” treatment by forcing her to choose between carrying a non‑viable pregnancy to term or travelling abroad for care, at personal expense and away from family and trusted clinicians. The panel said Ireland’s criminal framework prioritizes the rights of an inviable fetus over the woman’s rights, restricts clear information and state‑supported care for those who go overseas, and deters healthcare providers from giving full advice.

The committee called on Ireland to provide Mellet with compensation and state‑funded psychological support, to ensure remedies for similar cases, and to amend its laws (including, if necessary, the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment) to establish effective, timely and accessible termination procedures for pregnancies with fatal fetal abnormalities. The ruling does not have direct enforcement power but Ireland, as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, is obliged to provide an effective remedy and prevent future violations.

Reactions were mixed: rights groups including Amnesty International and the Center for Reproductive Rights urged prompt legal reform and decriminalization; pro‑life groups criticized the decision as biased and defended continued constitutional protection for the unborn. Irish politicians expressed concern and called for the matter to be addressed—some urging rapid constitutional and legislative change, others favoring the Citizens’ Assembly process already planned to examine the issue.

Rich Earth Institute (REI), a Vermont nonprofit, is investigating whether human urine can safely and effectively replace chemical fertilizers. Since 2012 the project has collected urine from volunteers (600 gallons in 2012; about 3,000 gallons in 2013 from 170 donors) and aims to reach roughly 6,000 gallons. Urine is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium—key plant nutrients—and when diverted from wastewater to farms could recycle those nutrients rather than letting them enter waterways.

REI is running field trials: early tests on hay fields at Fair Wind Farms showed urine-treated plots were about twice as productive as unfertilized controls, and the USDA’s SARE program funded further trials. This year urine will be applied on three farms. REI sanitizes donations by solar pasteurization or warm greenhouse storage (30 days at ≥20°C), and is studying pharmaceutical residues in urine with funding from the EPA and partnerships with the University of Michigan and SUNY Buffalo.

The institute recognizes practical and cultural barriers: the “ick factor” of collecting urine, legal and regulatory scrutiny, and lingering public skepticism. Few people will hand-carry jugs long-term, so REI promotes urine-diverting toilets—already used successfully in Sweden—which separate urine at the source for easier reuse. International studies (notably Swedish work and trials in Nepal, China, Mexico) have shown urine can substitute for mineral fertilizers and, in some cases, greatly boost yields when used with compost. However, other studies have found mixed results, and urine is not a complete soil amendment because it lacks organic carbon and beneficial microbes found in fecal compost.

REI is likely the only U.S. project legally returning human urine to soil; it continues outreach, trials, pathogen-safety work, and research on contaminants to evaluate urine’s practical role as an affordable, circular fertilizer.

Sen. Al Franken’s amendment to the FY2010 Defense appropriations bill — which bars the federal government from contracting with companies that prevent employees from taking workplace sexual-assault cases to court — survived conference with the House and remains largely intact, according to reporting by Sam Stein. The provision prohibits contracts with companies that restrict employees from suing over assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, or negligent hiring practices, and preserves a Title VII element allowing suits against both alleged perpetrators and their employers. It applies to contracts of $1 million or more. The amendment includes a narrow national-security waiver that would allow the Secretary of Defense to block a case only if doing so were necessary for safety; the Secretary must personally justify the waiver to Congress and make that explanation public.

Separately, a Dallas woman, Lynda Darden, filed suit against Halliburton alleging she was fired in June 2009 after notifying supervisors she was pregnant. Her attorney, Todd Kelly — who has represented other women with sexual-assault and harassment claims against Halliburton/KBR, including Jamie Leigh Jones — says Darden was the only employee in her area laid off despite less-experienced, nonpregnant employees being retained. Darden seeks back pay and front pay in lieu of reinstatement; the suit alleges the proffered layoff reason was a pretext for pregnancy discrimination. The piece highlights ongoing concerns about how Halliburton treats female employees and notes Kelly’s history of high-profile litigation against the company and its subsidiaries.

A Vivien Leigh dress worn as Scarlett O’Hara in the 1939 film Gone With the Wind sold for $137,000 at a Heritage Auctions sale in Beverly Hills. The gray two-piece outfit — originally slate blue-gray but faded with age — was the top lot among roughly 150 pieces from the large private collection of James (Jim) Tumblin, a former Universal Studios hair-and-makeup department head who began collecting screen costumes and props in the 1960s. Tumblin famously bought the dress for $20 after finding it about to be discarded at Western Costume; that purchase helped grow a collection of more than 300,000 items that he toured around the U.S.

Other notable sales included a straw hat worn by Leigh ($52,500), Clark Gable’s gray suit as Rhett Butler ($55,000), and a black bonnet worn by Leigh and Olivia de Havilland ($30,000). The auction also offered scripts, a typewriter used by screenwriter Sidney Howard, Leslie Howard’s Confederate uniform and many other film artifacts. Tumblin said he is keeping Leigh’s Oscar but hopes selling the collection will allow wider public display of the items.

A Broward Community Charter School teacher, 58-year-old Jennifer King Forshey, was arrested and charged with battery of a child after police say she ordered a 10-year-old student to unclog a classroom bathroom urinal with his bare hands. According to a Coral Springs police report, Forshey accused the boy of clogging the urinal with paper towels and told him to remove the soggy wad using his hands and a dry paper towel; the wet paper soaked through, leaving his hands "saturated in what smelled like urine." The bathroom allegedly had no soap and Forshey did not provide protective equipment. The student told police the urine was not his and that he did not know who had clogged the urinal. A fellow teacher reportedly witnessed Forshey give the instruction, and the principal said the child went to the office seeking soap because his hands smelled of urine.

Forshey admitted directing the child to clean the urinal but told police she only thinks what she did was wrong because she is in trouble. She was booked, released on $1,000 bond, and has been reprimanded by the school. The victim’s mother, through attorney Joshua Hertz, said they publicized the case to determine whether other children have been similarly treated and to protect her son’s privacy and wellbeing. Reactions from parents and colleagues were mixed: some said Forshey should be jailed, while others defended her as a dedicated teacher who has shown care for students.

On the eve of George Washington’s birthday, AP reporter Jesse Washington examines why the surname “Washington” is disproportionately African-American. The 2000 U.S. Census found 163,036 people with that surname, about 90% of whom were black—a far higher black share than any other common name. The article traces the phenomenon to slavery and Reconstruction-era choices about surnames: after emancipation many formerly enslaved people selected last names to assert identity, connect to ancestry, gain social advantages, or honor national figures. George Washington’s fame and the widely published fact that he freed his slaves likely made his name an attractive choice for some, though historians stress there is no direct evidence tying most black Washingtons to the president or to ownership by people named Washington. In fact, most enslaved people were recorded with only first names and only a few of George Washington’s slaves bore his surname.

The piece reviews George Washington’s complicated relationship with slavery—his inheritance and purchase of many enslaved people, efforts to recapture runaways, later opposition to the institution, and his will freeing his slaves after his wife’s death—and how that ambivalence may have influenced perceptions of his name. Scholars note multiple motives for choosing surnames (ancestral plantation names, tribute, or arbitrary selection) and emphasize that renaming was a common tool of self-definition during emancipatory moments.

The census data show the scale: of the roughly 146,520 Washingtons counted in 2000, 90% were black and only about 5% were white. Other historically white presidential surnames (Jefferson, Jackson, Lincoln) show varying black shares. The article also explores social effects: black people with “Black-sounding” names face documented hiring discrimination, while some white Washingtons have experienced misidentification or assumptions because of their name. Personal stories illustrate pride, ambivalence, and the name’s cultural weight across races. Historians conclude that whether by coincidence, convenience, or conscious choice, the predominance of the surname among African-Americans reflects the complex intersections of slavery, memory, identity, and nationhood.

Twin car bombs struck security and intelligence buildings in Damascus on Saturday, killing at least 27 people and wounding around 97, Syrian state media and the health ministry reported; the death toll could rise. The explosions — reported at about 7:30 a.m. and said by state TV and SANA to have targeted the aviation/air intelligence and criminal security (customs/air force intelligence) compounds — left scorched streets, mangled bodies and widespread property damage. Syrian state outlets said most casualties were civilians and blamed “terrorists,” while some witnesses and opposition activists described mass panic and shattered windows across nearby neighborhoods. SANA also reported a third blast near a military bus at the Yarmouk refugee camp.

No group immediately claimed responsibility. The attacks follow a string of large bombings against regime security installations since December, including twin suicide blasts in Aleppo in February, and have been variously blamed by the government on extremist “terrorists” and by some opposition figures as possibly staged by regime elements. U.S. intelligence has suggested al-Qaida in Iraq might be exploiting Syria’s turmoil; al-Qaida’s leader earlier called for Assad’s ouster. Opposition member Bassma Kodmani expressed doubt that groups like the Free Syrian Army could penetrate heavily guarded facilities without inside help.

The bombings come amid intensified government offensives in opposition strongholds (Homs, Idlib, Daraa) and rising casualties in the year-old uprising, which the U.N. estimates has killed more than 8,000 people. The attacks have heightened sectarian fears — Assad’s leadership is dominated by Alawites while the opposition is largely Sunni — and complicated international efforts to resolve the crisis. U.N. envoy Kofi Annan urged unified Security Council action and reiterated calls to end violence and secure humanitarian access; Russia and China have blocked stronger U.N. measures. International figures including U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and France condemned the bombings. Opposition networks reported additional killings around the country that day, including clashes and deaths in al-Raqqa.

Facebook has blocked all links and many mentions of the small, revenue-sharing social network Tsu.co across its platforms (Facebook, Instagram and Messenger), even deleting millions of past posts that referenced the site. Typing “Tsu” is allowed, but any “Tsu.co” link or that exact text is flagged as unsafe; Facebook says the move enforces its policy against developers or services that financially incentivize sharing because such programs drive spammy, bulk posting and a poor user experience.

Tsu, founded by Sebastian Sobczak and grown quickly to several million users, shares roughly 90% of ad revenue with its members (45% to the creator, the rest split among inviters), a model Tsu argues is fairer than Facebook’s. That structure gives users a financial motive to post links and invite others, and Facebook says that led to fake accounts and mass linking that triggered user spam reports. Facebook offered to unblock Tsu if it prevented users from cross-posting to Facebook.

Affected Tsu users—including photographers, artists and models—say the ban is heavy-handed and possibly aimed at stifling competition; many report having posts removed (estimates range from millions to about 10 million) and lost content or outreach. Tsu denies paying users to post on Facebook and likens its model to YouTube’s revenue-sharing. The dispute highlights the power large platform gatekeepers have to shape what can be shared and how rival business models are treated.

Former professional wrestler Bret "The Hitman" Hart, 58, announced on Instagram that he is battling prostate cancer and will undergo surgery in the coming days. A WWE Hall of Famer and five-time WWF/WWE world heavyweight champion (plus two WCW world titles and five U.S. heavyweight titles), Hart said this is his toughest fight and vowed to face it with determination. Hart previously survived a 2002 stroke and retired after a 1999 concussion. He is a member of Canada’s famed Hart wrestling family; his father Stu was a wrestler and trainer and his brother Owen died in a 1999 ring accident.

Brandon McGraw, a 33-year-old Marine from Camp Lejeune and veteran of Afghanistan and Iraq, died Saturday in a skydiving accident in Euroa, Victoria, Australia. He and his wife Cherilyn — who had won a trip for two on The Ellen DeGeneres Show in January — were jumping with Euroa Skydive. Cherilyn performed a tandem jump with an instructor seconds before Brandon exited the plane. Witnesses described his descent as initially “flawless,” with a good canopy and several minutes of glide, but during the final approach he suddenly veered side to side, slammed into the ground, went into cardiac arrest and was pronounced dead at the scene around 12:30 p.m. McGraw was an experienced extreme-sports enthusiast with numerous jumps; the skydiving school is investigating the unexplained complications that led to the crash — its first fatality in about 30 years. Cherilyn paid tribute to him on Facebook, posting the last photo taken of him aboard the plane and calling him her “hero” and “angel.”

This document is a collection of critiques and attacks on Newt Gingrich from conservative figures and outlets during the GOP 2012 primary, arguing he is unfit to be the Republican nominee. Key points:

- Elliott Abrams (former Reagan aide) charges Gingrich with frequently insulting Ronald Reagan and undermining Reagan-era anti‑Soviet policies despite sometimes voting with Reagan. Abrams cites a 1986 floor speech in which Gingrich called Reagan’s strategy a failure and even compared a Reagan–Gorbachev summit to 1938 Munich.

- Multiple conservative commentators and former officials (including Tom DeLay, Bob Dole, National Review editors, Ann Coulter, R. Emmett Tyrrell Jr.) warn Gingrich would be a liability in a general election. Criticisms include erratic, undisciplined leadership as Speaker, a history of personal scandals and divorces, and a pattern of self-promotion and opportunism comparable to Bill Clinton’s character flaws.

- Editorials and opinion pieces argue Gingrich is not a reliable conservative: he has made inconsistent policy statements (examples given on entitlement reform, the Paul Ryan plan, immigration and health-care mandates), accepted large payments from entities like Freddie Mac and lobbied for corporate interests, and lacks executive experience or success winning beyond a single House district. Those pieces contrast him with Mitt Romney, Rick Santorum and Ron Paul, suggesting Romney and Santorum are preferable choices for electability and governance.

- Gingrich’s supporters’ rhetorical framing (calling Romney the “establishment” candidate while portraying Gingrich as an outsider) is criticized as circular and hypocritical given Gingrich’s long Washington career.

- The conservative media backlash intensified with aggregators like the Drudge Report linking to these critiques, and GOP elders publicly urging Republicans to block Gingrich’s nomination because he could hurt down‑ballot Republican prospects.

Overall message: influential conservative voices contend Gingrich’s temperament, inconsistent record, ethical questions, and lack of broad electoral experience make him a risky general‑election nominee despite debate flair and appeal to some Republican voters.

Lawmakers, policy figures and experts warned Sunday that reaching a bipartisan compromise is essential to avoid the economic damage of the “fiscal cliff” — the automatic tax hikes and spending cuts set to take effect at year’s end.

Key views:

A CDC analysis of 1,075 contact lens–related infections reported to the FDA from 2005–2015 found that nearly 1 in 5 cases resulted in eye damage (such as corneal scarring, the need for a corneal transplant, or reduced vision). More than 10% required emergency or urgent care. Many infections involved easily avoidable behaviors — over one-quarter of reports noted risky practices like sleeping in lenses or wearing them longer than recommended.

Although contact lenses are a safe and effective vision correction for about 41 million U.S. users, improper wear and care can cause painful, disruptive infections that sometimes lead to long-term harm. Even “minor” infections can require daily clinic visits or hourly eye drops.

CDC and eye-care groups urge wearers to treat contacts as medical devices and follow proper hygiene: get annual eye exams, buy lenses from reputable sources, never share lenses, avoid tap water, disinfect nightly with prescribed solution, replace lens cases regularly, and do not sleep in lenses unless explicitly approved and supervised by an eye doctor. Three key risky behaviors to avoid are sleeping in lenses, “topping off” old solution with new, and failing to replace lenses as recommended.

In Chillicothe, Ohio, a small Rust Belt city of about 21,000, at least six women have disappeared in just over a year, and four bodies have been recovered—most found dumped along waterways outside town—prompting fears of a serial killer or organized trafficking. The victims share commonalities: many struggled with drug addiction, engaged in sex work to fund habits, and in some cases knew one another. Authorities from local police, county sheriffs, the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation and the FBI have formed a task force to investigate, re-examining cases previously ruled suicides or overdoses and looking for links to other disappearances in the region.

Key cases:
- Charlotte Trego, mother of two, last seen May 3, 2014; missing since.
- Tameka Lynch, 30 and mother of three, last seen May 3, 2014; body found May 24, 2014 in Paint Creek; autopsy cited probable multiple drug overdoses; family suspects foul play.
- Wanda Lemons, 37 and mother of five, last seen Nov. 3, 2014; still missing.
- Shasta Himelrick, 20 and pregnant, disappeared Dec. 2014; car abandoned on a bridge and her body later found in the Scioto River; coroner ruled it a suicide though friends dispute that.
- Timberly Clayton was found shot to death; a convicted sex offender has been named a prime suspect in that killing but not charged.
- Tiffany Sayre, 26 and mother of two, disappeared May 11 and was found June 20 wrapped in a sheet and concealed in a culvert; her death has been ruled a homicide and helped spur the multiagency task force.

Families criticize local law enforcement for initially downplaying or slow responses; some residents say police have long neglected problems tied to heroin and prostitution. Investigators have received many tips but say witnesses may be afraid to come forward; forensic analysis is ongoing. The community is frightened and grieving, holding vigils and calling for answers while authorities keep multiple possibilities—serial killer, traffickers, overdoses—under consideration.

Public Health England (PHE) is investigating a UK case of multidrug-resistant gonorrhea in a man who acquired the infection in Southeast Asia and sought treatment in early 2018. Laboratory analysis found the strain shows high-level resistance to the recommended first‑line combination therapy—azithromycin and ceftriaxone—as well as to most other commonly used antibiotics. PHE and international bodies (WHO, ECDC) say this is the first global report of such dual high‑level resistance.

The patient had a regular partner in the UK (who tested negative) and a recent sexual contact in Southeast Asia. Contact tracing is under way to limit onward spread. Clinicians report one remaining antibiotic option is being tried and the patient is being monitored to see if treatment succeeds. Experts warn this development is concerning because gonorrhea can cause serious complications if untreated and because rising antimicrobial resistance has long been anticipated; cuts to sexual health services were noted as intensifying the public‑health risk.

Sandra Bullock was not surprised or upset by ex-husband Jesse James’s quick engagement to tattoo artist Kat Von D. According to sources cited by PopEater, Bullock was given advance notice that the announcement would be made this week; she has accepted that Jesse is moving on and is focused on parenting their adopted son, Louis. Though she and James are not close, they have kept communication open enough for him to warn her when his relationship with Kat became serious.

Jesse James and Kat Von D, who began dating after James’s 2009 split and subsequent 2010 divorce from Bullock, announced their engagement. In a People statement, James praised Kat as his best friend and the love of his life; Kat called him “the one” and said they will maintain two homes for now. The couple, who have publicly exchanged affectionate messages on Twitter, appear committed and enthusiastic about their future together.

Cheryl Strayed’s memoir and the movie adaptation Wild—about her 1,100-mile, cathartic hike on the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT)—have sharply raised public interest in long-distance hiking. The publicity has driven large increases in PCT website traffic, permit requests and actual hikers; anecdotal and permit data show steep growth in thru-hike attempts over the past decade, with thousands seeking to walk sections or the full 2,650-mile route. Women appear to make up a growing share of hikers.

This surge has prompted both enthusiasm and concern. The PCT community celebrates the trail as a place for transformation—many hikers find walking healing and perspective—but warns against the idea that a long hike is a remedy for life problems if undertaken from a place of deliberate unpreparedness. Inexperienced or careless hikers can endanger themselves, strain rescue and community resources, degrade fragile environments (especially desert stretches), create human-waste and campsite impacts, and damage the reputation of hikers in towns. Even some experienced hikers sometimes behave irresponsibly.

To respond, the Pacific Crest Trail Association and land managers have introduced measures such as a daily permit quota (50 starts/day during the high window) to spread use and limit environmental damage; the PCTA also runs the #responsiblywild campaign to promote Leave No Trace, sanitation, safety and planning. The new management aims to maintain access while protecting the trail, but tensions remain: high demand pressures fragile ecosystems, increases rescues and costs, and has many long-time hikers nostalgic for quieter days. The consistent message: the PCT can transform lives, but prospective thru-hikers should prepare carefully—physically, financially, and environmentally—rather than setting out unprepared in search of salvation.

Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, 79, was found dead in his room at the private Cibolo Creek Ranch in Presidio County, West Texas, on February 13, 2016. Presidio County Judge Cinderela Guevara pronounced him dead at 1:52 p.m. and said his heart had stopped during sleep; she indicated the death certificate would list natural causes (myocardial infarction/heart attack) and that no autopsy was necessary after consultation with Scalia’s personal physician. Guevara reported Scalia had been visiting the ranch on a quail hunting and relaxation trip with a friend, had complained of not feeling well the night before, missed meals the following day, and was found unresponsive.

Scalia’s body was discreetly transported overnight to Sunset Funeral Home in El Paso with escorts from Texas DPS troopers and U.S. Marshals. Texas law required embalming before the remains could be moved out of state; the funeral home began that process early Sunday and collected information for the death certificate. Officials said there were no signs of foul play.

Contextual notes in the reporting: Scalia was the longest-serving justice on the current Supreme Court, appointed by Ronald Reagan in 1986. His death prompted immediate public and political attention, including President Obama’s statement that he would nominate a replacement before his term ended. The document also included an unrelated political commentary about Senator Bob Corker’s criticisms of President Trump and the limited actions by Republicans to constrain the president, but that material was separate from the reporting on Scalia’s death.

In June 2009 a mother of a fourth-grader at Miramonte Elementary discovered a disturbing series of notes and a drawing from a teacher’s aide, later identified as Areceli Luisjuan, who had been writing affectionate, intimate letters to her 11‑year‑old son. One letter described the aide crying and said she liked when the boy put his arm around her shoulder, urged secrecy and was signed “Sad Girl.” The mother found a crying‑woman drawing and a cell phone number after the picture frame fell. She says she first reported the matter to the child’s teacher and to the sheriff’s department but felt dismissed; a subsequent meeting at the school included the teacher, the aide, an assistant principal, the mother and her son, and the aide allegedly admitted to the letters and likened her feelings to a grandmother’s affection. The mother kept a written record of that meeting; the aide reportedly delivered a final letter and a candy‑filled heart bowl to the boy the same day. LAUSD later said Luisjuan no longer worked for the district, but officials had difficulty finding records of the employee or the incident and were researching it.

This episode surfaced amid a much larger criminal and administrative probe at Miramonte. The campus drew national attention after veteran teacher Mark Berndt was arrested and charged with numerous counts of lewd conduct, accused of binding, blindfolding and photographing students and of forcing some to ingest his semen as part of a “tasting game.” A second teacher, Martin Bernard Springer, was later arrested on suspicion of fondling a 7‑year‑old. Victims’ lawyers and parents have alleged additional staff misconduct and possible collusion: one attorney said two girls told him a female teacher regularly escorted them to Berndt’s classroom where he performed abusive acts, and claimed Berndt sometimes acted as that teacher’s substitute and brought food he had tampered with. Investigators have not publicly charged any other staff beyond Berndt and Springer, and prosecutors said they were unaware of a related case involving a female teacher. In reaction to the revelations and community outrage, LAUSD temporarily removed the entire Miramonte staff while authorities and the district continue reviewing personnel records, past complaints and how earlier reports were handled.

The document examines Donald Trump’s 2016-17 political persona and motives, arguing his candidacy is unusual because his basic aim—winning the presidency versus something else—remains genuinely uncertain. Evidence cited includes Trump’s extraordinary unpopularity outside a core base, his failure to perform routine nominee tasks (e.g., calling major donors), and behavior inconsistent with a rational, traditional campaign. Two main explanations are offered: incompetence and overconfidence, or a deliberate alternative plan to profit from his political brand.

Key threads:

- Business interests vs. campaigning: Trump’s campaign has damaged his licensing/branding business as companies distance themselves from his controversial image, making traditional consumer-brand monetization harder.

- Media venture hypothesis: Multiple sources report Trump has explored creating a media platform—a “mini-media conglomerate” or TV channel—targeting his enthusiastic base, possibly run through Trump Productions LLC and with involvement from Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner. The rationale: he generates massive ratings and ad revenue for existing outlets yet receives no cut, and he sees an opportunity to monetize a large conservative subculture that mainstream outlets (including Fox News) misread. Hope Hicks denied such plans, though Trump’s public complaints about biased press and his direct appeals to supporters via social media and rallies feed the idea.

- Trump as the breakout media star of 2016: The piece places Trump among past media breakouts (CNN, Drudge, Fox/MSNBC, Politico, BuzzFeed), noting his unprecedented ability to dominate coverage, manipulate the news cycle, and bypass or even punish media outlets. That direct connection to his audience could make a proprietary media platform viable.

- Foreign policy anecdote (Syria): A separate AP-based episode describes Trump’s decision to withdraw U.S. troops from Syria allegedly crystallizing during a December 14 phone call with Turkey’s Erdogan, who persuaded Trump—contrary to his own national-security team’s position—to commit to withdrawal. The report portrays the decision as hasty, taken without broad consultation, and surprising even to Erdogan; the White House denies AP’s account.

- Cultural parallel: The document closes by comparing Trump to the protagonist of Bob Roberts (1992), a satirical film about a wealthy, media-savvy conservative who manipulates populist resentments and celebrity status to pursue office. The comparison underscores themes of media manipulation, populist division, and spectacle-driven politics, suggesting Trump fits a familiar archetype of a celebrity-politician who leverages outrage and identity politics for influence—whether to win office or to build a media-enterprise empire.

Overall, the piece argues Trump’s candidacy may be less about a conventional presidential campaign and more about building a lasting media and political ecosystem centered on a large, insular conservative audience—and that his unorthodox behavior and decisions (domestically and in foreign policy) can be read through that lens.

A fatal head-on crash in November 2011 that killed Glen Walker, 35, and 16-year-old Joshua Jenkins and severely injured Walker’s wife, Sandra, concluded in court with a plea and a surprising moment of forgiveness. Police say Tamara Matthews’ minivan veered into oncoming traffic on Flat Shoals Road in south Fulton County, striking the Walker family’s van and causing it to flip. Eight people were hospitalized; Matthews’ son died at the scene, Glen Walker died weeks later, and Sandra Walker sustained a traumatic brain injury. Matthews pleaded guilty to misdemeanor counts of vehicular homicide and failure to maintain lane, receiving 36 months’ probation and 500 hours of community service; the judge urged that her service honor the lives of her son and Glen Walker. During sentencing, Sandra Walker gave a victim-impact statement forgiving Matthews and embraced her in court after Matthews apologized. (The Walkers’ two young children were not seriously injured.) Also noted in the report: a separate, brief item about a motorcycle crash in Surfside Beach that injured a man and a woman; the cause was not yet known.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor granted an emergency, temporary exemption late Tuesday to a small group of Catholic nuns, the Little Sisters of the Poor, shielding them from enforcement of the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive-coverage mandate. The stay, issued hours before the mandate was to take effect on Jan. 1, applies to the nuns and other Roman Catholic nonprofits that share their health plan (the Christian Brothers Employee Benefit Trust). Sotomayor gave the government until Friday to respond; the order is narrow and does not rule on the mandate more broadly.

The nuns had sought last-minute relief to avoid what their lawyers described as “draconian fines” if they did not provide or trigger contraceptive coverage. The administration contends such religious nonprofits can opt out by filing a self-certification form so that insurers provide the coverage instead—a so-called accommodation it says does not impose a substantial burden on religious exercise. The Becket Fund, representing the nuns, argues even that accommodation forces them to facilitate coverage they religiously oppose.

The decision comes amid a wave of legal challenges by religious groups and some private corporations over the contraception mandate. The Supreme Court has already agreed to hear related cases this term, including Hobby Lobby and Conestoga Wood Specialties, which raise whether for-profit companies can be exempted on religious grounds. The emergency stay affects only the Little Sisters’ case while the Court considers the appeals.

A suite of ocean measurements and satellite observations shows the Arctic Ocean—especially the eastern Eurasian Basin—is undergoing rapid “Atlantification,” with warm Atlantic waters intruding and mixing upward and undermining sea ice from below as well as from above. Moorings deployed since 2002, augmented by buoys and satellite data, reveal that a cold, fresh surface layer (the cold halocline) that once insulated surface ice from deeper, warmer Atlantic water has weakened or disappeared in winter in many places. The top of the Atlantic layer has shoaled (for example, from ~140 m to ~85 m at one site over a decade), enabling heat from ~4°C Atlantic currents to mix into the upper 200–250 m and reduce ice formation and thickness.

Across the Arctic Ocean sea ice extent is falling ~13% per decade since satellite records began and ice thickness has declined by ~1.7 m since the 1970s. In the eastern Eurasian Basin, summer ice persistence has shortened (annual ice-free periods jumping from under one month to more than three in some areas), and since about 2011 large parts have been essentially summer ice–free. The study finds that where air warming once dominated melt, ocean heat now contributes roughly equally, creating a feedback loop: less summer ice weakens the halocline, permitting more winter ocean mixing and further ice loss.

These shifts affect ocean chemistry and ecology (e.g., increased phytoplankton blooms), freshwater pathways, and potentially regional climate and human activities (shipping, resource access). One important uncertainty is how added freshwater from rivers and thawing permafrost will influence stratification—potentially promoting ice if it persists at the surface, or doing little if winds redistribute it. Overall, the Arctic is transitioning on a generational timescale toward conditions more like the Atlantic, with major consequences for sea ice, ecosystems, and climate feedbacks.

CBC radio star Jian Ghomeshi was fired after the broadcaster received information it says precludes continuing his employment. The Toronto Star reported allegations from three women — about 20 years younger than Ghomeshi — who say he physically assaulted them during dates or sexual encounters, describing striking, choking, biting, covering their mouths and noses, and verbal abuse. A fourth woman who worked at CBC accused him of workplace sexual harassment, saying he cupped her buttocks in the studio and told her “I want to hate f--- you.” None of the women filed police reports or went on the record because they feared lawsuits and online retaliation.

Ghomeshi denied non-consensual conduct, saying on Facebook that his sexual life can include role-play, dominance and submission but has always been consensual, and that an ex-girlfriend has orchestrated a smear campaign. He said he had voluntarily shown CBC evidence he says proves consent. CBC initially put him on indefinite leave, then dismissed him and said recently obtained information led to the decision. Ghomeshi’s lawyers announced he will sue CBC for $50 million for breach of confidence and bad faith and will pursue reinstatement under his collective agreement. Ghomeshi also retained crisis communications consultants.

The Star’s reporting involved detailed, repeated interviews with the women, who described being fans who met Ghomeshi at public events before encounters that turned violent, according to their accounts. The paper said some of its sources feared the same kind of online abuse faced by Carla Ciccone, who previously wrote about a bad date with an unnamed popular radio host and was subjected to vicious online attacks.

Separately, a first-person account (anonymized) by a woman called “Carla” (name changed) describes an unpleasant date with a well-known radio host (referred to as “Keith”), who groped and harassed her at a concert and afterward, making her feel unsafe and ashamed. She avoided escalation but later learned similar complaints about his behaviour from other women.

Ghomeshi’s firing also cost him other roles (he was removed as host of the Giller Prize ceremony). CBC spokespeople declined to comment on specific allegations citing privacy and legal considerations; Ghomeshi maintains there were no formal complaints to CBC HR. The situation prompted intense internal CBC discussions over brand risk and how to respond as the story unfolded.

Terry Wayne Ward, a 71-year-old Army veteran and longtime AT&T employee, was honored with an unconventional, laughter-filled funeral at Geisen Funeral Home in Crown Point that perfectly matched the tone of the widely shared obituary his daughter Jean Lahm wrote. Lahm—who works at the funeral home—crafted a humorous, personal obituary that reflected Ward’s irreverent, practical nature (including anecdotes about his 39 years at AT&T and his stash of electrical tape). The obit went viral, drawing hundreds of online condolences and comments from strangers, one floral tribute from Pennsylvania, and at least one couple who attended the service despite never having met him.

At the service, Lahm shared lighthearted stories—like her father’s colorblind quip while working on a tangle of wires—which echoed the obituary’s warm, funny portrait. Mourners celebrated his life with laughter, stories, and a reception where guests toasted him. Ward died Jan. 23 after a stroke; Lahm thanked hospital staff and noted that, in lieu of flowers, donations could be made “at your favorite watering hole.” The piece emphasizes how the obituary shifted focus from how he died to how he lived, inspiring others and illustrating the healing power of celebrating a life with humor.

Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, told RT in an exclusive interview that the cables his site has published are only the “tip of the iceberg” and that far more damaging, still-secret material exists. He argued WikiLeaks released only secret and confidential—but not “top secret”—documents and urged people not to assume mainstream media coverage reflects the full truth.

On the Middle East and North Africa, Assange said Egypt’s uprising reflected real, hard-to-reverse change, while Libya showed heavy involvement by external state actors. He warned that social networking sites—especially Facebook—act as vast surveillance tools: they compile comprehensive personal databases accessible to U.S. intelligence via built-in interfaces, he claimed, and users effectively help build that resource. He extended this critique to major tech firms and stressed the blurred boundary between state and corporate interests.

Discussing releases about Guantánamo and the UK, Assange said timing reflected WikiLeaks’ limited capacity under intense pressure and that many detainees remain wrongfully held. He criticized media partners, notably The Guardian and The New York Times, for over-redacting and self-censoring material—prioritizing commercial and legal concerns over the public’s right to know. On his legal situation, Assange said he fears a U.S. espionage indictment and views the Swedish extradition process as corrupted; he warned any country refusing U.S. extradition would face political pressure.

Finally, he called ignorance the primary enemy—fostered by secrecy and misleading media—and argued that most wars in the past 50 years were enabled by media lies that failed to challenge government propaganda.

An outing off Noank, Connecticut on June 26 turned terrifying for Clare Shaw and her family when their 8-month-old Shiba Inu, Ryder, slipped out of his harness and fell into the ocean. After hours of searching, back-tracking, and involving the Coast Guard, the family feared the worst and posted pleas on Facebook. Their post was shared widely.

Unbeknownst to them, boaters Phil Q. Bigelow, Patrick Jullarine and Tommy Nahornick found the soaking, shaking pup about a half-mile out near Fisher Island. They pulled him aboard, warmed and fed him, and tried to locate his owners—buying supplies and posting notices while they waited. An equine vet linked the boaters’ sighting to Shaw’s Facebook posts, enabling the reunion. Shaw expressed deep gratitude to the rescuers and the community, calling Ryder’s return a miracle and praising the power of social media. The rescuers downplayed their role, saying they were simply in the right place at the right time.
