Italy’s highest court is set to rule on the fate of Amanda Knox and her former boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito in the 2007 murder of Meredith Kercher. Kercher, a 21-year-old British student, was found sexually assaulted and with her throat cut in the Perugia apartment she shared with Knox.

Case history:
- Knox and Sollecito were convicted by a Perugia trial court in 2009.
- Their convictions were overturned on appeal and they were freed in 2011.
- Italy’s Court of Cassation vacated that acquittal in 2013 and sent the case back.
- In 2014 an appeals court in Florence again convicted them: Knox sentenced to 28½ years, Sollecito to 25 years. Co-defendant Rudy Guede was separately convicted and is serving 16 years.
- Knox (now living in the U.S.) spent nearly four years in custody during the earlier proceedings and has said she will not return voluntarily to Italy. Sollecito remains in Italy.

Possible outcomes from the high court:
1. Confirmation of the Florence convictions:
   - Florence prosecutors would move to execute the sentences. Police would likely arrest Sollecito in Italy.
   - For Knox, prosecutors would ask the Justice Ministry to seek extradition from the U.S.; extradition is legally possible but politically discretionary and could be slow. Italy could request she serve any sentence in the U.S.

2. Ordering a new appeals trial:
   - The Court of Cassation can annul part or all of the Florence verdict and remit the case for another appellate hearing. Its written reasoning (required within 90 days) would guide the new court. Multiple appellate rounds are not unprecedented in Italy.

3. Acquittal (no retrial):
   - The court could overturn the guilty verdict outright, effectively ending criminal proceedings against Knox and Sollecito. This outcome is rarer and also requires a full written rationale within 90 days. An acquittal would restore travel freedoms: Knox could return to Europe without arrest risk and Sollecito would regain his passport.

Other notes:
- A juror from the Florence verdict gave an interview saying she felt evidence was insufficient for such severe convictions; while the interview breaches deliberation secrecy and suggests the verdict wasn’t unanimous, unanimity isn’t required and this is unlikely to affect legal arguments or the high court’s decision.

This review panned Everybody’s Fine as an overly sentimental, inauthentic American remake of Giuseppe Tornatore’s 1990 Stanno Tutti Bene. Robert De Niro plays Frank, a widowed, unsophisticated retiree who, ignoring his doctor’s warnings, travels by bus and train to visit his four grown children unannounced. Each child — played by Kate Beckinsale, Sam Rockwell, Drew Barrymore and an absent New York artist son — is hiding unhappiness behind a false front. The film’s emotional beats are obvious and predictable: Frank gradually discovers the deceptions and ultimately confronts the consequences of his demanding parenting.

The critic faults director/writer Kirk Jones for a tone-deaf Americanization, weak characterization, syrupy scoring, and strained performances (notably an embarrassing scene where De Niro pretends not to know how to use a rolling suitcase). Despite attractive cinematography and a strong cast, the movie is called a cloying, phony melodrama with a banal payoff about truthfulness and family.

Twitter has sued the U.S. government to block a Department of Homeland Security / U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) summons seeking identifying records for the anonymous anti‑Trump account @ALT_uscis. The account, one of several “alt” or “rogue” government accounts that appeared after President Trump’s inauguration and which claims to represent dissenting federal immigration staff, has tens of thousands of followers and has posted criticism of Trump administration immigration agencies.

According to Twitter’s complaint filed in federal court in Northern California, a CBP agent faxed an administrative summons requesting the account’s login data, IP logs, phone number and mailing address. Twitter says the agency invoked an irrelevant customs statute and lacked authority to demand those records; the company argues the order would chill protected anonymous political speech under the First Amendment. The lawsuit names DHS Secretary John Kelly, acting CBP commissioner Kevin McAleenan and two special agents as defendants.

The ACLU is supporting the user and plans to defend the right to anonymous speech. DHS and CBP declined comment on pending litigation. Critics including Sen. Ron Wyden called the government effort a waste of resources. Twitter has a history of litigating government demands for user data and is represented by experienced First Amendment counsel in the case.

The High Court in London has ruled that Lauri Love, a 33-year-old British-Finnish man accused of hacking into multiple U.S. government systems in 2012–2013, should not be extradited to the United States. Lord Chief Justice Ian Burnett and Mr Justice Ouseley found extradition would be "oppressive" because Love—who has Asperger’s syndrome and severe depression—faced a real risk of suicide if sent to U.S. prisons, where psychiatric safeguards and the prospect of solitary confinement were judged inadequate. The judges said it would not be oppressive to prosecute Love in the UK and urged the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) to pursue domestic prosecution with assistance from U.S. authorities, noting the seriousness of the alleged offences.

The decision, met with cheers in court and welcomed by human rights groups such as Liberty, is seen as a precedent strengthening the forum bar introduced under the Extradition Act (following the Gary McKinnon case), which allows UK courts to keep trials at home where appropriate. Supporters had warned Love could face up to 99 years in the U.S.; his lawyers and psychiatric evidence emphasized the heightened suicide risk and the importance of family support available in the UK. The CPS has 14 days to decide whether to seek permission to appeal to the Supreme Court. Love said he hoped the ruling would set a humane precedent for others with neurodiversity and mental-health vulnerabilities.

Summary:

Texas’s new “campus carry” law (SB 11), signed by Gov. Greg Abbott, allows licensed Texans to carry concealed handguns into university buildings, classrooms and dorms beginning August 1, 2016 (community colleges in 2017). The law limits institutions’ ability to enact blanket bans and imposes penalties on those who try to prevent licensed carriers from bringing firearms into classrooms.

Faculty, students, staff and alumni at the University of Texas have mobilized in opposition. Gun Free UT — a group formed after the bill’s passage — has run petitions and organized rallies; roughly 200 UT faculty pledged to refuse guns in their classrooms. University leaders including UT System Chancellor William McRaven publicly opposed the bill, and administrators say they are soliciting campus input about implementation.

Opponents — including English professor Lisa Moore, emeritus economist Daniel Hamermesh, sociologist Javier Auyero and others — argue the law will chill classroom debate, undermine academic freedom, damage recruitment and harm campus safety. Moore, who teaches gay and lesbian studies, described past incidents (vandalism of her office and a semester when she taught with an armed guard after a disruptive student) to illustrate how the presence of firearms would change teaching: instructors may avoid provocative material, cancel discussions, dismiss class rather than confront disruptive armed students, or even grade leniently to reduce conflict. Hamermesh resigned from a teaching contract citing the heightened risk of large lectures. Other faculty say they fear losing colleagues to relocation and believe the law could deter prospective hires and students (some parents say they would not have sent children to UT had they known).

Proponents claim armed, licensed individuals could stop active shooters; critics counter that more guns don’t reduce violence and that law enforcement should handle such threats. Some faculty plan symbolic or civil-disobedience actions — posting “no guns” signs or cancelling class — even if those steps risk legal or employment consequences. University officials stress they are working to develop policies to comply with state law while addressing safety concerns. The recent mass shooting at Umpqua Community College — in a state that already permits campus carry — has intensified faculty opposition and urgency around the debate.

- Regional tensions and domestic politics: Turkish PM accuses Syrian President Bashar al-Assad of "state terrorism." Syrian rebels claim to have shot down a fighter jet over northern Syria. Egypt's President Morsi publicly told Assad "now is the time for change" and warned he would not remain in power long; Morsi also said Israel is not interested in peace with the Palestinians. China signaled support for a "political transition" in Syria. Hackers supporting the Syrian regime targeted Al-Jazeera's website.

- Israel and Palestinian developments: An Islamist extremist group said Hamas detained about 20 of its members amid a crackdown on rocket fire. Israel's Home Front Command will hold a drill at Hadassah Hospital in Jerusalem; the IDF began evacuating Migron caravans ahead of demolitions. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cut short a security cabinet meeting over a reported information leak. U.S. and Israeli politics intersected as Congressman Howard Berman urged continued U.S. support for Israel, and U.S. Democrats removed a reference to "Jerusalem as Israel's capital" from their party platform.

- Iran nuclear concerns and Israeli debate over military action: Israeli media reported, citing unnamed officials and a purported U.S. National Intelligence Estimate (NIE), that Iran has stepped up efforts toward a nuclear warhead and possibly ballistic missile warheads. Prime Minister Netanyahu warned that other threats to Israel are dwarfed by the prospect of an Iranian nuclear weapon and reiterated that Iran must not be allowed to obtain one. The government is investing heavily in home-front defenses and conducting emergency drills; the central bank also rehearsed major-crisis scenarios. U.S. officials have not confirmed the reported NIE and maintain the assessment that Iran is undecided about building a bomb and remains years away from such capability. The heightened public debate in Israel about possible preemptive military action has drawn criticism at home and concern from international partners, including the Obama administration, which urges patience for diplomacy. Some observers view wartime rhetoric as pressure to strengthen sanctions; others warn public discussion risks harming security.

- Other regional notes: Jordan's Muslim Brotherhood vowed mass protests to press for democratic reforms. Separately, notable U.S. political moves included Edward Kennedy’s call to support Barack Obama.

Media Rights Capital (MRC) and Netflix are responding after CNN published new sexual-harassment allegations against Kevin Spacey by multiple House of Cards crew members. Eight current or former crew members — speaking anonymously — described a pattern of predatory behavior on set, including nonconsensual touching, crude sexual comments and unwanted advances directed largely at young male staff. One former production assistant told CNN Spacey allegedly put his hands down the assistant’s pants while driving and later cornered and touched him in Spacey’s trailer; that assistant did not report the incident to police but told a coworker at the time, who corroborated parts of his account.

MRC acknowledged being “deeply troubled,” confirmed it investigated and took action after a 2012 complaint about Spacey (including his participation in training), and said it has set up an anonymous complaint hotline, crisis counselors and sexual-harassment legal advisors for the crew while it continues investigating current and any new formal claims. Netflix said it sent a representative to set, was only previously aware of one incident from five years ago that it was told had been resolved, and — working with MRC — suspended production on Season 6 (already designated the show’s final season) while evaluating next steps.

The reports follow earlier accusations by Anthony Rapp that Spacey made a sexual advance toward him in 1986 when Rapp was 14, which Spacey apologized for while saying he did not remember the incident and publicly came out as gay. Additional men have since made separate accusations dating back years, and Spacey’s representatives say he is seeking evaluation and treatment; his publicist and agency have since parted ways with him. The revelations arrive amid broader industry scrutiny of sexual misconduct following the Harvey Weinstein scandal.

TransCanada Corp. has launched two legal challenges after the Obama administration denied a permit for the proposed Keystone XL oil pipeline. The Calgary-based company filed a NAFTA Chapter 11 notice seeking more than US$15 billion in damages, saying the permit denial was “arbitrary and unjustified” and cost it billions in assets and expected value. Separately, TransCanada sued in U.S. federal court in Houston arguing President Obama’s rejection of the project exceeded constitutional authority; that suit seeks to invalidate the permit denial (not monetary damages) and to prevent future presidents from blocking construction.

TransCanada said it will take a C$2.5–2.9 billion after-tax writedown in the fourth quarter tied to the decision. The company contends its application met the same criteria used to approve other cross-border pipelines and that the denial was a symbolic, politically motivated act intended to bolster climate credentials—an outcome it attributes in part to environmental activists. Legal observers call the NAFTA claim uncertain but note TransCanada may have a viable argument that it was treated unfairly.

Opponents and environmental groups counter that the rejection was a legitimate policy decision driven by climate and spill-risk concerns. Canada’s federal government declined substantive comment on the lawsuit but reiterated disappointment at the permit denial while stressing broader North American energy cooperation continues. The dispute comes as U.S.–Canada relations and trilateral energy talks with Mexico move forward and ahead of a state visit by Canada’s prime minister.

Lawmakers in several U.S. states are revisiting alternative execution methods as lethal-injection drugs grow harder to obtain.

Wyoming: A legislative committee is drafting a bill to allow execution by firing squad after the state’s corrections director said Wyoming currently has no execution drugs. Wyoming law already allows gas-chamber executions if lethal injection is found unconstitutional, but the state lacks a gas chamber. Wyoming has one person on death row: Dale Wayne Eaton, convicted of a 2004 murder.

Utah: Rep. Paul Ray plans to introduce legislation to restore firing squads (which remain an option for inmates sentenced before a 2004 ban). He argues it is instantaneous and humane. Earlier attempts in both Wyoming and Utah stalled but were revived after a botched lethal injection in Oklahoma.

Tennessee: Gov. Bill Haslam signed a law permitting electrocution when lethal-injection drugs are unavailable. The bill passed with strong legislative support and, unlike some states, does not offer inmates a choice of method. Critics and legal experts predict court challenges on whether drugs truly were unobtainable and whether forced use of electrocution for already-sentenced inmates is constitutional; Tennessee’s attorney general said the law likely passes muster but may face litigation. Public polling in Tennessee showed modest majority support for the electric chair.

Background and legal context: States have struggled to obtain execution drugs amid European import restrictions. Thirty-two states retain the death penalty, relying mostly on lethal injection; fewer than a dozen regularly carry out executions. The U.S. Supreme Court has historically upheld various methods (firing squad 1879, electric chair 1890, lethal injection 2008) but bars punishments that inflict unnecessary or wanton pain under the Eighth Amendment.

Negotiators reached a tentative nuclear framework in Lausanne after late-night talks addressing several sticking points, but key details remain vague and politically contentious. The deal requires Iran to remove a larger number of centrifuges than earlier reports suggested, submits Iran to extensive IAEA inspections (some measures lasting up to 25 years), and mandates redesign of a reactor to prevent weapons-capable spent fuel. However, several unresolved or lightly specified issues drew criticism:

- Centrifuge research and development: The framework allows Iran to conduct “limited research and development” on advanced, more efficient centrifuges under an agreed schedule and parameters, and bars use of such centrifuges for enrichment for 10 years. The precise limits, oversight and timeline were not disclosed, prompting critics (notably in Israel) to warn this could accelerate Iran’s breakout potential.

- Low-enriched uranium stockpile: Iran must “reduce” its stock from over 10 tons to a few hundred pounds, but the fact sheet does not specify the method. U.S. negotiators had pushed for export of most material; Iran insisted on diluting much of it domestically. The framework allows either selling abroad or diluting on-site, a choice critics say could leave a path to reconversion, though some experts argue reconversion would be difficult and the dispute may be driven by Iranian domestic optics.

- Past weapons work and Parchin: The agreement states Iran will “implement an agreed set of measures to address the IAEA’s concerns,” but offers no public specifics about resolving allegations that Iran researched bomb design and tested detonators at sites like Parchin. The IAEA says Iran has not answered most questions; U.S. intelligence believes weaponization research continued until about 2003. Observers call this Iran’s “Achilles’ heel” in the pact.

Political reaction and congressional oversight:
- Congress from both parties responded cautiously, demanding detailed briefings and the right to review any final agreement. Senate Foreign Relations Chair Bob Corker and others planned legislation to require congressional review and delay lifting of sanctions; the White House warned it would veto measures that undercut negotiations. Lawmakers debated potential new sanctions or measures to require presidential certification of compliance every 90 days; such congressional moves could jeopardize a final deal by undermining foreign partners’ willingness to lift sanctions.
- Republican critics called the framework dangerously concessional; some Democrats urged caution so as not to derail diplomacy. The administration emphasized the importance of letting negotiations conclude and cautioned against premature congressional action.

Next steps:
- Negotiators have until June 30 to convert the framework into a detailed agreement. Much hinges on final technical language and verification measures governing centrifuge R&D, the disposition of enriched uranium, and resolution of the IAEA’s questions about past weapons-related activities.

USDA U.S. and world rice outlook (2014/15)
- U.S. total rice supplies for 2014/15 are projected at 282.6 million cwt, up 2.8 million from last month driven by a higher production forecast.
- USDA’s first survey-based U.S. crop forecast for 2014/15 is 228.8 million cwt, nearly 21% above 2013/14. Harvested area is unchanged at 3.03 million acres; average all-rice yield is 7,560 lb/acre (up 91 lb from last month but about 2% below last year’s record).
- By type: long-grain production is 169.3 million cwt (up 0.3 million), medium- and short-grain combined 59.5 million cwt (up 2.5 million).
- Imports are projected at 21.0 million cwt, down 9% from the prior year.
- Total use is forecast at 243.0 million cwt (up 3.0 million from last month), 12% above 2013/14: domestic/residual use 134.0 million cwt (up 1.0 million) and exports 109.0 million cwt (up 2.0 million). Long-grain exports 75.0 million cwt; medium/short combined 34.0 million.
- Ending stocks are projected at 39.6 million cwt (down 0.2 million from last month) but 21% above a year earlier.
- Season-average farm prices: long-grain $12.00–$13.00/cwt (unchanged); medium/short $17.50–$18.50/cwt (up $0.50); all-rice $13.80–$14.80/cwt (up $0.30 on both ends).

Global outlook (2014/15)
- World production is trimmed 2.1 million tons to a record 477.3 million tons, mainly because of lower forecasts for Bangladesh, Brazil, Indonesia and India; the U.S. forecast is a partial offset.
- India’s crop is lowered by 1.0 million tons to 103.0 million due to delayed planting from a late, weak monsoon.

- World consumption is trimmed slightly (down 0.3 million tons) to a record 482.1 million tons.

- World ending stocks are projected at 105.4 million tons, down 3.2 million from last month and down 4.7 million from the prior year; largest month-to-month stock declines are in Bangladesh, Brazil, Indonesia and India.

California drought and sushi rice market
- California’s historic drought has cut plantings of short- and medium-grain sushi rice by about 25% (only ~420,000 acres planted, roughly a quarter below normal), because growers received reduced or no water allocations.
- Sacramento Valley is the main U.S. source of high-quality Japonica varieties prized for sushi; reduced California output threatens higher prices and supply pressures for sushi rice domestically and for some export customers.
- Some California growers and mills that planted or ran full operations expect higher prices and improved returns; example estimates: from ~$20/cwt in 2013 to ~$24/cwt.
- Restaurants and sushi suppliers are bracing for higher input costs; some expect only modest menu price increases, others warn of margin pressure and potential substitution or reduced demand if prices rise too far.
- Meanwhile, overall U.S. rice production is forecast to rise sharply (about +21%) in 2014/15 because of larger Southern long-grain and increasing medium-grain output in Arkansas, Louisiana and other states, but Southern medium-grain may not fully substitute for California Japonica in sushi applications.

Bottom line
- U.S. rice production and supplies are up year-over-year, supporting higher use and exports and leaving larger ending stocks overall, but California’s severe drought tightens supplies of premium sushi rice and is likely to push prices and disrupt supply chains for sushi-focused markets even as other U.S. regions expand production. Globally, production remains a record but was trimmed this month; world ending stocks are lower month-to-month and down from a year earlier.

On New Year’s Eve, Mariah Carey’s live headlining set on Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve derailed when she complained she couldn’t hear through her in-ear monitors during “Emotions” and “We Belong Together.” The technical failure left her visibly frustrated and sparked widespread criticism and speculation about whether she had been lip-syncing.

Carey’s team (manager Stella Bulochnikov and publicist Nicole Perna) blamed production, saying they told stage managers the in-ears weren’t working before the set, production reassured them it would be fixed but went live anyway, and the singer was effectively “set up to fail” after cutting her vacation to perform. They also denied claims that she planned to lip sync and said she had rehearsed for the event.

Dick Clark Productions (DCP) strongly disputed those accusations, calling suggestions they intentionally compromised the performance “defamatory” and saying an initial investigation found no involvement in the issues. Production sources and some insiders told Billboard the audio feed had been set to the wrong frequency and placed blame on Carey’s tech team; others said all production systems were working and noted Carey used a body double for earlier rehearsals. Maryland Sound International’s audio producer said every monitor and in-ear device worked correctly.

The incident drew public reaction: Josh Groban posted (then deleted) a joke about lip-syncing, later apologizing for the mean tone, while Carey responded on Twitter with a lighthearted “Shit happens. Have a happy and healthy new year… Here’s to making more headlines in 2017.” Media outlets continue to report conflicting accounts and investigations into exactly what went wrong.

A leaked draft of a United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report warns that global efforts to curb greenhouse gas emissions are far too slow, making climate change risks increasingly critical and raising the chance of major economic disruption. If high emissions continue for another 15 years, limiting warming to internationally agreed targets may become effectively impossible with current technologies. That would likely force future generations to rely on large-scale carbon removal methods (e.g., bioenergy with carbon capture and storage), which are uncertain, costly, and would compete with food production.

The draft highlights that despite visible growth in solar and wind, fossil-fuel emissions—especially from rapidly developing countries such as China—have outpaced clean-energy deployment. Nuclear energy’s share is falling, and governments still subsidize fossil fuels more than clean energy, encouraging long-lived investments (e.g., coal plants) that lock in emissions. Apparent emissions reductions in wealthy countries are partially illusory because trade has outsourced production—and associated emissions—to other nations. The Kyoto Protocol has been inadequate, and a successor treaty won’t take effect until 2020 and may lack sufficient ambition or ratification by major emitters.

The IPCC emphasizes that staying within the 3.6°F (2°C) warming limit requires keeping atmospheric CO2 well under 500 ppm; current trends project exceeding that threshold within decades. Delaying action increases the scale, cost, and technical difficulty of mitigation and adaptation.

Separately, 18 leading U.S. environmental groups (including the Sierra Club and NRDC) urged President Obama to apply a strict “climate-impact” test to all energy decisions—such as the Keystone XL pipeline, Arctic drilling, hydraulic fracturing, coal mining on public lands, and LNG exports—arguing that the administration’s “all of the above” energy policy undermines its climate goals. The letter coincides with debates over the Keystone XL review and a State Department draft finding that the pipeline would not increase emissions, and comes as the Obama administration balances emissions-reduction initiatives (fuel efficiency, limits on coal pollution) with expanded domestic fossil-fuel production. Industry groups and some lawmakers are pushing back, campaigning to promote domestic oil and gas and to challenge administrative climate rules. The administration maintains it is pursuing emissions reductions while acknowledging continued use of oil and gas in the near term.

Thor: The Dark World remained No. 1 at the domestic box office for a second weekend, earning $38.5 million (a 55% drop) and bringing its two-week total to about $147 million against a $170 million production budget. The sequel is on track to surpass the original Thor’s domestic $181 million and is already outgrossing it internationally, with global receipts approaching $480 million and projections above $700 million.

The weekend’s breakout was Universal’s low-budget sequel The Best Man Holiday, which opened far above expectations with a studio estimate of $30.6 million from 2,024 theaters (about $15,115 per theater). The film—made for roughly $17 million—earned strong Friday-to-Saturday gains, drew an audience that was roughly 75% female and 87% African American, and received an A+ CinemaScore, signaling excellent word-of-mouth and potential for long legs. Its 1999 predecessor grossed $34 million total.

Other holdovers: Last Vegas continued steady with $8.9 million (third place) and a $47 million running total; Free Birds placed fourth with $8.3 million and $42.2 million to date; Jackass Presents: Bad Grandpa rounded out the top five with $7.7 million and $90.2 million cumulative, poised to pass $100 million.

In limited release, Nebraska opened strong with $140,000 from four theaters (high per-theater average), and Dallas Buyers Club expanded to 184 theaters, earning $1.8 million (~$9,700 per theater). Next weekend’s major release, The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, is expected to significantly reshape the box office, with early international openings already looking robust.

Summary:

- Major donations and aid: Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan pledged $25 million through their fund at the Silicon Valley Community Foundation to the CDC Foundation to support the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Ebola response in Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone and other threatened areas. This follows a $9 million donation by Microsoft co‑founder Paul Allen. The funds will support efforts to stop the outbreak at its source; CDC Director Tom Frieden emphasized early intervention to protect global health.

- Global outbreak scale and WHO warnings: The World Health Organization reported the outbreak’s death rate has risen to about 70 percent and warned that, without stepped‑up response, West Africa could see as many as 10,000 new cases per week within two months. WHO reported more than 4,400 deaths and roughly 8,900 suspected, probable and confirmed cases, with Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia hardest hit and urban spread a major concern.

- Health care worker infections and U.S. cases: In Dallas, roughly 70 staff at Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital were involved in caring for Thomas Eric Duncan, the Liberian patient who died of Ebola. One nurse (Nina Pham) later tested positive, prompting the CDC to expand monitoring of contacts and investigate potential breaches in infection‑control protocol. Medical records show caregivers used extensive personal protective equipment, and that Duncan suffered severe symptoms (profuse diarrhea, blood in urine), underscoring risks of exposure during care and challenges in tracking and monitoring all contacts.

- Impact on aid workers and journalists: Doctors Without Borders reported 16 of its staff infected and nine dead, criticizing inadequate on‑the‑ground international assistance despite public pledges. Freelance journalist Ashoka Mukpo, who contracted Ebola in Liberia and was evacuated to Nebraska, faced high medical and evacuation costs (evacuation alone about $150,000); a GoFundMe was launched and NBC later agreed to cover his medical expenses, with remaining donations redirected to replace contaminated equipment and support his recovery.

- Response priorities and challenges: WHO and public‑health experts stressed rapidly isolating and treating cases (aiming for 70 percent isolation within two months), strengthening basic care and protective measures for families and clinics, and improving tracking of contacts and proper donning/doffing of protective gear to prevent further spread among health workers and communities.

The American Farm Bureau Federation’s informal survey finds the cost of a classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10 has fallen to $49.04 in 2013, down slightly from $49.48 in 2012 and lower than the $49.20 in 2011. The meal includes turkey, stuffing, sweet potatoes, rolls with butter, peas, cranberries, a relish tray, pumpkin pie with whipped cream, coffee and milk, with enough for leftovers. The largest price drop came from a 16‑pound turkey, which cost $21.76 this year (about $1.36 per pound), roughly 47 cents less than in 2012. LPL Financial’s Jeffrey Kleintop quipped there’s “no inflation on the table.” The note also mentions page‑archiving efforts by the Internet Archive to preserve referenced pages and prevent broken links.

Two 29-year-old Australian twin sisters, Kristin and Candace (often spelled Candice) Hermeler, traveled to Colorado and carried out a planned suicide pact at the Family Shooting Center in Cherry Creek State Park. On the afternoon of the incident they rented handguns and shot themselves in lane 13; Kristin died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, while Candace survived but remained in serious condition at Swedish Medical Center. Because each shot herself, investigators ruled no crime was committed.

Officials found a May 1999 Time magazine cover depicting Columbine shooters among the twins’ belongings and located two 1999 letters Kristin had written to Columbine survivor Brooks Brown in which she described herself as having been “rejected, victimized and ostracized.” The correspondence and earlier phone contact indicate the twins felt connected to Columbine’s themes of bullying; Brown and his mother recall sympathetic exchanges with the twins in 1999, when the sisters were about 18. During interviews after the shooting, the surviving sister denied interest in Columbine and refused to discuss motives; authorities say she confirmed the suicide pact but would not elaborate on reasons.

Surveillance video, physical evidence, and the surviving twin’s statements led Arapahoe County investigators to conclude the event was a suicide and attempted suicide. The case has drawn international attention, with Australian reporters traveling to Colorado. Family members have thanked responders and requested privacy. Mental-health experts consulted in coverage noted that suicide pacts between closely bonded twins can reflect a belief that neither can live without the other and that such decisions often follow long-standing emotional pain, including histories of bullying.

This document compiles reporting, commentary, and reactions about an unverified dossier alleging ties between Donald Trump and Russia, and the fallout after its release.

Key facts and provenance
- The dossier was compiled as opposition research beginning in mid-2016. Initially commissioned by a Republican primary opponent, the work continued after that client dropped out and was later funded by a Democratic-aligned client (possibly a wealthy donor rather than the Clinton campaign or DNC).
- Fusion GPS, a U.S. research firm, retained Christopher Steele, a former MI6 Russia expert now at Orbis Business Intelligence, to investigate Trump’s Russian ties. Steele produced a series of memos between June and December 2016 based largely on Russian and émigré sources and intermediaries.
- The retired European counter-intelligence officer subcontracted on Russia-related matters also passed material to the FBI and reportedly to his own country’s intelligence service. Senator John McCain later received the documents via a trusted emissary at the Halifax security forum and on 9 December personally met FBI Director James Comey and handed the material to the bureau.
- U.S. intelligence chiefs included a summary of the dossier in a highly classified briefing to President Obama and President-elect Trump in mid-January 2017. CNN reported that intelligence officials briefed the White House that Russia had attempted to collect compromising information on Trump.
- BuzzFeed published an unredacted version of the dossier online after media reports signaled the existence of the material. Its origins and how that unredacted copy leaked remain unclear.

Contents and credibility issues
- The memos allege a multi-year Russian effort to cultivate Trump through kompromat, business deals, and possible embarrassing or salacious material (including an allegation about Trump with prostitutes in Moscow). They also allege meetings between Trump associates and Russian officials, including a claim that lawyer Michael Cohen traveled to Prague—an assertion strongly denied by Cohen and for which the FBI reportedly found no evidence.
- Many major news organizations declined to publish the dossier’s unverified allegations because they were anonymous and unsupported by direct evidence. BuzzFeed’s editor defended publication by saying readers should see the material despite “serious reason to doubt” it.
- The dossier’s author, Christopher Steele, is a former senior MI6 officer with Russia expertise; his memos drew on Russian sources and Orbis’s investigative work. Critics point out the anonymity of sources, payment by partisan clients, and apparent factual errors as reasons to treat the dossier cautiously.

Reactions and political fallout
- Jewish organizations (Anti-Defamation League, Anne Frank Center) condemned President-elect Trump’s public comparison of the dossier revelations and responses to Nazi Germany or Holocaust references, calling such analogies insensitive and inappropriate.
- The intelligence community’s involvement and media coverage sparked sharp partisan and normative debates:
  - Some commentators and former intelligence officials argued the dossier and its elevation by U.S. agencies showed necessary scrutiny of foreign interference and possible kompromat.
  - Others accused the “Deep State,” intelligence agencies, and sympathetic media of weaponizing unverified material to undermine a legitimately elected president, warning that endorsing anonymous claims without proof damages journalism and democracy.
- Democrats faced a dilemma: many urged investigation, sanctions on Russia, and stronger oversight, while most stopped short of openly delegitimizing Trump’s presidency. Some lawmakers pushed for an independent commission to probe Russia’s election interference and any links to Trump associates. Republicans and others warned against rushing to judgment without verified evidence.
- The episode intensified mistrust between Trump and the U.S. intelligence community and amplified calls across Congress for further probes into contacts between Trump’s circle and Russia.

Overall takeaway
- The dossier is a collection of unverified, anonymous intelligence reports compiled by a former British intelligence officer hired by a private research effort. It was circulated to U.S. and allied officials, summarized in an intelligence briefing, and eventually leaked and published in full by BuzzFeed.
- Its explosive allegations remain unproven, and its publication provoked intense debates about journalistic responsibility, political weaponization of intelligence, the proper response to foreign election interference, and the legitimacy and oversight of the incoming administration.

This compilation includes several short news items and a lengthy report about Bill Maher’s remarks on Islam following the Charlie Hebdo massacre.

- Headlines: Roy Moore said he would not be bound if the Supreme Court changed what he called God’s “organic law” on marriage; an Idaho woman was arrested for attempting to convert a Jewish acquaintance to Christianity by beating her; a woman tortured by her boyfriend was ordered by a court to write letters to her attacker or face jail.

- Bill Maher on Charlie Hebdo and Islam: On Jimmy Kimmel Live, HBO host and comedian Bill Maher condemned the murders at the French satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo and used the attack to criticize what he called liberal complacency toward illiberal elements of mainstream Muslim opinion. Maher argued that while most Muslims would not carry out such attacks, "hundreds of millions" allegedly support them or condone retaliation for insults to the prophet. He urged American liberals to defend free speech without special deference to religion, declaring that religions are dangerous and should be open to insult. Maher cited (unnamed) survey findings about poor treatment of women in many majority-Muslim countries and criticized practices like executions for apostasy or homosexuality. His comments—broad, provocative, and dismissive of religious sensitivities—drew criticism from some liberals and moderate Muslims; his on-air tone and language produced stunned silence at times. The segment also touched briefly on Maher’s harsh views of Bill Cosby amid the sexual-assault allegations against him.

An Aeroflot Boeing 777 flying from Moscow to Bangkok encountered a sudden patch of severe clear-air turbulence about 40 minutes before landing, injuring 27 people. The aircraft was carrying 313 passengers. Twenty-four of the injured were Russian and three were Thai; none of the injuries were reported as life‑threatening. Several passengers suffered broken bones, three required surgery (two for multiple leg fractures and one for broken ribs), and 15 people were admitted to Bangkok hospitals; by evening 14 remained hospitalized. Aeroflot and the Russian embassy said many of the injuries occurred because passengers were not wearing seatbelts when the unforecast turbulence struck in clear skies, giving crew no opportunity to warn them. Video and photos showed passengers thrown into aisles and luggage and food scattered around the cabin. The airline noted the crew were experienced (the pilot had over 23,000 flight hours) and said clear-air turbulence is difficult to detect by eye or radar; roughly 750 such events are recorded in civil aviation annually. Aeroflot said it will cover medical costs. The report also recalled the airline’s much-improved safety record since the Soviet era.

This document identifies the 12 jurors who found Casey Anthony not guilty of first-degree murder in July and provides brief biographical details for each: Joan Meier (late 60s, retired, graduate degree); Raymond Screen (mid-30s Black IT worker, two children); Jennifer Ford (32, white nursing student); Linda Bills (middle-aged Black female); Harriet White (50s, retired nurse); Brian Berling (33, white married chef, two children); Kimberly Kimball (41, divorced white female); Kathleen Nighland (50s, married white service representative); James Kearns (53, single, semiretired, caregiver); Ronald Robertson (57, single white billing rep); David Angelo (early 30s white male, high-school PE/health teacher); Mary Fuhr (white female, married 15 years, two children from prior marriage). Two alternate jurors (Elizabeth Jones, Heather Feuerhake) were named; two others (Dean Eckstadt, Russell Huekler) had already disclosed their identities.

The release of juror names had been delayed three months by Orange-Osceola Chief Judge Belvin Perry to allow tensions to cool and protect juror safety after intense public backlash to the verdict (including protests and threats). The jurors declined to speak to the media collectively or individually immediately after the verdict and had previously rejected offers to appear for paid interviews; some reportedly left the area following threats. The jury acquitted Anthony of first-degree murder, aggravated child abuse, and aggravated manslaughter, but convicted her on lesser charges of lying to law enforcement.

Police in the Bronx are investigating the death of a newborn girl found with her umbilical cord still attached outside a seven-story apartment building in Morris Heights. The infant was discovered unconscious in a courtyard alley behind 130 West 183rd Street just after 2:40 p.m.; she was pronounced dead at the scene. Police say surveillance video captured part of the fall from the building’s upper floors but have not determined exactly how the baby fell or whether she was alive when she fell. No arrests have been made.

Authorities located and took the baby’s mother to a hospital and were questioning her at the 52nd Precinct; the father was also questioned and released after saying he did not know the mother was pregnant. The Administration for Children’s Services is investigating but declined to comment on any prior involvement. Neighbors described shock and grief, and the building’s entrance was cordoned off while detectives and the Crime Scene Unit worked the scene.

Two months after United Airlines launched the first major-airline bug-bounty program, security researcher Jordan Wiens (owner of Vector 35) received its inaugural top reward: 1,000,000 MileagePlus miles. Wiens reported a remote-code-execution vulnerability in United’s customer-facing web systems after about six hours of testing. United validated his U.S. citizenship and location, remediated the bug, and deposited the miles — worth roughly $25,000 in cash equivalence — into his account. Wiens, who had never before participated in a commercial bounty, declined to disclose technical details per program rules.

United’s program, announced in May amid controversy over a prior researcher incident, awards miles rather than cash. Its published payout tiers are 1,000,000 miles for remote code execution; 250,000 miles for high-impact issues such as authentication bypass, brute-force attacks, PII disclosure and timing attacks; and 50,000 miles for lower-severity bugs like XSS and CSRF. The program covers United-operated, customer-facing sites and apps (with specific domains listed) and excludes internal systems, partner sites, on-board Wi‑Fi/entertainment/avionics, and other out-of-scope areas. The rules ban disruptive testing (brute force, code injection on live systems, DDoS, automated scans with certain tools), require researchers to be MileagePlus members not resident in sanctioned countries, and bar current/former United or partner employees and authors of the vulnerable code. United also requires confidentiality, may withhold or modify rewards at its discretion, and pays miles only after remediation.

Brandon Jenkins, a prospective student, has sued the Community College of Baltimore County (CCBC) after being denied admission to its radiation therapy program for Fall 2013. Jenkins, who met or exceeded the program’s minimum requirements, told a five-person interview panel that the most important thing in his life was “My God” when asked a personal question. According to the American Center for Law and Justice (ACLJ), which is representing him, that was the only time he mentioned his faith.

Afterward, program director Adrienne Dougherty allegedly told Jenkins in email and conversation that “this field is not the place for religion” and advised him to leave his beliefs out of future interviews, saying the program serves patients of many faiths and some who “believe in nothing at all.” CCBC’s attorney and staff also cited other reasons for the denial: Jenkins’ 3.2 GPA (reported as lower than other applicants), a decade-old criminal charge, and his stated preference to work in Maryland rather than relocate. CCBC declined to comment on the pending litigation but said the college is committed to diversity.

The ACLJ argues the college singled out Jenkins’ religion in violation of the First Amendment and is seeking a federal injunction ordering his admission and unspecified damages for delay and related expenses. ACLJ counsel called the rejection “flatly unlawful” and said the interview question was unrelated to academic qualifications. The case was filed in U.S. District Court in Maryland. Sources: ACLJ, The Christian Post, Reuters and Baltimore Sun excerpts.

A 2-year-old black Labrador named Bear, one of only a handful of dogs in the U.S. trained to detect the scent of electronic data devices, played a pivotal role in the investigation that led to former Subway pitchman Jared Fogle’s arrest on child-porn and related charges. Handled by trainer Todd Jordan, Bear located a thumb drive and other devices that human searchers had missed during a July search of Fogle’s Indiana home; those items contributed to the case. Bear has participated in five investigations, including the arrest of gymnastics coach Marvin Sharp, and routinely finds items like computers, iPads, flash drives and memory cards by scent. Jordan demonstrated Bear’s skill by having him quickly locate hidden devices and said Bear is rewarded with food when he indicates a find. After the Fogle raid, Seattle Police arranged to buy Bear; Jordan is training two more electronic-sniffing dogs for law enforcement. Prosecutors credited Bear as a valuable asset to the investigative team.

POLITICO’s weekly “Caucus” polling of Republican and Democratic insiders in Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina and Nevada — aggregated over seven months and updated for Thanksgiving week — shows growing GOP acceptance that Donald Trump is a durable contender, though his strength varies by state.

Republicans
- Trump is now the presumed favorite of roughly three-quarters of GOP insiders in New Hampshire and South Carolina, where many previously doubted his viability. Insiders cite voter anger on issues like immigration and reactions to global events as fueling his support.
- His position is weaker in Iowa and Nevada, where caucus mechanics and organization matter more. Iowa insiders now slightly favor Ted Cruz over Trump — the first time Cruz has led this measure — because Cruz has been building a strong ground operation. Some Iowa insiders still believe Trump can turn out nontraditional voters. Nevada insiders are split between Trump and Marco Rubio; Rubio benefits from a solid state organization and Mormon support.
- The landscape has shifted since before Trump entered the race (when Scott Walker and Jeb Bush were often favored in early states), and POLITICO notes Trump’s particular strength in South Carolina from October onward.

Democrats
- Democratic insiders across all four states overwhelmingly say Hillary Clinton would win if contests were held today, signaling that Clinton has largely blunted Bernie Sanders’s summer momentum. Sanders retains enthusiastic pockets of support, but insiders argue Clinton’s broader message, organization and perceived electability have reasserted her advantage — especially in New Hampshire and Nevada.

National polling note (Reuters/Ipsos)
- A separate Reuters/Ipsos rolling national GOP poll for the five days ending Nov. 27 found Trump’s support among Republicans fell from 43% to 31% over a week — his largest single-week drop since July — after controversial comments following the Paris attacks and an episode mocking a disabled reporter. Ben Carson also declined (to 15%), while Rubio and Cruz trailed with just over 8% each and Jeb Bush at 7%.

Hailstorms, wet weather and resulting fungus have slashed this year’s Champagne grape harvest by about 40% — the smallest yield in at least 40 years — and contributed to a roughly 20% drop in France’s overall grape harvest, with declines also seen in Burgundy, Bordeaux, Italy and England. Despite the shortfall, immediate supply disruptions are unlikely: Champagne requires at least 15 months’ aging, is typically blended from multiple vintages, and producers report more than a three-year reserve of finished/aging product and vats, built up during larger harvest years. A prior surplus—exacerbated by weaker demand in the U.S. and South America during the recession—also helps absorb this year’s loss. Demand appears to be recovering internationally (U.S. sales rose 14.4% in 2011, China grew strongly), but domestic French consumption has fallen (French sales down 2% in 2011, with steeper holiday declines) amid a sluggish economy and rising unemployment, which particularly hurts smaller houses. Major houses have offset declines through exports, while some distributors’ discounting to clear stock risks damaging Champagne’s image.

A Department of Homeland Security Inspector General (IG) report found that Secret Service employees improperly accessed and widely disseminated sensitive personal information about Rep. Jason Chaffetz while he was investigating the agency. Between March 24 and April 2, 2015, about 45 employees viewed Chaffetz’s 2003 Secret Service job-application file nearly 60–60+ times; the IG concluded only four accesses had a legitimate need. Some staffers shared the information internally via email and at least one acknowledged giving details to a reporter. The disclosures coincided with a March 24 House hearing in which Chaffetz criticized the Secret Service over security lapses.

The report singled out Assistant Director Edward (Ed) Lowery for an email saying “some information that he might find embarrassing needs to get out,” though Lowery denied directing leaks and said his message was a vent. The IG criticized the agency for violating the Privacy Act of 1974 and condemned the broad, inappropriate circulation of the file across headquarters, field offices and senior layers of the service. Investigators were unable to determine all external sources because so many insiders knew of the file.

Chaffetz called the actions intimidating and vowed to continue oversight. Secret Service Director Joseph Clancy apologized, promised disciplinary action and said he would review policies. DHS Secretary Jeh Johnson also apologized and urged accountability. The report noted that Clancy himself was reportedly unaware of the widespread sharing, and it raised concerns about potential conflicts in the IG probe after Secret Service internal-affairs inspectors participated in interviews, a decision criticized as compromising independence and possibly deterring whistleblowers.

A multinational team led by the British Antarctic Survey is racing to study a marine ecosystem that has been isolated beneath the Larsen C ice shelf for roughly 120,000 years. In July 2017 the trillion-ton iceberg A-68 calved from Larsen C, exposing about 2,200–3,600 square miles of seabed and surface water to sunlight for the first time in millennia. Scientists will spend three weeks aboard the research ship RRS James Clark Ross (starting Feb. 21) collecting seafloor animals, microbes, plankton, sediments, water samples and video to capture a baseline snapshot before the environment changes and new species colonize.

Leaders including expedition head Katrin Linse and BAS science director David Vaughan stress the urgency of studying how life responds to this dramatic change and using the opportunity to address questions about the resilience of polar continental shelves under climate change. The mission will be logistically difficult—very cold temperatures, heavy sea ice and rough seas—but is permitted under Antarctic conservation agreements.

Previous submarine work by Greenpeace showed Antarctic seafloor life can be diverse and abundant, prompting calls for large marine protected areas. While the Larsen C calving itself can’t be conclusively tied to human-driven warming, researchers note regional ice shelf retreat and accelerating ice-melt trends make understanding these ecosystems and their vulnerability increasingly important.

A Central California woman, Myrna Arias, has sued Intermex Wire Transfer LLC in Kern County Superior Court alleging she was fired after uninstalling a required job-management app (Xora/StreetSmart) from her company-issued iPhone because it tracked employees’ GPS location 24/7, including off-duty hours. Arias says she and co-workers asked whether off-duty monitoring would occur; her regional sales VP, John Stubits, allegedly admitted they would be tracked, boasted about knowing her driving speed at particular times, and told her to tolerate the intrusion. Arias complained that GPS monitoring continued even when using the app’s clock in/out feature and that the app could not be fully disabled. After she removed the app, she was reportedly scolded and then terminated weeks later despite meeting quotas and earning about $7,250 monthly.

The complaint alleges invasion of privacy, retaliation, labor-code and unfair business practices violations, intentional interference with contract (claiming Intermex’s CEO contacted Arias’s former employer NetSpend, leading to her termination there), and seeks an injunction plus over $500,000 in general, special and punitive damages. Arias’s attorney, Gail Glick, says the app let managers see employees’ every move and that the monitoring continued during personal time; Intermex had not commented.

Senators Heidi Heitkamp (D-N.D.) and Joe Donnelly (D-Ind.)—both from reliably Republican states—announced their support for same‑sex marriage, citing conversations with constituents, personal reflection, and prior pro‑LGBT actions (Donnelly noted votes to repeal “don’t ask, don’t tell” and support for workplace non‑discrimination). Their declarations add to a recent wave of Democratic Senate endorsements (including Tom Carper and Bill Nelson) and are notable because their states backed Romney in 2012.

The piece then analyzes why so many senators have shifted positions quickly. Using an expanded dataset of every senator-year since 1997 and variables including party, DW‑Nominate ideology scores, birth year, and modeled state and national public support for same‑sex marriage, a logistic regression shows ideology and state public opinion are the strongest predictors of a senator’s endorsement. Party adds little predictive power beyond ideology, and age has a small, insignificant effect.

A simple linear public‑opinion–based model underpredicts the recent spike in Senate endorsements. A refined “majority model” — which treats the key factor as the probability that same‑sex marriage has reached majority support (allowing for uncertainty in state polls) — fits the timing and rapid increase much better. The author argues senators are timing endorsements around perceived majority status: once support appeared to be a national majority (or near it) some senators felt politically safe to switch positions, creating a cascade as colleagues learned it was politically viable.

Going forward, the rate of new endorsements is expected to slow: the Senate is finite, many remaining opponents represent states where majority support hasn’t arrived, or oppose on principle or fear primary challenges. The recent surge thus reflects both genuine shifts in public opinion and strategic, threshold‑based decision‑making by senators.

Actor Wesley Snipes began serving a three-year federal prison sentence at the minimum-security Federal Correctional Institution McKean in Lewis Run, Pennsylvania, after being ordered to surrender by noon. Snipes, 48, was convicted in 2008 on three misdemeanor counts of willful failure to file tax returns; prosecutors say he failed to file returns for at least a decade and owed $2.7 million on $13.8 million of income from 1999–2001, and had allegedly not paid taxes on roughly $38 million earned since 1999. He was acquitted of more serious felony charges.

McKean is a low-security camp for about 300 nonviolent inmates with two-man barracks, daily showers, limited movie showings, organized sports and religious groups. Inmates earn only pennies an hour for chores, face five daily head counts, have restricted visitation contact, and a $290 monthly commissary limit. Snipes, who once said he relied on tax advisors and described himself as a “naive truth-seeker,” maintained he plans to seek Supreme Court review and filed a last-minute motion for a new trial alleging juror misconduct. The sentencing judge cited a “history of contempt” for tax laws and imposed consecutive one-year terms for the three convictions.

Robin Roberts made a celebrated return to Good Morning America after a 173–174 day absence following a bone marrow transplant to treat myelodysplastic syndrome (M.D.S.), a rare blood disorder likely linked to earlier breast cancer treatment. ABC promoted her comeback in advance; fans sent tens of thousands of well-wishes online and filled the studio. Roberts, 52, appeared emotional and grateful, saying faith, family and friends brought her to the moment. Doctors had cleared her after recent tests showed no abnormalities.

ABC kept Roberts involved while she recuperated—co-hosts frequently mentioned her and shared her messages—and maintained viewer engagement during her leave. The network plans a gradual return to on-air duties, with Roberts appearing initially only some days a week as she rebuilds strength; doctors will reassess day by day. Elizabeth Vargas and Amy Robach, who filled in while she was away, will continue to appear regularly. Roberts is scheduled to cover the Academy Awards and will air a behind-the-scenes special about her recovery on 20/20.

Her return renewed ABC’s optimism about Good Morning America’s competitive edge against NBC’s Today, though some critics accused the network of overcoverage. Colleagues on both shows expressed support, and Today sent a gift and public well-wishes. Roberts described the transplant recovery as harrowing—at one point feeling she might die—yet credited caregivers for pulling her back. She reported feeling not overly tired after her return broadcast but noted some vision issues under studio lights; her team will monitor her progress closely.

On Aug. 6–7, 2016, five members of the Short family — Megan (33), her husband Mark (40) and their three children Liana (8), Mark Jr. (5) and Willow (2) — were found shot to death in their Sinking Spring, Berks County, Pennsylvania home in an apparent murder‑suicide. Police responding to a welfare check after Megan missed a lunch date forced entry and discovered the bodies and a slain dog. Investigators reported a handgun near one of the adults and a handwritten note described as a “murder/suicide” note; they also said the couple had a history of domestic issues but have not disclosed who fired the shots.

Neighbors said Megan had posted on Facebook in late July that she planned to leave her 16‑year marriage and was seeking a rental, and a nearby friend provided screenshots of exchanges in which Megan referenced abuse and moving out. The community and the Wilson School District arranged counseling for students and families; local clergy asked for prayers.

The Shorts had been publicly known for their advocacy around congenital heart disease after daughter Willow underwent a heart transplant as an infant. Multiple profiles (Reading Eagle, The New York Times) described the family’s struggles obtaining Willow’s costly anti‑rejection medications, the stress and PTSD Megan reported following Willow’s care, and the family’s active involvement in organ‑donor awareness. Mark’s social media posts had portrayed a loving family, while neighbors recalled marital tension.

Authorities continued investigating and planned at least one autopsy; officials have urged anyone in crisis to seek help through suicide prevention resources.

An international enforcement operation led by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) called Operation Sunflower resulted in 245 arrests and the identification of 123 victims of child sexual exploitation and child pornography. Most arrests (222) occurred in the United States; others were made in six unnamed countries. Of the 123 victims, 110 lived in the U.S. across 19 states; ages ranged from infants/toddlers (five victims under age 3, nine ages 4–6) up through adults who were abused as children. Authorities directly removed 44 children from alleged abusers; the remainder involved victims exploited outside their homes or historical abuse now affecting adults.

The operation ran through November and December, with many arrests carried out in early December. California saw the most arrests (37), including multiple arrests in the Bay Area and Fresno—where three children, including a disabled 7-year-old, were rescued. Some suspects are registered sex offenders; one high-profile arrest was Michael Lindsay of San Jose, detained on allegations of child sex tourism involving the Philippines. Investigations are ongoing.

ICE emphasized the role of forensic image analysis and international cooperation (including the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children) in tracing where abuse occurred and identifying victims and perpetrators. Officials also released images of unidentified suspects in several open cases—one involving images believed to show a 13-year-old girl abused about 11 years ago in the Los Angeles/San Fernando Valley area—and asked the public for tips. Tips can be reported to ICE. Operation Sunflower was named in reference to a 2011 case in which forensic analysis of a sunflower-shaped road sign helped locate and rescue an intended rape victim.

Ken Bone, the mustachioed undecided voter who became an internet sensation for his red sweater after asking a question about energy policy at the St. Louis presidential debate, told CNN the debate “got very uncomfortable from up close,” likening it to “watching mom and dad fight.” He criticized the evening’s “bickering and name calling” but praised moderators Martha Raddatz and Anderson Cooper and said substantive answers could be found beneath the rhetoric.

Bone—who gained thousands of Twitter followers and widespread attention for photographing the emptying hall with what looked like a disposable camera—said he didn’t know Trump had invited several women alleging misconduct by Bill Clinton to the audience and called the move “uncalled for,” though he doesn’t expect it to determine his vote. He said the debate made him less certain rather than more: he had been leaning toward Trump but was impressed by Clinton’s composure and answers. Bone also explained the red sweater was a backup after he split the seat of his pants on the way to the event. Media and retailers quickly seized on his look, with outlets noting surging interest in similar sweaters.

A major new analysis published in Science Advances concludes that Earth is already undergoing a human-driven “sixth mass extinction.” Using conservative methods—the highest recent estimate of the pre-human (background) extinction rate (2 extinctions per 10,000 species per 100 years) and only IUCN-confirmed extinctions—the authors find modern vertebrate extinction rates over the 20th century are 8–100 times higher than the background rate. Key findings and points:

- Scale of loss: Since 1900, hundreds of vertebrate species have been lost (e.g., 477 vertebrates cited in one comparison versus ~9 expected under background rates). Including confirmed extinct, extinct-in-the-wild, and possibly extinct categories gives a total of hundreds of losses since 1500.
- Acceleration: Extinction rates have increased sharply over the last 200 years and especially since the mid-20th century; amphibians show marked recent acceleration.
- Time-comparison: The number of vertebrate extinctions in the past century would have taken roughly 800–10,000 years to occur at the background rate.
- Causes: The losses are attributed to human activities—habitat destruction and fragmentation, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species (including pathogens), and climate change—often interacting and driven by population growth, consumption and inequity.
- Consequences: Continued elevated extinction rates threaten ecosystem services (pollination, water purification, etc.) and human well-being; past mass extinctions required hundreds of thousands to millions of years for recovery.
- Conservatism and caveats: The study deliberately uses conservative assumptions (higher background rate and only well-documented extinctions) and therefore likely underestimates the crisis. Some scientists caution that declaring a full mass extinction depends on future trajectories (either rapid acceleration or sustained high rates).
- Call to action: The authors urge rapid, greatly intensified conservation efforts to protect threatened species and reduce pressures on populations; delaying action narrows the opportunity to avert a true mass extinction.

Overall, even with conservative metrics, the study presents strong evidence that modern vertebrate extinction rates are far above natural background levels and that urgent, large-scale conservation and policy responses are needed to prevent catastrophic biodiversity loss.

Two explosive devices detonated at separate Las Cruces, New Mexico, churches on Sunday morning; no one was injured and damage was relatively minor, but congregations were shaken and both buildings were temporarily closed while investigators searched the scenes.

Key points:
- First blast: about 8–8:30 a.m. at Calvary Baptist Church (a device in a mailbox near an administrative entrance). Worshippers were gathering; roughly 30 people were inside. Witnesses said they saw bomb parts.
- Second blast: roughly 20–30 minutes later at Holy Cross Catholic Church, about three miles away; an explosive went off in a trash can near the main entrance during the 8 a.m. Mass, shattering the glass front while communion was taking place. About 200 people were inside; because many were kneeling inside, the timing likely prevented injuries.
- Law enforcement response: Las Cruces PD, Dona Ana County bomb squad, New Mexico State Police, NMSU K-9, FBI, ATF and DHS are investigating. Authorities believe the two incidents are likely related and say the devices were more dangerous than fireworks; they have not labeled the acts terrorism or identified suspects or motives yet.
- Community reaction: Officials, including Gov. Susana Martinez, condemned the attacks and urged continued worship; local faith leaders called for forgiveness and vigilance. Churches were advised to monitor for suspicious items and increase security (parking patrols, cameras).

Researchers from Harvard (Andrew Reece) and the University of Vermont (Christopher Danforth) report that Instagram photos can reveal signs of depression. In a preprint study (not yet peer-reviewed) they analyzed roughly 44,000 images from 166 volunteers who also completed depression surveys and provided diagnosis histories. Images were evaluated two ways: human raters scored photos for happiness, sadness, likability and interest, while algorithms measured objective features such as hue, brightness, saturation, face count and filter use.

Key findings
- Depressed participants’ photos tended to be darker, bluer and less saturated (more gray), and they more often used the black-and-white “Inkwell” filter; nondepressed users favored warmer filters like “Valencia.”
- Algorithmic analysis outperformed average human raters at identifying depressed users and could identify signs before clinical diagnosis in some cases. The computer picked up systematic visual patterns that humans did not reliably perceive.
- Depressed users posted more images containing faces but with fewer people per photo, which may suggest smaller social gatherings.
- More post comments correlated with depression while more likes correlated with the absence of depression.

Implications and cautions
- The authors propose such image-based screening could augment early detection and prompt people to seek care rather than serve as treatment. They stress these tools should screen or assess, not replace clinicians, and caution against overinterpretation of single photos (a blue photo doesn’t necessarily mean depression).
- The study was posted on arXiv and is undergoing peer review; the computer’s performance was not directly compared with clinicians analyzing the same images. Ethical concerns (privacy, consent, commercial misuse) and the need for validation remain.

Broader context
- The work joins other AI efforts to detect health conditions from digital traces and suggests future opt-in screening tools that analyze social media to flag possible mental-health issues for follow-up by human professionals.

Dominique Venner, a 78-year-old far-right writer and former OAS member, shot himself at the altar of Paris’s Notre Dame Cathedral on Tuesday afternoon in an act he and supporters portrayed as political protest. The cathedral, holding about 1,500 visitors at the time, was evacuated; no one else was physically harmed. Venner left a final essay on his website and a recorded message read after his death in which he denounced France’s new law legalizing gay marriage and adoption and criticized immigration from North Africa, saying he “must sacrifice” himself to “awaken slumbering consciences.” 

Far-right figures, including National Front leader Marine Le Pen and MEP Bruno Gollnisch, praised his gesture as a political statement; others compared its symbolism to the suicide of Japanese nationalist writer Yukio Mishima. Church officials said Venner was not a regular at Notre Dame; masses were canceled and a vigil planned. Interior Minister Manuel Valls called the scene shocking given the cathedral’s national significance. Venner had a long career writing nationalist essays and military histories; his death followed weeks of protests over the gay marriage bill, which was recently signed into law.

Indiana resident James Wesley Howell, 20, who was arrested in Santa Monica, Calif., on June 12, 2016, faces multiple charges in two states. California authorities have charged him with three felony weapons and ammunition counts after finding a loaded assault rifle with modified high-capacity magazines and about 15 pounds of explosive-ready chemicals in his car. Howell pleaded not guilty in the California case and was held on $2 million bail; he told police he was headed to a large Los Angeles gay pride event. His arrest came hours after the Orlando nightclub attack and prompted heightened security at the parade.

Separately, Clark County, Indiana, prosecutors filed one count of child molesting against Howell, alleging he had sex with a 12-year-old girl on May 31 at a state forestry site after meeting her through an adult friend. The girl’s mother reported the incident June 2; Howell was interviewed by investigators June 7 and appears to have left Indiana afterward. Prosecutor Jeremy Mull said Howell likely fled to California after learning he was under investigation and is seeking his extradition. If convicted in Indiana, he faces up to 16 years in prison.

Background details include prior incidents in October in which Howell allegedly pulled a gun twice; he was convicted in April of misdemeanor intimidation and was on probation that barred him from possessing weapons or leaving Indiana. Federal agents also searched his Jeffersonville home, but provided no details.

Jeffrey Sandusky, 41, son of former Penn State assistant coach Jerry Sandusky, pleaded guilty to all 14 criminal counts Friday—one week before his scheduled trial. The charges, arising from incidents in 2013 and 2016 involving two teenage girls, include solicitation of statutory sexual assault and solicitation of involuntary deviate sexual intercourse (soliciting sex from a child under 16 and soliciting child pornography). Under a plea deal he faces up to six years in state prison (with a maximum possible sentence of eight years), and will be classified as a Tier III sex offender, the highest level in Pennsylvania. His lawyer had not immediately commented.

Bill Cosby was sentenced on Sept. 25, 2018, to three to 10 years in Pennsylvania state prison after being convicted of drugging and sexually assaulting Andrea Constand in 2004; the judge also labeled him a “sexually violent predator,” requiring lifetime monthly counseling. Moments after the sentencing, Cosby’s spokesperson Andrew Wyatt delivered an impassioned statement outside the courthouse, calling the trial “the most racist and sexist trial in the history of the United States,” characterizing the outcome as part of a broader “sex war” tied to the national conversation around sexual misconduct (invoking contemporaneous allegations against Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh), and alleging bias and falsified evidence. Wyatt and other members of Cosby’s team have repeatedly framed the case in racial terms, at times using incendiary comparisons. Cosby, 81 and legally blind, was processed into the Pennsylvania prison system and spent his first night at SCI Phoenix; officials said his needs and safety would be assessed and that corrections staff aim to place him in the general population when appropriate.
