The article explains why supermarket rotisserie chickens are often cheaper than buying and roasting a whole raw bird yourself. Grocery stores convert unsold or near-expiration fresh inventory—meat, produce, and other perishables—into prepared foods (rotisserie chickens, deli items, salad bars, hot bars, etc.) to avoid losses from spoilage. This reuse lets stores recover value from products they otherwise would discard and helps them offer low-priced prepared meals. Sell-by/use-by dates are intended as quality guides, not safety limits, and are often conservative; better consumer judgment could reduce waste. The practice of recycling near-expired items into prepared foods improves overall efficiency, lowers prices for consumers, and reduces food waste impact, while remaining safe when handled properly. The piece argues that such incremental operational innovations—like spit-roasting unsold chickens—are important contributors to rising living standards, alongside more visible tech innovations.

A U.S. Homeland Security intelligence report, shared with law enforcement in recent weeks, warns that Islamic State (ISIS) likely has the capability to produce authentic-looking Syrian passports. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) confirmed the report’s existence; the full document was not released publicly. Key points:

- ISIS reportedly seized passport printing equipment, blank passport books and access to passport offices in Syrian cities it controls (notably Deir ez-Zour and Raqqa), raising the possibility it can manufacture legitimate-looking travel documents.
- The group may also have access to biographical and fingerprint databases from Syrian government facilities, increasing the risk of identity theft and enabling passports tied to real identities.
- The Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) intelligence product noted sources at “moderate confidence” and warned that passports “issued” in ISIS-controlled areas or printed from captured blanks could already have been used to travel abroad, potentially to the United States.
- FBI Director James Comey told Congress the intelligence community is concerned about ISIS’s ability to manufacture fraudulent passports. State Department and DHS officials said they are aware of and taking the reports seriously.
- The report highlighted that fake Syrian passports are widespread, inexpensive in the region, and have already been used in past European attacks; it also cautioned that portable passport-printing machines make the situation fluid and dangerous, warning that uncontrolled passport production would enable ISIS operations beyond its territory.

Overall, U.S. authorities see ISIS’s access to passport materials and identity data as a significant security threat that could facilitate international travel by militants or operatives using authentic-looking or legitimately tied Syrian passports.

On Christmas Day The French Laundry in Yountville was burglarized; 76 bottles were stolen from the restaurant’s wine room, overwhelmingly high-end Burgundy from Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC) plus several cult Napa Cabernets (Screaming Eagle) and other rare bottles. The haul is valued at roughly $300,000 or more at retail — far higher at restaurant list prices — with individual DRC Romanée-Conti bottles worth about $11k–$15k retail. The thieves forced open a wine-room door and appear to have targeted specific, highly collectible labels.

Chef-owner Thomas Keller publicly appealed to the wine community via Twitter for information and said the restaurant is working with local law enforcement. The French Laundry — a three-Michelin-star restaurant that had just finished service for Christmas Eve before closing for a lengthy kitchen remodel — provided a detailed inventory of the stolen bottles, which includes multiple vintages of Romanée-Conti (Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg, Romanée St. Vivant, Grands Échézeaux), several Screaming Eagle vintages, multiple Dom Pérignon 2004 and a few other rare Burgundies. Keller said they look forward to rebuilding the cellar and urged anyone with tips to contact the restaurant.

Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams was arrested and questioned for four days at Antrim police station in connection with the 1972 IRA abduction and murder of Jean McConville, a widowed mother of 10 who was secretly buried and whose body was recovered in 2003. Adams voluntarily presented himself to police after contacting them about the case two months earlier; he says he went willingly, was then arrested under the terrorism act, denies any involvement and called the allegations a "sustained, malicious, untruthful campaign." Police have released him without charge and say they have sent a file to the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) for prosecutors to decide whether there is sufficient admissible evidence and whether prosecution would be in the public interest.

The arrest and its timing during an election campaign provoked political controversy. Adams criticized the timing and the use of coercive terrorism legislation; some unionist politicians and others said there is no reason to delay murder investigations for political calendars and questioned the propriety of his release. Sinn Féin reiterated its commitment to the peace process and Adams stated "The IRA is gone, it's finished."

The McConville family said they will continue to pursue justice after decades of campaigning. The case is linked to recent developments, including charges against former IRA leader Ivor Bell based largely on interviews from the Boston College oral-history tapes — a collection of confidential interviews with ex-paramilitaries — which have informed recent police activity related to the "Disappeared." Northern Ireland officials noted prosecutions will be handled by PPS lawyers; due to a conflict the director of public prosecutions will delegate the decision on Adams’s file.

At the fourth GOP debate in Milwaukee, Jeb Bush delivered his strongest performance yet—more assertive, better-prepared and less gaffe-prone—which reassured donors but didn’t materially change his weak standing in the field. The debate itself was more policy-focused and restrained than prior clashes, producing few fireworks or game-changing moments and unlikely to shift the overall race.

Winners
- Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz emerged as the night’s clear standouts. Both displayed poise, command of facts and effective messaging: Rubio on military policy, immigration and contrasts with Hillary Clinton; Cruz on entitlement reform, anti-"crony" rhetoric and defending a robust national defense. Their steady performances reinforced their roles as the field’s leading competitors.
- Rand Paul had a comparatively strong night, making libertarian arguments on the Fed, fiscal conservatism and challenging Rubio on defense spending.
- Carly Fiorina and, to a lesser extent, Ben Carson (who showed more energy early on) had moments that kept them viable, though Carson struggled with detailed foreign-policy questions.

Losers and weak performers
- Donald Trump reverted at times to combative, broad-stroke rhetoric and was less central to the debate’s substance than in previous nights; his foreign-policy answers were thin. Still, his poll position remained unaffected.
- John Kasich appeared peevish and often lost exchanges, undercutting his attempt to position himself as a pragmatic center.
- Jeb Bush, while improved and credited with a few crisp lines (notably rebutting Trump’s mass-deportation proposal), still lacked the stage mastery of Rubio and Cruz and failed to produce a breakout moment that would revive his campaign.
- Ben Carson struggled on substance, took little speaking time and faced questions about past anecdotal claims.

Main issues and dynamics
- Immigration and the role of America in the world dominated much of the debate, exposing the party’s divisions: Trump and Cruz backing hardline border measures, Kasich and Bush rejecting mass deportations, and Rubio largely staying out of the core immigration brawl.
- Defense spending and America’s global role produced a notable clash between Rubio (and Cruz) and Rand Paul, with Cruz framing strong defense as less costly than its absence.
- The debate’s tighter format and emphasis on substantive questions reduced chaotic exchanges and yielded fewer dramatic moments; moderators were praised for running a steadier, more issue-focused event.

Takeaway
The Milwaukee debate reinforced existing hierarchies rather than upending them: Rubio and Cruz continued to stand out, Bush showed recovery but not revival, Trump remained a dominant presence despite a muted night, and the overall race looked set for a slow, incremental slog into the primary season.

Shia LaBeouf has exited the upcoming Broadway revival of Lyle Kessler’s Orphans, citing "creative differences." The 26-year-old left about a month before previews, which begin March 19 at the Schoenfeld Theater, with an April 7 opening still planned. The Daniel Sullivan–directed production also stars Alec Baldwin as a powerful man held captive by two brothers; no replacement for LaBeouf has been announced and the statement gave no details about the disagreements.

Orphans, first staged in 1983 and previously adapted into a 1987 film, is a frequently revived play. LaBeouf — known for Transformers and the recent Indiana Jones film — had little theater experience and earlier this year said he would move away from big studio blockbusters toward riskier indie projects. His upcoming films include Robert Redford’s The Company You Keep and Lars von Trier’s Nymphomaniac.

The document also includes a separate piece about Tom Hanks preparing for his Broadway debut in Lucky Guy, Nora Ephron’s play about columnist Mike McAlary. Hanks discusses why he took the challenging, unflattering role, his collaboration with director George C. Wolfe, and Ephron’s influence and passing during the play’s development.

Afghanistan’s High Peace Council said it will accept a Taliban liaison office in Qatar to begin talks, but set strict conditions and rejected any foreign involvement in negotiations without Kabul’s consent. In an 11-point note to foreign missions, the council demanded that the Taliban stop violence against civilians, sever ties with al Qaeda and other terrorist groups, and accept the Afghan constitution and the rights it guarantees (including for women) before formal negotiations begin. The council also said Pakistan’s support would be necessary because many Taliban leaders are based there.

Kabul prefers a Taliban office in Saudi Arabia or Turkey but will accept Doha if Afghan sovereignty is respected and the office exists solely to facilitate talks. The council expressed anger that the United States, Qatar and Germany reportedly held secret contacts with the Taliban and that the U.S. considered moving some Afghan detainees from Guantanamo to Doha; Afghan officials insist any prisoners should be returned to Afghan custody.

The stance follows setbacks to reconciliation efforts, notably the September assassination of peace council head Burhanuddin Rabbani by a suicide bomber posing as a Taliban emissary, which hardened government demands that negotiators be properly authorized. U.S. and State Department spokespeople stress support for an Afghan-led reconciliation that brings fighters who renounce violence and respect the constitution back into society, and say Pakistan has an important role.

The Taliban, which reject the constitution and insist foreign troops must leave, showed no sign of accepting Kabul’s conditions and reiterated confidence in eventual victory. Separately, an insider-style shooting by a man in Afghan uniform wounded coalition troops in western Afghanistan, highlighting concerns about infiltration as NATO accelerates training Afghan forces ahead of its 2014 combat withdrawal.

The Supreme Court unanimously held in Bowman v. Monsanto (No. 11-796) that an Indiana farmer infringed Monsanto’s patent by using Monsanto’s Roundup Ready soybean seeds obtained from a grain elevator to grow and save new seeds without paying the company. Justice Elena Kagan’s opinion emphasized a narrow holding: the patent exhaustion doctrine allows a buyer to resell or consume a purchased patented item but does not permit the purchaser to create new copies of the patented invention. Bowman’s argument that the seeds “self-replicated” or that exhaustion should cover his conduct was rejected—Kagan said Bowman actively controlled and directed the reproduction over multiple generations, so his actions undermined Monsanto’s patent rights and the value of the patent would be destroyed if simple copying were permitted.

The decision protects inventors of self-replicating technologies (biotech, vaccines, cell lines, software, etc.) by confirming that patents can bar downstream reproduction of patented inventions, but the Court left open broader questions about other kinds of self-replicating products and scenarios where replication occurs outside a purchaser’s control. The ruling drew praise from biotech industry groups and Monsanto as supportive of innovation, and criticism from farm advocacy groups who view it as harmful to farmers.

Facebook analyzed about 1 million English-language U.S. status updates (anonymized) using the LIWC lexicon (68 word categories) to correlate language use with user age, friend count, time of day, and social feedback.

Key findings:
- Age differences
  - Older users: write longer updates, use more articles and prepositions, and more words about religion, social processes and family.
  - Younger users: use fewer articles/prepositions, more self-referential pronouns (“I”), more profanity, anger words and negative emotions, and more school-related language.
  - Update length was the single best predictor of age.

- Popularity (friend count)
  - More popular users: use more second-person pronouns (“you”), write longer posts, and mention music and sports more. They are less likely to discuss family, use fewer time-related words and fewer tense markers, and show less overall emotional language.

- Time-of-day patterns
  - Positive-emotion words peak in the morning; negative emotions rise after ~10 p.m.
  - Topic usage follows daily routines: sleep-related words peak at night/early morning, work and school words in the morning, and leisure/social words increase later in the day.

- Feedback (likes/comments)
  - Posts with more positive emotion words get more likes but fewer comments; negative-emotion posts get fewer likes but more comments (likely consoling responses).
  - Religious posts tend to receive likes rather than comments. Longer posts and posts with more pronouns get more engagement. Posts about sleep correlate negatively with both likes and comments, even after controlling for timing.

- Homophily
  - People’s word usage correlates with their friends’ usage: friends tend to use similar categories of words (not fully adjusted for shared demographics).

Methodology notes:
- Word-category percentages per update were computed automatically using LIWC.
- Analyses controlled for factors like time of year, friend count, age, and time-zone adjustments where noted.
- Results have potential applications for tailoring content or advertising to demographic and temporal patterns (e.g., timing promotions or matching tone to audience age).

Overall, Facebook’s linguistic analysis highlights predictable but quantifiable patterns linking language in status updates with age, popularity, daily routines, and social reactions.

One day before the 2014 Winter Olympics opening ceremony in Sochi, Google replaced its global homepage logo with a rainbow-colored Olympic-themed doodle and linked it to the Olympic Charter’s anti‑discrimination language: “The practice of sport is a human right…Every individual must have the possibility of practicing sport, without discrimination of any kind…friendship, solidarity and fair play.” The rainbow motif echoes the LGBT pride flag and was visible on Google’s sites worldwide, including Russia’s.

The doodle came amid international controversy over Russia’s law banning “homosexual propaganda” and President Vladimir Putin’s remarks seen as discriminatory. Some companies (notably AT&T and American Apparel) had publicly condemned the law or promoted Principle 6 of the Olympic Charter, but most official Olympic sponsors had not. Google declined to comment on the doodle, while IOC leadership publicly opposed discrimination. The action was widely read as a pro‑LGBT statement ahead of the Sochi Games.

Nicole Bahret of Cumming, Georgia, learned her 18-year-old son, Mackean Robertson, had been killed when she pulled up to the scene of a three-car crash in mid‑July and recognized his Honda. Deputies say a 17‑year‑old driver, Natalie D’Allen, in a Mercedes failed to yield, striking Robertson’s 2005 Honda, which slid into a westbound Nissan Pathfinder; Robertson was pronounced dead at the scene, while other drivers and passengers were hospitalized with non‑life‑threatening injuries. D’Allen later turned herself in and posted bond; the sheriff’s office said charges are pending the ongoing investigation. Bahret had spoken with her son about an hour before the crash; he had recently graduated from Georgia Cyber Academy and started a job. Hundreds attended his funeral, and Forsyth Central High School has scheduled a memorial for Aug. 12. A fundraiser for funeral costs has raised over $15,000. Bahret and family members described their grief and the support they’ve received.

Researchers report that people can partly infer personality from body odor. In a study to be published in the European Journal of Personality, 30 men and 30 women each wore a white cotton T‑shirt for three consecutive nights (avoiding fragrances, smoking and odorous foods) and completed a personality inventory. About 200 independent raters then smelled the shirts (each shirt smelled by 20 raters) and rated five personality traits on a 1–10 scale.

Raters’ judgments showed significant, though imperfect, agreement with donors’ self‑reports for three traits: extraversion (outgoingness), neuroticism (anxiety/moodiness) and dominance. Accuracy for extraversion and neuroticism was comparable to that seen when people judge personality from brief video clips. Dominance was judged most accurately when raters assessed the odor of an opposite‑sex donor, suggesting a possible role in mate selection.

Authors propose physiological mechanisms—stress‑related sweating, skin microbiome changes, or hormone‑linked sweat chemistry (e.g., testosterone effects)—that could link personality and scent. The researchers caution the findings are preliminary and may vary across cultures with different baseline body odors; further studies are needed.

Taylor Swift sparked intense speculation about new music after wiping her social media over the weekend and then posting a short, cryptic 10‑second video of a slithering serpent to Instagram and Twitter on Aug. 21, 2017. The blackout came three years to the day after her 1989 announcement, and the snake imagery — posted in multiple clips over subsequent days as tail, midsection and head were shown — fueled fan theories that she’s embracing the “snake” label from last year’s Kim/Kanye controversy and preparing a new era (widely suspected to be her sixth studio album).

Director Joseph Kahn, who has worked with Swift on several 1989 videos, boosted speculation by replying to her post with a smiley face and joking on Twitter, “In 30 minutes, as a show of power, @taylorswift13 will blot out the sun,” a quip tied to that week’s solar eclipse. Reports and industry sources (Us Weekly) had already suggested Swift had been quietly recording and was aiming for a fall release, and fans pointed to the Sept. 30 Grammy eligibility cutoff as a possible deadline.

Reaction online mixed excited conspiracy theories, jokes linking the teaser to the eclipse or Game of Thrones, and commentary about Swift reclaiming the snake image. Overall, the posts were widely interpreted as a deliberate, cryptic lead‑up to a major announcement — most likely new music — though Swift had not officially confirmed release details at the time.

Los Angeles prepared for a highly publicized, 53-hour closure of a 10-mile stretch of the I‑405 through the Sepulveda Pass so Caltrans crews could partially demolish a bridge and add an HOV lane as part of a long-term widening project. The shutdown—promoted in media and social channels and nicknamed “Carmageddon” or “Carpocalypse”—was expected to cripple traffic: roughly 250,000 daily users of that segment would be forced onto smaller freeways and surface streets, effectively hampering connections between the San Fernando Valley and Westside beach communities. City officials urged people to avoid the area or stay home; celebrities helped spread warnings.

Anticipating lost foot traffic, many local businesses rolled out special promotions and creative offers to lure customers or make the best of the disruption: discounted pet portraits, tattoo and piercing discounts, restaurant prix fixe deals, cocktail specials, jewelry markdowns, and amusement‑park incentives (including free rides for San Fernando Valley residents and a novelty “Caltrans Orange” cotton candy). Transportation alternatives included budget one‑way JetBlue hops and high‑end 15‑minute helicopter flights marketed as “Fly Over the 405.” A regional website aggregated events, deals and commentary tied to the closure.

The article also places the shutdown in historical context, recounting the Sepulveda Pass’s long evolution from Native trails and 18th‑century exploration through the 1935 Sepulveda Boulevard and the massive 1960s construction of the 405. That original freeway build was a major engineering effort celebrated at its 1962 opening; over decades the corridor became chronically congested, setting the stage for the contemporary widening project and the dramatic weekend closure.

On the two-month anniversary of Occupy Wall Street, protesters organized a citywide “Day of Action” in New York that tested the movement’s resilience after a pre-dawn eviction from Zuccotti Park. Actions began early with attempts to march on Wall Street and disrupt the Stock Exchange opening, continued with gatherings at Zuccotti and transit hubs across the five boroughs, student walkouts, and a planned convergence at Foley Square followed by a march over the Brooklyn Bridge. Some of the city’s largest unions backed the Foley Square rally.

Large crowds assembled and thousands marched; clashes with police occurred throughout the day. Police used barricades, mass deployments and occasional raids on Zuccotti Park; exits were closed at one point and officers entered the park. Arrests mounted—reports put the total at well over 100 in various updates and at least 242 by Thursday afternoon—and included protesters sitting in the roadway and City Councilman Jumaane Williams. Police reported several officers injured (including one hit by glass and others struck with thrown liquids), and protesters and bystanders were also hurt. Officials said some demonstrators deliberately sought arrest or engaged in violent acts, and authorities confiscated metal devices that could be used to lock people to objects.

Despite confrontations, much of the city’s daily functioning continued: the NYSE opened on time and most commuters were unaffected beyond localized disruptions. Protesters projected messages onto buildings, rang “people’s bells,” and marked their day with chants, sit-ins, and symbolic actions; they framed the eviction from Zuccotti Park as galvanizing, arguing it weeded out casual participants and strengthened commitment. City officials warned of large turnout and prepared significant policing resources, with overtime costs in the millions. The day ended with mixed assessments: protesters declaring tactical successes and renewed energy, while city leaders emphasized the need to maintain order and protect public safety.

The Internet Archive is running crawls to capture webpages as they are created and the pages they link to, so that when referenced pages change or disappear, archived versions corresponding to the time a page was written remain available. The initiative—part of a “No More 404” effort—aims to replace broken links with archived copies or provide companion links so readers can see what the original authors intended.

Separately, on Saturday, Feb. 17, a man camping at Little Harbor Campground on Catalina Island was injured after being gored by a bison. The attack occurred around 5:15 p.m. while the man sat on a log near a grazing bison; as he tried to move away the animal charged and gored his left arm. Los Angeles Fire Department personnel treated him on scene and he was airlifted to Harbor-UCLA Medical Center. Bison roam freely on the island’s back side and, while they can appear tame, attacks are very rare. The extent of the man’s injuries was not immediately known.

A North Carolina judge will decide whether to grant a new trial in the 1996 murder conviction of Daniel Green for the killing of James Jordan, Michael Jordan’s father. Green was convicted after co-defendant Larry Martin Demery testified that he and Green approached James Jordan’s car to rob him and that Green shot Jordan when he awakened. Green’s attorneys, Scott Holmes and Ian Mance, say Demery was the shooter and that Green was not at the scene. They filed for a new trial citing new evidence: a sworn statement from the jury forewoman saying she independently investigated the murder contrary to the judge’s instructions, and an affidavit from a former Robeson County newspaper editor who recounts an admission by Demery that he committed the killing. The defense also challenges a state forensic expert’s testimony that Jordan’s blood was found in Green’s car. North Carolina must respond to the filing by the end of April, after which Robeson County Superior Court Judge Robert Floyd will rule on whether to order a new trial.

Former Rhode Island governor and senator Lincoln Chafee, whose Democratic presidential bid struggled with near-zero poll numbers and only about $30,000 raised, announced he was ending his long-shot 2016 campaign at the Democratic National Committee’s Women’s Leadership Forum. Chafee—an anti‑war candidate known for his focus on foreign policy and opposition to the Iraq War—had fared poorly in a recent debate and faced tough questions from moderators about his viability. He declared his campaign in June but said after weighing the political landscape—citing Hillary Clinton’s strong week, Jim Webb’s withdrawal, and Joe Biden’s decision not to run—that he would stop pursuing the nomination while continuing to advocate for his “Prosperity Through Peace” message.

On a cold February day in 1944 in the eastern French village of Gemeaux, a gendarme seized two dolls from Jewish sisters Denise and Micheline Lévy — ages 10 and 9 — as the sisters were rounded up at their school and marched away with their parents, grandparents and other relatives to be deported to Auschwitz; the girls never returned. The dolls, one pink and one blue, were tossed into the street and picked up by a village shopkeeper, then kept by the family of Frédérique Gilles’ grandmother. Three generations preserved the dolls and the story; on Sunday Gilles, a teacher from Gemeaux, donated them to the Shoah Memorial (Holocaust museum) in Paris. 

(The document also contains an unrelated paragraph describing the Internet Archive’s efforts to crawl and preserve web pages to prevent broken links and maintain access to the versions of pages referenced at the time they were cited.)

Nebraska honored late punter Sam Foltz before/during its season opener vs. Fresno State by sending out a punt formation with no punter on a 4th-and-4 after its opening three-and-out. The remaining 10 players stood and the crowd and players applauded in remembrance of Foltz and former Michigan State punter Mike Sadler, who both died in a Wisconsin car crash about five weeks earlier. After roughly a minute and a delay-of-game penalty, Nebraska punted. Foltz was last season’s Big Ten Punter of the Year (44.2 yards per punt) and had been on the Ray Guy Award watch list this season.

Global Road Entertainment announced it will re-cut the family film Show Dogs and remove two scenes after parents and advocacy groups said they sent the wrong message about sexual abuse. The revised version will be in theaters starting the weekend after the announcement.

What prompted the change
- Two scenes show the movie’s protagonist, Max (a Rottweiler voiced by Ludacris), undergoing genital inspection by dog show judges. Although such handling is a routine part of real dog shows, critics said the way the film framed the scenes — telling Max to go to a “zen place,” rewarding him for tolerating the touching, and making it pivotal to his advancement — resembled grooming tactics used by sexual predators and could normalize unwanted genital touching for children.
- A viral essay by a parent and a statement from the National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE) called for distribution to stop and for the film to be recut. NCOSE argued children’s movies should teach bodily autonomy and the right to say “no.”

Responses
- Global Road defended the accuracy of its depiction of dog-show procedures but apologized to anyone who felt the original version sent an inappropriate message and announced the two scenes would be removed.
- Writer Max Botkin, whose original script was heavily rewritten, applauded the decision and said he did not write the deleted scenes.
- NCOSE asked for the film’s distribution to be halted until changes were made.

Context
- Show Dogs is a family comedy starring Ludacris as Max and Will Arnett as his human partner; the plot centers on infiltrating a dog show to solve the kidnapping of a baby panda. Other cast members include Natasha Lyonne, Stanley Tucci and Jordan Sparks.

Clint Eastwood’s American Sniper—a commercial hit that opened to record January box-office numbers, earned an A+ CinemaScore and six Oscar nominations—has sparked debate in Hollywood over its portrayal of war and its subject, Navy SEAL Chris Kyle. Some entertainers criticized the film or its themes on social media: Seth Rogen compared it to the propagandistic fictional movie-within-a-movie in Inglourious Basterds (then clarified he liked the film but felt a scene was reminiscent), and Michael Moore posted that snipers are “cowards” (noting his uncle was killed by a sniper in WWII). Moore later said his initial tweets weren’t about Kyle or American Sniper and posted a longer Facebook response that praised Bradley Cooper’s performance, acknowledged anti‑war elements in the film, but faulted Eastwood for conflating Vietnam and Iraq and for language in the film about Iraqis. The remarks drew pushback from others in public life. Bradley Cooper defended the project as a responsible effort to depict a soldier’s life and the toll on his family. Warner Bros. had no comment.

Russell Armstrong, 47, the estranged husband of Real Housewives of Beverly Hills cast member Taylor Armstrong, was found dead in Los Angeles in an apparent suicide in early August. Authorities reported he was discovered hanged at a friend’s home; the coroner’s office indicated suicide was likely and an autopsy and toxicology tests were pending. He is survived by a daughter with Taylor and two older sons.

The coverage and commentary around his death centered on whether participation in the Bravo reality franchise contributed. Reported factors that may have increased his stress included:
- Intense public scrutiny after the couple’s marital problems and Taylor’s on-camera disclosures, including her allegations of physical abuse (which Russell partly acknowledged as “in the heat of the moment” but which were not cited in the divorce filing).
- Financial strain: Russell had a history of bankruptcy and reportedly faced renewed money problems and a pending $1.5 million lawsuit alleging fraud, which his attorney and friends said were worsened by efforts to maintain a lifestyle expected of the show.
- Emotional strain from being portrayed negatively on camera and pressure from producers to deliver drama; friends and his attorney said he felt the show “pushed” the marriage to the limit and that he complained reality TV “ruined” his life.
- Broader concerns about reality-TV production practices: communications scholars and industry insiders note reality shows can create stress by manufacturing conflict, keeping participants emotionally vulnerable, and emphasizing dramatic narratives over nuance.

Accounts also included tabloid claims (unverified) about personal secrets and allegations from prior relationships. Bravo and spokespeople expressed sympathy; network decisions about the season’s premiere and edits were undecided at the time.

No official determination links the show to his death—investigations continued—but reporting emphasized multiple, converging pressures (marital breakdown, allegations of abuse, financial and reputational stress, and the spotlight of reality TV) that friends, his lawyer and observers say likely contributed to his deteriorating state.

A new study in Occupational & Environmental Medicine linked higher levels of pyrethroid insecticide metabolites in mothers and children to increased behavioral problems at age six. Researchers measured five pyrethroid metabolites in urine samples from pregnant women and their children, and assessed child behavior at home using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. Three metabolites (trans-DCCA, cis-DCCA, cis-DBCA) were most common. Findings included: higher maternal cis-DCCA during pregnancy associated with greater risk of internalizing behaviors; higher 3-PBA in children linked to more externalizing behaviors; and children with the highest metabolite levels were about three times more likely to show abnormal behavior. Authors suggest pyrethroids may affect neurochemical signaling in the brain.

The report is correlational, not proof of causation, and researchers call for more rigorous studies. Experts note prior research has also associated pesticide exposure with ADHD and other problems, though those studies were likewise correlational. Pyrethroids (e.g., permethrin) are widely used in over-the-counter lice treatments; alternatives include alcohol-based treatments, ivermectin, and non-pyrethroid products such as Sklice or more “natural” options. The study raises concerns for parents but is preliminary.

Researchers at UC San Diego report that cigarette smoke makes MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) markedly more virulent and harder for the immune system to kill. In laboratory experiments with human immune cells and in mice, MRSA exposed to cigarette smoke extract became more resistant to macrophage killing—about four times harder to clear—largely by altering its cell surface. Smoke-exposed bacteria resisted reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides (both key innate defenses), adhered better to human cells, and caused higher mortality in infected mice. The resistance increased with smoke dose and persisted for at least 24 hours, suggesting the effect can be passed to daughter cells. A related study found e‑cigarette vapor produced similar but much weaker surface changes. The authors conclude cigarette smoke not only damages host immunity but also directly stresses bacteria into more aggressive, immune‑resistant forms, offering an additional reason to avoid smoking. (Infection and Immunity, Crotty Alexander et al., 2015)

Sen. David Perdue (R-Ga.) drew criticism after quoting Psalm 109:8 during remarks at the conservative Faith & Freedom Coalition “Road to Majority” conference. He told attendees they should pray for President Obama “and we should pray like Psalms 109:8 says: ‘Let his days be few, let another have his office,’” pausing after the line while the crowd laughed. Perdue did not recite the subsequent verses, which explicitly invoke misfortune and bereavement on an enemy’s family.

Democrats accused him of effectively praying for the president’s death; Kristen Orthman, a spokeswoman for Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, framed the remark as further evidence of GOP extremism. Perdue’s office defended him, saying he was calling people to pray for leaders and did not wish harm on the president, and blamed the media for stoking controversy.

Religious scholars called the passage an “imprecatory psalm” — a biblical genre that calls for divine punishment of enemies. Harvard Divinity School’s Michael Coogan suggested Perdue’s use was likely tongue-in-cheek and not literal; Graham A. Cole of Trinity Evangelical Divinity School said the line is odd in context and doesn’t necessarily indicate a wish for Obama’s death. The incident echoes earlier controversies in which the same Psalm 109 verse — sometimes dubbed “the Obama Prayer” — has been used by critics of Obama.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie is expected to decide within days whether to enter the presidential race. He spent the weekend weighing the logistics of a late entry, consulting aides, his family and others in his inner circle, who are worried about the compressed political calendar and the difficulties of launching a last-minute campaign. Christie attended a National Guard event Sunday and declined to comment to reporters about his plans. The article also notes the source includes archived web content from various news and progressive outlets, with potential imperfections in how those sites were captured.

Two weeks after Molenbeek authorities ordered the closure of a neighborhood bar for drug use and dealing, the bar’s former co‑owner, Brahim (Brahim/Ibrahim) Abdeslam, detonated a suicide vest outside the Comptoir Voltaire café in Paris during the Nov. attacks, seriously wounding bystanders. Brahim had run Les Beguines, a low‑rent café on Rue des Beguines in Molenbeek, from 2013 until shortly after an August police raid found a “strong smell of drugs,” partially smoked joints and customers carrying drugs; the commune ordered a five‑month closure and the family sold the business at the end of September.

Brahim’s younger brother, Salah Abdeslam — who had been manager of the café until the sale — is now Europe’s most wanted man, believed linked to the Paris attacks and suspected of renting a vehicle used by the attackers. French and Belgian police have detained several associates; three people arrested in Belgium are connected to stops and checks after the attacks. A third brother, Mohammed, who works for the Molenbeek town hall, was briefly held and released with an alibi placing him in Lille.

Neighbors, friends and family describe the brothers as ordinary, social men who drank, smoked and ran a bar — lifestyles at odds with Islamist strictures — and express shock that they could be involved in extremist violence. Reports link Salah’s circle to known militants; media note past jail time for theft for Salah and a shared prison past with Abdelhamid Abaaoud, an alleged IS propagandist thought to have coordinated attacks from Syria.

Molenbeek, a deprived Brussels district long highlighted by Belgian officials as a hotspot for radicalization, is under heightened scrutiny. Belgian ministers and the interior minister have vowed to “clean up” the area amid an intensified manhunt for Salah and ongoing counterterror operations.

The House on Friday approved the "Keep Your Health Plan Act" (261–157), a Republican-led bill that would let insurers continue to renew and sell individual policies that were canceled because they don’t meet Obamacare’s new benefit standards. The measure drew bipartisan defections: 39 Democrats joined most Republicans (only four Republicans opposed), reflecting intense political pressure from constituents and tough 2014 re-election races. The White House threatened a veto and called the bill a threat to middle-class health security.

President Obama had announced an administrative fix Thursday allowing insurers, with state approval, to renew existing plans for about a year — a narrower, temporary remedy than the House bill, which would permit permanent sales of noncompliant plans. That executive action blunted but did not prevent a substantial number of Democratic defections. Democrats argued Upton’s bill would undermine the Affordable Care Act by creating a “shadow market” of plans lacking essential benefits, destabilizing new insurance marketplaces and driving up premiums; Republicans said it preserves affordable coverage people want.

The vote increased pressure on the Senate, where prospects for passage are uncertain and some Democrats have proposed alternative fixes. The episode underscored the political fallout from cancellation notices and President Obama’s earlier promise that “if you like your health plan, you can keep it,” which opponents say was broken. The White House met with insurers after the vote to discuss implementation and market stability, but administration officials and many Democrats maintained legislative fixes through Congress are preferable to the GOP bill.

Facebook has launched its App Center, a centralized discovery hub for apps across web, iOS, Android and mobile web. Rolling out first to U.S. users and then to Facebook’s full user base, the store debuted with more than 600 apps — including Draw Something, Pinterest, Nike+ GPS, Stitcher Radio, Path, Ghost Recon and new games like Jetpack Joyride. 

Key points:
- Purpose: a discovery portal (not a replacement for iTunes or Google Play) that links out to platform app stores for downloads and hosts web apps playable inside Facebook.
- Personalization: recommendations are tailored to each user based on their own app usage, ratings, engagement and what their friends use.
- Quality filtering: only higher-rated and more-engaging apps are listed.
- Access: available via Facebook’s iOS and Android apps and on the desktop/mobile web at facebook.com/appcenter; users can send links to mobile devices for easy downloading.
- Interface: desktop App Center offers category browsing (Games, Entertainment, Music, News, etc.), Friends’ apps and personalized suggestions; mobile is a pared-down experience focused on “Social Picks” and Top Apps, with more limited browsing and some UX issues (e.g., platform-compatibility visibility).
- Strategic context: aims to keep users within Facebook and expand its role as an entertainment platform; critics say this furthers a “walled garden” approach. The move comes as mobile apps grow rapidly in downloads and revenue potential.

Overall, App Center is a Facebook-curated app discovery layer that leverages social signals to recommend higher-quality apps while directing users to the appropriate app stores for installation.

Six students, all aged 14–15, from Toronto’s elite all-boys St. Michael’s College School were arrested and charged after a video of an alleged sexual assault was posted online. Police charged each youth with assault, gang sexual assault and sexual assault with a weapon in relation to a locker-room incident that a 22-second clip appears to show: a teen held down while allegedly assaulted with what looks like a broomstick. The six appeared in court, were released on bail with conditions barring contact with the complainant and the school, and face additional restrictions on social media.

Investigators said the school did not immediately notify police; police first learned of the video through media coverage. Toronto police are also probing at least three other hazing-related incidents at the school, including another alleged sexual assault, and warned anyone holding the clip to delete it because it may constitute child pornography. In response, St. Michael’s expelled eight students and suspended another in connection with separate videos, brought in counsellors, set up a confidential voicemail and said it has launched an independent third-party “Respect and Culture Review” to examine student traditions and attitudes. School principal Gregory Reeves acknowledged the school “has a serious problem,” defended his handling of communications with the victim’s family, and said the institution is cooperating with police. The case has prompted widespread criticism and a broader discussion about school culture and reporting obligations.

The Jets beat the Bengals 24-14 in an AFC wild-card game in Cincinnati, advancing to the divisional round and claiming their first playoff win in five years. Rookie quarterback Mark Sanchez completed 12 of 15 passes for 182 yards and a touchdown, becoming the fourth rookie QB in NFL history to win a playoff game. Running back Shonn Greene (mentioned in headline) and a strong defensive effort, including two late sacks in the fourth quarter, helped the Jets rally after an early 7-0 deficit. The victory followed a tense week after the teams met in the season finale and came amid emotion for owner Woody Johnson, who had recently suffered a family tragedy; coach Rex Ryan honored him publicly in the locker room. Ryan lauded the team's potential and reiterated his bold postseason predictions as the Jets prepare to face either the Colts or the Chargers next.

Michigan Governor Rick Snyder formally apologized to Flint residents and pledged to take “full responsibility” for resolving the city’s water crisis, calling it a “catastrophe” no one should have to endure. In his State of the State address he said, “I’m sorry I let you down,” promised to release his 2014–2015 emails about Flint, and vowed accountability for those responsible.

Snyder requested $28 million in immediate state funding to support emergency actions already underway—daily distribution of bottled water, filters and test kits, door-to-door visits to more than 21,000 homes, and National Guard assistance—and to pay for treatment and services for children with elevated lead levels, behavioral-health support, testing and replacing fixtures in schools, and an infrastructure integrity study. He said Flint would remain on Detroit’s water line through the end of 2016 and outlined additional budget provisions for pipe and fixture replacement and local follow-up care.

The crisis began in April 2014 when Flint switched from Detroit/Lake Huron water to the Flint River as a cost-saving temporary measure. The river water was highly corrosive and, officials say, was not properly treated for corrosion, causing lead to leach from old service lines. State and federal investigations, lawsuits, and criticism have focused on what officials knew and when—many residents and attorneys allege state agencies ignored or downplayed elevated lead levels and delayed action despite evidence in 2014 and 2015. Plaintiffs in multiple lawsuits seek damages and documents (including Snyder’s emails) to clarify responsibility.

Snyder defended the state’s response in interviews, saying he acted when he learned of unsafe blood-lead levels and blaming the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality for overly technical interpretations and slow responses. Critics, local leaders and protesters say the $28 million request is insufficient—Flint’s mayor and others estimate remediation and health costs could total $1 billion or more—and some demand his resignation. The Obama administration has declared a federal emergency and pledged continued support to state and local officials.

Two former classmates who studied in Australia are at the center of a high‑profile murder investigation in Jakarta after 27‑year‑old newlywed Wayan Mirna Salihin died after drinking a Vietnamese iced coffee that police say was laced with cyanide.

What happened
- Mirna collapsed and began convulsing after taking a single sip of the iced coffee at Olivier cafe in Grand Indonesia Mall; she later died in hospital. Police say cyanide was found in Mirna’s stomach and in the cup she drank from.
- Two friends were present: Jessica Kumala (also named as Jessica Kumala Wongso) and a woman known as Hani. Jessica reportedly arrived early and ordered Mirna’s drink. Hani also sipped from the same cup but survived.

Investigation and arrest
- After weeks of inquiries, Jakarta police arrested Jessica and named her a suspect, saying her statements as a witness were inconsistent with other evidence.
- Police say they have gathered around 20 witness statements, conducted a reenactment, and collected four of five items of evidence required under the Criminal Code to name a suspect. They plan a case expose to prosecutors that will include testimony from a forensic expert, a forensic psychiatrist and a criminal expert.
- Investigators have questioned Jessica multiple times, including sessions with forensic psychiatry experts, and have also re‑interviewed Hani, who police say panicked at the time and has given inconsistent details.
- Police sought assistance from the Australian Federal Police to obtain information about the trio’s relationship while studying in Australia (reports name Billy Blue College of Design and Swinburne University).

Defense and disputed points
- Jessica and her lawyer/uncle Yudi Wibowo deny involvement. Yudi has questioned aspects of the autopsy and called for a second autopsy, noting Hani’s sip from the same cup and denying rumors of a love triangle.
- Police say some forensic documentation from the national lab and psychiatric evaluation results were delayed, which slowed formal case filing. They also placed Jessica’s domestic worker (SR) under police protection as a witness; SR reportedly disposed of Jessica’s ripped pants at Jessica’s request and police have been unable to locate them.

Current status
- Jessica has been formally named a suspect; police intend to present their case to prosecutors and said they are prepared to respond to any pretrial motions. Investigation continues as authorities synchronize witness testimony, lab results, surveillance footage and reenactment findings.

Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio emerged rapidly as the consensus choice during the conclave that elected him Pope Francis. In private pre-conclave congregations and early ballots, cardinals increasingly shifted support to Bergoglio—seen as forceful but humble—after initial “courtesy” votes for several names. Reports indicate he secured the required two-thirds majority by the fifth round (some accounts say the third or final counted round), receiving at least 77 votes; the exact tally remains secret.

Observers and Vatican commentators said Bergoglio’s appeals for curial reform and a simpler, more pastoral leadership resonated with many cardinals, especially those from outside Rome critical of the Vatican bureaucracy in the wake of the Vatileaks scandal. His background as an Argentine of Italian descent and his perceived theological reliability combined with a down-to-earth style to attract broad support, including much of Latin America and many non-Italian cardinals. Italy’s usual voting strength was weakened, which undercut front-runners like Cardinal Angelo Scola; reports suggest some Italian and Vatican insiders, including Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone, opposed Scola, contributing to his loss.

Age was a debated factor—Bergoglio was 76—seen by reformers as prompting urgent action and by conservatives as possibly limiting his long-term impact. Cardinals recounted that much of the decision-making occurred in pre-conclave discussions and congregation speeches, where Bergoglio’s critiques of the Curia and emphasis on spiritual renewal impressed colleagues. He had been a strong contender in 2005 as well.

Francis’s initial public gestures underscored his modest style: he asked the crowd for blessings from St. Peter’s balcony, prayed at Santa Maria Maggiore, collected his luggage and paid his hotel bill, declined an elevated throne, and joined cardinals on a bus rather than a limousine. His election marked the first papacy from the Americas and the first non-European pope in over a millennium, signaling to many a potential shift in tone and priorities for the global church.

Conservative activist Andrew Breitbart, who initially reported that a photo of a man's crotch had been sent from Rep. Anthony Weiner’s Twitter account to a female college student, says he possesses a fully explicit photo he will publicize if Weiner retaliates. Weiner has admitted the original crotch photo was of him and acknowledged inappropriate contact with six women over three years via social media and sometimes by phone. Breitbart described the explicit image as an “insurance policy” against reprisals, though he hedged on that term and suggested more women could come forward if Weiner invites further scrutiny. Breitbart later showed the uncensored image on a radio show, where hosts photographed and circulated it online, raising the prospect of wider public exposure and further damage to Weiner’s reputation.

Nashua authorities believe a body recovered Sunday from the Merrimack River is likely that of 16-year-old Jacob Goulet, a Nashua High School North student who disappeared during an intense rainstorm Friday night. A Massachusetts State Police helicopter spotted the body near Parlee Farms in Tyngsborough; Tyngsborough and Nashua responders recovered it. The Massachusetts chief medical examiner must make a positive identification.

Goulet’s parents reported him missing Saturday morning after he failed to return from a friend’s house. Surveillance footage showed him near an open sewer at 75 Main St. Friday night, and callers reported personal items — a baseball cap and an umbrella — near an uncovered storm drain. Nashua police and officials believe he may have fallen into an interceptor sewer with a steep drop (possibly ~20 feet) that overflows into the Merrimack during heavy storms.

Search efforts over Saturday and Sunday involved Nashua and state police, the Nashua Fire Department dive team, public works, wastewater crews, Massachusetts Fish and Game, and private contractors using cameras; about 1,000 feet of sewer pipe had been searched. The sewer cover in question was resecured Sunday and officials said they are investigating how it came off. The city and school prepared grief counseling for classmates; a memorial grew at the site and community members expressed shock and sorrow. A GoFundMe for funeral costs had raised funds by Sunday evening.

Secretary of State John Kerry’s offhand suggestion that Syria could avoid U.S. military strikes by surrendering its chemical weapons quickly became a possible diplomatic alternative to President Obama’s threatened limited strikes after U.S. intelligence concluded the Assad regime used poison gas. Russia—Syria’s main ally and arms supplier—immediately endorsed the idea and urged Damascus to place chemical weapons under international control and destroy them. Syria and international figures including Ban Ki-moon and Britain’s David Cameron also welcomed the proposal, and the White House called it a “potentially positive development” worth examining.

The editorial argues the U.S. should pursue this route because verified removal and destruction of Syrian chemical stockpiles would better protect civilians, create longer-term deterrence, avoid more casualties from limited strikes, and might open a path toward a political settlement. For credibility, Syria must acknowledge its weapons and allow immediate inspections; Russia should cooperate with the U.S. and U.N. on a concrete, time‑bound plan and a U.N. Security Council resolution to authorize and enforce the process and set consequences for noncompliance.

The piece also reports skeptical views—chiefly from Michael Doran of the Brookings Institution—who warns the proposal could be a Russian and Syrian ploy to defuse U.S. pressure. Doran’s eight “truths” argue Assad won’t fully relinquish chemical weapons, Russia will drag out and manipulate inspections, and the U.S. has limited leverage after losing domestic political support for strikes. In an interview he suggested if the U.S. follows the diplomatic path it should demand immediate, verifiable steps (e.g., joining the Chemical Weapons Convention, full declarations, immediate U.N. monitors) and be prepared to follow up with a coherent policy—potentially including stronger support for vetted opposition forces—to prevent Assad from using the pause to continue atrocities. Doran cautions that even if Syria and Russia are sincere, embracing them would undercut prior U.S. demands that Assad step down and could signal weakness to allies and adversaries.

Overall, the consensus is that the Russian proposal offers a diplomatic pause that could avert unilateral U.S. military action and possibly lead to disarmament, but it will require strict verification, international cooperation and clear consequences to avoid becoming a sham that simply protects Assad while the conflict continues.

TerriLynn St. John, a 23-year-old mother of two from Middlesex County, Virginia, has been missing since early Tuesday morning. Family members say she was last seen around 7:30 a.m. preparing her car in the front yard of her Mill Wharf Road home; they believe a struggle occurred there. Her two young children, ages three and one, were found alone and unharmed at the house by relatives.

Middlesex Sheriff’s Major Michael Sampson called the case a missing person under suspicious circumstances. Investigators have identified and interviewed four persons of interest, including St. John’s boyfriend; those individuals have cooperated and submitted DNA samples now being tested at the Richmond crime lab. A K9 unit, air surveillance and searches on foot have been conducted, and neighboring jurisdictions and Virginia State Police are on standby to assist if needed.

Police described St. John as a white female, 5'6", 130 lbs, with blonde hair, blue eyes and several tattoos (including R.J.M. on her right wrist, a princess crown on her left wrist, and a cross on her ring finger). She was last seen wearing a blue Outer Banks hoodie. Authorities urged anyone with information to contact the Middlesex Sheriff’s Office at 804-758-5600 and asked residents to call tips rather than speculate on social media, which can distract the investigation.

On July 4–5, 2016, multiple suicide bombings struck three Saudi cities in what appeared to be coordinated attacks timed near the end of Ramadan and ahead of Eid al-Fitr. State-linked Saudi media and officials reported an explosion by a suicide bomber near a security building outside the Prophet Muhammad’s Mosque in Medina — one of Islam’s holiest sites — where several cars caught fire. Footage showed a fire near buildings overlooking the mosque; initial reports gave no clear casualty tally from that blast. Witnesses said worshippers had been breaking their fast when the blast occurred.

Separately, a suicide bomber detonated near the U.S. Consulate in Jeddah; the attacker died and two security guards were lightly wounded, with some vehicles damaged. Authorities said the bomber was a non-Saudi resident of the kingdom and security forces found and detonated additional explosive devices at the scene. In the eastern, Shiite-majority city of Qatif, a suicide bomber and a car bomb exploded outside a Shiite mosque while many residents were at home breaking the fast; that attack reportedly caused no immediate injuries. Local reporting noted the area’s history of previous IS-linked attacks on Shiite worshippers.

No group immediately claimed responsibility, though Islamic State has previously targeted Shiites and Saudi security sites and is widely suspected. The attacks killed four security officers overall, according to later reports, and unnerved Saudis given the rarity of strikes on Medina — a city that houses the Prophet’s tomb and is central to the kingdom’s religious legitimacy.

Saudi leaders condemned the assaults: King Salman vowed to “strike with an iron hand” against those who radicalize youth, and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef and other officials reassured the public that security was strong. The U.N. human rights chief called the bombing outside the Prophet’s Mosque “an attack on Islam itself.” The U.S. Embassy confirmed no consular staff were harmed and warned Americans in the kingdom to take precautions. Regional reactions included condemnation from Iran and arrests in neighboring Kuwait of suspects allegedly linked to IS plotting attacks on Shiite sites.

Philadelphia’s civic organizations are trying an unconventional tactic to boost the city’s chronically low voter turnout: a $10,000 lottery prize for one person who votes on Nov. 3. Announced by Larry Platt of the online publication The Philadelphia Citizen, former mayor John Street, and Republican Sam Katz, the prize is funded by the Pamela and Ajay Raju Foundation (Ajay Raju is a founder of The Citizen). Organizers will use a computer to pick one of Philadelphia’s 1,686 voting divisions at random, go to that polling place on Election Day, and give $10,000 to the first person seen leaving after voting (with eligibility checks to avoid conflicts of interest; if that person is ineligible they’ll select a random voter from the division’s turnout list).

Proponents say the lottery is a legal, nonpartisan way to spark discussion and increase participation after turnout plunged to about 27% in the May 2015 primary and has trended downward for decades. The idea takes inspiration from a Los Angeles “Votería” prize that reportedly increased turnout in one school-board contest. Critics call the scheme “icky” or demeaning—arguing voter engagement should come from information and civic education, not cash—and worry about the optics or ethics, though election-law experts at the announcement said it’s lawful so long as no candidate or issue is bought. The Citizen frames the giveaway as an experimental nudge amid broader efforts (education campaigns, registration reforms) to reverse declining participation.

Peggy Frank, a 63-year-old U.S. Postal Service carrier from North Hills with roughly 28–30 years on the job, was found unresponsive in her mail truck in Woodland Hills on Friday afternoon amid an extreme heat wave and was later pronounced dead. Temperatures that day reached about 115–117°F and an excessive heat warning was in effect. Paramedics attempted resuscitation; an autopsy was completed but the official cause of death remains pending pending further tests. Family members say Frank had recently returned from months off with a broken ankle, had suffered heat stroke the prior summer, and believe the heat — exacerbated by postal vehicles that lack air conditioning and can be 10–15°F hotter inside — may have contributed. Coworkers and relatives criticized the Postal Service’s protections for workers in extreme heat; USPS said employee safety is a priority, cited its Heat Illness Prevention Program and encouraged hydration, shade and carrying water/ice, and said the incident is under investigation. The case has drawn comparisons to past OSHA findings against USPS for heat-related worker deaths and illnesses.

Usaamah Rahim, a 26-year-old Boston security guard whom authorities say was radicalized by ISIS and other extremists, was fatally shot June 2, 2015, by an FBI-led anti‑terror task force after he waved a large military-style knife at officers. According to FBI affidavits and court documents, Rahim originally plotted to behead conservative activist Pamela Geller but told an associate he shifted plans to target police (“the boys in blue”) as easier targets. Rahim purchased three fighting knives online and discussed imminent attacks in recorded conversations with an associate, David Wright.

Wright, 25, was arrested and charged with obstructing a federal investigation for allegedly trying to destroy evidence on Rahim’s phone; a detention hearing was set for June 19. Authorities said Rahim had been under 24‑hour surveillance for suspected Islamist extremism and that a recent change in his behavior and social‑media threats prompted the confrontation. Video shown privately to community and civic leaders—though not released publicly—was described by police and some community figures as showing officers approach without drawn weapons, back away as Rahim advanced with a knife, then open fire when he refused to drop it. Rahim appears to have been shot multiple times; accounts differ on exact wounds.

Investigators searched locations in Massachusetts and Rhode Island and said they were probing two other associates, including a third person in Rhode Island. The shooting is under review by the Suffolk district attorney and the FBI; civil‑rights and Muslim community leaders attended a briefing and urged transparency. Rahim’s family initially alleged he was shot in the back while on a cellphone, but police and some community leaders said the video contradicted that claim. The case has prompted local concern about radicalization via social media and calls for independent review.

General Motors is recalling about 1.205 million late‑model pickup trucks and large SUVs worldwide (roughly 1.02 million in the U.S.) because an electronic power‑steering fault can cause a temporary loss of assist and then a sudden restoration, which can make steering difficult—particularly at low speeds. GM reported 30 crashes and two injuries linked to the defect but no deaths. Dealers will fix the issue by updating the power‑steering module software at no charge. GM previously issued a similar recall in 2017 for nearly 800,000 pickups.
