The New York Times reported that Sen. Ted Cruz failed to disclose two personal loans from Goldman Sachs and Citigroup on his 2012 Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings when he ran for the U.S. Senate. Cruz’s campaign has previously disclosed the loans on congressional financial-disclosure forms and says the funds were part of roughly $1 million in personal financing he used for the campaign. The loans — a Goldman Sachs “margin loan” and a Citigroup line of credit that together totaled between $500,001 and $1 million on his Senate disclosures — were revealed in July 2012 and were reported as paid off by the end of that year.

Cruz called the omission an “inadvertent filing question” or “filing error,” saying the underlying information has long been public and that the campaign will amend filings if necessary. His campaign noted the loan was listed on his Senate financial disclosures and said Cruz was unaware at the time that the loans had to be separately reported to the FEC; an aide called the issue one of “semantics.” Legal experts say candidates must disclose the original source of funds used in campaigns, so the omission could violate campaign rules. There is no allegation of wrongdoing by the banks, and Goldman Sachs and Citigroup declined to comment.

Betsy Davis, a 41-year-old artist who had lived with ALS since 2013, spent months planning a two-day “rebirth” gathering in Ojai, California, to say goodbye before using drugs prescribed under California’s new End-of-Life Option Act to end her life. In early July she emailed more than 30 close friends and family with a detailed schedule for the July 23–24 weekend, asking guests to be emotionally present and jokingly imposing one rule: no crying in front of her.

People flew in from across the U.S. for the event, held at a home with a wraparound porch. The weekend featured music (a cello and harmonica), cocktails and pizza from her favorite place, screenings of a favorite film, a fashion-show-style moment where guests tried on clothes Davis had selected, and the chance to take “Betsy souvenirs” marked with notes about their meaning. Davis, who had lost much physical control and communicated with difficulty, moved among guests in her electric wheelchair and kept the tone intentionally celebratory.

On the evening of July 24, dressed in a kimono from a bucket-list trip, Davis slipped into a canopy bed on a hillside, took a prescribed combination of morphine, pentobarbital and chloral hydrate at 6:45 p.m., and died about four hours later with her sister, her caretaker, her doctor and her massage therapist at her side. Friends described the gathering as her final performance and praised her choice to control the end of her life; supporters framed the weekend as joyful and intentional, while critics of assisted-suicide laws warn of risks to vulnerable people. Guests plan to reconvene next June to scatter her ashes.

Tom Hardy, 39, is a distinctive, tattooed British actor known for playing violent, complex characters rather than conventional heroes. Famous ink and recent addition: after losing a bet with co-star Leonardo DiCaprio over an Oscar nomination for The Revenant, Hardy got a DiCaprio-chosen tattoo reading a variation of “Leo knows everything/Leo knows all.” Hardy’s tattoos reflect personal loyalties (including his agent’s name) and his commitment to roles.

Raised in privileged west London but a poor student, Hardy fell into crime and severe substance abuse before training at the Drama Centre and landing early TV and film work (Band of Brothers, Black Hawk Down). Sober since 2003, he channels past addiction and brushes with darkness into intense, memorable performances (Stuart: A Life Backwards, Bronson, Legend, Mad Max: Fury Road, The Revenant). That lived experience gives him depth for roles as addicts, criminals and damaged men.

Hardy is combative and mercurial by reputation—he’s had well-publicized clashes on sets—but directors who handle him well (Christopher Nolan, among others) praise his leadership and risk-taking. He co-runs production company Hardy Son and Baker and is creator, star and executive producer of Taboo, a deliberately seedy, subversive 1814-set drama he developed over nearly a decade; production and editing have been intense, coinciding with the birth of a new baby with wife Charlotte Riley and ongoing sleep deprivation.

Despite mainstream success—box-office hits and an Oscar nomination—Hardy resists safe, crowd-pleasing choices and prefers exploring “nuttery” in darker, stranger parts (upcoming projects include Fonzo, as an ailing Al Capone, and producing/starring in McCullin). He describes acting bluntly and candidly, sometimes clashing with directors but delivering compelling work: “You don’t hire Tom Hardy if you don’t want Tom Hardy.” Taboo premiered on BBC1 from 7 January.

Researchers at NYU Langone conducted what is believed to be the first brain-imaging study of long-term Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) members to explore why many report little or no alcohol craving. Twenty long-term AA members (who reported no cravings the week before testing) viewed alcohol-related images while undergoing MRI scans. Each image set was presented twice: once after the participant read neutral newspaper text and once after they recited an AA abstinence-promoting prayer.

All participants reported some craving after viewing the images, but cravings were significantly lower after praying. MRI results showed increased activity after prayer in prefrontal cortex regions involved in attention, emotion regulation, and semantic reappraisal—areas linked to how situations are emotionally interpreted and controlled. The authors interpret this as evidence that AA experience (exemplified here by prayer) helps members reframe and emotionally regulate responses to drinking cues, reducing craving.

Senior author Marc Galanter notes these findings align with his decade-long work linking a “spiritual awakening” in AA to lasting reductions in craving and relapse risk. Prior studies cited by the team also showed prayer or spiritual awakening can reduce post-treatment drinking. The study, published in the American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse, suggests AA participation may produce measurable neurophysiological changes that mitigate cue-induced craving. The research was supported by the John Templeton Foundation.

Aslan Usoyan, 75 — a long-time and widely regarded mafia godfather in the post‑Soviet criminal world known as “Grandpa Hassan” — was killed by a sniper in central Moscow on Wednesday as he left the Karetny Dvor restaurant about 1.5 km from the Kremlin. Investigators say a single sniper shot struck Usoyan; he was rushed to hospital in a coma but died en route. A female bystander (reportedly a waitress) was also wounded and taken to hospital in critical condition.

Authorities have opened a murder probe and are considering several motives, including Usoyan’s extensive criminal activity. Police and media reports describe the attack as a professional, premeditated assassination: shots were fired from a stairwell between the fifth and sixth floors of a building across the restaurant, investigators recovered spent cartridges and other items, and witnesses said people had been seen photographing the street from that stairwell in preceding days. Some sources say the killer used a silenced Val-type 9mm weapon and armor‑piercing rounds; police also suspect the 2010 attempt on Usoyan’s life and this incident may be linked.

Born in Soviet Georgia in the 1930s and first imprisoned at 19, Usoyan rose to become one of the most influential figures of the Soviet/post‑Soviet criminal underworld, accused of controlling groups involved in illegal gambling, arms and drug trafficking and resource theft. His death has raised concerns among officials and observers that it could trigger turf wars and renewed violence among rival criminal clans.

Jan Chamberlin, a five-year member of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, resigned after the choir accepted an invitation to perform at President-elect Donald Trump’s January inauguration. In a letter she later posted on Facebook, Chamberlin said she wrestled with the decision, prayed, and concluded she could not in good conscience participate—writing she “could never ‘throw roses to Hitler’” or sing for him—and that doing so would damage her self-respect. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints said participation is voluntary, only a limited number of singers (about 215 of roughly 360) are expected to volunteer, and the choir’s performance is meant to honor freedom, civility and the peaceful transition of power rather than signal political endorsement.

The announcement prompted widespread debate within and beyond the LDS community. An online petition opposing the choir’s participation drew nearly 19,000 signatures, arguing the appearance misrepresents Mormon values and the church’s diverse 15+ million members, and could harm the choir’s image. Support and opposition have both been reported; choir members concerned about performing can opt out of the selection lottery. Chamberlin said she received hateful messages after posting her resignation. Nevada Senator and fellow Latter-day Saint Harry Reid publicly supported Chamberlin’s difficult choice. The church declined to comment on individual members’ status.

The NYPD is investigating Hollywood director Bryan Singer over an allegation that he forcibly sexually assaulted a man in his twenties on March 23, 2013, the department confirmed to BuzzFeed News. The complaint was filed May 9 and is being handled by the NYPD’s Special Victims Squad; Singer has not been charged. Singer’s lead attorney, Martin Singer, said neither Singer nor his representatives have been contacted by police and denied any criminal or inappropriate behavior, calling BuzzFeed’s reporting a “witch hunt.” Another Singer attorney disputed the outlet’s sourcing and details.

Separately, two civil lawsuits accusing Singer of sexual abuse of underage boys — notably one brought by Michael Egan, who alleged abuse beginning when he was a minor — have been dropped or dismissed without prejudice, meaning they could be refiled. The timeline of public developments includes:
- April 16: Egan files suit in Hawaii alleging abuse at 17.
- April–July: Reporting links other plaintiffs and longtime associates (e.g., Marc Collins-Rector) and uncovers documents and depositions that prompted motions to dismiss by Singer and co-defendant Gary Goddard.
- May–July: A separate John Doe suit was filed and later dismissed as to Singer (but continued against Goddard).
- Late July: Egan’s lawyer Jeff Herman dropped him as a client; documents showed Singer had attempted a $100,000 settlement offer.
- August 28: Egan’s suit was dismissed without prejudice, allowing potential refiling.

The NYPD noted the alleged victim in the current criminal complaint is a man in his twenties; New York’s criminal sexual act statute covers both sex with minors and nonconsensual acts between adults (forcible compulsion or incapacity). Singer’s public activity suggests he was in the New York area on the date of the alleged incident.

A set of six typewritten letters from Harper Lee to her close friend, New York architect Harold Caufield, failed to meet the reserve at a Christie’s auction in New York. The lot—estimated up to $250,000—included letters dated 1956–1961 (four written before To Kill a Mockingbird’s 1960 publication) and a signed 35th‑anniversary copy of Mockingbird inscribed to Caufield. The correspondence, eight pages total, is intimate and revealing: Lee uses playful pseudonyms, comments on creative struggles and homesickness while caring for her ailing father (the model for Atticus Finch), reacts with astonishment to the novel’s early praise, and voices opinions on religion and Southern politics. The letters surfaced as interest in Lee spiked ahead of the July release of Go Set a Watchman, and their appearance prompted discussion about privacy—Lee is famously reclusive and reportedly would be unhappy her private correspondence is being sold. Christie’s blurred some contents in its catalog; the consignor acquired the letters on the open market and remained anonymous.

A wave of angry protests over the anti-Islam film "Innocence of Muslims" spread across the Middle East and other Muslim-majority countries on Friday, Sept. 14, 2012, leading to violent clashes, attacks on diplomatic missions, and at least one death.

Key events and themes:
- Tunis: Thousands massed outside the U.S. embassy. Demonstrators scaled the outer wall, raised a black Islamist flag bearing the Muslim profession of faith, and fought with police; officers used tear gas and fired into the air.
- Sudan: Hundreds stormed the German Embassy after calls from a prominent sheikh; parts of the compound caught fire, vehicles were burned and protesters later moved toward other diplomatic missions.
- Libya: The consulate in Benghazi had been the site of a deadly attack earlier in the week; the airport was briefly closed Friday for security reasons.
- Egypt and Cairo: Hundreds — mainly hardline Islamists — protested after Friday prayers, clashed with police near the U.S. Embassy, and tore up an American flag. President Mohammed Morsi publicly urged protection of foreign diplomatic missions and condemned the Libya killings.
- Yemen: Thousands protested in Sanaa; security forces used tear gas and fired warning shots to keep crowds away from the U.S. Embassy. Earlier protests there had breached the embassy compound and burned the American flag.
- Lebanon: Clashes in Tripoli left one protester dead and dozens wounded after crowds set fire to fast-food restaurants and battled security forces.
- Other locations: Demonstrations took place across Pakistan (Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore, Peshawar), Indonesia, Malaysia (small peaceful rally in Kuala Lumpur), Iraq (Baghdad, Basra), the West Bank and Jerusalem, Bahrain and elsewhere. Responses ranged from peaceful marches to stone-throwing, flag-burning and assaults on foreign property.
- Official reactions: U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton denounced the film and emphasized the U.S. government had no involvement. Many governments increased security at diplomatic missions; Egypt’s president publicly condemned attacks and called for restraining protests.

Overall, numerically many protests involved hundreds rather than thousands, often dominated by ultraconservative groups, but the demonstrations were widespread and volatile, involving attacks on embassies and consulates, clashes with security forces, and at least one fatality.

Rep. Michele Bachmann, a leading 2012 Republican presidential contender who has championed sharp reductions in federal spending, and her family have nonetheless received substantial government funds, records and reporting show. Her husband Marcus Bachmann’s counseling clinic, Bachmann & Associates, received nearly $30,000 in state grants since 2006 (partly federally funded) to train staff, and has also been reimbursed through Minnesota Medicaid and related state care programs—totaling roughly $161,000 in state payments over several years for patient services. Those payments contradict public statements in which Bachmann said the clinic only got “one-time training money” that “didn’t help our clinic” and implied she and her husband did not get the funds.

In addition, the family retains a partnership in a Wisconsin farm that received almost $260,000 in federal farm subsidies from 1995–2008. Although Bachmann has said the subsidies went to her in-laws and that she personally did not receive money from the farm, her financial disclosures show she reported between about $32,500 and $105,000 in income from the farm between 2006 and 2009. Publicly, Bachmann has criticized farm subsidies and voted against the 2008 farm bill as “loaded with…pork,” yet she later urged USDA commodity purchases to support local pork and dairy producers during price troubles—actions that benefited constituents.

Bachmann has also opposed the 2009 federal stimulus, calling it an unacceptable direction for the economy, but requested stimulus funds for projects in her district and has differentiated transportation projects from what she labels earmarks. Critics and some Republican strategists say these contradictions between rhetoric and personal or constituent benefit could undermine her standing with fiscal conservatives. Bachmann’s office declined detailed comment in response to inquiries.

Here's a concise summary of the document:

- Background: The Simpsons character Apu Nahasapeemapetilon has become controversial after Hari Kondabolu's 2017 documentary The Problem with Apu, criticized for stereotyping Indian-Americans. The Simpsons’ attempts to address the controversy (notably the episode “No Good Read Goes Unpunished”) were widely seen as dismissive.

- Adi Shankar’s contest: Producer Adi Shankar launched a crowdsourced spec script contest to reimagine Apu—seeking scripts that would subvert, pivot, write out, or evolve the character into a more realistic, three-dimensional portrayal. He hoped Fox would produce the winning script as an episode.

- Allegation that Apu is being dropped: Shankar told IndieWire he’d heard from multiple sources that The Simpsons intends to quietly remove the Apu character rather than engage with the controversy. He condemned that as cowardice for a show known for cultural commentary. Fox’s only public response noted Apu’s brief background appearance in a recent episode; Simpsons executive Al Jean later pushed back on Shankar’s claim, saying Shankar does not speak for the show.

- Contest results and planned production: Shankar selected a winner—Vishaal Buch, an Indian-American family doctor—whose script depicts Apu evolving from Kwik-E-Mart owner into a thriving businessman and includes broader Indian-American representation. Shankar plans to produce Buch’s episode through his Bootleg Universe channel if Fox won’t; he’s helping polish the script and said he might involve Simpsons voice actors. A second-place winner was Tasha Dhanraj.

- Reaction and implications: The report notes mixed public reactions on Twitter—some view removing Apu as capitulating to “PC culture,” others will miss the character. Shankar and others view producing a thoughtful, inclusive episode as a missed opportunity for the show; Shankar intends to move forward independently to realize the winning script.

Researchers observed Cuban boas coordinating ambushes of Jamaican fruit bats at cave entrances in Cuba, forming a hanging “curtain” that intercepts bats as they emerge at dusk and return at dawn. Vladimir Dinets (Univ. of Tennessee) recorded snake positions and capture outcomes over eight days and reported in Animal Behavior and Cognition that individual boas positioned themselves sequentially so multiple snakes formed a barrier across the passage. Boas hunting together had higher success rates and captured prey more quickly than solitary snakes; with three or more snakes present bats were often forced into striking range or low flight. Dinets found no direct evidence of communication between snakes and thus stopped short of calling the behavior true social pack hunting, but he argued the positioning pattern and improved success imply coordination rather than coincidental use of preferred spots. Similar mass-ambush scenes have been reported anecdotally from Puerto Rico and Mexico, though quantitative studies are lacking. The finding challenges the long-standing view of reptiles as strictly solitary hunters, but some herpetologists caution that stronger experimental evidence is needed. Dinets also warns that cave populations of Cuban boas are declining from hunting and poaching, threatening these communal hunting events.

Comedian and actress Amy Schumer is taking a public stand on politics and protest while sharing personal news. She announced on Instagram that she will refuse to appear in any Super Bowl LIII commercials to show solidarity with Colin Kaepernick’s take-a-knee protests against racism and police brutality, challenging white NFL players to kneel and calling advertisers a means to pressure the league. Schumer said she told her reps she wouldn’t do a Super Bowl ad and framed the decision as the only leverage she has; celebrities including Diddy, Jessica Seinfeld and Christie Brinkley responded with support.

Separately, Schumer and husband Chris Fischer are expecting their first child — a pregnancy she revealed via Jessica Yellin’s #NewsNotNoise Instagram campaign. She used the announcement to urge followers to vote in the midterms and promoted Yellin’s effort to clarify political jargon and encourage civic engagement. The move fits Schumer’s recent pattern of activism: she’s protested Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination, advocated for gun control, supported transgender rights, and backed Kaepernick’s protest by urging performers to reconsider Super Bowl appearances.

ABC News aired an exclusive interview with First Lady Melania Trump during her first solo international tour of Africa (Ghana, Malawi, Kenya, Egypt), where she promoted her "Be Best" children's welfare initiative and visited orphanages, hospitals and conservation sites. Reporter Tom Llamas traveled with her and described the heavily secured motorcade and scenes from her visits, including feeding baby elephants in Kenya.

In the sit-down, Melania opened up about life in the White House and some obstacles she’s faced, saying she’s “sad” that some organizations declined to partner with her because of politics. She addressed sensitive topics including the #MeToo movement: she said she supports women and that they “need to be heard,” but also emphasized that accusations require evidence and warned the media sometimes portrays stories incorrectly. Asked about high-profile cases such as the Brett Kavanaugh investigation, she said she believed Dr. Ford was heard, noted the FBI investigation was completed and that the Senate voted, and declined to directly state whether she believed Ford. She also defended having her own views with President Trump, saying she gives him honest opinions though he does not always follow them.

The interview teased other personal topics—her husband’s alleged infidelities, criticism over the “I really don’t care. Do u?” jacket she wore on a Texas migrant visit, and misconceptions about her—but ABC previewed only fragments of her responses. Melania discouraged focus on her wardrobe (including debate about a pith hat in Egypt) and urged attention to the substance of her trip and aid initiatives. The program “Being Melania: The First Lady” was promoted to air in full on ABC.

Today Alaska will release 24,199 pages of emails sent to and from Sarah Palin during her first two years as governor (Dec. 2006–Sept. 2008). The disclosure, produced in response to a 2008 public-records request made after Palin was tapped as John McCain’s running mate, follows a nearly three-year effort complicated by Palin’s use of private email accounts, large volume, technical hurdles and repeated legal-review extensions.

Key points:
- The initial request was filed by Mother Jones in September 2008 after citizen requests revealed hundreds of withheld messages and suggested possible misuse of exemptions. Other news organizations later filed related requests.
- Palin used private Yahoo accounts for state business. Because the state could not directly access those accounts, it had to collect related messages from dozens of official state employee accounts, greatly increasing time and cost. After objections, the state ultimately dropped search fees; the final copying fee paid by the news organizations was $725.
- The review process was slow: IT issues (including changing email address formats), manual conversion of messages to PDFs, and prolonged legal review by the state Department of Law resulted in multiple deadline extensions and substantial staff hours and costs.
- The released set is not complete: communications sent between Palin’s private accounts and non-state recipients, and some exchanges among aides on private accounts, are not included. The state is withholding 2,353 pages (for reasons such as attorney-client privilege, work product or executive privilege) and redacting portions of other pages; an additional 140 pages were deemed unrelated to state business.
- Journalists will pick up the paper-only boxes in Juneau and plan to scan and publish searchable archives (joint efforts include Mother Jones, msnbc.com, ProPublica, The Washington Post, The New York Times, Anchorage Daily News/ABC and the Associated Press). The logistics of Juneau’s limited accessibility and bandwidth shaped the decision to release physical copies.
- Observers note the documents could yield revealing details about Palin’s administration—already scrutinized in earlier records and investigations (e.g., “Troopergate”)—but whether they will change public perception is uncertain. The release arrives as Palin has re-emerged in national headlines while hinting at possible further political ambitions.

President Trump planned to announce his Supreme Court pick to replace retiring Justice Anthony Kennedy on Monday night, having narrowed an initial list of seven interviewed candidates to three federal appeals judges: Brett Kavanaugh, Raymond Kethledge and Amy Coney Barrett. The selection, coming less than four months before midterms, drew intense pressure from conservatives pushing for a reliably originalist justice who would shift the Court rightward, and from Democrats and some Republicans who want assurances a nominee will not seek to overturn Roe v. Wade.

Key conservative endorsements and preferences:
- Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell privately urged Trump toward Raymond Kethledge or Thomas Hardiman, arguing they posed the fewest confirmation obstacles and warning that Kavanaugh’s extensive paper trail could complicate confirmation.
- Radio host Hugh Hewitt publicly promoted Kethledge as a “Gorsuch 2.0” and politically advantageous as a Michigan judge.
- ACU chair Matt Schlapp, Fox host Laura Ingraham and others backed Brett Kavanaugh for his judicial record and influence.
- Ben Shapiro favored Amy Coney Barrett as the strongest originalist choice among the three.
- Prominent conservatives including Mark Levin, Jim DeMint, Erick Erickson and FreedomWorks’ Adam Brandon pushed for Senator Mike Lee (not among the final three but still interviewed) or other originalist picks like William Pryor.

McConnell communicated repeatedly with Trump and White House counsel Don McGahn that Kethledge or Hardiman would be easier to confirm, citing concerns about Kavanaugh’s voluminous judicial and professional records from his years on the D.C. Circuit and prior White House and Starr investigation roles. Trump said he would not ask nominees about Roe v. Wade as he finalized his choice. The story was being updated as developments continued.

Doctors at Stony Brook University Hospital performed what appears to be the first-known operations on triplets born with craniosynostosis, a condition in which skull plates fuse too early and can restrict brain growth. The Howard triplets—Hunter, Jackson and Kaden, born Oct. 22, 2016 to Amy and Mike Howard of Center Moriches, N.Y.—were diagnosed within days of birth. Hunter and Jackson are identical twins; Kaden is fraternal. Craniosynostosis affects roughly 1 in 2,000–2,500 births, but the team estimated the odds of this combination in triplets at about one in 500 trillion.

When the boys were about 11 weeks old, pediatric neurosurgeon Dr. David Chesler performed three minimally invasive endoscopic procedures over two days in January. Surgeons removed fused bone strips to allow normal skull and brain growth; the infants went home within two days and are now wearing custom orthotic helmets 23 hours a day for six to nine months to help shape their skulls. Their head shapes have returned to normal, and the family reports the babies are doing well, showing normal recovery and distinct personalities. The parents conceived naturally and say life with three newborn boys is hectic but joyful.

A veteran Jackson, Mississippi detective and the murder suspect he was interviewing were both found dead after gunfire erupted inside Jackson Police Department headquarters on the evening of April 4, 2013.

Detective Eric Smith, 40, a Robbery‑Homicide Division investigator with the department since 1995, was interviewing 23‑year‑old Jeremy Powell on the third floor when shots were heard by other officers. When colleagues entered the interview room they discovered both Smith and Powell had been shot multiple times and were dead. Powell was being questioned in connection with the Monday killing of 20‑year‑old Christopher Alexander, whose body was found with a neck wound.

Police released few details about the sequence of events. The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation has taken over the inquiry. City officials and police leaders publicly mourned Smith, described as a decorated and well‑respected officer; Mayor Harvey Johnson Jr., Councilman Chokwe Lumumba and others expressed condolences and asked for the public’s patience while investigators determine what happened. The police headquarters was locked down and the scene secured following the shooting.

Actor Jon Bernthal said he observed troubling behavior from Kevin Spacey while working with him on the 2017 film Baby Driver, and that his respect for Spacey diminished as a result. Bernthal told SiriusXM he found Spacey “rubbing me the wrong way,” describing him as “a bit of a bully” who behaved poorly toward others on set; he said colleagues remember him commenting at the time. Bernthal added he never saw the kinds of sexual assault alleged in recent accusations, but was “enormously disappointed” because Spacey did not match the transformative stage performer Bernthal had admired earlier in his career.

The comments come amid a wave of allegations against Spacey that began Oct. 29 when actor Anthony Rapp accused Spacey of making sexual advances toward him when Rapp was 14. Rapp’s account prompted Spacey to apologize and publicly acknowledge he is gay. Since then more than a dozen men—some named, some anonymous—have accused Spacey of sexual harassment, groping, assault or attempted rape over several decades and in multiple locations (including the Old Vic theatre in London and sets or social situations in the U.S.). Allegations include unwanted touching, exposing himself, attempts to seduce or coerce young men, and predatory behavior alleged by current and former House of Cards staff.

Consequences for Spacey have been swift: Netflix announced he would be removed from House of Cards’ final season, and director Ridley Scott and Sony replaced him in All the Money in the World with Christopher Plummer and reshot Spacey’s scenes. Some accusers have filed police reports; at least one criminal investigation was reported in Nantucket. Spacey’s representatives have said he is seeking evaluation and treatment, while his lawyers have denied specific accusations.

Four women — 24-year-old Diana Carrillo of Irvine, her sister and two friends — left Saint Marc Pub-Cafe in Pacific City after a waiter asked to see their “proof of residency” before serving them. Carrillo, whose parents are immigrants, said the question felt hostile rather than joking and posted the incident on social media. The restaurant’s management apologized publicly three days later, said the waiter violated corporate policy, and fired him. Saint Marc offered to donate 10% of a weekend’s sales to a charity of Carrillo’s choice and invited the women as VIP guests; Carrillo declined the VIP offer but accepted the donation request, asking it go to Orange County Immigrant Youth United. The restaurant said it would comply. Carrillo tied the encounter to broader concerns about anti-immigrant sentiment.

Mariano Barbosa Jr., a 30-year-old hotel security director who worked at the SoHo Grand and later as director of security at Yotel in Manhattan, was arrested and charged with setting eight fires at the two hotels over a four-year period. Fire marshals say the fires began in February 2009 and continued through this month; they were set in hallways, stairwells and near exit doors between about 10:11 p.m. and 5:09 a.m. while Barbosa was on duty. The fires were quickly extinguished; two firefighters suffered minor injuries in a February blaze.

Authorities say Barbosa started the fires to make the hotels less popular so parties and bar crowds would be curtailed and his job easier. He allegedly used bedding materials, towels and sheets in several incidents. He was identified after submitting to voluntary questioning and was arraigned on charges including arson, reckless endangerment and criminal mischief.

Yotel is cooperating with investigators; the SoHo Grand declined comment. Fire officials condemned the actions as endangering guests and firefighters. Family members and some co-workers expressed shock and defended Barbosa’s character, noting his long employment and family responsibilities.

A popular odd-couple at a Russian safari park — Amur the tiger and Timur the goat — have broken up after the tiger attacked the goat. The pair, placed together in November near Vladivostok and unexpectedly becoming companions, drew wide attention and even merchandising. Staff initially reunited them after separation attempts because Amur reacted badly to being apart.

A 30-minute park video shows the relationship souring when Timur grew overly bold, repeatedly scratching his horns against Amur’s fur and annoying the tiger for hours. Amur eventually snapped, leapt on Timur, mauled him briefly, tossed him to the snow and walked away. Staff distracted the tiger with a live rabbit so they could retrieve the injured goat and take him to a vet. Park director Dmitriy Mezentsev reported Timur is now in good health but shaken and resting; it’s too soon to say whether he will be returned to Amur. The incident reinforced observers’ view that Amur did not intend to kill the goat but instead “gave him a lesson.” The pair have been separated for the time being.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s newly arrived ambassador to Germany, Richard Grenell, immediately warned German companies to wind down business in Iran after Trump announced the U.S. withdrawal from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and the reimposition of sanctions. Grenell—confirmed in April as the highest‑ranking openly gay official in the administration and a longtime critic of the deal—tweeted that U.S. sanctions would target “critical sectors” of Iran’s economy and urged German firms to halt operations, a message that alarmed German industry over potential U.S. fines if partners are blacklisted.

Grenell, a former U.S. U.N. spokesman and aide to John Bolton, took up the Berlin post about 16 months after his predecessor left. His nomination had been delayed by Democrats over past comments he said were intended as humor. Shortly after arriving he attended a high‑profile Washington send‑off featuring Trump allies and media figures, where supporters praised his appointment.

Angelyne—long a Los Angeles curiosity famous for dozens of pink billboards and for driving a pink Corvette—has been revealed by reporting in the Hollywood Reporter to likely have been born Ronia Tamar Goldberg (later Renee Tami Goldberg), the daughter of Polish Jewish Holocaust survivors who immigrated first to Israel and then to Los Angeles. Journalist Gary Baum and a genealogist compiled public records, yearbook photos and family testimony tying Angelyne to a 1950 birth in Poland, parents who survived ghettos and camps, childhood moves to Bnei Brak and then L.A., a mother’s death in 1965, and a youth in the San Fernando Valley. Baum corroborated the account with court papers including a recent Ventura County petition to change Renee Goldberg’s name to Angelyne Llyne and with interviews (including with a former husband and a stepsister).

Angelyne built a peculiar form of celebrity starting in the early 1980s by plastering billboards across Los Angeles of a glamorous, heavily made-up blonde in pink—“famous for being famous,” a prototype of later personal-brand stars. She monetized appearances, image licensing, merchandising and the mystique itself, appeared in small film roles, released records, ran quixotically for local office, and cultivated a tightly controlled public persona sustained by plastic surgery and careful secrecy. Her longtime assistant Scott Hennig has denied the Goldberg identification and dismissed investigators as stalkers; Angelyne herself has declined to discuss her past beyond saying she’ll save it for memoirs.

Profiles of her describe a mixture of theatrical self-invention, vulnerability and performance-art resonance: she both courts attention and guards mystery, seeing glamour as her “front stage.” Angelyne’s story raises themes of reinvention, the legacy of trauma and assimilation among Holocaust survivors, and the emergence of celebrity-by-branding that prefigured later reality- and social-media fame.
