Spinal Solutions LLC, a Southern California medical distributor led by founder Roger Williams, is at the center of a national scandal alleging it sold counterfeit and non–FDA-conforming spinal implants to surgeons and hospitals from about 1999 through its collapse in 2013. The company is accused of mixing fake screws with authentic implants in surgical kits, selling them at large markups (often billed to workers’ compensation), and steering business through lavish perks and alleged kickbacks to physicians—private plane trips, expensive consulting deals, cash-filled envelopes and other favors.

Discovery and scope:
- In 2009 Richard Walker of South African implant maker Ortho Sol identified fake copies of his titanium spinal screws among returns from a U.S. distributor. Two years later a Spinal Solutions employee gave suspected counterfeit parts to the FDA; the agency inspected the company and sent a warning letter in 2012 but did not shut it down. Spinal Solutions recalled some mislabeled items in 2013 and then folded under massive debt.
- Plaintiffs’ attorneys and company insiders say millions of dollars of implants were sold nationwide, and as many as thousands of patients may have received counterfeit parts. More than 30 lawsuits have been filed; a coordinated filing in Los Angeles added 28 plaintiffs, bringing the local total to 32 cases.

Allegations and evidence:
- Patients—including Derika Moses—found screws and rods removed from their spines that manufacturers (notably South Korea’s U&I Corp.) identified as fakes because of incorrect finishes, lot numbers and logos.
- An elderly machinist, William Crowder, has acknowledged making dozens (possibly hundreds) of copy screws after being given samples by Spinal Solutions’ operations manager; another contractor did laser engraving. Plaintiffs’ suits allege much larger production and distribution.
- A former employee presented suspicious screws to the FDA in 2011; inspectors later found poor inventory and quality-control practices. The FDA allowed the company to continue selling while it attempted fixes.

People and practices:
- Roger Williams lived a lavish lifestyle (multiple private jets, luxury cars, courtside seats) while the company accrued large debts, unpaid vendor bills, and high-interest financing; the IRS later found tax underpayments by Williams and his wife.
- Multiple surgeons did business with Spinal Solutions—some received consulting fees or trips. While doctors implicated deny knowingly implanting substandard devices, records show many operative reports listing Spinal Solutions implants. One high-profile surgeon later pleaded guilty to unrelated fraud.

Impact on patients:
- Plaintiffs describe chronic pain, infections, multiple revision surgeries, lost jobs and homes, and fear about the safety of metal still in their bodies. Lawsuits seek accountability for the alleged counterfeiting scheme, kickbacks, and fraudulent billing to insurers and workers’ compensation.

Status:
- Dozens of civil suits are pending; investigations by regulators and law enforcement have been referenced but not fully detailed publicly. Spinal Solutions ceased operations in 2013 amid debt; key figures have faced tax and other legal actions, and some defendants deny involvement.

Summary:

Cleveland police officer Timothy Loehmann has given his first public account of fatally shooting 12-year-old Tamir Rice on November 22, 2014, telling investigators and grand jurors he believed he was confronting an “active shooter situation” and thought Tamir was an adult. Loehmann said he and partner Frank Garmback repeatedly ordered Tamir to “show me your hands” as the patrol car drove onto park grass and slid to a stop beside him. Loehmann says Tamir reached into his waistband and pulled what he believed was a handgun; Loehmann fired two shots, killing Tamir, who was actually carrying an Airsoft pellet gun. Both officers provided written, unsworn statements that prosecutors released while presenting evidence to a Cuyahoga County grand jury weighing possible charges.

The officers’ accounts — which describe events that surveillance video shows unfolded in roughly two seconds — and the prosecutor’s release of expert reports finding the shooting justified have been sharply criticized by Tamir’s family and their attorneys. They call allowing unsworn officer statements before the grand jury “irregular” and argue the officers’ timeline and ability to observe the described motions in so little time are implausible. Family lawyers also contend key details from the 911 call (that the gun was “probably fake” and the suspect might be a juvenile) were not relayed to the officers. Prosecutor Timothy McGinty defended his handling as transparent; the family has requested a special prosecutor. The grand jury continues to consider whether to indict Loehmann and Garmback.

Search teams continued battling heavy weather Wednesday to recover victims and wreckage from AirAsia Flight QZ8501, which vanished Sunday en route from Surabaya to Singapore with 162 people aboard. Debris and seven bodies (four men, three women, including a flight attendant) were found floating on Tuesday 60–120 miles from the plane’s last known position; officials recovered additional bodies on Wednesday. Sonar has reportedly detected objects on the seabed thought to be wreckage, but Indonesian authorities said the main fuselage and the black boxes have not yet been located. Strong winds, rain, high waves and currents have hampered diving and helicopter operations and have caused wreckage to drift, complicating the search concentrated in the Karimata Strait near Borneo.

Relatives at crisis centers in Surabaya and Pangkalan Bun expressed grief, shock and anger over graphic coverage; many provided DNA samples and photos to help identification. International assistance, including U.S. naval and patrol assets, joined dozens of ships and aircraft in the effort. The Airbus A320 requested a climb to avoid bad weather shortly before contact was lost; investigators say recovering the cockpit voice and flight data recorders is crucial to determine causes. Possible scenarios discussed by experts include aerodynamic stall, instrument or engine damage from severe weather, or loss of speed/angle of attack, but authorities stressed conclusions await the black boxes. Public mourning and canceled or scaled-back New Year events followed as Indonesia grappled with the national tragedy.

Walt Disney Co. drew heavy criticism after filing 10 U.S. trademark applications on May 1 for “Día de los Muertos” — covering items like toys, cereal and jewelry — ahead of an untitled Pixar film inspired by the Mexican holiday. Disney said the filings were meant to protect a potential film title but that it has since withdrawn them because the movie’s title will change. 

The move provoked an online petition and widespread outrage from community leaders and activists who called the centuries-old, indigenous-rooted Day of the Dead a sacred cultural tradition not for corporate ownership. Critics noted past Disney trademark controversies (e.g., a withdrawn 2011 attempt to trademark “SEAL Team 6”) and argued religious and cultural observances shouldn’t be subject to trademarks. The petition had roughly 19,500 signatures by the following morning.

Reuters and commentary pieces report that Facebook planned to begin its IPO roadshow on May 7, which would put a likely public debut around May 18. Sources said founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg would participate in the roadshow after largely staying out of earlier investor events, a move that had irritated some Wall Street investors when he skipped a March analysts’ meeting. The company’s regulatory review of the IPO was said to be nearing completion, permitting the planned timetable; a recent flurry of acquisitions had briefly delayed the process while regulators signed off.

Facebook expected to raise at least $5 billion in what would likely be Silicon Valley’s largest IPO, drawing intense investor demand reminiscent of Google’s offering. However, updated filings and first-quarter results revealed decelerating revenue and user-growth trends and margin pressure that have raised questions about sustainability. Year‑over‑year revenue growth slowed materially (for example, from 154% in 2010 to much lower rates later), and operating margins and EPS showed notable compression—Q1 operating margin fell sharply versus the prior year.

Analysts and commentators flagged risks tied to Facebook’s heavy reliance on advertising (over 80% of revenue) amid a shift to mobile usage, where monetization remains a challenge. The acquisition of Instagram drew scrutiny for its valuation and for reinforcing concerns about Zuckerberg’s concentrated control over strategic decisions; reports that he led the deal with limited board pushback highlighted governance worries. Some investors and advisors suggested prudence—preferring another quarter to show margin recovery and a clearer mobile monetization path—rather than rushing to market immediately.

Pop star Justin Timberlake flew from Los Angeles to his hometown of Memphis to vote early and encouraged others to do the same. He posted an Instagram selfie at the polling place urging people to “rock the vote” and reminding them to vote on November 8 if early voting wasn’t available locally. Fans reacted excitedly to spotting him in line. The story notes that Tennessee prohibits ballot selfies and that Timberlake also owns property in Nashville.

This piece reviews 50 Cent’s 2009 album Before I Self Destruct and situates it against his recent work and persona. The writer begins by describing their expectations after reading 50’s book The 50th Law — fearless, streetwise hustler — and notes a disconnect between that image and much of his recent music, which at times sounds detached from the streets. Before I Self Destruct is an attempt to win back fans of his harder-edged early records rather than chase mass pop appeal. 

Pros:
- 50’s voice and menacing delivery remain potent on several tracks ("The Invitation," "Death to My Enemies"), and he convincingly returns to raw gangsta themes.
- The album’s production (Dr. Dre, Rick Rock, Polow Da Don, etc.) creates a cold, clinical sound that matches its amoral, transactional view of relationships and loyalty.
- Standouts include the provocative, confrontational "So Disrespectful" and the energetic collaboration with Eminem on "Psycho," which demonstrates what 50 can do when pushed by a strong partner.
- Lyrically the record alternates between playfulness and bitter anger, with money and betrayal as recurring motifs.

Cons:
- The album lacks consistent insight or emotional depth; some shock lines are disturbing rather than illuminating.
- The middle of the record drifts into generic, post-2001 Aftermath-style production, and by the second half he reverts to chasing hit formulas without the former inevitability.
- At times the album feels like transparent pandering to older fans, and 50’s attempts at romance or softer themes fall flat.

Overall assessment: Before I Self Destruct offers moments of ferocious return-to-form and solid production, but it doesn’t sustain interest across its runtime and often feels like a partial, uneven bid to reclaim street cred. The result is compelling in parts but ultimately falls short of revitalizing 50’s standing in hip-hop. Rating given in the review: about 2.5 stars out of 4.

Rupert Murdoch announced his engagement to former supermodel Jerry Hall in the births, marriages and deaths section of The Times (London) on 12 January. The 84-year-old media mogul and 59-year-old Hall, who have been dating for about four months after being introduced by Murdoch’s relatives in Australia, went public after appearing together at the rugby World Cup final in October and became engaged over a weekend in Los Angeles while attending the Golden Globes.

The Times notice—paywalled online—formally named their children and said the couple were “delighted” and “thrilled to be getting married.” Guardian Australia estimated a classified ad like that could cost close to £300; Murdoch or a representative paid extra for a black border. News Corp employees publicly congratulated them on social media.

This would be Murdoch’s fourth marriage (he was previously married to Patricia Booker, Anna Torv and Wendi Deng) and Hall’s second (her 1990 Bali ceremony with Mick Jagger has been disputed). Coverage includes both warm statements from a family spokesman and less flattering comments from some insiders; some commentators credit the relationship with giving Murdoch renewed energy. The report also recalls past tabloid controversies and Murdoch’s turbulent personal history, including his 2013 divorce from Wendi Deng amid rumors involving Tony Blair.

The document describes the Masters of Beef Advocacy (MBA), a beef-industry–funded training program launched in March 2009 that has trained nearly 3,000 students and farmers to promote beef and respond to critics of industrial livestock production. Funded and supported by the Beef Checkoff program and organized in part by National Cattlemen’s Beef Association communicators, the MBA targets young people on large land‑grant campuses—seen as the source of many future farmers and industry leaders—and teaches participants how to answer consumer questions, counter critics like Michael Pollan, and engage online and in person (social media campaigns, campus outreach, school and civic presentations, media interviews).

Profiles and viewpoints in the piece:
- Carrin Flores, a 26‑year‑old veterinary graduate student and MBA alum, embodies the program’s mission: proud of cattle and intent on a beef-industry career; she and others view critics such as Pollan as opponents and want to shape future narratives about beef.
- Other young participants express genuine concern about sustainability, environmental critiques, and their career prospects in farming, seeing advocacy as a way to reconcile criticism of conventional agriculture with the need to continue producing food.

The MBA curriculum (promoted as free and open to beef producers and allies) covers the beef lifecycle and addresses environmental sustainability, nutrition, animal welfare and safety through five online courses (e.g., Raising Cattle on Grass, Life in the Feedyard, From Cattle to Beef). The program promotes ongoing access to materials, alumni networks, classroom kits, and practical advocacy activities. Critics and observers note the program’s PR aims—framing it as industry-organized counter-messaging to skeptical voices—and raise concerns about corporate influence on campus debate, even as participants claim grassroots motives driven by livelihood concerns. The piece highlights the broader context: declining beef consumption, a shrinking and aging farm population, and heightened public scrutiny of modern agriculture.

Hurricane Isaac moved slowly over the northern Gulf Coast on August 29, 2012, causing widespread flooding, power outages and damage across Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and other states. Though weakened to a tropical storm at times, Isaac’s large size and slow motion produced prolonged wind, storm surge and heavy rain—resulting in overtopped levees, extensive rescues and major outages.

Key impacts and response
- New Orleans imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew; Mayor Mitch Landrieu warned of downed signals, strict anti-looting enforcement and urged caution during cleanup. At least 12 looting incidents were reported with arrests.
- Plaquemines Parish suffered severe flooding after multiple levees were overtopped. Residents were stranded in homes, attics and on roofs; hundreds were rescued by boats, National Guard and other responders. Officials considered intentionally breaching a downstream levee to drain trapped water.
- At least dozens of rescues occurred across the region (LaPlace, Braithwaite, Hancock County, Biloxi and elsewhere); nursing home evacuations were carried out.
- Federal response included FEMA coordinating with U.S. Northern Command and deployment of helicopters. More than 8,200 National Guard personnel were made available for relief operations.
- Utilities reported massive outages—more than 817,000 customers without power across five states at peak reporting, with Entergy and other companies mobilizing crews from many states; some outages could last up to a week.

Storm details and hazards
- Isaac’s center lingered near southeast Louisiana, producing storm surge (recorded surges as high as 11 feet at Shell Beach), widespread flooding (reports of 5–14 feet in places), and heavy rainfall (up to 17 inches reported at Audubon Park; other totals noted across the Gulf Coast).
- Tornado warnings and watches were issued across parts of Mississippi and Louisiana. Flood and flash-flood warnings affected numerous parishes and counties.
- Though largely a Category 1 storm (winds near 75–80 mph at times, later slipping to 60–70 mph), officials stressed that prolonged tropical-storm-force conditions and surge posed serious inland flooding risks—NOAA noted inland flooding is the leading hidden danger in such storms.

Local effects and damage
- Significant flooding and structural damage were reported in Plaquemines Parish and other low-lying areas; reports included floating coffins in inundated cemeteries and collapsed homes in New Orleans neighborhoods.
- Coastal towns from Louisiana through Mississippi and parts of the Florida Panhandle experienced beach erosion, flooded streets and infrastructure damage. Some evacuation shelters housed thousands; many schools and universities closed.
- Concerns were raised about possible reappearance of oil/tar residues from the 2010 BP spill along shorelines.

Government actions and advisories
- State and local officials closed roads (I-10 between Baton Rouge and New Orleans among them), activated shelters and urged residents to stay put until conditions improved. The White House and President Obama communicated with governors and local leaders; federal resources were on standby for search, rescue and recovery.
- Residents were reminded about the dangers of cleanup, the need to avoid flooded roads, and to report oil or hazardous debris.

Overall, Isaac’s slow, persistent passage caused extensive flooding and disruption across the central Gulf Coast region, prompting large-scale rescue operations, widespread power outages and significant local damage—especially in areas where nonfederal levees were overtopped.

Public Health England (PHE) confirmed that two children from the same family in Charnwood, Leicestershire, have died after developing hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a serious kidney complication of E. coli infection. The siblings were treated within the past two weeks. PHE said the cases are being investigated with local environmental health officers and partners, who are examining the family's recent movements and have taken samples from the home. Tests to identify the exact E. coli strain are underway and may take about a week. PHE stressed that E. coli infections are relatively rare, can range from mild to severe (often causing bloody diarrhoea), and can be acquired via contaminated food, contact with farm animals, or infected water; young children and the elderly are more at risk of complications. The incident is not currently being treated as an outbreak, and authorities expressed condolences to the family.

Michael Julian, the NYPD’s newly appointed deputy commissioner in charge of training, announced a campaign to curb officers’ use of profanity and reduce unnecessary force, saying both efforts will cut civilian complaints and improve police-community relations. Julian argued that many curse words are used for effect and can be unlearned through training; he cited that roughly 30% of Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) complaints involve a curse word and said eliminating that language could meaningfully reduce complaints. He also committed to retraining officers to manage adrenaline and emotional reactions that lead to “extra” kicks or punches during chases or arrests, stressing that officers need techniques for controlling themselves rather than just instruction on penal law. Julian noted that while New York officers are not “Rodney King”–style brutal, smaller acts of excessive force occur and can be corrected. The retraining initiative follows heightened scrutiny of NYPD use-of-force practices after Eric Garner’s death; Julian said new training would begin the following week. CCRB data in the piece indicate a modest drop in discourtesy allegations year-over-year, and the CCRB chair has publicly said foul language by officers is inexcusable.

Summary:

Two separate airline-related incidents occurred on Sunday.

1) Aldon Smith arrest at LAX: San Francisco 49ers linebacker/defensive end Aldon Smith was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport after, during random secondary screening in Terminal 1, he became belligerent and allegedly indicated he had a bomb before walking toward the gate. Los Angeles Airport Police detained him; he was booked on a charge of making a false bomb report (a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in jail) and posted $20,000 bail that night. The 49ers’ GM called the team “disappointed” and declined further comment while facts are gathered. Bystanders, including a former Marine, recorded the encounter. The arrest adds to Smith’s recent legal and personal troubles: he has pending felony charges from a 2012 weapons incident, and earlier this year missed five games while in alcohol treatment following DUI arrests.

2) Unruly passenger diverts Southwest flight: A Chicago-to-Sacramento Southwest flight was diverted to Omaha after passengers reported a man tried to open a cabin door midflight. The plane landed at Eppley Airfield so the unruly passenger could be removed; the flight later reached Sacramento about two hours late. Witnesses described the man acting strangely (one said he emerged from a lavatory soaking wet) and attempting to pry open the rear hatch; other passengers and a doctor helped restrain him until air marshals took him into custody. The airline provided few additional details.

A new study led by Columbia University and published in The Cryosphere finds Greenland’s summer surface albedo (reflectivity) has declined significantly since about 1996 and is likely to keep darkening through this century. Using multispectral satellite data from 1981–2012 and regional climate modelling, the researchers show summertime albedo fell at ~0.02 per decade (1996–2012) in melt-prone regions; modelled declines are smaller (~0.01 per decade) because the model lacks surface-impurity effects. Projected warming could reduce average ice-sheet albedo by roughly 0.08–0.10 by 2100 (with potential for larger declines).

Key mechanisms
- Exposure and concentration of light-absorbing impurities (dust, soot) at the surface as fresh snow melts. Warm summers can reveal years’ worth of buried impurities, darkening the surface.
- Snow/ice grain growth from melt–refreeze cycles: larger grains scatter less sunlight (especially in the infrared detectable by satellites), reducing albedo even if the snow looks “clean.”
These processes form positive feedbacks: warming → more melt → larger grains and more exposed impurities → lower albedo → more absorption and melt.

Additional findings
- The darkening signal is concentrated in areas that melt in summer; the high dry-snow zone showed no trend.
- Analyses of fire emissions and atmospheric aerosols do not show increasing deposition trends that could explain the surface darkening; instead, surface exposure and consolidation of existing impurities with melt are likely drivers.
- A 1996 shift in atmospheric circulation (favoring warmer, sunnier summers) likely initiated the accelerated darkening; episodic variability has since occurred but the ice sheet remains more sensitive to melt.
- Current models may underestimate future darkening and melt because they underpredict melting and generally omit impurity effects that amplify albedo loss.

Implications
- Lower albedo increases Greenland’s absorption of solar energy, accelerating melt, runoff, and sea-level contribution. The feedbacks make the ice sheet increasingly sensitive to warming and could hasten long-term mass loss unless countered by substantial snowfall and reduced warming—both unlikely under current greenhouse-gas trajectories.

Former Neighborhood Watch volunteer George Zimmerman, acquitted last year in the fatal shooting of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin, described his post-trial life in an Orlando Sentinel interview. Now 30, Zimmerman says his life is markedly different: he travels frequently, is in debt, receives continual death threats and carries a semi-automatic handgun for protection. He attended a firearms expo in Lake Mary—where he was photographed, hugged and greeted by some supporters—saying the event felt friendly and didn’t require extra security. Reactions from the public vary widely, from praise and invitations to parties to visible fear and hostility. Zimmerman says strangers often find him “soft-spoken” and kind, and that he resists hiding his identity or using aliases. He moves often, flying to states such as California, Texas and Virginia for speaking engagements and legal meetings. He recently launched a website to speak publicly, including a post about portraits he painted of the four Americans killed in Benghazi, which he plans to give to the families while selling replicas to raise money for wounded-veterans groups. He also noted a recent non-arrest incident in Lake Mary involving an alleged road-rage threat.

A large Danish cohort study published in JAMA Pediatrics suggests frequent prenatal use of acetaminophen (paracetamol/Tylenol) is associated with a higher likelihood that children will later be diagnosed with ADHD or related hyperactivity disorders. Researchers analyzed data from more than 64,000 mother–child pairs and found that about half of mothers reported some acetaminophen use during pregnancy. Any reported use was associated with a 29% higher risk of an ADHD diagnosis and a 37% higher risk of a diagnosis of hyperkinetic syndrome; longer use (e.g., ≥20 weeks) showed larger increases (including a reported 50% higher risk of ADHD medication use). The study could not assess dose and did not establish causation.

Investigators adjusted for fever and infection (which themselves can affect fetal brain development) but acknowledge residual confounding is possible. Other possible explanations include unrecognized infections, genetic predispositions that both increase pain complaints and ADHD risk, or continued acetaminophen use after birth. Animal data suggesting hormone-like effects of acetaminophen on the developing brain motivated the research, and prior human studies have reported similar associations.

Experts urge caution but not alarm: the findings do not prove acetaminophen causes ADHD, and clinicians would not recommend withholding necessary treatments for serious maternal illness. Authors and commentators advise pregnant women to avoid chronic or long-term use when possible, prefer minimal effective doses for short durations, and consider nonpharmacologic pain relief when appropriate. Tylenol’s manufacturer noted no randomized trials demonstrate a causal link and recommends consulting clinicians before use.

Background: Swaddling—wrapping an infant snugly with the head exposed—is a traditional practice that can improve calming and sleep but has uncertain effects on sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) risk. Because swaddling alters arousability and may affect sleep position stability, researchers conducted a systematic review and individual-level meta-analysis to quantify any association between swaddling and SIDS.

Methods: A comprehensive literature search to December 2014 identified four case–control studies (total 760 SIDS cases, 1,759 controls) from England, Tasmania (Australia), and Chicago. Investigators provided additional individual data on infant age and sleep position. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated and pooled using fixed- and random-effects models; analyses adjusted for infant age. Study quality was assessed with the Newcastle–Ottowa scale.

Main findings:
- Overall pooled association: Using a random-effects model (to account for heterogeneity, I2 = 65.5%), swaddling was associated with a borderline increased SIDS risk (age-adjusted OR 1.58; 95% CI 0.97–2.58). A fixed-effects pooled estimate (less heterogeneity) gave OR 1.53 (95% CI 1.18–1.97).
- When the most recent UK study was excluded (heterogeneity reduced), the pooled OR for the remaining three studies was 1.38 (95% CI 1.05–1.80).
- Risk by sleep position (position placed for sleep): swaddled infants placed prone had the highest risk (OR ≈ 13.0), swaddled side-placed infants had increased risk (OR ≈ 3.16), and swaddled supine infants still had a smaller but significant increased risk (OR ≈ 1.93).
- Position found: swaddled infants found prone were much more common among SIDS cases than controls and had markedly elevated risk.
- Age effects: swaddling was most common around 2 months of age but the association with SIDS increased with infant age; infants ≥6 months had higher risk (OR ≈ 2.5), possibly reflecting greater likelihood of rolling to prone.

Limitations: Only four observational studies with variable swaddling definitions and differing prevalence/times/locations were available; substantial heterogeneity existed. Many potential confounders (e.g., bed-sharing) were not uniformly adjusted for. Techniques and terminology for swaddling were inconsistently described. Small numbers limited some subgroup estimates.

Conclusions and implications: These analyses suggest swaddling may increase SIDS risk overall and that the risk is substantially amplified if the infant is placed—or rolls—onto the side or prone, and as infants get older. Practical implications include reinforcing existing advice to place infants supine to sleep, exercising particular caution when swaddling, and considering an age (commonly cited between 4–6 months) after which swaddling should be discontinued to reduce risk. Further well-designed studies with clear swaddling definitions and rigorous adjustment for confounders are needed.

Harper Lee has sued the Monroe County Heritage Museum in federal court, accusing the small nonprofit in Monroeville, Alabama, of improperly using the title, characters and imagery from her novel To Kill a Mockingbird to promote activities and sell merchandise. The complaint seeks to bar the museum from using the book’s name or related branding and accuses the museum of “trading upon” Lee’s fame and attempting to exploit her declining health to commercialize her work without compensation. The suit points to the museum’s website, gift shop items (t-shirts, mugs, etc.), local logos and annual theatrical productions as examples.

Museum attorney Matt Goforth and executive director Stephanie Rogers deny the allegations, say the institution has honored Lee’s legacy for decades, and warn that a successful suit could cripple the museum, which draws about 30,000 visitors a year and claims modest gift-shop income. Goforth also suggested Lee’s recent actions reflect influence from new “handlers.” The complaint notes past tensions—such as a 2002 dispute over a cookbook—and references Lee’s recent legal fights over her intellectual-property rights, including a separate trademark opposition by the museum and an earlier copyright-related suit she settled.

Background context: Lee, 87 and in poor health, is reclusive and deeply associated with Monroeville (the real-life inspiration for Maycomb). The town and museum have long celebrated her and the book, which has sold some 30 million copies and is widely required reading. Locals are divided over the lawsuit, which has heightened tensions in the small community and raised questions about who is making decisions for Lee as her health declines.

Researchers from MIT, the University of Sheffield and Tokyo Institute of Technology have demonstrated an ingestible origami robot that unfolds from a swallowed capsule and, guided by external magnetic fields, crawls across a simulated stomach wall to retrieve a swallowed button battery or patch tissue. Presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, this device continues Daniela Rus’s lab’s work on foldable robots and addresses the need for small, untethered, controllable devices for internal-body tasks.

Design and operation
- Structure: a three-layer laminated sheet — two structural outer layers with patterned slits and a central shrinkable layer (Biolefin). When the middle layer contracts the sheet folds into a rectangular, accordion-form robot with pinched corners for traction.
- Materials: after testing many options, the team used dried pig intestine (sausage casing) for the outer material for biocompatibility and malleability; the shrinking layer is biodegradable shrink wrap.
- Locomotion: combines stick-slip motion (primary, ~80%) and fluid thrust (~20%) to move in a liquid-filled stomach environment. A permanent magnet embedded in a forward fold responds to external rotating magnetic fields to steer, pivot, spin, and pick up metallic objects like button batteries.
- Deployment: folded small enough to be swallowed in a dissolvable capsule; the capsule dissolves and the robot unfolds under stomach-like forces.

Testing and motivation
- The team built a synthetic stomach model from silicone rubber tuned to a pig stomach’s mechanical properties and filled it with a water–lemon-juice mix to mimic acidic gastric fluids. In experiments the robot unfolded, navigated the environment, located a button battery and retrieved it using its embedded magnet.
- Removing ingested button batteries is a compelling clinical target: ~3,500 such incidents are reported annually in the U.S., and prolonged contact can cause severe tissue burns. The researchers demonstrated the battery’s rapid tissue-damaging potential with a simple ham test to underscore urgency.

Limitations and next steps
- The design is experimental and required structural trade-offs to work with biocompatible, less-stiff materials (fewer slits and fold-oriented stiffness).
- Current control relies on external magnetic fields; researchers plan to add sensors and pursue autonomous control and alternate materials (including non-animal options).
- The work is promising but preliminary; further development and safety testing would be needed before clinical use.

Experts have praised the concept as a creative, practical application of origami robots with clear clinical relevance.

Ford Motor Co. announced it will end vehicle production in Australia in October 2016, closing its Geelong engine plant and Broadmeadows assembly plant. The move ends more than 90 years of Ford car manufacturing in the country and will eliminate about 1,200 jobs. Ford Australia CEO Bob Graziano cited unsustainably high local business costs—particularly wages—sliding sales and a strong Australian dollar as the reasons, saying the company’s costs were roughly double those in Europe and nearly four times elsewhere. The decision is a setback for government efforts to support the domestic auto industry.

This long piece surveys and explains a recently prominent informal use of because in which it introduces a bare noun (or other short word/class) instead of a full clause or the usual because of + noun phrase—examples: “No work tomorrow because holidays,” “Because science,” “Can’t talk now because cooking,” “Going to bed early because exhausted,” “Because yay!” Linguists dubbed it “because NOUN” or “because+noun.” It’s terse, jocular, economical, spreads online, and often signals that the causal reasoning is obvious, trivial, playful, or being deliberately elided.

Key points:
- Traditional uses of because: subordinating conjunction (because + clause) and the compound preposition because of (because of + NP). The new pattern diverges by taking a bare NP (or even verbs, adjectives, interjections) directly after because.
- It’s widespread on social media (many Twitter examples) and shows recurrent nouns (science, school, people, bacon, etc.). Corpus evidence finds earlier instances in speech transcripts and reporting (Larry King, Dateline, etc.) and scattered written examples dating back decades.
- Linguists debate its precise grammatical status: some treat it as a new prepositional use; others argue it’s a different kind of elided/clausal construction. Analyses consider origins such as “because hey” (with discourse markers like hey/wow facilitating the shift), child–parent exchanges, meme forms (e.g., “because race car”), and pop-cultural precedents (e.g., Buffy).
- The form is highly adaptable: it can use bare nouns preferentially but also accepts verbs, adjectives, interjections, and occasionally longer phrases. Restrictions vary by speaker and context.
- Explanations for its popularity emphasize economy, humor from grammatical deviation, and the internet’s role in rapid diffusion. Cognitive accounts link its appeal to playful violations of grammatical expectations.
- Scholarly and popular attention has grown: coverage in mainstream and linguistic outlets, corpus studies (e.g., Twitter analyses), and recognition such as the American Dialect Society naming because its 2013 Word of the Year. Scholars continue to argue about its classification and historical trajectory.

Bottom line: “because X” is a productive, semantically transparent informal pattern that efficiently conveys a causal gist or stance. It’s not Standard English grammar, but it’s systematic, widespread, and linguistically unproblematic as an evolving informal usage—an example of how language innovates, especially online.

Lindsay Lohan is facing renewed pressure from prosecutors who will ask a judge to jail her for allegedly violating probation tied to a 2007 DUI and a May misdemeanor necklace theft. A probation progress report before L.A. Superior Court Judge Stephanie Sautner found Lohan in “substantial compliance,” but city prosecutors say that’s insufficient because she was terminated from required community service at the Downtown Women’s Center for repeatedly missing appointments. Lohan’s team says she completed a shoplifting course, has been attending therapy as ordered, and transferred the shelter hours to the American Red Cross—where she reportedly worked frequently last week. She was ordered to complete 480 hours of community service by April 2012 (360 at the shelter, 120 at the coroner’s office) but had logged only a small portion of the shelter hours. If the judge finds a violation, Lohan could be jailed but would likely be allowed to post bail pending a probation violation hearing. Lohan has defended her compliance on Twitter, saying her travel was approved and she’s trying to meet court obligations.

Here’s a concise, comprehensive summary of the document:

Inauguration schedule and events
- Donald Trump’s inauguration as the 45th U.S. president centered on multiple ceremonial events in Washington, D.C.
- Jan. 19: Public concerts at the Lincoln Memorial ("Voices of the People" and the "Make America Great Again! Welcome Celebration") with performers including the Republican Hindu Coalition, marching bands, Toby Keith and Lee Greenwood; wreath-laying at Arlington National Cemetery; Trump expected to stay at Blair House that night.
- Jan. 20 (Inauguration Day): Morning church service at St. John’s Episcopal, White House tea with President Obama and First Lady, motorcade to the Capitol. Ceremony on the Capitol west front begins 9:30 a.m.; Jackie Evancho to sing the national anthem; Mike Pence sworn in by Justice Clarence Thomas; Trump sworn in by Chief Justice John Roberts at noon using Lincoln’s Bible and his childhood Bible, followed by his inaugural address. Post-ceremony Congressional lunch, 3–5 p.m. parade along Pennsylvania Avenue, and evening inaugural balls across the city.
- Jan. 21: Interfaith National Prayer Service at the Washington National Cathedral.

U.S. withholding UNRWA funds
- The Trump administration reportedly froze $125 million in U.S. funding to UNRWA (one-third of annual U.S. contributions), pending a review of U.S. aid to the Palestinian Authority after Palestine cut contacts over U.S. recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital.
- Officials have considered cutting more—up to $180 million—raising concerns among Western diplomats, U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, and Israeli security officials about severe humanitarian consequences in Gaza, the West Bank and neighboring countries.
- Israeli leaders are cautious: Prime Minister Netanyahu supports scrutiny of UNRWA but prefers gradual disengagement rather than large sudden cuts, citing Israeli security interests tied to UNRWA’s role.

Areas where Trump and Democrats might cooperate
- Despite likely clashes, the piece outlines policy areas where Trump and congressional Democrats could find common ground: trade renegotiations (NAFTA, TPP exit), minimum wage increases, a major infrastructure/transportation package, allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices, and preserving Social Security/Medicare protections.
- Each area presents political and policy tensions—primary among them funding mechanisms for infrastructure, differing views on trade and tariffs, the labor stance of some Trump nominees (e.g., Andrew Puzder), and GOP resistance to entitlement expansions—yet Democrats might leverage cross-party splits to influence outcomes.

Market and public reaction
- Financial markets reacted to Trump’s comments favoring a weaker dollar, creating investor unease.
- An ABC News/Washington Post poll found Trump entering office with very low favorability compared with recent presidents: only 40% approved of his transition handling and 40% approved of his cabinet choices. Majorities distrust his decision-making and doubt his qualifications, though the public expects him to perform well on the economy and jobs.
- Polls show deep partisan and demographic divides on specific proposals (border wall, Obamacare repeal, Paris Agreement withdrawal), with majorities opposing some signature campaign ideas (e.g., banning entry for most non-U.S. Muslims, building the border wall).

Slow cabinet confirmations and transition challenges
- Trump’s Cabinet confirmations were proceeding slowly—projected to be the slowest since 1989—due to ethics issues, complex financial conflicts, Democratic opposition and scheduling. Some national security nominees might be fast-tracked, but many key posts faced delays.
- Democrats signaled they would use procedural tactics to slow confirmations, pointing to controversial nominees (Betsy DeVos, Tom Price, Andrew Puzder, Rex Tillerson) and unresolved ethics/financial disclosure issues. Republicans warned political costs if Democrats dragged out votes, but confirmation battles and extended vacancies in senior posts were likely.

Overall picture
- The document portrays a high-profile, event-filled inauguration amid significant policy uncertainty and political friction: potential humanitarian repercussions from changes to Palestinian aid, areas of possible bipartisan cooperation tempered by ideological constraints, market unease over Trump’s statements, weak public approval, and a fraught, protracted confirmation process for his Cabinet and senior appointees.

This document explains that while the NSA has extensive capabilities to collect Americans’ communications and metadata, there are practical tools and behaviors that can reduce what the agency (and others) can see. It presents five main defenses and important caveats:

Key tools and techniques
- Tor for anonymous web browsing: Tor routes traffic through multiple relays so destination sites see the exit node rather than your IP. The Tor Browser Bundle is an easy way to use Tor, but only traffic through the Tor Browser is anonymized, and traffic between the Tor exit node and the destination site is not protected — use HTTPS and other end-to-end protections for sensitive data.
- OTR for private instant messaging: Off-the-Record (OTR) is an end-to-end encryption extension for conventional IM networks. Both parties must use OTR-capable clients (e.g., Adium on macOS, Pidgin on Windows/Linux). When available, OTR prevents servers from reading chat contents.
- Silent Circle for secure calls: Silent Circle is an Internet telephony service offering end-to-end encrypted voice, with open-source clients and independent audits claiming no backdoors.
- RedPhone for secure calls: RedPhone (funded via the Open Technology Fund) provides end-to-end encrypted calls, is open source and audited, and was designed to be trustworthy even against government snooping.
- Physical phone control to avoid tracking: Cell networks inherently reveal tower/location data needed to route calls. To prevent location tracking you must turn your phone off, remove its battery, or leave it behind — there is no technical workaround that fully hides location from carriers.

Limits and caveats
- Metadata is hard to hide: Even if message contents are encrypted, metadata (who you call or message, when, and where) is often accessible and can be highly revealing. Encryption protects content but not necessarily calling patterns or other metadata.
- De-anonymization via contextual data: Simple operational security mistakes (e.g., logging in from multiple locations) can allow investigators to tie anonymous accounts to real identities by correlating logs and behaviors.
- Tool limitations: Tor protects origin IPs within its network but not traffic beyond the exit node; secure messaging and calling require both ends to use compatible, audited software; not all traffic or apps automatically benefit from these protections.

Practical advice
- Use Tor Browser for anonymized browsing, but combine it with HTTPS and other end-to-end protections.
- Use OTR-capable IM clients to encrypt chat contents.
- Use audited, open-source secure calling apps like Silent Circle or RedPhone for voice privacy.
- To prevent location tracking, power down or physically remove your phone’s battery (or avoid carrying it).
- Recognize that protecting metadata and operational security requires more than encryption — careful behavior and an awareness of what logs and patterns can reveal are essential.

The overall message: you can protect the contents of many communications with available, audited tools, but preventing collection or inference of metadata and location often requires behavioral changes or physical measures, and there are no perfect technological solutions.

Joe Miller formally conceded the Alaska U.S. Senate race to incumbent Lisa Murkowski, announcing he will not pursue further legal challenges after two months of post-election litigation. Miller, who won the Republican primary but lost the general election to Murkowski’s historic write-in victory of about 10,000 votes (the first successful Senate write-in since 1954), said at an Anchorage news conference he would “abide by the court’s decisions” though he remains critical of Murkowski’s ideology and plans to keep “sounding the alarm.” He emphasized the legal fight aimed to push for “more transparent, clearer standards” in counting votes and called the court battles important for the state, but declined to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Murkowski’s campaign quickly welcomed Miller’s decision, noting certification of her win allows her to be sworn in Jan. 5. Miller said he had not personally called Murkowski to concede and joked he didn’t have her number. He downplayed tensions with high-profile supporters such as Sarah Palin, saying post-race disputes were legal matters rather than campaign activity. Miller also said he hasn’t decided whether he’ll seek another office, including a possible 2012 House run.

Researchers and conservationists are using selective “back-breeding” to recreate a functional substitute for the auroch, a large wild cattle species that went extinct in 1627 and once shaped European ecosystems through intensive grazing. The Tauros Project, founded by ecologist Ronald Goderie in 2008 and allied with Rewilding Europe, is cross-breeding modern European cattle breeds that retain auroch ancestry (from Spain, Portugal, Italy and the Balkans) and comparing offspring DNA to the sequenced auroch genome. Now in its fourth generation, the program aims to reach its target phenotype and behavior by about the seventh generation (around 2025).

Tauros animals have been released on protected lands across Spain, Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic and Romania to test their self-sufficiency and responses to predators such as wolves. Project leaders report progress in appearance, behavior and “de-domestication,” with some herds learning to defend themselves and functioning as large grazers that can help restore mosaic habitats—open grasslands, scrub and wetlands—that many species need. Rewilding proponents argue that reintroducing a keystone herbivore can revive biodiversity and landscape processes lost after the auroch’s extinction.

The effort contrasts with earlier, ideologically driven attempts: in the 1920s–30s German zoologists (the Heck brothers) created aggressive “Heck cattle” partly using Spanish fighting breeds; one British farmer later culled half a Heck herd for dangerous behavior. Critics urge caution: the IUCN and some conservation scientists warn of potential ecological, agricultural and human-safety risks, and stress evaluating habitat suitability, impacts on native species, and whether complementary predators or other interventions will be needed. Supporters counter that restored large herbivores can be essential to re-establishing ecosystem function, as seen with successful bison reintroductions elsewhere.

Recent reporting and commentary have intensified criticism of the Catholic Church and Pope Benedict XVI for mishandling clergy sexual-abuse cases and failing to discipline church officials who enabled predatory priests. A New York Times editorial called the Pope’s apology inadequate because it did not address disciplining diocesan leaders who moved abusive priests between parishes. The Catholic League responded with a Times ad that blamed the scandal on homosexuality — a claim criticized as confused and unsupported; experts say pedophilia is driven by access to and control of children rather than adult sexual orientation. On Larry King Live, Catholic League president Bill Donohue downplayed the issue as not pedophilia because many victims were post‑pubescent, a remark criticized as deflecting responsibility.

In response to Times coverage, Cardinal William Levada, head of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, issued a lengthy defense of Pope Benedict on the Vatican website, calling the paper’s reporting and editorials unfair. Levada praised Benedict’s role in creating the 2001 Vatican norms that centralized and streamlined handling of abuse allegations and defended decisions in a high‑profile Wisconsin case involving Rev. Lawrence C. Murphy — who allegedly abused hundreds of deaf boys — arguing a canonical trial was suspended because the priest was dying and that some decisions were diocesan rather than papal. Levada nonetheless called the Murphy case “egregious” and insisted the priest would face divine judgment. The dispute highlights continuing tensions over accountability, media scrutiny, and the Church’s internal handling of abuse cases.

A Union County, SC teacher, Leigh Anne Arthur, resigned after a nude photo of her that had been stored on her phone was copied and spread by a student, according to district officials and multiple news reports. District interim superintendent David Eubanks said a student accessed Arthur’s unlocked phone, photographed an image from her gallery and distributed it via text and social media; the district learned of the incident on a Monday and Arthur resigned the following day. The Union County Sheriff’s Office is investigating and the student’s phone has been seized.

Arthur disputes the district’s characterization that she was at fault for “making the nude picture available,” saying the photo had been taken for her husband and that she left her phone on her desk briefly while on hall duty; she says the student took the phone, admitted to the principal, and two witnesses corroborated the account. Arthur says the principal asked for her resignation and that the district cited lack of policy but blamed her for allowing the phone to be accessible. She has filed a lawsuit against the school district and Eubanks claiming false accusations and procedural violations.

Students and parents have launched a petition (gaining thousands of signatures) seeking her reinstatement and criticizing the school’s handling; petitioners say the student(s) responsible have not been adequately punished. School officials have suggested Arthur may have exposed students to inappropriate material and noted potential disciplinary or legal consequences for the student. Arthur says she plans to press charges and has expressed forgiveness toward the student while emphasizing that he should be held accountable.

Shasta County authorities and Sherri Papini’s husband, Keith, have provided new details about her condition after she was found alive on Thanksgiving, three weeks after disappearing on Nov. 2 while jogging. Sheriff Tom Bosenko said investigators have conducted follow-up interviews with Papini and are treating the case as a kidnapping; they are searching for two Hispanic adult women driving an SUV based on her description. Officials say there is no known motive yet and no reason to doubt her account.

Keith Papini described reuniting with his wife in the hospital, saying she was severely injured: emaciated (about 87 pounds), with multicolored bruises, a broken nasal bridge, chopped-off long blond hair, burns, red rashes, chain markings, branding, and other wounds. He said she had been bound and had a bag over her head when dropped about 150 miles from home; she managed to flag down help after freeing a hand. Keith thanked supporters, condemned online accusations and rumors that the case is a hoax, and asked for privacy as the family begins a long healing process.

Hurricane Sandy, though not yet made landfall at the time of reporting, was already affecting the 2012 U.S. presidential campaign and could influence next week’s election in several ways.

Practical disruptions
- Campaigns had to alter schedules for Obama and Romney, and early voting in Maryland and D.C. was temporarily suspended.
- Polling has been disrupted: some polls (e.g., Investor’s Business Daily) paused tracking, and polls in hard-hit states will be harder to interpret. Large numbers of people without power or displaced could be unreachable, biasing results unless pollsters adjust with weighting.

Potential effects on polls and turnout
- A simple thought experiment: if 15 million (about 1/20 of the population) in Democratic-leaning Northeast areas were unreachable and leaned 20 points toward Obama, national poll totals could shift by roughly one percentage point. Polling firms’ weighting may mitigate this unpredictably.
- Turnout could be depressed along the East Coast, which would likely reduce Obama’s national popular-vote margin but might not change Electoral College outcomes in many states that are heavily Democratic anyway.
- Recovery capacity in the relatively wealthy Northeast may limit disruption by Election Day, but inland and less-prepared areas (including some Republican-leaning regions) could also be hit by flooding and rain, making state-level effects hard to predict.

Political psychology and incumbency
- Research (Reeves and Gasper, 2011) shows electorates tend to punish incumbents for severe weather damage but reward officials—especially governors—for competent disaster responses; presidents can gain from disaster declarations but less so than governors. Voters distinguish between uncontrollable events and governmental responses.
- Most academic studies assess disasters’ effects over months or years, so immediate political consequences are uncertain, though a well-managed response can help an incumbent and a botched one can hurt.

Other impacts
- The storm will change campaign plans and news coverage during the final stretch.
- Polling methodologies and cancellations could make late polls less reliable.

Advice
- The piece emphasizes public safety over politics: people in affected areas should prioritize safety and follow official guidance; political analysis can wait until recovery (and power) is restored.

Nestlé commissioned an independent Verité investigation that found indicators of forced labor, trafficking, child labor and other abusive practices in Thailand’s seafood supply chain. Migrant workers—largely from neighboring countries—were reportedly lured under false pretences, charged excessive recruitment fees, had wages withheld and identity documents confiscated, suffered verbal and physical abuse, and in some cases were sold to boat captains. These sea- and land-based abuses mirror long-standing findings about Thailand’s fishing sector and, the report notes, pose a systemic risk to virtually any company sourcing seafood there.

The revelations follow broader scrutiny of the Thai industry from media investigations, U.S. trafficking reports, EU warnings and civil lawsuits in the U.S. alleging products (including shrimp and pet/cat food) were linked to slave-staffed fishing boats and forced labor. Thailand’s government says it is taking enforcement action.

Nestlé has published an action plan based on Verité’s recommendations. Measures include improving traceability of seafood ingredients, training captains and boat owners, establishing grievance channels and an emergency response team for migrant workers, conducting audits and banning sourcing from illegal/unregulated fishing and trans-shipment at sea (for Purina). Nestlé intends periodic public updates and to work with the Thai government, suppliers, NGOs (e.g., Sustainable Fisheries Partnership) and multistakeholder groups (including the ILO working group) to address labor and sustainability risks. The company frames this as a difficult, multi-year effort similar to prior work on child labor in cocoa.

A June 5–8 Gallup poll found 29% of Americans support closing the Guantanamo Bay detention facility and moving detainees to U.S. prisons, while 66% oppose it — little changed from 2009 despite renewed attention after the exchange that freed Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl for five Taliban detainees. Partisan divisions persist: Republicans have long been the least supportive (support dipping as low as 8% in 2009), independents’ support has declined since 2007, and Democrats now show their lowest support yet (41% support, 54% oppose). Overall, public opinion on closing the prison has been steady since 2007, though it could shift if the detainee population continues to shrink or if released prisoners pose renewed threats.

Meanwhile, the White House reports 17 detainees were transferred in the past 13 months (including the five exchanged for Bergdahl), leaving 149 at Guantanamo. The administration is exploring further case-by-case transfers and is reportedly drafting options to override a congressional ban on bringing detainees to the U.S. — a move that would be a significant use of executive power and likely draw strong congressional opposition.
