China’s annual gaokao—the high-stakes national university entrance exam taken by nearly 10 million students this year—determines university placement and is seen as pivotal to future careers. Because gaokao results are released in late June, after many U.S. college admission deadlines, Chinese students who score poorly often must wait a year to reapply or pursue alternate tracks.

To attract top Chinese high-school graduates and international tuition revenue, several U.S. universities have begun accepting gaokao scores. The University of New Hampshire (UNH) announced it will accept gaokao results—becoming the first U.S. flagship state school to do so—and launched bilingual recruiting materials. UNH’s program requires gaokao scores plus an English test, video interview, and transcripts; admitted students could begin classes in January to avoid waiting until the regular autumn intake. The University of San Francisco already runs a similar Gaokao admission program, admitting students based on gaokao scores, school records and an English interview, sometimes allowing entry that same fall without SAT/ACT/TOEFL/IELTS.

International students—about 377,000 from China, over one-third of all international students in the U.S.—often pay full tuition and are an important revenue source. European, Canadian and Australian universities have long accepted gaokao scores. The move to accept gaokao in the U.S. occurs amid stricter U.S. visa policies for some Chinese students tied to national security concerns, including reports of shorter-duration visas for certain technical fields.

Cultural context: gaokao remains a life-defining, intensely competitive two- or three-day exam with deep historical roots. It draws widespread public attention and rituals—students and families wear symbolic clothing (often red) and brands market gaokao-themed apparel. About one in four test-takers may not secure a university place.

Apolipoprotein E (APOE) has three common alleles—e2, e3 and e4—yielding six possible genotypes. These variants influence risk for several conditions:

- Cardiovascular disease: Carrying at least one e4 allele increases the risk of atherosclerosis (fatty and scar-like buildup in artery walls), which raises the likelihood of heart attack and stroke.

- Hyperlipoproteinemia type III: The e2 allele strongly predisposes to this rare disorder, especially in individuals with two e2 copies. The condition causes elevated cholesterol, triglycerides and beta‑VLDLs, leading to xanthomas and early atherosclerosis.

- Age-related macular degeneration (AMD): Some studies suggest e4 may be protective or delay AMD, while e2 may increase risk or hasten onset; findings are inconsistent and further research is needed.

- Alzheimer’s disease and brain pathology: Having one or especially two e4 alleles substantially increases Alzheimer’s disease risk. People with e2 variants tend to have more brain plaques but are less likely to show clinical dementia symptoms.

Overall, APOE genotype affects lipid metabolism and disease susceptibility, but effects on some conditions (notably AMD) remain uncertain and are an active area of study.

Scout LaRue Willis, daughter of Bruce Willis and Demi Moore, staged a topless protest in Manhattan’s Lower East Side on May 27–28, 2014 to challenge Instagram’s anti-nudity policy. Willis tweeted two professional photos of her topless stroll—one captioned “What @instagram won’t let you see #FreeTheNipple” and another reading “Legal in NYC but not on @instagram”—as part of the #FreeTheNipple movement opposing social-media censorship of female nipples. She said public female toplessness is legal in New York City but repeatedly criticized Instagram for removing images (including ones of breast cancer survivors) and had her account disabled after changing her display name to “Areola.” Her action follows similar celebrity support for the campaign (e.g., Miley Cyrus, Cara Delevingne) and high-profile Instagram removals such as Rihanna’s suspended account. The protest drew broad online support while Instagram’s community guidelines prohibit nude or sexually suggestive content.

A Houston couple discovered a stranger had taken control of their internet-connected baby monitor and camera, using its speaker to shout insults and sexually explicit language at their sleeping 2-year-old and then at the parents. Marc Gilbert heard the voice coming from his daughter Allyson’s room on Aug. 10; the child—who is deaf and had her cochlear implants turned off—was unharmed. Gilbert unplugged the camera immediately. He says he used basic protections (router and camera passwords, firewall), but evidence suggests the family’s Foscam IP camera may have been exploited via a previously disclosed firmware vulnerability that allows remote takeover. Security researchers warned months earlier that many Foscam cameras were vulnerable and urged firmware updates and changing default admin credentials; Shodan shows tens of thousands of similar cameras online. Experts quoted advise changing default usernames/passwords, using strong, non-dictionary passwords, enabling strong Wi‑Fi encryption, keeping firmware up to date, and protecting any associated websites/accounts. Gilbert unplugged and will not reuse the device and is warning other parents about the privacy and safety risks of internet-enabled monitors.

Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son‑in‑law and senior adviser, has had his White House security clearance restored, ending months of uncertainty tied in part to Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation. Kushner twice met with Mueller’s team — a November interview focused largely on former national security adviser Michael Flynn, and a seven‑hour session in April — and his lawyers say he has fully cooperated, provided many documents, and believes he has finished all ongoing inquiries, including congressional probes.

Kushner’s interim clearance had been stripped in February amid a broader review of access procedures after staff secretary Rob Porter’s resignation. The delay in granting permanent clearance drew scrutiny because Mueller’s investigators were examining Kushner’s campaign and transition contacts (including with Russians) and early White House events such as James Comey’s firing. The process was also complicated by Kushner’s complex financial holdings and numerous foreign contacts; his initial clearance form omitted dozens of contacts later added in updated submissions. Kushner’s attorney disputes that the initial application caused the delay, saying the application was properly handled by career officials and that Kushner continued working on policy matters throughout. With the cleared status, Kushner can access highly classified briefings and sensitive intelligence used in policymaking and diplomacy.

French Green MP Véronique Massonneau was forced to halt her speech in the National Assembly after conservative UMP deputy Philippe Le Ray began imitating hen noises while she addressed planned pension reforms. Massonneau interrupted him—“That’s enough. Stop that, I’m not a hen!”—but the heckling continued until Assembly president Claude Bartolone intervened, calling the behaviour unacceptable and convening an extraordinary meeting of party whips. The episode, captured on video (though the noises are not audible), sparked national outrage and accusations of sexism—“degrading to the Republic,” said Pascal Canfin—and calls for Le Ray to be formally reprimanded. Massonneau suggested Le Ray was drunk; the incident has prompted debate over misconduct and misogyny in French politics.

Researchers from the U.S. Geological Survey and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service report high rates of intersex in bass from 19 National Wildlife Refuges across the Northeast: about 85% of male smallmouth bass and 27% of male largemouth bass showed ovarian tissue or immature eggs in their testes. Similar phenomena have been documented across the U.S. and worldwide in roughly 37 fish species.

Scientists link these abnormalities to exposure to estrogenic endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) entering waterways from multiple sources—synthetic pharmaceuticals (e.g., birth-control hormones), natural hormones in livestock manure, herbicides and pesticides (e.g., atrazine), and plastics-related compounds like BPA. These substances can act at very low concentrations to disrupt hormone regulation, affect reproduction, alter gene expression via epigenetic mechanisms, reduce fertilization rates across generations, and increase disease susceptibility.

The recent study mapped where intersex fish occur but did not include chemical analyses of water or tissue at sampling sites, so it cannot pinpoint specific compounds. Researchers and resource managers are concerned because refuges are managed for wildlife health; finding widespread intersex there indicates contamination is pervasive. Addressing the issue will be difficult and costly—potential responses include wastewater-treatment upgrades, tighter controls on agrochemicals and runoff mitigation—but specific sources need to be traced and management actions coordinated to reduce EDC inputs.

Two adults and two children were found dead Tuesday after a large house in Colts Neck, N.J., burned in a fire being investigated as a possible arson. Monmouth County Prosecutor Christopher Gramiccioni said three bodies were recovered inside the home and a fourth—a man—was found dead outside on the front lawn. Authorities have not released the victims’ names.

Local reporting identifies the deceased man found outside as 50-year-old homeowner Keith Caneiro. Sources say Keith, his wife Jennifer (45), and two of their children were killed in what investigators are treating as an apparent quadruple homicide, and that Keith suffered a gunshot wound that did not appear self-inflicted. The estate is on Willow Brook Road.

Earlier Tuesday morning, a separate fire broke out at the home of Keith’s brother, Paul Caneiro, in Ocean Township. That blaze is also under investigation for possible links to the Colts Neck fire; prosecutors said they are pursuing the connection as a possible angle but have not confirmed one. Neighbors said Paul appeared distraught at the scene and remained there through midday; he and his wife had not returned home as of Tuesday evening.

Background on Keith Caneiro reported by NJ Advance Media notes he owned a technology firm (Square One) and a pest control business (EcoStar Pest Management) in Asbury Park, had a real estate license, and grew up in Brooklyn. The family home was purchased in 1999 and the mortgage was paid off about two years ago. Prosecutors said more information would be released Wednesday as the investigation continues.

A newborn male infant was found alive but barely breathing inside a plastic trash bag in a dumpster at the Reserve at Windmill Lakes apartment complex in southeast Houston around 8 a.m. Tuesday. Maintenance worker Carlos Michel (Mitchell) heard crying while handling garbage, opened the bag and discovered the infant upside down with the umbilical cord still attached; he said the baby was cold and may have been only hours old. Paramedics took the baby to Hermann hospital, where he is reported to be recovering. Police and Child Protective Services are investigating and trying to locate the parents; investigators believe the mother may be a teenage resident of the property. Papers found in the bag included food leftovers and what appear to be homework assignments with a student’s name. The report notes Texas’s “Baby Moses” law, which allows a parent to safely relinquish an infant to any place that provides 24-hour medical care.

Taylor Swift discusses fame, privacy, friendship, and her shift to pop in a wide-ranging profile centered on the lead-up to her 2014 single "Shake It Off" and her album 1989.

Key points:
- Fame and privacy: Swift uses a vivid metaphor—“walking around with a cat on your head”—to describe being famous: she chose it and is grateful, but it brings intrusive attention. Her video shoot for "Shake It Off" (Project Sparrow) was run with extreme secrecy and heavy security because of fears about leaks, wiretaps, and hidden cameras. She employs staff whose job is to protect her image and prevent embarrassing exposures (e.g., in dressing rooms).
- New phase and music: Swift is excited about 1989, a deliberate, full-on pop album influenced by ’80s pop (Phil Collins, Annie Lennox, Madonna) and co-produced with Max Martin. She frames it as a departure from straddling country and pop, noting she won’t promote the record to country radio or attend country-award shows. The record contains fewer direct “diss” songs about exes; instead many tracks are wistful or reflective, though “Bad Blood” addresses a feud with another female artist and several songs seem inspired by her relationship with Harry Styles (e.g., “Out of the Woods,” “Style”).
- Personal life and dating: Swift, living happily single in New York, says she hasn’t dated since her split with Styles and is intentionally avoiding the pressure of public dating—cold approaches, scrutiny, jokes, and the way relationships become fodder for entertainment. She values romance but isn’t prioritizing relationships now and has poured energy into friendships and self-improvement.
- Friendships and feminism: Since moving to New York she’s cultivated close female friendships (Karlie Kloss, Lena Dunham, Lorde) and embraces feminism as equal opportunity for women. She also defends female solidarity but can be fiercely protective when crossed—explaining "Bad Blood" arose from a business betrayal (an unnamed female peer allegedly tried to undermine her tour).
- Personal details and lifestyle: Swift recently bought a Tribeca penthouse (and the unit across the hall for security), a Rhode Island home, and enjoys painting, working out, and domestic pleasures (cats Olivia and Meredith, a piano, rooftop garden). She describes lighter moments—hosting friends at Watch Hill, playing Celebrity, and a rainy Slip ‘N Slide incident.
- Public encounters: Despite precautions, she still faces intense public attention; she recounts a Central Park outing swarmed by paparazzi and fans, but also moments of generosity and warmth (giving money to a fan celebrating her birthday). She copes with crowds by retreating into music—Kendrick Lamar is mentioned as a go-to confidence booster.

Also noted: Media speculation around who the unnamed woman in "Bad Blood" might be—Katy Perry is suggested in the appended gossip item, with Perry tweeting a Mean Girls reference but not directly replying.

Overall, the piece paints Swift as a cautious, highly controlled public figure entering a creative and personal transition: confidently moving into mainstream pop, prioritizing close female friendships, asserting her privacy, and navigating the tradeoffs of immense fame.

This collection of reviews finds the 2017 Baywatch film a shallow, often crude reboot that never rises above its premise of slow‑motion beach bodies. Critics say director Seth Gordon leans into tasteless, R‑rated gross‑out humor and extended jokes about male anatomy, producing a movie that’s more dumb than cleverly self‑aware. Dwayne Johnson’s straight‑faced Mitch Buchannon and Zac Efron’s narcissistic Matt Brody have amiable chemistry early on, and the film initially evokes some of the TV series’ camp in playful banter and meta jokes about lifeguards acting like cops. But once a contrived plot about drugs, corruption and a resort owner (Priyanka Chopra) takes over, the fun deflates; cameos from original cast members are spoiled by early credit listings, outtakes aren’t funny, and the screenplay—credited to multiple writers—fails to deliver the sharp spoof many expected. The result: decent physiques and a few laughs, but little substance or satire. Overall grade in these reviews: mediocre (roughly C/C‑; 3/5 in one).

Midazolam (US brand Versed) is a short-acting benzodiazepine sedative given under physician supervision to produce drowsiness, amnesia, loss of consciousness for surgery or intensive-care sedation. A case report in Restorative Neurology and Neuroscience describes an unexpected "awakening" in a 43-year-old Italian man who had been in a minimally conscious state for nearly two years after a car accident.

Timeline and response:
- The man was comatose for 40 days, then emerged into a minimally conscious state—able to open/close eyes and make some simple movements but not communicate or follow commands. Over the following year he declined, showing slowed movements and repetitive behaviors.
- About two years after the injury, he was given a mild sedative, midazolam, to facilitate a CT scan. Minutes after administration he became fully interactive and verbal—recognizing places, speaking on the phone, answering questions—though he had no memory of the accident or its effects. The effect lasted about two hours, then he reverted to his prior condition.
- A repeated midazolam dose produced the same transient recovery. Pre-, during- and post-drug brain scans implicated regions associated with catatonia, a syndrome sometimes responsive to benzodiazepines.

Follow-up treatment:
- Continuous midazolam administration was not feasible outside an ICU. Doctors tried lorazepam (an oral/longer-acting benzodiazepine) but the patient became agitated and aggressive.
- Switching to carbamazepine (an anticonvulsant) allowed maintenance of improved interaction and communication.

Interpretation and limits:
- This is the first reported case of midazolam producing such an awakening. The authors suggest the patient may have had catatonic features that benzodiazepines can relieve, but it’s unclear whether he had true catatonia or overlapping symptoms. Midazolam produced only transient improvement and cannot be routinely used outside monitored settings; more research is needed to understand mechanisms and potential therapeutic paths.

At the 2016 Republican National Convention in Cleveland, delegates formally nominated Donald J. Trump as the GOP presidential candidate, ending a sustained but ultimately unsuccessful effort by conservative and NeverTrump delegates to deny him the nomination. Despite weeks of planning, social-media organizing and late attempts to change rules or unbind delegates, party leaders, an alliance of the Trump campaign and the RNC, and delegation majorities prevailed. High-profile challenges — including a symbolic Utah vote for Ted Cruz and a split Alaska delegation — were overruled under party rules, and convention officials awarded the contested votes to Trump.

The convention’s Tuesday program, themed "Make America Work Again," emphasized jobs and family but repeatedly returned to attacks on Hillary Clinton, including a forceful, theatrical indictment-style speech by Chris Christie that escalated accusations and evoked chants of "Lock her up!" Trump’s children, Tiffany and Donald Trump Jr., gave polished, sympathetic speeches that sought to humanize their father and highlight his business credentials; they were widely cited as among the night’s effective performers. Other Trump family members were scheduled to speak later in the week.

Winners and losers noted in coverage included: Trump himself (securely nominated); the prominence of Benghazi and criminalization rhetoric as campaign themes; the Trump children for strong performances; and Chris Christie for his dramatic, accusatory speech. Losers included Paul Ryan, whose formal declaration of Trump’s nomination undercut prior discomfort with the candidate; state delegates and rising politicians whose convention appearances tied them publicly to Trump; and figures like Michael Mukasey, criticized as hypocritical for past statements. Overall, the convention showcased party unity behind Trump despite visible dissent and procedural disputes.

John Sidney McCain Sr. (August 9, 1884 – September 6, 1945) was a U.S. Navy admiral best known for commanding the Fast Carrier Task Force in World War II. Born in Teoc (Carroll County), Mississippi, he attended the University of Mississippi before graduating from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1906. Early in his career he served with the Asiatic Squadron and on various battleships and auxiliaries; his first command was the cargo ship Sirius (AK-18). In 1936, at age 51, he became a Naval Aviator and from 1937–1939 commanded the carrier Ranger (CV-4), helping develop carrier tactics.

During the first year of WWII he was Commander of Air Forces for the Western Sea Frontier and the South Pacific Force. A controversial lapse in August 1942 — failing to order requested reconnaissance over the Solomon Islands and not informing commanders — contributed to the Allied surprise defeat at the Battle of Savo Island. He later served as Chief of the Bureau of Aeronautics (Oct 1942–July 1943) and Deputy Chief of Naval Operations (Air), becoming a vice admiral in July 1943.

In 1944 he succeeded Marc Mitscher as commander of the Fast Carrier Task Force (Task Force 38), leading sustained carrier operations that supported major amphibious campaigns across the Pacific (Peleliu, Philippine Sea, Leyte Gulf, Luzon, Formosa, the Ryukyus and raids on the Japanese home islands). His actions in protecting ships such as Canberra and Houston in October 1944 earned him the Navy Cross; he also received the Distinguished Service Medal with two Gold Stars. Under his command, carrier aircraft achieved massive successes, including sinking many enemy ships and destroying thousands of aircraft. McCain witnessed Japan’s surrender aboard USS Missouri on September 2, 1945, and died four days later after returning to the U.S.; he was posthumously promoted to admiral and buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

McCain is the patriarch of a notable naval family: his son John S. McCain Jr. also became an admiral (the only father–son pair of full admirals in U.S. history), his grandson John McCain III was a Navy captain and U.S. Senator, and his great-grandson John S. (Jack) McCain IV attended the Naval Academy. The destroyer USS John S. McCain (DDG-56) is named for him and his son.

At Harare International Airport Zimbabwe’s First Lady Grace Mugabe sustained a minor ankle injury when the presidential limousine moved suddenly as she was getting in; her shoe was run over and she was treated at a clinic and discharged. A police motorcyclist escorting the motorcade was also reported to have fractured his arm in a separate road collision.

Separately, Grace Mugabe was accused of assaulting 20‑year‑old South African model Gabriella Engels at the Capital 20 West Hotel in Sandton, Johannesburg. Engels says Mugabe entered a room where she was visiting Mugabe’s sons and repeatedly beat her with an extension cord, causing a head wound and bleeding; she posted photos of her injuries and says bodyguards did nothing. Engels filed a police complaint in South Africa alleging "assault with intent to do grievous bodily harm."

South African authorities gave mixed statements about Mugabe’s cooperation: Police Minister Fikile Mbalula said Mugabe handed herself over and would appear in court but was not under arrest; later officials said arrangements for her to surrender had not fully materialized. Police confirmed a case had been opened and that the investigation was advanced but could not name a suspect until a court appearance. Diplomatic immunity was raised as a possible issue only if she was on official business. Zimbabwean officials have not publicly commented on the hotel assault allegations.

A 23-year-old physiotherapy student from a poor family in Mandwara Kalan, Uttar Pradesh, who moved to Delhi with her family, died in Singapore after being gang-raped and severely injured on a private bus in New Delhi on December 16. Her family and villagers remember her as brave, full of life, determined to become a doctor, and intent on helping her ancestral village; they scattered her ashes in the Ganges and many are calling for the death penalty for the attackers.

Five men have been formally charged with murder, gang rape and criminal conspiracy; a sixth, a juvenile, will be tried separately. The accused were not present in court; prosecutors say the suspects admitted torturing and raping the woman “to teach her a lesson,” and bite marks and testimony from the surviving male companion and other witnesses form part of an extensive dossier. Murder in India can carry the death penalty, and public anger has fueled calls for harsh punishment.

The crime triggered massive protests across India, including student-led demonstrations, and sparked a national debate about violence against women and shortcomings in public safety. The government has created fast-track courts and set up review panels to recommend legal reforms; proposed measures under consideration include chemical castration and making harsher penalties for rape. Legal groups warn that speed must not compromise fair trials, and some lawyers oppose introducing the death penalty for rape on constitutional grounds. The case has also prompted solidarity protests in neighboring countries and intensified pressure to amend laws and strengthen enforcement to protect women.

Researchers have long observed that women outlive men worldwide; two recent studies explore when and why that gap widened and how sex influences aging.

1) Historical analysis of mortality trends
- A study led by USC gerontology researchers analyzed people born 1800–1935 across 13 developed countries and found that significant sex differences in adult mortality first emerged around the turn of the 20th century.
- For cohorts born after ~1880, female death rates among those over 40 fell about 70% faster than male rates. The divergence was strongest between ages 50–70 and narrowed after age 80.
- The researchers identify cardiovascular disease as the major contributor to excess male mortality in middle and early older age. Smoking explained only about 30% of the male excess after 1890.
- Authors suggest further work on diet, exercise, genetics, cellular biology, and links with later-life brain health to explain why men experienced higher heart-disease mortality.

2) Sex, stem cells and aging
- A commentary in Cell Stem Cell argues that sex differences in stem cell regulation and responses to sex hormones may help explain differing aging trajectories and longevity between men and women.
- Examples: estrogen boosts blood and neural stem cell function in female mice (important in pregnancy and estrus); estrogen supplementation extended male mouse lifespan in some studies, and historical data show eunuchs lived longer than intact men.
- Genetic manipulations in mice and human twin data hint at sex-specific effects (e.g., telomere differences) on aging. The authors call for more research into sex-specific stem cell aging and for controlling for sex in aging studies.
 
Taken together, these findings point to cardiovascular disease and sex-specific biology—including hormone and stem cell effects—as key factors in why the female longevity advantage expanded in the 20th century.

Daniel Perlman, a biophysicist at Brandeis University and prolific inventor, has designed a simple modification to wine bottles that prevents drips when pouring. After studying slow-motion footage and noting that glass’s hydrophilic nature makes wine cling to the lip and run down the neck, he added a tiny circular groove—about 2 mm wide and 1 mm deep—around the bottle’s opening. The groove interrupts the liquid’s path so the stream falls into the glass rather than bridging the gap and dripping. Tests show this minimal change is effective, but adoption requires manufacturers to build the groove into bottles, which could raise production costs and requires industry buy-in. Perlman is currently pitching the idea to bottle makers.

The piece argues that October’s disastrous rollout of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) has badly damaged public confidence in both the law and Democrats’ ability to expand healthcare. It notes two dominant problems: a malfunctioning HealthCare.gov and widespread cancellations/rate increases for individual-market plans, which undercut President Obama’s repeated promise that people could keep their coverage. While many canceled plans were low-value and some people will qualify for better, subsidized coverage, the public sees mostly broken websites and personal “rate shock” stories, which will dominate national and local news for months.

The author contends the ACA’s structure — a market-based, technocratic compromise shaped by conservative-leaning Democrats — guaranteed immediate, irritating disruptions for millions, producing resentment even when outcomes may be improvements. This design, intended to avoid the political cost of a more direct government program, obscures benefits while spotlighting coercive elements. Democrats, having refused larger changes like single-payer and passed the law without broader buy-in, now “own” its failures. Calls for Republican cooperation to fix the law are dismissed as unrealistic; the author argues concessions would have been needed when Democrats had greater leverage. The article criticizes the administration for insisting people wouldn’t lose plans and for resisting acknowledgment of trade-offs, concluding that the rollout’s problems and the law’s design are President Obama’s responsibility.

Selena Gomez revealed she underwent a kidney transplant over the summer because her lupus had damaged her kidneys. In an Instagram post she explained that this was why she stepped back from promoting her new music and thanked doctors, family and medical staff. Gomez said the donor was her longtime friend and actress Francia Raisa, calling the gift “the ultimate” and expressing deep gratitude. Gomez has previously spoken publicly about her lupus diagnosis, chemotherapy treatment, and periods of anxiety, panic attacks and depression linked to the disease; she has used her platform to raise awareness and has taken time off to focus on her health.

Google announced it has asked 34 cities across nine U.S. metro areas to complete readiness checklists as it explores expanding Google Fiber, its fiber-to-the-home gigabit internet and TV service. The metros under consideration are Phoenix; Atlanta; San Jose; Salt Lake City; Nashville; San Antonio; Portland, Ore.; and Charlotte and Raleigh‑Durham, N.C. Cities will provide maps of existing conduit, utility lines and other infrastructure so Google can assess local construction challenges, housing density and feasibility. Google said it will work with city leaders on planning and aims to announce which cities will get Fiber by the end of the year, but cautioned that no commitments have been made and not all evaluated markets will necessarily be chosen.

Background and implications:
- Google Fiber delivers 1 Gbps symmetrical speeds by running fiber directly into homes; Kansas City (and smaller deployments in Provo and an agreement in Austin) remain its primary live markets. Construction in Kansas City continues and uses contractors, so building elsewhere is unlikely to directly slow that project.
- Expanding would increase Google’s customer base and bargaining power for TV channel carriage; its current lineup still lacks some popular channels (e.g., AMC).
- Analysts view this move as both competitive pressure on incumbent cable/phone providers (notably Cox, Time Warner Cable and Comcast in the targeted markets) and a possible sign Google sees a profitable consumer broadband business rather than purely a strategic lever.
- Google’s rollout strategy targets neighborhoods with concentrated demand to avoid piecemeal costs; broader deployment could spur development of applications that use gigabit speeds.

No estimates were provided on customer counts or profitability timelines.

Former President George H.W. Bush, 91, was discharged after four days at Maine Medical Center following a fall at his Kennebunkport summer home that fractured a vertebra in his neck. His spokesman, Jim McGrath, said Bush was “very grateful” to return home. Doctors reported he never lost consciousness, suffered no nerve damage or spinal impingement, and will not need surgery; he will wear a neck brace for at least a couple of months. His physicians expect full recovery in about three to four months. Bush, who has a form of Parkinson’s and uses a scooter or wheelchair for mobility, is the oldest living former president and served as vice president under Ronald Reagan before his 1988 election.

North Korea announced on Jan. 6, 2016 that it had conducted a “successful” hydrogen (thermonuclear) bomb test at its Punggye-ri nuclear site. The underground explosion produced a magnitude-5.1 seismic event detected by US, Chinese, Japanese and South Korean monitoring agencies and prompted emergency national-security meetings, civilian evacuations near the Chinese border, and international condemnation.

Pyongyang’s state media called the device a “miniaturized H-bomb of justice” and framed the test as defensive and tied to leader Kim Jong Un’s authority; the announcement came two days before his birthday. The regime also reiterated its intent to continue developing advanced nuclear-strike capabilities while promising not to use nuclear arms unless attacked.

The claim that the device was a true hydrogen bomb was met with widespread skepticism. U.S. and South Korean officials and many independent experts said the measured yield and seismic signature were similar to North Korea’s earlier fission tests (2006, 2009, 2013), suggesting the detonation was more consistent with an atomic or “boosted” device rather than a full two-stage thermonuclear weapon. Analysts noted North Korea might have tested a boosted or partially fusion-augmented design or simply exaggerated the result for propaganda.

Reactions:
- The U.N. Security Council moved to draft significant new measures, likely expanding sanctions.
- China and Russia criticized the test; China said it would protest to Pyongyang.
- The United States confirmed a nuclear test had occurred but disputed the hydrogen-bomb claim and warned of appropriate responses; U.S. lawmakers pushed for tougher sanctions on entities doing business with North Korea.
- South Korea and Japan condemned the test and reinforced defense preparations.
- Global markets fell amid heightened geopolitical worries.

Implications:
- Whether or not it was a true H-bomb, the test signals continued advance in North Korea’s nuclear program and its intent to pursue miniaturization and missile delivery capability — goals that, if achieved, would substantially raise regional and global security concerns. Determining the device’s exact nature will take further technical analysis and monitoring.

The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA) exhibited material from Tomb 10A at Deir el-Bersha—an important Middle Kingdom (c. 2040–1640 BC) burial site for regional governors (nomarchs) of the Hare Nome. Excavated in 1915 by an MFA–Harvard team led by George Reisner, Tomb 10A contained the burial assemblage of a governor named Djehutynakht (uncertainly either Djehutynakht IV or V) and his wife (also called Djehutynakht). Although looted in antiquity, the tomb yielded one of the largest Middle Kingdom burial assemblages ever found, including decorated cedar coffins, pottery, canopic jars, nearly 60 model boats, daily-life models and the famed “Bersha procession” of a priest and offering bearers. The governor’s outer coffin is a masterpiece of Middle Kingdom art.

Because the tomb had been ransacked, the mummies were mutilated: a dismembered torso and a mummified, bandage-wrapped head were recovered (the head was found atop the governor’s coffin). CT scans in 2005 showed extensive post-mortem damage to facial bones that precluded reliable morphological sexing, though cranial features suggested a probable male. To resolve whether the head belonged to the governor or his wife, the MFA worked with the FBI Laboratory to attempt DNA analysis.

Ancient DNA work on Egyptian remains had a poor track record due to hot, arid conditions that fragment DNA to very short lengths and early studies plagued by contamination. Traditional forensic DNA methods rely on PCR amplification of relatively long targets (90–1200 bp), limiting their usefulness on highly degraded samples. High-throughput sequencing (HTS) and shotgun sequencing, however, can recover and sequence very short fragments without targeted PCR.

Using a small sample of tooth powder from a molar, FBI forensic scientists applied shotgun sequencing and successful ancient-DNA protocols. They recovered damaged DNA consistent with antiquity and determined the individual was biologically male. Independent confirmation by another group supported the result. The DNA evidence therefore indicates the head most likely belonged to the governor Djehutynakht rather than his wife, resolving a century-old question. The study also demonstrates that modern genomic methods (shotgun HTS) can recover usable genetic information from very old, environmentally degraded Egyptian remains, opening new forensic and archaeological possibilities.

This document combines a statement from the Paterno family with news reporting about the NCAA response to the Jerry Sandusky child-abuse scandal at Penn State.

Paterno family statement
- The family argues removing Joe Paterno’s statue does nothing for Sandusky’s victims or community healing. They say the priority should be uncovering the full truth.
- They criticize the Freeh report as an incomplete, prosecutor-like indictment rather than a fair adjudication: Joe Paterno never had a hearing, his counsel could not interview key witnesses (who are represented by lawyers), and critical evidence remains unreleased.
- The family contends the university should have insisted on due process and acknowledged ongoing legal matters instead of treating the Freeh findings as definitive. They stress the record on Paterno, the Board and other administrators is incomplete.

NCAA reaction and context
- The NCAA announced it would impose unspecified “corrective and punitive measures” on Penn State; details were to be disclosed by NCAA president Mark Emmert and executive-committee chair Ed Ray.
- The action follows Sandusky’s conviction on 45 counts involving 10 boys and the Freeh report’s conclusion that Joe Paterno and three administrators (Graham Spanier, Tim Curley, Gary Schultz) repeatedly concealed facts about the abuse.
- Emmert described the situation as unprecedented and systemic—more than a football scandal—and said the NCAA might use unusually harsh penalties (e.g., postseason and TV bans), noting that the traditional “death penalty” is limited by current rules.
- The Freeh report criticized Penn State’s decentralized, uneven compliance oversight and weak handling of Clery Act reporting. The NCAA wanted answers on institutional control and ethics compliance.
- Penn State President Rodney Erickson said the university was better positioned to respond to the NCAA after the report.

Two Steubenville, Ohio, high school football players, 17-year-old Trent Mays and 16-year-old Ma’Lik Richmond, were tried in juvenile court for raping a 16-year-old West Virginia girl after an alcohol-fueled party last August. Prosecutors say the girl, heavily intoxicated or incapacitated, was digitally penetrated first in a car and later in a basement; Mays also faced a charge for the illegal use of a minor in nudity-oriented material. If found delinquent, both could be detained in juvenile custody until age 21.

The accuser testified she remembers leaving the party around midnight, later waking up naked in a stranger’s basement with no memory of how she got there, missing personal items and a circulated photo and video that helped her piece events together. She described post-party texts from Mays pleading with her not to report the incident; one text acknowledged he took a naked photo and said it showed his semen, which he characterized as the result of a consensual act.

Several teenage witnesses who received immunity testified the defendants penetrated the girl with their fingers. Defense testimony sought to undermine the accuser’s credibility: two former friends testified she had a reputation for lying and heavy drinking, and an expert said she likely had a memory lapse from alcohol but not total loss of consciousness, implying possible consent. The case divided the community amid allegations that the town’s football culture shielded team members, while others argued the accuser, her supporters and media had exaggerated the incident. A judge ruled the defendants guilty in juvenile court.

Sergey Kislyak, Russia’s long-serving ambassador to Washington, has become a central figure in investigations into the Trump administration’s ties to Russia. A career diplomat fluent in English with decades of postings in the U.S., NATO and Moscow, Kislyak typically kept a low public profile while cultivating wide Washington contacts through embassy events, cultural outreach and regular meetings with officials and lawmakers.

His interactions with Trump associates have drawn intense scrutiny. Kislyak attended Trump’s April 2016 foreign policy speech and was later confirmed to have met with Michael Flynn and Jared Kushner at Trump Tower in December. Flynn resigned after misleading officials about his December contacts with Kislyak, and Attorney General Jeff Sessions recused himself from Justice Department inquiries after disclosing two 2016 meetings with the ambassador that he had not mentioned during his confirmation. Those revelations have prompted calls for further accountability and heightened interest in Kislyak’s role.

Observers describe Kislyak as intelligent, charming and a staunch defender of Kremlin policy—able to be personable yet unyielding in debate, especially on contentious issues like Ukraine. U.S. officials and some media reports have suggested he may have ties to Russian intelligence, an allegation Russian officials deny; experts are divided, with some noting it would be unsurprising for senior diplomats to have intelligence connections while others see him as a traditional envoy focused on diplomacy and arms-control issues.

Kislyak has publicly criticized U.S. policies toward Russia and lamented the low point in bilateral relations since the Cold War, yet he has also expressed hope for cooperation on shared challenges. Now at the center of the biggest Russia-related controversy in decades, his extensive Washington network and contacts with Trump insiders have made him a focal point of probes into whether and how Russia sought to influence the 2016 U.S. election and transition.

JetBlue is running a promotion for its “For Good Month” that will send 50 winners and their companions on a free three‑day volunteer trip dubbed “Destination Good” on Nov. 27. The airline will reveal the actual city only the morning winners depart from JFK; it says the mystery destination will be a city JetBlue already serves where the airline can make a visible impact. Activities will focus on JetBlue For Good’s pillars: youth & education, community and the environment, and volunteers will work alongside crew and nonprofit partners.

U.S. residents 18+ can enter through jetbluecheckinforgood.com by Oct. 26 by answering philanthropic questions (including a 150‑word essay) — winners will be notified by Nov. 20. Pop‑up check‑in kiosks will also appear in L.A. and NYC for on‑site entries.

Researchers studying invasive pythons in Florida’s Everglades have discovered that a small number of snakes carry mitochondrial DNA from the Indian rock python, indicating past crossbreeding with the established Burmese python population. USGS scientists analyzed tissue from 400 snakes captured across South Florida over a decade and found Indian-python genetic markers in at least 13 individuals. Because the markers were mitochondrial, they reflect maternal ancestry and likely result from hybridization that occurred before the snakes became established in Florida, perhaps via the pet trade or breeders.

Indian rock pythons tend to be smaller, faster and more adapted to drier, higher ground than the water-oriented Burmese python. Combining traits from both species could produce hybrids with broader habitat tolerance or faster range expansion — a phenomenon known as hybrid vigor — though researchers stress it does not automatically mean a new “super‑snake” has emerged. Behavioral effects and the overall impact on invasion dynamics remain uncertain and depend on which genes influence key traits.

The finding complicates already difficult control efforts: Burmese pythons have massively reduced native small-mammal populations and resisted numerous removal programs. The python population shows low genetic diversity consistent with a founder effect, but its large size still allows rapid adaptation. Scientists plan further work to assess how these genetic differences affect the snakes’ ecology and potential to expand their range, especially as climate change may open new areas for colonization.

Prince Andrew became the first senior royal to open a personal Twitter account, @TheDukeOfYork, debuting with the tweet "Welcome to my Twitter account - AY." The sign-off indicated tweets signed "AY" would be from him personally. His launch coincided with a visit to the Black Country University Technical College to introduce the Duke of York Award for Technical Education. The account drew mixed reactions: some followers offered friendly advice and support, while others posted critical or mocking messages referencing his friendship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and likening his sign-off to a comedy catchphrase. A royal spokesman said the duke embraces new technology, supports free speech, and aims to use Twitter to say what he is doing. Within two hours the account had over 3,000 followers, and he was following two golf clubs plus official royal accounts such as @BritishMonarchy and @ClarenceHouse.

Star Wars releases are scheduled annually for the next several years following The Force Awakens. Dates may change, but current plans outline five more films:

  - Director: Gareth Edwards. Writers: Gary Whitta, Chris Weitz.
