This long profile traces the life, career and struggles of violinist Rachel Barton Pine, centering on how a catastrophic 1995 Metra train accident reshaped a once-promising trajectory into a persistent fight to remain both an artist and a patient.

Early talent and rise
- Rachel Barton showed precocious musical talent from age 3, quickly advancing under notable teachers (Betty Haag, Almita and Roland Vamos) and performing demanding repertoire and concertos as a child.
- By her teens she won major international competitions (including the J.S. Bach International Competition, Szigeti, Kreisler, Paganini and a Queen Elisabeth bronze), made a praised 1994 recording, played with leading Chicago musicians and seemed poised for a top-tier international solo career.

The accident and its aftermath
- On Jan. 16, 1995, a commuter train dragged Barton when her shoulder strap snagged in automatic doors at Winnetka station. The injuries were horrific: her left leg was amputated above the knee; the right leg was badly crushed, losing toes and much tissue and bone; extensive reconstructive surgery followed.
- She endured dozens of operations, long hospitalizations, severe pain, narcotic withdrawal, PTSD and osteomyelitis (a chronic bone infection). Surgeons staged complex reconstructions using tissue and bone grafts; her medical bills mounted into the hundreds of thousands.
- The accident also caused intense psychological and family fallout: she severed ties with her father for years (they later reconciled), and for a time cut off contact with her mother and sisters. She struggled with body-image, intimacy, career setbacks and the public myth that the crash had somehow boosted her fame rather than devastating her prospects.

Legal and financial resolution
- Barton sued Metra and the Chicago & North Western, winning a jury verdict of roughly $29 million (plus punitive damages) before appeals and settlements. After legal fees, liens and expenses, she received about $15 million, which she uses as a safety net to cover ongoing, accident-related medical care.

Rebuilding life and career
- She gradually resumed performing, teaching and recording. Greg Pine, whom she met after the accident, became her husband and primary caregiver on tour; he helps her navigate inaccessible venues and carries her prized instruments when necessary.
- Physically and logistically limited, Barton nevertheless continues an intense schedule of concerts, teaching, outreach (her Rachel Elizabeth Barton Foundation donates instruments and supplies) and advocacy. She often performs sitting on a custom stool, and relies on wheelchairs and ongoing surgeries to manage pain and prevent complications.
- Despite continuing to display exceptional artistry—and receiving standing ovations and encores—she has not attained the international superstar bookings she might have expected pre-1995. She longs to play with top-tier orchestras and laments how much medical care and recovery time still intrude on her career and personal plans (including starting a family).

Legacy and present reality
- Barton remains one of the most accomplished violinists of her generation, admired for technical skill and expressive maturity. But her career has been irrevocably altered by the accident: years of recovery cost momentum and opportunities, while chronic medical management continues to shape her professional choices and personal life.
- Her story is one of resilience—a musician who rebuilt a life, continued to perform at a high level, and turned tragedy into sustained activism and teaching—yet it is also a study in ongoing loss, the limits of recovery, and the practical and emotional burdens of surviving a life-changing injury.

This document mixes two very different pieces: a short, provocative Twitter thread by rapper Azealia Banks about the 2016 presidential race, and a long Associated Press roundup of campaign developments in the final days before the Iowa caucuses.

Key points — Azealia Banks
- On Feb. 1, 2016 Banks tweeted that she planned to vote for Donald Trump.
- Her rationale was provocative and informal: she claimed Trump “has the balls to bust up big business,” said Hillary Clinton was too tied to corporate interests and Bernie Sanders lacked clout, and used coarse language to criticize other candidates and politics in general.
- Her comments elicited attention for their incendiary tone rather than policy detail.

Key points — AP campaign roundup (late January 2016, leading up to Iowa)
- The report compiles frequent updates from the presidential campaigns less than a week before the Iowa caucuses:
  - Donald Trump announced he would skip a Fox News debate amid a feud with the network (notably Megyn Kelly) and planned a simultaneous Des Moines event to benefit veterans; rivals criticized the decision and Ted Cruz challenged Trump to a one-on-one debate.
  - Two pro-Cruz super PACs offered $1.5 million to veterans’ charities if Trump agreed to a head-to-head debate before Iowa.
  - Trump defended his boycott, saying he had been treated unfairly and planned a veterans’ fundraiser near the debate site.
  - Republican rivals (including Chris Christie, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz) criticized the boycott and sought to redirect voters’ attention to campaign issues.
  - Bernie Sanders met with President Obama at the White House, played down negativity toward Hillary Clinton, and his campaign negotiated debate terms—willing to press for another New Hampshire debate if the DNC agreed to three more later.
  - Hillary Clinton sought an additional debate before New Hampshire and defended her campaign activities amid Sanders’ criticisms.
  - Campaign theatrics and outreach continued: Mike Huckabee released a parody video; John Kasich and others focused on Iowa and New Hampshire; endorsements and local alliances (e.g., Trump gaining Lt. Gov. Henry McMaster’s endorsement in South Carolina) were announced.
  - Miscellaneous items: an Iowa man was arrested for allegedly throwing tomatoes at Trump; light snow forecasts were not expected to hinder caucus turnout; Senate leaders made light and cautious public comments about the presidential field.

Overall tone and context
- The AP piece captures the chaotic, personality-driven nature of the 2016 campaign’s final stretch in Iowa—debate disputes, inter-candidate taunting, last-minute endorsements and events, and strategic maneuvering by both parties.
- The Banks tweets illustrate how celebrity commentary injected provocative, non-policy-driven voices into the broader public conversation about the election.

China plans to attempt the first-ever landing on the Moon’s far side (the “dark side”) before 2020, officials said. Zou Yongliao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ lunar exploration department told state TV the Chang’e 4 mission will study geological conditions there with the long-term goal of installing a radio telescope—an attractive site because Earth-based radio transmissions cannot reach the far side, giving it low radio interference. A successful landing will require relay communications via an orbiting spacecraft to pass signals between the far side lander and Earth. Chang’e 4 would follow China’s ongoing Chang’e program, which has launched orbiters, landed a probe with a rover in 2013, and plans a 2017 sample-return mission; China has also signaled interest in future crewed lunar missions.

Thirty-five years after William and Michelle Becker were found drowned near a Mattituck marina, New York conservation police are offering a $15,000 reward and re-opening public appeals for information about the couple’s 1981 deaths. The Beckers left a dinner party shortly before midnight on March 10, 1981; William, 43, a 15‑year DEC police veteran, was found the next morning tangled on a boat swim platform in his uniform with a head lump, and Michelle, 36, a local beautician and mother of three, was recovered about 20 hours later 40 feet away. Suffolk County police closed the case as an accident in 1983, saying William may have drowned trying to save his non‑swimming wife. Family members and some DEC investigators have long questioned that conclusion, citing odd details at the scene — a broken kitchen table on the boat, William’s clip‑on tie found on the floor — and the couple’s unlikelihood of visiting the cold, dark dock on foot. DEC Major Scott Florence and the department’s police union and fraternal group say the 35th anniversary is a chance to prompt witnesses to come forward; Homicide Squad detectives say they welcome any new information. The Beckers’ relatives, frustrated by what they view as a hurried initial inquiry, have pursued private investigators and hope the reward will encourage someone with answers to speak.

Study design and sampling
- The researchers conducted a randomized household survey in Puerto Rico, interviewing 3,299 households between January 17 and February 24, 2018. The target (~3,000 households) was set to detect a 50% increase in annual mortality (from a historic baseline of 8 per 1,000) with 80% power and α = 0.05.
- To achieve geographic representativeness, the island’s 900 administrative units (barrios) were assigned a remoteness index based on travel time to the nearest city of ≥50,000 people using population and road-network data. Barrios were grouped into eight remoteness categories (percentiles 1–8); 13 barrios were randomly chosen from each category. One additional barrio was sampled on each of the two inhabited offshore islands (Vieques and Culebra); largely uninhabited areas were excluded.
- Within each sampled barrio, 35 households were randomly selected using OpenStreetMap building layers. If a selected point was an abandoned or nonresidential structure, empty at the time of visit, or consent was refused, data collectors sampled a nearby visible house chosen at random. Empty homes were not revisited.

Survey instrument and procedures
- A single adult respondent per household completed a short (under 10-minute) hybrid census-style survey that collected information on all household members (including births, moves, deaths during 2017), demographic details, cause of death if after the hurricane, hurricane-related migration, neighborhood deaths, and monthly ordinal measures of access to electricity, water, and cellular service.
- Missing household members not known to be deceased were treated as alive. No personal identifiers were recorded; GPS coordinates were aggregated post-collection. No compensation was offered; consent was obtained; respondents were told there would be no direct benefit. Data collectors could provide information about health resources if requested.
- The study received a human-subjects research exemption from Harvard’s IRB.

Population weighting and estimation
- Survey weights were computed as the inverse probability of household selection (incorporating the sampling design) and were used with the most recent official 2016 population estimate to construct population-level estimates and excess-death estimates.

Statistical analysis and excess-death calculation
- Excess deaths were estimated by comparing the post-hurricane mortality rate (September 20–December 31, 2017) with the official mortality rate for the same period in 2016, since mortality showed stable seasonal trends 2010–2016.
- The researchers used unweighted crude rates for their principal post-hurricane mortality estimate because they found no remoteness-category clustering of deaths. The post-hurricane crude mortality rate (R_after) was calculated from observed deaths over the 102-day period; standard errors and 95% confidence intervals were computed assuming Poisson-distributed deaths and normal approximation for large rates.
- The household survey registered 38 deaths among respondents for the period studied; extrapolating to Puerto Rico’s population produced an estimate of 4,645 excess deaths (Sept 20–Dec 31, 2017). The 95% confidence interval was wide (approximately 800 to 8,500), and the authors rounded to “near 5,000” after accounting for certain assumptions.

Context, limitations, and findings highlighted
- The study notes major infrastructure disruption after Hurricane Maria—e.g., 83% of households lacked electricity for more than 100 days—and identifies interrupted or delayed medical care as a primary driver of sustained elevated mortality, estimating about one-third of post-hurricane deaths were due to healthcare interruptions.
- The household-survey methodology is an accepted approach for estimating disaster casualties but can underestimate deaths if whole households were destroyed or absent and therefore not sampled. The authors acknowledge this potential bias and suggest that their estimates are likely conservative and that larger surveys could narrow uncertainty.
- The findings contrast sharply with the official count of 64 direct deaths attributed to the storm and align with other independent excess-death analyses (e.g., media and academic studies), underscoring the broader public-health and policy implications of accurately estimating disaster mortality.

A row of newly built luxury houses on Water Street, Chesterton, Cambridge—marketed from about £1.25m each and built on the site of the former Penny Ferry pub—was daubed overnight with large Latin graffiti reading phrases such as “Locus in domos Loci Populum” (widely regarded as nonsensical Latin), plus slogans like “We [heart] our home” and currency symbols with “go away.” The stunt drew national attention partly because the message was in Latin and apparently mistranslated—many suspect the vandals used Google Translate to render “local homes for local people”—and partly because it highlighted local anger over unaffordable housing and perceived outsider investment. Cambridge’s average house price is around £475–500k (roughly 12–16 times local salaries), with a significant share of sales to overseas buyers, fueling resentment that new developments don’t serve the local community. Police are investigating the criminal damage; the developer HC Moss said it is removing the graffiti and reviewing security. Commentators (including classics academics) have noted the awkward Latin, the curious mix of political signals in the graffiti, and argued that the core issue is Cambridge’s housing crisis rather than the language used.

A gunman identified as 28-year-old Gene Evin Atkins was arrested after a deadly midday rampage and multi-hour hostage situation at a Trader Joe’s in Los Angeles’ Silver Lake on Saturday. Police say Atkins shot his grandmother seven times and wounded a woman at a South L.A. home, then fled in a car. Officers tracked the vehicle, exchanged gunfire during a chase, and the driver crashed into a pole outside the supermarket before running inside. During the chaos a 27-year-old Trader Joe’s employee, Melyda Corado, was shot and later died; it was not yet determined whether she was killed by police or the suspect. Atkins took roughly 40–50 people hostage; frightened customers and staff hid, climbed out windows or were evacuated as negotiators tried to resolve the standoff. After about three hours he handcuffed himself and surrendered, escorted out between hostages. Atkins was booked on suspicion of murder on $2 million bail. Atkins’ grandmother remained hospitalized in critical condition; another woman taken from the initial scene suffered a graze wound. Six other people (ages 12–81) were hospitalized in fair condition with non-gunshot injuries. Officials praised police, negotiators and first responders for preventing further loss of life.

Sen. Bernie Sanders used a Georgetown University speech to define and defend his “democratic socialism” as part of a long American reform tradition, casting himself as a successor to Franklin D. Roosevelt and invoking Martin Luther King Jr. He insisted his philosophy is not about government takeover of businesses or owning the means of production, but about guaranteeing economic rights—health care as a right, free college, jobs and a living wage, paid family leave, public financing of elections, and challenging economic inequality and political corruption. Sanders tied this agenda to FDR’s 1944 “second Bill of Rights,” arguing that economic security is essential to freedom, and urged building a political movement to confront a “ruling class” and restore an economy that works for all.

The speech, held amid response to the Paris attacks, also proposed a new, broader security organization involving NATO partners, Russia and some Arab League members. Sanders acknowledged some discomfort with the term “socialist” and sought to show his ideas fit within mainstream Democratic goals. His message resonated strongly with students and younger voters, while commentators noted he was trying to bridge pre–Cold War New Deal–era social democracy with contemporary liberal politics, reopening debates long muted by Cold War divisions.

The Metropolitan Opera’s 2014 staging of John Adams and Alice Goodman’s 1991 opera The Death of Klinghoffer provoked intense controversy, protests and heightened security. The work dramatizes the 1985 hijacking of the cruise ship Achille Lauro by members of the Palestinian Liberation Front and the murder of Leon Klinghoffer, a 69-year-old, wheelchair-bound American Jew. Opponents — including Jewish groups, some elected officials (former Gov. David Paterson, Reps. Carolyn Maloney and Peter King), former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, the Klinghoffer family, conservative religious organizations and smaller activist groups — accused the opera of glorifying or humanizing terrorists and being anti‑Semitic. Large demonstrations and a high-profile rally at Lincoln Center, attended by hundreds (including people in wheelchairs) and public figures, led to the Met canceling international HD cinema and radio broadcasts after pressure from the Anti-Defamation League and some donors; the New York run proceeded with heavy police presence and all bags checked.

Supporters of the production — including arts figures like Oskar Eustis, some critics, opera experts and the Met itself — argued the piece confronts the crime’s complexities, does not glorify terrorism, and portrays the Klinghoffers sympathetically. Defenders noted that the opera’s emotional center includes Marilyn Klinghoffer’s anguished final aria and that the work seeks to grapple with moral ambiguity rather than endorse violence. Critics countered that the libretto and staging create false moral equivalencies and present Palestinian suffering or rhetoric in ways that could be misused or felt as endorsement.

The opera’s fraught history dates to its 1991 premiere, which sparked protests and withdrawals by some co-commissioners; subsequent productions and controversies recurred over decades. Reactions have varied widely: some Jewish leaders condemned the work, others brokered compromises with the Met (e.g., dropping broadcasts), and some Reform Jewish leaders condemned it without calling for cancellation. The Met maintained that Klinghoffer is neither anti‑Semitic nor a glorification of terrorism and promoted the slogan “See it. Then decide.” The production ran in New York through Nov. 15, 2014, amid protests, counterprotests, disrupted performances and continued debate over artistic freedom versus the potential social impact of portraying real acts of terror.

After 53 days and an enormous multinational air-and-sea effort that logged more than 300 flights, 3,000+ flight hours and searched some 4.6 million sq. km of ocean with no confirmed finds, Australia, Malaysia and China announced a tougher, expanded next phase in the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370.

Key points:
- The next stage will broaden the search area into much deeper, previously unmapped ocean and will focus on detailed seabed mapping before intensive deep-water searches.
- Officials will audit and reanalyze all previously collected data—especially the satellite “ping” information and imagery—to ensure it was accurately interpreted when defining the search zone.
- New, highly specialized equipment will be sought from the private sector: deep-diving autonomous underwater vehicles (beyond the Bluefin-21’s ~4.5 km limit) and towed side-scan sonar capable of real-time mapping. Authorities say only a handful of suitable devices and vessels exist worldwide.
- The U.S. Navy’s Bluefin-21 will continue scanning the current area (it has covered ~400 sq. km so far; authorized for another month at about $40,000/day) while tenders are issued for deeper-capable hardware expected to enter the water within one to two months.
- Australia estimates the next phase will cost about $60 million; nations will consult on cost-sharing and expect significant private-sector involvement.
- A Canberra meeting of the three governments will convene experts to audit data, define resource needs, and invite other countries and research institutions to join the effort. Officials stressed they want to avoid long gaps in searching, learning from the lengthy Air France 447 recovery.

Despite confidence in the satellite-based analysis that led to the current search region, authorities acknowledge no wreckage has yet been located and say the coming phase will be more difficult, expensive and technically demanding.

AFP and Philippine media reported strong official backlash after Dan Brown’s new novel Inferno characterizes Manila as “the gates of hell,” describing six-hour traffic jams, severe pollution, massive poverty and a thriving child sex trade. Francis Tolentino, chairman of the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA), sent a public letter to Brown and his publishers demanding a correction, calling the depiction inaccurate and “diabolic.” Tolentino — who checked immigration records and said Brown has never visited the Philippines — defended Manila as a place of strong Catholic faith, compassion and hospitality, and disputed items such as the length of traffic jams. He noted past conflicts over Brown’s work, including Manila’s 2006 ban on screenings of The Da Vinci Code. Reactions among Filipinos were mixed: some agreed with Brown’s portrayal and urged reform, while others, including incoming local leaders, called for major rehabilitation of Manila’s infrastructure and services. The story comes amid official figures showing nearly 28 percent of Filipinos still live in poverty despite years of economic growth.

Summary:

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the most common form of cardiomyopathy, typically affecting adults aged 20–60. It begins most often in the left ventricle, where the heart muscle stretches, thins and the chamber enlarges; the disease can progress to involve the right ventricle and the atria. As the muscle dilates it loses contractile function, reducing the heart’s ability to pump blood and leading to heart failure. Typical heart-failure symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue and swelling of the ankles, legs, abdomen and neck veins. DCM can also cause valve problems, arrhythmias and intracardiac blood clots.

DCM has many names or subtypes depending on cause or context (alcoholic cardiomyopathy, congestive/idiopathic/familial dilated cardiomyopathy, ischemic cardiomyopathy, peripartum cardiomyopathy, primary cardiomyopathy, diabetic cardiomyopathy). Causes include coronary heart disease/heart attack, high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, viral infections (myocarditis), HIV, toxins (e.g., cobalt), certain drugs (cocaine, amphetamines) and some chemotherapy agents (doxorubicin, daunorubicin). Excess alcohol is a recognized cause; up to one-third of cases may be inherited, and in many cases the cause remains unknown.

The document also discusses alcohol-related fatty liver disease (ALD): heavy drinking can produce fat accumulation in liver cells, often initially asymptomatic but sometimes causing right-upper-abdominal discomfort and enlargement. ALD is preventable and usually reversible if alcohol use stops, but continued drinking can progress to alcoholic hepatitis (fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice) and ultimately alcoholic cirrhosis with complications such as portal hypertension, bleeding, confusion, enlarged spleen and liver failure. People who drink heavily are advised to seek confidential medical help.

Finally, the report covers the death of singer George Michael: a British coroner ruled his death natural, caused by “dilated cardiomyopathy with myocarditis and fatty liver.” He died at 53 on Dec. 25; an initial autopsy was inconclusive and toxicology tests delayed release of the body. The piece includes reactions from his former partner Kenny Goss, who described supporting Michael’s family, their longstanding relationship and philanthropic work, and his belief that Michael’s frail body “just gave up.”

Mantecore (often spelled Montecore in reports), the white tiger involved in the 2003 onstage incident that left entertainer Roy Horn partially paralyzed, died March 19 at age 17 after a short illness. Seventeen is at the low end of normal tiger lifespan, zoologists say. Mantecore was the tiger that bit Horn’s neck during the Oct. 3, 2003 show at The Mirage; Horn lost significant blood and subsequently suffered a stroke and brain swelling that ended his stage career. The tiger was quarantined for 10 days after the incident, then returned to The Mirage’s Secret Garden when no disease or abnormal behavior was found, and later split time between the attraction and Horn’s estate. Horn consistently maintained the animal did not “attack” him, saying Mantecore acted out of concern while he was having a medical emergency; Horn said he considered the tiger a brother and spent Horn’s final hours beside him. Siegfried & Roy announced the tiger’s death and noted his role in raising awareness for conservation.

Christopher Kennedy Lawford, an author, actor and addiction-recovery advocate born into the Kennedy political dynasty and Hollywood’s Lawford family, has died at 63. His cousin, former U.S. Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy, said Lawford suffered a fatal heart attack Tuesday in Vancouver, where he had been living with his girlfriend and working to open a recovery center. Local reports say he experienced a medical emergency at a yoga studio; an autopsy was planned.

The son of Patricia Kennedy (sister of John, Robert and Ted Kennedy) and actor Peter Lawford, Christopher drew early attention and later struggled with substance abuse beginning in his teens. He wrote candidly about addiction in several books, including the bestselling 2005 memoir Symptoms of Withdrawal and 2015’s What Addicts Know. He detailed years of heroin and opioid use, arrests, homelessness and eventual sobriety at age 30. After recovery he became a prominent advocate and mentor for others, including Patrick Kennedy, and worked on addiction policy and public education.

Lawford also had a steady acting career with roles on General Hospital, All My Children, appearances on series such as Frasier and The O.C., a small part in Terminator 3, and work as a correspondent. He earned a J.D. from Boston College Law School and was active politically and with organizations like the Special Olympics. He is survived by his sisters Sydney, Victoria and Robin, and his children David, Savannah and Matt.

Ariel Castro was arraigned in Cleveland on charges related to holding three women captive in his home for about a decade. He faces four counts of kidnapping and three counts of rape and was ordered held on $8 million bail. Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty said prosecutors will seek many additional charges — including repeated sexual violence, felonious assault, attempted murder and potentially aggravated murder under an Ohio law covering termination of pregnancies — after investigators say Castro repeatedly caused miscarriages and forced one captive, Amanda Berry, to deliver a daughter in captivity.

Victims Amanda Berry, Georgina “Gina” DeJesus and Michelle Knight (and Berry’s six-year-old daughter born in captivity) were rescued May 6. Reports and initial incident statements describe extreme abuse: the women were chained, confined, threatened, denied outdoor time, and repeatedly sexually assaulted. Knight told police she became pregnant at least five times and said Castro starved and beat her until she miscarried; she also said he forced her to assist in Berry’s delivery and threatened to kill the newborn if it did not survive. Investigators recovered over 200 items from Castro’s home, including writings—described as diary-like—detailing actions and alleged motives tied in part to his own history of abuse.

Castro has spoken with police, and DNA and other forensic tests are being expedited. Authorities are investigating whether anyone else was involved; two of Castro’s brothers were arrested then released when no link was found. The victims are receiving medical care and are with family; authorities say they need time and space to recover. Family reactions include Castro’s mother expressing sorrow and asking forgiveness, and his daughter saying she is disgusted and devastated by the revelations. Prosecutors describe the crimes as “beyond comprehension” and are pursuing extensive charges that could carry severe penalties.

When a jury acquitted Florida mother Casey Anthony of first-degree murder and manslaughter in the death of her 2‑year‑old daughter Caylee, public outrage followed—prompting calls for new laws. A central issue in the case was that Anthony never reported Caylee missing; the child was last seen June 16, 2008, but family members did not contact police until July 15. Anthony was convicted only on four misdemeanor counts of lying to investigators.

In response, Oklahoma mother Michelle Crowder launched a Change.org petition and Facebook page urging Congress to pass “Caylee’s Law,” which would make it a federal felony for a parent or guardian to fail to immediately report a child’s disappearance. The petition quickly drew large numbers of supporters, becoming one of the fastest‑growing campaigns on the site. A separate Facebook campaign has nearly two million people pledging to leave their porch lights on for Caylee.

A large RAND-led analysis of 67 studies, published in Pediatrics, found that serious vaccine complications are very rare and far outweighed by the benefits of immunization. The review updates prior assessments and reinforces that there is no credible evidence linking vaccines—especially the measles‑mumps‑rubella (MMR) shot—to autism or childhood leukemia. 

Key findings:
- Vaccines prevent vast numbers of illnesses, hospitalizations and deaths over lifetimes; the CDC estimates childhood immunizations given over the past two decades will avert hundreds of millions of illnesses, millions of hospitalizations and hundreds of thousands of deaths.
- Some vaccines are associated with uncommon adverse events:
  - MMR and some flu vaccines can trigger fever-related seizures in young children; these seizures are typically benign and leave no lasting harm.
  - Rotavirus vaccines (RotaTeq, Rotarix) are linked to a small increase in intussusception (about 1–5 additional cases per 100,000 doses). Experts note rotavirus infection itself can also cause intussusception and overall rates have declined since vaccine introduction.
  - Rare links were noted historically to conditions such as thrombocytopenic purpura, but serious outcomes remain extremely uncommon.
- The study stresses balancing these very small risks against the substantial protective benefits of vaccines.

Authors and public‑health experts say the report should reassure parents and help clinicians promote vaccination, though it may not change the views of strongly vaccine‑hesitant individuals. They also note that misinformation online contributes to vaccine doubts, and that physician endorsement remains crucial in persuading families.

The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) has raised the 30-year probability of a magnitude 8.0+ earthquake striking California to 7% (up from ~4.7%), primarily because modern models account for interconnected fault systems and the possibility of multi-fault ruptures. Large quakes that jump between faults release far more energy—an M8 would produce roughly 89 times the energy of the 1994 M6.7 Northridge quake—and while such “mega-quakes” are rare (now estimated about once every 500 years, versus 600 previously), smaller strong events are very likely: there is >99% chance of at least one M6.7+ in the next 30 years, a 93% chance of M7+, and a 48% chance of M7.5.

Key reasons for the revised forecast:
- Better mapping of faults (now ~300 included vs. 200 in 2007 and 16 in 1988).
- Recognition that faults are part of an interconnected system and earthquakes can jump from one fault to another (documented in several California events and major quakes elsewhere).
- Consideration of more than 250,000 fault-based earthquake scenarios in the new calculations.

Areas of greatest concern:
- Many high-risk faults lie under or near major urban areas, including Los Angeles.
- The southern San Andreas is singled out as most likely to host a large quake (19% chance of M6.7+ in the next 30 years for its southern section), since it has not ruptured in centuries and appears “locked and loaded.”

Implications:
- The forecast refines hazard estimates useful for designing critical infrastructure (hospitals, schools, bridges) but does not predict exact timing or location of earthquakes.
- Officials continue to urge residents to prepare for earthquakes; early-warning systems are being developed but need more funding to be deployed statewide.

The U.S. Navy is investigating whether a cyber intrusion contributed to the Aug. 21 collision of the guided-missile destroyer USS John S. McCain with a merchant tanker off Singapore. While investigators — including a cyber team from U.S. 10th Fleet (Fleet Cyber Command) dispatched to the ship — are collecting shipboard computer and network data to confirm or rule out cyber tampering, Navy leaders say there is currently no indication that a cyberattack caused either the McCain or the earlier June 17 USS Fitzgerald collision. The two accidents, which together killed 17 sailors, have prompted wider reviews of training, readiness and safety across the fleet, leadership changes in the 7th Fleet and an operational pause ordered by the Chief of Naval Operations.

Vice Adm. Jan Tighe and Vice Chief Adm. Bill Moran said cyber forensics will now be a routine element of mishap investigations, noting the Navy has invested in cyber defenses (about $1.5 billion from FY2014–2023) and needs the authorities and personnel to respond. Intelligence assessments have long warned that adversaries could potentially spoof or corrupt a ship’s systems (for example, navigation displays), which could contribute to collisions — a possibility the Navy must be prepared to “fight through.” The Navy is institutionalizing cyber checks in future accident probes to ensure such possibilities are neither overlooked nor casually dismissed.

Researchers from the University of Portsmouth analyzed Tor “hidden services” over six months and reported that a large share of traffic on those .onion sites goes to child sexual abuse content. Using 40 Tor relays (March–September) the team catalogued roughly 45–80k hidden services seen during the probe, crawled long‑lived sites to classify content, and measured visit counts. After excluding automated botnet polling, they found that about 75–83% of measured visits went to a small number of sites serving child‑abuse material, far more than visits to drug markets, whistleblower dropboxes, bitcoin services or other categories. Drug and contraband sites were the largest single category by number of sites but accounted for a much smaller share of measured visits.

The study also found that most hidden services are short‑lived (most disappear in days or weeks) and that a handful of sites account for the bulk of traffic. The researchers downloaded only HTML (no images) and warned they could not be certain that all measured hits were human visitors. Tor Project researchers and others cautioned several possible biases: law‑enforcement or monitoring crawlers, denial‑of‑service attacks, malware polling, and the study’s focus on long‑lived sites could all skew visit counts toward abuse sites. Tor’s leadership also noted hidden services make up only a small portion of total Tor traffic and stressed legitimate uses (e.g., secure whistleblowing, activist access).

The work raises questions about the prevalence and persistence of child‑abuse communities on Tor and about possible technical or policy responses (the presenter outlined a theoretical method to block access to particular hidden services), while also highlighting limits in measuring activity on anonymizing networks and the ensuing debate over interpretation and remedies.

A 10-year-old Houston girl, Britton Joniec, was rushed to Texas Children’s Hospital after swallowing a metal bushing (about the size of a nickel/quarter) from a fidget spinner she had put in her mouth to clean. Her mother, Kelly Rose Joniec, noticed Britton choking in the car; urgent care could not determine the object’s location and X‑rays at the hospital showed it lodged in her esophagus. Doctors removed the bushing endoscopically after emergency surgery; Britton recovered. The mother warned other parents that spinner bushings can pop out easily and pose a choking hazard for young children (particularly under age 8). The incident and her Facebook post drew widespread attention amid ongoing debates about fidget spinners’ safety and their bans in some schools.

On July 4, 2017 at Coney Island, Joey “Jaws” Chestnut won his 10th Nathan’s Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest, setting a new record by consuming 72 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes (up from 70 last year). Carmen Cincotti finished second with 62; Matt “The Megatoad” Stonie placed third with 48. Chestnut credited marathon-style training, gradually increasing intake before the contest.

In the women’s division, Miki Sudo won her fourth straight title, eating 41 hot dogs and buns; Michelle Lesco was second with 32 and record-holder Sonya Thomas finished third with 30 (Thomas’s record stands at 45).

The event drew thousands of spectators and TV coverage. During the men’s competition, police arrested five people who attempted to unfurl a banner in the crowd; PETA had been handing out free vegan hot dogs outside, but the arrested protesters were not linked to the group. Media noted the contest’s extreme numbers (Chestnut’s 72 dogs equate to roughly more than an average American’s yearly hot-dog consumption) and nutritional totals highlighted by commentators.

A new global study in Climatic Change warns that rising temperatures and more frequent heat waves will increasingly limit aircraft takeoff performance, forcing weight restrictions, delays or cancellations at many airports. Lead author Ethan Coffel and coauthor Radley Horton (Columbia University) modeled five common commercial jets at 19 major airports using 27 climate models and found that during the hottest part of the day 10–30% of fully loaded flights may need to offload fuel, cargo or passengers—or wait for cooler hours—to take off safely. 

Why: Warmer air is less dense, so wings produce less lift; combined with short runways or high-elevation airports, this can make some fully loaded planes unable to achieve safe liftoff. Heat-wave extremes matter more than mean warming: annual maximum daily temperatures at many airports are projected to rise 4–8°C (7–14°F) by 2080. If emissions continue unabated, some aircraft could require up to ~4% reductions in fuel/payload on the hottest days (about 12–13 seats on a 160-seat plane); with strong mitigation this falls to ~0.5%.

Impacts vary by aircraft and airport: short-runway sites like New York’s LaGuardia and constrained Reagan National, and very hot airports like Dubai, face the greatest risk; JFK, Heathrow and Charles de Gaulle are less affected. Economic effects include narrower airline profit margins and cascading delays across hubs. Possible adaptations include scheduling flights for cooler hours, redesigning aircraft (engines/wings), or extending runways—solutions that can be costly or impractical in dense urban airports. The study highlights an underexplored climate risk to aviation beyond emissions, joining other concerns like increased turbulence and sea-level threats to airports.

Trojan has launched a major advertising campaign for a new product, the Tri-Phoria, a vibrating "personal massager" (a vibrator) with three tips. To get broader TV placement, the company and ad agency used euphemistic language and pharmaceutical-style tropes—avoiding the word "vibrator" and implying sexual pleasure through lines about "screams of ecstasy" and other side effects—so some cable networks have approved the spot in daytime and evening slots. MTV, citing its younger audience, restricts the ad to 3:30–6 a.m., though other Viacom channels like Comedy Central and VH1 have been more permissive.

The campaign, produced by Sullivan Productions, is described by historian Rachel P. Maines as nearly explicit compared with early 20th-century "camouflaged" ads for similar devices; she notes there is still a thin layer of discretion. Trojan says it is spending millions—the largest vibrator ad push ever—and plans to seek broadcast-network approval and wider retail distribution (CVS, Walgreens, Wal‑Mart) in 2011. Company-funded research cited in the Journal of Sexual Medicine estimates the U.S. vibrator market at about $1 billion annually and finds substantial use: over half of women and nearly half of men have used vibrators, often with partners. The campaign has prompted debate over sexual content in advertising: some industry executives praise the subtle approach, while groups like the American Academy of Pediatrics have urged limiting suggestive sexual ads to late-night hours. Critics have also mocked the semantic dodge of calling a vibrator a "personal massager" to make it acceptable for broader audiences.

Sophia Chua-Rubenfeld, eldest daughter of Amy Chua (author of Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother), delivered the valedictory address at her high school graduation. Confirmed by an audience member, she was the class valedictorian and opened her speech with jokes gently poking fun at her mother, even quipping that she would read from her mom’s bestselling memoir. The school named one valedictorian for 2010–2011 (students selected the winner); the class president spoke as salutatorian. Earlier this year Sophia began a personal blog to address rumors about her family and chronicled her life; she applied to Harvard, Yale, and UVA and hinted on the blog she chose Harvard. The item also recalls Amy Chua’s controversial profile: a Yale law professor who faced heavy criticism after excerpts of her memoir—intended as satirical and self-deprecating—described strict parenting rules (no sleepovers, no play dates, only As).

Jack McCullough, 76, was ordered released and granted a new trial Friday after an Illinois judge threw out his 2012 conviction for the 1957 abduction and murder of 7‑year‑old Maria Ridulph. DeKalb County State’s Attorney Richard Schmack conducted a six‑month review of roughly 4,500 pages of records and concluded there was “clear and convincing evidence” that McCullough was wrongfully convicted. Schmack’s review found newly discovered materials — including AT&T phone records showing a collect call placed from a Rockford pay phone to McCullough’s home at 6:57 p.m. on Dec. 3, 1957, and other documents about his attempt to enlist in the U.S. Air Force that had been excluded at trial — that corroborate McCullough’s long‑asserted alibi that he was about 40 miles away when Maria was taken.

McCullough, who had served a life sentence, smiled and embraced family after the ruling. Opponents of the decision, including Maria’s brother and other family members, remain convinced of his guilt and have sought a special prosecutor to try to keep him jailed. The original case featured disputed timelines, eyewitness identification decades later from a six‑photo array, and no physical evidence tying McCullough to the crime. The girl disappeared while playing in the snow in Sycamore, Illinois; her body was found 144 days later about 100 miles away. McCullough’s conviction had been upheld on appeal before his jailhouse motion prompted the reexamination that led to his release.

A raft of unverified reports claimed a major explosion at Iran’s underground Fordow uranium enrichment site last Monday, but Iranian officials and independent sources have denied it and no confirmation has emerged.

Key claims and sources:
- Right-wing site WND and a defector (Hamidreza Zakeri, formerly of Iran’s intelligence ministry) reported a blast at about 11:30 a.m. that partially destroyed the facility, trapped roughly 240 people underground and caused wide disruption. WND described Fordow as housing ~2,700 centrifuges enriching to ~20% and said the explosion would be the most significant strike on Iran’s nuclear program if true.
- Some Israeli figures, including Home Front Minister Avi Dichter, publicly welcomed reports of an explosion (saying damage to assets is “welcome”), though Israel’s foreign ministry and other Israeli officials privately said they had no reliable intelligence confirming an incident.
- Experts noted possible motives for disinformation: Shlomo Aronson suggested Tehran might have leaked false reports to block inspectors, while others said sabotage or covert action against Iran’s program would benefit Israel.

Official denials and international reaction:
- Iran’s deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization, Saeed Shamseddin Bar Broudi (IRNA), and military commander Massoud Jazayeri denied any explosion, calling the reports Western propaganda intended to influence nuclear negotiations.
- Reuters and diplomats in Vienna said they could not verify the reports; the IAEA had no immediate comment. Western diplomats generally expressed skepticism.
- Coverage referenced past sabotage and cyberattacks (e.g., Stuxnet) and assassinations of Iranian nuclear scientists, and reiterated international concerns about Fordow’s 20% enrichment level.

Context:
- Fordow is buried under a mountain and houses centrifuges enriching uranium to 20%—a level that raises proliferation concerns though still below weapons-grade.
- The timing of the reports—on the eve of an Israeli election and amid stalled talks with world powers—fueled speculation about motives and consequences.

Bottom line: Dramatic claims of a damaging explosion and trapped personnel at Fordow circulated in media and were met with some Israeli officials’ approval, but Iranian authorities and independent observers have denied or been unable to verify the incident; its veracity remains unproven.

South Korean officials believe North Korea is moving an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), a lawmaker told CNN after a briefing by the National Intelligence Service (NIS). Details about when, where or how it was being transported were unclear. The report comes after North Korea’s sixth and largest nuclear test Sunday, which seismologists and North Korean state media described as a thermonuclear (hydrogen) bomb—potentially capable of being mounted on a long-range missile—though weapons experts say pairing a warhead and missile can’t be verified without an actual nuclear-tipped launch.

The NIS also warned that North Korea may conduct another ICBM test at a lower-trajectoried angle toward the North Pacific, and has dug additional tunnels at its test site that could enable another detonation “anytime.” Analysts note Pyongyang often times major tests around significant national dates—Sept. 9 was flagged as a possibility.

In response, South Korea’s military held joint live-fire drills (Air Force, Army, Navy) off the peninsula’s east coast, with the Navy threatening swift destruction of any North Korean provocation at sea. Diplomatically, the U.S. said it will circulate a UN resolution to impose the strongest possible sanctions; U.S. Ambassador Nikki Haley condemned the test. South Korea’s President Moon Jae-in and U.S. President Donald Trump spoke and agreed to lift payload weight limits on South Korea’s ballistic missiles, though public tensions between the allies have surfaced—Moon favors dialogue with Pyongyang while Trump has dismissed talks.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, attending international summits, condemned the test but urged dialogue over sanctions alone, warning sanctions won’t change North Korea’s security-driven behavior.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un delivered a televised New Year’s address — his first formal broadcast in 19 years — calling 2013 a year for “creations and changes” and urging a “radical turnabout” to transform North Korea into an “economic giant” and raise living standards. He stressed economic development as the country’s most important task while also reaffirming that military strength remains a national priority.

Kim appealed for an end to confrontation with South Korea and urged both sides to respect and implement prior inter-Korean agreements, a message coming just after conservative Park Geun-hye’s election in Seoul. However, he attached conditions likely unacceptable to Park, including implementing past pacts negotiated with previous liberal South Korean administrations. Park has signaled willingness to resume limited humanitarian and small-scale economic exchanges but insists on North Korean steps on its nuclear program before major cooperation.

The speech avoided direct mention of the United States or North Korea’s nuclear arsenal, but came amid UN Security Council deliberations about how to respond to Pyongyang’s recent long-range rocket launches — which the US, Japan and South Korea view as prohibited missile tests. Kim framed the December satellite launch as a source of national pride and inspiration for economic effort. The address also reinforced Kim’s more public leadership style compared with his father and grandfather; state media also published joint newspaper editorials and showed Kim watching a musical performance with his wife.

Gasoline prices have finally begun their usual autumn slide after a delayed and unusually steep run-up this summer and early fall. The national average fell to $3.72 after 11 straight days of declines, down from a summer peak near $3.87, but remains a record high for this time of year and about $0.27 above last year’s level. August and September saw atypical increases (9% and 7%) because refinery and pipeline problems tightened supplies during peak travel season.

Regional variation is large: California has been hit hardest—averaging about $4.51 and briefly surpassing Hawaii as the most expensive state—because West Coast refinery issues kept prices elevated and slowed the seasonal decline there. Other regions, including parts of the Midwest and several battleground states, are already seeing prices drop into the low-$3 range; some Ohio stations reported prices under $3.

Industry analysts expect a faster fall in pump prices over the coming weeks as inventories rebuild and demand slows, with wholesale prices already plunging in key markets. Forecasts point to further drops of roughly $0.30–0.50 from October peaks, bringing national averages into the $3.30–$3.35 range by late November and potentially holding there into early 2013 unless new supply disruptions or geopolitical shocks arise. The decline could modestly boost consumer spending and have political implications ahead of the election.

On June 10 The New York Times briefly posted — then removed — a Michael Barbaro article profiling several women whose names surfaced in Anthony Weiner’s sexting scandal. The Times replaced the piece with a production note and later republished the story; meanwhile, portions of the original draft were reconstructed from Google caches and reported by BuzzFeed.

The reconstructed 1,342-word piece portrays the women as varied individuals (a blackjack dealer, a college student, a fitness instructor, a porn performer and others) who have been publicly shamed and whose lives were disrupted after their online exchanges with Weiner became known. The article emphasizes the lingering indignity they face now that Weiner is again running for mayor: renewed media attention, mocking co-workers and customers, damaged careers and interrupted education. Several women describe emotional and practical fallout — harassment, lost jobs, estrangement and ongoing distress — and some formed an online support network to commiserate.

Profiles highlighted include Lisa Weiss, a 42-year-old blackjack dealer who leaked messages to RadarOnline and says the exposure led to heavy drinking, public humiliation and sustained obsessing over the episode; Gennette Cordova, a college student who withdrew from classes and moved after being mistakenly branded a participant; and Traci Nobles, a Georgia fitness instructor who lost her job after messages were leaked and is writing a book about the experience. Porn performer Ginger Lee staged a press conference and, through her lawyer, urged Weiner not to run, saying renewed headlines retraumatize the women. Some of the women nonetheless expressed mixed or even supportive feelings about Weiner’s candidacy.

Weiner issued statements of apology, saying he was sorry for the upheaval his behavior caused and that he would not discuss private exchanges; on the campaign trail he mixes contrition with humor. The Times defended its editorial process when the story was reposted, saying editors decide when stories are ready for publication.

South Korea’s Unification Ministry reported that North Korea issued an air-raid warning in a radio broadcast early Thursday; Yonhap described it as likely part of an air-raid drill. The alert came amid heightened tensions as North conducts large-scale exercises coinciding with annual South Korea–U.S. drills, which the allies say are defensive.

Pyongyang also intensified its rhetoric, warning that U.S. bases in Guam and Japan are within its “striking range” after the U.S. flew B-52 bombers over South Korea as part of those exercises. The North framed the moves as responses to U.S. “nuclear blackmail,” threatened corresponding military actions, and had previously warned of “strong military counteraction” if B-52 sorties continued. While analysts and U.S. officials say North Korea cannot strike the U.S. mainland, its conventional weapons could reach U.S. bases in the region.

Tensions have risen since North Korea’s most recent underground nuclear test—the first under Kim Jong Un—which prompted tougher U.N. sanctions that further angered Pyongyang. Observers note the regime’s aggressive posture serves domestic regime consolidation and reflects a continued “military-first” strategy: nuclear tests, rocket launches, and military leadership reshuffles under Kim. Analysts urge new strategies to address a more openly nuclear-capable North. In response, the U.S. is bolstering defenses, including deploying additional ground-based missile interceptors on the West Coast.

A Pakistani court on Wednesday sentenced four men to death for the May killing of 25–30-year-old Farzana Parveen, a pregnant woman who was beaten to death with bricks and sticks outside Lahore High Court after marrying the man of her choice. The convicted—her father, a brother and two cousins—were found guilty of murder; another cousin received a 10-year sentence for abetting. Prosecutors said DNA and forensic evidence proved guilt; defense counsel called the verdict politically motivated and said they will appeal.

The attack, carried out in broad daylight amid a clash between about 20 members of Parveen’s family and 10–15 supporters of her husband, Muhammad Iqbal, drew global outrage because it resembled a brazen “honour killing.” Parveen had gone to Lahore to testify in a case her family brought, accusing Iqbal of abducting her; she maintained she married willingly. The case gained further attention when it emerged Iqbal had earlier killed his first wife to be with Parveen but was released under an Islamic legal provision after relatives reportedly forgave him.

Rights groups estimate thousands of honour killings in Pakistan in recent years; such murders are more common in rural areas but several high-profile cases have occurred in Lahore, prompting criticism of societal norms and of law enforcement responses. The convicted men retain the right to appeal.

Pakistan’s military ordered a cutback in U.S. military personnel and warned it would review military and intelligence cooperation after a unilateral U.S. commando raid in Abbottabad killed Osama bin Laden, a move Pakistan framed as a violation of its sovereignty. The army said U.S. forces in Pakistan should be reduced to “minimum essential” levels and cautioned that any repeat raid would jeopardize cooperation, though it did not provide details on the drawdown. Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) acknowledged “shortcomings” in developing intelligence about bin Laden’s presence, asserted it had provided initial information to the CIA, and charged that the CIA failed to share subsequent developments “contrary to the existing practice” between the agencies.

The revelation that bin Laden lived for years in a garrison town near Islamabad intensified accusations in Washington that elements of Pakistan’s security establishment may have sheltered him, while in Pakistan the raid provoked anger and humiliation and put pressure on the army and government. U.S. officials and lawmakers reacted with a mix of skepticism and caution: some urged a firmer response to Pakistan’s apparent failures, while others warned against severing ties. Administration officials considered how strongly to press Pakistan, noting they have leverage (including U.S. aid) but want to use it carefully to avoid unraveling counterterrorism cooperation.

Pakistan pledged an investigation into how bin Laden remained undetected, but observers noted past probes have been limited. Meanwhile, U.S. officials sought more information about the Abbottabad compound and who had access, even as Washington publicly softened criticism to preserve an essential, if strained, partnership against militants.

An English historian, Dr. Paul Booth of Keele University, has identified what may be the earliest known sexual use of the word "fuck" in English records. While studying Chester county court plea rolls from Edward II’s reign, he discovered a man recorded three times (December 8, 1310; May 25, 1311; and September 28, 1311) under the name "Roger Fuckebythenavele" (variants spelled across the entries), part of a process that ended in his outlawry. Booth believes the name was likely a nickname and suggests two plausible meanings: either a literal (and clumsy) sexual act reported by a jilted partner or an insult meaning “dimwit” describing an inept way of attempting intercourse.

If Booth’s reading is accepted, this record predates previously cited sexual uses — notably a circa-1475 poem line — and would be the earliest clear sexual sense of the word in surviving English documents. Earlier appearances (for example John le Fucker, 1278) have been interpreted as different words or spellings (like the Germanic-derived fulcher “soldier”). Linguist Jesse Sheidlower notes that "fuck" is Germanic in origin and related to similar terms in Dutch, German, and Swedish with sexual and other meanings.

Booth, who is Honorary Senior Research Fellow at Keele and co-director of the Gascon Rolls project, plans to publish his findings in Notes and Queries and has informed the Oxford English Dictionary. He argues the repeated, slightly varied entries make a clerk’s joke unlikely. The discovery adds to a range of colorful medieval nicknames and swear-related names recorded in legal and local records.

A North Carolina judge, Superior Court Judge Greg (Gregory) Weeks, ruled that Marcus Robinson’s death sentence was tainted by racial discrimination in jury selection and converted it to life without parole—the first decision under North Carolina’s 2009 Racial Justice Act. Weeks found that race played a “persistent, pervasive and distorting” role in prosecutors’ peremptory strikes and that prosecutors struck black jurors at more than twice the rate of white jurors statewide (about 2.6 times in Cumberland County), based largely on a Michigan State University law study of more than 7,400 potential capital jurors. Weeks concluded the most plausible explanation was intentional discrimination by prosecutors, undermining jury neutrality and the integrity of Robinson’s trial.

Robinson, a Black man convicted of the 1991 murder of 17-year-old Erik Tornblom, will move from death row to the general prison population to serve life without parole. The ruling is the first evidentiary victory under the Racial Justice Act and potentially affects more than 150 pending challenges from other North Carolina death-row inmates. Prosecutors intend to appeal, arguing the Michigan State study was unreliable and that nonracial reasons could explain juror strikes. The decision drew mixed reactions: Robinson’s family and civil-rights advocates praised it as landmark reform, while the victim’s family left the courtroom distressed. The Racial Justice Act—one of only two such state laws in the U.S. (the other in Kentucky)—has been politically contested, with the Republican-led legislature having attempted to repeal it.

Eight bodies — ranging from infant to adult and in various stages of decomposition — were removed Tuesday from Johnson Family Mortuary in east Fort Worth after the building’s landlord discovered the unattended remains and called police. The landlord had asked the mortuary’s renters, owned by twins Dondre and Derrick Johnson, to vacate about two weeks earlier; officers executed a search warrant around noon on suspicion of abuse of a corpse. The Tarrant County medical examiner is handling identification and next-of-kin notification; anyone with concerns is asked to call 817-920-5700, ext. 5.

Co-owner Dondre Johnson called the situation a misunderstanding, saying some bodies were embalmed and in caskets (one intended for shipment to Nairobi) and others were covered in garbage bags. He said the business remains legal and would continue serving families. The mortuary’s state license is current through the end of the month, but the Texas Funeral Service Commission has five open investigations involving the business. No arrests had been made as of Tuesday evening and the investigation was ongoing.

A powerful wintry storm moving across the eastern U.S. this week brought a mix of snow, freezing rain and ice from the Midwest to New England, causing widespread travel disruption, power outages and at least eight deaths.

Impact and casualties
- Weather-related crashes and icy conditions contributed to at least eight fatalities across multiple states (including Indiana, Ohio, Maryland, Mississippi and Arkansas); a Mississippi tour bus crash killed two and injured others.
- About 200,000 utility customers were without power Friday evening across four states; Pennsylvania reported roughly 105,000 outages, mostly in the west.
- Snow and ice totals varied regionally: parts of northern New England saw 4–8 inches, some Massachusetts towns over nine inches, while Boston had under 3 inches.

Transportation and commuting
- The storm snarled road and transit systems: hundreds of crashes in New Jersey (555 incidents), massive backups on the George Washington Bridge, stalled traffic on I-78 and motorists stranded overnight on the Major Deegan Expressway.
- Air travel was severely affected Thursday with more than 8,200 delays and 1,900 cancellations nationwide; Newark Liberty and other hubs experienced the worst disruption. By Friday evening delays and cancellations had fallen but remained significant.
- Mass transit and bus services suffered; drivers and buses were sidelined because of conditions and federally mandated rest rules, producing long lines and hours-long waits at Newark airport and Manhattan’s Port Authority Bus Terminal. Some students were stranded at schools overnight or sheltered until parents arrived.

Government and response
- Officials acknowledged being caught off guard in some areas. New York Mayor Bill de Blasio and New Jersey officials said the storm outpaced preparations and promised reviews. Road crews and transit agencies scrambled to treat roads and restore service.
- The National Weather Service said snow would taper in the Northeast by Saturday morning but warned of lingering gusty winds, coastal flooding and additional snow from another cold front through Sunday.

Schools and local effects
- Numerous school delays and closures across the Northeast and upstate New York; some districts sheltered students when buses could not run. Speeds were reduced on interstates in parts of New Hampshire and Maine.

Overall, the early-season storm produced dangerous winter conditions over a broad area, disrupting travel, knocking out power for many and prompting emergency responses as communities worked to clear roads and account for stranded residents.

UPS has successfully tested a roof‑launched octocopter delivery system that could extend drone use into routine residential and rural deliveries. In Lithia, FL, UPS and supplier Workhorse Group demonstrated the HorseFly drone integrated with a custom electric delivery van: the octocopter docks on the truck roof, lowers a caged payload through a hatch where a driver loads it, then launches on an autonomous, preset route. After delivering to a home on a blueberry farm about a quarter mile away, the drone returned and was retrieved by robotic arms; it recharges while docked to the vehicle.

Key specs and capabilities: the 9.5‑lb carbon‑fiber HorseFly uses proprietary lithium 18650 batteries, has about a 30‑minute flight time, top speed near 45 mph, and can carry packages up to 10 lb. UPS says the approach could cut driven miles and emissions, especially for sparsely spaced rural stops, and aims for a system that can work from many vehicle types.

Challenges remain: FAA rules currently restrict commercial drones from flying over uninvolved people and require pilots to keep drones within visual line of sight, constraints that could limit operational scope. The concept echoes other industry efforts (e.g., Mercedes/Matternet); Amazon has also been piloting residential drone delivery abroad.

The Hollywood Reporter published a detailed investigative piece alleging that the American Humane Association (AHA)—the nonprofit that monitors animal safety on film and TV sets and approves the “No Animals Were Harmed” credit—has repeatedly concealed animal injuries and deaths to protect relationships with studios and producers. Reporter Gary Baum cites incidents beyond the well-known Luck horse fatalities, including a dog punched on Eight Below, a chipmunk dropped on Failure to Launch, and dozens of sheep and goats that died connected to The Hobbit. Sources (many anonymous) and critics say AHA excused or minimized these events by calling them accidental or “off-camera,” prompting calls for government oversight.

AHA responded with a long rebuttal denying the characterization, stressing a 99.98% on-set safety record over 70+ years and explaining its jurisdiction applies only while animals are on set. The statement disputes several specific claims (saying some deaths were unrelated to production or occurred outside AHA’s responsibility), describes steps taken after past incidents (including inspections and recommendations), and outlines reforms: creation of a Scientific Advisory Committee, hiring a veterinary director, recruiting licensed veterinarians as Certified Safety Representatives in key regions, and a policy to commission independent investigations for serious on-set injuries or deaths. AHA framed its work as prevention-focused and defended the credibility and importance of the No Animals Were Harmed® program while acknowledging ongoing improvements.

Buckingham Palace announced that 95-year-old Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, will stop carrying out public engagements this fall. The palace said he has the full support of Queen Elizabeth II and will continue as head of many charities but will no longer attend events in an active, public role. No new health details were provided; Philip has had past heart problems but was seen appearing well recently, including at the official opening of the refurbished Warner Stand at Lord’s cricket ground. Earlier reports and staff meetings had provoked speculation and false reports about the couple’s health, but both were photographed and carried out duties shortly before the announcement.

This document contains two unrelated items:

1) A technical note about a Wikipedia outlinks crawl started in March 2016. Key points:
- The crawl collected outlinks from wikipedia.org and the resulting files are not publicly accessible at present.
- Duplicate detection was turned off so the collection would be complete, because sharing data that contains pointers into other collections is complex.
- For the first time the crawl covered all language wikis rather than only English; the seed list was built from all 865 collections.

2) A CNN news summary (about six years ago) on Jerome Corsi’s book and the “birther” controversy:
- Jerome Corsi’s book Where’s the Birth Certificate? debuted at number six on the New York Times Best Sellers list and claims President Obama is not a natural-born U.S. citizen.
- Corsi asserts no legal authority has verified Obama’s eligibility; he is also the author of The Obama Nation and Unfit for Command.
- The birther issue had resurfaced earlier when Donald Trump raised it while considering a presidential run; Obama later released his long-form Hawaiian birth certificate (born August 4, 1961).
- Polling after the release showed 17% of Americans still thought Obama was definitely or probably not born in the U.S., down from 25% in March.

This document collects reactions and backstage anecdotes from the SNL 40th anniversary special, centered on Eddie Murphy’s much-anticipated return and a decision not to mock Bill Cosby.

Key points:
- Norm Macdonald tweeted a behind-the-scenes story saying SNL writers planned a “Celebrity Jeopardy!” bit in which Eddie Murphy would do a perfect Bill Cosby impression. Murphy reportedly declined after an hour-long conversation with Macdonald, deciding the laugh would be too easy and he “will not kick a man when he’s down,” given Cosby’s ongoing sexual-assault accusations.
- Piers Morgan and Cosby himself publicly praised Murphy’s decision; Cosby said he appreciated and applauded Murphy’s action.
- Murphy’s on-air appearance at SNL40 was brief and widely panned. He spoke for less than a minute, did not perform a classic character revival, seemed tentative on stage, and at one point appeared to pause and consult producers before the show cut to commercial.
- Critics and viewers reacted negatively online, calling the cameo awkward and disappointing. NBC later posted an edited version of Murphy’s segment that removed the most awkward moments.
- The piece frames Murphy’s refusal as an ethical choice around punching down, while noting the broader context of Cosby’s fame and the serious allegations against him.

A 62-year-old man, identified as Régis Levasseur, died after being gored by a deer while participating in a hunt in the Compiègne forest about 85 km (53 miles) northeast of Paris. The incident occurred around 10:00 a.m. while he was acting as a beater; he was not carrying a rifle. Police said the stag charged and pierced him with its antlers, causing fatal internal bleeding before emergency services arrived. Local hunters’ federation president Guy Harlé said the attack was a rare reminder of the dangers of wild animals and noted Levasseur was an avid hunter who was due to be married. 

The killing came a week after public anger over another nearby incident in which hunters and hounds chased a stag into a private garden and the animal was shot at close range; that episode prompted protests, petitions and criticism from France’s environment minister. Commenters on social media linked the two events. Authorities say hunting accidents in France—often involving firearm mishandling or shooting without a confirmed target—are uncommon but do occur: 18 people died in hunting accidents last year and 351 since 2001, mostly participants in hunts.

On 22–23 May 2013, 25-year-old British soldier Drummer Lee Rigby was murdered in broad daylight in Woolwich, southeast London. Two men, later identified as Michael Adebolajo (28) and Michael Adebowale (22), attacked Rigby with knives and a cleaver; witnesses filmed one attacker shortly after the killing declaring the act was revenge for British actions against Muslims. Armed police arrived minutes after emergency calls and shot both suspects; they were arrested and hospitalized in stable, non-life-threatening condition. Additional arrests were made as police searched multiple addresses and continued a counterterrorism investigation into possible wider conspiracies.

The two suspects had previously been known to MI5 and had surfaced in past probes of Islamist extremism, prompting calls for a Commons inquiry and public scrutiny of security services. Government ministers and security experts stressed the difficulty of detecting when radical views turn into violent action; former police and intelligence officials urged a prompt review to establish whether mistakes were made. Footage obtained by media showed the suspects allegedly luring police to ambush them after the killing and then charging at officers; officers fired multiple rounds as the men approached.

The attack shocked the country, prompted extra police and military security in London, and sparked condemnation from political leaders and Muslim groups. Local memorials and prayers were held for Rigby, who had served overseas and was remembered by family as a devoted son, husband and father. Investigations into motive, possible networks and any failures of surveillance continued.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Turkey has shared audio recordings related to the October 2 killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi with Saudi Arabia, the United States, Germany, France and Britain, and that those countries have listened to the material. Turkish sources earlier reported an audio purportedly documenting the murder; Erdogan’s comments were the first public confirmation that such recordings exist. He said the killer is among a 15-member Saudi team that flew to Istanbul before the killing and urged Saudi cooperation, asserting those individuals know who ordered the hit and where Khashoggi’s remains are.

Turkish authorities reportedly found traces of acid at the Saudi consul-general’s residence and allege the body was chemically disposed of; Istanbul prosecutors say Khashoggi was strangled on entering the consulate and his body dismembered. Turkey has carried out investigations and sought extradition of suspects; Saudi Arabia has arrested 18 people and dismissed five officials but has offered shifting explanations for the death, calling it at various times an accidental fight, then a premeditated murder by rogue operatives. Erdogan said some Saudi officials have impeded the probe and possibly tampered with evidence, while Turkish and Saudi teams have conducted joint inspections. Erdogan also said he may seek a bilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in Paris. U.S. and other officials have been cautious publicly—U.S. officials have denied certain claims that they have heard the tapes—while European leaders have pressed Riyadh to clarify the case.
