A previous article incorrectly claimed this winter solstice would be the longest night ever because Earth's rotation is steadily slowing. The correction explains that while Earth’s rotation is slowing on very long (geologic) timescales due to tidal friction from the Moon, short-term year-to-year changes in rotation — driven by factors like polar ice melt and mass redistribution — can speed or slow rotation. Over the past ~40 years the rotation has slightly sped up, and during much of the 20th century it fluctuated, so the longest night in recorded history likely occurred around 1912. The author apologizes and credits readers who pointed out the error.

The remainder of the piece explains why the winter solstice is the longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere: Earth’s 23.5° axial tilt makes December 21/22 the day when the Northern Hemisphere receives the least sunlight, producing the shortest day and longest night (conversely, the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day). It also covers related facts:
- Tidal friction from the Moon gradually lengthens days over billions of years and causes the Moon to recede slowly.
- Sunrise/sunset positions on the solstice are at their southernmost points; higher latitudes see the sun lower in the sky and longer shadows.
- The earliest sunset and latest sunrise do not fall on the solstice because of the combination of Earth's axial tilt and elliptical orbit, which shifts solar time relative to clock time.
- The coldest days typically occur weeks after the solstice because the Northern Hemisphere continues to lose more heat than it gains for a time; oceans and snow cover contribute to this seasonal lag.

Summary:

Demand for bourbon has surged over the past decade while traditional producers failed to forecast that growth, creating shortages of especially older, limited-release bottlings. Bourbon’s defining flavors develop slowly through chemical transformations—aldehydes turning to acids and then esters—as young spirit interacts with charred American oak over years. Because each new barrel restarts that long clock, conventional solutions take a decade or more to remedy supply gaps.

In response, many smaller distillers and start-ups are experimenting with accelerated aging techniques to produce drinkable bourbon in months or even days. Strategies include using much smaller barrels to increase the alcohol-to-wood surface ratio, adding toasted oak chips or oak sticks, agitating barrels and exposing spirits to heat/cold cycles, forcing wood segments under pressure in steel tanks, and employing rapid-oxidation or filtration systems that speed chemical reactions. Some companies claim success turning 4–6 month-old whiskey into acceptable products in short order; others use accelerated lots as components blended with longer-aged stocks.

Experts are divided. Proponents note financial necessity and report pleasing vanilla-forward flavors from some rapid methods. Critics—many from established distilleries and whiskey science—argue accelerated products often taste “hot,” “raw,” thin or lacking the roundness and complex esters produced by true long-term maturation. Research into techniques like ultrasonic treatment is ongoing, but most large producers remain skeptical and continue to emphasize time in barrel as essential to premium bourbon quality.

Researchers at the March of Dimes Prematurity Research Center Ohio Collaborative studied 3,485 Nordic mother–infant pairs and used genetic analyses (including Mendelian randomization and parental haplotype methods) to investigate how maternal height relates to birth size and gestational length. Main findings:

- Maternal height correlates with birth length, birth weight, and gestational age: each 1 cm increase in maternal height was associated roughly with +0.05 cm birth length, +10 g birth weight, and +0.34–0.4 days gestational age.
- Birth length and birth weight are largely determined by fetal genetics (the genes the baby inherits), not by maternal height acting as an intrauterine environmental factor. Evidence: fetal genetic scores and transmitted parental alleles strongly predicted birth size, while maternal non-transmitted alleles did not.
- In contrast, maternal height appears to have a causal effect on gestational length and preterm birth risk. Analyses showed associations with maternal genetic scores even after accounting for fetal genotype, and maternal non-transmitted haplotype scores were linked to gestational age and modestly to preterm birth risk. Shorter mothers have a higher risk of preterm birth (estimated ~3% increased risk per 1 cm shorter height).
- The mechanism linking maternal height to gestational length is uncertain; it may involve maternal genetics, lifelong nutrition, or other environmental/physiological factors.
- Results are based on relatively homogeneous, high-resource northern European cohorts where nutrition likely allowed genetic potential to be realized; findings about fetal vs. maternal environmental influences might differ in low- or middle-income settings.
- The authors note the association with gestational age needs further replication, as some cohort-specific variation and modest significance were observed.

Context and significance: Preterm birth is the leading cause of newborn death in the U.S.; identifying genetic and maternal factors that influence gestational duration helps clarify causes of prematurity and may guide prevention. The work was published in PLoS Medicine and is part of broader March of Dimes-funded prematurity research.

Sonya (Sonya) Thomas narrowly defended her women's title at the Nathan's Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog Eating Contest in Coney Island, consuming 36.75 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes to edge Juliet Lee, who ate 36. That was well below Thomas’s 2012 record of 45. Thomas, nicknamed the “Black Widow,” said the contest is more mental than physical.

In the men's contest, Joey Chestnut won his seventh straight title, breaking his own record by eating 69 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes (his previous record was 68). Matt Stonie finished second with 51, and Tim Janus took third with 50. Chestnut’s performance extended his dominance after the era of Takeru Kobayashi, who no longer competes due to a contract dispute.

The weigh-in featured lighthearted moments, including New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg delivering pun-filled remarks. The long-running event (nearly a century old) went on despite local amusement-park closures nearby.

This document is a compilation of tabloid-style celebrity gossip items focused on the Kardashian/Jenner family and associated stars:

- Kanye West and Kim Kardashian: At the after-party for Kanye and Jay-Z’s LA concert, eyewitnesses described Kanye as very affectionate and constantly touching Kim, though observers say public kissing was prevented by the crowd. Separately, Amber Rose—Kanye’s ex—tells Star magazine that Kim helped cause her breakup with Kanye by allegedly contacting him (calling, texting, sending provocative photos) while Kim was dating Reggie Bush and Kanye was with Amber. The piece mixes firsthand quotes, insider anecdotes, and sensational claims typical of celebrity tabloids.

Hurricane Sandy, which struck the East Coast days before Halloween 2012, disrupted celebrations, commerce and public safety across the region.

Economic and retail effects
- Halloween was expected to generate about $8 billion nationally, but Sandy threatened last-minute spending. Most consumers had already finished shopping, so major national losses were limited, yet small, family-run businesses that rely on final-day sales faced significant hits (one costume shop estimated up to $50,000 in losses). Pumpkin patches, takeout and restaurant sales, and seasonal fundraisers were also canceled or postponed.

Event cancellations and rescheduling
- Large events saw reduced participation or postponement: New York’s Greenwich Village Halloween Parade planned to go on despite rain but expected far fewer participants and roughly half the usual economic benefit. Numerous community parades, fundraisers and pumpkin-patch activities across the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast were canceled or moved.
- New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie issued an executive order postponing Halloween statewide to Monday, Nov. 5, citing unsafe conditions (flooding, downed trees and power lines, road closures). Many towns in Gloucester County and elsewhere postponed trick-or-treating to safer dates or the coming weekend; some municipalities left decisions pending.

Public safety, power outages and recovery
- Sandy caused catastrophic damage: widespread flooding, subway and road inundation, fires (notably Breezy Point), sinkholes, destroyed boardwalks and homes, displaced residents, halted mass transit and left millions without power. Officials urged caution about downed power lines, debris and dark neighborhoods; some communities closed daytime school events and parades.
- Authorities and child-safety groups advised parents to prioritize safety—avoid flooded or powerless areas, watch for hazards, keep costumes short and visible—and offered alternatives such as indoor candy hunts, trunk-or-treat gatherings, or postponing festivities. Mental-health experts recommended parents reassure children and restore routines to reduce anxiety.

Human impact
- The storm caused at least dozens of fatalities, extensive property damage, and large-scale displacement. Images and reports showed severe flooding, stranded residents, submerged vehicles and damaged infrastructure. Recovery and cleanup efforts were underway while officials assessed the full scope of losses.

Overall, Sandy significantly curtailed Halloween activities in hard-hit areas, forced cancellations and postponements to protect public safety, and threatened economic losses for small seasonal businesses even as many consumers had already completed holiday shopping.

A 20-year-old Burbank man, identified as Richard Pananian, died Friday morning after his 2004 Ford Fiesta rolled over on the southbound 5 Freeway near the 134/Colorado Boulevard overpass by Griffith Park. According to the California Highway Patrol, a witness said Pananian was driving at high speed and passing vehicles on the right shoulder when he veered left and struck the rear of a 2004 Ford F-150 traveling in the No. 4 lane. The Fiesta then went out of control, overturned multiple times, and as it climbed an embankment Pananian—apparently not wearing a seat belt—was ejected about 20–30 feet and landed on the walkway of an overhead Colorado Street exit sign. He was pronounced dead at the scene; CHP said the exact cause of death was unclear given the force of the collision. The F-150 driver and his two passengers were uninjured. It was not yet known whether alcohol or drugs were factors. Firefighters used ladders to retrieve the body, which remained on the sign for hours while lanes were closed; all lanes reopened by about 11 a.m. Pananian reportedly worked for a Van Nuys auto sales company, which posted condolences on Facebook.

The original illustrated map of the Hundred Acre Wood by E.H. Shepard—the iconic endpapers/map that opens A.A. Milne’s Winnie‑the‑Pooh—is being offered at Sotheby’s in July. Described by Sotheby’s senior specialist Philip Errington as “probably the most famous map in English literature,” the 1926 ink sketch (also used in the 1966 Disney cartoon) is estimated at £100,000–£150,000 ($133,000–$200,000). Four other original Shepard illustrations, including scenes of Christopher Robin and Pooh saying goodbye, Eeyore, Rabbit and Pooh Sticks, will be sold alongside it; the group is expected to fetch £310,000–£440,000. The images have not been publicly seen for nearly 50 years. Shepard collaborated with Milne on the Pooh books of the 1920s—Winnie‑the‑Pooh, The House at Pooh Corner, and poems in When We Were Very Young and Now We Are Six.

A Vancouver police officer, Const. Peter Colenutt, jumped into the frigid Lost Lagoon in Stanley Park to rescue a large dog that had crashed through thin ice after chasing a ball. Responding to a call at about 4:30 p.m., officers found the exhausted dog struggling to stay afloat. Colenutt removed parts of his uniform, took one end of a rescue rope while colleagues held the other, reached the dog and brought it and himself back to shore cold but uninjured. Photos of the rescue circulated on Twitter and drew praise. Colenutt recently received the Vancouver Police Board’s Chief Constable’s Commendation for a June 2016 water rescue in which he and a colleague swam 100 metres to assist a distressed swimmer.

Cardinal Donald Wuerl, the archbishop of Washington, D.C., said he will soon travel to Rome to discuss with Pope Francis the resignation he submitted nearly three years ago at age 75. Wuerl’s decision follows intense criticism after a Pennsylvania grand jury report on clergy sexual abuse found that, during his prior tenure as Bishop of Pittsburgh (1988–2006), he had notified the Vatican about accused priests but in some cases reassigned them, allowed early retirements, or approved financial assistance rather than removing them from ministry. The two‑year probe documented at least 1,000 victims and about 300 abusive clergy over seven decades and prompted widespread calls for accountability of bishops who mishandled abuse cases.

In response to the backlash, Wuerl asked to have his name removed from a Pittsburgh high school; Cardinal Wuerl North Catholic High School has been renamed North Catholic High School. He also canceled a planned speech at the World Meeting of Families. Wuerl says his meeting with Francis is intended to help the archdiocese move forward, and he acknowledged the need for discernment in light of “new revelations” about clergy abuse and episcopal failures. The grand jury did not accuse Wuerl of committing abuse himself.

President Obama on Thursday announced executive actions to halt deportations for millions of undocumented immigrants, drawing immediate praise from Democrats and fierce condemnation from Republicans. Democrats hailed the move as bold and necessary to keep families together while stressing it is only a first step and not a substitute for comprehensive immigration reform, which they urged Congress to pass. Leaders including Nancy Pelosi, Rep. Luis Gutiérrez and others welcomed the relief but emphasized the need for a permanent legislative solution.

Republicans called the president’s actions an unconstitutional overreach and vowed forceful responses. Speaker John Boehner, Sen. Mitch McConnell and other GOP leaders warned the unilateral move would complicate future negotiations and could prompt lawsuits, funding cuts, challenges to nominees, or other measures next year. Conservative House and Senate Republicans—led by figures like Ted Cruz, Steve King and Jeff Sessions—pushed for hard-line options, with some even mentioning impeachment or blocking nominees, while more moderate Republicans counseled restraint to avoid political fallout with Hispanic voters.

The announcement produced strong grassroots reactions: immigrant-rights activists and families celebrated and expressed relief, but many noted the action will still leave millions without status and urged a permanent fix. Opponents and some law-enforcement officials criticized the move as unlawful or premature, and some Republican officials worried the party’s response could be politically damaging ahead of 2016. Overall, Obama framed the step as a response to congressional inaction and called on lawmakers to pass legislation that would make his executive measures unnecessary.

This piece reviews predictions from The Simpsons episode “Lisa’s Wedding” (1995), which imagined life in 2010, and assesses which forecasts came true, which didn’t, and where reality still lags. Highlights:

Accurate or partly accurate predictions
- Soy-based snack foods and vending-machine credit card use arrived as expected.
- Widespread home satellite dishes became common (though not universal).
- Thousands of cable channels and news-channel proliferation occurred, but quality news hours remain limited amid lots of shouting.
- Celebrities being frequently arrested became common enough to be joked about.
- The Rolling Stones remaining active into old age proved prescient.
- Car designs resembling the Prius appeared; motion-controlled video games (Wii/Kinect) and e-readers/tablet-like devices (Kindle/Newton) materialized.
- Classroom networking and some sponsored influence in education happened to a degree.
- Vending-machine soy snacks and the general trend away from cash were correctly anticipated.

Wrong or overoptimistic predictions
- Human cryogenic freezing and revival are not possible yet.
- Video phones and ubiquitous face-to-face video calling flopped; people often avoid direct connection.
- Robot servants and sophisticated household robots remain far from the depicted reality—the best we have resembles rudimentary toys.
- Wristwatch communicators didn’t revolutionize life (limited to niche/ancillary uses).
- Big events like World War III obviously did not occur; the show’s quips about British rescuers were tongue-in-cheek.
- Some redesigns (airlines, clocks) and other fantastical touches were exaggerated or didn’t play out.

Mixed or humorous observations
- Fox’s franchise branching into hard-edged news and controversies mirrored media consolidation tensions.
- Jim Carrey’s career was lampooned; the writer argues he produced only a few truly classic films.
- Classroom overcrowding and the persistence of repetitive TV programming were noted as contemporary realities.
- Certain cut or obscure scenes (motion-game bit) were discussed as early nods to later tech.

Overall, the article praises The Simpsons for many surprisingly accurate cultural and tech predictions while acknowledging numerous missed marks and satirical exaggerations. It sets up a companion piece to cover the worst predictions from the episode.

House Speaker John Boehner and top House Republicans criticized President Barack Obama’s renewed focus on the economy as a pretext for seeking higher taxes and additional stimulus spending while urging that Congress should instead pursue spending cuts. Boehner said Republicans will not raise the debt ceiling without “real cuts in spending,” reiterating a hard-line negotiating stance ahead of an expected fall showdown over the debt limit and government funding. GOP leaders pointed to House-passed measures—such as approving the Keystone pipeline, reducing regulations and delaying parts of the 2010 health law—as actions they say would aid growth but which the White House opposes.

The White House and Senate Democrats rejected trading a clean debt-limit increase for spending cuts. Jay Carney stressed the U.S. must not default, and Senate leaders, including Harry Reid and Chuck Schumer, warned against attaching conditions to the debt ceiling. Republicans, including Budget Committee chair Paul Ryan, say they are preparing spending-cut and entitlement-reform proposals to accompany any debt-limit deal and have contemplated tax-code changes to raise revenue while lowering rates.

Background context: the 2011 Budget Control Act and subsequent sequestration created automatic cuts that Republicans now want replaced by targeted reductions; Democrats prefer a mix of spending cuts and new revenue. Treasury maneuvers can delay a default into the fall, but negotiations over replacing sequester cuts and funding the government for fiscal 2014 (starting Oct. 1) raise the risk of another high-stakes conflict similar to 2011’s debt fight and 2013’s “fiscal cliff.” Economic indicators show modest improvement and rising tax receipts, but the political standoff makes resolution uncertain.

Pentagon investigators concluded that Undersecretary of Defense for Intelligence Michael Vickers disclosed restricted information to the makers of the film Zero Dark Thirty and referred the matter to the Justice Department. Officials say Vickers identified by name a U.S. Special Operations Command planner (a SEAL Team operator, though reportedly not from the raid team itself) during discussions with director Kathryn Bigelow and writer Mark Boal. Revealing the identities of special-operations personnel can be classified or sensitive because of personal security risks.

The Justice Department received the referral in September but has not pursued criminal charges so far. The Defense Department inspector general is continuing its probe to see if there were other leaks; its report remains open and has not yet been issued. Investigators found no evidence White House officials leaked classified material, though that conclusion was reached without interviewing the White House or then‑CIA director Leon Panetta. Pentagon spokespeople and some officials characterize the matter as unlikely to result in prosecution and say interactions with filmmakers were meant to provide unclassified background for a high‑profile story.

Congressman Peter King requested the inquiry over concerns that classified details about the raid or agency methods might have been disclosed. Documents obtained via FOIA by Judicial Watch include a July 2011 transcript in which Vickers offered to make a planner available and mentioned the planner’s name; Pentagon officials later deemed that transcript unclassified. Filmmakers say they did not request classified material and were unaware of receiving any.

The episode highlights broader tensions over classification boundaries, leaks and what information should be shared with media or the public. Critics worry about potential risks to individuals and operational methods; classification reform advocates note the system’s inconsistencies. The investigation and referral add controversy around the acclaimed film, which has also drawn criticism for its depiction of CIA interrogation practices.

Johnny “Thumper” Duckworth, a long‑time busboy at Randy’s Southside Diner in Orchard Mesa/Grand Junction, found an envelope containing an ATM slip and $3,000 in cash behind a booth on 12/15/2015. Despite his own struggles—riding a bike to work, living temporarily with friends and family, working about 25 hours a week, and having wages garnished for medical bills—he turned the money over to his boss, Randy Emmons. The diner took the envelope to the bank, which identified and contacted the owner, regular customer Darrell Cox. Cox later rewarded Duckworth with $300 and a thank‑you note. In response to Thumper’s honesty, a GoFundMe page was created and raised more than $3,800 to help him with transportation, debts, and getting back into stable housing. Colleagues and the community praised his integrity and work ethic.

Summary:

A massive manhunt in northern New York ended with mixed results. Richard W. Matt, one of two convicted killers who escaped Clinton Correctional Facility with David P. Sweat, was found and fatally shot by a tactical team on Friday after being discovered inside a burglarized hunting camp near Owls Head/Malone. Investigators say Matt appeared sick, unbathed, and heavily intoxicated; DNA from soiled underwear in an earlier-burglarized cabin linked him to that site. Officials say Matt did not fire his shotgun before he was shot; an autopsy was pending.

Searchers continued to pursue David Sweat across roughly 22 square miles of rugged Adirondack terrain. On Sunday, State Police Sergeant Jay Cook spotted Sweat near the Canadian border in Constable. After Sweat ran, the sergeant fired, striking him twice in the torso. Unarmed, Sweat was taken into custody wounded, treated at Alice Hyde Medical Center and transferred to Albany Medical Center in critical condition. No officers were injured.

Authorities emphasized the importance of keeping Sweat alive to learn how the two men planned and executed the escape and who may have aided them inside the prison. Investigators are still testing DNA evidence from other burglarized camps to determine Sweat’s recent movements; there have been no confirmed sightings of him since Matt was killed, supporting the possibility they separated earlier. State police say the intensive search will continue until Sweat is captured or evidence shows he’s no longer in the area. Local residents expressed relief at the capture.

Cargill Meat Solutions of Fort Morgan, Colorado, is recalling about 132,606 pounds of ground beef produced and packaged June 21, 2018, because it may be contaminated with Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O26. The recalled products—sold under multiple brands (Our Certified, Excel, Sterling Silver, Certified, Fire River Farms) in various package sizes and bearing establishment number “EST. 86R” and July 11 use-or-freeze dates—were distributed to retailers nationwide. FSIS, CDC and state partners linked the recalled ground beef to an outbreak that has sickened 17 people (illness onset July 5–25) and is associated with one death. Some product may still be frozen in consumers’ homes; consumers are urged not to eat the product and to discard it or return it to the place of purchase.

FSIS reminds consumers to cook ground beef to an internal temperature of 160°F, avoid cross-contamination, and seek immediate medical care for signs of severe infection (including symptoms of hemolytic uremic syndrome). Cargill said affected products have been removed from stores and that food safety teams are reviewing facilities. Media and consumer contacts and FSIS resources for questions and complaint reporting were provided.

In late October 2015, Yale lecturer and Silliman College associate master Erika Christakis sent an email criticizing a college advisory that urged students to avoid Halloween costumes likely to be seen as racially insensitive. Her message, which defended students’ freedom to wear provocative or offensive costumes as part of campus life, ignited protests and intensified long‑standing debates at Yale over race, cultural insensitivity and free speech. The controversy coincided with other campus incidents — including complaints about a fraternity and concerns over a residential hall named for pro‑slavery politician John C. Calhoun — that spurred hundreds of students and faculty to march and demand action to improve the university’s racial climate.

In the wake of the unrest, Yale President Peter Salovey announced initiatives to strengthen faculty expertise in race and ethnicity and initially kept Erika and her husband, Nicholas Christakis (Silliman’s master and a sociologist who runs a lab at Yale), in their college roles. Dozens of faculty later signed a letter defending the Christakises’ free‑speech rights, while many more faculty expressed solidarity with students’ concerns about racism. Facing the fraught campus environment, Erika Christakis decided not to teach her seminars next semester and resigned from her teaching duties to return to work with young children and families; Nicholas Christakis said he will take a spring 2016 sabbatical and not teach his popular lecture. Students and colleagues praised Erika’s teaching but some said the campus climate made civil dialogue and open inquiry difficult, and others lamented the loss of her courses on child development and education.

A Michigan woman, Elizabeth Rathburn, 56, pleaded guilty to wire fraud for her role in operating a cadaver business that sold and rented human remains to medical and dental customers while concealing that many specimens were infected with HIV or hepatitis B. Prosecutors say Elizabeth and her husband, Arthur Rathburn, ran International Biological, Inc., buying diseased specimens cheaply, misrepresenting them as disease-free, and profiting from rentals and sales to researchers and conference attendees. Under a plea deal she agreed to testify against Arthur, faces 4–10 months in prison, and must pay $55,225 restitution to the American Anesthesiology Association, which had rented infected remains in 2012.

Arthur Rathburn is separately indicted on multiple charges including wire fraud, transporting hazardous materials and making false statements; he pled not guilty and faces up to 20 years if convicted. The indictment accuses him of disturbing practices—dismembering cadavers with chainsaws, stacking heads, shipping severed heads in blood-filled coolers on commercial flights (once allegedly labeling the blood as mouthwash), and storing more than 1,000 body parts in a Detroit warehouse. The FBI raided that warehouse in 2013 and seized over a thousand body parts. Arthur, a former University of Michigan anatomy program coordinator, is free on bond awaiting trial.

- National polling in mid-September 2016 showed a very close presidential race. In several polls, Hillary Clinton held a small lead over Donald Trump in two-way match-ups among likely and registered voters, but the margin narrowed or disappeared when third-party candidates were included.
  - CBS/New York Times (likely voters): Clinton 46%, Trump 44% (two-way); tied at 42% each when Gary Johnson and Jill Stein were included. Among registered voters Clinton led 46–41 (two-way).
  - Quinnipiac (likely voters): Clinton 48%, Trump 43% (two-way); in a four-way test Clinton 41%, Trump 39%, Johnson 13%, Stein 4%.
  - Other outlets (e.g., CNN) showed tightening in key battlegrounds (Florida, Ohio) and some national polls even favored Trump, contributing to perceptions of momentum for Trump and alarm among Democrats.

- Voter commitment and enthusiasm
  - Most supporters of both candidates were set in their choice (roughly 92% of Trump voters, 94% of Clinton voters said their choice was set).
  - Enthusiasm favored Trump’s side: 45% of Trump supporters were “very enthusiastic” to vote vs. 36% of Clinton supporters. Overall, enthusiasm among Democrats had declined since August (very enthusiastic Democrats fell from 47% to 38%), while Republican enthusiasm remained steady.
  - Many supporters cited opposition to the other candidate as their main reason for their vote rather than strong positive support (about half of each camp; Quinnipiac found 66% of Trump backers and 54% of Clinton backers motivated mainly by dislike of the other).

- Demographics and coalition dynamics
  - A persistent gender gap: Clinton led by double digits among women; Trump led by a similar margin among men.
  - Racial and education divides continued: Trump strong with white voters overall and especially whites without a college degree (about 58–59% for Trump); Clinton led among non-white voters and among whites with college degrees.
  - Clinton led among voters under 30 (about 48%), but notably below Obama’s 2012 levels among young voters.

- Health and transparency concerns
  - Following Clinton’s public illness at a 9/11 event and her pneumonia diagnosis, more than four in ten voters said each candidate should release more medical records. Responses were partisan: a majority of Republicans wanted Clinton to release more; a majority of Democrats wanted Trump to release more. The CBS/NYT poll was conducted before either candidate’s subsequent medical releases.

- Polling methodology and context
  - The CBS/New York Times poll (Sept. 9–13) surveyed 1,753 adults (1,433 registered voters) by random-digit-dial landline and cell phone; likely voter modeling was used. Margin of error ≈ ±3 points.
  - Quinnipiac surveyed 960 likely voters Sept. 8–13; margin of error ±3.2 points.
  - Polls showed tightening momentum for Trump but statistical aggregates and forecast models (e.g., FiveThirtyEight, NYT Upshot) still favored Clinton, albeit with reduced probabilities compared to earlier in the campaign.

Overall takeaway: As the first debate approached and with about eight weeks until Election Day, the race had become highly competitive—Clinton retaining a modest national edge in many polls but facing weakened Democratic enthusiasm and gains by Trump in several surveys, making the outcome less certain than earlier expectations.

One year after the brutal December 2012 gang rape and death of a 23-year-old student in New Delhi — a case dubbed “Nirbhaya” that ignited nationwide outrage — India has seen high-profile protests, legal reforms and increased public debate about violence against women, but mixed views on whether deeper attitudes have changed.

What happened and the immediate impact
- The woman and a male friend were assaulted on a private bus by six men; she suffered catastrophic injuries and died 13 days later. The attack provoked massive daily street demonstrations, sustained media attention, and international condemnation.
- Four perpetrators were later sentenced to death; one died in custody and a juvenile received a three-year sentence in a reform home.

Legal and institutional responses
- Parliament enacted tougher laws: mandatory minimum sentences (up to 20 years) for rape, criminalization of stalking, voyeurism, sexual harassment, acid attacks and trafficking, and creation of fast-track courts for sexual assault cases.
- Police and courts have been under pressure to act faster; some high-profile cases were tried relatively quickly.

Changes in reporting and public attitudes
- Reported rape cases rose sharply, which officials and activists largely interpret as increased reporting rather than only more incidents: in Delhi, reported rapes rose from 706 in 2012 to 1,330 in the first nine months of the following year; sexual assault reports also increased.
- Observers differ on outcomes: many women and campaigners say the case empowered victims to speak out and that public support for survivors has grown. Others say they still feel unsafe, and that legal changes may have unintended social consequences (some politicians warned new laws could be misused or harm women's employment prospects).

Broader context and lingering problems
- Long-term trends show reported rapes rose more than 50% from 2001–2012 while conviction rates fell (from about 41% to 24%), highlighting systemic weaknesses in policing, prosecution and social attitudes.
- Experts cautioned against treating the issue as uniquely “Indian,” noting gender-based violence is global, but emphasized India’s patriarchal norms need cultural change as well as legal reform.
- Family members of the victim and activists argue that laws alone are insufficient; shifting social mindsets is essential for real progress.

In short: the Nirbhaya case sparked unprecedented outrage, legislative change and greater willingness among survivors to report assaults, but significant doubts remain about whether these developments have produced meaningful, lasting shifts in safety, justice or societal attitudes toward women.

This compilation collects opinion and reporting after President Obama announced he would not release gruesome post-mortem photos of Osama bin Laden. Key viewpoints and points:

- Obama’s rationale: releasing graphic images of a man shot in the head could become propaganda, incite violence, and endanger U.S. troops and interests. White House spokespeople and some lawmakers (e.g., Rep. Mike Rogers) echoed concerns about inflaming anti‑American sentiment or giving bin Laden’s followers a rallying icon.

- Arguments against release voiced here:
  - Practical and strategic: the photos aren’t necessary to prove bin Laden’s death (conspiracy theories will persist regardless), and the “message” to jihadis has already been sent by the kill itself and years of U.S. action.
  - Moral and symbolic: releasing the images would elevate bin Laden’s significance and feed a spectacle—better to reduce him to an afterthought and move on.
  - Operational risk: graphic images could endanger troops or be used for propaganda.

- Arguments for release discussed:
  - Transparency and public record: photos would be part of the historical and journalistic record and might reduce doubts about the operation.
  - Evidence and accountability: viewing the images could reassure skeptics and families that bin Laden was actually killed.
  - Retributive satisfaction / “trophy” value: some want to see definitive proof and revel in it—though the author questions whether that merit outweighs harms.

- Criticisms of the administration’s handling of the body and evidence:
  - Some commentators (including a legal columnist) argue the burial at sea and suppression of photos destroy forensic evidence, foster suspicion about the circumstances of bin Laden’s death (e.g., whether he was resisting or executed), and set a troubling precedent for withholding information. They assert that forensic protocols and broader disclosure should have been followed and that Congress and the press should have a role in obtaining the materials.

- Media and public reaction: there were conflicting reports about who had seen what photos (e.g., Senator Scott Brown), and at least some photos were later sold to news agencies by a Pakistani official. Slate columnists and others debated related issues like the human‑shield claim, the raid’s narrative, and broader implications for the war on terror and press freedom.

Overall theme: the debate balances national security and operational concerns against transparency, public record, and accountability—many commentators accept the desire not to inflame violence, while others see the decision as an unnecessary suppression of evidence that fuels doubt and weakens democratic oversight.

Martin Shkreli, the controversial former pharma CEO convicted on three counts of securities fraud, is facing a renewed legal fight over his conduct while free on $5 million bail. Federal prosecutors have moved to revoke his bail and have asked a judge to detain him, arguing his recent social-media behavior — notably a deleted Facebook post offering $5,000 to anyone who would “grab a hair” from Hillary Clinton during her book tour — amounts to threats and harassment and makes him a danger to the community. The Justice Department says the post required Secret Service resources, risks inspiring followers to act on his offers (pointing to prior instances where people responded to his incentives), and follows other harassing public statements toward women. Shkreli declined to speak with the Secret Service about the post and later called it “just a prank” on Facebook. His lawyers must respond to the government’s motion by Tuesday, with a hearing scheduled for Sept. 14. Shkreli, who drew public outrage years earlier for raising the price of the drug Daraprim, faces up to 20 years on the convictions though his defense plans to appeal and he is expected to receive a lesser sentence given no prior record.

U.S. District Judge Brian Jackson is poised to hear testimony about whether Louisiana is adequately protecting death-row inmates from dangerous heat and humidity at Louisiana State Penitentiary (Angola) after the state refused to install air conditioning.

Background
- Three inmates with medical problems filed a lawsuit three years ago; Jackson ruled over two years ago that conditions become unconstitutionally cruel and unusual when the heat index exceeds 88°F. Death-row heat frequently tops that level and sometimes exceeds 100°F.
- The state’s current remediation measures include one cold shower per day, ice chests in cells and fans outside cells. Prison and state attorneys say those measures suffice; the inmates’ lawyers disagree and want AC installed.

Costs and litigation
- Public records obtained by the Associated Press show Louisiana has spent at least $1,067,000 fighting the case, largely on private attorneys and expert witnesses. That figure does not include some internal or future costs and, according to the judge, could grow substantially.
- Plaintiffs’ attorneys received $490,000 via a settlement with the current attorney general. Defense private law firms billed more than $424,000, including a Baton Rouge firm whose partner had been campaign treasurer to a former attorney general.
- The state has not publicly released its full estimate to install AC. Plaintiffs’ experts estimate about $225,000 (excluding engineering and operating costs) to cool death row’s six tiers; a state-hired engineer previously said nine units could cool all eight tiers and the state suggested the total remediation could cost roughly $1 million. Judge Jackson noted the litigation costs already rival or exceed the likely cost of installation.

Legal posture and broader concerns
- The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals partially upheld Jackson’s ruling but limited relief to the three plaintiffs and invited the state to provide solutions short of full AC installation.
- State attorneys warn that installing AC could prompt nationwide litigation by other prisoners; critics say the state’s refusal appears ideological or political and is wasting taxpayer money.

The hearing will address whether the current measures are adequate as Louisiana’s sweltering summer approaches and whether further relief — potentially including air conditioning — is required for the plaintiffs.

Footage and photos from Grandview Aquarium (Grandview Mall Ocean World) in Guangzhou, China, show animals kept in stark, inappropriate conditions inside a shopping mall. The facility houses two polar‑brown bear hybrids, six young belugas, five walrus calves, Arctic wolves and other species in small, barren, dimly lit enclosures. Visitors frequently bang on glass and shout to get photos, and animals have been observed pacing, swimming in repetitive circles and otherwise showing signs of stress and zoochosis.

The situation drew international attention after Animals Asia released video and launched a petition calling for the aquarium’s closure; the petition has gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures and prompted widespread media coverage and viral posts on Chinese social media. Animals Asia and the China Cetacean Alliance have criticized the facility for limited space, poor husbandry and treating animals as attractions for profit, and have reached out to the operator, Haichang Holdings, without substantive public response.

Animals Asia’s director Dave Neale reports that public pressure has led Grandview management to engage with the charity and implement some immediate measures (for example, providing snow and beginning enrichment for the bears), but the aquarium remains open and likely will not be closed soon. Animals Asia says it will continue to pressure the operators, monitor conditions and push for larger, lasting welfare improvements while acknowledging the tactical choice to work with management rather than walk away. The aquarium did not respond to requests for comment.

The Department of Justice has told a federal court it no longer needs Apple’s help to unlock the iPhone used by San Bernardino shooter Syed Farook because investigators, with assistance from an outside party, have successfully accessed the device and extracted its data. The DOJ asked the judge to vacate a February order that had compelled Apple to create software to disable iOS’s retry/auto‑erase protections so the FBI could brute‑force the passcode.

The development ends this particular legal battle between Apple and the FBI, but not the larger national debate over encryption, privacy and law‑enforcement access. Apple reiterated that compelling a backdoor would have set a dangerous precedent and said the case should never have been brought. The DOJ said it will continue pursuing all options—cooperation from manufacturers, court process, and technical assistance from public and private sectors—to obtain digital evidence when needed.

Officials have not disclosed which third party or technique was used, whether the method works on other iPhones, or whether the government will share details with Apple. Reports have named mobile‑forensics firm Cellebrite, but neither it nor the FBI has confirmed that. Security experts say the breakthrough implies a vulnerability in that iOS generation that Apple will need to address, likely without full government help. The case also prompted renewed legal and policy discussions about the scope of the All Writs Act and the balance between encryption, privacy and public safety.

This collection of reviews criticizes the 2010 remake of Clash of the Titans as a hollow, formulaic blockbuster that sacrifices story, character and logic for loud spectacle and market-tested elements.

Major points:
- Script and storytelling: The screenplay is a muddled, checklist-driven reworking of myth and the 1981 film. Key plot points are present but poorly connected, character motivations are thin or contradictory, and much of the film consists of filler set pieces with little narrative rhythm. Perseus’s arc is especially weak—he spends most of the film ineffective and whining, only “manning up” late when his companions have largely died to force the emotional beat.
- Characters and performances: Sam Worthington’s Perseus is wooden and underwritten; supporting actors (notably Mads Mikkelsen and Ralph Fiennes) do more with less, while the gods are treated as shouty, underexplained figures. Female roles (the princess, Io) are muddled by unnecessary changes and underuse. Calibos is retained but pointless.
- Direction and action: Louis Leterrier’s action scenes are frenetic, poorly staged and often incoherent; the film relies heavily on CGI monsters and noisy set pieces that feel interchangeable and sometimes incomprehensible.
- 3-D and production choices: The film was converted to 3-D post-shooting with unimpressive results—few shots feel immersive, so the premium ticket price isn’t justified. The remake also borrows visual and tonal cues from recent hits (Avatar, 300, LOTR), making it feel derivative and market-driven rather than inspired.
- Themes and tone: Attempts to modernize myths (angry demigod, gods losing power as humans stop worshiping them) are inconsistently handled and often reduced to macho self-reliance clichés, deus ex machina rescues, and spectacle over substance.
- Overall reception: Reviewers call it a loud, uninvolving mess—big on CGI and noisy set pieces, small on coherence, character, and genuine drama. It’s entertaining in sporadic moments (some monsters and performances) but ultimately feels soul-dead, derivative, and not worth the 3-D premium or the hype. Grades range around mediocre/C; many viewers would be better off skipping it.

Stiles Zuschlag, a senior from Lebanon, Maine, says Tri-City Christian Academy (TCCA) in Somersworth, N.H., where he attended since kindergarten, told him in August he could no longer attend after revealing he is transgender. Zuschlag, who transitioned from female to male in 2015 and began taking testosterone in 2016, had been on track to be valedictorian with a 3.89 GPA and was active academically and in sports. He and his mother met with TCCA administrator Paul Edgar to confirm the school would accept his male identity; according to Zuschlag, Edgar said he was “going down the wrong path,” urged him to repent, stop hormone treatment, suggested Christian counseling or homeschooling, and barred him from campus. Edgar declined comment citing privacy.

After being told to leave, Zuschlag transferred to Noble High School in North Berwick, Maine, where he says he has been welcomed, asked his preferred pronouns and facilities, and even was nominated for “Prince of Homecoming.” He said he misses TCCA but is relieved to be accepted.

Officials noted TCCA does not receive federal funds through the N.H. Department of Education’s state office; a New Hampshire education attorney, Andru Volinsky, said religious schools may legally ask students to leave regardless of federal funding and called the situation “heart-breaking.” The case highlights differing policies between private religious schools and public schools: Noble and several local districts have transgender-inclusive policies intended to protect students, while some private schools’ approaches vary. Zuschlag said he wants dignity, respect and acceptance as he finishes his senior year and intends to continue excelling academically.

Mariner Energy has a documented record of at least a dozen offshore accidents or pollution incidents in Gulf of Mexico waters investigated by federal regulators; inspectors recorded possible violations in at least six events and the company was fined three times. Incidents from 2006–2009 include a leaking, corroded storage tank damaged by Hurricane Katrina (May 25, 2006); an 11-foot fall with the worker not wearing required fall protection (May 29, 2006) that led to a $30,000 penalty; a welding accident fire (Oct. 28, 2006); a flash fire and tank explosion during decommissioning that burned a worker and violated Mariner’s own safety procedures (June 23, 2007); a derrick-barge strike causing minor damage (Mar. 1, 2008); a blowout from hitting a shallow gas zone on a drilling rig that forced evacuation (May 6, 2008); a drilling-related eye injury tied to unsafe operations (May 26, 2008); a cleaning-operation fire caused by hydrocarbons migrating into a scrubber (June 2, 2008); a pollution leak from a valve on a Rowan rig (Dec. 3, 2008); a contract worker fall during Hurricane Ike repairs with no violations found (Feb. 27, 2009); a methanol tank explosion during welding that burned a worker and prompted four possible violations (June 15, 2009); and an injury during crane decommissioning where safe practices were not followed (June 22, 2009).

A separate, widely reported 2010 incident on Mariner’s shallow-water Vermilion 380-A production platform produced a large smoke plume, forced 13 workers into the water (none fatally injured), and drew intense political and regulatory scrutiny amid the Deepwater Horizon fallout. The fire—on a decades-old platform with a prior history of maintenance problems and hurricane damage—renewed calls from environmental and some lawmakers for tougher oversight and complicated industry efforts to persuade regulators to lift a deepwater drilling moratorium. Mariner was in the process of being acquired by Apache Corp. at the time; officials noted the platform mainly produced natural gas and that little oil appeared to have spilled in that event.

Jon Gosselin, the 39-year-old former Jon & Kate Plus 8 star and father of eight, will make a one-night appearance as a performer in Caesars Atlantic City’s Dusk Nightclub “Untamed Male Revue” on April 1 (his 40th birthday). Gosselin — who says he works at Dusk as a member of the Senate DJ group, helps with promotion and DJs occasionally — told Entertainment Tonight the gig makes him feel part of a “fraternity or brotherhood” and called his role “integral” to the show. Club owner Eric Millstein told PEOPLE the R-rated performance will feature choreography by a former Vegas showgirl and costumes, and compared the revue to Magic Mike–style numbers; he said the event is meant to be more polished than sleazy and that the club plans to feature other celebrities in future editions. TMZ first reported the story.

A Grand Rapids woman, college student Hannah Pewee, says she was asked to leave Woodland Mall on a 90°F day for wearing typical summer clothes — denim cutoff shorts and a tank top — after an anonymous shopper reportedly complained about her “inappropriate dress.” Pewee posted a photo and account on Facebook, saying she felt humiliated and blamed what she called “slut‑shaming.” Her post went viral, drawing hundreds of supportive comments and thousands of shares.

Woodland Mall’s written code of conduct requires “appropriate attire, including shirts and shoes” and bans clothing with offensive graphics, but does not specify short length; Pewee noted there was no public rule about shorts and argued any dress code should be made clear. The mall apologized to Pewee, told her it would revise its online clothing policy for clarity, and said it would retrain security on handling such situations. Pewee and others urged that retailers update their policies to reflect current styles and avoid disproportionately policing women’s summer clothing.

Aubri Degeffered, a 3-year-old who turned three two weeks earlier, was abducted Sunday evening after a carjacker forced the driver out of a red Volvo SUV in the 4900 block of W. Chambers St. in Milwaukee at about 6:50 p.m. The suspect reportedly used the same red 2013/2014 Volvo XC60 (Wisconsin plates 409-XBP) in an attempted strong-arm robbery at a Brookfield gas station on W. Bluemound Road near Janacek Road around 7:30–7:35 p.m. An Amber Alert was issued that night; shortly after 11:00 p.m. police announced Aubri had been found safe in Lake Mills, Jefferson County, and a 32-year-old suspect was in custody. The Volvo was recovered in Jefferson County. Authorities say the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office located the child after receiving citizen tips; Milwaukee and Brookfield police continue investigating and plan to present charges to the Milwaukee County DA.

Gavin Paul Zimmerman, a 19-year-old Mormon missionary from West Haven, Utah, has died after slipping from a cliff at Cape Solander in Kurnell, a popular whale‑watching site in southern Sydney. Zimmerman, who had been serving in the Sydney Mission since August, was with fellow missionaries when he fell—reports say he slipped from near the cliff edge and fell roughly 10–30 metres into the water. Police recovered a mobile phone with photos taken moments before the fall showing he had been very close to the rocks’ edge. Lifeguards and emergency services retrieved him from the water and performed CPR, but he could not be revived.

Zimmerman’s parents, Raymond and Jeanette, and church leaders described him as a bright, committed young man who loved his mission, enjoyed sharing his faith, and was a positive influence on others. Friends recalled he had been excited about his time in Australia and had planned to send photos home. This is the second fatality at Cape Solander in about six weeks; local officials and police urged visitors to heed warning signs, remain on the whale‑watching platform and avoid climbing onto the rocks, and said they would discuss possible additional safety measures.

New York Times reporter James Risen defended his Page One story revealing large Pentagon-backed estimates of Afghanistan’s mineral wealth amid sharp online criticism that the piece was neither new nor an orchestrated PR push to bolster U.S. policy. Risen’s article reported Pentagon and survey findings — drawing on Soviet-era charts, USGS aerial surveys (2006–2007) and new ground work led by a Pentagon business-development team under Paul Brinkley — that U.S. officials value untapped deposits of copper, iron, lithium, rare earths, gold and other resources at roughly $900 billion–$1 trillion. Risen said his reporting tied together scattered data and new field work that earlier accounts had not synthesized, and denied the story was a planted Pentagon leak; he said sources who pushed him to pursue the material included retired CIA officer Milt Bearden and Brinkley.

Bloggers and other reporters challenged the story’s novelty and timing — published amid bad news about the Karzai government and just before Gen. David Petraeus’s congressional testimony — suggesting it could be intended to shape public opinion. Risen responded angrily to critics, disparaging bloggers before apologizing for his tone.

The reporting also highlighted major caveats: it could take decades to develop industry and infrastructure, and rapid mineral development risks intensifying conflict, corruption, provincial-central government disputes, and environmental damage. U.S. officials have been preparing Afghan institutions and hiring advisers and auditors to manage bidding and attract foreign investors, while acknowledging complex political and security challenges that could shape how, or whether, Afghanistan’s mineral potential is realized.

President Trump spent the weekend at his Bedminster, New Jersey golf club reviewing profiles, rulings and judicial philosophies of roughly five finalists to replace retiring Justice Anthony Kennedy, but had not interviewed any candidates as of Saturday evening. He told reporters he’s narrowed the search to “about five” and may consider up to seven candidates, including two women, and plans to announce his pick on July 9. The likely short list centers on five federal appeals judges: Brett Kavanaugh, Amy Coney Barrett, Thomas Hardiman, Raymond Kethledge and Amul Thapar. Several of those — Hardiman and Thapar — were previously interviewed when Trump picked Neil Gorsuch; Kethledge was also considered then.

White House Counsel Don McGahn has been advising the president, and the FBI background checks remain underway. Trump has been briefing and consulting with senators from both parties, including a bipartisan meeting with swing-state senators and Judiciary Committee members to build support. Senate Republicans hold a 51-49 majority, meaning confirmation hinges largely on a few GOP moderates, notably Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, who have expressed support for abortion rights.

Trump said he will not ask nominees whether they would vote to overturn Roe v. Wade, though he has previously pledged to nominate judges opposed to abortion rights. His published list of potential nominees includes six women (among them Barrett and Britt Grant). Profiles in the article note each leading candidate’s background: Kavanaugh’s work for Ken Starr and his controversial record; Kethledge’s conservative rulings including an IRS/Tea Party case; Barrett and Thapar as Trump appellate appointees (Thapar would be the first Asian‑American justice); and Hardiman’s working‑class background and pro‑gun rights record. The confirmation fight is expected to be highly partisan but Republicans control the Senate timetable.

When she was 10 years old Zoe Lemon (now Zoe Averianov), from Hebden Bridge/Salford, threw a message in a plastic bottle into the North Sea as she left Hull on a ferry on 12 September 1990. Her childish note asked the finder to write, gave her name, age and hobbies and mentioned her pets. More than 20 years later — about 350 miles from where it was launched — a Dutch couple, Piet and Jacqueline Lateur, found the bottle while walking the dikes of the Oosterschelde near Serooskerke. They replied and posted the original note and their letter to Zoe’s parents’ address; she received it at Christmas and was surprised and moved to see her childhood handwriting. She has since been in touch with Piet by email and asked for photos of the discovery; he says he keeps her letter on his piano.

Former Florida Governor Jeb Bush told WHAS11 News he is “not running for President,” denying recent speculation about a 2012 bid that would extend the Bush family’s presidential legacy. He was in Louisville to speak at the National Conference of State Legislatures about Florida’s education reforms, particularly gains among Latino students, and to emphasize state-led solutions over federal control. Bush praised aspects of President Obama’s education efforts, introduced by NCSL President Don Balfour as a leader who reversed a “generation of decline.” In his remarks Bush stressed accountability—“All kids can learn. Period.”—and argued that when students don’t learn, the responsibility lies with adults and systems, not the children. (The document also includes a note about archiving web pages to prevent broken links.)

Three French construction workers face court after finding and stealing a hidden cache of gold while working at a house in Normandy. The men, aged 20, 33 and 40, discovered jars containing gold—reported as either six 1‑kg bars and 600 US $20 gold coins or, in another account, 16 bars and 600 coins—valued at roughly €900,000–€1.2m. Instead of informing the homeowner, they sold the items to a local coin dealer and began spending and investing the proceeds (cars, motorcycles, life insurance, home improvements). Tax authorities were alerted when one worker deposited large cheques; an investigation led to confessions, seizure of vehicles and hundreds of thousands of euros, and charges of theft. The coin collector was also charged with handling stolen goods, which he denies. The owners, who believe the stash may date from World War II, were surprised and distressed by the incident.

A new Science paper reports that up to about half of Earth’s water predates the Sun. Researchers measured the deuterium-to-hydrogen (D/H) ratio in terrestrial water and found it is higher than what would be expected if water had been produced solely in the Sun’s protoplanetary disk. High deuterium enrichment requires very cold conditions and specific energy inputs, consistent with water formation in the earlier molecular cloud that collapsed to form the Sun and its disk. Because at least some water survived the star-formation process and was incorporated into the solar system, the study implies that water may commonly accompany planet formation in other stellar systems. That increases the chances that many exoplanets form in wet environments capable of supporting liquid water — and potentially life.

Jack Yufe, who died Monday at 82 in San Diego after a battle with cancer, was one half of an extraordinary identical-twin story that became central to the landmark Minnesota Twin Study on nature versus nurture. Born in Port of Spain, Trinidad, in 1933, Jack and his twin brother Oskar Stohr were separated at six months after their parents split: Jack was raised Jewish in Trinidad (later moving to Israel and serving in the Israeli navy before settling in San Diego as a retail proprietor), while Oskar was taken to Germany by their mother, raised Catholic and became a member of the Hitler Youth.

The brothers first met at age 21 in 1954 in an awkward encounter that left them distant for decades. They reunited as part of the Minnesota study, and researchers—especially psychologist Nancy L. Segal—documented their remarkable similarities despite divergent upbringings: identical dress and mannerisms at their reunion, shared habits (for example, flushing toilets before and after use, loud sneezes in elevators), temperaments, routines and quirks. At the same time, deep differences persisted on politics, religion and views of WWII, producing a complex “love-hate” relationship marked by fierce rivalry and mutual fascination.

Their case drew wide attention because it underscored genetic influences on behavior even when environmental backgrounds were starkly different, prompting psychologists to rethink explanations for personality and habits. Oskar died of cancer in 1997; Jack is survived by his wife Ruth, son Kenneth, daughters Anita Yufe, Hovi Reader and Debvra Gregory, and stepsons Renee and Enrique Vega.

Bobbi Kristina Brown, the 22-year-old only child of Whitney Houston and Bobby Brown, died on July 26, 2015, after nearly six months in a coma. She was found unresponsive in a bathtub at her Roswell, Georgia, home on January 31 and was initially placed in a medically induced coma to treat brain swelling. In March she was moved to a long-term care facility near Atlanta; on June 24 her condition worsened and her family transferred her to Peachtree Christian Hospice, where she died surrounded by family.

The Houston family released a statement saying she is “finally at peace in the arms of God” and thanked supporters for their love. Many celebrities and friends posted condolences on social media. Bobby Brown was reported to be grieving but taking comfort in the belief that his daughter is reunited with her mother, Whitney Houston.

Authorities said an autopsy will be performed; the Fulton County medical examiner noted that the long interval between when she was found unresponsive and her death will complicate efforts to determine what led to her condition. A police report had described the January incident as a drowning.

Sureshbhai Patel, a 57-year-old recent immigrant from India who had arrived in Madison, Alabama to help care for his grandson, was severely injured on February 6 after a police encounter. A neighbor had called about a “suspicious” person walking in the neighborhood. Dashcam and audio recordings show Madison officers — field trainer Eric Parker and trainee Andrew Slaughter — encountering Patel on a sidewalk. Patel, who does not speak English, could not understand officers’ questions. The interaction escalated when officers turned him around and Parker forcibly yanked his arm and slammed him to the ground. Patel could not brace his fall and suffered catastrophic neck injuries requiring cervical fusion surgery the next day at Huntsville Hospital; he has been left partially paralyzed and faces a long recovery, only beginning to regain some feeling in his arms and one leg.

Madison Police Chief Larry Muncey publicly condemned the officer’s actions, recommended Parker’s termination, and announced that Parker turned himself in on a third-degree assault charge. The FBI opened a parallel civil rights inquiry. Patel’s family has retained attorney Hank Sherrod and filed a federal lawsuit alleging excessive force and unlawful stop/search. The local Indian community and the Indian consul attended a press conference and support efforts have included a GoFundMe to help cover medical bills. Community leaders and organizers have discussed cultural and communication training between local police and Indian groups in response.

Wesley Morris’s piece reviews two new films, 42 and Trance, and also includes a short personal remembrance of meeting Jackie Robinson that doubles as a brief, positive capsule review.

On 42
- Morris argues biopics of sanctified icons often fail because reverence strips away the person’s quirks and inner life; 42 suffers that fate. 
- Brian Helgeland’s film focuses tightly on Jackie Robinson’s 1947 rookie season with the Brooklyn Dodgers but treats Robinson more as a moral symbol than as a fully realized human being. The movie makes Robinson (Chadwick Boseman) a model of restraint — “medicine” for racist America — and places dramatic emphasis on how white characters and the organization change rather than on Robinson’s interiority. 
- Morris praises certain scenes (e.g., racial taunts by Phillies manager Ben Chapman) and Boseman’s athletic, controlled moments, and notes strong work by Nicole Beharie, but criticizes thin, saintly portrayals of Black characters (Wendell Smith reduced to a deferential ally) and reliance on white characters (Branch Rickey, played by Harrison Ford) for drama. Ford’s forceful Rickey, while entertaining, further sidelines Robinson. 
- The film reads more like an allegory or an inspirational commencement speech than a penetrating sports drama, limiting complexity and emotional realism.

On Trance
- Morris contrasts Danny Boyle’s irreverent inventiveness with Helgeland’s reverence, praising Boyle for imaginative risks. 
- Trance is a high-style, twist-filled noir about an art heist gone wrong: auctioneer Simon (James McAvoy) suffers head trauma and forgets where he hid a stolen Goya; ringleader Franck (Vincent Cassel) hires a hypnotist, Elizabeth (Rosario Dawson), to recover the memory. 
- Boyle, with writer John Hodge, delivers sleek, kinetic visuals and a disorienting narrative that repeatedly reroutes the plot, using hypnosis, sex, and layered deceptions. Anthony Dod Mantle’s camerawork and Jon Harris’s editing create a sensory, sometimes intoxicating experience that keeps the viewer uncertain about truth and motive. 
- Performances by McAvoy, Dawson, and Cassel hold the film together even as the plot grows morally and narratively slippery.

Personal note / capsule review
- Morris closes with a short memoir of encountering Jackie Robinson as a child and a brief, more favorable take on 42: while acknowledging the film’s formulaic, TV-movie elements and its tendency to view a Black man’s story through white eyes, he also affirms Jackie Robinson’s historic importance and Chadwick Boseman’s strong, dignified performance. He gives 42 a modest positive rating.

Nokia (through HMD Global) has launched the Nokia 8, its first modern flagship Android smartphone aimed at reclaiming some mainstream presence against Apple and Samsung. Priced at €599 and due on sale in early September in Europe and other markets (US availability unclear), the 5.3-inch QHD device sits in the mid‑to‑high tier of 2017 flagships.

Key hardware and design
- Aluminum unibody, 7.3–7.9 mm thin, conventional bezels (not the ultra-slim look of some rivals).  
- Snapdragon 835, 4 GB RAM, 64 GB storage.  
- 5.3-inch high-resolution LCD.  
- No mention of waterproofing or wireless charging.  
- Pure Android software with an always-on display mode implemented for LCD.

Camera, audio and unique features
- Dual rear cameras: two 13 MP sensors (one color, one monochrome) developed with Carl Zeiss optics; 13 MP front camera.  
- “Dual‑Sight” or “bothie” mode: simultaneous use of front and rear cameras to capture or livestream split-screen photos/video directly to Facebook/YouTube — marketed as a new evolution of the selfie.  
- Ozo spatial/360-degree audio borrowed from Nokia’s OZO camera, enabling immersive sound capture and playback for recordings and live streams.

Context and challenges
- HMD Global, founded by former Nokia executives, has been reviving the Nokia name after earlier low- and mid-range reboots (Nokia 3, 5, 6) and the 3310 remake.  
- Analysts see interesting features (bothie, 360 audio) but question whether they’re compelling enough to pull customers from entrenched leaders; success likely depends on aggressive pricing and marketing.  
- The Nokia 8 competes in a crowded launch window alongside new Samsung and Apple flagships and faces established challengers like OnePlus, Huawei and others.  

Bottom line: the Nokia 8 pairs solid flagship internals with distinctive camera and audio gimmicks (bothie and Ozo audio) and leans heavily on Nokia brand nostalgia. It’s competitive on specs but not groundbreaking in design or features compared with top rivals, so its market success will hinge on marketing, price positioning and consumer appetite for its camera-focused differentiators.
