Grace Rebecca Mann, a 20-year-old junior and prominent member of Feminists United at the University of Mary Washington (UMW), was found murdered in April; a former rugby club member and her roommate, Steven Vander Briel, has been charged with first-degree murder and abduction. Mann had been a vocal critic of a rugby-team chant that referenced rape and necrophilia; after speaking out she and other Feminists United members say they were targeted by a sustained wave of abusive, sexist and threatening anonymous posts on the Yik Yak app. The group reports more than 700 hostile “yaks,” some naming members and including explicit threats of sexual violence and death, which created serious fear and changed students’ behavior on campus.

Feminists United, backed by the Feminist Majority Foundation and attorneys Debra Katz and Lisa Banks, has filed a Title IX complaint with the U.S. Department of Education accusing the university of failing to adequately protect students from the online harassment. The complaint says campus officials repeatedly told students to report the posts to Yik Yak and declined requests to block the app on campus Wi-Fi citing First Amendment limits and the fact that mobile access would still work. Yik Yak says it has added filters, warnings, reporting and moderation and is working to improve protections; it also says it can provide certain device and location data to law enforcement on request. Feminists United’s lawyers say Yik Yak bears some responsibility and want authorities to investigate whether threats on the app were connected to Mann’s killing, though they acknowledge there is no evidence so far linking the harassment directly to the murder. The case has renewed scrutiny of Yik Yak’s anonymous, location-based format as a facilitator of harassment and threats on college campuses.

Weight Watchers is struggling as consumers shift toward digital calorie- and activity-tracking tools. In its latest quarter the company reported its eighth consecutive revenue decline, a 15% drop in active subscribers to 2.51 million, and a holiday-quarter loss. Management said its turnaround will take longer than expected after a weak start to 2015, prompting plans to cut an additional $100 million in costs and the departure of North America president Lesya Lysyj. The company forecast 2015 earnings well below analyst consensus and noted restructuring costs aren’t included in guidance.

The downturn reflects increasing competition from inexpensive apps and wearables that let users monitor calories and exercise without a Weight Watchers subscription. Industry data show rapid growth in fitness trackers—from about 19 million in use now to a projected ~57 million by 2018—and accelerating smartwatch adoption once products like the Apple Watch arrive. Analysts say many consumers prefer digital, lower-cost or free options and that Weight Watchers has been slow to innovate. The company has begun integrating activity trackers (Fitbit, Jawbone, its ActiveLink) and relaunched marketing and its magazine, but results so far have been disappointing.

Analysts see the best growth opportunity for Weight Watchers in corporate and health-plan partnerships, where its structured programs could complement employer wellness and insurance offerings better than standalone apps. Management says the brand and offering will change going forward as it pursues its turnaround.

Mexico announced a major security reinforcement for its violent northeastern border region, deploying more troops and federal police in a new “Coordinated Operation Northeast” to reassert state control over Tamaulipas and Nuevo León. The move targets an area that has become a battleground since the split between the Gulf cartel and its former enforcers, the Zetas, and follows the recent deaths and arrests of key cartel figures. Officials declined to give force numbers, but said the buildup aims to prevent cartels from regrouping.

The states affected include Monterrey’s industrial hub in Nuevo León, which has seen roadblocks, political assassinations, shootouts and grenade attacks, and Tamaulipas, which borders Texas and has experienced school closures, blocked roads, killed civic leaders, mass civilian displacements (including a drug-war refugee shelter in Ciudad Mier), and the massacre of 72 migrants earlier this year. Local media have been intimidated, forcing some municipalities to use social media to warn residents. Authorities noted recent successes such as the killing of Gulf leader Antonio “Tony Tormenta” Cárdenas Guillén and arrests linked to migrant killings, but similar federal operations elsewhere (e.g., Ciudad Juárez) have so far failed to stop widespread violence that has left about 28,000 dead since 2006. Public opinion is divided, with nearly half of Mexicans calling the drug war a failure.

Separately, federal police arrested Carlos Montemayor, the newly identified leader of a faction of the Beltrán Leyva cartel once headed by Edgar “La Barbie” Valdez Villarreal. Officials say Montemayor admitted that 20 men who disappeared in Acapulco in September were mistakenly seized and killed, underscoring continued internecine cartel violence in Guerrero and Morelos. Texas officials expressed approval of Mexico’s increased border patrol presence.

The document recaps highlights from the 74th Golden Globe Awards (Jan. 8, 2017), blending ceremony moments, winners and notable speeches with behind-the-scenes gags.

Key winners and awards:
- La La Land was the night's big winner, taking seven Golden Globes including Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy, Best Actor (Ryan Gosling), Best Actress (Emma Stone), Best Director and Best Screenplay — a record sweep for one film.
- Casey Affleck won Best Actor – Drama for Manchester by the Sea.
- Isabelle Huppert upset Natalie Portman to win Best Actress – Drama.
- The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story and Sarah Paulson won in the limited-series categories.
- Tracee Ellis Ross won Best Actress in a TV Comedy for Black-ish, the first Black actress to win that category since 1983.
- The Crown won Best Television Drama; Westworld, Stranger Things and This Is Us were among notable nominees.
- Viola Davis won for Fences, and Meryl Streep received the Cecil B. DeMille Award.

Memorable speeches and moments:
- Meryl Streep delivered a stirring, politically charged acceptance speech about the presidential election and press freedom when receiving the Cecil B. DeMille Award.
- Viola Davis introduced Streep with an emotional tribute, praising Streep’s influence on artists and calling her an inspiration.
- Jimmy Fallon, the host, opened with a starry musical number and a monologue that included many jokes about President-elect Donald Trump, Russia, and pop culture; he also struggled early on with Teleprompter issues.
- Fallon referenced Mariah Carey’s New Year’s Eve technical mishap and later joked about speaking with her after the incident.
- Hugh Laurie joked about the Globes and the incoming administration while accepting Best Supporting Actor for The Night Manager.

Comedy bits and presenters:
- Amy Schumer and Goldie Hawn previewed their film Snatched while presenting and did a running “glasses/teleprompter” schtick that drew mixed reactions.
- Kristen Wiig and Steve Carell presented Best Animated Film with a darkly comic routine about their earliest animated-movie memories.
- Other comic highlights included surprise-win riffs (Billy Bob Thornton), celebrity cameos (Brad Pitt introducing Moonlight), and nostalgic tributes to Carrie Fisher and Debbie Reynolds.

Critical takes and low points:
- Reviewers and recaps noted both high and low moments: Meryl Streep’s speech and several winning performances were praised, while some skits (Fallon’s Teleprompter jokes, some of Amy and Goldie’s bits) and abrupt play-off music were criticized.
- The ceremony also included a brief in-memoriam tribute to the year’s losses, notably Carrie Fisher and Debbie Reynolds.

Overall, the Globes combined awards recognition (notably La La Land’s sweep) with political commentary, emotional tributes, and a mix of well-received and uneven comedic bits.

A Columbia University physician and professor, Dr. Prabhjot Singh, was the victim of a violent, presumably hate-motivated street assault after dropping off his wife and one-year-old son. Around 20 young men on bikes reportedly approached him on 110th Street near Lenox Avenue, shouted anti-Muslim/anti-“Osama” slurs, and repeatedly beat him—punching his face until he fell and continuing to strike him as he lay on the sidewalk. Singh sustained a fractured jaw, lost or displaced teeth, and other injuries; he was treated at a hospital where the NYPD Hate Crimes Task Force interviewed him.

Friends describe Singh as a devoted community physician and public-health scholar who works to improve care for underserved communities through roles at Columbia’s School of International and Public Affairs, the Earth Institute, and Mount Sinai. The attack fits a broader pattern of violence against Sikh Americans—often linked to ignorance that conflates turbans and beards with terrorism—cited alongside recent assaults elsewhere in the U.S. The piece calls for solidarity among marginalized groups and communities to counter hate and prevent further attacks.

Two opinion pieces criticize current airport security as intrusive, ineffective “security theater” and call for a risk-based overhaul.

The first piece, by Charles Krauthammer, uses the viral incident of a passenger (John Tyner) refusing a TSA full-body pat-down to illustrate a broader public rebellion against humiliating airport procedures. Krauthammer argues most post‑9/11 screening rituals—shoe removal, long lines, intrusive scans and groin pat‑downs—are pointless, degrade personal dignity, and persist only because officials refuse to use targeted profiling. He contends the public will tolerate only so much inconvenience and that the full‑body scan or pat‑down crosses the line: “Don’t touch my junk” has become a populist refrain against excessive government intrusion.

The second piece, by Robert W. Poole Jr., documents TSA growth since 2001 into a large federal force that subjects travelers (including children and clergy) to invasive searches and privacy‑violating body scans, yet still misses threats—citing GAO and internal TSA tests where fake bombs were smuggled past screeners. Poole argues the TSA’s assumption that all passengers present equal risk leads to wasteful, overbroad measures (e.g., liquids bans, universal scans, or mandatory pat‑downs). He proposes replacing one‑size‑fits‑all screening with a three-tier, risk‑based system: low‑risk travelers (e.g., vetted crew and trusted‑traveler participants) get minimal screening via biometric IDs; high‑risk individuals (watch‑listed by DHS) receive intensive scrutiny; everyone else faces standard checkpoint screening (walk‑through metal detectors and 2‑D X‑rays) with randomized secondary checks. Poole stresses this evidence‑based profiling wouldn’t be racial or religious stereotyping but intelligence‑driven targeting.

Together the pieces argue that current TSA practices are intrusive, often ineffective, and politically unsustainable, and that security would be both more respectful and more effective if focused on intelligence‑driven, risk‑based screening rather than blanket measures applied to all passengers.

Singer Etta James, 72, is gravely ill with dementia, an organic brain syndrome, and is undergoing treatment for leukemia, court documents reveal. Her Beverly Hills physician states she cannot sign her name or manage feeding, dressing and hygiene, though she recognizes family members; she receives round‑the‑clock in‑home care in Woodcrest (near Riverside) and has been hospitalized occasionally. James has not performed since early 2010 after a severe infection led to sepsis.

The medical disclosures emerged in a Riverside County civil case in which her husband of 41 years, Artis Mills, is seeking control over just over $1 million held in three of her accounts. Mills says the funds would be used to keep James at home—fulfilling her stated wish not to be placed in an institutional nursing facility—and seeks authority to move or transfer the money into a joint or his sole control with her as beneficiary. Their son Donto James, who along with his brother Sametto and Donto’s wife Christy was granted power of attorney in February 2008, does not oppose releasing funds for care but asks that a third party oversee the money to prevent family conflict. Mills has contested the power of attorney and had briefly filed for divorce in 2008.

A hearing in the matter is scheduled for Friday. Background notes: James is a celebrated R&B/soul singer best known for "At Last" and other 1960s hits; she wrote an autobiography, continued recording and touring, underwent gastric bypass surgery in 2001, and was portrayed by Beyoncé in the 2008 film Cadillac Records.

Sky 1’s screening of The Simpsons episode “Fraudcast News” sparked a Twitter frenzy, with viewers noting the episode’s timing as a pointed coincidence amid Rupert Murdoch’s unfolding troubles. In the episode Lisa Simpson launches a newspaper and labels tycoon Mr. Burns “a hateful man nobody likes.” Burns retaliates by buying up every Springfield media outlet, prompting residents to start their own paper; Burns quips that controlling all the media is impossible “unless of course you’re Rupert Murdoch.” Viewers praised the episode online as a clever jab at Murdoch, while Sky insisted the broadcast timing was coincidental and unrelated to News Corp.’s bid for BSkyB.

The story connects to wider developments in the phone-hacking scandal: Rupert and James Murdoch were summoned to appear before the UK Parliament’s Culture, Media and Sport Committee (along with News International CEO Rebekah Brooks) amid public pressure, though the summons is not binding on the Murdochs as non-British citizens. News International said it would cooperate if formally requested.

Separately, reporting revealed that during the initial 2006 Scotland Yard inquiry into phone hacking, five senior police investigators discovered their own mobile messages had likely been targeted, raising concerns that fear of tabloid retaliation may have led to a limited investigation. Allegations about some officers’ private conduct later surfaced in the press. Former lead investigator Andy Hayman left the Met under scrutiny, and Assistant Commissioner John Yates—criticized for the force’s early handling of the case—has apologized for describing the initial inquiry as a “success.” MPs will question senior officers, including Hayman and Yates, about whether being hacking victims or conflicts of interest affected the scope of the early investigation; some lawmakers have accused Yates of lying and renewed calls for his resignation.

Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) is recalling about 1.4 million vehicles to address a software security vulnerability after researchers demonstrated a remote hack of a Jeep that could control critical systems while the vehicle was driving. Wired reported that hackers Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek developed code that exploited the vehicle’s 8.4-inch infotainment system to access dashboard functions and, reportedly, brakes, transmission and other systems from afar; they plan to publish part of the exploit and present their work at Black Hat.

FCA says it has applied over-the-air patches and network-level protections and will send owners USB devices with additional security upgrades. The recall affects a range of 2013–2015 models (Dodge Viper; Ram 1500/2500/3500 and chassis cabs; 2014–2015 Jeep Grand Cherokee and Cherokee; 2014–2015 Dodge Durango; 2015 Chrysler 200/300, Dodge Charger, and Dodge Challenger). The company states it is unaware of any injuries, complaints, warranty claims or accidents tied to software exploitation and is proceeding “out of an abundance of caution.”

Gap Inc. announced it will raise U.S. hourly wages for store employees to $9 in June 2014 and $10 in June 2015, a move that will affect about 65,000 workers across its brands (Old Navy, Banana Republic, Gap, Athleta, Piperlime). The company said most of its store, call center and distribution-center employees already earn above the current federal minimum ($7.25) and framed the raises as a business investment rather than a political decision. The announcement followed President Barack Obama’s executive order to raise the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $10.10 an hour starting Jan. 1, 2015; Obama praised Gap’s decision. Separately, Wal‑Mart said it remains “neutral” on the federal minimum-wage proposal, noting most of its hourly associates already earn above that level and that it is examining the proposal’s impact on its business.

On July 26, 2017, Salt Lake City police Detective Jeff Payne unlawfully handcuffed and arrested University Hospital nurse Alex Wubbels after she refused his demand to draw blood from an unconscious, burned crash victim—explaining hospital policy and law require a warrant, patient consent, or that the patient be under arrest. Body‑camera footage of the incident was released by Wubbels’ attorney and sparked national outrage, widespread social media backlash, a Change.org petition, and protests.

City officials—including Mayor Jackie Biskupski and Police Chief Mike Brown—apologized after viewing the video, called the conduct unacceptable, and announced policy and training changes. Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill requested a criminal investigation; the Unified Police Department agreed to investigate and an internal affairs probe was already underway. Detective Payne and a second officer were placed on administrative leave.

Reports indicate Payne claimed he was ordered by a supervisor to arrest Wubbels; that supervisor later learned the hospital routinely draws blood and investigators often obtain a warrant to access such results. Police updated their blood‑draw policy to require subject consent or a search warrant (removing “implied consent”) and noted draws are subject to search-and-seizure law. The department also committed to additional training and improved coordination with the hospital.

Hospital leaders and nursing organizations defended Wubbels, saying she followed hospital protocol and patient‑advocacy duties. Wubbels accepted the apologies and expressed hope that the incident would prompt positive change. Prosecutors will determine if criminal charges against officers are warranted after the investigation.

Example item from People.com: Jennifer Aniston and boyfriend Justin Theroux have moved in together; they’ve rented a house while continuing to search for a permanent home.

Firefighter Michael R. Davidson, 37, a 15‑year FDNY veteran assigned to Engine Company 69, died after being critically injured fighting a five‑alarm blaze that broke out late Thursday night in a five‑story Harlem building where a film set for Edward Norton’s Motherless Brooklyn was located. Davidson, who had been cited for bravery four times in his career, was operating the hoseline (nozzleman) when crews encountered rapidly deteriorating conditions in the basement, became separated from his unit, and was later found unconscious. He was transported to Harlem Hospital and succumbed to his injuries.

Two other firefighters suffered serious burns and are being treated at a burn center; three civilians had minor injuries. The fire was brought under control around 2:30 a.m.; the cause remains under investigation. Davidson is survived by his wife Eileen and four young children (three daughters, ages 7, 3 and 1, and a 6‑year‑old son). He is the 1,150th member of the FDNY to die in the line of duty. Funeral arrangements are pending; the city’s mayor, the fire commissioner and community members have expressed mourning and support for his family. Film producers said they alerted the FDNY and residents as soon as they noticed smoke and expressed sorrow for the loss.

During Game 3 of the World Series, Houston Astros first baseman Yuli Gurriel made a racially insensitive gesture and mouthed a derogatory Spanish term after hitting a second-inning home run off Dodgers pitcher Yu Darvish. Television replays showed Gurriel pulling at his eyes in a mockery of Asian features. Gurriel, a Cuban who played in Japan in 2014, apologized through an interpreter, saying he did not intend to offend, explained he sometimes uses the word "chinito" in Cuba, and claimed frustration from a history of poor results against Darvish. Darvish, who is of Japanese and Iranian descent, called the act “disrespectful” but urged learning and moving forward; he later tweeted a conciliatory message. MLB said the commissioner intended to speak with Gurriel and could discipline him. Astros manager A.J. Hinch described Gurriel as remorseful; some Dodgers and Astros players expressed disappointment. MLB’s handling of similar incidents this season suggests discipline is possible, though punishments during the World Series present logistical challenges.

Japanese authorities are investigating after the badly decomposed remains of eight people were found on a roughly 7 m (23 ft) wooden boat that washed ashore near Oga city in Akita prefecture. The vessel — missing a rotor blade and navigational devices — was discovered Sunday and inspected on Monday, when some occupants were found reduced to bones. Officials suspect the boat and its occupants may have come from North Korea. The find follows several similar incidents in the same region: two skeletal bodies were recovered over the weekend on Sado Island with North Korean-style cigarettes and life jackets bearing Korean lettering, and eight men who said they were North Korean fishermen landed alive days earlier in Yurihonjo city after their boat drifted into Japanese waters. 

Japan frequently sees “ghost ships” — often uncrewed or with dead crews — wash up from the Sea of Japan, historically on the western coast facing North Korea. Observers link the pattern to North Korea’s pressure on fishermen to meet large seafood quotas despite using aging, poorly equipped vessels that venture far out to sea and lack distress equipment. So far this year, 44 wooden boats believed to be from the Korean peninsula have washed up on or drifted off Japan’s coast (compared with 66 in all of 2016). Authorities are continuing efforts to identify the deceased and determine the boats’ origins.

Former Massachusetts governor and GOP presidential contender Mitt Romney was heckled during a Des Moines Register “soapbox” appearance at the Iowa State Fair two days before the Ames Straw Poll, and the exchange turned into a tense, widely noticed back-and-forth.

At the start of the Q&A, audience members challenged Romney on entitlement and tax policy—asking why he wouldn’t raise the Social Security payroll tax cap or promise not to cut Medicare benefits. Romney responded brusquely, insisting it was his turn to speak and telling dissenters they could vote for someone else if they disliked his answers. He also defended low corporate taxes and delivered a line that drew heavy attention and Democratic criticism: “Corporations are people, my friend... of course they are. Everything corporations earn ultimately goes to the people.”

Democrats, including DNC communications director Brad Woodhouse, seized on the comment as evidence Romney is out of touch. Romney spokesman Eric Fehrnstrom later defended the remark, saying corporations are formed by people who create jobs. The incident follows other awkward moments for Romney on the trail and came just before a Republican debate and the Ames Straw Poll; Romney said he would not actively campaign in the straw poll, preferring to focus on winning delegates.

President Donald Trump sharply criticized Sen. Dianne Feinstein after she released the transcript of an August Senate Judiciary Committee interview with Glenn Simpson, co-founder of Fusion GPS, the firm that commissioned the anti-Trump dossier. On Twitter he labeled her "Sneaky Dianne Feinstein," accused her of releasing the transcript “totally without authorization,” and urged a tough primary against her. Trump reiterated his long-standing claim that the Russia investigation is a "witch hunt," insisted there was no collusion, and said Republicans should "finally take control." Feinstein, as the panel's top Democrat whose staff helped conduct the Simpson interview, had the authority to make the transcript public.

Tennessee Republican Senator Bob Corker, retiring chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, launched public criticisms of President Donald Trump—calling him unstable, likening his presidency to a reality show, saying White House aides must constantly "contain" him, and warning Trump’s behavior could push the U.S. toward "World War III." Corker’s comments, amplified in a New York Times interview and TV appearances, provoked an immediate Twitter broadside from Trump—who attacked Corker’s record, mocked him as “Liddle’ Bob Corker,” accused him of lacking the courage to seek reelection, and suggested Corker had sought Trump’s endorsement. The exchange highlighted fraying ties between the White House and Senate Republicans and exemplified Trump’s preference for loyalty as the main standard.

Commentary in the piece questions Corker’s timing and motives, noting he only became publicly critical after announcing retirement and after earlier having praised or enabled Trump when politically useful. Critics argue Corker and other establishment Republicans share responsibility for enabling Trump’s rise by failing to oppose him in the primary and by pursuing elite-friendly policies that alienated voters. The spat also dovetailed with concerns about GOP prospects in 2018: Steve Bannon plans to back primary challengers to establishment senators, exacerbating intra-party conflict as Republicans seek legislative wins (notably tax cuts) to shore up slim Senate and vulnerable House majorities. Journalists and some commentators urge other Republican leaders to state whether they share Corker’s assessment of the president, framing it as a pivotal moment for congressional Republicans.

Researchers at the Universities of Exeter and Zurich report that chestnut-crowned babblers, a highly social Australian bird, use a simple form of combinatorial vocal communication previously thought unique to humans. Instead of singing continuous melodies, these babblers produce discrete call elements (labelled A and B) and create different meanings by rearranging those elements. Field observations and playback experiments showed an AB call signals flight/locomotion (birds look to the sky), while a BAB arrangement signals feeding/chick prompts (birds look to nests). When researchers recombined the same elements into novel sequences, babblers still responded appropriately, demonstrating they interpret meaning from element order rather than from wholly different sounds. The authors suggest rearranging existing sounds is a quicker route to new signals than evolving new calls, and argue this simple “phoneme-like” structuring may represent an early step toward the capacity for language seen in humans. The study appears in PLOS Biology.

GQ profiles the week’s most powerful person in Washington as Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, highlighting a sudden cultural and political resurgence symbolized by the viral “Texts From Hillary” meme. Created by two D.C. communications pros, Stacy Lambe and Adam Smith, the Tumblr repurposes a November photo of Clinton texting aboard a military plane into humorous two-panel captions that cast her as calm, commanding and stylish — a departure from earlier caricatures of her as overly calculating or dour.

The piece argues the meme’s popularity underscores a broader rebirth in Clinton’s public standing. Serving as Secretary of State, she has benefited from lower visibility on partisan fights and a return to a policy-oriented, apolitical posture that voters admire. Recent polling shows unusually high favorability, including among Republicans, and commentators note that her performance in office has burnished her reputation rather than diminished it. This renewed respect has reignited 2016 speculation, though Clinton has largely downplayed plans to re-enter electoral politics.

Analysts quoted (including Benjy Sarlin and others) emphasize that Clinton’s rebound reflects both the nature of the State Department role and public nostalgia for a steady, experienced leader amid polarized politics. They also note the caveat that a formal presidential bid would likely erode some cross-party goodwill once she resumed a partisan role. Overall, the meme and the reaction to it are portrayed as symptomatic of Clinton’s shifted image from political bruiser to competent, even admired, stateswoman.

Bruno Mars dominated the 60th Grammy Awards in New York, winning all six of his nominations including album of the year (24K Magic), record of the year (title track), and song of the year ("That's What I Like"). Kendrick Lamar won five awards—mainly in rap categories including best rap album—and opened the show with a powerful, politically charged performance, but like Jay-Z (eight nominations) did not win in the top general-field categories. Kesha delivered a standout, emotional performance of "Praying" backed by prominent women and the Resistance Revival Chorus amid mentions of Time's Up and #MeToo; Janelle Monáe introduced her. The ceremony included other notable performances and tributes: a Las Vegas massacre memorial with "Tears In Heaven"; Logic’s suicide-prevention performance of "1-800-273-8255" with Alessia Cara and Khalid; Lady Gaga, Sam Smith, Pink, Chris Stapleton (who won three country awards), Little Big Town, Sting, and Childish Gambino. The Rolling Stones won for best traditional blues album in the pre-telecast; Ed Sheeran won best pop vocal album. Comedy and lighter moments included host James Corden’s skit with Hillary Clinton, Cher and others, and Dave Chappelle winning best comedy album. Posthumous Grammys went to Carrie Fisher, Leonard Cohen and engineer Tom Coyne. The show featured widespread displays of support for Time’s Up/#MeToo and several socially conscious performances.

Officials have reopened the investigation into actress Natalie Wood’s 1981 drowning after new information surfaced, prompting Los Angeles County sheriff’s homicide detectives to take another look at the case. Although Wood’s death was originally ruled an accidental drowning, detectives were prompted to reopen the matter following a “third party” letter and comments by the Splendour’s captain that suggested new recollections. Sheriff Lee Baca said homicide detectives want to speak with the captain based on remarks he made recounting the case on its 30th anniversary.

Much of the recent attention stems from a 2008 book co-authored by Marti Rulli and former Splendour captain Dennis Davern, Goodbye Natalie, Goodbye Splendour, which alleges circumstances inconsistent with the original accounts. The book recounts that on Thanksgiving weekend 1981, Wood, her husband Robert Wagner and guest Christopher Walken drank aboard the yacht after dinner; an argument erupted between Wagner and Walken, and later Wagner and Wood were heard arguing in their cabin. Davern says he heard loud noises and later was told by Wagner that Wood was missing and the dinghy was gone; he also claims Wagner initially refused permission to call the Coast Guard. The book alleges Wood had been taking Quaaludes and that Wagner became violent; it raises doubts about earlier statements by witnesses.

Sheriff’s investigators have interviewed sources connected to the book, traveled to multiple locations to follow leads, and assigned full-time homicide detectives to the inquiry. Officials stress no one has been formally named a suspect and say the investigation is ongoing. Wagner and his representatives say the family supports the sheriff’s review but caution that any new information must be credible and not driven by profit or anniversary publicity.

A Laysan albatross known as Wisdom — the oldest known wild bird in the United States, first banded in 1956 and now at least 63 years old — has hatched a healthy chick on Sand Island, Midway Atoll, despite surviving the tsunami generated by Japan’s 9.0 earthquake. Both Wisdom and her chick were observed alive about a week after 5-foot waves hit the atoll; the tsunami is estimated to have killed roughly 2,000 adult albatrosses and about 110,000 chicks at the refuge.

Wildlife officials note Wisdom’s remarkable longevity and reproductive success: she has likely raised at least 30–35 chicks over her lifetime and may fly some 30,000 miles a year. Midway Atoll hosts a huge portion of the global Laysan albatross population (about 71%); in 2008 there were over 450,000 breeding pairs across the atoll’s islands.

The release highlights Laysan albatross biology and threats: they are long-lived, monogamous surface feeders that lay one egg per year, incubate for ~65 days, and fledge chicks after 5–6 months. Major conservation threats include marine debris (an estimated five tons of plastic are fed to chicks at Midway annually), longline fishing bycatch, contaminants, invasive predators, and sea-level rise affecting low-lying nesting habitat. Midway is cooperatively managed to protect its ecosystems and cultural resources, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service monitors and cares for these seabird populations.

A Minnesota woman, 19-year-old Monalisa Perez of Halstad, was charged with second-degree manslaughter after her boyfriend, 22-year-old Pedro Ruiz III, was fatally shot during a failed YouTube stunt. Perez, who is pregnant, was released on $7,000 bail; the charge carries up to 10 years in prison.

According to the criminal complaint and media reports, Ruiz asked Perez to shoot a bullet into a book he held against his chest while filming. Perez says she fired from about a foot away using a .50-caliber Desert Eagle—a powerful semiautomatic pistol found at the scene. Ruiz had set up two cameras to record the stunt and had previously shown Perez a book he’d shot himself that hadn’t been penetrated. Perez had tweeted hours earlier that they were “probably going to shoot one of the most dangerous videos ever.”

Family members described Ruiz as a thrill-seeker who performed risky stunts and sought online attention; the couple posted prank and stunt videos on YouTube and discussed gaining subscribers. Authorities say Perez has posted multiple videos on her channel since May. Ruiz died from a single gunshot wound to the chest.

A Dallas priest long stationed at St. Cecilia Catholic Church, the Rev. Edmundo Paredes, is accused of molesting three teenage boys more than a decade ago and of stealing at least $60,000–$80,000 from his parish. The diocese says Paredes admitted the financial theft in 2017, was suspended and removed from ministry then, and was barred from representing himself as a priest after the sexual-abuse allegations were reported to the diocese in February. Those abuse claims were judged credible and referred to law enforcement, but Paredes is currently missing and may have fled to the Philippines; the Dallas Diocese has hired private investigators to locate him.

Bishop Edward Burns informed parishioners of the sexual-abuse allegations only recently after consulting the Diocesan Review Board and said the timing was partly prompted by the fallout from a high‑profile Pennsylvania grand jury report on clergy abuse. Survivors’ advocates and some parishioners criticized the diocese for waiting months to disclose the allegations, questioning whether the delay protected the church rather than victims. Diocesan spokespeople say the delay aimed to avoid compromising the police investigation and to respect victims’ requests for privacy.

Twelve hours after House Majority Leader Eric Cantor’s shocking primary defeat, a fast-moving scramble for GOP leadership roles began.

Pete Sessions (R-Tex.) is actively campaigning for the majority leader spot—calling, emailing and mass-texting colleagues for support. House Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) has also been sounding out members but says he won’t formally run until Cantor announces whether he will remain in leadership for the rest of his term. Other potential contenders for majority leader include Reps. Jeb Hensarling (R-Tex.), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) and Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-Wash.). GOP Vice Chair Lynn Jenkins was also mentioned as a possible mover-up.

The whip contest is already shaping up: Republican Study Committee Chair Steve Scalise and Rep. Peter Roskam (Ill.) have been openly lining up support, and McMorris Rodgers has told allies she’s considering either the leader or whip slot. Other names floated for whip include Sessions and Rep. Tom Price (Ga.). McCarthy and Roskam could benefit if races are held soon, since both already have whip teams in place.

Some conservatives are urging Cantor to step down immediately; others prefer he finish out his duties. Cantor had met privately with GOP leaders and planned, then canceled, a meeting with close allies. Speaker John Boehner is not believed to be under immediate challenge. House Republicans scheduled a conference meeting less than 24 hours after Cantor’s loss as the caucus begins to sort out the next moves.

This piece is a magazine-profile snapshot of Scarlett Johansson from Esquire’s November 2013 issue, mixing a playful opening anecdote about handwriting with broader observations about her career, public persona, and recent projects — interspersed with unrelated celebrity news snippets in the same archived page.

Main portrait of Scarlett Johansson:
- The article opens with a relaxed, intimate scene in a dim Manhattan hotel bar where Johansson cheerfully participates in a gimmick: providing handwriting samples for a graphologist. The playful exchange (writing “A bird in the hand…” twice, prompting the writer to try and fail at printing it) reveals a spontaneous, unguarded side of her.
- Contrary to common impressions of aloofness or boredom, Johansson is depicted as engaged, funny, politically aware, and generous — someone who enjoys ordinary pleasures (sharing a sandwich, horsing around in a bar) and is comfortable with light-hearted, self-aware stunts.
- At 28 she has a long, varied career: indie hits (Lost in Translation), mainstream films (the Avengers franchise), Broadway (Cat on a Hot Tin Roof), and a mix of roles from a seductive manipulator in Don Jon to an eerie predator in the upcoming Under the Skin. She’s been named “Sexiest Woman Alive” twice.
- She describes being exhausted from relentless work and longing for a simple staycation where she can sleep late and read — small luxuries she values given the demands and contrivances of film shoots (e.g., standing in uncomfortable conditions while costumed and jeweled).
- Johansson acknowledges the career pressures women face in Hollywood (“Pretty soon the roles you’re offered all become mothers”) and says she’s hustling — doing theater, producing, and branching out (e.g., a project with Esquire) to hedge against typecasting and career slowdown.
- Her demeanor in the interview is candid and self-aware; she rejects melodrama about celebrity loss of privacy and accepts the practicalities of sustaining a long career.

Other content on the archived page:
- A short Associated Press item noting that Johansson and fiancé Romain Dauriac welcomed a baby girl named Rose (mother and child doing well) and are seeking privacy; it lists recent credits like Lucy and Captain America.
- Brief celebrity items about Alyssa Milano welcoming a daughter, Elizabella Dylan Bugliari, and comments about pregnancy and motherhood.
- A note explaining that the crawl is part of an Internet Archive effort to preserve web pages to prevent broken links.

Overall tone and takeaway:
- The feature balances light, intimate anecdote and character detail with career context, presenting Johansson as competent, savvy, and sometimes weary but still playful and unpretentious — a star who treats celebrity pragmatically while protecting the life she values.

This document combines three related threads about preserving web content and conflicts in the craft-beer world.

- Internet Archive crawls: The Archive is running crawls to capture pages as they’re created and the pages they reference so that when linked content changes or disappears, a preserved copy is available. The aim is to replace broken links with links to the archived versions (or provide them as companions), ultimately to fix broken links across the web. These crawls include supported “No More 404” sites.

- Black Project/ Wicked Weed split: Black Project Spontaneous & Wild Ales announced it will sever business ties with Wicked Weed after Wicked Weed was acquired by Anheuser‑Busch InBev (AB InBev). Black Project cites deep ethical objections to AB InBev’s strategies toward craft beer, calling some practices predatory and saying they believe AB InBev intends to undermine American craft brewing. As a result Black Project will not attach its name to a collaboration beer aging in Asheville, will reblend and rebrand the beer brewed with Wicked Weed at their facility so it’s not a Wicked Weed collab, and will not attend the Wicked Weed Funkatorium Invitational. They express personal goodwill toward Wicked Weed’s people despite the decision.

- Budweiser Super Bowl ad controversy and craft-beer backlash: The piece critiques Budweiser’s recent Super Bowl ads that mock craft-beer culture—portraying Bud as “NOT SMALL,” “NOT SIPPED,” “NOT SOFT,” “NOT A FRUIT CUP,” “NOT IMPORTED,” and “NOT FOR EVERYONE.” The ads drew outrage because AB InBev has been buying craft brands and markets faux-craft products like Shock Top, making the anti-craft tone seem hypocritical. The analysis argues the ad’s goal is less to win over craft drinkers than to reassure and fortify mainstream Bud drinkers’ identity by positioning Bud as masculine, mainstream, and not trendy.

Overall, the document highlights efforts to preserve online records, a concrete repercussion of AB InBev’s craft acquisitions in the form of a collaboration split, and broader industry tensions amplified by provocative mainstream advertising.

Prosecutor Gerrie Nel told the Pretoria high court that Oscar Pistorius’ defense has relied on inconsistent and dishonest theories as the trial nears its conclusion. Nel said Pistorius’ lawyers have alternately argued he shot Reeva Steenkamp in self‑defense after mistaking her for an intruder and that he was not criminally responsible because he was startled and accidentally fired through a closed toilet door—two explanations Nel said cannot be reconciled.

The prosecution maintains Pistorius intentionally killed Steenkamp on Feb. 14, 2013 after a quarrel. Pistorius, who has pleaded not guilty, also faces three gun‑related charges, including an earlier alleged negligent discharge at a Johannesburg restaurant. South African cases have no juries; Judge Thokozile Masipa, aided by two assessors, will decide whether Pistorius is guilty of premeditated murder, murder without premeditation, culpable homicide (negligent killing), or should be acquitted. Conviction for premeditated murder carries a potential sentence of 25 years to life. The judge set a firm deadline for closing arguments to finish by the end of Friday.

A Pompano Beach man, 24-year-old Scott Simon, was arrested May 5 on a first-degree murder charge after he accidentally pocket-dialed 911 while apparently plotting to kill 33-year-old Nicholas Romondo Walker, authorities said. In the recorded 911 call made minutes before the fatal shooting, Simon is heard saying he would follow Walker home and kill him. Detectives say Walker was shot multiple times as he entered I‑95 south at Commercial Boulevard in Oakland Park; his Buick crashed into a guardrail and caught fire, and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Broward Sheriff’s Office homicide investigators believe Simon coordinated the attack but was not the triggerman. Surveillance footage from a Waffle House shows Simon and Walker arguing earlier that morning and captures a black 2012 Buick GS and a silver car leaving the restaurant; investigators are seeking two other suspects: the alleged shooter and a man seen with him in the black Buick. Two people seen speaking with Walker at the Waffle House have been interviewed and are cooperating.

BSO released surveillance videos and asked anyone with information to contact Detective Bryan Tutler or Broward Crime Stoppers (anonymous tips eligible for up to $1,000). The recorded 911 call will not be released publicly. Simon remains in Broward jail without bond.

Scotland Yard has contacted Australian authorities after nurse Jacintha Saldanha, 46, was found dead days after taking a prank call on behalf of the Duchess of Cambridge at King Edward VII’s Hospital. The call was made by 2Day FM DJs Mel Greig and Michael Christian, who impersonated the Queen and Prince Charles; the pair have been taken off air, placed on indefinite leave and are receiving intensive counselling. An inquest into the apparent suicide is to be opened.

Southern Cross Austereo, 2Day FM’s owner, held emergency board talks, suspended advertising and said it is reviewing broadcast procedures and will cooperate with investigations. The hospital’s chairman criticized the station for approving the spoof; the station says the segment had been legally cleared. New South Wales police said they have opened lines of communication with the Metropolitan Police but have not been asked to take action; legal analysts say prosecution is unlikely because no “guilty intent” is evident, though NSW surveillance laws on broadcasting private conversations could be relevant and regulators may investigate licence breaches. Several advertisers have pulled support from the station.

The royal couple scaled back public appearances—William canceled attendance at the British Military Tournament to stay privately with the Duchess as she recuperates from severe morning sickness. The loss has prompted widespread condemnation, calls for review of prank practices, and condolences to Saldanha’s family.

Michelle Obama made a lighthearted, upbeat final late-night appearance as First Lady on Jimmy Fallon’s Tonight Show the week before the Obamas left the White House. Fallon dedicated the episode to her, recalling how emotional he and the Obamas were after President Obama’s farewell speech. Michelle described the transition as “surprisingly emotional,” saying she’s been moved by concerns about children’s futures and urging young people to stay hopeful and resilient.

She pledged to stay active on her priorities — especially education and healthier school lunches — saying, “I’m not done.” She also said she offered Melania Trump transition advice about creating a safe family space in the White House and that she’d be willing to help Melania or Ivanka if asked.

The show mixed playful moments (a surprise meet-and-greet with fans, a competitive game of “Catchphrase” with Dave Chappelle and Jerry Seinfeld, and thank-you notes exchanged with Fallon) with affectionate tributes. It closed with Stevie Wonder performing a medley dedicated to her. The tone contrasted with the president’s more emotional public farewell the night before, giving Michelle’s final week in the White House a celebratory sendoff.

The United States announced a set of punitive measures against Uganda in response to a new anti-homosexuality law President Yoweri Museveni signed in February. The law—originally drafted with a death-penalty clause and later amended to allow life sentences for “aggravated homosexuality” (including sex with minors or while HIV-positive)—also criminalizes lesbianism and makes it illegal to assist people in engaging in homosexual acts. Human rights groups report increased abuses and arrests of LGBT people since the law took effect.

U.S. actions include:
- Cutting or redirecting portions of aid previously destined for Ugandan government institutions (including halting $2.4 million for a community policing program and reallocating $3 million for a planned national public health institute to another African country).
- Moving some funding for Ugandan health ministry salaries and travel to non-governmental organizations and shifting an NIH genomics meeting from Uganda to South Africa.
- Canceling a planned U.S.-sponsored regional military exercise in Uganda.
- Imposing visa restrictions on Ugandan officials believed to have been involved in human rights violations or corruption; specific targets were not named.

The White House emphasized these steps were intended to defend human rights for all Ugandans without ending humanitarian assistance or cooperation against threats such as the Lord’s Resistance Army and Somali extremism, where Uganda is a key partner. Uganda’s government rejected foreign pressure, saying it would not reverse the law. U.S. officials, including the president and UN Ambassador Samantha Power, called for repeal and reiterated that LGBT rights are human rights.

Former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates and former DNI James Clapper testified before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee on May 8, drawing intense media attention and renewed scrutiny of ties between the Trump administration and Russia. Yates said she met twice with White House counsel Don McGahn on Jan. 26–27 to warn that then–National Security Adviser Michael Flynn had misled Vice President Pence about calls with Russia’s ambassador and was vulnerable to Russian blackmail. Despite that warning, Flynn remained in his post for 18 more days and resigned only after The Washington Post reported he had lied to Pence. Yates characterized her meeting as urgent; the White House has downplayed it as a mere “heads-up.” Yates also testified she learned of Trump’s January 30 travel ban from the media and refused to defend it in court, which led to her firing days later.

Clapper corroborated some broader intelligence context: allied governments had passed along sensitive reports in 2016 about contacts between Trump associates and Russian officials, and he confirmed he had not been told about the FBI’s counterintelligence investigation until Director Comey disclosed it publicly. Both Clapper and Yates denied being anonymous sources for press reports and denied leaking classified material.

Republican senators pressed Yates over her refusal to defend the travel ban and suggested leaks harmed the administration; Democrats emphasized Flynn’s alleged deception and the administration’s delay in removing him. Yates declined to speculate on Trump’s motives; senators asked whether Flynn could face prosecution if he had lied to the FBI, to which Yates confirmed lying to the FBI is a crime.

The hearings produced no definitive “smoking gun” connecting the president to collusion, but Yates’s measured testimony, supported by Clapper’s presence, added credibility to concerns about the administration’s handling of Russia-related issues and raised fresh questions for the White House—especially why it kept Flynn in place after being warned. The episode came amid partisan exchanges and broader, ongoing FBI and congressional investigations that could continue into 2018. The hearings also generated a side-media story when President Trump briefly set a tweet denying collusion as his Twitter header, prompting widespread mockery online.

A 12-year-old boy attempted to drive alone from Kendall, on the mid-north coast of New South Wales, to Perth and was stopped by highway patrol in Broken Hill after covering about 1,300 km. Officers noticed the vehicle had a hazardous defect and, on checking, discovered the driver was a 12-year-old who had already driven across the state and was heading west to complete an approximately 4,000–4,300 km journey that would require crossing the remote Nullarbor Plain. The trip would take many days and poses serious risks (extreme remoteness, long distances between fuel stops, dangerous wildlife at night). The boy was arrested, taken to Broken Hill police station, and later released into his parents’ care; police inquiries are ongoing. The incident provoked public questions about how he refuelled, who taught him to drive, whether he had been reported missing, and whether deeper issues were involved. Authorities said the case is unusual and under investigation.

A 2-year-old girl, Leasia Carter, died after being left in a locked car for about 16 hours in Baltimore’s Belair-Edison neighborhood, police say. The child was found unresponsive around 5:15–5:30 p.m. Monday on Brendan Avenue and taken to Johns Hopkins Children’s Center in very serious condition; she later died. Investigators determined Leasia had been inside the vehicle most of Monday while temperatures reached about 89°F and that she suffered second-degree burns.

Her father, 31-year-old Wilbert Carter, who had sole legal custody, was arrested and charged with second-degree murder and child abuse. Police say Carter told them he drank about five alcoholic drinks Sunday, has periods when he passes out, and has little memory of events after late Sunday; family members said he returned home early Monday morning and only began searching for his daughter around 4 p.m. when he discovered the car still parked on Brendan Avenue. Neighbors reported he was distraught when he found Leasia.

Authorities stressed the rapid danger of leaving children in hot cars—the interior temperature can become life-threatening within minutes—and issued reminders not to leave children, elderly people or pets unattended in vehicles. The case is under homicide investigation.

Archaeologists excavating the ancient and medieval fortress and port of Burgos (Poros) on Cape Foros, near modern Burgas, Bulgaria, uncovered a rare 6th-century lead tube reliquary containing ashes claimed to be from the grave of John the Apostle (St. John the Theologian) in Ephesus. The tiny lead vessel (2.2 cm by 1.7 cm), decorated with crosses and bearing imagery matching clay reliquaries produced in Ephesus, was found within an Early Christian basilica dated to the 6th century. Museum director Milen Nikolov suggested a local pilgrim likely brought the relic back from Ephesus, where John’s tomb was a major healing pilgrimage site that produced a “manna” or curing powder collected by visitors.

Bulgarian archaeologists note lead tube reliquaries from this period are exceptionally rare (only about 43 known worldwide), and the Burgas find is unusual for its direct links to Ephesus. The discovery, made during 2014 excavations and announced in March 2015, joins other important finds at Burgos—structures from the 3rd–6th centuries, a Late Antiquity latrine, and a 10th-century Bulgarian royal seal—and follows earlier regional relic finds (notably a 2010 reliquary with remains attributed to St. John the Baptist from St. Ivan Island). The Burgos site has yielded extensive evidence of continuous occupation from Roman through medieval periods and multiple historical artifacts tying it to broader pilgrimage and trade networks.

Rescue excavations in Tulln, Lower Austria (2006–2007), conducted before construction of a shopping center, recovered a uniquely complete camel skeleton from a backfilled cellar dated to the late 17th century. Associated finds (a coin of Louis XIV’s era and a medicinal bottle from a Vienna apothecary active c.1628–1665) and historical records linking Ottoman troop activity in the region around the 1683 siege of Vienna place the burial in that period.

The almost-complete male skeleton—initially mistaken for horse or cattle—was identified as a camel by osteologists and subjected to detailed morphological, morphometrical and ancient-DNA analyses. These investigations showed mixed anatomical traits of both dromedary and Bactrian camels; molecular data confirmed it as an F1 hybrid (a “Tulu”): the mitochondrial DNA matched dromedary (maternal) lineages, while nuclear markers indicated a Bactrian paternal contribution. The animal was about seven years old, likely castrated, of relatively slender build, and bore a limited set of symmetric, stress-related bone lesions (scapulae, humeri, mandible, some thoracic vertebrae and acropodial changes) that the authors interpret as consistent with use as a riding animal rather than a heavily loaded beast of burden.

The find is exceptional for Central Europe—the first complete camel skeleton in the region—and provides archaeological and genetic evidence of Ottoman-era hybrid camels being present in Central European contexts. The authors suggest the camel may have been brought by Ottoman forces or acquired through contact with them, kept temporarily by townspeople who may not have known how to care for it, and then buried whole rather than butchered. The study highlights the value of combining archaeological and genetic methods and constitutes the first archaeozoological and genetic confirmation of a Tulu hybrid camel in the archaeological record.

Gabino Zavala, a 60-year-old auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, resigned after revealing to Archbishop José Gómez in December that he is the father of two minor teenage children who live with their mother in another state. The Vatican accepted his resignation; Zavala has been living privately and is no longer in ministry though he remains a priest and bishop. The archdiocese investigated and found no misuse of church funds, and it is offering the family spiritual support and financial help toward the children’s college.

Zavala, born in Mexico and ordained in 1977, ran the Archdiocese’s large San Gabriel pastoral region from 1994 and was widely known and popular, especially among Latinos. He was a prominent social-justice advocate—leading Pax Christi USA, opposing the death penalty, supporting immigrant rights and labor protections, and working on restorative-justice ministries—positions that made him a visible and sometimes controversial figure.

His fatherhood violates the Church’s canon law on priestly celibacy, and the disclosure has prompted shock and debate about celibacy’s relevance. Church officials declined to comment on Zavala’s involvement in the children’s lives or why the matter surfaced after many years. The Vatican did not name a successor; Archbishop Gómez called the news “sad and difficult” and asked for prayers for all affected. The episode is the first major local controversy under Archbishop Gómez and comes amid ongoing discussions about celibacy within and beyond the Church.

A symbolic bid to form a 51st state — dubbed North Colorado — failed to gain broad support after county ballot questions asking commissioners to pursue secession were rejected in six of 11 counties. Weld County, the most populous among those voting and led by commissioners who championed the idea, voted decisively against it (58% no, 42% yes), a result Commissioner Sean Conway described as halting the movement in his county while still prompting attention to urban‑rural grievances.

The measure passed in five counties: Kit Carson (52% yes), Washington (58%), Phillips (62%), Cheyenne (62%), and Yuma (59%), while voters in Elbert (74% no), Lincoln (55.5% no), Logan (58% no), Moffat (54.7% no) and Sedgwick (57% no) rejected it. The ballot question was intended as a straw poll asking whether county commissioners should pursue secession.

Supporters say the effort highlights rural frustration with Front Range–focused policy changes this year (including stricter gun laws and renewable‑energy standards) and aims to force attention on rural issues; organizers already plan further initiatives (such as proposing equal county representation in the state Senate) and backing sympathetic statewide candidates. Critics and some local leaders called secession unlikely to succeed given legal hurdles — any new state requires approval by the state and U.S. Congress — but proponents say the campaign has raised awareness of rural concerns.

Tracy Rosner, a white third-grade teacher at Coral Reef Elementary in Miami-Dade County, has filed a federal employment-discrimination suit after being denied reassignment in May 2015 to the school’s extended foreign language (EFL) track, which provides one hour of foreign-language instruction per day. Rosner says she requested the EFL reassignment and was rejected because she does not speak Spanish. Her complaint argues the principal enforced a policy requiring foreign-language teachers to actually speak the language and that this policy disproportionately disadvantages non-Spanish speakers in Miami-Dade, amounting to racial discrimination. Rosner’s lawyers say she was otherwise qualified and that the school could have assigned another teacher to deliver the one-hour Spanish portion. She also alleges retaliation after the denial: the principal doubled her workload, assigning her all subjects instead of just reading and language arts. Rosner filed a complaint with the district civil rights office, which found no probable cause and closed the case. She seeks damages for emotional pain, lost job quality and related harms. Miami-Dade School Board attorneys had not yet responded to the lawsuit.

- The single highest-calorie item at McDonald’s is the 40-piece Chicken McNugget order at 1,880 calories—close to an average person’s entire recommended daily intake and enough to feed multiple people.  
- The next largest item is the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes plus a large biscuit (1,310 calories). Many of the top calorie items are large sandwiches or large-portion items.  
- Size isn’t the only driver of calories: some beverages and desserts are calorie-dense too (e.g., a 16‑oz M&M’s McFlurry at 930 calories, Large Oreo Frappe at 810). A plausible single meal—one chicken sandwich, medium fries, and a McFlurry—can easily exceed 2,000 calories.  
- Calories measure energy but don’t fully describe nutritional quality: items with moderate calories can be extremely high in sodium (e.g., the Premium Grilled Chicken Bacon Clubhouse Sandwich has 630 calories and about 1,740 mg sodium).  
- 24/7 Wall St. reviewed roughly 500 McDonald’s menu items using McDonald’s nutritional data to compile the 50 highest-calorie items; fats, carbs, and sodium figures came from the same source.  
- While McDonald’s meals tend to be higher in calories than typical home-cooked or many non–fast-food chain meals, there is no direct evidence linking McDonald’s specifically to adverse health outcomes—research instead links higher local concentrations of fast-food outlets generally to increased obesity and related health problems.

A Florida woman was arrested after she shot two people — one a houseguest — during a dispute over visitors at her Bay County home. Authorities say 32-year-old Alana Annette Savell told investigators guests were drinking loudly and would not leave, so she armed herself with a .22-caliber handgun and fired toward their feet from her doorway. One guest was hit in the leg and taken to a hospital; Savell’s boyfriend was also struck in the leg. The boyfriend allegedly told investigators he had instructed Savell that after telling someone to leave three times she should retrieve the gun and shoot at the ground, and if that failed she should shoot them in the leg. Savell was booked on a charge of aggravated battery with a firearm; it’s not known if she has retained an attorney.

(Article also briefly notes, unrelatedly, that an e-cigarette exploded in a man’s pocket at New York City’s Grand Central Terminal, causing leg and hand burns.)

A 12-year-old male jaguar named Salman, on a one-year breeding loan from Thiruvananthapuram Zoo to Delhi’s National Zoological Park since October 2014, is being returned after staff concluded he is “too fat to breed.” Keepers say Salman has shown no interest in mating with the zoo’s lone female, Kalpana, instead prioritizing food and resting — reportedly eating more eagerly than other big cats and failing to respond to the female’s advances. Delhi Zoo officials tried a strict diet and more time in a larger enclosure to encourage exercise, but say he remained lethargic and gained no mating interest. Salman’s weight has not been officially recorded at Delhi (keepers estimate it exceeds 100 kg), and the originating zoo had certified him fit at transfer. Some staff suggest relocation stress could explain his behavior, noting other males in Delhi have also not sired cubs with Kalpana; nonetheless, officials decided to send Salman back since he hasn’t fulfilled the breeding purpose of the loan. Jaguars are native to the Americas and listed as “near threatened.”

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), a GOP presidential candidate, warned that Donald Trump is “a wrecking ball” threatening to dismantle the Republican Party, criticizing Trump’s recent rhetoric that broadly labels many immigrants as criminals and rapists. Speaking on CNN, Graham called the comments offensive and argued they alienate Hispanic voters, undermine the party’s moral authority to govern, and represent a “defining moment” requiring clear rejection of such demagoguery. While acknowledging border problems and endorsing tougher measures (more Border Patrol agents, more drones, addressing visa overstays), Graham urged Republicans not to embrace Trump’s tone because doing so would cost them elections.

Former Democratic Sen. Jim Webb, also a 2016 candidate, similarly condemned Trump’s abrasive immigration remarks as divisive and harmful to the presidential debate. Webb criticized inflammatory rhetoric from anyone seeking the presidency and said his own campaign offers a different tone for Democrats, appealing to working-class voters and opposing the party’s leftward shift. Both politicians reacted to Trump’s comments amid concerns within GOP leadership—who are courting Latino voters—that the rhetoric could hurt Republican prospects in key states.

A 22-year-old Australian, Mathew Carpenter, launched ShipYourEnemiesGlitter.com as a joking one‑service site that, for $9.99AUD, would anonymously mail an A4 note dusted with glitter to a target. The site’s irreverent copy (“We fucking hate glitter…people call it the herpes of the craft world”) and a single tweet/Product Hunt post went viral, generating millions of visitors, widespread media coverage (including late-night TV), and thousands of orders—reportedly over $20,000AUD in sales within days.

Overwhelmed by demand and the stress of continual media attention, Carpenter suspended new orders and publicly asked people to stop buying the “horrible product.” He then listed the business on Flippa and sold it in under two weeks for about $85,000 to an anonymous buyer. The sale included the website, domain, files and press contacts; Carpenter offered 30 days’ transition support and a three‑year non‑compete.

Carpenter detailed the simple business model: customers pay via PayPal, he prints a reproachful letter, sprinkles glitter, envelopes and ships. He estimated shipping costs of $2–$4, leaving roughly $6–$8 gross per sale, and noted options to outsource fulfillment to reduce his time commitment. He also highlighted growth opportunities—reopening orders, adding other annoying products, custom notes, and leveraging branding printed on each letter.

After the shutdown there was immediate competition from copycat sites. Carpenter framed the venture as a holiday side project that ballooned unexpectedly; despite his ambivalence about the product, he walked away with a substantial profit.

O.J. Simpson, the former NFL star acquitted in 1995 of the murders of ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, faced a Nevada parole hearing March/July (reported dates vary) that could lead to his release as early as Oct. 1. Now 70 and serving a nine-to-33-year sentence at Lovelock Correctional Center for a 2007 armed robbery and related charges (kidnapping, assault with a deadly weapon, conspiracy), Simpson previously won parole on some lesser counts in 2013. The parole board planned to hear him by video and rule the same day; no one had registered to testify against him.

Background: Simpson rose to fame as a Heisman Trophy winner, first overall pick in the 1969 NFL draft, 1973’s first 2,000-yard rusher, and a 1985 Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee. After football he worked as an actor and pitchman (notably for Hertz) and earned substantial income—Celebrity Net Worth estimated $10.8 million at his 1992 divorce. That wealth has largely dissipated: various reports now put his net worth near $250,000. In 1997 a civil jury found him liable for Brown and Goldman’s deaths and ordered $33.5 million in damages; the families have collected little. Some assets, such as his NFL pension (about $25,000/month), are protected from that judgment.

1994–1995 case: Nicole Brown and Ronald Goldman were found stabbed in June 1994; Simpson was charged and famously led police in a slow-speed Bronco chase before surrendering. The widely televised 1995 criminal trial ended in acquittal, a verdict that sharply divided public opinion along racial and other lines. Two years later a civil court held him responsible.

2007 robbery and imprisonment: In 2007 Simpson and accomplices entered a Las Vegas hotel room and used threats and weapons to seize sports memorabilia Simpson said belonged to him; the incident led to the 2008 convictions. Simpson has characterized the episode as a mistake, expressed remorse at earlier parole proceedings, and has maintained good behavior in prison. His lawyers argue his age, conduct and remorse make him suitable for parole; critics note public interest and the persistent controversy surrounding his past, urging privacy should he be released.

If paroled and released, Simpson would still face the civil judgment and public scrutiny; commentators have suggested he avoid the spotlight to reduce risk of further trouble and public spectacle.

The document is a multi-source, in-depth discussion of Hurricane Harvey’s immediate impacts and how the storm intersects with politics, disaster funding, climate science, and media coverage. Key points:

Immediate social response and political strains
- Local communities and ordinary people mounted a powerful, nonpartisan rescue effort during Harvey, but longer-term recovery will test national unity.
- Past post-storm aid fights (Katrina, Sandy) show Congress often becomes sharply partisan over disaster funding, with some conservatives demanding offsets that pit regions against one another and delay relief. That pattern could reappear after Harvey and would undercut national solidarity.

Costs and governance questions
- Harvey’s damages are expected to be in the tens of billions. Debates over whether to offset aid with cuts elsewhere would prolong and politicize recovery, and raise philosophical questions about government’s role in sharing risks that communities cannot bear alone.

Climate change and storm characteristics
- Scientists caution that no single storm can be said to be “caused” by climate change, but a broad and growing body of evidence shows anthropogenic warming is making certain storm characteristics worse:
  - Sea-level rise (including local subsidence) raised storm surge risk.
  - Warmer sea-surface and air temperatures increase atmospheric moisture (Clausius–Clapeyron), promoting heavier rainfall; Gulf waters were unusually warm when Harvey intensified.
  - Warmer oceans can increase storm intensity; deeper warm layers can sustain rapid intensification.
  - Some research suggests climate change may be making certain atmospheric patterns more “stagnant,” increasing the likelihood of storms that stall and dump extreme rain—though attribution of stalling to climate change remains less certain.
- Observational and climate-model analyses (including studies of quasi-resonant amplification, Arctic amplification, and meridional temperature gradients) indicate trends toward conditions that favor persistent, extreme summer weather, strengthening the plausibility of a human influence on events like the 2003 and 2010 heat/flood extremes and the 2011 Texas events.

Attribution and probabilistic framing
- The appropriate scientific framing is probabilistic: climate change increases the probability and severity of some features (rainfall, surge, possibly intensity and persistence), rather than being the sole proximate cause of any single hurricane. Formal attribution studies take time but initial physical reasoning and measurements indicate Harvey was exacerbated by recent warming.

Adaptation, mitigation, and justice
- Climate change is a “threat multiplier”; while local factors (development patterns, drainage, building codes, population growth in vulnerable areas) drive much of the damage, climate change increases future risks.
- Adaptation (sea walls, drainage, relocation) and mitigation (cutting emissions) are distinct: adaptation benefits are local and often regressive, while mitigation yields global, egalitarian benefits. Overreliance on adaptation without mitigation risks repeated, increasingly costly disasters and inequitable outcomes.
- Disasters expose and exacerbate systemic injustices (racial, economic), and the political aftermath can be used to push regressive policies unless advocates press for equitable, climate-aware reforms.

Media and political framing
- Coverage often avoids linking extreme weather to climate change out of sensitivity or fear of politicization, but ignoring the climate context is argued to be a journalistic failure that obscures root causes and future risk.
- The political environment (including the Trump administration’s skepticism of climate policy and withdrawal from the Paris Agreement) complicates national-level responses and long-term risk reduction, especially because some high-risk states are economically tied to fossil fuels.
- Partisan media sometimes weaponize climate discussion during disasters; critics argue honest discussion of climate drivers should happen promptly while public attention is high, to influence policy before the media spotlight moves on.

Overall conclusion
- Harvey should be seen both as an immediate humanitarian emergency demanding rescue and relief and as a revealing case that underscores how climate change is already amplifying certain hazards (storm surge, extreme rainfall, possibly intensity and persistence). The storm exposes governance, funding, media, and equity challenges: whether the nation will overcome political polarization to fund recovery fairly, integrate climate science into planning, and pursue mitigation and just adaptation remains an urgent test.

Researchers analyzing sediment from the bottom of the 1993 GISP2 ice core have discovered ancient tundra soil beneath Greenland’s Summit that dates to about 2.7 million years ago. Using beryllium-10 dating on silt and sand extracted from the lowest 30–50 ft of the core, the team found isotope concentrations characteristic of landscapes that were exposed at the surface for long periods—estimated at roughly 200,000 to 1 million years—before being buried by ice. Pollen and plant DNA from marine sediments offshore support a picture of tundra and patchy boreal-like vegetation on Greenland in the distant past.

The finding implies that at least at this Summit “pinprick,” the Greenland Ice Sheet has not fully melted for the last several million years, surviving earlier warm intervals that approached temperatures comparable to projections for this century. The preservation is explained by cold-based ice at the base of parts of the sheet: ice frozen to the ground deforms above but does little erosive scouring, allowing ancient landscapes to remain intact. The study highlights the ice sheet’s long-term resilience but also underscores uncertainty about its future under human-driven warming; the authors are now searching for similarly preserved landscapes in Antarctica.

A Pennsylvania couple who had married a week earlier were arrested after allegedly attempting to steal $1,049.26 worth of groceries and other items from a Wegmans to use at their wedding reception.

Police say 22-year-old Brittany Lurch and 32-year-old Arthur Phillips III filled two shopping carts with merchandise, including seafood from the seafood counter and, according to a source, items such as a shrimp platter, spiral hams, vegetable and appetizer trays, dinnerware, drinks and various household goods, then walked out to their car without paying. Officers stopped and arrested them after reviewing surveillance; the couple told police the items were for their reception scheduled that afternoon.

Both were booked on misdemeanor counts of retail theft and receiving stolen property and held in Centre County jail on $2,500 bail. Officers also found a glass smoking pipe with marijuana residue in the car; Phillips was charged with possession of drug paraphernalia. The couple waived their right to a preliminary hearing.

Summary:

The document reports multiple developments in ongoing sexual harassment scandals in Hollywood.

- Nickelodeon producer Chris Savino, creator of the animated series The Loud House, has been accused by as many as a dozen women of sexual harassment. Cartoon Brew detailed allegations including offers of work for sexual favors and explicit texts; at least one accuser publicly named Savino and others reportedly are part of an HR investigation. Nickelodeon confirmed Savino is no longer working with the network, saying it takes such allegations seriously. Savino issued a Facebook apology saying he was “deeply sorry,” ashamed, and respectful of the women who spoke out. The Loud House will continue production.

- New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman opened a civil rights investigation into The Weinstein Company after dozens of women came forward with allegations against co-founder Harvey Weinstein. The AG’s office subpoenaed company records to determine whether pervasive harassment or discrimination occurred at the company’s New York office. Weinstein has been fired by the company and has denied allegations of nonconsensual sex.

- Actress Ashley Judd, one of Weinstein’s early accusers, is scheduled for her first television interview since going public; she will appear with Diane Sawyer on ABC programs.

The piece situates these stories within a wider wave of public allegations against prominent figures in entertainment.

The U.S., France and Britain launched coordinated strikes on Syria on the night of April 13–14, 2018, aiming to punish and deter Syrian President Bashar al‑Assad for a suspected chemical weapons attack in Douma on April 7. Explosions and smoke were reported over Damascus as the allies carried out precision missile strikes, reportedly from outside Syrian airspace; Syrian state TV said air defenses responded.

President Donald Trump announced the operation from the White House, calling it a combined effort to degrade Syria’s chemical weapons capabilities and establish a strong deterrent. He warned Russia and Iran—key backers of Assad—about their association with “mass murder,” urged them to change course, and said the U.S. is prepared to “sustain” pressure until chemical attacks stop, while not seeking an indefinite ground presence in Syria. Trump also called for regional partners to take on more responsibility and resources in the region.

French President Emmanuel Macron said France joined the limited operation focused on Syria’s clandestine chemical arsenal and declared Assad’s “red line” crossed.
