The strikes came a year after a smaller 2017 U.S. missile attack meant to deter chemical weapons use; officials said the broader 2018 action targeted aircraft, depots and chemical facilities to more effectively degrade Assad’s ability to employ banned agents. Syrian and Russian positions complicate the conflict, and it remained unclear whether the strikes signaled a larger political strategy to end the war or were a limited punitive action.

UNICEF’s new report, released ahead of International Day of the Girl (11 October), finds that girls aged 5–14 spend far more time than boys on unpaid household work—an estimated 40% more, equal to 160 million additional hours per day globally. The burden begins early: girls 5–9 spend about 30% more time (≈40 million extra hours/day) on chores than boys, rising to 50% more for 10–14 year‑olds (≈120 million extra hours/day). Common tasks include cooking, cleaning, caring for family members, and collecting water and firewood; nearly two‑thirds of girls cook and clean, and almost half collect water or fuel. Much of this work is “less visible” (childcare, caring for elders) and is frequently undervalued or imposed as adult responsibility, limiting girls’ time to study, play and socialize. Collecting water and firewood can also expose girls to risks such as sexual violence.

Regional and country findings highlight particularly large gaps in South Asia and the Middle East and North Africa for 10–14 year‑olds, with the largest country‑level burdens in Somalia (10–14 year‑old girls spend about 26 hours/week on chores), Burkina Faso and Yemen. UNICEF emphasizes that measuring these disparities is a key step toward meeting Sustainable Development Goal targets on gender equality and related issues (violence, child marriage, FGM, education), and that empowering girls benefits societies economically and socially.

Researchers mined nearly 2,000 modern microbial genomes to infer traits of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA). Starting from about 6.1 million protein-coding genes grouped into ~286,500 clusters, they identified 355 gene families that meet strict phylogenetic criteria for having been inherited across both bacterial and archaeal lineages and so plausibly traceable to LUCA.

Analysis of those 355 proteins paints a detailed picture of LUCA’s biology and environment:
- Metabolism: autotrophic, CO2-fixing and H2-dependent, likely using the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway. Evidence also points to N2 fixation.
- Physiology: anaerobic (lived without oxygen) and thermophilic (heat-loving).
- Biochemistry: reliance on iron–sulfur clusters, radical reaction mechanisms, and cofactors such as flavins, S‑adenosyl methionine, coenzyme A, ferredoxin, molybdopterin, corrins and selenium; RNA required nucleoside modifications and SAM-dependent methylations.
- Environment: inhabited geochemically active settings rich in H2, CO2 and iron — consistent with hydrothermal vents or similar volcanic systems rather than oxygenated surface ponds.

The phylogenies also place modern clostridia and methanogens—organisms with lifestyles resembling these inferred traits—near the base of their domains. Overall, the genomic evidence supports an autotrophic, hydrogen‑driven origin of life in high‑temperature, anoxic, geochemically active environments such as hydrothermal vents.

Cyber-intelligence firm iSight Partners reported that a Russian-linked hacking group it calls “Sandworm Team” ran a sophisticated five-year cyber-espionage campaign targeting NATO, the EU, Ukrainian governments, energy and telecom companies, and related researchers. Attackers used phishing emails with malicious attachments and multiple exploitation methods, and beginning this summer they began exploiting a previously unknown vulnerability present in most Windows versions. iSight said the malware and code contained Russian-language clues and targeted subjects tied to Russian interests (notably the Ukraine crisis), leading researchers to conclude the actors likely have nation-state support, though direct government ties were not proven.

iSight notified Microsoft of the flaw and withheld public disclosure to allow a patch to be developed; Microsoft rolled out an automatic update. iSight found evidence some Ukrainian government systems were infected and said the Windows exploit was particularly potent, bypassing many defenses. The firm planned to distribute a detailed report to clients; some victims were notified privately. The research is part of a string of private-sector analyses linking advanced cyber-espionage operations to Russia.

Fox News host Laura Ingraham mocked Taylor Swift on Twitter after the Tennessee Senate race was decided, tweeting "Hey @taylorswift13, haters gonna hate. #shakeitoff" following the victory of Republican Rep. Marsha Blackburn over Democrat Phil Bredesen. Swift had publicly endorsed and said she voted for Bredesen (and Jim Cooper for the House), a rare overt political stance in which she explained she could not support Blackburn despite her usual preference for voting for women. Blackburn’s win all but ended Democrats’ hopes of taking control of the Senate.

A Massachusetts probate court released 192 pages of testimony that Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney gave in 1991 on behalf of Staples founder Thomas Stemberg during Stemberg’s divorce proceedings. The transcripts, released at the Boston Globe’s request and approved by the Norfolk Probate & Family Court, show Romney testifying that Staples had privately issued a new "D" class of shares prior to its IPO to help finance Stemberg’s divorce settlement. Romney characterized the share class as convertible to common stock (and said earlier rounds had greater voting rights) and portrayed Stemberg as an optimistic, risk-minimizing entrepreneur.

Romney’s campaign lawyer said he had no objection to making the testimony public and dismissed recent allegations as false; Staples and Stemberg’s camp likewise did not oppose release and said the matter is a private family issue. Maureen Sullivan Stemberg’s attorney, Gloria Allred, sought both release of the transcripts and lifting of a gag order preventing her client from speaking about the divorce; the judge allowed the transcripts to be released but kept the gag order in place, saying Sullivan Stemberg must file a separate request to lift it. Allred cautioned that without Sullivan Stemberg’s comments the testimony may lack context. The filings do not appear to present new, damaging information for Romney’s 2012 presidential campaign.

This document is a long, composite piece centered on Bob Dylan—his Nobel Prize in Literature, his artistry, career, persona, and fandom—interspersed with unrelated sections about web archiving, Twitter location info, and a long list of (mostly tongue-in-cheek) Nobel Prize betting odds for various writers.

Key points about Bob Dylan and the Nobel:
- The Nobel committee honored Dylan “for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition,” provoking familiar debates about whether song lyrics count as literature. Many defenders argue his words, inseparable from his music and voice, achieve sustained poetic power.
- Critics who dismiss Dylan are reminded of specific lyric examples (e.g., “It’s Alright, Ma,” “Visions of Johanna,” “All Along the Watchtower,” “Brownsville Girl”) and of his influence in reshaping American popular music by borrowing, reshuffling and reworking folk, blues and Tin Pan Alley traditions.
- Dylan’s career is described in phases: early acoustic protest/folk, the mid-60s electric trilogy, the Blood On The Tracks-era introspection, later creative periods (e.g., Tangled Up in Blue, Blind Willie McTell, Cross the Green Mountain), and a studio renaissance with Modern Times (2006) and Together Through Life (2009).
- The piece emphasizes that Dylan’s lyrics are experienced as part of performance—his voice and delivery are integral—so lines that may seem odd on the page work powerfully in song.
- It recounts his secretive, sometimes combative relationship with the media and obsessive fandom: stories of “Dylanologists,” collectors, intrusive fans like AJ Weberman, and the cult of memorabilia. The author notes both the burdens fame imposed and anecdotes showing Dylan’s dry humor and occasional warmth.
- The article covers touring practices (the “Never Ending Tour”), why Dylan keeps performing (creative drive, anonymity on the road), his elusiveness, and his continued productivity (tours, radio shows, planned volumes of Chronicles, sculpting, soundtrack work).
- Personal background and private life are sketched—birth name Robert Zimmerman, Jewish-Minnesotan roots, marriages and children, periods of reinvention (including retreat after a 1966 motorcycle accident)—and his complex reputation: admired as genius by peers (e.g., Steve Earle, Elvis Costello), yet criticized for personal failings and occasionally uneven output.
- Reflections from peers and collaborators (Bruce Langhorne, Joan Baez, Kinky Friedman, Allen Ginsberg) underline his influence and mystique. The piece repeats Dylan’s own refrain that he may not be understood until long after his lifetime.

Other content:
- Repeated short passages describe an Internet Archive crawl effort (“No More 404”) to archive newly created pages and their references to preserve links that would otherwise break.
- Brief note about adding location to Tweets and how to delete Tweet location history.
- A large, mostly satirical catalog of likely and unlikely Nobel Prize in Literature candidates and betting odds—covering international writers (e.g., Murakami, Atwood, Roth, Pynchon, Knausgaard, Elena Ferrante and many others)—used to frame public speculation about literary prizes and to suggest how unpredictable the Nobel can be.

Tone and framing:
- The piece blends serious literary defense of Dylan’s Nobel with cultural reportage, fan anthropology, critic commentary and anecdote. It pushes back on narrow definitions of literature by situating Dylan within American poetic and musical traditions and emphasizes that his gifts are best judged in performance context as well as on the page. The interspersed archival/web and betting-list items are peripheral and sometimes tongue-in-cheek additions.

Ana-Alecia Ayala, 32, who gained attention after posting a video dancing with her “chemo buddy” in a hospital room, has died after a year-long battle with uterine sarcoma. Diagnosed in December 2015 with a rare tumor that spread to her ovaries and the lining of her stomach, Ayala — a mother of a three-year-old — underwent surgery that removed most of the tumor, but a new growth on her spleen in July led to more aggressive inpatient chemotherapy. She spent much of her treatment trying to stay positive and connected to family, holding her child’s birthday in her hospital room and leaning on friends like Danielle Andrus, who supported and cheered her during chemo. Ayala used her viral dance video to encourage others not to see cancer as a death sentence, to find moments of joy, and to urge loved ones of patients to be present and playful. She died Wednesday surrounded by family, loved ones and the family priest. A GoFundMe was maintained to help her family.

A Georgia couple, Elrey “Bud” Runion, 69, and his wife June, 66, who disappeared after responding to a Craigslist ad to buy a 1966 Mustang convertible, were found dead near McRae, Telfair County. Their 2003 GMC Envoy was recovered in a nearby lake and two bodies discovered in woods were later positively identified as the Runions; both had been shot in the head with a small‑caliber handgun.

Investigators traced the last known contact on a cellphone to 28‑year‑old Ronnie Adrian “Jay” Towns of McRae. Towns initially was charged with making false statements and attempted theft by deception after reportedly answering the Craigslist ad for a car that likely didn’t exist. He was arrested after turning himself in and was later indicted on multiple counts including malice murder, armed robbery, making a false statement and criminal attempt to commit theft by deception; a magistrate judge denied him bond.

Sheriff Chris Steverson said robbery appears to be the motive. Authorities reported no evidence Towns owned the classic car sought by Bud Runion; they believe the suspect lured the couple to the rural meeting location. Towns’ family disputed the allegations and said he is innocent; they were present at his brief arraignment. Investigators said they are not seeking other suspects at this time and described having substantial evidence to review. The Runions — active in charity work for decades — have been mourned by family, friends and their Marietta community.

Rep. Elizabeth Esty (D-Conn.) has apologized and come under heavy criticism for her handling of sexual harassment, threats and alleged physical violence by her former chief of staff, Tony Baker. Newspaper reports said Esty learned in 2016 via a third party about misconduct toward a female staffer—who says she was punched in the back and received death threats—but did not suspend or fire Baker until about three months later after an internal review uncovered a broader pattern of alleged abuse. Esty said she demanded counseling for Baker, conducted an internal review, was advised by House counsel to enter a nondisclosure agreement, and later regretted “providing even the slightest assistance” as he sought another job. Baker has denied some allegations.

Esty, long a public supporter of #MeToo and stronger protections for congressional staff, apologized to victims, met with Connecticut women’s groups and domestic violence advocates, and asked the House Ethics Committee to investigate whether she violated any law, rule or standard in her handling of the case. She also announced she will not seek re-election and said she will work on improving workplace protections during her remaining months in office.

Reactions have included calls for her resignation from the Hartford Courant editorial board and Connecticut Republicans, mild criticism from state Democrats, and demands from advocacy groups for more information about what happened.

Scientists challenge the long-held view that black rats sustained repeated European outbreaks of the bubonic plague after the Black Death. A study led by Prof. Nils Christian Stenseth (University of Oslo), published in PNAS, found no correlation between European climate patterns and the timing of some 7,711 recorded plague outbreaks over 400 years, which would be expected if rat–flea dynamics in Europe had driven recurrent epidemics. Instead, the researchers link multiple waves of plague to population and flea booms in Central Asia’s great gerbils: wet springs followed by warm summers there favor gerbil and flea proliferation, increasing Yersinia pestis circulation. With high east–west trade (e.g., along the Silk Road), infected fleas or animals could have carried the bacterium to European port cities, then across the continent. The team plans to test the idea by sequencing ancient plague DNA from European skeletons; high genetic diversity between waves would support repeated Asian introductions versus a single European rat reservoir.

The article also summarizes general plague facts: Yersinia pestis is a zoonotic bacterium transmitted by flea bites, direct contact, or respiratory droplets (pneumonic form). Bubonic plague causes swollen lymph nodes (buboes); pneumonic plague is highly contagious and often fatal untreated. Modern antibiotics are effective if given early. From 2010–2015 there were 3,248 reported cases worldwide (584 deaths); WHO notes endemic hotspots include the DRC, Madagascar, and Peru. Prevention and outbreak control emphasize surveillance, vector and rodent control (vector control before killing rodents), safe clinical practices, isolation of pneumonic cases, chemoprophylaxis for contacts, and rapid laboratory confirmation. Separate research warns that agricultural expansion in East Africa may increase local plague risk by boosting rodent populations.

Researchers from Purdue University report that being your mother’s perceived favorite in adulthood can be linked to higher depressive symptoms. The study, published in the Journal of Gerontology: Social Sciences and led by Jill Suitor, used data from the Within-Family Differences Study: 725 adult children (average age ~49) across 309 families whose mothers were 65–75 at baseline. Data were collected in two waves seven years apart.

Key measures were adult children’s perceptions of four aspects of maternal favoritism/disfavoritism: emotional closeness, conflict, pride, and disappointment. The main findings:
- Adult children who believed they were emotionally closer to their mother than their siblings reported the highest levels of depressive symptoms.
- Elevated depressive symptoms were also found among those who saw themselves as the child their mother was most disappointed in or with whom she had the most conflict.
- The negative effect of perceived maternal disappointment was particularly pronounced among Black adult children; otherwise racial and gender differences were limited.
- Authors interpret these effects as driven by ongoing social comparison among siblings (not equity), producing strain whether the child is favored or disfavored.

The team plans to examine similar patterns for fathers and to study predictors of maternal favoritism. The paper situates its findings in broader literature linking parenting style and adult well-being.

Google UK marketing director Dan Cobley told Bloomberg TV that iOS 6 users can still “use Google Maps by downloading them or going to the Google Maps website” after Apple removed the built-in Google Maps app. That comment is puzzling: there is no standalone Google Maps app in the App Store (only Google Earth), nor is there a way to download maps from Google Maps in Mobile Safari, so it’s unclear what Cobley meant by “downloading them.” Google told SearchEngineLand it aims to make Google Maps available across devices, browsers and OSes, but provided no timeline or details about a new iOS Maps app or whether it would include turn-by-turn navigation. The piece also points readers to third‑party map app alternatives and links to related items mocking iOS 6 Maps and various gadget/product stories.

Inmates across multiple Florida prisons planned a coordinated, month-long strike beginning on Martin Luther King Jr. Day to protest unpaid labor, high commissary prices, lack of parole, violent and unsafe conditions, and broader criminal-justice policies. The action—called Operation Push and announced anonymously by organizers to avoid retaliation—calls for refusal to perform assigned work and to buy “overpriced” commissary items, aiming to force the state to hire outside contractors and thereby demonstrate the financial impact of losing inmate labor.

Key grievances cited:
- Unpaid labor: Florida largely pays prisoners nothing for in‑facility or outside work (3.15 million community work hours in 2017, per the DOC). Activists and inmates call this “slave labor” and seek meaningful pay rather than token sentence reductions.
- Price gouging in commissaries: Organizers allege extreme markups (e.g., soup sold for $17 vs. $4 outside), which burdens inmates’ families who must send money.
- Elimination of parole: Florida abolished parole for most offenses in 1984; prisoners want restored parole opportunities as an incentive and route to rehabilitation.
- Brutal conditions, violence, neglect and unexplained deaths: Reports and investigations have documented beatings, sexual assaults, cover-ups, suicides and deaths (notably Darren Rainey in 2012). Overcrowding and inadequate care have led to calls for federal investigation and systemic reform.
- Broader rights and policy demands: Restoration of voting rights for people with felony convictions, a moratorium on executions, and attention to environmental/health threats (e.g., nearby phosphate mining) affecting some facilities.

Context and responses:
- Florida runs the nation’s third-largest prison system (~97,000 inmates) and has seen repeated unrest: major nationwide prison strikes in 2016 included many Florida facilities; the DOC previously locked down all facilities in response to threats.
- Organizers contend retaliation is common (solitary confinement, transfers, limits on visitation/communication). Some leaders have already been punished.
- Advocacy groups (ACLU, Southern Poverty Law Center, Campaign to Fight Toxic Prisons, Human Rights Defense Center) support inmates’ demands and highlight systemic failures. They emphasize that fair pay, parole, and reduced incarceration would improve conditions and public safety.
- The Florida Department of Corrections has issued brief statements pledging to “ensure the safe operation” of facilities but has not publicly addressed specific reform requests or detailed strike responses.

Overall, the strike is framed by inmates and supporters as a nonviolent, coordinated effort to force public and governmental attention to what they call modern-day slavery, abusive and dangerous conditions, and entrenched policies that impede rehabilitation and basic human rights.

These articles collect reporting, eyewitness accounts and commentary surrounding the final days and death of Robin Williams.

Last known public appearance and last photos
- Photos and eyewitness accounts show Williams at a Bay Area art‑gallery reception about a day or two before his death. Attendees described him as frail but in good spirits, laughing and engaged, and not drinking. He attended with his wife and spoke with local students and an artist about a possible project.

Circumstances of death and scene
- Williams was found dead at his Marin County home on August 11. Marin County investigators reported he was discovered seated and unresponsive with a belt secured around his neck and wedged in a closet door; there was no suicide note. The person who found him was longtime assistant and friend Rebecca Erwin Spencer. Reports note superficial cuts on his wrist and a pocket knife near his body; toxicology results were pending at the time of reporting.

Mental and physical state before death
- Multiple sources describe Williams as suffering a severe, longstanding depression in the period before his death. Reports say he was sleeping excessively (sometimes up to 18–20 hours), had little appetite, and struggled to get out of bed. Friends and insiders linked his comedy to using laughter as a coping mechanism for private sadness. He had recently completed a short rehab stay that some sources said was for “deep depression,” not substance relapse.

Health concerns and medication theories
- After his death, it emerged Williams was in the early stages of Parkinson’s disease, a development that prompted speculation (including from friends and some outlets) that medication or the illness may have contributed to mood changes—an idea the press widely discussed while toxicology and medical details were unresolved.

Financial and estate matters
- Contrary to online rumors, Williams’ publicist said he had no crippling financial problems and his family was taken care of. Reporting cited Forbes’ estimated net worth (~$50 million) and the sale listings/mortgages on his properties. Estate experts suggested he likely had a living trust in place, meaning little probate drama was expected.

Work in his final months
- Williams had been working on projects shortly before his death, including voice work for the indie film Absolutely Anything and the TV show The Crazy Ones (canceled after one season). He had spoken publicly about appreciating steady work, though his publicist stressed his job choices were often artistic rather than purely financial.

Public reaction and broader context
- Coverage mixed factual reporting with speculation about causes and motives, and friends, colleagues and family mourned and recalled his generosity and comic genius. Many outlets emphasized understanding and awareness of severe depression and provided suicide-prevention resources.

Overall, the coverage paints a picture of a beloved, much‑loved entertainer who had been struggling privately with severe depression and health concerns in his final months, whose death was ruled an apparent suicide and whose work, legacy and estate left family members provided for.

Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine and Pike County Sheriff Charles Reader are leading the investigation into the execution-style slayings of eight members of the Rhoden family found Friday at four rural properties near Piketon, Ohio. All eight autopsies are complete; crime scenes remain closed and roadblocks will stay in place. More than 100 personnel from across southern Ohio are assisting; investigators have interviewed over 30 people and are pursuing numerous leads.

Investigators found marijuana grow operations at three of the four crime scenes — reportedly about 200 indoor plants — which appear commercial in scale. DeWine said it is unclear whether the grows are linked to the killings but they will be an important part of the probe. Officials are also considering other possible motives, including a drug cartel connection, turf war, or family dispute. DeWine described the attacks as a “sophisticated operation” and said those responsible took steps to hinder investigation and prosecution. No search warrants have yet been filed publicly, and authorities have not announced whether there is one or multiple suspects.

Law enforcement confirmed they are examining social media evidence, including a Facebook threat that specifically mentioned victim Christopher Rhoden Jr.; DeWine and staff are aware of that threat and say every piece of information is being considered. Sheriff Reader said the family was targeted and warned surviving members to take precautions, including arming themselves.

Victims are seven adults and a 16-year-old boy: Christopher Rhoden Sr. (40), Christopher Rhoden Jr. (16), Kenneth Rhoden (44), Gary Rhoden (38), Dana Rhoden (37), Clarence “Frankie” Rhoden (20), Hannah Gilley (20), and Hanna Rhoden (19). Some victims appear to have been killed while sleeping; one infant nearby was unharmed, as were two other small children. The community is shaken; a memorial fund has been set up at Fifth Third Bank and a $25,000 reward was offered by a Cincinnati businessman.

Authorities ask anyone with information to call 1-855-BCI-OHIO (224-6446) or the Pike County Sheriff’s Office at 740-947-2111.

Actor Ron Livingston defended his sister, Wisconsin news anchor Jennifer Livingston, after her on-air response to an insulting viewer email went viral. In a statement, Livingston praised Jennifer’s dedication to her job, family and community and called her a longtime role model. The email writer, Kenneth Krause, had told Jennifer she was “obese” and “not a suitable example” for local youth; his message urged her to “transform” herself publicly and offered unsolicited advice. Jennifer, a 37-year-old mother of three, said she felt bullied by the note; her husband posted the email to Facebook, prompting widespread support and media attention. News director approved her decision to address the letter on air. Krause later issued a statement repeating his plea that she use the moment to change, while many — including celebrities and her brother Ron — publicly backed Jennifer. The story was discussed on CNN’s Starting Point with Soledad O’Brien, who read Krause’s remarks and highlighted the public reaction.

A 10-year-old Guatemalan girl with cerebral palsy, Rosamaria (Rosa Maria) Hernandez, who was brought to the U.S. as an infant and has lived in Laredo, Texas, is facing deportation after federal immigration agents intercepted her transport to emergency gallbladder surgery in Corpus Christi.

Key points:
- Rosamaria needed specialized care unavailable in Laredo and was transported to Driscoll Children’s Hospital in Corpus Christi by her U.S.-citizen cousin after a notarized letter from Laredo doctors. Border Patrol stopped the vehicle at a checkpoint, permitted the transport but followed the ambulance to the hospital.
- Agents remained at the hospital outside her room through the night. Hospital officials declined to confirm or discuss the agency’s presence, citing patient privacy.
- After surgery and medical clearance, Border Patrol escorted Rosamaria and her cousin by ambulance to the Bexar County Juvenile Detention Center in San Antonio rather than releasing her to family. Officials later said she would be “processed accordingly” under immigration law; a hearing was scheduled to determine next steps.
- Rosamaria’s mother, Felipa Delacruz, is undocumented and was en route from Laredo; her grandfather (a permanent resident) was denied custody at discharge. Legal advocates argued the detention violated longstanding policies discouraging enforcement at “sensitive locations” such as hospitals and noted this case reflects a more aggressive immigration enforcement posture that has extended to schools, churches and hospitals.
- Rosamaria is reportedly in stable condition but frightened; visits at the juvenile facility are reportedly limited to U.S. citizens. Homeland Security/Custums and Border Protection involvement was clarified in later updates. Legal counsel is seeking expedited review and reunification, but the process may take weeks.

The case has drawn attention because it involves detention of a child who has lived in the U.S. for years and has serious medical needs, raising questions about enforcement near medical facilities and treatment of vulnerable migrants.

The piece is a first-person reflection by a former White House intern who was thrust into the 1998 Ken Starr investigation that led to President Clinton’s impeachment. Recounting a tense Christmas Eve 2017 encounter with Ken Starr in a Manhattan restaurant, the author describes mixed emotions—anger, discomfort, and an attempt to confront the man whose prosecutors had aggressively pursued her two decades earlier, jeopardized her family, and made her a public spectacle. Starr’s muted response—“it was unfortunate”—left unresolved feelings.

The author explains how the investigation and the subsequent media maelstrom devastated her life, leading to PTSD and years of therapy. She situates her personal trauma within a broader national wound: the 1998 scandal, amplified by the then-new internet and 24-hour media, blurred private and public boundaries, intensified partisan divisions, and reshaped public discourse. Using frameworks from George Lakoff and trauma experts, she argues the episode functioned like a “collective trauma,” altering cultural norms, encouraging scapegoating, and leaving many issues unexamined for decades.

The essay contrasts 1998’s isolating information environment with today’s social-media-enabled solidarity—particularly the #MeToo movement—which provides communal validation and empowers survivors to shape their narratives. The author acknowledges complexities in her own story (including debates over categorizing her experience), admits she is still unpacking and reprocessing what happened, and expresses cautious hope that cultural reflection and compassion can lead to healing and transformation.

The document mixes two topics. First, it describes an archiving effort—crawls that capture newly created web pages and the pages they reference so that when referenced pages change or disappear, links can point to the archived version. The Internet Archive hopes those archived links will replace broken links or serve as companions so readers can see what authors originally intended; the stated goal is to fix broken links on the web, including crawls of supported “No More 404” sites.

Second, it profiles Rep. Robert E. Andrews (D–N.J.), who announced his resignation after 23 years in Congress to join a law firm. Andrews introduced more bills than any other representative in that period—646 different measures on topics from pajamas to Taiwan, commemorative coins and tariff adjustments—but none became law (only four passed the House and none cleared the Senate). That unusually poor record, Andrews argues, masks his real influence: modern lawmaking tends to fold many ideas into large, must-pass “moving vehicle” bills rather than pass freestanding measures. Andrews says he deliberately drafts and stocks language so his ideas can be grafted onto larger bills; he estimates about 110 of his ideas have become law this way or via companion Senate measures. Examples include changes to Tricare and orthotic-device insurance rules, and his efforts helped prompt policy moves (such as short-sale decision rules by Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) even when his bills died on Capitol Hill. Critics note his reduced clout after Republicans took the House in 2011 and past allegations about campaign funds, but his output and strategy illustrate a shift in how congressional ideas get enacted.

Archaeologists and forensic experts have produced the first physical evidence confirming long-standing written accounts that some Jamestown colonists resorted to cannibalism during the "starving time" winter of 1609–1610. Bones discovered in 2012 during the Jamestown Rediscovery Project—most notably the skull, lower jaw and a tibia of a teenage English girl nicknamed "Jane"—bear cut and chop marks consistent with butchery using a light axe/cleaver and knife. Forensic analysis found four shallow frontal chops (possibly tentative attempts), deeper cuts splitting the cranium from the back, removal of jaw muscle and pry marks on the temporal bone to access the brain; the tibia shows a forceful break like animal butchery. The pattern and placement of cuts indicate human dissection rather than animal scavenging, and evidence suggests right-handed assailants and that multiple people may have been involved.

Jamestown, founded in 1607, suffered catastrophic losses that winter after supply failures and Native attacks: only about 60 of roughly 300 colonists survived. Contemporary colonial accounts had reported cannibalism, but this is the first archaeological confirmation in a New World colony. Chemical analysis of the bone implies Jane had a higher-protein diet before arrival, suggesting she belonged to a household of some standing; she was likely one of the new arrivals in 1609, possibly a maidservant or a colonist’s daughter. Her remains were found mixed with discarded animal bones in a cellar filled during a fort cleanup, and her cause of death is unknown though cut patterns indicate she was already dead when dismembered.

A facial reconstruction produced from CT scans and demographic data was unveiled at the Smithsonian; the remains and reconstruction will be exhibited at Jamestown’s Archaearium. Researchers say Jane was likely not an isolated case, reinforcing historical records that cannibalism occurred during the colony’s desperate famine. Identifying her exact identity remains unlikely given incomplete passenger lists and lack of comparative descendants.

Robin Williams’ death on August 11 at age 63 in his Tiburon, Calif., home was ruled a suicide by asphyxia from hanging, according to the Marin County coroner’s report and autopsy. He was found by his assistant in a bedroom about 11:45 a.m., seated on the floor with a belt around his neck and cuts on his wrist; no alcohol or illegal drugs were present. Toxicology showed therapeutic levels of prescription medications, including two antidepressants (mirtazapine and quetiapine/Seroquel), levodopa for Parkinson’s symptoms, and caffeine compounds. Williams had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in late 2013 and was being treated for severe depression; his widow said he had recently experienced increased paranoia and insomnia and had been sleeping in a stepson’s room.

Investigators noted several personal details: the night before he died he placed wristwatches with someone for safekeeping and called his wife briefly; he had been using an iPad with browser tabs about medications; his pill dispenser had been refilled the day before and pills remained in place. A pocketknife with dried blood was found nearby. Searches of his phone, iPad and computer uncovered no messages or search history explicitly indicating suicidal intent. The report mentions that a prior film role involving a hanging scene affected him emotionally, but there was no evidence of autoerotic activity. Williams’ death prompted widespread grief and remembrance for the acclaimed comedian and actor.

Researchers have found physical evidence in tree rings that Allied attacks on the German battleship Tirpitz during World War II damaged surrounding forests in northern Norway. Dendrochronologists led by Claudia Hartl (Johannes Gutenberg University) and Scott St. George discovered extremely narrow or absent growth rings for 1945 in pines and birches around Kåfjord, where the Tirpitz had sheltered. Sampling at sites from a few hundred metres to about 10 km showed severe growth suppression, tree mortality, and multi-year recovery—effects extending up to ~4 km from the fjord.

Archival and local accounts explain the cause: German crews generated dense artificial fog using chlorosulphuric acid to conceal the 250 m battleship from Allied aircraft. The acidic vapour stripped needles from evergreen pines, halting photosynthesis and biomass production and leaving a distinctive “fingerprint” in the rings. The Tirpitz was later damaged at Kåfjord and ultimately sunk by RAF Lancasters in late 1944 in Tromsø fjord.

Presented at the European Geosciences Union meeting, the study demonstrates how wartime chemical countermeasures produced long-lasting ecological impacts and suggests similar “warfare dendrochronology” signals may be found at other WWII sites.

French investigators reported that EgyptAir Flight 804 sent automatic warnings of smoke in multiple locations minutes before it vanished from radar over the eastern Mediterranean early Thursday, suggesting the start of a fire, though they stressed no conclusions have been drawn. The Airbus A320, en route from Paris to Cairo with 66 people aboard, suddenly lurched, spun and plunged about 38,000 feet into the sea without issuing a distress call. Debris was found about 180 miles north of Alexandria; photos and video released by the Egyptian military showed damaged seats, life jackets, a shoe, a handbag and a scrap of a child's blanket. Search teams from Egypt, Greece, Britain, France, the U.S. and Cyprus continued combing the deep waters for more wreckage and the plane’s black boxes, whose pings are detectable at those depths.

Egyptian authorities have said they consider terrorism more likely than mechanical failure, and some experts note the erratic flight could indicate an explosion or onboard struggle, but no group has claimed responsibility and no concrete evidence has been produced. European security officials said the passenger manifest contained no known terror suspects, and investigators in Paris are vetting passengers’ relatives and questioning all ground personnel who handled the aircraft at Charles de Gaulle. French officials met with about 100 family members in Paris and emphasized that all hypotheses remain under investigation.

The crash—coming after years of political and economic turmoil in Egypt and the October downing of a Russian jet—threatens further harm to Egypt’s fragile tourism and investment climate.

This collection of opinion and news items focuses on the controversy around Emma Watson’s recent Vanity Fair shoot and her role as Belle in Disney’s live-action Beauty and the Beast, using that controversy to question her feminist credentials.

Key points:
- A Vanity Fair photoshoot for Watson, which included a partly revealing shot, prompted online backlash and accusations of hypocrisy from critics who say it conflicts with her feminist and UN HeForShe work. Columnists like Julia Hartley-Brewer and commentators on social media mocked her, while others defended Watson, arguing feminism includes a woman’s right to choose how she presents herself.
- A commentator argues more broadly that Watson damaged her feminist credibility by taking a leading role in a Disney “princess” film. The piece criticizes Disney’s legacy as sexist and outdated, contending that despite superficial updates (Belle as an “inventor,” modern princesses like Frozen’s Elsa), Disney films still objectify and sidel ine female characters—citing statistics about female dialogue in Disney films and arguing that narratives still revolve around romance and male heroes.
- Supporters note Watson’s stated reasons for taking the role—that she believes Belle is not passive and can be influential—and defend her privacy choices (refusing selfies to avoid being tracked). Others point out the irony of objectifying Watson’s body to attack her feminism, underscoring feminist tensions over appearance, agency and public scrutiny.

Overall takeaway: The pieces debate whether Emma Watson’s participation in a high-profile Disney fairy-tale and a revealing magazine shoot undermines her feminist advocacy—raising larger questions about agency, celebrity responsibility, and whether reworking conventional “princess” stories is enough progress for women’s representation.

Two months before a 2-year-old boy, Lane Graves, was fatally attacked by an alligator at Walt Disney World’s Seven Seas Lagoon, Reedy Creek Emergency Services staff warned firefighters to stop feeding two alligators that had been frequenting a retention pond behind Fire Station 3 near the Magic Kingdom. Public-record emails obtained after the June 14 attack show communications captain Claude Rogers and dispatcher Dan Lewis complained that one juvenile and a 4–5-foot alligator were coming onto the station grounds—near dumpsters and parked cars—and making employees nervous. Rogers said Animal Control had been notified and asked crews to cease feeding the animals; Station leadership reportedly gave firefighters a verbal reprimand.

Feeding wild alligators is illegal in Florida because it removes their natural wariness of people and can create “nuisance” animals that become aggressive. Disney’s policy, according to the company, is to relocate small gators and bring in licensed trappers for larger ones, though it was unclear whether the station’s gators were removed before the fatal attack. Reedy Creek Administrator John Classe expressed skepticism that the pond gator could have been the attacker because it would have had to cross roadways to reach the Seven Seas Lagoon; experts note alligator movement varies widely, with some traveling little and others roaming miles. After the tragedy, Disney added warning signs about alligators and snakes and removed crocodilian characters; Lane’s parents have sought privacy.

A 25-year-old Maryland man, Ian Hawes, ran look-alike fundraising websites and Facebook ad campaigns that solicited donations by promising entry to a “Dinner with Donald Trump” raffle. His site (dinnerwithtrump.org) closely mimicked Trump’s campaign pages; donors overwhelmingly told POLITICO they believed they were giving to Trump. Hawes’ American Horizons PAC raised about $1.1 million from 21,253 donors (roughly $350,000 in its first three weeks), spending heavily on Facebook advertising and paying large sums—about $133,000—to CartSoft LLC, a payment company he founded. The fine print on Hawes’ site revealed the “dinner” was not a private meeting but two tickets to a sponsor-selected fundraising event; many donors said the solicitation was deceptive.

POLITICO found numerous donors who gave hundreds or thousands of dollars under the mistaken impression the money would go to Trump’s campaign; some received refunds after complaining. Hawes defended his operation as a legitimate PAC and said contributions would be used to create “value” for donors; he denied it was a scam and disputed some quoted communications. Trump’s campaign later accused Hawes of defrauding donors and issued a cease-and-desist.

Hawes also registered other politically themed domains (e.g., crookedhillary2016.org, imwithtrump.org) and amassed a large email list (over 410,000 sign-ups) he can use for future solicitations. The FEC has limited powers to police such consumer-facing fundraising tactics, and experts flagged the ease with which look-alike sites and targeted Facebook ads can mislead small-dollar donors.

Allen Christopher Ivanov, 19, is accused of killing three people and wounding a fourth at a house party in Mukilteo, Washington, after returning to the party armed with an AR-15 he bought a week earlier. According to a probable-cause affidavit and police statements, Ivanov told detectives he had broken up with his ex-girlfriend, Anna Bui, two months earlier, then decided he wanted to get back together. After seeing Bui at the party with another man, he went to his car, read the rifle’s owner’s manual, loaded a magazine, and reapproached the house around midnight.

Police say Ivanov was discovered hiding outside; he opened fire after a male partygoer said, “No, no, no.” He then entered the home, shot Bui twice (killing her), shot a man running toward the house, fired from a master-bedroom balcony at people in the driveway, climbed to the roof and realized his magazine was empty, returned to his car and drove away. He was arrested about 90 minutes later on Interstate 5. Victims killed were Anna Bui, Jake Long and Jordan Ebner (all 19); Will Kramer, 18, was critically wounded.

Investigators report Ivanov told them the attack was “about a girl,” that he viewed the rifle “as a symbol of power,” and that he had earlier bought a second magazine and signed up for a firearms safety class. A Kentucky-based witness said Ivanov had texted about committing a mass shooting days earlier; detectives also pointed to social-media posts suggesting premeditation.

Ivanov was held without bail and faces multiple counts including aggravated first-degree murder, first-degree murder, and attempted first-degree murder; formal charges were expected shortly. His parents have retained defense attorneys who say the family is devastated. The shootings have deeply affected the tight-knit high-school community where the victims and Ivanov were recent graduates.

On Feb. 4, 2004, Mark Zuckerberg launched thefacebook.com from his Harvard dorm as a college-only social network that combined profile pages, searchable class lists and friend linking. It stood out from competitors like Friendster and MySpace by restricting membership to students, offering a clean interface without spam, and emphasizing privacy controls—features that helped it grow rapidly (about 1 million users by December 2004) and eventually evolve into a global business that became profitable in 2009 and reported multibillion-dollar revenues later.

Facebook added many features over the years—some transformative for the web, such as News Feed and the Like button, others less successful (Beacon, Gifts, brief experiments)—and it has continually curated its public image, including through selective company timelines. For its 10th anniversary the company launched several user-facing items: a “timeline” of Facebook’s history, a new iPhone app called Paper, and “A Look Back,” a personalized video/slideshow that compiles each user’s most-liked photos, statuses and life events. Hundreds of millions of users received these short montage videos, which Facebook engineers optimized heavily (reducing per-video render time from 17 minutes to one) to generate and deliver them at scale. Zuckerberg marked the milestone with a statement about Facebook’s responsibility to connect people and serve its community, and the anniversary materials—complete with his signature on the videos—underscore how Facebook has both shaped online social life and curated its own narrative over its first decade.

This document reviews Kathryn Bigelow’s film Detroit, which dramatizes the July 1967 Algiers Motel killings during the larger Detroit riots. The film re-creates a notorious episode of white police brutality against mostly Black citizens in which three young Black men were killed and many survivors were tortured; official investigations eventually exonerated the Detroit police but left major questions unanswered. The riots themselves left dozens dead, many injured, and thousands arrested as the National Guard and police tried to restore order amid deep racial and economic inequities.

Bigelow and screenwriter Mark Boal (their collaborations include The Hurt Locker and Zero Dark Thirty) stage the story in a cinéma vérité style: a brisk historical prologue traces the Great Migration, white flight, segregation and the structural causes of urban unrest, then plunges into the chaos that culminates at the Algiers. The motel sequence—centered on a starter-pistol prank, an aggressively racist patrolman (Will Poulter), and a mixed group of unlucky bystanders including singer Larry Reed (Algee Smith), Melvin Dismukes (John Boyega), a Vietnam vet (Anthony Mackie), and others—is rendered as an extended, brutal, immersive ordeal. The film is relentless in its depiction of beatings, threats, and murder; its spare score often drops away to let the violence land starkly.

Critics praise the film’s visceral power, historical urgency and technical craft—Bigelow and cinematographer Barry Ackroyd capture escalating terror effectively, and performances (notably Boyega and Mackie) are widely admired. But the screenplay is criticized for trying to cover many perspectives while under-developing characters: it reads more as situational reenactment than deep character study. Bigelow and Boal also mix fact and invented elements, change some names, and fill legal or historical gaps imaginatively, which has prompted debate about accuracy and emphasis. The movie’s courtroom and aftermath scenes are viewed as less compelling than the motel sequence, though the coda about Reed’s survival and determination is noted as intentional rather than consoling.

Overall, Detroit is presented as a harrowing, morally urgent film that forces viewers to confront systemic racism and police violence—events that remain resonant today—while provoking discussion about how to dramatize and interpret historical injustice.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman drew global attention last year when he traveled to Pyongyang, sang “Happy Birthday” to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and participated in a high-profile exhibition basketball game between an ex-NBA squad and a North Korean team. The event highlighted the secrecy and personality cult surrounding Kim, whose exact birth year (commonly listed as 1982, 1983 or 1984) and even some family details remain opaque; Rodman once revealed the existence and name of Kim’s daughter, Ju Ae.

Kim’s birthday is believed to be Jan. 8 but, unlike the grand state holidays for his grandfather (Kim Il Sung’s “Day of the Sun”) and father (Kim Jong Il’s “Day of the Shining Star”), it has been observed in a low-key fashion during Kim Jong Un’s early years in power. Traditions such as distributing sweets to children continue, but large-scale national celebrations have not been evident, and the date is not a formal holiday. Analysts suggest the subdued approach may be intentional—to present Kim as modest or to avoid highlighting his youth and possible inexperience.

Since taking power after his father’s death in 2011, Kim has consolidated control, overseeing purges (notably the 2013 execution of his uncle Jang Song Thaek) and continuing North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs. His international profile rose further after the Sony Pictures hack tied to North Korea following the film The Interview. Chinese officials, meanwhile, publicly extended birthday congratulations and wishes for “new achievement” in socialism. Observers view 2015—after the official mourning period—as the start of Kim’s distinct era, with potential shifts in posture toward dialogue with the South still uncertain.

Study name and design
- ACOSOG Z0011 was a multicenter, randomized, phase 3 noninferiority trial (115 sites, 1999–2004) comparing completion axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) versus no further axillary surgery in women with early invasive breast cancer and 1–2 sentinel lymph nodes (SLNs) positive on standard histology.
- Eligible patients: clinical T1–T2 (≤5 cm) tumors, no palpable nodes, 1–2 SLNs positive by frozen section, touch prep, or H&E (immunohistochemistry-only positives were excluded). All underwent lumpectomy with whole-breast tangential-field radiotherapy; adjuvant systemic therapy was per treating physician.
- Planned accrual was 1,900 with 500 deaths for final analysis; the trial closed early because observed mortality was much lower than anticipated. Primary endpoint: overall survival (noninferiority margin: HR < 1.3). Secondary: disease-free survival and surgical morbidity.

Key results
- 891 patients were randomized (445 ALND, 446 SLND-alone). Median follow-up 6.3 years.
- Median nodes removed: 17 in ALND vs 2 in SLND-alone. Additional positive non-sentinel nodes were found in 27% of ALND patients; nonetheless, total nodal burden was low in the cohort (majority had only 1 involved node).
- Adjuvant systemic therapy rates and types were similar between groups (≈96–97% received systemic therapy).
- Overall survival: 5-year rates 91.8% (ALND) vs 92.5% (SLND-alone). Unadjusted HR for SLND-alone vs ALND = 0.79 (90% CI, 0.56–1.10); adjusted HR = 0.87 (90% CI, 0.62–1.23). Noninferiority was met (P = .008 for noninferiority).
- Disease-free survival: 5-year rates 82.2% (ALND) vs 83.9% (SLND-alone); no significant difference (adjusted HR ≈0.88).
- Locoregional and axillary recurrence rates were very low and similar (axillary recurrence ≈0.9% in SLND-alone).
- Surgical morbidity (wound infection, seroma, paresthesia, lymphedema, axillary web) was substantially higher after ALND; lymphedema rates were significantly increased with ALND.

Authors’ conclusions and implications
- For women with clinical T1–T2, SLN-positive (1–2 nodes) breast cancer treated with breast-conserving surgery, whole-breast radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, omission of completion ALND did not lead to inferior overall or disease-free survival at median 6.3 years and substantially reduced surgical morbidity.
- The only additional information gained from ALND is the exact number of positive nodes, which in contemporary practice seldom changes systemic therapy recommendations. Therefore ALND may be unnecessary in this well-defined group.
- Findings do not apply to patients undergoing mastectomy, those receiving no whole-breast radiation, those treated with partial-breast irradiation or prone positioning that spares the low axilla, patients with ≥3 positive SLNs, gross extranodal disease, or those receiving neoadjuvant therapy—for these groups ALND remains standard.

Limitations
- Early trial closure and fewer events than planned; median follow-up ~6 years (although axillary recurrences tend to occur early).
- Some missing follow-up data on a subset of patients.
- Results are specific to the trial’s inclusion criteria and contemporary multimodality treatment.

Practical impact
- The trial supports avoiding routine completion ALND in a large subset of women with early breast cancer and limited SLN metastasis who receive lumpectomy, whole-breast irradiation, and systemic therapy—potentially sparing many women the added morbidity of extensive axillary surgery without compromising survival or recurrence outcomes.

A nine-year-old girl, Maëlys De Araujo, vanished from a wedding hall in Pont-de-Beauvoisin, Isère, in southeastern France in the early hours of Sunday (about 03:00 local time). She was attending with her parents and sister. Guests searched for about an hour after the DJ announced she was missing, then alerted police.

A large search involving around 100 officers — including divers, cavers, firefighters, volunteer rescuers, sniffer dogs and a helicopter — has scoured the hall, its grounds, dense nearby vegetation, sewers and the nearby Guiers river, but has found no trace. Dogs reportedly lost the scent from the girl’s cuddly toy in the venue car park, which has led investigators to consider that she may have been taken by vehicle. Authorities have opened a kidnapping investigation but say they will not rule out other possibilities.

So far police have interviewed roughly 140–180 wedding guests and are also seeking to question about 70 people who attended two other nearby gatherings that night. They have searched the hall caretaker’s house and car and are checking criminal records and reviewing photos and videos from the event. Prosecutor Dietlind Baudoin urged caution but said the criminal hypothesis cannot be excluded. Maëlys is described as 1.30 m tall, 28 kg, with tanned/dark skin, brown eyes and chestnut hair, and was wearing a white sleeveless dress. Authorities have appealed for any witnesses to come forward.

Actors Alyssa Milano and Minnie Driver publicly criticized Matt Damon after he said in an ABC News interview that sexual misconduct exists on a “spectrum,” distinguishing between criminal acts like rape and child molestation and “shameful and gross” behavior such as groping. Damon called the #MeToo moment a “watershed” and said he supported women speaking out, praised Louis C.K.’s admission of wrongdoing as a basis for accountability, and warned that taking responsibility could end careers. He also discussed Harvey Weinstein, confidentiality settlements, and how social media changes reporting.

Milano tweeted that the “micro” incidents are what make the “macro” systemic — gaslighting, normalization and silencing are why women are rightly outraged — and invoked #MeToo. Driver called Damon “tone deaf,” argued men cannot properly judge or rank abuses they don’t experience, and said there should be no hierarchy of abuse: “it’s all f—ing wrong.” She urged men to listen rather than prescribe how women should feel. The backlash reflects broader debate over how to respond to a range of misconduct allegations and who gets to define or contextualize victims’ experiences.

Lemhi County Sheriff Lynn Bowerman has publicly identified DeOrr Kunz Jr.’s parents, Jessica Mitchell and DeOrr Kunz Sr., as suspects in the disappearance of their son, who vanished from a family camping trip near Leadore, Idaho, on July 10, 2015. Bowerman said investigators have found the couple to be “less than truthful,” noting repeated changes and inconsistencies in their accounts. He believes the parents know where DeOrr is and whether he is alive, but emphasized neither has been arrested and no warrants have been issued. The sheriff said he’s coordinating with prosecutors, the FBI and other agencies and is deliberately delaying charges to avoid jeopardizing the investigation or interfering with the possibility of finding the boy.

Family-hired private investigators have ruled out abduction and animal attack, while behavior analysts and the FBI recently reviewed interviews, prompting renewed questioning of the parents. The couple agreed to polygraphs, and authorities say responses raised concerns. Bowerman asked the public to report any observations of interactions between the parents and DeOrr that might aid the probe.

The sheriff also addressed public fundraising: after learning the parents are suspects, he told callers he could not unequivocally recommend donating. The family has raised about $15,000 for a private investigator, though the grandmother says they are no longer soliciting funds; the related website remains online and any future donations would go to other missing-children causes. DeOrr turned three on Dec. 30; finding him remains the sheriff’s stated top priority. Family members publicly maintain the parents’ innocence and urge the public to withhold judgment until facts are established.

Serena Williams has resumed on-court training after months away following a series of injuries and a serious medical issue. The 13-time Grand Slam champion, who hasn’t played since July, posted a photo on Twitter of herself serving in a hot-pink full-body suit while practicing in Palm Beach Gardens. Williams underwent an emergency procedure for a pulmonary embolism in February, remains on blood thinners, is avoiding long flights, and has only been cleared for light cardio. Her agent said she’s taking things day by day and will return to the tour only when her doctors and she agree she’s ready. Williams injured her foot on glass after Wimbledon last year, had two tendon-repair surgeries and long periods in a cast and walking boot; the resulting immobility may have contributed to the blood clots. She is still ranked No. 10 and has not withdrawn from the French Open, though a comeback at Wimbledon or the U.S. Open is considered more likely.

Belgium’s Kim Clijsters will also probably miss the French Open after a severe ankle injury sustained in a fall at a family wedding; she faces at least four to six weeks of recovery.

Other U.S. news: Ryan Sweeting of Fort Lauderdale won his first ATP title at the U.S. Clay Court Championship in Houston, jumping from No. 93 to No. 71 in the rankings after beating Kei Nishikori. For the U.S. Fed Cup team’s World Group playoff in Stuttgart, teenage players Christina McHale (18) and Melanie Oudin (19) will be relied upon after Bethanie Mattek-Sands withdrew with a hip injury; the German team views the young Americans as dangerous and motivated.

Tuesday night’s Mega Millions jackpot swelled to an estimated $636 million (annuity) after heavy last-minute ticket sales, producing at least two tickets that matched all numbers (8, 20, 14, 17, 39; Megaball 7). The lump-sum cash option would be roughly $341.2 million for a single winner; if unclaimed Tuesday, the jackpot would grow (state officials warned it could reach at least $950 million by Friday). Ticket-buying surged in the final days—one official said 65–75% of all number combinations were likely covered by Tuesday—pushing the prize near the U.S. record.

CNN’s coverage offered practical advice for any winners: sign and photograph the ticket immediately and secure it (safe deposit or home safe); consult a small, vetted team of professionals (an experienced attorney and a certified financial planner) to evaluate lump sum versus annuity, taxes, estate planning, and gifting structures; determine whether you can remain anonymous (only a few states allow it) and consider PR help or security if you cannot; consider laying low or traveling after claiming to avoid media and solicitations; and double-check your other tickets so you don’t miss smaller prizes—about $800 million in lottery prizes go unclaimed each year.

This document contains two distinct items: a brief note about web-archiving crawls and a detailed entertainment news piece about Kesha’s recent struggles and legal battle.

- Web-archiving initiative: The Internet Archive is crawling and archiving pages as they’re created and the pages they reference so that links will still point to the version live when a page was written. The aim is to preserve content and reduce broken links across the web by providing archived alternatives or companion links.

- Kesha profile and legal coverage:
  - Style and health: Singer Kesha, 28, has publicly shifted from her earlier glitter-and-party-girl image to a more natural look. In a Vogue interview she revealed she entered rehab for an eating disorder in January and stayed two months. She described using extreme thinness as a misguided source of validation, acknowledged being unhappy despite positive reactions to her appearance, and said she now focuses on health and self-acceptance while still occasionally embracing “hints of glitter.”
  - Past performance antics: Kesha nostalgically recalled earlier stage rituals—pouring beer on herself and rolling in glitter—that she no longer does because of skin irritation, but she doesn’t regret them.
  - Lawsuit and court developments: In October Kesha filed suit against producer Dr. Luke accusing him of sexual, physical, verbal and emotional abuse, including drugging and rape claims. A New York judge denied her request for a preliminary injunction that would have allowed her to record and release music without working with Dr. Luke.
  - Dr. Luke’s response: Dr. Luke publicly denied the allegations on Twitter, calling them untrue and motivated by money, saying Kesha was like a “little sister,” and insisting the truth will come out; he and his lawyer have also countered and countersued for defamation.
  - Industry and public support: Many artists mobilized behind Kesha after the court decision. Taylor Swift donated $250,000 to help her financially; other musicians voiced support on social media. Producers Jack Antonoff and Zedd publicly offered to produce music for Kesha to help her continue making music despite the legal entanglement. Numerous celebrities criticized the court ruling and praised Kesha’s bravery.

Overall, the piece combines a short technical note about archiving efforts with an in-depth look at Kesha’s personal recovery, public image change, the ongoing legal battle with Dr. Luke, his denials, and the music community’s response.

POLITICO obtained a sealed 1986 interim child-custody ruling that casts Democratic congressional candidate David Weprin in a harsh light amid a tight special election to replace Anthony Weiner. In that ruling, Justice Bruce Wright described Weprin as “heedless” of his infant son’s welfare, “extremely temperamental with a short fuse,” and engaging in both careless and “obsessive” behavior (including allegedly locking himself and the child in a bathroom and leaving the child with a doorman). Wright called the custody suit “rather useless” and ruled against Weprin at the time, criticizing both parents’ conduct in what he called “warlike” relations. The case was later resolved in Weprin’s favor: a 1989 decision by Judge Burton Sherman found the ex‑wife prone to “feign and exaggerate” complaints, said allegations of paternal abuse had “no basis in reality,” and ultimately granted Weprin custody; the parents later agreed to shared custody under New Jersey jurisdiction.

The custody documents surfaced as the heated Brooklyn–Queens special election between Weprin and Republican Bob Turner nears its conclusion. The campaign has included controversial tactics from the GOP, including a mailer tying Weprin and President Obama to support for the proposed Park51 Islamic cultural center near Ground Zero — distributed in the run‑up to the 10th anniversary of 9/11 — which Democrats condemned as incendiary. The district is safely Democratic by history but has been trending conservative; Obama’s weak approval and local demographics (notably a large Orthodox Jewish population) have made the race unusually competitive. Weprin has struggled on the campaign trail with gaffes and an unremarkable profile, while national Democrats have poured nearly $500,000 into ads to try to prevent a Turner upset. Observers warn that a Democratic loss would be politically damaging to Obama and could chill support for his agenda among vulnerable Democrats ahead of 2012.
