Texting while driving is widely illegal and dangerous, but recent court decisions have begun to consider whether people who send texts to drivers can share civil liability if the driver crashes after reading or replying. A Pennsylvania wrongful-death suit named two men who texted a distracted driver as defendants; the judge denied early dismissal, holding that a remote texter isn’t automatically immune simply because statutes ban only drivers from texting. The court relied on a 2013 New Jersey appellate decision (Kubert case), which similarly held that a remote sender can potentially be liable — but only if the sender knew or had “special reason to know” the recipient was driving and would likely read the message while driving, or if the sender actively encouraged the driver’s unlawful texting or otherwise had a special relationship enabling control.

The New Jersey ruling explained that liability requires traditional negligence elements: a duty, breach, causation and injury. It rejected the idea that merely addressing a message to a known driver creates liability, noting the sender should reasonably expect recipients to read messages when safe. It also distinguished ordinary, remote transmissions (like texts, emails, GPS prompts) from direct physical distractions or active encouragement: absent evidence that the sender knew the driver would immediately read/respond or that the sender substantially assisted or encouraged the illegal conduct, courts should dismiss claims. Applying that test, the New Jersey court affirmed summary judgment for a teen texter because plaintiffs failed to prove she knew the driver was driving or would read the text immediately.

Legal commentators see these rulings, plus cases like a lawsuit against Snapchat and proposals such as New York’s “textalyzer,” as signs the law is starting to treat distracted driving more seriously. Still, the knowledge/special-relationship threshold sets a high bar, so suits against remote texters will be difficult to win and are likely to be relatively rare. Practical concerns remain (privacy, evidentiary burdens, and broadening potential defendants), and courts emphasize the primary responsibility remains with drivers to obey the law and avoid distractions.

An unprecedented Ebola outbreak in West Africa—first reported in Guinea in February—has rapidly worsened, killing hundreds and infecting many more across Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea. Aid groups report the highest death toll on record for an Ebola outbreak (estimates in reports ranged from roughly 650 to 672+), and the World Health Organization and Médecins Sans Frontières say the epidemic is not under control.

Key developments and impacts
- Governments and leaders have mobilized emergency measures: Sierra Leone declared a state of emergency and announced house-to-house searches; Liberia closed schools, ordered many civil servants to stay home for 30 days, shut some markets, set aside a national disinfection day and said some communities would be quarantined. Security forces were deployed to enforce measures.
- Public fear, denial and hostility have hampered response: some communities have barred aid workers or hidden sick relatives rather than send them to treatment centers; at least one health ministry building was partly burned in anger after a relative died.
- International organizations pulled out or evacuated personnel: Peace Corps removed about 340 volunteers from the three countries; Samaritan’s Purse and other missionary groups recalled nonessential staff. Some humanitarian workers contracted Ebola.
- Two U.S.-affiliated aid workers (Dr. Kent Brantly and Nancy Writebol) tested positive and were in serious condition; an American man who traveled from Liberia to Nigeria died. Health workers have been heavily affected, including notable physician deaths.
- Transmission characteristics and risks: Ebola spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids of symptomatic patients; incubation is 2–21 days. Because early symptoms mimic malaria, flu and other illnesses and because people are contagious only once symptomatic, containment is challenging but risk to casual travelers is considered low. Authorities worried about regional or international spread given air travel links.
- No vaccine or specific cure exists; case fatality rates can be very high (reported as 60–90%). Supportive care (rehydration, symptomatic treatment) improves survival.

Overall assessment
Officials warn the situation is at a crisis point and likely to worsen before it improves. The outbreak has strained fragile health systems, prompted extraordinary public-health and security measures, and elevated international concern about further spread.

Johnson County, Tenn. — Authorities arrested two people this week in the January slayings of 36-year-old Billy Clay Payne Jr. and his 23-year-old girlfriend, Billie Jean Hayworth, whose 6–8-month-old baby was found alive in the mother’s arms. Marvin E. “Buddy” Potter Jr., 60, and Jamie Lynn Curd, 38, were taken into custody without incident and booked on two counts of first-degree murder.

Sheriff Mike Reece said the killings were “senseless and stupid” and stemmed from anger over communications between the victims and Potter’s daughter, who the couple had complained about for alleged harassment by phone and online after she was deleted as a Facebook friend. Curd, a second cousin of Payne, had defended Potter’s daughter in court and — according to investigators — had romantic feelings for her.

The bodies were found Jan. 31 at the couple’s home. Payne was discovered in his bedroom with a gunshot wound to the head and his throat cut; Hayworth was found shot in the head in the baby’s room. There was no sign of forced entry or an apparent struggle. The victims had been last seen by Payne’s father before he left for work early that morning; a neighbor discovered the scene about five hours later.

The Johnson County Sheriff’s Office and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation conducted an extensive probe, interviewing roughly 150–170 people. Potter and Curd remained persons of interest throughout; Curd began cooperating after a polygraph, which helped focus the case. Both were arraigned—Curd assigned a public defender and initially held with bond raised to $1.5 million; Potter is awaiting counsel and remains jailed on an initial $200,000 bond. The infant has been placed with family members. Sheriff Reece praised his deputies for the intensive investigative effort.

Arizona’s Republican-led Legislature approved Senate Bill 1062 (also cited as HB 2153 in the House) to allow individuals, businesses and religious organizations to cite sincerely held religious beliefs as a legal defense against government or private discrimination claims, and to seek injunctions if they show a burden on religious exercise. The measure passed the House 33-27 after a party-line Senate vote and heads to Republican Gov. Jan Brewer, who vetoed a similar bill last year and has given mixed signals.

Supporters—including the Center for Arizona Policy and some GOP lawmakers—say the bill protects religious liberty and clarifies existing law in the face of aggressive court actions. They point to cases where photographers, bakers and florists declined services for same-sex ceremonies and were sued.

Opponents—Democrats, civil libertarians, LGBT advocates, business groups (including the Greater Phoenix Economic Council) and the ACLU—call the bill a license for discrimination against gays and others, warning it could allow refusals of service (restaurants, medical care, wedding vendors, etc.), harm Arizona’s economy and reputation, and undermine local nondiscrimination laws. Critics argued it would create broad, potentially harmful religious exemptions; sponsors called such scenarios exaggerated. The debate has reignited national discussion on balancing religious freedom with anti-discrimination protections as courts and states confront same-sex marriage and related conflicts.

Camp Cloverleaf (also called Clover Leaf 4‑H Camp) is a year‑round traditional summer camp and retreat facility on Lake Francis in Highlands County, Florida. Operated with modern conveniences, it offers climate‑controlled cabins for up to 150 overnight guests, conference rooms (15–125 seats), a dining hall, auditorium, outdoor pavilion with barbecue, campfire circle (seating 150), waterfront with docks, canoes/kayaks, lighted recreational field, AV equipment and wireless internet. The site hosts school field trips, church retreats, family reunions, corporate meetings, teacher in‑service training, civic and athletic groups, weddings and more. Camp Cloverleaf also runs environmental education programs using 4‑H curricula or customized experiential lessons and offers food service on request. Resident Director: Steve Cooper (cloverleaf4‑h@ufl.edu, (863) 465‑4884); Assistant Director: Bill Tillett. Address: 126 Cloverleaf Rd., Lake Placid, FL 33852. 

Incident (June 22, 2018): More than two dozen people at the camp fell ill. Highlands County officials reported 33 children and three adults experienced symptoms including nausea, vomiting and headaches; one person briefly passed out. Victims were taken to at least two local hospitals; none of the cases initially appeared life‑threatening. Approximately 50 campers remained on site while the Health Department took over the investigation; no cause had been determined at the time of reporting. Camp officials did not immediately comment.

This piece criticizes former NFL coach and current NBC analyst Tony Dungy for saying he would not have drafted Michael Sam, the NFL’s first openly gay draftee, because he “wouldn’t want to deal with all of it” — the media attention and potential locker-room issues — even while insisting Sam should have a chance to play. The writer argues this stance is cowardly and inconsistent with Dungy’s record of supporting players who’d behaved badly by traditional Christian standards (e.g., Michael Vick). Rather than taking an honest, principled stand, Dungy is portrayed as caving to the discomfort of bigoted others and prioritizing convenience over fairness.

The piece also quotes radio host Rush Limbaugh reacting to the report. Limbaugh frames Dungy as the NFL’s moral authority and explains ( sympathetically) Dungy’s concern that Sam’s presence would turn team decisions into constant controversy—every roster move would be scrutinized through the prism of Sam’s sexuality. Limbaugh suggests the situation could be a marketing move for the Rams, and anticipates debate and media pressure no matter what happens to Sam’s roster status. Overall, the article condemns Dungy’s excuse as a cop-out and highlights the broader tension between doing what’s right and avoiding perceived “distractions.”

Greece confirmed it would miss a €1.6 billion IMF loan payment due June 30, underscoring the severity of its financial crisis. Government ministers have said they lack the funds unless creditors agree to release €7.2 billion in frozen bailout money; after talks collapsed over creditor demands, that release did not occur. The collapse of negotiations and the ECB’s decision not to expand emergency funding prompted capital controls and a six-day shutdown of Greek banks.

IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde said Greece would be in default as of July 1 if the payment was not made; an IMF spokesman described a missed payment as being “in arrears.” Missing the payment could push Greece closer to a euro‑zone exit if the ECB cuts off emergency liquidity that banks depend on, although the ECB was expected to maintain that lifeline at least for the short term and some analysts say Greece could default without immediately leaving the euro.

The country’s immediate fate is tied to a snap referendum called by the government for July 5 on creditor-imposed bailout terms. European leaders urged Greeks to vote “yes,” warning that a “no” would amount to rejecting engagement with creditors and increase the risk of leaving the euro. Reporting notes the unprecedented situation: as of the missed payment, Greece is cut off from international rescue loans for the first time in its modern bailouts.

ISIS released a propaganda video that threatens new attacks on Western targets, naming France, Italy, the United States and explicitly referencing Paris, Rome ("conquest of Rome") and the White House. The footage includes shots of homemade explosive devices and scenes of New York landmarks such as Times Square, Herald Square, Fifth Avenue and restaurants, and reprises some material from earlier releases. The group’s online magazine recently featured St. Peter’s Square, prompting Italy to deploy about 1,000 army personnel and increase security around Rome and the Vatican; the U.S. Embassy in Rome warned Americans to be vigilant around sites including St. Peter’s Basilica, Milan’s Duomo and La Scala and warned that general public venues (houses of worship, restaurants, theaters, hotels) could be targeted.

U.S. and New York officials said there is no specific, credible threat at this time but treated the video seriously. The NYPD and FBI reviewed the material and increased patrols and anti‑terror deployments as a precaution. City leaders — Mayor Bill de Blasio, Police Commissioner Bill Bratton and Governor Cuomo — urged residents and visitors to remain alert but not be intimidated, stressing the city is prepared and will not let terrorists disrupt normal life. Analysts warned authorities must take such propaganda seriously given ISIS’s resources and intent to strike Western cities.

Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck (dir. Brett Morgen) is a critically acclaimed, family-approved documentary portrait of Nirvana’s frontman that premiered in May 2015 (limited release) and on HBO. Running 132 minutes and unrated, the film draws extensively from Cobain’s personal archives—home movies, journals, drawings, music and audio tapes—plus interviews with close family and collaborators (including Courtney Love and Krist Novoselic) to present a textured, intimate chronology rather than a mythologized rock-star biography.

Morgen’s film opens with Super-8 home footage that humanizes the toddler Kurt and follows him through a fractured childhood, adolescent loneliness, the formation and rise of Nirvana, and the pressures of enormous fame. He uses haunting animation to bring journal entries to life and constructs a rapid, layered montage style—both visual and aural—that blends archival Nirvana music, private recordings and interviews. The result is an editing tour de force: immersive, often uncomfortable, and resolutely unsentimental. The film stops short of depicting Cobain’s 1994 death directly, noting it tersely, and instead assembles evidence of his insecurity, creativity, addiction and complicated personal relationships.

Critics praise the film for making the man more real than the myth, revealing private moments (including difficult home footage) and offering Frances Bean Cobain a way to “know” her father. Some note limitations—a relatively small set of interviewees, little exploration of Cobain’s musical development, and the necessarily selective narrative shaped by access to family archives—but overall Montage of Heck is regarded as revelatory, artful, and deeply affecting. Grade: A.

A recent cross-sectional study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics examined whether regular apple consumption is associated with better sexual function in women. Researchers surveyed 731 sexually active Italian women aged 18–43 (mean 31.9) with no history of sexual dysfunction, excluding those on certain medications or with depression. Participants reported their apple intake and completed the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), which measures domains including desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction and pain.

Women were divided into two groups: Group A (343 women) who ate one to two apples daily, and Group B (388 women) who ate fewer than one apple per day. Group A scored significantly higher on the total FSFI and specifically on the lubrication domain (both p = 0.001; Cohen’s d > 3), and multivariate analysis identified daily apple intake as an independent predictor of higher FSFI scores (p = 0.002).

Authors caution that the study is observational and cannot prove causation; sample size and cross-sectional design limit broad conclusions. They suggest possible mechanisms—apples contain antioxidants, polyphenols and phytoestrogens (e.g., phloridzin) that may enhance blood flow and mimic estrogenic effects, and apple peels are rich in phenolic compounds—warranting further research (including whether peels are especially important). Overall, the study found a notable positive correlation between daily apple consumption and several measures of female sexual function.

Natasha Exelby, a casual ABC contributor and former Wake Up! co-host, was taken off on-air newsreading duties after a viral weekend blooper showed her looking startled when cameras returned to her live. The clip, widely shared and met with public sympathy and support (including an online petition and endorsements from public figures), sparked debate after tabloids reported she had been “banned.”

ABC management say Exelby has not been sacked and deny she was punished for the mistake. Director of News Gaven Morris said slip-ups happen, presenters aren’t expected to be perfect, and the broadcaster does not publicly discuss confidential shift arrangements. He added Exelby has been offered further training, was “read the riot act” internally after a series of missteps, and may return to on-air shifts subject to normal performance management. ABC emphasized she is a casual contributor who works shifts on a needs basis.

The incident renewed criticism of the ABC’s consistency after a previous, more serious controversy over the vetting of a Q&A audience member. Colleagues in broadcast media shared their own bloopers in solidarity. Exelby declined to comment publicly.

Former New York governor George Pataki suspended his Republican presidential campaign Tuesday after a long-shot bid that never gained traction. Pataki, 70, aired a two-minute video statement on NBC affiliates in Iowa, New Hampshire and South Carolina — using equal-time rules after Donald Trump’s SNL appearance — saying the nation needs a leader who can defeat radical Islam, shrink federal power, and reunite the country. He tweeted his suspension and cited lack of resources and ground organization.

A three-term governor from 1995–2006 who defeated Mario Cuomo in 1994 and led New York after 9/11, Pataki had run unsuccessfully for president several times before and had been largely out of the national spotlight for years. His moderate positions — support for abortion rights and previous New York gun-control measures, and an emphasis on compromise with Democrats — were poorly suited to a GOP primary increasingly dominated by anti-establishment, hard-right sentiment. He seldom polled above 1 percent nationally, peaked at 2 percent in New Hampshire in July, raised only about $153,514 in Q3, and had roughly $13,570 cash on hand at the end of September. He never reached the main debate stage and was frequently overshadowed by better-known moderates like Marco Rubio and Chris Christie.

Pataki briefly criticized Trump’s immigration proposals, drawing a blistering public response from Trump, but the move did not boost his campaign. His exit marks the fourth current or former governor to leave the 2016 GOP field (after Rick Perry, Scott Walker and Bobby Jindal); the contest still contained a dozen candidates after his departure.

The Senate Intelligence Committee voted 10–5 to favorably report Gina Haspel’s nomination to be CIA director, clearing the way for a full Senate confirmation likely this week. If confirmed, Haspel would be the first woman to lead the agency. She has backing from most Republicans and at least five Democrats, making final confirmation highly probable.

Haspel, the agency’s deputy director and a 30-year CIA veteran, received public praise from committee chairman Richard Burr, who called her exceptionally qualified. Two committee Democrats, including ranking member Mark Warner, supported her after Haspel sent Warner a letter saying that, with hindsight, the CIA should not have undertaken the post-9/11 “enhanced interrogation” program (which included waterboarding) and that failing to brief Congress was a mistake. During her confirmation hearing she had stated she would not revive the program and said, “I don’t believe that torture works,” but stopped short of earlier, stronger criticisms.

Her career includes reported roles at a CIA “black site” in Thailand where detainees such as Abu Zubaydah were subjected to waterboarding and other harsh techniques—details declassified at Congress’s request. Opposition remains from some senators: Republicans Rand Paul and John McCain oppose her nomination (McCain has called for clearer explanations of her involvement), Sen. Jeff Flake was undecided, and several Democrats voiced serious concerns about accountability and the agency’s past abuses.

Seattle’s City Council voted 7-2 on June 12, 2018 to repeal a recently passed “head tax” on large employers — a levy of roughly $275 per employee at firms with at least $20 million in annual revenue that was projected to raise about $47–48 million a year for affordable housing and homeless services. The repeal followed intense public protest at a raucous council meeting and an aggressive opposition campaign funded by major local companies (including Amazon and Starbucks) and business groups that quickly raised several hundred thousand dollars and organized a referendum drive.

The move exposed sharp divisions over how to address Seattle’s worsening homelessness crisis, and highlighted the political influence of large employers in the city where Amazon is the largest private employer. Supporters said the tax was a progressive way to finance housing and services amid rising homelessness and deaths among the unhoused; critics argued the city had not shown accountability for existing spending and that the levy risked jobs and investment. Several council members who originally sponsored the tax voted to repeal it, saying they lacked the time and resources to defeat the well-funded referendum campaign.

Mayor Jenny Durkan supported avoiding a protracted political fight and pledged to pursue other partnerships and greater transparency in homelessness spending. The repeal raises questions about whether similar proposals elsewhere (such as a proposed “Google tax” in Mountain View) will proceed and underscores tensions between cities seeking revenue to mitigate growth-related problems and the corporate interests that shape local politics.

A retired nurse and longtime St John Ambulance volunteer, 77-year-old David Knowles, suffered a cardiac arrest while delivering a CPR refresher class at his Exeter church. Feeling dizzy and unwell, he warned his trainees the episode was real and instructed them on what to do before losing consciousness—students initially thought he was role-playing. Trainee Karol Chew and others called 999 and performed CPR until paramedics arrived. Knowles was taken to the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital, where he had a further cardiac arrest and a pulmonary embolism and was put into a medically induced coma. He spent about five weeks in hospital (waking roughly two-and-a-half weeks later) and was discharged in mid-March. Despite initial concerns about brain and organ damage and a lengthy recovery, doctors say he is making excellent progress: mentally alert, walking unaided, and continuing rehabilitation at home. Staff note that if he had collapsed alone while preparing the class he almost certainly would have died.

Escapologist Antony Britton narrowly survived a failed "Buried Alive" stunt at his Escape for Life festival in Slaithwaite Spa, West Yorkshire. Britton, handcuffed and buried under about six feet of soil in a standard grave without a coffin, lost consciousness roughly nine minutes into the attempt after the packed soil crushed his chest and compacted around an air pocket. Crew members, aided by a digger and hand-digging, pulled him out unconscious; paramedics gave him oxygen and he later regained consciousness. He sustained a cracked rib, scratches and bruises but said he felt he had been “seconds away from death.” Britton — who runs the charity events organisation and staged the stunt to raise funds for Leukaemia & Lymphoma Research (soon rebranding as Bloodwise) — said he won’t attempt the feat again and will take weeks to recuperate.

Britton is believed to be only the third person in a century to try the classic buried-alive escape, following Harry Houdini (1915) and Alan Alan (1940), both of whom were also rescued. The report notes past fatalities in related stunts, underscoring the danger. Britton praised his well-drilled crew and digger operator for the rescue and described the emotional experience of nearly dying before being recovered.

A 31-year-old Chinese tourist visiting Germany was accidentally registered as an asylum seeker and spent 12 days in the German refugee system before officials realized the error. Speaking only Mandarin, the man—identified as Mr. L—went to report a robbery early in his trip but ended up signing paperwork that triggered asylum processing. He was fingerprinted, medically examined, had his passport held, and was moved 220 miles to a refugee shelter in Dülmen, where he received food and allowances.

Staff noticed he behaved differently from typical refugees—well dressed, repeatedly asking for his passport and trying to explain he wanted to continue traveling to France and Italy. Communication failed until a local Chinese restaurant provided an interpreter (after attempts with translation apps), at which point officials understood the mistake and released him to resume his tour. German Red Cross officials said the case illustrated how language barriers and heavy bureaucracy can entangle unintended people during the country’s large refugee intake. An amendment to the report notes earlier location details were corrected: there is no police record of a robbery in Heidelberg and asylum cannot be applied for at Heidelberg town hall.

Eli Rosenbaum is a longtime Justice Department investigator who has spent his career tracking down suspected Nazi collaborators who entered the United States after World War II. Motivated by encounters with survivors and a personal awakening to the Holocaust, he joined the Office of Special Investigations (now part of the Human Rights Enforcement Section) as an intern in 1979 and rose to lead the unit’s work. Rosenbaum and a small team have pursued hundreds of cases—relying on sparse, often Cold War–era documents, forensic historical research, and survivor testimony—to strip alleged perpetrators of U.S. citizenship and seek their deportation. Since 1979 the office has succeeded in revoking citizenship in dozens of cases and deporting many accused collaborators.

The reporting centers on Jakiw Palij, an elderly man living in Jackson Heights, Queens, long accused of serving as a guard at the Trawniki camp in Nazi-occupied Poland. Palij maintains he was coerced into service and never participated in killings; prosecutors say his role helped facilitate mass murder. A federal judge revoked his citizenship in 2004, but deportation has not been completed because reluctant European countries refused to accept him, so he remains in the U.S. The piece highlights the practical and moral challenges Rosenbaum’s unit faces: aging suspects and witnesses, scarce and contested evidence (especially material from the Soviet bloc), public pressure, and the limitation that U.S. law generally allows only denaturalization and deportation rather than criminal prosecution for wartime atrocities. Rosenbaum sees pursuing every remaining suspect as an obligation to victims, despite the emotional toll and accelerating time pressures as the generation involved passes away.

David Welch, 54, left his Manhattan, Kansas, home without explanation on Sept. 2 and drove away in his maroon Pontiac Montana van. Family reported him missing within days; police initially found no indication he was in danger and notified other agencies. For nearly seven weeks there were no clues.

On Oct. 18 a passerby spotted an overturned vehicle in a deep ravine about 47 miles outside Green River, Utah — roughly 850–900 miles from Welch’s home on a desolate stretch of I‑70. Tire marks showed the van went straight off the road and rolled onto its passenger side; investigators believe he likely fell asleep at the wheel. Welch was found trapped and injured in the wreck and had written love notes to his wife of 32 years and their four sons during the time he was stranded. He was deceased when discovered; authorities do not know exactly how long he survived after the crash. The notes have been turned over to his family. His unexplained travel so far from home and the length of time he lived after the accident remain unanswered.

On April 7–8, 2017 a hijacked beer delivery truck was driven down Drottninggatan, a busy pedestrian street in central Stockholm, and crashed into the Ahléns department store, killing four people and injuring about 15 (ten remained hospitalized, including a child; several seriously). Police detained a 39‑year‑old man from Uzbekistan on suspicion of terrorism; authorities say he was previously known to security services as a “marginal” figure but had not been seen as a serious recent threat. Investigators found a suspicious technical device in the truck’s cab that may be an explosive or incendiary device; bomb-disposal and forensic teams were involved and investigators have not ruled out other accomplices. No claim of responsibility had been confirmed.

Government and public response was defiant: Prime Minister Stefan Löfven declared the act terrorism, ordered tightened border controls, visited the scene and urged people to continue life normally; Monday was declared a national day of mourning with a minute’s silence. The king and other senior figures expressed shock and solidarity; citizens left flowers at the site. Police increased patrols and conducted raids, but reported no further arrests. The attack echoed recent vehicle-ramming assaults in Europe (London, Nice, Berlin) and revived debate in Sweden about openness, integration and security after large recent migrant arrivals. International cooperation and investigations involving foreign security services were reported.

Papa John’s released its first advertisement since founder John Schnatter was forced to resign as chairman following revelations he used the N-word and earlier blamed NFL protests for hurting sales. The short video, posted to Facebook and Twitter, directly addresses customer outrage by showing real tweets accusing the company of racism and demanding change, and pledging that Papa John’s is “reviewing our culture from top to bottom” and will “earn back your trust through action.”

The move is part of a broader effort to distance the brand from Schnatter—removing his image from marketing, ousting him from his office, and attempting to limit his influence as he publicly challenges CEO Steve Ritchie and seeks to regain control. Schnatter’s spokesman criticized the ad as misleading and said some fans want him back.

Papa John’s announced mandatory bias training beginning in October at its corporate office and corporate-owned stores (about 20% of U.S. locations), after its leadership completed training two weeks earlier. The program will cover unconscious bias, racial and cultural sensitivity, and bias management. CEO Steve Ritchie published an open letter outlining additional steps: an internal diversity and inclusion audit, a listening tour of major cities, a minority-owned franchise support program, creation of a community-focused foundation, formation of an external DEI advisory group, and a pledge to diversify leadership.

The company has also hired Bank of America and Lazard to help stabilize the business amid declining sales. Observers note the ad mirrors crisis-response tactics used by other firms (e.g., Facebook, Uber, Wells Fargo, Starbucks) that acknowledged customer concerns and implemented anti-bias measures.

Former Massachusetts Republican senator Scott Brown has stayed active since leaving office, focusing on athletics and a low-key life in New Hampshire. A longtime triathlete and cycling enthusiast, Brown has been volunteering as a mechanic at Gus’ Bike Shop in North Hampton and remains a committed competitor—saying he “almost does a triathlon every day,” trains two to two-and-a-half hours daily, and has never failed to finish a race. He describes memorable rides in the Spanish Pyrenees and along Route 1A on the New Hampshire coast, enjoys tandem rides with his wife (including a rainy 111-mile Pan-Mass Challenge), owns four bikes (including two tandems and a Trek TTX 9.9), and wants to learn full bike maintenance. He recounts dangerous moments—high-speed descents, extreme-heat races requiring IV fluids, crashes that required knee surgery—and frequent run-ins with inconsiderate drivers. Brown contrasts triathlete camaraderie with some clique-y road-bike culture, names Lance Armstrong as an influential figure despite later disappointment, and says cycling is popular among politicians (he’s ridden with John Kerry and others). He encourages newcomers simply to start riding.

Separately, in April 2017 President Donald Trump nominated Brown to be U.S. ambassador to New Zealand; the Senate must confirm the pick. Brown had earlier backed Trump, briefly been considered for VA secretary, and worked as a Fox News contributor after losing his 2012 Senate reelection to Elizabeth Warren and a 2014 New Hampshire bid.

Also in the news, Brown was implicated by former Fox host Andrea Tantaros’ new lawsuit alleging that during an August 2015 on-set appearance he made sexually suggestive comments to her and touched her lower waist. Brown is not a defendant in the suit, has denied the allegations as false, and said his interactions with Tantaros were professional and in full view of staff. The suit forms part of broader allegations against Fox News figures and its workplace culture; Fox declined to comment on pending litigation. Brown’s past includes an unrelated, withdrawn 2000 defamation suit linked to an earlier harassment allegation.

Jennifer Love Hewitt and actor Brian Hallisay have welcomed their first child, a daughter named Autumn James Hallisay, born November 26. The couple, who secretly married recently, began dating in 2012 after reconnecting on the Lifetime series The Client List and were publicly revealed as engaged and expecting in June. They chose to keep the baby’s sex a surprise and held a gender‑neutral baby shower in October. Throughout her pregnancy Hewitt said she felt lucky and tried to stay stress‑free; she’s spoken about her desire to be a mother following the death of her own mother from cancer.

This document outlines the scale, causes, and institutional responses to child sexual abuse in India, placing it within a broader context of severe challenges facing the country’s children.

Scope and context
- India has about 430 million children and faces widespread child welfare problems: high under‑five mortality (1.7 million/year), widespread malnutrition and stunting, millions out of school, weak birth registration, early marriage, trafficking, homelessness, forced labor and drug abuse.
- An estimated 40% of children are considered vulnerable and in need of protection.

Prevalence of child sexual abuse
- A 2007 government survey—among the largest of its kind—found 53% of interviewed children reported one or more forms of sexual abuse and over 20% reported severe abuse. Of those reporting abuse, 57% were boys.
- Most victims do not report abuse: 72% told no one and only 3% reported to police. Perpetrators were usually known to the child (e.g., uncles, neighbors).
- Critics note methodological flaws in the 2007 survey (non‑random sampling and focus on vulnerable children), so its percentages cannot be generalized to all Indian children, but it signals a serious problem.
- NGO and smaller studies corroborate high prevalence: a 1998 RAHI study of middle/upper‑class women found 76% reported childhood abuse; a 2005 Chennai study found 48% of boys and 39% of girls reported sexual abuse, with 15% describing severe forms.
- Official record indicators: after a high‑profile 2012 adult rape case, UNICEF noted one in three rape victims is a child and cited over 7,200 child rapes a year (likely an undercount).

Public reaction and legal/institutional responses
- Media and NGOs have raised awareness and exposed protection failures, driving public pressure for reform.
- India enacted its first comprehensive child sexual abuse law in May 2012 (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act) after long‑running cases and public outrage—e.g., the Ruchika Girhotra case, in which a police officer abused a 14‑year‑old; he was convicted only decades later and received a limited sentence, highlighting systemic failures.
- The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), created in 2007, acts as a child‑rights watchdog, monitors legislation (including the 2012 Act and the Right to Education Act), and intervenes where police or authorities fail. It has campaigned against corporal punishment and taken up high‑profile failures.

Systemic shortcomings and consequences
- Despite legal advances and oversight bodies, India lacks an effective social services network to prevent abuse and support vulnerable children.
- High‑profile failures illustrate this gap: the Nithari murders (discovery of multiple raped and killed children in 2006) exposed police inaction and helped spur the NCPCR’s creation; the 2012 death of two‑year‑old Falak (abused while in the care of a severely traumatized 14‑year‑old) exemplifies absence of preventive social care and protection even where warning signs existed.
- Authorities remain under‑resourced and protection mechanisms spotty, leaving many children without timely help.

Overall message
The document argues that child sexual abuse in India is widespread and underreported, compounded by poverty, malnutrition, weak social services, cultural stigma, and institutional failures. While media scrutiny, NGOs, new legislation (2012), and the NCPCR mark progress, systematic gaps in prevention, reporting, investigation, and social protection leave large numbers of children vulnerable.

In April 2008 Rep. Dennis Kucinich bought a sandwich wrap at the Longworth House Office Building cafeteria and bit into an olive pit that allegedly cracked a tooth. This month he filed a $150,000 lawsuit against Restaurant Associates and three other companies that run and supply the cafeteria, alleging negligence and breach of implied warranty and claiming “serious and permanent dental and oral injuries requiring multiple oral and dental surgeries.” The complaint gives few details—no itemized dental costs, no explanation for the three-year delay in filing—and Kucinich has declined to comment beyond calling it a private legal matter. Video from five days after the incident shows him speaking normally on the House floor. The full lawsuit was made available online.

Researchers are disputing a high-profile identification of a mummified head long thought to be King Henry IV of France. The embalmed head with some vertebrae attached was discovered in 1919 at the Basilica of Saint-Denis and resurfaced in recent decades. In 2010 a multidisciplinary team led by French medical examiner Philippe Charlier used CT scans, digital facial reconstruction and anatomical comparisons to identify the skull as Henry IV. The reconstruction noted features such as a nasal growth and pierced ear that seemed consistent with historical descriptions.

A new genetic study from the University of Leuven analyzed ancient tissue from the head and compared Y-chromosome and matrilineal markers with samples from three living male Bourbon-line descendants. The head’s DNA did not match the descendants’ profiles. The Belgian team also tested a blood-stained handkerchief said to hold Louis XVI’s blood; its DNA did not match the Bourbon line either. The Leuven authors conclude the head is not Henry IV and cast doubt on the Louis XVI sample’s provenance.

The conflicting results have prompted two coauthors of the 2010 paper (and two other critics) to ask the British Medical Journal to retract the original identification, arguing the genetic evidence and other archaeological/historical concerns undermine the claim. Charlier defends his work, arguing that centuries of possible nonpaternity in royal lines and limits of ancient DNA make genetic matching uncertain; he also says morphological matches with Henry’s death mask support his identification.

Experts note facial reconstruction is better for excluding candidates than for definitive ID, and that ancient DNA is difficult to interpret. The head remains in a Paris bank vault pending reburial while the debate continues, leaving the specimen’s true identity unresolved.

This piece is a Q&A from New York magazine (June 3, 2013) with Will Smith and his son Jaden, conducted to promote their film After Earth. Will says he conceived the film’s premise while watching Jaden shoot The Karate Kid: a wounded, elite father must watch his son survive a hostile, postapocalyptic Earth—an allegory, Will explains, for the pain parents feel when letting kids face the world.

Much of the interview centers on Will’s idea that life is governed by “patterns” and his search for a unifying “theory of everything,” a view Jaden echoes with youthful, metaphysical speculation about a new, multidimensional mathematics. They talk about family dynamics: younger daughter Willow is the biggest star at home; Jada Pinkett Smith is the vigilant presence on set; Will describes a creative, efficiency-minded household stocked to capture ideas. Jaden describes the evolving father-son working relationship—teaching on Pursuit of Happyness, support on Karate Kid, collaboration on After Earth—and says he’d happily work with his dad again.

The pair address fame and parenting: Will insists his children choose their paths and says he won’t force them into show business; he also outlines efforts to teach them financial literacy. He admits to some “poor parenting moments” (e.g., pushing on with a scene despite snakes on location) and stresses discipline balanced with letting children “own themselves.” Jaden comments on fame’s downsides (rumors) and on his tastes and spending habits.

The article closes with a critical sidebar from the magazine’s writer, who ridicules elements of the interview: Will’s vague talk of “patterns,” Jaden’s abstract pronouncements, and the family’s ties to Scientology-adjacent education and celebrity culture. The critic portrays the exchange as emblematic of celebrity self-mythologizing and questions the coherence of their assertions.

On April 19, 2013, after a chaotic night in the Boston area, authorities apprehended 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev, a suspect in the Boston Marathon bombings, following a daylong manhunt that had shut down Boston and several surrounding communities. Earlier that morning his 26-year-old brother, Tamerlan Tsarnaev, was killed after a violent spree that included the fatal shooting of MIT police officer Sean Collier, a carjacking, assaults on officers with explosives, and a prolonged shootout in Watertown in which more than 200 rounds were fired. A transit police officer was also wounded.

Police found Dzhokhar hiding wounded in a tarp-covered boat behind a Watertown home and took him into custody after surrounding the area. The brothers, ethnic Chechens who had emigrated to the U.S., were identified from marathon surveillance photos released the prior evening. Investigators searched their home and questioned relatives while federal and local authorities probed possible motives, ties to extremist ideology, and whether anyone else was involved. The FBI confirmed it had interviewed Tamerlan in 2011 at the request of an overseas government but found no basis for further action then. Authorities said they had no evidence linking others to the attacks but continued to investigate. The Boston investigation and scene closure at Boylston Street remained active as officials restored public safety and examined the suspects’ backgrounds.

North Korea holds regular elections for local and national assemblies, but they are tightly controlled rituals rather than genuine democratic contests. Voting is compulsory for everyone over 17, turnout is routinely reported at near‑100% (state media often cites 99.7–99.97%), and ballots present a single, pre‑approved candidate chosen by the Democratic Front (dominated by the Workers’ Party). To vote “yes” citizens simply deposit an unmarked paper; to oppose a candidate they must cross out the name in a special booth — a highly dangerous act because voting lacks secrecy and is monitored.

Elections serve multiple regime purposes beyond façade legitimacy: they reaffirm loyalty to the Kim dynasty (Kim Jong Un has stood as a candidate), allow the state to showcase mass enthusiasm, and act as an informal census to verify residents’ whereabouts and detect defectors. Authorities organize voting by neighborhood units (inminban) and even use mobile ballot boxes for the elderly or sick. Dissent or absence can trigger investigations and punishment; many defectors in China return briefly for election days to avoid endangering relatives at home.

Legally the Supreme People’s Assembly and local people’s assemblies are the country’s legislative bodies, but real power rests with the supreme leader and the Presidium; the assemblies largely rubber‑stamp decisions. North Korea’s electoral system was modeled on the Soviet one but has been taken to extremes with near‑unanimous turnout and approval rates, and the state frames elections as patriotic and obligatory civic acts.
