In Bentonville, Ark., police arrested 31-year-old James Andrew Bates on suspicion of first-degree murder in the November 22, 2015 death of 47-year-old Victor Parris Collins, whose death was ruled a homicide by strangulation with drowning as a contributing cause.

Police say Bates called 911 the morning Collins was found floating in Bates’ hot tub. Investigators report signs of a struggle and an apparent attempt to wash down the patio: bloodied water, diluted blood spots on cushions, broken items in the spa (including Collins’ glasses and wedding ring), and a hose used despite freezing temperatures. Bates had visible bruises and scratches; Collins had facial injuries and bleeding. Witness interviews and evidence contradicted Bates’ account that Collins was alive when he went to bed and that subsequent late-night calls from his phone were accidental “butt dials.” A friend who left around midnight said Collins was alive then.

Crucially, utility records showed unusual water use at the residence: 50 gallons between 1–2 a.m. and 90 gallons between 2–3 a.m., consistent with spraying down the patio. Detectives also obtained data from Bates’ smart devices. Police recovered data from the Echo speaker on the premises and obtained Bates’ Amazon account and purchase records; Amazon declined to provide Echo-stored audio without a valid legal demand. Authorities are seeking any audio the “always on” device may have recorded (Echo records to the cloud only after hearing the wake word and stores clips until deleted). Bates also had other smart devices, including a water meter that produced the usage figures.

The case raises privacy questions about using smart-home data in criminal investigations. Bates’ attorney objects, arguing homeowners have an expectation of privacy and that technology shouldn’t be used against them; reliability of IoT device data can also be contested. Bates is jailed without bond. Collins, a former Georgia law-enforcement officer, was married with five children; friends and family have held memorial services and expressed shock.

A U.S. Air Force serviceman who disappeared from Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota 40 years ago has been located and charged with desertion. Jeffrey Michels, 64, was arrested on October 12 in Sanford, Florida, where investigators say he had been living with his wife and children under the alias Jeffrey Lantz. Records show he used that name to obtain a Florida contractor’s license in 1998 for Atlantic Development Corporation. Michels is being held by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations and will face a military trial for failing to report for duty on July 6, 1977. There is no statute of limitations for desertion; penalties range from dishonorable discharge and prison to, in wartime and extreme cases, execution—though severe punishments are rarely imposed. The arrest came days after Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl pleaded guilty earlier this week to desertion for leaving his Afghanistan post in 2009.

Bald eagles are increasingly visible across Massachusetts and other parts of the Northeast, including in and around Boston, as their population rebounds from near-extinction. Recent local sightings include two eagles on the frozen Charles River near the Longfellow Bridge, a pair at Spy Pond in Arlington, and Milton resident Tom Palmer’s first-ever eagle sighting along the Neponset River near Hutchinson’s Field. Social media and community boards have amplified reports, and conservation groups and park staff say sightings around Boston and nearby suburbs are becoming more common.

The comeback follows decades of recovery efforts: eagles were reintroduced to Massachusetts in 1982, produced their first wild eaglets in 1989, and were reclassified from endangered to threatened in 2012. State data showed 46 eagle territories in 2014 and reached a record 51 confirmed breeding pairs statewide recently, with growth especially rapid in eastern Massachusetts. Winter sees more eagles in the state as birds move south from northern New England and Canada for open water and food, and urban sightings reflect improving water quality, the presence of tall trees near shorelines, reduced shooting, and increased tolerance of humans.

Elsewhere along the Eastern Seaboard, higher eagle numbers have led to more human-wildlife conflicts and rehab cases. Wildlife centers report more admissions than a decade ago, including a notable share injured by vehicle strikes when scavenging roadkill. Lead poisoning — often from lead fragments in guts left by hunters field-dressing deer — is widespread in treated birds and can impair flight and make eagles more vulnerable to collisions. Experts urge hunters to use non-lead shot or properly bury gut piles to reduce risks. Overall, the increased presence of bald eagles is a conservation success but brings new management and safety challenges as the birds expand into urban and roadside habitats.

A north Metro Atlanta obstetrics/gynecology practice called Isis Women’s Health Care is changing its name after a decade because people are confusing it with the terrorist group ISIS and the clinic has received dozens of death threats. Founded by Dr. Hughan Frederick and named for the Egyptian goddess of motherhood, the practice grew from one employee to nearly 30 staff across three offices and built a reputation for “a better birth experience,” affiliated with North Fulton and Emory Johns Creek hospitals. Facing safety concerns and negative reactions after global news coverage of the militant group, the clinic has removed its signage and is rebranding rather than closing. Frederick says the decision is difficult and costly—requiring new signage, pamphlets, websites and business cards—but hopes to make the change positive by inviting community input on a new name. A public unveiling is scheduled for March 31 at their Mansell Road office.

- New meta-analysis (published in The American Journal of Gastroenterology) finds that people who both smoke and drink have nearly double the risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) compared with those who only smoke or only drink. This is the first meta-analysis specifically assessing the interaction between tobacco and alcohol for ESCC risk. Investigators conducted a systematic search of population-based case-control and cohort studies and calculated synergy factors to estimate multiplicative interactions. Both alcohol and tobacco were confirmed as independent, exposure-dependent risk factors, and their combined use markedly increases carcinogenic potency. The authors call for focused prevention efforts targeting people who use both substances. (Context: the U.S. expected >18,000 new esophageal cancer cases and >15,000 deaths in 2014.)

- A separate review discusses common beliefs about mixing alcoholic drinks and hangovers. Hangover symptoms are driven mainly by dehydration, hormonal changes, direct alcohol toxicity, and immune-system disruption. Key determinants of hangover severity are total alcohol dose and drinking speed; mixing different drink types does not inherently worsen hangovers. "Congeners"—non-ethanol byproducts of fermentation (e.g., acetaldehyde, fusel oils, tannins)—vary by beverage and can increase hangover severity; darker drinks like bourbon contain far more congeners than clearer spirits such as vodka. Experimental evidence shows bourbon produces worse self-reported hangovers than vodka at equivalent alcohol levels, though objective performance may not differ. No robust randomized trials have tested the effect of drinking order (beer then wine vs. wine then beer), and apparent differences likely arise from drink strength affecting judgment and subsequent consumption rather than mixing per se. Finally, reviews of proposed hangover cures find no proven effective remedies.

Maj. Nidal Hasan, the Army psychiatrist accused of the Nov. 5, 2009, Fort Hood shooting that killed 13 and wounded more than 30, rested his case without calling witnesses and declined to make a closing argument as the court-martial moved to jury deliberations. Hasan has been representing himself and repeatedly acknowledged during the trial that he was the shooter, but he largely remained silent in court, objecting little and presenting only one document — a favorable evaluation from his supervisor.

Prosecutors urged the 13-officer jury to unanimously convict Hasan of premeditated murder so the government could pursue the death penalty. In detailed closing arguments, they outlined evidence they say shows planning and intent: Hasan bought high-end weapons and practiced at a range, used laser sights, chose Nov. 5 because deploying units would be at the processing center, targeted soldiers rather than civilians, and told at least one person shortly before the attack that the Army would “pay.” Prosecutors portrayed Hasan’s conduct as the culmination of a progressive radicalization and said he believed he had a jihad duty to kill soldiers.

The defense did not present testimony; Hasan’s standby attorneys had sought to withdraw, arguing he was effectively aiding the prosecution. The judge barred certain defense claims and rejected some evidence the prosecution offered on motive (including emails with extremist cleric Anwar al-Awlaki and other background material), saying motive is not an element of the charged crimes. Prosecutors called 89 witnesses and submitted more than 700 items of evidence. The jury asked to have one officer’s testimony read back and a Fort Hood map shown during deliberations, which were paused overnight and set to resume the next day. If convicted unanimously on at least two counts of premeditated murder, Hasan would face a penalty phase where the death sentence is possible.

Summary:

Questions arose over whether any of Hillary Clinton’s private emails contained classified material. Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists said that if Clinton’s messages had been processed quietly through FOIA, some material would likely have been withheld as classified — noting that foreign-government information is an obvious classification trigger — but also observed that Clinton, as secretary of state, was the department’s top classification authority and thus unlikely to face charges for retention of classified information. Clinton’s aides said she often handled classified material via secure devices held by traveling aides or in hard copy, and her office said staff review found only one email with a foreign official (from the U.K.). Clinton has denied ever emailing classified information.

The State Department said it will speed the release of about 900 Benghazi-related pages from Clinton’s private account (roughly 300 Libya-related messages) before completing a months-long review of the full set of about 55,000 pages. Spokeswoman Jen Psaki said the review will apply standard FOIA redaction criteria (national security, privacy, privilege, trade secrets, etc.) and that the department plans a single full release at the end of the review, aside from the Benghazi subset. The review will include checking for classified national security information exempt from FOIA.

Charles Krauthammer argues that Americans prefer practical, tradition-based philosophy over rigid ideology and invokes Edmund Burke’s respect for circumstance. He analyzes Paul Ryan’s selection as Mitt Romney’s 2012 running mate, saying vice-presidential picks rarely matter but Ryan could be significant if Republicans successfully rebut Democratic “Mediscare” attacks about Medicare. Krauthammer outlines a two-pronged GOP response: stress Ryan’s plan doesn’t affect those over 55 and shift focus to Obama’s $700 billion Medicare cuts to fund Obamacare, forcing Democrats to defend their record.

He contends Ryan’s presence can nationalize and ideologicalize the campaign—reviving the 2010 dynamic that favored Republicans—while exposing Obama’s weak economic program and lack of vision. Ryan, 42, adds youth and vigor to the ticket and, beyond 2012, could become the long-term face of the Republican movement in the way Nixon, Mondale, and others rose from VP roles. Krauthammer frames Ryan as a movement conservative akin to Reagan: a proponent of constitutional, limited-government conservatism and structural reform, contrasting with both Obama’s “big-government” agenda and the prior era’s “compassionate conservatism.” If Ryan performs well, he could shape the GOP’s future for years regardless of the 2012 outcome.

Most Holy Redeemer, the Catholic parish in San Francisco’s Castro with a congregation of about 450–550 (more than 80% gay or lesbian), is facing anxiety and uncertainty after the archdiocese blocked drag-queen emcees from two charity events at the church’s community hall. The decision—initially blamed on incoming Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone, a vocal opponent of same-sex marriage and a key backer of Prop. 8—has stirred fears about anti‑gay sentiment, doubts about parish leadership, and even talk that the church could be closed by the archbishop.

The controversy began when parish leaders asked to allow drag performers at fundraising dinners tied to sobriety and wellness groups. The new pastor, Rev. Brian Costello, who publicly welcomed a diverse parish when he arrived in July, opposed the idea at first but relayed requests to the archdiocese; the request was denied. Church staff and parishioners stress that drag performers are a regular, accepted presence at the Castro parish and that the proposed appearances were not indecent. Some parishioners acknowledge past excesses—such as a drag performer waving a sexually shaped crucifix—that even longtime members found offensive—so tensions are not one-sided.

Despite the dispute, Most Holy Redeemer remains a vibrant community known for strong music and welcoming liturgies that draw visitors and renew faith for many. Still, parish leaders and local officials say paranoia is high given Cordileone’s national profile on gay issues. Cordileone, set to become archbishop, has publicly opposed same‑sex marriage and stated that Catholics in sexual relationships outside church teaching should not receive Communion; he led efforts supporting Proposition 8 and chaired the U.S. bishops’ marriage-defense subcommittee. His appointment signals to some that the Vatican and U.S. bishops are serious about reinforcing traditional teachings. Parishioners hope for openness from the new archbishop and worry about how his leadership will affect their long-standing, atypically gay Catholic community.

Donald J. Trump tweeted that Nykea Aldridge, a cousin of NBA star Dwyane Wade, had been shot and killed while walking with her baby in Chicago, initially misspelling Wade’s name and linking the killing to his appeal with African-American voters (“African-Americans will VOTE TRUMP!”). At first he did not offer condolences; he later posted a message expressing sympathy. The episode came amid Trump’s concerted effort to court Black voters by emphasizing crime and dysfunction in minority “inner city” communities.

This document compiles reactions to Mitt Romney’s speech at the NAACP convention, where he was frequently booed after criticizing Obamacare and promoting free-enterprise policies. Key themes and voices:

- MSNBC’s Lawrence O’Donnell suggested Romney’s appearance might be part of a GOP “Southern strategy,” implying he may have deliberately courted boos from an African-American audience to appeal to racist voters. Guest Goldie Taylor agreed, arguing Romney went to perform for parts of the GOP base rather than to genuinely engage the black community; she said true outreach would include rejecting voter ID laws she called discriminatory.

- House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi echoed that view, saying Romney’s being booed may have been “a calculated move” to gain political advantage.

- Rep. Emanuel Cleaver of the Congressional Black Caucus criticized Romney’s decision to oppose Obamacare at the NAACP, saying those who vetted the speech should be fired, though he gave Romney credit for showing up.

- Conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh offered a different reading: he defended Romney’s decision to attend and dismissed the boos as predictable given the audience’s attachment to Obama’s signature program. Limbaugh argued Romney used the forum to reach a broader media audience, not primarily to win over convention attendees. He portrayed Romney as a successful, hands-on businessman unfairly characterized as out of touch, and suggested Obama would not attend such an event because of poor black unemployment numbers. Limbaugh also implied Democrats were spinning the booing into an image of Romney wanting to take health care away from millions while favoring the rich.

Overall, the coverage highlights sharply divided interpretations: critics see Romney’s NAACP appearance as performative and possibly strategic pandering to racial resentment, while supporters view it as a legitimate campaign effort to present his economic message broadly despite predictable backlash.

The upcoming film Blind, which stars Alec Baldwin as a novelist who becomes blind after a car crash, is facing criticism for casting an able-bodied actor in a leading blind role. The Ruderman Family Foundation, a prominent disability-rights advocacy group, condemned the choice as “crip-face,” likening it to blackface and urging that portraying disability as a costume become unacceptable. The foundation notes that while people with disabilities make up nearly 20% of the U.S. population, 95% of TV disabled characters are played by non-disabled actors, and it has previously criticized films like Me Before You for similar casting. The film’s trailer debuted Wednesday; Demi Moore co-stars as a married socialite who cares for Baldwin’s character and becomes romantically involved with him. Directed by Michael Mailer, Blind premiered at the Woodstock Film Festival on Oct. 13 and is scheduled for worldwide release July 14 via Vertical Entertainment.

An 18-year-old African-American teen, Michael Brown, was fatally shot by a Ferguson, Missouri, police officer on Saturday, triggering protests, unrest and a federal civil rights and FBI inquiry. Accounts of the encounter differ sharply:

- Witnesses and Brown’s companion, Dorian Johnson, say Brown and Johnson were walking in the street when a white officer told them to move to the sidewalk, stopped his car, and an aggressive confrontation followed. Johnson and several bystanders describe the officer grabbing Brown, firing while Brown ran away with his hands raised, and then continuing to shoot as Brown turned and fell. Witnesses say Brown was unarmed; multiple people estimated several shots were fired.

- Police, including St. Louis County Police Chief Jon Belmar, say preliminary findings indicate a physical struggle began when Brown pushed the officer back into his vehicle, assaulted him and tried to seize the officer’s weapon. Belmar said a shot was fired inside the car, and Brown was later shot roughly 35 feet from the vehicle. Shell casings collected were from the officer’s weapon. The officer was treated for a swollen face and released; he is on paid administrative leave and will undergo psychological evaluations.

The shooting ignited intense community anger in Ferguson, a predominantly black suburb with strained relations with its largely white police force. Protests included peaceful vigils, hand-raising demonstrations, and violent episodes—looting, arson, and confrontations that led to dozens of arrests and injuries to officers. Local leaders, Brown’s family and civil-rights groups called for calm and a full, transparent investigation. Brown’s family retained attorney Benjamin Crump and urged witnesses with video or information to come forward. U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder said the case merits a thorough federal review. An autopsy was completed but details, including the exact number of gunshots and toxicology results, had not been released pending the investigation.

Mitch Daniels, the fiscally conservative governor of Indiana and a potential 2012 Republican presidential contender, delivered an education-policy speech at the American Enterprise Institute that surprised many conservatives by praising several Obama administration initiatives and urging a federal role in education and national standards. Daniels, a former Bush White House budget director and an intellectual, framed teacher evaluations around student growth, defended some collective bargaining, used the language of “social justice,” and limited voucher eligibility to students with two semesters in public school. He touted increased education spending in Indiana and full-day kindergarten expansion, while presenting himself with folksy humor and wonkish detail to appeal to moderates dissatisfied with the GOP field’s focus on cultural issues.

But Daniels’ moderation is qualified. Though he publicly urged Republicans to focus on fiscal issues over social ones, he backed measures at home that angered centrists: he planned to sign a restrictive anti-abortion bill in Indiana cutting Planned Parenthood’s Medicaid funding, banning abortions after 20 weeks, and requiring disputable medical assertions and warnings be provided to women seeking abortions. Critics say these actions undercut his image as a candidate who would move the party beyond the social-wars agenda. The coverage presents Daniels as a shrewd tactician — a disarming, wonky alternative to more combative GOP figures — whose professed pragmatism coexists with conservative stances that could trouble moderates and women’s advocates.

Headline: Sacha Baron Cohen’s Showtime series Who Is America? dupes Roy Moore with a fake “pedophile detector”; Moore threatens legal action

Summary:
- On July 29, 2018 Showtime released an episode of Sacha Baron Cohen’s satirical series Who Is America? in which Cohen, disguised as an Israeli anti-terrorism expert Col. Erran Morad, interviews former Alabama Chief Justice and ex-Senate candidate Roy Moore.
- During the segment, Cohen demonstrates a bogus device he claims detects a hormone associated with pedophiles. The device beeps when waved near Moore, prompting Moore to deny the allegation, call the device faulty and walk off the set.
- Moore had been accused during his 2017 Senate campaign of pursuing underage girls; he later issued a statement saying he was duped, condemning Cohen’s tactics as deceitful, and warning he might pursue legal action if Showtime airs a defamatory portrayal. Moore framed the stunt as an attack on his honor, Israel supporters and religious conservatives.
- The episode is part of the provocative, hidden-camera format of Who Is America?, which has also featured stings on Sarah Palin, Dick Cheney, Bernie Sanders and others. Critical coverage of the show highlighted how guests either expose objectionable views under Cohen’s prodding or simply reveal gullibility; one published ranking of episode three’s guests placed Moore mid-list, noting he largely reacted indignantly and may have suspected a prank rather than exposing new wrongdoing.
- The piece underscores the program’s pattern: public figures are often embarrassed or reveal extreme beliefs when confronted by Cohen’s elaborate disguises and staged scenarios.

The piece describes and mocks a Tumblr that posts selfies taken at funerals. It highlights public outrage—illustrated by a Good Morning America reading—while the Tumblr’s creator adopts a tongue-in-cheek, defiant tone. The page includes commentary about its blue template, links to press interviews for context, and a note that the blog likely won’t be updated (unless paid). The author closes with sarcastic options: follow them on Twitter or risk global mockery by posting a funeral selfie.

Alexander “Sasha” Shulgin (d. June 2, 2014; aged 88) was a pioneering chemist, psychopharmacologist and advocate for cognitive liberty best known for rescuing and popularizing MDMA (Ecstasy) for therapeutic use and for synthesizing and self-testing more than a hundred previously unknown psychoactive compounds. Working after an early career at Dow Chemical, he ran an independent backyard laboratory in California with his wife and collaborator Ann Shulgin. Together they documented their work and subjective reports in landmark books—PIHKAL (Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved) and TIHKAL (Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved)—which combine synthesis methods, experiential notes and psychotherapeutic reflections. Those volumes and their open dissemination made many novel substances widely known and sometimes rapidly spread into gray‑market production, provoking clashes with authorities: the DEA once licensed him as an expert analyst but later revoked his license and the Shulgins were fined after publishing Pihkal. 

Shulgin’s oeuvre includes compounds with diverse effects—psychedelics, entactogens, stimulants, aphrodisiacs and some toxic agents—and particular favorites like 2C‑B and DOM. He rigorously titrated doses, often tried new molecules on himself first (to protect others), and invited small groups of trusted colleagues into controlled trials. Ann applied some of these agents in psychotherapeutic settings, notably MDMA‑assisted therapy. Shulgin argued for legalization and regulated, informed access to psychoactive drugs, framing them as tools for personal and spiritual exploration rather than purely criminal matters. His work profoundly influenced recreational, therapeutic and scientific communities, while also fueling controversies over public safety and policy. He was remembered as a mentor, iconoclast and generous proponent of open research into consciousness.

Iran has executed a currency trader, Vahid Mazloumin—nicknamed the "Sultan of Coins"—and another member of his network after convicting them of “spreading corruption on earth.” Authorities say Mazloumin hoarded about two tonnes of gold coins to manipulate local prices; both men were hanged. Their arrests followed a July crackdown on speculators and an August directive from Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei authorizing special courts to try financial crimes. Those courts have rapidly tried and in some cases televised sentences, prompting criticism from Amnesty International, which called the executions “horrific,” a violation of international law for non-lethal offenses, and noted due-process concerns.

The backdrop is a severe economic crisis: US sanctions and other pressures have driven the Iranian rial down roughly 70% against the dollar in the latest round, increasing demand for gold coins and dollars as stores of value. The currency tumble and rising prices have fueled public anger over corruption and prompted arrests of many small currency and gold dealers, including a reported roundup of about 130 traders in Tehran’s bazaar. The rial was trading around 12,900 to the dollar at the time of the report, still far weaker than a year earlier.

A 35-year-old Evans, Georgia woman, Rachel Lehnardt, has lost custody of her five children (ages 4, 6, 8, 10 and 16) and was arrested on two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor after allegedly hosting a sexualized party at her home for her 16-year-old daughter and friends. Authorities say the incident came to light when Lehnardt confided in an Alcoholics Anonymous sponsor during a meeting; the sponsor reported the account to the Columbia County Sheriff’s Office.

According to the sponsor’s statements (summarized in the sheriff’s report), the daughter texted to ask if friends could "party" at Lehnardt’s house; Lehnardt agreed. The teens allegedly drank alcohol and smoked marijuana, played a game of naked Twister with Lehnardt, and used a hot tub. Lehnardt told the sponsor she had sex with an 18-year-old man in a bathroom and later awoke to find the daughter’s 16-year-old boyfriend having sex with her. She also reportedly showed her daughter pornographic photos and used sex toys in front of the group. No rape charges have been filed; authorities said 16 is the age of consent and there was “no evidence of rape.” Lehnardt posted $3,200 bond and her attorney says some allegations were exaggerated; Lehnardt has said she will seek counseling and continue AA.

Congressional negotiators unveiled a $1.1 trillion, 1,582‑page omnibus spending bill late Monday that implements the December budget agreement and would fund the federal government through the rest of fiscal 2014. Leaders aim to pass a short, 3‑day continuing resolution first to avoid a shutdown, then move the omnibus through the House and Senate this week.

Major features:
- Overall funding: $1.012 trillion in regular discretionary funding, plus $92 billion for overseas operations and about $6.55 billion for disaster relief.
- Sequester relief: Partially undoes sequester cuts, restoring Head Start to $8.6 billion (a roughly $1 billion, 13% increase) and partially restoring funding for medical research (NIH up to $29.9 billion) and job training. Federal civilian and military personnel get a 1% pay raise.
- Health care: Keeps appropriations for implementation of the Affordable Care Act frozen at post‑sequester levels, limiting new funding but not including riders that would block the law; the White House retains flexibility to finance health exchanges.
- Defense and war funding: Base defense funding reduced from earlier proposals but includes $92 billion in war/overseas contingency operations, about $10 billion more than the Senate sought.
- Regulators and agencies: Tight funding for Wall Street regulators — modest increases for the CFTC and SEC (with elimination of a $25 million SEC reserve). TSA funding reduced about $336 million overall, with policy changes favoring private screeners and capping screening personnel.
- Policy riders and restrictions: Dozens of contentious provisions remain, including bans on transferring Guantanamo detainees to the U.S., restrictions on aid to Libya until cooperation on Benghazi investigations, limits on certain gun‑tracking programs and DHS ammunition reporting, and a bar on enforcing incandescent bulb efficiency rules. Some conservative proposals (e.g., new greenhouse gas regulation bans, the global gag rule) were dropped.
- Veterans’ pensions: Exempts disabled veterans and survivors from a cost‑of‑living reduction included in the December deal, though the overall military retirement cut is not fully reversed.
- Other notable choices: No new funding for high‑speed rail, the IMF, or UNESCO; changes to Export‑Import Bank rules affecting coal projects; limits on conferences, travel and awards to curb excess agency spending.

Political context:
- The bill is a negotiated compromise praised by leaders of both parties and the White House as averting another shutdown and reflecting the December budget accord, but it leaves agency budgets well below the president’s requests — a win for Republicans who emphasize lower discretionary spending.
- Some conservatives and outside groups oppose the omnibus as too big or inconsistent with priorities, so final passage was uncertain though leaders expected bipartisan majorities.

Police released new surveillance footage and a sketch in the unsolved August 2, 2016 murder of 30-year-old Karina Vetrano, who disappeared while jogging in Spring Creek Park (Gateway National Recreation Area) in Howard Beach, Queens and was later found beaten, sexually assaulted and strangled in a marshy area off the trail.

Key points:
- The newly circulated video (released with the family’s approval) shows Vetrano jogging minutes before she vanished—earbuds in, hair in a ponytail—and is being used to keep the case in the public eye and prompt tips.
- Police also released a sketch of a man seen in the area that day wearing a woven wool cap; authorities say he is someone they need to speak with but have not labeled him a suspect or person of interest.
- Investigators obtained DNA from three locations (neck, phone and fingernails); fingernail DNA is the strongest and all samples point to the same individual, but searches of local, state and national databases have not produced a match.
- The NYPD and Vetrano’s family continue to seek public assistance; a reward totaling nearly $300,000 (including donations raised by the family) is offered for information leading to an arrest.
- Anyone with information is asked to contact NYPD Crime Stoppers at 1-800-577-TIPS (or Spanish 1-888-57-PISTA), via www.nypdcrimestoppers.com, or by texting tips to 274637 (CRIMES) then entering TIP577.

Japanese authorities upgraded the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear crisis from Level 5 to Level 7 on the International Nuclear and Radiological Event Scale (INES), the highest rating and the same category as the 1986 Chernobyl disaster. The decision was based on cumulative emissions data showing that the plant released on the order of hundreds of thousands of terabecquerels of radioactive iodine-131 after the March 11 earthquake and tsunami—exceeding the Level 7 threshold of “several tens of thousands” of terabecquerels. Officials estimate Fukushima’s total releases so far at roughly one-tenth of Chernobyl’s, though they warned releases could grow if the situation continues.

Authorities stressed differences with Chernobyl: Fukushima’s containment structures largely remain intact, no immediate radiation deaths have been reported, and current daily releases are far lower than early peaks. Still, the upgrade reflects widespread, long-lasting environmental contamination: tap water, vegetables and seawater have tested positive for radiation, hot spots have been found in soil and playgrounds, and authorities expanded evacuation recommendations to additional towns after finding elevated levels. Greenpeace reported contaminated vegetables and radiation at levels used as evacuation thresholds in Chernobyl.

The plant’s problems stem from tsunami damage that knocked out cooling and backup power, leading to reactor meltdowns, explosions and fires. Ongoing aftershocks, continuing releases, contaminated water pooling at the site and worker exposures complicate stabilization and cleanup, which experts say could take months to years. The upgrade heightened public anxiety and spurred large anti-nuclear protests in Tokyo, even as officials urged calm and emphasized efforts to prevent further health harm.

Summary:

Keith Olbermann’s abrupt departure from MSNBC followed weeks of negotiations rather than a sudden firing. Multiple outlets report longtime tensions with network management and stalled contract talks; Olbermann’s agent had been pressing for higher pay, and NBC declined raises. Sources say Comcast executives viewed him as a “loose cannon” and were uncomfortable with the publicity risk around the company’s takeover, which helped drive exit talks. Negotiations reportedly lasted weeks (about seven in some accounts) and produced an exit package reportedly worth well over $7 million that includes a short on-air blackout (variously reported at under 4½ months) and a likely non-television/gag clause. Attorney Patty Glaser helped negotiate the deal.

Media items note Olbermann may pivot to internet projects (he signaled an MLB.com “Baseball Nerd” blog return on his Twitter profile) and has been linked as a possible contributor or inspiration for an Aaron Sorkin cable-news drama. His Twitter activity dropped immediately after the announcement, consistent with claims of a temporary silence clause, though his bio was later updated.

Separate sports commentary in the document reviews American League East teams and broader MLB issues: it criticizes the Yankees’ weakened defense after injuries and roster moves (highlighting specific miscues in a game), worries their makeshift lineup and poor defense could doom them, and cautions about roster patchwork elsewhere. The piece assesses other division teams—Toronto (doubts about rotation and reliance on acquisitions like R.A. Dickey, with concern over painkiller Toradol use across baseball), Boston (mix of prospects and questionable veteran signings), Baltimore (emerging youth and prospects), and Tampa Bay (deep pitching depth despite trades)—and projects Tampa Bay as the class of the division with a likely chase for the second spot between Toronto and Baltimore.

Overall tone: Olbermann’s exit was negotiated amid mutual friction and corporate concern, producing a lucrative severance and a limited media blackout; meanwhile, the MLB coverage spotlights roster vulnerabilities, medical/drug concerns, and pennant-race expectations in the AL East.

This document compiles multiple Time magazine pieces profiling 2014’s most consequential people, events and movements. Key subjects include Alibaba’s founder Jack Ma, the Ebola fighters (Time’s Person of the Year), Iraq’s Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani, the Ferguson/Black Lives Matter protests, and Vladimir Putin — each presented through reporting, profiles and first-person accounts. Summaries below:

1) Jack Ma and Alibaba
- Alibaba’s Sept. 19, 2014 IPO was the largest ever, making founder Jack Ma extremely wealthy and positioning Alibaba as a global e-commerce giant. The company serves roughly a third of China’s population through marketplaces that host millions of merchants and via Alipay, its dominant payments service.
- Ma built Alibaba from 1999 by combining technical innovation with political and cultural savvy: prior government work helped secure Party backing; he pursued a strategy adapted to China’s market (e.g., keeping the site largely free to build scale), and deployed a distinctive management and marketing persona rooted in Chinese cultural motifs.
- Ma’s narrative and leadership helped Alibaba displace foreign competitors in China and become a major global internet player.

2) Time’s Person of the Year: The Ebola Fighters
- The 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa turned into an epidemic that exposed weaknesses in local health systems and global response mechanisms. The outbreak spread through Liberia, Guinea and Sierra Leone and reached other countries, stressing infrastructure and sparking fears and overreactions worldwide.
- Time honored the front-line responders—MSF, Samaritan’s Purse, local doctors, nurses, burial teams, ambulance drivers and volunteers—as the Person of the Year for their courage, sacrifice and the time they bought the world to improve defenses.
- The coverage includes moving first-person accounts from health workers and survivors (e.g., Kaci Hickox, Dr. Kent Brantly, Nina Pham, Salome Karwah, Dr. Jerry Brown, Dr. Mosoka Fallah, Dr. Philip Ireland, Iris Martor) describing conditions in treatment units, risks taken, personal losses, community denial and stigma, and the emotional and physical toll of caring for Ebola patients. Many recount extreme hardship, small victories, and the moral urgency of continuing to help despite personal danger.
- The piece also criticizes slow, disorganized international responses, bureaucratic obstacles, and irrational fear-driven policies (e.g., quarantines of asymptomatic volunteers), arguing the outbreak revealed global vulnerability to epidemics and the need to strengthen public-health systems and global coordination.

3) Massoud Barzani and the Kurds
- Massoud Barzani, leader of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) in northern Iraq, embodies Kurdish aspirations for statehood; under his rule the autonomous Kurdish region has its own army (peshmerga), economy, and political institutions.
- The rise of ISIS in 2014 put Kurdish gains at risk but also elevated Kurdish leverage: as Iraqi forces collapsed in parts of the country, Kurdish peshmerga both defended Kurdish territory and recaptured disputed areas like Kirkuk. U.S. airpower supported Kurdish defenses, and the KRG announced plans for an independence referendum.
- Barzani’s leadership is described as tribal but effective; his long experience navigating regional powers (Iran, Turkey, the U.S., Israel) has kept Iraqi Kurdistan relatively stable and economically improved. Yet independence risks destabilizing the region and complicates relations with Baghdad and neighboring states. By year’s end Barzani struck a pact with Baghdad under U.S. pressure, showing his pragmatic constraints.

4) Ferguson and the Rise of a New Civil Rights Movement
- The police killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, and the aggressive police response galvanized sustained national protests over police brutality and racial injustice in 2014. The movement coalesced around hashtags and local activists, spreading demonstrations nationwide and internationally.
- Activists (e.g., Johnetta Elzie, DeRay Mckesson) used social media to sustain attention, organize actions and build networks. The protests prompted broader conversations and some political responses about policing, accountability and criminal-justice reform.
- Coverage emphasizes the mix of peaceful protest, civil unrest, community anger, and the role of local history and systemic inequities that fueled the uprising. The movement’s persistence made police killings an ongoing national story rather than isolated incidents.

5) Vladimir Putin and Russia’s Assertiveness
- In 2014 Putin consolidated domestic popularity by seizing Crimea from Ukraine, an act many Russians saw as restoring national pride after the Soviet collapse. The annexation and Russia’s role in eastern Ukraine marked a bold reassertion of power.
- The move provoked international condemnation, sanctions, Russia’s diplomatic isolation (expulsion from G-8), and economic pain at home: a collapsed oil price, ruble devaluation, inflation and a looming recession. The downshift in Russia’s economic prospects contrasted with the surge in Putin’s approval ratings.
- The MH17 airline tragedy over eastern Ukraine and the strained G-20 summit highlighted the geopolitical costs. Yet for many Russians, restoring territory outweighed economic fallout—a reflection of Putin’s goal to reestablish Russia as a great power despite consequences.

Overall themes
- Leadership and sacrifice: Profiles highlight leaders and ordinary people whose decisions—whether entrepreneurial, political, or humanitarian—shaped 2014’s defining moments.
- Local action with global effects: Whether Alibaba’s global IPO, the Ebola responders, Kurdish defense against ISIS, Ferguson’s protests, or Russia’s moves in Ukraine, local actors and events had wide international consequences.
- Systemic vulnerabilities exposed: The Ebola crisis and the Ukraine conflict revealed weaknesses—in global health systems, international institutions, and regional stability—that demand better coordination and planning.
- The interplay of moral authority, political calculation and public narrative: Each story shows how narratives, symbolism and public perception (from Jack Ma’s persona to Putin’s Crimea move to the moral witness of Ebola fighters and Ferguson protesters) powerfully shape outcomes.

This collection underscores 2014 as a year when crisis and ambition forced difficult choices, elevated unexpected heroes, and reshaped global politics, economics and public consciousness.

At a recent Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation staff meeting, Bill Gates recounted two meetings he had with Donald Trump and described being unsettled by how much Trump seemed to know about his daughter’s appearance. Gates said Trump encountered his daughter Jennifer at a Florida horse show, later landed by helicopter at the same event, and during their first conversation in December 2016 Trump “knew” a lot about her looks, which Melinda Gates found objectionable.

Gates also said Trump asked him on two occasions whether vaccines were harmful — while considering a commission influenced by vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — and repeatedly asked whether there was a difference between HIV and HPV; Gates reportedly explained that the two are distinct. The remarks were broadcast by MSNBC’s All In with Chris Hayes. Commentators highlighted the contrast between Trump’s apparent focus on personal details and his lack of basic medical knowledge.

Australian TV presenter Karl Stefanovic conducted a year-long on-air stunt to expose gendered double standards in how broadcasters are judged for their appearance. Frustrated by the persistent fashion criticism aimed at his Today co-host Lisa Wilkinson (and other female presenters), Stefanovic wore the same inexpensive navy suit every day for a year (changing shirts and ties occasionally) and kept the experiment secret from everyone except Wilkinson and one colleague. He reported that no viewers complained or noticed, which he and supporters say illustrates that men are judged primarily on job performance while women are scrutinized for clothing, hair and appearance.

The story drew broad media attention and widespread social media support, with many feminists praising Stefanovic’s gesture as empathy-driven activism and a useful demonstration of everyday sexism. Some commentators and members of feminist communities welcomed the stunt, while a few critics called it a superficial stunt that doesn’t address deeper policy or economic inequalities. The coverage also appeared alongside unrelated material from activist groups documenting violence against women and resources for those affected by domestic or sexual violence.

Sen. Cory Booker, D‑N.J., delivered an unusual and emotional appeal to the Senate urging rejection of his colleague Sen. Jeff Sessions’s nomination for attorney general, saying his “conscience and country” outweighed Senate norms. Booker — the first sitting senator to formally testify against another senator at a Cabinet confirmation hearing — argued Sessions’ record shows hostility to civil‑rights protections and that he would not lead the Justice Department in addressing racial bias, voting rights, LGBT and immigrant protections, or mass incarceration. Booker acknowledged past collegiality with Sessions (they worked together on honoring Selma marchers) but said that history and the Justice Department’s stakes compelled him to speak.

Civil‑rights icon Rep. John Lewis and CBC Chair Rep. Cedric Richmond also testified against Sessions, framing the nomination as central to the nation’s direction on civil rights. Supporters of Sessions, including a former staffer and Republican senators, defended his character and record, calling attacks unfair and stressing his commitment to law enforcement and public service. Despite the Democrats’ arguments and emotional testimony, Republicans on the Judiciary Committee largely defended Sessions, and his confirmation appeared likely to succeed with the GOP Senate majority.

Booker’s testimony drew wide media and social‑media attention, with commentators debating whether his intervention was driven by principle, politics, or both and noting the national profile it lent him amid 2020 presidential speculation.

Vice reporter Simon Ostrovsky, who had been held by militia in eastern Ukraine, has been safely released and is in good health, Vice confirmed. The organization thanked supporters and said it would respect Ostrovsky’s and his family’s privacy. BBC’s acting Moscow bureau chief Kevin Bishop tweeted that the BBC had spoken to Ostrovsky and that he was en route to Donetsk. Mashable had reported he was held by militia.

Scientists have discovered an extensive network of liquid water beneath Antarctica’s ice sheets, kept from freezing by geothermal heat, pressure, ice insulation, and ice motion. In depressions beneath the ice there are hundreds of lakes—some isolated, many connected by channels and saturated sediments—that eventually drain toward the Southern Ocean where the ice becomes floating shelves.

The Whillans Ice Stream Subglacial Access Research Drilling (WISSARD) project is an interdisciplinary effort to directly study these subglacial environments. Using ground-penetrating radar, seismic profiling, GPS, and specialized drilling, WISSARD targets Subglacial Lake Whillans and the grounding zone at the southeastern Ross Sea. The grounding zone, where grounded West Antarctic ice meets the Ross Sea, is a key area for understanding ice-sheet stability because much of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet lies below sea level and could drive rapid future sea-level rise if the grounding line retreats. During the 2014–2015 season, WISSARD planned focused sampling: about eight days of work at a primary borehole to recover water and sediment from a water cavity ~750 m below the surface and additional basal ice cores nearby. Studies include geophysics, biogeochemistry, and microbial ecology.

A Nature paper reports definitive evidence of active microbial ecosystems under the West Antarctic Ice Sheet. Samples recovered from about a half-mile beneath the surface contained Archaea that metabolize ammonium and methane, demonstrating life in an ecosystem isolated from sunlight and wind for millions of years. The team, led by John Priscu with lead author Brent Christner, emphasizes careful drilling and contamination control to support the claim that these communities are indigenous and active. The finding expands ideas about life's limits on Earth and informs astrobiology, since analogous cold, subsurface aquatic environments are hypothesized on bodies like Europa and Titan. The discovery attracted attention both for its scientific implications and for the dramatic nature of retrieving living organisms from beneath Antarctic ice.

Researchers in an international project (RuminOmics, led from the University of Aberdeen and funded by the EU) have found preliminary evidence that methane emissions from ruminant livestock (cows, sheep, goats, deer) are consistent for individual animals and influenced by genetics. Methane—produced mainly by belching during digestion—represents both a potent greenhouse gas (≈25× CO2 global-warming potential) and an energetic loss for animals (about 2–10% of consumed energy). The team measured variability between individuals and observed in an initial sample of 25 dairy cows that animals identified as low emitters stayed low across different diets, and high emitters stayed high. If this pattern holds in a larger study (~1,400 animals planned), selective breeding could reduce herd methane output while improving feed efficiency and lowering costs. The researchers note diet can alter emissions but often with trade-offs (e.g., higher protein can cut methane per milk unit but raises nitrogen losses and nitrous oxide risk), so breeding low-emitting, efficient animals could offer a more sustainable solution. The project aims to quantify genetic influence, develop selection tools and models, and help the livestock industry reduce both methane and nitrogen environmental impacts.

Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker signaled interest in a 2016 GOP presidential profile, telling ABC that governors make better presidents than members of Congress because they bring fresh, executive experience from outside Washington and a “bottom-up” approach. Asked about Rep. Paul Ryan, Walker praised him but argued the GOP needs a message contrasting Hillary Clinton as the face of Washington. Democrats fired back: DNC spokesman Michael Czin said GOP governors’ records are “broken and dysfunctional,” noting Wisconsin’s weak job growth under Walker and criticizing other GOP governors’ records.

Separately, Rep. Darrell Issa, fresh from a trip to Iraq, criticized the Baghdad government’s insistence on long-term training before fighting ISIL and said he’s prepared to vote to authorize U.S. military action. Issa argued that Iraqis — particularly the Kurds with U.S. air support and technical help — should conduct ground combat against ISIL.

Severe flooding devastated large parts of Queensland, Australia, in January 2011, leaving Brisbane—Australia’s third-largest city—submerged in many neighborhoods and triggering a multi‑week emergency across the state. Floodwaters crested in Brisbane just under the 1974 record, forcing thousands into evacuation centers or to stay with relatives, closing the CBD, emptying skyscrapers and inundating about 30,000 homes and businesses (11,900 fully inundated, 14,700 partially). Rivers and roads carried cars, boats, debris and even buildings downstream; some properties were completely swept away.

The disaster followed weeks of heavy rain across northeastern Queensland and included catastrophic flash floods around Toowoomba and the Lockyer Valley. At least 25 people were confirmed dead with dozens more expected to be found as access to isolated towns improved; police reported 61 people missing, most near Toowoomba. Search-and-rescue teams—including more than 200 police and soldiers using helicopters and amphibious vehicles—methodically combed flattened floodplains littered with destroyed homes, crushed boats, snapped trucks and dead livestock. Officials warned more fatalities were likely.

Queensland Premier Anna Bligh called it possibly the worst natural disaster in state and national history and predicted a reconstruction task “of postwar proportions.” Early damage estimates were already in the billions (a $5 billion figure cited before Brisbane’s inundation), and wider economic impacts included a near shutdown of the state’s coal exports and massive crop losses (vegetables, fruit, sugarcane), which threatened higher prices.

Individual stories underscored the human cost: residents scrambling to pump out offices and homes, neighbors cooking on camp stoves amid ruins, accusations of slow emergency responses in remote areas, and heroic rescues—such as a mining company helicopter that evacuated dozens from stranded rooftops and a boy who sacrificed his life helping his younger brother and mother during a vehicle flood rescue.

Authorities cautioned that many homes would be uninhabitable and told evacuees it could be days before inundated neighborhoods were safe to re-enter. Cleanup, sewer and transport disruptions, looting incidents and ongoing patrols highlighted the continuing crisis as communities braced for long-term recovery.

Taylor Swift responded to accusations that she’s “terribly calculated and mean,” comments originally tweeted (and later deleted) by Grizzly Bear’s Edward Droste. Droste posted ambiguous tweets this summer implying a frightening, powerful celebrity and later shared gossip alleging Swift gave friends a list of rules before they joined her onstage. In a wide-ranging GQ cover interview with Chuck Klosterman, Swift—whose published remarks in the piece don’t name Droste—called such characterizations “highly offensive,” saying she plans and cares about her work but that planning is different from being mean or manipulative. She argued careers require hard work, and resentments about being labeled “calculating” stem from people misreading professional deliberation as a negative personal trait.

The interview covers much more: Swift discusses her creative choices (notably the conscious move to straight pop on 1989 despite label pressure), her habit of monitoring public perception after a period offline in 2013, and how she uses self-awareness to preserve her career. She addresses the public fixation on her personal life and songwriting—saying she rarely names subjects of songs and sometimes steers speculation deliberately (for example, calling “Bad Blood” a song about a lost friendship rather than a romantic dispute). Swift reflects on friendships and loneliness—describing demanding meet-and-greets and how TV sitcom reruns help her decompress—and revisits the Kanye West 2009 VMA incident as a career-altering “accident” that she later reconciled with. The profile portrays Swift as unusually controlled and self-aware for a pop star: strategic but also sincerely invested in her art and relationships, and frustrated by reductive tabloid readings of her motives.

The New York Daily News is cutting about half of its newsroom staff as part of a Tronc-led restructure to prioritize digital and breaking news coverage—especially crime, civil justice and public responsibility. Tronc, which bought the tabloid last September for $1 and absorbed its liabilities, announced the reductions in an internal memo and said the move was needed because the paper has not transitioned far enough to a digitally focused model amid falling revenue and print circulation. Revenue fell sharply in prior years and layoffs had already thinned the staff.

Editor-in-chief Jim Rich and managing editor Kristen Lee were among those laid off; Tronc named Robert York, editor of its Allentown Morning Call, to run the paper. Staff and former reporters warned the cuts will hamper ambitious watchdog and investigative projects—work for which the News has been recognized, including a 2017 Pulitzer shared with ProPublica. The decision has prompted sharp criticism inside and outside the paper about the future of local accountability journalism in New York.

The UN and eyewitnesses warn that the Iraqi operation to retake Mosul from the Islamic State (IS) could trigger one of 2016’s largest and most complex humanitarian crises. Lise Grande, the UN humanitarian coordinator for Iraq, said up to 1 million civilians could flee and as many as 700,000 might need shelter — far beyond current capacity. Only six emergency sites exist now for roughly 60,000 people; plans to expand to 22 sites would raise capacity to about 400,000, still well short of needs. The UN is especially concerned for the 1.2–1.5 million civilians still inside Mosul, where IS has reportedly booby-trapped areas, placed snipers, used civilians as human shields, and may even resort to chemical weapons as in the worst-case scenarios. Smugglers are charging large sums to evacuate people, but so far mass movements had not yet been detected.

On the ground, residents describe constant airstrikes, IEDs and IS fighters embedded in neighborhoods, making escape perilous; those who try to flee risk summary execution. Civilians report shortages, fear, and psychological trauma from IS atrocities. US forces have dropped leaflets urging people to stay indoors. Some residents say they want IS gone and are ready to rise up when possible, while many fear reprisals after liberation: local officials and displaced residents expressed deep concern about sectarian revenge if Shia militias participate in securing Mosul, and prefer Kurdish peshmerga or non-sectarian forces. The fall of Mosul would be a major blow to IS, but planners warn the humanitarian and security challenges during and after the assault could test response capacities to the breaking point.

Colin Kaepernick sat during the national anthem for the San Francisco 49ers’ first three preseason games to protest racial oppression and police brutality, and he plans to continue until he believes the country has changed. He met with teammates at a players-only meeting and spent nearly 20 minutes with reporters explaining that his action was intended to bring attention to systemic racism—not to disrespect the military—and that it was the result of long reflection and conversations with others, including team consultant Dr. Harry Edwards. Kaepernick said he won’t recruit teammates to join him but welcomes dialogue and will pursue additional, non-symbolic actions in the future.

Teammates expressed respectful, mixed reactions: many said they personally wouldn’t sit for the anthem and associate it with honoring soldiers, yet they largely respect Kaepernick’s right to protest, recognize the importance of the issues he raised, and emphasized unity and team cohesion. Some players (e.g., Daniel Kilgore) initially felt offended but came to understand his perspective after the meeting; others (NaVorro Bowman, Antoine Bethea, Bruce Miller) stressed supporting him as a teammate and avoiding division. Several noted the value of the team conversation and praised Kaepernick’s courage even if they disagreed with his method. Kaepernick acknowledged potential backlash, said he wouldn’t be deterred if adverse reactions occurred on the road, and indicated he’d accept consequences if they come.

This document combines a note about web archiving and a news report about Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s response to the Charlottesville violence.

- Internet Archive crawls: The Archive is proactively crawling and saving pages and the pages they reference so that when linked content changes or disappears, readers can access the version that existed when the referencing page was written. The goal is to reduce broken links across the web by replacing or supplementing fragile links with archived versions.

- McConnell on Charlottesville and white supremacists: After the violent “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Va.—which included neo-Nazi and KKK participants and resulted in the death of counterprotester Heather Heyer—President Trump drew criticism for saying there were “very fine people on both sides.” In response, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R‑Ky.) said there “are no good neo‑Nazis,” condemned the ideology of racial hatred, and urged everyone to stand against hate and violence. McConnell criticized the white supremacist groups planning a similar rally in Lexington, Ky., saying their messages of hate and bigotry are not welcome in Kentucky or anywhere in America. Though he did not name Trump in his remarks, McConnell has privately been upset by the president’s handling of the episode and concerned it could inflame tensions ahead of expected demonstrations.

Key points

- A major West African carrier, Asky, has suspended flights to Liberia and Sierra Leone to protect passengers and staff; Arik Air previously stopped flights to those countries. Passengers from Guinea will be screened. The move follows international concern as the Ebola outbreak spreads.

- The current West African Ebola outbreak, first reported in Guinea in February, is the deadliest on record: about 1,201 reported cases across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone and 672 deaths (WHO/UN figures at time of reporting). Guinea had the most deaths (319), followed by Sierra Leone (224) and Liberia (129). The outbreak’s fatality rate is roughly 50–90%; in this outbreak about 60%.

- Notable deaths among healthcare workers: Dr Sheik Umar Khan, Sierra Leone’s leading Ebola physician, died of the disease and was hailed as a national hero; Liberian doctor Samuel Brisbane also died. Two American health workers in Liberia (a doctor and a hygienist) were infected.

- International spread and response: Nigeria reported its first imported case — Liberian official Patrick Sawyer — who flew to Lagos and died in hospital; his arrival triggered contact tracing, quarantine of a Lagos hospital, closure for decontamination, and monitoring of contacts. WHO sent teams to Nigeria and Togo to assist tracing. Borders, airports and ports in affected countries have tightened screening; Liberia closed many border crossings and deployed police at its international airport.

- Public-health and social measures: Communities are being quarantined, football in Liberia was suspended to avoid crowding and contact, public-awareness campaigns and hygiene measures have been stepped up, and funerary practices are being warned against because dead bodies remain infectious. The incubation period can be up to 21 days; Ebola transmits via infected bodily fluids (vomit, diarrhea, blood, semen in some cases) and is not believed to be contagious before symptoms appear.

- Medical situation and outlook: There is no proven cure or licensed vaccine; treatment is supportive (fluids, symptomatic care). Experimental treatments and vaccines were under development. WHO and international partners urged multi-sector responses, as the outbreak overwhelmed national health systems. U.S. and other international actors increased assistance and were monitoring the situation closely.

Overall, the report describes an escalating, hard-to-contain Ebola epidemic with significant deaths including health workers, flight suspensions and international concern focused on rapid identification, contact tracing, quarantine measures and supportive care in the absence of a proven treatment.

Alan Dershowitz has joined Harvey Weinstein’s legal battle over access to The Weinstein Company (TWC) emails and records as a consultant. Weinstein, facing numerous sexual misconduct allegations and multiple investigations, is seeking old personal and business emails from TWC through Delaware Bankruptcy Court, arguing they could exonerate him and that his defense counsel needs them to perform constitutionally mandated duties. Dershowitz—Harvard Law professor and high-profile TV legal commentator who has recently been linked to Trump’s circle—filed a declaration supporting Weinstein’s bid, saying defense counsel Benjamin Brafman has a right to review potentially exculpatory material under Brady and related doctrines and that disclosure could prevent wrongful charges. Dershowitz said the emails have no legitimate commercial value to the bankrupt company and offered to submit a legal memorandum backing these claims. TWC has previously contended Weinstein’s request is unrelated to the bankruptcy.

Actress and neuroscientist Mayim Bialik wrote for Kveller about fertility, Jewish sexual ethics, and how traditional Jewish practice aligns with modern fertility awareness. Referencing the Torah’s instruction to “count seven days” (later extended by custom to 12 days), she notes this timing corresponds to the typical ovulation window—so historic Jewish ritual practices effectively flagged women’s most fertile time. She describes the mikveh immersion on the night of ovulation as a meditative, symbolic return to intimacy and explains how temporary abstinence before immersion can heighten desire and refresh marital sex.

Bialik stresses that Judaism values both procreation and sexual pleasure: sex is a mitzvah, encouraged especially on Shabbat, and a wife’s sexual rights are protected in the ketubah. She also affirms that birth control has a place in Jewish practice so families can plan responsibly, and that sex outside fertile periods (pregnancy, menopause) is fully endorsed—including playful imagery about enjoying sex freely. Overall her piece ties ancient ritual and modern fertility knowledge together, framing Jewish tradition as life-affirming and focused on how to live well.

At a Fox News/Google-sponsored Republican debate in Orlando, front-runners Mitt Romney and Rick Perry dominated a field of nine candidates with repeated, sometimes heated exchanges over immigration, health care and Social Security, overshadowing the rest of the contenders.

Key points:
- Romney and Perry targeted each other’s consistency and conservative credentials throughout the two-hour event. Romney pressed Perry over Texas’ policy allowing undocumented youths to qualify for in‑state college tuition, arguing it creates a “magnet” for illegal immigration and criticizing the subsidy. Perry defended the policy emotionally, saying children brought here through no fault of their own should be educated and accusing critics of lacking a heart; parts of the audience booed.
- The pair also traded accusations of flip-flopping: Romney cited Perry’s book to suggest Perry once favored letting state/local governments run retirement programs and questioned Perry’s stance on Social Security; Perry countered by alleging Romney revised editions of his book to remove praise of Massachusetts’ health‑care law (the model critics call “Romneycare”).
- Perry gave some uneven answers elsewhere, notably on foreign policy, which reinforced doubts about his preparedness despite leading in polls at the time. Romney generally emerged without major damage.
- Other candidates — Michele Bachmann, Rick Santorum, Newt Gingrich, Herman Cain, Ron Paul, Jon Huntsman and Gary Johnson — largely struggled for the spotlight. Santorum and Bachmann joined Romney in criticizing Perry’s tuition policy; Huntsman voiced frustration that the debate focused so heavily on the Romney‑Perry duel.
- The broader debate touched on entitlement reform, gun rights and the Obama administration’s economic record, but specific economic proposals received relatively little new attention. Audience participation and YouTube-submitted questions were notable features of the event.

Overall, the debate reinforced the head‑to‑head rivalry between Romney and Perry as the central story of the GOP primary contest, while other contenders failed to gain sustained traction.

Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, has publicly warned that an encrypted 1.3‑GB “insurance” file containing unredacted U.S. government documents will be unlocked and released if he is arrested, tried, killed, or otherwise silenced. The file—protected with strong 256‑bit encryption and already distributed to many supporters—purports to include the full set of U.S. documents WikiLeaks has received, including material withheld from publication to protect sources and individuals. Assange’s lawyer described the stash as a “thermonuclear device” in the information age, intended to protect WikiLeaks amid what they say are cyberattacks, censorship and calls for prosecution or worse.

The threats come as Assange faces a European arrest warrant from Sweden over sexual‑crime allegations (which he denies, saying the encounters were consensual), an Interpol alert, intense political pressure—some U.S. politicians called for prosecution or violent retaliation—and scrutiny from justice officials in the U.S., Australia and elsewhere over the publication of hundreds of thousands of leaked military and diplomatic cables. The leaks, reportedly provided by U.S. Army intelligence analyst Bradley Manning (now in custody), have embarrassed governments worldwide and revealed sensitive diplomatic communications.

Assange has accused critics of political motives, urged accountability from leaders (including suggesting President Obama and Secretary of State Clinton should answer questions or resign if implicated in illicit surveillance), and called out individuals who advocated harming him. His lawyers say they have faced surveillance and pressure, and have criticized what they view as attempts to criminalize journalistic activity. Swedish prosecutors insist their investigation is independent of the leaks. Investigations in the U.S. have explored possible charges under the Espionage Act, but legal experts note hurdles to prosecuting Assange, a non‑U.S. national who did not steal the documents himself.

This dispatch covers two CPAC-related items: an NRA “university” session and Sarah Palin’s speech.

NRA “university” at CPAC:
- The NRA ran an instructional session aimed at equipping supporters to counter “gun control myths” and reduce perceived links between guns and crime.
- Speakers argued against gun and ammunition registration, claiming it would only restrict law‑abiding citizens and not reduce violence.
- Claims included that guns account for only 0.5% of accidental U.S. deaths and that people are more likely to be hurt by a hammer than by an assault weapon.
- To mock the public image of “assault weapons,” an NRA presenter contrasted a movie clip of Arnold Schwarzenegger firing a machine gun with footage of people firing AR‑15–style semi‑automatics, drawing laughter.
- An NRA woman framed the moment as a fight for Second Amendment rights and urged attendees to help the NRA win over younger voters—acknowledging the group’s roughly four million members versus a U.S. population near 313 million—and tasked “NRA university” graduates with changing youth outreach outcomes.
- The session also claimed the NRA tried to defeat President Obama but failed to capture young voters.

Sarah Palin at CPAC:
- Former Alaska governor Sarah Palin gave a rousing CPAC speech noted for crowd-pleasing one‑liners. Ten highlighted lines included zingers about background checks, gibes about political consultants and pollsters, attacks on Obama for broken transparency promises, self-deprecating and populist advice to activists, and quips about her husband and political opponents.
- The piece notes Palin’s continued ability to work a crowd despite being semi-retired.

Overall tone: the report portrays the NRA session as a coordinated messaging effort to downplay gun‑control arguments and recruit younger supporters, and depicts Palin’s appearance as a lively, populist highlight of the conference.
