The California State Auditor’s office investigated 1,481 allegations of improper governmental activity from July 1, 2017, through June 30, 2018, and this report highlights seven substantiated cases showing misuse of state time, economically wasteful actions, and misuse of state property.

Key findings:

- Widespread time-and-attendance abuse:
  - Two California State University, Fresno facilities employees failed to account for more than 5,100 hours from 2013–2017, costing about $111,000; they concealed their absences.
  - At Kern Valley State Prison, an employee regularly left up to 45 minutes early over about two years, totaling an estimated 312 hours and nearly $9,000 in lost work.
  - A Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) key data operator slept at her desk for extended periods from February 2014 through December 2017, misusing more than 2,200 hours and costing the State over $40,000. She processed far fewer documents than expected and produced frequently inaccurate work. Supervisors were aware but did not properly document or pursue discipline, in part due to concerns about a possible medical condition; the employee remains employed and was eventually reassigned.

- Economically wasteful personnel decisions:
  - A nursing director at a Southern California prison assigned a licensed vocational nurse (a personal friend) away from patient care to perform scheduling duties for which she was overqualified, resulting in about $10,500 in unnecessary salary payments and roughly $18,700 in overtime paid to cover the vacant post — nearly $30,000 total waste.

- Payroll and procedural failures:
  - CDCR overpaid a staff services analyst nearly $3,000 (July 2016–March 2017) due to failures by the analyst, her manager, an associate warden, and a personnel specialist to follow pay and policy procedures. The associate warden then violated state law by not seeking recovery after audits identified the overpayments.

- Misuse of property and unauthorized construction:
  - A CAL FIRE assistant chief used on-duty staff to build an unauthorized 16x20-foot addition (with plumbing, electrical, sewer) onto a state residence he rented; it was decorated as a tiki room and used socially. He received a 30-day suspension and the structure has been demolished. He also failed to get required approvals.

- Wasteful procurement:
  - A manager at California State University, Dominguez Hills directed the purchase of a nearly $7,000 Nissan electric-vehicle quick charger without ensuring compatibility with campus energy plans. The charger sat unused for five years, its warranty lapsed, replacement parts are no longer available, and installation is uncertain until 2020–2021 at the earliest.

Other notes:
- The State Auditor also issued nonpublic reports addressing nepotism, bad-faith hires, improper promotions, and executive misconduct within two entities and shared them with parties who could remediate the issues and protect potential whistleblowers.
- The report underscores supervisory, procedural, and oversight shortcomings across multiple agencies that led to financial waste, misuse of personnel, and improper use of state resources.

Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump spent Saturday campaigning in Wisconsin amid fallout from a difficult week in his campaign. At rallies in Racine and Eau Claire he defended recent controversial remarks on NATO, abortion and nuclear weapons, blamed the press for misrepresenting him, and acknowledged one clear mistake—retweeting an unflattering photo of rival Ted Cruz’s wife. 

Trump faced particular backlash for comments on abortion, including saying “the laws are set” and initially suggesting women could be punished if abortion were banned; his team later issued clarifications and he described one exchange as hypothetical. Critics said the remarks worsened his already poor standing with women voters; Trump said he has no broad plan to change that beyond campaigning with his wife Melania and daughter Ivanka and “being myself.” 

Despite protests outside some events, the day’s appearances were peaceful. Trump also noted he benefits from massive free media coverage and repeatedly complained he’s held to a different standard than rivals.

At a January town hall in Council Bluffs, Iowa, 11-year-old Omaha fifth-grader Jacob Royal asked New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie what he would do about school lunches that have changed under First Lady Michelle Obama’s push for healthier meals. Royal said he missed pizza and “crispitos,” disliked gluten-free options and now brings his own lunch. Christie replied that he doesn’t think the first lady should be involved in school meal decisions and that parents — not the federal government or the White House — should decide what children eat. He said he personally supports healthier eating but would not use the presidency to mandate standards, promising to let schools return to previous offerings if elected. The exchange highlighted ongoing debate over the Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act nutrition standards adopted after 2010, which have drawn mixed reactions: some praise improved nutrition, while others note higher food waste and implementation costs. Christie has previously praised the goal of healthier eating but here emphasized parental control and criticized federal intervention. Jacob and several attendees welcomed his stance.

Summary:

Federal review of marijuana scheduling
- The FDA is conducting a scientific and medical review of marijuana at the Drug Enforcement Administration’s request. The review—an eight-factor analysis under the Controlled Substances Act—will inform HHS recommendations to DEA about whether to change marijuana’s Schedule I status. Schedule I denotes high abuse potential and no accepted medical use; rescheduling would not legalize marijuana but could ease research barriers, banking access for state-legal cannabis businesses, and some tax treatment.
- The eight factors include abuse potential, pharmacology, state of scientific knowledge, history/patterns of abuse, scope/duration/significance of abuse, public health risk, dependence liability, and whether it’s an immediate precursor to a controlled substance.
- Past DEA requests for FDA analysis (2001, 2006) left marijuana at Schedule I, largely citing insufficient evidence of medical efficacy. U.S. research has been constrained by federal controls—only one federally authorized cannabis grower (University of Mississippi, overseen by NIDA). NIDA has funded more marijuana-related research in recent years, but critics say federal funding and policy have focused disproportionately on harms and impeded broader study.
- Interest in medical uses is growing: some studies suggest potential benefits (anti-cancer properties of purified compounds, blood sugar control, slower HIV progression, links to lower suicide rates in medical-legal states). Currently 22 states plus D.C. allow medical marijuana; many more permit CBD oil. Public support for medical legalization exceeds 80% in polls. The FDA has not approved whole-plant marijuana for any medical indication.

UK research on high-potency cannabis and psychosis
- Independent studies from King’s College London report that use of high-potency “skunk-like” cannabis significantly increases risk of psychosis: users of potent cannabis had a roughly threefold higher risk compared with non-users; daily users faced about a fivefold increased risk. Researchers estimate smoking high-potency cannabis may account for about 24% of new psychosis cases in the studied sample.
- The multi-year study compared several hundred first-episode psychosis patients with healthy controls in south London and found the association depended on both frequency of use and potency. By contrast, lower-potency forms such as hashish—containing more cannabidiol (CBD), which may counteract THC’s psychotomimetic effects—showed no such link.
- Researchers and public-health officials urge clearer public messaging about potency-related risks, routine clinical questioning about cannabis type/frequency, and prevention efforts. Some commentators argue regulation could enable safer, lower-potency products.
- Experts note alcohol causes more physical harm overall, but cannabis—especially high-THC varieties—carries distinct psychological risks, including hallucinations and a potential contribution to schizophrenia in some users. The Home Office cited the findings to justify cannabis prohibition; public-health voices emphasize treatment availability for drug-related problems.

Overall picture
- In the U.S., federal agencies are re-examining marijuana’s scheduling amid growing evidence of medical potential and expanding state legalization, but federal restrictions still limit research. In the UK, new evidence ties high-potency cannabis to elevated psychosis risk, prompting calls for better public education and consideration of potency in policy and clinical practice.

Since the March 2011 Fukushima reactor crisis, U.S. consumer demand for Geiger counters and potassium iodide (KI) supplements has surged, with many stores quickly selling out and suppliers overwhelmed. Retailers and online sellers reported hundreds to thousands of orders as worried Americans sought protection against potential radioactive exposure.

Experts and government agencies, including the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman Greg Jaczko, stressed that any radiation reaching North America from Japan would be negligible and pose no health risk. Radiation and public-health specialists reiterated that KI only protects the thyroid from radioactive iodine and does not guard against other radiation or body parts; it must be taken shortly before or after exposure and is most important for children and pregnant women. Authorities in California, western Canada and Britain Columbia echoed warnings that routine KI use by people an ocean away is unnecessary.

Despite reassurances, panic buying has been reported in parts of the U.S., Russia and elsewhere. Some suppliers have sold out or are backordered; a few companies donated supplies to relief efforts in Japan. The episode revived debate in the U.S. over whether households – especially those near nuclear plants – should keep KI on hand. The federal government stockpiles KI for residents within 10 miles of reactors, but some experts argue for wider personal preparedness.

Roger Stone, a longtime adviser and friend of President Donald Trump, told TMZ that if Congress moves to impeach Trump it would trigger large-scale violence and could amount to a civil war. Speaking at an airport, Stone said those pushing impeachment “didn’t vote for him” and should “get over it,” arguing Democrats lost despite heavy spending. He warned, “Try to impeach him. Just try it. You will have a spasm of violence—an insurrection…Both sides are heavily armed,” and added that any politician who votes for impeachment “would be endangering their own life.” Stone said he was predicting, not advocating, violence.

The comments came amid limited impeachment efforts by some House Democrats—Rep. Brad Sherman introduced articles over Trump’s firing of James Comey, and Rep. Steve Cohen signaled plans to introduce articles over Trump’s remarks after violence at a white-supremacist rally. Democratic leadership, including Nancy Pelosi, has resisted immediate impeachment and instead called for an independent commission to investigate Trump’s ties to Russia.

The article profiles the Miami Caliente and the inaugural season of the Lingerie Football League (LFL), a women’s full-contact indoor football circuit that grew out of the one-off Lingerie Bowl halftime alternative. It juxtaposes the athleticism and violence of the game with the provocative, sexualized presentation that defines the league.

Key points:
- On-field intensity: The piece opens with a vivid play-by-play of Miami quarterback Anonka Dixon—described as an elite, multi-talented athlete—executing a bruising, athletic run while wearing the league’s minimal satin-and-lace uniform. The coverage emphasizes how physically brutal the league is: collisions, concussions, torn ligaments (Miami lost three players to ACL tears), broken bones and turf burns are common despite the skimpy attire.
- Players and image: The women are portrayed as highly trained, muscular competitors who embrace full-contact football, but must do so in revealing lingerie-style uniforms (bikinis, lace garters, clear facemasks). The league markets itself squarely to a Super Bowl demographic—“beautiful women and football”—a choice the founder, Mitch Mortaza, defends. Many players acknowledge the exploitative aspect, yet some frame participation as a form of empowerment similar to burlesque or the early, feminist-tinged evolution of roller derby.
- Business and culture: The LFL expanded from a single pay-per-view event into a ten-team league with a four-game season and a playoff/championship structure; its flagship event aired during Super Bowl week. Off-field issues include low pay, team drama, drunken fans, and “cheesy businessmen” running the league.
- Controversy over image control: Tensions between players, media, and league executives are highlighted by a dispute over a magazine photo shoot. Miami stars Anonka Dixon and Tina Caccavale—both top performers—were reportedly placed on probation by league officials for wearing shoulder pads during a New Times photo shoot. The league enforces strict image rules (contracts include “accidental nudity” clauses) and even banned the article’s reporter from credentialed coverage. The punishment underscores the league’s rigid control over how the players are presented, privileging sexualized imagery over depictions of athleticism.
- Contradiction at the core: The story frames the LFL as an uneasy mixture of elite athletic competition and overt sexualization. Players’ physical prowess and commitment to a dangerous sport clash with an organizational insistence on maintaining a Playboy-style aesthetic, producing both empowerment narratives and sharp criticism over exploitation and image policing.

Overall, the article paints the LFL’s inaugural season as a raw, conflicted spectacle—full-contact football that is legitimately brutal and athletic, yet tightly managed and marketed through a sexualized lens that provokes debate about exploitation, agency, and the cost of performing both athlete and object.

Netflix’s board has adopted a shareholder rights plan (a “poison pill”) days after activist investor Carl Icahn disclosed a roughly 9.98% stake in the company. The plan, approved unanimously by the seven-member board and effective through Nov. 2, 2015, issues one right per common share that allows holders to buy 1/1,000th of a new preferred share at $350 if an investor acquires 10% (20% for certain institutional 13G holders) or more of outstanding stock without board approval. The rights also grant holders, upon certain change-of-control transactions, the ability to buy common shares of the acquirer at favorable value—while the acquiring party cannot exercise the rights—making an unsolicited accumulation or takeover more costly and dilutive.

Netflix framed the move as protection against efforts to gain control that the board deems not in shareholders’ best interests. Icahn criticized the pill as poor corporate governance—particularly the low, discriminatory 10% threshold and that it was adopted without a shareholder vote—and reiterated governance complaints (including Netflix’s staggered board). He had said Netflix shares were undervalued and hinted at potential strategic moves after his disclosure. The action follows similar defenses at other companies targeted by Icahn and comes as Netflix faces intense competition and recent operational challenges after prior missteps that sharply cut its market value.

Egypt was rocked by major clashes between security forces and protesters in Cairo’s Tahrir Square ahead of parliamentary elections due to start on 28 November. Riot police used tear gas, rubber bullets and pellet cartridges to disperse thousands who had camped in the square after a large rally demanding that the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces (SCAF) hand power to civilians. At least one to two people were reported killed and hundreds—official tallies range around 650–676—were wounded, many with serious head injuries. Witnesses described running street battles, buildings and cars set on fire, protesters tearing up paving stones, and police firing from armoured vehicles.

Protesters briefly drove security forces from the square, captured and burned a police truck, and later rebuilt barricades as reinforcements including ultras and some Islamist groups swelled the crowds. Activists and journalists said the police assault mobilised broader public anger against SCAF and the interior ministry; some candidates and activists have frozen campaigns in the wake of injuries to peers. The interior ministry insisted its forces acted with restraint and blamed protesters for escalation.

The unrest came amid deep disputes over a draft constitutional framework that would give the military autonomy over its affairs and budget, and over the composition of the body to write the new constitution. Islamists—especially the Muslim Brotherhood and Salafi groups—look set to win a large share of parliamentary seats, raising stakes in negotiations with the government and military. Prominent figures, including Mohamed ElBaradei, proposed an alternative plan calling for postponing elections and transferring executive authority from the military while drafting a new constitution; the generals have not responded. The clashes cast doubt on whether the security forces can guarantee a credible, peaceful vote and highlighted the fragile, escalating confrontation between the military council and mass pro-change forces.

After years of requests, Facebook is testing a "Dislike" feature, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said at a company town hall. However, he emphasized it won't be a Reddit‑style downvote that lets people vote posts up or down. Instead, Facebook aims to offer a way to express other emotions—particularly empathy or sympathy when a simple Like is inappropriate (for example, in response to sad news). Details are sparse, but the company is likely to implement disliking as one of several reaction alternatives rather than a blunt negative button, both to avoid harassment and to prevent harming the experience for users and advertisers. Zuckerberg framed the change as a cautious effort to make the feature "a force for good" rather than a tool for abuse.

For the first time in over a decade the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) ran a public lottery to add thousands of “casual” longshore workers at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports. Entry required mailing 4x6 postcards; demand was enormous, with postal shops like Patrick Meehan’s in San Pedro selling out as hundreds of people rushed to apply before the deadline.

Background and process
- The last broad call for casuals was in 2004. This reopening is rare and highly sought because casual status is the only route into the union’s well‑paid, benefit‑rich full-time longshore positions.
- Officials arranged two pools of postcards (public and union‑distributed). A neutral firm, InterOptimis, will alternately draw from each pool until about 3,400 names are selected according to the ILWU timeline; union leaders said 2,400 names will be pulled to become casuals, though how many will ultimately be elevated to full time is unclear.
- Deadline extensions were granted for union‑issued cards; the drawing was scheduled to begin Feb. 6.

Why the lottery matters
- Full-time longshore workers can earn very high compensation (reports cite averages from roughly $123,000 to $161,000 and top earners near $200,000) plus medical and pension benefits.
- Casuals perform the same work but have inconsistent hours, no benefits, and much lower average annual earnings (about $31,000 for casuals who showed up for shifts in 2016). Casuals pick up work through a dispatch rotation and must often be physically present to claim shifts.

Worker perspectives and tensions
- Many applicants—including career casuals, multigenerational dock families, and others struggling in the broader labor market—see the lottery as a rare path to economic stability and respect. Interviewees recounted long waits, family traditions, and dramatic life improvements tied to union jobs.
- Longtime casuals are anxious and sometimes resentful: some have been waiting years or more than a decade to advance, and there are concerns employers favor keeping a large casual workforce rather than adding full-time positions. Economic shifts, automation, and post‑recession reduced hiring have slowed elevation to full-time status.
- Critics argue the system’s seniority and hours-based promotion can leave casuals stuck for many years; a 2015 petition opposed new lotteries for fear of reducing casuals’ chances to work and become registered members.

Broader context
- The intense interest in the lottery highlights shrinking opportunities for stable, well‑paid blue‑collar work in the U.S. and the declining share of unionized workers in manufacturing and related industries. For many applicants, even a tenuous route toward union membership and its lifetime benefits is worth the long odds.

In April 2008 diamond miners working in Namibia’s Sperrgebiet (a 10,000-square-mile restricted “forbidden territory” run by Namdeb/De Beers and the Namibian government) uncovered the remains of a 16th-century shipwreck that archaeologists identify as the Portuguese vessel Bom Jesus, which disappeared in 1533 while bound for India. The find—buried and exceptionally well preserved—includes about 5,438 artifacts: more than 2,000 mint-condition gold coins (Spanish and Portuguese) dated to c.1525–1538, Portuguese silver coinage, bronze cannons, muskets and swords, navigational instruments, pewter and copper tableware, five anchors, and tons of copper ingots, plus over 50 elephant tusks.

Experts say the weight and toxicity of the copper ingots likely inhibited microbial decay and helped preserve organic materials. Analysis of the coins and contemporary logs strongly points to Bom Jesus, making this the oldest known shipwreck found in sub‑Saharan Africa. Archaeologists suggest the ship struck rocks, broke up, and a coin chest from the captain’s cabin was buried intact by falling timbers—explaining the excellent condition of much of the treasure.

The site is protected and controlled by Namdeb; many items remain out of public view and conserved (timbers and weapons in damp storage). Officials have discussed exhibiting the wreck in a museum, but no formal plans have been confirmed.

Canada’s national police force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), has changed its uniform rules to allow Muslim women to wear a hijab on duty. Approved by the RCMP commissioner and announced by a spokesman for Public Safety Minister Ralph Goodale, the move aims to reflect Canada’s diversity and encourage more Muslim women to join the force. The RCMP tested several hijab designs and selected one intended not to interfere with officers’ duties; as of the announcement no officer had yet requested to wear it.

The decision follows earlier accommodation of religious dress by the RCMP, notably the 1990 allowance for Sikh officers to wear turbans, and mirrors policies already in place in Toronto and Edmonton police services, Police Scotland, and forces in parts of the U.S., U.K., Sweden and Norway. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau contrasted Canada’s inclusive approach with France’s recent controversies — including bans on burkinis — framed as attempts elsewhere to restrict visible expressions of Muslim faith. The policy change is presented as part of broader efforts to reduce barriers and promote representation within policing.

A multi-university study led by UC Davis researcher Cuihua “Cindy” Shen analyzed anonymized server data from more than 11,000 players in two massively multiplayer online games (EverQuest II in the U.S. and Chevaliers’ Romance III in China) to test the persistent stereotype that men are better gamers than women. Using players’ registered gender and controlling for confounding factors such as total play time, character class choice, current level, and guild membership, the researchers measured leveling speed (progress per unit play time) rather than raw level.

Key findings:
- Once differences in play time and game choices were accounted for, women advanced at least as fast as men — in some analyses they exceeded men’s progression rates. The apparent gap in raw levels reflected factors correlated with gender (for example, women on average played less and more often selected supportive/assistive classes), not innate skill differences.
- The results held across two games and two national cultures, making this the first large-scale longitudinal comparison of male and female performance in real MMOs.
- The stereotype that women are inferior gamers likely contributes to hostile gaming environments (e.g., GamerGate) and may discourage women from participating in gaming — a domain that can be an entry point into STEM careers.

Implications and recommendations:
- Debunking this stereotype could reduce a self-fulfilling cycle that deters women from gaming and related technical fields.
- Community and design interventions (female-supportive groups, reporting and moderation systems like Riot’s Tribunal) can help make gaming less hostile and more welcoming for women.

Bottom line: gender itself does not predict gaming performance in MMOs; observed disparities are driven by confounded behavioral choices and play patterns, not inferior ability.

USA TODAY coverage of opening night for the new Broadway jukebox bio The Cher Show focuses on two things: a minor celebrity kerfuffle and a mixed review of the musical.

At the performance, Kanye West and Kim Kardashian West attended. Jarrod Spector, who plays Sonny Bono, publicly called out Kanye on Twitter for being on his phone during the show’s opening night. Kanye quickly apologized on Twitter, saying the emotional dynamics of Cher and Sonny made him and Kim hold hands and sing “I Got You Babe,” and expressing appreciation for the cast’s work. Kim gushed that Cher is “seriously the most amazing beautiful person ever.”

The review of The Cher Show describes a production that aims to recreate the spirit of 1970s variety TV but rarely rises above clichés and broad comedy. The book by Rick Elice fractures Cher into three actresses — “Babe,” “Lady” and “Star” — representing different career stages, which allows for strong, distinct performances but leaves the script feeling sketchy and emotionally distant. Highlights include Bob Mackie’s lavish costumes, a standout dance number, Jarrod Spector’s Sonny, Emily Skinner as Cher’s mother, and the combined strengths of the three Chers (Stephanie J. Block, Teal Wicks, Micaela Diamond). Overall, while the show contains dazzling moments and solid performances, the reviewer finds it uneven and lacking a satisfying, heartfelt center.

John Bieniewicz, a 44-year-old experienced soccer referee and pediatric dialysis technician from Westland, Michigan, died after being punched in the head while officiating an adult recreational match in Livonia on Sunday. Witnesses say Bieniewicz was about to eject a player when 36-year-old Baseel Abdul‑Amir Saad of Dearborn allegedly struck him, knocking him unconscious; Bieniewicz never regained consciousness and was declared brain dead Tuesday. Saad surrendered and was arraigned on a felony charge of assault with intent to do great bodily harm; bond was set at $500,000 and prosecutors said charges may be amended as the investigation continues. Saad’s attorney has said his client is cooperating and that facts remain to be clarified.

Bieniewicz, a devoted husband and father of two boys, was a long‑time, highly respected referee (licensed at professional, collegiate, high‑school and youth levels) and president of the Metro Detroit Soccer Officials Organization. He worked as lead medical assistant in pediatric chronic dialysis at C.S. Mott Children’s Hospital and was active in the local soccer community. Friends described him as a devoted family man and mentor; they have organized a memorial and GoFundMe to assist his family. His organs are being donated.

The case has drawn attention to growing concerns about assaults on sports officials nationwide. National Association of Sports Officials representatives say assaults on referees have risen and deter people from officiating. Medical experts explained how a single unexpected blow to the head can cause fatal brain injury even without skull fracture, particularly when the victim is unable to brace. A preliminary hearing is scheduled for July 10.

A woman in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, was asked to leave a McDonald’s after bringing an eight-month-old joey named Jimmy into the restaurant in a child’s car seat following a customer complaint. Detective Ryan Klavekoske said deputies found the kangaroo with its owner; no tickets were issued. Owner Diana (Diane) Moyer and her husband Larry, who live on a 70-acre farm near Columbus, care for a menagerie including five kangaroos (ages 8 months to 7 years), sheep, goats, emu, deer, horses, poultry and peacocks. Moyer says Jimmy serves as a support/therapy animal for her disability and that she has taken him to church, a movie theater and the McDonald’s before without issue. The city, however, disagreed with her classification. Moyer has kept kangaroos for years, buying them from a Missouri livestock market; her farm is USDA-licensed and inspected, and she describes the animals as well cared for, housed in a barn in winter, and fed specialty diets that can be costly. She says she rarely receives negative reactions and plans to continue caring for and possibly expanding her collection of animals.

A veteran NYPD sergeant, 54-year-old Michael Iscenko of the Organized Crime Control Bureau, has been suspended after a female administrative aide alleged that he approached her from behind in January and tossed semen onto her leg in a hallway. The woman reported the incident immediately; the substance was tested and confirmed as semen, and DNA testing to link the sample to Iscenko is pending. He has not been criminally charged. Colleagues described him as professional in appearance. The article also notes the Internet Archive’s effort to crawl and preserve webpages to prevent broken links.

Florence Henderson, best known as Carol Brady on The Brady Bunch, has died at 82. She passed away at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles after suffering heart failure and was surrounded by family and friends. Henderson was hospitalized one day before her death.

Born February 14, 1934, in Dale, Indiana, she was the youngest of 10 children. After high school she studied at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York and built a career on Broadway in shows including Wish You Were Here, Fanny, The Girl Who Came to Supper and South Pacific. She also appeared in films and numerous TV guest roles and was the first woman to guest-host The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson (1962). From 1959–1960 she was one of the “Today” show’s early hosts covering fashion and human-interest stories.

Henderson rose to international fame as Carol Brady on The Brady Bunch (1969–1974), starring in every episode and later reprising the role in multiple spin-offs, reunion projects and The Brady Bunch Movie. After the series she remained a familiar presence on television—guesting on shows like The Love Boat, Murder, She Wrote, Ally McBeal and 30 Rock—appeared in reality TV (The Surreal Life, Dancing with the Stars) and hosted programs including Country Kitchen and The Florence Henderson Show. She received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1996.

She was married to Ira Bernstein (1956–1985), with whom she had four children—Barbara, Joseph, Robert and Elizabeth—and later to Dr. John Kappas until his death in 2002. Henderson is survived by her four children and five grandchildren. Colleagues and former co-stars paid tribute following the news of her death.

This document combines an explanation of web-archiving crawls and a short AP crime story.

- Web-archiving: Crawls are being run to archive pages as they are created and the pages they reference, so that when referenced pages change or disappear, links can point to the archived version that was live when the citing page was written. The Internet Archive’s aim is to repair broken links on the web by providing archived or companion links that show what a page’s authors originally intended. These crawls support the "No More 404" initiative.

- News item (Norwalk, Ohio): Police arrested 18-year-old Anthony Damante of Milan after surveillance showed he mistakenly left a 40‑gram bag of marijuana labeled “Sour Kush” on the front seat of the wrong car in a store parking lot. A woman who returned from buying lottery tickets found the suspicious-smelling bag and called police. Authorities say another woman in the lot paid Damante and went into the store while he placed the pot in the unlocked vehicle. Damante faces drug trafficking charges; court records don’t list an attorney. Source: Sandusky Register.

Brazil’s lower house of Congress began a heated, multi-day debate in mid-April 2016 on whether to impeach President Dilma Rousseff for alleged violations of budget laws, with a decisive roll-call vote scheduled for Sunday. Impeachment supporters accuse Rousseff of using accounting maneuvers in 2014 to hide deficits and bolster her re‑election; defenders say the practices were common to previous administrations and that she has not been proven guilty of graft tied to the Petrobras scandal. 

The proceedings unfolded amid large, often polarized street demonstrations and heightened tensions in Brasilia and other cities, with security measures (fences and police cordons) put in place to prevent clashes. Public opinion polls showed roughly two‑thirds of Brazilians backing impeachment. Many parties defected from Rousseff’s governing coalition, and analysts predicted her opponents would exceed the two‑thirds majority (342 of 513) needed to forward the case to the Senate.

Rousseff’s team sought a last‑minute injunction from the Supreme Court to suspend the lower‑house vote, but the court rejected the request, allowing the process to proceed. The attorney general called the impeachment a “violent act” and said Rousseff had been denied due process; opponents maintained the process reflected the people’s will. If the lower house approves impeachment, the Senate would decide whether to put Rousseff on trial. An affirmative Senate vote to try her would suspend her and install Vice President Michel Temer as acting president pending a possible six‑month trial. Temer, who lacks popular support, was already reportedly lining up potential economic ministers in case he assumes the presidency.

Retail retailer Yandy removed a “Brave Red Maiden” Halloween costume modeled on The Handmaid’s Tale after widespread backlash on social media. The costume turned the story’s red cloak and white bonnet—a recent symbol of protest against women’s oppression—into a revealing mini dress and cape. Yandy said the design was intended to reference the image’s use in protests and to be empowering, but acknowledged many viewers saw it as trivializing oppression and, after receiving numerous critical and personal responses, decided to pull the item. Reactions on Twitter ranged from disgust and bafflement to jokes and a few seeing accidental subversion.

NASA has renamed its Solar Probe Plus mission the Parker Solar Probe in honor of Eugene N. Parker, the University of Chicago astrophysicist who predicted the existence of the solar wind in 1958. It is the first time NASA has named a spacecraft for a living researcher. Parker, who is near age 90, attended the announcement and received a model of the probe, a chip of his photos and paper to fly on the spacecraft, and NASA’s Distinguished Public Service Medal.

Mission overview and goals
- Launch: planned summer 2018 (20-day window opening July 31, 2018) on a Delta IV Heavy.
- Duration: about seven years of solar orbits, ending ~2025.
- Trajectory: seven gravity-assist flybys of Venus to shrink the orbit and ultimately bring the probe within ~3.7–4.0 million miles (under 10 solar radii) of the Sun — roughly seven times closer than any prior spacecraft.
- Scientific objectives: trace the flow of energy that heats the corona and accelerates the solar wind; determine the structure and dynamics of plasma and magnetic fields at the solar wind source; study how energetic particles are accelerated and transported. Instruments will measure fields, particles and waves, and directly sample the near-Sun plasma.

Engineering and risks
- Spacecraft: car-sized probe with a 7.5-foot-wide, ~4.5-inch-thick carbon-composite heat shield and active thermal control so instruments remain near room temperature.
- Environment: will face temperatures up to ~1,370°C (about 2,500°F) and intense radiation; will retract/extend solar arrays during perihelion passes.
- Speed: will reach very high orbital speeds (hundreds of thousands of mph) and sample the region where solar wind transitions from subsonic to supersonic.

Scientific and practical importance
- The probe will address two longstanding puzzles: why the corona is millions of degrees hotter than the solar surface, and how the solar wind is accelerated to high speeds.
- Results are expected to advance basic stellar physics and improve understanding and forecasting of space weather (coronal mass ejections, solar energetic particles) that can damage satellites, threaten astronauts, disrupt aviation, and induce geomagnetically induced currents that can overload power grids on Earth. Studies cited estimate extreme space-weather events could cause enormous economic damage if unpredicted.

Context and legacy
- The mission (~$1.5 billion) represents a technically challenging, high-risk effort pushing the limits of spacecraft thermal protection; scientists expect surprises and major advances.
- NASA has previously renamed missions to honor scientists posthumously (e.g., Fermi telescope, Van Allen probes); naming this mission after Parker while he is alive marks a historic exception.

This collection of articles and recollections centers on the persistent risks of raw or undercooked animal foods and how past outbreaks shaped, but have not eliminated, unsafe practices.

Key points

- Jack in the Box, 1993: An E. coli O157:H7 outbreak from undercooked patties sickened over 600 people and killed four children. Restaurants were cooking burgers to 140°F (the federal standard then), which was insufficient to kill E. coli. Washington state had already raised its requirement to 155°F, but many operators didn’t adopt it. The incident prompted the industry to raise internal cooking temperatures and overhaul safety procedures.

- Recent trends and supply changes: Improvements in beef-supply safety have made many restaurants more willing to serve rarer, pink-center burgers (medium-rare), especially in gourmet and gastropub venues. Some operators mitigate risk by sourcing suppliers who test for E. coli O157:H7, but testing doesn’t eliminate other pathogens (Salmonella, Campylobacter) and cannot guarantee safety.

- Food code and safe temperatures: The federal food code requires ground beef to reach 155°F held for 15 seconds (or 158°F instant) to reliably kill pathogens. Lower temperatures require specific longer hold times (150°F for 60 seconds; 145°F for 3 minutes). Because grinding distributes surface bacteria throughout the patty, unlike whole steaks, undercooked burgers are uniquely risky. The code allows serving undercooked burgers only with clear written warnings on menus and verbal notification to customers.

- Enforcement and consumer information: Serving meat that contains E. coli is illegal; even if a customer requests medium-rare, a contaminated undercooked burger would make the restaurant liable. Experts note that server-to-patron risk communication often fails and that culinary terms like “medium-rare” don’t guarantee a specific safe temperature. The only sure consumer choice is to request the food be cooked to the safe internal temperature specified by the code.

- Outbreak examples since 1993: A 2014 recall of 1.8 million pounds of ground beef from Wolverine Packing Co. was linked to 12 E. coli cases across several states; health officials suspect undercooked burgers were involved. Separate incidents include outbreaks tied to raw milk (e.g., Moo View Dairy in South Australia linked to cryptosporidiosis) and to produce and shellfish.

- Practical safety advice (from food-safety experts): Use a meat thermometer (beef burgers: 160°F per some experts; food code: 155°F for ground beef), refrigerate perishables promptly, avoid washing raw poultry (it spreads bacteria), be cautious with sliced melons sold unrefrigerated, and avoid high-risk raw foods such as sprouts, raw shellfish, and raw milk. Commercial mayonnaise is generally safe; homemade versions carry more risk.

Takeaway
Although safer supply chains and consumer demand drive more restaurants to offer medium-rare burgers and other raw items, the biological risks remain real. Proper cooking to code temperatures, reliable supplier controls, clear consumer warnings, and honest server communication are the only dependable ways to reduce foodborne illness risk.

This collection of articles covers the controversy over Oxygen’s planned reality special All My Babies’ Mamas, which follows Atlanta rapper Shawty Lo and his 11 children by ten women. Critics say the show exploits children and promotes harmful stereotypes about unwed mothers, while supporters defend it as a legitimate depiction of one family.

Key points:
- Sabrina Lamb, a best-selling author and nonprofit CEO, launched a Change.org petition (nearly 28,000 signatures) calling for the show to be stopped. After seeing the pilot, she said it normalizes unprotected sex, demeans children with the slur “babies’ mama,” and exploits mothers and kids for entertainment — telling viewers the women “need therapy and condoms.”
- The Parents Television Council also condemned the premise as “crass, irresponsible and exploitative” and warned advertisers they would be held accountable.
- Oxygen responded that the special is intended as a look at one unique, complicated family and not a stereotype of any demographic; the network said development would continue.
- Shawty Lo defended himself in interviews, saying he provides for and cares for his 11 children and that critics should focus on responsible fatherhood rather than the number of his children.
- Commentators noted the broader debate: whether reality TV should be constrained when children are involved and whether viewers and parents should treat such programming as role models or merely representations of real-life situations.

The dispute centers on ethics, representation and the exploitation of children on reality TV versus creative freedom to depict unconventional family structures.

A gunman opened fire at Umpqua Community College in Roseburg, Oregon, Thursday morning at about 10:38 a.m., leaving multiple dead and injured. Officials reported 10 people killed and nine wounded; three of the wounded were in critical condition. The shooter was reportedly “neutralized” and later reported dead, though early counts of fatalities and injuries varied in initial reports. Identities of the shooter and victims were not immediately released.

The attack occurred in and around Snyder Hall; witnesses described hearing an initial shot through a window, then the shooter entering classrooms, forcing people to the floor and reportedly asking some to state their religion before firing. Survivors recounted chaos as students fled, hid or were locked down in buildings. Many victims were transported to Mercy Medical Center and other hospitals; several underwent surgery and most treated at Mercy were expected to survive. By the following morning three patients remained hospitalized.

Campus response included police clearing buildings, multiple ambulances on scene, evacuation of students to the Douglas County Fairgrounds where Red Cross counselors assisted, and an FBI response from regional offices. Local and federal officials, including Rep. Peter DeFazio, issued statements expressing condolences and praising first responders. The story remained developing as authorities continued to investigate.

At the closing ceremony of the 63rd Cannes Film Festival, Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives won the Palme d’Or. Charlotte Gainsbourg and jury president Tim Burton presented the award; Weerasethakul dedicated the prize to his home country. Match Factory will handle international sales for the film, which follows a man with acute kidney failure spending his final days with family.

Key awards and highlights:
- Palme d’Or: Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (Apichatpong Weerasethakul)
- Grand Prix: Of Gods and Men (Des Hommes et Des Dieux) — Xavier Beauvois; Sony Pictures Classics acquired U.S./Australia/New Zealand rights
- Jury Prize: A Screaming Man (Un Homme Qui Crie) — Mahamat-Saleh Haroun (Chad)
- Best Director: Mathieu Amalric — On Tour (Tournée)
- Best Screenplay: Lee Chang-dong — Poetry
- Best Actress: Juliette Binoche — Certified Copy (Copie Conforme) by Abbas Kiarostami
- Best Actor (shared): Javier Bardem — Biutiful, and Elio Germano — Our Life (La Nostra Vita)
- Camera d’Or (best first film): Leap Year (Año Bisiesto) — Michael Rowe

The jury was led by Tim Burton and included Kate Beckinsale, Benicio del Toro, Giovanna Mezzogiorno, Alexandre Desplat, Shekhar Kapur, Emmanuel Carrère, Alberto Barbera and Víctor Erice; jailed Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi was absent. The traditional red-carpet closing night featured international stars (including Penelope Cruz, Salma Hayek and Diane Kruger) and was followed by a gala, dinner and after-parties. Notably, no English-language film took a top prize this year.

A major Lancet study using 21 forecasting models and data from 35 high‑income and emerging industrialized countries projects substantial gains in life expectancy by 2030, with South Korea emerging as the world leader. Key findings:

- South Korean women are predicted to surpass 90 years (around 90.8–91) by 2030; South Korean men, and men in Australia and Switzerland, are forecast to reach about 84 years. Several other countries (France, Japan, Spain, Canada, New Zealand, the Netherlands) will also see notable increases for women and men.
- Overall, life expectancy is expected to rise in most studied countries and the female–male gap is narrowing as male lifestyles converge with female ones.
- The United States is an outlier with relatively small gains: U.S. life expectancy is projected to be among the lowest of rich countries in 2030 (about 79–80 for men and ~83 for women), similar to nations such as Mexico, Croatia or the Czech Republic for some groups. The study notes the U.S. already lags peers and that using data only through 2013 likely makes the U.S. projection optimistic (it doesn’t capture the 2015 life‑expectancy decline).
- Drivers of improvements in high‑performing countries include reductions in infant mortality, fewer cardiovascular deaths (especially stroke), declines in certain cancers, improved childhood nutrition, broad access to healthcare and rising living standards. South Korea’s gains are credited to equitable distribution of health benefits, low obesity and smoking, and strong investments in education and early‑life nutrition.
- Factors holding some countries back (notably the U.S.) include health inequality, limited universal healthcare coverage, high obesity, rising deaths from alcohol/drugs and mental‑health causes, higher homicide and maternal/infant mortality, and stalled progress on heart disease.
- The study cautions its projections assume continuation of current trends and cannot account for unforeseen events (epidemics, major policy changes). The authors emphasize policy implications: nations must prepare for larger elderly populations with strengthened health and social care, pension planning, and possibly new care models.

In short, the analysis predicts unprecedented longevity for parts of the world—led by South Korea—while highlighting widening international disparities driven largely by inequality and unequal access to health improvements, with the U.S. at risk of falling further behind.

Ford Motor Co. has demanded that supporters of Toronto Mayor Rob Ford stop using its script and oval logo after shirts reading “Ford Nation” with the automaker’s mark were signed by the mayor at a charity event. The company said the logo’s use was unauthorized.

Separately, newly released police search-warrant documents and media reports detail extensive allegations about Mayor Rob Ford’s conduct and substance use. Staffers interviewed by police described frequent heavy drinking, possible cocaine use, chaotic and abusive behavior, instances of alleged physical assaults on staff, and episodes suggesting impairment while working and driving. Specific incidents cited include drinking and driving (once in an Escalade with staff present), a drunken confrontation at city hall tied to a “Bier Markt” night, impaired behavior at the 2013 Garrison Ball (where he reportedly attended with his children and was later asked to leave), and involvement with associates under police scrutiny such as Alexander “Sandro” Lisi and Bruno Bellissimo. Staffers said they sometimes bought vodka for the mayor and sheltered him from scrutiny; some reported they feared or tolerated his conduct rather than reporting it.

The documents also describe strained dynamics between Rob Ford and his brother Doug, and recount internal staff tensions, firings (including chief of staff Mark Towhey after advising leave/resign/ fight options), and episodes of public and private misconduct. None of the allegations in the warrant materials have been proven in court; Ford has not been charged on those counts, though he has admitted to using crack cocaine and, in a later statement, said he had purchased illegal drugs while in office. The controversy has prompted calls from many city councillors for Ford to take a leave of absence and has drawn intense media and public scrutiny. Meanwhile, Ford Motor Co.’s own shares were noted in the report to have risen recently.

A coalition of environmental activists and celebrities staged a civil disobedience protest at the White House on Feb. 13, 2013, to urge President Obama to reject the proposed Keystone XL pipeline. More than 40 people—including Robert F. Kennedy Jr., actress Daryl Hannah, activist Bill McKibben, NASA climate scientist James Hansen, civil rights leader Julian Bond, and Sierra Club Executive Director Michael Brune—tied themselves to the White House gate or otherwise blocked access and were arrested on charges of failure to disperse and disobeying lawful orders; each was released on $100 bond.

The action marked a first for the Sierra Club in its 120-year history, with the board approving Brune’s participation to signal strong opposition to the $7 billion, 1,700-mile project that would carry tar-sands crude from western Canada to Gulf Coast refineries. Protesters argued the pipeline would transport “dirty oil” that emits substantially more greenhouse gases than conventional crude, risk spills, worsen local pollution near refineries (affecting many minority communities), and undermine efforts to address climate change. Kennedy and others said civil disobedience was justified given the pipeline’s environmental threat; organizers planned a larger rally on the National Mall expecting about 20,000 participants.

Supporters—including many business and labor groups and the American Petroleum Institute—back the pipeline as a source of jobs and a step toward North American energy independence. API argued Keystone XL has been thoroughly vetted and noted TransCanada agreed to many conditions to protect the environment. The project had previously been blocked twice by Obama over route concerns in Nebraska; the State Department has authority because the project crosses an international border, though the White House is expected to make the final decision.

The arrests came as Obama was campaigning on climate action in his State of the Union address and traveling to a manufacturing plant; opponents framed the pipeline as a major carbon threat, while proponents emphasized jobs and broader energy policy. The report also noted recent arrests of protesters trying to disrupt construction in Oklahoma.

Kensington Palace has announced that Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will marry on Saturday 19 May 2018 at St George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle. The Saturday date breaks with recent royal tradition (the Queen and the Duke of Cambridge married on weekdays) and coincides with the FA Cup Final, an event normally attended by the Duke of Cambridge as FA president. The Royal Family will cover the cost of the service, music, flowers and reception. Markle, who confirmed her engagement in November, will be baptized into and confirmed in the Church of England before the wedding. The couple have already begun public engagements together and will spend Christmas with the Queen at Sandringham. No extra Bank Holiday has been announced.

Vallejo authorities are searching for 29–30-year-old Denise Huskins, a physical therapist who was reportedly abducted from a Mare Island home early Monday and may be being held for ransom. Her boyfriend, identified in public reports as Aaron Quinn, told police he saw her forcibly taken and that a ransom demand was made; he reported the incident roughly 11–12 hours after it occurred. Police are interviewing Quinn but do not consider him a suspect or person of interest.

More than 100 search-and-rescue personnel, including dive teams, search dogs, sonar equipment, the FBI and county emergency teams, have been combing Mare Island and the Vallejo waterfront. Searchers focused on a waterfront area after spotting a possible object in the water during low tide. Investigators also found and recovered Huskins’ 2000 Toyota Camry at an undisclosed location in Vallejo and have examined the residence for evidence.

Huskins, described as about 5'7", 150 lbs, blonde with blue eyes, works at Kaiser Permanente Vallejo and previously lived in Southern California. Her family has traveled to Vallejo and is urging her safe return. Police released few details, asked the public for tips, and asked anyone with information to call the Vallejo Police Department.

TIME’s Fareed Zakaria interviewed President Barack Obama in the Oval Office, where Obama defended his foreign- and economic-policy record, outlined priorities, and responded to criticism heading into the 2012 campaign.

Foreign policy and national security
- Obama said he sought to change U.S. foreign policy trajectory by ending the Iraq War, refocusing on defeating al‑Qaeda, strengthening alliances and multilateral engagement, and restoring U.S. global leadership. He argued those goals have largely been achieved: Iraq is no longer a U.S. war, al‑Qaeda’s leadership and capabilities are severely degraded, NATO and Pacific alliances are strong, and the U.S. has reasserted influence in key multilateral forums.
- On Iran, Obama reiterated a policy of maximum pressure combined with a diplomatic path to peaceful nuclear energy under NPT constraints. He said Iran has been isolated and economically pressured, that serious negotiation proposals were rebuffed by Tehran, and that the U.S. would keep all options on the table to prevent a nuclear weapon.
- Regarding Afghanistan, he said counterterrorism efforts (targeting al‑Qaeda) have been highly successful but nation‑building and stabilization are harder, long‑term tasks. Progress has been made in several provinces and in building Afghan security forces, but full stabilization will take decades and require sustained international investment.
- On Asia and China, Obama denied the U.S. is pursuing a containment strategy. He framed the “pivot” as refocusing on the fast‑growing Asia‑Pacific where the U.S. has vital interests, while arguing a peacefully rising China is welcome but must play by common international rules.
- He defended his management of the foreign‑policy team and said his relationships with many foreign leaders are strong and based on trust, which has aided diplomacy.

Domestic politics and economics
- Obama dismissed Republican charges that he is timid or indecisive, saying the GOP would play to its base in primaries but that his record makes America safer and stronger.
- On fiscal policy, he said he created and embraced the Simpson‑Bowles commission and its balanced premise (spending cuts plus revenue). He argued he has offered balanced plans and made large cuts, but Republicans have refused to accept revenue increases. He rejected the notion that his administration walked away from deficit‑reduction.
- He emphasized that U.S. foreign policy rests on domestic economic strength—competitiveness, education, infrastructure, innovation—and defended his regulatory record and efforts to spur “insourcing.” He acknowledged more work is needed to reverse long‑term trends and boost growth.
- On relations with Congress, he said foreign policy benefits from a bipartisan, mission‑focused culture that allowed effective management, whereas domestic gridlock stems from a deeply ideological Congress that often prefers political advantage to compromise. He said personal rapport (e.g., with Speaker John Boehner) is not the problem; rather, Boehner struggles to bring his caucus to compromise—an assessment Boehner’s office disputed.

Personal image and leadership style
- Obama addressed perceptions that he is aloof, attributing them in part to avoiding Washington social life to spend time with his young daughters and family priorities. He argued that his style does not prevent him from forging substantive, trust‑based relationships with foreign leaders and managing complex policy effectively.

Overall tone and claim
- Obama portrayed the last three years as a successful reorientation of U.S. policy that left the country safer and better positioned for the future, while acknowledging ongoing challenges—particularly Iran, Afghanistan, and domestic economic competitiveness—and arguing those challenges require sustained, pragmatic leadership and international cooperation.

Jean S. Harris, the former headmistress whose 1981 trial for the killing of prominent cardiologist Dr. Herman Tarnower became a national sensation, has died at 89 in an assisted‑living center in New Haven, her son James confirmed.

Harris, a Smith College graduate and head of the Madeira School, was arrested March 10, 1980, after Tarnower was found dying of four gunshot wounds at his Purchase, N.Y., home. The long, publicized case centered on a 14‑year relationship between the divorced, 56‑year‑old Harris and the wealthy, 69‑year‑old Tarnower—author of the bestselling The Complete Scarsdale Medical Diet—and his growing involvement with his younger office assistant, Lynne Tryforos. Harris said she had gone to confront Tarnower and intended to kill herself but that the shooting occurred accidentally during a struggle for the gun; she also made incendiary remarks about her rival that figured in the trial.

Her eight days on the stand, the dramatic facts and competing portrayals—of Harris as a jilted, dependent woman victimized by a man and of her as a jealous, snobbish socialite—sparked wide debate among feminists, writers and social commentators and inspired TV films. A jury convicted her of second‑degree murder in March 1981; she received a 15‑to‑life sentence and served 12 years at Bedford Hills.

While incarcerated she counseled inmates, taught parenting skills, helped establish a center allowing infants to stay near their mothers, and later founded Children of Bedford Inc., raising funds and scholarships for children of incarcerated women. Cleared for parole after health issues and a clemency grant from Gov. Mario Cuomo, she was released in 1993 and continued to lecture and advocate on prison reform and related issues. She acknowledged at a parole hearing that she had "caused the man's death" though she maintained the shooting was not premeditated.

Former Alaska governor and 2008 GOP vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin drew thousands Friday at a Wisconsin Right to Life fundraiser, where she warned that the philosophy permitting abortion rights could lead to government rationing of health care for the elderly and disabled. Speaking to roughly 5,000 attendees at the fairgrounds near Milwaukee, Palin suggested that if policymakers don’t value unborn children, “perhaps the same mind-set applies to other persons,” and posed rhetorical questions about panels of bureaucrats deciding care for the elderly or children with special needs. Though she avoided explicitly reusing the incendiary “death panels” language she used earlier in the year, her remarks repeatedly implied a risk of de facto euthanasia under liberal policies.

The sold-ticket event highlighted Palin’s continuing popularity with conservative activists: long lines, enthusiastic promotional items, a pledge drive tied to an autographed copy of her forthcoming memoir, and supporters wearing “Palin 2012” shirts. Palin mixed prepared remarks with frequent off-script flourishes, personal anecdotes (including discovering her son Trig has Down syndrome), religious references, praise for the military, criticism of the “liberal media,” and calls to hold leaders like House Speaker Nancy Pelosi accountable on abortion-related votes. She took several jabs at President Obama without naming him and closed by urging supporters not to be silenced.

Palin also made an erroneous comment about newly minted dollar coins, asserting that the motto “In God We Trust” had been moved to the coin’s rim — a change she cast as a troubling trend and implicitly blamed on Democrats. Fox News and others later noted the coins were commissioned by Republican-led Congress in 2005 and enacted in 2007, countering her implication. The event reinforced Palin’s appeal to her base while also illustrating the limits of her rhetorical style: warm reception but stops and starts in delivery, and signs that not all attendees were deeply energized throughout.

Summary — Bruce v. Boardwine (Court of Appeals of Virginia)

Facts
- Joyce Bruce wanted to raise a child without a father’s involvement and asked longtime friend Robert Boardwine to donate sperm. They talked about a written agreement but never signed one.
- Bruce became pregnant in mid‑2010 after repeated at‑home insemination attempts using a turkey baster. She believed that because conception did not involve sexual intercourse or medical assistance, the donor would have no parental rights.
- Boardwine testified he intended to be involved in the child’s life. The friends’ relationship soured before the birth; Bruce did not list Boardwine on the birth certificate or notify him immediately. After the child’s birth Boardwine visited and later sought court action to establish parental rights.

Legal issue and statute
- Virginia law disclaims parentage for a “donor” who contributes gametes for a child “conceived through assisted conception,” unless the donor is the husband of the gestational mother. “Assisted conception” is defined to include pregnancies resulting from intervening medical technology (in vivo or in vitro) and lists medical and noncoital reproductive technologies such as artificial insemination by donor and in vitro fertilization.
- The court interpreted “medical technology” and held the statutory list confines the statute to procedures involving medical personnel and conventional medical treatment; it does not encompass home insemination with a kitchen implement (a turkey baster).

Holding and outcome
- The Court of Appeals affirmed that Bruce’s pregnancy was not the result of “assisted conception” as defined by the statute because no medical technology or personnel were involved.
- Robert Boardwine’s paternity was established by DNA (over 99.999% probability). As the child’s father, he was entitled to pursue and receive visitation (and joint custody rights as found by the trial court).
- The court’s decision turns on statutory interpretation rather than policy: the legislature’s exclusion of nonmedical home insemination from the assisted‑conception protection means donors in such cases can be recognized as parents with associated rights and obligations.

Practical significance
- Under current Virginia law, sperm donors who contribute outside the scope of medical/assisted‑conception procedures (e.g., at‑home insemination) may be treated as legal parents and can assert custody or visitation rights. The decision highlights a gap between the statute’s medical‑technology focus and situations involving informal, nonmedical gamete donation.

This long piece collects several perspectives and reporting about the decades-old allegations that Woody Allen molested his adopted daughter Dylan Farrow when she was seven, the family fallout that followed, and the ways the public has reacted.

Main themes and points

- Presumption of innocence versus public judgment: One piece argues that the presumption of innocence should apply to Dylan Farrow in the sense that, absent proof beyond a reasonable doubt, people should not default to assuming she is lying. The author criticizes a cultural double standard that protects famous men’s reputations while treating female accusers as inherently suspect, calling that dynamic a feature of “rape culture.” The piece also says ordinary observers (not jurors) are entitled to form opinions and weigh probabilities without the high legal standard required for criminal conviction, noting sexual violence is common whereas fabricated accusations are rare.

- Robert B. Weide’s account: Filmmaker Robert Weide—who made a PBS documentary about Woody Allen and later helped assemble a Golden Globes montage—describes his familiarity with Allen, his decision to comment amid online misinformation, and his attempt to separate two issues often conflated: Allen’s relationship with Soon‑Yi Previn and Mia Farrow’s 1992 molestation allegation regarding Dylan. Weide asserts many commonly repeated claims about Soon‑Yi are factually wrong (e.g., she was not Allen’s daughter or stepdaughter; she was an adult when her relationship with Allen began). He recounts his research into the custody dispute and the 1992–93 investigations: a Yale‑New Haven team and Connecticut police investigated and concluded findings that raised doubts about abuse, citing inconsistencies, possible coaching, and emotional dynamics in the household; no criminal charges were brought. Weide highlights contested elements—the videotaped interviews, destroyed notes, mixed medical findings—and stresses uncertainty, sympathy for Malone (Dylan), and the difficulty of knowing what truly happened. He defends checking facts and urges caution about online verdicts while noting Allen’s continuing career and family life.

- Family divisions and reporting from People: Coverage from People magazine focuses on how the allegations split the family. Moses Farrow, Dylan’s adoptive brother, now estranged from Mia Farrow and reconciled with Allen and Soon‑Yi, publicly defends Allen and accuses Mia of poisoning the children against their father. Moses says Dylan was never off alone with Allen and suggests she may have been influenced by their mother; Dylan strongly rejects that characterization, insisting her memories are true and calling Moses “dead to me.” Mia Farrow declined to comment directly in that report but publicly said she loves and will protect her daughter. The article reiterates the family’s deep divisions, the durable bitterness from the early 1990s custody fight, and the continuing emotional toll.

Contextual takeaways

- The documents stress two distinct but often conflated issues: Allen’s adult relationship with Soon‑Yi Previn (controversial but involving consenting adults) and the separate allegation that he molested Dylan as a child (investigated in the early 1990s with no criminal charges, but disputed findings and strong, lasting disagreements within the family).

- Evidence and interpretation remain contested: investigators raised questions about Dylan’s statements and possible coaching, while Dylan and supporters maintain her account; some family members support Allen, others support Dylan; public opinion has been shaped by decades of media coverage, social media, and renewed attention following public statements by Dylan and her siblings.

- The pieces reflect broader cultural debates about how to weigh accusations of sexual abuse, the appropriate standards for public judgment versus criminal conviction, and how fame and gender can shape credibility in the court of public opinion.

A 32-year-old Madison, Wisconsin man bought a camera designed to attach to a shoe intending to record “upskirt” videos of women. While testing the device at home, its battery exploded, causing minor burns to his foot. Troubled by the incident, he told a clergyman, who advised him to turn himself in and accompanied him to the West Police District station. The man admitted his intention to use the shoe camera for invasive recordings; officers counseled him and released him because no illegal recordings had been made. Police are continuing to investigate.

The report was included in a daily Madison Police Department log that also detailed other incidents from June 26–27, 2018, including domestic disturbances, weapons offenses, stolen vehicle, stalking and several sexual-assault reports, multiple traffic crashes, an attempted suicide, and armed robberies. The summary also notes that “upskirting” has risen with ubiquitous recording devices and that Wisconsin law (2015 Act creating statute 942.08(3)) makes intentionally installing or using devices to view, broadcast, or record under another’s clothing a Class I felony.

David Bowie’s comeback album The Next Day (released March 11) is widely praised as a startlingly strong return that both echoes his past and speaks urgently to the present. Produced with longtime collaborator Tony Visconti and recorded with familiar players (Gerry Leonard, Gail Ann Dorsey, Zachary Alford, Earl Slick, David Torn), the record deliberately references Bowie’s earlier eras—visually (a redacted Heroes cover) and sonically (nods to Berlin, Ziggy, Let’s Dance, Tin Machine and Lodger)—yet largely addresses contemporary concerns: celebrity culture, war, power, isolation and moral decay.

Musically the 14 tracks are lean, rock-driven and muscular: hard drums, sharp bass and fizzing guitars are punctuated by keyboards and occasional horns and strings. Bowie alternates jagged, confrontational numbers with melancholy and melodic pieces, using a mixture of witty, opaque and densely allusive lyrics that invite multiple interpretations but remain emotionally immediate.

Highlights and themes from key tracks:
- The Next Day: a stalking funk-rock opener about a fallen or tyrannical figure, mixing bitterness and doom-laden imagery.
- The Stars (Are Out Tonight): a catchy meditation on celebrity as minor gods; one of the album’s strongest songs.
- Where Are We Now?: the solitary, melancholic Berlin reflection that first announced Bowie’s return; delicate and ruminative.
- Love Is Lost, Dirty Boys and (You Will) Set The World On Fire: sharp critiques of fame, violence and ambition.
- I’d Rather Be High and You Feel So Lonely You Could Die: melodic, emotionally potent tracks—one regretful and jazzy, the other a climactic, vitriolic meditation on loneliness and self-destruction.
- How Does The Grass Grow?: unsettling juxtaposition of genocide-themed lyrics with an absurdist, la-la chorus.
- Heat: closes the album with introspective, ambiguous confession—“I am a seer, but I am a liar”—framing Bowie as storyteller and trickster.

Critics note the album’s balance of nods to past styles with fresh, contemporary production; it never feels merely retrospective or a museum piece. While some argue it doesn’t surpass Bowie’s 1970s masterpieces, most consider The Next Day an impressive, intellectually and emotionally charged comeback—rocky, inventive and full of memorable songs—offering more questions than answers in true Bowie fashion.

Campus Pride says it obtained Chick-fil-A’s WinShape Foundation 2011 tax (Form 990) records showing the foundation no longer funds some of the most controversial, politically active anti‑same‑sex‑marriage groups (previously cited beneficiaries included the Family Research Council, Eagle Forum and Exodus International). The records — filed Nov. 15 and public once released by the IRS — indicate nearly $6 million in grants focused on youth, education, marriage enrichment and local communities. 

Campus Pride executive director Shane Windmeyer, who received access to the forms, acknowledged WinShape still supports faith‑based groups that oppose same‑sex marriage for biblical reasons (for example, the Fellowship of Christian Athletes) but said these organizations do not pursue the same hard‑edged political agendas. Windmeyer, who began private conversations with Chick‑fil‑A president Dan Cathy after Cathy’s widely publicized comments opposing same‑sex marriage last July, says the two developed a personal relationship and that Campus Pride suspended a national college campaign against the chain to seek common ground around respect and dignity. 

The controversy over Chick‑fil‑A’s political donations and Cathy’s remarks sparked nationwide protests, calls for boycotts and counter‑demonstrations (including “Chick‑fil‑A Appreciation Day” and same‑sex kiss events). Chick‑fil‑A and WinShape did not comment for the story. The privately held chain operates over 1,615 locations and had roughly $4.1 billion in sales in 2011.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers in Pharr, Texas, seized 2,493 pounds of suspected marijuana hidden inside 2,817 carrot-shaped packages concealed within a commercial shipment of fresh carrots entering from Mexico. The tractor‑trailer was flagged by an imaging inspection system at the Pharr‑Reynosa International Bridge on Jan. 10; a secondary inspection with a canine unit uncovered the drug stash, which CBP estimates has a street value of about $499,000. Port Director Efrain Solis Jr. said the case illustrates smugglers’ creativity; Homeland Security is assisting the investigation. Local reports note a similar interception at the same bridge in December, when over $1 million in drugs disguised as carrots and cucumbers was stopped.

Capt. Bruce K. Clark, a 43-year-old Army nurse deployed to Tarin Kowt, Afghanistan, died April 30 while on a Skype call with his wife, Susan. She says he suddenly pitched forward on camera and that she and others later saw a bullet hole in a closet behind him. The Skype link reportedly stayed open for about two hours while Susan placed frantic calls to military authorities; two military personnel eventually arrived, checked his pulse, and he was pronounced dead. The Army initially described the death as non-suicide and non-combat related and said no bullet wound was found on Clark’s body; officials say the delay in response was due to Susan’s calls being routed through multiple stateside commands. The cause of death is still pending toxicology and autopsy results and remains under investigation. Clark joined the Army in 2006 after earning a nursing degree, had been deployed to Afghanistan in March, and is survived by his wife and two daughters. The family released Susan’s account to honor Clark and counter speculation surrounding his death.

LaVar Ball said he is not feuding with President Donald Trump but refused to publicly thank Trump for helping secure his son LiAngelo Ball’s release from China. In a CNN interview, LaVar insisted he and his own contacts were primarily responsible for getting LiAngelo — who, along with UCLA teammates Jalen Hill and Cody Riley, was detained for shoplifting in Hangzhou — home safely, and said he wouldn’t feel obligated to thank everyone who helped. He suggested Chinese President Xi might deserve thanks before Trump, questioned reports crediting Trump with preventing long jail terms, and downplayed any “war” with the president. The remarks follow a series of tweets from Trump saying he helped save the players from what he called potential 5–10 year sentences and criticizing LaVar as ungrateful.

Samantha Bee, host of TBS’s Full Frontal, is organizing a rival gala in Washington, D.C. called “Not the White House Correspondents’ Dinner,” to be held at the Willard Hotel on April 29—the same night the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) dinner is scheduled. Bee and her producers conceived the idea after the election as a way to create a joyful, journalist-focused event amid increasingly hostile relations between the Trump administration and the press. She said TBS is expected to broadcast the event, and all proceeds will go to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Bee emphasized the gala is not intended to supplant the WHCA dinner but to ensure a space to roast President Trump and spotlight “unsung journalists,” while offering an alternative if the WHCA dinner is altered or canceled. The move fits a broader trend of late-night hosts expanding beyond traditional TV—using live events and social media to reach fragmented audiences—and follows other high-profile political-comedy efforts such as Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert’s 2010 rally. Bee’s Full Frontal, renewed through 2017, plans to use the soirée to champion journalism and engage fans and journalists outside the conventional correspondents’ event.

Researchers at the University of Washington found that fruit flies (Drosophila hydei) perform ultra-fast, jet-like evasive maneuvers when they sense a threat. Using three high-speed cameras shooting 7,500 frames per second and an expanding-shadow stimulus (flies flew through crossing laser beams), the team recorded 3,566 wing beats across 92 escape events. Flies normally beat their wings ≈200 times per second and can reorient and execute banked turns—rolling and pitching nearly upside down—in under 0.01 seconds (often within one or two wing beats). Rather than simply yawing like a boat, they use subtle changes in wing motion to generate forces that rapidly change momentum, producing very fast and accurate responses.

The researchers replicated measured motions on a robot fly (tested in viscous fluid to match scaling) to directly measure wing forces, and derived mathematical rules governing the turns. The work highlights how a very small but neuron-dense brain can perform complex, high-speed sensorimotor computations. The next steps are to map the neural circuitry that translates visual input into these precise motor outputs. The study appears in Science.
