James D. Watson, the co-discoverer of the DNA double helix and 1962 Nobel laureate, has again stirred controversy with remarks published in Britain’s Sunday Times Magazine in which he suggested that black people are less intelligent than whites. The comments provoked immediate condemnation in the U.K., prompting cancellations of his scheduled public appearances (including events at the Science Museum and the University of Edinburgh), the withdrawal of a Bristol booking, and calls for action at his home institution. Watson issued an unreserved apology, saying he was mortified and that his words were not intended to imply genetic inferiority and that there is no scientific basis for such a belief. Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory suspended his administrative duties as the controversy unfolded.

The report notes broader problems with the claims Watson is reported to have made: there is no scientific consensus on definitions of "race" or "intelligence," and IQ testing is subject to cultural bias, making sweeping genetic assertions about populations unsupported by science. The article portrays Watson as a provocative, sometimes misguided figure — brilliant and visionary in his scientific achievements, yet prone to making inflammatory comments — and suggests hope that his remarks may have been misunderstood.

Separately, a Christie’s press release announced that Watson will sell his 1962 Nobel Prize gold medal at auction on December 4, with an estimate of $2.5–3.5 million. The sale, unprecedented for a living recipient, will include handwritten notes and manuscripts related to his Nobel speeches. The release summarizes Watson’s biography and scientific legacy: early aptitude and rapid academic rise, collaboration with Francis Crick leading to the 1953 discovery of DNA’s double-helix structure, influential books (including The Double Helix), leadership roles at Harvard and Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, and involvement with the Human Genome Project. Proceeds from the sale will be partially donated to scientific and local charities, the release says.

Following Whitney Houston's death at 48, sales and downloads of her music surged across major retailers. Seven of her albums were in Amazon’s top 10 best-sellers and several singles—most notably her cover of "I Will Always Love You" and "I Wanna Dance With Somebody"—shot up the iTunes charts and re-entered top lists. Observers expect sustained high chart positions as fans mourn.

Controversy arose when Sony Music reportedly raised the wholesale price of Houston’s Greatest Hits collection early Sunday, which briefly pushed the iTunes retail price of The Ultimate Collection from £4.99 to £7.99. Critics accused the companies of profiteering; Sony sources said the price change reflected an incorrect wholesale adjustment rather than a deliberate attempt to capitalize on the news. Apple and Sony declined to comment.

Former U.S. figure skater Tonya Harding expressed sympathy for Nancy Kerrigan and her family after the death of Kerrigan’s father, Daniel Kerrigan. Harding’s spokesperson noted she understands the grief, saying her own father died in April.

Daniel Kerrigan, 70, died after an altercation at the family home on Jan. 24; authorities charged his son Mark with assault and held him on $10,000 bail after a not-guilty plea. A cause of death has not been determined; family members told the Boston Herald it may have been a heart attack. Nancy Kerrigan has been “really struggling” but has responded gratefully to support from friends and fellow skaters.

The story also notes longstanding family troubles: in March 2008 Nancy’s parents sued her older brother Mark over $105,000 they said they lent him for mortgage, bills and other expenses while he was serving a two-year jail sentence on assault, drug and property-destruction convictions. Steven Avery, who in 1985 was wrongfully convicted of sexual assault in Manitowoc County, Wisconsin, was exonerated after DNA testing and became a national symbol of wrongful conviction reform. His release prompted apologies locally and helped spur an “Avery task force” whose recommendations were recently adopted by the state as criminal-justice reforms (formerly called the Avery Bill). Avery toured the Capitol, testified to lawmakers, and served as a prominent spokesman for reform.

Weeks after his exoneration, however, Avery was arrested and charged in the October 2005 disappearance and death of 25-year-old photographer Teresa Halbach. Investigators say they found her remains and vehicle at his salvage yard, blood from both Halbach and Avery in the car, her car key in his trailer with Avery’s DNA on it, and other incriminating evidence. The new charges stunned Avery’s supporters and the lawyers who had pursued his earlier civil suit; his lead civil attorney called the new allegations devastating and said they undermine the goodwill the case had generated for reform efforts.

The development provoked debate nationally among innocence advocates. The Innocence Project noted that post-exoneration convictions are rare and said Avery’s case should not derail efforts to free the wrongly convicted; Wisconsin Innocence Project leaders urged distinguishing the two sets of allegations and insisted their mission includes finding the truth and holding true perpetrators accountable. Still, critics and talk-show commentators have attacked innocence advocates, arguing that Avery’s prior record and convictions might indicate violent tendencies.

Locally, family members insist Avery is innocent and claim evidence was planted. The arrest has complicated Avery’s $36 million civil suit against former local officials and stalled some state payments and plans tied to his exoneration. It has also cooled local enthusiasm for a celebratory signing of the reform package, which lawmakers now refer to more generically as criminal-justice reforms. The case has renewed bitter divisions in Manitowoc and nationwide, raising fresh questions about possible evidence tampering, police conduct, the interrogation of co-defendant Brendan Dassey, and whether Avery’s earlier litigation against county officials motivated misconduct.

An unprecedented Ebola epidemic in West Africa—centered in Guinea and now spreading across Sierra Leone and Liberia—is the deadliest on record and remains out of control. As of late June 2014, WHO and reporting organizations put confirmed, probable and suspected cases at roughly 567–600 infections with about 338–390 deaths. The outbreak involves Zaire ebolavirus, the most lethal strain, and has reached large population centers for the first time, complicating containment.

Why it’s so severe
- Viral: Zaire ebolavirus is highly virulent and can evade immune responses; symptoms develop after a 2–21 day incubation and can include fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, in many cases, internal and external bleeding. Death typically occurs between days 6–16 from multi-organ failure and shock.
- Human and systemic factors: This is the first major Ebola event in West Africa, so many local health workers lack training and protective experience. Increased travel in the region, cross-border movement in the tri-border rural hotspot, unsafe burial practices, social stigma, denial, and distrust of health teams have all amplified spread and hindered contact tracing and care.
- Response strain: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) reports being overwhelmed and unable to open new treatment sites without more resources. WHO has deployed staff and plans a multi-country coordination meeting; officials warn the epidemic may continue for another three to four months unless responses are rapidly strengthened.

Transmission and risk outside West Africa
- Ebola is transmitted by direct contact with blood or bodily fluids of infected people or contaminated materials; it is not airborne and infected persons are typically contagious only when symptomatic. Because of this, international spread is considered unlikely to trigger a global pandemic. Air travel can export cases (e.g., likely routes from Conakry to Paris), but prior incidents show in-flight transmission is rare and robust public-health measures limit onward spread.

Treatment and containment
- Care is currently supportive (fluids, symptom management); some patients survive. Research on drugs and vaccines is under way, with increased funding and attention. Containment hinges on rapid diagnosis, isolation, infection-control practices, safe burials, effective public education, trained personnel, contact tracing and coordinated regional action.

Challenges ahead
- WHO and partners stress the need for a coordinated, well-resourced multi-country effort, better communication to overcome denial and harmful traditional practices, and mobilization of political, religious and community leaders to improve compliance with control measures. Without these steps and more resources, the outbreak risks further cross-border transmission and greater loss of life.

Headline: Cory Monteith died from a lethal mix of heroin and alcohol

Summary:
Canadian authorities have determined that 31-year-old Glee actor Cory Monteith died of mixed drug toxicity involving heroin and alcohol. His body was found in his Vancouver hotel room at the Fairmont Pacific Rim on July 13. Police indicated there was evidence in the room consistent with a drug overdose but did not detail specific items found. Monteith had a long history of substance abuse and had entered rehab earlier in the year; he has said his struggles began in his early teens. The investigation and reporting were ongoing at the time.

Two Fort Collins middle school students, both 11 years old, died by suicide within days of each other in November, bringing Larimer County’s total suicide count this year to 77, including three involving minors. The county coroner confirmed the students — a girl who attended Lincoln Middle School and a boy who attended Blevins Middle School — but has not released their names; the boy’s family asked for privacy. Last year Larimer County recorded 83 suicides, two of them youth, and 2014 was the highest in at least a decade.

The Poudre School District has provided extra counseling at the affected schools and says it has increased student mental-health supports and suicide-prevention training over the last five years. One victim’s family, whose daughter’s obituary and community vigils identified her as Ariana Cordova, said she had been bullied since elementary school and had received counseling and accommodations. Her family hopes her death will prompt stronger anti-bullying efforts and encourage students to seek help. A joint candlelight vigil was planned for the community, and families are raising funds to cover medical and funeral costs. Authorities have not confirmed bullying as a cause.

General Mills’ non‑GMO reformulation of Original Cheerios and Post Foods’ new non‑GMO Grape‑Nuts remove or greatly reduce several added vitamins, and neither company has explained why.

Key points
- Nutrition changes: Reformulated Original Cheerios have dropped riboflavin (vitamin B2) from about 25% of the daily value per 28 g serving to roughly 2%. Post’s new non‑GMO Grape‑Nuts no longer list vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin B12 or riboflavin.
- Company responses: General Mills declined to discuss formulation details and denied claiming non‑GM ingredients are “more wholesome.” Post confirmed the recipe change but did not explain the vitamin removals.
- Likely cause: Experts say sourcing vitamins that meet non‑GMO verification is complicated. Many vitamins are produced by or processed with microbes or feedstocks (corn, sugar, soy) that may be derived from genetically modified crops, and vitamin manufacturers often consider formulation details proprietary. Non‑GMO Project verification requires detailed supply‑chain information that can be hard to obtain.
- Industry context: Non‑GMO labeling has grown quickly as some consumers avoid GMOs, often citing health concerns. Still, most shoppers aren’t willing to pay more for non‑GMO products; a small segment will. Converting supply chains to non‑GMO standards is gradual and ingredient‑by‑ingredient.
- Nutrition concern: Nutrition experts and observers describe the result as ironic and potentially less healthy for consumers who avoid GMOs for health reasons, since some products lose significant micronutrient fortification in the switch.

Bottom line: Moving to non‑GMO formulations can complicate sourcing of fortified vitamins, and in these two high‑profile cereal reformulations that challenge appears to have resulted in reduced vitamin content—though the manufacturers have not publicly clarified the specific reasons.

This document stitches together Michael Wolff’s profile of Donald Trump from June 2016 (published in The Hollywood Reporter) with later reporting and excerpts from Wolff’s book and columns about the chaotic first year of the Trump White House and related breaking news about U.S. aid to Palestinians.

Key points from the Trump profile (June 2016):
- Wolff spent an evening with Trump at his Beverly Hills home during the final days before the California primary and portrays Trump as relaxed, self-satisfied and energized by his mass-media fame and campaign “phenomenon.”
- Trump revels in his celebrity and media relationships, praising figures like Rupert Murdoch, Sumner Redstone, Leslie Moonves and executives such as Roger Ailes and Jeff Zucker even while publicly attacking the “dishonest media.” He enjoys the media theater and sees his campaign primarily as a spectacle driven by his personal brand and “bigness.”
- In private he is warm and ingratiating toward the wealthy and powerful but deflects or minimizes policy specifics, foreign issues (e.g., Brexit) and nuanced discussion. He insists he need not “pivot” politically because he can “remake the electoral math” and broaden his appeal to women, Hispanics and blacks.
- Trump frames himself as a performer and natural campaigner who thrives without a teleprompter and whose chief appeal is authenticity and personal magnetism. He reads few books but cites Edward Klein’s Unlikeable and All Quiet on the Western Front.
- The profile emphasizes a divide between Trump the public snarling rhetorician and the congenial private figure, and highlights his confidence that the campaign’s success validates him above criticism.

Key points from Wolff’s White House reporting / Fire and Fury excerpts:
- Wolff had extensive access to the West Wing and reports pervasive dysfunction, factional infighting and a staff often baffled by Trump’s behavior.
- Many senior staffers were inexperienced around Trump, and the administration’s early months were marked by leaks, public embarrassments and rapid turnovers (Flynn, Spicer, Priebus, Bannon among others).
- Internal factions formed—Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump versus Steve Bannon and Reince Priebus—creating near-constant power struggles and public spectacle. Staffing churn and the lack of coherent policy direction made governance chaotic.
- Trump is portrayed as childlike in his desire for instant wins and photo opportunities, prone to repetition, impulsive phone calls to billionaire friends, and deeply self-focused. Several senior aides privately disparaged his competence.
- Appointments and removals often appeared ad hoc (e.g., John Kelly named chief of staff without prior notice to him). Hope Hicks rose as a central, soothing confidante. Anthony Scaramucci’s brief, tumultuous tenure is highlighted as emblematic of the administration’s dysfunction.
- By the end of the first year most experienced aides were gone; the administration’s notable legislative achievement was the tax bill, seen as a conservative victory that diverged from some of Trump’s populist rhetoric.
- Wolff and many insiders believed Trump lacked the discipline and credibility to withstand the Mueller investigation; discussions included possibilities ranging from impeachment to resignation or survival.

Additional breaking-news item included:
- The Trump administration was reported to have withheld up to $125 million (one-third) of annual U.S. funding to UNRWA (United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestinian refugees) pending a review of aid to the Palestinian Authority after the Palestinian decision to suspend contacts with Washington following U.S. recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. U.S. officials were also reportedly considering larger cuts (up to $180 million).
- Donor countries, U.N. officials and Israeli security officials were worried about humanitarian consequences in Gaza, the West Bank and refugee-hosting countries. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly preferred gradual disengagement rather than a sudden cut because UNRWA also serves Israeli security interests.

Overall takeaways:
- Wolff’s pieces portray Trump as a media-fueled, self-assured performer who prioritizes spectacle and personal loyalty over policy coherence, and they depict a White House riven by internecine conflict, turnover and managerial chaos.
- The news item about frozen UNRWA funding underscores how White House decisions and reviews on foreign aid were already producing potentially serious diplomatic and humanitarian consequences early in the administration.

Researchers have re-examined hair samples long claimed to be from the legendary Himalayan "yeti" and concluded they are not from an unknown primate or a lost polar-brown bear hybrid, but instead match Himalayan brown bear DNA. In 2014, Oxford geneticist Bryan Sykes and colleagues analyzed two hairs from the Himalayas and reported they matched an ancient polar bear sequence, suggesting a previously unrecognized bear species or a polar-brown bear hybrid that might have inspired yeti legends. Eliécer Gutiérrez (Smithsonian) and colleagues revisited the data and found that the short mitochondrial DNA fragment used in Sykes’ study is not informative enough to distinguish modern brown bears from polar bears; when properly compared, the hairs are consistent with Himalayan brown bears. This critique echoes an earlier 2014 letter by other researchers who said Sykes’ team did not analyze enough of the mitochondrial genome to support their controversial claim.

Sykes has defended the original work’s main point—that the samples were not from unknown primates—but acknowledges further work with fresh tissue is needed to resolve the identity conclusively. Other experts note that misidentified bear sightings are a plausible explanation for many yeti reports, and that cultural factors help perpetuate the legend regardless of genetic findings. The new paper was published in ZooKeys; related critiques have appeared previously in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

This document summarizes research and guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) about sleep-related infant deaths and safe sleep practices.

Key study findings (Pediatrics, Aug 2014)
- Researchers analyzed 8,207 sleep-related infant deaths reported from 24 states (2004–2012).
- Major risk patterns differ by age:
  - Younger infants (0–3 months): much more likely to be bed-sharing at time of death (≈74% vs 59% for older infants). “Bed-sharing” includes sleeping with a person or animal and on adult beds.
  - Older infants (4 months–1 year): more often found prone and/or in sleep areas with objects (blankets, pillows, stuffed toys); about 39% had objects present. About 18% had changed position to prone.
- Overall 69% of deaths involved bed-sharing; 58% of infants were male; most deaths occurred among non-Hispanic white infants.
- The study reports associations, not proven cause-and-effect, and emphasizes that risk factors vary with developmental stage.

AAP safe-sleep guidance and recommendations (for infants up to 1 year)
- Always place babies on their backs for sleep (naps and night). Back-sleeping markedly lowers SIDS risk.
- Newborns should have early skin-to-skin contact after birth; when not possible, place newborns on their backs in a bassinet.
- Use a firm sleep surface (crib, bassinet, portable crib/play yard) that meets CPSC standards, with a tight-fitting sheet and nothing else in the sleep space.
- Room-share (place baby’s sleep area in parents’ bedroom) for the first 6 months, ideally up to 1 year—reduces SIDS risk and aids feeding and monitoring. Room-sharing is safer than bed-sharing.
- Do not bed-share. It is especially dangerous for infants younger than 4 months, preterm/low-birth-weight infants, when caregivers smoke or used alcohol/drugs or sedatives, when the surface is soft (sofa, waterbed, old mattress), or when soft bedding is present.
- Keep soft objects, loose bedding, bumper pads, pillows, stuffed toys, etc., out of the infant’s sleep area to avoid entrapment, suffocation, or strangulation. Use wearable blankets if needed for warmth.
- If an infant falls asleep in a car seat, stroller, swing, carrier, or sling, move them to a firm back-sleep surface as soon as possible.
- Swaddling is acceptable if the baby is always placed on the back, the swaddle is not too tight and hips can move, and swaddling is stopped once the baby shows signs of trying to roll over.

Bottom line
Sleep-related infant death risk factors change with age: bed-sharing is the dominant risk for very young infants, while objects and prone positioning become more prominent risks as infants get older. Parents should follow AAP safe-sleep recommendations—back sleeping on a firm surface in a bare sleep space, room-sharing without bed-sharing, and avoiding soft bedding and objects—to reduce the risk across developmental stages.

Dartmouth College has accused 64 students of violating the school’s honor code after a widespread cheating scheme in Randall Balmer’s “Sports, Ethics and Religion” class last fall. The course—popular with student-athletes and expanded to about 280 students—used handheld “clicker” devices for participation. Balmer discovered that students were passing clickers to absent classmates so the absentees would appear present; he reported 43 students to the college judicial board and another 21 later confessed. An appeals process is underway and is expected to conclude by mid-January to determine sanctions, which can include suspension under Dartmouth’s honor code.

Balmer, chair of the religion department, said he had tried to handle the matter outside the judicial process but was required to report it; he later reduced the accused students’ marks by a full letter grade rather than failing them. Dartmouth officials have limited comment pending the appeals. The case is the latest high-profile academic-integrity scandal involving athletes—following incidents at Harvard (2012) and UNC (paper classes over many years)—and has prompted criticism about campus culture and students’ attitudes toward integrity. Dartmouth’s ethics institute director, Aine Donovan, said rising cheating reflects broader societal trends that de-emphasize self-regulation and collective responsibility.

When President Trump added chief strategist Steve Bannon to the principals committee of the National Security Council, the move provoked a sharp online backlash. The hashtag #StopPresidentBannon trended nationally on Twitter as thousands criticized Bannon’s increased influence, citing his background as head of the far-right site Breitbart News and accusing him of promoting racist, sexist and anti‑Semitic views. Social media users questioned his qualifications for national security policy and framed his new role as a dangerous shift in who actually shapes administration decisions.

Researchers have identified a novel tick-associated orthomyxovirus, named Bourbon virus, after isolating it from the blood of a previously healthy man from Bourbon County, eastern Kansas, who became ill in late spring 2014 and died 11 days after symptom onset.

Case summary
- Patient: previously healthy man in his 50s who worked outdoors and reported multiple tick bites, including an engorged tick found on his shoulder shortly before symptom onset.
- Clinical course: initial symptoms (day 1–3) included nausea, diarrhea, fever, myalgia, headache and fatigue. He was empirically started on doxycycline for presumed tickborne disease. By day 4 he was somnolent and hospitalized. Laboratory findings included leukopenia, lymphopenia, marked thrombocytopenia, mild hyponatremia, elevated AST/ALT, and progressive bone marrow suppression. He developed worsening respiratory failure, cardiogenic features (global hypokinesis), shock, multi-organ failure and died on day 11. An autopsy was not performed.
- Extensive testing for known bacterial, parasitic, fungal, and viral tickborne pathogens (including Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis, Heartland virus, tularemia, Q fever, babesiosis), and other common infections were negative.

Discovery and characterization of the virus
- A whole-blood specimen collected on illness day 9 was sent to CDC for Heartland virus testing. Although tests were negative for Heartland virus, plaque reduction neutralization tests revealed heterologous viral plaques and standard cell cultures showed cytopathic effect.
- Electron microscopy showed pleomorphic particles consistent with Orthomyxoviridae. Next-generation sequencing of culture supernatant revealed a novel orthomyxoviral genome with ~70% nucleotide identity to Dhori virus.
- Phylogenetic analysis grouped the novel virus with Dhori and Batken viruses (genus Thogotovirus), though with notable evolutionary distance. Real-time RT-PCR confirmed the virus in the patient’s blood and serum.
- The authors propose naming it Bourbon virus.

Significance and implications
- This is the first report of a Thogotovirus associated with human disease in the United States. Dhori- and Thogoto-like viruses have caused human illness elsewhere (including neurologic disease and laboratory-acquired infections).
- The patient’s tick exposure, seasonality, and clinical presentation (fever with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia unresponsive to doxycycline) suggest possible tickborne transmission, but vectors and reservoirs are not yet identified.
- The high viremia shortly before death suggests the virus may have contributed to the fatal outcome, though causality cannot be definitively proven from a single case.
- The finding highlights that additional, previously unrecognized tick-associated viruses may cause human disease and underscores the value of combining classical virology with nonselective molecular methods (NGS) for pathogen discovery.

Public health and next steps
- Clinicians should consider Bourbon virus in patients with febrile illness, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia who test negative for common tickborne diseases and who fail to improve with doxycycline.
- Ongoing work includes searching for additional human cases, determining geographic distribution, defining vector(s) and reservoir(s), and full virologic characterization to inform prevention and control measures.
- Meanwhile, standard tick-bite prevention measures (repellents, protective clothing, avoidance of tick habitats, and tick checks) are recommended.

Meryl Streep responded to criticism from Rose McGowan after McGowan slammed several actresses — including Streep and Jessica Chastain — for planning to wear black at the Golden Globes in protest of sexual harassment. McGowan accused them of silence and hypocrisy, saying accepting awards while doing little to change the industry was part of the problem. Streep issued a public statement saying she was hurt by McGowan’s attack, insisting she never knew about Harvey Weinstein’s abusive behavior, was not “deliberately silent,” and had only been to Weinstein’s office once in 1998 and never to his hotel room. Streep argued that Weinstein operated largely as a marketer and producer, so many collaborators would not have known about his misconduct, and she described efforts to help create a legal defense fund for victims. She said she tried to reach McGowan to explain and express sympathy but received no reply, and affirmed that they are ultimately on the same side opposing an industry culture that protects abusers. McGowan later deleted the tweet attacking Streep and apologized for a separate derogatory remark about the fashion label Marchesa. Weinstein has been accused by more than 50 women and has denied allegations of non-consensual sex.

A last-minute North Korean decision to send a delegation forced a minor change to the Winter Games opening ceremony. Director Song Seung-whan said he only adjusted one segment to reflect North Korea’s presence and spent much of the lead-up worrying about extreme cold and equipment reliability; dancers were given shoe spikes and electronics were tested for freezing temperatures. Despite concerns, the weather was milder than expected (around 28°F). The show involved about 1,300 performers plus 700 volunteers and was produced on a “very limited budget,” Song said, joking it was far less than Beijing’s.

IOC president Thomas Bach, introduced as a 1976 Olympic gold medalist, opened the Games. North Korean dignitaries Kim Yo-jong and Kim Yong-nam attended and briefly exchanged a handshake with South Korean President Moon Jae-in.

The Parade of Nations reflected the constraints of a winter ceremony (focus on warmth and practicality), but some delegations stood out for style: Sweden, Mexico and Tonga were highlighted for striking flagbearer looks; Belarus and Iran for outfits deemed stylish enough to buy at Nordstrom; and Jamaica and Bermuda were noted for braving the cold while looking good.

Windi C. Thomas, 44, of Erie pleaded guilty Monday to third-degree murder for the March killing of her boyfriend, 44-year-old Keeno Butler. Under a plea agreement accepted by Erie County Judge William R. Cunningham, Thomas faces a recommended state prison term of 18 to 36 years and will be sentenced Dec. 21. In exchange for the plea, prosecutors dropped charges of aggravated assault, reckless endangerment and possession of an instrument of a crime; the agreed range reduces the maximum by two to four years from the ordinary 20–40 year term for third‑degree murder.

According to police and the affidavit of probable cause, Thomas told investigators she cut Butler’s hand with a folding knife, struck him with a table leg and then placed part of her body on his head while she weighed about 300 pounds and he about 120. Butler was found dead in the living room after Thomas called 911. The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide caused by respiratory insufficiency secondary to blunt force trauma to the neck and thoracic compression, exacerbated by head trauma. Thomas remains jailed without bond pending sentencing. The victim’s family has expressed that they believe a harsher sentence is warranted.

Pope Francis, in a wide-ranging interview with Italy’s Corriere della Sera published as he nears his first anniversary, reaffirmed the Catholic Church’s teaching that marriage is between a man and a woman but signaled a more nuanced, pastoral approach to modern issues. He said the state has a responsibility to guarantee civil rights and suggested that some forms of civil unions — for example those providing economic or health-care protections to cohabiting couples — can be considered, a remark many outlets called the first tentative papal openness to civil unions. The Vatican later cautioned that the pope did not intend to enter a debate and that his words were general.

Francis reiterated themes from earlier comments: the church should be merciful and attentive to concrete situations, should avoid ideological or mythologized portrayals of the pope as a “Superman,” and should not unduly interfere in the spiritual lives of gays and lesbians. He praised Pope Paul VI’s courage in defending the contraception ban while noting the need for deeper reflection and mercy; topics such as contraception and Communion for divorced Catholics are expected to be discussed at upcoming bishops’ meetings.

On women’s roles, Francis said women should be present where decisions are made and that the church is engaged in deep reflection about more than merely functional roles for women. Addressing the clergy sexual-abuse crisis, he acknowledged the “very deep wounds” inflicted on victims, said the church has been open and transparent compared with other institutions, and noted the Vatican would study a recent critical U.N. report.

Francis also described Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI as a “wise grandfather,” explaining the two agreed Benedict should continue to participate in public church life rather than live cloistered. The interview avoided sensationalism: Francis rejected the “mythology” around him — including tales he sneaks out at night to feed the homeless — and insisted he is an ordinary man.

Separately, the Vatican marked Francis’s anniversary with commemorative coins, stamps and a DVD of behind-the-scenes footage, and announced that the expansive Barberini gardens and grounds of the papal summer residence at Castel Gandolfo would be opened to the public with guided tours, following Francis’s decision to make them accessible.

Rachel Borch, 21, of Hope, Maine, was attacked by a rabid raccoon while jogging on a narrow, overgrown trail on June 3. She spotted the raccoon acting strangely and charging at her; it latched onto her thumb and scratched her arms and legs. With no weapon and her phone lost in a puddle, Borch dragged the animal into a shallow muddy pool and held its head underwater until it stopped struggling. Bleeding and shaken, she ran home and was taken to Pen Bay Medical Center. Her family turned the carcass over to the Maine Warden Service; testing by the Maine CDC confirmed the raccoon was rabid.

Borch has begun post‑exposure treatment—rabies vaccine series, immunoglobulin and tetanus shots—and antibiotics for wounds; she is scheduled for her final injection soon. Hope Animal Control Officer Heidi Blood warned that one confirmed rabid animal usually indicates others nearby and reminded residents that rabies is fatal if untreated and that people and pets should avoid strange or dead wildlife. As of early June 2017, Maine had 20 rabid animals confirmed for the year (raccoons, red foxes and skunks), down from 64 in 2016.

This document summarizes a Humane Research Council (HRC) study and related commentary about why people adopt — and why most later abandon — vegetarian/vegan diets in the U.S., illustrated by a personal anecdote of someone who lapsed after many years.

Key findings from the HRC study
- Prevalence and churn: About 2% of U.S. adults are currently vegetarian/vegan, ~10% are former vegetarians/vegans, and ~88% have never been. Only about 1 in 5 people who try a veg diet remain on it long-term; roughly 84% eventually revert to eating animal products.
- Speed of transition matters: 65% of former vegetarians/vegans moved to the diet within days or weeks, compared with 53% of current vegetarians/vegans — suggesting rapid, abrupt changes are linked to higher lapse rates.
- Critical early window: One-third of lapses happen within three months and more than half occur within the first year.
- Motivations differ: Current vegetarians/vegans more often cite multiple motivations (animal welfare, environment, health). A majority (58%) of former vegetarians cited health as their main initial motivator, which may be less durable than ethical or environmental motivations.
- Social and cultural pressures: Social factors strongly influence lapses — about a third of former vegetarians lived with non-vegetarian partners when they returned to meat. Over 60% disliked standing out because of their diet and 58% said the diet was not part of their identity. Nearly half found maintaining a "pure" diet too difficult.
- Implications for advocacy: HRC argues that messaging stressing reduction rather than total elimination, encouraging slower transitions, broadening motivations, and addressing social/cultural barriers will likely be more effective in reducing overall animal-product consumption than pushing for dietary purity.

Illustrative personal account
- A long-term vegetarian who disliked vegetables and ate mainly pasta/cheese described gradual erosion of the diet driven by family, palate limitations (especially when accommodating a young child), pregnancy-related meat cravings in his partner, and one decisive meal out where fish satisfied a felt need for protein. He subsequently reintroduced processed meats like pepperoni and bacon but still avoids red-meat steaks. His story highlights practical, social, and craving-related triggers for lapsing.

Overall conclusion
- While meat consumption in the U.S. has begun to decline from a “peak meat” high, maintaining total abstinence is difficult for many. The HRC’s data suggest that slower, socially supported transitions, multi-faceted motivations (beyond health alone), and promotion of reduction rather than purity are promising strategies for moving animal-free diets closer to the mainstream.

This long excerpt—adapted from Chris Smith’s oral history of The Daily Show—traces the program’s evolution from Craig Kilborn’s original late-1990s format into the politically sharp, culturally influential show Jon Stewart shaped after taking over as host in 1999.

Key points:

- The Kilborn era (1996–1998) followed a conventional, pop-culture–heavy late-night news-parody template with field pieces, musical guests, and lighter satire. It drew a young-male audience but was not overtly political.

- When Kilborn left, Comedy Central recruited Jon Stewart. Stewart’s hiring raised internal tension: many Kilborn-era writers and producers resisted change, while Stewart wanted a new sensibility—less aimless mockery of eccentric people and more pointed satire directed at the media, politicians, and institutions.

- Early months were rocky. Stewart faced hostility from holdover staff, leading to confrontations (the infamous “fuck-you meeting”) and to his blunt assertion of authority over writers and the show’s direction. He recruited Ben Karlin as head writer and later David Javerbaum; together they pushed for sharper, deconstructive satire.

- On-air and off-air talent shifts were crucial. Stephen Colbert and Steve Carell (both recruited early) emerged as key correspondents whose performances expanded the show’s capabilities. Colbert’s scene-steady persona lent credibility to his satire; Carell’s field work helped shift the show’s political edge.

- Stewart radically reframed The Daily Show’s targets and methods: rather than lampooning obscure eccentrics, he emphasized critiquing the powerful—politicians and the news media—and exposing the gap between public messages and behind-the-scenes decision-making. The staff began to “deconstruct” how news and politics are produced.

- A turning point came during 1999–2000 campaign coverage. Field pieces in New Hampshire, including a now-famous Steve Carell exchange on John McCain’s bus, demonstrated how the show could both get candid moments from politicians and turn those moments into incisive satire. That episode signaled the show’s ability to be both funny and revealing.

- The changing media landscape (fragmentation of cable news, rise of Fox and MSNBC, internet growth) created fertile ground for Stewart’s approach; audiences were ready for a show that both mocked media tropes and offered a skeptical, informed perspective.

- Over time Stewart built a cohesive, opinionated staff and on-air cast who could consistently deliver pointed, intelligent satire—a transformation that made The Daily Show an influential cultural and political force.

The piece interweaves recollections from Stewart, producers, writers, and correspondents—Ben Karlin, David Javerbaum, Stephen Colbert, Steve Carell, and others—highlighting creative struggles, personnel changes, early production choices, and the strategic shift toward media- and politics-focused satire that defined The Daily Show under Jon Stewart.

A small landscape titled “On the Shore of the Seine,” attributed to Pierre-Auguste Renoir, has become the center of an FBI investigation and federal court dispute over ownership after being offered for auction in Alexandria this year. The painting, 5.5 by 9 inches in an ornate gold frame with a small “Renoir” plaque, was identified from Baltimore Museum of Art (BMA) records as having been stolen from the museum in 1951. The FBI seized the work before a Potomack Company auction.

Martha Fuqua (also known in press as “Renoir Girl”), a 51-year-old Loudoun County driving instructor and former teacher who filed for bankruptcy in 2009, brought the painting to auction houses this year. She initially told Potomack and the media she had bought the painting in a West Virginia flea market in a $7 box of junk. Earlier, however, she had taken the painting to Quinn’s Auction Galleries in June and told staff a different story — that she had obtained it from an estate and believed it was a genuine Renoir worth far more than the conservative estimate the auction house suggested. Quinn’s conservator neither confirmed nor dismissed authenticity and requested time to research the piece; Fuqua refused to leave the painting. Quinn’s staff later alerted the FBI after news broke of the Potomack sale.

Complicating Fuqua’s claim of innocent purchase is the long history of the painting in the household of her mother, Marcia Fouquet (who now uses the name Martha Fouquet). Fouquet, 84, is a Goucher College–trained fine-arts painter who ran a studio in Fairfax reproducing masterworks, including Renoir. Multiple former acquaintances and family friends — including a former tenant and boyfriend, a childhood friend of Fuqua’s, and a former student who lived with Fouquet — recall seeing the small framed painting displayed in Fouquet’s studio in the 1980s–1990s, often noting the ornate frame and “Renoir” plaque. These recollections raise questions about when and how the work entered the family’s possession and whether Fuqua’s flea-market story is accurate.

The BMA’s records show the museum had the painting on loan from longtime donor Saidie May in the 1930s and reported it stolen in November 1951. Potomack and Bernheim-Jeune (in Paris) had both taken steps to verify the painting; the Paris gallery confirmed it as a Renoir, while the Art Loss Register initially did not list it as stolen. Because the theft occurred decades ago, the statute of limitations for prosecuting the original theft has expired, though related charges (e.g., possession or transport of stolen property) remain possible.

A federal judge in Alexandria will decide whether the painting should be returned to the Baltimore Museum of Art or recognized as Fuqua’s property under the “innocent owner” provision of federal law. The FBI has shown interest in a mysterious middle-aged man who accompanied Fuqua to Quinn’s and in the inconsistencies between her accounts. Fuqua, her mother and family members have largely declined to comment amid ongoing litigation and investigation.

French authorities have charged a 23-year-old man with preliminary terrorism offenses for allegedly plotting an attack on President Emmanuel Macron and targeting minority groups. Arrested in the Argenteuil suburb after users in a videogame chat alerted police, he reportedly said he planned to target Macron on Bastille Day (July 14) on the Champs-Élysées and expressed nationalist, anti‑minority sentiments. Investigators found three kitchen knives in his vehicle and computer searches identifying possible targets; he told police he wanted to attack “Muslims, Jews, blacks, homosexuals.” The suspect had a 2016 conviction for condoning terrorism after praising Anders Breivik and received a three‑year sentence (half suspended). Authorities say his plans were vague and he appeared to be acting alone. The arrest comes amid heightened security for Bastille Day — when Macron will review the military parade and later visit Nice — and following recent attacks and attempts on the Champs-Élysées and police officers earlier this year.

Six people died and at least nine to ten others were injured after a police chase and rollover crash early Thursday morning near Edna, Texas, about 90 miles southwest of Houston. The incident began when Edna officers attempted to stop a 2003 Ford Explorer for a traffic violation on U.S. 59; the driver refused to stop and led police on a nearly 10-minute pursuit. Just after 1:30 a.m. the SUV apparently overcorrected, ran off the road and flipped multiple times, ejecting several occupants. Four people died at the scene; two more later died at hospitals. Three injured victims were airlifted to Memorial Hermann in Houston and the rest were taken to Jackson County Hospital; most surviving victims are in stable condition.

Authorities estimate the vehicle was carrying roughly 12–15 people. The Explorer’s seats had been modified (rear folded down, middle seat removed) to create more space, and several victims have been identified as nationals of Honduras and Guatemala. Two people who fled the crash on foot were later arrested; federal immigration and criminal investigators, including ICE, are involved and suspect human smuggling. Texas Department of Public Safety noted U.S. 59 is a common corridor for human and drug trafficking, and fatal crashes tied to smuggling have occurred previously in the region.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D–Nev.) and Sen. Jon Kyl (R–Ariz.) are quietly working together to add an online-gambling measure to a lame-duck legislative package tied to the federal budget. The proposal — discussed behind closed doors but not yet publicly introduced — would both expand and restrict certain types of online wagering. A key provision would establish an Office of Online Poker Oversight within the Commerce Department. Reid, who has strong backing from Nevada casino interests, and Kyl, a vocal opponent of some gambling, are shaping the language to strike a balance between enabling online poker and limiting other forms of internet betting.

In Irkutsk, Siberia, a mass methanol poisoning from a hawthorn-scented bath lotion sold and drunk as a cheap alcoholic surrogate has become the deadliest such incident in modern Russian history. Initial reports put the death toll around 49–55; later media cited at least 58 dead and about 37–40 people still ill, many in critical condition. Health minister Oleg Yaroshenko warned nearly half of the surviving patients are unlikely to survive because they sought treatment too late after ingesting large doses.

The product was mislabeled to suggest it contained potable ethanol; in fact it contained toxic methanol, which the body metabolizes to formaldehyde and formic acid, causing nausea, breathing problems, blindness and death. Survivors include a 33-year-old who lost his sight after drinking a small amount. Victims ranged from 25–62 years old and included a doctor and a kindergarten teacher; many bodies were found at home, indicating rapid fatalities.

Police uncovered an illicit workshop producing the contaminated bath oil and several brands of bootleg vodka; about 500 liters and multiple products were confiscated and seven people detained. Analysts note widespread use of surrogate household products (perfume, aftershave, antifreeze, window cleaner) as cheap alcohol in Russia — a problem worsened by economic pressures. Antidotes for methanol (fomepizole or ethanol) exist, but outcomes depend on dose and how quickly treatment is given, and permanent blindness is common among survivors.

Rush Limbaugh criticized the Republican establishment on his radio show after Rick Santorum won three states, calling party leaders “insulated” and “shocked” that Santorum had gained traction. Limbaugh rejected media suggestions that his show alone directed voters, saying that portraying conservative voters as “mind‑numbed robots” is insulting. He argued Santorum’s appeal stems from genuine dissatisfaction with Mitt Romney and from Santorum’s standing as a consistently conservative, minimally “corrupted” alternative. Limbaugh, who has pledged not to endorse a candidate, said Santorum’s rise was not surprising to him and reflected where the Republican base stands.

Separately, Santorum, fresh from victories in Missouri, Minnesota and Colorado, spoke to about 100 pastors (with a larger overflow crowd) in McKinney, Texas. He stressed he is not seeking to be “pastor in chief,” urged clergy to be more active, and framed his campaign around restoring the country’s moral foundations. Santorum criticized the Obama administration over religious‑freedom and contraception policy, decried the Proposition 8 ruling as intolerant toward opponents of same‑sex marriage, and recounted personal stories—including the loss of an infant son and caring for his daughter Bella, who has Trisomy 18—to explain his convictions. He said his campaign often benefits from being underestimated and noted his campaign raised $400,000 in two days. The event ended with attendees praying for him and his family.

A group of lesbian women, including Marianne and Erin Krupa of Montclair, N.J., sued the commissioner of the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance, arguing that the state’s insurance mandate for infertility treatment discriminates against nonheterosexual women. New Jersey law requires most insurers to cover medically necessary fertility treatments but defines infertility in terms that effectively exclude women who cannot become pregnant through heterosexual intercourse. The plaintiffs, represented by Grace Cretcher of Beranbaum Menken, seek damages for denied coverage of procedures such as artificial insemination and in vitro fertilization (IVF).

The complaint says the mandate treats same-sex couples like second-class citizens and forces them to pay substantial out-of-pocket costs. The Krupas report spending about $50,000 on multiple cycles of treatment and experiencing several miscarriages and an ectopic pregnancy; others in the suit describe emotional and financial strain from paying for failed cycles on credit. One plaintiff’s insurer, Horizon, said it covers infertility services regardless of sexual orientation and interprets the law in a gender- and orientation-neutral way. The Department of Banking and Insurance declined to comment on the litigation.

Fifteen states require insurer fertility coverage, and some (California, Maryland) have amended mandates to be explicitly orientation-neutral. New Jersey lawmakers have proposed bills to redefine infertility to allow physician determinations, but neither bill has advanced from committee. Reproductive specialists quoted in coverage say the mandate’s language creates a double standard that limits treatment options for same-sex couples and can force patients into less effective, less affordable care. The plaintiffs hope the lawsuit will change the law and relieve financial and emotional burdens on lesbian couples seeking to start families.

The Justice Department and FBI have launched the largest post-conviction forensic review in U.S. history to determine whether flawed FBI hair and fiber analysis contributed to wrongful convictions or warrants new trials. The review covers all FBI Laboratory hair and fiber examiners’ work since at least 1985 (and earlier where records exist) and begins from an initial pool of more than 10,000 referrals; roughly 2,500 cases with reported hair “matches” from 1972–1999 are being targeted. The Innocence Project and the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers are assisting.

Background and findings so far
- The review follows Washington Post reporting that Justice Department officials had long known about problematic forensic work but had not fully reviewed cases or notified many affected defendants. Two high-profile convictions highlighted by the Post (Santae Tribble and Kirk Odom) have since been vacated or moved toward vacatur after new testing.
- Early results show systemic problems: of 28 examiners in the FBI’s microscopic hair comparison unit, 26 overstated matches in ways favoring prosecutors in more than 95% of the 268 trials reviewed to date. Across reviewed transcripts and reports, examiners exceeded scientific limits in roughly 90% of testimonies, including dozens of death-penalty cases; 32 defendants in the reviewed set received death sentences, 14 of whom are already dead or executed.
- The FBI’s prior practice often presented hair “matches” as near-certainty and used misleading statistics, despite a lack of accepted research establishing how often hairs from different people can appear the same. The bureau has acknowledged that until 2012 hair examiners lacked written standards for testimony.

Scope, limits and consequences
- The review encompasses federal and state cases nationwide where FBI hair/fiber evidence was used—many predate routine DNA testing. It will focus on positive hair findings that contributed to convictions.
- Authorities have agreed to offer DNA testing where possible (if a judge or prosecutor allows) and to drop certain procedural objections to appeals in federal cases. But biological evidence is often lost or unavailable, and statutes governing retroactive appeals vary by state.
- Many procedural details remain unresolved: the exact number of cases to be reviewed, whether the review will scrutinize testimony by non-FBI analysts trained by the FBI or prosecutorial use of the evidence, and timing and scope of notifications to defendants and counsel. Past reviews were tightly controlled and results often not shared with defendants.

Government response and criticism
- The FBI and Justice Department say they are committed to notifying affected defendants and ensuring accurate future forensic testimony; the bureau is developing written standards for testimony across forensic disciplines.
- Critics call the revelations a “mass disaster” and lament long delays and inadequate earlier responses. The Justice Department had paused the review for nearly a year amid internal debate over standards; the inspector general later criticized delays and urged more prompt, comprehensive action.
- Lawmakers and forensic experts urge a root-cause analysis and broader reforms (including recommendations by the National Academy of Sciences to remove crime labs from police/prosecutor control or strengthen scientific standards). Several states have begun their own reviews, and the accreditation arm of crime-lab directors has recommended other labs assess whether similar reviews are needed.

Implications
- The admissions that nearly every examiner in the FBI hair unit overstated results for decades raise serious questions about convictions nationwide and about courts’ historical readiness to admit and police forensic testimony. The review may lead to additional exonerations, retrials, or post-conviction relief, but identifying and remedying harms will be complicated by lost evidence, differing state procedures, and legal doctrines limiting retroactive challenges.

The Congressional Budget Office released a report offering more than 100 deficit-reduction options, several of which would reduce military and veterans’ compensation and benefits. These are proposals for lawmakers to consider as they negotiate replacements for sequestration cuts; CBO stresses they are options, not recommendations.

Key proposals affecting service members, retirees and veterans:
- Cap military pay raises: Limiting annual increases to 0.5% below civilian wage growth could save about $25 billion from 2015–2023. Supporters note current pay for many servicemembers already exceeds civilian peers; critics warn of recruiting, retention and downstream retirement-pay impacts.
- Raise TRICARE fees: Two variants—one would require TRICARE-for-Life users (65+) to pay the first $550 of non‑Medicare costs and 50% of the next $4,950, saving ~$31 billion through 2023 but risking reduced preventive care. A second option would raise fees/deductibles for working-age retirees in TRICARE Prime, saving $2–11 billion depending on design.
- Reinstate partial ban on concurrent receipt: Restoring the pre-2003 rule that offsets retired pay by VA disability payments could save ~$108 billion (2015–2023). CBO notes retirees would still be better off after-tax than non-disabled peers, but opponents argue the two payments compensate different things and cuts could cause hardship; the option undercuts hopes for expanding concurrent receipt to those rated below 50%.
- Narrow VA compensation eligibility: Tightening the definition of “service-connected” and denying compensation for certain common conditions (e.g., COPD, heart disease, osteoarthritis, MS, Crohn’s) could save roughly $20 billion through 2023; broader eliminations would save more but be harder to administer. Supporters say civilian systems don’t compensate for all work-related conditions; opponents cite unique military risks.
- Restrict Individual Unemployability (IU): Ending IU payments for veterans over 65 (about one-third of IU recipients), which average $1,800/month boosts, could save about $15 billion by 2023. Critics point to the benefit’s role for those unable to work due to service-connected disabilities.

CBO also includes many other options impacting a wide range of federal beneficiaries (Social Security recipients, drug manufacturers, etc.). Separately, military leaders—including Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Martin Dempsey—have signaled willingness to curb growth in pay and benefits (housing, education, health) to manage shrinking defense budgets.

Mark Williams, a Sacramento-based conservative talk-radio host and prominent spokesman for the Tea Party Express, called President Barack Obama “our half white, racist president” in a September 2009 email to fellow Tea Party leaders obtained by TPMmuckraker. The remark came as part of a longer message in which Williams defended himself against what he said were out-of-context quotes and a CNN allegation that he had labeled Obama a “Nazi.” Williams asserted a long civil-rights record—saying he “marched for civil rights” during violent resistance to desegregation—and said he will “call out any racist, any time,” including the president.

Williams has a documented history of inflammatory descriptions of Obama, previously writing that the president is “an Indonesian Muslim turned welfare thug and a racist in chief,” and during a September 14, 2009 CNN interview acknowledged using the derogatory label “Mubarak Hussein Obama” and associating Obama with “the philosophy of fascism and national socialism.” The Tea Party Express, founded by a GOP consulting firm, is often criticized as “astroturf” because of ties to Republican operatives; some other Tea Party figures, such as Robin Stublen of the Tea Party Patriots, publicly distance themselves from Williams’ style and statements. TPMmuckraker reported Williams declined to comment.

Joy Milne, a 65-year-old from Perth, Scotland, may have sparked a new diagnostic approach for Parkinson’s disease after noticing a distinct, musky change in her late husband Les’s scent years before he was diagnosed. After noticing the same odor on other people with Parkinson’s, she mentioned it to researchers and was tested by Edinburgh University scientists. Using t-shirts worn by participants, Milne accurately identified people with Parkinson’s—initially scoring 11/12, with one control later diagnosed, effectively making her 12/12.

Researchers believe early Parkinson’s causes changes in skin chemistry—possibly in sebum—that produce a detectable molecular signature. Parkinson’s UK is funding expanded studies at Manchester, Edinburgh and London to recruit about 200 people with and without Parkinson’s. The work involves molecular analysis of skin swabs and evaluation by Milne and professional “smellers” from the food and drink industry.

If validated, a simple swab test based on this odor signature could enable earlier, more objective diagnosis, improve treatment planning and patient monitoring, and streamline recruitment for trials of disease‑slowing therapies. The research is still in early stages but is seen as potentially transformational for people with Parkinson’s.

California secession advocates (Yes California/“Calexit”) can now begin gathering the roughly 585,407 signatures needed to place a 2018 ballot measure that would remove language tying California to the U.S. Constitution. The campaign, energized by President Trump’s 2016 victory and widening cultural and policy gaps between California and federal policy—especially on immigration and the environment—says about 7,000 volunteers have begun collecting signatures.

The proposed measure would repeal state constitutional clauses declaring California an “inseparable part of the United States” and the U.S. Constitution the “supreme law of the land,” and would authorize a 2019 referendum on independence. Under Yes California’s rules, the referendum would require 50 percent turnout of registered voters and 55 percent voting for independence—thresholds that make success unlikely in an off-year election. Even if California voters approved secession, federal approval would be required: a constitutional amendment needing two‑thirds majorities in Congress and ratification by three‑quarters of states (or a constitutional convention), making unilateral secession effectively impossible.

The movement largely reflects protest and defiance against Trump-era policies and perceived threats to California priorities (sanctuary policies, environmental protections, reproductive rights), though state officials have avoided endorsing secession. Observers say Calexit is more a symbolic outlet for West Coast frustration than a realistic path to nationhood, but it has become a potent political lightning rod.

Newly released, heavily redacted documents and emails tie senior members of New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie’s administration and Port Authority appointees to the deliberate lane closures on the George Washington Bridge that created severe traffic jams in Fort Lee last September. Christie, a likely 2016 presidential contender, said he was “outraged” to learn he had been misled by a staffer and denied any prior knowledge of the closures, promising that “people will be held responsible.” He called the conduct “completely inappropriate and unsanctioned.”

The records, turned over under subpoena by Port Authority official David Wildstein, show close coordination among Christie aides, Port Authority appointees and the governor’s communications shop as the scandal unfolded. Emails include an exchange in which deputy chief of staff Bridget Kelly wrote, “Time for some traffic problems in Fort Lee,” and Wildstein replied, “Got it,” shortly before two Fort Lee lanes were closed for several days. When New York appointees later reopened the lanes, Wildstein and Kelly expressed panic; Wildstein said David Samson, Christie’s chosen Port Authority chairman, was “helping us to retaliate.” The staff then worked with Christie spokesman Michael Drewniak to craft a statement framing the action as a traffic safety review and ongoing contact with local police.

The closures caused major delays, reportedly affected emergency responses, and occurred in the run-up to Christie’s reelection — fueling allegations of political retribution after Fort Lee’s Democratic mayor did not endorse Christie. Two Port Authority officials, Wildstein and Bill Baroni, resigned in December after testifying they had violated protocols and tried to hide their plans. Christie’s statement did not name who he meant by the staffer who misled him, and his office did not clarify whether Kelly or others had been fired. Some Christie associates implicated in emails, such as Bill Stepien, have not faced immediate consequences. The revelations have damaged Christie’s reputation for blunt honesty and could complicate his national ambitions.
