Indian authorities arrested Sant Rampal, a 63-year-old self-styled guru, late Wednesday after a week-long standoff at his fortified ashram in Hisar, Haryana, about 200 km from New Delhi. The operation followed the Punjab and Haryana High Court’s order to produce him in court over contempt charges and a 2006 murder case. Rampal had repeatedly ignored summonses and sheltered thousands of followers who treated him as a divine leader.

Clashes between Rampal’s supporters and police turned violent in the days before the arrest. Devotees hurled petrol bombs and stones, fired shots, and allegedly used women and children as human shields, while police responded with tear gas, water cannon, bulldozers and forceful attempts to break into the complex. At least six people—including several women and an 18-month-old child—died (authorities say the bodies bore no visible injuries and may have died of illness), over 200 people were injured, and roughly 270 people were arrested on charges including rioting, illegal detention, attempt to murder and waging war against the state. Police evacuated more than 16,000 followers; several thousand reportedly remained inside when Rampal was taken into custody and later remanded until 28 November.

The episode has drawn comparisons to past religious sieges such as Waco and Operation Blue Star and highlights the difficulties Indian authorities face dealing with entrenched cult-like religious followings: devotees’ fervor can make arrests fraught, and using military force against citizens is politically and legally sensitive, so police and paramilitary units are tasked to limit bloodshed. Rampal denied the charges and any use of followers as shields, expressed regret over the deaths, and maintained his innocence. The incident revives debates about law enforcement’s handling of mass religious gatherings and the political risks of harsh crackdowns.

The Tarrant County Medical Examiner has determined that a 52-year-old Dallas woman, identified as Rosa Ayala-Goana (family has also used the name Rosy Esparza), died of “multiple traumatic injuries due to [a] fall from [a] roller coaster.” Her time of death is listed as 7:00 p.m. and the manner of death is ruled an accident.

The woman fell from the Texas Giant roller coaster at Six Flags Over Texas on Friday. Witnesses said she expressed concern that the safety bar had not fully engaged just before the 14-story ride began. Six Flags closed the Texas Giant immediately and said it will remain closed until internal and external investigations — including assistance from Gerstlauer Amusement Rides, the German manufacturer of the coaster’s cars — are complete; company leaders declined to provide further details during the inquiry. Arlington police have said they will leave the investigation to Six Flags and Gerstlauer.

State records show the Texas Giant had 14 reported injuries between April 2008 and April 2013 (three of those occurred before or after the ride); safety analysts note such self-reported figures undercount incidents and don’t capture “near misses.” The coaster had received a safety permit in February and met the state requirement for annual inspection by a qualified engineer. After the fatality, Six Flags also temporarily closed the Iron Rattler at Six Flags Fiesta Texas as a precaution.

Safety experts say fatal roller-coaster accidents are rare and often involve human error or restraint failure; investigators will examine whether a restraint malfunctioned or the rider slipped from the restraint. The company has expressed condolences and said it is supporting the family while investigations continue.

A Nebraska faith ministry, Lakota Hope, has launched a fundraising campaign to buy the four beer stores in Whiteclay, a tiny town on the edge of the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, aiming to raise at least $6.3 million to close them. Whiteclay—population about a dozen—sold 3.5 million cans of beer in 2015 despite the reservation being officially dry and suffering severe alcohol-related problems, including high fetal alcohol syndrome rates and extreme poverty.

Ministry founder Bruce BonFleur, who and his wife have worked in Whiteclay for nearly 20 years, says the owners are willing to sell; the effort is branded “B.O.B.S. Whiteclay P.L.A.N.” (Buy Out the Beer Stores / Promote the Lakotas As a Nation). The stores face mounting legal and political pressure, and the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission is scheduled to review their licenses. County officials recently recommended renewing the licenses, citing concerns that closures could increase intoxicated driving.

Reactions in the community are mixed. Some activists welcome the buyout idea but doubt it will work or prefer the state revoke licenses outright rather than pay owners; others warn that closures could simply move alcohol sales or result in increased bootlegging. Local observers describe visible poverty, public intoxication and neglected housing. Proponents suggest replacing the stores with community resources (e.g., recreation, arts, or a makerspace) to provide safer opportunities and economic options for residents.

Comedian and actress Amy Schumer surprised a Chicago mattress-store employee by buying her a pricey mattress as a thank-you after being allowed to use the store restroom. While jogging near Six Corners Mattress Firm, Schumer stopped in for the bathroom; employee Sagine Lazarre pointed her to it. On her way out Schumer asked which mattress was Lazarre’s favorite and then purchased that $2,000 mattress for her and her daughter, who had just moved into a new apartment. Lazarre only realized afterward that her benefactor was Schumer, after seeing the name on the card and searching online. Schumer’s publicist did not respond to WGN’s request for comment.

An anonymous hacker or group using the handle “thedarkoverlord” says it has stolen and begun leaking episodes of Orange Is the New Black season 5 after Netflix allegedly didn’t pay an extortion demand. The attacker posted the season premiere and, shortly before 6 a.m. ET Saturday, uploaded the first 10 episodes (about 11.46 GB) to Pirate Bay; neither Variety nor the Associated Press could verify the files’ authenticity. Netflix’s official release date for season 5 is June 9.

The intrusions appear to stem from a late‑2016 breach of post‑production vendor Larson Studios, and “thedarkoverlord” claims to hold other unreleased content from ABC, Fox, National Geographic and IFC. The hacker said only 10 of the 13 OITNB episodes were available because the attack occurred before the final three were completed. The group posted a taunting ransom message to Netflix and warned other networks they could also be targeted unless they “cooperate.”

Netflix confirmed a production vendor used by several studios had its security compromised and said law enforcement, including the FBI, is involved; the company had no further comment. Industry observers noted leaked episodes could hurt Netflix’s subscriber growth and stock performance—Netflix was relying on OITNB to help meet a strong quarterly subscriber target—but the ultimate motive for the leak may be extortion, bragging rights, or both. Netflix had previously renewed the series through season 7.

Global markets rose Tuesday as U.S. stocks continued a multi-session post-election rally that pushed the Dow Jones Industrial Average above 19,000 for the first time ever. The Dow had closed at a record 18,956.69 the prior day, and other major U.S. benchmarks—the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Russell 2000—also hit historic highs. Investors are pricing in potential fiscal stimulus from President‑elect Donald Trump, including deregulation and infrastructure spending, which has boosted equities.

European markets advanced (Stoxx Europe 600 +0.7%; France’s CAC 40 +0.8%; Germany’s DAX +0.6%; U.K.’s FTSE 100 +1.1%), and Asian bourses generally rose (Japan’s Nikkei +0.3%; South Korea’s Kospi +0.9%; Hong Kong’s Hang Seng +1.4%; Shanghai +0.9%; Australia +1.2%). Oil prices were firmer ahead of a possible OPEC production-cut decision, supporting commodity-linked shares. The Chinese yuan’s official fixing was set at 6.8779, slightly easing a recent weakening trend, while the dollar strengthened versus the yen. Analysts warned investors are trying to balance positioning for large U.S. fiscal stimulus against uncertainty about which policies will be implemented.

Sinéad O’Connor’s recent performance at Ireland’s Bray Music Festival has sparked widespread online backlash — not for her singing but for her changed appearance. Once famous for her shaved head, gaunt, androgynous look alongside a powerful voice (most notably on 1990’s “Nothing Compares 2U”), the 44-year-old showed up with a short dark bob, glasses, and a fuller figure in a belly-revealing top. Media outlets and social commenters reacted with shock, ridicule and schadenfreude, running galleries and slurs about her weight and style.

Commentary defending O’Connor argues the outrage exposes toxic double standards about aging women and celebrity appearance. Observers note she has long rejected conventional beauty norms, has continued to make music and tour (releasing albums regularly since 2000), and is also a mother of four who has been open about bipolar disorder — treatment for which can cause weight gain. O’Connor herself has acknowledged aging and body changes and said she’s entitled to have a belly. Writers compare the media’s fixation to the cruel scrutiny endured by other troubled stars, and emphasize that despite changed looks and past controversies (including outspoken criticism of the Catholic Church), her voice and songwriting remain powerful and emotionally resonant.

The broader point: the vitriolic focus on her appearance overlooks her continuing artistry and the realities of aging and health; growing older and taking medication that preserves life is not something to mock, and O’Connor’s talent and emotional intensity on stage remain intact.

Autumn Veatch, 16, survived a small-plane crash in the rugged North Cascades and hiked out after about two days before being found Monday. The Beech A-35, carrying Autumn and her step-grandparents Leland and Sharon Bowman, left Kalispell, Montana, Saturday and disappeared from radar near Omak. Autumn told family she survived the impact, tried to help the Bowmans at the wreck, stayed at the crash site for a day, then followed drainage to a river, found the Easy Pass trail, and walked downstream to Highway 20. Hikers gave her a ride to Mazama, where a motorist later drove her to the Mazama Store; she was taken to Three Rivers Hospital in Brewster with minor burns, dehydration, exhaustion and treatable rhabdomyolysis.

Authorities have not confirmed the condition of the Bowmans or located the downed plane as of Tuesday morning. Autumn’s cellphone data and descriptions helped narrow the search area; Civil Air Patrol and other aircraft and ground crews continued searching difficult, rocky, heavily forested terrain. Family and friends expressed relief at Autumn’s survival and concern for the grandparents.

Republicans abruptly pulled back from White House-led deficit reduction talks Thursday, halting negotiations as the debt ceiling deadline approaches. House Majority Leader Eric Cantor announced he was immediately withdrawing because Democrats insist on including tax increases in any deal, demanding that President Obama personally resolve “the tax issue” before discussions continue. Cantor’s exit led to the cancellation of a scheduled meeting with Vice President Joe Biden, Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner and other White House officials.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell publicly pressed for greater presidential involvement, accusing Obama of championing higher taxes instead of a bipartisan deficit plan. Shortly afterward, Sen. Jon Kyl likewise left the talks, leaving no Senate or House Republicans at the table; the remaining negotiators were four Democrats. Democrats criticized Cantor and Kyl, suggesting their departures were an attempt to avoid being the GOP members who would have to accept revenue increases. Cantor’s move surprised some GOP leaders and was widely seen as a high-stakes gambit to shift the talks’ dynamics and defend the party’s anti-tax stance even as pressure mounts to consider defense cuts and eliminating tax subsidies.

The American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI) 2015 automobile report finds overall U.S. car-owner satisfaction falling to 79/100, a 3–3.7% decline from a year earlier and the lowest level since 2004. Two main drivers are a record number of recalls (nearly 64 million vehicles in 2014) and rising vehicle prices after years of heavy incentives. Consumers now expect near‑perfect quality, so defects and long waits for recall repairs have reduced satisfaction.

Luxury brands scored best: Lexus (84) tops the list, followed by Acura, Lincoln and Mercedes-Benz (83), with BMW, Subaru and Toyota close behind. Asian and European manufacturers dominate the above‑average ranks. Domestic brands were weaker overall, with Fiat Chrysler (FCA) brands performing worst: Dodge (76), Jeep (75), Chrysler (74) and Fiat (73) occupy the bottom positions. ACSI notes Fiat/Chrysler’s low scores are part of a longer trend.

The rankings are based on about 4,294 owner surveys of vehicles purchased roughly six months to three years earlier. ACSI advises prospective buyers to consider long‑term trends and not just short‑term measures when evaluating brands.

President Trump warned he would be “very angry” if Republicans fail to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, saying he’s waiting for the bill to reach his desk and calling Obamacare a “failed experiment.” His remarks to televangelist Pat Robertson contrast with an earlier, more sanguine comment that failure would be “okay.”

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has stayed the Senate in session into August and pressed colleagues to allow debate and a vote, arguing blocking the measure would foreclose public consideration of GOP alternatives. Senate leaders including Majority Whip John Cornyn urged senators to at least allow the motion to proceed, saying tradition supports permitting amendments and votes.

However, key conservatives Sen. Ted Cruz and Sen. Mike Lee are pressing an amendment that would let insurers sell any plan alongside at least one that meets federal standards—a move critics say would siphon healthy people into skimpy plans and sharply raise premiums for older and sicker enrollees. The insurers’ trade group warned the Cruz-Lee change could jeopardize access and affordability for people with pre-existing conditions.

McConnell can only afford two GOP defections to pass repeal with 52 Republicans; Sen. Rand Paul is expected to oppose it and Sen. Susan Collins is seen as unlikely to support it. Several senators, including Lisa Murkowski, voiced frustration with leadership’s secrecy about final bill details and declined commitments. To entice moderates, Cornyn promised greater funding (he said “a substantial” increase) to a $62 billion state stability fund for high-cost, low-income enrollees.

GOP negotiators, including Sens. Mike Rounds and Bill Cassidy, are working with Cruz and Lee to modify the amendment—proposals include limiting how much insurers can charge for compliant vs. noncompliant plans—but it remained unclear whether conservatives would accept changes. McConnell planned a conference meeting and to release the bill publicly on Thursday.

Country music legend Merle Haggard, 79, died on April 6, 2016 — his birthday — at his home near Redding, California, surrounded by family. His manager, Frank Mull, and family said he succumbed to pneumonia after a prolonged battle that included recent hospitalizations for double pneumonia and canceled April tour dates with Willie Nelson. Haggard’s son Ben posted that his father had predicted he would die on his birthday. A pioneer of the Bakersfield sound and a figure in the Outlaw Country movement, Haggard had 40 No. 1 hits, numerous awards, and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1994; his song “Mama Tried” was recently added to the National Recording Registry. Colleagues including Willie Nelson paid tribute.

San Francisco moved quickly to rein in dockless electric scooter companies after hundreds of scooters flooded the city in March and April, creating complaints about unsafe riding and sidewalk obstructions. City Attorney Dennis Herrera sent cease-and-desist letters to Bird, Lime and Spin, citing violations of California law — riding on sidewalks, failing to wear helmets and carrying passengers — and providing photos of scooters blocking walkways and riders without helmets. Companies were given until April 30 to address the problems.

The Board of Supervisors unanimously approved an ordinance and permitting framework requiring scooter operators to obtain permits from agencies such as SFMTA or Public Works, educate users, allow city crews to remove unpermitted devices, and face fines starting at $125 per scooter. Supervisor Aaron Peskin (author of the ordinance) emphasized that sidewalks must remain safe for pedestrians, strollers and people with disabilities, while acknowledging scooters can offer transportation benefits. The Board also backed forming a working group to study emerging mobility technologies and unintended consequences.

The scooter firms say they are cooperating: Bird and Lime announced measures such as rider education, parking-photo requirements, suspending repeat offenders and offering helmets, and Santa Monica previously fined Bird for operating without permits. Some residents see scooters as a nuisance and safety hazard; others argue they are less dangerous than private cars and represent useful, eco-friendly short trips. The city is moving toward a formal permitting process expected to open soon to regulate operations and curb hazards.

This document contains three distinct items: a note about web-archiving crawls, a report on Heinz’s Super Bowl ad and its campaign, and a feature about mayonnaise’s rising popularity and divided opinions among chefs.

- Web-archiving effort: Crawls are being run to archive pages as they are created and the pages they reference so that links remain intact when original pages change or disappear. The Internet Archive hopes archived versions will replace or accompany broken links, aiming to “fix all broken links on the web.” These crawls include supported “No More 404” sites.

- Heinz Super Bowl ad: Heinz released its first Super Bowl commercial in 16 years, a 30-second spot (with a 50-second online version) from Cramer-Krasselt that blends humor and sentiment. Set to “If You’re Happy and You Know It,” people tap the bottoms of ketchup bottles to get sauce out, producing both wholesome Americana moments and comedic beats (e.g., a vendor apparently injuring himself with spilled ketchup; a grandmother making a long farting noise squeezing the last of a bottle). Tagline: “Where there’s happy, it has to be Heinz.” A “Show Us Your Heinz” campaign invites consumers to submit photos and to scan QR codes on specially marked bottles through Feb. 23 for a chance at over $400,000 in prizes, including five grand-prize trips to major sporting events.

- Mayonnaise trend and chef views: Mayonnaise recently outsold ketchup in the U.S., with Americans buying about $2 billion of mayo versus $725 million of ketchup, according to Euromonitor (which separates salsa as a dip, not a condiment). Chefs are split: many embrace mayo—praising its culinary versatility and encouraging customizations—while others dislike it strongly and replace it with flavored aiolis, yogurt, tomato, avocado, or other alternatives. Restaurateur Fabio Viviani praises mayo as a versatile “white canvas”; chef Stephen Jones and marketer Craig Horwitz are outspoken mayo detractors (Horwitz even founded a “holdthatmayo.com” site and co-directed a mockumentary). Chef Tim Love (a Hellman’s spokesperson) notes mayo is often present in dishes in less obvious ways and believes critics may have already enjoyed it without realizing.

San Francisco 49ers 36, New Orleans Saints 32
- San Francisco’s defense set the tone in a wild divisional playoff, delivering big hits, pressure and turnovers that fueled a fourth-quarter comeback and a 14-yard touchdown from Alex Smith to Vernon Davis with 9 seconds left.
- Early: Donte Whitner’s hard, legal hit knocked Saints RB Pierre Thomas out with a head injury and signaled the physical approach that disrupted New Orleans all day.
- Defense: The 49ers forced five Saints turnovers (interceptions by Dashon Goldson and Tarell Brown; forced fumbles by Blake Costanzo and Madieu Williams among others) while surrendering only one turnover themselves. Goldson’s first-quarter interception ended Drew Brees’ NFL-record streak of 226 postseason passes without a pick.
- Front seven: Justin Smith, Aldon Smith and others consistently pressured and sacked Brees (three sacks total), and Patrick Willis and NaVorro Bowman stifled the run, continuing a season-long stinginess vs. rushing attacks.
- Coaching/identity: Jim Harbaugh and DC Vic Fangio emphasized an old-school, physical defense that produced a plus-28 turnover differential in the regular season; that opportunism carried into the playoffs and sent the 49ers (14-3) to the NFC Championship to host the New York Giants.

Baltimore Ravens 20, Houston Texans 13
- Baltimore advanced to the AFC Championship (at New England) in a low‑scoring, defense-driven win over Houston, keyed by four takeaways and three interceptions of rookie QB T.J. Yates.
- Defense/control: Ed Reed and Ray Lewis led a unit that didn’t commit turnovers, wasn’t penalized, and came up with timely plays—Reed’s late interception near the goal line sealed the win. The Ravens finished 9-0 at home.
- Offense/boots-on-the-ground: Baltimore built an early lead (17-3) and then leaned on its defense; Joe Flacco hit Anquan Boldin for two early TDs, and Kris Wilson caught a 1-yard touchdown (his first catch of the season). Baltimore struggled to move the ball late, often going three-and-out, but the defense preserved the lead.
- Houston positives and miscues: Arian Foster ran for 132 yards (first 100-yard postseason rusher against Baltimore), and Andre Johnson had 8 catches for 111 yards, but Yates threw three interceptions and the Texans lost key chances (missed 50-yard FG). Despite injuries and instability at QB, Houston came close and owner Bob McNair praised the team’s season.
- Notes: Baltimore improved to 6-0 all-time vs. Houston (2-0 that season). With this home win, the first seven playoff games of the postseason were won by the home team—an NFL first since the current format began in 1990.

Overall theme
- Both games highlighted how elite defenses and turnovers decide playoff outcomes: San Francisco’s aggressive, takeaway-focused unit overcame New Orleans’ explosive offense, while Baltimore’s veteran defense protected a modest offensive output to reach the AFC title game.

Rapper Vanilla Ice (Robert Van Winkle) says he briefly dated Madonna in 1991 when he was 24 and she was 33. He called the relationship "exciting" and praised her as a lover, but says he ended it after Madonna published her 1992 coffee-table book Sex. He told News of the World he felt humiliated and exploited by the explicit photos—some of which featured him or made it look as if she was with other men—calling the book “disgusting and cheap” and likening his inclusion to being treated like a product. Vanilla Ice is currently appearing on the U.K. reality show Dancing on Ice.

A U.S. federal judge has ruled that the company long collecting royalties for "Happy Birthday To You" (Warner/Chappell) does not hold a valid copyright to the song’s lyrics. Judge George H. King found that the original 1935 copyright acquired by Clayton F. Summy Co. — later bought by Birch Tree Group and then Warner/Chappell — covered only specific piano arrangements and the melody (derived from the 1893 song "Good Morning to All" by sisters Mildred and Patty Hill), not the later "Happy Birthday" lyrics themselves.

Background: the Hill sisters wrote the melody and "Good Morning to All" in the 1890s and sold rights to Summy. References to "Happy Birthday" lyrics appear sporadically in early 20th-century publications, with the full lyrics first printed by 1911. Warner/Chappell had been licensing the song commercially since acquiring the successors' rights and was estimated to have earned about $2 million per year from fees for films, TV, ads and other public uses.

The lawsuit began in 2013 when filmmakers and musicians (including Jennifer Nelson, Rupa Marya and others) disputed Warner/Chappell’s demand for licensing fees — in one case $1,500 for a film sync license. Plaintiffs argued the lyrics were in the public domain and that any transfers to Summy did not include the words. King agreed, concluding the available agreements and 1935 registration do not show a transfer of the lyrics’ copyright and that the registration itself appears to have been limited to arrangements. He also noted unresolved questions about the lyrics’ authorship that could warrant further fact-finding.

Consequences and next steps: The ruling declares the "Happy Birthday" lyrics not owned by Warner/Chappell in the U.S. and opens the door for plaintiffs to seek restitution for licensing fees allegedly collected (the monetary claim will be decided later). Warner/Chappell said it is reviewing the opinion and may appeal. Intellectual property lawyers caution the decision applies to U.S. law only; rights or remaining copyright elements may persist in other countries, so commercial users outside the U.S. should be careful.

Researchers in the U.K. report that “temperature contagion” — the tendency to physically mirror another person’s cold exposure — occurs in healthy people. In a PLoS ONE study, 36 volunteers sat in a room at 21°C while watching short videos of actors placing a hand into visibly cold (ice) water, warm (steaming) water, or neutral water. Participants’ left and right fingertip temperatures and heart rates were recorded continuously with high-sensitivity thermistors.

Key findings
- Viewing cold videos produced a small but reliable drop in observers’ fingertip temperatures (mean drop ≈ 0.4°F in the left hand and ≈ 0.1°F in the right). Warm videos produced no significant temperature increase, and heart rate did not change.
- The cold effect was stronger for the observers’ left hand and was only seen for cold (ice) stimuli; the authors suggest steam and other warm cues were less visually salient and that temperature decreases are generally easier to elicit than increases.
- Individual differences mattered: scores on empathy measures predicted susceptibility to temperature contagion in a nuanced way (empathic concern positively predicted contagion, while one composite empathy score showed a negative relationship when modeled together).
- No evidence was found for strict left-right mirroring tied to which hand was observed.

Interpretation and context
- The authors frame the effect as an extension of emotional contagion and perception–action/mirror-neuron models: observing another’s peripheral physiological state can elicit congruent autonomic responses in the observer.
- Top-down cognitive influences on thermoregulation (e.g., imagery, suggestion) and prior cases of volitional limb temperature change support the plausibility of visually mediated temperature shifts.
- The selective effect for cooling and absence of heart-rate change align with known separable neural thermoregulatory pathways (cutaneous vasoconstriction vs. cardiac responses).
- The phenomenon may help social understanding and empathy, and variation in temperature contagion could be relevant to conditions with altered social cognition (e.g., autism, schizophrenia).

Limitations
- Small sample (n=36) and the visual potency differed between cold and warm stimuli (ice remained visible throughout while steam was transient), which may explain asymmetry in results.
- Effects were small in magnitude and limited to peripheral skin temperature changes.

Conclusion
The study provides experimental evidence that simply observing another person experiencing cold can produce measurable cooling in the observer’s own hands, supporting the idea that autonomic bodily states can be socially contagious and linked to individual empathy traits.

The American Chemical Society’s Reactions video (Nov 3, 2015) explains why some cheeses make better grilled cheeses than others by focusing on cheese chemistry. Key points:

- Cheese structure: Casein proteins form micelles (fat-filled, negatively charged spheres) held together in part by calcium.
- Role of acid/aging: As cheese ages, lactic acid builds up and lowers pH. Increased acidity reduces the negative charge on micelles, causing them to stick together, trap water and form a gooey network.
- Ideal melting pH: Cheeses with pH around 5.3–5.5 melt best for grilled cheese. Too acidic (lower pH) and the cheese will break down and release oil when heated, producing a curdled, oily mess.
- Recommendations: Choose cheeses with the right acidity and composition—Gouda, Gruyère, and Manchego are good choices. For cheddar, pick mild rather than sharp to avoid excessive breakdown.
- Additional resources: The episode references The Kitchen as Laboratory and provides links to sources on milk proteins, cheese texture, processed American cheese, and FDA standards.

The video also offers cooking tips in a related “We Tried It” segment for making the actual sandwich.

A full English translation of a letter British diplomats gave to Ecuador regarding Julian Assange has been released. The letter warns that Britain is obliged by law (the European Arrest Warrant framework and the UK Extradition Act 2003) to arrest and extradite Assange to Sweden, and that any Ecuadorian request for safe passage after granting asylum would be refused. It urges Ecuador to continue diplomatic negotiations to produce a jointly agreed text enabling Assange to leave the embassy and voluntarily surrender, warns that prolonged sheltering in diplomatic premises is incompatible with the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations and “not sustainable,” and notes the UK’s Diplomatic and Consular Premises Act could be used to remove diplomatic protection from the Ecuadorian embassy to allow arrest. The note frames these steps as undesirable but legally available if Ecuador cannot resolve Assange’s presence.

Context: Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, had been inside the Ecuadorian Embassy in London since June 19 to avoid extradition to Sweden over alleged sexual-assault offenses; Ecuador on Thursday announced it would grant him political asylum, saying his rights and fears of political persecution (including possible onward transfer to the U.S.) were legitimate. Britain responded that asylum would not alter its legal duty to extradite and said it might revoke the embassy’s diplomatic status—remarks that provoked strong rebukes from Quito and criticism from former diplomats worried about setting a dangerous precedent. Outside the embassy, police clashed with pro‑Assange protesters. Legal and diplomatic observers noted that even with asylum, Assange would face immediate arrest if he left the embassy and that practical options for getting him out (diplomatic car, bag, or appointment as a diplomat) are largely unworkable.

During Fox Sports’ live FS1 coverage of Round 2 of the 2018 U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills, an on-course microphone picked up and broadcast an exchange between two spectators in which one boasted about violent, rough sexual behavior toward an ex. The graphic, misogynistic comments were inadvertently aired to millions of viewers; the segment interrupted commentary by Joe Buck and was followed by an unrelated eight-minute audio outage. Fox Sports issued an apology, saying one of the many course microphones inadvertently captured offensive crowd chatter. The USGA also apologized, saying it “deeply regrets the inappropriate language and sentiment” and is working with Fox to address the issue. The incident renewed criticism of pervasive on-course miking and raised questions about crowd control and broadcast oversight at the tournament.

Former South Korean general I.-B. Chun, speaking at a London think tank, warned that a U.S. military attack on North Korea would encounter fiercely indoctrinated, well-armed defenders and enormous operational challenges. Drawing on nearly 40 years in South Korea’s military (including leading special forces and advising Moon Jae-in), Chun said North Korea functions like “one huge barracks” and the Kim family rule has created a cult-like devotion that would make invasion extremely difficult.

His key points:
- Much of North Korea’s military infrastructure is deeply hardened and underground.
- Civilians receive regular weapons and survival training from age 14; the country is highly militarized.
- The air force is outdated but could be used in kamikaze-style attacks.
- Pyongyang possesses chemical and biological stockpiles (estimated 2,500–5,000 tons), substantial artillery and rockets able to threaten Seoul, roughly 1.3 million active troops, 7.7 million reserves and some 200,000 special forces.
- A harsh domestic control system—collective punishment of family groups—maintains loyalty and internal surveillance.
- North Korea also has significant cyber capabilities and has been blamed for global attacks such as WannaCry.

Chun judged that North Korea’s recent ICBM tests suggest progress toward a missile that could reach the U.S., but he believes current warhead limitations leave a window for diplomacy. He urged preparing for worst-case scenarios while pursuing talks, calling military action a last resort — “like pulling out all of your teeth.” Other speakers noted China’s strategic tolerance for a nuclear North Korea to limit U.S. presence, and British MP Tom Tugendhat stressed Western stakes in upholding the international rules-based order regarding the peninsula.

Former South African president Nelson Mandela, 94, was readmitted to hospital late Wednesday for treatment of a recurring lung infection and “is responding positively” to care, the presidency said. He remains under observation and has “the best possible expert medical treatment and comfort,” officials added, while President Jacob Zuma and the African National Congress urged South Africans and the world to keep Mandela — widely known by his clan name “Madiba” — and his family in their thoughts and prayers and asked for privacy for medical staff.

Mandela’s lung problems date back to tuberculosis contracted during his 27 years as a political prisoner on Robben Island; he has had several hospital stays in recent years, including a lengthy December stay for a lung infection and gallstone surgery and a brief admission earlier in the month for a routine checkup. The White House said President Obama had sent best wishes and was being kept informed. Mandela, South Africa’s first black president (1994–1999) and a global icon of the anti-apartheid struggle and reconciliation, remains widely revered at home and abroad.

NOAA released the first high-resolution images from its new GOES-16 geostationary weather satellite (launched Nov. 19, 2016), showcasing dramatically improved detail and speed that NOAA calls a “game changer” for forecasting. GOES-16’s Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) delivers four times the spatial resolution, five times the coverage speed, and three times the spectral channels of previous GOES imagers. It can produce a full-Earth image every 15 minutes, a full-continental U.S. image every five minutes, and targeted regional imagery as often as every 30 seconds.

The initial photos (taken Jan. 15 and released later) include full-disk Western Hemisphere views, detailed views of storms across North America and Argentina, dust off Africa, fires in southern Mexico, and a Feb. 7 capture of a tornado outbreak over Louisiana. Compared side-by-side with GOES-13 imagery, GOES-16’s color-composite capability and clarity are markedly superior. NOAA says the enhanced imagery and faster data will improve warnings and forecasts for severe weather, hurricanes, wildfires and space-weather events.

GOES-16 will be positioned operationally (East or West) by late 2017; GOES-S (the next satellite in the series, later GOES-17) is undergoing testing and will follow about nine months after GOES-16’s commissioning.

A warrant was issued for 79-year-old singer Pat Boone after he failed to appear at a subpoenaed court hearing tied to a lawsuit over a luxury cruise-ship condo project. The ship’s developer lost a suit brought by some investors and was ordered to pay over $800,000 in attorneys’ fees. Those attorneys have sought to recover fees from purchasers of condos on the vessel, and Boone was subpoenaed as part of that effort. Boone missed the hearing because he was on vacation in Hawaii, prompting the judge to issue the warrant.

Boone told TMZ the warrant is based on a misunderstanding: his only connection to the project was an agreement to be a future spokesperson for the ship once it launched, and he says he knows nothing substantive about the development. He plans to appear in court but expects his testimony will be of little use to the litigant. He also made light of the situation with some self-deprecating humor.

This ProPublica–Houston Chronicle investigation examines a sharp decline in outcomes and trust at the once‑renowned heart transplant program at Baylor St. Luke’s Medical Center (affiliated with Baylor College of Medicine and the Texas Heart Institute). Historically celebrated for pioneering cardiac surgery, the program experienced a cluster of poor results, staffing losses, operational errors, and management changes that together produced worse‑than‑expected patient outcomes and growing alarm among clinicians, patients and regulators.

Key findings
- Measured over a recent SRTR reporting window (mid‑2014 through 2016), St. Luke’s one‑year heart transplant survival was about 85% versus a 91.4% national average; statistically, about twice as many patients died within a year as expected after adjusting for case mix.
- The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services formally cited the program for significantly worse‑than‑expected outcomes and threatened to cut Medicare funding; the hospital submitted a correction plan and avoided immediate funding loss.
- The program saw more postoperative complications and very long hospital stays: half of recipients between mid‑2016 and mid‑2017 stayed 27+ days vs. 16 days nationally.
- Multiple high‑profile clinicians left or reduced roles over several years; recruitment and organizational changes after a 2013 sale to Catholic Health Initiatives (CHI) and other transitions were cited by current and former staff as disruptive to care and institutional knowledge.
- Surgical leadership troubles: Dr. Jeffrey Morgan was hired as surgical director in 2016 amid earlier deaths and turnover. Several colleagues and internal reviewers described surgical errors and complications in specific cases after his arrival (sutures inadvertently occluding major veins, early lung transplant complications), and he has been named in malpractice suits from his prior work. The hospital and some colleagues defended him and reported improved survival since 2016, but others say concerns persisted and some physicians sought external reviews that administrators wouldn’t commission.
- Operational and equipment failures were reported in individual cases (e.g., a defibrillator malfunction or delayed backup during a transplant), with differing accounts between surgeons and the hospital about the accessibility and impact of backup equipment.
- Families of several patients described a lack of clear communication about intraoperative problems and complications; some patients suffered prolonged, complicated recoveries or died after multiple follow‑up operations, strokes, infections and organ failure. Individual stories (David Kveton, Lazerick Eskridge, James “Lee” Lewis and others) illustrate the human cost: unexpected complications, long hospitalizations, emergent reoperations, permanent disabilities and deaths.
- Despite the decline, the hospital at times continued to market the transplant center using its historical reputation, videos and charts that gave a more favorable impression; some promotional material was removed after reporters questioned administrators. Hospital leaders argued the program treats older, sicker, and higher‑risk patients and that outcomes have improved since leadership changes in 2016.

Contributing factors cited by sources
- Leadership and staffing turnover, including departures of experienced surgeons and specialty staff (infectious disease, critical care, pathology, nursing), and uneven surgical experience among replacements.
- Organizational disruption and cost pressures after CHI acquisition and expansion plans; clinicians described staff reductions and changing policies that affected clinical practice and research.
- Possible procedural or technical errors in individual surgeries and occasional equipment problems.
- Communication failures with families and reluctance (per some clinicians) to order external performance reviews earlier.

Hospital response and caveats
- St. Luke’s and Baylor College of Medicine acknowledged past poor outcomes, said they had made changes, and provided data showing improved one‑year survival since 2016 (hospital leaders contend 2015 was the anomalous year). They also stressed clinical complexity of their patients as a factor.
- The hospital defended individual clinicians’ competence, said internal investigations were underway where relevant, and disputed some characterizations of equipment access and other details.
- Some patients did have successful transplants and positive impressions; program leaders highlighted those cases in response.

Overall picture
The investigation portrays a program in transition: a storied center that widely promoted its past successes but that, amid leadership changes, staff losses and management upheaval, produced a period of unusually poor transplant outcomes and troubling case narratives. The mix of measurable declines in survival, accounts of surgical and equipment problems, clinicians’ requests for review, and families’ experiences of poor communication eroded confidence and prompted federal scrutiny. The hospital reports improvements and attributes problems to an earlier period of transition and high‑risk case mix, but the episode has already had lasting effects on patients, families and staff trust.

"Zebra" is American medical slang for diagnosing an exotic or rare condition when a common explanation is more likely. The term references Dr. Theodore Woodward’s aphorism, "When you hear hoofbeats, think of horses not zebras," taught to medical interns since the late 1940s as a warning against cognitive biases—especially the availability heuristic and the tendency to remember striking, novel cases—that can lead novices to overdiagnose rare diseases. In teaching diagnosis, the aphorism encourages prioritizing likelier causes, though clinicians also caution that rare conditions must be considered and ruled out when appropriate because, for an individual patient, rarity does not determine presence or absence.

The textbook term for an obscure, rare diagnosis is fascinoma. Examples of zebra-type misdiagnoses include attributing necrotic skin lesions to recluse spider bites even in areas where those spiders are absent, which can delay correct treatment. Some genuine but underrecognized conditions (e.g., Ehlers–Danlos and hypermobility syndromes) have adopted the zebra as a symbol of their awareness movements.

The zebra concept appears in popular culture (TV shows like Scrubs and House, a Law & Order: SVU episode, and a Harvard medical student video) and sits alongside other diagnostic aphorisms such as Sutton’s law, Occam’s razor, Leonard’s Law of Physical Findings, and Hickam’s dictum.

(The document also included an unrelated news item about two zebras that escaped from the UniverSoul Circus in West Philadelphia in November 2015; both were safely recaptured within hours and no injuries were reported.)

Marc Anthony and model Shannon de Lima have announced they are divorcing after two years of marriage. In a joint statement to Us Weekly on December 18 they said they “mutually and amicably decided to end our two‑year marriage,” asked for privacy and said no further comments will be made. Reports indicate the couple had decided to separate earlier in the year; legal documents show Anthony filed for divorce in Florida on December 16. 

Anthony, 48, and de Lima, 28, began dating in 2012 and wed in the Dominican Republic on November 11, 2014. They have no children together. Rumors of trouble intensified after Anthony shared a televised kiss with his ex‑wife Jennifer Lopez at the Latin Grammys in November; some sources have suggested Anthony still has feelings for Lopez. Anthony and Lopez share 8‑year‑old twins Emme and Max, and Lopez has spoken publicly about the difficulty of forgiving and moving past their marriage.

This document contains two loosely connected pieces: a personal reaction to a Budweiser Super Bowl commercial and a longer report about the NFL’s awkward branding problem with Roman numerals (specifically the upcoming Super Bowl L).

1) Budweiser “Flash Fans” ad
- The writer praises a Budweiser Super Bowl commercial called “Flash Fans.” Budweiser told two Port Credit, Ontario beer‑league hockey teams they were filming a documentary, then surprised them by filling the empty arena with passionate, body‑painted fans, thundersticks and banners.
- The players’ delighted reactions and the close 4–3 OT game made the stunt feel authentic and inspiring. The author notes the ad reminds viewers that many pro players started in small, love‑of‑the‑game settings and celebrates grassroots hockey. The piece ends by calling the ad refreshing and worthy of a celebratory Budweiser.

2) NFL and the “L” problem with Roman numerals
- The NFL uses Roman numerals for Super Bowls, a tradition meant to add grandeur since Super Bowl V (1971). But Super Bowl L (2016) poses a marketing dilemma: the single letter “L” is widely recognized as meaning “loser,” especially in pop culture and shows like Glee, risking awkward merchandising and messaging for the 50th game.
- Brand and advertising experts say the league may emphasize Arabic numerals for the 50th, reinterpret the L (e.g., “learning,” “love,” “largest”), or incorporate the numeral creatively into logos or the host city’s branding. The NFL has begun planning and discussing options.
- The story notes the Roman numerals’ historic place in Super Bowl branding, previous awkward sequences (e.g., IV, XXX), and mentions related business moves such as Nike replacing Reebok as the NFL’s apparel partner.

Overall takeaway: the first piece applauds a heartwarming, fan‑focused Super Bowl ad that celebrates amateur hockey and passion for sport; the second examines a real branding challenge facing the NFL as it approaches its 50th Super Bowl and the unintended cultural meaning of the Roman numeral L.

California Gov. Jerry Brown signed AB 60, a law allowing people in the U.S. illegally to obtain state driver’s licenses, making California the latest of at least 11 states to do so. The licenses—expected by late 2014 or early 2015—will carry a special marking and a notice that they are not federal ID or proof of work or benefit eligibility. The law lets any applicant who passes written and road tests obtain a license; officials estimate about 1.4 million people will apply in the first three years.

Supporters, including Latino advocates, police chiefs and insurance authorities, say licensing undocumented drivers will improve road safety, increase testing and insurance rates, and reduce hit-and-run incidents. The measure bans discrimination based on the license and prohibits using it as a basis for immigration arrest. Backers also hope the move will spur broader immigration reform.

Opponents raised concerns about fraud, racial profiling, conflicts with federal law, and public safety. Critics cite mixed results from other states—some reporting only small insurance gains or fraud problems—and studies with conflicting findings on uninsured-driver and crash rates. The DMV will develop eligibility guidelines and may open temporary offices to handle the influx; projected processing costs are $140–$220 million over three years, partly offset by applicant fees. The law is one of several pro-immigrant measures passed by California’s Legislature this year.

A group led by former Florida governor Jeb Bush and ex-New York Yankees captain Derek Jeter has won the auction to buy the Miami Marlins with a reported $1.3 billion bid, according to people familiar with the deal. The sale remains subject to a formal contract and MLB approval, and the identities and stakes of the other investors in Bush’s group have not been disclosed. Bush is expected to be the team’s “control person,” while Jeter plans to play an active role.

Current owner Jeffrey Loria bought the club in 2002 for about $158 million; Forbes had valued the franchise around $940 million. Loria does not plan to retain any ownership. Other bidders included Wayne Rothbaum and a group led by Tagg Romney. MLB approval is expected to be straightforward given Bush’s and Jeter’s prominence; commissioner Rob Manfred has expressed support for former players becoming owners.

The Marlins play in the relatively new Marlins Park (opened 2012) but have struggled with attendance (average ~24,313 this season, 24th of 30) and generate the lowest regional cable TV revenue in MLB (about $20 million annually under the current Fox deal through 2020). The team has a $120 million payroll this year—its highest ever—but has a long postseason drought and several backloaded contracts that could raise future payroll obligations. Potential revenue moves under new ownership could include stadium naming rights and renegotiating the local TV contract.

The transaction could trigger a payment to Miami-Dade County under the 2009 stadium-financing deal, though the amount would require complex calculation. Loria’s decision to sell reportedly reflects personal and business reasons, including his age, criticism from fans, and team struggles since the 2003 World Series. The sale process could take months to finalize.

Birds that eat winter berries can become intoxicated after frosts trigger fermentation in the fruit, and this year an unusually large number of such incidents has been reported. Early frosts convert berry starches to sugar; thawing then allows yeast to ferment the fruit into alcohol. Species that commonly gorge on these berries—Bohemian waxwings, robins, thrushes and similar songbirds—are most prone to becoming tipsy. A local official and a birding expert said calls came in about disoriented birds colliding with buildings and cars, but most simply sober up after a few hours and don’t require police intervention.

Wildlife rescue workers in places such as Whitehorse, Yukon, have admitted intoxicated waxwings into care; they show impaired flight and coordination but generally recover. Some intoxicated birds, however, die from collisions with buildings or hard surfaces. Scientific confirmation is limited because testing for alcohol in animals is costly and alcohol dissipates quickly, though postmortems in past cases have found fermentative alcohol in dead birds’ tissues. Young birds may be more vulnerable; species that rely on berries have relatively large livers that may confer higher tolerance.

Migration patterns and weather also play a role: many birds are still present in fall and unusual frost-thaw cycles or warmer trends may increase fermentation events. Experts note that migration “fallout” concentrates birds near roads and buildings, raising collision risk regardless of intoxication. Practical advice: don’t call police for loopy birds, but if you find an uninjured intoxicated bird, keep it in a ventilated box until it sobers; reduce window strikes by marking glass with stickers or suncatchers.

This collection compiles news coverage and social media posts from the run-up to the September 25, 2017 Kurdish independence referendum in Iraq. It gathers materials from regional news outlets aligned with different Kurdish political parties and from social accounts of influential figures involved in or commenting on the vote.

Key themes and content in the collection:

- Political mobilization and campaigning: Reporting and posts document intense campaigning by major Kurdish parties and civil society. The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) promoted a “yes” vote for independence; smaller parties and activists are also active, with some pushing for unity among Kurds and others criticizing the process or calling for broader dialogue. Coverage shows rallies, speeches, and messaging aimed at maximizing turnout and legitimizing the referendum.

- Official planning and logistics: Local authorities’ preparations are recorded—voter registration details, polling plans, deployment of security forces, and statements from the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) about conducting the vote despite Baghdad’s opposition. There is material on ballot design, voting locations (including disputed areas), and efforts to include Kurds in Syria and the diaspora.

- Regional and international responses: The collection captures reactions from the Iraqi federal government, which condemned the referendum and warned of legal and security consequences; statements and pressure from neighboring states (notably Turkey and Iran) opposing secession; and diplomatic moves by the United States and other international actors urging restraint and dialogue. Some local outlets reported on threats of economic and military measures and on attempts to isolate the KRG politically.

- Security dynamics and disputed territories: Coverage highlights tensions in Kirkuk and other mixed or disputed governorates, where control over oil fields and security forces (including Kurdish Peshmerga, Iraqi forces, and various militias) was contested. There are reports of skirmishes, mobilizations, and fears of escalation following the vote.

- Economic concerns and sanctions threats: News items and commentary document worries about economic repercussions—threats to close border crossings, suspend air links, impose trade restrictions, and withhold federal budget transfers—which could affect salaries and public services in the KRG. Some sources detail contingency planning and appeals to international partners.

- Legal and political debate: The collection records arguments used by pro-independence voices invoking self-determination and historical grievances, while opponents cite the Iraqi constitution, legal barriers, and risks of destabilization. Internal Kurdish debate is visible about timing, strategy, and the referendum’s scope (binding vs. consultative).

- Social media narratives and public sentiment: Posts from prominent individuals show efforts to shape domestic and international opinion—mobilizing supporters, broadcasting poll-day images and turnout claims, responding to allegations, and documenting incidents. Social media also captured grassroots sentiment, fears, and celebratory or defiant rhetoric.

- Aftermath indicators and anticipatory reporting: In the immediate lead-up, outlets focused on predicted outcomes, expected turnout, and contingency scenarios. Some content foreshadows rapid political fallout and the likelihood of strong pushback from Baghdad and regional powers.

Overall, the collection offers a multi-perspective portrait of the referendum campaign: organized KRG efforts to legitimize and execute a vote on independence; robust internal debate among Kurds about timing and consequences; strong external opposition and pressure from Iraq’s central government and neighboring states; security tensions in disputed areas; and widespread concern about economic and political repercussions. Social media amplifies real-time developments and partisan narratives, making the lead-up to September 25 a highly charged and closely watched episode in Iraqi-Kurdish relations.

Monterey County Superintendent of Schools Nancy Kotowski confirmed she had a long-term romantic relationship with Rev. Mike Manning, a Southern California priest who has taken a leave from ministry and stepped away from the Wordnet Catholic television ministry after the relationship was reported. Kotowski said the physical aspect of their relationship ended about three years ago; she described the bond as a 30-year, soul-mate commitment rather than an “affair.” The two are second cousins who did not grow up together; Kotowski attended Manning’s ordination but reconnected with him in her late 20s. Families on both sides were aware of and accepting of their closeness, she said.

Kotowski said she and Manning are now embracing celibacy because she supports his priestly calling, calling it a struggle but honoring what she sees as God’s call. She hopes the revelation will prompt discussion within the Catholic Church about mandatory clerical celibacy. Kotowski declined to specify how long the physical relationship lasted or to discuss other past relationships, and said she is not worried about legal or ethical repercussions.

President Vladimir Putin used his annual state-of-the-nation address—delivered 17 days before a presidential election he is expected to win—to showcase a new suite of Russian strategic weapons and make domestic policy promises.

Weapons and military messaging:
- Putin unveiled and displayed video/animations of several advanced nuclear-capable systems he said are operational or in testing, including:
  - A new intercontinental ballistic missile (RS-28 Sarmat reportedly) claimed to have the longest range and multiple warheads and described as able to reach almost any target.
  - The Avangard hypersonic glide vehicle and the Kinzhal air-launched hypersonic missile, both said to evade existing missile defenses.
  - A nuclear-powered, long-range cruise missile with theoretically unlimited range.
  - An autonomous, submarine-launched “doomsday” torpedo/underwater drone (Status-6/Kanyon).
  - Other systems including laser weapons and the Su-57 stealth fighter shown in deployment.
- Putin repeatedly asserted these weapons make missile defenses “useless” and warned that any attack on Russia or its allies would be treated as a nuclear attack and met with immediate response.
- He framed the developments as a response to years of Western policies (including the U.S. withdrawal from the ABM treaty) and stressed that attempts to contain Russia have failed. He insisted Russia has no plans to be an aggressor.

Domestic agenda and politics:
- The speech also covered domestic pledges: halving poverty within six years, raising life expectancy, boosting pensions, expanding daycare, doubling urban infrastructure spending over six years, raising GDP, and improving connectivity and healthcare in remote areas. No detailed funding plans were provided.
- Putin emphasized Russia’s “huge potential” and national security as a campaign theme to drive turnout; polls show him with broad support. Opposition leader Alexei Navalny is barred from running and has called for an election boycott.
- The presentation was staged in an exhibition space with large screens and animations, amplifying the military demonstrations to both domestic and international audiences.

Reactions and context:
- U.S. officials played down the speech, saying Russia’s capabilities are already factored into assessments and stressing U.S. defenses are aimed at other threats. The U.S. State Department criticized animated depictions of an attack on the U.S. as irresponsible.
- Analysts note some systems and tests were already known, while others remain claims or work-in-progress; similar hypersonic and advanced weapons programs are being pursued by the U.S. and China.
- The address combined nationalistic military theater with social-policy promises, serving both as strategic signaling to the West and as a campaign message to Russian voters.

Luis Vargas, a Mexican-born legal resident, was exonerated on Nov. 23, 2015, after spending 16 years in prison for three sexual assaults he did not commit. Vargas was convicted in 1999 and sentenced to 55 years to life based largely on victim identifications and the prosecution’s theory that the same person committed all three attacks. While Vargas was incarcerated, similar assaults continued in the same area by a serial attacker known as the “teardrop rapist” (named for a teardrop tattoo), who is believed to have committed more than 30 rapes in Los Angeles since 1996.

Vargas maintained his innocence and, with help from the California Innocence Project (CIP), obtained post‑conviction DNA testing of material from one victim’s kit and clothing. Advanced testing found genetic material from at least two people — the victim and the teardrop rapist — and excluded Vargas. The Los Angeles District Attorney’s office reviewed the evidence, noting victims’ earlier uncertainty in lineups and discrepancies in tattoo descriptions, and approved overturning the convictions. Judge William C. Ryan vacated the convictions and ordered Vargas released, though he was first transferred to federal custody because his green card was revoked after the original convictions.

Vargas’s family expressed relief and hope for reunification and normal life; CIP called the case its third DNA exoneration and 20th freed client. The teardrop rapist remains unidentified.

An anti-Muslim group in Irving, Texas, the self-styled Bureau of American Islamic Relations (BAIR), publicly posted names and addresses of more than 60 Muslims and “Muslim sympathizers” on Facebook after an armed BAIR protest at the Islamic Center of Irving. The list, copied from a public city document of people who signed up to speak at a March city council meeting opposing a state bill aimed at limiting Muslim influence, drew alarm because it exposed private contact information and could put those named at risk. Facebook initially left the post up (contrary to its policy against content that creates a genuine risk of physical harm), but removed at least one copy after complaints.

Background: Irving has been the focus of several recent Islam-related controversies — including Mayor Beth Van Duyne’s public warnings about “Sharia” tribunals and the high-profile arrest of 14‑year‑old Ahmed Mohamed over a homemade clock — and tensions rose after the November Paris attacks. BAIR members staged an armed protest outside the mosque, carrying rifles and signs reading “Stop the Islamization of America.” BAIR spokesman David Wright defended the group’s firearms and posted aggressive remarks about weapons on social media; he said the group was also protesting Syrian refugees.

Reactions: Local Muslim advocates and those named on the list expressed fear and outrage. Alia Salem of the Council on American‑Islamic Relations (CAIR) said it was the first time she’d felt “slightly alarmed” by public anti‑Muslim actions; CAIR reported a surge in Islamophobic incidents nationwide since the Paris attacks. Some who were listed reported misidentifications and warned the list could enable harm. City officials and critics condemned the armed protest at a place of worship and characterized publishing the list as intimidation. Organizers of a solidarity rally and many community members responded with offers of support for the mosque. Authorities (Irving police, Facebook) did not immediately comment beyond later removal of the posted list; CAIR said it planned to discuss the matter with federal authorities.

NBC’s rebooted Celebrity Apprentice, now hosted by Arnold Schwarzenegger, debuted Monday with middling ratings and lost the 8 p.m. primetime slot to ABC and CBS. The two-hour premiere averaged about 4.9 million viewers, trailing ABC’s The Bachelor (≈6.6M) and CBS’s sitcom block (≈6M). That figure is down more than 22% from Donald Trump’s most recent Celebrity Apprentice season premiere (2014–15), which averaged 7.6 million viewers, and its 18–49 demo score was about 46% higher than Schwarzenegger’s debut.

NBC heavily promoted the season and weathered earlier controversy over Trump retaining an executive producer credit, but stiff competition—The Bachelor and the Penn State–USC Rose Bowl on ESPN—likely suppressed viewership. Early reviews of Schwarzenegger’s turn were mixed. NBC noted the earlier Trump-season premiere had faced less sports competition, and observed the new Celebrity Apprentice provided a strong lead-in for The Wall, which retained much of its audience and performed well in the 10 p.m. key-demo slot.

A tailings dam at the Germano iron-ore mine in Minas Gerais, southeastern Brazil, collapsed on Thursday, sending a surge of water and clay-red mining waste down valleys and devastating nearby villages. Bento Rodrigues, about 7 km below the dam, was heavily flooded and dozens of homes and vehicles were destroyed; another settlement, Paracatu de Baixo, was also affected. Rescue teams, supported by nearby army units, searched for survivors into the night while authorities evacuated roughly 600 people to higher ground.

Local sources and the city hall of Mariana reported multiple casualties and many missing: initial counts cited at least one confirmed death, 15 believed dead in some reports, and about 45 people missing; official totals remained unconfirmed as searches continued. The dam, owned by Samarco (a 50:50 joint venture of BHP Billiton and Vale), held mining tailings—water mixed with metal filings and possible chemicals—raising fears of environmental contamination, particularly to the Gualaxo do Norte river. Samarco, BHP and Vale said they were assessing the situation, assisting affected people and could not yet determine the cause of the rupture. The disaster occurred amid industry-wide challenges, including a slump in iron-ore prices.

Jessica Simpson, 30, is engaged to former NFL player Eric Johnson, Us Weekly and Simpson’s representatives confirmed. The couple, who began dating in May 2010, moved quickly: Johnson accompanied Simpson to Italy for her 30th birthday in July, and his divorce from stylist Keri Johnson was finalized several months after their relationship began. Simpson was photographed wearing a sizable ruby-and-diamond ring on her left hand during a Kansas mall appearance the weekend the engagement was reported. Simpson’s father posted congratulations on Twitter. The announcement came days after Simpson’s ex-husband Nick Lachey became engaged to Vanessa Minnillo. Simpson has spoken publicly about her happiness with Johnson and her hopes for marriage and children; friends and family have also expressed support for the pairing.

The author announces they are ending their long-running project as they finish a master’s thesis and prepare to move abroad for a Ph.D. They thank readers for shaping their life and work, note the site and the Feminist Ryan Gosling book will remain available, and invite people to follow their personal projects on their website.

The rest of the document recounts Ryan Gosling’s heartfelt 2017 Golden Globes acceptance speech for Best Actor (La La Land). After a joking quip about being mistaken for Ryan Reynolds, Gosling thanked his partner Eva Mendes for managing family responsibilities while he filmed—raising their daughter, pregnant with their second child, and supporting her brother during his battle with cancer. He dedicated the award to her brother Juan Carlos Mendez, who died in April, and expressed love for his daughters. The speech prompted widespread online admiration, with many fans praising Gosling’s warmth and generosity.

A federal judge in Virginia refused to dismiss a lawsuit by Gavin Grimm, a transgender man who was barred from using the boys’ restrooms while in high school, finding he has plausibly alleged sex discrimination under federal law. U.S. District Judge Arenda L. Wright Allen ruled Grimm sufficiently pleaded a Title IX claim based on gender stereotyping and ordered the Gloucester County School Board and Grimm’s attorneys to schedule a settlement conference. Grimm sued in 2015 after the school barred him from boys’ bathrooms; his case has moved through appeals and was returned to the lower court. The decision follows similar federal appellate rulings recognizing federal protections for transgender students.

An inquest has concluded that Jane Wilson, 53, an experienced mountain walker from Stockport, died accidentally after falling on Tryfan in Snowdonia on March 25. She and her husband Gary, both regular scramblers, chose not to summit as dusk approached and attempted to descend across Tryfan’s west face using an Ordnance Survey app on his smartphone. Mrs Wilson went a short distance ahead to check a route; Mr Wilson asked if it was safe and they agreed to proceed. He then heard exclamations and rockfall; realising she had fallen, he climbed to a safer ledge and raised the alarm. Rescue teams found her body about 150 metres below, having first fallen 20–30ft down a vertical cliff and then tumbled into an area known as Notch arrete. She had a fractured skull and other severe injuries.

Rescuers noted the west face is loose and steep, with tricky rock steps, and said Mrs Wilson’s light boots may have been unsuitable and contributed to a slip. The rescuers and Mountain Rescue England and Wales warned that smartphone mapping can lack the detail of paper maps and that batteries can fail, urging use of map and compass alongside electronic aids. The coroner recorded accidental death and rescuers suggested it would have been safer to retreat the way they came or descend via the North Ridge. Tryfan is responsible for a high proportion of local rescue incidents, and less experienced walkers are advised to go with someone familiar with the routes.

Former Alaska governor Sarah Palin visited President Donald Trump at the White House Wednesday evening, bringing musicians Ted Nugent and Kid Rock. Palin posted photos of the visit on Facebook showing her with Trump, adviser Jared Kushner, and Nugent in the Oval Office; one image shows Palin and Nugent posing with a portrait of Hillary Clinton. The White House has not provided details about the meeting.

The appearance drew controversy because Nugent has a long history of violent, inflammatory rhetoric about Democrats: during the 2016 campaign he called Hillary Clinton a “devilbitch,” has called Clinton and Barack Obama deserving of treason charges and hanging, and previously called Obama a “subhuman mongrel” (for which he later offered an apology). Trump has defended Nugent in the past when Nugent’s remarks provoked backlash. The visit also reignited criticism over the Trump administration’s decision to stop routinely releasing detailed visitor logs.

Vice Adm. Scott Stearney, a 36‑year Navy aviator and native of Chicago, was found dead in his Bahrain residence on December 1, 2018. The Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Bahraini Ministry of Interior are investigating; officials have said there is no evidence of foul play at this time. Adm. John Richardson called the loss “devastating,” described Stearney as a decorated professional, devoted husband and father, and asked for privacy for the family. Rear Adm. Paul Schlise immediately assumed command of U.S. Fifth Fleet, with Vice Adm. Jim Malloy en route to Bahrain to take interim command.

Stearney graduated from the University of Notre Dame (B.A. in Economics), was commissioned in 1982, became a naval aviator in 1984, and graduated from the Navy Fighter Weapons School. He held an M.S. in National Resource Strategy. He flew the F/A‑18 in multiple strike fighter squadrons (VFA‑87, VFA‑136, VFA‑131), commanded Carrier Air Wing Seven aboard USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, and logged more than 4,500 mishap‑free flight hours and over 1,000 carrier arrested landings. He served ashore as an instructor at TOPGUN, aide to the CNO, and in senior joint staff and training roles.

His flag assignments included commander of Joint Enabling Capabilities Command (USTRANSCOM), Strike Force Training Atlantic, Carrier Strike Group 4, Navy Warfare Development Command, and director of operations for U.S. Central Command. From May 2018 until his death he served as commander, U.S. Naval Forces Central Command / U.S. Fifth Fleet / Combined Maritime Forces, responsible for more than 20,000 U.S. and coalition personnel. His decorations include the Defense Superior Service Medal, the Legion of Merit, and the Air Medal.

Norwood Thomas, a 93-year-old American World War II veteran, reunited with his wartime sweetheart Joyce Durrant Morris, 88, in Adelaide, Australia after more than 70 years apart. The two first met in London in 1944 — Thomas a 21-year-old paratrooper, Morris a 17-year-old — and parted when he left for Normandy. They exchanged letters but a misunderstanding ended their correspondence, and both later married others (Thomas’ wife died in 2001; Morris divorced). Last year Morris’ son found Thomas’ name online and the families reconnected by Skype, triggering an emotional revival of their longtime affection. After media coverage and hundreds of donations (plus complimentary first-class flights arranged by Air New Zealand), Thomas flew to Australia to spend time with Morris, and the pair plan to be together over Valentine’s Day. Both reflected on how different their lives might have been had they remained together.

Report title: Do Schools Challenge Our Students? What Student Surveys Tell Us About the State of Education in the United States
Authors: Ulrich Boser and Lindsay Rosenthal (Center for American Progress)

Summary:
Using student responses from the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) background questionnaires, the report analyzes students’ perceptions of challenge, engagement, and access to rigorous learning opportunities across grades and states. Key findings:

- Many students find schoolwork too easy. Significant shares across grades and subjects report low challenge: e.g., 37% of 4th-graders say math is too easy; 29% of 8th-grade math students say math is often/always too easy; 21% of 12th-graders say math is too easy. Even larger shares report civics and history as too easy.

- Low engagement in rigorous activities. Roughly one-third of 8th-graders read fewer than five pages per day in school/homework; about one-third rarely write long answers on reading tests. Among 12th-graders, 39% rarely or only monthly write about what they read; many rarely identify main themes or summarize passages.

- Limited access to science and technology learning. 72% of 8th-grade science students report not being taught about engineering and technology.

- Many students do not feel they are learning or do not understand instruction. Fewer than two-thirds of middle school math students say they almost always feel they are learning; under half of 12th-grade math students feel similarly. Large minorities report sometimes or hardly ever understanding teachers’ questions (25% middle school math; 36% 12th-grade math).

- Opportunity gaps by income and race. Higher-income students report better understanding of lessons and more access to rigorous opportunities than low-income peers (examples: 74% vs. 56% in 4th-grade science comprehension). Racial gaps also appear: in 4th-grade science and 8th-grade math, white and Asian/Pacific Islander students report higher rates of understanding than black, Hispanic, and Native students.

Caveat:
The data reflect students’ perceptions and frequency measures (e.g., pages read, types of tasks) but do not directly measure the quality of assignments or instruction. Nonetheless, given low achievement trends, these perceptions are seen as concerning indicators.

Recommendations:
- Strengthen and raise expectations through more rigorous standards (Common Core cited as a partial step).
- Expand students’ access to challenging, high-quality learning opportunities—especially in STEM.
- Use and further develop student surveys as a tool to assess classroom experiences and teacher effectiveness.
- Continue state and district reforms and use the report’s state-by-state data to drive policy and practice aimed at improving equity and rigor.

The authors urge policymakers, educators, and researchers to act on student-reported evidence to ensure all students receive the challenging education needed for college and the modern workforce.

An 8-year-old Canadian boy developed sudden, temporary allergies to fish and peanuts after receiving a blood transfusion while being treated for medulloblastoma. He had previously eaten these foods without problems but suffered anaphylaxis after eating salmon a few weeks post-transfusion and returned to the ER four days later after eating a peanut butter cup. Tests (blood and skin-prick) indicated IgE-mediated reactions to salmon and peanuts. Clinicians traced the plasma-containing transfusion to a donor with allergies to nuts, fish and shellfish; the donor’s remaining blood was not in the supply and they were barred from future donations.

Doctors concluded the boy acquired donor IgE antibodies via plasma, which can transiently sensitize recipients; because his own immune system had not produced those antibodies, the allergies were expected to wane. Indeed, by five months his IgE levels to salmon and peanut were undetectable, and by six months nuts and fish were reintroduced under supervision. Such transfusion-acquired allergies are rare but have been reported previously. Blood services in Canada and the U.S. do not routinely screen donors for allergy history, since IgE testing is not a reliable predictor and broad deferral could reduce the donor pool. Clinicians recommend awareness of the possibility, cautious reintroduction of foods under medical supervision, and more research to determine frequency and prevention strategies.

Summary:

A 2010 Wall Street Journal Magazine interview revealed designer Thom Browne’s critical take on President Obama’s style, saying Obama “could be dressed so much better” and suggesting politicians avoid dressing better than constituents; Browne compared this to the Queen Mother, who dressed up during the war because people expected to see a queen. Separately, at a later inauguration there was a minor oath gaffe: President Obama briefly cut off the word “States” during the oath (“The office of the president of the United Sta—”) and paused, echoing the well-known 2009 mistake when Chief Justice John Roberts misspoke part of the oath. The article notes the proper oath text and frames the moment as a small, human slip despite rehearsal.

New York’s highest court will hear a case over whether nude dancing at a suburban Albany strip club, Nite Moves, qualifies as exempt “live dramatic or musical arts performances” under state sales-tax law. The dispute stems from a 2005 audit that concluded the club owed roughly $124,000 (the audit initially alleged about $400,000) in unpaid sales taxes on its $11 cover charge and paid “couch” or lap dances. The club collects sales tax on nonalcoholic drinks but did not tax admissions and private dances.

Nite Moves argues the dances are choreographed artistic performances and presented expert testimony from cultural anthropologist Judith Hanna, who observed patterns she described as choreographic.
