An administrative law judge sided with the club in 2008, but the state Tax Appeals Tribunal reversed that finding, and an intermediate appellate court upheld the reversal, saying the club failed to prove the private dances were choreographed and noting dancers aren’t required to have formal training and the anthropologist didn’t observe private-room dances. The state also argued some dancers lack prior dance experience and some patrons merely seek conversation, so the performances shouldn’t receive the same exemption as theater or ballet.

The attorney for Nite Moves, W. Andrew McCullough, contends the tax department is acting like a dance critic and that skilled exotic dancers deserve the same exemption as other performers. The state Department of Taxation and Finance (represented by the attorney general’s office) seeks to prevent strip clubs from using the exemption. The case has broader implications as states increasingly target strip-club revenues; similar levies have appeared in several other states. The Court of Appeals typically issues a decision about a month after oral argument.

Summary:

American Cancer Society screening recommendations
- Begin cervical cancer screening at age 21.
  - Ages 21–29: Pap test every 3 years. HPV testing is not recommended for primary screening in this age group (it may be used for follow-up of abnormal Pap results).
  - Ages 30–65: Preferred option is co-testing (Pap + HPV) every 5 years. An acceptable alternative is a Pap test alone every 3 years.
  - High-risk women (e.g., immunosuppressed, exposed to DES in utero) may need more frequent screening as advised by their health care team.
  - Over 65: Routine screening can stop if there has been adequate prior screening in the past 10 years and no history of serious precancers (CIN2/3) in the last 20 years. Women with prior CIN2/3 should continue testing for at least 20 years after the abnormality was found.
  - Women who had a total hysterectomy (uterus and cervix removed) for benign reasons should stop screening; those who had a supracervical (cervix-preserving) hysterectomy should continue screening per guidelines.
  - Annual screening is not recommended. HPV-vaccinated women and women who have completed childbearing should still follow these guidelines.
  - These guidelines do not apply to women already diagnosed with cervical cancer, cervical pre-cancer, or HIV; such women should follow individualized recommendations from their care teams.

Why screening matters
- Screening historically cut cervical cancer deaths dramatically by detecting cancer early and identifying treatable precancers.
- Most cervical cancer is preventable with regular screening and HPV vaccination; symptoms often appear only in advanced disease, so prevention and screening are crucial.

New evidence on mortality and disparities
- A study in Cancer found U.S. cervical cancer death rates are substantially higher than earlier estimates because previous rates didn’t adjust for women who had hysterectomies (who are no longer at risk).
  - After adjusting for hysterectomy prevalence, mortality rose from about 5.7 to 10.1 per 100,000 for Black women and from 3.2 to 4.7 per 100,000 for White women in the analyzed data—meaning the Black–White disparity was underestimated by about 44%.
  - The adjusted mortality rate for Black women approaches levels seen in many low-income countries.
- The study used data from 12 states supplemented by behavioral risk surveys and highlights that disparities likely reflect differences in access to screening, HPV vaccination, and timely treatment.
- Experts emphasize that guideline-based screening remains appropriate but underused; increasing access to screening, vaccination (HPV vaccine coverage remains low among adolescents), and standard care is essential to reduce deaths and racial disparities.

John Travolta appears in Qantas’s new three-minute in-flight safety video—introduced as the airline’s ambassador—dressed in a captain’s uniform and delivering a light-hearted opening ("This is your captain speaking—well, maybe not today") while praising Qantas pilots and referring repeatedly to staff as "the team." Many Qantas cabin crew and pilots have reacted negatively, calling the video "cringeworthy," "corny" and "tacky." Criticisms include that a real pilot (several staff suggested Captain Richard de Crespigny, famed for handling QF32) should front the safety message, and that calling flight attendants "the team" is demeaning. Some staff also say the tone makes the safety message seem trite. Qantas, however, says feedback from staff and customers has been positive and that the airline is happy with the video.

The House passed its version of health-care reform late Saturday by 220–215 after approving an amendment that sharply restricts abortion coverage, marking a major victory for antiabortion forces and setting up a heated fight in the Senate and conference committee.

Key points:
- The amendment bars use of the new federal subsidies and the government-run plan to pay for elective abortions. It goes beyond the long-standing ban on direct federal funding of abortions by limiting coverage even for plans bought with private money if those plans are offered in the subsidized market.
- Supporters of the restriction credited intensive lobbying by the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops and the sway of conservative Democrats; 64 House Democrats backed the amendment.
- Abortion-rights groups warned insurers may drop abortion coverage from plans sold into the large subsidized market (anyone earning under $88,000 for a family of four could be eligible), which could effectively reduce access. Women could still pay out of pocket or buy separate riders, but advocates argued that those options are limited in practice.
- The bishops rejected an earlier Democratic compromise that would have required insurers to segregate federal subsidies for nonabortion services, calling it an accounting gimmick and insisting on stronger limits.
- The vote deepened fissures within the Democratic caucus; some House Democrats who voted for the bill say they will oppose any final legislation that includes the abortion restriction, and pro-choice lawmakers vowed to try to remove the provision in the Senate or conference.
- Senate Democrats face uncertainty: some senators are already pushing to include similar language; others oppose it. Legislative differences remain on several major issues—revenue sources (millionaire surcharge vs. excise tax on high-cost plans), the scope of a public insurance option, employer mandates, subsidy levels, and treatment of undocumented immigrants.

President Obama and Senate leaders sought to build momentum for completing reform, but the abortion provision has emerged as a potentially decisive hurdle as the debate moves to the Senate and final negotiations.

A record Powerball jackpot—about $550 million (with a $327 million cash option)—was drawing heavy attention as ticket sales surged, with officials estimating Americans would buy over $1 billion in tickets and about 105,000 tickets sold per minute. Despite the excitement and a 60% chance that the winning combination(s) will have been sold by the drawing, the odds of a single ticket winning the jackpot are astronomically low: roughly 1 in 175.2 million (slightly better than Mega Millions’ odds).

The report compares that improbability with far more likely events: dying from a bee sting (1 in 6.1 million), being struck by lightning (1 in 3 million lifetime; 1 in 10,000 over an 80-year lifetime per another stat), drowning in beach-related incidents (1 in 2 million), being attacked by a shark (1 in 11.5 million), hitting a deer in Hawaii (1 in 6,267), and an amateur golfer making consecutive holes-in-one (about 1 in 156 million)—all offered to illustrate how unlikely a jackpot win is.

The story also profiles recent winners Mary and Brian Lohse, who won $202 million and described the shock and sudden pressures of windfall wealth (unsolicited requests for money, hiring lawyers and financial advisers, and sharing some winnings with their community). Experts advise any winner to sign the ticket, wait before claiming, assemble trusted legal and financial counsel, and avoid immediately publicizing the win to manage the transition safely.

Actor Shia LaBeouf was involved in a physical altercation at the Hobgoblin pub in South London. Video obtained by TMZ shows LaBeouf, wearing a white cap, headbutting a bald man after a heated argument reportedly about the other man's comments regarding his girlfriend’s mother. A woman at the scene — likely the girlfriend — is heard pleading for him to stop. After the incident LaBeouf, appearing intoxicated, issued a rambling, remorseful-sounding apology in which he defended his reaction, saying he gets angry when people insult his girlfriend’s mother and insisting he’s “super normal.” The report notes LaBeouf has been in previous bar fights, including an encounter at the same pub in 2012 and a street fight outside a Vancouver bar in 2011.

John Mackey, co-founder and CEO of Whole Foods, argues against expanding government-run health-care entitlements and promotes market-based reforms. In a 2009 Wall Street Journal op-ed he warned that large deficits, rising entitlement costs from aging Baby Boomers, and unsustainable government spending risked higher taxes, inflation, or bankruptcy. Rather than creating a new government health entitlement, Mackey advocates strengthening individual choice and market mechanisms through eight reforms intended to lower costs and increase consumer responsibility:

- Expand high-deductible insurance and health savings accounts (HSAs); Mackey cites Whole Foods’ plan (employer-paid premiums plus personal wellness deposits) as an example that encourages careful spending and reduces costs.
- Tax parity between employer-provided and individually purchased health insurance.
- Allow insurance sales across state lines to increase competition and portability.
- Repeal government benefit mandates so coverage reflects individual preferences rather than lobbying-driven requirements.
- Enact tort reform to curb costly malpractice suits that drive up health-care prices.
- Require price transparency so patients know the full cost of care.
- Reform Medicare to address its impending insolvency and give beneficiaries more choice and responsibility.
- Add an easy, voluntary tax-deductible donation option to help uninsured people not covered by public programs.

Mackey rejects the notion of an intrinsic “right to health care,” noting that neither the Declaration of Independence nor the Constitution enshrine such a right; he argues health care is like food and shelter and is best delivered through voluntary market exchanges. He criticizes socialized systems (e.g., Canada and the U.K.) for rationing care and long wait lists, and says even citizens of those countries desire supplemental, controllable health-care dollars.

Mackey emphasizes personal responsibility for health, citing obesity and lifestyle-related diseases as major drivers of health-care costs. He points to evidence that plant-based, low-fat diets and healthy lifestyles can prevent or reverse many chronic conditions and advocates individual choices that promote long, disease-free lives.

Separately, in later interviews about the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare), Mackey escalated his rhetoric from calling it “socialism” to likening it—imprecisely—to “fascism,” arguing the government was controlling rather than owning health-care production. He later said that was a poor choice of words and sought a better term, while reiterating his view that government direction has reduced free-market innovation in health care. Mackey also discussed his broader philosophy of “conscious capitalism,” arguing that businesses should pursue higher purposes beyond profit, and expressed support for efforts to improve American diets.

On April 3, 2017, a bomb exploded aboard a St. Petersburg metro train, killing at least 11–14 people and injuring dozens (reports varied between 11 dead and up to 14). The blast occurred as the train traveled between stops; the driver continued to the next station, Tekhnologichesky Institut (Technological Institute), where wounded passengers were evacuated amid smoke and chaos. Authorities later discovered and defused a shrapnel-packed explosive at the busy Vosstaniya Square station, which investigators say may have been left there by the suspected attacker.

Russian investigators quickly focused on a 23-year-old suspect, Akbarzhon Jalilov, a Kyrgyz-born Russian passport holder from Osh in the Fergana Valley, who had rented a St. Petersburg apartment about a month earlier. Security services searched and sealed his flat, reportedly removing bags and containers with unidentified powders. CCTV footage allegedly showed him leaving home with a bag and rucksack. Officials and media cited links to radical Islamist groups and suggested the attack may have been a suicide bombing; several Central Asian nationals were detained on suspicion of recruiting for extremist groups, but no formal claim of responsibility was confirmed.

The attack occurred while President Vladimir Putin was visiting St. Petersburg; he offered condolences, visited the scene, and later said security services were investigating. Russian authorities shut down and evacuated the metro system temporarily and tightened security at transport hubs nationwide, including Moscow’s subway. International reactions included U.S. offers of assistance and condemnation; Hezbollah characterized the incident as the type of terrorism Russia confronts in Syria. The bombing revived concerns about Islamist militant attacks in Russia, recalling past subway, train and airline bombings linked to insurgents from the North Caucasus and foreign-based groups.

Researchers and reviewers tested a range of children’s headphones for sound quality, volume limiting and noise isolation, and found wide variation in safety and performance.

Key findings
- Most kid headphones can reach dangerously high levels when used with powerful sources (e.g., headphone amps or some AV receivers). That’s because many so‑called “volume‑limiting” models are passive: they rely on resistors in the cord to reduce level rather than an internal digital limiter. That reduction can be overridden by raising the source volume.
- Active, Bluetooth models with internal digital limiters (example: the Puro BT2200, $99.99) are far more reliable at preventing excessive volume in typical use. Testers found the Puro BT2200 well liked across ages (toddlers to tweens), good sounding, offered some noise‑cancelling/isolation, and limited volume safely in Bluetooth mode. Its battery life was ~18–22 hours. A wired connection is only a backup and must be plugged in the correct orientation—if reversed it can bypass the limit and play very loud.
- Several passive wired models sometimes failed to reduce volume effectively; some produced little or no attenuation in lab tests. However, two wired models tested as overall runners‑up kept maximum levels below 85 dB.
- The Wirecutter child‑panel liked Onanoff Buddyphones Explore ($29.99) for toddlers (but they’ll be outgrown and sound quality lags the Puro), and JLab JBuddies Studio ($29.99) was the corded pick for ages 4–11.
- Isolation varies widely. Only four models provided notably good isolation from typical low‑frequency background noise (50 Hz–2 kHz), and those were not necessarily the best volume‑limiters or children’s favorites. In‑ear models (Etymotic ETY‑Kids3 and Puro IEM200) reduced external sound most effectively; some large over‑ears (Direct Sound YourTones, Fuhu Nabi) also helped.

Testing approach and safety context
- Reviewers used objective lab measurements with pink noise (A‑weighted) and real music (a loud chorus from Major Lazer’s “Cold Water” and ZZ Top’s “Chartreuse”) played through an iPod touch as a representative loud source. An ear/cheek simulator and diffuse‑field calibration were used so results could be compared to the 85 dBA environmental guideline commonly referenced by hearing experts and the WHO.
- Because of measurement variability from fit and differing source devices, the team set an 88 dBA pink‑noise threshold as a pass/fail safety point; exceeding it doesn’t necessarily mean imminent harm but indicates less safety.
- Experts note the ear/brain can’t reliably judge dangerous loudness, and most earphones can be used unsafely; a practical safety strategy is combining sensible level limits with headphones that block out background noise so children don’t crank volume to hear.

Other notes
- Tests used sources children commonly use (iPod touch/iPhone), recognizing other devices (game consoles, receivers) can drive higher outputs and may be used by older kids.
- The Wirecutter article discloses it receives a percentage from linked product sales.
- The final recommendation: prefer active, internally limited headphones (especially Bluetooth models with reliable digital limiters and good isolation) and supervise overall noise exposure, because many inexpensive wired “limited” headphones can be defeated by source volume or misconnection.

Karl Smith, a 38-year-old identical twin, stunned a Chicago courtroom by confessing that he, not his twin brother Kevin Dugar, committed a 2003 shooting that left Antwan Carter dead and another man wounded. Kevin Dugar has been imprisoned since 2003 after a 2005 conviction and a 54‑year sentence based largely on eyewitness testimony; there was no confession or physical evidence against him and one witness recanted at trial.

Smith — who uses his mother’s maiden name and has long impersonated his brother — testified he wrote Kevin a confession letter in 2013, signed a sworn statement in 2014, and then took the stand saying, “I’m here to confess to a crime I committed that he was wrongly accused of.” He described the shooting in detail and said he consistently denied involvement earlier. Their mother supports Karl’s claim.

Prosecutors expressed skepticism, noting Smith is serving a separate 99‑year sentence for a 2008 armed-robbery/home‑invasion in which a child was shot and arguing Smith “has nothing to lose” by confessing now after his appeal failed. They also contend Smith’s account does not align with independent eyewitness descriptions. Kevin’s lawyer, a wrongful-convictions specialist, says Karl’s confession is newly discovered evidence that could warrant a new trial. Judge Vincent Gaughan has not yet ruled on the credibility of Smith’s confession or whether Kevin should get a new trial.

Former First Lady Michelle Obama, speaking at her first public event since leaving the White House — a 45-minute Q&A at the American Institute of Architects conference in Orlando — made no mention of President Donald Trump and signaled she won’t seek elected office again. She said presidential campaigns and holding office take a heavy toll on families and that she “wouldn’t ask my children to do this again.” Obama suggested she and her husband can do meaningful work as private citizens without “political baggage.”

She discussed adjusting to post-White House life — enjoying simple freedoms like opening windows and answering their own door — and described holding back emotions when saying farewell to White House staff on inauguration day. The former first lady emphasized continued commitments to public service, highlighting efforts to help girls access education worldwide (citing her Let Girls Learn initiative), to combat violence against women, and to improve women’s healthcare and economic opportunities. She also noted ongoing work with Barack Obama on planning the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago. Overall, she conveyed that the Obamas will remain active in social causes while keeping a relatively low public profile.

Researchers have reported compelling new evidence linking Zika virus infection during pregnancy to severe fetal brain damage and microcephaly.

Key findings
- An autopsy of a fetus from a European woman who was infected with Zika while pregnant in Brazil showed microcephaly, severe brain injury (smooth brain surface, lack of normal folds, calcifications, and fluid), and very high levels of Zika virus RNA concentrated in brain tissue. No other likely infectious causes (rubella, CMV, toxoplasmosis, dengue, yellow fever, West Nile, etc.) or genetic causes were identified.
- The team recovered a complete Zika viral genome from brain tissue; it closely matched strains from French Polynesia (2013) and Sao Paulo, Brazil (2015). Viral presence was limited to the brain, suggesting selective neurotropism.
- Ultrasounds were normal at 14 and 20 weeks but severe abnormalities were detected only around 29–32 weeks, implying some Zika-related damage may be detectable only late in pregnancy.
- Independent CDC work reported Zika in brain samples from Brazilian miscarriages and newborn deaths, and another Brazilian study found eye abnormalities in roughly one-third of 29 infants with microcephaly, indicating broader nervous-system/ocular involvement.

Implications and caveats
- This is among the strongest biological pieces of evidence to date that Zika can infect the fetus and replicate in fetal brain tissue, strengthening the hypothesized causal link between maternal Zika infection and microcephaly. However, it does not yet constitute definitive proof of causality; more studies are needed to establish risks, timing effects (trimester vulnerability), the role of asymptomatic infections, and mechanisms.
- The findings underscore serious lifelong disability risks for affected infants. There is no treatment or vaccine for Zika; the virus is mosquito-transmitted, and public health agencies have issued travel and pregnancy advisories while investigations continue.

Michael Brown, the 18-year-old shot and killed by a Ferguson police officer on Aug. 9, was mourned at a packed funeral Monday at Friendly Temple Missionary Baptist Church in St. Louis. Thousands filled the sanctuary (capacity ~2,500) and overflow rooms, with many more on church grounds. Family, community leaders, celebrities and White House representatives attended, including the Rev. Al Sharpton, Jesse Jackson, Spike Lee and Sean Combs. Brown’s casket was displayed with a St. Louis Cardinals cap and large photos; eulogies recalled him as a “gentle soul,” a devoted Christian who dreamed the world would know his name, and an aspiring HVAC technician and rapper.

Speakers blended grieving and calls for action. Family members urged peaceful protest, voter participation and a push for changes in policing; Rev. Charles Ewing said Brown’s “blood is crying…for justice.” Sharpton admonished destructive protest and called for sustained, peaceful efforts to reform how policing is done. The family asked for a day of silence during the funeral to grieve.

The service occurred amid ongoing investigations: a state grand jury and a federal probe are examining the shooting by Officer Darren Wilson. Police and witnesses have offered conflicting accounts; authorities say a scuffle occurred after Wilson told Brown and a friend to move from the street. Brown was unarmed and autopsy reports show he was shot multiple times. The funeral followed two weeks of protests and unrest in Ferguson; that day the mood in the community was calmer, schools reopened, and many hoped the service would help promote healing while keeping attention on demands for justice and reform.

Researchers report an association between consumption of milk contaminated decades ago with a pineapple pesticide and loss of brain cells linked to Parkinson’s disease. In a Neurology study, investigators analyzed brains from 449 Japanese-American men in Hawaii who had reported their milk intake in midlife and donated their brains after death. Men who drank more than 16 ounces (two cups) of milk daily at the study’s start had about 40% fewer neurons in the substantia nigra—an area damaged in Parkinson’s—than men who drank less. Residues of the banned organochlorine pesticide heptachlor epoxide were detected in many brains: about 90% of the highest milk consumers versus 63% of non‑milk drinkers. The pesticide was likely introduced to the milk supply in the 1980s via cattle feed contaminated by pineapple-industry use in Hawaii; commercial agricultural use was largely banned in the U.S. by 1988.

The study does not prove causation but shows an association between higher milk intake, brain pesticide residues, and neuronal loss decades later. Notably, the link between milk consumption and cell loss was not seen in men who had ever smoked—a finding consistent with prior observations of lower Parkinson’s incidence among smokers. Experts stressed limitations: milk intake was measured only once, the researchers lack direct samples proving the men’s milk contained the pesticide, and most milk drinkers do not develop Parkinson’s. The authors urge further investigation into dietary and environmental contributors to Parkinson’s and continued study of donated brains to clarify causal pathways.

Two sets of human remains were discovered in a rural area south of Kansas City in April. The Jackson County Medical Examiner confirmed one set belonged to 21‑year‑old Jessica Runions, who vanished Sept. 8–9, 2016 after leaving a party. Her burned 2012 Chevy Equinox was found Sept. 10 in a remote wooded area. Authorities have opened a homicide investigation into her death.

Friends say Runions left the party giving Kylr Yust, 28, a ride. Yust was arrested after the burned vehicle was found and charged with knowingly burning a vehicle; he has pleaded not guilty and is due to stand trial in October. Yust remains the only person charged so far; his attorney says he faces no additional charges at this time.

A second set of remains found nearby has not yet been identified. There is speculation—unconfirmed by investigators—that they could be 17‑year‑old Kara Kopetsky, who disappeared from Belton, Missouri in May 2007. Kopetsky had previously filed a protective order accusing Yust of kidnapping and assault days before she vanished. Yust has been a person of interest in her case for years.

Both families have connected and are working together to search, raise awareness and push for answers. Investigations are ongoing: local law enforcement and the medical examiner are continuing searches of the area, and identification of the second set of remains could take weeks to a year. No arrests have been made in either disappearance beyond the vehicle‑burning charge against Yust.

John Sandoval, 52, pleaded guilty March 31, 2017 to second-degree murder in the 1995 killing of his estranged wife, Kristina “Tina” Tournai Sandoval, after leading investigators to her remains as part of a plea deal. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison, with five years of parole; his sentence was backdated to his 2010 conviction, so time served counts toward it. Sandoval had been awaiting a second trial after the Colorado Court of Appeals overturned his 2010 first-degree murder conviction last year because of improperly admitted evidence.

Tina disappeared Oct. 19, 1995 after meeting Sandoval; despite circumstantial evidence and signs pointing to him (including scratch marks on his body and muddy items found soon after her disappearance), no body was found and the case went cold until Sandoval’s disclosure in March 2017. He told authorities the body had been buried beneath the grave of World War II veteran Arthur Hert at Sunset Memorial Garden cemetery in Greeley, in a spot where an open grave was later used for a burial. Her remains, wrapped in multiple layers of plastic and other coverings about 21 inches below the bottom of the grave, were exhumed; the veteran’s family was notified and his casket was reburied with honors.

Prosecutors and the family said Sandoval remained silent for 22 years and only revealed the location to avoid life imprisonment. The Tournai family agonized over accepting the plea—balancing the chance to recover Tina’s remains and obtain certainty against the prospect that Sandoval might serve less time than a life sentence—but ultimately agreed. District Attorney Michael Rourke and investigators stressed that Sandoval’s cooperation does not absolve him; prosecutors called him a stalker and murderer. The coroner performed a forensic autopsy; cause of death had not been publicly determined at the time of the hearing. The family plans a private burial for Tina.

A large Chinese prospective study of about 456,000 adults (ages 30–79) followed for roughly nine years found that drinking very hot tea raises the risk of esophageal cancer primarily when combined with smoking and/or regular alcohol use. Key findings:

- Drinking "hot" or "burning hot" tea alone was not linked to a higher risk of esophageal cancer.  
- Among people who both drank at least one alcoholic drink daily and drank very hot tea every day, esophageal cancer risk was about five times higher versus people who drank tea less than weekly at cooler temperatures.  
- For regular smokers who drank very hot tea daily, risk was about doubled compared with low-frequency, cooler tea drinkers. Intermediate increases were seen when only one additional risk (smoking or drinking) was present.  
- Mechanism: researchers suggest hot liquids damage or inflame the esophageal lining, making it more vulnerable to carcinogens in tobacco and alcohol. Prior work classifies beverages above ~149°F (65°C) as probably carcinogenic.  
- Limitations: tea temperature was self-reported, and the study is observational (cannot prove causation).  
- Takeaway: avoid drinking very hot tea if you smoke or drink alcohol regularly; quitting smoking and reducing alcohol remain the most important prevention measures. Tea still has reported health benefits for many people who do not combine it with those risks.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear challenges from Kansas and Louisiana seeking to bar Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood and similar providers that also offer abortions (which Medicaid already cannot fund). The court’s refusal leaves in place a split among lower courts: five federal appeals courts have ruled for providers’ right to retain Medicaid contracts and for patients to challenge state terminations, while at least one appeals court has ruled the opposite. That split affects Medicaid beneficiaries differently depending on their circuit.

Three conservative justices — Clarence Thomas, Neil Gorsuch and Samuel Alito — dissented, arguing the Court should resolve the conflict and asserting the cases are about patients’ rights to challenge provider exclusions, not abortion. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined the four liberal justices in declining review. Commentators and some justices framed the decision as part of a broader effort by the Court’s majority to avoid high-profile, politically fraught cases this term.

Background: The state actions trace to 2015 undercover videos (later found to be deceptively edited) that sparked state laws removing Planned Parenthood from Medicaid provider lists. Planned Parenthood sued, arguing it was being singled out for disfavored treatment for engaging in constitutionally protected abortion services. Planned Parenthood leaders praised the Court’s inaction as preserving patient access to care; anti-abortion groups expressed disappointment and urged administrative or legislative efforts to cut funding elsewhere. The decision leaves differing legal regimes intact across federal circuits until the Court or Congress acts.

Seattle implemented a 1.75-cent-per-ounce “sweetened beverage” tax on Jan 1, 2018 intended to reduce sugar consumption, fund priorities like a year of free community college for Seattle public high school graduates, and subsidize healthy food for low-income families. The tax applies to many sodas, sports drinks, kombucha and similar beverages that don’t list milk as the primary ingredient, but exempts certain milk-based drinks (a loophole noted by critics and firms like Starbucks).

Immediate effects and reactions
- Retail prices jumped sharply for bulk purchases: examples include a case of Gatorade rising from $15.99 to $26.33 at Costco. Costco and other retailers posted signage directing customers to stores outside city limits to avoid the tax.
- Customers and businesses reported shopping across city lines; early evidence suggests lost in-city sales and revenue leakage to suburbs, mirroring experiences in Philadelphia and Cook County, Ill.
- The tax has been criticized as regressive (hitting low-income families hardest), inconsistent (exempting some high‑sugar beverages), burdensome for businesses (especially restaurants that use syrups/powders), and likely to cost jobs or hurt local retailers.
- Supporters—public health organizations and some city leaders—argue the tax targets beverages linked to obesity, diabetes and other chronic diseases and will fund health and education programs; Seattle projected about $15 million in revenue in the first year to help programs including healthy meals for low‑income families.

Comparisons and controversy
- Critics point to Cook County’s experience: a similarly controversial penny‑per‑ounce tax (implemented Aug 2, 2017) prompted strong public backlash, lawsuits, significant drops in in-county beverage sales, cross-border shopping, and repeal on Dec 1, 2017. Opponents there included big beverage companies, retailers and restaurants; merchants reported large losses and logistical headaches from tax implementation and repeal.
- Analysts note legitimate public‑health arguments for taxing sugary drinks, but say Cook County’s policy was muddled (including diet drinks, initially unclear SNAP treatment) and that well-funded industry opposition and legal challenges undermined it.
- The debate nationally divides strange allies—progressive public‑health advocates and libertarians or business groups both oppose or question soda taxes for different reasons—while some argue that a tax must be large enough to change behavior to have health benefits, but that a large tax then risks driving economic harm and cross‑border sales.

Political fallout and broader debate
- In Washington state, a bill to make such a tax statewide has been introduced but faces skepticism about its prospects. Local voices in Spokane and elsewhere express concern for small businesses and restaurants; others support the tax on public‑health grounds.
- Commentators framed the Seattle tax as an example of “nanny state” social engineering and warned that abrupt, large price increases provoke strong consumer pushback and unintended economic consequences.

Bottom line: Seattle’s soda tax provoked sharp price increases, retailer and consumer responses that include cross‑border shopping, and heated debate over health benefits versus economic harm and regressivity. Experiences in Cook County and Philadelphia raise questions about whether such taxes will reduce consumption, raise stable local revenue, or instead shift sales outside taxed jurisdictions while disproportionately affecting lower‑income residents.

Salt Lake City police shot a male Saturday night who officers say was wielding a broomstick, leaving him in critical condition with two gunshot wounds to the torso. The Unified Police Department (which is investigating) and Salt Lake City police gave limited details: the shooting occurred around 8 p.m. as officers responded to a fight near a downtown homeless shelter adjacent to a mall and theater. Authorities say officers attempted to break up an altercation and that the man struck another person with a broomstick and then tried to attack an officer; one or two officers fired. Investigators have not released the victim’s identity or exact age (reports conflicted about whether he was a teenager), how many shots were fired, how far away he was, whether the broomstick was modified, or whether any other weapons were present. 

After the shooting, dozens of bystanders became hostile, shouting and throwing rocks and bottles; police called in nearly 100 officers from neighboring departments, some in riot gear, and detained multiple people. One officer was struck by a bottle, officials said. Streets were barricaded and a TRAX light-rail stop was temporarily closed; service resumed later that night. Authorities said more details would be released as the investigation continues.

Emojipedia updated three of its sample emoji designs after public feedback following the release of 157 proposed 2018 emojis.

- Skateboard: Skateboarding icon Tony Hawk criticized the original design as outdated and inaccurate. Emojipedia consulted him and replaced the old skateboard with a new design based on Hawk’s own board (adjusted for emoji scale).

- DNA double helix: The original sample showed a left-handed helix; Emojipedia corrected it to the anatomically standard right-handed double helix.

- Lobster: Observers, including Mainers and U.S. Sen. Angus King, pointed out the lobster emoji had only eight legs instead of 10 and a misshapen tail. Emojipedia added the missing pair of legs and tweaked the tail.

Emojipedia also noted that it displayed four hearts for the “Smiling Face With Smiling Eyes and Three Hearts” emoji for aesthetic reasons and will keep that version. These updated sample images are part of Emojipedia 11.1 and appear on the Unicode emoji charts; actual vendor implementations (Apple, Google, etc.) may differ. The emojis approved in Emoji 11.0 are expected to arrive on major platforms in the second half of 2018.

The United States and China — together responsible for about 40% of global greenhouse-gas emissions — announced coordinated post‑2020 climate targets aimed at spurring a strong global agreement in 2015. Their joint commitment is intended to build momentum ahead of international talks in Lima and the Paris summit next year, and signals leadership from the world’s two largest economies and emitters.

U.S. commitments
- Cut net greenhouse‑gas emissions 26–28% below 2005 levels by 2025 (up from an earlier U.S. goal of 17% by 2020).
- This target roughly doubles the annual reduction rate between 2020–2025 versus 2005–2020 and is projected to put the U.S. on a path toward ~80% reductions by 2050.
- The U.S. will submit the 2025 target as its intended contribution to the UNFCCC by Q1 2015.
- The pledge builds on domestic measures (clean‑energy growth, EPA power‑plant rules) and is presented as achievable with health, air‑quality and energy‑security co‑benefits.

China’s commitments
- Announce a peak year for CO2 emissions around 2030, with efforts to peak earlier if possible.
- Increase the share of zero‑emission energy (renewables and nuclear) to about 20% of total energy consumption by 2030.
- Reaching that share would require deploying roughly 800–1,000 GW of additional low‑carbon generation capacity — an amount comparable to China’s existing coal capacity and nearly equal to total U.S. generation capacity.

Significance
- The joint announcement is framed as a milestone in U.S.–China cooperation and a “fresh beginning” for climate diplomacy, intended to encourage other countries to present ambitious targets and help secure a comprehensive global climate agreement in Paris in 2015.

An Australian prospector has unearthed a 145-ounce (4.1 kg) gold nugget in Victoria’s famed Golden Triangle. Informally named “Friday’s Joy,” the find was made about 30 cm underground in an area previously worked over and is expected to fetch more than $250,000 at auction. The finder, who wished to remain anonymous, had been metal-detecting for over a decade and discovered the nugget using a Minelab GPZ 7000 detector—Minelab highlighted the discovery as proof their technology can still turn up major finds. The prospector initially mistook the object for scrap, washed and briefly stored it at home, and plans to sell the piece while continuing to prospect and travel. The nugget is now secured in a bank vault and a replica is being made. Minelab likened the discovery to other notable Victorian finds (including the 159.3-ounce “Cindy’s Pride” and last year’s 87-ounce “Fair Dinkum”), underscoring that significant gold remains in the region. A historical note: Victoria’s famous 69 kg “Welcome Nugget” (1858) remains one of the largest nuggets ever found.

Gov. Rick Scott ordered an emergency moratorium closing the Rehabilitation Center at Hollywood Hills after eight residents died and 115 were evacuated when the facility lost air conditioning following Hurricane Irma. The Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) removed all patients and barred new admissions while AHCA and the Department of Children & Families investigate; Hollywood police have opened a criminal probe.

Timeline and response
- Paramedics and Hollywood Fire Rescue were first called in the early hours Wednesday after a prolonged power failure disabled the nursing home’s AC. Three residents died at the facility; five died after being transported to hospitals across the street. The Broward Medical Examiner has identified the eight victims; causes of death remain under investigation.
- Memorial Regional Hospital and other area hospitals received evacuees, treating many for respiratory distress, dehydration and heat-related problems. Officials warned the death toll could rise.
- Larkin Community Hospital, adjacent to the home and linked by ownership, was also partially evacuated; 18 patients were relocated.
- Florida Power & Light said the nursing home was not designated a “top-tier critical infrastructure” site in county planning. Contractors reported a blown fuse that prevented AC restoration and said they had repeatedly sought FPL assistance.

Facility background and oversight
- The center and its owners have prior citations and at least one pending negligence lawsuit. The facility was acquired by Larkin Community Hospital interests in a 2015 bankruptcy sale; Larkin’s president is listed as the nursing home’s manager.
- Gov. Scott demanded answers and said anyone found not acting in residents’ best interests would be held accountable. AHCA cited the moratorium as necessary to protect frail elders; statewide inspections and welfare checks were conducted at dozens of long-term care facilities after the incident.

Family impact and follow-up
- Families scrambled for information and some reported repeatedly warning the facility and utility company about life‑threatening heat. Memorial Healthcare established a hotline for relatives. Local and state investigations are ongoing; causes of death and full circumstances remain under inquiry.

Homeland Security Adviser Tom Bossert defended President Donald Trump’s weekend tweet that showed a GIF of Trump body‑slamming and punching a person whose head was labeled “CNN.” On ABC’s This Week, Bossert said the image shouldn’t be perceived as a threat and framed Trump’s social media use as a legitimate response to what he called unfair cable coverage, praising Trump’s ability to speak “directly to the American people.” Bossert also called Trump “the most genuine…nonpolitician president” in his lifetime.

The GIF — taken from a 2007 WWE clip of Trump and WWE chairman Vince McMahon with the CNN logo superimposed — drew sharp criticism on the program. CNN contributor Ana Navarro called Bossert’s defense disgraceful, saying the tweet amounted to an incitement to violence and risked getting someone hurt. The exchange came amid broader debate about Trump’s Twitter use, which he defended as “modern day presidential” after attacking the “fake & fraudulent news media.” Some Republicans, including Sen. Ben Sasse and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, have said such tweets are beneath the dignity of the presidency.

A 16-year-old first-time skydiver, Mackenzie Wethington, survived a fall of about 3,500 feet in a January 2014 accident and is recovering in the ICU. Accounts differ about what happened: her father says only half the parachute opened and Mackenzie was unable to respond to ground instructions to cut away and deploy the reserve as she spiraled; the skydiving center owner contends the chute opened fully and then began rotating for technical reasons, possibly related to the jumper’s actions. Paramedics airlifted her to the University of Oklahoma Medical Center. Doctors called her survival “miraculous” given the likely bone and soft-tissue damage from such a fall. She sustained a lacerated liver and kidney, broken teeth and multiple fractures but is awake, breathing on her own, listed in fair condition, and expected to recover within about six to eight weeks. Experts note that survival from great-height falls depends on many factors—including air resistance, body position and luck—which can dissipate impact forces and sometimes produce unexpectedly survivable outcomes.

Scientists are hunting a distant, unseen ninth planet—often conflated with doomsday "Nibiru" rumors but entirely different. Caltech researchers Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown say there are now five independent lines of observational evidence that point to a massive, remote body (nicknamed Planet Nine) whose gravity explains several oddities in the outer solar system.

Key points:
- Planet Nine is hypothesized to be roughly 10 times Earth's mass and orbit about 20 times farther from the Sun than Neptune, placing it in the distant Kuiper Belt region.
- Initial evidence (2016) came from six trans-Neptunian objects with elongated, similarly aligned orbits tilted ~30° relative to the planets' orbital plane.
- Computer simulations including Planet Nine predict more high-inclination objects; five such known objects match that prediction.
- Additional studies suggest Planet Nine could have slowly tilted the entire planetary plane by about 6°, explaining the long-standing misalignment between the planets' orbital plane and the Sun's equator.
- Planet Nine's gravity also offers a natural explanation for some Kuiper Belt objects that orbit in the opposite direction to most bodies.
- Alternative analyses (e.g., the Outer Solar System Origins Survey) say a random distribution might also account for some observations, so the case isn't settled.

Batygin and Brown are actively searching for the planet with the Subaru Telescope on Mauna Kea. If found, it would likely be the solar system’s long-missing "super-Earth" and help reveal whether it formed here or was captured. Importantly, such a distant planet poses no near-term threat to Earth; the catastrophic Nibiru-style scenarios are misinformation.

A fierce power struggle has erupted in Iran between President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad and Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, centered on Ahmadinejad’s close ally and chief of staff Esfandiar Rahim-Mashaei. Mashaei, widely seen as Ahmadinejad’s preferred successor for the 2013 presidential race, is accused by clerical hardliners of undermining the clerical establishment and even of promoting heterodox religious ideas — including links to a documentary about the imminent return of the Hidden Imam and alleged use of “supernatural” practices. Conservatives say Mashaei and his circle seek “Islam without the clergy,” and have labeled them a “deviant current.”

Tensions escalated after Ahmadinejad and Mashaei tried to assert control over the intelligence ministry, prompting the resignation of intelligence chief Heydar Moslehi; Khamenei publicly refused the resignation and reinstated Moslehi, an unusual rebuke to the president. Ahmadinejad briefly boycotted cabinet meetings, returned with ostentatious declarations of loyalty to Khamenei, and has faced calls for impeachment from MPs and stern warnings from clerics that defying the supreme leader amounts to apostasy. In the aftermath, dozens of Ahmadinejad allies and journalists close to Mashaei have been arrested on charges ranging from political deviation to “magical” practices.

Complicating the domestic fight are reports that Mashaei has sought contact with U.S. representatives, part of a broader strand in Ahmadinejad’s circle favoring limited outreach to the West — a policy previously attempted in 2009 and rejected by Khamenei. U.S. officials say no formal meetings have taken place and are wary of engaging a single Iranian faction. Observers link the infighting to broader regional unrest following the Arab Spring, with both Ahmadinejad’s camp and the clerical establishment worried about regime legitimacy. The dispute highlights deep fissures over clerical authority, foreign policy orientation, and succession politics inside Iran’s ruling elite.

Summary:

Angelina Jolie was promoted from U.N. goodwill ambassador to special envoy days after her engagement to Brad Pitt, a role that will involve representing the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees on complex displacement crises and occasional diplomatic messaging. Tabloids immediately speculated about the safety of Jolie’s large, custom engagement ring—reportedly designed by Pitt, valued in estimates from $250,000 to $500,000, and publicly shown at a private museum viewing—and offered tongue-in-cheek advice about protecting it while she continues refugee travel.

Media outlets also debated the potential value of the couple’s wedding or baby photos, with estimates for worldwide wedding-photo rights ranging from around $2 million to $5 million (noting the market has cooled since their twins’ 2008 photos fetched $14 million, which the couple donated to charity). Coverage touched on likely prenuptial arrangements given their combined wealth, speculation about wedding details and Jennifer Aniston’s reaction, and family aspects of the proposal—reported as an emotional, family-centered event in which their children celebrated Angelina’s ring.

Scientists have discovered a 99-million-year-old juvenile dinosaur tail preserved in Myanmar amber, providing an unusually detailed three-dimensional view of feather structure and arrangement. Found by Lida Xing at an amber market and described in Current Biology, the 1.4‑inch tail contains eight articulated vertebrae and highly preserved feathers. CT scans and microscopy show the tail likely belonged to a small coelurosaur (a sparrow-sized theropod outside the avian lineage) because its vertebrae are unfused (no pygostyle), unlike birds and their close Cretaceous relatives.

The feathers are bushy, with poorly developed central shafts (rachises) and an upper-dark/lower-light color pattern, resembling modern ornamental rather than flight feathers. Their structure implies limited aerodynamic function, suggesting roles such as signaling or thermoregulation. Chemical analysis of a cross-section shaped by a jeweler revealed ferrous iron—degradation product of hemoglobin—hinting that further pigment or keratin studies may be possible.

Because amber preserves three-dimensional anatomy and chemistry, this specimen overcomes key limits of flat fossil impressions and links feathers directly to a dinosaur tail. The find indicates similar specimens may be misidentified as plant debris in amber markets and underscores the potential for additional discoveries from the Hukawng Valley amber deposits as access improves.

Three thin women dominated the U.S. Professional Wing Eating Championship Sunday at Coca-Cola Field in Buffalo, consuming nearly 500 chicken wings in 12 minutes and easily outpacing seven men. Miki Sudo, 28, of Las Vegas — a 115‑pound newcomer who turned pro in April — won with 178 wings; Michelle Lesco of Tucson finished second; five‑time champion Sonya “The Black Widow” Thomas was third with 141. Joey Chestnut, last year’s winner, did not appear.

Sudo also won Saturday’s Buffet Bowl contest featuring Buffalo foods such as beef on weck. The three women’s combined weight (345 lb) was noted as lighter than some male contestants; the field included 19‑year‑old Yasir Salem, who placed fourth after recently completing an Ironman. Organizers reported higher Sunday attendance though overall festival turnout (72,000) was down from last year’s 80,000.

The National Buffalo Wing Festival featured 32 vendors, long lines for popular booths like Dinosaur Bar‑B‑Que and Anchor Bar, new items (spicy Buffalo Rolls, vegetarian “wings” made with green beans and gouda), and lively emceeing by George Shea. Festival founder Drew Cerza called it “one of the best.”

Audrey Parker, a 57-year-old Halifax woman with Stage 4 breast cancer, chose a medically assisted death on Nov. 1 after publicly urging lawmakers to amend Canada’s 2016 Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) law. Parker said she was forced to schedule her death earlier than she wanted because the law requires patients to be mentally competent and able to give consent at the moment the procedure is carried out (“late-stage consent”). Fearful that advancing cancer and medications could rob her of lucidity, she wanted the option to make an advance request so she could live longer—she hoped to see Christmas—but ultimately decided not to risk losing eligibility.

Her final Facebook post, urging Canadians to contact MPs to remove the late-stage consent requirement for people already assessed and approved for MAID, drew thousands of reactions and widespread support. Friends, advocates and groups such as Dying with Dignity Canada have used Parker’s case to press for legislative change—some calling for an “Audrey’s Law” to permit advance requests in cases like hers.

Federal Justice Minister Jody Wilson‑Raybould said the government had no plans to change the legislation, though Liberal MP Darren Fisher and other local politicians signaled openness to listening to constituents. The government has commissioned evidence reviews: the Council of Canadian Academies is due to publish a December report summarizing evidence on advance requests and other excluded groups, but it will not make policy recommendations and the government is not obliged to act.

Parker’s situation highlights the ethical and policy tensions in MAID: balancing safeguards to protect vulnerable people (notably concerns about advance directives in dementia) against cases in which terminally ill, competent patients fear premature death or forced suffering to preserve moment-of-decision capacity. Her death has renewed national debate over whether Canada should allow limited advance requests for those already assessed and approved for MAID.

Summary:

- The U.S. Army awarded the Medal of Heroism to three JROTC students killed in the Feb. 14 Parkland, Florida, school shooting: Alaina Petty (presentation made to her family), Peter Wang (to be presented at his memorial), and Martin Duque (to be presented to his family later). The medal recognizes cadets whose actions involved acceptance of danger and extraordinary responsibility. All three were reportedly killed by fellow student Nikolas Cruz. Witnesses say Wang held a door open to let classmates escape; Petty was active in the female color guard; Duque was remembered as a devoted churchgoer and football fan.

- Overview of the Parkland shooting: The attack at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School left 17 dead and more than a dozen wounded. The suspect, 19-year-old Nikolas Cruz, allegedly triggered fire alarms to draw students into halls and used an AR-15-type rifle; he was arrested about an hour later.

- Community response and assistance:
  - Comfort dogs: At least 18 therapy dogs and 33 handlers from Lutheran Church Charities arrived to support students, staff, families and first responders.
  - Fundraising: The Broward Education Foundation set up an official Stoneman Douglas Victims’ Fund (GoFundMe), which rapidly raised over $1.5 million toward an initially increased goal. A steering committee led by former U.S. Senator George LeMieux and the National Center for Victims of Crime were named to oversee transparent distribution; donations were accepted through June 30 with distributions planned thereafter. Individual memorials and scholarship/safety funds (e.g., the Alex Schachter fund) were also created.
  - Blood donations: OneBlood requested donors, especially O negative, to replenish supplies after the incident.
  - Financial and logistical aid: Florida Attorney General Pamela Bondi pledged to cover funeral expenses for the 17 victims. JetBlue offered free flights for victims’ family members and partnered with Lyft to provide ground transportation; JetBlue also organized a blood drive with the Florida Panthers.

- Personal remembrances and local effects: The report includes tributes for victims (including a detailed memorial excerpt for freshman Alex Schachter, who played in the school marching band) and notes veterans and community members attending services and supporting families.

Overall, the piece combines recognition of heroic actions by student JROTC members, details of victims’ lives, the immediate facts of the shooting and arrest, and a summary of community, organizational and governmental relief, fundraising and support efforts following the tragedy.

The CDC released draft federal guidelines saying medical evidence shows the benefits of male circumcision outweigh the risks and that insurers should cover newborn circumcision. The guidelines do not tell parents they must circumcise—decisions may reflect personal, cultural or religious beliefs—but they urge clinicians to counsel parents of newborn boys and sexually active uncircumcised men (especially those at higher HIV risk) about benefits and harms.

Key findings cited:
- Circumcision reduces a heterosexual man’s risk of acquiring HIV from a female partner by about 50–60%.
- It lowers risk of genital herpes and some high‑risk HPV strains (roughly 30% or more) and reduces infant urinary tract infections and lifetime risk of penile cancer.
- It does not appear to lower HIV transmission risk during anal sex or clearly reduce HIV spread from infected men to women.
- Complication rates are low: under 0.5% in newborns, about 9% in children ages 1–9, and roughly 5% in adults; most problems are minor (bleeding, inflammation).

Context and response:
- These are the first federal circumcision guidelines and draw on studies—including randomized trials from Africa—that strengthened evidence of protective effects against HIV and other STIs.
- U.S. newborn circumcision rates fell over recent decades (about 58% by 2010), influenced by changing demographics, shifting medical stances and some state Medicaid programs ceasing coverage.
- The draft mirrors the American Academy of Pediatrics’ 2012 position and begins a 45‑day public comment period before finalization. The guidance is expected to provoke opposition from “intactivist” groups who argue the procedure is an unnecessary, nonconsensual surgery and that risks may be minimized in the CDC statement. Some HIV/AIDS advocates also note limited relevance for men who have sex with men, the primary group driving U.S. HIV incidence.

Police responded to Oakdale Elementary in Rock Hill, S.C., after a 9-year-old student became violently disruptive when a teacher confiscated iPads from several noisy pupils. According to the police report, the boy crawled under a desk, flipped multiple chairs, and when escorted into a hallway repeatedly stomped on the teacher’s foot. Two other teachers and an assistant principal restrained him; the teacher’s left foot was reported bruised and swollen. By the time officers arrived the student had calmed and was released to his mother. Two other students were also disorderly during the September 26 incident but were separated and calmed. No arrest was made.

This document contains three main pieces:

1) Web crawl seed description
- A seed named Wide00014 was defined to crawl “slash pages” and top pages across the web using the Wide00012 inter-domain link graph. It included:
  - A ranking of all URLs with more than one incoming inter-domain link (ranked by incoming-link count from Wide00012), with up to 100 top-ranked URLs per domain.
  - For every domain that is linked-to, the top-ranked pages (up to 100) were also included using Wide00012’s navigational link graph.

2) Summary of a study on “hearing voices” (Lancet Psychology)
- An online survey and detailed analysis of 153 people who hear voices found large variation in these experiences.
- Many voice-hearing experiences differ from the stereotypical portrayal (e.g., angry, commanding voices in schizophrenia). Voices are often internal, conversational, and experienced more like distinct “characters” or parts of self rather than purely auditory phenomena. Some people experience physical sensations alongside voice-hearing.
- Up to ~15% of people who report hearing voices have no psychological diagnosis.
- The researchers (led by Angela Woods, Durham University) argue voice-hearing is more complex than commonly assumed and call for broader, more nuanced research to inform interventions; therapies can help some people reinterpret voices as aspects of themselves.

3) Article on dreams and the origins of religious concepts
- Discusses how vivid REM dreaming likely contributed to religious beliefs in many cultures: dreams were often treated as communications from deities or spirits because of their emotional intensity and involuntary nature.
- Cites a paper by Patrick McNamara and Kelly Bulkeley arguing dreams foster “supernatural agent” concepts for three reasons: they generate alternate realities, elicit theory-of-mind attributions, and allow experience of value (linked to forebrain dopaminergic systems).
- From this perspective, humans are neurologically predisposed to generate god concepts in dreaming, which may have influenced the historical evolution of religion.

Sources noted: The Lancet Psychology study (lead Angela Woods) and McNamara & Bulkeley (Frontiers in Psychology, 2015).

A man disrupted a U.S. Supreme Court oral argument on Wednesday by shouting slogans protesting the 2010 Citizens United campaign‑finance decision. The protester, identified by court spokeswoman Kathy Arberg as Noah Newkirk of Los Angeles, rose from the public gallery during argument in a patent‑fee case and yelled phrases including "Money is not speech," "Corporations are not people," and "Overturn Citizens United." Police removed him after a brief scuffle; he was charged under a federal statute prohibiting "loud threatening or abusive language" or "haranguing" in the Supreme Court building. The justices did not comment and the official transcript does not record the interruption. Court officials noted such outbursts are rare; the courtroom holds about 330 public seats and spectators are routinely warned against speaking, demonstrating, bringing signs, electronics or cameras.

Ivanka Trump attended the new Broadway musical Come From Away Wednesday night alongside Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Nikki Haley, part of a larger political/diplomatic crowd including cabinet members, former PM Jean Chrétien and about 150 UN ambassadors. Trudeau introduced the show, joked about the snowy welcome and spoke about the close Canada–U.S. relationship, receiving a standing ovation. The musical — created by Canadians Irene Sankoff and David Hein and recently opened at the Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre — tells the true story of Gander, Newfoundland, which sheltered 6,579 passengers from 38 planes after the Sept. 11 attacks; it mixes poignant moments with humor and includes a subplot about prejudice against Muslims. Trudeau and Ivanka had met previously at a White House roundtable on women in the workforce; the Canadian consulate had arranged a ticket block but did not disclose the guest list.

Nearly four years after her death, the U.S. Army has released the last photograph taken by Spc. Hilda I. Clayton, a 22‑year‑old combat photographer from Augusta, Ga., who was killed on July 2, 2013, while documenting an Afghan National Army mortar validation exercise in Laghman Province. A mortar tube accidentally exploded, killing Clayton, an Afghan photographer she was training, and several ANA soldiers. The image and related photographs appeared in the May–June issue of Military Review, which highlighted the U.S.–Afghan partnership and gender equality in the force.

Clayton, assigned to the 55th Signal Company (Combat Camera) and attached to the 4th Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division, was documenting efforts to train and enable ANA forces—a mission the journal described as emblematic of the partnership central to stabilizing Afghanistan. Military Review and colleagues said Clayton’s death underscored that female soldiers increasingly face the same hazards as male counterparts. She was honored in memorial ceremonies at Forward Operating Base Gamberi and at the Defense Information School (DINFOS), where her name was added to the Hall of Heroes. Combat Camera named its annual best combat camera competition the Spc. Hilda I. Clayton Best Combat Camera Competition in her honor.

The release of her final image drew widespread public attention and remembrance, echoing precedent cases—such as LIFE photographer Paul Schutzer in 1967—where photographers’ final rolls documented their last moments. Colleagues and the public have paid tribute to Clayton’s dedication to documenting military work and to training Afghan partners.

One week after the Oct. 1 Route 91 Harvest festival shooting in Las Vegas that killed 58 and injured hundreds, country star Jason Aldean visited critically injured patients at University Medical Center on Sunday. The hospital thanked him on Facebook, saying his visit helped "heal hearts and cheer" the wounded. Aldean’s pregnant wife, Brittany, posted an Instagram photo of the couple looking toward the Mandalay Bay hotel and wrote that returning to Vegas felt surreal, praising the strength of the patients and saying they would "never forget." Aldean had performed on Saturday Night Live the night before and was the artist on stage when the shooting began; he declined to attend a UFC ceremony honoring victims and first responders, UFC president Dana White said.

Three cardboard effigies depicting lynched African-Americans were found hanging by nooses at prominent locations on the University of California, Berkeley campus on the morning of a nationwide #BlackLivesMatter protest. Two were on Sather Gate arches and a third in a tree near Bancroft Lane; the cutouts bore names and dates of historical lynching victims and, on one, the hashtag #ICantBreathe. Campus and city police removed two effigies; students removed the third. Authorities are investigating and have not determined who put them up or their intent.

The images sparked heated debate: some community members and observers called them inflammatory, traumatic and racially terrorizing, while others — including an academic who studies African American history — suggested they might be guerrilla or protest art intended to connect historical lynching and contemporary police violence. Hundreds of people nonetheless took part in a largely peaceful Berkeley protest that afternoon and later joined a larger Oakland demonstration; authorities made 45 arrests in Oakland. Campus officials said they are treating the incident seriously and are seeking to learn the motivation behind the display.

NASA-supported observatories report that the Sun is entering the polarity reversal of its magnetic field — a routine event that occurs about every 11 years and marks the midpoint of the solar cycle’s maximum. Stanford’s Wilcox Solar Observatory director Todd Hoeksema estimated the complete flip to occur within three to four months. The Sun’s polar fields weaken to zero and then re-emerge with opposite polarity; the north pole has already switched and the south is nearing reversal.

The flip makes the heliospheric current sheet (a vast, wavy surface extending billions of kilometers from the Sun’s equator) more rippled. As Earth moves through those waves, we can expect increased “stormy” space weather that can affect satellites and astronauts. The more wrinkled current sheet also provides greater shielding from high-energy cosmic rays, reducing that hazard. The effects extend across the heliosphere, even influencing spacecraft near interstellar space like the Voyagers.

This solar maximum is relatively weak—one of the least active in about a century—with fewer sunspots and less eruptive activity than typical peaks. Nevertheless, the magnetic reversal itself is a normal part of the solar cycle and not a cause for alarm.

A Quinnipiac University poll of 832 likely Iowa Democratic caucus-goers (Aug. 27–Sept. 8; ±3.4 pts) finds Bernie Sanders narrowly ahead of Hillary Clinton 41%–40%, with Joe Biden at 12% and Martin O’Malley at 3%. The lead marks a big shift since Quinnipiac’s July survey, when Clinton led 52%–33%. The margin is within the poll’s error, but the result — and similar polls showing Sanders gaining in New Hampshire — highlights growing momentum for Sanders amid lingering fallout from Clinton’s email controversy.

The survey shows a large gender split: Clinton leads among women 49%–35%, while Sanders leads among men 49%–28%. Favorability and trait ratings also favor Sanders on honesty and caring: Sanders posts a +72 net favorability and 86% seen as trustworthy; Clinton’s favorability is +56 and 64% seen as honest. Clinton continues to score highest on leadership and crisis temperament (92% and 89% positive). Biden registers high favorability (+70) and especially strong marks on honesty.

Other findings: 54% of likely caucus-goers prefer a nominee with Washington experience; voters broadly support the Iran nuclear deal (66%); strong support exists for Planned Parenthood and opposition to cutting its federal funding. A majority (66%) prioritize a nominee closest to their views over electability.

The report also notes that Clinton’s recent endorsement of small-dollar federal matching for donations — intended to curb big-money influence — could disproportionately boost Sanders, who relies heavily on small donations (67% of his fundraising last filing came from contributions of $200 or less, versus 18% for Clinton). While such reform could advantage Sanders, it is unlikely to be enacted before the 2016 contest.

British Airways suffered a major IT outage over the weekend that disrupted around 75,000 passengers, grounding hundreds of flights at Heathrow and Gatwick and causing long queues, cancelled services and many travellers sleeping in terminals. CEO Alex Cruz apologised “profusely,” called the failure a “tragedy,” and said BA was making progress toward normal operations—about 95% of flights were running by Monday, with all Gatwick and long‑haul Heathrow services restored and most short‑haul services resuming. Cruz blamed a short, catastrophic power surge at about 09:30 on Saturday that damaged communications hardware and prevented the backup system from operating correctly; he said there was no evidence of a cyberattack and no passenger data breach.

Cruz rejected union claims that the outage resulted from past cuts and outsourcing of IT staff, asserting the teams handling the incident were local and not involved with foreign outsourcing. He promised an exhaustive investigation into root causes and pledged to honor compensation rules; industry estimates suggest BA could face a bill in the tens of millions, perhaps over £100m. Affected customers can rebook over the next six months and are entitled to reimbursements for essentials and hotels, though BA may argue “extraordinary circumstances” to limit liability.

The outage had worldwide knock‑on effects (including cancellations at sister airlines), left many passengers without luggage, and provoked widespread criticism over communication and contingency planning. Technology experts and commentators questioned why disaster‑recovery systems did not kick in and suggested loss of in‑house IT expertise after outsourcing could be a factor, a point BA denies. Rival carriers and social media also reacted, and disruptions were expected to take several days to clear completely.

This document combines background about the End of Term Web Archive pre-inauguration web crawls and a news report about a fatal accidental shooting during a Punta Gorda, Florida citizen police academy.

Key points about the web archive:
- The crawls were done in Fall–Winter 2016 as a pre-inauguration capture for the End of Term Web Archive, which preserves U.S. federal government web content around changes of administration.
- Content archived includes .gov and .mil sites, relevant non-.gov domains, and government social media.
- The project aims to capture pages and the pages they link to so future readers can access the versions that existed at the time and to reduce broken links (“No More 404” effort). More information: http://eotarchive.cdlib.org/.

Key points from the Punta Gorda citizen police academy shooting:
- On the evening of the citizens police academy session in Punta Gorda, 73-year-old Mary Knowlton, a retired librarian and community volunteer, volunteered to role-play as a victim in a lethal-force simulation.
- During the simulation, an officer’s handgun was fired and Knowlton was struck by a live round; she died after being rushed to a hospital.
- The officer has been placed on administrative leave. Punta Gorda Police Chief Tom Lewis said the department was unaware that live ammunition was available to the officer and has asked the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) to investigate how live rounds ended up in the weapon.
- Knowlton’s family and the community are grieving; the city is offering counseling. Her son publicly said he forgives the officer.
- The citizen academy was organized by the chamber of commerce and mirrors the city’s Citizens Academy program designed to increase civic engagement and improve police-community relations. Such academies, which often include nonlethal use-of-force simulations, are common and promoted by law-enforcement associations.
- Authorities were still investigating details, had not released the officer’s name, and witnesses and participants were being questioned by FDLE.

The piece juxtaposes the web-archiving project’s purpose—preserving official pages and context at transitions of government—with a specific news story captured in those crawls: a tragic accidental death during a community police training event.

An Oklahoma man, Benjamin Lawrence Petty, 36, pleaded guilty to raping a 13-year-old girl at the Falls Creek Baptist church camp in June 2016 and was sentenced to probation under a negotiated plea. Petty, who was working at the camp as a cook, reportedly tied the girl’s wrists with a rope, raped and sodomized her, and threatened her to keep her silent. He pleaded guilty to three felonies—first-degree rape, forcible sodomy and rape by instrumentation—and received three concurrent suspended 15-year prison sentences, placed on 15 years’ probation. Conditions include life registration as an aggravated sex offender, treatment, strict reporting and assessment requirements, and wearing an ankle monitor for 24 months.

Murray County Assistant District Attorney David Pyle has said Petty’s legal blindness was a major factor in negotiating a plea that spared prison time and that the victim’s family, who live out of state, consented to the arrangement to avoid repeated travel. Petty had no prior felony convictions.

The plea and probation have drawn criticism from advocates and the victim’s representatives. The Oklahoma Coalition Against Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault argued the deal sends the wrong message and noted monitoring does not prevent assaults and agencies are under-resourced. The victim’s family has also filed a civil lawsuit against the Baptist General Convention of Oklahoma and two churches, alleging negligent hiring, supervision and failure to run background checks that might have prevented the attack. Prosecutors and defense counsel differ on whether the negotiated sentence constitutes appropriate accountability; the county district attorney said he was not aware of the plea details and will review the case.

Three college friends in New Paltz, N.Y. — SUNY New Paltz student Reese Werkhoven and roommates Cally Guasti and Lara Russo — bought a beat-up couch from a Salvation Army thrift store for $55 in March 2014. While sitting on it weeks later they discovered envelopes of cash hidden in the cushions. After probing the seams they unearthed roughly $40,000 in bills.

Initially unsure what to do, they debated ethical, legal and safety concerns and consulted their parents. A deposit slip bearing a woman’s name provided a lead; Werkhoven called her the next day and she confirmed she had left money in the couch. The students drove to her home and returned the full amount. The woman, a 91‑year‑old widow who had hidden weekly savings in the couch over decades after her husband’s failing health, had the couch donated while she was hospitalized and recovering. Grateful, she rewarded each student with $1,000. The three say they returned the money because it didn’t belong to them and keeping it would have felt wrong.

Sony today unveiled the PlayStation 4, positioning the console around the player and developer experience rather than a raw specs race. Lead architect Mark Cerny said PS4 development began early in the PS3 era; the goal was an accessible, developer-friendly platform that emphasizes experience and ease of creation. To that end the PS4 is effectively a high-end x86 PC: an 8-core CPU/GPU combination with 8 GB of unified GDDR5 memory and a local hard drive, which should make development easier compared with the PS3’s tricky architecture.

Key hardware and features
- Controller: A redesigned DualShock 4 with a Vita-style touchpad, a share button, a headphone jack, and an LED light bar for motion tracking (working with a stereo 3D camera accessory). Movement gestures are integrated into the controller itself.
- Performance: Demos (Unreal Engine 4, Killzone, Quantic Dream, Capcom) showed much improved lighting, facial detail and larger environments—visually impressive though not a revolutionary leap beyond high-end PCs.
- Background/system features: Quick suspend/resume (save states), background downloads and a secondary processor to let you play while content downloads, and fast wake-from-sleep booting.
- Social and streaming: Built-in tools for pausing and uploading gameplay video, spectator modes, Ustream integration, and a dedicated video-processing chip for easy streaming and sharing. PSN will emphasize real names/profile pictures and integrate Facebook; mobile apps will tie into the ecosystem.
- Remote play & Vita: Remote play to handhelds (Vita emphasized) with the goal of making every PS4 title playable on Vita, though initial connections may be wired.
- Backwards compatibility & cloud: No native PS3 hardware backwards compatibility; Sony plans PlayStation Cloud streaming for older titles but provided few details.

Other notes
- The PS4 is due Holiday 2013. Sony did not show the final console design or price.
- Sony emphasized personalization (predictive downloads based on habits) and broader social integration—features that may appeal or be intrusive depending on execution.

Bottom line: The PS4 is a developer-friendly, x86-based next-gen console focused on improved visuals, faster performance, seamless background systems, and heavy social/streaming features. It advances the PS3’s strengths without a dramatic break in concept, leaving questions about price, final hardware design, and certain cloud/remote play details.
