President Trump’s lawyers are advising him not to agree to a broad, face-to-face interview with special counsel Robert Mueller, fearing he could incriminate himself by making false or contradictory statements and risk charges for lying to investigators, The New York Times reports. Counsel hope that by refusing an extensive interview, Mueller may be reluctant to subpoena the president, avoiding a protracted court battle over whether a sitting president can be compelled to testify. 

This legal advice conflicts with Trump’s public statements that he is willing and eager to speak under oath, insisting there was no collusion or obstruction. If Trump declines and Mueller subpoenas him, the resulting legal fight could stretch for months, possibly reach the Supreme Court, and carry significant political fallout—raising accusations the president is concealing information and prolonging the investigation into the Russia ties and obstruction questions as midterm and future campaigns approach.

The University of Canterbury (UC) is digitising and translating the 15th-century Canterbury Roll—a unique, visually striking 5-metre medieval English genealogical scroll dating from the Wars of the Roses and the only roll of its kind in the southern hemisphere. Acquired by UC in 1918 and once owned by Sybilla “Nurse” Maude, the Roll traces English lineage from mythical origins through the late Middle Ages and uniquely bears contributions from both Lancastrian and Yorkist sides.

As part of the Canterbury Roll Project, UC academics and students are producing a new, advanced digital edition with a fresh English translation and an interactive, scrollable, zoomable online presentation (planned for full public release in 2018). Much of the Latin transcription and translation work has been done by UC students through internships, providing them with research, coding and teamwork experience.

A UK scientific team led by Professor Haida Liang (Nottingham Trent University) will visit Christchurch in January to apply new imaging and sensing techniques—groundbreaking tests never before used on this manuscript—to search for hidden writing and other features, potentially revealing further information about the Roll’s origins and history. The project also reframes the Roll’s cultural role: from a symbol of British colonial identity to a teaching resource for comparing Western genealogy concepts and Māori whakapapa.

This piece explains that “greenness” can be measured many ways—building efficiency, per-person carbon footprints, cultural indicators—but event-finding app Gravy ranked U.S. cities by the number of “green-friendly” events they host annually. While a high count of environmental festivals and awareness events doesn’t guarantee real-world environmental progress, it does reflect a city’s public commitment to environmentalism, which often correlates with other green rankings. The article presents Gravy’s list of the five “Most Earth-Friendly Cities” and pairs each city with a suggested Earth Day activity. (A separate note mentions that Alexa Internet has donated web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996 for use in the Wayback Machine.)

Families of Sandy Hook victims asked the Connecticut Supreme Court to revive their lawsuit against Remington Outdoor Co., arguing the gunmaker’s military-themed marketing of the AR-15-style Bushmaster rifle helped attract and radicalize young men like shooter Adam Lanza. The families — nine victims’ relatives and one survivor — seek to overcome federal immunity under the 2005 Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (PLCAA) by advancing claims of negligent entrustment and violations of Connecticut consumer-protection law. Negligent entrustment is an exception to PLCAA and normally applies where someone supplies a dangerous instrument to a person they know or should know is likely to misuse it.

At Tuesday’s hearing in Hartford, attorneys for the families said Remington deliberately marketed the AR-15 to a “younger demographic,” linking it to militarism, macho vigilantism and phrases such as “perform under pressure” and “consider your man card reissued,” which they say increased the risk the weapon would fall into dangerous hands. Lead counsel Joshua Koskoff urged the court to allow discovery so the families can probe Remington’s marketing and internal documents. If reinstated, the case would move to discovery and possibly a trial; legal observers say the U.S. Supreme Court could ultimately be asked to weigh in.

Remington’s lawyer argued the PLCAA bars this suit and that manufacturers aren’t legally responsible for criminals’ actions; he contended any liability would rest with the retail seller. Justices focused heavily on whether negligent entrustment can apply to a manufacturer and how advertising factors into that doctrine, questioning the link between marketing and the legal elements required to overcome PLCAA immunity. Observers note negligent entrustment has been used against sellers but not previously against manufacturers, making the families’ argument novel and legally challenging. The court did not announce a decision.

Civil liberties groups say the NSA’s mass-surveillance programs unlawfully invade privacy. In response, an anonymous group of anti‑NSA pranksters in New York has been trying to dramatize that point by doing similar, low‑tech surveillance themselves: over the past year they secretly planted dozens of tiny tape recorders under benches and tables around the city, retrieved recordings, and posted some clips on a website called WeAreAlwaysListening.com.

The posted audio ranges from trivial (a woman at the gym discussing evening plans) to intimate (a man describing a lover’s sexual fetish). The group claims—ironically—that they are “pro bono contractors” aiding the NSA’s mission, and they label their devices “PROPERTY OF THE NSA.” Their site links to an ACLU petition urging Congress to let parts of the Patriot Act (Section 215) expire; the project’s stated goal is to raise awareness about how mundane conversations reveal personal patterns and to push people to protest mass surveillance.

They say they avoid publishing names and have redacted sensitive numbers, but they do publish recording locations and photos, which could allow identification. Their operatives remain anonymous, partly to avoid legal exposure: New York law requires at least one-party consent to record private conversations, and stealth planting and later retrieval of recorders almost certainly violates that statute. The ACLU is not formally affiliated (though it allowed a link to its petition), and the group says it would stop if the tactics were ruled illegal or unconstitutional. The stunt has ignited debate about whether the demonstrators’ illegal invasions of privacy are justified as political protest against government surveillance.

President Obama announced two U.S. actions in Iraq: targeted military strikes to protect American personnel and facilities, and an urgent humanitarian operation to aid thousands of Iraqi civilians—mainly Yazidis—trapped on Mount Sinjar without food or water.

Key points:
- Authority and purpose: Obama authorized targeted airstrikes against ISIL/ISIS convoys if they threaten U.S. personnel, the consulate in Irbil, or the U.S. embassy in Baghdad. He emphasized limited, carefully calibrated action and said no U.S. combat troops would return to fight in Iraq.
- Humanitarian mission: U.S. aircraft have begun airdrops of food and water to civilians stranded on Mount Sinjar; initial drops included roughly 8,000 meals and 5,300 gallons of water in 72 bundles delivered by one C-17 and two C-130s escorted by F/A-18s. Strikes may be used if necessary to help break the siege and allow relief to reach those trapped.
- Rationale: The Yazidi population on Sinjar faces potential mass slaughter or death by dehydration; ISIL rhetoric against Yazidis was described as genocidal. The Iraqi government requested assistance, and the U.S. acted to avert a possible massacre.
- Wider U.S. posture: Several hundred U.S. advisers remain in Iraq to train and assist Iraqi and Kurdish forces; U.S. surveillance assets monitor militant movements. The administration frames military action as limited support for moderate forces while insisting the long-term solution is Iraqi political reconciliation and stronger indigenous security forces.
- International and political context: The intervention follows rapid ISIL advances in northern Iraq, including capture of towns and threats to Irbil. The administration consulted Congress and allies and intends to coordinate with the UN and regional partners. Commentators note risks of mission creep but observe the situation has deteriorated enough to prompt intervention.

Obama closed by stressing the gravity of military decisions, the U.S. responsibility to protect its citizens and vulnerable populations when capable of doing so, and pride in the personnel carrying out the missions.

Iceland has become a global travel hotspot: visitors have jumped from under 500,000 in 2010 to an expected 2.4 million this year. The surge followed wide coverage of the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption, exposure in movies and TV (including Game of Thrones), music tourism, and quirky, effective promotion by Iceland’s tourism authorities. Authorities and industry partners responded to the 2010 crisis by promoting Iceland as a year‑round destination and encouraging travel beyond Reykjavik, using campaigns such as the Iceland Academy and home‑host initiatives.

Expanded air service and low‑cost stopover options from Reykjavik‑based carriers Wow Air and Icelandair—both offering convenient North American connections and free stopovers—have helped drive demand. Icelandair also markets the country onboard with themed planes and stopover promotions. Growth in accommodations and vacation rentals has kept pace with demand (HomeAway listings rose 68% in a year, with stays up 81%).

Visitors are drawn to Iceland’s glaciers, waterfalls, volcanoes, lava fields, geothermal pools (like the Blue Lagoon), geysers, the Northern Lights, and film/music‑related sites. Increased tourism has led to more tour offerings and infrastructure work (including construction near attractions), though seasonal changes (melting glaciers) and private‑property issues can affect visitor experiences.

The Senate unveiled the final details of a year-end tax deal and began floor debate, putting in motion a package with a 10-year cost of about $858 billion (roughly $801 billion in tax provisions plus $57 billion for 13 months of extended unemployment benefits). The agreement, brokered between President Obama and Republican leaders, would:

- Extend current income-tax rates for all brackets for two years (preventing Jan. 1 tax increases for nearly all Americans).
- Continue jobless benefits for the long-term unemployed and implement a one-year payroll (Social Security) tax cut.
- Make the estate tax permanent at a top rate of 35% with a $5 million exemption indexed for inflation (a more generous provision than many Democrats wanted).
- Renew and extend numerous energy-related tax incentives — including a one-year, 45-cent-per-gallon ethanol credit, credits for wind and solar, biodiesel, hybrid production, energy-efficient appliances and transit benefits (largely at reduced/pre-stimulus levels).

The measure was expected to pass the Senate with support from most Republicans and a substantial number of Democrats after farm- and energy-state sweeteners were added; a key procedural vote was scheduled for the following Monday. Republicans generally backed the bill as necessary to avoid economic harm from tax hikes, though some conservatives worried about added deficits.

House Democrats reacted angrily to the deal — chanting “Just say no” in closed-door sessions and passing a nonbinding resolution urging changes before the House consider it — primarily objecting to extending tax cuts for higher incomes and to being sidelined during negotiations. Speaker Nancy Pelosi sought modifications rather than outright rejection, but many rank-and-file Democrats viewed the package as unacceptable and a sign of internal frustration after heavy midterm losses. Vice President Biden privately warned Democrats that opposing the deal could derail it.

The bill contains no identified spending offsets, so it would increase the federal deficit significantly. The standoff highlighted the emergence of divided government after the midterms and illustrated the White House’s willingness to accept a temporary compromise on tax policy to try to bolster the sluggish recovery and avoid immediate economic disruption.

A gunman, identified as 26-year-old Christopher Sean Harper‑Mercer, opened fire Oct. 1 at a writing class at Umpqua Community College in Roseburg, Oregon, killing nine people and wounding several others before killing himself as officers arrived. Police say they received the first 911 call and were on scene within six minutes and exchanged gunfire with the shooter two minutes later. Harper‑Mercer entered the classroom armed with multiple weapons, wore a flak jacket and carried several magazines. Authorities recovered a multi‑page document described as a “manifesto,” but have not disclosed its contents or a motive.

Survivors’ accounts relayed by relatives describe brutality and calculated behavior: students were ordered to crawl to the center of the room; some were asked about their faith and then shot; at least one student was told he would be spared and given a package to deliver to police. Several witnesses report Harper‑Mercer shot a pleading victim despite promises to spare them, and that one student who later died may have shielded others. One male student reportedly was spared and handed an envelope or backpack said to contain information for authorities.

Victims ranged in age from late teens to 67. Hospitals treated multiple wounded; two remained hospitalized in critical and fair condition at the time of reporting, and Mercy Medical Center saw hundreds come to donate blood. Families of victims and survivors described traumatized loved ones — including a 16‑year‑old nursing student who survived but lost a kidney — and community mourning in the rural timber town.

Harper‑Mercer had moved to Oregon with his mother several years earlier; his online profiles showed an interest in previous shootings and extremist subjects. His family issued a statement expressing shock and sorrow and said they were “deeply saddened” by the events. Law enforcement continues its investigation.

House Republicans nominated Rep. Paul Ryan (R‑Wis.) as their candidate for Speaker of the House, moving him one step away from formally taking the gavel from John Boehner when the full House votes to elect him the following morning. Ryan, 45, won the closed secret-ballot nomination 200–43 over Rep. Daniel Webster; he will need a floor majority of 218 to be elected. His selection follows weeks of Republican turmoil after Boehner’s abrupt resignation and comes with expectations that Ryan—widely viewed as the party’s fiscal policy leader and the GOP’s 2012 vice presidential nominee—will try to unify a fractured conference and change how the House operates by giving rank-and-file members more influence over legislation and committee representation.

Ryan initially resisted the job, citing family time and preference to remain Ways and Means chairman, but agreed to run after securing assurances from GOP factions, including an endorsement from conservative Rep. Trey Gowdy. Nevertheless, a sizable right‑wing bloc signaled dissent (43 votes for Webster), indicating Ryan will face ongoing challenges from the conservative Freedom Caucus. Early tests include responding to a recent bipartisan budget deal struck by Boehner—Ryan criticized the process but said he would back the deal—and passing detailed FY spending bills in December to avert a government shutdown. Separately, Ryan requested that official House records reflect his name as Paul D. Ryan.

Summary:

Melania Trump broke her public silence after the release of a 2005 videotape in which Donald Trump made lewd remarks about women, giving multiple interviews to Fox News and CNN. She described the comments as offensive and inappropriate, said Donald apologized and she accepts that apology, and declared “we are moving on.” Melania characterized the remarks as “boy talk,” saying she had never heard her husband speak that way and suggested he had been “egged on” by the host. She defended her husband against sexual misconduct allegations as politically motivated and unsupported by evidence, saying accusations should be handled in court and attacking media coverage as dishonest and biased toward damaging her family.

Melania disputed specific accuser accounts she called false, defended Donald as a gentleman who respects women, and urged him to “be himself” in debates and focus on issues. She also pushed back on what she called unfair treatment of her modeling past and complained about negative stories and imagery used against her during the campaign.

Separately, TMZ reports Billy Bush and NBC have reached a confidential financial settlement that ends his employment with the network. Bush — who was implicated in the same 2005 tape and felt he was made a “scapegoat” — is said to be satisfied with the settlement amount.

President Trump and former aide Omarosa Manigault Newman engaged in a volatile public dispute after Omarosa’s new memoir Unhinged and a series of media appearances in which she accused Trump of racism and alleged he used the N-word on recordings from his Reality TV days. Trump responded on Twitter with personal attacks, calling her “that dog” and “a crazed, crying lowlife,” prompting widespread criticism for the crude presidential rhetoric directed at a Black woman who once served in his administration.

Omarosa released multiple secret recordings she says relate to her firing and to discussions about an alleged tape of Trump using the racial slur. CBS obtained a recording of a 2016 campaign conference call in which aides, including Katrina Pierson and Lynne Patton, discuss how to handle such a tape; on that call Pierson appears to acknowledge Trump “said it” and was “embarrassed.” Pierson initially denied the call took place but later said she had been trying to placate Omarosa. The White House and campaign have not produced or verified any tape of Trump saying the slur. At a briefing, press secretary Sarah Sanders said she could not guarantee no such recordings exist but insisted Trump has never used the word and denied the president’s comments were racially motivated.

Omarosa also confirmed she has been interviewed by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, though she declined to discuss details. The Trump campaign filed arbitration with the American Arbitration Association alleging Omarosa breached a 2016 nondisclosure agreement. Omarosa contends the campaign’s legal action is an attempt to silence her and argues Trump is a misogynist and racist who disrespects women and African Americans; she also accused White House staff of mistreating her when she was fired. The dispute has drawn scrutiny over the recordings’ legality and authenticity, the campaign aides’ earlier denials, and the White House’s inability to categorically rule out the existence of tapes containing racial epithets.

A middle-school boy from Knoxville, Tennessee, Keaton Jones, went viral after his mother Kimberly posted an emotional Facebook video on Dec. 8, 2017 in which he described persistent bullying at Gibbs Elementary. In the clip Keaton tearfully says classmates call him ugly, make fun of his nose, tell him he has no friends and escalate to physical humiliation—pouring milk on him, putting ham down his clothes and throwing bread. His mother wrote that Keaton had asked to be picked up because he was too afraid to go to lunch.

The video rapidly spread across social media, amassing tens of millions of views and the hashtag #StandWithKeaton. It drew widespread public sympathy and outreach from athletes and celebrities: Tennessee Titans and University of Tennessee football players invited Keaton to a game and to visit his school; Snoop Dogg, Chris Evans, Mark Ruffalo, Kelsea Ballerini and Dale Earnhardt Jr. were among the high-profile figures who offered support, invitations and messages encouraging him to stay strong. Keaton and his mother urged other bullying victims to stay strong and hoped things would improve. The story prompted discussions about bullying and prompted offers of in-person support for Keaton.

Ten years after Hurricane Katrina, National Weather Service meteorologist Robert Ricks remembers the agonizing decision he made on Aug. 28, 2005, to issue an unusually blunt urgent bulletin warning New Orleans area residents of an unprecedented, catastrophic storm. As the forecast coordinator at the Slidell, La., office responsible for New Orleans, Ricks crafted a stark “URGENT... SPECIAL MESSAGE” describing widespread uninhabitability, massive structural failures, snapped or uprooted trees, and severe water shortages that would make human suffering “incredible by modern standards.” That message — and another more personal forecast in which he wrote “Godspeed to all those in the path of this storm” — are now preserved in the Smithsonian Museum of American History, along with a rosary Ricks held during the storm.

Ricks says he reviewed every line and removed nothing because local expertise and his experience living through prior storms (Betsy and Camille) convinced him the language was necessary. He reluctantly acknowledges he would have preferred to be wrong, but the devastation proved the warnings justified. His forthright language reflects a broader recent shift at the NWS toward more direct, sometimes emotional messages in true emergencies to motivate people to take life-saving action — similar to the well-known plea issued during Hurricane Sandy in 2012. Ricks, a lifelong New Orleans resident who returned to work amid colleagues who had lost homes, says seeing the human response and the damage was heartbreaking.

The document is a multi-source critical roundup of the 2011 film adaptation of Sara Gruen’s novel Water for Elephants, directed by Francis Lawrence and scripted by Richard LaGravenese, starring Robert Pattinson (Jacob), Reese Witherspoon (Marlena) and Christoph Waltz (August), with Hal Holbrook framing the story as an elderly Jacob. It summarizes plot and production details and presents mixed-to-negative reviews that converge on a few key points:

- Story and tone: The film condenses Gruen’s Depression-era circus tale and its central love triangle—Jacob, Marlena, and the cruel ringmaster August—while keeping the novel’s main incidents. Reviewers note the movie is faithful to the book in plot and scenic pleasure but lacks the novel’s quirky intimacy, period grit and emotional spark. Some critics call it decorous, respectable and old-fashioned; others find it timid, monotonous and overly “nice.”

- Performances: Christoph Waltz is widely praised for bringing menace and intensity to August, providing most of the film’s tension. Reese Witherspoon is seen as visually appropriate and capable but underplayed—too refined to fully convey Marlena’s lower-class roots. Robert Pattinson’s Jacob is criticized as bland and insufficiently lived-in; his narration is described as plodding and juvenile in tone. Hal Holbrook’s framing performance is appreciated.

- Rosie the elephant and animal elements: The elephant Rosie is identified as the film’s emotional centerpiece; her presence supplies many of the movie’s highs and the sense of wonder missing elsewhere. Some scenes of circus life (arrival, tent-raising, smells and chores) work briefly, but the film overall shies away from the harsher realities of circus cruelty.

- Direction, script and craft: Francis Lawrence’s direction is competent and visually polished; production design, cinematography (Rodrigo Prieto) and costumes are consistently praised for period atmosphere. Screenwriter LaGravenese is credited with streamlining the novel for a two-hour film but is criticized for cramming in too many minor episodes and dropping characters without developing them. The score by James Newton Howard is called overbearing by one critic and lush but lacking a clear theme by another.

- Pacing and climax: A common complaint is that the film’s pacing is flat, its narration interrupts momentum, and the climactic rampage—central to the book’s catharsis—plays out perfunctorily and too quickly, leaving audiences feeling cheated out of emotional release.

- Overall verdicts: Reviews range from mildly favorable to critical. Some find it pleasant, family-friendly entertainment that will satisfy fans and benefit commercially; others see it as a bland, timid adaptation that sacrifices the novel’s charm, grit and emotional core despite strong production values and Waltz’s standout turn.

Practical info included: PG-13 rating, two-hour runtime, production credits, and principal cast/animal performers.

Richard Dunn, stuck overnight at Las Vegas’ McCarran Airport, used his iPhone to film a self-made, lip-synced music video of Celine Dion’s 1996 hit "All By Myself" while the terminal was nearly empty. Working alone, he improvised camera rigs—taping his phone to a wheelchair pole, to the extended handle of his computer bag and placing it on moving walkways for dolly shots—and even sprinted to catch an escalator shot. Mid-video he humorously recreates the waterfall silhouette from Flashdance using a water bottle. The cleverly produced clip was uploaded to Vimeo, drew roughly half a million views soon after, and reportedly drew Celine Dion’s interest.

On August 12, 2017, violent clashes erupted in Charlottesville, Virginia, during a “Unite the Right” white nationalist rally protesting the planned removal of a Confederate statue. Hundreds of rally supporters and counter-protesters confronted one another: there were chants, physical fights, chemical sprays, and armed militia-style presence. Authorities declared an unlawful assembly and ordered people to disperse; the governor declared a state of emergency.

At about 1:30 p.m. a silver Dodge Charger drove into a crowd of counter-protesters on the Downtown Mall/Water Street. Thirty-two-year-old Heather Heyer was killed and dozens were injured; initial reports said at least 19–26 people required hospital treatment. Witnesses described the car accelerating into the march, reversing, and fleeing; police arrested 20-year-old James Alex Fields Jr. of Maumee, Ohio, after a short chase. Fields was charged with second-degree murder, multiple counts of malicious wounding and leaving the scene; a bond hearing was set and a civil rights investigation was opened by the U.S. Attorney’s Office, the FBI and the Justice Department.

Later in the day, a Virginia State Police helicopter that had been assisting law enforcement crashed outside Charlottesville, killing two troopers: Lt. H. Jay Cullen and Trooper-Pilot Berke M.M. Bates. Their deaths were linked to the day’s response activities.

Additional arrests were made for related violent incidents: Troy Dunigan (disorderly conduct), Jacob L. Smith (assault and battery), and James M. O’Brien (possession of a concealed handgun). Event organizer Jason Kessler and alt-right leader Richard Spencer publicly disavowed the vehicular attack and urged dispersal, while criticizing police handling; the White House and First Lady called for unity and peace, and President Trump tweeted condemning hate and violence. Vigils were held that night in McGuffey Park and on the Downtown Mall. The FBI’s Richmond field office confirmed it would collect evidence for the ongoing civil rights inquiry.

At a public Senate Intelligence Committee hearing where Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey and Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg testified on misinformation, content moderation and foreign interference, Infowars host Alex Jones — recently banned or suspended by multiple platforms — showed up and provoked a confrontation with Sen. Marco Rubio (R‑Fla.). Reporters say Jones livestreamed his arrival, sat in the front row near the witnesses, and accosted Rubio in a hallway during a recess, interrupting an interview, taunting the senator and calling him names. When Jones touched Rubio’s shoulder, Rubio recoiled and warned him, “Don’t touch me again,” later saying he’d “take care of” Jones; Jones accused Rubio of threatening him. The incident underscored Jones’s attempts to remain in the public eye after platform removals, even as data indicate Infowars’s audience has been shrinking.

Summary:

As the 2018 midterms approach, President Trump is publicly framing the elections as a referendum on himself—urging supporters at rallies to “vote for me”—but privately he is preparing to distance himself from any large GOP losses. Insider accounts say Trump tells confidants the “real election” is 2020 and plans to blame congressional leaders (notably Paul Ryan and Mitch McConnell), the media, and other factors if Democrats gain control. White House aides expect impulsive, blame-shifting tweets and no unified post-election messaging from the administration.

Trump nevertheless remains confident about GOP prospects, credits McConnell for energizing voters during the Kavanaugh fight, and is campaigning heavily—especially on immigration—to boost turnout. At a Texas rally for Sen. Ted Cruz, he escalated hard-line immigration rhetoric around a migrant caravan, attacked Democrats and prominent liberals, touted tax cuts and the economy, and urged a swift border wall. His appearance underscored his role in energizing the GOP base, though the tone risks alienating moderates in suburban House battlegrounds.

Democrats, for their part, are downplaying expectations of a “blue wave” to motivate turnout and avoid complacency. Leaders including DNC chair Tom Perez and Sen. Bernie Sanders emphasize that races will be close and stress turnout strategy over certainty. Polls have generally favored Democrats on the generic ballot, and many Democrats argue that flipping 23 House seats would still constitute a wave.

However, there are growing warning signs for Democrats: Trump’s rising approval, a strong economy, fallout from the Kavanaugh confirmation (which energized some GOP voters), and early voting trends showing GOP-affiliated voters outpacing Democrats in several key states (Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Montana, Tennessee and Texas), according to TargetSmart/NBC analysis. Early voting data also show variations by gender, region and state; only Nevada shows Democratic-affiliated voters leading early turnout so far. Concerns persist about voter suppression risks in places like Georgia.

Both parties are intensely mobilizing in the final weeks: Democrats aim to convert enthusiasm into votes without overpromising, while Republicans, led by Trump’s rallies and immigration messaging, are working to close the enthusiasm gap. The midterms could therefore be decided by narrow margins in crucial House and Senate contests.

On May 18, 2018, a mass shooting at Santa Fe High School, near Houston, Texas, left 10 people dead—mostly students—and about 10 wounded. The suspected shooter, 17-year-old student Dimitrios Pagourtzis, surrendered and was taken into custody; he has been charged with capital murder and was denied bond. Authorities said Pagourtzis used a sawed-off shotgun and a .38 revolver reportedly obtained from his father and that explosive devices (including pipe bombs, pressure-cooker–style devices and a Molotov cocktail) were found at the school and nearby. Officials also said Pagourtzis had journal entries and digital material indicating he intended the attack and initially planned to commit suicide but claimed he lacked the courage.

Eyewitnesses described chaos in art classrooms where the attack began; several students and substitute teachers were among the dead and injured. Two substitute teachers and multiple teens were confirmed killed. Victims identified included 15– and 16–17-year-old students and an exchange student from Pakistan, Sabika Sheikh. Families, classmates and community members mourned; stories highlighted how ordinary students’ lives and plans were cut short. Thirteen others were reported injured overall and many treated at local hospitals; a school resource officer who engaged the shooter was shot and underwent surgery.

Local, state and federal officials responded: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, law enforcement leaders and members of Congress commented, with federal prosecutors reportedly exploring additional charges. President Trump and Vice President Pence expressed condolences; Trump ordered flags at half-staff and reactivated a federal school-safety commission. The shooting renewed debate over school security and gun policy—students at Santa Fe voiced mixed views on solutions—and reignited national grief following the Parkland massacre earlier that year. Community support included offers such as NFL player J.J. Watt offering to pay victims’ funeral costs. Schools in the Santa Fe district closed for several days as investigations continued.

The SEC suspended trading in Cynk Technology Corp. after an unprecedented run-up in the company’s penny stock raised concerns about market manipulation and the accuracy of public information. Regulators cited potentially manipulative transactions and inadequate marketplace information; FINRA and OTC Markets had already flagged and halted the stock before the SEC action.

Cynk purports to operate Introbiz.com, a social-network/contact-selling site, but the company has no revenue, no assets, and—according to SEC filings—only one employee. Its filings showed a $1.5 million loss (mainly from stock-based compensation) through the first nine months of 2013, and a principal owner listed with a large stake. Public records and on-the-ground checks cast further doubt on the company: its claimed Belize office suite does not exist, its website registration is masked, and corporate leadership is murky—reporters encountered conflicting identities associated with the CEO listing.

The share price exploded from $0.06 on May 15 to an intraday high near $22 in mid-June, a rise of tens of thousands of percent, before the trading suspension. Market participants and regulators noted that the surge could have been exacerbated by shorting difficulties and brokerage compliance locks after sharp, suspicious price moves. Observers warned that penny-stock manipulation harms investor confidence and can stigmatize legitimate small companies. The SEC is investigating how a firm with essentially no operations reached a multibillion-dollar market valuation.

Here are the main points from the document:

- Timothy Geithner criticized Mitt Romney’s claim that most jobs lost under Obama were among women, calling it a “ridiculous” and misleading political argument. Geithner said the financial crisis began in early 2008 and early job losses disproportionately hit men in construction and manufacturing, and noted Romney’s claim has been largely debunked.

- RNC Chairman Reince Priebus dismissed President Obama’s proposed “Buffett Rule” (a minimum tax rate on millionaires) as a minor change that wouldn’t significantly reduce the deficit, calling it a “shiny little object” and saying the revenue would cover only about 11 hours of federal spending.

- Rep. Darrell Issa said the Secret Service misconduct scandal from Obama’s Colombia trip likely isn’t an isolated incident and promised broader investigation into how often such lapses have occurred and whether systemic changes are needed. Eleven Secret Service members and five military personnel were relieved or implicated after allegations involving local prostitutes.

- Rep. Michele Bachmann condemned Hilary Rosen’s remark that Ann Romney “has never worked a day in her life” as insulting to women. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand noted Rosen apologized and called the comment inappropriate. Bachmann and Gillibrand clashed over Republicans’ and Democrats’ records on women’s issues, including contraception; Bachmann said she is seriously considering endorsing Romney to help unite the GOP.

44-year-old outdoorsman Marco Lavoie was rescued alive after surviving more than three months in remote northwestern Quebec, but he is in very serious condition.

What happened
- Lavoie left on a planned two-month canoe/hiking trip from July 16 in the Lake Matagami/Nottaway River region. He was expected back in mid-September; family reported him missing Oct. 21.
- Sometime during the trip—likely mid‑August—a bear attacked his campsite, eating his food and destroying his equipment. The bear did not directly injure Lavoie; his German shepherd intervened.
- With food and gear gone, Lavoie was stranded in harsh terrain and onset of winter. He became hypothermic, dehydrated and severely starved; reports say he lost roughly half his body weight (about 90 lbs).

Rescue and condition
- Police searches over eight days were hampered by weather. On Oct. 30 a helicopter crew spotted him; rescuers hiked in because they could not safely land. Officers carried him about a mile (one report said nearly two miles) to the chopper.
- Lavoie was barely able to speak and initially could not drink; he was hospitalized and put on IV fluids. Authorities said he likely would have died within 24–48 hours without rescue.

Contested reports
- Some outlets reported that Lavoie killed and ate his German shepherd to survive; police have not confirmed that detail. Survival experts said extreme measures are sometimes necessary in such conditions and that his endurance was remarkable.

Context
- The Nottaway River area is remote and dangerous; locals warned it’s not suitable for solo travel. Lavoie is an experienced hiker who often took long trips alone. Police plan to interview him once he recovers to get full details.

Susan Schneider Williams recounts the last year of her husband Robin Williams’s life, describing how diffuse Lewy body disease (LBD) overtook a brilliant, larger-than-life man and ultimately led to his suicide in 2014. She writes to clinicians and researchers to put a human face on the disease and to urge continued work toward better recognition, treatment, and cures.

Key points:
- Robin experienced a constellation of seemingly unrelated and progressively severe symptoms over about ten months: constipation, urinary difficulty, loss of smell, insomnia, severe anxiety and panic, paranoia and delusions, memory loss, motor symptoms (tremor, shuffling gait, masked face), visual-spatial problems, freezing, and extreme medication sensitivity. Many symptoms fluctuated unpredictably even within a single day—a hallmark of LBD.
- Early signs (sudden prolonged anxiety/fear, high cortisol) were not recognized as part of a unifying neurodegenerative process. He was initially diagnosed clinically with Parkinson disease; only three months after his death did an autopsy reveal diffuse LBD with widespread α-synuclein Lewy bodies and severe neuronal loss. Pathologists said his brain showed one of the worst LBD pathologies they had seen.
- Treatments were limited and sometimes harmful: antipsychotics can worsen LBD, and medication sensitivities complicated care. Despite following medical advice—therapy, physical therapy, sleep management, medication adjustments, and lifestyle measures—his decline was rapid and inexorable.
- Robin often hid symptoms (likely including hallucinations), and he experienced the profound anguish of recognizing his own cognitive and functional deterioration. Susan describes the emotional devastation for both of them: losing not only a spouse but a best friend and confidant.
- After his death, Susan educated herself about the disease, learned that LBD and Parkinson’s share the Lewy-body pathology but are distinguished clinically by which symptoms appear first, and found that earlier diagnosis likely would not have changed the outcome in Robin’s severe case. Still, she emphasizes the value of research and hopes that clinicians and scientists will continue pursuing better diagnostics, treatments, and cures.
- Susan now works with the American Brain Foundation and calls on medical professionals to carry forward the humanity behind their research—turning Robin’s suffering into meaningful progress.

Overall message: LBD can present with varied, fluctuating neuropsychiatric and motor symptoms that are easily misinterpreted; it can progress rapidly and be devastating even in people who appear highly functional. Susan’s personal story underscores the urgent need for awareness, careful diagnosis, safer treatment strategies, and accelerated research into LBD and related disorders.

Summary:

The notion of “digital natives” — people born around 1980 or later who supposedly possess innate, superior facility with digital technology — has become influential in education, marketing and business. Proponents argue that this cohort learns, works and buys differently and therefore requires different teaching methods, workplace norms and products. The label originated with Marc Prensky’s 2001 essay and has been widely repeated by commentators, institutions and advertisers. Prensky himself later framed the terms as a cultural metaphor rather than a literal claim about skills.

Recent reviews and research challenge the idea. A June paper in Teaching and Teacher Education and a 2011 Higher Education Academy review conclude there is little evidence for a distinct generation of information-savvy learners or superior multitasking ability among younger people. Studies show many younger people use technology much like older generations (often passively) and that multitasking carries cognitive costs for all ages. Critics argue that treating students as inherently tech-proficient can lead to misguided education policies, wasted resources on unproven e-learning reforms, and unrealistic expectations in workplaces and marketing.

That said, some researchers note generational differences do exist in values, preferences and behaviors (workplace expectations, life goals, religiosity, substance use, institutional trust), so generational categories can be useful in some contexts. The main takeaway: while younger cohorts may be more immersed in digital culture, basic human cognition doesn’t change by birth year—educational and organizational decisions should be guided by evidence of how people actually learn and work, not by the myth of innate digital competence.

Summary — Tomah VA over‑medication / infection‑control timeline and response

What happened
- From October 2015 through October 2016 a dentist at the Tomah VA Dental Clinic used his own reusable instruments rather than the VA’s required sterile/disposable equipment and sterilization procedures.  
- The practice was discovered when a substitute for the dentist’s assistant observed and reported it. VA investigators concluded the violations were purposeful.  
- The dentist was removed from patient care and reassigned to an administrative role; the matter has been referred to the VA Inspector General for possible criminal review.

Who may be affected
- The Tomah VA identified and is notifying 592 patients who received care from that provider during the period. They may be at risk for hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV. The VA says there is no confirmed infection reported yet and that overall risk is low, but is treating the notifications as a precaution.

VA response and patient support
- The VA is offering free screening for the affected veterans and will provide free medical treatment for anyone who tests positive. Screening site: Tomah VA campus, Building 400, Room 1054 — Mon–Fri 8:00 a.m.–5:30 p.m., Sat 8:30 a.m.–noon; testing available through Dec. 22.  
- A 24‑hour hotline is available for questions or to schedule tests: 888‑598‑7793.

Context and reaction
- The announcement renewed local concern about care quality at Tomah VA; the facility has faced previous scrutiny over prescribing practices. VA leaders say improvements are underway but acknowledged remaining issues to address.

Prosecutors at London’s Old Bailey told jurors that the now-defunct News of the World illegally intercepted voicemail messages belonging to Kate Middleton and Prince Harry while Middleton was dating Prince William. It was the first time the Murdoch tabloid was accused of accessing a royal family member’s phone directly; earlier allegations had focused on aides’ phones. Prosecutors said private messages between William and Middleton — including affectionate nicknames and details of a military training mishap — were among about eight voicemails recovered by private investigator Glenn Mulcaire, who has pleaded guilty to phone-hacking charges.

Evidence presented also included a 2006 “target evaluation” list seized from Mulcaire naming royal aides, and police testimony that hundreds of attempts were made to hack phones of aides to Princes Charles, William and Harry. The prosecution linked some royal stories in the paper to payments (about $5,000) to Mulcaire and other sources; editors’ emails and columns were shown to suggest the paper used hacked material. Prosecutors additionally alleged that News of the World obtained royal phone directories during a 2006 raid on former royal correspondent Clive Goodman’s home.

The allegations emerged in the trial of former News of the World editors Rebekah Brooks and Andy Coulson and others, who are charged with conspiring to intercept communications between October 2000 and August 2006; they deny the charges. The case has already seen guilty pleas from Mulcaire and several journalists. Brooks faces separate charges including conspiracy to obstruct police; Coulson later served as Prime Minister David Cameron’s communications chief. The scandal prompted the Leveson inquiry into press ethics and relations among media, police and politicians.

A small preliminary study from France’s Center for Cognitive Neuroscience, published in PNAS, found that intranasal oxytocin improved social behaviors in 13 adults with high‑functioning autism or Asperger’s. After inhaling oxytocin, participants made more eye contact when viewing faces and behaved more socially in an interactive ball‑tossing game. These results add to prior research showing oxytocin can improve emotion recognition and reduce repetitive behaviors in some people with autism.

Oxytocin is a naturally produced hormone and neurotransmitter linked to bonding, trust, maternal behavior and social sensitivity. Some people with autism appear to have lower oxytocin levels, which has prompted interest in whether oxytocin or related drugs could treat core social deficits in autism. Experts not involved in the study called the findings promising but preliminary; oxytocin’s short-lived effects mean drug development might focus on longer‑acting alternatives. Researchers cautioned more and larger studies—including pediatric trials—to confirm safety, efficacy and optimal timing of treatment, though some investigators speculate early intervention could substantially alter social development if benefits are validated.

Target is launching a $5 private-label wine line called California Roots, debuting Sept. 3 at about 1,100 Target stores that sell alcohol. The California-grown collection includes five varieties: Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Moscato, Cabernet Sauvignon and a Red Blend, each described with tasting notes and suggested pairings. Target positions the line as an exclusive, high-value offering aimed at growing its fast‑expanding alcohol business. The rollout ties into a broader strategy to expand beer, wine and spirits assortments—adding alcohol to about 300 stores via remodels, increased footprints and new licenses—and to emphasize local craft beers. The move also comes amid Target’s ongoing store remodel program and push into small-format urban and campus stores in Southern California and elsewhere. The launch evokes comparisons to Trader Joe’s low‑priced Charles Shaw (“Two‑Buck Chuck”), whose price has since risen.

A Secret Service prostitution scandal stemming from an April 11 incident in Cartagena has led to multiple dismissals, suspensions and a broad investigation. At least 11 Secret Service employees and about 10 military personnel are accused of heavy drinking, visiting a strip club and bringing prostitutes to hotel rooms while preparing for President Obama’s arrival at the Summit of the Americas. The episode became public after a payment dispute drew hotel staff and Colombian authorities’ attention. Eleven recalled agents were placed on administrative leave and had their top-secret clearances revoked; three Secret Service employees have been fired or forced out so far and a third voluntarily resigned. More firings are widely expected as the probe continues.

Among those removed was David Randall Chaney, a 48-year-old supervisor in the agency’s international programs division. Chaney posted several photos on Facebook from his protective duties, including shots beside Sarah Palin during the 2008 campaign, and joked in comments about “checking her out” and about a woman in a revealing costume “not in front of my son.” Chaney retired under pressure; another senior supervisor, Greg Stokes of the K-9 division, faces dismissal but can contest the charges. Both men have nearly two decades of Secret Service service and had worked on presidential protection details.

The scandal has prompted bipartisan criticism and calls for accountability. Lawmakers overseeing the Secret Service expect further personnel actions; investigators in Colombia have interviewed numerous hotel staff and Secret Service employees, conducted drug tests and polygraphs, and sent military investigators to assist. The White House said presidential security was not compromised and urged patience while investigations proceed. The episode has become an embarrassing political distraction in an election year and raised broader questions about judgment and oversight within the agency.

NBC10 Investigators exposed a man using a handheld cell-phone jammer on a SEPTA 44 bus to silence passengers he found rude. The man, who identified himself as “Eric,” admitted repeatedly activating the device when people talked on their phones and defended his actions as “taking the law into my own hands.” An undercover reporter documented him using a walkie‑talkie‑like unit with multiple antennae to block calls. After being informed on camera that jammers are illegal, he later said he researched the law and would dispose of the device.

Federal law forbids possessing, selling or using cell-phone jammers; penalties include fines and jail time. Experts warn jammers can interfere with GPS, two‑way radios and emergency communications, potentially creating public‑safety hazards by blocking calls to 911 or disrupting police and dispatch channels. SEPTA said its systems (including panic buttons and driver-dispatch methods) have been tested and would require far more than a handheld jammer to be affected, but riders remain alarmed.

The report also noted the practice is not unique to Philadelphia—commuters in New York, New Jersey and DC have admitted using similar devices to silence loud or lengthy conversations on trains, justifying the behavior as enforcing courtesy despite legal and safety risks.

Multiple Yale Law students say professors Jed Rubenfeld and Amy Chua privately warned them that then-D.C. Circuit Judge Brett Kavanaugh preferred female clerks who had a “certain look,” and Chua allegedly offered to coach students on appearance and clothing to help them win clerkships with him. The accounts, first reported by HuffPost and the Guardian, describe Rubenfeld telling a prospective clerk that Kavanaugh “hires women with a certain look,” and Chua advising another student to dress “outgoing” and offering to evaluate photos of outfits. Students who spoke insisted they feared professional repercussions and requested anonymity.

Neither professor accused Kavanaugh of sexual misconduct; Chua and Rubenfeld have defended Kavanaugh publicly—Chua calling him a mentor to women and praising the excellence and diversity of his clerks—and Chua said in a statement that he hires only the most qualified. A former Kavanaugh clerk called the suggestion absurd and emphasized professional standards in chambers. Observers note that giving interview-attire advice is not unusual, but singling out a judge in this way and focusing on students’ physical appearance raised red flags and sounded sexist to some.

The reporting surfaces amid intense scrutiny of Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court nomination following an allegation by Christine Blasey Ford that he sexually assaulted her in high school (which he denies). Yale is reported to be conducting an internal review into Rubenfeld’s conduct toward female students; Yale officials said they will look into the claims about Chua if substantiated, while noting Chua is currently hospitalized. The story highlights students’ discomfort with the perceived role of appearance in elite clerkship selection and the influential role Rubenfeld and Chua have long played in placing students with prominent judges.

A growing market for on‑demand IV “hangover cures” is catering to affluent, time‑pressed customers—especially finance workers and tourists—in cities and resort areas. Doctors and entrepreneurs like New York urologist Dr. Elliot Nadelson and his son Adam have launched mobile IV services (and small clinics) that send nurses with IV fluids plus anti‑nausea, antacid and anti‑inflammatory medications to homes, offices, hotels and Hamptons rentals. Treatments take about 35–40 minutes, cost a few hundred dollars for a full cocktail (about $249 in New York), and clients say they feel dramatically better afterward—enough to return to work or events the same day.

Providers pitch the service for hangovers, food poisoning, flu recovery and athletic rehydration. Operators frame it as both effective and a new revenue stream for physicians as traditional practice gets squeezed; critics note it’s not medically essential. Similar businesses, like Las Vegas’s Hangover Heaven, offer clinic and hotel‑visit options with varying price add‑ons. The model is expanding to other cities (Chicago and broader Hamptons marketing), and many users endorse it as a convenient way to recover quickly.

Divers from the Gran Acuifero Maya (GAM) project have confirmed that two extensive flooded cave networks off Tulum, on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, are connected, creating the world’s longest known underwater cave system. After months of exploration and 10 months of focused searching, the Sac Actun system (previously ~263 km/163 mi) was found to link with Dos Ojos (~83 km/52 mi), producing a combined mapped length of about 347 km (216 miles). By speleological convention the merged system retains the name Sac Actun.

GAM director and underwater archaeologist Guillermo de Anda and lead diver Robert Schmittner stressed the find’s archaeological, hydrological and ecological importance. The network—averaging about 20 meters deep but reaching up to 100 meters and with shallower sections—contains more than 100 documented archaeological contexts, including remains of extinct fauna, early human evidence, Maya artifacts, cave paintings, human burials and man-made structures in dry or partially dry chambers. The caves and their associated cenotes historically supplied freshwater and held deep religious significance for the Maya; studying them can illuminate settlement patterns, rituals and regional development from the Pleistocene through the colonial era.

The discovery also highlights the aquifer’s biodiversity and freshwater value and will prompt further mapping, water-quality and conservation studies. GAM aims to search for additional connections to nearby systems (including Ox Bel Ha and a so-called “mother of all cenotes”) to better understand the full subterranean network; the region already hosts hundreds of submerged cave systems totaling many hundreds of kilometers of passages. The achievement is the culmination of decades of exploration and was dedicated to longtime cave mapper Bil Phillips.

Saudi Arabia will change its official weekend from Thursday–Friday to Friday–Saturday beginning June 29, a royal decree announced, aligning the kingdom with other Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The move is framed as economically motivated—intended to improve coordination with international markets, eliminate lost business hours with global partners, and ease the path for opening the Tadawul stock market to foreign investors.

Analysts and bankers see the switch as a meaningful step toward broader market liberalization that could precede direct foreign access to the $400 billion Saudi exchange. Global banks and asset managers have already been positioning for liberalization, and index providers such as MSCI have signaled pressure on Saudi Arabia after upgrading peers like the UAE and Qatar. Direct foreign entry to the market has been forecast by some banks as early as next year and could draw substantial inflows.

The change will apply across ministries and monetary agencies; schools will adopt the new weekend in the next academic year. The decree was described by Saudi officials as ending negative effects and missed opportunities from differing regional workweeks. The Tadawul All-Share Index was modestly down on the news; regulators have also been pursuing other market reforms this year, including new corporate and trading rules.

An 11-year-old girl, Evha Jannath, died after falling from the Splash Canyon rapids ride during a school trip to Drayton Manor Theme Park in Staffordshire, England. Evha, a Year 6 pupil at Jameah Girls Academy in Leicester, was rescued from the water by park staff and airlifted to Birmingham Children’s Hospital but was pronounced dead shortly after arrival. Her family described her as “a beautiful little girl” and the school and local mosque held prayers; the park and her school closed for the day as a mark of respect.

Staffordshire Police said the Health and Safety Executive has opened an investigation. Park director George Bryan said staff alerted emergency services as soon as she fell. Witnesses and relatives expressed shock and grief; a classmate noted Evha had almost missed the trip because she lacked suitable clothing and had to borrow some from school. Earlier incidents and safety concerns around similar rapids rides were recalled: a 2016 accident in Australia that killed four people, past falls on the same Drayton Manor ride reported by visitors, and recent temporary closures of similar attractions at other UK parks as a precaution. Authorities will investigate the exact cause and whether further action is required.

Barnes & Noble is rethinking its Nook hardware strategy after a 34% drop in e-reader and tablet sales in its fiscal fourth quarter (ended April). While the company says it is not exiting the device business, it will stop producing its own color tablets (like the Nook HD) and instead pursue partnerships to have future tablets manufactured and possibly co-branded with third parties. The company will continue to sell Nook tablets in stores and keep designing and manufacturing its black-and-white e-readers. CEO William Lynch said more details on the device strategy will be released in coming months.

The move follows heavy losses in the Nook digital business—losses more than doubled in the quarter—contributing to an overall fourth-quarter net loss of $118.6 million and a 7.4% revenue decline to $1.3 billion. Barnes & Noble cut Nook-related spending by $26 million year-over-year but digital sales still fell nearly 9%, partly due to weaker device sales and the absence of last year’s big-title bestsellers. The company’s stock dropped about 18% after the earnings release. Separately, Microsoft, which holds a 17.6% stake from a 2012 investment, has been rumored as a potential buyer of Nook; Microsoft declined to comment. Barnes & Noble plans modest brick-and-mortar changes—opening about five stores and closing 15–20—as in prior years.

- Twitvid is rebranding as Telly; an early preview is available at telly.com where Twitvid users can log in with existing accounts and find all their videos migrated.

- Separately, Stefanie Gordon, an event planner from New York, unexpectedly documented the space shuttle Endeavour’s last launch. While flying to Palm Beach she photographed and filmed the launch, posted a photo to her ~1,800 Twitter followers, and saw the post go viral.

- Within hours she received media inquiries (ABC, BBC, CNBC), gained about 1,000 new followers, and had to disable @mention notifications to preserve her phone battery. Gordon says others on the plane took photos but she appears to have been the only one who posted them to Twitter. She found the experience awe-inspiring and has since tweeted her LinkedIn resume as she’s job hunting.

Alex van der Zwaan, a London-based attorney formerly at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, pleaded guilty to making false statements to the FBI and special counsel Robert Mueller’s office in the Russia investigation. A federal charging document says van der Zwaan lied about his communications with former Trump campaign aide Rick Gates and another individual, deleted or failed to produce relevant emails, and secretly recorded calls about a 2012 report his firm prepared for Ukraine’s Justice Ministry on the trial of former Ukrainian prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko. Prosecutors say the report was produced as part of work arranged by Paul Manafort for pro‑Russia Ukrainian interests; Manafort and Gates have been indicted previously on charges including money laundering and acting as unregistered foreign agents. Skadden has said it fired van der Zwaan in 2017 and is cooperating with authorities. The plea was filed ahead of a scheduled hearing and comes as Gates is reportedly nearing a plea deal with Mueller. The story appeared alongside routine political coverage, including President Trump’s comments criticizing Barack Obama’s response to Russian interference.

This piece profiles White House Counsel Kathryn “Kathy” Ruemmler and the controversy over how the Obama White House handled an inspector general’s report that found the IRS had improperly targeted conservative groups. After learning of an April 24 preview of the IG’s findings, Ruemmler and Chief of Staff Denis McDonough decided not to brief President Obama until the investigation was complete, to avoid any appearance of interference. That cautious, lawyer-first approach was upended on May 10 when IRS official Lois Lerner publicly acknowledged extra scrutiny of conservative tax-exempt applicants, creating a communications crisis and criticism that the White House had been out of the loop.

The article emphasizes Ruemmler’s legal mindset: deliberate, risk-averse about disclosures, protective of executive-privilege interests, and focused on insulating the president from potential scandal. Colleagues and outside lawyers largely defend her decision as the correct legal posture, arguing she could not pursue facts that might jeopardize the independent audit and that briefing the president prematurely could itself have been improper. Critics, however, including some former political aides and commentators, contend she lacked political and media savvy and should have at least given Obama a heads-up to enable crisis planning. The White House’s inconsistent public accounts—led by press secretary Jay Carney and senior adviser Dan Pfeiffer—further eroded credibility, prompting McDonough to convene veteran political operatives for damage-control advice.

The profile also touches on Ruemmler’s personality and background: a former federal prosecutor known as a “lawyer’s lawyer,” cool-headed and methodical, with little campaign experience and a preference to “stay in her lane.” It notes the challenges of an insular West Wing without certain first-term political figures who might have bridged legal and political strategy.

A secondary commentary in the piece criticizes media fixation on trivial personal details—specifically a follow-up Washington Post story about Ruemmler’s shoes—arguing such coverage demeans women in power by focusing on appearance rather than professional substance. The columnist calls out broader gendered double standards in political reporting and urges more substantive coverage until women are better represented in leadership settings.

Swedish freelance journalist Kim Wall (30) disappeared after boarding the privately built UC3 Nautilus submarine owned by Danish inventor Peter Madsen on the evening of 10 August. Madsen was rescued alone after the submarine sank in Køge Bay/Øresund on 11 August; Wall was missing. Police raised the submarine, found no body on board, and later charged Madsen with manslaughter.

Court proceedings have been held behind closed doors, but Copenhagen police say Madsen told investigators and the court that Wall died in an accident aboard the Nautilus and that he subsequently "buried" her at sea at an unspecified location in Køge Bay. He denies confessing to wrongdoing and maintains his not-guilty plea, according to his lawyer. Authorities have mapped the submarine’s route that night and launched an ongoing search along that path (using divers, ships, helicopters and sonar) to locate Wall’s remains.

Investigators believe the submarine was deliberately sunk shortly before Madsen’s rescue. He initially told police he had dropped Wall ashore that night but later gave a different account. The investigation remains active and details are being withheld to avoid prejudicing the case.
