Raymond Reinke, 55, of Pendleton, Oregon, pleaded guilty August 23, 2018, in federal court in Mammoth Hot Springs, Wyoming, to four Class B misdemeanor counts stemming from multiple incidents in Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks, including an incident in which he aggressively provoked a bison captured on video. Two other charges (public intoxication in Grand Teton on July 28 and a July 31 disorderly conduct count in Yellowstone) were dismissed as part of the plea agreement.

Sentence and conditions:
- 130 days incarceration (with credit for 21 days already served: imposed as 60 days for harassing wildlife, 60 days for interfering with law enforcement, and 10 days for disorderly conduct)
- $70 in court fees and assessments (no additional fines)
- Five years unsupervised probation
- Alcohol and bar ban, plus prohibition on drug or alcohol use during probation
- Substance abuse evaluation and required treatment if indicated; alcohol testing and searches for alcohol/controlled substances on reasonable suspicion
- Five-year ban from entering Yellowstone, Grand Teton, and Glacier National Parks (the latter was added because the arrest occurred there on August 2)

Court remarks noted Reinke’s apology to the bison and his history of alcohol problems; the judge and prosecutor described the wildlife harassment as among the most egregious they’d seen in Yellowstone. Park officials underscored the sentence as reinforcing stewardship and visitor safety.

Related incident: Separately, a 10-year-old boy from a Washington family was injured in a bear attack on the Divide Trail near Old Faithful the same week; he suffered puncture wounds and was treated at Big Sky Medical Center. Park officials reminded visitors not to run from bears and to stand their ground if charged; Yellowstone averages about one bear attack per year. The report also referenced other recent animal-related injuries in the park earlier that season.

Police in El Cerrito, California, are asking the public for help identifying a woman they say violently robbed a teenage girl of her phone and backpack outside El Cerrito High School. According to authorities, the attacker jumped out of a car, demanded the student’s belongings, and when the girl refused, repeatedly struck her in the head, knocking her unconscious before taking the items and fleeing. Days later the victim found photos of a smiling woman on her iCloud account and recognized her as the assailant. Investigators believe the suspect unknowingly uploaded the selfies from the stolen phone to iCloud, and have released the images to the public to generate tips. Students commented about smartphone safety and called the suspect’s action of taking selfies “dumb.”

The Skagit County sheriff’s office says the owner of Lucky Teriyaki in Sedro‑Woolley asked local law enforcement not to dine at the restaurant after four deputies finished lunch there. Sheriff Will Reichardt posted that deputies were told other customers “didn't like law enforcement” and that the owner later confirmed and asked that he pass the message to other agencies. The post drew wide attention and mixed public reaction online.

Through an interpreter the restaurant owners later said a language barrier likely caused a misunderstanding. They explained an employee saw other patrons upset after spilling soup and water, wondered if the deputies’ presence was the reason, and then asked the deputies if they were leaving—an exchange that was later misconstrued. The owners say they have received death threats, feel terrible about the incident, and invited law enforcement to eat for free at the restaurant on Monday, July 18, welcoming officers to return.

Local business owner Dave North said he will still hold a planned police appreciation fundraiser for the Behind the Badge Foundation in early August. The Sedro‑Woolley Police Department said it is disappointed but will continue to respond to businesses regardless of their requests.

Paula Deen has lost a string of corporate partnerships after acknowledging during a deposition that she used a racial slur in the past and faced allegations in a racial and sexual discrimination lawsuit. QVC said it and Deen agreed she would “step back” from broadcasts and the network will phase out her products online while she addresses the allegations; QVC’s CEO called Deen’s statements and the lawsuit “troubling” but noted people deserve second chances. The Food Network already declined to renew her contract, and Ballantine Books (Random House) canceled a five‑book deal including a top‑selling cookbook. Retailers Sears, Kmart, Target and Walmart are phasing out her merchandise, and other partners such as Smithfield Foods, Caesars Entertainment and diabetes‑drug maker Novo Nordisk have suspended ties or activities.  

Despite widespread defections, some projects remain intact: Deen’s magazine publisher has not made a final decision publicly, her annual fan cruise has strong demand (prompting an extra 2014 sailing), and the Metropolitan Cooking & Entertaining Show is keeping her on its fall tour, saying it accepts her apology and supports offering a path to forgiveness. Deen has publicly apologized, denied being racist, and said she will work to earn forgiveness.

Twin blasts struck Syria’s army command headquarters near Omayyad Square in Damascus before 7 a.m., triggering hours of heavy gunfire, a large fire inside the fortified compound, and widespread damage to nearby buildings, witnesses and state media said. Authorities said the blasts were caused by a car bomb and an explosive device; the army reported some guards wounded but said no senior commanders were hurt. Residents described windows shattered several miles away and panicked soldiers firing in the area. The British-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported heavy clashes inside the compound with casualties on both sides and said rebels may have been inside.

State TV and the Information Minister portrayed the incident as a “terrorist” attack by opponents of President Bashar al-Assad, while witnesses and activists described the attack as part of an escalating rebel campaign targeting regime security sites. Ambulances and police sealed off the area and checkpoints snarled traffic into Damascus.

The blasts come amid an 18‑month civil war that began with 2011 protests and has since turned into a broader armed conflict with tens of thousands killed. Rebels have increasingly struck symbols of regime power in Damascus this year, including a July bombing that killed senior officials. The incident also reportedly cost the life of Maya Nasser (also spelled Naser), a 33‑year‑old correspondent for Iran’s Press TV, who was killed in the fighting around the blasts; Press TV blamed regional backers of the militants. World leaders were discussing Syria at the U.N. General Assembly as the violence continued, with U.N. Secretary‑General Ban Ki‑moon urging action while Russia and China have repeatedly vetoed Western resolutions aimed at pressuring Assad.

Investigators released, for the first time, a description of a man involved in an attempted chemical-soaked-rag abduction of a 22-year-old woman near Ketner Lake on May 28 and said they are exploring whether that incident is connected to the Oct. 5 abduction and murder of 10-year-old Jessica Ridgeway.

Key points:
- The May 28 victim was jogging near Ketner Lake Open Space (about half a mile from Jessica’s home and just south of Witt Elementary) when a man grabbed her from behind and tried to put a rag—described as having a chemical smell—over her mouth. She escaped and called 911.
- The suspect was described as white or light-skinned, 18–30 years old, about 5'8", brown hair, medium build. No vehicle description is available.
- Westminster police said they are reviewing this and other attempted abduction cases in the Denver metro area to identify any links to Jessica’s Oct. 5 disappearance; her body was found Oct. 9 in an Arvada open space about 11 miles away.
- Authorities ask the public to report anyone exhibiting unusual behavior or abrupt changes in routines around Memorial Day or Oct. 5, and to contact Westminster police at 303-658-4336 or PDamberalert@cityofwestminster.us with tips.
- Police also requested help locating a specific type of cross seen or possibly associated with the suspect—asking people to report anyone wearing, carrying, recently purchasing, or connected to such a cross or a local business that sells them.

Contact info for tips and the reporting officer (Joey Bunch) were provided in the bulletin.

Air Force Staff Sgt. Luis Walker, a basic training instructor at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio, was convicted by a military jury on all 28 counts against him—including rape, aggravated sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact—and faces the start of his sentencing phase. Prosecutors said Walker victimized at least 10 female recruits between October 2010 and January 2011, using his position to gain trust, isolate trainees in offices or empty dorms, and force kissing, touching or intercourse. Four recruits were alleged to have had sexual intercourse with him; prosecutors also said he threatened some recruits’ careers to coerce sex and intimidated others into lying.

Walker’s case is part of a broader scandal at Lackland that involves investigations of 12 instructors and allegations affecting at least 31 female trainees; several other instructors have been charged or pleaded guilty (including Staff Sgt. Peter Vega‑Maldonado, who admitted sex with a trainee, and Staff Sgt. Craig LeBlanc, who faces charges referred to a general court‑martial). Victims testified they initially did not report abuse out of fear of reprisal or being recycled in training.

The trial featured graphic, emotional testimony and competing narratives: prosecutors portrayed Walker as a predator who exploited trainees’ vulnerability and the hierarchical nature of basic training, while the defense emphasized inconsistencies in testimony and the absence of physical evidence such as DNA or surveillance video. The scandal prompted wider Air Force and Pentagon attention, including expanded reviews of other training bases and new DoD measures to improve handling of sexual assault complaints amid concerns that military sexual assaults are vastly underreported.

Artist Ryan Mendoza, who rescued the dilapidated Detroit home where civil rights icon Rosa Parks once lived by dismantling its facade and shipping it to Berlin, says he now wants to return the rebuilt house to the United States.

Mendoza, 45, who lives in Germany, removed the 21-by-21-foot house’s facade about a year ago after Detroit issued a demolition order. He paid more than $130,000—largely from selling other artwork—to disassemble, move and reconstruct the structure in his Berlin studio, where it has been displayed to thousands of visitors. Mendoza has framed the project as an artwork intended to make Parks’s legacy more visible at a time when the U.S. is grappling with Confederate monuments and a resurgence of white nationalism.

While Mendoza originally planned a European showing before returning the house, Detroit cultural institutions have shown limited interest so far. The Nash Family Foundation has pledged up to $40,000 to help ship the house back, and numerous U.S. museums have expressed receptivity to displaying it—likely in a major venue such as Washington, D.C., or New York if Detroit won’t host it. Mendoza says German officials, including Vice Chancellor Sigmar Gabriel, have advocated for returning the house and even wrote to former first lady Michelle Obama to help the effort.

The house’s removal was arranged with consent from Parks family members who had tried to preserve the property; Parks lived in Detroit after leaving the South in 1957 and died in 2005. Mendoza argues the house should serve as a monument to Parks and the civil rights movement amid national debates over which histories are commemorated.

Researchers at the University of Tokyo and Kyoto University have used human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells to grow a life-sized human ear-shaped cartilage structure and successfully implanted it under the skin of a rat. The process converted iPS cells into cartilage cells, formed them into many small spherical aggregates, packed those into thin biodegradable tubes shaped into an ear form, and implanted the forms under the animal’s skin. After about two months, the tubes dissolved and a roughly 5‑centimeter (2‑inch) human‑ear–shaped cartilage remained. The team says because the construct is living tissue it could grow with a child and hopes to begin human clinical trials in about five years to treat congenital ear absence or deformities.

The article places this result in the broader context of regenerative bioengineering advances: efforts to make artificial kidneys (UCSF), lab‑grown intestines and “gut‑on‑a‑chip” models (Cornell, EPFL, Harvard), intervertebral disc therapies (Cornell, Duke), a bioengineered windpipe transplant in a toddler, miniature liver buds (Yokohama City University), bioartificial heart scaffolds and biologically enhanced mechanical hearts (Carmat, MGH, MIT), lab‑grown blood vessels (Cytograft, MGH), successful bioengineered bladders (Wake Forest/Anthony Atala), 3‑D printed ears with electronic capability (Princeton), and scalable artificial skin production (Fraunhofer). These developments target organ shortages and disorders ranging from congenital malformations to organ failure; clinical progress varies by tissue and remains challenging, especially for large organs like the liver.

Florida Gov. Rick Scott and top state lawmakers unveiled what they called the most significant Florida gun-safety proposal in decades in response to the Feb. 14 mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School that killed 17. The Republican governor—who said he is an NRA member but did not consult the NRA on the plan—proposed a three-part package that broke with some traditional GOP positions (and with President Trump’s suggestion to arm teachers) but stopped short of an assault-weapons ban demanded by students and many Democrats.

Key elements of Scott’s plan:
- Raise the minimum age to purchase any firearm, including semiautomatic rifles, from 18 to 21 (with exemptions for active-duty military, National Guard, spouses, and law enforcement).
- Strengthen restrictions to keep weapons from “dangerous” people: create a Violent Threat Restraining Order allowing family, welfare experts or law enforcement to ask a court to bar someone from buying or possessing guns; require people involuntarily committed under Florida’s Baker Act to surrender firearms until cleared by a court; and bar people subject to injunctions for stalking, domestic violence, etc., from possessing guns.
- Ban bump stocks and propose tougher background checks, waiting periods and enhanced penalties for threats to schools and for possessing firearms after being legally prohibited.
- Expand school safety measures with a proposed $450 million: place a law-enforcement officer in every public school (one per 1,000 students), mandatory active-shooter drills, infrastructure upgrades (metal detectors, reinforced doors), anonymous reporting tools, threat assessment teams and additional mental-health counselors.
- Commit $50 million to broader mental-health initiatives, including embedding Department of Children and Families case managers in sheriff’s offices and grants for law-enforcement teams to work with DCF.

Reactions and context:
- Stoneman Douglas survivors and many student protesters welcomed some measures (age increase, more resource officers, mental-health funding) but were disappointed Scott did not seek an AR-15–style ban and vowed to keep pressing for one.
- Democrats argued the plan didn’t go far enough, urging assault-weapons bans and comprehensive federal background checks. Senator Bill Nelson criticized it as minimal.
- Sheriff Scott Israel and some local law enforcement supported the plan as a useful step.
- The NRA’s Florida lobbyist called the proposals “gratuitous gun control.”
- Scott explicitly rejected arming teachers, saying trained law enforcement should protect schools—a position at odds with President Trump’s suggestion to arm some teachers.
- National experts, educators and advocacy groups widely criticized the idea of arming teachers as dangerous and unrealistic, arguing it risks accidents, confusion in crises and harms school climate. Others supported increased training for some school staff in rare cases.

Broader debate:
- The announcement has fed a larger national conversation about solutions to mass shootings: whether to tighten gun access (age limits, bans, background checks), invest in mental-health and school security, or arm school staff. Critics of “hardening” schools also warn of increased policing’s disproportionate harms to marginalized students and potential erosion of civil liberties.

Overall, Scott’s plan represents a significant, if politically cautious, move toward gun restrictions in Florida—prioritizing age limits, mental-health restrictions and school security funding—while avoiding a ban on semiautomatic rifles and drawing mixed responses from students, politicians, law enforcement and advocacy groups.

Seven men have been charged in the 2014 hazing death of University at Albany student Trevor Duffy; prosecutors allege the men forced Duffy to drink a 60‑ounce bottle of vodka, which caused his death. The national fraternity Zeta Beta Tau (ZBT) has publicly disavowed the group accused in the case, saying the men were not members of the recognized Epsilon Gamma chapter at UAlbany and were an unauthorized "rogue" group illegally using the ZBT name and marks. ZBT, based in Indianapolis, has retained counsel and plans to sue the individuals for falsely representing themselves, damaging the fraternity’s reputation, and infringing its copyrights and trademarks. One defendant, Joseph Angilletta, is represented by attorney Paul DerOhannesian, who said he was informed of the new civil action and declined to comment on the merits. ZBT noted it is a national organization founded in 1898 with chapters across North America.

Researchers have concluded that the Bramble Cay melomys (Melomys rubicola), a small mosaic‑tailed rodent found only on Bramble Cay at the northern tip of the Great Barrier Reef, has been extirpated from its only known habitat and most likely driven to global extinction primarily by human‑induced climate change.

Key points:
- Extensive, targeted surveys in August–September 2014 using traps, cameras and searches failed to find any individuals; previous surveys in 2011 and repeated declines since the 1990s had already indicated a shrinking population (estimates: several hundred in 1978, ~93 in 1998, then 10–12 in 2002–2004).
- The species’ tiny, low‑lying coral cay home (about 340 × 150 m, only ~3 m above high tide) experienced repeated seawater inundation over the previous decade, greatly reducing its herbaceous vegetation (the rodent’s main food and shelter) and the island’s available area (from ~4 ha in 1998 to ~2.5 ha by 2014).
- The study by Queensland’s Department of Environment and Heritage Protection and the University of Queensland concludes sea‑level rise and increased frequency/intensity of extreme weather and storm surges — linked to anthropogenic climate change — were almost certainly the primary drivers of the population’s decline and loss.
- While the report notes a small chance another population might persist in nearby Papua New Guinea (Fly River delta), surveys of other Torres Strait islands have found no additional populations; the species is listed as extinct in the wild in Queensland.
- The loss is significant because it likely represents the first documented mammalian extinction caused primarily by human‑driven climate change. Conservation groups have warned it exemplifies Australia’s broader mammal extinction crisis and called for greater funding and action to protect threatened species.

Background: The Bramble Cay melomys was first recorded by Europeans in 1845, was larger than other Australian melomys, foraged nocturnally on island vegetation (notably Portulaca oleracea), and coexisted with seabird colonies and nesting turtles. Its restricted single‑island range, small population size, possible inbreeding, and vulnerability to introduced predators, habitat erosion and sea inundation made it especially susceptible to extinction.

Sebastian Gorka, a deputy assistant to President Trump and a former Breitbart national security editor aligned with Steve Bannon, has left the White House. Gorka’s departure was announced Friday; a resignation letter he sent (published by The Federalist and confirmed by POLITICO) blamed “forces” inside the West Wing that do not support Trump’s “MAGA” agenda and said those who best represented the campaign’s policies had been “countered, systematically removed, or undermined.” He criticized the administration’s Afghanistan speech for omitting references to “Radical Islam” and for failing to define strategic victory conditions.

A White House official, however, said Gorka was forced out: “Sebastian Gorka did not resign, but I can confirm he no longer works at the White House.” His exit came one week after Steve Bannon’s ouster and is seen as part of new Chief of Staff John Kelly’s reshaping of the staff; allies said anti-Bannon factions had been erecting internal roadblocks. Gorka opposed the decision to send more U.S. troops to Afghanistan.

The departure drew criticism from Trump loyalists who fear the administration is shifting toward military and establishment advisers (e.g., Kelly and H.R. McMaster) and away from the populist base. Controversies surrounding Gorka include past accusations about ties to extremist symbols and organizations (which he and some outlets have disputed or pushed back against), and questions about whether his wife, a DHS official, will remain. Separately, two House Democrats introduced amendments to bar federal pay for Gorka and Stephen Miller, accusing them of promoting white supremacist views—though such measures are unlikely to reach the floor.

On the morning of Dec. 18, 2017, Amtrak Cascades Train 501 derailed on its inaugural run over the new Point Defiance Bypass near DuPont, Washington, throwing 13 cars off an overpass onto southbound Interstate 5. At least three people were killed and more than 70 were hospitalized, including about 10 with serious injuries; 19 people were uninjured. The train carried 80 passengers, five crew members and a technician.

Data from the event recorder and NTSB statements showed the train was traveling about 80 mph in a 30-mph curve where the derailment occurred — roughly 50 mph over the posted limit. Witnesses and an NTSB consultant said the train appeared to miss the curve, suggesting excessive speed was the primary factor. Speed-limit signs are posted two miles before and immediately before the slowed zone. Investigators continued on-scene work, including inspecting the bridge and recovering cars with cranes.

The derailment occurred on a newly upgraded 14.5-mile corridor that cost roughly $180–181 million to shift passenger service inland alongside I-5, shorten the Seattle–Portland trip by about 10 minutes and raise line speeds to 79 mph on most segments. The corridor had been equipped for positive train control (PTC) hardware, but Amtrak said PTC was not yet activated on that stretch; the system could automatically slow or stop a train and has been urged federally after several prior fatal speed-related crashes. Congress had mandated PTC implementation years earlier but deadlines were pushed back.

Emergency response involved local fire and rescue, Good Samaritans and medical volunteers; hundreds assisted at the scene. Southbound I-5 was closed for an extended time; authorities established a passenger reception center and a public hotline. Washington Gov. Jay Inslee declared a state of emergency. The NTSB and other federal agencies led the investigation; as of initial reports investigators said it was too early to determine why the train was travelling at excessive speed.

A 5-year-old girl in Portland, Texas, is being praised as a hero after home surveillance showed her rescuing her unconscious mother from the bottom of a backyard pool. On a recent mommy-daughter swim day, 34-year-old Tracy Anderwald had a seizure, blacked out and sank to the pool floor. When five-year-old Allison realized her mother had not surfaced for more than five minutes, she dove down, pulled Tracy to the shallow end and turned her so her head was out of the water.

A nearby aunt, Tedra Hunt, heard children screaming, ran over, called 911 and emergency crews took Tracy to Christus Spohn Hospital Corpus Christi-Memorial. Doctors said Tracy likely would not have survived much longer underwater; she initially faced concerns about possible neurological damage but awakened the next day and was released after tests a few days later. Tracy has never had a seizure before and will see a neurologist to determine the cause.

Family members credit Allison’s early swim training—she’s been swimming since about 2½—and called her calm, capable response extraordinary. They hope the story highlights the importance of teaching children water safety and swimming skills.

US Ambassador to New Zealand Scott Brown acknowledged he was the subject of a US State Department investigation after complaints about remarks he made during a July trip to Samoa, where he also serves as the US representative. Brown, speaking with his wife Gail Huff, said the inquiry followed allegations that at a party in Apia he told attendees they looked “beautiful” and suggested they could earn “hundreds of dollars” working in the US hospitality industry. Brown and Huff said they did not intend to offend and stressed they would be more careful about cultural sensitivities going forward. The Guardian reports the complaints came from two serving female Peace Corps members. The US State Department and related missions did not respond to the paper’s earlier requests for comment; the Wellington embassy said only that the ambassador had nothing further to add.

A Baltimore judge ruled Wednesday that the criminal cases against six police officers charged in the arrest and death of Freddie Gray will proceed in separate trials and that Baltimore State’s Attorney Marilyn Mosby will remain the lead prosecutor.

At the first motions hearing, Circuit Judge Barry Williams issued three key rulings from the bench: he denied defense requests to dismiss the charges, refused to recuse Mosby despite defense allegations of prosecutorial misconduct and potential bias, and ordered the cases split because much evidence admissible against some officers would be prejudicial or inadmissible against others. Williams said he was troubled by some of Mosby’s public comments but found they did not deprive the defendants of a fair trial and rejected arguments that Mosby’s marriage to a city councilman required recusal.

The six officers—Caesar Goodson Jr., Sgt. Alicia White, Lt. Brian Rice, William Porter, Edward Nero and Garrett Miller—face charges ranging from second-degree assault and misconduct in office to manslaughter and, for Goodson, second-degree depraved-heart murder. Prosecutors had sought some joint trials, but Williams concluded separate proceedings were necessary; his decision effectively means six trials.

Outside the courthouse, dozens of protesters held peaceful demonstrations and marches, briefly blocking traffic and resulting in one arrest. The proceedings followed months of contentious filings focused largely on Mosby’s actions; Williams admonished both sides for overheated rhetoric and emphasized maintaining courtroom order. Gray, 25, suffered a severe spinal cord injury while in police custody on April 12 and died a week later, sparking protests and a wider national debate over police treatment of black citizens.

A short piece reports Facebook data showing “LOL” has declined as a way to show laughter on the social network and is now used mostly by older users. The article suggests the drop is tied to changing online language and emoji’s rise among younger people, while variants like “haha” and “hehe” remain common. It notes the report doesn’t account for ironic uses but concludes that “LOL” is aging out as emoji (notably the 😂 face) becomes dominant.

New Johns Hopkins research finds that about 47% of the U.S. edible seafood supply—roughly 2.3 billion pounds out of an estimated 4.7 billion pounds—goes to waste each year due to losses at multiple points in the supply chain.

Key findings
- Consumer-level waste is the largest share: about 1.3 billion pounds (51–63% of total seafood loss).  
- Bycatch (fishers discarding unintended species) accounts for about 573 million pounds (16–32%).  
- Distribution and retail losses total about 330 million pounds (13–16%).  
- The discarded seafood contains enough protein to meet annual needs for roughly 10 million men or 12 million women, and could close about 36% of the gap between current consumption and the 2010 U.S. Dietary Guidelines, which recommend 8 ounces of seafood per person per week.

Context and implications
- Policymakers and the public are increasingly focused on reducing food waste; the federal government has a goal to halve food waste by 2030.  
- Demand-side guidance to increase seafood consumption conflicts with pressures on supply from overfishing, climate change, pollution, habitat loss and diversion of fish to nonfood uses.  
- Reducing waste could help meet dietary recommendations without further straining aquatic resources, but not all lost seafood is recoverable or appropriate to redirect to human consumption (e.g., bycatch is often better left in the water).

Recommendations
- The study’s authors suggest prevention-oriented strategies across the chain: reducing bycatch through fishery limits or gear changes, smaller portion packaging at processing, encouraging frozen purchases to extend shelf life, and broader actions by governments, businesses and consumers to reduce losses.

Source: “Wasted seafood in the United States: Quantifying loss from production to consumption and moving toward solutions,” Global Environmental Change (Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future).

At the 18th annual Critics' Choice Movie Awards in Santa Monica, the Broadcast Film Critics Association honored Argo and its director Ben Affleck — awarding Argo Best Picture and Affleck Best Director — a strong sign for the Oscars given the Critics' Choice record as a predictor. Affleck joked about the Academy in his acceptance.

Other major winners included Daniel Day‑Lewis (Best Actor for Lincoln), Jessica Chastain (Best Actress for Zero Dark Thirty) and Anne Hathaway (Best Supporting Actress for Les Misérables). Jennifer Lawrence had a standout night, winning two genre acting awards (Best Actress in an Action Movie for The Hunger Games and Best Comedic Actress for Silver Linings Playbook); Silver Linings Playbook also won Best Comedy and Bradley Cooper took Best Actor in a Comedy. Judd Apatow received the Louis XIII Genius Award. Wreck‑It Ralph won Best Animated Feature and Amour earned Best Foreign Language Film.

The ceremony, hosted by Sam Rubin at Barker Hangar and televised on The CW, came the same day Oscar nominations were announced, producing an upbeat mood on the red carpet as nominees and winners reacted to both honors and to how critics’ reviews influence their work.

A powerful winter storm swept across northern Europe and the United States, causing widespread flooding, wind damage, travel disruption and fatalities.

Northern Europe and Britain
- A storm with hurricane-force gusts drove the largest tidal surge in Britain in 60 years, swamping stretches of the east coast. About 1,400 properties were flooded, several coastal communities faced exceptional tides and waves, and some houses eroded into the sea at Hemsby. Evacuations were ordered along the Roskilde fjord in Denmark and elsewhere.
- The Thames Barrier in London closed twice in two days to protect against the surge. Britain’s Environment Agency said sea levels in parts surpassed those of the deadly 1953 flood, but stronger defences and evacuations limited UK storm-related deaths to two.
- The wider storm system killed at least eight people across northern Europe (including Sweden, Denmark and Poland). Tens of thousands lost power, road and rail services were disrupted, and dozens to hundreds of flights were cancelled across Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Germany and Poland. Hamburg saw tidal flooding comparable to 1962 but suffered little major damage due to improved defences; another surge was expected.
- Cultural sites and local infrastructure were threatened (e.g., Viking ships on display in Roskilde), and wind farms in Germany produced a large surge of electricity output during the storm.

United States
- A separate frigid winter storm gripped large swaths of the U.S., bringing snow, ice and dangerously low temperatures. Major East Coast cities (Washington, Philadelphia, New York, Boston) were forecast to see wintry precipitation on Sunday with a warm-up on Monday.
- The storm caused record-cold highs in places like Dallas/Fort Worth, widespread travel disruption with hundreds of flight cancellations, numerous vehicle crashes, and at least seven storm-related deaths across several states (Texas, Arkansas, Oklahoma, New Mexico).
- Very cold conditions persisted across the High Plains and Great Lakes—10–35 degrees below average—with extreme wind chills in some areas. Governors in Tennessee and Arkansas declared states of emergency.

Overall impact
- Significant coastal flooding and storm surge in northern Europe, major travel and power disruptions, multiple fatalities, and in the U.S. a severe early winter outbreak producing record cold, travel chaos and additional deaths.

The piece notes that while Beyoncé and Jay‑Z’s daughter Blue Ivy might invite teasing (e.g., during color lessons), her name isn’t the most unusual in Hollywood. It points out that many celebrity kids have far more unconventional names—examples include Audio Science, Pilot Inspektor, Moon Unit and Apple—and directs readers to a HuffPost Parents slideshow of the strangest celebrity baby names.

U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, 40, is continuing rehabilitation after being shot in the head during the Jan. 8 Tucson supermarket attack that killed six and wounded 13. Rabbi Stephanie Aaron of Giffords’ congregation reported visiting her at TIRR Memorial Hermann in Houston, where Giffords is recovering with husband Mark Kelly. Aaron said Giffords sang a prayer and the song “American Pie,” knew all the words, and responded when Aaron brought matzo-ball soup. Giffords has been encouraged by therapists to mouth song lyrics to help rebuild speech and brain function; reports also noted she has asked for toast and mouthed “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.” Aaron described Giffords as determined but experts warn recovery from such traumatic brain injury will be long and difficult.

Separately, internal Tucson Fire Department memos show veteran firefighter Mark Ekstrum refused to go on duty for the Jan. 8 response, citing “political bantering,” which his captain said caused confusion and delay in preparatory work; an engine had to stop to pick up replacement personnel. Ekstrum, a 28-year veteran, retired two days later while discipline was being considered. He later told the department he was distraught and distracted by the shootings and had voted for Giffords in the past; supervisors had recommended a 20-day suspension and one official said he might have faced termination absent retirement. Ekstrum’s record was otherwise positive, and city officials said they would have handled the matter differently after receiving his statement.

Ben Bernanke will hold the first-ever Federal Reserve news conference Wednesday at 2:15 p.m., following the Fed’s recent decision to keep the federal funds target at 0–0.25% and to end its $600 billion bond-buying program (quantitative easing) as scheduled on June 30. The Fed described the recovery as progressing at a “moderate pace,” said the recent rise in inflation is likely temporary, and reiterated that rates are likely to remain very low for an “extended period.” It added flexibility to “adjust” its holdings of Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities as needed, but gave no clear guidance on policy after QE ends. Updated economic forecasts for 2011–2012 will be released before the press conference.

An accompanying editorial urges the media to press Bernanke about why, despite his own view that the Fed “retains considerable power” to reduce unemployment even at near-zero rates, he has been reluctant to take more aggressive measures. The piece argues that the Fed could commit to keeping rates at zero for years, tolerate somewhat higher inflation temporarily, or explicitly reject prolonged high unemployment — yet Bernanke has emphasized the risks of more aggressive easing (chiefly inflation and higher government borrowing costs) without weighing those risks against the far greater and more certain costs of sustained high unemployment: lost incomes and savings, worsened public finances, long-term damage to workers’ skills and health, and political fallout. The editorial credits Bernanke for greater transparency and calm crisis leadership but criticizes recent policy restraint and urges journalists to challenge him at the news conference.

China’s official economic data are widely viewed as unreliable and potentially manipulated, analysts say, a concern highlighted by a 2007 remark from Li Keqiang—then a regional Party chief and now a vice premier—saying GDP figures are “man-made” and “for reference only.” That skepticism is timely after official data showed second‑quarter GDP growth slowed to 7.6% year‑on‑year, the weakest quarterly pace in three years and the sixth consecutive quarter of deceleration.

Sources of mistrust
- Provincial GDP totals exceed the national aggregate by roughly 10%, partly from double‑counting, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
- Some series (registered urban unemployment, electricity consumption) have behaved inconsistently with GDP: electricity growth has lagged GDP, and unemployment has held low and stable, raising questions about whether headline figures are being “smoothed,” especially around leadership transitions.
- China’s statistical strengths lie in industrial metrics (production, profits) that benefit from long‑standing corporate reporting systems; by contrast, services and household consumption are harder to measure accurately (e.g., informal services, restaurant and leisure spending).
- State purchases can inflate retail‑sales figures, masking true household demand.

Alternative indicators and efforts to improve data
- Economists and banks use other proxies—bank lending, electricity use, rail freight, equipment sales, and survey products such as the China Beige Book—to gauge activity and turning points.
- The NBS has taken steps to centralize and standardize reporting, work with international agencies (UN, IMF, OECD), and reduce local filtering of data, but transparency remains limited (for example, CPI weighting is not published).

Current economic backdrop and outlook
- Q2 growth of 7.6% matched expectations but reflected weak external demand, a cooling property market, and lower consumer and producer prices. H1 growth was 7.8%.
- Authorities characterize the slowdown as a move toward more sustainable, lower growth; the government set a modest official target of 7.5% for the year.
- Policymakers have eased monetary conditions with rate cuts and reserve requirement reductions, but say they will not repeat the large 2008 stimulus. Analysts expect further monetary easing but disagree on timing and strength of a rebound—many see a possible pickup in Q3 but note downside risks.
- Investment remains strong (fixed‑asset investment up ~20% year to June), while retail sales and industrial output growth have softened.

Bottom line: While headline growth has moderated to multi‑quarter lows, data quality concerns mean investors and economists increasingly rely on alternative indicators to read China’s economy. The government is making incremental improvements to statistics, but opacity and incentives for local officials to hit targets continue to fuel skepticism.

Most modern Thanksgiving foods — turkey, cranberry sauce, mashed or sweet potatoes, pumpkin pie, and cider — were not necessarily what the 1621 Plymouth feast actually featured. Contemporary pilgrim accounts mention “wild fowl” and plentiful venison (a gift from Wampanoag leader Massasoit), plus lots of fish and shellfish; turkey is not explicitly recorded. Turkey later became the holiday’s emblem because it’s native to America, large enough to feed a family, nonessential to everyday farm labor, and was promoted as Thanksgiving became a national holiday (Bradford’s journals were reprinted in 1856 and Lincoln declared Thanksgiving in 1863). Literary and cultural cues (e.g., A Christmas Carol) also helped cement its role.

Cranberry sauce as we know it likely wasn’t served in 1621 because sugar was scarce and the sweetened boiled-berry sauce wasn’t attested until decades later. Native peoples, however, had long used wild cranberries fresh, dried, in pemmican (a nutrient-dense mix of dried meat, fat, and berries), as dyes, and medicinally. European colonists adapted cranberries to Old World recipes once sweeteners and bee-hives became common; commercial cultivation and the cranberry industry grew by the 19th century.

Pumpkins were available but pies probably were not at the first feast because of limited flour, butter, and ovens; pumpkins were more likely baked in coals or stewed. Pumpkin pie became common on American tables later in the 17th century.

Apples and hard cider were widespread in New England from early colonial times and were very likely the pilgrims’ drink at that harvest celebration. Cider had a long European history and dominated colonial beverage consumption (by 1775 many New England farms ran cider mills). Although cider consumption later declined with beer’s rise, there’s a modern revival in American craft cider, with producers reviving heirloom varieties and producing diverse styles influenced by French and Spanish traditions.

In short: the first Thanksgiving likely featured diverse native foods—venison, seafood, wild fowl, pumpkins, and cider—rather than the standardized modern menu; many classic dishes and preparations evolved later through cultural, economic, and technological changes.

While having electricians install power for a table-tennis room, Wiltshire rug designer Luke Irwin made a chance discovery that has been hailed as one of the most important British archaeological finds in recent years. Insisting the cable be buried rather than run overhead, workmen uncovered fragments of a high-quality mosaic about 18 inches down. Irwin stopped the work and called Historic England; archaeologists found the mosaic to be part of an exceptionally well-preserved, vast Roman villa dated to about AD 175–220, remodelled through into the fifth century.

Initial excavations revealed a three-storey, elite country house—comparable to major sites such as Chedworth—built with premium materials from many quarries. Finds include a fine mosaic floor, a large slab of probable Roman Purbeck marble beneath the modern house, a perfectly preserved Roman well, a stone coffin of a Roman child (previously used as a planter), hundreds of discarded oyster and whelk shells (imported live from the coast), high-status pottery, brooches, coins, wild animal bones and pig remains. Walls more than a metre high are thought to survive beneath river-borne sediment, and timber structures from the fifth century indicate continuity of use after the Roman withdrawal — a rare window into the little-understood Romano–post-Roman transition.

Historic England describes the undisturbed site as “of national significance” with “incredible potential” for understanding Roman and post-Roman Britain. The site has been protected; further research will proceed as funding allows.

British Prime Minister Theresa May said it was "highly likely" Russia ordered the March 4 nerve-agent attack on former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter in Salisbury, and announced the expulsion of 23 Russian diplomats, asset freezes, and a ban on government and royal attendance at the 2018 World Cup. The pair remain hospitalized in critical condition after exposure to Novichok, a Soviet-era nerve agent.

The UK’s measures — the largest diplomatic expulsions in decades — prompted strong reactions. Russia denied involvement and called the expulsions a provocation. Former U.S. diplomats criticized President Donald Trump’s initial public reticence to directly blame Moscow, arguing the administration should have stood immediately and unequivocally with Britain. Trump said he would "condemn Russia or whoever it may be" once facts were clear; Secretary of State Rex Tillerson had earlier said Russia was "clearly" responsible before being fired by Trump.

U.S. officials subsequently made stronger statements: UN Ambassador Nikki Haley declared at a Security Council meeting that the United States believes Russia is responsible and urged the UN to hold the Kremlin accountable, warning that failure to act would risk future chemical attacks elsewhere. The White House later issued a statement of solidarity with the UK, framing Russia’s behavior as part of a broader pattern of violating international norms. Russian UN Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia dismissed allegations and suggested the UK explain the evidence.

This document combines a CDC/NCHS analysis of newborn male circumcision in U.S. hospitals (1979–2010) with a short news item about Danish public opinion and political debate on banning male circumcision.

CDC/NCHS report (Owings, Uddin, Williams)
- Scope: Uses National Hospital Discharge Survey (NHDS) data to estimate rates of circumcisions performed during birth hospitalizations from 1979 through 2010. These figures exclude procedures done outside the birth hospitalization (ritual/community setting or later in life) and therefore do not represent total male circumcision prevalence.
- National trend: The hospital-based newborn circumcision rate fell about 10% over the 32-year period, from 64.5% in 1979 to 58.3% in 2010. Peak was ~64.9% (1981); low point ~55.4% (2007). Rates fluctuated—declining in the 1980s, rising in the 1990s, then declining again in the 2000s—concurrent with changing AAP guidance (1970s: no routine indication; 1989: potential benefits; 1999: insufficient evidence to recommend routine circumcision).
- Regional patterns: Distinct regional differences emerged:
  - Northeast: Relatively flat trend; annual rates varied roughly 60.7%–69.6%.
  - Midwest: Trends mirrored the national pattern (decline in 1980s, rise to late 1990s, decline after), rates between ~68.8% and 82.9%.
  - South: Increased until 1998 then declined; rates ranged ~53.8%–66.1%.
  - West: Large decline (about 37%) from 63.9% (1979) to 40.2% (2010), with most of the drop in the 1980s and a low near 31.4% in 2003.
- Methods: NHDS (1965–2010) is a stratified, clustered, multistage national sample of nonfederal short-stay hospitals. Circumcision identified via ICD-9-CM code 64.0 on discharge records. JoinPoint software was used to detect statistically significant trend changes; reported trends were tested at α = 0.05. Comparison with other data sources shows differences of under 6% for overlapping years.
- Limitations: Only captures circumcisions performed during the birth hospitalization in sampled hospitals; excludes out-of-hospital procedures and later-age circumcisions.

Denmark news item
- A YouGov/Metroxpress poll of ~1,000 Danes found 74% support a full or partial ban on male circumcision; only 10% supported parental right to circumcise.
- The poll coincides with planned parliamentary hearings. Some parties favor a ban; others are divided. The Danish Health and Medicines Authority (2013) concluded evidence does not justify outlawing circumcision nor broadly recommending it.
- Estimated 1,000–2,000 circumcisions occur yearly in Denmark, mostly among Jewish and Muslim boys. The debate touches human rights concerns (Convention on the Rights of the Child) and community-religion arguments urging caution about using polls to shape policy.

Overall takeaway
- In the U.S., hospital-based newborn circumcision rates declined modestly from 1979 to 2010 with pronounced regional variation, especially a large decline in the West. Trends reflect changing medical guidance and regional practice patterns. Separately, Denmark is experiencing strong public support for restricting or banning nonconsensual male circumcision, fueling political debate despite health authority findings of neither clear harm nor clear broad benefit.

Hurricane Sandy briefly paused intense campaigning in the final days of the 2012 presidential race, but the pause was short-lived as both campaigns balanced disaster response appearances with renewed electoral activity.

Immediate response and optics
- President Obama stayed in Washington to oversee federal relief efforts, visited the Red Cross, and planned a New Jersey damage tour with Republican Gov. Chris Christie — who publicly praised the president’s handling of the storm. The administration emphasized rapid, unbureaucratic aid delivery. Obama’s storm-focused duties won bipartisan attention but kept him off the campaign trail for several days.
- Mitt Romney canceled a planned rally in Ohio and turned it into a storm-relief event, helping load supplies and urging donations. He resumed traditional campaigning on Wednesday with events in Florida.

Campaign competition and strategy
- Both campaigns quickly resumed normal political fighting. Romney and his allies bought new TV and radio ads to try to expand the battleground map into states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Minnesota; operatives tracked roughly $4.5 million in Republican spending in Pennsylvania this week. Obama’s campaign responded with its own ad buys and denounced the moves as signs of Republican weakness.
- The campaigns clashed over Romney’s charge that Obama’s auto bailout benefited China because of alleged Jeep production there; Chrysler executives and spokesmen disputed the claim, and Obama’s team called the ads misleading. Romney continued to air radio ads reiterating the point.

Electoral logistics and risks
- Northeastern storm damage threatened voting logistics: possible relocation or consolidation of polling places, paper-ballot use in some Maryland locations, and extended voter registration in Connecticut.
- Strategists noted trade-offs: managing a credible federal response can yield political benefits for an incumbent (“good government is good politics”), but staying off the trail so close to Election Day risks losing momentum and early voting organization. Both sides tried to adopt a measured, largely positive tone in public events given the disaster context.

Outlook
- Obama planned a late-campaign blitz beginning Thursday to re-engage directly with voters; Romney pressed aggressive final-week campaigning in key states. The storm offered both a political risk and opportunity — for Obama to display leadership and for Romney to demonstrate compassion and recover momentum.

President Donald Trump used Twitter to accuse the media of treating his son unfairly and “distorting democracy” after coverage of Donald Trump Jr.’s meeting with a Russian lawyer. Trump contrasted his son’s scrutiny with Hillary Clinton’s controversies and thanked former adviser Michael Caputo for defending the administration, as well as attendees of the U.S. Women’s Open. 

Separately, CNN interviewed Michael Caputo, a former Trump campaign communications aide with extensive past ties to Russia, who said he never heard anyone in the campaign discuss Russian involvement in the 2016 election. Caputo—who lived and worked in Russia in the 1990s, ran a PR firm with Moscow ties, and has been linked publicly to figures such as Roger Stone—testified behind closed doors to the House Intelligence Committee and publicly insisted he had no knowledge of collusion. He defended Donald Trump Jr.’s decision to meet a person described in email exchanges as a “Russian government lawyer,” saying campaigns would pursue leads offering damaging information on an opponent. Caputo acknowledged past business dealings in Russia but denied working to improve Vladimir Putin’s image, criticized the investigations as a “Russia collusion delusion,” and remained supportive of President Trump. Lawmakers attending his three-and-a-half-hour closed-door testimony called it notable.

Howard Stern gave a wide-ranging, three-hour interview to Neil Strauss for the new Rolling Stone cover story, discussing his traumatic divorce from his first wife Alison, the chaotic period that followed before he met his second wife Beth, longtime therapy, and his future plans for the radio show. Stern said he considered quitting radio after re-signing his contract and expects to cut back from four taped days to roughly three shows a week as time goes on. He defended his interview style—saying interrupting guests keeps things fresh—and recounted an on-air exchange with Strauss that led the writer to reveal a very personal detail about his girlfriend. Stern also addressed former sidekick Artie Lange’s 2017 suicide attempt: Lange has told Stern he might return and explain what happened, but Stern said he’s cautious about bringing him back because he doesn’t want to do anything that could harm Lange and wants him to stay alive. The story and related archival pieces appear in Rolling Stone and online.

A group of 18 House Republicans formally nominated President Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize, filing a letter to the Norwegian Nobel Committee praising his efforts to push for denuclearization and a formal end to the Korean War. Led by Rep. Luke Messer (R-Ind.), the letter credits Trump’s “maximum pressure” campaign and international coordination—including with China—for creating one of the most effective sanctions regimes in history and helping bring North Korea to the negotiating table.

The move followed a historic inter-Korean summit where Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae‑in pledged to pursue complete denuclearization and to enter talks with the U.S. about formally ending the 1950s armistice. Trump is scheduled to meet Kim in late May or June, the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. North Korea has halted nuclear and missile tests and announced it would close a nuclear site ahead of that meeting.

Sen. Bob Corker and retired Gen. Michael Hayden both praised aspects of the administration’s pressure campaign and diplomatic coordination that produced the talks, while cautioning skepticism about North Korea’s promises and criticizing some of Trump’s past rhetoric toward Kim.

This piece reviews the film adaptation of Elizabeth Gilbert’s Eat Pray Love, starring Julia Roberts and directed by Ryan Murphy. Both reviews praise the movie’s visual pleasures—Roberts’s charismatic screen presence, lush cinematography of Italy, India and Bali, enticing food scenes, romantic locales, colorful supporting players, and pleasing wardrobe and production design—making it an attractive, easy-to-watch armchair travelogue likely to appeal to fans of the bestselling memoir.

However, both critics find the film shallow and uneven. The movie is criticized for sanitizing and idealizing Gilbert’s journey into a series of comfortably familiar, touristic vignettes that gloss over deeper emotional complexity. The screenplay struggles to translate Gilbert’s intimate, confessional prose to film, leaving many plot elements (notably the collapse of Liz’s marriage and subsequent romances) underexplained and the spiritual quest clichéd and flattened into types: handsome Italians, earnest ashram mates, and exoticized Eastern mentors. Richard Jenkins’s performance as a fellow seeker is singled out as a notable, more fully realized exception; Javier Bardem adds romantic chemistry but can’t rescue the film’s “navel-gazing” flatness. Overall grade: pleasant and visually seductive but emotionally shallow—good for light viewing but not a faithful or intellectually deeper rendering of the memoir.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said President Donald Trump’s abrupt firing of FBI Director James Comey raises serious concerns about a cover-up of the FBI’s probe into Russian interference and possible ties to the Trump campaign. Schumer questioned the timing and rationale—Justice Department officials cited Comey’s handling of the Hillary Clinton email investigation—but argued that if that were the true reason, Comey could have been dismissed earlier. Schumer and many Democrats demanded a special, independent prosecutor to take over the Russia investigation; he and other critics warned the dismissal could chill future FBI leaders and pointed to recent removals of officials probing Trump as a troubling pattern.

Trump announced Comey’s immediate removal in a letter saying new leadership was needed to restore public trust; the White House attributed the action to a memo from Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein criticizing Comey’s public handling of the Clinton probe. Rosenstein said Comey overstepped DOJ norms by holding a public news conference and announcing investigative steps. Republicans were split in reaction: some supported Rosenstein’s rationale and continued to back DOJ leadership, while others—including Sen. Richard Burr and Sen. John McCain—expressed concern about the timing and impact on ongoing investigations.

Comey learned of his firing while speaking in Los Angeles; Deputy Director Andrew McCabe became acting FBI director. The dismissal intensified calls across the political spectrum for independent oversight of the Russia probe, with legal analysts and Democrats likening the move to Watergate-era actions and warning of abuse of presidential power. The firing occurred amid other developments—grand jury subpoenas in the Michael Flynn probe and an announced Oval Office meeting between Trump and Russia’s foreign minister—heightening scrutiny of the administration’s handling of the Russia investigations.

Researchers from the U.S. Army (including RDECOM), MIT, Special Operations Command, industry and universities are collaborating on TALOS (Tactical Assault Light Operator Suit), a high-tech combat exoskeleton intended to greatly improve ballistic protection, survivability and combat effectiveness for special operators. Inspired in part by battlefield casualties, the program is exploring a range of technologies: liquid/solid-transforming magnetorheological or nanoparticle “liquid ceramic” armors that stiffen on impact and can be integrated with Kevlar; attachable exoskeleton frames (hydraulic or powered) to amplify strength and load-carrying; integrated sensors and cameras (including night vision and heads-up displays similar to Google Glass) for situational awareness; medical sensors and automatic wound-sealing foams; advanced communications and antenna systems; and compact power and electronics. 

Developers stress TALOS is not a flying Iron Man suit and faces major practical limits—most notably power supply and weight (heavy pumps or batteries)—and many components remain experimental. Timelines given range from a prototype within about a year to more capable demonstrators two to three years out, but full operational capability is further off. The project has drawn both excitement for its potential and criticisms about new risks and unrealistic expectations.

Archaeologists have uncovered a previously unknown grave on Beacon Island in the Houtman Abrolhos, tied to the 1629 wreck of the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia and the subsequent mass murders among its survivors. The Batavia ran aground on Morning Reef during its maiden voyage; survivors reached nearby islands but a mutiny led by undermerchant Jeronimus Cornelisz resulted in the systematic killing, rape and abandonment of many shipwrecked people. More than 120 victims were killed in July 1629 by musket fire, stabbing, strangling, poisoning, drowning and throat cutting.

The newly discovered skeleton — the 11th found on Beacon Island since the 1960s and the first intentionally excavated there by archaeologists — was recovered about 1.5 metres down and appears to be an adolescent. Two musket balls were found beside the body. A tooth found in 2013 helped pinpoint the area, and analysis suggests there may be another nearby grave. Forensic teams are examining the remains to learn more about the individual’s origin, diet and cause of death; the skull’s position and associated artifacts may shed light on burial practices and the violent events.

The find forms part of the Australian Research Council-funded Shipwrecks of the Roaring Forties project led by University of Western Australia archaeologist Alistair Paterson, with international collaborators. Researchers say the site is historically significant as the earliest known European habitation in Australia (albeit on islands), and further work — including a planned virtual-reality reconstruction of Beacon Island — aims to deepen understanding of the Batavia story and its place in Dutch, Western Australian and wider maritime history.

An anonymous donor has given $34 million to the San Francisco Foundation to benefit underserved residents of Oakland, with the foundation directed to get the money "in the streets" by summer. Announced at an East Oakland press event, the donation will be invested in jobs, housing, education, health care and technology skills. Key allocations include $6 million for Oakland public schools (early-childhood education, African-American student achievement and community coordinators), $4 million for Oakland Codes, $1 million to the Ella Baker Center for a restaurant worker training program for formerly incarcerated residents, and significant funding targeted to East Oakland nonprofits.

Citywide impacts projected by the foundation: about 731 new affordable housing units, roughly 2,500 jobs, and additional support for re-entry programs and other housing initiatives. About one-third of the funds are earmarked specifically for East Oakland, where the foundation estimates 813 jobs and 136 affordable units will be created in that area.

City leaders — including Mayor Libby Schaaf, Councilman Larry Reid and others — praised the donation as timely given rising rents and displacement pressures from the Bay Area tech boom, and emphasized that philanthropy must partner with government to promote equitable growth. The San Francisco Foundation, led by CEO Fred Blackwell (an Oakland native), will disburse the grants to local nonprofits; a full recipient list is posted at sff.org/oaklandannouncement.

About 1 million gallons of acidic, metal-laden mine water were accidentally released from the abandoned Gold King Mine near Silverton, Colorado, on Wednesday morning when an EPA-contracted crew working to access and treat the mine pool triggered a collapse. The orange-brown plume flowed into Cement Creek and downstream into the Animas River, reaching Durango by Thursday evening and continuing toward New Mexico.

Local and state officials closed the Animas to recreational use (tubing, rafting, kayaking) in La Plata County and advised the public, pet owners and agricultural users to avoid the river until test results are available. Durango stopped pumping raw river water to its reservoir and suspended some outdoor water uses (parks, golf course, college) and urged residents to conserve water; stores reported spikes in bottled-water sales. Farmington, N.M., shut down river intake pumps as the plume approached.

Preliminary concerns focus on iron, aluminum, cadmium, zinc and copper and a large drop in pH where the plume arrived (from about 7.8 to 5.8). Officials said previous mining had already impaired fish populations in Cement Creek and upper Animas; Colorado Parks and Wildlife placed caged fish in the river to monitor impacts. The EPA and state agencies are sampling downstream locations to determine metal concentrations and when the river will be safe; results were expected within 24–48 hours. New Mexico officials criticized the EPA for delayed notification.

Ryan Lock, a 20-year-old chef from Chichester, died on 21 December while fighting with the Kurdish YPG near Raqqa, ISIL’s stronghold in northern Syria. Lock, who had no prior military experience, traveled to the region in August after telling family and friends he was going on holiday to Turkey. Kurdish sources and the YPG say he and four comrades were surrounded by IS fighters in the village of Ja'bar during heavy fighting; when their bodies were recovered, a gunshot wound beneath his chin led investigators to conclude he shot himself to avoid capture. Rights activists and fellow fighters have praised his bravery, saying his action denied IS a propaganda opportunity. Lock is the third British national reported to have died fighting alongside Kurdish forces against IS. His family have expressed gratitude to the YPG for repatriating his body; the Foreign Office continues to advise against all travel to Syria.

San Bernardino police expanded a search Wednesday for 22-year-old Sahray Astina Barber, an Art Institute of California–Inland Empire graphic design student who was last seen around 6 a.m. Monday near her apartment complex on Northpark Boulevard across from Cal State San Bernardino. Roommates reported several of her belongings—including a laptop and cellphone—scattered on the lawn and some items were later found about 30 yards from a nearby bus stop. Mounted and motorcycle units searched hills north of the campus; as of Wednesday no sign of Barber had been found.

Her disappearance comes amid a recent string of violent incidents at CSUSB, including two attacks in the Pfau Library and an attempted kidnapping on campus; university officials have increased police presence and issued warnings. Investigators are treating Barber’s case seriously—assigning more than a dozen detectives, interviewing her roommates and ex‑boyfriend, and sending her laptop to a high‑tech crime unit—but have not established a concrete link to the campus attacks or determined foul play. Barber is described as about 5'8", 125 lbs., with long red‑brown hair and green eyes. Anyone with information is asked to call the San Bernardino Police Investigations Bureau (case #2015-26028).

NBC's three-hour live staging of The Sound of Music, led by Carrie Underwood as Maria and Stephen Moyer as Captain von Trapp, was a high‑budget, ambitious production that split critics. The broadcast boasted a huge, movie‑scale set, impressive technical execution with few visible mishaps, and strong support from seasoned performers — notably Audra McDonald’s powerful “Climb Ev’ry Mountain,” Laura Benanti’s scene‑stealing Elsa Schraeder, and a competent supporting ensemble including Christian Borle.  

However, most reviewers agreed the leads were miscast for the dramatic demands of the role: Underwood sang well and belted powerfully, but her acting was widely described as thin, mannered, or emotionally underdeveloped, and Moyer’s sternness read as self‑conscious rather than richly textured. Critics also argued the stage version’s plotting and tone (long, didactic, and stagebound) made the telecast feel uneven, and the hybrid film‑style staging—large soundstage, no visible audience, movie camerawork—diminished theatrical energy.  

Overall, the event was technically impressive and intermittently moving thanks to its supporting cast and the strength of Rodgers & Hammerstein’s score, but many felt it ultimately played like expensive, well‑sung karaoke rather than a fully convincing dramatic live musical.

This piece outlines a high-profile disagreement between Paul Krugman and Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke over how aggressively the Fed should try to reduce persistently high unemployment. Both are prominent economists; Krugman urges the Fed to aim for noticeably higher inflation (3–4% annually for several years) to lower real interest rates, weaken real debt burdens, encourage spending, and boost growth and jobs. Bernanke and many Fed officials reject that approach as “reckless,” arguing that deliberately raising inflation risks unanchoring inflation expectations, which would make wages and prices more volatile, force investors to demand higher nominal interest rates, and could produce perverse effects (greater saving, reduced spending) as happened in past high‑inflation episodes.

The column reviews the Fed’s aggressive post‑2008 actions—near‑zero short‑term rates, emergency lending, and more than $2.5 trillion in asset purchases—which have helped but not produced a strong recovery; unemployment remained stubbornly high. It explains the mechanics behind Krugman’s proposal and Bernanke’s counterarguments, and notes other possible unintended consequences (wage lagging price increases, loss of policy credibility, higher long‑term rates). The author sides with Bernanke, warning that flirting with higher inflation is dangerous because shifts in expectations have unpredictable, possibly severe costs, and that the Fed cannot solve every economic problem. The piece closes by praising candid, substantive debate over monetary policy.

Ken Stern, drawing on a decade at NPR, criticizes the U.S. nonprofit sector in his book With Charity for All: Why Charities Are Failing and a Better Way to Give. He argues that many charities are financially inept or outright dubious. Some organizations are clearly fraudulent—high executive pay and heavy fundraising costs with little reaching beneficiaries—but such cases can be hard to spot because IRS charity status is easy to get, state oversight is weak, and donors are easily swayed by emotive labels like “veteran” or “cancer.” Investigating charities’ finances is often time-consuming and difficult.

Stern also challenges organizations that are legally nonprofits but function little like true charities. He cites non‑profit hospitals, which on average do not provide more charity care than for‑profit hospitals yet enjoy tax advantages, and college football bowl organizations that spend on events, travel, and entertainment while claiming charitable status. He also notes arts organizations (e.g., opera companies) that primarily benefit donors. The accompanying note clarifies that the source itself recommends few charities by design, focusing on identifying and deeply investigating a small number of top giving opportunities rather than broadly rating many organizations.

Two former bodyguards of Gisele Bündchen and Tom Brady were sentenced to five years in prison in Costa Rica for shooting at photographers during the couple’s April 2009 wedding celebrations at a seaside home. A court in Puntarenas found Costa Rican guard Miguel Solis and Colombian Alexander Rivas guilty of attempted murder; a third man, Manuel Valverde, was acquitted. The court also ordered the two convicted men to pay five million colones (about $10,000) each in damages to each of the two photographers. According to the complaint, the bodyguards confronted the photographers and demanded their camera memory cards; as the photographers drove away, at least one bodyguard fired shots. No one was injured. Neither convicted defendant testified at trial.
