An Associated Press Twitter account was hacked on Tuesday and a false tweet claimed there had been two explosions at the White House and that President Barack Obama had been injured. The bogus message was widely retweeted (about 1,849 times) before it was taken down and AP suspended the account. AP and its staff quickly confirmed the tweet was fake and said hackers had attempted to steal journalists’ passwords via a convincing phishing email. White House press secretary Jay Carney publicly confirmed the president was safe.

The fake alert briefly spooked financial markets: the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which had been up about 130 points, plunged roughly 125–145 points within two minutes after the tweet, then bounced back once the story was proven false. The Syrian Electronic Army claimed responsibility for the attack; the same group has been linked to recent hacks of several CBS News Twitter feeds.

A Newaygo County jury has convicted Glenna Duram of first-degree murder and a felony firearm charge in the 2015 killing of her husband, Martin Duram. Martin, 46, was found shot five times in the couple’s Ensley Township (Sand Lake area) home on May 13, 2015; Glenna survived a gunshot wound to the head that prosecutors say was a suicide attempt. The jury deliberated more than eight hours before returning the guilty verdict. Family members noted the couple’s African grey parrot later mimicked what sounded like an argument—saying phrases including “Don’t f—ing shoot”—but prosecutors did not introduce the bird as evidence. Authorities previously said financial problems, including the home’s foreclosure, may have contributed to the incident. Glenna Duram’s sentencing is scheduled for Aug. 28.

Organizers formally launched a campaign to recall Santa Clara County Superior Court Judge Aaron Persky, who drew national outrage for his 2016 sentence of former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner for sexually assaulting an unconscious, intoxicated woman. On Monday about 35 people filed a notice of intent with the county registrar of voters and submitted a 198-word statement condemning Persky as lenient toward athletes and privileged defendants; if accepted it and Persky’s response will appear on recall petitions to be circulated starting in August.

The campaign, led by Stanford law professor Michele Dauber (a friend of the victim’s family and longtime anti–campus sexual assault activist), must gather 58,634 valid signatures within 160 days to qualify the measure for the June 2018 county ballot. Dauber said supporters have raised about $450,000 and have hired a firm to collect signatures. Supporters include elected officials, academics and women’s-rights leaders; opponents argue the recall threatens judicial independence. A committee defending Persky said removing a judge over a single sentencing decision sets a dangerous precedent.

Background: Turner was convicted of three felonies in 2016; prosecutors sought six years in prison but Persky followed a probation recommendation and sentenced Turner to six months in jail and three years’ probation; Turner served three months and must register as a sex offender for life. The high-profile sentence prompted legislation mandating prison terms for sexual assault of unconscious or intoxicated victims, national debate, more than 1.3 million signatures on a Change.org petition, and thousands of complaints to the state Commission on Judicial Performance— which closed its preliminary investigation unanimously, finding insufficient evidence of misconduct.

Persky has largely remained publicly silent; he requested transfer to civil court last summer and recused himself from at least one criminal case amid the controversy. If the recall qualifies, county voters would decide Persky’s fate and, on the same ballot, pick his replacement (the winner needs only a plurality). Cost estimates to place the recall on the June 5, 2018 ballot are about $1.1 million, though proponents dispute that figure. Supporters and detractors alike warn the campaign’s broader impact could reshape how judges exercise discretion.

This document presents two sharply contrasting takes on U.S. energy policy and rising gasoline prices.

1) Critique of President Obama’s energy stance (Charles Krauthammer-style)
- Argues Obama is hostile to oil despite claiming an “all of the above” approach, citing restrictions on drilling off the Mid-Atlantic and Florida coasts, reduced Gulf production, blocking Arctic drilling, and a 70% drop in Rockies leases.
- Highlights Obama’s veto of the Keystone XL pipeline as a defining example of anti-oil policy, saying it costs jobs, strengthens rivals (China, Venezuela, Russia), harms allies, and prolongs dependence on foreign oil.
- Credits recent production gains not to Obama but to past administrations’ permits and to fracking technology developed outside his policies.
- Calls Obama’s emphasis on reducing demand or developing future fuels (e.g., algae) unrealistic, noting failed or troubled green projects (Solyndra, Ener1, Chevy Volt) and portraying Energy Department spending on algae as misplaced.
- Concludes high gas prices politically damage Obama and reflect what the author calls an ideological, impractical energy policy that ignores abundant domestic fossil-fuel resources.

2) Counterpoint skeptical of “drill more” as a cure (New York Times-style)
- Notes Republicans’ mantra linking tax cuts and more drilling to economic recovery, including claims that restricted drilling causes high gas prices and lost jobs.
- Argues recent data undercuts that message: the U.S. is in a hydrocarbon boom—oil and especially natural gas production have risen and imports fallen—largely thanks to fracking and horizontal drilling, not deregulation.
- Points out that despite higher domestic production and lower import dependence, gasoline prices have still climbed and the recovery hasn’t yielded the expected employment boom, suggesting U.S. energy policy has limited effect on global oil prices and overall job creation.
- Observes environmental costs of fracking have been inadequately addressed, and that the industry has largely been allowed to expand even while environmental concerns were downplayed.

Overall synthesis
- Both pieces agree the U.S. has experienced rising oil and gas production driven by fracking. They diverge sharply on interpretation: critics of Obama see his policies and decisions (e.g., Keystone veto) as ideologically anti-fossil-fuel and politically damaging, while skeptics of the “drill, baby, drill” prescription argue that increased domestic production has not lowered gas prices or meaningfully improved employment, and that environmental and global-market realities limit the impact of U.S. drilling.

What happened to Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370) remains unknown, and statistical methods cannot yet provide a definitive answer. However, Bayesian statistical techniques have proven valuable in focusing and updating search efforts for missing aircraft and shipwrecks by converting expert judgment and varied evidence into probability maps that point searchers to the most likely locations.

How Bayesian search works
- Bayesian methods start with a prior probability distribution (e.g., uniform or informed by past cases) over where the object might be. New information — radar, communications, ocean currents, unsuccessful searches, and hypotheses about cause — is used to update that distribution, producing revised probabilities for each grid cell or three-dimensional location.
- The approach formalizes and quantifies subjective judgments (expert testimony, sensor reliability, assumptions about beacons or debris behavior) so they can be combined, compared and updated as fresh information arrives.
- Bayesian searches were used successfully in locating wreckage of Air France Flight 447 in 2011. Analysts at Metron and others re-evaluated assumptions (for example, whether black-box pingers were functioning), revised probability maps, and within days of a targeted search found the wreckage on the ocean floor after prior searches had failed.

Strengths and limitations
- Strengths: flexibility to incorporate conflicting theories (e.g., northern vs. southern arcs for MH370), to account for uncertainty and past search coverage, and to adapt when new evidence or revised hypotheses appear. It helps avoid cognitive biases by forcing “slow” analytical updating rather than instinctive judgments.
- Limitations: it depends on expert judgments and assumptions that can be subjective; poor record-keeping about prior searches or optimistic sensor-performance estimates can skew outcomes. Quantified probabilities themselves carry uncertainty and can be misinterpreted as precise. Some statisticians caution Bayes is less suitable when new evidence radically changes the scenario, though proponents argue that is precisely when Bayesian updating is useful.

Application to MH370
- For MH370, evolving evidence — including how communications were turned off and patterns suggesting deliberate diversion — shifts prior beliefs and therefore changes where searches should concentrate (deliberate diversion makes locations far from Kuala Lumpur more plausible).
- Analysts must account for which areas have already been searched and with what effectiveness (e.g., acoustic beacon detection ranges and failure rates). That requires making informed but subjective estimates about sensor performance and crash effects on beacons and wreckage.
- There is no public evidence Malaysia or Malaysia Airlines has formally used Bayesian search methods, though French investigators with Air France experience have been assisting.

Outlook
- Without a significant new breakthrough (debris that narrows search areas, new telemetry, or credible intelligence), many experts fear MH370 likely lies on the floor of the Indian Ocean in terrain that could make detection extremely difficult or impossible. Even if surface debris were found now, it might only indicate a general body of water rather than pinpoint the wreck.
- Bayesian search theory remains one of the best disciplined tools available to refine where to look and to combine uncertain information methodically, but it cannot by itself overcome fundamental lack of data or very long elapsed time since disappearance.

A small brown pebble found on a Sussex beach in 2004 by fossil hunter Jamie Hiscocks has been identified as the first likely example of fossilized dinosaur brain tissue. Most likely from an iguanodontian (a dinosaur closely related to Iguanodon) from the Early Cretaceous (~130–133 million years ago), the specimen preserves mineralized remnants interpreted as meninges (the brain’s protective membranes), tiny capillaries, strands of collagen, and possible fragments of cortical (neural) tissue. Researchers propose the brain was preserved because the animal’s head settled in acidic, low‑oxygen water (a bog‑ or swamp‑like environment) that “pickled” soft tissues and allowed early mineralization before decay.

The find was studied using environmental and scanning electron microscopy; the preserved structures show similarities to the brains and meningeal blood-vessel patterns of modern birds and crocodiles, dinosaur descendants. In this specimen the tissue appears pressed against the skull roof, which could reflect postmortem collapse rather than a naturally larger brain, so the team cautions against inferring greater intelligence from this single example.

The work, coordinated by the late Martin Brasier and colleagues at Cambridge and other institutions, is published in a Geological Society of London special volume. Experts call the claim compelling but extraordinary and expect close scrutiny—issues raised include the need for broader comparative anatomy, detailed vessel branching data, and public access to the specimen. If upheld, the discovery will prompt reexamination of other fossils and could open new windows into dinosaur neuroanatomy and evolution.

Ignite Restaurant Group, parent company of Joe’s Crab Shack, is testing a no-tipping policy at 18 of its 131 locations as a response to rising minimum-wage debates. Under the pilot, restaurants in 10 states (Utah, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Michigan, Nebraska and Kansas) have eliminated tips and raised fixed hourly wages for staff based on past pay and job importance; Joe’s declined to disclose exact pay levels. The company says it will not add service charges to checks, though some menu prices have increased. CEO Ray Blanchette called tipping “antiquated” and said the change should reduce turnover by giving employees stable pay (he cited examples like $14/hour versus $2.25/hour tipped rates). The two Orange County Joe’s locations are not included in the trial. The move follows a similar no-tipping shift by New York restaurateur Danny Meyer, who is phasing out tips at his restaurants and raising menu prices to cover fair wages. (The latter part of the document contains unrelated notes about web-archiving efforts.)

Susan Carland, a Muslim sociologist who lectures at Monash University and is married to TV host Waleed Aly, has been receiving persistent, often violent and racist online abuse because she wears a hijab and speaks publicly about Muslim rights. After finding that blocking, arguing or ignoring trolls achieved little, she chose a constructive response: for every hateful tweet she receives she donates A$1 to UNICEF. Motivated by the Quranic idea of “repel evil with what is better,” she sees donating to aid children harmed by war, poverty and injustice as a tangible way to turn virtual hate into real good. Carland began the pledge months ago and — within a few weeks of renewed attention — had already raised over US$1,000. She says the practice has helped her remain grounded in her faith and identity, refuse to be defined by others’ prejudice, and feel more secure and peaceful in public life.

On Tuesday morning, Jan. 14, 2014, a 12-year-old seventh-grader, identified as Mason Campbell, opened fire at Berrendo Middle School in Roswell, N.M. He smuggled a sawed-off 20‑gauge shotgun into the school in a bag or band instrument case and fired in the gym as classes were starting. Two students were seriously wounded: an 11- or 14-year-old boy (reports vary) shot in the face who was flown to University Medical Center in Lubbock and remained in critical condition after surgery, and a 13-year-old girl (identified by family as Kendal Sanders) shot in the arm and later listed in satisfactory condition. Campbell was disarmed after teachers intervened — notably eighth-grade social studies teacher and coach John Masterson — and taken into custody; he was later transferred to a psychiatric hospital. Authorities executed search warrants on his locker, home and the bag and were working with prosecutors on charges.

The school was locked down, students were bused to a nearby mall for reunification, and parents were urged not to come to the campus. Officials noted staff had received active-shooter training and praised their response. A prayer vigil and community services were planned; state and federal officials were monitoring the situation. Materials from the Associated Press were used in reporting.

UPMC Presbyterian has closed its 20-bed cardiothoracic ICU after discovery of mold in toilets and behind walls and is investigating whether the contamination is linked to fungal infections in three transplant patients over the past year.

Key facts
- Two heart transplant patients who died (one in June 2014 with rhizomucor, one in October 2014 with rhizopus) had stayed in the same CTICU room where mold was recently found. A third patient, a lung transplant patient detected Sept. 3 with lichtheimia, is still being treated.
- All three fungi are related (zygomycetes) but preliminary testing indicates they are not the same species as the mold found in drywall; UPMC has not identified the wall mold publicly.
- The earliest in-hospital detection this month (Sept. 3) prompted immediate transfer of the infected patient and nearby patients and eventual closure of the unit for cleaning and remediation by UPMC infection-prevention staff and a private remediation company.
- UPMC says it cannot definitively determine whether the mold contributed to the two deaths and notified the families; it began a full review only after the most recent case suggested a possible link between the three infections.
- Of 56 patients in the unit over the prior year, eight were transplant patients; three transplant patients developed fungal infections and five did not; none of the other 48 non-transplant patients were infected.
- UPMC officials defended their timing of public disclosure as driven by clinical complexity and family notification priorities; they have launched an online blog to report investigation updates.
- Outside experts note such invasive mold infections are rare and most often affect severely immunocompromised patients (like transplant recipients). Possible contributing factors cited include water intrusion or recent construction/deconstruction near the hospital, though the source of the contamination remains undetermined.
- The investigation falls under Pennsylvania’s health department; Allegheny County health officials note mold is usually an allergic risk for healthy people but can threaten immunocompromised patients.

UPMC continues remediation and investigation; the reopening date for the CTICU is unclear.

Researchers have uncovered two striking fossil discoveries that illuminate ancient predator and arthropod evolution.

1) A 100-million-year-old predatory cockroach in amber
- Scientists described a tiny, previously unknown cockroach species, Manipulator modificaputis, preserved in Myanmar amber. At just under 1 cm, it combines features unlike any modern cockroach—long neck, triangular mobile head with large lateral eyes, an extra pair of modified eyes on top of the head, elongated mouthparts and legs, narrow body and wings—giving it a chimera-like appearance (mantis/crane fly/cockroach).
- The specimen belongs to the extinct Manipulatoridae. Researchers (Peter Vršanský and Günter Bechly) interpret many of its traits as adaptations for hunting—likely nocturnal, solitary, able to take flight, and using spined long legs to seize prey—although some paleontologists argue its legs were weak and it may have ambushed prey or moved between leaves rather than running.
- The find adds to evidence that many Cretaceous cockroach lineages were predatory; most of these ferocious forms went extinct, with the praying mantis (in the same superorder) the main surviving predatory lineage today.

2) A giant Ordovician filter-feeding arthropod from Morocco
- Paleontologists reported Aegirocassis benmoulae, an anomalocaridid up to ~7 feet long that lived about 480 million years ago in what is now the Sahara. Unlike earlier predatory relatives, Aegirocassis evolved mesh-like frontal appendages to filter plankton, showing a shift to large-scale suspension feeding during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event.
- Dozens of well-preserved specimens were found, indicating it was relatively common and that a rich plankton ecosystem already existed then. Exceptional soft-tissue preservation allowed researchers to identify a second set of dorsal swimming flaps previously unseen in anomalocaridids.
- This discovery helps resolve how the double-branched (bifurcate) arthropod limb evolved: the dorsal flaps are precursors to the upper branch of modern biramous limbs. The Moroccan site has thousands more fossils (early arthropods, horseshoe-crab-like forms, jellyfish relatives, starfish and snails) promising further insights.

Together, these finds—one in amber, one in ancient marine deposits—reveal surprising diversity and ecological specializations among ancient arthropods and shed light on the evolutionary origins of key anatomical features.

At the 2014 Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas automakers and tech companies pushed hard to make connected cars mainstream, highlighting plans to integrate smartphones, apps and built-in 4G broadband into vehicle infotainment systems. Google unveiled the Open Automotive Alliance—a coalition including GM, Honda, Audi, Hyundai and Nvidia—to adapt Android for cars. Automakers see Android as an attractive common platform because of its mobile dominance, broad supplier support, large developer base and existing use of Google services (maps, search) in many marques.

The move reflects pressure from rapidly evolving consumer devices: smartphone and tablet mapping, streaming and entertainment have made costly, proprietary in‑dash systems look obsolete. Carmakers historically favored bespoke, stable software (MyFord Touch, QNX, Linux variants) to meet safety and reliability demands, but those fragmented approaches force app developers and suppliers to support many incompatible systems. Past collaboration efforts such as the Genivi Alliance produced limited results, so many in the industry view Android as a more pragmatic standard.

Tesla and other innovators have demonstrated the appeal of car‑centered computing (e.g., the Model S’s large touchscreen and integrated apps), while startups like CloudCar offer modular, upgradable infotainment hardware that can be added to vehicles. Ford has also expanded R&D in Silicon Valley and opened parts of its vehicle software to outside developers. Overall, 2014 was positioned as the year the auto industry accelerates its embrace of smartphone‑style ecosystems to keep vehicles current and competitive.

A Balch Springs, Texas, police officer, Roy Oliver, was charged with murder in the April 29 killing of 15-year-old Jordan Edwards and surrendered Friday, posting $300,000 bond. Edwards was a passenger in a car of teenagers leaving an unruly house party when officers fired; initial police claims that the vehicle was backing up aggressively were revised after body-camera video showed it was driving away. An affidavit says another officer broke the car’s rear window and Oliver then fired multiple rounds into the vehicle, fatally wounding Edwards.

Oliver was fired by the Balch Springs Police Department for violating policies in the shooting. His personnel file shows a prior 16-hour suspension in 2013 following a prosecutor’s complaint about his courtroom conduct and at least one reprimand in 2017 for being disrespectful to a civilian. Oliver served previously with Dalworthington Gardens police and in the U.S. Army, including two tours in Iraq.

The shooting prompted protests and renewed national scrutiny over police shootings of black people. Jordan’s family has filed a wrongful-death lawsuit and their attorneys welcomed the murder charge as a sign the state may not “sweep this clear wrong under the rug,” while noting a conviction is not yet assured. Local officials said the criminal investigation will continue; the Balch Springs chief acknowledged the department’s earlier public account was wrong and called the incident a tragedy.

A quirky, cavern-like one-bedroom house in Malibu that resembles something from The Flintstones is listed for $3.5 million. Per public records the property is owned by longtime television personality Dick Clark and his wife. The custom, free-form mountaintop home sits on nearly 23 acres and features vaulted ceilings in the living and dining areas, large glass expanses with ocean views, a fireplace, a wine cellar and two bathrooms—an interior described as a bright cave. Diane Carter of Coldwell Banker’s Malibu Colony office is the listing agent, according to the MLS. The piece also includes boilerplate about Trulia and notes the article’s author is a Forbes contributor, with opinions their own.

A British magazine claims to have a new Jay-Z poem in which he vows to stop using the word “bitch” now that daughter Blue Ivy Carter has arrived, with lines suggesting he regrets normalizing the slur after becoming a father. The piece notes the irony for Kanye, who recently used the term on Watch the Throne. 

Separately, in her first interview since giving birth, Beyoncé says she and Jay-Z will raise Blue in a “normal loving family” and that Jay will be a hands-on, “inspirational” dad who will change diapers. Beyoncé also says celebrity friends like Kelly Rowland are eager to babysit and denies some tabloid claims about extravagant hospital arrangements, calling many reports exaggerated. The interview appears in Star magazine.

Jeff Herman, a Florida attorney known for representing alleged sexual-abuse victims, has become the public face of recent lawsuits accusing high-profile Hollywood figures—most notably director Bryan Singer and producer Gary Goddard—of sexual assault of minors. Herman has litigated roughly 800 abuse cases over his career, gaining prominence for suing institutions like the Catholic Church and the Boy Scouts, and for holding frequent, high-profile press conferences to encourage other victims to come forward.

Two major suits Herman filed are highlighted: Michael Egan’s claims that he was drugged and coerced into sex as a teenager by Singer and others in the late 1990s, and a separate anonymous British plaintiff (identified in filings as John Doe No. 117) who alleges being groomed and sexually abused as a teenager by Singer and Goddard after the London premiere of Superman Returns in 2006. Herman presented photos, a teenage shirtless image, emails and handwritten notes allegedly from Goddard, and other souvenirs (like an envelope containing a premiere ticket) as evidence. The new plaintiff says he was plied with alcohol and Quaaludes, subjected to unwanted sexual acts and psychological harm; his lawyers say other alleged victims have contacted Herman and that more suits — including claims of a Hollywood “sex ring” — are forthcoming.

Singer, Goddard and their lawyers strongly deny the allegations, calling them fabricated, defamatory, or opportunistic attempts to profit from public accusations. Critics also accuse Herman of grandstanding at press conferences and of damaging reputations without due process. Herman acknowledges using publicity strategically to encourage other victims and admits to being “opportunistic,” arguing that public exposure is necessary to empower victims and break institutional silence.

The profile also traces Herman’s background and motivations: his career shift into abuse litigation after a 1997 child-abuse school case, intensive forensic training, and personal history that includes family revelations of abuse by his grandfather and a fragmented memory that may indicate his own early abuse. He survived an 18-month suspension in 2009 for undisclosed conflicts tied to a business competing with a client; he returned to practice in 2011 and continued handling high-profile abuse suits (some later dismissed on statute-of-limitations grounds).

Herman’s methods—creating a child-friendly interview room, offering medals to survivors, and advising parents to trust instincts about potential predators—reflect his single-minded focus on protecting children, though some of his views (e.g., broad cautions about adult males) have been criticized as sweeping or fear-inducing. He says he remains vigilant about false claims but operates with a presumption of skepticism while zealously advocating for clients. The litigation over Singer and Goddard is ongoing, and Herman says more allegations tied to Hollywood abuse will be pursued.

The document critiques the political theater around the 2011 U.S. debt-ceiling standoff, focusing on President Obama’s prime-time address and House Speaker John Boehner’s response. Key points:

- Tone and rhetoric: The author objects to what they see as condescension in Obama’s remark that “most people outside of Washington” hadn’t heard of the debt ceiling, arguing ordinary citizens are informed and entitled to be treated as adults. Obama’s explanation that raising the debt ceiling merely lets the government pay previously incurred bills is called misleading in the context of the specific $2.4 trillion increase he sought, which would permit additional spending into the next fiscal year.

- Political tactics and responsibility: The piece portrays Republicans, especially Boehner, as escalating demands to sabotage compromise and politically corner Obama. It recounts a history of shifting GOP positions after gaining power in 2010—from talk of an adult “first big moment” on the debt limit to later threats of attaching large concessions—culminating in Boehner’s push for extreme measures like a balanced-budget amendment and repeated short-term debt hikes that would risk recurring crises.

- Negotiation dynamics: Obama argued for a balanced approach—major spending cuts, entitlement reforms, and revenue increases from the wealthy—while Republicans insisted on cuts-only. The author criticizes both sides’ negotiation style: Boehner for performative, Tea-Party-driven maximalism aimed at political victory over policy; Obama for sometimes undercutting his own position with folksy analogies (household budgets) and rhetoric that may overstate popular demand for compromise.

- Policy substance and stakes: The writer emphasizes the real economic danger of default and condemns tying the debt ceiling to unrelated concessions (like a balanced-budget amendment). They note Obama’s efforts to remind voters where deficits originated (tax cuts, wars, Medicare prescription program, and the recession) and to mobilize public pressure on Congress, a tactic that briefly overwhelmed GOP websites.

- Political consequences: The author judges the Republicans as taking greater political damage and suggests Obama’s speech likely resonated more with centrists than Boehner’s message did with broader audiences. Still, they warn the opposition is willing to risk economic harm to score political points, making a clean up-or-down vote on a debt increase unlikely.

Overall, the piece denounces Washington posturing, accuses Republicans of bad-faith tactics to force political defeat, and questions some of Obama’s rhetorical choices while endorsing his substantive call for a balanced mix of spending cuts and revenue increases to address the deficit.

Celia Barquín Arozamena, a 22-year-old Spanish golfer and standout student at Iowa State University, was found murdered on 17 September 2018 at Coldwater Golf Links in Ames, Iowa. She suffered multiple stab wounds to her head, neck and upper body. Barquín was a rising star—2018 Big 12 champion, Iowa State Female Athlete of the Year, European Ladies’ Amateur champion in July 2018, and had earned invitations to major professional events. She was completing a civil engineering degree and widely mourned by teammates, coaches, Spanish sports authorities and the international golf community.

Authorities arrested 22-year-old Collin Daniel Richards, whom they describe as homeless, and charged him with first-degree murder; bond was set at $5 million. Investigators say a police dog tracked the victim’s scent to a nearby homeless encampment where Richards had been staying. The criminal complaint cites witnesses who reported Richards had expressed an “urge to rape and kill a woman,” and officers found him with fresh scratches and a laceration; police recovered blood-stained clothing and a knife allegedly discarded after the attack. Officials have called the killing a random act of violence and say no connection between victim and suspect is known. Richards has a prior record including domestic-abuse and other charges; he faces life in prison if convicted.

Iowa State and the wider golf community have paid tribute to Barquín; the university postponed team events, plans campus memorials, and will honor her at an upcoming football game. Funeral arrangements were pending. The slaying followed another high-profile killing of a University of Iowa student earlier that summer, prompting broader concern about community safety.

On Jan. 31, 2018 a rare “Super Blue Blood Moon” will occur: a total lunar eclipse of a Blue Moon (the second full moon of a month) that also happens near lunar perigee (a supermoon). It’s the first total eclipse of a Blue Moon in about 152 years.

Visibility and timing
- Totality lasts about 77 minutes and the Moon will pass through the southern part of Earth’s umbra, making the lower limb brighter while the rest takes on a reddish “blood moon” hue.  
- The eclipse is best seen from eastern and central Asia, Indonesia, New Zealand and most of Australia in the evening; Alaska, Hawaii and northwestern Canada will see it start-to-finish; much of North and Central America will see the eclipse in progress at moonset. Specific event start and maximum times were published in multi–time-zone timetables (beginning around 11:48–11:30 UTC depending on phase referenced; maximum near 01:30 UTC).  

Supermoon context
- This eclipse is the culmination of a winter trilogy of visible supermoons (Dec. 3, 2017; Jan. 1, 2018; Jan. 31, 2018). Visible supermoons can appear roughly 14% larger and 30% brighter than full moons at apogee.

Viewing and outreach
- The Virtual Telescope Project organized free livestreams: an Australia-based live webcast of the Jan. 31 eclipse starting ~11:30 UTC, and a Rome Supermoon rise broadcast the same day beginning ~16:00 UTC. Multiple astrophotographers and observatory partners contributed imaging support. Space.com and NASA provided visibility maps, schedules and guidance; Space.com solicited reader photos of the event.

Photography and safety tips
- For smartphones: tap and hold to lock focus on the Moon and lower exposure as needed. For DSLRs: use daylight white balance, fast shutter speeds to counter lunar motion, and include landmarks for context.  
- No special eye protection is needed—unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses and supermoons are safe to view with the naked eye.

Since late 2014 Florida’s coral reefs have been struck by a multi-year, high‑mortality disease outbreak that is unprecedented in scale for the Florida Reef Tract. Initially detected near Key Biscayne, the outbreak spread rapidly: by fall 2015 it covered roughly 55 linear miles from Pompano Beach to Biscayne National Park, continued moving north and south through 2016–2018, and by 2018 reached Looe Key in the lower Keys. The event has affected many coral species (notably brain and star corals) across much of the 360‑mile reef tract and is estimated to have killed millions of corals, producing local extirpations in some areas.

Causes and impacts:
- The precise cause remains unresolved; investigators suspect a bacterial agent but recognize coral disease is typically driven by multiple interacting biological (bacteria, viruses, fungi) and non‑biological (warm sea surface temperatures, poor water quality, UV, sedimentation) stressors.
- Infected corals often lose tissue rapidly, sometimes dying within weeks, and exposed skeletons are colonized by algae and invertebrates, preventing recovery.
- Longstanding pressures—pollution, coastal development, warming—have weakened reef resilience and likely contributed to the outbreak’s severity.

Response and research:
- Since 2015 state (DEP) and numerous federal, academic, NGO and community partners have coordinated monitoring, sampling, pathogen identification, environmental factor studies, treatment trials, and public outreach.
- Efforts include regional coordination calls, disease and planning workshops (2017), priority sampling plans, intervention-methodology reviews, and citizen-science reporting programs (SEAFAN, C‑OCEAN) and a Reef Ambassador initiative.
- Experimental interventions under exploration include topical antiseptics (e.g., chlorine‑laced epoxy) and antibiotic applications, along with laboratory analyses (including DNA work) to identify pathogens.
- Restoration work is intensifying: institutions such as Mote Marine Laboratory are culturing and outplanting lab‑raised corals (tens of thousands planned) that so far show some resistance, offering a possible path to bolster reef recovery.

Outlook:
- Determining exact causes will take years. Meanwhile managers stress reducing known stressors (improving water quality, limiting turbidity and sedimentation) to enhance coral recovery potential. Reporting observations to regional monitoring programs and supporting restoration and water‑quality improvements are among recommended public actions.

Verizon agreed to buy Yahoo’s core Internet business for about $4.8–4.83 billion in cash, ending Yahoo’s run as an independent company. The deal transfers Yahoo’s web properties—mail, news, sports, Finance, Yahoo Answers, fantasy sports, Tumblr, Flickr, ad technology and some real estate—to Verizon, while excluding Yahoo’s stakes in Alibaba and Yahoo Japan (worth roughly $40 billion combined) and certain intellectual property, which remain with the standalone public company that will likely be renamed.

Strategic context
- The acquisition follows Verizon’s purchase of AOL in 2015 and is intended to expand Verizon beyond connectivity into mobile content, video and advertising, leveraging Yahoo’s large audience (about 1 billion monthly users) and AOL’s ad tech to better compete with Google and Facebook in digital advertising.
- Tim Armstrong (AOL) and Verizon executive Marni Walden are key figures in shaping Verizon’s media push. Verizon hopes combining AOL and Yahoo will create scale for mobile media and ad offerings across its subscriber base.
- Regulators’ proposed privacy rules and net-neutrality debates pose potential challenges to Verizon’s ability to monetize combined ad inventory using user and location data.

Financial and corporate notes
- Yahoo shareholders will retain the company’s Asian investments and cash; Yahoo’s stock rose modestly on the news. Marissa Mayer is expected to depart after closing.
- The deal is expected to close early the following year and reshapes Verizon into a larger player in digital media and advertising while marking the end of Yahoo as a standalone internet pioneer.

Lady Gaga delivered a powerful, widely praised performance of her Oscar-nominated song "Til It Happens To You" at the 2016 Academy Awards, seated at a white piano and surrounded by survivors of sexual assault whose bare arms displayed messages of resilience. The performance, from the documentary The Hunting Ground, spotlighted campus sexual assault and was one of the night's most stirring moments. 

In a subsequent Instagram post, Gaga revealed the performance surprised some family members—her grandmother and aunt learned for the first time that Gaga is a survivor of sexual abuse when they saw her onstage. Gaga, born Stefani Germanotta, said she had long kept the abuse secret out of shame and religious guilt; she initially disclosed the assault publicly in a 2014 Howard Stern interview. Although she did not win the Oscar (Sam Smith's "Writing's on the Wall" took the award), Gaga said performing lifted a weight off her and credited the survivors who joined her for helping her feel less alone. She also thanked her fiancé, Taylor Kinney, for his support. The performance and her openness were widely covered as a milestone moment for sexual assault survivors.

At the start of 2013, thousands of state-level laws quietly went into effect alongside high-profile federal actions like the “fiscal cliff.” Many new statutes range from pragmatic policy changes to quirky local rules, and together they reflect lawmakers responding to public concerns as well as cleaning up older laws.

Notable and unusual examples highlighted:
- Illinois: strip clubs must charge a $3 “skin” tax that funds rape crisis centers; sale and trade of shark fins banned; popping motorcycle wheelies outlawed; employers may no longer request applicants’ social media passwords.
- California: “driverless” cars are permitted on roads only with a human in the passenger seat; K–12 and higher-education employees with regular child contact must now report suspected abuse; expanded authority to investigate mortgage fraud and restrictions on foreclosure during loan-modification review; hunters banned from using dogs to chase bears or bobcats.
- Kentucky: releasing feral hogs into the wild is illegal.
- North Carolina: stealing unused cooking oil worth more than $1,000 is a felony.
- Kansas (Wellington): households limited to four cats.
- Massachusetts (Concord): outlawed plastic water bottles in certain contexts.
- New York: selling e-cigarettes to minors can carry fines up to $1,000.
- Maine and Maryland: same-sex marriage legalized (Maine also recognizing out‑of‑state unions).
- New Hampshire and Montana: new abortion restrictions (partial‑birth ban in NH; parental notification in MT).
- Pennsylvania and other states: expanded use of E-Verify for public‑works contractors and measures targeting services to undocumented immigrants.

Context and trends:
- Overall state lawmaking has slowed since 2009, but many bills address contemporary scandals or policy debates (e.g., child abuse reporting after the Sandusky case, “Caylee’s Laws” after the Casey Anthony trial, protections for homeowners and oversight of mortgage fraud).
- Observers note state legislatures are active on a wide variety of issues, though debate remains over whether legislation is the best tool for every problem.

Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives won a majority in the June 7, 2018 Ontario provincial election, unseating the Liberals after 15 years and making Ford the new premier. Ford, 53, had become PC leader only in March after Patrick Brown’s abrupt resignation and ran a populist, tax-cutting campaign promising income tax and hydro cuts, lower gas and beer prices, and billions for transit and infrastructure while pledging to eliminate the deficit by finding government “efficiencies.” His victory united rural conservatives with “Ford Nation” supporters in Toronto and was aided by widespread desire for change and frustration with outgoing Liberal Premier Kathleen Wynne.

Observers note Ford ran a controlled, message-focused campaign that downplayed media exposure and avoided policy specifics until late; critics say many promises were uncosted and lacked details about how they would be paid for. Despite controversies — associations with his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford (whose substance scandals and 2016 death loomed large), internal PC nomination disputes, legal disputes with Rob Ford’s widow, and other campaign headaches — Ford overcame doubts, presenting himself as sensible during debates and assembling a ministerial bench including former rivals Christine Elliott and Caroline Mulroney.

The NDP, led by Andrea Horwath, became the official opposition and gained seats; the Liberals were routed and reduced to a small rump, with Wynne resigning as leader. The Green Party won its first seat. Analysts caution Ford’s win was not an overwhelming personal mandate — a majority of voters did not support him — but it does give his government wide latitude to implement its agenda amid skepticism about how promised cuts and expansions will be financed.

Rachel Uchitel, who rose to fame after a widely publicized affair with Tiger Woods, quietly married boyfriend Matt Hahn in Nevada. County records show they obtained a marriage license one Sunday night and filed it the next morning. Uchitel is 36; Hahn, a former Penn State football player turned San Francisco businessman, is 26. The couple had been living together in San Francisco for several months. Uchitel, previously married in 2004 for about 16 months, has also been linked to actor David Boreanaz and has appeared on reality shows such as Celebrity Rehab With Dr. Drew and Famous Food. She is currently pregnant and publicly shared a photo of Hahn rubbing her five-month baby bump.

JBS Tolleson, Inc. of Tolleson, Arizona recalled roughly 6.5–6.94 million pounds of raw, non‑intact beef products (including ground beef and patties) packaged July 26–Sept. 7, 2018, because they may be contaminated with Salmonella Newport. Affected products bear establishment number “EST. 267” inside the USDA inspection mark and were distributed to retailers and institutions nationwide.

The recall followed an investigation by FSIS, CDC and state partners after epidemiological traceback using receipts/shopper cards from eight patients linked illnesses to raw ground beef supplied by JBS. As of the report, 57 confirmed Salmonella infections were reported across 16 states (illness onset Aug. 5–Sept. 6); 14 people were hospitalized. FSIS continued to update the recall’s scope and poundage in early October 2018.

Symptoms of salmonellosis include diarrhea, abdominal cramps and fever beginning 12–72 hours after exposure; most recover in 4–7 days but young, elderly or immunocompromised persons can develop severe disease. Consumers are urged not to eat, but to throw away or return, any recalled product (or check freezers), and to cook ground beef to 160°F (other beef cuts to 145°F with a 3‑minute rest) using a food thermometer. For questions, consumers may contact JBS USA’s hotline or FSIS resources (Ask Karen, USDA Meat & Poultry Hotline).

Edvard Munch’s 1895 pastel-on-board version of The Scream sold at Sotheby’s in New York for $119,922,500 (including buyer’s premium), the highest price ever paid for a work at auction. Five bidders competed and the winner participated by telephone. This was the only one of Munch’s four versions that remained in private hands; the others are in Norwegian museums (one at the National Museum and two at the Munch Museum). Sotheby’s noted this version is the most colorful and the only one with a hand‑painted frame that includes Munch’s poem describing "the great scream in nature."

The seller, Norwegian businessman Petter Olsen — son of a friend and patron of Munch — said proceeds will fund a new museum, art center and hotel in Hvitsten, Norway. The sale surpassed the previous auction record of $106.5 million (Picasso’s Nude, Green Leaves, and Bust, 2010) and is among a small number of works sold at auction for over $100 million. The Scream, an enduring symbol of human anxiety, has immense popular‑culture recognition comparable to the Mona Lisa.

"O: A Presidential Novel" is a 368-page political fiction set during the 2012 presidential election and published anonymously by Simon & Schuster, which teases that the author "has been in the room with Barack Obama" and "spent years observing politics." The book mixes real-life figures and events with fictionalized characters and plotlines in the vein of Primary Colors. Its anonymity has provoked intense speculation in Washington about the author's identity, with frontrunners including:

- Joe Klein (who wrote Primary Colors and has denied involvement)  
- Former White House press secretary Robert Gibbs (the publisher’s description seems to match him, and his resignation shortly before publication fueled rumors)  
- Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel (named by some pundits as a possibility)  
- Politico correspondent Ben Smith (who has led the hunt and denied authorship, though some note he fits the profile)  
- President Barack Obama himself (suggested because he’s an experienced writer and might control his narrative, though White House spokespeople declined comment)  
- Jokes have even proposed Obama’s teleprompter (“TOTUS”) as the author.

A reviewer who read the novel called it a fast, well-plotted campaign thriller that leans more on press-campaign dynamics than deep presidential character study, evoking the brisk pacing of Game Change rather than the depth of What It Takes. The anonymous author demonstrates strong insider knowledge of campaigns and the press—suggesting a political reporter or press staffer—and sketches recognizable stand-ins for Obamaland figures (e.g., David Axelrod as “Avi Samuelson”). Distinctive clues noted in reviews include a vividly drawn Arianna Huffington–like character (Bianca Stefani) and the specific detail that one character’s mother suffers from myelodysplastic syndrome—both details readers and sleuthing journalists have examined for hints to the author’s identity.

US lawmakers and U.S.-Pakistan tensions

U.S. senators from both parties sharply criticized Pakistan after a tribal court in Khyber sentenced Dr. Shakeel Afridi to 33 years for treason for helping U.S. intelligence collect DNA used to confirm Osama bin Laden’s presence. Senate Armed Services Committee leaders Carl Levin and John McCain called the verdict “shocking and outrageous,” called Afridi’s actions heroic, and urged Pakistan to pardon him immediately. They warned that keeping Afridi jailed could further damage U.S.-Pakistani relations and reduce Congress’s willingness to provide financial aid. The U.S. has provided Pakistan more than $18 billion since 2001, but concerns persist about elements of Pakistan’s establishment supporting extremists. After bin Laden’s May 2011 death near a Pakistani military academy, lawmakers tightened aid conditions.

Separately, tensions were heightened by continued U.S. drone strikes in northwest Pakistan. Pakistani intelligence officials reported a drone attack in North Waziristan that killed 10 people, following another strike the day before. Drone strikes, seen by Washington as an effective tool against militants, provoke strong anti‑American sentiment in Pakistan and are viewed as sovereignty violations that risk civilian casualties. Pakistan has demanded an end to strikes and closed NATO supply routes to Afghanistan after a NATO air raid killed Pakistani soldiers in November. U.S. officials have pushed Pakistan to take action against the Haqqani network, but strained relations and disagreements over drones and other issues have made cooperation difficult.

President Petro Poroshenko cancelled a planned working visit to Turkey after a sharp escalation in Donetsk region, citing reported entry of Russian troops into Ukraine around Amvrosiivka and Starobeshevo. He said the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) will meet urgently in Kyiv, he will remain in the capital, and Ukraine will push for emergency meetings of the UN Security Council and the EU Council to secure international assessment and response.

The situation on the ground: pro-Russian separatists appear to have seized control of the strategically located southeastern port town of Novoazovsk after days of shelling. Observers and local reports describe rebel checkpoints and restricted access; Ukrainian officials and some sources describe the forces as Russian troops, while rebels and their leaders claim many fighters are Russian citizens volunteering or on leave. Rebel leader Alexander Zakharchenko claimed 3,000–4,000 Russians were fighting with separatists. Ukrainian forces reportedly withdrew from Novoazovsk to preserve lives and reinforced defenses at nearby Mariupol as rebels threatened to advance on the key Azov Sea port.

International reactions include US, German and French concern and calls for explanations from Moscow; the OSCE held a special meeting in Vienna. Kyiv and Western leaders expressed alarm that the incursion could be intended to divert Ukrainian forces from Donetsk and Luhansk or to create a land corridor between Russia and Crimea. The fighting has contributed to heavy civilian and military casualties and large displacement since April.

During a Salvation Army fundraiser at the Tega Cay Wal‑Mart, an anonymous donor dropped a coin into a red kettle that was later appraised at Brownlee Jewelers as being worth about $1,200. The coin is expected to be sold and the proceeds donated to the Salvation Army. The report was by David Thackham.

The Air Force is warning service members to protect operational and personal information on social media under the slogan “Loose Tweets Destroy Fleets,” a modern take on WWII’s “Loose Lips Sink Ships.” AFCENT officials stress that while social media helps stay connected, posts can reveal sensitive details—location, unit ties, schedules or personal data—that adversaries (including ISIS sympathizers and lone actors) can exploit to target personnel and jeopardize missions. Recent incidents include online releases of names and contact information for military and diplomatic staff.

OPSEC (Operations Security) guidance: use strict privacy settings; check with supervisors before posting work-related material; encrypt emails; use secure phone lines; shred sensitive paper; and follow your unit’s Critical Information List. Public affairs handles media contacts, and suspected OPSEC violations should be reported to unit OPSEC managers. The message, echoed by other services, has drawn media attention and mixed public reaction. For more, consult Air Force Instruction 10-701 or your unit OPSEC manager.

An iron gate bearing the Nazi slogan "Arbeit macht frei" — stolen from the Dachau concentration camp memorial in November 2014 — has likely been recovered in western Norway, Bavarian and Norwegian police say. The find came after an anonymous tip to police in Bergen, who photographed the largely intact, mostly black gate in a storeroom; no arrests have been announced. German authorities had installed a replica at Dachau in 2015 after the theft. Dachau, opened in 1933 near Munich, was the prototype Nazi concentration camp and by liberation on April 29, 1945 had seen more than 200,000 prisoners pass through and over 41,000 deaths. The gate is to be returned to German authorities as soon as practical. The story recalls a similar 2009 theft of an "Arbeit macht frei" sign from Auschwitz, which was later recovered.

A 45-year-old man was arrested after trying to smash the protective display case of the Salisbury Cathedral copy of the 1215 Magna Carta with a hammer on Thursday afternoon. Alarms and a silent alert were triggered shortly before Evensong; staff, volunteers and members of the public restrained the suspect and held him until police arrived. The outer layer of the two-layer glass case sustained three holes, but the inner layer and the document itself were undamaged. No one was injured. The suspect is in custody at Melksham police station on suspicion of attempted theft, criminal damage and possession of an offensive weapon.

The cathedral has removed the Magna Carta for safe-keeping while the case is refurbished; a facsimile will be displayed and the visitor centre will reopen when possible. The Salisbury copy — one of only four surviving original 1215 Magna Cartas and described by the cathedral as its most beautiful — has been on display in the 13th-century Chapter House since 2015. Police have asked witnesses who have not yet spoken to them to call with the crime reference number.

Minnie Driver, 42, speaks candidly about her career, private life and new film in a wide-ranging Observer interview. Promoted early as a rising Hollywood star after an Oscar-nominated turn in Good Will Hunting, Driver says her trajectory stalled after a string of missteps and negative press—most notably the flop Hard Rain, on-set tensions, and a tabloid row over comments about Judi Dench that she says were taken out of context. She describes that period as “awful” but not bitter, accepting it as part of the job.

Driver is currently promoting Hunky Dory, a small British indie high-school musical set in 1976 Wales; she’s proud of her performance and the live-singing approach but frustrated by limited budget and a cut singing scene. She still aspires to big projects—an Oscar and work with directors like Danny Boyle and Martin Scorsese—but also craves the stability of US television: she wants a regular paycheck and to be able to pick up her son from school.

Much of the piece revisits her private life. Driver, who has long guarded the identity of her son Henry’s father, reveals he was a writer on her former US series The Riches; she declines to name him but says she no longer needs to protect him and that he’s become more involved in Henry’s life. She reflects on motherhood as changing her priorities—making her take work less seriously—and on her unconventional upbringing and life in Los Angeles, where she feels at home in outdoor pursuits but finds Hollywood culture difficult.

Driver presents herself as resilient and grounded: physically similar to her younger self and still British in accent, she says she’s learned to let negative things affect her briefly and move on, and is proud she hasn’t succumbed to self-destructive reactions. Hunky Dory is due in cinemas on 2 March. An editorial note clarifies a prior reference to Judi Dench.

Headline: Drudge amplifies Trump allies’ attacks on Ted Cruz after Colorado delegate sweep; Cruz fires back

Summary:
- The Drudge Report ran multiple provocative headlines accusing Ted Cruz of “rigging” Colorado’s GOP delegate process after Cruz’s campaign secured all 34 delegates at the state assembly. Zignal Labs analytics show Drudge’s coverage shaped social conversation about the win, with words like “cheating” prominent.
- Cruz publicly blamed Drudge for acting as an attack site for Donald Trump’s campaign in a radio interview, saying the site has been recycling old anti-Cruz pieces and downplaying Cruz victories (he cited a lack of “red siren” coverage after Colorado). Drudge responded by linking to a prior interview in which Cruz had praised the site.
- Commentary in the piece argues Drudge and other right-wing outlets (and Trump allies) are trying to delegitimize Cruz’s grassroots-organizing victories to prevent his ability to unite the conservative base at a contested convention. It notes Trump and his surrogates have loudly decried Colorado’s process as “crooked,” despite rules being set months earlier and similar caucus outcomes in other states.
- The article defends the Colorado outcome: Cruz invested organization and showed up; Trump largely didn’t. It criticizes Drudge’s headlines as misleading or sensationalized (e.g., claims of mass disenfranchisement) and frames the attacks as distraction from scrutiny of Trump’s charitable giving.
- Broader context: The piece also summarizes related campaign news — DNC criticism of Cruz, delegate shifts favoring Cruz in some contests, Trump discussing Ayn Rand, polling in New York showing Trump and Clinton leads, and various other political and national headlines.

An 8-year-old girl testified at the murder trial of her mother, 25-year-old Jessica Dutro, saying Dutro and her then-boyfriend, 24-year-old Brian Canady, regularly beat the children and gave them “lickins” and painful punishments. Dutro is charged with murder, murder by abuse and second-degree assault in the August 2012 death of her 4-year-old son, Zachary Dutro-Boggess, who was hospitalized with abdominal trauma that tore his bowel and was taken off life support two days later. Canady has pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter and second-degree assault.

The daughter — who was 7 when Zachary died and testified in soft, one-word answers — described prolonged time-outs where children had to “face the wall” with their hands raised and were hit if their arms dropped, and said both adults hit the children until they were sick. She told investigators “Jessica and Brian” beat Zachary and that Dutro warned her not to talk about being hit. The three surviving children now live with Dutro’s relatives.

Prosecutors introduced a Facebook message from Dutro to Canady in which she described putting Zachary in timeout because he “made her mad,” used a slur suggesting she believed he would be gay, and wrote that Canady would have to “work on” him. The judge ruled the message admissible, as were web searches prosecutors say Dutro made the day Zachary’s life support was terminated (including searches for anger management, parenting classes, free items and sex with strangers). Prosecutors say the evidence shows a pattern of torture and neglect that led to Zachary’s death.
