An Egyptian court on Tuesday sentenced 25-year-old pop singer Shaimaa Ahmed (known as Shyma) to two years in prison and a 10,000‑Egyptian‑pound fine after finding her guilty of “inciting debauchery” and publishing an indecent film over a recent music video. The clip for her song "I Have Issues" showed her in underwear and included sexually suggestive actions—most notably eating a banana—and drew more than a million viewers as well as strong conservative backlash. The video’s director was also sentenced to two years in prison in absentia and fined. Shyma, who was arrested Nov. 18, denied intent to offend and said some controversial scenes were added without her consent; she has the right to appeal. Observers note the verdict fits a pattern in Egypt of legal action against women over perceived moral transgressions—recent cases include prison terms for dancers in videos and sanctions against another singer, Sherine Abdel Wahab, over remarks about the Nile.

Leslie Kahn, 61, of Epping, New Hampshire, got stuck in her backyard pool on Aug. 11 after a ladder step broke while she was trying to get out. With no one else home and her cellphone inside, the breast cancer survivor used a pool pole to drag a chair holding her iPad within reach and posted a “911” plea for help on a local Facebook group, Epping Squawks. Neighbors and police responded quickly. After several attempts to improvise a solution failed, a step ladder was brought and Kahn was able to climb out safely. She thanked the community for their prompt help and reflected on the give-and-take of asking for and offering assistance.

The Federal Reserve rejected parts of Citigroup’s capital plan following this year’s bank “stress tests,” blocking the New York-based lender from raising its dividend or expanding share buybacks as it had proposed. CEO Vikram Pandit said internally that Citi still believes it can return “meaningful” capital to shareholders and will work with regulators on an acceptable plan.

Key points:
- Citigroup passed the stress test overall but its projected Tier 1 common capital ratio would fall to 4.9% under the Fed’s severe-recession scenario—below the Fed’s 5% minimum—if it pursued dividend increases or buybacks. The Fed did not object to Citi keeping its existing 1-cent quarterly dividend.
- The Fed’s scenario assumed a 13% unemployment rate, a 50% drop in stock prices and a 21% fall in home prices, producing aggregate losses of $534 billion across the 19 tested firms over nine quarters.
- Other firms whose capital plans were objected to included SunTrust Banks, Ally Financial and MetLife. SunTrust’s ratio would drop to 4.8% under its proposed capital actions; Ally’s ratio was estimated at 2.5% under the stress scenario regardless of its planned actions. MetLife’s total risk-based capital ratio would be 6% versus the Fed’s 8% threshold in the test.
- Most of the 19 banks did pass, allowing some (notably JPMorgan and Wells Fargo) to raise dividends or authorize buybacks; JPMorgan announced a 20% dividend increase and a $15 billion buyback authorization.
- Market reaction: Citigroup stock fell about 3.2% on the news; results helped lift the KBW Bank Index overall after positive outcomes for other big banks.
- Background context: Citi still carries more than $200 billion of unwanted assets in its Citi Holdings unit, including over $100 billion of mortgages. Ally and others argued the Fed’s analysis overstated certain risks or failed to credit management actions and other capital sources.

Overall, the Fed’s stress tests largely affirmed improved industry capital levels versus 2009 but constrained several banks’ immediate plans to return capital to shareholders by finding their proposed dividend or buyback programs would leave them short under the Fed’s severe-stress scenario.

Cory Booker, the 44-year-old mayor of Newark, handily won the Democratic primary for New Jersey’s special U.S. Senate election, taking 59% in a four-way race. He will face Republican Steven Lonegan in the October special election and is heavily favored in a state that hasn’t sent a Republican to the Senate since 1972. Booker’s victory was decisive despite sustained criticism from the progressive left.

Progressive critics argue Booker is too close to Wall Street and Silicon Valley, portrays himself as a populist while being an elite technocrat, and favors pragmatic, neoliberal solutions over structural reforms. Some commentators say his appeal to the party could be more about his race and celebrity than left-leaning policy reliability. Others counter that Booker’s pragmatism and ability to get things done make him a valuable Democratic senator who will vote reliably on many issues.

Booker’s biography—son of pioneering Black IBM executives, standout student-athlete, Stanford class president, Rhodes Scholar at Oxford, Yale Law graduate, anti-corruption Newark councilman and mayor—underscores his establishment credentials and cultivated public profile. He campaigned as a unifier and pragmatist rather than an ideologue, positioning himself for general-election appeal.

Observers debate his national ambitions: supporters see a potential next-generation Democratic star with broad appeal; detractors fear he will be a media-focused, elite-oriented senator more interested in profile than progressive policy. Booker will have to run again next year for a full term after winning the special election.

Colin Kaepernick’s national-anthem protest — kneeling to draw attention to racial injustice and police brutality — has spread beyond him. Seahawks cornerback Jeremy Lane joined the protest by sitting during the anthem, and teammates including linebacker Bobby Wagner and receiver Doug Baldwin are considering joining or staging a team-wide action. Wagner emphasized any action would be collective, not individual, saying the team wants to show unity. Baldwin said the locker room has discussed it, has heard support from veterans, and has been in contact with Kaepernick. Coach Pete Carroll expressed support for Lane’s right to protest and left the decision to players; other teammates such as Michael Bennett publicly backed Lane. The Seahawks will host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday (the season opener, coincidentally on September 11), and attention will be on whether the team will sit or otherwise act together during the anthem. The piece notes Kaepernick’s stated reason for kneeling — protesting a country that oppresses black people and people of color — and cites President Obama framing the tactic as a messy but valid part of democracy.

A Brussels appeals court has ordered retired Belgian King Albert II to take a DNA paternity test to determine whether he is the father of 50-year-old artist Delphine Boël. Albert, who abdicated in 2013 and is no longer immune to legal proceedings, must submit to a saliva test within three months or be legally presumed her father; his lawyers may still challenge the ruling. Earlier court-ordered testing in 2013 established that Jacques Boël — previously thought to be her father — is not biologically related to her. Boël has pursued legal recognition of her parentage for more than a decade; her lawyers welcomed the court’s emphasis on “acting in the interests of the child.” The matter first drew public attention after a 1999 biography alleged an extramarital relationship by Albert in the 1960s. There was no immediate comment from the royal household.

Democrat Jon Tester was declared the winner of Montana’s U.S. Senate race over Republican Rep. Denny Rehberg after a close, expensive contest. Speaking in Great Falls, Tester urged lawmakers to set aside partisanship and address pressing national issues—particularly the federal deficit, taxes, the economy—and to curb the “relentless, secretive political spending” that flooded his race. Tester (56), a farmer, led by about 16,000 votes late Wednesday with 48.5% to Rehberg’s nearly 45% and Libertarian Dan Cox taking a notable 6.5%. Rehberg, a long-time Montana politician, conceded Wednesday, praising Tester and underscoring their shared commitment to the state.

Tester called for greater transparency of outside and “dark” money in federal elections; observers estimated outside spending on the matchup exceeded $30 million, making it the costliest in Montana history when combined with roughly $20 million the candidates spent themselves. Tester also expressed hopes Congress will pursue deficit reduction, tax reform, and consider his stalled wilderness/jobs bill that would add protected wilderness and identify new logging acreage.

The Associated Press called the race early Wednesday, though some county counts—most notably in Yellowstone (Billings)—continued into the evening due to machine problems and late registrants. The document also briefly notes other Senate outcomes: Democrat Heidi Heitkamp’s narrow win in North Dakota over Republican Rick Berg, who conceded pending final canvass results.

Tsai Ing-wen of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) won Taiwan’s presidential election decisively, poised to become the island’s first female president. Early returns showed Tsai with about 60% of the vote to Kuomintang (KMT) candidate Eric Chu’s roughly 30% with about half the ballots counted. Chu conceded, apologized to supporters and resigned as KMT chair; Premier Mao Chi-kuo also resigned. The KMT also lost its legislative majority, though final seat distribution remained uncertain amid strong showings by independents and smaller parties.

Tsai campaigned on preserving the status quo—de facto independence—while refusing to endorse the idea that Taiwan and China are one nation to be reunified. She urged dignity and reciprocity in cross-strait ties, warned against provocations, and pledged cooperation with other parties and to uphold Taiwan’s democracy. Beijing, which views Taiwan as a breakaway province and has warned it could use force if Taiwan declares formal independence, has largely taken a wait-and-see stance; analysts expect China may respond with diplomatic or economic pressure if Tsai is perceived to move toward formal independence.

Economic concerns—stagnant growth, low wages and housing affordability—played a major role in voters’ dissatisfaction with the KMT, which had overseen improved ties with China under outgoing President Ma Ying-jeou. The vote signals Taiwanese desire to keep distance from Beijing while maintaining stable relations. The campaign also briefly united politicians in condemning the online bullying of a 16-year-old pop singer who was compelled to apologize in a China-related controversy.

A high-speed passenger train derailed near Santiago de Compostela, Spain, on the night of July 24, 2013, killing about 80 people and injuring dozens more (around 94–95 hospitalized; many critically). The eight-carriage Renfe train, carrying some 218–247 people on a Madrid–Ferrol service, left the tracks on a curve about 2–3 miles from Santiago, hit a concrete wall, caught fire and piled up; security footage shows carriages jack‑knifing, overturning and one carriage propelled into the air. Many victims were recovered at the scene; hospitals and emergency services were overwhelmed and blood drives and other aid efforts were mounted.

Investigators quickly focused on excessive speed as a likely cause. Witnesses and media reports — including video analysis — said the train may have been traveling roughly 120–190 km/h (about 75–120+ mph) where the limit was about 80 km/h (50 mph). The 52‑year‑old driver, Francisco José Garzón Amo, a 30‑year Renfe veteran who reportedly posted about high speeds on social media, survived with minor injuries and was under police guard in hospital and formally under investigation though not initially arrested. Officials also probed why speed‑control systems did not prevent overspeeding.

Spain’s prime minister and the king visited the site; national and regional mourning was declared and scheduled festivities for St. James’s feast day were canceled. One U.S. citizen and at least one Mexican were among the dead; several foreign nationals were injured. Renfe and infrastructure manager Adif launched inquiries; authorities said initial checks showed no obvious train maintenance fault, and multiple investigations aimed to establish the precise causes. The crash was described as one of Europe’s worst rail disasters in recent decades.

A 22-year-old Disneyland outdoor vendor, Christian Barnes of Long Beach, was arrested Wednesday on suspicion of possessing a destructive device after a small explosion in a trash can in Mickey’s Toontown Tuesday evening. The blast, believed to have been caused by dry ice placed inside a plastic bottle, caused no injuries or significant damage but prompted a roughly two‑hour evacuation of the Toontown area. Barnes, held on $1 million bail, is cooperating with investigators; police said the incident appears isolated and not tied to other recent dry‑ice explosions in Anaheim. Disneyland said it is working closely with authorities.

Summary:

- Humanitarian and military action in Iraq: The U.S., joined by Australia, France and the UK, conducted humanitarian airdrops and coordinated airstrikes to assist and protect the town of Amerli, which has been besieged by ISIS since mid-June. Amerli, about 70 miles north of Baquba, is home to fewer than 20,000 residents, many Shiite Turkmen, who face severe shortages of food, water, power and medical care and feared an “imminent massacre.” U.N. and Iraqi video showed desperate scenes reminiscent of the Sinjar crisis for Yazidis. U.S. Central Command also reported additional strikes near Mosul to support Iraqi and Kurdish forces and humanitarian efforts, bringing CENTCOM’s total to 115 strikes across Iraq.

- Yazidi women and girls trafficked: The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that ISIS has abducted and moved hundreds of Yazidi women from Iraq into Syria and “distributed” roughly 300 women among its fighters. SOHR said it confirmed at least 27 cases where women were sold or forcibly married to ISIS militants for about $1,000; some victims have reportedly been forced to convert to Islam. The Yazidi population suffered mass displacement to Mount Sinjar and Kurdistan, prompting air drops and later intervention; about 122,600 people from Sinjar district have sought refuge in Kurdistan, according to USAID.

- Continued violence and attacks: Multiple attacks across Iraq were reported, including suicide bombings and roadside bombs that killed and wounded Iraqi soldiers near Baghdad and in southern towns such as Yousifiya, Mahmoudiya and Latifiyah. Sectarian tensions and the ongoing power struggle since 2003 were cited as background to ISIS gains.

- Regional and international concern: Saudi King Abdullah warned that extremist advances in Iraq and Syria pose a threat to Europe and the U.S. and urged stronger international response. Western governments were deliberating responses; President Obama was awaiting military options from his defense team while surveillance flights over Syria had been ordered. Britain raised its domestic terror threat level to “severe.”

- ISIS brutality and regional spillover: In Lebanon, ISIS released a video showing the beheading of a captured Lebanese soldier from an earlier Arsal clash; militants had briefly seized the border town and taken 19 soldiers hostage, demanding prisoner releases. The group’s brutality and territorial gains have increased regional alarm.

- Broader context: The reporting underscores ISIS’s campaign of territorial expansion across parts of Iraq and Syria, associated mass displacement, sectarian persecution (especially against Yazidis and Shiite communities), and the international community’s increasingly active—though cautious—military and humanitarian responses.

Cell-phone use in theaters has erupted into a high-profile debate as increasingly common disruptions — texting, ringing phones and even an audience member storming the stage to plug in his charger — collide with traditional expectations of a dark, quiet auditorium. The flashpoint events this summer included a 19-year-old, Nick Silvestri, who jumped onstage at the Broadway play Hand to God and tried to plug his iPhone into a prop outlet (it was fake). Silvestri later apologized at a publicity-stunt-style press conference, saying he had been drinking, didn’t realize the stage was off-limits and that he’d learned about theater etiquette from the reaction. Producers used the incident to generate publicity for the show, which has struggled at the box office despite critical praise.

Also grabbing headlines was veteran actress Patti LuPone, who, without breaking character, took a texting patron’s phone during her Off-Broadway show Shows for Days and later warned that phone distractions “destroy” the world actors work to create — saying the problem has made her question continuing to work onstage. The piece notes similar past confrontations (e.g., Frances McDormand stopping a show when a phone rang) and points to a generational divide: younger, mobile-native audiences and tourists are more likely to treat devices as indispensable, while theater professionals and many long-time patrons see such use as rude and corrosive to live performance.

Overall, the incidents underline growing tension over theater etiquette in the mobile era, with performers increasingly taking direct action and producers sometimes turning disruptions into publicity — but also renewing discussions about how to enforce norms and protect the live-theater experience.

A 10-year-old family beagle named Bailey was killed after four dogs from a neighboring yard—three pit bulls and a mixed breed—escaped through a hole in a shared fence and attacked the dog in the 2900 block of Ninth Street North in Texas City. Thirteen-year-old Brittany Baker witnessed the attack when she arrived home from school; her father, Steve Baker, described the dogs “shaking [Bailey] like a rag doll.” Police and animal control responded and eventually secured the dogs; the neighbor boarded up the hole afterward.

Texas City police declared all four dogs “dangerous” under the city ordinance. That designation requires owners to keep animals in a secure, at least six-foot enclosure with a mechanical lock, microchip/tagging, visible warning signs, annual registration and $100,000 liability insurance; the owner has 15 days to appeal. Two dogs were initially taken by animal control, later retrieved by the owner.

Following the attack, grieving owners hoped the incident would raise awareness about dangerous animals. In a surprising turn, the neighbor and owner of the four dogs, Emerald White, has filed a lawsuit in 405th District Court seeking up to $1 million, claiming she was bitten and injured when she entered the Baker yard to retrieve her dogs after they escaped. White’s suit also alleges the Bakers failed to confine Bailey. The Bakers say they had repaired fence slats for their side and had urged the neighbor to fix his portion. Police say this was the first reported problem with the four dogs.

A State College police detective testified at a preliminary hearing for 18 members of Penn State’s Beta Theta Pi fraternity in the death of 19-year-old pledge Tim Piazza, saying surveillance video from the fraternity house showed Piazza “looked dead, he looked like a corpse.” The footage, shown at the Bellefonte hearing to decide whether to send the case to trial, documents Piazza’s severe intoxication and injuries after a Feb. 2 hazing event that prosecutors say forced him to consume a life-threatening amount of alcohol. Detective David Scicchitano described Piazza as unconscious and limp after an initial serious fall around 11:22 p.m., later left alone on a couch, and repeatedly falling, hitting his head and stomach, and staggering toward the basement stairs. He was not seen again for about two hours until brothers found him in the basement and carried him upstairs, by which time he had labored breathing, had “lost all color,” and some members believed he might be dead. Piazza died Feb. 4 of a traumatic brain injury and severe abdominal bleeding; his blood-alcohol level was dangerously high. The defendants face charges ranging from involuntary manslaughter to felony aggravated assault, and the Beta Theta Pi chapter has also been named as a defendant. Penn State has permanently banned the chapter, citing a persistent pattern of excessive drinking, drug use and hazing.

A major eruption of Kilauea on Hawaii’s Big Island forced widespread evacuations, caused earthquakes and destroyed structures as lava and hazardous gases spread through residential areas.

Key events and impacts
- Beginning in early May (reports span May 3–8, 2018 with follow-ups into 2019 updates), Kilauea’s east rift zone produced multiple fissures in Lower Puna, notably in Leilani Estates and Lanipuna Gardens. More than 110 earthquakes occurred in 24 hours; one strong temblor was upgraded to magnitude 6.9 (the largest since 1975) and earlier quakes reached ~5.0.
- Lava erupted from multiple fissures, sometimes fountaining tens to 150 feet and advancing across streets, woodlands and yards. At least one home and other structures were destroyed; dozens to hundreds of residents evacuated (orders affected about 1,500–1,700 people in Leilani Estates alone).
- Five or more vents opened in unusual locations far from Kilauea’s summit; new ground cracks, steaming, ash and continued seismicity were reported. Scientists warned additional vents and outbreaks were possible and that the duration was uncertain.
- Sulfur dioxide (SO2) and other volcanic gases reached hazardous concentrations in evacuation zones. Authorities warned elderly people, children and anyone with respiratory problems to leave immediately. Laze plumes (acidic steam + glass particles) formed where lava entered the ocean, presenting further health and safety hazards.
- Utilities and infrastructure were impacted: about 14,000 Hawaii Electric Light customers initially lost power (half later restored), and Puna Geothermal Venture shut down. Road closures and temporary flight restrictions were put in place. The Coast Guard set marine exclusion zones near ocean lava entries.
- Emergency response: Hawaii County activated full emergency operations; Gov. David Ige signed an emergency proclamation, activated the Hawaii National Guard for evacuations/security, and shelters were opened (Pahoa and Keaau community centers). The American Red Cross and FEMA were assisting. Authorities restricted access to affected neighborhoods and warned against sightseeing and drone flights.

Scientific status and hazards
- The eruption followed intense seismic swarms and collapse/explosive events at summit craters (including Halema‘uma‘u), which increased magma movement downrift into the east rift zone. USGS/Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO) noted ongoing intrusion, subsidence, ash bursts, and high earthquake rates; future vent locations were unpredictable.
- Primary hazards: lava inundation and fire, gas exposure (SO2), ash and vog, ground cracking, methane explosion risk in some areas, unstable lava deltas and dangerous laze at ocean entry points. N95 masks may filter ash but do not protect against volcanic gases.

Human stories and guidance
- Residents described dramatic, noisy eruptions, strong shaking, burning vegetation and sulfurous air. Many fled with little time, helped evacuate elderly neighbors, or lost homes. Officials allowed limited, vetted access for residents to retrieve items when conditions permitted.
- Authorities urged preparedness: follow evacuation orders, bring emergency supplies and medications, avoid affected areas, stay indoors during ashfall, and seek medical attention for severe gas exposure. Looting and vandalism would be prosecuted.

Overall picture
Kilauea’s eruption in Lower Puna produced rapidly changing, dangerous conditions—lava flows, multiple fissures, strong earthquakes and toxic gases—prompting mandatory evacuations, infrastructure disruptions and an extended emergency response. Scientists emphasized the unpredictability of new vents and the need for residents to remain alert and follow official guidance.

Jon Gosselin is at the center of competing media stories involving girlfriend Hailey Glassman and Octomom Nadya Suleman. Glassman publicly accused Gosselin of emotional abuse on television, but a source close to Gosselin tells Fox411 the segment was staged: the pair allegedly agreed to have her make the accusations to generate TV appearances and income while Gosselin pursues another reality show. That same source says Gosselin was indeed negotiating a stunt-oriented reality project with Suleman—despite his public denials—and hoped to be paid heavily for staged dates. Insiders portray Gosselin as financially strained, relying on managers and publicists to broker deals, and blaming youthful marriage and too many children for his personal problems; his relationship with estranged wife Kate is described as estranged and compartmentalized. Meanwhile Gosselin has tweeted gratitude to Glassman for helping him reform, apologized publicly (including at a synagogue appearance where he said he’s seeking spiritual growth), and said he and Glassman were "slowing things down" rather than breaking up. Glassman posted on Twitter that she’s “semi-single” and taking time for herself.

No ticket matched Tuesday night’s Mega Millions numbers (7, 25, 43, 56, 59; Mega Ball 13), so the jackpot rolled to an estimated $502 million for Friday’s drawing (cash option $301 million). This marks the fourth time the 16‑year game’s jackpot has climbed past $500 million. The current roll began after the last jackpot win on Jan. 5 ($451 million, claimed by Shane Missler), and since then there have been 33 winners of $1 million or more. Only three Mega Millions jackpots have been larger: $656 million (2012, split), $648 million (2013, split), and $536 million (2016). Mega Millions is played in 44 states, Washington, D.C., and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

A Pete Hoekstra Super Bowl ad attacking Democratic Sen. Debbie Stabenow has drawn widespread criticism for racial insensitivity. The 30-second spot, filmed in California, depicts a young Asian woman riding a bike past rice paddies and speaking in broken English to thank “Debbie Spenditnow” for weakening the U.S. economy and “taking our jobs.” The ad never names China but uses Asian-themed imagery on a campaign site and accuses Stabenow of sending American dollars to China.

Republicans and Asian-American groups condemned the commercial: GOP consultant Nick De Leeuw called it “appalling,” the Michigan chapter of the nonpartisan Asian & Pacific Islander American Vote group said it promotes harmful stereotypes, and other Republican strategists also criticized the creative. Democrats labeled the ad hypocritical, noting Hoekstra’s long House tenure and recent work for a Washington lobbying firm, and launched counter-sites and ads.

Hoekstra defended the spot as satirical and focused on spending and jobs lost to international competitors, saying it had generated strong positive reaction and “jump started the debate.” His campaign began airing the ad statewide and plans further cable buys. Critics argue Hoekstra could have made his economic point without the racial caricature; the backlash has become a campaign issue as Stabenow leverages it for fundraising.

Daybreakers is a 2010 R-rated action-horror take on the vampire genre from Australian brothers Michael and Peter Spierig. Set in 2019, a vampire plague has turned most of humanity undead and transformed society into a dark mirror of the old world — corporate-suited vampires commuting at night, blood-spiked coffee chains, blood farms that treat humans as livestock, and an emerging underclass of feral “subsiders” born when vampires go without blood. The central crisis is a global shortage of human blood, a thinly veiled metaphor for resource depletion.

Ethan Hawke plays Edward Dalton, a vampire hematologist who despises preying on humans and is trying to develop a synthetic blood substitute for his blood-provision corporation run by Sam Neill’s profit-driven executive. Edward switches to animal blood and, after encountering a human resistance group led by Claudia Karvan’s Audrey and Willem Dafoe’s raspy, charismatic Elvis (who has somehow reverted to human), becomes embroiled in a plot about a possible cure and the fate of both species.

Critics praise Daybreakers for its inventive concept, satiric tone, punchy visual style and unapologetic gore — a welcome counterpoint to more romantic, sanitized vampire fare — and for lively performances by Hawke and Dafoe. However, many reviews note the film’s B-movie sensibility, script holes, and a mid- to late-film sag in momentum and engagement: the Spierig brothers’ worldbuilding is strong and imaginative, but the story devolves into familiar horror-chase rhythms and a climax that some found underwhelming. Overall, it’s regarded as smart, entertaining exploitation cinema that refreshes classic vampire tropes even as it struggles to fully deliver on its promise.

On August 7, St. George mother Deborah Skouson posted on Facebook asking for help finding a specific pink, flowered Target shirt her 10‑year‑old daughter Cami—who has autism and is strongly attached to that exact shirt—would wear. After a few matches on eBay proved insufficient, Skouson offered to pay for shirts and shipping. The plea went viral (more than 22,000 shares, picked up by a local anchor and pages with millions of followers), and offers arrived from around the world. Within days she had been promised or received more than 135 identical shirts, sent even from Germany, England and the Philippines; Target also offered to make larger versions so the shirt will fit Cami as she grows. Skouson said the outpouring restored her faith in the internet and community kindness, though some critics urged she not reinforce her daughter’s fixation—an opinion she respectfully rejected, saying she knows what’s best for her child.

Danish inventor Peter Madsen was sentenced to life in prison by Copenhagen City Court after being found guilty of premeditated murder, aggravated sexual assault and desecration of a corpse in the death of Swedish journalist Kim Wall. Wall, 30, disappeared after boarding Madsen’s private submarine on Aug. 10; Madsen initially gave conflicting accounts, later admitting he dismembered her body and threw parts into the sea. Her remains were recovered in Køge Bay over subsequent weeks.

Prosecutors argued the killing was sexually motivated and planned, presenting recovered deleted messages in which Madsen described fantasies of tying, torturing and murdering a woman and evidence he brought tools and heavy objects consistent with planned assault and disposal. A court-ordered psychiatric report described him as having psychopathic traits and lacking empathy but not psychotic. The judge rejected Madsen’s claim that Wall died accidentally from exhaust fumes, calling his explanations implausible and noting his repeated changes of story.

The verdict, unusually severe for Denmark, followed an 11-day trial spread over seven weeks that drew international attention. Madsen, who admitted only to mistreating the corpse, said he would appeal; he was also ordered to pay damages to Wall’s boyfriend. Wall’s parents attended much of the trial; she had been an internationally published journalist.

On the evening of June 2, 2015, an articulated Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) Route 148 bus ran a red light at Michigan Avenue and Lake Street during rush hour, striking two pedestrians and several vehicles before mounting the curb and coming to rest on the sidewalk near 205 N. Michigan Ave. One pedestrian, 51-year-old Aimee Coath of Flossmoor, was pinned beneath the bus, taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital and pronounced dead. Eight others, including the bus driver (48), were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries.

Witnesses described chaotic scenes: the bus reportedly hit cars, went up on the curb and struck a concrete wall; bystanders attempted rescue and paramedics freed the woman from under the bus. At least 10 ambulances responded; parts of Michigan and Lake were closed for hours and buses rerouted. The driver, employed by CTA for under a year as an operator, was ticketed for failing to stop at a red light and for “failure to exercise due care.” Police said no criminal charges had been filed at that time and investigators were reviewing onboard video and awaiting final drug-test results. CTA officials said it was too soon to determine disciplinary action.

Two recent college alumni have embraced the tiny-house-on-wheels lifestyle and hit the road with their dogs, trading traditional homes for compact, mobile living to pursue work and adventure.

Kelly Tousley (’11) and Curtiss O’Rorke Stedman converted a utility trailer into a 98-square-foot, roadworthy home in June and left Juneau, Alaska, to tour for about a year supporting Curtiss’s growing music career. Their trailer, built in eight months for about $8,600, includes vinyl floors, lime-green walls, solar electricity, a kitchenette, a curtained bathroom (no running water) and a bench that folds into a queen bed. They sold or gave away most belongings to downsize, found the purging emotionally challenging (plants and sentimental clothes were hardest to part with), and plan to try the tiny lifestyle for at least a year before reassessing. They tow the trailer around Alaska’s road system and into the Lower 48; updates are on paygasnotrent.com.

The story also notes another couple, Kristin Connolly Schillaci (’05) and Tony Schillaci (’06), who spent a year traveling in an 18-foot 1980 Coachman, driving 25,000 miles to 30 juried art shows in 35 states to sell Kristin’s fine art photography, also accompanied by two large dogs.

Both examples illustrate the do-it-yourself, downsizing ethos of the tiny-house movement: choosing mobility and minimalism to pursue creative careers and a nomadic lifestyle.

A powerful 7.2-magnitude earthquake struck eastern Turkey near Van on Sunday, killing at least 265 people and injuring around 1,140, officials said. The quake’s epicenter was about 16 km northeast of Van at a shallow depth, and roughly 200 aftershocks—including a magnitude-6.0 event—followed. The worst damage concentrated in the town of Ercis, where many multi-storey buildings and a student dormitory collapsed; Van city and surrounding villages were also hit. Official tallies reported about 970–1,000 buildings destroyed across the affected zone.

Rescue operations continued amid a race against time to find survivors trapped under rubble. Crews—including 2,400 rescue workers, 680 medics, 12 rescue dogs, cranes and heavy machinery—were cutting through concrete and rebar; teams pulled several people alive from ruins, including one who called for help on his mobile. Authorities warned the death toll could rise as more outlying areas are reached; officials estimated dozens to perhaps a few hundred people remained trapped at certain sites. Many scenes showed desperate relatives and survivors sleeping outdoors in freezing conditions.

Local and national authorities mobilized emergency response: tents and supplies were being distributed, the Turkish Red Crescent set up shelters (including in a stadium), and ambulances and air ambulances were deployed. The airport at Van sustained damage, hampering logistics. The government said it could handle the response but accepted international offers of help from multiple countries.

Commentators and officials noted vulnerabilities that worsened the impact: some rural buildings of mud brick were almost entirely destroyed, and building regulations have often been ignored, increasing collapse risk. Van province is seismically active, and the quake was the strongest in Turkey since the devastating 1999 events that killed nearly 20,000 people.

Funny or Die launched "Live Funny or Die" on Nov. 8 to provide dedicated comedic coverage of the 2012 presidential campaign. The debut video features comedians impersonating many GOP contenders — including Mitt Romney, Ron Paul, Michele Bachmann, Rick Perry and a Herman Cain parody — and a cameo by an Obama impersonator. The sketch lampoons campaign personas and modern internet culture: Romney is portrayed as flat and tone-deaf, the Herman Cain bit (played by Mike Tyson) jokes about Cain’s simplistic "1-1-1" style while breaking into a pizza jingle, Darrell Hammond riffs on Perry with a hybrid Clinton/Trump impression, Bachmann’s bit references Marcus Bachmann and Craigslist, and Ron Paul frets about camera framing. The Obama impersonator (Reggie Brown) closes by joking that viral attention boils down to "cats and breasts." The piece ends by undercutting traditional political rhetoric with internet-savvy, irreverent humor.

Former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner, convicted in the sexual assault of an unconscious, intoxicated woman after a January 2015 fraternity party, was sentenced on June 2 to six months in county jail and three years' probation — a punishment that sparked widespread outrage for being too lenient. Prosecutors had sought six years. Jail booking records indicate Turner, 20 at the time of sentencing, is expected to be released on Sept. 2 after serving roughly half his term (three months) for good behavior, and will be kept in protective custody while incarcerated.

The case drew further criticism after Turner’s statement blaming Stanford’s “party culture” and peer pressure for his actions and his father’s remark that the conviction was “a steep price to pay for 20 minutes of action.” Witness accounts say Turner penetrated the unconscious woman until two Swedish students intervened and tackled him as he tried to flee. The light sentence and the tone of the statements intensified public outrage over perceived special treatment for a privileged, high-profile athlete.

In August 2014, Lund University chemistry professor Charlotta Turner received an urgent text from her PhD student Firas Jumaah saying he might not finish his thesis because he and his family were trapped in Iraq and in immediate danger from ISIS. Jumaah, a Yazidi, had returned to visit family when ISIS attacked Sinjar and nearby areas, massacring and enslaving civilians. He and his wife and two small children were hiding in a disused bleach factory as ISIS fighters roamed nearby.

Distressed, Turner contacted the university’s security chief, Per Gustafson, who quickly arranged a private security firm and armed transport. Within days four mercenaries in two Land Cruisers extracted Jumaah and his immediate family and took them to safety at Erbil airport. Jumaah later completed his PhD in Sweden and now works for a pharmaceutical company in Malmö; the family survived the occupation and have nearly finished repaying the university for the rescue. Gustafson called the operation unique, and Turner described her intervention as an obvious moral duty to save her student.

The document argues that the early 2000s will be remembered as a Superhero Era and warns that the current boom is likely to peak and then decline, as similar fads have. It criticizes Warner Bros.’ aggressive plan to release about 10 DC films from 2016–2020 as short-sighted and potentially accelerating audience fatigue amid an already crowded superhero slate (studios have 20+ such films planned). While Marvel has built hits on humor, strong casting and steady quality (Iron Man, Guardians of the Galaxy), Warner’s track record beyond Batman and Superman is inconsistent (Catwoman, Jonah Hex, Green Lantern). Warner’s DC strategy leans toward darker tones, heavy use of new or lesser-known actors (Gal Gadot as Wonder Woman, Ezra Miller as The Flash, Jason Momoa as Aquaman, Ray Fisher as Cyborg) and rebooting failed properties, which the piece suggests is risky.

The article also summarizes recent blockbuster-era news: Warner’s announced DC schedule (Suicide Squad, Batman v Superman, Wonder Woman, two Justice League films, The Flash, Aquaman, Shazam, Green Lantern reboot, a Cyborg movie), Marvel developments (possible Civil War-based Captain America 3 with Robert Downey Jr. in a pivotal role), Michael Keaton saying he’d reprise Batman if Tim Burton directed, Jeremy Renner expressing interest in a Hawkeye solo film, and a fast-tracked Lego Batman spin-off. Overall the piece urges Warner to consider stepping back and diversifying rather than racing Marvel into an oversaturated market.

Netflix will release the award-winning documentary Virunga, teaming with Leonardo DiCaprio’s Appian Way (DiCaprio as executive producer). Directed by Orlando von Einsiedel, the film follows the embattled park rangers of Virunga National Park in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo as they protect endangered mountain gorillas from poachers, armed militias and industrial encroachment. Virunga profiles rangers including an ex–child soldier, a gorilla carer and a Belgian conservationist, and highlights the broader threats to biodiversity and local communities. The documentary, which has won prizes at festivals including Tribeca and DOXA, will debut simultaneously on Netflix and in select New York and Los Angeles theaters on November 7. Netflix says the partnership aims to bring the story to a global audience; DiCaprio framed the release as an opportunity to inform and inspire action on conservation issues. The deal also adds to ongoing tensions between Netflix and exhibitors over theatrical windows.

Former Secretary of State and retired four-star general Colin Powell confirmed that personal emails leaked online by hackers are authentic. The messages, first reported by BuzzFeed and posted on DCLeaks.com (a site U.S. officials have linked to Russian-linked actors), span mid-2014 to August 2016 and reportedly total thousands of items.

Key revelations from the leaked correspondence:
- Harsh criticism of Donald Trump: In a June 17 email Powell called Trump a “national disgrace” and “international pariah,” saying Trump was “in the process of destroying himself.” In other messages he condemned Trump’s role in promoting the “birther” movement as racist, said Trump “takes us for idiots,” and argued Trump’s overtures to Black voters were futile.
- Views on Benghazi and Hillary Clinton: Powell described the prolonged investigations into the 2012 Benghazi attacks as a “stupid witch hunt,” while assigning some blame to the ambassador on the ground and to leaders including the intelligence community and “yes, HRC.” He also expressed frustration at being linked to Clinton’s private-email controversy and lamented personal and professional fallout from the broader controversy.
- Private politics and endorsements: Powell, who has called himself a lifelong Republican but twice endorsed Barack Obama previously, said in 2014 he would “rather not have to vote for” Hillary Clinton despite respecting her. Leaked exchanges show friends and advisers pressing him about a possible endorsement of Clinton; Powell indicated he was delaying any decision.
- Other context: The leaks were publicized amid broader concerns about websites (including DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0) that security experts and some U.S. officials believe are tied to Russian intelligence and have released hacked Democratic Party-related materials to influence the 2016 election. Powell said his privacy had been violated and warned journalists to respect it. The story continued to develop as additional documents were examined.

Michael Lohan has proposed to Kate Major, Jon Gosselin's ex. Lohan, 49, said their five-year relationship is built on friendship and waited to announce the engagement until his daughter Lindsay’s situation improved; he has been urging her to seek rehab. He described getting Major’s father's approval during a visit to Florida and confirmed the couple plans to have children. Major, 27, said she’s “really happy,” has begun wedding planning—mentioning talks with bridesmaids and a possible late-year ceremony at Oheka Castle in New York—and praised the ring. She added she and Jon Gosselin do not speak but wished him and Kate Gosselin well. The article also notes the crawls are part of an Internet Archive effort to preserve referenced web pages to prevent broken links.

Netflix’s political drama House of Cards will end with its forthcoming sixth season, TVLine reports. The decision was made months earlier and is not a reaction to recent allegations against star Kevin Spacey, a Netflix rep confirmed. Production on Season 6 began earlier this month and the final season is slated to premiere in 2018.

The announcement came shortly after actor Anthony Rapp accused Spacey of making a sexual advance toward him when Rapp was 14. Spacey issued a statement saying he did not recall the encounter, apologized if he behaved as described, and said he now lives as a gay man. That prompted criticism—GLAAD’s president warned against using a coming-out as a way to deflect sexual-assault allegations. House of Cards creator Beau Willimon also issued a statement on the matter.

Creators Melissa James Gibson and Frank Pugliese had previously discussed the show’s future, noting Season 5’s pivot—Claire Underwood (Robin Wright) taking the presidency from Spacey’s Frank—and indicating there was more story to explore beyond the presidency, a direction Season 6 will conclude.

Secretary of State John Kerry said U.S. intelligence strongly points to pro-Russian separatists, likely aided by Russian forces, as responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine. Speaking on multiple Sunday shows, Kerry said it is “pretty clear” the missile system used was transferred from Russia to separatists, Ukrainians did not possess such systems in the area, and a recent convoy of armored vehicles and heavy weapons crossed from Russia into separatist-held territory. He cited video evidence of a launcher returning to Russia with a missing missile, reports that separatists moved through towns near the launch site, and accounts of separatists tampering with the crash site and removing bodies and plane parts—actions he warned have “seriously compromised” the investigation. Kerry called for full access to the site and described the episode as “a moment of truth for Russia.”

Kerry also addressed the Gaza conflict, saying the U.S. is hopeful for a near-term ceasefire and backing an Egyptian initiative while insisting that “you cannot reward terrorism” and that Israel has the right to defend itself against rocket attacks. He said he and President Obama have been in active contact with regional leaders and that he may soon travel to the region to press for a ceasefire. Kerry was briefly caught on an open mic criticizing aspects of Israel’s operations; on-air he defended his reaction as emotional but reiterated support for Israel’s security needs.

The World Food Programme (WFP) produced a July assessment warning of severe food and nutrition deficiencies in northern Rakhine State, Myanmar, finding more than 80,000 children under five in majority‑Muslim areas were "wasting" and calling for assistance for over 225,000 people. That six‑page report was removed from public view after the Myanmar government requested a joint review; WFP replaced it with a statement that a revised, government‑aligned version was being prepared and should not be cited. WFP leadership later directed the original assessment be republished and said the findings stood, but said a fresh evaluation was needed because the situation deteriorated sharply after insurgent attacks on August 25 triggered a military crackdown and widespread displacement.

The episode has intensified criticism that UN agencies prioritized relations with Myanmar’s government and donor access over documenting and responding to Rohingya needs. Sources said prior WFP food‑aid reductions to some internally displaced Rohingya had likely worsened hunger, and the original assessment reported movement restrictions, blocked market access and military presence limiting food access. Since the August violence, humanitarian agencies have been denied free access to the conflict zones, a restriction WFP and others urge authorities to lift.

The broader crisis has driven more than half a million Rohingya into Bangladesh, where authorities are registering arrivals, restricting movement, and creating concentrated camps. Bangladesh provides temporary IDs and basic aid but does not formally recognize the Rohingya as refugees and is increasingly anxious about long‑term burden, security risks, and the difficulty of providing adequate shelter, nutrition, health care and education in overcrowded camps. Humanitarian actors warn of disease, recruitment risks by extremists, and the likelihood that many refugees will not return to Myanmar given the reported abuses.

Three inmates — Hossein Nayeri (37), Jonathan Tieu (20) and Bac Duong (43) — escaped from the Orange County Central Men’s Jail on a Friday after cutting through steel bars and plumbing ducts, accessing an unsecured recreational roof, and rappelling to the ground. The escape occurred sometime after a 5 a.m. head count and went unnoticed until an evening count about 16 hours later. Authorities say the cuts appeared professionally made, and investigators believe the men had outside help and possibly inside assistance.

Sheriff Sandra Hutchens described the fugitives as armed and dangerous, called the situation “every sheriff’s nightmare,” and said the department is reviewing jail policies and procedures. Hutchens identified Nayeri — who faces charges including kidnapping and torture and was extradited from Iran in 2014 — as the likely mastermind because of his background; prosecutors have described him as especially dangerous. Tieu and Duong are documented gang members with violent charges; Duong’s gang tattoos were released to aid identification. ICE had been unable to deport Duong due to his country of origin not accepting him.

Since the escape, deputies have served at least 30 warrants and arrested five people Wednesday believed to be connected to the breakout; more arrests were expected. Officials said some of those arrested are gang members, but names and details were withheld to protect the investigation. A $200,000 reward was offered for information leading to the inmates’ capture. Hutchens also visited Vietnamese-American neighborhoods appealing for community help.

The incident prompted immediate changes to inmate-count procedures to prevent a repeat, and renewed scrutiny of the aging Central Men’s Jail (built 1968), which lacks modern security technology. Tips can be reported to the Orange County Sheriff’s hotline at 714-628-7085 or anonymously to Crime Stoppers at 855-847-6227.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said on CNN that there is no evidence the missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 was the result of terrorism. Speaking three weeks into the search, she called the operation “a very difficult mission,” noted the multinational effort and declined to discuss U.S. intelligence capabilities, saying American intelligence is not geared toward plane crashes and that she would not detail what assets exist. 

Separately, Russia’s U.S. ambassador Sergey Kislyak told ABC that Crimea is now part of the Russian Federation and that Russia has no intent to cross Ukraine’s border, framing Russian forces in Crimea as operating on Russian territory and defending Russia’s regional role. He reiterated Russia’s view that resolving Ukraine’s crisis requires addressing rifts between the interim Kyiv government and the rest of the country, including constitutional changes, and expressed some hope for a diplomatic solution.

Freedom Industries Inc. — the company linked to a Jan. 9 chemical spill that contaminated Charleston, W.Va.’s, main water supply — has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of West Virginia. President Gary Southern signed the petition, which lists assets and liabilities each in the $1 million–$10 million range, names at least 200 creditors, and shows the top 20 creditors are owed $3.66 million.

The filing recounts details of the spill: a chemical used in coal-cleaning leaked from a storage tank and its containment area at Freedom’s facility, flowed into the Elk River and tainted the state’s largest water system. The petition notes the storage tank appears to have been pierced through its base by an object and cites a working theory that a nearby broken water line, causing ground freezing just before the spill, may have contributed to the failure.

In the aftermath, residents across a nine-county area were told not to use tap water except for flushing toilets; some schools and businesses closed for days. Restrictions have since been lifted for most people. The terminal that leaked had not been inspected by state officials since 2001, when it was under different ownership and stricter regulations; Freedom Industries bought the terminal the month before the incident. The company now faces multiple lawsuits and state and federal investigations.

Researchers measured tiny tidal tilting in Scotland’s Loch Ness caused not by the moon directly tugging the loch’s water but by ocean tidal loading: when North Sea tides (about 13 km east) press on the seafloor, they deform the Earth and slightly tilt the land on which the loch sits. Using distributed pressure sensors along the 35 km length of the loch, the team achieved depth measurements accurate to about 0.1 mm and demonstrated a net tilt signal corresponding to depth differences of roughly 1.5 mm between the loch’s ends depending on North Sea tide phase. The authors report a tilt accuracy better than 10−8 over 35 km, making Loch Ness effectively one of the longest and most precise natural tiltmeters, and this may be the first European lake observation of land-shifting tides from ocean tidal loading.

Multiple news reports and anonymous officials allege that Susan Rice, President Obama’s National Security Adviser, requested the unmasking of the identities of U.S. persons mentioned in intelligence reports that pertained to the Trump transition and campaign. Those unmasked names were reportedly distributed to senior National Security Council staff, some Defense Department officials, DNI James Clapper, CIA Director John Brennan and others. The underlying intelligence largely consisted of incidental collection — foreign-to-foreign or foreign-to-U.S. communications picked up during surveillance of foreign targets — in which U.S. identities are normally redacted unless unmasked for valid foreign-intelligence, national-security, or law-enforcement reasons.

The disclosures emerged from an NSC review of unmasking procedures conducted by Ezra Cohen-Watnick and from reporting by Bloomberg and other outlets. White House lawyers were said to have learned Rice requested identities on “dozens of occasions.” Supporters of Rice and some former officials say unmasking is a lawful practice when justified and there is no proven partisan motive. Critics argue the pattern raises civil-liberties and politicization concerns, noting the documents reportedly contained political details about Trump transition meetings and policy thinking and that some recipients beyond intelligence professionals may have seen the names.

The matter has become entangled with congressional oversight: House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes publicly revealed that Trump transition officials were incidentally collected and has been criticized for his handling of sensitive material after he viewed records at the White House. Democrats on the committee say they were shown the materials later and questioned why Nunes alone had access initially. The reports do not substantiate President Trump’s earlier tweet accusing President Obama of wiretapping Trump Tower; there is no evidence of an illegal wiretap or that Rice’s actions amounted to unlawful surveillance. Investigations by congressional intelligence committees into both possible ties between Trump associates and Russia and the unmasking/dissemination practices are ongoing. Rice has declined to comment beyond earlier statements that she was surprised by reports and knew nothing about specific allegations.

President Barack Obama used his final U.N. General Assembly address to defend globalization, democracy and cooperation while warning against rising nationalism, isolationism and strongman rule. He argued that open markets, accountable governance and international law remain the best foundations for progress, but acknowledged that globalization has exposed deep fault lines—economic dislocation, cultural anxieties and inequality—that require a “course correction” so the benefits of integration are more broadly shared.

Key themes and assertions:
- Diplomacy over military solutions: Obama reiterated that diplomatic engagement, not force, is the right path for resolving conflicts such as Syria’s civil war and for containing extremism, which he said cannot be solved by walls or simple isolation.
- Refugee crisis and humanitarian responsibility: He urged wealthy and well-positioned nations to do more for refugees, praising pledges at the U.N. and noting U.S. efforts to increase refugee admissions.
- Critique of authoritarianism and populism: He warned against the appeal of “aggressive nationalism,” crude populism and the “strongman” model — implicitly criticizing figures like Donald Trump and contrasting that approach with democratic norms, free media and human rights.
- Russia and international order: Obama rebuked Russia for using force to regain influence, warning such behavior diminishes long-term stature and security; he also stressed resolving disputes by law rather than militarization (citing the South China Sea).
- Record and legacy: He highlighted achievements of his presidency—restoring relations with Cuba, the Iran nuclear agreement, climate cooperation, reducing terrorists’ safe havens and progress in Myanmar—while conceding limits and unfinished business, including Middle East peace, Guantanamo closure and fully addressing refugee flows and rising extremism.
- Economic message: He defended free markets and innovation over protectionism, cautioning that trade wars and state control are counterproductive; he stressed the need to address inequality through policies like stronger labor rights and education.

Overall, Obama framed the choice facing the world as moving forward with reformed global integration and cooperative institutions versus retreating into isolation, division and authoritarianism, urging nations to choose the former.

Twitch streamer AnaPlaying accidentally set her hair on fire during a live League of Legends stream while casually flicking a lighter near her head. She didn’t notice for several seconds, then quickly patted out the flames. Though startled, she appeared unhurt and laughed off the mishap on camera as viewers looked on.

Justice Anthony Kennedy’s retirement highlights how broken Supreme Court nominations have become after recent partisan escalation. The process deteriorated in 2016 when Senate Republicans refused to consider Merrick Garland, citing an invented “election-year” rule, and Democrats retaliated by filibustering Neil Gorsuch—prompting Republicans to eliminate the Supreme Court filibuster. That tit-for-tat “Senate syndrome” has left the minority with virtually no check on confirmations when its rival controls the Senate, but also created a pattern where opposing control of the White House and Senate often means seats will remain vacant.

The stakes are unusually high: justices serve life terms often spanning decades, and a single vacancy can shift the Court’s balance permanently on issues from campaign finance to abortion and health care. That high-stakes randomness incentivizes extreme strategy—justices delay retirement for political reasons, presidents name younger nominees, and nominations become existential battles. The author argues this dynamic is understandable on both sides—Republicans for blocking Garland, Democrats for opposing Gorsuch—but destructive in consequence.

A proposed fix is to deescalate by instituting fixed, nonrenewable terms for justices (for example, 10 or 18 years), which would regularize vacancies, reduce the individual stakes of any single nomination, discourage politically timed retirements, and potentially draw bipartisan support. Without reform, confirmations will remain bitter, seats may stay open for long periods, and nominees will skew more ideologically extreme.

In the immediate politics of Kennedy’s retirement: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell vowed to confirm a Trump nominee before the midterms; Democrats, led by Chuck Schumer, demanded the vote wait until after the election, calling quick action hypocritical given the Garland blockade. Republicans hold a narrow majority and face some vulnerable senators who may be pressured either way. The confirmation fight is expected to be intense and expensive, with abortion rights and Roe v. Wade central issues. Trump has a short list of potential nominees, and timeline estimates based on past confirmations suggest a vote could occur in October; Kennedy’s resignation takes effect July 31.

A McDonald’s drive-thru worker in Doral, Fla., Pedro Viloria, jumped through the service window Tuesday morning to help an off-duty Miami-Dade police officer who lost consciousness while ordering breakfast with her two children. Surveillance footage shows the officer’s foot slipped off the brake and her SUV began rolling; Viloria chased the vehicle, pulled the woman from the SUV as it stopped against a curb, and comforted her children while bystanders and emergency responders arrived. A second McDonald’s employee performed CPR and paramedics took over; the officer was transported to a hospital. McDonald’s praised Viloria and the team for their quick action; officials have not released updates on the officer’s condition.

Central Europe is facing widespread, severe flooding as swollen rivers — chiefly the Danube and Elbe — reach record or near‑record levels, prompting large evacuations, extensive defense work and rising concerns about health, environmental and economic impacts.

Hungary
- The Danube is forecast to reach unprecedented highs over the coming days, peaking near the Slovak border (Nagybajcs) and in Budapest. Authorities reported new all‑time highs at Nagybajcs and Komarom; Budapest’s mayor estimates a peak near 8.95 m but expects existing flood defenses to hold with limited margin. Prime Minister Viktor Orban declared the situation potentially Hungary’s worst flood ever and a state of emergency is in effect.
- Nearly 400 people have been evacuated so far and about 70 communities affected; some villages (e.g., Kisoroszi) are cut off and reachable only by boat/helicopter. Military units and volunteers are reinforcing dams and building sandbag barriers; helicopters and amphibious vehicles stand ready.
- Environmental concerns center on a toxic sludge reservoir at Almasfuzito near Komarom. Greenpeace and a Hungarian Academy of Science report warn groundwater or breaches could mobilize toxic waste; the site is under close monitoring.

Germany
- The Elbe’s high waters threaten Saxony‑Anhalt and other regions. Thousands have been evacuated, including from Halle and Bitterfeld; Dresden’s historic center was spared major harm but surrounding areas are inundated. Aerial footage shows widespread flooding and industrial debris, raising contamination and safety worries.
- Damage to homes, businesses and agriculture is expected to run into hundreds of millions of euros; Chancellor Angela Merkel pledged 100 million euros in emergency aid. The Elbe is still cresting as it flows toward the North Sea, with a peak expected in Saxony‑Anhalt.

Czech Republic, Slovakia, Austria and broader region
- The Danube passed Bratislava without major damage but an extreme flood alert remains in western Slovakia. Czech authorities report eight deaths, ~700 affected communities and about 20,000 evacuated; focus is now shifting to draining and clean‑up, with pumps, international offers of help, and army units assisting.
- Austria reported four deaths and three missing; southwestern Germany reported three deaths. Across the region at least 15 people have died.
- Flooding follows heavy recent rains on already saturated ground. Some river levels are beginning to fall in parts of Bavaria, though towns such as Passau remain severely impacted. Forecasts call for scattered showers that could complicate recovery.

Overall impact
- Tens of thousands have been evacuated across multiple countries. Emergency services, military units and volunteers are heavily engaged in sandbagging, pumping and evacuations. Environmental contamination concerns, infrastructure and utility disruptions, and large economic losses—potentially exceeding costs from the 2002 floods—are mounting as waters crest and clean‑up begins.

Researchers analyzing data from the nationally representative Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2007–2009; 10,711 adults aged 19–64) examined links between diet, instant noodle consumption and cardiometabolic risk. Using a 63‑item food‑frequency questionnaire and principal components analysis, they identified two major dietary patterns: a “traditional” pattern (rice, fish, vegetables, fruit, potatoes) and a “meat and fast‑food” pattern (more meat, soda, fried/fast foods including instant noodles).

Key findings:
- The “meat and fast‑food” pattern (highest quintile) was associated with higher odds of abdominal obesity (OR 1.41) and elevated LDL cholesterol (OR 1.57), but lower odds of low HDL and of high triglycerides.
- The “traditional” pattern was associated with lower odds of elevated blood pressure and marginally lower abdominal obesity.
- Neither overall dietary pattern was associated with prevalence of metabolic syndrome as a whole.
- Independent of the major dietary patterns, women who ate instant noodles at least twice weekly had a substantially higher prevalence of metabolic syndrome (OR 1.68); this association was not seen in men (interaction p = 0.04).

Authors and outside experts note limitations: cross‑sectional design cannot prove causation, and higher sodium and unhealthy accompanying foods could explain some effects. The study highlights that frequent instant‑noodle consumption—especially in women—may be linked to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes, and that instant noodles are not part of a healthy diet when eaten several times per week. The report provoked strong reactions in South Korea, where instant noodles (ramyeon) are culturally ubiquitous and widely consumed.

A 35-year-old caterer, Tyonne Johns, was fatally stabbed after a wedding reception at Ellanor C. Lawrence Park in Chantilly, Va., following a dispute over folding chairs. Johns, owner of Chef Tyonne catering, was packing up chairs into her company truck late Saturday when 19-year-old Kempton A. Bonds, a Fairfax County Park Authority facilities attendant working the event, claimed the chairs belonged to the park. Witnesses say tensions had been brewing all evening—Bonds earlier cut power to the reception and called police about disorderly conduct and noise; officers found the situation resolved. Minutes after the chair argument, police say Bonds pulled a pocketknife and repeatedly stabbed Johns in the upper body. She was taken to a hospital and died. Bonds remained at the scene, was arrested, charged with second-degree murder, is being held without bond, and has been fired pending the investigation. Friends, colleagues and family remembered Johns as a talented, driven chef and business owner; the park authority and community expressed shock and condolences.

Facebook announced it will begin using face-recognition technology to make photo tagging easier, rolling out the feature gradually in the U.S. starting next week. The system will compare faces in newly uploaded photos to a limited subset of a user’s friends (likely those communicated with most often) and suggest tags, but tagging is not automatic: Facebook will prompt the uploader to confirm any match, and if nothing is done the photo will remain untagged. Users keep existing tag-notification and removal controls, can control who may tag them, and can opt out of having their name suggested via a “Suggest photos of me to friends” setting. Experts note face recognition is still error-prone, especially across large populations, and welcome Facebook’s “human-in-the-loop” confirmation approach; prior manual tags improve future accuracy. Facebook will initially launch to a small U.S. user group.

Separately, Facebook’s ad and virtual-goods revenue is surging: sources say 2010 revenue will be about $2 billion—more than double 2009—driven by advertiser interest from major brands and growth in display advertising and its credits program. The company’s rapid growth has increased its market valuation and attracted investor interest, but has also intensified privacy scrutiny. Facebook has recently simplified privacy controls and reduced public exposure of some user data in response. Mark Zuckerberg was named Time’s Person of the Year amid the company’s expansion.

Sausage Party, an R-rated animated comedy produced by Sony and Annapurna Pictures, opened strongly with $33.6 million, giving a rare box-office win to Sony amid a summer of flops. Released in 3,103 theaters, the $19 million film — featuring voices like Seth Rogen, Kristen Wiig and Jonah Hill — set the record for the biggest August opening for an animated film. Critics responded well (about 82% on Rotten Tomatoes) and analysts credited its success to fresh, adult-targeted comedy.

Top of the weekend box office was Suicide Squad, which held No. 1 with $43.8 million in its second weekend but suffered a steep 67% drop from its huge opening, signaling that poor reviews may be denting its legs despite a hefty domestic total ($222.9M) and $465.4M worldwide. Disney’s Pete’s Dragon opened to about $21.5–21.6 million in 3,702 theaters — critically praised but a disappointing start against its $65M budget; Disney expects foreign grosses and word-of-mouth to help.

Other holdovers and new releases: Jason Bourne added $13.6M (domestic total $126.8M); Bad Moms grossed about $11.4–11.5M, bringing its total to $71.5M on a $20M budget; Florence Foster Jenkins opened modestly with $6.6M, skewing older audiences and hoping awards attention will boost returns. In limited release, Hell or High Water earned $592,000 from 32 theaters (strong per-screen average) and WWII thriller Anthropoid made $1.2M in 452 theaters.

Overall weekend receipts rose nearly 15% from the prior year, and analysts noted August is increasingly a viable launch window for original, offbeat films that offer an alternative to franchise-driven summer fare.

Planned for about 1:17 a.m. Eastern, the Curiosity rover’s Mars landing will be confirmed on Earth roughly 13 minutes and 48 seconds later—the light-time delay for radio signals from Mars—if everything goes well. However, silence after the expected time would not necessarily mean mission failure: several factors can interrupt communications.

Curiosity has multiple transmitters. It will send direct X-band status messages to Earth until the landing site rotates out of Earth view a few minutes before touchdown. Most of the detailed telemetry will be sent via a UHF link to NASA’s Mars Odyssey orbiter, which will relay it to Earth in real time. If Odyssey cannot point toward Curiosity—an open risk because Odyssey had a reaction-wheel glitch two months earlier and is operating with a spare—those relays could be missed. The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter will also be listening, but it will record data for later playback rather than provide live relays. If both orbiters miss the signal, Curiosity can speak directly to Earth later that day when geometry permits.

NASA says a successful landing could occur and go unconfirmed for hours; if no signal arrives via the orbiters and the Deep Space Network within about 18 hours, concern would grow that something went seriously wrong. The rover’s descent is fully preprogrammed, so mission control cannot intervene and must “ride along” as the Entry, Descent and Landing (EDL) sequence plays out. Because Curiosity is larger and more complex than previous Mars rovers, it uses a novel—and untestable on Earth—“sky crane” hovering-rocket stage to lower the rover, making the landing more hazardous. NASA leaders have characterized Curiosity as one of the agency’s most important missions in a decade.

The landing drew global attention, with public watch events scheduled worldwide, including a large gathering in New York’s Times Square. Historically, Mars missions are difficult: only about one-third of global attempts since the late 1960s have succeeded, and the United States remains the only nation to have repeatedly landed and completed missions on Mars (six successes out of seven attempts).

The University of Alberta has canceled a scheduled “Spoon Bending and the Power of the Mind” workshop after the presenters withdrew. The event had been listed as part of Pediatric Integrative Medicine rounds and was to be led by Anastasia Kutt, an Edmonton “energy healing therapist” and registered reiki master. The flyer promised an experiential guided meditation/“energy transfer” technique intended to let most participants bend cutlery with their minds, and explicitly stated it would not be a scientific evaluation.

The workshop announcement drew widespread criticism from scientists, doctors and skeptics—spurred in part by law professor Timothy Caulfield’s tweet of the poster—and prompted a campus protest poster decrying “unethical institutional support… for medical quackery.” Commentators compared the event to classic spoon‑bending tricks popularized by Uri Geller and criticized its inclusion in an academic medical program as an example of how some “integrative” or complementary medicine initiatives incorporate non‑evidence‑based practices like reiki and acupuncture. Critics argued that basic scientific skepticism ("Bigfoot skepticism") should have prevented the program from inviting an energy‑healing demonstration in a medical setting. The cancellation followed the public backlash.

Law enforcement mounted a massive, multi-agency manhunt in the snowy San Bernardino Mountains around Big Bear Lake for Christopher Jordan Dorner, a 33-year-old former LAPD officer accused of a vengeful killing spree. More than 100 officers, including SWAT teams, search-and-rescue teams and federal agents, combed about eight square miles of forest, cabins and backcountry after Dorner’s burned Nissan Titan was found on a Forest Service road. Footprints were seen leaving the truck, but searches Friday turned up no sign of him.

Police say Dorner has admitted in an online manifesto to targeting people he blamed for his 2008 firing, and investigators believe he killed three people and wounded others in separate attacks, including the slayings of a retired LAPD captain’s daughter and her fiance in Irvine and an ambush that left a Riverside officer dead and another seriously wounded. The manifesto, apparently posted on Facebook and accompanied by a mailed package to CNN that included a bullet-pierced coin belonging to former LAPD Chief William Bratton, threatened “unconventional and asymmetrical warfare” against officers and families; authorities are guarding more than 40 people named in it.

Snow and freezing temperatures hampered the search, grounding helicopters and limiting aerial sensors, but also helped tracking teams. Authorities checked dozens of tips and false sightings across Southern California and beyond and searched Dorner’s and his mother’s homes for evidence. Officials warned the public, closed local schools, and urged vigilance; some residents armed themselves amid concern Dorner could be hiding in vacant cabins or using the terrain and his military and law-enforcement training to evade capture. Investigators considered the burned truck possibly a diversion, and police planned to resume and broaden the hunt with daylight and clearer skies.

Rebel fighters from the Seleka coalition seized the Central African Republic’s capital, Bangui, over the weekend, forcing President François Bozizé to flee and prompting international alarm. Seleka leader Michel Djotodia declared himself president and said he would form a power-sharing government, keep Prime Minister Nicolas Tiangaye in place, and hold elections after a two- to three-year transition, while pledging to respect the January Libreville accord that had briefly brought rebels into government.

The African Union immediately suspended the CAR from its activities and imposed sanctions, travel bans and asset freezes on Seleka leaders. The United Nations, France, the United States and regional actors also condemned the coup and urged respect for the peace deal and protection of civilians. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called for a swift restoration of constitutional order.

Fighting during the takeover killed and wounded many: South Africa reported 13 soldiers killed and 27 wounded among its deployed troops that had been assisting the national army. Looting and insecurity spread through Bangui after the government’s collapse; utilities were disrupted and humanitarian and human-rights concerns were raised by the US State Department and others.

Bozizé—who himself took power in a 2003 coup—left the country; reports placed him in neighboring states but his location was initially unclear. Seleka said it launched the offensive after accusing Bozizé of reneging on the January peace deal (which had integrated some rebel figures into government) and of failing to meet demands including prisoner releases. The CAR, a poor, landlocked former French colony with significant untapped mineral resources, now faces deep uncertainty over governance, security and humanitarian conditions.
