Oscar Pistorius, the South African Paralympic sprinter convicted last year of culpable homicide in the February 2013 shooting death of his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp, is expected to be released from prison on parole in August after serving about 10 months of his five-year sentence. A family member and reports say a parole date of August 21 has been set; corrections officials did not comment. Under South African rules he was eligible for “correctional supervision” after serving one-sixth of his term. Pistorius was originally found not guilty of murder but guilty of culpable homicide after a lengthy trial; prosecutors are appealing and will again seek a murder conviction at the Supreme Court of Appeal in November, which, if successful, could raise his sentence substantially.

Pistorius has been held in a single cell in Pretoria for safety and is reported to have spent long periods isolated, with limited exercise time. His lawyers say parole conditions will include psychological and anger-management programmes and other restrictions. The Steenkamp family expressed dismay, saying 10 months is insufficient punishment. Pistorius’s legal team say he has declined book and movie deals, is financially depleted, and hopes to do community work on release.

Pacific Life said Friday it will pull its ads from Tucker Carlson’s Fox News program after an ad ran directly after Carlson’s opening monologue in which he called the “immigration crisis” making the U.S. “poorer and dirtier and more divided” and referred to immigrants as “cynical shake-down artists.” The company, whose spot touted “protecting generations of families for 150 years,” said on Twitter it “strongly disagree[s] with Mr. Carlson’s statements,” that its customer base and workforce reflect national diversity, and that it will suspend advertising on the show “in the coming weeks as we reevaluate our relationship with his program.” Fox News called the backlash “unfortunate and unnecessary distractions,” accusing left‑wing groups of weaponizing social media to pressure advertisers. Critics on Twitter had urged sponsors to drop Carlson’s show after the remarks.

Amazon’s Prime Day began in 2015 as a mid‑July experiment—code‑named “Piñata”—to drive summer sales, promote Prime memberships and test systems and new shopping behaviors. Since then it’s grown into one of Amazon’s biggest retail events, running roughly 30 hours with tens of thousands of limited‑time “lightning” deals across many countries. Amazon doesn’t release exact revenues, but analysts and the company say Prime Day sales have grown rapidly year‑over‑year and generate significant device and third‑party seller volume; Prime members (now tens of millions in the U.S.) spend far more on average than non‑members.

Prime Day’s purposes: boost otherwise slow July sales, expand brand and ecosystem engagement (notably with Echo/Alexa and other Amazon devices), encourage Prime signups and collect customer data while stress‑testing systems ahead of the holidays. Early events suffered website crashes and criticism that many “deals” were poor or inventory clearances, prompting improvements—such as Amazon’s promise that lightning deals will be the lowest price on the site in the prior 365 days—and expanded inventory and deal scheduling.

Operationally, Amazon and many third‑party sellers prepare months in advance; sellers often plan inventory to hit Prime Day demand. Some retailers run competing promotions, though major players like Walmart and Target at times have sat out. Technical glitches have recurred (notably checkout and cart problems), but Amazon typically recovers and reports record sales and device adoption (Echo, Fire TV, Kindles, etc.) during the event.

For shoppers: Prime Day deals are exclusive to Prime members (free trials and student promotions apply), deals rotate rapidly (sometimes every five minutes), and supplies are limited. Tools and tactics to navigate Prime Day: use the Amazon app to “watch” deals and receive notifications, add items to wishlists, employ price‑tracking services (CamelCamelCamel) or browser extensions (Honey) to verify true discounts, join waitlists for sold‑out lightning deals, and ask Alexa for exclusive offers. Also note that as of 2017 Amazon collects sales tax in most U.S. states, so purchases are usually subject to tax.

A Laurel County, Kentucky man, Ernest (Chris) Chumbley, has been charged with murder after admitting he shot and killed his wife, Virginia Chumbley, at their Greenlawn Subdivision home in the early hours of Wednesday, Aug. 28, 2013. Deputies say Virginia was found with two gunshot wounds; her body was sent to Frankfort for autopsy. Ernest called 911 after the shooting and told dispatchers he had shot his wife. From the Laurel County Detention Center he told reporters he carried out what he described as a “mercy killing” at Virginia’s request because she was suffering from breast cancer and had asked him to “stop the pain.” Neighbors said the couple had been married more than 20 years and that Virginia’s condition had worsened recently. Chumbley pleaded not guilty in Laurel District Court, is jailed on $200,000 cash bond, and is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Sept. 5. Authorities say the investigation is ongoing.

Brazil’s Senate voted 61–20 to convict and remove President Dilma Rousseff on charges of manipulating the federal budget to hide worsening economic problems. Rousseff, Brazil’s first female president, had been suspended since May while facing the trial. The Senate’s decision ends 13 years of rule by the leftist Workers’ Party, a period of rapid growth that expanded the middle class but ended amid economic decline and political scandal.

Rousseff denied wrongdoing, called the impeachment a coup and testified for 14 hours during a marathon trial in which many senators spoke. Emotions ran high on both sides. Although removal from office was approved, a subsequent Senate vote failed to reach the necessary majority to bar her from holding public office for eight years (42–36), so she retains the right to run again. Rousseff is expected to appeal to Brazil’s highest court. Interim president Michel Temer was sworn in after the decision.

Original report: TeNiya Jones, a 19-year-old University of Kentucky student from Fort Myers studying abroad in a CIEE program, went missing after a swimming accident in the Mediterranean off Tel Aviv. She and several other students were caught in a strong current Saturday evening; two students reached shore but Jones did not. The Jones family had suffered a prior tragedy when TeNiya’s brother Samuel was fatally shot in Lehigh Acres last December.

Three new papers in Science report that people in the Olorgesailie Basin of southern Kenya were making sophisticated Middle Stone Age (MSA) tools and transporting exotic materials at least ~320,000 years ago—tens of thousands of years earlier than many had thought. The discoveries include small, standardized, retouched blades and points (some clearly hafted), abundant obsidian artifacts whose raw material came from 25–50+ km away, and 88 lumps of pigment (red ochre, some ground). These finds contrast with the earlier, long-lived Acheulean tradition at Olorgesailie (1.2 million–~500 thousand years ago) dominated by large hand axes and cleavers.

Well-dated volcanic layers (argon and uranium methods) bracket the MSA deposits; however, a gap in the sedimentary record between ~499,000 and 320,000 years ago leaves the timing of the transition unclear. No hominid fossils have been recovered at Olorgesailie, so it’s not certain whether Homo sapiens or a close relative made the tools. The timing roughly coincides with other evidence for the emergence of H. sapiens in Africa (350–260 ka).

The authors link technological change to highly variable local climate and tectonic activity—frequent, rapid shifts between wet and dry conditions and landscape reworking—which would have made resources less predictable. They argue greater mobility, information sharing and long-distance exchange networks (evidenced by transport of large obsidian cores rather than only finished flakes) helped these populations cope. Pigments may indicate symbolic behavior and group identity. Critics note alternative drivers (population change, other social factors) and caution against directly equating MSA technology with modern human cognition since similar behaviors appear at different times and with different hominins across Africa.

Taken together, the Olorgesailie findings add strong evidence that many behaviors once framed as a late “human revolution” were present much earlier in Africa, supporting a gradual, regionally varied emergence of complex technology, social networks and symbolic practices linked to environmental pressures long before 40–50 ka.

This article summarizes CareerCast’s “Best Jobs of 2017” (as reported by 24/7 Wall St.), highlighting ten top occupations by pay, growth outlook and work environment. Key points:

- Methodology: CareerCast ranked jobs using four criteria — environment, income, outlook, and stress — and provided median wages and projected 2014–2024 employment growth; employment data came from the BLS (May 2016).

- Overall findings: The best jobs tend to be high-paying, in demand, and low-stress. Four of the top 10 require advanced math skills and three are in health care. Growth drivers include digitization/data needs and an aging population.

  - Work primarily in schools and hospitals treating communication disorders; most positions require a master’s degree.

  - Help patients with disabilities perform daily tasks; high demand and pay.

Context: CareerCast’s full list identified statistician as the best job overall and newspaper reporter as the worst, noting that many of the worst jobs are low-paid, shrinking, or hazardous. The BLS projects 7% average employment growth across all occupations for 2014–2024.

A military transport plane crashed near the Boufarik air base southwest of Algiers on Wednesday shortly after takeoff en route to Bechar (with a planned stop in Tindouf). The Soviet-designed Ilyushin Il-76 was carrying soldiers. Emergency teams and more than 300 responders converged on the agricultural crash site, where thick black smoke and a fuselage fire were reported.

Officials gave escalating casualty figures: Algerian state radio and later reports initially said more than 100 dead; the civil protection agency later put the provisional death toll at 181. Some passengers were rescued with severe burn injuries. The Defense Ministry offered condolences and opened an investigation; the cause of the crash remains unclear. Footage from the scene showed ambulances and Red Crescent vehicles and body bags in a field.

Study objective and methods:
- Researchers analyzed U.S. national mortality data for children aged 5–11 years across 1993–2012 (grouped into 5-year periods) to examine trends in suicide counts, crude rates, and methods. Negative binomial regression produced incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for period trends.

Key findings:
- Overall suicide rate for ages 5–11 was essentially stable over the 20 years (1.18 to 1.09 per million; IRR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.03). A total of 657 suicides occurred in this age group during 1993–2012 (≈33 per year); 84% were boys.
- Racially divergent trends masked by the stable aggregate rate:
  - Black children: suicide rate rose from 1.36 to 2.54 per million (IRR 1.27; 95% CI 1.11–1.45).
  - White children: suicide rate fell from 1.14 to 0.77 per million (IRR 0.86; 95% CI 0.79–0.94).
  - These significant changes were driven mainly by boys: black boys increased (1.78 → 3.47 per million) and white boys decreased (1.96 → 1.31 per million). Changes among girls were not statistically significant.
- Methods of suicide:
  - Hanging/suffocation accounted for the majority (78.2%); firearms 17.7%; other methods 4.1%.
  - Firearm suicides declined overall (IRR 0.69; 95% CI 0.57–0.85) and among white boys (IRR 0.72; 95% CI 0.59–0.88).
  - Hanging/suffocation increased significantly in black boys (IRR 1.35; 95% CI 1.14–1.61); overall rates by hanging/suffocation or other methods did not change significantly.

Conclusions and implications:
- Although the aggregate suicide rate in U.S. elementary-aged children was stable from 1993–2012, a substantial and significant increase among black children (especially boys) and a decrease among white children reveal an emerging racial disparity. The authors call for ongoing surveillance and research to identify risk, protective, and precipitating factors to guide early detection and culturally informed prevention efforts for children under 12.

Researchers studying Antarctic notothenioid fishes report that their antifreeze proteins (AFPs), while essential for preventing fatal freezing by binding and halting growth of internal ice crystals, also strongly inhibit ice melting. Laboratory and field work showed AFP-stabilized ice can remain “superheated” (stable above the normal equilibrium melting point) both in AFP solutions and inside fish tissues and serum. Experimental fishes retained internal ice at temperatures more than 1 °C above the expected melting point for at least 24 hours and at slightly lower temperatures for days; wild-caught fish also contained superheated ice. A 1999–2012 temperature record from a shallow McMurdo Sound habitat showed summers routinely exceeded the fishes’ equilibrium melting point but never reached temperatures high enough to overcome the AFP-induced melting inhibition observed in experiments. Thus seasonal warming is unlikely to reliably clear internal ice. The work reveals an antagonistic pleiotropic cost of AFPs: they protect against freezing but promote lifelong accumulation of potentially damaging internal ice crystals (notably concentrated in the spleen), a trade-off whose long-term effects on fish health remain to be determined.

The U.S. lost 33,000 payroll jobs in September — the first monthly decline in nearly seven years — largely because Hurricanes Harvey and Irma shut thousands of businesses in Texas and Florida and forced mass evacuations. The storms kept about 1.5 million people from working during the month, the largest such disruption in 20 years, and drove steep job losses in leisure and hospitality (restaurants and bars shed roughly 105,000 jobs). Many hourly workers temporarily off the job were counted as unemployed in the payroll survey, which depressed the jobs total.

Despite the payroll drop, the unemployment rate fell to 4.2% (the lowest since February 2001) because the household survey, which is used to compute the rate, counted many storm-affected people as employed. Labor-force participation rose and the employment-population ratio climbed to 60.4%, the highest since January 2009, signaling underlying strength outside the storm zones. Average hourly earnings rose 2.9% year-over-year (and 0.5% month-to-month), but economists caution that wage figures were likely boosted by the temporary loss of lower-paid workers in affected areas.

Other indicators also point to solid economic momentum: services-sector activity expanded in September at its fastest pace since 2005, manufacturing grew at the fastest rate in over 13 years, and auto sales jumped 6.1% year-over-year as storm replacement demand picked up. Economic-loss estimates from Moody’s put Harvey’s damage at roughly $76–87 billion, Irma at $58–83 billion, and Puerto Rico’s Maria preliminarily at $45–95 billion. Job growth is expected to rebound as businesses reopen and reconstruction accelerates.

This document combines two items: an explanation of a web-archiving effort and a news report on the Bastille Day truck attack in Nice.

- Web-archiving: Crawls are being run to archive newly created pages and the pages they reference, preserving the versions that existed when content was published. The Internet Archive hopes archived links will replace broken links or serve as companion links so readers can see what authors originally intended. The stated aim is to eliminate broken links across the web, including crawls of supported “No More 404” sites.

- Nice attack (report by Camilla Turner and others): On Bastille Day in Nice, a 19-ton refrigerated truck driven by 31-year-old Mohamed Lahouaiej Bouhlel plowed through crowds on the Promenade des Anglais, killing 84 people and injuring 256 (85 hospitalized, 12 victims not yet identified; a 6-month-old child among the critically injured). Bouhlel was shot dead by police. French authorities widened the probe after arresting additional suspects — including an Albanian couple accused of supplying weapons and a man believed to have received a text from Bouhlel (“Bring more weapons”) sent about 30 minutes before the attack. CCTV showed Bouhlel driving the truck along the promenade two days earlier, suggesting premeditation; investigators say he had emptied his bank account and was to have returned the truck the day before. The Islamic State declared Bouhlel one of its “soldiers,” but investigators are still determining whether the attack was directed, inspired, or opportunistically claimed. The attack follows earlier major assaults in France (Charlie Hebdo and the Nov. 2015 Paris attacks) and has provoked public anger over perceived security lapses. Amid mourning and vigils at the promenade, life began to return to normal with people returning to beaches and daily routines.

U.S. President Donald Trump said he would consider intervening in the Justice Department’s prosecution of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou if doing so served U.S. national security interests or helped secure a major trade deal with China. His remarks, made in a Reuters interview before a Canadian court granted Meng US$7.5 million bail pending an extradition hearing, heightened concerns that her December arrest in Canada (on U.S. charges of misleading banks about Iran-linked transactions) could be seen as politically motivated in Beijing. The arrest has strained diplomacy, and coincided with the detention in China of former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig; Canada says it is providing consular assistance and engaging with Chinese officials. Trump said the White House has discussed the case with the Justice Department and with Chinese officials, though he had not personally spoken to President Xi.

Summary:

Pennsylvania imposes an inheritance tax on the value of a decedent’s estate transferred to beneficiaries. Rates depend on the recipient’s relationship to the decedent:
- 0%: surviving spouse and parents receiving from a child age 21 or younger.
- 4.5%: direct descendants and lineal heirs.
- 12%: siblings.
- 15%: all other heirs (except charitable organizations, exempt institutions, and tax-exempt government entities).

Spousal jointly owned property is exempt. Since July 1, 2012, certain farmland and agricultural property may be exempt when transferred to eligible recipients (see Inheritance Tax Informational Notice 2012‑01). Tax payments are due on death and become delinquent nine months afterward; a 5% discount applies if paid within three months. Additional details and FAQs are available in the Pennsylvania Inheritance Tax brochure and the Tax Compendium.

Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) devastated large parts of the central Philippines in mid-November, leaving widespread destruction, a rapidly rising death toll and millions in urgent need of aid. Official figures at the time exceeded 2,300 confirmed dead, with the UN estimating more than 11 million people affected; aid workers feared the real toll was far higher, particularly on Leyte and Samar where the storm first made landfall with 195 mph winds and huge storm surges.

Damage and humanitarian needs
- Whole villages, infrastructure and hospitals were flattened; Tacloban airport, roads, ports and power systems were badly damaged, complicating relief delivery.
- Immediate priorities included search-and-rescue, clean drinking water, shelter, food, sanitation and emergency medical care; health experts warned of imminent disease outbreaks (cholera, dengue, respiratory infections).
- Large numbers of injured, elderly, pregnant women and people with chronic illnesses crowded makeshift clinics and airport treatment centers where supplies and staff were stretched thin.

Security and logistics challenges
- Massive logistical bottlenecks slowed distribution: aid stockpiles were often stuck in Manila or Cebu while roads, bridges and airstrips needed clearing.
- Law-and-order problems emerged in Tacloban amid shortages: reports of looting, violent incidents, stampedes at food stores and attacks on convoys led to curfews and additional troop deployments; some aid agencies temporarily withdrew staff over safety concerns.
- Mass burials began where bodies had been left in the open; authorities attempted to take samples for later identification.

International and UK response
- A large international relief effort mobilized: US military forces (including aircraft carriers, destroyers, helicopters and transport aircraft), European field hospitals, and aid from many countries and institutions were deployed. The UN and NGOs scaled up emergency deliveries.
- The UK committed over £20m in aid, sent the aircraft carrier HMS Illustrious (with helicopters, water-purification capability and 900 crew) to relieve HMS Daring, deployed medical teams and RAF transport aircraft, and the UK Disasters Emergency Committee appeal raised tens of millions of pounds within days.
- Other contributors included Japan, Australia, China, South Korea, the Asian Development Bank, the UAE and many NGOs supplying money, supplies, water, shelter materials, vehicles and personnel.

On-the-ground situation and outlook
- Some aid was reaching hardest-hit areas as military and humanitarian actors cleared access and opened logistics hubs (notably Cebu), and initial deliveries of food, water, medical supplies and heavy equipment began. Nevertheless, large gaps remained in coverage for outlying islands and smaller towns.
- Humanitarian leaders emphasized the need to rapidly scale up water, sanitation, shelter and medical services to prevent secondary health crises and to sustain longer-term recovery and rebuilding efforts.

Overall, the response was being ramped up but faced unprecedented logistical and security challenges as relief agencies worked to move large volumes of aid into devastated communities and to stabilize a fragile, fast-changing situation.

Donald Trump’s presidential campaign is planning a Republican National Convention in Cleveland (July 18–21) that will feature not just politicians but a lineup of sports figures and entertainers, aiming for a “winners” theme, Ivanka Trump said. Campaign aides have been contacting retired athletes, coaches and sports leaders to appear; names reported as being targeted or affiliated include Mike Tyson, Mike Ditka, Bobby Knight and NASCAR CEO Brian France. Organizers have not finalized roles or whether any will speak on stage.

Attempts to secure some high-profile sports appearances have been uneven: Tyson and France both announced through spokespeople they would not attend, while Ditka said he would be willing but hadn’t been asked. Trump later tweeted Tyson was not asked to speak, though he has publicly touted Tyson’s endorsement in the past. The involvement of some figures has drawn criticism given past controversies.

Separately, third-party groups have booked musical acts to perform around the convention—reported names include Journey, Bret Michaels, Rick Springfield, Martina McBride, Rascal Flatts and The Band Perry—though at least one band (The Beach Boys) denied participation. Concert costs will be covered by private groups, not the RNC or host committee. Organizers also unveiled a convention stage design featuring large LED screens and curving staircases.

A powerful tornado struck Joplin, Mo., on Sunday, devastating neighborhoods, killing more than 120 people and leaving many unaccounted for. As officials worked Thursday to reconcile an unaccounted-for list of roughly 230 people, the Associated Press found multiple cases where people listed as missing were in fact alive but out of contact because of destroyed phones and spotty service. Examples include 75-year-old Sally Adams, who was rescued from her destroyed home and had no way to notify family; she remained on the list despite relatives reporting her safe. A hotel housed survivors whose names appeared on the list after family Facebook posts or hotline calls. 

Authorities said some of those on the missing list are dead, and the death toll rose (officially reported at 126 in one update). Identification of victims has been slow and cautious after an early misidentification; a federal forensic team is using dental records, DNA, fingerprints and other markers to confirm remains. Nursing home losses added to the confusion: 12 Greenbriar residents were listed as missing while officials had earlier reported 11 deaths. Officials urged survivors to check the list and report themselves as safe, while families continued to wait for remains and funeral arrangements.

NASA announced that after 35 years of travel, Voyager 1 has entered an unexpected transitional region near the edge of the heliosphere that scientists call a "magnetic highway." In this region the Sun’s magnetic field lines connect with interstellar magnetic field lines, letting lower-energy particles from inside the heliosphere stream outward and higher-energy cosmic-ray particles from outside stream inward.

Charged-particle instruments on Voyager 1 recorded a dramatic change: a roughly fivefold rise in high-energy particles and about a thousandfold drop in low-energy solar particles beginning with an entry into the region on July 28, 2012, with re-entries and a stable stay since August 25. The magnetic field strength also increased each time the craft entered the region. However, the magnetometer still shows an East–West field orientation consistent with the Sun’s influence rather than the expected North–South interstellar orientation. Because the magnetic direction has not changed, scientists conclude Voyager 1 remains inside the heliosphere—likely within the heliopause layer—and are calling this the last region it must cross before reaching true interstellar space.

Mission scientists estimate Voyager 1 could cross into interstellar space within months to a few years, but the timing is uncertain. Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object (about 122 AU from Earth) and continues to return data, though power limitations will force instrument shutdowns over the coming decade.

Conservative host Sean Hannity publicly sparred with Fox colleague Megyn Kelly on October 6, 2016 after Kelly criticized both presidential candidates for avoiding tough interviews. On her show she said Hillary Clinton avoids “unsafe” settings and suggested Donald Trump mainly appears on friendly programs like Hannity’s. Hannity fired back on Twitter, accusing Kelly of “clearly” supporting Clinton and telling her she should be mad at the Democratic nominee. The exchange prompted widespread reaction across media and social networks, with commentators debating its significance for Fox News amid the post-Ailes era and questioning network control over on-air personalities. An update noted the two appeared to have reconciled later that night.

A photograph of an elderly man eating alone at an In-N-Out in California with a laminated photo of his late wife beside him touched many online viewers. Posted to Twitter and imgur by different users in October 2014, witnesses say diners approached him and he happily shared the story behind the picture: he met his sweetheart at 17, lost contact during the war, then spent a decade searching for her. A chance barber-shop reunion led to a proposal; they were married for 55 years until she died in 2009. He now takes her photo everywhere and keeps it with him while he eats. Observers described the scene as both heartbreaking and beautiful; the man offered simple wisdom about love—calling himself “rich… not with money, but with love,” and urging people to tell their spouses they love them every day.

A Las Vegas justice of the peace denied Floyd Mayweather Jr.’s emergency request to be released to house arrest or moved to the general population, rejecting his claims that jail food and water threatened his health and endangered his boxing career. Judge Melissa Saragosa said water is available 24 hours and that Mayweather is refusing to eat the provided meals; she also found he has sufficient space and time for physical activity despite it differing from his usual regimen. Mayweather’s team had argued his physician found he’d lost muscle tone and was eating under 800 calories a day versus his usual 3,000–4,000, and that lack of bottled water and training could cause withdrawal and anger. Prosecutors and the judge characterized the complaints as self-inflicted and inappropriate for jail, and ordered him to serve the remainder of his three-month sentence. Mayweather pleaded guilty last year to reduced domestic battery charges and began the sentence after being allowed to postpone surrender to make a fight.

Danish police announced divers found the head and both legs of Swedish freelance journalist Kim Wall, who disappeared after boarding inventor Peter Madsen’s homemade submarine on August 10. The remains — found in Koege Bay in weighted bags alongside some of Wall’s clothes, a knife and lead pieces — were identified by dental records. A headless torso had washed ashore in late August, and police say blood in the submarine matched the torso. Investigators continue searching for remaining body parts and are focusing on the neck and throat to determine cause of death; initial autopsy of the head showed no skull fractures.

Madsen, who was rescued after the submarine sank and is in custody, is charged with killing Wall but denies the charge, saying she died in an accidental hatch injury and that he later panicked and disposed of the body. Police also reported finding images on a computer from a laboratory Madsen ran that they “presume to be real” showing strangulation and decapitation; Madsen says the computer was shared. Prosecutors are pursuing the investigation; if convicted of murder he faces five years to life. Next pre-trial hearing is scheduled for October 31.

Former White House press secretary Sean Spicer used a surprise Emmys comedy skit to lampoon his six-month tenure and made news again by saying he regrets one of his most infamous moments. In a Monday interview he told The New York Times he does regret charging into the briefing room on Inauguration Day to dispute accurate news reports that President Obama’s inauguration crowd had been larger than President Trump’s — a confrontation that produced his “largest audience” line and later drew the phrase “alternative facts.” Spicer resigned this summer after repeated clashes with the press and a public dispute over Anthony Scaramucci’s appointment as communications director. His Emmys appearance — attended and playfully embraced by entertainment figures such as James Corden, who joked about kissing him onstage — was widely discussed as an attempt to rehabilitate his image and court the entertainment and media industry for speaking gigs and paid TV work after leaving the White House.

A 16-year-old student, identified as Alex Hribal, carried out a roughly five-minute stabbing rampage at Franklin Regional High School in Murrysville, Pennsylvania, shortly before classes on April 9, 2014. Armed with two kitchen knives about 8–10 inches long, he ran down a crowded hallway and into classrooms, stabbing and slashing students and a security officer. In total 22 people were injured by cuts or puncture wounds; at least four were reported in critical condition (one described as “eviscerated”), and several required surgery. Victims were ages 14–17. An assistant principal, Sam King, tackled Hribal and a school resource officer handcuffed him; Hribal sustained a minor hand wound and was treated. Teachers, students and first responders administered immediate aid—teachers used students’ hoodies as tourniquets and classmates helped apply pressure to wounds—while a pulled fire alarm helped evacuate the building.

Hribal was charged as an adult with four counts of attempted homicide, 21 counts of aggravated assault and possession of a weapon on school grounds, and jailed without bail. Authorities said he made statements indicating he wanted to die; motive remains unclear. Investigators, including the FBI, searched his home and computer and were probing reports of a threatening phone call the night before. Classmates described Hribal as shy and relatively quiet; neighbors called the family ordinary and stunned.

The attack shocked the suburban, upper-middle-class community of about 20,000. School officials paused in-person classes for several days and offered counseling; officials and medical staff praised students, staff and first responders for actions that likely prevented further loss of life.

Arnold Schwarzenegger is preparing a return to films now that his term as California governor has ended. He tweeted that he has given his agency, Creative Artists Agency (CAA), the go‑ahead to take offers seriously after seven years. Best known for the Terminator franchise, Schwarzenegger mostly did cameos during his governorship (e.g., Around the World in 80 Days, The Expendables) and has not had major roles since his 2003 election.

He’s been reading scripts — one reportedly about a compassionate Nazi soldier — but says he’ll adapt roles to his age, avoiding extreme fighting or heavy action and focusing more on character work, citing Clint Eastwood as an example. Schwarzenegger expressed eagerness to learn and grow as an actor. The piece also notes his past high popularity as governor, subsequent decline in approval, and past speculation about a presidential bid (which would be constitutionally barred because he was born in Austria).

Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.) announced he will not run for president in 2012. In a statement posted Feb. 22, 2011, Thune said he and his wife Kimberley had considered encouragement from supporters but concluded he can best serve the country “in the trenches of the United States Senate.” He cited three reasons for declining a bid: his Senate role and opportunities for increased leadership (including a new Finance Committee assignment and the impending retirement of Sen. Jon Kyl), family considerations around the demands of a presidential campaign, and timing. Thune has told donors and supporters of his decision and said he wants to help Republicans focus on regaining the Senate majority in 2012. He did not indicate whom he might support in the GOP primary.

Pressure is growing on the Metropolitan Police to broaden its phone-hacking inquiry after MP Tom Watson named private investigator Jonathan Rees in the House of Commons, accusing him of illegally targeting politicians, royals and sensitive intelligence sources while working for Fleet Street papers including the News of the World and Mirror Group titles.

Key allegations and background
- The Guardian’s inquiries suggest Rees may have targeted many high-profile figures, including former prime minister Tony Blair; ministers Jack Straw, Peter Mandelson and Alastair Campbell; the then-girlfriend Kate Middleton (now the Duchess of Cambridge); Prince Edward, the Countess of Wessex, and the Duke and Duchess of Kent; former Met commissioner Sir John Stevens and assistant commissioner John Yates; and senior Bank of England officials.
- Rees reportedly ran a network that obtained confidential material by burglary, computer intrusions, blagging (social-engineering to extract data from banks, phone companies and government agencies), and through corrupt police and other public servants. Journalists and investigators who worked with him say he used specialist hackers and “blaggers” to steal information that was then sold to newspapers.
- In July 2006 a hacker working for Rees allegedly installed a Trojan on the computer of former intelligence officer Ian Hurst, copying emails that exposed the identities and locations of MI6 informants inside the Provisional IRA—raising serious national security concerns.
- Rees worked freelance for several papers from the mid-1990s, earning substantial sums. He was jailed in 1999 for conspiring to plant drugs on a woman; after his release in 2004 the News of the World continued to hire him. He was acquitted in March 2011 of murder charges in the 1987 killing of his former business partner Daniel Morgan, but Scotland Yard is reported to have seized “boxloads” of paperwork in earlier inquiries into Rees’s links with corrupt officers and illegal activities.
- Southern Investigations, Rees’s agency, has been implicated previously in handling stolen documents for newspapers. Associates say Rees exploited masonic and other contacts inside the police to buy intelligence; some officers were later convicted of unrelated offences.

Investigations and responses
- Operation Weeting is the Met’s inquiry into News of the World phone hacking (launched January 2011). Several News of the World staff have been arrested. However, Watson was told some Rees-related evidence “may be beyond [Weeting’s] terms of reference” because it concerns illegal intrusions other than voicemail hacking.
- Scotland Yard acknowledged it had “received a number of allegations regarding breach of privacy which fall outside the remit of Operation Weeting” and is considering them.
- News International said Rees and Southern Investigations worked for many newspapers and denied the specific allegations, noting that Watson made them under parliamentary privilege. The Met says it is cooperating with Operation Weeting but has not asked News International for information about Rees.

Significance
- If the Met’s seized paperwork corroborates the Guardian’s claims, it could reveal extensive illegal news-gathering beyond voicemail hacking—implicating journalists, private investigators and corrupt public servants and affecting senior political and royal figures, as well as vulnerable intelligence sources. Calls are growing for investigators to expand the inquiry to cover these broader allegations.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating its daily web crawl data to the Internet Archive; after an embargo period those captures are added to the Wayback Machine.

Separately, police in Spokane arrested 50-year-old Carlo M. Cerutti at his duplex near NorthTown Mall after his neighbor reported an assault. Court documents say the incident began when Cerutti’s wife argued with a neighbor, accusing him of putting trash in her can. The neighbor told officers Cerutti rushed out wielding “a large sword-type weapon with multiple blades” and swung it like a hatchet. The victim blocked the blade with his hands, managed to pull the weapon away, and a second neighbor witnessed the fight. Cerutti was arrested and faces assault charges.

On March 24, 2015, Germanwings Flight 4U9525, an Airbus A320 flying from Barcelona to Düsseldorf with 144 passengers and six crew, crashed into a remote, snow-dusted ravine in the French Alps, killing all 150 people aboard. The impact scattered pulverized debris across steep mountainsides; investigators recovered a black box and launched a difficult search-and-recovery operation in challenging weather and terrain. The aircraft went into an unexplained eight-minute rapid descent from cruising altitude and lost radio contact without sending a distress call.

Among the victims were two opera singers, two babies and 67 Germans, including 16 tenth-grade students and two teachers from Josef-Koenig-Gymnasium in Haltern am See, who were returning from a Spanish language-exchange trip. The small town and the Spanish partner town of Llinars del Vallès were plunged into shock and grief: students and residents gathered at the school and local churches with candles and embraces, flags were lowered to half-mast, and officials arranged crisis support. German, French and Spanish leaders called for thorough investigations; early statements from authorities and the White House said there was no indication of terrorism. French officials said the recovered black box(s) — flight and/or cockpit voice recorders — would be examined to establish what happened. Lufthansa and Germanwings described the day as a tragedy and emphasized that flying remains safe as investigations continued.

Google’s year-end search roundup for 2014 showed what captured the world’s attention, with the biggest spike in queries tied to Robin Williams’ suicide — people sought his films, quotes (notably “carpe diem”) and information about depression. Google published two trending lists (U.S. and global) based on year-over-year increases in searches rather than raw volume; the U.S. and global lists were largely similar, differing mainly where the world searched more about bearded drag queen Conchita Wurst and the Sochi Winter Olympics, while U.S. searchers looked more for Ferguson/Michael Brown and the Ukraine conflict.

Other major global trending topics included the Ebola outbreak, the World Cup, the Ice Bucket Challenge, the smartphone game Flappy Bird (one of the first apps to break into Google’s top 10), ISIS, Disney’s Frozen, and the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. Notably, no Apple product made the top 10 this year, and indie games like 2048 and Flappy Bird outpaced big-budget titles.

Google’s list, reflecting roughly two-thirds of all internet searches, echoed recent annual summaries from rivals: Yahoo’s top searches skewed heavily toward celebrities (with Ebola at No. 1), while Microsoft’s Bing released category-specific top lists (celebrities, athletes, destinations, etc.).

PayPal has terminated its payment-processing relationship with Infowars and related sites, notifying the outlet that after “a comprehensive review” its content “promoted hate and discriminatory intolerance against certain communities and religions,” which PayPal says violates its acceptable use policy. Infowars was given 10 days to switch processors. No specific violations were publicly detailed by PayPal; Infowars says it was told off the record that criticism of Islam and opposition to transgender instruction were cited. InfowarsStore.com—whose merchandise the company says contains no political content—will be affected, and Infowars is exploring legal options.

The article frames the decision as politically motivated censorship and economic sabotage timed ahead of midterm elections, alleging coordination with left-leaning organizations and media. It cites recent pressure from Right Wing Watch and coverage in the Washington Post as contributing factors and accuses lawmakers and Big Tech of colluding to silence conservative voices, drawing comparisons to social-credit–style suppression. The piece warns other conservative groups they could be targeted next, calls for executive action to protect conservatives from deplatforming and anti-trust intervention against PayPal, and urges readers to support Infowars financially.

Context noted in the piece: PayPal’s move follows a broader set of deplatforming actions against Alex Jones and Infowars by Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, and app stores after longstanding controversies—such as Jones’s false claims about Sandy Hook—prompted public criticism and prior calls for enforcement of platform policies. PayPal confirmed its decision and reiterated it was based on its values and findings from its review.

A French court found Air France guilty of discrimination for removing Horia Ankour, a 30-year-old nursing student and pro-Palestine activist, from a Nice–Tel Aviv flight in April 2012 after staff asked if she had an Israeli passport and whether she was Jewish. When she answered no, she was escorted off the plane. The court fined Air France €10,000 and ordered it to pay Ankour €3,000 in damages and legal fees. Prosecutors had backed Ankour’s case as discriminatory; Air France said it had acted because her name appeared on a list of people deemed undesirable by Israeli authorities amid a wider “Welcome to Palestine” campaign that led to about 300 canceled tickets after pressure from Israel.

Swiss mountaineer Erhard Loretan, one of the few climbers to have summited all 14 peaks over 8,000 meters, died in a climbing accident on his 52nd birthday. Police in the Valais canton said Loretan and a 38-year-old Swiss client fell while ascending the summit ridge of the Gruenhorn in the Bernese Alps; they fell about 200 meters from roughly 3,800 meters on the 4,043‑meter peak. Loretan died at the scene and his client was airlifted to hospital in serious condition.

Born in the canton of Fribourg, Loretan began climbing at 11 and reached his first 8,000‑meter summit, Nanga Parbat, in 1982. He completed all 14 such peaks by 1995, becoming the third person after Reinhold Messner and Jerzy Kukuczka to do so. He was famed for a 1986 ascent of Everest done in 40 hours, at night and without supplemental oxygen.

Loretan’s reputation was marred by a 2001 family tragedy: he shook his seven‑month‑old son to stop crying, and the infant died. Loretan pleaded guilty to negligent manslaughter and received a four‑month suspended sentence; the high‑profile case helped spur research and awareness about the dangers of shaking infants.

This piece examines Jerry Seinfeld’s new web series Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee—its tone, production, place in the evolving media landscape, and what it signals about established stars moving online.

Show basics and tone
- Format: Each ~13–15 minute episode finds Seinfeld picking up a fellow comic in a vintage car, driving to a café or diner, and having an often meandering, conversational meal or coffee. The debut guest is Larry David.
- Content: Conversation skews toward everyday minutiae (e.g., cigars vs. cigarettes, underwear, dietary quirks) with occasional weightier asides, but largely feels like “a show about nothing,” distilled to its essence: skilled comedians riffing on life’s trivialities.
- Feel: The show aims for a casual, fly-on-the-wall vibe, but is highly produced—crisp, tightly edited cinematography and deliberate aesthetic choices sometimes make it feel polished to the point of distancing the viewer. Still, the chemistry between Seinfeld and David is engaging and the episode is enjoyable for fans.

Production and comparisons
- The series’ visual style and editing give a commercial sheen; sequence choices and detail shots make the conversation feel curated rather than wholly spontaneous.
- It recalls other formats: dashboard GoPro car chats (e.g., Carpool) and semi-improvised dining journeys (e.g., The Trip), while echoing Seinfeld’s earlier TV work and the improv-feel of Curb Your Enthusiasm.

Context and significance
- Platform choice: Seinfeld released the series online (Crackle and its own site) rather than on broadcast TV—despite his ability to secure traditional network deals. That choice reflects both practical and artistic reasons.
- Broader trend: High-profile talents (Tom Hanks, Larry King, Will Ferrell, etc.) are increasingly launching projects online. The web offers freedom from network constraints—no fixed timeslots, fewer executive interventions, flexible episode lengths—plus access to growing ad revenue and audiences on mobile devices.
- Artistic motive: For established stars “who don’t need the Web,” online platforms are attractive for experimentation and creative control; they can pursue low-stakes, personal projects that recall their roots in stand-up and smaller-scale comedy.

Assessment and outlook
- Strengths: The series showcases veteran comedic talent, relaxed camaraderie, and entertaining conversation; it’s a pleasant, low-pressure watch for fans.
- Limitations: The production’s polish can create distance, and the format may meander or feel self-indulgent to viewers not invested in Seinfeld-style banter.
- Future curiosity: How the show will play with guests less familiar to Seinfeld (e.g., Ricky Gervais) will test whether the format remains compelling beyond comfort-zone pairings.

Bottom line: Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee is a nicely produced, character-driven web series that leverages the internet’s freedom to let a comedy legend play and experiment. It’s emblematic of a larger shift: big-name creators using online platforms to make intimate, flexible projects that traditional TV might not accommodate.

President Trump reacted to reports that an FBI informant contacted Trump campaign aides in 2016, saying on Twitter that if the FBI or DOJ "was infiltrating a campaign for the benefit of another campaign" it would be a major scandal. The New York Times reported an unnamed informant—described as an American academic teaching in Britain—had contacted advisers George Papadopoulos and Carter Page after allegedly suspicious ties to Russia. Conservative outlets have circulated the informant’s name.

Trump shifted language from saying a representative was “implanted” to saying the campaign was “infiltrated,” alleging the action was politically motivated without providing evidence. He said the truth will emerge only if Congress is given the documents the House Intelligence Committee and Senate Judiciary are seeking. Republicans, including Rep. Jim Jordan, have pushed for access to sensitive classified materials and expressed outrage if the reports are true. The Papadopoulos interaction with an Australian diplomat in April 2016 is tied to the FBI probe that led to Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into possible coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia.
