Sen. Elizabeth Warren sharply confronted Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf during a Senate hearing over the bank’s fake-accounts scandal, saying he should resign, return ill-gotten pay, and be criminally investigated by the DOJ and SEC. The scandal involved roughly 5,300 fired employees who created millions of unauthorized customer accounts as part of a cross-selling push tied to performance targets. Warren highlighted Stumpf’s repeated public praise of cross-selling on earnings calls, argued those metrics helped boost Wells Fargo’s stock and enriched Stumpf by hundreds of millions, and called the leadership “gutless” for not holding senior executives accountable. Other senators pressed Stumpf on whether the behavior amounted to fraud, whether the bank would claw back pay from retiring executive Carrie Tolstedt (nearly $125 million), and how harmed customers would be assisted. Stumpf frequently disclaimed legal, compensation or credit-expert knowledge in his answers. Sen. Patrick Toomey expressed skepticism that thousands of employees could have acted independently without systemic pressure from the bank’s culture and incentives.

Separately, the report notes President-elect Donald Trump was expected to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital while postponing an embassy move by signing another six-month waiver. The anticipated recognition—seen as a partial but provocative shift—drew international criticism (including from Pope Francis) amid warnings it could derail peace talks and spark violent protests. The item also mentions reporting that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman allegedly proposed a U.S.-backed peace plan heavily favoring Israel (denied by Saudi officials), underscoring regional realignments that may affect U.S. impartiality in Israeli-Palestinian negotiations.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle released additional details about their May 19 wedding at Windsor Castle.

Guests and family roles
- Both of Meghan’s parents, Doria Ragland and Thomas Markle, will attend. They will arrive in the UK during the week before the wedding to meet senior royals, including Queen Elizabeth II, Prince Philip, Prince Charles, Camilla, Prince William and Kate.
- On the wedding day Meghan and her mother will travel by car to Windsor; her father will walk her down the aisle at St. George’s Chapel at noon (7:00 a.m. ET).
- Harry’s family will also be represented: all three of Princess Diana’s siblings will attend, and Diana’s sister Jane Fellowes will give a reading to honor Diana’s memory.
- Harry has chosen his brother William as best man. Meghan will have no maid of honor.
- All bridesmaids and page boys will be children (possibly including Prince George and Princess Charlotte); newborn Prince Louis will not attend.

Ceremony, logistics and traditions
- Meghan will spend her last night single at an undisclosed hotel; Harry and Meghan will spend their first night as a married couple at Windsor Castle and will not leave immediately on honeymoon. They plan their first public appearance as a married couple during the week following the ceremony.
- The palace will post the Order of Service online the morning of the wedding for viewers at home.
- The bride’s dress designer and style will be kept secret until Meghan exits the car at the chapel.
- Alexi Lubomirski, who shot the couple’s engagement photos, will be the official wedding photographer.

Other notes
- The palace expressed hope that 96-year-old Prince Philip—recovering from hip surgery—will be well enough to attend.
- Officials emphasized plans for a celebration that will be shared widely via television and the internet.

The Navy completed a review of Aaron Alexis’s military record after he shot 12 people at the Washington Navy Yard and was killed by police. The review found multiple missed warning signs and recommended that future security-investigation reports include any available police documents—even if they did not lead to charges or convictions.

Key findings:
- Alexis had a 2004 Seattle incident in which police say he fired a .45 and shot out tires; the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) knew of the arrest from fingerprints but its report to the Navy omitted references to gunfire and used Alexis’s account that he merely deflated tires. Seattle police would not supply records, and Alexis denied the weapon on his security questionnaire.
- OPM interviewed Alexis when he joined the Navy Reserve in 2007 and cleared him for a Secret clearance in 2008; the only flag then was his credit history. His clearance was valid for 10 years.
- Additional incidents included a 2008 arrest in Georgia for disorderly conduct (resulting in administrative punishment), a 2009 drunken/disorderly punishment later removed on appeal, and a September 2010 Fort Worth report of discharging a firearm at home (no charges filed). After the Fort Worth incident, commanders began proceedings to separate him, but the process ended when police did not charge him; Alexis left the Navy three months later with an honorable discharge.
- Alexis had reported hearing voices and complained of microwave attacks; his contractor job required a clearance and gave him access to the Navy Yard.

The Navy recommended to Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel that personnel-investigation reports always include any available police documents so that adjudicators have fuller information when granting security clearances.

Over the 2016 holiday weekend, a predominantly white armed militia occupied the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge in Oregon, demanding that federal public lands be transferred to local ranchers, loggers, and miners. Leaders Ammon and Ryan Bundy warned they would not rule out violence if law enforcement tried to remove them. Despite the clear threat and takeover of a federal facility, much media coverage initially framed the event as a “peaceful protest” or treated it with relatively little alarm, prompting public outcry and the trending tag #OregonUnderAttack.

Many critics argued the subdued or sympathetic coverage reflected racial and religious bias: social media commentators noted the disparity between how this incident was handled and how the media and authorities have treated armed or confrontational protests led by Black or Muslim Americans. They pointed to past coverage of Black Lives Matter protests—often depicted in harsher terms, with protesters labeled “thugs” or blamed for broader crime trends—and to the quick attribution of blame to Muslim communities after terrorist attacks, as evidence of uneven standards.

The piece links these differences to implicit bias—subconscious attitudes that shape perception and behavior. It summarizes research showing that such biases affect police and public perceptions, including studies where officers dehumanized Black people, or where people perceived Black children as less innocent, and experiments showing faster shooting decisions against Black suspects in simulations. The argument is that these ingrained biases likely influence media framing and public reaction, consciously or not, and that journalists and pundits should be aware of them when reporting on racially charged events.

The Florida chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-FL) filed a federal lawsuit on July 29, 2015, against Florida Gun Supply in Inverness after owner Andy (Andrew) Hallinan posted a Facebook video declaring his shop a “Muslim-free zone.” Hallinan said the policy was a response to the July 16 Chattanooga shootings and claimed a duty to protect his customers by refusing to “arm and train” people he believed might harm others.

CAIR argues the policy violates federal public-accommodations law and seeks an injunction preventing the shop from discriminating or segregating customers on the basis of religion. CAIR-FL leaders, including Hassan (Hassan) Shibly and civil-rights director Thania Diaz Clevenger, said American Muslims have the same rights to browse, purchase firearms, take safety classes and use ranges without being profiled or excluded, and said they tried to resolve the matter before suing.

Hallinan’s attorney, Robert Muise of the American Freedom Law Center, called the lawsuit frivolous and argued Hallinan is acting out of public-safety concerns rather than religious animus; he suggested CAIR might be sanctioned and pointed to past allegations involving CAIR in other cases. Hallinan initially invited Shibly to a training session but later rescinded the invitation amid backlash and claims that CAIR was listed as an unindicted co-conspirator in a prior terrorism case. CAIR disputes the significance of that listing and framed the litigation as necessary to prevent religious discrimination and “segregation” in Florida.

Summary:

Multiple recent studies and reviews raise concern that widely used proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)—drugs such as omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole and esomeprazole that reduce stomach acid—may be associated with several serious adverse outcomes, including chronic kidney disease (CKD), increased amyloid-beta production relevant to Alzheimer’s disease, and elevated dementia risk in older adults. Key findings and caveats:

1) Association with chronic kidney disease (JAMA Internal Medicine, Jan 11, 2016)
- Two large observational analyses: the ARIC cohort (10,482 participants, ~14 years median follow-up) using self-reported PPI use, and Geisinger Health System data (248,751 patients, ~6 years median follow-up) using prescription records.
- PPI users had higher rates of incident CKD in both datasets. Estimated 10-year absolute CKD risk rose from 8.5% to 11.8% among ARIC baseline users, and from 13.9% to 15.6% in the Geisinger replication.
- PPI users tended to have higher BMI and more comorbid medication use.
- Authors emphasize observational design and residual confounding; results do not prove causality. They call for limiting unnecessary PPI use given widespread prescribing and potential public-health impact.

2) PPI use, amyloid production and animal/cell models (PLOS ONE, Badiola et al.)
- Systems-biology work predicted lansoprazole could affect Alzheimer’s-related pathways. In cell models expressing human APP/PS1, lansoprazole and other PPIs (5–50 µM) increased Aβ40 and Aβ42 production, decreased Aβ38, and altered Aβ species patterns—changes consistent with modulation of γ‑secretase and increased BACE1 (β‑secretase) activity.
- Acute intraperitoneal lansoprazole in wild-type and 3xTg-AD mice increased soluble brain Aβ40 (dose-dependent) and produced modest Aβ42 increases.
- Authors propose PPIs can alter amyloid metabolism in vitro and in vivo, suggest potential mechanisms (inverse γ‑secretase modulation, increased BACE1/meprin β activity), and note relevance given PPIs cross the blood–brain barrier. This is preclinical evidence; implications for humans remain uncertain.

3) Epidemiologic link to dementia (JAMA Neurology, Feb 15, 2016; German cohort)
- Analysis of 73,679 AOK-insured German adults aged ≥75 (2004–2011): regular PPI users (defined by repeated quarterly prescriptions) had a higher risk of incident dementia versus non-users (adjusted hazard ratio 1.44; 95% CI 1.36–1.52).
- Authors and commentators stress observational limits, possible confounding (diet, body weight, comorbidities), and that association ≠ causation. They call for randomized prospective trials and adherence to prescribing guidelines to avoid unnecessary long-term PPI use.

Clinical context and recommendations from commentators and editorials:
- PPIs provide major symptomatic benefit and can be essential (e.g., severe GERD, Barrett’s esophagus, prevention of NSAID-induced ulcers), but evidence is growing that long-term or inappropriate use carries risks (nutrient deficiencies, infections, CKD, possible cardiovascular and cognitive associations).
- Many patients are prescribed PPIs without clear indication, and a substantial fraction of long-term users might be able to stop therapy.
- Clinicians should reassess indications and duration of PPI therapy, consider nonpharmacologic measures for mild reflux, monitor for side effects, and avoid unnecessary chronic use while awaiting stronger causal evidence.

Overall takeaway:
Emerging observational and preclinical data link PPIs to potentially serious outcomes including CKD and increased amyloid-related biology and dementia risk in the elderly. These findings are not definitive proof of harm but strengthen calls to limit inappropriate long-term PPI use, reassess ongoing need in patients, and pursue randomized or mechanistic studies to clarify causality.

Summary:

Major U.S. news outlets reported that the CIA concluded Russia actively intervened in the 2016 presidential election with the intent of helping Donald Trump win. The Washington Post revealed the agency’s assessment, and the New York Times added that Russian hackers also breached the Republican National Committee but did not publicly release Republican materials—raising concerns Russia might retain leverage. Both reports relied on anonymous intelligence sources; Russia and WikiLeaks denied state involvement.

The revelations triggered intense political fallout. Critics accused Republican leaders, notably Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, of downplaying or suppressing warnings before the election—reportedly arguing that going public would look partisan. McConnell later faced scrutiny because his wife, Elaine Chao, was nominated for Transportation Secretary and he has not recused himself from her confirmation. Former CIA officer Evan McMullin and others called for investigations; Trump and his transition team dismissed the CIA’s conclusions as politically motivated, likening the agency to those who incorrectly asserted Saddam Hussein had WMDs and calling the stories “fake news.” Trump responded on Twitter by deflecting to his TV show, The Apprentice, and has said a press conference would be held on December 15.

The reports prompted debate over next steps. Commentators urged the Obama administration and intelligence community to declassify and publicize evidence. Many called for congressional hearings and investigations, though partisan divisions—exemplified by McConnell’s earlier resistance—make a quick bipartisan probe unlikely before the Electoral College meets. Some observers warned it may be difficult to prove Russia’s actions directly changed the election outcome absent evidence of vote tampering.

Separately, there is discussion about how Congress and Republicans might pressure or steer a potentially Russia-friendly President Trump. Options outlined include aggressive hearings to publicly build the case and persuade Trump, passing and enforcing sanctions or Ukraine/Syria-related measures that constrain Russian influence, public rebukes from Republican leaders, and waiting for further Russian behavior to demonstrate hostility. The situation was framed as urgent: if verified, foreign interference intended to favor one candidate is an extraordinary attack on U.S. democracy, demanding investigation and potential retaliation—though any response risks escalation in cyber and geopolitical arenas.

President Obama said he wants a “thorough and rigorous” investigation into a prostitution scandal in Cartagena, Colombia, that led to 11 U.S. Secret Service agents being sent home. Speaking at the close of the Summit of the Americas, Obama said he expects agents to act with “dignity and probity,” praised the agency’s difficult work, and pledged to reserve final judgment until the internal probe is complete. The agents were placed on administrative leave and interviewed by the Secret Service’s Office of Professional Responsibility after allegations that they and five Defense Department personnel — all part of the presidential advance team — brought prostitutes to a hotel and violated curfew. The matter came to light after a dispute over payment prompted Colombian police to notify the U.S. Embassy.

The scandal drew heavy U.S. media attention and diverted coverage from summit topics, angering many Colombians who felt it tarnished their country’s image as it seeks to showcase security and progress. House Oversight Chairman Darrell Issa said lawmakers want details and suggested more people may have been involved, warning of potential risks such as blackmail. Officials say the implicated Secret Service members include both special agents (protective detail) and uniformed division personnel (logistics and security). The Defense Department has opened a separate inquiry into its personnel.

Donald Trump is scheduled to receive his first classified intelligence briefing tomorrow at the FBI’s New York Field Office, which has the secure facilities required for such sessions. Career staff from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) will lead the briefing on major global threats; the FBI will simply host. Trump plans to bring New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and retired Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn. Both have supported him publicly and their presence has prompted speculation they might be considered for administration roles; unlike Trump, they would need—and would have—security clearances to attend.

The briefings are part of a long-standing tradition of providing classified intelligence to major-party presidential nominees; DNI Director James Clapper and White House officials have defended continuing the practice despite partisan objections. Candidates do not need formal security clearances to receive the briefings, which typically cover analytic assessments and emerging threats but avoid the most sensitive details about sources and methods. Both Trump and Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton are expected to receive two to three such briefings before the election.

The visit comes amid heightened debate over candidates’ fitness to receive secret information—critics have questioned Trump’s suitability because of his statements, while Republicans have urged limiting Clinton’s access after the FBI’s finding that she had been “extremely careless” with a private email server. Clapper and administration spokespeople emphasized the importance of briefing nominees to ensure a smooth transition and expressed confidence intelligence officials can protect sensitive information while informing both candidates.

Josephine Crook, 49, was arrested Friday night, Oct. 24, 2014, on suspicion of commercial burglary after allegedly stealing women's undergarments from the Kohl’s on South Fremont Avenue in Alhambra. Police say she concealed the items in an empty purse and failed to pay. Officers also allege she possessed burglary tools—a pair of wire cutters and scissors. Crook was taken into custody about 7:15 p.m., booked at the Alhambra Police Department, and held on $20,000 bail; she was scheduled to appear at Alhambra Municipal Court the following Wednesday. No further details were released.

More than 1,000 metres of overhead electrical cable were stolen overnight Friday from land off the A1133 at Newton-on-Trent in Lincolnshire, leaving the village without power for several hours. This is the second recent overhead cabling theft in the county, following a similar incident in August at Normanby-Le-Wold. Police warn the crime is extremely dangerous and ask anyone with information to call 0300 111 0300.

Bloomberg reported that Russian hackers infiltrated Dow Jones servers to obtain prepublication material and other nonpublic information to trade on. Four people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the intruders sought stories being prepared for publication and other data that could give traders an edge. The FBI’s New York office confirmed it is aware and investigating; the Secret Service and SEC are also said to be involved, and the White House was briefed. Authorities have been probing the case for at least a year and have been assessing how the stolen information could be monetized.

Dow Jones has disputed Bloomberg’s account, saying it has found no evidence of such an investigation and is looking into the report. The company had earlier disclosed a separate, lower-grade breach affecting contact and payment information for about 3,500 customers and said that incident appears part of a broader campaign targeting multiple companies.

The episode highlights a growing law-enforcement focus on cyber-enabled insider trading: previous cases have involved Russian-speaking hackers breaking into news-distribution services to steal unreleased press releases and earnings data, which were then used to make profitable trades. Investigators say journalists and data providers are attractive targets because market-moving information often exists in-house well before publication.

This collection of clippings and notes centers on Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise amid their high-profile separation, and on Cruise’s early life and development into a movie star.

Katie Holmes
- After filing for divorce from Tom Cruise and seeking sole legal custody of their daughter Suri, Holmes remained publicly active and professionally busy. She was seen out with Suri and made media appearances while preparing to resume acting and fashion work.
- Holmes is set to begin production on Molly, a film she co-wrote and co-produces about a single mother and daughter, with filming in New York through August. She also completed a modern adaptation of Chekhov’s The Seagull in May and is slated to shoot the romantic comedy Responsible Adults in the fall. Holmes plans her first New York Fashion Week show for her clothing line Holmes & Yang.
- Lawyers for both Holmes and Cruise were negotiating a divorce settlement; sources said neither wanted the process litigated publicly.

Tom Cruise: background and character profiles
- Several pieces revisit Tom Cruise’s upbringing and path to stardom. Before Scientology, Cruise (born Thomas Mapother IV) spent time at St. Francis Seminary and was raised in a Roman Catholic environment. Priests and classmates recall he attended seminary largely for education and structure rather than from a strong priestly calling.
- Former instructors (notably Father Aubert) and classmates remember a shy but cocky, attention-seeking youth who benefitted from speech and drama training. He left the seminary after his freshman year and later adopted the stage name Cruise.
- Former manager Eileen Berlin, who mentored Cruise in his late teens and early 20s, describes him as ambitious, physically proud, private, moody, and prone to quick anger—traits she links to a difficult childhood marked by dyslexia, bullying, and an abusive or absent father. She believes those scars and his difficulty opening up contributed to his troubled relationships and eventual embrace of Scientology, which he later credited with helping him overcome learning problems.
- Former seminary classmates and friars were surprised by Cruise’s adoption of Scientology and by his later public persona; some expressed dismay at his early risqué roles compared with his seminary past.
- Anecdotes include a priest sending Cruise an old seminary photo around the time of his 50th birthday and the note that Holmes’s family and faith background contrasted sharply with the Scientology milieu, which factored into Holmes’s decision to leave with their daughter.

Contextual notes
- The material appears drawn from archived web crawls (Wayback Machine/Alexa), with WARC files currently not publicly available. The Karlbox is a limited-edition collaboration between designer Karl Lagerfeld and 255-year-old art-supply maker Faber‑Castell. Housed in a black lacquered, beech‑wood cabinet (reminiscent of a Chinese wedding chest) and designed by Lagerfeld, the Karlbox contains 350 premium art tools—Albrecht Dürer water‑soluble color pencils (all 120 shades), Polychromos pencils, Pitt Artist pens and crayons, Castell 9000 graphite pencils, pastels, watercolor brushes and accessories (eraser, sharpeners, foldable water cup), all organized in removable drawers and sorted by color families. Each box is serialized and comes with a certificate of authenticity; production is strictly limited (reported as 2,400–2,500 pieces) and the retail price is about $2,850–$3,000. Initially sold at select Faber‑Castell shops, Karl Lagerfeld boutiques, Harrods and Gump’s (and later other specialty stores), the set reflects the intersection of fashion, art and design and Lagerfeld’s longtime practice of drawing as a central creative tool.

Archbishop Charles J. Chaput of Philadelphia issued new pastoral guidelines, effective 1 July, instructing priests and parish leaders how to apply Pope Francis’s Amoris Laetitia in the archdiocese. The six‑page document affirms mercy and pastoral accompaniment but emphasizes that existing Catholic doctrine and canonical discipline on marriage remain unchanged.

Key points:
- Divorced Catholics who have civilly remarried without an annulment may be welcomed back to the sacraments only if they abstain from sexual relations and “live as brother and sister.” Reconciliation in the sacrament of penance, predicated on that commitment, could open the way to receiving the Eucharist.
- Persons in active, public same‑sex relationships “offer a serious counter‑witness” to Catholic teaching and should not hold positions of parish leadership (parish council, lector, instructing the faithful) or distribute Communion. Those with predominant same‑sex attractions are called to live chastely, seek support and, when chastity is difficult, frequently seek penance. The guidelines acknowledge some with same‑sex attraction may still be able to marry heterosexually and have children.
- Cohabiting unmarried couples should be encouraged to marry; if one partner is unwilling or seriously incapable of commitment, pastors are advised to urge separation. If a couple is preparing for marriage but delaying, they should practice chastity as part of preparation.
- The document directs priests to accompany and guide people in “irregular” situations toward holiness while upholding doctrine. It forbids persons in those situations from certain parish roles to avoid confusing witness.
- Chaput praises parts of Amoris Laetitia but insists local application must remain consistent with Church teaching. Commentators note the exhortation leaves room for differing diocesan interpretations; some bishops may take more permissive approaches while others, like Chaput, will apply stricter norms.

Reactions quoted include supporters who see continuity with longstanding Church practice on the need for a state of grace to receive Communion, and critics who question enforcement and the exclusion of people in irregular situations from parish ministry.

An adult film star, Kacey Jordan, told ABC News she attended an all-night party at Charlie Sheen’s Los Angeles home the night before he was hospitalized with “severe abdominal pains.” Jordan said she was paid $5,000 to attend and described Sheen as disheveled, heavily intoxicated and repeatedly smoking large chunks of cocaine from a pipe. She claimed a man later arrived and dumped “tennis ball–size” amounts of cocaine on a table and that Sheen used the pipe every few minutes. Jordan said she feared Sheen was on a “suicide binge.”

Jordan also alleged Sheen was setting up a rented $250,000-a-month mansion to host constant parties, offered to let several porn stars move in, promised cars and other perks, and even asked Jordan if she would babysit his children. She said Sheen wrote her a check for $30,000 when she left; TMZ published an image of a check made out to cash. Jordan declined payment for the interview, has no plans for legal action, and said she’s glad he’s sought rehab.

Sheen is reported to be in an undisclosed rehab facility and production on Two and a Half Men is on hold. His representatives issued a statement saying he is getting medical attention and accusing “opportunistic women” of exploiting the situation. The report prompted a strong reaction from ex-wife Denise Richards, who publicly barred Sheen from being alone with their daughters while he completes treatment.

Researchers at Nationwide Children’s Hospital tested 100–101 breast‑milk samples purchased from public milk‑sharing websites and compared them with unpasteurized donor milk from screened milk banks. They found high levels of bacterial contamination in the internet‑purchased milk: about 74% of samples would have failed milk‑bank safety criteria. Specific findings included higher rates in web‑purchased milk of gram‑negative bacteria (72% vs. 35% in bank samples), Staphylococcus (63% vs. 25%), Streptococcus (36% vs. 20%), and three samples with Salmonella (none in bank milk). Nine percent of online samples contained dangerous staph levels; some showed signs of fecal contamination. All samples tested negative for HIV.

Investigators attributed the contamination mainly to poor hygiene during expression, unclean containers or pump parts, inadequate cooling during shipping (19% of sellers did not use dry ice or other cooling), and long transit times. Milk‑bank donors are screened and their milk is pasteurized, which reduces bacterial risk; however, bank supplies are limited, costly (about $6/oz), and prioritized for premature or medically fragile infants. Professional organizations (FDA, American Academy of Pediatrics) discourage feeding infants breast milk obtained directly from individuals or via the Internet, and experts warn buyers cannot reliably verify quality, contents, or handling of online purchases. Researchers noted the study may not apply to milk shared among known friends or relatives, and emphasized safer alternatives such as regulated milk banks or screened sharing arrangements.

Researchers presented several advances and findings around detecting and managing Alzheimer’s disease at the Alzheimer’s Association International Conference in London.

1) Promising blood test for amyloid
- A team led by Randall Bateman (Washington University) described a simple blood test that measures ratios of different beta‑amyloid forms to indicate whether amyloid plaques are accumulating in the brain—a hallmark associated with Alzheimer’s.
- The test was developed by comparing blood ratios with PET-scan measures in 41 people. If validated, it could be used widely by primary care clinicians—analogous to routine cholesterol checks—to screen for Alzheimer’s risk and identify people who might benefit from earlier interventions or further testing.
- Experts caution the sample was small and larger validation (an additional ~180 people) is underway. A positive amyloid test does not guarantee someone will develop symptomatic Alzheimer’s, since plaques begin forming 15–20 years before symptoms.

2) IDEAS PET‑scan study: many patients with suspected Alzheimer’s lack brain amyloid
- Interim results from the large IDEAS study (over 18,000 Medicare beneficiaries enrolled; ~4,000 analyzed so far) show that only 54.3% of patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and 70.5% of patients diagnosed with dementia had amyloid plaques on PET imaging.
- A negative amyloid PET effectively rules out Alzheimer’s; a positive result raises the risk but is not definitive. These PET results led physicians to change care plans for about two-thirds of patients—often involving starting or stopping Alzheimer’s symptom drugs—far more than expected (planned ~30%, observed ~66%).
- The findings suggest many people on Alzheimer’s medications may not have amyloid pathology and thus might be receiving inappropriate treatment. The study aims to show whether PET imaging changes outcomes and inform Medicare coverage decisions; CMS funded much of the study by reimbursing PET scans.

3) Clinical and policy implications
- PET scans that detect amyloid are informative in diagnostically uncertain cases (atypical presentations, puzzling MCI) and may help avoid harmful or useless treatments (e.g., for Lewy body dementia patients who shouldn’t receive certain Alzheimer’s drugs). However, scans are costly ($3,000–$6,000), invasive CSF tests exist, and Medicare has limited coverage pending stronger evidence.
- Experts advise against using amyloid PET as a general screening tool for asymptomatic people or those who can be reliably diagnosed by standard methods.

4) Lifestyle prevention trial and broader research context
- The Alzheimer’s Association launched a $20 million, two‑year POINTER clinical trial in the U.S. to test whether a combined lifestyle intervention (exercise, nutrition counseling, social/cognitive stimulation, self‑management) can prevent cognitive decline in 2,500 at‑risk older adults. This follows positive results from a Finnish trial and mirrors similar studies internationally.
- Researchers emphasize a multipronged approach—combining lifestyle measures with future drug therapies—may be the best path to reducing Alzheimer’s risk or slowing progression.

Overall, these developments point to improved, less invasive screening (blood tests) and better-targeted use of expensive diagnostics (amyloid PET) that can refine diagnoses, prevent inappropriate treatment, and identify people who might benefit from early lifestyle or future disease‑modifying interventions—while larger validation and outcome data are still needed.

A WISE (domestic violence prevention) survey given to fifth-graders at Windsor Elementary School in Vermont asked about sexual history, sexual orientation and gender identity, prompting complaints from parents. Parent Vanessa Beach said her 10-year-old daughter and classmates were too young for such questions and that a sexual partner at that age would constitute abuse. Officials said parents were sent an opt-out notice but Beach said she did not receive it; a researcher noted passive-consent policies are common in Vermont. WISE says students are told participation is voluntary and that the survey questions were developed with University of New Hampshire researchers with whom data are being shared. School administrators and WISE are addressing parental concerns and hope to use the issue to open dialogue; Beach said she supports much of WISE’s domestic-violence work despite her objections.

The piece profiles the three Huntsman sisters—Mary Anne, Abby, and Liddy—daughters of Republican presidential candidate Jon Huntsman Jr., who have gained attention as the @Jon2012girls for tweeting candid, snarky campaign-trail updates. In New York for a karaoke-themed photo shoot, the twentysomething sisters come off as playful, media-savvy and earnest: they rehearse together (even singing Wilson Phillips to psych up before debates), parody political ads (their viral Funny-or-Die–style spoof of a Herman Cain spot brought them brief fame), and consciously use social media and off-the-cuff sass to reach young, disillusioned voters. They insist they aren’t aiming to be reality stars or cable pundits but were raised to give back, and see campaigning for their father as an extension of that ethic. The story also shares a light, embarrassing anecdote—Mary Anne once went on a single date to see Elf with NBA player Kris Humphries, who ate an enormous tub of popcorn—which underscores their informal, relatable public persona.

George C. Brinkman Jr., 45, of Brunswick, is in custody after a nearly nine-hour standoff and is a suspect in multiple recent killings in northeastern Ohio.

Key facts:
- Police arrested Brinkman early Tuesday morning at a friend’s home in Brunswick after a SWAT standoff; officers used a stun gun when he was found holding a gun. He was evaluated at a hospital and is being held by North Royalton police.
- Investigators have charged him with murder in the shooting deaths of Rogell Eugene John II, 71, and Roberta Ray John, 64, found Monday at their Lake Township home. The sheriff’s office says Brinkman had been house-sitting for the Johns and had previously dated their daughter; he worked at the Johns’ business.
- Brinkman is also a suspect in the deaths of Suzanne Taylor, 45, and her daughters Taylor Pifer, 21, and Kylie Pifer, 18, whose bodies were discovered Sunday at their North Royalton home. Police say Suzanne Taylor was stabbed and had her throat cut; the daughters showed no outward signs of trauma as reported. Formal charges in the North Royalton deaths had not been announced at the time of the reports.
- Before his arrest Brinkman messaged WOIO Channel 19 reporter Lacey Crisp on Facebook—he is friends online with the North Royalton victims—and initially agreed to an on-camera interview. The station alerted police because Brinkman revealed he was at the standoff location and it was unclear whether others were at risk; the conversation ended at police request. The station says Brinkman later accused the reporter of betraying him.
- Brinkman’s record includes past convictions for bad checks, criminal mischief, disorderly conduct, and a 1999 conviction for receiving stolen property and unauthorized computer access, with time served for violating community control.
- Family members said Brinkman and Suzanne Taylor were longtime friends and former classmates; relatives speculate possible jealousy but police have not confirmed motive.
- A vigil for the North Royalton victims was planned for Wednesday evening.

Investigations into motive and causes of death for all victims are ongoing.

House Republicans pulled their long‑sought Obamacare repeal vote Friday after Speaker Paul Ryan concluded he did not have the votes, handing a major setback to President Donald Trump and GOP leaders. Facing defections from both conservative hardliners in the House Freedom Caucus (who said the bill didn’t go far enough) and moderate Republicans (who feared Medicaid cuts and constituent harm), leadership abandoned the American Health Care Act just before a scheduled floor vote. Trump had pressed members to support the measure and lobbied heavily, but acknowledged afterward he was “10 to 15 votes” short.

Republican leaders had hoped a vote would force members to show their loyalties, but Ryan decided cancelling would avoid an even larger, more embarrassing defeat. Democrats celebrated the collapse as a victory for protections in the Affordable Care Act. GOP reactions were mixed: some architects of the bill were angry, Freedom Caucus leaders vowed to keep pushing for repeal, and moderates urged regrouping and bipartisan talks. Leaders on both sides said repeal remains a priority, but the failure exposed deep divisions within the Republican conference and left Obamacare intact “for the foreseeable future.”

Munich police evacuated the city's main train station and the Pasing station after receiving tips about a possible bomb attack, a police spokeswoman told ABC News. Both stations were cleared and later reopened after officers — including those called in from New Year’s Day duty — conducted searches. Authorities reported finding nothing suspicious so far and urged the public to avoid crowds, public transport and train stations. The situation is developing.

Federal prosecutors say they seized about $20 million in cash hidden under a mattress in a Westborough, Massachusetts, apartment as part of their probe of TelexFree, an alleged international pyramid scheme that posed as a VOIP telecom company. Agents arrested 28-year-old Brazilian Cleber Rene Rizerio Rocha after following him from New York; he is charged with conspiracy to commit money laundering and is being held pending a detention hearing.

Prosecutors allege TelexFree generated little legitimate revenue and primarily paid returns to earlier investors with funds from new recruits; nearly 965,225 victims worldwide lost about $1.76–$1.8 billion before the company filed for bankruptcy in 2014. Co-founder James Merrill pleaded guilty to fraud charges and awaits sentencing; co-founder Carlos Wanzeler fled to Brazil and has not been extradited.

According to the criminal complaint, Rocha acted as a courier for Wanzeler’s nephew. He flew from Brazil, met a cooperating witness in Massachusetts and handed over $2.2 million in a suitcase. After agents followed him to the apartment and arrested him, they recovered the larger stash beneath the mattress. Authorities say Rocha was involved in a scheme to launder millions in hidden TelexFree assets through Hong Kong and transfer them to Brazil.

Actor Scott Wilson, best known recently for his role as Hershel Greene on AMC’s The Walking Dead, has died at 76 from complications of leukemia. His representative said Wilson passed peacefully at his Los Angeles home. A veteran film and TV actor with a career beginning in 1967 (notable early work includes In the Heat of the Night and In Cold Blood), Wilson earned a Golden Globe nomination for The Ninth Configuration and appeared in films such as The Great Gatsby, Dead Man Walking and Pearl Harbor, and on series including CSI.

Wilson’s return to The Walking Dead season 9 had been announced at New York Comic-Con and he had already completed filming his scenes. AMC and many cast and crew members paid tribute, and the show honored him with an on-screen memorial during the season premiere. Tributes poured in from colleagues and fans remembering him as a gifted actor and a gentle, generous person.

Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders said he will treat the Democratic convention as "contested" unless Hillary Clinton wins enough pledged delegates to secure the nomination without relying on superdelegates. At a Washington press conference he urged superdelegates—especially from states he won decisively like Washington and Minnesota—to switch their support to him, arguing they should reflect the will of voters in their states and consider electability against Donald Trump. Sanders acknowledged he faces a steep climb—needing roughly 65% of remaining pledged delegates to overtake Clinton—but vowed to fight for every vote and delegate remaining.

ABC/Washington Post analysis noted that under the Democratic proportional system, it is unlikely either candidate will reach a majority of delegates without superdelegates: about 15% of delegates are unbound superdelegates. Clinton already has a large lead among pledged delegates and about 520 superdelegates committed, while Sanders has roughly 39. Analysts say Sanders’ path is mathematically difficult because many remaining delegates are in California (and D.C., which favors Clinton), and proportional allocation makes it hard to swing enough delegates even with strong showings. Clinton also leads by several million votes overall, a gap Sanders’ arguments (momentum, superior general-election performance in some polls, and state wins) have not closed. The consensus: Sanders can force a contested convention by continuing his campaign, but actually prevailing there or persuading enough superdelegates to overturn Clinton’s delegate and popular-vote advantages is unlikely.

Summary:

Congress required the military in 2007 to test troops’ brain function before deployment and again after return to detect traumatic brain injury (TBI). ProPublica and NPR found the program largely failed: more than 1 million service members took the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) at a taxpayer cost exceeding $42 million, yet the military still lacks a reliable system to identify many TBIs.

Key findings and problems
- ANAM was chosen quickly and without strong scientific backing. It was developed in-house at a military lab, then licensed to outside organizations, and some developers who stood to profit were involved in the selection process—raising conflict-of-interest concerns. A top Army neuropsychologist called the selection “nepotistic.”
- Many military medical experts warned ANAM was not validated to screen or diagnose combat-related concussion and that its results were sensitive to non-injury factors (fatigue, distraction). Senior clinicians described the test as “fraught with problems” and no better than a “coin flip” in congressional testimony.
- The military often did not follow recommended protocols for using ANAM. Troops typically received only a single pre-deployment baseline (though multiple baselines produce more reliable results). The Army restricted use of baseline results: a policy explicitly barred sending soldiers with low “red” baseline scores for medical follow-up, even though other services (Navy/Marines) do refer low scorers.
- Implementation was poor: there is no integrated digital system for storing and accessing results; retrieving a baseline for clinicians in theater requires manual requests and paperwork. Despite tens of thousands of TBIs in theater, requests for past scores have been very few.
- Costs were mischaracterized. ANAM was presented as “free” because it originated in a military lab, but the Army had licensed it, and the Defense Department has paid contractors and the licensee roughly $42 million (including millions annually in user fees and large contracts to administer the test).
- Promised comparative research was delayed. A head-to-head study to evaluate ANAM against other tests was supposed to be completed around 2009 but remained unfinished; the GAO reported results weren’t expected until 2015, years after the initiative began and after the wars wind down.
- Some evidence suggests ANAM can be useful if used appropriately (for instance, to help assess immediate post-blast fitness for duty), and other tests (e.g., ImPact, used by the NHL and some professional teams) had stronger supporting research. Critics say the military prioritized speed, cost and ownership over rigorous comparison and validation.

Consequences and reactions
- Critics inside and outside the military say the program offers the appearance of help but little real protection for soldiers with invisible brain injuries. Former program managers and clinicians described missed diagnoses, inadequate follow-up, and frustrated caregivers and families.
- Congressional sponsors and members expressed anger and disappointment that the program did not meet the statute’s intent (especially the lack of consistent post-deployment testing and meaningful follow-up).
- Military leaders defended the program as a first step and said they are working to improve the test and to study alternatives.

Bottom line
The military’s rapid adoption and flawed implementation of ANAM—chosen amid political pressure and without robust validation or consistent clinical use—has left a large database of largely underused baseline tests and has not delivered the reliable, systemwide screening Congress intended to protect troops from undiagnosed TBIs.

A 73-year-old man with a spotless driving record was stopped by Seattle officer Nic Abts-Olsen Tuesday night for driving with his headlights off near Martin Luther King Jr. Way South and South Massachusetts. When the officer returned to the vehicle after checking the man’s license and registration, he watched the driver portion cocaine from a small glass vial. Startled by a knock on the window, the man spilled powder on his hands and the car floor, initially claiming the substance was “vitamins” before admitting the truth and complimenting the officer’s detection. What would have been only a warning due to the driver’s clean record turned into an arrest; the man was booked into King County Jail for narcotics possession. The encounter was recorded on patrol car video. The item also notes it was posted alongside other City of Seattle archival content.

Anthony J. Lescowitch Jr., 35, of Drifton/Freeland, was arrested after sharing a police department's Facebook post showing his wanted photo. Freeland police had posted the photo seeking help locating him on charges including aggravated assault related to a July 14, 2013 attack in which the victim was struck, robbed and later had cash withdrawn via the victim’s ATM card. Minutes after the department’s post, Lescowitch reposted and mocked it. An undercover officer using a fake female Facebook profile conversed with him for about 30 minutes, obtained his location, arranged a meeting and had officers arrest him there without incident. Lescowitch, also wanted by Luzerne County probation, was arraigned and jailed on $25,000 bail (he could not post 10%) and faces multiple charges; a preliminary hearing is scheduled. Several others have also been charged in the same assault case.

Donald Trump said the U.S. should "seriously" consider racial and religious profiling as a counterterrorism tool following the Orlando nightclub massacre. In a CBS "Face the Nation" interview, the presumptive Republican nominee said he dislikes profiling but argued other countries (like Israel) use it successfully and the U.S. must use "common sense" over "political correctness." Trump reiterated his proposal for a temporary ban on foreign Muslims entering the country—claiming it would have prevented the Orlando attack despite the shooter being U.S.-born—and urged Muslim communities to report suspicious behavior, citing San Bernardino as an example where neighbors allegedly saw warning signs. He also said he is working with the NRA on a policy to bar people on the no-fly/terror watch lists from buying guns, acknowledging complications because some on the lists shouldn't be there. Trump criticized fellow Republicans for talking too much about his positions instead of focusing on governing. Civil libertarians have called profiling discriminatory.

A Connecticut man already facing burglary charges was arrested on new counts after a victim recognized his stolen sweatshirt in the man’s mug shot. Police say Derek Benson, 30, was linked to a July 2014 Glastonbury home burglary after the homeowner saw Benson’s booking photo from a separate late‑year arrest and noticed Benson wearing the victim’s gray Coco Libre–branded sweatshirt. The homeowner alerted police, and investigators connected Benson to the earlier break‑in, during which the sweatshirt and jewelry were taken. Benson was arrested last week on charges of burglary, larceny and criminal mischief and is being held on $125,000 bond.

Apple will begin selling the iPhone 4S in mainland China on Jan. 13 through its partner China Unicom, adding China to a 22-country rollout that makes this the fastest iPhone launch in Apple's history. The iPhone now represents nearly half of Apple’s revenue and a majority of its profits, and China—home to roughly 960 million mobile subscribers and the world’s largest smartphone market—is seen as a major growth opportunity. China Mobile (over 630 million subscribers) and China Telecom remain potential future partners, but no deals have been announced; many China Mobile users already run iPhones through unofficial workarounds. Siri will not support Mandarin at launch, though Apple plans to add Chinese language support in 2012. Analysts expect strong demand in China, citing the rapid Hong Kong sell-out and a sizable high-end phone market; expected unsubsidized prices mirror prior iPhone pricing in China.

Granville P. Swift (1821–1875) was a Kentucky-born California pioneer, early Bear Flag Revolt participant and successful Gold Rush miner who amassed and then largely lost a vast private hoard of gold. Arriving in California as a trapper in the 1840s, he helped seize Sonoma in 1846, served as a captain in the California Battalion, then turned to mining after gold was found at Sutter’s Mill. Swift proved an exceptionally productive prospector and reportedly made enormous sums—contemporaries estimated up to $100,000 (or more) apiece for him and two partners. He had much of his gold minted into distinctive octagonal $50 slugs marked as his.

Because there were no secure banks, Swift buried large portions of his wealth around the Bay Area—primarily Sonoma—and kept a crude handwritten inventory listing bottles, jugs and a tin box. He was notoriously absent‑minded about the locations, however, and much of the buried treasure was forgotten. Several recoveries occurred in the early 20th century (notably about $7,000 found in 1903, roughly $30,000 uncovered from a chimney in 1904, and $42,600 dug up by a rancher in 1914 after a vivid dream), but a substantial remainder is believed still undiscovered.

Swift’s later life was marked by misfortune: he lost money in a Comstock Lode swindle, his sister’s large cache was washed away in a flood, he sold much property and moved to Solano County, and his marriage ended in divorce. He returned to prospecting for quicksilver but died in 1875 after a fatal riding accident. Swift is remembered as a bold, generous, and often unlucky figure whose buried gold remains part history, part local legend.
