Two former friends and Senate allies of the late Sen. John McCain — GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham and former independent Sen. Joe Lieberman — praised McCain’s daughter Meghan for her sharp rebuke of President Donald Trump during McCain’s memorial speech, saying her words reflected her father’s character. Meghan’s comment that “The America of John McCain has no need to be made great again” underscored the differences between McCain and Trump; Trump was not invited to the service. Graham and Lieberman, longtime companions of McCain often dubbed the “three amigos,” reminisced about McCain’s courage, love of the Senate and legacy, with Graham predicting McCain will be a foundational figure in Senate history.

Separately, former Secretary of State John Kerry criticized current political leaders for fostering a “fact-less world,” contrasting today’s partisan climate with the bipartisan outreach exemplified by McCain. Kerry, a frequent Trump critic, defended statesmanlike engagement and pushed back against Trump’s past attacks on him.

Former Defense Secretary Leon Panetta urged Democrats to wait for special counsel Robert Mueller’s report before pursuing impeachment, arguing Mueller’s findings should guide any next steps. Panetta warned that efforts by Trump’s team to undermine Mueller’s credibility could backfire and said evidence was accumulating that could support obstruction-of-justice charges.

ESPN commentator Rob Parker sparked controversy on December 13–14, 2012 by questioning Washington Redskins quarterback Robert Griffin III’s racial authenticity on the ESPN2 show First Take, suggesting RGIII “is kind of black” because he has a white fiancée and calling him a “cornball brother” who’s “not one of us.” Parker defended himself on Twitter, calling critics “uneducated” and promising further discussion on First Take, but then stopped tweeting and was later suspended indefinitely by ESPN while the network conducts a review; ESPN called his comments “inappropriate.” The incident drew widespread criticism — including from NFLPA executive director DeMaurice Smith — and was positioned by critics as part of a recurring pattern of racially tinged commentary in sports media (examples noted include earlier criticism of Colin Kaepernick’s tattoos and debates over Cam Newton). RGIII’s father said the remarks seemed intended to stir controversy rather than reflect overt racism. The story highlights lingering racial issues around black quarterbacks despite their growing prominence in the NFL.

A catastrophic fire ripped through the Kiss nightclub in Santa Maria, a university city in southern Brazil, in the early hours of Sunday, killing at least 233 people (some reports later cited up to 245) and injuring many more. The blaze was ignited when pyrotechnics used by a performing band set the club’s ceiling soundproofing alight; toxic smoke spread rapidly and most victims died of asphyxiation, while others were crushed in a panicked stampede.

Witnesses and officials said the venue was overcrowded—estimates ranged from about 1,000 up to 2,000 people—and at least one exit was locked. Security staff initially blocked fleeing patrons, reportedly mistaking the rush for an attempt to avoid paying tabs, and only reacted when flames became obvious. Firefighters described encountering bodies blocking exits and had to break through walls to reach victims. Many victims were moved to a gymnasium used as a makeshift morgue; identification was hampered, especially for female victims whose personal items were scattered in the wreckage.

Local and national officials, including President Dilma Rousseff, traveled to Santa Maria. Authorities said the club’s operating permit was in renewal and pointed to safety violations—locked doors, flammable ceiling material, and the use of indoor pyrotechnics—as likely contributors. Investigations and questioning of club owners and staff were under way.

The disaster recalls other deadly nightclub fires worldwide caused by indoor fireworks igniting flammable materials, and has intensified scrutiny of venue safety ahead of Brazil’s upcoming major international events.

An orca known as J35 (Tahlequah), a 20-year-old member of the endangered Southern Resident killer whales’ J pod, carried her dead newborn calf for at least 17 days and about 1,000 miles through waters off Washington and British Columbia. The calf was born July 24 and was seen alive only briefly; J35 balanced and pushed the body on her rostrum while other pod members accompanied her and at times shared the responsibility of holding the carcass. The prolonged behavior—an unprecedentedly long documented case of cetacean mourning—generated worldwide attention and audio and photographic documentation. Researchers interpret the actions as grief and note orcas’ strong parental bonds, particularly when a calf lived even briefly after a 17-month gestation.

Scientists worried the exertion could harm J35, but shore-based telephoto images showed she remained in good physical condition, supported by family members who appeared to feed her. The event has intensified concern about the Southern Residents’ precarious status: the three pods number 75 whales, have not had a surviving birth since 2015, and are declining largely because their primary prey, Chinook salmon, is also endangered. Observers are particularly worried about other underweight individuals (notably J50). Authorities have been urging boats to keep distance, enforcing restrictions to avoid disturbing the pod, and continuing conservation measures—including cuts to Chinook catch limits and noise and pollution mitigation—while researchers stress urgent stewardship to try to restore the population’s reproductive viability.

Mike Megna, 44, a former Pompton Lakes police officer and Marine who spent about three weeks helping at Ground Zero after 9/11, is battling a very rare kidney disease he believes was caused by exposure to World Trade Center dust. He began urinating blood in 2007, became chronically anemic and disabled, and after years of tests was diagnosed at the Mayo Clinic with "monotypic atypical anti-GBM (anti–glomerular basement membrane) nephritis," a newly named, extremely rare autoimmune kidney disorder documented in only a few dozen people worldwide. Mayo clinicians say the disease is slow-moving and currently best managed by monitoring rather than aggressive treatment.

Megna has exhausted savings, sold his business, fallen behind on his mortgage and faces foreclosure on his West Milford home. He has received limited compensation from the DOJ Victim Compensation Fund for earlier respiratory and digestive ailments but his kidney condition is not on the official list of illnesses covered under the Zadroga Act–administered World Trade Center health programs. Those programs require published, peer‑reviewed epidemiologic evidence showing a higher rate of a condition among 9/11 responders versus the general population before adding it to the covered list. Researchers at Mount Sinai are studying kidney disease in responders; preliminary work prompted a petition to add kidney disease to the list and a published study is expected before reconsideration.

Frustrated by the wait, Megna put up billboards and a website (DoRightByMike.com) to press officials for recognition and compensation. Federal officials say they must follow the statutory scientific process; clinicians say causation in an individual case is plausible but proving it statistically will be difficult because the disease is so rare. Megna’s doctors and family note his physical decline and depression; he hopes that if kidney disease is later certified he can amend prior claims to receive additional compensation before he becomes sicker.

New U.S. guidelines — the first update in nearly three decades, issued by the National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer’s Association — recast Alzheimer’s disease as a continuum that begins years before dementia appears and divides it into three stages: a pre-symptomatic phase with brain changes but no outward symptoms, a middle phase of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) with subtle problems but preserved daily function, and the dementia phase. The change reflects mounting evidence that Alzheimer’s-related brain changes (amyloid and tau pathology, neuronal loss, brain shrinkage) can start five to 10 years before current clinical detection.

While the guidelines formally recognize earlier-stage disease and emphasize the promise of biomarkers (brain imaging and cerebrospinal fluid tests, and ultimately blood tests) for earlier, objective detection, they do not call for immediate change in routine clinical practice. Diagnosis will remain clinician-driven for now, and the guidelines advise that biomarkers be used primarily for research and clinical trials because tests lack standardized methods and clear cutoff values, and because abnormal biomarkers do not always predict symptomatic disease. There is also no proven therapy yet to prevent or substantially delay progression, so telling asymptomatic people they are likely to develop Alzheimer’s has uncertain benefit.

The update aims to accelerate research, identify earlier-stage patients for trials, and ultimately enable earlier intervention if disease-modifying treatments become available. Short-term practical impacts include greater attention to people with MCI — potentially as many as the 5.4 million Americans estimated to have Alzheimer’s dementia — and encouragement for such patients to seek testing in research settings. Policymakers are also responding: proposed Medicare coding for Alzheimer’s diagnostic discussions would recognize the importance of early diagnosis and caregiver involvement. The authors stress the guidelines are iterative, anticipating further revisions as biomarker science and treatments advance.

Paul Ceglia, a 39-year-old man from western New York who filed a 2010 lawsuit seeking 84% of Facebook (and claiming Mark Zuckerberg promised him a large stake in return for 2003 work), has been federally indicted for allegedly faking evidence in that case. Prosecutors say Ceglia did hire Zuckerberg for work on a project, but fabricated a contract that purported to give him at least 50% of Facebook, created fake emails, and destroyed evidence. He was arrested last month, has pleaded not guilty, and faces wire- and mail-fraud charges that each carry up to 20 years in prison; he is due in Manhattan federal court on Nov. 28.

Separately, Ceglia’s then-current lawyer, Ohio attorney Dean Boland, has sought to withdraw from the case (filing reasons privately), joining several prior attorneys who left; Facebook has asked the court to disclose the reasons but won’t oppose the withdrawal if it doesn’t delay proceedings. Facebook has urged dismissal of Ceglia’s civil suit, arguing forgery, fabricated emails, spoliation of evidence, and that the claim is time-barred. Facebook has previously called the lawsuit fraudulent and described Ceglia as a convicted felon and scam artist.

Police in Kabul fired warning shots and into the air to disperse large, sometimes stone-throwing crowds protesting reported Quran burnings in the U.S., in the latest wave of unrest that has swept Afghanistan. Crowds — estimates ranged from hundreds to over 10,000 in some accounts — chanted anti‑American and anti‑government slogans, burned tires, waved Taliban flags and hurled rocks at police in several parts of the capital. Security forces responded with baton charges and gunfire into the air; at least five people were wounded (including two with apparent gunshot wounds) and one person was reported killed. Officials said some protesters fired pistols at police and accused Taliban elements of exploiting the anger ahead of parliamentary elections this weekend; the Taliban denied directing the protests but acknowledged sympathy. The demonstrations follow earlier deadly clashes tied to threatened and copycat Quran burnings in the U.S., and come amid concerns the unrest could destabilize polling and broader security ahead of an upcoming U.S. strategy review.

Amanda Palmer and Jason Webley’s new concept album Evelyn Evelyn — a theatrical, genre-hopping record about fictional conjoined twins Eva and Lyn Neville — features a wide range of collaborators, including Frances Bean Cobain. Cobain, then 17, contributed guest vocals on the song “My Space,” but Palmer stresses Frances is as much a visual artist and graphic-novel fan as a singer. Palmer praises her as smart, funny and determined to make art on her own terms.

Evelyn Evelyn frames its songs with spoken-word interludes that tell the twins’ picaresque, often dark backstory (circus life, abuse, marginalization), and mixes cabaret, folk, country and ’80s-style tracks. The record includes cameos from “Weird Al” Yankovic, Tegan and Sara, Gerard Way and Andrew WK; many guest parts are blended into choruses, so individual voices are not always distinct. Highlights cited include the cabaret tune “Have You Seen My Sister Evelyn,” the country-tinged “You Only Want Me ’Cause You Want My Sister,” the guest-heavy “My Space,” and a stripped-down cover of Joy Division’s “Love Will Tear Us Apart” that closes the album. Reviews call the project eccentric and theatrical but emotionally compelling, rewarding listeners who give it time. The album was released on 11 Records.

On Nov. 21, 2012, then-16-year-old Ivins Rosier admitted on video to shooting a retired Florida Highway Patrol K-9, Drake, who was later euthanized. Rosier faced trial as an adult and was found guilty by a Palm Beach County jury of felony cruelty to animals with a firearm, burglary of a dwelling with a firearm, and shooting into a building. Circuit Judge Robin Rosenberg ordered the now-17-year-old held without bail. Defense attorneys said they will seek a new trial and challenge the adult indictment, arguing his right to juvenile sentencing was violated and again contesting the sufficiency of the evidence despite Rosier’s confession and GPS ankle-monitor records placing him inside Trooper Robert Boody’s home that night.

House Democratic leaders Nancy Pelosi and Chuck Schumer said they reached an agreement with President Donald Trump to quickly enact legal protections for DACA recipients and to negotiate a separate package of border security measures that would not include funding for Trump’s proposed border wall. The announcement followed a White House dinner where Trump, Schumer and Pelosi discussed DACA, border security and other priorities; aides said the plan discussed would follow a bipartisan DREAM Act-style approach providing protections and potentially a path to citizenship for young undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children.

The White House called the meeting “constructive” and Trump said he favored bipartisan action on DACA and “massive border security,” while maintaining he would pursue the wall later. Democrats emphasized the wall would be excluded from the immediate deal. Senate Majority/Minority conversations have noted support for technology, agents and other non-wall security investments. White House spokeswoman Sarah Huckabee Sanders disputed that excluding the wall was agreed, and Trump later tweeted that “no deal” had been finalized, while still urging protections for “good, educated” young people.

The outreach to Democrats continues Trump’s recent pattern of bipartisan talks after Republican setbacks on health care and other goals. Republican leaders, including Speaker Paul Ryan, signaled support for protecting Dreamers but stressed border security must be addressed; many House conservatives oppose granting legal status and could resist any bill that includes a path to citizenship. The timing and details remain to be negotiated, and passage could create intra-party tensions for House Republicans if leadership moves a Democratic-backed package to a floor vote.

Leaked emails from the recent AshleyMadison hack suggest the company’s former founding CTO, Raja Bhatia, hacked a competing dating site in 2012.

Key points:
- In a November 30, 2012 email to AshleyMadison CEO Noel Biderman and COO Rizwan Jiwan, Bhatia said he had found a security vulnerability in Nerve.com’s dating platform, exfiltrated its entire user database, and could modify records (e.g., toggle paying status, send/compose messages). He included a link to a GitHub sample that is no longer available.
- Bhatia had been ALM’s CTO from 2007–2010 but was not employed there when he sent the message. Months later Biderman asked Bhatia, “Should I tell them of their security hole?”—no reply appears in the leaked archive and it’s unclear whether ALM disclosed the issue.
- If true, Bhatia’s actions could constitute criminal unauthorized access under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.
- The emails also show ALM considered buying Nerve.com in 2012 and that internal ALM staff were aware of security weaknesses at AshleyMadison itself. Bhatia acknowledged earlier that AshleyMadison stored passwords insecurely and that security had been neglected.
- The leaks come amid a massive breach by the Impact Team that exposed millions of AshleyMadison users’ records and a separate release of CEO Biderman’s emails and documents. The breach has led to extortion attempts, public fallout, and unconfirmed reports of related suicides. ALM offered a $500,000 reward for information on the attackers; ALM, Bhatia, and Nerve’s CEO did not comment in the reports.

An annual Chronicle of Higher Education report on 212 public university presidents found that in fiscal year 2011–12 Graham B. Spanier of Pennsylvania State University was the highest‑paid public university president, receiving $2.9 million—largely due to $1.2 million in severance and $1.2 million in deferred compensation—after his November 2011 ouster related to the Sandusky child‑abuse scandal. The survey highlighted that lucrative severance and deferred‑compensation arrangements have boosted some packages into seven figures. Three other public presidents earned more than $1 million: Jay Gogue (Auburn) $2.54 million, E. Gordon Gee (Ohio State) $1.90 million, and Alan M. Merten (George Mason) $1.87 million. E. Gordon Gee had the highest base salary at $830,439 and is noted for substantial fundraising and lavish perks. The report also showed growth in the $600,000–$700,000 compensation band (28 presidents, up from 13), with median total compensation for public research university presidents rising 4.7% to $441,392 and median base salary up 2% to $373,800. The rest of the top ten included leaders from Ball State, Michigan, Virginia Tech, UC, Florida, and Texas, with totals ranging from about $815,000 to $985,000.

Archaeologists from the University of Buckingham say Amesbury in Wiltshire — the parish that includes Stonehenge — is Britain’s oldest continuously occupied settlement, with evidence of habitation back to about 8820 BC. Carbon dating of aurochs (giant wild cattle) bones and other finds from the Blick Mead/Vespasian’s Camp excavations indicate continuous use of the site across every millennium since then, predating the previous record-holder Thatcham (occupied from c.7700 BC). The site has been recognised by the Guinness Book of Records.

Led by David Jacques, the team uncovered huge quantities of Mesolithic material: about 31,000 worked flints from a 16 sq m area, bones of large game (aurochs, red deer, wild boar), evidence of extensive feasting (including frogs’ legs), burnt flint from cooking fires, and signs of land clearance. Some flints show a distinctive pink colouring produced by algae and the unusually warm spring water, which may have made the site visually special and a long-standing attraction. The River Avon nearby likely served as a major travel route.

Researchers argue these finds change the narrative about Stonehenge’s origins: rather than being a Neolithic construction placed into an empty landscape by incoming farmers, the monuments appear to be a later development (around 3000 BC) built by communities who had lived and used the area for millennia. The discoveries thus provide a missing link between early Mesolithic activity (c.8820–6590 BC) and the later Neolithic monument-building at Stonehenge. The project was filmed for forthcoming documentaries and has attracted local pride and interest.

Old Rag Mountain, a popular and challenging hike in Shenandoah National Park, is a roughly 9-mile circuit featuring significant elevation change and a strenuous rock scramble that requires upper-body strength and careful planning. Hikers should be physically prepared, carry at least 2 quarts of water per person, wear sturdy ankle-supporting shoes, allow 7–8 hours (and bring a headlamp), avoid hiking in wet or icy conditions, stay with their group and on the trail, pack lightly (many prefer fanny packs), and hike on weekdays to avoid crowds. Pets are prohibited. Parking is at the Old Rag Fee Station lot (free, but an entrance permit is required); the small trailhead lot is closed to the public and roadside parking is forbidden. The park has increased patrols and reserves the trailhead lot for staff and search-and-rescue personnel; the fee station lot is about 0.8 miles from the trailhead. Overnight camping is limited and restricted above 2,800 feet; a backcountry permit is required for legal sites. Resources include Old Rag Mountain Stewards, guidebooks, and online hiking reports.

Separately, authorities searched Shenandoah National Park in April 2016 for 31-year-old Nicole K. Mittendorff of Woodbridge, Virginia, a Fairfax County firefighter and triathlete reported missing after she failed to show for a shift. Her 2009 Mini Cooper was found near White Oak Canyon/Old Rag on Saturday night; she was last in contact with family on Wednesday, April 13. State and park police searched by ground and air; family and community members organized a Find Nicole webpage and social media efforts, and asked anyone with information to contact Virginia State Police.

A scientist has developed a simple mathematical model to guide people and authorities on when to leave initial, poor-quality shelter after a small urban nuclear detonation to minimise radiation exposure from fallout. Michael Dillon of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory published the analysis in Proceedings of the Royal Society A.

Key points:
- Taking immediate cover in nearby buildings is critical, but deciding how long to stay depends on shelter quality and travel time to better shelter.
- Poor-quality shelters (lightweight homes, no basements) are more easily penetrated by fallout; adequate shelters include underground concrete spaces or the cores of large buildings.
- Dillon’s model finds that if an adequate shelter is reachable within 15 minutes, people in poor shelters should wait up to 30 minutes after detonation before moving. If an adequate shelter is within 5 minutes, they should move immediately and skip inferior nearby shelters.
- Prompt movement to adequate shelter could save tens of thousands of lives in a single low-yield (0.1–10 kiloton) detonation.
- Practical considerations such as traffic and shelter distribution complicate real-world response; preliminary work suggests many U.S. households may have adequate shelter within 15 minutes, but further assessment is ongoing.

The guidance is intended to aid emergency planning for low-yield nuclear detonation response.

The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) reported that the Islamic State (IS) executed 1,878 people in Syria between June 28, 2014 (when IS declared its “caliphate”) and December 27, 2014. Key details:

- Total executed: 1,878.
- Civilians: 1,175 (including four children and eight women). Of these, 930 were members of the Shaitat (al-Shaitaat) tribe from eastern Deir Ezzor, many killed after the tribe’s uprising against IS; a mass grave of 230 Shaitat was later reported.
- Regime forces and allied militiamen: 502, captured and executed after clashes with IS.
- Rival fighters: 81 members of Jabhat al-Nusra, rebel and Islamic battalions, executed after capture.
- IS militants executed by IS: about 120 (mostly foreign fighters attempting to return home) plus a few others on other charges.

SOHR cautioned the real death toll is likely higher due to hundreds missing or detained in IS jails, loss of contact with roughly a thousand Shaitat members, and dozens of Kurds still missing since IS attacks on Kobani in mid-September. Executions included beheadings, shootings and stoning across Aleppo, Deir Ezzor, Raqqa, Hassakeh, Homs and Hama. International reporting noted that IS has publicized many such executions in videos and that coalition air strikes were being carried out against IS targets in Syria and Iraq.

Former President George H.W. Bush, who died at 94, was a World War II Navy pilot and the last U.S. president to serve in that war. After the war he built a broad public-service résumé—oil businessman, U.S. representative, U.N. ambassador, Republican National Committee chair, envoy to China, and CIA director—before serving two terms as Ronald Reagan’s vice president (1981–89) and winning the presidency in 1988.

As president (1989–1993) Bush presided over major foreign-policy successes: he assembled a broad international coalition that achieved a swift victory in the 1991 Persian Gulf War to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait; he managed the delicate diplomacy surrounding the fall of the Berlin Wall and the peaceful dissolution of the Soviet Union and German reunification; and he ordered the 1989 removal of Panama’s Manuel Noriega. Those accomplishments made him highly popular at the time and prompted talk of a “new world order.”

Domestically, however, Bush’s presidency was undermined by a downturn and rising unemployment. His famously broken 1988 pledge—“Read my lips: No new taxes”—and the resulting 1990 tax increases alienated conservative Republicans and contributed to a primary challenge by Pat Buchanan and to Bush’s defeat by Bill Clinton in 1992. Historians have grown more favorable about his presidency over time.

Bush was noted for personal dignity and bipartisanship: he handled his 1992 loss with grace, later forged a friendship with Clinton, and collaborated with former rivals on humanitarian efforts. In retirement he remained active in occasional diplomacy, charitable work, and public life, while largely staying out of the political spotlight even as his sons pursued political careers—George W. Bush became president in 2000, and Jeb Bush later ran for president.

Born June 12, 1924, in Milton, Massachusetts, to Senator Prescott Bush, he married Barbara Pierce after WWII; she preceded him in death earlier the same year at 92. Remembered for public service, international leadership, and personal decency, Bush leaves a legacy shaped by wartime valor, extensive government experience, major foreign-policy achievements, and the political costs of difficult domestic choices.

Three Israeli teenagers — Eyal Yifrach (19), Gilad Shaar (16) and Naftali Frenkel (16, U.S.–Israeli) — who were abducted while hitchhiking home from West Bank religious schools on 12 June were found dead on 30 June in a shallow grave near Halhul, close to Hebron. Israeli authorities say the youths were likely shot soon after being abducted; their discovery followed a massive two‑week search that included raids across the West Bank and the detention of some 400 Palestinians, during which at least several Palestinians were killed.

Israel blamed Hamas for the kidnappings and murders and vowed retaliation. The Israeli military conducted dozens of air strikes on Gaza overnight — saying they were in response to rocket fire from Gaza — and demolished the homes of two men named as suspects, Marwan Kawasme and Omar (Amer) Abu Aysha, whose whereabouts remain unknown. Hamas denied involvement and rejected Israeli claims, while a small group calling itself Ansar as‑Dawla al‑Islamiya later claimed responsibility; that claim could not be independently verified.

The killings provoked intense national mourning in Israel, large funerals, and strong political rhetoric from leaders including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who promised to pursue and punish those responsible. International reactions condemned the murders and urged restraint; U.S. President Barack Obama and other leaders offered support for efforts to find the perpetrators and called for calm to avoid broader escalation. The UN and rights groups urged all parties to exercise restraint and warned against collective punishment.

Researchers analyzing data from 4,676 healthy women in the Nurses’ Health Study report that greater adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet is associated with longer leukocyte telomeres — protective DNA structures whose length is considered a biomarker of cellular aging. Measured cross-sectionally and adjusted for age, BMI, smoking, physical activity, calorie intake and other factors, women with the highest Mediterranean diet scores had significantly longer telomeres than those with the lowest scores. The average difference corresponds to about 1.5 years of biological aging per one-point increase on the diet score (roughly 4.5 years for a three-point change), an effect comparable to differences seen for smoking and physical activity.

The Mediterranean diet in this study was defined by a nine-point score emphasizing vegetables, fruits, nuts, whole grains, legumes, fish, a favorable monounsaturated:saturated fat ratio, lower red/processed meat, and moderate alcohol. No single food component explained the association, suggesting the benefit stems from the overall dietary pattern. The authors propose antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of the diet as plausible mechanisms, since oxidative stress and inflammation accelerate telomere shortening.

Strengths of the study include its large, well-characterized cohort and validated dietary assessments. Limitations include its cross-sectional design (preventing causal inference or measurement of telomere attrition over time), reliance on a single telomere measure, possible residual confounding, and a predominantly white female sample that may limit generalizability. Independent experts called the findings interesting but not conclusive. Overall, the results add to evidence that a balanced Mediterranean-style diet may help protect cellular aging and support long-term health.

- The Alaska primary for U.S. Senate remains undecided: Republican Joe Miller leads incumbent Sen. Lisa Murkowski by 1,668 votes, but the Division of Elections says more than 20,000 ballots remain to be processed (11,266 absentee returned so far, 658 early votes, and 8,972 questioned ballots). Absentees can arrive up to 15 days after the election; state officials plan counts on Aug. 31, Sept. 3 (questioned ballots) and a final count on Sept. 8.

- Most of the outstanding ballots appear to be Republican, and if three-fourths of the 20,896 remaining ballots are Republican, Murkowski would need roughly 55% of them to overtake Miller.

- Miller, backed by Sarah Palin, says he expects to keep his lead (citing military absentee voters and his volunteer network) and warned against protracted legal challenges, accusing opponents of “lawyering up” and likening potential tactics to the 2008 Minnesota recount. He criticized the NRSC sending an attorney to Alaska as potential meddling. Murkowski’s campaign says it’s focused on the remaining ballots and calls speculation premature.

- There is active discussion of a possible alternate path for Murkowski if she loses the Republican primary: running on the Libertarian ticket. The Alaska Libertarian Party and its Senate candidate David Haase have indicated openness to talks, and Murkowski ally Andrew Halcro has discussed the option with both Haase and Murkowski. Murkowski has said she is “considering all the options,” according to Halcro.

- National attention is high: Democrats are framing the race as GOP infighting and a Tea Party-fueled upset, while both campaigns continue to observe counting closely and prepare for possible legal or strategic moves depending on final results.

Researchers at the University of Lincoln used a fully counterbalanced, improved version of the Ainsworth Strange Situation Test (SST) to examine whether adult domestic cats form a “secure attachment” to their owners (i.e., view them as a source of safety and security in unfamiliar or threatening situations) in the same way dogs and human infants do. Twenty cat–owner pairs were tested in two versions of the SST in unfamiliar rooms, and a range of behaviours were recorded and analysed with controls for order effects and measurement reliability.

Key findings
- Vocalisation: Cats vocalised more when left with a stranger after the owner had departed, but vocalisation alone is ambiguous: it may reflect frustration or learned reinforcement (e.g., attention, feeding) rather than separation distress rooted in attachment.
- No secure‑base effect: Cats did not explore or play more in the presence of their owner than in the presence of a stranger, which would be expected if the owner functioned as a secure base. Passive behaviour results were inconsistent and difficult to interpret.
- Proximity/contact measures: Many proximity/contact measures were unreliable. Marking (rubbing) showed shifting patterns—initially directed more at the stranger, later more at the owner—consistent with familiarisation and social preference, not clear attachment based on safety.
- Separation distress indicators (door‑orientation, vigilance) were inconsistent and generally did not support the idea that cats rely on owners for reassurance in a strange environment.

Conclusions
- The study found no convincing, consistent behavioural evidence that the typical adult cat–owner relationship meets the operational criteria for a Bowlby-style secure attachment as demonstrated by the SST in dogs and children.
- Cats do show social preferences for their owners and can form close bonds, but these relationships tend to be more autonomous and not primarily based on dependence for safety and security. Some behaviors interpreted elsewhere as “separation anxiety” may instead reflect frustration or other affective states.
- The SST has limits for assessing cat–human bonds because many cat behaviors are variable or unreliable in this context; alternative methods are needed to characterise the normal psychological features of the cat–owner relationship.

Contextual points
- Cats’ evolutionary history (largely solitary hunters), domestication differences from dogs, and varied socialisation histories likely contribute to generally more independent social relationships with humans. Individual variation exists; some cats may form stronger attachments, but this does not appear to be the norm.

A suspected drunken driver drove through temporary police barricades into a crowd on Red River Street during the South by Southwest festival in downtown Austin in the early hours of March 12–13, 2014. The vehicle struck many pedestrians, killing two people—a Dutch cyclist and an Austin woman on a moped—and injuring 23 others (five critically). Witnesses and bystanders provided first aid while emergency responders treated and transported victims. The suspect, identified as Rashad Charjuan (Rashad) Owens, 21–22, of Killeen, attempted to flee a police checkpoint, was tased and taken into custody, and faces capital murder charges; authorities say the act appeared intentional. Austin officials, including Police Chief Art Acevedo, Mayor Lee Leffingwell and SXSW managing director Roland Swenson, held press conferences and a vigil was held for the victims. Despite the tragedy, SXSW organizers said the festival would continue. The coverage includes numerous photos of the crash scene, victims being treated, the arrest, vigils and memorials.

British prime minister David Cameron was heard briefly humming to himself as he returned to 10 Downing Street after announcing he would resign on Wednesday, following the Brexit vote. The short, jaunty tune—captured on his microphone before he removed it—prompted wide speculation and mock analysis online. Twitter users compared it to everything from the West Wing theme, Winnie-the-Pooh, and the Dam Busters theme to a Shostakovich opening. Classic FM and others described it in grand musical terms (“Wagnerian fanfare,” “Beethoven‑esque”), while commentators suggested his relaxed, even cheerful demeanour signalled relief at leaving office. Media and commentators playfully dissected the phrase’s rhythm, harmony and possible meanings, treating the moment as a quirky coda to Cameron’s premiership.

Paramount has closed a high-profile deal to adapt Erik Larson’s nonfiction book The Devil in the White City, with Leonardo DiCaprio set to star as H.H. Holmes and Martin Scorsese directing. The long-gestating project, which DiCaprio first joined in 2010, follows two interwoven 1893 Chicago stories: architect Daniel H. Burnham’s role in the World’s Fair and Holmes’s construction of a “murder castle” near the fair where he preyed on dozens (estimates range from about 27 to as many as 200) of mostly young single women.

Paramount acquired the rights after a competitive auction that included Universal and Fox; the studio previously held the rights twice. Billy Ray (Captain Phillips) will write the screenplay. Producers include DiCaprio and his Appian Way partner Jennifer Davisson, Stacey Sher, Scorsese, Rick Yorn and Emma Tillinger Koskoff; Elizabeth Raposo and newly minted Paramount Film Group president Marc Evans will oversee the project at the studio.

The film reunites DiCaprio and Scorsese following The Wolf of Wall Street; they’ve collaborated on five prior features. The move marks a notable, darker turn for DiCaprio’s career and represents a significant financial commitment by Paramount. Agents and reps mentioned include LBI (DiCaprio, Appian Way, Scorsese), WME (Scorsese), CAA, APA (Larson) and others. Deadline Hollywood first reported the news.

A 36-year-old Colorado woman, Michelle Marie Thompson of Arvada, was arrested Feb. 28 in Port St. Lucie, Florida, and charged with trespassing after repeatedly returning to the New York Mets’ First Data Field despite being told to leave. Mets staff had first confronted Thompson on Feb. 26 after she had been wandering the complex asking about Tim Tebow, who was at the facility for Minor League camp. Thompson told officers she was in a relationship with Tebow—at one point saying the relationship was “all of the above”—and claimed she was living with him in Jacksonville. Staff instructed her to leave the property and an officer suggested she leave St. Lucie County; she returned two days later and was arrested. She remained in the county jail with $750 bail. Tebow said he hopes she gets help and that he and the team take fan safety and security seriously; Mets players noted the proximity of fans at the spring training facility and the team’s security procedures.

This collection of short tech pieces and an article excerpt looks back at how photography, Apple’s software strategy, and platform competition have evolved, arguing for perspective over complaint.

- On photography and cameras: The author urges readers to adopt a long view. After decades of living with photographic technologies, current gripes about Apple and imaging should be weighed against historical progress—how cameras and image-making have changed over time—rather than treated as uniquely dire today.

- On CloudKit and iCloud: Developers and users have a love/hate relationship with Apple’s cloud services. While iCloud can be powerful, it’s been plagued by intermittent outages and cryptic errors that frustrate developers. The piece explains why CloudKit matters as part of Apple’s cloud strategy and why attention to its reliability and developer experience is important.

- On Apple’s public betas and openness: Apple’s decision to offer a public beta of its Mac OS X (now macOS) recalls a similar opening in 2000 when OS X first appeared. The comparison highlights a shift toward more openness and user involvement in pre-release testing, signaling a cultural change at Apple since its leadership transition years earlier.

- News excerpt (mobile competition): Samsung and Google jointly unveiled the Galaxy Nexus smartphone running a new Android version, part of Samsung’s push to expand in a fiercely competitive, litigious smartphone market. That launch followed closely after Apple’s rollout of the iPhone 4S, underscoring ongoing rivalry between Android handset makers and Apple.

Overall, the pieces encourage perspective on technological complaints, emphasize the practical importance of cloud tools like CloudKit, note Apple’s increased openness with public betas, and situate device launches within intense platform competition.

The document criticizes the MPAA’s film-rating practices after it gave the quiet, nonviolent drama Love Is Strange an R rating—officially “for language”—while films with explicit nudity, graphic gore and extreme violence (Sin City: A Dame to Kill For and Jersey Shore Massacre) received the same R rating and other violent films have gotten less restrictive ratings. Love Is Strange stars John Lithgow and Alfred Molina as a long-term gay couple facing housing upheaval; it contains no sex, nudity or violence, only some strong language and tender intimacy. Critics and commentators argue the MPAA is inconsistent and biased—often stricter on sexual content and especially LGBT themes than on violence—and accuse it of effectively penalizing depictions of homosexuality. The MPAA has not publicly rebutted charges of homophobia beyond noting the film was rated R for language; the British and Canadian boards rated the film less restrictively (15 in the UK, PG in Canada). The piece frames the rating as part of a broader, longstanding controversy over the MPAA’s unequal treatment of sex and violence and its perceived harshness toward LGBT-related material.

Cobalt, a silvery-blue metal essential for lithium-ion batteries in phones, laptops and electric cars, is experiencing a global boom. Demand has risen sharply—consumption grew from about 75,000 tonnes in 2011 to an expected 122,000 tonnes this year—and prices have roughly doubled in recent years. That has transformed cobalt from a secondary by-product of copper and nickel mining into a primary target: roughly 300 companies worldwide are now hunting cobalt deposits, and established miners are expanding output, especially in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which supplies over 60% of raw cobalt. China dominates cobalt refining.

The surge has spurred renewed mining interest in the United States and elsewhere. Small Canadian and US companies are developing projects in Idaho, Montana, Missouri, Alaska and other sites aiming to produce “made in America” cobalt that can command premiums because buyers want to reduce geopolitical and ethical risks. The U.S. recently listed cobalt as a critical mineral. However, building mines is costly and prices are volatile, and analysts say the U.S. will still need imports; the DRC and China are likely to remain central to supply chains.

The boom has serious human-rights and ethical implications. Widespread reports document hazardous, exploitative and often illegal child labour in artisanal and small-scale cobalt mines in the DRC, where children and adults work long hours in dangerous conditions with little protection. Rights groups and former child miners describe life-threatening risks, long shifts and the extreme poverty that drives families to mine. These abuses have increased pressure on companies and governments to trace and clean up supply chains.

Responses include corporate efforts to source ethically and government measures such as modern slavery legislation under consideration in Australia—requiring large companies to audit and report on supply-chain abuses. Researchers are also working to reduce cobalt usage in batteries, but alternatives at automotive scale are likely five to ten years away, so cobalt demand—and the associated economic and ethical challenges—look set to continue for the foreseeable future.

Two female capybaras that escaped Toronto’s High Park Zoo on May 24 have remained at large for more than two weeks. One was spotted June 5 and another was seen June 10 swimming and climbing a bank at the south end of High Park near The Queensway by a Breakfast Television cameraman. City staff have placed traps in the park to try to capture them.

The escape occurred while zoo staff were moving a third capybara into the enclosure. The animals—nicknamed “Bonnie and Clyde” by the public—have prompted a social-media stir (parody accounts, a video game) and lighthearted comments from Mayor John Tory. But an animal-welfare group, ZooCheck, warned the zoo could face charges under Ontario’s anti-cruelty legislation, citing the facility’s history of past escapes (including a peacock last year and several animals in 2009).

Background on capybaras: they are the world’s largest rodents, semi-aquatic, good swimmers, and can be deceptively stealthy despite their size (up to four feet long and well over 100 pounds). Experts note they adapt to varied habitats and can evade capture by plunging into water, but they are unlikely to survive a harsh Canadian winter. The main immediate dangers are vehicle traffic and eventual cold weather if they are not recaptured.

National Louis University (Chicago) is offering a Groupon for a graduate-level introductory teaching course — the first time an academic university has used Groupon to promote enrollment. The three-credit course, aimed at people with no prior teaching experience and open to anyone with an undergraduate degree, normally costs $2,232; the Groupon cuts the price to $950 (about a 60% discount). The offer goes live Tuesday, runs through Wednesday or until it sells out, has 25 slots (and requires 15 buyers to “tip”), and the class meets Monday evenings from late September to December. The course counts for 3 of the 36 credits needed for the university’s graduate teaching degree; students must complete regular admissions and pay full price for additional coursework. University officials say the promotion is intended to let prospective teachers test the profession’s realities and attract new talent amid discouraging trends in K–12 education. Groupon describes the deal as an experimental way to help people take a first step toward a new career.

Former President Barack Obama publicly criticized President Donald Trump’s Jan. 27 executive order restricting immigration, breaking the usual practice of former presidents avoiding direct criticism of a successor. Obama’s spokesman Kevin Lewis said the former president “fundamentally disagrees” with discriminating against people based on faith and praised the airport protests as an appropriate civic response when American values are at stake.

The executive order indefinitely bars Syrian refugees, pauses all refugee admissions for 120 days, and temporarily bars entry for 90 days from seven predominantly Muslim countries (Iraq, Syria, Iran, Sudan, Libya, Somalia and Yemen). Its initial implementation caused confusion at airports, detentions and deportations of some travelers, and prompted a temporary federal court order allowing those already en route or in the U.S. to stay. The administration later said lawful permanent residents (green card holders) would be admitted on a case-by-case basis after additional screening.

The White House framed the policy as a security measure, with President Trump claiming it was “similar” to a 2011 Obama administration action on Iraqi refugees. Detailed reporting and government testimony show that the 2011 measure was a limited, targeted response to a specific threat—rescreening Iraqi refugees after two admitted refugees in Kentucky were linked to attacks—and applied only to Iraq. It led to an overhaul of refugee screening and a temporary slowdown that reduced Iraqi admissions in 2011. By contrast, Trump’s order is broader, affects multiple countries and faiths, and was not tied to a single identified threat—making the comparison to 2011 misleading.

The FBI’s annual Crime in the United States report found that violent crime rose in 2015 but remained well below the highs of the 1990s. Key points:

- The national violent-crime rate increased to 372.6 incidents per 100,000 people in 2015, up from 361.6 in 2014, a 3.9% rise in estimated violent crimes (about 1,197,704 incidents). Property crime fell by 2.6%.
- There were an estimated 15,696 murders in 2015 versus 14,164 in 2014. Despite the uptick, 2015 violent crime totals were still lower than in 2012 and far below the 1996 peak of 636.6 per 100,000.
- The rise in violent crime was concentrated in large cities, particularly in segregated, impoverished neighborhoods. Chicago saw a notable increase in murders (54 more homicides, a 13% jump in 2015).
- The South had the highest crime levels: a murder/manslaughter rate of 45.9 per 100,000—more than double rates in other regions—and higher rates of rape, assault and property crime.
- The report intersected with 2016 presidential campaign debates on public safety. Donald Trump cited rising crime to support aggressive policing measures like stop-and-frisk; Hillary Clinton emphasized gun control and national guidelines on police use of force.
- Experts and officials urged community policing and alternatives to incarceration for nonviolent offenders. FBI Director James Comey had previously warned that scrutiny of policing might have discouraged some aggressive tactics, while others called for shifting law enforcement from a “warrior” to a “guardian” mentality.

Overall, the FBI report signals a modest rebound in violent crime concentrated in urban, disadvantaged areas, prompting debate over policing tactics and crime policy.

Uber is expanding a one-day on-demand flu vaccination service called UberHEALTH across more than 35 U.S. cities. On Thursday from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., Uber users can select "UberHEALTH" in the app and pay $10 to receive a wellness pack (water bottle, tissues, hand sanitizer, lollipop, recyclable tote) delivered by an Uber. With that request, up to ten people at the same location can also receive a Fluzone® flu shot administered free of charge by a registered nurse from Passport Health; nurses handle all consent and paperwork. Vaccinations are for ages 4 and up; maximum one wellness pack and up to ten free shots per request. Organizers expect high demand, have prepared thousands of doses and hundreds of nurses, and note the $10 covers part of the cost with the rest subsidized by Uber, Passport Health, and partners.

The service scales up last year’s pilot (which provided >2,000 vaccinations in several cities) after a study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found convenience strongly influences whether people get vaccinated—about 80% of prior users said they wouldn’t have been vaccinated without the service. Epidemiologist John Brownstein, PhD, has joined Uber as an advisor to help identify further health initiatives. A full list of participating cities spans major metropolitan areas in the Northeast, South, Midwest and West. Users who can’t access UberHEALTH are directed to VaccineFinder to locate nearby providers. Note: FluMist availability is limited nationwide.

An 18-week-old Irish baby, Megan Hui, survived after doctors at Dublin’s Rotunda Hospital declared her twin dead and gave her mother the abortion pill following a miscarriage. Michelle Hui, 31, had five scans that reportedly showed fetal loss at about six weeks’ gestation. She was given mifepristone/misoprostol to clear the uterus and later returned for a D&C when a post-treatment pregnancy test remained positive. During preparation for the surgical procedure, clinicians detected a fetal heartbeat — 10 days after the presumed miscarriage — revealing she had been carrying twins and one had been missed on scans, likely obscured by blood and clots.

Megan was born healthy on February 25, weighing just under 6 pounds, and is thriving at 18 weeks. Her mother expressed relief and anger that the fetus had been overlooked and worried about potential effects of the abortion drugs, which carry some risk of congenital anomalies in surviving pregnancies. Medical commentators called the case extraordinary and extremely rare; it has been written up in medical journals. The Rotunda Hospital declined to comment.

President Obama announced that the U.S. now formally recognizes the National Coalition of Syrian Revolutionary and Opposition Forces as the legitimate representative of the Syrian people opposing President Bashar al‑Assad. He said the coalition is sufficiently inclusive and representative and that recognition will help the U.S. support the opposition’s political organization and future role in governing liberated areas and coordinating humanitarian relief. The move follows similar recognition by Britain and the EU and does not currently include weapons transfers, air strikes, or legal state authority for the coalition (e.g., control of Syrian embassy assets). Administration officials left open the possibility of future arms provision but said any support must promote a political solution.

Obama emphasized responsibilities for the coalition — organizing effectively, representing minorities and women, and committing to a political transition — and warned the U.S. will distinguish and not support extremist elements among anti‑Assad fighters. He specifically singled out Jabhat al‑Nusrah, which the U.S. recently blacklisted as a terrorist organization for attacks it says were intended to hijack the Syrian uprising. The recognition is intended to bolster the opposition politically, though critics say it may be too little, too late for armed rebels who have expressed frustration at limited U.S. assistance and it does not change the military balance inside Syria.

A video filmed at a San Antonio Whataburger on July 4 went viral showing a man approach a group of teenage boys, throw a drink at them, shout a racial slur, and walk off wearing one teen’s "Make America Great Again" hat. The teenager whose hat was taken identified himself as 16-year-old Hunter Richard; he later posted on Instagram downplaying the incident and defending political conversation over confrontation. The footage drew more than 2 million views, widespread online outrage, and social-media attention from Trump supporters. San Antonio police arrested 30-year-old Kino Jimenez in Universal City and charged him with theft of a person. Whataburger said employees were not involved, condemned the behavior, and urged questions be directed to police; reports say the man in the video has been fired from his job.

James Robert Jones, 59, a former Army private convicted of premeditated murder and aggravated assault in 1974 at Ft. Dix and sentenced to 23 years, was captured by U.S. Marshals in South Florida after living under an assumed identity for decades. Jones escaped from the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Ft. Leavenworth in 1977 and had been on the run for 37 years. Army investigators contacted the Marshals in January after determining he likely lived in Florida; a prison photo matched a Florida driver’s license issued in 1981 under the name Bruce (Walter) Keith. Marshals observed him living in Deerfield Beach (since at least 2005) and arrested him Thursday morning outside his Pompano Beach workplace. Jones surrendered peacefully and said he expected it would “catch up to” him. He will be extradited to Kansas to resume his sentence and likely face additional charges related to the 1977 escape.

On April 7, 2017, the United States launched a decisive missile strike on the Shayrat airbase in Homs province, Syria, firing about 60 Tomahawk cruise missiles from two U.S. destroyers in the Mediterranean. The strike—ordered by President Donald Trump in retaliation for an earlier chemical attack in Khan Sheikhoun that killed scores (reported as at least 70–87 people, including many children)—targeted runways, hangars, a control tower and ammunition areas. Syrian state media and opposition monitors reported several military and civilian deaths and damage to aircraft and infrastructure; Russia disputed U.S. claims about damage and casualty figures.

The action marked the first direct U.S. attack on forces loyal to President Bashar al-Assad and a clear policy shift by the Trump administration. Washington called the strike a measured response intended to deter further use of chemical weapons, while stressing it was limited in scope. The White House urged other nations to join in efforts to stop Syrian atrocities.

Reactions were sharply divided internationally and domestically:
- Russia condemned the strike as “aggression” and a violation of international law, suspended a deconfliction memorandum with Washington governing Syrian airspace, and warned of damage to U.S.-Russia ties; Moscow said it had been notified in advance and disputed U.S. accounts of effectiveness.
- Assad’s allies Iran and Hezbollah denounced the attack; Iran called it dangerous and counterproductive.
- Many Western and regional governments— including the UK, France, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and others—welcomed or supported the strike as an appropriate response to chemical weapons use, though some urged renewed political efforts and UN-led solutions.
- Global bodies: NATO’s Jens Stoltenberg and EU officials criticized chemical weapon use and some backed the strike, while calls were made for legal and UN scrutiny.

In the U.S., Congressional reaction crossed party lines. Senior leaders in both parties largely supported the action but cautioned that any further military escalation should involve Congress. Libertarian and some progressive lawmakers (e.g., Rand Paul, Mike Lee, Barbara Lee, Tim Kaine) protested that the president acted without congressional authorization and raised constitutional and legal concerns. Defense hawks like John McCain, Lindsey Graham and Marco Rubio praised the strike.

Analysts and commentators warned of risks: potential deterioration of U.S.-Russia relations, the strike complicating efforts to defeat ISIS or stabilize Syria, uncertainty about a wider strategy to resolve the conflict, and the possibility of further escalation in the region. The U.S. initially sought diplomatic measures at the UN after the chemical attack but moved to a unilateral, limited military response when a Security Council resolution did not proceed.

The strike prompted emergency sessions at the UN Security Council, varied international statements, and heightened regional tensions, with many observers noting it as a significant but uncertain turning point in the six-year Syrian war.

Rough Night is a raunchy R-rated comedy about five college friends — Scarlett Johansson (Jess), Kate McKinnon (Pippa), Jillian Bell (Alice), Ilana Glazer (Frankie) and Zoë Kravitz (Blair) — who reunite for a bachelorette weekend in a Miami beach house that spirals disastrously out of control when an encounter with a male stripper ends in his accidental death. Directed and co-written by Lucia Aniello (with Paul W. Downs), the film flips the premise of dark bachelor-party thrillers into a female-led farce that mixes elements of The Hangover, Bridesmaids and Very Bad Things.

Critics note the movie’s derivative plot but praise the fresh “female gaze” and the cast’s chemistry, especially Bell’s manic comic timing and McKinnon’s scene-stealing exuberance. Johansson provides a grounded lead as a career-minded bride-to-be trying to loosen up, while Glazer and Kravitz add distinct comic flavors. The screenplay gives the ensemble room for broad, often bawdy set pieces and sight gags, though many jokes and plot turns — especially once the story shifts into black-comedy cover-up territory — are uneven or predictable. Supporting bits (including Ty Burrell and Demi Moore as sleazy neighbors) are underused.

Overall reception is mixed: the film delivers some genuine laughs and a satisfying female-centered take on a familiar formula, but it doesn’t fully sustain its darker comic ambitions. Reviewers generally found it entertaining enough as a “girls’ night out” crowd-pleaser, though not especially original or deeply satisfying. Grade examples given include about a C–/C+.

A KTVU investigation found that BART janitor Liang Zhao Zhang, who earned $271,243 in 2015 (about $57,945 base pay plus roughly $162,050 in overtime and additional benefits), spent significant stretches of his shifts in a storage closet at San Francisco’s Powell Street station and accumulated unusually high overtime over multiple years.

Key findings
- Public records from Transparent California show Zhang earned $271,243 in 2015; BART said he was paid every day that year and worked large amounts of overtime.
- Timecard data indicate Zhang worked long shifts—often about 17 hours—and was paid every day in 2015. Transparent California noted a stretch of 18 consecutive days in July 2015 with 17-hour days.
- KTVU reviewed BART surveillance video from random days and observed Zhang enter a Powell Street storage closet for long periods (examples: 54 and 90 minutes in one day; 90 and 78 minutes on another).
- Zhang told investigators he was taking meal breaks in the closet; BART policy gives a 30-minute lunch and has a separate break room, though BART does not systematically track breaks.
- KTVU also found Zhang failed to clock in or out 16 times in one year, and over two months had three missing punches.
- BART confirmed 49 other janitors made over $100,000 in 2015 and said no laws prevent employees from taking voluntary overtime. BART has not audited Zhang or other high-earning custodians and told KTVU no comprehensive audit is planned.
- BART officials defended Zhang as a frequent volunteer for overtime and said supervisors approve his timesheets. Management acknowledged station cleanliness issues and that janitorial staff often must prioritize dealing with human waste and drug-related messes.
- Critics, including Transparent California, called the pay and management oversight “obscene” and a “catastrophic management failure,” arguing the overtime and timecard discrepancies warranted an audit.

Overall, the investigation raises questions about oversight of overtime, timekeeping practices, use of break areas, and whether supervisors adequately monitor custodial duties and pay.

On August 3, 2012, LGBT advocacy group Rights Equal Rights (led by Fred Karger) launched a global boycott of Amway/Alticor and related family businesses in response to a $500,000 donation from the Doug and Maria DeVos Foundation — tied to Amway president Doug DeVos — to the National Organization for Marriage (NOM), an organization that campaigns against same-sex marriage. The donation was disclosed in the foundation’s IRS Form 990. Rights Equal Rights said the boycott aims to hold donors accountable for funding groups that oppose LGBT equality and to pressure other major contributors to anti-gay campaigns, especially ahead of November 6 marriage votes in Minnesota, Maryland, Maine and Washington. The group published boycott resources at boycottamway.com.

The action came amid wider public controversy over corporate and executive positions on same-sex marriage (for example Chick‑fil‑A, whose CEO’s comments provoked boycotts and counterprotests). Supporters of the boycott cite NOM’s defense of anti-LGBT companies; Amway responded that the DeVos family makes personal political contributions and that Amway’s business is open to everyone. Media coverage and commentary linked the DeVos donation to broader debates about corporate involvement in marriage-equality issues and noted other companies’ public stances (Chick‑fil‑A, Google, Kraft/General Mills, Ben & Jerry’s) and the reactions those stances have sparked.

This collection of articles and interviews revisits the long-unsolved 1981 death of actress Natalie Wood, who disappeared from the couple’s yacht near Catalina Island and was later found drowned. Initially ruled an accidental drowning, the case was reopened in 2011 and the cause later listed as drowning with “undetermined factors”; Los Angeles investigators have since named her husband, actor Robert Wagner (now 88), a person of interest.

New coverage and audio reporting include:
- An exclusive interview on the podcast “Fatal Voyage: The Mysterious Death of Natalie Wood” in which Lana Wood, Natalie’s sister, says she was blacklisted in Hollywood after Natalie’s death—allegedly by Wagner—and describes how her acting/production career ended, forcing her into retail and other jobs. Lana reiterates long-held suspicions that Wagner had something to hide.
- Appearances on Dr. Phil by Lana Wood and Dennis Davern (the yacht’s skipper), in which Davern now asserts he believes Wagner murdered Natalie. Davern claims he heard a loud fight that night, later found Wagner alone on deck, and alleges Wagner prevented him from calling for help and coached him on an accident narrative. Lana Wood told Dr. Phil she believes Wagner “something like” knocked her sister out and threw her in the water.
- Wagner has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and generally declines media comment. His representative condemned Davern and Lana Wood as exploiting the tragedy.

The renewed scrutiny, investigative reporting, and testimony from those involved continue to fuel public interest and controversy around the unresolved circumstances of Natalie Wood’s death.

The South Park season 21 premiere, “White People Renovating Houses,” lampooned white nationalism and also featured repeated spoken commands to Alexa and Google Home devices. Characters yelling voice-activated phrases during the 30-minute episode caused many viewers’ smart speakers to wake up, add items to shopping lists, set alarms, and otherwise respond — sometimes repeatedly — prompting users to post videos and complaints on Twitter and even unplug devices. The stunt generated amusement and annoyance; creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone often push boundaries, and the episode was largely a one-off after last season’s serialized arc. The incident echoes prior cases where TV ads and shows inadvertently triggered voice assistants (notably a Burger King commercial), and reporters contacted Amazon and Google for comment.

A PBS NewsHour investigation and interviews with 34 current and former women who worked for the U.S. Forest Service detail widespread sexual harassment, sexual assault, gender discrimination and retaliation across the agency, particularly in the wildland firefighting divisions. The reporting includes multiple firsthand accounts:

- Michaela Myers, a 22-year-old seasonal firefighter, says a veteran supervisor repeatedly groped her after a crew pizza party. She reported the abuse to USDA investigators after the season; the Forest Service later told her the investigation found no misconduct and closed the case. She says she faced informal blacklisting afterward.

- Other women described routine demeaning sexual comments, groping at after-hours gatherings, several reported rapes by coworkers or other firefighters, and physical endangerment tied to gender hostility (including an incident where a falling tree injured a female hotshot crew member). Many who reported misconduct say they then faced retaliation: threats, anonymous notes, demotions, removal of duties, negative reviews, and social isolation.

- Several women described longstanding institutional problems: a “boys’ club” culture, remote mixed-sex crews that socialize with heavy drinking, and a reporting system federal employees distrust. A USDA OIG survey of nearly 2,000 Forest Service employees in California found most knew of the agency’s “zero tolerance” policy but most victims did not report harassment because they didn’t trust confidentiality or feared job consequences.

- Women who tried to pursue complaints say the federal EEO process is slow, opaque and often unsatisfying; average complaint processing times can be long. Many felt the agency’s new hotline and policy changes (a hotline created in late 2017 and planned uniform training) have not fixed the culture or ensured follow-up.

- Several long-running class-action suits and consent decrees since the 1970s and 1990s were recounted, showing decades of attempts to address gender disparity and harassment—some improvements in hiring numbers followed, but many women say misogyny and retaliation persist. Multiple interviewees said harassment continued covertly and that speaking up often brought reprisals.

- The reporting coincided with revelations about Forest Service leadership: in 2018 Chief Tony Tooke stepped down amid a USDA investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct, including relationships with subordinates prior to his appointment. His resignation came as the agency faced increased public scrutiny.

The piece emphasizes fear as a common theme—many women declined to be named—and shows that while many love the Forest Service mission, harassment and retaliation have driven some from their careers. Interviewees and advocates call for stronger accountability, transparent investigations, improved protection from retaliation, and cultural change so employees can report misconduct without fear. The Forest Service says it takes reports seriously, has launched a hotline, completed many inquiries, and found misconduct in some cases, but many women remain skeptical that those steps are enough. The story invites current and former employees to come forward via a NewsHour tipline.

President-elect Donald Trump announced he will nominate David M. Friedman, a bankruptcy lawyer and close adviser with strongly pro-settlement, far-right Israeli views, as U.S. ambassador to Israel. Friedman has questioned the need for a two-state solution, has compared left-leaning American Jews to Jews who aided the Nazis, supports Israeli settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, and has said Israeli annexation of the West Bank would not necessarily be illegal—positions that diverge sharply from long-standing U.S. policy.

In his transition statement Friedman said he looked forward to serving “from the U.S. embassy in Israel’s eternal capital, Jerusalem,” signaling an intention to shift American policy. The U.S. embassy is currently in Tel Aviv because the U.S. has long held that Jerusalem’s final status must be resolved through negotiations; moving the embassy would be politically explosive, anger Palestinians and many international partners, and break with almost all other countries’ practice.

Trump and aides have repeatedly said he intends to move the embassy; one discussed option would be to have the ambassador operate out of the U.S. consulate in Jerusalem and treat it as the embassy. It is unclear how advanced those plans are or whether Trump has been fully briefed. The nomination drew immediate criticism from liberal Jewish groups and others who view Friedman’s views and lack of diplomatic experience as reckless and likely to undermine U.S. mediation credibility.

Molly Shattuck, 47, a well-known former Baltimore Ravens cheerleader and estranged wife of former Constellation Energy CEO Mayo Shattuck III, has been indicted in Sussex County, Delaware, on nine counts related to a sexual relationship with a 15-year-old boy. A grand jury returned charges including two counts of third‑degree rape, four counts of unlawful sexual contact, and three counts of providing alcohol to a minor. She was arraigned, pleaded not guilty, and released on $84,000 bail with conditions barring contact with the alleged victim and other minors (except her own children) and requiring surrender of her passport.

According to police affidavits and court records, the relationship began after Shattuck contacted the teen on Instagram in late May; her son later gave the boy her phone number. Over the summer their interactions allegedly escalated from messages to physical encounters: kissing and groping in the backseat of Shattuck’s Cadillac, meetings at a movie-theater parking lot and a middle-school lot, and repeated lunch pickups during which they made out. Over Labor Day weekend at a rented beach house in Bethany Beach where the teen stayed with Shattuck’s children and friends, investigators allege Shattuck gave alcohol to the teen and others, performed oral sex on the boy outside and again in her bedroom, and offered intercourse, which the boy declined.

Baltimore-area schools and police were notified when the McDonogh School learned of allegations involving a parent and referred the matter to police. Delaware State Police executed a search warrant at Shattuck’s home in early October, seizing phones, computers and other items described as relevant. Shattuck’s attorneys say she maintains her innocence. The Delaware case is pending; local Baltimore prosecutors have declined to pursue parallel charges while Delaware’s investigation proceeds.

Actor Charlie Sheen has sued adult film actress Capri Anderson for extortion, alleging she demanded $1 million to keep silent about the October incident at New York’s Plaza Hotel and stole a $165,000 watch from his room. Anderson, who was found in Sheen’s suite when police responded to a disturbance and later filed a police complaint accusing Sheen of second-degree harassment, has gone public with detailed interviews about the night.

Anderson told ABC’s Good Morning America and Nightline she was paid $3,500 to escort Sheen to dinner and stay with him; she said he became increasingly intoxicated, used a white powdery substance, grew abusive, hurled racial slurs, put his hands around her neck, threw objects (including a lamp) and trashed the room, leaving her frightened and locked in the bathroom when police arrived. She said Sheen later texted her offering $20,000 for silence; she also says she never received the promised $3,500. Photos circulated showing a trashed room; Sheen was taken to a hospital for a psychiatric evaluation after police arrived.

Sheen’s attorney Yale Galanter denied the allegations, accused Anderson of attempting to “cash in” on his client’s fame and said they will vigorously defend the suit and “never pay her a dime.” Anderson’s lawyer said a civil suit in Los Angeles was expected; Anderson’s criminal complaint could lead to prosecution by the Manhattan DA, though the alleged harassment charge carries a relatively light maximum jail term.
