Malaysian authorities say Kim Jong-nam, the estranged half brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, was killed on Feb. 13 at Kuala Lumpur airport by the nerve agent VX. Preliminary toxicology detected VX on his eyes and face; one of the two women accused of smearing the substance was reported to have vomited afterward. Malaysian police have detained three people (including the two women) and are seeking several North Koreans, among them a diplomat and an Air Koryo employee. CCTV shows a woman wiping something on Kim’s face; he convulsed and died en route to hospital.

VX is an extremely toxic, persistent V‑type agent banned under the Chemical Weapons Convention; minute amounts absorbed through skin can cause rapid seizure and death. Experts note puzzlement about how the alleged attackers reportedly avoided severe symptoms, suggesting possible rapid washing or medical treatment/antidote. The airport and other locations Kim visited may have been contaminated; Malaysian authorities moved to decontaminate affected areas.

North Korea, which has not signed the Chemical Weapons Convention and is widely believed to possess large chemical stockpiles (estimates range from a few thousand to over 10,000 tonnes in crisis), denied involvement, accused Malaysia of fabricating evidence, and asserted Malaysia bears responsibility because the death occurred there. Malaysia has demanded cooperation, including questioning a senior embassy staffer; Pyongyang has refused and protested strongly. The case has triggered a diplomatic row between the two countries and intensified international scrutiny and speculation about North Korean assassination capabilities.

Multiexport Foods, Inc. (Miami, FL) expanded a voluntary recall announced Dec. 22, 2012 for cold‑smoked salmon sold under the "Paramount Reserve" brand because of possible Listeria monocytogenes contamination. The recall covers 12‑oz twin packs (two 6‑oz vacuum packs in a cardboard sleeve; UPC 6 88264 86705 0) and 1.25‑lb packs (UPC 6 88264 86664 0), with specific lot/sublot/batch codes printed on stickers on the back of the packages. The products were distributed to retail outlets between Nov. 12 and Dec. 21, 2012, in 42 states and Puerto Rico (list includes, among others, CA, FL, NY, TX, WA) and include items sold at Wal‑Mart’s Sam’s Club stores. The bacteria was detected during routine testing on a shipment that had not yet reached stores; no illnesses have been linked to the product. Consumers may return affected packages for a full refund. Tampa Bay Fisheries and Multiexport Foods are cooperating with the FDA.

The trial of Samsung vice-chairman Lee Jae‑yong (Jay Y. Lee), widely regarded as the de facto head and heir of the Samsung conglomerate, has begun in Seoul on charges including bribery, embezzlement, perjury and concealing assets. Lee was not present at the preliminary hearing; his lawyers denied all charges on his behalf and challenged aspects of the special prosecution’s case and legitimacy. Four other Samsung executives also deny wrongdoing.

Prosecutors allege Lee conspired to funnel tens of billions of won (prosecutors cite roughly 41–43.3bn won or about $36–38m; Samsung has acknowledged payments of 20.4bn won) to foundations and individuals tied to Choi Soon‑sil, a confidante of President Park Geun‑hye, in exchange for government support for a 2015 corporate merger that strengthened Lee’s control of Samsung. Lee has said the donations were customary, made under government request, and has expressed regret for assisting Choi’s daughter’s equestrian career. The case is part of a broader corruption scandal that led to Park’s impeachment; Park and Choi deny criminal wrongdoing, though Park has apologized for her relationship with Choi.

The hearings at Seoul Central District Court are expected to run months under an expedited process; a ruling from the district court is anticipated in late May. If convicted, Lee faces a lengthy prison term and appeals through Korea’s multi-tier judiciary. The trial has drawn intense domestic and international attention because of Lee’s prominence, the role of chaebol in South Korea’s economy, and the political implications for Park’s presidency and Samsung’s succession and management. Samsung maintains it did not pay bribes and expects the courts to reveal the truth.

President Trump sowed confusion Friday by telling Fox & Friends he would not sign a “more moderate” immigration bill, touching off a day of frantic damage control as House Republicans prepared to vote on two GOP proposals: a hard-right Goodlatte bill and a negotiated, middle-ground leadership compromise that would protect Dreamers and include tougher border measures. The comments threatened GOP unity and delayed vote plans because many Republican lawmakers said they would not back legislation the president opposed.

Hours later the White House reversed course. Spokesman Raj Shah said Trump had misunderstood the morning question and that the president “fully supports both the Goodlatte bill and the House leadership bill” and would sign either. The leadership bill largely reflects Trump’s stated priorities—border-security funding (including money for the wall), an end to the visa-lottery, limits on chain migration, and a pathway to citizenship for immigrants brought to the U.S. as children—so White House officials, including Stephen Miller, had helped craft and promote it.

Despite the formal endorsement, the episode left Republicans nervous: some conservatives praised Trump’s initial remarks, hardliners still oppose protections for Dreamers as “amnesty,” and some centrists worry about enforcement provisions. Even with White House backing, the compromise was still expected to face defections from both immigration hardliners and some moderates, making passage uncertain. Democrats opposed both GOP bills. The scramble highlighted the fragility of Republican cohesion on immigration and the outsized impact of the president’s off-the-cuff comments on Capitol Hill.

At Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court confirmation hearing, Fred Guttenberg — father of Jaime Guttenberg, a 14-year-old killed in the Parkland school shooting and now a prominent gun-control advocate — said he extended his hand and identified himself to Kavanaugh, who looked at him but walked away without speaking or shaking his hand. The exchange was widely photographed and filmed. The White House spokesman said an “unidentified individual” had approached Kavanaugh and that security intervened “before the Judge was able to shake his hand,” a claim Guttenberg says video disproves; the spokesman stood by his statement.

Guttenberg, invited to the hearing by Senator Dianne Feinstein, had hoped to put a human face on the consequences of Kavanaugh’s pro-gun positions. Kavanaugh has a record critical of assault-weapon bans and is supported by the NRA, which ran a major ad campaign for his confirmation. After the lunch break, Guttenberg was escorted out by security for about 15 minutes and questioned; he believes Kavanaugh may have pointed him out. Critics said Kavanaugh’s refusal to acknowledge the victim’s father reflected poor character and underscored concerns about his stance on gun rights; others, including a more conservative Parkland parent, defended Kavanaugh and said his confirmation should not be politicized.

Consumer and safety groups say some fidget spinners sold at Target contain dangerously high levels of lead. U.S. PIRG Education Fund tested 12 spinners bought from Target and found two models distributed by Bulls-i-Toy with extremely elevated lead: the Fidget Wild Premium Spinner Brass tested at 33,000 ppm in the center and 22,000 ppm in an arm, and the Fidget Wild Premium Spinner Metal tested at 1,300 ppm in the center and 520 ppm in an arm. By comparison, federal limits for accessible parts of children’s products are 100 ppm.

U.S. PIRG retested samples to confirm results, notified Target and the CPSC, and called for recalls and for the CPSC to classify fidget spinners as toys so they must meet children’s product lead standards. The CPSC has so far classified most fidget spinners as “general use” products, not toys; companies (Target and Bulls-i-Toy) have pointed to age labeling (14+) and CPSC guidance to say the items aren’t subject to children’s product lead limits. U.S. PIRG disputes that classification, noting spinners are sold in toy aisles and sometimes marketed as suitable for younger ages on retailer sites.

Health experts and advocates warn that no level of lead is safe for children and that lead exposure can cause irreversible developmental harm. The CPSC has also issued separate warnings about other spinner hazards (choking, coin-cell batteries, fire risk when charging). U.S. PIRG recommends consumers stop using the affected spinners, calls for immediate recalls, public disclosure and investigation by Target and Bulls-i-Toy, expanded CPSC testing and reclassification of fidget spinners as toys, and broader testing of metal/brass models for lead. Target and Bulls-i-Toy have not recalled the products and did not agree to reclassify them; Bulls-i-Toy did not respond to some requests for comment.

Pedro Aguayo Ramírez, the 35-year-old Mexican wrestler known as Hijo del Perro Aguayo and son of lucha libre legend Pedro “Perro” Aguayo, died early Saturday after suffering a neck injury during a match in Tijuana. Video shows Aguayo falling unconscious on the ropes, apparently after taking a flying kick from Oscar Gutierrez (Rey Mysterio Jr.). The match continued for nearly two minutes before participants and the referee realized he was seriously hurt; paramedics and a spectator doctor attended him and he was taken to a nearby hospital, where he died about 1:30 a.m. Local prosecutors said an autopsy found trauma to the neck and a cervical fracture and have opened a possible manslaughter investigation. The event promoter could not be reached for comment; the Tijuana Boxing and Wrestling Commission called it an unfortunate accident and said medical response was prompt though the ringside doctor was treating another wrestler. Aguayo, a popular 20-year veteran who led the group Los Perros del Mal and held multiple national and international titles, was mourned across the wrestling community.

Retired Gen. Alexander M. Haig Jr., a prominent military officer and White House insider, died at 85 at Johns Hopkins Hospital of complications from a staphylococcal infection. Haig rose from West Point graduate and combat service in Korea and Vietnam to senior roles in government: military assistant to Henry Kissinger, White House chief of staff for President Richard Nixon during Watergate, supreme allied commander in Europe under Presidents Ford and Carter, and U.S. secretary of state under Ronald Reagan. He also made an unsuccessful Republican presidential bid in 1988 and later worked in the private sector and as a commentator.

Haig’s most consequential period was as Nixon’s chief of staff (May 1973–October 1974), when he helped manage the government through Watergate’s climax. Uninvolved in the break-in itself, he defended Nixon but came to see resignation as inevitable after reviewing the Oval Office tapes; he organized meetings to persuade Nixon and informed Vice President Gerald Ford to prepare to assume the presidency. He was criticized for urging Nixon to destroy tapes and for his role in events surrounding the firing of special prosecutor Archibald Cox (the Saturday Night Massacre). Haig always denied brokering a pardon-for-resignation deal, though Ford pardoned Nixon after he succeeded to the presidency.

As Reagan’s first secretary of state (1981–1982), Haig clashed with White House aides, declared himself a dominant voice on foreign policy, and served a turbulent 17 months before being dismissed. His tenure coincided with intense Cold War confrontations and covert operations in Central America, and critics said tensions between the State Department and the White House hindered coherent policy.

Haig was known for his disciplined military bearing, close ties to powerful mentors (notably Kissinger), a rapid rise in rank largely through White House service, and a distinctive rhetorical style sometimes called “Haigspeak.” He is survived by his wife, Patricia, three children and eight grandchildren. Funeral arrangements included a Mass at Fort Myer and interment at Arlington National Cemetery, delayed due to military commitments overseas. President Obama praised Haig as exemplifying the “warrior-diplomat” tradition of public service.

Here are the key points from the document:

Clinton Foundation memo
- A November 2011 memo from Douglas Band, a top aide to Bill Clinton, published by WikiLeaks, says two leading Clinton Foundation fundraisers pressured corporate donors to steer paid speaking engagements and other business to former President Bill Clinton. The memo details extensive fundraising activities and how they sometimes translated into lucrative paid work for him.

Fox News, Megyn Kelly, Gingrich, Trump
- Newt Gingrich criticized Megyn Kelly on her show, accusing her of being "fascinated with sex" and uninterested in public policy. That attack drew further criticism of Kelly from Donald Trump and others.
- Karl Rove appeared on Kelly’s show to defend her and criticized Trump for spending time promoting his new Washington, D.C. hotel and praising Gingrich instead of campaigning effectively with 13 days until the election.
- Kelly’s program also covered WikiLeaks’ DNC/Podesta emails, countering Gingrich’s charge that she ignores policy.

Trump rallies and supporter sentiment
- Reporting based on interviews at Trump rallies across six states showed that many supporters distrust polls, believe in a “silent majority,” and think the election is or will be rigged.
- Some supporters expressed fear, anger, and apocalyptic rhetoric about a potential Hillary Clinton presidency, with a few making violent or vigilante comments; others said they would accept the election result peacefully.
- The coverage highlighted divisions, anxiety among Trump backers, and the influence of pro-Trump media outlets in shaping supporter beliefs.

Trump’s hotel ribbon-cutting and branding efforts
- With the campaign floundering in polls, Trump held an “official opening” for his renovated D.C. hotel to tout his executive/business credentials, framing it as “under budget and ahead of schedule.”
- The event was presented as non-campaign but blurred lines with campaign activity: it was on his campaign website, used campaign staff, and handed out hotel promotional materials.
- Critics, including Hillary Clinton, used the event to attack Trump’s record (e.g., labor practices, sourcing, taxes). Protesters gathered outside the hotel.
- Ivanka Trump spoke to promote a softened, entrepreneurial image for the family brand.
- Observers questioned whether the hotel appearance was an effective use of the candidate’s limited campaign time.

Overall themes
- The documents and reporting underscore controversies around the Clinton Foundation’s fundraising practices and paid engagements for Bill Clinton; tensions and media battles involving Megyn Kelly, Gingrich and Trump; strong, sometimes extreme reactions among Trump supporters; and Trump’s attempt in the campaign’s closing days to rehabilitate his public and business image via high-profile branding events.

This compilation of reviews describes The Grey as a lean, wintry survival thriller built around a restrained, brooding Liam Neeson. Directed by Joe Carnahan from a story by Ian Mackenzie Jeffers, the film strands Neeson’s grim sharpshooter John Ottway and several oil-field coworkers in an unforgiving Alaskan wilderness after a plane crash. Pitted against brutal weather, terrain and a relentless pack of wolves, the survivors must improvise shelter, weapons and food while confronting physical danger and existential questions about death, faith and masculinity.

Strengths highlighted:
- Neeson: multiple critics praise his gravitas, emotional core and suitability for this kind of spare, angry-everyman role, noting he finds soul in Ottway’s melancholy and moral toughness.
- Tone and craftsmanship: Carnahan’s direction is steadier and more thoughtful than his earlier, noisier films; the movie often reads like Jack London– or Hemingway-inspired man-vs.-nature fiction, mixing practical survival detail with reflective dialogue and moral weight.
- Supporting cast and realism: the ensemble (Dermot Mulroney, Frank Grillo, Nonso Anozie, Dallas Roberts, and others) is generally solid; much location shooting and physical detail heighten the film’s immediacy.
- Themes: reviewers appreciate the film’s willingness to treat mortality seriously and to explore masculine behavior under duress without overstatement.

Criticisms noted:
- Wolves and CGI: several critics found the wolf behavior exaggerated or implausible and some computer-generated effects unconvincing; at times the wolves feel stylized or over-the-top.
- Pacing and characterization: one critic called the film tedious and felt many survivors were underwritten, making some scenes feel repetitive or rote; a few dramatic beats (e.g., Ottway’s suicidal moment) are said to be underexplained.
- Occasional melodrama: a minority view finds some of the film’s poetry, spiritual discussions and sentimental moments heavy-handed.

Overall impression:
The Grey is described as a technically assured, often grimly powerful survival drama anchored by Neeson’s intense performance and Carnahan’s unexpectedly austere direction. It works best as a brooding, elemental man-vs.-nature tale that balances visceral action with existential reflection, though its depiction of wolves and uneven characterization keep it from universal acclaim. Running time is about 1:57; rated R.

Former Sicilian Mafia member Vincenzo Calcara, now a police collaborator, has told investigators that the 1981 assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II was orchestrated by Cosa Nostra and carried out by Mehmet Ali Ağca as a Mafia hitman. Calcara implicated jailed Mafia boss Salvatore "Toto" Riina and former local mayor Antonio Vaccarino, and named a third man, "Antonov," whom he said Riina and Vaccarino later murdered and secretly buried near Milan; prosecutors in Sicily have forwarded Calcara’s testimony to Rome, but searches based on his claims have found no body and investigators have voiced doubts about parts of his account. Calcara has also written a six-page letter to Pope Francis seeking a private meeting to reveal three “very important secrets,” including alleged information about the 1983 disappearance of 15-year-old Emanuela Orlandi, the daughter of a Vatican employee. Calcara asserts exposing these truths would reveal disturbing links between the Vatican and criminal elements. Separately, reports note Ali Ağca visited Palermo months before the shooting, and that jailed Mafia financier Pippo Calò faces a new arrest warrant. Authorities remain cautious about Calcara’s allegations.

A large new PayScale analysis of about 1.4 million full-time employees over two years finds that the gender pay gap persists even after controlling for many variables (job, industry, seniority, geography, education, marital/family status and generation). Key findings:

- Overall controlled gap: women earn 2.7% less than comparable men.
- The gap appears in every industry and nearly every occupation tracked. Controlled differences range from about 1.3% (real estate) to 5.4% (mining/quarrying/oil & gas).
- Education does not close the gap: a wage gap exists at every education level and grows at the top (2.2% for Associate’s holders, 4.7% for MBAs, 5.1% for PhDs).
- The gap widens with rank: entry-level women earn ~2.2% less than comparable men, while executives earn ~6.1% less.
- Life stage and family matter: the controlled gap is largest between married men with children and married women with children; mothers face penalties while fathers often receive boosts. Women’s median pay also peaks much earlier (around age 40 at ~$49,000) vs. men (continuing to rise into their 50s to ~$75,000).
- Occupational segregation contributes (female-dominated jobs often pay less and have fewer pay-premium career paths), but segregation doesn’t fully explain the disparity—PayScale and experts point to discrimination and gendered expectations (e.g., men viewed as primary earners) and pay-setting practices that disadvantage women.
- The overall 22% raw gap for white women understates wider gaps experienced by women of color.

In short, PayScale’s controlled analysis shows the gender pay gap is widespread across sectors, education levels, and seniority, and grows for more educated and higher-ranking women—indicating that job choices alone do not explain the disparity.

"The Way, Way Back" is a warm, well-acted indie coming-of-age comedy set at a Cape Cod beach house, written and directed by Nat Faxon and Jim Rash. The film centers on 14-year-old Duncan (Liam James), an awkward teen caught between his insecure, recently divorced mother Pam (Toni Collette) and her overbearing, smug boyfriend Trent (Steve Carell). Early scenes establish Trent’s antagonism and Duncan’s isolation, which deepen the home-front tension.

Duncan finds refuge and a surrogate family at a shabby local water park, Water Wizz, run by the charming, Peter Pan–type Owen (Sam Rockwell). Owen gives Duncan a job and steady encouragement, helping him grow in confidence; the movie hinges on the contrast between Owen’s easy, wisecracking mentorship and Trent’s bullying control. Strong supporting turns include Allison Janney as the boozy next-door neighbor Betty, Maya Rudolph as Owen’s long-suffering lieutenant, and AnnaSophia Robb as a girl who sparks Duncan’s first tentative romance.

Critics praise the screenplay’s authenticity, conversational dialogue, and balanced handling of humor and heartbreak; Faxon and Rash—previously Oscar winners for co-writing The Descendants—avoid teen-movie clichés and keep the tone heartfelt rather than raunchy. Technical elements (cinematography, production design, score) enhance the film’s nostalgic summer vibe. At 1h 43m and rated PG-13, the movie is broadly accessible and recommended as a wistful, family-friendly summer alternative that captures the small but formative moments of adolescence.

Matt "Megatoad" Stonie, one of Major League Eating's top competitors, set a new bacon-eating world record in Daytona, Fla., by consuming 182 slices — an estimated more than six pounds — of cooked bacon in five minutes. The event, sponsored by Smithfield, delivered roughly 28,000 mg of sodium in the total haul. Stonie said the bacon was cooked to his liking (slightly crispy) and that his experience in longer contests left him prepared; he described focusing on texture and saltiness rather than flavor while competing and stressed that the bacon must be cooked properly. MLE had not previously sponsored a bacon contest, and unofficial prior tallies were far lower (around 54 slices). Stonie, who is second only to Joey "Jaws" Chestnut on MLE’s rankings and frequently trades records with him, has had a strong month of records in Florida (including a 14.5-pound birthday cake record on Feb. 14). It was unclear whether Chestnut would attempt to reclaim the bacon mark.

In early June 2013 a four-story wall of a building at 2136 Market Street in Center City Philadelphia, which was being demolished, collapsed onto the neighboring Salvation Army thrift store, killing six people and injuring 13. The collapse triggered multiple investigations, lawsuits, and intense scrutiny of demolition practices in the city.

Ronald Wagenhoffer, a 16‑year veteran inspector with Philadelphia’s Department of Licenses & Inspections (L&I) and the lead inspector tied to the site, was found dead June 12 in an apparent suicide. NBC10 obtained a cellphone video in which Wagenhoffer apologized and said, “It was my fault,” admitting he had not truly inspected the adjacent demolition site after a May 14 citizen complaint about worker safety and sidewalk protection. City records show he completed an initial inspection of 2136 Market Street in February and that L&I had told officials no violations were found after the May complaint. City leaders, including Mayor Michael Nutter, L&I Commissioner Carlton Williams and Deputy Mayor Everett Gillison, defended Wagenhoffer’s character and the department’s procedures, while the mayor’s press secretary disputed NBC10’s reporting. L&I colleagues and officials offered support and counseling to staff.

Criminal and civil inquiries followed. Excavator operator Kane R. Robert (aka Sean Benschop) was charged; prosecutors say he tested positive for Percocet and marijuana the day of the collapse and a grand jury was convened. Plaintiffs—including Salvation Army employees and customers who were buried or injured—filed lawsuits against demolition contractor Griffin Campbell and building owner Richard Basciano, alleging gross negligence and violations of safety regulations. Lawyers noted Campbell’s troubled past and argued owner selection of the contractor was negligent.

Regulatory fallout included inspections of hundreds of demolition permits across Philadelphia, discovery of violations at some Campbell sites, and calls from city council members for stricter oversight and licensing of demolition contractors. Federal OSHA had an open May 15 complaint about worker fall risks at the site; its standards bar unbraced multi‑story walls standing alone. Videos taken before the collapse showed bricks falling onto the sidewalk while pedestrians and traffic remained nearby. The incident prompted debate over demolition oversight and worker and public safety in the city.

Jennifer Lawrence was on a private Beechcraft 400 Beechjet that made an emergency landing at Buffalo Niagara International Airport on Saturday after engine trouble. The jet, en route from Louisville, Kentucky, to Teterboro, New Jersey, experienced an apparent left-engine failure while cruising (reported at about 31,000 feet); reports say the second engine failed during the diversion. The plane landed safely at about 1:15 p.m. with two crew and two passengers aboard; Lawrence was confirmed as a passenger and was uninjured. After landing the aircraft went to Prior Aviation. It is not yet clear when the plane departed Buffalo.

A federal judge in Texas, U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor, ruled Dec. 14, 2018, that the Affordable Care Act (ACA) is unconstitutional after Congress zeroed out the tax penalty for the individual mandate. He declared not only the mandate but the entire 2010 law invalid, reasoning the rest of the statute could not be severed from the now‑penaltyless mandate.

The ruling has no immediate effect: the ACA remains in force while appeals proceed and people who enroll by current deadlines will have coverage starting Jan. 1. The Justice Department under President Trump declined to defend the mandate earlier this year, and Democratic state attorneys general led by California AG Xavier Becerra have vowed to appeal; the case is expected to move next to the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and could eventually reach the Supreme Court.

Politically, the decision puts Republicans in a bind. Public support for key ACA provisions—protections for people with pre-existing conditions, Medicaid expansion, allowing young adults on parental plans—has grown, and Democrats made health care a pivotal issue in the recent midterms. Many Republicans offered mixed reactions: some praised the ruling, others urged bipartisan work to preserve popular elements of the law. Democrats condemned the decision and plan to defend the ACA in court and push votes in Congress to put Republicans on record.

Legal scholars say O’Connor’s severability analysis is weak because Congress itself removed the penalty but left the rest of the statute intact; many expect the ruling to be stayed and overturned on appeal. Still, experts warn the uncertainty could disrupt insurance markets, raise premiums later, reduce consumer enrollment, and divert policymaking toward litigation rather than improvements. The most stable remedy would be legislative action, but crafting bipartisan fixes—while preserving popular protections—faces political challenges.

BP’s board is weighing three options for its next $10.5 billion annual dividend as it faces intense pressure from the Obama administration, Congress and angry Gulf Coast residents after the Deepwater Horizon spill: suspend the dividend for two quarters, pay the dividend in bonus shares, or escrow the dividend while using operating cash for cleanup unless the escrow is needed. The discussions come ahead of a White House meeting called for midweek between President Obama and BP chairman Carl‑Henric Svanberg and CEO Tony Hayward.

The administration has demanded that BP post “a faster” and more reliable plan to collect leaking oil and has pushed for BP to deposit a substantial sum into an independent escrow or claims fund to compensate affected fishermen, workers and businesses. White House advisers did not specify an amount; Senate Democrats proposed a $20 billion fund. The administration also wants BP to be liable for economic losses tied to the spill response, including lost wages from the federal deep‑water drilling moratorium—a stance that roiled markets and prompted a sharp one‑day drop in BP’s stock.

BP says it will discuss options constructively but will not agree to an open‑ended blank check; it insists it will pay claims tied directly to oil damage and prefers a claims process based on transparent, pre‑agreed rules. The meeting follows heightened government oversight: Adm. Thad Allen is the federal response chief, government scientists have revised spill estimates to the mid‑30,000s of barrels per day, and BP has been installing sensors and improving its oil‑collection systems. Obama is using a more assertive posture—traveling to the Gulf, planning an Oval Office address and pressing BP to fund an escrow and expedite containment and compensation.

A small Pike County, Ky., church that voted to bar interracial couples from membership and from participating in services has reversed course after regional church leaders found the vote invalid.

On Nov. 27 the 42–44–member Gulnare Free Will Baptist Church approved a motion, 9–6, declaring it does not condone interracial marriage and that such couples would not be received as members or used in worship (funerals excepted). The measure was prompted after 24‑year‑old congregant Stella Harville brought her fiancé, 28‑year‑old Ticha Chikuni, a black student she met at Georgetown College, to sing at a service; a former pastor, Melvin Thompson, raised objections and pushed for the motion. The vote shocked Harville’s longtime‑member parents and drew condemnation from other local churches.

New pastor Stacy Stepp, who opposed the ban, asked the Sandy Valley Conference of Free Will Baptists to review the matter. The conference’s parliamentary committee concluded the vote was not carried out according to Robert’s Rules of Order and would have required a bylaw change — which needs a majority of the entire membership (about 23 votes) or two‑thirds of those voting (10 votes). Because those thresholds were not met, the conference declared the action null and void and called for rebuilding the damaged relationships.

Stepp said he will formally nullify the vote at a church meeting and intends to move forward with a statement welcoming all people regardless of race. Other area ministers condemned the ban as an anomaly that does not reflect local churches’ values. Stella Harville said she hopes the church follows through with overturning the decision.

Hadiya Pendleton, a 15-year-old King College Prep sophomore and majorette who had performed at President Obama’s inauguration events, was fatally shot in a Chicago park after seeking shelter from rain with friends. The gunman reportedly jumped a fence, ran toward the group and opened fire; Hadiya was hit in the back and died at Comer Children’s Hospital. Two teenage boys were also wounded but not fatally. Police say none of the teens were involved with gangs and believe the shooter may have mistaken them for rival gang members; the suspect fled in a white Nissan. No arrests have been reported. The city increased the reward for information to $24,000.

Four years earlier Hadiya had appeared in an anti-gang public service video as a sixth-grader urging peers to choose a better future. Her father and officials described her as a talented, ambitious student who hoped to attend Northwestern and become a pharmacist, journalist or lawyer. The killing, Hadiya’s being the 42nd Chicago homicide so far in 2013, drew national attention: the White House expressed condolences and activists including Rev. Jesse Jackson and Rev. Al Sharpton planned a march to the site, with Jackson emphasizing broader causes of gun violence such as weapons flow, poverty, jobs and drugs.

European Council President Herman Van Rompuy called an emergency coordination meeting for Monday morning to bring together top euro-zone officials — including ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet, Eurogroup chair Jean-Claude Juncker, European Commission President José Manuel Barroso and Commissioner Olli Rehn — amid market turmoil that has sharply pushed up Italy’s borrowing costs. While Van Rompuy’s office described the session as preparatory rather than a crisis meeting, officials expect Italy’s deep sovereign debt (about 120% of GDP), political tensions between Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi and Finance Minister Giulio Tremonti, and the recent sell-off in Italian assets to be discussed. Italy’s 10-year bond spread versus Germany reached euro-era highs, and Italian bank and equity prices fell sharply amid fears that yields near 5.5–5.7% could place severe strain on the country’s finances.

The meeting precedes a scheduled euro-group finance ministers’ discussion on finalizing a second bailout for Greece and on forthcoming EU bank stress-test results. Officials are alarmed progress on a second Greek rescue has been too slow; proposals under consideration include private-sector involvement, bond rollovers, maturity swaps, or buybacks via the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF). However, there is no consensus: Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Finland insist private creditors bear some cost, while the ECB is wary of measures that would amount to debt reduction and risk a selective default and downgrade by ratings agencies. Talks with banks’ representatives (the IIF) have made little headway, leaving officials close to “square one.”

The broader concern is contagion: while Greece, Ireland and Portugal are relatively small, Italy (and Spain) are large enough that a rescue would dwarf existing funds; estimates suggest multi-hundred-billion euro needs if either required full support. German commentators and some EU leaders have urged a long-term, comprehensive strategy rather than short-term fixes. In Italy, government figures sought to present unity behind austerity and support for Tremonti, but political uncertainty persists, feeding market anxiety about whether Italy could become the next major epicenter of the euro-zone debt crisis.

A solid-gold, 5-inch replica of the Apollo 11 Lunar Module was stolen from the Armstrong Air & Space Museum in Wapakoneta, Ohio, after an alarm sounded shortly before midnight Friday. The 18-karat models were made by Cartier in 1969—one presented to each Apollo 11 astronaut (Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins) and containing microfilm naming contributors to the gift. The museum, in Armstrong’s hometown, said the missing piece—one of only three—represents a public loss; police say its monetary value is difficult to determine.

Wapakoneta police are investigating with assistance from the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation and the FBI. Retired NASA agent Joseph Gutheinz, who has helped recover stolen lunar material, believes the thieves likely intend to melt the piece for gold rather than sell it intact, which would make recovery much harder. Authorities noted a moon rock remained at the museum; notable Apollo artifacts have fetched millions at auction, underscoring both historical and potential monetary value. No further details or surveillance information have been released.

Archaeologists using ground-penetrating radar at William Shakespeare’s grave in Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon, say their survey shows signs the head end of the burial was disturbed, lending new support to a long‑standing (but previously discredited) story that the playwright’s skull was stolen by trophy hunters in 1794. 

Led by Kevin Colls of Staffordshire University, the non‑invasive investigation also produced other findings: Shakespeare and his wife Anne Hathaway appear to have been buried in shallow, roughly one‑metre‑deep graves beneath the church floor and wrapped in shrouds rather than placed in coffins (the radar showed no coffin nails or metal). The team also examined a skull kept in St Leonard’s church about 15 miles away—part of a local legend that it was Shakespeare’s—and concluded it belonged to an elderly woman, not the playwright.

Colls called the evidence that the grave was disturbed “very convincing,” though Holy Trinity’s vicar Patrick Taylor urged caution, saying the evidence is not definitive and the mystery may remain. The results are featured in a Channel 4 documentary marking the 400th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death.

Aretha Franklin delivered a hugely extended, church-like rendition of the national anthem before the Detroit Lions–Minnesota Vikings Thanksgiving game at Ford Field, stretching to 4 minutes 35 seconds — well over the typical two-minute expectation. Seated at a grand piano and wearing a fur coat and Lions knit hat, the Queen of Soul slowed and elongated the song, drawing loud applause from the Detroit crowd and widespread reaction online.

Twitter exploded with jokes about the length (delayed warmups, Colin Kaepernick kneeling, Thanksgiving chores, time-of-possession quips and comparisons to short NFL careers), but commentary was mixed: many mocked the excess while others defended and praised Franklin’s status and artistry, insisting she can sing as long as she likes. Observers also contrasted the anthem with a criticized halftime set by Andy Grammer, and noted Franklin’s legendary career—six decades, 20 Grammys, a Kennedy Center Honor and a Presidential Medal of Freedom—and past high-profile performances (including stepping in for Pavarotti and singing "Nessun Dorma").

New University of Chicago research finds that hearing a job candidate speak can make them seem more intelligent, thoughtful and competent—and more hireable—than reading the exact same words on a résumé or transcript. In a series of experiments, Booth School MBA students prepared written and spoken “pitches.” Evaluators who listened to audio versions rated candidates higher on intellect and competence and were more likely to want to hire them than evaluators who only read transcripts. Watching video added no benefit beyond audio alone. The effect held when actors read pitches aloud and when professional recruiters evaluated Booth candidates. Lead researcher Nicholas Epley says speech conveys not just specific ideas but a speaker’s underlying capacity to reason, making voice an important asset in conveying intelligence during hiring. The study appears in The Journal of Psychological Science.

The Spanish-language version of the federal health insurance marketplace, CuidadoDeSalud.gov, launched more than two months after HealthCare.gov and has suffered many of the same technical and usability problems — plus additional language and navigation issues — leaving many Spanish-speaking Americans unable or discouraged from enrolling during the first enrollment wave.

Key points:
- CuidadoDeSalud.gov went live on Dec. 6 after an initial promised three-week delay turned into more than two months. That left little time for people seeking coverage starting Jan. 1.
- Users and enrollment navigators reported technical failures (site outages, inability to upload scanned documents, long or dropped hotline calls) and navigation problems specific to the Spanish site (slower page transitions, links that pointed to English pages).
- Translations were frequently awkward or inaccurate — described as “Spanglish” or computer-generated — producing confusing terms (e.g., rendering “premium” as “prima”) and grammatical errors that made plan details hard to understand.
- The site’s shortcomings exacerbated existing barriers for many Latinos: limited internet access, low digital literacy, fear of government scrutiny (especially in households with undocumented members), and shortage of Spanish-speaking navigators and call-center staff.
- Enrollment data showed low Spanish-language uptake in several large states: in October–November fewer than 1,000 signups in New Mexico, under 5,500 Spanish signups in California, and limited Spanish-only calls nationally (about 3.5% of calls).
- Advocates and providers say the failures undermined outreach efforts by Spanish-language media and community groups and hurt confidence in federal responsiveness. Federal officials acknowledged problems, said improvements were underway, and noted phone- and paper-based enrollment options remained available.
- Community clinics and local navigators have stepped in as trusted in-person resources, helping some people enroll and obtain coverage, but capacity is strained and many eligible people still face affordability or access hurdles.

Bottom line: Delayed launch, technical glitches, poor translations, and limited local support meant the Spanish-language marketplace underdelivered at a critical time, leaving many Spanish-speaking, low-income, and less tech-savvy people behind in the initial rollout of the Affordable Care Act.

Fred Beckey, a celebrated and eccentric American mountaineer and prolific author, died in Seattle at 94 of congestive heart failure, according to friend and manager Megan Bond. A German immigrant raised in Seattle, Beckey made as many as a thousand first ascents over a seven-decade career across the Pacific Northwest, Alaska, the Canadian Rockies, Wyoming and beyond, and climbed in the Himalayas and China. He established major new routes on Alaska peaks including McKinley, Deborah and Hunter (1954) and helped define the “golden age” of American first ascents.

Beckey authored more than a dozen books—most notably the three-volume Cascade Alpine Guide—that are considered definitive references for North American mountaineering. Known for his rawboned persistence, mordant humor and uncompromising dedication to climbing, he continued to plan and undertake climbs into his 90s. He is survived by his brother Helmut. Private burial services were planned, with a public memorial to follow.

Researchers analyzing over 10,000 ancient zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia report finding graphite inclusions inside a zircon dated to 4.1 ± 0.01 billion years. The graphite is completely encased in crack-free zircon, making modern contamination unlikely. Measurements show the graphite is isotopically light (high 12C/13C), a signature commonly associated with biologic carbon because metabolic processes preferentially use 12C. If produced biologically, this would push evidence for life back to about 4.1 Ga—roughly 300 million years earlier than prior geochemical indications (~3.8 Ga) and soon after planetary formation.

The team (Bell, Boehnke, Harrison, Mao, Lao) emphasizes the robustness of the inclusion’s primary nature and the zircon’s U–Pb age. They note, however, that isotopically light carbon is not an unambiguous biosignature: abiotic processes (e.g., Fischer–Tropsch-type reactions) can also produce 12C-enriched organic molecules. Thus the finding is suggestive but not definitive proof of Hadean life. If biogenic, it implies life arose very early and could have persisted or re-emerged quickly after heavy early bombardment. The study is published in PNAS and funded by NSF and a Simons fellowship.

A national shortage of intravenous sodium bicarbonate (medical-grade baking soda) has forced U.S. hospitals to conserve supplies, delay some procedures, and, in rare cases, transfer patients. The two U.S. suppliers, Pfizer and Amphastar, fell short after an undisclosed problem at one of Pfizer’s suppliers and a surge in demand that stretched Amphastar’s capacity. Both companies say they don’t know when normal supplies will resume, estimating not before June or August.

Sodium bicarbonate is inexpensive but widely used — to correct blood acidity, treat certain poisonings, support chemotherapy and open‑heart surgery, relieve pain during suturing, and as a staple on emergency crash carts. Its low price reduces manufacturers’ incentives to invest in production or redundancy, and industry-wide issues — limited suppliers, aging facilities, raw-material and quality-control problems, and overseas manufacturing pressures — have contributed to recurring shortages of basic generics.

Hospitals are responding by prioritizing use for critical needs and conserving stock; some systems report only delays and partial fills rather than widespread cancellations. However, some facilities have had to postpone major surgeries and cancer treatments or transfer patients. The FDA is working with manufacturers on mitigation options, including temporary importation, and notes overall progress on shortages over the past decade, though about 50 drugs remain listed as in short supply.

This Economic Policy Institute (EPI) briefing paper analyzes how Wal‑Mart’s import activity contributed to the growing U.S. goods trade deficit with China and the associated loss of U.S. jobs between 2001 and 2013.

Key findings
- The U.S. goods trade deficit with China rose from $84.1 billion in 2001 to $324.2 billion in 2013, and EPI estimates this growing deficit eliminated or displaced about 3.2 million U.S. jobs over 2001–2013.
- Wal‑Mart was a major conduit for Chinese imports. Using company reports, ocean‑freight data and other sources, the paper conservatively estimates Wal‑Mart accounted for roughly 11.2% of U.S. goods imports from China over the period—about $11.4 billion in 2001 rising to $49.1 billion in 2013.
- Because Wal‑Mart exports to China are negligible (estimated at ~1% of U.S. exports to China), its expanding imports drove a disproportionate share of the bilateral deficit growth. EPI attributes a $36.7 billion increase in the U.S. trade deficit with China to Wal‑Mart between 2001 and 2013.
- Wal‑Mart’s share of the import growth is estimated to have displaced at least 415,400 U.S. jobs over 2001–2013—about 13.2% of total jobs lost due to the rising China deficit. In 2013 terms, Wal‑Mart’s trade flows were associated with roughly 541,300 displaced jobs (125,800 in 2001).
- Manufacturing bore the brunt: 75.7% of the jobs displaced attributable to Wal‑Mart were in manufacturing (about 314,500 jobs). These losses are especially damaging because manufacturing jobs typically pay higher wages and offer better benefits, particularly for workers without a college degree.
- Wal‑Mart’s 2013 pledge to buy $250 billion of American‑made goods by 2023 has produced relatively few confirmed manufacturing jobs to date—EPI documents fewer than 4,100 specific U.S. manufacturing jobs tied to the program (many of them future promises)—and estimates that since 2001 Wal‑Mart’s growing China trade displaced more than 100 U.S. jobs for every job the program has created or promised.

Methodology and caveats
- Employment effects are estimated using an input‑output model across 195 U.S. industries (77 manufacturing industries) to calculate direct and indirect labor requirements displaced by imports and supported by exports. Estimates are counterfactual — what employment would have been absent the growing trade deficits — and focus on domestic exports (excluding re‑exports).
- The paper treats Wal‑Mart’s share of China imports as constant at 11.2% for conservatism, though evidence suggests the share likely grew; therefore the job‑loss figures are described as lower‑bound estimates.
- The estimates exclude impacts in wholesale/retail, advertising, re‑spending multipliers, and second‑round wage effects; they also do not quantify reductions in wages and bargaining power for non‑college‑educated workers broadly caused by competition with low‑wage countries. Prior EPI work suggests many more workers experienced indirect wage losses.

Broader context and policy implications
- EPI places responsibility for the bilateral imbalance partly on Chinese policies—currency management that increased dollar holdings and suppressed the yuan, large purchases of U.S. Treasuries and other foreign assets, and labor‑rights and wage repression—that made Chinese exports artificially cheap.
- Wal‑Mart is characterized as a major facilitator of distribution for those artificially cheap imports. EPI argues the U.S.–China trading relationship requires fundamental change, including addressing China’s exchange‑rate practices and labor standards, since current imbalances damage U.S. manufacturing capacity, wage levels, and macroeconomic health.
- The paper notes that many powerful U.S. actors (retailers, importers) benefit from inexpensive imports, but those benefits do not translate into net national gains when accounting for lost production capacity, jobs, and wage erosion.

Author and data sources
- Author: Robert E. Scott, Director of Trade and Manufacturing Policy Research at EPI. Analysis relies on U.S. Census, USITC, BLS, Wal‑Mart reports, Journal of Commerce import rankings, and prior EPI research (notably Kimball & Scott 2014).

Overall conclusion
- Between 2001 and 2013 the growing U.S. goods trade deficit with China displaced millions of U.S. jobs; Wal‑Mart alone is estimated to have been responsible for the loss of over 400,000 jobs (mostly in manufacturing). The report calls for policy changes to address currency manipulation and labor standards in China and highlights the tension between corporate gains from low‑cost imports and broader national economic costs.

Adrian Lamo, the former hacker who reported Army intelligence analyst Bradley (now Chelsea) Manning to authorities, says he doubts Manning acted entirely alone in leaking a classified helicopter video and tens of thousands of diplomatic and battlefield documents to WikiLeaks. Lamo told investigators he knows of several Boston-area people — including MIT and Boston University students and recent graduates — whom Army and FBI investigators have interviewed about possible ties to Manning and WikiLeaks. Lamo alleges some local information‑security specialists provided Manning with encryption tools, helped him avoid detection on Defense Department networks, and in at least one case physically transferred material to WikiLeaks. He declined to name individuals publicly but said they opposed the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and had connections to WikiLeaks.

Those interviewed by investigators have denied any role; a recent MIT graduate acknowledged exchanging emails and meeting Manning but denied involvement. Pentagon officials said the questioned civilians are not currently considered accomplices. WikiLeaks declined to discuss source identities.

Separately, U.S. authorities have increased scrutiny of WikiLeaks volunteers and associates. Jacob Appelbaum, a U.S. WikiLeaks volunteer and Tor project researcher, was detained, questioned, and had devices inspected by customs and FBI agents when returning from Europe and later approached at the DefCon conference. Appelbaum, who has spoken publicly for WikiLeaks, defended the organization’s mission and rejected claims that volunteers were responsible for endangering lives. The FBI is assisting Defense Department investigators exploring whether civilian associates in the hacker community aided Manning’s disclosures.

Sen. John McCain said it’s “worth looking into” whether Sen. Ted Cruz is constitutionally eligible to be president because Cruz was born in Canada to an American mother and held dual U.S.-Canadian citizenship until 2014. Speaking on KFYI’s Chris Merrill Show, McCain—who faced similar questions in 2008 after being born at a U.S. military base in the Panama Canal Zone—said he isn’t a constitutional scholar but thinks the issue could merit review and possibly a Supreme Court decision. His comment follows Donald Trump and others raising the question publicly; McCain suggested Cruz might do well to address the matter preemptively. The exchange also highlights McCain’s longstanding antagonism toward Cruz and how establishment figures can shape primary narratives.

An active shooter incident occurred Friday morning at Noblesville West Middle School in Noblesville, Indiana. At about 9:06 a.m. dispatchers received reports; police responded immediately. A male student returned to class carrying two handguns and opened fire, injuring a teacher and a student. A male student suspect was detained at the scene; authorities say there are no further suspects and the school is being treated as a crime scene.

The teacher who intervened has been identified by parents as Jason Seaman, a science teacher and former college football player; he was shot three times and underwent surgery and was awake and speaking en route to the hospital, according to family. Both injured victims were transported to IU Health hospitals; officials have not released their conditions.

Students were evacuated and bused to Noblesville High School where parents reunited with them; one other unrelated threat locked down the high school briefly but is not believed to be connected. Multiple law-enforcement agencies are assisting in the investigation.

Local and state officials, including Vice President Mike Pence and Gov. Eric Holcomb, issued statements of support; lawmakers and educators renewed calls for stronger school-safety measures and limits on access to guns. The American Red Cross is available to assist. The investigation remains active and details continue to be updated.

On April 1, 2011, Southwest Airlines Flight 812, a 15-year-old Boeing 737-300 en route from Phoenix to Sacramento with 118 passengers and five crew, suffered a sudden fuselage rupture at cruise altitude that created a several-foot hole in the mid-cabin. Oxygen masks deployed, some passengers and a flight attendant fainted or felt lightheaded, and the pilots made an emergency rapid descent from about 34,400 feet to about 11,000 feet and diverted to Yuma Marine Corps Air Station, where the aircraft landed safely. No serious injuries were reported; a few people received minor treatment.

The National Transportation Safety Board dispatched investigators; they retrieved the flight recorders and planned to cut a section of the fuselage for fracture analysis. Boeing confirmed a depressurization event but did not speculate on a cause. Southwest grounded and inspected 79 similar 737-300s (about 80 planes cited in some reports), canceling roughly 300 flights on Saturday and possibly a similar number on Sunday, while coordinating with the FAA and NTSB. Southwest noted the affected aircraft had passed required inspections, including a routine check days earlier and a heavy check in March 2010. FAA records showed several frame-crack repairs in March 2010 for this airplane.

Investigators and safety experts noted metal fatigue and maintenance issues as possible factors, pointing to a 2009 Southwest 737 fuselage hole caused by fatigue and to past industry accidents (Aloha 1988, Helios 2005, Qantas 2008) to underscore risks of pressurization failures. Southwest is phasing out older 737-300s but still operates many; inspections and Boeing-devised checks were being applied to airplanes with original aluminum skin. Passengers praised the crew’s quick response as key to the safe outcome.

A third passenger from Asiana Airlines Flight 214 died Friday from injuries sustained when the Boeing 777 crashed while landing at San Francisco International Airport last Saturday. The victim, described as a girl under 18 and confirmed by the Chinese consul as a Chinese national, died at San Francisco General Hospital; her family requested privacy and no further details were released.

Separately, police confirmed that one of the earlier fatalities, 16-year-old Ye Meng Yuan of China, was run over by an airport fire truck while responders were spraying foam on the burning jet. Investigators say the rig was repositioning after the evacuation when it struck her; it is unclear whether she was already deceased at that time. An autopsy found extensive crushing injuries but did not determine the exact cause of death. Ye’s friend, 16-year-old Wang Lin Jia, was also killed; she was found near the seawall the plane clipped on landing.

In total, dozens were treated at San Francisco General — 31 children and 36 adults among the injured — with six patients remaining hospitalized, two in critical condition. NTSB teams have begun cutting up the wreckage to move it to a hangar, and runway 28L was reopened Friday. Investigation into the crash and the circumstances of the victims’ deaths continues.

After President Donald Trump announced the U.S. would withdraw from the 2015 Paris climate agreement, the French government publicly rebuked that decision by re-editing and reposting the White House’s explanatory video with counterpoints added to refute U.S. claims. France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs tweeted the revised video, changing lines such as “The Paris Accord is a bad deal for America” to “Leaving the Paris Accord is a bad deal for America and the world,” replacing “badly negotiated” with “comprehensively negotiated,” and adding rebuttals noting that major U.S. companies (ExxonMobil, Schneider Electric, Microsoft) disagree with Trump’s assessment. The French edits also corrected U.S. assertions about the climate fund’s size and disputed the administration’s use of an MIT study, citing MIT researchers who said Trump had misinterpreted their findings and that Paris was “a step in the right direction.”

President Emmanuel Macron amplified France’s response with a high-profile address urging scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs disappointed by the U.S. move to consider France “a second homeland,” and coin­ing the slogan “Make our planet great again.” France, Germany and Italy issued a joint statement calling the Paris Agreement irreversible and not open to renegotiation. EU and U.N. officials, Pacific island leaders and a range of other countries including China, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and South Korea also criticized the U.S. withdrawal as a major disappointment and reiterated their commitment to the accord.

Brussels’ Zaventem airport planned a limited restart of passenger operations 12 days after suicide bomb attacks destroyed its departures hall and killed 35 people in Brussels (including three bombers). Airport CEO Arnaud Feist said the airport would partially reopen on Sunday with a very small number of flights (three Brussels Airlines short‑haul services initially) and a temporary check‑in zone able to process roughly 800 departing passengers per hour—around 20% or less of normal capacity (normal throughput about 5,000/hr). The operator aims to restore much greater capacity by late June or early July, with a full reopening of the departure hall before the summer holidays.

Security will be substantially tightened: initially access only by car/taxi with number‑plate cameras and random vehicle checks, no drop‑off zone, passenger and baggage screenings in tents outside the main building and a second security barrier, and increased armed police and military patrols. The new measures were agreed after negotiations with police unions and may further limit throughput. Train and bus links will resume later.

The closure has hit airlines and the local economy: Brussels Airlines, the airport’s largest carrier, estimated losses of €5 million per day and will gradually add services (including some long‑haul) while it positions aircraft and crews at other hubs; several carriers (Ryanair, Jetairfly/TUI, Thomas Cook) are operating from alternative Belgian airports for at least the next week. Hotel stays in the city fell sharply amid the disruption.

This document summarizes research on how Facebook use after a breakup affects recovery and how Facebook behaviors map onto stalking-like behaviors.

Study 1 (Facebook harassment and stalking behaviors)
- Sample: 411 participants reporting how they communicated with ex-partners on Facebook.
- Factor analysis of Facebook harassment produced three categories: Covert Provocation (e.g., surveilling photos, posting to provoke), Public Harassment, and Venting.
- Each Facebook-harassment category was associated with higher rates of cyber obsessional pursuit (COP) and offline obsessive relational intrusion (ORI).
- Individuals who engaged in COP were nearly six times more likely to also perpetrate ORI.
- Those who admitted to stalking behaviors tended to do so across contexts: online, on Facebook, and offline.
- Conclusion: Facebook can facilitate stalking-like behaviors; the colloquial idea of “Facebook stalking” has empirical support.

Study 2 (Facebook exposure and postbreakup adjustment)
- Sample: 464 participants (mostly young adults) who had experienced a breakup with someone having a Facebook account.
- Measures included current breakup distress, negative feelings, sexual desire, longing, and personal growth following the breakup; assessed offline contact with the ex, whether participants remained Facebook friends with the ex, and frequency of Facebook surveillance (checking ex’s page/friends list).
- Main findings (controlling for personality, relationship history, offline contact, and other predictors):
  - Facebook surveillance (frequent checking of an ex’s profile or friends list) was associated with greater current distress, more negative feelings, increased sexual desire and longing for the ex, and lower personal growth.
  - Remaining Facebook friends with an ex showed a mixed pattern: such participants reported less negative feeling, sexual desire, and longing than those who were not Facebook friends, but they also reported lower personal growth.
  - Offline contact predicted greater distress, desire, and longing—consistent with prior research—but Facebook surveillance explained additional variance beyond offline contact, suggesting weak-tie online exposure can independently prolong distress.
- Interpretation:
  - Frequent exposure to an ex via Facebook can sustain or reignite emotional attachment and impede meaning-making and growth after a breakup.
  - Remaining Facebook friends might blunt longing by exposing one to banal, everyday updates that reduce mystique, but this same exposure may hinder the personal-growth process.
- Limitations: Correlational design prevents causal conclusions; those hung up on an ex may simply seek more Facebook contact. Experimental or longitudinal work is needed.

Practical takeaway
- Monitoring an ex on Facebook is common and perceived as harmless, but it correlates with worse emotional recovery and, in some cases, with stalking-like behaviors. Avoiding online and offline exposure to an ex is likely the better strategy for healing.

WWF’s Greater Mekong program says scientists described 208 new species from the Greater Mekong region in 2010 — 145 plants, 28 reptiles, 25 fish, 7 amphibians, 2 mammals and 1 bird — discoveries that include striking finds such as a new monkey with an “Elvis-like” hairstyle, a psychedelic gecko, a self-cloning skink, five carnivorous plants and a distinctive leaf warbler. The finds underline the region’s exceptional biodiversity across Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar (Burma), Thailand, Vietnam and Yunnan province in China.

WWF cautions that these newly documented species exist amid severe and accelerating threats: habitat loss, deforestation, unsustainable development, overexploitation and climate change. The recent extinction of the Javan rhinoceros in Vietnam is cited as a stark example of the region’s biodiversity decline. WWF urges Greater Mekong governments to prioritize biodiversity in regional planning and economic decisions, calling on leaders meeting in Myanmar in December 2011 to incorporate the value and costs of biodiversity loss into policy to safeguard the region’s natural heritage.

Authorities uncovered 13 severely malnourished and neglected Turpin children in a Perris, California home after a 17-year-old daughter escaped and alerted police. Deputies found six minors and seven adults—who appeared childlike due to stunting and malnutrition—living in squalid conditions; three were reported chained to furniture. Parents David Allen Turpin, 56, and Louise Ann Turpin, 49, were arrested and jailed on high bail; investigators believe the couple are the biological parents of all 13 and are conducting a “meticulous” probe into when and why the abuse occurred. 

Medical experts warned the children will likely need prolonged, careful physical rehabilitation (including monitored nutritional refeeding) and long-term psychological care for trauma and developmental delays. Riverside County hospitals told reporters the patients are stable and being guarded; minors are in county care and could be placed with relatives pending background checks. Child Protective Services and the sheriff had no prior contact with the family.

The Turpins had registered an in-home private school, Sandcastle Day School, with California’s Department of Education; the state noted it lacks authority to inspect private or home schools. Local residents expressed shock, and officials cautioned against donating to unvetted online fundraisers. State lawmakers called for greater oversight of private and home schooling in response to the case.

Summary:

Security researchers found serious cybersecurity weaknesses in RF-enabled St. Jude/Abbott pacemakers and associated hospital systems. Independent teams were able to obtain programmer devices cheaply on auction sites and discovered multiple issues: programmers could be used without strong manufacturer controls, monitoring systems sometimes required no logins, patient data (including names, SSNs, phone numbers and conditions) were stored unencrypted, and researchers demonstrated that third parties could remotely access and send programming commands to pacemakers. Experts caution that clinicians resist security measures that impede care (e.g., simple passwords), but multiple researchers have warned manufacturers for years and few firms had adequately secured devices.

In response, the FDA approved and Abbott issued a corrective firmware update (treated as a recall) on August 29, 2017 for about 465,000 RF-enabled St. Jude/Abbott pacemakers (models Accent, Anthem, Accent MRI, Accent ST, Assurity, Allure, and related CRT-Ps). No ICDs/CRT-Ds are affected. The update adds authorization checks so only Merlin Programmer/Merlin@home transmitters can communicate with implants. There have been no reported patient harms linked to these vulnerabilities.

Key points about the firmware update:
- Available beginning Aug. 29, 2017; devices manufactured after Aug. 28, 2017 will ship with the update pre-installed.
- Update requires an in-person clinic visit, takes about three minutes, during which the device runs in a backup mode with life‑sustaining functions maintained.
- The FDA and Abbott do not recommend prophylactic device replacement.
- Small risks from the update include possible reload of prior firmware (0.161%), loss of programmed settings (0.023%), and a very low chance of complete device failure (0.003%).

Recommendations:
- Patients should discuss timing and suitability of the update with their physicians; clinicians should weigh patient dependency, device age and risks/benefits.
- Providers should back up device settings and be prepared to manage pacing‑dependent patients during the update.
- Questions/resources: www.sjm.com/cyberupdate, Abbott hotline 1-800-722-3774, and FDA DICE contact.

The FDA emphasized that networked medical devices can have exploitable vulnerabilities but also provide benefits, and pledged continued monitoring, collaboration with manufacturers, researchers and providers, and guidance on reporting adverse events.
