Youngjoo Hwang, a wardrobe crew member on Fox’s 2015 series The Grinder, filed a lawsuit alleging that co-star Fred Savage created a hostile work environment, verbally abused and intimidated female crew, and physically assaulted her. According to the complaint and statements at a news conference, Hwang says Savage repeatedly gave her dirty looks and profanities, told crew not to look at or follow him, and on one occasion “violently struck” her arm three times after she brushed dandruff from his jacket. She alleges supervisors discouraged reporting, citing an executive producer who told her the conduct might not constitute harassment and advised against contacting HR. Hwang is seeking unspecified damages for emotional distress.

Savage and Fox strongly deny the claims. Savage called the allegations “completely without merit and absolutely untrue,” saying he fully participated in an internal Fox investigation that allegedly found no evidence to support the accusations. Fox issued a statement saying it conducted a thorough investigation and found no wrongdoing and will vigorously defend against the suit. Hwang’s attorney contends Fox did not perform an independent investigation and that Savage’s lawyers have declined to speak with them; she also says other women on the set filed complaints, without naming them.

The Grinder ran from 2015–2016. The filing follows a separate, previously settled 1993 sexual harassment lawsuit against Savage from his time on The Wonder Years.

On Aug. 27 in Berkeley, Calif., Reveal host and journalist Al Letson intervened to protect a right-wing demonstrator who was being attacked by a group of black bloc/antifa protesters during a “Rally Against Hate” that mostly failed to draw the planned right-wing crowd. Letson, who was filming the event for Reveal, saw a man fall and be surrounded and struck—reportedly with a flagpole—and dove on top of him to shield him from further blows. The moment was captured on video and widely shared.

Letson said he acted out of basic humanity and fear someone would be killed—citing Charlottesville as part of his motivation—and chose to set aside journalistic nonparticipation to prevent serious harm. He stressed that his action didn’t change his overall view of antifa; he still sees a distinction between those fighting white supremacy and the supremacists themselves, but worries that violent tactics by the left create a false equivalency in public perception. Letson also described his approach to covering the alt-right as exposing figures in the open so the public can see who they are, rather than giving them an uncritical platform.

The man Letson protected later identified himself as Keith Campbell, a 54-year-old Trump supporter and video blogger who said he was targeted because antifa members recognized him from his channel. Campbell suffered bruised ribs and kidney damage, has since temporarily relocated, and says he only learned Letson protected him after seeing video. Reveal’s editor noted that while their policy is nonparticipation, Letson’s response was a human reaction to someone in distress. The incident has been used in debates about antifa tactics and media coverage of political violence.

Thai officials will test human feces found at a campsite in Thungyai Naresuan wildlife sanctuary to try to link construction tycoon Premchai Karnasuta to a suspected poaching incident. Premchai — president of Italian-Thai Development, builder of Suvarnabhumi airport — and three companions were arrested earlier this month after rangers found their camp with guns and carcasses of protected species: a black leopard, a Kalij pheasant and a red muntjac. Chaiwat Limlikitaksorn, head of the parks’ special task force, said the feces were found near spent bullet casings and where the panther was skinned; DNA testing may place Premchai at the scene. Premchai has denied the poaching charges; he and his colleagues have been released on bail while investigations continue. The article also notes a broader context of powerful Thais avoiding justice amid other recent scandals involving military and police figures. The final paragraphs shift to an unrelated note about web archiving efforts to preserve pages and prevent broken links.

Margaret Thome Bekema, 97, of Walker, Michigan, received an honorary high school diploma from Catholic Central High School on Oct. 29, 2015—79 years after she left school during her junior year. Bekema quit at 17 to care for her mother, who had cancer, and her three younger siblings; the sacrifice prevented her from graduating with the Class of 1936 and "broke her heart." The school presented the diploma, a graduation cap and alumni certificate at the Yorkshire and Stonebridge Manor senior community in front of family and friends. Principal Greg Deja praised her lifetime of sacrifice and service; relatives and community members had nominated her for the honor. Bekema later worked in clerical roles during World War II and as a preschool teacher, raised a family, and remained active in her faith community. She was emotional and grateful at the ceremony. (Reporting by The Associated Press and MLive.)

A federal judge has ordered Disneyland to pay Jose R. Martinez $8,000 after he was trapped for more than 30 minutes on the “It’s a Small World” ride on Nov. 27, 2009. Martinez, a San Pedro resident in his early 50s who uses a wheelchair after a spinal cord injury and has chronic conditions including diabetes, hypertension and anxiety, was stuck in the ride’s “Goodbye Room” when it malfunctioned the day after Thanksgiving. While other riders were evacuated, staff could not assist Martinez and did not call firefighters; the ride’s music played loudly on repeat and was only turned off after complaints. Martinez experienced increased anxiety, autonomic dysreflexia from a full bladder, and was later treated at a Disneyland first-aid station.

U.S. District Judge James Selna found Disneyland breached its duty to provide safe premises and failed to warn disabled guests they might be trapped in the event of a breakdown. The $8,000 award comprises $4,000 for pain and suffering and the remainder for violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act. Disneyland said it believes it provided appropriate assistance and was disappointed the court did not fully agree; the company notes it has addressed first-aid access issues highlighted at trial. Martinez sued in 2011; parts of his complaint were previously dismissed on summary judgment.

Students at Pittsburg High School in Kansas uncovered questionable credentials for their newly hired principal, Amy Robertson, leading to her resignation from the $93,000-a-year post days after her March 6 hiring. A six-student team from the school paper, the Booster Redux, spent weeks investigating Robertson’s background and found that her claimed MA and PhD from Corllins University appeared suspect: the school’s website was nonfunctional, it was not listed by the U.S. Department of Education or recognized accreditation databases, and online sources described Corllins as a possible diploma mill. The students also found past Gulf News reports tying Robertson to a Dubai English-language school that had its license suspended and later closed.

Robertson, who has lived much of the past two decades in Dubai and said she runs an education consulting firm, denied wrongdoing and said her degrees had been authenticated by the U.S. government. The district said Robertson would have needed to obtain Kansas licensure before formally taking the principal role. After a closed special school-board session, the superintendent announced Robertson’s resignation, and the board said it would reopen the position and contact other applicants.

The story drew local, state and national attention; advisers and professional journalists praised the student reporters for thorough, persistent investigative work. The superintendent acknowledged responsibility for the oversight and planned to meet with the students to thank them.

Panic! at the Disco frontman Brendon Urie has publicly identified as pansexual in a new Paper interview. Urie said he’s married to a woman and very much in love with her, but isn’t opposed to men — “I like a person” — and that he’s “definitely attracted to men.” He called the interview his coming out as pansexual.

Urie reflected on the band’s 2013 song “Girls/Girls/Boys,” which was written about a threesome but has been embraced as a queer anthem and a message of self-acceptance. He also recalled a playful “stage gay” persona early in the band’s career — kissing bandmates and friends onstage or when drinking — which sometimes made others uncomfortable. Urie recently appeared on Broadway in Kinky Boots, a show with LGBT themes, and Panic!’s latest album, Pray for the Wicked, was released June 22.

Howard G. Buffett, son of investor Warren Buffett, has purchased hundreds of Rosa Parks artifacts that had been held in a New York warehouse for years amid legal disputes over her estate. Buffett told the Associated Press his foundation plans to donate the materials— which include Parks’ Presidential Medal of Freedom, Congressional Gold Medal, photographs with presidents, a pillbox hat, a signed postcard from Martin Luther King Jr., meeting documents, clothing and household items— to a museum or institute yet to be selected so they can be publicly accessible. The collection, inventoried by Guernsey’s auction house at more than 1,000 items, was removed from Parks’ Detroit home after a protracted fight between her heirs and friends and had been held since 2006. While Buffett declined to confirm the price, a lawyer for Parks’ heirs said the sale was for $4.5 million; 12.5% goes to the auction house, 20% to Parks’ relatives, and the remainder to the Rosa & Raymond Parks Institute for Self Development. Guernsey’s president and Buffett emphasized the goal of preserving the materials for public benefit and education.

Hospitals: Big not-for-profit systems are profitable largely because of Wall Street and consolidation
- Axios reviewed financial filings from 84 of the largest not‑for‑profit health systems (combined revenue $535.5 billion). On patient care alone they earned $14.4 billion in operating profit (2.7% margin). When investment income, trading, accounting gains from mergers/acquisitions and other non‑operating items are included, their total surplus rose to $35.7 billion (6.7% margin), more than double year‑over‑year.
- Much of the extra gain came from financial investments, stocks, bonds, derivatives and merger accounting, as well as revenue boosts tied to consolidation. Some systems also run insurance arms. Academic systems such as Northwestern Memorial and University of Colorado Health posted among the highest margins; Kaiser Permanente is very healthy, while others (e.g., Partners) showed losses.
- The piece stresses that modest margins on huge revenues still produce large profits. Critics and researchers say consolidation has increased hospitals’ market power, raised prices and insurance premiums, and usually does not lower costs. Experts note the top tax‑exempt systems now operate like Fortune 500 companies, wielding substantial financial and political clout.
- The American Hospital Association defended hospitals’ need for positive margins to fund medical advances and blamed Medicare/Medicaid for underpayment; it also said investment income is reinvested, though some funds go to revenue‑generating projects.
- Caveat: the analysis focuses on the wealthiest systems; many smaller, rural and public hospitals continue to struggle with low payments, fewer patients and weaker negotiating power with insurers.

White House: Communications director Mike Dubke resigns amid broader shakeup talk
- Mike Dubke resigned as President Trump’s communications director after just over three months on the job. Sean Spicer will resume dual duties as acting communications director while the White House sorts out replacements.
- Dubke cited personal reasons; he offered to stay through Trump’s foreign trip. He plans to return to his private communications firm. Chief of Staff Reince Priebus thanked him and said Dubke will assist with transition.
- Dubke’s departure comes amid mounting scandals — congressional probes and Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia investigation — and reports that Trump is considering a wider staff reshuffle. Trump has been speaking with former campaign aides Corey Lewandowski and David Bossie about possible crisis‑management roles; both are seen as aggressive loyalists though their effectiveness and potential conflicts are uncertain.
- The White House is also reportedly frustrated with Jared Kushner amid reporting about his contacts with Russians, though removing a family member is uncertain. Kellyanne Conway downplayed a major shakeup, saying Dubke left professionally.
- Dubke was seen as an establishment figure who didn’t fully fit the chaotic White House culture; his role was unusual (in some ways subordinate to Spicer), and he struggled to generate consistently positive press. The communications shop is a focal point for possible changes, with Spicer likely to remain but possibly in a reduced public role and Conway perhaps expanding duties.

Bottom line: Leading nonprofit hospital systems are generating sizable overall surpluses driven by investment returns and consolidation, prompting concerns about market power and affordability; separately, the Trump White House’s communications team is in flux as staff departures and potential returns of campaign loyalists signal broader personnel and political turbulence.

Pat Roberts narrowly fended off a right-wing primary challenge from Milton Wolf in Kansas on Aug. 5, 2014, a victory credited in large part to an organized intervention by national Republican groups. Roberts won 48% to Wolf’s 41% (two minor candidates split the rest). With Sen. Lamar Alexander expected to hold off a challenge in Tennessee, this left 2014 as the first cycle since 2008 with no incumbent Republican senator losing a renomination.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), chaired by Kansas Sen. Jerry Moran, concentrated resources in Wolf’s suburban Johnson County base — sending staff to knock on tens of thousands of doors and running a massive phone bank — and helped Roberts essentially tie Wolf in that county (Roberts trailed there by only 147 votes). Roberts’ campaign said it reached over 200,000 GOP households in the closing weeks. The NRSC also provided regional staff and messaging support.

Roberts, a long-serving politician who moved right during the race, warned against intraparty infighting after the win, arguing such divisions waste resources. Wolf, a radiologist and distant relative of President Obama who campaigned as a hard-line conservative backed by tea-party groups, attacked Roberts as too Washington-oriented but was hurt by campaign controversies (including criticized Facebook posts) and Roberts’ targeted campaign.

The result was part of a broader pattern that night in which establishment Republicans prevailed in several primaries (including in Michigan, where businessman Dave Trott defeated Rep. Kerry Bentivolio), signaling a push by GOP leadership to protect incumbents and mainstream candidates ahead of competitive general-election contests.

The piece criticizes prominent progressives — especially Michael Moore and, to a lesser extent, Keith Olbermann — for defending WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange after two women in Sweden accused him of sexual assault. It frames this as part of a broader problem: most rapes go unreported and very few perpetrators are ever punished, so public figures should take accusations seriously rather than dismissing or minimizing them.

Key points:
- Rape prosecution statistics (from RAINN) show low reporting and conviction rates: factoring in unreported cases, only about 6% of rapists ever serve time. The author uses this to argue why supporting victims and pursuing allegations matters.
- Assange is accused by two women of multiple acts in Sweden, including holding a woman down, having sex without a condom despite her express wish, and having sex with an unconscious woman. He fled and is fighting extradition; Michael Moore posted $20,000 bail for him.
- Moore’s public defense — urging distrust of “official stories” and emphasizing Assange’s right to bail — is portrayed as dismissing the accusers and enabling victim-blaming. The author argues Moore should not ask progressives to ignore allegations against a powerful man merely because he’s a left-wing hero.
- The article condemns the progressive tendency to protect high-profile men, warning that such responses harm survivors, discourage reporting, and erode the credibility of the movement. It calls for a strict requirement that progressive leaders unequivocally take rape allegations seriously regardless of the accused’s status.
- It recounts the Twitter backlash (hashtag #Mooreandme) urging Moore to apologize and donate the bail money to an anti-sexual-assault organization, and criticizes Olbermann’s handling of criticism and earlier inaccurate reporting that helped spread misunderstandings about the charges (e.g., “sex by surprise”/condom-break framing).
- The piece acknowledges Assange’s right to legal defense and presumption of innocence but stresses that this does not justify dismissing or smearing his accusers.

Overall, the author demands accountability from progressive public figures: standing against rape and supporting survivors must be non-negotiable, even when the accused is a political ally.

On Nov. 1, 2013, 23-year-old Paul Anthony Ciancia opened fire at Terminal 3 of Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), pulling a .223-caliber semiautomatic rifle from a bag and shooting through a security checkpoint. A Transportation Security Administration behavioral detection officer, 39-year-old Gerardo I. Hernandez, was killed—the first TSA officer to die on duty—and at least two others were wounded (officials reported seven injured overall, with some injuries later clarified). Law enforcement shot Ciancia in the chest; he was taken into custody in critical condition.

Witnesses described travelers diving for cover and evacuating onto the tarmac as shots rang out around 9:20 a.m. Ciancia walked through an exit lane toward the checkpoint, and one witness said the shooter calmly asked “TSA?” as he approached. Airport police pursued and shot him near a cluster of restaurants behind the terminals. Officials recovered more than 100 rounds and written anti-government material critical of the TSA on the suspect.

Authorities said Ciancia, a Los Angeles resident originally from Pennsville, New Jersey, had texted his brother before the shooting saying he was thinking about killing himself; his father had notified Pennsville police asking for help locating him earlier that day. Investigators continued to probe his background and motive, which officials said appeared linked to anti-government views but remained unclear. The shooting halted operations at LAX for hours—746 flights were affected, including diversions and a temporary ground stop—and federal and local officials, including President Obama, were briefed.

An Oakland County woman, Lori Cichewicz, has filed a "wrongful conception" lawsuit against her doctor after he told her in 2008 that her fallopian tubes were blocked and she could not get pregnant, so she did not need contraception. Contrary to that advice, she became pregnant and in April 2011 gave birth to a daughter, Reagan, who has Down syndrome.

Cichewicz, now 50, says the unplanned pregnancy and its emotional and financial consequences—especially concerns about raising a special-needs child at her age—caused significant distress. She emphasizes she never questioned giving birth and describes her daughter as much loved. Her attorney argues the doctor’s advice misled her and caused harm. The doctor and his lawyer did not respond to requests for comment.

A Michigan appeals court ruled 3-0 that Cichewicz may seek damages for the emotional distress tied to the unplanned pregnancy (consistent with medical malpractice-type claims), but cannot recover costs for raising the child with Down syndrome. The case was returned to Oakland County Circuit Court and is expected to go to jury trial in the coming months unless settled. Legal analysts say her claim appears viable under wrongful conception principles.

Uber announced a strategic partnership with Carnegie Mellon University to create the Uber Advanced Technologies Center in Pittsburgh to research mapping, vehicle safety and autonomous driving technology, and to fund faculty chairs and graduate fellowships. The center will leverage CMU’s robotics expertise and NREC ties, hire senior scientists, and develop core technology, vehicles and infrastructure for a future fleet of driverless cabs.

The move comes amid growing tension with major investor Google. Google has invested in Uber, provided Google Maps integration, and had David Drummond on Uber’s board, but is reportedly developing its own ride-hailing service tied to its advanced self-driving car program. That prospect—combined with Google’s superior mapping/data assets and many accident-free miles of driverless testing—raises a strategic threat to Uber. Uber’s Pittsburgh lab is therefore both a long-term investment in autonomy and a bid to catch up or compete in a future where autonomous vehicles could replace human drivers and reshape on‑demand transport.

Researchers at the University of Florida have confirmed via DNA analysis that three Nile crocodiles (Crocodylus niloticus) were captured in South Florida between 2000 and 2014, demonstrating the species can survive — and grow quickly — in the state’s subtropical environment. The three juveniles, found in the Miami/Everglades region (one on a house porch, one in a park, and a female recaptured in Everglades National Park), were genetically identical to each other and matched populations from South Africa, but did not match Nile crocodiles sampled from U.S. zoos and attractions. That pattern suggests an introduction from a common, likely unpermitted source—most plausibly the pet trade—rather than escape from licensed collections.

Nile crocodiles are large, opportunistic predators responsible for many attacks and fatalities in Africa; UF researchers warn that if established in Florida they could prey on native birds, fish, mammals and even other crocodilians, outcompete or hybridize with the smaller American crocodile (an endangered species in South Florida), and pose risks to people and livestock. One juvenile in the study grew about 28% faster than juveniles in parts of the species’ native range, underscoring Florida’s suitability.

While there is no confirmed breeding population yet, scientists recommend a formal risk assessment because Florida’s Atlantic and Gulf coasts provide favorable climate and more individuals may be present. The findings add Nile crocodiles to Florida’s long list of invasive species and raise concern that illegal trade or releases could lead to a new, potentially dangerous invader in the Everglades ecosystem.

A prostitution scandal involving U.S. Secret Service personnel in Cartagena, Colombia has prompted expanded congressional investigations and internal disciplinary action. Agencies say 12 Secret Service employees have been implicated and 11 U.S. military members are also under review. Six Secret Service members have left the agency, one was cleared of serious misconduct but faces administrative action, and five remain on administrative leave with suspended clearances.

Senate Homeland Security Chairman Joe Lieberman said his committee will send initial questions and pursue broader inquiries to determine whether the incident was an isolated lapse or part of a pattern; he and others stressed there is currently no evidence that classified information was compromised. House Homeland Security Chairman Peter King has requested a minute-by-minute timeline of actions and locations and has assigned investigators to probe the matter, warning more firings are likely. Committees may hold public hearings.

Officials across party lines, including Rep. Darrell Issa and Sen. Tom Coburn, expressed confidence in Secret Service Director Mark Sullivan’s handling of the case and in the agency overall. White House adviser David Axelrod called the conduct disappointing but urged that the actions of a few not denigrate the many professionals in the agency. Some lawmakers, including Sen. Susan Collins and Rep. Carolyn Maloney, suggested increasing the number of female agents as one measure to reduce the risk of similar incidents. The White House demanded a thorough investigation, and former Secret Service director Ralph Basham warned the behavior could have endangered the president’s security.

A Texas state representative from Cypress filed a resolution (HCR 75) urging Texans to stop using the Chilean flag emoji as a substitute for the Texas (Lone Star) flag. The item appears amid other content — a photo gallery about Houston rapper Trae Tha Truth’s custom emoji set and a short note about the Internet Archive’s “No More 404” crawls, which archive web pages and their references so links remain viewable even if originals change or disappear.

The remains of the 298 victims of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 were transported from the crash area held by pro-Russian separatists into Ukrainian government-controlled Kharkiv by refrigerated train, then prepared for transfer to the Netherlands. Recovery efforts were hampered by an unsecured crash site in rebel-held farmland near Hrabove, where wreckage remained scattered, some bodies unaccounted for, and evidence apparently treated haphazardly — fueling international frustration.

The disaster intensified calls in Brussels for tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Western officials have accused Russia of supplying advanced Buk surface-to-air missiles to separatists; Russia denies this and has presented an alternate narrative blaming Ukrainian forces. Russian military briefings and state media claimed radar and satellite data showed a Ukrainian fighter near MH17 and alleged Ukrainian missile-unit movements, while urging Kiev to explain radar activity and the removal of missile batteries. Moscow also suggested the jet deviated from course and questioned intercepted audio evidence circulated by Ukraine.

The U.S. and EU dismissed Russia’s claims as propaganda and reiterated that intelligence points toward Russian involvement in arming the separatists; Ukraine says its fighters were grounded and denies responsibility. The UN Security Council adopted a resolution calling for an independent international investigation. The competing claims have deepened the diplomatic standoff amid pressure to broaden sanctions on Russia as investigators work to secure the site and establish the facts.

The House Intelligence Committee voted unanimously to release a classified Democratic memo that rebuts a recently published GOP memo alleging FBI and Justice Department abuses in surveillance tied to the Russia probe. The Democratic document now goes to President Trump for a five-day security review; the White House said it would “consider” the release as it did the Republican memo.

Rep. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), the memo’s lead author and the committee’s top Democrat, said the Democratic memo provides a point-by-point rebuttal and noted Democrats had submitted it to the FBI and Justice Department for review—something Republicans declined to do. Schiff urged that any redactions be made by the professional agencies rather than the White House. GOP chairman Rep. Devin Nunes and other Republicans backed making the Democratic memo public; one Republican, Rep. Tom Rooney, warned it might “muddy the water” but supported transparency.

The action follows intense partisan dispute over the earlier GOP memo, which accused the FBI of improperly relying on a dossier funded by Clinton-linked sources to obtain a surveillance warrant for former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page. Democrats and some Republicans counter that the FBI did disclose potential bias in its application, and many lawmakers from both parties expressed skepticism that the GOP memo “clears” the president. President Trump meanwhile attacked Schiff on Twitter, calling him a liar and leaker; Schiff dismissed the tweets as “false smears.” Lawmakers on both sides said they hope special counsel Robert Mueller’s probe will continue without interference.

A hate crime investigation is underway after the Chicago Loop Synagogue at 16 S. Clark St. was vandalized early Saturday. Police say surveillance footage shows a white male in dark clothing and a face mask exit a dark SUV (possibly a Toyota Highlander), place two swastika stickers on the front doors, smash a plate-glass window with a metal object, then flee. Officers responded at 12:20 a.m.; no arrests had been made as detectives treated the incident as a hate crime. Community activist Raul Montes Jr. offered a reward for information leading to arrest and conviction. The American Jewish Committee’s Chicago office condemned the attack, noting it comes amid a rise in anti-Semitic incidents nationwide and emphasizing that the Jewish community will not be intimidated.

The report also includes related accounts of swastika and anti‑Semitic graffiti in other cities over the weekend. One New York subway incident drew widespread attention when commuters, led by a rider named Mr. Nied, quickly wiped Nazi symbols off a train using hand sanitizer and other supplies; photos and a social‑media post about that cleanup went viral. Police in New York said other anti‑Semitic markings have been reported recently, highlighting a broader pattern of such offenses.

Facebook on Wednesday disavowed and condemned tweets by board member Marc Andreessen that appeared to endorse colonialism in reaction to India’s ban on Facebook’s Free Basics program. Andreessen posted and then deleted tweets saying India’s rejection of Free Basics — a service that offered a limited set of free internet sites to the poor — was “morally wrong” and that “anti‑colonialism has been economically catastrophic for the Indian people for decades.” He apologized, withdrawing his comments “in full and without reservation.” 

CEO Mark Zuckerberg publicly called Andreessen’s remarks “deeply upsetting” and said they did not reflect his or Facebook’s views; a company spokeswoman reiterated that Facebook strongly rejected the sentiments. The incident follows India’s Telecom Regulatory Authority ruling on net neutrality that blocked Free Basics for violating equal‑access principles, and comes amid broader tech‑industry efforts to expand internet access in developing regions.

The Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) warned that 2012 could see the beginning of the euro’s breakup, forecasting a 60% chance that at least one country will leave the euro area by year-end and raising the decade-long breakup probability to 99%. CEBR said the crisis could force many French and German banks — and others across Europe — into writedowns, bailouts or even nationalization, and predicted further banking turmoil.

The warning comes as European leaders work to stabilize Spain and Italy’s debt and preserve the single currency in its 10th anniversary year. The euro suffered consecutive annual losses against the U.S. dollar and fell to record lows versus the yen amid sovereign-debt downgrades, EU divisions and recession risks. Safe-haven demand lifted the Swiss franc while Italy endured its worst year for its bond market since at least 1992.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel acknowledged expected turbulence in 2012 but vowed to do everything to save the euro and strengthen European cooperation. She planned talks with French President Nicolas Sarkozy on fiscal-rule revisions, with euro leaders aiming for a March accord. Greek Prime Minister Lucas Papademos said the coming months would be crucial for Greece, as his interim government seeks to secure a €130 billion bailout and a debt-swap cutting €100 billion from Greek debt.

German public opinion was divided: polls showed a slim majority thinking a fundamental solution is possible, while notable shares expect countries to abandon the euro or require aid. Finance Minister Wolfgang Schäuble urged calm and Germany moved to accelerate payments into the permanent bailout fund to boost confidence. Overall, policymakers warned of a pivotal period ahead as Europe tries to contain contagion and preserve the monetary union.

Forbes’ 2018 list of the world’s 100 highest-paid athletes—led by Floyd Mayweather’s $275 million—contained no women, the first time in eight years. NBA players dominate the list, followed by football and baseball stars. Serena Williams, the top-earning female athlete in 2018 with $18 million, fell roughly $5 million short of the $22.9 million cutoff, a shortfall Forbes attributes in part to her time away after having a baby. The omission spotlighted persistent pay gaps in sports: women’s teams like the U.S. Women’s National Soccer Team and U.S. Women’s National Hockey Team have recently fought for better pay and won new agreements, but many athletes and advocates say progress is insufficient. Retired soccer star Abby Wambach and tennis pioneer Billie Jean King urged continued action and male allyship; Olympic bobsledder Kaillie Humphries called for renewed public conversation and accountability to drive change.

La-Sonya Mitchell-Clark, 38, of Youngstown was reunited with her biological mother, Francine Simmons, after nearly 40 years when the Ohio Department of Health released birth records for adoptees born between Jan. 1, 1964 and Sept. 18, 1996. Mitchell-Clark received her original birth certificate showing Simmons' name, searched for her on Facebook and discovered they both work at InfoCision in Boardman — though neither had realized the family connection despite being at the company for years. A day after contacting colleagues, Mitchell-Clark got a call from Simmons; the emotional reunion revealed they live just six minutes apart. The search also uncovered three biological sisters, including co-worker Kamala Cummings. Both women expressed shock and joy at reconnecting; Mitchell-Clark’s adoptive parents are supportive. The story highlights how newly available adoption records can help people access family medical history and reconnect, while officials note outcomes vary and provide guidance on requesting records.
