Raul Ramirez, a 32-year-old Salvadoran immigrant, pleaded guilty in March to sexually penetrating his female roommate and will be sentenced to three years in California state prison under a plea deal overseen by Santa Clara County Judge Aaron Persky. Ramirez was arrested in November 2014 after his roommate called police; he admitted the assault and used a Spanish interpreter in court. The three-year term is the statutory minimum for the felony conviction Ramirez accepted, and prosecutors say Persky agreed with their position that prison was appropriate.

The Ramirez case has been widely compared to the high-profile Brock Turner case, in which Persky sentenced a 20-year-old former Stanford swimmer convicted of sexually assaulting an unconscious woman to six months in county jail and probation rather than the two-year state prison minimum. Critics argue the very different outcomes highlight bias and the role of race, class and privilege—Turner is white and from a privileged background, while Ramirez is poor and Latino. Supporters of Persky note legal differences (Ramirez pleaded to a charge with no probation option; Turner's case involved dropped counts) and argue judges must retain discretion. Some defense attorneys contend Ramirez’s sentence is the standard outcome and that Turner’s sentence was the anomaly.

The Turner sentence prompted national outrage, a victim impact statement that went viral, calls for investigation and a recall campaign against Persky led by Stanford law professor Michele Dauber. A separate open letter from 53 recent Stanford Law graduates urged restraint, warning that recalling a judge over sentencing decisions threatens judicial independence and could chill legitimate exercises of mercy.

A June poll of Santa Clara County voters found strong support for recalling Persky (66% of 776 respondents), with many respondents believing race and privilege affected sentencing outcomes. Support dipped after respondents read anti-recall messaging, and older voters—who are likelier to decide a low-turnout local election—were more evenly split. The debate continues over whether Persky abused discretion in Turner’s case or whether his decisions reflect broader systemic disparities in sentencing.

Vicki Gardner, executive director of the Smith Mountain Lake Regional Chamber of Commerce, survived the on-air shooting at Bridgewater Plaza that killed WDBJ reporter Alison Parker and photojournalist Adam Ward. Gardner was shot in the chest and taken to Carilion Roanoke Memorial Hospital, where she underwent emergency surgery. She was listed as stable Wednesday night and was upgraded to good condition on Thursday morning. Her husband, Tim Gardner, said she is recovering and the family has received strong community support; he asked that people continue to visit and enjoy Smith Mountain Lake as a way to help. A prayer vigil was held for her Wednesday night. The shooter, Vester Flanagan, later died by suicide; police found items in his car including a wig, extra magazines, and other personal effects.

Nevada’s pension chiefs, former CIO Ken Lambert and current CIO Steve Edmundson, have quietly shifted the state’s public employee retirement assets away from active stock- and bond-picking toward near-total indexing. Since 2014 they moved most equity and fixed-income allocations into funds that track market indexes (about 42% to the S&P 500, 18% to international stocks, 30% to U.S. Treasuries, plus modest private equity and real estate), effectively removing large discretionary bets and cutting reliance on outside active managers.

Their rationale: most active managers fail to outperform long-term after fees, hiring and firing managers consumes resources, and excessive short-term reactions undermine a pension’s long-duration obligations. Cost savings matter: with roughly $35 billion under management, each basis point saved equals about $3.5 million; their changes are expected to save roughly $4 million annually and have helped the fund outperform many peers over the past decade. They emphasize discipline and temperament—avoiding frequent trading and sticking to a long-term allocation—even when markets panic.

Nevada’s approach mirrors broader skepticism about expensive active management (echoed in critiques of New York and CalPERS practices), and stands out because few large public pension systems have moved so comprehensively to indexing. The managers’ low‑key, frugal style and focus on doing little rather than active tinkering underline their belief that, for long-term pension liabilities, simple, low-cost indexed investing often trumps attempts to beat the market.

Scholarly debate has intensified over whether five “Additional Passages” (about 325 lines) added to an early 17th-century printing of Thomas Kyd’s The Spanish Tragedy were written by William Shakespeare. Douglas Bruster, an English professor, published a detailed textual study arguing they are Shakespeare’s work. Building on earlier claims by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, stylistic and computational work by scholars such as Darren Vickers, and prior authorship-attribution efforts, Bruster focuses on spelling habits and printer misreadings tied to Shakespeare’s known handwriting.

Bruster compares idiosyncratic spellings and orthographic patterns found in the Additional Passages with those in the handful of manuscript lines commonly attributed to Shakespeare (notably in Sir Thomas More). He identifies 24 recurring spelling features (e.g., shortened past tenses like “blest,” single medial consonants) and points to nine textual corruptions in the quarto that plausibly result from a compositor misreading Shakespeare’s hand. He contends that resolving such misreadings restores awkward lines into fluent, characteristically Shakespearian verse. Bruster calls the aggregate of these features the “DNA” of Shakespeare’s pen.

Some prominent editors and scholars—Eric Rasmussen and Jonathan Bate among them—are persuaded enough to include the passages in forthcoming editions (the Royal Shakespeare Company edition and the new Riverside/Bankside edition). If broadly accepted, the additions would be the first largely uncontested enlargement of the Shakespeare canon since mid-1990s editorial acceptance of Shakespearean material in Edward III.

Caveats remain: the evidence is largely circumstantial and contested; individual spelling traits are not uniquely Shakespearean; and skepticism persists about editorial motives to “add” Shakespeare. Critics warn of over-enthusiastic attribution in a field where collaboration and textual revision were common. Still, Bruster’s methodical combination of historical context, linguistic patterns, and handwriting-based explanations has shifted opinion among some leading scholars and renewed interest in Shakespeare’s collaborative role within Elizabethan theater.

President Trump said he is “looking at the possibility” of meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in July, prompting concern among U.S. and European officials given Putin’s pariah status over election meddling, the Salisbury nerve‑agent attack and aggression in Ukraine and Syria. The White House confirmed National Security Adviser John Bolton will visit Moscow later this month, accompanied by NSC aides including Fiona Hill, to discuss logistics for a potential summit—likely timed just before or after the NATO summit in Brussels on July 11–12. Vienna has been mentioned as a possible venue, though Moscow (home to the World Cup final on July 15) and other sites are also under consideration.

Critics warn a U.S.–Russia summit would allow Putin to normalize relations and seek relief from sanctions, and could undercut allied unity at NATO and in responses to Russian actions. Trump has repeatedly pushed for friendlier ties with Russia—recently urging Russia’s readmission to the G7—arguing cooperation is preferable, while many experts and other Western leaders view Moscow as untrustworthy and continue to press sanctions and other countermeasures. The planned outreach comes amid ongoing investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election and broader transatlantic tensions over how to handle Russia.

This document profiles the destructive rise of modern electronic slot machines through the tragic case of Scott Stevens, a former chief operating officer who became a compulsive gambler and died by suicide after losing millions. Once successful and family-focused, Stevens developed a gambling habit after early wins in Las Vegas (2006). Over six years he hid his addiction, embezzled nearly $4 million from his employer to fund play, drained family savings and retirement accounts, and continued gambling even after being fired. On August 13, 2012, after losing thousands at the Mountaineer Casino, he wrote a final letter to his wife, called lawyers, phoned 911, and killed himself.

Stevens’s widow sued the casino and International Game Technology (IGT), alleging that slot machines and casino practices intentionally exploit vulnerabilities and create addiction. The piece places his story in a broader context: U.S. casino expansion since the 1980s, the dominance of electronic gaming machines (EGMs)—now nearly a million nationwide—and research showing that a small share of problem gamblers account for a large portion of casino revenue. It describes how casinos and manufacturers employ data, loyalty programs, targeted marketing, perks, and hosts to cultivate “whales” (big losers) and sustain “continuous gaming productivity.”

The report explains key technological and design features that amplify addiction:
- Virtual reel mapping: computer-driven “virtual reels” let designers weight symbol frequency and mask true odds, enabling outcomes far less likely than they appear and producing “near misses” that encourage continued play.
- Near misses and “losses disguised as wins”: visual and auditory feedback (lights, sounds, celebratory animations) treats small or net losses as wins, triggering reward responses and prolonging play.
- Multiline and multihand video formats: many paylines or simultaneous hands create frequent small “wins” while producing steady net losses.
- “Starved” or unbalanced reels: uneven symbol distributions that appear fair but limit winning combinations.

The article summarizes scientific findings on gambling addiction: 1.1–1.6% of U.S. adults meet criteria for gambling disorder (3–4 million people), with another several million at risk; addicts show brain changes in reward and impulse-control systems similar to substance addictions; one in five gambling addicts attempts suicide. It also recounts prior legal efforts by attorney Terry Noffsinger to hold casinos accountable—lawsuits alleging that casinos knowingly enticed vulnerable gamblers—which have largely failed in court, often on grounds that regulation and voluntary exclusion programs place responsibility on individuals.

Critics quoted argue manufacturers and casinos intentionally design machines to be addictive and to target high-value patrons, while industry groups downplay increased prevalence. The piece notes regulatory choices—some countries ban certain deceptive features, while U.S. regulators approved virtual reel mapping decades ago—and highlights the ethical and public-health implications of a business model that depends heavily on addicted gamblers’ losses.

Overall, the document presents Stevens’s death as a human tragedy that raises systemic questions: whether modern slot-machine design and casino practices manufacture or exploit addiction, and whether legal and regulatory structures adequately protect vulnerable players.

A former Bronx-Lebanon Hospital doctor, identified as 45-year-old Dr. Henry Bello, carried out an attack inside the Bronx hospital on Friday afternoon. Wearing a lab coat and carrying a rifle concealed beneath it, he opened fire around 2:50 p.m., killing at least one woman and wounding several others—reports indicate six people were shot on the 16th floor, five seriously. Officers found Bello on the 17th floor dead of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot; a female victim’s body was found nearby. Witnesses described chaotic scenes as staff and patients sheltered or aided victims; medical personnel performed emergency care amid the attack. Authorities say Bello had previously worked at the hospital and appears to have acted alone; officials noted past allegations against him. City leaders called the incident a horrific workplace-related act; the investigation is ongoing.

President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama reported combined assets valued between $1.8 million and $7 million for 2013 on financial disclosure forms released by the White House. The forms, which list holdings in broad ranges, show their largest jointly held asset is Treasury notes worth between $1 million and $5 million. Other holdings reflect a middle‑aged family’s needs, including Vanguard retirement funds, college savings plans and a 30‑year mortgage on their Chicago home valued between $500,000 and $1 million at a 5.625% rate.

Most of the president’s reported income came from book royalties—Dreams From My Father ($50,001–$100,000), The Audacity of Hope ($15,001–$50,000) and Of Thee I Sing ($5,001–$15,000)—totaling between $70,000 and $165,000 in 2013 (down from $250,000–$2.1 million in 2011). The Obamas’ previously released 2013 tax return showed $98,169 paid in federal taxes on $481,098 of adjusted gross income.

Vice President Joe Biden and his wife Jill reported assets between $276,000 and $940,000, including a Wilmington rental property. Biden reported refinancing mortgages at a lower 3.375% rate and listed modest book royalties (Promises to Keep earned less than $201). The Bidens paid $96,378 in federal taxes on $407,009 in adjusted gross income.

The White House noted the reports were reviewed by the Office of Government Ethics and reiterated the administration’s practice of posting disclosure forms online for transparency.

Actress Marcia Strassman, best known as Julie Kotter on the 1970s sitcom Welcome Back, Kotter and as the mother in Disney’s Honey I Shrunk the Kids (and its sequel), died Oct. 25 at her Sherman Oaks, Calif., home after a seven-year battle with breast cancer. She was 66.

Born April 28, 1948, in New York City and raised in New Jersey, Strassman moved to Los Angeles at 18. She began her career as a singer in the late 1960s and moved into television, with early appearances on The Patty Duke Show and a recurring role as Nurse Margie Cutler on M*A*S*H before her breakout as Julie Kotter (1975–79). Over a five-decade career she worked steadily in TV and film, including roles on Booker, Tremors, Third Watch, Providence and voice work on Aaahh!!! Real Monsters, and appeared in films such as The Aviator (1985).

Active offscreen, Strassman served on the Screen Actors Guild national board (elected to a three-year term in 2010) and was a longtime fundraiser for breast cancer research and other progressive causes. Friends and colleagues—among them director Bob Weide and singer/actress Cher—publicly mourned her passing. Her sister Julie described her as gifted, resourceful and widely loved.

She is survived by her daughter, costume designer Elizabeth “Lizzie” Collector, her brother Steven, and sister Julie. Services are pending; the family has asked that donations in her name be made to cancer organizations in lieu of flowers.

The document compiles reporting from the Los Angeles Times and The Washington Post on the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ demographics and the fallout from two consecutive years of all-white acting nominees that fueled the #OscarsSoWhite controversy. Key points:

- Persistent imbalance: Studies show the academy remains overwhelmingly white and male. From 2012 to the time of reporting membership shifted only slightly (e.g., about 91% white and 76% male). Blacks, Asians and Latinos each make up only a few percent of voters.

- Institutional limits: The academy’s roughly 6,200 members serve for life and are organized into 17 branches with strict, experience-based membership requirements. That structure, plus Hollywood’s underrepresentation of women and minorities in key roles, makes rapid change difficult.

- New commitments and controversy: Under pressure, the academy pledged to double its number of women and minority members by 2020 and adopted rules to revoke voting rights from inactive members. Critics say the targets are unrealistic given current industry demographics; some veterans argue the changes unfairly penalize older members (calling it ageism) or were enacted hastily without member input.

- Concentrated power in homogeneous branches: Branches that shape what gets made and promoted—executives and public relations—are especially white (executives ~98% white in 2012; PR ~95% white). Directors and other craft branches are also heavily male. This concentration helps perpetuate hiring patterns that limit diverse storytelling and career pathways into the academy.

- Industry root causes: Multiple interviewees and studies argue the problem originates with Hollywood’s hiring and greenlighting practices—studio executives, producers and decision-makers tend to favor familiar networks, making it hard for diverse talent to establish the credits needed for academy membership. Data cited include low percentages of women and people of color among directors, writers, lead actors and studio leadership.

- Internal debate and mixed reactions: Some industry figures applaud the academy’s moves as necessary; others warn against tokenism or “social engineering.” High-profile protests and calls to boycott continue, with some performers and filmmakers declining to attend or criticize the Oscars. The academy has added more diverse members recently but its board and ruling bodies remain largely white.

- Stakes and implications: The controversy has reputational and commercial consequences—the telecast’s viewership has declined and black viewership dropped markedly. Reforming the academy alone won’t fix systemic exclusion; sources argue studios and employers must change hiring and financing to create a pipeline of diverse filmmakers and craftspeople who can later be invited into the academy.

Overall, the articles conclude the academy mirrors a broader “inclusion crisis” in Hollywood: meaningful change will require both internal reforms to membership and far deeper shifts in who gets hired, financed and promoted across the business.

Dabbing (the dab) is a simple hip‑hop dance gesture—dropping the head into the bent crook of a slanted, upward‑angled arm while extending the other arm straight—that became a youth fad and internet meme from about 2015 onward. Originating in the Atlanta hip‑hop scene in the mid‑2010s, attribution initially varied (Migos, Skippa Da Flippa, Peewee Longway, Jose Guapo, Rich the Kid), with Skippa Da Flippa later acknowledged as the originator. The move evolved through summer 2014 and bears a resemblance to sneezing into one’s elbow; some disputed claims link it to the cannabis‑dabbing subculture.

Dabbing spread rapidly through music, sports and popular media. High‑profile moments boosting its popularity included NFL quarterback Cam Newton’s televised touchdown celebration in November 2015, Jason Derulo teaching James Corden to dab on Carpool Karaoke, and appearances in K‑pop, club scenes and goal celebrations (e.g., Paul Pogba, Jesse Lingard). Politicians and public figures worldwide also mimicked the gesture—Hillary Clinton, several European presidential candidates, UK and Australian politicians, Kenya’s president, and others—sometimes generating controversy or ridicule. Responses have ranged from playful adoption to accusations of disrespect depending on context.

The dab has been incorporated as a quick celebratory element in dance and performance, often marking musical drops or endings, and has been popularized through celebrity use and memes. In some places the gesture provoked stronger reactions: Saudi Arabia’s authorities associated it with drug culture and the move was effectively banned by the National Committee for Drug Control, leading to at least one arrest and public apology after a public performance.

Joy Dianne Covey, 50, a self-made tech executive best known as Amazon’s first chief financial officer, died in a bicycle crash on a rural stretch of Skyline Boulevard in San Mateo County when a minivan turned in front of her. The driver remained at the scene; police said drugs or alcohol do not appear to be factors and the collision remains under investigation.

Covey rose from an unconventional start—she dropped out of high school at 15, worked as a grocery clerk, then completed a bachelor’s at Cal State Fresno in 2½ years and earned both a J.D. and an M.B.A. from Harvard in 1989. She joined Amazon in late 1996 and served as CFO and vice president of finance and administration through 1999, and remained with the company until 2000. She played a central role in Amazon’s rapid expansion, international growth, and its 1997 IPO, and was noted for advocating long-term business decisions over short-term Wall Street pressures. Fortune named her one of the 50 Most Powerful Business Women in America.

After leaving Amazon, Covey focused on family, travel, environmental work and philanthropy. She founded the Beagle Foundation, served on boards including JetBlue and the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC)—where she was treasurer—and supported NRDC fellowships for Harvard Law graduates. Colleagues remember her as an independent, analytical thinker who thrived in the tech world’s meritocratic environment. She is survived by her son.

Facebook’s highly anticipated IPO on Friday fell short of expectations amid trading glitches, heavy supply and a late-day market selloff. The stock, priced at $38, opened about 11:30 a.m. ET after a 30-minute Nasdaq delay, briefly rose as much as 18% (to about $45) but slid through the day and closed at $38.23—just $0.23 above the offer price—after volatile trading in which more than 570 million shares changed hands.

Key factors in the weak debut:
- Nasdaq technical problems and a delayed open caused confusion and late trade confirmations, hampering orderly demand and execution.
- A broad market downturn late Friday reduced gains across the board and pressured Facebook’s shares.
- The IPO’s massive size—421.2 million shares, plus a 63.2 million-share overallotment—put substantial supply into the market; some analysts say the market couldn’t absorb that volume.
- Pricing at the top of the range ($38) and a relatively large percentage of total shares sold (est. ~18%) left little room for a strong first-day “pop,” unlike some recent internet IPOs.
- Underwriters, led by Morgan Stanley, intervened during the day—using the overallotment to stabilize the price and prevent it from falling below the offer.

Financial context and reactions:
- The IPO raised roughly $16+ billion for Facebook and valued the company at about $104–105 billion—making it the largest tech IPO ever by dollars raised (second-largest U.S. IPO including overallotment).
- Concerns cited by analysts include questions about valuation, advertising effectiveness (notably GM’s recent pullback), mobile strategy, and recent quarter-over-quarter profit softness.
- Facebook’s debut also weighed on related social stocks—Zynga, Yelp and LinkedIn all fell on the day.
- Despite the muted market reaction, Facebook’s IPO was a major liquidity event for early investors and employees; Mark Zuckerberg rang Nasdaq’s opening bell remotely and company morale at the campus was celebratory.

Bottom line: While the IPO was historic in scale and left Facebook with a huge market capitalization, technical issues, heavy supply and market headwinds produced a muted first-day performance, forcing underwriters to support the stock through stabilization measures.

Iranian authorities have postponed the trial of two Americans, Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, detained since July 2009 after being arrested near the Iran-Iraq border. Judiciary spokesman Qolamhossein Mohseni-Ejei said the delay was due to the absence of the third suspect, Sarah Shourd, who was released on $500,000 bail in September and returned to the U.S.; officials said the court will wait for her return or decide how to proceed without her. The trio maintain they were hiking in northern Iraq and unaware they crossed into Iran; U.S. officials have not determined exactly where they were when taken into custody and have criticized Iran’s continued detention.

The case has become intertwined with broader U.S.–Iran tensions, including stalled nuclear negotiations. President Ahmadinejad previously floated linking the Americans’ release to a prisoner swap for Iranians detained in the U.S. Iranian state media spotlighted claims of mistreatment by at least one jailed Iranian, and Tehran says publicity could help secure returns. Shourd has described the group’s trip as an innocent hike to a Kurdish waterfall area, encountering local soldiers and then Iranian guards; she said they were misled into Iranian custody and labeled suggestions they intended to agitate or create publicity as illogical. Bauer and Fattal remain in Evin prison.

These articles examine revelations from the Panama Papers — some 11.5 million documents leaked from Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca — that expose how offshore companies and secrecy jurisdictions are used by the wealthy and well connected. Key points:

- The leaks implicate relatives and associates of senior Chinese Communist Party figures. Among those linked to British Virgin Islands (BVI) companies are Jasmine Li, granddaughter of former Politburo Standing Committee member Jia Qinglin; Xi Jinping’s brother-in-law Deng Jiagui; Li Peng’s daughter Li Xiaolin; the son-in-law of senior leader Zhang Gaoli; the brother of ex–vice-president Zeng Qinghong; and others. Many are part of China’s “red nobility.” The documents show family members acting as shareholders or directors of BVI entities that in some cases held Chinese businesses or Swiss bank accounts. There is no document evidence that the officials themselves were beneficial owners, but the disclosures highlight opaque links between politics and business in China.

- Mossack Fonseca had extensive business in China and Hong Kong (tens of thousands of companies), and used standard offshore structures (BVI, Liechtenstein, Samoa, Niue, etc.). Mossack Fonseca says it applies anti–politically-exposed-person (PEP) checks, and insists it complies with laws, while noting clients seek legal secrecy and compliance advice. Critics point out that such services, even when lawful, enable tax avoidance, concealment of wealth, and can facilitate corruption and money-laundering.

- The Panama Papers more broadly reveal the scale and mechanics of the global offshore industry: Mossack Fonseca helped create over 214,000 shell companies; the files have names and links implicating politicians, businesspeople and celebrities worldwide. Estimates of wealth hidden offshore vary widely (from trillions to tens of trillions of dollars), and significant sums — especially from developing countries — are believed to be siphoned into secrecy jurisdictions annually.

- Political and public fallout has been substantial: media investigations and public anger have prompted probes in multiple countries, the resignation of Iceland’s prime minister, and calls for greater transparency and reform. Panama announced plans for an international panel to strengthen oversight of its offshore industry. Mossack Fonseca has accused hackers of stealing the files and denies wrongdoing.

- The coverage stresses that while many offshore arrangements are legal and used for legitimate cross-border business, the leaks expose ethically questionable practices, conflicts of interest, and the ease with which politically connected people can hide assets — fueling demands for stronger enforcement, transparency, and international reform of secrecy jurisdictions.

Chiapas state police in southern Mexico discovered 513 migrants packed inside two trailer trucks on May 17 while scanning the vehicles with X‑ray equipment at a checkpoint near Tuxtla Gutiérrez. The migrants — primarily from Guatemala (410) but also El Salvador (47), Ecuador (32), India (12), Nepal (6), China (3), and one each from Japan, the Dominican Republic and Honduras — included 32 women and four children. Many were dehydrated after hours of travel, clinging to cargo ropes strung inside the containers; the trailers had air holes punched in the roofs but lacked sufficient ventilation and water, according to those rescued. Migrants said smugglers charged about $7,000 each and planned to move them onward to Puebla for transfer toward the U.S. border. Four alleged smugglers were arrested after attempting to flee. Authorities called the seizure one of the largest migrant shipments detained in Mexico in recent years; it follows an incident in January when 219 migrants were found in a trailer in Chiapas. The discovery was made using backscatter X‑ray scanners, highlighting their growing use in vehicle inspections.

John Goodlett, a 25-year-old recent hire at Enterprise Rent-A-Car in Tulsa, Oklahoma, drew national attention for a small act of kindness. While helping Coty Vincent, a mother of 11-month-old twins whose car had been damaged in a hit-and-run, Goodlett picked one child up from a car seat and held him with one arm while he processed Vincent’s rental at the counter. Vincent photographed him typing with one hand and holding her son with the other, posted the picture to Facebook with the caption praising his compassion, and the post went viral—receiving hundreds of thousands of reactions and tens of thousands of shares.

Goodlett, who is a twin himself, said he was surprised by the attention and hoped the story would encourage everyday kindness. Enterprise offered him a gift card, which he donated to a local Boys & Girls Club run by the Salvation Army; Enterprise also sent Vincent a double stroller. Vincent said the public response has been uplifting and called the moment a reminder that simple, humane gestures can make a big difference.

An Arizona state trooper unexpectedly helped deliver a baby on the side of State Route 80 near Bisbee on Nov. 14. Trooper Miguel Rincon was conducting a traffic stop when a car pulled up and a woman said her granddaughter, Courtney Benavidez, was rushing to the hospital after her water broke. Benavidez’s labor progressed so quickly the baby, named Carter Jett (nicknamed “Jet” for his speedy arrival), was born in the car before Rincon reached her. Rincon left his stop, called for medics and retrieved blankets and gloves; by the time he returned Benavidez was already holding the newborn. He wrapped the baby and cared for mother and son until emergency crews arrived. Both were taken to Canyon Vista Medical Center, released the next day, and are doing fine. Rincon, a DPS trooper since 2008, called the incident his most surprising on the job.

Summary:

A new startup, Fantex Holdings, announced a trading exchange that will offer tracking stocks tied to individual athletes’ future earnings, starting with NFL running back Arian Foster. The firm plans to sell 1.06 million shares at $10 each, using proceeds to pay Foster $10 million in exchange for 20% of his future brand and playing income; shares will trade only on Fantex’s own exchange and the company expects to pay dividends linked to Foster’s earnings. Fantex is backed by Silicon Valley, Wall Street and sports figures, including co-founder/CEO Buck French, former athletes like John Elway on its board, and executives from hedge funds and brokerage firms. The offering carries heavy risks—injury, performance slumps, non-guaranteed NFL contracts, insider-trading concerns, illiquidity, and lack of governance or recourse for investors—and Fantex’s filings list many such risk factors. The concept echoes prior celebrity-backed finance ideas (e.g., Bowie Bonds) and aims to capitalize on NFL and fantasy football fan interest, though critics call it speculative.

An opinion piece in the document criticizes this and similar novel investment products as part of a broader post-crisis surge in flashy, often risky offerings—enabled by a recovering market, the JOBS Act, and financial innovation—that make it easier for unsophisticated investors to lose money. The writer warns that vehicles like athlete tracking stocks, Bitcoin-related funds, themed investing platforms, and art-as-investment reflect a return of “bullshit investments” and that deregulation and new crowdfunding rules are shifting wealth toward information-rich insiders. The recommended prudent response is caution: favor low-cost index funds or simple, well-known advice and avoid speculative gimmicks.

Separately, the document reports that Motif Investing, a Silicon Valley startup offering theme-based baskets of stocks (“motifs”), raised $25 million in a Series C round led by Goldman Sachs, bringing total funding to $51 million. Motif—positioning itself as an accessible thematic-investing platform without management fees—has attracted diverse users, created thousands of motifs, and plans to expand products for financial advisors and grow its engineering staff. The CEO says the company aims to remain independent but acknowledges it could be an attractive acquisition target for established financial firms.

Viktor and Amalija Knavs, the parents of first lady Melania Trump, were naturalized as U.S. citizens in a private New York ceremony, their immigration attorney Michael Wildes said. The Slovenian-born couple had been U.S. permanent residents for more than a decade and reportedly obtained green cards after being sponsored by their adult daughter, Melania Trump — the same family-sponsored visa category the Trump administration has sought to curtail. Wildes said the Knavses followed the same process as other applicants and praised family reunification as a core immigration principle. The White House and the first lady’s office declined to comment beyond noting the family’s privacy. The Knavses, in their early 70s and often seen traveling with the first family, moved to the Washington area after the inauguration. The case highlights tension between the administration’s push to reduce family-based immigration in favor of a “merit-based” system and the continued use of family sponsorship channels that currently supply the largest share of green cards.

This document details the public clash between Goop, Gwyneth Paltrow’s wellness brand, and Dr. Jen Gunter, a San Francisco obstetrician-gynecologist who has become a prominent critic of Goop’s health and sexual wellness claims.

Key points:

- Dr. Jen Gunter, a credentialed gynecologist and author, has repeatedly criticized Goop content she considers medically unsound or dangerous—examples include promotion of jade (yoni) eggs for vaginal health, vaginal steaming, claims linking bra-wearing to breast cancer, and other alternative remedies promoted on the site. Her critiques, posted on her blog, blend clinical evidence with sharp commentary and have drawn wide attention and professional support.

- Goop has grown from a personal newsletter into a lucrative wellness empire that markets and promotes many alternative therapies and products (supplements, crystal therapies, “earthing,” oxygen bars, specialty foods, etc.). It drew 1.8 million unique U.S. visitors in June (comScore) and runs paid wellness summits with high-priced tickets.

- The site has faced repeated external scrutiny for unproven or deceptive health claims. TINA.org documented over 50 instances where Goop or products it promoted were presented as treating or preventing medical conditions without sufficient scientific evidence (e.g., infertility, depression, psoriasis, cancer). TINA.org warned Goop and later filed complaints with California prosecutors after limited corrective action.

- Goop responded publicly with a post titled “Uncensored: A Word From Our Doctors,” defending discussion of alternative health approaches and featuring contributions from Goop-affiliated practitioners (including Dr. Steven Gundry). That post indirectly targeted Gunter and defended featuring nontraditional viewpoints; one Goop-contributor criticized Gunter for tone rather than substance. One physician quoted in the piece later said she did not consider herself a Goop “doctor” and urged an audit of Goop content.

- The dispute intensified into a “flame war,” with Goop and its contributors pushing back and Gunter replying with pieces such as “Goop’s Misogynistic, Mansplaining Hit Job,” asserting her expert authority and criticizing Goop’s framing and claims. Her posts have generated substantial traffic (one cited as 157,000 views) and support from other medical professionals.

- Critics (including media figures and scientists) and consumer-rights groups argue that Goop’s marketing sometimes crosses legal and ethical lines by implying medical benefits without competent scientific substantiation, potentially exploiting vulnerable consumers. TINA.org and regulatory bodies have previously intervened or inquired about Goop’s product claims.

Overall message: The piece frames a broader conflict between celebrity-driven wellness marketing that blends alternative and lifestyle advice with limited scientific backing, and evidence-based medical professionals like Dr. Jen Gunter who publicly challenge misleading or potentially harmful claims. The article calls for greater accuracy and accountability in Goop’s health-related content and marketing.

CIA Director John Brennan held an unusual on-camera news conference to respond to a Senate Intelligence Committee report that condemned the CIA’s post-9/11 interrogation program. Speaking at Langley with senior officers behind him, Brennan took a defensive but measured tone: he praised the agency’s workforce and said most employees acted faithfully, but acknowledged that some officers used techniques that were unauthorized, “abhorrent,” and should be repudiated. He admitted the agency fell short in oversight and accountability and said the CIA was unprepared to run a detention-and-interrogation program.

On effectiveness, Brennan said detainees subjected to “enhanced interrogation techniques” (EITs) provided “useful and valuable” information that was used in operations, including the hunt for Osama bin Laden, but insisted it is “unknown and unknowable” whether the harsh methods were the cause of that intelligence. He repeatedly avoided calling the practices “torture,” leaving labels to others, and declined to endorse the Senate panel’s public release of its summary, saying there has already been “more than enough transparency.”

Brennan disputed the Senate report’s implication that the CIA deliberately misled officials and the public, though he acknowledged the report aligns with many internal CIA findings that criticized program management. He noted the EIT program ended in 2007 and urged moving past the debate to current national-security challenges. Senate Intelligence Committee chair Dianne Feinstein rebutted many of his claims in real time via Twitter, defending the committee’s methods and conclusions. Critics, including some lawmakers, have called for Brennan’s resignation, but the White House has expressed confidence in him.

CNN is reformatting its 8 p.m. program “Parker Spitzer” into an ensemble show called “In the Arena,” replacing co-host Kathleen Parker with a rotating panel centered on Eliot Spitzer. Effective Monday, E.D. Hill and Will Cain — both conservative commentators — and other guests and contributors “within and outside the CNN family” will join Spitzer nightly, CNN U.S. executive Ken Jautz announced.

The change follows four months of backstage tensions, critical reviews that Spitzer often dominated the show, and weak ratings: the program struggled to gain viewership in the key 25–54 demographic and lagged behind competitors. CNN executives said the new format will present multiple points of view and broaden debate-style discussion; they emphasized they were not making the hour solely “The Eliot Spitzer Show,” though Spitzer’s role will grow.

Parker, a Pulitzer Prize–winning columnist who had cut back her newspaper schedule earlier, said she is stepping away to refocus on her syndicated column and other writing but will appear on CNN occasionally. Both Parker and Spitzer issued cordial statements about one another. The rebranding evokes debate-roundtable programs like the former “Crossfire” and aims to strengthen CNN’s prime-time performance against Fox News and MSNBC.

The document rebuts claims that recent cold snaps disprove global warming. It criticizes media and politicians who conflate short-term, regional weather with long-term, global climate trends—highlighting examples from the Express, Telegraph, Mail and MPs who used local snowfall and cold in Britain to argue against climate science. The author notes that the Met Office’s seasonal outlook was cautious (near or above average with a one-in-seven chance of a cold winter), so accusations that forecasts were politically manipulated are unsupported.

Scientists explain the current wide temperature contrasts as natural weather variability: a pronounced meandering of the large west-to-east airflows has allowed Arctic air to plunge south in some regions (causing extreme cold and snow in parts of Europe, the U.S. and China) while other areas (Alaska, northern Canada, North Africa, the Mediterranean) are unusually warm. Experts emphasize that single events or short-term extremes do not negate the long-term warming trend—2009 ranked among the planet’s warmest years—and that climate change can increase the frequency and severity of extremes but does not eliminate cold spells. The piece underscores the distinction between weather (variable, regional, short-term) and climate (long-term, global trends) and warns against politicized confirmation bias that mistakes isolated events for evidence against global warming.

Chelsea Manning, the former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who leaked hundreds of thousands of classified documents to WikiLeaks in 2010 and was imprisoned in 2013, is the subject of a high-profile Vogue feature accompanied by photos by Annie Leibovitz, including an image of Manning in a red swimsuit that she captioned on Twitter, “guess this is what freedom looks like.” The long profile traces Manning’s troubled childhood in Oklahoma, her struggles with gender identity and sexuality, her enlistment in the military in 2007, and the 2010 disclosures — including the “Collateral Murder” video — that made her a polarizing figure. The piece recounts her guilty pleas, 35‑year sentence, coming out as transgender the day after sentencing, legal battles in prison to receive hormone therapy, repeated suicide attempts, and her commutation and release by President Obama in May 2017. 

Since her release, Manning has been living in New York, cultivating a public persona that mixes activism, fashion interest, social outings, teaching herself programming, and plans to write a memoir. The Vogue story follows her reemergence into public life — from an after-party for the Lambda Literary Awards to visits with LGBTQ elders — and captures her reflections on responsibility for her actions, the limits of official channels for reporting government wrongdoing, and uncertainty about future plans.

The profile and photo spread generated mixed reactions: praise for Manning’s bravery and visibility, along with criticism and outrage from detractors who view her leaks as treasonous and object to Vogue featuring a trans woman who received clemency. Commentators such as the National Review argued the coverage glamorizes a traitor and exemplifies what they see as identity‑politics–driven double standards. The article situates Manning at the intersection of debates over whistleblowing, national security, transgender visibility, and celebrity.

The romantic musical Once was the big winner at the 2012 Tony Awards, taking home eight trophies including Best New Musical and Best Actor for Steve Kazee. Based on the 2006 indie film about an unlikely Dublin romance between a Czech flower seller and an Irish street musician, the stage version uses the film’s songs by Glen Hansard and Markéta Irglová (including the Oscar-winning “Falling Slowly”) and stars Cristin Milioti opposite Kazee. Once also won awards for director John Tiffany, book writer Enda Walsh, scenic design (Bob Crowley) and lighting (Natasha Katz), among others.

The ceremony, hosted by Neil Patrick Harris at the Beacon Theatre, saw other major winners including Clybourne Park (Best Play), Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman (Best Revival of a Play), The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess (Best Revival of a Musical), and James Corden and Nina Arianda taking Best Actor in a Play and Best Actress in a Play, respectively. Notable winners in musical categories included Alan Menken and Jack Feldman for Newsies (Original Score) and Audra McDonald for Best Actress in a Musical (The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess). The full list of nominees and winners spanned play, musical, revival, performance, design and score categories.

A 25-year-old man deliberately jumped from a moving, open-sided monorail at the Bronx Zoo into the Wild Asia tiger exhibit, clearing a 16-foot perimeter fence and landing in the enclosure. He spent about 10 minutes alone with an 11-year-old male Siberian tiger named Bashuta before zoo staff used a fire extinguisher to drive the animal away and called it into a holding area. The man suffered multiple bites and punctures, a broken arm and leg, and was hospitalized in stable condition; his family asked for privacy.

Zoo Director Jim Breheny said the tiger would not be euthanized, calling Bashuta blameless because the incident resulted from the visitor’s deliberate act. Staff credited quick emergency response for preventing a worse outcome and said they did not have to use deadly force. Bashuta, who has lived at the zoo three years and has sired cubs there, will be returned to exhibit. The zoo — which has no surveillance cameras in that part of the exhibit and had only Bashuta on display at the time — plans to review safety procedures but characterized the event as an extraordinary, self-endangering act rather than a security failure.

This document mixes two distinct topics: technical notes about a web crawl and multiple overlapping obituary/news pieces about writer-filmmaker Nora Ephron. Summary:

Web crawl notes
- A crawl of outlinks from wikipedia.org began in March 2016. The resulting files exist but are not publicly accessible.
- For this run several changes were made compared with prior crawls: duplicate-detection was disabled to produce a complete collection (facilitating possible future data sharing), and for the first time seeds were built from all 865 Wikimedia collections rather than just the English Wikipedia.

Nora Ephron obituary and career overview
- Nora Ephron (May 19, 1941–June 26, 2012) was a celebrated essayist, journalist, novelist, screenwriter, director and producer known for sharp, witty, personal writing in the Dorothy Parker tradition and for romantic-comedy screenplays and films.
- Cause of death is reported variously in the excerpts as complications from myelodysplasia/acute myeloid leukemia and pneumonia; one account says she had been diagnosed with myelodysplasia six years earlier.
- Career highlights: early journalism at the New York Post and magazine work (Esquire, New York), bestselling essay collections (e.g., Crazy Salad, I Feel Bad About My Neck), novels (Heartburn), and prominent screenplays/films including Silkwood (1983), When Harry Met Sally (1989), Sleepless in Seattle (1993), You’ve Got Mail (1998), and Julie & Julia (2009). She also directed and produced films and wrote candidly about aging, gender, and culture.
- Awards and recognition: Three Academy Award nominations for writing (Silkwood — with Alice Arlen; Sleepless in Seattle — with David S. Ward and Jeff Arch; and When Harry Met Sally). She was praised as an influential woman in film history and notable for bringing women’s experiences and humor to mainstream cinema.
- Personal life: Born in Manhattan, raised in Beverly Hills, Wellesley College graduate (1962). Daughter of Hollywood playwrights Henry Ephron and Phoebe Wolkind; eldest of four sisters (all writers). Married three times (Dan Greenburg, Carl Bernstein — their public divorce inspired Heartburn — and later Nicholas Pileggi). Survived by husband Nicholas Pileggi, two sons (Jacob and Max Bernstein), and her sisters.
- Style and themes: Known for mordant wit, self-deprecation, cultural commentary, and turning personal pain into comic, incisive copy; memorable cultural moments (e.g., the deli orgasm scene in When Harry Met Sally) and reflections on food, aging and feminism were recurring subjects.
- Legacy: Widely admired as a prolific, influential writer and filmmaker who bridged journalism, essays, novels and Hollywood, and who helped shape contemporary romantic comedy and candid female voices in American letters and film.

Comedian Russell Brand has been publicly discussing his recently finalized 14-month marriage and divorce from pop star Katy Perry, repeatedly expressing affection and care for his ex. In back-to-back interviews with Piers Morgan and Howard Stern, Brand said he still feels “compassion and warmth” for Perry and emphasized he doesn’t want to say anything that might hurt her. He described falling deeply in love and later realizing marriage wasn’t working—largely for practical reasons such as their conflicting careers and time apart—while denying tabloid claims about feuds with Perry’s parents or other sensational causes.

Brand confirmed he’s enjoying single life and acknowledged press reports linking him to Isabella Brewster, but declined to elaborate to protect those involved. He rejected attempts to frame Perry’s song “Wide Awake” as a pointed message about their split, calling it “a nice song” and resisting detailed interpretations. Brand also said he isn’t interested in claiming money from Perry in the divorce and reiterated respect for her ambition and talent. Overall, his public comments strike a conciliatory tone, combining honesty about the marriage’s breakdown with a desire to avoid causing Perry pain.

This site argues that the mainstream media built and perpetuated a false, sensational narrative around the Jerry Sandusky case that unfairly “framed” Joe Paterno, destroyed his legacy, and unduly harmed Penn State’s university and football program. The authors deny defending child abuse or promoting conspiracy theories; instead they claim media incompetence and ratings-driven bias led to a one-sided story that ignored facts and basic logic. The project—centered on documentary work (The Framing of Joe Paterno), books, interviews, and research—says two years of investigation, including interviews with Sandusky in prison, convinced its creators that both Paterno and Sandusky were badly wronged and that key evidence and testimony were misreported or overlooked.

The site collects and promotes a wide range of materials aimed at undermining the prevailing narrative: long-form interviews, press conferences, polls about public knowledge, op-eds, legal updates, analyses of the Freeh report and Board of Trustees actions, timelines, transcripts, videos, and public events (town halls, screenings). It highlights perceived media errors and institutional failings—criticizing reporters, the Freeh investigation, the Penn State Board of Trustees, the NCAA sanctions, and prosecutors’ handling of documents and testimony (e.g., Mike McQueary, the “Schultz file,” victim statements, and settlements). The site also publicizes support for the Paterno family lawsuit from former players and others, petitions, and criticism of mainstream outlets.

Recent and notable items featured include John Ziegler’s media appearances (Blaze TV, Glenn Beck network, Today Show segment), a Sandusky prison interview, new allegations about the origins of accuser Aaron Fisher’s claims, a judge’s rulings affecting Sandusky appeals, and local controversies over released transcripts and BOT communications. The site promotes events and media (mini-movie acceptance at festivals, town halls with Franco Harris), and runs opinion pieces by contributors (Ray Blehar, Eileen Morgan) that reexamine testimony, timelines, and the Freeh report.

An anecdote cited near the end: Penn State mistakenly mailed a mass season-ticket renewal letter to Jerry Sandusky’s home in 2015, which the university called a database error from a mass mailing to roughly 30,000 recent ticket holders; Sandusky remains incarcerated and maintains his innocence. Overall, the site’s mission is to challenge mainstream accounts, press for reassessment of the case and sanctions, and publicize alternative evidence and commentary supporting Paterno (and, it contends, Sandusky).

The FDA announced that breast implants—both saline and silicone—may carry a very small but measurable increased risk of anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL), a rare immune-system cancer distinct from breast cancer. The FDA has reviewed approximately 34–60 cases worldwide (depending on reports) among an estimated 5–10 million women with implants. ALCL linked to implants typically arises in the scar tissue capsule around the implant and presents years after surgery with symptoms such as lumps, pain, asymmetry, fluid buildup, or swelling.

In many reported cases removal of the implant and surrounding scar tissue has been sufficient; some patients have required chemotherapy or radiation. The FDA noted limited data and cannot yet recommend a specific treatment approach; affected women should be evaluated by both a breast surgeon and an oncologist. Because the observed number of cases is so small, the FDA said current evidence supports continued marketing and use of implants but urged that women considering implants discuss the potential risk with their doctors. Women with implants and no symptoms need no change in routine care but should promptly report symptoms.

The agency is asking clinicians to report confirmed cases to MedWatch and is working with the American Society of Plastic Surgeons to create a registry; labeling for implants will be updated to include information on the possible link. The biological mechanism is unclear; one hypothesis is that silicone around implants might stimulate nearby cells, but this remains speculative. Industry and professional groups have acknowledged the rarity of the cases and expressed support for the registry; implant makers and societies emphasize implants’ overall safety while noting known surgical risks (e.g., seroma, hematoma, rupture, and capsular contracture).

Nevest Coleman, 49, returned Monday to his old job on the Chicago White Sox grounds crew at Guaranteed Rate Field after spending 23 years wrongfully imprisoned for a 1994 rape and murder. Prosecutors vacated his conviction last November after new DNA evidence, and a Cook County judge recently granted him a certificate of innocence. Coleman’s childhood priest and other advocates helped secure an interview with the team; the White Sox hired him back and welcomed him as part of the “family.”

Coleman described emotional reunions with former colleagues, including longtime head groundskeeper Roger “The Sodfather” Bossard, and began his first day by power-washing an entrance near the team’s 2005 World Series plaza. He said family support and the belief in his innocence sustained him in prison, where he read extensively and kept busy with work programs. Since his release he’s reconnected with siblings, two children and three grandchildren, and hopes to move to full-time status with the club.

The White Sox expressed gratitude that justice was served and said they look forward to having Coleman back at the ballpark for the season.

On Saturday, a gunman in an armored van attacked Dallas police headquarters before leading officers on a vehicle chase that ended on I‑45 in Hutchins. Police negotiators had tried for hours to communicate with the suspect, who identified himself as 35‑year‑old James Boulware and told authorities he wanted to “blow up police” because they had taken his child and accused him of being a terrorist. A police sniper later shot the man through the van’s windshield; explosive‑ordnance concerns and the presence of suspected pipe bombs delayed recovery of the body until a robot could approach the vehicle. At least two pipe bombs were found inside the van, which had ports in its walls for firing weapons, and officials reported loud detonations as they worked to neutralize explosives. No other injuries were reported.

Family members declined to discuss the incident at length. Boulware’s father said his son blamed police for losing custody of his middle‑school‑aged child; he had seen his son the night before and did not anticipate such an attack. Police have given the name and motive but are awaiting medical examination to definitively identify the deceased. (Separately noted: Alexa Internet has been donating crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996; those data are added daily to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.)

- International diplomacy: The U.S. and China jointly announced a new round of U.N. sanctions on North Korea intended to substantially hinder Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs in response to its recent atomic-bomb test.

- Agriculture — GM corn and rising pest resistance:
  - Reports detail growing problems with pests overcoming genetically modified (GM) crops. The western corn rootworm, a major U.S. pest, has been found damaging Bt corn engineered to produce a bacterial toxin intended to kill it.
  - Iowa State researchers identified Bt-resistant rootworms in four Iowa fields; laboratory tests show these bugs can pass resistance to offspring. Illinois fields also saw similar damage, and past examples include bollworm resistance to Bt cotton in India.
  - Causes likely include repeated planting of the same trait year after year and inadequate use of mandated “refuges” (non-Bt corn planted to dilute resistance genes). Where farmers planted Bt corn consecutively, resistance was more likely to emerge.
  - If resistance spreads, farmers may need to return to heavier pesticide use and other control measures.
  - Monsanto’s position: existing products still work on the vast majority of acres; the company is trying to make refuge compliance easier (mixed-seed bags), offers alternative products, and is developing new traits. Monsanto acknowledges the issue and is researching next-generation technologies (e.g., RNA interference) to combat pests.

- Wider critique and industry implications:
  - The broader commentary argues that reliance on single herbicides (Roundup) and single-trait GM crops has driven the evolution of “superweeds” and now “superinsects.” Overuse of uniform technologies across millions of acres creates strong selection pressure that accelerates resistance.
  - Despite these biological setbacks, Monsanto’s stock and investor sentiment remain strong because the company is developing and selling new patented technological fixes, effectively creating a cycle in which farmers must adopt ever-more advanced (and costly) solutions to evolving pest problems.
  - The piece urges regulators and the public to scrutinize this cycle and consider integrated resistance-management strategies rather than relying solely on successive high-tech remedies.

At the Feb. 2 National Prayer Breakfast, President Donald Trump mixed humor and policy while framing religious freedom as central to his agenda. He joked about Arnold Schwarzenegger’s Apprentice ratings, defended his “tough phone calls” with foreign leaders, and repeated calls to fight terrorism to protect religious liberty. Most consequentially, Trump vowed to “get rid of and totally destroy the Johnson Amendment,” the 1954 tax-code provision that bars tax-exempt organizations, including churches, from directly engaging in partisan campaigning. He said repeal would let “representatives of faith” speak freely and insisted his actions would protect religious and personal liberty.

The pledge drew sharp criticism from church-state advocates, legal experts and many clergy who warn repeal would invite unchecked, tax-advantaged political activity through houses of worship, risk turning them into conduits for “dark money,” undermine religious freedom by politicizing congregations, and damage democracy. Polling and critics cited by multiple outlets indicate most Americans and many clergy oppose pastors endorsing candidates from the pulpit. Legal scholars note Trump cannot unilaterally erase the amendment — Congress must act — although a president can direct enforcement practices to blunt its effect.

Trump also defended his immigration executive order at the event, arguing for stricter vetting to prevent extremists from entering the U.S. and saying new systems would ensure arrivals embrace American values of religious and personal liberty. Outside the Washington Hilton, about 150 faith leaders and activists, including Christian author Ann Voskamp and former Obama faith adviser Michael Wear, protested the travel ban and urged compassion for refugees, contending security and humanitarian obligation are compatible.

Commentary and analysis linked Trump’s Johnson Amendment attack and the broader speech to a vision of religious nationalism that appeals to white evangelical supporters and the religious right. Critics say the move chiefly serves those who want to build church-based political machines and could lead to greater partisan influence and less transparency in campaign funding if churches were allowed to engage openly in electoral politics while retaining tax-exempt status.

Poland’s deputy defense minister Bartosz Kownacki drew criticism after he insulted France following a diplomatic spat over a cancelled defence event invitation. France revoked Poland’s invite to the Euronaval 2016 maritime defence exhibition in Paris after talks between Warsaw and Airbus over a planned purchase of 50 Caracal helicopters broke down. Kownacki told TVN24 the French were “showing us the door” and taunted that “these are the people we taught to eat with a fork a couple of centuries ago,” implying historical Polish superiority. 

His remarks were condemned by Poland’s liberal opposition and even by a spokeswoman for the governing Law and Justice (PiS) party as “unfortunate” and undiplomatic; some opposition MPs demanded his dismissal. The episode—mockingly dubbed “forkgate”—comes amid heightened tensions after Poland halted the Airbus talks and moved to buy U.S. Black Hawks, prompting threats of legal action from Airbus and the postponement of a presidential visit by France’s François Hollande. Historical claims in Kownacki’s comment are dubious; forks likely spread to northern Europe later. The incident adds to a string of diplomatic controversies involving PiS ministers.

Standard & Poor’s on Monday downgraded Italy’s long-term sovereign rating one notch to A (from A+) and cut the short-term rating to A-1, citing weak growth, high debt and political gridlock; it placed the rating on negative outlook, signalling further cuts are possible. The move surprised markets that had been focused on Moody’s, which is still reviewing Italy.

The downgrade pushed Italy’s 10‑year bond yield up (peaking +16 basis points, trading around 5.6%) and widened the spread over German bunds to about 382 basis points. Officials and analysts warned higher borrowing costs come at a bad time, with nearly €30 billion of gross bond issuance due in October–November and roughly €100 billion still to be raised before year-end. ECB purchases of Italian and Spanish bonds earlier this month had reduced yields but haven’t stopped recent increases; talk of further ECB buying helped trim the rise after the downgrade.

Rome angrily rejected S&P’s assessment, saying the agency was out of touch and politically influenced, and stressed recent fiscal measures and a parliamentary majority. Markets, however, remain nervous because Italy’s debt is large (around 120% of GDP) and the country is considered too big to be easily rescued if stress intensifies.

The downgrade also heightened concerns about the broader euro‑zone banking sector—especially French banks exposed to Greek risk—and about the limits of rescue resources. European equity markets were relatively resilient on the day amid positive signals on Greek aid talks and speculation the U.S. Federal Reserve would ease policy. Separately, Greece continued negotiations with the IMF/ECb/Commission troika over further aid disbursements, Spain sold higher‑yielding Treasury bills as its banking woes persist, and ECB officials warned the growth outlook has deteriorated.

This long piece charts how online streaming and Twitch have remade chess from a quiet, niche pastime into a fast, social eSport with diverse personalities, new formats, and broader audiences.

Key points

- Streaming transformed chess’s image. Eric Hansen’s Chessbrah channel exemplifies a brash, party-friendly, interactive style—long streams with trash talk, music, and irreverent antics—that intentionally rejects old stereotypes of chess as stodgy or antisocial. Chessbrah drew controversy but also a large following by making chess feel accessible and fun for younger viewers.

- Different streaming styles coexist. John Bartholomew represents a calmer, instructional approach: clear, beginner-friendly YouTube lessons and analysis that helped grow a teaching-focused audience. Chess.com and Danny Rensch occupy the middle ground, producing structured programming, leagues, and mass participation features while encouraging player–viewer interaction.

- Chess.com and leagues helped professionalize online chess. Chess.com evolved into a hub (play, lessons, broadcasts) and pushed shorter time controls, audience-friendly commentary, and Twitch partnerships. The PRO Chess League and Speed Chess Championship—featuring top pros like Magnus Carlsen and Hikaru Nakamura—drew large Twitch audiences and signaled chess’s emergence as an eSport.

- Stream formats and viewer preferences. Fans prefer interactive commentary at an understandable level, faster games that create more mistakes and suspense, and personalities who engage with chat. Twitch monetization (subscriptions, donations) makes streaming viable for players.

- Inclusion challenges persist. The gender gap and misogynistic harassment remain real problems on Twitch. Alexandra Botez’s experience—earning substantial donations but facing sexualized, abusive chat—illustrates the cost female streamers can pay; moderation and community-building help but don’t erase the issue.

- Real-world events and crossover appeal. Streamed chess now includes IRL finals and celebrity appearances (e.g., John Urschel), bridging online audiences to live events and exposing chess to new demographics.

Additional brief news items included at the end (chess roundup)
- Delhi International Chess Festival: GM Levan Pantsulaia won the main event; Category C set a world record for most participants in a FIDE-rated Swiss.
- Computer championships: Stockfish won the Rapid Computer Championship; Lc0 emerged as a strong challenger; bullet events upcoming.
- Features and historical pieces: Articles on prearranged draws’ effects, Deep Blue vs Kasparov, and Anand’s notable games.
- Tata Steel: Ian Nepomniachtchi joined Magnus Carlsen and Vishy Anand in the lead in round nine.
- Arena Kings Streamers Championship leaderboard: Hikaru Nakamura leading season 3 standings.
- PRO Chess League: Matches and schedules previewed, including Chessbrahs participation.

Bottom line: Streaming has modernized chess’s presentation, expanded its audience, and turned players into entertainers and teachers—while raising persistent issues around culture and inclusion as the game integrates into mainstream eSports.

Chef Tom Colicchio has renamed his Beekman Hotel restaurant from Fowler & Wells to Temple Court after learning the original name’s connection to 19th-century phrenologists. Colicchio said research revealed Fowler & Wells promoted beliefs that conflict with the restaurant’s values. The article explains phrenology — the pseudoscience of reading skull shapes to infer mental traits — was widely accepted in the 1800s and was used both to justify slavery and, paradoxically, to support abolitionist arguments.

It gives historical examples: slaveholders like Charles Caldwell used phrenology to claim Africans were naturally “tameable” and thus fit for enslavement; his writings echoed the racist scenes depicted in Django Unchained. At the same time, many prominent abolitionists and reformers, including Lucretia Mott, George Combe, and Horace Mann, embraced phrenology. They argued that perceived weaknesses in enslaved people meant they would not seek violent revenge if emancipated and therefore deserved aid, not continued bondage. The piece emphasizes that phrenology is now thoroughly discredited, and that 19th-century scientific racism and abolitionist sentiment were sometimes intertwined in complex and contradictory ways.

Chinese state media announced that senior politician Bo Xilai has been expelled from the Chinese Communist Party and will be handed over to judicial authorities to face criminal charges. Xinhua and other outlets said the party’s Politburo concluded that Bo committed repeated violations over a long career—taking large bribes (personally and through his family), abusing power (notably in the handling of the murder case involving his wife), mishandling personnel promotions, and maintaining improper sexual relationships with multiple women. The move follows months of investigation that began after Chongqing police chief Wang Lijun sought refuge in a U.S. consulate in February and culminated in guilty verdicts for Bo’s wife Gu Kailai (convicted of murdering British businessman Neil Heywood and given a suspended death sentence) and for Wang (sentenced to 15 years). State media framed the expulsions and impending prosecution as necessary to address corruption, abuse of power and damage to the party’s reputation.

The announcement came just before Xinhua set Nov. 8 as the opening date of the 18th Party Congress, the once-a-decade leadership transition expected to confirm a new top team, and signaled party unity ahead of that meeting. Observers say the strong action aims to crush Bo’s lingering public support—partly rooted in his populist, Maoist-tinged Chongqing policies—and to defuse a scandal that had threatened the succession. Analysts note the case raises broader questions about how Bo rose so high despite alleged long-running misconduct; factional debates over whether to limit punishment or pursue criminal charges reportedly delayed the congress timetable. Bo is believed to be detained or under house arrest; formal charges and a trial timetable have not been announced.
