Iranian military officials warned that Tehran makes no distinction between U.S. and Israeli interests and would retaliate against both if attacked. IRGC naval commander Ali Fadavi said Israel cannot be seen as separate from the United States and threatened U.S. forces in the region. The remarks followed a denied Israeli report of U.S.-Iran talks aimed at keeping Washington out of any future Israel-Iran conflict, and came amid U.S. domestic debate over President Obama’s Iran policy. Iran has demonstrated upgraded weapons and exercises to signal deterrence; Israel views a nuclear-capable Iran as an existential threat while Iran denies weaponization.

U.S. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, General Martin Dempsey, publicly distanced Washington from any Israeli unilateral strike, saying an Israeli attack would likely delay but not destroy Iran’s nuclear program and that he did not want to be complicit. Dempsey argued sanctions and international pressure should be given time, warned that a premature attack could undermine the coalition, and reiterated U.S. reluctance to be drawn into conflict over Iran.

Dempsey also addressed Syria and Afghanistan. On Syria he cautioned that creating humanitarian zones would oblige their protectors to defend them comprehensively (including against missiles), noted U.S. support to neighboring countries and non-lethal aid to rebels, and warned of the risk of Syria becoming a failed state exploited by extremist groups. On Afghanistan he said NATO must help build vetted Afghan forces so combat roles can end by the 2014 target, noting vulnerabilities from rapid force expansion and “green-on-blue” insider attacks. NATO’s Admiral James Stavridis echoed that measurable progress has been made in Afghanistan—reduced terrorist safe havens, improved Afghan forces and sustained international partnership—while acknowledging continued challenges ahead.

Comedian Kevin Hart launched a Hurricane Harvey Relief Challenge on Instagram, urging fellow celebrities to donate and match his $25,000 gift to the American Red Cross to help victims of the storm in Texas. His appeal named peers such as Beyoncé, Jay‑Z, Dwayne Johnson, Chris Rock, Jerry Seinfeld, Dave Chappelle and Justin Timberlake and encouraged public support with messages of solidarity for Houston. Other celebrities responded: Kim Kardashian and her family pledged $500,000 to the Red Cross, Sandra Bullock donated $1 million (noting she owns a home in Austin), and Coldplay performed a one‑off song called “Houston” at their Miami concert as a tribute to the flood‑hit city. Proceeds from these efforts are intended to aid relief and recovery for those left homeless, injured or without power.

Ryan Seacrest has been named the new permanent co-host of ABC’s Live with Kelly and Ryan, joining Kelly Ripa and helping launch a new phase in the morning TV ratings battle. The announcement aired on Monday’s show after Ripa teased the reveal; the pair greeted each other onstage. Seacrest — a high-profile broadcaster and former American Idol host who has guest-hosted Live multiple times during the yearlong search for Michael Strahan’s replacement — will also serve as an executive producer, giving him a role similar to Ripa’s.

Live airs in many markets at 9 a.m., directly against the third hour of NBC’s Today; NBC plans a new 9 a.m. program this fall led by Megyn Kelly, creating fresh competition. Seacrest will relocate from Los Angeles to New York (where Live is based), though he will keep his numerous existing roles, including syndicated radio shows for iHeartMedia and hosting E! red carpet specials. ABC is building a new radio studio in the ABC building for him, and the deal could lead to further partnerships with Disney, ABC’s parent company.

The seat beside Ripa drew many high-profile contenders after Michael Strahan abruptly left Live for Good Morning America; during the interim Ripa had several guest co-hosts, including Andy Cohen and Anderson Cooper. Representatives for Ripa, Seacrest and ABC did not comment before the official announcement.

News Corporation has increased its cash offer to take full control of the 61% of BSkyB it does not already own, raising its bid from 675p to 700p per share (valuing the stake at £7.8bn / $11.5bn). BSkyB’s independent directors again rejected the proposal as significantly undervaluing the company and said regulatory and pre-financing conditions create uncertainty about any formal offer. They said they would consider a proposal above 800p per share.

Despite the impasse on price, both sides agreed to enter talks and a cooperation agreement to pursue the necessary regulatory approvals. News Corp said it would fund a significant portion of the deal from cash reserves (around $8.2bn at end-March) and argued full ownership would diversify revenues away from advertising into subscriptions and expand its global footprint. BSkyB appointed a board committee to handle the possible offer; it is advised by Morgan Stanley and UBS, while News Corp’s advisers are Deutsche Bank and J.P. Morgan Cazenove. BSkyB’s shares jumped about 21% on the news.

Here are concise summaries of the two reports:

1) Trump’s uncomfortable interview with Hugh Hewitt
- Republican front-runner Donald Trump faced a difficult interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, who pressed him on foreign-policy knowledge. Trump appeared flustered and at one point confused “Quds” (the IRGC Quds Force) with the Kurds. He resisted detailed answers on how he would respond if China sank an allied ship, citing the value of unpredictability. When Hewitt asked whether Trump could name regional militant leaders (Nasrallah, Zawahiri, al-Julani, al-Baghdadi) Trump admitted he did not know them all “without a scorecard,” saying many would be “gone” by the time he took office and promising strong military leadership. Hewitt treated the exchange as substantive questioning rather than a “gotcha” attempt; Trump disagreed. Hewitt asked the same lineup of questions to Carly Fiorina, who performed better, recognizing Soleimani and the Quds Force and differentiating groups like Hamas and Hezbollah. Hewitt will pose similar foreign-policy questions at the next Republican debate.

2) NYPD trains media on active-shooter response
- The NYPD held an active-shooter training session for members of the media after a recent live-broadcast newsroom killing. The department stressed that mass shootings now occur frequently and often end before police arrive, leaving a critical 4–9 minute window. Officers urged civilians to follow police directions immediately and emphasized the ABCs of response: Avoid, Barricade, Confront (as last resort). The NYPD is expanding patrol officer training and rescue-task-force concepts that pair officers with EMS and fire personnel. The department recommends businesses and families run drills and directs the public to NYPDshield.org for guidance.

Little Caesars is launching a limited-time Bacon Wrapped Crust DEEP!DEEP! Dish pizza nationally on Feb. 23. The Detroit-style, 8-corner deep-dish pizza features more than 3½ feet of bacon wrapped around the crust, bacon sprinkled on top, and pepperoni; it was developed by the chain’s R&D team and replaces the Soft Pretzel Crust Pizza. Priced at about $12 (plus tax) at participating locations, it will be available by request from 4–8 p.m. through late April. One slice contains roughly 450 calories, 23 g fat, 830 mg sodium and 40 mg cholesterol. Industry analysts say the move taps into America’s ongoing bacon craze and could attract indulgence-seeking customers, though it may add kitchen complexity and may not travel well.

Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, 27, who is suspected of deliberately crashing an Airbus A320 in the French Alps and killing all 150 on board, had a history of significant depression, German media report. Bild and other outlets say Lubitz received psychiatric treatment for a “serious depressive episode” about six years earlier and underwent roughly 18 months of treatment; his aviation file reportedly recommended regular psychological assessments. Lufthansa confirmed his training was interrupted several months during that period but said he was later cleared to resume training and passed all subsequent tests.

French prosecutors, citing cockpit voice recorder data, say Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and initiated a controlled descent, and have offered no motive. Searches of Lubitz’s residences in Germany recovered items including boxes and a computer; investigators reportedly found material indicating mental-health issues, though nothing publicly identified as a suicide note. The crash has prompted airlines to revise cockpit procedures to ensure two crew members are present at all times. Investigations continue, including recovery of the flight-data recorder and examination of Lubitz’s medical and training records.

Researchers have found evidence that excess vitamin B12 can alter the behavior of Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes), a common skin microbe, in ways that may promote acne in some people. Comparing bacteria from acne-prone and clear-skinned individuals, the team observed differences in bacterial gene expression, notably in the pathway that produces vitamin B12. When volunteers received B12 injections, the vitamin suppressed the bacteria’s own B12-synthesis genes and in at least one participant led to a gene-expression shift resembling that seen in acne patients and to a breakout.

Lab experiments showed that adding B12 to P. acnes cultures increased production of porphyrins—compounds that trigger inflammation, a key driver of acne. The proposed mechanism is that excess external B12 causes the bacteria to downregulate their B12 synthesis and switch metabolic activity toward making inflammatory porphyrins, which in some people may contribute to pimples.

The study provides a plausible bacterial pathway linking B12 supplementation to acne but does not prove causation. It involved a small number of human subjects (10 given injections, with one developing pimples) and needs confirmation in larger, controlled trials. Experts caution against stopping B12 supplementation based on this work alone—B12 is essential for nerve function and blood health, and prior studies have shown mixed effects on inflammation. The findings highlight how diet and supplements can affect skin health via changes to resident microbes and may inform future targeted acne therapies.

Airbnb is running a contest offering one overnight stay for two in Paris’ Catacombs on Halloween (Oct. 31). The Catacombs are a public ossuary containing the remains of about six million Parisians. The prize includes access to the subterranean tunnels, a private concert and dinner in the catacombs’ acoustically notable spaces, a storyteller session with scary tales, and the opportunity to spend the night and emerge at dawn. Entrants must apply on Airbnb’s site by telling the host why they’re brave enough to sleep there before the Oct. 20 midnight deadline. Rules require respecting the site (no pets) and the experience is limited to two people.

With less than two weeks until the U.S. presidential election, Donald Trump’s campaign released a targeted TV ad aimed at Indian Americans in which he speaks some Hindi and borrows Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 2014 slogan, “Ab ki baar Modi sarkaar,” swapping in his own name. The ad features footage from a recent Edison, New Jersey, rally where Trump praised Modi and pledged closer U.S.–India ties, and it highlights his tough rhetoric on “radical Islamic terrorism,” showing images such as the 2008 Mumbai Taj Mahal hotel attack.

This outreach is part of broader multilingual campaign efforts (Hillary Clinton has run Spanish and Creole spots), and appears to be the first major Hindi-targeted ad. It is driven in part by the Republican Hindu Coalition and donor-organizer Shalabh Kumar, who has spent millions to support Trump’s engagement with the community. Despite that, polls show Trump far behind Clinton among Indian Americans (one survey cited 7% for Trump vs. 70% for Clinton), and the group represents a small voting bloc nationally.

Reactions in India were largely negative: quick street interviews in Delhi conveyed that many saw the ad as pandering to Hindus, ignoring India’s diversity, and were unconvinced by Trump’s Hindi or his sincerity. Critics called the move ignorant, opportunistic, and inconsistent with his prior rhetoric on immigrants and minorities, and doubted he would be a trustworthy or appropriate U.S. president.

A Las Vegas blackjack dealer who uses the handle @liberallisa has gone public with what RadarOnline says are Facebook messages she exchanged with Rep. Anthony Weiner, part of a broader scandal in which Weiner admitted to engaging in “inappropriate” online conversations with six women but denied meeting any of them or having physical relations. RadarOnline published a September 28 Facebook exchange in which the woman and Weiner trade sexually explicit messages; the dealer is reported to be a Milwaukee native who studied at UW–Milwaukee and has in the past done Democratic campaign work, though Nevada Democrats say they have no record of her volunteering.

Another woman, Meagan Broussard, a 26‑year‑old single mother from Texas, also went public via Andrew Breitbart’s BigGovernment and TV interviews, saying she exchanged dozens of sexually charged photos and messages with Weiner over about a month; Breitbart’s site was where the shirtless photos of Weiner first appeared, prompting his admission.

The controversy has led top Republicans to call for Weiner’s resignation and left most Democrats reluctant to defend him. The story also generated satire: Jon Stewart staged a mock “resignation” on The Daily Show, lampooning himself for not being tougher on Weiner and injuring his hand in the course of an elaborate gag; John Oliver then took over the show’s anchor duties in the bit.

Wells Fargo is facing major fallout after admitting that thousands of employees opened millions of unauthorized customer accounts over several years to meet aggressive sales targets. The bank has fired about 5,300 workers, was fined $185m by regulators, and is under multiple reviews including by the Labor Department and federal prosecutors.

In a public response, Wells Fargo’s board announced clawbacks and other penalties for senior management: CEO John Stumpf will forfeit about $41m in unvested stock awards, receive no salary during an independent investigation and won’t get a 2016 bonus; Carrie Tolstedt, former head of community banking, will forfeit roughly $19m in unvested awards, receive no 2016 bonus and left without severance. The board said further compensation clawbacks or employment actions are possible depending on investigation results.

The scandal has prompted strong political backlash. California dropped Wells Fargo as a bond underwriter for a year, and lawmakers including Senator Elizabeth Warren have demanded resignations and further accountability. Stumpf has apologized and accepted responsibility but has not stepped down; he is due to testify before the House Financial Services Committee. Wells Fargo also pledged to contact customers to verify accounts and to send confirmation emails after new account openings.

The board launched an independent probe into retail practices; meanwhile lawsuits and regulatory scrutiny continue, and the company may face additional penalties or legal action as investigations proceed.

Terry Jones, a fringe Florida pastor who drew global attention by threatening to burn Qur'ans on the ninth anniversary of Sept. 11, may have claimed a deal to relocate a nearby Muslim community center — a claim that appears unfounded — and then announced he was suspending the burn. His stunt became a major story this summer after he repeatedly promoted it in interviews and linked it to wider debates over the proposed “Park 51” center near ground zero, free speech, and religious freedom. International reactions, including protests in Afghanistan and warnings from military leaders, amplified the controversy.

Mainstream U.S. media largely decided not to help stage the event: Fox and CNN said they would not show images of any burning, the Associated Press barred distributing photos, audio or detailed descriptions of the act, and NBC said it would film but not broadcast live. News executives and editors framed these decisions as reasonable restraint — arguing that publishing images would be gratuitous and risked further provocation — and many journalists acknowledged media coverage had inflated Jones’s influence.

The episode highlighted how a marginal figure can exploit the 24-hour news cycle to gain disproportionate attention, and prompted some editorial soul-searching about the media’s role. Other extremist groups (e.g., Westboro Baptist Church) have attempted similar stunts but now attract little coverage, suggesting Qur’an-burning provocations may be losing their shock value and media traction.

This document mixes information about web archiving with excerpts and commentary about fascism and a 2016 Merriam-Webster popularity story.

Key points:

- Alexa Internet has been donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996. Those daily crawls are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo, as part of an effort to preserve pages and the pages they reference so links remain accessible even if originals change or disappear. The Internet Archive aims to reduce broken links (the “No More 404” initiative) and to have archived versions linked as companions or replacements for dead links.

- Several quoted passages illustrate historical and literary reflections on fascism: Anne Applebaum on the polarized propaganda of World War II; Al Gore on early Western reluctance to confront Hitler; and fictional references from John Grisham and a general note about the rise of fascism in pre–World War II Europe.

- A separate, contemporary thread recounts Merriam-Webster’s 2016 “word of the year” dynamics: “fascism” became the dictionary’s most-looked-up word that year. Merriam-Webster’s Twitter account tried to encourage people to look up other words to prevent “fascism” from topping the list, promoting playful alternatives like “flummadiddle” and engaging followers to boost other lookups.

Overall, the document connects internet preservation efforts with historical and current discourse about fascism, and ends with a light social-media anecdote about dictionary lookups in 2016.

Summary:

A wave of drug- and crime-related violence in northern Mexico has escalated into attacks on public officials and citizen vigilantism. In Nuevo León, Mayor Prisciliano Rodriguez of Doctor González (30 miles east of Monterrey) was shot dead by suspected drug gunmen while driving to his ranch; another passenger was also reportedly killed. Rodriguez’s slaying is the fourth public-official murder in just over a month—mayors were also recently killed in Santiago (Nuevo León), Hidalgo (Tamaulipas) and San Luis Potosí—reflecting rising attacks on officials, police and journalists amid a violent struggle between the Gulf cartel and its former enforcers, the Zetas. President Felipe Calderón, who sent tens of thousands of troops and federal police into the drug war in 2006, condemned recent killings and said the surge shows cartels are desperate; nevertheless more than 29,000 people have died since his campaign began and violence around Monterrey has driven away tourism and investment. Monterrey and Nuevo León have seen over 450 drug-related killings this year, and the U.S. advised consulate staff to send their children out of Monterrey.

Separately, in Ascensión, Chihuahua, extreme frustration with chronic kidnappings and perceived inadequate security led about 200–1,000 residents to pursue alleged kidnappers who had taken a 16-year-old girl. The girl was rescued, several suspects were captured by the military, but mobs later seized two teenage suspects, who were beaten, held in a vehicle and died; residents also stormed a military base and city hall. The town’s mayor fired the local police force and requested state and federal help; investigations are ongoing. Locals say persistent kidnappings (about three a week) and extortion have driven them toward forming neighborhood watches and, in some cases, taking justice into their own hands.

Researchers observing Chromodoris reticulata, a thumb-sized red-and-white nudibranch from Pacific coral reefs, report it detaches, sheds and then regenerates its penis repeatedly — a behavior not previously documented. These sea slugs are simultaneous hermaphrodites: during mating each individual donates and receives sperm. In 31 recorded matings, after a brief copulation (seconds to minutes) each slug left its penis behind, then regenerated a new external penis within about 24 hours by uncoiling and differentiating an internal spiral structure. They could do this up to three consecutive times. The penis bears backward-pointing spines, which the authors suggest help displace rival sperm from a partner and make withdrawal difficult, explaining why the organ is discarded. The discarded-and-regrown penis may therefore give a reproductive advantage despite the short-term cost of reduced mating opportunity. The study appears in Biology Letters.

A primetime interview and Amanda Knox’s upcoming memoir, Waiting to Be Heard, have renewed attention on her account of four years in Perugia’s Capanne women’s prison after her 2007 arrest in the Meredith Kercher case. The memoir contains vivid descriptions of prison life and alleges inappropriate behavior by staff—most notably that a male guard made sexual advances and that officials once falsely told her she was HIV positive. It also describes humiliating medical examinations and emotional pressure during interrogations that led her to name Patrick Lumumba.

However, contemporaneous documents and Knox’s own handwritten prison diary, letters to lawyers and state department records paint a more mixed picture and, in some places, contradict the memoir. Her diary repeatedly describes friendly, attentive prison staff, decent facilities (library, TV, private bathroom), supportive embassy visits and upbeat interactions with fellow inmates and children in the facility. In the diary she notes a male guard who “winked” and mentioned her sexuality, and she recounts the false HIV scare there too, but she often presents a calmer perspective than in the memoir. Her letter to lawyers after her arrest also describes having time to write down statements—contrasting with the memoir’s depiction of being hurried or coerced into accusations—and gives a less harrowing account of the medical checks.

Other corroborating sources include testimony from a former fellow inmate who remembered Knox as popular, involved in cultural activities, and employed doing dispensary deliveries, and U.S. embassy consular cables showing multiple visits by high-level diplomats between 2007 and 2009. Italian lawyers and embassy records show no formal complaints by U.S. officials about mistreatment.

The discrepancies between Knox’s later memoir and records from the time—over the nature and severity of harassment, the interrogation and the medical exam—have generated debate over which account is truer. With a retrial ordered by Italy’s Supreme Court and expected to resume in Florence, passages from Waiting to Be Heard are likely to be re-examined in court.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev is set to be formally sentenced to death for his role in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings that killed three people and injured more than 260. At Wednesday’s hearing up to 20 victims will speak, but it is unclear whether the 21-year-old will use the court’s opportunity to address the judge. Defense lawyers have suggested Tsarnaev feels remorse—citing visits from Sister Helen Prejean and a written note—but prosecutors showed video suggesting a lack of remorse. Legal experts say there is little to gain and significant risk in speaking: the judge must impose the jury’s death recommendation, remarks could be perceived as too little or backfire if they justify the attack, and wouldn’t affect the mandatory sentence though a sincere, sustained display of remorse might help a future clemency bid. Many victims and attorneys expect Tsarnaev will remain silent; historically, defendants’ statements at sentencing have ranged from apologetic to defiant.

An actress who says Harvey Weinstein raped her at Sundance two decades ago responded with disbelief and relief to his early-morning arrest, echoing widespread Hollywood reaction to his fall from power.

Separately, eight women told CNN that veteran actor Morgan Freeman, 80, engaged in inappropriate behavior over many years — including unwanted touching and comments about women’s bodies — often during professional settings like press junkets. Several accusers said they didn’t report incidents for fear of losing work. Freeman issued an apology to anyone who felt uncomfortable, saying he never intended to offend or make anyone feel uneasy.

The CNN piece cites past interview footage and first-hand accounts. Author/activist Janet Mock recalled Freeman commenting on her appearance during a 2015 ET interview, calling the encounter an example of men in power treating women’s bodies as theirs. Entertainment reporter Chloe Melas described a 2017 junket incident while pregnant in which Freeman allegedly ogled her and made comments; Warner Bros. HR later said it could not corroborate the account.

The stories are part of a broader reckoning in Hollywood over sexual misconduct by powerful men.

A CDC and Colorado health-department report details the March 2014 death of a 19-year-old Colorado resident after he consumed an entire marijuana edible cookie containing about 65 mg of THC (labeled 6.5 servings). A 23-year-old friend purchased the cookie from a licensed store and was instructed to cut it into six pieces of ~10 mg THC each. After eating one piece and feeling no effect within 30–60 minutes, the man ate the remainder. Over the next few hours he exhibited erratic speech, hostility, incoherence, severe agitation and destructive behavior. About 2.5 hours after consuming the remainder of the cookie, he jumped from a fourth-floor balcony and died of traumatic injuries. Toxicology showed delta-9-THC of 7.2 ng/mL—above Colorado’s 5 ng/mL per se driving limit—and no other drugs or alcohol were detected. The decedent reportedly had no history of substance abuse or mental illness.

The report highlights key issues with THC edibles: oral THC has delayed onset (peak 1–2 hours) and variable absorption, which can lead consumers—especially inexperienced users—to ingest multiple servings before feeling effects, increasing the risk of severe anxiety, psychotic-like symptoms, and dangerous behaviors. In response to similar concerns, Colorado implemented new rules (effective Feb 2015) requiring edibles to contain no more than 10 mg THC per package or to be clearly marked by 10-mg servings and to undergo potency testing. The authors call for improved public health messaging and product labeling to reduce overconsumption risk; this was the first reported Colorado death linked solely to marijuana since recreational legalization.

A woman from Manlius, N.Y., Sally Hootnick, tracked her missing iPad after leaving it on an American Airlines flight that landed at JFK. After leaving messages with the airline’s lost and found, she used MobileMe’s GPS tracking and located the device at a Long Island house. She alerted American Airlines and Port Authority police but felt they did not act. When the device later moved between JFK, Los Angeles and San Francisco—suggesting airline-employee use—she remotely sent messages to the iPad and made it beep every two minutes to harass whoever had it. Only after threatening to contact a consumer protection agency did American Airlines corporate security follow up and a detective speak with her; the Port Authority did not respond to requests for comment. Hootnick has since replaced the iPad and disabled service on the old unit, so she can no longer track it; she believes the device is now unusable to the finder because its serial number is flagged as stolen. American Airlines declined to comment on the ongoing investigation.

An 87-year-old Grand Rapids man, Howard Arthur Klein, was arrested in a late-June prostitution sting near Leonard Street and Broadway Avenue but prosecutors later dropped the charge. Police said the operation targeted a recurring prostitution problem on the West Side and involved undercover female detectives; several people were arrested during two related operations. Klein was cited for solicitation after allegedly approaching a woman he says he thought was someone from his church. Kent County Prosecutor William Forsyth declined to pursue the case, noting Klein’s age, lack of prior criminal history, possible dementia, and the absence of a compelling reason for prosecution. Other arrestees from the stings faced solicitation or related charges.

A 27-year-old Trader Joe’s assistant manager, Melyda Corado, was fatally struck by a bullet fired by Los Angeles police during a shootout with 28-year-old suspect Gene Evin Atkins in Silver Lake on Saturday, LAPD Chief Michel Moore announced. Atkins had allegedly shot his grandmother and a 17-year-old girlfriend at a home, then kidnapped the teen and led police on a roughly 15-minute chase. After crashing his car into a light pole outside the Trader Joe’s on Hyperion Avenue, Atkins ran toward and into the store, firing at officers. Two pursuing LAPD officers returned fire—firing eight rounds—and investigators determined one officer’s round hit Corado as she exited the store near Atkins; she ran back inside and collapsed behind the manager’s desk and later died. About 40 people were in the store; several customers and children were rescued or escaped, some as hostages were released. Atkins held a standoff for hours, surrendered after being shot in the arm, and was taken to a hospital. He faces more than 30 charges, including murder, attempted murder, false imprisonment and felony evading; bail was set at roughly $18.7 million and arraignment was postponed to Aug. 14.

Chief Moore expressed sorrow and defended officers’ actions as defensive given the deadly threat, while community reaction was mixed. The Trader Joe’s remained closed briefly and a memorial grew outside; a GoFundMe for Corado’s funeral raised significant support. The LAPD released dash- and body-camera footage of the pursuit. Several others—including Atkins’ grandmother and girlfriend—were hospitalized, some in critical condition; multiple people were treated at the scene with mostly non-life-threatening injuries.

The annual Canadian UFO Survey, compiled by Winnipeg-based researcher Chris Rutkowski and Ufology Research, found that reported UFO sightings in Canada rose slightly in 2015 to 1,267 cases—the second-highest annual total since the survey began in 1989 (only 2012 was higher, with 1,981 reports). Reports came from coast to coast, with Quebec accounting for an unexpectedly large share (35% of reports) and notable increases in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. Major cities with the most reports were Montreal (97), Toronto (78) and Vancouver (69). The average sighting lasted about 16 minutes.

Most reports describe lights or unusual aerial shapes (orbs, triangles, discs, diamonds) and can be attributed to stars, planets, aircraft, fireballs, drones or other explainable sources. About 12% of reports remained unexplained overall; when restricted to higher-quality cases with corroborating information or investigator follow-up, the unexplained fraction falls to roughly 1–3%. The survey includes several intriguing high-quality unexplained incidents, including a Manitoba October 2015 account of a silent, dark triangular object with colored lights that has not been explained after investigation.

The dataset (1,267 reports in 2015; 16,905 since 1989) was compiled from 17 sources such as Transport Canada, National Defence, the National UFO Reporting Center and public submissions including YouTube. Researchers caution many accounts are anecdotal or poor quality, and they discuss cultural and psychological factors that may influence reporting (increased public interest, media attention, prevalence of cameras and drones). Rutkowski emphasizes ongoing skywatching and investigation but notes there is no proof of extraterrestrial visitation.

The document reviews the 2010 remake The Wolfman (dir. Joe Johnston), surveying multiple critics’ perspectives and comparing it to Universal’s 1930s–40s horror canon—especially Lon Chaney Jr.’s 1941 Wolf Man. Key credits: Benicio Del Toro, Anthony Hopkins, Emily Blunt, Hugo Weaving, Geraldine Chaplin; screenplay by Andrew Kevin Walker and David Self (based on Curt Siodmak); makeup by Rick Baker; music by Danny Elfman.

Main points:
- Premise and setting: Victorian England, 1890s. Lawrence Talbot (Del Toro) returns to his family estate after his brother’s gruesome death, is bitten by a werewolf at a gypsy camp, and becomes the cursed Wolf Man, attacking villagers at each full moon. Supporting roles include Hopkins as Sir John Talbot, Blunt as Gwen, Chaplin as the gypsy Maleva, and Weaving as a Scotland Yard inspector.
- Tone and goals: The film attempts to bridge the atmosphere and gothic storytelling of the original Universal horror classics with modern graphic violence and CGI—retaining period detail and familiar beats while adding explicit gore and digital effects.
- Critical consensus (mixed-to-negative):
  - Many critics feel the remake fails to live up to the original’s iconic status. Del Toro’s performance, in trying to echo Lon Chaney Jr., is judged muted and lacking emotional connection; the human Talbot elicits little empathy.
  - The film’s hybrid approach is uneven: earnest attempts at gothic atmosphere are undercut by gratuitous gore, intrusive CGI, and moments of unintended camp.
  - Rick Baker’s makeup and creature design drew criticism for looking campy or dated in places; some set pieces (notably the climactic werewolf-on-werewolf fight) were compared to comic or low-budget visuals.
  - Supporting cast are underused—Hopkins provides occasional menace but is more plot necessity than character; Blunt is attractive and the film’s most credible human presence but is limited by a thin love-interest role; Weaving’s inspector is peripheral.
  - Production values (cinematography, period sets) and some effective sequences (e.g., moon-transformation/amphitheater scene) are praised, and the film is often described as visually beautiful and moodily shot—but those strengths don’t fully overcome narrative and tonal problems.
- Comparative context: Reviewers place The Wolfman alongside other Universal remakes (Dracula, Frankenstein, The Mummy) and argue it’s largely unnecessary—familiarity with the original didn’t translate into a superior remake. The film’s R-rated violence doesn’t add depth, merely shock value.
- Range of reactions: Some critics were harsher—calling it toothless, muddled, and an unfulfilled promise—while others found it an enjoyable, affectionate throwback with campy pleasures and faithful homage to old-school monster-movie tropes, if not a great film.

Overall takeaway: The 2010 Wolfman is a handsome, well-made period horror with moments of genuine atmosphere and a reverence for the 1941 original, but it is undermined by uneven tone, underwhelming central performance, dated or campy creature effects, and gratuitous gore. It’s generally seen as unnecessary and mediocre by many critics, though a few find it a fun, nostalgic creature feature rather than a total failure.

Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, sharply criticized President Donald Trump’s decision to withdraw the United States from the 2015 nuclear agreement (JCPOA), saying Trump “can’t do a damn thing” and calling his remarks “ludicrous and shallow” and containing “more than 10 lies.” Speaking to teachers in Tehran a day after Trump announced the U.S. would reimpose sanctions, Khamenei warned the U.S. threatened both Iran’s people and its system and insisted Iran would not continue full implementation of the deal unless Britain, France and Germany provided credible, practical guarantees that they could withstand U.S. pressure.

Hardliners welcomed the U.S. exit, with the Revolutionary Guards’ commander praising Washington’s withdrawal as proof the U.S. is not trustworthy, and some hardline MPs staged a dramatic protest in parliament—burning a paper U.S. flag and a copy of the JCPOA while chanting “death to America.” State-aligned papers and conservative commentators framed the move as vindication of long-held anti-U.S. views, bolstering hardliners politically and weakening reformists who supported the deal.

President Hassan Rouhani and others said Iran would try to salvage the agreement if European partners defy U.S. sanctions; Europe’s governments expressed support for keeping the deal. The IAEA had repeatedly verified Iranian compliance, most recently in February. Still, Tehran faces economic and political uncertainty: the rial plunged to record lows, and ordinary Iranians voiced fears about economic hardship, psychological stress, and the potential for increased domestic repression or even conflict. Analysts warned the crisis strengthens hardliners and could undercut moderates’ future influence, including over succession for the aging supreme leader.

International reactions were mixed: European powers, Russia and China expressed regret and a desire to preserve the deal; Israel and Saudi Arabia welcomed the U.S. move. The Trump administration framed the withdrawal as correcting a “one-sided” agreement and signaled plans to reimpose sanctions on key Iranian sectors, while urging a broader deal to address Iran’s missiles and regional behavior. Iran has said it could resume higher-scale uranium enrichment if the JCPOA collapses.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) prepared to vote on strong net neutrality rules after a year-long, highly publicized process sparked by President Obama’s call for tougher protections. Chairman Tom Wheeler’s proposal would reclassify broadband providers as common carriers under Title II of the Communications Act, giving the FCC clearer authority to stop ISPs from blocking, slowing or favoring online traffic (including banning “fast lanes”). The draft rules extend fully to wireless service, a notable shift from 2010 rules and one that mobile carriers say complicates congestion management; the FCC plans to treat practices like zero‑rating on a case‑by‑case basis.

The debate has been deeply polarized. Tech giants (Google, Netflix, Amazon, Facebook), civil‑rights groups and many consumer advocates back the Title II approach as necessary to preserve an open Internet and protect competition and free expression. Major ISPs and many Republicans argue Title II is government overreach that could chill investment, raise prices, and hinder network management; some lawmakers are pushing alternative legislation that bans blocking and paid prioritization without full utility regulation.

More than 3.7–4 million public comments were filed—the largest response ever—and the industry expects court challenges regardless of the vote. Even supporters acknowledge the rules change the regulatory framework more than consumers’ day‑to‑day experience: prices and access likely won’t shift immediately, but the FCC will have stronger jurisdiction to review practices and adjudicate disputes. Ultimately the policy’s final shape and impact will be determined in the courts, Congress and the marketplace.

President Trump announced his support for the bipartisan First Step Act, a major overhaul of federal criminal justice policy that pairs prison-reform measures with sentencing changes. The bill aims to improve prison conditions and re-entry outcomes by requiring Justice Department risk-and-need assessments, expanding time credits for good behavior and participation in job-training and other programs, banning the shackling of pregnant women, and seeking to place inmates closer to home when possible. It would also reduce certain mandatory minimums for nonviolent and drug offenses (including curbing life sentences under “three strikes” for third drug convictions except for serious violent felonies), eliminate “stacking” of gun charges, and retroactively extend parts of the 2010 Fair Sentencing Act to address the crack/powder disparity.

Support for the measure is broad and cross‑partisan: the House passed a prison‑reform-only version earlier, the Fraternal Order of Police and other law‑enforcement groups have signed on after negotiated exceptions (notably excluding some fentanyl offenders from credit eligibility), and public advocates and celebrities have urged action. Key backers inside the White House include Jared Kushner; the recent firing of Attorney General Jeff Sessions and the more open stance of acting AG Matthew Whitaker reduced a major internal block. Opposition persists among some conservative lawmakers and law‑enforcement officials who fear risks to public safety. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has said he will consider bringing the bill to a floor vote if 60 votes can be secured. Proponents say the bill could release some thousands of people serving long sentences, provide relief for elderly and terminally ill inmates, and invest in re‑entry programs.

A 19-year-old UCSB junior, Lucas Ransom, was fatally attacked by a large shark off Surf Beach near Lompoc on the morning of Oct. 22. Ransom and a friend, Matthew Garcia, had been about 100 yards offshore in six-foot surf when the shark surfaced and pulled Ransom under after about 45 minutes in the water. Garcia said Ransom looked at him and called “Help me, dude” before disappearing. Ransom’s parents said his left leg was ripped off at the pelvis; he bled profusely and was pronounced dead at the scene by Vandenberg Air Force Base responders. Witnesses and officials closed Surf Beach and two nearby beaches for at least 72 hours.

Shark experts and wildlife officials said the behavior and the severity of the injury point to a great white, likely 14–20 feet long; great whites commonly attack from below and can mistake surfers or bodyboarders for seals. Authorities noted such fatal attacks are very rare in California. Ransom, described by his mother as a fearless athlete with a “sweet” heart, was a chemical engineering major from Riverside County.

HBO Now, HBO’s standalone streaming service that doesn’t require a cable subscription, launched in April exclusively for Apple devices (iPhone, iPad, Apple TV) and Cablevision Optimum Online customers, with viewing also possible via HBONow.com. It costs $14.99/month and offered a 30-day free trial at launch. The service provides access to HBO’s full catalog of original series (e.g., Game of Thrones, The Sopranos), movies (about 2,000 titles at launch), sports and comedy specials, and lets you add items to a Watchlist.

The Apple TV/iOS apps are essentially HBO Go without the need for a cable login—familiar, straightforward, and functional. Navigation is split into Watchlist, Series, Movies, More, Search, and Settings; playback in early testing was HD and reliable, though the Apple TV interface is plain and can be clunky for browsing compared with iOS devices. Account setup initially experienced some signup glitches for some users.

The terms of service reserve HBO’s right to change limits on simultaneous streams and registered devices and to restrict password sharing; “authorized users” living in the same household can be added, but enforcement details are unclear. HBO hints it may eventually offer exclusive programming for HBO Now, and the service is expected to expand to other platforms (Android, consoles, set-top boxes) over time. For users in Apple’s ecosystem, signing up—especially with the free trial—is an easy way to get HBO without cable.

Donald Trump intensified intra-party tensions by refusing to endorse two senior GOP leaders — House Speaker Paul Ryan and Sen. John McCain — in their upcoming Republican primaries. In a Washington Post interview, Trump said he was “not quite there yet” on endorsing Ryan in Wisconsin and confirmed he had not backed McCain in Arizona, criticizing McCain’s record on veterans’ care. The non-endorsements followed public criticisms from both Ryan and McCain of Trump’s recent attacks on the parents of Army Capt. Humayun Khan — remarks that prompted a strong rebuke from President Obama, who called Trump “unfit to serve.”

Trump praised Ryan’s primary opponent Paul Nehlen’s campaign and thanked Nehlen on Twitter after Nehlen defended Trump’s Khan confrontation; Nehlen has drawn support from figures such as Ann Coulter and Sarah Palin. Ryan’s team denied seeking Trump’s endorsement and expressed confidence in victory. McCain faces a three-way primary; Kelly Ayotte and other GOP senators who criticized Trump were also singled out by him for disloyalty.

The episode highlights deep divisions within the Republican Party weeks after a convention meant to show unity. Trump defended his behavior as justified pushback and blamed the media for bias, said he wants control over general-election debate terms, and threatened to fund super PACs to target Republicans or Democrats in future races if he loses. The dispute has already driven at least one Republican congressman, Richard Hanna, to declare he will vote for Hillary Clinton.

Judge Brett Kavanaugh spent a contentious second day before the Senate Judiciary Committee answering questions on abortion, presidential power, judicial independence and sexual misconduct allegations involving a former mentor.

Abortion: Kavanaugh called Roe v. Wade an “important precedent” that has been repeatedly reaffirmed and described Planned Parenthood v. Casey as “precedent on precedent,” but he declined to preview how he would rule on future cases. Democrats pressed him as advocacy groups warned his confirmation could threaten abortion rights.

Presidential power and investigations: Kavanaugh repeatedly declined to answer hypothetical questions about the president’s powers — including whether a president can pardon himself, trade pardons for silence, or be compelled to respond to a subpoena — saying such issues might come before the court and are inappropriate to decide in the hearing. His past writings, however, have raised questions about his views on whether a sitting president can be criminally prosecuted.

Judicial independence and record: Kavanaugh emphasized judicial independence as the foremost quality of a judge and cited a ruling for a Guantanamo defendant to illustrate impartiality. He said he stopped voting after becoming a federal judge and invoked the “no hints, no forecasts” approach to discussing future cases.

Alex Kozinski and sexual misconduct issues: Kavanaugh described the public allegations against former judge Alex Kozinski — his onetime mentor and colleague — as a “gut punch,” said he was shocked and unaware of the misconduct before it surfaced, and supported efforts to improve harassment reporting and protections in the judiciary. He could not recall receiving offensive emails from Kozinski.

Fact-check and hearing logistics: Senator Dianne Feinstein misstated historical figures about deaths from illegal abortions, conflating the number of illegal procedures with deaths; actual deaths were far lower. The day included protests and arrests, procedural disputes that briefly adjourned the Senate, and public attention from President Trump, who praised Kavanaugh.

Overall context: The hearings were framed by Democrats’ intense scrutiny over Kavanaugh’s potential impact on issues such as abortion, guns and executive power, while Republicans largely signaled support; Kavanaugh’s refusal to answer many hypotheticals followed typical nominee practice but left major questions unresolved as the committee’s deliberations continued.

Marcela Franco, a 26-year-old student who had registered for summer classes at Santa Monica College, died Sunday from wounds sustained during a shooting rampage on Friday, college officials said. Her father, 68-year-old Carlos Navarro Franco, a 22-year groundskeeper at the college, was killed at the scene when a gunman opened fire on their SUV as they were driving on campus to buy textbooks. The college has created the Carlos Franco Family Memorial Fund.

Authorities identified the shooter as 23-year-old John Zawahri, who was killed by police after a confrontation in the college library. Investigators say the violence began shortly before noon at a house that was set on fire, where Zawahri’s father, Samir Zawahri, 55, and brother, Chris, 25, were found dead. Over a roughly 10–13 minute rampage through Santa Monica, Zawahri allegedly carjacked a woman, fired into a public bus (wounding riders), shot multiple people at random, and killed another unidentified woman near the library. Several others were wounded; four others died in total including Carlos and Marcela Franco and two members of the Zawahri family.

Police described Zawahri as heavily armed with high-powered weapons including an AR-15–style rifle and possibly up to 1,300 rounds of ammunition, and wearing a ballistic vest. Law enforcement sources say he had a history of emotional and mental health problems and past contact with police, but investigators have found no links to domestic or international terrorism. The motive remains under investigation. The college plans a campus memorial for the Francos.

Keith Urban and Nicole Kidman keep their romance private and connected despite busy, separated schedules: Urban says they avoid texts and email, preferring phone calls and even sexting while he tours and shoots American Idol in the U.S. and Kidman films in London.

In a Vanity Fair cover interview, Kidman (reflecting on her past marriage to Tom Cruise) says she was very young during that time and values the growth and solitude she experienced afterward. Playing Virginia Woolf in The Hours helped her appreciate life during a difficult period. She describes extreme fame as intoxicating when shared only between partners, but says she no longer seeks that intensity and is often surprised by public recognition—something she must explain to her children.

Now living in Nashville with Urban and their two daughters, Kidman says she doesn’t miss Hollywood’s all-consuming business side and appreciates the quieter, more idiosyncratic life there. Motherhood has strengthened her marriage, providing “glue” that helps them heal and grow together, though she admits struggling to balance family life with her artistic ambitions. Overall she calls her marriage peaceful and deeply connected, even as she navigates tensions between creative desire and protecting her family.

A software error in American Airlines’ pilot schedule-bidding system allowed many pilots to remove holiday flights from their rosters, leaving thousands of December flights without assigned cockpit crews. The Allied Pilots Association (APA) says about 15,000 flights (roughly 19,000 cockpit seats) were initially unstaffed, affecting major hubs including Miami, Dallas–Fort Worth, Chicago O’Hare, LaGuardia and others. American says the glitch has been fixed, reserve pilots are being used, and the carrier is offering pilots 150% of hourly pay (the maximum allowed under the contract) to pick up open trips. The APA has filed a grievance, arguing the carrier’s remedy and how overtime pick‑ups are being allocated violate the union contract and urging crews to be cautious about accepting assignments. American says it is working with the union to resolve the issue and expects to avoid holiday cancellations; the cost impact is unclear. Competitors’ shares rose modestly while American’s stock showed little net change after the reports.

Jacob Brundage, a 39-year-old professional poker player from Lakeland, Florida, said he nearly had a panic attack when he discovered his black tote containing $7,000 in cash and playing chips was missing after an Uber ride June 1 from The Venetian to the Rio for the World Series of Poker. He initially couldn’t reach the driver through the app’s masked-caller feature; after finding Uber staff at the Rio, they helped track down the driver. More than an hour later the driver—whose phone had died—called back, returned to the casino, and handed Brundage the bag intact. Brundage rewarded the driver $200 and gave $100 to the Uber employees who assisted. Uber noted that while riders frequently leave items in cars, this was likely the most valuable item left in a Las Vegas Uber.

Filmmaker Quentin Tarantino joined hundreds of demonstrators in New York on Oct. 24 to protest police brutality, taking part in a Washington Square Park rally and a roughly two-mile march up Sixth Avenue organized by RiseUpOctober. Speakers — including activist Cornel West and organizer Carl Dix — and relatives of people killed by police shared stories and called for justice. Tarantino, who flew in from California, said he felt compelled to speak out against what he called “murder,” acknowledging the rally’s timing was “unfortunate” because it came days after NYPD Officer Randolph Holder was fatally shot while chasing a suspect. The protest remained peaceful and produced no arrests.

The march drew sharp criticism from police and the officer’s family. Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association president Patrick Lynch condemned Tarantino and urged a boycott of his films, calling his remarks slanderous. Holder’s relatives called the demonstration disrespectful, and a retired officer staged a solo march in support of the NYPD. Organizers and participants said the event focused on those killed by police and the need for accountability despite sympathy for the slain officer’s family.

A West Long Branch, New Jersey homeowner, Joe Hornick, was ticketed for flying Donald Trump “Make America Great Again” flags outside his home more than 30 days before the state primary. The borough’s ordinance bans political signs earlier than 30 days before an election and requires removal within five days afterward; borough officials consider flags to be political signs. Hornick has flown two Trump flags since February, says they’ve been torn down repeatedly, and says he will not remove them even if fined or jailed — he faces a municipal hearing where penalties could include a $100–$2,000 fine, up to 90 days in jail, or both.

The ACLU of New Jersey (deputy legal director Jeanne LoCicero) has called the ordinance unconstitutional because it time-limits political speech; the group has won similar challenges in other New Jersey towns. Legal commentary notes that Reed v. Town of Gilbert (2015) and City of Ladue v. Gilleo (1994) establish that content-based restrictions on signs—like singling out political signs—are likely unconstitutional, though governments may impose content-neutral limits (e.g., size). The borough’s attorney had not commented publicly at the time of reporting.

Two men, father and son Flint Wayne Harrison, 51, and Dereck James “D.J.” Harrison, 22, were taken into custody after a day-long manhunt in Sublette County, Wyoming, linked to the alleged kidnapping and assault of a Utah woman and her four daughters (ages 13–18).

According to Centerville, Utah, police, the men allegedly lured the family to a home in Centerville earlier this week for a barbecue, then tied them up with wire and duct tape. As some of the victims tried to escape, they were reportedly struck with a baseball bat; the girls broke free, fled and one called 911. The suspects had already fled by the time officers arrived.

Flint Harrison surrendered to authorities in Sublette County early Saturday and immediately cooperated to help locate his son. Dereck Harrison was found and arrested without incident Saturday night near the Half Moon Lake area northeast of Pinedale after a search that included evacuating a campground and a shelter-in-place order for the town. Deputies said Dereck was found walking about a mile from a roadblock; he was believed to have been armed with two knives, a .300 Winchester Magnum, a .22 Remington rifle and multiple high-capacity magazines, and had made threats against law enforcement. Centerville police said Dereck appeared to have been using methamphetamine heavily and that the motive appears to have been retaliation against the mother.

Both men will be extradited to Utah to face charges. Flint Harrison is registered in Wyoming as a sex offender for an attempted forcible sexual abuse conviction from 2001; it is unclear whether additional Wyoming charges will be filed.

Wheaton College has removed former U.S. House Speaker J. Dennis Hastert’s name from its Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy after he was federally indicted for hiding $3.5 million in payments to a longtime acquaintance and lying to the FBI about suspicious bank withdrawals. Hastert, a 1964 Wheaton graduate who had donated his congressional papers and served on the center’s advisory board, resigned from that board and from several other positions (including roles at CME Group and a law firm) after the indictment. The college re-designated the J. Dennis Hastert Center as the Wheaton College Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy, said the center will continue its mission consistent with the college’s values and ethical standards, and noted it was praying for all involved. Wheaton has not yet decided what to do with Hastert’s donated papers. Separately, plans for a proposed $500,000 statue of Hastert in the Illinois state Capitol were earlier deferred at his request.

Jonathan Brussow, a 19‑year‑old from Rockford, Michigan, died after being swept into the sea by a massive wave while vacationing with his girlfriend’s family on Eleuthera in the Bahamas. Brussow, who had been dating Athena Williams since middle school, had recently asked her family for permission to marry her while on the trip. In the early hours of March 5 he and Athena’s brother, Eric, climbed a cliff near the Glass Window Bridge to talk; a rogue wave struck the pair, sweeping them into the water. Eric survived with serious injuries after clinging to rocks and making it ashore; Brussow was missing.

Family, friends, local residents and authorities mounted an intensive multi‑day search despite stormy conditions. On March 9 searchers recovered Brussow’s body hundreds of yards from the impact site, in a depression that had held surge water. His family described him as adventurous and loving—nicknamed “Stormy”—and expressed gratitude for the Bahamians who helped in the search.

The families have shifted a GoFundMe originally aimed at finding him alive toward covering repatriation expenses, reimbursing search costs, and funding safety improvements near the Glass Window Bridge (including warning signs and rescue gear) and medical equipment for the local hospital. Williams, devastated but thankful for local support, said she and Brussow had planned a life together and hope to honor him by helping the island community that aided them.

Rochester-area Assemblyman Bill Nojay, a 59-year-old conservative Republican first elected in 2012, apparently died by suicide Friday morning at Riverside Cemetery after an officer responding to a welfare check saw him shoot himself. Colleagues described the outspoken lawmaker as a staunch defender of conservative, pro–Second Amendment positions and a frequent critic of both Democrats and establishment Republicans. He served as an election attorney for GOP leader Brian Kolb, co-chaired Donald Trump’s New York campaign committee, hosted a conservative radio show, and was active on issues such as opposing New York’s SAFE Act.

News reports tied his death to mounting legal troubles. The Rochester Democrat & Chronicle said Nojay failed to appear in court to turn himself in on charges alleging he embezzled $1.8 million from a legal client; federal agents had also been probing his involvement in a business linked to Rochester’s school modernization program. Separately, Cambodian prosecutors had pursued fraud allegations since 2014 from a dentist who accused him of misappropriating $1 million tied to an agricultural-marketing company (Akra Group) he helped start. Nojay had downplayed the Cambodia matter and other overseas ventures, but they had drawn scrutiny and subpoenas.

His primary and general-election challengers suspended campaigns following his death. Colleagues expressed shock and noted his combative, unapologetic style in Albany; investigators gave no public explanation for what drove him to take his life.
