Bloomberg News reporters used internal Bloomberg Terminal functions to view subscriber usage data — such as who at a firm was logged in, when they last logged on, which terminal functions they used and frequency of use — by employing a “Z function” to list subscribers and a UUID function to view individual background and activity. While the terminals never showed specific securities or trades, the usage hints could reveal Wall Street thinking and proved valuable for reporters. The practice, first publicized after a New York Post report about Goldman Sachs, was found in a preliminary Bloomberg analysis to have been used by “several hundred” reporters; Bloomberg has about 2,400 journalists worldwide.

Goldman Sachs complained after a reporter phoned an employee noting a partner’s lack of terminal activity; Bloomberg disabled the newsroom’s access to those functions and said it changed policies so reporters now see only the same customer-relationship data as clients. Bloomberg executives, including editor-in-chief Matt Winkler and CEO Daniel Doctoroff, apologized and emphasized client trust; the company also created a client data compliance officer role and centralized data security.

The issue prompted scrutiny beyond banks: Federal Reserve regulators are examining whether Fed employees were tracked, and former Bloomberg staff recalled browsing senior officials’ usage data. Bloomberg denied some reports and declined to detail investigations. Competitor Thomson Reuters highlighted its separation of editorial and customer data. Media accounts and insiders say the capability was used in multiple stories (including at JPMorgan during its trading losses) though there is no public evidence that the data were used to access specific trades or included in published reporting.

President Trump currently says he has confidence in Veterans Affairs Secretary David Shulkin “at this point in time,” White House deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley told Fox News, while acknowledging the president can replace anyone at will. Gidley and deputy Raj Shah declined to discuss personnel plans; Shah said there would be “no personnel announcements.” Gidley stressed Trump wants the “right people” in place and can act whether or not a replacement is ready.

Despite that public show of support, multiple reports from CNN and the AP say Trump has told associates he is preparing to remove Shulkin and that the White House is vetting possible successors. The ouster could be announced as soon as this week, though no decision is final until made public. Shulkin has faced internal rebellion at the VA and damaging watchdog inquiries: a February inspector general report found improper acceptance of Wimbledon tickets and doctored emails to justify his wife's travel on the taxpayer dime, and another probe is examining alleged misuse of his security detail. He has denied wrongdoing and blamed internal political appointees for undermining his efforts.

Potential replacements under consideration include Pete Hegseth, former Rep. Jeff Miller, retired Lt. Gen. Keith Kellogg, Michael Kussman, Toby Cosgrove and Leo Mackay Jr. If Shulkin departs, Deputy Secretary Tom Bowman would serve as acting head until a Senate-confirmed nominee is in place.

A Southwest Airlines flight from Seattle to Dallas returned to Seattle after crew realized a “life‑critical” shipment — a donated human heart or heart tissue — had been left on board. The heart had arrived in Seattle earlier from Sacramento and was supposed to be unloaded; the pilot announced the turnback while over Idaho. Southwest said the decision to return was made to deliver the shipment within the required time window. Passengers reacted with shock and concern because of transplant time limits; some researched viability online.

Initial reports left details unclear (whether it was a whole heart, its exact destination, and whether anyone’s life was at risk). Regional organ-procurement organizations said they typically use private flights for whole‑heart transplants and do not use commercial carriers for such operations. Subsequent reporting clarified the shipment was tissue—heart valves—sent by Sierra Donor Services to LifeNet Health in Seattle for processing; tissue has a much longer allowable transport/storage window than a whole organ (processed donated valves can be stored for years). The tissue traveled in a temperature‑controlled cargo box and was left behind like other checked cargo while a courier waited in Seattle. Sierra Donor Services and LifeNet said the donation process was not compromised and the tissue ultimately reached its destination on time.

The plane landed after about three hours airborne, the cargo was unloaded, passengers deplaned during a further delay for an unrelated mechanical issue, and the flight departed for Dallas about five hours later. Passengers and a doctor on board called the incident “gross negligence,” though officials maintain the shipment was recovered without harming the donation.

ABC News reporter Sheila Marikar covered an incident in which Sarah Palin, while visiting Paul Revere’s house in Boston, offered a confused and incorrect version of Revere’s famed midnight ride. Palin said Revere “warned the British” by “ringing those bells” as he rode through town to send “warning shots and bells” so Americans “were gonna be secure… and we were gonna be armed.” Marikar and others note this contradicts the historical record: Revere’s mission was a covert effort to warn colonial leaders like John Hancock and Samuel Adams of the approaching British, not to alert the British or use bells. The report highlights Palin’s misstatement and the factual inaccuracies in her account.

Security firm Trend Micro says the hacker groups known as Pawn Storm, Fancy Bear and APT28—believed by U.S. intelligence and many experts to be linked to Russian espionage—used phishing tactics similar to those employed in the DNC breach to target Emmanuel Macron’s presidential campaign and German political foundations.

Key findings:
- Trend Micro discovered multiple fake domains created to mimic Macron’s En Marche! campaign and services (examples: onedrive-en-marche.fr, mail-en-marche.fr), intended to trick staff into giving up credentials.
- The firm identified related attacks on German groups linked to major parties (Konrad Adenauer Stiftung for the CDU and Friedrich Ebert Stiftung for the SPD). Germany faces federal elections in 2017.
- Fancy Bear typically uses phishing as an entry point and deploys bespoke malware (X-Agent). Trend Micro has tracked many reused command-and-control servers for the group; their unusually long-lived and increasingly numerous servers suggest the group operates loudly and persistently rather than stealthily.
- Trend Micro could not confirm whether any Macron staffers actually fell for the lures or whether data was exfiltrated. Macron’s digital campaign manager, Mounir Mahjoubi, confirmed attempted hacks but said they were unsuccessful and that staff are trained to report such attempts. No supporter data was reported compromised.
- The report raises concerns that the same playbook used in attacks on U.S. political targets may be applied to influence European elections. Russian President Vladimir Putin has denied interest in interfering in France’s vote.

Federal and industry officials are considering controlled burns of an expanding oil slick in the Gulf of Mexico after a drilling rig explosion and sinking left a deepwater well leaking roughly 42,000 gallons a day about 50 miles off Louisiana. The spill has spread into an area roughly 42 by 80 miles and moved to within about 20 miles of the Mississippi River Delta, putting fragile marshes and important coastal wetlands at risk. Officials said winds may keep the slick offshore for about three days but could shift and push oil ashore thereafter.

Federal, state and industry responders (Coast Guard, NOAA, BP and Transocean) have deployed nearly 50 vessels, pre-positioned booms along sensitive shoreline areas and established five staging sites from Venice, LA to Pensacola, FL. Controlled burning using fire-resistant booms is being weighed because it can remove 50–95% of surface oil and may reduce shoreline impacts—though it produces a heavy smoke plume and leaves waxy residue that must be skimmed or will sink. Any burn would be daytime, offshore, and limited to protect land visibility and safety; no final decision had been made.

Attempts to stop the leak are ongoing but so far unsuccessful. Teams are using remote-controlled submersibles to try to operate the blowout preventer on the wellhead about 5,000 feet down, and BP is preparing a large dome to capture oil (a method not previously used at this depth) and has permits for drilling a relief well—a months-long remedy. The rig’s wreckage lies nearby and 11 workers remain missing and presumed dead after the explosion; 115 others survived.

The incident has sparked expanded federal investigations with subpoena power into possible criminal or civil violations by the rig operator and related companies. Officials warn the spill could have serious ecological and political consequences if oil reaches Louisiana and Mississippi shores.

A small funk band, Vulfpeck, released Sleepify — an album of 10 silent tracks — as a deliberate business experiment to generate streaming royalties while fans sleep-stream the “songs.” The stunt is less a musical statement than a creative workaround to low streaming payouts: with roughly 1.1 million plays, Sleepify earned an estimated $6,700–$9,400 from Spotify, money the band plans to use for touring. The move also drove listeners back to the band’s real music and drew a wry response from Spotify, which called the idea “clever” while noting its similarity to John Cage’s 4’33”.

The article places Sleepify in a broader context of distributed computing and digital-era gaming of attention: legitimate crowd-computing projects exist, and so do frauds that use bots to inflate ad or play counts. While bot-driven streaming could in theory boost payouts, practical and technical barriers exist (Spotify limits concurrent plays per account), and Spotify’s payout system — it distributes about 70% of revenue proportionally based on total plays — means gaming would divert money from other artists as well. Overall, Sleepify is framed as an ingenious publicity stunt and commentary on how music is valued in the streaming age.

Former White House executive chef Walter Scheib, 61, was found dead late Sunday in the mountains near Taos, New Mexico, authorities said. Scheib, who moved to New Mexico recently, was reported missing after setting out alone on a hike June 13 near the Taos Ski Valley; his girlfriend reported him missing the next day and his vehicle was located at the Yerba Canyon trailhead on June 16. Search teams including ground crews, aircraft, National Guard members and dogs had been combing rugged terrain that reaches above 12,000 feet; police said rescue workers found his body about 1.7 miles from the base of the Yerba Canyon Trail but provided no cause of death or further details.

Scheib served as White House executive chef for 11 years (1994–2005) under Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush after being hired by then–First Lady Hillary Clinton. He later ran a private chef business and co‑authored White House Chef: Eleven Years, Two Presidents, One Kitchen. Authorities continue to gather information about the circumstances of his death.

This collection of pieces examines the political and legal fallout from the 2010 Supreme Court decision Citizens United v. FEC, which granted corporations broad First Amendment free-speech rights and helped enable unlimited political spending by outside groups—most visibly through “super PACs.” The 2012 Iowa caucuses provided the first major presidential test of that new environment, as super PAC ad spending—most notably Restore Our Future backing Mitt Romney—played a decisive role in reshaping the Republican contest and damaging Newt Gingrich’s campaign.

Observers note ironies and consequences: several Republican figures (including Gingrich) who once praised the Citizens United reasoning found themselves hurting from pro-Romney outside spending, yet many conservatives publicly remain committed to the decision as a free-speech victory. Analysts and former officials warn that super PACs have altered campaign dynamics (massive, often negative ad buys, coordination gray areas, and opaque funding disclosures) and create risks for nominees who may be “defined” or undermined by allied outside groups.

Legal pushback is emerging in some states. The Montana Supreme Court upheld a long-standing state ban on corporate election spending, arguing Montana’s unique history of corporate domination justifies stricter limits and rejecting the national implication of Citizens United in that context. Montana’s ruling emphasized corruption risks and the need for transparency; dissenters warned the U.S. Supreme Court is likely to reverse it. Commentators criticized the Citizens United majority—especially Justice Kennedy’s claim that independent corporate expenditures don’t create corruption—and highlighted practical problems: apparent coordination between campaigns and super PACs and the ease with which donors can shield their identities.

Overall, the pieces portray a nation wrestling with the effects of deregulated campaign spending: immediate electoral impacts in Iowa, legal challenges at state levels, growing calls (including from Bernie Sanders and reform advocates) for constitutional or statutory fixes, and intensifying debate over whether corporate political spending undermines democracy and transparency.

Two-time Oscar winner Tom Hanks served on a Los Angeles jury in a misdemeanor domestic assault case last week. The defendant faced up to a year in jail; closing arguments were imminent when prosecutors disclosed that a lawyer from the City Attorney’s Office had spoken with Hanks outside the courtroom to thank him for his service. Defense attorney Andrew Flier moved for a mistrial, citing prosecutorial misconduct. At a hearing the next morning, both sides agreed to resolve the case with a reduced charge—disturbing the peace—and a $150 fine.

City Attorney’s Office spokesperson Frank Mateljan confirmed the outside interaction and said the office will review the matter. CNN sought comment from Hanks’ representatives but received none. Flier said he had initially been concerned Hanks’ celebrity could influence the jury but found him to seem fair during voir dire; Hanks was attentive on the bench and cordial with other jurors and members of the public outside the courthouse. The alleged victim’s reaction was not available, and prosecutors do not identify domestic violence claimants.

Jane Fonda’s life and career—profiled in Susan Lacy’s HBO documentary Jane Fonda in Five Acts—has been marked by reinvention, controversy, tragedy and activism played out in the public eye. A focal point remains her 1972 trip to Hanoi during the Vietnam War, when photos of her sitting on a North Vietnamese anti‑aircraft gun sparked decades of outrage and the enduring nickname “Hanoi Jane.” Fonda has repeatedly said the image was a grave mistake and a lapse of judgment; she has expressed regret for that specific act while defending her decision to go to Vietnam and the lessons she learned there. On The Late Show with Stephen Colbert she reiterated that she knew the moment was wrong but does not regret the visit itself. The episode and other coverage note how the photo overshadowed her long history of antiwar work, her continued activism (including participation in the Women’s March), and how the incident has continued to provoke veterans and critics even decades later. The reporting also recalls Nixon-era efforts to silence her and includes Fonda’s own reflections that she may have been set up for the photograph.

This document collects multiple posts and news items about two-year-old Rumer (Rumer Rose) Maujean, who was diagnosed with an aggressive neuroblastoma (an 11 cm tumour on her adrenal gland) in December 2014. Her parents, Sacha Maujean (a sole parent in one account) and Adam Koessler (in other entries), describe urgent tests and transfer to Brisbane’s Lady Cilento Children’s Hospital for treatment. Rumer’s cancer was staged as advanced (stage 3 in one post, stage 4 mentioned in another account) and her prognosis was described as serious (a cited 50% chance of recovery in one post). She began chemotherapy aimed at shrinking the tumour, with treatment and a lengthy hospital stay (up to around two years) separating the family from their home in Cairns.

The posts ask for community and online support—financial donations via GoFundMe pages and emotional backing—because the family faces accommodation, travel and living costs while one parent gives full-time care and has left work. Local media reported more than $8,000 raised so far and a fundraising goal around $20,000 to cover expenses. Additional material in the document advocates for decriminalising medicinal cannabis in Australia and recounts a related legal case in which a father (Adam Koessler in some entries) was arrested for administering cannabis oil to his child; that text argues for parental rights and broader access to medical cannabis as a complementary therapy. Links to the GoFundMe pages and a Facebook progress page are provided for donations and updates.

CNN suffered a severe ratings collapse in Q2 2012, recording its worst quarter in primetime since 1991 and its weakest Total Day numbers in over a decade. Primetime averages fell to about 446,000 total viewers and 129,000 adults 25–54 (down roughly 35% and 41% year‑over‑year). Daytime averaged 319,000 total and 95,000 in 25–54, also steep declines. CNN’s prime‑time lineup saw especially large drops: Piers Morgan Tonight, Anderson Cooper 360 (both airings), Erin Burnett OutFront and Wolf Blitzer’s programs all lost large shares of total viewers and the key 25–54 demo. For example, Piers Morgan’s 9 p.m. was down about 32% in the demo to ~137,000 — the worst quarterly 9 p.m. performance in CNN history.

All three cable news networks declined in the demo that matters to advertisers, but CNN’s losses were far larger than Fox News (down ~14% in 25–54) and MSNBC (down ~18%). In total viewers Fox remained far ahead (about 1.79–2.14 million in primetime depending on the report), while CNN averaged roughly 470,000 total viewers in some reports and was only a fraction of Fox’s audience.

CNN attributes much of the drop to a quieter news quarter compared with Q2 2011 (which included events such as Osama bin Laden’s death and the Royal Wedding) and says its ratings reflect the news environment; the network also emphasizes a commitment to nonpartisan journalism over opinion-driven programming. Critics and some insiders argue CNN faces an identity crisis: competitors have boosted audiences with personality- and opinion-driven shows, a direction CNN has largely resisted.

There were modest signs of recovery in June 2012: month‑over‑May gains in Total Day and weekday primetime, with individual shows showing small month-to-month increases (Burnett, Cooper and Morgan all up to varying degrees). Nevertheless, the quarter’s results intensified concerns about CNN’s strategy and long‑term relevance in a cable-news landscape that increasingly rewards opinionated, personality-led programming.

About 15 armed men ambushed two vans carrying jewelry on the A6 motorway (Paris–Lyon) in central France in the early hours of March 11, forcing the drivers out unharmed and fleeing with an estimated haul (reported in some accounts as about €9 million). The attackers abandoned and set fire to the two vans near a toll exit in the Burgundy region; forensic teams later examined the charred vehicles amid nearby vineyards. No shots were fired and no injuries were reported. Police, including gendarmes, searched the area and have handed the case to the unit that investigates organized crime, but the thieves and the jewels remain at large.

Authorities noted the robbery resembles earlier high-profile jewelry heists in France — including those attributed to the so-called Pink Panther gang — and comes amid a series of spectacular thefts over the past decade (notably the 2007–2008 Harry Winston double heist and other Cannes and Paris robberies). Investigators describe the culprits as well-equipped, “battle-hardened” organized-crime figures; inquiries are ongoing.

A student at Butler High School in Matthews, North Carolina, was shot and killed Monday morning after a fight in a crowded hallway as students were arriving for the day. A school resource officer quickly arrested a male student suspected of firing the fatal shot; authorities recovered the weapon and describe the incident as isolated. The victim, also male, died at a hospital. Surveillance video showed the shooting occurred during a fight between the two students. The school — about 2,000 students — was placed on lockdown for roughly two hours; counselors were made available and classes resumed for those who stayed on campus after families were allowed to pick up students. Dozens of parents gathered outside during the lockdown, and many students were seen leaving crying and hugging relatives. Officials have not released names or ages and are reviewing security procedures.

Andy Roddick announced on his 30th birthday that he will retire from professional tennis after the 2012 US Open. Speaking to reporters at Flushing Meadows, he said injuries and waning ability to commit physically and emotionally led him to the decision — he didn’t want to “disrespect the game by coasting home.” The announcement came after he had considered the idea since Wimbledon and following a first-round win over Rhyne Williams; he was set to face Bernard Tomic in the second round.

Roddick finishes a career with a 610–212 record, 32 singles titles, more than $20 million in prize money, a 2003 US Open title (the last Grand Slam won by a North American man), four other major finals, year-end No. 1 in 2003, a 2007 Davis Cup championship, nine straight years in the top 10 (2001–2009) and 12 consecutive seasons with at least one ATP title. Praised for his competitiveness, work ethic and honesty, he served as the face of American men’s tennis, mentored younger players, and plans to focus on his foundation, media work and family after retirement — while still expecting to play tennis for enjoyment.

A government shutdown began after Congress failed to agree on a short-term funding bill tied to efforts by House Republicans to delay or defund the Affordable Care Act. The impasse forced implementation of agency contingency plans, furloughing roughly 800,000 federal employees and halting many nonessential services while legally required functions—national security, protection of life and property, benefit payments, and similar excepted activities—continued.

Key impacts and operational details
- Scope: About 800,000 federal workers faced furloughs out of more than 2 million employees; many excepted employees (e.g., air-traffic controllers, prison guards, Border Patrol agents, military personnel) remained on duty but could see pay delayed. The U.S. Postal Service and programs funded outside annual appropriations (Social Security, Medicare, most federal retirement payments) continued.
- Agency effects: Massive reductions at NASA (only ~549 of ~18,250 staff continued), the National Park Service (all sites closed), Smithsonian museums and the National Zoo (panda cam and exhibits dark), the FDA and EPA (large furloughs), the Defense Department (400,000 civilian employees furloughed, troops continued to serve), State Department consular work curtailed (visa/passport delays), SBA, FHFA, USDA loan and guarantee processing slowed or stopped, and many research and regulatory activities suspended.
- Public services: Veterans’ benefit payments and some VA programs could be affected within weeks; WIC payments and certain welfare grants faced immediate interruptions unless states stepped in; routine food inspections, safety inspections, and infectious-disease surveillance would be curtailed; processing of FOIA requests and many customer hotlines (IRS, others) were closed.
- Contractors: Contractor work depended on contract terms and agency decisions; historically contractors have not been reimbursed for lost revenue during shutdowns.
- Pay and benefits: Excepted employees are legally entitled to pay for work performed once appropriations are restored, but paychecks could be delayed. OPM guidance preserved health and life insurance coverage (employee shares may accrue) but required cancellation of scheduled leave during furloughs. Congress has in past reimbursed furloughed workers, but that was uncertain given the political climate.
- How shutdowns are managed: Agencies followed OMB guidance and updated contingency plans; managers notified employees who must report. Excepted functions—national security, benefit payments, and protection of life/property—continued. Shutdowns end only when Congress enacts funding.

Political context and dynamics
- The shutdown arose from a partisan fight centered on the Affordable Care Act. The House repeatedly passed stopgap measures that included provisions to delay the individual mandate and strip congressional staff subsidies; the Democratic-led Senate rejected those additions and passed a “clean” continuing resolution, which the House refused to accept.
- Leaders traded blame: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and others warned that Republicans would be held responsible; Speaker John Boehner defended his conference’s demands as fairness. Divisions existed within the GOP—some moderates urged a clean bill to avoid shutdown consequences.
- A looming debt-ceiling deadline raised the stakes: lawmakers warned the budget fight could merge into even more damaging fights over the nation’s borrowing authority if the shutdown persisted.

Practical consequences and timelines
- Employees were given brief windows to secure workspaces before leaving and were legally barred from working while furloughed. Agencies provided Q&A guidance on status, pay, benefits, and procedures.
- Some programs funded outside annual appropriations (military pay after an emergency measure, Social Security, federal retiree annuities) continued; other services and payments could be delayed within days to weeks depending on cash reserves and program funding structure.
- The shutdown’s economic and public-service effects were immediate for many communities—tourism businesses near parks, small businesses reliant on agency loans, and individuals awaiting critical services faced disruptions.

Overall, the shutdown produced broad, immediate interruptions across federal programs and workplaces, with long-term effects dependent on its duration and whether Congress later votes to reimburse furloughed employees or restore interrupted programs. Political fractures—within and between parties—shaped both the onset of the shutdown and prospects for a quick resolution.

A powerful late-December storm system spawned multiple tornadoes across the South and Midwest on Dec. 31, 2010–Jan. 1, killing at least seven people, injuring dozens and leaving widespread damage from Arkansas and Missouri to parts of Illinois and Mississippi.

Key impacts
- Fatalities: Six people died on Friday — three in northwestern Arkansas (Gerald Wilson, 88; Mamie Wilson, 78; and 78-year-old Dick Murray) and three in Missouri (including 21-year-old Megan Ross and her 64-year-old grandmother Loretta Anderson). A seventh storm victim died Saturday in a Columbia, Mo., hospital. These were the first U.S. tornado deaths since mid-September and the first in Missouri this year.
- Serious damage: Tornadoes and severe winds demolished homes and trailers, scattered debris long distances (frames and appliances found hundreds of yards away), and demolished about a dozen homes at Fort Leonard Wood where winds were estimated 136–165 mph. Mobile homes were especially hard hit in rural areas near Rolla and Lecoma, Mo., and in the tiny Arkansas hamlet of Cincinnati.
- Injuries and displacement: Dozens were injured (some hospitalized), many were left homeless, and communities spent New Year’s Day cleaning up. Reports described scenes of devastation in Sunset Hills and other St. Louis County areas, Petersburg, Ill., and along Table Rock Lake where docks and boats were damaged.
- Conditions and outlook: The outbreak was fueled by unusually warm, moisture-rich Gulf air ahead of a sharp cold front, producing instability unusual for winter. Tornado watches were issued into Saturday for parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Louisiana; flash flooding and additional storm damage were reported in Alabama and central Mississippi.

Human stories
- Residents recounted dramatic escapes: Chris Sisemore of Cincinnati, Ark., said a twister lifted him out of his house and carried him across the road; he survived with only bumps and bruises. Other survivors and volunteers sifted through debris, searching for belongings and coping with loss.

Weather context
- Though most U.S. tornadoes occur in spring, winter outbreaks are not unprecedented (notable examples in 1999 and 2008). Meteorologists noted links between large-scale oceanic patterns and jet-stream shifts that can increase severe weather risk in the central U.S.

Officials continued damage assessments and recovery efforts as the system pushed eastward. Associated Press reporters contributed to the coverage.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid named Democratic Sens. Patty Murray (WA), Max Baucus (MT) and John Kerry (MA) as his three appointees to the 12-member "super committee" created under the recent debt-limit agreement to identify more than $1 trillion in deficit reductions by year-end. Murray will serve as one of the committee’s co-chairs; the House Speaker will name the other co-chair and two House members, while House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell will each pick three members.

Reid described the panel’s mission as producing a balanced, bipartisan deficit plan and said his picks have budget expertise and bipartisan experience. Murray (a senior appropriator, Budget Committee member and chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee), Baucus (Finance Committee chair) and Kerry (2004 presidential nominee) issued a joint statement committing to pragmatic, bipartisan work.

Republicans criticized Murray’s appointment as politically motivated because of her role in Democratic fundraising; RNC Chair Reince Priebus called for her removal. Democratic leaders emphasized the need for members who will defend revenue measures and protect entitlement programs if Republicans refuse to consider new taxes. Pelosi told her caucus she will aim to protect Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security and urged public deliberations by the panel. 

(Additional unrelated material about a large web crawl dataset and its parameters was included in the document but is not directly connected to the super committee story.)

The Chronicle of Higher Education analyzed federal graduation-rate data for more than 1,000 four‑year U.S. colleges (research, master's, and baccalaureate arts & sciences institutions) to compare six‑year bachelor’s completion rates for cohorts entering in 1996 (reported as the six‑year period ending 2002) and 2002 (ending 2008). Key points:

- Top performers: Harvard led all research universities with a 98% six‑year graduation rate for the 2002 cohort. Yale (97%) and Notre Dame (96%) followed. Among public research universities, the University of Virginia topped the list at 93%, with William & Mary and UC‑Berkeley close behind.
- Overall trends: About one‑third of institutions (33%) had lower graduation rates in 2008 than in 2003. The Chronicle noted the recession as a likely contributor to falling rates and also cited the possibility that some students are taking longer than six years to finish.
- Method and caveats: Rates reflect first‑time, full‑time students seeking bachelor’s degrees who graduated within six years, and can omit sizable groups (e.g., part‑time students). To smooth year‑to‑year spikes the analysis also compared averages of 2001–02 vs. 2007–08. Small cohort sizes at some institutions (e.g., Golden Gate, Alliant International) can produce large swings in reported rates. The Chronicle also flagged schools whose admissions selectivity changed (per Barron’s tiers), since greater selectivity tends to raise graduation rates.
- Details and lists: The report includes sortable tables by institution type, lists of the 12 highest‑ and lowest‑graduating institutions, and a full searchable dataset showing year‑by‑year rates and changes in averaged rates and selectivity for each school.

Bottom line: Many top private and public research universities show very high six‑year graduation rates, but a significant minority of colleges experienced declines between the early 2000s and 2008; methodological limits (definition of cohorts, small sample sizes at some schools, changing selectivity, and longer time‑to‑degree) complicate interpretation.

Interviews Before Execution was a weekly Henan Legal Channel talk show (launched 18 November 2006) in which reporter Ding Yu interviewed convicted murderers on death row, sometimes hours or days before their executions. The programme—aimed at deterring crime and urging viewers to “perceive the value of life”—was regionally very popular, drawing about 40 million viewers in a province of 100 million and running for just over five years before being abruptly canceled this week by the station for “internal problems.”

Format and content
- Ding and her team selected cases from court reports, with prisoners chosen in consultation with the Henan high court; the show never covered political prisoners or contested convictions.
- It focused on violent murder cases—many motivated by money—and featured over 200 interviews. Ding sometimes conveyed final messages to victims’ families and at times expressed no sympathy for the condemned, arguing they deserved punishment.
- The programme produced high-profile episodes (including a multi-part series on Bao Ronting, an openly gay man who murdered his mother) and showed emotional encounters such as a mother’s reunion with her child when a death sentence was suspended.

Context and controversy
- The series has prompted international coverage and a documentary (Dead Men Talking) picked up by the BBC and PBS International. Critics view the format as exploitative; Ding and producers defended it as giving prisoners a final chance to speak and serving as a public warning.
- China’s criminal justice context is relevant: 55 crimes carry the death penalty (though the exact number of executions is state secret and estimated to be the world’s highest). Confessions sometimes occur before suspects see lawyers, and executions are carried out by a gunshot to the head or lethal injection.
- Legal reforms are mentioned: since 2007 all death sentences must be reviewed by the Supreme Court, and some judges involved with the show have publicly expressed hopes to reduce or eventually abolish capital punishment, citing its violence.

Cancellation
- The show was taken off air after recent international attention; the station plans a different legal affairs programme in its place. Ding’s interviews and the behind-the-scenes documentary have sparked renewed debate about media ethics, the death penalty in China, and the human impact on both inmates and journalists who document their final hours.

Vint Cerf, a founding Internet pioneer and Google vice president, warned at the AAAS annual meeting that relying chiefly on digital storage risks creating a "digital Dark Age" that future archaeologists and historians will struggle to interpret. Over centuries, files can vanish, become unreadable, or be tied to obsolete software and operating systems, leaving large gaps much as the post‑Roman written record does today. Cerf urged planning for long‑term preservation—especially for photographs and legal documents—and suggested practical steps such as keeping physical copies of important images. He highlighted a proposed approach called "digital vellum," being explored at Carnegie Mellon, which records a full snapshot of the environment (software, OS and processes) needed to reproduce a digital object later. Cerf argued that even apparently mundane digital items can gain historical importance, so failure to preserve them could permanently erase context and perspective.

Google’s new social network Google+, launched in late June, appears to be losing early momentum in the U.S., Experian Hitwise data shows. For the week ended July 23, U.S. visits to Google+ fell about 3% to 1.79 million (after a 283% jump the prior week) and average time on site dropped about 10% to 5 minutes 15 seconds. Experian’s measurements exclude mobile and third‑party app traffic.

Google announced it had topped 10 million users in mid‑July. Early enthusiasm—driven by novelty and features like Hangouts and Circles—helped initial signups, but usage and referral traffic are slipping as the “new car smell” fades. Critics and some users report stale content, limited sharing, and friction around maintaining Circles. Google’s integrated toolbar may help retention short‑term, but sustaining engagement and retention remains the critical challenge as Google moves into the next phase of Google+.

Two former Hard Rock Café servers at the Universal Studios location in Orlando, Christopher Grant and Benjamin Aguda, sued Hard Rock Café International in Orange Circuit Court, alleging the company failed to pay required minimum wage. The complaint says the restaurant unlawfully used the tip credit by paying servers and bartenders below minimum wage while requiring them to share tips with kitchen staff—specifically “expediters” who garnish and prepare plates. Plaintiffs and their attorneys contend tip-sharing with kitchen employees violates Florida and federal law because tip credits or pooling are only lawful when tipped employees retain all tips or pools are limited to employees who customarily receive tips. The suit argues servers were deprived of needed earnings and that Hard Rock should have known the arrangement was illegal.

Researchers report that some of the water found on the Moon originates from the solar wind. Analysis of tiny glassy grains of lunar regolith (from Apollo samples) shows traces of water and hydroxyl (200–300 ppm) whose hydrogen is depleted in deuterium — matching the Sun’s low-deuterium signature. The team concludes hydrogen ions carried by the solar wind implant in the Moon’s surface and bond with oxygen in rocks, producing water and hydroxyl. Published in Nature Geoscience, the study identifies this process as a previously unrecognized source of lunar water, complementing known reservoirs such as polar ice.

Implications: the finding reshapes ideas about inner Solar System water sources, suggests other airless bodies (e.g., asteroids, moons) could host surface water produced the same way, and raises the possibility—though technically challenging—of using in-situ water for life support or as feedstock for rocket fuel. Critics note the sample set is tiny (a few grains from Apollo soils), so the global abundance and practical extractability of this solar-wind–derived water remain uncertain.

The White House circulated a memo of talking points urging allies to defend President Donald Trump’s handling of the violent “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, insisting “the president was entirely correct” when he said “both sides” shared blame. The talking points praised Trump as a voice of unity who condemned hate groups, cited law-enforcement and journalist reports of clashes between counter-protesters and white nationalists, highlighted DOJ and ICE actions, and attacked media coverage. 

The memo drew immediate criticism because it downplayed explicit rebukes of white supremacists, neo-Nazis and the KKK—the groups that organized the rally that left a counter-protester dead and two police officers later killed in a helicopter crash. Trump’s initial comment that “many sides” were to blame, followed by a later but brief denunciation of hate groups, prompted rare, widespread rebukes from Republicans (including Paul Ryan, Marco Rubio, John McCain and others) and Democrats, who said the president failed to unequivocally condemn white supremacy. The controversy led to political fallout, with calls for clearer moral leadership and some businesses distancing themselves from the administration.

Paris Saint-Germain will replace its Emirates sponsor on the front of its shirts with the message “JE SUIS PARIS” (“I AM PARIS”) for its next two matches — Wednesday’s Champions League game against Malmö and Saturday’s Ligue 1 home match against Troyes. The larger tribute, agreed with sponsor Fly Emirates, follows an earlier, smaller memorial inscription beneath the club crest and honors the victims of the Nov. 13 Paris attacks that killed more than 129 people. Saturday’s game will be the club’s first home match at the Parc des Princes since the attacks; players and officials observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims.

Rapper Eminem’s headlining set at the Bonnaroo music festival in Tennessee drew backlash after loud blasts that many concertgoers said resembled gunshots rang out during his performance of “Kill You.” Videos show fans screaming and ducking; attendees and social media users described being frightened or traumatized, with some saying such realistic effects were inappropriate without warning given recent mass shootings and attendees’ PTSD. Supporters noted Eminem has used similar effects in live shows for years and as recently as other 2018 festival appearances. Eminem’s representatives responded that the sound was not gunshot effects but a pyrotechnic concussion — a loud boom used by him and many artists in live shows for over a decade. The incident sparked debate over the timing and sensitivity of using gun-like sound effects at concerts.

Summary:

Islamic State (ISIS) released a video showing the beheading of Peter (Abdul-Rahman) Kassig, a 26‑year‑old former U.S. Army Ranger turned humanitarian who was captured in October 2013 while delivering aid in Syria. U.S. officials and the White House reviewed and confirmed the video; President Obama and other leaders condemned the killing and praised Kassig’s humanitarian service. His parents and supporters had publicly campaigned for his release and said his conversion to Islam in captivity was genuine.

The video is unusually long and graphic: it combines lengthy propaganda celebrating ISIS’s rise with extremely grisly executions, including a mass beheading of Syrian soldiers. Kassig himself appears only near the end already dead; unlike earlier Western victims, he is not shown speaking or being filmed during the act. Analysts and U.S. officials speculated he may have refused to read forced statements; ISIS’s choice not to show a Western woman hostage who remains captive also departs from its previous pattern of foreshadowing subsequent executions.

ISIS still holds other Western captives, including a 26‑year‑old American woman taken in August 2013 (whose identity is being withheld for safety) and British photojournalist John Cantlie. The group has demanded large ransoms (reported over $6 million) for American hostages, but U.S. policy forbids ransom payments and discourages families from doing so. Officials and hostage‑negotiation experts say inflated ransom demands often indicate hostage propaganda is the primary goal rather than genuine release for payment. Some countries and intermediaries have, however, reportedly arranged payments for other Western hostages.

The video and killings come amid intensified U.S.-led airstrikes and military pressure that have cost ISIS territory and revenue (notably oil facilities). Observers view the elaborate, brutal video as both a recruitment and morale tool for ISIS and as a sign of desperation in the face of mounting military setbacks. The killings also highlighted frustrations and complications in U.S. efforts to free hostages, including interagency differences over ransom tactics and the opaque role of intermediaries in prior releases.

A ceasefire and evacuation deal for rebel-held eastern Aleppo — brokered by Turkey and Russia to allow civilians and opposition fighters safe passage to Idlib — collapsed into confusion and resumed violence as parties on the ground refused to comply.

Key points:
- The agreement, struck late Tuesday by Turkish intelligence and the Russian military, aimed to evacuate thousands of civilians and fighters. It reportedly excluded direct assent by the Assad government and Iran, fueling objections from Iran-backed militias and some pro‑government elements.
- Implementation stalled Wednesday: evacuation buses waited idle, and shelling and air strikes in the besieged enclave resumed. Both sides blamed the other: Russia and the Syrian government accused rebels of breaking the truce; opposition activists, civilians and Turkey blamed Iranian-backed militias and pro-government forces for continuing attacks and blocking exits.
- Iran‑aligned militias and Hezbollah — heavily involved in the assault on Aleppo — were reported to be imposing new conditions, holding people at checkpoints and demanding reciprocal evacuations (including wounded from Shiite villages Foua and Kefraya). The UN and rebel sources said Iranian militias were obstructing the deal.
- The United Nations reported summary executions of civilians by pro‑government forces in recently recaptured districts, increasing fears of reprisals and possible war crimes. The UN said it was not part of the evacuation talks but stood ready to help; Western officials urged UN observers and humanitarian agencies to oversee any evacuation.
- Negotiations continued through Wednesday and late reports indicated a revised agreement might include reciprocal evacuations and could begin within hours or on Thursday. Estimates of those to be moved varied; figures cited ranged up to tens of thousands from both sides.
- The failed/fragile ceasefire highlighted fractures among Assad’s backers (Russia, Iran and allied militias), the humanitarian catastrophe in eastern Aleppo after weeks of siege and bombardment, and the likely political consequence: the evacuation would hand full control of Aleppo to the Assad government, marking a major victory for his coalition.

Civilians remained trapped and terrified amid ongoing bombardment; evacuation plans were uncertain, contested, and subject to last‑minute changes as international and local actors jockeyed over terms and guarantees.

Medicinal Genomics, a startup founded by Kevin McKernan, has released the raw DNA sequence reads of the Cannabis sativa genome to the public via Amazon’s EC2 cloud. The data—more than 131 billion bases of shotgun reads—are not yet assembled into contiguous sequences; McKernan estimates the genome is about 400 million bases, roughly three times the size of Arabidopsis. The DNA was prepared in an Amsterdam lab. 

McKernan, who previously co-founded Agencourt Biosciences and worked on sequencing technologies and the Human Genome Project, financed the roughly $200,000 project himself with angel investors. He envisions the genomic data enabling scientific study of the plant’s roughly 60 cannabinoids (beyond THC), guiding breeding or bioproduction to enhance therapeutic compounds (e.g., CBD) while minimizing psychoactive effects, and supporting regulation through genetic “fingerprinting” of strains. Medicinal Genomics plans to provide genome annotations and tools, including an iPad app.

Experts note the work shifts cannabis study toward pharmacology and could aid drug development, though some researchers point out that active compounds are already known and the genome is not strictly necessary to study them. The sequence release has not yet undergone peer review or assembly into a published draft genome.

Justin Timberlake tells Vanity Fair he hasn’t spoken to ex Britney Spears in about nine or ten years, wishing her well but saying their teenage relationship grew out of extraordinary circumstances that didn’t translate into adulthood. Reflecting on his early fame with other former Mouseketeers, Timberlake calls them “little kids with big toys,” noting that newfound celebrity and lifestyle made normal growth impossible.

He praises current (at the time) ex Jessica Biel as the most significant person in his life and says he wants a family someday. Timberlake argues celebrities often date each other because they understand the pressures of fame and provide refuge, and he believes lasting relationships require both partners to change together. Professionally, he’s focused more on acting than music for now—appearing in Friends with Benefits with Mila Kunis—though he doesn’t rule out future music projects. The piece also includes anecdotes about his Mouseketeers days and a discussion of performing a sex scene in the film.

Alaska Governor Bill Walker said he will use his executive authority to expand Medicaid under the federal Affordable Care Act, aiming to cover more than 20,000 uninsured Alaskans in the first year. Walker — an independent whose earlier expansion efforts were blocked by the Republican-led legislature — will accept $146 million in federal funds and apply directly for the expansion. He cited examples of nearly 30 other states that have adopted Medicaid expansion and highlighted projected benefits: about $1 billion in federal healthcare dollars over six years, $100 million in state savings, and roughly 4,000 new jobs.

Because the legislature is not in session, the Legislative Budget and Audit Committee must review the federal funding request; it has until Sept. 1 to either support the request or recommend a special legislative session. Committee chairman Rep. Mike Hawker called the committee’s role largely procedural. Opponents, including Republican state Sen. John Coghill, warned of fiscal risk if federal support wanes and said future taxpayers could be burdened.

Police and CNN issued an all-clear after CNN's New York offices and studios were evacuated Thursday night following a phoned-in bomb threat. CNN Worldwide president Jeff Zucker said in an internal memo that the NYPD had declared the building secure and employees could return the next morning, thanking authorities and staff for their response. The NYPD tweeted the threat was not substantiated; a law enforcement source said the caller claimed there were five devices in the building.

A new report from the special inspector general for Afghanistan reconstruction finds that large U.S.-funded infrastructure projects meant to aid counterinsurgency are delayed, may be unsustainable for the Afghan government, and could create harmful “expectations gaps.” The review focuses on the Afghan Infrastructure Fund and related U.S. efforts to build roads, power plants and other big projects designed to win local support for the Afghan government.

Key findings and concerns:
- Major projects are so behind schedule that many benefits will not materialize until after most U.S. combat forces leave (expected end-2014).
- The Afghan government likely lacks the financial resources and technical capacity to operate and maintain some projects, risking rapid decline in services once U.S. support ends.
- The “Kandahar Bridging Solution” — costly diesel generators supplying roughly 25 MW each to Kandahar until a hydropower turbine is installed — may be ineffective and unsustainable. Critics, including Maj. Gen. Kenneth Dahl, found no evidence the extra electricity produced employment, stability, or greater support for the government; the planned turbine will produce less power than the generators, and diesel subsidies cannot be sustained by Afghan budgets.
- A $23 million road in Helmand may have adverse effects because landowners have not been compensated for lost property.
- Four electricity projects totaling over $300 million remain unawarded to contractors despite prior claims they would deliver counterinsurgency benefits.
- The report warns that implementing projects the Afghan state cannot sustain could be counterproductive, eroding both U.S. and Afghan legitimacy if promised goals are unmet.

Reactions:
- Senator Claire McCaskill said the findings question the strategic rationale of large-scale spending, noting a lack of evidence these projects improve security.
- The U.S. Embassy defended big projects as signals of long-term U.S. commitment; Pentagon officials said announcements alone have generated goodwill and criticized the inspector general’s conclusions as premature.

Context:
- The U.S. has spent nearly $90 billion on Afghan reconstruction over a decade. This report, initiated under new inspector general John Sopko, shifts scrutiny from contracting waste and fraud to the conceptualization and sustainability of projects, challenging the longstanding assumption that large infrastructure spending is an effective counterinsurgency tool.

President Barack Obama on March 18, 2011 urged Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi to immediately halt attacks on civilians and comply with a new U.N. Security Council resolution aimed at protecting civilians. Citing Gadhafi’s threats against cities like Benghazi and the risk of regional destabilization, Obama said the council’s terms—including an immediate cease-fire, withdrawal of forces from populated areas, and restoration of power, water and humanitarian access—are “not negotiable.” He warned that if Gadhafi refuses to comply, the resolution will be enforced through military action by an international coalition; the U.S. would participate but would not deploy ground troops.

Obama noted sanctions, asset freezes and humanitarian aid already imposed, and said Secretary of State Hillary Clinton would travel to Paris for an allied meeting. U.S. officials have indicated American forces could help enforce a no-fly zone (e.g., by targeting Libyan air defenses), though the president did not spell out specific U.S. responsibilities. Britain, France, NATO and Arab partners were coordinating plans and preparing for action, and an emergency international summit on Libya was set for Paris the following day.

Portugal and Spain played a classic 3-3 draw in Sochi as Cristiano Ronaldo stole the show with a late hat-trick that rescued a point for Portugal. Ronaldo opened the scoring from a penalty after just minutes, added a second before halftime when David de Gea fumbled his shot, and sealed the comeback with a sublime free-kick in the 88th minute — his first direct free-kick success in major tournaments after 44 attempts. The display pushed his international tally to 84, making him one of the few to score in four World Cups and the oldest World Cup hat‑trick scorer.

Spain fought back strongly, powered by Diego Costa’s physical, clinical two-goal performance and a brilliant strike from Nacho that briefly put them ahead 3-2. Spain controlled much of the match despite off-field turmoil after sacking their manager a day before the tournament; they created more chances but were undone by individual errors on two goals. The game was widely hailed as one of the tournament’s best openers, boosting Portugal’s hopes in a congested group and showing Spain remain dangerous despite recent upheaval. Media and pundits celebrated Ronaldo’s landmark night and the match’s entertainment value, while both teams take encouraging points and lessons as they prepare for upcoming group fixtures.

A 2-year-old boy, Yoshiki Fujimoto, who went missing on Aug. 12 on Yashiro (Suo-Oshima) Island in Yamaguchi Prefecture, was found safe on Aug. 15 about 560 meters from his great‑grandfather’s home. Yoshiki had been walking toward a nearby beach with his grandfather and 3‑year‑old brother when he turned back toward the house and disappeared after roughly 100 meters. A large search involving hundreds of police, firefighters, volunteers, drones, search dogs and helicopters failed to find him until 78‑year‑old volunteer Haruo Obata climbed a mountain trail near the last known location, called out repeatedly and heard Yoshiki respond. Obata found the boy sitting barefoot on a mossy rock in a mountain stream at about 6:30 a.m.; Yoshiki accepted candy and was wrapped in a towel and reunited with his family.

Medical checks found only dehydration, scratches and tick bites; he was coherent, able to converse with his mother, and remained hospitalized for observation. Experts called the rescue a “miracle,” noting favorable conditions likely helped—shade by the stream, access to water, and the toddler’s limited stress response and unpredictable movements. Rescuers later said the exact mountain area had not been thoroughly searched earlier, and some officers expressed regret that it wasn’t covered sooner. The family thanked rescuers and the volunteer who found him; the grandfather apologized for taking his eyes off the child.

Harry Shearer, the longtime voice actor behind key Simpsons characters including Mr. Burns, Ned Flanders and Principal Skinner, announced he is leaving The Simpsons after 26 seasons. In a tweet he said he wanted the freedom to do other work and suggested a contract dispute prompted the departure, claiming a producer’s lawyer told him, “Harry will not be part of it, wish him the best.”

Showrunners Matt Groening, Al Jean and producer James L. Brooks confirmed Shearer was offered the same deal accepted by the rest of the cast but declined; they said the series will continue and will recast his characters “with the finest voiceover talent available.” Fox had recently renewed the series for two more seasons (through 2017) and the rest of the voice cast signed two-year extensions for seasons 27 and 28. Production on season 27 has already begun without Shearer.

Brooks publicly urged continued talks on Twitter, saying negotiations were still possible. The article notes the series has faced contract disputes before (notably a 2011 pay-cut negotiation) but had retained its cast. The season 26 finale was scheduled to air Sunday.

Summary:

Severe flooding in southeastern Louisiana has created an urgent need for blood donations. The South Texas Blood and Tissue Center (STBTC) in San Antonio is ready to help but is already facing a seasonal summer shortfall—many regular donors are students on break—and additional restrictions tied to the Zika outbreak have further reduced usable inventory. STBTC’s Julie Vera noted people who recently traveled to Zika-affected areas must wait 28 days before donating; the center can now test for Zika but requires an extra consent form. All blood types are needed; donors can find locations at southtexasblood.org.

Experts also warned the flood could raise mosquito-borne disease risks once waters recede. Peter Hotez said eggs sheltered in containers may hatch after flooding, potentially boosting Aedes aegypti populations (the mosquito that spreads Zika). CDC’s Ben Beard said increases in Aedes are uncertain and that the agency would respond aggressively if monitoring shows higher numbers. No locally transmitted Zika cases had been reported in Louisiana at the time, though experts cautioned some cases might be unreported; flooding can also increase risk of other mosquito-borne illnesses such as West Nile.

BuzzFeed’s CEO Jonah Peretti told employees the company has canceled a $1.3 million advertising agreement with the Republican National Committee and will not accept ads for Donald Trump’s presidential campaign. Peretti said the decision was made because Trump’s rhetoric and proposed policies—such as a proposed ban on Muslim travel and other statements targeting immigrants, women and the press—are “directly opposed to the freedoms” of BuzzFeed employees and could make it difficult for some to do their jobs. Peretti framed the move as a business choice rather than an editorial one, drawing an analogy to refusing cigarette ads for health reasons. Editor-in-chief Ben Smith reiterated it was a publisher’s business decision and would not affect BuzzFeed News’s campaign coverage; reporters said it likely won’t change their already strained relationship with the Trump campaign. The RNC’s Sean Spicer said the committee never intended to use the reserved BuzzFeed ad space and criticized BuzzFeed for not ruling out taking money from a candidate under FBI investigation. BuzzFeed declined to comment further on the size or specifics of the buy.

Since the Harvey Weinstein allegations and the #MeToo movement, public attention to sexual harassment and assault has intensified. The piece recalls Anita Hill’s 1991 testimony accusing Clarence Thomas of sexual harassment and how then-Senate Judiciary Committee chair Joe Biden handled the hearings. In a Teen Vogue interview, Biden said he believed Hill, voted against Thomas, pushed to add women to the Judiciary Committee afterward, and regrets not doing more to shield Hill from aggressive questioning. He said he unsuccessfully tried to prevent attacks by some Republican senators and decided against subpoenaing certain witnesses for fear they might undermine Hill’s testimony and cost them a close vote. Biden apologized, calling his inability to do more his one regret.

Anita Hill and others have criticized Biden’s past conduct and apologies as insufficient, arguing the hearings modelled poor treatment of women and missed an opportunity to lead on gender-equal practices. Hill says the core problem is that women weren’t truly heard. Biden emphasized the need for cultural change, pointing to his work on college sexual-violence prevention and his “It’s on Us” campaign, and said success would be when no abused woman blames herself.

Apple rejected the first “fart” app submitted for Apple Watch. The app, Fart Watch, let users remotely trigger fart sounds from an iPhone using the Watch as a wrist-mounted remote (a digital whoopee cushion). Apple’s rejection cited guideline 2.11 (apps that duplicate many existing, low-value apps such as fart, burp, flashlight, and Kama Sutra apps may be rejected) and 8.1 (trademark/copyright compliance), explicitly noting the Watch app was “primarily a fart app” and that such apps are not accepted on Apple Watch. The developer plans to pivot to a bracelet-bling product for the Watch. The piece notes the move aligns with Apple’s effort to cultivate a more upscale image for the Watch, though jailbreaks and sideloading could eventually enable such novelty apps.

A Maine innkeeper’s essay contest to give away her 210-year-old Center Lovell Inn and restaurant has drawn an official probe and complaints from losing entrants. Janice Sage, who said she acquired and later ran the inn after winning it in a contest herself 22 years ago, held a recent contest that drew fewer than the 7,500 hoped-for entries; entrants each paid a $125 fee and submitted 200-word essays. A local panel picked Prince and Rose Adams, a 45-year-old couple from the U.S. Virgin Islands who operate a Caribbean-style restaurant on St. John, as winners; they plan to close their St. John restaurant and open the Maine inn by July 10.

Dozens of unsuccessful entrants have formed the Center Lovell Contest Fair Practices Commission and allege deceptive advertising and unfair advantage for restaurant or inn owners, saying Sage had promised no such advantage. Maine State Police are investigating whether the contest violated a state “games of skill” law that bars operators from partially or completely controlling outcomes; the inquiry is narrowly focused on that statute and expected to conclude within a week. Sage and the Adamses did not comment, and authorities suggested contestants seeking other remedies consult private counsel.

Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas) withdrew Thursday night from the race for House majority leader, saying continuing his campaign would create “unnecessary and painful division” within the Republican conference. His exit leaves Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) as the clear front-runner to succeed Rep. Eric Cantor (R-Va.), who lost a historic primary on Tuesday and will remain majority leader until July 31 to aid transition. 

Sessions, chairman of the House Rules Committee and former head of the House GOP campaign committee, launched his bid immediately after Cantor’s loss but could not overcome McCarthy’s advantages as the party’s chief vote counter and top fundraiser. McCarthy further consolidated support in the quick turnaround to a secret-ballot leadership vote set for June 19 by Speaker John Boehner, which left little time for challengers to organize.

Other potential contenders — Reps. Jeb Hensarling, Paul Ryan, Tom Price and Jim Jordan — declined to run. Rep. Raúl Labrador is considering a challenge but would face long odds. With McCarthy likely to move up, the contest to replace him as majority whip is now the competitive race, featuring Rep. Peter Roskam, Rep. Steve Scalise and Rep. Marlin Stutzman.

Two friends, Vicky Torres (Cabazon) and Juanita Salas (Beaumont), have been camping outside the Best Buy at 1650 Second St. since last Wednesday to secure a spot for Black Friday sales. Wrapped in blankets and equipped with mittens, snacks and hot coffee, they rotate overnight so one can rest while the other holds their place; Salas’s husband, Jacob Alva, also helps by holding her spot sometimes and providing support (food, phone charging, bathroom breaks). They say camping is cold but fun, helps stretch a fixed income to buy gifts (they hope to buy a 50-inch HDTV for $199), and attracts attention from passersby—some admiring their dedication, others calling them “stupid,” and some asking them to save spots (which they refuse). Store manager Eric Tschudy noted the number of campers grows each year and praised regulars like Torres; Alva said he isn’t worried about safety because police and store security are present. The scene underlines that even weeks before Thanksgiving shoppers are lining up for steep Black Friday discounts as retailers vie for holiday sales.

A Los Angeles jury awarded casino magnate Steve Wynn $20 million in his defamation suit against "Girls Gone Wild" founder Joe Francis. Wynn sued after Francis repeatedly claimed Wynn had threatened to have him killed and buried in the desert over a roughly $2 million gambling debt. The jury assigned $5 million for statements Francis made to a TMZ producer in a courthouse hallway and $11 million for remarks on Good Morning America; punitive damages up to another $60 million may be decided separately.

Wynn testified the killing allegation was a "terrible lie" that damaged his reputation; Francis has insisted the threat was real and said music producer Quincy Jones told him Wynn wanted him dead. Jones denied telling Francis that and said Wynn never made such a threat. Francis’s team has not produced the alleged email he cited. Francis’s attorney says the judge erred by allowing the GMA claim late in the trial and that some statements were made during a court proceeding and thus privileged; Francis plans to appeal. The two have a long history of disputes, including earlier litigation over allegations that Wynn supplied prostitutes and drugs during Francis’s gambling losses. Francis’s net worth has been reported at about $150 million.

This collection of reviews and reporting summarizes the release and early reception of James Cameron’s Avatar (2009). Key points:

- Premise and plot: Avatar follows paraplegic marine Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), who uses a genetically engineered Na'vi-human "avatar" to interact with the indigenous Na'vi on the alien world Pandora. Initially part of a human effort to secure a valuable mineral (unobtanium), Sully becomes sympathetic to the Na'vi, falls in love with Neytiri (Zoe Saldana), and ultimately opposes the military and corporate forces led by Colonel Quaritch (Stephen Lang) and Administrator Parker Selfridge (Giovanni Ribisi). Sigourney Weaver plays scientist Grace, who prefers coexistence and relocation over annihilation.

- Production and release: This was James Cameron’s first film in 12–15 years and a major studio gamble—reported budgets range widely but are large (commonly cited around $230m–$300m, with rumors higher). The world premiere was in London; the film opens in both 2D and Cameron’s heavily promoted 3D version.

- Visuals and 3D: Critics praise Avatar’s technical achievements and immersive 3D, calling it a potential milestone that could reinvigorate theatrical exhibition. The motion-capture/“emotion capture” performances and richly realized alien world are highlighted. The 3D is described as used judiciously rather than gimmicky; standout sequences include the scene where Sully first awakens in his avatar and a long, spectacular final battle.

- Performances and tone: Sam Worthington is noted as a believable leading man, Zoe Saldana’s role is singled out as challenging and award-worthy, and Sigourney Weaver provides strong supporting presence. The narrative blends action, romance and emotional beats; some critics find the script cheesy or conventional at times, with familiar clichés and an old-fashioned good-versus-evil structure.

- Themes and politics: Reviewers identify clear anti-colonial and environmental themes, with parallels to historical colonization, Vietnam, and recent political rhetoric about pre-emptive military action. Cameron frames the film as a critique of human entitlement toward other peoples and nature.

- Reception and impact: Early critical reaction was largely positive—many reviewers said the film exceeded hype, offering both spectacle and emotional engagement. Some viewers experienced mild eye strain or discomfort from long 3D viewing, but major nausea reports were dismissed. Observers predicted strong box-office success and multiple Oscar nominations; Cameron indicated he has stories plotted for sequels.

Overall assessment across the pieces: Avatar is a technically groundbreaking, visually stunning and emotionally engaging blockbuster that, despite some narrative clichédness, delivers a powerful cinematic experience and may mark a turning point for 3D filmmaking.

A London lawyer, Matthew Dick, proposed to his girlfriend Delyth Hughes by hiding the message in The Times cryptic crossword. Dick worked with crossword editor Richard Rogan to include clues whose answers and wording — including a six-letter clue for "Delyth" and one reading "'Will you marry me,' say, that's forward also rude" (answer: "proposal") — spelled out the proposal in Tuesday’s puzzle. The couple were in Cornwall celebrating Hughes’s birthday when Dick underlined key words in the puzzle and produced a ring; Hughes, 39, was initially stunned, joked “No” and then accepted. Rogan said it was likely the first proposal in the paper’s 85‑year crossword history and called it a one‑off.

Comedian Stephen Colbert’s May 1 “Late Show” monologue about President Trump’s first 100 days — which included a bleeped, crude metaphor suggesting a sexual relationship between Trump and Vladimir Putin — prompted more than 5,700 complaints to the Federal Communications Commission. POLITICO obtained 100 redacted samples of complaints filed between May 2 and May 17 showing objections from across the political spectrum: parents upset their children might hear it, conservatives who said the joke was disrespectful and biased against Trump, and LGBT viewers who called the line homophobic for using accusations of being gay as an insult.

Many callers urged the FCC to fine Colbert and CBS, but broadcast lawyers say that is unlikely. The Late Show airs at 11:30 p.m., within the FCC’s “safe harbor” when indecency rules are relaxed, and the disputed line was bleeped. Legal experts say the agency would have to prove obscenity — a very high bar that this segment likely would not meet, especially given its political context and lack of explicit sexual appeal. FCC Chairman Ajit Pai confirmed the agency is reviewing the complaints, noting that such reviews are routine and do not indicate merit. The complaint volume is far smaller than past high-profile cases, such as the 2004 Super Bowl incident.

Liam Neeson’s 31-year-old nephew, Ronan Sexton, is in critical condition after suffering serious head injuries when he fell about 20 feet from the top of a telephone kiosk on Brighton’s seafront promenade. The incident occurred at about 4 a.m. last Sunday while Sexton was out with friends; police say the fall is not being treated as suspicious and no further investigation is planned. He was first taken to the Royal Sussex County Hospital and later transferred to Hurstwood Park Hospital in Haywards Heath, where his mother, Bernadette Sexton (Neeson’s sister), has been at his bedside. Neeson, who lives in New York with his two teenage sons, has been in contact with his sister. The report also recalls Neeson’s past tragedy: the 2009 death of his wife Natasha Richardson from a head injury sustained in a skiing accident.

North Korea carried out a third nuclear test, provoking global condemnation and putting China — its sole major ally — in a difficult position. Beijing summoned Pyongyang’s ambassador, issued unusually stern public rebukes, and joined other Security Council members in condemning the test, yet stopped short of specifying punitive steps. Chinese statements emphasized opposition to nuclear proliferation and urged calm and a return to the stalled six-party denuclearization talks, reflecting Beijing’s dual aims of denuclearization and regional stability.

Analysts say China’s response will be decisive for the international reaction: while Beijing is likely to support tougher U.N. measures, it is unlikely to abandon North Korea, which it sees as a strategic buffer and a fraternal party ally. The Chinese military and Communist Party institutions favor keeping Pyongyang close despite growing frustration over its provocations. Xi Jinping’s new leadership may tighten policy somewhat, but major shifts are unlikely in the near term.

For the United States and its allies, the test raises pressure to strengthen deterrence and missile defenses and to push additional sanctions — a difficult task because North Korea is already heavily sanctioned and has few economic levers. Pyongyang framed the test as self-defense against U.S. hostility and threatened further steps. Experts warned the test advances North Korea’s status as a nuclear contender and risks a destabilizing cycle of sanctions and provocations, while options for the international community remain limited.

China surprised markets by changing how it sets the yuan’s daily reference rate, prompting a devaluation of about 1.9% on Aug. 11 and a further 1.6% drop the next day. The move—presented by the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) as a step toward a more market-oriented exchange rate that takes greater account of the previous day’s close and market supply-and-demand—pushed the onshore yuan to four-year lows and the offshore rate lower still. Over two days the yuan fell roughly 3.5% onshore and about 4.8% offshore.

Markets reacted sharply: global stocks and commodity prices declined, safe-haven bond yields fell, and several Asian currencies also weakened. The shock intensified concerns about China’s slowing economy—exports plunged and domestic activity data disappointed—and reignited fears of a competitive devaluation or “currency war.” Policymakers and analysts are divided: some see the change as a technical liberalization toward a floating exchange rate (the IMF called it a welcome step), while others view it as an “engineered” depreciation to support exporters and jobs.

The move complicates geopolitics and policy: U.S. lawmakers condemned it as currency manipulation, though the U.S. Treasury was measured and the IMF urged careful implementation. It could influence U.S. Federal Reserve timing for rate hikes by adding downward pressure to global inflation and the dollar’s strength. China says it does not intend a sustained depreciation and has used state banks to stabilize the market, but internal voices reportedly favor a larger overall devaluation to aid growth. The episode also risks undermining China’s push to internationalize the renminbi and its bid for IMF Special Drawing Rights inclusion, depending on how the policy evolves.
