A prison letter written by Tupac Shakur to Madonna has surfaced and is scheduled for auction. In the 1995 letter, Tupac explains ending their relationship partly because of concerns about his public "image" and how being seen with a white woman might affect his standing with his audience. He apologizes for any hurt he caused, says he’s grown “spiritually and mentally,” and describes himself then as a young man with limited experience dating a major celebrity. The note, which TMZ reported on and which Gotta Have Rock and Roll will list with a $100,000 starting bid, underscores the personal insecurities behind a high-profile breakup and has drawn attention for both its candid content and Tupac’s handwriting.

Italy’s national statistics agency Istat will, beginning with 2014 data published in September, include estimates of illegal activities—prostitution, illegal drug sales and trafficking, and contraband cigarettes and alcohol—in its calculation of GDP. The update follows Eurostat/EU guidelines and replaces the previous national accounts methodology from 1995. Istat warns these activities are hard to measure, but estimates they could raise GDP by about 1–2%. The revision (with prior years to be adjusted) also brings research & development and arms into GDP by reclassifying R&D as investment rather than an intermediate cost. The larger measured output will make Italy’s deficit look smaller as a share of GDP, a politically useful development as Prime Minister Matteo Renzi seeks to meet deficit targets.

Sen. Rand Paul defended and stood by longtime aide Jack Hunter amid controversy over Hunter’s past as a provocative South Carolina radio personality who praised John Wilkes Booth, disparaged Abraham Lincoln, adopted a “Southern Avenger” persona (including a Confederate-flag ski mask), and voiced other racially charged comments. Paul called many of those past statements “absolutely stupid,” said he is not a fan of secession, and emphasized that Hunter has recanted some remarks and never acted discriminatorily on the job. Paul argued that youthful provocations shouldn’t automatically disqualify capable staffers and insisted he would immediately fire anyone who showed evidence of white supremacist behavior — a charge he says he has seen no proof of in Hunter.

Under pressure from the publicity, Hunter left Paul’s office to resume work as a pundit, saying he did not want to be a distraction and that his earlier persona was “campy” and politically incorrect rather than racist. He said he’s become more libertarian and tolerant over time, will retire the “Southern Avenger” moniker, and wants to defend himself outside a senatorial staff role. Supporters and former colleagues offered mixed views: some defended Hunter’s professionalism and evolution; others criticized his past and saw the episode as embarrassing for Rand Paul and illustrative of tensions between libertarian/tea-party roots and efforts to mainstream within the GOP. The episode also revived broader debates about the linkage between states’ rights rhetoric and defenses of the Confederacy.

Astronomers have spectroscopically confirmed the most distant galaxy yet detected: z8_GND_5296. Its light left when the universe was about 700 million years old (a redshift of z ≈ 7.5), so we see it as it was 13.1 billion years ago. The object was first identified as a faint infrared “red” candidate in deep Hubble images; its distance was confirmed using Keck Observatory’s MOSFIRE spectrograph by detecting Lyman‑alpha emission.

Key findings and context
- z8_GND_5296 breaks the previous spectroscopic record (z ≈ 7.2) and provides a direct probe of the era of reionization, when the first stars and galaxies ionized the early neutral hydrogen fog.  
- It is a small, early galaxy but unusually vigorous: the team estimates a star-formation rate of order a few hundred solar masses per year—far higher than the Milky Way—suggesting plentiful gas in the young universe.  
- Many earlier candidates at similar redshifts were only photometric selections and later proved to be nearer objects (e.g., brown dwarfs) when not spectroscopically confirmed; spectroscopy is therefore essential to reliably measure distance.  
- Detecting Lyman‑alpha at such times is difficult because neutral hydrogen can obscure it; finding this line in z8_GND_5296 may indicate a locally ionized region or particular conditions that let the emission escape.

Implications and next steps
- This confirmed detection helps map galaxy formation during the first billion years and informs models of reionization and early star formation.  
- Pushing to yet higher redshifts (z ≳ 10, corresponding to ≈350 million years after the Big Bang) is believed possible in principle but limited by current telescope sensitivity; upcoming facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope and next-generation ground-based telescopes will be crucial to find and confirm earlier objects.  
- The team searched 43 Hubble-selected candidates and obtained spectroscopic data over two nights at Keck; they plan further observations to study other candidates and better characterize early galaxy populations.

President Obama’s likely choice of former Republican Sen. Chuck Hagel for secretary of defense drew mixed reactions across Capitol Hill as his nomination loomed.

Key Republican responses were skeptical or hostile:
- Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) said Hagel should receive a “fair” confirmation hearing but would withhold full endorsement, saying he’ll review Hagel’s record and whether his views fit the job—noting the nominee must understand the U.S.–Israel relationship, the Iranian threat and the need for a robust military. McConnell had praised Hagel when he left the Senate in 2009 but has pulled back amid GOP concerns about Hagel’s past comments on Israel and Iran.
- Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) called Hagel an “in-your-face” and “out of the mainstream” nomination, accusing him of unusually antagonistic views toward Israel and criticizing his past positions on Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah.
- Freshman Rep. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), an Iraq/Afghanistan veteran, said he would oppose Hagel’s confirmation, citing Hagel’s past opposition to the Iraq surge and comments on Iran, Hezbollah, Hamas and Israel, and suggested Obama could have nominated qualified Democrats instead.
- Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) also criticized the pick, saying the president ignored bipartisan concerns about Hagel’s record.

Democratic and leadership defense:
- Senate Majority Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) defended Hagel as a “serious candidate,” highlighting his Vietnam service and committee experience on Foreign Relations and Intelligence, and urged respect for the president’s prerogative to lead.

Overall, Hagel’s anticipated nomination was expected to trigger a contentious confirmation fight focused on his past foreign policy statements—especially regarding Israel and Iran—while some leaders urged a fair hearing to evaluate his qualifications.

Libya abruptly announced a cease-fire hours after the U.N. Security Council approved a broad no-fly zone and authorization to use “all necessary measures” to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe. Military experts, rebels and activists expressed deep skepticism, calling the move tactical brinksmanship by Col. Moammar Gadhafi intended to buy time, confuse the West and protect his forces. Reports from Misrata and other areas said government bombardment continued; activists claim Gadhafi is concealing heavy weapons among civilian housing to create human shields. Rebel leaders and analysts suggested the cease-fire announcement—delivered by deputy foreign minister Moussa Koussa rather than Gadhafi himself—could be a psychological ploy or a way for factions inside Libya to distance the leader from the pledge.

Despite the announcement, Britain, France, NATO and the U.S. prepared forces for enforcement: fighters were repositioned to bases in Italy and Cyprus, naval vessels massed off Libya, and emergency meetings convened about the no-fly zone’s scope. Some analysts warned that a genuine cease-fire could reduce the immediate justification for strikes against Gadhafi’s air and ground defenses, while others predicted the West would proceed.

Commentary in the piece framed the intervention as a fraught, high-stakes gamble. Supporters argue intervention was forced by Qaddafi’s likely victory and potential reprisals, and that a quick success could reinforce a “Responsibility to Protect” norm and boost uprisings elsewhere. Critics worry about a protracted air campaign devolving into a costly quagmire, fueling anti-Western sentiment if civilians are killed or ground troops are required, and undermining regional stability. Questions remain about the political endgame after intervention—what happens if Qadhafi falls or if the no-fly zone fails—and whether similar crises in Bahrain and Yemen will be addressed consistently. The piece ends with cautious hope that the U.N. resolution and reports of a cease-fire might create space for a rapid political settlement, while underscoring the many unresolved risks.

President Barack Obama condemned the violence in Bahrain, urging restraint and accountability after security forces opened fire on protesters. In a phone call Friday with King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, Obama called for those responsible for the shootings to be held accountable and for Bahrain to respect universal rights and pursue meaningful reform. The White House also expressed condolences for the dead and urged governments in Yemen and Libya to show restraint amid region-wide protests.

In Bahrain, clashes left dozens wounded after soldiers and armored vehicles fired on largely Shiite anti-government demonstrators demanding greater representation and political reform. After several days of heavy-handed tactics, the crown prince, Salman bin Hamad al-Khalifa, ordered the military to withdraw and appealed for all political factions to begin sincere dialogue. His statement marked a sharp policy reversal and raised the possibility of talks, though opposition parties such as al-Wefaq say conditions must improve before negotiating and significant divisions remain among protesters. The unrest in Bahrain—home to the U.S. 5th Fleet—occurred alongside violent crackdowns across the region, prompting international criticism and temporary suspension of some arms sales by European countries.

The document is a critique of the 2015 Academy Award nominations, arguing they largely got many picks right (Boyhood, Laura Dern, Edward Norton, Mark Ruffalo, Birdman, etc.) but also revealed persistent problems—especially a lack of diversity and what the author views as unfair snubs.

Key points:
- Some misses were minor surprises or overhyped narratives (e.g., Jennifer Aniston’s expected Cake nomination that didn’t materialize; Marion Cotillard’s win of critics’ prizes made her Oscar nod less surprising).
- More serious snubs include the omission of the Swedish film Force Majeure from Best Foreign Language Film, which the writer calls one of the year’s best films.
- The biggest perceived injustice is the limited recognition for Selma: although it received a Best Picture nomination (helped by the expanded field), it was largely shut out of directing, acting, screenplay, editing, and cinematography categories. Ava DuVernay was not nominated for Best Director, and David Oyelowo was left off Best Actor—both seen as glaring omissions.
- The author connects Selma’s shortchanging to broader issues: the Academy’s whiteness and male dominance (voting membership cited as ~93% white, 76% male), a failure to reward black filmmakers and performances, and a tendency to favor films about white men. The piece notes the historical underrepresentation of black nominees in directing and the fact no black person has ever won Best Director.
- The author argues that Selma’s lack of nominations is partly due to a successful smear/controversy campaign over purported historical inaccuracies and possibly to studio campaign failings, but primarily reflects systemic bias that can hamper future opportunities for DuVernay. By contrast, white male directors of flawed or disputed biopics face fewer professional consequences.
- The piece laments that the nominations send a message that the Academy doesn’t care about diversity despite public efforts by Academy president Cheryl Boone Isaacs to change that, and worries about the negative impact on Selma’s legacy and DuVernay’s career.

Overall, the article praises many of the year’s nominees but frames the Academy’s choices as evidence of a persistent, structural problem of racial and gender bias that produced unjust exclusions—most notably Ava DuVernay’s omission from Best Director despite Selma’s critical acclaim.

The mayor of Kharkiv, Hennadiy (Gennady) Kernes, was critically wounded by a gunshot to the back on Monday while jogging and underwent a two-hour operation for chest and abdominal wounds; doctors said his life remained in danger. Kernes, a wealthy and controversial former Yanukovych supporter who later backed a united Ukraine, has faced accusations linking him to organized crime, which he denies. Kharkiv also saw clashes between pro-Ukrainian and pro-Russian protesters, with several injured.

Separately, masked pro-Russian militants seized the local government building and police station in Kostyantynivka and continue to occupy administrative buildings across eastern Ukraine, including Sloviansk and Donetsk. The insurgents are holding multiple hostages, notably seven OSCE observers (one Swedish observer was released for medical reasons); captured observers were paraded publicly by the militants, who accuse them of spying.

The events come amid Western moves to punish Moscow: the US announced expanded sanctions targeting seven new Russian officials (including two close to President Putin) and 17 companies linked to his inner circle, with asset freezes and visa bans; the EU was also preparing additional sanctions. Western governments and Kyiv accuse Russia of backing the separatists and using the unrest as a pretext for intervention; Russia denies direct involvement. The situation remains volatile with kidnappings, armed occupations and rising diplomatic pressure.

Ugandan army leaders and U.N. officials say recent changes in the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) point to a weakened but still dangerous group. Joseph Kony has named his son, Salim Saleh (about 22), as deputy and given him field-command duties. Uganda’s top general, Sam Kavuma, said that placing Kony’s son in a leadership role reflects Kony’s loss of contact with senior commanders—some killed, others in disarray—and increasing fragmentation of fighters into autonomous gangs. Intelligence from defectors reportedly identifies Salim as the second-most influential figure in the movement.

The LRA, long notorious for extreme violence, child abductions and sexual slavery, now operates in remote border forests of the Central African Republic (CAR), South Sudan, Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo after being driven out of Uganda. U.N. Regional Office head Abou Moussa and other U.N. reporting note a marked decline in killings, abductions and displacement following an African-led military campaign and rebel defections: displaced people linked to the LRA fell from about 420,000 in March 2013 to 160,000 by March of the reported year. Moussa and others say Kony remains mobile and elusive—possibly recently seen in Kafia Kingi, an area controlled by Sudan—and stressed there is “no room for complacency” until Kony is captured or removed. U.S. Ambassador Samantha Power urged Sudan not to shelter the group. Kony is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes and crimes against humanity and is believed to command only a few hundred fighters.

The ACLU of Michigan says Detroit police have been picking up homeless people in the busy Greektown entertainment district, forcing them into vans and abandoning them miles away — sometimes outside Detroit — leaving them with no money or means to return. After a year-long investigation and multiple complaints, the ACLU filed a complaint with the U.S. Justice Department and sent a letter to Detroit police calling the practice illegal, inhumane and discriminatory.

The ACLU documented five individual cases in which people who were not committing crimes were repeatedly taken “for a ride” and dumped in unfamiliar or unsafe neighborhoods, including locations on Detroit’s east side, Dearborn and Allen Park. Reported incidents include being dropped at the Detroit–River Rouge boundary, forced to discard personal money, and being left to walk for hours back to shelters or warming centers; one man with health problems said he had to cross a freeway and walk two hours to return downtown. Warming center staff say many victims then spend long hours walking back to get meals or services.

Detroit Police Chief Chester Logan said the department had not yet received the ACLU’s complaint and would review the allegations. The ACLU calls for an end to the practice and argues that homelessness does not remove a person’s right to dignified treatment.

The Supreme Court on Monday declined Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli’s request to bypass the normal appeals process and fast-track review of the constitutionality of President Obama’s health care law. The one-line order means challenges will proceed through federal appeals courts, where hearings are already set in May and June in several circuits. The Justice Department opposed Virginia’s plea. 

So far, five federal judges have ruled: two Republican appointees (Florida and Virginia) have found parts or all of the law unconstitutional, while three Democratic appointees (Michigan, Virginia and D.C.) have upheld it. The Virginia and Florida district-court rulings striking down the law are stayed pending appeal. Separate suits include Cuccinelli’s Virginia case and a larger Florida-led challenge joined by 26 states that targets the individual mandate requiring most Americans to obtain insurance or face a penalty. 

The appeal schedules could still allow the Supreme Court to hear the matter and issue a decision by early summer 2012. Virginia officials expressed disappointment at the denial. The court’s brief order did not indicate any justice recused; Justice Elena Kagan, who previously served as solicitor general, apparently participated. Meanwhile, parts of the law—such as Medicare payment changes and an extension allowing children to stay on parents’ plans until age 26—are already being implemented.

Mischa Barton has sued her mother and one-time manager, Nuala Barton, in Los Angeles Superior Court, accusing her of long-term financial exploitation, fraud and abuse of managerial power. The complaint alleges Nuala misrepresented Mischa’s earnings (including for the film The Hoarder), pocketed the undisclosed difference plus a 10% management fee, and forged Mischa’s signature on documents. Mischa also claims Nuala created companies that controlled her money, launched a Mischa Barton handbag line and a London boutique using her name without paying her, and entered her into endorsement deals without informing her.

The lawsuit further alleges Nuala engineered joint ownership of the $7.8 million Beverly Hills house Mischa bought in 2006, borrowed against the property and then barred Mischa from the home while Nuala and Mischa’s father continue to live there. Mischa says both parents have not worked outside of managing her for more than a decade and have relied on her income to support their lifestyle. The filing asserts ongoing verbal abuse and bullying led to the breakup of their personal and professional relationship.

Mischa seeks unspecified actual damages (the suit references claims over $25 million) plus treble punitive damages, fees and other relief under counts including breach of fiduciary duty, breach of oral contract and conversion. Nuala’s attorney declined comment, saying they had not yet received the complaint. Mischa is now represented by new industry agents and Venable LLP attorneys. The suit situates itself within broader celebrity “momager” controversies, noting similar disputes between talent and parent-managers.

A new Global Slavery Index from Walk Free estimates about 29.8 million people are living in modern slavery worldwide — higher than other recent estimates — including victims of sex trafficking, forced labour, debt bondage, forced marriage and hereditary chattel slavery. Nearly half of the victims are in India (about 13.9 million). Other countries with the largest absolute numbers are China (2.9 million), Pakistan (2.1 million), Nigeria (701,000), Ethiopia (651,000), Russia (516,000), Thailand (473,000), the Democratic Republic of Congo (462,000), Myanmar (384,000) and Bangladesh (343,000).

The index also ranks prevalence per capita: Mauritania has the highest proportion (about 151,000 people, roughly 4% of its population) where hereditary chattel slavery persists, followed by Haiti, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Moldova, Benin, Ivory Coast, Gambia and Gabon. The report highlights that slavery takes many forms — people born into servitude, kidnapped and sold, coerced through false job offers, forced into domestic work or exploitation on fishing boats — and occurs in all 162 countries surveyed, including wealthier nations where hidden cases appear to be far higher than previously recognized. Walk Free’s authors say the index provides a baseline for governments and activists to measure and address modern slavery.

A March 31 heat burst in Southeast Alaska broke a 101-year-old statewide March temperature record. Klawock on Prince of Wales Island reached 71°F, surpassing the previous March record of 69°F set in Ketchikan in 1915. The National Weather Service called it the warmest official March temperature in Alaska to date. Other Southeast communities also set March 31 daily records: Juneau, Yakutat, Sitka and Ketchikan (Ketchikan hit 65°F, Yakutat 57°F). March 2016 was already the warmest monthly average on record for several Southeast Alaska locations, including Juneau, Sitka, Klawock, Haines, Petersburg, Skagway and Ketchikan. (Twitter post from NWS Alaska confirmed the preliminary record.)

At the Milwaukee debate two days after Bernie Sanders’s New Hampshire win, Sanders and Hillary Clinton largely agreed on policing reform but diverged on health care and immigration. Clinton delivered what many observers called her strongest debate performance of the campaign: calm, controlled, and effective at framing Sanders as idealistic but politically unrealistic and insufficiently loyal to President Obama—an argument aimed at African-American voters. She pressed Sanders on his health-care plan and Wall Street critiques, defended Obama’s legacy, and avoided major gaffes on sensitive topics.

Sanders showed improved foreign-policy fluency and energized supporters but struggled to expand his appeal beyond his base. He relied heavily on his familiar themes—attacking billionaires, Wall Street, and income inequality—and failed to land decisive blows on Clinton. A notable misstep was claiming he could handle race relations better than Obama, which Clinton exploited. Sanders scored a strong moment attacking Henry Kissinger, which played well with younger liberals.

Policy and political takeaways: both candidates embraced police-reform rhetoric, reflecting the Black Lives Matter movement’s influence. Clinton used Obama as a political shield, aligning herself with his accomplishments (notably the ACA) to undercut Sanders’s critiques. The debate reinforced Clinton’s electability narrative and left Wall Street donors uneasy, while Republicans faced a less advantageous matchup should Clinton be the nominee. Overall, Clinton emerged stronger; Sanders maintained momentum but left questions about electability and broader appeal unanswered.

News Corp is selling a controlling stake in three Chinese TV channels and the Fortune Star film library to China Media Capital (CMC), a state-backed private equity fund, marking a clear retreat from its attempt to build a major broadcasting business in China. The assets include Xing Kong, Xing Kong International, Channel [V] Mainland China and a 757-title Chinese film library (Fortune Star). CMC is backed by Shanghai Media Group and China Development Bank and is seen as seeking overseas distribution channels to help Chinese media internationalise.

News Corp will retain close to 50% of the assets (reports value the combined assets at $300m and the deal at roughly $160m), and the new joint venture will be led by Jack Gao from Beijing with offices across China, Hong Kong and Singapore. The transaction follows earlier reorganisations of News Corp’s pan-Asia operations and reflects growing recognition—inside and outside the company—that regulatory and commercial realities make local control preferable. Observers say the move signals frustration with Chinese government media controls and may reflect James Murdoch’s skepticism about building a profitable China business, though News Corp stresses it will keep a significant stake and other regional interests (including Star India, a stake in Phoenix Satellite TV, and Chinese operations of Dow Jones and MySpace) remain. The deal aligns with Beijing’s policy of consolidating media into commercially viable but state-aligned groups that can project Chinese content abroad.

A 40-year-old zookeeper, Akira Furusho, was fatally mauled by a rare white tiger at Hirakawa Zoological Park in Kagoshima, Japan. He was found bleeding from the neck in the tiger’s display cage by a colleague after the zoo closed; he was taken to hospital and pronounced dead. The 5-year-old male tiger, Riku (about 1.8 m long and 170 kg), was later sedated by a zoo veterinarian with a tranquilizer gun. Under normal procedure keepers are supposed to remove tigers to a separate sleeping chamber before entering the display pen; police and labor authorities are investigating the zoo’s handling of its four white tigers and whether safety rules were violated. The zoo — run by a public corporation under contract with the city and open since 1972 — will keep Riku alive at the family’s request. The incident echoes previous fatal and non-fatal tiger attacks on keepers abroad.

Republicans strengthened their position in Congress and held off a high-profile Wisconsin challenge as they build momentum toward a Senate majority and a larger House advantage. Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker — a potential 2016 Republican presidential contender who drew Democratic ire for curbing public‑sector unions and survived a 2012 recall — beat a recall effort. GOP House gains included upsets of veteran Democrats: former Democrat Evan Jenkins defeated 19‑term West Virginia Rep. Nick Rahall, and Rick Allen unseated five‑term Georgia Rep. John Barrow.

Hillary Clinton was briefly interrupted by a protester who threw a shoe and some papers at her while she was opening remarks Thursday at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries’ annual convention at Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas. The woman, wearing sandals, had reportedly evaded security, rushed past staff and tossed the items a few minutes into Clinton’s speech to an audience of more than 1,000. Clinton was not hit, was momentarily startled, joked (“Is that a bat?,” “Thank goodness she didn’t play softball like I did”), and quickly resumed her address; the protester was escorted out and taken into custody by hotel security and Secret Service agents. Organizers said the woman was not credentialed for the event and police were to be called.

Clinton, the former secretary of state and likely 2016 Democratic front-runner, delivered the rest of her keynote and a Q&A with ISRI chair Jerry Simms, discussing the recycling industry, international trade, Syria, Russia’s annexation of Crimea, U.S.-Israel relations and political polarization in Washington. She emphasized recycling’s environmental and economic benefits, urged tougher trade enforcement against countries that block markets, supported economic backing for Ukraine and fair elections, and criticized extremes in politics that refuse compromise. The appearance was part of a multi-state paid-speech tour; she did not announce any 2016 plans. Audience members praised her composure and command of the issues.

A 62-year-old Federal Protective Service employee, Eulalio “Leo” Tordil, was arrested Friday in Aspen Hill, Maryland, after authorities say he carried out three separate shootings over about 24 hours that left three people dead and three wounded.

Thursday afternoon: Prince George’s County police say Tordil followed and fatally shot his estranged wife, 44-year-old Gladys Tordil, in the High Point High School parking lot in Beltsville as she waited to pick up her children. A man who tried to intervene was shot and injured. Gladys had earlier obtained a protective order against Tordil; the FPS had removed his duty weapon and placed him on administrative leave.

Friday morning: About 11:13 a.m., an off-duty officer reported shots in the Westfield Montgomery Mall parking lot in Bethesda. Three people were struck — one man died, another man was critically wounded, and a woman sustained non-life-threatening injuries. Investigators said two victims may have been shot while coming to the first victim’s aid.

About 11:50 a.m.: A woman was found fatally shot in her car outside a Giant grocery store in the Aspen Hill area.

Manhunt and arrest: Police linked the vehicle seen at the shootings to Tordil (a silver 2015 Hyundai Elantra with Pennsylvania plates) and issued an alert. Officers located his car in a Northgate shopping center parking lot; plainclothes officers kept him under surveillance for roughly an hour while he moved among businesses and ate at a Boston Market. When he returned to his vehicle, officers boxed it in, rammed it, and ordered him out; Tordil surrendered without incident and a weapon was found in the car. He reportedly had threatened “suicide by cop.” No shots were fired during the arrest.

Charges and status: Prince George’s County charged Tordil with first-degree murder and related counts for his wife’s killing and with assault for shooting the Good Samaritan. Montgomery County is pursuing charges related to the mall and grocery-store shootings; as of Friday night he was being interviewed by Montgomery detectives and was to be arraigned in district court.

Community impact: The incidents prompted shelter-in-place orders at Montgomery County schools and temporary lockdowns of businesses and government buildings; all orders were lifted after the arrest. Authorities noted the arrest location’s proximity to sites from the 2002 Beltway sniper case, increasing local alarm. Investigators continue to probe motive and the connections among the three shootings.

China has released hundreds of high-resolution photos, video clips and scientific data from its 2013 Chang'e-3 lunar mission, a rare display of openness from its normally secretive space program. The mission’s rover, Yutu (“Jade Rabbit”), landed December 14, 2013 and became the third unmanned spacecraft to reach the Moon. The rover experienced power and mobility problems within a month—stopping movement on January 25 after 42 days of a planned three-month mission—but continued transmitting observations and data until October of the following year. Although it never covered the intended three square kilometers, Yutu holds the record for the longest operational period of a lunar rover, surpassing the Soviet Lunokhod. The newly released high-definition images reveal detailed views of the lunar surface.

A strong solar flare and associated coronal mass ejection (CME) from sunspot AR2665 in mid-July 2017 is bringing a geomagnetic storm that should make the aurora borealis visible across much of Canada and the northern United States on the night of Sunday, July 16 into Monday morning. The flare produced X-rays that caused a minor radio blackout over parts of Asia and launched a cloud of charged particles; part of that cloud is sweeping past Earth.

NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center issued a geomagnetic storm watch, forecasting mainly G2 (moderate) activity (2/5), with possible brief rises to G3 (strong). Aurora visibility was expected as far south as much of the northern U.S. — including Montana, the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern Illinois, Michigan, northern New York and much of New England — putting cities such as Minneapolis, Chicago, Detroit, Buffalo, Syracuse, Albany and Boston within reach. The timing of peak activity was predicted between about 8 p.m. and 2 a.m. EDT, tapering off by Monday morning.

Tips for viewing: seek dark, clear skies away from light pollution (provincial parks and rural areas recommended), allow 30–40 minutes for eyes to adjust, and avoid bright lights or camera flashes; auroras can be faint or suddenly bright and are often unpredictable.

Summary:

On the GOP debate stage, Brian Williams asked Gov. Rick Perry whether he had ever struggled with the idea that someone put to death might have been innocent, but failed to name Cameron Todd Willingham or present the scientific evidence that later undermined the arson conviction. Perry responded defensively, praising Texas’s capital punishment process and insisting its decisions reflect citizens’ wishes, allowing him to avoid addressing Willingham’s case specifically.

The piece then recounts the Willingham house fire of December 23, 1991, in Corsicana, Texas. Cameron Todd Willingham returned to his burning home and pleaded that his three young children were trapped inside; firefighters recovered the children but all three died of smoke inhalation. Willingham, a young unemployed father, was distraught and restrained by bystanders. The economically depressed community rallied to help with funeral costs.

Investigators Douglas Fogg and deputy fire marshal Manuel Vasquez led the arson inquiry. Vasquez was a highly regarded, confident specialist who believed fires “tell the story” and rarely acknowledged error. The article implies that the original arson investigation and ensuing prosecution rested on interpretations by such experts—interpretations that later scientific analysis would call into question—while noting the failure of media questioning to press Perry on the specific case of a possibly wrongful execution.

A UPS driver who noticed "call 911" written on a package alerted police during a scheduled pickup at a Robertsville, Missouri, home, prompting a response that freed a woman who said she had been beaten, held captive and sexually assaulted. Deputies say 33-year-old James Tyler Jordan had allegedly forced the woman to strip, assaulted her, threatened her with a .45-caliber handgun and made her talk to the driver while he stood behind her with the gun. A 3-year-old child was also in the house; deputies allege the child was locked in a room for hours. Jordan surrendered before a SWAT team entry and was taken into custody without incident. He faces charges including domestic assault, sodomy, felonious restraint, unlawful use of a weapon and endangering the welfare of a child; bond was set at $100,000 cash. The sheriff’s office credited the UPS driver as “a huge help.”

Brad Pitt used the publicity around the Oakland premiere of his new film Moneyball to clarify recent remarks about his marriage to Jennifer Aniston that sparked controversy. Speaking at the Coliseum and later to Matt Lauer on TODAY, Pitt said his original comments had been misconstrued and that he never intended to criticize Aniston. He emphasized that his point was about parenting — that the best thing he did as a father was ensure his children have a good mother — and called Aniston “a dear friend,” saying she didn’t deserve negative spin. Pitt also noted Aniston did not contact him after the Parade quotes came out.

Tabloid coverage pushed the story further: some outlets reported that Aniston’s team “went ballistic,” contacted Pitt’s camp, and “read him the riot act,” prompting his apology. Gossip pieces speculated Pitt might be jealous of Aniston’s new relationship with Justin Theroux, while other pieces framed the flap as routine Hollywood drama. Pitt, meanwhile, stayed focused on Moneyball and downplayed awards talk, saying it’s too soon to dwell on that.

Israeli police arrested a woman after CCTV footage showed her allegedly setting fire to a fuel pump at the Paz gas station on Derech Bethlehem in Jerusalem. According to police, she approached a man who was filling his car, asked for a cigarette, and when he refused she produced a lighter and ignited the pump. The vehicle caught fire within seconds; the driver pulled the burning pump away, and gas station workers extinguished the flames. The driver’s brother had been in the car but was unharmed. The suspect, reported to be in her mid-thirties, was detained shortly after the incident, denied involvement during questioning, and has had her arrest extended by five days while being sent for psychological evaluation.

Two New York City elementary schools recently restricted Rainbow Loom bracelets and kits after the toy craze disrupted school routines. P.S. 87 on the Upper West Side banned both bracelets and kits, citing conflicts and distractions during recess and class; P.S. 107 in Park Slope still allows students to wear bracelets but forbids bringing looms and related supplies after kids began arriving with large bags of bands and equipment. Administrators and some parents said the kits interfered with teaching, created divisions between kids who had them and those who didn’t, and sometimes became obsessive. Other parents criticized the bans as overreactions, arguing Rainbow Looms are inexpensive, creative, and foster collaboration and pride — and noting the activity is popular with both boys and girls, challenging gendered toy norms.

The Rainbow Loom phenomenon—small plastic looms used to weave multicolored rubber-band bracelets—exploded nationwide over the summer. Invented by Cheong-Choon Ng, the kits have spurred a huge online community (YouTube tutorials, patterns) and supply shortages at stores. Reactions nationwide vary: some schools prohibit wearing or trading bracelets, while many allow them with limits (e.g., one bracelet worn at school). Supporters praise the fine motor skill, concentration and cross-gender appeal of the craft; critics say it distracts from learning and can be disruptive.

Sébastien Bras, 46, chef of the famed three-Michelin-starred restaurant Le Suquet in Laguiole, France, has asked the Michelin Guide to remove his restaurant from its next edition because he can no longer bear the pressure that comes with the rating. Bras—who took over the family establishment from his father about a decade ago and whose restaurant earned three stars in 1999—said in a Facebook video and to AFP that he wants to “give a new meaning” to his life, cook with a freer spirit and without the constant anxiety of anonymous inspectors who may appear at any service. He acknowledged he might lose fame but accepts that outcome and cited, as a background concern, the 2003 suicide of chef Bernard Loiseau amid fears about losing stars, though he said he is not in that mental state.

Michelin said it had never before had a chef request exclusion for reasons other than a change of concept or closure and that Bras’s request would be considered but would not automatically lead to removal; a Michelin executive stressed the guide is made for diners, not restaurateurs, and that the scrutiny is part of what drives culinary standards. The move echoes earlier cases where chefs relinquished stars by closing or radically changing their restaurants (e.g., Alain Senderens, Olivier Roellinger), but Bras’s request is notable for seeking delisting while remaining open and keeping the same concept.

A large cache of LinkedIn account credentials tied to the company’s 2012 breach has resurfaced and is being sold on the dark web. A seller using the name “peace” listed a dataset for 5 BTC (about $2,200) that reportedly contains 167 million LinkedIn account records; roughly 117 million of those include both email addresses and passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-1. Security researcher Troy Hunt and the paid breach-search site LeakedSource obtained and sampled the data; LeakedSource says it cracked about 90% of the passwords within 72 hours.

The discovery means the 2012 incident was far larger than the ~6.5 million credentials publicly known at the time. LinkedIn has confirmed the data appears to come from the 2012 theft, says there is no sign of a new breach, and is invalidating exposed passwords and contacting affected members. The company noted it has since adopted stronger protections (salted hashing, email challenges, two-factor authentication) and urged users to enable two-step verification and use strong, unique passwords.

The leaked dataset highlights weak password choices and reuse: common passwords like “123456,” “linkedin,” and “password” appear frequently, and some victims were still using their old passwords years later. Recommended actions for users are to change any old LinkedIn passwords (and any other sites where the same password was reused) and enable two-factor authentication.

The White House is preparing to include, at least conceptually, a fee on large banks in President Obama’s upcoming budget to help recoup taxpayer costs from the financial rescue programs (notably TARP). Administration officials say the exact form is undecided but it will stop short of a financial transactions tax and avoid a compensation tax deemed too evadable. Options under consideration include a levy on bank liabilities (to reflect risk-taking) or on profits; officials want a structure that is hard to pass on to customers and that shields smaller, struggling community banks. The fee would target firms that benefited most and could raise billions to offset losses elsewhere (auto aid, housing programs, AIG), though questions remain about who precisely would be covered and timing; auto companies and AIG are unlikely targets while the proposal would require congressional approval.

The proposal comes amid rising public and political anger over large Wall Street bonuses as banks begin bonus season; lawmakers and the administration are debating bonus taxes or other measures. Banks warn a new levy could reduce lending and be passed to customers, and some employees face liquidity issues because bonuses are increasingly paid in restricted stock.

Separately, New York Fed general counsel Thomas Baxter told Rep. Darrell Issa that Treasury Secretary Tim Geithner had no role or knowledge of AIG disclosure decisions; Issa disputed the narrowness of that account. The White House and Senate Democrats expressed continued confidence in Geithner.

Economic and regulatory context: White House economist Christina Romer said the administration favors more action after disappointing jobs data but still expects recovery to begin by spring. Regulators are taking a stronger role in bank staffing decisions. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission and other hearings will draw testimony from major bank CEOs and regulators this week. Broader coverage notes improving corporate earnings (largely versus weak 2008 comparatives), concerns about China’s fast-rising property market, and continued debate about regulators’ and Fed Chairman Bernanke’s roles during the crisis.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 85, told an audience in New York she hopes to remain on the bench until about age 90 and has already hired clerks for at least two more terms. Speaking after a performance of the play The Originalist — about the late Justice Antonin Scalia, a frequent ideological foil and personal friend — Ginsburg reflected on her working relationship with Scalia, saying their exchanges sharpened her arguments. She discussed recent court politics amid conservative appointments (including Neil Gorsuch and the nomination of Brett Kavanaugh after Anthony Kennedy’s retirement) and defended the Constitution’s gradual broadening of rights, citing Obergefell v. Hodges and her dissent in the 2013 Voting Rights Act decision. Noting the “pendulum” nature of U.S. politics, she emphasized that courts follow social change rather than lead it. The appearance underscored her celebrity status, public recognition, and continued role as a leading liberal voice on the Court.

An online hunting controversy erupted after American hunting-show host Larysa Switlyk posted photos from an Islay, Scotland trip showing her and companions posing with dead wild goats. The images prompted widespread condemnation on social media — users called them “disgraceful” and “sickening” — and drew responses from Scottish leaders. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon and Environment Secretary Roseanna Cunningham said the reaction was understandable, noted that hunting goats and deer is legal in Scotland, and said they would review whether legal changes are needed.

The incident fed into a larger, ongoing debate over trophy hunting. Critics point to a string of high-profile cases (most famously the 2015 killing of Cecil the lion) and to online displays of trophies by wealthy hunters as evidence that paid big-game hunting is ethically dubious and damaging to wildlife. Defenders argue hunting can provide economic benefits — a 2015 report cited country sports tourism bringing about £155 million (~$200 million) annually to Scotland — and can serve conservation or herd-management purposes in places where predators are absent and hunting revenue supports reserves.

Switlyk, a former California accountant who hosts “Larysa Unleashed,” defended her actions on Instagram as connecting with nature and conservation, and said she would be offline for a while; critics replied that killing animals contradicts that claim. The episode highlights tensions between cultural attitudes, legal frameworks, economic incentives, and conservation arguments surrounding hunting and trophy displays.

Robin DiMaggio, a 47-year-old professional drummer and former musical director for United Nations events and “The Arsenio Hall Show,” was arrested on a federal wire-fraud charge after prosecutors say he misappropriated $750,000 meant for a charity concert to benefit homeless and displaced children.

Key points:
- The Bulgaria-based Peace for You Peace for Me Foundation’s financial sponsor wired $750,000 in August 2016 to an account controlled by DiMaggio as a guarantee for artist deposits. DiMaggio had told the foundation he would place the funds in escrow and secure high-profile performers for a Sofia benefit concert.
- Prosecutors allege DiMaggio never opened an escrow account. Instead he deposited the money into his personal bank account and used it for cars, credit-card debt, living expenses, and to buy a Calabasas home for his ex-wife (about $251,370). He also transferred $150,000 to his company, DiMagic Entertainment, Inc.
- None of the funds were paid to artists. When the sponsor demanded a return, DiMaggio allegedly claimed deposits had been sent to artists and later suggested postponing the event; he also at one point told investigators a third party had used his email to withdraw funds, though he admitted using some money for the home.
- Civil actions followed: the sponsor sued in 2016, DiMaggio filed for bankruptcy, and a $1.2 million summary judgment was awarded in bankruptcy court though not yet formally entered at the time of reporting.
- The FBI investigated the matter. DiMaggio was released on bond with a tracking device; if convicted of wire fraud he faces up to 20 years in federal prison.

Background: DiMaggio has a long music career, having performed or recorded with artists such as Paul Simon, David Bowie, Diana Ross, Dr. Dre and others.

Andrew Gillum, the progressive mayor of Tallahassee, won the Florida Democratic gubernatorial primary in an upset, becoming the party’s nominee and putting himself one step from potentially being Florida’s first Black governor. Backed by progressive leaders including Bernie Sanders and outside liberal groups, Gillum prevailed despite raising far less money than several rivals and facing an FBI-related probe into Tallahassee city government that touched associates. He campaigned on Medicare for All, decriminalizing marijuana, abolishing ICE, and other progressive priorities.

On the Republican side, U.S. Rep. Ron DeSantis easily won the GOP nomination after receiving a high-profile endorsement from President Donald Trump, who repeatedly promoted DeSantis and credited his support with helping put the congressman "on the map." DeSantis defeated establishment favorite Adam Putnam and will face Gillum in the November general election, converting the contest into a high-profile referendum on Trump in a pivotal swing state.

The primary night also produced other consequential results: Gov. Rick Scott won the Republican Senate nomination and will challenge Democratic Sen. Bill Nelson in a closely watched race; GOP Kevin Stitt won Oklahoma’s GOP runoff for governor; and in Arizona, Republican Senate primaries—affected by Sen. John McCain’s death—saw candidates align more with Trump than with McCain’s legacy. The outcomes in Florida and Arizona are being watched for signals about national political trends heading into 2020, including turnout among minorities and the strength of Trump’s influence.

Relatives of a family killed in a high‑speed crash that helped expose Toyota safety problems have sued Toyota and a Lexus dealership for product liability and negligence. The suit, filed in San Diego County Superior Court, names Toyota Motor Corp., Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A., other Toyota U.S. entities and El Cajon Luxury Cars, Inc. (Bob Baker Lexus). Plaintiffs include the parents of CHP Officer Mark Saylor, his in‑laws Fe and Cleto Lastrella, and his brother. They seek unspecified damages.

On Aug. 28 the plaintiffs’ suit says a 2009 Lexus ES350 loaned to Officer Saylor for service “began to accelerate on its own” while traveling on State Route 125 near Santee, California. Saylor, his wife Cleofe, their 13‑year‑old daughter Mahala and Cleofe’s brother Christopher Lastrella died after the car reached speeds above 120 mph, struck an SUV, tumbled down an embankment and caught fire. Investigators later concluded a wrongly sized floor mat could have trapped the accelerator, and the plaintiffs contend Saylor was unable to stop the car despite attempts to brake.

The crash prompted Toyota’s large recalls: in late September a 3.8 million‑vehicle recall to address floor‑mat interference and in January a further 2.3 million‑vehicle recall for sticking gas pedals. The case has drawn national attention; Fe Lastrella testified before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee during hearings probing Toyota’s safety issues, and Toyota’s president apologized to Congress and to the Saylor family. Toyota declined to comment on pending litigation. The automaker also faces numerous federal class‑action suits that may be centralized by a judicial panel.

Violent clashes between police, military forces and protesters in Egypt have escalated into the worst unrest since the February uprising that toppled Hosni Mubarak. Demonstrations centered on Tahrir Square in Cairo and spread to cities including Suez, Alexandria and Ismailiya. Protesters—many unaffiliated with political parties—demand an end to prolonged army rule under the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces (SCAF) and reject delays in transferring power to civilians. They accuse the generals of trying to enshrine military autonomy in a new constitution and of perpetuating elements of the old regime.

Over several days of confrontations, security forces used batons, tear gas, birdshot and armored vehicles; witnesses and morgue reports indicate many victims with bullet wounds. Reported death tolls range up to 33 and injuries exceed a thousand. Soldiers and police stormed and briefly cleared Tahrir Square, attacked a makeshift hospital, and clashed with protesters; troops later pulled back and crowds returned. Protesters chanted against Field Marshal Mohamed Hussein Tantawi and the ruling council, and some called for continued sit-ins and wider demonstrations.

Political parties and Islamist groups face tensions about joining protests: the Muslim Brotherhood condemned the crackdown but did not endorse the demonstrations; other Islamist leaders voiced support but urged caution because national parliamentary elections are due to begin. The military refused to postpone the vote and intends to retain key powers until a new constitution is finalized and a president elected, likely in late 2012 or 2013. Activists and secular forces fear the military and Islamists alike; the Brotherhood could win a substantial share of parliamentary seats, deepening polarization.

The unrest has prompted domestic cabinet resignations, international calls for restraint (from the U.S., EU and U.N.), and concern about worsening economic fallout—tourism, investment and currency stability are already strained. The military issued measures aimed at curbing “corrupt” political actors, but activists described them as inadequate. With the army maintaining authority and elections scheduled to proceed, the crisis of legitimacy and public anger suggest continued protests and political volatility ahead.

The piece is a light, humorous take on the viral sites Hipster Puppies and Hipster Kitty, which parody hipster culture by attributing pretentious, trendy tastes and behaviors to pets. The author riffs on the trope—dogs that listen to Radiohead, wear American Apparel, nap on indie magazines, or eat Olive Garden breadsticks “ironically”—and names sample characters from the sites (Clara, Bailey, Cosmo, Daisy) to illustrate the joke. The article notes how the simple formula—combining cute animals with ridicule of hipsters, à la LOLcats and Hipster Bingo—rapidly spread online and explains why such mash-ups become popular: they pair two widely loved (and sometimes mocked) internet obsessions. The tone is playful and self-aware throughout.

A single ticket matching all six numbers won the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot from the Aug. 23, 2017 drawing — the largest grand prize ever won by a single ticket in U.S./North American lottery history. The winning numbers were 6, 7, 16, 23, 26 and Powerball 4. The ticket was sold at the Pride Station & Store on Montgomery Street in Chicopee, Massachusetts; the store will receive a $50,000 commission.

The winner, 53-year-old Mavis Wanczyk of Chicopee, came forward within a day to claim the prize, chose the lump-sum cash option (reported earlier as $443.3 million before taxes) and said she planned to retire and keep a low profile. Wanczyk said she discovered the win after comparing numbers with a coworker as she left work.

The Massachusetts State Lottery initially misidentified a Watertown convenience store as selling the jackpot ticket; that shop did sell a $1 million winning ticket, and another $1 million ticket was sold in Dorchester. Lottery officials attributed the error to human transcription mistakes when recording retailer names. Powerball officials also noted six other tickets won $2 million and 34 more won $1 million in the drawing. Local police said they would keep an extra eye on Wanczyk following her public claim.

A Michigan GOP-funded campaign mailer asked voters to call Democratic state House candidate Rev. John Fisher to complain about the Affordable Care Act, but directed them to a phone number that actually connects to Fisher’s 91-year-old mother, Isabel Kramb, who is in hospice care at a Portage nursing home. Fisher’s campaign said the number is listed under his name in an online directory but rings his mother’s room; they called the tactic beyond the pale and asked Republican opponent Brandt Iden to denounce the party’s actions. Iden said he did not condone the GOP’s tactics and that the mailer was not from his campaign. The Michigan Republican Party acknowledged responsibility and apologized, saying it did not intend for people to reach Fisher’s mother. Local reporters confirmed the number is publicly listed and that Kramb has received calls intended for her son.

Researchers tracing HIV’s genetic history conclude the global AIDS pandemic began in 1920s Kinshasa (then Leopoldville) in what is now the Democratic Republic of Congo. An international team led by Oxford and Leuven analyzed hundreds of archived HIV sequences with phylogeographic methods and combined the genetic “family tree” with historical data to date and map the virus’s early spread. Their work shows HIV-1 group M—the single cross-species transmission that became pandemic—was present in Kinshasa in the 1920s and then spread via rail and river networks to other Congolese cities (including Mbuji-Mayi, Lubumbashi and Kisangani) between the late 1930s and early 1950s.

The researchers argue a “perfect storm” of factors in Kinshasa enabled the jump from isolated infections to a sustained epidemic: rapid urban population growth and a male-skewed labor force that expanded the sex trade; extensive colonial transport links moving roughly a million people through the city annually; and unsafe medical practices (notably reuse of unsterile needles) that could have amplified transmission. Although multiple simian-to-human transmissions of related viruses occurred in central Africa, only group M expanded globally—likely because these social, demographic and infrastructural conditions favored its sustained spread. Experts call the study a detailed, persuasive reconstruction of HIV’s early pandemic phases, while acknowledging some causal elements remain necessarily inferential.

Reports of forcible sexual assaults on U.S. college campuses have risen sharply in recent years, but experts say the increase likely reflects greater reporting rather than a sudden spike in incidents. NPR’s analysis of Department of Education data found a 49% rise in reported forcible rapes at four-year colleges from 2008 to 2012. The DoE reported a roughly 50% increase in campus forcible sex crimes from 2,200 in 2001 to 3,300 in 2011. Similar upticks were documented by other investigations.

Advocates view higher reporting as a positive sign that survivors feel safer coming forward and are getting institutional support. Campaigns such as bystander training, clearer consent education and improved investigatory procedures—along with pressure from students and new federal guidance and laws (including the Campus SaVE Act)—have encouraged schools to address sexual assault more seriously. The University of Michigan, which expanded prevention education and investigations, saw reported incidents jump 113% from 2010–2012; administrators say that increased awareness and responsiveness naturally raise reported numbers.

Still, challenges remain: many assaults continue to go unreported, investigative processes can be slow or opaque, and schools have been criticized for handling high-profile cases poorly. Surveys suggest prevalence of sexual violence on campus is far higher than official police-report-based rates, because anonymous studies capture incidents that never reach authorities. Federal and campus reforms aim to improve prevention, reporting and adjudication so survivors receive support and campuses become safer.

An agency nurse accidentally switched off the ventilator of 37-year-old tetraplegic Jamie Merrett at his Wiltshire home in January 2009, an act captured on a camera he had installed after raising concerns about his care. Merrett, who has been ventilator-dependent since a 2002 road accident but previously could speak, use a wheelchair and operate a voice-activated computer, was without the machine for about 21 minutes before paramedics restarted it. He subsequently suffered serious brain damage and now has much reduced cognitive function; his sister says his understanding has regressed to that of a young child.

The nurse, Violetta Aylward, who was supplied by agency Ambition 24hours, has been suspended and is under investigation by the Nursing and Midwifery Council. A confidential Wiltshire social services report, leaked to the BBC, found the agency knew it was required to supply staff trained on ventilator use but lacked adequate systems to verify staff training. NHS Wiltshire Primary Care Trust said it had implemented actions to prevent a recurrence but is limited in comment because litigation is likely. Merrett’s solicitor describes the case as extreme negligence, and the family is considering legal action. The BBC’s Inside Out programme will broadcast the footage.

North Korea’s state media reported that Kim Jong Un has assumed “the supreme commandership” of the armed forces, a transfer of power said to have occurred on October 8 at the request of his father, the late Kim Jong Il. The announcement followed elaborate public mourning ceremonies that elevated Kim Jong Un as the country’s new “supreme leader.”

The powerful National Defence Commission (NDC) issued a blunt statement saying the leadership change does not signal any policy shift: “foolish politicians around the world, including the puppet group in South Korea,” should expect no change from Pyongyang. The NDC declared it would “never deal” with South Korean President Lee Myung-bak and sharply criticized Seoul for allowing only selected private delegations to visit Pyongyang to pay respects. North Korea also denounced leaflet drops by groups in the South and Seoul’s decision to put its military on alert after Kim Jong Il’s death, calling the situation “war‑like” and warning of retaliatory reprisals in strong rhetoric.

Seoul’s Unification Ministry said it regretted Pyongyang’s statement but reaffirmed its commitment to easing inter‑Korean tensions and dialogue. Regionally, governments are watching closely whether the succession will change North Korea’s stance on issues like denuclearization. In response to concerns, the U.S. plans a senior diplomatic visit: Assistant Secretary Kurt Campbell will travel to China, South Korea and Japan in early January to discuss developments related to North Korea and broader regional issues. U.S. and South Korean defense chiefs have emphasized maintaining close cooperation to preserve peace and stability on the peninsula.

Sam’s Club, the Walmart-owned membership warehouse chain, is closing 63 U.S. clubs (plus three in Puerto Rico) as part of a “right‑sizing” of its real estate portfolio aimed at concentrating a stronger, more future‑fit fleet of clubs, CEO John Furner said in a companywide memo. Furner said the company’s review found some locations cannibalized others or were in areas where population growth fell short of expectations; Walmart will try to place affected associates in nearby roles and will provide support and severance where eligible.

Walmart said the closures will produce a charge of about $0.14 per share, mostly hitting fourth‑quarter results, and will provide more details with its Feb. 20 earnings. Analysts expect Sam’s Club to accelerate efforts on e‑commerce, higher‑quality grocery assortments, private‑label marketing and member growth, targeting households with roughly $75,000–$125,000 in annual income. Cowen analyst Oliver Chen framed the moves as preparation for faster, delivery‑driven competition; he noted Sam’s has improved recently but still lags peers like Costco and BJ’s.

The announcement lists affected locations across many states—including multiple closures in Alaska, Illinois and California—and three Puerto Rico clubs. Walmart also recently raised its starting hourly wage (reported elsewhere), and the Sam’s Club cuts are tied to broader restructuring that may include converting some stores to distribution centers.

On a busy Friday morning near the Empire State Building, 58-year-old Jeffrey T. Johnson, a former Hazan Import Co. employee who had a long-running dispute with co-worker Steven Ercolino, fatally shot Ercolino and then confronted two police officers. The officers fired a total of 16 rounds (one fired nine, the other seven) and killed Johnson. Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly said Johnson had pointed a .45-caliber pistol at officers and that at least seven of the officers’ rounds struck the gunman. However, Kelly confirmed that nine bystanders were wounded by police gunfire—either by direct hits, bullet fragments, or shrapnel from ricochets—and not by shots from Johnson. Three people sustained direct gunshot wounds and six were hit by fragments; six were treated and released the same day and three remained hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries.

Witnesses described the encounter as extremely brief and chaotic; surveillance video shows Johnson draw and aim as officers approach, then collapse after being shot. Victims included commuters, a Bronx mother of two, and a tour guide; several did not realize immediately they had been hit. Some bystanders criticized the officers’ accuracy and tactics, while police and experts emphasized the split-second nature of such confrontations and that courts typically side with officers who use deadly force when pursuing an armed suspect.

Background details: Johnson, who legally purchased the handgun in Florida in 1991 but had no New York carry permit, reportedly lost his job the previous year and kept confronting Ercolino, who had filed prior complaints about him. The shootings prompted street closures and renewed debate over police shooting protocol in crowded urban areas; NYPD policy states officers should avoid firing when it would unnecessarily endanger bystanders, though officials said the officers “had absolutely no choice.”
