Uber Technologies Inc. has confidentially filed its S-1 registration for an initial public offering with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, according to people familiar with the matter. The move puts Uber in close competition with smaller rival Lyft, which also filed an S-1 and is reportedly targeting a March or April debut. Both IPOs are expected to be among the largest in a wave of offerings planned for 2019 as ride-hailing companies race to be first to market.

Lieutenant Scott Sears, a 27-year-old officer in the 1st Battalion Royal Gurkha Rifles and brother-in-law of tennis star Andy Murray, completed a solo, unsupported trek to the South Pole on Christmas Day. Over about 38 days he skied and hauled a sled across roughly 700–702 miles of Antarctic plateau, crevasse fields and glaciers in temperatures around −50°C and winds up to 150 mph. He arrived more than 12 days earlier than expected and described hitting a severe physical and mental wall with about 38 km to go before recovering after food and music. Guinness World Records has not yet confirmed his claim to be the youngest person to reach the Pole solo. Sears, who played tennis internationally until age 19 before joining the Army, raised over £30,000 (reported as about £33,500) for the Gurkha Welfare Trust to help rebuild schools in Gorkha, Nepal, after the 2015 earthquake. He said the achievement followed two years of planning and training and that the experience would take time to sink in after nearly six weeks alone in a tent.

Summary:

Kenneth Starr, a New York investment adviser to celebrities and wealthy clients, was arrested at his Manhattan apartment and charged in federal court with running at least a $30 million fraud involving wire fraud, investment-adviser fraud and money laundering. Authorities say Starr ran a complex scheme since early 2008 that siphoned and misappropriated client funds for personal use (including a $7.5 million Manhattan apartment purchase) and operated like a Ponzi scheme, using some clients’ money to repay others. The criminal complaint names a network of associates including Starr’s son and wife, former New York City council president Andrew Stein (who was charged with lying to the IRS but released on $250,000 bail), an unidentified former national political official, and a partner at a major law firm.

Prosecutors allege numerous high-profile clients or targets of the fraud—described anonymously in filings as “an actress,” “an elderly heiress,” “a retired prominent basketball player,” and “a jeweler.” Lawyers and reporting have since associated some victims with real names: heiress Rachel Mellon’s lawyer said she was shocked; jeweler Jacob Arabov and his wife say they were defrauded and recorded conversations with Starr; and media reports and insiders indicate actress Uma Thurman and former talent-executive Jim Wiatt may have been among clients questioned. Other celebrities previously linked to Starr in civil suits or reporting include Martin Scorsese, Mike Nichols, Neil Simon, Diane Sawyer, Hal Prince, Wesley Snipes and Annie Leibovitz, some of whom withdrew funds amid suspicions.

Court details include agents finding Starr hiding in a dark closet during the arrest; Starr was detained without bail as a flight risk and his attorney said they would appeal. The U.S. Attorney characterized some clients as “pawns” in the scheme. The Securities and Exchange Commission has also filed a civil action against Starr and associates. The cases are being prosecuted in the Southern District of New York (USA v. Kenneth Starr and Andrew Stein) and in a parallel SEC matter.

On Oct. 10, 2017 the U.S. Men’s National Team suffered a historic collapse, losing 2-1 to already-eliminated Trinidad & Tobago and failing to qualify for the 2018 World Cup — the first time the United States will miss the tournament since 1986. The defeat, sealed on the CONCACAF Hexagonal’s final day, erased three decades of progress in U.S. men’s soccer and sparked immediate outrage and calls for leadership change.

Key facts and context
- The U.S. needed only a draw in Couva but conceded two first-half goals (an Omar Gonzalez own goal and a long-range strike) and managed a solitary Christian Pulisic goal in the second half. They finished fifth in the hexagonal; Mexico, Costa Rica and Panama took automatic spots, Honduras goes to an intercontinental playoff.
- Other results — Mexico losing late to Honduras and Panama defeating Costa Rica (on a controversial “phantom” goal) — combined with the U.S. loss to eliminate the team.
- The loss has broad repercussions: damage to the sport’s momentum in the U.S., financial implications for broadcasters (Fox paid large sums for 2018/2022 World Cup rights expecting U.S. games), and blows to the reputations of players, coaches and administrators.

Accountability and fallout
- Immediate blame was directed at multiple levels:
  - Players: Numerous individual errors, poor performances across qualifying, an aging core (Tim Howard, Michael Bradley, Clint Dempsey) and inconsistent strike options left the team short.
  - Coaching: Bruce Arena was criticized for selection and tactical choices (notably starting Omar Gonzalez over in-form Geoff Cameron and favoring attack when a draw would suffice). He was expected to be dismissed.
  - Administration: U.S. Soccer president Sunil Gulati faced scrutiny for hiring decisions (Jurgen Klinsmann earlier) and for perceived underinvestment or mismanagement of youth development.
  - Systemic issues: Critics highlighted structural problems in U.S. player development — a pay-to-play youth model that limits the talent pool, weak scouting, uneven coaching, and a “missing” 23–27 age cohort — as root causes.

Controversy over Panama’s first goal
- Panama’s opening goal against Costa Rica appeared not to cross the line. Without goal-line technology, the score stood; some suggested CONCACAF or FIFA appeals could be pursued, but overturning match results is unlikely.

Longer-term implications
- Missing the World Cup denies U.S. soccer a major global showcase that has historically driven participation, fandom and commercial growth (examples cited: the 2010 Donovan winner and 2014 Brooks goal). The absence could set back momentum, youth inspiration, and broadcast/marketing value for years.
- Many commentators argued this failure exposes the need for a reboot: overhaul youth development, broaden talent ID, and restructure how the national program is run. The immediate cycle gives the U.S. four years to rebuild ahead of 2022.

Overall assessment
- The elimination was framed as the most embarrassing moment in U.S. soccer history — a complex failure with multiple culprits from players to federation leadership and underlying structural flaws in American soccer development. While it may spur necessary reforms, the immediate consequence is lost opportunity for growth and the need for a comprehensive rebuild.

Newly released police, medical and investigative documents in the killing of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin flesh out the contested sequence of events and investigators’ early views of the case.

Key facts and evidence
- George Zimmerman (28), a neighborhood-watch volunteer, is charged with second-degree murder for fatally shooting Martin on Feb. 26. Zimmerman says he shot Martin in self‑defense after the taller teen attacked him during a confrontation; Zimmerman has pleaded not guilty.
- Two police officers who arrived at the scene reported Zimmerman had a bloody, possibly broken nose, abrasions on his forehead, a small laceration on the back of his head and grass on his clothing. Investigators note Zimmerman could be heard yelling for help repeatedly on a 911 tape.
- Multiple witnesses (names redacted) described seeing a man on the ground with another person in a hoodie straddling him and throwing punches; one heard a “pop” and then saw the person in the hoodie laid out, consistent with Zimmerman’s account of a close struggle.
- The medical examiner ruled Martin’s death a homicide from a gunshot wound fired from “intermediate range” (within 36 inches; one passage says 1 to 18 inches). The autopsy noted a small abrasion on Martin’s left fourth finger, suggesting a struggle.
- Toxicology found THC and a marijuana metabolite in Martin’s system at low levels; experts cautioned those findings don’t indicate intoxication and can persist or redistribute after death.
- Video of Martin buying Skittles before the incident was released. Records also show Martin had been suspended from school earlier for nonviolent offenses; his family says the THC was a trace amount.

Investigative and prosecutorial context
- A March 13 “capias request” from police urged prosecutors to arrest Zimmerman, criticizing his decision to follow Martin contrary to the dispatcher’s instruction and calling the encounter “ultimately avoidable.” The request emphasized there was no indication Martin was engaged in criminal activity.
- Controversies persist about evidence interpretation: FBI audio analysis could not definitively identify alleged racial language on a 911 call or conclusively determine whether screams on bystander calls were Martin’s or Zimmerman’s because of poor audio quality. There is dispute over whether Trayvon’s father initially identified his son’s voice on noisy 911 tapes; his attorney says a later “cleaned” tape showed it was Trayvon.
- The case ignited national debate over racial profiling, gun rights and Florida’s self‑defense/"Stand Your Ground" doctrines. Zimmerman’s arrest came weeks after local police initially declined to charge him, prompting protests and a special prosecutor’s involvement. The trial date has not been set.

The document profiles the Sentinelese, an exceptionally isolated indigenous people living on North Sentinel Island in the Andaman archipelago. Likely direct descendants of some of the earliest humans leaving Africa up to ~60,000 years ago, the Sentinelese have resisted outside contact for millennia and number perhaps 50–200. They survived the 2004 tsunami and repeatedly repel outsiders with arrows; their hostility is framed as a defensive response to a history of violent, exploitative and disease-causing contacts with outsiders (colonial kidnappings, shipwreck salvagers, epidemics, and later exploitation of other Andaman tribes).

Anthropologists and Indian authorities have oscillated between contact attempts and a policy of non‑interference. Early expeditions met with arrows; later gift-based approaches in the 1970s–1990s led to rare, cautious interactions but no sustained integration. The tribe is described as healthy, alert and self-sufficient—living in small palm shelters, hunting turtles, fish, pigs and monitor lizards, using iron salvaged from wrecks for arrow tips, and keeping fire they did not learn to make. They lack agriculture, formal chiefs or witchdoctors; their language, counting and songs are highly distinctive, reinforcing long isolation.

Incidents recounted include the 2006 killing of two illegal fishermen who drifted to the island—attempts to recover their bodies were frustrated by Sentinelese resistance and controversy over whether outsiders should respect the islanders’ exclusion zone. The piece contrasts the Sentinelese’s relative well‑being with the demographic collapse and dependency of other Andaman tribes (Onge, Great Andamanese, Jarawa) after contact. It outlines the ethical and practical dilemma facing officials and scientists: whether and how to protect the Sentinelese from harm and disease while preserving their autonomy, acknowledging that past contact has often brought devastation. The prevailing contemporary stance urged by activists and many officials is to respect the tribe’s desire for isolation and to enforce exclusion to let them decide their own future.

These leaked military and intelligence files, published by news organizations after being obtained by WikiLeaks, portray a bleak, complicated picture of the Afghan war and of Pakistan’s role in it.

Key findings about Pakistan and the ISI
- Multiple reports allege that elements of Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) have cooperated with Taliban and Al Qaeda figures—sometimes to plan or facilitate attacks in Afghanistan. Some accounts describe ISI officers or former ISI chiefs meeting insurgent and Arab extremists and helping to recruit, train, move or protect fighters and suicide bombers.
- Experts and U.S. officials caution that proving direct, centralized ISI orchestration is difficult; the agency’s hierarchical nature and plausible deniability (notably via the autonomous “S Wing” and retired operators who retain networks) complicate attribution.
- Senior U.S. military and administration officials repeatedly confronted Pakistani leaders about suspected ISI ties to militants, sometimes presenting lists of suspected operatives. Pakistani leaders and the ISI have routinely denied current complicity and said the leaked documents misrepresent realities.
- The files highlight longstanding U.S. frustration with Pakistani forces’ unwillingness or failure to stop cross-border insurgent movement: militants allegedly attacked from near Pakistani positions, moved truckloads across the frontier, and retreated into Pakistani tribal areas where they found sanctuary.
- Prominent Pakistani figures named in the logs include former ISI chief Lt. Gen. (ret.) Hamid Gul, who is depicted as maintaining and reactivating old mujahedeen/Taliban networks and meeting insurgent and Arab leaders. Gul denies the allegations.

Operational details from the logs
- The records contain detailed, sometimes granular accounts of plots and networks: recruitment and training cycles for suicide bombers in Pakistan, planned truck- and vehicle-borne attacks into Afghanistan, and coordination of larger offensives timed to exploit border geography.
- Some reports connect ISI operatives to the planning or facilitation of specific attacks or offensives (for example, meetings in Quetta urging attacks in Kandahar and detailed threat warnings about suicide operations). In some instances the planned attacks did occur; in others the outcome is unclear.
- The files mix credible, corroborated reporting with material that U.S. analysts regarded as less reliable or possibly disinformation, and occasionally include implausible-sounding plots (e.g., poisoned alcohol or a remote-controlled bomb disguised as a golden Koran).

Wider revelations about the Afghan war
- The trove includes more than 90,000 incident and intelligence reports from 2004–2009 and gives a granular account of fighting, intelligence operations, and failures.
- They portray coalition shortcomings—rising Taliban attacks (notably a huge escalation in roadside bombs), the use of secret special forces “black” units for kill-or-capture missions, and increasing reliance on armed drones.
- The logs document civilian harm and alleged cover-ups: multiple “blue on white” incidents (coalition forces killing civilians), detailed cases of civilian casualties from air strikes and ground fire, and accounts of other lethal errors by coalition partners. The published excerpts list hundreds of admitted civilian deaths and injuries, though the true toll is likely higher.
- The disclosures also reference serious tactical and intelligence concerns (e.g., Taliban access to surface-to-air missiles) and reveal tensions between NATO/US commanders and neighboring states suspected of fueling the insurgency.

U.S.-Pakistani strategic context and reactions
- Despite the secret reports’ troubling portraits of Pakistani duplicity or at least tolerance for insurgent sanctuaries, U.S. officials publicly continued to emphasize partnership—driven by mutual interests such as counterterrorism operations, drone strikes against Al Qaeda havens, and keeping nuclear-armed Pakistan aligned for logistic routes into Afghanistan.
- The Obama administration and senior U.S. officials publicly urged Pakistan to do more to eliminate militant havens, while continuing military assistance. Congressional members said briefings from U.S. agencies on Pakistani complicity have often been vague, though many lawmakers expressed strong belief Pakistan was aiding insurgents.
- Pakistan’s government and military denied the leaks’ implications; the ISI declined comment pending review and Pakistan’s ambassador to Washington said the documents did not reflect current realities.

Limitations and caveats
- The logs combine validated intelligence, routine reporting, analysts’ judgments, and some items of uncertain credibility; some reports may reflect deliberate disinformation, incomplete information, or misidentifications.
- U.S. officials have found it difficult to produce incontrovertible evidence tying Islamabad’s highest levels to specific attacks, even as patterns in the documents suggest troubling overlaps between Pakistani intelligence actors and militant networks.

Overall impression
- The leaked files portray a war being fought amid deep intelligence ambiguities, growing civilian costs, and strategic friction: U.S. forces and diplomats repeatedly confronted Pakistani counterparts over suspected links between parts of Pakistan’s security apparatus and insurgent groups, while publicly maintaining a working partnership to pursue counterterrorism objectives and preserve regional cooperation.

Researchers at Simon Fraser University have developed an inexpensive, effective chemical lure and trap for detecting and monitoring bedbug infestations after eight years of study. The interdisciplinary team — biologists Regine and Gerhard Gries, chemist Robert Britton, and students — identified a blend of airborne pheromones plus a previously undetected histamine and three novel fecal compounds that together attract bedbugs and then cause them to remain on contact. Regine Gries served as a host to the colony during experiments (reportedly enduring about 180,000 bites) to collect shed skin and feces for analysis. The trap, tested successfully in infested Vancouver apartments, uses the pheromone mix to draw bugs in and histamine on filter paper to keep them there; the chemical components cost under a dime. The work, funded by NSERC with industry partner Contech Enterprises, is published in Angewandte Chemie and is being commercialized, with products expected next year to help early detection and treatment monitoring.

Kanye West has been discharged from UCLA Medical Center and is back home with his wife Kim Kardashian and their children after more than a week of treatment following what sources describe as a mental breakdown. He was admitted on November 22 after showing signs of extreme exhaustion, paranoia and difficulty distinguishing reality; his personal physician, Dr. Michael Farzam, and Kim were involved in his care. Insiders link the episode in part to the emotional aftermath of Kim’s October 3 Paris robbery and the anniversary of Kanye’s mother Donda’s death. Family and friends say he still needs ongoing psychological and medical treatment.

Kanye’s Saint Pablo Tour has been suspended indefinitely; promoters and sources say there’s no set date for a return as he’s in a fragile state, though an insurance policy may cover financial losses from canceled dates. Kim has been by his side throughout the hospitalization, and friends hope the treatment will help both his health and their marriage.

On July 24, the first day New York's same-sex marriage law takes effect, Mayor Michael Bloomberg will officiate the wedding of two of his senior aides — Chief Policy Adviser John Feinblatt and Consumer Affairs Commissioner Jonathan Mintz — who have been together for 14 years and have two daughters. The ceremony will be held at Gracie Mansion. Bloomberg, who has only officiated two weddings while mayor (his daughter’s and Rudy Giuliani’s), said the couple helped him "see the issue of marriage equality in very clear terms" and called the day historic. The city extended City Clerk hours on the Sunday to accommodate couples seeking licenses; New York became the sixth state to legalize same-sex marriage after Gov. Andrew Cuomo signed the bill on June 24.

Saudi billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal was released on January 27, 2018, more than two months after being detained in Saudi Arabia’s wide-ranging anti-corruption purge. A senior official said his release followed a financial settlement approved by the attorney general; terms were not disclosed. The official and other sources indicated some detainees have been freed after settlements while others remain in custody or face trial.

In an interview with Reuters conducted at the Ritz-Carlton hotel hours before his release, Prince Alwaleed denied wrongdoing, called his confinement a “misunderstanding,” and said he expected to retain full control of his global investment vehicle, Kingdom Holding Co. He described his detention conditions as comfortable, said he had communicated with his business executives and family, and voiced support for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s reform efforts. Saudi authorities previously alleged charges against him including money laundering, bribery and extortion; Forbes has estimated his net worth at about $17 billion.

The detentions and subsequent settlements have unsettled foreign investors — Alwaleed’s prominence as an investor in firms such as Twitter and Citigroup heightened those concerns — and Saudi officials appear keen to signal a shift from the crackdown toward broader economic reform. Authorities have suggested they aim to raise substantial sums through settlements, though analysts question how much will be recovered. After his release, Alwaleed said he would remain in Saudi Arabia and continue managing his global investments.

Casey Affleck has withdrawn from presenting the Best Actress award and will not attend the 2018 Oscars, saying he did not want to become a distraction and wanted the focus to remain on the actresses. The move, first reported by Deadline and confirmed by the Academy, came amid renewed scrutiny from the #MeToo movement over settled 2010 lawsuits by two women who worked on Affleck’s film I’m Still Here. The women accused him of sexual harassment and other misconduct; the suits were settled out of court and Affleck has denied the allegations. His lawyer said Affleck originally considered counter-suing. The decision ends the customary practice of the previous year’s Best Actor handing the Best Actress trophy and was seen as a way to avoid creating controversy or awkwardness for the nominees. Public pressure—including petitions and reactions like Brie Larson’s muted applause when Affleck won Best Actor—had highlighted concerns about him presenting onstage.

Caitlyn Jenner unveiled details about choosing her new name and life as a transgender woman in interviews and media appearances following her Vanity Fair cover. She described picking “Caitlyn” as difficult—she considered names like Heather and Cathy, watched Miss America for inspiration, and ultimately chose Caitlyn after her assistant Rhonda independently suggested it; she deliberately used a C rather than a Kardashian-style K. Jenner, formerly Bruce, will also star in E!’s documentary series I Am Cait, which follows her adjusting to life publicly as a woman, learning makeup and wardrobe, and reflecting on gender identity and authenticity. Her mother, Esther Jenner, praised Caitlyn’s debut and said she’s happy though she’ll initially struggle to change how she refers to her child.

Separately, media reports claim Kim Kardashian is privately pregnant with twins after in vitro fertilization; only close family allegedly know and she is waiting to see whether both embryos are viable before announcing. Kim has been keeping a low profile to let Caitlyn have her moment, plans a staged family outing likely to be photographed, and said publicly she’s experiencing morning sickness and laryngitis while asking to be addressed as Mrs. West at an event.

Joshua Holt, a 26-year-old former Mormon missionary from Utah who has been held without charge for two years at Venezuela’s notorious El Helicoide prison, posted emotional cellphone videos and written pleas on Facebook saying his life is in danger amid a prisoner uprising. Holt — detained in 2016 after Venezuelan police said they found weapons in the Caracas apartment he shared with his wife, Thamara Candelo — said he has been “begging” the U.S. government for help and pleaded that fellow Americans not let him “continue suffering.” In posts he described guards attempting to enter his cell and inmates trying to kill him.

The disturbance at El Helicoide, the Caracas headquarters of the intelligence agency SEBIN, was confirmed by videos posted by people identifying themselves as inmates who said they had taken control of parts of the facility to protest torture and human-rights abuses. Venezuelan officials, including Attorney General Tarek William Saab, said a commission was sent to negotiate and later claimed the situation had “normalized,” though inmates and some outside observers disputed that account. The U.S. Embassy in Venezuela warned Holt and other U.S. citizens were in danger and said the Venezuelan government is directly responsible for their safety.

The riot came as Venezuela prepared for a presidential election widely denounced by regional leaders as illegitimate amid a deep economic and humanitarian crisis. Opposition figures jailed at El Helicoide as well as other inmates called for greater public support; authorities denied allegations of torture, extortion, and detention of minors. U.S. diplomats and local sources expressed uncertainty about the true status of control inside the prison.

David Goldberg, 47, the chief executive of online-survey company SurveyMonkey and husband of Facebook Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg, died suddenly Friday night. His brother announced the death on Facebook Saturday morning and Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg shared the post.

A longtime tech entrepreneur, Goldberg sold his first startup, Launch Media, to Yahoo at age 26, then ran Yahoo Music and worked at Benchmark Capital. In 1999 he acquired a small survey firm and built it into SurveyMonkey, a company valued at around a billion dollars.

Goldberg and Sandberg met in Los Angeles in 1996, remained friends while she moved to Washington, D.C., and began dating six years later. He frequently credited her as a trusted sounding board and described their partnership as one where work and family advice are shared freely.

As a leader, Goldberg emphasized work–life balance and leading by example: he and Sandberg sought to leave the office by 5:30 p.m. to be with their children, with work often continued later at night. He encouraged giving employees room to fail so they can learn, kept regularly scheduled meetings to a maximum of three per week to avoid wasted time, and remained accessible for informal conversations.

Saudi Arabia announced it will not take up its newly won non‑permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council, in an unprecedented public rebuke of the Council and the wider international response to Middle East crises. Riyadh cited “double standards” and the Council’s failure to resolve the Israeli‑Palestinian conflict, curb nuclear proliferation in the region (implicitly referencing Israel), or halt Syria’s civil war — especially after the regime of Bashar al‑Assad avoided strikes by agreeing to surrender chemical weapons. The decision signals deep frustration with the Security Council’s inability to act and constitutes a demand for reforms to enable it to “effectively and practically” maintain international peace and security.

The move reflects widening Saudi disillusionment with U.S. policy since the Arab Spring and recent U.S.–Iran rapprochement following President Obama’s phone call with Iran’s new president, Hassan Rouhani. It also coincides with broader regional tensions, including U.S. cuts to aid for Egypt. Within Riyadh, reactions were mixed: some officials and observers saw the withdrawal as a return to Saudi traditional reluctance to occupy high‑profile, public diplomatic roles; others viewed it as a sudden, king‑led slap at the U.N. and the United States. Russia criticized the decision as puzzling. Diplomats do not expect Saudi Arabia to reverse course, and the U.N. has not yet received formal notification or scheduled action to fill the seat.

Rolling Stone’s August 5, 2010 issue features an interview with Leonardo DiCaprio in which the actor opens up about his anxiety, early fame, and the losses among his peers. Fresh from the success of Inception, DiCaprio says he still gets irrational stomach-churning worries over small, arbitrary things and must consciously tell himself to stop stressing. He reflects on the wild period after Titanic, saying he “got to be wild and nuts” for a few years but avoided the more destructive excesses that ruined some young stars’ lives. He contrasts his choices with the tragic fates of contemporaries—noting that two blond peers he’d auditioned with, Jonathan Brandis and River Phoenix, died young—saying he never got into drugs or self-destructive behavior. He also observes that Titanic changed his dating life, as interactions with women became colored by his fame. The full interview and more are available to Rolling Stone All Access subscribers.

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas announced he will seek full UN membership for a Palestinian state when he addresses the UN General Assembly on Sept. 23 and will take the bid to the UN Security Council. He said the request seeks recognition of a state within the pre-1967 borders (East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza), not immediate independence on the ground, and stressed the move aims to strengthen negotiations on final-status issues (Jerusalem, borders, refugees, prisoners) and to delegitimize Israeli occupation policies rather than Israel itself. Abbas urged peaceful public demonstrations and acknowledged that recognition would not end occupation overnight.

The announcement sets up a diplomatic clash: the United States has signaled it will veto any Security Council resolution granting full membership, arguing statehood must come through direct talks with Israel, while Israel opposes unilateral UN moves and favors keeping many settlers and control over Jerusalem and borders. Arab states and the Arab League broadly back Abbas, but Hamas criticized the effort and banned Gaza demonstrations. U.S. diplomats had tried to dissuade the Palestinians and promote an international statement endorsing President Obama’s negotiation framework, but Palestinians found it insufficient.

Procedurally, Security Council approval (including no veto from any of the five permanent members) is required for full UN membership; the likely U.S. veto means the bid probably will not pass the Council, though delays and alternative diplomatic paths (including a General Assembly route) remain possible. Israeli authorities worry the UN push could spark unrest in the West Bank and have placed IDF forces on alert. Observers warn the move could heighten regional tensions and confrontation rather than revive negotiated peace.

Researchers report that optimism and overall happiness are strongly linked to better cardiovascular health. Multiple analyses — including a large review of more than 200 studies and a specific study of 5,100+ adults from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) — found that people with higher levels of optimism were significantly more likely to meet “ideal” heart-health criteria. In the MESA analysis, the most optimistic participants had about twice the odds of ideal cardiovascular health (measured by the American Heart Association’s Life’s Simple 7: blood pressure, BMI, fasting glucose, cholesterol, diet, physical activity and smoking) compared with the least optimistic, and were 50–76% more likely to have intermediate or ideal total health scores. Optimists showed better blood sugar and cholesterol, were more physically active, had healthier BMIs and smoked less. These associations remained after adjusting for age, race/ethnicity, income, education and poor mental health, suggesting optimism’s link to heart health is not solely due to socioeconomic or behavioral differences. While causality is not established — it’s unclear whether optimism directly protects the heart or reflects healthier lifestyles — investigators note potential biobehavioral mechanisms and suggest that promoting psychological well‑being could be a promising strategy for improving population cardiovascular health.

Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales opened at No. 1 domestically but with weaker-than-expected returns that underscore franchise fatigue. The Johnny Depp-led sequel is estimated to earn $62.2 million over its first three days and about $77–76.6 million across the four-day holiday weekend from 4,276 locations — modest against its reported $230 million production budget. It is the lowest opening for a Pirates film except the original; the series has trended downward in U.S. grosses while remaining highly profitable thanks to massive overseas appeal (an estimated $208.4 million internationally this weekend), pushing global weekend receipts to roughly $270–300 million. Disney’s distribution chief stressed the franchise’s continued global resonance; the series has generated over $4 billion worldwide.

Paramount’s Baywatch, starring Dwayne Johnson and Zac Efron, underperformed, projected at about $18.1 million for the three-day and $22 million for the four-day frame against a budget above $60 million. Poor reviews (around 19% on Rotten Tomatoes) likely hurt the film, and Paramount hopes international grosses will help. Baywatch’s weak start adds to a string of misses for Paramount this year.

Other box office notes: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 continued strong, adding roughly $19–24 million this weekend and nearing $340 million domestically; Alien: Covenant is expected to finish fourth with about $13.1 million in its second weekend; and the YA film Everything, Everything should deliver around $7.6 million. Milestones this weekend included Fate of the Furious topping $1 billion overseas, Beauty and the Beast passing $500 million domestically, and Disney becoming the first studio to clear $1 billion in 2017 so far.

A standoff threatened Friday between Occupy Wall Street protesters and the NYPD after the city and Brookfield Properties — which owns privately controlled-but-public Zuccotti Park — announced the plaza would be temporarily closed for power-washing and sanitation. Officials said protesters could return afterward but would not be allowed to bring back tents, sleeping bags and tarps. Protesters called the move a pretext for eviction, vowed to resist, and organized an early-morning human chain to “defend the occupation,” warning it could lead to mass arrests.

Brookfield cited allegedly unsanitary and unsafe conditions; Mayor Bloomberg and Police Commissioner Ray Kelly backed enforcement of rules banning camping gear. Protest leaders and civil liberties lawyers countered that an on-site sanitation crew has been cleaning the park since the occupation began and that protesters had stepped up efforts — sweeping, filling buckets from nearby businesses, renting power washers (which were unusable due to lack of water), hiring sanitation workers and allocating $3,000 from donations for cleaning supplies. Union leaders and several city council members publicly supported the protesters and urged the mayor not to evict them. The dispute raised concerns that arrests or forceful removal could amplify public sympathy and attention for the movement.

Noel Cintron, who served as Donald Trump’s personal driver for roughly 25–30 years until the Secret Service took over in 2016, has sued the Trump Organization in Manhattan state court alleging unpaid overtime, inadequate raises and other wage violations.

Key claims:
- Cintron says he was paid a fixed salary that rose only twice over more than a decade: $62,700 (2003), $68,000 (2006) and $75,000 (2010).
- He alleges the 2010 increase was conditioned on surrendering his health insurance, which the suit says saved the company about $17,866 a year.
- He claims to have worked roughly 3,300 hours of unpaid overtime during his last six years on the job and seeks about $200,000 in damages (including roughly $178,000 calculated for overtime).
- He also alleges the Trump Organization failed to provide annual wage notices required under New York law.
- Cintron’s suit is limited to the most recent six years by the statute of limitations.

The Trump Organization disputed the claims, saying Cintron “was at all times paid generously and in accordance with the law” and expects to be vindicated in court. The case is Cintron v. Trump Organization LLC, Supreme Court, State of New York (Manhattan).

Spanish authorities say remains found on a rural property in northwest Spain are likely those of Denise Thiem, a 41-year-old American from Arizona who went missing April 5 while walking the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route. Interior Minister Jorge Fernández Díaz said evidence points to the remains being Thiem’s and that there are “well‑founded suspicions” the prime suspect arrested this week, Miguel Ángel Muñoz, is responsible for her death. Muñoz was arrested in Grandas de Salime, Asturias, after investigators led to his small farm; officials said the suspect was little known locally. The search, which at one point involved about 300 police and military personnel, helicopters and FBI cooperation, focused on the area around Astorga, where Thiem was last seen. Spanish TV aired footage of a bearded man in his 30s being taken into custody; U.S. Embassy officials declined to comment. Thiem’s disappearance raised safety concerns about the popular Camino, which draws tens of thousands of pilgrims and hikers each year.

Thousands gathered in Soho on Monday night to honor the 49 victims of the Orlando Pulse nightclub shooting. The vigil on Old Compton Street drew LGBT people, supporters and public figures including Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and London Mayor Sadiq Khan. Attendees held Pride banners and observed a silence before releasing 49 rainbow balloons — one for each person killed — amid applause and cheering. The London Gay Men's Chorus performed Simon & Garfunkel’s "Bridge Over Troubled Water" for the emotional crowd. Vigils like this have been held worldwide in the aftermath of the attack.

Rush Limbaugh told the author he recently urged listeners to call Congress about health care legislation — a rare move for him. He noted he almost never directs coordinated political action from his show and recalled one prior instance in the 1990s when he gave out the Capitol switchboard to prove how quickly it would be overwhelmed. He said the numbers he provided this time were similarly tied up, requiring alternate toll-free and toll-call numbers. When asked why he was taking this step now, Limbaugh said the situation is urgent ("This is ball game") because Republicans lack the votes to stop the bill and the American people must make their opposition heard about both the substance and the process. He framed the legislation as a transformational threat to the country, saying listeners want to preserve America "as it was founded" and avoid turning it into a "third world country." He also acknowledged that answering on air would cost the author exclusivity, but that getting the message out was the priority.

A New Jersey couple, Kathryn M. Schurtz, 35, and her fiancé Joseph D. Kearney, were killed Wednesday afternoon in a fiery, chain-reaction crash on westbound I‑78 in Windsor Township, Berks County, while driving to their wedding in Pittsburgh. Heavy traffic from an earlier collision had slowed vehicles; a westbound tractor‑trailer was unable to stop and struck the couple’s car, pushing it into the rear of another tractor‑trailer and triggering collisions with three additional trucks. The couple’s vehicle and two tractor‑trailers caught fire. Three other people were injured.

Schurtz, a Jersey City resident originally from Fanwood, was a Union Catholic High School alum, graduate of George Washington University and holder of an MBA from Notre Dame. She worked as Head of Platform Partnerships for Oracle Data Cloud. Visitation services will be held at Immaculate Heart of Mary R.C. Church in Scotch Plains; donations may be made to the Kathryn M. Schurtz Scholarship Fund at Union Catholic High School.

The crash shut I‑78 for hours between Hamburg and Lenhartsville, caused major diversions onto local roads and strained volunteer emergency crews, who worked through the night to clear wreckage and assist investigators.

Eli Manning returned from Disney World to join the New York Giants' Super Bowl XLVI victory parade in Manhattan. The procession began at Battery Place and Washington Street, moved up through the Canyon of Heroes, and concluded at City Hall Plaza where Mayor Michael Bloomberg presented the team with the Key to the City. All Giants players participated and large crowds lined the route. Ongoing coverage included photos, quotes and videos. Separately, some returned soldiers questioned holding such celebratory events amid ongoing conflicts—arguing it could imply the U.S. considers the wars finished—while others noted that honoring service members need not wait until wars end, a point highlighted by Leslie Gelb of the Council on Foreign Relations.

Attorney General Eric Holder said the Obama administration will soon issue federal guidance to make it easier for banks to serve state-legal marijuana businesses. Holder told an audience at the University of Virginia that getting large amounts of cash out of dispensaries and growers and into the banking system is a public‑safety and law‑enforcement priority. He said the Treasury and Justice Departments are developing rules or guidance “very soon,” though the Justice Department later clarified he meant guidance for prosecutors and federal law enforcement rather than legally binding protections for banks.

Banks have largely shunned marijuana businesses for fear of violating federal law and money‑laundering statutes, leaving many dispensaries operating on large cash reserves that create security and operational problems (no loans, difficulty paying bills or keeping accounts). Industry and banking groups say they need detailed assurances — more than a nonbinding memo — before they will provide routine services. Holder did not specify whether the guidance would cover only states that legalized recreational use (Colorado, Washington) or also those allowing medical marijuana. The move follows the administration’s earlier decision not to block Colorado’s and Washington’s legalization measures and reflects an effort to address the practical tensions between state legalization and federal prohibition.

North Korea fired short-range missiles into the Sea of Japan (East Sea) over the weekend, according to South Korean reports and defense officials. On Saturday Pyongyang launched three short-range guided missiles in a northeasterly direction away from South Korean waters, and on Sunday fired another similar missile from its east coast. South Korea has increased monitoring and remains on high alert.

Short-range guided missiles travel less than about 1,000 km; analysts say such launches are routine for other countries but attract concern because they come from North Korea. Regional tensions have eased compared with a period last month when Pyongyang issued near-daily threats and officials feared tests of longer-range Musudan missiles (estimated range ~3,500 km). The recent flare-up followed North Korea’s December long-range rocket launch and a February underground nuclear test, and was compounded by tightened U.N. sanctions and large U.S.-South Korea military drills.

International reactions included U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon expressing concern and urging North Korea to refrain from further launches and return to stalled nuclear talks. South Korea’s Unification Ministry called the tests deplorable and urged de-escalation and talks over the suspended Kaesong industrial complex, which was closed after both sides withdrew workers amid the crisis.

Israeli air and artillery strikes on Gaza and intensified rocket fire from militants escalated into the deadliest confrontation between Israel and Gaza militants in years. Israel launched Operation Pillar of Defense on Wednesday, killing Hamas military commander Ahmed Jabari, and over several days struck hundreds of targets across the Gaza Strip. Hamas and other Gaza groups responded with an unprecedented barrage—including rockets aimed toward Tel Aviv and, for the first time in decades, alarms in Jerusalem (one rocket reportedly landed in the West Bank). Casualties and damage: Gaza health officials reported dozens killed (reports vary around 29–30 dead, including many civilians and children) and hundreds wounded; Israel reported several civilian deaths (including three in Kiryat Malachi) and dozens of injuries from rocket attacks. Israel said hundreds of rockets were fired from Gaza, many intercepted by the Iron Dome system.

In response, Israel’s cabinet authorized mobilizing up to 75,000 reservists (about 16,000 had already been called), moved heavy forces to the border, and restricted key roads near Gaza—steps seen as preparing for a possible ground invasion. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu convened extended strategy meetings; officials said the mobilization did not automatically mean all reserves would be called up.

Regional and international reactions: Egypt’s Islamist government sent Prime Minister Hesham Kandil to Gaza and pledged to mediate a truce and provide humanitarian support; President Mohamed Morsi denounced the strikes and recalled Egypt’s ambassador to Israel. The United States and other Western allies backed Israel’s right to self-defense while pressing for de-escalation and urging contacts with Hamas to stop rocket fire. The U.N. and many nations expressed concern over civilian casualties; the Non-Aligned Movement condemned Israel’s actions.

Context and risks: The flare-up followed months of increasing rocket attacks from Gaza and came amid sensitive regional dynamics after Egypt’s political shift and the broader Arab Spring. Observers warned the confrontation could widen quickly and recalled the heavy toll of the 2008–09 Gaza war if a ground offensive occurs. Diplomatic efforts (including planned visits by the U.N. secretary-general and other delegations) aimed to halt the violence, but at the time of reporting no durable cease-fire had been reached.

A Florida woman, 26-year-old Felicia Nevins, says the Pasco County Sheriff’s Office publicly detailed a private incident on Facebook after she called for help storing sperm with dry ice for at-home artificial insemination. Nevins told deputies she had forgotten to remove a rubber O‑ring from a thermos, creating a risk the container could explode; responders safely removed and opened it and treated the matter privately. The sheriff’s office posted a brief account (with a stock photo) describing the unusual, potentially dangerous call. Although Nevins was not named, she says the post included enough identifying details—age, location and timing—that reporters and neighbors were able to identify her; a TV crew later came to her home. The post was widely shared and drew many rude comments, prompting Nevins to say she feels humiliated and exposed, including that medical information became public. The sheriff’s office defended the post as part of its social-media strategy and a way to share safety information, adding it does not publish names and that identifying details became available through public-records requests and media reporting. Nevins has asked that the post be removed and said she will unfollow the department’s Facebook page. The episode has drawn attention to Pasco’s prolific and sometimes controversial use of social media to publicize police calls.

French nuclear safety institute IRSN says a significant release of the radioactive isotope ruthenium‑106 detected across Europe in late September/early October 2017 most likely came from an accident at a nuclear fuel‑treatment facility or a centre for radioactive medicine in the region between the Urals and the Volga (southern Ural area) — i.e., most plausibly Russia or possibly Kazakhstan. IRSN ruled out a nuclear‑reactor accident (which would have produced other radionuclides) and the crash of a ruthenium‑powered satellite. 

European monitoring networks measured trace but widespread ruthenium‑106 with peak detections in early October and steady decline after Oct. 6; by mid‑October it was no longer detected in France. IRSN estimates the release magnitude at about 100–300 terabecquerels and places the likely release during the last week of September 2017. Were such an event to have occurred in France, local protective actions (sheltering/evacuation) within a few kilometres would have been required; food contamination above legal limits could occur within a few tens of kilometres of the source. However, IRSN assesses that concentrations recorded in Europe posed no health or environmental consequences and that the risk of contaminated food imports (e.g., mushrooms) into France is extremely low. Russian authorities have said they are unaware of an accident; IRSN had not contacted Kazakh authorities.

7-Eleven will begin selling ready-to-drink Soylent at 18 stores in the greater Los Angeles area starting Monday, July 10. This is Soylent’s first placement in traditional brick-and-mortar retail (previously sold only through its website and Amazon) and is described by both companies as the first step in Soylent’s retail distribution plan.

The test rollout will offer three flavored bottled varieties—Cacao, Cafe Coffiest and a new Cafe Chai—positioned as convenient, nutritionally complete meal replacements for on-the-go, millennial customers. 7-Eleven and Soylent executives framed the move as expanding demand beyond e-commerce; no pricing details were provided (a case of 12 bottles sells for $39 online).

Background context: Soylent (Rosa Labs/Rosa Foods) is a Silicon Valley–born meal-replacement brand known for powdered and ready-to-drink products geared toward efficiency-minded consumers. The product has a somewhat mixed reputation—comments about its taste and reports of digestive issues (and several recalls in recent history) have circulated among users—so retail exposure may broaden appeal but also bring more scrutiny. The companies did not announce plans to expand beyond Los Angeles.

Hillary Clinton’s campaign on Wednesday released a letter from her physician, Dr. Lisa Bardack, detailing a recent diagnosis of “mild, non‑contagious bacterial pneumonia” and summarizing her overall medical status to address concerns after she became ill at a Sept. 11 memorial and left the campaign trail. Bardack said Clinton was diagnosed last Friday after a non‑contrast chest CT showed a small right middle‑lobe pneumonia, has been treated with a 10‑day course of the antibiotic Levaquin (about halfway through), and has been examined several times since. Bardack reported normal vitals (blood pressure 100/70, pulse 70, temperature 97.8, pulse oximetry 99%), routine lab results and up‑to‑date vaccinations (including Prevnar and Pneumovax). She listed Clinton’s medications (including Coumadin and Armour Thyroid) and noted prior 2016 sinus and ear infections treated with antibiotics, steroids and a myringotomy tube; a March CT of brain/sinuses showed no abnormalities. Bardack concluded Clinton is “recovering well” and “healthy and fit to serve as President.”

The release came amid criticism of the campaign’s delayed disclosure after Clinton was seen staggering into a van at the memorial. Independent physicians who reviewed the letter said the results overall appear reassuring: the pneumonia is small, vitals and labs are good, and the CT scan was appropriate given her history of blood clots. Some doctors noted Levaquin can cause dizziness and raised questions about specific long‑term medication choices and the absence of certain tests (e.g., an ECG baseline or colon‑cancer screening).

The campaign also published a brief health letter for vice‑presidential nominee Tim Kaine from Dr. Brian Monahan, who pronounced Kaine in “overall excellent health,” recommended a vitamin D supplement, and reported normal labs and a structurally normal heart aside from mild left atrial enlargement.

The disclosures coincided with Donald Trump offering limited new medical information on a taped appearance with Dr. Oz; physicians and commentators reiterated calls for more comprehensive, standardized health reporting for presidential candidates.

In the run-up to Facebook’s $16 billion IPO in May 2012, research analysts at the lead underwriters—chiefly Morgan Stanley, and also JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and Bank of America—unexpectedly lowered revenue and earnings forecasts while the IPO roadshow was underway. Morgan Stanley’s consumer internet analyst Scott Devitt cut his Q2 and full-year 2012 revenue estimates (e.g., Morgan Stanley’s 2012 revenue view fell to about $4.85 billion from just over $5.0 billion; Q2 to $1.111 billion from about $1.175 billion). The cuts followed Facebook’s May 9 amended SEC prospectus that warned of slower revenue growth due to a shift to mobile, where advertising was less lucrative.

Those revised forecasts were conveyed verbally and quickly to institutional and large clients—investors who normally get privileged access to underwriter research—but not broadly disclosed to retail investors. Several sources say a Facebook finance executive told at least one underwriter analyst to reduce estimates. Institutional demand reportedly weakened after the news; some large investors reduced or hedged allocations. By contrast, retail demand remained very strong. Reported book indications suggested institutions were comfortable around roughly $32 a share, while retail interest was nearer $40, and the IPO was priced at $38. Shares opened above the IPO price but plunged in the following days, trading more than 18% below the IPO price by the third day.

The episode raised concerns about selective disclosure and fairness—privileged verbal guidance to big clients that small investors lacked—and prompted scrutiny by regulators (SEC, FINRA) and a Massachusetts subpoena to Morgan Stanley. Underwriters say multiple syndicate analysts cut estimates and that procedures complied with regulations; firms declined detailed comment. Critics argue the practice of quietly disseminating underwriter forecasts during IPO roadshows is opaque and potentially unfair, and that this case may merit regulatory investigation.

This document stitches together several related news threads about political donations, alleged corruption tied to Florida businessman Harry Sargeant III, and the role of former CIA official Marty Martin in both private-sector controversies and the long hunt for Osama bin Laden.

Key points:

- Questionable campaign donations: Dozens of Californians — including Jihan and Waleed Nassar and others — were listed as $500 donors to Florida Gov. Charlie Crist’s 2006 campaign, allegedly bundled by businessman Harry Sargeant III. Many donors say they didn’t or couldn’t have given the money or were recruited under pressure. The McCain presidential campaign returned $50,000 in funds tied to Sargeant after media reports raised legality concerns; campaigns warned donors that foreign nationals cannot contribute and that reimbursement schemes violate limits. Crist’s campaign manager said they processed many checks and would review the flagged contributions.

- Harry Sargeant III and International Oil Trading Co.: Sargeant, a wealthy Florida businessman and former Florida GOP finance chair, ran International Oil Trading Co., which held large Pentagon fuel contracts supplying U.S. forces in Iraq. Congressional and Pentagon probes found the company overcharged the government (a Pentagon audit cited potential overpayments up to $204 million). Sargeant has been accused in a civil lawsuit by ex-partner Mohammad al-Saleh (brother-in-law to Jordan’s king) of cutting him out of a one-third share and of involvement in bribery and fraud related to obtaining a Jordanian authorization to ship fuel. Sargeant denies wrongdoing; his lawyers say disputed wire transfers were legitimate subcontractor payments.

- Bribery and payments in Jordan: Court documents and emails cited in the lawsuit allege two $4.5 million wire transfers (total $9 million) were routed “for the Pasha’s attention,” which plaintiffs say went to Jordan’s General Intelligence Directorate (GID) chief (possibly Gen. Mohammad Dahabi) to secure shipping rights. Plaintiffs argue this may violate the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act; Sargeant’s lawyers claim payments were to a Jordanian subcontractor (Taurus Trading Co.) and not illicit.

- Marty Martin’s involvement and allegations: Marty Martin, a retired CIA officer who later worked for Sargeant’s firm, is identified in court filings and press accounts as a former CIA Middle East station chief who helped Sargeant leverage contacts in Jordan. Separately, press commentary alleges Martin participated in questionable conduct after leaving the agency: joining the fuel firm implicated in overcharging the Pentagon, helping launder campaign contributions via straw donors for GOP fundraising, allegedly arranging the Jordan payments, and celebrating violence in Iraq. Martin and Sargeant’s representatives largely declined comment.

- Context and political fallout: Sargeant was a major GOP fundraiser and bundler for candidates including Charlie Crist and John McCain; the donation controversies surfaced while Crist was being considered as a possible McCain running mate. Some GOP officials defended returning McCain-linked funds as an ethical stance; others continued to back Sargeant within the state party despite probes.

- Bin Laden hunt and CIA intelligence: Interwoven with these accounts is reporting on the long CIA hunt for Osama bin Laden. The breakthrough came by tracking one of bin Laden’s couriers, aided by detainee interrogations and surveillance of a phone call. That lead identified a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, which U.S. intelligence and the White House judged likely to hide a “high-value target.” President Obama authorized a Navy SEAL raid; bin Laden was killed, identified by DNA and other means, and his body buried at sea. Marty Martin (named in some accounts as a former head of the CIA bin Laden unit) publicly defended aggressive interrogation programs as contributing to the success, further complicating perceptions of his post‑CIA activities.

Overall, the pieces portray a network of fundraising and business relationships tying a high-profile GOP fundraiser (Sargeant), an ex-CIA officer (Martin), questionable international payments and subcontracting in Jordan, and campaign contribution irregularities — all unfolding alongside the backstory of the CIA’s pursuit of bin Laden and the public roles of those involved. Investigations by congressional committees, Pentagon auditors, and ongoing civil litigation have probed alleged overbilling, bribery, and improper influence; many key figures have denied wrongdoing or declined comment.

The New York Times Book Review published an interview with Alice Walker in which she listed David Icke’s And the Truth Shall Set You Free among books on her nightstand. That passing mention prompted sharp criticism because Icke is a well-known conspiracy theorist whose work is widely condemned as antisemitic—recycling tropes from The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, alleging Jewish control via the Rothschilds, and promoting Holocaust denial-adjacent claims and other bigoted conspiracies. Critics, notably Tablet’s Yair Rosenberg, argued the Times should have warned readers or contextualized Walker’s recommendation instead of relaying it unqualified.

The piece recounts Walker’s long history of engagement with Icke’s work—public praise in 2013 and later promotion of his lectures and interviews—and points to a 2017 blog poem of hers attacking the Talmud that has itself been labeled antisemitic. Rosenberg and others argue that cultural elites have repeatedly overlooked Walker’s antisemitic statements, sometimes excusing them as anti-Zionism, and that media platforms like the Times have failed to hold her accountable by ignoring or not interrogating these views. The New York Times defended its approach by saying the "By the Book" feature reflects subjects’ personal tastes and is not an editorial endorsement, and that the column does not provide background on books named by interviewees.

The controversy raises broader questions about when publications should add context or challenge bigoted claims when public figures recommend or praise extremist material, and about distinguishing legitimate criticism of Israel from expressions that smuggle in antisemitic tropes.

Summary:

Federal agents investigated Novus Health Care Services, a Frisco, Texas hospice founded in 2012 by accountant Brad Harris, after an FBI affidavit alleged Harris directed nurses to hasten patients’ deaths to maximize Medicare/Medicaid payments. The probe, opened in October 2014 and focused on alleged improper recruitment and billing of patients who did not qualify, expanded after multiple employees told investigators Harris ordered overdoses of palliative drugs (including morphine) or instructed staff to increase dosages—one text message quoted in the warrant read, “You need to make this patient go bye-bye.” Harris allegedly asked executives to “find patients who would die within 24 hours” to avoid Medicare/Medicaid “aggregator cap” penalties that can force hospices to repay funds when average stays exceed caps. At least one nurse refused to comply; the affidavit says Harris ordered overdoses for several patients and one alleged instance involved a requested quadrupling of a medication dose. FBI agents executed searches of Novus in September 2015 and sought emails and records from a data storage vendor in February 2016. No criminal charges have been filed, and the FBI declined to comment. After the raid, Novus filed civil suits against departing employees and executives (some later dropped), and attorneys for former staff accused Novus of failing to disclose the FBI investigation in its filings.

Herman Cain campaigned in Nashua, N.H., asserting he still hopes to finish first — or at least gain momentum with a second-place finish — despite recent controversies. In a 22-minute speech to about 250 people, he defended himself against allegations of sexual harassment and criticism over a shaky answer on Libya, arguing that presidents need leadership and judgment rather than encyclopedic foreign-policy knowledge. Cain also drew negative attention by canceling a scheduled interview with the influential Union Leader after attempting to restrict C-SPAN coverage and shorten the meeting; the paper ran a “no-show” headline. Those developments, combined with growing concerns among state GOP figures about his perceived foreign-policy weaknesses and character questions, have eroded his standing in New Hampshire, where recent polling places him fourth with roughly 8 percent, well behind Romney, Ron Paul and Newt Gingrich, even as he remains more competitive nationally and in Iowa. The Union Leader’s endorsement is considered a key prize in the New Hampshire GOP contest.

16-year-old New Zealand singer Lorde (Ella Yelich-O’Connor) was named VH1’s You Oughta Know artist for September after her breakout single “Royals” became an international hit. The track — the first by a female to top the Billboard Alternative chart in 17 years and one of the fastest-rising alternative hits since Gotye’s “Somebody That I Used To Know” — was inspired by a National Geographic photo of a baseball player with a shirt that read “Royals,” plus Lorde’s longtime fascination with historical aristocracy. Separately, San Francisco radio station 96.5 KOIT temporarily pulled “Royals” from its playlist at listeners’ requests until the end of the World Series, as San Francisco Giants fans wanted to avoid airing a song that could be seen as supporting the opposing Kansas City Royals. The World Series between the Giants and Royals began with Game One on October 21.

President Obama ordered flags at the White House and other federal buildings lowered to half-staff through Saturday to honor five service members killed in the July 16 Chattanooga shootings, issuing a proclamation calling the violence senseless and praising first responders and national unity. The move came after criticism from Republican leaders, veterans and others who noted governors and the U.S. Capitol had already ordered flags lowered. Earlier Tuesday, House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell announced flags at the Capitol would be at half-staff; White House aides had initially declined to say whether the presidential flag would be lowered, prompting public backlash until Obama’s proclamation. The shootings, carried out by Mohammad Youssuf Abdulazeez, killed four Marines at a Navy facility and one sailor wounded later dying, and remain under FBI investigation.

Former U.S. Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr. and his wife, former Chicago 7th Ward Ald. Sandi Jackson, were sentenced in federal court after pleading guilty to crimes involving misuse of campaign funds and false tax returns. Jesse Jackson Jr. received 30 months in prison for using roughly $750,000 in campaign funds for personal expenses; Sandi Jackson was sentenced to one year for filing false joint federal tax returns and for extensive personal use of campaign credit cards and funds. U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson rejected defenses based on Jesse Jr.’s bipolar disorder and Sandi’s need to care for their two children, calling their conduct “knowing, organized” misconduct that was repeated and covered up. The judge allowed the couple to stagger their sentences so one parent can remain with the children, and gave Jesse Jackson Jr. until around Nov. 1 to report. Prosecutors had sought longer terms (four years for him, 18 months for her); the judge credited their guilty pleas in imposing sentences at the low end of guideline ranges. Jackson Jr. must forfeit $750,000; Sandi was ordered to pay $22,000 restitution. The hearing marked a dramatic fall for a once-prominent political couple from the Jackson family dynasty, drawing emotional statements from both defendants and public comments from family members. Prosecutors and the judge emphasized the breach of public trust and the need for equal application of the law.

A Kissimmee office of the Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration (PRFAA) closed after a rat infestation contaminated donations—boxes of water, food and other supplies collected after Hurricane Maria—that were meant for Puerto Rico but never shipped. PRFAA executive director Carlos Mercader said the agency lacks the budget to cover shipping costs and past attempts to forward the donations through other organizations failed. He also said many donations will instead be distributed to Puerto Rican families displaced to Central Florida and that an inventory will be done to determine which items remain usable.

The Kissimmee office had shown rodent problems since August, before the hurricane, and Mercader said the facility is deteriorated and will be relocated. Former local PRFAA director Juan Hernandez Mayoral called the situation government negligence, questioning why staff did not act earlier. The episode is part of wider criticism over aid failures to Puerto Rico after Maria, including congressional scrutiny of FEMA’s food contract controversies.

Newly released deposition videos from civil litigation in the 2013 “affluenza” case provide the first on‑the‑record account from Ethan Couch and his parents about the fatal drunk‑driving crash that killed four people and injured others near Fort Worth, Texas.

Key points:
- Ethan Couch, 16 at the time, admitted to heavy drinking and drug use (listing Valium, hydrocodone, marijuana, cocaine, Xanax and ecstasy) and said he “most of the time” drank at the family’s second home. He remembers almost nothing of the crash other than “waking up handcuffed to the hospital bed.” Police reported his BAC was 0.24, about three times the legal limit.
- Couch had pleaded guilty to four counts of intoxication manslaughter and two counts of intoxication assault and received 10 years’ probation plus treatment rather than the 20‑year prison term prosecutors sought. The defense had argued he suffered from “affluenza,” a condition promoted by psychologist Dr. G. Dick Miller, who said the family’s wealth and lack of consequences enabled Ethan’s behavior.
- Depositions of parents Tonya and Fred Couch show they allowed Ethan unsupervised access to a second home and early driving privileges. Tonya acknowledged sometimes disciplining him but could not recall the last time she punished him; she admitted she “never saw the child drink,” though others testified she knew he drank. Fred Couch denied believing “affluenza” is real and downplayed being permissive.
- The tapes revisit a prior incident four months before the crash in which a drunk 15‑year‑old Ethan was given a summons and minimal consequences; Tonya later said Ethan did not complete required community service, and Ethan denied a punishment his father described (walking to work).
- The McConnell family—whose son Lucas was severely injured—pursued a civil suit that prompted these depositions; the Couch family has since settled all related civil claims without admitting wrongdoing.
- Victims’ families remain critical of the criminal sentence and feel the tragedy was preventable, though some say they are working toward forgiveness.

The depositions, obtained by ABC News, deepen public insight into the couple’s parenting, Ethan’s substance use, and the circumstances leading up to the crash that sparked national outrage over privilege, accountability and the “affluenza” defense.

Memories Pizza was a small, family-owned pizza and ice cream shop in Walkerton, Indiana run by the O’Connor family for about nine years. The business drew sharply divided reactions: many local patrons and some visitors praised the friendly service, nostalgic small‑town atmosphere, and liked the pizza, breadsticks and staff; others criticized the food harshly, calling the pizza doughy, greasy or undercooked and reporting poor quality or even food‑illness.

The shop became a national flashpoint after the owners publicly said they would refuse to cater a gay wedding, citing Christian beliefs and support for Indiana’s Religious Freedom Restoration Act. That stance prompted strong responses online and off—some supportive commenters praised their religious conviction and noted a large GoFundMe that raised substantial donations, while many others left negative reviews or condemned the decision as discriminatory. The controversy, coupled with intense public attention and backlash, coincided with the restaurant’s closure; reviewers report it is now permanently closed.

Amazon is expanding beyond retail fulfillment into general business shipping, the Wall Street Journal reports. The new service, called "Shipping with Amazon," will pick up packages from businesses (initially third-party merchants on Amazon) and deliver them to customers, starting in Los Angeles and expanding to other cities. Amazon intends to undercut traditional carriers on price, directly challenging FedEx and UPS. The announcement knocked down FedEx and UPS shares in pre-market trading; UPS said it remains an Amazon partner but declined to comment on Amazon’s strategy.

Two new Pediatrics studies link common plastic-associated chemicals to metabolic problems in U.S. children and teens, but do not prove these chemicals cause the problems.

Key findings
- DEHP (a phthalate used in some plastics and food packaging): In 766 adolescents (ages 12–19), higher urinary DEHP metabolites were associated with greater insulin resistance — a precursor to Type 2 diabetes. The association persisted after adjusting for factors such as calorie intake and weight. Other phthalates (commonly in personal-care products) were not linked to insulin resistance in this study.
- BPA (bisphenol A): In a sample of over 10,000 children (ages 6–18), those with the highest urinary BPA had about double the odds of obesity versus those with the lowest levels.

Caveats and alternative explanations
- Both studies are observational and cannot establish causation. Reverse causation or confounding is possible: obese or insulin-resistant children may store or excrete more of these chemicals, or they may consume more packaged foods that contain them.
- Urinary measures reflect recent exposure and rapid metabolism; critics note urine levels may not represent active blood levels where hormonal effects would occur. Some experts argue metabolism may inactivate BPA’s endocrine-disrupting properties.
- Prior research is mixed; regulatory agencies (e.g., FDA) generally consider current adult exposures low and safe, though some jurisdictions have restricted BPA use (e.g., in baby bottles).

Implications and practical advice
- Food packaging and processing are likely major exposure routes for DEHP and BPA; canned and packaged foods can contribute to higher body burdens.
- Reducing exposure may be possible by choosing fresh foods over canned/wrapped products, minimizing use of unnecessary personal-care products (to reduce some phthalates), and using packaging materials that don’t contain DEHP.

Overall, the studies add to growing concern about links between endocrine-disrupting chemicals and metabolic health in youth, but further research (especially longitudinal and mechanistic work) is needed to determine whether these chemicals contribute causally to obesity and insulin resistance.

The Commerce Department’s annual revision and first estimate for Q2 paint a weaker picture of the U.S. economy. Real GDP grew at an annualized 1.3% rate in April–June, below economists’ median 1.8% forecast, and the first-quarter growth figure was sharply revised down to 0.4% from 1.9%. Lower-than-expected inventory accumulation, reduced federal and consumer spending, and higher gasoline prices were cited as factors behind the slowdown.

The annual revisions also worsened the damage from the 2007–2009 recession: output from its start to finish fell 5.1% (versus the prior 4.1% estimate), with 2009 contracting 3.5% (previously -2.5%) and 2008 down 0.3% (previously flat). The revisions attributed the deeper decline to weaker consumer spending and business investment than earlier estimated. On the brighter side, 2010 growth was nudged up to 3.0% from 2.9%. Unemployment remains elevated at about 9.2%.

A 911 call about shots fired at Virginia College in west Spartanburg Tuesday morning triggered a large, rapid law enforcement response; deputies described preparing for a mass-casualty event. The call came after 54-year-old Angela Timmons texted her daughter saying she was hiding in a bathroom and had heard gunshots. When the daughter called 911, deputies swarmed the campus, but while still on the phone the daughter got another text from Timmons saying it was an April Fools’ joke.

Sheriff Chuck Wright and other officials condemned the prank as dangerous and “not funny,” noting deputies risked their lives responding. Timmons, who works in the college’s financial aid office, was arrested and charged with disturbing schools, aggravated breach of peace, and two counts of unlawful use of a telephone; she was released on personal recognizance bond. She apologized, saying it was a one-second prank and she didn’t intend harm, and said she plans to hire an attorney. Virginia College expressed disappointment and said it is cooperating with the sheriff’s office; the school did not comment on Timmons’ employment status.

President Donald Trump publicly criticized Attorney General Jeff Sessions and the Justice Department, accusing them of harming Republicans' midterm prospects by moving forward with two long-running "Obama era" investigations and indicting two GOP congressmen shortly before the November elections. In tweets, Trump said recent charges put "two easy wins" in doubt and faulted Sessions for not intervening.

The indictments referenced were likely Rep. Duncan Hunter (R-CA), charged with using campaign funds for personal expenses from an investigation that began in June 2016, and Rep. Chris Collins (R-NY), indicted on insider trading-related charges stemming from 2017; both deny wrongdoing. Collins suspended his reelection bid after his indictment; Hunter remains in his race. While both seats are expected to remain Republican, the charges give Democrats some hope.

Trump’s attack underscores his repeated expectation that the Justice Department should be politically deferential — a stance at odds with norms of DOJ independence. Sessions has defended the department’s impartiality and indicated he will not resign, despite Trump’s repeated public criticisms and frustration over Sessions’ recusal from the Russia probe. Some allies have counseled against firing Sessions before the midterms, though talks of replacing him after the elections have surfaced.

A Palestinian sniper shot and killed a 22-year-old Israeli Bedouin civilian, Salah Shukri Abu Latyef, on Tuesday while he was working on the Gaza border fence; Israeli and Palestinian sources gave differing accounts of the shooter’s affiliation. Israel responded with air and tank strikes across Gaza targeting sites it described as weapons facilities, rocket launchers and terror infrastructure; Hamas said some strikes hit al Qassam (Hamas) camps and that a 4‑year‑old girl was killed and 11 others wounded. Israel said it held Hamas responsible and vowed a forceful response; Defense Minister Moshe Ya’alon and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Gaza’s rulers not to “test our patience.” The U.N. secretary‑general expressed concern, condemning the Israeli death and deploring Palestinian civilian casualties. Israeli officials emphasized the incident violated understandings that had eased restrictions near the fence since the 2012 ceasefire and moved to restrict access for workers; Kerem Shalom crossing was closed. The episode heightened tensions amid a recent spike in attacks and political debate in Israel over security measures and prisoner releases.

Francesco Schettino, captain of the Costa Concordia that ran aground off Giglio in January, apologized in his first full TV interview since the disaster, saying he constantly thinks about the victims and accepts responsibility as the ship’s captain. He acknowledged being “distracted” and admitted he failed to act decisively once the 144,500-ton vessel struck rocks, but maintained that at the moment of impact another officer was actually commanding the ship and that he had ordered manual navigation from the deck. Schettino, who faces charges including multiple manslaughter, causing a shipwreck and abandoning ship, was recently released from house arrest with travel restrictions. Investigators and critics accuse him of bringing the ship too close to shore, delaying and mismanaging the evacuation, and abandoning ship before all passengers and crew were safe. He denied suggestions he sailed close to Giglio to impress a woman and broke down when asked about the youngest victim, a five-year-old girl. Other officers and Costa Cruises personnel are also under investigation.
