During a “March 4 Trump” rally at the Minnesota State Capitol on March 4, 2017, roughly 400 Trump supporters and about 50 counterprotesters clashed in and around the Capitol rotunda. Video shows a black-clad person throwing a smoke bomb or similar device that struck a 61-year-old woman (who was unhurt). St. Paul police and the Minnesota State Patrol identified five people they believed had lit off fireworks or a smoke device inside the rotunda; six people in total were detained that day.

Linwood “Woody” Kaine, 24, son of U.S. Senator Tim Kaine, was among five people arrested on suspicion of second-degree riot. Police say officers located the suspects near a park, identified themselves, and when confronted Kaine refused orders to the ground, struggled with officers, required a chemical spray and a knee strike before being subdued and handcuffed. The Ramsey County attorney declined to file felony charges, saying there were insufficient facts to prove felony-level riot, and referred the matter back to investigators; the St. Paul City Attorney was reviewing the case for possible misdemeanor charges. As of the report, none of the five had been formally charged and the investigation remained active.

The arrests and charging decisions drew political commentary. Local Republican officials accused prosecutors of political bias for not pursuing felony charges and asked for federal review; Ramsey County Attorney John Choi and St. Paul City Attorney Samuel Clark said they were unaware of Kaine’s relation to Sen. Tim Kaine until media reports and defended the decision to follow evidence, noting they would revisit the case if new evidence warranted. The Pioneer Press was unable to reach Kaine or the other arrestees for comment.

German police have recovered about 100 items stolen in 2006 from Yoko Ono that belonged to John Lennon, including three leather-bound diaries (1975, 1979 and 1980), two pairs of his round metal-rimmed glasses, a cigarette case, a handwritten music score, contract documents, a 1965 Beatles concert tape and other memorabilia. The recovered objects were displayed at Berlin police headquarters after many were found in July in storage at the Berlin auction house Auctionata; police confiscated them and opened an investigation. A 58-year-old man (a German businessman of Turkish origin) was arrested in Berlin after searches of his home and cars turned up further items; a second suspect, reportedly Ono’s former chauffeur now living in Turkey and with a prior related conviction in New York, is currently out of reach. German prosecutors and police flew to New York so Ono could verify the items from photos; she identified them and was reportedly emotional. Authorities are still examining computer files and contracts to determine how the goods reached the auction house and whether Auctionata knew they were stolen. It is not yet clear when the items will be returned to Lennon’s estate.

North Korea launched an unidentified projectile from Pyongyang that flew over Japan and landed in the Pacific, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs said while U.S. and South Korean forces analyzed the launch. Japanese officials reported the missile passed over Hokkaido, caused no damage, and appeared to break into three parts. The test follows recent North Korean activity including three short-range ballistic missile launches and a second intercontinental ballistic missile flight test last month. Tensions are heightened amid ongoing U.S.–South Korea military exercises that Pyongyang condemns as provocative; the North has also threatened possible strikes toward Guam, while Washington and Seoul say the drills are defensive.

This document covers two related justice-system stories: a developing New York legislative deal to expand the state DNA database and accompanying reforms, and a long-running controversy in Virginia over delayed DNA retesting, poor notification of potential exonerees, and systemic failures in handling evidence of wrongful convictions.

New York: lawmakers and Gov. Cuomo are negotiating a package of end-of-session deals—including the state budget, redistricting, pension changes and a DNA database expansion. Assemblyman Joseph Lentol said parameters of a DNA bill are in place that would require DNA samples from all convicted people (the current law covers fewer than half of statutory crimes and has been expanded several times since the 1990s). Proponents, including Manhattan DA Cyrus Vance Jr., argue that collecting DNA from low-level offenders has helped solve many cold cases (cited: links to 48 murders and 220 sexual assaults) and can also exonerate the wrongly convicted. Defense and innocence advocates warn that access to evidence and testing must be made easier for defense lawyers; Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver supports defendant access, while Senate Majority Leader Dean Skelos is open to limited access but opposes broader wrongful-conviction measures (e.g., mandatory videotaped interrogations). Some Assembly members want to attach a decriminalization-style tweak (making possession of small amounts of marijuana in public view a violation rather than a misdemeanor), but its inclusion is uncertain. The negotiations occur amid budget talks in which the governor is seeking a new pension tier for future hires; he reportedly may drop a proposed 401(k)-style option if leaders accept reduced benefits for new employees.

Virginia: the piece recounts the case of Bennett Barbour—convicted in 1978 of a rape he did not commit—who was cleared by DNA testing years later but was not notified by state authorities. Virginia began a large-scale DNA retesting initiative after old biological evidence was rediscovered; what was meant to be an 18-month, $1.4 million project has stretched years and costs rose to about $5 million. Of roughly 800 samples, 214 yielded usable results and more than 70 people (commonly cited as 76–79) were excluded as the source of biological evidence. Yet only a handful have been formally exonerated; many excluded individuals were not told they’d been cleared.

Problems identified:
- Secrecy and poor administration: the audit’s case selection, procedures, and timelines remain opaque. Freedom of Information requests were resisted; notification practices were inadequate.
- Faulty notification process: the Department of Forensic Science and prosecutors largely controlled testing and notification. In 2008 the legislature ordered notification, but the state used legalistic letters and pro bono lawyers who were barred by confidentiality agreements from explaining results or representing recipients. Many letters frightened or confused recipients; some were never delivered. Families of deceased suspects sometimes were not notified at all.
- Conflicted roles and incentives: critics say letting the crime lab and prosecutors manage notification is problematic because those offices are not structured to seek exonerations and may have pro-prosecution biases; officials argue labs should only provide analysis and that prosecutors/police are responsible for legal follow-up.
- Grassroots remediation: private attorney Jonathan Sheldon, frustrated by state inaction and limited disclosures, used public records and detective work to locate many excluded individuals and notify them—often succeeding where state agencies failed. His actions prompted scrutiny from the lab (reports suggested inquiry into whether he breached confidentiality agreements).
- Human cost: the article illustrates the life-destroying effects of wrongful convictions (Barbour lost years, relationships, and suffers serious illness) and highlights claims that Virginia’s error rate may be far higher than acknowledged—some experts estimate exclusion rates implying possible wrongful-conviction rates in the single digits to teens of percent among tested cases. Only a few formal exonerations have resulted despite dozens of exclusions.

Conclusion: Both accounts show DNA testing’s dual power to solve crimes and to expose wrongful convictions, but they also reveal major policy and procedural gaps—New York’s debate balances crime-solving gains with safeguards for defendants and access to evidence; Virginia’s saga exposes bureaucratic opacity, ineffective notification, and possible institutional resistance that has delayed or denied redress to many people whom DNA excluded as perpetrators. The piece calls into question who should manage DNA retesting and notifications and urges reforms to ensure timely, transparent exonerations and fair defense access.

Summary:

Union Street Guest House is a boutique inn in Hudson, NY, near Warren Street’s shops. Guests’ experiences reported here are sharply divided. Positive comments praise the building’s vintage decor, antique furnishings, a cozy lounge with an honor bar, the spacious “Gallery/Presidential Suite,” and reasonable rates when available. Criticisms are numerous and recurring: dirty or poorly maintained rooms, creaky floors and thin walls, pest/odor issues, bathroom cleanliness problems, noisy neighbors and dogs, cheap supplies (one-ply toilet paper, poor pillows), billing errors, and unresponsive or rude management and staff.

A major controversy centers on the inn’s policy of charging a $500 fee—deducted from a wedding deposit—whenever a guest or anyone in a wedding party posts a negative online review. Multiple reviewers allege the owners threatened or actually attempted to collect that fee; several guests also claim unresolved refund disputes and erroneous credit-card charges. Some guests report being charged nonrefundable amounts after early departures for emergencies. Local press coverage amplified the backlash, while the inn says it will refund the $500 if a negative review is removed.

Overall, while some visitors enjoy the place’s character and location, many recent reviewers warn against staying due to cleanliness, noise, management practices, billing problems, and the contentious $500 negative-review policy.

Hillary Clinton and her campaign sharply criticized FBI Director James Comey after he informed Congress that the FBI had discovered new emails "pertinent" to the closed probe of her private server while investigating Anthony Weiner. Speaking in Florida, Clinton called the timing "unprecedented" and "deeply troubling," urging Comey to release full details immediately. Her campaign accused Comey of providing "selective information" and potentially influencing the election; chairman John Podesta said Comey should have reviewed the material more thoroughly before going public, and campaign manager Robby Mook said the Justice Department historically avoids actions that could affect elections.

Clinton’s team stressed the additional emails may be duplicates and might not reveal new information, and vowed not to be distracted in the campaign’s final days. Top surrogates including Tim Kaine and Brian Fallon demanded more transparency about whether the FBI has reviewed the content or determined if messages involve Clinton. Huma Abedin, whose emails on a device shared with estranged husband Anthony Weiner spurred the discovery, was defended by the campaign; Robby Mook said he is confident she complied with prior probes.

Republicans reacted predictably: Donald Trump pressed the issue on the campaign trail and questioned Abedin’s role and potential immunity; supporters like Newt Gingrich urged the FBI to release emails. Trump allies argued Comey was in a difficult position — either risk accusations of interfering by publicizing the probe or of concealing information. The controversy elevates Comey as a central figure in the closing days of the 2016 campaign and raises partisan disputes over the FBI’s timing and handling of the disclosure.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds were photographed having a friendly, laughter-filled dinner at New York City’s Blue Ribbon restaurant just a week after announcing their separation. Both released a statement saying they would treat each other with "love and kindness" while ending the marriage, and sources say the meal was simply a civil, lighthearted attempt to connect — not a reconciliation. Insiders suggest busy, conflicting work schedules strained the marriage; Reynolds was in New York for a photo shoot between movie commitments, and Johansson recently returned from vacation. Some tabloids framed the outing as Johansson managing her public image, while other sources quoted friends who said Reynolds had complained privately that Johansson didn’t make him a priority. Neither partner has commented on plans beyond maintaining civility; they have no children together.

The Gravity blanket is a high-tech weighted duvet launched via Kickstarter that uses “deep pressure touch stimulation” (also called deep touch/proprioceptive input) to simulate being hugged. It’s filled with high-density plastic pellets and comes in 15, 20 and 25 lb options—roughly 7–12% of a user’s body weight—with a cotton inner shell and removable fleece cover. The makers claim the pressure can raise serotonin and melatonin, lower cortisol, slow heart rate and blood pressure, reduce movement and promote deeper REM sleep, and help with insomnia, anxiety, PTSD, OCD and ADHD. Gravity raised millions on Kickstarter and was marketed as a “therapeutic” product priced from about $169 (projected retail up to $279), with shipping planned for autumn.

Independent reporting and experts caution the scientific evidence is limited. Small, non‑controlled or unblinded studies have shown calming effects in some settings, but rigorous randomized controlled trials identifying who benefits have not been done. After queries from STAT, the campaign removed or softened explicit treatment claims on its Kickstarter page because such language violated Kickstarter’s rules (and ran counter to FDA guidance that wellness products should not claim to treat disorders). Weighted blankets are already used in some clinical contexts (e.g., autism, dementia) and lower‑cost alternatives exist, but buyers are advised to be skeptical of broad medical promises until stronger evidence is available.

The piece also noted other novelty travel/comfort items recently marketed—duvet suits (padded wearable blankets) and the Slanket (a large fleece blanket with sleeves)—as part of a broader trend in sleep/comfort products.

This document compiles reporting and commentary from multiple outlets about the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign, focusing on Hillary Clinton, an endorsement from a prominent Republican foreign‑policy figure, and fact-checking of Donald Trump’s attacks.

Key points

- Republican national-security veteran Brent Scowcroft endorsed Hillary Clinton. Scowcroft, who served as National Security Adviser under Presidents George H. W. Bush and Gerald Ford (and worked in other Republican administrations), said Clinton “brings truly unique experience and perspective” and “deep expertise in international affairs,” directly rebutting Trump’s claims that she lacks the temperament for high‑pressure foreign-policy responsibilities. Richard Armitage, another Republican national-security official, had also announced support for Clinton earlier.

- The document includes excerpts analyzing President Obama’s Syria policy and the 2013 decision to call off strikes after the Assad regime’s use of chemical weapons. It outlines Obama’s reluctance to use large-scale force (rooted in opposition to Iraq and prior frustrations), his misreading of the Arab Spring, and his regret over Libya intervention—factors that led him to reverse course on Syria. The episode drew strong reaction from officials including Hillary Clinton, who criticized the decision.

- A long Associated Press fact-check of Donald Trump’s June 22, 2016, speech finds numerous distortions and inaccuracies in Trump’s attacks on Clinton and other claims:
  - Trump overstated Clinton’s responsibility for Middle East instability, misstated U.S. involvement in Libya, and wrongly tied her to decisions (like Iraq troop withdrawal dates) driven by others.
  - His assertions about denied security requests before the Benghazi attack and that Clinton “left [the ambassador] there to die” are exaggerated or contradicted by congressional investigations and records.
  - Claims that Clinton planned to spend “hundreds of billions” on refugee resettlement, or that she would allow unscreened refugees, are false or misleading; the refugee resettlement budget is under $1.2 billion and Clinton supported existing screening processes and a proposal to take up to 65,000 Syrian refugees.
  - Trump misstated trade and tax facts: the U.S.–China trade deficit rose by about 17.6% during Clinton’s time as secretary of state (not 40% in the relevant period), and the U.S. tax burden is lower than many developed countries, not the “highest.”
  - On immigration, Clinton’s proposals (pathway to citizenship, targeted enforcement) do not amount to “open borders” or blanket amnesty as Trump claimed.
  - Trump’s economic claims—about Obamacare’s impact, his own business record and wealth, and the effects of his proposed tax cuts—were flagged as inaccurate or overstated. Independent estimates found his tax plan would greatly increase deficits absent offsets, and independent valuations show his net worth is substantially less than his claim.

Overall takeaway

The assembled pieces emphasize that Hillary Clinton attracted cross‑party endorsements from experienced Republican foreign‑policy figures, that debates over U.S. intervention (notably in Syria and Libya) were central to critiques of Obama-era decision‑making, and that many of Donald Trump’s rhetorical attacks and factual claims in the campaign were challenged by reporters and investigators as exaggerated, misleading, or false.

Forrest Sanco and Donna Grant, both 56 and high‑school friends who recently reconnected and fell in love, disappeared while flying their privately owned Cessna 150 in the Bahamas. The couple planned to elope in Rum Cay after flying from Fort Worth. On Sept. 26 they flew from Fort Pierce, Florida, to Freeport, Grand Bahama, cleared customs and spent the night. The next day they landed in North Eleuthera about 1:30 p.m., purchased fuel, and filed a flight plan that Forrest closed at 4:58 p.m., indicating he was nearing Rum Cay. They departed North Eleuthera around 2:30 p.m. for Rum Cay—121 miles away—but never arrived and have not been heard from since. Their last social post was an Instagram sunrise on Sept. 26.

The family did not report them missing until about Oct. 6, roughly ten days later, because they expected limited communication on the romantic trip. Local searches have been conducted by private pilots and crews hired by relatives, funded via a GoFundMe that exceeded its $10,000 target. Bahamian authorities, including the Royal Bahamas Defence Force, are leading official search efforts with assistance from the U.S. Coast Guard; debris sighted near Cat Island was later determined not to be related. Bad afternoon weather and recent repairs to the aircraft are noted as concerns. Families continue to search and hope for answers.

Caitlyn Jenner reveals in her memoir The Secrets of My Life that she underwent gender confirmation surgery in January 2017. She describes the operation as successful and says it left her feeling “wonderful” and “liberated,” calling the decision “complex” because of the health risks involved. Jenner says she disclosed the procedure to stop public speculation and to be candid, adding it was partly motivated by wanting “all the right parts” and frustration with tucking. The book also recounts earlier procedures: breast augmentation and facial feminization in March 2015, and notes that she legally changed her name to Caitlyn Marie and her gender marker to female in October 2016. The memoir is due April 25.

Researchers report that commonly used proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)—over‑the‑counter and prescription drugs for reflux and heartburn—may harm blood‑vessel cells and be linked with higher risks of serious illnesses.

Laboratory study (Houston Methodist Research Institute, published in Circulation Research, May 2016)
- Long‑term exposure of human endothelial cells (which line blood vessels) to PPIs accelerated cellular aging (senescence). Healthy endothelium repels blood; aged/diseased endothelium becomes “sticky,” promoting blockages.
- PPIs impaired lysosomal acidification in these cells. Lysosomes, which clear cellular waste, failed to produce enough acid, causing waste buildup and accelerated cell aging.
- An H2‑antagonist (a different class of antacid) did not show these harmful effects in the lab.
- Limitations: only two PPIs were tested (one commercially available, esomeprazole/Nexium), the exact mechanism by which PPIs reduce lysosomal acidity was not shown, and in‑vivo effects in humans remain unproven—clinical trials are needed.

Epidemiologic findings and related studies
- Observational and preliminary clinical data have linked long‑term PPI use with increased risks of heart disease, kidney disease, dementia and infections; a Danish study reported an increased ischemic stroke risk among PPI users (overall ~21% higher; higher at large doses and varying by PPI brand).
- Another study found increased risks of kidney disease and kidney failure among PPI users compared with alternative medications.

Implications and recommendations
- Investigators warn against long‑term, unsupervised PPI use. PPIs are effective short‑term but were not tested for extended, widespread OTC use.
- Physicians should reassess chronic PPI prescriptions and consider alternatives where appropriate: lifestyle changes (diet, weight loss, smoking/alcohol reduction), H2 blockers, antacids for occasional heartburn, or surgical options for severe GERD.
- Further research, including long‑term clinical trials, is required to confirm whether PPIs produce the same vascular effects in humans and to clarify mechanisms.

Funding and disclosures: Study funded by NIH and Swiss National Science Foundation; author disclosures are in the manuscript.

After the US women’s national team beat Japan 5-2 to win the 2015 Women’s World Cup, a small but vocal group of Twitter users tried to frame the victory as "payback" for Japan’s 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor and even invoked the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. “Pearl Harbor” trended heavily in the US, driven both by provocative posts (some from parody or hyper‑patriotic accounts) and by the large number of people condemning those posts. Many users criticized the wartime references as inappropriate and racist, defending Japanese fans and calling the jokes “not funny” and “awful.” Analytics showed mentions of “Pearl Harbor” jumped from roughly 500 a day to over 50,000 that evening, with much of the activity expressing outrage rather than endorsement.

Evelynn M. Hammonds, a historian of science and African‑American studies who had served as Harvard’s senior vice provost for faculty development and diversity, was appointed dean of Harvard College — becoming the first Black person and the first woman to hold that post. Her appointment, announced while Harvard was continuing to break gender and racial barriers after Drew Gilpin Faust became the university’s first female president, placed Hammonds in charge of undergraduate academic life and administration. Hammonds came to Harvard in 2002 from MIT, was named senior vice provost in 2005, and has been noted for initiatives supporting faculty diversity and programs to help women balance family and career.

Hammonds’ deanship was later engulfed by controversy over searches of Harvard e‑mail accounts during the fallout from a large cheating investigation in an introductory government course. Administrators, concerned about leaks of confidential disciplinary information, examined e‑mail accounts of resident deans; what was initially described as limited searches was later acknowledged to have been broader. The episode prompted apologies from Hammonds and other administrators, an outside inquiry into electronic‑communication policies, and significant campus debate about privacy, process, and responsibility. Many colleagues praised Hammonds’ accomplishments — including curricular innovations and residential life reforms — and defended her motives, while others and student commentators criticized her role and effectiveness.

Amid that controversy, Hammonds announced she would step down as dean (taking leave and then returning to faculty work), transition to a program at the W.E.B. Du Bois Institute studying race and gender in science and medicine, and return to teaching and research after a sabbatical. Her departure was framed both as a personal decision to resume academic work and, in many accounts, the culmination of the difficult episodes of the academic year. Harvard said it would search for a successor to her prior senior‑provost role when she assumed the deanship. The reporting also noted broader efforts at peer institutions — notably Yale — to increase racial diversity in senior administration.

Fifteen former staffers of the 1970s Church Committee — the bipartisan Senate inquiry that exposed wide-ranging CIA, FBI and intelligence abuses — have written an eight-page letter to President Obama and Attorney General Loretta Lynch urging leniency for NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden and proposing negotiated settlement that would allow his return to the U.S. without prolonged prison time.

Key points from their appeal:
- The signatories, led by former Church Committee chief counsel Frederick Schwarz Jr. and ex-staff director William Green Miller, argue Snowden’s 2013 disclosures sparked important public debate and bipartisan reforms (including changes to the Patriot Act and an end to bulk metadata collection) and increased protections for foreigners targeted by U.S. surveillance.
- They acknowledge Snowden broke the law but say past cases of mishandling classified information (e.g., Sandy Berger, David Petraeus, John Deutch) show a record of leniency and that Snowden’s motives were reformist rather than personal gain.
- Drawing on their committee’s history of uncovering abuses (COINTELPRO, domestic spying, CIA experiments), they stress the dangers of secret intelligence operations and the public benefit of disclosure in prompting accountability.
- The group stops short of asking for a full pardon — which Obama has rejected — and instead urges negotiation of a plea or settlement that balances legal consequences with recognition of Snowden’s public service.
- They also note geopolitical risks as U.S.-Russia ties cool and imply concern about Snowden’s safety in Russia, though they avoid direct criticism of President-elect Trump.

Overall, the letter brings influential, historically grounded voices to calls for a pragmatic resolution that would allow Snowden to return and face mitigated consequences in light of the public reforms his disclosures produced.

A national investigation by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution and reporting by the Associated Press found hundreds of U.S. doctors accused of sexual misconduct in 2016–2017 and revealed systemic leniency in how the medical profession disciplines them. The AJC identified 450 cases brought to regulators or courts; about half of those doctors remain licensed. Even some criminally convicted physicians have returned to practice.

Common outcomes for accused doctors include short suspensions, probation, mandatory therapy, or referral to “impaired physician” programs rather than permanent license revocation. These programs and guidelines often treat sexual misconduct as illness or impairment and are largely nondisciplinary. State boards sometimes accept settlements that do not require admissions of guilt; patients are rarely guaranteed apologies or restitution. High-profile cases such as Larry Nassar stand in contrast to the everyday pattern in which many physicians sanctioned by employers or civil suits never face medical board discipline. A study cited found two-thirds of doctors disciplined by employers or who paid settlements for sexual misconduct never faced state board action.

Victims and advocates say the personal nature of the doctor–patient relationship makes these harms especially severe. The reports detail multiple examples of doctors who kept practicing after criminal convictions or repeated allegations, including a gynecologist in California, a Tampa-area physician convicted of misdemeanor battery, a family doctor in Arkansas facing sexual-assault charges, and an Idaho psychiatrist whose license was later reinstated. Investigations cite hospitals’ reluctance to report abusive physicians, gaps in interstate reporting systems, and patients’ reluctance to challenge clinicians as factors favoring doctors.

Critics — including some former board members — blame institutional bias by physician-dominated boards, inconsistent punishments, administrative-law processes, and overloaded regulatory systems that often do not pursue harsher penalties or appeals. Rehab and physician-health programs vary widely, are sometimes opaque about methods, and may not be equipped to evaluate or treat sexual misconduct appropriately. Researchers say the typical treatments focus on addiction models rather than restitution or victim-centered interventions; there is little evidence about effective therapies for physician sexual misconduct.

Advocates call for stronger, consistent policies (including zero-tolerance approaches and permanent revocation for sexual abuse of patients), better reporting by hospitals, and reforms to medical board and physician-health program practices to increase accountability and protect patients.

This collection of TIME pieces profiles several defining people and stories of 2013 and their wider significance.

Pope Francis — TIME’s Person of the Year
- Jorge Mario Bergoglio, the first pope from the Americas, quickly reshaped the papacy’s tone and global resonance in his first nine months. Emphasizing humility, mercy and identification with the poor, he modeled simplicity (living modestly, driving an old car, wearing a simple cross) and dramatic public gestures (washing feet of women and non-Catholics, embracing outcasts) that amplified the Church’s pastoral mission.
- Francis has not changed core Catholic doctrine on issues like priestly celibacy, abortion or marriage, but he has shifted priorities away from doctrinal policing toward compassionate outreach—calling the Church a “field hospital.” He attacked the “idolatry of money,” pushed for Vatican transparency, and encouraged bishops who are “gentle, patient and merciful.”
- His style has energized many lapsed Catholics and attracted global attention, while provoking criticism from traditionalists and scrutiny from conservatives and abuse-victims advocates. As a media-savvy moral voice, his influence may be especially important as Catholicism grows in the developing world.

Edward Snowden in exile
- The profile of Edward Snowden describes his cautious life in Moscow after leaking vast NSA surveillance documents. Surrounded by allies and guarded by Russian security, Snowden has accepted asylum, kept a low public profile, and continued to argue that mass surveillance threatens basic freedoms.
- His revelations sparked international debates, diplomatic tensions, legal actions and changes in behavior by some groups and technology companies. Critics, including U.S. intelligence officials, warn about security harms and increased risks to counterterrorism. Snowden sees his disclosures as a necessary warning about the balance between government power and individual rights.

Bashar al-Assad — “Michael Corleone” transformation
- A long-form profile traces Bashar al-Assad’s evolution from a mild, Western-educated doctor who seemed ill-suited to rule into a ruthless wartime leader. The Assad regime’s brutal repression since 2011—including massive casualties, chemical-weapons attacks and large refugee flows—has made Bashar more brutal than his father.
- Assad has survived international pressure and even a threatened U.S. military response by making calculated concessions (e.g., agreeing to give up chemical weapons) that preserved his core military capabilities and forced world powers to negotiate with him, thereby shoring up his survival.

Edith Windsor and the marriage-equality milestone
- Edith Windsor, who sued the U.S. government over estate taxes and won in the Supreme Court’s 5-4 ruling that struck down key parts of DOMA, is depicted as an unlikely civil-rights icon. Her case secured federal recognition of same-sex marriages and unlocked many federal benefits for married same-sex couples.
- Windsor’s life story—growing up Jewish in Depression-era Philadelphia, living much of her life discreetly as a lesbian, and later becoming an outspoken, public figure—illustrates the personal and generational dimensions of the LGBTQ rights movement and the cultural shifts that made the Supreme Court victory possible.

Ted Cruz and the U.S. government shutdown
- Senator Ted Cruz led a high-profile effort to shut down the federal government in 2013 in an attempt to defund the Affordable Care Act. The tactic provoked widespread public disgust and strained relationships within the GOP, yet Cruz views the backlash as evidence that he is challenging a disconnected political establishment and mobilizing a new, direct form of political engagement.

Across these profiles TIME highlights themes of moral authority, the power of symbolism and media, the tension between rhetoric and institutional constraint, and how individuals—through style, leaks, legal fights or brinkmanship—shaped major political and cultural debates in 2013.

Lena Dunham praised Glamour for running an unretouched February 2017 cover showing her cellulite, posting an emotional Instagram note about body acceptance and the harm of a culture that pressures women to hate their appearance. She recounted being mocked in adolescence but said she never hated her body itself, only the messages telling her to. Dunham thanked women in Hollywood and Glamour for normalizing diverse female bodies and vowed not to be shamed into hiding. The cover image features Dunham in purple metallic shorts with her Girls co-stars Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Allison Williams.

The piece also reflects on Girls’ cultural impact since its 2012 debut: its realistic, imperfect portrayals of young women, frank nudity and controversial storylines helped shift TV representation and spurred conversations about feminism and politics. The cast—Dunham, Kirke, Mamet and Williams—have engaged in activism and projects beyond the show. In an exit-style interview conducted by executive producer Jenni Konner, the actresses discuss the highs and lows of working on Girls: creative growth, close but sometimes fraught relationships (including moments of loneliness and tension for Dunham), and the challenges of certain seasons. They note how the show shaped their careers and helped open the door for later female-driven series. The final season of Girls premiered on HBO February 12, 2017.

A group calling itself Truckers for the Constitution (also promoted as Truckers Ride for the Constitution or Truckers to Shut Down America) organized a planned protest for Oct. 11 to intentionally slow or clog the inner loop of I-495, the 64-mile Capital Beltway around Washington, D.C. The organizers say the multi-day convoy will travel “three lanes deep,” keep the left lane open for emergency vehicles, and display supporter markings to allow some motorists through. They framed the action as a Tea Party–style, coast-to-coast effort to draw attention to trucker grievances and broader political complaints.

Motivations cited include low pay for independent truckers, high diesel prices and fees, new EPA fuel-efficiency and anti-idling rules, insurance and technology mandates, perceived erosion of Fourth Amendment protections, anger over alleged government spying, and concern about national debt. Organizers also accused top officials (a flyer named President Obama, Secretary of State John Kerry and Sens. John McCain and Lindsey Graham) of being “domestic enemies” and urged Americans to take back the country from “global banking cartels.”

Some organizers went further, threatening to seek the “arrest” of elected officials they say violated their oaths—citing citizens’ grand juries as a proposed mechanism—and saying they would present demands to lawmakers and could trigger a shutdown if officials did not comply. Prominent logistics coordinator Earl Conlon described confronting members of Congress directly; a promoter said thousands had RSVP’d and social media interest was large. Organizers insisted the action would be “peaceful” but warned they would resist interference.

Authorities noted that any attempt to physically detain lawmakers would be illegal, and observers pointed out the protest’s actual impact would depend on turnout and commitment; past similar actions had not produced the worst-case traffic disruptions. An update to the story later noted that truckers were no longer planning to arrest members of Congress.

The Syrian Centre for Policy Research (SCPR) report Confronting Fragmentation finds Syria’s human and economic losses far greater than widely cited figures: it estimates 470,000 war-related deaths since March 2011 (about 400,000 from direct violence and 70,000 from indirect causes such as lack of healthcare, food, water and shelter), versus roughly 250,000 used by the UN before it stopped compiling Syrian casualty data in mid-2014. The report says 11.5% of the population have been killed or injured, with roughly 1.9 million wounded. Life expectancy fell from 70 in 2010 to 55.4 in 2015; poverty rose sharply (an 85% increase in 2015); 45% of Syrians have been displaced (6.36 million internally and over 4 million abroad); 13.8 million lost livelihoods; consumer prices surged and basic services—health, education, sanitation—have deteriorated. Total economic losses are estimated at $255 billion.

SCPR, which conducted field research across Syria, attributes the collapse of institutions, infrastructure and national wealth to prolonged conflict, coercion, smuggling and exploitation of resources (notably oil by ISIS and other armed groups). It warns indirect deaths will likely rise and criticizes uneven humanitarian access and global complacency, noting international attention increased mainly after the crisis affected developed countries.

The report’s release coincides with renewed diplomatic activity and a precarious military situation around Aleppo: Russia proposed a ceasefire beginning March 1, a move U.S. officials view skeptically as potentially allowing government and Russian forces to defeat moderate rebels beforehand. The U.S. has demanded an immediate ceasefire with full humanitarian access and is pressing for resumed peace talks aimed at a political transition and ultimately Assad’s removal, though U.S. policy has grown ambiguous and fragmented amid competing priorities to combat IS and manage regional allies.

Study overview and key findings
- A University of Southern California analysis of 5,490 adolescents from the Children’s Health Study (cohorts reaching 11th–12th grade in 1995, 1998, 2001, 2004 and 2014) examined trends in cigarette and e‑cigarette use and prospective associations between adolescent vaping and later cigarette initiation.
- Cigarette smoking among Southern California high‑school seniors fell from 19% in 1995 to ~9% in 2004, then plateaued (~7.8% in 2014). However, when combined with e‑cigarette use, the 2014 past‑30‑day prevalence rose to 13.7% among 12th graders — substantially higher than cigarette use in 2004 and similar to smoking prevalence around 2001.
- The authors conclude e‑cigarettes are not simply replacing cigarettes; they appear to be recruiting new adolescent nicotine users who likely would not have smoked combustible cigarettes in the absence of e‑cigarettes.

Vaping and later smoking
- In a prospective follow‑up of 298 never‑smoking adolescents (baseline mean age 17.4), 40.4% of baseline e‑cigarette users reported initiating cigarette use ~16 months later vs. 10.5% of never‑vapers.
- After adjustment for demographics and potential confounders, baseline e‑cigarette users had about six times the odds (OR ≈ 6.2) of initiating cigarette use compared with never‑vapers. The association persisted when restricted to youth who had never used any combustible tobacco at baseline.
- The association was especially strong among adolescents who initially reported no susceptibility or intention to smoke, suggesting vaping may prompt cigarette initiation even in those considered low‑risk.

Health and regulatory context
- E‑cigarette liquids are sold in many youth‑oriented flavors (fruit, candy, dessert) and with variable, often unregulated nicotine content; some products labeled “nicotine‑free” have been found to contain nicotine.
- Nicotine is highly addictive and harmful to the developing brain; vapor can contain solvents, formaldehyde and other potentially harmful chemicals. Long‑term health effects remain uncertain.
- The FDA has asserted jurisdiction over e‑cigarettes, but comprehensive regulation, labeling and enforcement were still developing at the time of these studies. States (e.g., California) have moved to raise the tobacco purchase age to 21.

Debate and implications
- Some experts argue many teens vape non‑nicotine flavors socially and may not become addicted. Others point to accumulating evidence that vaping can be a gateway to smoked tobacco.
- The USC team and accompanying commentaries warn that rising youth e‑cigarette use threatens to reverse decades of progress in reducing adolescent nicotine use and could produce new generations with nicotine dependence.
- The authors call for longitudinal monitoring of youth e‑cigarette/topography/nicotine dose, stronger regulation (product content, flavoring, marketing, sales to minors), and targeted prevention efforts to reduce youth initiation.

Bottom line
- Between 1995 and 2014 cigarette smoking among adolescents declined, but the emergence of e‑cigarettes has increased overall youth nicotine product use. Evidence from trend and prospective data indicates e‑cigarettes are recruiting adolescents who would not otherwise have used tobacco and substantially increase the odds of subsequent cigarette and other combustible tobacco initiation.

Summary:

A U.S. Navy Blue Angels F/A-18 crashed Thursday during a practice takeoff near Smyrna, just outside Nashville, Tennessee, killing the pilot, identified by a U.S. official as Marine Capt. Jeff Kuss. Kuss, a Durango, Colorado native who joined the Blue Angels in 2014 and had more than 1,400 flight hours, was the only casualty; no civilians on the ground were injured. Five other Blue Angels jets landed safely shortly after the accident. Navy leadership said the crash will be fully investigated. Local residents described witnessing the plane’s sudden descent and a resulting fireball; the crash occurred days before a scheduled weekend air show. The incident came the same day as a separate, nonfatal crash involving an Air Force Thunderbirds pilot in Colorado.

Separately, heavy rains and flooding in Texas created deadly conditions at Fort Hood, where an Army truck (a Light Medium Tactical Vehicle) was swept off a low-water crossing into a swollen creek, killing three soldiers and leaving six missing. Three other soldiers were rescued and remained hospitalized in stable condition. Extensive emergency search efforts—including aircraft, canine teams and swift-water craft—were deployed. Much of Texas was under flood watches or warnings after storms that have driven rivers, including the Brazos, to record or near-record levels; hundreds to thousands of homes have been affected and more heavy rain was forecast, raising fears of worsening flooding.

CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta drew attention after complaining on Twitter about loud music at a Trump rally in Missoula, Montana making live TV difficult and potentially creating a security concern for the Secret Service and local law enforcement. GOP consultant and former Melania Trump aide Justin Caporale mocked the comment with “Dear Diary….” Caporale later shared a screenshot showing Acosta had sent him a blunt direct message reading “F**k you,” then blocked him. The DM’s authenticity was confirmed by Daily Caller reporter Peter Hasson. Conservatives amplified and mocked the exchange. Acosta later apologized publicly, saying he had mistaken Caporale for an old campaign friend and expressing regret for any offense. CNN did not comment.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who has publicly defended North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and criticized President Trump’s Twitter attacks, was arrested for DUI in Newport Beach. Police stopped Rodman late Saturday for a traffic violation, administered field sobriety tests which he failed, and he blew over the legal limit on a breathalyzer. He was handcuffed, held in custody for about seven hours, then released when officers deemed him sober enough to care for himself. Rodman’s rep told TMZ that alcoholism has been an intermittent struggle for him over the past 15 years amid personal issues, and they’re considering sending him back to rehab. Rodman previously had a DUI arrest in 1999.

The USDA and EPA announced the United States’ first national food-waste reduction goal on Sept. 16, 2015: cut food loss and waste 50% by 2030. The initiative will be a public–private partnership including charitable and faith-based organizations, industry, and state, local and tribal governments to improve food security, conserve resources and reduce climate-harming methane from landfills.

Key facts and rationale
- U.S. food loss and waste equals roughly 31% of the retail-and-consumer food supply—about 133 billion pounds annually—and is the largest single component of municipal solid waste.  
- Food decomposing in landfills is a major source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas.  
- Even a 15% reduction could free enough food to feed more than 25 million Americans each year.  
- An average U.S. family of four wastes about 2 million calories worth nearly $1,500 yearly. About 14% of U.S. households are food insecure.

Federal and partner actions
- The U.S. Food Waste Challenge (launched 2013) provides a platform for sharing best practices; it had over 4,000 participants by end of 2014.  
- USDA has rolled out consumer tools (an app on storing food and understanding date labels), guidance to encourage donation of misbranded or substandard food, research into loss-reduction technologies, and a new consumer education campaign and ChooseMyPlate.gov resources on reducing waste.  
- USDA and EPA will urge private-sector actors (restaurants, grocers, institutions, food-service firms) to set aggressive reduction targets; some industry groups (e.g., Consumer Goods Forum) and companies (Albertson’s, FreshDirect, Sodexo) have pledged actions such as diverting food to hunger relief and reusing scraps.

Context
- The goal aligns with broader U.S. climate and sustainability efforts under the Obama administration and was announced ahead of a U.N. General Assembly discussion on sustainable production and consumption.

Overall, the plan frames food-waste reduction as a way to strengthen food security, cut greenhouse gases, conserve resources and spur innovation through coordinated federal leadership and multi-sector partnerships.

Federal land managers abruptly halted a weeklong Bureau of Land Management (BLM) roundup of cattle tied to Nevada rancher Cliven Bundy, citing "serious concern" for the safety of employees and the public after tensions escalated and armed supporters converged on the site.

Key points:
- The BLM stopped the operation Saturday and released roughly 300–400 of the gathered cattle back to the range; their original target had been about 900 head the agency said were trespassing on public land.
- The roundup centered on a long-running dispute: the federal government says Bundy's cattle have illegally grazed on public lands for about 20 years and that he owes roughly $1 million in unpaid grazing fees; Bundy argues Nevada, not the federal government, has authority and cites his family's long history on the land.
- The standoff drew armed militia and out-of-state supporters. Protesters briefly shut down northbound I-15 near Bunkerville; authorities later reopened the highway. A videotaped scuffle earlier in the week between protesters and federal rangers—during which rangers used Tasers and dogs and officials say a police dog was kicked—sparked further unrest and is under federal investigation.
- BLM Director Neil Kornze said the decision to end the gather was made after consulting law enforcement and because of escalating tensions. Nevada Gov. Brian Sandoval praised the move as prioritizing safety. Clark County Sheriff Douglas Gillespie said he helped mediate the agreement and emphasized his duty to maintain public safety even though federal land is under BLM jurisdiction.

Thae Yong-ho, the No. 2 North Korean diplomat in Britain and deputy ambassador at the Pyongyang embassy in London, has defected to South Korea with his wife and children. The 55-year-old, who had lived and worked in London for about a decade and publicly promoted North Korea, arrived in Seoul recently and is under South Korean government protection. His defection — the highest‑ranking North Korean official to flee in nearly 20 years — came as a surprise given his outwardly comfortable life in London, which included social activities such as tennis and dining locally, and duties like escorting a sibling of Kim Jong‑un to an Eric Clapton concert. South Korean officials say Thae cited disillusionment and disgust with Kim Jong‑un’s isolated, repressive regime, admiration for South Korea’s democratic system, and concern for his family’s future. The circumstances of how he evaded embassy monitoring and left Britain have not been disclosed.

This document compiles reporting and excerpts about Jeffrey Tambor’s public response to sexual harassment allegations that cost him his role on Amazon’s Transparent, reactions from colleagues, and the broader fallout.

Key points:
- Tambor was fired from Transparent after former assistant Van Barnes and actress Trace Lysette (both transgender) accused him of inappropriate behavior on set, including unwelcome touching, sexual comments, and other misconduct. Barnes also alleged propositioning, “butt pats,” and once watching her sleep; Tambor denies the most serious claims while admitting he could be “volatile,” “mean” and “difficult.”
- The allegations were made amid the #MeToo movement and sparked intense debate because Tambor, a cisgender man, played the show’s transgender lead, Maura Pfefferman. That casting had already been contentious for some in the trans community.
- Tambor granted a rare, emotional interview (The Hollywood Reporter) in which he expressed shock at being fired, acknowledged temper problems, apologized for yelling and being tactless, denied being a predator, and said he’s learning and trying to change. He also described his grief over losing the Maura role and the effect on his life.
- Amazon conducted a lengthy investigation; Tambor was interviewed for many hours but disputes parts of the inquiry’s outcome. Jill Soloway, showrunner and creator, texted him that his option would not be renewed and later publicly sided with the accusers; she and Tambor have not spoken since.
- Cast reactions are mixed: some colleagues (e.g., Jason Bateman, David Cross) have defended or supported Tambor, citing context and his value as a collaborator; others (Alia Shawkat, Jessica Walter implicitly) have expressed support for victims and discomfort with his behavior. On-set dynamics and accumulated tensions were cited by some as context for outbursts, not as excuses for harassment.
- After the controversy, Transparent will end with a final season without Tambor; he remains in Netflix’s Arrested Development and participated in promotion for its fifth season, where cast members addressed the issue at publicity events.
- The accusers’ post-allegation paths diverged: Lysette continues acting and activism; Barnes returned home and enrolled in cosmetology school. Barnes says she received little support from the show or Amazon beyond a GoFundMe offer.
- The story underscores complexities raised by #MeToo — power dynamics, cumulative workplace behavior, the particular sensitivities around trans representation, and tensions between public accountability and claims of misinterpretation — while leaving unresolved disputes over specific allegations.

Banks joins returning judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Heidi Klum and Howie Mandel and said she’s excited to connect with contestants and encourage them to “smize.” The summer series, in which performers compete for a $1 million prize, will air live from the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles.

The World Anti‑Doping Agency (WADA) said a Russian-linked hacking group known as Fancy Bear (aka APT28/Tsar Team) breached its ADAMS athlete database and published confidential medical records on several high‑profile U.S. Olympians, including Serena and Venus Williams, Simone Biles and Elena Delle Donne. The leaked files mainly show Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) — official permissions that allow athletes to take otherwise banned medicines for verified medical reasons. Fancy Bear claimed the TUEs prove widespread U.S. doping and threatened further releases.

WADA, USADA and national federations condemned the release as a criminal privacy breach aimed at undermining anti‑doping work. USADA chief Travis Tygart and USA Gymnastics stressed the athletes had followed rules and obtained proper approvals; the IOC said none violated anti‑doping regulations at Rio. WADA said the attackers likely used spear‑phishing to steal passwords (including that of whistleblower Yuliya Stepanova) and warned the incidents compromise efforts to rebuild trust after its investigation into Russian state‑sponsored doping. The hack is seen by analysts as part of a broader campaign of strategic leaks tied to Russian cyber‑operations.

The Israeli military launched a limited ground offensive into the Gaza Strip late Thursday, escalating an 11-day exchange of air strikes and rocket fire aimed at inflicting “a significant blow to Hamas.” Israel said troops and tanks entered areas near the border to destroy cross-border tunnels used by militants; the operation followed repeated failed de‑escalation efforts and came after militants attempted a tunnel attack earlier the same day.

Casualties and damage
- Gaza health officials reported at least 24 Palestinians killed and about 200 wounded since the ground phase began overnight; Gaza authorities say roughly 258 Palestinians (about three‑quarters civilians) have died since the wider campaign began on 8 July. Reports include children among the dead and dozens of homes destroyed, with more than 18,000 people displaced.
- Israel reported its first military fatality in the operation and said 14 “terrorists” were killed overnight; at least one Israeli civilian was killed by mortar fire and others seriously injured.
- Human Rights Watch and Gaza medics said a hospital (Wafa) was hit with patients inside; other strikes hit populated neighborhoods and a beach incident that killed four children drew Israeli acknowledgment of a tragic misidentification.

Military posture and tactics
- Israeli forces described the initial phase as focused on border tunnel networks and said troops remained largely in sparsely populated northern border zones while testing opposition before deeper incursions. The IDF warned residents to evacuate operational areas and approved calling up another 18,000 reservists (bringing the total mobilized since 8 July to 65,000).
- Militants continued rocket fire into Israel—more than 50 rockets were reported after the ground operation began—and vowed to resist. Hamas spokesmen called the invasion a dangerous step and vowed retaliation; Hamas leadership publicly asserted it would not accept defeat.

Diplomacy and truce efforts
- The ground offensive interrupted ongoing ceasefire negotiations in Cairo. A temporary five‑hour truce earlier in the day allowed limited aid deliveries and civilian movement; Egyptian-mediated talks involved Palestinian Authority and Arab League officials, who stressed stopping the bloodshed as a priority. Hamas had rejected an earlier Egyptian ceasefire proposal as insufficient.

Context and concerns
- Israeli officials framed the action as necessary to stop ongoing attacks and restore security for Israeli communities; spokesmen emphasized striking Hamas’s military capacity. Observers cautioned the operation is risky for Israeli forces and could cause heavy civilian harm if it expands into Gaza’s densely populated areas, as seen in past conflicts (2008–09, 2012). Humanitarian access remained restricted and urgent amid continued bombardment and displacement.

Key points:

After Sandra Bland was found dead in a Waller County, Texas, jail cell on July 13, 2015—three days after being arrested during a traffic stop—social media widely circulated a conspiracy theory that her mugshot shows her already dead. The theory pointed to the photo’s low resolution, alleged floor-like background, shoulder positioning, flat-looking eyes, and Bland wearing an orange jumpsuit as suspicious signs of a cover-up.

Leading forensic pathologists including Dr. Michael Baden, Dr. Adel Shaker, and other experienced practitioners dismissed the claim as without merit. They said a low-resolution mugshot cannot reliably indicate life or death unless extreme decomposition is present and called the speculation “ridiculous” and “alarmist.” Baden and others noted that a deceased person can appear to be sleeping and that mugshots commonly show somber or angry expressions; many alleged irregularities can’t be judged from the image alone.

Theories intensified amid other controversies: inconsistencies in booking documents (medical history, suicide-attempt notations and dates), dashcam footage and booking-video “glitches,” questions about where and how Bland could have hanged herself with a trash bag, and odd details reported about the cell (e.g., a Bible placed on the bed). Authorities and prosecutors responded by explaining procedural reasons for some document differences, releasing additional booking photos and security footage showing Bland walking and posing for her mugshot, and saying the case would undergo a thorough review. The Harris County medical examiner ruled Bland’s death a suicide; Waller County officials said she died by asphyxiation with a trash bag. Forensic experts and released booking footage have largely undercut the claim that the mugshot depicts a dead person, while broader questions about the circumstances of her death remain under investigation and continue to fuel public scrutiny.

Donald Trump posted and then deleted a campaign tweet that showed Hillary Clinton over a pile of $100 bills with a six‑point star (widely interpreted as a Star of David) and the caption “Most Corrupt Candidate Ever!” Critics — including the Clinton campaign, the Anti‑Defamation League, Jewish outreach director Sarah Bard, and some congressional leaders — called the image blatantly antisemitic and part of a pattern of racially charged messaging from Trump. The image was traced by Mic to an alt‑right / white‑supremacist message board and to racist Twitter accounts; Mic reported the file name and watermark suggested ties to extremist sources.

The Trump campaign initially defended the graphic as using a generic or “sheriff’s” star and later replaced the image with one overlaid by a circle (observers noted star points still showed). Dan Scavino, the campaign’s social media director, said the image was “lifted from an anti‑Hillary Twitter user,” and other surrogates dismissed criticisms as political correctness. Some white‑nationalists praised the original tweet, intensifying concerns. The ADL’s Jonathan Greenblatt urged Trump to apologize and disavow bigotry; others said the episode raised questions about the campaign’s sourcing practices and tolerance of extremist content.

Trump moved on publicly to other topics (vice‑presidential speculation, condemning Islamist terrorism) while the controversy unfolded on the same day Clinton was interviewed by the FBI about her private email server.

President Barack Obama used his weekly radio and internet address to mourn the victims of the mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary in Newtown, Connecticut, and to call for unity and "meaningful action" to prevent future tragedies. He expressed deep sympathy for the families—noting most victims were young children—and described how he and Michelle Obama were comforting their own children. Obama repeated his request to set aside politics but did not specify any particular gun-control measures. The shooting, in which a 20-year-old gunman killed 20 children and six adults at the school before killing himself (26 dead at the scene, two more died at hospital), reignited debate over gun policy. New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg urged immediate leadership on gun control, criticizing past inaction. In Washington, partisan disputes over the fiscal cliff were briefly set aside: House Speaker John Boehner canceled the Republican weekly address so Obama could speak for the nation and offered condolences.

Prince Alireza (Ali-Reza) Pahlavi, the 44-year-old youngest son of the late Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, was found dead of an apparent self-inflicted single gunshot in his South End/Boston home in the early hours of Jan. 4, 2011. Boston police and Suffolk County officials said the wound appeared to be self-inflicted; his brother Reza Pahlavi announced the death on his website, saying Ali‑Reza had “struggled for years to overcome his sorrow” and finally succumbed.

Born in Tehran in 1966, Alireza left Iran with his family after the 1979 revolution. He lived for many years in Boston, kept a low public profile, and pursued academic studies in ancient Iranian languages and civilizations at institutions including Princeton, Columbia and Harvard (he enrolled in a Harvard doctorate program in 1993 but did not complete it). Neighbors described him as reserved and private.

Family friends and associates said Alireza suffered long-term depression, deepened by the deaths of his sister Leila in 2001 (found dead in a London hotel room from an accidental overdose) and his father in 1980. Reza Pahlavi, who lives in the U.S. and is active in opposition to Iran’s clerical regime, and other family members planned to travel to Boston; the family asked for privacy while mourning. Authorities continued an investigation but treated the death as an apparent suicide.

Vice President Joe Biden officiated his first-ever wedding Monday, marrying longtime White House staffers Brian Mosteller and Joe Mahshie at the Naval Observatory. Biden obtained a temporary D.C. certification to preside over the private ceremony, attended only by the grooms’ families. He posted a photo on Twitter saying he was "proud to marry Brian and Joe," and his wife Jill Biden tweeted, "Love is love!" Biden had publicly endorsed same-sex marriage in 2012.

Poland summoned the US ambassador and demanded an apology after FBI Director James Comey wrote in a Washington Post piece (adapted from a Holocaust Memorial Museum speech) that “the murderers and accomplices of Germany, and Poland, and Hungary, and so many, many other places” had convinced themselves their actions were right. Polish leaders — including President Bronislaw Komorowski and Prime Minister Ewa Kopacz — protested strongly, saying Comey’s formulation falsely implicated Poland and insulted Poles who helped Jews; Poland emphasized it was a victim of Nazi occupation, not a perpetrator. U.S. envoy Stephen Mull attended Warsaw Ghetto Uprising ceremonies, told Warsaw he had made clear that “Nazi Germany alone” bears responsibility for the Holocaust, and apologized for the misunderstanding while noting the article’s broader point that many people in various countries either aided the Nazis or failed to do enough. The controversy prompted a Washington Post column criticizing Comey’s wording, arguing it blurred the crucial distinction between Germany’s state-engineered extermination and the different circumstances in occupied countries like Poland and, later, occupied Hungary. Comey’s original commentary stressed the Holocaust’s lessons about human capacity for moral surrender and the need for Holocaust education and institutional checks on power; critics say his phrasing risked historical falsification by suggesting collective culpability of Poles. A correction clarified an earlier attribution error about comments by the Polish ambassador.

This piece centers on a four-minute video Glamour posted of supermodel Gigi Hadid simply staring into the camera. The article opens with a playful memory of childhood staring contests and positions Hadid — a 22-year-old model with major commercial and editorial credentials, a large social following, and a history of speaking out on social issues — as an expert at prolonged eye contact. Glamour framed the clip as “weirdly mesmerizing” and even slowed it down for effect; the video was promoted alongside Hadid’s inclusion in Glamour’s 2017 Women of the Year.

A critical voice in the piece questions the stunt as emblematic of larger trends in digital media: publishers pivoting to video without clear ideas, repurposing photo-shoot footage as low-effort content, and elevating celebrity for doing “nothing.” The critic finds the video underwhelming — full of blinks, minimal movement, and a contrived eerie soundtrack — and uses it to argue that outlets are baffled by nontraditional stars like Hadid, who gain fame largely through presence rather than conventional talents. Overall, the article mixes admiration for Hadid’s status and work ethic with skepticism about the video and what it says about modern media priorities.

Researchers analyzing the 2013–2016 West African Ebola epidemic found evidence that a substantial minority of infections may be asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, implying the outbreak was more widespread than case counts indicate and that undetected transmission may have occurred.

Study details and key findings
- A serosurvey (Oct 2015–Jan 2016) in Sukudu, Sierra Leone—a village (~900 residents) classified as an Ebola “hotspot”—tested 187 people who had been quarantined because they lived with or shared a latrine with confirmed Ebola cases.
- Using ELISA assays for Ebola glycoprotein and nucleoprotein IgG (validated against positive and negative controls), researchers identified 14 seropositive individuals (7.5% of tested). Of these, 12 reported no Ebola-like symptoms during the outbreak and 2 recalled only fever.
- Counting these 14 alongside the village’s reported 34 EVD cases implies roughly 25% of infections there were minimally symptomatic, and raises the symptomatic case fatality ratio for that village to about 78%.

Implications and caveats
- The findings support the idea that Ebola infection can present across a clinical spectrum, including asymptomatic or very mild cases. Similar observations date back to early Ebola work and other regional serosurveys.
- If asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic infections can transmit Ebola, standard surveillance relying on symptomatic case detection could miss a meaningful fraction of transmission events—complicating containment, contact tracing, and modeling.
- Important limitations: small, single-village sample; retrospective symptom recall and possible underreporting due to stigma; IgG indicates past infection but not timing; some potential assay cross-reactivity or misclassification of controls. The study did not determine whether asymptomatic individuals can transmit the virus or whether they develop long-term sequelae.
- The results affect definitions of survivorship, surveillance strategies, vaccine study design, and planning for future outbreaks.

Conclusion
The study provides serologic evidence that minimally symptomatic Ebola infections occurred during the West African epidemic and may have accounted for a meaningful share of infections in at least one hotspot. Broader serosurveys and research on transmission potential and clinical outcomes in seropositive but asymptomatic people are needed to refine outbreak detection, containment, and survivor support policies.

Summary — Belgorod shooting, April 22 (developing)

- Incident: On the afternoon of April 22 a gunman opened fire in central Belgorod (southwest Russia, ~40 km from the Ukrainian border) outside and then inside a shop. The attack occurred at about 14:00 local time (10:00 GMT).

- Casualties: Six people were killed (including a 14‑year‑old girl); one other wounded who later died in hospital. Five victims died at the scene.

- Suspect and manhunt: Authorities identified the suspect as Sergey Pomazun, about 32, with a prior criminal record. He reportedly fled the scene in a dark BMW X5; his car and residence were later found but no weapon was recovered. Police initially (and mistakenly) announced his detention, but he remained at large while a large-scale search continued. Local police mobilized roughly 1,200 officers, special forces were deployed, border/customs checks were heightened and descriptions were sent to nearby Ukrainian regions. A reward was offered for information.

- Weapons and motive: Tabloid reports alleged the shooter used a 7.62mm Saiga carbine; officials also warned he might be armed with a gas pistol and a semi‑automatic rifle. Media suggested conflicting theories including an attempted robbery of an arms shop and possible psychiatric history; investigators had not confirmed motive or mental‑health claims. Some reports mentioned a possible second suspect, but police had not confirmed this.

- Local reaction and response: Belgorod authorities imposed a shelter‑in‑place advisory during the special operation, declared two days of mourning (April 23–24), and said funeral costs and aid to victims’ families would be covered. President Putin was being kept informed. Psychologists were sent to assist relatives; churches held memorial services. Residents described panic and shock; crowds later laid flowers and candles at the scene.

- Context: Mass shootings are rare in Russia but several high‑profile cases have occurred in recent years (including a November 2012 Moscow office massacre). Russian gun laws restrict civilian access to rifles and require hunting‑club membership for some firearms, though illegally obtained weapons have been used in prior attacks.

Note: This was a developing story with some conflicting reports; details (including suspect status, motive and weapon type) were subject to confirmation.

Pope Francis told reporters aboard the papal plane returning from Armenia that Christians should apologize to groups the Church has offended or exploited, specifically mentioning gay people, the poor, exploited women, child labor victims and those harmed by the Church’s blessing of weapons. Reiterating the Catechism, he said homosexuals must not be discriminated against, should be respected and accompanied pastorally, and asked, “Who are we to judge?” While he has not changed Church doctrine that calls homosexual acts sinful, his repeated emphasis on mercy and this explicit call to apologize drew praise from LGBT advocates and more liberal Catholics as a breakthrough; some conservatives say his remarks are ambiguous on sexual morality.

In the same news conference Francis addressed other topics from the Armenia trip: he defended using the word “genocide” for the World War I-era mass killings of Armenians (noting his long usage and past papal references), urged creative reform and greater flexibility within the European Union after Brexit, and dismissed suggestions of there being “two popes,” calling Benedict XVI “Pope Emeritus” and “the wise grandpa.” Vatican spokesmen later stressed the Pope’s intent to build bridges, not provoke Turkey.

Researchers analyzed data from the Pittsburgh Youth Study to examine whether adolescent marijuana use predicts physical or mental health problems in midlife. The sample comprised 408–506 males (depending on follow-up) who were first assessed as seventh‑graders in 1987–88 and followed with frequent interviews through age 25 and again around age 35. Using detailed longitudinal records, participants were classified into four marijuana-use trajectories: low/never users (46%); adolescence‑limited users (11%); late‑increasing/adult‑onset users (21%); and early, chronic users (22%).

After controlling for potential confounds (including tobacco and other drug use and socioeconomic factors), the study found no significant differences across these trajectory groups on a range of self‑reported and diagnostically assessed outcomes in their mid‑30s. Measured outcomes included lifetime depression and anxiety, psychotic symptoms, respiratory problems (e.g., asthma), cardiovascular indicators (e.g., high blood pressure), allergies, and headaches. Results held even in models without covariate adjustment, and did not differ by race in this sample (about 54% Black, 42% White).

The authors note the findings contrast with some prior work linking chronic marijuana use to later psychiatric disorders but align with other studies that found no such effects. They emphasize strengths of the design—prospective measurement of use and health across development—while acknowledging limitations: the sample included only men, follow‑up extended only into the mid‑30s (before many cardiovascular illnesses typically emerge), relied in part on self‑reported health measures, and may miss subtler symptoms (e.g., transient paranoia). The authors also suggest that individual differences (including genetic vulnerability) may moderate risk, and that marijuana might accelerate onset in susceptible people rather than cause disorders broadly.

Their conclusion cautions that this single study is not definitive for policy decisions on legalization; its results should be considered alongside the broader, mixed literature on long‑term consequences of early chronic marijuana use.

A Mountain View police traffic officer stopped a slow-moving Google self-driving car on El Camino Real near Rengstorff Ave after noticing it was causing traffic to back up. The car was traveling about 24 mph in a 35 mph zone. When the officer approached he identified the vehicle as a Google Autonomous Vehicle, contacted the onboard operators to discuss how the car selects speed and to inform them about impeding traffic (California Vehicle Code 22400(a)). A passenger — not the car — took control and pulled the vehicle over. No citation was issued; Mountain View PD noted the vehicles are classified as neighborhood electric vehicles under California law and are permitted on roads with posted speed limits of 35 mph or less, so the car’s presence on El Camino Real was lawful. Mountain View PD meets regularly with Google about safe operation of the fleet. Google’s Self-Driving Car Project said its prototypes are speed-capped at 25 mph for safety and noted they have not received tickets after 1.2 million autonomous miles. Media inquiries go to policepio@mountainview.gov.

Researchers report that reduced eye contact in infancy is the earliest measurable behavioral sign yet linked to later autism. Using eye-tracking, teams at Emory’s Marcus Autism Center followed 110 infants (59 high-risk because they had an autistic sibling, 51 low-risk) across ten sessions from 2 months to 2 years while the babies watched videos of caregivers. At age 3, 13 children were diagnosed with autism (11 boys analyzed). Infants who later developed autism showed normal levels of eye looking at birth but began a steady decline in attention to people’s eyes between about 2 and 6 months; this decline continued into toddlerhood. By contrast, typically developing infants increased eye looking until ~9 months and then remained steady. Greater and faster declines in eye fixation predicted more severe autism. Babies who developed autism spent relatively more time looking at mouths, bodies, and—after the first year—objects, suggesting they miss social learning opportunities that typically come from face-focused attention.

Experts call the study a major advance because it documents a developmental shift rather than a single snapshot, and it points to a possible early window (before 6 months) for intervention. However, the differences are subtle and detectable only with specialized eye-tracking equipment; parents are unlikely to notice them unaided. The authors and commentators stress the need for larger replication studies and caution that eye-tracking will not identify all autism cases, but they see potential for very early screening tools and for developing interventions aimed at preserving or boosting early social engagement.
