More than 200 people attended the unveiling of a new Confederate monument, “Unknown Alabama Confederate Soldiers,” Sunday at the privately owned Confederate Veterans Memorial Park near Brantley in Crenshaw County, Ala. The modest stone marker, placed among existing monuments, replica cannons and tall flagpoles, is dedicated to “unknown Confederate soldiers” from the Civil War, particularly those from the local area.

Organized by park owner and Sons of Confederate Veterans member David Coggins, the ceremony included speeches, a flag-raising, the naming of Confederate veterans, an unveiling with blank gunfire and firing from replica cannons. Attendees — many wearing Confederate-themed clothing, period costumes or uniforms — waved Confederate flags; members of the Daughters of the Confederacy and re-enactors participated. About 10 people affiliated with the Three Percenters militia were present in camouflage and body armor, carrying firearms; organizers said they were there for security.

Speakers repeatedly said the event was meant to honor ancestors and heritage, not to respond to recent racial unrest or the violent Charlottesville clashes; organizers said the dedication had been planned months earlier. The memorial, surrounded by a black metal fence and flanked by other monuments, bears the inscription “Unkown AL Soldier CSA” and the quote “Mother, I have been found, I am home.” Organizers also solicited donations for a future Confederate Navy monument.

A 106-year-old woman, Virginia McLaurin, joyfully met President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama at a White House event for Black History Month. A video shows McLaurin excitedly entering the room, squealing and telling the president, "It's an honor," as the Obamas warmly greet her. Michelle hugs her and says, "I want to be like you when I grow up," and the three dance together in the Blue Room, laughing. McLaurin expressed disbelief and happiness at being in the White House and seeing "a black president."

Islamic State (IS) fighters overran the Yazidi-majority town and district of Sinjar in northern Iraq in a rapid weekend offensive that routed Kurdish peshmerga defenders, captured towns and oil fields, and left tens of thousands displaced and surrounded. The Yazidis—an ancient, mostly Kurdish minority whom IS brands “devil worshippers”—fled en masse to nearby Mount Sinjar, where between 10,000 and 40,000 civilians were reported trapped, exposed and running out of water, food and medicine.

Witnesses, Yazidi MPs and U.N. agencies reported mass suffering and killings after IS seized Sinjar. Reports cited about 50 people killed when IS entered the town, and UNICEF and local officials said dozens of children (UNICEF reported some 40 children dead in the 48 hours to Monday night) died from dehydration, hunger and the harsh conditions on the mountain. Families buried victims in shallow graves; aid airdrops reached few of those stranded. Survivors described forced compliance measures—such as placing white flags on homes—and accounts of abductions and killings of those who stayed behind.

The IS advance highlighted the collapse of Iraqi security forces earlier in the campaign, the failure of some Kurdish units to hold the town, and the broader political paralysis in Baghdad as Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki resisted calls to step aside. Kurdish forces pledged counter-attacks and sought to reopen routes to the stranded on Sinjar; various Kurdish factions, including groups from Syria and the PKK, signaled willingness to assist. U.N. agencies warned that large-scale humanitarian flights and evacuations were urgently needed to avert further catastrophe for the displaced Yazidis.

A California federal judge dismissed a $42 million copyright lawsuit filed against Taylor Swift by R&B artist Jessie Braham (who records as Jesse Graham). Braham alleged that Swift’s 2014 hit "Shake It Off" lifted distinctive lyrics from his 2013 song "Haters Gone Hate," claiming a 22-word phrase and asserting that 92% of her song derived from his work. 

U.S. District Judge Gail Standish threw out the complaint for failing to plead sufficient factual detail beyond conjecture, giving Braham leave to amend if he can cure the deficiencies. In a lighthearted ruling, Standish repeatedly quoted Swift’s lyrics — including lines from "Shake It Off," "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together," "Blank Space," and "Bad Blood" — to illustrate her points, closing with the quip that, for now, the defendants have “shaken off” the lawsuit.

Neiman Marcus disclosed late in December that customer payment-card data had been stolen after purchases at its stores, but investigators briefed on the case say the company’s network was first breached in mid‑July and the intrusion was not fully contained until January 1. Neiman publicly acknowledged the theft only after inquiries by security journalist Brian Krebs; it informed credit-card companies around Christmas. The firm says it has no evidence Social Security numbers or birth dates were taken, does not collect PINs in stores, and has offered affected customers one year of free credit monitoring. Neiman has defended its delay in public disclosure as necessary to confirm evidence; critics and some law‑enforcement sources questioned the timing, noting the announcement came after the holiday shopping season.

Investigations of the Neiman Marcus breach are ongoing, and state attorneys general from multiple states are coordinating probes of both the Neiman and Target incidents to determine any links. Neiman has said it has “no knowledge of any connection” to Target’s breach.

Separately, reports about the Target breach (which affected far more people) and an iSight forensic report filed with the U.S. Secret Service describe sophisticated point‑of‑sale (POS) malware that scraped unencrypted card data from cash-register memory during authorization. The iSight analysis highlights operational sophistication, notes POS‑memory‑scraping malware has roots in Eastern Europe (with similar techniques also seen in Brazil), and warns this method is likely to be used more widely because it yields high rewards with relatively low risk. Federal and private investigators view the Target attack as part of a broader international campaign against multiple retailers; investigations into attribution and connections among incidents remain active.

Vincent van Gogh’s reputation as perhaps the greatest colourist is complicated by new scientific findings showing that some of his original pigments have faded or chemically altered, changing the appearance of many works from their 1880s state. The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam presents this research in a new exhibition, Van Gogh at Work, which combines technical, historical and personal insights into his practice: the types of canvases he used (including reused supports and paintings applied on the reverse), his close exchanges with contemporaries such as Toulouse-Lautrec, and interactive displays that let visitors inspect paint texture and microscopic detail. The show also displays personal artefacts—his palette, tubes of paint and a loaned Sunflowers—and emphasizes that, despite colour loss, Van Gogh’s expressive power endures.

Complementing the museum’s findings, scientists in Belgium have identified a chemical pathway explaining why some of Van Gogh’s reds—notably red lead (minium) used in paintings such as Wheat Stack Under a Cloudy Sky—are turning white. Using x‑ray powder diffraction tomography on minute white globules from the painting, researchers found a core of minium surrounded by degradation products including plumbonacrite (a rare lead carbonate hydroxide), hydrocerussite and cerussite. They propose that light-driven conversion of minium produces plumbonacrite, which then reacts with CO2 to yield the white carbonates that bleach the red pigment. This “missing link” finding is important for conservation practice, reinforcing the need to control light exposure in museums. Overall, the technical revelations deepen understanding of Van Gogh’s methods and materials without diminishing his artistic stature.

Kanye West performed a private, reportedly multimillion-dollar gig in Almaty, Kazakhstan over the Labor Day weekend for the wedding of a grandson of Kazakh president Nursultan Nazarbayev. The show took place at the Hotel Royal Tulip and included hits like "Can't Tell Me Nothing"; video and photos of the performance circulated online. Reports estimate Kanye was paid around $3 million. The piece notes Nazarbayev’s wealth and controversial reputation—his family’s business ties, Kazakhstan’s low corruption rankings, and past artists declining paid appearances for his circle. The wedding is believed to have involved members of Nazarbayev’s extended family, including relatives of his daughter Dinara and her husband Timur Kulibayev.

Death Valley recorded an average temperature of 107.39–107.4°F in July, the highest monthly average ever measured at a single location in U.S. (and Western Hemisphere) history, breaking the previous U.S. record of 107.2°F from 1917. The average daily high was about 119.6°F; nighttime lows never fell below 89°F for the entire month and rose above 100°F on three nights. The hottest day was July 7 (127°F). While this is a U.S. and Western Hemisphere record, it is slightly below the global warm-month record of 107.44°F set at King Khaled, Saudi Arabia in August 2015. Death Valley National Park—uninhabited except for staff—also joined other Western U.S. locations and Miami in posting record-warm months that July.

A white sample bag flown to the lunar surface on Apollo 11 in June 1969—used by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to collect the mission’s first lunar material—has become the subject of a legal dispute after it was mistakenly sold at a government auction.

The bag was seized in 2003 during the criminal investigation of Max Ary, founder and longtime director of the Kansas Cosmosphere, who was convicted in 2005 of stealing and selling hundreds of space artifacts (many loaned by NASA). Ary was sentenced to three years in prison and ordered to pay restitution; he has denied intent, saying he mixed museum pieces with his personal collection.

Federal prosecutors say an internal clerical error led to two distinct lunar sample bags being conflated under the same inventory number. One was an Apollo 17 bag Ary sold in 2001 for $24,150; the other was the Apollo 11 bag found in Ary’s garage. Because of the misidentification, NASA was not properly notified before the Apollo 11 bag was forfeited and sold at a government auction on Feb. 15, 2015, for $995 to Nancy Carlson of Illinois. Carlson later sent the bag to NASA’s Johnson Space Center for authentication; NASA then learned the bag had been sold without its notice or permission and has withheld it. Carlson sued NASA in Illinois federal court seeking its return.

On July 15, federal prosecutors asked the Kansas federal judge who handled Ary’s case to set aside the forfeiture, rescind the sale and refund Carlson, calling the Apollo 11 bag “a rare artifact, if not a national treasure.” The dispute centers on correcting the clerical misidentification and resolving ownership and restitution of the historic artifact.

Two 33-year-old friends from Middlesbrough, company director Phillip Boyle and rigger Jamie Blyth, made headlines after a drunken late-night decision to fly to Pattaya, Thailand. What began as a “quiet pint” at a local pub escalated into buying last-minute tickets at Manchester Airport the next morning, with Boyle admitting he’d packed only a carrier bag of T‑shirts and underwear. They endured two long flights (with a stop in Abu Dhabi), spent a couple of days in Pattaya visiting bars and restaurants, slept little, and had a generally wild but enjoyable short break—though Boyle says he’s fallen behind at work and had a newly bought pair of trainers stolen. Both men say they had a great time despite initial regrets on the flight, and Boyle recommends the spontaneous trip. The episode drew comparisons to similar drunken travel stunts reported in the press.

Maine voters will decide a Nov. 7 referendum to expand Medicaid, which supporters say would extend free health care to roughly 70–80,000 low-income Mainers and bring federal funds and jobs to the state. The nonpartisan state fiscal office estimates about 80,000 more people would become eligible and that expansion would bring roughly $525 million per year in federal dollars while costing Maine taxpayers about $54 million annually; the federal government would cover about 90% of the expansion population’s costs.

Supporters — including hospitals, Maine Equal Justice Partners, and others — argue expansion will improve health outcomes, increase preventive care access, reduce the uninsured rate (Maine’s was 9.1% in 2016), stabilize struggling rural hospitals, help address workforce shortages, and create about 4,000 health-care jobs. Hospitals have backed expansion for years and say it would ease the financial burden of uncompensated care.

Governor Paul LePage strongly opposes expansion, calling it “pure welfare” and arguing it would unfairly burden Maine taxpayers and divert resources from the elderly and disabled. He has repeatedly vetoed legislative expansion efforts and attacked hospitals for supporting the referendum, claiming (incorrectly, according to the state fiscal office) that expansion would cost taxpayers $100 million per year or $500 million over five years. LePage says hospitals would gain financially at taxpayers’ expense; proponents counter that expansion would not reduce services for the elderly or intellectually disabled and that state Medicaid choices can protect those programs.

Campaign organizers face turnout challenges because there are no statewide or national races this year to drive voters to the polls, and LePage retains strong support in many rural areas. Senator Susan Collins is not taking a position on the ballot measure, though campaign leaders hope her past support for Medicaid during repeal debates may help. If voters approve the referendum, LePage could not block it.

Tesla has filed an international patent for an automated turn-signal system that uses its Autopilot sensors and onboard processor to detect when a vehicle is about to cross a lane line or make a turn, and then activate the turn signal for the driver. The system would infer intent from measured steering angles and surrounding-vehicle detection rather than relying on the driver to physically move the stalk. Tesla envisions the tech helping forgetful or lazy drivers and could also apply to autonomous lane changes; the company is already developing Autopilot features that handle on/off-ramps and automated lane changes. The patent may never reach production—manufacturers often patent ideas defensively—and Tesla has not yet commented further. The article notes this is no substitute for proper signaling before maneuvers, but it could reduce un-signaled lane changes if implemented.

A University of North Carolina–led analysis published in the Journal of Cancer Policy estimates that indoor tanning in the U.S. caused about 263,600 skin cancer cases in 2015 (including ~8,947 melanomas, >168,000 squamous cell carcinomas and ≥86,000 basal cell carcinomas). Direct medical costs to treat those cases totaled about $343 million that year (average Medicare-based costs: $5,054 per melanoma case and $1,168 for other skin cancers). When the authors also estimated lifetime economic losses from premature death and lost productivity using a GDP-based value per lost life-year ($55,266/year), they projected over $127 billion in lifetime losses among people currently diagnosed with tanning-related cancers.

The study combined published risk increases linked to tanning beds with tanning prevalence (roughly 30 million U.S. users and ~25,000 salons) to attribute cases and costs to indoor tanning. Authors note their estimates may undercount cases and omit some long-term care and productivity costs; outside experts cautioned the economic figures could be overstated and emphasized that UV exposure from natural sun also carries risks. Dermatologists stress that tanning beds increase melanoma risk—particularly for young women—and that even one session raises squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma risks. Regulatory moves (FDA warnings, a 10% excise tax under the ACA) aim to curb indoor tanning, and the study’s authors hope their cost estimates will help reduce use.

Julian Assange—founder of WikiLeaks and then holed up in the Ecuadorian embassy to avoid extradition—publicly rejected a meeting with Benedict Cumberbatch and sharply criticized DreamWorks’ film The Fifth Estate, in a letter to the actor released in January and reiterated in October. Though he praised Cumberbatch personally and said he might have enjoyed meeting him, Assange said he could not meet because doing so would legitimize a film he considers misleading, defamatory and politically motivated. He accused the production of basing its script on “toxic” books by authors with vendettas against him, distorting events, reviving disproven allegations, and strengthening arguments used by governments prosecuting WikiLeaks and its sources. Assange warned the film would harm WikiLeaks’ staff and sources at a moment of intense government pressure and called the project “political opportunism, influence, revenge and, above all, cowardice,” later dismissing the movie as a “geriatric snoozefest.” Cumberbatch reportedly responded courteously and admitted parts of the script troubled him. The Fifth Estate, directed by Bill Condon and based partly on Daniel Domscheit-Berg’s book, premiered at Toronto and attracted both praise and strong criticism from WikiLeaks for its accuracy and depiction of people involved.

Summary:

The document profiles Twitter’s evolving identity, leadership and product strategy. Flipboard’s Mr. McCue describes Twitter as a new kind of company—neither purely a tech nor a media firm—and praises CEO Dick (Dick Costolo) and the company’s unapologetic approach. Twitter has taken public stances defending user privacy, fighting court and government demands for user data; chief lawyer Alexander Macgillivray framed the company as protecting users’ ability to speak freely.

Leadership history and dynamics: Twitter’s early rapid growth is recalled by co-founder Biz Stone; Dick Costolo, who joined as COO in 2009 and became CEO in 2010, now steers the company. Costolo rehired Jack Dorsey, whose role was reduced after managerial complaints; Dorsey remains influential on strategy though less involved in day-to-day reporting. Colleagues say Costolo drives fast decisions and has shaped Twitter’s culture, sometimes brusquely—examples include firing a senior employee by phone and pushing some board members out. He has also pushed third-party apps away, a move critics say alienates early, enthusiastic developers in favor of a broader consumer base.

Product direction — in-house video hosting: Twitter is weighing building its own video-hosting capability so users could upload video directly through official mobile apps, similar to its recent move to internalize photo hosting. The goal is to improve consistency, user experience, stability across clients, and to better control how media appears in the timeline. Owning video delivery could also enhance ad products (promoted tweets) and monetization. However, the change would hurt third-party video hosts (yFrog, TwitVid, Vodpod). The plan is under internal discussion and, if approved, likely to be rolled out quietly in a future update.

The FDA announced it has approved Teva’s Plan B One-Step (levonorgestrel) for over‑the‑counter sale to females 15 years and older; girls under 15 must get it by prescription. Previously the pill was OTC only for ages 17+. The agency said studies showed females 15+ could understand proper use and labeling, and that broader OTC access can help reduce unintended pregnancies. Packaged product will carry a “not for sale to those under 15—proof of age required” label, include a product code prompting cashiers to verify age, and have security tags; retailers with onsite pharmacies will stock it in family‑planning/female‑health aisles and sell during normal hours whether the pharmacy is open or not. Teva plans education for consumers and staff and offered audits of age‑verification practices.

The decision falls short of a federal judge’s April order to remove all age and point‑of‑sale restrictions for emergency contraception; the Center for Reproductive Rights said it will continue litigation, arguing remaining ID and access barriers are still significant. Senator Patty Murray praised the move as science‑based progress. The FDA noted the action is independent of the court case and that other emergency contraceptives (generic two‑dose Plan B and prescription ulipristal/ella) retain their current statuses. The pill is most effective if taken within 72 hours of unprotected sex and does not prevent STDs or terminate an existing pregnancy.

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan disclosed that Michael Cohen, President Donald Trump’s personal lawyer, has been under a criminal investigation for months focused on his personal business dealings. This was revealed after FBI raids Monday on Cohen’s home, hotel room, office, safety deposit box and two cell phones; earlier covert warrants had also yielded multiple email accounts. Prosecutors say their review of those emails showed Cohen did “little to no legal work” and exchanged “zero emails” with Trump.

Cohen has not been charged. His lawyers and Trump’s counsel moved in court to block prosecutors from using some seized material, arguing much of it is protected by attorney‑client privilege and asking that lawyers or a special master, rather than the government’s filter team, perform the initial privilege review. Prosecutors asked the court to permit a standard “taint” or “filter” team — a segregated group that vets potentially privileged documents before investigators see them — and said they are confident most seized material will not be covered by privilege. They also noted Cohen told at least one witness his only client was Trump, and that Mueller’s office had previously dropped a records request about Cohen’s business dealings and referred related matters to Manhattan.

The search reportedly targeted communications about efforts to suppress negative pre‑election information, including the “Access Hollywood” tape and a nearly $130,000 payment to Stormy Daniels said to have been made to silence an alleged affair, as well as records tied to Cohen’s taxi medallion business. Prosecutors suggested communications about the Daniels payment may not be privileged, citing the President’s public statements.

A hearing in Manhattan federal court over access to the seized records was adjourned to Monday so Cohen must appear; Trump’s newly engaged lawyer expressed concern about fairness if the government’s filter team handles the review. News organizations successfully argued to keep most of the proceedings public.

A senior North Korean diplomat, Vice Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui, sharply rebuked recent U.S. comments and threatened to pull out of the planned June 12 summit between Kim Jong-un and President Donald Trump. Responding to Vice‑President Mike Pence and others who invoked the “Libya model” of denuclearization, Choe called Pence’s remarks “ignorant” and “stupid,” labeled him a “political dummy” in some reports, and warned that if diplomacy failed the U.S. could face a “nuclear-to-nuclear showdown” or “an appalling tragedy.” Analysts note Choe is a top aide whose statements likely reflect Kim’s thinking.

Her attack follows rising tensions after U.S. officials, including National Security Adviser John Bolton and Pence, referenced Libya as a precedent — a comparison Pyongyang views as deeply insulting because Libya’s leader was later overthrown and killed. The exchanges have raised doubts about whether the Singapore summit will proceed, though both sides still appear to want talks. North Korea meanwhile is pressing ahead with a public dismantling of its Punggye-ri nuclear test site and has invited international journalists to observe the event. U.S. and North Korean teams reportedly plan further preparatory meetings in Singapore.

Police say a 39-year-old man, identified as Joshua Corbett, was arrested early Sunday after breaking into Sandra Bullock’s home and searching through her belongings. Authorities suspect the incident may have been driven by an obsession: sources told Today that Corbett might have kept a diary devoted to the Oscar-winning actress. The break-in occurred around 6:30 a.m., hours after Bullock attended the Spike TV Guys' Choice Awards; she and her 4-year-old son Louis were inside the house at the time. Her representative confirmed she was unharmed.

A Texas death-row inmate, Robert Roberson III, has been granted a stay of execution and his case sent back to a trial court, halting a scheduled June 21 execution. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals based its decision on a new state law allowing challenges that rely on new scientific evidence potentially showing wrongful convictions. Roberson, 49, was convicted in 2002 of killing his 2-year-old daughter, Nikki Curtis, after prosecutors said he caused fatal head trauma; experts at trial testified she died of shaken baby syndrome and prosecutors at one point alleged sexual abuse (an element later dropped). 

Roberson’s lawyers argued the conviction rested on “junk science,” asserting that modern research shows the classic triad of brain swelling, subdural bleeding and retinal hemorrhages long attributed to deliberate shaking can also result from short falls, medical conditions, birth trauma or other causes. They also noted the absence of neck injuries expected if a child were fatally shaken and raised alternative explanations offered by Roberson—an accidental fall from a bed, a high fever or an earlier injury or illness. The Texas attorney general’s office maintains the conviction and death sentence were proper. 

The appeals court returned the case for further review; there is no timetable for resolution. One of nine judges dissented from the reprieve.

Slate’s analysis of the Supreme Court’s decision on the Affordable Care Act highlights two distinct outcomes in one ruling. Chief Justice John Roberts joined the Court’s liberal justices to uphold the individual mandate, but he did so by recharacterizing it as a tax rather than relying on Congress’s Commerce Clause power. At the same time Roberts joined the conservative justices in rejecting a broad reading of the Commerce Clause and limiting Congress’s authority to regulate “inactivity.” 

That dual move produced a 5–4 result that preserved Obamacare but also marks a significant rollback of longstanding Commerce Clause doctrine—exactly the goal of conservative legal networks like the Federalist Society. Slate argues Roberts knowingly split the difference: he saved the ACA from being struck down while advancing a narrower vision of federal power that could constrain future legislation. The piece warns this creates political and legal consequences: Democrats lose a clear doctrinal win to defend future statutes, while Republicans gain arguments and campaign talking points about new taxes and limits on federal authority. Slate also comments on Roberts’s public persona—how his affable image helped mask a conservative jurisprudential project now evident in the decision.

A Taunton, Massachusetts woman escaped seconds before her home exploded and burned Sunday after an apparent gas leak, authorities said. Police identified the homeowner as 52-year-old Laurie Beliveau. Investigators believe she had removed a gas shut-off valve while attempting to repair a natural-gas hot water heater, allowing gas to fill the basement and be ignited by an unknown source. Neighbors reported feeling the ground shake and seeing smoke; one neighbor said Beliveau ran to his house screaming and warned she had “done something to the furnace” and that her pet cockatoo remained inside. The two-story single-family home was destroyed; officials said it is “a pile of lumber” and nothing is salvageable. Fire marshal, state police, utility and Columbia Gas investigators responded. Columbia Gas noted such explosions are rare but reminded residents to evacuate and avoid operating utilities if they suspect a leak. An affidavit filed in August indicates the home was in foreclosure. The incident is under active investigation.

A federal judge in Hawaii, U.S. District Judge Derrick Watson, issued a nationwide temporary restraining order blocking President Trump’s revised travel ban less than two hours before it was to take effect, finding an objective observer could conclude the ban was meant to disfavor a particular religion. At a Nashville rally the same evening, Trump called the ruling “an unprecedented judicial overreach,” accused the court of acting for "political reasons," and said the decision made the administration look weak. He defended the revised order as a narrowed version tailored to address the 9th Circuit’s earlier objections to his January 27 ban (which had been blocked after widespread protests and lawsuits) and vowed to continue fighting the case in court, including up to the Supreme Court, insisting the measures are needed to protect the nation.

Also at the Nashville event, Trump honored Andrew Jackson on the 250th anniversary of Jackson’s birth, toured the Hermitage, laid a wreath at Jackson’s tomb, praised Jackson as an inspirational populist who opposed the “arrogant elite,” and noted increased interest in Jackson since the election.

A photo circulating on social media shows a Royal Air Force bomb with “LOVE FROM MANCHESTER ❤” written on its side; the RAF confirmed the image is genuine. The picture surfaced shortly after the Manchester Arena attack, prompting outrage. Critics — including a writer who says they work for a humanitarian charity in the Middle East — call the message sickening and disrespectful to Manchester residents mourning the victims. The piece argues that celebrating airstrikes is morally wrong because bombs kill civilians and worsen humanitarian crises in places like Syria and Iraq. It also cites Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn’s remarks that Britain’s foreign policy and wars overseas have helped create conditions for terrorism at home (not as sole causes, but as contributing factors) and references the Chilcot inquiry’s finding that the 2003 Iraq invasion substantially increased the terrorism threat to the UK. The author urges that military retaliation will not bring back victims or aid healing, and demands that bombing not be done “in the name of Manchester.”

The Comedy Central Roast of Justin Bieber assembled a high-profile, eclectic panel — including Kevin Hart (roastmaster), Hannibal Buress, Chris D'Elia, Snoop Dogg, Natasha Leggero, Ludacris, Shaquille O’Neal, Jeff Ross, Martha Stewart and surprise guest Will Ferrell — to take aim at the 21-year-old pop star. While there were many funny moments and strong individual sets (Hart’s hosting, Buress’s sharp barbs, Pete Davidson’s opening, and Ferrell’s Ron Burgundy bit), the event largely felt less like a roast of Bieber and more like a networking/spotlight opportunity for the performers. 

Several comics traded easy stereotypes and recycled targets (age, race, celebrity careers), and some jokes misfired or were tone-deaf — for example, D’Elia’s string of extreme tasteless bits (touching on rape, ISIS, Eric Garner, Bill Cosby and more) alienated and embarrassed at times, while a few Paul Walker jokes and a risky line about Hart drew negative reaction. Conversely, Snoop’s off-teleprompter rant about Bieber’s use of a racial slur and Davidson’s personal material landed well. Bieber himself appeared uncomfortable and used his rebuttal to issue a halting plea for a second chance, which undercut the roast’s ostensible purpose.

Overall, the show delivered some memorable roasting moments and showcased the comedians more than it did the honoree; rather than a focused takedown of Bieber, it felt like a platform for established performers to score laughs and promote themselves, leaving the star largely spared and visibly uneasy.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel and U.S. President Barack Obama held a phone call after media reports, based on leaks by former U.S. intelligence contractor Edward Snowden, alleged U.S. surveillance of European allies and EU institutions. Merkel told Obama she expected answers and said spying on friends and EU bodies was unacceptable; Obama assured her the U.S. took concerns seriously and agreed to high-level bilateral talks as well as joint U.S.-EU discussions on intelligence collection, oversight, privacy and data protection starting early July. Germany will send Interior Minister Hans-Peter Friedrich to the United States next week.

The revelations have provoked broad European unease: the European Parliament voted overwhelmingly to launch an in-depth inquiry by its Civil Liberties Committee into U.S. programs such as PRISM and alleged bugging of EU premises, and urged U.S. authorities to provide full information. Some leaders, including France, called for delaying the transatlantic trade talks; the European Commission said negotiations would proceed but stressed the need for confidence and transparency. Polling showed a sharp drop in German trust of the U.S. The EU will sweep its offices for bugs, and some German politicians suggested contacting Snowden in Moscow to take his testimony or even consider witness protection. Obama maintained that intelligence services routinely seek information about foreign capitals while promising to supply requested information as allegations are assessed.

Sen. John McCain said he would withdraw support for Indiana Senate candidate Richard Mourdock unless Mourdock apologized for his remark that pregnancies from rape are “something God intended,” telling CNN he’d forgive Mourdock if he “owns up” and asks for forgiveness. McCain’s comment came as Democrats and the Obama campaign pressed Mitt Romney to retract his endorsement and pull a TV ad featuring him. Romney’s campaign has continued to back Mourdock while distancing Romney from Mourdock’s views, saying they disagree on rape/incest exceptions but still support him.

Mourdock resisted an apology at a Wednesday press conference, saying he regretted being misinterpreted. A day later McCain’s spokesman clarified that McCain still supports Mourdock, noting McCain hadn’t seen Mourdock’s full remarks before his CNN interview and that McCain welcomed Mourdock’s clarification and apology.

President Obama criticized Mourdock on “The Tonight Show,” calling rape “a crime” and using the episode to argue against politicians—mostly male—making decisions about women’s health, framing Mourdock’s comments as part of what’s at stake in the election. The Obama campaign also released a video juxtaposing Romney’s pro-Mourdock ad with Mourdock’s remarks to underscore the contrast with Romney’s positions.

Brazil’s extremely high cesarean (C‑section) rates — driven by cultural preferences, convenience, provider incentives and systemic factors — have prompted new rules and campaigns to curb unnecessary surgical births and better inform women.

Scope of the problem
- Nationally more than half of births in Brazil are by C‑section; roughly 84–90% in private care and about 40–45% in public hospitals. These rates far exceed WHO guidance (10–15%) and those in many other countries.
- Factors fueling high rates include maternal preference for scheduled births, perceptions of C‑sections as more modern/“civilised,” fear of pain or pelvic changes from vaginal birth, and practical benefits for families (e.g., planning maternity leave).
- Provider- and system-level drivers include: convenience and scheduling for physicians and hospitals, higher profitability or lower disruption for surgical births, medico‑legal fears that favor intervention, reserved beds for scheduled C‑sections in private hospitals, and loss of skills or infrastructure needed for safe vaginal or assisted deliveries.

Government response and new rules
- Brazil launched a campaign (“Childbirth is normal!”) and regulations requiring that doctors and hospitals disclose their C‑section rates and provide detailed information about risks; patients must sign informed consent, and physicians must document and justify indications for C‑section.
- Health insurers face fines for failing to provide requested information. Pregnant women receive portable medical notes recording pregnancy history.
- The aim is to empower women through information and change institutional incentives and practices.

Perspectives and consequences
- Advocates and clinicians warn C‑sections carry risks for mothers and potential long‑term health impacts for children (e.g., higher obesity and chronic illness risks) and increase costs.
- Many women report pressure from doctors toward C‑sections; others choose them for control and convenience. Doulas and childbirth education are less common but growing as supporters of vaginal birth.
- Experts say information provision alone is insufficient; cultural change, hospital policy, availability of trained staff and infrastructure for natural labor, and broader societal debate are needed.

Evidence from implementation research (Quebec/Canada)
- A qualitative study of obstetricians’ views on implementing guidelines to reduce C‑sections identified barriers and facilitators across four levels: hospital (management, policy), departmental (leadership, staffing, equipment, economic incentives), clinicians (skills, medico‑legal concerns, acceptance of guidelines) and women (knowledge, preferences).
- Specific challenges include weekend staffing and induction policies, reliance on continuous fetal monitoring (linked to higher intervention rates), loss of operative vaginal skills, lack of anaesthetist availability for safe vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC), and time required to counsel women.
- Facilitators: standardized protocols, education for clinicians and patients, audit and feedback (peer review), local evidence and opinion leaders, second‑opinion processes, and aligned financial/payment structures.
- Conclusion: implementing guideline‑based change is complex and must address local contexts, clinician motivations, organizational factors and women’s information and choices.

Overall takeaway
Brazil’s C‑section epidemic is multifactorial — cultural, economic, clinical and organizational. New disclosure and consent rules aim to reduce unnecessary surgeries by informing women and increasing institutional transparency, but sustained reductions will require systemic reforms: better infrastructure and staffing for vaginal birth, changes in financial and legal incentives, clinician training and leadership, and public education to shift expectations about childbirth.

A 72-year-old Plano man, identified as Rex Benson, died early Thursday after re-entering his burning home on Haggard Street to retrieve a cell phone. The fire began shortly after 1 a.m.; Benson, his adult daughter and a male roommate initially escaped, but Benson and the other man went back inside to get a phone to call 911. Firefighters arrived about three minutes after the call to find the single-story house fully engulfed; crews could not reach Benson, who was found dead inside. The roommate and daughter survived. Plano Fire and Rescue emphasized that people should never re-enter burning buildings—about nine out of 10 who do do not survive. Neighbors expressed shock and sorrow. The cause of the fire remains under investigation; no foul play is suspected.

A manhunt is underway after a weekend shooting in Montpelier that left 33-year-old Markus Austin dead. Vermont State Police have issued a second-degree murder warrant for 29-year-old Jayveon Caballero of Barre and say he may have fled the state — possibly on a Greyhound bus from White River Junction headed toward New York City. Bail for Caballero is set at $500,000.

Investigators say Caballero and Austin knew each other and were involved in an altercation earlier Sunday outside Gusto’s bar in Barre. Witnesses and court documents indicate Austin allegedly struck Caballero’s girlfriend, Desiree Cary, 22, during that fight. Police say Caballero later confronted Austin outside an apartment on Barre Street in Montpelier and shot him; Austin’s body was found in the complex parking lot around 4:30 a.m. Witnesses reported seeing a man fire the shot, show concern, then leave the scene.

Authorities executed a search warrant at Caballero’s residence but did not find him. Cary was arrested Sunday evening on unrelated drug-distribution charges tied to an ongoing investigation and has pleaded not guilty; she was held for lack of $10,000 bail. Police are contacting other states about Caballero’s possible movements and are asking anyone with information to come forward.

The slaying is notable as reportedly the first murder in Montpelier — the nation’s smallest state capital — since the 1920s. Austin is a former player for the Vermont Frost Heaves, a defunct semi-pro basketball team.

Tim Cook used a major executive reshuffle at Apple — amid fallout from the Maps debacle and as Hurricane Sandy dominated headlines — to refocus the company on product quality and teamwork over internal politics.

Key moves and context
- Scott Forstall, longtime iOS chief, will leave Apple next year and serve as an interim advisor to CEO Tim Cook. Forstall reportedly clashed with other executives, resisted signing Apple’s public apology for Maps, and overstated Maps’ readiness. His departure removes a powerful, polarizing figure tied closely to Steve Jobs.
- Jony Ive will take responsibility for Human Interface across the company, aligning industrial design and UI under a single, design-driven vision.
- Craig Federighi will run both OS X and iOS engineering teams, unifying software development efforts.
- Bob Mansfield, who had signaled retirement, will lead a new “Technologies” group combining wireless and semiconductor teams to drive ambitious future hardware and mobile initiatives.

Implications
- The changes emphasize Apple as a software-and-experience company where design and software must tightly integrate. Ive’s broader role could produce more unified, minimal, highly refined user experiences across devices.
- Consolidating OS teams under Federighi and grouping wireless/semiconductor efforts under Mansfield signals focus on cross-platform unity, mobile hardware leadership, and new product families — with the smart home and connected devices cited as likely strategic areas.
- Cook’s reorganization aims to curb internal politicking, enforce accountability (e.g., being honest about product readiness), and align leadership behind a single customer- and product-focused mission: making Apple’s products “the best in the world.”

Overall, the shakeup is presented as a decisive move by Cook to streamline leadership, reduce infighting, and position Apple to innovate beyond the iPhone/iPad era while maintaining its tightly controlled customer experience.

Pope Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio to Italian immigrants in Argentina, was officially installed as the 266th pope in a simplified inauguration Mass in St. Peter’s Square that stressed humility, service and care for the poor, weak and the environment. He is the first pope from Latin America and the first Jesuit chosen for the role. Speaking on the Feast of St. Joseph, Francis emphasized that “authentic power is service,” urged protection of “the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and those in prison,” and called on political and social leaders to be “protectors” of people and creation.

The Mass—shorter and less ornate than Benedict XVI’s—drew an estimated 150,000–200,000 people and representatives from about 130 countries, including heads of state and leaders of other faiths. Francis received the pallium and the Fisherman’s Ring (a modest gold-plated-silver version reflecting his simplicity), toured the crowd in an open vehicle, kissed babies, and kissed the head of a disabled man. He kept symbolic signs of a simpler papacy (black shoes, plain vestments) and continued staying at the Vatican hotel rather than immediately moving into papal apartments.

Francis paid public tribute to his predecessor Benedict XVI—calling him, sending warm greetings and asking for his prayers—and the Vatican reported Benedict’s supportive, cordial participation. The new pope’s message of pastoral simplicity and outreach won broad public approval and raised expectations that his style could lead to substantive changes in Vatican priorities and personnel, even as he inherits deep challenges including clergy sexual-abuse scandals and internal Vatican tensions. Back in Argentina, large crowds watched the inauguration and heard a phone message he recorded thanking them and asking their prayers.

The Weinstein Company (TWC) has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Delaware amid the sexual‑misconduct scandal surrounding co‑founder Harvey Weinstein. The company listed $500 million–$1 billion in both assets and liabilities and between 200 and 999 creditors. TWC said an affiliate of private‑equity firm Lantern Capital Partners will serve as a “stalking horse” bidder to buy substantially all assets, setting a floor for a court‑supervised auction that could attract other suitors (including Lionsgate, Miramax or movie producer Killer Content).

In a statement the board announced it will immediately release all employees from non‑disclosure agreements tied to Weinstein, calling the move “an important step toward justice for any victims who have been silenced by Harvey Weinstein.” New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, who had sued the company on behalf of employees and had urged the NDA releases, called the decision a “watershed moment.”

TWC’s collapse follows months of failed sale efforts — including a terminated bid led by Maria Contreras‑Sweet after previously undisclosed liabilities surfaced — and the mass of allegations from more than 70 women accusing Harvey Weinstein of sexual harassment and assault. The Chapter 11 filing pauses pending civil actions (including Schneiderman’s suit) and allows an auction process whereby assets may be sold “free and clear” of claims; plaintiffs will generally be unsecured creditors. The filing also appoints restructuring officers and leaves open the possibility of creditor investigations, adversary proceedings to recover assets, and parallel criminal or arbitration proceedings involving Harvey Weinstein and others.

Robert B. Sherman, one half of the famed Sherman Brothers songwriting team, died in London at age 86. With his brother Richard, he wrote hundreds of songs and scores for films and stage, including Mary Poppins, The Jungle Book, The Aristocats, Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, Winnie the Pooh and Charlotte’s Web. The brothers won two Academy Awards for Mary Poppins (including “Chim Chim Cher-ee”), a Grammy, 23 gold/platinum albums, a Hollywood Walk of Fame star, the National Medal of Arts and induction into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. Their most ubiquitous tune is “It’s a Small World (After All),” which plays continuously at Disney parks worldwide.

Born in New York in 1925 and raised in New York and Beverly Hills, Robert learned songwriting from his father, Tin Pan Alley composer Al Sherman. He served in World War II (recovering in England after being wounded) and later settled in Britain, where he spent his final years. Colleagues noted the brothers’ gift for writing simple, singable songs that work for children and adults alike; their creative process often involved quick collaborations and title-driven brainstorming. Sherman is survived by his brother Richard and four children.

President Barack Obama announced he will visit Havana, Cuba on March 21–22, becoming the first sitting U.S. president to visit the island in 88 years. He tweeted the trip and White House officials said he will meet Cuban President Raúl Castro, Cuban entrepreneurs and members of civil society, and will then continue to Argentina on March 23–24. First Lady Michelle Obama will accompany him to Cuba and the rest of the First Family will join in Argentina.

The trip is part of the Obama administration’s effort to normalize relations after secret talks that led to the December 2014 rapprochement, reopening of embassies in 2015, and recent agreements such as restored commercial air service. Deputy National Security Adviser Ben Rhodes said the visit aims to press for additional reforms, expand opportunities for U.S. businesses and travelers, and improve the lives of the Cuban people, while also raising U.S. concerns about human rights directly with Cuban leaders. Rhodes and officials said Obama will meet dissidents but is not expected to meet Fidel Castro.

The announcement drew mixed reactions: Cuban officials welcomed the visit and called for lifting the U.S. embargo and returning Guantánamo, while some U.S. politicians—especially Republican presidential candidates and Cuban-American lawmakers—criticized the trip, saying it rewards an oppressive regime. Travel and trade restrictions remain in place unless Congress acts to lift the long-standing embargo.

Summary:

The Internet Archive is conducting crawls to preserve newly created webpages and the pages they reference so that links remain accessible even if original content changes or is removed; archived versions can replace broken links or serve as companions to show what authors originally intended. The broader goal is to eliminate broken links across the web through "No More 404" site crawls.

Separately, a criminal complaint describes a fatal on-the-job attack near River Falls on County Road FF. Four men were replacing shingles when Miguel Navarro allegedly cut co-worker Valles-Flores with a circular saw, causing him to fall backward onto a garage roof where Navarro continued to cut him. Two other crew members reportedly jumped off the roof and hid until police arrived. There was no apparent argument beforehand; in a recorded jail call Navarro allegedly said he had been teased, wasn't being paid, and suspected he had been drugged to work more. Valles-Flores died on the garage roof from multiple sharp-force injuries—including 10 wounds to face, neck, back and extremities—and a transection of the jugular vein and carotid artery, according to a provisional autopsy. Navarro faces possible charges including first-degree intentional homicide (which carries a life sentence) and mayhem (up to 40 years and a $100,000 fine) and was held on $500,000 cash bond in Pierce County Jail.

Najim Laachraoui, a 24–25-year-old Belgian, has been identified by authorities as one of the suicide bombers in the March 2016 Brussels airport attack and is suspected of having been the bomb-maker for the November 2015 Paris attacks. Belgian prosecutors said his DNA matched evidence from an explosive belt used at the Bataclan and was found in several safe houses; he was also filmed pushing a luggage trolley containing an explosive at Brussels airport. Laachraoui traveled under the false name Soufiane Kayal and was seen with Paris suspect Salah Abdeslam driving from Hungary into Austria in September 2015. He is believed to have been a veteran fighter in Syria and may have recently returned to Europe.

His family and former teachers describe him as a clever, quiet youth with no visible signs of radicalization before he left for Syria in 2013 and cut off contact. Mourad Laachraoui, Najim’s younger brother and a Belgian taekwondo athlete, said the family had alerted police when Najim went to Syria; police visited and later searched their home after the Paris attacks. Mourad and the family say they are shocked and devastated, insist Najim gave no warning signs, and worry about preventing radicalization of their remaining children. Authorities have not publicly confirmed Najim’s death to the family.

Newly recovered documents from the collapse of the Rana Plaza building in Bangladesh — which killed more than 1,100 garment workers — show that jeans produced for Wal‑Mart’s supply chain were manufactured at Ether Tex, a factory housed on the building’s fifth floor. The documents, provided to the New York Times by an advocacy group and not disputed by Wal‑Mart, include a 2012 purchase order from Canadian contractor Fame Jeans for jeans to be delivered to Wal‑Mart and pricing sheets. Wal‑Mart and Fame Jeans deny authorized production at Rana Plaza at the time of the collapse, with Fame’s CEO blaming a “rogue employee.” Wal‑Mart says its investigation found no evidence of production at the time of the disaster.

In the wake of the disaster, European retailers and labor groups negotiated a legally binding five‑year Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh requiring independent inspections, public reporting and financial contributions to safety upgrades (e.g., fire escapes). Many major European chains — including H&M, Inditex (Zara), Marks & Spencer, Benetton, Carrefour and others — signed the Accord; PVH and Canada’s Loblaw are notable non‑European signatories.

Wal‑Mart declined to join the Accord, saying it prefers a unilateral plan it believes will deliver faster results and objects to the Accord’s governance and dispute‑resolution provisions that could create legal liability. Instead Wal‑Mart announced it will hire Bureau Veritas to conduct in‑depth safety audits of the 279 factories it uses in Bangladesh, publish results on its website, require urgent fixes or halt production, set up an independent worker hotline, and provide fire‑safety training. Wal‑Mart will pay for audits but says it will not underwrite renovations, expecting safety costs to be reflected in prices.

Other large U.S. retailers, notably Gap, have also balked at signing the Accord, citing fears of legal exposure and proposing to limit remedies to public expulsion. Critics and labor advocates argue the Accord’s legally binding framework is necessary to ensure enforceable, transparent improvements and fault U.S. retailers for fragmented, nonbinding alternatives. Observers warn multiple competing, voluntary initiatives may weaken overall effectiveness.

This document describes a collection of periodically archived websites related to labor unions in the New York City metropolitan area and selected national labor organizations. Key points:

- Archived content focuses on NYC-area labor unions whose records are held by the Tamiment Library’s Robert F. Wagner Labor Archives (the official repository designated by the New York City Central Labor Council).
- Includes websites of selected national unions and labor-movement organizations that support organized labor, social and economic justice for workers, and internal democracy within unions.
- Archived sites may not be exact replicas of the originals due to technical, privacy, or other limitations.
- Users can add location information to Tweets (city or precise location) from the web or third-party apps and may delete their Tweet location history. A link to learn more is provided.

Three women—Ashley England, Mary Jordan and Sammie Whaley—were arrested in Bellevue, Ohio after they allegedly assaulted a female McDonald’s employee on June 8 because they thought she was serving them and their children too slowly. The attack occurred in the restaurant parking lot; security video identified the suspects and they were arrested the next day. England faces charges of assault, theft and child endangerment; Jordan is charged with assault and child endangerment; Whaley is charged with assault. Child endangerment counts stem from England and Jordan having their children present and reportedly participating in the incident. All three have pleaded not guilty. Booking photos show two of the women smiling. The article also includes unrelated news blurbs and ads.

Overview:
On May 28–29, 2016 a 3-year-old boy (initially reported as 4) fell into the moat of the Cincinnati Zoo’s Gorilla World after climbing through barriers. A 17-year-old, 450‑lb western lowland gorilla named Harambe grabbed, dragged and at times appeared to shield the child. After roughly ten minutes and amid loud, agitated crowds, the zoo’s dangerous-animal response team shot and killed Harambe to protect the boy, who was taken to Cincinnati Children’s Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries and later released.

Key facts:
- The child climbed through the barrier and fell about 10–15 feet into the shallow moat surrounding the gorilla habitat. Video of the incident circulated widely online.
- Harambe initially appeared to stand over and sometimes tend to the child, but responders later reported that he was “violently dragging and throwing” the boy, creating a life‑threatening situation.
- Zoo officials said a tranquilizer would not act quickly enough and might further agitate the gorilla, so the response team used lethal force. The team includes keepers, veterinarians, maintenance, leadership and security and is certified annually by the county sheriff’s office.
- The zoo temporarily closed Gorilla World, received public sympathy and criticism, and said it would review procedures and safety measures. Gorilla World had been in operation since 1978 and is inspected by the Association of Zoos & Aquariums and the USDA; the zoo had planned a new, larger gorilla habitat.

Public reaction and aftermath:
- The killing triggered intense public debate and social media outrage. Supporters of the zoo argued the decision saved the child; critics condemned the shooting and blamed the parents for inadequate supervision.
- Petitions and online groups calling for charges against the parents and “justice for Harambe” garnered tens of thousands of signatures. Demonstrations and a memorial vigil were organized, and visitors left flowers at a statue outside the closed exhibit.
- Animal-rights groups such as PETA called for secondary barriers and argued captivity itself is unsafe for primates.
- The boy’s family released a statement saying the child was “doing well,” thanked the zoo, declined interviews, and asked that donations be made to the zoo in Harambe’s name rather than to them.

Context and commentary:
- Zoo director Thane Maynard called the decision agonizing but necessary given the child’s imminent danger and the risks of using a tranquilizer. The incident renewed discussions about zoo enclosure design, emergency protocols, parental supervision in public venues, and the ethics of keeping endangered animals in captivity.

GOBankingRates.com data conflicts with a recent America Saves survey that found Americans’ personal saving attitudes rose substantially in September. America Saves — a campaign run by the Consumer Federation of America (CFA) — conducts a triannual Personal Savings Index (PSI) of 1,000 adults to measure self-reported interest, effort and effectiveness in saving. ORC International ran the latest interviews Sept. 10–13; the survey has a ±3 percentage-point margin of error.

Key PSI findings (Sep. 2015 vs. May 2015):
- Interest: up from 63% to 75% (highest in seven surveys)
- Effort: up from 58% to 65%
- Effectiveness: up from 55% to 62%

The PSI also shows a clear income gradient: higher earners report stronger saving interest, effort and effectiveness. In September, respondents earning over $100,000 reported 84% interest, 76% effort and 71% effectiveness, while those under $25,000 reported 68%, 58% and 55%, respectively. CFA notes the results are encouraging but cautions that broader factors (perceptions of personal and macroeconomic conditions, actual income) influence the measures and no multi-year trend is yet established. America Saves aims to promote saving among low- and moderate-income households using behavioral-economics–based outreach.

On Jan. 23–24, 2014, 19-year-old pop star Justin Bieber was arrested in Miami Beach after police say he participated in a pre-dawn drag race in a rented yellow Lamborghini. Witnesses and officers reported that members of his entourage blocked a residential street to create a drag strip and that Bieber and another driver in a red Ferrari (rapper Khalil Amir Sharieff) raced at roughly 55–60 mph in a 30 mph zone. Police stopped Bieber around 4:30 a.m.; according to arrest reports he was belligerent, cursed at officers, initially refused orders and resisted arrest without violence. Officers said he appeared incoherent, had bloodshot eyes and the odor of alcohol, and admitted to having smoked marijuana, had a beer and taken prescription anti‑depressants. He failed field sobriety tests; breath tests showed a blood‑alcohol level below .08 but above Florida’s zero‑tolerance threshold for those under 21. Bieber was booked on charges including DUI, drag‑racing and resisting arrest (and driving on a suspended license); Sharieff also faced DUI charges.

Bieber spent the required lockup period, appeared via video for bond court where bail was set at $2,500, posted bond and was released. After release he briefly waved to fans atop an SUV. The incident prompted an Opa‑locka Police internal probe into an alleged unauthorized police escort of Bieber’s party at the airport. The arrest added to a series of recent legal and public‑behavior incidents involving Bieber, including prior complaints about reckless driving, alleged vandalism in Los Angeles and earlier seizures of drugs from a tour bus.

President Trump asked his lawyers about the possibility of pardoning Paul Manafort and others linked to probes of his 2016 campaign, attorney Rudy Giuliani said. Giuliani and other White House lawyers advised against pardoning anyone connected to Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia investigation—at least until Mueller finishes—because such pardons could raise obstruction concerns. Giuliani said Trump accepted that advice and did not press the matter further.

Timing and scope are unclear: Giuliani said the discussion occurred several weeks earlier and involved pardons for a range of people under investigation, not only Manafort. White House spokespeople subsequently denied the matter was under active consideration. A senior official confirmed the president had weighed pros and cons a few weeks earlier. Inside the West Wing, senior aides including Chief of Staff John Kelly, White House counsel Don McGahn and others oppose any pardon; staff are trying to keep Trump from raising it.

The discussion arose after a wave of summer pardons by Trump and shortly after Manafort’s conviction on eight tax- and bank-fraud counts. Trump has publicly expressed sympathy for Manafort, praising him for refusing to cooperate with Mueller. Legal experts warn pardoning witnesses could increase legal exposure for the president. Other Trump associates who pleaded guilty in Mueller’s probe include Michael Flynn, George Papadopoulos and Rick Gates.

Separately, Trump’s former lawyer Michael Cohen pleaded guilty to tax crimes, false statements to a bank and campaign finance violations tied to hush-money payments. Trump has sought to minimize Cohen’s plea’s implications for himself, tweeting support for Manafort and stating the payments came from his personal funds (campaign finance rules still apply). White House lawyers view Cohen’s admissions as hurtful but not dispositive, and are reviewing defense options.

Key points
- A CDC/Pew analysis of 2010–2011 national ambulatory care data estimated outpatient oral antibiotic prescribing and judged appropriateness by diagnosis using guidelines and regional variation.
- About 13% of outpatient visits (~154 million visits/year) resulted in an antibiotic prescription. The study estimated 506 antibiotic prescriptions per 1,000 population annually, of which 353 per 1,000 (≈70%) were likely appropriate — meaning roughly 30% (~47 million prescriptions/year) were unnecessary.
- Acute respiratory conditions (sinusitis, suppurative otitis media, pharyngitis, colds, bronchitis, influenza, etc.) were the largest contributors: they accounted for 44% of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions and roughly half of those prescriptions were unnecessary. Per 1,000 population, respiratory conditions led to 221 antibiotic prescriptions annually but only 111 were estimated appropriate.
- The single diagnoses producing the most antibiotic prescriptions per 1,000 population were sinusitis (56), suppurative otitis media (47), and pharyngitis (43).

Implications
- Antibiotic overprescribing in outpatient settings is substantial and drives antibiotic resistance; CDC estimates ~2 million antibiotic‑resistant infections and ~23,000 deaths annually in the U.S.
- The White House National Action Plan aimed to halve inappropriate outpatient antibiotic use by 2020. Based on these estimates, achieving that goal would require an overall reduction in outpatient antibiotic prescribing of about 15% (≈23 million fewer prescriptions annually).

Recommended actions and stewardship opportunities
- Target stewardship toward acute respiratory conditions where most unnecessary prescribing occurs.
- Interventions suggested include provider self-audit and feedback, practice‑level stewardship activities, health system support, payer data and feedback, state/local technical assistance and regional coordination, national tracking and metrics, and guidance from professional societies.
- Clinician–patient communication and pharmacist counseling at dispensing can reduce inappropriate use and educate about harms (allergies, adverse events, resistance).

Conclusion
- The study provides a national baseline showing roughly one-third of outpatient oral antibiotic prescriptions in 2010–2011 were unnecessary, highlighting the need for focused outpatient antibiotic stewardship to preserve antibiotic effectiveness.

In April 2014 Boko Haram abducted more than 200 schoolgirls from a boarding school in Chibok, Nigeria; roughly 60 have escaped but most remain missing. The kidnappings have worsened fear, disrupted girls’ education in northern Nigeria, and raised concerns about a “lost generation.” Jubilee Campaign USA, a U.S.-based human rights and religious freedom nonprofit, launched the “Education After Escape” fundraiser to support 10 of the girls who escaped by placing them in specialized boarding schools abroad or in safe locations where they can continue their education and receive trauma support. The group set a target of $125,000 (with an early one-month effort already raising over $20,000) to cover tuition, travel, and related costs, and emphasizes that helping these girls is both a practical response to Boko Haram’s violence and a way to sustain the Chibok community’s future. Jubilee Campaign notes its prior work assisting victims of northern Nigeria violence, its nonprofit credentials, and appeals for donations and awareness while urging continued pressure on authorities to locate the remaining abducted girls.

Sunni extremist militants from the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIS/ISIL) claimed in mid-June 2014 to have executed large numbers of captured Shiite Iraqi security personnel—posting graphic photographs from Tikrit that purportedly show mass shootings and bodies dumped in mass graves or the Tigris River. ISIS’s claim of 1,700 killed could not be independently verified; Iraqi officials, Human Rights Watch and others said the images and death toll remained unconfirmed though consistent with the group’s pattern of atrocities. Witness accounts and local officials said many captured were air force cadets from Camp Speicher; some Sunni captives were reportedly released. Government sources reported recoveries of a smaller number of bodies and denied large-scale executions, while tribal and security leaders warned the militants were targeting anyone affiliated with the government.

The assertions and images heightened fears of sectarian reprisals between Iraq’s Shiite majority and Sunni communities, and there were appeals for restraint from Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani even as he urged Iraqis to defend the country—sparking mobilization of volunteers and militias that raised concerns about renewed sectarian bloodletting reminiscent of 2006–2007. Iraqi forces, allied militias and tribal fighters mounted counterattacks and regained some territory in places, but ISIS continued to score gains: it seized Mosul and later Tal Afar (near the Syrian border) and was pushing toward Baghdad, prompting heavy fighting, mortar strikes on civilian areas, and large population displacements.

The crisis drew urgent international attention. The U.S. repositioned forces and sent the carrier USS George H.W. Bush and escorts to the Gulf, reinforced embassy security and increased diplomatic engagement; President Obama ruled out ground troops but said options were being prepared. U.S. officials explored direct talks with Iran to coordinate responses, as Tehran—an ally of Shiite Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki—was reported to be providing support to Iraqi forces and militias (which Iran publicly denied sending in large numbers). Regional concerns included the risk of Iraq fracturing, rising oil prices, and the diplomatic complication of potential U.S.-Iran cooperation amid ongoing nuclear negotiations.

Terrorist attacks continued in Baghdad and elsewhere—suicide and car bombs and mortar strikes killed and wounded dozens, including volunteer recruits—underscoring the growing instability and the danger of the conflict spiraling into broader sectarian civil war. Political and military leaders both in Iraq and internationally warned that ISIS’s apparent aim was to provoke sectarian conflict to further its goal of establishing a cross-border Sunni Islamist state.

More than 200 bottlenose dolphins were corralled and held for a second day in Taiji Cove, Japan, where local fishermen select some animals for sale to aquariums and prepare the remainder for slaughter, U.S. conservationists reported. The Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, which is monitoring and live-streaming events, said fishermen had already taken 37 dolphins for captivity (including a rare albino calf), two dolphins had died, and many others were bloodied and stressed from attempts to escape. The group described the capture process—hundreds of dolphins driven into subgroups by nets, pushed into shallow water under tarpaulins where trainers and hunters pick the “prettiest” for sale while allegedly killing the less desirable animals out of view—and warned the cove would likely be filled with blood once slaughter begins.

Taiji’s dolphin drive hunt, a longstanding local practice, draws international condemnation but is defended by local officials as legal, traditional fishing. The practice was thrust into the spotlight by the documentary The Cove and continues to provoke disputes between Western activists and Taiji authorities; Wakayama Prefecture has called outside criticism biased and harassment. Activists also warn that dolphin meat sold for consumption can contain dangerously high mercury levels. Prominent opponents include Richard O’Barry and Sea Shepherd; U.S. Ambassador Caroline Kennedy publicly expressed concern about the hunts’ inhumaneness. The story was highlighted on CNN after being reported via a citizen iReport.

Here are the key developments from the roundup:

Zara Phillips — Olympic debut
- Zara Phillips, 31, made her Olympic debut Sunday in the dressage phase of the equestrian three-day eventing on High Kingdom.
- She received warm home support, including husband Mike Tindall (who greeted her with a kiss), and family members including Prince Philip, Princess Anne, and siblings in the stands. Princes William and Kate are expected to attend the cross-country phase.
- A former European and World champion, Phillips said she was “really pleased” despite a few mistakes and described the experience of riding for Team GB at the Games as “incredible.” She returns Monday for the much tougher cross-country leg.

Paula Radcliffe withdraws from Olympic marathon
- Marathon world-record holder Paula Radcliffe (38) has been ruled out of the London 2012 Olympic marathon because of a persistent foot injury/osteoarthritis after a test run deemed her unfit.
- Radcliffe said withdrawing was painful but she has tried everything and did not want to compete if not at her best. UK Athletics and the British Olympic Association will nominate Freya Murray as her replacement under the Late Athlete Replacement policy; Murray will join Claire Hallissey and Mara Yamauchi for the race on August 5.
- Coaches and commentators noted Radcliffe’s disappointment but urged that her career be judged on her broader achievements (world record, world championship, multiple major-marathon wins), not by Olympic medals she never secured.

Kimberly Rhode wins skeet gold for USA
- American shooter Kimberly Rhode won gold in women’s skeet, becoming the first U.S. athlete to earn an individual-sport medal at five consecutive Olympics.
- Rhode tied the world record and set an Olympic final record with 99 points; Wei Ning (China) took silver and Danka Bartekova (Slovakia) bronze after a shootout.
- Rhode shot near-perfect qualifying rounds (65 straight hits before one miss) and dominated the final, extending the USA’s notable achievements in shooting.

Atmosphere
- Fans continued to enjoy the Games atmosphere in London’s Olympic Park amid variable weather, with sunny moments during some events and later rain during others.
