Following North Korea’s threats to test a missile near Guam, the island’s Office of Civil Defense reiterated guidance—matching Ready.gov—that survivors of a nuclear blast should not use hair conditioner when decontaminating. Nuclear detonations create fallout: fine, radioactive dust that can settle on skin and hair. Human hair has overlapping protein “scales” that can open and trap tiny particles. Shampoo and soap are designed to rinse away particles, but many conditioners contain cationic surfactants, silicones and cationic polymers that smooth scales and leave oily, positively charged residues that bind to negatively charged fallout particles, making contamination harder to remove. Experts therefore advise removing outer clothing and taking a decontamination shower with soap or mild shampoo (avoiding protein-based conditioner-containing products) to shed most contamination; lotions or other oily or sticky cosmetics should also be avoided during exposure because they attract dust. While the exact increase in risk from using conditioner is uncertain, it’s a simple precaution to skip conditioner until decontamination is complete. The Ready.gov warning traces back to public-health research and messaging tested by CDC/FEMA.

President Trump threatened to withdraw federal funding from the University of California, Berkeley after the campus canceled a scheduled speech by Breitbart editor Milo Yiannopoulos following violent protests. In a tweet he wrote, “If U.C. Berkeley does not allow free speech and practices violence on innocent people with a different point of view - NO FEDERAL FUNDS?”

The event was called off about two hours before it was to begin after clashes involving about 150 masked agitators (per the university) amid a crowd of roughly 1,500 protesters. Demonstrators threw smoke bombs, flares, rocks and commercial-grade fireworks, smashed windows, started a bonfire on Sproul Plaza and reportedly used Molotov cocktails and other projectiles; at least six people were injured. UC Berkeley police and university officials said the violence by a small group disrupted what had otherwise been lawful protest and forced the cancellation on safety grounds.

Yiannopoulos, a provocative right‑wing commentator associated with Breitbart and the alt‑right, condemned the shutdown as political violence. Critics of Trump’s tweet, including Rep. Barbara Lee, called the threat to cut funding an abuse of power. Berkeley, historically linked to the 1960s Free Speech Movement, receives substantial federal research funding (about $370 million in 2015–16). The incident follows other violent protests tied to Yiannopoulos appearances elsewhere.

Brittany Williams, a Texas mother who ran a mud-run event in Dallas, developed severe eye pain hours after the race. Emergency-room doctors initially noted corneal abrasions and a chemical-burn–like injury and sent her home, but within about 24 hours her condition worsened and she was hospitalized. Doctors say flesh-eating bacteria entered a cut in her eye, rapidly destroying the cornea; she is now blind in her left eye and faces uncertain prospects for saving or restoring vision. Williams spent a week in the hospital and needs further antibiotics and treatment to prevent the infection from spreading. Uninsured and working two jobs, she faces more than $100,000 in medical bills; several local doctors have declined treatment because she lacks insurance. Her family has launched a GoFundMe campaign and had raised nearly $10,000 from about 170 donors. Officials have noted that mud races can harbor harmful bacteria, and similar outbreaks have occurred at other events. Williams says she’s trying to stay positive despite the ordeal.

A long-term study of nearly 75,000 U.S. nurses, published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, links rotating night-shift work to modestly higher risks of death from all causes, cardiovascular disease, and lung cancer. Using 22 years of Nurses’ Health Study follow-up, researchers defined rotating night shifts as working at least three nights per month along with days or evenings. Key findings:
- Working rotating night shifts for 6–14 years was associated with an ~11% higher all-cause mortality and a 19% higher risk of fatal cardiovascular disease.
- Working rotating night shifts for 15+ years was associated with a similar increase in cardiovascular mortality (about 23%) and a 25% higher risk of lung cancer mortality.
- No overall association was found between rotating shift work and mortality from all cancers combined.

The study cannot prove causation. The authors note these results add to evidence that rotating night work may harm health and call for further research on how duration, intensity, and individual traits (e.g., chronotype) influence risk.

A 17-year-old girl has died after a shark attacked her while she was surfing with her father at the popular Kelp Beds surf break at Wylie Bay, about three kilometres east of Wylie Bay near Esperance on Western Australia’s south coast. The attack occurred around 4pm; witnesses report the father heard her scream and, with help from another teenager, pulled her to shore after she resurfaced. Paramedics treated her on the beach and she was taken to Esperance Hospital in critical condition with major blood loss; she later died. Authorities believe a great white shark was likely responsible.

Wylie Bay Beach was closed and the Department of Fisheries advised no swimming, surfing or diving in the area for at least 48 hours and planned patrols. The site has a history of shark activity, including a 2014 attack at the same beach in which surfer Sean Pollard lost both arms. The department had previously used drum lines in the area after earlier incidents; officials did not immediately confirm whether deterrent gear would be deployed following this attack. Local reactions included shock and calls for caution; some fishers say great white numbers have increased. The report also noted a list of previous fatal shark attacks in WA since 2000.

With NFL officials locked out during a labor dispute, replacement referees are working preseason games — and for the first time a woman will be on an NFL officiating crew. Shannon Eastin, an Arizona-based official with experience in the Mid-Eastern Athletic Conference and other high school and small-college leagues, will serve on the replacement crew for Thursday’s preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and San Diego Chargers. Replacement officials already worked the Hall of Fame Game and have had early miscues (for example, a mistaken coin-toss announcement). Talks between the NFL and the officials’ union are ongoing while the league trains replacement refs; the lockout of regular officials began in June and is the most serious such labor standoff since 2001.

An investigative film by the Guardian and reporting reveal that Bradley Manning, detained a year ago on suspicion of supplying thousands of sensitive military and diplomatic documents to WikiLeaks, displayed serious mental-health and behavioral problems long before his Iraq deployment. Officers at Fort Leonard Wood in 2007 described him as a "mess of a child": he wet himself, threw chairs, shouted at superiors, and was repeatedly escorted to psychiatric evaluations and diagnosed with an adjustment disorder. Despite concerns from some senior officers and these incidents, Manning kept his security clearance and was deployed to Forward Operating Base Hammer in Iraq.

Eyewitnesses and colleagues at FOB Hammer say security around intelligence computers was extremely lax: about 300 soldiers had access to the computer room, SIPRNet laptops were left unsecured with passwords on sticky notes, and many troops viewed violent combat footage on equipment connected to the secure network. Two months after arriving in Iraq, Manning’s rifle bolt was removed because he was considered a potential danger, and various accounts describe further volatility, including violent outbursts. Manning denies the charges; he faces multiple counts that could carry up to 55 years in prison. The Defense Security Service is investigating why he was allowed to work in intelligence after earlier psychiatric counseling. No other personnel at the base have been charged.

A federal survey by the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics, based on in-person interviews with about 13,500 Americans aged 15–44 (2006–2008), offers a detailed picture of U.S. sexual behavior and some surprising trends.

Key findings
- Rising abstinence among youth: Among 15–24-year-olds, 29% of females and 27% of males reported never having any sexual contact (oral, anal, or vaginal), up from 22% for both sexes in 2002. The increase was concentrated among 15–19-year-olds.
- Prevalence of sexual acts among adults: For ages 25–44, roughly 98% of women and 97% of men reported having had vaginal intercourse; oral sex with an opposite-sex partner was reported by about 89% of women and 90% of men; anal sex with an opposite-sex partner was reported by 36% of women and 44% of men. Overall, about four in ten adults have had anal sex.
- Same-sex experiences and fluidity: Women (ages 15–44) were more than twice as likely as men to report same-sex experiences (≈12.5% vs. 5.2%). Women also reported bisexual identity at higher rates than men. Same-sex reporting among women was higher in less-educated groups; among men, same-sex activity was more common in higher-educated groups. The authors emphasize that sexual behavior and identity are not neatly separable categories.
- Patterns and implications: The data suggest oral sex can be a gateway to vaginal sex for some but a stopping point for others; most adults report monogamous behavior. The findings are intended to inform sex education, STD prevention, and public-health policy.

Methods and caveats
- Data were collected during one-on-one household interviews by female interviewers. Sensitive questions were presented via laptop with audio (respondents entered answers directly), a method intended to improve reporting accuracy.
- The survey excluded institutionalized or high-risk populations (e.g., homeless, incarcerated). Researchers note possible influences on reported trends include sex-education messages, abstinence promotion, or reporting biases; they caution against overinterpreting causes.

Overall conclusion
The survey documents notable increases in sexual nonexperience among teens and young adults and highlights greater-than-expected diversity and fluidity in sexual behavior—especially among women—information valuable for shaping education and prevention efforts.

Pete Davidson has spoken publicly about using medical marijuana to manage Crohn’s disease and has criticized New York State’s medical marijuana program as difficult to navigate. He told High Times that prescription medicines and medical visits didn’t help as much as cannabis did—smoking allowed him to eat, feel well enough to perform, and get through SNL. Davidson says performing while sober “has gone awful” for him, and he opposes keeping therapeutic cannabis hard to obtain or illegal.

Separately, Davidson announced on Instagram that he’s been sober for the first time in eight years, crediting supportive relationships (a girlfriend and friends) and urging fans not to give up hope. He’s also spoken about Kid Cudi’s music as life-saving for him and younger listeners. Longtime SNL producer Lorne Michaels has praised Davidson’s focus despite his public jokes about cannabis. Season 42 of SNL premiers October 1, and Davidson’s first hour-long standup special “SMD” airs October 29.

Hillary Clinton, speaking at a Women for Women International event in New York, said she accepts responsibility for losing the 2016 presidential election but argued outside factors swung the result. She noted she won the popular vote by more than 3 million and said, "If the election had been on October 27, I would be your president," blaming the timing of FBI Director James Comey's late October letter and Russian-linked WikiLeaks releases for scaring off some supporters in the final 10 days. Clinton also took a jab at President Donald Trump, saying she’s “happy to be the diversion” if he tweets about her and suggesting he should focus on issues more important to the country. She is currently writing a book that will partly reflect on the 2016 loss.

The program opens with discussion of President Obama’s second-term agenda and the political obstacles it faces in a sharply divided Washington. Panelists — including Jim DeMint, Ben Jealous, Bob Woodward, Andrea Mitchell and Ted Koppel — weigh how much of Obama’s inaugural priorities can survive partisan budget fights and whether impending fiscal battles will shape or constrain his administration going forward. They also examine the aftermath of the Benghazi hearings and what departing Secretary of State Hillary Clinton can expect as she leaves office.

Separately, the show covers Michele Bachmann’s presidential campaign and recent remarks: when pressed on Meet the Press about what office she’s seeking she reiterated she’s running for president, not to “be anyone’s judge.” Bachmann drew attention and criticism for refusing to call gay couples with kids “families” and for insisting that social issues of that nature are “the defining political issue of our time,” despite public focus elsewhere.

A 22-year-old Davenport woman, Ashley R. Hautzenrader, is charged with one count of child endangerment after she gave birth in a University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics (UIHC) bathroom late on May 8 and, believing the newborn was stillborn, attempted to flush the infant down a toilet and then placed the baby in a pillowcase and left it in a trash can. UIHC employees found the newborn alive shortly after delivery. Hautzenrader admitted to placing the baby in the trash can and was arrested; she has been placed on supervised release and will be appointed a public defender. The charge is an aggravated misdemeanor carrying up to two years in prison. Hospital and police officials declined to release further details, citing privacy and an ongoing investigation. Officials reminded the public that Iowa’s Safe Haven law allows parents to leave newborns (up to 14 days old) at hospitals without prosecution. The baby’s current condition has not been disclosed.

Giorgio Armani used his finale show at Milan Fashion Week to publicly criticize the industry and organizers after Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour skipped his presentation to attend Paris shows. Armani, who has anchored Milan’s calendar for decades and currently stands as one of the few major designers on the event’s last day, said Wintour’s absence left him “penalized” and blamed the National Chamber of Italian Fashion (Camera della Moda) for failing to ensure high-profile names remain on the closing day. Vogue defended Wintour, saying the extended fashion calendar makes it impossible to attend every show.

On the runway, Armani’s Fall-Winter 2014-15 collection emphasized subtle tailoring and wearable innovation: ankle-length pleated trousers, rounded single-button jackets, lime accents, sporty side stripes, luminous grays for evening pieces and a notable wispy gray fur with lime highlights. Backstage he lamented what he called excessive, fantastical showmanship by some peers that sacrifices commercial functionality and economic value, arguing that fashion must produce functional products to merit government support.

Also featured on the last day, DSquared2 staged a theatrical, asylum-themed show mixing glamor and madness—mini dresses, heavy embellishment, locks and syringe-like straps—portraying a fallen Hollywood diva in a glamorous rehabilitation setting. Armani’s remarks stirred discussion about scheduling, industry priorities and the balance between creativity and commerce in Italian fashion.

Actor Shia LaBeouf was removed from a Thursday night performance of the Broadway musical Cabaret at Studio 54 and arrested after allegedly disrupting Act I. Police say the 28-year-old was smoking in the theater, slapping other audience members on the buttocks and heads, and became “incoherent” and “very agitated” when officers intervened. He was escorted out at intermission, fell as police approached, and was taken to the Midtown-North station.

While in custody he reportedly demanded his handcuffs be removed, spat at officers, had to be fitted with a face mask, and hurled threats and a homophobic slur at arresting officers, saying he had “millions and millions of dollars and attorneys” and would “ruin” one officer’s career. He was charged with criminal trespass and disorderly conduct (reports also cite harassment), and was released from custody early Friday with a court date set for July 24. The incident follows several prior episodes of erratic behavior by LaBeouf, including past arrests and public incidents.

The summary:

A partial government shutdown entered its third day as Senate and House Republicans blamed Democrats for rejecting a plan by Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell to link a short-term funding extension with a later floor debate on immigration. McConnell said he would consider allowing debate on immigration proposals in mid- to late February if leaders do not reach a deal sooner. Democrats, led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, insisted no agreement had been reached and doubted McConnell’s pledge was a firm commitment to include protections for DACA “dreamers” in must-pass funding.

Republican leaders, including President Trump (via Twitter) and House Speaker Paul Ryan, accused Democrats of siding with their “far left base” and prioritizing undocumented immigrants over citizens; Trump urged use of the “nuclear option” to pass spending with a simple majority if the stalemate continued. Democrats countered that they had made concessions — reportedly agreeing to significant wall funding after Trump “picked a number” — but Republicans said that offer fell short of immediate funding levels the president demanded. Republicans also sought changes in family-based immigration and the diversity visa program, complicating compromise.

Moderate senators from both parties met to try to craft a path forward, discussing a proposal to extend funding through Feb. 8 while guaranteeing consideration of immigration legislation in the interim. Progress was reported by some negotiators and White House legislative director Marc Short, but no firm deal emerged. Lawmakers warned the longer the shutdown continued into the workweek, the greater the impact: hundreds of thousands of federal workers would remain furloughed or unpaid, some services (e.g., trash pickup on National Park Service land) had already been disrupted, military reservists’ drills were canceled, contractor payments delayed, and IRS tax-season preparations slowed.

Party leaders remained divided over strategy and concessions. Some Republicans opposed yielding on immigration while the government was closed; Democrats questioned whether moderates would accept wall funding and other GOP demands. With March 5 looming as the DACA-related deadline for protected status expirations, uncertainty persisted about whether either side would yield or whether the Senate would muster the votes to break the impasse.

Three-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Vittorio Storaro, a longtime collaborator of Bernardo Bertolucci, has defended the making of Last Tango in Paris amid renewed outrage over the film’s infamous 1972 “butter” scene. The controversy reignited after a resurfaced 2013 interview in which Bertolucci said he and Marlon Brando devised the use of butter on the morning of the shoot and did not tell 19‑year‑old Maria Schneider, prompting critics to call the scene nonconsensual and many Hollywood figures to condemn Bertolucci and the late Brando.

Storaro, who was on set for the production and spoke exclusively to The Hollywood Reporter from Rome, called the recent media reaction “ridiculous” and “made up by a journalist.” He said the film crew always treated it as acting and that nothing violent occurred during filming. According to Storaro, last‑minute adjustments to scenes—often discussed each morning by Bertolucci and Brando—were a normal part of their process; Schneider knew the script’s explicit nature, understood the scenes, and became emotionally attached to the shoot, even lamenting its end. Storaro described a positive, creative atmosphere on the small set and said Brando was generous and intelligent.

The renewed uproar followed Bertolucci’s own clarification (and earlier comments) that the simulated rape was written in the script and that the only surprise was the butter; Bertolucci has expressed some regret for how he handled the situation. Schneider, who died in 2011, had previously said she “felt a little raped” by the experience. Storaro maintains the scene was simulated and not malicious, while acknowledging Bertolucci may have felt guilty for not fully explaining some last‑minute details. The debate underscores how the film’s provocative scenes and themes continue to provoke strong reactions more than four decades after its release.

Summary:

President Barack Obama’s tough remarks and proposal on Jan. 21 to curb risky behavior by large financial institutions—which would bar banks from proprietary trading and investing in hedge funds and private equity—triggered a sharp market reaction. Stocks fell sharply that day (S&P 500 closed down 1.9%), with major banks and Wall Street firms such as Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America posting notable declines. Observers said it was as much Obama’s confrontational tone—“If these folks want a fight, it’s a fight I’m ready to have”—as the details of his plan that unnerved investors.

Market strategists noted that political developments increased investor uncertainty: the Jan. 19 special-election victory of Republican Scott Brown in Massachusetts reduced Democrats’ legislative leverage and may have pushed Obama to target Wall Street. Analysts emphasize that markets hate uncertainty; even when investors favor some regulation, the legislative horse-trading and unclear outcomes create short-term pain. Traders reacted by taking profits, and some described the sell-off as an emotional, knee-jerk response. Others argue that better regulation could strengthen the system over the long run.

House Financial Services Chairman Barney Frank sought to calm markets by saying any new rules would be phased in slowly—perhaps over five years—to avoid fire-sale conditions, and suggested some firms might avoid restrictions by changing their corporate status. This eased financial shares somewhat. Other influences on the Jan. 21 drop included worries about China’s economy and a technical pause after recent gains.

Commentary in the piece stresses that political headlines increasingly matter because of the scale of the nation’s problems, though some experts caution that political events typically cause short-term, sector-specific moves while corporate earnings, economic data, employment and Fed policy remain the primary long-term market drivers. Nonetheless, with tougher regulation on the horizon and bankers politically unpopular, Washington is likely to be a less friendly backdrop for financial firms going forward.

(Separate section) Web-crawl dataset description:

A wide web crawl using Heritrix (Mar–Dec 2011) captured 2.7 billion records across 2.27 billion unique URLs from ~29 million hosts. The seed list used Alexa’s top 1 million sites. The crawl was experimental with new distributed crawling software and had operational issues (missed embedded resources, queue sizing problems, repeated crawls of some Argentine government sites), so results are “warts and all.” The maintainers have since improved their process; researchers can request access by contacting the archive, subject to approval.

Summary:

Candida auris is an emerging fungal pathogen that poses a serious global health threat because it is often multidrug-resistant, can be misidentified by standard laboratory methods, and has caused outbreaks in healthcare settings. Rapid, accurate identification is critical so hospitals can implement infection control measures. The CDC has updated guidance and resources: as of December 21, 2018, recommendations for laboratorians and health professionals (including environmental disinfection, species identification, and screening) were revised and webpages reorganized; the case count was updated to 523 on that date; and on July 20, 2018, fact sheets for patients, laboratory staff, and infection preventionists were added. U.S. laboratories that identify C. auris are urged to notify state or local public health authorities and to contact CDC at candidaauris@cdc.gov. The CDC provides expert commentary and ongoing resources on detection and containment.

Three days after voters signaled anxiety about the economy, the government reported solid October job growth: employers added 214,000 jobs and revised August–September payrolls up by 31,000. That marks the ninth consecutive month with at least 200,000 jobs added, the longest streak since 1995, and pushed the unemployment rate down to 5.8% (its lowest since July 2008).

Broad economic indicators show acceleration: GDP grew at about a 4.1% annual rate over the past six months, manufacturing is expanding at its fastest pace in three years, service-sector activity is healthy, and home sales picked up in September. The Federal Reserve recently ended its bond-buying stimulus in light of the stronger picture.

Despite the hiring boom, wage growth remains weak for most workers—real average hourly pay rose only 0.3% year-over-year through September—and income gains since 2010 have skewed heavily to the wealthiest 10%. Exports fell in September and the trade deficit widened, prompting many economists to trim third-quarter growth estimates to around 3% annualized or less. Voters’ continued economic pessimism suggests many Americans have not yet felt the improvements.

Summary:

Mylan bought the EpiPen auto-injector in 2007 and turned an otherwise low‑revenue, decades‑old product into a billion‑dollar franchise through aggressive marketing, lobbying and distribution efforts. Under CEO Heather Bresch the company promoted public‑entity stocking (schools, theme parks, cruise ships), changed labeling and packaging (switching to two‑packs after 2010 guidance recommending two doses), ran heavy TV advertising and donated devices to thousands of schools—moves that helped make EpiPen the dominant, “Kleenex‑like” brand and grow users about 67% over seven years.

At the same time Mylan sharply raised prices: wholesale and retail costs rose several hundred percent since 2008 (a commonly cited increase from roughly $57–$100 to $400–$600+ for a two‑pack). Margins jumped (estimated to about 55% in 2014) and EpiPen became a major profit driver for Mylan. The increases have left many patients and families struggling to afford the life‑saving device, prompting public outcry, media scrutiny and calls from lawmakers for investigations. Mylan says it does not set final retail prices, offers coupons and has invested in awareness and access; critics counter that the device’s active drug costs only a few dollars and argue the price hikes are unethical.

Competition has been limited—rivals have struggled to gain market share and a delayed competitor recall left Mylan with near‑monopoly power—though a potential Teva generic and other entrants could pose a future threat. The controversy led to Congressional attention and a House Oversight hearing on the price increases.

Republican New York gubernatorial candidate Carl Paladino, a Tea Party favorite, sparked controversy after a speech to Orthodox Jews in Brooklyn in which he criticized homosexuality and said he didn’t want children “brainwashed” into thinking it is an equally valid lifestyle. He said children would be better off getting married and raising families, opposed gay marriage, and disparaged public displays at Pride parades. Portions of his prepared remarks—some of which he said were written by members of the audience and that he later crossed out—included harsher language he said he did not read aloud.

On NBC’s Today show Paladino attempted to clarify and soften his remarks, saying discrimination against gays is “horrible,” that he is “not anti-gay,” and that he would recruit qualified gay people for his administration, though he reiterated his opposition to exposing young children to homosexuality and to gay marriage. His campaign manager framed Paladino’s views as aligned with Catholic teaching.

The remarks drew strong criticism from gay-rights advocates and Democratic rival Andrew Cuomo’s camp, who called the comments homophobic and intolerant. Paladino’s campaign defended him and claimed many New Yorkers agree with his stance, though polls show a majority favor gay marriage and Cuomo’s lead expanded following the controversy. The article also notes Paladino’s own personal controversies, including an extramarital child, past obscene and racist emails, and unsubstantiated attacks on Cuomo’s personal life.

(The document also includes unrelated metadata about a large web crawl conducted March–December 2011 by Archive.org describing its scope, tools used, operational issues, and contact info for access to the dataset.)

Summary:

This document compiles several pieces focused on corporal punishment in public schools, centered on the U.S. Supreme Court decision Ingraham v. Wright (430 U.S. 651, 1977), followed by commentary, state law examples (especially Alabama), medical and psychological guidance, and news reporting.

1. Ingraham v. Wright (1977) — Supreme Court majority opinion (Powell, J.)
- Facts: Two Florida junior high students sued Dade County school officials under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, claiming excessive paddlings violated constitutional rights. Florida law and local policy then authorized limited paddling (but forbade degrading or unduly severe punishment); evidence at trial showed unusually harsh paddlings at one school.
- Issues: Whether corporal punishment in public schools violates the Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause, and whether the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause requires prior notice and hearing before corporal punishment.
- Holdings:
  - Eighth Amendment: Not applicable to typical school disciplinary corporal punishment. The Court tied the Eighth Amendment historically and doctrinally to the criminal process and protections for those convicted of crimes, so it should not be extended to traditional school discipline. The openness of schools and common-law constraints (civil and criminal liability for excessive force) provide adequate safeguards.
  - Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process: The liberty interest in freedom from bodily restraint and punishment is implicated when school officials deliberately restrain and inflict appreciable physical pain. But longstanding common-law privilege allowing reasonable corporal punishment, plus available post-deprivation civil/criminal remedies and the openness of schools, make additional constitutional requirements for pre-punishment notice or hearing unnecessary. Requiring prior hearings would unduly intrude on school administration and likely curtail or eliminate corporal punishment even where traditionally permitted.
- Result: Affirmed the Fifth Circuit’s en banc judgment; no constitutional relief for petitioners under the Eighth Amendment or procedural due process as litigated.

2. Dissents (White, joined by Brennan, Marshall, Stevens; Stevens separate)
- Main points:
  - Justice White: The Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment should not be confined to punishments labeled “criminal” — the Amendment’s plain language forbids inhumane punishments regardless of context. Corporal punishment in schools is “punishment” and, if severe, can be as inhumane as punishments held unconstitutional in other contexts. On due process, White argues Goss v. Lopez requires at least an informal “give-and-take” before deprivation of liberty; post-hoc tort remedies are inadequate because physical pain is irreparable and state immunities and good-faith doctrines may leave injured students uncompensated.
  - Justice Stevens: Agrees with White’s critiques on both Eighth Amendment scope and the insufficiency of post-deprivation remedies for protecting liberty from bodily punishment.

3. Historical and legal background from the majority opinion
- Corporal punishment in schools has deep colonial and common-law roots; most states historically allow reasonable corporal punishment by teachers, subject to civil/criminal remedies if excessive.
- By the 1970s, about 21 states had statutes authorizing moderate corporal punishment in schools; only a few states had banned it.
- The common-law test: force is privileged if the educator reasonably believes it necessary for control, training, or education; excessive force is actionable.

4. Broader materials: reporting, state law, and professional guidance (focused on Alabama and medical/psychological positions)
- Alabama context:
  - Alabama law (since 1995) allows corporal punishment in public schools and directs local boards to set codes; it disclaims liability for employees acting within law and rules, except for “excessive force or cruel and unusual punishment.”
  - Many Alabama districts use paddling (often a wooden paddle, typically limiting number of “licks”); parents in many districts may opt out; refusal to submit can lead to suspension in some places.
  - Federal Civil Rights Data (2013–14) showed Alabama among states with high paddling rates (~18,749 students paddled that year; a long-term decline from ~40,000 in 2000). Usage is regionally concentrated and shows racial and gender disparities (boys, and Black students in particular, paddled at higher rates).
  - Local reportage and officials often defend paddling as a disciplinary tool; some districts are moving away from it and adopting alternatives like PBIS.
- Research, professional associations, and medical/psychological guidance:
  - Major medical and child-development organizations (American Academy of Pediatrics, American Psychological Association, American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, etc.) oppose corporal punishment in schools, citing limited effectiveness and harmful long-term effects (increased aggression, poorer attitudes toward school, lower academic performance).
  - Pediatric and psychological guidance emphasize positive, relationship-based discipline: proactive reinforcement of desired behaviors, clear consistent rules, time-outs, removal of privileges, and teaching skills — recommending nonphysical alternatives to spanking.
  - Resolutions (e.g., from the APA) condemn institutional corporal punishment and encourage humane, effective behavior-management strategies.

5. Commentary and anecdotes
- Personal narratives and op-eds in the document describe cultural persistence of corporal punishment, regional pride in its use, and the tension between tradition and modern research/policy trends.
- Observations note that corporal punishment is often used because it is cheap, quick, and administratively convenient rather than demonstrably effective.

Overall synthesis:
- Legally, Ingraham v. Wright holds that the Eighth Amendment does not apply to disciplinary corporal punishment in public schools and that, under the Fourteenth Amendment, pre-punishment hearings are not constitutionally required so long as the practice remains governed by common-law reasonableness and subject to civil/criminal remedies for excess. Dissenters argued the decision leaves students unprotected from severe or mistaken corporal punishment and that minimal pre-punishment procedural safeguards (an informal opportunity to explain) should be constitutionally required.
- Practically and policy-wise, corporal punishment remains legal and prevalent in parts of the U.S. (notably many Southern states, including Alabama), but is declining and widely opposed by medical, psychological, and child-advocacy organizations, which recommend nonphysical disciplinary methods and point to evidence of harms and racial disparities in application.

President Trump, in a Fox News interview with Laura Ingraham, defended the administration’s sparse slate of State Department nominees and broader staffing choices, saying vacancies won’t derail his agenda because “the one that matters is me.” He framed the approach as deliberate cost-saving and business-like—saying he tells subordinates not to fill unnecessary slots—and blamed Senate Democrats, particularly Chuck Schumer, for obstructing confirmations. Trump acknowledged he has nominated fewer people than prior presidents and said he’s “filling up roles,” praising Secretary Rex Tillerson’s work while noting he is unhappy with the thinking of some potential nominees.

The interview covered many other topics: Trump called the Steele dossier “fake” and a disgrace after Democratic financing revelations; said Donna Brazile’s claims of a rigged DNC primary were a major, potentially illegal story unfair to Bernie Sanders; described the U.S. justice system as too slow and in some respects a “joke”; and reiterated that any DACA/Dreamer deal would include curbs on chain migration and funding for his border wall. He touted the economy—claiming big growth, deregulation wins, job creation and corporate repatriation—defended his trade posture and Asia trip (stressing North Korea as the key issue), signaled toughness on China enforcement, and said he may meet Putin. He also complained about what he described as biased media treatment of him and his family, praised his regulatory and judicial record, and reaffirmed confidence in his leadership and accomplishments. The document also contains a long list of diplomatic and executive positions and notes many unfilled or pending nominations across departments.

The MPAA and the National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO) have adopted a zero-tolerance policy banning wearable recording devices—like Google Glass and smartwatches—from movie auditoriums. Moviegoers must turn off and stow any such devices or face being asked to leave; if staff suspect recording, police may be called. The rule, approved at the ShowEast meeting, extends existing anti-piracy measures for phones and other recording gear and formalizes policies many theaters already enforced individually. Critics note that determined pirates likely have better ways to rip films than a shaky Glass recording, but the policy aims to prevent in-theater recording and protect films from illegal copying.

Hugh Hefner and ex-fiancée Crystal Harris traded public barbs after Harris told Howard Stern she found their sex life disappointing. On the Sirius XM show Harris, 24, said they had sex only once, that it “lasted like two seconds,” and that she’d “never seen Hef naked” and wasn’t attracted to him. Hefner responded on Twitter, calling her interview untrue, suggesting she was trying to impress a new boyfriend, and insisting their first night together was satisfying enough that he kept her for additional nights. The piece also notes Harris has been seen socializing with Jordan McGraw following the breakup and that she partied with Heidi Montag on the day her wedding was to have taken place.

A large prospective study of 9,509 adults (ages 35–75) with stable coronary artery disease followed weight an average of 12 times over about 4.7–5 years and found that greater weight variability (“yo-yo” or weight cycling) was linked to substantially worse outcomes. After adjusting for average body weight and other risk factors, those in the highest quintile of weight variability versus the lowest had markedly higher risks: new-onset diabetes (+78%), heart attack (+117%), stroke (+136%), and death (+124%). The highest-fluctuation group experienced median per-visit weight swings of roughly 3.9 kg (about 8.6 lb) versus ~0.9 kg (2 lb) in the lowest group.

The study, led by Dr. Sripal Bangalore and published in The New England Journal of Medicine (sponsored by Pfizer), is observational, so it cannot prove causation. The authors note limitations, including not knowing why participants gained or lost weight (illness could drive changes). Still, the findings raise concern that repeated weight loss and regain may be especially harmful for people with existing coronary heart disease and reinforce the importance of sustained weight loss and weight maintenance in this high-risk population.

Summary:

The FDA has warned that some homeopathic teething tablets and gels may be dangerous for infants and toddlers and is investigating reports of seizures and other serious effects after their use. Homeopathic products are marketed as “natural” and are not evaluated by the FDA for safety or effectiveness under current policy; some labeled homeopathic remedies have been found to contain substantial, inconsistent, or toxic amounts of active ingredients (for example, belladonna/atropine), which can cause seizures, breathing difficulty, lethargy, muscle weakness, flushing, constipation, urinary retention, agitation, or other harms. Consumers should seek immediate medical care if these symptoms occur after using such products.

Evidence and regulation:
- There is little reliable evidence that homeopathy is effective for any condition. Major reviews (including Australia’s NHMRC) found no reliable efficacy.
- Safety data are limited; some homeopathic products contain non-dilute active ingredients (including heavy metals or alcohol) and have caused adverse events or interactions.
- The FTC requires substantiation for health claims; the FDA proposed (2017) a risk-based enforcement approach focused on products that pose greater risk (vulnerable populations, safety concerns, non-oral/topical routes, poor quality, or claims to treat serious diseases).
- Homeopathic products are legally regulated as drugs but, under FDA policy, many may be marketed without preapproval if they meet certain listing and labeling conditions (HPUS ingredients, specified labeling). State rules on practice/licensing vary.

Teething guidance and safer alternatives:
- The FDA and pediatric authorities (AAP) note there is no proven benefit from homeopathic teething products. Teething can usually be managed without drugs.
- Recommended non-drug measures include giving babies firm objects to chew (teething rings, hard unsweetened crackers), cold items to numb gums (refrigerated—not frozen—teething rings; note AAP warns against frozen toys that can injure the mouth). Suggested safe items include pacifiers, spoons, clean wet washcloths, refrigerated teething rings, and chilled—not frozen—foods.
- If analgesics are needed, caregivers should be instructed on proper dosing of OTC acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
- Topical teething gels can carry risks: benzocaine-containing gels should not be used in children under 2 because of risk of methemoglobinemia; overdoses of topical agents have been linked to seizures and other serious effects.

Bottom line: Homeopathic teething products have no proven benefit and can contain harmful or inconsistent amounts of active substances. Parents should avoid these products, use safer non-pharmacologic measures for teething, follow dosing guidance for any necessary analgesics, and seek immediate medical help for concerning symptoms after exposure.

A tenant in an Oswego, Illinois apartment building intervened in a knife attack Monday by retrieving his AR-15 and ordering the attacker to stop. Witness Dave Thomas said he saw a bloody confrontation in a hallway, went home, chose his AR-15 over a handgun for greater intimidation, and stopped the assailant without firing. Police later apprehended the suspect; the stabbing victim was hospitalized and expected to recover. Thomas holds a valid FOID and concealed-carry permit and is a firearms instructor. The report frames the incident as an example of an armed civilian stopping a violent attacker without shots being fired.

Apple offers free nationwide recycling of its products and provides state-specific program details and battery/component removal guidance for independent recyclers via Apple Support.

In its annual environmental report, Apple said it recovered more than 61 million pounds of materials (steel, aluminum, glass, etc.) from old devices. Notably, the company recovered 2,204 pounds of gold—about one ton—worth roughly $39.5 million at recent spot prices (~$1,230 per troy ounce). Most of that gold likely came from circuit boards and other internal components of millions of recycled iPhones and computers (an average smartphone contains about 30 mg of gold, per Fairphone). While some gold could come from high-end gold Apple Watches, it’s unlikely many such expensive watches were recycled quickly. The piece also referenced a Conan O’Brien sketch tied to Apple’s past gold-colored iPhone announcement.

Researchers and conservationists warn that growing whale- and dolphin-watching tourism may be harming cetacean populations. Attendance has risen from about 4 million people in 1991 to 13 million in 2008, creating an industry worth roughly $2.1 billion. While collisions with vessels do cause direct injuries and deaths, scientists at the International Marine Conservation Congress emphasized subtler impacts: repeated disturbance can change animal behaviour (interrupting feeding, increasing swimming speed and respiration, displacing animals from preferred areas) and raise stress and energy expenditure. These small effects can accumulate and, in some cases, drive local declines—examples include bottlenose dolphins in New Zealand’s Doubtful Sound (numbers fell from 67 to 56 between 1997 and 2005) and endangered Irrawaddy dolphins in the Mekong, which face heavy boat traffic. Studies of minke whales in Iceland show predator-like responses to tour boats, though impacts on overall population there remain uncertain.

Experts say more rigorous, long-term population modelling is needed to determine which populations are most at risk and whether behavioural changes translate into lasting declines. Short-term measures—minimum approach distances, speed limits, and no-go zones—can help, but many guidelines are voluntary or inconsistently enforced; in some areas they have not prevented boat strikes or deaths. Stakeholders note tension between tourism income and conservation: in some regions dolphin-watching is an alternative livelihood to fishing, which also threatens animals (e.g., entanglement). Most delegates urged better management, stronger regulations, funding for monitoring, and public education so whale watching can be sustained without causing a "death by 1,000 cuts."

A shooting occurred Saturday morning around 9:30 a.m. in the food court of Melbourne Square Mall (1700 W. New Haven Ave.), leaving two men dead and one woman wounded. Police identified the shooter as 57-year-old Jose Garcia‑Rodriguez of Palm Bay. Investigators say he shot his 33‑year‑old wife, Idanerys Garcia‑Rodriguez, a food‑court employee, and another man—identified later as 36‑year‑old Leonardo Coppola, a food‑court restaurant operator—before apparently shooting himself. Jose Garcia‑Rodriguez and Coppola died (one at the scene, the shooter later at a hospital); Idanerys Garcia‑Rodriguez survived and is reported in good condition.

About 100 people were in the mall when the shots were fired; witnesses described panicked evacuations and hiding. Responding officers heard shots on arrival, cleared the mall and evacuated people from stores and hiding places. Police recovered three handguns and substantial ammunition believed to belong to the shooter. Authorities say the incident appears to stem from domestic violence, with Coppola reportedly trying to shield or move the victim out of harm’s way when he was shot.

The response included multiple agencies (Melbourne PD, FBI, Florida FDLE, ATF, neighboring police agencies and mall security); the bomb squad searched a vehicle connected to one victim but found nothing suspicious. The mall closed for the remainder of the day and reopened Sunday. Local officials and neighbors expressed shock; police are continuing their investigation and have asked witnesses to contact Melbourne Police.

Researchers at Baylor University studied how to make workday breaks more restorative. In a five-day diary study of 95 employees (959 breaks recorded), Emily Hunter and Cindy Wu found that the quality — not just the quantity — of breaks drives recovery of energy, concentration and motivation, with downstream benefits for health and job attitudes.

Key findings:
- Best timing: Mid-morning breaks are more effective than waiting until lunch or later. Breaks taken earlier in the day replenish resources before depletion sets in; breaks later in the day were less restorative and linked to more symptoms of poor health.
- Activity matters less than preference: The most restorative breaks are those people choose and enjoy. There was no evidence that non-work activities are inherently better than work-related ones; preferred activities (even work-related passion tasks) provide autonomy and recovery, whereas chores and errands do not.
- Frequency over single long breaks: More frequent short breaks were associated with higher resource recovery than fewer long ones. The study did not specify an optimal length, but suggests regularly “recharging” before energy hits zero is better than waiting for long recoveries.
- Consequences: Better breaks (earlier, preferred, and more frequent) led to fewer somatic symptoms (headache, eyestrain, back pain), reduced emotional exhaustion, greater job satisfaction and more organizational citizenship behavior.

Practical takeaways: Encourage mid-morning, self-chosen, reasonably frequent short breaks to sustain energy, focus and motivation and to improve well-being and workplace behavior.

Wynonna Judd says she’d back her sister Ashley Judd if the actress-activist ran for the U.S. Senate in 2014, despite their differing views. Speaking to Us, the country singer — who recently married Cactus Moser and appeared on Dancing With the Stars — emphasized family loyalty and support, noting Ashley was among the first she told when Ashley and Indy 500 racer Dario Franchitti announced their amicable split. Wynonna praised Ashley’s compassion, citing how Ashley helped Cactus after his motorcycle accident.

Separately, Democratic operatives are quietly recruiting alternatives to Ashley Judd in a potential challenge to Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell in Kentucky. Some party figures fear Judd’s liberal activism and lack of political experience could jeopardize Democratic chances in the conservative state and harm down-ballot races. One possible alternative is 34-year-old Kentucky Secretary of State Alison Lundergan Grimes, who has been courted by Bill Clinton and met with Democratic Senate campaign officials; her lack of political baggage and family ties in state politics make her an attractive option. The maneuvering highlights Democratic concern that nominating the wrong candidate or having a messy primary could squander their best opportunity to unseat McConnell.

Eva Longoria and husband José “Pepe” Bastón welcomed their first child together, a son named Santiago Enrique Bastón, on June 19 in Los Angeles. The newborn weighed 6 lbs., 13 oz. and the couple shared the first photo with HOLA! USA, saying they are “so grateful for this beautiful blessing.” Longoria, 43, who remained active professionally and in advocacy throughout her pregnancy—supporting Time’s Up, premiering Overboard and receiving a Hollywood Walk of Fame star—has moved into a Bel Air Crest home where she and Bastón will raise their son.

Bastón, 50 and president of Televisa, already has three children from a previous marriage, giving Santiago older step-siblings. Longoria, who married Bastón in 2016 after dating since 2013, spoke during pregnancy about raising a feminist son surrounded by strong female role models. In the months before the birth she held a pajama-themed baby shower attended by friends and family. Days before Santiago’s arrival she also experienced the loss of her longtime dog Jinxy.

Russian ski-cross racer Maria Komissarova, 23, suffered a severe spinal injury during a training crash at the Rosa Khutor Extreme Park above Sochi on Feb. 15. She fractured and dislocated her T12 vertebra and was rushed to Krasnaya Polyana Hospital No. 8, where surgeons performed an immediate 6½-hour operation that officials described as successful. Doctors reconstructed the vertebra and inserted a metal implant; Komissarova remained in serious but stable condition and conscious at times, though some reports said she was on a ventilator. Transfer to Moscow was ruled out because of the emergency nature of the surgery; further prognosis was expected to become clearer over the next several days and will depend on any spinal-cord damage. President Vladimir Putin visited her in hospital. Komissarova is out of the Sochi competition; she had a World Cup podium (second place in 2012) but was not viewed as a medal favorite. The accident highlights the risks of newer Olympic freestyle disciplines, where serious training injuries, while relatively rare at these Games, have occurred.

Major central banks—the U.S. Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of England, Bank of Canada, Bank of Japan and Swiss National Bank—announced coordinated measures to ease strains in global financial markets by enhancing their ability to provide liquidity. Key steps include:

- Cutting the cost of temporary U.S. dollar liquidity swap lines by 50 basis points so the new price is the U.S. dollar overnight index swap (OIS) rate plus 50 bps, effective December 5, 2011, and extending authorization of the swap lines through February 1, 2013.
- Establishing temporary bilateral swap arrangements as a contingency to provide liquidity in each other's currencies if market conditions require (currently no need beyond U.S. dollars).
- The Bank of England, Bank of Japan, ECB and Swiss National Bank will continue three-month tenders until further notice.
- The Fed extended and reduced pricing on existing dollar swap lines with those central banks and stands ready to use additional tools to backstop U.S. short-term funding if needed.

The coordinated move aimed to mitigate a worsening credit squeeze driven by the spreading European sovereign-debt crisis and to prevent a contraction in bank lending to households and businesses. Markets reacted positively: stocks and futures rose sharply (e.g., Germany’s DAX up ~4%). The action was intended to reassure markets and ensure banks can access dollar and, if necessary, other-currency liquidity quickly.

Dustin Snyder, 19, a longtime Valrico resident, was diagnosed with synovial sarcoma—a rare soft-tissue cancer—one day before his 18th birthday. After surgery, chemo and radiation, the cancer returned multiple times, ultimately spreading through his stomach and pelvis. Recently placed in hospice, doctors say he has only weeks to live.

Snyder and his girlfriend, Sierra Siverio, 21, reconnected after middle‑school romance and had been together over two years. They decided to marry as soon as possible; Snyder proposed after dinner. Within hours of Snyder’s sister Brittany Hails publicizing their situation and requesting help, community members and businesses donated virtually everything needed for a wedding: a donated diamond ring, a tuxedo from Men’s Warehouse, a sequined wedding dress and bridesmaid dresses from a Tampa company, venue and reception space at the Big Red Barn in Plant City, flowers and additional dresses from LifePath Hospice, and photography and other services. A GoFundMe set up by Hails raised over $13,000–$14,000 to cover remaining costs and to help the family with end‑of‑life expenses.

The couple—focused on living positively—were overwhelmed by the community support. They married on Sunday, Jan. 28, 2018, surrounded by friends and family.

Zynga priced its IPO at $10 a share Thursday, the top of its $8.50–$10 range, selling 100 million shares (with a 15 million‑share overallotment option) and raising about $1 billion. The stock (ticker ZNGA) will begin trading on Nasdaq Friday. The $10 price values Zynga at roughly $7 billion by one measure (about $8.9 billion including unexercised options and warrants), below earlier $20 billion speculation but on par with large traditional game publishers such as Electronic Arts.

Zynga, best known for Facebook titles like FarmVille, CityVille and Mafia Wars, reported nine‑month revenue through Sept. 30 of $828.9 million (more than double year‑earlier revenue) and net income of $30.7 million, down from $47.6 million due to higher marketing and R&D spending. The company has about 227 million average monthly users and earns most revenue from a small percentage of players buying in‑game items.

Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs led the underwriting syndicate. Zynga said proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes and potential acquisitions; roughly $83.6 million will cover tax withholding on vesting restricted stock units. Observers noted the pricing was conservative relative to some recent internet IPOs, leaving room for potential future offerings.

Roberto Unger, a longtime Harvard Law professor who once advised Barack Obama and taught him courses like Jurisprudence and “Reinventing Democracy,” publicly urged voters to defeat Obama in 2012. In a YouTube video titled “Beyond Obama,” the 65-year-old Brazilian politician and intellectual — who has run for Brazil’s presidency and served as a minister — argued that Obama failed to advance a progressive agenda and had betrayed liberals.

Unger’s criticisms include:
- Prioritizing bailouts for financial interests while neglecting workers and homeowners.
- Relying on “financial confidence and food stamps” and limited fiscal/monetary stimulus instead of broadening economic and educational opportunity.
- Subordinating economic and educational reform to the secondary issue of healthcare reform to avoid a fight.
- Practicing a politics of “hand-holding” rather than struggle and bold change.
He acknowledged that a Mitt Romney victory would bring costs in judicial and administrative appointments but said those risks were preferable to another Obama term because only a political reversal could revive progressive possibility in American life.

The video, posted in May and viewed thousands of times, marked a sharp break between Unger and his former student; Unger has been a Harvard faculty member since 1976 and received tenure unusually early in his career.

Researchers in Pretoria used gas chromatography–mass spectrometry to analyse organic residues from 24 clay tobacco-pipe fragments excavated from William Shakespeare’s Stratford-upon-Avon garden and nearby sites (artefacts loaned by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust). The sensitive forensic technique identified a variety of smoked plants in early 17th‑century England: cannabis residues in eight samples, nicotine in at least one, and definite chemical evidence of Peruvian coca (cocaine) in two pipes (the cocaine-positive pipes were not from Shakespeare’s garden). Other reports of camphor or nutmeg-type residues have also been suggested in related coverage.

The study’s authors and commentators link these chemical findings to contemporary botanical and literary sources (e.g., John Gerard’s Herbal and Shakespeare’s Sonnet 76) to speculate that cannabis was used as a smoked “weed” that could aid creativity, while “compounds strange” might allude to foreign drugs such as coca. The work demonstrates how forensic chemistry can illuminate historical smoking practices and raises questions about whether Elizabethan theatrical life was frequently tobacco- or drug‑tinged. The results were published in the South African Journal of Science (July 2015).

This piece examines why housework remains largely women’s responsibility despite gains in men’s involvement with childcare and cooking. It opens with a statistic that only about 2% of commercials showing men depict them doing domestic tasks and cites Arlie Hochschild’s argument that cleaning is emotional as well as physical work—women often feel that maintaining an orderly home signals safety and that they will be judged first for domestic messiness. That social expectation reduces men’s incentives to take on chores: even when men do more cleaning, women frequently receive the credit.

Proposed fixes are debated. Philosophers suggest formal chore negotiations, but the author finds that impractical. Jenny Anderson’s comparative-advantage approach—assigning tasks based on who’s relatively better and letting repetition improve skill—is presented as a pragmatic alternative. Other suggestions include lowering women’s “filth thresholds” where feasible, hiring help when possible, and making cleaning more appealing through gadgets.

Jessica Grose’s view—that women’s disproportionate housework is driven by male free-riding—is countered by the claim that men and women often simply have different standards of cleanliness: people who care more about tidiness will clean more. The author and a male commentator describe negotiated compromises in their own marriages: splitting tasks unevenly but acceptably, paying for weekly cleaning, and tolerating a less-than-perfect home. They stress that household tasks differ in kind (drudgery vs. enjoyable childcare, stressfulness of finances, etc.), so simple hourly comparisons are misleading.

Overall, the article argues the solution isn’t only to demand parity but to acknowledge differing preferences and task types, use comparative advantage, lower standards where acceptable, outsource when possible, and make chores less onerous—while also recognizing the broader cultural pressures that still put the burden on women.

This long profile traces Bruce Jenner’s decades-long struggle with gender identity, his public life as an American sports hero, and his transformation into Caitlyn Jenner. It blends intimate recollection, family testimony, and reporting on surgery, media strategy and fallout.

Key points

- Early life and identity: Growing up dyslexic and privately cross-dressing, Jenner felt female from childhood but buried that identity while building an elite athletic career. Winning the 1976 Olympic decathlon made him a symbol of American masculinity even as his inner conflict persisted.

- Attempts to transition: Jenner first pursued transition in the mid- to late-1980s—taking hormones, removing facial hair, and having surgeries—then stopped because of fear, career considerations, and concern for his young children. That period was described as “the dark years,” marked by isolation and career decline.

- Family and marriages: Jenner’s complex family life included three marriages and six biological children (plus stepchildren via Kris Jenner). His second and third marriages ended amid strain over his gender issues and shifting family dynamics. Many of his children experienced long periods of distance from him; some believe Kris Jenner’s role in the family/business dynamic widened that gap. Several of his children now describe the relationship improving as he moves toward authenticity.

- Recent transition and surgery: In early 2015 Jenner completed facial-feminization surgery and breast augmentation after living more openly as a woman for some time. The immediate postoperative period included acute pain, medication-induced panic, and counseling; she emerged resolute, saying she could not be lying on her deathbed having never addressed this truth.

- Public reveal and media: Jenner chose to tell her children privately after a leak to TMZ forced the issue. She then appeared in a high-profile Diane Sawyer interview and planned an E! docu-series produced by Bunim/Murray. Some of Jenner’s older children declined participation, worried the show would trivialize the story and undermine its potential positive impact for the transgender community. Jenner insists the show aims to help others, not merely to profit or entertain.

- Personal reflections and motives: The profile conveys ambivalence among family and friends about motives and timing. Jenner’s mother and others wondered whether fame and money played roles, while Jenner denies that the transition was for publicity. Caitlyn expresses remorse for past absences as Bruce and hopeful intent to rebuild relationships and use her platform for transgender advocacy.

- Cultural significance: The piece situates Jenner’s transition within broader shifts in visibility and acceptance of transgender people, noting the severe employment discrimination and high attempted‑suicide rates many face. Jenner received widespread celebrity support after the televised interview and planned to spotlight suicide prevention and support for transgender youth in her media projects.

Overall impression
The article presents a layered portrait of a public legend confronting a lifelong private truth: the costs and consequences of living as Bruce, the complexity of family wounds and reconnections, and the fraught but potentially influential way Caitlyn Jenner intends to use fame to raise awareness about transgender lives.

Last month’s Hurricane Maria severely damaged Puerto Rico’s communications and power infrastructure. In response, Alphabet’s Project Loon partnered with AT&T, federal and local authorities (FCC, FAA, FEMA), aviation regulators, and several private companies to launch stratospheric balloons that deliver basic LTE internet and voice/text services to hard-hit areas.

Key points:
- Project Loon has deployed multiple high-altitude balloons (e.g., HBAL199 and HBAL237) over Puerto Rico more than 60,000 ft up; several more were launched from Nevada and the FCC authorized up to 30 balloons for the relief effort.
- The balloons provide basic internet access (texts, emails, light web use) to AT&T customers with compatible 4G LTE phones by linking with temporary ground infrastructure installed by partners such as SES Networks and Liberty Cablevision.
- This deployment uses new machine-learning algorithms to cluster and station balloons over needed areas by riding stratospheric winds; the team is still learning to adapt to the region’s shifting winds.
- Project Loon is experimental but has prior disaster use (flood relief in Peru, early 2017). Balloons are solar-powered and typically provide daytime service; many can stay aloft 100+ days (record 190 days).
- The effort involved spectrum support from multiple companies and coordination with Pan-American and Puerto Rican aviation authorities and air traffic controllers.
- The response supplements other restoration efforts: AT&T has deployed temporary cell sites and other tech firms (Cisco, Facebook, Tesla) have also contributed to communications and power recovery. Puerto Rico continues to face widespread outages—limited electricity, many nonworking cell towers, closed schools, and shelters—following the storm.

Summary:

Facing three scandals—Benghazi, the IRS’s targeting of conservative groups, and the Justice Department’s seizure of Associated Press phone records—President Obama and his team moved aggressively midweek to contain political damage. The White House released 100 pages of Benghazi emails to show how talking points evolved, and Obama directed Treasury Secretary Jack Lew to request the resignation of acting IRS Commissioner Steven Miller, who resigned; a new acting commissioner will be named and a permanent nominee will require Senate confirmation. The administration also signaled plans to revive legislation to protect journalists.

Republicans immediately intensified scrutiny and demanded more, with GOP leaders calling for an apology and promising continued investigations, including a scheduled hearing on the IRS. Democrats and White House aides argued the administration chose to act deliberately rather than rush and risk errors—waiting for an inspector general report and declassification before responding.

Commentators and some Republicans view the AP phone-record seizure as a lower-tier concern compared with Benghazi and the IRS, but all three warrant Congressional investigation. Opinion pieces urged Republicans to pursue inquiries vigorously but warned against relying on scandal alone as a political strategy or prematurely speculating about electoral effects or impeachment.

Behind the scenes, aides acknowledge Obama’s constrained second-term agenda: while he can still act on immigration, parts of the budget, executive steps on climate, healthcare implementation, judicial nominations, and troop withdrawals, his ability to set the agenda is limited by political realities and ongoing controversies. Obama and his advisers emphasize measured responses, long-term perspective, and a desire to refocus on governing despite frustration over the political distractions.

Pop star Justin Bieber posted an Instagram photo showing him FaceTiming Malala Yousafzai and wrote that he admires her story and looks forward to meeting her to discuss how he can support the Malala Fund. Malala, the Pakistani education activist who survived a 2012 assassination attempt by the Taliban, has been campaigning globally for girls’ schooling, including attention around the kidnapped Nigerian schoolgirls and related summits. The post signals Bieber’s interest in the cause, though he gave no details about any partnership; the outreach comes amid recent tabloid controversies involving Bieber and actor Orlando Bloom.
