The mysterious dimming of star KIC 8462852, first flagged by citizen scientists using Kepler data for its deep, irregular dips in brightness (up to ~22%), has been further investigated with infrared observations. A team led by Massimo Marengo (Iowa State University) analyzed 2015 data from NASA’s Spitzer Space Telescope and found no significant excess infrared emission that would be expected from warm dust produced by a major planetary or asteroid collision. Combined with earlier null results from WISE, this absence of an infrared signature makes catastrophic rocky collisions unlikely.

The Spitzer results support the leading non‑artificial explanation: a family or swarm of cold comets on a long, eccentric orbit producing varying, irregular transits that caused the observed dimming in 2011 and 2013. By the time Spitzer observed the system the cometary material would have moved away and would not be detectable in infrared. SETI radio searches have also found no signals indicative of intelligent activity, and while the possibility of an artificial “megastructure” cannot be strictly ruled out by these observations, the comet swarm remains the preferred explanation. Researchers emphasize the star remains unusual and worthy of further observation.

Starbucks appears to be rolling out a limited-edition "Unicorn Frappuccino," a pink-and-blue, unicorn-themed variant of its popular blended drink. Images have begun appearing on Instagram and Twitter, and baristas and customers have been discussing it on Reddit. Early tasting reports (one from blogger Mike Fahey, whose wife works at Starbucks) describe a sour raspberry/fresh-fruit profile layered with a strong sour syrup—some liken it to Tropical Skittles. The drink was rumored to debut around April 19–20, 2017; Starbucks had not issued an official announcement at the time of these reports. Links to Reddit and early coverage circulated alongside the rumors.

Sen. John McCain’s announcement that he will oppose the latest GOP Obamacare repeal bill (the Graham-Cassidy measure) dealt a major — likely fatal — blow to the seven-year Republican effort to dismantle the Affordable Care Act, but did not end the fight. With McCain’s “no,” Republicans likely lack the votes needed before the Sept. 30 budget-rule deadline that would allow repeal to pass without a Democratic filibuster. Senators Rand Paul and possibly Susan Collins also oppose the bill, and other GOP defections are possible.

Republicans remain interested in repeal — Vice President Pence said the administration is “undeterred” — and some Republicans have floated alternative routes (e.g., pairing repeal with tax reform under a new budget resolution). But attention is also shifting toward bipartisan talks led by Sens. Lamar Alexander and Patty Murray to stabilize insurance markets, especially by resolving the legal certainty of cost-sharing reduction (CSR) payments that insurers rely on. McCain cited those bipartisan negotiations in explaining his opposition, and Democrats pressed to resume them.

Democrats welcomed McCain’s stance cautiously and warned the law remains vulnerable while President Trump can still take administrative steps — such as threatening to end CSR payments or cutting outreach and enrollment funding — that could undermine the exchanges. Activists and Democratic leaders plan continued protests and pressure on vulnerable GOP senators until repeal is unequivocally off the table. Congressional leaders have not formally declared the issue settled; GOP leaders could still attempt another repeal push before or even after Sept. 30, keeping uncertainty about the ACA’s future alive despite market signs of stabilization.

NBC News, Sky News, CNN and other outlets have obtained thousands of purported ISIS internal documents — including a 23-question recruitment/registration form — that illuminate the group's personnel records, routes, and organizational practices. The trove, reportedly stolen from a senior ISIS internal security official by a disillusioned defector, contains names, addresses, phone numbers, family contacts and other personal data for more than 22,000 jihadis from at least 51 countries. Media reports and German authorities say many entries match known extremists (e.g., Londoner Abdel Bary, former ISIS media head Junaid Hussain), while others identify previously unknown recruits and recruiters across Europe, North America, the Middle East and North Africa.

The standardized form asks routine biographical details (name, alias, birth date, nationality, education, blood type, address, family contacts) plus organization-specific items: countries traveled, point and date of entry, who recommended the applicant, prior jihad experience, field of specialty, "Sharia level," level of obedience, whether the applicant seeks to be a fighter or a suicide attacker, personal property left behind, and space for date/place of death. Some entries are strikingly candid — including candidates requesting immediate suicide missions or noting combat injuries. Separate batches reportedly focus specifically on would-be suicide attackers.

Intelligence and law-enforcement agencies view the cache as a potentially valuable source for tracking foreign fighters, identifying recruitment networks, prosecuting returnees, and mapping routes through transit countries that often went unchecked. German officials consider the documents likely authentic, and Sky and other outlets have shared the material with authorities. The leak is also a reputational blow to ISIS, suggesting internal dissent and operational vulnerabilities just as the group faces intensified military pressure and recent high-profile strikes against its leadership.

This document combines a 1990s-era column by Michael Schrage about Pizza Hut’s PizzaNet experiment with a long Gizmodo feature ranking the 100 most significant websites.

Michael Schrage — PizzaNet (1994)
- Pizza Hut launched PizzaNet in a Santa Cruz pilot that let customers order pizza via the World Wide Web using Mosaic browsers. Orders were routed to a centralized PizzaNet server in Wichita and then relayed to local restaurants; staff called to verify orders and payment was collected on delivery.
- Pizza Hut framed this as a low-cost, straightforward technical effort, but Schrage argues the pilot only automated an existing commodity transaction. He urges focusing on what networked computing can uniquely deliver: interactivity and design value rather than merely replacing the phone. For example, let customers visually design pizzas on-screen (place toppings where they want), gamify family pizza-making, or sell design tools—ideas he calls “computer-aided pizza engineering.”
- Schrage broadens the point: the same “Media Fab” potential applies to other customized products (e.g., T‑shirts designed online and shipped). None of this requires new technology—entrepreneurs just need to invest to blend designability and delivery.

Gizmodo — The 100 Most Significant Websites (selection and themes)
- Gizmodo presents a ranked list of 100 websites that shaped the Web’s culture, commerce, and politics. The list spans early web pioneers, social platforms, content hubs, tools, and controversial or novelty sites. It evaluates influence rather than quality and mixes nostalgia, utility, and social impact.
- Highlights and takeaways:
  - Early infrastructure and pioneering projects: The WWW Project (Tim Berners-Lee), W3Catalog, Project Gutenberg, NASA, Internet Archive (Wayback Machine), and AltaVista.
  - Foundational commerce and services: Amazon, eBay, Craigslist, PayPal’s ecosystem origins, Expedia, MapQuest, and Seamless—sites that changed retail, travel, classifieds, and delivery.
  - News, satire, and fact-checking: New York Times, Drudge Report, The Onion, Snopes—illustrating web influence on journalism, propaganda, and satire.
  - Social and community platforms: Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, MySpace, Tumblr, LinkedIn, Friendster, LiveJournal—credited with reshaping social interaction but also criticized for harms (privacy, political manipulation, harassment).
  - Media, entertainment, and fandom hubs: YouTube, Netflix, Twitch, Vimeo, Giphy, SoundCloud, Bandcamp, Pitchfork, TV Tropes, Wookieepedia—sites that enabled new creator economies, fandoms, and distribution models.
  - Creative and user-generated culture: Blogger, GeoCities, DeviantArt, Newgrounds, Neopets, FanFiction, Imgur, Flickr—platforms that democratized content creation and community.
  - Search, developer, and productivity tools: Google, GitHub, Stack Overflow, DuckDuckGo, Dropbox—critical infrastructure for information discovery, collaboration, and coding.
  - Controversial or disruptive actors: WikiLeaks, The Pirate Bay, 4Chan, Megaupload, PornHub—sites that challenged legal, ethical, or social norms and sparked debates about free speech, piracy, and harm.
  - Niche but influential services: Kickstarter (crowdfunding), Kickstarter’s role in projects like Oculus; Bandcamp’s support for indie musicians; WhoSampled, HaveIBeenPwned, OpenSecrets—sites serving specialized investigative or cultural purposes.
  - Nostalgic/time-capsule sites: Space Jam’s promo page, Hampsterdance, Hamsterdance, GeoCities—examples of early web aesthetics and meme culture.
- Top-ranked: Wikipedia (#1) is praised for collective knowledge-building and staying true to its ideals; Google (#2) for transformative search technology and subsequent dominance; YouTube (#3) for democratizing video and spawning new industries.
- The list balances admiration and critique—many entries are acknowledged for both their innovations and negative consequences (monopolistic tendencies, privacy intrusions, culture wars, or decay over time).

Overall synthesis
- Together, the pieces illustrate two linked truths about the web’s history: early experiments (like PizzaNet) showed how the internet could digitize ordinary transactions, but the web’s deeper value lies in enabling new forms of interactivity, community, and creative expression. The Gizmodo list maps how dozens of sites executed those possibilities—some realizing Schrage’s vision for designable, participatory services, others illustrating unintended consequences and cultural shifts as the web matured.

About 10 people reported illness after a suspicious package arrived in the mailroom of a large IRS building in downtown Kansas City, Missouri. Symptoms included vomiting and sweating; two people were taken to St. Luke’s Hospital and are in good condition. Firefighters checked for gases and fumes, isolated the package from the public, and have not identified its contents. The building was not evacuated and has since returned to normal operations. The investigation has been turned over to the IRS and other federal authorities.

Golf publications and sponsors are distancing themselves from Tiger Woods amid his recent personal scandal and indefinite break from the PGA Tour. Golf Digest said it will suspend Woods’ bylined instruction articles while he’s away, though it will keep him on the masthead and has no current plans to end their long-standing relationship; Woods reportedly has an exclusive deal with the magazine worth about $3 million a year. Observers note the move reflects broader commercial pressure as advertisers and partners react to reputational risk.

Major corporate sponsors have already pulled back: Accenture ended its relationship, Gatorade stopped producing his sports drink, Gillette suspended ads featuring him, and AT&T said it was re-evaluating ties. That backlash has severely damaged Woods’ endorsement income (Forbes estimated his annual earnings around $110 million). 

Not all partners cut ties — Swiss watchmaker TAG Heuer removed photos of Woods early in the controversy but then reposted them with a “TAG Heuer stands with Tiger Woods” message, emphasizing a professional ambassador relationship. The actions follow media reports about an early-November car crash and multiple women alleging affairs, which led Woods to acknowledge marital infidelity and take an indefinite leave to focus on family.

The U.S. Under-23 men’s team was eliminated from CONCACAF Olympic qualifying after a dramatic 3-3 draw with El Salvador on March 26. Needing a win to reach the semifinals and keep Olympic hopes alive, the Americans surged ahead almost immediately when Brek Shea’s cross found Terrence Boyd in the 2nd minute. Bill Hamid injured his ankle in the first half and remained in goal until the 39th minute; El Salvador scored twice in quick succession (Lester Blanco, Andres Flores) to take a 2-1 lead before halftime. Sean Johnson replaced Hamid.

In the second half Freddy Adu set up Boyd’s 65th-minute equalizer, and Joe Corona headed in a go-ahead goal in the 69th to make it 3-2. The U.S. then ceded momentum, and in stoppage time Jaime Alas struck a bouncing shot that Johnson failed to hold; the ball ricocheted over him into the net for a 3-3 finish, eliminating the U.S. The result, combined with Canada’s earlier draw with Cuba, knocked the Americans out of contention for the 2012 Olympics.

Match context and fallout: the U.S. struggled to maintain possession and control, especially after Hamid’s injury; coaching decisions about keeping Hamid on drew criticism. Key performers: Boyd (two goals) and Adu (two assists) were bright spots; several defenders and both goalkeepers were criticized in postgame grades. El Salvador, who had limited preparation time, advanced to the semifinals and moved one win away from an Olympic berth. U.S. players and coach Caleb Porter expressed devastation, with captain Freddy Adu calling it one of the worst feelings of his career.

Study and purpose
- A secondary analysis of the prospective Coping with Cancer cohort examined whether terminally ill adults with metastatic, chemotherapy‑refractory cancer who were receiving palliative chemotherapy months before death experienced different end‑of‑life care and place of death than those who were not.
- 386 patients (recruited 2002–2008) whose physicians estimated ≤6 months to live and who later died were analyzed; 56% were on palliative chemotherapy at study enrollment (median 4.0 months before death).

Key methods
- Baseline clinical, sociodemographic and psychosocial data were collected, including performance status, treatment preferences, advance care planning and whether patients had discussed end‑of‑life wishes.
- Primary outcomes: use of intensive interventions in the last week of life (CPR, mechanical ventilation) and place of death (ICU, hospital, home, hospice, nursing home).
- Secondary outcomes: survival, late hospice referral (≤1 week before death), and whether patients died in their preferred place.
- Propensity score weighting was used to adjust for measured differences between patients who were or were not receiving chemotherapy.

Main findings
- Patients on chemotherapy differed at baseline (younger, better performance status and quality of life, more likely to prefer life‑extending care, less likely to acknowledge terminal illness or have end‑of‑life discussions).
- After propensity adjustment, receiving chemotherapy at enrollment was associated with:
  - Greater use of intensive interventions in the last week of life: 14% vs 2% (adjusted risk difference 10.5%; 95% CI 5.0% to 15.5%).
  - Higher rate of feeding tube use in the last week: 11% vs 5% (adjusted risk difference 7.1%; 1.7% to 12.5%).
  - More late hospice referrals (≤1 week before death): 54% vs 37% (adjusted risk difference 13.6%; 3.6% to 23.6%).
  - Greater likelihood of dying in an ICU: 11% vs 2% (adjusted risk difference 6.1%; 1.1% to 11.1%).
  - Lower likelihood of dying at home: 47% vs 66% (adjusted risk difference −10.8%; −1.0% to −20.6%).
  - Lower likelihood of dying in preferred place: 68% vs 80% (adjusted risk difference −9.4%; −0.8% to −18.1%).
- There was no significant survival advantage for those receiving chemotherapy (hazard ratio 1.11; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.38).

Interpretation and implications
- Among patients recognized as terminal (≤6 months prognosis), use of palliative chemotherapy months before death was associated with more aggressive, medicalized care near death, later hospice enrollment and higher likelihood of dying in an ICU rather than at home, without measurable survival benefit in this cohort of decedents.
- Patients receiving chemotherapy were less likely to have had end‑of‑life discussions or advance directives, suggesting treatment may delay advance care planning and affect goal concordance.
- Findings do not establish causation (observational design; possible unmeasured confounding) but point to the need for better communication and advance care planning when considering or continuing palliative chemotherapy near the end of life.
- Clinicians and patients should weigh the potential for increased intensive end‑of‑life care and reduced chance of dying in the preferred setting against unclear survival benefit when deciding about continuing chemotherapy for patients with limited life expectancy.

Summary:

- A U.N. independent commission investigating human rights violations in Syria heard testimony suggesting rebel forces have used the nerve agent sarin. Commission member Carla Del Ponte said investigators, after interviewing victims and medical staff in neighboring countries, have "strong, concrete suspicions" based on how victims were treated, but no incontrovertible proof and no evidence so far pointing to government use. She gave no specifics on timing or locations. This inquiry is separate from a U.N. investigation into alleged chemical attacks that has stalled. Both the Syrian government and rebels have accused each other of multiple chemical attacks; the U.S. has said it has varying confidence that the government used sarin. President Obama had warned that chemical-weapons use would be a "red line."

- Fighting continued across Syria: Rebels reportedly shot down a government helicopter in Deir el-Zour province, killing eight troops, and have been assaulting and occupying parts of several air bases, including heavy clashes at the Mannagh base near the Turkish border where rebels seized a tank unit and killed a base commander. Government warplanes have been striking rebel positions; the conflict has killed more than 70,000 people and displaced or driven over a million from their homes.

- Israel conducted air strikes around Damascus targeting what it said were Iranian-supplied guided missiles destined for Hezbollah. Syrian state media condemned the strikes; Israel publicly framed them as aimed at preventing advanced weapons transfers to Hezbollah, not at toppling Assad, and sought to avoid escalating into broader conflict. Israel deployed Iron Dome batteries as a precaution. Tehran denied the strikes were against arms shipments; Hezbollah did not comment.

Courtney Stodden, 21, is pregnant with her first child, confirmation she gave to FOX411 after a video of her holding a positive pregnancy test circulated. The clip, reportedly sent to friends and family by a source close to Stodden, shows husband Doug Hutchison, 55, filming her in their bathroom; Stodden says she feels “a little overwhelmed.” Us Weekly reports she’s about four weeks along and said the news was bittersweet and that they hadn’t planned to go public so soon. Stodden called the leaked video an invasion of privacy; her estranged mother and former manager, Krista Keller, told FOX411 she learned of the pregnancy through media coverage.

The story also revisits long-running controversies around Stodden’s marriage to Hutchison, whom she married in 2011 at age 16 with Keller’s consent. On Lifetime’s The Mother/Daughter Experiment: Celebrity Edition, Keller stunned viewers by admitting she told Hutchison she loved him and, in another episode, by suggesting he had a sexual “fantasy” involving her and Courtney. The revelations have further strained the turbulent mother-daughter relationship—Keller defended the marriage at the time by calling an older partner “more responsible”—and fueled sensational coverage of the family’s dynamics on reality TV.

British researchers at Imperial College London report evidence that human intelligence is influenced not by a single “intelligence gene” but by at least two large, distinct gene networks—named M1 and M3—potentially coordinated by a shared regulatory system. Using data from mouse and human brain samples, postmortem brains, and genetic and cognitive data from thousands of living volunteers (including the Generation Scotland cohort and the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936), the team found that genes associated with variation in cognitive abilities (memory, attention, processing speed, reasoning) in healthy people overlap with genes that, when mutated, contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders such as epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder. One network contains roughly 1,000 genes and the other a few hundred; their functions appear non‑overlapping and remain to be defined.

About 40% of intelligence variation is attributed to heredity; environmental factors remain uncertain. The authors suggest that because many of the implicated genes may share common regulation, it could eventually be possible to influence cognitive performance pharmacologically—initially a theoretical prospect aimed at helping people with learning disabilities or cognitive impairments. The discovery relied on large datasets and heavy computation; researchers still need to determine how the genes interact, which are the key drivers, and the precise mechanisms linking these networks to both normal cognition and disease.

The article also notes related research funded by the Wellcome Trust (STRADL) studying depression subgroups to better understand causes and develop diagnostics and therapies. An editorial amendment clarified that autism is a disorder rather than an illness.

Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.), a Foreign Relations Committee member, told Fox News Sunday that President Trump’s tariff-driven trade policies helped prompt General Motors’ recent decision to close five plants (in Ohio, Michigan, Maryland and Ontario), cut 15% of its North American salaried workforce and potentially lay off up to 14,000 workers. Cardin and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau both tied GM’s restructuring to the steel and aluminum tariffs the U.S. has imposed. Trump angrily threatened to cut GM subsidies after the announced closures and model discontinuations including the Chevrolet Cruze and Buick LaCrosse.

Cardin welcomed the 90-day U.S.-China tariff truce struck by Trump and Xi—during which planned tariff increases on $200 billion of Chinese goods were delayed—for reopening negotiations on technology transfer, intellectual property and agriculture, but criticized the administration’s earlier decision to use national security as a basis for tariffs on U.S. allies, saying it fractured unity needed to pressure China. Sen. Roy Blunt (R-Mo.) also called the China pause positive while urging more specifics and noting that removing other trade disputes would give the U.S. more leverage with China. Bipartisan concern about Chinese intellectual property theft was noted, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer previously endorsing tougher action.

Separately, former Vice President Dick Cheney addressed criticism from the late President George H.W. Bush—who had called Cheney an “iron ass” after 9/11—saying 9/11 had changed his approach and that any rift was smoothed over by a later conciliatory note and social gestures from Bush.

International Women’s Day (IWD) on March 8 is both a celebration of women’s cultural and economic achievements and a moment when many corporations launch campaigns and products to align with the pro-woman conversation. This year’s IWD saw a wave of brand activity—some praised, some mocked—and highlighted tensions between inspirational messaging and the demand for concrete action in the #MeToo/Time’s Up era.

Notable brand moves:
- Mattel unveiled 17 “role model” Barbie dolls depicting historical and contemporary women (e.g., Amelia Earhart, Katherine Johnson, Patty Jenkins, Chloe Kim). The dolls aim to respond to parental concerns about role models for girls, but critics noted the dolls all share the same slim body type, undermining the message for some.
- Nike ran an Oscars ad with Serena Williams declaring “there’s no wrong way to be a woman,” a feel-good spot that fits the motivational genre.
- Google published an interactive Doodle featuring stories from 12 women artists and encouraged public contributions via #HerStoryOurStory.
- Uber released a video in Asian markets countering myths about female drivers; Facebook rolled out IWD-themed cards and photo frames.
- McDonald’s flipped the golden arches to a “W” at one California location and on its digital channels, a stunt that drew ridicule from portions of social media.
- Diageo rebranded Johnny Walker as “Jane Walker” for a limited release; the launch backfired after remarks and the concept were perceived as patronizing.

Context and critique:
- The #MeToo and Time’s Up movements have raised expectations for corporate responses: audiences now look for tangible actions (internships, hiring practices, inclusion riders) rather than only inspirational slogans. Erin Keeley, CMO at Mono, says the conversation has shifted from awareness to “what happens next.”
- Some campaigns that coupled messaging with substantive initiatives (e.g., Getty Images’ female-focused sports photography internship; actors advocating for inclusion riders) were singled out as better models.
- French daily Liberation used pricing (charging men 25% more) to dramatize the gender pay gap, and France announced tougher wage-gap screening and penalties for companies with unjustified disparities.

Broader cultural reckoning:
- Media institutions are also reconsidering how women are represented and remembered—examples include projects like The New York Times’ “Overlooked” obituaries series, which reclaims the histories of notable women long omitted from mainstream remembrance.

Overall, IWD 2018 demonstrated both the commercial eagerness to associate with women’s empowerment and the higher bar demanded by a public newly attuned to systemic inequities: brands are rewarded for meaningful, sustained commitments but criticized for superficial or tone-deaf gestures.

Violence and unrest intensified in Kiev after months of anti-government protests sparked by President Viktor Yanukovych’s decision to reject an EU association and accept closer ties with Russia and a Russian bailout. Clashes between protesters and riot police escalated over several days, with burning buses, cobblestones hurled, stun grenades and rubber/plastic bullets used, dozens injured and roughly 1,500 activists seeking medical help. Protest encampments in Independence Square remained active despite freezing weather.

The government passed new anti-protest laws criminalizing participation in violent demonstrations, and protesters reported threatening text messages warning against “mass disturbance” that echoed the new law’s language; mobile operators denied providing location data or sending the messages. Opposition figures said the authorities were tolerating radical elements while intimidating moderates; some protesters detained youths they said were paid to provoke violence, and opposition leaders accused the government of bus­ing in thugs to discredit the movement. Radical protesters and some opposition members embraced more confrontational tactics, arguing peaceful protest had been exhausted; others publicly condemned the violence.

Ukraine’s opposition sought negotiations—Vitali Klitschko met only with presidential aides after attempting to see Yanukovych—and the government said it would use force if provocations continued, while denying plans to declare a state of emergency. Orthodox priests briefly helped calm clashes on one occasion.

Russia criticized Western involvement: Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov blamed certain EU and U.S. politicians for encouraging the unrest by engaging with protesters and warned events were “getting out of control.” EU officials denied condoning violence and reiterated support for Ukraine’s eventual political association with the EU. Moscow framed the unrest as justification for firm measures and emphasized concerns about “radical opposition” actions, while many protesters viewed government moves as repression aimed at silencing pro-European sentiment.

A nurse identified in German media as Niels H. (Niels Högel) — aged 40 and serving a life sentence since 2015 for two murders and two attempted murders — is now suspected of killing at least 84 additional patients, investigators said. He was convicted of giving lethal overdoses of heart medication at intensive-care units where he worked; judges concluded he created cardiac crises so he could then resuscitate and gain praise. During his 2015 trial he admitted administering the drug to roughly 90 people at a Delmenhorst clinic, and he later told police he had also killed patients at an Oldenburg hospital where he worked earlier.

A special commission formed in 2014 has reviewed hundreds of medical records and exhumed 134 bodies to test for drug residues; many potential victims were cremated, hampering evidence collection. Authorities say abnormalities go back to 2000, and staff meetings as early as 2001 had discussed unusually high numbers of deaths and resuscitations but did not notify police, allowing him to move between clinics. Oldenburg police chief Johann Kuehme warned the true total may be higher and blamed local health authorities for acting too slowly. Prosecutors plan further charges against Högel and are also pursuing cases against former hospital staff, though any additional convictions will not extend his current life sentence. Identities of the newly suspected victims have not been released.

This document examines how President-elect Donald Trump’s tax proposals and the Republican congressional agenda could deliver large benefits to wealthy families while posing political and fiscal challenges.

Key points

- Estate tax repeal: Republicans, buoyed by control of the White House and Congress, aim to repeal the federal estate tax (the “death tax”), which now applies at a 40% rate only to very large estates (exemptions were $5.45M per person/$10.9M per couple). Repeal would save roughly $20+ billion a year and largely benefit a tiny share of estates (about 0.2% of deaths). Republicans can try to pass long-term repeal via budget reconciliation, but need to manage narrow Senate margins and political optics given Trump’s populist rhetoric.

- Who benefits: Eliminating the estate tax would create large windfalls for ultra-wealthy families and many in Trump’s circle. Estimates cited (Bloomberg) suggest Trump’s family could save hundreds of millions to over $1 billion depending on his true net worth; nominees and allies (Wilbur Ross, Richard DeVos, Linda and Vince McMahon, Steven Mnuchin, Gary Cohn) also stand to gain substantially.

- Other major Trump proposals and estimated impacts (based on his 2005 return and journalistic analyses):
  - Repeal of the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) could reduce Trump’s taxes by roughly $31 million (2005 basis).
  - A new 25% rate on certain pass-through/business income could save him tens of millions (est. ~$16M).
  - Cutting the top individual rate to 35% could save high earners modestly (~$0.5M in the cited calculation).
  - Repealing the estate tax was estimated to be the biggest single saving (~$1.1B in one analysis).
  - Eliminating many deductions could raise his taxable income modestly (estimated $3–5M higher taxes in one scenario).

- Winners and losers under the GOP framework:
  - Winners: Corporations (corporate rate cut to 20%), many small businesses (25% rate), heirs to large estates, some high-income households (AMT repeal, lower rates), and some low- and middle-income taxpayers via a doubled standard deduction and larger child tax credit.
  - Losers: Taxpayers in high-tax states if state and local tax deductions are removed (notably affecting blue states like NY and CA); accountants/tax preparers if filing is simplified; and the federal budget—analysts project roughly $2.2 trillion in net tax cuts, worsening the national debt and potentially pressuring spending on domestic programs.

- Politics and debate:
  - Democrats strongly oppose repeal; some proposed raising estate rates on the very richest. Public opinion shifts depending on framing: people favor repeal when told it’s a “death tax” but are likelier to support it (or higher rates) when told who would be affected.
  - Some conservatives urge a populist-focused reform that visibly helps middle-income voters rather than front-loading benefits to the wealthy.
  - GOP leaders are aware of political risks and are waiting for guidance from Trump on package details; some want estate repeal via reconciliation, others prefer a comprehensive overhaul.

Overall, the piece argues that Trump’s plan and Republican priorities would disproportionately help the very wealthy—delivering substantial tax savings to heirs and high-net-worth individuals—while raising questions about political coherence with Trump’s populist appeals and increasing federal deficits unless offset by other measures.

Thom Hartmann argues that the true original purpose of the Second Amendment was to preserve Southern slavery by protecting state-controlled militias—often functioning as slave patrols—not to guarantee individual recreational gun use. He documents colonial and early state practices (e.g., Georgia militia laws requiring plantation inspections and punishments for fugitive slaves) and dozens of slave revolts that made Southern elites fear both internal uprisings and the possibility that a federal military could emancipate slaves by enlisting them. At the 1788 Virginia ratifying convention, Patrick Henry and George Mason warned that Article I, Section 8’s federal militia powers could be used to disarm state militias and enable emancipation; Henry explicitly linked the militia question to protecting slave “property.” James Madison, who initially drafted the amendment, altered wording to emphasize a “free State” (changing “country” to “State”) to reassure those concerns—Hartmann contends this change helped secure Southern support for ratification.

Hartmann contrasts that historical context with modern debates: he says the Amendment’s original aim was collective, anti-tyranny defense, not sport or personal self-defense, and thus contemporary gun-control measures intersect with deep constitutional principles. He notes political risks Democrats face when proposing restrictions, cites historical parallels of governments curtailing rights by first restricting arms, and reminds readers the Constitution can be amended if society decides to change the balance between gun rights and regulation.

A key Senate procedural vote to advance the Defense Authorization bill — which included a provision to repeal the military’s 17-year-old "Don't Ask Don't Tell" (DADT) policy — failed Thursday, 57-40, falling three votes short of the 60 needed to overcome a filibuster. The defeat is a major setback for President Obama and Democrats pushing repeal, though proponents pledged to keep fighting.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid called the cloture vote without completing negotiations with moderate Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who supports repeal but had sought a negotiated process for amendments and debate. Collins voted yes but criticized Reid for walking away from talks; other Republicans who had raised similar procedural concerns, including Scott Brown and Lisa Murkowski, voted no. One Democrat, newly elected Sen. Joe Manchin, also voted against advancing the bill.

Shortly after the vote, Collins and independent Sen. Joe Lieberman announced plans to introduce a stand-alone repeal bill, with Reid said to support bringing it to the floor during the lame-duck session. Reid’s spokesman indicated Reid would co-sponsor the measure, but a standalone bill faces challenges, including potential amendment fights.

Supporters of repeal — including military leaders like Adm. Mike Mullen and Defense Secretary Robert Gates — warned that congressional failure could force a rushed, disorderly implementation if courts overturn DADT first. Opponents argue repeal during wartime could harm troop effectiveness and safety. Advocacy groups expressed anger at the filibuster, calling the failure a betrayal of troops and promising continued efforts to repeal. President Obama called the outcome disappointing and urged the Senate to revisit the issue in the lame duck session.

BuzzFeed News and the BBC have published leaked documents (the “Fixing Files”) and new betting analysis revealing long‑standing, widespread suspicions of match‑fixing at high levels of men’s professional tennis. Key findings:

- A core group of roughly 16 players — all at some point ranked inside the world top 50, including Grand Slam title winners — repeatedly appeared on lists of suspected fixers handed to tennis authorities over the last decade. More than half were still active and many were due to play the Australian Open.
- The material includes a 2007–08 inquiry triggered by highly abnormal betting on the Nikolay Davydenko vs. Martin Vassallo Arguello match in Sopot. Investigators linked large bets from syndicates in Russia, northern Italy and Sicily to suspicious match patterns across dozens of matches (72 flagged in the original probe), and identified 28 players for further disciplinary inquiry.
- Investigators recovered deleted texts, phone contacts and betting links implicating gambling rings and showing how players could be approached in hotel rooms and offered large sums (reported offers of ~$50,000+) to influence matches, often by “tanking” sets or matches. Betting patterns frequently matched on‑court anomalies (e.g., favourites winning the first set then collapsing).
- Despite the investigators’ report and evidence handed to authorities, no full disciplinary action followed against the implicated top players. Reasons given included legal advice that a new 2009 anti‑corruption code could not be applied retrospectively and, according to whistleblowers and some former investigators, a Tennis Integrity Unit (TIU) that was underpowered, secretive and often failed to follow up bookmaker intelligence.
- Independent betting analysis by BuzzFeed of ~26,000 matches identified 15 players with repeated losses in matches showing heavy, lopsided betting; four displayed patterns so extreme their performances were statistically highly improbable. Several of those players overlap with names previously flagged to the TIU.
- The TIU’s position: it says it takes a zero‑tolerance approach, assesses all credible intelligence and has prosecuted lower‑ranked players (including life bans). TIU officials and ATP leadership emphasize the difficulty of proving corruption and defend confidentiality and current investigative practices. Critics — including former integrity reviewers and investigators who led the 2008 work — say the TIU lacks resources, refused to use proactive betting analysis, and missed a chance to “nip it in the bud.”
- Multiple bookmakers, the European Sports Security Association and foreign police claim they repeatedly alerted the TIU about suspicious matches and were sometimes rebuffed or not asked for crucial account/computer records needed to pursue cases. Some Italian criminal investigations since then have produced arrests and local sanctions, but the TIU has not publicly sanctioned many high‑profile names from the leaked lists.
- The reporting does not name current players implicated because BuzzFeed/BBC lack direct access to phone, bank or computer records necessary to prove individual guilt; the TIU has the authority to demand such records.

Overall: the documents and analysis portray a pattern of suspicious betting and potential corruption reaching into elite men’s tennis over many years, assert that early, strong investigative leads were not fully pursued, and raise questions about whether the sport’s current anti‑corruption structures and resourcing are adequate to detect and deter organized match‑fixing.

A national outbreak of cyclospora, a microscopic intestinal parasite that causes watery diarrhea and other gastrointestinal symptoms and is treated with antibiotics, has sickened 397 people across 16 states (with at least 22 hospitalizations). Iowa first detected the outbreak in late June after a parasitologist identified Cyclospora cayetanensis in a patient sample; cases later appeared in neighboring Nebraska and other states. Iowa and Nebraska investigators have linked many illnesses there—about 80% in Iowa—to a specific brand of prepackaged bagged salad mix (iceberg and romaine lettuce, carrots and red cabbage) that moved through national distribution, but they have not named the company or product lot, saying the tainted lot appears to be out of the market and legal restrictions in many states limit public naming when the immediate public-health threat has passed.

Federal agencies (CDC and FDA) are continuing investigations to determine whether the bagged salad link explains cases in other states; they caution that different states’ epidemiologic patterns suggest there may be multiple sources. Food-safety experts and advocates have criticized the pace and transparency of the probe, arguing the source should have been identified sooner and calling attention to “culture of non-disclosure” tied to state laws that can hinder public identification of implicated producers. Investigators note difficulties in traceback—short shelf life of bagged salad means implicated packages were often discarded—and that contaminated ingredients could come through common processors or distributors rather than a single brand. Patients continue to recover after antibiotic treatment, and officials say they are narrowing possibilities though no single national source has yet been confirmed.

Jann Wenner, co-founder and longtime publisher of Rolling Stone, confirmed that he is exploring a sale of his 51% stake in the iconic music and culture magazine. Wenner, 71, told The New York Times that although he still loves the job, selling is “just the smart thing to do.” Wenner Media said it is considering “strategic options” to position the brand for growth; the company’s president and Wenner’s son, Gus, is credited with engineering the planned transaction.

Rolling Stone, founded by Wenner and Ralph Gleason in 1967, helped define rock journalism and published major cultural and political writers (Hunter S. Thompson, Joe Klein, P.J. O’Rourke, Tom Wolfe). But the magazine’s influence and finances have waned in recent years. Its reputation suffered a major blow after a 2014 article about a gang rape at the University of Virginia was discredited; a Columbia Journalism School review called it a “failure of journalism,” and subsequent libel suits resulted in a multimillion-dollar jury award. Circulation, newsstand sales and print ad revenue declined as readers moved online, and critics say Wenner was slow to adapt and favored legacy artists on covers.

Wenner has been paring assets: he sold a 49% stake in Rolling Stone to digital music startup BandLab in 2013 and recently sold Us Weekly and Men’s Journal to American Media Inc. Those titles had generated about three-quarters of Wenner Media’s revenue, leaving the company smaller and more vulnerable. Wenner’s sale would mark the end of an era for the magazine he built from a $7,500 loan into a cultural institution, though its present value is far below a previously rumored half‑billion-dollar offer.

Republican and Democratic national committee leaders reacted differently after Michael Bloomberg signaled he is “looking at all the options” — including an independent 2016 presidential bid — saying the campaign debate so far is “distressingly banal.” DNC Chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz told CNN Bloomberg’s priorities (education, consumer protection, gun safety, etc.) are already reflected in the Democratic platform and argued Republicans in the field would roll back that progress. RNC Chair Reince Priebus welcomed a Bloomberg run, calling him effectively “another Democrat” who would siphon votes from the eventual Democratic nominee and make a contested outcome more likely; he predicted Bloomberg couldn’t reach 270 electoral votes and could hand the decision to a Republican-controlled House.

Bloomberg’s openness follows strong early showings by outsiders Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump in New Hampshire, which advisers say may have increased the opportunity for an independent candidacy. Bloomberg has reportedly told aides to prepare a possible run and would need to begin getting on state ballots by early March. Analysts say an independent Bloomberg could draw more from Democrats than Republicans because of his liberal stances (e.g., gun control, climate), potentially helping the Republican nominee — though structural barriers make a third-party victory unlikely. Reactions among campaigns and voters were mixed: Trump welcomed the idea, Sanders criticized it as oligarchic, and Clinton’s team declined comment.

Researchers from the UK and US report that boys born to older fathers scored higher on a composite “Geek Index” (GI) at age 12—made from non‑verbal IQ, strong focus on interests, and relative social aloofness—than boys of younger fathers. The study used data from the Twin Early Development Study (TEDS): roughly 7,800 British twins with full data (and broader analyses on ~15,000 twins). Key findings:

- GI increased with paternal age, especially after about age 45; in boys the GI rose ~1.5 points per five years of paternal age. Maternal age had little effect. The association was sex‑specific: it was observed in males but not clearly in females.
- Higher GI predicted better academic outcomes at 16, particularly greater uptake and success in STEM GCSEs. Children of fathers aged 50+ were more likely to achieve high STEM grades than those of fathers under 25.
- Genetic modeling estimated GI to be substantially heritable (~57%); the genetic contribution to GI variance increased with paternal age. The authors suggest both familial inheritance (men who delay fatherhood may themselves have “geeky” traits) and potential de novo genetic factors related to older paternal age may contribute.
- There may be partial overlap between genes linked to higher GI and genes implicated in autism. The researchers propose that a modest inheritance of such variants could bolster school success, while a higher “dose” together with other risk factors might raise autism risk—offering a possible explanation for prior links between advanced paternal age and autism. The male‑specific effect could relate to the known male‑bias in autism or to measurement issues (girls’ “geekiness” may manifest differently).

Limitations and cautions:
- The GI was measured at age 12 and linked to school results at 16; the study cannot show whether GI advantages persist into adulthood, long‑term career success, or whether higher GI associates with adverse social/emotional outcomes.
- The observational twin design cannot fully disentangle all familial, environmental, and de novo genetic causes. The authors controlled for SES, maternal age, and parental qualifications, and ran sensitivity analyses excluding very old fathers and autism diagnoses, but caution that effects at the individual family level are small and should not guide personal decisions about timing of parenthood.

Overall conclusion: while advanced paternal age has documented risks (e.g., higher rates of autism and some psychiatric disorders), this study identifies a small but measurable association between older fathers and a cluster of traits—higher non‑verbal IQ, intense interest focus, and social aloofness—that predict better academic (especially STEM) performance in boys. The effect likely reflects a mix of inherited traits in men who delay fatherhood plus possible age‑related genetic changes; further work is needed to clarify mechanisms, sex differences, long‑term outcomes, and potential trade‑offs.

This long profile examines Bernie Sanders’s position within the Democratic Party nearly two years after his 2016 presidential run and as he weighs a possible 2020 campaign. It highlights three central tensions: his deep satisfaction that ideas long associated with him—especially Medicare for All and a $15 minimum wage—have moved into the Democratic mainstream; his discomfort with the trappings of fame, party politics, and media scrutiny; and the strategic, personal, and political calculations behind whether to run again.

Key points:

- Influence and agenda-setting: Sanders has successfully shifted Democratic debate on health care, labor, taxation, and party rules. His advocacy helped popularize Medicare for All, press employers on wages (e.g., Amazon, Disney), and contributed to changes like limiting superdelegates. His extensive digital operation and mass online viewership amplify his message.

- Relationship with the Democratic establishment: After 2016 tensions, Sanders has tried to build working ties—joining Senate leadership efforts to defend the Affordable Care Act, collaborating with figures like Chuck Schumer and DNC chair Tom Perez, and cultivating alliances with labor and grassroots groups—while still being distrusted by many centrists and Clinton loyalists who view him as divisive or narcissistic.

- The question of running in 2020: Sanders says he will probably run only if he is the best candidate to defeat Donald Trump. Advisors see both opportunity (a more favorable climate for his ideas, a loyal base) and risk (age concerns, negative opposition research, the cost and complexity of a national primary, and stronger centrist pushback). His likely path would rely on a committed base to win early contests and build momentum, but that strategy is fragile if rivals (e.g., Warren, Biden, Booker) chip away at his support.

- Strengths and vulnerabilities: Sanders’s strengths are his message, energized grassroots following, and media savvy. His weaknesses include challenges reaching beyond economic issues to address identity and racial politics convincingly, past controversies (old writings, media appearances), organizational frictions (polarizing former staff), and the practical demands of a modern primary campaign.

- Personal dimension: The profile conveys Sanders’s mix of pride in policy wins and discomfort with celebrity and inside-the-Beltway politics. Allies debate whether he should run again or focus on building a movement and grooming younger leaders; Sanders himself frames the choice around effectiveness in beating Trump.

Overall, the piece portrays Sanders as a transformed yet conflicted figure: a potent force reshaping Democratic priorities whose decision on 2020 could either culminate in a presidential bid shaped by lessons from 2016 or redefine his role as the ideological architect for a younger generation of progressive leaders.

Pierre D. Fulton, the passenger in the car Walter Scott was driving when he was stopped by North Charleston police on April 4, was publicly identified and issued a single written statement through his lawyer. Fulton described Scott as a "dear friend" who had helped him become a better man over the past five years, said he doesn't know why Scott ran from Officer Michael Slager, and added, "I know he didn't deserve to die." He asked for prayers for Scott's family and for privacy; his lawyer said that will be his only public comment. Slager, 33, is charged with murder after video showed him firing eight times at the unarmed Scott, 50, as Scott ran away. Slager has not entered a plea and his attorney says they are conducting an independent investigation.

Michael Bloomberg has offered to cover the roughly $15 million the United States would have contributed to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change’s operating budget after President Trump announced the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement. Bloomberg said Americans are “forging ahead” and argued that cities, states, businesses and civil society—the “non-state actors”—can collectively meet the U.S. 2025 emissions target even without federal participation. He proposed a “parallel” pledge and suggested his group’s submission could be reflected in U.N. reports on Paris signatories’ progress.

Former U.N. climate chief Christiana Figueres noted, however, that there is no formal mechanism for non-country entities to become full parties to the Paris accord, so it was unclear how such a submission would be handled. She also said the U.S. government must continue reporting emissions to the U.N. for several years because formal withdrawal cannot take effect immediately. Bloomberg’s move underscores a shift in U.S. climate leadership from the federal government to states, cities, academia and industry. His stance is part of broader business and public backlash to the withdrawal, exemplified by figures like Elon Musk and Bob Iger leaving presidential advisory councils and companies such as Google and Shell criticizing the decision.

Trigger warning: child loss

This document tells the stories of two mothers who lost young children to drowning and are now urging parents and medical organizations to take drowning prevention far more seriously.

Nicole Hughes recounts the sudden drowning of her 3-year-old son, Levi, on June 10, 2018, while the family was on vacation in Fort Morgan, Alabama. Despite wearing a life jacket in many photos and having physicians present who immediately performed CPR and intubation, Levi was found face-down in the deep end and could not be revived. Hughes highlights startling facts—that drowning is the leading cause of death for children ages 1–4, that most child drownings occur when the child is not expected to be swimming, and that a child can drown in less than a minute, often silently without splashing or calling for help. Overwhelmed with grief and anger, Hughes founded a nonprofit, Levi’s Legacy, to eradicate drowning and promote designated supervision. She calls on the American Academy of Pediatrics to prioritize drowning prevention in well-child visits and parent resources, arguing that water safety should be as prominent as guidance on SIDS prevention, vaccinations, and car seats.

The piece also profiles Morgan Beck Miller (wife of Olympic skier Bode Miller), who lost her 19-month-old daughter, Emeline, in a backyard pool drowning in early June. Beck Miller shared a message urging parents to focus more on drowning prevention than on topics like organic foods or screen time, stressing how quickly drowning can occur and asking followers to read Hughes’s account to raise awareness. Both mothers emphasize that drowning is highly preventable and call for greater public education and systemic attention to protect children.

Austrian daredevil Felix Baumgartner postponed his planned record‑breaking stratospheric skydive by one day because of an incoming cold front. The Red Bull Stratos mission moved the jump from Monday, Oct. 8 to dawn Tuesday, Oct. 9, expecting calmer conditions for the fragile, 55‑story‑tall helium balloon and its 2,900‑lb fibreglass capsule to lift Baumgartner to about 120,000 ft (≈36,600 m). Winds at ground level must be under 2 mph for launch.

If successful, the 43‑year‑old will exceed the 1960 record of 102,800 ft set by Col. Joe Kittinger (now an adviser and in radio contact during the jump), become the first person to break the sound barrier in freefall, and set records for longest freefall and highest manned balloon flight. Baumgartner — a veteran of some 2,500 jumps who has trained and rehearsed for five years — will wear a highly flexible, pressurized suit with life‑support systems, cameras and monitoring gear. The 11‑ft by 8‑ft capsule is reinforced, has a large exit hatch, and was designed to avoid past failures such as the 1962 Dolgov accident.

The mission carries substantial risks: at extreme altitudes there is little atmosphere and one small failure (ripped suit, helmet crack, or an uncontrolled high‑speed spin) could cause ebullism, anoxia, the bends, barotrauma or loss of consciousness from high g‑forces. To mitigate danger the suit has safety systems including a drogue parachute that deploys if sensors detect loss of consciousness. Baumgartner will accelerate to supersonic speeds (reaching ~700 mph within ~40 seconds), then transition to a stable freefall position as atmospheric density increases, freefall for several minutes, deploy his main parachute around 5,000 ft, and be expected to land near Roswell, New Mexico. The team plans to livestream the jump.

Actor-author Carrie Fisher, best known as Princess Leia, died Dec. 27 at age 60 after suffering a heart attack on a flight from London to Los Angeles and being treated at a hospital. Her death prompted widespread tributes from friends and co-stars. Star Wars creator George Lucas remembered Fisher as a longtime friend who was “extremely smart” and “feisty, wise and full of hope,” offering condolences to her family. Harrison Ford called her “one-of-a-kind…brilliant, original,” and Mark Hamill expressed he was “devastated.” Peter Mayhew, who played Chewbacca, called her “the brightest light in every room.”

Fisher had completed filming for Star Wars: Episode VIII (directed by Rian Johnson), which wrapped production in July 2016 and is scheduled for release Dec. 15, 2017. Sources say she had finished her scenes, though the effect of her death on future installments—particularly any planned role in Episode IX—remained unclear at the time. Fisher’s career included her breakout in 1977’s Star Wars and numerous later film and TV roles, as well as work as a writer and comedian.

Four U.S. senators have placed friendly bets on the NBA Finals between the Golden State Warriors and the Cleveland Cavaliers: California Democrats Kamala Harris and Dianne Feinstein are backing the Warriors, while Ohio Democrats Sherrod Brown and Republican Rob Portman are rooting for the Cavaliers. If Golden State wins, Brown and Portman will each deliver a case of beer (Platform Brewing for Brown, Great Lakes for Portman) to the California senators. If Cleveland wins, Harris will send a case of Anchor Brewing and Feinstein a case of California Chardonnay to the Ohio senators.

The article also recaps Game 1 of the Finals in Oakland, a 124-114 Warriors overtime win over the Cavs. Key points:
- Stephen Curry scored 29 points; Kevin Durant added 26. Klay Thompson returned from a leg injury to score 24.
- LeBron James had a 51-point performance with eight assists and eight rebounds, his eighth straight Finals appearance and eighth 40-point game this postseason.
- The game went to overtime after a costly late-game mistake by J.R. Smith, who grabbed a rebound and dribbled away from the basket thinking the Cavs were ahead instead of attempting a shot or calling timeout.
- A review overturned an on-court charging call on James late in regulation, changing it to a foul on James that tied the game; Tristan Thompson was later ejected for a Flagrant 2 foul with 2.6 seconds left.
- Kevin Love returned from a concussion to contribute 21 points and 13 rebounds for Cleveland. Andre Iguodala remained out for Golden State with a knee bone bruise.
- Both teams had endured seven-game conference finals to reach the Finals, and players and coaches predicted more intense competition ahead as the series continues.

The US military’s assumption of control over Haiti’s main airport and emergency operations after the magnitude-7 quake has sparked diplomatic and humanitarian tensions as flights from other countries and aid agencies were diverted to the Dominican Republic. Brazil and France lodged formal protests after US military aircraft were prioritized at the congested Toussaint L’Ouverture runway; Brazil warned it would not relinquish UN command responsibilities and France accused the US of treating the airport as a Washington “annexe.” NGOs including the Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières also complained that medical and relief flights were turned away.

The disputes unfolded as Haiti struggled to respond to catastrophic damage in Port-au-Prince six days after the quake, which Haitian authorities say killed more than 100,000 people and left hundreds of thousands homeless. Aftershocks, blocked roads, a ruined port, fuel shortages and a short-staffed, damaged government hampered distribution. Looting, crowding at helicopter drops and chaotic food distributions meant many vulnerable people — the elderly, sick and weak — were being pushed aside.

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, who arrived in Port-au-Prince, said the UN was feeding 40,000 people and aimed to reach 1 million within two weeks, stressing priorities of saving lives, scaling humanitarian assistance and coordinating incoming aid. The UN mission itself suffered heavy losses, including several senior officials, weakening its capacity.

The US dispatched a vanguard of troops, aircraft carrier-based logistics and air-traffic control authority (with FAA guidance prioritizing rescue, military and humanitarian flights) and defended its efforts to clear sites and open alternative ports and landing zones. US agencies reported significant aid deliveries and systems installed, but much relief remained stuck at the airport pending ground transport and distribution.

Haitian president René Préval urged calm and coordination as international power struggles over command and access played out amid urgent life-and-death needs across the country. Aid groups increasingly sought alternate routes into Haiti via the Dominican Republic and overland convoys to bypass airport bottlenecks. Overall, the crisis combined massive immediate humanitarian needs with complex logistical, security and diplomatic challenges.

The Voyage of the Dawn Treader (2010) is the third film in the Chronicles of Narnia screen series, directed by Michael Apted from C.S. Lewis’s novel and scripted by Christopher Markus, Stephen McFeely and Michael Petroni. Returning to Narnia are siblings Lucy (Georgie Henley) and Edmund (Skandar Keynes); their cousin Eustace Scrubb (Will Poulter) joins them along with King Caspian (Ben Barnes) aboard the ship Dawn Treader to search for seven lost lords and confront a dark force emanating from a mysterious island. The cast includes voices by Liam Neeson (Aslan) and Simon Pegg (Reepicheep); Tilda Swinton makes a brief cameo as the White Witch.

Critical reaction was mixed. Some reviewers found the film bland and uneven compared with the first Narnia installment and competing fantasy franchises, criticizing its episodic plotting, overreliance on special effects (including a largely wasted 3-D presentation), and a generic, faith-tinged tone that fails to connect deeply with human emotion. Will Poulter’s performance as the obnoxious, talkative Eustace drew particular notice—grating to some but ultimately providing the film’s most memorable energy and a satisfying character arc when Eustace is transformed into a dragon and learns humility. Other praised elements included Apted’s steadier hand compared with the previous director, quieter human moments amid the effects, and generally serviceable family-adventure entertainment suitable for children. Running about 1 hour 52–55 minutes, the film is rated PG for fantasy action and frightening images.

This document collects several commentaries and excerpts criticizing how U.S. political, media, and policy elites handle questions about radical Islamists, national security, and related counterterrorism diplomacy. Key points:

- Political attacks on lawmakers: The author argues the severe backlash against Rep. Michele Bachmann and four GOP colleagues (the “National Security Five”) for probing Huma Abedin reflects elite efforts to shut down inquiry into Islamist influence in government. The piece frames the response as an attempt to silence uncomfortable questions rather than address possible security risks.

- Failures of institutional vigilance: Citing Cold War espionage scandals (Aldrich Ames, Robert Hanssen), the writer warns that political correctness and a reluctance to conduct rigorous counterintelligence screening have replaced past tough-minded security practices, increasing risks of bad analysis and flawed policy regarding radical Islamist threats.

- Media criticism and Islamophobia debate: The document condemns Politico for publishing a lengthy Newt Gingrich op-ed defending Bachmann and warning about Muslim influence, calling the outlet sensationalist. It also notes widespread condemnation of the Bachmann-Abedin accusations from figures like John McCain and others, and questions whether similar outrage would follow if surveillance and law enforcement targeted marginalized Muslim communities.

- Summarized FDD material on counterterrorism politics:
  1) Global Counterterrorism Forum (GCTF): The forum, launched by Turkey and the U.S., excludes Israel—an omission criticized by some U.S. lawmakers (e.g., Sens. Lieberman, Kirk). Disputes stem from Turkey–Israel tensions after the 2010 Mavi Marmara incident. The State Department defended the forum’s limited founding membership but said Israel could participate in relevant activities.
  2) Engagement with the Taliban: U.S. officials, including Secretary Clinton and VP Biden, pursued talks with the Taliban as a difficult but necessary step; discussions have included potential detainee transfers and efforts to distinguish Taliban factions from direct U.S. enemies.

Overall, the document argues that elites—political, media, and policy—are often unwilling to confront uncomfortable questions about Islamist extremism and counterterrorism, sometimes suppressing debate and risking poor analysis and policy as a result. It also highlights controversies in U.S. counterterrorism diplomacy, including exclusions from international forums and engagement strategies with adversaries.

Comedian and Friends star Matthew Perry told a story on Jimmy Kimmel Live! that he and a friend once beat up a third‑grade Justin Trudeau for "excelling in a sport" when Trudeau’s father was prime minister and the boy didn’t have security. Perry joked that the incident may have helped push Trudeau into politics. Trudeau playfully replied on Twitter (on April Fools’ Day), offering a rematch and quipping “who hasn’t wanted to punch Chandler?” Fans suggested a charity pay‑per‑view or other fun rematch ideas; Perry had not publicly answered the invitation.

Norwegian Air Shuttle plans to offer ultra-low-cost one-way transatlantic fares—potentially as low as $69—starting as early as 2017 by operating nonstop flights between small U.S. regional airports with low fees (e.g., Westchester County, Bradley International) and smaller European cities such as Edinburgh, Bergen and Birmingham. CEO Bjørn Kjos said average fares on such routes would likely be closer to $300 round trip, significantly undercutting many current long‑haul prices that are higher due to busy airport fees. The strategy—part of a broader push to take market share from traditional flag carriers—relies on using smaller, fuel‑efficient aircraft (Norwegian has 100 Boeing 737 MAX on order and expects five in 2017) to serve point‑to‑point markets and keep costs down. Regulatory arrangements (customs facilities at regional U.S. airports) would be needed but are expected to be achievable. Norwegian faces competition from other low‑cost long‑haul players like Iceland’s Wow Air and Eurowings, though Kjos questioned Eurowings’ ability to match Norwegian’s cost base with larger widebody jets. Norwegian also reported a 96% long‑haul seat load factor in September, contributing to better‑than‑expected results.

Support for the death penalty in the United States has fallen below 50% for the first time since 1971, according to an Aug. 23–Sept. 2 Pew Research Center poll. Only 49% of Americans now favor capital punishment for people convicted of murder, a seven-point drop since March 2015 and the lowest level in more than four decades. Opposition (42%) is the highest since 1972.

Long-term trend: support peaked at 80% in 1994 and has declined steadily since the mid-1990s. Executions have also declined sharply (98 in 1999 versus 15 this year).

Partisan and demographic divides remain:
- Republicans: 72% favor the death penalty; Democrats: 34% favor it.
- Independents are split (44% favor, 45% oppose), with those leaning Democratic showing notable declines in support.
- Men (55%) favor it more than women (43%).
- Whites (57%) are more supportive than Black (29%) and Hispanic (36%) respondents.
- Younger adults (18–29) are less supportive (42%) than older groups.
- Those without a college degree (51%) are more likely to support it than college graduates (43%).
- Religious variation: white evangelical Protestants strongly favor it (69%); Catholics and the unaffiliated are more divided.

Contributing factors: High-profile botched lethal injections and the lack of an agreed alternative have reduced the number of executions and likely contributed to declining public support. Public concerns include risks of wrongful execution and doubts that capital punishment deters serious crime.

Hostess Brands is voluntarily recalling about 710,000 cases of specific snack cakes and donuts after its flour supplier, Grain Craft, recalled certain flour lots for undeclared peanut residue. Affected products (single-serve cakes, multipacks and bagged donuts such as Ding Dongs, Zingers, Chocodiles and various chocolate, powdered, glazed, maple and crunch donuts) were sold nationwide in the U.S. and in Mexico at mass merchandisers, grocery and dollar stores, drug stores, distributors and convenience stores. A full list of SKUs, UPCs, batch codes and best-by dates is available on the FDA website.

Risk and reports: People with peanut allergies or severe sensitivities risk serious or life‑threatening reactions if they consume these products. Hostess says the amount of peanut residue is believed to be low and “not expected to cause adverse health effects in the vast majority” of allergic consumers, but it has received reports of two allergic reactions to products covered by the recall.

What to do: Consumers with peanut allergies should discard affected items or return them to the place of purchase for a full refund. Questions can be directed to Hostess at 1-800-686-2813 or via www.hostesscakes.com. More details and the complete product list are posted on the FDA recall page.

An increasing number of people—mostly in the U.S.—have developed a serious, often lifelong allergy to mammal meat after being bitten by the Lone Star tick. The reaction is triggered not by meat protein but by a sugar called galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal), found in beef and pork (and present in the cancer drug cetuximab). In affected people, antibodies to alpha-gal provoke massive histamine release hours after eating meat, producing itching, hives, stomach cramps and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis.

The alpha-gal link was identified in 2004 by University of Virginia immunologist Thomas Platts-Mills, who noticed a geographic overlap between cetuximab reactions, meat-allergy reports and regions where Lone Star ticks and Rocky Mountain spotted fever occur. Subsequent work by Platts-Mills, Scott Commins and colleagues found that about 80% of meat-allergy patients recalled tick bites and that tick exposure dramatically increases alpha-gal antibody levels. The precise mechanism remains unknown: researchers suspect something in tick saliva (a bioactive molecule, microbe, or residual blood proteins) primes the immune system to target alpha-gal.

Historically concentrated in the southern and central U.S., cases are now being reported farther north and northeast, raising questions about changing tick ranges or other tick species acquiring the same ability. Alpha-gal syndrome appears to affect anyone regardless of genetic predisposition, and there is currently no cure—management relies on avoidance of mammal meat and emergency treatments like epinephrine for severe reactions. Public-health tracking is limited because reporting isn’t mandatory, so researchers are compiling incidence maps and collecting blood samples to trace the cause and spread. Preventive advice: take standard tick-avoidance measures, check thoroughly after outdoor activities, and seek immediate medical help for post-meat symptoms such as sweating, itching, or breathing difficulty.

Turkish prosecutors have sought more than four years in prison for New York Knicks center Enes Kanter, accusing him of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in a series of tweets from May–June 2016. An Istanbul indictment says Kanter would be tried in absentia; he is in the United States and cannot easily return after Turkey canceled his passport last year (he was briefly detained in Romania in May before U.S. officials intervened).

Kanter, a vocal critic of Erdogan and a supporter of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, downplayed the indictment, saying it doesn’t bother him and that his focus remains playing basketball and helping the Knicks make the playoffs. He said he speaks out to be “the voice” for Turks he says are suffering—journalists and others jailed, tortured or disappeared—and called Erdogan “maniac,” criticizing Turkey’s restrictions on free speech. The report notes Kanter’s outspoken profile and large Twitter following.

Rolling Stone’s profile of Donald Trump gives a close, often intimate portrait of the candidate on the campaign trail and in his gilded private world, arguing that his success rests less on policy detail than on personality, performance and a deep political instinct.

Key scenes and impressions
- The piece opens with an on-board tour of Trump’s lavish private 757 and a flight from New York to a New Hampshire rally, capturing his mercurial, digressive conversational style: one moment rehearsing notes, the next puncturing rivals, debating policy shorthand, or asking crude rhetorical questions.
- On stage in Hampton, Trump delivers his familiar, unscripted populist message: he presents himself as a tough, successful outsider who will reclaim jobs, punish corporations that move jobs abroad, and confront elites and weak politicians. His delivery—an aggressive, schoolyard brogue and relentless attack mode—electrifies the crowd and translates well on television.
- The reporter documents how Trump’s wealth, celebrity and self-branding function as political assets: flaunting success while posing as an anti-elite champion who can “beat the hell out of” party insiders and corporate interests. Trump repeatedly frames himself as “owned by the people,” not by donors.
- The profile traces Trump’s biography and business career—his Queens upbringing, the influence of his father Fred, his Wharton education, his Manhattan real-estate triumphs (Commodore/Grand Hyatt, Trump Tower), and his evolution into a brand-licensing tycoon—showing how those experiences shaped his instincts and tactics.
- The story highlights contradictions in his positions (e.g., promising big domestic spending, defense build-ups and tax increases for the wealthy while offering few concrete policy mechanics) and notes his tenuous financial liquidity despite huge reported income and branding revenue.
- It documents his media strategy: dominating coverage through provocative comments and feuds (notably with Megyn Kelly and Fox News), treating appearances like episodes of his own reality show, and relying on earned media instead of early ad buys.
- The piece emphasizes both his strengths (a near-perfect feel for a resentful electorate, uncanny ability to command attention, persuasive stump performance) and vulnerabilities (high negatives within the GOP, late development of a ground operation, thin policy scaffolding, and propensity for alienating comments that could provoke coordinated opposition).

Controversy and tone
- The article quotes an on-air remark by Trump about Carly Fiorina—“Look at that face! Would anyone vote for that?”—which generated sharp criticism and coverage. Trump later said he meant Fiorina’s persona, not her physical appearance.
- Rolling Stone frames Trump as both uniquely gifted at political showmanship and dangerously unmoored from orthodox campaign mechanics and policy rigor. The author warns that while Trump’s approach has so far outmaneuvered rivals and held up under controversy, sustained, coordinated attacks from party elites and the need for concrete campaign infrastructure and funding pose significant tests.

Bottom line
- The profile argues that Trump’s candidacy is sustained by performance, branding, and a visceral connection with a broad swath of angry, underemployed and disaffected voters rather than by detailed policy or party backing. That combination makes him a serious and durable political force—but one with glaring institutional and strategic liabilities that could surface if the race becomes a protracted, conventional primary fight.

CNN is investigating allegations that Dr. Sanjay Gupta, its chief medical correspondent, misrepresented his role in a post-earthquake surgical intervention in Nepal. Reporting from the aftermath of the April 7.8 magnitude quake that killed more than 8,000 people, Gupta appeared on air saying he helped save an eight‑year‑old girl with a life‑threatening brain clot and was shown examining scans and operating at Bir Hospital in Kathmandu. His account drew global attention.

An independent probe by the Global Press Institute, which trains and publishes work by local journalists, found conflicting accounts: doctors and families told the institute Gupta actually assisted on a different patient, a 14‑year‑old, and that the eight‑year‑old named in CNN’s broadcast had not suffered serious injuries. GPI also reported that a CNN text story initially described the girls’ conditions accurately, then was altered hours later to match the broadcast’s version.

Gupta acknowledged on CNN’s New Day that the patient he operated on “may not have been this eight‑year‑old girl but rather…a 14‑year‑old” and said chaos in the hospital could have caused confusion. CNN’s statement defended Gupta, saying he assisted surgeons by performing a craniotomy on a young victim, that the network would try to verify the exact identity, and expressing full support for him.

Bir Hospital’s senior neurosurgeon, Dr. Rajiv Jha, told the Guardian Gupta repeatedly offered to help and was permitted to assist in one case after some hours. Jha said he had not authorized broadcasting the surgery and believed footage came from a cellphone filmed by a colleague. Gupta maintains he was asked to intervene.

The episode has reignited ethical debate over physician‑journalists: critics argue filming medical interventions risks confidentiality breaches and self‑promotion and that celebrity correspondents reporting in crises can displace or outreport local journalists. The Global Press Institute’s founder called the error “grave” and said local reporters would not have made such mistakes, framing the investigation as a prompt to reassess how foreign and celebrity journalists cover the developing world.
