A San Jose Mercury News report says Apple is expected to announce a newspaper subscription plan tied to tablets like the iPad, which publishers hope will help offset falling print circulation and ad revenue. Key claims include that Apple will take about a 30% cut of subscriptions sold through its App Store and possibly up to 40% of in-app advertising revenue; Apple has reportedly agreed to provide an opt-in feature allowing subscriber data to be shared with publishers. Many large newspapers are preparing tablet apps and negotiating with Apple; publishers prefer paying a flat fee and bundling digital app access with print subscriptions, but current terms would make Apple the intermediary for subscriber access. Analysts see tablet editions as a short-term risk but a longer-term opportunity to create richer, more valuable advertising, which would also benefit Apple. Competition from Android-based tablets could give publishers more leverage later.

Media critic Ryan Chittum questions the Mercury News story’s sourcing and framing, calling much of it speculative and noting the pattern of rapid, often under-sourced coverage around Apple. He argues outlets chase pageviews and fear being scooped, which lowers reporting standards; he also doubts publishers would accept giving Apple a near-third cut of recurring subscription revenue.

As part of the national “A Day Without Immigrants” protest, groups of workers in multiple states were fired after skipping shifts to participate. In Nolensville, Tennessee, 18 employees of Bradley Coatings, Inc. — described as team leaders — informed supervisors they would join the protest and were terminated the next day. A former employee called the dismissals unfair and said they had planned to make up the time; the company’s attorney said the firings were due to time-sensitive client schedules and a prior warning that missing work would lead to termination, not the protest itself. Tennessee’s Department of Labor noted the state’s at-will employment rules, while acknowledging legal limits like civil rights protections.

Separately in Catoosa, Oklahoma, a dozen Hispanic kitchen staff at I Don’t Care Bar and Grill were fired (some notified by text) after not showing up for work to support the protest. The restaurant owner cited a zero-tolerance no-show/no-call policy; the workers said they felt compelled to participate to show immigrants’ importance to the community and were surprised by the firings but plan to keep supporting immigrant causes.

Both employers said their actions were about attendance and contractual obligations rather than the political nature of the protest.

Brown University announced sanctions against two fraternities for hosting unregistered parties last fall that created conditions facilitating sexual misconduct, and said it will review alcohol and social event policies.

Key points:
- Sigma Chi (Olney House): On Oct. 3, 2014 an unregistered basement party was broken up by Public Safety after a student reported non‑consensual sexual contact while exiting the crowded space; the complainant could not identify the individual. Sigma Chi was found responsible for holding an unauthorized party, serving alcohol to minors, and creating an unsafe environment. Sanctions: probation, loss of social and University privileges through fall 2016 (no social events, loss of chapter room/lounge/library/basement access, and barred from recruitment/initiations). Members must attend educational programs. Sanctions were upheld on appeal and the national chapter was notified. No individual members were charged.

- Phi Kappa Psi (Sears House): On Oct. 17, 2014 two students reported receiving alcoholic drinks that allegedly contained GHB; one student later experienced non‑consensual sexual contact outside the chapter house while incapacitated. The chapter was found responsible for creating an environment that facilitated dangerous/possibly criminal behavior, drug possession/use and violations of operational rules. Because the organization controlled beverage service, it was held responsible for provision of a drink that contained GHB. Sanctions: loss of University recognition and housing for four years. The decision was upheld on appeal and the national chapter was notified. After appeal, questions arose about one lab test used as evidence; a final review of physical evidence will determine whether findings/sanctions should be modified. No individual members were charged.

- Broader response: Brown will conduct a comprehensive spring review of alcohol and social event regulations with students, faculty and staff. Meanwhile, parties with alcohol are prohibited in Greek or program houses; registered events with alcohol may occur only in approved campus spaces, for those 21+, with required security and safety measures. The university emphasized prevention efforts, increased reporting, bystander training availability, and resources for reporting/support.

The university framed the sanctions as accountability for organizations that create unsafe environments, while noting not all members were individually culpable.

Comedian Bill Cosby was the subject of false death rumors that trended on social media Monday, with "Bill Cosby died" topping Twitter and related searches high on Google Trends. The 73-year-old responded around 4 p.m. on his Twitter account, saying he was "rebuttalling rumors about my demise." This was not the first time — in February he also tweeted to deny similar reports, joking about using "rebuttal" as a verb and asserting, "I don't care, because I'm alive!"

Heavy fighting erupted in Juba, South Sudan in early July 2016 during a meeting of President Salva Kiir and First Vice‑President Riek Machar, prompting fears the country is sliding back into full-scale war. Clashes between forces loyal to Kiir and those backing Machar involved heavy gunfire, mortars and grenades, hit UN compounds and humanitarian facilities, and forced tens of thousands to flee. Estimates of casualties vary but run into the hundreds; some reports cite about 272 dead. Roughly 30,000 people were newly displaced in Juba and many more were already sheltering in UN “Protection of Civilian” sites.

Humanitarian responders describe dire needs and huge operational challenges. Aid organizations such as World Vision and the International Medical Corps face overwhelming demand for food, clean water, emergency medical care and trauma and sexual assault supplies; a maternity ward inside a Protection of Civilians site was shelled and workers were injured. The UN’s humanitarian coordinator warned that South Sudan’s crisis predated the Juba fighting—millions already faced acute food insecurity and one in five people were displaced—and appealed for unimpeded access and far more donor funding (the 2016 response plan was only about 40% funded at the time).

The immediate trigger for the violence is disputed. South Sudan’s embassy alleged a false Facebook post from an SPLA‑IO spokesman claiming Machar had been detained provoked the attack; the spokesman says his post came after fighting began and was intended to warn supporters. Political analysts and local figures point to deeper issues: weak control of forces by both Kiir and Machar, the outsized influence of SPLA chief of general staff Paul Malong and his loyalist militias (Mathiang Anyoor), ethnic divisions within the army, and failures to implement the 2015 peace agreement (notably demobilization and reintegration of combatants).

The international community condemned the violence, urged restraint, and discussed peacekeeping measures and targeted sanctions; several countries began evacuating nationals. Observers warn that unless command-and-control is restored, key peace‑implementation steps are accelerated, and donors fund a sustained humanitarian response, South Sudan risks renewed, widespread conflict with catastrophic humanitarian consequences. Despite the bleak situation, aid workers on the ground report glimmers of hope in displaced children and communities and stress the need for continued assistance and long‑term reconciliation.

Early on Feb. 21, 2013 a dispute that began at a Strip hotel escalated into deadly gunfire and a multi-vehicle crash on Las Vegas Boulevard at Flamingo Road. Police say occupants of a black Range Rover Sport with tinted windows, custom black rims and paper dealer plates pursued a gray Maserati. At a traffic light someone in the Range Rover opened fire, striking the Maserati. The Maserati then ran a red light and crashed into a taxi, which erupted in flames.

Three people died: the Maserati driver, later identified as 27-year-old Kenneth Wayne Cherry Jr., and the taxi driver, Michael Boldon, along with a taxi passenger. The Maserati’s passenger was shot and taken to University Medical Center; several other people (reports say at least six) were injured. Six vehicles were involved in the resulting crash. Witnesses, traffic and hotel surveillance and traffic-camera footage are part of the investigation; video will not be released publicly. Authorities described the Range Rover occupants as armed and dangerous and alerted law enforcement in neighboring states while canvassing Strip resorts for leads. By evening investigators had interviewed the Maserati passenger and continued collecting evidence; the intersection was reopened after CSI work.

Officials emphasized the incident was isolated and stressed visitor safety, noting a recent uptick in violent incidents on the Strip but that suspects have been identified or arrested in other cases. The shooting recalled past high-profile drive-by violence in the area; investigators were still piecing together the motive and exact sequence of events.

Summary — Is Guinness vegan?

- Background: Historically, Guinness brewed in Dublin used isinglass (a fish-bladder fining agent) to help clarify beer. Because traces may remain, Guinness traditionally was not considered vegetarian/vegan when produced in Ireland. Messaging from the company and different regional brewers over the years was inconsistent, causing confusion about which specific products/markets were isinglass-free.

- Change in process: Guinness invested in a new filtration system at St. James’s Gate to eliminate isinglass. Company communications from 2016–2018 indicate that this new state‑of‑the‑art filtration has removed isinglass from beers produced at St. James’s Gate and that draught, bottle and can formats of several core products (including Guinness Draught, Guinness Original, Guinness Extra Stout, Guinness Foreign Extra Stout and Hop House 13) are now suitable for vegans. The company’s FAQ and direct emails (January 2018) confirm these products are brewed without isinglass.

- Regional exceptions and prior variations: Earlier emails and statements show variability by region and product:
  - Guinness brewed in Australia (and some Canadian/Canadian‑brewed Extra Stout batches) historically did not use isinglass and were labeled vegan/vegetarian in those markets.
  - Up through mid‑2017 some bottle/can formats were still being transitioned; keg draught became vegan earlier in some markets.
  - Guinness advised checking lot codes (e.g., any L‑code after L7300 — Oct 27, 2017 — indicates the new process) if consumers worry about older stock. They also note optimal taste is 9–12 months and recommend not consuming products past best‑by dates.

- Takeaway: After installing the new filtration system, Guinness has moved away from isinglass at its main Dublin brewery and now markets many of its flagship beers as suitable for vegans. Confusion in the past stemmed from different production sites and changing processes, but as of early 2018 Guinness states that draught, bottled and canned versions produced at St. James’s Gate are isinglass‑free.

The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America named Louisville, Kentucky the worst U.S. city for spring allergies in 2014, moving up from No. 5 the previous year. Louisville’s river basin, mild climate and precipitation trap and encourage pollen growth; local allergists report a roughly 20% rise in visits over three years. NBC medical commentator Dr. Nancy Snyderman notes a longer growing season and vegetation in new areas likely extend and increase pollen exposure for the roughly 40 million Americans with seasonal allergies. Typical symptoms include coughing, sneezing, itchy eyes, runny nose and sore throat; avoiding exposure (for example, exercising early when morning dew suppresses pollen) can help most sufferers. The AAFA’s top 10 spring-allergy cities—all in the South—are: 1) Louisville, KY; 2) Memphis, TN; 3) Baton Rouge, LA; 4) Oklahoma City; 5) Jackson, MS; 6) Chattanooga, TN; 7) Dallas; 8) Richmond, VA; 9) Birmingham, AL; 10) McAllen, TX. The piece also briefly outlines allergy types and notes people with allergies can lead healthy lives with proper management.

San Francisco is experiencing an epidemic of vehicle "smash-and-grab" thefts — in 2017 there were about 31,122 reported car break-ins and fewer than 2% resulted in arrests. Inside Edition sent investigative reporter Lisa Guerrero to Alamo Square to demonstrate the problem by parking a bait car containing a Michael Kors purse and a $250 speaker rigged with GPS trackers and hidden cameras. Within seconds a man and woman smashed a window, grabbed the purse and speaker, and fled. Guerrero tracked them via the GPS to public transit, confronted the suspects on camera, recovered the purse from a trash can and watched surveillance footage of the initial theft. While she was interviewing a neighbor who had also recorded the theft, thieves broke into Inside Edition’s crew vehicle and stole thousands of dollars of equipment. The segment highlights how quick and brazen these break-ins are — often lasting only about 20 seconds — and underscores the scale of the problem across the Bay Area.

Authorities probing Wednesday’s murder-suicide at UCLA discovered a “kill list” in the Minnesota apartment of the shooter that led them to the body of his estranged wife.

What happened
- On Wednesday at UCLA, former Ph.D. student Mainak Sarkar, 38, shot and killed mechanical engineering professor William S. (Bill) Klug, 39, in a campus office, then fatally shot himself.
- Los Angeles police found a note at the UCLA scene asking that Sarkar’s cat be checked on; that led investigators to his St. Paul residence.
- In Sarkar’s apartment they found a “kill list” naming two UCLA professors and a woman. The second professor was off campus and is safe.
- Following that lead, Brooklyn Park, Minn., police conducted a welfare check early Thursday at a home on Pearson Parkway and found 31-year-old Ashley Hasti dead of an apparent gunshot wound. Authorities believe Hasti was killed before the UCLA shooting, though timing remains under investigation.

Key details about the people involved
- Mainak Sarkar earned a Ph.D. in mechanical engineering from UCLA in 2013. He apparently believed Professor Klug had stolen his computer code or other intellectual property; Sarkar posted a blog in March accusing Klug of stealing his work and calling him “a sick person.”
- Sarkar arrived at UCLA armed with two semi-automatic pistols and multiple rounds. LAPD Chief Charlie Beck said Sarkar was prepared to engage multiple victims and that mental-health problems appear to have been a factor.
- Ashley Hasti and Sarkar had been married in 2011 and separated about a year later. Hasti, a Minnesota native, was a University of Minnesota medical student and described by family and former professors as an excellent, well-liked student. Her motive for being on the list is unclear.
- Sarkar left a note at UCLA requesting that authorities check his cat, which prompted the search of his St. Paul apartment. A suspicious package near that apartment was rendered safe by a bomb squad.

Community response and investigation
- UCLA held a candlelight vigil for Professor Klug; his wife requested privacy to mourn.
- Police are seeking to trace Sarkar’s movements (at one point appealing for help locating a 2003 Nissan Sentra) and continue investigating motives and timing of Hasti’s death. Authorities say there were no significant prior police contacts for Sarkar aside from a 2006 traffic accident.

Former U.S. intelligence contractor Edward Snowden’s father, Lon Snowden, arrived in Moscow to visit his son after Russia granted Edward temporary asylum following his leak of extensive U.S. surveillance programs. Speaking at Sheremetyevo airport, Lon said he had had no direct contact with Edward for months but felt “extreme gratitude” that his son was safe. Russian authorities and Snowden’s lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, have kept Edward’s location secret; state media later reported the father and son did meet, though details were withheld for security.

Edward Snowden, 30, faces U.S. charges including theft of government property and unauthorized disclosure of national defense information, each carrying up to 10 years in prison. He fled to Hong Kong in June after accessing and sharing thousands of NSA documents revealing wide-ranging internet and phone surveillance; he then traveled to Moscow and remained in the airport transit zone until Russia granted asylum on August 1. The disclosures triggered international controversy, earning him praise from some as a whistleblower and condemnation from others as a traitor, and strained U.S.-Russia relations.

Kucherena said Snowden is living modestly on donations and savings, avoiding publicity under security constraints, and may seek work in Russia in IT or human rights. He has met with supporters, received an integrity-in-intelligence award from former U.S. officials, and reportedly is adapting to life in Russia (learning the language, has a girlfriend). Lon Snowden expressed doubts that his son will return to the U.S., defended his actions as exposing injustices, thanked Russia and President Putin for offering asylum, and said he hopes to explore legal options and learn more about Edward’s circumstances while in Russia.

The new head of the British Army, General Mark Carleton-Smith, has warned that Russia now poses a greater threat to the security of the UK and its allies than Islamist extremist groups such as al-Qaeda and IS. In his first interview since becoming Chief of the General Staff, he said the physical Islamist threat has diminished and that Moscow has embarked on a systematic effort to probe and exploit Western vulnerabilities—especially in non-traditional domains like cyber, space and undersea warfare. He stressed Britain and its partners must not be complacent or leave Russia’s actions uncontested.

Carleton-Smith’s remarks come amid heightened tensions over Russia’s annexation of Crimea, its role in Ukraine, alleged interference in Western elections, a series of high-profile cyber-attacks blamed on Russian actors, and the Salisbury Novichok poisonings for which Britain has blamed Russian military intelligence (GRU). Russia denies involvement in these incidents and has dismissed Western accusations as fantasy or hysteria; its embassy and senior officials publicly mocked the general’s comments. UK Defence Secretary Gavin Williamson has made similar statements earlier this year.

The document provides instructions and messages related to embedding Twitter content (a Tweet and a video) into a website. It mentions copyable embed code snippets and links to learn more. It also includes a Tamil error message indicating an issue accessing the service and asking to try again ("மீண்டும் முயற்சிக்கவும்?"), plus a note about including the original key/media when embedding. Finally, it reminds that by embedding Twitter content you agree to the Twitter Developer Agreement and Developer Policy.

Weeks before Reeva Steenkamp was killed, she sent Oscar Pistorius texts saying she was "sometimes scared" of him, the murder trial in Pretoria heard. In a January 27 message displayed in court, Steenkamp accused Pistorius of picking on her "incessantly," being "nasty" and throwing tantrums in public, and described their relationship as having a "double standard"—he would be "quick to act, cold and off-ish when you are unhappy." She complained about his jealousy and said, "I just want to be loved and to love. Maybe we cannot do that for each other."

For his part Pistorius apologized in one message, admitting he was "tired and sick" but saying that was no excuse for jealous behaviour; he also accused Steenkamp of ignoring him when she talked to another man. Other exchanged messages included pet names and a reference by Pistorius to Steenkamp smoking "weed." Police IT expert Capt. Francois Moller testified he had "jailbroken" both phones to extract SMS and WhatsApp conversations and said many normal and affectionate messages were also found. More messages are due to be revealed as the trial continues.

The court also heard from neighbour Annette Stipp, who said she awoke around 3 a.m. on Valentine’s Day to three sounds like gunshots followed immediately by a woman's terrified screams, then another set of shots and silence. Stipp told the court the bathroom lights at Pistorius's home were on from when she first heard the noise. Under cross-examination she admitted a discrepancy in her earlier police statement and could not confirm seeing a male figure in the bathroom; the defence suggested what she heard as a second volley of shots might have been the sound of a cricket bat as Pistorius forced the bathroom door.

Pistorius faces charges of premeditated murder for the shooting of his girlfriend on February 14, 2013, plus counts of illegal ammunition possession and two separate public shooting incidents; he pleads not guilty and says he shot Steenkamp by mistake, believing she was an intruder. The prosecution's case is expected to finish this week, and the trial—originally to be brief—has been extended into May.

An ArmaLite advertisement showing Michelangelo’s David holding an AR-50A1 rifle has provoked strong backlash in Italy. The image, part of the company’s “A Work of Art” campaign and originally tweeted in May 2013, depicts David replacing his sling with a large American-made rifle. Italy’s culture minister Dario Franceschini condemned the ad on Twitter, calling it offensive and illegal and saying authorities will act to have it withdrawn. Florence officials and the Accademia Gallery’s director also criticized the campaign; the city’s historical heritage superintendent Cristina Acidini has issued a legal notice demanding removal. Some commentators called the depiction an assault on the sculpture’s dignity, while others argued that iconic artworks are fair game for playful reinterpretation. ArmaLite has used similar provocative imagery elsewhere in the campaign.

North Korea invited foreign journalists and experts to its Sohae (Tongchang-ri) Satellite Launching Station as it prepared to launch an Unha-3 rocket between April 12–16 to mark the April 15 centennial of founder Kim Il Sung. Pyongyang insists the flight is a peaceful satellite mission to gather forestry, disaster, crop and weather data; international observers were shown the 30-meter rocket, control center and the satellite. Journalists were restricted in equipment but allowed to film; a visiting European analyst said the vehicle appeared to be a space launcher.

South Korea, the U.S., Japan and other countries view the launch as a veiled long-range ballistic missile test that would violate U.N. Security Council resolutions. Japan warned it would shoot down any falling parts, and Washington suspended a food-aid deal in response. South Korean officials reported that rocket fueling—the last prelaunch step—was imminent, typically taking two to three days, making a launch possible within days. Tensions were heightened by indications North Korea may also be preparing a nuclear test: satellite imagery showed work at the Punggye-ri test site consistent with final preparations for an underground blast.

A "Blue Moon" is the informal name given to an extra full moon in a year; in popular modern usage it refers to the second full moon occurring within a single calendar month. Because the average lunar (synodic) month is about 29.53 days, most months have one full moon, but the extra half-days accumulate and occasionally produce 13 full moons in a year. In 2015 those dates included full moons on July 2 and July 31, making the latter a Blue Moon under the now-common definition that originated from a 1946 Sky & Telescope article (earlier definitions identified a Blue Moon as the third full moon in a four-full-moon season). By this calendar-based definition a Blue Moon happens about once every 2.7 years.

The full moon is technically an instant—when sun, Earth and moon align—but is visible for a night; the July 31 full moon occurred at 6:43 a.m. EDT (1043 GMT). Despite the name, a Blue Moon normally has no unusual color (though atmospheric effects can sometimes make the moon appear bluish). The article was provided to Space.com by Simulation Curriculum and invited readers to submit photos.

Fifty-seven people (35 passengers and 22 crew) aboard the Russian-operated, ice-strengthened research cruise ship MV Akademik Shokalskiy were trapped in pack ice off the Antarctic coast on Christmas after issuing a satellite distress call. The ship, built in 1984 and operating a privately funded “Spirit of Mawson” expedition commemorating Douglas Mawson’s centenary, became beset about 1,500 nautical miles south of Hobart, Tasmania, after southeasterly winds pushed ice into its path and blocked its route to open water. Passengers and crew reported no immediate danger, adequate provisions, and high morale; expedition leader Chris Turney and others posted updates saying all were well and celebrating Christmas aboard. Australian Maritime Safety Authority officials said the location is remote and normal aircraft or rescue vessels cannot reach it quickly; three ice-capable ships—the Chinese Xue Long (Snow Dragon), the French Astrolabe and the Australian Aurora Australis—were tasked to assist but were at least two days’ sailing away, making the operation complex and lengthy. The voyage had been conducting scientific work (marine mammal, ornithology, glaciology, oceanography and geology) around Mawson’s Hut and nearby islands before encountering heavy ice.

Inorganic (metallic) mercury is used illegally in some skin-lightening, anti-aging, acne and antiseptic creams because it inhibits melanin and lightens skin. However, mercury is toxic, banned in cosmetics, and harmful to users, their families, and the environment.

Key facts:
- Absorption and exposure: Mercury in creams is absorbed through the skin; absorption varies by compound, formulation and amount used. Repeated use leads to accumulation because inorganic mercury is excreted slowly (half-life ~1–2 months). Urine testing shows elevated mercury in users. Children can be exposed by contact with users or contaminated household items; some creams have been applied directly to children.
- Health risks: Use has been linked to kidney damage and impaired renal function, various skin injuries (rashes, uneven pigmentation), and possible central nervous system injury with prolonged exposure. Reported symptoms include metallic taste, excessive salivation, mouth sores, nausea, tremors, irritability, memory/vision/hearing problems, depression, numbness/tingling, difficulty concentrating, insomnia, headaches, weight loss, fatigue; infants and young children are especially vulnerable.
- Prevalence and enforcement: Studies (e.g., from Norway and the U.S. FDA) and public-health alerts (including California) have found numerous illegal products containing mercury—often imported, unlabeled or mislabeled, sold through ethnic shops, online or brought in personally. Analyses have found some creams with mercury levels far above legal limits (e.g., up to 200,000 times California’s limit). Because these products are illegal and unlabeled, mercury-related illness is likely underdiagnosed.
- Regulatory and public-health response: Mercury is generally banned in cosmetics; FDA and state health agencies issue import alerts, seize products and can take enforcement action. Consumers should avoid creams without proper English labeling or ingredient lists and stop using products listing mercury or related compounds (mercurous chloride, calomel, mercuric, mercurio). Sellers can face seizure, injunctions or prosecution.
- What to do: Stop using suspected products, wash skin and contaminated items thoroughly, seek medical advice or contact poison control (1-800-222-1222 in the U.S.), and preserve the product (don’t discard) for possible testing; follow local hazardous-waste guidance for disposal.

Illustrative cases: California reported at least 60 mercury-poisoning cases over four years linked to imported or homemade creams, including children hospitalized after household exposure.

Bottom line: Do not use unlabeled or imported skin-lightening/anti-aging creams that may contain mercury. Mercury in cosmetics poses serious health risks to users and household contacts and should be reported to health authorities.

Rick Perry, Texas’ longest-serving governor, announced July 8, 2013 that he will not seek reelection in 2014, ending a 13-year run that began when he succeeded George W. Bush in 2000. Speaking at a Caterpillar dealership in San Antonio, Perry emphasized his record on jobs, the economy and states’ rights, said he will spend the next 18 months continuing to lead the state, and that he will “pray and reflect” before deciding his future. He declined to make any firm commitments about 2016 but called a presidential bid “certainly…an option.”

Perry’s decision clears the path for Texas Attorney General Greg Abbott to pursue the Republican nomination; Democrats may coalesce around figures such as state Sen. Wendy Davis, who led a high-profile filibuster against proposed abortion restrictions. The announcement came amid ongoing political fights in the Texas Capitol over abortion legislation.

The report recalled Perry’s political arc: elected to the Texas House in 1984, switching to the GOP in 1989, rising to agricultural commissioner, lieutenant governor and then governor, and winning full terms in 2002, 2006 and 2010. It also noted high-profile controversies that marred his 2012 presidential campaign—most famously his debate “oops” moment when he couldn’t recall a federal department he’d vowed to eliminate—and other headline-making episodes from his tenure. Perry leaves office with a strong conservative record and a substantial donor network, and he retains the option of seeking higher office in the future.

This document combines metadata about a large web crawl from March–December 2011 and a collection of news/opinion excerpts about Mitt Romney’s defense of “Romneycare” compared with Obamacare.

Crawl dataset (March–December 2011)
- A web-wide crawl ran from March 9 to December 23, 2011 using Heritrix (3.1.1-SNAPSHOT) with a seed list derived from Alexa’s top 1 million sites.
- Scale and scope: 2,713,676,341 captures across 2,273,840,159 unique URLs on 29,032,069 hosts. The crawl respected robots.txt and had no broad scope limits apart from a few manually excluded sites.
- The crawl used new distributed “HQ” software by Kenji Nagahashi and was somewhat experimental. Operational issues occurred: large URL queues sometimes prevented crawling embedded/linked resources; repeated crawls of some Argentine government sites skew country-level results.
- The archive team has since changed its wide-crawl methods but released this dataset “warts and all” for research; access requests can be made to info@archive.org and will be considered case-by-case.

Political commentary on Romneycare vs. Obamacare
- Multiple commentators criticized Mitt Romney’s public defense of his Massachusetts health-care plan (Romneycare) and its similarity to the national Affordable Care Act (Obamacare).
- Critics argue Romney more effectively articulated the rationale for an individual mandate than President Obama, endorsing mandates to address “free-rider” issues and asserting Romneycare’s broader applicability to other states.
- Opponents (including conservative pundits and Rick Santorum) said Romney’s defense deepened conservative distrust: they see individual mandates as an infringement on freedom and argue Romneycare increased costs and did not improve Massachusetts outcomes.
- Some commentators noted Romney’s inconsistent positioning—claiming Romneycare was a state-specific solution while elsewhere suggesting its features could apply nationally—and questioned his political judgment and alignment with the Republican primary electorate.
- Observations included Romney’s praise for aspects of foreign systems (notably Switzerland), awkward small-room speech optics, and concerns that his defense made him sound more like a technocrat than a conservative.

Overall, the document juxtaposes technical information about a large, imperfect web crawl dataset made available for research with a set of media reactions to Romney’s public defense of his health-care policies, emphasizing both the archive’s experimental dataset limitations and the political controversy surrounding the individual mandate.

Online ticket sites crashed Monday as fans rushed to buy presale tickets for Star Wars: The Force Awakens after tickets unexpectedly went on sale hours early. Users reported Fandango showing a “site maintenance” message and MovieTickets displaying server errors; IMAX pages blamed heavy traffic and directed customers to other vendors. The outage coincided with the release of the third trailer — premiered during ESPN’s Monday Night Football halftime — which highlights new characters (Poe, Finn, Rey) and returning favorites (Han, Leia, Chewbacca), teases Kylo Ren’s connection to Darth Vader, and keeps Luke Skywalker’s role mysterious. The film, directed by J.J. Abrams and starring Oscar Isaac, Daisy Ridley and John Boyega, opens December 18, 2015.

Mike Evans, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers wide receiver who signed a five-year, $82 million extension in March and pledged to "help a lot of people," donated $11,000 to the family of Gregory Hill Jr. on Saturday. Evans found the family’s GoFundMe after asking how he could help; his contribution helped push the campaign close to $100,000.

Gregory Hill was shot and killed by a St. Lucie County deputy in January 2014 after officers responded to a loud-music complaint. Officers fired through Hill’s garage door as it was opening; Hill was hit three times and later found to have an unloaded 9mm in his back pocket and a blood-alcohol level near 0.40. Hill’s mother sued the sheriff’s office and a trial was held in May. A federal jury found Hill 99% responsible for the incident and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office 1% liable, awarding $4 in damages ($1 each to his three children and $1 for funeral expenses). Because of the 1% apportionment, the sheriff’s office’s share amounted to four cents. The family created a GoFundMe to cover their children’s needs, repair the home, and pursue appeal and related costs; attorney John Phillips will oversee the funds. Evans and his wife Ashli also run the Mike Evans Family Foundation, which offers scholarships and support for victims of domestic violence.

Nintendo warned of a surprise full-year net loss after the Wii U failed to meet expectations, prompting President Satoru Iwata to say the company is rethinking its business model. Nintendo cut its Wii U hardware sales forecast for the year to March 31 from 9 million to 2.8 million units and halved game-sales forecasts; 3DS hardware and software forecasts were also reduced. The company now expects an operating loss of ¥35 billion and a net loss of ¥25 billion, versus earlier projected profits, and trimmed its dividend to ¥100 from ¥260.

Poor Wii U demand has been blamed on delayed titles, loss of casual players to smartphones and tablets, and core gamers favoring Sony’s PS4 and Microsoft’s Xbox One. Nintendo has resisted putting its key franchises (Mario, Zelda, Pokémon, etc.) on mobile devices, limiting its ability to tap the fast-growing mobile-games market. Iwata said Nintendo is studying how smart devices could help grow its business but cautioned that it’s not as simple as porting characters to phones.

The profit downgrade and bleak hardware outlook hit the stock sharply (ADR fell 17% in New York), increased pressure on management, and raises questions about Nintendo’s strategy in an industry shifting toward mobile and new consoles. Iwata apologized to shareholders, ruled out an immediate management shake-up, and said any announcement on pay cuts will come with third-quarter results. Nintendo will use cash reserves to cover losses and revised its currency assumptions to reflect a weaker-yen environment.

Zynga has hired Don Mattrick, formerly president of Microsoft’s Interactive Entertainment Business (Xbox), as its new CEO, replacing founder Mark Pincus in the top operating role. Mattrick, 49, will start next Monday, join Zynga’s board and the company’s new executive committee. Pincus will remain chairman and take the title chief product officer so he can focus on game development; he retains 61% of voting control and supported the hire.

The move responds to Zynga’s post-IPO struggles: weak mobile performance, declining Facebook/web engagement, a roughly 70% stock drop since late 2011, recent layoffs and office closures. The board pushed for a veteran manager to scale the company; Pincus framed the change as a deliberate step to revive Zynga and called Mattrick the right leader.

Mattrick brings a long track record in games—founding Distinctive Software, 15 years at Electronic Arts, and overseeing major Xbox growth (Xbox 360 installed base and Xbox Live expansion). Critics note his limited mobile-games experience, the arena where Zynga most needs hits. His departure from Microsoft comes amid internal restructuring at Microsoft and followed some high-profile Xbox One controversies, though those are not believed to be the primary reason for his move.

Investors reacted positively, with Zynga shares rising about 9% on the news. Observers say the hire follows a common pattern of bringing experienced executives into founder-led tech companies to manage growth; whether Mattrick can deliver mobile hits and full operational independence under Pincus’s voting control remains an open question.

Swiss scientists using Rosetta’s ROSINA instrument have analyzed the gases in the coma of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko and described what the comet would “smell” like. Even at ~400 million km from the Sun, ROSINA’s mass spectrometers have detected a surprisingly rich mix of molecules beyond the expected CO and CO2. Confirmed species include water, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, ammonia, methane, methanol, formaldehyde, hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen cyanide, sulfur dioxide and carbon disulfide.

Project lead Kathrin Altwegg summarized the detected mix as odors of rotten eggs (H2S), horse-stable ammonia, pungent formaldehyde, bitter-almond hydrogen cyanide, a whiff of alcohol (methanol), vinegar-like SO2 and a sweet-scented carbon disulfide—though the overall gas density is very low and the coma remains dominated by water and carbon dioxide. Monitoring how this composition changes as 67P heats toward perihelion will help determine the comet’s makeup, compare Kuiper-belt and Oort-cloud comets, and inform models of the solar nebula and the origins of the Solar System.

The findings come as Rosetta prepares to deploy the Philae lander to 67P on Nov. 12; Rosetta will continue orbital observations for over a year while accompanying the comet around the Sun.

Jared Fogle, the former Subway pitchman convicted on child pornography and related charges, has appealed his 15-year, 8-month federal prison sentence, arguing the judge improperly based the punishment in part on his fantasies and uncharged conduct. Under Fogle’s plea deal prosecutors had asked for about 12½ years (and Fogle agreed not to seek less than five), but U.S. District Judge Tanya Walton Pratt exceeded that recommendation in November. Fogle’s lawyers contend the judge relied on statements about his “obsession” with child pornography, fantasies of sex with minors and discussions with third parties—none of which, they say, amounted to criminal acts—and that punishing him for thoughts or uncharged allegations violates plea-bargain principles and legal limits on sentencing. The appeal asks the Seventh Circuit to vacate the sentence and order a resentencing focused on Fogle’s admitted actions. Background: investigators seized computers and DVDs after a July raid; Fogle admitted paying for sex with 16- and 17-year-olds, possessing child pornography he received from Russell Taylor, and paid $1.4 million total in restitution to victims. Taylor received a 27-year sentence for extensive child-exploitation offenses. Subway severed ties with Fogle amid the case.

This review of Saturday Night Live’s recent episode, hosted by Steve Carell with musical guest Ella Mai, finds the show largely listless and uneven despite a few bright moments. Carell’s opening monologue riffed on a rumored reboot of The Office—complete with surprise appearances by former castmates—but his performance and much of the episode felt uncommitted, with many sketches suffering from weak premises, slack pacing, and unfinished endings.

Highlights and low points:
- Best bits: a dark, physical-space-station sketch featuring floating, frozen monkey props and a dead cosmonaut (Kate McKinnon) that leaned into transgressive, risky comedy; a surreal Thanksgiving/“kern” space sketch that spectacularly fell apart but showed ambition; and a filmed Amazon parody with Carell as Jeff Bezos that landed several pointed digs at Donald Trump.
- Strong supporting turns: Kenan Thompson’s LaVar Ball, Heidi Gardner’s quietly excellent performance in an RV-marriage sketch, and Aidy Bryant’s reactions in a “Beauty School Drop Out”–style number.
- Weaknesses: many sketches were thin, over-explained, or ended abruptly (notably a clueless-dad Disney sketch and a sputtering “GP Yass” GPS commercial). Carell often matched the material’s dullness instead of elevating it. Weekend Update stayed conservative and safe, choosing low-hanging political targets (including a Bigfoot-porn joke about a newly elected Republican) over sharper satire.
- Recurring bits: Kate McKinnon’s Laura Ingraham cold open skewered Fox News with several absurdist “feel facts” and parody ads; Cecily Strong returned as Jeanine Pirro; the Bezos sketch doubled as a Trump takedown but was critiqued for ignoring Amazon/Bezos’ own problematic power dynamics.

Overall verdict: An ambitious but sloppy episode that produced occasional moments of genuine comic risk and visual invention, yet mostly stalled on unimaginative writing and flat execution. SNL goes on hiatus next week, returning December 1 with Claire Foy.

Newly filed court papers detail that Paul Manafort, President Trump’s former campaign manager, has been held in near-total solitary confinement at the Northern Neck Regional Jail in Virginia since June 15, locked in his cell roughly 23 hours a day aside from attorney visits. A judge revoked his bail after allegations he tried to influence witness testimony while under house arrest; Manafort faces charges including bank fraud and money laundering and has two trials pending, the first starting July 25.

Manafort’s lawyers, led by Kevin Downing, say the restrictive conditions and the jail’s roughly two-hour distance from his legal team are preventing adequate trial preparation and ask that he be released. They also argue the witness-tampering allegations did not involve threats of physical violence. Prosecutors from Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s office oppose release, contending clandestine witness tampering is as harmful to the justice system as overt violence and noting such restrictions are common for defendants detained pending trial. Critics including John Dowd have called the confinement harsh and a violation of civil liberties.

After President Trump told a New York audience of police officers to be “rough” with suspects and joked about removing officers’ hands when they shield a detainee’s head, acting DEA Administrator Chuck Rosenberg circulated a memo rebuking the remarks. Rosenberg wrote that the president “condoned police misconduct regarding the treatment of individuals placed under arrest” and used the message to reaffirm the agency’s operating principles — including rule of law, respect and compassion, service, integrity, accountability, leadership, courage and diversity. He emphasized that DEA agents should “act honorably” to earn public trust, that law enforcement must speak out when something is wrong, and that he did not believe DEA personnel would mistreat defendants. The memo followed public distancing by other officials: law enforcement agencies said they do not tolerate roughing prisoners, White House spokeswoman Sarah Huckabee Sanders called Trump’s comment a likely joke, and Attorney General Jeff Sessions pledged to prosecute officers who abuse their authority while defending lawful use of force.

Store-bought microwave popcorn is convenient, but you can easily make it at home with popcorn kernels, a little oil, salt, and a brown paper bag or a pot/air-popper. Homemade popcorn lets you control flavors (kettle corn, herbs, low-salt options) and avoid many health concerns tied to commercial microwave popcorn.

Key health risks associated with many microwave popcorn products:
- PFOA/PFAS (perfluoroalkyls such as PFOA/PFOS): used in grease-resistant bag linings; linked in some studies to cancer, endocrine and thyroid disruption, infertility, and reduced vaccine effectiveness. Many major brands now use PFOA-free bags and regulators have moved to phase out these chemicals, but some exposure concerns remain.
- Diacetyl (2,3-butanedione) and substitutes: a buttery flavoring that, when inhaled as vapor, has been linked to severe, irreversible bronchiolitis obliterans (“popcorn lung”) in factory workers. Diacetyl is safe to eat but can be harmful when heated and inhaled; substitutes like 2,3-pentanedione may cause similar effects in animal studies. Labeling often hides these flavorings under “natural and artificial flavors.”
- Trans fats: partially hydrogenated oils appear in some microwave popcorn varieties to achieve desired texture and shelf life; trans fats raise heart disease, stroke, and diabetes risk. The FDA has moved to ban or limit artificial trans fats and many brands now offer zero–trans-fat options.
- Saturated fat: some microwave popcorn varieties contain high levels of saturated fat that can raise LDL cholesterol and increase cardiovascular risk.
- Sodium: many products are high in salt; eating a whole bag can deliver a large fraction of the recommended daily sodium limit.

Practical advice:
- Make your own popcorn (brown paper bag in microwave, covered bowl, skillet, pressure cooker, or air popper) to reduce exposure to questionable additives, control fat and salt, and customize flavors.
- If buying commercial microwave popcorn, check labels for PFOA-free packaging, low or zero trans fats, lower saturated fat and sodium, and choose brands that disclose ingredients clearly.

Overall: Homemade popcorn is simple, customizable, and generally healthier than many commercial microwave options that can contain problematic chemicals, unhealthy fats, and excess salt.

At the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation dinner, President Barack Obama delivered a pointed, energetic appeal urging African-American voters to turn out for Hillary Clinton and reject Donald Trump. He warned that, although his name won’t be on the ballot, the progress of his presidency — on issues from tolerance and democracy to criminal-justice reform and good schools — is at risk. Obama said he would view low black turnout as “a personal insult…to my legacy,” and framed the election as a choice between hope and fear.

Mixing humor and scorn, he mocked Trump’s late concession on the birther controversy and lampooned Trump’s suitability to criticize the black community (“we’re not stupid”), noting Trump’s long record opposing civil-rights and equality measures. Obama invoked the new Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture and the sacrifices of civil-rights activists to argue that voting and voter-registration efforts are moral obligations; he also condemned voter-ID laws as voter suppression and highlighted partisan priorities that put a higher fear on the ballot than gun violence (“apparently more afraid of a ballot than a bullet”).

Hillary Clinton, who received a “Trailblazer Award” that night, praised the Obamas and echoed the message that the election isn’t about trivialities like birth certificates but about who will fight for the forgotten. The speech was part of broader efforts by Barack and Michelle Obama to mobilize the coalition of minorities, young people and women who helped elect Obama to back Clinton in 2016.

Donald Trump’s for-profit real estate seminar business, Trump University (later renamed Trump Entrepreneur Initiative), is the subject of three major civil lawsuits brought by former students and the New York attorney general. Two federal class actions in California (Tarla Makaeff v. Trump University, filed 2010; Art Cohen v. Donald J. Trump, filed 2013) and a 2013 New York state suit by Attorney General Eric Schneiderman (seeking about $40 million) allege deceptive practices affecting thousands of consumers.

Key allegations and facts:
- Plaintiffs say Trump University misled students by claiming Donald Trump handpicked instructors and that attendees would get access to private financing; former employees and sworn statements contradict those claims and describe unqualified instructors and unethical sales tactics.
- The business used aggressive “upsell” tactics: free seminars funneled attendees into a $1,495 “apprenticeship” (a three-day program), then into mentorships costing $10,000+, and a top “Gold Elite” package at $35,000.
- Unsealed sales playbooks show pressure-based rebuttals and scripts pushing consumers to go into debt to enroll.
- The New York Department of Education warned the company as early as 2005 that calling itself a “university” violated state law; the name was later changed.
- Trump has denied wrongdoing, called the cases baseless and politically motivated, and said he could have settled but chose not to. In deposition he downplayed involvement in selecting instructors, and Trump University’s president similarly testified that instructors were not handpicked by Trump.
- Courts have already ruled against Trump on some points: a 2014 New York trial court found Trump University and Trump liable for operating an unlicensed school; a New York court refused to dismiss Schneiderman’s fraud case on statute-of-limitations grounds; and Trump lost a countersuit against Makaeff and was ordered to pay $800,000 in her attorneys’ fees.
- Trial timing is uncertain and may extend beyond the presidential election; one California case is set for Nov. 28, where Trump is expected to testify. Plaintiffs’ leadership changes and other developments continue (e.g., Makaeff withdrew as lead plaintiff).

Additional context: numerous former students and even instructors have reported manipulated reviews and pressured endorsements. The Better Business Bureau reports Trump University does not have an A rating and has been unrated since September.

Overall, the suits accuse Trump University of running a bait-and-switch, high-pressure sales operation that sold expensive real-estate programs under misleading claims about Trump’s direct involvement and the quality of instruction. Trump disputes the claims and has not settled; litigation is ongoing.

On Oct. 22, 2014, a gunman fatally shot Cpl. Nathan Cirillo, a 24-year-old reservist on ceremonial guard at Ottawa’s National War Memorial, then stormed the Centre Block of Parliament. Dozens of shots were fired inside Parliament; the attacker was shot and killed there by House of Commons sergeant-at-arms Kevin Vickers with assistance from RCMP. Three other people suffered minor injuries and were treated and released.

Authorities identified the shooter as Michael Zehaf-Bibeau, a Canadian born in 1982 with past criminal convictions in Quebec and British Columbia. Police initially treated the incident as an unfolding, possibly multi-assailant situation but by late evening said there was no ongoing public threat. RCMP and Ottawa police said the attack “caught [them] by surprise”; investigators continued background checks into the suspect and possible motives, with some reports saying he was a recent convert to Islam.

Prime Minister Stephen Harper called the assault “brutal and violent,” pledged that Canada “will not be intimidated,” and offered condolences to Cirillo’s family and to the family of Warrant Officer Patrice Vincent, a soldier killed two days earlier in a separate attack in Quebec. Opposition leaders condemned the attack and voiced support for government efforts. The shootings prompted lockdowns on Parliament Hill, elevated security at government sites nationwide, and international offers of support, including from U.S. President Barack Obama and NATO.

Summary:

An outbreak in Illinois of severe, unexplained bleeding has been traced to synthetic cannabinoids (sold as K2, Spice, “fake weed,” etc.) laced with a long-acting rat-poison anticoagulant, brodifacoum. Synthetic cannabinoids are human-made psychoactive chemicals sprayed on plant material or sold as liquids; they are often more potent and unpredictable than cannabis.

Timeline and toll:
- Initial cluster grew rapidly; hospitalizations involved spontaneous, severe bleeding (coughing up blood, bloody urine/stools, bleeding from eyes/ears/nose/gums).
- Early reports cited dozens of cases; by April updates the outbreak had expanded widely:
  - Reports grew from 38 to 56 and then to 153 cases across 13 counties.
  - At least four deaths (two men in their 20s, a man in his 40s, and a woman in her 30s) have been linked to the tainted product.

Cause and clinical course:
- Several hospitalized patients tested positive for brodifacoum, a “superwarfarin” anticoagulant that blocks vitamin K–dependent clotting and has an extremely long duration of action.
- Brodifacoum causes life‑threatening bleeding, shock, stroke and death if untreated. Treatment requires high‑dose vitamin K (intravenous initially, then prolonged oral therapy — sometimes many tablets daily for months) and supportive care; therapy is expensive and prolonged.

Public health response and guidance:
- Illinois health officials have warned people not to use synthetic cannabinoids, to seek immediate emergency care (do not self-transport) if severe bleeding or unexplained bruising occurs, and to inform clinicians about possible synthetic cannabinoid exposure.
- The state is working to avoid financial burdens for treatment; the Bausch Foundation donated nearly 800,000 vitamin K tablets to assist care.
- Federal charges have been filed against individuals alleged to have sold the tainted product.

Bottom line: Synthetic cannabinoids are not safe substitutes for marijuana—these products can contain highly dangerous additives. In this outbreak, contamination with a potent rat poison has caused hundreds of illnesses and multiple deaths; anyone who used these products in the past month and develops bleeding should get immediate medical attention.

Spain formally welcomed King Felipe VI after King Juan Carlos abdicated, marking a generational transition amid economic hardship and questions about the monarchy’s future. Felipe, 46, in military uniform, was proclaimed and swore to uphold the constitution before Parliament, pledging a modernized, transparent, and unifying monarchy “for new times.” He paid tribute to his father’s role in Spain’s return to democracy and thanked Queen Sofia. Crowds cheered as Felipe, Queen Letizia and their daughters appeared on the royal palace balcony; their elder daughter Leonor, 8, becomes Princess of Asturias.

The handover took effect at midnight when Juan Carlos signed the abdication law; he later removed the military sash and placed it on his son. The proclamation and related events were deliberately austere—no foreign heads of state, limited pomp and modest receptions—to reflect public sensitivity during Spain’s deep economic crisis and high unemployment. Observers say Felipe, seen as untainted by recent scandals that have damaged the royal family’s image (including Princess Cristina’s legal troubles and Juan Carlos’s controversial 2012 hunting trip), faces urgent tasks: increasing palace transparency, limiting costs to taxpayers, and helping preserve national unity amid separatist pressures in Catalonia and the Basque region. Polls show mixed public attitudes toward the monarchy, though many favor Felipe personally.

Authorities in Miami, Oklahoma, arrested 23-year-old Gregory Arthur Weiler II of Elk Grove Village, Illinois, after motel workers discovered dozens of Molotov-style bottles and other suspicious items in and near his room. Police say searches uncovered bomb-making materials, a funnel, a 5-gallon gasoline can, torn documents that when assembled contained instructions for making Molotov cocktails, a hand-drawn map, a list of 48 area churches and journal entries describing a plan to destroy church buildings over time. Weiler was charged with threatening to use an explosive or incendiary device and violating the Oklahoma Anti-Terrorism Act; he is being held without bond and is due back in court Oct. 22. Family members and acquaintances told reporters he has a long history of mental illness and substance problems; local church leaders said the community remains calm and prayed for him. Authorities say he had the means to carry out attacks but investigators continue to assess the threat.

A 220–227 pound Fukang pallasite meteorite—an eye-catching, gold-flecked slab discovered in China and prized by collectors—has become the subject of a federal ownership dispute and a possible theft investigation.

Key facts:
- Seller/believed original owner: Stephan (Stephen) Settgast of Novato/Marin County, a long‑time collector.
- Buyers: Lawrence Stifler and Mary McFadden (founders of the under‑construction Maine Mineral & Gem Museum) of Brookline, Massachusetts.
- Broker: A New York meteorite dealer, Darryl Pitt, who helped arrange the transaction.
- Preparers: Keith and Dana Jenkerson of KD Meteorites in Osawatomie, Kansas, who cleaned and restored the specimen.

Timeline and claims:
- Settgast acquired the Fukang slice in 2004. In 2014 he agreed to sell it to Stifler and McFadden for $425,000; payment was routed via the New York middleman.
- The Jenkersons spent nearly two years preparing the meteorite and valued it as high as $1 million; they also sought a larger fee for their work.
- In January (year not specified), after restoration, the meteorite was taken from the Jenkersons’ studio while they were away. Stifler and McFadden allege Settgast reclaimed the rock in what they call a theft motivated by “seller’s remorse.” The Kansas sheriff’s office suspects Settgast but is deferring a criminal determination pending resolution of civil ownership.
- Settgast sued in federal court to void the sale and retain the meteorite, asserting he never formally transferred possession and that the buyers intended to display it publicly—allegedly violating an oral sale condition. The buyers and broker counterclaimed, seeking the meteorite and calling the act a blatant theft.

Context and valuation:
- Pallasites like the Fukang are visually spectacular and highly sought by collectors; values are subjective and debated. Experts say while visually significant, Fukang‑type pallasites are not especially scientifically novel.
- Parties also dispute fees owed to the Jenkersons (they sought 5% of value vs. a smaller promised fee).

Status:
- A federal hearing was scheduled for late June (judge: U.S. District Judge Saundra Brown Armstrong). Local law enforcement is awaiting the civil decision before pursuing any criminal charges.

In short, the case centers on conflicting accounts over a multimillion‑dollar (disputed) space rock sale, disputed sale terms about public display, restoration fees, and whether the seller lawfully reclaimed the meteorite—issues now being litigated in federal court.

On Feb. 27 President Donald Trump met with leaders of historically black colleges and universities in the Oval Office. During the meeting Kellyanne Conway briefly knelt on the Oval Office couch to take a candid photo, with her heels touching the cushions. The posture struck many observers as awkward and led to a surge of jokes and memes online. Commenters warned, however, that while the moment was cringeworthy, it is trivial compared with more serious issues for which the administration should be held accountable—“shoes on the Oval Office couch” being “least of our concerns,” as one Twitter user put it. The item also notes that these social-media snapshots and pages are being archived (by efforts such as the Internet Archive) to preserve the original content and prevent link rot, so readers can see the posts as they appeared when written.

Students, performers and venues are testing a simple tool to curb smartphone distraction: a lockable neoprene pouch made by San Francisco startup Yondr. The pouch locks like a retail security tag and keeps phones inaccessible during events or classes unless owners step outside to unlock them. Teachers at Mercy High in Burlingame use them to keep students “in the moment,” and artist-driven, phone-free policies have been adopted at shows by Dave Chappelle, Alicia Keys, the Lumineers and others to prevent recording, leaks and audience distraction.

Founder Graham Dugoni created Yondr after seeing how phones interrupted live experiences; he piloted the pouches in clubs and schools and has since expanded into concerts, comedy clubs and large venues. Artists say the system lets audiences engage more fully and protects new material, while some fans object—citing memories captured on their phones, the desire to share with friends, or safety concerns about restricted access. Users who try Yondr often report initial anxiety followed by greater enjoyment and presence once the novelty wears off. Overall, the pouches are presented as a practical compromise that preserves personal possession of phones while enforcing device-free zones to improve live social interaction.

Former Nevada Assemblywoman and GOP Senate nominee Sharron Angle gave her first mainstream interview since clinching the Republican nomination, moderating some primary rhetoric while holding firm on key conservative positions.

What she softened
- Social Security: Angle backed away from earlier talk of “phasing out” the program. She now says current benefits should be protected, more funding added, and future workers offered a choice between Social Security and personal accounts.
- Violent rhetoric: She acknowledged her comment about citizens resorting to “Second Amendment remedies” if conservatives lose was too strong and revised her language to focus on defeating Harry Reid electorally.

What she did not change
- Unemployment benefits: Angle opposed extending unemployment aid in Nevada, arguing benefits discourage job-seeking and should instead be restructured to supplement lower wages once people are employed.
- Abortion: She reiterated a staunch anti-abortion stance, has previously suggested no exceptions for rape or incest (saying she believes in God’s plan), and framed abortion as an issue the government improperly entered after Roe v. Wade. She has sponsored legislation linking abortion to increased breast cancer risk.
- Social conservatism and church-state views: Angle defended bringing religious values into politics, described the separation of church and state as intended to “protect the church,” and sidestepped past comments calling the doctrine unconstitutional.

Other positions and campaign strategy
- Yucca Mountain: She suggested accepting the nuclear waste could create jobs, urging Nevada to “make lemonade out of lemons.”
- Campaign focus: Throughout the interview she attacked Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, blaming him for high unemployment, foreclosures, and deficits, and asked for a debate on these issues.

Reaction and context
- The interview marked a rare mainstream-media appearance after mostly speaking to conservative outlets. Critics, including Reid’s camp and some Republicans, have labeled her views extreme and questioned their electoral appeal; some GOP figures have expressed reservations about supporting her. Conservative radio hosts and far-right groups have embraced her positions, while advisers have urged she move toward the center for the general election.

Comedian and former Daily Show host Jon Stewart returned to late-night on Tuesday as a guest on CBS’s The Late Show with Stephen Colbert to deliver a blistering, comedic critique of President Donald Trump’s first 10 days in office. Stewart called the early Trump administration “purposeful, vindictive chaos,” and used a recurring sketch—mocking future executive orders—to lampoon Trump’s policies and persona. In the bit he pretended the president would (among other things) declare the official language of the U.S. “bull—-,” demand China send its Great Wall to replace a border barrier, and admit “I, Donald J. Trump, am exhausting,” quipping that the presidency is supposed to age the president, not the public.

The segment mixed sharp political satire with affectionate banter between Stewart and Colbert and brief homage gags to Johnny Carson and Jerry Lewis. Stewart ended on a serious note, urging “relentless stamina and vigilance and every institutional check and balance” to contain the administration’s agenda and warning that preserving the country’s institutions will require continued action. The appearance also renewed interest in Stewart’s post-Daily Show projects: he remains under an HBO production deal developing timely animated programming, though no material has yet appeared.

The article reports on campaign activity April 2016 as Republicans and Democrats crisscrossed Northeastern primary states. Donald Trump, campaigning in Waterbury and Bridgeport, Connecticut, rejected calls to tone down his brash style despite his new campaign chairman Paul Manafort telling Republican officials Trump could appear more restrained in private. Trump said being “presidential” is easy but that he needs to “rant and rave” on the stump to energize supporters, and insisted he would carry out contentious policies such as building a southern border wall. He also revived attacks on Ted Cruz’s eligibility. Ted Cruz campaigned in Pennsylvania and Indiana, calling the coming contests pivotal and arguing localities should decide on transgender bathrooms.

On the Democratic side, front‑runner Hillary Clinton campaigned in Connecticut, focusing on raising wages, early childhood education and closing the gender pay gap, and reiterated support for a higher federal minimum wage. Bernie Sanders spoke to a young crowd in Baltimore, attacking trade agreements and big banks and contrasting his positions with Clinton’s. The piece notes the high stakes for Republicans as Trump seeks the delegates to clinch the nomination while rivals aim to force a contested convention.

Marine archaeologists working at the famed Antikythera shipwreck, off the small Greek island of Antikythera, have recovered a sediment-encrusted bronze right arm from a large Roman‑era cargo vessel that sank around 1 BC. Using a bespoke underwater metal detector, the team—from the Greek Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities, Lund University and partners—has detected multiple large metal targets under and among multi‑ton boulders on the sloping wreck site. Project divers and directors say the signals indicate at least seven, and possibly up to nine, additional bronze statues remain buried there.

The 2017 season’s other finds included a patterned slab of red marble, a silver tankard, ship timbers, pottery shards, human bone and a small bronze disc about the size of a gear wheel. Preliminary x‑ray imaging suggests the disc is decorative (it bears a bull motif) rather than a toothed cog, though its size and context link it to the Antikythera mechanism (the ancient geared device earlier recovered from the wreck). The team previously recovered human skeletal remains and has extracted DNA from a skull, which has yielded sex and origin information pending publication.

The Antikythera wreck has been intermittently excavated since sponge divers discovered it in 1900 and yielded spectacular bronzes and the Antikythera mechanism. Bronze statues are rare because metal recycling in antiquity destroyed many works; intact bronzes from shipwrecks are therefore exceptionally valuable for study. Recovering the newly indicated statues will be challenging: large boulders—likely displaced onto the wreck by earthquakes centuries after the sinking—must be moved or fractured by mechanical, grout‑expansion, or shaped‑charge techniques, and any retrieved bronzes will require extensive conservation and reconstruction.

Investigators plan to return in spring to continue excavation, with hopes not only of recovering statues but also further parts of the ship’s cargo and possibly additional elements related to the Antikythera mechanism.

An online Crimson survey of more than 1,300 incoming Harvard freshmen (about 80% of the class) finds notable levels of self-reported academic dishonesty and outlines students’ academic priorities, extracurricular backgrounds and athletics.

Key findings on cheating and integrity
- 10% admitted to cheating on an exam; 17% said they cheated on a paper or take‑home; 42% admitted to cheating on homework or problem sets.
- Recruited varsity athletes reported higher rates: 20% had cheated on an exam and 26% on papers/take‑homes (vs. 9% and 16% for non‑recruits). Men reported cheating more than women.
- These rates are higher than those reported in a Crimson survey of Harvard’s Class of 2013.
- Harvard has stressed academic integrity since a large 2012 cheating scandal; administrators say they are addressing cheating through faculty actions, student presentations and a joint committee.

Academics and academic plans
- 84% of respondents said academics would be their top priority at Harvard.
- 26% plan to concentrate in economics or government (more than current shares); only 11% plan arts & humanities (below current 16%). No incoming students indicated plans to concentrate in African & African American Studies, Germanic Languages & Literatures, or South Asian Studies.
- 59% plan a secondary field and 36% a language citation; 23% plan both.
- 82% cited their own expectations as their main source of pressure; most expect to study more hours in college than in high school (largest group anticipating 20–29 hours/week).

Extracurriculars and leadership
- 84% participated in community service in high school; many were active in music, student government and academic clubs.
- Leadership was common: 27% led two clubs; 26% led one; 19% led none.
- 79% of former student-government participants believe student government can effect change (60% of non‑participants agree).

Athletics
- 69% played sports in high school; 12% are recruited to varsity squads at Harvard and another 9% plan to try as walk‑ons.
- Recruited athletes are much likelier to expect four‑year varsity participation (93% vs. 47% of intended walk‑ons).
- Concussions: 22% of incoming athletes reported at least one; most said it did not change their desire to play.
- Academic differences: recruited athletes were more likely to list BC Calculus as their highest pre‑college math (33% vs. 43% for non‑athletes at lower levels), and more recruited athletes planned to concentrate in economics (32% vs. 15% of non‑athletes); only one recruited athlete planned government.

Context and response
- The survey is part II of a four‑part Crimson series on the Class of 2017. Harvard officials noted the results align with the College’s recent efforts to curb cheating and to strengthen a culture of integrity.
