Comedian Russell Brand was arrested at LAX on September 17 after allegedly striking several paparazzi who were trying to photograph fiancée Katy Perry. According to law enforcement and reports, Brand shoved and hit photographers when one attempted an upskirt shot of Perry. A victim performed a citizen’s arrest; Brand was interviewed by airport police, booked at the LAPD Pacific Division on a misdemeanor simple battery charge, released on $20,000 bail, and has not publicly commented. Perry tweeted support, saying her fiancé would “do his job & protect me.” Legal sources note that while an attempted upskirt photo is not a legal defense to battery, prosecutors would expect strong jury sympathy for a celebrity protecting his partner. The incident caused Brand and Perry to miss their flight; Brand is based in New York while filming the Arthur remake.

Former nanny Hailey Glassman has publicly described emotional strain from her relationship with Jon Gosselin, saying she feels emotionally abused, has put her life on hold, and is exhausted by public accusations that she’s a “homewrecker.” In response, Jon told The Insider he’s grateful for Hailey’s support, regrets the pain his actions have caused her, and wants the chance to make things right with Hailey, his estranged wife Kate, and their children.

Stephanie Santoro, another former nanny and Jon’s reported ex-lover, told RadarOnline.com she fears Jon may have suicidal tendencies. Santoro said that after Jon and Hailey briefly split, Jon called her saying he planned to “end it all” and couldn’t handle the pressure of his life and relationship. Santoro hopes he’s not still in that state and noted a recent meeting with rabbi Schmuley might help. The coverage includes multiple interviews and photos documenting the couple’s public struggles.

Google has begun publishing, for the first time, aggregated figures showing how often governments requested user data or removal of content from its services between July 1 and Dec. 31, 2009. The company launched an online country map listing those requests (excluding some countries for legal or safety reasons, notably China) and said it will later report how often it hands over user data. Google’s legal team reviews each request and complies only when legally required, and it tries to notify affected users when possible.

The disclosure was positioned as a transparency measure to highlight the scale of government censorship and data demands amid criticism of Google’s own privacy practices. Privacy advocates welcomed the step as putting numbers behind anecdotal reports, though observers warned the raw counts are imperfect and hard to interpret (a single request can cover multiple URLs or accounts, and some types of requests are excluded).

Key reported figures for the six-month period: Brazil made the most user-data requests (3,663), followed by the U.S. (3,580). Brazil also led in content-removal requests (291); Germany and India ranked ahead of the U.S. on removals. Google stressed limitations in the data (omitting low-volume countries, information that could harm investigations, and YouTube copyright takedown requests).

The announcement came while Google faced criticism from international privacy commissioners (Canada, France, U.K., others) over services such as Buzz and Street View. Those regulators pressed Google to adopt more privacy-protective defaults and clearer account-deletion procedures. Google responded that it has addressed these issues publicly but offered no new commitments in its reply.

North Korea conducted another ballistic missile test on Sunday, firing a Pukguksong-2 solid-fuel medium/medium‑range missile from Pukchang that South Korea said flew about 310 miles (500 km) and reached roughly 560 km altitude before splashing into the Pacific. Pyongyang hailed the test as confirming combat readiness, said leader Kim Jong Un approved deployment and mass production, and promised more launches in response to U.S. policies. State media claimed technical successes including solid‑fuel operation, stage separation and guidance; outside experts cautioned the program still needs more tests to prove reliability, especially for re‑entry of nuclear warheads.

The launch was the second in a week (following a Hwasong‑12 test that flew farther and raised concerns about progress toward an ICBM) and the 10th this year, prompting condemnation from the United States, South Korea and Japan. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson called the testing “disappointing” and “disturbing” but said diplomatic and economic pressure—including efforts to get China to support tougher U.N. sanctions—remains Washington’s course. Seoul held security meetings and criticized the provocation; Tokyo urged cutting North Korea’s revenue sources. The U.N. Security Council agreed to meet behind closed doors to discuss stronger measures. Analysts note solid‑fuel missiles are tactically significant because they enable faster, harder‑to‑detect launches, but say longer‑range, reliable ICBM and solid‑fuel capabilities will require more time and testing.

French authorities continued hunting accomplices after a wave of attacks that left 17 victims and the three gunmen dead. Prime Minister Manuel Valls said there was “without a doubt” at least one accomplice and vowed the search would continue, noting the threat remained. France mobilized large security forces — Defense Minister Jean‑Yves Le Drian said 10,000 troops would be deployed to protect sensitive sites, while Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve assigned 4,700 officers to guard 717 Jewish schools.

Turkish officials said Hayat Boumeddiene, the common‑law wife of Amedy Coulibaly (who killed a policewoman and later four hostages at a kosher supermarket), entered Turkey from Madrid on Jan. 2 and toured Istanbul with a companion identified by French sources as Mehdi Sabri Belhoucine. Turkish intelligence reportedly tracked her by cellphone, reviewed CCTV showing the pair at Sabiha Gokcen airport, followed them to a hotel in Istanbul, then to Sanliurfa near the Syrian border, where their signals ceased and Turkish officials say she crossed into IS‑held Syria on Jan. 8. Authorities also seek a Mini Cooper registered to Boumeddiene; some reports say up to six members of the terror cell may still be at large.

The attackers’ ties to international jihadist networks were highlighted: Coulibaly pledged allegiance to ISIS in a video verified by SITE, while the Kouachi brothers claimed links to al‑Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula and had prior convictions connected to networks that sent fighters abroad. The attacks began with the Charlie Hebdo massacre, prompting massive solidarity rallies (“Je suis Charlie”) and a planned unprecedented print run for Charlie Hebdo’s next issue. Investigations continued amid intelligence cooperation between France and Turkey and ongoing searches for additional suspects.

Summary:

- A Star magazine report claiming Tom Cruise is working with lawyers to reunite with his daughter Suri and negotiating with ex-wife Katie Holmes is false. Holmes’ representative denied the story. Gossip Cop notes Star has a history of repeatedly publishing unverified reunion claims about Cruise and Suri that never materialized.

- Scarlett Johansson publicly rejected a former Scientology member Brendan Tighe’s claim that she “auditioned” to date Tom Cruise after his 2001 divorce from Nicole Kidman. Johansson called the idea demeaning and denied the accusation.

- Actress Erika Christensen discussed her Scientology upbringing on Dax Shepard’s Armchair Expert podcast. She described being raised with Scientology-influenced parenting, having taken introductory courses from about age 12, and endorsed personal responsibility and skepticism toward outside claims. Christensen said drinking is allowed in Scientology but illicit drugs are not, and she dismissed criticism of the church—specifically the documentary Going Clear—by questioning the credibility of its sources.

- Brendan Tighe, a former Scientologist who left in 2011, has spoken publicly about his time in the Sea Org and about discovering alleged internal documents (which he says suggested “auditions” to date Cruise) that led him to recount the Johansson story; his claims have been refuted by Johansson and are disputed.

Following numerous reports of hoverboards catching fire and several high-profile incidents (including explosions in a Washington state mall and at least 10 fires reported to U.S. authorities across nine states), major retailers and regulators have cracked down on the battery-powered self-balancing scooters.

- Amazon has removed many hoverboard listings in the US and UK and told sellers they must provide documentation proving compliance with safety standards (UN 38.3 for batteries, UL 1642 for batteries, and UL 60950-1 for chargers). Amazon also requested sellers indemnify Amazon against patent litigation (noting a potential claim by Razor USA). Listings for several popular brands disappeared; Razor and Jetson models remained in some markets. Amazon held seller accounts under review until required paperwork is provided.
- Other retailers acted similarly: Overstock discontinued hoverboard sales and offered refunds; Walmart halted in-store sales (while still selling some Razor models online). eBay continued to list many units and reported heavy sales before the crackdown.
- Regulators and investigators: The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission opened a formal investigation into the product line; airlines banned hoverboards from flights citing battery watt-hour limits; Britain’s trading standards found a high failure rate in imports and warned consumers to look for proper UK plugs and safety markings.
- Cause and safety issues: Many problematic units are cheap imports or knockoffs made in China with substandard battery packs and chargers. UL (an independent testing lab) does not certify whole hoverboards but can list components (batteries/chargers); some fires involved units whose battery packs lacked proper UL certification. Beyond fire risk, the CPSC noted dozens of fall-related injuries.
- Additional complications: A patent dispute (Razor’s patent acquisitions) has raised legal risk for sellers and was cited by Amazon in its seller requirements. Counterfeits and unauthorized branding further complicate consumer safety.

Advice implicit in actions and warnings: buy from reputable, authorized retailers; seek products with appropriate component safety certifications; be aware of legal restrictions on use (e.g., in the UK) and of travel restrictions (airlines).

Luca Guadagnino’s films celebrate nature’s ability to reveal and transform people, and that theme is central to his lush, patient adaptation of Andre Aciman’s novel, Call Me By Your Name. Set in the sun-drenched, sensory-rich countryside of northern Italy in the summer of 1983, the film traces a quietly devastating first love between 17-year-old Elio (Timothée Chalamet) and Oliver (Armie Hammer), a charismatic American doctoral intern staying with Elio’s family.

Guadagnino lingers on place and mood—peaches, warm breezes, tree-lined roads and a chic pool—making the environment feel like a character that encourages risk and self-reckoning. Chalamet and Hammer share electric chemistry as their initially guarded, competitive rapport slowly becomes intimate. Writer James Ivory’s faithful, nuanced screenplay paces their emotional arc so that when they finally confess feelings—well into the film—the payoff is earned and deeply affecting.

Visually and sonically, the film is immersive: Sayombhu Mukdeeprom’s 35mm cinematography gives tactile, sensory detail without becoming fussy, while a carefully chosen soundtrack (from John Adams to Sufjan Stevens and the Psychedelic Furs) heightens moments of joy and melancholy. Guadagnino uses long takes and silence to underscore the impermanence of the affair, making the sense that it cannot last one of the story’s most resonant notes. A heartfelt monologue from Elio’s father (Michael Stuhlbarg) provides emotional closure and wisdom.

Overall, Call Me By Your Name is a richly rendered, emotionally precise film about desire, self-discovery and loss—visually sumptuous, sensitively acted (notably Chalamet’s multilingual, complex Elio), and, according to the reviewer, the year’s best movie.

Toughie, the last known Rabbs' fringe-limbed tree frog (Ecnomiohyla rabborum), has died at the Atlanta Botanical Garden, marking the extinction of his species. Collected during a 2005 rescue in central Panama as the chytrid fungus devastated amphibian populations, Toughie was at least 12 years old and became a widely recognized symbol of the extinction crisis. His species was formally described in 2008 after he was already in captivity.

Toughie drew public attention—he was named by Mark Mandica’s young son, photographed for Joel Sartore’s Photo Ark project, and even projected onto St. Peter’s Basilica—helping personalize the broader loss of biodiversity. In 2014 Mandica recorded the frog’s call, the only known recording. Scientists say the species’ tiny range and the deadly impact of chytrid likely eliminated any wild survivors. Toughie’s death highlights how many species are vanishing, often before people even know they exist, and underscores concerns about cascading effects on ecosystems and the urgency of conservation.

Cosmetic foot surgery to accommodate fashionable shoes — often called “Cinderella” procedures — is on the rise and drawing heated debate among podiatrists and orthopedists. Many surgeons report increasing numbers of women seeking elective operations (toe shortening/lengthening, bunion correction, hammertoe repair, fat-pad augmentation via collagen or other injections) so they can wear high heels or designer footwear. Some practitioners and clinics market these services aggressively with cosmetic names and media promotion; doctors report practices expanding, and some patients pay cash or receive insurer coverage when pain is claimed.

Critics — including leaders of the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society and other foot specialists — warn these medically unnecessary procedures are risky and can produce lasting disability. The foot’s complex anatomy makes even small changes potentially destabilizing; complications cited include nerve damage, chronic pain and loss of function. Professional groups are preparing statements discouraging elective cosmetic foot surgery and studying how common the procedures are. Many physicians argue conservative measures (changing shoes, wider lasts, orthotics, exercises) should be tried first.

Proponents and some patients defend the surgeries as legitimate quality-of-life or career choices: many women feel shoes are essential to appearance and confidence, and some report relief of gait or back problems after correction. Clinics offer a range of interventions — from toe surgery to injections or PRP — and some surgeons brand and promote aesthetic procedures with appealing names. The debate centers on balancing personal aesthetic desires and social pressures with medical ethics and long-term foot health.

Zig Ziglar, the iconic motivational speaker and self-help author known for his homespun, relentlessly upbeat advice, died Nov. 28 in Plano, Texas, at age 86 after suffering pneumonia. Born Hilary Hinton Ziglar on Nov. 6, 1926, in Coffee County, Alabama, and raised in Yazoo City, Mississippi, he served in the Navy after World War II, worked in sales, and began speaking at churches and civic groups. He launched Zigmanship (now Ziglar Inc.) in the late 1960s after moving to Dallas and made a fulltime speaking career in his 40s.

Ziglar built a vast following through his “Success Rallies,” seminars such as “Born to Win,” more than 30 books (including the best-seller See You at the Top, later retitled Biscuits, Fleas and Pump Handles), audiotapes and corporate events for companies like IBM and J.C. Penney. His message mixed goal-setting, positive thinking, Christian faith and memorable one-liners (“You can get everything in life you want if you will just help other people get what they want,” “Failure is an event, not a person,” “money’s not the most important thing in life, but it’s reasonably close to oxygen”), and he remained a popular draw into the 2000s, sometimes commanding large fees though he also waived them.

Devoutly religious after a 1972 conversion, Ziglar incorporated faith into many books (Confessions of a Happy Christian; Confessions of a Grieving Christian, written after his eldest daughter Suzan’s death in 1995) and daily routines. He was known for a buoyant persona—an “opportunity clock” morning ritual, clipping inspirational newspaper stories, and an indefatigable optimism—and for mentoring through Ziglar Inc., which continues to promote the “Ziglar Way.”

He kept a busy touring schedule until retiring in 2010 and continued writing after a 2007 fall that caused a brain injury (he co-wrote Embrace the Struggle). Survivors include his wife Jean (they were married more than 66 years), three children (including son Tom Ziglar, CEO of Ziglar Inc., and author Julie Ziglar Norman), seven grandchildren, 12 great-grandchildren and a great-great-grandson. A memorial service was planned at Prestonwood Baptist Church.

All Nashua public schools were closed Monday after officials received a detailed threat of violence aimed at both city high schools. Superintendent Mark Conrad and Nashua police said the threat — reportedly specific to Monday and received by a school administrator via email — was concerning enough that they could not rule out credibility, so they closed all district schools out of caution and notified parents with automated calls. The FBI, State Police, the state Homeland Security and Emergency Management office, and a state bomb squad assisted local authorities in the ongoing investigation. More than 11,400 students, teachers and staff across 17 public schools (about 12,000 students reported in some accounts) were affected; some private parochial schools also closed. Officials said schools were expected to reopen Tuesday but stressed they would continue working with state and federal partners to determine the threat’s credibility and keep the community safe. Parents expressed fear and frustration over the disruption and uncertainty.

Several hundred — later reports up to about 2,000 — Pacific walrus hauled out on a narrow barrier island near Point Lay on Alaska’s Chukchi Sea coast in the first week of August, the earliest recorded haulout there since the animals began coming ashore in 2007. Federal and local officials link the early arrival to unusually rapid summer sea-ice retreat: ice this year has moved beyond the continental shelf earlier than in past years, forcing walrus that normally rest on sea ice between foraging dives to come to shore. Large haulouts have become common when ice retreats (as many as tens of thousands have gathered in previous years), raising risks from overcrowding and fatal stampedes if animals are disturbed by people, boats, or aircraft. Point Lay leaders and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service are urging people to stay away; the village lacks infrastructure for tourists. The agency is also weighing whether to list the Pacific walrus under the Endangered Species Act amid concerns that long-term sea-ice loss threatens the population. (Correction: spokesperson Andrea Medeiros’ name was previously misspelled.)

Chelsea Manning, the transgender Army private serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents to WikiLeaks, was found guilty of four disciplinary infractions at the military prison in Fort Leavenworth after a closed, four-hour board hearing. Manning tweeted that the board imposed 21 days of restrictions on recreational activities — no gym, library access or outdoor time. Possible harsher penalties, including indefinite solitary confinement, were reportedly avoided.

Charges included disrespect, disorderly conduct and “medicine misuse” after a cell search found an expired tube of toothpaste. Prison staff also confiscated reading material and magazines from her cell, including I Am Malala, the novel A Safe Girl to Love, Out magazine, the Caitlyn Jenner cover of Vanity Fair, and a Cosmopolitan containing an interview with Manning. Her lawyers say some confiscated items also related to trans rights and government transparency.

ACLU attorney Chase Strangio criticized that Manning faced the board without counsel and warned the infractions will follow her through parole and clemency processes, potentially extending her time in more restrictive custody. A petition with over 100,000 signatures was delivered to Congress asking that the charges be dropped, and supporters say public scrutiny helped prevent solitary confinement. Military officials did not immediately comment.

Tropical Storm Harvey forced widespread shutdowns across the U.S. Gulf Coast energy system, knocking about a quarter of U.S. refining capacity offline and disrupting major fuel pipelines, spurring supply and price pressures nationwide.

Key impacts
- Motiva’s Port Arthur, Texas refinery (603,000 bpd, the nation’s largest) was shut by flooding; assessment and repairs could take up to two weeks or longer depending on receding floodwaters. Many other Gulf refineries were closed or operating at reduced rates.
- Colonial Pipeline, the largest U.S. refined-product system, suspended key segments after refinery outages reduced supply. Lines from Houston remained down; Colonial estimated service from Houston could resume by Sunday pending inspections and startup. Line 1 (gasoline) supplies roughly 40% of the South; Line 2 carries diesel and jet fuel.
- Explorer and other regional pipelines and terminals also were disrupted, causing supply tightness for some East Coast and Midwest markets.

Government and market responses
- The Department of Energy announced a 500,000-barrel emergency draw from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to supply the Phillips 66 Lake Charles refinery and help alleviate short-term supply strain; officials said further assistance could follow.
- Markets reacted sharply: U.S. gasoline futures and regional wholesale margins surged, retail averages rose (AAA reported nationwide averages up about 10–11 cents week-over-week), and analysts warned prices could jump further (estimates as high as ~35 cents/gal) if outages persist.
- International flows shifted as traders sought gasoline/diesel from Europe and Asia to fill gaps, but logistics and transit time limit the immediacy of that relief.

Outlook
- Recovery timing is uncertain; historic flooding and access issues mean some capacity could remain offline for an extended period (analysts warned portions may stay shut for months). The situation threatens localized shortages ahead of the Labor Day holiday and has already pushed gasoline prices higher nationwide.

Former Minnesota Vikings punter Chris Kluwe recounts events from the 2012 season through his April 2013 release, arguing his outspoken support for same-sex marriage led to his dismissal. He describes being cleared by the Vikings’ legal department in summer 2012 to speak as a private citizen, then writing a viral letter in September defending equality. After that, head coach Leslie Frazier privately told him to stop speaking about the issue; team owner Zygi Wilf privately expressed support. Special-teams coach Mike Priefer repeatedly used homophobic language around Kluwe, escalated to a comment about “rounding up all the gays” and nuking an island, and began treating him coldly. Kluwe says Priefer began marking him down unfairly on internal “Production Point” sheets and berated him publicly after a poor game. Despite reasonable season statistics and complying with coaching requests to change punt style, the team drafted a punter in the fifth round in April 2013 without notifying Kluwe, then released him in May. Kluwe details other signs of being sidelined (limited contact from coaches after surgery, a text from GM Rick Spielman asking him to “fly under radar” regarding tweets about the pope) and argues Frazier and GM Rick Spielman lacked the backbone to resist Priefer’s bias. He calls for Priefer to be removed from coaching, defends the importance of speaking out for equality, and concludes that his activism likely cost him his NFL career even though he says the league itself is not institutionally homophobic.

Oscar Pistorius, the 26-year-old South African Paralympic star, has been charged with the murder of his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp, who was shot dead at his home in the early hours of Valentine’s Day. Pistorius wept in court as prosecutors indicated they would pursue a premeditated murder charge. He is being held at a police station pending a bail hearing.

Pistorius’ family strongly denies he intended to kill Steenkamp, saying they have “zero doubt” he mistook her for an intruder and acted instinctively. His father, uncle and sister read statements expressing shock and grief, insisting police forensic evidence “strongly refutes” premeditation. Family members and his agent have visited him and said supporters worldwide remain behind him. His agent cancelled all upcoming races and appearances while the legal process continues; sponsors have said they are waiting on the outcome before altering commitments.

Accounts from friends, neighbours and media reports describe chaotic scenes: Pistorius allegedly shot Steenkamp through a bathroom door, firing multiple times; she was reportedly still alive when carried downstairs and Pistorius attempted resuscitation. A close friend, Justin Divaris, said Pistorius phoned him at 3:55 a.m. claiming, “I shot Reeva,” and later sobbed “My baba, I’ve killed my baba.” Forensic teams removed the bathroom door and blood evidence was reported along the route Pistorius carried Steenkamp.

Background details include Steenkamp’s profile as a model, law graduate and reality-TV contestant; her family is focusing on the criminal process and has arranged a private funeral. Reports also note Pistorius’ past brushes with police and that he kept multiple firearms and had pending gun-license applications. The case has shocked South Africa, with wide media attention and uncertain implications for Pistorius’ athletic career.

Researchers who reviewed video of an April 10 incident at Royal Burgers’ Zoo in Arnhem conclude a female chimpanzee, Tushi, deliberately planned and used a stick to swat down a documentary drone. Published in Primates, Jan van Hooff and Bas Lukkenaar recount that a TV crew’s drone attracted the chimps’ attention during practice. Several animals picked up long willow twigs; Tushi and another female, Raime, climbed scaffolding where the drone hovered. Tushi brandished a roughly 6-foot stick and made two sweeping strikes; the second hit and broke the drone. Her facial grimace that coincided with the strikes, lack of fear, and the fact she obtained and carried the stick to a position where the drone could be hit led the authors to describe the action as deliberate and planned rather than reflexive. The authors argue the episode adds evidence that chimpanzees engage in forward planning of tool use and select implements (sticks, wood, stones) for particular purposes, reflecting spontaneous, innovative tool behavior observed previously at the zoo. The full study (van Hooff & Lukkenaar 2015) is available in Primates.

Updated forecast: a major nor'easter is expected to slam the U.S. Northeast beginning Monday night and into Tuesday, bringing blizzard conditions, hurricane-force gusts in places, and heavy snowfall measured in feet.

Key points
- Scope: Blizzard warnings/watches and winter-storm warnings cover a large swath from the mid-Atlantic into New England, including New York City, northern New Jersey, southern Connecticut, and areas from Maryland to Maine.
- Snow totals: Forecasts show widespread 12–18 inches possible in New York City and Boston, with isolated amounts up to 2 feet in parts of northeastern Massachusetts. Maryland through Maine could see more than a foot; Philadelphia 6–12 inches; Washington, D.C. 6–10 inches.
- Timing and character: Snow begins late Monday night (first reaching D.C.), peaks Tuesday morning into afternoon in NYC, then tapers off across New England by Tuesday evening. The storm is fast-moving with intense narrow bands producing very high snowfall rates (2–5 in/hr) over roughly nine-hour bursts at each location. Thundersnow is possible.
- Impacts: White-out conditions, extreme winds (gusts 40–50+ mph), heavy coastal flooding along parts of the Jersey shore, widespread travel bans/closures (NYC schools closed; Connecticut travel ban), risk of widespread power outages due to leaves on trees, and roads becoming impassable. Authorities urge avoiding travel and carrying winter survival kits.
- Meteorology: The storm is a rapidly intensifying “bomb” nor’easter driven by a cold pulse from the Great Lakes tapping subtropical moisture from a warm Gulf Stream—creating near-ideal conditions for heavy East Coast snows. Some modeling and comparisons rate it among the strongest March storms on record for NYC; if realized, it would be the city’s second-biggest March snowstorm since 1869.
- Context: Follows an unusually warm late winter with blossoms and 60s–70s temperatures; studies suggest warming oceans and a shifting climate may be making large East Coast snowstorms more likely, and many of NYC’s largest storms have occurred since 1996.

Officials and forecasters emphasize preparation and caution as the storm approaches.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam allowed a legislative resolution authorizing the state to sue the federal government over refugee resettlement to proceed without his signature, saying he has “constitutional concerns” about one branch directing another. Haslam asked Attorney General Herbert Slatery to clarify whether the legislature can hire outside counsel to represent the state; sponsors say the Thomas More Law Center has offered to take the case pro bono if the attorney general declines. The measure stems from post–Paris and San Bernardino attack fears and supporters’ claims that federal vetting of refugees is inadequate. Opponents — including immigrant-rights groups and the ACLU of Tennessee — say the resolution is discriminatory, constitutionally suspect, undermines separation of powers, and could make the state appear unwelcoming; Slatery previously noted states cannot refuse refugees admitted by the federal government without violating the Supremacy Clause. Tennessee has not participated in the federal resettlement program directly since 2008, when Catholic Charities of Tennessee began administering placements.

Secretly recorded phone conversations that aired on Dr. Phil appear to capture Jared Fogle, the former Subway spokesman, admitting sexual interest in children and describing methods for approaching and abusing minors. The recordings were made over several years by Rochelle Herman-Walrond, a former Florida radio host who said she secretly taped Fogle and provided the tapes to federal investigators. In the clips aired, the speaker—identified as Fogle—says he likes “all ages,” asks about 7‑ and 8‑year‑old children Herman‑Walrond knew, urges her to wear revealing clothing to “sex” children up, suggests targeting a child from a “broken home,” and outlines how he would groom kids by getting “a little closer” until abuse occurs. He also references flying to Thailand to make it “easier” to get young children and, in previews, appears to ask about watching 10‑ and 11‑year‑olds naked and installing cameras. Herman‑Walrond says she first warned Subway about concerns in 2011; the company says the complaint was not escalated properly. Fogle pleaded guilty in August to paying for sex with minors and child pornography and faces sentencing next month (reports vary between September/November). The FBI confirmed receiving tapes before raiding Fogle’s home but has not publicly confirmed Herman‑Walrond’s role as an informant. Additional audio was scheduled for a subsequent Dr. Phil episode.

On March 21–22, a military coup in Mali toppled President Amadou Toumani Touré. Capt. Amadou Sanogo and a junta calling itself the CNRDRE seized power in Bamako, citing failures in the army’s campaign against a renewed Tuareg insurgency in the north. The coup created a power vacuum that Tuareg rebels—primarily the National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad (MNLA), but also Islamist groups such as Ansar Dine—exploited to capture the entire northern third of the country within days, taking key towns including Kidal, Gao and Timbuktu.

The insurgents’ objectives differ: the MNLA seeks an independent Tuareg state (Azawad), while Ansar Dine wants Sharia law imposed across Mali. In captured towns residents report Islamist fighters destroying or banning music and alcohol and enforcing strict Islamic practices. The takeover has already displaced hundreds of thousands: UN agencies say over 200,000 people uprooted since January, with some 100,000 fleeing abroad. Aid agencies warn of a widening humanitarian crisis across the Sahel, where around 13 million people need food aid after drought.

Regional leaders and organizations reacted swiftly. West African heads of state, led by figures such as Ivory Coast’s Alassane Ouattara, formed an emergency diplomatic committee and, through ECOWAS and the African Union, imposed sanctions and an embargo to force the junta to restore civilian rule. Sanctions include border closures and freezing Mali’s regional central bank accounts; ECOWAS gave the junta a 72-hour deadline that was not met. The junta has resisted stepping down and has not dispatched forces north to repel the rebels. Neighboring capitals worry that the collapse of Mali could encourage unrest at home.

Sanctions are having immediate domestic effects: long fuel lines, panic buying, and fears of power outages and unpaid civil servants as Mali imports all its fuel and its central account is frozen. The disruption threatens agriculture (diesel for irrigation), electricity generation, and basic services.

Internationally, there has been relative indifference so far, but the UN Security Council planned an emergency meeting. UNESCO warned that the conflict endangers Timbuktu’s unique mud-and-wood architecture and its 700,000 ancient manuscripts—cultural treasures at risk from conflict and restricted access. Diplomacy is complicated: the MNLA says it will negotiate about Azawad’s future but refuses to recognize the junta as a legitimate interlocutor.

In sum, the coup compounded an existing insurgency and produced a rapid territorial loss in northern Mali, creating political instability, humanitarian displacement, threats to cultural heritage, regional security concerns across the Sahel, and economic hardship inside Mali—developments that West African leaders and international actors deem dangerous for the wider region.

Researchers reconstructed 1,112 years of warm-season moisture in central Mongolia from Siberian pine tree rings and find that the climate during the rise of the 13th‑century Mongol Empire was unusually wet and productive, not dry as sometimes supposed. The tree‑ring reconstruction explains 56% of regional water‑balance variability and correlates with steppe productivity. It shows a 15‑year run of above‑average moisture coinciding with Genghis Khan’s rise and the empire’s early conquests (≈1211–1225) that is unprecedented in the past millennium. The authors argue this persistent wet spell would have boosted grassland productivity and horse fodder, facilitating mobilization, cavalry strength, and the formation of Mongol political and military power. By contrast, the decades immediately before saw severe drought (circa 1180–1190), so the abrupt shift from drought to sustained moisture likely helped create conditions for unification and expansion. The study also shows that the early‑21st‑century drought in central Mongolia was the hottest in the 1,112‑year record, consistent with anthropogenic warming, and warns that future warming could produce severe “heat droughts” that outweigh higher precipitation, with major implications for semiarid ecosystems and societies. The tree samples—long‑lived, slow‑growing pines from lava‑flow rock—provided the high‑resolution moisture history used in the analysis.

JK Rowling has launched legal action seeking £24,000-plus from her former personal assistant, Amanda Donaldson, alleging the assistant wrongly used Rowling’s funds and took merchandise. Donaldson worked for Rowling from February 2014 until her dismissal for gross misconduct in April 2017. Court papers lodged at Airdrie Sheriff Court claim Donaldson improperly benefited by £23,696.32 through unauthorised spending on a business credit card and removal of Harry Potter memorabilia.

Alleged unauthorised transactions include purchases at bakeries, Jo Malone (£1,482), Molton Brown (£3,629), Paper Tiger (£2,139), Starbucks (£1,636) and other retailers; alleged thefts of collectible Harry Potter items (including a motorised Hogwarts Express and other sets); purchase of two cats (£1,200); a £400 cash withdrawal purportedly for a restaurant deposit that was not paid; and taking £7,742 in foreign currency from a safe. Rowling says the purchases and removals were without her knowledge or consent. The alleged irregularities were reportedly uncovered during an accountant’s review of statements and spreadsheets.

Donaldson denies the claims and says Rowling has suffered no loss and is not entitled to damages. A spokeswoman for Rowling confirmed legal action has been taken but otherwise declined comment. The case, before Sheriff Derek O’Carroll, is due back in court later this year.

Tens of thousands of mostly young people took to U.S. streets for several nights after Donald Trump’s election, chanting “not my president” and staging spontaneous demonstrations in cities from New York and Los Angeles to Portland, Seattle, Chicago, Boston, Columbus, Minneapolis, Madison, Milwaukee and Oakland. Many protesters were high‑school and college students; some walked out of class. The movement, energized by social media hashtags like #notourpresident and a Change.org petition that drew millions of signatures, lacked clear national coordination but planned more actions over the coming days, including targeting the Dec. 19 meeting of the Electoral College.

Most protests were peaceful but several turned violent. Portland police declared a “riot” after a crowd of about 4,000 included a small group they described as “anarchists” who smashed cars, threw rocks and Molotov cocktails, spray‑painted graffiti and led to 26 arrests. Oakland police reported putting out dozens of fires amid vandalism; Los Angeles saw an effigy burned and authorities reported as many as 185 arrests. New York’s protests around Trump Tower drew large crowds and about 65 arrests.

Political leaders urged calm: President Obama and Hillary Clinton urged acceptance of the result, while Trump initially derided protesters as “professional” and later sent a conciliatory tweet. Some activists discussed pressuring faithless electors, though experts say defections are rare and unlikely to change the outcome. The protests reflect deep youth dismay at Trump’s victory and signal a new, still‑unstructured anti‑Trump movement.

A former student allegedly stabbed two people at Rutgers Business School on the Livingston Campus in Piscataway on Friday afternoon, Nov. 4, 2016. The victims — a faculty member and a student — were attacked inside an office on the fifth floor around 2:30 p.m.; witnesses reported screams and saw a woman bleeding as professors applied towels to her wound. The suspect fled but was quickly taken into custody with self-inflicted injuries. All three injured individuals were transported to Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital for treatment. Rutgers issued shelter-in-place alerts and briefly locked down the New Brunswick campus; the lockdown was lifted once authorities secured the scene. The university described the stabbing as unprovoked and isolated. The Middlesex County Prosecutor’s Office is investigating and no charges had been filed at the time of the reports.

A Jefferson Parish magistrate on Aug. 7 found probable cause to hold Shantel Parria Wagner on a second-degree murder charge in the June death of her husband, Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office Sgt. Troy Smith. Magistrate Commissioner Paul Schneider reduced her bond from the usual $500,000 to $300,000 and ordered GPS monitoring and home confinement except for medical appointments if she posts bond.

Smith, 44, an academy instructor and former NOPD officer, was found June 17 after Wagner called 911 saying he had shot himself; he died about a week later. Detectives arrested Wagner July 11 after forensic testing and interviews led them to conclude the wound was not self-inflicted. Prosecutors say Wagner gave multiple inconsistent statements and that a witness reported she confessed to shooting Smith. Defense attorneys maintain Wagner consistently said Smith committed suicide, note Smith’s PTSD, depression and a prior suicide threat, and point out Wagner’s DNA was not found on the gun.

During a two-day probable-cause hearing, forensic pathologist Dr. Dana Trosclair testified about the entry wound (right parietal scalp) and exit on the top of the head with a right-to-left, slightly front-to-back and upward trajectory, but said the final autopsy opinion is pending pending toxicology. The sheriff’s crime-lab commander testified reconstruction is in preliminary stages and that the totality of evidence contradicts a self-inflicted wound. The magistrate relied on Wagner’s inconsistent statements and the alleged confession to find probable cause. Wagner faces a mandatory life sentence if convicted.

A nearly 100-year-old Dutch woman named Annie fulfilled a bucket-list wish to experience being arrested and spend time in a police cell. At her niece’s request, officers from Nijmegen-Zuid cooperated, handcuffed and booked her into a cell, and photographed her smiling during the visit. The department shared the story and pictures on Facebook, calling it “a day to remember” after helping the centenarian cross that unusual item off her list.

Gossip roundup: Heidi Montag has released her debut pop album Superficial after three years of work and is promoting it on radio, telling Ryan Seacrest she’s focusing on her music for now and putting plans for children with husband Spencer Pratt “kind of on hold.” The album and its club-ready, provocative lyrics—highlighted by the single “I’ll Do It,” which includes lines like “come eat my panties off of me”—are described by Montag as personal, empowering and a tongue-in-cheek take on Hollywood’s surface focus; she calls the title a double entendre about superficiality and inner life. Montag also says she and Pratt have been into yoga lately to help them relax. The item opens with snarky commentary about the song’s cringeworthy lyrics and general celebrity Schadenfreude.

A man attempted to jump the north perimeter fence of the White House on Friday afternoon, prompting a lockdown and a temporary closure of pedestrian Pennsylvania Avenue. Secret Service and U.S. Park Police officers pulled him down, checked a briefcase, and took him into custody. Officials had not identified him or announced charges at the time. President Barack Obama was not at the White House during the incident; he was in Michigan. Authorities declared the situation over after the man was apprehended.

The 25th annual amfAR Gala Cannes (Cinema Against AIDS) was held May 17, 2018 at the Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Cap d’Antibes, France. The black-tie benefit, produced by AAB Productions and presented by Bold Films and Chopard, combined high-profile entertainment, fashion and auctions to raise funds for amfAR.

Highlights
- Performances by Sting and Shaggy, Grace Jones, Ellie Goulding and Jason Derulo.
- A fashion show curated by Carine Roitfeld; the looks were auctioned as a collection for $1.7 million.
- Major auction items and results included:
  - Pierce Brosnan’s original Bob Dylan painting (which included a lunch with the actor) — sold for $1.4 million (reported buyer: Ukrainian collector Marina Acton).
  - A restored 1964 S3 Bentley Convertible — sold for over $800,000 (introduced by Heidi Klum and Benicio Del Toro).
  - A Joe Bradley painting — nearly $1 million.

Notable honorary chairs and celebrity supporters included Alessandra Ambrosio, Linda Evangelista, Kate Hudson, Scarlett Johansson, Heidi Klum, Katy Perry, Aishwarya Rai, Donatella Versace, Michelle Yeoh, Carine Roitfeld and many others.

Contacts for sponsorship, tickets and press were listed by the organizers.

Elon Musk tweeted that he plans to start a tunnel-digging venture called The Boring Company to ease Los Angeles traffic, saying he’ll begin digging “in a month or so” and even specifying a start near SpaceX by Crenshaw and the 105 Freeway. His comments followed earlier complaints about LA congestion and came alongside other provocative tweets (e.g., about a “neural lace”), so observers questioned whether he was serious or joking.

Skeptics note Musk’s many commitments (Tesla, SpaceX, OpenAI, recent SolarCity ties) and the logistical, legal and engineering challenges of urban tunneling—especially in an earthquake-prone area—but others point out LA already has subway tunnels and past expert testimony that modern tunneling can address seismic concerns. Musk has repeatedly insisted he isn’t just trolling, while his team had not immediately commented.

Summary:

U.S. birthrates have fallen sharply, reaching a 30-year low in 2017 with 3,853,472 births — down 2 percent from 2016. The general fertility rate declined to a record low of 60.2 births per 1,000 women aged 15–44, and the CDC’s total fertility rate dropped to 1,764.5 births per 1,000 women, well below the 2,100 replacement level and marking the largest single-year decline since 2010. The decade-long decline since the 2007 peak has been especially pronounced for minority groups: Hispanic women’s fertility fell more than 27% from 2007–2016, Black women’s by about 11%, while smaller declines occurred for white and Asian women.

Birthrates fell across almost all age groups in 2017. Teen births plunged to a record low (18.8 per 1,000, a 7% drop and down 55% since 2007), and rates fell for women ages 20–24 and 25–29 (each down 4%). Women in their early 30s saw a slight 2% decline but remained the highest-rate group (100.3 per 1,000). The only rise was among women aged 40–44 (up 2%).

Social and economic factors appear to be driving delayed childbearing: many millennial women are prioritizing career establishment, financial stability and paying off debts before starting families, and research suggests a marital pay gap that emerges after a first child born between ages 25 and 35 often does not close. Health outcomes showed mixed worsening trends in 2017: preterm births rose (driven by late preterm births), low birth weight reached a new high for the period, and cesarean rates edged up slightly.

Demographers note the long-term implication that U.S. population growth will increasingly rely on immigration if low fertility persists, bringing U.S. rates closer to those of other low-fertility countries.

La Casa Pacifica is a historically significant, fully walled 5.45-acre oceanfront estate in San Clemente with about 450 feet of beachfront and expansive coastal gardens. The estate, once President Richard M. Nixon’s “Western White House,” sits at a preferred elevation with panoramic ocean and sunset views. Its restored and modernized Spanish Colonial Revival main residence (circa 1927) — roughly 9,000 sq. ft. — and other gleaming white structures set amid exotic palms, Monterey cypress, emerald lawns and manicured gardens have been featured in Architectural Digest multiple times.

The property’s built area totals about 15,000 sq. ft., including the main house, a 3,000-sq.-ft. entertaining pavilion with guest wing, a two-bedroom guest house, and multiple staff quarters. Recreational amenities include an oceanfront swimming pool, lighted north-south tennis court, and putting green. The compound is secured behind three gated entrances and carries a storied political and social history. It has returned to the market with an asking price of $63.5 million, reduced from $75 million three years ago.

Russia’s consumer-rights watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has opened an inquiry into fidget spinners after state TV segments and complaints from parents and teachers suggested the toys might harm children or be used politically. The agency said it will study spinners’ effects on children’s health, possible negative impacts, and urged parents to supervise purchases and buy from trusted sellers.

The inquiry follows repeated reports on pro-Kremlin Rossiya24 claiming spinners can “zombify” or make people impressionable and alleging they are being promoted by the non-systemic opposition to influence youth. Hosts and guests argued spinners dull critical thinking or are being distributed at opposition events; critics and independent journalists mocked those claims as absurd.

Internationally, concerns about spinners are not unique to Russia: some have been modified into weapons, small parts can be choking hazards (German customs seized tons), schools in the U.S. have banned them as distractions, and therapists debate their benefit for attention disorders. The story also noted the toy’s recent global craze and media attention, including a Saturday Night Live spoof.

Afghan President Hamid Karzai has appointed a delegation to investigate a United Nations report that found torture and other severe abuses in Afghan-run detention facilities. The delegation — which includes advisers from the Interior Ministry and the National Directorate of Security (NDS), both named in the UN report — was ordered on January 22 to examine allegations of torture, mistreatment, death threats, sexual abuse and procedural misconduct, and to report back within two weeks.

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) issued the report on January 20 after interviewing 635 detainees held in 89 facilities from October 2011 to October 2012. It documents 14 abusive practices, including genital twisting, fingernail extraction, electric shocks and transfers to hidden locations; one unnamed NDS operative is quoted alleging the agency has secret places used for detention and torture. The report also recounts threats of sexual violence and other coercive methods used to extract confessions.

Afghan authorities have denied the findings. NDS officials and presidential spokespeople questioned the report’s methodology and the credibility and motives of interviewees, saying observers (including the ICRC and rights groups) have access to facilities and that documented evidence should be shown. The International Committee of the Red Cross confirmed it has access to detention facilities and would intervene if it witnessed abuse.

Local lawyers, a judge speaking anonymously, and former detainees dispute the denials, arguing oversight is limited, visits are controlled, and interrogations in terrorism-related cases are effectively beyond scrutiny. Lawyers and survivors cited multiple cases of severe physical abuse, sleep deprivation, electric shocks, suspension by the hands, and coerced confessions leading to wrongful convictions. Critics warn the presidential inquiry — involving agencies implicated in the report — may be limited in independence and effectiveness.

Families of about 800–850 victims (and roughly 1,500 injured responders/others) of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks have filed a consolidated federal lawsuit in Manhattan seeking to hold the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia liable for aiding the hijackers and funding al-Qaeda. Brought by aviation firm Kreindler & Kreindler under the authority of the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), the complaint alleges multiple forms of support from elements of the Saudi state:

- Saudi embassy and consular officials in the U.S. and Germany allegedly provided logistical help to some hijackers (finding apartments, helping them learn English, assisting with credit cards/cash) in the 18 months before 9/11. The suit also claims a Saudi official stayed in the same Virginia hotel as several hijackers the night before the attacks.
- Saudi charities and government-supported organizations are accused of serving as fronts that funneled money to al-Qaeda, funded training camps, and facilitated travel and paperwork; the complaint names groups including the Al-Haramain Islamic Foundation and the Saudi Red Crescent Authority.
- The filing cites FBI findings and alleges deliberate concealment of money trails and even coded passport markers used to ease al-Qaeda members’ international travel.

Plaintiffs’ attorneys say the suit is the culmination of years of work and aims to prove Saudi government complicity; they did not specify a damages amount. The lawsuits proliferated after Congress overrode President Obama’s veto of JASTA last year, removing sovereign-immunity barriers to suing foreign governments in terrorism cases. The Kingdom has not commented in the filing; court proceedings to coordinate related cases are underway.

Former Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight has pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter for a January 2015 hit-and-run in Compton, California, in which his pickup truck struck two men after an argument on a film/commercial shoot tied to the Straight Outta Compton project. One victim, Terry Carter, died; the other, Cle "Bone" Sloan, survived with serious injuries. Security-camera footage shows a confrontation at a drive-in, a struggle at Knight’s window, the truck reversing and then moving forward over one man and into the other.

Under a plea deal, murder and attempted murder charges and separate robbery and criminal-threats counts were dismissed. Knight admitted using a "deadly and dangerous weapon" and accepted terms calling for 22 years for voluntary manslaughter plus six years under California’s three-strikes law; a judge later sentenced him to 28 years in state prison (including enhancements for a prior strike, the serious-violent-felony finding, and a deadly-weapon use). He will begin serving the term in October.

Knight, 53, once helped launch artists such as Dr. Dre, Tupac Shakur and Snoop Dogg. His past includes multiple arrests, parole violations, and a 1996 era marked by Tupac’s killing while in his car and later litigation around Biggie Smalls’s death. Knight turned himself in after the 2015 incident; his defense characterized the episode as self-defense and fleeing alleged armed attackers, claims Sloan denies. Under California law a no-contest plea is treated as a guilty plea.

Eric W. Deaton, a 42-year-old New Lebanon resident and Constitution Party candidate for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Sen. George Voinovich, was indicted Aug. 31 by a Montgomery County grand jury on one count of unlawful sexual conduct with a minor, a third-degree felony. The indictment alleges Deaton engaged in sexual conduct with a girl aged 13–15 between March 20, 2006 and March 25, 2007. If convicted he faces up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine; he is scheduled for arraignment Sept. 14.

Perry Township police say Deaton met the girl while serving as a church elder, tutored her, invited her to his home, paid her for odd jobs, and that investigators have hotel receipts and video. Deaton, who is married with three children and has listed roles such as Cub Scout leader on his site, denies the allegations, calling them lies and politically motivated because of his campaign. Speaking with attorneys, he said he will remain in the Senate race and defend himself in court; his lawyer noted Deaton passed a four-hour polygraph and suggested evidence (surveillance video and receipts) will support his innocence. Deaton has reported backing from Tea Party and other conservative groups.

President Obama and Vice President Biden unveiled a sweeping gun-violence initiative in January 2013 combining 23 executive actions and several major legislative proposals, framed as the most ambitious federal effort on gun safety in nearly two decades following the Newtown school massacre.

Key executive actions (selected highlights)
- Strengthen background checks and data sharing: presidential memoranda and agency directives to get federal agencies and states to provide more data to the national background-check system, remove legal barriers (including HIPAA-related issues), improve incentives for state reporting, and require federal law enforcement to trace guns recovered in crimes.
- Enforcement and prosecution: tougher penalties for lying on background checks, steps to prevent “straw purchasers,” maximize enforcement against gun crime, and propose rulemaking allowing background checks before returning seized guns.
- Research and public health: a presidential memorandum directing the CDC and scientific agencies to research causes and prevention of gun violence (reversing a long-standing de facto chill on such research) and a call for Congress to fund the work; expand the National Violent Death Reporting System to all states.
- Regulation, guidance, and safety measures: nominate an ATF director, review gun-lock and safe standards, issue ATF guidance to dealers about private-sales background checks, promote a national safe-gun-ownership campaign, and direct training for law enforcement, first responders and school officials on active-shooter scenarios.
- Mental health and schools: clarify Medicaid and ACA mental-health coverage rules, finalize mental-health parity regulations, encourage hiring school resource officers, and develop model emergency-response plans.

Major legislative proposals the White House sought from Congress
- Universal criminal background checks for all gun sales (closing private-sale/gun-show loopholes).
- Reinstate and strengthen a ban on military-style assault weapons.
- Reinstate a limit on high-capacity magazines (10-round cap proposed).
- Ban armor-piercing bullets and strengthen tools to prevent/prosecute gun crimes.
- Expand funding and policies for mental-health treatment and school safety.

Context, reaction, and politics
- The package was prompted by the Sandy Hook elementary school shooting and included an overall $500 million proposal for implementation and related measures. Obama stressed that while many executive actions could be done without Congress, substantial, lasting change required legislation.
- The restoration of CDC research into gun violence was a notable reversal of the post-1996 chilling effect; the White House requested initial funding (e.g., $10 million for CDC research and $20 million to expand death reporting).
- The plan drew widespread public support in polls but immediate and fierce opposition from the NRA and many Republicans, who argued it infringed on Second Amendment rights and would not stop mass shootings. The NRA ran an ad attacking Obama and opposed many measures while claiming alternate priorities such as increased armed protection of schools.
- Congressional prospects were uncertain: some Democrats and gun-control advocates prioritized background checks as both effective and politically viable, while Republicans and some Democrats who support gun rights signaled resistance, particularly to an assault-weapons ban. The White House planned national outreach and lobbying to build support, while congressional leaders signaled a slow legislative timetable.

Overall, the initiative combined enforcement and administrative steps aimed at tightening background checks, improving data and research, and enhancing enforcement, paired with an ambitious legislative push for universal background checks, renewed assault-weapons and magazine limits, and other statutory changes — setting up a likely protracted political battle.

Three of Kandahar province’s top officials were killed Thursday when members of the governor’s own guard opened fire during a high-level security meeting ahead of Afghanistan’s parliamentary elections.

Victims and injuries
- Provincial police chief Brig. Gen. Abdul Raziq (often reported as Razik), Governor Zalmay Wesa and provincial intelligence chief Abdul Mohmin were killed; Wesa died of wounds at a nearby hospital. A provincial military corps commander was also reported among the dead by a local MP.
- Three Americans (one service member and two civilian contractors) were wounded; their conditions were not immediately known.
- NATO said U.S. Gen. Scott Miller, commander of U.S. and NATO forces in Afghanistan, was present but unhurt.

Circumstances and claims
- The shooting occurred inside the governor’s residence during a security conference; the attackers were members of the governor’s elite guard who turned their weapons on colleagues. Afghan forces cordoned off the area and a gun battle lasted more than an hour; one of the original attackers was reported killed.
- The Taliban claimed responsibility and said Gen. Miller was the intended target. The slain figures were among the most powerful local security actors in southern Kandahar and close U.S. allies; Raziq had survived earlier assassination attempts and was accused widely of authoritarian tactics and corruption.

Context and related violence
- The attack came amid sharply rising violence ahead of Saturday’s parliamentary elections, which the Taliban have vowed to disrupt and have warned civilians and schools to avoid.
- Separate incidents the same day included a Taliban-claimed suicide attack on a NATO convoy near Bagram (Parwan province) that killed two civilians and injured several Czech soldiers, a bombing in Helmand that killed an election candidate, attacks in Baghlan that killed six policemen, and a suicide car bombing in Maidan Wardak that killed two Afghan soldiers.
- Afghan security forces have faced near-daily attacks in recent months; NATO’s role is mainly training and air support since 2014. This year several NATO and U.S. service members have been killed in Afghanistan.

This article by Simon Maloy criticizes conservative media attacks on Michelle Obama’s anti-obesity campaign and examines James O’Keefe’s recent defenses of a failed sting against a CNN reporter.

Key points:
- Conservative commentators have responded to Michelle Obama’s nutrition and fitness efforts with sexist and juvenile attacks, including Rush Limbaugh’s nickname and an Andrew Breitbart-affiliated cartoon that the author calls playground-level mockery.
- The piece then turns to James O’Keefe, the conservative activist known for deceptively edited ACORN videos. O’Keefe’s attempted prank on CNN’s Abbie Boudreau—which involved luring her onto a boat and allegedly planning a “seduction” stunt—backfired and drew criticism.
- O’Keefe posted a defense on BigGovernment arguing the explicit prank memo was a draft he never intended to follow and that any plan would have been tame, consensual, and satirical. Maloy finds O’Keefe’s explanations unconvincing, noting the memo was written by Ben Wetmore (a longtime associate) and pointing out inconsistencies and implausibilities in O’Keefe’s account.
- The author argues that even if O’Keefe objected to the memo’s excesses, the basic intent—to trick and film a reporter under false pretenses—remains problematic. He also suggests O’Keefe’s past behavior makes it likely that more sensational footage would have been used.

Overall, Maloy condemns the tone and tactics of the conservative response to Michelle Obama and casts doubt on O’Keefe’s credibility and excuses regarding the failed CNN sting.

ABC has acquired the rights to revive American Idol, with the reboot slated to premiere in March 2018. The show, which ran for 15 seasons on Fox before ending in 2016, will be produced by Fremantle and 19 Entertainment (and/or Core) and was the subject of a brief bidding war that ABC won over Fox and NBC. ABC executives framed the move as bringing back a pop-culture staple and said the series will join their reality lineup; the season is expected to be shortened and heavily promoted.

Hosts, judges and exact format have not been finalized, but Ryan Seacrest — now a co-host of ABC’s Live with Kelly & Ryan and already associated with other high-profile gigs (including New Year’s Rockin’ Eve) — is widely reported as the likely host and appears open to returning. Logistical challenges remain if Seacrest stays on Live in New York while Idol films in Los Angeles: reports say the plan may require him to fly coast-to-coast twice in as many days for live shows, or producers could relocate Idol production to New York. No official deals for judges have been announced; key former figures like Simon Cowell are now tied to other networks and projects.

Background and context: Idol was once a ratings juggernaut but experienced steep declines and high production costs toward the end of its Fox run. Industry observers have questioned whether a quick revival is wise, but ABC hopes the brand’s built-in audience will help shore up its Sunday lineup.

James Debney, CEO of American Outdoor Brands (formerly Smith & Wesson), addressed the company’s sharp profit and sales decline while responding to the recent Parkland, Florida, school shooting in which a Smith & Wesson M&P15 rifle was used. Debney expressed sympathy for the victims and said the company shares the desire to make communities safer, while reiterating support for lawful Americans’ right to own firearms and for “effective solutions” that protect responsible gun owners.

Financial results: AOB reported a dramatic drop in quarterly profit to $4.7 million from $37.6 million a year earlier and sales down about one-third to $157.4 million. Debney attributed the downturn to “challenging market conditions,” forecasting flat revenues for the next 12–18 months. The company has cut jobs, repaid $75 million of debt, extended a $75 million note to 2020, and trimmed its fiscal-year sales and earnings guidance repeatedly.

Industry context: The decline is part of a broader “Trump slump” in gun purchases that followed a surge during the Obama years. Lower demand reflects eased fears of imminent gun restrictions, fewer hunters, and falling crime rates. Firearm background checks—a sales proxy—fell 8.4% last year and were the lowest in six years in January. The sector faces heavy discounting and excess inventory; rivals include Remington, which filed for bankruptcy.

Political and retail fallout after Parkland: The shooting intensified scrutiny of the gun industry and prompted major retailers (Dick’s, Walmart, Kroger) to raise minimum purchase ages to 21 and to stop selling assault-style rifles. Corporations and others have cut ties with the NRA. The political environment remains fluid, with competing pressures from calls for stricter controls and strong pro-gun lobbying.

Debney background: British-born, a Manchester Institute of Science and Technology graduate and a long-time NRA fundraiser, Debney has acknowledged he had not fired a gun before taking the job but has received the NRA’s Golden Ring of Freedom for fundraising.
