Shoukhrat Mitalipov, an OHSU professor, published a Nature paper on Aug. 2 reporting a major advance in using CRISPR gene editing to correct a disease-causing mutation in human embryos. The work, which was accidentally leaked in late July, targeted a common mutation that causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), a leading inherited cause of sudden death in young people. Mitalipov’s team selected HCM because of its severity and prevalence and obtained institutional approval after a two-year review, arguing that embryo research can reveal DNA repair behaviors not modeled well in stem-cell-derived “embryo-like” cells.

Instead of introducing CRISPR after fertilization (an approach in three prior Chinese studies that produced low success rates, mosaicism, and off-target effects), Mitalipov co-injected CRISPR with sperm during fertilization. The strategy appears to have leveraged the egg’s high-fidelity DNA-repair machinery: the maternal healthy DNA served as a template to correct a four–base-pair deletion in the paternal genome. Across 163 viable embryos, nearly 50% were fully corrected, only one showed mosaicism, and none showed detectable off-target edits. Independent experts contacted by Quartz raised methodological questions—particularly whether mosaicism was thoroughly excluded and whether evidence proves the specific repair pathway was used—so some uncertainty remains.

Mitalipov, known for developing mitochondrial replacement techniques (“three-parent” embryos), sees clinical applications as the goal and believes it could take about a decade to reach clinics. The article emphasizes that CRISPR embryo editing is more complex than mitochondrial replacement and not yet applicable to polygenic traits (e.g., intelligence), so “designer babies” remain far off. It also warns of risks from unregulated or premature clinical uses—mosaicism, off-target effects, and unknown harms—and notes regulatory differences worldwide (U.S. FDA bars clinical trials using edited embryos; the U.K. offers a model of extended public debate and regulated licensing).

Separate human-interest reporting describes Russell Cruzan III, an infant from the Kalamazoo area diagnosed with mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome (a progressive, often fatal mitochondrial disorder similar to the case of Charlie Gard). Russell’s parents are pursuing experimental care at Boston Children’s Hospital and raising funds via crowdfunding to cover treatment and travel costs. The broader text also includes background on mitochondrial disease—its symptoms, inheritance patterns, diagnostic challenges, variability, lack of cure, and the need for better awareness, support, and research.

The parents of U.S. Olympic swimmer Ryan Lochte are facing foreclosure on their Florida home. CitiMortgage filed suit in Volusia County alleging Steven and Ileana (also spelled Ileane/Illeana in reports) Lochte took out a $258,000 mortgage in 2007, stopped making payments in February 2011, and now owe roughly $242,000-plus interest (the bank seeks about $250,000). The lender is asking to foreclose and, if a sale doesn’t satisfy the debt, to pursue the Lochtes for the remaining balance. Ileana Lochte filed a motion to dismiss the case last month; a judge has not yet ruled. Attempts to reach the Lochtes and their attorneys were not immediately successful. The couple divorced last year and both were recently in London watching their son Ryan, who won five medals (including two golds) at the London Olympics.

Emma Coronel Aispuro, wife of Mexican drug lord Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán, gave her first on-camera interview to Telemundo journalist Anabel Hernández, aired in a special titled “The Queen of El Chapo.” Coronel—an American-born former beauty queen who married Guzmán in 2007 when she was 18—said she has not seen her husband since his recapture on January 8 and fears for his life and health in the maximum-security Altiplano prison. She accused Mexican authorities of effectively punishing him for his 2015 escape by restricting basic needs and monitoring him constantly.

The interview, filmed in Sinaloa on Feb. 12 and produced with UC Berkeley’s Investigative Reporting Program, also covered family life, their twin daughters (now 4), and Coronel’s concerns that they may be judged or suffer for their father’s crimes. She described Guzmán as intelligent and outwardly untroubled even under stress, but upset about becoming a narco-legend and losing control of his own story. Coronel discussed Guzmán’s desire to collaborate on a film to tell his version and defended his interactions with actress Kate del Castillo, who had sought to help develop a movie and later met Guzmán with Sean Penn. Coronel said she saw del Castillo’s role as professional, called the publication of a video used with a Rolling Stone piece a "betrayal," and denied jealousy over del Castillo.

Actress Angelina Jolie was a standout at San Diego Comic-Con, appearing with Salt co-star Liev Schreiber to promote their upcoming film. Dressed in a fitted leather jacket, pencil skirt and heels, the 35-year-old discussed on-set mishaps—including a fall that briefly left her deaf until she realized she still had earplugs in—and shared anecdotes about the weapons used in filming (even an unconventional use of a fire extinguisher). Jolie described Salt as “meaner, harder and darker” than her previous action films like Wanted and Tomb Raider and called it a better action movie.

Separately, Jolie and Brad Pitt quietly resolved false breakup rumors in court after the British tabloid News of the World ran a January story claiming the couple had met a divorce lawyer to arrange asset division and custody. The paper removed the article but did not retract it publicly, so the couple sued. Their London lawyers accepted an undisclosed settlement (to be donated to charity), and their attorney said the settlement ends the litigation.

A Honolulu medical examiner concluded that 3-year-old Finley Puleo Boyle of Kailua likely died from the sedatives and local anesthetic given during a December dental procedure, ruling the death accidental. Finley lapsed into a coma on Dec. 3 at Island Dentistry for Children during treatment by Dr. Lilly Geyer and died a month later on Jan. 3. The autopsy found no underlying heart condition or allergic reaction; it says she received five drugs (including Demerol, hydroxyzine, chlorohydrate), nitrous oxide, and a lidocaine-with-epinephrine injection. According to the report, she became unresponsive and suffered cardiopulmonary arrest immediately after the lidocaine injection.

Her parents filed a negligence lawsuit while she was in a coma. Their lawyer and the family allege lapses in monitoring and care during sedation; the family says oxygen levels were not checked for an extended period and that CPR was not promptly administered. Dr. Geyer’s attorney has called allegations unproven and declined further comment due to the lawsuit. There were no prior state complaints on file against Geyer, and no criminal charges have been filed. New Hawaii rules tightening dental sedation oversight took effect in January.

More than three dozen La Salle University students and three staff on an annual spring-break mission trip in eastern Kentucky were found safe after becoming lost on a late-afternoon hike near Bad Branch Falls on Pine Mountain.

The group of 37 students and 3 staff left a volunteer site in Harlan County for a customary hike to a popular overlook called High Rock. They arrived late (around 5 p.m.), became disoriented as darkness fell on a wooded, uneven “lollipop” trail, and could not locate the way down. Most were wearing light clothing and few had flashlights; temperatures fell into the low 20s. They called 911 around 7 p.m. and stayed together near a campfire while guiding rescuers by cellphone.

Search-and-rescue teams located them by about 11 p.m., but it took until roughly 3:30–3:45 a.m. Friday to walk all members down an alternate, less obstructed route. All 40 were evaluated at Appalachian Regional Hospital in Whitesburg; most were treated for cold, exhaustion or possible hypothermia. One person remained hospitalized briefly for observation (reported in good/ stable condition) and others received soup, dry clothes and phones to call family. The group was expected to return to Philadelphia on Saturday. Rescuers described the terrain as rough and noted the trail has warnings to stay on it.

SmartAsset analyzed 100 largest U.S. cities to identify the worst places to own a car, using seven factors: annual hours spent in traffic, annual cost of traffic (time + fuel), commuter stress index, non‑driving options (average walk/bike/transit scores), motor vehicle thefts per 1,000 residents, repair shops per 10,000 drivers, and parking garages per 10,000 drivers. Non‑driving options were double‑weighted; thefts, repair shops and garages were half‑weighted; other factors had single weight. Data sources included the Texas A&M Mobility Score Card, WalkScore, the FBI and Census business data.

Key findings
- The worst cities are coastal or near coasts, especially older East Coast cities that weren’t designed for heavy car traffic.
- Some places with terrible traffic don’t rank highest because driving is still the primary way to get around (e.g., parts of the Los Angeles metro).

Top 10 worst U.S. cities to own a car (ranked worst to least bad)
1. Newark, NJ — severe metro traffic from being inside the NY metro area and a high auto‑theft rate.
2. San Francisco, CA — heavy traffic with an average commuter traffic cost of about $1,600/year and high auto‑theft rates.
3. Washington, D.C. — average commuter spends ~82 hours/year in traffic, costing about $1,834/year.
4. Oakland, CA — highest auto‑theft rate in the study and ~78 hours/year in traffic, though many repair shops per driver.
5. Arlington, VA — shares D.C. metro’s ~82 hours/year and $1,834 cost; car ownership is more necessary than in D.C.
6. Portland, OR — lowest traffic burden in the top 10 (≈52 hours/year, ~$1,200 cost) but few parking garages and relatively few repair shops per capita.
7. Anaheim, CA — severe traffic and the highest commuter stress index; low non‑driving score makes car ownership more necessary.
8. New York, NY — highly walkable and transit‑accessible (making cars unnecessary), but drivers still face about $1,700/year in traffic costs.
9. Seattle, WA — ~63 hours/year in traffic and a high auto‑theft rate.
10. Boston, MA — very walkable with strong transit (MBTA), helping residents avoid ~64 hours/year in traffic.

Bottom line: Coastal, densely populated, and older cities—especially those with costly congestion, high commuter stress and elevated auto‑theft rates—tend to be the worst places to own a car; strong non‑driving options make car ownership less necessary and can lower a city’s ranking.

A major global study in Lancet using data from 188 countries (1980–2013) finds obesity rising everywhere and now affects nearly 30% of the world — about 2.1 billion people (up from 857 million in 1980). The U.S. contains the largest share of the world’s obese (87 million, 13% of the global total) despite having ~5% of the world population, but two-thirds of people with obesity live in developing countries. No country has reduced its obesity rate in the past 30+ years.

Highlights:
- Worldwide overweight/obese population grew from 857 million (1980) to 2.1 billion (2013).
- About one-third of U.S. adults are overweight and another third are obese (CDC figures).
- Some countries show even higher prevalence: e.g., male obesity >50% in Tonga; female obesity >50% in Kuwait, Kiribati, Micronesia, Libya, Qatar, Samoa and Tonga.
- Regional hotspots include the Middle East/North Africa, Central America, and Pacific/Caribbean islands; biggest female rises in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Honduras, Bahrain; biggest male rises in New Zealand, Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, USA.
- Child/adolescent overweight and obesity rose ~47% globally; ~22–24% of children in developed countries and ~13% in developing countries are overweight/obese.
- In rich countries adult obesity increases have slowed recently; in developing countries rates are accelerating.
- Causes were not definitively analyzed but likely include cheaper, more available high-calorie processed foods, reduced physical activity, dietary changes, and possible microbiome shifts. Weight gains tend to track income gains.
- Health consequences are serious: obesity increases risks for heart disease, stroke, diabetes, some cancers and contributes to millions of deaths annually. The WHO has launched a commission to study childhood obesity and propose solutions.

More than half of global obesity is concentrated in ten countries: USA, China, India, Russia, Brazil, Mexico, Egypt, Germany, Pakistan and Indonesia.

A 3-year-old boy fell about 15–16 feet into the jaguar enclosure at the Little Rock Zoo on Oct. 10, 2014. Witnesses say the child’s feet went over the railing; one jaguar was reported with its mouth around the boy’s neck and another reportedly bit the back of his neck before zoo staff and the father managed to free him. Zoo employees used a fire extinguisher to keep the cats at bay while a staffer lowered a ladder and retrieved the conscious, responsive child. An ambulance that had been staged at the zoo reached the scene quickly; the child was taken to Arkansas Children’s Hospital with extensive scalp lacerations, a depressed skull fracture and minor puncture wounds. Doctors said the wounds were not life-threatening and on Saturday the hospital reported the child was stable and expected to improve. The city and zoo say staff followed training during the rescue, an investigation is underway, and the zoo is accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums; USDA inspections recently found no violations. The family’s privacy is being respected.

A Bend, Oregon woman, 32-year-old January Irene Neatherlin, was sentenced March 9 to 21 years and 4 months in prison after pleading guilty to 11 counts of first-degree criminal mistreatment and one count of third-degree assault for operating an unlicensed day care, Little Giggles, and repeatedly endangering children in her care.

Case facts and conduct
- Police found seven children under age 5 alone in Neatherlin’s home on March 15, 2017; surveillance and tips from a former roommate and boyfriend showed she repeatedly left children unattended while going to a tanning salon, gym, or running errands.
- Investigators and prosecutors say she regularly gave children melatonin to keep them asleep during those absences. Parents were told not to drop off or pick up children between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. (“nap time”).
- Allegations include a range of injuries and neglect over several years: an 11-month-old taken to a Portland hospital with bleeding and swelling in the head consistent with shaken-baby injuries; a child scalded by overheated milk; bruises; persistent sleep problems in children given melatonin; and other signs of mistreatment.
- Neatherlin allegedly misrepresented qualifications (claimed to be a registered nurse and to be licensed), created fake documents, and has a long criminal history of theft and ID theft.

Sentencing hearing and reactions
- The sentencing hearing featured emotional testimony from many parents and grandparents describing lasting physical, emotional and financial harm: sleep-cycle disruption, ongoing therapy, loss of trust, marital/job impacts, and fear for their children’s safety.
- Prosecutors sought a 35-year sentence, characterizing her conduct as a prolonged, systematic scheme putting children at risk. Defense acknowledged guilty pleas and Neatherlin apologized repeatedly in court, expressing remorse and saying she loved the children but made “very poor calls.”
- Deschutes County Circuit Judge Wells Ashby said the testimony revealed “very tragic” consequences and “carnage” for families, noted Neatherlin’s pattern of lying and prior convictions, and emphasized community safety in imposing the 21-year-plus sentence. He also said Neatherlin has “a very long way to go” toward rehabilitation.
- Some parents urged the maximum punishment and said they feared she could not be rehabilitated; others expressed hopes of moving on and protecting their children.

Legal notes
- Neatherlin entered negotiated guilty pleas to 12 of 122 charges and faces a possible maximum of 60 years and substantial fines per her plea petition; she has 30 days to appeal.
- Prosecutors cited additional concerning post-arrest behavior, including attempts to recruit inmates to support false claims and solicit bail money through promises of offshore funds.

Overall, the case exposed an extended pattern of deception and child endangerment at an unlicensed day care, resulting in long prison time and broad emotional and practical fallout for affected families.

Israel expanded a ground offensive into the Gaza Strip amid continuing rocket fire by Hamas and no diplomatic breakthrough to halt fighting. The operation, launched late Thursday after 10–12 days of air and naval bombardment failed to stop rockets, aims to destroy Hamas’s tunnel network and weapons caches. Israeli forces reported uncovering at least 13 cross-border tunnels (some up to ~30 m deep), destroying dozens of rocket launchers and hitting hundreds of targets. Israel says the campaign has severely degraded Hamas’s arsenal, though militants continue to fire rockets into Israel (hundreds since the fighting began) and stage ground attacks.

Fighting on the ground has been fierce and at times audacious: Hamas fighters disguised in Israeli uniforms infiltrated through tunnels, ambushed patrols and killed Israeli soldiers; another attempt reportedly carried handcuffs and tranquilizers suggesting kidnapping intent. Israeli forces reported militants using antitank missiles, small arms, explosives and even an explosives-laden donkey. Since the ground offensive began, three Israeli soldiers and two civilians have been reported killed; dozens of soldiers were wounded. Israel says it has hit more than 300 Hamas targets during the ground phase.

Palestinian casualties and humanitarian distress have soared. Gaza Health Ministry tallies exceeded ~330–336 deaths (including large numbers of children) with thousands injured; UN and local officials say roughly 80% of casualties are civilians. Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced, with more than 60,000 seeking shelter in UN facilities and many areas without electricity or adequate water and medical supplies. Israel briefly opened the Erez crossing for medical aid amid concerns about shortages.

Diplomatic efforts to end hostilities have so far failed. Egypt’s ceasefire proposal was rejected by Hamas; mediators including Egypt, Qatar, France and the UN have been unable to secure a truce. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon planned to travel to the region to press for a ceasefire. Regional politics complicate the picture: while Hamas has expanded its military capabilities since earlier conflicts (2009, 2012), it faces weakened political and financial support from key allies after regional shifts following the Arab Spring.

The violence sparked international protests and strained press coverage in the area, with media organizations adjusting correspondents’ deployments after security concerns and public controversy. Both sides signaled readiness for continued operations: Israel warned the campaign could last up to weeks, while Hamas said it was replenishing weapons and prepared for a prolonged fight. Humanitarian agencies and world leaders expressed urgent concern about rising civilian tolls if the ground offensive pushes deeper into populated Gaza.

Two years after buying Tidal for $56 million, Jay Z has secured a major lifeline: Sprint has acquired a 33% stake in the streaming service, enabling Tidal to remain independent and better compete with larger rivals. Sources report the purchase was about $200 million. Under the deal, Tidal will be offered to Sprint’s roughly 45 million retail customers, Sprint CEO Marcelo Claure will join Tidal’s board, and the partners will collaborate on artist exclusives and marketing. A dedicated annual marketing fund for artist initiatives and exclusives is said to be $75 million. Current Tidal subscribers (around one million) will see no immediate service change, and Jay Z and the platform’s artist-owners remain stakeholders.

The alliance gives Tidal capital, distribution and promotional reach that analysts say it lacked compared with Spotify, Apple and Amazon, and comes amid prior reports of early struggles, mounting losses, subscriber-number scrutiny and takeover rumors. Jay Z described the partnership as aligned with Tidal’s goal to let artists connect directly with fans; Sprint framed it as a way to offer exclusive content and entertainment experiences to customers.

A Schenectady man, Michael Briggs, 38, has pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and attempted burglary in the December 2012 killing of 82-year-old retired nun Mary Greco. Briggs admitted strangling and stabbing Greco in her apartment; her body was found on New Year’s Day 2013. He had been doing snow-shoveling work for her days before the murder and later stole her car.

Investigators linked Briggs to the crime with multiple pieces of evidence: surveillance video showing him leaving home with a shovel and walking toward Greco’s residence; his fingerprints on a toilet seat, a coffee mug, a glass, and inside her car; and his DNA on the blanket covering her body. A rosary and crucifix given to Greco shortly before her death were missing.

Briggs, who lived nearby, was on parole at the time for a prior robbery and had a history of violent offenses, including a 1997-2007 prison term for robbery and a sexual assault allegation involving a minor. He accepted the plea a week before trial and is scheduled to be sentenced in June to 30 years to life. District Attorney Robert Carney said Briggs’ record and parole violation make future release unlikely.

The three-part Netflix series The Day I Met El Chapo: The Kate del Castillo Story, which premiered Friday, provoked objections from Sean Penn, who unsuccessfully sought edits to how his October 2015 meeting with Sinaloa cartel leader Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán is portrayed. Penn did not try to block the series, sources say; his primary concerns were that the show inaccurately suggests he alerted the U.S. Department of Justice about the meeting and that its depiction could endanger him. Penn’s spokesperson called the series’ allegations “fabrication[s]” and “bald-faced lie[s].” Producers and Netflix did not accede to his requests; producers say they never claimed Penn was “in cahoots” with the DOJ and say Penn was invited to participate but largely did not.

The series centers on Mexican actress Kate del Castillo’s role in arranging contact with Guzmán and includes interviews with her, family, journalists and officials. It was produced by 25/7 Productions and David Broome, and Netflix says it aimed to present del Castillo’s side of a story already widely reported, including Penn’s own Rolling Stone piece, which had been criticized.

Included in publicity for the project is Sean Penn’s lengthy first-person Rolling Stone account of his trip to meet El Chapo: vivid detail of clandestine travel into Sinaloa, his impressions of Guzmán and a recounting of their conversations and a later videotaped interview Guzmán provided. Penn’s article and the meeting previously sparked controversy over whether his contacts led to Guzmán’s capture; Penn has denied that he alerted authorities. Legal letters exchanged between Penn’s lawyers and the producers warned of danger and called del Castillo’s account “reckless,” while Netflix maintained Penn had multiple opportunities to participate and that the series’ purpose was to tell del Castillo’s perspective.

A Gold Coast lifeguard, Nick Malcolm, rescued 10-year-old Prince Christian of Denmark after the boy was swept off his feet by a strong current at Mermaid Beach on Thursday. The prince was swimming with his family between the flags in a patrolled area when a likely “flash rip” pulled him out; Malcolm paddled out on his board, put the boy on it and brought him back to shore. Malcolm did not initially know the identity of the child; Prince Frederik personally thanked him afterwards. Malcolm, a New Zealander based on the Gold Coast who trains in surf lifesaving sports, has declined media comment and returned to patrol duties. Officials stressed the incident highlights the importance of swimming in patrolled areas and the danger of rips, which cause many drownings in Australia each year. The Danish royal family is holidaying on the Gold Coast and will visit Tasmania next; Princess Mary is Australian-born.

Apple announced the long-delayed white iPhone 4 will be available starting tomorrow through Apple, Verizon, AT&T and authorized resellers in 16 GB ($199) and 32 GB ($299) models with two‑year contracts. The company framed the launch as finally getting “every detail right.”

Separately, Apple sought to clarify concerns about how iOS devices handle location data after researchers found a stored location-related cache. Apple said it never tracks customers’ iPhone locations and that some public confusion stems from users not understanding technical details of fast, accurate mobile location services. The company explained it maintains a crowd-sourced database of Wi‑Fi hotspots and cell towers gathered anonymously and encrypted from millions of iPhones; the cached data researchers saw are locations of nearby hotspots and towers (which can be far from the device), not a history of the device’s own movements.

Apple acknowledged bugs: the device cached the hotspot/tower database for too long, continued updating that data even when Location Services was turned off, and the cache wasn’t encrypted or excluded from backups. Apple committed to an iOS update within weeks to reduce the size of the cached database, encrypt it, stop backing it up, and delete it when Location Services are disabled.

The disclosure comes amid a class-action suit alleging invasion of privacy and “secretly recording movements,” and investigations by regulators in France, Germany, Italy and South Korea. Apple’s statements aim to reassure users, but questions remain about transparency and handling of the cached data.

A 16-year-old girl was killed Friday night after being ejected from a Sizzler carnival ride at a Dia De Los Niños Fiesta held at St. Thomas Aquinas Catholic Church in east El Paso. Two other teenage girls, ages reported between 15 and 18, were on the ride: one was also ejected and taken to University Medical Center with injuries described as non-life‑threatening; the third was not ejected and was treated at the scene. The fatality was transported to Del Sol Medical Center where she later died; friends and local reports identify her as Sam Aguilar, a Hanks High School student. Witnesses told reporters the girls had complained that a seat belt would not buckle and were told by the operator they were OK; the aunt of the uninjured teen said only two people were supposed to be in the ride at a time and her niece held on to the handle bar. El Paso Police’s Crimes Against Persons unit is investigating, and officials say the cause and whether required inspections were performed remain under review. The ride operator was Playtime Amusements Inc.; the Sizzler model has about 200 units in the U.S.

A Georgia Tech fraternity email instructing pledges how to “lure” and hook up with women has sparked an investigation and widespread condemnation. The message, reportedly sent last month by a member of Phi Kappa Tau’s Alpha Rho chapter and later circulated online, reads like a step‑by‑step “how‑to” for approaching women at parties: offering drinks, encouraging dancing that includes explicit touching, escalating to kissing and sexual contact, and advising to give women more alcohol if “anything ever fails.” It includes a seven‑step “7 E’s of Hooking Up” that culminates in “Ejaculate” and “Expunge (send them out of your room…when you are finished),” and signs off “in luring rape bait,” language students and observers described as explicitly rape‑apologetic and deeply offensive.

Women on campus called the email disturbing and threatening; one student said the tone essentially instructs men to keep intoxicating women until they can be taken to bed. The phrasing “rape bait” was singled out as particularly sickening. The fraternity’s national office called the email “extremely inappropriate” and said it does not reflect Phi Kappa Tau’s values. The chapter suspended the member who sent the email and placed the chapter on suspension while the fraternity and Georgia Tech investigate. Georgia Tech’s Office of Student Integrity and the campus Interfraternity Council are reviewing the matter; the university said it does not condone such behavior and is determining the facts. The incident prompted strong reactions online and comparisons to other fraternity/sorority controversies.

A college friend of Brock Turner, drummer Leslie Rasmussen, drew national outrage after a letter she wrote to the judge before Turner’s sentencing suggested the assault was “a huge misunderstanding,” blamed alcohol and cautioned against being “politically correct,” and argued Turner “is not a monster.” Judge Aaron Persky read portions of that and other character letters at sentencing; critics said the letters helped justify his light sentence of six months in county jail (rather than the statutory two-year prison minimum) after a jury convicted Turner of three felony sexual-assault counts for attacking an unconscious, intoxicated woman behind a dumpster on Stanford’s campus.

Rasmussen’s letter went viral and provoked accusations of victim-blaming and perpetuating rape culture. In the backlash, her band Good English was dropped from multiple festival and venue lineups and from its PR firm. Rasmussen issued an apology (first shared by the band and later on her personal Facebook), said she did not mean to minimize the victim’s suffering, acknowledged Turner’s conviction, and called her original comments a mistake she’d learn from.

Sentencing documents and reporting painted a broader pattern of concerning behavior by Turner: several incidents at parties where women felt uncomfortable or were grabbed, evidence of heavy drinking and drug use, and texts and phone content prosecutors cited. The documents also say Turner minimized his responsibility in statements to probation. Activists, including Stanford law professor Michele Dauber, have criticized Persky for weighing the character letters heavily and are leading a recall campaign against him; Persky has not publicly commented while appeals proceed.

Legally, Turner was convicted of assault-related charges (including sexual penetration with a foreign object of an intoxicated and unconscious person and intent to commit rape), not statutory “rape” under California’s narrower legal definition, though he is required to register as a sex offender for life. The case has sparked wide public debate about campus sexual assault, sentencing, victim-blaming, and the role of social media in amplifying and punishing out-of-court statements.

সংক্ষেপে: কমেডি সেন্টারের নতুন “The Daily Show” হোস্ট হিসেবে নিয়োগপ্রাপ্ত দক্ষিণ আফ্রিকান কমেডিয়ান ট্রেভর নোআকে তার পুরনো টুইটের কারণে তীক্ষ্ন সমালোচনার মুখে পড়তে হচ্ছে। অনেকে তাঁর টুইটে ইহুদী, ইস্রায়েল এবং নারীদের নিয়ে আপত্তিজনক কটাক্ষ এবং স্টেরিওটাইপিক মন্তব্য খুঁজে পেয়েছেন — উদাহরণ: ইহুদী ও ইস্রায়েল সম্পর্কিত অশ্লীল/নির্মম রসিকতা, ‘ওজনজুড়ে’ নারী ও যৌনকর্মী নিয়ে অবমাননাকর টপিক ইত্যাদি। রোজান বারসহ কয়েকজন সমালোচক সরাসরি নিন্দা জানিয়েছেন। কমেডি সেন্টার নোআকে সমর্থন জানিয়ে বলেছেন যে তিনি সীমা ধাক্কা দেন ও সকলকেই টার্গেট করে; কয়েকটি টুইটের ভিত্তিতে সমগ্র চরিত্র বিচার করা অনুচিত। নোআ নিজে প্রথমে একটি দ্রুত মুছে ফেলা টুইটে ইঙ্গিত করলেও পরে এক বিবৃতিতে বলেছে যে কিছু সতর্ক ব্যর্থ রসিকতা দিয়ে তাঁকে গণ্য করা তার প্রকৃত চরিত্র বা বিকাশকে প্রতিফলিত করে না। সংবাদপত্র ও কলামিস্টদের মধ্যে বিতর্ক আছে—কিছু লেখক বলেন এসব টুইট নব নিয়োগের ন্যায্যতা ও কমেডি সেন্টারের বিচার প্রক্রিয়া প্রশ্নবিদ্ধ করে, আবার কেউ এধরনের রসিকতাকে কমেডিয়ানদের টুইট পরীক্ষা-নিরীক্ষার অংশ হিসেবে দেখেন।

Pippa Middleton, 28 and sister of the Duchess of Cambridge, was photographed in Paris this weekend laughing as a male companion in her car pulled what looked like a semi-automatic pistol from the glovebox and aimed it at a paparazzo following them. The shot, taken while she rode in an Audi convertible with three male friends after attending a lavish costume party hosted by French designer-aristocrat Arthur (Vicomte) de Soultrait, prompted immediate media uproar and reports that French police might open a probe and that those involved could face charges.

Subsequent reporting tempered the alarm: ABC News said the photographer later told acquaintances the gun was fake and he never felt scared, and friends of one passenger said they now possess the toy weapon. De Soultrait’s company called the incident “a stupid joke.” Paris police told ABC News there is no formal investigation because no complaint has been filed; other outlets said at least one member of the public did file a complaint and judicial authorities were reportedly considering a preliminary inquiry.

The episode has drawn criticism because it came amid heightened concern about shootings in France and because Pippa — a high-profile private individual who has previously tried to curb paparazzi attention through legal warnings — appeared to smile in the photos, which some commentators called a misstep. Buckingham Palace declined to comment, noting Pippa is not a working royal. French law carries penalties if a real weapon was displayed (up to seven years’ imprisonment) or for using a fake gun in public (up to two years), so the legal outcome would depend on prosecutors’ assessment if and when a formal complaint is pursued.

California’s State Water Resources Control Board says Nestlé may lack legal rights to withdraw most of the water it bottles as Arrowhead from the San Bernardino National Forest. After a nearly two-year investigation prompted by complaints during the drought and reporting by the Desert Sun, regulators concluded that Nestlé’s average claimed extraction of 62.6 million gallons per year (1947–2015) far exceeds the roughly 8.5 million gallons (26 acre-feet/year) the company appears to have a valid right to take. The board says a “significant portion” of current diversions lacks a valid basis of right, and has ordered Nestlé to submit an interim compliance plan within 60 days and an investigation and monitoring plan within 90 days. Nestlé disputes the findings in part, saying the report affirms it holds valid rights to a “significant amount” of water and that it will comply with California law. Activists who sued or filed complaints welcomed the report; a related lawsuit and permit-renewal issues with the U.S. Forest Service remain part of broader challenges over the company’s historic claims and environmental impacts. The archive preserving these state agency documents is maintained by various California and university libraries and the California State Archives.

Tulane physical anthropologist John Verano joined Peruvian archaeologist Gabriel Prieto this year to expand excavations at a coastal dune site near Huanchaquito, Peru, where Prieto in 2011 uncovered a mass ritual sacrifice dated to about 600 years ago. The original find included 42 children and 76 young llamas; the new work has revealed additional sacrificial victims. The site dates to the Chimú state (ca. 1100–1470 A.D.). Researchers note the unusual nature of a large-scale child sacrifice on the Peruvian coast and suggest the event may have been an offering to the sea or a response to catastrophic flooding tied to an El Niño event; llamas may have been included to carry the dead to the afterlife. Erosion and local construction exposed bones on a sandy ridge roughly 100 yards from the beach. Multiple labs are now analyzing the bones and teeth to reconstruct the event and learn more about its meaning. Verano called the discovery exciting and atypical compared with previous finds of captive-killed adults.

The document argues that Hillary Clinton’s reputation as a policy wonk has long been undermined by a pattern of politically driven reversals that leave observers doubting whether she’ll make the right choices when under pressure. It recalls 2008, when many Democratic policy experts backed Barack Obama not because he knew more, but because they trusted him more to resist popular pressures — citing Clinton’s support for a temporary federal gas tax holiday (despised by economists) and her votes on Iraq as key examples. 

The piece then catalogs recent shifts by Clinton in the 2016 cycle — opposition to Obamacare’s “Cadillac tax,” breaking with earlier support for the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), and a wavering stance on the Keystone XL pipeline — arguing these moves look like poll-driven positioning rather than principled policy changes given her prior endorsements, advisers, and writings. While some reversals (e.g., opposing TPP) have short-term political benefits — shoring up unions and fending off left-wing challengers like Bernie Sanders — they reinforce the central political problem the author identifies: Clinton is perceived as overly calculating and unwilling to make unpopular but sensible choices. That perception, the piece contends, undermines her chief asset — her deep policy expertise — and raises doubts about how she would govern. 

The document also touches on related political news (Republican House speaker contest, Marco Rubio scrutiny) but centers on the argument that Clinton’s pattern of flip-flops damages trust among policy elites and voters who want leaders willing to act against short-term pressures for better long-term policy.

Christopher “Big Black” Boykin, best known as Rob Dyrdek’s friend and co-star on MTV’s reality series Rob & Big, died Tuesday at age 45, his representative confirmed. No official cause of death has been released; some sources connected to Boykin told TMZ they believe it was a heart attack. 

Boykin and Dyrdek starred together on Rob & Big from 2006–2008, documenting their day-to-day adventures (from adopting a mini-horse to breaking Guinness records). After leaving the shared household when Boykin became a father, he later appeared on Dyrdek’s follow-ups Fantasy Factory and Ridiculousness. Before television, Boykin served in the U.S. Navy and launched a clothing line called “Do work” in 2007.

MTV issued a statement expressing sadness and condolences. Celebrities who worked with him, including Chanel West Coast, tweeted tributes. Boykin is survived by his nine-year-old daughter, Isis.

Judy Shalom Nir-Mozes, a prominent Israeli media personality and wife of Interior Minister Silvan Shalom, sparked widespread outrage after tweeting a racist joke about U.S. President Barack Obama—“Do u know what Obama coffee is? Black and weak.” The post, seen and screen‑shot by many of her roughly 75,000 followers, drew hundreds of condemnatory responses calling it explicitly racist and especially insensitive in the wake of the racially motivated Charleston church massacre. Nir‑Mozes quickly deleted the tweet, apologized publicly—first calling it “a stupid joke somebody told me,” later addressing President Obama directly to say she “likes people no matter about their race and religion”—and made a light‑hearted remark hoping her husband would not divorce her over the incident. The episode revived scrutiny of past social‑media controversies involving her, including an earlier deleted tweet aimed at Obama and previous inflammatory comments about Palestinians that cost her a UNICEF Israel role.

A bill to lower Washington, D.C.’s voting age from 18 to 16 cleared the D.C. Council’s Committee on the Judiciary and Public Safety by a 3-0 vote and will move to the full Council for final consideration. If approved by the Council in the required two votes, signed by Mayor Muriel Bowser, and cleared through a 30‑day congressional review, the Youth Vote Amendment Act of 2018 would make D.C. the first U.S. municipality to allow 16- and 17‑year‑olds to vote in all elections, including federal contests such as the presidential race. 

Introduced in April by Ward 6 Councilmember Charles Allen and co‑sponsored by several colleagues, the measure draws on momentum from youth activism (notably after the Parkland shooting) and organized advocacy by Vote16DC. Supporters argue 16‑ and 17‑year‑olds shoulder adult responsibilities, vote at higher rates when enfranchised, and are more likely to form lifelong voting habits; opponents cite concerns about teens’ political knowledge and parental influence. About 70 public witnesses—mostly young people—testified in favor; none testified against. The DC Office of Planning estimates roughly 10,400 residents ages 16–17 (about 80% youth of color) would be newly eligible to vote. The full Council is expected to take up the bill later this month.

Archaeologists working at the Rimrock Draw Rockshelter near Riley in southeastern Oregon have uncovered a small orange agate scraper found about 12 feet down and roughly 8 inches beneath a layer of Mount St. Helens volcanic ash dated to about 15,800 years ago. If the stratigraphic context is secure, the tool would predate the Clovis horizon (~13,000 years ago) and could represent the oldest human occupation yet documented west of the Rockies.

Excavations by the Bureau of Land Management, the University of Oregon Archaeological Field School, and volunteers—ongoing since 2011—have also produced dozens of stemmed stone points (similar to those found at nearby Paisley Cave) and tooth enamel fragments likely from extinct camels. Blood-residue tests on the agate scraper showed proteins consistent with bovids, most likely Bison antiquus. The site sits against an ancient lava flow with deep, blackened deposits and an old streambed—features favorable for long-term human use.

Researchers describe the find as “tantalizing” but caution that extraordinary claims will require thorough testing: demonstrating the ash layer is continuous and undisturbed, ruling out vertical movement of the artifact, expanding the excavation, obtaining additional controlled finds, and publishing results for peer review. Two pre-Clovis sites (Paisley Cave and Monte Verde) are already well accepted, and Rimrock’s evidence, if validated, would push human presence in the region back by roughly 1,000–1,500 years. The team plans more excavation and analysis in upcoming field seasons.

An 11-year-old Northern California girl, Paige Warner of Roseville, died after a sudden, severe allergic/respiratory reaction while on a family Thanksgiving trip to Oahu, Hawaii. Paige, who had a history of food allergies and environmental sensitivities, swam in a pool at a Thanksgiving gathering on Nov. 27. Within 10–15 minutes of leaving the water she complained of a burning nose and throat swelling, used her inhaler without relief, and rapidly worsened. An EMT at the scene gave diphenhydramine and a first dose of epinephrine; 911 was called and paramedics arrived within minutes. In the ambulance and at Kapiolani Children’s Hospital she suffered respiratory failure and cardiac arrest, received prolonged CPR, was resuscitated, intubated, placed on life support and cooled to protect her brain.

Despite intensive care, repeat MRIs and tests showed progressive, catastrophic brain injury. After failing brain-death tests, she was pronounced medically dead on Dec. 4. Her family—mother Karin Carpenter, father Hank, sister Violet and relatives—spent her final hours with her. The exact trigger of the reaction remains unknown; the family and doctors have speculated about multiple possible contributors including the flight, new environmental allergens in Hawaii, a large feral cat population near where they stayed, possible pool pesticides/chemical runoff from an adjacent golf course, or a bronchospasm from cold water. Family members recounted her love of art and Christmas, and a GoFundMe for the family raised tens of thousands of dollars. A funeral was planned for January.

Here are the key stories and highlights from Mendocino County Today (July 23, 2015):

Bowe Bergdahl spotted during Redwood Valley marijuana raid
- Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl, the former POW now facing a military desertion charge, was visiting friends at a remote property in Redwood Valley when Mendocino County’s drug task force raided the site on July 21. Deputies seized 181 marijuana plants and made arrests, but Bergdahl was not involved in the grow. He presented military ID and an Army leave pass. County authorities contacted the military, and at the Pentagon’s request Bergdahl was escorted by Army personnel back to his duty station; he was not arrested.

Plowrights fined for creek damage
- Thomas R. Plowright III and Patricia Plowright must pay $25,000 after violating a 2011 Cleanup and Abatement Order for earthmoving and road work that caused sediment to discharge into Little Mill Creek (a Navarro River tributary important for steelhead and coho). The Regional Water Board found they failed to complete required cleanup and monitoring; all violations have since been remedied and the court adopted the judgment.

Obituaries and community notes
- Michael Albert Kisslinger, 60, former reporter for Mendocino County Public Radio and community activist, died July 20. Survived by his wife Anne Molgaard and two children; memorial details provided.
- Reminder: two Mendocino County Library workshops on communication/conflict management were canceled.

Local government and development concerns
- A proposed coast trash transfer station project (about $5 million) did not get final approval at a joint supervisors/City Council meeting; the hearing was postponed to Aug. 18 amid threatened Fish & Wildlife legal action and arguments that existing Pudding Creek facility could absorb the load.
- Friends of Outlet Creek raised alarm that the County approved a 500,000-ton-per-year asphalt plant in the Outlet Creek floodplain without CEQA review. They cite over $2 million spent on salmonid habitat restoration in the watershed and have filed suit seeking CEQA compliance; they requested support from CA Dept. of Fish and Wildlife.

Crime log and arrests
- Notable arrest: John Cooley Jr., 38, arrested in Fort Bragg for two counts of burglary, possession of burglary tools, offenses while on bail, and probation violation; bail set at $45,000. A roundup of other recent bookings was listed (DUIs, probation revocations, vehicle theft, meth sales, etc.).

Remembering Rosie Marie Grover (30th anniversary)
- Long feature recalling the 1985 rape and murder of 15-year-old Rosie Grover in Ukiah, the community response, conviction of Richard Dean Clark (on Death Row since 1987), and a new memorial dedication on the 30th anniversary. The case prompted changes in CHP policy on responding to calls for assistance.

Laytonville murders and wider coverage
- Local and Canadian coverage of a brutal attack that killed two and critically injured others in Laytonville. Suspect Talen Barton, 19, charged with murder, attempted murder and false imprisonment; one victim, Teo Palmieri, remembered as a promising Laytonville High senior.

Statewide wildlife policy debate
- California Fish and Game Commission scheduled to consider a statewide ban on commercial bobcat trapping (or a zonal buffer approach) at an Aug. 4–5 meeting in Fortuna. Environmental groups back a ban (citing international pelt markets and ethics), while some county boards and the Department of Fish and Wildlife favor zonal protections and better population data. Advocates say better bobcat population surveys are needed.

Health advisory
- First West Nile virus human case in Mendocino County since 2014 was reported; the patient is recovering and may have been infected out of county. Statewide first WNV death reported in Nevada County. Officials reminded residents about mosquito-avoidance precautions.

Other items
- An editorial-style online comment about Donald Trump’s 2015 presidential campaign tone was featured.
- A playful reprint of Gilbert & Sullivan’s “I Am the Very Model of a Modern Major-General” and a few photos and links punctuate the edition.

Overall tone: a mix of local crime and court reporting, environmental and land-use disputes, community remembrances, and regional/state policy debates.

Vili Fualaau has filed for legal separation from his wife Mary Kay Letourneau, according to Washington State court records dated May 9 and confirmed by RadarOnline. Fualaau, 33, told Radar the filing is intended to protect business interests and does not mean the marriage is over — he said they remain in love and that rumors of trouble are false. He explained the move is tied to background checks required for his potential licensing as a distributor for marijuana-cigarette brand “Cigaweed,” which would vet both spouses; Letourneau’s criminal history (she served over seven years in prison for a sexual relationship with Fualaau when he was her sixth-grade student) could complicate that process.

Letourneau, 55, reportedly filed paperwork seeking dismissal of the separation petition just hours after news broke; her filing did not state a legal basis. Vili’s attorney said he intends to proceed with the petition and declined to comment on whether it signals a future divorce. The couple married in 2005 and have two children; Letourneau has four children from a previous marriage. Story is developing.

- As of Jan. 13 (reporting week Jan. 7–13, 2018) the CDC had recorded 30 pediatric flu-associated deaths; the true number may be higher because of reporting delays and variable state reporting. The CDC planned to release updated pediatric death data on Jan. 26.

- Experts say it’s too early to know whether this season will produce more child deaths than usual. Historically the U.S. records about 100–300 pediatric flu deaths per season (likely an underestimate). Officials expect the count to rise as the season continues and believe the season may not have peaked.

- Vaccination remains the primary protection for children. Although this season’s vaccine is a poor match for one severe strain (estimated 10–30% effectiveness against that strain), it can lessen illness severity and overall reduce risk (the CDC cites up to ~60% reduction in some contexts). About 80–85% of children who died from flu in past seasons were not vaccinated.

- There is enough vaccine supply nationally; providers may need to source different brands or presentations if their usual supply is unavailable.

- Local reports (Cuyahoga County/Cleveland Clinic area) note increased hospitalizations—around 930 this season including Akron General totals—and several adult deaths. Clinicians stress watching for warning signs in children (persistent/recurrent fever, difficulty breathing, trouble staying awake) and that vaccine protection takes about two weeks to develop.

- Conclusion: the season is active and potentially severe; vaccination and prompt medical attention for concerning symptoms are recommended while more weeks of data are needed to determine the season’s eventual severity.

The AFAJP posted a video urging support for an Onion Pulitzer via a petition and user-uploaded videos. The organization’s president, Stephen Forbeck, was interviewed on ABC Nightly News. Though the reporter treated the issue somewhat lightly, the appearance demonstrated that AFAJP has a composed, determined leader and that awareness of the group is growing — signaling momentum for changing how journalism awards are decided.

This roundup looks at people and brands whose “fame stock” rose sharply this week thanks to publicity, celebrity attention or tragic news.

- AshleyMadison: The adultery website sponsored Howard Stern’s “Miss Mistress” pageant, a move its founder says produced millions in free advertising. The company claims a 22% revenue increase and 27% growth in memberships in the 55 days after the announcement versus the 55 days before.

- Sarah Killen and associated vendors: When Conan O’Brien made Sarah the single person he follows on Twitter, her profile exploded—roughly 19,000 new followers and a cascade of gifts and offers (a new iMac, wedding gown, rings, donations, connections such as meeting Ludacris). Dressmaker Kelima K donated a wedding dress in return for Sarah promoting The Children’s Hunger Fund, showing how small vendors can gain exposure via celebrity attention.

- Corey Feldman: The death of Corey Haim has prompted renewed attention on Feldman, who has given high-profile interviews (Larry King) about his late friend. Though the circumstances are tragic, Feldman’s visibility has increased—raising questions about whether he’ll continue to capitalize on the attention.

- Steve Holmes: A 19-year-old U.S. student suddenly gained fame when Kanye West followed him on Twitter and sent a cryptic message. Holmes’s followers jumped from about 60 to thousands within hours, drawing global media attention and an overwhelming influx of messages.

The piece highlights how modern media—especially Twitter and televised stunts—can quickly elevate obscure people and businesses, turning fleeting attention into tangible gains for some and complicated publicity for others.

TMZ and Los Angeles County officials report that actress Brittany Murphy's autopsy is complete and showed no signs of trauma or foul play; the body appeared "normal" and not overly thin. The coroner is deferring an official cause of death pending toxicology, histopathology and neuropathology results, which are expected in about 4–6 weeks. Authorities say Murphy, 32, died suddenly of cardiac arrest and reportedly experienced internal bleeding before death; she was taking prescription medications for medical conditions. The LAPD has finished its initial inquiry and found no evidence of a crime.

In a cave called Bruniquel in southwest France, researchers have determined that two stone rings made from hundreds of deliberately broken and arranged stalagmite pieces were constructed about 176,500 years ago — far older than any previously well-dated human-built structures. The features, discovered in 1990 but long understudied, lie deep in the cave (about 336 meters/368 yards from the entrance), are composed of cut and similarly sized stalagmite pillars laid into two ovals up to 40 cm high, and show traces of fire. Early work had carbon-dated a burned bear bone to about 47,600 years, but that method was near its limit; a 2013 team led by stalagmite specialists used uranium-series dating on stalagmite cross-sections to date when the formations were broken and found the much older age.

Because modern humans were not in the region then, the builders must have been Neanderthals. The find implies Neanderthals could control fire, penetrate and navigate deep, dark caves, organize cooperative activity, and create structured constructions—behaviors long underappreciated for the species. The purpose of the rings remains unknown; researchers suggest symbolic or ritual functions are possible but unproven. The discovery, published in Nature, challenges assumptions about Neanderthal cognitive and social complexity and suggests their material culture — much of which would not survive in open sites — may be richer than previously recognized.

Canadian pop star Justin Bieber and his entourage were asked to leave the Mayan archaeological site at Tulum after he reportedly tried to climb onto one of the ruins, a National Institute of Anthropology and History official said. The official, speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to be named, did not identify which structure was involved. While some pre-Hispanic pyramids in Mexico are open for visitors to climb, others are roped off or marked “no entry” due to fragility; those protections were in place at Tulum. The visit occurred Thursday, and comes after other incidents involving Bieber in Latin America in recent years.

GQ published a provocative piece titled “21 Books You Don’t Have to Read,” in which writers argue that many canonical “Great Books” have not aged well—some because they’re racist or sexist, many because they’re simply boring—and suggest contemporary or overlooked alternatives. Contributors pair 21 classics with recommended replacements, often favoring more diverse, modern, or emotionally nuanced works. Examples include replacing Lonesome Dove with Jean Stafford’s The Mountain Lion, The Catcher in the Rye with Dorothy Strachey’s Olivia, The Old Man and the Sea with Tove Jansson’s The Summer Book, The Lord of the Rings with Ursula K. Le Guin’s Earthsea series, and the Bible with Agota Kristof’s The Notebook. The piece’s claim that readers don’t need to read the Bible—calling it “repetitive, self-contradictory, sententious, foolish” and suggesting Kristof’s novella instead—provoked sharp backlash from Christian figures and social media users. Critics including Fox’s Father Jonathan Morris and evangelist Franklin Graham defended the Bible’s importance; others condemned GQ’s judgment as offensive or dismissive. GQ did not immediately comment.

Aldabra giant tortoise Abuh (also reported as “Abu”), a roughly 35-year-old, ~1‑metre, 55‑kg female, has been found safe two weeks after escaping Shibukawa Zoo in Okayama Prefecture. Abuh had been allowed to roam the park during visiting hours and slipped away on August 1. The zoo offered a ¥500,000 (≈$4,500) reward; a local — variously reported as a “bounty hunter” or a family — spotted her within a short distance of the zoo (reports say about 50–140 metres away) on August 16. Abuh was in good health, ate pears and watermelon on return, and this was her second disappearance in under a month. Zoo staff said they were relieved and will introduce new measures to prevent further escapes. Reports also discussed how far a giant tortoise could theoretically travel in that time, noting their slow but steady pace.

Researchers from the University of Nottingham and the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare swabbed frequently touched surfaces and the air at Helsinki-Vantaa airport during winter 2016 to identify respiratory viruses. Using genetic detection methods, they found viral material on about 10% of samples, most often on the plastic security-check trays used for hand luggage. Other contaminated sites included shop payment terminals, staircase rails, passport counters, children’s play areas and the air; toilet surfaces showed no respiratory viruses. Rhinovirus (common cold) was the most frequently detected pathogen and influenza A was also found. The study emphasizes that the detection of viral genetic material does not prove those viruses were infectious, but prior research shows many microbes can survive on surfaces for days. Authors say the findings support stronger public-health measures at busy transport hubs—improved hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, more frequent cleaning of high-touch surfaces, and provision of hand-sanitizing stations—plus consideration of design or technical changes in airports to reduce transmission risk. The work was part of the EU-funded PANDHUB project and is published in BMC Infectious Diseases.

The Walton family and the Walmart Museum have sued Helen Huff, widow of Arkansas photographer David A. Huff, seeking possession of about 200 photographs, negatives and proofs taken of the Walton family and early Wal‑Mart from 1950–1994. The Waltons (filing as Crystal Lands, LLC, and Wal‑Mart Stores, Inc.) say the studio kept the materials only “as a courtesy” and that the images are company/family property and should not be sold or commercially used by Huff. Huff counters that she holds the copyrights; she says her husband and father‑in‑law worked as independent contractors who supplied equipment, controlled shoots, developed film and even gave the Waltons copyright notices asserting the studio’s rights. Huff has filed a federal counterclaim seeking to stop Wal‑Mart from using the photos without permission.

The dispute centers on whether the photos were “works for hire” (which would vest ownership with the Waltons absent a written contract) or independently created photographs owned by the photographers. The Professional Photographers of America supports Huff, calling the case a “David vs. Goliath” fight and citing precedent (Natkin v. Winfrey) where courts ruled photographers owned copyrights when no work‑for‑hire agreement existed. Wal‑Mart says it tried to resolve the matter privately; PPA reports an alleged $2,000 offer to Huff that she declined. The federal court scheduled case management and set a trial term for April 2015 (case management hearing July 7 noted earlier). The outcome could affect photographers’ copyright rights in similar situations.

A British self-described “email prankster” using the handle @SINON_REBORN duped multiple Trump White House figures by impersonating senior officials over email, CNN reports. Posing as Jared Kushner, the prankster convinced Homeland Security Adviser Tom Bossert to reply and even provided his personal email address. Using other fake identities (including Reince Priebus, Jon Huntsman Jr., Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr.), he engaged White House Communications Director Anthony Scaramucci in heated exchanges and tricked Huntsman and members of the Trump family into correspondence. Scaramucci’s responses to the bogus Priebus and Huntsman messages are shown in the shared emails.

White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the administration is taking the incidents seriously and is investigating. Cybersecurity experts told CNN the episodes illustrate how vulnerable officials are to spear-phishing and social-engineering attacks, even when no malicious links were clicked in these cases. The prankster told CNN his intent was mischief rather than harm; he said he received no law-enforcement contact after emailing Eric Trump.

Scientists have reconstructed global sea-level changes over roughly the last 3,000 years and find that the 20th-century rise was exceptionally rapid and largely driven by human-caused warming.

Key findings
- Global mean sea level (GSL) was relatively stable for millennia with natural variability of roughly ±7–11 cm before the 20th century. Small multidecadal rises and falls corresponded to known climate fluctuations (e.g., a decline 1000–1400 CE tied to ~0.2 °C cooling).
- The 20th century saw a GSL rise of about 14 cm (1.4 mm/yr on average), and statistical analysis shows with ≥95% probability that this century-scale increase was faster than in any of the previous 27 centuries for which data are available.
- Semiempirical modeling calibrated to the reconstructed GSL and temperature records indicates it is extremely likely that without anthropogenic warming the 20th-century rise would have been between a 3 cm fall and a 7 cm rise—far less than observed.
- Combining diverse proxy records (from salt marshes, coral, archaeological indicators) at 24 locations with 66 tide gauges, the authors produced a spatiotemporal hierarchical reconstruction that accounts for regional effects (land motion, ocean dynamics, gravitational fingerprints).
- The dominant contributors to 20th-century rise were thermal expansion of warming oceans and mountain-glacier loss; however, in the 21st century large ice sheets (Greenland, Antarctica) may play an increasingly important and uncertain role.

21st-century projections and implications
- Using the semiempirical model with RCP temperature scenarios, projected GSL rise by 2100 (relative to 2000) is:
  - RCP8.5 (high emissions): likely 52–131 cm
  - RCP4.5 (moderate mitigation): likely 33–85 cm
  - RCP2.6 (strong mitigation): likely 24–61 cm
- These projections overlap more with the IPCC AR5 process-model ranges than earlier semiempirical studies, but both approaches may underestimate risk if rapid ice-sheet processes (e.g., West Antarctic instabilities) accelerate.
- Even a few inches of human-caused sea-level rise already have substantial impacts: a companion analysis found that thousands of U.S. “nuisance” coastal floods since 1950 would not have occurred without the human contribution to sea-level rise. In many U.S. locations, recent decades’ floods are now tipped into occurrence largely because of the added inches from warming.

Methods and robustness
- The reconstruction integrates high-resolution proxy records and long tide-gauge records using a Gaussian-process–based empirical hierarchical model that separates global mean sea-level signal from regional linear and nonlinear components, with sensitivity tests across multiple priors and data subsets.
- Two independent temperature reconstructions were used to calibrate the semiempirical model; results are robust to various sensitivity checks though spatial proxy coverage is incomplete (notably sparse in much of Asia, South America, and Africa).

Conclusions
- The 20th-century sea-level rise is exceptional in the context of the last three millennia and is largely attributable to anthropogenic warming. Future sea-level rise this century is projected to exceed that of the 1900s under all emissions scenarios considered, and strong mitigation could substantially reduce—but not eliminate—century-scale rise. Major uncertainties remain about contributions from rapid ice-sheet disintegration, which could increase risks beyond modeled ranges.

Spencer West, a 31-year-old born with sacral agenesis who had both legs amputated below the pelvis as a child, successfully reached the summit of Mount Kilimanjaro to raise awareness and funds for clean water in Kenya. Over eight days (reported as seven in some accounts) he covered roughly 20,000 “steps,” spending about 80% of the climb propelling himself hand over hand, sometimes using a custom wheelchair or riding on porters when terrain allowed. He trained for a year with two friends and a support team of about 50 people, including guides and porters.

West’s climb was part of his “Redefine Possible” campaign and a fundraising effort to raise $750,000 (about $500,000 raised before the ascent) for Free the Children to build boreholes and provide clean water to tens of thousands affected by severe drought in Kenya and neighboring countries. He hopes his achievement will inspire others to overcome challenges; he now works as a motivational speaker with Me to We and uses his story to promote service and possibility. Despite fatigue, bruised hands and teammates’ altitude sickness, West described summiting as humbling and life-changing.

Records released by the Seminole County Sheriff’s Office show that while out on $1 million bond and wearing a court-ordered GPS ankle monitor, George Zimmerman sought to buy a bulletproof vest and an infrared home-security device, saying they were for his protection. The 57‑page monitoring log—active from July 6, 2012, through July 13, 2013—also documents routine check‑ins by phone every other day, multiple moves by Zimmerman and his wife Shellie, and frequent trips outside Seminole County to meet with attorneys in Orlando (permitted under his release conditions). Deputies were alerted to the vest and security device purchase by a sales representative from a police-supply store; Zimmerman later confirmed the purchases. The log contains other minor entries, such as Zimmerman changing phone numbers after media exposure and deputies reviewing sporting‑goods store surveillance to confirm he did not enter a firearms area. Zimmerman was acquitted last month in the 2012 fatal shooting of 17‑year‑old Trayvon Martin.

Iowa police are handing out colorful thumb bands reading "TXTNG KILLS" to discourage texting while driving as part of the statewide "X the TXT" awareness push tied to a new law that took effect July 1. The state ordered 30,000 bands (with plans for 30,000 more) in black, blue and bright pink and is distributing them at places like the Iowa State Fair, high school and college football games, and during traffic stops; some counties have given batches to deputies to hand out. For the first year of the law officers can only warn offenders; fines start next year. Officials say catching people in the act is difficult—drivers often warn others when police are nearby—and hope the bands provide a visible, youth-friendly reminder. The effort mirrors national campaigns (including Allstate’s "X the TXT") and comes amid broader trends: 30 states ban texting while driving and distracted driving contributed to nearly 6,000 deaths in 2008.

A government shutdown grew increasingly likely as conservative activists and tea-party House Republicans pressured Speaker John Boehner to refuse the Senate’s stopgap funding bill because it preserves funding for the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare). The Senate passed a two-month continuing resolution Friday that funds the government and does not defund or delay Obamacare; Senate Democrats, led by Harry Reid, say any House alterations would be the cause of a shutdown. Conservatives warn Boehner’s leadership would be at risk if he accepts the Senate bill, and activists have mobilized nationwide calls urging House Republicans to demand Obamacare defunding or delay. Hardliners including Sens. Ted Cruz and Mike Lee and a faction of House members pushed amendments to block or delay the law’s individual mandate starting Oct. 1.

Boehner faced competing pressures: rank-and-file conservatives demanding tougher language (options under consideration included delaying the mandate, cutting lawmaker/staff subsidies, repealing the medical device tax, or eliminating the IPAB) and Senate Democrats and the White House refusing to accept policy riders to the short-term funding measure. With both sides unwilling to yield and little active negotiation, aides in both parties increasingly expected a partial shutdown beginning Tuesday if Congress did not approve funding. Even if a shutdown is averted, leaders face a separate debt-limit showdown expected by mid-October.

Agencies spent the week preparing for shutdown contingencies. A partial closure would furlough large portions of the civilian federal workforce (estimates around 40% of nondefense employees), suspend many services (national parks, some permits, passport/visa processing, certain courts), and complicate Defense Department civilian operations though active-duty troops would remain deployed. Entitlement programs (Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid) would continue. The Treasury warned the government could hit the borrowing limit by Oct. 17, raising stakes for a looming debt-ceiling confrontation.

Max Lomas, a longtime friend and one-time housemate of Bobbi Kristina Brown, has died of an apparent drug overdose. Lomas — who lived off and on with Brown, her partner Nick Gordon, and others after Whitney Houston’s death — first spoke publicly about the chaotic, drug-fueled environment surrounding Brown in the weeks before he found her unconscious in a bathtub on January 31, 2015. In an exclusive PEOPLE interview, he described heavy drug use, parties, frequent fights (often over jealousy) between Brown and Gordon, and a failed attempt at sobriety shortly before the incident. Lomas said Gordon at times became abusive toward Brown, a claim Gordon’s lawyers have denied.

Lomas had been romantically involved with Brown earlier and said Houston had taken him in as a troubled teen. He recalled that family members, including Brown’s aunt Pat Houston and her father Bobby Brown, planned an intervention that ultimately never occurred. Lomas and Gordon performed CPR on Brown after pulling her from the tub; she later remained in a coma for six months and died in hospice care at 22 on July 26, 2015. Brown’s family later won a $36 million wrongful-death civil suit against Gordon; no criminal charges were filed against Lomas.

According to reports, Lomas was found unconscious in a friend’s bathroom with a syringe nearby and was taken to a Mississippi hospital, where he died. Page Six contacted his attorney for comment.

Joel Davis, a General Studies student at Columbia who had been a prominent sexual-assault-prevention activist — cofounder of Youth to End Sexual Violence, chairman of the International Campaign to Stop Rape and Gender Violence, and a 2017 Spectator columnist — was arrested in Manhattan on June 26, 2018 on federal charges of possessing child pornography and attempting to sexually exploit minors, including children as young as two. Authorities say Davis confessed to prior sexual abuse of a 13-year-old boy and admitted to keeping child porn on his phone; an affidavit alleges weeks of explicit text exchanges with undercover officers in which he sought photos and videos of a nine-year-old and described intended sexual acts involving a nine‑year‑old and a two‑year‑old. FBI officials called the alleged conduct a profound hypocrisy given his advocacy work. Davis could face up to 70 years in prison. The article corrects an earlier erroneous claim that he was a Nobel Peace Prize nominee.

The piece also contains a separate, personal column describing life at Columbia’s School of General Studies: its student body of nontraditional students who often carry histories of trauma, the challenges of belonging between traditional and nontraditional campus cultures, and the importance of peer support among GS students. A byline identifies Joel Davis as an ancient studies major, chair of the International Campaign to Stop Rape, author, and (incorrectly, as corrected) a Nobel nominee — details reflecting that portion’s original publication as a personal column.

Video of Pope Francis laying hands on a wheelchair-bound Mexican man during Mass in St. Peter’s Square sparked debate over whether the pope performed an exorcism. The man convulsed and heaved after Francis prayed over him; the Italian bishops’ TV station initially reported several exorcists said there was “no doubt” it was an exorcism or a liberation prayer, but its director later apologized for mischaracterizing the event. The Vatican said Francis did not intend to perform an exorcism, only to pray for a suffering person, and the priest who brought the man also called it a prayer for liberation rather than a formal rite.

Former Vatican exorcist Gabriele Amorth insisted the event was an exorcism, claiming he later performed his own exorcism on the man and found four demons, linking the case to Mexico City’s abortion legalization. Other theologians and exorcists said the pope’s touch and words could constitute an exorcism or a simpler “liberation” prayer; the Vatican stresses intention and cautions distinguishing spiritual problems from psychological illness. The episode highlights Pope Francis’ frequent references to the devil and a renewed interest in exorcism within parts of the Church.
