Republican nominee Donald Trump made a surprise visit to Mexico City to meet President Enrique Peña Nieto — his first foreign trip as the party’s nominee — and afterward and at a joint news conference struck a markedly more diplomatic tone than in much of his campaign rhetoric. Both described the meeting as “open,” “constructive” and substantive. Trump defended the U.S. right to build a secure border and said each country has the right to erect a physical barrier to stop illegal movement of people, drugs and weapons, but he declined to press his repeated campaign promise that Mexico would pay for a U.S. border wall, saying financing “didn’t come up.” Peña Nieto stressed shared interests, highlighted the mutual economic ties and jobs created by trade, challenged Trump’s depiction of the border situation (noting illegal immigration has fallen) and said many of Trump’s past comments “have hurt” Mexicans, while also calling the discussion sincere and constructive.

The visit provoked protests and criticism in Mexico and from political figures including former presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón, who called Trump unwelcomed and untrustworthy. Back in the U.S., Democrats seized on the trip: Hillary Clinton said a short visit cannot undo a “year of insults,” and Tim Kaine and others said Trump’s record makes softening unlikely. Trump’s running mate Mike Pence defended the trip as evidence of decisiveness and said the wall’s logistics would be discussed; campaign officials later insisted Trump still intends that those here illegally must leave.

The trip came hours before Trump’s much-anticipated immigration speech in Phoenix and followed weeks of mixed signals from his campaign on deportations and border policy. Observers saw the Mexico visit as a calculated attempt to show presidential composure and frame immigration messaging, even as many doubt it will repair damage done with Hispanic voters.

This article compiles reactions from many entertainers who said they would leave the United States if Donald Trump were elected president. Published amid the 2016 campaign and updated after Trump’s victory, it catalogs dozens of celebrities—actors, musicians, comedians and activists—who jokingly or seriously pledged to relocate to places such as Canada (Vancouver, Nova Scotia), Europe (Spain, France, Italy, Iceland), Africa, Australia, the Caribbean, or even another planet (Jon Stewart/Jon Stewart’s rocket, Cher’s Jupiter). High-profile names include Lena Dunham, Miley Cyrus, Jon Stewart, Chelsea Handler, Neve Campbell, Raven-Symoné, Whoopi Goldberg, Samuel L. Jackson, George Lopez, Amy Schumer, Barbra Streisand, Cher, Spike Lee, Al Sharpton, Barbara Streisand, Rosie O’Donnell and others. The piece notes gag campaigns like “Cape Breton If Donald Trump Wins,” reports responses from Trump’s sons (offering to buy airfare), and highlights several colorful quotes—ranging from practical plans to hyperbolic reactions—illustrating celebrity alarm and outrage at the prospect of a Trump presidency.

From today the opioid-receptor drug nalmefene (brand name Selincro) is recommended by the UK’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and may be prescribed for people who regularly drink above low‑risk levels (defined here as about 7.5 units/day for men and 5 units/day for women). It is intended for people who want to reduce their drinking rather than for those who need to stop immediately; it reduces the urge to drink and is licensed to be taken up to once daily on days when the patient feels at risk of drinking. NICE recommends nalmefene be used alongside psychosocial support or counselling; clinical-economics assessment found the combination is cost‑effective for the NHS compared with counselling alone.

The pill is supplied in 14‑tablet packs (about £42.42 per pack, roughly £3 per day). NICE expects up to about 35,000 people might receive nalmefene in the first year based on estimates of those receiving psychosocial interventions, though early uptake in Scotland was low (53 prescriptions in 2013/14), and actual numbers may be lower if patients opt for non‑pharmacological routes. Experts emphasise it targets people who regularly drink above recommended limits and who have already engaged with brief advice or therapy, not casual moderate drinkers.

On March 22, 2016 Arizona’s presidential primary produced unusually long voting lines in Maricopa County after officials cut polling places from 200 in 2012 to just 60 this year, citing budget limits and an expectation of increased mail voting. The Associated Press obtained county records showing many sites stayed open long after the official 7 p.m. closing time: voters were still casting ballots at 10 p.m. or later at 20 locations, five sites remained open past midnight, and the last ballot in one location was cast at 12:58 a.m. Some voters waited up to nearly six hours; one man spent four hours in line and others waited until 1 a.m.

The long waits have prompted a U.S. Justice Department inquiry seeking documents and explanations — including how officials decided the number of polling places and whether minority voters were disproportionately affected — after a complaint from Phoenix’s mayor. Arizona Secretary of State Michele Reagan certified the primary results for Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump despite acknowledging problems (including some voters being left off rolls), noting she had no authority to reject county canvasses; certification opens a five-day window for legal challenges. Lawyers for Bernie Sanders are considering a challenge, arguing provisional ballots and mislisted voters may have affected delegate allocations.

A bankrupt New Mexico peanut-processing company, Sunland Inc., is at the center of two linked developments: the destruction of nearly a million jars of peanut butter and renewed bidding over the shuttered Portales plant.

Peanut butter disposal
- Trustee Clarke Coll arranged for about 950,000 jars (roughly 25 tons) of peanut butter to be hauled to the Curry County landfill in Clovis and buried because Costco, which had supplied $2.8 million worth of Valencia peanuts used to make the product, refused to accept further shipments.  
- Costco initially agreed by court order to take and test the product, but after receiving eight loads rejected it as “not merchantable” due to leaky peanut oil and stated during a conference call it would only accept destruction.  
- Coll and others maintain the product presented no health or safety issue; its estimated value was about $2.6 million, and the estate is paying roughly $60,000 to dispose of it. Requests to donate, repackage or sell to institutional brokers were declined.  
- Sunland’s plant was previously linked to a 2012 salmonella outbreak that led to widespread recalls and a temporary shutdown; the company filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy last October.

Asset sale and reopened auction
- After an initial courtroom auction in which Hampton Farms outbid Ready Roast Nut Co. with $20.05 million, a late $25 million offer from Canadian company Golden Boy Foods arrived minutes before final approval. Golden Boy wired the funds and asked to reenter bidding.  
- Bankruptcy Judge David Thuma reopened bidding, saying he could not ignore the extra $5 million that would better serve creditors. Golden Boy’s $25 million will serve as the opening bid when the auction resumes; final approval will be considered in a later hearing.  
- Both Hampton Farms and Golden Boy say they would resume production at the Portales facility. Trustee Coll and counsel say the higher bid will help pay secured and unsecured creditors; Sunland’s debts include about $21 million in secured claims and an estimated $40 million in unsecured claims.  
- Golden Boy had previously expressed interest and visited the facility last year but withdrew during its own corporate sale; it renewed its bid after getting corporate approval.

Background
- Sunland, once the nation’s largest organic peanut butter producer and a supplier to retailers including Costco, Trader Joe’s and Target, was linked to a 2012 salmonella outbreak affecting dozens of people and recalled hundreds of products. The plant later briefly resumed production but ultimately entered Chapter 7 liquidation amid financial troubles.

Overall, the case highlights continued fallout from the 2012 outbreak: large quantities of finished product are being destroyed amid liability/merchantability disputes, while creditors and potential buyers contest the best path to maximize value from the company's assets.

MaineDOT ran a “My Maine Sign” contest inviting the public to submit short, safety-themed, punny messages for the electronic highway message signs. The contest, which drew more than 2,000 entries and closed March 18, sought messages that discourage distracted or impaired driving, speeding, seatbelt neglect and other road hazards. Officials selected finalists and put them to a public vote; finalists received transportation-related prizes and the two grand-prize winners (one per sign size) got a personalized street sign. Six winning messages were announced in late May — three for small signs and three for large signs — including entries such as “Put Down UR Cell — Or You May End Up In One,” “Spend Money On Lobstahs — Not Speeding Tickets,” “Little Known Fact — Snow Is Really Slippery,” “A Cold Suppah Is Bettah Thana Hot Ticket,” “Be Protected — Not Projected – Buckle Up,” and “Keep In Mind — Moose Eyes Don’t Shine.” The DOT plans to rotate sign messages every couple weeks and archive good submissions for future use.

Police on Mackinac Island are investigating an alleged barroom assault between campaign aides for Republican presidential hopefuls. Early Friday, John Yob — national political director and Michigan strategist for Rand Paul — posted that Rich Beeson, deputy campaign manager for Marco Rubio, punched him at Horn’s Bar during the Mackinac Republican Leadership Conference. Yob said he has video from multiple angles and later provided a grainy clip to CNN; police say they have not yet reviewed that footage but have taken witness statements and bar security video. Mackinac Island Police Chief Brett Riccinto said the matter and Yob’s complaint have been forwarded to the county prosecutor, who will decide whether charges are filed. Beeson did not comment, and Michigan State Police are not involved; the incident echoes a past well-known Horn’s Bar altercation.

A New Jersey mother, Tricia Fraser, has sued anti-abortion ad firm Heroic Media (Majella Cares) and the group Life Always after a 2009 photo of her then-4-year-old daughter Anissa was used without her approval on a controversial billboard near Manhattan’s Holland Tunnel reading, “The most dangerous place for an African American is in the womb.” Fraser says she responded to a NYCastings posting for family modeling and only signed a release for stock family photos; Getty Images later licensed the image to Heroic Media with a restriction against use “in connection with a subject that would be unflattering or unduly controversial.” The suit alleges those terms were violated and that neither she nor her daughter consented to association with an “offensive, defamatory, and racist” political campaign aimed at discouraging abortion access. Fraser says the ad—also displayed in Jacksonville, Fla.—triggered widespread media attention and protests, forced awkward conversations with her child, caused emotional distress, and damaged Anissa’s budding modeling career. The complaint seeks punitive damages under New York civil rights law, disgorgement of any profits, and an injunction barring further use of the child’s image. Heroic Media, Life Always and pastor Stephen Broden have not yet commented.

The Federal Reserve left policy unchanged at its two-day meeting, taking no new stimulus measures but signaling readiness to act if labor-market gains falter. In a firmer-than-June statement, the Fed noted that economic growth had slowed and would likely remain “moderate over coming quarters,” and that unemployment was expected to fall only slowly. It reaffirmed its near-zero federal funds rate target (0–0.25%) and its pledge to keep rates exceptionally low “at least until late 2014,” and repeated ongoing balance-sheet measures (including Operation Twist and continued bond purchases through year-end).

The FOMC vote was 11–1, with Richmond Fed President Jeffrey Lacker dissenting. Markets reacted negatively, with major U.S. stock indices slipping after the announcement. Officials and outside economists are divided on whether further easing is inevitable: many expect the Fed to act at its September meeting if July–August jobs reports show weak employment, while others say the central bank’s tools have limits and may not materially offset weak fiscal policy, tight credit or high household debt. Chairman Bernanke will have the opportunity to clarify policy thinking at the Jackson Hole conference in late August.

Britain flew an RAF plane to Cyprus carrying one million euros in cash as a contingency to give emergency loans to roughly 3,000 UK service personnel and their families if Cypriot banks or ATMs become inaccessible amid the island’s bailout crisis. The Ministry of Defence is also offering to pay March and future salaries into UK bank accounts and says it will compensate any military or government staff fully for losses arising from the proposed EU/IMF bailout levy on deposits. The move follows wider concern about Cyprus’s plan to tax bank deposits to meet part of a €15.8bn rescue package—an unprecedented step that has closed banks temporarily, sparked depositor outrage, raised fears of capital flight and undermined confidence in eurozone deposits. UK ministers (including the Chancellor) reaffirmed a promise to protect personnel posted to Cyprus, while analysts and former officials warned the levy could trigger runs, capital flight, prolonged capital controls and damage European financial stability.

Researchers at UCSF report that habitual consumption of caffeine from coffee, tea, or chocolate is not associated with increased premature heartbeats or palpitations. The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, analyzed 1,388 community-dwelling participants (average age 72) from the NHLBI Cardiovascular Health Study. About 60% consumed at least one caffeinated product daily. Participants completed food-frequency surveys and 24-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring; investigators measured premature atrial contractions (PACs) and premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). No relationship was found between frequency of coffee, tea, or chocolate intake and PACs or PVCs per hour.

The findings challenge the common clinical recommendation to avoid caffeine to prevent arrhythmias. The authors note prior beliefs that extra heartbeats were harmless have changed—PACs and PVCs can predict more serious conditions—so the null association is especially relevant. They acknowledge limitations: they did not assess energy drinks, did not ask whether symptomatic people had already reduced intake, and cannot speak to acute effects of a single caffeinated dose. The study adds to growing evidence that moderate coffee consumption may have cardiovascular and metabolic benefits, while cautioning that very high caffeine doses (e.g., powdered caffeine) can be dangerous and children should limit intake.

German prosecutors have indicted two nonagenarian former SS guards from the Stutthof concentration camp near today’s Gdansk, Poland, on charges of being accessories to murder. The men — a 93-year-old from Borken who served at Stutthof from June 1942 to September 1944 and a 92-year-old from Wuppertal who served from June 1944 to May 1945 — were charged last week in the state court in Münster; the announcement was delayed until they were notified. Both deny knowing about killings at the camp.

Prosecutors say the guards knowingly supported hundreds of killings by performing guard duties and supervising prisoners who were taken to forced labor, and that the camp’s routine mass killings could only have occurred with such helpers. During the men’s periods at Stutthof, about 65,000 people died there by gassing, shooting, injections (including phenol and gasoline), starvation and exposure; documented atrocities in 1944–45 included gas-chamber killings of Polish and Soviet prisoners, shootings of Jews, and medical staff-administered lethal injections.

The indictments rely on legal reasoning German authorities have used since 2011 to prosecute former Nazis who cannot be tied to a specific killing but who materially helped camps operate. The case was aided by testimony from survivors, including St. Louis Park resident Judith (Judy) Meisel, who identified one of the accused from a photo as Johann Rehbogen and provided detailed eyewitness accounts of abuse and killings. Meisel, whose mother was murdered at Stutthof, may join the prosecution as a co-plaintiff and could testify; other U.S.-based survivors have also been interviewed.

Defense and procedural steps remain: the defendants can challenge the indictment and will likely undergo medical evaluations to determine fitness for trial; a trial could begin next summer if they are deemed competent. For survivors like Meisel, the prosecution offers a chance for answers and public reckoning, and she has said she welcomes speaking out to preserve the memory and lessons of what happened.

Italian police say they have deciphered a coded text written in a special alphabet used by the 'Ndrangheta, a powerful Calabrian mafia network. The handwritten three-sheet document, found with weapons and ammunition during an investigation into a high‑profile Rome murder in January last year, appears to contain the oath recited when new members join the San Luca clan. Two police officers who enjoy crosswords spent weeks cracking a script described as a mix of Arabic, Cyrillic and Chinese‑style characters. The translated content is rich in symbolism and details how to recognize a "Man of Honour." Officials say the find highlights the group's use of archaic, quasi‑mystical rites even as it operates globally and dominates Europe’s cocaine trade.

A parked Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 787 Dreamliner caught fire at London’s Heathrow Airport, forcing both runways to close for about 90 minutes before operations resumed. The empty aircraft, reportedly the Dreamliner named "Queen of Sheba," was on a remote stand; no passengers were aboard and no injuries were reported. Images showed foam on the fuselage and scorching near the tail. British police are treating the blaze as unexplained and the UK Air Accidents Investigation Branch has sent a team. Heathrow and London Fire Brigade crews attended.

The incident revived concerns about the 787’s lithium-ion batteries: fifty Dreamliners were grounded in January after two battery-related incidents (including a fire at Boston’s Logan Airport) and returned to service in April/May following Boeing’s redesign and regulator approvals. Ethiopian was among the first carriers to resume 787 flights. Boeing said it has staff on site at Heathrow; its shares fell roughly 6–7% on the New York market after news of the fire. Separately, Thomson Airways returned a 787 to Manchester as a precaution for an unrelated technical issue. Airline and pilot groups have called for a rapid, transparent determination of the cause.

On the evening of June 17, 2015, a white 21-year-old, later identified as Dylann Storm Roof, entered a Bible study at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church—“Mother Emanuel,” a historic Black congregation in downtown Charleston—and sat with the group for about 40–50 minutes before opening fire. Nine people were killed, including the church’s pastor and state senator Rev. Clementa Pinckney, and victims ranging in age from 26 to 87: Cynthia Hurd, Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, Tywanza Sanders, Ethel Lance, Susie Jackson, DePayne Middleton-Doctor, Myra Thompson and Daniel Simmons Sr. Several people survived by hiding or playing dead; one survivor said the gunman told her to live so she could tell what happened.

The attack stunned Charleston and the nation. Local leaders, activists and elected officials—including President Obama, Gov. Nikki Haley and U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch—called the killings a hate crime and vowed vigorous investigation and support for the community. The massacre revived painful historical echoes for Emanuel AME, founded in the early 19th century and long central to Black civic life in Charleston (notably associated with Denmark Vesey), and heightened concerns about racial violence and gun access.

Following a large multi-agency manhunt that circulated surveillance images and the suspect’s vehicle, Roof was recognized by a motorist and arrested on June 18 during a traffic stop in Shelby, North Carolina. Authorities said Roof had expressed racist views and shown interest in segregation and Confederate symbolism; records cited prior minor arrests and unsettling behavior. The FBI and other federal agencies investigated potential civil rights and hate crime charges. In the days after the shooting, vigils and prayers drew hundreds while the city grappled with grief, security threats (including bomb threats to other AME sites) and calls for reflection on race relations and gun laws.

Bryshon Nellum, a 2012 Olympic silver medalist who survived being shot in the legs in 2008 and was once told he might never be an elite athlete again, was selected by his U.S. teammates to carry the American flag at the London Games’ closing ceremony. Nellum helped the U.S. men’s 4x400 relay to silver and reached the 400m semifinals, and was praised by the U.S. Olympic Committee for embodying the Olympic spirit.

The U.S. surged late in London—largely on the strength of track and field—to overtake China in both total medals and golds heading into the final weekend. By Friday the Americans led China 94–81 in total medals and 41–37 in golds. The track team accounted for 26 medals (including eight golds) and helped push the U.S. toward projections that it could finish atop the medal table overall and possibly match the highest U.S. gold totals on foreign soil (45). Standout nights included Ashton Eaton and Trey Hardee 1–2 in the decathlon, Christian Taylor and Will Claye 1–2 in the triple jump, the women’s record-setting 4x100 relay (Jeter, Madison, Felix, Knight), and Jordan Burroughs’ wrestling gold.

China, which led early and had strong showings in diving, table tennis and badminton, fell behind as medal opportunities dwindled in swimming and track; some Chinese officials and media complained of judging bias. Britain enjoyed a home boost, set for third in golds with its best performance in over a century, fueled by rowing and track cycling backed by heavy investment from U.K. Sport. Russia underperformed in golds for the first time since the pre-Soviet era, signaling a rebuilding phase, while South Korea emerged as an unexpected Asian power. Australia and Germany fell short of their targets.

Other notable results: Oscar Pistorius competed in the men’s 4x400 final for South Africa after his team was advanced following a late-race collision; France’s Renaud Lavillenie set an Olympic pole vault record; Meseret Defar won the women’s 5,000m; Turkey’s Asli Cakir Alptekin won the women’s 1,500m; Russia took synchronized swimming gold; New Zealand and Australia won sailing titles; Latvia’s Maris Strombergs repeated as BMX champion; and Tunisia’s Oussama Mellouli won the 10 km open-water swim, adding to his pool medal. Overall, the late U.S. charge made the medals chase an unofficial but compelling storyline as the Games closed.

President Trump’s nominee for Navy secretary, Philip Bilden, withdrew from consideration, saying he could not meet federal ethics requirements without “undue disruption and materially adverse divestment” of his family’s private financial interests. Bilden, a former Army Reserve intelligence officer who ran HarbourVest Partners’ Hong Kong office and recently retired after 25 years in private equity, informed Defense Secretary Jim Mattis of his decision. The Pentagon had tried to counter earlier reports that he might drop out, and Mattis said he would recommend a new nominee soon. Bilden’s withdrawal echoes the recent resignation of Vincent Viola as Army secretary nominee, another wealthy businessman who stepped aside after concluding he could not disentangle his business holdings to satisfy conflict-of-interest rules.

A Memphis teenager, Chauncy Jones Black (15–16), whose family lives in severe poverty, was helped after he approached shopper Matt White at a Kroger asking to carry groceries in exchange for doughnuts. White learned Chauncy lives with his disabled mother, sleeps on pallets on the floor, had an empty fridge and almost no possessions after a robbery, and is a straight-A student who wants to work to help his mom and eventually run a business. Touched by their situation, White bought groceries, drove them home, publicized the encounter on Facebook and created a GoFundMe initially seeking $250 to buy Chauncy a lawn mower so he could earn money. The story went viral; donations—reported in updates at various points as tens of thousands up to nearly $92,000—have funded clothes, household items and other help, and spurred efforts to secure ID, jobs, mentors, furniture and possibly a new home. White continues to coordinate donations, volunteer help and mentoring opportunities for Chauncy and his mother.

The article outlines a central paradox in today’s music industry: albums generate ever-smaller shares of artists’ total income, yet they remain crucial as the organizing, branding and promotional centerpiece for broader revenue streams (touring, endorsements, merchandise, etc.). Lady Gaga’s Born This Way exemplifies this dynamic. The album sold 1.108 million U.S. copies in its first week—an enormous total that outsold the next 42 albums on Billboard combined—largely thanks to an intensive, months‑long marketing campaign planned around a fixed release date and leveraging TV appearances, retail tie‑ins, branded promotions and manager Troy Carter’s coordinated push.

A major driver of the million‑plus figure was a two‑day Amazon promotion that sold the digital album for 99 cents. Amazon reportedly paid the distributor the full wholesale price (about $8–$9) and absorbed the loss to attract users to its Cloud Drive service; Billboard estimated about 440,000 downloads came from that sale. Brick‑and‑mortar retailers protested, saying deep discounts devalue music and hurt store sales. Industry observers note that recorded‑music revenue is now a smaller part of an artist’s earnings, but albums remain the essential anchor for marketing and long campaigns. The piece concludes that Gaga’s campaign—though boosted by Amazon’s promotion—demonstrates how an album release can still drive massive attention and underpin a complex, multi‑stream business strategy.

Hispanic community leaders, immigrant advocates and legal groups are scrambling to calm widespread fear after the Trump administration began enforcing President Trump’s broad Jan. 25–26 executive orders on immigration. The early, high‑profile deportation of Arizona resident Guadalupe Garcia de Rayos — a working mother with U.S. citizen children who had been convicted years earlier of using a false Social Security number — has intensified anxiety among undocumented immigrants and mixed‑status families, who worry the administration will not limit removals to violent criminals.

Trump’s orders expanded who counts as a “criminal alien” and widened deportation priorities to include people charged but not convicted, those with minor offenses (including illicit entry), and immigration‑related fraud. Legal experts estimate millions more could be vulnerable under the new definitions. Community organizers say that even routine interactions with federal officers can trigger detention, and that ICE/CBP institutional incentives for high removal numbers may drive aggressive enforcement.

In the days after the orders, ICE conducted coordinated operations in multiple states (including California, Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, New York and Kansas) that resulted in hundreds of arrests. Officials say most detainees had prior convictions; advocates report many without criminal records were also rounded up, fueling fears that the enforcement sweep is broader than the Obama‑era focus on serious criminals. Reports of workplace and home raids, alleged denial of lawyer access, traffic checkpoints and daytime sweeps have contributed to panic and reduced trust in law enforcement.

Immigrant rights groups and Spanish‑language media have mobilized rapid legal responses: “know your rights” trainings, hotlines, legal triage, and public town halls (e.g., Telemundo’s event) to inform communities about their options. Legal advocates warn shortages of immigration judges and use of expedited removal procedures could further limit due process, and caution that targeting low‑risk individuals risks driving people into hiding, undermining community safety and isolating victims and witnesses.

Activists plan protests and continued legal challenges to the orders. Meanwhile families like Garcia de Rayos’s and others facing ICE appointments are organizing support amid widespread uncertainty about how aggressively the administration will pursue deportations going forward.

Researchers at the MRC Toxicology Unit (University of Leicester) reported in Science Translational Medicine that an orally delivered compound can halt neurodegeneration in mice by blocking a stress pathway triggered by misfolded proteins. Instead of removing amyloids, the drug inhibits the enzyme PERK, preventing an overactive cellular defense response that shuts down protein synthesis and leaves neurons unprotected. In prion-diseased mice the treatment restored protective protein production, prevented memory loss and other symptoms, and extended survival.

The findings are presented as an important proof of principle that a small-molecule, brain-penetrant, orally administered drug can arrest amyloid-driven neuron death — a mechanism shared across prion disease, Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. However, the treated mice suffered significant side effects (notably weight loss and impaired glucose regulation from pancreatic damage), and researchers emphasize human trials are still a long way off. Experts called the results highly encouraging and potentially a turning point, while cautioning that translation from mice (prion model) to common human neurodegenerative diseases will require more work to confirm efficacy and to eliminate harmful side effects.

A new dating site, Maple Match, launched in early 2016 to connect Americans with Canadians who might want to move north if Donald Trump wins the U.S. presidency. Branded with the slogan “Making dating great again,” the site frames itself as a way for Americans to find Canadian partners and potentially relocate to escape a Trump administration. Founder and CEO Joe Goldman says the service is serious despite its tongue-in-cheek premise and is not funded by any anti‑Trump group. After media attention, traffic and signups surged—reports cite thousands of hits and several thousand signups in days—so Maple Match is currently operating a waiting list and plans to begin matching soon. The site markets Canada’s perceived advantages (universal health care, left‑leaning politics, cultural ties) and presents the platform as both a practical and romantic route for those considering emigration.

A recent detailed Hollywood salary report from The Hollywood Reporter reveals surprising disparities in how much celebrities earn across movies, TV, endorsements and reality shows. Key findings:

- Movie paydays can be enormous: Robert Downey Jr. reportedly earned $75 million for Iron Man (including 7% of box office gross) plus $12 million from an HTC endorsement. Liam Neeson made about $20 million for Taken 3.
- Huge co-star gaps: On The Wolf of Wall Street Leonardo DiCaprio made over $25 million while Jonah Hill accepted roughly $60,000, a 416× difference.
- Top actresses vary: Jennifer Lawrence’s Hunger Games earnings put her at about $35 million versus Jennifer Aniston’s $15 million.
- Endorsements are extremely lucrative: Celebrities often make as much or more from product deals than from films; Bethenny Frankel reportedly made $100 million from her Skinnygirl brand.
- TV salaries can outpace film: Ashton's Two and a Half Men pay was reported at $750,000 per episode; Big Bang Theory leads with main cast members around $1 million per episode. Alex Trebek earns roughly $10 million a year; Jon Stewart made $25–30 million annually, topping late-night hosts.
- Reality TV pay is uneven: A few franchises (the Kardashians, Duck Dynasty) command massive deals, but most reality participants earn little.
- Industry averages are stark: Though a few stars earn millions, SAG stats show the average union member earns about $52,000 yearly, and most make less than $1,000 a year from acting work.
- Extras and animals: Background extras earn modest daily rates (about $148/day plus overtime/conditions pay); perverse examples include a TV monkey reportedly being paid $108,000 for nine episodes.

The piece also includes celebrity gossip snippets about private habits and staff anecdotes, underscoring Hollywood’s mix of astronomical top-tier pay, wide internal inequalities, and many performers earning very little.

A Republican amendment from Rep. Ron DeSantis (R‑Fla.) would halt funding for Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia investigation 180 days after the measure becomes law and bar the probe from examining any matters predating June 2015 (the month Donald Trump announced his presidential campaign). DeSantis filed the amendment as part of an upcoming House spending package; POLITICO noted it’s one of many proposed amendments and faces uncertain prospects in committee, passage in the House, and survival in the Senate.

Separately, federal investigators working for Mueller are focusing on President Trump’s role in drafting the White House’s initial response to a New York Times story about the June 2016 Trump Tower meeting involving Donald Trump Jr., Paul Manafort, Jared Kushner and Russian contacts. Prosecutors want to know what Trump knew about the meeting and whether he tried to conceal its purpose. The White House has said Trump “weighed in” on the statement drafted aboard Air Force One; Trump aide Ty Cobb maintains the statement was not untruthful and that the president’s role was minimal. Investigators are interested in whether any knowingly false statements were made, which could be relevant to potential charges or to show Trump’s conduct to a jury.

The report describes a photographic expedition to the remote Great Bear Rainforest on Canada’s central coast to document the region’s rare “spirit” bears—black bears with a genetic white coat—whose population is under 500. The rainforest, roughly the size of Switzerland, is roadless and accessible only by air or water. The spirit bear is a flagship species in a biologically rich ecosystem that also supports whales, wolves, eagles, sea lions and abundant marine life.

Conservationists and First Nations view the bears and forest as sacred and are fighting a proposed massive oil pipeline and tanker traffic that would link Alberta’s oil fields to B.C.’s coast. Opponents say the pipeline would turn the coast into a “superhighway for supertankers” and risk catastrophic spills; proponents argue the route largely skirts the rainforest, would use double-hulled tankers and tug escorts, and would bring jobs. Skepticism is intensified by Enbridge’s recent pipeline spills in the U.S., which local fishers fear could destroy their livelihoods.

To raise awareness, conservation groups enlisted the International League of Conservation Photographers—a high-profile team including National Geographic and other documentary photographers—to create striking imagery of the landscape, wildlife and spirit bears. The story follows the photographers and a Gitga’at Nation bear tracker, Marven Robinson, into remote, off-limits areas. The Gitga’at revere the spirit bear (moskam al) and have historically spoken of them quietly. After patient, difficult searching amid lush, silent forest and salmon-rich rivers, the team finally encounters a spirit bear—an eerie, ghostlike sight that underscores both the rarity and symbolic power of the animals in the campaign to protect the Great Bear Rainforest.

An international team of scientists led by Stephanie Jenouvrier (WHOI) used long-term field data and IPCC-based sea-ice projections to model the future of all 45 known emperor penguin colonies across Antarctica. The study, published in Nature Climate Change, finds that emperor penguins—about 600,000 today—are highly dependent on sea ice for breeding and foraging and are therefore vulnerable to climate-driven changes in sea-ice concentration.

Key findings
- By 2100 the global emperor population is projected to decline by at least 19% from current levels; two-thirds of colonies are expected to shrink by more than 50%.
- All colonies are projected to be in decline by the end of the century under IPCC sea-ice scenarios; even southern refuges like the Ross Sea are unlikely to remain viable long-term.
- Some colonies may increase briefly (through mid-century) before later collapsing as sea-ice patterns change.
- The species faces a “Goldilocks” dependency on ice: too much sea ice forces longer foraging trips; too little reduces krill habitat and can cause colony breakup by waves.

Conservation implications
- The authors argue the emperor penguin merits endangered status (including consideration under the US Endangered Species Act) because future climate change places the species at significant risk.
- Designating the species as endangered could enable protections (e.g., restrictions on fishing and tourism, management of US vessels) and support broader conservation actions.
- The paper recommends focusing conservation efforts on potential refuges (notably the Ross Sea) and creating new international strategies to address threats from future climate change.

Context and methods
- The work builds on a 50-year study of the Terre Adélie colony and leverages satellite mapping (including detection of colony guano) to provide a continent-wide baseline.
- Population models incorporate observed relationships between penguin demography and sea-ice concentration and apply projected SIC changes from climate models.

Bottom line
Emperor penguins, currently one of the more stable penguin species, are forecast to face widespread and severe declines this century as sea-ice conditions shift with climate change. The study calls for listing the species as endangered and for targeted international conservation measures to try to safeguard remaining populations.

Heavy fighting raged in the northern oil town of Malakal as South Sudan’s conflict entered its second month. The army reported intense street battles — including reported tank clashes — and denied rebel claims they had captured the town, while rebels said they had “recaptured” it. Malakal, a strategic gateway to Upper Nile oilfields, has changed hands multiple times since fighting began on December 15 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir (a Dinka) and troops backing former vice-president Riek Machar (a Nuer).

The violence has caused large-scale displacement and heavy civilian losses. UN figures and aid sources say hundreds of thousands have fled their homes (estimates in reports ranged from about 350,000 to 400,000), and casualties are high: estimates of deaths vary from around 1,000 to as many as 10,000 including reports of ethnic killings. More than 200 civilians reportedly drowned when an overloaded ferry sank on the Nile as people tried to flee Malakal; thousands have sought shelter at UN bases in the area.

Separately, government forces say they are advancing on Bor in Jonglei state, another key contested town. Regional mediators from IGAD are holding ceasefire talks in Addis Ababa, but progress is stalled over core issues — notably the rebels’ demand for the release of political detainees held in Juba. Both sides have linked a cessation of hostilities to the prisoner issue, and despite some optimism from government officials, no durable truce had been reached.

A planned TV series about Selena Quintanilla’s romance with husband Chris Perez, announced by Endemol Shine North America after it optioned Perez’s memoir To Selena With Love, is facing a legal challenge. Selena’s father, Abraham Quintanilla Jr., sued Perez and Endemol in Texas, asking the court to halt production. The suit asserts that a 1995 Estate Properties Agreement—signed shortly after Selena’s death—grants Quintanilla Jr. exclusive, perpetual global rights to Selena’s name, image, voice, signature, photographs and other “Entertainment Properties,” as well as related publicity, copyright and trademark rights. The complaint alleges Perez agreed to the deal and accepted 25% of net profits from exploitation of those properties, so his 2012 book (which features Selena’s photo on the cover) and the proposed TV adaptation were unauthorized and breach the agreement. Selena’s estate seeks a judicial declaration that Perez and Endemol have no rights to exploit her likeness or produce the series.

This document recounts the controversy at the New York Review of Books (NYRB) that led to the resignation of editor Ian Buruma after the magazine published a first‑person essay by Jian Ghomeshi, the former CBC broadcaster accused by many women of violent sexual misconduct.

Key facts about Ghomeshi included in the piece:
- Ghomeshi was fired from the CBC in October 2014 after executives saw evidence he had caused physical harm to a woman. Over twenty women subsequently accused him of sexual abuse and harassment, alleging hitting, biting, choking and verbal abuse during sex. Many allegations appeared in reputable outlets such as The Toronto Star.
- In November 2014 he was charged with sexual assault relating to three women; additional charges from three more women followed in January 2015. He was acquitted in March 2016 of the criminal charges that went to trial, and later settled a separate allegation involving a CBC coworker out of court with a peace bond and a public apology.
- The document notes Canada’s sexual‑assault law differs from U.S. “rape” statutes, and that “sexual assault” under Canadian law can include threats and nonconsensual physical contact.

The controversy at NYRB:
- Buruma commissioned and published Ghomeshi’s essay “Reflections from a Hashtag,” in which Ghomeshi expressed remorse but called the accusations “inaccurate” and sought to present a “nuanced” view of events.
- The publication drew immediate and intense criticism on social media and from staff and readers, who objected that a high‑profile literary magazine had given an allegedly violent, extensively accused man an unchecked first‑person platform. Critics argued the piece lacked sufficient fact‑checking and context about the breadth and seriousness of allegations.
- Several NYRB staffers opposed publication; after publication, university presses that advertise in the Review reportedly threatened a boycott, and academic advertisers pressured the magazine.
- Buruma defended his decision publicly, saying he intended to spark discussion about how to treat figures accused but not convicted and arguing he had been “convicted on Twitter” without due process. He says he stood by his editorial judgment but felt compelled to resign amid social media backlash and advertiser pressure.
- The magazine later appended an editorial note clarifying details about the Ghomeshi allegations and legal proceedings. The NYRB declined further comment; readers and commentators called for greater transparency and better editorial judgment.

Broader reactions and context:
- The controversy was tied to #MeToo debates about platforms, due process, victim accountability and how institutions should handle accused but unconvicted figures.
- Commentators and academics quoted in the document argued that while there is space to examine cultural forces and include perspectives of accused men, prestigious outlets should not publish unchallenged first‑person defenses without rigorous context and fact‑checking. Some said the episode undermined trust in the NYRB and reflected resistance to gender‑equality progress among some opinion leaders.

The document also notes that the NYRB planned to publish readers’ letters responding to the article in a forthcoming issue (October 25, 2018), and concludes with references to unrelated book titles.

Document is two parts: metadata about a Wikipedia outlink crawl, and a longer article about controversy over a New York Times Book Review line.

1) Wikipedia outlinks crawl
- A crawl of outlinks from wikipedia.org began March 2016.
- The resulting files are not currently publicly accessible.
- For this collection several deliberate choices were made:
  - Duplicate detection was disabled to keep the collection complete, since the team may share the data and managing pointers into other collections would be complex.
  - For the first time the crawl used seeds from all 865 Wikimedia collections (not just enwiki), whereas earlier runs targeted only enwiki.

2) Controversy over calling Jodi Kantor’s book “chick nonfiction”
- The New York Times Book Review published Douglas Brinkley’s largely positive review of Jodi Kantor’s book The Obamas, but included the phrase “Call it chick nonfiction, if you will; this book is not about politics, it’s about marriage,” which provoked criticism for seeming dismissive and gendered.
- Critics (including writers Jennifer Weiner, Rebecca Traister, and Ezra Klein) argued the phrase diminishes both Kantor’s work and Michelle Obama as a serious political actor, reflecting a double standard when women write about or are the subjects of political biographies.
- The book, though focused on the Obamas’ marriage, contains reporting on Michelle Obama’s influence and tensions within the White House (e.g., over health care and immigration) — material other reviewers and outlets treated as serious political reporting.
- Defenders note Brinkley’s review otherwise praised Kantor’s reporting and prose, calling some anecdotes riveting and the author a strong reporter; but he also characterized parts as “gossipy” or having a “tabloid scent,” and described Kantor as a “reportorial wunderkind,” language critics found condescending.
- Commentators pointed out that similar books about male politicians or books by men are rarely labeled dismissively, and that Michelle Obama’s role as professional equal to the president makes the subject historically significant.
- Neither Brinkley nor the Times Book Review editor had responded to requests for comment at the time.

Key points

- The New York Times reported that in February President Trump asked then-FBI Director James Comey to end the FBI’s investigation into ousted National Security Advisor Michael Flynn. Comey memorialized the exchange in a memo quoting Trump: “I hope you can see your way clear to letting this go, to letting Flynn go. He is a good guy. I hope you can let this go.” Comey has written memos of all his interactions with Trump; House Oversight Chair Jason Chaffetz has requested those memos and Democrats are accusing the president of obstruction of justice.

- Comey’s abrupt firing has become a major political controversy and has begun to disrupt the Republican policy timetable on Capitol Hill. Issues that were GOP priorities—health care repeal, tax reform and regulatory rollbacks—have been at least temporarily pushed down the agenda as Capitol Hill focuses on the firing and ongoing investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 election.

- The Senate must confirm a new FBI director, a process likely to be contentious because Democrats are demanding answers about the timing of Comey’s dismissal and the status of the Russia probe. Several Democrats say they will not consider a new FBI director until a special counsel is appointed; Sen. Mark Warner urged delaying confirmation until a special prosecutor is in place.

- Republicans argue the controversy will not derail their agenda, pointing out Senate rules and partisan opposition already slow progress. Some Republican senators say they’ll continue health-care negotiations and other work, while others acknowledge the distraction has already consumed time and attention (e.g., hearings delayed, conference meetings diverted to briefings on the firing).

- Democrats are using procedural tools to slow the Senate schedule and press for accountability; Republicans counter that the controversy could even reduce scrutiny on policy items by shifting public attention. Overall, the Comey firing has intensified scrutiny of the administration, raised questions about obstruction, and complicated Senate business at a critical legislative juncture.

Demi Moore resurfaced in public and online following a recent hospitalization, rehab stay and her split from Ashton Kutcher. She attended a Beverly Hills event celebrating the launch of the TV show The Conversation, which she executive produced. On Twitter she returned using the handle @MrsKutcher and asked followers for suggestions for a new screen name, despite not having filed for divorce yet. The piece also notes speculation about Ashton Kutcher’s dating life after he was reportedly seen dining and shopping with former That ’70s Show co-star Mila Kunis; Mila is set to take part in the show’s 25th anniversary FOX special on April 22.

A Connecticut dentist, Dr. Rashmi Patel, 45, was arrested Feb. 17 and charged with criminally negligent homicide (misdemeanor) and tampering with evidence in the death of 64-year-old Judith Gan, who stopped breathing while undergoing conscious sedation for a full-mouth extraction and implant work at his Enfield office on Feb. 17, 2014. Patel turned himself in, posted $25,000 bail, and is due in Superior Court on Feb. 24.

State Department of Public Health inspectors and the State Dental Commission found that Patel failed to properly respond when Gan’s oxygen levels and vital signs deteriorated during what was intended to be a 20-tooth extraction. According to reports, dental assistants repeatedly warned him, one begged him to stop and another ran to call 911 after the patient “flat-lined,” but Patel continued the procedure. Gan had a significant cardiac and stroke history and was on medications that could affect sedation response; regulators concluded he should not have planned so many procedures in one visit.

The Dental Commission suspended Patel’s license in April, later banning him permanently from performing conscious sedation and ordering five years of monitoring, though it did not revoke his license after a proceeding in which defense experts said he met the standard of care. Patel’s attorney disputes the criminal charges and says the commission’s findings support that defense; Gan’s family plans to pursue civil action.

Regulators also cited prior safety problems in Patel’s practice: a December 2013 incident in which a patient aspirated a throat pack during sedation and required hospital treatment, improper delegation of sedation tasks and monitoring to assistants on multiple occasions, and the presence of expired medications in his office. Patel previously lost a 2011 malpractice jury verdict that was later settled on appeal.

This document is a comprehensive Phoenix-focused guide to evidence, procedure, and legal issues in Arizona personal injury cases, produced by the Lamber Goodnow Injury Law Team, followed by a short unrelated news item about the Vacca family.

Key points about evidence and preservation
- Medical records are often admissible via Arizona hearsay exceptions (Rule 803(6) for regular business records; Rule 803(4) for statements made for medical diagnosis/treatment). Seek prompt medical care after an accident and preserve all treatment records (including bills, discharge summaries, therapy notes, imaging, prescriptions).
- Police reports are typically hearsay and usually inadmissible at trial, though parts can be admissible under the public records exception (Rule 803(8)). Police reports remain valuable for investigations and settlement negotiations because they document time, place, weather, witness names/statements and an officer’s initial assessment of fault.
- Digital evidence and chain of custody: Arizona courts recognize the importance of digital evidence. Preservation, collection, and documentation (chain of custody) are critical to ensure evidence is admissible and unaltered. Non-electronic evidence (photos, vehicle parts, physical debris) should be preserved and catalogued quickly before it degrades or is repaired.
- Parties’ own out-of-court statements are generally admissible; hearsay is excluded because statements made outside court lack oath and cross-examination, making credibility harder to assess.

Practical post-accident steps
- Notify police immediately when an accident causes injury or death (ARS § 28-666). Obtain the police report from the responding agency or online portal. Preserve photos, witness contact information, physical evidence, and all medical documentation. Work with an attorney to ensure evidence is catalogued and chain of custody is preserved.

Arizona personal injury law overview
- Statute of limitations for personal injury: two years (ARS § 12-542). Other relevant provisions summarized include comparative negligence rules (pure comparative negligence, ARS § 12-2505), mandatory auto insurance minimums (ARS § 28-4009), wrongful death statute (ARS § 12-611), product and premises liability references, and more.
- Auto insurance minimums: $15,000 per person bodily injury; $30,000 per accident for two or more persons; $10,000 property damage. Uninsured/underinsured coverage is not mandatory but insurers must offer it in writing (ARS § 20-259.01).
- Healthcare provider liens and insurer reimbursement: Hospitals and providers commonly record liens (balance liens) for unpaid charges related to third-party claims (ARS § 33-931–33-936). Liens attach only to recovery proceeds, are capped at a provider’s “customary charges,” and can often be negotiated or challenged on procedural or substantive grounds (e.g., imperfect perfection, lack of necessity or causal relation, incorrect amounts). Health plan reimbursement issues can be complex due to ERISA preemption for large self-funded plans.
- Lamber Goodnow emphasizes that liens and insurer reimbursement demands should be carefully reviewed by counsel — they do not automatically override a plaintiff’s rights.

Court options and procedure
- Most Phoenix cases are resolved in settlement, but when necessary, cases may be filed in state or federal court.
- State courts: Most Phoenix personal injury cases begin in Maricopa County Superior Court. Appeals proceed to the Arizona Court of Appeals and potentially the Arizona Supreme Court.
- Filing a civil case generally requires: filing a complaint, serving the defendant, answering, discovery, and trial (jury or bench). Arizona civil juries are eight persons and may render verdicts with up to two dissenters.
- Federal court: The District of Arizona handles federal cases; federal jurisdiction requires a federal question or diversity (amount in controversy over $75,000 and complete diversity). Federal juries may require unanimity unless otherwise stipulated.
- Practical choice: Many Phoenix lawyers prefer state court to avoid the unanimity requirement of federal juries.

Lamber Goodnow’s capabilities and recognition
- The firm highlights its use of advanced technology (VR, 3D printing, mobile devices) in case presentation, media recognition (national media appearances), and legal rankings and awards. They emphasize a proactive, thorough investigative approach and willingness to pursue legislative solutions when appropriate.

Separate news item
- The four children of Charles Vacca, an instructor killed when a nine-year-old girl lost control of a Uzi at an Arizona gun range, released a video message to the unnamed child offering compassion and forgiveness. Their attorney noted the family’s awareness of the national gun debate but asked that the personal tragedy not be overshadowed. The video was released by the family’s counsel.

Overall takeaways
- After an accident in Arizona, obtain prompt medical care, preserve all records and physical/digital evidence, obtain the police report, and consult an experienced personal injury attorney to protect admissibility, manage liens/reimbursements, determine proper venue, and pursue settlement or litigation.

Pvt. Arthur “Bud” Kelder, who died in 1942 as a POW at Cabanatuan after surviving the Bataan Death March, is believed by his relatives to be one of 10 Americans buried as an “unknown” (Manila X-816, grave A-12-195) after postwar attempts at identification. Kelder’s cousin John Eakin, working from declassified records and dental evidence (including distinctive gold inlays), and two forensic dentists concluded X-816 is likely Kelder. They say JPAC (Joint Prisoner of War/Missing in Action Accounting Command) repeatedly refused requests to disinter and DNA-test the remains, citing an unusually high burden of proof and the agency’s risk-averse disinterment policies. Former JPAC investigator Rick Stone also reports that he narrowed many WWII unknowns (notably 94 Tarawa cases) to small candidate pools suitable for targeted disinterment and DNA testing, but that his recommendations were ignored or buried by senior officials. Critics charge JPAC is hampered by poor management, turf fights, outdated methods and a growing backlog; independent reviews and the GAO have documented dysfunction, and JPAC admitted to staging false repatriation ceremonies in the past.

JPAC and DOD officials say they are expanding research and disinterment programs (including work at the Punchbowl and other cemeteries) and stress the need for strong circumstantial and anatomical evidence before disturbing unknowns; they note logistical and record limitations for WWII cases and a relatively small number of WWII disinterments and identifications in recent years. Stone and families argue the standard is set too high and that modern forensic DNA and documentary analysis could identify many unknowns quickly if pursued.

After litigation by Kelder’s family and recent media coverage, the Pentagon reversed course and authorized exhumation of X-816 and the other 10 remains from common grave 717. The timing and results of testing were not yet known; if confirmed, the family intends to rebury Kelder in the family plot in Chicago. The case has become a focal point in calls for sweeping reforms to the U.S. accounting-for-the-missing mission, which the Defense Secretary has pledged to restructure amid forthcoming inspector general and congressional scrutiny.

An annular ("ring of fire") solar eclipse traveled across a narrow path from southern China, over Tokyo, across the Pacific and the Aleutians, and made landfall in the western United States before ending east of Lubbock, Texas. The Moon was near apogee, so it did not fully cover the Sun and left a bright ring visible along a roughly 240–300 km–wide track; partial phases were seen across much of East Asia and North America.

Millions witnessed the event. Tokyo enjoyed near-ideal viewing — despite brief rain — with live TV coverage, school and public viewing events, pleasure-boat and private-plane excursions, and Panasonic filming from Mount Fuji. Hong Kong viewers were largely clouded out, while hundreds attended viewing sites in U.S. locations such as Reno, Oakland, northern California, southern Oregon, Albuquerque (praised as an excellent vantage), and other parts of the Southwest. Observers reported strong emotional reactions and striking visual effects (including crescent-shaped light patterns from tree shadows). Experts cautioned against looking at the Sun without proper filters. The Slooh network provided online coverage, and NASA notes the next solar eclipse will be on 13 November, visible over northern Australia.

An Ohio inmate, Dennis McGuire, was executed using a two-drug combination—midazolam (a sedative) and hydromorphone (an opioid painkiller)—that had never before been used in a U.S. execution. The method was adopted after supplies of previously used drugs, like pentobarbital, became unavailable. The U.S. Supreme Court denied McGuire’s last-minute appeals and a federal judge allowed the execution to proceed while ordering the state to photograph and preserve the drugs’ packaging and syringes.

McGuire, 53, was convicted in 1994 of the 1989 rape and stabbing murder of Joy Stewart, who was eight months pregnant. The case was unsolved for months until McGuire—then jailed on an unrelated charge—offered information that led to his being accused; DNA later confirmed his guilt and he acknowledged responsibility in a recent letter to Gov. John Kasich. Prosecutors described the crime as particularly heinous.

Defense attorneys argued McGuire’s traumatic, abusive childhood and impaired brain function made him impulsive and mentally vulnerable, and they warned the new drug cocktail could cause “air hunger,” a terrifying difficulty breathing, resulting in a painful death. The state disputed those claims and said the appeal was untimely. The execution reportedly took more than 15 minutes and witnesses said McGuire made several loud snorting or gasping sounds as it progressed; his adult children were present. McGuire had requested a last meal and met with family before being moved to the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility for the execution.

McGuire also sought a stay to pursue organ donation, but Gov. Kasich denied requests because McGuire could not identify a family member who would receive his organs. The case highlighted broader issues facing death-penalty states as pharmaceutical suppliers restrict sales of drugs for executions and prompted debate over the humaneness and transparency of new lethal-injection protocols.

NATO decision and the end of the mission
- NATO was poised to formally end its U.N.-mandated Libya air campaign at the end of October, with ambassadors due to meet in Brussels to confirm a prior recommendation to wrap up operations. NATO said pro‑Gaddafi forces no longer had the command-and-control or capabilities to pose an organized threat to civilians; remaining NATO activity would be limited to intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, with strike capability retained if needed. Libya’s interim oil and finance minister asked for a short extension to ease sanctions and free funds for salaries and reconstruction.

Fall of Sirte and the capture/killing of Gaddafi
- Anti‑Gaddafi forces captured Sirte, the deposed leader’s hometown and the last major stronghold, after a brief final assault. Fighters raised the new national flag and celebratory scenes spread across Libya, though isolated pockets of fighting and reports of fleeing convoys continued.
- Conflicting, rapidly changing accounts surrounded Muammar Gaddafi’s fate. NTC sources, Libyan officials and international outlets ultimately reported that Gaddafi was captured alive after his convoy was attacked near Sirte, then died of wounds while being transported. Graphic mobile phone and broadcast footage of his corpse circulated, reportedly showing abuse and his body paraded in Misrata. Gaddafi and his son Mo’tassim were buried in a secret desert location to prevent their graves from becoming shrines.
- Numerous senior regime figures were reported captured or killed in the fighting: Mo’tassim Gaddafi was reported wounded and captured; spokesman Moussa Ibrahim, cousin/adviser Ahmed Ibrahim, intelligence chief Abdullah al‑Sanusi and others were reported detained; former defence minister Abu Bakr Yunis was reported killed. Saif al‑Islam was reported on the run in the southern desert.

Concerns about rule of law and human rights
- The violent and publicly humiliating treatment of Gaddafi’s body — and videos showing him alive after capture but later dead — alarmed Western governments and rights groups. Under pressure, the National Transitional Council (NTC) pledged to investigate the circumstances of Gaddafi’s death. U.S. and other Western officials urged the NTC to demonstrate respect for human rights and the rule of law, noting this moment as a test for Libya’s transition.
- Human Rights Watch and others stressed that alleged war crimes by Gaddafi’s regime should still be investigated even if he was dead, and that suspected crimes by all sides warranted scrutiny and fair trials where appropriate.

Political transition and outlook
- The NTC declared Libya liberated and moved to consolidate control nationally, while acknowledging major challenges ahead: regional and tribal rivalries, political infighting, security and economic strains, and the need to rebuild institutions and hold credible elections (planned for 2013).
- Interim leader Mahmoud Jibril signaled frustration with the political power struggle and hinted at stepping down as transitional arrangements were formalized. International leaders and the UN welcomed the end of Gaddafi’s rule but cautioned that reconciliation, inclusion and adherence to the rule of law would be vital for a stable transition.

Wider regional notes (brief)
- The document also relayed concurrent Middle East developments reported that day, including violence in Syria and Libya’s interim government recognizing the Syrian opposition.

In short: NATO prepared to end its Libya operation after pro‑Gaddafi forces were routed and Sirte fell. Muammar Gaddafi’s capture and death — amid graphic footage and disputed accounts — marked a dramatic end to his 42‑year rule, prompting jubilation in Libya but also international concern about summary violence, the need for investigations, and the difficult path ahead toward reconciliation, rule of law and democratic transition.

Rajan Zed, president of the Universal Society of Hinduism, delivered the Idaho Senate’s opening invocation on March 3, 2015, offering a lengthy prayer in Sanskrit and English drawn from ancient Hindu scriptures that emphasized selflessness, service and peace. Most senators greeted him warmly—shaking his hand and thanking him—but three Republican senators (Steve Vick, Sheryl Nuxoll and Lori Den Hartog) stepped out during the invocation and returned only after it concluded, citing objections on religious grounds; Nuxoll said she believes the U.S. is a Christian nation and called Hinduism a “false faith.” Four other senators were briefly absent for unrelated reasons. Zed, who has given invocations in Congress and other state legislatures, said he was unbothered by the walkouts and stressed Hinduism’s inclusiveness. The Idaho Legislature regularly opens with prayers from various faiths when guest chaplains are invited.

Anthony Weiner’s mayoral campaign suffered another blow as campaign manager Danny Kedem abruptly resigned after a week of damaging revelations that Weiner continued sending explicit online messages and photos to women after leaving Congress in 2011. Two campaign insiders said Kedem, 31, informed Weiner of his decision within 24 hours; Weiner confirmed the departure saying Kedem “did a remarkable job.” Kedem had helped elevate what was once a long-shot bid to the top of the polls and previously worked on John DeStefano’s New Haven re‑election and Hillary Clinton’s 2008 campaign. His exit leaves an already thin and reportedly difficult campaign understaffed just as doubts about Weiner’s viability grow internally.

Prominent Democrats and Republicans called for Weiner to withdraw. David Axelrod said on Meet the Press that Weiner should “go away” and is not fit to be mayor, while Rep. Peter King called him “not psychologically qualified” and urged him to step aside, calling Weiner’s remaining poll strength a “terrible aberration.” Weiner, however, insisted his campaign still has “an excellent staff” and volunteers continue to show up.

Activists in the Philippines marched on China’s embassy in Manila Friday to protest Chinese actions around the disputed Scarborough Shoal (called Panatag Shoal by Filipinos and Huangyan Island by China). About 400 protesters carried signs such as “China Back Off,” calling attention to what they say are ongoing Chinese intrusions that threaten Filipino fishermen’s livelihoods. The standoff intensified in early April after China sent maritime surveillance ships and the PLA Navy blocked a Philippine attempt to arrest crews of Chinese fishing boats near the shoal, about 220 km from Luzon.

China’s foreign ministry blamed the Philippines for encouraging anti-China protests and said Manila must protect Chinese nationals and institutions in the Philippines; Beijing also warned its citizens to stay indoors and several Chinese travel groups postponed trips. Small counter-protests occurred in Beijing. The dispute has regional implications—Vietnam, Brunei, Malaysia and Taiwan also claim parts of the South China Sea, a strategic trade route and potential hydrocarbon area—and Chinese state media have issued strong warnings, even alluding to a “small-scale war” if Manila does not back down.

Economic and diplomatic tensions have followed: Chinese authorities are reportedly holding 1,200 Philippine banana containers citing quarantine concerns, and civic groups in the Philippines plan further protests outside Chinese missions in New York, Singapore and Rome. Philippine organizers emphasized the protests target Chinese government policy and actions, not Chinese residents in the Philippines.

A 34-year-old substitute teacher, Lacey Sponsler, was arrested in Pawhuska, Oklahoma, after police say she exposed herself while performing a cartwheel in a junior high/high school choir class. Authorities allege Sponsler wore a long dress with no underwear; a student filmed the cartwheel, which reportedly flipped the dress and exposed her buttocks and genital area. A 17-year-old student told police Sponsler had said beforehand that she wasn’t wearing underwear and later discussed drugs and made inappropriate comments about minors. When questioned, Sponsler initially denied the act and later said she did not remember performing the cartwheel or exposing herself, claiming she was “just dancing with the students” and trying to be “a cool teacher.” She was booked on a complaint of indecent exposure. Court records show prior drug-related convictions and probation violations from 2008–2011.

A study by Anirban Mukhopadhyay at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology suggests forcing a smile when you’re unhappy can backfire. Across three experiments (surveys about smiling frequency and life satisfaction, responses to amusing images, and facial-muscle exercises), researchers found that the emotional effect of smiling depends on why someone smiles. People who naturally smile when they’re happy tend to feel better when they smile often. But people who smile to mask or try to induce happiness—i.e., who don’t usually smile from genuine joy—may come to associate smiling with their underlying unhappiness, making them feel worse. The author’s recommendation: don’t push a grin on someone who’s down; wait for the negative emotion to lift or address the cause, and consider personal beliefs about smiling when deciding whether to try smiling as a mood-regulation strategy. The study appeared in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

Miley Cyrus told Billboard she’s “completely clean” after quitting marijuana for several weeks and described a period of personal change as she prepares a new, more singer‑songwriter–leaning album. Living on a Malibu compound she shares with fiancé Liam Hemsworth, pets and her recording studio “Rainbow Land,” Cyrus says she’s moved away from shock tactics and some hip‑hop collaborations, aiming for music that’s more personal, twangy and DIY. The lead single “Malibu,” out May 11, is a breezy, unadorned love song about Hemsworth; the rest of the album mixes acoustic and pop elements and includes songs about Hillary Clinton and women in the workplace.

Cyrus explained the creative shift as part of an evolution—wanting clarity, sharper focus and to surround herself with people who push her to grow. Her time on The Voice broadened her audience and drove her desire to connect with fans who don’t share her politics; after campaigning for Democrats in 2016 and launching the Happy Hippie nonprofit, she says she now seeks to engage people compassionately rather than “preach to the choir.” She reflected on past controversies (the 2013 VMA performance, accusations of cultural appropriation), her openness about gender and sexuality, and her intention to use visibility for activism rather than spectacle.

Pope Francis made history on Sept. 24, 2015 as the first pope to address a joint session of the U.S. Congress. His visit drew tens of thousands to the Capitol grounds, heavy security, and bipartisan fanfare and was tightly choreographed (Speaker Boehner and other leaders escorted him, and members were urged to show decorum).

Key themes of his speech and visit:
- Climate change: Citing his encyclical Laudato si’, Francis urged a “courageous and responsible” effort to slow environmental deterioration and called on the U.S. and Congress to take action. Democrats applauded; many Republicans remained silent.
- Poverty, refugees and immigration: He pleaded for compassion toward the poor and refugees (calling the Syrian exodus a crisis on a WWII scale) and urged the nation not to be afraid of immigrants, reminding lawmakers that America was built by immigrants and appealing to the Golden Rule.
- Death penalty and human dignity: Francis called for abolition of capital punishment worldwide, urging rehabilitation and respect for every human life—echoing recent U.S. bishops’ calls and energizing faith-based abolition efforts.
- Arms trade and war profiteering: He condemned the global arms industry—saying weapons are often sold “for money that is drenched in blood”—and urged an end to the arms trade.
- Family and marriage: He warned that the family is “threatened” and alluded to concerns about changes to the basis of marriage, reaffirming traditional Catholic teaching even as he remains pastoral toward individuals.
- Religious extremism and freedoms: He cautioned against simple bipolar worldviews, called for a balanced fight against ideological violence, and stressed safeguarding religious, intellectual and individual freedoms.
- Reconciliation and bridge-building: He acknowledged painful historical contacts with indigenous peoples and praised efforts to overcome historic differences, calling for politics that serve the common good rather than being “a slave to the economy and finance.”

Notable moments and reactions:
- The pope opened and closed his address warmly, later appearing on a Capitol balcony to bless the crowds and ask for prayers (he also asked nonbelievers to send “good wishes”).
- His remarks touched on, but did not dwell on, abortion or same-sex marriage; he reiterated the church’s pro-life stance and concern for the family but avoided detailed policy prescriptions.
- The speech produced partisan reactions—strong applause from many Democrats for his climate and immigration remarks, more muted responses from Republicans—though some Republican figures (including immigrant-background lawmakers) did applaud portions.
- Before and after the address he met privately with Speaker Boehner and participated in ceremonial events (offering a special Bible to the Library of Congress and visiting a statue of Junipero Serra).

Overall, Francis used the historic forum to press for compassion, conscience-driven politics, care for the environment and marginalized, opposition to the death penalty, and critique of war profiteering—urging lawmakers to pursue policies that protect human dignity and the common good.

A Middle Tennessee family is raising awareness and funds after their son, Owen Torti, was diagnosed as a newborn with LCHAD (long‑chain 3‑hydroxy acyl‑coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency), a rare genetic metabolic disorder that prevents the body from converting certain fats into energy. Owen, now about two years old, must be fed almost constantly (hourly during the day, continuous at night) because if his energy stores run out his body begins breaking down muscle, which can lead to organ damage, seizures, coma or death. He was born nine weeks premature after his mother developed HELLP syndrome; newborn screening identified his condition at seven days old.

Owen has been hospitalized repeatedly (about 12 times in 20 months) for metabolic crises. He receives specialized formula (Lipistart) and, because of severe oral aversion and frequent vomiting, has had a G‑tube placed and is fed almost entirely through it. His care includes plans for an intensive inpatient feeding program at Baylor in Dallas. Medical costs, special formula not covered by insurance, and program fees have created financial need.

Owen’s parents, Kayla and Tyler Torti, are both carriers of the gene; future children would have a 25% chance of having LCHAD. The family found little public information when Owen was diagnosed—LCHAD was first described in the 1990s and was added to newborn screening only about six years ago—so they are working to share their story to help other families feel less isolated.

Community support has grown: coworkers and local runners formed “All In for Owen” teams that ran the Ragnar Relay and raised about $15,000 to help with medical bills and to raise awareness. The family hopes their visibility will connect and comfort other families facing LCHAD and attract broader attention and resources for this orphan disease.

Authorities plan to demolish two East Haven, Conn., homes this week that were badly damaged when a 10-seat propeller plane crashed into them on approach to Tweed New Haven Airport, a crash that killed four people. The victims were pilot and former Microsoft executive 54-year-old Bill Henningsgaard and his 17-year-old son Maxwell, and two children who lived in one struck home: 13-year-old Sade Brantley and 1-year-old Madisyn Mitchell. Emergency repairs were made after the crash so crews could recover the bodies.

Neighbors and community members held a vigil at Margaret Tucker Park; the children’s mother, Joann Mitchell, who escaped the burning house, attended but did not speak. Local officials, including Mayor Joseph Maturo and Gov. Dannel Malloy, praised the community’s response and offered condolences.

NTSB investigators said the plane was upside-down when it hit one house at about a 60-degree angle during its first approach and that the pilot did not declare an emergency. After initial wreckage removal, investigators found no immediate indication of mechanical problems; a preliminary NTSB report is expected within 10 business days, with a full report potentially taking up to nine months.

The pilot, Henningsgaard, was a noted philanthropist and community leader who had worked at Microsoft and later led civic initiatives such as Eastside Pathways and served with Social Venture Partners. He had survived a 2009 crash-landing on the Columbia River with his mother. Colleagues and community organizations remembered him for his civic commitment and leadership.

Bitcoin experienced a dramatic intraday collapse after a recent parabolic rise.
