Seventeen-year-old Johran McCormick was fatally shot early on March 13 after being found in a 16-year-old girl’s bedroom in a Spring-area home off FM 2920. According to investigators, the girl let Johran into the house around 2:30 a.m. Her younger brother spotted feet under the bed and alerted their father. The father confronted Johran in the girl’s room; the girl reportedly denied knowing him, and an argument ensued. The father told deputies Johran dropped his hands as if reaching for something, so he fired one shot that struck Johran in the head. Johran died at the scene.

Johran’s parents, Zakia McCormick and Shawn Curley, dispute parts of the account and say they were told Johran may have been in bed with the girl when her father entered. They want the 55-year-old father prosecuted for murder and petitioning for a life sentence, arguing the killing was not accidental. Community activists and supporters also want criminal charges filed against the girl, seeking accessory or involuntary manslaughter charges on the theory her alleged lie to her father contributed to the death.

Harris County investigators continue to probe the case; it will be forwarded to a grand jury to decide whether to indict the father. Legal experts noted that if the father reasonably perceived a threat to himself or his child, a claim of self-defense or defense of others could make murder charges difficult to obtain or sustain. Meanwhile, family, friends and classmates have mourned Johran at vigils, and his parents describe him as a typical teen with plans for the Air Force or a mechanic career.

Deadpool 2 is a loud, gory, wildly self-aware sequel that mostly delivers more of what made the first film a hit: raunchy, fourth‑wall‑breaking comedy, hyperviolent set pieces, and Ryan Reynolds’ charismatic, wisecracking lead. The movie gleefully lampoons superhero conventions and pop culture — skewering earnest comic‑book tropes, fan culture, and even its own “lazy writing” — while piling on absurd, over‑the‑top mayhem and provocative gags.

Plotwise it’s straightforward in intent but convoluted in execution: after losing his love Vanessa, Wade Wilson/Deadpool (Reynolds) cycles briefly through despair thanks to his instant‑healing power, then seeks a surrogate family by training with the X‑Men and mentoring a troubled teen mutant, Firefist (Julian Dennison). Their relationship draws the attention of a time‑traveling, Terminator‑like killer, Cable (Josh Brolin), who’s come to stop Firefist’s dark future. Domino (Zazie Beetz), whose power is extreme luck, joins the ensemble and delivers a standout, effortlessly charming turn. The film mixes its action and comedy with topical jabs — from gun violence to the dour tone of some rival superhero movies — and revels in sophomoric provocation and celebrity cameos.

The movie’s strengths are Reynolds’ magnetic, cheeky performance and the film’s fearless, satirical energy; its weaknesses are that it often feels like “more of the same” — repeating gross‑out gags, irreverent jokes and regrowing‑limb set pieces from the first film. Still, for viewers who enjoy unpredictable, shocking, and frequently hilarious takes on the superhero genre, Deadpool 2 is a must‑see.

DineEquity, parent of Applebee’s and IHOP, said it will close as many as 160 restaurants — roughly 105–135 Applebee’s and 20–25 IHOPs — while opening 125 new locations globally between the two brands. The increased closures, up from earlier guidance, reflect struggles in the casual‑dining segment as customers shift to quick‑service chains like Panera and Chipotle; Applebee’s has been particularly hard hit. DineEquity reported Q2 net income of $20.9 million (down from $26.4 million year‑over‑year), with comparable same‑restaurant sales falling 6.2% at Applebee’s and 2.6% at IHOP. Management said shuttering underperforming stores and investing in franchisee financial health, supply chain improvements and brand changes are necessary for long‑term recovery. The company reiterated plans to open 20–30 Applebee’s (mostly abroad) and revised IHOP openings to 80–95 (mostly U.S.), and recently named Stephen Joyce as CEO. DineEquity operates over 3,700 restaurants in 19 countries.

A Dartmouth College study published in the Journal of Digital Forensics, Security and Law has confirmed the authenticity of the famous backyard photograph showing Lee Harvey Oswald holding the same model rifle used in the JFK assassination. Using advanced digital image-forensics methods and a physiologically plausible 3‑D model of Oswald, researchers led by Hany Farid and Emily Whiting recreated Oswald’s pose, added mass to body segments, and performed a balance (stability) analysis. Their work found the pose—though it looks off‑balance—is physically stable. They also reaffirmed earlier findings that the photo’s lighting and shadows are consistent and showed the rifle’s measured length matches the known weapon. The study therefore refutes long‑standing claims that the image was faked and demonstrates that detailed 3‑D modeling can be a powerful forensic tool for evaluating the physical plausibility of images.

First piece — Baltimore riots and response (April 2015)
- Severe unrest erupted in Baltimore following the April 19 death of Freddie Gray, a 25‑year‑old Black man who suffered a spinal injury while in police custody. What had been largely peaceful protests for nearly a week culminated after Gray’s funeral in a night of rioting, looting and arson that burned 19 buildings, injured about 20 officers, and led to more than 250 arrests.
- Local, state and federal responses: Baltimore deployed more than 3,000 police from Maryland, New Jersey and D.C. and National Guard troops to secure streets, enforce a one‑week, 10 p.m.–5 a.m. curfew and protect businesses and hospitals. Maryland’s governor declared a state of emergency and criticized Mayor Stephanie Rawlings‑Blake for delaying her request for the Guard as looting escalated; the mayor defended her cautious approach as a “delicate balancing act” to avoid overreaction that could inflame tensions.
- Investigations and accountability: Six officers were suspended and the U.S. Justice Department opened a civil‑rights investigation into Gray’s death. The ATF sent teams to investigate the fires.
- Community and national reaction: Volunteers began cleanup and some peaceful protests continued, while local leaders and President Obama condemned the violence but urged broader attention to the long‑standing social problems—poverty, crime and lack of opportunity—that underpin unrest. The disturbances disrupted daily life—schools, businesses and some government services closed, and a scheduled MLB game was to be played without fans.

Second piece — Proposal to build a connected regional trail network in Baltimore (Dec 2015)
- Argument: The Baltimore region trails network is fragmented and lags behind peer Northeastern metro areas. Investing in a connected set of high‑quality trails would boost health, transportation, tourism and quality of life at much lower cost than major highway projects.
- Six priority projects proposed (collective cost argued to be less than one basic highway interchange):
  1. Gwynns Falls/Middle Branch Trail to BWI/B&A Trail — ~10 miles, ~$10M: fills a missing link to create a continuous spine from Mt. Washington to Greater Annapolis; largely follows river valleys and is feasible with minimal property acquisition.
  2. Baltimore Trail “Beltway” — ~15 miles new (35‑mile loop), $10–20M: a citywide loop analogous to I‑695 that would connect neighborhoods, spur tourism and economic development but requires coordination with rail/utilities.
  3. Jones Falls Trail to Torrey C. Brown Trail — ~14 miles, $15–20M: links city to northern suburbs and fills a key gap in the East Coast Greenway; may face neighborhood resistance and challenges crossing I‑695.
  4. Middle Branch Loop Trail — ~3 new miles (4 total), $4–10M: waterfront loop linking downtown and industrial/Under Armour area; opportunities and design challenges include bridge access and coordination with private interests.
  5. Towson Run Trail — ~5 miles, $6–8M: connects Towson University and downtown Towson to regional trails, improving access for a large suburban population; may require bridges and face local opposition.
  6. Patapsco Trail — ~16 new miles (18 total), $15–20M: parallels the Patapsco River to Ellicott City, sharing sections with Project 1; largely feasible using existing public rights‑of‑way and attractive for tourism and day trips.
- Conclusion: The author urges creation of a regional trail plan and investment from state, county, corporate or private sources to build a coherent network that enhances competitiveness, recreation and transportation for future residents and visitors.

A charter bus operated by OGA Charters rolled over Saturday morning, May 14, 2016, on U.S. Highway 83 about 45–46 miles north of Laredo, Texas, while en route to a casino in Eagle Pass. Seven people died at the scene and an eighth died later at a Laredo hospital; 44 others were injured and taken to hospitals in Laredo, Carrizo Springs and San Antonio. Trooper Conrad Hein said the driver — who survived — “lost control” of the single vehicle; it was raining at the time but investigators have not determined whether weather was a factor.

The National Transportation Safety Board dispatched investigators to the scene to determine the cause and will examine company operations. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration records show OGA Charters, a small San Juan, Texas–based company with two buses, had been ordered twice in 2015 by Louisiana inspectors to take one of its buses out of service for brake and emergency-exit defects (including brake leaks and automatic-adjustment problems); the inspections also cited a discolored windshield and other violations. The records do not confirm whether the sidelined bus was the one that crashed. OGA had a “satisfactory” rating in 2014 but had six inspections since 2014 showing 15 violations, including hours-of-service and maintenance issues.

The Laredo Morning Times identified the eight victims by name and age. Local and federal authorities continue to investigate.

President Trump suggested on Friday that war with North Korea was a possible outcome, telling reporters in Bedminster, New Jersey, “I think you know the answer to that,” when asked whether the U.S. would go to war after he referenced a potential “bad solution.” Flanked by Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Nikki Haley, Trump said his Cabinet is unified on the North Korea crisis even though senior officials have emphasized diplomacy. Tillerson and Defense Secretary Jim Mattis have urged combined messaging and diplomatic efforts, but Trump has repeatedly issued tough warnings—saying there would be “big, big trouble” if North Korea threatened Guam and earlier warning of “fire and fury” that he later doubled down on. North Korea has announced plans to launch rockets over Japan toward waters near the U.S. base on Guam as a warning.

Trump also refused to rule out military intervention in Venezuela, calling a military option “certainly something that we could pursue,” while declining to say whether U.S. forces would lead any operation. He cited the humanitarian suffering in Venezuela and reiterated U.S. demands that President Nicolás Maduro restore democratic norms. The White House declined Maduro’s request for a call and said Trump will speak to him once democracy is restored. The administration recently imposed sanctions on Maduro after a contested vote that created a pro-government constituent assembly.

Latin American governments and regional bodies reacted strongly against Trump’s threat of force, with Peru, Mexico, Colombia and others condemning any military option as contrary to U.N. principles. Venezuela’s government dismissed the warning, called for regional unity against the U.S., and portrayed the remarks as aggressive interference. Meanwhile, Venezuela’s new constituent assembly moved up governors’ elections to October amid ongoing protests, shortages of food and medicine, high inflation and months of deadly unrest that have left more than 120 dead.

On July 23, 2015, a gunman opened fire during a showing of the comedy Trainwreck at the Grand Theatre in Lafayette, Louisiana. The shooter, later identified as 59-year-old John Russell (or Russel) Houser, fired about 13 rounds, killing two female moviegoers (33-year-old Jillian Johnson and 21-year-old Mayci Breaux), wounding nine others, and then fatally shooting himself. Initial reports said three people were dead including the shooter; later confirmed two victims and the gunman were deceased. Several wounded were taken to hospitals, at least one in critical condition.

Police described Houser as a transient who had been in the Lafayette area since early July; he parked near the exit and appeared intent on fleeing before encountering officers. Investigators searched a Motel 6 room where he had stayed and found wigs and disguises; bomb squad and K-9 units checked suspicious items and a backpack in the theater.

Background checks and court records show a history of arrests and troubling behavior: past charges (including arson and selling alcohol to a minor), traffic citations, eviction in 2014 accompanied by property damage, and a 2008 family-filed petition for a temporary protective order stating he exhibited “extreme erratic behavior,” had mental-health issues (manic depression/bipolar), and that his wife had removed weapons from their home; she later filed for divorce.

An extensive online footprint tied to the name Rusty or John Russell Houser showed frequent, strongly conservative and racially charged postings on forums and social sites. His comments expressed fears about America’s future, distrust of mainstream media, advocacy of censorship conspiracies, interest in the Greek nationalist group Golden Dawn, and hostile rhetoric toward minorities. He had also appeared on local TV in the 1990s as a provocative commentator.

President Obama was briefed on the attack and asked to be kept updated. Authorities continued the investigation into motive and Houser’s recent movements. Witnesses described hearing multiple pops and seeing muzzle flashes; some escaped uninjured, though many were traumatized.

This document combines three main items: an explanation of web crawls by the Internet Archive, a detailed report on the murder of Colorado’s corrections chief Tom Clements, and a longer feature on Governor John Hickenlooper’s shift to championing new gun-control legislation in Colorado.

Internet Archive effort
- The Archive is crawling and saving web pages as they are created and archiving pages they reference so that links remain functional even if the original pages change or disappear. The initiative—part of a “No More 404” effort—aims to preserve the specific versions of pages cited by others and to replace or supplement broken links with archived versions.

Murder of Tom Clements
- Tom Clements, 58, executive director of the Colorado Department of Corrections, was shot and killed at his home in Monument (north of Colorado Springs) around 8:30 p.m. A dark, boxy car with its engine running was seen near the house; a witness reported one person driving away. Law enforcement has not ruled out any motive, including a connection to his job; the FBI and Colorado Bureau of Investigation are involved.
- Clements was appointed by Gov. John Hickenlooper in 2011 after a long career in Missouri corrections, overseeing state and private prisons and parole. Gov. Hickenlooper praised him as kind and thoughtful and ordered flags at public buildings lowered until after Clements’ funeral. Clements is survived by his wife and two daughters.
- Investigators searched the wooded Black Forest neighborhood, canvassed neighbors and used search dogs. Clements’ address was easily found online, highlighting privacy concerns.
- The killing raised scrutiny of a recent professional decision: Clements denied a request by Saudi national Homaidan al-Turki—convicted in Colorado of sexual assault and other crimes—to be transferred to Saudi Arabia. Al-Turki’s case previously drew international attention. Officials said a State Department call to Colorado corrections after the shooting was likely a courtesy and not tied to the investigation.
- Colorado increased security for top appointed officials and the governor’s mansion as a precaution. The article notes historical parallels—another state prisons director was murdered in Oregon in 1989 and remains a controversial case—and mentions an unsolved 2008 killing of a county prosecutor as a similar unresolved political-era slaying.

Hickenlooper and Colorado’s new gun laws
- The piece traces Gov. Hickenlooper’s evolution on gun policy after the Aurora movie-theater mass shooting. Initially skeptical that tighter laws could prevent such violence, Hickenlooper nonetheless pursued pragmatic reforms—seeking data, consulting stakeholders across urban and rural Colorado, and balancing political and economic concerns.
- Colorado passed one of the nation’s tougher gun packages (expected to be signed by Hickenlooper), including expanded background checks and a 15-round magazine limit. The governor deliberated carefully—hesitating over magazine limits due to political and job-loss risks but ultimately supporting them after reviewing studies on officer fatalities and other evidence.
- The reforms drew fierce opposition (NRA ads, hall protests, a banner plane) and political risk for Democrats in a state with many gun owners and a large unaffiliated electorate. Still, polls cited show broad public support for expanded background checks (about 80%) and significant support for magazine limits (about 61%).
- Supporters portray the package as a pragmatic, potentially national model; critics warn of political backlash and overreach. Hickenlooper frames the effort as common-sense, evidence-based policymaking and expressed a desire to move past the gun debate.

Overall, the document covers an archival web-preservation initiative, a high-profile murder investigation that could implicate official duties or other motives, and the political story of a governor who, after tragedy and study, embraced significant gun-control measures despite controversy.

China warned it will retaliate if the U.S. imposes further tariffs, after reports the Trump administration plans to raise proposed duties on an additional $200 billion of Chinese imports from 10% to 25%. Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang said Beijing is open to "dialogue and consultation" but warned that unilateral U.S. pressure would be counterproductive and promised to defend China's rights without detailing measures.

The move would follow the U.S. imposition of 25% tariffs on $34 billion of Chinese goods (announced July 6) and China’s matching tariffs. A second U.S. tranche targeting about $16 billion in goods could take effect imminently. Reports say U.S. officials are privately discussing restarting talks — Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and Chinese Vice Premier Liu He representatives have been in contact — but formats, timetables and issues remain unresolved. High-level negotiations stalled after the initial tariffs and subsequent retaliatory measures.

Domestic U.S. divisions complicate diplomacy: Treasury engages in talks while U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer continues a tougher stance based on a 301 finding that China misappropriates U.S. technology. The trade conflict has disrupted markets, affected deals (notably contributing to the collapse of Qualcomm’s $44 billion bid for NXP), and prompted Chinese leaders to signal a policy shift toward supporting growth amid risks from the trade dispute and deleveraging efforts.

The American Psychiatric Association has released DSM-5, the fifth major revision of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. The APA describes it as a clinician’s guide reflecting current knowledge; the revision process involved unprecedented public review (three drafts and more than 13,000 comments). DSM-5 has three main sections: an introduction/how-to-use guide, Section II with categorical diagnoses, and Section III with self-assessments and conditions needing more research.

Key structural and diagnostic changes
- The multiaxial system was eliminated and chapters reorganized to show relationships among disorders; diagnoses are now framed across age, gender and developmental characteristics.
- The overall number of disorders is similar to DSM-IV, but several diagnostic definitions and categories were revised.

Major disorder-level changes
- Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD): Four previous diagnoses (autistic disorder, Asperger’s, childhood disintegrative disorder, and PDD-NOS) were combined into a single ASD category defined by deficits in social communication/interaction plus restricted, repetitive behaviors; Social Communication Disorder is used when repetitive behaviors are absent.
- Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder: A new diagnosis intended to address possible over-diagnosis of bipolar disorder in children; for youth up to 18 with persistent irritability and severe behavioral dyscontrol.
- ADHD: Revised to emphasize persistence into adulthood. Age-of-onset criterion changed from symptoms before age 7 to before 12; adult diagnosis may require one fewer symptom than for children, while cross-situational requirements were strengthened.
- Bereavement exclusion removed: Major depressive episode can be diagnosed in bereavement; a detailed footnote helps clinicians distinguish normal grief from depressive episodes. Persistent Complex Bereavement Disorder is included in Section III as a condition for further study.
- PTSD: Reorganized into four symptom clusters (reexperiencing, arousal, avoidance, and persistent negative alterations in cognition/mood), with developmentally sensitive criteria and separate rules for children 6 and younger.
- Neurocognitive disorders: Dementia and amnestic disorder are subsumed under Major Neurocognitive Disorder; a new Mild Neurocognitive Disorder was added to encourage early detection and intervention.
- Other additions: Binge Eating Disorder, Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder, and Hoarding Disorder are now officially recognized.

Reception and controversy
- APA leaders emphasized DSM-5’s role as a clinical guide and noted that it reflects current knowledge rather than creating new science. They argued clinicians need the manual now despite ongoing research into biological markers.
- Critics argue DSM-5 lowers diagnostic thresholds and may broaden diagnoses, risking over-diagnosis and over-treatment. Prominent voices—including former DSM-IV lead Allen Frances and others—warn of medicalizing normal states and of potential impacts on care priorities and resources.
- The NIMH, led by Thomas Insel, has publicly criticized DSM-5’s lack of validity (no objective biological markers) and announced a research shift toward the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework, which encourages studying underlying biological and behavioral dimensions across DSM categories. NIMH says this is a research reorientation, not necessarily a clinical repudiation of DSM use.
- Commentators and some psychiatrists note DSM-5 remains primarily symptom-based and is unlikely to incorporate the biological classification many hoped for; it will likely continue to guide clinical diagnosis and insurance reimbursement for years while research (RDoC, biomarker work) seeks more etiologic classifications.

Overall, DSM-5 updates definitional criteria and several diagnoses, reorganizes the manual’s structure, and formalizes some previously used clinical diagnoses. Its release has intensified debate about psychiatric classification, the balance between pragmatic clinical needs and ambitions for biologically grounded diagnostic systems, and the risks of over-diagnosis versus the benefits of earlier detection and treatment.

On June 27, Singapore Airlines flight SQ368, a Boeing 777-300ER en route from Singapore to Milan with 222 passengers and 19 crew, turned back to Changi Airport about two hours after takeoff when an engine oil warning was triggered. Passengers reported vibrations, a faint fuel smell and strange noises before landing. After touchdown, the right engine caught fire; airport emergency services arrived quickly and extinguished the blaze within minutes using water and foam. All occupants disembarked safely and no injuries were reported. Singapore Airlines towed the aircraft away and offered passengers options to reschedule; a replacement flight departed later that morning. Singapore’s leaders and aviation authorities said they were investigating the cause and reviewing procedures.

American sprinter Manteo Mitchell broke his left fibula during the leadoff leg of the U.S. men’s 4x400m relay at the Olympics but, despite intense pain, completed the remaining 200 meters so the team could qualify for the final. He reported feeling a snap halfway through his leg and later described wanting to lie down; an X-ray after the race confirmed a complete fibula fracture. Doctors said the bone should heal in four to six weeks. Mitchell ran his half-lap in about 46.1 seconds—tying for fifth in that leg—and the U.S. finished the heat in 2:58.87 to advance. Mitchell said the injury likely stemmed from a prior misstep on stairs; he remained in good spirits afterward. USA Track and Field had not named his replacement; options included 400m hurdlers such as Angelo Taylor or Kerron Clement, as some other relay-pool athletes were already injured.

Vice President Joe Biden is not immediately joining other Cabinet members in voluntarily returning part of his salary in response to the automatic sequester cuts that began March 1. Biden’s office said he will share the burden with his staff and will take a pay reduction if and when his own employees are affected by furloughs, but for now is holding off while they assess whether his office will face cuts.

President Obama, Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel, Secretary of State John Kerry and others have pledged to give back portions of their pay (Obama 5% of his $400,000 salary; Hagel and Attorney General Eric Holder the equivalent of 14 days’ pay; Kerry 5% to charity), a symbolic gesture intended to show solidarity with federal workers hit by the roughly $85 billion in sequestration cuts. That pressure to “lead by example” is amplified by public relations considerations, since many Cabinet members are substantially wealthier than Biden.

Biden, who earns $230,700 as vice president and has far more modest personal finances than many Cabinet colleagues, has made other symbolic moves (saying he would return to riding Amtrak to Delaware). His office clarified that earlier reports saying he had declined to take a pay cut were incorrect — he has only deferred a decision pending whether his staff will be furloughed.

Google admitted that its Street View cars unintentionally collected fragments of payload data transmitted over unencrypted (open) Wi‑Fi networks for about three years. The company had previously said it only gathered network identifiers (SSID and MAC addresses) to improve location services, but a German data protection authority’s inquiry prompted a deeper review and revealed that a piece of code—originally written in 2006 for an experimental project—sampled all publicly broadcast Wi‑Fi data. That code was incorporated into the Street View software a year later, despite the mobile team not intending to collect payload data.

Key points:
- The data collected were limited fragments (not continuous streams), because cars were moving and the monitoring system cycled channels roughly five times a second; Google says it never used these payload snippets in any products.
- Once the error was discovered, Google grounded the Street View fleet, isolated the data, and pledged to delete it while working with regulators on disposal.
- Google will commission an independent third-party review of the software and said it has stopped collecting Wi‑Fi network data and is reviewing internal controls to prevent recurrence.
- The disclosure could prompt regulatory and legal scrutiny (including potential wiretapping concerns), and highlights the risk of unencrypted Wi‑Fi—users are urged to password‑protect their networks.

Google apologized for the mistake and has provided a third‑party report to data protection authorities confirming the collection occurred only from unencrypted networks.

Gil Scott-Heron, the influential poet and musician often credited as a progenitor of hip-hop, died in New York at 62, his publisher reported. Best known for his 1970 spoken-word piece "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised," Scott-Heron first recorded with the album Small Talk at 125th and Lenox and became widely known for that seminal track, which entered popular culture through many references and parodies. Born in Chicago in 1949, he grew up in Jackson, Tenn., attended high school in the Bronx and studied at Lincoln University before settling in Manhattan.

A prolific young writer—by 23 he had published novels, poetry and recorded several albums—Scott-Heron continued recording through the 1970s and early 1980s, later taking a long hiatus. He returned with 1994’s Spirits, which included a cautionary track to the then-new hip-hop generation, and after a period of public struggles with substance abuse and legal trouble in the 2000s he resumed performing following his 2007 release from jail. His 2010 album, I’m New Here, received critical acclaim. Artists across generations, including Kanye West, have cited his influence and used his voice in later work.

Profiles of Scott-Heron portray a complex, charismatic figure who called himself a "bluesologist," lived modestly in Harlem, and loved watching boxing and older TV shows. He inspired admiration for his biting social commentary and artistic originality but also suffered visibly from crack addiction, which markedly affected his appearance and life. Despite personal challenges, his cultural legacy endures through his music, poetry and lasting impact on contemporary music, especially hip-hop.

Mitt Romney won the Illinois Republican primary handily, extending his delegate lead and reinforcing his front-runner status. With 55% of precincts reporting, Romney led with about 48% to Rick Santorum’s 34%, Ron Paul’s 9% and Newt Gingrich’s 8%, making Illinois one of Romney’s largest state wins since Florida. Exit polls showed voters prioritized electability (37%) over ideological purity (20%), a dynamic that favored Romney.

Romney’s financial advantage was decisive: his campaign and the super PAC Restore Our Future spent roughly $3.7 million on Illinois advertising versus about $532,000 for Santorum and allied groups, particularly dominating the costly Chicago media market. Romney campaigned in Illinois on election day, including a Google office visit and an online event, and framed the victory as part of a national tide in his direction.

Santorum, who had campaigned in Illinois but also spent time elsewhere (including Puerto Rico, where he lost big), conceded the state to Romney and used his post-primary remarks to insist he would stay in the race. Delivering a populist, conservative-focused speech from Gettysburg, Pa., Santorum congratulated Romney while arguing he’d performed well where conservative Republicans live and vowed to press on to Louisiana and his home state Pennsylvania. He emphasized themes of freedom, limited government, opposition to Obamacare/Romneycare and skepticism of climate science, portraying the contest as a foundational struggle for the party’s direction.
