Charlie Gard, an 11-month-old British infant with a rare genetic mitochondrial disease that left him brain-damaged and unable to breathe unaided, attracted international attention and widespread public support—raising more than £1.3 million and hundreds of thousands of supporters. His parents, Connie Yates and Chris Gard, campaigned to take him for experimental treatment in the United States and received offers of assistance from Pope Francis and U.S. President Donald Trump, as well as interest from hospitals including NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia and Italy’s Bambino Gesù.

British doctors at Great Ormond Street Hospital and successive courts, including the U.K. Supreme Court and the European Court of Human Rights, ruled that the experimental therapy would be futile and could cause Charlie suffering, and authorized withdrawal of life support. Legal and ethical debate centered on parental rights versus the child’s best interests, with U.K. law giving primacy to the child’s welfare when parents and doctors disagree.

Charlie’s parents announced they would establish The Charlie Gard Foundation to support research into mitochondrial and other rare childhood illnesses, provide information and guidance to families facing similar situations (including clarifying parental rights and access to treatment), and serve as a legacy honoring Charlie. They said all donations from their GoFundMe (including a £10,000 donation from GoFundMe itself) will go to the foundation. The family later announced with great sadness that Charlie had died; they asked for privacy and thanked supporters.

Researchers conducted a large meta-analysis of 88 studies (148 samples, >8,000 participants) to estimate the association between in vivo brain volume (measured by MRI) and intelligence (IQ). They found a small but reliable positive correlation (r = .24; R2 ≈ .06), which held across ages (children and adults), IQ domains (full-scale, verbal, performance), and sexes. However, multiple tests indicate that the literature is affected by dissemination/publication bias: studies reporting stronger positive correlations are overrepresented, and reported effect sizes have declined over time. Even after accounting for bias, the modest association remains, but brain volume explains only a minor portion of IQ variance and has limited practical predictive value.

The authors caution against interpreting brain size as a direct or causal proxy for intelligence. Comparative and within-human examples support this: species or individuals with larger brains do not necessarily show higher cognitive performance, and men’s larger average brain volumes do not translate into higher IQ than women. Instead, brain structure and integrity (microarchitecture, connectivity, etc.) likely matter more for cognitive differences than gross brain size.

The Utah Legislature approved HB277, eliminating the civil statute of limitations for child sexual abuse and sending the measure to Gov. Gary Herbert. Under current law, victims have four years after their 18th birthday to file civil suits; the new law would instead allow a four-year window to sue beginning when a victim discovers or remembers the abuse. Supporters, including Rep. Ken Ivory and bill floor sponsor Sen. Aaron Osmond, said the change lets survivors take needed time to heal and pursue accountability for crimes often not processed until decades later. Deondra Brown, co‑founder of the Foundation for Survivors of Abuse and a survivor who watched the vote from the Senate gallery, praised the bill for giving victims options to address lifelong medical and financial harms. Opponents raised concerns about reliability of late-discovered memories; the final Senate vote was 24-2.

Separately, a retired Rich High School teacher, 60-year-old Michael Layne Williamson, was sentenced July 27 to one to 15 years in prison (plus up to five years concurrent) after pleading guilty to aggravated sexual abuse of a child for assaults committed 22 years earlier. During sentencing, Judge Thomas Willmore rejected defense requests for a short or home-confinement term despite Williamson’s stage 4 prostate cancer, calling the crimes far beyond a mere “indiscretion.” The victim, now 35, delivered an emotional impact statement describing long-term trauma, secrecy, and the courage to report after two decades; Williamson offered apologies and asked for forgiveness. The judge ordered Williamson to complete sex-offender treatment while incarcerated.

Federal and state investigators have determined that 13 bald eagles found Feb. 20 near Federalsburg on Maryland’s Eastern Shore did not die of natural causes, though officials are not publicly disclosing how they died or releasing suspect information to avoid compromising the probe. The birds showed no external trauma, and necropsies ruled out disease, including avian influenza. Authorities now are focusing on prosecuting anyone responsible; killing a protected bald eagle carries penalties up to a year in prison and a $100,000 fine. Maryland Natural Resources Police and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service are investigating, and a $25,000 reward has been offered for information leading to a conviction. This event is the state’s largest bald-eagle die-off in about 30 years.

A 36-year-old woman developed an itchy, pimple-like lesion on her left groin about two months after a honeymoon in Belize. After an initial primary-care visit and a course of sulfamethoxazole with only partial improvement, she sought further evaluation at Florida wound clinics. Clinicians noted a small central punctum with pus and a firm, beanlike subcutaneous nodule; a surgeon suspected a living organism. Under local anesthesia a 5 mm incision revealed and allowed removal of a tapered, spiny larva that pathology identified as a human botfly (Dermatobia hominis) — a maggot that causes cutaneous myiasis. The lesion had an air hole the larva used to breathe; botfly larvae in the tropics live under skin for 27–128 days before dropping out to pupate. The woman’s wound healed completely within a week. The report notes botfly infestations are uncommon in the U.S. but common in tropical regions, can sometimes be self-extracted after occlusion (petroleum jelly, bacon, nail polish, plant extracts) that forces the larva to surface, and represent a frequent travel-related skin complaint from developing countries.

European political and financial leaders warned that Greece’s growing instability could trigger a catastrophic shock to the eurozone and the global economy, prompting urgent contingency planning in London and elsewhere.

Key developments
- Political uncertainty in Greece: After inconclusive elections on 6 May and failed coalition talks, new elections were called for 17 June. An interim technocratic government led by Panagiotis Pikrammenos was appointed to run until then. The left-wing Syriza, opposed to austerity and renegotiation of the bailout, was polling strongly.
- Capital flight and bank pressure: Large withdrawals accelerated after the election, with reports of billions of euros taken from Greek accounts in short order. The Bank of Greece reported substantial ECB lending outstanding and large TARGET2 liabilities. The ECB restricted some funding until Greek banks are recapitalised using parts of the €130bn EU/IMF bailout.
- Financial contagion risks: Analysts and officials warned that a disorderly Greek exit from the euro could cause losses of up to €hundreds of billions across the ECB, national central banks and euro-area institutions, potentially amounting to roughly $1tn (about 5% of EU output) in a worst-case scenario. Losses could force recapitalisation of the ECB or national central banks, erode the firewall’s capacity (EFSF/ESM), and spark depositor flight from other periphery countries.
- Systemic channels of exposure: The ECB/Eurosystem are exposed via Greek sovereign bonds they hold, ECB loans to Greek banks (distributed through national central banks), and TARGET2 cross-border claims and liabilities. An exit might convert Greek assets and liabilities into a devalued new currency, leaving other euro-area central banks with losses and raising difficult legal, monetary and political choices.
- International responses: The UK government and Bank of England are drawing up contingency plans to protect the British economy—already in a double-dip recession—should eurozone fragmentation occur. Bank of England governor Sir Mervyn King warned the euro area “is tearing itself apart” and indicated further UK stimulus might be needed if Europe fails to resolve the crisis. US President Barack Obama described the crisis as a “headwind” to US recovery and was expected to press European leaders at the G8 for pro-growth measures rather than more austerity, though US leverage is limited.
- European politics and markets: French and German leaders met to seek calm; the ECB signalled preference to keep Greece in the euro and said Greek banks should be recapitalised with bailout funds before additional ECB support. Markets reacted nervously with falls in equities and the euro amid reports of ECB restrictions on Greek funding.

Outlook and stakes
Officials and economists stressed the choices facing Europe are stark: either implement stronger fiscal burden-sharing, well-capitalised and regulated banks and credible firewalls to preserve the eurozone, or face “uncharted territory” with potentially huge social, political and economic costs. Many warned that a disorderly Greek exit could be catastrophic for Greece and inflict severe damage across the euro area and beyond.

President Donald Trump delivered a prepared speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos on Jan. 26, 2018, pitching an upbeat, business-friendly case for his "America First" economic agenda while insisting the U.S. remains a partner on the world stage.

Key points from the speech:
- Economic accomplishments: Trump touted U.S. growth since his election—2.4 million jobs created, record stock-market gains, low unemployment (including historic lows for African‑American and Hispanic unemployment), high consumer and business confidence—and credited tax cuts and deregulation for restoring U.S. competitiveness.
- Tax and regulatory changes: He emphasized the 2017 tax overhaul (corporate rate cut from 35% to 21%, middle‑class and small‑business relief), claimed millions of workers received bonuses, and highlighted large repatriation and investment plans (e.g., Apple). He said his administration cut far more regulations than it initially pledged, calling regulation "stealth taxation."
- Trade and energy: Trump reaffirmed support for free trade only if it is fair and reciprocal, criticized unfair practices (IP theft, industrial subsidies, state-led planning) and said the U.S. will enforce trade laws and pursue bilateral agreements (including with TPP countries). He also said the U.S. lifted self-imposed limits on energy production to boost security and reduce dependence on single suppliers.
- Security and foreign policy: He framed military strength as necessary for prosperity, urged allies to share defense burdens, praised international efforts against ISIS and pressure on North Korea and Iran, and stressed preventing Afghanistan from becoming a terrorist safe haven.
- Immigration and workforce development: Trump advocated replacing "chain migration" with a merit-based immigration system and urged investment in people and workforce development as the best anti-poverty measures.
- Tone and reception: Trump repeatedly defended his record and attacked the media as purveyors of "fake news," drawing hisses from parts of the audience. Reaction from attendees and commentators was mixed—some praised his pro-business focus and restraint relative to expectations, while others called the speech self-centered or tone‑deaf. The address came amid news reports about Trump’s past desire to fire Special Counsel Robert Mueller and controversy over his comments about certain countries; Trump responded to some criticisms with brief denials or conditional apologies in separate remarks and interviews.

Overall, the Davos speech presented a promotional case for the U.S. economy under Trump—urging business investment in America—while reiterating themes of fair trade, deregulation, national security, and immigration reform.

Nathan “Bodie” Barksdale, a notorious 1980s Baltimore drug dealer long associated with HBO’s The Wire, has died at age 54 in a federal medical prison in Butner, North Carolina. Authorities and a Baltimore City Health Department spokesperson said he died of natural causes after a period of illness. 

Barksdale ran a violent heroin operation in West Baltimore public housing, survived being shot more than 20 times and had his right leg amputated. Convicted in the mid-1980s for torturing three people and later acquitted in the 1982 killing of a mentor, he served prison time and afterward worked with the city’s Safe Streets anti-violence program. In 2014 he was arrested in a DEA wiretap investigation, pleaded guilty to participating in a heroin conspiracy with members of the Black Guerrilla Family, and was sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison. At his plea hearing he acknowledged relapsing into addiction and running a scam to feed it.

Barksdale is widely thought to have inspired elements of characters on The Wire — most notably the drug lord Avon Barksdale and the dealer “Bodie” Broadus — though series creator David Simon has said the show’s characters were composites drawn from many stories and not direct representations of one man. Barksdale himself embraced the connection at times, releasing a DVD about his life that included an interview with Wood Harris, who played Avon on the series.

A 32-year-old Florida man, Joseph Michael Schreiber, was arrested and charged with arson after investigators say he set fire to the Islamic Center of Fort Pierce late on Sept. 11–12, 2016. The blaze, which heavily damaged the mosque, occurred on the 15th anniversary of 9/11 and during the Muslim holiday Eid al-Adha; no one was inside and services were relocated. Deputies say a tip led them to Schreiber, whose motorcycle matched surveillance footage of a rider fleeing the scene. A search of his home produced additional evidence, and an examination of his social media showed multiple anti-Islam posts. Schreiber reportedly confessed, saying he did not intend to hurt anyone and felt embarrassed. He was held without bond; under Florida law his status as a prison-release re-offender and as a habitual felony offender could expose him to a mandatory minimum 30-year term or, if deemed a habitual offender, life in prison. The FBI is also investigating for possible federal charges. The mosque had previously faced threats and intimidation after being publicly identified as the place of worship attended by Orlando gunman Omar Mateen.

This article describes human-rights lawyer Amal Clooney’s efforts, alongside Yazidi survivor-activist Nadia Murad, to seek international justice for atrocities committed by ISIS against the Yazidi community. Clooney visited refugee camps in northern Greece and met survivors who described mass killings, rape, sexual slavery and family separations—horrors the U.N. and U.S. State Department have characterized as genocide. More than 5,000 Yazidis have been killed and at least 3,200 remain missing or held, per a U.N. inquiry.

Clooney and Murad are working to gather evidence (survivor testimony, exhumations, etc.) and press the U.N. and key governments to refer the situation to the International Criminal Court so perpetrators can be prosecuted. Because Iraq and Syria are not ICC members, an ICC probe would require either Iraq’s invitation or a U.N. Security Council referral—a diplomatic hurdle complicated by past resistance from permanent members such as Russia and China. Clooney has lobbied U.N. officials and ambassadors and plans further outreach.

The piece highlights Murad’s personal story—captured in 2014, enslaved and repeatedly raped before escaping—and her advocacy (U.N. testimony, congressional testimony, U.N. goodwill ambassadorship, Nobel nomination). Survivors remain at risk and traumatized; some still receive threats. Clooney emphasizes the need for accountability and international justice, invoking Nuremberg as precedent, and says she and Murad will persist despite challenges to secure prosecutions that would bring survivors recognition and redress.

Brussels officials say chronic traffic jams and repeated closures of key road tunnels are being worsened because original construction plans for the city’s 7.1 miles of underground tunnels cannot be found — reportedly because they were stored in a pier under a viaduct in 1989 and were "apparently eaten by mice" before being moved to proper storage in 2010. The revelation came during a parliamentary inquiry into the tunnels’ dilapidated condition and the long-delayed repairs, which are estimated to cost about €1 billion. Former officials told MPs they had warned ministers as early as 2013 about urgent repair needs, a shortage of engineers and technicians, and the high cost and traffic disruption deeper renovations would cause; emergency patching was routinely done but comprehensive renewals were repeatedly postponed for budgetary and logistical reasons. The rodent-eaten-plans explanation has provoked ridicule and frustration domestically and abroad, and underscored wider criticisms of Brussels’ fragmented political structure and deteriorating infrastructure.

Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, sought asylum in Ecuador’s London embassy in June 2012 to avoid extradition to Sweden over allegations of sexual assault and rape he denies. After more than three years inside the embassy, a UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention concluded that his confinement amounted to “arbitrary detention.” The panel’s finding — disclosed to the UK and Sweden in late January and published in early February 2016 — is not legally binding but increases political pressure on both states.

Assange said via WikiLeaks he would surrender to British police at noon the Friday after the ruling if the UN rejected his claim, but if the UN ruled in his favor he would expect his passport returned and arrest attempts to cease. His lawyers argued that changes in UK law since 2012, and his inability to exercise asylum outside the embassy, supported the UN’s view; they asked Sweden to drop its outstanding extradition request and the UK to guarantee he would not be arrested or extradited, including over potential U.S. investigations into WikiLeaks’ publications.

The UK government maintained Assange was voluntarily avoiding lawful arrest and said the UN opinion would not be legally binding while a European Arrest Warrant remained in force; Downing Street and Scotland Yard warned he would be arrested if he left the embassy. Sweden said the UN finding differed from its position and planned to respond, noting its prosecutors still handled the legal process. Supporters called on the UK and Sweden to comply with the UN panel, while Assange’s team sought assurances of meaningful liberty and potential compensation if the panel’s standard was met. Concerns also persisted about possible U.S. interest in prosecuting Assange.

A Dallas County lawsuit filed Sept. 6, 2017, alleges the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) was negligent in the June heat-stroke death of 15-year-old Reid Comita at Buffalo Trail Scout Ranch. The suit claims Reid, who was enrolled in an introductory backpacking class intended to be under adult supervision, was instead sent on an "extremely aggressive" hike in near-100°F conditions with a high heat index, lacked proper training, and was accompanied by only two other teens rather than the required two adults. The family also alleges poor communication—being notified of his death more than four hours later. Reid, who was completing requirements for Eagle Scout and was posthumously awarded the rank by his troop, is remembered by his parents as a talented, nonathletic student who sought the safer introductory course. The BSA issued a statement expressing sympathy, saying youth safety is paramount. The Comitas say they have not heard from BSA leadership and blame the organization for Reid’s death.

Major Japanese stock indexes plunged last week—Japan’s Nikkei fell more than 10% in its biggest weekly slide since 2008—after the March 11 earthquake and tsunami and the ensuing Fukushima Daiichi nuclear crisis. Despite the rout and widespread concern about reconstruction costs and radiation, billionaire investor Warren Buffett said the sell-off represents a buying opportunity. Speaking in Daegu, South Korea, Buffett said the disaster “will take some time to rebuild, but it will not change the economic future of Japan,” and that he would not sell Japanese stocks if he owned them. He expects the global economic impact to be limited and noted that extraordinary events often create buying opportunities.

Others echoed his long-term optimism: overseas investors were active buyers, and analysts noted reconstruction spending could support a recovery. Estimates for rebuilding range widely—Japan’s economy minister put costs above 20 trillion yen (~$247 billion), and the World Bank suggested rebuilding could take up to five years and cost as much as $235 billion. Reconstruction-related firms (homebuilders, contractors) have already seen strong gains. Buffett, who has large cash reserves and recent acquisition activity, also said Berkshire Hathaway is seeking large acquisitions globally, including in South Korea, where it already holds stakes. He canceled a planned Japan visit because of the quake and was scheduled to meet South Korean President Lee Myung-bak before heading to India.

Newsmax CEO Christopher Ruddy set off a media storm when he told PBS’s Judy Woodruff that President Trump was “considering perhaps terminating” special counsel Robert Mueller, who is overseeing the Russia investigation. Ruddy later said he had not directly discussed firing Mueller with Trump and was interpreting comments from others (including Trump lawyer Jay Sekulow). The White House and Press Secretary Sean Spicer denied Ruddy spoke to the president about the matter.

Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein told a Senate subcommittee he has not seen “good cause” to fire Mueller and stressed that he—not Attorney General Jeff Sessions—has authority over hiring or firing the special counsel. Rosenstein said Mueller would have sufficient independence and that federal rules require written justification for removal and permit dismissal only for cause; he also said he would not follow any order he deemed unlawful or inappropriate. Senators criticized Sessions for skipping the hearing and sending Rosenstein in his place.

Separately, on ABC’s “This Week,” attorney Jay Sekulow declined to rule out the possibility Trump could fire Mueller, noting the president is the “unitary executive” and would consult advisers. Ruddy, a Trump confidant and Mar-a-Lago member who has previously floated ideas publicly, has been reported to have visited the West Wing recently, though accounts conflict on whether he met the president that day.

Background: Mueller was appointed in mid-May to investigate Russian interference in the 2016 election and any links to the Trump campaign. The controversy reflects mounting congressional and media scrutiny over whether the administration might attempt to curtail the special counsel’s work.

Rare photos from Nirvana's first concert (March 1987, Raymond, Washington) have surfaced after being shared by Maggie Poukkula, daughter of Tony Poukkula, whose basement hosted the fledgling band's debut. Maggie, 19, posted a three-photo strip on Twitter showing her father with Kurt Cobain; she discovered the images tucked inside her father's Cobain/Nirvana biographies and only realized their significance after media coverage. That night Nirvana’s lineup was Cobain, Krist Novoselic and drummer Aaron Burckhard; Tony reportedly joined them on guitar for at least two Led Zeppelin covers. An incomplete set list from the show lists Zeppelin jams (“Heartbreaker,” “How Many More Times”) and early versions of originals like “Aero Zeppelin,” “Mexican Seafood,” “Pen Cap Chew,” “Hairspray Queen,” “Spank Thru” and “If You Must.” A “Heartbreaker” jam appears on the 2004 box set With the Lights Out; a bootleg of “If You Must” circulates online. The photos follow a wave of newly revealed Cobain artifacts showcased in Brett Morgen’s documentary Montage of Heck, which drew on extensive archival material and is returning to theaters on August 7. The piece also briefly references Internet Archive efforts to preserve web pages and prevent broken links.

This document contains two separate pieces about Gwyneth Paltrow and a reported medical incident linked to a treatment she has promoted.

1) Gwyneth Paltrow — lifestyle and beauty practices
- At 43, Gwyneth Paltrow is widely known for her wellness and lifestyle website Goop.com and for branching into beauty products (a makeup line with Juice Beauty and a Goop skin-care line).
- She lives in Los Angeles and is the mother of two children, Apple (11) and Moses (9).
- Paltrow favors serums, facial and body oils, and says she uses an “Instant Facial” product with gentle fruit acids and exfoliating beads (non-plastic) that tingles and gives a glow; although recommended for thrice-weekly use, she admits using it more often, then following with day/night cream, oil and eye cream.

2) Reported death after live bee acupuncture (bee venom apitherapy)
- A separate medical report describes a 55-year-old woman in Spain who died after an allergic reaction to live bee acupuncture, an alternative therapy that Paltrow has promoted.
- The patient had been receiving monthly treatments for two years. Immediately after a live bee sting she developed wheezing, difficulty breathing, and loss of consciousness; she was hospitalized at Ramón y Cajal University Hospital in Madrid and later died of multiple organ failure.
- Doctors reported she suffered a massive watershed stroke and permanent coma due to severe anaphylactic shock. The 2015 case is thought to be the first reported death from live bee acupuncture in a patient without a prior allergy; repeated exposure to bee venom likely increased the risk of a severe reaction.

Overall, the document juxtaposes Paltrow’s public wellness and beauty activities with a serious, potentially precedent-setting medical case linked to an alternative therapy she has promoted.

A New Jersey Transit train crashed into Hoboken Terminal at about 8:45 a.m. Thursday, killing a 34-year-old woman and injuring 108 others, Governor Chris Christie said. The train struck the station at high speed, crashing through barriers and leaving severe damage to the platform and terminal ceiling. Most of the injured were aboard the train; the fatality was a person on the platform struck by debris. The engineer was initially hospitalized, later released, and is cooperating with investigators. The National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation; officials are not speculating on cause. Hoboken Terminal’s structural integrity must be evaluated and no timeline for reopening was given; PATH service was expected to resume the afternoon of the crash. NJ Transit opened a Family Reunification Center in Jersey City and a hotline (855-336-1774). Eyewitnesses described a sudden, violent impact, chaos and panic as passengers escaped through windows and doors amid collapsed ceilings and wreckage.

At Yahoo’s annual shareholder meeting — the company’s first under CEO Marissa Mayer — the proceedings were largely uneventful. Shareholders re-elected directors up for re-election and approved the executive compensation plan. Mayer touted product progress and user growth since taking the role in July, highlighting a 70% increase in Yahoo mobile email usage after an April redesign and a 50% rise in photo uploads via the redesigned Flickr mobile app; she framed product improvements as the path to increased traffic, advertising and revenue. Yahoo shares traded up about 3% to $24.87 in afternoon trading.

The meeting did include several off-topic and crass interruptions. An elderly shareholder, self-identified as Greek, loudly told Mayer she was “attractive” before asking about dividends; Mayer ignored the remark and continued. Other distracting questions ranged from which football team she’d root for to complaints from Walmart employees (Mayer sits on Walmart’s board), which she deflected by focusing on Yahoo business. Overall the tone was mild aside from those incidents.

Summary:

President Obama has taken a deliberately low-profile, multilateral approach to the Libyan crisis, preferring to let other nations—especially European partners—publicly lead efforts while the U.S. works behind the scenes. His advisers say this reflects his preference for coalition-based diplomacy and a cautious assessment of limited intelligence about Libyan rebels, the uncertain post‑Gaddafi political landscape, and the complex military options available. Privately, the administration has pushed strong financial sanctions, supported NATO planning, and considered non‑kinetic measures such as jamming regime communications, using naval assets to deliver aid, and humanitarian relief teams for eastern Libya. Publicly, however, Obama has made few statements and has not endorsed specific measures such as a no‑fly zone, attracting criticism from conservatives and some interventionists who view his stance as weak or indecisive.

Meanwhile, France broke from most other countries by becoming the first to formally recognize the Libyan National Council in Benghazi and to meet its representatives, prompting a threatened break in relations from Tripoli. European and NATO officials debated options including a UN‑mandated no‑fly zone, stepped‑up surveillance of Libyan airspace, and humanitarian assistance, while noting any action would need legal backing and regional support. Germany froze Libyan assets and Russia banned arms sales; the U.S. has frozen billions in regime assets and suspended operations at Libya’s Washington embassy.

On the ground the conflict remained violent and fluid. Gaddafi’s forces retook Zawiya after heavy fighting, and assaults continued at Ras Lanuf and other towns, with reports of civilian casualties, mass graves, house‑to‑house searches and arrests. Rebel forces were described as poorly organized and underequipped compared with Libya’s substantial military and air defenses. The war has caused thousands of deaths (estimates varied widely) and displaced roughly a quarter‑million people, many stranded at borders. Both sides continued diplomatic maneuvers—Gaddafi sending envoys and the rebels pressing for aid—while international bodies (UN, NATO, EU, AU, Arab League) coordinated deliberations over possible responses.

Reynolds American agreed to buy Lorillard for about $25 billion in cash and stock (about $27.4 billion including debt), a deal that would reshape the U.S. tobacco industry by leaving two dominant players—Reynolds and Altria—controlling roughly 90% of the market. Reynolds would add Lorillard’s Newport (the No. 2 U.S. cigarette brand and the leading menthol) to its portfolio alongside Camel and Pall Mall, creating a company with more than $11 billion in annual revenue and roughly $5 billion in operating income.

Key terms and partners
- Purchase price: $68.88 per Lorillard share (cash and stock).  
- British American Tobacco (BAT) will fund $4.7 billion of the deal and keep a 42% stake in Reynolds.  
- Imperial Tobacco will buy several Lorillard brands (including Salem, Winston, Maverick) and the Blu e‑cigarette line for $7.1 billion to reduce antitrust concerns; Imperial will also acquire Lorillard’s Greensboro manufacturing/research facilities and about 2,900 employees.  
- Reynolds expects about $800 million in annual cost synergies and says the deal will be accretive in year one. Reynolds CEO Susan Cameron will remain in place; Lorillard CEO Murray Kessler will join Reynolds’s board.

Strategic rationale
- The acquisition gives Reynolds a much stronger position against Altria (whose Marlboro controls ~44% share), especially in menthols (about one-third of the U.S. cigarette market), and boosts Reynolds’s total U.S. market share to roughly 33%.  
- The deal also expands presence in e‑cigarettes (Vuse for Reynolds; Blu to Imperial) and includes R&D and next‑generation tobacco product collaborations with BAT (heat‑not‑burn and vapor products).

Challenges and market reaction
- Shares of Lorillard and Reynolds fell after the announcement, reflecting investor concern about deal risk and regulatory approval.  
- The transaction faces significant antitrust scrutiny from the FTC because it would further consolidate a market already under pressure from decades of anti‑smoking efforts and declining shipments; selling brands to Imperial and other divestitures may not be sufficient.  
- E‑cigarettes remain a growing but uncertain segment because of evolving FDA regulation and local restrictions.

Advisers
- Lazard (lead) and JPMorgan advised Reynolds; Centerview Partners and Barclays advised Lorillard. Credit Suisse and Goldman Sachs advised Imperial.

Bottom line: The deal would create a much stronger Reynolds with dominant menthol strength via Newport and expanded scale versus Altria, but it carries substantial regulatory and execution risk and will likely face intense FTC scrutiny.

RadarOnline reports Whitney Houston had Valium, Xanax and alcohol in her system when she died at the Beverly Hilton. Sedatives and booze—found in her hotel room—are believed by a source to have suppressed her respiration and stopped her heart, likely causing death before she was found partially submerged in the bathtub; final toxicology and blood alcohol results are pending and expected in several weeks.

The article also recounts Houston’s troubled final days, including an incident at Tru Hollywood nightclub where she appeared disheveled, intoxicated and injured, with eyewitnesses saying she was drinking heavily. It mentions fallout after her death: reports about daughter Bobbi Kristina’s behavior at the burial, reactions from celebrities, and speculation that ex-husband Bobby Brown might pursue a tell-all book—though a confidentiality agreement and concerns for their daughter could complicate that.

Transport for London (TfL) has refused to renew Uber’s licence to operate in London, ruling the company is not a “fit and proper” private hire operator because of failures in corporate responsibility that can affect public safety. TfL cited shortcomings in reporting serious criminal offences, obtaining medical certificates and conducting driver background checks, and raised concerns about Uber’s use of “Greyball” software that could block regulators and law enforcement.

The decision, supported by Mayor Sadiq Khan and groups including black-cab drivers and employment-rights campaigners, stops short of an immediate ban: Uber’s current licence runs until 30 September and the company can continue operating while it appeals the ruling in court. Uber’s new CEO Dara Khosrowshahi—who acknowledged the verdict reflects the “cost of a bad reputation”—said the company will challenge TfL’s decision and pledged to rebuild trust. Uber urged users to back drivers and petition the mayor.

The ruling drew divided reactions: critics and unions hailed it as a needed check on Uber and a warning to gig‑economy firms over worker rights and safety; many users and some ministers warned it could leave millions of Londoners and about 40,000 drivers disadvantaged. The dispute may take months of appeals and is seen as a major setback for the company in one of its largest markets.

With six days left before a July 20 deadline, negotiations in Vienna between Iran and the P5+1 (the U.S., Britain, France, Germany, Russia and China) were stalled and facing “huge” remaining gaps, especially over how far Iran would be allowed to enrich uranium. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry met repeatedly with Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif as other ministers joined talks, but by the end of the day no breakthrough had been reached.

Background: under a six-month interim agreement reached in January, Iran accepted limits on its nuclear activities in exchange for partial sanctions relief; July 20 is the target date for a comprehensive deal. An extension is possible and increasingly likely, though some parties prefer a final agreement by the deadline and Iranian officials signaled any extension would be short.

Complicating factors:
- Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei publicly emphasized Iran’s need to continue enrichment, a statement interpreted by some analysts as undermining Iranian negotiators’ flexibility.
- Core disputes remain over the scope and level of uranium enrichment and the duration and intrusiveness of inspections and monitoring.
- Broader regional crises (Israel–Gaza, Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan) both complicate and, in some areas, create overlapping U.S.-Iran interests (e.g., stemming Sunni extremist flows into Iraq), expanding the agenda beyond strictly nuclear issues.
- Domestic pressures constrain both sides: Iranian hardliners oppose major concessions to Rouhani’s government, and some U.S. lawmakers threaten to reject any deal perceived as allowing meaningful Iranian enrichment.

Stakes and outlook: Western aims are a long-term agreement that imposes clear limits on Iran’s nuclear capabilities and an enduring monitoring regime; failure risks renewed isolation of Tehran and potential escalation. Observers noted the talks’ success depends in part on whether Iran wants a deal badly enough to accept significant constraints. With differences large and political pressures intense on both sides, negotiators were likely headed either to a short extension past July 20 or to last-minute intensive bargaining.

Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson reassigned Acting TSA Administrator Melvin Carraway after a Homeland Security Inspector General “red team” probe found widespread screening failures at dozens of major U.S. airports. Undercover testers were able to smuggle mock explosives or banned weapons through checkpoints in 67 of 70 trials (about 95%). In one cited case, screeners missed a fake explosive taped to an agent’s back even after a pat-down prompted by an alarm.

Johnson moved Carraway to the DHS Office of State and Local Law Enforcement and named Acting Deputy Director Mark Hatfield to lead TSA pending a new appointment. He released a six-point directive ordering immediate revisions to TSA screening procedures to address identified vulnerabilities, nationwide retraining of officers and supervisors, tests of screening equipment, and increased covert testing. Johnson also urged prompt Senate confirmation of President Obama’s nominee for TSA administrator, Vice Admiral Pete Neffenger. He framed the tests as a critical but constructive part of improving aviation security as threats evolve.

Images and a video posted to Reddit ignited an online uproar over alleged unsanitary conditions at a Golden Corral in Port Orange, Florida. A Reddit user, GCWhistleblower, shared photos showing food stored near overflowing trash; a cook, identified as Brandon Huber, posted a video claiming the restaurant kept raw and cooked food by the dumpster before health inspections. Huber says he raised concerns internally first but then went public after failing to get media attention.

Golden Corral responded that the footage showed improper food handling at that location, but none of the items were served to customers and all were destroyed within an hour under management direction; the company said Huber took part in the disposal. Management has fired the manager involved for not following food‑handling procedures. Huber’s father reportedly attempted to sell the video to the company for $5,000, an offer the company says it rejected. Huber’s current employment status was not disclosed. The incident drew comparisons to past viral restaurant sanitation scandals and highlights how social media can rapidly damage a chain’s reputation.

Comedian Joan Rivers, 81, remains on life support at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York after going into cardiac and respiratory arrest during a throat procedure at an Upper East Side clinic on Aug. 28. She was placed in a medically induced coma and has been kept alive by machines while doctors assess potential brain and other damage. Her daughter Melissa Rivers has been at her bedside, issuing brief statements thanking supporters and asking for prayers; family and friends have surrounded Joan. Reports about her condition have varied—sources told E! News she is making slow, small improvements and is “on the road to recovery,” while other outlets have cautioned her prognosis is uncertain and, if she survives, recovery and rehabilitation could take months or years. The incident prompted widespread celebrity and public support, and a scheduled taping of Fashion Police was canceled.

The piece argues Hillary Clinton clearly won the first 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra, largely by forcing Donald Trump into defensive, ineffective responses. Observers heard Trump’s supporters groan during the debate; Clinton’s team entered the spin room energized while Trump’s camp seemed deflated. Moderator Lester Holt is credited with keeping the exchange disciplined.

Five key takeaways:
- Trump appeared weak and defensive when under attack. Instead of his usual bluster, he often bellowed, interrupted or retreated into meandering answers, which made him seem rattled and inexperienced.
- Clinton targeted Trump’s persona effectively, contrasting her modest, middle-class roots with Trump’s privileged start (noting his father lent him startup money). Those personal jabs undermined his “self-made” image.
- Trump failed to press hard on the Clinton Foundation and other lines that could have helped him; he spent too much time self-justifying and missed opportunities to land more damaging attacks.
- One of Trump’s successful lines—arguing Clinton hadn’t produced results over “30 years”—is likely to recur and resonated as a simple, fact-checkable critique of her long public career.
- Clinton’s most damaging attacks focused on Trump’s business record: his refusal to release tax returns, past promotion of the birther conspiracy, and, especially, anecdotes about stiffing contractors. Trump’s dismissive replies (e.g., “That makes me smart,” or blaming poor workmanship) reinforced the criticisms and played into concerns about his treatment of working people.

Overall, the debate highlighted preparation versus bombast: Clinton’s rehearsed, targeted assaults and steadier delivery contrasted with Trump’s inconsistent performance. While the result may not immediately reverse campaign dynamics, the night strengthened Clinton’s standing and exposed vulnerabilities in Trump’s debate approach.

A US Secret Service agent, Special Agent Noel E. Remagen, has died after suffering a stroke while on duty during President Donald Trump’s weekend visit to the Turnberry golf resort in Ayrshire, Scotland. The 42-year-old was part of the presidential protection detail and had been working the midnight shift protecting national security adviser John Bolton when colleagues found him unresponsive on Saturday night. He was treated onsite by a White House doctor and Secret Service personnel, then taken to Queen Elizabeth University Hospital in Glasgow, where he died surrounded by family. The Secret Service said he had served 19 years and praised the care he received from medical teams and Scottish police. Remagen is survived by his wife and two young children and was the son of a retired Secret Service employee. The President and First Lady traveled to Joint Base Andrews to see Remagen’s family.

President-elect Donald Trump sparked alarm and confusion in Washington and abroad with a series of offhand remarks and a tweet suggesting the United States should “greatly strengthen and expand its nuclear capability” and that, if necessary, “let it be an arms race … we will outmatch them at every pass and outlast them all.” His comments contradicted longstanding U.S. nonproliferation goals and drew immediate criticism from arms-control experts who warned that openly advocating an expansion of the U.S. arsenal could provoke a nuclear arms race and undermine treaties such as New START.

Trump’s team issued inconsistent explanations: some aides said he meant modernization or stronger nonproliferation efforts (including preventing proliferation to terrorists and rogue states), while incoming press secretary Sean Spicer alternately called the arms-race remark a private comment and insisted there would be no arms race—yet also said Trump would not “take anything off the table.” Advisers such as Kellyanne Conway framed the tweet as rhetorical rather than policy.

Experts and former officials condemned the public, informal treatment of nuclear policy—saying it’s too consequential for 140-character proclamations—and warned about financial, strategic and diplomatic consequences. The controversy unfolded against a background of similar statements by Russian President Vladimir Putin calling for strengthened nuclear forces; Putin downplayed the risk of an arms race and noted U.S. superiority in some platforms. Putin and Russia’s defense chief also highlighted Moscow’s recent military activity in Syria and plans to bolster strategic forces and deployments along Russia’s western and Arctic fronts.

Overall, the episode exposed unclear intentions from the incoming administration on nuclear policy, prompted fears of a major departure from decades of U.S. arms-control posture, and provoked international unease and calls for clarification.

A 2012 national survey of 534 U.S. pediatricians and family physicians (66% response) found that requests from parents to delay childhood vaccines are common: 93% reported at least one such request in a typical month and 21% said ≥10% of parents in their practice made the request. Most physicians believe delaying vaccines puts children at risk (87%) and causes more pain (84%), yet many acquiesce to requests to preserve trust and retain families (82% and 80% respectively). Overall, 37% said they often/always agreed to spread out vaccines and another 37% sometimes did. Very few routinely dismiss families over delayed schedules (2% often/always dismiss; 12% rarely dismiss).

Physicians use varied counseling strategies—sharing personal vaccination choices, warning about outbreaks, etc.—but generally find them ineffective and report vaccine discussions consume substantial visit time (10–14+ minutes for hesitant parents, often more than half of an average 18-minute visit). Forty percent said these issues reduced their job satisfaction. Experts note a lack of evidence-based communication strategies and suggest systemic changes: reimbursing extended vaccine counseling, starting education during pregnancy, public pro-vaccine messaging to normalize vaccination, and keeping hesitant families in care to allow ongoing dialogue. Some physicians do dismiss families who refuse all vaccines but are more flexible about delayed schedules.

Ohio Gov. John Kasich postponed the scheduled execution of Ronald Phillips one day before it was to occur so medical experts could determine whether Phillips could donate nonvital organs or tissues to his ailing mother (who needs a kidney) or to others. Phillips, 40, was sentenced to death for the 1993 rape and murder of a 3‑year‑old and had exhausted appeals; his execution was rescheduled for July 2, 2014 at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility.

Kasich said the matter is “uncharted territory” for Ohio but that saving another life justified the delay. Under Department of Rehabilitation and Correction policy, state officials will perform initial compatibility testing; if feasible, the transplant(s) would be done at Ohio State University’s Wexner Medical Center and Phillips would return to death row afterward. The department requires transplant costs be covered by Phillips or recipients and noted such donations are rare in Ohio but have occurred in other states.

The stay also drew attention because Phillips would have been the first in Ohio executed with a new two‑drug lethal‑injection cocktail (midazolam and hydromorphone) adopted amid pentobarbital shortages; with his execution delayed, another inmate, Dennis McGuire, may be the first to face that protocol. Phillips’ attorney says Phillips sought the donation as a final, remorseful gesture rather than a delaying tactic. Observers noted this is an unprecedented last‑minute stay in the U.S. context of imminent execution to allow organ donation.

Demi Lovato candidly detailed her past substance abuse in an interview with Access Hollywood, saying at age 19 she was so dependent on cocaine that she smuggled it onto airplanes, used in airplane bathrooms and hid her use even from a 24/7 sober companion. She described addiction as making her manipulative and prone to lying to appear “okay,” and said she also abused alcohol—recalling drinking vodka from a soda bottle in the morning to catch a flight—before realizing her behavior matched alcoholic patterns and deciding to get sober.

Lovato also discussed long‑standing eating‑disorder struggles that began in childhood and became life‑threatening, and noted that a 2010 stint in an Illinois rehab helped her confront those issues. Her mother, Dianna, who later sought help for her own eating disorder and depression after an intervention, said she suspected Demi’s drug use but was initially in denial. Both say getting treatment brought them closer and improved family wellbeing; Lovato expressed pride and love for her mother.

Exploding Kittens is a humorous, strategic card game created by Elan Lee (Xbox/ARGs), Matthew Inman (The Oatmeal), and Shane Small (Xbox/Marvel). Modeled on Russian roulette, players take turns drawing cards until someone draws an exploding kitten and loses. The deck includes cards that let players avoid exploding (peek, shuffle, defuse) or force opponents into danger, and tension rises as the deck thins. The concept evolved from an earlier “Bomb Squad” idea; the creators chose to portray kittens as accidentally self-destructive via typical feline antics rather than malicious harm. The game’s art features Inman’s signature Oatmeal illustrations and reused comic imagery. Launched on Kickstarter to fund production and community-driven improvements, the campaign rapidly surpassed its $10,000 goal (reached in minutes) and quickly raised six-figure sums. The team markets the game with playful, irreverent humor and invites backers to help bring it to life.

An investigation by Channel 4’s Dispatches found that dozens of NHS trusts have been disposing of aborted and miscarried fetal remains by burning them as clinical waste, in some cases in hospital “waste‑to‑energy” incinerators that generate power. The programme said 27 trusts burned about 15,500 fetal remains over two years, with examples including 797 fetuses incinerated at Addenbrooke’s and 1,101 at a waste‑to‑energy facility serving Ipswich. Some women were reportedly not told their baby would be incinerated and were given forms saying the remains would be “cremated,” a term charities say should not be used for incineration alongside rubbish.

The revelations prompted an immediate government response. Health minister Dr Dan Poulter called the practice “totally unacceptable” and asked NHS medical director Prof Sir Bruce Keogh to tell all trusts to stop. The chief medical officer asked the Human Tissue Authority (HTA) to issue clear guidance; the Care Quality Commission said it may investigate trusts that failed to inform and consult families. Prof Keogh stated that, while incineration is not illegal, existing guidance deems it inappropriate and that burial or cremation should be used to provide greater dignity.

Charities including Sands argued that incineration is unacceptable and that parents’ grief is not related to gestational age; they urged cremation where possible. The story was highlighted by Channel 4 host Amanda Holden, who has personal experience of pregnancy loss. NHS trusts named defended their practices, saying options are discussed with families and that they respect parents’ wishes. NHS figures note that nearly 190,000 abortions took place in 2011 in England and Wales and that miscarriages and stillbirths are common, underscoring the scale of the issue.

More than a week after announcing the FBI had discovered emails potentially related to its probe of Hillary Clinton’s private server, FBI Director James Comey informed Congress that the agency’s review found nothing to change the conclusion reached in July: no recommendation for criminal charges against Clinton.

Comey’s initial Oct. 28 letter—sent shortly before the election and revealing newly found emails on a laptop tied to Anthony Weiner—had provoked intense controversy. Critics said it violated Justice Department norms about election timing and upended the campaign; supporters of Trump argued it could harm Clinton’s prospects. After an expedited, around-the-clock review, the FBI concluded the newly found emails were largely personal or duplicates and that intent to mishandle classified information remained unproven. The Justice Department was notified; Attorney General Loretta Lynch and Deputy AG Sally Yates had disagreed with Comey’s earlier decision to notify Congress but were informed before the clarifying letter.

The reversal set off a firestorm on social media and among politicians and pundits. Reactions ranged from condemnation of Comey for needlessly disrupting the race to accusations he had “caved” to pressure. Democrats said the latest letter should put the matter to rest, while Republicans and Trump allies continued to attack Clinton and the FBI’s handling. Some commentators (including Rush Limbaugh) suggested Comey’s initial disclosure had distracted from damaging WikiLeaks releases and indirectly benefited Clinton when the FBI cleared her again. Campaigns on both sides seized the moment: Clinton’s team framed the letter as validation; Trump and his allies called the system rigged and renewed criticism of Clinton’s handling of classified materials.

Observers noted the damage from Comey’s first disclosure — internal polling reportedly showed some voters shifted away from Clinton — may not be fully reversible even after the FBI’s clarification two days before the election.

Wonder Woman continued to dominate the North American box office in its second weekend, outpacing new releases and pushing its domestic total past the $190–205 million range and its global total beyond $300 million. The Patty Jenkins–directed, Gal Gadot–starring DC film earned roughly $16–57 million on Friday and was projected to finish the weekend with about $53–57 million, bringing its two‑week domestic cume to roughly $192–205 million.

Universal’s Tom Cruise reboot The Mummy opened far below expectations. The $125 million tentpole earned about $12–32 million on Friday and was projected to finish the weekend around $30–32 million, a weak start that undermines Universal’s plans for a connected “Dark Universe.”

Fox’s animated Captain Underpants slipped to third, adding about $13 million for a two‑week total near $42 million. Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales dropped to fourth with an estimated $10.5 million for the weekend, though its worldwide haul remained strong (about $384.5 million). A24’s low‑budget psychological horror It Comes at Night performed respectably for its scale, earning roughly $2.4–2.5 million on Friday and projecting to about $6–6.5 million for the weekend.

Other films rounding out the top 10 included Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, Baywatch, Megan Leavey, Alien: Covenant, and Everything, Everything.

Researchers Jon Kleinberg (Cornell) and Lars Backstrom (Facebook) analyzed anonymized Facebook data (1.3 million users, ~379 million nodes, 8.6 billion links) to study signals in social networks that identify romantic partners and predict relationship stability. They found that simple mutual-friend counts ("embeddedness") are a mediocre predictor of partners, while a measure they call "dispersion" is far better. Dispersion captures how a person’s mutual friends span and connect different social circles — a partner typically links otherwise separate groups (family, college, work, etc.). Using dispersion, the researchers correctly identified a user’s spouse about 60% of the time (and the top dispersed friend as the partner ~50% for people “in a relationship”); embeddedness performed much worse (~25% accuracy). They also found that couples with low dispersion were more likely to break up: among non-married declared relationships, low-dispersion pairs were about 50% more likely to split within two months than high-dispersion pairs. Facebook can use these signals to better tailor News Feed content and ads by prioritizing people who occupy central, cross-cutting positions in a user’s network. The authors note this isn’t necessarily causal, but it empirically supports the idea that partners who bridge multiple social worlds tend to have more durable relationships.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Washington on May 10, meeting first with Secretary of State Rex Tillerson at the State Department and later with President Donald Trump in a closed Oval Office session that also included Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak. The visit came a day after Trump abruptly fired FBI Director James Comey, who had been overseeing investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election and possible ties to the Trump campaign.

At the State Department photo opportunity, Lavrov responded sarcastically when asked about Comey’s dismissal—“Was he fired? You’re kidding”—then left with Tillerson, who declined to comment on Comey and framed Lavrov’s visit as a continuation of broad talks begun in Moscow. In the Oval Office, Trump described the meeting as “very, very good,” said the Comey firing had no effect on the meeting and defended the dismissal as due to poor performance. The White House said Trump and Lavrov discussed Syria (including Russia’s, Turkey’s and Iran’s plan for “de‑escalation zones”), Ukraine, the Middle East, and improving bilateral relations.

Lavrov and Russian officials denied discussing election interference with Trump and dismissed allegations of Russian meddling as unsupported, echoing Trump’s characterization of the story as “fake news.” Russian spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Comey’s firing was a U.S. internal matter and should not affect bilateral ties. The meetings drew scrutiny because Kislyak’s presence links to probes of former national security adviser Michael Flynn and because Comey’s firing prompted renewed calls in Congress and the public for an independent investigation into Russia’s election activities. U.S. lawmakers warned the administration to be cautious in dealings with Russia.

A teenager was discovered impersonating a doctor at St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach after staff received a Jan. 13 call about a youth in a white lab coat and stethoscope claiming to be a physician. The juvenile’s age was redacted in the police report; police and the hospital agreed not to press charges.

A patient in the OB/GYN office reported that the youth, who “appeared to be a child,” wore a lab coat bearing the St. Mary’s logo and “anesthesiology.” Security staff said they had seen him around the hospital for about a month and had observed him accessing secured areas. Security footage captured him entering from the parking lot; officers noted a white lab coat hanging in a car parked outside.

When confronted, the teen told police he had been a doctor “for years” and that his family could vouch for him. An OB/GYN who found the youth in an exam room said the teen had left a note asking to “shadow” him. Hospital officials later stated the individual never had contact with any hospital patients or entered patient care areas. The teen’s mother said he is under medical care for an undisclosed condition but had been refusing medication. Local authorities took the juvenile into custody but, in coordination with the hospital, did not pursue charges.

A 20-year-old woman (identified as Ms Jackson) has appealed a Family Court order that bans her from breastfeeding her 11-month-old son after she had a finger and foot tattoo on May 6 without telling the tattooist she was breastfeeding. The boy’s father (Mr Macek), separated from the mother, removed the child to his care citing the mother’s alleged mental health and drug issues. Ms Jackson sought the child’s return; in an interim Newcastle hearing on June 5, Federal Circuit Court Judge Matthew Myers ruled the mother should have primary care and the father regular contact, but barred her from breastfeeding. 

The judge found that, although the mother’s HIV and hepatitis tests were negative, she remained within a potential “window period” during which infection might not yet be detectable, creating an unacceptable risk of transmitting a blood-borne disease to the infant via breast milk. The ruling referenced guidance that hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV can be transmitted through improperly sterilised tattoo equipment and material from the Australian Breastfeeding Association about HIV transmission via breast milk. Judge Myers weighed breastfeeding benefits against the lifelong harm of a possible HIV infection and also noted the mother had smoked cannabis while breastfeeding on May 22. Both parents produced clean drug screens in court; the judge ordered both to abstain from illicit drugs in the 48 hours prior to or during child care, to avoid criminal activity while caring for the child, and required the mother and father to live with maternal and paternal grandmothers respectively so a “responsible adult” would be present. The mother, who has postnatal depression, was ordered to obtain and follow a mental health plan. An apprehended domestic violence order against the father remains in place.

The decision prompted criticism from breastfeeding advocates and experts, who argue the risk from regulated tattoo parlours is very low and that prohibiting breastfeeding absent evidence of infection could set a worrying precedent restricting women’s behaviour. A full bench of the Family Court in Sydney agreed to hear an urgent appeal of Judge Myers’ orders.

Al Jazeera America (AJA) launched in the U.S. by replacing Al Gore’s Current TV, debuting in roughly 45–48 million homes after Al Jazeera bought Current for $500 million. Housed in a temporary New York office with plans for a larger space and 12 U.S. bureaus, the network staffed heavily with U.S. television veterans — including John Seigenthaler, Joie Chen, Antonio Mora and Ali Velshi — and built a news operation of about 900 employees (400 newsroom staff) funded by the Qatar government.

AJA’s stated mission is to offer substantive, in-depth journalism with less punditry and fewer commercials (about six minutes an hour), emphasizing documentaries, investigative reporting (a 16-person team), and domestic coverage beyond New York and Washington. Executives promise programming geared to American tastes: an 8 p.m. nightly newscast, a 9 p.m. newsmagazine and a 10 p.m. talk show among other shows, though daytime and morning schedules were still unclear at launch.

The rollout faces challenges: limited carriage (not yet carried by some major providers like Time Warner at launch), often-high channel placement that reduces discoverability, and the requirement to block U.S. viewers from Al Jazeera English’s live online stream as a condition of broader cable carriage. Internally, some Al Jazeera staff expressed concern that the U.S. channel’s American-heavy staffing and audience-testing could dilute the network’s original editorial boldness. Observers note both the advantage of deep funding and the potential reputational baggage from past controversies over Al Jazeera’s independence.

Reception among U.S. media insiders was cautiously optimistic: many hires are respected journalists, and the editorial focus could fill a niche left by opinion-driven cable rivals. But industry skeptics expect modest initial ratings; Current had low prime-time viewership, and AJA must still secure wider distribution and advertiser confidence to realize its ambitions.

President Donald Trump told Fox News’ Bill O’Reilly that he “respects” Vladimir Putin and dismissed calls that Putin is a “killer” by saying “there are a lot of killers. We’ve got a lot of killers. What, do you think our country’s so innocent?” The remarks, aired in excerpts ahead of a Super Bowl interview, appeared to place the U.S. and Russia on the same moral plane and revived criticism of Trump’s warm rhetoric toward the Russian leader amid ongoing probes into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump said he might or might not get along with Putin but prefers better relations—especially if Russia helps fight ISIS—and expressed willingness to work with both Kiev and Moscow to try to restore peace in eastern Ukraine.

His comments drew rebukes from Republicans including Sen. Marco Rubio, who tweeted that the U.S. is not comparable to Putin, and more measured criticism from Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who called Putin a “former KGB agent and a thug” and rejected equivalency between U.S. and Russian behavior. The Kremlin demanded an apology from Fox for O’Reilly’s initial “killer” characterization. The interview also reiterated Trump’s unproven claims of widespread voter fraud in the 2016 popular vote and his intent to investigate it—an effort that Senate leaders have been reluctant to fund. Background noted that dozens of journalists have been murdered in Russia since 1992, many during Putin’s rule, and that U.S. intelligence concluded Russia sought to influence the 2016 election.

This long piece critiques Hillary Clinton’s 2015 presidential campaign launch and places her prospects in the broader political context. The author (former Clinton adviser Bill Curry) argues Clinton’s campaign strategy and the Democratic party’s broader deficits threaten her standing, while two other excerpts discuss structural reasons she might still be the likely nominee and possibly the favorite in a general election.

Key critiques of Clinton’s campaign and political style
- Poor launch choices and optics: Clinton’s decision to announce via a pre-taped video and rely on staged “listening” sit‑downs and elite events (e.g., a high‑priced Global Women’s Summit) reinforces an image of distance from ordinary voters. Leaks about the campaign (including a $2.5 billion fundraising goal) and habitually insulated entourages make her seem part of an out‑of‑touch elite.
- Legacy of leaking and staff dynamics: Persistent leaks—used historically by Clinton insiders to gain status—preempt and politicize her every move, harming authenticity.
- Messaging and money problems: Modern campaigns’ dependence on big donors, polling, focus groups and data-driven messagecraft produces bland, risk‑averse “vaporware” messaging that avoids substantive policy debate. This dynamic pushes Democrats toward the status quo, alienating their base and failing to offer real solutions.
- Policy vacuum: Democrats are weak on clear, substantive policies to address major structural problems (particularly economic reform). Without real answers, scripted listening tours and soft biography-focused appeals won’t satisfy voters hungry for solutions.
- Need for intra-party challenge: Curry argues the party would benefit from a vigorous primary debate to force policy confrontation and refresh ideas; unopposed coronation risks complacency and decline.

Polling, fundamentals, and the electoral outlook
- Toss-up fundamentals: Another analysis argues that, despite punditry, a general election with Clinton is about a 50/50 proposition given key fundamentals: no incumbent running, President Obama’s middling approval, and an economy growing at roughly average rates. Those fundamentals tend to produce close contests.
- Clinton’s strengths:
  - Institutional advantages: Name recognition, experience, credentials and likely fundraising capacity make her the dominant Democratic nominee and a safe general‑election pick.
  - Structural Democratic advantages: Some commentators argue an “emerging Democratic majority” (demographic trends and a larger Democratic coalition) favors her, and Pew data suggest public opinion didn’t shift dramatically between 2012 and 2014 — turnout differences explained the midterm losses.
  - Relative alternatives: Many plausible Republican nominees also have middling or negative favorability; Clinton’s current favorability is roughly break‑even and comparable to Obama’s at similar phases, so she may still fare well against GOP rivals.
- Risks and uncertainties:
  - Personal negatives: Clinton’s favorability hovers around break‑even and perceptions of untrustworthiness persist; scandals (e.g., email) and revelations about fundraising could amplify negatives.
  - Economic and political swings: A recession, a significant drop in Obama’s approval, or a successful Republican nominee could change the race. Also, “electorate exhaustion” after two Democratic terms could matter, though evidence is thin.
  - Electoral College fragility: The Democratic “blue wall” is not ironclad; small shifts in coalition composition or turnout could reverse narrow advantages.

Overall assessment and prescription
- The campaign’s current approach — elite venues, carefully scripted outreach, and heavy reliance on fundraising and consulting — risks reinforcing perceptions of Clinton as part of the privileged establishment and leaves her without the substantive policy narrative needed to persuade anxious voters.
- Democrats need a substantive debate over policy and direction. Clinton would benefit from confronting big issues directly, offering concrete policy reforms (especially on economic inequality), and engaging in real contests within the party to sharpen ideas and credibility.
- Despite substantial vulnerabilities, structural advantages (name recognition, organization, fundraising, demographics) make Clinton a strong favorite to win the Democratic nomination and a competitive general‑election candidate; absent a major economic downturn or a gaffe that dramatically shifts public opinion, she remains a plausible front‑runner for the presidency.

Valedictorian Colin Yost of Portsmouth High School (NH) surprised his classmates and families at the class of 2015 graduation by ending his speech with the line “all you have to do is shake it off,” then launching into a choreographed flash mob to Taylor Swift’s “Shake It Off.” Yost and a small organizing team created the routine, made an instructional video, rehearsed during five scheduled graduation practices with administration approval, and coordinated music cues so the whole class of about 235 students could join in from their seats. The performance—meant to reinforce his message about embracing your “inner nerd” and being proud of who you are—moved the crowd and went viral after parents and a teacher posted videos. The clip drew national attention (including MTV) and hundreds of thousands of views. Yost, who will study chemical and biological engineering at Princeton and hopes to become a heart surgeon, said the moment of collective joy and positivity will be a lasting memory.

A South Korean news report says one of the North Korean soldiers who defected in 2017 was found to have anthrax antibodies, indicating he had either been exposed to or vaccinated against anthrax and had developed immunity. A South Korean intelligence source told Channel A the discovery has heightened concern in Seoul about North Korea’s biological-weapons capabilities. Suspicion that Pyongyang pursues biological agents stems from disclosures about the Pyongyang Biological Technology Research Institute (linked to military Unit 810) and reporting that North Korea has researched ways to protect anthrax from the extreme heat of missile re-entry, potentially to weaponize it for ICBMs.

Anthrax can be rapidly fatal without antibiotics or vaccination; South Korea’s military does not yet have an anthrax vaccine but expects one by the end of 2019. The report arrives amid broader worries—cited in a recent U.S. White House report—that North Korea may be developing chemical and biological weapons deliverable by missile. The story also notes related South Korean reporting that the U.S. forces in Korea have been conducting biological detection work and have imported anthrax samples multiple times since 2009, with one 2015 shipment reportedly exposing up to 22 people.

Jennifer Lawrence told Elle she refuses to starve herself for roles and dislikes Hollywood body standards that label her “obese” or “fat,” saying she aims to be fit and strong rather than thin. Discussing preparation for The Hunger Games, she emphasized setting a healthy example for young fans. She also described her down-to-earth relationship with boyfriend Nicholas Hoult — they enjoy low-key nights in, joking and watching TV — and admitted she often says the first thing that comes to mind under media pressure. Despite fame and big paychecks, she’s not eager to buy a mansion and continues to prefer modest living situations.

Bloomingdale’s faced a major social media backlash after a holiday catalog ad showing a laughing woman and a man was captioned “Spike Your Best Friend’s Eggnog When They’re Not Looking.” Over 3,800 social posts in 48 hours—mostly negative—called the copy “creepy” and accused the retailer of promoting date-rape behavior. Bloomingdale’s apologized, calling the wording inappropriate and an error in judgment. Branding experts note the pressure on marketers to stand out during the crowded holiday season can push them toward risky creative choices. The episode underscores how quickly controversies amplify on social platforms, similar to recent social-media debates over Starbucks’ holiday cups.

In November 2013, Hallie Twomey of Auburn, Maine launched "Scattering CJ," a Facebook campaign asking volunteers worldwide to scatter small amounts of her son Christopher John (CJ) Twomey’s ashes so he could “see the world” after his 2010 suicide at age 20. CJ, a former U.S. Air Force aircrew member who loved travel and adventure, had remained in an urn on the mantel; Hallie wanted to give him the journeys he never had.

The response far exceeded expectations. Within a year thousands offered to help and more than 9,000 people volunteered (the page later had over 17,000–18,000 followers). Hallie selects volunteers headed to unique or previously unvisited places, sends a small sealed packet of ashes along with CJ’s photo and a letter asking that they tell him he was loved and that she is sorry, and requests a photo and brief note after scattering. The Facebook page documents hundreds of scatterings—at famous landmarks, remote sites, all seven continents (including Antarctica), underwater dives, skydives, hot-air-balloon drops and more. Destinations include Machu Picchu, Cappadocia, Namibia, the Zugspitze, Hainan, and even a payload on a civilian memorial rocket flown from New Mexico to the White Sands range.

Logistics have been broadly manageable though occasional mail damage or lost packets occur; some donations are returned when offers cannot be fulfilled. About two-thirds of the ashes the family planned to share had been sent by early 2015, with Hallie keeping a portion at home and some incorporated into jewelry. The project has brought Hallie comfort and community support, prompted people affected by suicide to share their stories, and helped her feel CJ will not be forgotten. The family continues to accept offers for a few remaining dream locations (eg. Christ the Redeemer, Galapagos, Great Pyramid) while Hallie prepares for the emotional moment of sending off the final packets.

Researchers at Noldus Information Technology investigated the phenomenon known as “resting bitch face” (RBF) to see why some neutral expressions are perceived as annoyed or judgmental. Using FaceReader software—which maps 500 facial points and classifies expressions across basic emotions plus contempt—the team first established a baseline: genuinely neutral faces registered about 97% “neutral” and roughly 3% incidental emotion. When they analyzed photos and videos of people commonly labeled with RBF (examples included Kristen Stewart, Queen Elizabeth II, Anna Kendrick, Victoria Beckham and Kanye West), the non-neutral component rose to about 6%, driven largely by subtle signals of contempt (one-sided lip tightening, slight squinting, a raised corner of the mouth). FaceReader’s results matched human perception and indicated that RBF is detectable equally in men and women; the perception that it mainly affects women likely stems from social expectations that women should appear more smiling and approachable. The researchers published their findings, invited the public to submit neutral-face photos for analysis, and advised against worrying about RBF—there’s no simple “fix,” and the effect is largely an unconscious facial cue rather than intentional.

Disney CEO Bob Iger told ABC employees that hackers claim to have accessed a Disney feature and threatened to release it online in increments unless the studio paid a large ransom in bitcoin. Iger said Disney refused to pay and is cooperating with federal investigators. Reports identify the film as Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, due in theaters in late May and starring Johnny Depp; the extortionists allegedly threatened to post an initial five-minute clip and then successive 20-minute segments until paid.

The incident follows a series of recent Hollywood-targeted attacks—most notably the posting of Orange Is the New Black episodes after Netflix declined a ransom and earlier breaches involving agencies such as UTA, ICM and WME—and echoes high-profile cyber extortion cases like the 2014 Sony Pictures hack. The report notes the broader context of a global ransomware outbreak affecting many organizations and underscores why Disney, with its valuable upcoming releases and franchises, is an attractive target.
