U.S. Rep. Trey Radel (R-Fort Myers), a 37-year-old freshman elected in 2012, was arrested on Oct. 29 in Washington, D.C., and charged in D.C. Superior Court with misdemeanor possession of cocaine. He faces up to 180 days in jail and a $1,000 fine and is scheduled to appear in court the day after the charge. According to reports, a federal probe led authorities to a suspected dealer who identified Radel as a buyer; Radel allegedly purchased cocaine from an undercover agent in Dupont Circle and was later notified at his apartment that he would be charged. Radel issued a public statement apologizing to his family and constituents, acknowledging a struggle with alcoholism, and saying he will seek treatment and counseling. House Speaker John Boehner’s office said the matter will be handled by the courts and is between Radel, his family and constituents. Colleagues and local officials expressed surprise and disappointment; Radel has missed recent House votes and has not indicated any plans to resign.

Israeli police, working with the FBI and other agencies, arrested a 19-year-old dual U.S.-Israeli citizen in southern Israel in connection with a months‑long international wave of bomb threats against Jewish institutions, community centers and other sites in the U.S., Australia and New Zealand. Authorities say the suspect used sophisticated “camouflage” and network‑evasion techniques and that computers, antennas and other equipment were seized; police allege he may have carried out hundreds of calls over two to three years, though officials have not specified how many threats are directly tied to him.

The arrest followed a multi‑country investigation after many threatening calls were traced to Israel. Some incidents caused major disruptions, including an emergency airplane landing. Israeli investigators also detained and questioned the suspect’s father; both were ordered held pending further inquiry. Police have accused the teen of extortion through threats and false reporting and are examining a bitcoin account to see whether he was paid.

The suspect’s attorney and family say he has a history of behavioral problems and was diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor in his teens; his lawyer requested a medical evaluation. Israeli authorities say the suspect refused to cooperate with computer searches. Motive has not been determined.

The arrest brought relief and condemnation from Jewish organizations and U.S. officials. JCC leaders and the Anti‑Defamation League called the acts anti‑Semitic and praised the investigative effort. U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions commended the FBI and Israeli police, reiterating the Justice Department’s commitment to protecting civil rights. Law enforcement also emphasized that other perpetrators have been implicated in some threats (notably a separate arrest of a former U.S. reporter), and investigations into all incidents continue.

Here’s a concise summary of the updates from Monday’s pretrial hearing in the Hannah Graham case:

- A pretrial hearing for Jesse LeRoy Matthew Jr., charged with capital murder in the 2014 disappearance and death of 18-year-old University of Virginia student Hannah Graham, was held in Albemarle County. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Matthew also faces first-degree murder charges in the 2009 death of Morgan Harrington and is serving a life term for a 2005 attempted murder and sexual assault.

- Key testimony came from former Louisa County detective Buck (Stuart/Buck) Garner, who handled a bloodhound named Shaker. Garner testified the dog tracked Graham’s scent over several days, locating a strong scent at an industrial/mulch area about a mile from downtown (which the detector characterized as indicating “fear and adrenaline”), at the Hessian Hills apartments, at the passenger-side door of Matthew’s car, at the entrance to his building, and at the doorframe of his apartment. He said the dog did not detect scent near other apartments.

- Detective Sgt. Mooney testified about Graham’s phone records and surveillance footage. Texts and video show Graham lost and wandering downtown the night she disappeared; video places her in different areas but contains unexplained time gaps. Some surveillance footage also showed a vehicle resembling Matthew’s near the time Graham was walking eastbound. Mooney said the surveillance video was consistent with the canine’s scent trail.

- The bloodhound’s findings formed the basis for search warrants of Matthew’s apartment and vehicle. The defense challenged those warrants, arguing the dog’s alerts conflicted with witness accounts and video, that detectives may have misled the magistrate, and that probable cause was lacking.

- Albemarle County Circuit Judge Cheryl Higgins denied the defense motion to invalidate the search warrants. She found no evidence of deliberate misstatements or reckless disregard in the affidavit and concluded that, despite possible inconsistencies in the dog’s work, other facts in the six-page affidavit (witnesses placing Graham and Matthew together, at least one witness saying they went to a downtown bar, and transaction records showing Matthew bought drinks with his debit card) could establish probable cause.

- Additional procedural note: A mental health expert had been authorized previously to examine Matthew before trial.

Coverage is ongoing as more evidence and testimony are presented.

A massive volcanic ash cloud from Iceland’s Eyjafjallajökull eruption has shut much of Northern and Central Europe’s airspace for several days, disrupting at least 63,000 flights and affecting more than 6.8 million passengers. Major hubs including Heathrow, Frankfurt and Amsterdam were closed or operating only limited services; over 300 airports have been impacted and overall flight numbers fell from about 24,000 to 5,000 on Sunday.

Airlines and industry groups have questioned the blanket closures and their cost — estimated at about $200 million (£130m) per day. Several carriers, including KLM, Air France-KLM and Lufthansa, conducted empty test flights and reported no apparent damage, and KLM said it completed 10 test flights at normal altitudes without problems, sharing results with Dutch authorities. IATA urged a move from blanket bans to a step‑by‑step reopening of airspace. National transport ministers and EU transport ministers planned emergency video talks to consider easing restrictions and co-ordinating responses.

Regulators and air-traffic bodies, notably Eurocontrol, have advised caution because volcanic ash — a mix of glass, sand and rock — can seriously damage engines. Eurocontrol notes some parts of Europe may be ash-free but that does not automatically mean flights can resume. Scientific test flights gave mixed findings; scientists warned the ash distribution is patchy and can remain “very worrying” and invisible at various altitudes.

Economic fallout is mounting: large carriers face steep daily losses (British Airways reportedly losing ~£25m/day, EasyJet up to £5m/day), perishable exports such as Kenyan flowers and vegetables are at risk, supply chains and businesses that rely on air freight are under strain, and events (e.g., Japanese MotoGP) have been postponed. Governments are exploring measures including deploying ferries/trains for stranded passengers, using Spanish airports as entry hubs, and discussing possible financial support for the industry. No clear timeline for full resumption of normal services was available; some politicians suggested partial resumption might be possible sooner in less-affected areas, but safety remains the overriding concern.

A disturbing shrine and a history of troubling behavior have emerged in the aftermath of the January 2011 Tucson shootings carried out by Jared Lee Loughner, who is accused of wounding U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords and killing six people. Reporters found a camouflage tent in Loughner’s Tucson backyard containing an eerie altar: a skull replica atop a pot of shriveled oranges, ceremonial candles, potting soil and other items that experts say appear in various occult practices. Investigators had been focusing on Loughner’s online anti-government postings as motivation, but the shrine raises questions about other influences on his state of mind.

Classmates, instructors and friends describe Loughner, 22, as increasingly alienated, strange and intellectually obsessed. At Pima Community College he was known for odd classroom outbursts, questions about mind control and seminars about semantics; faculty once warned he must produce a mental-health clearance before returning. Neighbors and classmates said he was “not normal” and that some feared he might be violent.

A close friend, Bryce Tierney, recounted that Loughner long harbored a grudge against Rep. Giffords after an encounter at a town-hall style event where, in Loughner’s view, she failed to answer a philosophical question he posed about the meaning of words and government. Tierney described Loughner’s growing preoccupation with lucid dreaming—treating dream life as an alternate reality—and keeping a dream journal that he believed revealed much about Loughner’s mindset. Over time Loughner became more isolated, embraced nihilistic and semantic theories (claiming words meant nothing), and flirted with provocative material and rhetoric; he listed Mein Kampf among favorite books on YouTube and posted rambling videos and MySpace messages, some referencing violence or conspiratorial ideas like mind control.

Authorities charged Loughner with attempted assassination of a member of Congress and related federal counts; investigators found in his home a letter from Giffords’ office confirming he had attended an August 2007 event. Friends say he had flirted with guns recently but had not been an established gun user. Tierney and others speculate Loughner sought to create chaos and media spectacle rather than acting from coherent political ideology. The shrine, his online postings, dream fixation, social withdrawal and prior campus concerns together paint a portrait of a deeply disturbed young man whose exact motives remain subject to ongoing investigation.

A Wichita mother and son, 62-year-old Huong (Houng) Pham and her 23-year-old son Cody Ha, were found shot to death late Saturday in their home on the 7500 block of East Huntington. Police were called around 11 p.m. after a family member returned home and discovered the bodies; no motive has been released and investigators are asking for tips.

Cody had been playing an online multiplayer video game with several friends that night, including Ashley Martinez in Houston and longtime friend Tommy Ong. While on a group voice call, the players heard loud popping noises—at least two shots—that sounded like gunfire and then heard Cody’s phone ringing repeatedly. One friend said he later heard Cody’s sister in a panicked phone call saying she didn’t feel safe. Martinez and another player spoke with a Wichita detective early the next morning to report what they heard.

Neighbors reported unusually frequent car traffic at the house, and friends said people sometimes came to the front door to buy prescription pills; Cody would briefly leave the game to answer the door. Cody worked days in the family’s dry-cleaning business and played games at night; friends described him as easygoing.

Court records show Huong Pham had been involved in prior civil stalking-related disputes years earlier, but those matters were dismissed and it is unclear whether they relate to the slayings. The killings were reported as the city’s 29th and 30th homicides of the year. Police continue to seek information; tips can be given to Wichita police or Crime Stoppers.

A Bernalillo, N.M., middle school teacher, 63-year-old Benjamin Nagurski, was arrested after allegedly threatening a student with a knife during a pop quiz. School officials removed him from the classroom after students reported he turned toward chatting pupils holding a knife and told one student to stop talking; when confronted the teacher allegedly said, "Maybe next time I'll pull a machete on you." Students interviewed by police corroborated the accounts. The school principal told police Nagurski had a rounded steak knife and another knife with a sharp tip and wooden handle; Nagurski told investigators he had been shaking the knife and apologized, saying he was removing staples from a bulletin board. He is charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and unlawful/unauthorized possession of a weapon on school grounds (reported alternatively as carrying a weapon onto school grounds), was booked, and held on bond ($10,000 reported in one account; another reports release on a $5,000 cash/surety bond). It was not known if he has an attorney; the school district superintendent had not immediately commented.

A 9-year-old girl, Jordan Landon, survived nearly two days trapped in an overturned 1995 Chevrolet Monte Carlo after a crash on Highway 55 in rural Craven County, N.C., that killed her father, 39-year-old Douglas Landon. The wreck likely occurred late Friday night after the pair stopped at a convenience store; surveillance captured them together minutes earlier. Jordan was pinned by a seatbelt and remained trapped in the mangled, upside-down car until about 5:45 p.m. Sunday, when a passerby spotted the vehicle about 48 hours after the crash. Rescuers initially thought both occupants were dead but discovered Jordan alive; it took three fire-and-rescue teams over an hour to free her.

Jordan survived on Pop-Tarts, water and Gatorade and endured subfreezing nights; she reportedly cried for help at times but was not heard. She sustained non-life-threatening injuries and was taken to Pitt County Memorial Hospital; she is expected to recover. Her father was found curled protectively over her and died in the wreck.

Investigators recovered a speedometer stuck at 110 mph and say speed was a factor; troopers do not suspect alcohol or mechanical failure. Jordan’s mother, Cissy (Claudette) Leohmann, who had filed a missing person report, disputes the high-speed finding and believes a tire blowout caused the crash—pointing to damage on the rear wheel—while troopers counter that mechanical failure was unlikely. Leohmann also crashed her own car Saturday while searching near the scene; those responders did not spot the overturned vehicle. Family and friends praise Douglas Landon’s protective actions and Jordan’s resilience.

A group of relatives of passengers on Malaysia Airlines flight MH370, joined by American investigator Blaine Gibson, have been conducting grassroots searches for debris on Madagascar’s beaches after official underwater searches yield no wreckage. Over a week on Île Sainte-Marie and other Indian Ocean coasts, seven relatives — including Jiang Hui, who found a small white/sand-coloured board thought possibly to be aircraft debris — plus Gibson (who has previously recovered multiple suspected MH370 parts) located several items that may be from the missing Boeing 777. Families have handed finds to Malaysian investigators and worked with local officials, fishermen and tourism bodies to raise awareness, distribute laminated guides and videos explaining how to identify, photograph and preserve potential debris, and recruit locals to keep searching after the relatives leave.

Beach debris recovered around East and southern Africa (Réunion, Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania, Mauritius) has been important to investigators: analyses of items such as a flaperon have suggested the aircraft entered the sea out of control. Ocean drift modelling supports how pieces could travel thousands of miles from a likely crash zone in the southern Indian Ocean.

Meanwhile, the official underwater search — coordinated by Australia with Malaysia and China — has narrowed to a final sweep by a single vessel, the Dutch-owned Fugro Equator, which left Fremantle for what is likely its last deployment. The deep-sea search has scanned some 120,000 sq km with autonomous vehicles and multibeam sonar, recovered wrecks of historic ships and other non-airliner items, but not the MH370 fuselage or black boxes. The operation (costing roughly $150m) is scheduled to finish in early 2017 unless “credible new evidence” prompts a resumption. Families express frustration that they have had to lead much of the debris effort and are pressing authorities to collect and analyse finds as the official search winds down.

Here are the key points from the document, summarized clearly and concisely:

Return of fallen Navy SEAL and Trump’s Dover visit
- President Donald Trump made a secret, unannounced trip to Dover Air Force Base to honor the remains of Chief Special Warfare Operator William “Ryan” Owens, a 36-year-old Navy SEAL killed during a pre-dawn raid in Yemen.
- Owens was the first known U.S. combat fatality since Trump took office. The raid killed more than half a dozen militants and wounded three other U.S. service members; it also reportedly caused civilian casualties, including the 8-year-old daughter of Anwar al-Awlaki.
- The mission, described by a defense official as planned under the Obama administration and authorized by Trump, underscores ongoing U.S. counterterrorism operations in hotspots such as Yemen, Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria.
- Trump and his daughter Ivanka met Owens’ family during a private, two-hour visit. The family had requested privacy; media coverage of casualty returns is allowed unless families object.
- Owens’ service record included two Bronze Stars and other honors. His death highlighted the human cost of U.S. military operations as the new administration considers shifting military strategy against groups like ISIS.
- The raid prompted debate because of Trump’s past statements about targeting terrorists’ families and White House assurances that U.S. citizens would not be targeted.

Melania Trump’s delayed White House move and staffing
- Two weeks into Trump’s presidency, First Lady Melania Trump had not moved into the White House, was largely absent from official events, and was still assembling her East Wing staff, raising questions about how she will define the role.
- The White House announced she will move to Washington at the end of the school year so her son Barron can finish school, and she named Lindsay Reynolds as her chief of staff. Stephanie Winston Wolkoff is a senior adviser.
- Many key East Wing positions remain unfilled (press, scheduling, correspondence, social secretary). Residence staff and outside helpers have covered some duties so far.
- Observers note that first ladies often take a low public profile at the start and reshape the role to their preferences; Melania has signaled interest in issues like cyberbullying but given few concrete indications of an agenda. Ivanka Trump, by contrast, has taken on some public ceremonial duties and already moved to Washington with her family.
- The slow start has drawn media scrutiny and commentary about whether this represents a break from modern expectations for a visible, active first lady or a deliberate redefinition of the office.

Mirror Mirror is Tarsem Singh’s glossy, candy-colored 2012 retelling of Snow White that leans into whimsy and visual spectacle more than emotional depth. Starring Julia Roberts as a narcissistic Queen, Lily Collins as a more proactive Snow White, Armie Hammer as Prince Alcott and Nathan Lane as the Queen’s flustered henchman Brighton, the film recasts Snow White as a 2012-style would-be heroine who can fence and helps shape her own fate. The seven “dwarfs” are reimagined as a ragged band of outlaw-ish, comic antiheroes (including memorable turns by Mark Povinelli and Jordan Prentice) who train and aid her.

Critics agree the movie is sumptuous to look at — Tarsem’s eye for fantastical production design and the late Eiko Ishioka’s opulent costumes are frequently singled out as the film’s crowning achievements — and it often plays as a playful, Disney-referencing confection with slapstick and anachronistic jokes. Julia Roberts chews scenery enjoyably as the vain, scheming queen, and Nathan Lane provides the best comic lift.

But most reviewers also note the picture’s weaknesses: its story and characters are light and often one-dimensional, dialogue is hit-or-miss, and Tarsem’s fetish for striking images sometimes overwhelms narrative momentum and emotional engagement. Lily Collins is appealing in her first major lead role, but her “Groucho eyebrows” and limited chemistry with the prince are distractions to some. Overall, Mirror Mirror is visually inventive and intermittently funny—a pretty, airy fairy tale meant for family viewing—but it sacrifices heart and substance for style. Running time ~95–106 minutes (sources vary); rated PG.

A Syracuse-area couple sued their 30-year-old son, Michael Rotondo, to force him out of their Camillus home after he ignored repeated written demands to leave. In a widely covered, half-hour hearing in Onondaga County Supreme Court, Justice Donald Greenwood rejected Rotondo’s request for more time and ordered that the parents be allowed to obtain an enforceable eviction order; he also asked adult protective services to investigate, expressing concern about conditions in the home.

Key points:
- Parents Mark and Christina Rotondo say they began telling Michael to leave as early as Feb. 2, 2018, offered $1,100 to help him relocate, and claim he does not contribute to expenses or household chores.
- Michael, who moved back in eight years ago after losing a job and runs a website business, refused to go voluntarily and argued he was entitled to six months’ notice based on a legal precedent he found online. The judge provided an appellate decision that undercut Michael’s cited case and called his six-month demand “outrageous.”
- Michael repeatedly challenged procedural details in court, declined to speak directly to his parents when asked by the judge, sought media attention after the hearing, said he would appeal, and insisted he was not ready to leave home.
- No specific vacate deadline was set in court; the parents’ attorney was asked to prepare an eviction order that the judge would sign and that would include reasonable time for Michael to move.
- The story drew national and international media attention, with camera crews present at the hearing.

A Florida appeals court on Wednesday overturned the 2008 second-degree murder conviction of former FBI agent John J. Connolly Jr., who had been convicted for his role in the 1982 killing of Boston businessman John Callahan. By a 2-1 decision the Miami court found prosecutors relied on a flawed theory—charging Connolly with second-degree murder with a firearm (a crime without a statute of limitations) even though it was undisputed that hitman John Martorano used his own gun and that Connolly neither carried nor fired the weapon. Without the firearm element, Florida’s four-year statute of limitations would have barred the charge when Connolly was indicted in 2005.

Connolly, 73, who served as the handler for mobster James “Whitey” Bulger and had previously been convicted on federal racketeering charges in 2002, was sentenced in 2009 to 40 years for the Callahan murder after jurors heard he tipped off Bulger and others. The appeals court sent the case back to the lower court and stayed it pending post-appeal motions; Connolly’s lawyers sought immediate release but were denied. Florida’s attorney general is considering an appeal to the state Supreme Court.

Reactions were sharply divided: victims’ families and prosecutors decried the ruling as letting a corrupt agent evade accountability and cited broader FBI corruption that enabled Bulger’s crimes, while Connolly’s defenders called the decision vindication, arguing prosecutors overreached and that Connolly was scapegoated for flaws in the FBI informant program. The split decision featured a dissent arguing the evidence supported conviction because Connolly aided and facilitated the murder even if he did not pull the trigger.

A curling team skipped by Jamie Koe and including Olympic gold medallist Ryan Fry, Chris Schille and DJ Kidby were ejected from the Red Deer Curling Classic (a World Curling Tour event in Alberta) after complaints from opponents and spectators about drunken, abusive behaviour. Organizers said the players were “extremely drunk,” swore, broke brooms and caused some locker-room damage; the team forfeited their final match and a notice was posted that they were removed from the competition (and potentially barred from future club events). Fry — who had been playing as a spare and won Olympic gold with Canada in 2014 — issued a public apology, called his conduct “disrespectful and embarrassing,” offered to pay for damages and said he will take steps to improve. Koe, not on the ice for the last game, and Canadian skip Brad Jacobs said the team does not condone the behaviour and will handle the matter internally. The World Curling Tour requested a formal complaint from the event committee.

Beijing authorities have destroyed more than 500 illegal outdoor barbecue grills as part of a three-month crackdown aimed at cutting PM2.5 and easing the city’s frequent hazardous smog. State media showed workers cutting up grills seized largely from outdoor vendors, many operated by ethnic Uighur Muslims from Xinjiang. Officials say the action is part of broader emergency measures to fight air pollution — including alternating driving days by license plate, school closures, factory shutdowns and traffic limits when pollution is severe. Critics online argued the raids target small sources while major contributors—factory emissions, coal heating and vehicle exhaust, and dust from the Gobi—remain the primary causes of Beijing’s recurring “airpocalypse” episodes and rising health risks such as lung cancer.

Sen. Ted Cruz’s new memoir, A Time for Truth, was omitted from The New York Times bestseller list despite publisher HarperCollins and Nielsen BookScan reporting roughly 11,800 first-week hardcover sales—enough to place it high on other industry lists. The Times told HarperCollins its “uniform standards” review found the “overwhelming preponderance of evidence” that the book’s sales reflected “strategic bulk purchases,” a common tactic in political publishing, and therefore excluded it. Cruz’s campaign and HarperCollins vehemently deny any bulk orders and have demanded the Times produce its evidence or apologize. The dispute has generated substantial publicity for Cruz—boosting attention and likely sales—and his team and allies are using the controversy to portray the paper as biased. Cruz’s book has outpaced recent first-week sales by some other GOP rivals and the campaign is benefiting from the heightened media coverage.

An American Airlines captain died after becoming ill during an overnight Flight 550 from Phoenix to Boston. About four hours into the flight the captain became incapacitated; the first officer declared a medical emergency and diverted the Airbus A320 with 147 passengers and five crew to Syracuse, landing there around 7:10 a.m. The first officer safely flew the plane, and after about four hours on the ground a replacement crew continued the flight to Boston.

Recordings of ATC communications and onboard reports indicate the captain was unresponsive; a flight attendant who is a nurse attempted to assist. American Airlines confirmed the captain’s death, expressed condolences and said it is supporting the family and crew. The airline did not disclose the cause of death. Officials noted that regulations require two pilots in the cockpit and that first officers are trained to handle pilot incapacitation; no passengers were reported at risk.

A Green Bay "creepy clown" that had residents alarmed and photos circulating widely on Facebook was revealed to be a staged marketing stunt. Filmmaker Adam Krause posted on the "Gags - The Green Bay Clown" Facebook page claiming he created the character "Gags" as part of a 10-day campaign to promote his upcoming short film, also titled Gags. Krause said the photos were taken in May 2016, that safety was prioritized during the shoots, and no one was ever in danger.

The stunt followed reports that a clown in a soiled jumpsuit, ruffled collar, heavy makeup and carrying four black balloons was seen walking near Mason and Adams Street around 2 a.m. on Aug. 1. The original Facebook post was widely shared and spawned a fan page for sightings; police received calls but said there was little they could do because the person was not breaking the law. Green Bay Police Captain Kevin Warych and others noted the figure appeared unarmed and not overtly dangerous, and some suspected it was related to a horror film before Krause’s admission.

Amanda Knox, 24, has started a new relationship in Seattle with 24-year-old James Terrano, a classical-guitar student at the University of Washington. The Mail on Sunday reports the pair — longtime acquaintances — have been spending a lot of time together, often in Terrano’s modest rented flat in Seattle’s Chinatown, and have been seen walking and shopping there with Knox’s mother. Terrano’s brother confirmed the relationship; both Knox and Terrano have been discreet when approached by photographers.

The story notes Knox’s effort to resume a “normal” life after an Italian appeals court overturned her 2009 murder conviction in the death of Meredith Kercher. The article also covers the end of Knox’s relationship with former boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito, 27. In his first extensive interview since their release, Sollecito said the couple’s romance is over, described the impact of their imprisonment as having “brutally stamped” their relationship, and expressed sympathy for Knox while saying he still hopes for truth and closure for Kercher’s family. The piece summarizes key background: Knox and Sollecito were convicted in Kercher’s 2007 killing, later freed after doubts about the police evidence; a third defendant, Rudy Guede, was also convicted in the case.

Researchers have identified Saccorhytus coronarius, a tiny, 540‑million‑year‑old marine animal from central China, as the oldest and most primitive known deuterostome—the group that ultimately gave rise to vertebrates and therefore humans. Published in Nature, the study is based on exquisitely preserved microfossils recovered from limestone deposits in Shaanxi Province and examined with electron microscopy and CT scanning.

Key findings:
- Saccorhytus was about 1 mm long, likely living between grains of sand on the early Cambrian seabed.
- Its body was bilaterally symmetrical and covered by a thin, flexible skin with musculature, suggesting it wriggled to move.
- It had a relatively large mouth and probably fed by engulfing particles or tiny prey.
- No evidence of an anus was found, implying ingestion and egestion may have used the same opening.
- Small conical structures around the mouth may have allowed expelled water to escape and could represent an early precursor to gill slits.
- The fossils predate previously known deuterostomes (circa 510–520 million years ago), helping fill a gap between molecular-clock estimates and the sparse early fossil record; their tiny size supports the idea that many early animals left few fossils.

The international team (UK, China, Germany), including Simon Conway Morris and Degan Shu, conclude Saccorhytus may approximate the common ancestor of a wide range of deuterostome lineages—from echinoderms and hemichordates to vertebrates—offering new insight into the very earliest stages of the evolutionary path that eventually led to fish and humans.

A Saratov Airlines Antonov An-148 passenger jet carrying 71 people (65 passengers and six crew) crashed shortly after takeoff from Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport on Feb. 11, 2018, en route to Orsk. The aircraft disappeared from radar minutes after departure and plunged into a snowy field near Ramenskoye/Argunovo, about 40–50 km southeast of the airport. Wreckage and debris — including at least one engine — were scattered over roughly a one-kilometer radius; state and emergency officials reported no survivors. Early recovery teams found bodies and a flight recorder.

Russian authorities opened a criminal investigation and said all possible causes were being examined, including weather, human error and the aircraft’s technical condition; some reports suggested a technical malfunction or an engine problem, though officials had not confirmed a cause. The seven-year-old plane had been manufactured in 2010, spent time in storage, and entered service with Saratov Airlines in 2016. President Vladimir Putin ordered a special investigative commission and offered condolences; relatives waited at Orsk airport as psychologists and emergency crews responded. The crash is one of several recent high-profile Russian air disasters cited in coverage.

A Louisiana middle school yearbook is attracting attention for including Presley, a 5-year-old female golden doodle who is the service dog of 14-year-old Joseph “Seph” Ware. Seph, a seventh-grader at Good Hope Middle School in West Monroe, was diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy at age 3 and relies on Presley to help with tasks his weakened muscles can’t manage. School officials photographed Presley alongside Seph on picture day with his permission; students adore the dog and often sneak pets despite rules. Seph signs classmates’ yearbooks with a paw print for Presley. Seph’s mother, Lori Ware, said the warm reception at Good Hope is especially meaningful after earlier difficulties getting Presley accepted at his elementary school. Presley has a canine sibling, Elvis, who also works as a service dog for another boy with muscular dystrophy. The story has gained traction online and in local media. The piece also notes Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a genetic disorder that primarily affects boys, causing progressive muscle, heart and respiratory weakness, with improved care extending many patients’ lifespans into their 30s and beyond.

Belgian authorities captured Salah Abdeslam, the main fugitive linked to the Nov. 13, 2015 Paris Islamist attacks that killed 130 people, in a major anti-terror raid in the Molenbeek neighborhood of Brussels on March 18, 2016. Abdeslam, 26, was wounded in the leg during a gunbattle and taken alive. The operation involved heavy armed police, explosions and helicopters; at least five people were arrested in related raids and three are being held on suspicion of sheltering him. One man, Mohamed Belkaid (alias Samir Bouzid), was killed earlier in a separate raid after police found Abdeslam’s fingerprints and explosives-related evidence in a Brussels apartment. Belgian and French officials said Abdeslam is believed to have driven some of the attackers on the night of the Paris attacks and to have slipped back to Brussels afterward; French prosecutors moved to seek his extradition. Authorities continue investigating ties to other suspects, including Mohamed Abrini and an individual known as Soufiane Kayal, whose whereabouts remain unknown. The arrest was hailed as a major intelligence opportunity amid ongoing concerns about jihadist networks centered in Molenbeek.

Surgeons at Glenfield Hospital in Leicester have successfully treated a newborn girl, Vanellope Hope Wilkins, who was born with ectopia cordis — an extremely rare condition in which the heart (and part of the stomach, in her case) develops outside the chest. Detected at a nine-week scan, doctors had warned her parents that survival chances were below 10% and advised termination; the couple chose to continue the pregnancy after further testing showed no chromosomal abnormalities.

Vanellope was delivered by Caesarean on Nov. 22 to reduce infection and trauma. A multidisciplinary team of about 50 staff immediately cared for her; within roughly 50 minutes she underwent the first of three operations to relocate her heart. Over subsequent procedures surgeons gradually created space in her chest, used a protective mesh (and later her own skin) to cover the defect — since she lacks a breastbone — and monitored her in pediatric intensive care. She remains ventilated and faces ongoing risks, particularly infection, but has defied expectations and is recovering.

Medical staff say this appears to be the first successful neonatal repair of ectopia cordis in the UK, though a few pediatric survivors have been reported in the United States. Clinicians caution that long-term outcomes are uncertain and further interventions (for instance to provide bony protection that grows with her) may be needed. Her parents named her Vanellope for the resilient Disney character and say they hope the case offers encouragement to other families facing similar diagnoses.

Raffaele Sollecito has spoken publicly for the first time since his release, telling Italian weekly Oggi that he and Amanda Knox remain in daily contact and that he plans to visit her in Seattle—possibly before Christmas. Sollecito said they “need each other” to try to understand what happened, to talk and to rebuild lives after “four years in a circle of hell” that brought them immense suffering.

His interview recalls details of the case and investigation: he wore the same gray fur-lined coat that figures in the evidentiary record to symbolize alleged sloppy police work. The piece also revisits conflicting witness claims about Knox’s clothing the day after Meredith Kercher’s murder and notes arguments that some evidence was contaminated.

Knox and Sollecito were sensationally cleared on appeal of the 2007 murder and sexual assault of Meredith Kercher after judges accepted that key forensic evidence—DNA on a knife and on a bra clasp—was unreliable or possibly contaminated. Ivory Coast national Rudy Guede was convicted in a separate fast-track trial and remains imprisoned. Perugia prosecutors say they will appeal the acquittal once the written ruling is published. Meanwhile Knox has returned to Seattle, kept a low profile while negotiating possible TV interviews, and is being protected amid threats and intense media attention.

Roger Ebert, the celebrated film critic who spent 46 years with the Chicago Sun-Times and became a national figure through television, blogging, and a Pulitzer Prize, died at 70. A passionate champion of movies, Ebert combined scholarship, wit, and biting humor in reviews that could be rapturous or brutally blunt. The piece highlights ten of his most admired reviews—raves for E.T., Casablanca, Toy Story, Raging Bull, Platoon, Beauty and the Beast, Titanic, Hoop Dreams, Star Wars, and Fargo—showing his range: from praise of family-friendly wonder and technical achievement to deep readings of character, theme and social meaning.

It also collects some of his sharpest one‑liners aimed at bad films, including memorable lines about Last Rites, Baby Geniuses, The Brown Bunny, Mad Dog Time, Valentine’s Day, Deuce Bigalow: European Gigolo, Little Indian, Big City, Battlefield Earth, Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen, and North—demonstrating his talent for withering, memorable criticism.

The document includes a personal profile tied to Ebert’s memoir Life Itself and a TV interview excerpt. It covers his long partnership with Gene Siskel, Siskel’s death in 1999, and Ebert’s own battle with thyroid and salivary‑gland cancer, which cost him his lower jaw and the ability to speak and eat. Despite these losses, Ebert remained active: he adapted to a computerized voice, continued to write popular blog posts read by millions, won a Webby, traveled to festivals, attended frequent screenings, and co-produced Ebert Presents at the Movies with his wife Chaz, who he credits with helping him continue his work and life. Candid about his condition, Ebert embraced honesty online (sometimes controversially), treasured vivid childhood memories that shaped his love of film, and urged contributing joy to the world despite hardship—saying he wasn’t being courageous, just continuing to do what he always did.
