Initial reports that Gal Gadot earned only $300,000 for Wonder Woman while Henry Cavill was paid $14 million for Man of Steel sparked outrage about a gender pay gap for superhero leads. However, the $14 million Cavill figure has been called unconfirmed and “ridiculous” by sources; the Elle piece that spurred the story conflated upfront salaries with bonuses and backend deals. A source told The Hollywood Reporter that Gadot’s upfront pay for Wonder Woman was equal to or slightly higher than Cavill’s Man of Steel base pay. 

Context: It’s common for emerging stars to receive low- to mid-six-figure salaries on tentpole debuts (e.g., Chris Hemsworth earned ~$150k for Thor; Adam Driver ~ $500k for The Force Awakens). Upfront pay often excludes box-office bonuses and backend points, and actors typically earn much more for sequels or after breakout success. Wonder Woman has been a major hit ($574M+ worldwide to date), so Gadot’s compensation is likely to be renegotiated. Separately, some producers and a few established actors receive large backend payouts (e.g., producer Jon Peters received $80–85M across Superman projects; Robert Downey Jr. has been reported to command huge sums for Avengers films).

At the Beach to Beacon 10K in Cape Elizabeth, Maine, 23-year-old Jesse Orach — last year’s top Maine finisher and a recent University of Maine track graduate — collapsed from heat stroke just short of the finish while leading the Maine field. Windham runner Robert Gomez, 34, found Orach lying in the grass, helped him to his feet, and supported him across the line; both were credited with 31:31. Orach later collapsed again and spent about an hour in the medical tent; he said his core temperature peaked at 107.3°F. Gomez, who finished his best-ever Beach to Beacon as a result, said camaraderie trumped competition. Officials declined to disqualify either runner for providing or receiving assistance. Among Maine women, Emily Durgin won in 34:43, edging last year’s champion Michelle Lilienthal (35:11); Tracy Guerrette was third (36:43).

Researchers have grown functional jawbone in the lab from pigs’ own stem cells and used it to replace large jaw defects in a pig model—a step toward human clinical use. The team removed 6-cm, load-bearing portions of the pigs’ jaws and replaced them with patient-specific scaffolds made from decellularized cow bone, machined to match CT-derived 3‑D models. Mesenchymal stem cells harvested from each pig’s fat were seeded into the scaffolds and cultured for three weeks inside a custom bioreactor that forced nutrient medium into the scaffold’s interior, producing provisional bone tissue before implantation.

In a 14‑pig study, six animals received their own cell-seeded scaffolds, six received identical scaffolds without cells, and two were left to heal untreated. After six months, all groups showed some regrowth, but the cell-seeded grafts performed best: they restored and maintained original bone height, integrated with host tissue, and matched the mechanical strength of native bone. Unseeded scaffolds tended to shrink, suggesting host bone formation couldn’t keep up with matrix degradation. Animals recovered quickly with no rejection.

The advance supports the idea that cultivating bone in a scaffold prior to grafting improves outcomes compared with implanting empty scaffolds or simply adding cells at the time of surgery. Experts note remaining questions: optimal scaffold composition (for example whether to add bone morphogenetic proteins), comparative benefit versus other experimental methods and current autografts, and extensive safety testing before human trials. The lead investigator’s company aims to seek human trials in roughly three years.

This document contains two unrelated pieces: a description of the University of Wisconsin’s Archive-It partnership and a news report on the global distribution of ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs).

University of Wisconsin — Archive-It
- The University of Wisconsin–Madison has been an Archive-It partner since August 2007. Its archived holdings are organized into two sub-collections:
  - The UW–Madison Collection: web captures documenting campus life, administration, colleges/departments, major organizations, student life, research, buildings, events, UW System and Colleges administration, and UW Extension sites.
  - The Stem Cell Research Archives Project: a targeted collection preserving records of stem cell research at UW–Madison and public reactions across Wisconsin.
- For more information or inquiries, the archives website is http://archives.library.wisc.edu and contact email is uwarchiv@library.wisc.edu.

Global wealth trends and city rankings for the ultra-rich
- Hong Kong overtook New York in 2017 as the city with the largest number of ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs; defined as net worth of $30 million+), rising nearly one-third to about 10,000 people, according to Wealth-X.
- Hong Kong’s gain was attributed to a strong stock market and deeper financial ties with mainland China. Notably, no single mainland Chinese city made Wealth-X’s top 10 because China’s wealth is widely dispersed across the country.
- The United States still hosts the largest share of the world’s UHNWIs (nearly one-third), but Asia—especially China—is rapidly closing the gap. Asia saw a 20% increase in UHNWIs in the prior year.
- Globally, the ultra-rich population grew 13% to over 250,000 persons with combined wealth of $31.5 trillion, helped by a stronger global economy and equity markets.
- Other top cities for UHNWIs include Tokyo, Los Angeles, Paris and London.
- Caveats and risks: China faces near-term headwinds—trade tensions with the U.S., high domestic debt, a falling currency and a weaker stock market—that could slow wealth growth despite longer-term trends of rapid wealth creation across the country.

On Father’s Day evening in New Smyrna Beach, 46-year-old Eugene Blackwell Sr. allegedly shot his 18-year-old son, Eugene Blackwell Jr., four times during a domestic dispute at the family’s Edward Street home. Police say the confrontation began when Blackwell Sr. argued with his wife, Windy Blackwell, after she mentioned divorce; he reportedly grabbed her by the throat and the son intervened. After the mother left, the father shot his son multiple times; as the wounded teen fled, the father fired once more but missed.

Neighbors heard gunshots, called 911 and helped the bleeding teen, who collapsed in a neighbor’s driveway and shouted that his father had shot him. He was airlifted to Halifax Health Medical Center in critical condition; doctors reported bullets struck his abdomen, leg, hip and arm, with one bullet damaging several organs and another lodged in his hip. By Monday he was reported in satisfactory condition.

Blackwell Sr. initially drove away but later turned himself in; he was arrested and charged with attempted first-degree murder (and battery), denied bond, and held without bail. The mother told police the marriage included a long history of domestic abuse and that Blackwell Sr. had previously been arrested and convicted for related offenses. Authorities recovered unspecified items from the home and are still seeking the gun used in the shooting. The victim is a recent New Smyrna Beach High graduate and accomplished weightlifter.

President Donald Trump escalated tensions with U.S. trading partners after announcing 25% tariffs on imported steel and 10% on aluminum by threatening on Twitter to impose retaliatory taxes on European car imports if the European Union responded with its own punitive measures. Trump cited a “big imbalance” and complained EU barriers prevent U.S. cars from selling there. His warning targeted major European automakers such as Volkswagen and BMW; in 2016 the EU exported over 6 million cars, more than 1 million to the U.S.

The tariffs prompted sharp reactions: EU officials discussed countermeasures including a possible 25% tariff on a range of U.S. goods (e.g., Harley-Davidson motorcycles, Kentucky bourbon, blue jeans), while Canada called the measures “absolutely unacceptable” and warned it would defend its trade interests. Canadian PM Justin Trudeau and Foreign Minister Chrystia Freeland signaled readiness to retaliate; Canada is the largest supplier of steel to the U.S. Trump’s move revived concerns about a widening trade war and a “spiral of protectionism” that critics say could cost jobs on both sides of the Atlantic. Reports indicate the White House may apply the tariffs globally without exempting close allies.

At a March 22, 2012 charity launch for her fragrance True Reflection at the London Hotel in West Hollywood, Kim Kardashian was hit with a bag of flour thrown by a young woman while doing red-carpet interviews. Kim laughed it off, joked about needing more powder, left briefly to clean up, then returned to the carpet to applause. Security detained the suspect and the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department filed a non-criminal battery report; Kim declined to press charges and the woman was later released. The fire department checked the powder and confirmed it was ordinary flour. Family members reacted on Twitter—Kris Jenner warned to call security, Khloé said she wished she'd been there, and Kourtney criticized the stunt as classless at a charity event. The incident followed other recent celebrity public pranks, such as Sacha Baron Cohen dumping fake ashes on Ryan Seacrest.

At the South by Southwest premiere of Get Hard, a Will Ferrell–Kevin Hart comedy about a wealthy hedge-funder (Ferrell) who hires a law-abiding car-wash owner (Hart) to “toughen him up” for prison, audience members loudly accused the film of racism and questioned its treatment of homosexuality. Early reviews amplified that criticism, calling out scenes built on “gay-panic” humor and stereotypes. 

Filmmakers and stars have defended the movie as satire: director/co-writer Etan Cohen, Ferrell, Hart and producer Adam McKay say the film skewers the deluded attitudes of a privileged one percent and aims to provoke by holding a mirror to prejudice rather than endorsing it. McKay criticized coverage as “lazy journalism” and argued the film’s core is a satirical take on income inequality and fear about prison violence, not homophobia. Some critics and commentators were less offended than underwhelmed, calling it mean-spirited or simply not very funny.

Despite the negative headlines and debate, Ferrell and Hart’s star power and promotional appearances may blunt the impact; industry groups had not publicly weighed in, and the film’s box-office effect remained uncertain.

Neil Newhouse, Mitt Romney’s lead pollster, circulated a memo on September 10, 2012 arguing that the fundamentals of the presidential race remain favorable to Romney despite an Obama convention bounce. Newhouse emphasizes economic indicators—43 months of unemployment at 8% or higher, 23 million people struggling to find work, and 47 million on food stamps—as the central liabilities for President Obama and contends those realities will reassert themselves and cost him reelection.

Key points from Newhouse’s memo:
- The convention-related polling boost for Obama is temporary—a “sugar-high”—and recent tracking shows his approval already slipping.
- The contest is tight and competitive across an expanding battleground. He cites Pollster.com statewide polls showing margins under three points in eight states, and notes previously Democratic strongholds (e.g., New Jersey, Connecticut) have tightened.
- Romney is running targeted, local ad and field operations across many states (including ads in Wisconsin), backed by substantial fundraising (Romney Victory raised $111 million in August) and intense grassroots activity (door knocks, volunteer contacts far exceeding 2008 levels in several states).
- Newhouse claims Romney leads on the economy in some polls and that the campaign’s combination of message, organization, money, and enthusiasm will produce a Romney victory.

The report also relays a blunt, unnamed Romney adviser’s dismissal of media and some Democratic polls suggesting Romney is losing (specifically in Ohio), calling those narratives “horses**t.” That adviser argues the race is a “dogfight,” that Obama’s convention bounce will fade, and that the underlying map and campaign efforts favor Romney.

By contrast, independent aggregate polling models (e.g., HuffPost Pollster’s model) showed Obama ahead by about three points after the conventions, reflecting the genuine competitiveness Newhouse acknowledges even as he projects confidence in a Romney win.

A private baby shower at Club Luis de Camoes in Stoughton, Mass., erupted into a large brawl after a fight between two men at the bar. The altercation escalated into a 200-person melee that involved children and prompted Stoughton police to call three neighboring police departments, state police and the sheriff’s office for backup. Officers attempting to break up the fight were reportedly surrounded by guests who threw bottles and chairs; officers deployed tasers and at least one attendee was tased. Four people—Paulo Depina, Aderito Deandrade, Patrick Lopes and a teenager—were arrested and charged with assault and battery on a police officer. Several police and partygoers sustained minor injuries; officials said protecting the many children present was a primary concern. The suspects are expected to appear in court.

At the 50th annual Country Music Association Awards at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena, Garth Brooks won entertainer of the year, beating Carrie Underwood, Chris Stapleton, Keith Urban and Luke Bryan. Taylor Swift presented the top prize. Chris Stapleton took male vocalist and music video of the year; Carrie Underwood ended Miranda Lambert’s six-year streak by winning female vocalist of the year; Eric Church won album of the year for Mr. Misunderstood; Maren Morris was named new artist of the year; and Thomas Rhett’s “Die a Happy Man” won single of the year. Lori McKenna won song of the year for writing Tim McGraw’s “Humble and Kind.” Little Big Town won vocal group, Brothers Osborne won vocal duo, and Dierks Bentley with Elle King won musical event of the year; Kenny Chesney received the Pinnacle Award.

The show celebrated the CMA’s 50th anniversary with a multi-artist opener featuring Randy Travis, Vince Gill, Charley Pride, Roy Clark, Alabama, Charlie Daniels, Ricky Skaggs, Alan Jackson, Dwight Yoakam and others. Dolly Parton received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award and was honored by Reba, Carrie Underwood, Martina McBride, Jennifer Nettles and Kacey Musgraves performing “I Will Always Love You.” High-profile presenters and attendees included Matthew McConaughey, Peyton Manning, Nicole Kidman and the U.S. Olympic gymnastics team’s Final Five.

The night also featured a controversial and widely talked-about performance by Beyoncé singing “Daddy Lessons” alongside the Dixie Chicks — marking Beyoncé’s first CMA appearance and the Dixie Chicks’ return — which prompted both praise and backlash from segments of country music fans. Other performances included George Strait, Brooks & Dunn, Jason Aldean, Dwight Yoakam and Little Big Town (performing “Better Man,” written by Taylor Swift). Hosts Brad Paisley and Carrie Underwood returned for their ninth time, mixing musical banter with topical jokes.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu retracted and clarified controversial remarks in which he suggested that Haj Amin al-Husseini, the former mufti of Jerusalem, had prompted Adolf Hitler to adopt the Final Solution. In a Friday Facebook post in Hebrew and English, Netanyahu said he never meant to absolve Hitler or the Nazis of responsibility for the Holocaust and affirmed that the decision to move from deportation to systematic extermination was made by the Nazis themselves, beginning in June 1941. He repeated that the mufti supported Nazi aims—broadcasting anti‑Semitic propaganda from Berlin, recruiting Muslims to the SS, opposing Jewish emigration—and called his wartime behavior “murderous,” but stressed that the Nazis did not need outside influence to decide on genocide.

The clarification came after widespread domestic and international criticism of a World Zionist Congress speech on Oct. 20 in which Netanyahu recounted an account of a 1941 meeting between Hitler and Husseini in which, he said, Husseini told Hitler to “burn” the Jews—an assertion historians condemned as inaccurate and potentially encouraging Holocaust denial. Netanyahu’s initial comments prompted rebukes from historians, political analysts, Palestinian officials and the German government, which reiterated that responsibility for the Holocaust lies with the Germans.

Seven-year-old Grayson Powell was disqualified from a youth bowling tournament in St. John’s, Newfoundland, immediately after helping his three-person Riverdale team win the provincial title. Grayson bowled a career-best 171 and participated in warm-ups and three games without issue, but was pulled aside at the medal ceremony and told by Newfoundland & Labrador Youth Bowl Canada (NL YBC) provincial director Gord Davis that his faded black jeans did not meet the tournament’s dress code requiring black pants.

Grayson’s father, Todd Powell, said the timing of the disqualification ruined the kids’ moment and accused Davis of bias because the teams moved up into first and second place after Riverdale was removed both came from lanes Davis coaches in Corner Brook. NL YBC defended the decision, saying the dress code for Provincial A tournaments had been in place for decades and that parents were aware of it; Davis said he delayed action during play to avoid embarrassing the children and later apologized for communication failures. He also said Grayson and his teammates would receive gold medals in a special ceremony. The dispute sparked community criticism about rule enforcement and fairness, with family and supporters portraying the penalty as overly harsh and ill-timed.

The University of Texas at Austin will remove the statue of Confederate president Jefferson Davis from its prominent location on the South Mall and relocate it to an exhibit at the Dolph Briscoe Center for American History, UT President Greg Fenves announced. The move follows recommendations from a 12-member advisory panel that solicited more than 3,100 public responses and reviewed options for dealing with campus monuments tied to the Confederacy.

Fenves said Davis “is in a separate category” because he had few ties to Texas and his role is best presented in an educational context; the Davis statue will be taken down within days, refurbished, and moved to the Briscoe Center within about 18 months. For symmetry, the campus statue of U.S. President Woodrow Wilson, which faces Davis, will be relocated to another outdoor site. Four other contested statues—Confederate generals Robert E. Lee and Albert Sidney Johnston, Confederate Postmaster General John Reagan, and former Texas governor James Hogg—will remain on the South Mall. Fenves said those four have strong or complex ties to Texas and he will consider adding contextual plaques (including on the Littlefield Fountain).

The decision follows student pressure—student government leaders who campaigned to remove Davis served on the panel—and incidents of vandalism that heightened controversy. State lawmakers urged similar review of Confederate monuments at the Texas Capitol. The university framed the compromise as preserving historical heritage while providing appropriate educational context.

Researchers led by Victor Velculescu developed and validated an ultrasensitive sequencing method, targeted error correction sequencing (TEC-Seq), to detect tumor-derived cell-free DNA (ctDNA) in blood for potential early cancer detection and monitoring.

Key points:
- TEC-Seq targets 58 cancer-associated genes (~81 kb) and uses deep targeted capture (~30,000×) plus endogenous and a small set of exogenous barcodes, redundant sequencing, and strict filtering to suppress sequencing and amplification errors. Analytical sensitivity reaches detection of mutant allele fractions down to ~0.1% (100–200 copies per 100,000), with an empirical false-positive rate <3.3 × 10−7 per base.
- In 44 healthy individuals, TEC-Seq found no driver-gene tumor mutations but identified clonal hematopoiesis–related DNMT3A mutations in 16% (allele fractions 0.16–5.3%), underscoring the need to distinguish blood-cell–derived variants from tumor-derived ctDNA.
- In 194 cancer patients (breast, colorectal, lung, ovarian; majority stage I–II), TEC-Seq detected tumor-specific alterations in plasma in 62% overall of stages I–II and >75% in stages III–IV. Detection by cancer type for stage I–II patients was ~71% (colorectal), 68% (ovarian), and 59% (breast, lung). cfDNA concentrations and ctDNA allele fractions were higher in metastatic disease.
- Concordance with tumor tissue: among 100 patients with matched tumor sequencing, 72% of plasma-detected alterations tested were identical to tumor mutations; 82% of patients had at least one plasma alteration matching the tumor. Higher plasma allele fractions (>1%) were almost always found in the tumor.
- TEC-Seq performance was reproducible across serial blood draws, and ddPCR confirmed many plasma calls. Some plasma-only mutations reflected intratumoral heterogeneity or subclonal/metastatic lesions not present in the initial biopsy.
- Clinical implications: preoperative ctDNA quantity correlated with recurrence and poorer survival in resectable colorectal cancer, suggesting prognostic value. TEC-Seq’s broader gene panel improved detection versus hotspot-only approaches.

Limitations and next steps:
- Sensitivity is not yet complete—many early cancers remain undetected. Larger population studies are needed to validate screening utility and to evaluate specificity and positive-predictive value at population scale.
- Distinguishing clinically significant tumors from indolent lesions will be essential to avoid overtreatment.
- Further optimization and clinical trials are required before routine clinical use; initial applications may focus on higher-risk populations.

Overall, TEC-Seq demonstrates a feasible, specific, and sensitive approach to detecting ctDNA from many early-stage tumors and shows promise for future noninvasive cancer screening and management, while highlighting challenges (blood-cell mutations, tumor heterogeneity, and incomplete sensitivity) that must be addressed.

Firefighters near Grande Prairie, Alberta, used specialized large-animal rescue training to free 10 horses that fell through thin spring ice on a dugout about 65 km west of Grande Prairie on Sunday. The call came late afternoon; roughly 35 regional firefighters and search-and-rescue members from Hythe, Beaverlodge, La Glace and Grande Prairie responded. Working amid thin ice, melting edges, cold water and the danger posed by frightened, partly feral broncing horses, crews cut paths with chainsaws and used slings and boards to get the animals over mud and slush to shore. All 10 horses were pulled from the water by about 6 p.m.; three later died (two from exhaustion, one from injuries caused by other horses). A veterinarian reported the seven survivors were in good condition. Fire Chief Trevor Grant warned landowners to be cautious around sloughs in warming weather, noting ice conditions can change within hours.

Ruth Ann (Ruth Catherine) Steinhagen, the Chicago woman who in 1949 lured Philadelphia Phillies first baseman Eddie Waitkus to a hotel room and shot him, has died at 83. The shooting, carried out when she was 19 and nearly fatal for the 29‑year‑old player, became a sensational national story and helped coin the era term “baseball Annie” for obsessive, often relentless fans. Waitkus survived, returned to play and later inspired Bernard Malamud’s novel The Natural and the 1984 film starring Robert Redford.

Steinhagen had become fixated on Waitkus as a teenager—building a shrine of photos and clippings, learning Lithuanian radio programs and even collecting ticket stubs—and escalated to violence after he was traded to the Phillies. On June 14, 1949, she summoned him to the Edgewater Beach Hotel with an unsigned note, shot him with a .22 rifle just below the heart, then knelt at his side. Declared legally insane at her hearing, she was committed to Kankakee State Hospital for nearly three years and was released in 1952 when doctors deemed her sane.

After release, Steinhagen withdrew from public life. She lived quietly in a modest Northwest Side Chicago home with her family, rarely spoke about the incident and otherwise remained obscure—so much so that neighbors only learned of her past years later. Waitkus chose not to press charges when she was released, and he died in 1972. Steinhagen died Dec. 29 at Swedish Covenant Hospital of a subdural hematoma from an accidental fall; her death went unreported until discovered in records months later. Authors and historians note the case’s mix of obsession, mental illness and celebrity that embedded it in both Chicago crime lore and baseball history.

A vandal spray-painted Pablo Picasso’s 1929 portrait "Woman in a Red Armchair" at Houston’s Menil Collection. A bystander recorded the attack and posted it to YouTube; surveillance footage also captured the incident. The perpetrator stenciled the word “Conquista” and a small bull/bullfighter image on the canvas, then fled. Museum staff quickly moved the painting to chief conservator Brad Epley, who began immediate restoration; Menil officials say the work has an “excellent prognosis” and that all spray paint has been removed but the painting must rest. Houston police are investigating the case as criminal mischief; no arrests have been made. The painting has been in the Menil since 1956 and is one of several Picassos in its holdings. Museum leaders noted the episode echoes past high-profile art vandalism.

Summary:

On October 21 a massive distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack against Dyn, a major DNS provider, caused widespread outages and severe slowdowns for many popular sites (Twitter, Spotify, etc.). The attack came in multiple waves and was highly distributed, involving large numbers of IP addresses. Investigation and outside analysis point to the Mirai botnet — malware that infects poorly secured Internet of Things (IoT) devices (DVRs, IP cameras and similar)—as the attack vector. The Mirai source code had been publicly released earlier on hackforums.net, allowing many actors to build botnets from vulnerable devices.

Cybersecurity firm Flashpoint and other researchers believe the likely perpetrators were non-state, English‑language forum-based hackers — often called “script kiddies” — motivated by notoriety or disruption rather than political or financial goals. Flashpoint found links to attacks against a video-game company (possibly PlayStation Network around a big game release), suggesting the game firm was the intended target and Dyn was collateral because it provided DNS services for that target.

The attack highlighted systemic problems: many IoT devices are shipped insecure, often unpatchable, and therefore can be repeatedly conscripted into large botnets. Even if Dyn and others harden defenses, the rapidly growing and largely unregulated IoT ecosystem (Intel projects huge device growth) makes future large-scale DDoS attacks likely. Recommended mitigations include resetting devices to factory settings, changing default passwords, and broader measures — though manufacturers, ISPs, regulators and consumers all share responsibility. In response, Sen. Mark Warner urged federal agencies to consider whether ISPs can and should block insecure IoT devices from networks, framing the issue as a “tragedy of the commons.”

Dyn and law enforcement continue technical analysis; Dyn initially estimated tens of millions of infected devices but later revised its figures. Investigation may identify methods and vulnerabilities to address, but preventing similar assaults at scale remains a major challenge so long as insecure IoT devices persist.

Donald Trump sparked a major intra-party and bipartisan backlash after saying in an MSNBC interview that if abortion were outlawed “there has to be some form of punishment,” implying women who obtain illegal abortions could be penalized. Trump quickly sought to walk back the remark, issuing a campaign statement that placed legal responsibility on providers rather than women (“The woman is a victim in this case”), reiterated he is “pro-life with exceptions,” and claimed the comment was misconstrued.

Republican rivals and party leaders immediately condemned the original comment. Ted Cruz and John Kasich, among others, said women should not be punished and emphasized focusing on providers. Democrats, including Hillary Clinton and DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz, used the episode to attack GOP positions on abortion and tie Trump to other party figures who oppose exceptions for rape and incest. Conservative and pro-life leaders also criticized Trump’s framing, saying punishing women is out of step with the mainstream pro-life movement.

The controversy came amid other Trump controversies—attacks on a reporter who accused his campaign manager of battery and remarks about the Geneva Conventions—that deepened concerns among Republicans about his electability and the party’s unity. Polling showed Trump trailing with many female voters and facing a competitive Wisconsin primary. Critics also questioned the sincerity of Trump’s recent shift from a previously pro-choice stance to a pro-life position, and commentators rejected his comparison of that evolution to Ronald Reagan’s historical record. Overall, the episode intensified GOP angst over Trump’s rhetoric and its potential to fracture the party heading into the convention and general election.

A 25-year-old Israeli woman told police she was gang‑raped early one morning after accepting a lift near Manali, Himachal Pradesh, while trying to reach Kaza/Keylong. She said a vehicle without number plates carrying six men offered to take her to Manali; two of the men allegedly raped her at an unidentified location and then dropped her in town. She and a friend reported the assault to police later that morning; she underwent a medical exam and was being moved to a larger hospital for further tests. Authorities recovered the vehicle, examined CCTV—including night‑vision footage—and by Monday had arrested two local men, while searches continued for the remaining suspects. The Israeli embassy was informed and the case file was sent for expert opinion in Mandi. Police say the area’s extensive CCTV coverage should help crack the case. The report notes similar attacks on foreign women in the Kullu–Manali area in 2012 and 2013.

Coach is acquiring rival handbag and accessories maker Kate Spade & Co. for $2.4 billion, paying $18.50 per share in cash. The deal, expected to close in Q3 2017, will preserve Kate Spade’s brand independence and key staff and is projected to be accretive to adjusted earnings in fiscal 2018. Coach expects about $50 million in annual cost savings from combined inventory and supply-chain efficiencies, which it says will reduce the need for heavy discounting at Kate Spade and help reinforce its luxury positioning.

Coach CEO Victor Luis said the acquisition targets younger, millennial consumers, leveraging Kate Spade’s strong brand awareness and lifestyle assortment. The move advances Coach’s longer-term strategy to build a global, multi-brand luxury group following prior purchases such as Stuart Weitzman and amid earlier acquisition speculation including Jimmy Choo. Analysts view the deal as a sensible brand fit that could benefit from Coach’s sourcing, distribution and design resources.

Market reaction: Kate Spade shares jumped over 8% on the news and Coach shares rose nearly 5% that day. Coach has been recovering financially after cutting U.S. discounting; its stock is up over the past year, while Kate Spade’s had lagged.

Michael and Cynthia Rondini have filed a federal wrongful-death lawsuit alleging that mishandling by University of Alabama officials and Tuscaloosa law enforcement — and an alleged sexual assault by a well‑connected local man — led their daughter, Megan Rondini, to commit suicide in February 2016.

Key allegations:
- Megan Rondini, a 20-year-old UA junior, reported being sexually assaulted in July 2015 after meeting a man at a Tuscaloosa bar; she said she may have been drugged.
- The suit asserts investigators and some university staff treated Megan like a suspect rather than a victim, focused on her actions (including taking a handgun and $3 for cab fare), failed to properly investigate (allegedly not testing a rape kit, not interviewing witnesses, and not recording all interviews), and were unduly sympathetic to the accused.
- Defendants named include the alleged assailant (not criminally charged), Tuscaloosa County Sheriff Ron Abernathy, investigator Adam Jones, deputy Joshua Hastings, UA Title IX coordinator Beth Howard, and a Women & Gender Resource Center staffer, Cara Blakes.
- The complaint says university counselors denied or delayed care, that Megan’s requests for help went unanswered, and that these failures caused severe depression, anxiety, PTSD and ultimately her suicide.
- The suit seeks unspecified damages and asks the court to order better sheriff’s office training and safer investigative practices; no dollar figure is requested in the filing.

Responses and context:
- The alleged attacker’s attorney called the lawsuit “baseless” and emphasized a grand jury declined to indict after review. The sheriff said the matter was referred to a grand jury because of conflicting statements.
- The University of Alabama said it was “deeply saddened,” disputes some media accounts, and maintains it provided information and referrals to counseling and accommodations.
- The case drew public attention after a BuzzFeed News report using interviews, texts and interrogation videos; the story provoked criticism in Congress and among advocacy groups about law enforcement treatment of sexual-assault survivors.
- The lawsuit is pending in federal court; no hearing date has been set.

Mitt Romney won the Nevada Republican caucuses easily Saturday, marking his second straight victory after winning Florida four days earlier and reinforcing his front‑runner status. With returns from 14 of 17 counties showing Romney at about 42 percent, Newt Gingrich about 25 percent, Ron Paul about 20 percent and Rick Santorum about 13 percent, Romney held a double‑digit lead as results continued to come in (Clark County, which often supplies a large share of votes, was still outstanding). Nevada awarded 28 delegates proportionally.

Romney used his victory to attack President Barack Obama’s economic record and to cast the 21st century as “an American century.” Nearly half of Nevada Republicans surveyed said the top factor in their vote was a candidate’s ability to beat Obama in November; about one quarter of caucusgoers identified as Mormon, a bloc that helped Romney win Nevada in 2008.

The Nevada contest was low‑key compared with Florida: little advertising, no debates, and modest candidate time spent in state. Donald Trump’s high‑profile endorsement of Romney in Las Vegas was a notable event of the brief campaign. Romney’s super PAC also ran ads targeting Gingrich’s claims about ties to Ronald Reagan.

Other candidates responded by shifting focus to upcoming contests. Gingrich planned to campaign in Ohio; Santorum and Paul headed to Minnesota and Colorado. Santorum hopes to outlast Gingrich and position himself as the conservative alternative to Romney; Paul aimed to mobilize libertarian and anti‑war GOP voters. At the time of the Nevada results, the AP delegate tally showed Romney with 87 of the 1,144 delegates needed for the nomination, Gingrich 26, Santorum 14 and Paul 4. The nominating calendar moves next to Minnesota and Colorado caucuses and a nonbinding Missouri primary.

A bright lunar occultation of Aldebaran will occur overnight Oct. 18–19. A lunar occultation happens when the Moon passes in front of a star; this event will hide 1st‑magnitude Aldebaran (the orange “eye” of Taurus) from viewers in parts of Mexico, Central America, the eastern U.S., southeastern Canada and southern Europe. Most observers in the eastern and southern U.S. will see a total occultation (the star disappears behind the bright lunar limb and reappears up to about 75 minutes later). A narrow “graze line” a few hundred yards wide—running roughly through Los Angeles, near Las Vegas, Denver and southeast of Minneapolis—will experience grazing events where Aldebaran appears to wink in and out as lunar limb mountains cross the star; these are especially striking through small telescopes. Binoculars or a telescope are recommended (the disappearance on the bright limb requires magnification). Exact disappearance/reappearance times and maps are available from the International Occultation Timing Association and related resources. This monthly series of Aldebaran occultations began in January 2015 and ends in September 2018; after that the next series won’t begin until 2033. Weather should be mostly clear across the southern U.S. for the event, though local conditions vary.

President Trump and Republican congressional leaders unveiled a broad tax-reform framework seeking to simplify the tax code, cut rates, and spur economic growth. Key elements:

- Individual taxes: Collapse seven brackets into three (12%, 25%, 35%), with Congress allowed to add a higher fourth bracket if needed. The plan doubles the standard deduction to $12,000 for singles and $24,000 for married couples, increases the child tax credit (amount unspecified), and creates a $500 credit for non-child dependents. The alternative minimum tax and the estate tax would be repealed. Many itemized deductions—including the state and local tax deduction—would be eliminated, though mortgage interest, charitable giving, education and retirement incentives, and some business credits would be preserved.

- Business taxes: Cut the corporate tax rate from 35% to 20% and create a 25% top rate for pass-through businesses (partnerships, sole proprietorships). Republicans propose moving from a worldwide to a territorial system for multinationals, with a one-time repatriation tax and new taxes on foreign profits to limit base erosion. Businesses could immediately expense new investments for five years; deductibility of interest would be limited (details TBD).

- Process and politics: The framework is a joint Republican proposal; many details remain to be written by congressional committees. Administration officials offered no official cost estimate. Senate budget instructions would permit up to $1.5 trillion in tax cuts over 10 years, though outside analyses of similar plans project much larger deficits ($3–7 trillion). Republicans argue growth will offset revenue losses; critics — Democrats and fiscal watchdogs — say the plan disproportionately benefits the wealthy and risks enlarging the deficit. Trump pressed lawmakers and voters to support the plan, urged some Democrats to join, but also hinted at bypassing Democrats using budget rules and threatened political consequences for wavering Democrats.

Overall, the proposal aims to deliver middle-class tax relief and business incentives to stimulate jobs and wages, but major specifics on bracket thresholds, transition rules, anti-abuse safeguards for pass-throughs, and deficit impacts remain unresolved and politically contentious.

This document centers on Beloit College’s long-running “Mindset List” project, founded in 1998 by Tom McBride and Ron Nief to describe the cultural touchstones and taken-for-granted realities shaping each incoming college class. Originally intended as a faculty reminder about dated references, the Mindset List quickly became a popular annual catalog (widely trafficked on Beloit’s site, webcast, and social media) that highlights how generational experience shifts over time and what teachers should know when educating new students.

The piece includes the full Mindset List for the Class of 2014 (students born in 1992), a 75-item inventory that illustrates how this cohort grew up with digital technologies and globalized culture as norms. Key themes from that list:
- Digital nativity: email is seen as slow, cellphones (smartphones) replace watches, many never learned cursive, CD-ROMs and early home computers are already museum artifacts, and instantaneous online access shapes expectations about information.
- Media and pop culture: references and celebrities shift—some older pop-culture icons mean little to them (e.g., Dirty Harry, dial-up modem noise), while others (Nirvana on “oldies” stations, Buffy, pop singers) are familiar.
- Globalization and geopolitics: Korean cars, U.S. business in Vietnam, U.S.-Russia cooperation in space, and the economic rise of China are long-standing realities; the Cold War nuclear threat is not part of their lived memory.
- Social change and institutions: expanded disability accommodations, legal and cultural shifts (e.g., assisted living, hospice, women priests in Anglican Church), DNA fingerprinting and the human genome, and evolving consumer/habits (many cable channels but little to watch).
- Education and pedagogy implications: because the generation conflates information access with knowledge, professors must teach patience, research skills, and critical evaluation beyond online searches.

Beyond the 2014 list, the document references subsequent Mindset List releases and related Beloit material: excerpts and announcements for later classes (2021, 2022), talks and essays by McBride (on topics like “Nintendofy”ing the Gen Z classroom, the decline of dormitory life, and economic virtues of Millennials), the Mindset List speakers’ program, companion publications (e.g., The Millennial Promise), and resources such as WeRHistory study guides. Also noted briefly is Alexa Internet’s donation of crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996 (tied to Wayback Machine archiving).

Overall, the Mindset List functions as a widely used, periodically updated tool that captures generational shifts in technology, culture, and expectations—intended to help educators, institutions, and the public better understand and teach successive cohorts of college students.

RedState, the influential conservative blog owned by Townhall Media (part of Salem Media Group), laid off several prominent writers and editors on Friday in what many observers say was at least partly a purge of anti‑Trump voices. Confirmed dismissals included Caleb Howe, Jay Caruso, Ben Howe, Patrick “Patterico” Frey, Neil Stevens, and Susan Wright. Some staffers discovered their firings when their accounts were locked; others received a brief memo from Townhall general manager Jonathan Garthwaite saying the outlet “can no longer support the entire roster of writers.”

Former RedState editor Erick Erickson and multiple current and ex‑staffers told The Daily Beast and CNN that the cuts appeared driven by both financial and political considerations: higher per‑click contracts were reportedly terminated and, among lower‑paid writers who remained, pro‑Trump contributors were largely retained while frequent critics of President Trump were let go—even when those critics produced strong traffic. Fired contributors framed the move as signaling that criticism of the president will no longer be tolerated at the site, reflecting a broader shift in parts of the conservative media ecosystem toward protecting Trump. Townhall/Salem did not offer detailed public comment.

Johnny Bobbitt Jr., a homeless Marine veteran who became nationally known after he gave his last $20 for gas to stranded motorist Kate McClure, is suing McClure and her boyfriend Mark D’Amico in New Jersey Superior Court. McClure’s Nov. 2017 GoFundMe raised more than $400,000 from over 14,000 donors to help Bobbitt, but his attorneys say the couple have refused to give him access to the bulk of the funds, spent more than half of the money on themselves and treated the campaign as a “personal piggy bank.” The suit seeks compensatory damages, an accounting of the donations, counsel fees, appointment of a receiver and for the funds to be deposited with the court; it also requests an injunction barring McClure and D’Amico from dissipating the money.

McClure initially used some funds to help Bobbitt—food, clothes, a bank account for daily needs and plans for trusts and long-term support—and the couple bought him a camper and appeared with him on national media. But Bobbitt says no formal trusts were created, he was later forced off the land where the camper was parked, and has relapsed into drug use and returned to the streets. D’Amico acknowledges controlling the money and has told reporters he would rather “burn it” than give large sums directly to Bobbitt because of his addiction; he has also asserted substantial spending by Bobbitt on drugs, legal bills and family support. McClure and D’Amico deny wrongdoing; D’Amico has said more than $150,000 remains. A court hearing is pending.

Former Toronto mayor Rob Ford put several personal items on eBay under the username "torontorobford." Listings included the tie he was wearing when he admitted to smoking crack cocaine, moose-print pajama pants (advertised as the ones he wore on a Wal‑Mart shopping trip), a size 4XL football jersey, and a novelty poster. Each listing claimed a connection to Ford's time in office, but the seller had a feedback score of zero, a warning for potential buyers. The post also included standard eBay bidding and checkout notices.

A non-binding United Nations agreement called the Global Compact for Migration was adopted in Marrakech on Dec. 10, 2018 by 164 of the 193 UN member states. Framed as a voluntary pact to promote “safe, orderly and regular” migration, it emphasizes international cooperation, protection of migrants’ human rights and measures to curb human smuggling and the deadly journeys many migrants face. The compact grew out of a 2016 UN declaration recognizing that migration affects nearly every country and cannot be managed unilaterally; the International Organization for Migration estimates about 1 billion migrants worldwide.

Supporters, including German Chancellor Angela Merkel and UN Secretary‑General António Guterres, argued the compact addresses the human cost of unregulated migration, helps economies through labor mobility and remittances, and does not create a new right to migrate. Opponents — notably the United States under President Trump and several mostly eastern European and other countries (e.g., Hungary, Poland, Austria, Australia, Czech Republic, Dominican Republic, Latvia, Slovakia) — rejected the pact, saying it could impose policies, blur distinctions between legal and illegal migration, or conflict with national sovereignty. The agreement’s adoption highlights global divisions over migration amid political backlash in some countries after large refugee arrivals to Europe in 2015.

Prosecutors from six California counties announced they will combine charges against Joseph James DeAngelo Jr., the 72-year-old former police officer arrested in April on suspicion of being the "Golden State Killer," into a single trial to be held in Sacramento. An amended complaint alleges 13 counts of murder plus multiple kidnapping and weapons charges spanning northern, central and southern California; DeAngelo, who remains in custody and has not yet pleaded, is to be arraigned on the amended complaint this week.

The move unifies prosecution teams so victims and families from multiple jurisdictions can be tried together; Sacramento County District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert called it a fitting end to a more-than-40-year quest for justice in what she termed one of California’s most notorious unsolved serial-rape and killing sprees. The crimes attributed to the Golden State Killer—rapes, burglaries and murders—occurred mostly in the 1970s and 1980s, with the last known offense in 1986.

Investigators linked DeAngelo to the crimes through DNA. Early evidence included DNA recovered from the 1980 double murder of Lyman and Charlene Smith. This year, investigators used genetic genealogy—searching a public genealogy database to build family trees from DNA matches—to identify likely relatives and narrow suspects based on age and location. Surveillance and recovery of DeAngelo’s discarded DNA (from a tissue) produced a match tying him to DNA evidence from multiple crime scenes, leading to his arrest. The document also recounts one specific 1975 murder charge in Tulare County: Claude Snelling was shot in his Visalia backyard after a masked intruder forced Snelling’s daughter from her bed; she escaped unharmed.

Harper Lee, the 87-year-old author of the Pulitzer Prize–winning 1960 novel To Kill a Mockingbird, filed suit in federal court in Manhattan alleging her former agent’s son-in-law, Samuel Pinkus, and related entities improperly obtained and profited from the book’s copyright.

Key allegations:
- After longtime agent Eugene Winick (of McIntosh & Otis) fell ill around 2002, Pinkus took over handling some clients and allegedly diverted commissions and clients to companies he controlled.
- In 2007, while Lee—then living in assisted care and suffering from poor eyesight and hearing after a stroke—signed a document assigning the novel’s copyright to Pinkus’s company. Lee says she did not understand she had assigned the copyright and that Pinkus exploited her infirmities and his position of trust.
- Although the copyright was reportedly reassigned to Lee last year and Pinkus was discharged as her agent, the complaint alleges he continued receiving royalties this year.
- McIntosh & Otis previously won an arbitration judgment against a Pinkus-controlled company over diverted commissions.
- The suit seeks unspecified damages and requests reassignment/confirmation of Lee’s copyright and forfeiture of commissions; it calls the transfer “self-dealing” incompatible with an agent’s duty of loyalty.

Defendants also include Leigh Ann Winick (Pinkus’s wife and president of Keystone Literary LLC) and Gerald Posner (who is said to have incorporated one of Pinkus’s businesses). Calls and messages to the defendants were reportedly not immediately returned.

Background: To Kill a Mockingbird is Lee’s only published novel, has sold over 30 million copies, is widely taught in schools, and the film adaptation won multiple Academy Awards. The case is Lee v. Pinkus, filed in the Southern District of New York.

Former New York governor Eliot Spitzer, who resigned more than five years ago amid a prostitution scandal, appeared on MSNBC’s Morning Joe as he pursues a comeback running for New York City comptroller. On-air he became emotional when asked how the scandal changed him, saying “a lot of pain” and choking up; hosts and panelists debated whether his tears were genuine but praised him for facing questions publicly.

Spitzer repeatedly acknowledged wrongdoing, calling his actions the product of “hubris” and poor judgment, and asked voters to judge him on the “totality” of his record. He framed his candidacy around his past achievements as attorney general and governor — from Wall Street enforcement to progressive stances on issues such as same-sex marriage and drivers’ licenses for undocumented immigrants — arguing that those accomplishments show he can be a tough, substantive public official rather than a traditional politician.

If elected comptroller, Spitzer said he would use the office’s control over roughly $140 billion in pension assets to pressure corporations on governance reforms (for example, separating CEO and board chairman roles) and to act as an activist investor and watchdog over financial firms that do business with the city. He acknowledged the difficulty of changing public perception in a short campaign period and conceded that voters will decide whether he has earned a second chance.

Commentary in the piece placed Spitzer’s return in the broader context of numerous recent political sex scandals. Observers noted a cultural shift that makes it easier for politicians implicated in moral failings to attempt comebacks: lowered public expectations, pervasive bad behavior across public life, and a pragmatic voter focus on competence over personal character.

This piece—excerpted from a Boston Globe–produced book celebrating Fenway Park—profiles the century-old ballpark as an enduring, beloved Boston icon and the oldest stadium in Major League Baseball. Built in 1912, Fenway’s distinctive features—the brick Yawkey Way entrance, the manual scoreboard, Pesky’s Pole, and the idiosyncratic, tightly confined field with its odd angles and minimal foul territory—give it a one-of-a-kind playing character and intimate fan experience. Its quirks (the Green Monster, narrow streets, and close-in seats) produce unusual plays, constant fan interaction, and memorable sensory moments from scalpers to the eighth-inning “Sweet Caroline’’ singalongs and “Dirty Water’’ after wins.

Fenway is woven into Boston and baseball lore: writers and entertainers have likened its charm to a cultural landmark comparable to the Freedom Trail; it has appeared in films and TV; and generations of fans — including families across decades — treasure its continuity. The stadium has hosted countless historic athletic and civic events: legendary players (Babe Ruth, Ted Williams, DiMaggio, Hank Aaron, and many others) performed there; baseball milestones and dramatic moments from 1912 through 2004 are etched into its history (e.g., the 1912 World Series, Fisk’s 1975 homer, Roger Clemens’s 20-strikeout game, Dave Roberts’s 2004 steal). Fenway has also hosted football, hockey, presidential speeches, and major concerts.

Beyond statistics and events, the park’s lore—chants, on-field antics, famous incidents, and colorful personalities—defines its appeal. With relatively few structural changes since opening, Fenway remains a living museum of baseball history and a continuing pilgrimage for fans worldwide.

Harris County deputy Darren Goforth, 47, was fatally shot outside a northwest Houston gas station on Friday night after finishing at a pump. Prosecutors say the gunman, 30-year-old Shannon Jaruay Miles, ran up behind Goforth, shot him in the back of the head and then stood over him and fired until the weapon was empty — 15 rounds from a .40-caliber semi-automatic. Ballistics matched a .40 Smith & Wesson found in Miles’ garage and a witness identified him in a video lineup. Miles was arrested Saturday, appeared in court Monday on capital murder charges, did not enter a plea, and was held without bail; defense attorneys indicated they will investigate mental-health issues.

Court records show Miles spent four months in a mental hospital in 2012 after being declared incompetent in an aggravated assault case; that assault was later dismissed after he was returned to competency. Records also document multiple prior run-ins with police, including convictions or pleas for resisting arrest, misdemeanor firearm and other offenses. Authorities continue to investigate motive; officials have noted it’s unclear why Goforth was targeted, though Sheriff Ron Hickman said investigators initially believed the uniform may have made him a target.

Goforth was a 10-year veteran with a wife and two children. The killing prompted large community response: a vigil and walks drew more than 1,000 people, and donations for the family exceeded $150,000. President Obama called Goforth’s widow to offer condolences. Funeral services were scheduled for Friday at Second Baptist Church with burial at Woodlawn Cemetery.

A New Hampshire jury on Friday returned a split verdict in the case of former St. Paul’s School senior Owen Labrie, acquitting him of the most serious rape charges but convicting him on one felony and four misdemeanors related to a sexual encounter with a 15-year-old freshman in May of the previous year.

Key findings and outcomes
- The 12-person jury found Labrie guilty of: one felony count of using a computer or internet service to entice a child under 16 (maximum seven years), three counts of misdemeanor sexual assault, and child endangerment. The jury acquitted him of aggravated felonious sexual assault and a simple assault count.
- Sentencing is set for Oct. 29. Labrie faces up to 11 years in prison under one news account (combined maximums cited) and will be required to register as a sex offender. He remains free on bail with a nightly curfew; prosecutors asked for higher bail.
- The jury concluded intercourse occurred but was not convinced the prosecution proved it was without the girl’s consent. Defense counsel J.W. Carney argued the convictions stemmed largely from the victim’s age and that the internet statute was overbroad when applied to consensual teen encounters; he signaled a possible appeal and said he would seek probation.
- Both teenagers were emotional at the verdict: Labrie wept and his Harvard acceptance had already been rescinded; the victim and her family also wept and called the convictions “a measure of justice.”

Evidence and trial themes
- Testimony and emails showed Labrie had pursued the younger student for months, invited her to a secluded mechanical/attic room, and brought a blanket and a condom. The victim testified Labrie ignored her objections and removed her bra and underwear; Labrie testified the encounter was consensual and later said he lied to friends to boast.
- DNA evidence: semen and sperm were found on the victim’s underwear, and some biological material matched Labrie’s DNA; a cervical swab showed no sperm.
- The trial exposed campus sexual culture at the elite boarding school, including references to a “senior salute” tradition in which seniors sought underclassmen partners. The victim’s family faulted the school for fostering a “toxic culture”; school officials praised the victim’s courage, denied condoning such behavior, and said they had taken disciplinary and handbook actions.

Reactions
- Prosecutors praised the victim’s courage and said the convictions vindicated her; the victim’s family said the outcome held Labrie accountable though their daughter cannot be made whole.
- Carney characterized the verdict as finding “one teenager guilty of having consensual sex with another teenager” and criticized application of the computer-enticement law to high-school social planning.

The verdict leaves Labrie’s future altered by criminal convictions and lifetime sex-offender registration while highlighting contested factual claims about consent and broader concerns about student sexual culture at an elite boarding school.

Elon Musk announced he will not take Tesla private. After exploring the idea with advisers (Silver Lake, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley) and gauging investor interest, Musk concluded most existing shareholders prefer Tesla to remain public, many institutions face compliance limits on investing in a private company, and retail shareholders would have no clear path to ownership. He also determined that pursuing a go-private transaction would be more time-consuming and distracting than expected—an unacceptable distraction as Tesla must focus on ramping Model 3 production and reaching sustainable profitability. Musk said the board agreed with him, and Tesla will remain public while focusing on building products, improving Model 3 production, and achieving financial sustainability. He thanked investors, customers and employees.

Belgium has opened its first criminal trial over a euthanasia case since the practice was legalized in 2002. Three East Flanders doctors are accused of improperly euthanizing Tine Nys, a 38-year-old woman who was diagnosed with Asperger’s two months before she was killed in 2010. Prosecutors say there are sufficient indications to refer the case to the Assize Court in Ghent on charges of “poisoning.” The family filed a criminal complaint alleging procedural irregularities during the death and subsequent attempts by doctors to block the investigation; emails obtained by the AP show at least one doctor, psychiatrist Dr. Lieve Thienpont, disparaging the family and urging colleagues to “stop these people.”

Belgium is one of a small number of countries (along with the Netherlands) that allow euthanasia for psychiatric suffering when patients meet strict criteria of “unbearable and untreatable” suffering. Still, euthanasia for mental disorders remains rare (about 40 cases per year of roughly 2,000 total) and controversial. Critics question whether conditions like autism should qualify and whether psychiatric patients always have the decisional capacity to request death. Concerns have centered on Thienpont, a prominent psychiatrist and euthanasia advocate whose practice approved a high number of psychiatric euthanasia requests; some colleagues, including Dr. Wim Distelmans (chair of Belgium’s euthanasia review commission), have refused to accept her referrals, saying patients arrived expecting automatic approval and that independent consultations required by law were undermined.

The case has fueled calls for tougher oversight and clearer rules. Critics cite vague legal provisions, limited transparency from Belgium’s single review commission, and occasional procedural lapses; some Belgian psychiatric bodies are drafting stricter guidance requiring demonstration that all proven treatments were tried. Supporters of psychiatric euthanasia argue denying it singles out mentally ill patients and infringes autonomy. The Nys prosecution, and a concurrent Dutch prosecution of a euthanasia-for-dementia case, underscore the ethical and legal tensions as countries extend end-of-life laws to psychiatric and non-terminal conditions.

A gunman opened fire at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh during Saturday morning Sabbath services, killing 11 people and wounding six others, including four police officers. Authorities arrested 46-year-old Robert Gregory Bowers, who was shot by police and faces multiple federal and state charges — including murder, weapons counts and hate crimes — after reportedly telling officers he wanted all Jews to die and that Jews were committing genocide against his people.

The attack is believed to be the deadliest targeting the Jewish community in U.S. history, the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) said. The ADL and other Jewish organizations highlighted the shooting amid a documented surge in anti‑Semitic incidents and online harassment: the ADL reported a nearly 60% rise in anti‑Jewish incidents from 2016 to 2017 (1,267 to 1,986 incidents), and FBI statistics show Jews were the most frequent religious targets in 2016. Law enforcement cautioned that bias motivations can be complex and underreported, but the FBI is treating and investigating the case as a hate crime.

The shooting exploited a common security vulnerability: synagogue doors are often left unlocked on the Sabbath. The massacre prompted nationwide condemnation, calls for increased protection at houses of worship, extra patrols at synagogues in major cities, and renewed debate over hate speech and gun safety in the U.S. Local leaders and national organizations described the incident as part of a troubling rise in hate‑based violence and urged unity and stronger measures to prevent similar attacks. Authorities pledged a swift, severe prosecution.

Josh Hardy, a 7-year-old cancer patient at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, will receive the experimental antiviral brincidofovir after drugmaker Chimerix and the FDA arranged a new open-label trial that begins with him as the first participant. Josh, who has battled multiple cancers since infancy and became severely immunocompromised after a bone marrow transplant, developed a disseminated adenovirus and is critically ill in the ICU with heart and kidney failure.

Chimerix had initially declined the family’s and physicians’ requests for compassionate-use access to the unapproved drug, saying individual emergency use could slow broader development. After intense media coverage and a high-profile social media campaign (“Save Josh”) that mobilized public pressure, Chimerix and the FDA finalized a plan to release brincidofovir to Josh and enroll up to 20 patients in the pilot study; the company said this approach enables help for multiple patients while advancing clinical evaluation. St. Jude expected to receive the medication within 48 hours but cautioned the drug’s safety and efficacy in children remain unproven.

Chimerix CEO Kenneth Moch called the arrangement a way to help Josh and other patients; Josh’s parents and supporters praised the decision. The case highlighted tensions between compassionate-use requests and drug development priorities, and prompted widespread community support, protests, and online activism that company officials said both aided the outcome and sometimes produced hostile responses.

Megyn Kelly returned to Fox News’ The Kelly File after a 10-day family vacation, and Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump immediately criticized her on Twitter. Trump complained that Kelly was “off her game,” said he preferred the show without her and suggested she take another unscheduled vacation. He also retweeted a follower who called her a “bimbo.” Kelly has not responded directly on Twitter.

Kelly’s vacation had prompted speculation that she was stepping away because of backlash after she questioned Trump about past sexist remarks during a GOP debate; Trump himself suggested there “probably” was a connection. Fox News pushed back, saying her time off was pre-planned and dismissing conspiracy theories, while asserting network support for Kelly and noting other anchors had recently taken vacations.

The episode is part of an ongoing feud dating to the debate, when Trump made a crude remark about Kelly having “blood coming out of her…wherever.” The story also notes Trump’s broader pattern of refusing to apologize for past controversial comments, with only an apology from his lawyer (not him) mentioned in connection with a decades-old allegation.
