A viral claim that Neville "Bunny Wailer" Livingston — the songwriter of "Electric Boogie" (commonly known as "The Electric Slide") — confirmed the song is about a vibrator circulated online and in some outlets. The story originated with an Aazios item quoting an unnamed source close to Livingston and spread widely on social media. In response, EDM.com contacted Livingston, who issued a clear denial: he says he has never said the song was inspired by anything other than Eddie Grant’s "Electric Avenue," and called the vibrator interpretation a falsehood that offends his and Marcia Griffiths’ legacies and tarnishes the song beloved by millions. The rumor had prompted many amused and shocked reactions online, but the songwriter himself has put it to rest.

CNN reports that U.S. investigators placed former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort under court-authorized electronic surveillance under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) both before and after the 2016 election. The wiretaps began after Manafort became a target of an FBI probe rooted in his work for Ukraine’s pro‑Russian Party of Regions (investigated since at least 2014). Surveillance was halted last year for lack of evidence, then resumed under a new FISA warrant that extended into early 2017 as the FBI expanded its focus to ties between Trump campaign associates and suspected Russian operatives.

Sources told CNN that intercepted communications included exchanges that led investigators to worry Manafort may have encouraged Russian assistance to the campaign, though two sources cautioned that the evidence is not conclusive. Some of the intercepted material reportedly renewed FBI interest last fall after communications between Manafort and suspected Russian operatives, and among Russians themselves, were picked up. As part of the FISA-authorized effort, the FBI searched a storage facility belonging to Manafort earlier this year; what was seized, if anything, is not known.

Surveillance continued into the early months of the Trump administration and overlapped a period when Manafort was known to speak with President Trump; it stopped only after lawyers for the President and Manafort insisted it cease. It is not known whether President Trump’s communications were captured. The White House and Manafort declined comment.

Background: The Manafort inquiry originated from long-running probes of his consulting work in Ukraine, including potential violations of the Foreign Agents Registration Act; several U.S. firms later filed retroactive registrations. Justice Department prosecutors earlier determined there was insufficient evidence to charge Manafort or related U.S. subjects, prompting the temporary suspension of monitoring. The FBI renewed surveillance amid broader counterintelligence concerns about Russian election meddling, fueled by CIA and other intelligence indicating a Kremlin-directed operation.

Separately, Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s team — which took over the Russia probe in May 2017 — has been given details from these intercepts and has pursued aggressive investigative steps: grand jury subpoenas for several Manafort associates and for figures tied to Ukraine-related consulting firms, and an unusual subpoena to a former Manafort lawyer. Mueller’s office has also sought documents and voluntary interviews from White House officials while trying to avoid forcing them into subpoenas. The reporting notes gaps in surveillance timing (notably no FBI monitoring in June 2016 during the Trump Tower meeting involving Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner and a Russian lawyer) that could affect prosecutorial efforts.

Sophie the Giraffe is a 7.5-inch natural-rubber teether made by French firm Vulli that has become a ubiquitous and fashionable baby gift in the U.S. over the past decade. Imported to the U.S. in the early 2000s by Hélène Dumoulin‑Montgomery, Sophie’s popularity grew after placement in high-end gift baskets in Los Angeles, celebrity exposure, and demand spikes following safety scares over Chinese-made toys. Roughly 500,000 Sophies are sold annually in the U.S.; she’s sold in about 75 countries and priced variably (cheaper in Europe, more expensive in places like Brazil).

Despite its fame and the brand’s emphasis on 100% natural rubber and food-grade paint, parents have reported mold growing inside Sophies. Several caregivers — including a pediatric dentist who cut open the toy after detecting a musty smell — found black mold or mildew in the hollow interior where moisture can collect. Others posted photos and accounts on Amazon and parenting forums. Vulli responded that Sophie should only be cleaned on the surface with a damp cloth and not submerged, to avoid water entering the hole; they said they hadn’t been contacted about specific complaints and that they take safety seriously. Cleaning experts and pediatricians note that mold inside toys is a known risk when moisture becomes trapped; it’s more concerning for children with mold allergies or immune issues but generally avoidable with proper cleaning and drying.

Practical takeaways: hollow, punctured, or “squeaker” toys that can trap drool are prone to internal mold if moisture gets inside. Manufacturers’ cleaning instructions should be followed; for toys that can be submerged, recommended methods include hot soapy water, bleach solutions, dishwasher runs, vinegar soaks, or boiling, followed by thorough drying. Many parents now avoid toys with interior cavities or holes for this reason.

Ricki Lake announced that her ex-husband, jewelry designer Christian Evans, has died. In an emotional Instagram post on Feb. 14 she said Evans, 45, “succumbed to his life long struggle with bipolar disorder” and that knowing him made her a better person. Lake and Evans married in April 2012 after dating since 2010, separated after his first major manic episode in 2014, and finalized their divorce in 2015, though they continued an on-and-off relationship and even lived together again at times. Lake says Evans was open with her about a bipolar diagnosis but resisted medication and treatment; he was hospitalized under a 5150 hold in 2014 and later entered a treatment facility. His mania returned last September, and on Feb. 11 Evans emailed a note to family; he was found dead two days later from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Lake described him as loving and misunderstood, said she plans to honor him and scatter some of his ashes in Ibiza, and urged awareness and early treatment for bipolar disorder. Hotlines and resources for mental-health crises were shared.

A U.S. congressional report and multiple security firms say that on April 8, 2010, routing announcements from a small Chinese ISP (IDC China) — picked up and propagated by China Telecom — caused roughly 18 minutes during which routes to a large portion of the Internet were redirected through Chinese servers. The commission’s report described that route hijack as affecting routes to many U.S. government and military sites (Senate, DOD, services’ networks, NASA, NOAA, etc.) and major commercial sites (Dell, Yahoo, Microsoft, IBM). Security researchers (including McAfee) characterized it as one of the largest BGP/IP hijacks recorded and warned it could have enabled eavesdropping, data manipulation, diversion to spoof sites, or later decryption of captured traffic; however, there is no public evidence confirming misuse of the data. China Telecom denied any hijack. The incident highlights structural vulnerabilities in global routing (BGP), risks from improperly trusted certificate authorities, and broader U.S.–China tensions over cyber activity and Internet control; experts warn similar incidents can recur and called for improved safeguards.

Henry Rayhons, a 78-year-old former Iowa state representative and lifelong northern Iowa farmer, is awaiting trial on a felony charge that he raped his second wife, Donna Lou Young, at a nursing home where she was a resident. Donna, four days short of her 79th birthday, died in August of complications from Alzheimer’s disease; Rayhons was arrested one week after her death and pleaded not guilty.

Background and relationship
- Rayhons and Donna married in 2007 after both were widowed; they were publicly affectionate and active together—singing in church choir, attending fairs, and spending summers on Rayhons’s farm. Friends and many family members described them as deeply in love.
- Donna developed progressive Alzheimer’s over several years. As her condition declined, her daughters (from a prior marriage), Linda Dunshee and Suzan Brunes, became worried about her safety and care. They ultimately moved her into Concord Care Center in Garner in late March.

Events leading to the investigation
- Tensions rose between Rayhons and Donna’s daughters over visitation, outings and how Donna should be cared for. Staff and the daughters recorded incidents of confusion and risky behaviors by Donna.
- Concord staff used the BIMS (a brief cognitive screening) in Donna’s chart; she scored very low on tests in April and May. Based on those results and clinical impression, physician John Brady initialed a care plan on May 15 marking Donna as not mentally able to consent to sexual activity.
- Donna was moved to Room 12 North and on the evening of May 23 Rayhons visited. Shortly after he left, Donna’s roommate reported being distressed and said she had heard sexual noises behind the privacy curtain. Staff called police; Donna was taken for a sexual-assault exam that night. Bedding and panties were sent to the state crime lab.

Investigation and evidence
- A hallway camera captured Rayhons dropping Donna’s underwear into a hamper after the visit. Donna’s sexual-assault kit later showed a stain in her underwear that “indicated the presence of seminal fluid,” though no spermatozoa were identified and no foreign DNA was found on vaginal or oral swabs.
- Rayhons told a state special agent he sometimes could not recall specific visits but said Donna had sometimes asked for sex and that he would only respond when she wanted it. Prosecutors say Rayhons confessed to having sex with Donna; Rayhons’s attorney says his statements are vague and taken out of context.
- The resident who initially complained later told an investigator she heard whispering rather than sexual noises. Donna’s daughters, who initiated the guardianship proceedings and limited Rayhons’s contact, would not be interviewed for the story.

Legal and ethical issues
- Prosecutors must prove a sex act occurred on May 23 and that Donna lacked the mental capacity to consent because of Alzheimer’s. Iowa’s sexual-assault statute criminalizes sex with a person who has a mental defect or incapacity precluding consent; the statute treats spouses and cohabitants differently in some provisions, creating legal complexity when a spouse lives in a nursing home.
- Experts note dementia is variable: a person can lack short-term memory yet still be able to express desires, including sexual ones. Critics argue brief cognitive screens like the BIMS don’t measure decision-making capacity about sex; thorough clinical assessments of judgment and understanding are more relevant.
- The case highlights profound tensions among love, intimacy, elder autonomy, dementia, family gatekeeping, nursing-home procedures, and criminal law. Some geriatric and nursing-home experts warn that blanket bans on sexual contact can deprive dementia patients and their partners of meaningful intimacy; others emphasize protecting vulnerable residents.

Aftermath and status
- Donna was moved to a facility with an Alzheimer’s unit, visited by Rayhons shortly before she died Aug. 8; he was arrested Aug. 15 and released on bond. Trial was scheduled for late January in Hancock County; prosecutors sought a change of venue citing local publicity.
- The dispute also produced family rifts (over nursing-home bills, Donna’s belongings, guardianship decisions) and raised questions about whether nursing homes and police are equipped to assess capacity and handle alleged sexual activity involving residents with dementia.

Overall, the Rayhons case is being watched as a rare, fraught test of how the criminal-justice system, families and care institutions should treat intimate relations when one partner has dementia—balancing protection of the vulnerable with respect for long-standing marital intimacy and personal autonomy.

Steven Avery, the central figure of Netflix’s Making a Murderer, has filed a broad appeal in Wisconsin seeking release on bond and challenging his 2007 first-degree intentional homicide conviction in the 2005 death of photographer Teresa Halbach. The pro se filing, signed by Avery and containing numerous spelling and grammar errors, alleges multiple legal failings: that investigators executed an improper search across several properties (making discovered evidence “fruit of the poisonous tree”); that a juror improperly influenced others by repeatedly declaring Avery “is f------ guilty”; that Judge Angela Sutkiewicz made misleading statements; and that his trial attorneys were ineffective.

Avery had previously served 18 years for a wrongful rape conviction and later sued Manitowoc County for millions before he and his nephew Brendan Dassey were arrested in Halbach’s death. Dassey, a teenager at the time, is serving time as an accessory.

The case drew national attention after the documentary raised questions about the investigation and trial, prompting public debate, petitions, and “armchair” inquiries; authorities call the series biased, while filmmakers defend it. Kathleen Zellner, a high-profile Illinois attorney known for pursuing wrongful-conviction reversals, recently took over Avery’s defense and says she has new evidence that will exonerate him (details not disclosed). Manitowoc County officials deny impropriety; Gov. Scott Walker has publicly said he would not pardon Avery and pointed to a 2011 appeals-court ruling that upheld key aspects of the conviction.

South Korea announced it will send $8 million in humanitarian aid to North Korea — $4.5 million via the World Food Programme for nutritional products for children and pregnant women and $3.5 million via UNICEF for vaccines and medical treatments — marking the first Seoul-to-Pyongyang aid package in nearly two years. Seoul’s Unification Ministry said the move separates humanitarian assistance from politics; timing and delivery details remain to be confirmed. The plan dented President Moon Jae-in’s approval rating and provoked concern in Japan and the United States, coming shortly after new UN sanctions imposed over North Korea’s sixth nuclear test on Sept. 3.

Tensions on the Korean Peninsula intensified amid sharp rhetoric between Washington and Pyongyang. At the UN General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump warned he would “totally destroy” North Korea if it threatened the United States or its allies and dubbed Kim Jong Un “rocket man.” North Korea’s Foreign Minister Ri Yong-ho, attending the UN, derided Trump’s speech as “the sound of a dog barking” and dismissed the insults. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson played down prospects for dialogue, while Trump discussed the crisis with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

China urged restraint, with Foreign Minister Wang Yi warning the situation was worsening and calling on all parties to avoid escalation; Wang also repeated Chinese demands that South Korea remove the U.S.-deployed THAAD missile-defense system. Chinese state media criticized U.S. rhetoric, urging dialogue instead of threats. The international community remains alarmed by North Korea’s accelerated missile and nuclear activity, including recent ICBM launches and the September nuclear test, which prompted the latest UN sanctions. Humanitarian groups, including UNICEF, warned of acute malnutrition affecting hundreds of thousands of North Korean children, underscoring Seoul’s stated rationale for the aid.

Loretta E. Lynch, President Obama’s nominee for U.S. attorney general and the first African-American woman nominated for the post, testified at an all-day Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearing that showcased deep Republican criticism of the Justice Department under outgoing AG Eric Holder. Lynch, a longtime federal prosecutor and current U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, emphasized her independence, law-enforcement credentials, and intent to be “Loretta Lynch,” not Eric Holder.

Major points:
- Immigration: Republicans pressed Lynch repeatedly about the administration’s executive actions on immigration. She said she was not involved in those decisions but found the Justice Department’s legal rationale “reasonable” and stressed the importance of ensuring any executive action is lawful. Her responses frustrated some GOP senators who view the administration’s moves as unconstitutional.
- Key policy positions: Lynch said waterboarding is “torture and thus illegal,” supports the death penalty as an effective punishment, does not favor marijuana legalization and disagrees with President Obama’s comment that marijuana is no more harmful than alcohol, and indicated she believes NSA surveillance programs are constitutional and effective.
- Prosecutorial discretion and national security: She defended prosecutorial discretion, expressed willingness to use all available tools — including military commissions in certain terrorism cases — and highlighted her office’s extensive terrorism prosecution record.
- Relations with Congress and communities: Lynch pledged to foster a better relationship with Congress and to repair strained ties between law enforcement and minority communities, making community-police relations a priority.
- Background and demeanor: Her testimony was calm and polished. She frequently avoided taking firm stances on contentious administration decisions, citing her role as a career prosecutor. She spoke personally about her family’s civil-rights history and values. Supporters praised her qualifications and independence, while several Republicans signaled they would oppose her nomination.

The committee delayed any vote; Lynch will need at least some Republican support to advance. The hearing underscored partisan tensions over the Justice Department’s recent policies even as Democrats urged senators to judge Lynch on her record rather than use the nomination to score political points.

This document stitches together three related but distinct political developments and perspectives from late 2017:

1) Media bias and the Alabama GOP primary
- The piece argues Washington media favor establishment figures like Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and oppose Donald Trump, so they portrayed Roy Moore’s primary victory over Luther Strange as a rebuke of Trump rather than of McConnell.  
- It contends Moore’s supporters believed Trump actually preferred Moore and only backed Strange superficially to appease the GOP establishment. Moore ran explicitly against McConnell and cast himself as authentically “Trumpian.” Strange, an appointee unpopular with Alabama voters, lost despite heavy spending by a pro-McConnell super PAC and Trump’s late endorsement.  
- The writer says the DC press corps mischaracterized the result; Moore’s base sees him as aligned with Trump and likely to face weak Democratic opposition in the general election, especially if Trump actively campaigns for him.

2) McConnell’s political troubles and GOP dynamics
- Reporting summarizes the immediate political fallout for McConnell: Strange’s loss, failure to pass a GOP Obamacare repeal-replace measure, and Sen. Bob Corker’s retirement combined to make a bad day for the Majority Leader.  
- Trump privately criticized McConnell as “weak” for failing on health care and for opposing changes to Senate filibuster rules; Trump has periodically attacked McConnell publicly. Still, McConnell’s Senate colleagues publicly back him, praising his leadership record (including shepherding Neil Gorsuch’s confirmation) and downplaying his culpability for recent GOP legislative setbacks.  
- McConnell pledged to support Moore in the general election despite Moore’s vows to oppose his leadership. Internal GOP views presented: problems blamed on fractious Senate dynamics, specific bills and personalities rather than on McConnell alone.

3) U.S. funding to UNRWA and Israeli reactions
- The Trump administration reportedly froze a scheduled Jan. 1 transfer of $125 million to the U.N. Relief and Works Agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) while reviewing U.S. aid to the Palestinians following the U.S. recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. Officials were reportedly considering cutting up to $180 million (about half of U.S. contributions).  
- Diplomats and analysts warned that a major cut would be catastrophic for UNRWA’s operations and could worsen humanitarian conditions in Gaza, the West Bank and refugee-hosting states. U.N. Secretary-General and other donors were engaged on the issue.  
- Israel’s leadership had mixed instincts: while Netanyahu supports Trump’s critical stance toward UNRWA and Palestinian policy, Israeli security officials cautioned against sharp cuts because UNRWA’s services affect regional stability. Israel reportedly urged the U.S. toward a “gradual disengagement” rather than abrupt funding cuts.

Overall: the excerpts highlight tensions within the Republican coalition (populist insurgents vs. establishment), strained relations between Trump and congressional GOP leaders, and consequential shifts in U.S. policy toward Palestinian aid that have diplomatic and humanitarian implications.

A Canadian fMRI study (Psychology and Aging) finds older adults perform better on attention-demanding memory tasks in the morning than the afternoon. Researchers tested younger (19–30) and older (60–82) adults on distracting picture–word memory tasks and scanned brain activity. When tested in the afternoon, older adults were about 10% more likely than young adults to attend to distractions and showed reduced activation in attentional control regions, instead exhibiting default‑mode “idling.” However, a separate group of older adults tested in the morning (8:30–10:30 a.m.) performed much better: they ignored fewer distractors, closed the performance gap with younger adults, and activated the same rostral prefrontal and superior parietal regions young adults used to suppress distraction. The authors conclude time of day affects cognitive performance and brain activity in older adults and recommend scheduling mentally demanding tasks in the morning and accounting for time-of-day when testing cognitive function in aging studies.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, facing a torrent of scandals after admitting he smoked crack cocaine, has doubled down instead of stepping aside, drawing public outrage and political maneuvers to limit his role. At a veterans’ event he was jeered and one WWII veteran refused to shake his hand, calling him a “druggie.” Undeterred, Ford declared “I’m not going anywhere” and the next day was at City Hall signing and selling “Robbie Bobbie” bobblehead dolls—hundreds of people lined up and proceeds went to charity.

The controversies, including reports of a videotape showing Ford smoking from a crack pipe and other episodes of erratic behavior, have eroded his ability to lead. Council members say his moral authority and capacity to build consensus—the main sources of the mayor’s power—have evaporated, leaving a functional power vacuum that hampers work on major issues like transit. With no legal mechanism to remove an unconvicted mayor, Toronto’s 44-member City Council is pursuing two strategies: asking Ford to take a leave, apologize and cooperate with police (and, if he refuses, asking the Ontario government to legislate his removal), and seeking to curtail his powers—removing his ability to appoint or dismiss the deputy mayor and executive committee or to set the council agenda. Both moves face obstacles: reluctance to invite provincial intervention and procedural delays on stripping powers.

Some former allies, such as Councillor Denzil Minnan-Wong, say Ford has lost the authority to lead; others, like Councillor Adam Vaughan, favor internal measures over provincial involvement. Ford retains a devoted core of supporters—“Ford Nation”—and his brother Doug vowed to defend him. Meanwhile, councilors warn the scandal has disrupted decision-making on key priorities, notably the contentious transit plan, and created instability that they are trying to contain while the city approaches next year’s municipal election.

Professor Will Brooker, a film and cultural studies academic at Kingston University, is spending a year immersing himself in David Bowie’s life and personas to research the musician for a commissioned monograph, Forever Stardust. Adopting a “method” approach, Brooker lives through distinct phases of Bowie’s five-decade career—Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane, the Thin White Duke, the 1983 comeback era and others—by copying Bowie’s appearance, diet, music, reading, films and daily routines for months at a time.

His immersion ranges from sourcing period clothing and makeup (sometimes with help from makeup artists and a tailor) to replicating habits such as sleep deprivation, extreme diets (weekend red peppers and milk), and high caffeine intake to approximate Bowie’s stimulant use. Brooker studies writers and thinkers who influenced Bowie (e.g., William Burroughs, Aleister Crowley, Michael Moorcock, Nietzsche), watches films Bowie watched, visits places associated with him (Brixton, Bromley, Beckenham, and soon Berlin), and takes singing lessons to learn key songs. He describes the method as trying to “inhabit Bowie’s head space” while retaining critical distance.

Brooker says the project helps him understand Bowie’s creative life and its costs—commenting on the heavy drug use and instability of Bowie’s 1970s period—while acknowledging one cannot truly become Bowie. He hopes Bowie would find the study amusing; Bowie's camp had no comment. Brooker’s students haven’t seen him teach since the project began, and he promises not to lecture in full Ziggy regalia.

A 32-year-old woman, Cherie Amoore, was arrested and charged after allegedly abducting 7-week-old Ahsir Simmons from the King of Prussia Mall on the evening of March 31, 2016. The baby was taken from his stroller in the mall’s food court after Amoore — who had been talking with the mother, Malika Hunter, and following the family around the mall — allegedly picked him up while the mother was distracted and then walked out with him. Surveillance video showed Amoore leaving the mall with the infant.

Ahsir was found safe later that night in a home above a barber shop in Tredyffrin Township after family members and others identified Amoore from released surveillance images. Police say Amoore had shown the baby to relatives and friends at several locations; when officers knocked, she reportedly said, “I took the baby and I am sorry.” Amoore was arraigned on charges including kidnapping of a minor, unlawful restraint, false imprisonment and interference with custody, and held on $500,000 bail.

Investigators say Amoore told them she had given birth to a son on Feb. 11 who died hours after birth and that she “wanted” to hold a baby again; police are attempting to verify her claimed pregnancy through medical records. Amoore told detectives she did not intend to steal the child and described the episode as an “out of body” experience. Her family has asked for privacy; her mother, Renee Amoore, is a prominent Pennsylvania Republican official.

The infant’s mother expressed gratitude that her son was returned but said the episode left her traumatized and fearful about taking her children out in public. Mall officials and police emphasized their security response and cooperation with law enforcement in locating the child. Authorities and media also noted a delay in the nationwide Amber Alert reaching smartphones due to procedural steps required to activate and disseminate the alert.

Russia blocked U.S. diplomatic access to two properties in Moscow on and before Aug. 1, 2017: a weekend recreation compound (a dacha) on the outskirts of the city and a 2,000 sq. m. warehouse in southern Moscow. The moves were announced as retaliatory measures after the U.S. Congress codified new sanctions on Russia; Moscow also ordered the U.S. to cut about 755 diplomatic and locally hired staff in Russia by September. The U.S. embassy said it had been promised access until noon on Aug. 1 to remove belongings but had been denied entry for two days; a Reuters witness reported U.S. vehicles with diplomatic plates being refused at the dacha. Russian officials told state media that the Americans failed to obtain required permits for the properties (one is in a conservation area) and characterized complaints of blocked access as a “pre‑meditated provocation.” The actions follow reciprocal measures at the end of 2016, when the Obama administration expelled 35 Russian diplomats and closed two Russian recreational facilities in the U.S. Both sides described the situation as a serious diplomatic escalation.

A two-century-old shipwreck roughly 150 miles off Galveston, Texas, has been located about 3,000–4,300 feet below the Gulf surface and is now the subject of a high-tech, remotely guided salvage and research operation led by Texas A&M Galveston and NOAA. Discovered by a Shell survey crew in 2011, the copper-sheathed hull’s wooden structure has mostly disintegrated, but the copper plating preserves the vessel’s form. Remotely operated vehicles have returned a range of artifacts dated to about 1800–1830: muskets, pistols, swords, cannons (some believed British), anchors, navigational instruments, ceramic plates, glass bottles (one still sealed and containing yellow ginger), a leather-bound book, clothing and a galley stove with a protective lead plate.

The mix of Spanish, Mexican and British items has led researchers to hypothesize the ship may have been a warship or arms transport involved in early 19th-century conflicts in the region (possibly linked to Spain, Mexico or the Texas independence era), but its identity and origin remain unresolved. The wreck also supports abundant marine life—anemones, corals, crabs—and sits amid unique seafloor features such as brine rivers.

The expedition is notable for its shore-based command center at Texas A&M Galveston that, via satellite video and audio, lets dozens or hundreds of scientists participate remotely while guiding ROVs from the surface vessel Nautilus (operated with equipment and support from ocean explorers including Bob Ballard). Recovered items are being sent to A&M’s Cultural Resources Laboratory for study; investigators hope the artifacts and context will solve the ship’s mystery.

A fast-moving brush fire named the La Tuna Fire erupted in La Tuna Canyon north of Burbank, California on Friday, Sept. 1, rapidly forcing large-scale evacuations, shutting an interstate and becoming the largest wildfire by acreage in the city’s history.

Key facts
- Growth and scope: The blaze expanded from a 1-acre vegetation fire to more than 5,000 acres within a day and later was reported at about 5,895 acres. At its peak it was burning in multiple directions through the Verdugo Mountains and into canyon areas above Burbank.  
- Evacuations and damage: Mandatory evacuations affected roughly 300 homes in Burbank, 250 in Glendale and 180 in Los Angeles; police conducted door-to-door evacuations. Early reports noted at least one home destroyed; later counts indicated three homes destroyed and one damaged. A few minor injuries (dehydration, minor burns) were reported.  
- Firefighting response: More than 500 firefighters were initially deployed, growing to over 1,000 personnel statewide, with 206 engines and nine helicopters assigned. Crews from other missions (including some returning from Hurricane Harvey relief) were recalled. The state of emergency for Los Angeles County was declared by Governor Jerry Brown, and Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti declared a local emergency.  
- Conditions and challenges: Extreme heat (temperatures up to 106°F), gusty winds (reported up to 50 mph), unstable air and canyon topography produced erratic, rapid fire behavior and spot fires (embers crossing I-210). These factors hampered containment; the fire was roughly 10% contained at one point. Rain later brought moisture but also wind shifts that complicated suppression.  
- Public impact: Portions of Interstate 210 were closed, heavy smoke prompted health advisories to stay indoors, and mandatory evacuations were expected to remain in force into Sunday. Officials said containment plans were in place despite the fire’s size and volatility.

Officials emphasized the dynamic nature of the incident and the potential for rapid changes in behavior, while committing significant local and state resources to protect lives and property.

Sears’ largest shareholder and CEO Edward “Eddie” Lampert, through his hedge fund ESL Investments, has proposed buying key Sears assets to raise cash and shore up the struggling retailer. In a letter to Sears’ board dated April 20, ESL said it is interested in acquiring the Kenmore appliance brand, the Home Improvement business (SHIP), and Parts Direct — valuing SHIP and Parts Direct together at an enterprise value of $500 million — and said it would consider buying some Sears real estate (including assuming about $1.2 billion of debt) and entering into master leases so stores could continue operating.

ESL’s proposal is nonbinding but says it could close quickly (within about 90 days for Kenmore) and would finance the purchase with ESL equity plus third‑party debt. ESL also outlined an exchange offer and tender offer structure to address roughly $1.5 billion of Sears debt (including an exchange of 2nd‑lien debt for equity and a tender for unsecured debt), and said proceeds from divestitures would be used to reduce leverage and improve liquidity. ESL signaled willingness to accept an independent review process and a “go shop,” and said Lampert and another ESL principal would recuse themselves from related Sears deliberations.

The announcement lifted Sears shares. It comes amid years of declining sales, numerous store closures and prior brand sales (e.g., Craftsman), as Sears seeks ways to monetize brands like Kenmore and DieHard and unlock value from its real estate holdings. ESL framed the plan as a way to create runway for Sears’ transformation while maximizing the value of its assets.

Senate Democratic leaders have decided to delay debate on a major climate-change (cap-and-trade) bill until the spring of 2010, prioritizing health care, financial-regulatory reform and a jobs package first. The postponement reflects growing political and practical obstacles: concerns about harming the economy and jobs, voter backlash in coal- and industry-dependent states, and uncertainty among some senators and constituents about how cap-and-trade works.

Key figures are split on timing. Advocates like Sens. Barbara Boxer and John Kerry want to move quickly; Boxer said the Finance Committee may begin deliberations in January and hoped for action in 2010. Others representing coal states—Sens. Max Baucus, Jay Rockefeller and Jeff Bingaman—favor caution and more time to win local support. Blanche Lincoln and other centrists also urged attention to jobs and economic impacts. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid indicated action “sometime in the spring,” but said financial reform and a jobs bill will come first, making an earlier vote unlikely.

The delay complicates President Obama’s domestic priority to curb greenhouse gases and could weaken U.S. leverage in international talks (Copenhagen in December and follow-ups to Kyoto). The administration argues climate legislation would spur clean-energy investment and jobs; critics warn of higher energy costs and political vulnerability ahead of the 2010 midterms. Meanwhile, the EPA is moving toward declaring greenhouse gases a public-health danger, which could trigger regulations independently of new legislation.

French lawmakers voted overwhelmingly to approve a new intelligence law that greatly expands state surveillance powers, passing the National Assembly 438–86. Backed by both the ruling Socialists and the centre-right UMP, the bill now goes to the Senate in June. Drafted after the January 7–9 Paris attacks that killed 17 and amid ongoing jihadist threats, the government says the law modernizes a 1991 legal framework to address mobile and internet-era communications and improve counter‑terrorism capacity.

Key provisions authorize interception of mobile communications, geo‑location of private residences, bulk collection of metadata via internet providers, and installation of “black boxes” — algorithmic filters on servers to flag suspicious online behavior. The bill also creates a supervisory body, the National Commission for Control of Intelligence Techniques (CNCTR), with broader remit to oversee intelligence activity and handle complaints.

Civil liberties groups, internet advocates and some companies sharply criticize the measure as excessive, dubbing it the “French Patriot Act” or “French Big Brother.” They warn the law’s broadly defined purposes could be used beyond terrorism — for industrial, scientific espionage or monitoring social movements — and argue it risks mass surveillance and threats to privacy and the digital economy. Supporters reject claims of intent to carry out generalized monitoring, saying the focus is on targeted surveillance of identified threats. Public opinion polls show many French people favor tighter security measures, though opposition is stronger among younger people. The debate has largely sidelined civil liberties voices in parliament, though external protests and critiques remain vocal.

Apple recently reversed course and restored MassRoots — a cannabis-focused social app — to the iPhone App Store after previously removing it in November 2014. MassRoots founder Isaac Dietrich had proposed geo-restricting the app to jurisdictions where marijuana is legal; after a campaign and petition, Apple accepted geo-restrictions covering the 23 states (plus D.C.) where medical cannabis is legal, and the app is again available. MassRoots said it will add further compliance features and stressed its responsibility to promote safe, legal cannabis use.

The move highlights a broader conflict between Apple and the growing “weed tech” industry. Many marijuana-related apps, from social networks to dispensary directories, have been rejected or forced to alter features with little explanation. Companies say Apple’s enforcement is unpredictable and hampers businesses that operate legally in states where cannabis is permitted. Examples include Weed Firm (a banned game), Weedmaps (told to change how it labels dispensaries), and other startups that have had apps blocked or approved only after restrictive workarounds (e.g., pushing transactions to web pages).

The sector is expanding rapidly — a $2.7 billion market with substantial VC interest — and pot-tech firms are petitioning Apple to allow lawful cannabis apps in the App Store, arguing customers should have the choice to download them and that app approval should be consistent and fair. Apple has not publicly commented on the controversy.

Several celebrity babies made headlines over the weekend. Sienna Miller and her fiancé Tom Sturridge welcomed their first child, a daughter, in London. Miller, 30, who had kept the pregnancy private for months, revealed in an April British Vogue interview that everything was progressing well. The couple, who became public with their relationship over the past year and showed Miller’s engagement ring in February, celebrated with a babymoon in Portofino in May and attended social events in London before the birth.

Separately, Kourtney Kardashian and Scott Disick introduced their newborn daughter, Penelope Scotland Disick. Kourtney, 33, told E! News both mother and baby are resting comfortably after an all-natural delivery; Penelope weighed 7 lbs., 14 oz. Family members expressed joy—Kris Jenner noted the baby looks like big brother Mason. The couple had announced the pregnancy last November; Penelope is their second child after Mason.

Summary:

Apple
- Apple’s cash and investments surpassed $200 billion for the first time, with roughly 89% held overseas (about $202.8 billion total at the end of June). The offshore portion has risen from 72% two years earlier.
- Strong international iPhone sales—e.g., greater China revenue more than doubled year-over-year—are driving the cash buildup, which the company shelters in foreign affiliates to avoid immediate U.S. taxes.
- CEO Tim Cook has urged comprehensive U.S. tax reform to allow easier repatriation; until that happens Apple is limited in how it can use onshore cash. Investors and activists (e.g., Carl Icahn) have pressed the company to return more capital.
- Apple increased its capital-return program in April by $70 billion (including a $50 billion boost to buybacks and an 11% dividend increase). By the end of the June quarter it had returned $126 billion of a planned $200 billion program, including $90 billion in repurchases.
- To fund returns and obligations, Apple has issued nearly $50 billion of debt globally and used $10 billion in cash for U.S. taxes last year. Accounting assumptions suggest limited earnings impact if cash were repatriated; Apple estimated repatriating $69.7 billion would trigger about $23.3 billion in U.S. taxes.
- Apple’s lobbying on tax and related issues has increased, reaching historically high levels as it hires lobbyists focused on tax and international tax reform. Policymakers (including the White House and Congress) have considered one-time tax measures to encourage repatriation and overhaul the system that incentivizes offshore profit accumulation.

Gilead Sciences
- Gilead’s rise—driven by high-priced hepatitis C drugs (Sovaldi, Harvoni, Epclusa)—has brought scrutiny for tax strategies and pricing. Revenues tripled since 2012 to $32.6 billion, while the company reportedly shifted assets to Ireland and kept substantial profits abroad.
- An advocacy report says Gilead held $28.5 billion overseas in 2015 and would face about $9.7 billion in U.S. tax on repatriation; its effective tax rate fell to 16.4% in 2015 from 27.3% in 2013. Such transfer-pricing and offshore strategies are common among large pharma and tech firms.
- A Senate Finance Committee investigation found Gilead intentionally set high prices for Sovaldi (considering $50k–$115k scenarios) to maximize revenue and establish a pricing benchmark for future drugs. Executives weighed shareholder value against reputational risk and largely prioritized revenue.
- The report highlighted consequences of the pricing strategy: restricted access by insurers and Medicaid (leading to “warehousing” of patients), substantial public and governmental backlash, and questions about priorities (price/revenue vs. access and R&D).
- Key findings: pricing was driven by perceived “value” and revenue potential rather than development costs; executives planned to set a high price floor for future treatments; access restrictions followed due to cost; and the company defended its pricing citing clinical value and long-term system cost reductions.
- The Gilead case is presented as representative of broader issues around corporate tax avoidance and drug pricing, prompting ongoing congressional attention.

Overall themes
- Large U.S. corporations are accumulating trillions in foreign profits, motivated by the U.S. tax system that taxes repatriated income at a high rate, which encourages profit shifting and offshore holdings.
- Policymakers and activists are debating one-time repatriation taxes and comprehensive tax reform to address offshore hoards and perceived tax avoidance, while companies push lobbying and seek ways to return capital to shareholders without onerous tax costs.
- In pharmaceuticals, aggressive pricing strategies combined with tax optimization have heightened scrutiny over corporate behavior, access to medicines, and whether corporate priorities favor shareholder returns over patients.

Sherri Papini, a 34-year-old mother from Mountain Gate near Redding, who disappeared on Nov. 2 after going for a jog, was found alive early Thanksgiving morning on the side of Interstate 5 in Yolo County. Papini was discovered around 4:30 a.m. after she flagged down a passing motorist; she was reportedly bound with restraints and “heavily battered.” She was treated at a Sacramento-area hospital for unspecified injuries and released. Shasta County Sheriff Tom Bosenko said investigators are looking for two Hispanic women armed with a handgun who were driving a dark-colored SUV, based on Papini’s description.

Papini’s sister, Sheila Koester, said the family is “elated and relieved” and thanked investigators, search teams, media and the motorist who helped. Koester declined to give details about Papini’s physical or emotional condition, whether she has seen her two young children, or what happened during the roughly three weeks she was missing, saying Sherri needs time to recover with family. Bosenko said Papini was emotional when reunited with her husband and that investigators have interviewed her and hope for more information as follow-up work continues.

Authorities conducted extensive investigative work while Papini was missing — including nearly 20 search warrants, interviews with friends, acquaintances and past relationships, and out-of-state follow-ups — and had received more than 400 tips. Officials have not disclosed a motive or further corroborating details, and the investigation remains active. Family members and some online commenters expressed gratitude to those who reported sightings or called authorities.

On March 22–23, 2016, coordinated suicide bombings at Brussels’ Zaventem airport and the Maelbeek metro station killed at least 34 people (including three suicide bombers) and wounded over 270. Islamic State claimed responsibility. Belgian authorities launched a large manhunt and raised the national terror alert to its highest level, conducting raids in Brussels and seeking at least one suspect seen on airport CCTV who fled after abandoning a large bomb-laden bag that later detonated harmlessly during a controlled disposal.

Investigators identified two attackers as brothers Ibrahim (29) and Khalid El Bakraoui (27): Ibrahim was identified by fingerprint as an airport suicide bomber and Khalid blew himself up at Maelbeek. A suicide note and partial will by Ibrahim were found on a laptop in a trash can near an apartment linked to the attackers; a taxi driver who had transported the suspects led police to that apartment in Schaerbeek. At that site police discovered about 15 kilograms of TATP and other bomb-making materials, nails and an IS flag; one detained person remained in custody.

Belgian and international officials continued investigations and intelligence cooperation. Turkish officials said Ibrahim El Bakraoui had been detained at Turkey’s Syrian border in June and deported to the Netherlands in July, and that Turkey had warned Belgium and the Netherlands he was a foreign fighter. European leaders called for better intelligence sharing and increased security funding; France, Germany, Poland and other countries tightened security and held moments of silence. The U.S. House condemned the attacks and Secretary of State John Kerry planned to visit Brussels. Sporting events and flights were disrupted, and Belgium observed national mourning.

Ridley Scott’s Alien: Covenant revitalizes the Alien prequel series, delivering the most satisfying installment since the first two films. Directed with visual flair and tight pacing, the 122-minute R-rated sci-fi horror mixes philosophical ideas from Prometheus with the visceral terror fans expect: face-huggers, chest-bursters and other Giger-inspired creatures.

Plot/characters
- The colony ship Covenant is transporting 2,000 passengers and 1,140 embryos to Origae-6. After damage in a space storm and the death of the captain (James Franco, brief), second-in-command Christopher (Billy Crudup) — an uncertain, faith-oriented man — assumes command and opts to divert to a nearer habitable planet.
- Daniels (Katherine Waterston) is the emotionally affected terraforming officer and one of the film’s central survivors. Other crew include pilot Tennessee (Danny McBride) and flier Farris (Amy Seimetz).
- The crew finds a seemingly inviting world that quickly proves deadly when alien contagions begin infecting humans.
- A major highlight is Michael Fassbender’s dual performance as David (his Prometheus android) and the updated synthetic Walter. Their interplay raises questions about creation and playing God and culminates in a dark, diabolical twist.

Strengths
- Scott, with writers John Logan and Dante Harper, restores narrative momentum lost in Prometheus, balancing intelligent speculation, genre thrills, philosophical beats and grisly set pieces.
- The film is lean, tense, and visually striking, aided by Dariusz Wolski’s cinematography, Jed Kurzel’s score, strong effects, and solid supporting performances (notably Fassbender and Waterston).
- It ties into Prometheus while setting up further prequels — Scott has indicated at least two more films before reaching the original 1979 timeline.

Weaknesses
- The faith-versus-science element implied by Crudup’s character is introduced but underexplored, and his portrayal as a weak leader may alienate some viewers.

Bottom line
Alien: Covenant successfully reinvigorates the franchise by combining philosophical ambition and satisfying horror, and it leaves audiences eager for the next chapter.

President Obama cut short his campaign swing to visit St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana, on Monday to survey damage from Hurricane Isaac, reassure residents of federal recovery aid and praise first responders for preventing loss of life. Touring the hard-hit Ridgewood neighborhood in LaPlace, he saw widespread debris, uprooted trees, ruined household goods and standing floodwater, and spoke with residents who were evacuated or rescued by boat when waters rose rapidly in an area that had not flooded in 17 years.

Briefers told Obama the most urgent needs are returning roughly 3,900 evacuees, providing temporary housing and transportation, and reopening public facilities such as schools and fire stations. He pledged a swift federal response to determine why a local levee failed and to help prevent future failures, and lauded FEMA and the National Guard for their coordination.

The visit followed a similar trip by Republican nominee Mitt Romney and was accompanied by a bipartisan group of state and federal officials, including Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal. The White House emphasized the visit was not a photo opportunity and framed it as bipartisan crisis management; aides also contrasted the response posture with criticisms of the federal handling of Hurricane Katrina. At the time about 125,000 people in Louisiana remained without power and roughly 2,600 were in shelters; Isaac caused limited deaths compared with Katrina but still produced widespread flooding and disruption, including temporary refinery shutdowns that were largely being restored.

U.S. Olympic swimmer Ryan Lochte apologized for his role in a widely publicized incident in Rio de Janeiro, saying he was not “more careful and candid” in describing events from early Sunday morning and that he regretted diverting attention from other athletes. Lochte reiterated that the situation was “traumatic” — describing armed men and a language barrier — but accepted responsibility, said the episode could and should have been avoided, and asked the focus return to the Games.

Lochte and teammates Gunnar Bentz, Jack Conger and Jimmy Feigen had initially said they were robbed at gunpoint after stopping at a gas station. Rio police disputed that account, saying the swimmers vandalized a bathroom after leaving a party, were confronted by security, and then paid to leave; officials recommended false-reporting charges against Lochte and Feigen and opened an investigation. Bentz and Conger have returned to the U.S.; Feigen remained in Brazil while resolving a payment requirement tied to the case. The U.S. Olympic Committee and USA Swimming criticized the swimmers’ conduct and said they would review possible consequences. The IOC opened a disciplinary inquiry. The matter remains under investigation.

The Emoji Movie (directed by Tony Leondis) is an 86‑minute Sony Pictures Animation film set inside a teenager’s smartphone in a city called Textopolis, where each emoji is expected to display a single, fixed expression. The protagonist, Gene (voiced by T.J. Miller), is a “Meh” emoji who’s born able to show many emotions. After failing on his first day, he becomes targeted for deletion by the relentlessly cheerful supervisor Smiler (Maya Rudolph). Gene teams up with the overenthusiastic Hi‑5 (James Corden) and a hacker named Jailbreak (Anna Faris) to escape the phone, reach the cloud, and be “fixed.”

Critics panned the film for weak writing, clumsy plotting, shallow character motivations and heavy-handed product placement — it serves as a parade of branded app set pieces (Candy Crush, Spotify, Instagram, Dropbox, etc.) that critics saw as cynical advertising rather than imaginative worldbuilding. Reviewers also faulted the movie’s visual design for making the emojis generic rubber‑faced CGI, its humor and dialogue for feeling dated and manufactured, and its moral (“be yourself”) for being trite and undermined by the film’s commercialism. Performances from a large voice cast (including Anna Faris, James Corden, Patrick Stewart, Maya Rudolph, Steven Wright, Jennifer Coolidge and others) did little to rescue the film.

Some reviewers noted brief positives — bright visuals that may hold young children’s attention and an unrelated short film (Puppy! from Hotel Transylvania) shown with it — but overall the consensus frames The Emoji Movie as a cynical, uninspired, and largely unsatisfying children’s feature that sacrifices creativity to branded tie‑ins.

This piece criticizes Muslim groups and leaders for responding to the film American Sniper by claiming it spurred threats and anti‑Muslim hate. The author argues this reaction is part of a recurring "victim" strategy—what he calls “victim jihad”—that distracts from confronting jihadist doctrine inside Muslim communities. He contrasts this with expectations from the Bush Doctrine that moderates would oppose radicals, saying that unity against extremism never materialized. The author defends American Sniper as a respectful portrayal of a decent patriot and mocks calls for the film’s director and star to denounce alleged hateful speech. He accuses Muslim organizations of seeking censorship and submission to protect their image, and contends that mainstream media and elites sanitize or ignore jihad and Islamist extremism. Quoted commentary claims that once Muslim populations reach a “critical mass” in non‑Muslim countries they try to dominate, and that free speech is anathema in the Muslim world. The article references a Reuters item reporting that an Arab‑American civil rights group asked Clint Eastwood and Bradley Cooper to denounce hateful language directed at U.S. Arabs and Muslims after the film’s release.

North Korea’s UN ambassador in Geneva, So Se Pyong, used a February 27 Conference on Disarmament session to blame the United States for creating an “unpredictable” situation on the divided Korean Peninsula and for abusing the U.N. Security Council to enforce a hostile policy against Pyongyang. His remarks followed North Korea’s recent provocative steps: a December long‑range rocket launch and its biggest nuclear test to date on February 12, actions that prompted tighter U.N. sanctions and international condemnation.

So framed the nuclear test as a defensive response to U.S. hostility and defended North Korea’s right to peaceful satellite launches, while warning South Korea to avoid stirring “Pandora’s box.” South Korea’s delegate urged Pyongyang to abandon its nuclear program and pursue peace, and Ireland’s foreign minister called on North Korea to stop nuclear and missile activities and return to stalled six‑party denuclearization talks.

Separately, North Korean state media and a commentator on the Uriminzokkiri website claimed the DPRK is now a “fully‑independent rocket and nuclear weapons state” and warned the U.S. mainland is “well within” the range of its strategic rockets — a claim viewed skeptically by many experts despite the December launch (which South Korea estimated could reach about 10,000 km) and growing concerns that Pyongyang is advancing toward a miniaturized warhead capable of long‑range delivery. State media also condemned upcoming U.S.–South Korean military drills and warned the peninsula was “an inch away from explosion.”

The Wall Street Journal fired longtime chief foreign affairs correspondent Jay Solomon after an Associated Press investigation found emails and texts showing he discussed prospective business deals with Farhad Azima, an Iranian‑born aviation magnate and long‑time source allegedly involved in arms and covert aviation activities. Washington Bureau Chief Paul Beckett informed staff at a sudden meeting; the Journal said Solomon “forfeited” its trust, violated ethics and standards, and was not forthcoming about his actions.

The AP report — based on tens of thousands of messages it obtained (which Azima’s lawyers say were stolen by hackers) — describes Solomon discussing a potential 10% stake in a company, business opportunities with Azima, and being asked to “ferry” a $725 million UAE proposal involving surveillance planes to government representatives. Azima emailed, “We all wish best of luck to Jay on his first defense sale.” Solomon told the AP he “clearly made mistakes,” denied ever entering into business with Azima or intending to, apologized to colleagues, and conceded his emails could look troubling.

Solomon, a veteran national security reporter and author of a 2016 book on Iran, had been well regarded internally but had faced prior criticism over perceived bias on the Iran nuclear deal. Staff reacted with shock and concern about potential fallout, including reviews of his past reporting. The Journal’s internal investigation continues while the AP’s reporting provided the basis for his dismissal.

Ken Taylor, Canada’s ambassador to Iran during the 1979 hostage crisis, and his colleagues at the Canadian Embassy in Tehran played the central, high-risk role in sheltering six American diplomats who escaped the storming of the U.S. Embassy and in arranging their clandestine departure from Iran. Over several tense months Taylor and other Canadian staff hid, moved and supported the six fugitives amid the pervasive danger of discovery, collected intelligence for Washington, and coordinated escape plans with Ottawa and the U.S. State Department.

Taylor recounts that other escape options—overland to Turkey or by tanker through the Persian Gulf—were too dangerous. Ultimately Canada supplied authentic documentation and devised exiting strategies so the six could travel as Canadians; the CIA provided forged exit visas and sent agent Tony Mendez for a brief on-the-ground role. A potentially disastrous passport error (the wrong Iranian calendar) was spotted and fixed by a Persian-speaking Canadian official, avoiding detection that could have aborted the operation. On the appointed pre-dawn day in late January 1980, Taylor organized transport to the airport, ensured the flight departed before he and remaining Canadian staff left Iran, and the six boarded safely for Zurich.

Taylor has been critical of the Ben Affleck film Argo, which dramatizes Mendez’s book and emphasizes the CIA and an American agent as principal heroes while minimizing the extended Canadian contribution—Taylor calls the CIA a “junior partner.” He accepts that Argo is entertaining Hollywood, but stresses the historical record: Canada furnished most of the logistics, documents and months of shelter and risk (including notable contributions by John and Zena Sheardown), whereas Mendez’s actual time in Tehran was brief. Affleck later added a postscript acknowledging Canada’s role, but Taylor and some Canadians feel the film still shortchanges them.

Taylor’s actions in Tehran made him a public figure; he later served as Canada’s consul-general in New York and had a career in the private sector. The episode stands as a notable example of international cooperation and the vital impact of diplomacy under danger.

On the morning of March 30, 2015, two men in a dark, unmarked SUV attempted to enter the restricted National Security Agency (NSA) campus at Fort Meade, Maryland, shortly before 9 a.m. Authorities say the vehicle failed to obey routine NSA police instructions to exit, barriers were deployed, and the SUV accelerated toward an NSA police vehicle blocking the road. NSA officers opened fire; the SUV then crashed into the police vehicle. One occupant of the SUV was killed at the scene, the other was critically injured and taken to a hospital; an NSA police officer was also injured and hospitalized. The FBI is leading the investigation, which federal officials said does not appear to be terrorism-related.

Later reporting indicated the SUV had been stolen from a Jessup motel earlier that morning after an overnight stay involving three men (two dressed as women). Investigators believe the vehicle’s presence at the NSA gate may have been a wrong turn following the theft and that the suspects might not have stopped because of drugs in the car. The FBI’s evidence response team processed the scene, interviewed witnesses, and coordinated with U.S. prosecutors to determine possible charges. Fort Meade authorities said the incident was contained, residents and employees were safe, and security measures at access points remained in force.

Context: The shooting drew wide media attention and follow-up by investigators; it came amid other recent security incidents in the region, including earlier gunfire at an NSA building this month by a suspected shooter who claimed he heard voices. The White House and Defense Secretary were briefed. Identities of those involved have not been released.

This document reports on the environmental and human costs of China’s dominant rare-earth industry, focusing on Baotou in Inner Mongolia—the country’s largest processing hub. Ore from nearby Bayan Obo is concentrated and refined in Baotou using acid baths and hydrometallurgical processes that generate vast quantities of toxic, sometimes radioactive, waste. A 10 km² tailings pond of black, sludge-like effluent coats the shore with a walkable crust; tests found elevated radiation and the wastes contain thorium and other hazardous chemicals. Locals say crops failed, livestock died, and soil and groundwater are saturated with contaminants. Villages near the refineries have largely depopulated (one example fell from 2,000 to 300 residents in a decade), and remaining residents report widespread illness (diabetes, respiratory problems, bone disease) and difficulty obtaining adequate compensation or relocation. Attempts by villagers to profit from selling waste for reprocessing were recently curtailed by authorities, with at least one person on trial.

The piece also describes the industrial landscape of Baotou—an expanded, polluted city driven by the rare-earth boom, with plants, pipes, coal-fired power, and housing built alongside heavy industry. Visitors found some processing plants unusually quiet or guarded, and guides evasive about production details. The article emphasizes that many “rare earths” (e.g., cerium, neodymium) are actually relatively abundant; China’s global dominance (roughly 90–97% of production in the period cited) stems largely from its willingness to carry out the hazardous refining processes that produce toxic byproducts other countries avoid.

Finally, the report connects these local harms to global consumption: rare earths are essential in consumer electronics, electric cars, wind turbines and other technologies (neodymium for strong magnets, cerium for polishing screens, europium/yttrium/terbium for displays and lasers, etc.), so the environmental damage in Baotou underpins products sold worldwide. The article calls attention to the hidden environmental price of modern tech and the need for more sustainable supply chains, recycling, and substitutes.

Karlie Hay, an 18-year-old from Tomball, Texas, was crowned Miss Teen USA at the pageant in Las Vegas. Background: Many people with chronic, life-limiting illness experience repeated hospital admissions near the end of life, yet hospitals are typically geared to aggressive, life‑prolonging treatment rather than comfort-focused care. Clinicians find it hard to judge when to continue active management or to shift to palliative pathways, and existing prognostic tools are often subjective, require specialist judgement or depend on data not routinely available in emergency settings. This contributes to unnecessary, costly, and sometimes distressing interventions that often do not improve quality of life and may undermine bereavement outcomes.

Purpose and rationale: Researchers at the University of New South Wales developed CriSTAL (Criteria for Screening and Triaging to Appropriate aLternative care) to help identify hospitalized elderly patients (65+) at high risk of dying within days to months. The tool aims to prompt timely, honest conversations with patients and families about prognosis, limits of treatment and alternative end‑of‑life care (for example home or hospice), not to mandate withholding care. It also seeks to reduce futile interventions, change hospital culture toward earlier end‑of‑life planning, and better allocate resources.

Methods: The team performed a narrative review of 112 articles and 18 validated prognostic instruments to identify objective predictors of short- and medium‑term mortality that are routinely available at point of care. They prioritized items that are easily retrievable from records, do not require specialist judgement or value judgements, and independently predict death. Clinicians (doctors and ICU nurses) were consulted on feasibility.

Tool composition: CriSTAL initially consists of 29 items drawn from evidence-based predictors, including:
- Acute deterioration indicators on presentation or after a rapid response call (e.g., low systolic BP <90 mmHg, extreme heart or respiratory rates, decreased consciousness, low oxygen saturation, abnormal MEW/SEWS scores)
- Demographics and history (age ≥65, emergency admission, recent hospitalizations, prior ICU admissions)
- Advanced comorbidities (advanced cancer, chronic kidney disease, chronic heart failure, COPD, recent stroke or MI, moderate/severe liver disease)
- Frailty markers (unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow gait, inability for activity), nursing home residence
- Evidence of cognitive impairment
- Simple test findings (e.g., proteinuria, ECG abnormalities)

A slightly modified checklist is proposed for use after a Rapid Response Team attendance to reassess ongoing need for hospitalization or escalation.

Validation and planned testing: Recognizing limitations (length, potential overfitting, reliance on a narrative review), the authors plan retrospective validation using RRT-attended deaths as cases with matched controls, followed by prospective testing in ED admissions and after RRT calls. They will refine items based on predictive performance (aiming for AUROC >80%) and limit the error such that predicted-to-die patients have at most a 5% chance of surviving to discharge. The tool’s scores are intended to inform shared decision‑making, not to replace clinical judgement.

Implications and cautions: If validated and shortened, CriSTAL could support earlier, more appropriate triage to palliative or alternative care, reduce futile intensive interventions, and improve patient and family experience. Proper training in communication about prognosis is essential to ensure sensitive use. The authors emphasize ethical safeguards: the tool should not be used to ration care solely for cost reasons and predictive accuracy may vary by setting and population, so local validation is recommended.

Dissemination and trials: CriSTAL is being trialled in selected Sydney emergency departments. The research has been published in a supportive and palliative care journal and has drawn interest from clinicians and patient‑advocacy groups, who welcome improved identification provided discussions are handled compassionately and adequate alternative care services exist.

Wisconsin voters face a high-stakes recall election Tuesday to decide whether to remove Republican Gov. Scott Walker and replace him with Democratic Milwaukee Mayor Tom Barrett. The contest has drawn intense national attention and roughly $63.5 million in spending. Walker is a slight favorite; Democrats privately say a Barrett win would be an upset.

Key stakes and players:
- Scott Walker: A loss would be a major setback for a once-rising conservative star, difficult to recover from; a win would elevate him as a national conservative hero and fuel speculation about future presidential runs.
- Organized labor: Unions, energized by opposition to Walker’s 2011 law stripping many public-sector collective-bargaining rights, have been central to the recall effort. Another failure after recent setbacks would raise serious questions about their political clout.
- President Obama and national Democrats: The DNC and White House have provided money and organizational help, but Obama declined to campaign in person. If Walker prevails, Democrats will face criticism for not doing more and worry Wisconsin could be more competitive in the presidential race.
- Tom Barrett: A defeat would likely end Barrett’s statewide ambitions after multiple gubernatorial losses; a win would vindicate Democrats’ efforts.
- Bill Clinton: His late-campaigning for Barrett is low-risk—success would be credited to him, failure unlikely to be blamed.

Broader implications:
- The recall’s outcome could reshape the fall presidential map. Wisconsin was crucial to Obama’s 2008 win and is viewed as essential to his re-election prospects. Republicans, buoyed by a Walker victory, plan to press Wisconsin as a targeted state for Mitt Romney, potentially expanding GOP opportunities.
- The recall has intensified polarization in Wisconsin, sapping resources and possibly affecting independent voters who were pivotal to Obama’s earlier win.
- The campaign atmosphere is bitter and highly mobilized, illustrated by scenes like both candidates crossing paths while campaigning at a local dairy breakfast.

Overall, Tuesday’s vote is a consequential, closely watched referendum with major implications for state politics, labor’s influence, national Democratic strategy, and the 2012 presidential race.

A widely shared video from Yueyang, China, shows a 2-year-old girl named Tutu walking ahead of her mother and being struck and crushed by a car after entering the driver’s blind spot; she died. The Shandong prosecutor’s office and social media users condemned the mother’s phone use, urging people to “put down your phone” and warning of the parenting dangers of smartphone obsession.

Chinese news reports and officials say the case is part of a pattern of “distracted walking” tragedies: similar recent incidents include two other toddlers killed while parents were absorbed by phones (in Henan and Anhui provinces). Experts and advocates say distracted walking is under-recognized compared with distracted driving, even as cities like Shanghai have taken measures against phone use while driving and elsewhere (Hong Kong, Seoul) post warning signs about phone use on escalators or streets.

Researchers note pedestrian-crash data are limited, making causation harder to prove, but scholars of digital behavior urge creating phone-free norms and “sacred spaces” (no phones at meals, in cars, classrooms) to reduce risks. Polling shows heavy smartphone use in China, and child-safety groups warn that parental distraction by devices contributes to serious child injuries and near-misses. Public reaction on Weibo has been highly critical, calling for greater awareness and parental responsibility.

Nearly nine years after her abduction, Elizabeth Smart confronted her kidnapper, Brian David Mitchell, in a packed Salt Lake City courtroom just before he received two life sentences. Mitchell, a homeless street preacher convicted in federal court of kidnapping and transporting a minor for sexual purposes, spent much of the proceedings silently singing hymns and rocking in his chair; when asked if he had anything to say he continued singing.

Speaking directly to Mitchell for the first time since her rescue, Smart — who was 14 when Mitchell seized her at knifepoint on June 5, 2002, and endured what she called “nine months of hell” — delivered a calm, brief statement. She told him she knows what he did, that he knew it was wrong, and that although he took nine months of her life they cannot affect the wonderful life she has now. Her father, Ed Smart, also addressed Mitchell, calling on him to face his guilt.

At trial Smart testified to repeated rape, sexual assault, forced drug and alcohol use, being tethered to a tree, threats to kill her and her family, and being forced into a polygamous “marriage.” She described narrowly missed opportunities for rescue and recounted years of legal delays due to disputes over Mitchell’s competency. Mitchell’s defense argued insanity; a jury rejected that defense in December and convicted him. A federal judge, calling the crimes “unusually heinous and degrading,” imposed life sentences without parole.

Mitchell’s estranged wife and accomplice, Wanda Barzee, pleaded guilty and received a 15-year sentence in 2010. Smart, now in her early 20s and recently returned from a Mormon mission, said outside court that the sentencing marks the end of a long chapter and the start of a new one; she plans to work as a child advocate and help other victims.

Dave Asprey, creator of Bulletproof Coffee, has launched FATwater — a bottled “near-water” beverage that contains about 2 grams of medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil (from coconut) in tiny emulsified droplets, plus flavoring and a sweetener. Asprey markets it as a more hydrating alternative to plain water and sugary coconut/energy drinks, claiming the fat droplets help water enter cells more effectively, provide a small energy bump, increase thermogenesis and suppress appetite. He’s selling it locally now with plans to expand.

Nutrition experts and scientists are skeptical. MCTs are metabolized differently from long‑chain fats and can increase thermogenesis in studies, but those effects have been observed at much higher doses (typically 18–60 g/day), so 2 g is unlikely to affect fat burning. There is no research showing that adding tiny fat droplets improves hydration. Taste tests of lemon and berry flavors were mixed to negative, with some testers noting odd mouthfeel. Critics including a water sommelier call it a “near water product,” and dietitians question the need for it.

Bottom line: FATwater is a novel, marketed product that uses MCT oil as a selling point, but current evidence doesn’t support its key hydration or metabolic claims — and experts say if you’re thirsty, plain water will do.
