Researchers report successful binary communication with four advanced ALS patients, two permanently in complete locked-in state (CLIS) and two transitioning into CLIS, using a functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS)–based brain–computer interface (BCI) and an implicit, attention-light task. Background: CLIS patients are fully paralysed but cognitively intact; conventional neuroelectric BCIs (EEG/ECoG/P300/SCP) have repeatedly failed to establish reliable communication in CLIS, possibly because those methods require explicit, effortful control and residual somatic/motor mediation that CLIS patients lack. Approach: The team used a bedside, portable fNIRS system to record frontocentral cortical oxygenation (oxyhemoglobin, O2Hb) while patients listened to auditorily presented personal “known-answer” question pairs and open yes/no questions. Patients were instructed to mentally answer “yes” or “no” during 15 s response intervals. Training sessions (questions with known answers) allowed mutual adaptation of patient strategy and an SVM classifier; after reaching above-chance performance, sessions with online feedback and then open questions were performed. EEG and EOG were recorded concurrently for comparison. Results: Across many sessions over weeks (three patients completed >46 sessions; one completed 20), online fNIRS classification (linear SVM on O2Hb features) discriminated “yes” versus “no” with daywise accuracies typically above chance and often exceeding 70–75% (feedback/open-question correct response rates: F 78.6%, G 78.8%, B 75.8%; W trained but had more variable results). fNIRS oxygenation increased for “yes” and decreased for “no” in most patients; semantic concordance between paired true/false questions was well above chance (≈67–70%). EEG oscillations (0–30 Hz) and EOG did not reliably discriminate answers at group level, although occasional EOG or EEG differences occurred; overall fNIRS classification outperformed EEG and EOG (statistically significant in most comparisons). Analyses linked lower-frequency EEG power (delta/low-theta) — markers of reduced vigilance — to poorer fNIRS BCI performance in three patients, suggesting that drowsiness/low arousal impairs communication; one long-term CLIS patient showed a different pattern, possibly reflecting altered baseline rhythms. Implications and limitations: This is the first systematic demonstration that fNIRS-based BCI with an implicit, overlearned yes/no paradigm can enable above-chance binary communication in multiple CLIS ALS patients, potentially offering a route to restore at least minimal communication. Findings support the hypothesis that hemodynamic signals and implicit processing tasks can succeed where neuroelectric, attention-demanding BCIs failed. Major caveats include small sample size (four patients), variable individual results (one patient less robust), incomplete understanding of the cognitive/physiological basis of the fNIRS yes/no differences, and sensitivity to vigilance/sleep–wake fluctuations. The authors propose hybrid EEG–fNIRS systems to monitor and mitigate low-vigilance periods and call for replication and further investigation into the underlying mechanisms and scalability. Data and materials: All data are publicly archived; the study was ethically approved and funded by multiple agencies. Overall conclusion: fNIRS-based binary BCI communication delivered sustained above-chance yes/no answers in four CLIS ALS patients, representing an important proof-of-concept step toward restoring basic communication for patients otherwise unable to express thoughts or preferences.

Emma Kelty, a 43-year-old British adventurer from Finchley, London, has been reported missing and is believed to have been murdered while kayaking the Amazon. Kelty, who resigned as a primary school head in 2014 to travel and was known for solo exploits (including skiing alone to the South Pole and hiking across the US), began paddling the Amazon in February from its Peruvian source toward the Atlantic.

In late August and early September she posted online about repeated unsettling encounters after entering Brazil’s Amazonas state — men with machetes, silent boats lingering near her camp at night, and armed strangers that disrupted her sleep. On 10 September she joked about warnings for the Coari area; two days later she reported encountering dozens of men in motorboats, some with arrows and rifles. Nearing Coari on the Solimões river, she sent a distress signal and has been missing since.

Brazilian police arrested three men — two 17-year-olds and an adult named Erinei Ferreira da Silva — on suspicion of her murder; they are seeking four more suspects. According to one arrested teenager, Kelty camped on Boieiro island near Lauro Sodré, where she was approached by two people, then five others who stole her belongings, shot her twice with a sawn-off shotgun and dumped her body in the river. The suspects allegedly tried to sell her phones, tablet and GoPro in local communities. Authorities launched a search with divers, the navy and fire officers, and residents reported seeing her canoe earlier.

The area is known for river piracy and drug-trafficking violence; officials and local sources linked such criminal activity and violent disputes among gangs to attacks in the region, including previous high-profile disappearances. The UK Foreign Office is assisting Kelty’s family, who described her as an “active and determined” explorer. Police continue investigations and searches for further suspects and for Kelty’s body.

President Trump hailed a federal-court ruling allowing his administration to proceed with construction of parts of the U.S.–Mexico border wall, calling it a “big legal win.” U.S. District Judge Gonzalo Curiel denied lawsuits from California and environmental groups that sought to block the administration’s waiver of environmental reviews for barrier construction in southern California. Curiel’s 101‑page opinion said courts should not substitute themselves for political branches on such matters and found plaintiffs had not shown Homeland Security exceeded its statutory authority under a 1996 law that permits expedited construction and waivers in certain border areas.

The lawsuits alleged violations of the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act and the Coastal Zone Management Act and warned construction could harm the Tijuana Estuary and threatened species. Curiel acknowledged procedural shortcomings in stakeholder consultation but concluded they did not meet the high threshold to enjoin work. California Attorney General Xavier Becerra said the state would evaluate options and that it opposed the wall; the Center for Biological Diversity said it would appeal.

Trump’s praise of the ruling did not mention his long‑running, personal criticism of Judge Curiel during the 2016 campaign—when Trump attacked Curiel as “Mexican” and questioned his impartiality despite the judge being U.S.-born—a remark that drew bipartisan condemnation at the time. The decision clears the way for projects including a recent contract to replace a Calexico barrier with 30‑foot bollards and comes amid Trump’s broader request to Congress for roughly $23 billion for border security.

Baltimore police finished the first phase of their probe into Freddie Gray’s death a day early and turned their investigative file over to City State’s Attorney Marilyn Mosby, who is reviewing the evidence and has urged the public to remain patient and peaceful while deciding whether to bring charges. Gray, 25, suffered catastrophic spinal injuries and died April 19, a week after being arrested April 12 in West Baltimore. Police and bystander videos show officers putting Gray into the rear of a transport van; police have said he was not buckled in and that officers failed to provide timely medical care.

Investigators said new findings include one serious head wound consistent with striking a protruding bolt in the van and a previously undisclosed additional stop the van made after picking up Gray; that stop was captured on private surveillance video. The department said it has “exhausted every lead” in this phase but is keeping the investigation active and declined to release all findings. Six officers involved have been suspended with pay; five had given statements the day Gray was injured.

Mosby reiterated her office is conducting an independent review and will not rely solely on the police file. Maryland’s chief medical examiner has not yet finalized the autopsy report, which will go to Mosby’s office. The case has sparked intense unrest in Baltimore and nationwide protests; most demonstrations were peaceful though some arrests occurred. City leaders, Gray’s family and their attorneys stressed the need for a thorough, not rushed, investigation. The Justice Department is also conducting an independent probe.

A Rosenberg man, Jason Griffin, 39, has been charged with manslaughter, felon in possession of a weapon and unlawful possession of body armor after a man was shot and killed at a party in the Heights, Houston police said.

The FBI has issued a confidential “flash” alert warning state election officials that foreign hackers breached two state election systems this summer, prompting a nationwide advisory to strengthen election cybersecurity. The bulletin, from the FBI’s Cyber Division and first reported by Yahoo News, said investigators found cyberintrusions against two state voter registration systems; one resulted in exfiltration of voter data. Sources identified the affected states as Illinois—where the voter registration system was shut down for about 10 days after attackers downloaded personal data on as many as 200,000 voters—and Arizona, where malware was found but no confirmed data theft.

The FBI listed eight IP addresses tied to the attacks, noted one address was used in both incidents, and asked states to check their logs for similar activity (while advising not to probe the listed IPs directly). Officials said the perpetrators are believed to be foreign hackers; investigators are exploring possible links to other politically motivated intrusions (including the DNC hack), though no attribution has been confirmed. Cybersecurity experts who reviewed the alert said the methods and at least one IP have ties to known Russian-linked activity, but they also noted data theft could be the work of ordinary cybercriminals seeking fraud gains.

The alert came days after Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson convened state election officials to offer DHS support—such as vulnerability scanning—while stressing that DHS had no specific, credible threats targeting the election. The FBI declined to discuss details beyond noting it routinely shares advisories to help system administrators defend against persistent cyber criminals.

The Paradise Papers leak—about 13 million documents from offshore law firm Appleby and other registries—exposes widespread tax avoidance by billionaires, corporations and public figures, and has provoked strong political reaction.

Key themes and revelations
- Bernie Sanders: The US senator called the papers evidence of a “rapid movement toward international oligarchy,” arguing a tiny number of billionaires and multinational firms hide wealth in tax havens to avoid paying their fair share. He blamed both Congress and the Trump administration for enabling tax breaks that benefit the wealthy and criticized proposed Republican tax reforms as favoring billionaires over the middle class.
- Wilbur Ross: Documents show Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross retained investments linked to Russian interests (including ties to the Sibur gas group, part-owned by Kirill Shamalov, Putin’s son-in-law) after joining the administration, prompting Democratic calls for explanation, hearings and possible investigation.
- Corporate mechanisms: The papers detail how major multinationals use complex structures to shift profits and reduce taxes:
  - Nike: Sales revenue is routed through a Belgian logistics hub and Dutch entities, then to Bermuda and later to a “stateless” Dutch CV structure, enabling a dramatic fall in its effective global tax rate and accumulation of offshore profits (over $12bn). The OECD and EU measures aim to phase out such “reverse hybrid” arrangements by 2021.
  - Apple: After the “double Irish” loophole was restricted, Apple reportedly sought a new tax residency and moved key Irish-managed entities to Jersey, where a 0% corporate tax for foreign companies could preserve low tax rates on overseas profits. Apple disputes that the move reduced taxes and has resisted the EU’s ruling that it received illegal state aid from Ireland.
- High-net-worth individuals:
  - Lewis Hamilton: Paradise Papers reveal advisers (Appleby and EY) helped set up Isle of Man-based leasing arrangements allowing jet and motorhome imports with large VAT refunds. Experts describe the leasing structures as artificial and potentially abusive; HMRC has been asked to review Isle of Man refunds. Hamilton says he relied on professional advice and that arrangements were lawful; his representatives deny wrongdoing.
  - Other wealthy clients and celebrities also appear across the files using BVI, Guernsey, Malta, Isle of Man and other jurisdictions for image rights, leasing and other arrangements to lower tax bills.

Political and regulatory fallout
- US Democrats (including Chuck Schumer and Ron Wyden) seized on the leaks to argue Republican tax proposals extend benefits to those dodging taxes while burdening the middle class.
- Calls for investigations, inspections and hearings: Senators and critics demanded answers and potential resignations in cases like Wilbur Ross; the Isle of Man’s handling of VAT refunds is under review by UK tax authorities.
- International response: The leaks feed ongoing global debates about closing loopholes—OECD and EU anti-avoidance initiatives are targeting schemes such as reverse hybrids and stateless entities, but multinationals have often stayed a step ahead with new structures.

Overall picture
The Paradise Papers reveal how law firms, accountants and advisers help wealthy individuals and corporations exploit cross-border legal and regulatory gaps—using shell companies, leasing chains, intellectual-property flows, and “stateless” entities—to minimize taxes and move profits to low- or zero-tax jurisdictions. While many arrangements are claimed to be legal, experts and politicians say they underline systemic inequities and regulatory failures, prompting renewed calls for reform and enforcement.

An Amtrak passenger train derailed Dec. 18 in DuPont, Washington, when several cars plunged from a bridge onto I‑5, killing three rail enthusiasts and injuring more than 70 others, some critically. The deceased were identified as Jim Hamre, 61, and Zack Willhoite, 35, both Tacoma‑area members of All Aboard Washington, and Benjamin Gran, 40, of Auburn.

A preliminary NTSB review of data from the lead locomotive’s event recorder and onboard cameras shows the engineer warned of an “over speed condition” about six seconds before the derailment. The recorded final locomotive speed was 78 mph—acceptable for the approach but well above the posted 30 mph limit for the upcoming curve where the derailment occurred. The train’s brakes were reported to have engaged automatically; investigators noted none of the crew were seen using personal electronic devices. The train was on the inaugural run of a new, faster route south of Tacoma and was not equipped with positive train control, a technology that can prevent speed‑related derailments. The NTSB’s full investigation is expected to take up to two years.

Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker suspended his Republican presidential campaign on Sept. 21, 2015, saying he would “clear the field” so a positive conservative alternative to front-runner Donald Trump can emerge. Once a leading hopeful—especially in Iowa after a January speech—Walker's bid collapsed within weeks of formally entering the race due to poor debate performances, inconsistent positions (notably on birthright citizenship), and plunging poll numbers (a CNN/ORC poll showed him under 1% nationally). Fundraising and cash-flow problems compounded the decline: his well-funded super PAC could not substitute for hard campaign dollars, and donations and momentum dried up after August's Cleveland debate. Many staff and supporters learned of the decision only at the announcement; his super PAC said it will wind down and return remaining resources.

Walker's exit, the second notable GOP withdrawal after Rick Perry, leaves 15 candidates in the field and sparked immediate jockeying for his staff and donors—especially big backers like the Ricketts family. Rival campaigns moved quickly to recruit former Walker aides and appeal to his Iowa organization. Reactions were mixed but mostly respectful from fellow Republicans; critics on the left celebrated his departure. Overall, Walker’s rapid rise and fall highlighted the limits of early momentum, the central role of debates and media performance in 2016, and how fundraising shortfalls can doom even seemingly well-backed campaigns.

A Brenham veterinarian accused of killing a cat with a bow and arrow will not face charges after an Austin County grand jury returned a "no-bill," finding insufficient evidence to prosecute. The case stemmed from an April Facebook photo—later deleted—showing the vet holding an orange cat with an arrow through its head and a boastful caption. Investigators received an unsworn hearsay report that she acted to protect her pets from a potentially rabid stray, but could not verify when or where the photo was taken, obtain usable data from the deleted Facebook account, or establish probable cause to search local properties. The county DA noted the state lacked proof the incident occurred in Texas and could not prove cruelty beyond question (noting some euthanasia methods can involve a head bolt when done correctly). The veterinarian has been fired from the Washington Animal Clinic. The cat, named Tiger by his pet sitter, prompted protests at the courthouse and widespread online outrage, with many calling for indictment and harsher accountability.

Shannon Egeland, a 43-year-old convicted mortgage fraudster, was sentenced Wednesday to an additional 3 years and 10 months after admitting he staged an insurance scam by having his 17-year-old son shoot him in the legs the day before he was to report to serve a 10-year federal sentence for a high-profile mortgage-fraud scheme. The July 31, 2014 shooting near Caldwell, Idaho—a week after Egeland applied for disability insurance—resulted in the amputation of his left leg. Egeland directed his son to obtain and fire a 20-gauge shotgun, then falsely reported to police that he had been assaulted while helping a pregnant motorist. The fraud was quickly uncovered and Standard Insurance suffered no loss.

U.S. District Judge Anna J. Brown called the plot “an unthinkable kind of situation.” Prosecutors, who had sought five years for the insurance conspiracy, described Egeland as a “menace to society” and said he had a long record of criminal behavior dating to 2004; defense counsel urged leniency, noting Egeland’s medical, mental-health and financial struggles and the difficulty of his existing 10-year sentence. Egeland, who appeared in court on a prosthetic and said he’s been receiving mental-health treatment in custody, expressed remorse and said the harm to his son “will haunt me the rest of my life.” He was also ordered to pay $90,011 in back child support and was urged to continue mental-health care and re-evaluation.

Fans of the struggling 2016 Cleveland Browns had organized a tongue-in-cheek "Perfect Season" parade to mark an 0–16 campaign, raising over $10,000 through a GoFundMe intended to cover parade costs. After the Browns won their first game on Christmas Eve, the parade was canceled and organizers pledged the collected funds to the Greater Cleveland Food Bank. Cleveland Pizza had also donated, bringing the total to more than $8,000, and the Browns announced they would match the donation with an additional $10,000. The fundraiser had originally targeted $1,999 for event expenses.

The National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO) announced at CinemaCon that it will pilot off‑night, discounted movie tickets in a single U.S. state later this year as an experiment. NATO chief John Fithian said the idea—already used in Latin America and Canada—could begin soon; studios must approve the plan and NATO will avoid any role that could imply price‑setting to sidestep antitrust concerns. The trial will be limited in scope and duration, and the specific state was not disclosed.

The move marks a notable shift for U.S. exhibitors, who have long resisted discounting because studio revenue shares are tied to ticket prices and discounts directly reduce theater and studio income. Past attempts by startups (e.g., Groupon, MoviePass) largely failed amid industry pushback. NATO argues weeknight discounts have helped theaters abroad and is pursuing the pilot because many seats remain unused on off nights. The announcement reflects growing willingness among some exhibitors to experiment with pricing as ticket sales volumes stagnate while higher prices and premium formats have driven revenue increases.

Martha Stewart partnered with Triscuit to create a limited-edition Toasted Coconut & Sea Salt Triscuit that hit stores in early May 2015. Stewart said the flavor—chosen after extensive testing—is a balance of savory and sweet she believes will be “habit forming.” She’s fond of salt and keeps a variety of crackers in her pantry, though she says she isn’t much of a snacker.

The cracker’s toasted-coconut taste is described as mild and not overly perfumed, with a pleasant salty-sweet contrast that complements Triscuit’s whole-grain texture. Stewart recommends serving the crackers with toppings like crab and lime, avocado and hot pepper, melted cheese, or an indulgent dessert version—melted milk chocolate and a marshmallow—for a s’mores-style treat. The launch leaned into contemporary food trends—coconut, avocado, artisanal collaborations and Pinterest-friendly recipes—and included tie-ins with small “artisan” producers. Overall reviewers found the Martha Triscuit a successful, on-trend limited-edition flavor that plays well both solo and as a vehicle for toppings.

Netflix warned its customer-service team to expect angry callers before it announced a price change that splits its streaming and by-mail DVD service into two $7.99 plans (up from a single $9.99 plan), meaning customers who want both will pay $15.98 starting in September. The announcement generated roughly 4,000 mostly negative blog responses and heavy call volume; Netflix added extra phone staff, but callers still faced long holds. A Wall Street analyst (Rich Greenfield, BTIG) tested the lines, reporting 35 calls over two hours with 9–15 minute holds and said reps offered no retention discounts, merely advising disgruntled customers to wait until September. Netflix spokesman Steve Swasey said the company anticipated some backlash and had "tested, researched, [and] analyzed" reactions, adding bluntly, "These are our prices."

At the same time, Netflix has renewed a multi-year licensing deal with NBC Universal, keeping and adding content to its Watch Instantly library (titles like Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, The Motorcycle Diaries, and episodes of The Office, Law & Order: SVU, and 30 Rock), though some shows such as new SNL episodes reportedly won’t be available for now. Netflix has also recently lost some Sony content and had other studio disputes, so retaining NBCU programming helps justify higher licensing costs tied to the rate increase — though added titles may not placate many subscribers upset by the higher combined price.

A stunt performer was seriously injured during a Monday night performance of the Broadway musical Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark at the Foxwoods Theatre. Around seven minutes before the finale, a line or harness meant to secure a Spider-Man stunt double snapped as he jumped from a platform during a rescue scene; the performer plunged into a stage pit and was taken on a stretcher to Bellevue Hospital with broken ribs and some internal bleeding. Audience members reported screams, a blackout and falling equipment; the performance was stopped and later cancelled.

The show — a $65 million production that has experienced multiple preview-period accidents (including previous broken bones and a concussion) — had already delayed its official opening to Feb. 7 for revisions. After this incident OSHA, Actors’ Equity and the New York State Department of Labor met with the company; Actors’ Equity later said performances would not resume until backup safety measures were in place and the state labor department inspected the equipment involved. The injured actor was identified in later reporting as Christopher Tierney; director Julie Taymor visited him in the hospital.

This article compiles numerous accounts—many from prominent Republicans and people who knew him—portraying Senator Ted Cruz as widely disliked for his abrasive personality rather than his ideas. After Cruz’s alliance with Donald Trump soured, Trump began attacking him personally; that echoed a long history of former colleagues and political figures criticizing Cruz as arrogant, self-centered, and difficult to work with.

Key critiques and incidents cited:
- Former Bush 2000 campaign aides and other Bush insiders recall Cruz as hyper‑arrogant, a team‑breaker who sent unsolicited memos, barged into meetings, and was broadly shunned—so much so that he wasn’t offered a White House job.
- Bob Dole condemned Cruz for his role in defeating a disability rights treaty and for mocking past GOP nominees, saying “nobody likes him.”
- John McCain publicly disparaged Cruz as a “wacko bird,” questioned his tactics, and was offended by Cruz’s treatment of Dole and past criticism of McCain.
- George W. Bush said he didn’t like Cruz; aides and allies viewed him as self‑serving and divisive.
- John Boehner called Cruz a “jackass” and blamed him for empowering the House Freedom Caucus and pushing damaging shutdown stances.
- Other Republicans—Peter King, Lindsey Graham and others—have labeled Cruz a “carnival barker,” opportunist, or “poison” for the party, faulting his tactics on shutdowns and national‑security debates.
- Former colleagues from law school, Supreme Court clerkship, Princeton and Harvard law describe Cruz as pompous, abrasive, and socially awkward—examples include elitist study‑group behavior, odd personal habits, and a reputation for alienating peers. His Princeton roommate and classmates gave especially scathing personal recollections.

The piece closes with a lighter anecdote: a newly surfaced 30‑second video of an 18‑year‑old Cruz joking that his ambitions included “take over the world, world domination… rich, powerful, that sort of stuff,” which the campaign dismissed as evidence of his longstanding sense of humor.

Overall, the article argues that much of Cruz’s political vulnerability stems less from policy differences than from a widely reported pattern of abrasive, alienating personal behavior.

Four Florida A&M University juniors — Isaiah Butterfield, Stephen Brooks, Joshua Cosby, and Fitzroy Rhoden — say they were confronted by a white man outside an off‑campus apartment building in Tallahassee late Saturday after waiting to enter a friend’s unit. Butterfield recorded part of the roughly 10‑minute encounter and posted the video to Twitter, where it went viral. In the clip, the man, later identified by social media and local outlets as Don Crandall, claims to live in the building, tells the students they cannot enter without a key, then returns and pulls a gun while trying to block them from the elevator. Another bystander (identified by Butterfield as “Chad”) intervenes on the students’ behalf.

Crandall has been named a general manager at the Baymont Inn & Suites; the Pax Hotel Group, which owns the property, confirmed his involvement, condemned his actions, and says it has fired him. Stadium Centre management, where the incident occurred, told residents Crandall is not a resident and emphasized that firearms are prohibited on the property and that the complex is committed to an inclusive community. Butterfield and his friends described feeling targeted and shaken by the encounter, which they and others have framed as racially motivated.

Jennifer Herold, Republican candidate for Ohio House District 7, issued a statement condemning comments by Senate Majority Leader Tom Patton made on a January 18 radio show in which he questioned her fitness to serve because she is a 30‑year‑old mother of two young children. Patton said a state representative must spend three nights a week in Columbus and noted he waited until his children were grown before running; he also called Herold “the gal” and used the term “sweetie.” Herold called the remarks “insulting and discriminatory,” argued motherhood is a strength not a liability, and cited examples of women and men who have successfully served while raising children (Sarah Palin, Cathy McMorris Rodgers, Lt. Gov. Mary Taylor, Rep. Christina Hagan, Gov. John Kasich, Paul Ryan). She urged local and state Republican organizations to reconsider endorsements that tacitly support Patton’s views and invited supporters to sign a petition and use the hashtag #ISupportJen. Patton later said his remarks were “misunderstood,” apologized for “poor choice of words,” and said it was not his intention to imply young mothers couldn’t serve. The GOP primary winner on March 15 will face Democrat David Thurau in November.

Researchers at Queen Mary University of London demonstrated that bumblebees can learn a novel string‑pulling task and socially transmit that skill through their colonies, challenging the idea that large brains are required for spreading new behaviors.

Key findings
- Task and training: The experiment used blue artificial “flowers” with sugar reward hidden underneath a clear Plexiglas table and attached to strings. Bees were first trained stepwise (flower progressively moved under the table) until many learned to pull the string to extract the reward.
- Individual innovation: Spontaneous innovators were rare—only a few bees solved the task without training, usually after much exploration or luck.
- Social learning: When untrained bees watched a trained demonstrator (visual-only observation), about 60% learned to pull the string on their next trial. Observers typically needed ~5 demonstrations on average, though some learned after 1–2 observations.
- Mechanisms: Learning involved simple associative processes—local enhancement (bees attracted to the location of the demonstrator), stimulus enhancement (attention to the string), and perceptual feedback-driven trial-and-error. Observers failed coiled-string tests where early tugs produced no visible movement, indicating they did not gain an abstract means-end understanding from observation alone.
- Diffusion and persistence: In seeded colonies (one trained demonstrator per colony), the behavior spread quickly across many foragers (dozens learned within a few hundred paired foraging bouts), producing up to four sequential “learning generations.” The behavior continued to spread and persist even after the original demonstrator died. Control colonies without a demonstrator showed no diffusion.
- No cooperation: Paired experienced bees were slower than solitary skilled bees, suggesting they do not cooperate to pull strings.
- Scale and rigor: The work involved hundreds of bees and used network‑based diffusion analysis and social-network models to show social transmission best explains the spread.

Implications
- Cognitive capacity: The study shows small insect brains can support flexible problem solving and social transmission of foraging techniques.
- Culturelike phenomena: Because learned behaviors propagated across individuals and generations and persisted beyond the original demonstrator, the results suggest bees can exhibit rudimentary culture-like transmission via simple associative mechanisms rather than high-level insight.
- Future directions: Authors plan to investigate neural bases of these abilities and note that lack of such behaviors in the wild may reflect limited opportunity rather than inability.

William Morris Endeavor Entertainment (WME) and private-equity firm Silver Lake announced on Dec. 18, 2013 they have agreed to acquire IMG Worldwide, a leading global company in sports, event management, talent representation, fashion and multimedia rights. WME co-CEOs Patrick Whitesell and Ariel Emanuel said IMG’s global reach and management complement WME’s business; Whitesell and Emanuel will serve as co-CEOs of the combined company. Silver Lake’s Egon Durban highlighted IMG’s growth potential and plans to expand its digital platform. The combination creates a worldwide sports-and-entertainment platform spanning North America, Europe, Asia, South America and Africa with an expanded client roster and assets across sports, events, film, TV and fashion. Terms were not disclosed; the transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and includes Mubadala Development Company as a minority investor. J.P. Morgan, Barclays, RBC, Deutsche Bank and other advisers and financiers supported WME and Silver Lake; Evercore and Morgan Stanley advised seller Forstmann Little. The release also summarized WME and Silver Lake’s business profiles.

A Travis County jury convicted 69-year-old James Miller of criminally negligent homicide in the 2015 stabbing death of 32-year-old musician Daniel Spencer and acquitted him of murder and manslaughter. Miller was sentenced to 10 years probation, six months in the county jail, 100 hours of community service, an alcohol monitor for at least a year, payment of about $10,000–$11,000 in fines/restitution, and court costs.

Prosecutors portrayed Spencer as an upstanding community member and disputed Miller’s claim of self-defense, citing blood-evidence inconsistencies with Miller’s account. The victim’s mother testified about her loss. Miller, a retired Austin police officer, said he and Spencer had been drinking and playing music the night of the killing and that Spencer made a sexual advance; Miller said he acted in a so-called “gay panic” and stabbed Spencer. Defense counsel argued the act was uncharacteristic and justified probation.

The outcome—much lighter than a murder conviction—drew criticism from LGBT advocates who contend “gay panic” defenses perpetuate bias and should be banned; the American Bar Association has urged curtailing such defenses, and several states are considering legislation to restrict them.

A family’s dog, Jade, went missing in Yellowstone National Park after a July 23, 2015 head‑on collision in which the driver who fell asleep at the wheel severely injured Jade’s owner, David Sowers. David was medevaced for treatment; when rangers tried to free Jade from a crushed crate she bolted and has been missing since. Multiple sightings—most recently near Canyon Village—indicate Jade is still alive. Friends, family (David, his partner Laura Gillice, and his daughter Angie Sowers) and numerous volunteers are making repeated trips from Denver (about 550 miles) and conducting daily trapping and search efforts, despite medical, travel, and other expenses. The group is asking for donations and help from park visitors to support search efforts and bring Jade home safely. Contact organizers include Kat Brekken and Sandy Monville.

Rupert Murdoch filed for divorce from his wife of 14 years, Wendi Deng Murdoch, in New York, citing an irretrievable breakdown. Sources say the couple had been living increasingly separate lives, and Wendi was reportedly surprised when served papers. News Corp’s planned split into two companies was not thought to be the main cause.

Speculation about reasons for the split quickly surfaced. Reports point to tensions from Wendi’s active social life and high-profile friendships — names repeatedly linked in gossip include MySpace co-founder Chris DeWolfe, former British prime minister Tony Blair, and Google executive chairman Eric Schmidt — though those ties were denied or remain unproven. Past rumors of an affair with DeWolfe date to 2008. Journalists and commentators, including BBC correspondent Robert Peston and biographer Michael Wolff, hinted that there could be “jaw-dropping” or undisclosed reasons behind the divorce, which has fueled intense media and public speculation.

Background: Rupert met Wendi in 1998 in Hong Kong; they married in 1999 and have two daughters. Wendi became prominent in News Corp.’s China business, produced films, and played an energetic social and philanthropic role. Their marriage had long-standing tensions — reports of separate bedrooms, friction with Rupert’s older children, and Wendi’s gatekeeper role at times strained family relations. The couple reportedly have prenuptial and postnuptial agreements; Rupert retained prominent divorce counsel, and Wendi has her own attorney. Observers note that Wendi’s deep knowledge of Murdoch’s affairs and her close involvement in his world complicate the fallout and have contributed to intense media interest.

U.S. and Cuban officials say an American contractor working under a U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) program was detained in Havana on Dec. 5 while distributing cellphones, laptops and other communications equipment to Cuban activists. The man, who worked for Development Alternatives Inc. (a Bethesda-based contractor awarded a USAID democracy and human-rights support contract), has not been publicly identified; U.S. Interests Section consular officers have requested access. Cuban authorities have not released charges.

The detention risks straining ties between Havana and the Obama administration, which has signaled a cautious, conditional opening toward Cuba—saying Washington will reciprocate only if Cuba makes concrete human-rights concessions. U.S. officials were encouraged the arrest had not been publicized and hoped for a quiet release; some U.S. congressional and administration sources questioned the circumstances, including reports the contractor used a tourist visa and worked covertly.

Cellphones and computers have become more available in Cuba but internet access remains limited and monitored; authorities have shown particular sensitivity to dissidents such as blogger Yoani Sánchez. Human-rights advocates say Cuban law can be used broadly to criminalize aiding government critics, while some analysts argue the U.S. democracy-promotion programs in Cuba—historically routed through Miami exile groups and criticized by government audits—have been controversial and sometimes poorly managed.

The case underscores lingering tensions over U.S. efforts to promote access to information in Cuba, the Cuban government's continuing hard-line measures against perceived dissent, and the delicate balancing act in U.S.-Cuba relations as Congress debates broader travel restrictions.

Baltimore County investigators are examining a black Ford F-150 after a 16-month-old girl, identified as Sabriya Towels, was found in cardiac arrest inside the truck on McDowell Lane in Lansdowne and later died at the hospital. Neighbors say a relative — not a parent — had been asked to drop the child off at the Highland Village Head Start Center but instead drove to a home on South Paca Street and went inside to sleep. About four hours later he attempted to pick her up, discovered her in the vehicle and ran back out. Police currently treat the incident as likely accidental; the relative has not been named and no charges have been filed. It was about 88°F outside and investigators have removed the child car seat from the truck; the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner will determine the cause of death.

The report also references a separate, similar case in Alexandria in which a mother, Zoraida Magali Conde Hernandez, was charged with felony child neglect after her 8-month-old died after being left in a hot car; that child was taken to Inova Alexandria Hospital and pronounced dead. Temperatures on the relevant days were around 88–90°F. Employees at the Head Start did not comment.

Students, teachers, parents and other supporters staged a nationwide Day of Action on March 4 against deep public-education budget cuts, holding rallies, marches, teach-ins, walkouts and other protests on college and K–12 campuses from California to Wisconsin, Texas, Illinois, Washington and Alabama.

Most events were peaceful and often festive, featuring signs, chants, poetry and personal testimony about tuition hikes, class reductions and layoffs. Large gatherings took place in California (Berkeley, Sacramento, Oakland, UC campuses, Cal State schools), with hundreds rallying at the state Capitol and thousands participating across the Bay Area. Demonstrations also included faculty actions (University of Illinois instructors urging “Furlough Legislators”), a mock “R.I.P. Education” coffin in Olympia, and campus protests over tuition increases at UT Austin and financial-aid shortfalls in Wisconsin.

Several actions turned disruptive or violent: arrests were made after protesters attempted to enter an administrative building at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee; protesters smashed a car window and blocked gates at UC Santa Cruz; more than 150 were arrested after shutting down Interstate 880 in Oakland; and smaller clashes and safety concerns prompted campus advisories. Officials and some university leaders voiced support for peaceful protest but warned against violence.

Organizers said the demonstrations aimed to protest cuts that have reduced course offerings, raised fees, furloughed staff and strained access to higher education amid state budget shortfalls and dwindling federal stimulus support. Protesters called for restored funding and policy changes to prioritize public education funding.

Time (Dec. 27, 2016) argues the U.S. should abolish the penny because producing it costs more than its face value. In 2016 the Mint’s unit cost for a one-cent coin rose to about 1.5 cents (it produced more than 8.4 billion pennies), generating an estimated $69 million loss due to rising metal costs—chiefly zinc. Nickels have long cost more than five cents to produce (about seven cents each in the referenced year) because copper and nickel prices have climbed, driven in part by demand from electronics and electric vehicles and use in stainless steel. Dimes and quarters remain profitable to produce, and seigniorage from those coins helped the Mint report $391.5 million in net earnings last year. The piece notes that U.S. military bases abroad and many other places already operate without pennies, suggesting eliminating the coin would save money and simplify transactions.

Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke has recommended cutting or altering nearly half of the 27 national monuments the Trump administration reviewed, according to a memo to President Trump reported by the Wall Street Journal and obtained by the AP. Zinke proposes reducing the boundaries of six terrestrial monuments — including Utah’s Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, Nevada’s Gold Butte, and Oregon’s Cascade-Siskiyou — and two large Pacific marine monuments, and suggests changes at others such as New Mexico’s Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks and Rio Grande del Norte and Maine’s Katahdin Woods and Waters.

The review was ordered by Trump amid complaints that past presidents overused the Antiquities Act to create overly large protections. Zinke says his recommendations will include unspecified boundary adjustments while preserving public access for activities like hunting, fishing and grazing and protecting tribal interests and historical land grants. He declined to specify whether areas would be reopened to energy development, mining or logging; the memo emphasizes increased public access.

Conservation groups condemn the proposals as an unprecedented assault on public lands and say they will sue if protections are reduced or designations rescinded. Zinke previously announced six monuments would see no changes. The White House had no immediate comment.

Auctioneers sold a rare photo album containing informal images of Adolf Hitler and his inner circle, likely taken by someone very close, possibly Eva Braun, and discovered in the Führer bunker in 1945. The album, reportedly first obtained by British Fleet Street photographer Edward Dean from a Russian soldier who found it in a drawer after the suicides of Hitler and Braun, mostly contains relaxed, early- to mid-1930s snapshots — including a striking image of Hitler strolling at the Berghof — that would not normally have passed Nazi image control. Bidding was highly competitive, drawing telephone and online interest from multiple countries. The auction house’s military-history specialist said buyers of Nazi memorabilia tend to be historians and collectors rather than sympathizers, and noted the ethical sensitivities around ownership of Nazi-era items. Institutions such as the Auschwitz memorial have urged private holders to donate documents and personal artifacts to preserve Holocaust history and context.

Peaches Geldof, 25, was found dead at her home in Wrotham, Kent on Monday with her 11-month-old son Phaedra nearby. Her husband, Thomas Cohen, had been away overnight with their older child and asked a friend to check on Peaches when she did not answer her phone. Sources said Phaedra was likely too young to understand what happened and that the family may take some comfort that she was not alone. Peaches’s body has been released by coroners so funeral arrangements can proceed; the cause of death remains unexplained pending toxicology results, which may take weeks.

In the weeks before her death, concerns were raised about Geldof’s dramatic weight loss and extreme dieting—she had publicly described lengthy juicing regimens and subsisting on items such as miso soup. Medical commentators and members of the public had warned such habits risk electrolyte imbalance, muscle and organ wasting, and heart problems. A U.K. doctor suggested signs consistent with long-term bulimia and said sudden cardiac issues related to eating disorders or other heart conditions could explain an otherwise unexplained sudden death. Official investigations, including toxicology, are ongoing. Story developing.

Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, and the American Cancer Society (ACS) released a report, “The Global Burden of Cancer in Women,” highlighting that the four leading causes of cancer death in women—breast, colorectal, lung and cervical cancers—are largely preventable or can be detected early when treatment is more effective. The research, published at the World Cancer Congress, warns that cancer’s impact on women is rising, especially in low- and middle-income countries: female cancer deaths worldwide rose from 3.5 million in 2012 and are projected to reach about 5.5 million by 2030 (a >57% increase), driven by population growth and aging. The study also underscores a large economic toll—globally about $286 billion in 2009—with much of the cost stemming from premature deaths and lost productive life (for example, $82 billion in the U.S. in 2008).

The Merck–ACS public–private partnership aims to boost awareness, advocacy, prevention and early detection. It will support initiatives such as expanding the ACS “All of Me Young Scholars” program to train young health and civil-society professionals in Brazil, Mexico, Colombia and India to promote prevention and early detection in low- and middle-income settings. The work ties into Merck’s Healthy Women, Healthy Economies initiative, which links women’s health to economic growth and promotes policies to increase women’s participation and well‑being.

Commentators in the release emphasized shared responsibility across public and private sectors to increase prevention and treatment. The report and release also reiterated common evidence-based prevention measures highlighted by health authorities: avoid tobacco, participate in recommended screening (e.g., Pap smears, HPV vaccination, age‑appropriate mammography), maintain healthy diet and regular exercise to prevent obesity-related cancers, and protect skin from sun damage. The World Health Organization estimates about one-third of cancers are preventable through such measures. The full report is available from the American Cancer Society.

Studios sometimes back films that fail to recoup their costs, producing high-profile box-office flops. Examples mentioned include Cowboys & Aliens, The Lone Ranger, Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within, and The Adventures of Pluto Nash. Failures can come from poor audience interest, wrong casting or story choices, or simply budgets so large they’re impossible to recover.

Box-office snapshot:
- The Fate of the Furious dominated, grossing $38.7M in its second North American weekend for a 10-day domestic total of $163.6M and $908.4M worldwide; it held well overseas, led by $318M from China.
- The Boss Baby and Beauty and the Beast continued strong runs ($137M domestic/$358.1M worldwide for Boss Baby; $1.1B global for Beauty and the Beast).
- Disney’s Born in China was the strongest new release, opening to $5.1M from 1,508 theaters.

Notable underperformers:
- Unforgettable (Warner Bros.), starring Katherine Heigl, opened to a career-worst $4.8M from 2,417 theaters; studio cited poor resonance with target audience. The film’s modest $12M budget limits the damage.
- The Promise, a $100M Armenian-genocide drama starring Christian Bale and Oscar Isaac, grossed just $4.1M from 2,251 theaters. Financed by the late Kirk Kerkorian, its backers emphasize the film’s role in raising awareness and supporting a $20M donation to establish The Promise Institute for Human Rights at UCLA.
- Phoenix Forgotten opened to $2M from 1,592 theaters; Free Fire earned $1M from 1,070 theaters. Both failed to attract sizable audiences despite notable producers and casts.

Other specialty releases: Fox Searchlight’s Gifted crossed $10M after adding $4.5M; The Lost City of Z expanded to 614 theaters and earned $2.1M in its second weekend.

Overall, the report contrasts blockbusters that continue to earn strongly with several new releases and prestige pictures that underperformed or risk becoming costly flops.

Researchers at the University of Warwick have produced the first international standard charts for normal infant crying during the first three months, based on a meta-analysis of nearly 8,700 infants from industrialised countries (including the UK, Canada, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany and Japan). Key findings:

- Typical pattern: average crying is about 2 hours per day in the first two weeks, rises to a peak of ~2 hours 15 minutes per day at six weeks, then falls to ~1 hour 10 minutes by 12 weeks.
- Wide individual variation: some infants cry as little as 30 minutes per day, others over 5 hours.
- Geographic differences: highest crying and colic rates were observed in the UK, Canada, Italy and the Netherlands; lowest in Denmark, Germany and Japan. Colic (defined as >3 hours/day, ≥3 days/week) was most common in the UK (28% at 1–2 weeks), Canada (34.1% at 3–4 weeks) and Italy (20.9% at 8–9 weeks); lowest in Denmark (5.5% at 3–4 weeks) and Germany (6.7% at 3–4 weeks).
- Rationale: existing colic criteria date to the 1950s (Wessel criteria) and may not reflect modern, cross-cultural norms; new charts aim to help clinicians reassure parents or identify excessive crying that needs evaluation and parental support.
- Implications: cultural or parenting practices (e.g., Danish parents waiting to let babies self-soothe) and possibly genetic or prenatal factors may explain differences. The lead author warns against unproven parenting remedies and notes parental stress can exacerbate problems; health professionals can use the charts to guide reassurance and intervention.

The study, “Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Fussing and Crying Durations and Colic Prevalence in Infants,” was published in The Journal of Pediatrics (April 2017).

Researchers at Stanford (Barragan & Dweck) tested whether very simple reciprocal interactions—not just an innate disposition—trigger altruistic behavior in young children. Across four studies with 1–2-year-olds and preschoolers, they compared brief reciprocal play (e.g., rolling a ball back-and-forth) to friendly but nonreciprocal “parallel” play (experimenter and child play with separate toys).

Key findings:
- Study 1 (34 one- and two-year-olds): Children who engaged in 6 minutes of reciprocal play helped an adult retrieve out-of-reach objects on many more trials than children who experienced parallel play.
- Study 2 (30 one- and two-year-olds): A single reciprocal warm-up increased helping not only toward the original experimenter but also toward a new adult; control (no play) and parallel play did not produce similar helping. Differences in how much “fun” children had did not explain the effect.
- Study 3 (30 four-year-olds): Even a very brief (1-minute) reciprocal interaction increased generosity (allocations of stickers) relative to parallel play.
- Study 4 (20 four-year-olds): After brief reciprocal versus parallel interactions with two different assistants, children expected the reciprocal partner to be more likely to act benevolently (give a gift, help open a door, share a toy).

Conclusions:
- Simple reciprocal interactions powerfully prime both the enactment and the expectation of altruism in young children. The effect generalizes across partners and persists into preschool age.
- These results challenge claims that early helping is purely innate and unaffected by social experience; instead, subtle social cues (reciprocity) can rapidly create a “benevolent” norm that children adopt.
- Practical implication: caregivers and experimenters can foster helping by engaging children in brief reciprocal activities that communicate mutual care.

Vice President Mike Pence represented President Trump at a Capitol ceremony Friday honoring the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.), who is lying in state under the Capitol dome. Pence, speaking on behalf of a grateful nation, praised McCain’s long record of service—in the Navy, where he was a Vietnam-era POW, and in Congress—and honored his commitment to country, limited government, tax reform and the military. Pence acknowledged he did not always agree with McCain but stressed McCain’s example of putting country first; he also reiterated that President Trump “respected his service,” though Trump did not attend at the family’s request.

Thousands queued to pay respects as McCain’s flag-draped casket was carried into the rotunda. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House Speaker Paul Ryan delivered tributes celebrating McCain’s courage and character. The two-day Washington observances will include a procession past the Vietnam Veterans Memorial and a funeral at Washington National Cathedral on Saturday, where former presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama will speak per McCain’s wishes. High-ranking Trump administration officials attended Friday’s service; Trump, who had a fraught relationship with McCain, was absent. McCain, 81, died last Saturday after being diagnosed last year with an aggressive brain cancer; he is survived by his wife, seven children and his mother.

A Russian court on August 17, 2012 found three members of the feminist punk group Pussy Riot—Nadezhda Tolokonnikova, Maria Alyokhina and Yekaterina Samutsevich—guilty of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred for staging an anti‑Kremlin "punk prayer" in Moscow’s Christ the Saviour Cathedral in February. Judge Marina Syrova sentenced each to two years’ imprisonment; having already been jailed for about five months, they face roughly 19 more months behind bars unless pardoned. The defense plans to appeal.

The case became a global cause célèbre, drawing support from Western celebrities and international criticism: the U.S. and EU called the sentences disproportionate and urged review, and human‑rights observers warned of a blow to freedom of expression. In Russia, however, public sympathy was limited—an independent poll found only about 6% supported the women—while many viewed their act as sacrilegious. Outside the courthouse, supporters chanted “Shame” and scuffles with police led to dozens of detentions, including several opposition figures.

Critics of the verdict portrayed it as part of a broader Kremlin crackdown on dissent under Vladimir Putin’s renewed presidency and a reprisal for winter protest movements. The Orthodox Church condemned the stunt but later appealed for mercy, leaving open the possibility of supporting a pardon—though that would likely require admissions of guilt. The trial intensified tensions over protest laws, Internet controls and limits on civil liberties in Russia.

Former lead prosecutor Marcia Clark reacted with skepticism and cautious interest to reports that a folding Buck knife allegedly recovered from property once owned by O.J. Simpson is being tested by the LAPD. Clark said she was stunned that what may be evidence was kept by an off-duty officer for years, noted the possibility it could be a hoax or planted, and urged thorough testing to determine the truth. She also said DNA recovery is possible with modern techniques but that prosecution is unlikely given the passage of time and Simpson’s 1995 acquittal; she expressed sympathy for the victims’ families.

According to reports, a construction worker found the knife around 2002 and gave it to a retired LAPD officer who kept it in his toolbox; it only reached investigators when the officer later asked a colleague for the Simpson case number. LAPD confirmed the knife is under investigation and will undergo fingerprint, hair and serology/DNA testing. Forensic experts say the blade’s size could have inflicted the wounds on Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman, and that Buck knives were long suspected by some investigators.

However, experts caution that contamination and degradation over many years — and handling by non-gloved individuals — may limit what usable fingerprints or DNA can be obtained. Mitochondrial DNA from hair shafts might be possible, and eliminating contamination could involve obtaining reference samples from the finder and the officer who had the knife. Even if the knife yields incriminating material, double jeopardy bars retrying Simpson on the murder charges. The knife’s discovery is therefore potentially significant for historical and evidentiary clarity, but unlikely to lead to new criminal charges.

The articles mark the eighth anniversary of the U.S. stock-market rally that began after the March 9, 2009 lows and note that, by the standard rule (no 20% decline since the rebound), the S&P 500’s roughly 250% gain makes this the second-longest post‑war bull market. But analysts disagree about when the “real” bull market began: commonly cited alternative start points include September 2011 (a recovery after a deep correction), March 2013 (the breakout above the 2007 high and the end of a “secular bear”), and February 2016 (a broad washout that some view as a cleansing that renewed the advance). 

Coverage highlights several consistent themes:
- Endurance and performance: The rally has been unusually persistent, delivering some of the best eight‑year returns on record and large gains for many major stocks and sectors (notably consumer discretionary and several blue‑chips and new Dow additions like Apple, Visa and UnitedHealth).
- Valuation and risk: Valuation metrics (forward P/E, Shiller CAPE, Q ratio) are elevated versus long‑run averages, prompting caution that prospective returns over the next several years may be muted and that a correction is likely at some point.
- Low volatility and investor behavior: The market has seen surprisingly low volatility and relatively little investor participation (household equity ownership is low), raising concerns about complacency and herding/fear‑of‑missing‑out dynamics.
- Catalysts and outlook: Strategists generally don’t expect the bull to “die of old age”; rather, a recession, financial panic or policy shock would end it. Many expect further gains driven by improving earnings, low interest rates (though the Fed is tightening) and potential fiscal reforms, but most also warn a 5–10% pullback is plausible and that larger declines would follow if growth or earnings falter or Fed tightening, political disappointments, or global risks materialize.

Bottom line: The market’s age depends on the chosen start date, but regardless of when the bull “officially” began, stocks are richly valued after a rare, long run of gains. That argues for cautious positioning—expect more gains is a plausible base case, but also expect corrections and elevated risk.

Walmart is offering to send rapper Pitbull to the store that receives the most Facebook "likes" by July 16. A joke campaign led by Boston Phoenix writer David Thorpe (and amplified online) pushed the remote Kodiak, Alaska Walmart, which by Monday had amassed over 35,000 likes—far exceeding Kodiak’s population—and leads the contest. Walmart confirmed other stores have until July 16 to catch up. Pitbull, touring in Europe, has reacted good-naturedly—tweeting about Kodiak (“I hear there's bear repellant…”) and saying he'll go “wherever the fans want to have a party.” The visit would be his first to Alaska.

Dr. Fredric Brandt, a high-profile Miami dermatologist known as the “Baron of Botox,” died by suicide at his Coconut Grove home at age 65. Police said a friend found him hanging in the garage; he had been under psychiatric care for depression. Friends, family and his longtime publicist emphasized that he had struggled with depression for some time and that, while a recent parody of a plastic surgeon on Netflix’s Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt upset and “devastated” him, it was not the sole cause of his death.

Brandt built a prominent career treating celebrities such as Madonna, Kelly Ripa and Stephanie Seymour, teaching dermatologists, running clinical trials for injectables, authoring books on anti-aging, hosting a radio show, and launching the Dr. Brandt Skin Care line sold internationally. Trained in multiple medical specialties, he completed his dermatology residency at the University of Miami and opened practices in Coral Gables and New York City. Colleagues praised his innovations, teaching and personal warmth, while friends remembered his generosity, love of show tunes and art collecting.

He is survived by his brother Paul and his three dogs. Those who knew him stressed that his professional success and public persona belied long-standing personal pain from depression.

Former James Bond actor Pierce Brosnan, 62, was stopped by Transportation Security Administration (TSA) agents at Burlington International Airport, Vermont, after screening detected a 10-inch hunting knife in his carry-on. The blade was confiscated (or, per one report, Brosnan chose to put it in checked baggage) in line with post-9/11 rules that ban sharp objects from cabins. Police said the matter was resolved at the checkpoint and Brosnan was allowed to continue his journey; there were no arrests or citations. His publicist had not responded to requests for comment. Photos show Brosnan interacting with security and removing his belt during screening.

This document chronicles the case of Crystal Mason and situates it within the broader problem of felony disenfranchisement in the U.S.

Key facts about Mason’s case
- Crystal Mason, a Black woman from Rendon near Fort Worth, cast a provisional ballot in the 2016 election after her name did not appear on voter rolls. She says she was never told that being a felon on supervised release (she had been sentenced to 60 months for tax fraud and released in early 2016) made her ineligible to vote under Texas law. Her provisional ballot was never counted.
- Mason was later arrested for illegal voting. On March 28, 2018, State District Judge Ruben Gonzalez convicted her and sentenced her to five years in prison. Her motion for a new trial was denied in a 16-page ruling; her attorney has filed an appeal and seeks release on bond.
- The prosecution argued the court could not consider an amicus brief from the Texas Civil Rights Project and the ACLU, which contended a 2002 federal statute allows voters who reasonably believe they are eligible to cast a provisional ballot, shifting the burden to the state. The judge sided with the state.
- Public reaction included an online petition (over 38,000 signatures) comparing Mason’s sentence with lighter sentences in other cases (including a white woman in Iowa sentenced to probation and a fine for attempting to vote twice), and criticism that Mason’s punishment is disproportionately harsh.

Broader context on felony voting rights
- An estimated 6.1 million Americans are disenfranchised due to felony convictions; incarceration and supervision disproportionately affect people of color, which critics argue functions as a modern mechanism of political marginalization.
- Voting eligibility for people with felony convictions varies widely by state:
  - Some states restore voting rights automatically upon release (e.g., Massachusetts, Hawaii).
  - Others restore rights after completion of parole/probation, or require an application to regain rights (e.g., Kentucky, Iowa, Florida, Wyoming, Nevada, Delaware).
  - A few allow voting while incarcerated (Maine and Vermont allow prisoners to vote; California relaxed some rules in 2016 for county jail inmates).
- The patchwork of rules creates confusion, deters risk-averse formerly incarcerated people from voting, and fuels claims of unequal enforcement and racial disparities in prosecutions.

Claims and calls to action
- Advocates and Mason’s supporters argue her conviction and five-year sentence are unjust and disproportionate, emblematic of racial disparities in enforcement of voting laws.
- The document demands that all charges against Crystal Mason be dropped and calls for steps to ensure incarcerated and formerly incarcerated people on supervision are clearly informed about their voting eligibility.

Overall message
The case of Crystal Mason is presented as an example of how inconsistent state-level felony disenfranchisement laws and uneven enforcement can criminalize attempted civic participation—disproportionately affecting people of color—and spark legal, civil-rights, and public debates over voting access, fairness, and reform.

At a high-profile UFO conference in Mexico City, journalist-producer Adam Dew and UFO researcher Jaime Maussan unveiled two Kodachrome slides they say show a dead extraterrestrial recovered in the 1947 Roswell incident. Dew claims Kodak dated the film to the late 1940s and says the slides were found in a trunk of photos belonging to deceased oil geologist Bernard Ray and his wife Hilda. The images have not been publicly released in high resolution and are slated for sale alongside a documentary, prompting accusations the event was commercial.

The presentation divided opinion. Prominent UFO advocates and some speakers (including former astronaut Edgar Mitchell and researcher Gary Heseltine) endorsed the slides as genuine evidence of nonhuman remains. Maussan insisted forensic and photographic experts supported their authenticity and denied the event was motivated by profit.

Skeptics quickly dismissed the claim. Experts and critics noted that Kodak dating only proves the film stock is old, not that the subject is extraterrestrial. Many commentators and scientists argued the photos more plausibly depict a mummified human—likely a child with a proportionally large skull or intentionally deformed cranium—rather than an alien. Comparisons were made to known mummy and child-mummy images, and some noted the figure appeared displayed in a case with a label, suggesting a museum or curiosity rather than crash evidence.

The reveal also raised credibility concerns: attendees paid large fees to view the slides, high-resolution images weren’t released for independent analysis, and similarities to earlier hoaxes (notably a 1990s “alien autopsy” film) fueled suspicion—some pointed out the same name “Hilda” appears in related claims. Former UK MoD UFO investigator Nick Pope and others called the presentation underwhelming or likely a hoax or stunt.

Overall, while the slides generated intense media and public attention and reinforced beliefs on both sides, independent verification is lacking; many experts regard the simplest explanation—mummified human remains or a period model/hoax—as far more probable than authenticated Roswell aliens.
