Reports surfaced that Madonna had applied in a Malawian court to adopt two more children while visiting the country. Malawian court and government spokespeople originally said the 58-year-old pop star appeared before the High Court in Lilongwe and that a ruling would follow within about a week. Media accounts noted she already adopted two Malawian children, David (2006) and Mercy (2009), and described her long-running charity work there through Raising Malawi, including fundraising for schools and a pediatric ICU in Blantyre.

Soon after those reports, Madonna denied applying to adopt additional children, telling Us Weekly the rumors were untrue and that her visit was to inspect the children’s hospital in Blantyre and other Raising Malawi projects. The story circulated alongside background about her previous adoptions, her family, and earlier comments she’s made about Malawi’s conditions and adoption challenges. The report also referenced unrelated recent controversy over her remarks at the U.S. Women’s March, which drew Secret Service attention.

This document covers two major freshwater-landscape stories: a new global lake census and the long-term desiccation of the Aral Sea.

Global lake census
- A study published in Geophysical Research Letters used high-resolution satellite imagery and supercomputing to count lakes worldwide by checking every cloud-free pixel. It found 117 million lakes on Earth, far fewer than some previous statistical estimates (a widely cited 2006 study put the number at 304 million), but the total lake-covered area is larger than earlier estimates.
- Lakes occupy about 2 million square miles (5 million km²), roughly 3.7% of ice-free land. About 90 million lakes are very small (0.2–1 hectare); most lakes are concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere between ~45° and 75°N (Canada, Russia, Alaska, Northern Europe, Great Lakes region), largely because of glacial and tectonic history.
- Most lakes (85%) lie below 500 m elevation. The study excluded the Caspian Sea and ice-covered regions (Antarctica and Greenland). The authors plan to release the dataset publicly and update it with higher-resolution Landsat 8 data.
- Accurate counts matter for understanding lakes’ roles in the global carbon cycle and greenhouse-gas budgets: lakes emit CO2 and methane but also sequester carbon in sediments. Lakes are dynamic—many are shrinking or disappearing due to warming-driven permafrost thaw, drought, and overuse (e.g., >100 Chinese lakes lost in the 2000s).

Aral Sea collapse
- Satellite images (MODIS/Terra) document dramatic shrinkage of the Aral Sea since the 1960s, when Soviet irrigation projects diverted the Syr Darya and Amu Darya rivers to support cotton farming. By 2000 the Aral was already a small remnant; over the 2000s the southern basin split and the eastern lobe progressively dried, disappearing entirely by the mid-2010s.
- Kazakhstan built a dam in 2005 to preserve the Northern Aral Sea, but overall retreat has devastated local communities and ecosystems. Exposed, contaminated lakebed dust (from fertilizers and pesticides) causes public-health problems and has driven further water use to try to remediate affected croplands.
- Regional climate extremes intensified (colder winters, hotter, drier summers). Health impacts include large rises in respiratory and other illnesses and higher infant mortality in the region; the Aral Sea’s collapse is frequently cited as a major ecological and humanitarian disaster.

Together these pieces highlight the power of modern satellite data to clarify water-land dynamics worldwide and the severe, often human-driven, consequences when lakes and inland seas shrink or disappear.

A light aircraft was safely landed at Humberside Airport after its pilot collapsed in-flight, but police later confirmed the pilot has died. The Cessna 172, which had taken off from Sandtoft and was returning from Skegness, made a distress call at about 18:25 BST. The sole passenger—an inexperienced flyer identified as "John"—was talked down by two flying instructors contacted by air traffic control and guided to make several circuits before landing at about 19:30. An RAF Sea King helicopter was scrambled to assist. Eyewitnesses reported sparks and a bumpy touchdown; the aircraft was later removed and two incoming flights were delayed.

Humberside Police said a post-mortem will be carried out and the death is not being treated as suspicious; the pilot’s identity will not be released at the family’s request. Friends described the pilot as a very experienced aviator and praised the passenger’s calm, heroic handling of the emergency. Roads around the airport were briefly closed but have since reopened and operations resumed.

Marcus M. Stanley, a senior economic adviser to Sen. Barbara Boxer, resigned after being arrested Tuesday for attempting to bring marijuana into the Hart Senate Office Building. Capitol Police stopped Stanley at the Constitution Avenue security checkpoint when they say he tried to "remove and conceal" a leafy green substance from his pocket; the material later tested positive for marijuana. Stanley, who has worked for Boxer since 2009, earned a six-figure salary and previously served on the Environment and Public Works Committee and the Joint Economic Committee. Boxer accepted his resignation, with a spokesman calling his actions "wrong and unacceptable." The incident adds to a string of drug-related stops at the Capitol since the Visitor Center opened; more than a dozen people have been stopped for marijuana and other drugs in the past year and a half. The arrest comes amid debate in California over Proposition 19, which would legalize and tax marijuana — a measure Boxer opposes. Stanley is the fourth Hill aide arrested this year; Boxer’s office has previously fired another senior aide after a separate criminal charge.

A 23-year-old student who was gang-raped and brutally assaulted on a moving bus in New Delhi on December 16 remains "extremely critical" at Mount Elizabeth Hospital in Singapore. Upon her arrival by air ambulance, doctors found she had suffered a prior cardiac arrest, significant brain injury, and infections in her lungs and abdomen; much of her intestines had been removed earlier at Safdarjung Hospital in Delhi. A multidisciplinary team is working to stabilise her; the High Commission of India is assisting the family and hospital. Security at the hospital has been tightened and the family is aided by interpreters and a liaison officer.

The attack has intensified public outrage in India over police and societal mistreatment of rape victims. Demonstrations in New Delhi have demanded better protections for women and harsher punishment for rapists. Political leaders, including Congress chief Sonia Gandhi and Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, pledged to see the perpetrators punished and to ensure the victim receives the best care. Six people have been arrested in connection with the bus attack.

The case has also prompted administrative action elsewhere after reports of other mishandled rape complaints: in Punjab, following the suicide of an 18-year-old who had alleged gang rape and accused police of harassment and inaction, one officer was suspended and two fired; the suspects in that earlier case were arrested only a month after the crime was reported. In Chhattisgarh another officer was suspended for refusing to register a rape complaint. The incident has generated broader criticism of officials whose comments demeaned protesters; a national lawmaker apologised for insulting remarks about women demonstrators.

Croatia opened a new transit route for migrants on Wednesday after Hungary sealed its Serbia border, allowing hundreds to enter from Serbia and continue toward northern Europe. About 150–600 migrants crossed into Croatia on foot or by bus, where authorities registered them and said they would receive or direct them onward — many aim for Germany or Scandinavia. Croatian PM Zoran Milanovic said the country was ready to help and set up reception and registration centers, while warning of local hazards such as marked landmine fields from the 1990s war.

The Hungarian closure triggered violent clashes at the Serbia–Hungary frontier. Hungarian riot police used tear gas, pepper spray, water cannons and batons to push back migrants who tried to breach a sealed crossing near Roszke/Horgos; protesters threw bottles and lit small fires. Hungary has declared a state of emergency in the border zone, deployed troops and police, and begun criminal proceedings against people entering illegally. The UN secretary-general and neighboring governments criticized the crackdown; Croatia and others denounced barbed wire fences as unacceptable.

The wider context: EU border agency Frontex reports more than 500,000 migrants have reached EU borders this year (up from 280,000 in 2014), many fleeing Syria and other conflict zones via Turkey, Greece, Macedonia and Serbia. Previously most transited Hungary into Austria and Germany, but Austria and Germany have tightened controls, halting some train routes and creating bottlenecks. Serbia warned Hungary’s closure is unsustainable and could strain its capacity and social tolerance as refugees accumulate.

Separately, Egyptian billionaire Naguib Sawiris proposed buying or leasing Greek islands to house Syrian refugees, suggesting a $100m joint-stock vehicle to manage donations and the islands as assets, pending Greek government approval.

During French President Emmanuel Macron’s state visit to Washington, President Donald Trump displayed several awkward, headline-grabbing gestures that drew wide reaction on social media.

- Hand-hold with Macron: As the leaders left the White House, Trump grabbed and continued holding Macron’s hand while leading him away. The brief moment was widely mocked and GIF’d on Twitter as “weird” and overly familiar.

- Oval Office dandruff incident: During remarks in the Oval Office, Trump joked about “a little piece of dandruff” on Macron’s shoulder, then reached over and brushed it off while cameras clicked. Observers interpreted the move as a clumsy “power play” or an attempt to belittle the French president; Macron appeared initially surprised but then smiled and laughed.

- Awkward moment with Melania Trump: Earlier, Trump made several tentative attempts to take First Lady Melania Trump’s hand during the South Lawn welcome; she appeared reluctant before briefly allowing contact. Melania’s wide-brimmed white hat also drew attention and comparisons on social media as it complicated greeting gestures and cheek kisses.

The visit included substantive meetings—discussions ranged from the Iran nuclear deal and Paris climate accord to trade and North Korea—but much of the media and public conversation focused on these personal, awkward interactions and the viral reaction they generated online.

This document is a compiled gallery and caption list of archival photographs of U.S. Senator Orrin Hatch spanning several decades. Key points:

- The images document Hatch’s long public career from at least the 1970s through the 2010s, showing him with presidents (Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald Trump), fellow senators (Bob Dole, Bob Bennett, Mitch McConnell, Diane Feinstein), judiciary figures (John Roberts, Samuel Alito, Elena Kagan), and public figures (Muhammad Ali, Mitt Romney).
- Photos highlight roles and moments including Hatch as Senate Judiciary Committee chairman, involvement in Supreme Court nomination hearings, campaigning and debates, fundraising events, receptions, memorial and public speeches, and bipartisan legislative efforts (e.g., co-sponsoring bills with Sen. Ted Kennedy).
- Several captions note specific occasions: oath-taking by Vice President Nelson Rockefeller, honorary degree ceremonies, discussions about land swaps and Forest Service issues, and policy appearances (State Children’s Health Insurance Program).
- The collection emphasizes Hatch’s prominence in Washington, his interactions across the political spectrum, and his visibility at both national and Utah-focused events over a multi-decade Senate tenure.

Overall, the document serves as a visual record of Orrin Hatch’s extensive political career and public life.

President Donald Trump criticized Nike’s decision to feature Colin Kaepernick in its 30th‑anniversary “Just Do It” campaign, calling it a “terrible message” and saying “there’s no reason” for the endorsement. He noted, however, that Nike has the right to make its own business decisions, framing that freedom as part of what the country is about, and acknowledged he personally would not have chosen Kaepernick. 

Kaepernick began kneeling during the national anthem in 2016 to protest police brutality and racial injustice and later accused NFL owners of colluding to keep him off rosters. Nike renegotiated a multiyear deal with him, posting an image reading “Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.” The announcement briefly rattled Nike’s stock and prompted mixed reactions: the NFL issued a statement saying the social justice issues raised by Kaepernick deserve attention and action, while some public figures, like country singer John Rich, criticized Nike and encouraged boycotts. The NFL supplies Nike with team apparel under a partnership through 2028.

This article is a media-focused roundup that centers on several recent stories and trends in journalism and popular culture.

- Denis Finley tweet controversy: Denis Finley, executive editor of the Burlington Free Press, sparked outrage after a string of ill-judged tweets, most notably mocking Vermont’s move to add an “X” gender marker on driver’s licenses by calling it “one step closer to the apocalypse” and later comparing recognition of trans people to recognizing pedophiles. The piece uses the episode to warn about newsroom leaders tweeting impulsively, arguing that conventional editorial processes and restraint protect journalistic reputations. Colleagues and retired reporters lament the impulse to share quick takes on social media rather than producing reported, edited work.

- Jake Tapper vs. Stephen Miller: A high-profile TV clash on CNN ended abruptly when anchor Jake Tapper cut off White House aide Stephen Miller after a combative exchange about Trump, Michael Wolff’s book, and CNN’s coverage. The segment illustrated the performative nature of cable confrontations, and while Trump later attacked Tapper on Twitter, the piece notes Tapper’s growing role as a skeptical interlocutor.

- The New York Times Golden Globes ad: The Times ran a minimalist “The Truth is Hard” ad during the Golden Globes, invoking its recent investigative reporting (e.g., on sexual harassment). The article praises the intent but questions the ad’s reach and impact, suggesting a broader, sustained campaign is needed to rebuild public willingness to pay for quality journalism.

- Decline in TV news viewership: Citing Pew and Poynter, the author notes an accelerated drop in local TV news viewers from 2016–2017, especially among younger Americans, and suggests ideology may play a role in shifting trust.

- Other media and culture notes:
  - Coverage of Oprah Winfrey’s Golden Globes speech prompted renewed speculation about a presidential run.
  - The Associated Press published a photo gallery of Golden Globes fashion history.
  - Sarah Stillman (Columbia) has documented cases of deportations that expose people to grave harm, illustrating systemic problems in immigration enforcement.
  - Recognition of women broadcasters in English soccer coverage (Rebecca Lowe, Kate Abdo) but an observation that men still dominate on-field and officiating roles.
  - Discussion of regional sports-media tensions around the New England Patriots and ESPN, and defense of reporter Seth Wickersham’s work.
  - Jack Goldsmith (Lawfare) raises doubt about whether Robert Mueller’s investigation includes a formal obstruction probe, based on Rosenstein’s apparent lack of recusal.
  - Patricia O’Conner highlights Robert Graves’s writing guide “The Reader Over Your Shoulder,” urging writers and readers to prioritize clarity and critical reading in an era of misinformation.
  - ESPN is marketing the College Football Playoff more aggressively to female viewers, using new audience data to tailor ad inventory.

The piece frames these items around themes of media responsibility, the consequences of impulsive social-media behavior, the evolving economics and audience strategies of news and sports media, and the continuing need for careful journalism and critical readership.

A 13-foot, 1,500-pound male great white shark carcass washed ashore on a rocky stretch of Westport, Massachusetts—less than half a mile from Little Compton, Rhode Island—late Friday and was discovered Saturday. State marine biologist Greg Skomal performed a necropsy and found no obvious trauma, leaving officials unable to determine the cause of death. Because of the shark’s size and its location below the high-tide line, authorities plan to leave the body where it is in hopes the tide will carry it back out; moving it was deemed impractical. Little Compton briefly closed Goosewing and South Shore beaches; both reopened Sunday with a police patrol boat monitoring for other sharks.

The stranding comes amid an uptick in shark activity off Massachusetts, particularly Cape Cod, where Labor Day weekend sightings prompted beach closures and raised safety concerns after a July incident in which a man was bitten off Truro. Experts attribute increased white shark presence to rising populations of their prey—especially grey seals, protected since the 1970s and now abundant along the North Atlantic coast—meaning sharks are likely to remain nearshore until their seasonal migration to warmer waters.

A Suncor Energy employee, 36-year-old Lorna Weafer of Fort McMurray, was killed by a large male black bear on May 8 at the company’s oil sands base camp about 25 km north of Fort McMurray, Alberta. Co-workers who witnessed the midday attack tried to intervene and called RCMP; Weafer was pronounced dead at the scene. RCMP and Alberta wildlife officers shot and killed the bear; authorities described it as an above-average-sized male and believe the attack may have been predatory. Traps and cameras were deployed and another bear was later captured.

Suncor said the company is shocked and has launched a full investigation; Alberta Occupational Health and Safety will also work with Suncor to determine if anything could have prevented the incident. Colleagues and family remembered Weafer as warm, compassionate and well-liked; Suncor and officials urged increased vigilance around wildlife as bears emerge from hibernation. This was the third employee death at Suncor’s oil sands site so far this year, though the other two were work-related.

A completed toxicology report and French prosecutor’s statement confirmed that U.S. celebrity chef and TV host Anthony Bourdain, who died by suicide on June 8 in a hotel near Strasbourg while filming an episode of Parts Unknown, had no narcotics or toxic products in his system. Investigators found only traces of alcohol and a non-narcotic medicine at therapeutic doses, and no signs of violence or third-party involvement. Bourdain, 61, had been candid about past heroin and cocaine addiction but had long been in recovery. The story also notes his relationship with Italian actress Asia Argento—who posted a grieving message and photo following his death—and recalls his celebrated career and outspoken public life. Crisis resources were provided.

President Trump cut federal advertising and outreach for the 2018 open-enrollment period for the Affordable Care Act by roughly 90 percent—reducing the federal budget from about $100 million to $10 million for the 39 states that use HealthCare.gov—part of an effort critics say aims to undermine Obamacare. The move, along with a halved enrollment window (six weeks, ending Dec. 15) and reductions in navigator grants, has raised public confusion about whether subsidies and coverage remain available and prompted insurers to adjust marketing, pricing and market participation.

Insurers and state exchanges have responded unevenly:
- Many carriers are stepping up their own outreach and advertising to fill the gap. Examples include Independence Blue Cross deploying mobile enrollment teams in Philadelphia, Centene expanding TV/print advertising as it enters three new states, and Oscar Health running TV spots promoting easy, tech-driven enrollment.
- Some Blues plans and insurers increased local online, grassroots, and in-person efforts (e.g., Florida Blue hiring 700 temporary staff and planning 1,000 enrollment events). Others, squeezed by higher costs, are cutting recruitment spending and focusing on helping existing members choose cheaper options rather than aggressively attracting new enrollments (e.g., Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan).
- Several carriers have raised premiums—about 20 percent on the popular “silver” plans—after uncertainty and the administration’s reduction of cost-sharing payments and other support. Some insurers have also exited markets or counties.

Forecasts and early signals are mixed:
- The Congressional Budget Office pared its 2018 enrollment projection to 11 million (from a higher prior estimate) after federal actions; private forecasters like S&P predict potential declines of up to 1.6 million signups. Outreach groups founded by former Obama officials expect fewer enrollees and say insurer-led local efforts can’t match a national campaign.
- Despite concerns, early days of enrollment showed a surge: reporting indicated record first-day activity on HealthCare.gov (over 1 million visitors and about 200,000 plan selections on Nov. 1, compared with ~100,000 selections and 750,000 visitors last year). Officials cautioned early data often reflect renewals rather than new enrollees, and final totals remain uncertain.

Overall, insurers are spending more in many local markets to counter federal pullback and combat consumer confusion, but financial pressures from reduced federal support and shortened enrollment could still depress total 2018 sign-ups and reshape local market offerings.

Three conservative House Republicans—Reps. Matt Gaetz (Fla.), Andy Biggs (Ariz.) and Louie Gohmert (Texas)—introduced a nonbinding resolution calling for special counsel Robert Mueller to resign or recuse himself from the Russia investigation, alleging conflicts of interest tied to his prior role as FBI director. The measure accuses Mueller of being “compromised” because the FBI, while he led it, allegedly withheld information about Russian-linked corruption tied to the 2010 Uranium One sale and silenced a confidential informant with a nondisclosure agreement. The move comes the same week Mueller’s team announced its first indictments and a guilty plea in the probe (charges against Paul Manafort and Rick Gates, and George Papadopoulos’s plea), and reflects growing GOP frustration and efforts by some conservatives to curb the investigation. Most GOP leaders have not joined calls to remove Mueller; some senators have instead pursued legal protections for special counsels. The resolution also urges scrutiny of the FBI’s handling of the uranium matter and ties the controversy to broader Republican criticisms of the Obama-era approval of the Uranium One transaction.

A series of recent reports and studies link marijuana use to cardiovascular complications, including rare but sometimes fatal events in young and middle-aged adults.

Case report from Germany
- Two young men (ages 23 and 28) were found dead with evidence of recent cannabis use; THC was detected in blood and brain tissue.
- Postmortem investigators concluded other causes were excluded and attributed both deaths to cardiac complications—likely arrhythmias—precipitated by smoking cannabis, while acknowledging possible underlying predispositions.
- The authors cautioned that the absolute risk in the general population is low but higher in people with cardiovascular disease. The paper prompted criticism from some drug-policy experts and an appeal for more awareness and testing in death investigations.

French national surveillance study (Journal of the American Heart Association)
- Analysis of 2006–2010 reports to the French Addictovigilance Network found 1,979 marijuana-related complications; 35 (about 1.8%) involved cardiovascular or vascular conditions.
- Of the 35, 22 were heart-related (including 20 myocardial infarctions), 10 involved peripheral arterial disease, and 3 were cerebrovascular. Nine patients (≈25.6%) died.
- Most cases were male with a mean age of 34.3. The proportion of reported cardiovascular complications rose more than threefold from 2006–2010.
- Researchers noted likely underreporting and recommended clinicians consider cannabis use when assessing cardiovascular events, especially in younger patients and those with preexisting cardiac risk.

Expert perspectives and implications
- Forensic toxicologists and medical examiners have reported cardiotoxic effects of cannabis in some individuals and urge routine testing in relevant deaths.
- Other experts emphasize that while marijuana is not typically directly lethal like some substances, it can trigger harmful cardiovascular responses in susceptible people; duration/frequency of users in the cases was not always specified.
- Authors and commentators call for continued surveillance, more research into mechanisms, and public and clinical awareness that cannabis can pose cardiovascular risks for certain users.

This document profiles conservative commentator and filmmaker Dinesh D’Souza, tracing his rise, controversies, ideas, and resurgence after being pardoned by President Trump.

Key points:

- Background and career: D’Souza is an Indian-American conservative author, longtime public intellectual and former Reagan White House staffer who held fellowships at AEI and Hoover and briefly served as president of The King’s College. He’s written 16 books and produced several commercially successful right‑wing documentaries (notably 2012’s 2016: Obama’s America and 2016’s Hillary’s America).

- Political style and influence: Once a mainstream conservative figure, D’Souza shifted toward conspiratorial, provocative rhetoric after 2007. His work often attacks liberal policies on race and education and advances controversial interpretations of history and presidents (notably an “anti‑colonial” explanation for Barack Obama). While many establishment conservatives criticized or distanced themselves from him, he found a large, receptive audience among populist and conspiracy‑oriented conservatives and expanded his reach under the Trump era.

- Major ideas and books: His early works (Illiberal Education) criticized campus “political correctness.” The End of Racism (1995) and later books argued against liberal racial policies and were polarizing. The Enemy at Home (2007) blamed the cultural left for fueling anti‑American anger abroad and drew widespread condemnation, contributing to his estrangement from some conservative institutions.

- Scandals and conviction: In 2012 D’Souza resigned from The King’s College after a personal scandal. More consequentially, in 2014 he was indicted for using “straw donors” to funnel roughly $20,000 to Wendy Long’s 2012 Senate campaign. He pled guilty to one count of making illegal contributions, was fined $30,000, sentenced to community confinement (halfway house) for eight months, and received five years’ probation. He maintained the prosecution was politically motivated; the judge rejected that claim.

- Pardon and reaction: On May 31 (year implied 2018 in context), President Trump pardoned D’Souza. D’Souza publicly taunted Preet Bharara, the prosecutor who brought the case (and was later fired by Trump), while Bharara defended the conviction’s facts. Trump framed the pardon as correcting unfair treatment.

- Public persona and methods: D’Souza is known for attention‑grabbing provocations on race and politics (e.g., inflammatory tweets, combative films that link Democrats to racist eras), and for turning controversies into commercial success. He argues his approach hasn’t changed from earlier work, claiming consistent provocation to challenge liberal orthodoxies; critics see increasing conspiratorial and extreme positions.

Overall, the piece argues D’Souza evolved from a respected conservative intellectual to a polarizing provocateur whose controversial theories and tactics gained renewed mainstream acceptance and influence with the rise of Trump, culminating in a presidential pardon that ignited debate about law, politics, and selective clemency.

A 46-year-old British woman, identified as Kay Longstaff, was rescued after spending about 10 hours in the Adriatic Sea following a fall from the aft deck of the cruise ship Norwegian Star late on Saturday. The ship was sailing toward Venice, roughly 60 miles off Croatia. CCTV allowed rescuers to determine the exact time and location of her fall; a Croatian coastguard patrol and other vessels and aircraft joined the search. She was spotted about 1.3 km from the fall site and reached by a rescue swimmer around 9:40 a.m. the next day.

Longstaff, who said she practices yoga and sang to stay awake while floating, was exhausted but conscious when found. She was taken to a hospital in Pula for observation and considered in stable condition; doctors noted she was young, healthy and a sports person. Officials said warm summer sea temperatures may have helped her survival. Norwegian Cruise Line and the British embassy in Croatia have been notified and the incident is under investigation. The report notes similar recent overboard incidents involving cruise passengers and crew.

Advertising this season shows a clear shift back to using the word "Christmas" rather than neutral terms like "holidays" or "season's greetings." The American Family Association (AFA), which has campaigned for retailers to explicitly say "Merry Christmas," says retailer recognition of Christmas rose from about 20% to 80% over five years and predicts its campaign may be nearing an end. Only a handful of national retailers remain on the AFA’s "Companies Against Christmas" list.

Despite that trend, the AFA continues to press campaigns and will target Dick’s Sporting Goods for using the phrase "Holiday Shop," urging its supporters to boycott the chain and contact executives. The group frames its efforts as consumer advocacy, arguing retailers shouldn’t advertise Christmas imagery without naming the holiday.

Retailers have responded in recent years when criticized: examples cited include Lowe’s renaming "Family Trees" to "Christmas Trees," Walmart switching "Holiday Shop" to "Christmas Shop," and Target and Gap making more explicit use of "Merry Christmas" after past boycotts. The National Retail Federation notes most consumers plan to celebrate Christmas (91% in a cited survey) and says holiday language is now a strategic, C-suite decision rather than an afterthought.

The AFA publishes a detailed "Naughty or Nice" listing that categorizes large retailers as Christmas-friendly, marginal, or against Christmas based on their advertising across print, broadcast, web and in-store materials; it updates and promotes that list and encourages supporters to report companies it deems censoring the word.

Multiple massive pileups and several smaller crashes on the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276) between Willow Grove and Bensalem on Friday morning closed the roadway for hours and involved dozens of vehicles. The incidents began around 8:30 a.m.; at peak one eastbound crash area involved about 75 cars plus several tractor-trailers, and another near the Route 1 exit involved roughly 30 cars and a jackknifed tractor-trailer. Overall reports cite up to 100 vehicles across multiple wreck sites, with many towed and numerous cars heavily damaged or totaled.

Emergency responders transported about 27–30 people to area hospitals; five were initially reported in serious condition but none had life‑threatening injuries. Hospitals reported treatment mainly for blunt-trauma soft-tissue and bone injuries and one closed-head injury that appeared to be improving; most patients were later treated and released.

Icy roadway conditions, packed ice from a recent snowstorm and sun glare (and road spray reducing visibility) are being blamed for the chain-reaction crashes. The Turnpike Commission had lifted storm restrictions only two hours before the pileups; investigators and officials emphasized driver responsibility to adjust speed to conditions. The eastbound lanes were reopened just before 4 p.m., roughly 7½ hours after the first crash. Tow yards collected dozens of vehicles, and cleanup required removing disabled commercial trucks and portions of the median to let trapped motorists exit.

A rare case of heteropaternal twins in northern Vietnam has prompted a wave of concerned calls to the Center for Genetic Analysis and Technologies (CGAT) in Hanoi. A couple from Hoa Binh Province had fraternal twins tested after relatives noted the children looked very different. DNA results showed the mother is the biological parent of both infants but the husband is the father of only one child — a first documented Vietnamese case of “heteropaternal superfecundation” (twins by different fathers). The story, reported widely, led many other fathers to call CGAT worried their twins’ differing appearances meant different fathers.

Experts emphasized that such cases are extremely rare globally (only about ten reported instances), though biologically possible when two ova released in the same fertile period are fertilized by sperm from different men. Specialists also stressed that fraternal twins commonly look quite dissimilar even with the same parents, and warned that DNA testing based solely on appearance can harm family ties. Authorities have kept the family’s identity confidential.

Hillary Clinton spoke at the Professional Business Women of California conference in San Francisco, using her closing remarks to call attention to everyday "indignities" faced by women and to urge Silicon Valley to do more on diversity and inclusion.

Key points:
- She cited recent examples of women being undermined while doing their jobs: White House reporter April Ryan being patronized and cut off by Sean Spicer in the press room, and Fox host Bill O’Reilly’s racist remark about Rep. Maxine Waters’s hair.
- Clinton argued such treatment—especially toward women of color—should not be normalized and warned that any woman could be targeted.
- She pressed tech companies to adopt stronger policies, especially paid parental leave, and to address workplace bias and harassment.
- Clinton referenced Uber’s recent sexual-harassment scandal and praised companies like Salesforce and Gap for making concrete commitments on equal pay and family leave.
- Her message emphasized that “corporate feminism” or symbolic gestures aren’t enough; Silicon Valley should use its resources and influence to implement practical, inclusive solutions that improve life for women broadly.

Hawaii conservationists are increasingly alarmed that feces from the islands’ large feral and free-roaming domestic cat population are contaminating coastal waters with the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and other pathogens, contributing to deaths and reproductive losses in Hawaiian monk seals and other native species. Monk seals are one of the world’s most endangered pinnipeds (about 1,100–1,300 individuals), and toxoplasmosis has been implicated in multiple mortalities: NOAA attributes at least eight confirmed seal deaths since 2001 to toxoplasmosis or contaminated prey/water, and researchers estimate the parasite has killed several more seals and affected seabirds and endangered land birds. Recent suspected cases include Hoku, a 10-year-old male that died last spring of severe brain inflammation consistent with protozoal infection, and a stillborn pup found in January whose mother may have transmitted toxoplasmosis in utero.

Cats in Hawai‘i—numbering in the hundreds of thousands (estimates of 300,000 on O‘ahu and 300,000–400,000 on Maui) and lacking natural predators—shed T. gondii oocysts that reach the ocean via runoff, sewage spills, wastewater injection plumes, and improper disposal (e.g., flushing cat litter). Oocysts are hardy and can survive in seawater for years. Other pathogens of concern for seals include Sarcocystis neurona, Neospora caninum, and leptospirosis (the latter linked to contaminated surface water and relatively high human incidence in Hawai‘i).

The disease threat compounds other pressures on monk seals—low juvenile survival (possibly linked to food competition and overfishing), human-seal interactions, and environmental contaminants—and could undermine recovery goals that require growth to roughly 2,900 animals before downlisting. Managers say toxoplasmosis is now among the primary concerns for seals on the main Hawaiian Islands.

Responses are contentious. NOAA and many conservationists advocate reducing feral-cat numbers via adoption programs and "humane euthanization" in some cases to protect native species and ecosystems. Animal welfare groups and humane society leaders oppose killing healthy cats, urging more use of trap-neuter-return (TNR), adoption, and nonlethal controls. Political efforts such as a proposed ban on feeding feral cats on state land have faced fierce public pushback.

Gaps in knowledge hamper targeted action: there are few Hawai‘i-specific studies mapping how and where T. gondii enters coastal waters, and necropsy challenges (decomposition) often prevent definitive cause-of-death determinations. Ongoing efforts include pathogen and contaminant screening of seals, mapping seal movements relative to sewage outflows and pollution sources, public outreach, and planning for a monk-seal hospital. Scientists stress the difficulty of generating political will to control free-roaming cats—citing prior failures to protect other native species—and warn that without better mitigation, disease and other threats could reverse tenuous population gains.

Key points

- In 2017 the CDC recorded 918 cases of congenital syphilis in the United States — the highest in 20 years — up 46% from 628 in 2016 and up from 362 in 2013. The rise has more than doubled cases since 2013.
- The 918 cases included 64 stillbirths and 13 infant deaths; overall syphilis (and other STD) diagnoses also surged in 2017, with 30,644 syphilis diagnoses (a 76% increase from 2016) and nearly 2.3 million cases of chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis combined — the fourth consecutive year of sharp rises.
- Congenital syphilis is preventable: pregnant women who test positive can be cured with penicillin, which prevents transmission to the fetus. Untreated maternal syphilis carries about an 80% chance of transmission and can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, infant death or severe lifelong disabilities.
- Contributing factors cited include failures in prenatal screening and treatment (women tested early can later acquire infection or not be treated in time), reduced access to prenatal care, declines in STD prevention funding and condom use, and the opioid crisis — substance use increases risky sexual behavior and reduces care-seeking.
- Cases were reported in 37 states; the South and West were hardest hit. Louisiana had the highest rate (93.4 cases per 100,000 births); California had the most cases in absolute numbers and faces barriers reaching marginalized populations without stable housing or prenatal care.
- Public health leaders call the trend a systemic failure and urge enhanced testing (early and again later in pregnancy), improved access to prenatal services, targeted outreach to at-risk women (including those with substance use disorders), stronger surveillance and increased funding — some advocate declaring a public health emergency and creating programs like those that virtually eliminated mother-to-child HIV transmission.

Bottom line: A preventable disease is resurging among pregnant women in the U.S., producing a record rise in infants born with syphilis and preventable deaths, driven by gaps in screening, treatment access, funding, and intersecting social and substance-use problems.

A day after NBC News reported that Flint’s corroded lead service lines have not been removed, Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder acknowledged a “trust issue” but said he has no immediate plan to replace the pipes. Snyder defended a short-term strategy of adding phosphates to coat pipes and limit lead leaching and said the state is still working to identify where lead lines are and will use third-party experts to verify corrosion control. He called full pipe replacement a large, complex planning task not on the short-term agenda.

Flint Mayor Karen Weaver and city officials have proposed a “Fast Start” plan to remove and replace up to 15,000 lead service lines—at an estimated cost of $55 million—prioritizing high-risk households (pregnant women, young children, seniors, those with compromised immune systems or elevated tap or blood-lead levels). The plan, which the city says would be provided at no cost to homeowners who authorize access, would replace lines with copper, install temporary kitchen filters, and could be executed in two phases using up to 32 crews; officials say work could begin within weeks though details and timelines remain provisional. The city seeks state and federal funding and partnership; Weaver insisted pipe replacement is essential to restore public trust.

Background: Flint’s water became contaminated with lead after a 2014 switch to Flint River water without adequate corrosion control. Residents rely on bottled/filtered water, numerous investigations (including federal) and lawsuits are underway, and lawmakers have proposed emergency funding to address pipe replacement and other recovery needs.

U.S. News & World Report evaluated 41 popular diets (detailed profiles on 20 reviewed by a 22‑expert panel) and ranked them across seven criteria: short‑ and long‑term weight loss, ease of following, nutritional completeness, diabetes prevention/management, and heart‑disease management. Key findings:

- Best overall diet: DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension).  
- Second best overall: Mediterranean Diet.  
- Best commercial weight‑loss plan: Weight Watchers (followed by Jenny Craig and the Raw Food Diet for weight loss).  
- Best for diabetes: DASH, then the Mayo Clinic diet.  
- Best heart‑healthy: Ornish Diet, followed by the TLC (Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes) diet.

Report emphasizes there is no one ideal diet for everyone; choice should match individual goals (weight loss, blood pressure, diabetes, heart health) and that exercise, while important, was outside the scope of the diet rankings. The findings come amid high U.S. overweight and obesity rates (about 34% overweight and 34% obese among adults, per 2007–2008 CDC data).

Researchers at Leiden University Medical Center tested the long-held notion that extreme fear can “curdle” blood by measuring coagulation markers in young, healthy adults exposed to a horror film versus a neutral documentary. In a crossover trial, 24 volunteers (≤30 years) watched the horror movie Insidious and the documentary A Year in Champagne one week apart (order determined by availability). Blood was drawn within 15 minutes before and after each 90-minute film and analyzed for coagulation markers (factor VIII, D-dimer, thrombin–antithrombin complexes, and prothrombin fragments 1+2). Participants rated their fear on a visual analogue scale.

Results from 21 participants (three were excluded for unreliable samples or procedural complications) showed that the horror film was rated substantially more frightening. Watching the horror movie was associated with a mean increase in coagulant factor VIII of 11.1 IU/dL compared with the documentary; factor VIII rose in 57% of participants during the horror film versus 14% during the documentary. No significant differences were found for D-dimer, thrombin–antithrombin complexes, or prothrombin fragments 1+2, indicating that increased factor VIII did not progress to thrombin formation or fibrin generation. No thrombotic events occurred.

The authors propose this acute coagulation response may be an adrenergic or stress-mediated physiological preparation for potential injury. Limitations include small sample size, nonrandomized movie order, a nonvalidated fear scale, and modest fear intensity. Clinically, while every 10 IU/dL rise in factor VIII has been associated with increased venous thrombosis risk, the study found no evidence of clot formation in healthy young adults. The paper wryly concludes that “bloodcurdling” has some literal basis, while advising relaxation during holidays to minimize thrombosis risk.

The Walt Disney Company announced it is parting ways with Pixar co‑founder and longtime chief creative officer John Lasseter after he took a sabbatical six months earlier amid accusations of inappropriate workplace behavior. Disney CEO Bob Iger praised Lasseter’s creative legacy but did not specify the misconduct behind his exit. Lasseter acknowledged “missteps,” apologized last fall for unwanted hugging and said he will remain involved as a consultant through year’s end before pursuing new creative work.

The decision followed internal reviews and a “day of listening” at Walt Disney Animation in February, during which employees raised concerns about a culture at Pixar and Disney Animation that some described as domineering and protective of powerful, mostly male creative leaders. Multiple current and former employees told reporters that crude remarks, inappropriate touching and a work environment that made it hard for women to advance were long‑standing problems. Pixar has been criticized as a “boy’s club”: only one of its 20 features has had a credited female director, and that director was removed midproduction after clashing with Lasseter.

Disney weighed allowing Lasseter to return in a reduced or nonmanagerial role—arguments in his favor included his creative importance and the risk he might join a competitor—but many employees, activists and online campaigns (including #LoseLasseter and a Change.org petition) opposed that, and some reportedly threatened to quit if he returned. Women in Animation and others welcomed the outcome as part of a broader shift toward holding senior figures accountable.

Leadership changes are expected: Jennifer Lee (Frozen) may be promoted at Walt Disney Animation and Pete Docter may take on more responsibility at Pixar. Lasseter’s departure comes as Pixar prepares to release Incredibles 2 and follows intensified scrutiny of workplace culture in Hollywood and beyond.

U.S. stocks fell on Wednesday, Jan. 20, 2016, but recovered sharply from steep intraday losses to close well above session lows as buyers stepped in around the S&P 500’s 1,800 technical level. Major indexes finished down: the S&P 500 lost about 1.2% to roughly 1,859 (its lowest close since April 2014), the Dow fell roughly 250 points after an earlier 566-point drop, and the Nasdaq finished mildly lower after attempting a late rally. Earlier intraday declines exceeded 3.5% for the majors, putting the market in correction territory year-to-date. Trading volume was heavy—about 12.4 billion shares, the busiest session since late August—and new 52-week lows on the NYSE (1,357) and Nasdaq (853) were the most on a single day since November 2008.

Sector action was volatile: small caps and biotech led the rebound, with the iShares Nasdaq Biotechnology ETF reversing a 3% drop to finish up ~2.75% after reaching +4% intraday; energy plunged nearly 3% on the day after briefly dipping 6%. Stocks that had fallen sharply, including Netflix and Apple, also pared losses into the close. Market participants and strategists attributed the late bounce largely to short-covering and bargain hunting once the S&P hit the 1,800 area, though some remained skeptical the rebound would hold.

Veteran investor Mark D. Cook argued the market is in a bear phase, pointing to persistent selling in oil and emerging problems in China. He highlighted technical signs—short-lived “one-day wonder” rallies and lack of institutional buying activity—and outlined the four psychological stages investors go through in a bear market (denial, high anxiety, fear, panic). Cook believes the market is still in the early (denial) stage and warned broader capitulation and deeper losses could follow before a true bottom is reached.

Michael James “Mike” Rogan, 42, of Stratford, Wisconsin, died April 17, 2015, after a deer struck his family’s van on a rural Marathon County highway while he was driving his pregnant wife and seven children to the hospital. Mike was pronounced dead at St. Joseph’s Hospital in Marshfield; his wife Niki and their children (ages 2 to 15) sustained only minor injuries. Niki gave birth hours later to their eighth child, a son named Blaise.

Born March 20, 1973, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, he was the son of Ronald and Susan (Rogan) Bornbach. Mike served in the U.S. Marine Corps (and later in the reserves). He married Nicole S. Richardson on July 11, 1998. For about eight years he owned and operated Arnie’s Farm Care, helping organic farmers across Wisconsin. He was active in St. Mary’s Oratory in Wausau—singing in the choir, participating in The Holy Name Society and youth work—and enjoyed beer making, hunting, and time outdoors with his children.

Survivors include his wife Niki and their children Anne, Jon, Claire, Ben, Luke, Jacob, Gemma and Blaise; his parents Ron and Sue Bornbach; sister Beth Bornbach (and daughter Johanna); brothers Joseph and Gabriel Bornbach; and mother‑in‑law Kathleen Richardson. He was predeceased by grandparents John and Sylvia Rogan, several aunts and uncles, and his father‑in‑law Arnold Richardson.

A Mass of Christian Burial was held April 25, 2015, at St. Mary’s Roman Catholic Oratory in Wausau with burial at St. Mary’s Catholic Cemetery in Marathon, where military rites were performed by VFW Post 6352. Visitations were held April 24–25. A memorial fund has been established to support Mike’s widow and children; friends and community members organized additional fundraising and support efforts after the crash.

Jared Fogle has filed court documents seeking to withdraw his guilty plea and challenging one of his charges — “traveling for the purpose of engaging in illicit sexual conduct.” In the filing (reported by The Blast), Fogle argues the charge was improperly applied to him and points to former Team USA doctor Larry Nassar as a comparative example, saying Nassar, who also traveled while committing sexual crimes, was not charged with that specific offense. Fogle claims this shows a divergent application of the law and asks that the travel charge be dropped.

He also contends he was pressured into pleading guilty, accusing prosecutors of modifying charges to force a plea and alleging his expensive attorneys pushed him toward the deal to avoid financial ruin. Fogle mentions struggles with “alcohol and sex addictions” and says doctors later medicated him to control his libido. The court has not yet ruled on his motion.
