Reports say 18-year-old Justin Bieber annoyed fellow passengers on an Air New Zealand flight returning from a promotional tour to Australia/New Zealand by loudly swearing in first class while surrounded by his entourage. A female passenger, described as a mother of two, confronted him and asked him to stop using profanity on the plane; sources claim Bieber was embarrassed, apologized, and briefly sang a cappella — though that last detail is likely apocryphal.

Separately, actors Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard, promoting their film Hit & Run, said living near Bieber has been disruptive. Shepard complained that music, parties and paparazzi since Bieber moved into a nearby rental have made their neighborhood chaotic, while Bell noted they can’t be sure which house the noise is coming from but have noticed the blaring music.

A California couple walking their dog found a buried cache of rare U.S. gold coins on their rural Northern California property last year. The hoard—dug from eight cans beneath a tree—contains 1,427 coins dated 1847–1894: four $5 pieces, fifty $10 pieces and 1,373 $20 double eagles, most minted at the San Francisco Mint. Many are in near-mint condition, likely stashed soon after minting, which makes them especially valuable; the collection has been appraised at about $11 million. One standout, an 1866-S "No Motto" $20, is valued at over $1 million. The find is described by numismatist Don Kagin, who is handling sales and marketing, as the largest such U.S. coin discovery; comparable past finds were far smaller or were located with known provenance (e.g., shipwrecks). Several coins were auctioned at the Old San Francisco Mint, where an 1874 $20 double eagle sold for $15,000, and many others were later listed for sale online. The discoverers, a middle‑aged husband and wife who asked to remain anonymous to avoid prospectors, plan to keep a few coins, pay off debts and donate proceeds to local charities; funds from the recent auction will help efforts to convert the Old Mint into a museum. The origin of the buried stash remains unknown, and speculative links to outlaws or thefts have not been substantiated.

This document combines two items: a note about web archiving crawls and a CNN report on new UN sanctions against North Korea.

Web-archiving note
- The Internet Archive is crawling and saving web pages as they are created and archiving the pages those pages reference. The aim is to preserve the exact versions cited by authors so links do not break when source pages change or disappear. Archived links can replace or accompany original links to show what authors originally intended. The broader goal is to eliminate broken links across the web; these particular crawls support “No More 404” sites.

UN Security Council resolution on North Korea (CNN)
- On August 5, 2017, the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2371 (15-0) imposing tougher sanctions on North Korea in response to recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) tests and UN-resolution violations.
- Key measures: bans on major North Korean exports (coal, iron, iron ore, lead, lead ore, seafood), restrictions on banks and joint ventures, prohibition on hiring additional North Korean workers abroad, asset freezes and travel bans on nine individuals and four entities (including a major North Korean bank). The sanctions aim to cut more than one-third of North Korea’s estimated $3 billion annual export revenue.
- The US described the sanctions as among the strongest in a generation; Nikki Haley and President Trump welcomed China and Russia’s support. China resisted harsher measures (e.g., cutting oil supplies).
- Reactions and rationale: US and other Western envoys framed the sanctions as necessary to curb North Korea’s missile and nuclear programs; China and Russia cautioned against escalatory military responses (criticized deployment of THAAD in South Korea). China’s leadership emphasized that sanctions are not the ultimate goal but a means to bring North Korea back to negotiations.
- North Korea’s state media warned the US against “hostile policy,” threatening severe retaliation if attacked.
- Analysts were divided on effectiveness: some said the measures would hurt elite revenues and could pressure Pyongyang, while others argued the regime is willing to endure hardship and is determined to keep its nuclear program, so sanctions alone are unlikely to force denuclearization. Some experts urged further actions (e.g., cutting oil and repatriating workers) if North Korea continues tests.

Researchers report that genetic risk factors for schizophrenia also predict likelihood and heavier use of cannabis, suggesting part of the well-established association between cannabis use and schizophrenia may reflect shared genetic influences rather than cannabis solely causing the disorder. The study published in Molecular Psychiatry analyzed about 2,082 healthy Australians (1,011 cannabis users), calculating each person’s genetic risk score for schizophrenia and finding those with higher scores were more likely to try cannabis and to use it more heavily.

The finding does not rule out that cannabis can increase schizophrenia risk—especially in genetically vulnerable people—but implies the relationship is bidirectional and more complex than simple cause-and-effect. Experts note that schizophrenia and cannabis use are polygenic and influenced by many environmental factors; some evidence shows cannabis worsens illness course or accelerates onset in high-risk individuals, while other analyses reduce that apparent effect after controlling for confounders. Because schizophrenia affects roughly 1% of the population, most cannabis users will not develop it.

Authors argue the genetic overlap matters for understanding public-health impact and policy: any benefit from restricting cannabis to prevent schizophrenia is likely small, though people with family histories of psychosis should still avoid cannabis as a precaution. The study needs replication, and experts caution that causality remains unresolved and multiple mechanisms (genetic predisposition, environmental exposure, and interactions) likely contribute to the observed association.

Senate Republicans narrowly passed a resolution under the Congressional Review Act that overturns an Obama-era rule preventing states from withholding Title X family-planning funds from providers that also perform abortions, such as Planned Parenthood. The measure passed 51–50 after Vice President Mike Pence cast the tie-breaking vote; two Republican senators, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, joined all Democrats in opposing it. Georgia Sen. Johnny Isakson, recovering from back surgery, returned to vote and helped create the 50–50 tie.

The bill now goes to President Trump, who was expected to sign it. Supporters say it restores state authority to direct Title X dollars to providers that don’t offer abortions (Title X funds cannot be used for abortion itself) and lets states steer money to community health centers and other clinics. Opponents — including Democratic senators and Planned Parenthood leaders — called the action an attack on women’s access to contraception, cancer screenings and other reproductive-health services, warning it will reduce care for low-income patients (Title X served about 4 million clients in 2015, most of whom were low-income women).

The vote is a political win for anti-abortion groups after the collapse of the House GOP’s broader health-care repeal effort. It follows a recent pattern of Congress using the Congressional Review Act to overturn late-administration regulations and marks Pence’s second tie-breaking vote early in the Trump administration. Critics warned Republicans will continue attempts to cut funding to Planned Parenthood through other measures.

A Danish cohort study of 55,502 adults (aged 50–64 at baseline) suggests moderate chocolate consumption is associated with a modestly lower risk of developing atrial fibrillation (AF). Using diet data collected between 1993–1997 and linked to national health registries over an average 13.5-year follow-up, researchers identified ~3,346 AF cases. Compared with eating chocolate less than once a month, participants who ate about 1 ounce (~28 g) once per week had ~17% lower AF risk; those eating 2–6 ounces per week had ~20% lower risk; and daily consumers had ~16% lower risk. Women saw the largest reduction at one serving per week; men at 2–6 servings per week.

Authors note possible biological mechanisms (cocoa flavanols’ anti-inflammatory, vasorelaxant and antioxidant effects) and point to prior evidence linking dark chocolate with better cardiovascular measures. But the study is observational and cannot prove causation. Limitations include lack of data on chocolate type or flavanol content, potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., sleep apnea, kidney disease), possible diet changes over time, and a relatively homogeneous Danish population. Commentators call the findings interesting and say randomized trials with quantified cocoa doses would be needed to assess causality. Overall message: moderate chocolate intake, particularly higher-cocoa varieties, may be a reasonable snack option within a healthy lifestyle, but it’s not a substitute for proven preventive measures (healthy diet, exercise, no smoking).

Key points

- Brazil sharply cut Amazon deforestation from a 2004 peak (27,772 km2/yr) to a 2012 low (4,575 km2/yr) through protected areas and indigenous lands, stronger enforcement, supply‑chain and credit measures, fines and embargoes. This reduced land‑use CO2 emissions by about 63% (2005–2012) and supported Brazil’s Paris commitments.

- Since 2012 deforestation has been rising again. Official satellite monitoring (PRODES) reported 7,900 km2 lost between Aug 2017 and Jul 2018—a 13.7% increase year‑on‑year and the largest annual loss since 2008. Most losses occurred in Mato Grosso and Pará. Authorities attribute much of the rise to illegal logging and organised crime.

- The incoming president (election runoff 28 Oct; inauguration Jan) Jair Bolsonaro campaigned on weakening environmental protection: proposals include closing or subsuming the environment ministry, weakening enforcement and licensing, opening indigenous reserves to mining, banning some international NGOs, and withdrawing from the Paris Agreement. He has strong agribusiness backing.

- Modeling by the commentary’s authors projects that removing Brazil’s environmental protections would rapidly raise primary‑forest loss in the Amazon to about 25,600 km2/yr—comparable to early‑2000s rates and a 268% increase from 2017. Within a decade that would total areas the size of the UK or Oregon; about 18% of projected clearing would occur inside protected areas and indigenous lands.

- Carbon consequences: the model estimates cumulative emissions from 2021–2030 of ~13.12 GtCO2e (average ~1.31 GtCO2e/yr), roughly 3% of current global emissions and a substantial share of the remaining carbon budget for the 1.5°C target. Such emissions would make Brazil’s Paris targets effectively unattainable.

- Ecological and climate risks extend beyond carbon: the Amazon recycles regional moisture and helps sustain rainfall over large parts of South America; substantial additional loss could weaken those moisture cycles, reducing regional (and potentially extra‑regional) rainfall, harming agriculture and cities, and contributing to shifts toward a drier, savanna‑like state.

- Scientists warn the Amazon may be near a “tipping point.” Some estimates place the threshold at 20–25% loss of original forest; Brazil’s estimates already show ~17% loss. Continued deforestation, fires and warming together increase the risk of an abrupt biome shift with global biodiversity and climate consequences.

- Policy implication: strong political will and continued enforcement, protected area expansion and restoration are essential to prevent rapid forest loss, protect indigenous lands and biodiversity, and avoid large carbon releases that would undermine global climate goals.

Sources & authors: commentary and modeling by Aline C. Soterroni, Fernando M. Ramos, Michael Obersteiner and Stephen Polasky (Soterroni et al., Environmental Research Letters 2018), plus reporting from The Guardian, BBC and others summarizing 2017–2018 official PRODES data and expert analyses.

Former President George W. Bush made light of an awkward moment at Donald Trump’s inauguration when he struggled to put on a poncho — a scene Ellen DeGeneres joked about on her show, where Bush laughed it off and blamed “genetics” after seeing his late mother Barbara Bush in a similar picture. On Ellen he was given an official presidential poncho with instructions.

Bush has been promoting his new art book Portraits of Courage, a collection of paintings of veterans, and spoke warmly about his friendship with former First Lady Michelle Obama, saying they bonded over humor and often sat together at public events. He said he’d be open to collaborating with Barack and Michelle Obama on causes for service members, veterans and families.

Separately, attendees reported Bush privately described Trump’s inaugural ceremony as “some weird shit” after leaving the dais. The poncho moment quickly became an internet meme and part of broader commentary on the unusual tone of the inauguration.

Harold Lyle Hayes, a 21-year-old medic with the Army Air Forces’ 807th Medical Air Evacuation Transport Squadron, survived a 63‑day ordeal behind German lines in Albania after the C-53D transport plane carrying 30 Americans (13 nurses, 13 medics, and four crew) crash‑landed there on Nov. 8, 1943. Blown far off course by a storm, attacked by German fighters and antiaircraft fire, the crew made a belly landing in a marsh. One crewman was injured; the rest had no weapons and little idea where they were.

Albanian partisans and villagers hid, guided and fed the Americans—often at grave risk to themselves—leading them through brutal mountain terrain, blizzards, hunger, illness, lice and diarrhea, and occasional crossfire between rival partisan groups. The group endured thefts, near‑rescues (including a failed air pickup) and the separation of three nurses who hid in Berat for months. British and American intelligence organized rescue efforts: OSS Capt. Lloyd G. Smith and British agent Lt. Gavan Duffy helped coordinate the eventual extraction. On Jan. 9, 1944, after trekking more than 600 miles in harsh conditions, 27 Americans reached the coast and were ferried back to Italy; the remaining three nurses were rescued in March.

Afterward the survivors were ordered to keep their experiences and the identities of their Albanian helpers secret, both to protect escape routes and because Albania fell under Enver Hoxha’s repressive postwar regime; some collaborators were later imprisoned or executed. Hayes rarely spoke of the episode for decades. His firsthand recollections are a key source for Cate Lineberry’s book The Secret Rescue: An Untold Story of American Nurses and Medics Behind Nazi Lines, and for earlier memoirs and accounts. Hayes went on to a civilian career as an aeronautical engineer, married in 1944, and is the last living member of the group, preserving their story for posterity.

Over two days of heavy bombardment in late February 2018, Syrian government forces and allied groups launched intense airstrikes, rocket and artillery attacks on the besieged rebel-held enclave of eastern Ghouta, just outside Damascus, killing and injuring hundreds of civilians and prompting warnings of an imminent humanitarian catastrophe. Local monitors and rescue workers reported roughly 194–200 deaths in 48 hours (other tallies cite about 98–127 on individual days), including many children; local counts say more than 700 people have been killed in the past three months. Exact figures remain uncertain because rescue operations continue and some families buried victims privately.

Humanitarian and rights organizations condemned the assaults as potential war crimes. Amnesty International said “flagrant war crimes” were being committed; the White Helmets described the bombardment as apocalyptic. Medical facilities were heavily hit—at least five to seven hospitals and clinics, including a maternity center, were bombed, forcing some to suspend operations and hampering treatment of the injured amid acute shortages of supplies. Aid agencies warned that the enclave’s six-year siege, collapsing medical capacity and rising malnutrition had left its roughly 400,000 civilians “boxed in” with nowhere safe to flee.

The strikes included barrel bombs, air-to-ground attacks and mass rocket fire, and came amid reports that regime forces were preparing for a ground offensive to retake the last major rebel pocket near the capital. Rebel groups returned fire, shelling parts of Damascus and killing and wounding civilians there. The escalation drew urgent UN appeals to stop targeting civilians; the UN and child-protection agencies expressed outrage and described the situation as among the worst of the war. Observers warned the assault risked producing atrocities comparable to earlier high-casualty events in Syria’s conflict.

Elsewhere, the report noted related developments in northern Syria where pro-government fighters were said to be moving into Afrin amid Turkey’s offensive against Kurdish YPG forces, raising the prospect of a wider confrontation.

Between Aug. 29 and Aug. 31, 2015, the Arizona Department of Public Safety investigated four shootings in which bullets struck vehicles along an eight-mile stretch of Interstate 10 through central Phoenix.

- Aug. 29, ~11:03 a.m.: An eastbound SUV was shot; a 13‑year‑old female front-seat passenger suffered a cut to her right ear, was treated on scene and not hospitalized.
- Aug. 29, ~11:09 a.m.: A westbound passenger bus between 35th and 59th avenues was struck; only the driver was aboard and he was uninjured.
- Aug. 29, ~10:15 p.m.: A motorist heard a loud bang and later (the next day) discovered bullet holes on the passenger side of her vehicle near 16th Street.
- Aug. 31, ~4:25 a.m.: A work truck eastbound near 24th Street/14th Avenue was struck; damage consistent with a bullet hit was found on the driver‑side front headlamp after the driver initially thought a rock had struck the truck.

All incidents occurred within the same general stretch of I-10. DPS Director Frank Milstead said it is unclear whether the shootings are related or random and warned motorists to stay vigilant. Detectives are investigating and asking anyone with information to contact DPS or Silent Witness; a web tip form and phone numbers were provided. Photos related to the incidents were released by DPS.

Researchers reported tiny tube-, filament- and knob-like structures in 3.77–4.28 billion‑year‑old rocks from the Nuvvuagittuq belt in Quebec that they interpret as microfossils of iron‑oxidizing bacteria that lived on ancient seafloors near hydrothermal vents. The structures are hematite‑filled, consistent in size and shape despite later metamorphism, and are accompanied by carbon‑rich material with isotope ratios falling within the biological range and magnetite‑ringed blobs thought to reflect interactions between organic matter and vent iron precipitates. If confirmed, these would be the oldest direct evidence of life and would, along with recently reported 3.7‑billion‑year‑old Greenland stromatolites, imply diverse microbial ecosystems existed very early in Earth’s history and support hydrothermal vents as plausible cradles for life.

However, the claim is controversial. Critics call the features “dubiofossils” and note that ancient, highly metamorphosed rocks can produce mineral structures that mimic biology; past assertions of the oldest fossils (e.g., Schopf’s 3.46‑billion‑year‑old putative bacteria) have been disputed as abiotic mineral forms. Some researchers welcome the multiple lines of evidence and find the morphologies suggestive of biological origins, but many urge caution, calling for better regional geologic context, tighter age constraints, and more definitive exclusion of nonbiological explanations before a consensus can be reached.

Investigators arrested 72-year-old Joseph James DeAngelo on April 24 as the suspected Golden State Killer/East Area Rapist, accused of roughly 12 murders, at least 45 rapes and hundreds of burglaries in California from the mid-1970s to 1986. The breakthrough came after cold-case detectives used forensic genealogy: DNA from crime scenes was uploaded in GEDmatch, a public, volunteer-run genealogy site that aggregates raw profiles people export from commercial services. GEDmatch returned distant relatives (third- and fourth-cousin matches), allowing investigators and a genetic genealogist to build extensive family trees—more than 25 branches and one with ~1,000 people—and progressively narrow suspects by cross-referencing demographics, locations and surveillance. Authorities then collected discarded items from DeAngelo for direct DNA matches; two independent samples produced overwhelming matches to decades-old crime-scene DNA and led to his arrest in Citrus Heights.

The case highlights both the power and privacy concerns of open-source genetic databases. Unlike commercial firms that typically require legal process for law-enforcement access, GEDmatch’s public uploads enabled familial searching without statutory limits, meaning people can be implicated by relatives’ uploads even if they never submitted DNA themselves. Experts note this creates promising investigative tools but also potential for broad, unregulated use of genetic information; some companies may be compelled to produce data via warrants. Prosecutors are coordinating prosecutions across multiple counties; some rape charges may be barred by statutes of limitations, but several jurisdictions plan to pursue murder and remaining viable sexual-assault cases.

Defense Secretary Ash Carter told the Senate Armed Services Committee that only about 60 vetted Syrian opposition fighters had been enrolled in the U.S. train-and-equip program as of early July, far below the program’s goal of roughly 5,400 fighters in the first year. The revelation, following President Obama’s recent Pentagon briefing defending the overall strategy against the Islamic State (IS/ISIL), sparked sharp criticism from Republicans — notably Sen. John McCain — who argued the low turnout shows the administration’s approach is failing. Democrats urged patience, saying rigorous U.S. vetting and other valid constraints explain the slow start.

Carter said roughly 7,000 volunteers are being screened, but stringent background checks, documentation requirements, and pledges to obey the laws of war have eliminated many candidates. Another major hurdle is the U.S. requirement that recruits agree to fight ISIL only and not target the Assad regime; many Syrian fighters resent Assad more than ISIL and refuse to accept that limitation. Uncertainty about what support the U.S. would provide (air cover, resupply, protection from Assad’s forces) also discourages recruits, and officials acknowledged internal debate within the administration over the extent of U.S. commitments.

Carter and Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. Martin Dempsey defended the broader campaign, noting thousands of coalition airstrikes and tactical gains, but acknowledged setbacks and that efforts to train Iraqi and Syrian forces remain early and behind expectations. Pentagon officials said they expect throughput to improve as vetting and training processes are refined and relationships with opposition groups grow, but critics warned the program is unlikely to meet its stated goals without clearer commitments and more robust support.

This piece criticizes House Republicans’ recent priorities and tactics as Congress approaches automatic across-the-board federal spending cuts known as the sequester. It describes H.R. 667, a measure to rename NASA’s Dryden Flight Research Center after Neil Armstrong, as an emblematic example of lawmakers’ deliberate idleness: taking up a symbolic renaming at a moment when tougher fiscal choices loom. Sponsored by Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy, the bill prompted lengthy floor praise for Armstrong while Congress largely avoided substantive action on the looming sequester.

The article outlines how House Republicans have effectively embraced inaction because doing nothing will trigger a 2.5 percent cut in all federal spending without any new tax increases—an outcome they prefer to another negotiated deal that raised taxes last year. Speaker John Boehner urged President Obama to negotiate with Senate Democrats, while House Republicans scheduled minimal floor time and planned recesses that coincide with key budget deadlines.

Detailed color from a single afternoon in the House highlights procedural delays and ceremonial remarks, culminating in extended debate over the NASA renaming—a bill that had previously passed the House overwhelmingly. Democrats, represented in the debate by Rep. Donna Edwards and Minority Whip Steny Hoyer, warned that the sequester would force damaging cuts to an already strained NASA budget and other programs. The narrative also satirically notes that members of Congress won’t suffer salary cuts under sequestration, while staff face furloughs and many public services would be reduced, arguing that lawmakers have little immediate incentive to avert the sequester.

Overall, the story uses the Armstrong renaming and congressional behavior to illustrate a broader critique: that Republicans are using procedural delay and symbolic measures to avoid decisive budgeting, effectively welcoming across-the-board cuts rather than negotiating alternatives.

A 95-year-old former New York City resident, Jakiw Palij, believed to have been a guard at the Nazi-run Trawniki labor camp in occupied Poland, has been deported from the United States to Germany, U.S. officials and Reuters report. Palij’s presence at Trawniki is tied to one of the largest single massacres of the Holocaust—about 6,000 Jewish men, women and children were shot there on Nov. 3, 1943. He emigrated to the U.S. in 1949, became a citizen in 1957, but lied about his wartime activities; his U.S. citizenship was revoked in 2003 and a deportation order issued in 2004.

After years in which no European country would accept him, Germany agreed—following talks between U.S. and German officials—and Palij was placed in an elderly care home in Ahlen. U.S. officials, including Ambassador Richard Grenell, said President Trump prioritized getting Palij out of the country. The U.S. Justice Department and the White House say Palij admitted training at the SS-run Trawniki camp in 1943 and served as an armed guard who prevented prisoners’ escape.

German authorities have not opened criminal proceedings; investigators say membership or training alone is not enough under German law to prosecute without proof of specific participation in or facilitation of killings. Jens Rommel, head of Germany’s office that investigates Nazi crimes, said there are currently no preliminary proceedings or arrest warrant and that evidence tying Palij to specific units or actions remains insufficient. Germany has a complex postwar record on prosecuting Nazis, though recent precedent (e.g., the 2011 conviction of John Demjanjuk) has allowed convictions based on service at extermination camps without proving individual acts.

The Palij case emerged as part of broader U.S. efforts dating to the early 1990s—after records surfaced following the Cold War—to denaturalize and deport former Trawniki guards. U.S. prosecutors successfully denaturalized 16 former SS members who served at Trawniki.

California officials are considering easing statewide drought mandates and letting local water agencies set their own conservation targets. The State Water Resources Control Board is weighing a proposal that would require cities and districts to compare their expected water supplies to projected demand over a potential three‑year drought and set conservation goals based on that gap; the rule would run through January. The change — backed by agencies like Irvine Ranch Water District — would allow some areas to loosen restrictions if local supplies look sufficient, while others, particularly hard‑hit Southern California, could keep strict limits. Permanent statewide bans on obvious waste (e.g., washing sidewalks with a hose or washing cars without a shutoff nozzle) would remain. Officials say recent El Niño precipitation helped Northern California reservoirs, but the drought is ongoing and local control acknowledges differing regional conditions while relying on continued public conservation.

Here are concise summaries of the two human‑interest stories:

1) Paddleboard crossing from Cuba to Key West
- Ben Friberg, a 35‑year‑old guitarist from Chattanooga, became the first person to paddleboard the full Florida Straits, completing an approximately 110–111 mile crossing from Cuba to Key West in about 28 hours on Aug. 2, 2013.
- He arrived dehydrated and exhausted but otherwise in good condition; his father watched from an accompanying support boat that carried a medic and navigator.
- Friberg stood on a 14‑foot board for most of the trip, pausing only briefly to snack. He wore sun protection, gloves and special socks.
- He said the trip aimed to promote peace and understanding between Cuba and the U.S. and a healthy lifestyle. He previously set a 24‑hour paddleboard distance record (238 miles on Canada’s Yukon River).
- The report notes others have crossed the Straits by board or surfboard (including a 1992 windsurfer and a 2011 paddleboard attempt from 14 miles off Cuba), and that swimmer crossings are rare (Australian Susan Maroney succeeded in 1997 using a shark cage).

2) Freshwater diving record in Tennessee
- Jerry Hall, 49, set what is believed to be a new freshwater dive record by remaining submerged in South Holston Lake, Tenn., for 6 days, 1 hour and 42 minutes (dive began July 27; he surfaced Aug. 2, 2013).
- Hall had previously held a five‑day record (2008). He remained on liquids only, expected to have lost about 30 pounds, and had gained weight beforehand to offset loss.
- He emerged weak, cold and emotional, hugged his son, and asked for simple comforts (a hot dog, a beer, hot shower). The dive was monitored around the clock by other divers and medical staff and served as a fundraiser for the Bristol Motor Speedway children’s charity.
- The time will be submitted to Guinness World Records for certification.

Massachusetts Republicans are struggling to find a candidate for the upcoming special Senate election to fill John Kerry’s seat. Many prominent GOP figures have declined to run, leaving the party with only little-known potential contenders and uncertainty about whether they can field anyone. Tagg Romney, Mitt Romney’s eldest son and a visible surrogate during his father's presidential campaign, announced he will not run, saying he’s focused on his business and family despite being flattered by outreach urging him to run. The seat is currently occupied temporarily by William “Mo” Cowan until a special election in June.

A 2012 incident resurfaced this week after the widow of Anthony Hensley filed a wrongful-death lawsuit in Cook County Circuit Court. Hensley, 37, a father of two from Villa Park, drowned April 14, 2012, after a mute swan attacked and overturned his kayak in a deep retention pond at the Bay Colony condominium complex in unincorporated Maine Township. According to the complaint, Hensley—who frequently visited the complex to feed and tend swans placed there to deter geese—was repeatedly lunged at by a nesting, territorial swan as he tried to swim to shore and did not reach safety. Dive crews recovered him from the roughly 50-foot-deep pond; he was later pronounced dead at a hospital. OSHA investigated but closed the matter with no violations found involving Knox Swan and Dog (the company that places swans to control geese), and that company is not a party to the suit.

Hensley’s widow, Amy, alleges negligence by the property management companies and the condominium and homeowners’ associations that owned and operated Bay Colony, arguing they “should have known” mute swans are territorial and dangerous and therefore are liable for “knowingly keeping dangerous animals on the premises.” She seeks at least $50,000 in damages. Named defendants have not commented. The article also includes unrelated material about methods to deter geese (including use of swan decoys), which provides context on why properties sometimes keep swans.

A DeKalb County, Georgia, firefighter, Robert Sutton, is being hailed a hero after catching an infant tossed from a second-floor window of a burning apartment complex on Glenwood Road in Decatur. The fire erupted on a Tuesday afternoon; when a father, trapped by flames and smoke, handed his baby out the window, Sutton—one of the first responders on scene—caught the child “like a football pass.” Contractors renovating the next building recorded the rescue on a cellphone. The family escaped without injuries; the father was later removed by ladder. Sutton, a 10-year veteran with two young children, credits training, teamwork and being in the right place at the right time rather than personal heroism. Fire department leaders praised his situational awareness and the crew’s preparedness. The footage has circulated widely and prompted public admiration for the firefighters’ training and swift actions. 

(Note: the document also contains unrelated brief news items and background about web archiving efforts to preserve referenced pages.)

Researchers at the Scripps Research Institute have developed a novel approach that may enable a blood test for Alzheimer’s disease by detecting disease-specific antibodies. Instead of hunting for the native antigens that trigger immune responses, the team screened thousands of synthetic molecules (peptoids) that act as antigen surrogates and bind antibodies. In a small study published in Cell, three peptoids captured antibodies that were present in blood from six Alzheimer’s patients but not from healthy controls or Parkinson’s patients; follow-up testing reportedly found similar signals in people with mild cognitive impairment. In a separate screen of 200 elderly non‑demented volunteers, about 8% showed elevated levels of the same antibodies, suggesting potential as an early predictor.

The technique is rapid, adaptable to other diseases, and has been licensed to OPKO Health for development of diagnostic kits potentially available within months. However, results are preliminary: the sample size was small, patients already had diagnosed disease, and larger studies are needed to confirm specificity, timing of antibody appearance, and clinical utility—especially given the current lack of disease‑modifying Alzheimer’s treatments.

On August 31, 2014, China’s top parliamentary body, the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (NPC), endorsed a tightly controlled framework for Hong Kong’s 2017 chief executive election that requires candidates to win majority support from a nominating committee likely dominated by Beijing loyalists. The decision—portrayed by Beijing and Hong Kong Chief Executive Leung Chun-ying as a milestone toward “one person, one vote”—was denounced by pro-democracy activists as a move to effectively bar opposition candidates and produce a constrained, “Chinese-style” democracy.

Pro-democracy groups, led by the founders of the Occupy Central civil disobedience movement (Benny Tai, Chan Kin-man and Reverend Chu Yiu-ming), vowed to launch peaceful non-violent occupation actions aimed at Hong Kong’s Central financial district, saying dialogue had been exhausted. Hundreds of protesters and large police deployments, fences and barricades around government sites signaled preparations for possible large-scale demonstrations. Organizers warned the nominating rules would make it “almost impossible” for genuine opposition candidates to appear on the ballot; they said the movement would press on though it had not yet secured broad middle-class backing.

The NPC framework must still pass a two-thirds vote in Hong Kong’s 70-seat legislature, where pro-democracy camps hold enough seats to block it; if blocked, the leader would likely again be chosen by a small, pro-establishment election committee. Beijing officials defended the decision as legal and prudent, while Chinese authorities warned against “illegal” protests and foreign interference. The U.S. urged respect for freedoms of assembly and expression and said the chief executive’s legitimacy would be strengthened by genuine voter choice.

Separately, Macau’s chief executive Fernando (Dr.) Chui Sai-on was “re-elected” unopposed by a 400-member pro-Beijing election committee, receiving about 96% of votes amid protests calling for universal suffrage. The vote followed an unofficial civil referendum favoring direct elections for 2019 and arrests of some referendum organizers over data-law allegations. Chui pledged to focus on economic diversification away from gambling and acknowledged shortcomings in his first term. Activists warned lack of sincere reform could fuel further political activism.

Belgium has reformed the royal allowance and tax rules so members of the royal household will for the first time since 1830 pay taxes and lose some state benefits. The government approved changes that restrict state payments to the monarch, the heir (and spouse) and the widow/widower of a monarch; an abdicated monarch would also receive an allowance. Other family members will see their stipends cut or eliminated: Crown Prince Philippe’s income will be converted from a large tax-free allowance (previously about €923,000) to a taxable gross salary of €180,000, with job-related staff and expense costs paid separately and closely scrutinized; his siblings Laurent and Astrid will receive gross wages of €90,000. Queen Fabiola’s allowance will be sharply reduced (to roughly €450,000 from about €1.3–1.4 million in earlier reports) and surviving spouses’ allowances will be reduced to two-thirds of an heir’s for 10 years, then half thereafter. The royal household will also lose income- and VAT-exempt status. The move followed media and political pressure after reports that Queen Fabiola planned to use a foundation or trust to avoid Belgian inheritance tax. The changes align Belgium more closely with other European monarchies that limit allowances and apply taxes. King Albert II remains exempt from the new rules due to constitutional protections for the reigning sovereign.

A Chicago kayaker fishing near Waukegan Harbor discovered a 4-foot American alligator floating in Lake Michigan around 9:30 a.m.; he initially thought it was a dead fish. Waukegan Animal Control responded after the kayaker called 911 and retrieved the animal, which had its mouth taped shut. The alligator was transferred to the Wildlife Discovery Center in Lake Forest, where staff and a veterinarian will assess its condition; the curator said the animal appeared thin and likely had limited time in cold lake water but could recover if there are no major infections. City officials said they will investigate possible abandonment (which is a crime). The city initially misidentified the animal as a caiman but was later told it was an American alligator. Officials noted stricter state regulations have reduced such exotic-animal abandonments in recent years; past local incidents included a large Burmese python in 2012 and an alligator found in the Chicago River in 2010.

A second girl linked to the 2014 Chibok abductions was reported freed this week amid a broader military operation against Boko Haram, though details and claims remain disputed.

Key points:
- The Nigerian military said on Thursday that Serah Luka was among 97 women and children freed in operations in Borno’s Demboa area; they also reported 35 militants killed. The army described Luka as a Chibok school pupil abducted in April 2014 and said she is receiving medical care.
- Activists from the #BringBackOurGirls campaign disputed that Luka was among the mass April 14, 2014 Chibok school kidnappings, saying she had been taken from her home in Madagali, Adamawa, though she did attend the Chibok school briefly.
- The announcement came two days after Amina Ali Darsha Nkeki — the first of the so-called Chibok girls to be found since 2014 — was located by a civilian vigilante group on the edge of Sambisa Forest. She was reunited briefly with family, flown to Abuja, met President Muhammadu Buhari, and introduced her four-month-old baby, born in captivity.
- Buhari pledged medical, psychological and educational support for Amina and said her testimony could help locate other missing girls. Activists and relatives hope the escapes will lead to finding more of the more than 200 girls still missing from the Chibok abduction.
- The handling and public presentation of Amina by security forces drew criticism from commentators and rights activists, who warned against politicizing survivors and stressed the need for trauma-sensitive care and careful investigation.
- The broader context: Boko Haram has abducted thousands of women and girls in northern Nigeria since 2009. The Chibok case drew international attention via the #BringBackOurGirls campaign; 219 of the 276 originally seized were held after immediate escapes, and around 218 remain unaccounted for from Chibok.

Summary:

In October 2009, 28-year-old Crissita Elaine Cage-Toaster was reported missing after her car was found abandoned on Belle Isle in Detroit with her ID, purse and cellphone inside. Her parents, Rosita and Johnny Toaster, provided police with detailed identifying information including a distinctive shoulder tattoo — a large red rose with her parents’ nicknames.

Five months later, on March 30, 2010, a body was recovered from the Detroit River. The Wayne County Medical Examiner’s Office and Detroit police recorded the remains as possibly Caucasian or Hispanic; the decedent was actually Black. The body was fingerprinted, cataloged as Jane Doe 10-3047, photographed (the tattoo was documented, the ME office says), and after remaining unclaimed for about a year, was buried in an unmarked grave in Knollwood Cemetery, Canton Township, in March 2011.

The Cage-Toaster family learned only in late 2017 — after Rosita contacted the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System and pressed for a tattoo-focused review — that the Jane Doe and their daughter were the same person. The medical examiner’s office says Detroit police ultimately made the identification and notified them in 2017; the ME office says it followed standard procedures (fingerprints, DNA, dental, NAMUS entry) when it received unidentified remains. Police acknowledge decomposition can alter complexion and complicate ID but insist the current team connected the case quickly once alerted.

The parents say investigators were negligent, pointing to miscoding of ethnicity, lack of a full autopsy (the cause of death remains “undetermined” or reported as drowning in some accounts), missing personal effects that were in the car, and years of agonizing uncertainty. Wayne County officials have notified the family they will exhume the remains so the parents can arrange a proper burial and memorial. Survivors of one of Australia’s deadliest wildfires have won the country’s largest class-action settlement: defendants agreed to pay about A$494.7–497.4 million (roughly US$467–470 million). The payment resolves claims by more than 5,000–10,000 plaintiffs who accused electricity provider SP AusNet, its contractor Utility Services Corporation Ltd., and the Victorian government of negligence over the Kilmore East blaze on Black Saturday, Feb. 7, 2009. That fire killed 119 people in Kilmore East (part of 2009 Black Saturday fires that overall killed 173 and destroyed thousands of homes) and was found by a 2009 Royal Commission to have been sparked when an electricity line failed and arced against a pole stay. SP AusNet agreed to the settlement without admitting liability, saying the conductor had been damaged by lightning in a way that compromised its fail-safety. The settlement still requires final court approval and payouts are expected to be distributed in 12–18 months. Plaintiffs’ lawyers called the award “a measure of justice,” while survivors described it as some relief for immense loss.

Bristol Palin and husband Dakota Meyer are expecting a child in spring, the couple announced to Entertainment Tonight. The baby will be Palin’s third; she and Meyer have a daughter, Sailor Grace, born last December, and Palin also has a son, Tripp, from a previous relationship with Levi Johnston. Palin, 26, and Meyer—who married in June after a contentious period that included a custody dispute—said they feel blessed and thankful for “grace and new beginnings.” Palin has publicly thanked Meyer for supporting their blended family.

A Fresno man, 37-year-old Bobby Pearson, was released from jail after a jury mistakenly signed a not-guilty verdict in a burglary trial despite an 8-4 vote favoring guilt. Judge W. Kent Hamlin recorded the acquittal after jurors nodded when polled, though jurors later disclosed during lunch they had been confused by the forms and one said he had voted guilty. Because the not-guilty verdict was entered, retrial would likely violate double jeopardy protections.

Less than two hours after his midnight release, Pearson was found lying in the road with fatal wounds and died at Community Regional Medical Center. Police say he had gone to his mother's home, got into a fight with his sister’s boyfriend, Willie Gray, with whom he reportedly had long-standing problems. Witnesses reported a loud pop; investigators noted one wound that appeared to be a stab and another possibly a gunshot. An autopsy was scheduled.

Willie Gray, a Big Fresno Fair landscaper whom coworkers remembered as a hard worker, was arrested about a mile from the scene at an apartment complex. Police seized a gun and towed a minivan believed to be a getaway vehicle. Gray was being treated for injuries and is expected to face murder charges once booked; the investigation is ongoing.

Legal analysts noted Gray might claim self-defense, but leaving the scene could be used at trial as evidence of consciousness of guilt. Prosecutors and observers described the sequence—Pearson’s accidental acquittal followed by his killing—as bizarre and tragic.

Researchers say this winter could start relatively mild for the U.S. Northeast but grow stormier and colder later on because of how the polar vortex behaves.

- Current state: The polar vortex — a ring of fast, high-altitude winds that normally traps Arctic air — is stronger than average now, which should keep extreme Arctic cold bottled up through early winter (around the start of the Christmas season). That supports broader forecasts for a warmer winter tied to a strong El Niño.

- Later-season risk: Scientists warn the vortex is typically weakest and most likely to wobble from late December through February. A strong early-season vortex can become increasingly unstable as winter progresses; if it weakens or becomes distorted, it can send late blasts of cold air and snow into more southerly regions. Researchers will be watching for that increased volatility.

- Long-term influences: Declining Arctic sea ice has been linked to a looser, more variable vortex in recent years, a factor behind the deep cold outbreaks in some winters and unusual warmth elsewhere (e.g., warmer, low-snow Alaska).

- Practical impacts: Regardless of vortex behavior, consumers should see lower heating costs this winter. Propane, heating oil and natural gas prices are down and inventories are high—propane supplies in particular have surged because of increased natural gas production from shale. New York state forecasts significant reductions in average winter heating bills compared with 2013–14.

- Expert perspective: Seasonal forecasters who use different techniques—such as Judah Cohen, who emphasizes Siberian October snow cover to predict winter patterns—have successfully anticipated active, snowy winters in the past and caution that above-normal precipitation and snowfall remain possible along the East Coast.

In short: Expect a potentially mild start to winter due to a strong polar vortex and El Niño, but remain aware of a credible chance for late-season cold and snow if the vortex weakens or becomes distorted; economically, lower fuel prices should ease heating costs.

A rare fatal chain‑reaction crash in the Everglades killed three people and injured eight after an SUV struck and killed a roughly 300‑pound black bear Sunday night on Snake Road (near mile marker 49 on Alligator Alley) on the Big Cypress Seminole Reservation.

According to Seminole and Broward officials, a Cadillac SUV (possibly an Escalade) hit the bear and became disabled. A second car stopped to assist the SUV’s occupants; while they were out of that vehicle, a third car (reported as a Mercedes) plowed into the stopped vehicle and then struck the three Good Samaritans, killing them. Of the 13 people across the three vehicles, eight were injured and two walked away unhurt, including the SUV driver. Six injured were taken to Broward Health Medical Center and two to Memorial Regional Hospital. The victims’ identities have not been released. The bear was killed in the initial collision. Officials called the involvement of a black bear in a traffic fatality unusual for the area.

Summary:

The document describes two separate stories about government overreach and political media behavior.

1) Municipal code enforcement abuses and legal challenge:
- Ebony Conner, a single mother of five in Cahokia, Illinois, was arrested and briefly jailed for failing to mow her lawn and clean her yard without first receiving a citation or a court date; authorities only cited a village complaint. Conner says she should have been issued a ticket and given a court appearance rather than arrested.
- The piece notes similar incidents elsewhere: a 70-year-old in Prichard, Alabama, was arrested over a lawn citation for property she no longer owned, and a 75-year-old in Riesel, Texas faced a warrant after allegedly failing to respond to a court letter about mowing.
- The Institute for Justice (IJ) has sued Pagedale, Missouri, over aggressive and profit-driven municipal enforcement practices. Pagedale historically raised a large share of revenue from fines and fees (nearly 20% in 2013), and non-traffic tickets rose sharply from 2010–2014.
- Plaintiffs describe a cycle of fines that residents cannot escape: fines for minor or vague violations prevent homeowners from making repairs, which triggers more fines; inability to attend court leads to warrants and jail time.
- Individual plaintiffs include Vincent Blount (thousands in fines, jail time, threats to demolish a non-dangerous home), his partner Valarie Whitner (vague “house not up to code” tickets, arrested, forced to take a payday loan to pay fines), and 84-year-old Mildred Bryant (facing a list of onerous and sometimes absurd demands like repainting a two-story house and having matching curtains). These plaintiffs represent a class seeking to end what they allege is unconstitutional, punitive ticketing since 2010.

2) Rudy Giuliani media tour criticized by Samantha Bee:
- Comedian Samantha Bee mocked Rudy Giuliani, President Trump’s personal lawyer on the Russia investigation, for openly admitting his media appearances are “a big PR campaign” to undermine Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s probe.
- Bee argued Giuliani is being used to spread propaganda—particularly the “spygate” theory—and often slips into telling truthful or revealing moments while otherwise promoting false narratives. She ridiculed the “spygate” claim and dismissed its substance, noting the FBI informant wasn’t “implanted” in the campaign and mocking Trump’s performance as president.

Overall, the document highlights alleged abuses of municipal code enforcement that trap vulnerable residents in cycles of fines and punishment, and separately relays a critical media take on Giuliani’s public role undermining the Russia investigation.

The Air Force Academy said a racial slur incident that prompted a widely shared, blistering address from superintendent Lt. Gen. Jay Silveria was staged by one of the cadet candidates who was allegedly targeted. In September, racist epithets were found outside dorm rooms at the academy’s prep school; the student later admitted responsibility and has left the school (the academy did not specify whether the student withdrew or was expelled). Silveria’s speech—urging anyone who can’t treat others with dignity and respect to leave and telling listeners to record his remarks—came amid national racial tensions following Charlottesville and NFL anthem protests. The academy, which enrolls about 4,000 students and a roughly 240‑student prep program, reiterated that racism has no place at the institution.

A 3-year-old girl, Mariah Woods, has been missing from her Jacksonville, North Carolina home since her mother, Kristy Woods, put her to bed Sunday night and discovered her gone the next morning. The Onslow County Sheriff’s Office, the FBI and multiple local agencies launched ground and air searches, issued an AMBER Alert, and released surveillance photos of a woman and child seen at a Walmart the morning after the disappearance as investigators seek to identify them.

Mariah is described as a white female, about 2 ft. 9 in., 30 pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes, and wears leg braces to assist walking. Authorities say they are following tips and leads, interviewing family members (including the mother’s partner and Kristy’s mother), searching the home, vehicle and surrounding wooded areas with K9 units and drones, and asking neighbors to check yards and outbuildings. Officials have not disclosed many case details, saying they will explore every lead and are using all available resources.

Family members have made emotional public pleas for Mariah’s return; her biological father expressed skepticism about how a child could be taken without anyone hearing. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Onslow County Sheriff’s Office at 910-989-4070.

Dennis Lee Thian Poh, a 47-year-old businessman and experienced trekker from Kuala Lumpur, has been missing since April 5 after separating from his group while descending from Khopra Danda toward Bayeli in Nepal’s Annapurna region. He was due to return March 28 + planned trek; last seen between Ghorepani and Ghundrung. Rescue efforts began April 7 and have intensified, with SAR Dogs Nepal, local villagers, Sherpas, police and international volunteers searching areas between Khopra and Bayeli and around Dobasto and Tadatani. Poor weather — heavy fog, snow, hail and freezing nights — plus difficult terrain, ravines and limited visibility have hampered searches and prevented helicopter use; army rappel teams were being deployed.

Lee’s wife, Jennifer (Eileen Peters), flew to Nepal to help coordinate the rescue and has distributed flyers and appealed for help; the family hopes he will be found in time for their second wedding anniversary. SAR Dogs Nepal are using scent items from Lee’s gear and have identified several locations of interest, but conditions remain dangerous. The family has urged more experienced volunteers to assist and provided contact numbers and an email for tips; friends set up a Facebook page “Find Dennis” for information and support. Authorities and rescuers warn that despite some survivors lasting weeks if fit and uninjured, the odds are challenging given the terrain and worsening weather.

Key points

- An Iranian parliamentary security committee spokesman, Hossein Naqvi Hosseini, said Iran currently does not need more 20-percent enriched uranium because Tehran reactor fuel has been supplied. He added Iran is willing to convert its 20-percent stockpile into fuel rods to allay concerns about non‑peaceful use, though he gave no implementation details. Hosseini is not a government spokesman or on the nuclear negotiating team.

- Halting production of 20-percent enriched uranium is a central Western demand because enrichment above that level makes further progress toward weapons-grade material much easier. Western diplomats say Iran offered to stop 20-percent enrichment at recent Geneva talks, but Tehran has not publicly confirmed that offer.

- Negotiations: Iran met with the P5+1 (U.S., Russia, China, Britain, France, Germany) in Geneva as it seeks relief from crippling sanctions. Further talks were scheduled for Nov. 7–8. U.S. officials described discussions as detailed and constructive, while Israel and some hardliners remain highly skeptical and press for tougher demands (including elimination of fissile material and underground sites).

- Breakout time and proliferation risk: Independent analysis (Institute for Science and International Security, David Albright) warns Iran’s “breakout” time—the time to convert stockpiles into weapons‑usable material—has shortened and could be as little as a month under some scenarios. Iran’s centrifuge numbers rose (from ~12,000 in 2012 to ~19,000) and its medium‑enriched uranium stockpile has nearly doubled, increasing concerns. Experts urge negotiators to lengthen breakout times and improve detectability.

- Political context: President Hassan Rouhani and Foreign Minister Javad Zarif present a more moderate negotiating face, but hardliners and Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei retain final authority and send mixed signals. Economic sanctions are pressuring Iran, yet domestic politics and regional security concerns (notably Israel’s insistence on preventing a nuclear weapon) complicate prospects.

- Outlook: There are signs of progress, but significant distrust, technical risks (rapid breakout capability), and political obstacles on all sides mean the durability and scope of any agreement remain uncertain.

Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds are reportedly growing closer and have been visiting each other on film sets. Insiders say their relationship is becoming "more serious." Lively visited Reynolds in Boston—where he’s filming R.I.P.D.—after he reportedly stopped by her Gossip Girl set in New York. They were seen dining romantically at Boston’s Mistral Bistro, where Lively allegedly picked up the check. She stayed only one night, returned to NYC on Oct. 11, and was later seen buying men’s clothing (possibly gifts) at Bergdorf Goodman and spending about $5,000 at Chanel SoHo.
