A pat-down and private search uncovered 1.79 pounds of heroin, with an estimated street value of over $70,000. He was held without bail, turned over to Homeland Security Investigations, and faces federal narcotics smuggling charges that carry up to 10 years in prison. Officials praised the seizure as an example of vigilant border screening.

Keith Schiller, Donald Trump’s longtime bodyguard and aide, privately told House Intelligence Committee investigators that he rejected an offer—made by a Russian associate during Trump’s 2013 trip to Moscow for the Miss Universe pageant—to send five women to Trump’s hotel room. According to multiple bipartisan sources, Schiller said he treated the offer as a joke, told Trump about it (they laughed), waited outside Trump’s door for several minutes as was his security practice, then left and did not see anyone enter the room. He could not recall who specifically made the offer but testified it did not come from Emin Agalarov; Agalarov’s attorney denied his client’s involvement.

The committee raised the matter because it appears in the unverified Christopher Steele dossier, which alleges salacious conduct in Moscow and that Russia holds kompromat on Trump. Schiller denied knowing about those dossier allegations and denied knowledge of other alleged interactions between Trump associates and Russians. He also said he was unaware of deliberations around FBI Director James Comey’s firing and only delivered the termination letter when asked.

Schiller’s lawyer criticized committee leaks about the testimony as misleading and indefensible. The FBI has corroborated some dossier material and used parts of it in a surveillance warrant for Carter Page, but investigators have not verified the dossier’s most sensational Moscow claims. Trump and the White House have repeatedly denied the dossier’s allegations.

Sen. John McCain’s family, colleagues and constituents gathered at the Arizona State Capitol on Wednesday—the day he would have turned 82—for the first of two days of memorials in Arizona before his body is flown to Washington and then to Annapolis for burial. A private morning ceremony in the Capitol rotunda, where his flag-draped casket lay in state, included remarks by Gov. Doug Ducey, former Sen. Jon Kyl and a benediction by Sen. Jeff Flake. Cindy McCain kissed and pressed her cheek to the casket; several children, including Meghan and sons in uniform, and other dignitaries paid their respects amid visible emotion.

By midmorning military honor guards stood at the Capitol and a motorcade brought the hearse under escort. Hundreds of Arizonans—veterans, Democrats and Republicans alike, some traveling hours or arriving before dawn—waited in the heat under canopies to view the casket. Volunteers handed out water and flags; organizers said the public viewing would continue as long as lines remained. A public procession and a memorial service at North Phoenix Baptist Church are scheduled for Thursday, followed by viewings and services in Washington, D.C., and a private burial at the U.S. Naval Academy. McCain died Saturday at 81 of an aggressive brain cancer.

NASA's Curiosity rover has returned its largest science downlink to date, summarized in six papers in Science that together reshape our picture of early Mars (about 3.5–4+ billion years ago). Key findings:

- Gale Crater was once habitable. Curiosity found sedimentary mudstones and clay minerals indicating a long-lived, shallow freshwater lake (possibly 50 × 5 km), fed by streams and groundwater. Chemical ingredients essential for life—S, N, H, O, P and C—were present, so the environment could have supported chemolithoautotrophic microbes for tens of thousands to millions of years.

- Surface water was widespread. Ground-truthing of orbital observations confirms many features identified from orbit (streams, deltas, channels, lakes) were indeed aqueous, implying a wetter early Mars than previously thought.

- Organic carbon detected but origin uncertain. The SAM instrument has identified up to six organic compounds and rising concentrations across samples, but two complications remain: chlorine-bearing minerals can destroy organics during heating, and contamination from an organic solvent used in SAM’s wet chemistry. Results are promising but not yet definitive for indigenous Martian organics.

- High surface radiation. Curiosity’s RAD instrument measured surface radiation from cosmic rays and solar events; levels would likely sterilize exposed microbes within a few million years (modeled on Deinococcus radiodurans). However, life could potentially survive subsurface or survive in long dormancy if it originated in the earlier, more protected environment.

- Radiation-driven chemical damage informs drilling strategy. Radiation also degrades surface organics over time. Using cosmogenic decay measurements, Curiosity’s team dated Yellowknife Bay exposure at ~80 million years, demonstrating a method to find recently shielded rocks (e.g., under overhangs) that may better preserve organics for future drilling.

- Productive detours. A detour to Yellowknife Bay before heading to Mount Sharp proved scientifically valuable, yielding the habitability results; the rover is now on a faster transit toward Mount Sharp but continues to examine interesting targets en route.

Overall, Curiosity has confirmed Gale Crater hosted an Earth-like, habitable lake environment and validated orbital evidence for widespread ancient water on Mars. While definitive proof of past Martian life remains out of reach for Curiosity, these findings significantly increase the plausibility that life could have existed there and help guide future searches for preserved organics.

Nelson Mandela’s death at 95 prompted an outpouring of tributes from musicians and world leaders, highlighting his enduring legacy as a symbol of equality, freedom and revolution.

Music tributes:
- U2 — "Ordinary Love": Written for the film Mandela: Long Walk To Freedom; Bono evokes Mandela’s belief in ordinary love.
- Hugh Masekela — "Mandela (Bring Him Back Home)" (1987): A South African plea to see Mandela free.
- The Special A.K.A. — "Free Nelson Mandela" (1984): A buoyant protest single calling for his release.
- Youssou N'Dour — "Nelson Mandela" (1986): A tribute album by the Senegalese star.
- Public Enemy — "Prophets of Rage": Hip‑hop political commentary that namechecks Mandela.
- Santana — "Mandela" (1988): Instrumental tribute performed at Mandela’s 70th birthday.
- Simple Minds — "Mandela Day": Performed at Mandela’s 70th birthday as a hopeful anthem.
- 2pac — "Just a Breath of Freedom (4 Nelson Mandela)": A poem praising Mandela’s struggle.
- Tracy Chapman — "Freedom Now": Performed at Mandela’s 70th birthday, calling for his release.
- Johnny Clegg — "Asimbonanga": A Zulu/English protest song (“We have not seen him”) that Mandela later joined onstage to perform.

Global reaction:
- President Barack Obama eulogized Mandela at the White House, calling him “one of the most influential, courageous and profoundly good human beings” and saying “he no longer belongs to us. He belongs to the ages.” Obama praised Mandela’s moral courage, humility and the example he set to choose love over hate, and ordered U.S. flags lowered to half-staff. He said Mandela’s life shaped him personally and pledged to carry forward Mandela’s example; he is expected to travel to South Africa for the state funeral.

Overall, artists across genres and nations joined political leaders in mourning Mandela and celebrating a life that inspired protest music, celebration and a global commitment to justice and reconciliation.

Two Ohio men, Ricky Jackson and Wiley (Wylie) Bridgeman, were released this week after spending nearly four decades imprisoned for a 1975 Cleveland murder they did not commit. Cuyahoga County prosecutors dropped charges after the key eyewitness, Edward (Eddie) Vernon, who was 12 at the time, recanted. Vernon said he was coerced and given information by detectives and admitted in a recent affidavit and courtroom testimony that he lied to help police; he first told the truth after confiding in his pastor and contacting the Ohio Innocence Project.

Jackson, convicted at 19 and incarcerated for 39 years, walked out of the Justice Center on Friday, calling his release “extraordinary” and expressing no bitterness toward Vernon, whom he praised for the courage to recant. Bridgeman, who had remained imprisoned while his brother Ronnie (now Kwame Ajamu) was paroled in 2003, was also freed after the charges were dropped. The Ohio Innocence Project handled the case and noted Jackson had been the longest-held U.S. prisoner later exonerated. Jackson’s original death sentence was vacated on a technicality, and the Bridgeman brothers were removed from death row after Ohio banned capital punishment in 1978.

Prosecutor Timothy McGinty acknowledged that without the eyewitness testimony the state’s case had “evaporated.” The case drew renewed scrutiny after a 2011 Scene Magazine article questioned the convictions. Ohio provides compensation to some wrongfully convicted people but not all; an Ohio Innocence Project fund has been set up for Jackson. Attorneys representing the brothers had sought a new trial based on Vernon's new statements; Ronnie Bridgeman is pursuing clearing his record. Prosecutors said they will not charge Vernon.

Investigators probing the April 21 death of music superstar Prince are focusing on a possible drug overdose and whether a physician prescribed medications to him in the weeks before he died. Law enforcement sources told the Associated Press that Prince was found unconscious on his private plane during an emergency stop in Moline, Illinois, on April 15; first responders reportedly administered naloxone (Narcan) on the tarmac. Authorities say prescription pills were found at his Paisley Park home, and investigators are trying to determine what drugs were involved, whether an overdose occurred on the plane or at Paisley Park, and how Prince obtained any medication.

Local prosecutors obtained and then won a court order to seal the search warrant for Paisley Park, citing the intense media scrutiny and the risk of compromising the ongoing criminal investigation; the warrant will remain sealed for 180 days or until criminal proceedings begin. Carver County officials have said the federal DEA is not currently involved. The county’s incident report on the 911 response shows the emergency call came at 9:43 a.m., responders reached Paisley Park within five minutes, and Prince was pronounced dead at 10:07 a.m.; the cause of death remains “unknown” pending autopsy and toxicology results, expected in several weeks. Authorities say neither foul play nor suicide is suspected. Prince, 57, was cremated and a private memorial service was held; the investigation continues.

Summary:

Over 75 women have accused film producer Harvey Weinstein of sexual harassment and assault, with accounts spanning decades and sharing disturbing commonalities: unwanted advances in hotel rooms and offices, demands to disrobe or give massages, coerced sexual contact, and in some cases rape. Many survivors carried long-standing shame and isolation before recent news reports prompted more to speak publicly.

Three women—actress Alice Evans, actress/photographer Katherine Kendall, and psychologist Tomi-Ann Roberts—joined a conversation about their encounters, how those experiences shaped their careers and lives, and what the recent cascade of revelations has meant for them. Roberts described a college‑age encounter in New York in which Weinstein appeared naked in a bathtub and pressured her to undress; she stopped pursuing acting and later researched sexual objectification. Kendall recounted a Miramax meeting in the early 1990s that ended with Weinstein appearing naked, demanding massage and touching; she resisted, left terrified, and felt the episode chilled her career prospects. Evans described an encounter at Cannes in 2002 where Weinstein publicly propositioned her at a bar and tried to coax her into a bathroom—she escaped but was left worrying that mentioning her boyfriend might have cost him a role. All three discussed the psychological aftermath—shame, self-blame, re-examining past actions—and the relief and validation of seeing many other women come forward. They critiqued perfunctory public apologies, stressed that genuine apology requires acknowledging harm, and discussed forgiveness as a private healing choice. They emphasized the need to amplify voices without large platforms and to push systemic change so future victims are protected. They also debated responses to bullying and the limits of “taking the high road,” arguing for stronger defenses and support.

The reporting also reviews how Weinstein and The Weinstein Company’s corporate governance enabled his longevity. Investigations (and plaintiffs’ accounts) revealed that Weinstein and his legal team used nondisclosure agreements and secret settlements for decades to silence accusers and conceal misconduct. Examples include Ambra Battilana Gutierrez, who recorded Weinstein admitting to groping her but was pressured, smeared, and ultimately settled under an agreement that restricted her ability to speak and destroyed evidence; and former assistant Zelda Perkins, who settled in the U.K. and later criticized the secrecy and company inaction. Private investigators and a high-powered legal team were used to discredit accusers and influence prosecutors.

Internally, TWC’s board structure and contracts concentrated control with the Weinstein brothers and limited directors’ ability to rein him in. Two long-time directors, Tarak Ben Ammar and Lance Maerov, describe efforts in 2014–15 to change governance, investigate alleged misuses of company funds and personnel, and deny Harvey a renewed contract—efforts that were repeatedly thwarted by Weinstein allies, board dynamics that favored the Weinsteins, and interventions by powerful lawyers. In 2015 Weinstein repaid millions the board said he had improperly used, and negotiations over his contract included disputes about access to his personnel file. Lawyers resisted full disclosure; an outside review letter (very brief) claimed no unresolved claims implicating TWC. The board later adopted a code of conduct in 2015, which ultimately provided the basis used in October 2017 to place him on leave and then fire him after The New York Times exposé. Ben Ammar and Maerov argue that had governance changes succeeded earlier, the company—and its reputation—might have been spared much damage and some abuses curtailed.

Finally, reporting notes a high-profile bid to buy The Weinstein Company led by Maria Contreras-Sweet that proposed majority female control and set-aside funds to address future claims, positioning itself as a potential “white knight” to salvage assets without bankruptcy. The overall narrative ties Weinstein’s pattern of abusive sexual behavior to systems of secrecy, corporate enabling, and the cultural mechanisms that allowed powerful men to evade accountability for years.

Ohio voters will decide on Nov. 3 whether to legalize recreational marijuana under a constitutional amendment submitted by the private investor group ResponsibleOhio. Secretary of State Jon Husted certified that the group submitted 320,267 valid signatures—more than the 305,591 required—after a petition drive that cost over $2 million and used about 200 paid circulators. ResponsibleOhio’s backers have pledged at least $20 million for the fall campaign and have built a professional political operation, including prominent legal and data teams.

If approved, Ohio would become the sixth U.S. jurisdiction to legalize recreational marijuana (joining Colorado, Washington, Oregon, Alaska and D.C.) and the most populous to do so. The proposal would allow adults 21+ to possess, permit individuals to grow a small number of plants for personal use, authorize 1,150 commercial licenses across cultivation, processing and retail, and levy a 15% transaction tax (plus sales and business taxes). Revenue projections from a ResponsibleOhio task force estimate industry revenue exceeding $2 billion by 2020 and annual tax receipts of more than $500 million, with funds partly used for a state regulatory body and distributed to local governments.

The plan’s most controversial feature is a constitutionally specified limit on commercial cultivation to 10 named farms — an oligopoly structure that opponents decry as unfairly favoring wealthy investors. Those investors include local celebrities and business figures; all 10 operators have pledged to allow unionization. ResponsibleOhio also plans a future 2016 ballot initiative to permit expungement of convictions for acts that would be legal under legalization.

The initiative faces organized opposition from a broad coalition: the Republican state leadership (including Gov. John Kasich and Attorney General Mike DeWine), the Ohio Farm Bureau, many marijuana reform activists who object to the investor-centered model, and others. The Ohio Legislature preemptively put Issue 2 on the same ballot; that measure would ban “a monopoly, oligopoly or cartel” involving federally controlled substances. Secretary Husted has said if both measures pass the legislative measure would take precedence; ResponsibleOhio disputes that and legal challenges are expected if both pass.

The petition phase also produced controversy: Husted flagged problems with ResponsibleOhio’s voter-registration forms and hired an investigator; subpoenas and disputes over signature validity delayed certification earlier this summer. Polling has shown modest majority support for legalization in Ohio (around 52% in a July Quinnipiac poll), but margins could tighten by Election Day.

A coroner’s inquest in Billings, Montana found that Officer Grant Morrison was justified in fatally shooting 38-year-old Richard Ramirez during an April 2014 traffic stop. Morrison, a five-year veteran who had previously been involved in another fatal shooting (cleared in 2013), testified that he believed Ramirez — who had methamphetamine in his system — was reaching for a gun at the time and that he fired three times to protect himself. Dashcam and police videos shown to the seven-person jury captured Morrison repeatedly ordering occupants to raise their hands and then firing; Ramirez’s movements in the car were largely obscured on video. The jury deliberated about an hour before returning the ruling, and Yellowstone County Attorney Scott Twito said no criminal charges are expected.

Family members expressed disappointment and plan to sue the officer and the department for excessive force, criticizing the inquest as one-sided because most witnesses were law enforcement and testimony about Ramirez’s drug use and past interactions with police featured prominently. Investigators later found a small amount of methamphetamine and a syringe near Ramirez’s seat, and an autopsy confirmed a significant methamphetamine level in his bloodstream. Dashcam footage released afterward also showed Morrison emotionally distraught immediately after the shooting, saying, “I thought he was gonna pull a gun.” The shooting was one of several officer-involved shootings in Billings deemed justified by the department.

Summary:

Western governments have accused Russia’s military intelligence service (the GRU) of a global campaign of cyber-operations and recently disrupted a close-access plot to hack the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) in The Hague. In April Dutch military intelligence, with British help, intercepted four Russian operatives who had diplomatic passports and a hire car parked near the OPCW containing specialist hacking gear, laptops, cash and travel evidence linking operations in Switzerland, Malaysia and Brazil. The suspects were expelled; their equipment was seized.

The US Department of Justice subsequently indicted seven GRU officers, charging them with computer hacking, wire fraud, identity theft and money laundering for targeting the OPCW, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and other organizations (including anti-doping agencies, FIFA, a US nuclear company and US political targets). Canada, the UK, NATO and the EU also condemned the alleged operations, which investigators say aimed to discredit institutions investigating Russian wrongdoing (such as the Skripal novichok poisoning, the Douma chemical attack and doping scandals) and to interfere with probes into MH17’s downing.

Russian officials denied the accusations as baseless “spy mania” and propaganda. Western leaders — including Theresa May, Mark Rutte, Jeremy Hunt and NATO figures — described the evidence trail as detailed and unprecedentedly public, warned of consequences and said they would consider further sanctions and countermeasures. Independent investigators (like Bellingcat) have also published material linking many GRU cyber operatives to broader campaigns. The episode has intensified diplomatic tensions and framed Russia as engaging in a pattern of reckless cyber activity against international institutions.

Summary:

Fan Bingbing, one of China’s highest-paid and best-known actresses (featured in X-Men: Days of Future Past and ranked No.1 on Forbes China 2017 with reported earnings of 300 million yuan), has been at the center of a major controversy and a publicity blackout since early July. Academics at Beijing Normal University published a widely circulated 2017–18 "China Film and Television Star Social Responsibility Report" that assessed 100 Chinese celebrities on professional work, charity and personal integrity. Only nine stars scored above the 60% passing threshold; actor Xu Zheng topped the list (78%). Fan received a score of 0%, fueling speculation that the rating reflects allegations she and others used "yin-yang" dual contracts to underreport income and evade taxes.

The controversy began in May when former CCTV presenter Cui Yongyuan posted contracts that appeared to show secret payments. Fan’s studio called the claims slander but did not dispute the documents’ authenticity; Fan has since largely disappeared from public view and stopped posting to Weibo. State media and other outlets later reported she was "under control" and possibly detained pending legal action, reports that were briefly published and then removed. Local authorities reportedly probed tax practices in Jiangsu — where Fan has business registrations — and state bodies vowed crackdowns on excessive pay and tax evasion in entertainment. Major producers and video sites announced moves to boycott "unreasonable" actor pay.

The report’s publication and state attention to celebrity conduct have intensified online debate: some fans defended Fan’s prior charity and public work and questioned the zero score and the transparency of the report’s methodology (authors cited "research and web-scraping" without full details). The episode highlights tightening official scrutiny of China’s entertainment industry and the high reputational risk celebrities face from tax and integrity allegations.

House Republican leadership publicly backed House Majority Whip Steve Scalise after reports that he spoke at a 2002 event organized by a white nationalist group founded by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke. The disclosure threatened Scalise’s standing just days before Republicans take full control of Congress.

Scalise acknowledged appearing at the event while serving in the Louisiana state legislature, called it a “mistake I regret,” and insisted he opposes the group’s views. His first statement — blaming sloppy staff work for his appearance — frustrated GOP aides, prompting coordinated expressions of support from Speaker John Boehner and Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy, who said Scalise has their full confidence.

Details remain disputed: Scalise and aides say he frequently spoke to many groups while barnstorming the district and likely did not know the group’s white-supremacist ties; organizers and Stormfront posts described his remarks favorably; a 1999 Roll Call item suggests Scalise knew and criticized David Duke then. Louisiana politicians, including Gov. Bobby Jindal and Democrat Rep. Cedric Richmond, defended Scalise’s character, while national Democrats and civil-rights advocates condemned the appearance and pressed for accountability. Conservative commentators were split, with some calling his explanation implausible.

The episode adds a politically sensitive distraction for House Republicans amid leadership transitions and follows other ethics and legal troubles affecting GOP members.

President Obama used today’s press conference to pick a public fight with House Republicans over deficit reduction by making a forceful moral case for raising revenue — specifically by ending high-end tax breaks — and framing the debate as one about national priorities.

Key themes and lines of attack
- Obama repeatedly argued that protecting tax breaks for millionaires, billionaires, corporate-jet owners and large oil and gas companies forces painful cuts to priorities like college scholarships, medical research, food safety and Medicare. He stressed that the wealthy have unusually low tax burdens and can afford to pay more.
- He singled out a $3 billion tax perk for corporate jet owners and mentioned it multiple times to draw a stark contrast between protecting such benefits and preserving programs for students and seniors. The line was designed to cast Republicans as defenders of the wealthy if they refuse revenue options.
- Obama said deficit reduction must be “balanced” — including both spending cuts and revenue increases — and that Democrats have already shown willingness to make painful spending cuts. He also opposed shifting health-care costs onto seniors as a way to reduce Medicare spending, insisting instead on actual cost reductions.
- While he did not categorically rule out a final deal that lacks higher-end tax increases, he clearly intends to keep relitigating the issue and to make the moral argument central to the political fight.

Reactions in the document
- Critics accused Obama of “class warfare,” complained there was little focus on growth or business-tax reform, and doubted the credibility of some proposed spending cuts.
- Supporters said the administration effectively boxed Republicans: either agree to a balanced approach that includes revenue, or be seen as protecting wealthy interests at the expense of broader national needs.

Bottom line
Obama’s presser aimed to reframe the debt-ceiling and deficit talks from a fight over spending cuts into a contest over who will fairly share sacrifice and defend core investments. By repeatedly invoking the corporate-jet tax break and the wealthy’s low tax rates, the White House sought to put Republicans on the defensive and make revenue increases — especially at the top end — a central, moral issue in the coming negotiations and political debate.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has overturned lifetime Olympic bans and reinstated results for 28 Russian athletes who had been sanctioned over alleged state-backed doping at the 2014 Sochi Winter Games, while partially upholding 11 other appeals (those 11 remain found guilty of anti‑doping violations but had life bans reduced to bans only from the 2018 Pyeongchang Games). CAS said evidence was insufficient, on an individual-case basis, to prove anti‑doping rule violations for the 28 athletes; it emphasized it was only deciding those specific appeals, not adjudicating whether a systemic manipulation occurred.

The ruling restores multiple Sochi medals (including Alexander Tretiakov’s men’s skeleton gold and other podium places), likely promoting Britain’s four-man bobsleigh team into the bronze position, and returns Russia to the top of the Sochi medal table. CAS noted much of the evidence was circumstantial and that there was no direct positive test or confession in those 28 cases.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) reacted with mixed emotion and strong concern. While it welcomed CAS confirmation of wrongdoing for 11 athletes, it said overturning the other 28 “may have a serious impact on the future fight against doping,” accused CAS of applying a higher standard of proof than the IOC’s Oswald Commission, and warned it could appeal to the Swiss Federal Tribunal. The IOC also stressed that CAS clearing does not automatically entitle those athletes to invitations to compete at Pyeongchang; the Russian Olympic Committee remains suspended and about 160 Russians have already been cleared to compete as neutrals.

Reactions were polarized: Russian officials and athletes hailed the decision as justice and sought entry for the cleared competitors at Pyeongchang; whistleblowers, athletes affected at Sochi, and many international figures condemned the CAS outcome as a blow to anti‑doping efforts and to sporting integrity. CAS maintained its remit was limited to individual appeals rather than ruling on the broader question of institutional doping at Sochi.

A Badlands National Park Twitter account briefly posted climate-change facts — including that atmospheric CO2 is higher than at any time in the last 650,000 years — then deleted the tweets after a few hours. The National Park Service (NPS) said the messages came from a former employee who was no longer authorized to use the park’s account and that the park removed the tweets when it realized the account had been compromised. The NPS added that park social media managers should continue posting public-safety and park information but avoid content related to national policy issues.

A high-school student discovered an exceptionally complete baby Parasaurolophus fossil in Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument in 2009. Kevin Terris, then 17 and a student at The Webb Schools, spotted the first bone during a field trip led by paleontologist Andrew Farke. Subsequent excavation (including a helicopter airlift) and 1,300 hours of preparation revealed an almost whole skeleton nicknamed "Joe" (in honor of donor Joseph Augustyn). The specimen is the smallest, most complete and youngest Parasaurolophus known.

Bone histology from a leg sample shows no annual growth rings, indicating Joe was under one year old at death but already about 6–8 feet (1.8–2.5 m) long—roughly a quarter the size of an adult. Joe already bore a small, hollow crest bump, implying Parasaurolophus began developing its distinctive tube-shaped crest much earlier in life than related hadrosaurids. CT scans and 3-D models of the skull and skeleton were produced and made available online at DinosaurJoe.com; the physical specimen is on display at the Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology.

The find, excavated under federal permit and described in a PeerJ paper authored by Farke, Sarah Werning and several students, sheds light on growth and crest development in Parasaurolophus and suggests juveniles produced higher-pitched calls (“tweeters”) compared with adults’ deeper tones (“woofers”), helping age and social status recognition in groups. The fossil cannot be sold because it was collected from public land; its principal value is scientific.

Three months ago Harvard student Aran Khanna built and published a Chrome extension called “Marauder’s Map” that pulled Facebook Messenger’s embedded geolocation tags from messages and plotted them on a map. Messenger (since its 2011 launch) attached precise location coordinates to many messages by default on Android (and with permission on iOS). Khanna’s extension made that hidden historical location data obvious and easy to explore — revealing dorm rooms, daily routines, and meter‑level precision even for people he barely knew or wasn’t friends with, simply because group chats delivered the same location metadata to all chat participants.

Khanna published a blog post, released the code on GitHub, and shared the extension on Medium, Reddit and Twitter on May 26, 2015. The story quickly went viral: the extension was downloaded over ~85,000 times, generated hundreds of tweets and more than 170 news stories worldwide. Facebook contacted Khanna within a day, asked him not to speak to the press, and then asked him to disable the extension; he complied. Facebook also changed its desktop code to stop sending location data to browsers (which broke the extension) and, nine days after Khanna’s post, issued a Messenger update making location sharing opt‑in. Facebook told media it had been working on changes for months; it later rescinded Khanna’s summer internship offer, citing violations of its terms (scraping) and ethical concerns over his public description of how Facebook collected and shared location data.

Khanna framed the project as a public‑interest demonstration: his tool exposed what users were unknowingly sharing so they could judge the privacy implications themselves. In an academic case study he documents methods, timeline, media impact, and Facebook’s response, and argues that making data practices transparent — and generating public attention — prompted product change where earlier reporting had not. The episode raises questions about default privacy settings, corporate responsiveness, the ethics and risks for researchers and students who publicize platform flaws, and the protection of vulnerable users from inadvertent geolocation exposure.

Researchers at UC Berkeley report that “postural expansiveness” — sitting or posing with limbs spread and torso stretched — boosts romantic interest in quick dating situations. Across two field studies (144 speed-dates and a 3,000-person experiment on a GPS-based dating app), people who adopted expansive, “power” postures were more likely to be chosen as potential partners than those who held closed, contractive poses. In the speed-dating videos, each unit increase in coded expansiveness nearly doubled the odds of getting a “yes” for another date; in the online experiment, expansive photos generated about 25% more interest overall. Expansion signaled greater perceived dominance (and openness), which likely conveys resource abundance and willingness to share — traits that make quick impressions favorable. The effect appeared for both sexes but was stronger for men: a larger share of men’s positive responses came when they used expansive poses. Authors caution that, as with earlier “power pose” claims, findings should be interpreted carefully, but they conclude that taking up more physical space can improve brief, first-impression romantic outcomes.

Human Rights Watch and multiple reporting pieces document that Afghanistan’s rapid revival and expansion of irregular, locally recruited security forces — militias and the U.S.-backed Afghan Local Police (ALP) — have produced widespread abuses, weak oversight, and impunity, undermining both Afghan civilians’ safety and longer-term stabilization efforts.

Key findings
- Human Rights Watch’s 102‑page report, “Just Don’t Call It a Militia,” documents killings, rape, arbitrary detention, abductions, forcible land grabs, illegal raids and other abuses by militias in Kunduz province and by ALP units in Baghlan, Herat and Uruzgan. The report is based on 120+ interviews with victims, witnesses, officials and other sources.
- Many armed groups have been reactivated, funded and armed by elements of the Afghan state (notably the National Directorate of Security and networks linked to Shura-e-Nazar/Jamiat-i-Islami) with little vetting or accountability. Patronage links to senior officials often protect perpetrators from investigation or arrest.
- The ALP, created in July 2010 at U.S. urging to provide village-level security, expanded fast (7,000 recruits by August with plans for up to 30,000). Units receive only short training (about 21 days), are vetted by village shuras, and report to district police — but oversight is weak, national police command structures are inadequate, and ALP units often outnumber official forces locally.
- Human Rights Watch documented specific ALP abuses: house raids, beatings, unlawful detention, gang rape (a 13‑year‑old abducted and raped in Baghlan), forced recruitment, extortion and land grabs. In many cases no one was held accountable because of powerful connections.
- Past community defense programs (ANAP, AP3) were likewise hijacked by strongmen and factions, becoming corrupt, abusive and destabilizing. Human Rights Watch warns the ALP risks repeating these mistakes unless vetting, oversight, investigation and complaint mechanisms are rigorously enforced.
- Human Rights Watch urges Afghanistan and the U.S. to cut ties with abusive irregular groups, investigate allegations of abuse, create external complaint bodies, allocate resources to probe complaints, and avoid rushed expansion of ALP units without proper safeguards.

Context and broader concerns
- U.S. military and Afghan officials acknowledge improvements in some local security situations after ALP deployment, but also accept risks: infiltration by criminals/insurgents, inadequate vetting, and insufficient accountability. U.S. Special Forces mentor many ALP units; broader training responsibility remains contested.
- Separate reporting highlights chronic weaknesses in Afghan national forces: training shortfalls, literacy problems, high attrition among soldiers and police, and continued dependence on U.S. support for logistics and sustainment. Lt. Gen. William Caldwell said only a tiny number of Afghan army battalions could operate without U.S. assistance, and that full self-sufficiency could take years.
- The case of Brig. Gen. Abdul Raziq in Kandahar exemplifies the dilemma: a powerful local strongman and U.S. ally credited with combat effectiveness against the Taliban, yet long accused of corruption, drug trafficking, extrajudicial killings and torture. Investigative reporting describes accounts of severe torture, unlawful detention and a 2006 massacre allegedly carried out by forces tied to Raziq. Despite credible allegations, he has received U.S. training, equipment and public praise; his promotions and appointments reflect political and military expediency that may have bypassed human-rights safeguards.

Implications
- The mixing of patronage, rapid militarization at the village level, inadequate vetting and weak oversight is producing abuses that fuel local grievances and can strengthen the insurgency rather than weaken it.
- Human rights abuses by pro-government forces may expose U.S. and Afghan authorities to legal and moral risks and hinder efforts to build legitimate, accountable Afghan security institutions.
- Reforming or replacing abusive local forces requires halting expansion until robust vetting, training, command and control, investigation procedures and independent complaint mechanisms are in place.

Bottom line
Short-term security gains from militias and hastily formed local police have come at the cost of serious human-rights violations and impunity. Both Afghan and U.S. authorities need to stop supporting abusive irregular forces, improve vetting and oversight, investigate and hold perpetrators accountable, and invest in properly trained, accountable security forces if stability and legitimacy are to be achieved.

This document traces Barack Obama’s rapid immersion into foreign policy after arriving in Washington in 2005, and then presents a strongly critical conservative reaction to his approach—especially the phrase “leading from behind” used by an Obama adviser to describe actions in Libya.

Key points about Obama’s development on foreign policy
- Background and early limits: Before the Senate, Obama’s career was primarily domestic—part-time lawyer, law professor, and state legislator—with limited formal training in international affairs despite travel in his youth.
- Deliberate education: Upon entering the Senate and joining the Foreign Relations Committee, Obama sought out experts (Anthony Lake, Susan Rice, Samantha Power) and read widely to build expertise. He hired Samantha Power as a foreign-policy fellow after being influenced by her liberal-interventionist arguments in A Problem from Hell, which urged a moral imperative to prevent genocide.
- Positioning in a divided Democratic debate: Obama arrived during intense soul‑searching in the Democratic Party after Iraq. There was tension between realist critics—who warned against intervention driven by ideals—and humanitarian liberals who argued failures in Iraq shouldn’t end liberal internationalism or efforts to stop mass atrocities.

Critical response and “leading from behind”
- Origin of phrase: An adviser’s description of U.S. action in Libya as “leading from behind” became shorthand for an Obama style that emphasizes modesty, coalition work, and caution, rooted in two perceived beliefs: U.S. relative power is declining and America is widely reviled.
- Conservative critique: Columnists (notably Charles Krauthammer and others quoted) use the phrase to condemn Obama’s foreign policy as passive, indecisive, and abdication of leadership—citing episodes like the 2009 Iran Green Revolution and Libya. They argue “leading from behind” rationalizes weakness, confuses the implications of China’s rise, misreads historical anti‑American sentiment, and reflects elite liberal antipathy toward U.S. power rather than global reality.
- Political consequences: Critics warn the style risks strategic failure and domestic political fallout, urging Republicans to present a contrasting “leader from the front” who embodies strength and decisive defense of liberty.

Overall framing
- The document presents two intertwined narratives: a descriptive account of Obama’s rapid self-education and evolving approach to foreign policy amid Democratic debate over intervention and realism; and a sustained conservative denunciation that portrays his cautious, coalition‑centered tactics as dysfunctional “leading from behind” that amounts to abdication rather than prudent, consequence‑based leadership.

Jeb Bush entered the 2016 Republican primary as the establishment favorite: a two-term Florida governor from a presidential dynasty who raised more than $100 million through his campaign and the super PAC Right to Rise. He ran a policy-focused, wonkish campaign—rolling out detailed plans and emphasizing experience and competence—and adopted a patient “slow and steady” approach.

But his campaign faltered badly. Donald Trump’s insurgent, anti-establishment, often personal style reshaped GOP politics and seized angry voters’ attention. Trump labeled Bush “low energy,” relentlessly attacked his record and family ties, and made Bush’s careful, policy-driven message look out of step. The Bush team largely underestimated Trump early on, debated internally whether to engage, and failed to mount an effective, timely response. That indecision let damaging narratives stick.

Three other key problems compounded Bush’s decline:
- “Bush fatigue”: Many Republican voters had an aversion to the Bush family brand tied to George W. Bush’s presidency and its fallout, which polls showed was a major liability.
- Misuse of time and money: The campaign and super PAC prioritized massive fundraising early rather than building Jeb’s distinct personal brand or adapting to changing dynamics; huge ad spending and a delayed offensive failed to move voters.
- Campaign style and organization: Bush was an uneven performer on TV and debates, stumbled on issues like Iraq and immigration, and was surrounded by loyalists who sometimes shielded him from tough feedback. Strategic disagreements among advisers hindered nimble responses to new threats (notably Trump and rising rivals like Marco Rubio).

Attempts to pivot—hiring a debate coach, shifting messaging, deploying family surrogates including George W. Bush and Barbara Bush, and focusing on South Carolina—were too late. Losses in early contests (sixth in Iowa, fourth in New Hampshire, disappointing South Carolina) and high-profile setbacks (e.g., Nikki Haley endorsing Rubio) ended his campaign. He suspended his bid on Feb. 20, 2016.

Analysts conclude Bush’s defeat was both personal and structural: a skilled, policy-minded candidate whose approach and pedigree were mismatched to a Republican electorate craving insurgent, emotional leadership. The campaign’s failures—strategic misreads, timing mistakes, and an inability to neutralize anti-establishment energy—turned what looked like a likely nomination into one of the most notable modern collapses of an establishment favorite.

Researchers and reporters have highlighted that castoreum — a fragrant brown secretion from beavers’ castor sacs (located near the base of the tail) — has a musky, vanilla-like aroma and has been used for decades in perfumes and as a flavoring in foods. The U.S. FDA classifies castoreum as “generally recognized as safe,” and historical sources say manufacturers have used it for at least 80 years. Castoreum is a mix of castor sac secretions plus nearby anal-gland material and sometimes urine; it smells pleasant mainly because of the beaver’s diet of leaves and bark. Collecting it requires anesthetizing and “milking” the animal’s glands, which is unpleasant and limits production — annual use is very small (a few hundred pounds). Because the FDA permits it as a safe “natural flavoring,” manufacturers may not list castoreum explicitly on ingredient labels.

A 14-year-old boy, Stephen J. Brumby, died July 3 after being accidentally shot at about 3:15 p.m. at High Noon Gun Range in Sarasota. According to the Sarasota County Sheriff’s Office, Stephen was struck in the neck after his father, 64-year-old William C. Brumby, was removing a spent shell casing that had deflected off a nearby wall and fallen into the back of his shirt. While using his right hand (which was holding the handgun) to clear the casing, he inadvertently pointed the firearm behind him and it discharged, fatally wounding his son. William Brumby was at the range with two other children, aged 24 and 12, who were uninjured. Detectives, citing witness statements and surveillance video, determined the shooting was accidental. No charges have been filed and the investigation remains open. A GoFundMe memorial fund has been established to help the family. The report notes High Noon Gun Range has previously been described as a highly safety-focused facility; this incident is the second gun-range death in the area in the past year.

Billboard has raised its first-week sales forecast for Taylor Swift’s new album 1989, now predicting it will sell at least 1 million copies in its debut week (tracking Oct. 26–Nov. 2). If SoundScan’s final tally, due Nov. 5, confirms that figure, 1989 would be the 19th album since Nielsen SoundScan began tracking sales in 1991 to top 1 million in a week—and would make Swift the first act in pop history to have three consecutive albums debut with million-plus weeks (Speak Now in 2010 and Red in 2012). The album has shown particularly strong sales through iTunes and Target (which offers an exclusive bonus-track edition). 1989 is also projected to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, become 2014’s first new-release to hit a million, and instantly become one of the year’s best-selling records after a heavy week of promotion by Swift on major TV and radio platforms. Final numbers and chart placement were expected to be announced Nov. 5.

An Ontario judge sentenced former North York General Hospital anesthesiologist Dr. George Doodnaught, 65, to 10 years’ imprisonment after finding he sexually assaulted 21 sedated female patients during surgeries between about 2006 and 2010. Justice David McCombs called the offences “reprehensible in the extreme,” stressing Doodnaught’s exploitation of patients’ trust and the profound, lasting psychological harm—shame, panic attacks, loss of self-worth, distrust of physicians and damaged relationships—described in victim impact statements. Many victims attended sentencing; some applauded as Doodnaught was handcuffed and led from court.

McCombs found Doodnaught used decades of operating-room experience and a permissive “touchy-feely” manner to avoid detection while concealed behind surgical drapes, kissing women, fondling breasts and forcing oral sex or masturbation. The assaults escalated before he was stopped: six occurred over three-and-a-half years at the start, and 15 in the six months before his arrest. Hospital records show multiple prior internal complaints; senior administration only learned of them after the 2010 complaint that triggered the criminal probe. The hospital has apologized and changed how it tracks complaints.

Doodnaught was convicted in November after a 76-day trial. He remains free on bail and intends to appeal his convictions; a Court of Appeal bail application was scheduled. His lawyer said he and his supporters are disappointed by the sentence; the defence has filed many letters of support. The College of Physicians and Surgeons has suspended his medical licence and will hold a disciplinary hearing that could lead to revocation—the College’s notice alleges up to 30 patient victims, including one alleged incident from 1992. Victims and advocates said the 10-year term was insufficient and called for legal changes.

Police and city officials announced the identification and later arrest of 27-year-old Daniel St. Hubert as the suspect in the June 1 elevator stabbings at the Boulevard Houses in East New York that killed 6-year-old Prince Joshua “P.J.” Avitto and critically injured 7-year-old Mikayla Capers. At a Wednesday press conference, NYPD Chief of Detectives Robert Boyce, Commissioner Bill Bratton, Mayor Bill de Blasio and Brooklyn Borough President Eric Adams called the public to submit tips and warned that St. Hubert—described as 5'9", 210 pounds, formerly on parole and with a history of violent arrests—was armed and dangerous and might have changed his appearance.

Officials said forensic evidence and a DNA hit linked St. Hubert to the crime; police later tracked and arrested him in South Ozone Park shortly after 8 p.m. using his cell phone location. A knife was recovered on him. He is wanted for the children’s stabbings and has not been charged but has not been ruled out in a separate nearby fatal stabbing of 18-year-old Tanaya Copeland. The killing sparked community outrage, a large manhunt with a reward that grew to $69,000, and renewed calls from city leaders for increased safety measures in NYCHA buildings. Family members and neighbors expressed relief and grief after the arrest; Mikayla remains hospitalized and P.J.’s family is planning his funeral.

BP will show live video of its planned "top kill" attempt to stop the Gulf of Mexico oil leak after pressure from the Obama administration and discussions with Coast Guard Adm. Thad Allen. The operation — set to begin as early as dawn Wednesday and possibly take up to two days — involves pumping heavy drilling mud and cement into the leaking well to choke off the flow. BP warned seabed flow appearances may change during the procedure and will not necessarily indicate overall progress; the company said it will report on progress and the outcome when complete. Multiple ROV live feeds of the leak are being made available (though they may freeze or be unavailable at times).

An international surrogacy scandal unfolded after Australian couple David and Wendy Farnell returned from Thailand with only one of their newborn twins. The healthy twin daughter, Pipah, came to Western Australia with the couple; her brother Gammy, born with Down’s syndrome, a congenital heart defect and a lung infection, remains in Thailand in the care of surrogate mother Pattaramon (Pattharamon) Chanbua.

The Farnells told Australian media they wanted both children but say the surrogate threatened to involve police and to keep both babies if they tried to take Gammy. They also said they were told too late in the pregnancy about Gammy’s condition and were angry the surrogacy agency had not done earlier testing; David Farnell said that had they known earlier they likely would have terminated the pregnancy, though he denies asking the surrogate to abort. The surrogate says she refused an abortion for religious reasons and has said the parents rejected Gammy, later telling reporters she would not have returned him because she feared he would be placed in an institution.

The story prompted a large fundraising effort—over A$241,000 (about $224,000) has been raised—to pay for Gammy’s care. It also intensified scrutiny of international surrogacy: commercial surrogacy is effectively banned in Australia, many couples travel abroad (notably to Thailand and India), and Thailand lacks a clear legal framework. Thai authorities are preparing legislation to outlaw commercial surrogacy; Australia has requested a transitional period to allow ongoing arrangements to be completed.

Public outrage was fueled further by revelations that David Farnell has prior convictions for sexual offences against young girls in the 1990s; he has acknowledged the convictions, said he has reformed, and denied posing a danger to his daughter. The case sparked calls in Australia for stricter regulation of cross-border surrogacy and raised questions about agency practices and surrogate protections in Thailand.

Blue Origin, the private space company founded by Amazon's Jeff Bezos, successfully launched its New Shepard rocket to the edge of space and landed the booster upright back on its West Texas pad in the company’s first successful uncrewed reusability test. The flight reached about 100.5 km (329,839 feet), peaked near Mach 3.72, and carried a crew capsule—designed for six passengers—to suborbital altitude; the capsule returned under parachute. The booster reignited its engine about 5,000 feet above the pad, deployed landing legs and touched down softly at roughly 4.4 mph, within 4.5 feet of the pad center.

Bezos called full reuse a “game changer,” saying reusable rockets can dramatically cut access-to-space costs and are central to Blue Origin’s long-term vision of millions living and working in space. The company plans suborbital tourist flights on New Shepard and is developing an orbital launcher for Florida launches. The flight follows an April New Shepard launch that failed to recover the booster due to hydraulic issues.

Rival firms such as SpaceX and Virgin Galactic are pursuing related goals. Elon Musk congratulated Blue Origin while noting the difference between suborbital “space” flights and orbital velocity requirements. Blue Origin is accepting names of prospective passengers but has not announced pricing or bookings; Bezos says he intends to fly on his vehicles himself.

Miranda July, filmmaker and author, candidly recounts a long history of shoplifting in a New Yorker piece. Her first theft—stealing Neosporin as a 19-year-old freshman at UC Santa Cruz—ended with her being caught, wetting herself, arrested, fingerprinted and mug-shot, and learning she was legally an adult. Rather than stopping, she escalated into a habitual, calculated shoplifter after dropping out and moving to Portland: stealing groceries (cheese, bread, soy products), using large purses to conceal goods, cutting alarm tags, resetting copy counters, and even orchestrating insurance scams and thefts of luggage. She worked at Goodwill and stole from the charity—slipping books, clothes and small items into her bag and once staging a stunt to get a pink blouse for a coworker, which led to her being called in and weeping when not fired but rebuked. July frames theft as part of a rebellious identity and a way to feel free and in control, likening the necessary mindset to surfing. Eventually she stopped, prompted by a relationship that made her feel she should “straighten out,” and by realizing she could channel rebellion into art. She reflects that people often feel secretly fraudulent as adults. The piece exposes her youthful transgressions, the moral ambiguity of her actions, and how they intertwined with her formation as an artist.

Voters around the country faced dozens of ballot measures in a midterm election that produced several notable results and illuminated larger political trends.

Colorado
- Following last year’s legalization of recreational marijuana, Colorado voters approved a special tax on marijuana by about 65%–35%. The measure imposes a 15% excise tax (for school construction) plus a 10% sales tax (for marijuana-related law enforcement). The Colorado Legislative Council estimates nearly $70 million in additional state revenue next year. Opponents argued it unfairly singles out marijuana relative to products like beer, but the revenue potential largely drove support.
- In 11 mostly rural and conservative counties in northern Colorado, voters were asked whether they favor seceding from the state to form a new entity (proposed “North Colorado” of ten counties, plus Moffat County joining Wyoming as a panhandle). The plan has no realistic path to becoming law because it would require statewide and congressional approval, but the measures serve as a signal of grassroots conservative frustration with liberal Denver policies. Early returns in Weld County showed 58% opposed and 42% in favor.

Washington
- Initiative 522, which would require labeling of foods containing genetically modified ingredients, was closely contested. With about 800,000 votes counted, 53% opposed and 47% supported the measure, but it was still too early to call. The campaign drew massive out-of-state spending: $22 million was raised to oppose the initiative (only $550 from in-state donors), the largest amount ever spent by one side in an initiative race. Major contributors opposing the measure included the Grocery Manufacturers Association and Monsanto. Proponents also received substantial out-of-state funding. The influx of external money highlights how state initiatives are becoming national battlegrounds and raises concerns about outside influence in local democratic processes.

Other notable measures
- New Jersey voters considered a constitutional amendment to raise the state minimum wage from the federal $7.25 to $8.25 per hour, with future increases tied to cost-of-living adjustments. Eighteen states already have higher minimums than the federal level.
- New York voters were asked to amend their constitution to allow the legislature to authorize seven casinos to generate revenue for public schools and potentially reduce property taxes.

Broader themes
- The ballots reflected growing ideological polarization (e.g., secession votes) and the nationalization of state and local ballot campaigns. Outside interests and wealthy donors are increasingly funneling money into state initiatives and small local races—sometimes dwarfing in-state contributions—which experts say could undermine the intent of citizen-led initiative processes. Examples include heavy outside spending on GMO labeling in Washington, a high-profile SeaTac minimum-wage fight, and targeted funding in local county races.

Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi and longtime boyfriend Jionni LaValle are officially married. The Jersey Shore alum and LaValle wed on Saturday, Nov. 29, at The Venetian in Garfield, New Jersey, in a Great Gatsby–themed ceremony and reception. The couple—who have two children, son Lorenzo (2) and daughter Giovanna Marie (3 months)—exchanged vows after getting engaged in March 2012.

Polizzi, 26, wore two gowns from Bridal Reflections (an off‑white lace dress for the ceremony and a Gatsby‑themed reception dress) and later a blinged Ines DiSanto party dress in photos she shared on her website. Bridesmaids, including BFF Jenni “JWoww” Farley, wore black gowns with bows. The celebration featured an 18‑piece band, Time Machine, and amenities such as a cigar and scotch bar. Polizzi said she stayed relaxed during planning, focusing on enjoying the moment.

President Donald Trump publicly supported calls for a boycott of Harley-Davidson after the company announced it would shift production of motorcycles destined for Europe to non-U.S. plants. Harley says the move is a response to EU retaliatory tariffs imposed after the Trump administration levied tariffs on various EU goods; Harley estimated the new tariffs could cost up to $100 million a year. On August 12, 2018 Trump tweeted that many Harley owners plan to boycott the company if manufacturing moves overseas and called that "great," saying competitors are moving in the U.S. direction and predicting a more level playing field. His comment followed a weekend meeting with about 180 "Bikers for Trump" supporters at his Bedminster, New Jersey golf club. Harley-Davidson declined to comment.

Former Winnipeg broadcaster and former Red River College journalism instructor Stephen (Steve) Vogelsang, 53, has been charged with two counts of robbery in connection with separate bank robberies in Medicine Hat, Alberta. Police say a man passed notes to tellers and took cash from a Royal Bank on Oct. 19 and a Bank of Montreal on Oct. 20; no weapons were seen. Vogelsang was arrested without incident at a Medicine Hat hotel early Saturday and remains in custody awaiting court.

Vogelsang is a well-known local figure who served as news director and longtime sports anchor at CKY/CTV Winnipeg (1992–2002) and taught journalism at Red River College from 2002 to 2011, returning part-time from 2014 until this past summer. Red River College confirmed he is no longer employed there.

Court records and reporting outline a string of financial and legal problems: a divorce, foreclosure and mortgage disputes over properties in Nelson, B.C., and Winnipeg (including allegations his ex-wife’s signature was forged), claims he had been sleeping in his vehicle, and prior criminal matters in Winnipeg — a sexual‑assault charge that was stayed in October 2017, a protection order granted in March 2017 by a former student he had been dating, and charges for disobeying court orders filed in August 2017. The former student alleges persistent unwanted contact despite police warnings; Vogelsang denies violent conduct and disputes her claims. Former students have expressed shock at the allegations.

A Brooklyn woman and New York law school graduate, Anna Lushchinskaya (also known professionally as Lushchinsky), was arrested after a racially charged, violent subway attack that was widely shared on social media. Videos from a northbound D train (around 8:30 a.m.) show the 40-year-old shouting profanities and racial slurs at a 24‑year‑old Asian woman, spitting, and striking her with an umbrella and keys; the victim suffered facial lacerations. A male passenger who intervened (who identifies as Dominican) and another Good Samaritan were also scratched. Witness Juan Ayala helped restrain Lushchinskaya until police arrived; bystanders criticized others for mostly recording rather than intervening.

Police apprehended Lushchinskaya at the 36th Street station. Criminal court records list five misdemeanor charges in one account (including menacing with a weapon and attempted assault); other reports cite two counts of felony assault. She pleaded not guilty, posted $1,000 cash bond, and is due back in court. State bar records show she graduated from New York Law School and was admitted in 2004, though her current registration status is unclear.

The incident drew comparisons to an earlier 2018 viral case involving attorney Aaron Schlossberg and prompted discussion about possible professional discipline. Experts noted that a criminal conviction would make bar discipline against Lushchinskaya more likely. This is at least her second subway-related arrest this year: a June complaint alleges she pepper‑sprayed passengers at the same station and faced related charges then as well.

South Korean film legend Choi Eun-hee has died at age 91 (reported as 92 by some sources) after chronic illness; she was receiving kidney dialysis and passed away in hospital on April 16, her eldest son Shin Jeong-gyun said. Born in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, in 1926, Choi began acting in 1947 and became one of Korea’s most celebrated actresses of the 1950s–70s, appearing in about 130 films. In 1954 she married director Shin Sang-ok; together they founded Shin Film and made many seminal works such as The Houseguest and My Mother (1961) and Red Scarf (1964).

In 1978 Choi was abducted from Hong Kong by North Korean agents and taken to Pyongyang; Shin was abducted months later. The couple were forced to make films for Kim Jong Il’s regime, winning international recognition (Choi earned Best Actress at the 1985 Moscow Film Festival for Salt). In 1986 they escaped while in Vienna, sought asylum at a U.S. embassy, lived in exile in the United States for about a decade, and returned to South Korea in 1999. Choi later led a theater company, produced a musical, and published an autobiography, Confessions, in 2007.

She is survived by two sons and two daughters. Her life—marked by stardom, abduction and escape—garnered wide public attention and mourning in South Korea.

Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, 92, was treated for dehydration Thursday in Winnipeg while volunteering with his wife Rosalynn on a Habitat for Humanity build. After working in the sun—sawing wood for a staircase—Carter appeared to wobble and then collapsed; Secret Service agents helped him to his motorcade and paramedics later attended. He was taken to St. Boniface Hospital for rehydration and observation; Habitat officials said it was precautionary, his wife accompanied him, and Carter reported he is feeling fine and encouraged volunteers to continue.

The Carters had led a morning devotional before joining about 500 volunteers at the Lyle Street site, part of the Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter Work Project and a Canada-wide Habitat blitz to build 150 homes (25 in Manitoba) for Canada 150. The couple are long‑time Habitat volunteers (since 1984) and previously worked in Winnipeg in 1993. Habitat International CEO Jonathan Reckford said further updates would come from the Carter Center.

An Ohio man who went missing on Mount St. Helens was found alive Wednesday after nearly a week lost on the volcano’s flank. Matthew B. Matheny, 40, of Warren, Ohio, set out alone on a day hike from the Blue Lake Trail area last Thursday and did not return. Friends reported him missing after he failed to come back; a deputy later found the borrowed Subaru Outback he had driven parked at the trailhead.

About 30–40 search-and-rescue personnel, aided by helicopters, tracking dogs and a drone, searched daily. Investigators narrowed their search to a roughly 1-square-mile area using cellphone data, witness reports and a computer model predicting his likely movements. A Skamania County–based rescue crew located Matheny about three miles from the car on Wednesday morning.

Rescuers found him conscious, talking and in satisfactory condition; he was airlifted to a Vancouver, Washington, hospital and treated mainly for dehydration and scrapes. His parents said he survived by eating berries (huckleberries) and killing and eating bees; his sandals reportedly broke during the ordeal. Authorities described his survival as “extremely unusual” given the circumstances. Family and officials thanked the search teams and volunteers.

Former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney addressed the NAACP annual convention in Houston, attempting to woo African-American voters by arguing his policies would better help black families than President Obama’s. He framed education as a central civil-rights issue, highlighted higher Black unemployment (14.4% vs. 8.2% overall), invoked his father’s civil-rights record, and pledged to work with black leaders and defend traditional family values.

Romney repeatedly stuck to his standard stump-line economic message—including a pledge to repeal the Affordable Care Act (“Obamacare”) and cut “non-essential” spending—which drew loud boos, jeers and audible disapproval from parts of the audience. He acknowledged the Republican Party’s imperfect racial record, asked for a “fair hearing,” and said he would not tailor different speeches to different audiences. His advisers called the appearance important and “courageous,” arguing that showing up matters even if he won’t win the bulk of the black vote.

The Obama campaign and NAACP attendees criticized Romney’s proposals as harmful to working families and out of step with the audience, while some credited him for engaging the community despite the rocky reception. Vice President Biden, not Obama, was scheduled to address the convention later.

Researchers have documented the rapid origin of a new bird species on Daphne Major, a small Galápagos island, providing the first direct, field-observed example of speciation confirmed by genomic data. In 1981 a large, non-native male (a large cactus finch, Geospiza conirostris) arrived on the island and mated with a resident medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis). That mating founded a "Big Bird" lineage whose descendants were tracked by B. Rosemary and Peter Grant over decades.

Genetic analyses by Uppsala University and collaborators show the immigrant came from Española (~100+ km away), so it could not return to its home population and instead bred with the local species. The hybrid offspring differed in song and beak morphology from resident finches—traits crucial for mate choice—so they tended to mate assortatively within their lineage. Within two generations the lineage was reproductively isolated from the other island species, and subsequent generations remained a closed breeding group. The Big Bird finches occupy a distinct ecological niche (larger body and beak allowed access to different food), survived environmental challenges (including near-collapse during a drought, then recovery), and numbered roughly 20–30 individuals with several breeding pairs when last counted.

This case demonstrates that hybridization can produce a viable, ecologically competitive new lineage quickly—much faster than traditional views of speciation—and suggests hybrid speciation may have contributed repeatedly to the diversity of Darwin’s finches. The study, “Rapid hybrid speciation in Darwin’s finches,” was published in Science (Nov. 23, 2017) and was supported by multiple institutions including Princeton, Uppsala University, and Galápagos conservation organizations.

The document compiles brief news items. Highlights include:

- A 2012 profile revisited: Shanyna Isom, who reportedly grows fingernails through hair follicles in her skin, remains seriously ill and financially strained two years after the initial report.

- Law enforcement actions: 16 people with alleged gang ties were arrested in a multi-agency sting in Tucson; police say the group is suspected of drug trafficking, money laundering, homicides and other violent crimes. In Ohio, three inmates—including a convicted high school killer—escaped over a prison fence but were recaptured; a guards’ union said prison officials were warned about an escape plan a day earlier.

- Science: Large coronal mass ejections on Sept. 10 are headed toward Earth, with significant geomagnetic activity expected.

- Crime: In Orem, Utah, police arrested a man, Bryan Ford (30), and a passenger, Christina Schlegel (25), after a Zales employee identified Ford as the man who stole an expensive ring from University Mall. Schlegel reportedly swallowed the ring to hide it; an X-ray at a hospital confirmed the ring was in her stomach. Both were booked on investigation of theft.

Oprah Winfrey is consolidating her media operations in Los Angeles and closing her Chicago Harpo Studios production complex by year’s end. Winfrey told Harpo staff in person that production will move to OWN’s new West Hollywood headquarters, where many shows and corporate teams are already based. Although the Chicago lease runs through April 2016, active shooting at Harpo stopped immediately and most production will end by mid-December; about 200 Harpo employees will be affected, with a small number offered roles or freelance work in L.A. and a skeleton Chicago crew remaining to close the facility.

Winfrey described the decision as bittersweet—Chicago and Harpo were central to her career and helped revitalize the West Loop—but said consolidating all teams under one roof makes sense as OWN expands. OWN, co-owned with Discovery, has posted consecutive years of growth and performs particularly well with African-American viewers. The network’s West Hollywood space on The Lot includes sound stages and post-production facilities Harpo lacked.

Winfrey will continue to focus on OWN while pursuing on-camera and film projects. She’s set to appear in Ava DuVernay’s Queen Sugar (DuVernay is finalizing the pilot), will reteam with director Lee Daniels for the Pryor biopic as Richard Pryor’s grandmother, and maintains Harpo Films’ development slate (including Henrietta Lacks at HBO and Oprah’s Book Club picks). She declined to take a role in the Broadway revival of ’night, Mother, citing the emotional toll of nightly portrayals of suicide, but will explore other New York theater opportunities and plans to do international speaking engagements rather than another domestic arena tour.

OWN’s scripted push will expand: Queen Sugar will join multiple Tyler Perry series (recently extended), an Octavia Spencer-led Tulsa miniseries about the 1921 race massacre, and Belief, a spirituality event series. Several remaining shows—Master Class, Iyanla: Fix My Life and others—will now be produced in L.A.

The Harpo campus, opened in 1990 and sold in 2014 to Sterling Bay (which leased space back to Harpo), played a major role in Chicago’s TV economy and neighborhood revitalization. Its closure threatens jobs in the city and marks a notable shift of Winfrey’s production footprint to the West Coast, though local boosters hope the West Loop will continue to thrive with new tenants and productions.
