Madonna’s 15-year-old son Rocco Ritchie has been at the center of a public custody clash after refusing to return to New York from his father Guy Ritchie’s home in London. Multiple insiders tell tabloids Rocco — who spent months traveling with Madonna on her Rebel Heart tour — grew increasingly unhappy with her strict, controlling parenting, frequent fights during the tour, and her frequent public sharing of his images on Instagram. He reportedly told his father he felt like “a trophy” rather than a son and preferred the more stable life with Guy.

Tensions escalated in Stockholm and London when Rocco “ran away” to his dad’s house and later blocked his Instagram. Madonna sought legal action in New York; a Manhattan judge ordered Rocco to return to New York before school resumed in January and to face his mother. Guy Ritchie’s camp says Rocco expressed clearly that he did not want to go back, and Rocco has separate legal representation in the U.K. Sources characterize Madonna as loving but “mega controlling”; others say Guy may have influenced Rocco’s decision. The dispute remains active, with outcomes of the court processes and whether Rocco will comply still unclear.

At a lunch at New York’s Lotte New York Palace during a United Nations gathering, President Donald Trump hosted and addressed leaders from several African nations and the African Union. He praised Africa’s economic potential, touted expanding U.S. trade and investment across sectors (agriculture, energy, transportation, healthcare, travel and tourism), and cited US initiatives such as potential Millennium Challenge Corporation investment in Côte d’Ivoire and Sasol’s U.S. petrochemical project. He also emphasized health and security cooperation — praising progress against HIV/AIDS, Ebola response, and Namibia’s growing health self-sufficiency — and highlighted U.S. partnerships to counter terrorism and respond to humanitarian crises in countries including the Central African Republic, Congo, Libya, Mali, Somalia and South Sudan. Trump named North Korea as a global security threat and said Ambassador Nikki Haley would visit Africa to work on peace and prevention efforts.

The speech drew attention, and ridicule, after Trump twice mispronounced “Namibia” as “Nambia,” a non‑existent country, prompting viral social‑media reaction and debate. Some observers defended his broader points about economic opportunity and partnership; others mocked the gaffe and questioned aspects of his remarks about Africa.

Miss World has announced it will end its swimsuit round after 63 years. Chairwoman Julia Morley said the organization no longer wants to evaluate women on their bodies and instead will emphasize other attributes—intellect, interview performance, charity work and “Beauty with a Purpose” service projects. The change was revealed privately to international directors after the 2014 pageant; Rolene Strauss of South Africa, crowned Miss World 2014, is the last winner to have competed with a swimsuit segment. Going forward, competitions will still include talent, top model/fashion, sports, social media challenges and in-depth interviews; a beachwear or fashion-style presentation may replace the bikini portion. Organizers frame the move as modernizing pageantry and shifting Miss World’s image from a beauty contest to an ambassadorial role focused on outreach and purpose.

A Brooklyn father and son, Joseph Andrade, 44, and his 22-year-old son Carlos, died of an apparent double opioid overdose after briefly leaving a family birthday party Sunday to “go for a smoke.” Police said both likely snorted a heroin–fentanyl mix. Carlos — who was not known to use drugs and had driven from Maryland with his girlfriend and their two young children for the celebration — was found inside his building’s foyer by his girlfriend, turning blue and unresponsive; Joseph was discovered a short distance away on the street. Distressed relatives called 911 and officers administered Narcan, but both men were pronounced dead at Lutheran Medical. Neighbors said Joseph had a history of addiction; Carlos was described as a devoted father. The deaths are under investigation and the medical examiner will determine the official cause. The report notes the broader context of the U.S. opioid crisis, with thousands of overdose deaths annually.

Donald Trump told CNN’s Jake Tapper that he believes the world would be better off if brutal leaders like Saddam Hussein and Moammar Gadhafi had remained in power. He argued that Iraq and Libya are more fractured and have become breeding grounds for terrorism since those dictators were removed, saying Hussein “would kill the terrorists immediately” and that both countries are now “broken up” and out of control. Trump acknowledged those leaders were “horrible,” but maintained their removal made the region less stable.

He also criticized partisan rancor in Washington—pointing to the Benghazi committee’s hearing with Hillary Clinton as an example of extreme partisan “hatred”—and presented himself as a potential unifier who has worked with both Democrats and Republicans. Trump said the country is deeply divided under President Obama and denied considering Clinton an “enemy,” calling her an opponent.

Bob Dylan was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature on Oct. 13 — the first time the prize has been given mainly to a musician — honored “for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition.” The 75‑year‑old, who won a Pulitzer Prize in 2008 and has 11 Grammys, has not publicly acknowledged the win. His official website briefly added the phrase “winner of the Nobel Prize in literature” in the lyrics section and then removed it. The Swedish Academy says it has been unable to reach Dylan or his representatives and has stopped trying to confirm whether he will attend the Nobel ceremony and banquet in Stockholm on Dec. 10. Dylan is known for avoiding awards recognition.

This piece contrasts the popular outcry over Conan O’Brien’s 2010 exit from The Tonight Show with classic labor-hero stories like Norma Rae, arguing the furor is disproportionate but revealing. The author says Conan was cast by fans as a working-class martyr—an everyman standing up to corporate injustice—because his public removal felt emblematic of a larger sense of unfairness: powerful executives keep their jobs while talented people get downsized or sidelined. That emotional resonance, coupled with Conan’s relatively classy and funny response and Jay Leno’s awkward image, fueled protests and sympathy.

At the same time the article explains the business reality behind NBC’s decision: Conan’s ratings, particularly in key advertising demographics (18–49 and 25–54), were inconsistent and often trailed competitors, and his advantage among younger viewers was smaller than expected. Attracting and holding 18–34 viewers late at night is increasingly difficult—cable channels, niche programming, sports, DVR playback, web clips and streaming, and video games all compete for that audience. NBC’s earlier experiment of putting Leno at 10 p.m. also undermined Conan by airing a stylistically similar show ahead of him. The piece concludes that while Conan became an unlikely symbol of the aggrieved worker, the situation reflects broader shifts in viewing habits and the coming generational change in late-night audiences.

Jack Ma, executive chairman of Alibaba, says he can no longer fulfill a January 2017 pledge to help create one million U.S. jobs because the current U.S.–China trade conflict has destroyed the “basis” for that promise. Ma made the commitment after meeting then-president-elect Donald Trump, proposing to stimulate American employment by helping U.S. small businesses sell on Alibaba’s e‑commerce platforms rather than by building factories or fulfillment centers in the U.S. In a Xinhua interview Ma confirmed the pledge is now unachievable but said Alibaba will continue to promote healthy China‑U.S. trade. He has warned the trade war could last many years and recently announced he will step down as Alibaba’s executive chairman next year to pursue work in education. Alibaba confirmed Ma’s remarks; the company earlier held outreach events in the U.S. to encourage small businesses and farmers to sell to Chinese consumers, though it has not disclosed how many U.S. jobs those efforts created.

Salon offers a personal list of "trippy" films to mark the rerelease of Nicolas Roeg’s The Man Who Fell to Earth and Terrence Malick’s The Tree of Life rollout. The piece teases a mix of well-known classics, experimental works, a feature-length montage, and a lesser-appreciated recent film by a surrealist evocatively likened to "Wavid Clynch." It playfully invites readers to add their own picks while riffing on parallel-universe imagination. The excerpt highlights Disney’s Fantasia as a standout: an experimental anthology of animated sequences set to orchestral music (conducted by Leopold Stokowski) that treats imagery as the mind’s eye made visible. Fantasia fuses music and animation so closely it feels hallucinatory—at times silly, sometimes terrifying, and often breathtaking—making it a rare Disney film that provokes questions about meaning and perception.

A South Korean-owned very large ore carrier, the Stellar Daisy, went missing in the South Atlantic after sending a distress message indicating it was taking on water on the port side. The Marshall Islands–flagged VLOC was en route from Brazil to China with iron ore and sent the alert Friday; a text to its operator said the ship was sinking. Two Filipino crew members were rescued Saturday from a life raft, but 22 crew remain unaccounted for (eight South Koreans and 14 Filipinos). Additional empty lifeboats and a raft were found in the area. South Korea has requested search-and-rescue help from Brazil and Uruguay, and Brazil dispatched a C-130; commercial ships located the rescued sailors. The ship’s exact fate has not been confirmed.

Georgia state Rep. Jason Spencer is facing calls to resign after a segment on Sacha Baron Cohen’s Showtime series Who Is America? showed him participating in humiliating, racist and homophobic stunts. Cohen, in character as Israeli “anti-terrorism expert” Erran Morad, persuaded Spencer to role-play a Chinese tourist by shouting racist gibberish and to shout the n-word as a ploy to attract attention during a fake kidnapping scenario. Spencer also obliged Cohen’s suggestion to threaten an assailant by baring and thrusting his buttocks, and performed other degrading actions. Spencer, who previously proposed a 2016 bill targeting Muslim head coverings, said the footage was presented to him as an “educational aid,” claimed he asked for provocative language to be removed, and said he’s seeking legal counsel. Georgia lawmakers have urged his resignation; Spencer has declined, saying he lost his primary and will serve out the remaining five months of his term. The episode joined other controversial Who Is America? segments in which Cohen reportedly duped public figures and everyday people into revealing bigoted or extreme views.

Campbell Soup is reformulating some of its soups to respond to changing consumer preferences and stagnant soup sales. Under CEO Denise Morrison, the company has been removing ingredients consumers distrust (like MSG and certain flavor enhancers), simplifying labels, and emphasizing more recognizable, “kitchen-style” ingredients. A limited-edition line (branded with Star Wars characters) debuted a revised chicken-broth product that reduced listed ingredients from 30 to 20 by eliminating items such as MSG, disodium inosinate/guanylate, vegetable oil and cornstarch, and by adjusting yeast extract and other flavorings to preserve taste. Campbell emphasizes innovation, perimeter grocery growth and digital marketing—buying brands such as Bolthouse, Plum Organics and others to reach millennial and health-conscious shoppers and to expand beyond canned soup. The company has launched new formats (Slow Kettle tubs, Skillet Sauces), pushed social and digital advertising, and introduced an ad campaign (“Made for Real, Real Life”) reflecting diverse family types. The changes are risky because longtime products are beloved and cost/texture/taste trade-offs can matter to consumers. Campbell has clarified it is initially changing a kids’ chicken-in-broth product in themed cans and is still evaluating timing for any changes to its classic red-and-white chicken noodle soup. The moves come as global soup sales have plateaued or declined and smaller organic brands gain share.

Claims resurfaced that a hidden planet called Nibiru (also promoted as “Planet X”) will collide with Earth or trigger apocalyptic events on September 23, 2017. The prediction, advanced by David Meade and promoted in viral videos and articles, links a specific alignment of the constellation Virgo, planets, and biblical numerology—especially the number 33 and Revelation 12—to the start of end-times events. Meade says the world “as we know it” will begin to change around that date, though he does not always claim instant annihilation.

Scientists and many faith leaders strongly reject the theory. NASA senior scientist David Morrison has repeatedly debunked Nibiru as a hoax: a massive planet or brown dwarf that close would be easily visible and would already have disrupted the orbits of inner planets and the Moon. Historical versions of the same doomsday idea have failed before (e.g., 2003 and 2012). Evangelical scholars like Ed Stetzer criticize the use of “biblical numerology” and call such sensational claims misleading and unhelpful to believers, urging critical thinking amid viral fake-news cycles.

Four-year-old Eli Waller of Hamilton Township, New Jersey, died in his sleep on Sept. 25 after showing only mild pinkeye the night before. The Mercer County medical examiner determined his cause of death was Enterovirus D68 (EV‑D68), confirmed by the CDC; brain and lymph‑node swelling were attributed to the virus. Eli, a youngest triplet with no known underlying health problems, had been well enough to attend preschool the two previous days.

EV‑D68 reemerged in the U.S. in August and has since been detected in at least 43 states. It typically begins like a common cold but can cause severe respiratory illness, hospitalizations for breathing difficulties, and, in rare cases, paralysis. The CDC has identified several deaths of patients who tested positive for EV‑D68, though the virus’s exact role in some fatalities is still under investigation.

Health officials say there are no specific treatments or vaccines for EV‑D68; prevention focuses on routine hygiene—covering coughs, frequent handwashing (20 seconds), and staying home when ill. Eli’s family announced plans to start The First Day of School Foundation to support students in special education, honoring his memory.

Little Fockers (2010) is the third installment in the Focker franchise, directed by Paul Weitz, written by John Hamburg and Larry Stuckey, and starring Robert De Niro, Ben Stiller, Owen Wilson, Dustin Hoffman, Barbra Streisand, Blythe Danner, Teri Polo, Jessica Alba and Laura Dern. The plot revolves around Greg Focker (Stiller) trying to prove to his father-in-law Jack Byrnes (De Niro) that he can be the family patriarch, a quest complicated by Jack’s spying and jealousy—especially after Greg’s interactions with pharmaceutical rep Andi Garcia (Alba). Returning subplots and characters from Meet the Parents and Meet the Fockers are recycled, with new bits (an erectile-dysfunction drug called “Sustengo,” an enema gag, and other gross-out jokes) thrown in.

Critics found the film dispiriting and largely unoriginal. Many reviewers criticized the movie as a thin, mostly predictable cash-grab that rehashes humor and dynamics already mined in the earlier films, offering little character development or fresh comedic insight. De Niro’s performance as the paranoid, controlling Jack drew particular scorn: reviewers lamented that his once-great dramatic stature has been undermined by repeated self-parody in these comedies. Other high-profile talents (Hoffman, Streisand, Blythe Danner, Owen Wilson, Laura Dern, Harvey Keitel in a brief bit) are underused; Alba offers little beyond sex appeal. The humor is uneven—occasionally genuinely funny (notably one outrageous scene involving an injection), but mostly relying on lowbrow, juvenile gags that will please broad audiences but disappoint those hoping for smarter or more original comedy.

Overall verdict: Little Fockers is an intermittently amusing, safe holiday crowd-pleaser that exists primarily to capitalize on franchise familiarity rather than to take creative risks; it will likely return modest box-office but frustrate viewers seeking daring or fresh comedy.

Jelinajane Bedrijo Almario, arrested in May 2016 in Hanford, California, was sentenced to 13 years in prison after being tried as an adult for organizing a prostitution and human-trafficking ring that involved 14- and 15-year-old girls. Prosecutors say the then-16-year-old posted victims' photos on prostitution websites, drove them to motels in Tulare County to meet clients, and recruited them via friends, acquaintances and social media. She also sent threatening messages to a victim’s family member and was charged with making terrorist threats. Hanford detectives said the operation lasted several weeks, that they recovered the victims and provided them help, and called the case an eye-opener because the alleged ringleader was a juvenile.

Researchers in Ottawa report that cardiotrophin‑1 (CT‑1), a naturally occurring protein, can stimulate a healthy, reversible form of heart growth and improve blood flow in animal models of heart failure. Published in Cell Research, the study—led by Lynn Megeney and Duncan Stewart and involving The Ottawa Hospital, the University of Ottawa, the Heart Institute and partners—shows CT‑1 promotes formation of longer, better‑organized heart muscle fibers and stimulates growth of blood vessels, boosting pumping function after damage from heart attack (left‑sided failure) or pulmonary hypertension (right‑sided failure).

Key findings:
- CT‑1–treated cardiac cells form elongated, functional fibers and induce accompanying blood vessel growth; by contrast, phenylephrine (PE), which drives the harmful hypertrophy seen in heart failure, produces wider, dysfunctional enlargement without new vessels.
- The beneficial remodeling induced by CT‑1 is reversible after treatment stops—similar to physiological enlargement from exercise or pregnancy—whereas PE‑induced pathological enlargement is irreversible.
- CT‑1 produced marked improvements in heart function in multiple rodent models (left and right heart failure) and appears to better control apoptosis‑related signaling pathways involved in muscle growth.

Implications:
- CT‑1 could offer a regenerative therapy for both left and right heart failure; right heart failure currently has no medical treatments beyond transplant for many patients.
- In animal studies CT‑1 was delivered via a small subcutaneous pump; short treatment courses produced durable benefits but were not permanent. Dose, duration, and safety thresholds remain to be established.
- The investigators have patents pending and hope to advance to human trials; if successful, clinical availability would likely take several years to a decade.

Funding came from Canadian research bodies, Heart and Stroke Foundation, and industry partner Fate Therapeutics. The authors emphasize this is a translational advance grounded in basic molecular and cellular research.

This document collects information and announcements related to the February 14, 2018 mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida and the FBI’s handling of a January 5, 2018 tip about the shooter, Nikolas Cruz.

Key points:
- The FBI provided an online form for the public to submit information about the Parkland shooting (name, contact, narrative, and file uploads—limit 4 files, max 512 MB each).
- On January 5, 2018, someone close to Nikolas Cruz contacted the FBI Public Access Line (PAL) and reported serious concerns: Cruz’s gun ownership, expressed desire to kill people, erratic behavior, disturbing social media posts, and a possible plan to conduct a school shooting.
- Under FBI protocols, that tip should have been treated as a potential threat to life and forwarded to the Miami Field Office for further investigation.
- The FBI determined those protocols were not followed: the PAL did not forward the January 5 information to the Miami Field Office and no follow-up investigation occurred at that time.
- FBI Director Christopher Wray said the Bureau is still investigating the matter, committed to determining what happened, reviewing response processes, and improving how tips from the public are handled. He expressed regret to victims and families and reiterated the FBI’s commitment to public safety.

Police in Surrey condemned motorists who taunted a woman threatening to jump from a bridge after the M3 at Sunbury was closed for more than two hours while officers talked her down. The woman was rescued from the footbridge and later detained under the Mental Health Act. During the incident, several motorists posted abusive tweets — one telling police to “tell her to get on with it” and another suggesting the woman be shot with a rubber bullet or forced into a net to clear traffic — prompting police to explain and ask for patience. Inspector Julie Hillman and Chief Constable Lynne Owens defended the road closure as necessary to save the woman’s life and called the public’s comments “completely unacceptable.” One of the tweeters later deleted her remarks and apologised. The summary notes that people in distress can contact the Samaritans for support.

Greece
- A plan to form a national unity government collapsed amid fierce party feuding, leaving Greece dangerously close to running out of money next month unless a new government secures emergency funding from the EU and IMF.
- Prime Minister George Papandreou resigned and tried to hand over to a coalition that was not agreed. Veteran technocrat Lucas Papademos (former ECB vice‑president and former Bank of Greece governor) re‑emerged as the leading candidate, but he insisted both main parties (PASOK and New Democracy) give written commitments to back the €130 billion bailout and its austerity measures before taking the job.
- An alternative candidacy—parliament speaker Filippos Petsalnikos—was floated but was rejected by large parts of both parties as too close to Papandreou. Talks were chaotic, repeatedly delayed and ultimately unresolved.
- Political paralysis has triggered a bank run: Greeks withdrew large amounts of euros in cash (estimates of up to €5 billion over a week), with some ordering very large withdrawals amid fear of a return to the drachma. The Bank of Greece warned that uncertainty was harming the economy and banking system.
- Parties did agree on early elections for February 19, 2012, though Papademos reportedly would accept a government that could extend beyond that date if needed. Urgent tasks for any new government include securing the bailout tranche, passing the 2012 budget and arranging €8 billion in previously pledged rescue funds to avoid imminent default.
- European leaders are pressuring Greece for clarity; there is concern that continued indecision could prompt lenders to withdraw support and increase the risk of Greece exiting the euro.

Italy
- The government presented economic overhaul measures in amendments to the 2012 budget to reassure markets and accelerate reforms amid rising yields (10‑year rates around 7%).
- Key measures include raising the retirement age to 67 by 2026 and plans to privatize state real estate via special‑purpose funds (first fund by April 2012 to buy at least 20% of unused prisons and barracks), with net proceeds dedicated to reducing public debt (about €1.9 trillion, ~120% of GDP).
- Local administrations will be ordered to reduce debt from 2013; companies running local public services may bid across jurisdictions to gain scale and efficiency. Transfers of public‑sector staff rules will be loosened, with hiring freezes applied where administrations have excess employees.
- The budget would incentivize infrastructure investment through tax cuts, encourage apprenticeships with payroll tax credits, ease use of part‑time contracts, boost women’s workforce participation, and liberalize some professional services by abolishing mandatory tariffs for groups like lawyers and notaries.

Overall: Greece faces acute political and financial crisis with stalled coalition talks threatening bailout support and prompting bank runs; Italy is pressing through structural and fiscal reforms (pensions, asset sales, labor and service liberalization) to stabilize markets and reduce debt.

A U.S. consulate employee, Raymond Davis, was arrested in Lahore on Jan. 27 after he shot and killed two armed men he says tried to rob him, a case that has deeply strained U.S.–Pakistan relations and provoked public outrage. Pakistani police and some witnesses dispute Davis’s self-defense claim, saying he continued firing as one suspect fled; a bystander was also killed when an American vehicle rushed to the scene. The U.S. insists Davis has diplomatic immunity and demands his release; Pakistani authorities have been reluctant to make a definitive ruling on his status, leaving the decision mired in legal and political dispute between federal and Punjab provincial officials.

Davis was moved from police custody to 14 days of judicial remand while his lawyer filed a petition challenging the court’s jurisdiction and asserting immunity; a hearing was set for Feb. 25. U.S. officials, including Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and Ambassador Cameron Munter, have pressed Pakistani leaders for his release, and some U.S. lawmakers warned of possible cuts to aid if Davis is not freed. Pakistan’s government faces a dilemma: handing Davis over risks domestic accusations of capitulating to Washington, while refusing could harm ties with a crucial ally that provides billions in aid.

The case has sparked protests and inflamed anti-American sentiment. Relatives of the dead men have demanded justice; demonstrators staged rallies and reenactments portraying Davis as a killer. The situation worsened when Shumaila Kanwal, the wife of one of the slain men, committed suicide by ingesting rat poison, telling doctors she had no faith in Pakistan’s justice system and demanding “blood for blood.” The U.S. Embassy contends the two men had criminal records and had just robbed another person in the area, while Pakistani officials emphasize unresolved legal questions and ongoing investigations into the deaths.

Summary:

The document contains two distinct pieces.

1) George Zimmerman MySpace and defense’s social media use:
- A 2005 MySpace page attributed to George Zimmerman, under the name "Joe G." and titled "only to be king again," was confirmed by Zimmerman's attorney to be genuine but abandoned in 2005. The page includes photos (one showing the same orange polo as his 2005 mug shot), a biographical post, references to 2005 legal troubles, and disparaging, anti-Mexican remarks written in street slang. It also brags about having two felonies reduced to misdemeanors and mentions a court dispute with an ex-girlfriend.
- This revelation came amid a broader social media battle around the Feb. 26 shooting of Trayvon Martin. Both sides have used online platforms: Martin’s family to raise funds and petition for charges, and Zimmerman’s defense—led by attorney Mark O’Mara—to raise money, post updates, and attempt to counter rumors. O’Mara initially ordered Zimmerman to remove his online presence, but then launched a polished site and a Facebook page (managed by a digital marketer) when online donations proved substantial.
- The defense’s social media activity drew criticism: comments on the Facebook page included attacks on Martin’s family, and the page later required moderated comments. Social media experts warn that an attorney’s active hosting of client social channels is unusual, may prejudice a jury, and could conflict with American Bar Association rules against facilitating extrajudicial comments. The ABA is revising its guidance to address social media use by lawyers.

2) Importance of estate planning (separate article excerpt):
- The piece argues that estate planning is necessary for people of all wealth levels, not just the very rich. Without a will or plans, state laws can force estates into probate, potentially delaying distribution and causing family disputes.
- An estate plan—wills, advance directives, and designated executors—lets individuals control distribution of assets, make medical and funeral decisions in advance, and reduce the likelihood of familial conflict and prolonged probate. It emphasizes meeting with an estate planning lawyer to ensure clear, specific instructions for handling possessions, finances, and appointed managers of the estate.

Busy Philipps alleges in her forthcoming memoir, This Will Only Hurt a Little (out Oct. 16), that James Franco physically shoved her to the ground while they were filming the 1999 TV series Freaks and Geeks. In an excerpt obtained by multiple outlets, Philipps says a scene required her character to gently nudge Franco’s character; she writes that he “grabbed both my arms and screamed in my face, ‘DON’T EVER TOUCH ME AGAIN!’” and “threw me to the ground. Flat on my back. Wind knocked out of me.” She describes the cast as horrified, says she tearfully told co-star Linda Cardellini (who advised she contact her manager), and that Franco later apologized only after being told to do so by the director and producers. Philipps calls him a “f***ing bully” and notes he was never punished. She has previously mentioned the incident publicly and told The Hollywood Reporter the two have discussed it over the years and that Franco at one point apologized; she also contextualizes her behavior at 19 as shaped by feeling expendable early in her career. The revelation comes amid broader sexual-misconduct allegations against Franco, which he has denied. Philipps’s memoir also addresses other personal traumas, including being raped at age 14. Franco’s representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Billy Joel and Alexis Roderick were married in a surprise ceremony during their annual July 4th party at Joel’s Long Island estate. The intimate nuptials were officiated by New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo and attended by family and close friends, including Joel’s daughter Alexa Ray and actor Kevin James. Joel, 66, and Roderick, 33 — an equestrian and former Morgan Stanley executive who has been with Joel since 2009 — are expecting a baby girl this summer. Joel’s ex Christie Brinkley shared a photo congratulating the couple. This is Joel’s fourth marriage; he is currently on tour with an upcoming Fenway Park date on July 16.

Researchers report in Biology Letters that male black widow spiders sometimes mate with immature females by piercing their hardened exoskeletons to reach internal genitalia and deposit sperm. These subadult females have fully developed reproductive organs and later produce the males’ offspring after molting; the procedure appears not to injure them if timed a few days before the molt. Field sampling found about one-third of immature females showed evidence of such mating. The behavior likely functions to let normally monogamous males avoid postcopulatory sexual cannibalism by mating when females are too young to eat them, increasing individual male reproductive success. Authors note this tactic alters male mating preference and could influence the species’ evolutionary trajectory, though it may or may not spread widely given the adaptive reasons for sexual cannibalism.

The Obama administration announced that Washington and Wisconsin have been granted federal waivers freeing them from many core requirements of the No Child Left Behind (NCLB) law, bringing the total to 26 states — more than half the nation. The waivers suspend NCLB’s unachievable 2014 mandate that all students reach math and reading proficiency and instead require states to adopt new accountability systems, show progress for historically underperforming subgroups, link teacher evaluations more closely to student achievement, and set college- and career-ready targets.

Washington’s waiver lifts the 2014 proficiency requirement, gives districts more flexibility with certain federal funds, requires improvement for disadvantaged subgroups, and commits the state to halve achievement gaps by 2018. It also mandates annual identification of Title I priority (bottom 5%), focus (next 10%), and reward schools. Wisconsin’s application was approved after requested detail was added. Ten states and D.C. still have pending applications; six states were approved in the prior month.

The waivers are an executive action intended as a temporary fix while Education Secretary Arne Duncan continues pushing Congress to reauthorize the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. Supporters say waivers relieve impossible mandates and let states target the lowest-performing schools; critics argue the administration is circumventing Congress and that the reforms still over-rely on standardized testing and may not address deeper problems in education.

Since 1996 Alexa Internet has donated its web crawl data daily to the Internet Archive, where it’s added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo. The rest of the document criticizes Discovery Channel’s Shark Week for sacrificing science and conservation messaging for sensationalism. The 2013 opener, a fictionalized “documentary” titled Megalodon: The Monster Shark Lives, blurred fact and fiction—reviving an extinct two‑million‑year‑old shark as if it might still exist—and exemplified a broader trend of fear-driven, dramatized programming. While Shark Week once promoted marine biology and helped raise awareness, recent specials rely on horror tropes, misleading reenactments, celebrity cameos, and sensational titles (e.g., “Sharkpocalypse,” “Top Five Eaten Alive”), undermining credibility and misrepresenting sharks as man‑eating monsters. Critics argue Discovery should return to substantive science storytelling: showcase shark diversity and behavior (thresher tails, wobbegongs, cookiecutter sharks, porbeagles, social lives of great whites), highlight real conservation needs, and stop trading accuracy for ratings if it wants to retain viewers and serve sharks responsibly.

Rep. Thaddeus McCotter (R–Livonia) wrote a crude TV pilot after his failed 2012 presidential bid and subsequent political troubles, The Detroit News reported. The 42-minute script, titled "Bumper Sticker: Made On Motown," casts McCotter as the humiliated host of a deliberately “train wreck” variety/talk show populated by offensive caricatures based on his congressional staff, his brother and others. The script’s humor includes explicit jokes about sex, drinking, race, flatulence and vomiting; a character nicknamed “Wardo” (widely identified as District Director Paul Seewald) is shown vomiting onstage after binge drinking, and another staff-based character (“Chowsers,” linked to Deputy District Director Don Yowchuang) leers at women and brags “I’m Thai.”

A former staffer leaked the script to the paper; McCotter says the draft was unfinished, given to a reporter without permission, and written as a cathartic outlet after his campaign embarrassment. He denies using taxpayer time to write it and says much of his writing occurs at home. The pilot name-checks media figures S.E. Cupp and Stephen K. Bannon (portrayed as the show’s reluctant producer); both say they were surprised by their inclusion and treated McCotter’s material as personal musings.

The script drew scrutiny because some staffers depicted in it were the same longtime employees who handled the petition drive that failed to place McCotter on Michigan’s primary ballot—87 percent of his signatures were invalidated—and the Michigan attorney general is investigating. Records show pay increases for Seewald and Yowchuang in early 2012.

McCotter has pursued other creative projects—he leads a band, formed Screaming Lemur Productions in 2010 to register music, contributed to media outlets and published a 2011 book. He says he planned to leave Congress in 2014 and was preparing post-congressional work, cultivating Hollywood conservative contacts. Local Republicans criticized him for appearing disengaged from constituent work after the ballot fiasco; McCotter rejects that claim, describing creative work as his personal outlet. Colleagues describe him as quirky and serious about policy, though some doubt a TV career is likely.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak unexpectedly refused to resign in a late televised address, instead saying he would remain president until September elections while delegating most—but not all—presidential powers to Vice President Omar Suleiman. The announcement sparked immediate anger and confusion among hundreds of thousands of protesters massed in Cairo’s Tahrir Square, who had expected Mubarak to step down. Demonstrators chanted “Leave, leave” and vowed larger protests; opposition leaders such as Mohamed ElBaradei denounced both Mubarak and Suleiman as unacceptable and warned the situation was volatile.

The speech intensified uncertainty about who actually holds authority—Egypt’s ambassador to the U.S. said Suleiman was now “de facto” president but that three key powers (amending the constitution, dissolving parliament and firing the cabinet) remained with Mubarak. The army publicly moved to “protect the nation” and met without Mubarak, signaling a potentially greater military role. Suleiman’s subsequent remarks failed to distance him from Mubarak and further angered protesters.

The U.S. government expressed disbelief and called for clarity, saying the transition’s immediacy and sufficiency were unclear; Washington found itself squeezed between regional allies and critics at home. The turnout and anger in Tahrir underscored the breakdown between the regime’s limited concessions and protesters’ demands for immediate change, leaving Egypt in a precarious, tense standoff.

A widely shared photograph of a bedraggled white cockatoo—nicknamed "Debbie" after Tropical Cyclone Debbie—showed the bird stripped of most of its feathers and clinging in a storm-hit Queensland forest. Rescuers found and placed the injured cockatoo in a box on Tuesday, but the Townsville Bulletin later reported it was discovered dead in the box on Thursday and was buried in the forest. A wildlife carer said the bird had likely been injured during the cyclone; photographer Alix Sweeney said she noticed the distinctive white bird amid the gale-force winds.

Cyclone Debbie caused extensive damage across Queensland: heavy rains (some areas received over 15 inches), widespread flooding, power outages affecting roughly 50,000 homes, and many schools closed. Emergency crews continued rescue operations. Viral, lighter‑tone coverage also noted a 5-foot bull shark found dead in a puddle in Ayr—near the cyclone’s landfall—and a brewery fire at the XXXX Brewery; authorities warned people to avoid floodwaters but said the brewery blaze would not affect beer supply. No serious human injuries were reported.

A Los Angeles street artist known as XVALA plans to include life‑sized reproductions of recently leaked nude photos of Jennifer Lawrence and Kate Upton in his upcoming show “No Delete” at The Cory Allen Contemporary Art Showroom (CACA) in St. Petersburg, Florida. XVALA, who has for years assembled and publicly displayed “compromised” celebrity images as part of his “Fear Google” series about digital privacy, says the additions fit the exhibit’s critique of loss of privacy. Cory Allen, the gallery publicist, defended the choice as part of a larger art project and said the gallery would not be posting the images online.

Representatives for Lawrence and Upton have warned they will pursue legal action against anyone who disseminates the stolen photos; the images are also part of an active federal criminal investigation. Critics note XVALA’s decision to show the work in Florida rather than California — where distributing nude images without consent with intent to distress can be illegal — and question whether exhibiting hacked images constitutes legitimate commentary or exploitation. The show was scheduled to open October 30.

Katharine F. Lemansky, who used the name “Katie Brown” on Facebook, was charged with misdemeanor animal cruelty in Cary, North Carolina after posting a photo showing her chocolate lab-mix with its mouth taped shut. The image, posted Friday with the caption “This is what happens when you don't shut up!!!,” went viral and generated hundreds of thousands of shares and numerous calls and messages to police departments, including from abroad.

Cary police say Lemansky told them the incident occurred in North Carolina; animal control officers who examined the dog and its littermate found them to be well cared for—vaccinated, spayed, microchipped, clean, well-nourished and with no signs of muzzle injury. Capt. Randall Rhyne called taping the muzzle “a terrible decision” and supported the cruelty charge. Lemansky was not jailed (the misdemeanor carries up to 150 days) and must appear in Wake County court on Dec. 14.

Law enforcement across multiple jurisdictions, including Avon, Torrington and South Daytona, investigated tips about Lemansky’s location; some agencies reported she no longer lived in their towns. The case drew strong public reaction—some urging further action and others warning that a single photograph lacks context. Authorities want to speak with Lemansky and see the dog to complete their inquiry.

Don Miller, owner of a small graphic printing business in Norfolk, Va., is facing higher costs at a time his sales have fallen 15% and he’s had to lay off staff. Virginia’s unemployment insurance trust fund has been drained by the recession, forcing the state to more than double the average employer tax per worker from about $95 in 2009 to an estimated $171 this year, and to cut benefits for some recipients. Virginia expects to borrow heavily to replenish the fund.

Nationwide, 36 states have raised the annual payroll tax employers pay to finance unemployment benefits; increases range from modest amounts to nearly $1,000 per worker in some states. So far 25 states have borrowed more than $25 billion from the federal government to keep benefit checks flowing, and analysts expect several more states will need to borrow soon. Some states have also cut benefits: examples include Pennsylvania (a 2.3% benefit cut), Hawaii (huge employer tax increases and proposed benefit reductions), and Texas (large shortfall and higher employer taxes).

The combination of higher employer payroll taxes and reduced benefits is creating hardships for businesses and unemployed workers. Small employers say higher taxes make rehiring harder during a downturn, while laid-off workers — including seniors who rely on unemployment to supplement Social Security — face sharply reduced income. Observers note many states entered the recession with trust funds well below recommended reserve levels, exacerbating the crisis. The article highlights the tension between fiscal necessity and the risk that raising taxes or cutting benefits during a recession could further suppress employment and economic recovery.

D.C. Council members Elissa Silverman and David Grosso introduced the Universal Paid Leave Act of 2015, a proposal to create one of the nation’s most generous paid-leave programs. Key points:

- Coverage and benefits: Nearly all full- and part-time employees of private entities based in D.C. would be eligible for up to 16 weeks of paid leave for family or medical reasons (birth, adoption, fostering, caring for an ill family member, recovery from illness, military-related leave). D.C. residents who work outside the city and federal employees who live in D.C. could opt in by paying into the fund; Maryland and Virginia residents who work for the federal government in D.C. would be excluded.

- Financing: The program would be funded by a new employer contribution to a city-run Family and Medical Leave Fund, modeled like unemployment insurance. Contributions would be on a sliding scale by salary (e.g., about 1% for high earners, down to 0.6% for minimum-wage workers in some estimates). Self-employed residents could opt out. Benefit payments would cover 100% of the first $1,000 of weekly earnings and 50% of earnings above that, capped at $3,000 per week.

- Rationale: Supporters argue the program addresses a major gap in U.S. social policy (the U.S. lacks national paid parental leave), helps low-income workers most, supports family stability, and aids women’s labor-force participation and re-entry after childbearing. The bill grew from a DOL-funded study and consultations with states that have paid-leave programs; the administration has backed local/state experiments to advance paid-leave policy.

- Cost and opposition: The D.C. Chamber of Commerce and some businesses warn the employer-funded approach could burden employers, raise costs, and drive businesses out of the city. Council supporters counter that pooled coverage spreads risk, increases employee loyalty and productivity, and that prior D.C. labor protections had minimal negative business impact.

- Legislative status: The bill has committee assignment and bipartisan co-sponsors sufficient for Council passage pending two required votes and mayoral approval. An official cost estimate from the D.C. Chief Financial Officer will be prepared as the measure proceeds.

- Broader context and personal stories: The coverage references national debates over declining labor-force participation, especially among working-age women, and research that links universal paid leave with higher female employment. Personal anecdotes (e.g., Charlotte Brock) illustrate how lack of paid parental leave forces difficult choices, can push women out of the labor force, and hinder career recovery.

Overall, the proposal would make the District a national leader in paid family and medical leave by offering lengthy, broadly available, and relatively generous wage replacement funded primarily by employer contributions.

Chris Urmson, director of Google’s self-driving car project, describes a July 1, 2015 rear-end collision in Mountain View that highlights how often Google’s autonomous vehicles are struck by distracted human drivers. While driving autonomously with a safety driver aboard, a Google Lexus stopped at a green light because traffic ahead was backed up; a following car failed to brake and hit it at about 17 mph. Occupants suffered only minor whiplash and the damage was limited, but the incident was one of 14 collisions involving Google’s fleet since 2009 — 11 of them rear-endings — and none caused by the self-driving systems. Urmson uses these incidents to argue that many minor crashes go unreported (NHTSA estimates up to 55%), so police-based crash rates undercount real risk; because Google’s cars now drive roughly 10,000 miles per week, the program can begin to estimate true crash exposure. He emphasizes that autonomous vehicles can monitor the environment 360 degrees without fatigue or distraction, contrasting them with human drivers who are increasingly inattentive due to phones and other distractions. Urmson notes the team is exploring ways the cars might alert distracted motorists before impacts but is cautious about nuisance measures (e.g., honking). The coverage also mentions broader debate over autonomy’s regulatory, insurance and cybersecurity challenges and that all test cars are accompanied by safety drivers per California rules.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced nominees for the 89th Oscars. La La Land led with a record-tying 14 nominations; Moonlight and Arrival followed with eight each. The Best Picture field (9 films) includes: La La Land; Moonlight; Arrival; Manchester by the Sea; Hell or High Water; Lion; Fences; Hidden Figures; Hacksaw Ridge.

Key category nominees:
- Best Director: Denis Villeneuve (Arrival); Mel Gibson (Hacksaw Ridge); Damien Chazelle (La La Land); Kenneth Lonergan (Manchester by the Sea); Barry Jenkins (Moonlight).
- Best Actor: Casey Affleck (Manchester by the Sea); Denzel Washington (Fences); Ryan Gosling (La La Land); Viggo Mortensen (Captain Fantastic); Andrew Garfield (Hacksaw Ridge); Tom Hanks (Sully) [note: list included Hanks in initial roster].
- Best Actress: Isabelle Huppert (Elle); Ruth Negga (Loving); Natalie Portman (Jackie); Emma Stone (La La Land); Meryl Streep (Florence Foster Jenkins).
- Best Supporting Actor: Mahershala Ali (Moonlight); Jeff Bridges (Hell or High Water); Michael Shannon (Nocturnal Animals); Dev Patel (Lion); Lucas Hedges (Manchester by the Sea) [original list also names Jeff Bridges, Ali, Dev Patel and Shannon].
- Best Supporting Actress: Viola Davis (Fences); Naomie Harris (Moonlight); Nicole Kidman (Lion); Octavia Spencer (Hidden Figures); Michelle Williams (Manchester by the Sea).

Other major categories and nominees (high-level highlights):
- Adapted Screenplay: Moonlight; Lion; Arrival; Fences; Hidden Figures.
- Original Screenplay: Hell or High Water; La La Land; The Lobster; Manchester by the Sea; 20th Century Women.
- Cinematography: Arrival; La La Land; Lion; Moonlight; Silence.
- Film Editing: Arrival; Hacksaw Ridge; Hell or High Water; La La Land; Moonlight.
- Production Design, Sound Mixing, Sound Editing, Original Score, Original Song, Costume Design, Makeup/Hairstyling, Visual Effects, Animated Feature, Documentary Feature, and short film categories each featured multiple nominees (notable entries include Kubo and the Two Strings, Moana, Zootopia in animation; Fire at Sea, I Am Not Your Negro, OJ: Made in America, 13th in documentary; Rogue One and The Jungle Book in visual effects).

Context and industry notes:
- The nominations were viewed as a test of the Academy’s recent push for diversity after the “OscarsSoWhite” controversy; the field was notably more diverse this year.
- Mel Gibson’s directing nomination for Hacksaw Ridge was a notable surprise given his prior ostracism.
- Many nominees are modest box-office earners; none had topped $100 million domestically at the time, reflecting the awards’ continued focus on smaller, critically acclaimed films rather than blockbusters.
- Amazon earned its first Best Picture nomination with Manchester by the Sea. The show (hosted by Jimmy Kimmel) and the nominations format were also adjusted this year amid ongoing debates about Hollywood’s inclusivity and declining TV ratings for the telecast.

Law enforcement and marine researchers are investigating the death of a juvenile male great white shark that washed ashore at Seascape/Beer Can Beach in Aptos, California, on June 17, 2018. The shark measured about 8–9 feet long and weighed roughly 500 pounds. Initial on-site observations noted fresh puncture wounds, scars consistent with feeding on sea lions (including sea lion fur in its jaws), and other cuts; researchers said it otherwise appeared well-fed and healthy, suggesting a rapid cause of death.

A necropsy was performed by UC Santa Cruz–affiliated researchers (California Department of Fish and Wildlife handled coordination). Necropsy findings prompted the California Department of Fish and Wildlife’s law enforcement division to open a criminal investigation; officials have not disclosed what in the necropsy led to that decision. Researchers have suggested possible natural causes such as bacterial infection (Carnobacterium and other pathogens previously implicated in shark deaths), ingestion of debris or hooks, or injury from a fight, though some investigators doubt sea lion wounds were fatal.

The incident generated controversy after a photo circulated showing a marine biologist posing beside the carcass for scale; the photographer defended the action as necessary to document size before the tide could carry the shark away. Authorities urged the public to report stranded marine animals to lifeguards or officials, noting that great whites are protected and that intentional harm could carry significant penalties. The stranding is considered notable by researchers because few great whites wash ashore in the area; investigators continue to probe whether foul play was involved.

The document contrasts the fading “chick lit” trend—urban, fashion- and romance-focused novels—with an emergent cultural and literary shift toward “farm lit,” stories about women leaving city life for rural farming, small-scale food businesses, and community-centered lives. Examples of such novels feature heroines who trade careers and high-powered relationships for farming, baking, oyster tending, or raising goats and discovering new romances and meaning in the countryside.

That fictional trend mirrors a real and growing movement: women are increasingly becoming farmers and farm operators across the United States. Citing a USDA Economic Research Service study, the text reports that the number of woman-operated farms more than doubled between 1982 and 2007; counting all primary and secondary female operators, nearly one million women are involved in U.S. farming—about 30 percent of farmers. Women are entering farming from diverse backgrounds: midlife career changers seeking tangible work and family connection, younger graduates motivated by food justice and sustainable agriculture, and older women who inherited land. Many operate small farms, specialize in livestock or niche produce, and form cooperative networks and organizations to overcome barriers.

Profiles of individual women—Tammy Burnell, Hannah Breckbill, Pilar Rebar, and others—illustrate motivations (loss or life-change, desire to work “in something real,” commitment to clean food) and the variety of enterprises (organic seedlings, flower production, diversified fruit, livestock, farm B&Bs). Female farmers confront distinct challenges: smaller-scale operations that need help with financing, equipment access, marketing, and business planning. In response, organizations such as the National Women In Agriculture Association, Women, Food and Agriculture Network, Annie’s Project, Soil Sisters, MOSES, and local initiatives provide training, tours, networking, and technical assistance.

USDA leaders quoted in the piece emphasize the momentum behind the trend, note women’s increasing land ownership (higher rates than men), leadership in livestock, and the fact younger women are entering farming faster than older women leave. They also acknowledge remaining constraints—many women rely on off-farm income and few women-operated farms exceed $100,000 in sales—and describe USDA efforts to improve women’s representation and access to programs through initiatives like Know Your Farmer, Know Your Food and County committee reforms.

Overall, the piece links a cultural shift in popular fiction to a substantive rise in women’s participation in agriculture, portraying female farmers as diverse, committed, collaborative, and increasingly influential in rebuilding local and sustainable food systems.

David Goodall, a 104-year-old Australian botanist and ecologist who had long campaigned for legal assisted dying, ended his life Thursday at the Life Circle clinic in Basel, Switzerland, using a lethal drug under medical supervision. Not terminally ill, Goodall traveled from Perth after euthanasia remains illegal in Australia; he and supporters raised over $20,000 to fund the trip. In interviews and at a news conference the day before his death, he said his abilities and eyesight had declined, he no longer wished to continue living, and he wanted the freedom to choose the timing of his death. Wearing a shirt reading “Ageing Disgracefully,” he sang a few bars of Beethoven and requested doctors decide the method. He hoped his decision would help “free the elderly” and spur legalization elsewhere; Exit International said he died listening to Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy.” Goodall, a respected academic who edited the 30-volume Ecosystems of the World series and received an Order of Australia Medal, was accompanied in Basel by four relatives and a close friend and had previously bade farewell to family in Australia and France. The report notes evolving laws elsewhere—Victoria, Australia, recently passed a bill allowing assisted dying for terminally ill patients starting in 2019, and several U.S. states and countries permit forms of physician-assisted suicide.

Debra Long, mother of Matt (born Matt Heichel), has not seen or spoken with her son for years and fears she might not recognize him. She keeps faded photos of him from childhood, prom and early marriage. Long says Matt’s behavior changed after he moved into the home of former Penn State assistant coach Jerry Sandusky in 1996: she opposed the foster placement, accused Sandusky of stalking-like behavior and suspected abuse, and later preserved court and probation documents reflecting concerns about the placement and how Matt became estranged from his biological family.

Matt, now 33, went to live with the Sanduskys after being held in juvenile detention for setting a barn on fire. He was later formally adopted as an adult. Records and interviews describe a rocky, controlling relationship: runaways, a 1996 suicide attempt while at the Sandusky home, theft accusations and other disturbances. Long says she once asked Matt if Sandusky had touched him; he replied, “I don’t want to talk about it.” Matt initially declined public comment and previously denied abuse, but later—through his attorney—told prosecutors he is a molestation victim of Jerry Sandusky and said he would testify truthfully if called, asking the media for privacy. During the trial, one other victim testified that Matt was present at a shower when an assault began and left before it occurred.

Several family members recall strained dynamics: Matt’s ex-wife Jill Thomas told police he was estranged from Sandusky and became physically sick after calls with him; Matt’s brother Ron Heichel says he felt unwelcome in the Sandusky home and later was convicted of an unrelated murder. Long was subpoenaed and testified before the grand jury; the FBI also received her documents and is conducting a parallel investigation focused partly on possible cover-up.

Legal observers reviewed the 1990s foster-care records and noted some red flags—probation officers’ concerns, a psychologist’s input favoring Sandusky’s home, and admitted procedural lapses—though they cautioned that practices then varied and records are limited. Sandusky and his charity The Second Mile were trusted in the community and had relationships with child services, which likely influenced placements.

The context: Jerry Sandusky faces more than 50 counts of child sex abuse involving boys connected to The Second Mile; his arrest led to charges against Penn State officials, caused major upheaval at the university, and prompted multiple state and federal inquiries into Penn State and The Second Mile. Matt’s situation became a focal, complicated subplot in the broader investigation and trial—highlighting family ruptures, contested foster-care decisions from the 1990s, and unanswered questions about what Matt experienced and told investigators.

A 46-year-old South Carolina mother, Debra Harrell, was arrested and charged with “unlawful conduct toward a child” after leaving her 9-year-old daughter alone at a park while she went to work at McDonald’s. The child, who had a cellphone and sometimes walked to the McDonald’s inside Walmart for lunch, had been at the park for several hours over multiple days. On the third day a passerby questioned the girl, reported the situation to police, and officers took the child to headquarters, contacted Harrell, and arrested her after she admitted leaving her daughter there. The Department of Social Services then took custody of the child.

The case has prompted widespread criticism that authorities overreached. Legal experts note state neglect laws are typically vague—requiring “appropriate” supervision for a child’s age and development but rarely specifying ages or time limits—leaving broad discretion to police, child welfare workers, judges, and prosecutors. Critics argue that arresting Harrell and placing the child in foster care likely inflicted more harm than the parenting decision itself, risked costing the mother her job, and came amid shortages of foster families and overburdened child-protection staff. Commentators also link such prosecutions to class and race dynamics—Harrell is Black and low-income—and to welfare-era pressure that pushed single mothers into low-paying work without affordable childcare.

Broader debate centers on a cultural shift toward zero-tolerance, constant supervision of children that many say isn’t supported by statistics about actual risks (for example, the rarity of stranger abductions). Advocates for “free-range” parenting contend that some everyday choices carry small risks either way, and question why certain ordinary parenting decisions are criminalized while others that carry greater everyday risks (like driving with children) are socially accepted.

Researchers combined a large new anatomical dataset with molecular data to reconstruct relationships and timing of early placental mammal evolution and to infer the likely form of the placental ancestor. Over six years they scored 4,541 phenomic characters across 86 living and fossil species, assembled these data in the MorphoBank database, and analyzed them together with DNA sequences to produce a fossil-calibrated phylogeny.

Major findings
- Timing: Crown Placentalia and the major placental orders originated after the Cretaceous–Paleogene (K–Pg) boundary (~66 Ma). The placental common ancestor is inferred to have arisen within a few hundred thousand years after the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, and modern orders appeared within a couple million years thereafter — supporting a “post‑K–Pg explosive” radiation rather than a deep Cretaceous origin implied by some molecular clock studies.
- Ancestral reconstruction: The hypothetical placental ancestor resembled a small, insectivorous, roughly rat‑sized mammal with a long furry tail, fleshy nose, light underbelly, and reproductive anatomy indicating full-term live birth (e.g., a two-horned uterus and close maternal–fetal blood contact).
- Phylogeny and relationships: Many molecularly recovered nodes were confirmed, but the combined analysis overturned some molecular results. Notable placements include Sundatheria (Dermoptera + Scandentia) as sister to Primates, a close relationship between Proboscidea and Sirenia, monophyly of echolocating bats (Chiroptera), and a basal split of Placentalia into Xenarthra and Epitheria. The oldest known afrotheres in their tree are extinct New World taxa, challenging the idea that Afrotheria arose in Africa tied to Gondwanan breakup.

Implications and debate
- The results argue against a Gondwana-driven vicariance model and push the origin and diversification of placentals into the Paleocene, about 36 million years later than some molecular-only estimates.
- The study showcases MorphoBank and integrated phenomic–genomic analysis as a powerful approach for deep-time phylogeny reconstruction, but the conclusions remain contested. Critics note possible problems with convergent morphological traits and the difficulty of fully reconciling fossil and molecular signals; the authors acknowledge debate but contend the fossil record increasingly supports a late, post‑K–Pg origin.

Overall, this integrated fossil-plus-molecular study supports a rapid Paleocene diversification of placental mammals from a small, insectivorous ancestor soon after the end‑Cretaceous extinction and proposes several revised interordinal relationships.

Felicia "Snoop" Pearson, 31, known for playing a cold-blooded assassin on HBO’s The Wire, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute heroin the day before her trial was to begin in connection with a multistate drug investigation dubbed "Operation Usual Suspects." Judge Lawrence Fletcher-Hill accepted the plea, gave Pearson credit for time served, suspended a seven-year sentence, and ordered three years’ supervised probation with permission for provisional out-of-state travel for work. 

Prosecutors say Pearson was caught on a wiretap and accused of storing drugs and cash in her Baltimore apartment, occasionally selling heroin for co‑conspirators, and being involved in activities tied to a network that bought heroin from New York and marijuana from California for sale in Baltimore. She was one of 64 people indicted in March. Outside court her attorney framed the plea as a way to move forward with her acting career; Pearson insisted she would have been acquitted and said she plans to move to Los Angeles. 

Pearson has a prior criminal history—including a juvenile conviction for second-degree murder for which she served time—and was previously arrested on a minor drug charge in 2008 but acquitted. She told followers on Twitter she was "FREE" and said she is working on two movies.

Roger Ebert, the influential and widely read film critic and longtime Chicago Sun-Times columnist, died in Chicago at 70. His death was announced by the Sun-Times; no cause was given, though he had battled cancer and related health problems since 2002. 

Ebert helped bring film criticism into the mainstream, most famously alongside Gene Siskel on television, where their thumbs-up/thumbs-down verdicts reached a broad audience and shaped public taste. In 1975 he became the first film critic to win a Pulitzer Prize; his columns were widely syndicated, he wrote more than 15 books, and in 2005 he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Colleagues and readers praised his clear, witty, conversational prose, emotional sensibility, and willingness to engage with both popular and art-house cinema.

Despite severe surgeries that robbed him of much of his jaw and his ability to speak and eat, Ebert remained prolific: continuing to write reviews and essays, maintaining an active online presence—blogging and tweeting to large followings—and even publishing a rice-cooker cookbook. Public figures including President Obama and many fellow critics and writers lauded his influence, generosity, and enduring voice. Editorial tributes highlighted his passion for movies, his work ethic, his mentorship of younger critics, and the rare combination of erudition and accessibility that made him a defining voice in film criticism.

Researchers scanning infants’ brains have identified early neuroanatomical changes that can predict later autism in babies at high familial risk. In an NIH-funded Infant Brain Imaging Study, teams led by Joseph Piven and Heather Cody Hazlett used MRI to scan 106 infants who had an older sibling with autism (and 42 low‑risk controls) at about 6, 12 and 24 months. Fifteen of the high‑risk infants were diagnosed with autism at 24 months.

Key findings
- Infants later diagnosed with autism showed accelerated cortical surface‑area growth between 6–12 months (increased expansion of the brain’s folded outer surface), followed by an overall brain-volume “overgrowth” between 12–24 months that coincided with the emergence of behavioral symptoms.
- A deep‑learning algorithm applied to 6‑ and 12‑month MRI data (plus sex) correctly predicted 30 of 37 autism cases among high‑risk infants (about 81% sensitivity) and produced few false positives (~3%). Behavior-based predictions at that age perform much worse.

Implications and caveats
- The work suggests autism‑related brain changes begin in the first year of life and raises the possibility of identifying high‑risk infants months before behavioral symptoms appear, which could enable earlier intervention research.
- Major limitations remain: the results are from a relatively small, high‑familial‑risk sample and must be replicated in larger, independent cohorts. It’s unclear whether the biomarkers apply to the general population. Differences in MRI equipment and processing, and the need for a population‑wide “brain growth chart,” pose practical hurdles to clinical use.
- Even if prediction improves, there is currently no proven way to prevent autism; the immediate benefit would be informing families earlier and enabling trials of early interventions while the brain is highly plastic.

Bottom line: Early MRI markers show promise for predicting autism in infants with an affected sibling, but further replication, broader testing, and practical validation are required before clinical adoption.

Billionaire hedge-fund manager David Tepper has moved his residence and his firm, Appaloosa Management, from New Jersey to Florida, a shift that is likely to cost New Jersey hundreds of millions in tax revenue. Tepper, who registered to vote in Florida, listed a Miami Beach condo as his address, filed legal paperwork declaring Florida residency, and relocated Appaloosa effective Jan. 1. People close to him say family ties motivated the move, but Florida’s lack of personal income and estate taxes (and lower corporate taxes) offers large financial incentives compared with New Jersey’s high tax burden.

Tepper has earned several billion dollars in recent years—Institutional Investor’s Alpha put his gains at more than $6 billion over three years—and with New Jersey’s top marginal income-tax rate at 8.97 percent, his state tax liability over that period could have exceeded $500 million before deductions. New Jersey depends heavily on income taxes (about 40% of revenue), and a tiny share of taxpayers provide a large portion of collections; the state’s nonpartisan budget office warned Tepper’s departure creates “unusual” income-tax forecast risk and could widen budget shortfalls. The move highlights tensions in tax policy: how reliance on a small group of very high earners makes revenue vulnerable, and the broader debate over taxing the wealthy versus boosting middle-class wages and economic growth.

Chicago officials, led by Mayor Rahm Emanuel, pledged to keep the city a sanctuary for undocumented immigrants despite President-elect Donald Trump’s stated plans to crack down on illegal immigration and threaten funding for sanctuary jurisdictions. Sanctuary policies generally limit local law enforcement cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The decision follows fears among immigrants — including DACA “Dreamers” — who worry about deportation; Emanuel directed residents seeking help to call 311. Chicago aldermen plan a news conference and want Illinois Gov. Bruce Rauner to oppose federal interference. Illinois Comptroller-elect Susana Mendoza also urged Rauner to speak out.

Trump told CBS’s 60 Minutes he intends to deport “probably 2 million, it could be even 3 million” immigrants with criminal records and that DACA could be ended; he reiterated plans to build a border wall. Experts note Trump’s deportation figures are uncertain: DHS counts about 1.9 million noncitizens with convictions (a mix of legal and undocumented residents), while the Migration Policy Institute estimates about 820,000 undocumented immigrants have criminal records. Past federal policy under Obama prioritized deporting criminals, producing high deportation numbers early in his presidency; more recently enforcement focused on more serious offenders and deportations declined.

Legal and practical constraints mean mass deportation of all undocumented people is implausible, though accelerating removals to reach about 2 million over a term is feasible under existing resources. Much attention centers on the likely rollback of Obama-era programs—especially DACA—which could put hundreds of thousands of young immigrants at risk. Nationally, many cities (New York, Los Angeles, Seattle, Philadelphia, San Francisco, among others) have reaffirmed sanctuary commitments since the election; immigrant-rights groups and unions like the United Farm Workers are mobilizing to resist harsh enforcement. President Obama urged Trump to “think long and hard” before jeopardizing the status of DACA beneficiaries.

Jerry Buss, the longtime majority owner of the Los Angeles Lakers, was hospitalized for several months with an undisclosed form of cancer and had spent time in the intensive care unit at Cedars‑Sinai, according to multiple reports. The family kept his illness private; team representatives declined to comment further out of respect for the family. Buss, 79 (later reports noted he died at age 80), had a history of recent hospital visits for other issues, including dehydration and blood clots.

Current and former Lakers—including Kobe Bryant, Pau Gasol, Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul‑Jabbar and Shaquille O’Neal—expressed support and concern; Bryant spoke publicly about Buss’s enormous impact on his career and on the game, crediting Buss with taking a chance on him as a 17‑year‑old and creating the “Showtime” Lakers brand that helped globalize basketball. Team officials noted that Buss’s children, Jim (basketball operations) and Jeanie (business side), had been running team affairs.

Buss bought the Lakers (and the Forum and the NHL’s Kings) in 1979 and transformed the franchise into an NBA powerhouse and cultural icon, assembling eras led by Kareem Abdul‑Jabbar and Magic Johnson in the 1980s and later Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant. Under his ownership the Lakers won 10 NBA championships. A former aerospace engineer and real‑estate developer, Buss was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2010 and was widely credited with making the Lakers an entertainment spectacle and model franchise.

This document criticizes CNN’s coverage of the Steubenville rape verdict for centering sympathy on the convicted teens rather than the 16-year-old victim. It uses transcripts and episode descriptions to show CNN anchors (Candy Crowley, Poppy Harlow) and legal commentator Paul Callan emphasizing the emotional breakdowns of defendants Trent Mays (17) and Ma’lik Richmond (16), their “promising futures” as star football players and students, and the lifelong consequences of sex-offender registration for the boys. Critics say that tone minimized the gravity of the crime and sidelined the victim’s trauma.

Key points:
- CNN repeatedly highlighted the defendants’ tears, family pleas and future losses while giving far less attention to the victim’s experience and the long-term impact of rape on survivors.
- Legal analysis focused on the defendants’ label as registered sex offenders and its effects on employment and housing, which many viewers found disproportionately sympathetic.
- The coverage fit a broader pattern in mainstream media that has at times privileged narratives about accused athletes’ potential and reputations over victims’ stories, encouraging accusations of victim-blaming and reinforcing “rape culture.”
- Media critics and journalists (including Salon, Gawker, the Women’s Media Center and others) argued CNN’s framing was tone-deaf and that balanced reporting should center the crime’s seriousness, the victim’s trauma, and cultural questions about masculinity and accountability.
- The report notes substantive facts of the case: Mays and Richmond were found guilty of raping a heavily intoxicated 16-year-old at multiple parties, with social-media evidence (photos, texts, videos) playing a central role in public outrage. The state planned a grand jury to consider further charges.
- The piece also documents additional media failures: several networks aired the victim’s name and CNN’s segment selection favored footage of crying defendants (because the victim’s identity was protected), producing visually sympathetic material about the boys.
- Some outlets and writers (e.g., Dan Wetzel at Yahoo Sports) were praised for contextualizing the crime, condemning victim-blaming, and exploring the town’s football-centric culture that critics say enabled the behavior.

Overall, the document calls for more responsible, victim-centered reporting that explains rape’s severity, avoids normalizing sympathy for perpetrators as the primary story, and uses coverage to examine cultural and systemic issues that contributed to the crime.

Actress Nastassja Kinski has publicly supported her half-sister Pola after Pola revealed in Stern magazine that their late father, celebrated German actor Klaus Kinski, sexually abused her from about age five to 19. Nastassja told Bild she was “deeply shocked,” called Pola a “heroine” for speaking out, and said the disclosure—and Pola’s forthcoming autobiography—could help other victims who hide abuse.

Pola says she was abused repeatedly and that Klaus tried to normalize it, even treating her as his “little sex object.” Christian David, a Kinski biographer, noted rumors about Klaus’s relationship with Pola had circulated for years.

The article places the revelations in context of Klaus Kinski’s legacy: a brilliant but volatile actor known for intense roles in Werner Herzog films (Aguirre, Nosferatu, Fitzcarraldo) and for scandalous off-screen behavior. The piece explores the moral dilemma fans and colleagues face now—can one still appreciate Kinski’s art given the allegations—and notes how the abuse colors memories of his work and of directors like Herzog, who documented Kinski’s volatility in My Best Fiend. The author concludes that the new revelations make it impossible to remember him uncritically.

Apple filed a U.S. patent application, “Protective Mechanism for an Electronic Device,” describing a system to reduce drop damage to portable electronics (specifically citing the iPhone). The concept uses sensors (gyroscopes, accelerometers, possibly GPS or imaging) and a processor to detect freefall, estimate orientation, fall speed, distance to impact and time-to-impact, and consult stored fall statistics to choose a response.

Responses proposed include methods to change the device’s orientation or reduce impact on fragile components: shifting a weighted internal mass to alter center of gravity, extending aerodynamic foils or lift members, deploying small thrust mechanisms (e.g., gas canister), retracting vulnerable parts, or gripping/ejecting attached cables that might pull a device off a surface. The patent also mentions motors to clamp plugs/cables to prevent a fall or forcefully jettison them if they cause a pull-down.

Apple acknowledges many embodiments; the filing notes the complexity and practical hurdles—particularly for very thin devices—so integration into current iPhones is unlikely in the near term. The application was filed in September 2011 and lists Nicholas V. King and Fletcher Rothkopf as inventors.
