U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) chief Travis Tygart publicly accused Lance Armstrong of attempting to influence and undermine antidoping efforts and of offering money to testing bodies. Tygart told CBS that an Armstrong representative offered USADA more than $150,000 (he later estimated about $250,000) in 2004, an offer USADA rejected as a conflict of interest; he also said Armstrong donated roughly $100,000 to the International Cycling Union during his career. Tygart said Armstrong tried to intimidate former teammates who testified to a federal grand jury and that Tygart himself received death threats during the investigation.

The allegations come after USADA’s October report, which described what it called “the most sophisticated, professionalized and successful doping program that sport has ever seen,” and resulted in Armstrong being stripped of his seven Tour de France titles and given a lifetime ban. The World Anti‑Doping Agency and the International Cycling Union declined to appeal USADA’s sanctions.

Armstrong, 41, who has long denied doping, has reportedly told associates he is considering publicly admitting to using performance‑enhancing drugs and blood transfusions; such a confession could potentially affect reinstatement under WADA rules. He has also been in talks with antidoping officials reportedly seeking meetings with WADA leadership. Legal questions remain about possible perjury consequences for past sworn denials.

Oprah Winfrey’s network announced a 90‑minute “no‑holds‑barred” interview with Armstrong to air January 17 from his Austin home; the interview is expected to cover the USADA report and the allegations. The announcement prompted commentary about past ties between Armstrong, Discovery (a former team sponsor), and Winfrey. Armstrong has been training in Hawaii and competing in non‑sanctioned triathlons since being banned; he has stepped down from the Livestrong board.

President Obama pushed ahead with efforts to secure fast-track trade authority to complete the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), as bipartisan legislation was introduced in the Senate Thursday and a companion bill by Rep. Paul Ryan is expected in the House. The Hatch (R-Utah)–Wyden (D-Ore.) bill would give the president “trade promotion authority,” allowing a final agreement to come to Congress for an up-or-down vote without amendment. Hatch plans a committee markup April 23.

Administration officials say fast-track is essential to conclude TPP negotiations with 11 Pacific nations and to lock in U.S. influence in the region amid rising Chinese competition. Obama framed the deal as a priority to expand opportunities for American workers, while cautioning that past pacts have not always delivered.

The measure includes Wyden-won transparency provisions, a mechanism allowing the Senate to revoke fast-track if the administration fails to meet negotiating commitments, and language calling for worker, environment and human-rights protections (though specifics are limited). Opponents — including many House and Senate Democrats, labor unions and environmental groups — argue the TPP will cost U.S. jobs and favor multinational corporations. The AFL-CIO will run a six-figure ad campaign targeting lawmakers to fight the bill.

Senate Democrats remain deeply divided: leaders such as Chuck Schumer and Dick Durbin have expressed skepticism, with Schumer conditioning support on a strong separate anti–currency-manipulation measure. Republicans are broadly supportive, and backers expect the Senate to pass the bill in May, setting up a tougher battle in the narrowly divided House where Obama would likely need more than 30 Democrats to win final passage.

Most U.S. Independence Day fireworks — from consumer sparklers and bottle rockets to many professional show shells — are made in China. Since U.S.-China trade normalized in 1979, Chinese producers have come to supply roughly 98–99% of consumer fireworks and about 75% of display-grade pyrotechnics, driven by labor-intensive manufacturing and much lower costs than would be possible under U.S. environmental and safety regulations. U.S. imports rose from tens of millions in the early 1990s to more than $200 million by 2013.

Quality and safety have improved as U.S. buyers and the American Fireworks Standards Laboratory began inspecting tens of thousands of shipments from China and enforcing stricter standards; some non-Chinese sources (Thailand, a few U.S. and European firms) supply a small share of product. Industry leaders note longstanding personal and multigenerational business ties between U.S. importers and Chinese makers.

Meanwhile, U.S. research and military labs continue to drive pyrotechnic innovation. The Army’s Picatinny Arsenal and commercial firms (e.g., Fireworks by Grucci) are developing greener, less smoky formulations, non-toxic colorants, lead-free primers and technologies that enable brighter colors and complex aerial shapes or letters. Chemists still face challenges — notably producing a vivid true blue that remains stable at the high temperatures fireworks require — and commercial makers closely guard many color formulas. The result: while the bulk of production is overseas, U.S. expertise and military-driven R&D continue to influence safety, environmental improvements and new visual effects used in modern displays.

The Phunky Elephant, a gastropub in Staten Island, removed a dessert called the “Roofie Colada” from its menu after widespread criticism on social media and from local patrons who called the name offensive and trivializing of date-rape. The dessert—coffee ice cream, Kahlua, vanilla vodka, caramel and chocolate syrup, topped with donuts and whipped cream—was named as a nod to a Family Guy joke. The owner, Patricia Gaja, said the name was meant as homage to the cartoon and not malicious, but acknowledged complaints that began when the item debuted in June and said the restaurant would rename the item while preparing a new seasonal menu.

Critics argued the reference normalized “roofies” and made light of sexual assault; some described staff responses to early complaints as dismissive. After mounting backlash, the restaurant issued a public apology stating it did not support date rape or violence, that it regretted any offense caused, and that the dessert would be taken off the menu until an appropriate new name is chosen. Community reaction was mixed, with some defending the joke and others urging the restaurant to be more sensitive.

Brew Guru (from the American Homebrewers Association) highlights Zymurgy magazine’s 15th annual Best Beers in America survey results. Bell’s Two Hearted Ale dethroned long-time No. 1 Pliny the Elder (Russian River), taking the top spot. The survey—voted on by AHA members—also placed Founders Breakfast Stout third, Three Floyds Zombie Dust fourth, and Bell’s Hopslam fifth. Ties appear at sixth (Founders KBS and The Alchemist Heady Topper) and eighth (Deschutes Fresh Squeezed IPA and Sierra Nevada Celebration). Ballast Point Sculpin rounded out the top ten.

Top breweries ranked: 1) Bell’s Brewery, 2) Founders, 3) Russian River, 4) Sierra Nevada, 5) Stone, followed by Firestone Walker, Deschutes, Dogfish Head, Lagunitas and Ballast Point. Stone led in number of beers on the list (31), followed by Bell’s (27) and Firestone Walker (25).

The full list and clone recipes are available at HomebrewersAssociation.org. The AHA (publisher of Zymurgy and operator of the Brew Guru app) represents over 46,000 homebrewers and runs events like Homebrew Con and the National Homebrew Competition.

The Connecticut Supreme Court unanimously ruled that state officials may forcibly medicate Lishan Wang, a mentally ill physician accused of murdering Yale doctor Vajinder Toor, to restore his competency to stand trial. Wang, who has pleaded not guilty and refused medication, is also charged with attempted murder for allegedly shooting at Toor’s pregnant wife (who was not injured). 

The court found prosecutors satisfied the legal standard from a 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision: it is “substantially likely” (defined by Connecticut justices as a greater-than-50% probability) that the recommended antipsychotic medications would restore Wang’s competency, and that the expected benefits outweigh risks and no less-intrusive alternatives exist. A state psychiatrist testified the chance of restoration ranged from the mid-50s to about 70 percent. 

Wang’s attorney argued that such a success rate is too low to justify involuntary medication and said he may seek federal review; prosecutors maintain the decision is supported by medical experts and falls within the rare circumstances permitting forced treatment.

The 2012 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the European Union in recognition of its decades-long role in promoting peace, reconciliation, democracy and human rights across the continent. The EU—an unprecedented supranational union where member states share sovereignty, citizens can live and work across borders, and a near-equal, transnational parliament shapes legislation—was credited with turning a historically violent region into one of the longest eras of peace in modern European history. Its achievements include integrating former dictatorships in Southern Europe and post‑communist states in Central and Eastern Europe, advancing enlargement into the western Balkans, and neutralizing historic enmities—most notably between Germany and its neighbors.

The award highlights the EU’s unique institutions, such as the European Parliament and the European Court of Justice, and recognizes that Europeans themselves—who supported integration, reforms and the costs of enlargement—are among the true beneficiaries. The decision was also controversial: critics point to the EU’s bureaucratic complexity, perceived democratic deficits, and the serious challenge posed by the 2012 sovereign debt and eurozone crisis, making the timing and choice seem odd to some. Giving the prize to an organization is rare but not unprecedented; some commentators saw the award as both recognition of past achievements and a morale boost amid current troubles. The prize announcement was unusually leaked early by Norwegian media.

U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo made a high-profile visit to Pyongyang in early July to press North Korea for concrete steps on denuclearization and the return of U.S. Korean War remains following the Trump–Kim summit in Singapore. Pompeo met senior North Korean officials including Kim Yong Chol for nearly three hours, stayed overnight in Pyongyang, and said he aimed to “fill in” details of the leaders’ vague summit commitments and keep momentum toward implementation. U.S. aims include agreeing an initial, verifiable list of nuclear sites and arranging the handover of remains; U.S. officials warned verification is difficult because Washington lacks a high-confidence accounting of North Korea’s arsenal and suspects hidden facilities.

The visit came amid concerns in U.S. government circles that President Trump has overstated summit results and that U.S. language has softened from “complete, verifiable and irreversible denuclearization (CVID)” to “final, fully verified denuclearization,” which some see as a weakening of leverage. Pompeo planned further regional consultations with South Korea and Japan.

Separately, multiple media reports—partly disputed by the State Department—said Pompeo would deliver two gifts from Trump to Kim Jong Un: a letter and a signed Elton John “Rocket Man” CD, a tongue-in-cheek reference to Trump’s earlier nickname for Kim. The CD story produced conflicting accounts; the State Department said only a letter was left, while Trump later confirmed having the CD and said it had not yet been delivered. The visit underscored both cautious optimism about diplomacy and skepticism over North Korea’s seriousness and verifiability.

This dataset is a large, experimental web-wide crawl run with new distributed crawling software by Kenji Nagahashi, using Heritrix 3.1.1-SNAPSHOT and an initial seed list of Alexa’s top 1 million sites (retrieved near the start of the crawl). Key metadata:
- Crawl period: 09 March 2011 – 23 December 2011
- Total captures: 2,713,676,341
- Unique URLs: 2,273,840,159
- Hosts crawled: 29,032,069
- Scope: effectively unlimited except for a few manually excluded sites; robots.txt was respected

Notes and caveats:
- The crawl was experimental: new HQ software fed URLs to crawlers and experienced operational issues (e.g., URL queues grew too large, so many embedded and linked resources were never fetched).
- The dataset includes repeated crawls of some Argentinian government sites, which can skew geographic analyses.
- The team has since changed their wide-crawl procedures but released this “warts-and-all” snapshot for researchers.

Spanish researchers at the University of Granada report that lying and other emotional states produce measurable changes in skin temperature detectable with thermal imaging, a phenomenon they call the "Pinocchio Effect." In doctoral research by Emilio Gómez Milán and Elvira Salazar López, volunteers monitored with thermal cameras showed that anxiety (for example when lying) raises the temperature at the tip of the nose and affects temperature around the inner corner of the eye. Conversely, exerting strong mental effort can cool the nose. The team links these peripheral thermal changes to activity in the brain’s insular cortex, which regulates body temperature: greater insular activity corresponds to smaller surface temperature changes and vice versa. They also found thermal “footprints” for physical activities and sexual arousal—chest and genital warming in both sexes—and distinct patterns for different dances (e.g., lower buttock and warmer forearm temperatures in Flamenco). Parts of the work have been published; other results remain unpublished.

A University of Colorado Boulder study’s Humor Research Lab has ranked Chicago the funniest city in the U.S., placing it ahead of Boston and Atlanta. Using an algorithm that combined measures such as number of comedy clubs, famous comedians from each city, comedians’ ratings of local audiences, residents’ visits to comedy sites, and Twitter humorists, researchers identified a top-10 list that also includes Boston, Atlanta, Washington, Portland (Ore.), New York, Los Angeles, Denver, San Francisco and Seattle.

The team then surveyed more than 900 residents across those cities about the types of comedy they enjoy, the importance of humor in relationships, personality traits, descriptions of their city’s humor, and favorite jokes. The study found Chicagoans favor deadpan, quick-witted observational humor—often aimed at the city’s harsh weather and the CTA—and are strong on improv and stand-up. Paradoxically, many Chicago respondents couldn’t cite specific one-liners, preferring situational, observational wit over classic zingers.

The research was led by Peter McGraw of CU-Boulder and grew from his book The Humor Code, co-authored with Joel Warner. The study also characterized other cities’ comedic flavors (e.g., Boston’s mix of highbrow and rowdy humor, D.C.’s political absurdity, and Portland’s eccentricity).

An explosion in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood on Saturday night injured 29 people (mostly minor injuries); all have been released from hospitals. The blast occurred about 8:30 p.m. on West 23rd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues and is believed to have come from an explosive device in or near a dumpster. A second suspicious device — described as a pressure cooker with wiring taped to what appeared to be a cellphone — was found about four blocks away on West 27th Street and was safely removed and rendered safe by NYPD and FBI bomb technicians; a third suspicious item proved to be trash.

Surveillance footage shows the same man near both the 23rd and 27th Street locations, including footage of a duffel bag being left and later two men removing a white bag believed to contain the pressure cooker. Investigators have not determined motive or confirmed links to other incidents, including an earlier pipe-bomb explosion in New Jersey; officials say similarities are being examined but there is no evidence tying the Manhattan blast to international terrorism so far.

Mayor Bill de Blasio called the incident an “intentional act” but said it’s too soon to label it a terror attack. Governor Andrew Cuomo announced deployment of an additional 1,000 state police and National Guard personnel to transit hubs and said enhanced policing citywide will accompany the ongoing investigation. The FBI is conducting forensic analysis of the devices at its Quantico laboratory. Officials urged public vigilance while assuring New Yorkers the city remains operational.

Nationwide anger erupted after a controversial final call in Monday Night Football gave the Seattle Seahawks a 14-12 win over the Green Bay Packers, a result many blamed on replacement officials working while regular referees were locked out. The NFL said it was negotiating with the referees’ union and hoped to reach an agreement; spokesman Brian McCarthy noted officiating controversies are part of sports. President Obama, asked about the finish, called it “terrible” and said “we’ve gotta get our refs back.”

New Jersey Senate President Stephen Sweeney — a Packers fan — announced plans to introduce state legislation that would bar professional sporting events from using replacement officials, arguing inexperienced refs jeopardize player safety, reduce game quality and devalue fans’ investments. Sweeney compared the need for trained officials to workplace safety supervision.

The botched ruling had big gambling fallout. Sportsbooks and bettors reported massive swings: Nevada bookmakers estimated tens of millions shifted in-state, while estimates of the worldwide money swing ranged from about $150 million (R.J. Bell and some Vegas books) to as high as $200–250 million from an online operator — and one oddsmaker even suggested up to $1 billion. The call also affected betting lines and futures: some sportsbooks reversed bets after the score, and Green Bay’s Super Bowl odds lengthened (from 7-1 to 9-1 at one Las Vegas hotel).

Vanity Fair profiles Blackwater founder and CEO Erik Prince, portraying him as a driven, polarizing figure who has lived a double life as both a public corporate CEO and a covert asset for U.S. intelligence. Prince is presented as vain, evangelical-tinged, intensely driven, and litigious, yet also confident that his work served vital national-security aims.

Key revelations and allegations:
- Prince claims to have worked closely with the CIA for years, running clandestine paramilitary and intelligence operations—ranging from inserting personnel into “denied areas” to assembling hit teams targeting al‑Qaeda affiliates.
- He recounts a specific alleged operation in which a Blackwater team traveled to Germany to surveil and prepare to assassinate al‑Qaeda financier Mamoun Darkazanli without informing the CIA station chief or the host country—an act that would violate NATO intelligence‑sharing norms and contradict official assertions (including from CIA Director Leon Panetta) that the targeted‑assassination program was never operational.
- Prince says he and teams were still overseeing intelligence missions as recently as months before the new administration took office, including operations aimed at countries like Iran.

Context and controversies:
- Blackwater and Prince have faced intense criticism and legal scrutiny over conduct in Iraq, including accusations of excessive force, multiple deaths, bribery allegations reported by the New York Times (which Prince denies), pending trials, and civil suits.
- He has become a cultural shorthand for private military power—appearing as inspiration for fictional villains—while simultaneously cultivating a self-image as a patriotic fixer willing to take big risks for U.S. interests.
- The article highlights Prince’s contradictory persona: a conservative, religiously inclined but self-described libertarian and practicing Catholic; a family man who trains his children in emergency skills; and a publicity‑shy but outspoken operator who prefers to fly coach to avoid attention.

Implications:
- If Prince’s account is accurate, it exposes previously secret, potentially unauthorized paramilitary activity conducted by a private contractor on behalf of U.S. intelligence, raising legal and diplomatic questions about oversight, accountability, and the use of contractors for covert lethal operations.
- The piece frames Prince as both a valuable asset because of his resources and reach and as a liability whose methods and secrecy increased controversy inside the CIA and in public debate over the role of mercenary contractors in America’s post‑9/11 wars.

Summary:

Two convicted murderers, Richard Matt (49) and David Sweat (35), escaped from Clinton Correctional Facility in Dannemora, N.Y., after cutting through cell walls and a 24-inch steam pipe leading to a sewer. The breakout occurred from an "honor block" tier where inmates had looser restrictions; the pair used a hand-held electrical saw powered by an improvised extension-cord splice and a 20-pound sledgehammer. They hid tools in a guitar case and concealed their absence by piling clothing under their beds. They emerged from a sewer hole near the prison around midnight and were discovered missing during a 5:30 a.m. wake-up check.

Investigators are conducting a massive manhunt in nearby forested areas with the FBI assisting and believe the fugitives may still be within a five- to ten-mile radius. Authorities are probing possible outside help: attention has focused on a female civilian employee who worked in the prison tailor shop and had contact with the inmates; investigators have searched her home and are examining whether she supplied tools or a cellphone. Correction officers say five weapons were found in limited searches after a June 1 yard fight between rival inmate groups (some Muslim, some suspected Bloods) that led to a partial lockdown; some officers question whether a full-facility search request was denied by DOCCS headquarters. DOCCS has declined to release operational details while the investigation continues.

Prison staff are not required to pass through metal detectors, though bags and purses are supposed to be searched; a size limit on employee bags is rarely enforced, according to an official. Manhole covers are locked from the inside, but the inmates apparently used the sledgehammer to break a lock. Witnesses reported seeing two men carrying a guitar case near a nearby house just after midnight.

Coverage includes personal background on Matt from his son, Nicholas Harris, who described Matt’s violent history, prior escapes, and a troubled childhood. Authorities warned the public the two are very dangerous and offered a $100,000 reward; residents have reported sightings, and police continue door‑to‑door inquiries in surrounding rural communities.

Summary:

Recent polls show the presidential race tightening: Hillary Clinton’s national lead over Donald Trump has narrowed from more than 8 points after the Democratic convention to about 4–5 points now. Models still favor Clinton — roughly a 70–74% chance to win — but her margins in key swing and tipping-point states have fallen in step with the national shift. State-level polling averages that were strongly pro-Clinton in mid‑August have compressed, with several battlegrounds (Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Florida, etc.) now showing much smaller Clinton leads or near ties. The forecasting model applies a trend adjustment that expects state polls to follow national movement; recent high-quality state surveys have borne that out.

On the Republican side, Trump’s campaign is described as disorganized and behind on critical field operations. Internal confusion over leadership and implementation — worsened by Paul Manafort’s abrupt resignation in August and turnover among staff — has delayed a coherent swing‑state deployment plan. Jared Kushner and other aides have pressed the RNC for progress, but major GOP donors remain reluctant to provide significant new funding, and some prominent conservatives (including the Koch network) are withholding full support. The campaign has tried to professionalize messaging and control surrogates, and Trump’s on‑the‑trail discipline has improved, producing some polling gains. Still, operatives warn time is short: with early voting imminent, Republicans see the path to 270 electoral votes as narrow and requiring luck or a major reset for Trump to prevail.

Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia told CNN’s Piers Morgan he sees no personal or ideological “falling out” among justices after the recent 5–4 Affordable Care Act decision and was offended by media criticism of colleagues—especially Chief Justice John Roberts. He declined to discuss internal deliberations or recent cases in detail, criticized anonymously sourced press reports about the Court, and said justices do not decide cases for political reasons.

Promoting his new book Reading Law (co‑authored with Bryan Garner), Scalia reiterated his textualist philosophy: judges should interpret statutes and the Constitution by the text itself rather than legislative history or foreign law. He warned that nontextual interpretation erodes confidence in the rule of law.

On hot-button issues, Scalia said Roe v. Wade should be overturned and that abortion and the death penalty are questions best left to states rather than the Court; he insisted he is not personally “pro” death penalty but opposes removing such decisions from democratic processes. He defended the Court’s 2000 Bush v. Gore ruling and dismissed ongoing criticism of it.

The hourlong interview mixed seriousness with Scalia’s trademark blunt humor. He described himself as engaged and has no near‑term plans to retire, saying his proudest judicial contribution is moving colleagues toward greater attention to legal text.

Groupon is facing a second federal class-action over unpaid overtime, this time from about 50 former "deal vetters" in Chicago who say they weren’t paid overtime for working more than 40 hours a week. Deal vetters reviewed the company’s merchant contracts; the role has since been eliminated. The suit follows an August class action by over 1,000 salespeople seeking overtime pay (recently amended to add details such as a $32,000 starting salary). The new filing alleges violations of federal and state wage laws; a judge has allowed discovery to begin. The suits come amid a turbulent month for Groupon marked by executive departures, SEC scrutiny, a delayed IPO and controversy over large pre-IPO executive bonuses. Groupon did not comment.

Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) faced major regulatory and market fallout in January 2017 after U.S. and California regulators accused the company of failing to disclose software in about 104,000 2014–2016 Jeep Grand Cherokee and Ram 1500 vehicles with 3.0-liter diesel engines that can increase NOx emissions. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and California Air Resources Board issued notices of violation after enhanced testing prompted by the Volkswagen diesel scandal; the EPA said it found eight undisclosed control functions and warned FCA could face penalties up to $44,539 per vehicle (roughly $4.6 billion total).

CEO Sergio Marchionne strongly rejected parallels to Volkswagen, calling FCA’s case different and denying any deliberate cheating or use of software to detect test conditions. He said FCA had discussed emissions with the EPA for more than a year, planned software updates to address concerns, and would contest the allegations with the incoming Trump administration. Still, U.S. and Milan-listed shares fell sharply (U.S. trading down about 10–18% intraday; Milan down ~16%), and New York Attorney General and the U.S. Justice Department signaled investigations.

Background context in the reporting noted FCA’s recent stock listing in New York, its sales recovery—especially in trucks and Jeeps—and Marchionne’s announced plan to retire at the end of 2018. Analysts suggested the issue might be primarily a failure to disclose software rather than deliberate deception like VW’s case, but regulators treated it as a serious Clean Air Act violation and continued to probe the nature and impact of the undisclosed devices.

A Tempe woman, 25-year-old Alaina Marie Limpert, was arrested on one count of child abuse after her nearly two-year-old daughter ingested mac and cheese made with THC butter. According to the police report, Limpert prepared the THC-laced macaroni for her husband; neither parent sought immediate medical care when the child showed effects. Witnesses said the parents laughed about the child’s symptoms and placed her in the backyard pool to “shock” her. The Department of Child Safety was notified two days later and removed all three children from the home. Hospital testing confirmed THC in the toddler’s system. Police also found two marijuana grow tents in the garage, mushrooms, bongs and pipes, containers of hash oil, other drug paraphernalia, and three large tubs of THC butter in the refrigerator. Limpert admitted making the mac and cheese with THC but said she did not know her daughter had eaten it. She is due back in court April 19.

A Tulane medical student, 25-year-old Peter Gold, is in guarded but improving condition after being shot early Friday while intervening in an attempted abduction Uptown New Orleans. Surveillance footage shows a hooded man dragging an apparently intoxicated woman toward an SUV in the 1000 block of St. Mary Street around 4 a.m. Gold turned his car around, rushed to help and was confronted by the assailant, who demanded money. The attacker shot Gold in the abdomen; several subsequent attempts to shoot him in the head failed when the gun jammed. The woman suffered minor injuries and was treated and released.

Police released clear images from private security cameras of the suspect and his getaway vehicle and initially offered a $10,000 Tulane reward. On Sunday authorities identified 21-year-old Euric Cain as the suspect; his SUV was located and he is wanted on charges including attempted first-degree murder, second-degree kidnapping and armed robbery. Tulane, Crimestoppers and the city have raised the reward to up to $12,500 for information leading to his arrest. Police are asking anyone with information to contact Crimestoppers.

A veteran Boston police officer, Michael Doherty, 40, was arrested after an early-morning assault on an Uber driver in South Boston in which prosecutors say Doherty used racial slurs against the driver and a Good Samaritan who intervened. The incident occurred about 2:45 a.m.; prosecutors say Doherty became upset about the pickup location, hurled profanity and a racist epithet at the driver, then struck him when the vehicle stopped at East 2nd and M streets. The driver flagged down another motorist for help; Doherty briefly drove off in the Uber, was chased, then stopped at East 1st Street and Farragut Road, where he allegedly again used a racial slur at the Good Samaritan and began striking both men. The Uber driver was knocked to the ground; Doherty fled but turned himself in later that morning.

Doherty, a 16-year Boston Police Department veteran, faces two counts of assault and battery while using a racial slur and a charge of using a motor vehicle without authority. He posted $500 bail and was released with conditions including staying away from the victims, drug testing and a ban on using Uber. The department’s Anti-Corruption Unit is investigating and has placed him on paid administrative leave; Uber has barred him from its platform and offered cooperation. Doherty’s attorney disputes the prosecutors’ account, saying Doherty was the “real victim” and describing his injuries (a black eye, stitches, and a torn biceps tendon). An unrelated brief hearing involving Doherty’s ex-girlfriend, charged separately in a nighttime breaking-and-entering case, occurred prior to his arraignment.

Actor and singer-songwriter Jackson Odell, best known for playing Ari Caldwell on ABC’s The Goldbergs, has died at 20. He was found unresponsive at his Tarzana home in the San Fernando Valley on June 8; the Los Angeles County Coroner’s Office said the cause of death is pending an autopsy and that no foul play is suspected. Odell began working in entertainment at age 12 and also appeared on shows including The Fosters, Modern Family and iCarly, and in the 2011 film Judy Moody and the Not Bummer Summer. As a songwriter he contributed original songs to the 2018 film Forever My Girl—among them “Wings of an Angel,” performed in the film by American Idol alum Lauren Alaina—and shared covers and originals on his YouTube channel.

A Canadian meta-review led by Dr. Meghan Azad (University of Manitoba), published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, evaluated 37 studies involving over 400,000 people to assess long-term effects of artificial (non-nutritive) sweeteners (e.g., aspartame, sucralose, stevia). Key findings:

- No convincing evidence that regular consumption of artificial sweeteners promotes weight loss. Seven randomized controlled trials (about 1,000 participants, median follow-up ~6 months) showed no significant weight-loss benefit.
- Longer observational studies (30 studies, average follow-up ~10 years) found associations between frequent sweetener use and modest increases in weight and waist circumference, plus higher risks of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and some cardiovascular events. Because these are observational data, they show associations but cannot prove causation.
- Possible mechanisms discussed include alterations to gut microbiota, metabolic responses to sweet taste, and behavioral compensation (eating more because calories were “saved”). However, evidence is limited and causal pathways remain unclear.
- The reviewers emphasized a scarcity of rigorous long-term randomized trials and called for more research comparing different sweeteners and investigating biological mechanisms.

Implications: Given the lack of proven long-term benefit and some evidence of potential harm, Azad advises caution about daily use of artificial sweeteners and suggests people trying to reduce sugar might prefer alternatives like water until stronger evidence is available. Some clinicians share caution but note confounding factors in observational studies; some consumers remain unconcerned and continue regular use.

Polish cybersecurity researcher Krzysztof Szczypiorski has proposed and tested a steganography method called “StegIbiza” that hides Morse code–style messages in subtle tempo changes within Balearic/club music. In his system, a tiny tempo increase represents a dot and a slight decrease a dash; by modulating beats per minute over time a DJ can encode whole sentences. Szczypiorski says such adjustments are easily implemented in digital audio workstations or via a DJ controller’s tempo slide, limited mainly by the DJ’s manual skill.

In two experiments described in an arXiv paper (not peer reviewed), he found that tempo shifts under about 1% went unnoticed: in a lab test with 20 listeners (half musicians), none detected differences when the tempo was altered that slightly, and in a live open-air DJ set of ≈70 attendees the manipulations were also largely imperceptible—until he pushed the tempo changes too far and partygoers reacted negatively. He notes that musical steganography is centuries old, but applying it to trance-oriented club music offers a novel vehicle because the genre’s rhythm-focused, immersive nature helps mask modest tempo modulation. The implication: subtle tempo tweaks at raves could be used to convey hidden messages without most listeners noticing.

British sandwich chain Pret a Manger says a second customer has died after eating a product that contained an undeclared allergen. The company is investigating a December 2017 incident in which a customer in Bath collapsed and died after consuming a “super-veg rainbow flatbread” that was labeled dairy-free but was later found in testing to contain dairy protein. Pret says the dairy protein came from a mis-sold dairy-free yoghurt supplied by vegan brand CoYo; Pret has ended its contract with CoYo and is taking legal action. CoYo disputes Pret’s claim as unfounded, says Pret did not provide essential batch information needed for its own probe, and denies the recalled product it pulled in February 2018 is the same one involved in the death. The Food Standards Agency and local councils have been involved previously after dairy traces were found in CoYo products. Pret previously pledged to implement full ingredient labeling on all freshly made items following the 2016 death of 15-year-old Natasha Ednan-Laperouse from undeclared sesame in a Pret baguette; her parents, who campaign for stronger allergen warnings, expressed sorrow at the new fatality. Coroner investigations into the second death are ongoing.

The Senate narrowly approved a sweeping Republican tax overhaul after late-night negotiations, clearing a major step toward revamping the U.S. tax code for the first time in decades. The 51–49 vote, with Sen. Bob Corker the only Republican opposed, advances a bill that would cut about $1.4–$1.5 trillion in taxes, including a permanent corporate tax rate cut to 20% (from 35%), changes to international taxation, and temporary individual tax cuts. It also includes GOP policy priorities such as allowing drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and repealing the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate.

Leaders won key holdouts by making last-minute concessions: a $10,000 cap on state and local property tax deductions (secured for Sen. Susan Collins), an expanded deduction for pass-through businesses (raised to ~23% to gain support from Sens. Ron Johnson and Steve Daines), an expanded medical expense deduction, and limits rather than full repeal of the alternative minimum tax to finance some changes. Other amendments adopted included allowing 529 plans for K–12 spending.

Democrats strongly criticized both the bill’s substance—arguing it favors corporations and the wealthy and will increase deficits—and the rushed process, mocking handwritten last-minute edits. Nonpartisan analysts project the legislation would add about $1 trillion to the federal deficit over ten years even after growth effects; Republicans argued it will spur growth and help voters ahead of the 2018 midterms.

The House and Senate must reconcile differences before the final bill reaches President Trump, who welcomed the Senate vote. Some Republicans sought automatic "trigger" provisions or further deficit protections but were blocked by procedural limits. Several senators obtained commitments on unrelated issues (e.g., immigration protections) in exchange for support. The bill’s mix of permanent corporate cuts and temporary individual changes, and its projected fiscal impact, leave political and policy debates unresolved as lawmakers move toward conference negotiations.

A magnitude-6.5 earthquake struck offshore near Eureka, Northern California, late Saturday afternoon (about 4:27–4:30 p.m.). The temblor lasted roughly 30 seconds, was centered west-northwest of Ferndale at about 13 miles depth, and was strongly felt across the region (reports as far north as central Oregon, south to Santa Cruz and east to Reno). Dozens of aftershocks followed, the largest about magnitude 4.2.

Damage and impacts
- No major injuries reported; roughly 30 people sought care for minor injuries. Hospitals and major institutions (Humboldt State University, St. Joseph Health System) reported no serious casualties.
- Significant but mainly minor-to-moderate property damage: toppled chimneys, broken water pipes, fallen ceiling plaster, dislodged light fixtures and floor tiles, merchandise knocked off shelves, damaged traffic signals, and broken windows in towns such as Eureka, Ferndale and Redway.
- Several commercial buildings and an apartment building were declared unsafe; residents were referred to Red Cross for temporary shelter.
- Bayshore Mall in Eureka was closed after reports of injuries and ceiling debris; individual businesses (grocery stores, hardware, bakeries, pet supply and antique shops) reported extensive interior damage.
- Isolated communities (e.g., King Salmon) lost power and saw downed lines; some residents temporarily moved to higher ground out of tsunami concern (no tsunami occurred).

Utilities and emergency response
- Initially more than 25,000–28,000 PG&E customers lost power across Humboldt County and surrounding areas; power restoration was completed by early the next morning after crews, including mutual-aid teams, worked through the night.
- The county Office of Emergency Services and other local agencies conducted inspections; state officials said local authorities appeared capable of managing the response without additional state assistance.
- Common emergency calls included reports of broken gas lines and downed power lines; residents were warned to avoid downed lines and to report hazards to 911 or PG&E.

Context and reaction
- Residents described intense, rolling shaking; some compared it to prior large quakes (Loma Prieta, 1989) or noted this as their strongest experience.
- Seismologists noted the quake occurred in the seismically active Mendocino Triple Junction area; magnitude-6.5 events are large but not uncommon there.
- Social media (notably Twitter) played a prominent role in rapid reporting and sharing images and reactions during and after the event.

Overall, the earthquake caused widespread disruption and localized structural damage around Eureka and Humboldt County, produced numerous aftershocks, briefly knocked out power to tens of thousands, but resulted in no confirmed major injuries or fatalities.

A mountain lion entered a Boulder, Colorado, home—apparently by pushing through a window screen—and spent more than an hour roaming two levels of the house before officers hazed it with nonlethal beanbag rounds and chased it back into nearby wilderness. The big cat killed the homeowner’s 10‑year‑old cat, Klondike, during the incident. Neighbors watched from their windows and recorded the animal inside. Animal control and police used beanbag rounds to scare the cougar out; it was not captured and appeared uninjured. Authorities urged residents to keep ground‑level windows and doors secured at night. The homeowner said the family will be more vigilant about closing windows after the loss.

Rutgers University’s Board of Governors approved a 2.3% increase in undergraduate tuition and fees for 2015–2016, raising the typical in-state New Brunswick student’s bill by $318 to $14,131. Room and board will rise about 2.6%, bringing the average New Brunswick student’s total cost to $26,185—an increase of $624. Comparable tuition hikes (about 2.3%) were approved for most graduate students; out-of-state students face about a 3.4% increase. The board also approved a $3.8 billion university budget.

University officials say the increases are needed to cover rising costs, including union contract raises and a 3.7% reduction in state funding. Rutgers remains one of the nation’s costlier public universities, but officials note substantial institutional aid: less than half of students pay full sticker price and the typical in-state New Brunswick undergraduate receives about a 45% reduction through grants and scholarships. The board boosted university financial aid by 3.2%, allocating $32.5 million to the Rutgers Assistance Grant to help low-income students.

Separate reporting highlights graduate borrowing concerns: a Center for American Progress study found 20 universities accounted for $6.5 billion—one-fifth—of federal graduate loans in 2013–2014; Rutgers ranked 19th and was the only public university on the list. Critics point to cuts in state support that have pushed public colleges to raise tuition and reliance on student loans, and policymakers are urged to reassess the sustainability and value of expanded graduate lending.

The Labor Department reported 160,000 new nonfarm payrolls in April, well below the roughly 205,000 economists expected, and the smallest monthly gain since September. The unemployment rate held at 5.0%. The three‑month average job gain is about 200,000. Hourly earnings rose 2.5% year‑over‑year, while labor force participation ticked down to 62.8%.

The report arrives amid mixed economic signals. GDP grew at a tepid 0.5% annual rate in Q1, and inflation remains persistently low, muting growth prospects. Financial markets show divergent views: oil prices and the S&P 500 have rebounded in recent months as recession fears eased, while 10‑year Treasury yields have fallen to around 1.8% as investors buy safe government debt. Labor market indicators are bright in some respects—long‑term unemployment has declined, initial jobless claims hit multiyear lows, more people report jobs as “plentiful,” and voluntary quits have risen—helping push modest post‑recession wage gains. 

Taken together, the data are contradictory and have led the Federal Reserve to pause further rate hikes after its December increase. With another jobs report due before the June Fed meeting, continued mixed readings would complicate the Fed’s policy decisions.

An overturned oil tanker on a national highway near Bahawalpur in Pakistan burst into flames on June 25, 2017 after villagers who had rushed to collect leaking fuel were engulfed by a sudden fire and explosion. Local officials and hospital staff said at least 150–153 people were killed and many more — dozens critically — suffered severe burns; the toll could rise as some remain in critical condition. The tanker, en route from Karachi to Lahore with roughly 6,600 gallons of oil, overturned when a tire blew. A mosque loudspeaker and word of mouth drew crowds carrying jerry cans and pots to siphon fuel despite police warnings. Witnesses and officials said the blaze spread rapidly — one account blamed a lit cigarette — incinerating motorcycles and several cars and leaving many bodies burnt beyond recognition, necessitating DNA identification. Emergency teams declared a state of emergency at Bahawalpur’s Victoria Hospital, airlifted the worst cases to hospitals in Multan and Lahore, and called in extra staff. Firefighters took over two hours to control the blaze. Pakistan’s prime minister cut short a trip abroad and returned to respond to the disaster. The incident occurred on the eve of Eid al-Fitr, compounding local shock and grief.

A widely shared video showed Chicago police forcefully removing and bloodying a passenger from a United Airlines flight after he refused to be bumped so four crew members could take the seats. The footage caused immediate public outrage and made United’s initial responses—anodyne PR statements and a poorly worded apology from CEO Oscar Munoz—look tone-deaf. Munoz later defended staff, calling the passenger “disruptive,” and explained the crew needed seats after the flight had been boarded, which raised questions about why United chose to remove paying, seated customers rather than use alternatives (driving the crew, chartering, or offering more compensation).

Accounts say United first sought volunteers and offered up to $800 plus hotel and a next-day flight; two accepted, then four passengers were randomly selected to be involuntarily bumped. One refused, reportedly a doctor with patients the next day, and was forcibly dragged off, delaying the flight two hours. The incident exposed failures in United’s handling and training and intensified scrutiny of airline overbooking practices.

The piece places the event in context: overbooking is legal and common because carriers want to maximize load factors, and federal rules require airlines to seek volunteers first and set mandatory compensation levels for involuntary denial of boarding (200–400% of fare, up to statutory caps). Critics say airlines exercise excessive latitude in choosing whom to bump and in using force when customers refuse. The article argues the rules and carrier practices need updating, and notes public anger has led to calls for boycotts and demands for better customer treatment and higher compensation to avoid such confrontations.

The National Park Service (NPS) proposed on October 24, 2017 to institute higher “peak-season” entrance fees at 17 highly visited parks to raise revenue for urgent infrastructure repairs (roads, bridges, campgrounds, waterlines, restrooms, visitor facilities) and to standardize and increase fees for road‑based commercial tours.

Key points
- Parks affected (17): Arches, Bryce Canyon, Canyonlands, Denali, Glacier, Grand Canyon, Grand Teton, Olympic, Sequoia & Kings Canyon, Yellowstone, Yosemite, Zion, plus Acadia, Mount Rainier, Rocky Mountain, Shenandoah, and Joshua Tree.
- Peak season: each park’s busiest contiguous five‑month period (timing varies; many begin May 1 or June 1, Joshua Tree “as soon as practicable” in 2018).
- Proposed peak-season fees: $70 per private non‑commercial vehicle, $50 per motorcycle, $30 per person on foot or bike; park‑specific annual pass for any of the 17 parks: $75.
- The all‑lands America the Beautiful annual pass would remain $80; children under 16 and holders of Senior, Military, Access, Volunteer, and Every Kid in a Park passes remain exempt.
- Most parks remain free: only 118 of 417 NPS sites charge entrance fees and this proposal affects only the 17 fee‑charging parks.
- Commercial operators: proposed increases and standardized commercial use authorization (CUA) application/management fees; all CUA fees stay in the collecting park. Commercial fee changes would take effect after an 18‑month implementation window.
- Financial impact: estimated additional revenue of about $70 million per year (a 34% increase over FY2016 collections). Under the Federal Lands Recreation Enhancement Act, 80% of an entrance fee stays in the collecting park; 20% funds projects in other parks.
- Public comment: 30‑day comment period from Oct 24–Nov 23, 2017 via the NPS PEPC website or by mail to the NPS Recreation Fee Program.

Reactions noted in coverage
- Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke framed the increases as necessary to preserve parks for future generations and improve visitor experience.
- Critics, including the National Parks Conservation Association, argued such steep hikes could make parks unaffordable for some visitors and that the administration should address maintenance needs through budgetary means rather than primarily shifting costs to visitors.
- Visitor numbers have continued to grow despite past fee increases (2016 saw a record 331 million visits).

investigators said one of three conductors on Amtrak Train 188 reported overhearing the engineer say the train had been struck by something shortly before the fatal derailment in Philadelphia. NTSB member Robert Sumwalt said the conductor heard radio transmissions between Amtrak engineer Brandon Bostian and a SEPTA engineer; the SEPTA engineer reported being hit by a rock or shot at, having a broken windshield and putting his train into an emergency stop. NTSB recovered outward-facing video from the SEPTA train and is reviewing radio traffic; the FBI is examining a distinctive circular damage pattern on the lower left of the Amtrak windshield.

Bostian, 32, was interviewed by the NTSB for the first time since the crash. He cooperated but has no memory of events after passing North Philadelphia station; he suffered a concussion. Investigators continue to consider all causes—speed, track condition and human factors—and have noted Train 188 accelerated into a 50-mph curve at about 106 mph. NTSB and others say positive train control (PTC), which could have overridden the speed, would have prevented the derailment; Amtrak and safety advocates have pushed for wider PTC implementation.

Passengers on two other trains in the area reported similar projectile strikes shortly before the derailment, including an Amtrak Acela with a window cracked in a circular pattern. SEPTA says projectiles have struck trains in the area before. Bostian’s colleagues describe him as professional; his attorney says he was not impaired. The crash killed eight people, injured more than 200, and prompted intensive recovery and repair work at Frankford Junction, while Congress and transportation officials face renewed scrutiny over rail safety funding and PTC deployment.

Ricky Gilmore, a 49-year-old paraplegic from Newcomb on the Navajo Nation, was left without his wheelchair and stranded on a seldom-traveled dirt road near Tocito/Shiprock after a man and woman he had been hitchhiking with allegedly forced him from their white pickup on Oct. 16. With no wheelchair, food, water or coat, Gilmore crawled and dragged himself roughly four miles over three days and two cold nights, sustaining severe abrasions to his buttocks and legs, a sprained wrist, shoulder soreness and dehydration. He was found by a passing motorist, Wilfred Sisco, with a body temperature of 94°F and taken to Northern Navajo Medical Center, where he was treated two days in intensive care for acute kidney failure from dehydration and a blood infection. Gilmore said several vehicles passed him without stopping during his ordeal; he filed a police report naming the suspects as Native American, the man in his mid-20s with a cursive neck tattoo and a heavyset woman in her 40s, believed to be from the Shiprock or Kirtland area. Recovering in hospital, he said he plans to go home, rest and stop hitchhiking for a while. Authorities have not publicly confirmed details of the report.

Thai wildlife officials have begun removing tigers from the controversial "Tiger Temple" in Kanchanaburi province after complaints from tourists and concerns about animal welfare and illegal breeding/trafficking. The Wildlife Conservation Office (WCO) says the temple held 137 tigers in conditions that posed risks to visitors and violated regulations. When WCO teams arrived Monday to begin relocation, temple staff initially blocked entry and—according to WCO director Teunjai Noochdumrong—apparently released some animals to obstruct the operation; officials described the scene as “mayhem.” After a standoff and a court order, authorities sedated several animals (reports cite three to eight tigers tranquilized on the first day) and began transporting them to government animal refuges in other provinces. The operation involves roughly 1,000 state personnel and is expected to continue about a week. The temple had attempted to re-register as a zoo but failed to meet government requirements. More than 300 officials stayed overnight at the site to secure the remaining tigers.

Here’s a concise summary of the document’s stories:

Mariah Carey & Nick Cannon
- Sources tell TMZ Mariah Carey and Nick Cannon have been separated since May and are living in separate New York City homes. Divorce lawyers have reportedly been negotiating a property and custody settlement for months, and the divorce is described as "a done deal."
- Tensions escalated after a March radio appearance by Cannon in which he played a game naming celebrities he had slept with; one answer reportedly humiliated Carey and triggered weeks of arguments. Additional fallout came when Cannon discussed Carey’s pre-marital sexual history on air.
- Carey is said to be angry that Cannon takes many work gigs—despite not needing the money—because it keeps him away from their children. Cannon contends Carey is surrounded by "yes men" and reacts poorly to disagreement, and he says he has earned $75 million for the family since 2011.

- Ronnie Ortiz-Magro confirmed to PEOPLE that he and Sammi Giancola have permanently split after a five-year, on-and-off relationship that played out on Jersey Shore. Meg Ryan & John Mellencamp
- Meg Ryan and John Mellencamp quietly ended their three-year relationship. A source cited long distance—Ryan in New York, Mellencamp in Indiana—as the cause. A 25-year-old American woman, identified as Lauren Mann of Colorado, was found dead in her Vienna apartment on Tuesday evening after her employers alerted police when she failed to show up for work as an au pair. Officers and firefighters forced open her door and found her half-naked on a mattress in a pool of blood. Initial autopsy results were inconclusive, ruling out stabbing, shooting and strangulation; a later report from prosecutors and police said the cause of death was suffocation. Authorities have not determined whether a third party was involved and continue to treat the case as a potential homicide while awaiting toxicology results, which could take days to weeks. No suspects or arrests have been announced. The U.S. Embassy is providing consular assistance; Mann was a 2012 graduate of the University of Colorado–Boulder’s College of Music and had lived in Vienna for several years.

Norway will become the first country to switch off national FM radio and move fully to digital audio broadcasting (DAB), beginning January 11, 2017 (starting in Bodø/Nordland) and completing nationwide by year’s end, with the far-north counties aimed for Dec. 13, 2017. The government says the move—official since 2015 after years of planning—will cut transmission costs (DAB is roughly eight times cheaper than FM), saving about 200 million NOK (~$23.5m) a year, free funds for programming, and provide many more channels (25 national DAB channels now, capacity for 20+ more), better sound quality and improved emergency preparedness.

The transition is contentious: opinion polls show about two-thirds of Norwegians oppose switching off FM. Critics, including some government MPs and local radio leaders, warn the country isn’t ready—about 2 million cars lack DAB receivers and millions of home radios will stop working without adaptors (car adaptors cost roughly 1,500 NOK / ~$176). There are safety concerns that people could miss emergency alerts unless they upgrade or rely on local FM stations (some local FM will continue). The government and Digital Radio Norway have run public information campaigns and set criteria for the switchover (coverage of 90%+ population, significant daily digital listenership, affordable car reception solutions).

Other countries (Switzerland, Britain, Denmark, Sweden, parts of Southeast Asia and South Korea) are watching Norway closely as they consider similar moves; Britain plans to review switchover once digital listening hits 50%. The U.S. did not adopt DAB, using HD Radio instead.

A taxi driver in Chengdu, Sichuan province, Wang Mingqing, has been reunited with the daughter who went missing from the family’s roadside fruit stall in January 1994. Wang and his wife Liu Chengying (also reported as Liu Dengying) lost sight of three-year-old Qifeng when she wandered off; despite years of searching, the couple never found her. Wang later became a Didi driver and used passengers’ phones, social media, 10,000 printed leaflets and a rear-window sign to publicize the case. A police artist’s age-progressed sketch circulated online late last year, and in March a 27-year-old woman living about 20 km away in Jilin province — raised by adoptive parents as Kang Ying and told she had been found on the roadside — recognized the image and contacted the Wangs. Shared physical traits and a DNA test confirmed she is their missing daughter. Kang flew to Chengdu with her husband and two children to meet her birth parents, and the long-running search ended in a tearful reunion after 24 years. The story has drawn wide attention in China, highlighting the nation’s ongoing issue of child disappearances and abductions.

White House and national security officials held a 90-minute unclassified conference call Thursday with members of Congress to present evidence and discuss possible U.S. military action in response to Syria’s alleged chemical-weapons attack. Senior officials on the call included Sec. of State John Kerry, Sec. of Defense Chuck Hagel, NSA Susan Rice, DNI James Clapper and Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Adm. James Winnefeld. Lawmakers were told the president remains “weighing his options,” that the administration’s objective is preventing further use of chemical weapons, and that it is seeking international support while not letting other countries dictate U.S. policy.

Officials reportedly presented intercepts — including an alleged intercepted phone call from a high-level Syrian official — as part of the evidence tying the Assad regime to the attack. The briefing produced no timeline or detailed plan, and provided no immediate answers on how any military action would be funded; Hagel promised to supply more information before or soon after any strike.

The call did little to change members’ positions. Some lawmakers, including Sens. Bob Menendez and Carl Levin and Rep. Eliot Engel, said the evidence justifies a decisive response and urged targeted strikes and continued efforts to gain allied support. Others, such as Sen. Jim Inhofe, reiterated opposition to military intervention without a clear strategy and funding plan. Sen. Bob Corker said he would back “surgical, proportional” strikes but opposed deploying U.S. ground forces and urged seeking congressional authorization. Separately, growing congressional unease was reflected in an expanding number (137) of lawmakers pressing the president to seek a formal authorization vote before taking military action. The White House said 15 members asked questions on the call and that consultations would continue.

Researchers from Australia, France and Japan have found that Adelie penguin numbers in East Antarctica are far higher than previously believed. Using aerial and ground surveys, tagging and resighting, and automated cameras across multiple breeding seasons, the team estimated about 5.9 million Adelies along a 5,000 km stretch of East Antarctic coastline — roughly 3.6 million more than earlier counts that only included breeding pairs. Extrapolating from this, they place the global population at about 14–16 million.

The key difference is inclusion of non-breeding birds, which spend much time foraging at sea and were largely missed by earlier colony-based counts; the study suggests non-breeders may be as numerous as breeders and are an important reserve of future breeders. The researchers also estimated prey needs for East Antarctic breeders during the breeding season: about 193,500 tonnes of krill and 18,800 tonnes of fish. These figures will inform the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources when setting sustainable krill fishery catch limits.

The findings have conservation implications: many penguin colonies are close to permanently occupied research stations (over one million breeders within 10 km of nine stations in the region), highlighting areas that may need enhanced protection.

Venezuela’s contested May 20, 2018 presidential election delivered a declared landslide victory for incumbent Nicolás Maduro, who claimed nearly 68% of the vote and a new six‑year term. The vote was boycotted by much of the mainstream opposition, marred by widespread allegations of irregularities — including “red tents” near polling places where government-issued “Fatherland Cards” were scanned and benefits offered — and saw turnout reported by the electoral board at 46.1% (opposition figures and some sources put it much lower). Major opposition figures Henri Falcón and Javier Bertucci rejected the process as illegitimate and called for a new ballot; domestic critics and many international actors described the election as a sham that props up an increasingly authoritarian regime.

Internationally, the U.S. and many regional governments refused to recognize the result. U.S. Deputy Secretary of State John Sullivan said Washington would not accept the outcome and that oil sanctions were “under active review” as a possible response; the Lima Group and Canada also declined to recognize the vote and signaled diplomatic measures. Maduro dismissed criticism, celebrated the win before supporters, pledged economic recovery and dialogue with opponents, and framed his victory as resistance to “imperialist” pressure.

The contested re‑election comes amid Venezuela’s deepening socio‑economic collapse — including hyperinflation, massive food and medicine shortages, declining oil production and mass migration — raising prospects of intensified international isolation and further domestic instability.

Fresh heavy fighting erupted in South Sudan’s capital, Juba, leaving at least 66 soldiers dead and an unknown number of civilians wounded or killed, after President Salva Kiir said security forces had foiled an attempted coup by supporters of his sacked deputy, Riek Machar.

Key points:
- Clashes began Sunday evening and resumed with heavy weapons and sporadic shelling; communications and phone networks in Juba have been unreliable and the international airport remained closed.
- Local medical sources reported 66 soldiers killed (seven dying awaiting care and 59 killed outside), while hospitals have admitted more than 300 wounded; the ICRC and hospitals are overwhelmed. The overall death toll is uncertain but described by UN and Security Council officials as “heavy” with “dozens and dozens” of casualties.
- Around 15,000–20,000 civilians are sheltering in two UNMISS compounds in Juba, straining food, water, sanitation and medical supplies; about 16,000 were also reported taking refuge in UN sites by other UN officials.
- Kiir accused troops loyal to Machar of attempting to seize power; authorities say around ten senior former officials have been arrested. There are conflicting reports about Machar’s whereabouts.
- International response: the UN urged restraint and protection of civilians; the African Union expressed deep concern. The US Embassy suspended normal operations, ordered non-emergency staff departures, and warned US citizens to leave immediately, promising evacuation guidance. The US Department of State issued or reiterated a travel warning and evacuation guidance for Americans in the country.
- Background: tensions rose after Kiir dismissed Machar and the entire cabinet in July. The rivalry—partly along Dinka (Kiir) and Nuer (Machar) lines—comes amid South Sudan’s continuing struggles to build stable governance since its 2011 independence.

The situation remains fluid and dangerous; aid agencies and UN missions are responding to urgent medical and humanitarian needs while calling for an immediate end to hostilities and protection of civilians.

A member of Canada’s elite Joint Task Force 2 (JTF2) made a confirmed world-record sniper kill in Iraq, hitting and killing an Islamic State insurgent from 3,540 metres (about 2.2 miles). The Canadian Special Operations Command verified the shot but gave no operational details for security reasons. Military sources and media report the sniper fired from a high-rise with a McMillan TAC-50 during an operation in the last month; the round reportedly took under 10 seconds and disrupted an ISIS attack on Iraqi security forces. Verification reportedly relied on video and other sensor data, and coalition partners observed the engagement.

The shot surpasses the previous confirmed record of 2,475 metres set by a British sniper in 2009 and follows earlier long-range records held by Canadian snipers in Afghanistan. JTF2’s remit includes counterterrorism, sniping and hostage rescue; in Iraq Canadian special forces are officially in an “advise and assist” role supporting and training Iraqi forces and Kurdish units. Sources emphasized the extreme technical challenge—ballistics, wind, altitude, angle and even the Earth’s curvature must be accounted for—and highlighted Canada’s strong sniper training programs. For operational security, the unit did not identify the sniper, his observer, exact location or timing. Some commentators urged caution pending full technical details, but Canadian veterans and experts called the feat extraordinary and likely to stand as a lasting record.

Juan Jose Vidrio Bibriesca, 43, who was already in Eagle County, Colorado, court on a felony drug-related bond-violation, was charged with two additional felonies after a folded paper bindle of cocaine fell from his hat while he stood at the podium before Judge Katharine Sullivan. A law-enforcement officer in the gallery saw the item fall, and courtroom surveillance video confirmed it came from Bibriesca’s hat. He was taken to the county jail and later appeared before District Court Judge Paul Dunkelman. Bibriesca, born in Mexico and reportedly in the U.S. illegally, may also face attention from Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Booking records do not list an attorney. (Source: Vail Daily/AP)

A nationwide class-action lawsuit (Meghan DeVries v. Ulta Beauty, Inc.), filed February 8, 2018 in Cook County, Illinois by attorney Thomas Zimmerman Jr., accuses Ulta of routinely repackaging, resealing and reselling previously purchased and used beauty products. The complaint alleges store managers are given quotas limiting how many returned items may be discarded, and staff were instructed to clean obviously used items (for example with cotton swabs or alcohol) so they could be placed back on shelves without disclosure. The suit cites employee statements and social-media posts claiming the practice is widespread and references an undercover investigation that reportedly found harmful bacteria (including E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus) and viruses on returned products, raising sanitary and health concerns. DeVries seeks damages for consumers who bought used items and injunctive relief to stop the alleged practice; a separate similar suit was filed earlier by another woman. Ulta spokesperson Karen Twigg May and another company statement say Ulta’s policy forbids resale of used products, the company prioritizes guest health and safety, and it intends to vigorously defend against the allegations.

John Stamos and fiancée Caitlin McHugh are expecting their first child. Stamos, 54, told People he and McHugh, 31, had talked about starting a family and everything “fell into place.” The pregnancy prompted Stamos to propose—he called McHugh’s parents before proposing—and the couple are keeping the baby's sex private. Both expressed excitement: Stamos said he’s always wanted to be a dad and plans to be a playful parent, while McHugh praised his generosity and suitability for fatherhood. Newt Gingrich vowed to stay in the 2012 Republican presidential race after losing key Deep South primaries in Alabama and Mississippi to Rick Santorum. Though he finished behind Santorum in both contests, Gingrich placed ahead of front-runner Mitt Romney in those states and his campaign has shifted its short-term aim from winning the nomination to denying Romney an outright delegate majority before the convention. Campaign advisers argue that dragging the contest into a contested convention would undercut Romney’s inevitability.

Gingrich’s continued candidacy reflects personal ambition, financial independence, and a willingness to press on despite mounting doubts about his viability. His operation carried debt and has limited geographic success (victories only in South Carolina and Georgia), and exit polls showed declining support among very conservative, evangelical and Tea Party voters compared with earlier Southern contests. Critics and some conservative activists urged Gingrich to withdraw so Santorum could consolidate the anti-Romney vote, but Gingrich’s team insists accumulating delegates now helps block Romney.

Santorum’s back-to-back wins reinforced his status as the conservative alternative to Romney and bolstered his argument that Gingrich should step aside. Romney’s campaign framed the outcomes as preserving his delegate-position momentum. With Romney ahead in delegates (about 459 to Santorum’s 203 and Gingrich’s 118 at the time), the path to a convention showdown remains difficult but central to the strategies of Santorum and Gingrich, who hope to prevent Romney from reaching the 1,144-delegate threshold and force a contested convention.
