Rick Santorum’s Ohio campaign failed to properly file full delegate slates in multiple congressional districts, jeopardizing as many as 18 of Ohio’s 66 delegates (63 being awarded on Super Tuesday). The Ohio GOP says Santorum submitted no delegate names in three districts (losing eligibility for those nine district delegates) and filed incomplete slates in six other districts, making him eligible only for the partial number of delegates he named there. Opponents (Romney, Gingrich, Paul) submitted full slates in all districts.

Practically, if Santorum wins a district where he filed no or only partial slates, he would only receive the delegates he actually submitted; any unsubmitted delegates would remain unallocated unless claimed through a party challenge process. The state party can convene a three-member “committee on contests” to resolve disputes, with appeals possible to the RNC.

The filings were owed both to the Ohio secretary of state and the state party; Santorum’s campaign filed only with the secretary of state, which merely certifies ballot eligibility, and the omission was spotted when the Ohio GOP reviewed slates this week. Santorum’s campaign defended itself, saying votes will count toward at-large delegates and blamed being a small operation focused on Iowa earlier. Romney’s campaign framed the lapse as evidence of organizational weakness. The misfilings are especially consequential because several affected districts are areas where Santorum expected to perform well.

This article reviews the idea that an advanced civilization could become a galactic (or universal) superpower by progressively harvesting ever-larger energy sources, a framework originating with Nikolai Kardashev in 1962 (Type I: planetary, Type II: stellar, Type III: galactic). It highlights a recent preprint by Dan Hooper (Fermilab/Univ. of Chicago) that revives and adds an urgent twist: because dark energy will accelerate cosmic expansion, stars outside our Local Group will eventually cross the cosmic horizon and become forever inaccessible. To maximize usable energy before that happens, sufficiently advanced civilizations would aggressively secure and pull in stars from other galaxies—using swarms of solar collectors (Dyson-sphere-like statites) both to harvest and to propel those stars toward the home system.

The piece discusses how such megastructures (ideas traced from Olaf Stapledon to Freeman Dyson) would be built from millions of individual satellites rather than a rigid shell, and how star-moving activities could produce observable signatures—accelerated, radiating stars en route, or galaxies missing certain mid-mass stars—detectable by their altered spectral and infrared profiles. Hooper notes only stars of certain masses (roughly tens to ~100 solar masses) would be useful, producing characteristic light spectra. Humans are far from this level (Carl Sagan placed Earth at ~0.7 on the Kardashev scale), but older alien civilizations might already be Type II–III and potentially observable if astronomers develop sufficiently sensitive instruments. The article also references related science-fiction and historical scientific ideas about Dyson spheres and megastructures.

A Pew Research Center telephone survey (March 21–April 8, 2013; n=1,983; margin of error ±3 points) finds that 60% of Americans say “humans and other living things have evolved over time,” while 33% say “humans and other living things have existed in their present form since the beginning of time.” These overall levels are similar to 2009, but the partisan gap has widened: 67% of Democrats versus 43% of Republicans now say humans have evolved (Republican acceptance fell from 54% in 2009). 

Views vary sharply by religion and demographics:
- White evangelical Protestants are most likely to reject evolution (64% say humans have always existed in present form); half of black Protestants hold that view. By contrast, majorities of white mainline Protestants (78%), the religiously unaffiliated (76%), and white non-Hispanic Catholics (68%) say humans have evolved.
- Among those who accept evolution, about one-third of the public (32%) attributes it to natural processes such as natural selection, while roughly one-quarter (24%) say a supreme being guided evolution.
- Younger people, men, and those with more education are more likely to accept evolution.

Pew notes these partisan differences persist even after accounting for religious, racial/ethnic, and other demographic differences. The survey used both landline and cellphone RDD sampling with weighting to produce nationally representative estimates.

Eman Ahmed Abd El Aty, a 36-year-old Egyptian woman who has been bedridden for about 20–25 years and is reported by her family and treating doctors to weigh roughly 500 kg (about 1,100 lb), is being brought to Mumbai for high‑risk weight‑loss treatment. Renowned bariatric surgeon Dr. Muffazal (Muffi) Lakdawala of the Centre for Obesity and Digestive Surgery volunteered to treat her pro bono after Eman’s sister contacted him; he has experience operating on extremely heavy patients and on prominent Indian politicians. Egyptian physicians had said little more could be done locally; Eman’s condition has been described variously as massive obesity with lymphoedema and possible elephantiasis/parasite involvement.

Transport and logistics are major challenges: moving her may require home demolition/crane or a specially equipped charter aircraft. A visa hiccup arose because she could not present herself in Cairo for fingerprinting; Dr. Lakdawala appealed on Twitter to India’s External Affairs Minister Sushma Swaraj, who intervened and secured a medical visa within 24 hours. Dr. Lakdawala expects to fly her to Mumbai within days and anticipates she will need months of inpatient recovery there; he estimates surgery could reduce at least 200–300 lb initially, but full long‑term weight reduction would take years and carries very high risk.

Two pilots in the helium-filled Two Eagles balloon—American Troy Bradley and Russian Leonid Tiukhtyaev—are nearing the end of a record-setting trans-Pacific flight that began from Saga, Japan. By Thursday they had passed the previous gas-balloon distance record of 5,209 miles (8,383 km) set in 1981 and reached about 5,260–5,261 miles (≈8,465–8,467 km), the distance needed to meet international rules for a new record. They were also poised to break the traditional gas-balloon duration mark (about 137 hours) set in 1978; that milestone was expected Friday.

The team had planned to land in Canada but shifting weather—a high-pressure ridge off the U.S. West Coast—pushed them south toward Baja California, where they expected to touch down Saturday. Mission control in Albuquerque monitored and adjusted the flight as the pilots traded altitude and ballast to catch favorable winds; chase crews were being organized to assist the landing. Two Eagles’ carbon-fiber capsule and large helium envelope were built for up to 10 days aloft, though some gas and ballast losses have shortened endurance. Official certification of any new records must still be completed by the U.S. National Aeronautic Association and the Federation Aeronautique Internationale.

Workers in Cristovo de Cea, Galicia, Spain accidentally destroyed and covered a believed 6,000‑year‑old Neolithic tomb after mistaking its granite slabs for a broken picnic bench. Parks-and-recreation staff poured concrete into the burial chamber and placed a new picnic table on top. The site had heritage status and should have been protected and marked, but local officials, including the mayor, say they were not informed; an investigation is underway. Archaeologist Juan Barceló called it a "monumental error," attributing the breakdown in communication partly to summer holidays and stressing such accidents are not the norm in Spain. The report notes similar incidents elsewhere—both accidental and deliberate—where ancient sites have been destroyed, including examples from Nanjing, California, Belize and a botched restoration attempt.

Comedy Central marked Newt Gingrich’s May 2 withdrawal from the 2012 Republican presidential race with a satirical take on the children’s book Goodnight Moon. The “Goodnight Moon Colony” image gallery — seven illustrated “pages” posted on Comedy Central’s Indecision site — depicts Gingrich in bed with a lunar base visible through his window and lampoons his campaign remarks. Slides say “goodnight” to items tied to Gingrich’s campaign and record (e.g., “Dirty Unwashed Occupy Wall Street Protestors,” “Bankrupt Health Care Think Tank”), while the intro jabs that the campaign will be remembered mostly for his moon-colony proposal. Gingrich had proposed establishing a permanent U.S. lunar base by 2020 and later missions to Mars — a plan experts questioned for its cost and timeline, especially alongside his promises to shrink NASA and cut its budget. The piece notes rival Mitt Romney’s different approach of strengthening NASA-private partnerships and convening a cross-sector coalition on space policy.

- Health advisory on copper mugs and Moscow mules: Iowa's Alcoholic Beverages Division advised against serving Moscow mules and other acidic beverages (pH below 6.0, e.g., drinks with fruit juice, vinegar, wine) in unlined pure copper mugs because acidity can cause copper to leach into the drink. Excess copper intake can cause copper poisoning, with symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting and jaundice. Because Moscow mules (vodka, ginger beer, lime) are acidic, pure copper mugs are not recommended. Safe alternatives include mugs with a copper exterior but a lined interior (nickel or stainless steel), which are widely available. (Original reporting: Live Science; NIH cited for symptoms.)

- UCSF Food Industry Documents Archive: There is a collection of web resources related to the UCSF Food Industry Documents Archive, which preserves internal documents from food industry companies (for example, the U.S. sugar industry) that are relevant to public health.

Houston police have identified 62-year-old Joseph James Pappas as the suspect in the July 20 daylight killing of prominent Houston cardiologist Dr. Mark Hausknecht, who was shot while bicycling to work near the Texas Medical Center. Authorities say Pappas may have harbored a 20-year grudge: his mother died on the operating table while under Hausknecht’s care two decades earlier. Surveillance footage showed the gunman ride past Hausknecht, turn around and fire; a tip after police released images led them to Pappas.

Chief Art Acevedo described Pappas as dangerous, skilled with firearms, possibly suicidal and likely armed; police found evidence at Pappas’s Westbury home during a search but he was not there. Following the shooting, ads using a phone number linked to Pappas listed multiple weapons, ammunition and tactical gear for sale; investigators are examining whether any of those items relate to the murder. Pappas previously served about 30 years in Harris County law enforcement and held a real estate license.

Dr. Hausknecht, 65, a respected interventional cardiologist who once treated former President George H.W. Bush, was mourned by colleagues and family. Police continue to search for Pappas and have charged him in the homicide. Authorities stress he should be considered armed and dangerous.

A staffing-firm survey of more than 600 U.S. office workers and managers (companies of 20+ employees) found significant on-the-clock personal activity:

- Employees spend an average of 56 minutes per workday (about 4.7 hours/week) using mobile phones for non-work purposes — mainly personal email and social media — which is 43% more than managers estimate (39 minutes).
- They also spend an average of 42 minutes per day (3.5 hours/week) on other personal tasks (errands, etc.).
- Combined, that totals nearly 8 hours of lost productivity per week for the average worker.
- Younger employees (ages 18–34) spend the most time: about 70 minutes/day on mobile devices plus 48 minutes/day on other personal tasks — roughly 10 hours/week.
- More than half of workers say they use personal devices to access websites blocked by company IT; managers are less likely to think this occurs.

OfficeTeam cautions that occasional personal use is understandable but can become a major distraction and recommends using breaks and lunch to handle non-work matters.

A near-21-hour insurgent siege on a high-rise near Kabul’s diplomatic and military district began just after lunch on Tuesday and ended Wednesday morning when Afghan and NATO special forces killed the last of six attackers. The assailants, at least three of whom were suicide bombers detonating elsewhere in the city, occupied an under-construction 15-story building overlooking the U.S. Embassy and NATO headquarters, firing rockets and rifles into the heavily fortified enclave. Authorities found burqas in the attackers’ van and say the men likely used them to smuggle a large cache of weapons into the building.

At least seven Afghan civilians were killed and 17 injured; NATO reported six coalition personnel wounded. No casualties were reported inside the embassy or NATO compound, though hundreds of diplomats and staff spent the night in bunkers. NATO helicopters and Western forces provided aerial support while Afghan forces led the clearance operation, which proceeded floor by floor. The Taliban claimed responsibility; U.S. Ambassador Ryan Crocker and Afghan officials pointed to the Haqqani network as the likely perpetrator.

The attack highlighted security and intelligence shortcomings in Kabul—and raised concerns about the capacity of Afghan forces as NATO transitions security responsibilities and U.S. troop withdrawals continue. The government has launched an investigation into how weapons breached checkpoints and whether insiders aided the attackers. The assault was the third major strike in Kabul in four months and temporarily paralyzed central parts of the city.

DARPA has issued a request for ideas to explore turning existing large aircraft (e.g., B-1, B-52, C-130–type airframes) into airborne “motherships” that can carry, launch and recover unmanned aerial systems (UAS). The goal is to extend the reach and mission set of smaller drones—reconnaissance, strikes, etc.—by bringing them much closer to targets without needing nearby airfields, using minimal modifications to planes already in the inventory.

The effort is currently conceptual—“float-the-idea” stage, not a prototype program—and seeks technical approaches for safe midair launch and recovery, a major technical challenge. The idea revives an old concept (1920s airships that carried biplanes, 1960s D‑21 drones launched from B-52s) and fits into broader Pentagon investments in robotic “marsupial” systems that carry and deploy smaller robots. Observers note parallels in foreign developments and other domains: China showed vehicle-carried robots at Zhuhai, and U.S. researchers have also pursued underwater “carriers,” including demonstrations of a drone launched from a submerged torpedo/missile tube.

Steve and Terri Weaver of Stuttgart, Arkansas, won a total of $1,050,000 in lottery prizes over one weekend. On Saturday Steve bought a $1 million scratch-off and won; the next day Terri purchased a $250,000 “Taxes Paid” scratch-off and won $50,000. The couple said they were shocked and briefly worried about the claiming process, joked about lie detector tests, and plan to invest the money. They also said they will continue to play and will go to work the next day.

Researchers have used modern imaging and genomic sequencing to reveal new details about Ötzi, the 5300-year-old "Tyrolean Iceman" found on an Alpine glacier. A 3D CT study of his mouth shows severe dental disease: advanced gum disease, deep cavities, heavy wear on front and back teeth from chewing coarse, stone‑ground grain and using teeth as a tool, a discolored front tooth likely lost in trauma, and a broken molar probably caused by a grit-containing diet. The authors link rising cavity rates in the Neolithic to increased consumption of coarsely ground starches.

Whole-genome sequencing provides further insights: Ötzi carried a genetic predisposition to arteriosclerosis, despite lacking modern lifestyle risk factors, suggesting some cardiovascular risk may be hardwired. His paternal lineage falls in the rare G2A4 Y‑chromosome haplogroup tied to Near Eastern Neolithic migrants into Europe, and his overall profile is most similar to small, relatively isolated modern populations in Sardinia, Corsica and parts of the Caucasus—likely the closest living relatives of early farmers who entered Europe. The genome indicates brown eyes and hair, type O blood, lactose intolerance, and the presence of Borrelia burgdorferi DNA (about 60% of a genome), making Ötzi the earliest known carrier of Lyme disease. Taken together, these findings deepen understanding of Ötzi’s health, lifestyle and ancestry and offer data on ancient disease and population movements.

Here are the key points across the stories:

Wendy Davis and Texas abortion bill
- Texas Democratic Sen. Wendy Davis criticized Gov. Rick Perry and Lt. Gov. David Dewhurst for using a 20-week abortion ban and related omnibus legislation to advance political ambitions, saying they’re willing to “put women in harm’s way” to climb the political ladder.
- Davis warned Republicans will be more strategic in a special legislative session but said national attention will hold them accountable. She emphasized the bill is broader than a 20-week ban and contains provisions likely to close many Texas clinics.
- Davis, who rose to national prominence after a filibuster against the bill, rejected Perry’s personal attack referencing her past as a teenage mother and vowed to continue fighting when the Legislature reconvenes.

Nancy Pelosi on Edward Snowden and surveillance
- House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi questioned the substantive value of NSA leaker Edward Snowden’s disclosures, suggesting he may know the surveillance “machinery” but not the content, and criticized his reported willingness to share information with Russia and China.
- Pelosi reiterated that Snowden broke the law, defended the surveillance programs as balanced with civil liberties protections (citing FISA amendments, inspectors general, congressional oversight, and the Privacy and Civil Liberties Board), and said the current programs are not comparable to the broad, unchecked surveillance under George W. Bush.

Ralph Reed on opponents of gay marriage
- Faith and Freedom Coalition leader Ralph Reed pushed back against framing opponents of gay marriage as bigots, noting many prominent Democrats (including President Obama, Vice President Biden, Sen. Patrick Leahy and Bill Clinton) once supported the Defense of Marriage Act and asking whether that made them intolerant then.

Michael Hayden on NSA revelations and public trust
- Former CIA and NSA director Gen. Michael Hayden said the Snowden disclosures have done “significant” damage to President Obama and urged the administration to better educate the public about surveillance to build comfort and consensus.
- He argued that while secrecy protects operational advantage, democracies need national consensus for sustained surveillance programs or they risk a backlash.

Overall themes
- Political fallout and strategy around contentious national issues (abortion and surveillance) are prominent: Davis accuses Texas leadership of politicizing abortion, Pelosi and Hayden debate the impact and oversight of NSA disclosures, and Reed defends the motives of those opposing gay marriage. Each story centers on accountability, public perception, and how political actors frame or respond to controversy.

Rapper T.I. (Clifford “Tip” Harris) was arrested early Wednesday near his Atlanta-area gated community on charges of disorderly conduct, public drunkenness and simple assault after an altercation with a security guard who would not let him in because he had lost his key, Henry County deputies said. He and a friend were taken into custody around 4:30 a.m. and later released on bail.

T.I. told The Blast he had returned from the studio, found the guard allegedly sleeping in the gatehouse, and confronted him; the verbal dispute escalated but, he insists, never became physical. He suggested race and the predominantly white local police played a role in the arrest, noting the guard was Black and the responding officers were white. T.I. said he may have “hurt [the guard] by [his] words” but denies any physical assault and plans legal action against his homeowners association; his attorney has issued a statement backing his claim that the arrest was wrongful.

The article also notes T.I.’s past legal history: a 2009 federal gun conviction that resulted in about seven months’ imprisonment and an 11-month federal sentence around 2010 after a probation violation tied to a drug arrest. After posting bail Wednesday, T.I. spent time with family and celebrated his son Major’s 10th birthday. Representatives had not immediately responded to requests for comment.

Early Thursday morning during a Ferguson protest, at least three shots were fired at a line of roughly 25 officers outside the Ferguson Police Department. Two officers—a 41-year-old St. Louis County officer (wounded in the right shoulder) and a 32-year-old Webster Groves officer (wounded below the right eye with a bullet lodged behind his ear)—were hit, treated at Barnes-Jewish Hospital and released. Authorities described the incident as an ambush and said the shots appeared to be aimed at officers from about 125 yards away, likely fired from a handgun. No suspects have been identified; shell casings were recovered and police conducted searches and questioned several people near a home four blocks from the station.

The shooting occurred hours after Ferguson Police Chief Thomas Jackson and the city manager resigned following a DOJ report finding widespread racial bias in the Ferguson force. Protests in Ferguson, sparked last August by the police killing of Michael Brown, had dwindled before the gunfire; witnesses say the crowd split into largely peaceful demonstrators and a smaller, volatile group. Video of the shooting exists and multiple departments responded to secure the scene.

Federal and local leaders condemned the attack. Attorney General Eric Holder called the shooter a “damn punk,” said the violence threatened reforms sought by nonviolent protesters, and offered Justice Department investigative resources. Other officials—including President Obama, Missouri’s governor, U.S. senators and representatives—condemned the ambush, urged information sharing, and offered rewards (CrimeStoppers $10,000; two congressmen added $3,000). The Missouri Highway Patrol and St. Louis County Police took over protest security that night.

Officials warned the shooting complicates policing of demonstrations and raised concerns about escalating violence. Investigations and a manhunt are ongoing; tip lines and rewards have been publicized for information leading to arrests.

- The U.S. Marshals Service is holding an online auction of Ted Kaczynski’s personal effects to help satisfy a $15 million restitution order to his victims. Kaczynski, the “Unabomber,” conducted a mail bombing campaign from 1978–1995, killing three and injuring 23; he is serving life in federal prison.

- High-interest items include his 35,000-word handwritten manifesto (top bid about $17,525), his iconic hoodie made famous by an FBI wanted poster (about $20,025, with sunglasses included), and his Smith-Corona typewriter (around $11,000). Lesser items—such as a hand-bowed wood saw and letters to his aunt—have drawn only modest bids. The most valuable asset, his Montana cabin, is not for sale; it is displayed at the Newseum in Washington, D.C.

- Appraisers and collectors offer differing perspectives. Appraiser Elyse Luray acknowledges historical and collectible value in the manifesto and typewriter but dismisses much of the lot as appeal for “weird” collectors and notes hype inflates prices. Crime-memorabilia collector Scott Michaels sees value in ownership for storytelling and cites the hoodie as iconic but says he’d prefer the saw for its direct human connection. Criminologist Jeffery Ian Ross frames interest in crime memorabilia as a centuries-old public fascination driven by voyeurism and a desire to connect with headline events. Collectors warn buying such items is not a reliable investment but rather a way to own an object of morbid history.

- Separately: Actor Kellan Lutz is participating in a celebrity baggage auction with JetBlue and DoSomething.org, donating luggage and items to raise funds for youth groups; earlier rounds raised more than $15,000, and Lutz’s items join a second round of auctions on eBay.

- Also noted: A 1917 film reel, Charlie Chaplin in Zepped—the only known surviving copy, depicting Chaplin bringing down a German Zeppelin and containing early animation—was purchased in 2009 for its tin but is expected to command a six-figure price.

A US jury has ordered Facebook, its Oculus unit and certain executives to pay $500m to video game publisher ZeniMax, finding that Oculus breached a contract and infringed some copyrights when launching its Rift VR headset. The court rejected ZeniMax’s main claim that Oculus stole trade secrets, but found co‑founder Palmer Luckey violated a non‑disclosure agreement; Oculus said it was disappointed and will appeal.

The ruling came just before Facebook reported strong fourth‑quarter results: net profit more than doubled to about $3.6bn and revenue rose sharply (Q4 revenue roughly $8.8bn, up from $5.8bn), driven by robust mobile advertising (now ~84% of ad revenue). Facebook reported roughly 1.86 billion monthly users and said it expects to reach 2 billion in 2017. Management signalled increased hiring and spending for video and related priorities, and pledged more AI work to combat fake news. Despite legal and regulatory challenges — including privacy issues in Europe, concerns about fake news and slowed ad growth prospects — analysts called the quarter “stellar,” and Facebook reiterated it will appeal the Texas verdict.

Greg Gianforte, Montana’s congressman-elect who was accused of body-slamming Guardian reporter Ben Jacobs the night before a special congressional election, pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault. Judge Rick West imposed a 180‑day deferred sentence, 40 hours of community service, 20 hours of anger‑management classes, a $300 fine and an $85 court fee. West had initially sentenced four days in jail (partly through a work program) but replaced that with community service and anger management because those convicted of assault are ineligible for the work program. In Montana, misdemeanor assault carries up to six months in jail and a $500 fine. Gianforte has apologized to Jacobs and pledged $50,000 to the Committee to Protect Journalists.

The episode drew national attention and commentary: President Trump praised Gianforte after the assault, calling him “a tough cookie,” remarks that prompted criticism from the White House Correspondents’ Association for appearing to celebrate violence against a journalist. The incident and its fallout occurred amid broader political activity in Montana, where Trump campaigned on other issues (immigration, support for Republicans in a competitive Senate race) while the state’s Senate contest remained closely contested.

A Cooke Aquaculture net pen near Cypress Island failed over the weekend, releasing thousands of farmed Atlantic salmon into waters between Anacortes and the San Juan Islands. The pen, holding roughly 305,000 fish and an estimated 3 million pounds of biomass, suffered anchor and walkway failures; Cooke initially blamed “exceptionally high tides and currents coinciding with the solar eclipse,” though tide and wind records and local experts dispute that explanation. Cooke later estimated 4,000–5,000 fish escaped, but final losses won’t be known until harvesting and inventory are complete.

State and federal agencies and Cooke are coordinating a response. The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) has urged recreational and commercial fishers to harvest as many of the nonnative Atlantics as possible (no size or bag limits; a license required), and buyers may legally purchase them. Tribal and commercial fishers have been recovering escapees from areas as far as Bellingham Bay and Samish; some have also been found in rivers. Tribal leaders and conservation groups called the spill “devastating” and an “environmental nightmare,” expressing fears about competition with and disease risks to imperiled Pacific salmon, impacts on juvenile migration routes, and long-term ecosystem effects. Others, including a NOAA scientist and some researchers, note Atlantic salmon typically fare poorly in the wild and have not established breeding populations or repeatedly hybridized with native species.

Critics note past maintenance issues at the site and contest Cooke’s tide-based explanation, pointing to previous net problems and monthly stronger currents earlier in the year. Concerns were also raised about the ad hoc public-harvest approach—some urge contracting experienced commercial or tribal fishers to remove escapees to avoid unintended impacts on other species and to ensure proper handling and accountability. WDFW said the escaped fish were treated for bacteria earlier in the season and currently show no disease signs; penalties for the farm are under review. The incident has intensified opposition to Cooke’s proposed expansion of net-pen farming in Puget Sound.

Ringing Bells, a Noida-based startup, says it will begin shipping its heavily scrutinized Freedom 251 smartphone — touted as the world’s cheapest at Rs. 251 (~$4) — on June 30. CEO Mohit Goel told IANS the company is ready with about 200,000 units and will open another registration phase after this initial dispatch, though the firm originally promised to deliver 2.5 million (or had stated plans for 25 lakh) units by June-end. The February launch drew massive interest (reports of roughly 70 million registrations) but also intense skepticism, a police FIR and controversy after demo units shown to media were alleged to be rebranded phones from another maker.

The 3G dual-SIM device has a 4-inch screen, 1.3 GHz quad-core processor, 1 GB RAM, 8 GB storage (expandable to 32 GB), Android 5.1, an 8 MP rear camera with flash, a 3.2 MP front camera and a 1,800 mAh battery. Ringing Bells claims the phones are manufactured in Haridwar under “Make in India” and display the Indian tricolour at startup; IANS was shown only a photograph, not a review unit. Goel admits the company will incur a loss of about Rs. 140–150 per phone but expects profitability from scale and app partnerships.

The company also plans to launch a “Freedom” 32-inch HD LED TV in early July for under Rs. 10,000, claiming one lakh units in stock. Critics remain unconvinced about the phone’s feasibility and authenticity, given earlier doubts that a smartphone could be produced at such a low price and the controversies surrounding the prototype demonstrations.

Summary:

In August 2018, Christopher Watts murdered his pregnant wife Shanann, 34, and their daughters Bella, 4, and Celeste, 3, in Frederick, Colorado. He later pleaded guilty to multiple counts—including five counts of first-degree murder, unlawful termination of a pregnancy and tampering with bodies—and in November 2018 was sentenced to life without parole plus additional years.

Released investigation files and phone records reveal a deteriorating marriage in the weeks before the killings. Shanann, about 15 weeks pregnant, and the girls spent most of the summer visiting family in North Carolina; Watts joined them for the final week. While they were apart, investigators found Watts was having an affair with co-worker Nichol Kessinger and went on dates. Friends reported that Watts became distant and cold after rejoining the family; Shanann canceled a planned gender-reveal party and texted friends that Chris said they were “not compatible,” that he refused counseling, and that he told her he didn’t want the third child.

Phone messages between the couple show escalating tension from mid-July through early August: Shanann repeatedly pressed for communication and expressed fear their marriage was failing; Watts alternately apologized, minimized problems, and at times said he was “not sure what’s in my head.” Investigators’ analysis documents Watts juggling simultaneous conversations with his wife and the other woman.

On Aug. 13 a friend reported Shanann and the children missing. Watts publicly pleaded for their return but was later arrested after a lengthy interview and polygraph administration on Aug. 15. He initially denied involvement, but the polygraph indicated deception on key questions; after sustained questioning and a call to his father, Watts confessed to killing Shanann (claiming a false story that she harmed the children) and admitted placing Bella and Celeste in oil tanks and burying Shanann in a shallow grave. Autopsy and crime-scene reports show Shanann was strangled and the children suffocated; their bodies were hidden at a remote oil site where Watts worked.

The released files—nearly 2,000 pages—include interviews with friends, family and coworkers, details of Watts’ lies about his movements (including fabricating an outing to a baseball game), evidence of financial stress, and Kessinger’s account of their relationship. The records also document investigators’ methods (including polygraph results) used to obtain Watts’ confession and provide a detailed timeline of the family’s final days.

Emmanuel Macron won France’s presidential runoff decisively over far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, prompting rapid international congratulations and relief across Europe and beyond. EU leaders — notably Germany’s Angela Merkel, European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker and EU Council President Donald Tusk — welcomed a pro-European result, seeing Macron’s victory as a boost for EU unity after Brexit. World leaders including U.S. President Donald Trump, former U.S. figures like Hillary Clinton, Canada’s Justin Trudeau, Brazil’s Michel Temer and Australia’s Malcolm Turnbull also offered congratulations and signaled readiness to work with him. British Prime Minister Theresa May spoke with Macron and briefly discussed Brexit and future UK–EU partnership.

Macron, 39, delivered his victory speech at the Louvre — a symbolic, stage-managed opening that emphasized European commitment (he entered to Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy”) and a return to a dignified presidential style. He presents himself as a centrist reformer promising a youthful “revolution” while restoring a unifying republican leadership. His agenda includes labor-law liberalization (potentially via presidential decrees), public spending cuts, tax and pension reform, measures against nepotism and corruption, support for small businesses and targeted education reforms.

But Macron faces immediate and deep challenges: persistent high unemployment, economic malaise, social division between prosperous urban centers and struggling peripheral areas, a state of emergency and ongoing counterterrorism and military commitments (including operations in the Sahel). Large protests, led by unions, signaled resistance to planned labor reforms. Domestically, his ability to deliver reforms hinges on winning a parliamentary majority in June; without one he will need to build novel coalitions. He has kept the choice of prime minister secret while promising a balanced, partly novice government and gender parity among candidates.

Analysts view Macron’s victory as a significant pushback against the populist wave that produced Brexit and Donald Trump, though observers including Condoleezza Rice warned that the broader populist and nativist influence persists even when candidates lose. Macron’s campaign combined grassroots tactics, data-driven outreach and optimistic messaging to capture support from voters intent on blocking the far right as well as those seeking change. Internationally, Macron is expected to move quickly to engage with Angela Merkel and to signal continuity in France’s global and military commitments, while carefully navigating relations with the Trump administration on areas of both cooperation (security) and disagreement (e.g., climate policy).

The article reports on the immediate aftermath of President Donald Trump’s July 26, 2017 tweets declaring that transgender people would not be allowed to serve “in any capacity” in the U.S. military. The announcement surprised Pentagon leaders and left policy and personnel questions unresolved.

Key points:
- Gen. Joseph Dunford, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told all service chiefs and commanders there would be no changes to current policy until Defense Secretary Jim Mattis receives presidential direction and issues implementation guidance. Meanwhile, service members should be treated with respect and remain focused on missions.
- Mattis was reportedly on vacation and had not received specific direction when Trump tweeted. Pentagon officials said they would work with the White House to provide guidance “in the near future,” but a timetable was unclear; implementation guidance could take weeks or months.
- The Navy issued an internal message saying no transgender sailors would be discharged and health care would continue until further guidance is given.
- Trump justified the action by citing “tremendous medical costs and disruption,” a claim disputed by a RAND Corp. study estimating annual medical costs for transgender troops at no more than about $8 million and noting replacement and recruitment costs could be far higher.
- Estimates of transgender service members range from roughly 1,300 to 6,600 among 1.3 million active-duty troops.
- Reaction in Washington was sharply divided: critics including Sen. John McCain opposed the move, arguing qualified service members should be allowed to serve; supporters like Rep. Duncan Hunter praised restoring “warrior culture.” Transgender service members expressed fear and uncertainty.
- The announcement halted a recent trend toward inclusion that began under Clinton and accelerated under Obama (repeal of the gay ban, opening more roles to women, and allowing transgender troops to serve openly in 2016). The services had been given time to implement policies; Mattis had earlier extended an implementation deadline to Jan. 1 to study readiness impacts.

Overall, military leaders temporarily maintained the status quo while awaiting clear presidential instructions and formal policy guidance.

Alaska State Troopers report two men skiing in the Rainbow Mountains were caught in an avalanche Saturday afternoon. One skier, tentatively identified as 35-year-old Eric Peterson of Delta Junction, was found deceased by the other skier but his body has not yet been recovered; next of kin have been notified. The surviving skier is 63-year-old Fairbanks resident Michael Hopper, who dug himself out after 2–3 hours, located Peterson’s glove, and then found him. Hopper, who owns nearby Black Rapids Lodge and is experienced in local mountains, was later spotted near the Richardson Highway and was able to summon help. Troopers say the avalanche struck just behind the pair and that the slope remains unstable with heavy snowfall; recovery will be attempted when conditions allow. Multiple agencies, including AST, military personnel from Black Rapids, Fort Greely Fire Department and Rural Delta Fire and Rescue, responded. This is a developing story.

A Human Rights Watch report by Jamie Fellner finds that in 2012 just 3% of federal drug defendants went to trial, with 89% of those convicted and receiving sentences averaging more than three times longer—about 11 years more—than defendants who accepted plea deals. Fellner argues this is largely driven by prosecutors’ use of mandatory-minimum sentencing and charge-stacking to threaten vastly longer terms if defendants refuse pleas, effectively coercing guilty pleas and removing meaningful judicial discretion. The report documents extreme examples—first-time or low-level offenders receiving decades in prison after trial because mandatory minimums constrained judges—and links the rise in pleas to mandatory minimums enacted in the 1980s. The Justice Department responds that its charging policies aim to reserve enhancements for serious offenders and not to coerce defendants; Attorney General Eric Holder has directed prosecutors to avoid charging low-level drug offenders with mandatory-minimum offenses. Fellner and reform advocates call for restoring judges’ discretion by reducing or eliminating mandatory minimums or allowing greater departures from guidelines to prevent prosecutorial overreach and protect the integrity of the justice system.

Researchers at Charles University (Prague) report in PLoS ONE that people can, above chance, judge a man’s measured intelligence from a single neutral-expression facial photograph, but the same is not true for women. The study used 80 photographed students (40 men, 40 women) who completed an IQ battery, and 160 independent raters who scored those photos for perceived intelligence and attractiveness.

Key findings
- Perceived intelligence from men’s faces correlated significantly with measured IQ (particularly fluid and figural intelligence). No such correlation was found for women’s faces.
- Both male and female raters performed similarly; both sexes’ ratings were highly correlated.
- Perceived intelligence and perceived attractiveness were positively correlated for both sexes, but that link was much stronger for women’s faces (suggesting a stronger “halo” of attractiveness for women).
- Geometric morphometric analysis identified facial shapes associated with perceived intelligence (the “intelligence stereotype”): longer/narrower faces, wider eye distance, larger/prolonged nose, slight upturn at mouth corners, and a sharper chin were rated as more intelligent; broader, rounder faces with closer-set eyes, shorter noses, downturned mouth corners, and heavier round chins were rated as less intelligent.
- Crucially, those morphological features did not correlate with actual IQ for either men or women. In other words, raters used visual cues that matched cultural stereotypes of a “smart face,” but those cues don’t explain the real IQ differences—except that people nevertheless judged men’s intelligence with some accuracy via cues not captured by face-shape measures.

Possible explanations offered
- Cues that genuinely track intelligence may be sexually dimorphic or linked to male development (e.g., hormonal factors), making them visible in men’s faces but not women’s.
- The strong attractiveness halo for women may mask or override subtle cues to intelligence, preventing accurate judgments.
- Evolutionary or signaling explanations: accurate signaling of intelligence may have been more adaptive for men in mate or social contexts, so honest cues persisted more in male faces.

Other observations
- Fluid and figural intelligence (problem-solving and spatial/figural reasoning) showed the clearest links with perceived intelligence from men’s faces; verbal/crystallized intelligence did not.
- The relationship between perceived intelligence and measured IQ in men showed some nonlinear pattern (very high IQs >140 were not perceived as increasingly more intelligent).
- The authors stress that the “intelligent-looking” face likely reflects a cultural stereotype rather than a reliable morphological marker of intelligence.

Limitations and future directions
- Small, homogeneous sample (university students) and static neutral photographs limit generalizability.
- The visual cues that permitted accurate judgments of men’s IQ were not identified by the geometric shape analysis; possibilities include skin texture, subtle expressions, eye gaze, color, or dynamic/behavioral cues—areas for future research.
- The stronger attractiveness-intelligence correlation for women needs further study to disentangle perceptual bias from genuine cues.

Bottom line
People can modestly and unexpectedly infer men’s IQ from a single neutral photo, but not women’s. The features that make a face look intelligent map onto a clear stereotype (longer, narrower faces with certain nose, mouth, chin proportions), yet those shape traits do not explain real IQ differences. The authors suggest sexual dimorphism of cues, attractiveness halo effects, or signaling differences as possible reasons for the male-only effect, and call for more research into the actual visual cues and their developmental or social origins.

Jamaica’s two-man bobsled team returned to the Winter Olympics in Sochi after a 12-year absence, and the Jamaican Tourist Board promoted a new reggae tune, “The Bobsled Song,” as a theme for their run. Written by Sidney Mills and Jon Notar and performed with Groove Guild, the song is designed to sync with the 1,500‑meter, 17‑turn Sochi track—if you start it the moment pilots Marvin Dixon and Winston Watts begin their run it reportedly matches the course’s twists and turns and finish. An eight‑bit animated video illustrates the course and lyrics (including the “It’s bobsled time” chorus). Jamaica qualified for the two‑man event without World Cup starts by earning points in lower‑tier North American races and are considered long shots for a medal.

Derrick Henry, Alabama’s bruising workhorse and Heisman finalist from Yulee, is expected to enter the 2016 NFL Draft regardless of Saturday’s award result. Scouts and draft analysts will face several questions about him: the effect of an enormous college workload, how much his success depends on Alabama’s elite blocking, his size and injury risk, and how scheme-specific his skills are.

Dan Hatman, a former NFL scout who watched four Henry games, offered a measured evaluation. Hatman sees Henry as a power, scheme-dependent back rather than a one-on-one playmaker who can routinely create when blocks break down. He praised Henry’s balance, vision, patience and ability to finish runs once he gets a head of steam, but noted limited lateral agility and few big, sudden cuts. Hatman believes Henry fits best in offenses that mix power runs with inside zone blocking (examples: Oakland, San Francisco, Pittsburgh, Carolina), and compared him to recent late-round rookies Matt Jones and Karlos Williams—players who can produce big plays when blocking is right despite not being highly graded for elusiveness.

Workload is a major concern: Henry totaled 339 carries in the season (breaking Alabama’s single-season record and ranking near historic SEC highs), and Hatman calls that “absolutely” an issue when projecting how much wear he brings into the NFL and what teams can expect from his rookie contract. Because Hatman (who generally devalues the position) and other evaluators see value late in drafts for productive, lower-cost backs, he would place Henry in roughly the 100–150 pick range (around the fourth round), though many mocks have him higher.

Henry himself has downplayed concerns about carries, saying he wants the ball and to help his team, noting injuries to teammates (e.g., Kenyan Drake) increased his workload late in the season. Overall, Henry projects as a physically impressive, downhill runner who can break long runs when blocking and scheme fit are right, but whose heavy college usage, limited lateral quickness and scheme dependence may push him out of the early draft rounds.

On Sunday morning, Nov. 5, 2017, a gunman opened fire during services at the First Baptist Church in Sutherland Springs, a tiny, close-knit community about 30–40 miles southeast of San Antonio. Authorities identified the suspected shooter as 26-year-old Devin Patrick Kelley. He arrived at a Valero station across the street, then crossed into the church wearing tactical gear and a ballistic vest and began shooting. Law enforcement later found Kelley dead in his vehicle after a brief pursuit; investigators recovered multiple weapons and have not said whether his death was self-inflicted or caused by a civilian who engaged him.

The attack left 26 people dead and about 20 others wounded, with victims ranging in age from young children (reported as 5 or as young as 17 months in some accounts) to elderly parishioners in their 70s. Among the dead was 14-year-old Annabelle Pomeroy, the daughter of Pastor Frank Pomeroy. Several families suffered multiple losses; survivors and injured included children and infants. Local hospitals, including Connally Memorial and University Hospital in San Antonio, treated many of the wounded. First responders, federal agents (FBI, ATF) and state officials assisted at the scene.

Sutherland Springs residents—described as tightly bonded and centered on the church, which provided community services and outreach—reacted with shock, grief and vigils. Images of candlelight services, memorial crosses and a community center filled with families waiting for news of loved ones captured the town’s mourning. Governor Greg Abbott and President Trump expressed condolences; investigators continued on-scene work and family notifications. The mass shooting was among the deadliest in recent U.S. history and left a small town reeling.

The Navy has for the first time advanced female candidates into the selection pipeline for its two elite special-warfare communities previously closed to women: a prospective SEAL officer and at least one candidate for the Special Warfare Combatant-Craft Crewman (SWCC) enlisted program. The service confirmed the candidates but declined to identify them for operational-security reasons. One woman is a junior in an ROTC program who will attend SEAL Officer Assessment and Selection (SOAS) and compete for SEAL officer slots; one or more enlisted women have entered the SWCC accession pipeline and recruit training.

These developments follow the Pentagon’s decision more than a year ago to open previously restricted combat and special-operations jobs to women. Naval Special Warfare officials emphasize that women must meet the same standards and complete the same demanding training as men: Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL training (BUD/S) for SEALs and the SWCC pipeline for boat operators. Attrition is high—about 73–75% for enlisted SEAL candidates and 63% for SWCC; SEAL officer selection historically has a higher pass rate (roughly 65%). Officials warn it may take months or years before a woman actually graduates as a SEAL or SWCC.

The command reports it has prepared for integration—reviewing curriculum, facilities and policies, making minor lodging and uniform adjustments, and placing female staff in the training pipeline—while stressing discretion to protect candidates’ identities. Officials also noted that the SWCC community now includes a sailor who is transgender. Overall, the steps mark a milestone for Naval Special Warfare but do not guarantee when the first female operator will ultimately be produced.

A campaign in South Korea led by the Society for Textbook Revise (STR) has succeeded in persuading the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (MEST) and several publishers to remove specific examples of evolution from high-school textbooks — notably the evolution of the horse and examples tied to Archaeopteryx. STR, an offshoot of the Korea Association for Creation Research (KACR), frames its goal as deleting the “error” of evolution to “correct” students’ worldviews; it says its membership includes some biology professors and high-school science teachers. The group is also pushing to eliminate material on human evolution and classic demonstrations such as finch-beak adaptation.

The move alarmed mainstream scientists, who say they were not consulted and warn that STR is using legitimate scientific debates (for example, revised interpretations of Archaeopteryx as one of many feathered dinosaurs rather than a direct ancestor of modern birds) as a tactic to undermine evolution teaching. Creation science — the effort to provide evidence supporting the Genesis creation account — has been growing in visibility in South Korea, aided by activities such as a widely attended KACR exhibition and even campus creationist displays at major institutes.

Surveys show substantial skepticism about evolution in South Korea: roughly one-third of respondents in a 2009 documentary’s survey rejected evolution for reasons including perceived lack of evidence, religious conflict, or lack of understanding. Similar proportions reject evolution in the United States. Contributing factors include strong religious — particularly Christian — influence and limited capacity in evolutionary biology education: only a handful (about 5–10) of evolutionary scientists teach the subject at South Korean universities. Many biology teachers also expressed doubts about evolution in trainee-teacher surveys.

Some scientists fear that engaging creationists could lend them undue legitimacy, but others argue silence has failed. In response, evolutionary scientists and sympathetic theologians led by Dayk Jang of Seoul National University are organizing to counter STR’s campaign and to improve evolution education in classrooms and public discourse.

Police in Tennessee are investigating whether an attempted attack on a woman in Centerville is related to the April 13 disappearance of 20-year-old nursing student Holly Bobo from her Parsons home. Heather Sullivan, 31, says a "tall, skinny man" grabbed her arm around 5:30 a.m. in January as she was getting out of her car, causing her to drop a lamp; her boyfriend’s arrival frightened the man away. Bobo, a cousin of country singer Whitney Duncan, was allegedly taken from her Parsons home about 7:30 a.m. by a man in camouflage; both homes are near wooded areas. Tennessee Bureau of Investigation director Mark Gwyn says investigators are considering all possibilities. An $80,000 reward (including $50,000 from the state) has been offered. Hundreds of residents have searched nearby woods; a blood sample found was tested but results have not been released. Bobo’s family continues to appeal for her return.

Nielsen’s “Women of Tomorrow” study of nearly 6,500 women in 21 developed and emerging countries (Feb–Apr 2011) found high levels of stress worldwide, with women in emerging markets notably more time-pressed. Top findings:

- Stress levels by country (highest to lower): India 87%, Mexico 74%, Russia 69%, Brazil 67%, Spain 66%, France 65%, South Africa 64%, Italy 64%, Nigeria 58%, Turkey 56%, U.K. 55%, U.S. 53%, Japan 52%, Canada 52%, Australia 52%, China 51%, Germany 47%, Thailand 45%, South Korea 45%, Malaysia 44%, Sweden 44%.
- Indian women were the most stressed and felt they had the least time to relax (82%). Despite this, they were most likely to spend disposable income on themselves—96% on clothes, 77% on health/beauty, 44% on home electronics.
- Spending patterns differ by market: women in emerging economies tend to spend extra cash on clothes, health/beauty, groceries and children’s education; women in developed markets prioritize vacations, savings and debt repayment.
- Women globally are achieving higher education and workforce participation, increasing their financial influence but also their stress as they juggle multiple roles; in emerging markets traditional social expectations often lag behind workplace changes, intensifying pressure.
- Women in emerging markets are more optimistic about prospects for their daughters (e.g., ~80% expect greater financial stability and 83% more education) than women in developed markets.
- Social media and mobile tech are central: women use social networking more than men (talk 28% more, text 14% more monthly), follow brands online, and view digital devices positively. TV remains the top source for learning about new products in 17 of 21 countries, but word-of-mouth is highly trusted (70%+ in developed, 80%+ in emerging markets).
- Implication for marketers: engage women with socially relevant, integrated strategies that respect their time pressures and trusted channels.

Overall, the report highlights growing female consumer power and optimism—especially in emerging markets—paired with significant time-related stress that shapes spending and media habits.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev’s body was transferred from the Boston medical examiner to a Worcester funeral home after sitting unclaimed for almost two weeks. His relatives have demanded a second independent autopsy; his death certificate (obtained by CNN) lists the cause as gunshot wounds and blunt trauma, notes he was shot by police and run over/dragged by a car, and classifies the manner as homicide/DOA. Funeral director Peter Stefan of Graham Putnam & Mahoney is handling the remains and says his staff can perform Muslim funeral rites, but no burial plot or service date has been set. Several cemeteries in Massachusetts, Connecticut and New Jersey declined to accept the body, citing fear of reprisals; Stefan said burials should proceed regardless and is prepared for protests and to request government help if no plot is found.

Background from the investigation: Tamerlan and his younger brother Dzhokhar are accused of the Boston Marathon bombings that killed three and wounded more than 260. Tamerlan died April 19 after a shootout and subsequent events in which police say the brothers killed a campus officer, carjacked an SUV and used explosives against pursuing officers. Dzhokhar, 19, is hospitalized and detained on federal charges including use of a weapon of mass destruction; investigators found explosive residue in Tamerlan’s Cambridge apartment and believe the brothers built the devices there. Officials say the Marathon may not have been the original target and are reviewing whether agencies could have done more to prevent the attack. Three friends of Dzhokhar have been charged with helping dispose of potential evidence from his dorm room. Authorities currently believe the brothers acted alone but are probing possible outside influence or assistance.

Thousands participated in a daylong Occupy Oakland general strike that began peacefully Wednesday and culminated in chaotic clashes late Wednesday night after protesters occupied a vacant building near 16th and Telegraph and police moved in.

Morning–afternoon: Large, mostly peaceful demonstrations
- Demonstrations began at Frank H. Ogawa Plaza with several rallies and marches through downtown. Estimates ranged from several thousand to about 7,000 at peak.
- Protesters targeted banks, corporate offices and city institutions. Many downtown businesses closed or limited services; union groups provided food and support.
- Small-scale vandalism occurred at times (notably a window-smashing and paint attack at a Whole Foods and graffiti at other sites), but the broad crowd largely remained nonviolent. Organizers and “peace teams” repeatedly urged restraint.
- A significant march to the Port of Oakland successfully disrupted port operations by late afternoon. Protesters blocked entrances, stopped trucks, and prevented some workers from entering; port officials said maritime operations were effectively shut down until safe to resume.
- There were confrontations with drivers: a silver Mercedes struck two protesters at 11th & Broadway; they were injured and taken to hospital. Reports that one victim died were false.
- City leaders (Mayor Quan, Interim Police Chief Howard Jordan, city administrators) largely maintained a minimal, background police presence early in the day and urged peaceful protest while preparing mutual-aid options. The city set up an emergency operations center and coordinated briefings.

Evening–early morning: escalation and police action
- Around 10:30–11:30 p.m., roughly 100–300 protesters entered and occupied the foreclosed Traveler’s Aid building near 16th & Telegraph, posted fliers declaring it reclaimed for community use, and hung banners.
- Police massed in riot gear nearby, and a large crowd gathered. Barricades were built and set on fire on Broadway/16th; reports of fireworks, M‑80s, flash-bangs and tear gas followed. Police issued dispersal orders.
- Interim Chief Jordan said officers reclaimed the Traveler’s Aid building and that 30–40 people were arrested overall; he reported some identified agitators among the crowd and blamed a small group for vandalism. Protesters and medics reported at least one person wounded — possibly struck by a rubber bullet — who was taken to an ambulance.
- By early Thursday morning the crowd thinned; police lines partially dispersed and the scene calmed. Volunteer medics and ambulance crews treated injured demonstrators; organizers and many protesters emphasized nonviolence and cleanup.

Context and reactions
- The strike was organized in response to economic inequality, cuts to services, and recent police actions (including a previous clearing of the plaza in which Iraq War vet Scott Olsen was seriously injured). Speakers such as Angela Davis and local activists participated.
- City officials praised much of the day’s peaceful participation but warned against fires, vandalism and assaults on officers; they planned to identify those they said instigated violence.
- The action drew broad local support, including some unions and community groups, while a small minority engaged in property damage that critics feared would overshadow the protest’s goals.

Overall: A large, largely peaceful general strike that succeeded in shutting down parts of Oakland—including the Port—during the day, but ended with late-night confrontations after an occupied building and subsequent police intervention led to injuries, arrests, and fires.

A convicted murderer who escaped a Michigan prison Sunday was captured in Indiana Monday evening after a roughly 24-hour flight that included multiple car thefts and a carjacking.

- Suspect and capture: Michael David Elliot, 40, serving five life sentences for four 1993 murders (and additional terms for arson, robbery and firearm use), escaped from the Ionia Correctional Facility around 6–7 p.m. Sunday. He was arrested Monday evening in Kankakee Township, LaPorte County, Ind., after allegedly stealing four vehicles during his run. Deputies used Stop Sticks; his car lost control and slid into a snowbank, and deputies pulled him from the vehicle without injury. He was arraigned in Indiana on auto-theft and resisting charges and is being held without bond.

- Escape and movements: Corrections staff did not notice the escape until a 9 p.m. count. Elliot reportedly left through the facility sally port, went through a hole in the perimeter fencing, then walked into Ionia, carjacked a woman at knifepoint (box cutter) and forced her to drive more than 100 miles toward Elkhart County, Ind. The victim escaped at a gas station by locking herself in a bathroom and calling 911; Elliot fled in her Jeep Liberty, which was later found in Shipshewana, Ind. Authorities say Elliot stole additional vehicles in northern Indiana and may have been in several areas during the manhunt.

- Prison and investigation details: Elliot was serving sentences for the Aug. 8, 1993 killings of four people in Midland County. He has maintained his innocence and previously sought release based on new evidence, which was denied. Michigan officials, including Gov. Rick Snyder, praised law enforcement for the capture and promised a thorough review of how the escape occurred. Corrections officials noted Elliot was seen in a white kitchen uniform during the escape—despite not being assigned to the kitchen—which may have helped him avoid detection on cameras.

- Public safety response: The escape prompted widespread searches across Michigan and northern Indiana, school lockdowns in some areas, and alerts warning the public he should be considered dangerous. Local and federal agencies, including the U.S. Marshals Service, assisted in the response.

The document reports on the New Hampshire primary outcomes and reactions across both parties.

Republican side
- Donald Trump won the New Hampshire GOP primary, leading with about 34% of the vote (with 76% reported). In his victory speech in Manchester he returned to populist themes — promising to rebuild the military, protect the Second Amendment, be a jobs president, and build a border wall — and attacked Bernie Sanders, accusing him of wanting to "give away our country." Trump also touted his self-funding and independence from lobbyists.
- John Kasich finished a strong second (about 16%), positioning himself as a moderate, compassionate alternative to the negative tone of the campaign. He emphasized a positive, heart-driven leadership style, vowed to continue campaigning in South Carolina, and criticized Democrats while avoiding heavy attacks on GOP rivals.

Democratic side
- Bernie Sanders scored a decisive victory over Hillary Clinton in New Hampshire, with roughly 60% to Clinton’s 38% (with 93% of precincts reported). He framed the win as a rejection of establishment politics and a mandate for sweeping change, celebrated high turnout and grassroots support, and urged small donations nationwide.
- Sanders’ team hailed the margin as historically large for a contested Democratic primary and warned tougher attacks were likely ahead.
- Hillary Clinton conceded and called for regrouping. Her campaign stressed that the nomination would likely be decided in March, pointed to Clinton’s strengths with minority voters and data-driven operation, and vowed to push forward and adapt messaging (including on Wall Street and foreign policy). Clinton emphasized resilience and promised to fight for votes nationwide.

Context and tensions
- The Democratic race had become bitter in the final week, with clashes over Clinton’s paid speeches and heated exchanges between surrogates and supporters on both sides (including debates about gender and generational divides).
- Clinton’s campaign released a memo outlining a path forward focused on upcoming diverse primary states and Super Tuesday where they expect to regain ground.

Overall, the results strengthened Trump’s front-runner status on the GOP side, elevated Kasich as a notable second-place moderate, and marked a major boost for Sanders on the Democratic side while forcing Clinton to recalibrate her strategy for the coming contests.

President Trump on Tuesday sharply attacked Deborah Ramirez, the second woman to accuse Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh of sexual misconduct, calling the allegations a “con game” by Democrats and questioning Ramirez’s memory and credibility after she told The New Yorker that a drunken Kavanaugh exposed himself to her at a Yale dorm party. Trump dismissed her account as uncertain and emphasized Republicans’ determination to move the confirmation forward.

Republicans largely rallied behind Kavanaugh amid mounting pressure from conservatives to secure his confirmation before the Supreme Court’s new term. Senate Judiciary Committee leaders scheduled a committee vote for Friday morning and signaled a full Senate vote could follow the next week. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell defended the nominee and predicted confirmation, while the White House said withdrawal was not under consideration.

To avoid the optics of an all-male GOP panel questioning an accuser, committee Republicans hired Arizona sex-crimes prosecutor Rachel Mitchell to question Christine Blasey Ford and Kavanaugh at Thursday’s public hearing. Democrats objected to the process in other ways, pressed for an FBI background investigation, and planned to question both witnesses themselves. Kavanaugh has denied both Ford’s allegation that he assaulted her in high school and Ramirez’s account.

Several GOP senators remained undecided and urged Ramirez to provide sworn testimony and evidence; some said an FBI probe would be useful. Meanwhile, attorney Michael Avenatti said he represents a third woman who may come forward soon with allegations from Kavanaugh’s high school years. The confirmation fight intensified both on Capitol Hill and in the public sphere, with partisan accusations exchanged between Senate leaders.

The NTSB released a preliminary report on the August 9 small-plane crash in East Haven, Conn., that killed four people: pilot William Henningsgaard, his 17-year-old son Maxwell, and two children from a struck home, 13-year-old Sade Brantley and 1-year-old Madisyn Mitchell. The twin‑engine aircraft had departed Teterboro around 10:49 a.m. and was on approach to Tweed‑New Haven Airport (HVN).

Radio transcripts show that about two minutes before impact the pilot acknowledged being in visual contact and was instructed to land on runway 20. At 11:20:55 a.m. the tower made a truncated call to the airplane’s call sign “622,” and no further communications were received. Radar’s last target placed the aircraft 0.7 miles north of the runway at about 800 ft.

Multiple witnesses reported the airplane was inverted and descending nose‑first at high speed just before the crash. One student pilot on I‑95 said he saw the airplane at the end of a right roll, inverted and heading toward the ground; a nearby resident described the airplane descending right‑side down at a steep angle into two homes on Charter Oak Avenue. The aircraft struck two houses, destroying much of the front fuselage and cockpit, and wreckage was largely consumed by fire. Weather at the time included winds from 170° at 12 knots gusting to 19, visibility 9 miles, and an overcast ceiling at 900 ft.

Environmental cleanup at the site is ongoing and the homes will be demolished when complete. Funeral services for the victims have been held, and community fundraisers have been organized. The NTSB posted the full preliminary report on its website.

Comedian Jimmy Kimmel criticized Sen. Bill Cassidy and the GOP’s Graham-Cassidy bill in a widely watched monologue, arguing the proposal would break Cassidy’s promises to protect people with pre-existing conditions and that it would lead to large coverage losses. Kimmel, whose infant son has a congenital heart defect, accused Cassidy of lying after the senator had earlier proposed a “Jimmy Kimmel test” — that reforms should protect kids like Kimmel’s — and appeared on Kimmel’s show in May. Cassidy, Lindsey Graham and President Trump defended the bill, saying it preserves protections and expands coverage; Graham called Kimmel’s attacks “garbage.”  

Health-policy experts, advocacy groups and analysts largely backed Kimmel’s critique, saying Graham-Cassidy’s state waivers, deep Medicaid cuts and block-grant–style funding would create wide variation in protections and could allow insurers to raise premiums or limit coverage for people with prior conditions. Critics warned the bill risks reducing coverage for millions and would force states to cut enrollment, benefits, or provider payments. Conservative voices offered mixed views: some argued state flexibility could expand coverage, while others said the bill’s consequences are uncertain and complex. The CBO said it could not yet score the bill before the legislative deadline.  

Commentary noted the tension between celebrity advocacy and policy expertise: supporters applauded Kimmel’s emotional, high-profile intervention; critics argued he oversimplified complexities and that policy debates require technical understanding. Overall, the news coverage framed Kimmel as a prominent public critic whose claims about the bill’s impacts were echoed by many analysts, even as defenders insisted the legislation could protect those with pre-existing conditions if implemented by states.

A federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging former University of Illinois graduate student Brendt Christensen, 28, with kidnapping resulting in the death of 26-year-old visiting scholar Yingying Zhang, whose body has not been found. The four-page indictment includes a special finding that the offense was “especially heinous, cruel or depraved,” involved torture or serious physical abuse, and was committed after substantial planning and premeditation. It also alleges use of a cellphone and vehicle in interstate commerce and adds two counts of making false statements to FBI agents.

If convicted on the aggravated kidnapping count, Christensen could face the death penalty (a decision on seeking capital punishment will be made later by the U.S. Attorney General); if the death penalty is not sought, the conviction would carry mandatory life without parole. Christensen, held without bond in Macon County jail, is tentatively scheduled for trial Feb. 27 before U.S. District Judge Colin Bruce. His attorney declined comment.

Prosecutors say Zhang disappeared June 9 while walking to a bus stop or an apartment lease signing; surveillance shows her speaking with a driver and entering the front passenger seat. Investigators identified Christensen’s Saturn Astra as the vehicle, found evidence its passenger area had been cleaned, and discovered his internet visits to a sadomasochism site with kidnapping fantasies. Audio and other surveillance allegedly captured Christensen describing an “ideal victim,” admitting to the kidnapping, and recounting Zhang fighting him; authorities have not disclosed the source of those recordings. Zhang’s family remains in the Urbana area awaiting further developments.

The Director of National Intelligence’s office said the Sept. 11 attack on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya, that killed U.S. Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans was “deliberate and organized.” That public revision reflects evolving intelligence gathered in the investigation and is the most direct U.S. assessment to date that extremists carried out a coordinated terrorist strike, with some participants linked to or sympathetic to al‑Qaeda affiliates in North Africa. 

The DNI statement emphasized that initial reports — which suggested the violence began spontaneously amid protests over an anti‑Islam video that also touched off demonstrations in Cairo — were preliminary and revised as more information (intercepts, informants, photos, videos) emerged. Officials say it remains unclear whether any single group exercised overall command or whether the attack was planned well in advance; current consensus is that the assault was highly organized but may have been planned “on the fly” during the day’s unrest, possibly by local militias such as Ansar al‑Shariah with some ties to al‑Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb.

The changing public characterizations have generated sharp political controversy. Republicans have accused the Obama administration of downplaying terrorist involvement to avoid exposing security failures or political damage; some lawmakers have demanded more information and briefings. The White House says its statements tracked evolving intelligence and that officials — including President Obama in an early remark calling it an act of terror — did not intentionally mislead. U.S. investigative efforts have increased, with CIA personnel and federal agents assisting despite challenges at a looted crime scene; a State Department review led by Tom Pickering is also underway.

Sofia Vergara and Joe Manganiello are engaged, according to multiple outlets. Manganiello proposed on Christmas Day while the couple and their families were vacationing in Hawaii; Vergara has been seen wearing a large diamond ring. The pair went public as a couple in June after being introduced in May at the White House Correspondents Dinner and have had a fast-moving romance. They celebrated Manganiello’s 38th birthday during the trip, and spent the following week with family at the St. Regis Princeville Resort in Kauai marking the engagement. Vergara’s ex-fiancé Nick Loeb expressed support, saying she deserves happiness. Manganiello has previously praised Vergara publicly, calling her his “dream girl.”

U.S. Senator Barbara Boxer publicly urged San Diego Mayor Bob Filner to resign in an open, personal letter, saying he betrayed women and San Diegans and should get long-term help. Her call came as Filner — facing accusations from about 14 women of unwanted sexual advances, inappropriate comments, kissing and touching, and a civil sexual-harassment suit from former communications director Irene McCormack Jackson — left an intensive behavioral-modification therapy program earlier than planned and will continue outpatient treatment. All nine San Diego City Council members, made unanimous when Councilwomen Marti Emerald and Myrtle Cole joined calls for his resignation, have urged him to step down, citing new allegations including advances toward two women who were military sexual-assault survivors at a conference meant to help them. Local and state investigators are interviewing alleged victims, and the mayor’s office changed the locks on his City Hall office while he is away. Filner’s lawyers say he will take personal time and return to City Hall on Aug. 19.

Actress Skye McCole Bartusiak, 21, was found dead Saturday at her home in Houston; the cause of death has not been determined. Her mother said Bartusiak—who had a history of epileptic seizures—had suffered seizures in recent days and they believe she may have choked after a seizure while alone; paramedics were unable to revive her. Her boyfriend discovered her sitting up in the garage apartment beside her parents’ home; her mother performed CPR before emergency crews arrived.

A Texas native, Bartusiak began acting at age 6. Her notable film roles included The Cider House Rules (1999), playing the young daughter of Mel Gibson’s character in The Patriot (2000), and a role opposite Michael Douglas in Don’t Say a Word (2001). She appeared on TV series such as 24, Lost and House M.D., and later produced and starred in short films; her last feature role was the lead in the 2012 thriller Sick Boy. Her mother said Bartusiak had been preparing to produce and direct her first feature and remembered her life and career fondly.

Johnny Strange, a 23-year-old adventurer from Malibu known for extreme stunts and for becoming the youngest person to complete the Seven Summits at 17, died Thursday in a wingsuit BASE-jumping accident in the Swiss Alps. Swiss police said he crashed seconds after launching from Mt. Gitschen around noon; authorities are investigating and noted strong winds had been reported that day. Strange had recently called into KROQ’s Kevin & Bean from Switzerland to describe filming a dangerous wingsuit proximity video, then posted footage showing him flying over a mountainside and deploying a parachute; that video was his last YouTube upload. He had publicly acknowledged the risks of wingsuit BASE jumping and mourned other jumpers killed doing similar stunts, including Dean Potter. Friends and acquaintances, including model Gigi Hadid, remembered his adventurous spirit and prolific record of risky exploits. TMZ and family sources confirmed the death.

Donald Trump will moderate a Newsmax-hosted presidential debate in Des Moines on Dec. 27, to be broadcast on Ion Television, Newsmax CEO Christopher Ruddy confirmed. Newsmax billed Trump as “a truly great American” in invitations sent to campaigns; it’s unclear which, if any, candidates have accepted. The event comes a week before the Iowa caucuses and will not be limited to a single topic.

The arrangement highlights Trump’s unusual influence with segments of the conservative base—especially the Tea Party—despite controversies around his behavior and past flirtations with running for president.
