Candidates have courted him this year (some meeting privately), and many may feel compelled to appear given his media pull and willingness to criticize opponents. Newsmax itself has strong reach into conservative audiences, second in monthly web traffic only to Fox News among like-minded sites.

The profile notes that Trump’s role in the primary has grown unexpectedly prominent: other GOP hopefuls have echoed elements of his message and sought his endorsement. Whether his presidential interest is earnest or publicity-driven, his celebrity and ability to command attention make his participation a notable, spectacle-like moment in the 2012 primary season.

Mexican president Enrique Peña Nieto publicly reaffirmed that Mexico “will not pay for any wall” after US president Donald Trump signed executive orders including one to begin construction of a border barrier. In a short televised statement Peña Nieto said he “regrets and rejects” the US decision but also emphasized Mexico’s willingness to maintain friendly ties and negotiate with the US. He left undecided a planned 31 January meeting with Trump, saying the trip would depend on evaluations by officials; aides said the visit was being considered but not cancelled, which prompted criticism at home.

Peña Nieto faces heavy domestic pressure to call off the trip and stronger criticism for lacking a decisive response to Trump’s confrontational agenda. Voices from across Mexico’s political spectrum urged cancellation as a dignified stance; former president Vicente Fox and others publicly condemned Trump. Analysts note Peña Nieto’s options are limited: outright paying for the wall would provoke domestic outrage, while refusing could worsen relations with an administration seen as unusually hostile. His low approval rating (around 12%) further weakens his ability to rally a united national response.

Trump’s executive order orders “immediate construction” of a physical wall and gives DHS six months to plan how to stop “all unlawful entries,” though building a continuous wall along the nearly 2,000-mile border is costly (estimates $12–38 billion plus maintenance) and practically difficult. The order also signals expanded deportations, larger detention capacity, and sanctions on sanctuary cities. Some initial funding could come from existing federal budgets, but large-scale construction would require more congressional appropriations. Administration aides have floated mechanisms—like taxing remittances or using NAFTA leverage—to shift costs, ideas Mexican officials reject.

Experts and officials note that barriers are only one piece of border security and that technology, personnel, and other resources are often more effective. Deportation priorities were broadened under Trump to allow immediate removal of many more unauthorized migrants, increasing the number vulnerable to expedited deportation and detention. The orders also push for expanded detention and faster processing of cases, raising concerns from advocates about conditions and legal access for detainees.

Mexico is simultaneously trying to protect key economic ties—NAFTA supports roughly $500 billion in trade—while exploring diversifying partnerships in the hemisphere. Mexican ministers met with Trump officials the same day as the orders; Mexico has said it would seek negotiations that address cross-border crime, gun trafficking, and migration cooperation but has warned it will not accept paying for the wall. The standoff leaves Mexico balancing domestic political pressures, economic interdependence with the US, and limited leverage in confronting the new US administration.

Lady Gaga's album Born This Way debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 1,108,000 copies sold in its first week in North America (reported as about 1.11 million), per Nielsen SoundScan. It is only the 17th album to sell a million in a week since SoundScan began in 1991, the biggest weekly total since 50 Cent’s The Massacre (1.141 million in 2005), and the largest digital-week ever: 662,000 downloads (about 60% of the total). The sales surge was driven largely by Amazon’s promotional 99-cent digital sale on May 23 and again May 26, which is estimated to have moved roughly 440,000 downloads; Amazon absorbed the wholesale cost and temporarily encountered distribution delays. Born This Way is Gaga’s first No. 1 album (previous releases had peaked lower), and Gaga is only the fifth woman to post a million-plus week. Industry context notes million-plus weeks are rare in the SoundScan era and have become less common as sales decline; the last such week before Gaga was Taylor Swift’s Speak Now in 2010.

Federal agents arrested 29-year-old Ross William Ulbricht at San Francisco’s Glen Park Branch Library, accusing him of operating Silk Road, a large anonymous online drug marketplace run through the Tor network that used Bitcoin for payments. Authorities say Ulbricht operated under the alias “Dread Pirate Roberts” and oversaw a sprawling “black-market bazaar” that from 2011–2013 facilitated hundreds of kilograms of illegal drugs, generated roughly $1.2–$1.6 billion in sales and about $80 million in commissions, and had hundreds of thousands of registered users and over a million transactions.

The FBI’s case rests on more than 100 undercover buys and server evidence obtained from foreign law enforcement; agents also tracked online postings and other digital traces linking Ulbricht to early forum promotions of Silk Road under the username “altoid” and to administrator accounts. Investigators say he ran the operation from San Francisco, paid administrators, and concealed activity via Tor and Bitcoin.

The indictment accuses Ulbricht of narcotics trafficking, money laundering and soliciting murders-for-hire to protect the site. Prosecutors allege two separate murder-for-hire plots: one in which Ulbricht paid an undercover agent $80,000 to torture and kill a Silk Road employee accused of stealing Bitcoins, and another in which he allegedly paid $150,000 to have a user who threatened to expose thousands of users killed; in both cases the purported victims were later shown in staged photos, and there is no confirmed homicide. Authorities say Ulbricht told associates he was creating an “economic simulation” to demonstrate a world without institutional force, reflecting his libertarian views.

Ulbricht was remanded pending further hearings; his attorney declined comment. The takedown prompted political praise and a plunge in Bitcoin’s value after news of the arrest. Friends and some acquaintances have expressed disbelief, noting his academic background in physics and engineering and previous public libertarian activism.

Researchers analyzed 183 hours of Oakland Police Department body-worn camera transcripts from 981 routine traffic stops (36,738 officer utterances) to measure how respectfully officers speak to white versus Black community members. Using a three-part approach, they first showed human raters could reliably infer respect-related qualities (respect, politeness, friendliness, formality, impartiality) from short transcribed utterances and that language directed at Black drivers was judged less respectful. They then built computational-linguistic models, trained on those human ratings, that predict Respect and Formality from measurable language features (e.g., apologies, gratitude, safety-oriented phrases increase Respect; informal address, disfluencies, negative wording decrease it). Applied to the full corpus, the models found a consistent racial disparity: officers’ language scored higher in Respect toward white drivers than toward Black drivers even after controlling for officer race, driver age/gender, stop outcome (warning/citation/arrest), searches, offense severity, location, and neighborhood crime/business metrics. Formality did not differ by race. The disparity was widespread across many officers rather than driven by a few outliers, and the gap in Respect grew over the course of stops because Respect increased more quickly in interactions with white drivers. The study demonstrates body-camera footage can be a rich source of large-scale, objective data about everyday police–community interactions, suggests linguistic markers that could inform training, and calls for broader use of such methods while noting privacy and scale challenges. The authors released their code and emphasize the findings do not by themselves prove intent or bias but reveal systematic differences in treatment with implications for procedural justice and public trust.

This document recounts the scandalous life and notorious 1859 murder trial of Congressman Daniel E. Sickles, who shot and killed Philip Barton Key—son of the author of “The Star-Spangled Banner” and Washington’s U.S. attorney—after discovering Key’s yearlong affair with Sickles’s much younger wife, Teresa.

Key facts of the murder and investigation
- Sickles received an anonymous letter detailing the affair and investigated; witnesses confirmed meetings between Key and Teresa.
- On February 27, 1859, Sickles confronted Key in Lafayette Square, shot him multiple times in public, then confessed at the attorney general’s office. He retrieved Teresa’s wedding ring and her diamond earrings before surrendering.
- The shooting was highly public and sensational, occurring in sight of the White House and lending itself to broad press coverage.

The trial and legal significance
- Sickles assembled a high-profile defense team and became the central, theatrical figure of the trial. Public sentiment initially sided with him, seeing the killing as a “natural revenge” for adultery.
- Defense strategy: argued that Sickles acted in a “heat of passion” and was temporarily insane—an early, successful use of the insanity/temporary insanity defense in U.S. murder law. Attorneys invoked moral, literary, and religious arguments to justify the killing as an understandable, even justifiable, response to dishonor.
- Prosecution emphasized premeditation: Sickles had planned revenge, carried multiple pistols, discussed his intentions beforehand, and recruited witnesses.
- Emotional testimony and Sickles’s courtroom performance swayed the jury; after twenty days of arguments, they acquitted him in under an hour.

Immediate and long-term consequences
- Public approbation was fleeting. The initial adulation turned to ostracism; Sickles and Teresa became social pariahs. Teresa later died of tuberculosis; Sickles reportedly resumed serial affairs.
- Legally, Sickles’s verdict popularized the insanity defense in America and inspired satire and critique (notably by Mark Twain). Over time, controversies about the defense led to reforms; notably, the Insanity Defense Reform Act of 1984 shifted burdens of proof after the Hinckley verdict, and several states have narrowed or abolished the defense.

Broader biography and legacy
- The piece situates the murder within Sickles’s larger life of scandal and political ambition: early predatory sexual behavior, ties to Tammany Hall, flamboyant and often reckless public life, and repeated controversies.
- During the Civil War Sickles raised a brigade, rose to major general, lost a leg at Gettysburg (his amputated limb is preserved in a museum), and was later diplomat to Spain. His military career was mixed—bold but insubordinate—and his postwar life included triumphs and humiliations (financial losses, scandalous relationships, and alleged misuse of public funds).
- Biographical assessments (drawn from Keneally’s American Scoundrel and contemporary commentary) paint Sickles as charismatic, willful, and often immoral: a figure who generated both political success and personal ruin, and whose most infamous act reshaped American legal and cultural attitudes toward crime, passion, and responsibility.

The National Liberation Front of Corsica (FLNC), the island’s main armed separatist group, has announced it will abandon its decades-long armed campaign and begin demilitarization, saying it will shift to conventional, public political action. The FLNC’s unilateral communiqué—confirmed authentic by a journalist who has had contact with the group—declared no preconditions for the move and framed recent political gains as part of the reason for stepping back from clandestine violence.

The FLNC’s announcement ends nearly 40 years of low-intensity conflict that began with attacks in 1976 and included bombings, robberies, murders, and rocket strikes targeting French institutions on Corsica and the mainland. Notable incidents cited in the group’s history include more than 50 bomb explosions in one day in 1997 and a violent escalation after a senior French official’s 1998 killing. A faction had suspended military actions in 2003, but attacks continued intermittently.

The group pointed to recent legislative progress—such as a local assembly law restricting property purchases to residents of at least five years, aimed at curbing speculative second-home buying—as evidence that political channels can advance Corsican interests. FLNC members reportedly number more than 100; the island’s population is roughly 320,000. The announcement follows similar recent moves by other separatist groups in Europe (for example ETA), and signals a turn toward building “a true Corsican political power” through public politics rather than armed struggle.

Two 29-year-old Australian twin sisters carried out a suicide pact at the Family Shooting Center in Cherry Creek State Park near Denver, Colorado, investigators say. Surveillance footage and physical evidence indicate both sisters simultaneously put .22-caliber pistols to their heads after shooting targets for roughly 80–90 minutes; one died at the scene and the other survived and later told investigators what happened. The surviving twin, described as distraught, declined to explain their motive during a two-hour interview and is in stable condition at Swedish Medical Center. The sisters were traveling on cultural exchange visas and had been in Colorado about five weeks; one’s visa expired the day after the shooting. Authorities have not released names pending fingerprint confirmation by ICE; a search-warrant copy and relatives identified them as Candace and Kristin Hermeler. Investigators found no suicide note or obvious explanation in their hotel room. This incident is at least the seventh suicide at U.S. shooting ranges this year and the third at this facility since 2004.

Adele’s second album, 21, released yesterday, is a raw, bluesy breakup record inspired entirely by one painful relationship. The 22-year-old singer describes the collection as “cheap therapy,” drawn from candid, diary-like, sometimes drunken writing as she works through heartache. Songs such as “Someone Like You” and “Rolling in the Deep” showcase her powerful, emotive voice and frank lyrics — so honest some tracks may become too painful for her to perform in future. Adele hopes the album will help listeners heal as it has helped her, and says she’s also been exploring American musical styles like country and bluegrass as influences for her evolving career.

Kim Cattrall told Piers Morgan she was never friends with her Sex and the City co-stars — they were colleagues — and thinks that professional distance is healthy. The 61-year-old repeated that she did not make demands that killed a proposed third film, calling reports that she was a “diva” and asked for money or projects “ridiculous.” She said she had been saying “no” to a third installment for about a year and blamed negative press partly on Sarah Jessica Parker, saying Parker “could’ve been nicer” and that none of the cast reached out to check on her, calling the dynamic “toxic.”

Cattrall also revealed she considered IVF after marrying Mark Levinson in 1998 but decided against it because of the intense Sex and the City shooting schedule; she said she channels maternal instincts by mentoring younger actresses. Media reports and anonymous sources, however, have claimed Cattrall made “outrageous demands” that contributed to the film being canceled shortly before filming; Parker has said any possibility of a third movie is “over.” The full Morgan interview airs in the U.K. on Monday.

LulzSec announced it is disbanding after a 50-day run of high-profile hacks and released a large final data dump. In its farewell statement the group framed the operation as a planned “50 day cruise,” celebrated AntiSec goals, urged others to continue the movement, and posted links to its releases and torrent mirrors before shutting down hosting.

Overview of the final dump (initial pass):
- AOL: Highly technical network-engineering document (layer 4–7 switching best practices).
- AT&T: Large RAR containing many internal LTE-rollout items (memos, emails, presentations, reports).
- Battlefield Heroes: Text file with account details for ~550,000 users.
- Hackforums.net: CSV with about 200,000 user records.
- NATO-bookshop.org: ~220,000 user logins for a NATO online bookshop.
- US Navy: Image showing “Pablo Escobar AntiSec” inserted in a Navy salary-grade list (evidence of site defacement).
- Office networks: Text file listing internal IP addresses for companies including Disney, EMI and Universal.
- “Silly routers”: IPs for routers with default/weak passwords like “root” or “admin.”
- Private investigators: Supposed email login credentials.
- Random gaming forums: User login dumps (unspecified forums).
- FBI-related file: Output from an FBI URL (not further analyzed).

Context and questions raised:
- LulzSec had previously signaled longer-term intent, promised regular releases and teamed with Anonymous on “AntiSec,” so the abrupt retirement raises speculation: a genuine planned end, pressure from law enforcement, or a deception/decoy while members continue covertly.
- The group claimed responsibility for multiple high-profile intrusions (FBI, CIA, US Senate, Arizona DPS) and encouraged others to mirror its materials because it won’t renew hosting.

Takeaway: The group ceased public activity and posted a sizeable archive of stolen data spanning corporate, governmental and consumer targets. Further forensic analysis will be needed to validate and assess the full impact of the released material.

Sen. Rand Paul has asked Kentucky Senate GOP leaders to pursue legislation that would clarify state law so a candidate could appear on the ballot for both the U.S. Senate and the presidency in the same year. Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer confirmed he is considering a bill to resolve what Paul believes is an ambiguous—and potentially unconstitutional—statute that currently could bar simultaneous runs. Thayer said Paul raised the issue with the Senate Republican caucus after testifying on felon voting-rights legislation and that Thayer would decide whether to file the bill before the filing deadline.

The change would let Paul “hedge his bets” in 2016: seek the GOP presidential nomination while also running for Senate re-election. If he won both, he would vacate the Senate seat upon becoming president; if he lost the presidential race but won the Senate race, he would remain a senator. The proposal faces political obstacles: the Kentucky House, controlled by Democrats (and reportedly opposed by House Speaker Greg Stumbo), may block the measure, and intra-party dynamics—particularly around Sen. Mitch McConnell’s contested position—add complexity. Paul has not formally announced a presidential campaign.

A Tennessee teenager, 16-year-old Emily Gipson of Lebanon High School, posted a spoken-word anti-bullying video to YouTube on Jan. 22 that has drawn hundreds of thousands of views and widespread attention. Prompted by a classmate’s suicide, her free-verse piece criticizes student behavior and the school’s response to bullying—saying “smiles are fake and suicide prevention is something to laugh at”—and calls out administrators for dismissing complaints with lines like “kids will be kids.” The video contains no profanity or explicit calls for violence, but school officials suspended Gipson for two in-school days, saying she recorded the piece in a classroom without a teacher’s permission; principal Scott Walters also said the video hurt teachers’ feelings. Gipson and her grandfather dispute aspects of the school’s account but say they accept the punishment; Gipson has since posted a follow-up poem urging teens to speak up and says the episode revealed the issue is broader than her school.

Two men with nearly identical lives—Jeremy Lewis, 27, of Alabama, and Josh Potter, 25, of Georgia—suffered catastrophic, on-the-job amputations of their left arms yet received vastly different workers’ compensation outcomes because of where they were injured.

Facts and outcomes
- Both were married with two young children and worked in Southern industrial plants. Both received prostheses and faced major life disruptions.
- Jeremy Lewis (Alabama) lost his arm in 2006 at a poultry feed mill. After years of litigation and delay, Alabama’s scheduled-benefit system awarded him roughly $45,000 (lump sum), leaving him with about $33,500 after fees. The low award helped push his family into foreclosure and long-term financial hardship; he now relies on his wife’s wages and Social Security disability.
- Josh Potter (Georgia) lost his arm in 2007 in a factory accident just 15 miles from Lewis’s injury site. Georgia classifies severe amputations as “catastrophic” and pays far higher benefits: a larger lump amount plus two-thirds of wages until return to work or for life if the worker cannot return. Potter receives weekly benefits that have allowed his family to remain financially stable.

Broader issue: geographic lottery and the schedule of benefits
- The U.S. system lets each state set its own workers’ compensation rules and benefit “schedules” that assign dollar values or weeks of pay to lost body parts. There are no federal minimums, so identical injuries produce widely different awards across state lines (e.g., value of a lost arm ranges from ~$48,840 in Alabama to $439,858 in Illinois).
- Schedules often result from decades-old political deals rather than current medical or economic analysis; some states have not indexed amounts for inflation (Alabama’s $220 weekly cap dates to 1985).
- The “permanent partial disability” category—meant to compensate for lasting impairment and future lost earnings—is especially controversial and inconsistent. Studies show these benefits typically fall far short of replacing lost earnings long-term.
- Courts in some states, including Alabama, have limited judges’ ability to consider factors like age, education, or occupation when awarding more than schedule amounts. As a result, workers with the same physical loss but different return-to-work prospects receive the same meager scheduled payout.

Policy and politics
- Over the past decade many states have reduced workers’ comp benefits under pressure from employers and insurers seeking lower costs; employers are paying the lowest workers’ comp rates since the 1970s.
- Critics argue these rollbacks shift costs to injured workers, families, and taxpayers. Even some defense lawyers and judges in Alabama call the state’s schedule inadequate and unfair.
- Employers counter that raising one benefit without broader reform would hurt competitiveness, and some propose commissions to negotiate balanced changes. Advocates argue injured workers should not be forced to give up protections elsewhere to improve the most obviously unfair payouts.

Human consequences
- The article contrasts Lewis’s loss of home and financial security with Potter’s relative stability to show how state law can determine whether a life-altering workplace injury leads to poverty or survivable hardship.
- Anecdotes illustrate the dehumanizing arithmetic of valuing body parts and the arbitrary outcomes that result from state-by-state variation.

Conclusion
- The cases of Lewis and Potter demonstrate a “geographic lottery” in U.S. workers’ compensation: two identical catastrophic injuries kilometers apart can produce dramatically different life trajectories because state laws differ widely, are often outdated, and in many places have been narrowed in recent years—leaving many injured workers undercompensated and vulnerable.

Employees at a Wells Fargo branch in the San Fernando Valley allegedly opened premium checking and other accounts for Latino immigrants and small-business customers without proper consent, according to former employee Siham El-Dahan and customer Frank Ahn. The promoted premium accounts could be opened with $50 and enabled free cross‑border transfers, but carried a $30 monthly fee if the customer did not place $25,000 in Wells Fargo deposits within three months. 

El‑Dahan, a business banker with more than 20 years’ industry experience who joined Wells in May 2013 and was fired two weeks ago, says she repeatedly raised concerns with HR beginning in September about managers playing favorites, denying legally required breaks, and pressuring staff with sales quotas. She and other employees began opening bogus accounts for customers "on a daily basis," she said. After her complaints — including an emailed letter to bank directors and a signed note to CEO John Stumpf — she believes she was retaliated against; the bank cited a customer loan default as the reason for her termination, which she disputes.

Customer Frank Ahn described being repeatedly enrolled in unwanted accounts and a credit card over several years despite protests and cancellations; improper fees were largely reversed but some remained and account entanglements prevented him from switching banks. Wells Fargo declined to comment on the allegations.

A marine engineer from Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, says his life and career have been derailed by his name—Saddam Hussain—given by his grandfather with good intentions. After graduating from Noorul Islam University in 2014 (ranked second in his class), he has been repeatedly rejected—about 40 times—by multinational shipping companies, which told him his name raises security and immigration concerns for crews who travel internationally. 

To overcome the problem he legally changed his name to Sajid and updated identity documents (passport, voter ID, driving licence), but employers still require educational certificates in the new name. His university insists it cannot change his degree without updated Class 10 and 12 certificates; the CBSE has not yet acted. He has petitioned the Jharkhand high court to direct the CBSE to amend his school records; a hearing was set for May 5. Meanwhile he remains unemployed while classmates have found jobs.

The article notes this is not an isolated issue: other people named Saddam have faced prejudice, suspicion or even violence because of association with the former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein, who was executed in 2006. The piece highlights bureaucratic hurdles to changing names on academic records and the real-world consequences a controversial namesake can bring.

Emmis Digital used a social-media–driven competition called the "Intern Games" to fill an unpaid summer internship at its Chicago office. More than 25 students applied, 10 were interviewed and three finalists—Jake Bouvy (marketing, Indiana University), Kelsey Halverson (journalism, Iowa State) and Katie—were pitted against each other for two weeks. Each finalist rallied friends and followers under hashtags (#TeamJake, #TeamKelsey, #TeamKatie), posting videos, photos and updates to drive traffic and likes for Emmis sites. Katie was eliminated mid-contest; Halverson ultimately generated the most measurable social impact, while Bouvy impressed with creative technical work. Rather than pick one, Emmis hired both Halverson and Bouvy (they receive college credit). The stunt highlights how digital-era hiring favors social-media savvy and real-world experience over traditional resumes, and it comes amid broader scrutiny and decline in unpaid internships nationally.

Summary:

Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, a Boeing 777 carrying 239 people from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing, vanished early Saturday about an hour after takeoff. As of more than two days into the search, multinational teams (roughly 9–10 countries, dozens of ships and aircraft) have found no confirmed wreckage or emergency signals. Search areas have expanded from the Gulf of Thailand/South China Sea toward the Andaman Sea after radar suggested a possible turnback; authorities say the search area now spans hundreds of miles and grows each day.

Key investigative developments and leads:
- Two passengers boarded using passports reported stolen in Thailand (one Italian, one Austrian). CCTV images and thumbprints have been shared with international agencies; the FBI and Interpol are checking biometrics and records. U.S. officials say the stolen-passport pattern resembles human-smuggling activity and may be unrelated to the disappearance, but terrorism has not been ruled out.
- Ticket-purchase leads link the two to a Thai booking agent and a man who bought their tickets, but authorities caution these leads remain unconfirmed.
- Five checked-in passengers did not board; their luggage was removed.
- Several reported debris sightings and an oil slick have been investigated and disproven (oil traced to a ship; a reported life raft was a cable-reel cap; reported door/tail sightings unverified).

Official stance and concerns:
- Malaysian aviation authorities say all possibilities (mechanical failure, hijacking, terrorism, pilot action, etc.) remain under consideration; they emphasize there is no distress call and that the disappearance is “unprecedented” and puzzling.
- Family members have been told to prepare for the worst; many relatives—particularly the large number of Chinese passengers’ families—are frustrated and demanding answers and faster action. China urged Malaysia to accelerate search and rescue efforts.

Search challenges and outlook:
- Ocean search and recovery are difficult and time-sensitive; experts warn that with each day the search area widens and chances of locating wreckage or flight recorders diminish. Authorities say finding debris or the “black boxes” is necessary to determine what happened.

At the time of reporting, no definitive cause has been identified and the plane has not been found. Investigations into the stolen passports and other leads continue.

For the first time in 146 years of records, Chicago went through both January and February without an inch of snow on the ground at the official measurement site at O’Hare Airport. The National Weather Service records depth at 6 a.m., so very small amounts that fell later and melted (a trace on Feb. 25 and 0.1 inch on Jan. 30) were not counted. The unusually snow‑free winter followed a snowy early December; from Dec. 18 to March 11 O’Hare recorded only 0.7 inches, well below the typical late‑winter total.

The near‑record thaw coincided with severe spring storms and tornadoes in mid‑March (including a fatal tornado in Ottawa) that produced snow again — ending the no‑snow streak when Winter Storm Stella and subsequent lake‑effect snow brought several inches and a reported 6 inches of snow cover by March 14.

Local meteorologists link the anomaly to broader climate change trends but caution that single-season events and short warm spells can reflect natural variability as well. Impacts of the warm winter include earlier budburst and possible crop losses from late frosts (as happened in 2007 and 2012), greater insect survival, disrupted bird migration timing, and economic effects that are mixed (lower heating bills and more outdoor activity vs. risks to fruit growers). Residents expressed relief and enjoyment at the milder weather, though experts warned snow or cold could still return in March.

Queen Elizabeth II used her pre-recorded annual Christmas message to emphasize the importance of family, friendship and community. Wearing a red dress, she said family strength had been highlighted by two grandchildren’s marriages that year and noted that friendship often arises during hard times; she also cited the Commonwealth as an example of a family-like community beyond blood ties. The message was recorded Dec. 9, before the Queen’s husband, Prince Philip, was hospitalized following a heart procedure.

On Christmas Day the royal family attended the traditional morning service at St. Mary Magdelene Church on the Sandringham estate without the Duke of Edinburgh, who remained in hospital recovering after a coronary stent was fitted for a blocked artery. Buckingham Palace said Philip was “in good spirits” and family planned hospital visits after the royal lunch. The Queen led the procession to the church in a lavender coat and hat; other attendees included Prince Charles and Camilla, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge (William and Kate), Prince Harry, and granddaughter Zara Phillips with her husband Mike Tindall. After the service the Queen accepted bouquets from children and later gave them to Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie. The Queen, who writes her own broadcasts and has delivered them on radio since 1952 and television since 1957, focused this year’s address on family and community ties.

Thieves used Paris’s off-limits catacombs to steal about 300 bottles of fine wine — roughly €250,000 (£230–231k) worth — from a private apartment cellar near the Jardin du Luxembourg (6th arrondissement). Investigators say the culprits entered the catacombs through a secret or sealed access, drilled through the cellar wall, removed the grands crus and slipped back underground. Police suspect the gang was well informed and may have scouted the location beforehand; the Paris criminal investigation department is handling the case. The heist highlights how the vast labyrinth beneath Paris — roughly 150 miles of former quarries and ossuaries (only a small section is open to tourists) — is sometimes used illicitly by “cataphiles” despite restrictions and police patrols.

PITTSFIELD — Two men, Joseph E. Van Wert, 65, of Becket, and Randy W. Lambach, 45, of Pittsfield, have been arrested and charged in connection with an alleged citywide prostitution and human trafficking ring. Police say the investigation, begun in spring 2017 after complaints of increased prostitution, found activity concentrated around First, Adam, North, Linden and Wahconah streets and involved multiple women, some recruited because of drug addiction; one witness estimated a victim might have been as young as 15.

Authorities allege Lambach recruited addicted women, photographed them, posted ads (including on backpage.com), arranged appointments and transported women—sometimes out of town—often keeping 50–90% of fees or paying them with heroin, crack or prescription drugs. He allegedly threatened women who tried to stop or speak to police and reportedly had trafficked some former foster children. Lambach is accused of shuttling women in a blue station wagon and of supervising or watching some encounters. Van Wert is accused of allowing meetings to occur in his third‑floor apartment at a North Street senior living facility in exchange for cash and drugs.

Police arrested Lambach and Van Wert in mid‑November. Lambach pleaded not guilty to four counts of human trafficking; Van Wert pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to commit human trafficking, deriving support from prostitution, maintaining a house of prostitution and sexual conduct for a fee. Both are being held pending a dangerousness/bail hearing. The investigation is ongoing and further charges are possible. Anyone with information was asked to contact Pittsfield Police.

Alexandria Duval, 37, who is accused of killing her identical twin sister, Anastasia, when their SUV plunged about 200 feet off a cliff on Maui on May 29, is fighting extradition from New York to Hawaii on a second-degree murder charge. Duval was arrested in Albany on Nov. 11 after investigators located her there; she had been injured in the crash and was earlier released in Hawaii when a judge found no probable cause for murder. A Hawaii grand jury later indicted her, and Maui police issued a warrant. At a Nov. 18 appearance in Albany County Court, Duval — described by her public defender Terry Kindlon as “profoundly distraught” and a “soul mate” to her sister — declined to waive an extradition hearing, which is scheduled for Dec. 16. Her attorney says the evidence assembled so far is insufficient for extradition and maintains the crash was a tragic accident; authorities say the sisters were fighting over the steering wheel when the vehicle went over the cliff.

Charlotte, N.C. — Police have charged 23-year-old Reco Latur Dawkins Jr. with attempted murder, felony breaking and entering, and conspiracy after an early‑morning home invasion left 21‑year‑old Army National Guard combat medic Semantha Bunce critically wounded.

Incident details
- The attack occurred Tuesday morning at a home on Matlea Court in east/northeast Charlotte while Bunce was feeding her infant. Intruders knocked, rang the doorbell, then kicked in the front door.
- Family members say Bunce retrieved a gun and exchanged fire with the intruders in a stairwell. She was shot several times (reported wounds to the stomach and arm) and transported to Carolinas Medical Center, where she was recovering in the ICU; her baby was not injured.
- Neighbors reported hearing gunfire and later found bullet holes in nearby homes. Police initially indicated multiple intruders but had not publicly named other suspects at the time of reporting.

Arrest and investigation
- Dawkins surrendered to Charlotte‑Mecklenburg police’s violent criminal apprehension team on Sunday. He has a prior criminal history, including multiple breaking‑and‑entering arrests and a 2010 conviction with probation.
- Authorities described the attack as apparently random; the investigation remains active and detectives have asked the public for tips.

Community response
- The case drew national attention. Friends, fellow soldiers, and Bunce’s husband’s employer set up crowdfunding pages to help cover medical bills, household expenses, and lost wages. Family members and neighbors have expressed concern and called for greater neighborhood vigilance.

A 14-year-old boy, identified as Georta Mack, was fatally shot by his father early Tuesday morning in their East Price Hill home on Blanchard Avenue in Cincinnati. The father, who had recently dropped his son at the bus stop and believed he was at school, returned home and heard a noise in the basement around 6:30 a.m. He grabbed a handgun, was startled when the teen returned and mistakenly shot him in the neck. The father called 911, pleading for help; neighbors later described the scene as tragic and said Georta was a helpful, well-liked youth who lived with his 73-year-old father. Georta was transported to Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center and pronounced dead shortly after 8:15 a.m. Police say the father is cooperating with investigators; officers are consulting with the Hamilton County prosecutor’s office and have not announced whether charges will be filed. Cincinnati Police Chief Eliot Isaac called the incident a "terrible, terrible tragedy," urging responsible gun ownership and awareness in homes where firearms are kept. No names were initially released by police.

Toya Graham, a Baltimore single mother of six, was filmed pulling her 16-year-old son Michael out of a protest crowd during riots sparked by the death of Freddie Gray and repeatedly striking him while scolding him. Speaking to CBS, she said she acted to protect him and prevent him from becoming another Freddie Gray, calling herself “no-tolerant” and saying her son knew he was in trouble and considered running when he saw her. Graham condemned the violence and vandalism and hopes the episode will be a lesson for her son. The widely circulated video drew praise from Baltimore Police Commissioner Anthony Batts, who said he wished more parents had intervened; he also said many rioters were local high school students. The disturbances left at least 20 officers injured, one person critically hurt in a fire, and resulted in 235 arrests (34 juveniles). The National Guard was deployed and a curfew remained in effect.

Prime Minister Theresa May survived a December 12, 2018 Conservative Party no-confidence vote, but the result exposed deep Tory division over her Brexit strategy: 200 MPs backed her and 117 voted against, meaning more than a third of her parliamentary party rejected her leadership. The challenge followed her decision to postpone a Commons vote on the withdrawal agreement she negotiated with the EU amid clear defeat, and came after Eurosceptic backbenchers demanded she go, arguing her deal betrayed the 2016 referendum (notably over the Northern Ireland "backstop").

May had campaigned to remain in post, warning that removing her would risk delaying or stopping Brexit; she pledged to resign before the next scheduled general election in 2022 if she survived. Cabinet ministers rallied to her defense, but hardline Brexiteers called for her immediate resignation. The vote’s scale leaves her weakened: although party rules bar another internal challenge for 12 months, her authority to pass the current deal is diminished—about the same number of MPs who opposed her leadership had planned to oppose the meaningful vote on the deal, effectively blocking it unless she secures significant concessions from Brussels, which EU leaders have said are unlikely.

The crisis raises broader risks: uncertainty for the March 29, 2019 Brexit timetable, potential for a change of leader if she eventually loses a later contest, and economic and political consequences domestically and for UK-EU relations. Markets reacted modestly, with sterling initially rising then settling up around 1% on the day. European leaders, including Angela Merkel, stressed they would not renegotiate the withdrawal agreement, while EU institutions stepped up no-deal contingency planning. The contest also highlighted possible future leadership contenders and deep divisions within the Conservative Party over the Irish backstop, no-deal Brexit, and whether to pursue another referendum.

Summary:

Two separate news items are reported.

1) Mo Ibrahim Prize for African Leadership: No winner
- The 2012 Mo Ibrahim Prize, worth $5 million paid over 10 years plus $200,000 annually for life, was not awarded because no former democratically elected African leader met the foundation’s strict criteria for exceptional governance, improvement of living standards, and voluntary departure from office. The prize’s founder, telecoms entrepreneur Mo Ibrahim, emphasized maintaining high standards and credibility by not compromising. This is the third year (after 2009 and 2010) with no winner; previous recipients include Pedro Verona Pires (Cape Verde), Festus Mogae (Botswana) and Joaquim Chissano (Mozambique). Separately, the foundation gave a special $1 million award to Archbishop Desmond Tutu for “speaking truth to power.” Ibrahim has argued the prize is needed because many African leaders, often from poor backgrounds, fear losing income and cling to power.

2) Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences: Roth and Shapley honored
- The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2012 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences to Lloyd Shapley (UCLA) and Alvin Roth (Harvard/soon Stanford) for their work on the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design. Shapley’s theoretical work (with David Gale) established algorithms for stable matching; Roth applied and extended these ideas to real-world problems, improving systems that match students to schools, medical graduates to residency programs, and donated kidneys to patients. Their work has been implemented in places like New York City and Boston, substantially improving allocation outcomes (e.g., reducing students assigned to undesired schools). The economics prize carries roughly $1.2 million.

A Texas judge has ruled that Sofya Tsygankova, the estranged 32-year-old wife of concert pianist Vadym Kholodenko, is mentally incompetent to stand trial on charges that she smothered the couple’s two young daughters. Tsygankova, charged with two counts of capital murder for the deaths of Nika, 5, and Michaela, 1, was ordered committed to a state mental health facility for 120 days of treatment so she might regain “a reasonable degree of rational understanding.” She will remain in the Tarrant County jail until a bed is available. Prosecutors did not object to the order. Police say Kholodenko found Tsygankova covered in blood with wrist cuts and the children dead in their beds on March 17; an empty bottle of the antipsychotic quetiapine was found in the home and Tsygankova had been at a mental health facility the day before. Tsygankova has pleaded not guilty. Kholodenko, a Ukrainian pianist who won the Van Cliburn competition in 2013, resumed performing a month after the killings and has asked audiences to focus on the music amid his family’s loss.

At Alan Shepard Elementary School in Bourbonnais, Illinois, longtime custodian Steve Weidner—known affectionately as "Mr. Steve"—was treated like a rock star on June 2 as students lined up for him to sign their yearbooks. Weidner, who has worked at the school for more than 15 years and is known for looking out for the kids, was seated on the playground while children waited in a line that wound around the play area so he could autograph their books. The school said he was touched and amazed by the display of affection. A photo of the scene was posted to Reddit and quickly rose to the site’s front page, drawing thousands of upvotes and comments.

Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin’s Institute on Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault released “The Blueprint for Campus Police,” a detailed report the UT System will use to train nearly 600 campus police officers across its eight institutions. The guide emphasizes that sexual-assault survivors often present differently from victims of other crimes because of trauma, and urges officers to be victim-centered, science-based and trauma-informed. It provides concrete language and procedures for first contact (e.g., reassure victims they are safe and will not be judged; view intoxication as vulnerability not culpability), explains how trauma can affect memory and behavior (omissions, inconsistencies or emotional flatness do not mean an assault did not occur), and debunks common rape myths. The Blueprint draws on prior survivor data and interviews with campus leaders and police, and aims to translate neurobiology and victimology research into practical policing changes.

Separately, a 21‑year‑old UT‑Austin student identified as John Doe filed suit seeking to halt a campus disciplinary hearing that could expel him over an alleged off‑campus, alcohol‑involved sexual encounter with a non‑student. No criminal charges were filed and the alleged victim did not file a police report; the university opened a Title IX investigation after the woman’s father complained. The lawsuit contends Doe was denied due process (no cross‑examination, no subpoenas, limited ability to present witnesses) and that the university’s broad definition of consent and investigative practices are biased and threaten students’ constitutional rights. Doe’s attorney and other defense lawyers argue a national trend of campus procedures—spurred by federal Title IX enforcement—has led to rushed or unfair disciplinary actions against accused men. The case joins numerous similar lawsuits challenging universities’ handling of sexual‑misconduct allegations.

More than 100 former NFL players, including Jamal Anderson, Chris Doleman and O.J. Santiago, have joined a lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Atlanta alleging the league concealed the dangers of concussions; they add to over 1,500 players already pursuing similar claims. Filed by attorney Mike McGlamry, the suit accuses the NFL of repeatedly denying links between concussions and long‑term brain injury, failing to protect players, and downplaying risks. The NFL denies intentionally misleading players and reiterates that player safety is a priority.

The filing cites recent studies linking repeated head trauma to chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)—a progressive, Alzheimer's‑like disease marked by memory loss and mood changes that can only be diagnosed postmortem—and notes 12 confirmed CTE cases in deceased NFL players. Boston University’s Center for Traumatic Encephalopathy has consistently found brain damage consistent with repeated head blows in studied players and is seeking to examine the brain of Junior Seau, who died by suicide. The article highlights the growing public awareness of CTE and suggests that confirmation of CTE in high‑profile cases like Seau’s could significantly change how the sport and its long‑term risks are perceived.

Alexandra Nicole Laird, a 21-year-old woman from Pleasant Grove, has been indicted and faces multiple charges after giving birth in March 2015 to a daughter who tested positive for opiates and amphetamines and required about a month in intensive care for neonatal withdrawal. A Jefferson County grand jury indicted Laird on April 15, 2015; police say she admitted using heroin one to two times weekly for at least five months of that pregnancy, leading prosecutors to pursue an enhanced Class B felony charge of chemical endangerment of a child. Laird does not have custody of that child.

She also faces an unrelated drug-possession matter from a traffic stop in which 38 hydrocodone pills were found in a vehicle; neither occupant claimed them. After missing a court appearance and testing positive on a court-ordered drug test, Laird was jailed in September 2015; officers say she then admitted to using heroin three times a day and to being pregnant again (estimated 18–20 weeks). Authorities obtained a formal warrant and a judge ordered her jailed without bond until the new baby is born, citing the unborn child’s risk from continued heroin exposure. Laird has claimed financial hardship and is self-employed cleaning houses; she is due back in court on the original child-endangerment charge in July.

Context: The case comes amid national attention on opioid-exposed newborns. In 2016 President Obama signed the Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act, which includes steps to protect drug-dependent newborns and assist families by enforcing a 2003 reporting law and promoting non-punitive “safe care plans,” though advocates note the law lacks significant new funding.

India’s Supreme Court has unanimously struck down the colonial-era adultery law (Section 497 IPC), ruling it unconstitutional and discriminatory. A five-judge bench found the provision—which criminalised a man having sex with a married woman without her husband’s consent and punished the man with up to five years’ jail—archaic, arbitrary and based on the notion that a wife is her husband’s property. The court said adultery can be addressed as a civil matter (e.g., divorce) but not as a criminal offence; Chief Justice Dipak Misra declared “husband is not the master.” Justices stressed women’s sexual autonomy and equality.

The challenge was brought by Joseph Shine, an Indian businessman in Italy, who argued the law treated women as objects and discriminated on gender grounds. The central government had opposed repeal, saying criminal sanctions protect the sanctity of marriage. Some feminists and officials argued instead for a gender-neutral offence to deter abandonment and protect vulnerable women; others welcomed the decolonising move, noting Britain had long removed such laws.

The judgment follows other recent progressive rulings by the court (notably decriminalising homosexual acts) and bolsters arguments against remaining marriage-based exceptions in sexual offence laws, including ongoing challenges to the marital-rape exception. Reactions are mixed but largely supportive; debates continue over whether adultery should ever be criminalised or whether reforms should focus on protecting disadvantaged spouses through other means.

A Mississippi school district abandoned a long-standing practice of assigning some student offices by race after public outcry. The Nettleton School District had used a 30-year-old system that alternated which races could run for specific class positions—e.g., one year certain offices reserved for white students and others for black students—to assure minority representation following court-ordered desegregation efforts decades ago. When Brandy Springer, a mother of mixed-race children who recently moved to the area, learned her 12-year-old daughter was ineligible to run for sixth-grade class reporter because the slot was designated for black students this year, she contacted an online mixed-race families group. The story spread online, drew criticism from advocacy groups and the NAACP (which called for a Justice Department inquiry), and provoked wider concern that the policy erased multiracial, Hispanic and Asian students and taught division rather than inclusion. The district acknowledged growing ethnic diversity and said the caucasian/african-american classifications no longer reflected its student body; by Friday it posted that it would stop using race in school elections. Springer has since moved her children out of the district. The episode highlights tensions between efforts to enforce minority representation and the complexities of race in increasingly diverse and multiracial communities.

President Donald Trump announced on May 8, 2018 that the United States is withdrawing from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, calling it “defective” and “the worst deal ever,” and pledged to reimpose “the highest level” of sanctions — including secondary measures that would penalize foreign companies and countries doing business with Iran after legally required wind-downs. The move reverses a major Obama-era foreign policy achievement in which Iran agreed to curb its nuclear program and accept inspections in exchange for sanctions relief.

Trump framed the decision as necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, criticized Iran’s regional behavior, and said he had consulted U.S. allies. He argued the agreement was too one-sided and insufficiently addressed Iran’s ballistic missile program, support for proxy groups, and cyber activity. Administration hardliners, including new national security adviser John Bolton, supported the withdrawal; congressional Republicans, Saudi Arabia and Israel praised it. Critics — including former President Barack Obama and European leaders such as Emmanuel Macron — warned it undermines U.S. credibility and the global nonproliferation regime and could strain relations with Britain, France, Germany, Russia and China, all original signatories.

Immediate consequences and uncertainties highlighted in reporting:
- The U.S. will reimpose complex primary and secondary sanctions, putting foreign companies and governments at risk if they continue buying Iranian oil.
- Iran said it would remain engaged with the other signatories, but responses could range from continued compliance to steps like expelling inspectors or resuming nuclear activities.
- The decision raises regional security concerns (Israel put forces on heightened alert amid reported Iranian activity in Syria) and could complicate U.S. diplomacy with North Korea by undercutting trust that agreements with Trump will be honored.
- Some U.S. lawmakers urged working with allies to renegotiate a stronger deal, while others supported the withdrawal absent proof of violations.

Overall, the U.S. exit creates diplomatic and strategic uncertainty: it punctures the existing multilateral accord that had verifiably constrained Iran’s nuclear program and sets the stage for renewed sanctions, potential Iranian retaliation or noncompliance, and a test of whether Europe, Russia and China will maintain the agreement without the United States.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has ordered a temporary freeze on grants and contracts as the Trump administration takes charge, several news outlets and agency sources report. Staff were instructed to suspend all contract and grant awards immediately, including task orders and work assignments, and to keep the directive internal. Communications from agency public affairs also imposed tight controls on external messaging—no press releases, social media, blogs or new website content—until the transition “Beach Team” reviews activities.

Key points:
- The freeze affects a broad array of EPA funding programs (research, site redevelopment, air/water monitoring, state and tribal assistance, environmental justice projects, etc.). The EPA awards billions annually in grants and contracts (reported figures: more than $4 billion a year in some accounts; historical totals cited up to $9.6B in grants and $1.4B in contracts for 2013).
- The scope and duration are uncertain: officials said a review was underway and aimed to be completed within days, but it was unclear whether the halt applied only to new awards or also to existing contracts and payments.
- Transition officials, led at EPA by Myron Ebell, described the pause as a precaution to prevent actions the incoming administration does not want to proceed. Ebell and others framed it as similar to prior administration reviews, though former EPA officials called the breadth and communication restrictions “extreme” compared with typical transitions.
- The freeze comes amid broader Trump administration moves affecting agencies (a federal hiring freeze and proposed budget cuts to the EPA reportedly totaling $815 million). Scott Pruitt, an EPA critic nominated to lead the agency, has a history of legal challenges to EPA regulations.
- The action has raised concerns about impacts on state programs, vulnerable communities, ongoing environmental work and agency transparency. Other federal agencies reportedly received similar communication restrictions.

The situation remained fluid as of reporting, with agency spokespeople indicating grants and some state/tribal funding were being processed while other categories were under review.

Former New York governor and former state attorney general Eliot Spitzer defended his record of prosecuting corporate wrongdoing in a Slate column, pushing back against what he called repeated misrepresentations—especially by the Wall Street Journal—about cases he brought against AIG, its former CEO Hank Greenberg, and the insurance broker Marsh & McLennan. Spitzer argued critics are trying to rewrite the narrative of the financial crisis to protect an anti-regulatory ideology. He recounted key facts: Greenberg was removed by AIG’s board amid questions about fraudulent reinsurance contracts; five people were convicted in Connecticut in 2008 related to those frauds; a federal prosecutor labeled Greenberg an unindicted co‑conspirator; New York’s state case was called “devastating” by the judge and AIG settled with Spitzer’s office in 2006 by restating results and paying $1.6 billion, with an additional $750 million shareholders’ settlement pending approval. He defended the prosecutions as proper and necessary.

On Marsh & McLennan, Spitzer noted that although two employee convictions were later thrown out due to disclosure failures, many Marsh employees were convicted and the company admitted wrongdoing—paying an $850 million settlement for price‑fixing, bid‑rigging and kickbacks—leading to leadership changes and the resignation of then‑CEO Jeff Greenberg. Spitzer condemned corporate leaders who oppose measures like taxing private equity fees and criticized rhetoric such as Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman’s extreme comparison of tax proposals to Nazi aggression.

Following the Slate column, two former Marsh executives—William Gilman and Edward McNenney—filed libel suits seeking $60 million and $30 million respectively, claiming they were defamed by Spitzer’s piece (though not named) after their 2008 convictions on antitrust charges were later vacated and dismissed in 2010. Both men had been indicted in Spitzer’s probe; Marsh paid the $850 million settlement in 2005, and while many defendants pleaded guilty or were convicted, several convictions were overturned or dismissed. The plaintiffs allege Spitzer’s statements were defamatory and identify him as acting recklessly despite outcomes favoring them; they also have separate litigation accusing Marsh and Spitzer of using them as “scapegoats.” Slate’s parent company and Slate Group LLC are defendants in the libel suits.

A coordinated York County drug investigation led to the Dec. 29 arrest of three California men in West Manheim Township/Hanover after officers seized 247 pounds of marijuana (double-wrapped, street value about $2 million), $11,000 in cash, three duffel bags, a Glock handgun and other items. Authorities charged Christopher Heath, 37; Ryan Falsone, 27; and Tyler Long, 31, with delivery of marijuana, conspiracy to deliver marijuana and possession with intent to deliver. Heath is a Yuba County Sheriff’s drug task force agent; he had his badge and service weapon on him at the time of the stop and was reportedly on vacation. York County District Attorney Tom Kearney said the stop was part of a coordinated, intelligence-driven operation (not a routine traffic stop) and that investigators did not know Heath was a law‑enforcement officer before the arrest. Officials said the operation appears to be interstate—possibly originating in California—and federal charges are likely; all three were out on bail. Multiple local and state agencies assisted in the investigation.

Joe Jackson, the 89-year-old patriarch of the Jackson family and the early manager who launched The Jackson 5 and helped shepherd the careers of Michael and Janet Jackson, has died. Reports say he died on Wednesday, June 27, in Las Vegas after a battle with cancer; family sources and media cited hospice care and prior hospitalizations. 

Born in 1928, Joe married Katherine in 1949 and fathered 11 children (one of whom, Marlon’s twin, died at birth). He formed The Jackson Brothers in the 1960s that became The Jackson 5 with Jackie, Tito, Jermaine, Marlon and Michael; the group signed with Motown and scored four consecutive No. 1 Billboard singles in 1970. Joe later managed other family acts and was honored in 2002 as Best Entertainment Manager of All Time by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Joe’s parenting and management style—strict and sometimes physically disciplinary—was long controversial; he acknowledged disciplining his children and defended his methods as necessary to keep them out of trouble and to create successful careers. Family members and grandchildren posted tributes after his death. He had suffered health problems in recent years, including a 2015 stroke and other hospitalizations. His relationship with his family was complicated but he remained a central figure in the rise of one of music’s most famous families.

Sally Jewell, 57, was confirmed by the Senate 87–11 to serve as U.S. Secretary of the Interior. The former CEO of outdoor retailer REI, Jewell previously worked as a petroleum engineer and commercial banker and has served with conservation groups such as the National Parks Conservation Association. She pledged to resign from REI upon confirmation and to balance competing uses of the Interior’s portfolio—recreation, conservation, mining, forestry and offshore and onshore energy development—across the department’s management of roughly 500 million acres of federal land and extensive offshore resources.

Her nomination won broad bipartisan support, including endorsements from Democrats and some Republicans who praised her business experience and outdoor credentials; 11 Republicans opposed her confirmation, citing concerns about her ties to environmental organizations and perceived restrictions on oil and coal development. Senators emphasized the importance of the Interior secretary’s “landlord” role for western and Alaskan states. Jewell succeeds Ken Salazar as head of the sprawling, 70,000-employee department that also serves federally recognized tribes.

Researchers studying Easter Island (Rapa Nui) challenge the long-standing narrative that its early inhabitants collapsed through resource depletion and internecine conflict. A new paper in the Journal of Pacific Archaeology analyzes basalt carving tools (toki) recovered during recent excavations of four moai and finds that most of the tools came from a single quarry complex. Chemical (mass spectrometer) sourcing of 17 tool fragments indicates the islanders repeatedly used one preferred quarry rather than exploiting multiple sources locally.

Authors interpret this pattern as evidence of craft specialization, information exchange and coordinated activity—signs of a socially complex and organized society with chiefs, priests and worker guilds who farmed, fished and produced nearly 1,000 large statues—rather than simple competitive collapse. The study’s leaders stress caution: exclusive quarry use could reflect cooperation but might also reflect coercion, and further mapping and sourcing work is needed. They also note that later population decline on Rapa Nui is linked to European contact, colonization and slavery, not necessarily internal collapse, and that Rapa Nui culture and people persist today.

Alan Rickman’s most iconic role is widely considered to be Professor Severus Snape in the Harry Potter films. Rickman portrayed Snape’s complex arc—from brooding antagonist to tragic hero devoted to Lily Potter—with subtlety, using looks and small gestures to hint at the character’s deeper loyalties long before audiences learned them.

J.K. Rowling privately told Rickman that Snape was secretly working for Dumbledore, a detail he often had to conceal from directors, journalists, and cast while the series was still being published. Rickman said Rowling gave him one small, non-plot but crucial piece of information that shaped his performance; otherwise he learned developments along with readers as new books came out. Producer David Heyman recalled directors sometimes clashing with Rickman because he knew things they did not.

After Rickman’s death at 69 from cancer, fans have revisited his portrayal—compilations and videos collecting Snape’s key scenes underscore how effectively Rickman conveyed the character’s love for Lily, his moral ambiguity, and his ultimate sacrifices. The piece also notes the contrast between actors’ on-screen personas and real life, as with Tom Felton (Draco Malfoy), who is described as a very different person off-screen.

New analyses of large cancer datasets reinforce a small but consistent link between adult height and cancer risk: roughly a 10% increase in overall cancer risk for every additional 10 cm of height. Leonard Nunney (UC Riverside) compared observed cancer incidence in several very large studies (including the UK Million Women Study and cohorts from the US, Europe and Korea) with predictions based on body cell number, using height as a proxy. His model—grounded in the idea that cancers arise when somatic cells acquire the right set of mutations—found that increased cell number with greater body size explains the height–cancer relationship for most tumor types (18 of 23 cancers examined). Predicted and observed effects were similar (about 11–13% predicted for a 10 cm increase, vs ~9–12% observed).

Exceptions and contributors:
- Some cancers (stomach, mouth and cervical) showed little or no height effect, likely because strong environmental or infectious drivers (e.g., HPV for cervical cancer) mask any size-related signal.
- Melanoma and thyroid cancer (especially thyroid cancer in women, driven largely by Korean data) showed larger-than-expected height associations. Nunney and other experts suggest additional influences—higher IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) levels in taller people, differences in cell turnover, geography, or other factors—may help explain these outliers.
- IGF-1, a growth-promoting hormone correlated with taller stature, is a plausible complementary mechanism: it raises cell division rates and has been linked to cancer susceptibility, while populations with very low IGF-1 show reduced cancer incidence.

Takeaways and caveats:
- The effect size is modest compared with major, modifiable risks (e.g., smoking, obesity, sun exposure). Height itself is not a modifiable risk factor, but the findings suggest that having more cells contributes materially to cancer risk.
- The study relies on simplifying assumptions (e.g., proportional scaling of cell number with height) and some geographic and cancer-specific variation remains unexplained.
- Practical advice remains unchanged: regardless of height, reducing known lifestyle risks and regular screening when appropriate are the most effective ways to lower cancer risk.

Hurricane Harvey stalled over Texas in late August 2017, dumping unprecedented rain and causing catastrophic flooding across southeastern Texas—especially in Houston—and parts of southwest Louisiana. The slow-moving storm inundated neighborhoods, swelled rivers and reservoirs, forced mass evacuations, and prompted large-scale rescue operations that continued as waters rose.

Human impact and rescue efforts
- Thousands of people were rescued from rooftops, vehicles and homes by federal, state, local, volunteer and military teams. The U.S. Coast Guard reported rescuing over 3,000 people in one day; Houston police and fire units also conducted thousands of rescues. Calls to 911 and to the Coast Guard surged, overwhelming systems at times.
- There were confirmed storm-related deaths (reports varied as officials investigated), many people displaced into shelters (tens of thousands in Houston alone), and more than a million people estimated displaced across the region.
- Rescuers faced chaotic, sometimes hostile conditions: volunteers described panicked crowds rushing boats and isolated incidents of boats being shot at, which at times forced rescues to pause.
- Citizens and businesses pitched in—boat owners, volunteers like the “Cajun Navy,” and local businesses opening space and supplies helped augment official response.

Rain, flooding and infrastructure
- The National Weather Service warned of continuing heavy rain—15 to 25 inches more along the upper Texas coast and southwest Louisiana through the week, with isolated totals possibly reaching 40–50 inches in some spots—threatening to exceed state records.
- Major rivers and reservoirs were at record or near-record levels. Authorities made controlled releases from Addicks and Barker reservoirs (and other dams such as Lake Conroe) to avoid uncontrolled overtopping or failures; those releases flooded downstream neighborhoods and prompted evacuations.
- Buffalo Bayou and other waterways surged, some above all-time peaks. Floodwaters persisted and were expected to recede slowly, keeping communities at risk for days to weeks.
- Roadways, airports and ports were heavily impacted; thousands of flights were canceled and significant portions of U.S. refinery capacity along the Gulf Coast were shut or curtailed, creating gas supply concerns and pushing prices higher.

Government response and forecasts
- Federal, state and local officials mobilized resources: the National Guard was activated, FEMA warned recovery would be long and large-scale, and the Pentagon identified potential support assets. President Trump pledged federal support and asked Congress for rapid disaster relief funding (initially requesting $7.85 billion).
- Officials estimated hundreds of thousands would need disaster assistance and that housing and recovery efforts could take years.
- Forecasts showed Harvey meandering between land and the Gulf, reloading with moisture and repeatedly striking already flooded areas, prolonging the event and complicating response.

Economic and secondary effects
- The storm disrupted oil and gas production (platform evacuations and refinery shutdowns), shipping and supply chains, contributing to gasoline price spikes and prompting release from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
- Insurance and insured-loss estimates varied; flood damage—often not covered by standard homeowner policies—posed major financial risk to homeowners and the National Flood Insurance Program.

Local stories and aftermath
- Dramatic personal accounts highlighted fear, loss and resilience: residents clinging to roofs, families rescued by dump trucks and boats, people losing homes and possessions, and volunteers and businesses providing shelter and supplies.
- Evacuation orders—mandatory and voluntary—were issued across many counties and cities; curfews and shelter operations were in place for large numbers of evacuees.
- Officials urged those awaiting rescue to make themselves visible (hanging sheets/towels) and asked the public to donate money and volunteer through official channels to aid what FEMA described as a multiyear recovery.

Overall, Harvey produced historic, widespread inland flooding that overwhelmed infrastructure and emergency systems, caused extensive human and economic damage, and set the stage for one of the largest disaster recovery efforts in recent U.S. history.

LoJack’s 2013 Vehicle Theft Recovery Report — compiled from LoJack-equipped recoveries in 27 states plus California — found the Honda Accord was the most stolen and recovered vehicle for the fifth consecutive year. LoJack-tracked recoveries in 2013 totaled $121 million; the priciest recovered vehicle was a 2011 Porsche Panamera (~$103,400).

Why the Accord tops theft lists: it’s one of the best-selling, longest-running models in the U.S., so there are many on the road and many compatible parts across model years. That makes Accords lucrative for thieves who strip cars for parts. LoJack and the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) both report similar findings, though NICB’s data includes all reported thefts (not just LoJack-equipped vehicles); NICB noted the 1996 Accord as a particularly commonly stolen year.

Honda points out the Accord’s popularity, reliability and large in-service fleet (over 10 million built in Marysville, Ohio) as factors, and notes newer models include security features like immobilizer systems.

LoJack’s top 10 most stolen/recovered models in 2013:
1. Honda Accord
2. Honda Civic
3. Toyota Camry
4. Toyota Corolla
5. Chevy Silverado
6. Acura Integra
7. Cadillac Escalade
8. Ford F350
9. Nissan Altima
10. Chevy Tahoe

Residents of Wukan, a village in Guangdong province, appear to have reached a tentative compromise with provincial authorities after nearly two weeks of protests over alleged illegal land sales and the death of a village negotiator in police custody.

Background
- Villagers say local officials sold communal farmland to developers without proper consultation or compensation. Thousands of land-related protests occur annually in China, but Wukan drew unusually large attention because villagers expelled local officials and police and blocked access to the town.
- Tensions escalated after the detention and death of village negotiator Xue Jinbo on 11 December. Police said he died of a “sudden illness”; his family and many villagers say he was beaten to death and demand an investigation.
- Villagers also sought the release of detained local leaders and the return of confiscated land.

Recent developments and outcome
- Deputy provincial Communist Party secretary Zhu Mingguo met village representatives in Lufeng. Village leaders reported concessions by authorities: the release in the coming days of several detained villagers (reports say three to four detainees), return of land from at least one development project, withdrawal of police roadblocks into the village, and release of Xue Jinbo’s body.
- Protest leaders described the agreement as a beginning rather than a final victory and warned villagers would resume protests if promises are not kept. Villagers later met to discuss the developments.
- Authorities had urged residents not to march; villagers had planned a demonstration through police barricades but stood down after the meeting.

Context
- The standoff comes amid wider social unrest in southern China, including labour strikes and other local protests (for example, a separate protest in nearby Haimen over a planned power plant). The Wukan outcome is notable for the relative concessions granted by provincial officials.

Nearly a month after SAT answer sheets from a Broad Run High School administration on May 2 went missing, Loudoun County officials found them Monday in the school’s shipping area. A sealed box containing 236 answer sheets was discovered on the bottom shelf of a cart; an ETS representative collected the box and plans to take it to an ETS/College Board facility in Princeton for validation. Initially administrators believed UPS had picked up and lost the exams — video was thought to show a UPS employee leaving with a box and a tracking number — but UPS said the shipment never entered its system. School officials now say a mix-up likely occurred when several boxes were moved from the guidance office to the shipping area on May 4: one similar box left with UPS while the box of answers remained on a cart and was overlooked. The tests will be validated so affected students (about 200–300) will not need to retake the SAT; the district will investigate the handling and delivery procedures.

Researchers at Colorado College found that simply being told you slept well can boost cognitive performance—a “placebo sleep” effect. In the study led by Christina Draganich and Kristi Erdal, 164 students were told a fabricated technique measured their prior-night sleep and were randomly assigned to receive feedback that their REM sleep was either above average (28.7% of total sleep time) or below average (16.2%). All participants heard a brief lecture about sleep’s importance before being shown faux measurement equipment and data. Those told they had above-average sleep performed significantly better on the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test, which assesses attention and information-processing, than those told they had poor sleep. The authors conclude that mindset about sleep can positively or negatively influence cognitive function, suggesting beliefs alone may help control aspects of health and cognition. The study, “Placebo Sleep Affects Cognitive Functioning,” appears in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

On March 10, 2014, aviation photographers including Steve Douglass and Dean Muskett were at Rick Husband Amarillo International Airport when they noticed contrails from three high‑flying, distant aircraft and photographed them with 300 mm lenses. At first the group thought the silhouettes might be B‑2 bombers, but closer inspection of the images revealed a smooth, slightly curved trailing edge—“almost boomerang shaped”—not the B‑2’s distinctive W‑shaped trailing edge. Whiteman AFB (which houses B‑2s) said no B‑2 flight over Texas occurred that day.

Aviation Week’s Bill Sweetman and colleagues reviewed the photos and concluded the images likely show a real, unidentified aircraft rather than a camera artifact. Voice signals picked up during the sighting suggest the planes may have been piloted. Observers noted the shape loosely resembles the Navy’s X‑47B UAV but appears larger; Douglass speculated it might be a stealthy transport. The identity and origin of the three “black” aircraft remain unknown, prompting speculation about a classified test or demonstration.
