Cuba’s National Assembly conducted a historic two-day transition in April 2018 that will for the first time in nearly 60 years place someone outside the Castro family in the presidency. First Vice President Miguel Díaz-Canel, 57, was named the sole candidate and is all but certain to be approved by the largely controlled, unanimous-voting legislature to succeed 86‑year‑old Raúl Castro, who is stepping down after two five‑year terms. Raúl Castro will remain head of the Communist Party, preserving his ultimate authority.

State media framed the change as continuity of the revolutionary, single‑party system while presenting Díaz‑Canel as a younger, low‑profile technocrat with regional party and education ministry experience. Officials and commentators stressed generational renewal and the need to maintain socialist governance amid economic stagnation, an aging population and growing discontent among youth. Cubans interviewed urged economic improvements but voiced caution about preserving the revolution’s ideals.

The selection followed Cuba’s usual tightly managed process: a government-appointed candidacy commission, ballots that offer approval or disapproval, and near‑unanimous results. Alongside Díaz‑Canel, the assembly approved other Council of State leaders, mostly non‑revolutionary figures, signaling a broader leadership turnover while keeping the party’s institutional continuity intact. International and domestic observers expect close scrutiny of Díaz‑Canel’s actions once he formally assumes the presidency.

Samuel Shaffer, 34, a self‑proclaimed prophet and co‑leader of the doomsday polygamist sect called the Knights of the Crystal Blade, was convicted and sentenced for abusing children in his group. He pleaded guilty to felony child sodomy in Sanpete County and was sentenced June 2026 to 15 years to life; that sentence will run concurrent with an earlier Iron County judgment that requires a minimum of 26 years behind bars after Shaffer was previously sentenced for first‑degree rape of a child and child abuse. Other charges in Sanpete County were dismissed.

Investigators say Shaffer and fellow member John Alvin Coltharp (34) had illegally “married” each other’s underage daughters — Shaffer admitted he was married to Coltharp’s 8‑year‑old, and Coltharp has pleaded guilty to child sodomy and child bigamy and faces sentencing in August. The case began after Coltharp’s ex‑wife reported he had taken their four children in December 2017. Police found two girls inside empty 50‑gallon water barrels exposed to subfreezing temperatures and two others in poor health inside an abandoned mobile trailer; all four received emergency medical care. A third man has also been charged in the investigation. Shaffer’s attorney has not publicly indicated whether he will appeal.

Masafumi Nagasaki, an 82-year-old Japanese man, lived alone as a voluntary castaway on Sotobanari, a tiny, waterless island in Okinawa Prefecture, for nearly 30 years (arriving in 1989). Famously dubbed the “naked hermit,” Nagasaki abandoned city life—reportedly quitting jobs including photography and entertainment—after being disturbed by pollution and seeking solitude. He survived with minimal supplies, collecting rainwater, buying provisions and 10,000 yen sent by family once a week, and kept a strict daily routine of exercise and beach cleaning. A typhoon early in his stay destroyed his belongings and prompted him to adopt nudity as his island “uniform.” He refused to harm wildlife (declining turtle eggs), expressed a wish to die on the island, and said living there let him escape social pressures and “follow nature’s rules.”

Documentarian Alvaro Cerezo lived on Sotobanari with Nagasaki for five days and filmed his last interviews. In April 2018 authorities removed Nagasaki—reportedly after someone noticed him weakened—and returned him to civilised life in a government house in nearby Ishigaki; he is now reportedly not allowed to return to the island. Nagasaki’s decades-long isolation made him one of the world’s longest-lasting voluntary castaways.

A sudden eruption of Mount Ontake in central Japan on Saturday killed or is feared to have killed dozens of hikers and forced rescue teams to suspend recovery efforts because of toxic gas and heavy ash. Authorities on Monday said five more bodies were located near the summit, bringing the presumed death toll to 36; 12 bodies have been recovered and taken down for examination, leaving others still near the peak. Rescuers—including soldiers and firefighters—airlifted eight bodies by helicopter before halting operations around 1:30 p.m. as sulfur smells, rising ash and noxious fumes made the summit unsafe.

The 3,067-meter volcano erupted without warning around noon when many people (estimates ~250) were hiking and enjoying fall foliage. The blast sent plumes of gas and ash into the sky, showered the slopes with rocks and left ash deposits up to about 50 cm in places. Hundreds were initially trapped; most descended by nightfall, while about 40 stranded overnight came down the next day. Japan’s Fire and Disaster Management Agency reported at least 63 injured (including several serious cases) and had been trying to confirm missing persons.

Mount Ontake’s eruption appears to have been a sudden, steam-driven explosion—difficult to predict even though there were tremors in the area earlier this month. Officials said the Japan Meteorological Agency may review monitoring practices but stressed forecasting such eruptions is inherently challenging. Families of the missing gathered nearby as recovered bodies were examined in a local school gymnasium. This is Japan’s first fatal volcanic eruption since 1991.

Three people were wounded in a shooting at Washington Square Mall in Indianapolis Wednesday evening. Police say a male suspect entered the mall around 6:30 p.m., confronted a man he knew, and shot him; two nearby bystanders—a second man and a woman—were also struck by gunfire. The victims are young adults: two men (ages 25 and 26) and a 20-year-old woman. All were taken to hospitals; one 26-year-old remained in serious but stable condition and the other two have been released. Investigators say the attack was not random and appears to stem from an existing dispute between the shooter and the primary victim. The suspect fled; police were searching for him and possibly a second male suspect. The mall and police responded quickly, and no juveniles were involved. Authorities ask anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

A SEPTA worker in suburban Philadelphia who found a bag containing more than $15,000 in cash and turned it in to police has been awarded the money after no one proved ownership. In March 2016, 62-year-old Bob Tracey spotted a Wells Fargo bank bag in the road, opened it and found stacks of $100 and $20 bills. He immediately called Upper Darby police and surrendered the cash. The bag also contained a digital scale, a crack‑cocaine pipe and a vial, making it unlikely the true owner would come forward. Although police superintendent Michael Chitwood supported returning the funds to Tracey if unclaimed, Tracey had to file a court petition under state lost‑property law. On Monday, Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Charles Burr II ordered the $15,200 returned to Tracey after claimants failed to prove ownership. Police and Chitwood said bureaucratic delay forced Tracey into court despite expectations the money would be returned sooner.

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met in Singapore on June 12, 2018, for a historic summit at the Capella resort on Sentosa Island — the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. Their day included a long handshake and photo ops, a roughly 40–45 minute private one-on-one meeting with only interpreters, followed by a bilateral meeting with senior aides and a working lunch. Trump described the meetings as “very, very good,” said the two had developed an “excellent” and “very special” relationship, and declared the summit “better than anybody could have expected.” Kim expressed that getting to the meeting had not been easy and said they had “decided to leave the past behind.”

The leaders signed a joint statement pledging to “work toward complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula,” with Trump committing to provide “security guarantees” to North Korea and Kim reaffirming his commitment to denuclearization. The document provided no definitions or specifics about what “complete denuclearization” or the promised “security guarantees” would entail, and critics noted similar vague agreements in the past. The statement also called for new U.S.–North Korea relations aimed at peace and prosperity and cooperation on recovering Korean War POW/MIA remains.

The summit was heavy on ceremony and symbolism but light on concrete substance. Trump and aides framed the meeting as the start of a negotiating process rather than a finished deal; Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said sanctions would remain until denuclearization occurred but that the U.S. was prepared to provide North Korea with “sufficient certainty” that denuclearization would not end badly for the regime. Observers and former officials voiced skepticism that Kim would relinquish his nuclear arsenal, noting the challenge of verification and North Korea’s likely desire for security guarantees, possible U.S. troop reductions in Korea, and economic benefits in return.

Reactions were mixed: some praised the diplomatic opening and urged sustained negotiations and verification; others criticized the summit for elevating Kim’s international stature without securing concrete commitments on weapons, human rights, or a timeline. International figures including the U.N. secretary-general urged both leaders to pursue verifiable denuclearization. The White House indicated Trump would depart Singapore earlier than planned and visit U.S. military bases in Guam and Hawaii on the return trip. Overall, the summit produced a symbolic breakthrough and a joint pledge to negotiate, but left major questions about details, verification, and outcomes unanswered.

Summary:

Eleven Secret Service personnel (special agents and Uniformed Division officers), part of an advance team securing a Cartagena hotel before President Obama’s arrival for the Summit of the Americas, were recalled to Washington amid allegations they brought women—believed to be prostitutes—back to their hotel rooms and engaged in misconduct. The incident reportedly involved heavy drinking, at least one payment dispute when an agent initially refused to pay a woman, and a hallway disturbance that drew local police. Because foreigners were involved, police filed a report that reached the U.S. Embassy and prompted a Secret Service inquiry; the case was turned over to the agency’s Office of Professional Responsibility.

None of the recalled agents were assigned to Obama’s immediate protective detail. At least one supervisor was among those implicated; several agents are married. The Secret Service and White House say the matter did not affect the President’s security and that Obama has confidence in the agency, though the agency expressed regret for the distraction. Author Ronald Kessler and Rep. Peter King (R-N.Y.), who was briefed on the probe, called the episode embarrassing and potentially compromising.

Separately, U.S. Southern Command reported five service members staying at the same hotel were confined for curfew violations and may be under investigation for related misconduct. The episode drew criticism in Cartagena, a city known for tolerated prostitution zones, and threatened to overshadow Obama’s diplomatic visit.

Facing criticism over its overwhelmingly older, white, male membership and the high-profile #OscarsSoWhite backlash, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a major membership expansion, sending 683 invitations — the largest and most diverse class to date. Nearly half of the invitees are women and 41% are people of color. The list mixes longtime Hollywood figures who had not been members, international auteurs, and rising stars. Directors invited include Park Chan-wook, Lucrecia Martel, Abbas Kiarostami, Hou Hsiao‑Hsien, the Wachowskis, Patty Jenkins, Ryan Coogler, Nuri Bilge Ceylan and many others beyond the traditional older white-male cohort. Acting invitees include Idris Elba, Oscar Isaac, Michael B. Jordan, Tessa Thompson, Regina King, Eva Mendes, Kate Beckinsale, Luis Guzmán and Ice Cube, among others. The move is part of the Academy’s pledge to double the number of women and people of color in its membership by 2020 in response to criticism and calls for greater diversity.

Summary:

American journalist James Foley, kidnapped in Syria on Nov. 22, 2012, was murdered by Islamic State militants in a graphic video posted Aug. 19, 2014. Foley’s captors emailed his parents on Aug. 12, 2014, warning they would execute him in retaliation for recent U.S. airstrikes in Iraq; GlobalPost published the message with the family’s permission. The email mixed extreme rhetoric with factual errors (the family disputes claims they were given many opportunities to negotiate). After proving they held Foley the militants demanded an exorbitant ransom (100 million euros) or prisoner releases—terms most experts believe were never intended to be met.

The executioner, a masked militant with a British accent dubbed “Jihadi John,” emerged as a notorious figure; British foreign fighters are estimated to number in the hundreds or low thousands within ISIS and are thought to be used for particularly brutal acts. Former hostages described Foley being singled out for harsher treatment—beatings, mock executions and degradation—partly after militants found photos linking his brother to the U.S. Air Force.

ISIS held up to 20 Western hostages in Syria and Iraq, including American freelance reporter Steven Sotloff (who was later threatened), two young Italian aid workers, and three ICRC staff abducted last October. Families of hostages defended their loved ones’ humanitarian motives while authorities and charities worked privately to secure releases.

Global reaction included expressions of condolence and condemnation; Pope Francis personally called Foley’s parents to offer comfort. Foley’s family and former fellow captives remembered him as compassionate and devoted to bearing witness in conflict zones.

Summary:

Twelve boys (ages 11–16) and their 25-year-old football coach remain trapped deep inside the Tham Luang Nang Non cave in Chiang Rai, northern Thailand after heavy rains flooded the system on June 23. They were found alive by British cave divers nine days later, huddled on a muddy ledge about 4 km (2.5 miles) from the entrance. Medical teams have been supplying food, blankets and basic care; video footage shows the boys in good spirits but weak. A new medical assessment said two boys and the coach show exhaustion from malnutrition and that it would be too dangerous to attempt an evacuation on Thursday.

Rescuers face narrow, winding, dark, flooded passages that require expert diving and up to six hours to reach the group and five hours to return. Pumping operations have removed large volumes of water (reported as tens of millions of gallons), clearing roughly 1.5 km of the route and lowering water at about 1.5 cm per hour in places, but many passages remain submerged. Teams aim to drain the third chamber so the boys might be able to walk or wade out without full diving, but monsoon rains forecast for the weekend could rapidly refill the cave and force a decision to evacuate under far riskier conditions.

Options being pursued:
- Continue massive pumping to make the route walkable.
- Teach the boys basic diving using full‑face masks and guide them out with expert divers and a static guide line—considered highly risky for non-swimmers and narrow, low-visibility squeezes.
- Search the surface for natural chimneys or shafts that could provide an alternative entrance; drilling has been abandoned in favor of locating existing openings.
- Maintain the boys’ health and morale by supplying oxygen to the chamber, bringing in medical staff and two Thai Navy SEAL divers to stay with them, and attempting to install a communications line to their families.

International support includes divers, equipment and personnel from Australia, the UK, the US, China, Israel, Laos, Myanmar and others. Rescue teams continue rehearsals and contingency planning; time and weather are the critical constraints as officials race “against the water” to choose the safest viable extraction before heavier rains arrive.

The California Supreme Court unanimously overturned a lower-court ruling that had required the City of Los Angeles and the Los Angeles Zoo to change how they care for elephants, a setback for animal-rights advocates. The dispute began in 2007 when L.A. resident Aaron Leider sued the zoo director and the city over the elephant exhibit expansion, alleging elephants were subjected to cruel treatment (chains, drugs, bullhooks, electric shocks). In a 2012 bench trial, Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge John Segal ordered the city to stop using bullhooks and shocks and to exercise the elephants; a divided appeals court affirmed that injunction.

The state high court reversed, holding that Leider’s taxpayer suit improperly sought to enforce criminal animal-abuse statutes through an injunction. Justice Carol Corrigan wrote that taxpayer actions cannot be used to enforce criminal law, and the trial court’s findings implicated criminal penalties without providing a jury trial or the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard—effectively usurping prosecutorial discretion. The case was remanded for further proceedings.

Plaintiff’s attorney called the decision “extremely disappointing” and signaled plans to seek retrial or legislative remedies; the zoo celebrated the ruling, saying it affirms the quality of its elephant care. The city did not comment.

A new report from Transportation for America finds that at least 66,405 U.S. bridges — about 11% of the national total — are classified as "structurally deficient," meaning they need significant maintenance, rehabilitation or replacement. These bridges are heavily used: roughly 260 million daily trips cross them. The average age of structurally deficient bridges is 65 years, and the Federal Highway Administration estimates repairs would cost about $76 billion (a figure likely to grow as many busy, interstate-era bridges near the end of their service lives).

The study follows the May 23 Interstate 5 span collapse over the Skagit River in Washington — a high-profile incident caused by an oversized truck striking the span — but that bridge was not on the deficient list. Transportation for America warns the problem has worsened since 2011 (15 states have more deficient bridges now) and projects that in a decade one in four bridges will be 65 or older. It notes federal policy changes in the recent transportation funding law eliminated a dedicated bridge-repair fund and rolled money into a program limited to the National Highway System; nearly 90% of structurally deficient bridges are outside that system, reducing their access to federal dollars.

Recommendations include creating new dedicated transportation revenues, expanding eligibility for federal programs to cover about 180,000 bridges, and making bridge and highway repair a national priority. Views differ on urgency: some experts call the system better than ever and favor greater state-level responsibility and funding, while advocates emphasize the risks of deferred maintenance — more closures, weight limits and deterioration short of dramatic collapses — and the need for increased investment. The report highlights many high-traffic, non-iconic overpasses in poor condition and stresses that aging infrastructure will pose growing challenges without stepped-up repair and replacement.

J.C.X. Simon, one of four men convicted in the racially motivated "Zebra" killing spree that terrorized San Francisco in 1973–74, was found dead and unresponsive in his San Quentin cell Thursday night and was pronounced dead at 11:59 p.m. The 69-year-old was serving a life sentence with the possibility of parole; the official cause of death is pending an autopsy.

Simon was convicted in 1976 of two counts of first‑degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder and assault with a deadly weapon. He and accomplices Larry Green, Manuel Moore and Jessie Lee Cooks were tied to a six‑month campaign of random attacks that targeted white victims, leaving 14 people dead and seven wounded, many shot execution‑style. The manhunt that followed was one of the largest in the city's history and drew intense scrutiny after authorities briefly authorized widespread stops and questioning of Black men.

Key testimony at the trial came from Anthony C. Harris, an alleged participant who cooperated with prosecutors and said the group called itself an offshoot of the Fruit of Islam. The other three convicted members remain incarcerated at separate California prisons; all received life sentences with repeatedly denied parole.

The document profiles Kim Kardashian and her family’s highly successful, diversified branding machine built around their reality show Keeping Up With the Kardashians. Kim, her sisters Kourtney and Khloé, and their mother Kris Jenner have turned celebrity into a wide-ranging business empire—fashion lines, jewelry, fragrances, skin care, self-tanner, fitness videos, credit cards and endorsements (from QuickTrim to Carl’s Jr.). Despite her origins in a widely publicized sex tape, Kim remains popular and trusted by many consumers; Brand Keys research ranks her at the top of its celebrity loyalty index (tied with Snooki), with Kourtney and Khloé also near the top. Consumers often see Kim as entrepreneurial and relatable rather than purely glamorous.

At public appearances and on social media she cultivates engagement: using Twitter and other channels as real-time focus groups, responding to fans’ questions and shaping products to fit their preferences. Her merchandise tends to reflect a Southern California nightclub aesthetic—slinky dresses, leggings, hoop earrings and jewelry with Armenian influences—rather than high-fashion craftsmanship. The sisters’ marketing works because each targets different demographics (Khloé to married women, Kourtney to new moms and women who empathize with relationship struggles, Kim to single women), and because the family framing makes them broadly relatable. Observers call their operation savvy and tightly managed—so much so that commentators speculate the sisters’ personal lives can be leveraged strategically to sustain audience interest and product sales.

A University of Cambridge study, published in Neurology, found that sleeping more than eight hours per day is linked to a higher risk of stroke, particularly in older adults. Researchers followed 9,692 stroke-free adults (age 42–81) from the EPIC-Norfolk cohort for about 9.5 years. After adjusting for multiple risk factors, long sleepers (>8 hours) had a 46% greater stroke risk than people who slept six to eight hours; short sleepers (<6 hours) showed an 18% higher risk, but that association was not statistically significant in this cohort. Persistent long sleep (reported at both survey points) doubled stroke risk versus persistent average sleep, and people whose sleep rose from short to long had nearly four times the risk. Age-specific patterns emerged: excess sleep raised risk mainly in those aged 63+; short sleep appeared riskier in younger people. The researchers also ran a meta-analysis of 11 other prospective studies (about 560,000 participants), which supported the associations: pooled hazard ratios were roughly 1.45 for long sleep and 1.15 for short sleep.

The team cautions that causality is unclear — long sleep might be an early marker or consequence of underlying health problems rather than a direct cause. The association persisted after controlling for common cardiovascular risk factors and among participants without preexisting disease. Authors recommend clinicians consider unusually long sleep in older patients as a potential warning sign and call for further research to clarify biological mechanisms and directionality. The study was supported by the Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK.

University of Missouri President Tim Wolfe resigned after escalating campus protests over systemic racism and the administration’s perceived inaction. His decision followed sustained pressure from students, faculty, donors and community leaders, and came amid a week of intense unrest sparked by multiple racist incidents — including racial slurs directed at students and faculty and a swastika drawn in feces in a dorm bathroom — and long‑standing complaints about an inhospitable climate for minority students.

The immediate catalyst was a high-profile hunger strike by graduate student Jonathan Butler, who vowed not to eat until Wolfe was removed. Butler’s protest, organized with Concerned Student 1950, highlighted repeated racist episodes and institutional failures (including controversial administrative decisions earlier in the year). Momentum surged when black members of the Missouri football team announced they would not practice or play until Wolfe left; their boycott drew national attention and broadened support. Faculty walkouts, a student government demand for Wolfe’s ouster, public teach‑ins, and criticism from deans and external groups further isolated the administration.

In response to the resignations (which also included another official, with one remaining in a research role), the Board of Curators announced new measures: hiring a university‑system diversity, inclusion and equity officer; offering more support to those experiencing discrimination; forming a task force to improve diversity and inclusion; and requiring diversity training for all faculty, staff and incoming students. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest praised the protests as an example of how vocal civic action can prompt change. Butler ended his hunger strike after Wolfe’s resignation and vowed the movement would continue pushing for reform.

Lionsgate and AMC have signed Mad Men creator Matthew Weiner to a long-term deal worth about $30 million that keeps him as showrunner for two more seasons with an option for a third (which would carry the series through a seventh season). Weiner said he expects Season 7 to be the show’s last and is “thrilled” to finish it.

The agreement resolves a recent standoff after Weiner’s prior contract expired and discussions about cost-cutting and shorter episodes. The deal guarantees the current cast will not be cut for financial reasons—only for creative ones—and pays Weiner roughly $10 million per season. As a compromise, most episodes will be shortened for broadcast to 45 minutes to accommodate more commercials, while the first and last episode of each season will remain 47 minutes; Weiner will produce 47-minute “final cut” versions for digital/DVD/VOD. AMC also confirmed Season 5 will not premiere until early 2012. Weiner emphasized the fight was about preserving the show’s creative integrity rather than money.

Summary:

A mass shooting at a Waffle House in Nashville left four people dead and several wounded. Suspect Travis Reinking, 29, is the subject of a large manhunt involving more than 80 Nashville police officers plus FBI, ATF and state troopers; he was added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation’s Top 10 Most Wanted list. Reinking allegedly arrived nearly naked, armed with an AR-15–style rifle, opened fire in the restaurant’s parking lot and then inside. A quick-thinking customer, James Shaw Jr., wrestled the gun away, limiting further casualties; Shaw suffered minor injuries.

Victims killed included employees and patrons: Taurean Sanderlin, 29; Joe Perez, 20; DeEbony Groves, 21, a Belmont University student; and Akilah Dasilva, 23, a music-engineering student and producer. Several others were injured, including Tia Waggoner and Sharita Henderson, both treated at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

Reinking, who had recently moved from Morton, Illinois, has a history of disturbing behavior and run-ins with authorities: in 2017 Secret Service agents detained him after entering a restricted area near the White House; earlier local police reports described paranoid delusions (including claims that Taylor Swift was stalking him), and he was once evaluated for mental-health concerns. Illinois authorities had previously seized four firearms from him after the White House incident; those weapons were later given to his father, who now acknowledges returning them to Travis. Police have recovered three of the four earlier-seized guns and believe Reinking may still be armed with at least one handgun.

Officials warned nearby residents to be cautious; schools were to go into lock-out if the suspect was not found before classes. Authorities have not established a clear motive.

USS Independence (CVL-22) was a World War II light aircraft carrier converted from the cruiser USS Amsterdam (CL-59). Launched August 1942 and commissioned January 14, 1943, she was the lead of a new class of carriers built on cruiser hulls and joined the Pacific Fleet in mid-1943.

Wartime service
- Early 1943–44: After training at Pearl Harbor, Independence took part in carrier strikes across the central and South Pacific, including Marcus and Wake Islands (August–October 1943), where the Grumman F6F Hellcat saw its first combat. In November 1943 she helped strike the heavily fortified Japanese base at Rabaul.
- Tarawa and damage: During preinvasion strikes on Tarawa (November 1943) she was torpedoed, suffering serious damage and undergoing repairs in Funafuti and San Francisco. While repaired she received an extra catapult and pioneered night carrier operations.
- Leyte Gulf and late‑1944 operations: In 1944 she operated in the fast carrier task forces striking Luzon, Formosa, Okinawa and the Philippines. Planes from Independence’s group helped locate and attack Admiral Kurita’s force and participated in the strikes that contributed to sinking the battleship Musashi and multiple Japanese carriers in the Battle of Leyte Gulf, a decisive blow to the Imperial Japanese Navy. She also endured the December 1944 typhoon that caused heavy fleet casualties.
- 1945: Independence supported the Okinawa campaign (March–June), took part in final strikes on Japan in July–August, and after Japan’s surrender carried out surveillance for POW camps and supported occupation landings. She then joined Operation Magic Carpet, returning U.S. servicemen home into early 1946.

Postwar tests and sinking
- Operation Crossroads: In 1946 Independence was used as a target ship in Bikini Atoll atomic tests, placed about 500 yards from blasts (Able and Baker). Heavily damaged and contaminated but not sunk, she was towed to Kwajalein and decommissioned on August 28, 1946. Further radiological testing followed at Pearl Harbor and San Francisco.
- Disposal: In January 1951 the hulk was scuttled off the California coast near the Farallon Islands.

Modern rediscovery
- Discovery and imaging: Oceanographer Robert Ballard and the Ocean Exploration Trust, working with NOAA and the U.S. Navy, conducted a 20‑hour expedition that produced the first images of the wreck in over six decades. The ship lies about 30 miles west of Half Moon Bay at roughly a half‑mile depth. High‑resolution photos and video captured intact features—flight deck, anti‑aircraft guns, hatches, ladders, letters of the ship’s name, and even a Grumman Hellcat fighter with markings still visible. The wreck is unusually well preserved in deep, cold waters.
- Environmental and safety notes: Past records indicate the ship was carrying concrete-filled 50‑gallon drums of low‑level radioactive waste when sunk; current surveys found no trace of these barrels. Experts say remaining radioactivity is negligible after 70 years, and expedition teams collected sediment and biota samples for testing.

Legacy
- Independence earned distinction for combat service across major Pacific battles and for pioneering night carrier operations. Its well-preserved wreck now provides historical insight and detailed 3‑D imaging opportunities while raising interest about deep‑sea heritage and stewardship.

An 18-year-old student, identified as Vladislav Roslyakov, carried out a deadly combined bomb-and-shooting attack at Kerch Polytechnic College in Crimea on Wednesday, killing 20 people and wounding dozens before taking his own life. Authorities say a nail-filled explosive detonated in the cafeteria and the gunman then moved through the building shooting victims at close range; a second device was found and disarmed. Many victims suffered catastrophic blast and shrapnel injuries; some critically wounded were flown to hospitals in Moscow.

Roslyakov, a fourth-year student described by classmates and relatives as quiet, withdrawn and with few friends, had recently obtained a shotgun permit and bought ammunition days earlier. Investigators recovered little useful data from his computer, and local officials are probing whether he acted alone or had accomplices. Crimean and Russian officials have deployed security forces to schools across Kerch and declared days of mourning; funerals were planned on the Russian mainland.

The attack, the deadliest student-led school massacre in Russia since Beslan (2004), has prompted debate over school security, gun controls and cultural influences. President Vladimir Putin characterized the assault as a consequence of “globalization” and harmful online subcultures that glorify violence, drawing parallels in state media to U.S. school shootings such as Columbine. Kremlin spokesmen say any policy changes on gun ownership will await the outcome of the investigation.

A large copper bull sculpture mounted on top of Barista’s restaurant in Hurricane, Utah — which drew local outrage because of an oversized, cone-shaped depiction of male genitalia — had its prominent feature removed by owner Stephen Ward on Friday. Ward says he made the change for aesthetic reasons, not due to neighbor complaints, and that the altered sculpture displays more of the bull’s belly and plate work. The sculpted genitalia had prompted residents to ask the city to revoke the restaurant’s business license; city officials say the sign had been approved but the installed proportions differed from submitted plans.

The dispute comes amid longer-running tensions between Ward and the Hurricane community over his business practices, pricing and a March 14 altercation between an employee and a patron. Ward claims the city has harassed his business for years and has begun legal action against the city over denial of a liquor-license upgrade and against a man who initiated a petition opposing the restaurant’s license renewal. Despite the controversy, Ward and his wife say the publicity has boosted customer traffic. City planning officials and Ward disagree on whether the city had adequate opportunity to inspect the sculpture before installation. The story is developing.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman led a team of retired American basketball players to Pyongyang for an exhibition game and publicly sang “Happy Birthday” to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un before about 14,000 spectators. Rodman dedicated the event to Kim and bowed to him; Kim and his wife watched from a special box. The Americans—including Kenny Anderson, Cliff Robinson, Vin Baker, Craig Hodges, Doug Christie and Charles D. Smith—played cooperatively with North Korean players in the second half. Rodman called the visit “historic” and framed it as “basketball diplomacy,” aiming to build cultural ties rather than engage in politics.

The visit drew heavy criticism in the U.S. from lawmakers, the NBA and human rights groups, who say Rodman’s friendliness with Kim risks legitimizing a repressive regime. Controversy intensified after Rodman, in a CNN interview, appeared to suggest Korean‑American missionary Kenneth Bae—held in North Korea since 2012 and sentenced to 15 years of hard labor—was to blame for his detention. Bae’s family and critics condemned Rodman for making damaging and uninformed remarks and urged him to use his access to advocate for Bae’s release. Former New Mexico governor Bill Richardson and members of Congress said North Korea was exploiting Rodman as a conduit to the U.S. The White House declined to engage with Rodman’s comments, reiterating concern for Bae’s health and urging his amnesty and return.

The Trump administration has refused a Turkish proposal to link the release of U.S. pastor Andrew Brunson to relief for Halkbank, a major Turkish state bank facing potential U.S. fines and investigations, a senior White House official said. Brunson’s detention in Turkey—he has been accused of links to outlawed groups, denies wrongdoing, and is under house arrest after nearly two years—has provoked the sharpest U.S.-Turkey crisis in decades, contributed to a sharp fall in the Turkish lira, and prompted U.S. sanctions and tariffs against Turkey.

U.S. officials have told Ankara that negotiations over Halkbank, which U.S. authorities allege helped Iran evade sanctions and which is under subpoena and scrutiny by the Justice Department, are off the table until Brunson is freed. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and other senior U.S. officials have signaled additional sanctions could follow if Brunson is not released; Turkish officials reject U.S. pressure and deny wrongdoing by the bank.

Beyond humanitarian concerns, U.S. pressure has political dimensions: freeing Brunson would allow President Trump to claim success for his tough tactics and please evangelical supporters who have rallied for the pastor. If convicted, Brunson could face up to 35 years in prison.

A Fort Worth police report and media accounts detail an alleged early-morning January 30 incident in the Dallas area involving Cleveland Browns quarterback Johnny Manziel and his ex-girlfriend, Colleen Crowley. Crowley told police Manziel became aggressive in his Hotel ZaZa room after she tried to leave, forced her through a stairwell and into a vehicle, struck her multiple times (including on her left ear, which she said left her temporarily deaf), dragged her by the hair, smashed her phone and threatened her — allegedly saying “shut up or I’ll kill us both” and at one point saying he would kill himself. She described Manziel as appearing “on some kind of drugs” or in a possible psychotic state. Crowley said she fled to her Fort Worth apartment, tried to contact family by FaceTime, armed herself with a kitchen knife out of fear, and that Manziel then ran off; she later sought an order of protection.

Manziel denied the assault and the suicide threat to TMZ, saying “it didn’t happen” and that he is “completely stable.” The Dallas Police Department said investigative follow-up has not produced a criminal complaint and the case is closed; Fort Worth originally filed an “information only” report, citing jurisdictional issues and Crowley’s reluctance to cooperate further. The NFL said it is aware of the police report and had begun a review when the incident occurred. The Browns indicated Manziel’s continued off-field incidents undermine team expectations and said his status will be addressed when league rules permit; he is not expected to return to the team next season. The story follows prior off-field incidents involving Manziel, including an October stop in Ohio after an interstate altercation with Crowley.

Chelsea Clinton, speaking on NBC’s Today ahead of the Democratic National Convention, said Donald Trump’s rhetoric paints a country she couldn’t imagine raising her children in, calling his insults of women, minorities, Muslims and immigrants far more upsetting than attacks on her mother. She said Hillary Clinton is resilient from years in politics and can withstand partisan attacks; Chelsea plans to introduce her mother in Philadelphia and expects an emotional moment as a new mother herself, saying the election is fundamentally about her children.

Chelsea emphasized she will present the Hillary she knows—contrasting the candidate Republicans portrayed—and said her mother won’t engage in the divisive, bigoted rhetoric of Trump. She noted a cordial personal relationship with Ivanka Trump despite stark political differences and joked about what her father would be called if he returned to the White House.

The piece also touches on broader convention themes: Chelsea’s effort to unify Sanders supporters (“Your cause is our cause”), Democrats’ spotlight on countering Trump’s proposed Muslim ban (notably through Khizr Khan’s speech), and the party’s emphasis on public safety and reclaiming traditional Republican themes. Finally, both Chelsea and Hillary highlighted the milestone of the first woman nominated for president and framed that achievement as advancing opportunity for all.

This document reviews international responses to Ebola outbreaks—primarily the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic and later flare-ups in the Democratic Republic of the Congo—and highlights humanitarian organizations’ roles in treatment, prevention and longer-term recovery.

Key points:

- The 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic was unprecedented: more than 26,900 infections and over 11,100 deaths, including heavy losses among health workers (869 infected, 507 killed), which further weakened already fragile health systems and disrupted care for other illnesses.

- AmeriCares response: beginning April 2014, AmeriCares focused on protecting health workers, expanding Ebola treatment capacity and restoring health services. Actions included:
  - Delivering millions of protective supplies and medical items to over 100 health facilities across Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea; in total more than 7 million units shipped, including 3.3 million pieces of PPE and large quantities of medicines and bleach.
  - Recruiting and managing clinical staff (over 180) and supplying the U.S. Department of Defense-built Ebola treatment unit (ETU) in Buchanan, Liberia, and supporting other IOM-run ETUs.
  - Running mobile clinics, measles vaccinations, psychosocial support for schools, and infection prevention & control (IPC) training.
  - Initiating longer-term health system strengthening: an 18-month maternal-newborn care project in Grand Bassa County (facility upgrades, equipment, staff training), IPC training programs in Sierra Leone’s Bonthe District, PPE and reunification kits for children in interim care centers, and large PPE/bleach shipments in Guinea to rebuild trust and IPC capacity.

- Other humanitarian responses:
  - World Food Programme (WFP): scaled up food assistance to prevent a food crisis, targeting more than one million people across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone (distributions to quarantined households, patients and affected communities), and coordinating logistics for the humanitarian response (Logistics Cluster, UNHRD, UNHAS).
  - Samaritan’s Purse: provided community protection programs, hygiene training, care centers, airlifted nearly 200 tons of supplies, public education campaigns and hospital reconstruction to aid recovery and rebuild trust.
  - International Medical Corps: operated ETUs, trained frontline workers and treated patients (example: Bong County ETU in Liberia discharged survivors, including infants).
  - UNICEF: major role in West Africa response delivering thousands of tons of supplies, community engagement, WASH (water, sanitation, hygiene) interventions, and vaccination and information campaigns in later DRC outbreaks.

- DRC outbreaks: The document summarizes responses to Ebola outbreaks in DRC (2018–2019), noting initial containment efforts, later escalation in conflict-affected eastern provinces (North Kivu, Ituri), high child vulnerability, and coordination of vaccination and response by WHO, UNICEF, MSF and national authorities.

- Ebola basics and ongoing needs: The text reiterates transmission (direct contact with bodily fluids and contaminated materials), clinical care measures (IV fluids, electrolyte balance, oxygen and blood pressure support), variable case-fatality rates, and the availability of vaccines for high-risk groups. It emphasizes continuing needs even as outbreaks ebb: PPE, medicines, IPC training, logistics and long-term health system strengthening to restore services and prevent future epidemics.

- Calls to action: The piece notes multiple ways the public can support relief efforts—donations, volunteering, and local Red Cross/Red Crescent engagement—and emphasizes the importance of protecting frontline workers and rebuilding community trust in health systems.

Overall message: International NGOs and UN agencies provided broad emergency and follow-up support—clinical staffing and ETUs, supplies and PPE, food assistance, logistics, training and community engagement—to control Ebola outbreaks, protect health workers and begin rebuilding health systems to prevent and respond to future epidemics.

Germany failed to win agreement from Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland to accept EU-wide relocation quotas for migrants, after Berlin warned of a sharp surge in arrivals and growing strains on public order. Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said the crisis was “the greatest challenge the EU has faced,” and that Germany now expects about 800,000 asylum-seekers this year and up to 40,000 could arrive in a single weekend. He urged a fair distribution of those still en route rather than leaving the burden to frontline states.

Talks in Prague ahead of a planned meeting of EU interior ministers produced no consensus on the European Commission’s proposal to relocate 160,000 migrants, and officials even raised the unusual possibility of using majority voting instead of the usual consensus. Germany signaled increasing preparedness to use domestic resources — Defense Minister Ursula von der Leyen put 4,000 troops on standby — and politicians warned the open-border humanitarian gesture the previous weekend may have encouraged more people to travel.

Eastern and Central European leaders reiterated migration as a matter of national sovereignty and resisted quotas. Hungary’s Prime Minister Viktor Orbán vowed tougher laws and arrests for illegal border crossings. Czech officials made similar sovereignty claims. Steinmeier countered that closing borders would betray European values. The U.N. said the Juncker plan would help but was insufficient and urged swift, broad participation.

Meanwhile, transport disruption escalated: Austria suspended regional rail traffic with Hungary and migrants were reported marching toward Vienna; Macedonia reported huge daily inflows and debated fence-building; and Mediterranean crossings hit record levels. The episode also featured a widely circulated video of a Hungarian camerawoman, Petra Laszlo, tripping and kicking fleeing migrants; she was fired, faces criminal charges, apologized publicly and said she panicked, while drawing intense public condemnation.

When Fox announced on May 6, 2015 that The Mindy Project would be canceled after three seasons, fans erupted online. That same day Mindy Kaling — vacationing in Montana with friends — posted a short, upbeat Instagram video that playfully referenced the news: “Hey guys, I'm in Montana, is anything happening in LA? #themindyproject.” The clip shows sweeping Montana twilight scenery and ends with Kaling smiling and winking, a cryptic but hopeful response amid reports that Hulu was in talks with Universal TV to pick up the series for additional seasons. The piece also notes the source’s broader effort to archive pages to prevent broken links.

Researchers have identified a new tyrannosaur species, Timurlengia euotica, from fossils unearthed in the Kyzylkum Desert of northern Uzbekistan. Dated to about 90 million years ago, Timurlengia fills a roughly 20-million-year gap in the tyrannosaur fossil record and sheds light on how small-bodied ancestors evolved into giant apex predators like Tyrannosaurus rex.

Key findings:
- Timurlengia was roughly horse-sized (around 200–250 kg), with long legs, blade-like teeth, and likely a fast, nimble pursuit-hunting lifestyle.
- CT scans of its braincase show a relatively large brain and inner-ear structures adapted for balance and low-frequency hearing—sensory capabilities similar to those of later, much larger tyrannosaurs.
- These features indicate that advanced senses and neuroanatomy evolved in tyrannosaurs before the dramatic increases in body size seen near the end of the Cretaceous. In short, they “got smart before they got big.”
- The timing suggests tyrannosaur gigantism occurred rapidly late in their history, possibly after other large predator groups declined, allowing tyrannosaurs to occupy apex niches.

The study was led by the University of Edinburgh with collaborators from Russian and U.S. institutions and is published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The discovery helps explain the evolutionary pathway that produced T. rex and increases understanding of tyrannosaur diversity during the late Mesozoic.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has opened a formal investigation into the Tesla Model S after two U.S. incidents this year in which road debris punctured the vehicle’s underbody and led to battery fires; a third fire in Mexico is outside NHTSA’s jurisdiction. In both U.S. cases, Tesla’s battery monitoring system alerted drivers, who stopped and exited before smoke or fire caused injury. Tesla reported no deaths or serious injuries from these fires.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk publicly defended the Model S’s safety, arguing that gasoline cars experience far more fires, injuries and deaths than Teslas, and pointing to the Model S’s structural protections (firewalls between battery modules and the cabin). Musk said Tesla requested a federal investigation to clear up public concerns—though NHTSA says its probe was an independent decision—and pledged to implement any regulator-recommended safety improvements.

Tesla is taking three immediate steps:
- A software update to increase highway ground clearance (reducing the chance of undercarriage strikes); a later update will let drivers set ride-height preferences.
- Asking NHTSA for a prompt, full investigation and promising to apply any warranted fixes to new and existing cars.
- Expanding warranty coverage to include fire-related damage (except deliberate arson), even if driver error is involved.

The incidents briefly affected Tesla’s stock price. Musk emphasized that, by Tesla’s metrics, Model S fires are far less frequent and less severe than gasoline-vehicle fires, and that the company will bear costs where appropriate to reassure buyers and protect the electric-vehicle adoption narrative.

In July 2016 a faction of the Turkish military launched a violent, overnight coup attempt that brought tanks and helicopters onto the streets of Ankara and Istanbul, struck Parliament and other targets, and left hundreds wounded and at least 160–265 people dead (Turkish official counts varied). President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who returned quickly from holiday and used smartphone video appeals to mobilize supporters, blamed followers of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gülen — long a onetime ally turned opponent — calling them the “parallel” network behind the plot and formally asking the U.S. to extradite Gülen. Gülen and his movement condemned the coup and deny any role; U.S. officials said Turkey had not yet presented evidence sufficient to warrant extradition.

The coup collapsed within a day as pro-government crowds, police and loyal military units confronted the plotters; large numbers of soldiers surrendered or were detained. Turkish authorities detained thousands: reports cited roughly 1,500–2,800 military personnel arrested, along with sweeping purges of the judiciary and civil service — thousands of judges and prosecutors were removed or detained and senior officers arrested. The government also moved quickly to purge suspected Gülenists across the police, intelligence and judicial ranks.

Background context: Fethullah Gülen is a moderate Sunni cleric who has promoted education, interfaith dialogue and secular-style curricula through a global network of schools and institutions (including more than 100 U.S. charter schools). He lived in self-imposed exile in Pennsylvania since 1999. The Gülen movement (Hizmet) was an influential ally of Erdoğan and the AK Party for years, helping weaken Turkey’s secular establishment through influence in police and judiciary; the relationship broke down after 2013 corruption probes and policy clashes, and Turkey designated the movement a terrorist organization in May 2016.

The immediate aftermath: The failed coup gave Erdoğan political cover to intensify a long-running consolidation of power. The government pledged to “cleanse” the military and judiciary of Gülenists and promised severe punishment for plotters. International reactions ranged from condemnation of the coup and support for Turkey’s elected government to caution from allies (notably the U.S.) about accepting Turkish allegations against Gülen without evidence. The upheaval strained Turkey’s institutions, threatened economic and tourism sectors, and raised concerns about broader instability and an intensified domestic crackdown that could further polarize Turkish society.

An Alaska Bureau of Land Management employee filmed a 22‑second clip of a 12–15‑foot long, icy, undulating object in the Chena River near Fairbanks that quickly went viral after being posted to the agency’s Facebook page. The footage, slightly sped up and given ominous music but otherwise unaltered, sparked hundreds of speculative comments and wide media pickup — suggestions ranged from giant sturgeon, lost sharks or seals, to fantastical “river monsters” and even “zombie salmon.” Federal and state experts, however, say the simplest explanation is most likely correct: frazil ice (loose, slushy river ice) accreted on a rope snagged on a bridge pier, which made the stationary rope appear to “swim” in the current. BLM and Alaska Department of Fish and Game officials shared that conclusion; while less sensational, it ended the mystery for authorities.

Executives of Wheel of Fortune are apologizing after an episode aired on about 200 local stations that included a puzzle answer reading “The Fast and The Furious” shortly after actor Paul Walker’s death in a high‑speed car crash. The show called it an “unfortunate coincidence,” saying the episode was taped weeks earlier. Host Pat Sajak also addressed the timing, noting the episode had been recorded long before the accident and expressing regret. The program extended condolences to Walker’s family, friends and fans.

The USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) has issued guidance recommending that meat and dairy producers adopt a single, consumer-friendly date label phrase—“Best If Used By”—to reduce confusion and curb food waste. Date labels like “Sell By,” “Use By,” and “Best Before” are voluntary and set by manufacturers; they often indicate quality rather than safety. FSIS says “Best If Used By” best communicates that the product will be at peak quality by that date but can remain wholesome and safe to eat if it shows no signs of spoilage. “Use By” should be reserved for infant formula, the only food currently required by law to carry a safety-related date.

The guidance is part of USDA efforts to cut food loss—about 30% of the U.S. food supply is estimated to be lost or discarded at retail and consumer levels—and complements past USDA/EPA initiatives and the national goal to halve food waste by 2030. FSIS is soliciting public comments for 60 days; the guidance is voluntary and applies primarily to products under USDA jurisdiction (meat, poultry, some egg and dairy items), while most packaged foods fall under the FDA. Advocates say unified labeling could reduce unnecessary disposal of edible food and associated environmental and economic costs. Legislative efforts to standardize date labeling have stalled, but industry could also adopt the phrasing voluntarily.

The document combines two linked pieces about how big, franchise-driven entertainment is reshaping Hollywood and what that means for filmmakers and mid‑budget films.

1) Disney’s success and the franchise model
- The Walt Disney Company has been thriving: stock near all‑time highs, EPS up 26% over nine months, and large investments (e.g., $1 billion Cars Land) paying off.
- Much of Disney’s growth is fueled by its film studio. Park expansions like California Adventure’s Pixar rebranding (Toy Story Mania, Cars Land) attract visitors by immersing fans in movie worlds, boosting attendance and revenue from parks, merchandise, TV spinoffs and licensing.
- Blockbuster films such as The Avengers create multiple revenue streams — box office, toys, TV projects, potential park attractions — illustrating why studios prioritize tentpoles that can be leveraged across businesses.
- That cross‑platform logic makes mid‑budget films harder to justify unless very low cost; studios now favor big global blockbusters that support broad merchandising and ancillary plays.

2) The decline of mid‑budget, adult‑oriented films and its human cost
- Over the past 15–20 years the industry shifted from a varied slate (many mid‑budget adult films) to a polarized model: very high‑budget tentpoles and micro‑budget indies, squeezing out the traditional mid‑budget range ($5M–$60M).
- Causes include skyrocketing production and especially marketing costs, the need for worldwide appeal and ancillary exploitation (theme parks, franchises), the collapse of reliable ancillary revenue streams (DVD market), and studio consolidation into conglomerates focused on cross‑vertical returns.
- Consequences:
  - Established auteur filmmakers (John Waters, David Lynch, Francis Ford Coppola, Steven Soderbergh, Spike Lee, James Toback and others) struggle to finance projects at the budgets they need or refuse to compromise artistically. Many have reduced output or left features altogether.
  - Independent producers face increased competition, lower budgets, and tighter margins; many projects must be made for far less than in past decades, if at all.
  - Some veteran filmmakers migrate to television and streaming, where serialized storytelling, creative freedom and new financing can be found, but TV is a different medium with its own limits and instability.
- Illustrative data: a comparison of Paramount’s 1997 slate (broad variety, 19 films including many mid‑range budgets) with a recent slate (fewer films, more $100M+ tentpoles) shows the industry’s consolidation toward big blockbusters.
- Industry observers warn the model is vulnerable: overreliance on franchises and foreign grosses could falter, potentially prompting another cycle of change (as happened in the 1960s–70s), but many filmmakers and films may be lost if that retrenchment continues.

Overall thesis
- The entertainment business increasingly prioritizes franchise films that can be monetized across parks, merchandise and TV, producing short‑term profitability and investor reward (as with Disney) but eroding the middle of the film ecosystem. That shift sidelines mid‑budget, adult‑oriented cinema and strains the careers of established auteurs, driving some to TV or out of filmmaking altogether — a cultural loss that could persist until the industry’s economic logic changes.

A former North Korean soldier, Lee So Yeon, and other defectors have testified that women in the North Korean military face severe neglect, widespread sexual violence and harsh living conditions. Lee, who served nearly a decade and is now a South Korea-based activist, described crowded concrete barracks, inadequate washing facilities (no hot water, contaminated hoses), rice-hull mattresses that retain foul odors, and chronic food shortages. Malnutrition and stress commonly caused female recruits to stop menstruating; sanitary provision was poor and reusable cloth pads were frequently washed in secret.

Defectors and researchers say sexual harassment and rape are endemic: commanders and squad leaders have raped low-ranking women with little likelihood of punishment because victims rarely testify. Other witnesses reported sexual assaults in civilian jobs (trains, border work) and in prison camps for repatriated escapees; forced abortions have also been reported. Observers caution that defector testimony should be treated carefully given incentives to sensationalize, but independent researchers’ interviews corroborate many of the claims.

Recent policy changes include mandatory seven-year military service for women and government claims of improved sanitary distribution and cosmetics for female units—moves some analysts interpret as morale-building or overcorrection rather than comprehensive reform. Overall, scholars and defectors portray a patriarchal, militarized system where women bear heavy physical burdens, face sexual abuse, and have limited recourse.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has proposed removing the Oregon chub—a small minnow endemic to Oregon’s Willamette Valley—from the Endangered Species Act protections, marking the first time a fish would be delisted due to recovery. The chub was listed as endangered in 1993 after widespread floodplain habitat loss and predation by introduced fish left fewer than 1,000 fish in about eight populations. A 1998 recovery plan emphasizing habitat restoration, private‑land partnerships, translocations, modified dam flows and monitoring led to steady gains: the species was reclassified as “threatened” in 2010 and now numbers roughly 150,000–180,000 individuals across about 80 sites. The delisting proposal opens a 60‑day public comment period and would be followed by nine years of post‑delisting monitoring; final removal is contingent on that process. Officials credit collaborations among federal and state agencies, landowners and conservation groups for restoring chub habitat in ways compatible with agriculture and other land uses. The chub’s recovery has also benefited other native species (salmon, pond turtles, red‑legged frogs) and joins a small group of animals that have been downlisted or delisted after population recoveries.

This article analyzes the first trailer for Peter Jackson’s film adaptation of The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey and highlights five key takeaways:

1. New material appears in the first film
- Jackson and the writers have expanded Tolkien’s story using material from other Tolkien works. Elements of a side-quest involving Gandalf, Galadriel and other powers confronting a dark threat in Mirkwood—material not in the original Hobbit novel—are present in the trailer, so that added storyline is introduced in the first movie rather than being held for the second.

2. Middle-earth feels authentic
- The trailer preserves the look and tone of Middle-earth fans expect. Hobbiton, Bag End, Gandalf and cameo appearances from actors associated with the earlier films (brief glimpses of Elijah Wood and Ian Holm) recreate a familiar, comfortable sense of place.

3. The dwarves read as dwarves in context
- Early images had raised concerns that the dwarves looked too modern or "sexy," but the trailer shows them behaving and feeling like dwarves—gruff, bearded, proud, and given a stirring group song—so their characterization works in motion.

4. Gollum’s cave is more illuminated
- The critical Bilbo–Gollum scene, which is pitch-black in the book, appears to have been brightened for the film. That makes the sequence visible in 3D but moves away from the book’s “inky” darkness.

5. Tolkien-style songs are prominent
- The trailer features the dwarves’ song “Misty Mountains,” suggesting music and the characters’ songs will play a more prominent role in the adaptation, echoing Tolkien’s frequent use of verse.

Overall, the trailer is praised as cinematic and faithful-feeling while signposting the film’s expanded narrative choices and stylistic adaptations for 3D cinema.

Justice Clarence Thomas asked questions from the Supreme Court bench for the first time in about 10 years during oral arguments in Voisine v. United States, a challenge to a federal law that bars people convicted of domestic violence misdemeanors from possessing firearms. Thomas intervened late in the hour while U.S. government attorney Ilana Eisenstein was defending the law, pressing whether a misdemeanor conviction should be able to “suspend a constitutional right” (the Second Amendment) and asking for other examples where a misdemeanor does so. He probed whether the statute’s reach to reckless, not just intentional, conduct was justified and how long any suspension of rights lasts. The case arises from two Maine men—Stephen Voisine and William Armstrong—who entered conditional guilty pleas to reckless/simple assault and later were charged under the federal firearms ban when guns were found or turned in; they argue that reckless conduct should not qualify as a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” that triggers the ban.

Thomas’s break in silence was notable because he has rarely spoken at oral argument (his last question was Feb. 22, 2006) and has said he relies on briefs and chamber deliberations rather than courtroom questioning. The appearance came shortly after the death of Justice Antonin Scalia, Thomas’s close friend and frequent interlocutor at arguments. Other justices’ questioning during the session largely favored the government’s view that recklessness can fall under domestic-violence statutes, and the wider argument focused on statutory interpretation—whether “use” or related language requires intent—or should encompass reckless acts.

Flamingo Air, a small Cincinnati-based charter company led by CEO David MacDonald, has for decades offered private “romantic flights” that let couples have sex in the air—essentially a legal, marketed pathway to join the “mile high club.” The idea began as a bet and has become a niche, sustainable sideline: for about $425–$495 couples get a one-hour private flight in a small plane, served with champagne and chocolates, a discreet pilot up front, and a cushioned rear area where the pair can be intimate. MacDonald emphasizes marketing the experience as romantic and classy rather than overtly sexual, a strategy he credits for steady demand—often from straightlaced, middle-aged or older couples and frequently booked by women—especially around anniversaries and Valentine’s Day. Flamingo Air averages a few such flights weekly and also runs a flight school and other aviation training services. A Las Vegas operator, Love Cloud, offers a similar product and has found similar customer patterns. Accounts from customers note practical awkwardness (small cabin, turbulence, pilot nearby), but many callers treat the flights as memorable, bucket-list experiences rather than sleazy adventures.

Scientists have described a new, unusually feathered dinosaur from northeastern China—Changyuraptor yangi—dating to about 125 million years ago. The meat-eating microraptorine measured roughly 1.2–1.3 m (about 4 ft) long and weighed around 4 kg (9 lb), making it the largest known “four-winged” dinosaur. Its body, forelimbs and hind limbs were covered in feathers, and it possessed exceptionally long tail feathers—about 30 cm (1 ft), the longest known among non-avian dinosaurs.

Changyuraptor’s anatomy closely resembles primitive birds such as Archaeopteryx, blurring distinctions between birds and bird-like dinosaurs. Bone microstructure indicates the specimen was fully grown. Researchers believe it was unlikely to have achieved sustained, powered flight like modern birds but could probably flap and perform gliding or controlled descents—its long tail feathers may have helped slow descent and enable safer landings. Feathers may also have served roles in display, species recognition or mating.

The fossil was found in Liaoning Province, a prolific region for feathered dinosaur discoveries. The study detailing Changyuraptor was published in Nature Communications.

A Queensland teenager suspended after a Vegemite (or possibly chicken) sandwich was thrown at Prime Minister Julia Gillard says he’s innocent and phoned a radio station to protest the school’s decision. Sixteen‑year‑old Kyle Thomson was suspended for three weeks after the incident at Marsden State High School during Gillard’s visit, but he and his mother, Anna, say Kyle only knocked a sandwich out of another student’s hand to stop a second throw and was wrongly blamed. Gillard laughed off the episode on air, declined to intervene with the school’s punishment and urged Kyle to speak with the principal. The episode drew widespread media and online attention—nicknamed “#sandwichgate”—with conflicting accounts about what happened and debate over whether the school overreacted because the target was the Prime Minister.

The FBI’s annual Hate Crime Statistics report for 2017 shows a roughly 17% increase in reported hate crime incidents—7,175 in 2017 versus 6,121 in 2016. Part of the rise reflects improved reporting: about 1,000 more law enforcement agencies submitted data in 2017. Of the incidents, 7,106 were single-bias and 69 involved multiple biases. The leading bias categories in single-bias incidents were race/ethnicity/ancestry (59.6%), religion (20.6%), and sexual orientation (15.8%). About 5,000 incidents were crimes against persons (e.g., intimidation, assault) and roughly 3,000 were crimes against property (e.g., vandalism, robbery); some incidents fall into both categories.

The FBI is working to increase and improve reporting by training officers on identifying and reporting bias-motivated incidents and by supporting DOJ resources such as a new hate crimes webpage. The report’s data are intended to inform the public, researchers, community leaders, and law enforcement so they can better understand, prevent, and investigate hate crimes, which remain a top priority for the FBI’s civil rights program.

Australia, at Malaysia’s request, is leading the underwater search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 via the Australian Transport Safety Bureau and the Joint Agency Coordination Centre (JACC). As of 11 January 2017 the international search effort continues in the southern Indian Ocean and is being conducted methodically; progress can appear slow but work is ongoing.

Current operations and status:
- Fugro vessels are conducting underwater searches. The Fugro Equator is completing final survey “swings” with an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV); five AUV missions were completed in the past week though some recoveries and maintenance were delayed by weather. Weather in the immediate forecast was not expected to significantly affect AUV operations.
- Fugro Equator’s current search work was expected to conclude in January 2017.
- International ministers (Malaysia, Australia and China) agreed on 22 July 2016 that if the aircraft is not found within the agreed search area and no credible new evidence pinpoints a location, the search will be suspended when the current area is completed. That decision is a suspension, not a permanent termination: credible new information would prompt reconsideration and possible resumption.

Incidents and setbacks:
- A towfish (a towed sonar vehicle) being used by Fugro Discovery struck a 2,200-meter-high mud volcano, causing its cable to break and the towfish plus about 4.5 km (2.8 mi) of cable to sink to the ocean floor. No crew were injured; the JACC reported it may be possible to recover the towfish later. A spare towfish was being prepared and the towing vessel returned to Western Australia for replacement cable.
- Separately, the vessel Havila Harmony sustained damage when a fishing net bent its underwater communications pole; it underwent repairs in dry dock and was expected to resume searching after repairs.
- Despite these setbacks, roughly 70% of the internationally agreed 46,000-square-mile search zone had been covered. The operation was projected to continue until mid-2017 unless credible new information alters plans.

Findings to date:
- The only confirmed aircraft debris recovered so far is a flaperon that washed ashore on Réunion Island in July. Sonar searches have also located a 19th-century shipwreck and other seabed features, but not the MH370 wreckage.
