The South African government has begun using existing laws to seize privately owned farmland where purchase negotiations have stalled, as part of broader plans to accelerate land reform and test arguments for expropriation without compensation ahead of a proposed constitutional amendment. City Press and other outlets report that two game farms in Limpopo—owned by Akkerland Boerdery—were selected for unilateral takeover after the owners rejected a government offer roughly one-tenth of their asking price. The owners obtained an urgent court injunction to halt eviction; the Department of Rural Development and Land Reform is opposing that application and says courts will determine what is “just and equitable” compensation.

This action is framed by the ANC as addressing apartheid-era land imbalances: a 2017 audit found white people own about 72% of private farmland, though whites are under 9% of the population. The government has reportedly drawn up lists of farms to test seizure procedures; Afriforum published a purported list of some 190 targeted farms, prompting accusations and denials—department officials called the list fake, while Afriforum and farm groups say its authenticity is vindicated by the targeting of named properties. Agricultural unions and some media have criticized the publication as inflammatory or misleading.

The moves have stoked fear among farmers and investors about property rights and agricultural investment; some farmers report falling land values and canceled sales. The ANC and President Cyril Ramaphosa argue constitutional clarity and accelerated land reform are necessary to redress historical injustice, while opponents warn of economic harm amid already weak growth and high unemployment.

A Colorado first grader, 6-year-old Elijah Thurston, was suspended one day from Stratton Meadows Elementary after pointing his finger like a gun at a classmate and saying “You’re dead.” School staff explained the meaning of “dead” to him and warned him not to confuse play with reality; the suspension will be recorded on his permanent record. His father, Austin Thurston, called the punishment excessive and said the family had already taught Elijah that school isn’t the place for gun play and that he understands the difference between pretend and real violence. Elijah is writing an apology to the school voluntarily. The district defended the suspension as appropriate and declined further comment citing student privacy.

The article places this incident alongside another recent case in Virginia: an 11-year-old sixth grader (identified as RMB) was suspended for 10 days, expelled for a year, and had marijuana charges filed after school staff found plant material and a lighter in his backpack. Subsequent tests showed the plant was not marijuana; the school cited a zero-tolerance policy that also bans lookalike substances. RMB’s parents say he may have been the victim of a prank and that the ordeal has harmed his mental health; they seek his return to his original school and expungement of his record. Both stories are used to critique broad zero-tolerance school policies that can produce severe punishments for young children over ambiguous or noncriminal behavior.

A man who heckled Bristol Palin at a Sunset Strip bar in September 2011 has sued her and Lifetime/A&E for defamation, invasion of privacy and emotional distress. Talent manager Stephen Hanks says video of the incident — in which he shouted that Palin’s mother was “a whore” and she confronted him, asking if he was gay — was used in publicity for Palin’s upcoming Lifetime reality show without his permission. Hanks alleges Palin later told In Touch magazine the encounter helped prompt her move back to Alaska, but he says she had already bought a home there two months earlier, so her statements harmed his reputation and career. The suit, filed in federal court in Los Angeles seeking more than $75,000, claims Hanks never consented to be filmed and that Palin’s public comments were defamatory and degrading. Representatives for Palin and Lifetime did not comment.

Bill O’Reilly announced at the end of his broadcast that he is taking a planned vacation and will return April 24. The break comes amid a widening advertiser boycott and reports that O’Reilly paid roughly $13 million in settlements to several women who accused him of sexual harassment. About 60 companies have pulled ads from The O’Reilly Factor, and paid ad time on the show has fallen by more than half, according to Kantar Media. Despite the controversy, his ratings remain strong: the show averaged about 3.7 million viewers last week (up from the prior week and year) and posted its best quarter ever for the first three months of 2017.

Speculation has grown that the vacation could be a de facto suspension or prelude to his departure. New York magazine’s Gabriel Sherman, citing unnamed and “highly placed” Fox sources, reported internal talk that the episode might be O’Reilly’s last and that 21st Century Fox CEO James Murdoch wants him off the air, while Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch are reportedly more hesitant. Fox has denied that the break is punitive. Meanwhile, Paul, Weiss — the law firm retained over the Roger Ailes scandal — is reported to be investigating additional harassment claims, including one flagged through Fox’s anonymous hotline.

A series of low‑intensity bombs detonated at and around the Mahabodhi (Bodh Gaya) temple complex in Bihar, eastern India, injuring two people and causing minor damage. Four of the eight or nine blasts occurred within the UNESCO World Heritage site—near the Bodhi tree believed to be a descendant of the tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment—while the others struck nearby sacred locations; the tree and the main temple were not damaged. A 50‑year‑old Tibetan and a 30‑year‑old Myanmar national were hurt. Authorities described the devices as timed and treated the incident as a terror attack; no group claimed responsibility, though police suspected the home‑grown Islamist group Indian Mujahideen, which has been blamed for numerous past bombings in India. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh condemned the attacks. The event came amid rising regional tensions involving Buddhists in neighboring countries.

A temporary ceasefire between Israel and Gaza militants collapsed as rocket fire from Gaza resumed and Israel carried out airstrikes in response. Hamas said the wife and child of its military commander Mohammed Deif were killed. Israeli officials reported dozens of rockets — initially three that landed in open areas near Beersheba and later many more, some reaching Tel Aviv and Jerusalem — but few or no Israeli casualties were reported. Israel said roughly 50 rockets were launched on one day and later military statements described more than 25 airstrikes across Gaza.

Egypt-hosted talks in Cairo aimed at a longer truce ended without agreement and both Israeli and Palestinian delegations withdrew. Negotiators remained far apart: Palestinians demanded a lifting of the Israeli and Egyptian blockade and reconstruction measures including a seaport and airport; Israel insisted on Gaza’s demilitarization and control over crossings to prevent rearmament. Palestinian negotiators accused Israel of undermining the talks; Israel blamed renewed rocket fire for making talks impossible. The US expressed concern and blamed Hamas for breaking the ceasefire, while affirming Israel’s right to defend itself.

The conflict, which began with Israel’s Operation Protective Edge on 8 July to stop rocket attacks and destroy cross-border tunnels, has produced heavy casualties and destruction: Palestinian health authorities reported about 2,016 deaths including many civilians, while Israeli authorities reported roughly 66–67 deaths, mostly soldiers. Observers note both sides face domestic pressures—Hamas for tangible gains for Gazans, Israel to avoid appearing to reward militants—and analysts warn that without international pressure a fragile informal truce or controlled, unilateral steps may replace a formal agreement, leaving Gaza’s humanitarian crisis and political impasse unresolved.

Intensified Russian and NATO military exercises are increasing tensions in Europe and raising the risk of miscalculation, a report by the London-based European Leadership Network (ELN) finds. Both sides say their drills are defensive, but the scale, scope and focus suggest they are training with the other’s capabilities and likely war plans in mind: Russia’s large, often unannounced snap exercises this year have ranged from the Arctic to the Far East and have included strategic aviation, naval missile and nuclear-capable forces; NATO has responded with increased activity and command units in eastern Europe and sizable multinational exercises such as Allied Shield, BALTOPS and Saber Strike.

The ELN does not claim war is inevitable, but says the “changed profile” of exercises sustains a climate of fear and unpredictability—especially when drills are not pre-notified—creating a dangerous dynamic where each side’s preparations provoke the other. Examples of risky incidents, such as close encounters between Russian military aircraft and civilian airliners, underscore the danger.

Reactions differ: NATO’s deputy spokesperson argued the report unfairly equates the two sides and stressed Russia’s exercises are larger and less transparent; Moscow frames NATO expansion as a threat and justifies its own posture. The ELN recommends improved communication and prior notification of exercises, limits on large drills near borders, renewed incident‑prevention links, and longer-term arms‑control measures to reduce the risk of accidental confrontation.

At the 2015 Emmy Awards, organizers drew widespread criticism after airing a montage that included series finales and revealing scenes from recently ended shows such as Mad Men, Boardwalk Empire, Nurse Jackie and Parenthood. Viewers took to Twitter to complain that the segment spoiled key finales they had not yet seen; host Andy Samberg jokingly acknowledged the backlash, quipping “Welcome back to the spoiler awards” after the clip. Some defended the Emmys, noting many of the series concluded months earlier, but many fans said the ceremony had ruined the chance to watch those finales unspoiled. The controversy came amid a night of wins including Game of Thrones, Jon Hamm’s long-awaited lead-actor Emmy, and other major awards.

President Trump reacted to Tuesday’s Alabama special Senate election, in which Democrat Doug Jones defeated Republican Roy Moore. On Wednesday Trump tweeted that he initially backed Luther Strange because he believed Moore “will not be able to win the General Election,” saying he was “right” and that “the deck was stacked against him.” He also argued the result shows the GOP needs “GREAT Republican candidates” to protect narrow House and Senate margins. Trump had at first urged Moore to step aside after molestation allegations surfaced, then endorsed him late in the race, recording a robocall and holding a rally for him.

Moore, a former Alabama Supreme Court chief justice twice removed from the bench, faced multiple accusations that he sexually assaulted girls as young as 14 when he was in his 30s; he denied the allegations. Jones’s victory makes him the first Alabama Democrat elected to the Senate in 25 years and narrows the GOP Senate majority to 51–49.

Reactions included praise for Trump’s initial support of Strange from Sen. Lindsey Graham and criticism of Steve Bannon for backing Moore. Media figure Matt Drudge tweeted that Strange “would have won in a landslide.” Democrats framed the result as a response from women and African-American voters unhappy with the tone of Trump’s presidency; Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Vice President Joe Biden both lauded Jones and suggested Senate Republicans were relieved not to be tied to Moore.

German officials responded to a suspected terror threat that forced the cancellation of a Germany–Netherlands friendly in Hanover on Tuesday night, prompting heightened security and political debate.

Key developments:
- Authorities evacuated thousands from the Hannover stadium after a tip—reported to have come from foreign (French) intelligence—warning of a possible attack on a German sporting event. Police searched the city overnight but found no explosives and made no arrests; patrols continued in a reduced form.
- State leaders said there was currently no further specific threat to Hanover or to large public events. Hanover’s mayor and Chancellor Merkel praised residents and security services for calm and professionalism; ticket refunds for evacuated fans were announced.
- Security responses: North Rhine-Westphalia said it would boost policing at Christmas markets; the Bundesliga’s weekend matches were planned to go ahead, though with consideration of increased security measures. Germany’s domestic intelligence chief, Hans-Georg Maaßen, warned Germany is a target for ISIS and called the threat “very high,” while advising against blanket cancellations of large events.
- Political fallout: Opposition figures criticized Interior Minister Thomas de Maizière for withholding details of the threat, accusing him of stoking fear by not being transparent; defenders argued disclosure could endanger sources.
- Related incidents and context: Berlin-born rapper Denis “Deso Dogg” Cuspert may still be alive in Syria despite U.S. claims he was killed. Turkey arrested eight men in Istanbul allegedly planning to travel to Germany, with documents indicating a route through Greece to Germany. Sweden raised its terror alert following concrete information of a plot. A false-alarm police operation at a Stuttgart-area school (a man with a toy gun) underscored a tense national atmosphere.
- Institutional responses: The German Police Union rejected proposals to use soldiers for police duties, citing constitutional limits and a need for better police resourcing.

Overall, officials stressed vigilance and proportional security measures while trying to balance public information, civil liberties and protecting intelligence sources amid elevated terror concerns following recent European attacks.

A high-profile sale of a tiny pour of purportedly ultra-rare Macallan 1878 ended in embarrassment after forensic tests showed the bottle was a fake. In late July at the Devil’s Place bar in the Waldhaus am See hotel, St. Moritz, Chinese novelist Zhang Wei paid about CHF10,000 (≈$10,000 / £7,600) for a three-quarter‑ounce dram poured from an unopened bottle claimed to be the last 1878 Macallan in circulation. Experts quickly raised doubts about the bottle’s label, cork and historical details, noting inconsistencies (eg. references to a nonexistent “Macallan and Talisker Distilleries Ltd”) and similarities to batches of fake Macallans that surfaced in the early 2000s.

The hotel sent samples to Rare Whisky 101 and to laboratories in Scotland and Oxford. Carbon dating gave a 95% probability the liquid dated from around 1970–72, and further analysis suggested the spirit was likely a blended Scotch (about 60% malt, 40% grain), not a single malt from 1878. The bottle was therefore judged essentially worthless as a collector’s item. The Waldhaus accepted the findings, refunded Zhang in full (the manager flew to China to return the money and apologize), and said it would continue investigations and destroy confirmed fakes. Macallan owner Edrington and industry specialists urged buyers and sellers to authenticate rare bottles and warned of increasing fraud in the rare-whisky market.

South Korea and Japan announced a landmark agreement to resolve the long-standing dispute over “comfort women” — women, mostly Korean, forced into sexual slavery by Japan’s Imperial Army during World War II. Announced after a meeting of the two countries’ foreign ministers in Seoul, the deal includes a formal apology from Japan and a government-funded payment of about 1 billion yen (≈ $8.3 million) to a fund administered by South Korea to support the surviving victims and finance projects to restore their dignity and provide psychological care.

Both governments characterized the accord as a “final and irreversible” resolution if Japan fulfills its pledges. The agreement also commits both sides to refrain from criticizing each other internationally over the issue and envisions consultations in Seoul about a contentious statue of a girl erected outside the Japanese embassy. Japanese leaders framed the deal as closing a painful chapter so it will not be passed to future generations; South Korean leaders stressed urgency because most survivors are elderly (only a few dozen remain).

Reactions were mixed: the U.S. and U.N. welcomed the accord as promoting reconciliation and regional security cooperation (important given North Korea’s threats), while some survivors and activists criticized it for not guaranteeing direct individual government compensation and questioned whether victims were fully consulted. The deal was seen as politically timely — marking wartime anniversaries and easing bilateral tensions that have impeded deeper security cooperation between two key U.S. allies.

Hostess Brands, maker of iconic snacks like Twinkies, Wonder Bread and Drake’s Devil Dogs, told a federal bankruptcy court it must liquidate and close operations after a nationwide bakers’ strike over a court-imposed contract. The shutdown will cost nearly 18,500 employees their jobs, close 33 bakeries, 565 distribution centers and 570 outlet stores, and halt production immediately (final deliveries were made Thursday night). Outlet stores will sell existing stock for about a week and retail shelves may still contain products until sold.

Hostess, which had about $2.5 billion in annual sales and produced roughly 500 million Twinkies and 127 million loaves of Wonder Bread a year, will seek court approval to sell its assets to the highest bidders; brands could be revived under new owners, but displaced workers would not automatically be rehired.

The Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers and Grain Millers union (about 5,000 Hostess employees) refused a concession contract that management obtained permission from the bankruptcy court to impose. Union leaders called the liquidation a failure of management and investor owners, criticizing repeated restructuring and cuts demanded of workers. The Teamsters (representing 6,700 employees) narrowly approved a separate concessions deal; they blamed mismanagement but said their vote protected jobs.

Hostess filed for bankruptcy in January (its second since 2004) and is controlled by investment firms including Silver Point Capital and Monarch Alternative Capital. The company had sought worker concessions including an 8% salary cut in year one (with modest increases later), reduced pension and health contributions, in exchange for equity and board representation for workers. CEO Gregory Rayburn said the company lacked the resources to survive an extended strike and regretted the outcome.

About 10,000 people fled from Myanmar into Thailand after heavy fighting broke out along the Thailand–Myanmar border around the town of Myawaddy, opposite Mae Sot, following Myanmar’s highly criticised national election. Clashes involved Myanmar government forces and a breakaway faction of the Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA) that opposes the junta and objects to alleged coercion of voters and attempted integration of ethnic forces into a state-controlled border guard. Myanmar troops reportedly retook Myawaddy after reinforcements; both sides suffered casualties and at least five Thai civilians and several Myanmar refugees were wounded when shells and a stray rocket-propelled grenade struck Thai territory. Thailand did not return fire and prepared to provide humanitarian assistance as refugee numbers rose.

The violence erupted after polls closed in Myanmar’s first election in 20 years, a vote widely condemned by Western governments and the UN as neither free nor transparent. Opposition parties were constrained or boycotted, international monitors were barred, and many seats were uncontested or skewed toward the pro-military Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP). Observers and opposition figures alleged vote rigging and advance-ballot abuses. Global leaders — including US President Barack Obama, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon — denounced the election; sanctions and international pressure were signalled. The post-election period also focused attention on whether detained opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi would be released when her house-arrest term ended.

The Senate Commerce Committee released a report and held a hearing after a year-long probe of nine major data brokers and testimony from privacy groups, revealing widespread collection and sale of highly detailed, sensitive consumer profiles. Companies queried included Acxiom, Experian, Epsilon, Reed Elsevier, Equifax, TransUnion, Rapleaf, Spokeo, and Datalogix; some cooperated (notably Equifax), while others (Acxiom, Experian, Epsilon) refused to disclose collection and sales practices, citing confidentiality.

Findings and testimonies show brokers compile massive dossiers—Acxiom claims multi-sourced insight on roughly 700 million people—and sell lists sorted by thousands of attributes (Equifax described a taxonomy with more than 75,000 data points). Examples include purchases (soft drinks, shampoo), health-related product use (laxatives, yeast infection treatments), medical visit counts (OB/GYN visits), travel and alcohol consumption, and lifestyle indicators (pet owner, smoker, veteran, donation behavior). Privacy groups and the World Privacy Forum uncovered and testified that brokers sell lists identifying rape victims, people with HIV/AIDS, seniors with dementia, domestic violence shelter contacts, police officers’ home addresses, and those with addictions—sometimes enabling harm or identity theft. Experian’s subsidiary reportedly sold social security and banking data to an alleged identity-theft ring and sought gun-permit data.

Current U.S. law protects consumer data only in limited contexts (credit, employment, insurance, housing); medical privacy rules don’t cover information gathered from non-medical sources (e.g., over-the-counter purchases). Opt-out mechanisms are inconsistent or opaque, and consumers generally cannot learn what is held or who buys it. The probe highlights a large, growing industry (estimated $156 billion) operating with little transparency or consumer control. Senators and privacy advocates called for stronger regulation and oversight to remove harmful lists and increase transparency; committee chair Jay Rockefeller described the practices as a “dark underside” that merits government action.

President Trump, traveling in Europe ahead of a high-stakes summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin, gave interviews in Scotland and the U.K. in which he criticized several Western institutions and leaders and discussed topics from trade to domestic politics.

Key points:

- Trump called the European Union “a foe” on trade grounds, arguing EU countries — including NATO members — have taken advantage of the U.S. and failed to meet defense spending commitments. He singled out Germany for striking a natural-gas pipeline deal with Russia (Nord Stream 2), saying it gives Moscow leverage and amounts to “waving a white flag.” German Chancellor Angela Merkel pushed back, stressing Germany’s independent policy decisions.

- He reiterated a tough stance toward NATO allies for underfunding defense, while claiming his pressure at the recent Brussels summit produced increased financial commitments.

- On Russia and his upcoming meeting with Vladimir Putin in Helsinki, Trump said he had “low expectations” but hoped for positive outcomes. He criticized the special counsel’s Russia investigation as a “witch hunt” that harms U.S. relations with Russia and other countries and called aspects of the probe partisan and disgraceful.

- In other interviews (with Piers Morgan and the Daily Mail) Trump discussed multiple issues: he called Putin “probably” ruthless but said better U.S.–Russia relations would be beneficial; defended aspects of his immigration enforcement while disputing claims about family separations; discussed his Supreme Court pick Brett Kavanaugh and the odds Roe v. Wade might be revisited; praised his meeting with Queen Elizabeth II but declined to discuss details; and described his tweeting habits as highly hands-on.

- The interviews and comments aggravated diplomatic tensions with close allies, came after contentious NATO and U.K. visits (including criticism of British Prime Minister Theresa May’s Brexit approach and his reported advice that she “sue the EU”), and preceded his Helsinki summit with Putin.

Overall, Trump framed trade competition and defense spending shortfalls as central grievances with Europe, reiterated skepticism about the Russia probe, and stressed a transactional view of alliances while signaling cautious optimism about talks with Putin.

President Obama told Afghan President Hamid Karzai by phone that he has ordered the Pentagon to plan for a full U.S. troop withdrawal from Afghanistan by Dec. 31 if Kabul does not sign the bilateral security agreement (BSA) Washington negotiated. The White House said Karzai’s prolonged refusal to sign—or to grant U.S. forces immunity from Afghan prosecution—has made a post-2014 U.S. presence increasingly difficult to plan. Obama left open the possibility of a smaller, narrowly focused mission after 2014 (training, advising Afghan forces and limited counterterrorism) if a BSA is eventually concluded, but warned the longer talks drag on the smaller and less ambitious any mission will be.

Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel began contingency planning for the “zero option” and was taking that posture to NATO defense ministers in Brussels. White House Press Secretary Jay Carney and other officials stressed that without a signed BSA Congress and the Pentagon are unlikely to approve keeping troops in-country. U.S. commanders say Afghan forces have improved tactically but still lack institutional capacity (logistics, sustainment, ministerial budgeting and advanced capabilities) and will need continued international support to avoid instability that could create terrorist safe havens. The impasse has prompted congressional scrutiny and scheduled hearings on Afghanistan’s future.

Six Russian military aircraft were intercepted off Alaska this week by U.S. and Canadian fighters after entering North American Air Defense Identification Zones (ADIZ), officials said. Two Alaska-based U.S. F-22s intercepted six Russian planes—identified as two IL-78 tankers, two MiG-31 fighters and two Bear long-range bombers—about 55 nautical miles off Alaska Wednesday evening; the Russian aircraft looped south and returned to base. More than six hours later, two Canadian CF-18s intercepted two Bear bombers roughly 40 nautical miles off the Canadian Arctic coast in the Beaufort Sea. In both cases the aircraft entered the ADIZ (which extends roughly 200 miles from the coastline) but did not cross into sovereign U.S. or Canadian airspace (which extends 12 nautical miles). NORAD said such intercepts are not uncommon (occurring up to about 10 times a year and more than 50 Russian bomber approaches in five years). U.S. officials suggested the incidents may have been related to a visit by Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko to North America. Separately, Sweden reported two Russian military aircraft violated its airspace near the island of Öland, calling it a “serious violation” and summoning the Russian ambassador.

The Pentagon’s Office of Net Assessment (ONA) has funded a long-running program, called the Body Leads Project, that analyzes leaders’ body movements to infer decision-making styles and predict likely actions. Using movement pattern analysis—a method originating with Rudolf Laban and expanded by Warren Lamb that treats each person’s “body signature” of linked movements as a window into thinking and truthfulness—the project has studied more than a dozen foreign leaders, including Vladimir Putin (studied in reports from 2008 and 2012), Dmitry Medvedev, Saddam Hussein and Osama bin Laden.

ONA has supported Brenda Connors of the Naval War College since the mid-1990s and paid outside experts such as Warren Lamb, psychiatrist Richard Rende and Harvard’s Timothy Colton for related work; contracting records show roughly $300,000 a year has been spent on the effort since 2009. Connors and colleagues published an academic paper on movement pattern analysis and decision-making in Frontiers in Psychology, and Connors has previously commented publicly about Putin’s gait and its possible psychological implications.

Pentagon officials said the studies are intended to provide insight into leaders’ attitudes and mindsets rather than to make direct policy recommendations. Although the reports are not classified, ONA and Pentagon spokespeople have said they will not be released publicly; Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel and other senior officials have not been directly involved in using the studies to shape policy. The program drew attention amid the 2014 Russia–Ukraine/Crimea crisis as U.S. policymakers sought better ways to anticipate Putin’s actions.

An interaction between an Indiana State Trooper and a Muncie man, Greg Barnes Jr., has gone viral after Barnes posted a selfie of the two following a traffic stop. Barnes was pulled over on State Road 332 for speeding; after the trooper ran his information and issued a warning, they talked for several minutes about their days and the broader tensions around policing that sometimes lead to hostile or deadly encounters. Barnes asked to take a selfie to show children and others that not all police encounters are negative. He posted the photo and a message urging mutual respect — “not as ‘black man’ and ‘blue police officer,’ but as humans” — ending with the hashtag #Respect. Trooper Shawn Cosgrove said he agreed to the photo because of its positive intent. The post has resonated widely, garnering hundreds of thousands of shares, and both men noted that respectful behavior can make traffic stops go much more smoothly, though it won’t always prevent a ticket.

Texas Children’s Hospital cared for and then successfully separated conjoined twin girls Knatalye Hope and Adeline Faith Mata, born April 11, 2014, at 31 weeks gestation. The twins, from Lubbock, were discovered to be conjoined at a 19-week ultrasound on Jan. 13, 2014. They were joined at the chest and abdomen and shared multiple structures — including liver, diaphragm, pericardial sac, portions of intestine and colon, pelvic structures and some lung tissue.

After multidisciplinary prenatal planning and neonatal care in the hospital’s Level IV NICU, the team prepared for separation by placing custom tissue expanders in December 2014 to grow extra skin for closure. A multidisciplinary surgical team of more than 26 clinicians (including 12 surgeons from pediatric surgery, plastic surgery, cardiovascular surgery, urology, liver transplant, orthopedics and pediatric gynecology, plus anesthesiologists and nursing staff) performed the separation on Feb. 17, 2015. The official separation occurred about 18 hours into the complex operation; surgeons worked roughly 18 hours to separate them and spent about 23 hours operating on Knatalye and 26 hours on Adeline. The hospital called it the first successful separation for twins with that particular thoraco‑omphalo‑ischiopagus configuration.

Both girls are recovering in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit and are expected to remain hospitalized for months; additional surgeries and rehabilitation (to develop mobility and other skills) are anticipated. Their parents, Elysse and John Eric Mata, expressed gratitude to the care teams and supporters. Fundraising efforts helped the family with relocation and expenses during the hospitalization and recovery period.

Indie band Stargroves released “Westfjords” (Sept 14, 2012), a twangy track written by Teddy Watson and featuring 16‑year‑old Oscar nominee Abigail Breslin on vocals. Produced at Threshold Recording Studios by Jeremy Sklarsky and mastered by Fred Kevorkian, the recording credits Teddy Watson (vocals, banjo guitar), Abigail Breslin (vocals), Enrico de Trizio (piano/keys/synth), Charlie Rauh (electric guitar), Bryan Percivall (bass) and Andrea Belfiore (drums). The post includes full lyrics and links to the band’s website and social media. The article notes Breslin’s musical debut follows a trend of actors exploring music—citing Ryan Gosling’s Dead Man’s Bones and Michael Cera and Christopher Mintz‑Plasse’s indie projects.

Michelle Williams spoke about still struggling to find meaning in the 2008 death of her then-fiancé Heath Ledger during her first network interview since his passing. Though she appears happier and professionally successful—promoted by her work in Blue Valentine and collaboration with Ryan Gosling—she says the event itself remains without meaning: “I can’t find a meaning for it.” Williams described how the loss made her obsess over how life can change in an instant and how many aspects of her life “died.” A comforting line from a book helped: “when you’ve truly lost everything, then at least you can become rich in loss.” She also reflected on the surreal feeling after Ledger’s death, saying she misses the year when it felt possible he might reappear and the “magical thinking” that came with it. Gosling, who joined the interview, praised working with her and downplayed dating rumors, calling their relationship a creative, professional partnership.

Researchers from Spain report in Nature that lethal violence between members of the same species is unevenly distributed across mammals and appears to track evolutionary relationships: closely related species tend to have similar rates of killing their own kind. Examining cause-of-death data for more than 1,000 mammal species and archaeological evidence from some 600 human populations, the team estimated ancestral levels of intraspecific lethal violence across the mammalian family tree.

Key findings
- Mammals overall average roughly 3 lethal deaths per 1,000 deaths. Rates are higher in social, territorial groups and in lineages that include primates.  
- Ancestors of primates and apes show substantially higher inferred rates: about 18 per 1,000 for great apes and roughly 20 per 1,000 (≈2%) for the earliest humans—more than six times the root mammal rate.  
- Historical and archaeological evidence indicates human lethal-violence rates have fluctuated: roughly 2% in prehistoric hunter-gatherers, higher in some historical periods (e.g., medieval times), and substantially lower in contemporary societies (modern global average cited ~13 per 1,000 from WHO data, though estimates vary).
- The authors stress that the pattern does not prove a purely genetic cause: inherited ecological contexts, social organization and culture also shape violence. They argue lethal violence is part of our evolutionary history but socially modifiable and reversible.
- Commentators: Steven Pinker praised the study as supporting the view that humans have natural tendencies toward lethal violence that modern institutions can reduce. Others (e.g., Douglas Fry, Richard Wrangham) caution against overgeneralizing from primate infant-killing to human adult-on-adult violence and emphasize social organization’s role.

Takeaway
The study suggests humans evolved within a relatively violent mammalian clade, implying an ancestral propensity for lethal interpersonal violence, but also shows that social, ecological and cultural factors can amplify or suppress that tendency—meaning violence is not strictly hardwired and can be mitigated by societal change.

Yahoo announced it will “free up” Yahoo IDs that have been inactive for at least 12 months and make them available for new sign-ups: in mid‑July anyone can try to claim released IDs, and in mid‑August claimants will learn which addresses they received. Yahoo says inactive users can simply log into any Yahoo product before July 15 to keep their IDs.

Security concerns: critics warn this policy could enable account takeover and identity theft. Dormant Yahoo addresses are often tied to other online services (password resets, legacy Flickr accounts, backup emails), so reassigning those addresses could let attackers reset passwords and gain access to users’ active accounts (email, banking, social media) via social engineering. Wired sought comment; Yahoo responded with a statement from SVP Jay Rossiter expressing confidence the transition can be made securely and framing the change as a way to give users desirable, shorter IDs.

Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders posted surprisingly close fundraising totals in Q3 2015, underscoring Sanders’ growing strength and challenging assumptions about his viability. Clinton’s campaign raised just over $28 million in the quarter — bringing her six‑month total to roughly $75 million after a $47.5 million Q2 — while Sanders pulled in about $25–26 million for Q3 and reported $15 million raised in Q2 and roughly $25 million cash on hand. Clinton’s haul included more than $3 million from a joint fundraising committee and was largely made up of small donations (93% under $100); her campaign expected a summer dip amid email controversy. Sanders’ fundraising was driven almost entirely online — he hit one million individual contributors in Q3 and took in $2.07 million in online donations on Sept. 30 alone — despite hosting very few in‑person fundraisers. The close gap highlights Sanders’ momentum in early states and raises questions about whether establishment concerns over his ability to compete financially in a general election are justified. Clinton’s allies point to large affiliated super PAC resources (e.g., Priorities USA Action) as an advantage Sanders rejects. Full disclosures for the quarter were due the following week and were expected to be examined for contribution sources and spending.

An English Springer Spaniel named Hendrix, 6, was mistakenly placed on the wrong United Airlines cargo flight at Newark this week and sent to Shannon, Ireland instead of Phoenix. United discovered the error and took steps to return him; staff walked and fed Hendrix during the detour, and he reunited with his owner in Newark before being flown on to Phoenix, where he arrived Friday night. Owner Meredith Grant (and her mother, identified in some accounts) said she learned of the mistake only shortly before the Phoenix flight was due to land and was upset by the airline’s handling and response. United apologized and offered a full refund; the family wants stronger consequences for whoever was responsible.

Amazon’s new AmazonBasics Microwave is a $59.99, 700W countertop microwave designed to demonstrate Amazon’s Alexa Connection Kit rather than to be a premium appliance. It has minimal local controls and no onboard microphones or speakers (just a beeper). Instead, it pairs with your Alexa system as “the microwave,” letting you control it via voice through your Echo devices. An Alexa button on the microwave signals your Echo to listen in the microwave-control context (so you can say things like “stop” without the wake word). Presets and quick-cook settings are stored in Amazon’s cloud and accessed via Alexa.

A notable feature is an optional subscription popcorn-reordering service: Alexa counts how often you say “make popcorn” and can auto-reorder Amazon popcorn when you’re low; there’s also a physical popcorn button. The unit is a straightforward black, boxy microwave with a turntable, vents and metal enclosure, shipping November 14 for preorder now.

More broadly, the device showcases Amazon’s Alexa Connection Kit — a compact module (with real-time OS, Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth, etc.) intended to make it easy and inexpensive for manufacturers to add Alexa voice control to everyday appliances. Amazon aims to expand its lead as the smart-home hub by offering a plug-and-play way for makers to integrate Alexa into low-cost devices.

Summary:

Internal emails from leaders of the Miss America Organization revealed sustained, vulgar, misogynistic and fat‑shaming commentary about former Miss Americas by then‑CEO Sam Haskell and others, including board members Tammy Haddad and Lynn Weidner and telecast writer Lewis Friedman. Examples include jokes about renaming past winners “cunts,” repeated insults and sexualized comments about specific former winners (notably Mallory Hagan, Kate Shindle and Gretchen Carlson), discussion of blacklisting critics, and strategizing to undercut Hagan’s coaching business. The messages span roughly 2013–2015 and show senior leaders treating alumnae as “malcontents” and “has‑beens,” at times proposing investigations or ostracism to silence dissent.

HuffPost published the emails, prompting an internal investigation, the suspension and then resignation of Haskell, and the resignations or departures of other senior executives (including chairman Lynn Weidner and president/COO Josh Randle). The disclosures also contributed to Dick Clark Productions resigning its board seats and terminating its production relationship with Miss America after being “appalled” by the emails. Several former Miss Americas and outside observers called for broader leadership changes and reforms; the organization said it would institute new communication policies and investigate the matter. Haskell has disputed aspects of the reporting, calling the emails private and saying they were stolen. The scandal prompted widespread condemnation for the contrast between the organization’s stated mission of empowering young women and the conduct revealed in the messages.

In a high-profile Indiana U.S. Senate debate, Republican Richard Mourdock—who defeated longtime GOP Senator Richard Lugar in the primary and is backed by the Tea Party—said pregnancies resulting from rape are “something that God intended to happen,” framing his opposition to abortion around his belief that life is a gift from God and begins at conception. He said he would allow abortion only to save the mother’s life. Mourdock later tried to clarify, saying he did not mean God preordained rape and that critics’ interpretations were “sick and twisted,” but he reaffirmed that God creates life.

Democratic challenger Rep. Joe Donnelly, also personally pro-life but supporting exceptions for rape and incest, rejected Mourdock’s remarks as disrespectful to survivors. National Democrats and the DNC seized on the comments to paint Mourdock as extreme. The controversy drew comparisons to Missouri GOP candidate Todd Akin’s widely condemned remarks earlier in the cycle.

The fallout included public distancing by Mitt Romney’s campaign—Romney’s spokesperson said the comments do not reflect the former governor’s views—raising questions about continued Republican support and advertising. The episode adds turbulence to a closely watched Senate race where Republicans have invested heavily, with national figures and groups campaigning and spending to support Mourdock while polls showed him underperforming Romney in Indiana.

This document combines two items: (1) a report from the Texas Policy Evaluation Project (TxPEP) about self‑induced abortion in Texas, and (2) the full text of a Texas legislative bill imposing new abortion restrictions.

Key findings from the TxPEP study
- Scope and methodology: TxPEP surveyed nearly 800 Texas women aged 18–49 during 2014–2015, asking whether they had ever attempted to end a pregnancy on their own or knew/suspected a close friend had.
- Estimated prevalence: Applying survey proportions to Texas’s roughly 6 million reproductive‑age women, researchers estimate between 100,000 and 240,000 Texas women have attempted self‑induced abortion.
- Trend and context: The report suggests the incidence may be rising in Texas after clinic closures linked to laws such as HB2 (2013). Prior studies are cited showing higher self‑induction after increased restrictions (national 2008 estimate ~2%; 2012 Texas clinic sample ~7%).
- Most common groups affected: Self‑induction was most prevalent among Latina women in border counties (rural areas with clinic closures) and women reporting difficulties accessing reproductive health care.
- Methods used: Two main categories—home remedies (herbs, teas, vitamins) and medications, primarily misoprostol obtained without prescription in Mexico. Misoprostol alone often resulted in complete abortion but with varied dosing, methods, and reports of intense cramping/bleeding and uncertainty about normalcy and safety.
- Motivations: Primary reasons given were lack of money to travel/pay for clinic care, local clinic closures, recommendations from friends/family, and fear of stigma. Poverty was identified as a common underlying factor amplifying barriers.
- Expert reactions: Study co‑author Dr. Daniel Grossman and providers like Amy Hagstrom Miller (Whole Woman’s Health) framed the findings as evidence that restrictions like HB2 place economically disadvantaged women and women of color at risk and drive unsafe self‑care.

Summary of the legislative bill (excerpted Texas statute)
- Purpose: The bill amends Texas law to regulate abortion procedures, providers, facilities, and abortion‑inducing drugs; establishes penalties and enforcement mechanisms.
- Major provisions:
  - Preborn Pain Act: bans abortions at or after 20 weeks post‑fertilization except to avert death or substantial and irreversible physical impairment of the woman, or for severe fetal abnormalities. Requires physicians to determine probable post‑fertilization age before abortion and to use methods that maximize the unborn child’s chance of survival when the fetus is 20+ weeks (subject to exceptions for maternal health).
  - Physician requirements: Physicians performing abortions must have active admitting privileges at a nearby hospital (within 30 miles) that provides obstetrical/gynecological services, and must provide 24‑hour telephone access and emergency hospital information. Violations may be Class A misdemeanors or subject to medical board discipline.
  - Regulation of medical (drug) abortion: Defines “abortion‑inducing drug” and requires physicians to follow FDA‑approved protocols (or certain ACOG guidelines as of 2013), verify gestational age and intrauterine location, provide the FDA label and 24‑hour contact, schedule and document a follow‑up within 14 days, and report serious adverse events to FDA MedWatch.
  - Facility standards: Abortion facility standards are raised to ambulatory surgical center level by specified dates.
  - Reporting and privacy: Expands reporting requirements (including probable post‑fertilization age) and includes privacy protections for women in legal proceedings.
  - Enforcement and severability: Texas Medical Board enforcement, penalties for providers violating provisions, and broad severability clauses directing courts and officials to preserve and enforce as much of the law as constitutionally possible.

Overall picture
- The TxPEP study documents a substantial number of Texas women attempting self‑induced abortions—often using misoprostol obtained abroad or home remedies—linked to clinic closures, cost, stigma, and access barriers. The legislative text reflects the opposite policy direction: tightening abortion regulations, restricting later abortions, imposing facility and provider requirements, regulating drug abortion protocols, and expanding enforcement—measures that advocates argue have contributed to reduced clinic availability and increased self‑managed abortion attempts.

Hassan Mustafa Osama Nasr (Abu Omar), the Egyptian cleric kidnapped in Milan by the CIA in 2003, has defended Sabrina De Sousa — a former U.S. State Department official later revealed to be an undercover CIA officer — as she faces imminent extradition from Portugal to Italy. De Sousa, a dual U.S.-Portuguese citizen convicted in absentia in 2009 (one of 26 Americans) for her role in the “extraordinary rendition” of Abu Omar to Egypt, faces a four-year sentence. Portugal rejected her appeal; she was detained in Lisbon after traveling there to see family.

In a Guardian interview, Abu Omar called De Sousa and the convicted operatives “scapegoats,” saying senior U.S. officials who authorized the rendition enjoy immunity and should be tried instead. He said he did not personally know De Sousa and was unsure of her role, but urged Italy’s president, Sergio Mattarella, to pardon her on humanitarian grounds. Abu Omar reiterated that he was abducted in Milan, transported via Germany to Cairo, and allegedly tortured there; Italian prosecutors later convicted 22 CIA operatives and other officials for orchestrating the abduction.

De Sousa denies significant involvement, saying she was a minor translator in early planning and has long sought to defend herself; she also accuses the U.S. of abandoning her by not invoking diplomatic immunity. She has appealed publicly (including an open letter to Pope Francis) and asserted the U.S. government declined to intervene. The U.S. has largely stayed silent; some pardons were granted to other defendants previously, and the case has been politically sensitive for Italy given wider tensions with Egypt (e.g., the Giulio Regeni affair). Observers note the case highlights accountability issues around the Bush-era rendition program and the diplomatic dilemmas it still creates for both Washington and Rome.

Barbara and Chad Soper of Rockford, Michigan, have three children born on consecutive numeric dates: Chloe on 8‑8‑08, Cameron on 9‑9‑09 and newborn Cearra on 10‑10‑10. None of the births were scheduled to hit those dates — Chloe and Cameron were induced for medical reasons, and Cearra was delivered early after Barbara developed blood clots. Statisticians note the sequence is attention‑grabbing but not astronomically improbable once you account for timing and many births occurring in those years. The family says they won’t have more children; commentators pointed out the practical challenges of closely spaced pregnancies and parenting several very young children.

Security researchers are warning Mac users about a new Trojan called OSX/Sabpab that targets Macs running Java and Microsoft Word. Discovered by Sophos and Kaspersky Lab, one variant exploits the same Java vulnerability used by the Flashback malware; another spreads as a boobytrapped Word attachment named “10th March Statemnet” (misspelled), a lure linked to a Dalai Lama/Tibetan statement. If a vulnerable user opens the malicious document, the Trojan installs silently—dropping a decoy Word file while opening a backdoor for attackers to steal data or install further code.

Experts urge users to install available patches (Microsoft issued an Office for Mac update in 2009 that addresses the Word vulnerability and confirmed coverage for Sabpab) and update Java and Apple software. Anti-virus tools can detect and remove Sabpab; Symantec/Norton provide removal guidance and both free and paid Mac antivirus options are recommended. While there’s no evidence Sabpab is widespread, analysts say these incidents mark an increase in targeted Mac attacks and underscore the need for Mac users to take malware protection seriously.

A 40-year-old man, Jason Luis Rivera, was arrested early Saturday at singer Miley Cyrus’s Studio City home after jumping the fence and hiding in bushes on the property. He was found carrying a pair of scissors, told police he was friends with and “married” to Cyrus, and was tasered when he didn’t immediately comply with officers’ orders. The incident began with a 911 call from someone at the house; Cyrus was not home. Rivera was booked on trespassing and burglary charges at LAPD Valley Jail on $1,000 bail.

A 1999 photograph by German artist Andreas Gursky, titled "Rhein II," sold at Christie’s in New York for $4.3 million, setting a new auction record for any photograph. The chromogenic color print face-mounted to acrylic glass had been estimated at $2.5–$3.5 million; the buyer was not disclosed. "Rhein II" is a panoramic image of the Rhine and one of an edition of six, with four copies held by major institutions including MoMA and Tate Modern. The sale surpassed the previous photography auction record held by Cindy Sherman’s "Untitled" (1981), which fetched about $3.8–$3.9 million. Gursky, known for large, disorienting landscapes, has said his work aims to make viewers aware of their place on a rapidly moving planet. The WARC files for the referenced web crawl are not publicly available.

Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette announced criminal charges July 29, 2016, against six current and former state employees in connection with the Flint water crisis. The defendants include three Michigan Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) employees — Liane Shekter-Smith (former chief of the Office of Drinking Water and Municipal Assistance), Adam Rosenthal (water quality analyst) and Patrick Cook (community drinking water specialist) — and three Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) employees — Nancy Peeler, Corinne Miller and Robert Scott.

Prosecutors allege these employees altered, buried or otherwise concealed reports that showed dangerous lead levels in Flint’s water and rising blood-lead levels in children. Key allegations include:
- MDEQ: Rosenthal, Cook and Shekter-Smith are accused of manipulating Lead and Copper Rule monitoring reports, excluding samples to keep lead levels below the federal action level, misleading the EPA about corrosion-control practices, and concealing compliance problems. Rosenthal faces counts including tampering with evidence; Shekter-Smith, the highest-ranking defendant charged, faces misconduct and willful neglect counts and has been fired.
- MDHHS: Prosecutors say an epidemiologist’s July 28, 2015 report showing a significant year-over-year spike in children’s blood-lead levels was “buried.” Peeler and Scott are accused of producing a “bogus” report and misrepresenting data; Miller is accused of ordering staff not to act and of directing deletion of emails related to the findings. All three face misconduct, conspiracy and willful neglect charges.

This second round of charges follows earlier prosecutions in April that named two MDEQ employees (Stephen Busch and Michael Prysby) and a Flint city worker (Michael Glasgow), the latter of whom pleaded no contest and is cooperating with investigators. Schuette characterized the motive as arrogance and treating Flint residents as expendable; special prosecutor Todd Flood noted the apparent coordination between the two agencies around the same date as particularly significant.

Schuette’s office has also filed civil suits against consulting firms Veolia and Lockwood, Andrews & Newnam for their roles in consulting on Flint’s water treatment; those firms deny wrongdoing. The investigation — described as possibly the largest in Michigan history — remains active, and additional charges could follow. Flint has since returned to the Lake Huron water supply, but residents are still advised to use filters and bottled water while long-term remediation continues.

On April 1, Forbes.com published an April Fools’ Day blog by contributor Len Burman headlined “Romney drops out of race, endorses Santorum” that briefly ran at about 10:40 a.m. and was taken down roughly 30 minutes later. The post included fabricated quotes suggesting Mitt Romney would leave the GOP race and back Rick Santorum; despite Burman saying it was meant as obvious satire and even dated April 1, the headline spread quickly on Twitter and reached the top of Google News before its removal. Burman, an economics professor and 10-month Forbes blogger, said he intended the piece to satirize the Republican right and did not expect editors to pull it; he later posted (and then had removed) an explanation claiming Forbes had an unannounced ban on April Fools’ content. Forbes executive producer Coates Bateman, who removed the posts, did not respond to inquiries. Burman has reposted the piece on his personal blog and said the episode taught him about how headlines travel on the Internet.

Separately, Mitt Romney himself was the target of an internal April Fools’ prank during a Milwaukee campaign event. Aides staged a fake, sparsely attended set with recorded applause to embarrass him as he was introduced; Romney, surprised and calling himself “the April fool,” later entered the real room and spoke to a large crowd and joked that he would “forgive but remember.”

Question
Does initiating opioid therapy, compared with nonopioid medication, improve pain-related function for patients with moderate to severe chronic back pain or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain despite prior analgesic use?

Design
The SPACE trial: a pragmatic, randomized, 12‑month trial in Veterans Affairs primary care clinics (n = 240 randomized; 234 completed). Patients with chronic (≥6 months), moderate–severe back or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain were randomized to a treat‑to‑target opioid strategy (starting with immediate‑release morphine, oxycodone, or hydrocodone/acetaminophen, with escalation options) or a nonopioid medication strategy (starting with acetaminophen or NSAIDs, then adjuvants/topicals, then pregabalin/duloxetine/tramadol if needed). Outcome assessors were blinded; patients and clinicians were not.

Primary and key secondary outcomes
- Primary: pain‑related function (Brief Pain Inventory [BPI] interference scale, 0–10; higher = worse).
- Main secondary: pain intensity (BPI severity).
- Primary adverse outcome: medication‑related symptoms (patient checklist).

Main results
- Pain-related function over 12 months did not differ: mean 12‑month BPI interference 3.4 (opioid) vs 3.3 (nonopioid); difference 0.1 (95% CI −0.5 to 0.7); overall P = .58.
- Clinically meaningful functional improvement (≥30% reduction) at 12 months: 59% opioid vs 61% nonopioid (P = .79).
- Pain intensity was slightly better in the nonopioid group over 12 months: mean BPI severity 4.0 (opioid) vs 3.5 (nonopioid); difference 0.5 (95% CI 0.0 to 1.0); overall P = .03. The magnitude was small and below the trial’s prespecified 1‑point MCID.
- Medication‑related adverse symptoms were greater with opioids: mean symptoms 1.8 vs 0.9 at 12 months; overall P = .03.
- No significant between‑group differences in hospitalizations, ED visits, deaths, doctor‑shopping, diversion, or opioid use disorder diagnoses were observed, though the trial was not powered to detect rare serious harms.
- Secondary outcomes largely similar; only anxiety showed a small advantage for opioids.

Other points
- Most opioid patients received low to moderate doses; fewer than 15% had a mean dispensed dose ≥50 morphine‑equivalent mg/day in any 90‑day window.
- Trial was pragmatic with flexible, treat‑to‑target medication management delivered primarily by pharmacists; nonpharmacologic therapies were permitted.
- Limitations: unblinded patients, VA population (mostly men) may limit generalizability, excluded patients already on long‑term opioids, and limited power to detect rare serious harms.

Conclusions
Over 12 months, initiating opioid therapy did not improve pain‑related function versus a structured nonopioid medication strategy for moderate to severe chronic back or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain. Nonopioid therapy produced slightly better pain intensity and fewer medication‑related symptoms. Findings do not support initiating opioid therapy for these conditions when alternatives are available.

A Le Sueur County judge has sentenced 48-year-old Susan Ann Russo to probation, community service and four days in jail for a 2015 crash that killed 79-year-old New Prague school bus driver Joseph “Joe” Tikalsky. The collision occurred Oct. 28, 2015, as Tikalsky was retrieving his newspaper near his mailbox while wearing a reflective jacket. Prosecutors say Russo was distracted — likely texting — when she struck him.

Russo pleaded guilty as part of a deal and was ordered to complete 40 hours of community service with Minnesotans for Safe Driving, two years’ probation (including a ban on active electronic devices in her vehicle and on drugs/alcohol), a $3,000 fine to be used for distracted-driving awareness (such as a billboard), and four days in county jail split into two-day stints on the anniversary of Tikalsky’s death in 2016 and 2017. A forensic exam later found no phone activity, and Russo unsuccessfully sought to withdraw her plea; the judge said she should have seen Tikalsky regardless.

At sentencing, family members urged action rather than anger. Tikalsky’s widow and children forgave Russo and are lobbying for stricter distracted-driving laws and tougher consequences. Russo tearfully apologized in court, saying she will live with the mistake and try to make amends. The judge and family emphasized treating distracted driving with the seriousness once reserved for drunk driving.

A farmer in Gansu province, Guan Quanzhi, has been awarded 520,000 yuan (about $83,000) in compensation after being seriously injured by a wild giant panda in March 2014. According to local reports, a panda chased by officials into Liziba (Li Baizi) village bit Guan’s right leg; villagers eventually freed him by covering the animal’s head. The attack required multiple surgeries (reports cite seven to eight hours of surgery and subsequent operations over the year) and may still necessitate further operations or even amputation. Guan’s son sued the provincial and Longnan city forestry bureaus and the Baishuijiang National Nature Reserve management; following negotiations the agencies agreed to pay the settlement, which will cover medical costs. The reserve is home to over 100 wild pandas. The item notes that despite their cuddly image, giant pandas are bears capable of inflicting severe injuries; China’s wild panda population was reported at 1,864 in 2013, up nearly 17% over the previous decade, due to conservation efforts.

Vice President Joe Biden said on Tuesday there is "no doubt" Syrian President Bashar al-Assad was responsible for the Aug. 21 chemical attack near Damascus. Speaking at the American Legion convention, Biden argued the Syrian regime uniquely possesses the weapons, delivery capabilities, a history of chemical use, and motive — and has impeded investigation by shelling attack sites and blocking access for five days. He said the U.S. national security team is consulting with allies and that those who use chemical weapons must be held accountable.

At a White House briefing, spokesman Jay Carney said the U.S. must respond because allowing large-scale chemical attacks without consequence would threaten U.S. security interests, but President Obama has not decided what action to take and is considering a range of options, not all of them military. Concerned lawmakers have urged that any military action receive prior congressional authorization; nearly two dozen had signed a letter insisting the president seek Congress if he deems force necessary. President Obama told PBS NewsHour interviewers he had not made a decision and that alleged chemical-weapons use would factor into his calculus.

Mercedes-Benz unveiled an ultra-luxury open-top G-Class at the Geneva Motor Show: the Mercedes‑Maybach G650 Landaulet. Limited to 99 units and priced around $500,000, it will be the world’s most expensive production SUV. Built on an extended G‑Wagen platform, the G650 pairs a twin‑turbo V12 (the G65’s unit) with portal axles and 17.7 inches of ground clearance to keep true off‑road capability while delivering Maybach‑level rear‑seat luxury.

Key features include:
- Landaulet body with a covered front row and a retractable fabric roof over the rear.
- Long wheelbase (about 22.8 inches longer than standard) with first‑class reclining, massaging rear captain’s chairs, inflatable support chambers, heated/ventilated leather, folding tables and retractable footrests.
- Electric, dimmable glass partition between passengers and driver, heated/cooled (thermal) cupholders, premium audio and high‑resolution displays.
- Off‑road hardware: three locking differentials, low‑range gearing, and a V12 producing roughly 630 hp and very high torque (reported 737 ft‑lb).
- Production to begin in autumn in Graz, Austria, deliveries after September.

The G650 continues Mercedes’ strategy of pushing the Maybach sub‑brand into extreme, high‑margin derivatives to fund costly investments in electric, autonomous and shared‑mobility tech. It follows a trend among luxury marques (Bentley, Rolls‑Royce) of expanding into very high‑end SUVs and underscores the enduring appeal of the rugged, boxy G‑Class platform.

Longtime Republican operative Roger Stone, a close Donald Trump confidant, has repeatedly denied colluding with Russia in the 2016 election while publicly discussing alleged contacts with WikiLeaks and its founder Julian Assange. Stone appeared on Alex Jones’ Infowars wearing an eccentric pilot-style outfit, drawing mockery, and later told CBS This Morning he has repeatedly denied any collusion, is aware he’s likely been under surveillance, has not spoken to the FBI, and is preserving documents at the Senate Intelligence Committee’s request.

CNN reviewed Stone’s public statements from August to October 2016 showing he frequently claimed some form of communication with Assange or intermediaries and predicted WikiLeaks would release damaging material on Hillary Clinton’s campaign—statements that have heightened scrutiny amid FBI and congressional probes. Stone acknowledged exchanges with the persona Guccifer 2.0 but called them “benign” and denied knowledge of specific hacked materials, even as U.S. officials link Guccifer 2.0 and the Podesta/DNC hacks to Russian intelligence. WikiLeaks later denied ever communicating with Stone.

Stone also echoed White House claims that President Obama ordered a wiretap of Trump Tower, saying it was “certainly possible,” and accused the intelligence community of being politicized. FBI Director James Comey has said there’s no evidence supporting the wiretap allegation. Stone has defended Trump aides such as Paul Manafort and Michael Flynn, denied contact with Russians to influence the election, and insisted on having a chance to respond to allegations.

People magazine named Ryan Reynolds its 2010 Sexiest Man Alive the same day the first trailer for his superhero film Green Lantern was released. The trailer offers the first official look at Reynolds in the green suit and teases the plot: Hal Jordan (Reynolds) learning to use his powers and confront his fears to protect the Green Lantern Corps from the villainous Parallax. It also shows Blake Lively as Carol Ferris, Jordan’s fellow test pilot and love interest, and Peter Sarsgaard as antagonist Hector Hammond.

The People feature highlights Reynolds’s humor and life—he grew up the youngest of four brothers in Canada, is married to Scarlett Johansson, and jokes about the new title bringing family teasing and perks at home. The article notes some reaction and debate over the choice, with readers suggesting other contenders (e.g., Jon Hamm), and points readers to the full People issue for more photos and the full interview.

CBS News chief foreign correspondent Lara Logan was brutally assaulted while reporting in Cairo’s Tahrir Square on Feb. 11, the day Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak resigned. According to CBS, Logan and her crew were caught in a crowd of more than 200 people that became violent; she was separated from her team and suffered a sustained sexual assault and beating. She was rescued by a group of women and about 20 Egyptian soldiers, rejoined her team, returned to her hotel and flew back to the United States the next morning for medical care. Logan is recovering in the U.S.; CBS and her family have asked for privacy and declined further comment.

The attack occurred amid widespread celebration in Tahrir Square after 18 days of protests, a setting that had generally seen less harassment earlier in the uprising but where assaults and groping resurfaced in the final days. Logan’s assault was among at least 140 attacks on journalists covering the Egyptian unrest since Jan. 30, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. A week before the assault, Logan and two CBS colleagues had been detained by the Egyptian military for a day; she returned to Cairo shortly before Mubarak stepped down. Logan has been with CBS since 2002 and a "60 Minutes" correspondent since 2006.

The document contrasts two ways of viewing U.S. air travel: the widespread passenger perception that “flying sucks” and the industry-expert case that flying is objectively better than ever. It argues the experts are right on key measures: flying is far safer, more reliable, and dramatically cheaper and more accessible than in the regulated, high-price era before 1978. After deregulation, airlines competed on price, expanded capacity, unbundled amenities, merged, and introduced fees — trade-offs that made travel affordable to many more people while shifting comfort and service into paid premium tiers.

The piece traces how air travel expectations and complaints evolved culturally. In the past, when flying was expensive and rare, jokes and anxieties centered on safety. As safety improved, humor and gripes shifted to quality and inconvenience (airplane food, legroom, fees). The author explains that much of modern complaining stems not only from genuine annoyances (crowding, lost bags, delays, occasional high-profile incidents) but from psychological and social dynamics:
- Powerlessness: the highly controlled experience of flying (security, crew instructions) breeds feelings of lack of control that trigger complaints and heightened vigilance.
- Social signaling: complaining is a communal activity — people share and one-up grievances, reinforcing the narrative that “flying sucks.”
- Boredom and internal focus: long waits and repetitive procedures make travelers dwell on discomfort and amplify annoyance.

The article notes airlines still offer choices — premium seats, meals, checked bags — for those willing to pay, and even fully upgraded fares are often cheaper today (even adjusted for inflation) than mandatory regulated fares from decades ago. It also points out that more people fly than ever (passenger volumes have grown substantially), which increases scale-related impersonality and the frequency of bad experiences.

In short: objectively, commercial air travel today is safer, cheaper, and more reliable than in earlier eras; subjectively, many travelers feel it’s worse because of reduced comfort in basic economy, the scaling and depersonalization of the system, and social/psychological drivers of complaining. The article ends by noting that airline workers have additional, often unspoken, practical insights for passengers.

WSB‑TV Atlanta traffic reporter Mark Arum paid an impromptu on‑air tribute to Malik “Phife Dawg” Taylor after learning the A Tribe Called Quest rapper had died of diabetes complications. Arum, who says he’s long enjoyed slipping hip‑hop lyrics into his reports, mixed multiple Phife references into his traffic update rather than his usual one or two lines. The tribute echoed several iconic lines—e.g., “more hits than the Braves or the Yankees,” “tell your mother, tell your father, send a telegram,” and others—and was shared via WSBTV’s Facebook. The story notes social‑media condolences from artists including Jill Scott and Chuck D and suggests watching the band’s Beats, Rhymes, and Life documentary to further honor Phife.

UN chemical weapons experts entered Damascus suburbs to investigate an alleged large-scale chemical attack on August 21 after their convoy was fired on by unidentified snipers. Inspectors visited Moadamiyet al-Sham and other sites, interviewed survivors and medical staff, and collected samples, though officials warned shelling and the delay could have degraded or contaminated evidence. Reports of casualties vary widely; aid groups and activists cited hundreds to over a thousand victims with thousands showing “neurotoxic” symptoms, while opposition and state sources blamed each other.

The United States and several Western governments say there is strong intelligence suggesting the Syrian regime under President Bashar al-Assad was responsible; Secretary of State John Kerry called the attack a “moral obscenity.” The Obama administration moved naval forces and consulted allies as it weighs options, including limited strikes (e.g., Tomahawk cruise missiles) intended to punish and deter use of chemical weapons without becoming further embroiled in the civil war. UK leaders likewise signaled readiness to respond even without a UN Security Council resolution, citing humanitarian need; David Cameron cut short his holiday to chair a security meeting and William Hague said action could proceed without full UN unanimity. France pushed for action; Russia, China, Iran and Syria warned against intervention and urged full UN vetting of evidence.

Russia and Syria rejected Western accusations and questioned the timing and credibility of the Syrian government’s late permission for inspectors, accusing opponents and foreign backers of fabricating or staging evidence. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon emphasized inspectors’ safety and urged cooperation from all sides.

International reactions are mixed: some nations (UK, France, U.S.) press for accountability and possible military response; Germany urged caution but signaled it might consider consequences if use is confirmed; many countries and analysts warned of risks and legal objections to unilateral action without Security Council authorization.

Key issues remaining: verification of chemical agent use and responsibility, potential degradation of evidence due to continued shelling and time delay, possible international military responses (limited vs. broader), and the diplomatic/legal debate over acting without UN Security Council approval.

German authorities are considering a music‑identification tool — nicknamed “Nazi Shazam” — to let police instantly recognize neo‑Nazi and other far‑right songs. A prototype developed by Saxony’s regional police registers audio fingerprints of indexed “rechtsrock” tracks so they can be identified on internet radio, at concerts, clubs or demonstrations, allowing rapid intervention and conserving investigative resources.

Interior ministers from Germany’s 16 states will discuss the proposal. The aim is to combat music seen as a “gateway” into the neo‑Nazi youth scene: the Federal Review Board for Media Harmful to Minors currently indexes hundreds to over a thousand far‑right or racist songs, restricting their sale and access for under‑18s. Supporters say the app would help police and watchdogs at events and curb recruitment of young people via music.

Legal issues remain unresolved — notably whether automatically identifying music in a public venue counts as acoustic surveillance — so adoption is not yet decided. Critics also note far‑right groups increasingly use non‑indexed or newer nationalist folk/punk material to evade restrictions.
