On Friday a gunman opened fire during a midnight screening of The Dark Knight Rises in Aurora, Colorado, killing 12 people and wounding 58. Investigators say the shooter demonstrated an unusually high hit rate for an amateur, suggesting extensive target practice. He used multiple weapons — an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle with a high-capacity magazine (which later jammed), a 12‑gauge shotgun, and a Glock .40-caliber pistol; police also recovered a second Glock in his car. The suspect set off gas canisters inside the dark theater and had apparently booby-trapped his nearby apartment with explosives and chemicals. Police arrested him outside the theater within minutes before he could reach his car.

Authorities are searching the suspect’s apartment and records for evidence of range practice (receipts, internet searches, calls) to establish premeditation and mental state. A local range owner says the suspect, identified as James E. Holmes, applied for membership in June but never followed through; the owner described an odd, rambling answering‑machine message.

Holmes, 24, was a neuroscience graduate student at the University of Colorado who abruptly dropped out in June after failing part of his first‑year oral preliminary exam. He had been receiving a $26,000 annual federal stipend. University officials say he had strong academic credentials on paper but classmates and some former mentors described him as a mediocre, socially awkward student. Police reported that about 90 packages containing ammunition and other items were shipped to campus in the weeks before he left.

Holmes appeared in court with orange hair and a dazed demeanor and faces multiple first‑degree murder charges; his next hearing was set for July 30. Investigators are also checking whether materials from campus labs contributed to the explosives found in his apartment.

Fort Lee, N.J., has begun issuing $85 fines to pedestrians caught texting while walking after three fatal pedestrian-related accidents this year, police said. Officers handed out pamphlets during a brief grace period in March and have since issued more than 117 tickets. Borough police chief Thomas Ripoli called texting while walking a serious distraction that makes people unaware of their surroundings; some residents questioned the fines’ necessity or cost.

The crackdown follows research from Stony Brook University showing that cell-phone use while walking disrupts gait and memory. In a study published in Gait & Posture, researchers Eric Lamberg and Lisa Muratori had participants walk an 8-foot course while talking or texting. They found that both activities reduced walking speed, but texting caused greater disruption: texters veered off course (about a 61% increase in lateral deviation), traveled farther (13% increase), and made more navigational errors than talkers. The authors say dual-tasking with phones increases cognitive distraction and reduces situational awareness, and suggest the findings could be used in rehabilitation to prepare patients for real-world walking demands. They emphasize the intent is to raise awareness, not to ban texting while walking. The report notes isolated incidents and urban rumors about bans elsewhere but underscores that texting while walking does lead to more collisions and unsafe behavior.

Sixteen U.S. Postal Service employees in the Atlanta area were sentenced to federal prison after admitting they accepted bribes to hand-deliver kilogram-sized packages of cocaine on their routes. Federal agents uncovered the scheme in 2015 while investigating a drug trafficking ring; traffickers targeted postal workers believing their jobs made them less likely to be stopped. Undercover investigators used a confidential source who posed as a trafficker and recorded negotiations in which carriers and clerks agreed to deliver cocaine (often preferring it over marijuana because they could charge higher bribes) for payments sometimes as low as $250. Some defendants recruited coworkers and negotiated kickbacks for recruits’ deliveries.

All 16 postal employees pleaded guilty and received prison terms ranging from about three years to nine years, followed by periods of supervised release and various forfeiture or restitution orders. Sentences and financial penalties varied by defendant; an additional non‑employee intermediary, Dexter Bernard Frazier, was also sentenced to nine years. The case was investigated by the FBI, the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General, and the DeKalb County District Attorney’s Office and prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Atlanta. Officials stressed the breach of public trust and the danger posed to communities and fellow postal workers.

On Sept. 24 the Texas State Board of Education narrowly approved (7-6) a nonbinding resolution directing textbook publishers to correct what board members described as a “pro-Islamic/anti-Christian” bias in future world history and social studies textbooks. Supporters—mostly social conservatives—said the measure is meant to ensure more balanced coverage that gives Christianity and other non-Muslim faiths at least equal treatment and to warn publishers they could reject texts that demonize or lionize religions or give unequal space to major faiths. The resolution cites past examples (including older Texas texts no longer in use) and even mentions foreign investment in a U.S. publisher as a possible influence.

Opponents—three Democrats and three moderate Republicans, plus two absent Democrats—called the action politically motivated, offensive, and a distraction that damages the board’s reputation. Critics said the resolution rests on unproven accusations, is largely cosmetic (not legally binding on publishers), and diverted the board from adopting more neutral language urging balanced treatment of all religions. The vote split highlighted deep ideological divisions on the board over how religion should be portrayed in textbooks.

A major dispute erupted within the Democratic presidential race after the Bernie Sanders campaign accessed and saved portions of Hillary Clinton’s voter-file data following a software glitch at vendor NGP VAN. Audit logs show four Sanders staffers conducted 25 targeted searches over about 40 minutes, viewing lists of high-priority Clinton supporters and wavering voters in multiple early states. Sanders fired one staffer involved, said the access began as an effort to probe a security problem, and contended the DNC and its vendor were at fault.

The DNC temporarily suspended Sanders’ access to the shared voter database, prompting Sanders’ campaign to sue the committee and accuse it of trying to favor Clinton. The cut-off hampered Sanders’ field operation and inflamed long-standing suspicions among his backers that the party favors Clinton. Clinton’s team called the incident theft of “fundamental” strategic data and demanded assurance the proprietary information had been deleted.

After negotiations and a court’s involvement, the DNC restored Sanders’ access early Saturday after the campaign provided requested information and agreed to an independent audit by Kroll and to sign an affidavit about staff actions; Sanders said it would continue its lawsuit. Both sides stressed further investigation and possible disciplinary action may follow. The episode intensified rancor between the campaigns just weeks before early voting in Iowa and New Hampshire and highlighted tensions over DNC neutrality and data-security practices.

Summary:

- Alexa Internet has been donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996. The donated data arrive daily and are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.

- Separately, GQ published a provocative photo shoot and cover story featuring Lea Michele, Dianna Agron, Cory Monteith and other Glee cast members. The actors posed in revealing shots by photographer Terry Richardson and discussed the racy shoot and their rise to fame. Michele recalled early career pressure to get a nose job and credited her mother for discouraging it; Monteith, who left school in ninth grade, cautioned against viewing his path as a model for teens. Glee co-creator Ryan Murphy said he aimed to create a responsible take on a family show. The cast described surreal moments from their sudden fame, including performing at the White House Easter Egg Roll and watching Amber Riley sing the national anthem for President Obama.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the NSA continued to monitor Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders even after the Obama administration publicly pledged to curb surveillance of allied heads of state following the Snowden revelations. Officials say Israel was kept under closer watch because of concerns it might attack Iran and, later, because U.S. negotiators feared Israel was spying on and trying to undermine the Iran nuclear talks.

Intercepts reportedly showed Israeli knowledge of the negotiations and intentions to leak details. When Netanyahu and aides lobbied Jewish-American groups and members of Congress against the deal, some conversations involving members of Congress were allegedly swept up. White House officials worried those intercepts could expose accusations that the executive branch was spying on Congress, yet wanted the intelligence to counter Netanyahu’s efforts. To limit traces, the NSA reportedly removed members’ names and personal attacks before sharing material.

The National Security Council declined to comment on the WSJ specifics but reiterated that foreign intelligence collection has validated national security purposes and affirmed U.S. support for Israel. The Office of the Speaker and the House Intelligence Committee said they are looking into the report; Rep. Devin Nunes requested additional information. Republicans including Sen. Ted Cruz criticized the administration. An Israeli embassy spokesman called the allegations “total nonsense.” The report also notes that U.S. officials used media reports to confront Netanyahu about potentially revealing negotiation positions without disclosing the source of the information.

In an interview on Australian TV’s Sunday Night, Sir Elton John reignited a long-running feud with Madonna, calling her a “f***ing fairground stripper,” saying “her career is over,” and criticizing her treatment of Lady Gaga — who is godmother to Elton’s son, Zachary. Elton argued Madonna should have stuck to making great pop records rather than the dance direction of her MDNA tour, which he called a disaster, and referenced past tensions including Madonna’s comments about Gaga’s “Born This Way” and her winning a Golden Globe over work connected to Elton. The interview, conducted by friend Molly Meldrum, also touched on Elton’s family life, his son conceived via surrogate with husband David Furnish, and his upcoming world tour marking 40 years since “Rocket Man.”

New Yorkers with caffeine cravings are being offered a new option: caffeinated beef jerky called Perky Jerky. Invented by Tribeca resident Matt Keiser (38) — who says the idea came after spilling a Red Bull on jerky while skiing — and co‑founded with ski partner Brian Levin (37), Perky Jerky launched online in August and is about to appear in Sports Authority stores. The snack, sold for $2.99 (1 oz) and $4.99 (2 oz), contains about 60 mg of caffeine per ounce (roughly a small coffee or one Red Bull) and is teriyaki‑pepper flavored with guarana. Reactions from New Yorkers were mixed: some found it unpleasant, while others reported an effective, longer‑lasting lift without the post‑workout crash associated with energy drinks. The product is marketed as an all‑natural, high‑protein, low‑fat snack for active professionals.

Lululemon pulled a shipment of its popular black Luon yoga pants after customers reported some pairs were overly sheer, prompting a recall and refunds and cutting its first-quarter sales forecast by about $20 million. The issue marked at least the fourth quality-control problem for the premium apparel company in about a year, following earlier complaints about color-bleeding and transparency in other items. Shares fell early in trading.

Lululemon blamed its Taiwanese supplier Eclat Textile Co., but Eclat responded that all shipments were certified and produced to contract specifications and said Lululemon had approved the batches. Lululemon said it is working with the manufacturer to determine the cause and has a sourcing manager on-site in Taiwan. Analysts warned the string of glitches highlights weaknesses in Lululemon’s supply-chain oversight and reliance on a small number of suppliers for key fabrics.

Tiger Woods, 37, has begun a reportedly serious romance with Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn, 28. Sources say they met through the ski community (Vonn has been teaching Tiger’s children to ski), started dating in November, and have been balancing busy sports schedules while keeping in frequent contact. Tiger visited Vonn in Austria in mid-January and the pair took a romantic trip to Antigua. Vonn was initially wary because of Tiger’s well-publicized infidelity and 2010 divorce from Elin Nordegren; her friends are reportedly concerned about her involvement with someone with that history. Some sources suggest Tiger is more committed now and even entertains thoughts of marriage, but others remain skeptical given his past.

The piece describes American culture’s celebration of fame, wealth and power but notes how quickly those can vanish. 24/7 Wall St. compiled a list of 50 well-known people who recently suffered sharp declines in influence, reputation, or career standing across politics, business, sports and media. The excerpt profiles five individuals whose prominence collapsed amid scandal, poor performance, or abrupt dismissals:

- Anthony Scaramucci — Appointed White House Communications Director in July 2017, Scaramucci was fired less than two weeks later. His chaotic, profanity‑filled media interview, reported protocol breaches, public disputes with other Trump aides, and a concurrent divorce highlighted the brief, turbulent tenure.

- Chris Christie — The two‑term New Jersey governor and 2016 presidential hopeful saw his approval ratings plummet. His reputation was damaged by the Bridgegate scandal, and despite briefly leading Trump’s transition team he was sidelined and not included in the administration. Christie attracted criticism for appearing to use state perks during a government shutdown.

- James Comey — The FBI director since 2013, Comey drew controversy for his public handling of the investigation into Hillary Clinton’s emails during the 2016 campaign. He was fired by President Trump in May 2017 amid conflicting White House explanations, cementing his fall from power.

- Mark Fields — CEO of Ford (CEO since 2014, with the company veteran hired in 1989) was ousted in 2017 after a nearly 40% drop in Ford’s share price under his leadership. His push into electric and autonomous vehicle development, plus cost-cutting moves, failed to reassure shareholders.

- Tiger Woods — Once dominant in golf with 14 majors, Woods’ career and reputation suffered after a 2009 infidelity scandal and subsequent personal problems. A 2017 incident involving a roadside stop and failed field sobriety testing (later tied to prescription medications) led to rehab and his lowest professional ranking ever.

The article implies that while public figures may face higher scrutiny, some falls are deserved; the full list and methodology are available through the original 24/7 Wall St. links.

Juneau police defended their handling of the investigation into newly elected Mayor Stephen “Greg” Fisk’s death after his bruised, bloodied body was found in his home Nov. 30. Authorities initially did not rule out foul play while awaiting autopsy results, which fueled widespread speculation and national attention. Preliminary autopsy findings later indicated Fisk, 70, died of natural causes and his injuries were consistent with falling or stumbling into objects; he had a history of heart problems. Police chief Bryce Johnson said investigators had to consider all possibilities because no one witnessed the death and the scene initially suggested an assault to the person who found him (his son). There was no sign of forced entry, no apparent gunshot wound, and no indication of drugs or suicide. Deputy Mayor Mary Becker was named acting mayor; Fisk’s family is grieving privately.

Lady Gaga honored David Bowie with a high-tech, theatrical tribute at the 2016 Grammy Awards that blended elaborate costumes, choreography, special effects and multiple costume changes. The segment — one of the night's largest — was directed in part by Nile Rodgers and spanned Bowie classics including "Space Oddity," "Changes," "Ziggy Stardust," "Suffragette City," "Rebel Rebel," "Fashion," "Fame," "Under Pressure," "Let's Dance" and "Heroes."

The performance was produced in collaboration with Intel as part of its Experience Amazing campaign and the Recording Academy’s Next Generation of GRAMMY Moments initiative; Intel provided new technology showcased in the broadcast. A teaser featured Gaga saying the tech gave her the power to “invent the un-inventable” and to reveal “the wizard behind the curtain, the mind behind the machine.”

Gaga’s Bowie tribute built on a long-standing artistic debt: she has publicly cited Bowie as an inspiration since early in her career, referenced him in liner notes and interviews, and earlier at Grammys week signaled the homage with Ziggy Stardust–inspired red-orange styling and a Bowie tattoo. The tribute followed recent high-profile appearances for Gaga, including singing the national anthem at Super Bowl 50 and winning a Golden Globe.

Robin Williams, who died at 63, was widely adored by peers and audiences across generations, but he held a special place for people now in their mid‑20s to early 30s who grew up on his 1990s family films. Already an acclaimed actor in the 1980s and early 1990s (Good Morning, Vietnam; Awakenings; Dead Poets Society), Williams shifted into children’s entertainment with a humility and generosity that endeared him to a younger audience. His work in Hook, his electrifying voice performance as the Genie in Aladdin, and transformative roles in Mrs. Doubtfire, Jumanji, Jack and Flubber showed him willingly erasing his celebrity to create joyous, child-centered performances. Those films, frequently replayed on VHS or rented from Blockbuster, made him feel “like us” to kids—innocent of adult concerns and eager to please.

Later in his career Williams returned to serious adult work (earning four Oscar nominations and winning for Good Will Hunting), though mid‑budget adult dramas waned and some projects like Jakob the Liar and Bicentennial Man missed the mark. Still, for a generation raised on his movies, his legacy is measured in the comfort and delight his performances provided.

The author also recalls personal encounters with Williams from his early stand‑up days at the Comedy Store and the Mork & Mindy breakout, describing Williams’ astonishing improvisational gifts and restless creativity that fueled both his comedy and his dramatic turns. A memorable, whispered “Help me” to the author amid a flashbulb frenzy stayed with him, and in learning of Williams’ apparent suicide by asphyxia, that moment took on a tragic resonance.

Oakleigh Ryan Nance is an 11-month-old who was born premature at 3 pounds and initially did well—quickly coming off oxygen and thriving despite early NICU days where staff nicknamed her “Miss Sassy.” Several months ago she developed a sudden high fever and was found to have a severe urinary tract infection that likely reached her kidneys. She has had recurrent infections and was hospitalized for testing.

Findings:
- Grade/stage 3 vesicoureteral reflux (kidney reflux), putting her at risk of ongoing kidney infections. The left kidney is poorly functioning (~22%) and appears duplicated (two renal units with two ureters).
- Infection with a dangerous, antibiotic‑resistant bacterium (Pseudomonas reported in one account; another report cites a “super strain” of E. coli and notes CDC investigation). Because of prior heavy antibiotic exposure, treatment options are limited.
- Cardiac abnormalities discovered on testing: moderate atrial septal defect (ASD) and pulmonary stenosis; these raise additional concern given the infection and kidney involvement.

Planned care and prognosis:
- Oakleigh is scheduled for surgery at the end of the month (news item also mentions a surgery planned for the second week of August) to correct reflux in her left kidney. The planned 4.5-hour procedure will shorten and reposition duplicated ureters to prevent reflux and remove a pocket on the kidney. After recovery, she will see a cardiologist for further heart evaluation.
- The family is concerned about the resistant infection and the limited antibiotic options. They are fundraising to help cover medical costs and say their faith and family support are sustaining them through the struggle.

Background on Pseudomonas/E. coli in the report:
- Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common environmental bacterium that often causes mild problems in healthy people but can cause severe, difficult‑to‑treat infections in sick or hospitalized patients because it resists many antibiotics.
- Serious bloodstream or organ infections can produce high fever, chills, confusion, and shock. The reports also reference a resistant E. coli strain in media coverage, which can likewise cause severe, hard‑to‑treat disease.

Overall, Oakleigh faces surgery to protect her kidneys and further cardiac evaluation, while clinicians contend with a serious, antibiotic‑resistant bacterial infection and limited treatment options. The family is seeking support and remains hopeful.

- At a CNN town hall in Columbia, South Carolina, Donald Trump conceded he “could have” signaled support for invading Iraq during a 2002 Howard Stern interview, but reiterated his broader claim that by the time the war began he was opposed. He said he “wasn’t a politician” then and argued that as a private-sector figure his remarks weren’t widely tracked by the press.

- BuzzFeed published the full 2002 Stern interview in which Trump, asked if he would support an invasion, replied, “Yeah, I guess so,” and added “I wish the first time it was done correctly.” CNN pointed out that Trump has repeatedly asserted he opposed the Iraq War before the 2003 invasion, though contemporaneous public evidence of that position is scarce. Earlier remarks from 2003 and interviews with Neil Cavuto show Trump offering mixed or qualified comments about whether and how the U.S. should act.

- Trump criticized former President George W. Bush for launching the Iraq War and said he didn’t know why Bush went in; a member of the town-hall audience confronted him over alleging that Bush lied about WMDs.

- On comments by Pope Francis that a candidate who wants to deport undocumented immigrants and build a border wall “is not Christian,” Trump called the pope “a wonderful guy,” downplayed the clash as overblown by media, and said he’d meet the pope anytime. Other GOP candidates (John Kasich and Jeb Bush) declined to join the dispute; Kasich praised the pope’s humility, and Bush said it’s inappropriate to question someone’s faith.

- Trump used the event to attack rivals, especially Ted Cruz, accusing him of truth problems and backing Marco Rubio after Rubio accused Cruz’s campaign of photoshopping an image. Trump displayed his usual mixture of combative and self-promotional rhetoric and said he can switch between being politically correct and blunt. He also discussed personal habits like eating fast food on the road.

- John Kasich shared a personal campaign moment—comforting a tearful young man—and emphasized listening and compassion. He downplayed expectations for a strong South Carolina showing while expressing respect for other candidates and naming Chris Christie as someone he’d consider for his administration.

- Jeb Bush shrugged off Nikki Haley’s endorsement of Rubio, asserted he has momentum, highlighted Sen. Lindsey Graham’s endorsement, and said drug policy should emphasize treatment over punishment. He also offered a personal anecdote about meeting his wife as a poignant moment.

- The article notes Trump’s past writings (The America We Deserve, 2000) advocating firmness toward “outlaw” states, and cites several past interviews showing varying stances on Iraq and the timing/quality of any opposition before the 2003 invasion.

Men in Black 3 (2012) revisits the secret agency that monitors Earth’s extraterrestrials, reuniting Agents J (Will Smith) and K (Tommy Lee Jones). The plot centers on Boris the Animal (Jemaine Clement), a vengeful alien who escapes a lunar prison and travels back to July 1969 to kill young K, averting the shield K once erected that keeps Boris’s species out of Earth’s atmosphere. To stop him, J uses a time-travel device to rescue K in 1969, producing encounters with many Rick Baker-designed creatures, a Hitchcock-like freefall on the Chrysler Building, and a climactic sequence at Cape Kennedy tied to the Apollo 11 launch.

Critical reaction is mixed but leans positive overall. Strengths highlighted: an inventive, occasionally touching story that brings fresh emotional depth to J and K’s relationship; inspired period set pieces (1969 scenes, Andy Warhol cameo); playful, bizarre alien designs; and especially Josh Brolin’s performance as young K — widely praised for capturing Tommy Lee Jones’s mannerisms and adding energy and charm. Michael Stuhlbarg’s Griffin provides whimsical, existential comic relief with his ability to foresee time-travel outcomes.

Criticisms focus on uneven tone, creaky sequelitis, and plot contrivances around time-travel logic (notably how K’s disappearance in the present is handled). Some reviewers found much of the franchise banter diminished and several effects or creature designs unappealing in 3-D. Still, many conclude the film is better than expected—often more enjoyable than Men in Black 2—and succeeds as a fun, occasionally poignant blockbuster that justifies its return to the series for fans and mainstream audiences alike. Running time: 106 minutes. Rated PG-13.

Attorney General Eric Holder told the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee that the Justice Department is not engaged in a cover-up of Operation Fast and Furious, calling the congressional investigation politically motivated and saying he has "nothing to hide." He repeatedly denied personally authorizing the controversial "gunwalking" tactics and said that when he learned of them he ordered they stop. Holder said he first learned of Fast and Furious in early 2011, and that he did not know about Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry’s December 2010 killing until a day after it occurred.

Republicans on the committee, led by Chairman Darrell Issa, pressed Holder over production of subpoenaed documents and accused the department of withholding tens of thousands of records and of greater Justice Department involvement in the operation than acknowledged. Issa threatened contempt proceedings over documents created after problems with the program surfaced; Republicans also released a report alleging higher-level knowledge. Democrats on the committee defended Holder, saying no evidence contradicts his testimony.

Holder said internal reviews are ongoing and promised that culpable officials will be removed from federal service and possibly charged when sufficient evidence exists, but acknowledged no one has yet been disciplined. The Justice Department and committee have exchanged sharply worded letters about recently produced documents, including one in which Assistant Attorney General Lanny Breuer discussed a plan with Mexican officials that critics characterized as endorsing "gunwalking"—a claim the department disputes. The hearing showcased partisan disagreement over who knew what and when about the flawed operation that allowed hundreds of firearms to be lost or trafficked to Mexican cartels, some later recovered at crime scenes including where Agent Terry was killed.

President Trump publicly attacked Nordstrom on February 8 after the retailer decided not to carry his daughter Ivanka Trump’s apparel line for the season. Nordstrom had confirmed on February 2 that it was dropping the brand “based on the brand’s performance.” Trump waited almost a week to tweet that his daughter had been “treated so unfairly,” and the White House amplified the complaint via the @POTUS account and press secretary Sean Spicer, who framed the retailer’s decision as a “direct attack” on Trump administration policy rather than a business choice.

Despite the president’s criticism—echoed on official channels—Nordstrom’s stock rose roughly 5% by the close of trading, reversing an initial dip. Observers suggested the rally could reflect investor expectations of free publicity, stronger sales, or reputational gains from opposing the president. T.J. Maxx also announced it was dropping Ivanka’s line the same day; the president had not tweeted about that decision. The piece also includes unrelated text about web archiving and Twitter location features.

The International Professional Surrogates Association (IPSA), founded in 1973, is a nonprofit and the leading authority on Surrogate Partner Therapy. IPSA’s mission is to advance the science, art, availability and professional standards of surrogate partner therapy worldwide by supporting surrogate partners, therapists, clients and researchers. Its goals include ensuring ethical, qualified surrogates for therapists, increasing public and professional acceptance, promoting training and certification standards, providing training and referrals, supporting research and continuing education, and fostering member cooperation. IPSA requires prospective surrogates to complete substantial human sexuality training and connects clients to certified surrogates through therapists.

The article profiles Larry Villarin, a 62-year-old California-based surrogate certified by IPSA and one of only about ten male surrogates in the U.S. His paid work—helping clients overcome sexual dysfunctions and intimacy blocks through stepwise, therapeutic physical and emotional exercises—often looks unconventional and intimate (nude sessions, guided touch, mirror work, blindfolded trust exercises), but is structured, gradual, and goal-oriented. Clients, referred mainly by therapists, include people with disabilities, abuse survivors, those from strict religious upbringings, late-life virgins, and individuals with conditions like vaginismus. Sessions begin with non-sexual assessment and goal-setting, proceed through progressive exercises (talk, modeling openness, non-genital touch, guided movement, use of dilators when indicated), and can span weeks to years. Villarin emphasizes trust-building, emotional boundaries, and modeling openness to help clients gain body image acceptance, sexual confidence, and real-world intimacy skills.

The practice raises legal and ethical challenges: paying for sex is illegal in the U.S., and surrogates sometimes risk arrest; IPSA navigates this legally by framing its work as therapeutic and not centered on intercourse. Emotional complications also arise when clients develop romantic attachments; surrogates must maintain strict boundaries and ethical safeguards (separate therapy rooms, clear rules, therapist involvement). Proponents view surrogate therapy as a controlled, therapeutic intervention that can produce transformative outcomes—reduced shame, new sexual function (including first orgasms), and increased confidence—though many benefits are realized after clients leave the surrogate’s care.

The article profiles widespread Tunisian anger focused especially on Leila Trabelsi, wife of ousted President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, and her extended family—the Trabelsis—whose rapid rise from modest origins to dominating large parts of Tunisia’s economy made them a powerful symbol of corruption and cronyism. Leila, once a hairdresser, married Ben Ali in 1992; her siblings, nephews and other relatives allegedly used political influence to extort businesses and secure stakes in banks, airlines, media, car dealerships, hotels and more, depressing domestic investment and contributing to high unemployment. That resentment helped fuel the uprising that began in December and culminated in Ben Ali fleeing to Saudi Arabia in January.

After the regime fell, Tunisians targeted Trabelsi properties: villas and businesses were looted and burned, and some family members were reportedly attacked or arrested. Tunisian authorities detained dozens of Ben Ali relatives, displayed seized gold and jewelry on state television, and launched investigations into crimes and illicit enrichment. State control was also imposed on Zitouna Bank, linked to Ben Ali’s son-in-law Sakher Materi.

Internationally, Switzerland moved quickly to freeze assets belonging to Ben Ali and others to prevent flight of funds while awaiting formal requests for assistance. Domestically, interim ministers resigned from Ben Ali’s ruling party amid efforts to restore confidence in the government. Observers and a co-author of a book on Leila argue the Trabelsi clan’s excesses played a central role in catalyzing popular outrage, though Ben Ali himself enabled their behavior.

Bordering Tunisia, Libya’s two-month civil war has driven a massive refugee flow and spilled occasional violence across the frontier, straining local resources and drawing international attention.

Refugee situation in Tataouine, Tunisia
- About 30,000 Libyans—many from the western mountain region under attack by Col. Muammar Qaddafi’s forces—fled into southern Tunisia; U.N. estimates put total entries to Tunisia at roughly 276,000 (mostly foreign workers) since the conflict escalated.
- Instead of large camps, most newcomers have been absorbed into local communities around Tataouine: only ~2,500 live in two small tent clusters, while the majority are hosted by Tunisian families (many descendants of earlier Libyan refugees). Aid workers called the welcome unusually generous given Tunisia’s own revolutionary transition and economic difficulties.
- Local authorities, volunteers and international agencies have set up three coordination centers to place families, distribute basic food and bedding, enroll Libyan children in schools, and run a free clinic. The government has kept borders open.
- Despite generosity, the influx magnifies existing problems in the impoverished south: limited infrastructure, unemployment, reduced police presence after Tunisia’s revolution, and frustrations with the transitional government’s response.

Cross-border fighting and wider conflict
- Fighting briefly crossed into Tunisia near the Dehiba–Wazin crossing when Gaddafi’s troops and rebels clashed over the strategic post. Artillery struck Tunisian soil; Gaddafi forces briefly hoisted their flag then apologized locally. Tunisia lodged formal protests.
- The Dehiba–Wazin fighting typified the fluid frontlines: advances, retreats and confusion as both sides sought control of supply routes into the Western Mountains.
- In Libya, fighting around Misrata worsened. Rebels reported heavier rockets and continued shelling of residential areas; they appealed to NATO to stop bombardment and protect civilians. Gaddafi’s government denied targeting civilians, calling opponents militants and foreign-backed.
- NATO continues air strikes under a U.N. mandate to protect civilians, but the campaign has deepened international rifts, with critics accusing the alliance of overreach.
- Reports from state media claimed government forces had captured towns (e.g., Kufra); rebels disputed some of those claims. Explosions and NATO activity were reported in Tripoli.

Overall, the Libyan conflict has produced substantial humanitarian displacement into Tunisia, showcased notable local solidarity amid Tunisia’s fragile transition, and highlighted the conflict’s spillover risks and ongoing military stalemate inside Libya.

A 41-year-old homeless man, identified by the Secret Service as James Dirk Crudup, jumped the White House fence Tuesday evening and was quickly apprehended by uniformed Secret Service officers who approached with guns drawn, ordered him to lie down, handcuffed him and took him into custody. He will be charged with unlawful entry and contempt of court for violating a previous order to stay away from the White House. A backpack found near the fence was being examined; authorities did not believe he was armed. The area was briefly locked down and an all-clear was issued shortly after 9 p.m. The motive for the fence-jump was unknown. The incident was broadcast live on CNN.

Jurgen Klinsmann was dismissed as U.S. men’s national team coach Monday, days after returning from a Berlin gala where he dined with President Obama and Angela Merkel. His firing followed media criticism after two recent losses that harmed — but did not eliminate — the team’s chances of qualifying for the 2018 World Cup. Klinsmann had defended his record and said he felt “very comfortable” in the job on Sunday. U.S. Soccer made the decision after top executives Sunil Gulati and Dan Flynn met with Klinsmann in Los Angeles; Gulati cited the team’s form and development as reasons for needing “to go in a different direction.” A replacement was not immediately named, though Bruce Arena is expected to take over through the current World Cup cycle. Gulati planned to explain the decision further in a media call.

Republican presidential advisers defended Mitt Romney’s forceful criticism of President Obama after deadly anti-American protests erupted across the Middle East, arguing the unrest and the attack that killed the U.S. ambassador to Libya reflected weaker U.S. leadership under Obama and would not have occurred under a President Romney.

Key points:
- Romney foreign-policy advisers (Richard Williamson, Eliot Cohen, Mitchell Reiss) portrayed the situation as evidence of waning U.S. influence and “lead-from-behind” caution by Obama, citing attacks and demonstrations in Egypt, Libya and Yemen and the Syrian civil war as examples of missed U.S. leadership.
- Williamson and others faulted the Obama administration’s rhetoric and responses, including a White House comment calling relations with Egypt a “work in progress” and an Embassy statement criticizing an anti-Muslim video while referencing free speech. They said such messaging signaled a lack of American resolve.
- Romney’s camp argued he would have pursued a clearer, more consistent U.S. vision—championing pluralism, rule of law and stronger support for favorable forces in the region—and suggested he would draw tougher lines on threats like Iran’s nuclear program, though advisers were vague about specific thresholds or use of force.
- The Obama campaign responded that the protests were triggered by an inflammatory video, not U.S. policy, and accused Romney of politicizing a sensitive international crisis. Obama avoided attacking Romney directly while pledging to pursue those responsible for the Libyan attack.
- Republicans who had criticized Romney’s initial responses largely rallied behind him as influential party foreign-policy voices defended his aggressive stance. Romney himself emphasized the need for a stronger America to shape events rather than be at their mercy.
- The episode brought foreign policy to the forefront of the campaign. Romney’s team hopes to turn perceived Democratic weaknesses on global strategy into political advantage despite polling that generally favors Obama on foreign-policy competence.

Four bystanders helped prevent Saturday’s shooting at a Tucson shopping-center “Congress on Your Corner” event from becoming even deadlier after gunman Jared Loughner opened fire, killing six people (including a federal judge and a 9-year-old girl) and wounding 14 others, among them Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, who was the apparent target.

Authorities say Loughner, 22, used a 9mm Glock and tried to reload; four civilians—Bill Badger (74, retired Army colonel), Patricia Maisch (61), Roger Salzgeber, and Joseph Zamudio—intervened. Maisch says she grabbed the magazine as Loughner tried to reload, creating a distraction that allowed Badger and Salzgeber to tackle him; Zamudio helped hold him down. None of them sought recognition; Maisch repeatedly called the two men “the heroes” and described holding the shooter’s ankles and helping secure the scene while another man treated a head wound with paper towels.

Federal prosecutors charged Loughner with multiple counts including attempting to assassinate a member of Congress and killing federal employees; investigators recovered a letter and writings in his home suggesting he planned to target Giffords. FBI Director Robert Mueller confirmed Loughner acquired the weapon in November.

Pima County Sheriff Clarence Dupnik, emotional after the attack, criticized vitriolic political rhetoric and Arizona’s permissive gun laws as potentially contributing factors. His remarks drew rebuke from some national politicians who cautioned against speculative links to motive while noting Loughner’s apparent mental instability.

Lexington School District Two says a substitute teacher arrested for allegedly being intoxicated at Brookland-Cayce High School was not a district employee but worked for Kelly Services, which supplies subs to the district. On March 10, 2017, school administrators removed the substitute after she appeared erratic and sent her to the School Resource Officer; law enforcement charged her, and she was later found with an open container and charged with disorderly conduct before paramedics took her to a hospital. The sheriff’s department declined to release further information.

Actor James Gandolfini, best known for his Emmy-winning portrayal of mob boss Tony Soprano on HBO’s landmark series The Sopranos, has died at 51 of an apparent heart attack while on holiday in Rome. The death was later confirmed by autopsy. He had been scheduled to appear at the Taormina Film Festival in Sicily.

Gandolfini played Tony Soprano for six seasons (1999–2007), winning three consecutive Emmys and becoming the emotional and commercial core of one of TV’s most influential dramas. Creators, co-stars and industry figures—including David Chase, HBO, Brad Grey and Edie Falco—paid tribute, calling him a genius, generous colleague and central figure in the show’s success.

Beyond The Sopranos, Gandolfini had a varied career in film, television, stage and producing. His credits include True Romance, Get Shorty, The Man Who Wasn’t There, The Taking of Pelham 123, Zero Dark Thirty, The Incredible Burt Wonderstone, and recent films Violet & Daisy and Not Fade Away. He returned to Broadway in God of Carnage, earning a Tony nomination, and produced HBO documentaries such as Alive Day Memories: Home from Iraq and Wartorn: 1861–2010. He was attached to several upcoming projects, including an HBO miniseries adaptation, Criminal Justice, and films Enough Said and Animal Rescue.

Born Sept. 18, 1961, in Westwood, New Jersey, Gandolfini was a Rutgers graduate and former bouncer who rose from character roles to become a defining figure in modern television. He is survived by his wife Deborah Lin, their infant daughter Liliana, his son Michael from a previous marriage, and two sisters. HBO and colleagues expressed profound sorrow at the loss.

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met in Singapore for a historic summit aimed at addressing Pyongyang’s nuclear program. After nearly four hours of talks on Sentosa Island, the two leaders signed a document committing to work together for peace, held a public handshake and lunch, and Trump described the meeting as having gone “better than expected.” Officials from both sides conducted last-minute staff-level sessions; Trump expressed optimism about a potential breakthrough while Secretary of State Mike Pompeo cautioned that Kim’s sincerity on denuclearization remained uncertain and emphasized the need for complete, verifiable, irreversible denuclearization. U.S. sanctions would stay in place until progress was demonstrated, Pompeo said.

Kim made rare public outings in Singapore before the summit, projecting a more affable image since earlier diplomatic moves (including a recent meeting with South Korea’s president). Observers and experts warned that North Korea has little history of relinquishing weapons it sees as essential to regime survival, and skepticism remains that Kim will fully abandon nuclear arms. Analysts cautioned that if the two sides do not reach a shared understanding of denuclearization, any process begun by the summit could quickly falter. Trump tempered earlier grand expectations, framing the talks as the start of a potentially longer negotiation process rather than an immediate, total denuclearization.

France’s National Assembly approved a landmark bill to legalize same‑sex marriage and allow joint adoption by same‑sex couples, voting 329 in favor, 229 against, with 10 abstentions. The legislation, a key campaign promise of President François Hollande and described by supporters as France’s biggest social reform in decades, must still pass the Senate before becoming law.

The measure would redefine marriage as a contract between two people rather than between a man and a woman and extend full spousal and adoption rights to same‑sex couples. It follows France’s 1999 civil‑union law (PACS), which granted many but not all marriage rights. If enacted, France would join a growing list of countries that permit same‑sex marriage.

The proposal has split public opinion and provoked sustained, large protests led chiefly by the Roman Catholic Church and social conservatives; religious leaders (including the archbishop of Paris) and many mayors and lawmakers argue it undermines traditional family structures and child welfare. Some provisions—such as access to medically assisted procreation for lesbian couples—were deferred for later debate. Gay‑rights groups hailed the bill as a major advance for equality.

The French debate mirrors broader international contention over marriage equality: the UK and parts of the US have recently moved toward legalization amid strong political and social divisions, while many countries still criminalize same‑sex relations.

Christina Grimmie’s family expressed deep gratitude for the overwhelming love, memorials, donations and tributes they’ve received since her June 10 killing. In a statement Bud, Tina and Marcus Grimmie said Christina’s joyful spirit, voice and faith touched many and that they will take time to decide how best to honor her. Manager Brian Teefey (via Laura Worley/LH7 Management) said he created a GoFundMe to help the family; donations have surpassed $100,000. Marcus Grimmie posted that Maroon 5 frontman and former The Voice coach Adam Levine personally offered to pay for Christina’s funeral and her plane flight. Christina, 22, was shot and killed by 27-year-old Kevin James Loibl after a meet-and-greet following a show; her brother tackled Loibl before he turned the gun on himself. Family, friends and the entertainment community continue to mourn and support them.

Actor Harrison Ford, a longtime pilot, crash-landed a single-engine World War II–era plane on the Penmar Golf Course in Venice, Los Angeles on March 5, 2015 after reporting engine trouble shortly after takeoff from Santa Monica Airport. Witnesses said the aircraft clipped a tree before coming down; Ford was the sole occupant. Two doctors golfing nearby and other bystanders helped pull him from the aircraft and first responders treated him on scene. He was conscious and breathing when taken to a hospital with moderate, non–life-threatening injuries (including head lacerations) and was expected to undergo surgery but to make a full recovery. Fire, FAA and NTSB officials praised the skill of the emergency landing; the exact cause of the incident was undetermined at the time. Ford’s family and son Ben Ford described him as “battered, but OK.”

On November 22, 2013 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a formal warning letter to 23andMe ordering the company to stop marketing its Saliva Collection Kit and Personal Genome Service (PGS) because the product is being sold as a medical device without required marketing authorization under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

Key points:
- The FDA considers the PGS a medical device because it is marketed to provide health-related reports (e.g., carrier status, disease risk, and drug response) for more than 200 conditions, including high‑risk areas such as BRCA-related cancer risk and pharmacogenetic results (warfarin, clopidogrel, 5‑FU). Such results could lead to harmful decisions if false positives or negatives occur (unnecessary surgery, missed risk, inappropriate medication changes, bleeding or thrombosis).
- 23andMe submitted 510(k) premarket notifications in 2012, but the FDA says the company failed to provide required additional information and validation data despite extensive interactions (meetings, emails, guidance) dating back to 2009. As a result the 510(k)s were treated as withdrawn and FDA has not received new supporting data.
- The agency is concerned 23andMe expanded its intended uses and marketing (including TV ads) without authorization and that it has not shown analytical or clinical validation that the tests perform as claimed.
- FDA classified the device as class III and concluded it is adulterated and misbranded because there is no approved PMA or cleared 510(k). The letter demands 23andMe stop marketing the PGS immediately and respond in writing within 15 working days with corrective actions and timelines, warning of possible enforcement (seizure, injunction, fines) if it fails to comply.
- 23andMe acknowledged receipt and said it regrets missed expectations on timeline and communication and is committed to engaging with FDA.
- The action underscores FDA’s caution about direct‑to‑consumer genetic tests: the agency supports consumer access to genetic information in principle but requires evidence of test accuracy, proper validation, and adequate risk mitigation and communication before allowing companies to market interpreted genetic health reports directly to consumers.

An Egyptian man, Taymour el-Sobky, was sentenced to three years in prison with hard labor after saying on a December TV talk show that a large share of married Egyptian women are prone to infidelity. State media say he claimed roughly 30–45% of women have a “readiness for immorality.” Video of the remarks circulated on social media, sparking public outcry and complaints that led prosecutors to charge him with “spreading false news” and harming public peace; he can appeal.

Rights lawyers and observers criticized the prosecution as part of a broader climate of shrinking free expression in Egypt under President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, noting recent convictions of writers, presenters and intellectuals for alleged offenses against public modesty or religion. Critics argue such cases are often driven by public pressure rather than consistent legal standards.

Rosemont police have officially closed the investigation into 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins’ death, ruling it accidental and saying there is “no evidence that indicates any other conclusion.” Jenkins was found dead Sept. 10 inside a walk-in freezer in an unused kitchen at the Crowne Plaza near O’Hare, roughly 21–24 hours after she left a ninth-floor party. The Cook County medical examiner already ruled the death accidental from hypothermia, listing acute alcohol intoxication and the prescription drug topiramate as contributing factors and finding no trauma or common “date-rape” drugs.

In closing the case, police summarized their work: 135 reports, interviews with 44 people (30 confirmed to have been in the room that night), review of dozens of hours of surveillance, five photo lineups, forensic analysis of four cellphones, and multiple warrants. Investigators retraced Jenkins’ path through the hotel, noting surveillance that shows her impaired and alone entering the kitchen area around 3:32 a.m., but no camera view directly captures her entering the freezer. Motion-sensor footage indicates no one else approached the freezer area between when she entered the kitchen and when her body was found; only a security guard was later seen in the area and did not approach the freezer. Police also say the hotel room had been booked with a fraudulent credit card and they have identified two alleged perpetrators linked to a gang and ongoing fraud investigation.

As part of the case closure, Rosemont published a large set of records, videos and numerous postmortem photographs—some showing Jenkins’ clothing partially displaced—which family attorneys called “graphic and disturbing” and said raise further questions. They also criticized what they described as earlier denials of requests to review investigation materials. Defense of the police conclusion includes reference to “paradoxical undressing,” a documented hypothermia phenomenon where cold victims remove clothing. Police emphasized that investigators found no evidence of forced intoxication or foul play despite widespread social-media conspiracy theories. Jenkins’ mother declined comment and attorneys for the family have signaled continued concerns about the circumstances and released materials.

A drunken male passenger attempting to enter an aircraft cockpit to charge his mobile was removed from a Mumbai‑to‑Kolkata IndiGo flight on September 24. The captain of flight 6E‑395 initiated offloading on grounds of a security violation while the plane was still on the ground. The about-35-year-old man was handed to airport police, questioned and then released without charges. IndiGo confirmed passengers are not permitted to enter the cockpit.

The report notes similar recent incidents in India: a first‑time flyer on a GoAir flight from New Delhi to Patna tried to open a rear door mid‑flight thinking it was the lavatory and was taken into custody after landing (the door could not have been opened due to cabin pressure), and over 30 passengers on a Jaipur‑bound flight suffered nosebleeds, headaches and ear pain after cabin pressurization was reportedly forgotten.

The U.S. Olympic Committee (USOC) has initiated a formal process that could strip USA Gymnastics of its status as the sport’s national governing body (NGB) after the federation refused to voluntarily relinquish recognition. The action follows the Larry Nassar sexual-abuse scandal—Nassar, a former national team doctor, is serving an effective life sentence after admitting to child pornography and sexual-abuse charges, and more than 350 survivors have come forward.

Sixteen days after filing a Section 8 complaint to revoke USA Gymnastics’ recognition, the USOC said USA Gymnastics responded by declining to give up its NGB status and instead raised questions about the allegations and the hearing process. USOC CEO Sarah Hirshland said revocation was not a decision taken lightly but is the correct step given repeated organizational failures.

Next steps: a three-person hearing panel (chaired by a USOC board member with representatives from the NGB and athlete advisory councils) will be selected. USA Gymnastics may present evidence and legal arguments; the panel will report and recommend to the USOC board, which will issue the final decision. The bylaws set no firm timeline; Hirshland said it could take weeks to months. While the process proceeds, USA Gymnastics will continue operating; if recognition is revoked, the USOC would assume control of elite programs until a new NGB is named. USA Gymnastics could persist as an organization, but members would likely move to the new governing body.

Background context: USA Gymnastics has endured leadership turmoil—multiple CEOs since 2016—and heavy criticism over handling of the Nassar crisis, loss of major sponsors, ongoing survivor mediation, and revelations that medical records from the Karolyi ranch were found after executives had told Congress they were missing. These failures, including an indictment of a former CEO for alleged evidence tampering, prompted the USOC’s intervention. USA Gymnastics says its current board inherited a crisis and is pursuing reforms, but the USOC judged those steps insufficient.

The piece is a positive review of Creed (officially Rocky 7), a spin-off/sequel to the Rocky franchise directed by Ryan Coogler. Unlike the brutal, melodramatic boxing film the trailers implied, Creed honors the series’ traditions while introducing fresh characters and emotional depth. Michael B. Jordan plays Adonis “Donnie” Johnson Creed, the out-of-wedlock son of Apollo Creed, who leaves juvenile facilities to pursue boxing and seeks out Apollo’s old friend Rocky Balboa (Sylvester Stallone) to train him. Jordan gives the conflicted, likable protagonist real texture—torn between a combative nature and reluctance to follow the sport that killed his father—while Stallone, at 69, delivers a touching, understated turn as an aging Rocky who becomes a mentor and sentimental anchor.

The film leans into classic fight-film conventions—training montages, personal sacrifice, and three pivotal fights (including one long, uncut brawl)—yet avoids cliché by playing its emotional beats openly and earnestly. Tessa Thompson provides strong support as Donnie’s girlfriend. The review highlights the movie’s moral clarity, its crowd-pleasing catharsis in the title fight, and an especially stirring, nostalgic final image of Rocky and Adonis climbing the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps. Verdict: formulaic and cornball but genuinely effective and enjoyable; 3½ out of 4 stars. Rated PG-13.

RadarOnline.com reports that Tiger Woods is undergoing a six-week sexual addiction treatment program at Pine Grove Behavioral Health and Addiction Services in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, run by Dr. Patrick Carnes. A source says Woods is “devastated,” hopes rehab will let him get his life back on track and plans to return to the PGA Tour in the spring — possibly aiming for events such as the Masters — though no public schedule has been announced.

The site also reports that his wife, Elin, has not visited him at the clinic, has been photographed without her wedding ring, and has not made any public statement or filed for divorce. RadarOnline notes Woods requested no roommate while in treatment and recounts that his admission to rehab followed revelations of multiple extramarital affairs and a late-November car crash. Local outlets have placed him at the closed treatment facility, but the clinic maintains privacy about patients.

Summary:

Investigators retraced the route and final days of the Hart family after a 2003 GMC Yukon carrying two mothers, Jennifer and Sarah Hart (both 38), and their six adopted children plunged off a cliff on California’s Pacific Coast Highway. The SUV was discovered overturned March 26; Jennifer and Sarah and three children (Markis, 19; Jeremiah, 14; Abigail, 14) were found dead at the scene. Three other children (Devonte, 15; Hannah, 16; Sierra, 12) remain missing and are presumed dead, possibly swept out to sea.

Using cellphone pings and surveillance footage, authorities say the family was near Newport, Oregon, about 8:15 a.m. on March 24, drove south on US-101 into Northern California, turned onto Highway 1 at Leggett, and reached the Fort Bragg area around 8 p.m. on March 24, where they stayed until about 9 p.m. March 25. A grainy Safeway surveillance image from Fort Bragg taken at 8:05 a.m. March 25 may show Jennifer Hart buying groceries; investigators and the FBI have been working to enhance the footage. Beyond that point the family’s movements are unclear until a German tourist spotted the SUV after it had gone over the cliff.

CHP investigators say physical evidence — no skid marks at a turnout, data from the vehicle indicating it stopped then accelerated straight off the cliff, and an SUV speedometer pinned at 90 mph — suggest the plunge may have been intentional. Crews have been searching roughly 20 miles of shoreline from the crash site toward Fort Bragg for the missing children.

Authorities searched the family’s Woodland, Washington home and served a warrant; no suicide note was found. The Harts had earlier lived in West Linn, Oregon, and Minnesota. Records show a 2011 Minnesota conviction: Sarah Hart pleaded guilty to a gross misdemeanor domestic assault related to hitting a child. Neighbors in Woodland reported concerns and called Child Protective Services days before the crash after one son, Devonte, repeatedly sought food at their house; a former friend says she reported alleged emotional abuse and food deprivation to Oregon child welfare officials in 2013, but investigators said there was insufficient evidence at the time.

The investigation is ongoing as officials continue searches and attempt to piece together the family’s final movements.

Two Chechen-origin brothers living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Tamerlan (26) and Dzhokhar (19) Tsarnaev, who had appeared to be assimilating successfully, became the suspects in the April 15, 2013 Boston Marathon bombings that killed three people and wounded many more. Tamerlan, a talented heavyweight boxer who aspired to the Olympics, had quit college, married and had a daughter; friends described him as intense, increasingly devout and somewhat isolated ("I don't have a single American friend"). Dzhokhar was a recent Cambridge Rindge & Latin graduate, a scholarship recipient, a wrestler and a quiet, popular student who worked as a lifeguard and used social media. Neighbors and classmates reacted with shock and disbelief.

After the bombings a massive manhunt unfolded: Tamerlan was killed in an overnight shootout with police; Dzhokhar was captured wounded in Watertown after hiding in a boat. The family’s backstory is the familiar immigrant arc: fleeing violence in the Caucasus, moving through Russia and eventually settling in the U.S. The brothers’ home life included signs of religious conservatism and, according to acquaintances, growing religiosity in the parents.

U.S. authorities revealed the FBI had interviewed Tamerlan in early 2011 after a foreign government warned he was a follower of radical Islam and might leave to join underground groups. That inquiry — which included checks of travel, internet activity and associations — reportedly found no terrorism links at the time. Tamerlan had traveled to Russia in 2012. Investigators continued probing whether the brothers acted alone, were radicalized domestically, or had outside accomplices; they also reviewed whether any intelligence failures occurred. Public reaction mixed grief, relief at the capture of the surviving suspect, and debate over how warning signs were handled.

A retrospective cohort study published in BMJ examined longevity among 9,889 athletes who competed in the Summer Olympics from 1896–1936, classifying their sports by cardiovascular, static and dynamic intensity, risk of bodily collision, and level of physical contact. After adjusting for birth year, sex and nationality, the investigators found:

- No survival advantage for athletes in high–cardiovascular-intensity sports (e.g., cycling, rowing) versus low–intensity sports (e.g., golf, cricket). Hazard ratios for moderate and high cardiovascular intensity were essentially neutral (≈1.00).
- A higher long-term mortality among athletes in sports with high physical contact (HR ≈1.13–1.16) and, in univariate analysis, for high risk of bodily collision (HR ≈1.11), though the collision effect weakened in multivariate models and was closely related to contact level.
- These contact-related excess risks persisted for deaths after age 50, suggesting cumulative injury rather than only early traumatic deaths.

Authors note limitations: the cohort reflects training and medical care practices from 70–110 years ago; many potential confounders (years/intensity of training, post-career activity, sport-specific behaviors, substance use) weren’t measured; and results should not be taken as discouraging exercise generally. The study adds to evidence that extremely intensive exercise may not provide additional longevity benefits beyond moderate activity and highlights potential long-term harms associated with repeated collisions and physical contact.

Meteorologist Scott Sutherland explains how to view the Eta Aquarid meteor shower, a yearly display produced when Earth passes through debris left by Halley’s Comet. The shower is active from mid‑April to late May, with this year’s main viewing window on the pre‑dawn hours of May 5 and May 6 (best visibility from about 3 a.m. local time until dawn). NASA predicts May 5 may offer slightly more meteors, though the absolute peak is expected during daylight hours that day. Observers away from light pollution with clear skies can expect roughly 10–20 meteors per hour.

The shower’s radiant rises with the constellation Aquarius, so look east in the early morning. If local weather or timing prevents in‑person viewing, the Slooh Community Observatory planned a live webcast beginning at 8 p.m. EDT on May 5.

A notable feature of the Eta Aquarids is their high speed (about 240,000 km/h or ~148,000 mph), which can create "persistent trains": faint, colorful glowing trails that linger from seconds to minutes (rarely longer). Scientists propose two possible causes for these trains — ionization of air molecules with delayed light emission as electrons recombine, or chemiluminescence from vaporized meteoroid metals reacting with atmospheric oxygen/ozone — but more observations are needed to fully explain them.

Sources: NASA, Slooh, The Weather Network.

The piece is a gossipy, tongue-in-cheek roundup of high-profile "kiss" moments involving Barack Obama and other political figures, mixing commentary, anecdotes, and tabloid-style reactions. It opens with an account of Obama unexpectedly kissing Jill Biden at the Democratic National Convention—presented ambiguously as a possible accidental peck—and uses that to riff on awkward “accidental” mouth kisses in social situations (with three humorous scenarios: a crush, a family friend, and an inappropriate person like a boss).

The article then lampoons media coverage of Obama’s on-camera interactions, claiming he has a history of using affectionate kisses to charm or disarm women in public: references include a playful description of an Obama-Diane Sawyer moment before an ABC interview, an instance with Hillary Clinton during a health-care address, and the earlier Jill Biden moment. It also notes a time Carla Bruni, France’s first lady, initially did not kiss Obama at a NATO summit—creating tabloid scrutiny—but later exchanged polite kisses at a dinner, after Michelle Obama and Bruni had met and reconciled any awkwardness. The piece closes with lighter fashion commentary about Michelle Obama’s and Bruni’s outfits at the event. Overall, it’s a satirical take on political optics and media obsession with intimacy and image.

A Dallas grand jury has indicted former police officer Amber Guyger on murder in the Sept. 6 fatal shooting of 26-year-old Botham Shem Jean, who was unarmed and inside his own apartment. Guyger, who was off-duty but in uniform, says she mistakenly entered Jean’s unit believing it was her own, encountered him in the dark, gave commands he did not follow and fired two shots, one of which fatally struck him. She called 911, began first aid, and later said she realized she was in the wrong apartment only after an officer asked for the address.

Guyger was initially arrested on manslaughter charges, posted a $300,000 bond, and was fired by the Dallas Police Department on September 24. Dallas County DA Faith Johnson said prosecutors presented extensive evidence and witness testimony to the grand jury and concluded the shooting was “knowing,” supporting a murder charge rather than manslaughter. Guyger surrendered on the murder indictment and was released on bond; her attorney insists the shooting was a tragic mistake and expects a not-guilty verdict from a fair jury.

The case sparked days of protests and renewed calls for police accountability. Jean’s family and civil-rights groups welcomed the indictment as a step toward justice; the family has also filed a federal lawsuit alleging excessive force and accusing the city and police department of pattern and practice failures. Dallas police leadership said the department is working on reforms including implicit-bias training and citizen oversight, while noting the broader strain between law enforcement and the community. The trial could still be many months away, and the incoming district attorney will oversee prosecution.

Coca-Cola has introduced its first alcoholic beverages in Japan — a trio of fizzy lemon-flavored alcopops released this week, marking a global first in the company’s ~125–132‑year history. The drinks, modeled on Japan’s popular canned Chu‑Hi (shochu highball) category, come in three alcohol strengths (about 3%–8%) and target younger consumers, particularly women who are a key Chu‑Hi market. The recipe is proprietary, but the flavors follow the strong citrus profile (especially lemon) that leads the segment. Major domestic producers such as Suntory, Asahi and Kirin currently dominate Chu‑Hi sales. Coca-Cola says it has no plans to launch the range outside Japan. The move echoes the 1990s alcopop boom in Europe and the UK — products that drew both popularity and controversy for appealing to young drinkers.

A broad UN climate package—the "Cancún Agreements"—was adopted at the two-week summit in Cancún, Mexico, restoring momentum to the international process after the Copenhagen dysfunction. More than 190 countries agreed, over the objections of Bolivia, to a compromise set of decisions that stop short of a binding global treaty but create frameworks for future action.

Key elements:
- All countries committed, for the first time in a UN decision, to take actions to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and to strengthen mitigation pledges. The package anchors and fleshes out pledges from the Copenhagen Accord and establishes clearer rules for monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) of emissions and support.
- A new "green" climate fund and mechanisms for technology transfer and adaptation finance were agreed in principle to help developing countries cope with climate impacts; wealthy countries pledged long-term support that could eventually approach $100 billion annually, but details and funding sources remain unresolved.
- A mechanism to reduce emissions from deforestation (REDD-plus) and compensation arrangements were outlined.
- The agreement endorses the 2°C goal but contains no binding global emissions treaty, no specific global peaking date, and many mitigation targets remain vague or voluntary. Developed countries acknowledged the need to cut emissions 25–40% by 2020, but second Kyoto Protocol commitments were not fully specified; Japan initially resisted but ultimately accepted compromises.

Reactions:
- Delegates and many governments hailed the outcome as a necessary, pragmatic step that salvages and rebuilds confidence in the UN process and provides a foundation for negotiating a legally binding agreement in future meetings (e.g., Durban 2011).
- Critics—including Bolivia and several environmental groups—called the package weak and insufficient to prevent dangerous warming, arguing it could allow temperature rises far above safe limits and that consensus procedures were improperly overridden when Bolivia’s objections did not block adoption.
- Observers noted the agreement’s importance lies in process and institutional advances (finance, MRV, REDD) rather than immediate cuts in emissions; much of the substantive work and ambition will depend on follow-up negotiations and national commitments.

Researchers report that the elaborate, colorful facial patterns of guenon monkeys likely evolved to prevent crossbreeding between closely related species that live and travel together. Guenons (a tribe of more than ~25–35 African forest monkey species) often share groups, feeding sites and sleeping trees, creating opportunities for interspecies mating that could produce infertile or less-fit hybrids. 

To test the long-held hypothesis that distinctive faces function as “I’m different” signals, teams from New York University, Exeter and the University of Hull photographed 22 guenon species (over 150 individuals) in zoos, sanctuaries and the wild. They applied human face-recognition methods (the eigenface technique) to quantify facial features and compare similarity within and between species. Results showed each species has consistent, species-specific facial patterns and that species in geographic or social contact are especially visually distinct from one another.

The authors interpret this as strong evidence of visual character displacement: selection has favored facial divergence to ensure species recognition and reproductive isolation where interbreeding risk is high. The study, published in Nature Communications, is presented as some of the clearest evidence that visual signals can act as barriers to hybridization. Ongoing work will examine whether modern distinctiveness reflects present-day neighbors or historical sympatry during species formation.

A new ABC News/Washington Post poll (June 2–5, 2011; n=1,002; ±3.5 points) finds a pessimistic electorate and mixed prospects for Republicans vying to challenge President Obama in 2012.

Top-line findings
- Mitt Romney and Sarah Palin lead GOP nomination preferences: Romney 21% and Palin 17% among Republicans and GOP-leaning independents; all other potential contenders are in single digits.
- In general-election matchups, Romney is the only tested Republican who runs even with Obama (47–47% among all adults; 49–46% among registered voters). Obama leads the other Republicans tested (Palin, Newt Gingrich, Tim Pawlenty, Michele Bachmann, Jon Huntsman).
- Palin fares worst against Obama (trailing by ~15–17 points) and faces large levels of rejection: 64% of Americans say they definitely would not vote for her, 63% say she is unqualified, and 41% of Republicans say they would rule her out.

Economic discontent and political vulnerability
- National mood: 89% rate the economy negatively; 57% say recovery has not begun; among those who see a recovery, 81% call it weak.
- The ABC Frustration Index (economy, presidential approval, anti-incumbency, dissatisfaction with government) is high at 68 overall — 80 among Republicans and 72 among independents — levels associated historically with electoral trouble for incumbents/major-party officeholders.
- Obama's approval has returned to pre–bin Laden levels (47% approve, 49% disapprove); 59% disapprove of his handling of the economy (a new high). Only 33% approve of his handling of the deficit (career low).
- Trust on the economy is essentially tied: 42% trust Obama and 45% trust congressional Republicans.
- Anti-incumbent sentiment is strong: 55% say they would look for a new representative in Congress; 66% say the country is on the wrong track; 69% are dissatisfied or angry with federal government performance.

Candidate-specific notes
- Romney: Gains from independents and many conservative voters; pulls 87% of Republicans and 48% of independents in an Obama matchup. He does especially well with higher-income and college-educated GOP voters. Potential liabilities include lingering Republican opposition to the Massachusetts health-care law he signed (41% of leaned Republicans oppose it; 37% have no opinion) and weaker support among evangelical white Protestants.
- Palin: Strong name recognition but deep negatives across the electorate and sizable defections inside the GOP. She does better among lower-income GOP voters and some evangelicals but has high flat-out rejection.
- Other Republicans: Obama leads Gingrich and Huntsman by ~10 points and leads Pawlenty and Bachmann by double digits in the poll.

Implications
- Romney currently looks like the strongest GOP general-election alternative to Obama, largely because of independent support and gains among several voter groups where McCain underperformed in 2008. Yet neither GOP frontrunner commands the bulk of possible primary voters; most potential GOP voters have not locked in a choice, and fewer than a quarter of Americans are following the race very closely.
- Obama retains a core base (86% of Democrats, strong support from minorities, young voters, liberals and lower-income groups) but his standing is tightly tied to perceptions of the economy: among those who believe recovery has not begun, 64% would not consider voting for him and Romney leads 63–29 in that group.
- The electorate’s widespread economic frustration leaves room for a challenger to unseat Obama if economic trends do not improve; but Obama’s base and his remaining favorable personal ratings (55% see him as a strong leader) mean re-election is still possible if conditions don’t deteriorate further.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, publicly accused the CIA of improperly searching a standalone computer network set up for her panel’s review of the agency’s Bush-era detention and interrogation program. Feinstein said the CIA searched the committee’s computers in January, potentially violating a prior agreement, the Constitution’s separation-of-powers and speech-and-debate protections, the Fourth Amendment, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, and an executive order barring domestic CIA searches. She said the CIA removed documents and that the agency’s inspector general has referred the matter to the Justice Department.

CIA Director John Brennan denied the agency spied on the committee, said the matter is being investigated and pledged cooperation with efforts to determine wrongdoing. Feinstein said she has sought an apology and acknowledgment the action was wrong but received none. The dispute centers on how committee staff obtained draft internal CIA materials amid a review of interrogation practices; Feinstein emphasized the committee has been provided over 6.2 million pages of documents and framed the episode as a serious threat to congressional oversight. Senators including Patrick Leahy and Majority Leader Harry Reid praised Feinstein’s disclosure; Sen. John McCain suggested an independent probe may be needed. The White House expressed confidence in Brennan but declined to comment on potential legal violations.

Researchers led by Brian Wansink of Cornell analyzed 14 studies covering 1,179 adult diners across eight developed countries and found adults consume about 92% of what they serve themselves. Results were consistent across the U.S., Canada, France, Taiwan, South Korea, Finland and the Netherlands and did not differ by gender or whether people ate at home or in a lab. Slight variations emerged: distracted adults ate a bit less (about 89% of what they took), people ate a larger share of meals (92.8%) than snacks (76.1%), and those eating fruits, vegetables, whole grains and lean proteins consumed more of their portions (91.2%) than those eating less healthy foods (80.6%). By contrast, children (326 participants under 18) ate only about 59–60% of what they served themselves. The authors note the findings help clarify how portion size translates into actual intake and suggest that awareness of the tendency to eat most of what you plate might encourage more mindful portion control.
