A Colorado neighbor is suing Oprah Winfrey after she bought a $10.9 million parcel above Telluride, alleging the purchase and a prior undisclosed correction to property records effectively blocked long-standing public access to hiking trails. Retired physicist Charles D. Goodman says Winfrey’s Yellow Brick Road company, the land’s former owners (Hoyt and Carol Barnett) and the town of Mountain Village conspired to erase easements that allowed nearby residents access to trails established in 1989 after negotiations with the U.S. Forest Service. The Barnetts requested a correction to the records shortly before selling the land. Mountain Village officials say the correction only cleared ambiguities and deny closing access; the town and Winfrey’s team say they intend to maintain “reasonable” neighbor access. Winfrey plans to build a mansion and guest home on the property, a project that would require a bridge over a ski run and removal of roughly 800–1,000 trees for wildfire mitigation. 

Separately, the document briefly criticizes actress Katherine Heigl for suing Duane Reade for $6 million over a tweeted photo, calling the lawsuit excessive and noting similar frivolous celebrity image lawsuits exist.

KPCC’s AirTalk featured Mark Gold, owner/chef of Eva Restaurant in West Hollywood, who instituted a policy offering diners a 5% discount if they check their cell phones at the door. Gold’s aim is to reduce “distracted dining” and encourage conversation and a home-like, relaxed dining atmosphere. About half of patrons accept the offer, and no one has reacted negatively; Gold admits he’s guilty of phone use himself and uses the policy as a reminder.

The story went viral after the Associated Press picked it up, producing global media attention—Gold has since done roughly 40 interviews with outlets including Marketplace, CNN and Good Morning America, plus requests from radio stations in Germany, Ireland and India. Despite the publicity, Gold reports only a modest uptick in business so far. The station invited listeners to weigh in on whether distracted dining is a problem and whether restaurants should curb cell-phone use.

Air France and Germany’s largest carriers canceled more flights to Tel Aviv amid safety concerns after fighting between Israel and Hamas, following a Hamas rocket that exploded about a mile from Ben Gurion Airport. Lufthansa (and subsidiaries Germanwings, Austrian, Swiss and Brussels), Air Berlin and several other European carriers extended or suspended services; Air France halted flights “until further notice.” The European Aviation Safety Agency strongly recommended airlines avoid Tel Aviv, and the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration barred U.S. carriers for 24 hours (through midday Thursday), citing a “potentially hazardous situation” and pending review of new information from Israel.

Reactions were mixed: British Airways continued its twice-daily Tel Aviv service, saying it had judged the risk acceptable; aviation experts noted airlines make independent risk assessments and pointed to Israel’s Iron Dome and airport defenses as reducing the likelihood of a strike on aircraft. Critics, including Michael Bloomberg, called the FAA ban an overreaction that rewards Hamas, while Israeli officials and Ben Gurion airport authorities insisted the airport is highly secure. Hamas hailed the flight disruptions as a victory.

Operational impacts included dozens of canceled flights from major European cities, Air Canada suspending at least one rotation, and Polish LOT suspending flights through July 28. Ben Gurion still expected over 200 flights despite cancellations, but some travelers were stranded and others sheltered briefly when sirens sounded. Israel opened the small Uvda airport to help capacity. Authorities warned the suspensions threaten tourism and the economy; last year Israel saw record inbound visitors, and the conflict is likely to reduce arrivals. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited on a military flight amid diplomatic efforts to halt hostilities.

The New York Jets cheerleaders settled a 2014 class-action wage suit for $325,000, approved by a New Jersey court. The suit, filed by a former cheerleader identified as Krystal C., covered the 2012–13 and 2013–14 seasons and alleged cheerleaders earned only about $150 per game, low pay for appearances, and no compensation for practices or rehearsals. Under the settlement each of the 52 squad members will receive $2,500 per season worked (with final amounts including interest and varying by seasons worked) and up to $400 per photo shoot. The Jets denied the claims but said they settled to avoid litigation. The case is part of a broader wave of similar lawsuits around the NFL — including settlements with the Buccaneers, Raiders and tentative deals with the Bengals — and ongoing litigation by the Buffalo Bills’ cheerleaders. State Sen. Diane Savino praised the deal and urged the Bills and the NFL to adopt uniform rules to ensure fair pay and protections for cheerleaders.

New Mexico obstetrician-gynecologist Christopher Driskill, 42, has been suspended by the New Mexico Medical Board and is under investigation after a board report accused him of multiple serious professional and ethical violations.

Key allegations:
- Sex with multiple patients and some former staff members, including having a sexual encounter that coincided with leaving another patient unattended during labor.
- Repeatedly abandoning women in labor at Lea Regional Medical Center and other facilities, including instances that delayed or required emergency C-sections.
- Keeping and drinking alcohol at work, working while under the influence, and stashing liquor in his office.
- Inappropriate behavior documented in charts, including lewd personal notes.
- Casual or improper prescribing practices, including prescribing drugs to a girlfriend without proper records.
- Failure to report his termination and leave of absence to the medical board as required; he was fired from Premier Health in August and subsequently informed Lea Regional Medical Center.

The board determined Driskill posed a “clear and immediate danger to the public.” His medical license is suspended and now faces potential revocation; a hearing has not yet been requested or scheduled and he has not publicly commented. Driskill was president-elect of the New Mexico Medical Society and was expected to assume the presidency in May; the society declined to comment until after the hearing.

A New Zealand father, Samuel Forrest, is urgently arranging to bring his newborn son Leo home from Armenia after the baby, born on January 21 with Down syndrome, was rejected by his mother. According to Forrest and a GoFundMe page he created, Leo’s mother told him to either send the child away or divorce her; she later filed for divorce and has left the family. Forrest says hospital staff in Armenia initially prevented him from seeing the baby and that, in that country, children with disabilities are often abandoned or stigmatized.

Forrest, from Auckland, has pledged to keep and care for Leo and is seeking funds to return to New Zealand and support them while he finds part-time work so Leo can be cared for at home. His online fundraiser, picked up internationally, quickly raised large sums—surpassing NZ$160,000 after an initial jump from $10,000 to $80,000. The New Zealand government has fast-tracked Leo’s citizenship and passport, enabling their planned return. Forrest is also working with disability-awareness groups to challenge stigma and advocate for children with special needs. The baby’s mother confirmed she has left her husband and declined further comment.

News reports say the online auction for the Kel-Tec PF-9 pistol George Zimmerman used to fatally shoot Trayvon Martin in 2012 involved both a public, fake listing and a simultaneous private, verified auction.

United Gun Group, which hosted the sale, told WKMG/News 6 it ran two auctions "to troll the trolls": a public page that attracted many bogus bids (a top displayed bid near $138,900 and a winning name of “John Smith”) and a private, pre-qualified-bidder auction that produced legitimate offers. United Gun Group said the real auction had about 22 bidders, 42 total bids, and at least one verified offer of $120,000; TMZ reported roughly seven verified users and a leading verified bid over $120,000. The site later added private email verification to filter fake bids.

Zimmerman acknowledged the auction’s close in a statement thanking supporters and said the winning bidder would be notified and could remain anonymous; he also offered to be interviewed only under specified conditions (four-star hotel and $1,000/day). United Gun Group tweeted Zimmerman was vetting offers and verifying funds. The Trayvon Martin Foundation declined to comment.

Background: Zimmerman shot Martin after a confrontation in 2012; he was acquitted in 2013. Zimmerman said the pistol had been returned to him by the Department of Justice and described it as “a piece of American history.” Reports differ on the final sale price because of the fake public bids; at least one verified offer was reported at $120,000, while inflated figures near $138k appear to be from the fake listing.

This document contains several distinct news items and an editorial apology, summarized below:

1) PennLive/The Patriot-News editorial apology and policy clarification
- After the U.S. Supreme Court’s 5–4 Obergefell v. Hodges ruling legalizing same-sex marriage nationwide, a PennLive editor posted a statement saying the paper would “very strictly limit” op-eds and letters opposing same-sex marriage, equating such pieces with racist, sexist or anti‑Semitic content, while still allowing discussion of the decision’s legal merits for a limited time.
- The statement provoked heavy backlash accusing the paper of censoring free speech. The editor responded: affirmed commitment to the First Amendment, clarified the intent was to preserve civil discourse and to refuse publication of slurs or abusive language (e.g., homophobic epithets), and acknowledged that reasoned opposition grounded in conscience or religion remains welcome. The editor apologized to anyone offended by the attempt to foster civil debate.

2) Entertainment item — Seth Meyers/Amy Poehler segment mocking sportswriter
- Seth Meyers and Amy Poehler reprised their “Really?” bit to mock an online remark by Sports Illustrated contributor Andy Benoit, who tweeted that “women’s sports in general [are] not worth watching.” The segment ridiculed and advised Benoit about tweeting, prompted by a tweet highlighting a remarkable Women’s World Cup goal.

3) Wal‑Mart cake controversy in Slidell, La.
- A local man filmed that a Wal‑Mart refused to make a cake bearing the Confederate battle flag but later sold a cake with an ISIS battle flag image. Wal‑Mart apologized, calling the ISIS cake a mistake by a store associate who did not recognize the image. The company reiterated its policy of not selling Confederate-flag merchandise, a policy many retailers adopted after the Charleston church shooting, which had renewed scrutiny of Confederate symbols.

4) Takata airbag crisis — CEO addresses public
- Takata’s chief executive, Shigehisa Takada, publicly apologized for deaths and injuries tied to defective Takata airbag inflaters, but defended the company’s products and declined to resign. The company faces the largest automotive safety recall in history—about 35 million vehicles affected so far—and mounting lawsuits and regulatory scrutiny.
- Takata has acknowledged manufacturing failures in some inflaters (“alpha cases”), linked to careless handling at two North American plants, and is still investigating other failures (“beta cases”) that may involve long-term exposure to heat and humidity. The use of ammonium nitrate as a propellant (avoided by some competitors) is under scrutiny; Takata maintains it has used and tested the compound for years and deems it safe.
- Replacement inflaters also sometimes use ammonium nitrate, raising concerns about the durability of repairs. Automakers and regulators have criticized Takata’s response as slow and poorly communicated; the company has lost market value and suspended dividends. Takata forecasts a return to profit, but analysts are skeptical given ongoing recalls and litigation.

Archaeologists using non‑invasive particle physics techniques have discovered a large, previously unknown void inside the Great Pyramid of Giza (Khufu’s Pyramid). The cavity, detected with three independent muon‑imaging methods by an international team (ScanPyramids, with Japanese and French collaborators), lies directly above the Grand Gallery and appears to be at least ~30 m long with dimensions comparable to that gallery. This is the first major internal structure found in the pyramid since the 19th century.

Muon tomography maps density by counting high‑energy muons from cosmic rays that penetrate rock; fewer muons are absorbed where empty space exists. All three muon systems showed a consistent “hotspot” indicating a significant low‑density region, though the technique’s resolution cannot yet reveal the void’s exact shape, orientation (horizontal or inclined), or whether it is a single chamber or a series of cavities.

Researchers emphasize that the feature’s purpose and contents are unknown. Hypotheses include a structural role (e.g., relieving weight above the Grand Gallery) or an unknown corridor or chamber; some experts note its size may argue against purely stress‑relief use, but opinions vary. The team plans no invasive entry; they are developing tiny flying robots that might one day explore the space subject to Egyptian authority approval. The discovery, reported in Nature, is widely regarded as significant for understanding the pyramid’s architecture and construction, though it does not immediately answer questions about burial goods or Khufu’s mummy.

Denver police pursued a stolen tractor towing an attachment through central Denver on the night of July 20/21, 2018. The tractor had been taken from a Denver Water facility in the Lincoln Park area near 1600 W. 12th Ave. Video shows the tractor driving on busy streets and sidewalks, including crossing Park Avenue, before the chase ended in Lower Downtown near 15th and Market. More than a dozen police vehicles and a helicopter were involved. The pursuit concluded when a police cruiser rammed the tractor; the impact deployed the cruiser’s airbags and officers then used a Taser to subdue the driver. Two officers were taken to hospital with injuries and were treated and released the next morning. Police say they did not fire their weapons. The suspect’s identity has not been released and the investigation is ongoing; Denver Water referred questions to Denver Police. Fox31 and Channel 2 are seeking further details.

Researchers at Brigham Young University report that groundwater-driven chemical weathering, not surface erosion, is the dominant process destroying Oahu’s mountains. By sampling groundwater and stream water and combining those data with U.S. Geological Survey estimates, the team quantified how much mineral mass each pathway removes annually and found that more material is being dissolved by groundwater than transported away by erosion. Because the Hawaiian Islands are composed of similar volcanic rock but experience variable rainfall, they provide a useful natural laboratory for such comparisons. Taking plate tectonics into account — Oahu’s slow uplift as it moves northwest — the authors estimate the island will continue to gain elevation for up to about 1.5 million years; after that, continued groundwater dissolution will outpace uplift and reduce the mountains (Koolau and Waianae) to a low, nearly flat island like Midway. A surprising mineralogical finding was abundant quartz in a saprolite sample taken at 1 m depth. The study appears in Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta.

A new Gallup poll finds U.S. congressional approval at a record low: only 10% of Americans approve of Congress, the lowest in nearly 40 years of Gallup polling. Gallup’s editor-in-chief noted that only historically reviled figures (e.g., Fidel Castro, Saddam Hussein, Osama bin Laden) have been rated worse.

The story highlights many surprising things and people that score higher than Congress in various polls:
- BP during the 2010 Gulf oil spill: 16% approved of its response (June 2010 Gallup).
- Socialism: 33% of Americans view it positively (CBS/New York Times).
- Waterboarding: 50% said it should be allowed against suspected terrorists (CNN/ORC), though 68% called it torture.
- Abortion: 19% support legality “in all cases” (ABC/WP), nearly double Congress’s approval.
- President Richard Nixon: 24% approved him at the height of Watergate (1974 Gallup).
- People who never believed in Santa: 16% reported not believing in Santa as a child (AP/GfK).
- Greek PM George Papandreou: 21% worldwide approval during Greece’s debt crisis (2011 Gallup).
- Grassroots movements: 24% supported Occupy Wall Street and 27% identified with the Tea Party (NBC/WSJ).
- Celebrities: Even widely disliked Paris Hilton had a less unfavorable rating than Congress—60% unfavorable for Hilton vs. 86% who disapproved of Congress (Ipsos).

Overall, the piece underscores deep American discontent with Congress by comparing its record-low approval to a range of policies, public figures and even nonpolitical categories that poll better.

The documents describe the Supreme Court oral argument over Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act, which requires certain jurisdictions (mostly in the South) to obtain federal preclearance before changing voting rules. A conservative majority of justices signaled strong skepticism about the continued need for that burden, and appeared inclined to invalidate or narrow Section 5 and require Congress to devise a new coverage formula. Chief Justice Roberts, Justices Kennedy and Scalia pressed whether the covered jurisdictions still merit special treatment based on decades-old data, with Scalia calling the statute a “perpetuation of racial entitlement.” Liberal justices and defenders of the Act argued Congress reasonably reauthorized Section 5 in 2006 based on evidence that racial discrimination in voting persists; they emphasized history and ongoing problems in minority access to the franchise. The challengers (Shelby County, Ala.) said the preclearance regime has outlived its usefulness and stigmatizes covered areas. If the Court strikes Section 5, nine states would no longer need preclearance and could more easily adopt changes such as stricter voter ID laws, polling-place moves, or redistricting. The decision was expected to be close (likely 5–4) and could leave it to Congress to craft a new formula, though that would be politically difficult. The case’s outcome was uncertain until the term’s end.

The Ig Nobel Prizes, organized by the Annals of Improbable Research and co‑sponsored by Harvard student groups, are annual spoof awards that honor research and achievements that “first make people laugh, and then make them think.” Held each September in Harvard’s Sanders Theatre, the theatrical ceremony (with paper airplanes, genuine Nobel laureates presenting the prizes, and a live online broadcast) celebrates imaginative, unusual, and often absurd but thought‑provoking science, medicine and scholarship. Winners receive modest gag prizes (notably a $10 trillion Zimbabwean note) and then give 60‑second talks; longer “Ig Informal Lectures” follow a few days later for fuller explanations.

The event began awarding ten prizes a year in 1991. Nominees are judged solely on whether their work elicits laughter and thought; most winners are contacted privately in advance and accept. The Ig Nobels maintain an archive of past ceremonies, videos, press clips, books, and an email list and social channels for updates.

Illustrating the tone and scope, the 2016 (26th) ceremony honored diverse studies and actors: Volkswagen received the Chemistry prize for cheating emissions tests; a German team won Medicine for finding that scratching the non‑itching arm while watching a mirror can relieve an itch; physics prizes went to researchers who showed dragonflies are attracted to polarized light from black tombstones and white horses attract fewer horseflies; a Biology prize was shared by Charles Foster and Thomas Thwaites for living as wild animals (badger, goat, etc.); other awards recognized work on rats’ sexual behavior in different trouser fabrics, the perceived personalities of rocks, how often people lie, susceptibility to pseudo‑profound nonsense, and how viewing objects between your legs changes perception. The ceremony blends satire, genuine curiosity, and peer‑reviewed research, aiming to spark public interest in science through humor and surprise.

An improvised explosive device partially detonated on a District Line train at Parsons Green station, west London, at about 08:20 BST on Friday, injuring 29 people (including schoolchildren and a young boy). There were no life‑threatening injuries. Witnesses described a fireball, smoke and panic as passengers fled; many were treated for flash burns and crush injuries. Photos and video showed a white plastic bucket inside a supermarket bag smouldering on the carriage floor with wires protruding.

Police and counter‑terrorism teams launched a major investigation, reviewing extensive CCTV from the Underground and nearby businesses and appealing for public information and images. Forensics are examining the device to determine its construction and origin; investigators believe the initiator exploded but the main charge failed, and that the device may have been remotely triggered, suggesting the bomber could have left the train before detonation.

Islamic State’s Amaq agency claimed responsibility; analysts cautioned such claims should be treated carefully. The attack is the fifth terrorist incident in the UK within six months and the first this year without fatalities.

Prime Minister Theresa May raised the UK threat level from severe to critical, saying an imminent further attack could not be ruled out. She announced increased visible security: more armed police on transport and streets and military personnel temporarily replacing police at some protected sites to free up officers for patrols. Senior police said hundreds of detectives and MI5 are involved and that the suspect(s) remain at large. The response prompted an appeal for calm from the mayor and criticism of premature public speculation about suspects.

A Facebook-driven boycott movement has formed against Spirit Airlines after the carrier refused to refund a $197 ticket for Jerry Meekins, a 76-year-old former Marine with terminal esophageal cancer whose doctor advised him not to fly to New Jersey to see his daughter for surgery. A long-running "Boycott Spirit Airlines" Facebook page surged from about 700 likes to over 18,000, with much of the backlash coming from current service members and veterans. Veterans groups including the Veterans of the Vietnam War and the Veterans Coalition sent a letter to Spirit. Spirit did not comment for the story.

Separately, Spirit is changing its carry-on baggage fees effective November 6: gate-purchased overhead carry-ons will rise to $100 (up from $45), and online/reservation/airport kiosk fees will increase by $5–$10. The new fee range for carry-ons will be $25–$100, and Spirit said the adjustments standardize fees for domestic and international travel.

A refrigerated trailer carrying more than 20 tons of confectionery — including Nutella, Kinder Surprise eggs and other chocolates — was stolen in Neustadt, Germany over the weekend. Police estimate the haul is worth roughly €50,000–€70,000 (about $80,000) and say removing that much cargo would have required another truck rather than a car. Authorities are investigating whether the theft was planned or opportunistic and whether it is connected to other recent trailer thefts in the region (including an empty trailer stolen in Weimar and a separate disappearance of a trailer loaded with 30 tons of fruit juice in Wittenberg). Police urged anyone offered large quantities of chocolate through “unconventional channels” to report it and warned against discarding any found sweets. The incident follows other recent food-related thefts in Germany and abroad.

An Air Algerie MD-83 (flight AH5017), operated by Spain’s Swiftair, disappeared over northern Mali on Thursday while en route from Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso to Algiers with 110 passengers and six crew. Officials said about half the passengers were French (51); the manifest also included citizens of Burkina Faso, Lebanon, Algeria, Canada, Germany and several other countries. Contact was lost roughly an hour after takeoff; Burkina Faso said the crew asked to change route due to a storm.

Search efforts by French warplanes and U.N. helicopters concentrated in sparsely inhabited desert and scrubland in northern Mali near the Algerian border. French and regional officials gave conflicting accounts of the crash site—Mali’s president said wreckage was spotted between Aguelhoc and Kidal, while Burkina Faso authorities and local officials near Gossi said remains were found about 50 km from the Burkina border. By midday French ministers reported no confirmed wreckage despite intensive searches. An Algerian official and other sources indicated the aircraft had likely crashed, but no cause had been determined; bad weather is suspected though all hypotheses remained open.

The region’s difficult terrain, limited Malian government presence, Tuareg rebel control of much territory and the need to rely on French and U.N. assets complicated operations. The incident came amid heightened concerns over air safety after recent high-profile crashes. The MD-83 type has a relatively clean record; Swiftair’s safety history is limited. French President François Hollande canceled travel plans and pledged full military support for the search.

A 21-year-old Mississippi State University student, John Sanderson of Madison, was fatally shot Saturday night in Evans Hall, a male residence hall, university officials said. Campus police were notified at about 10 p.m. and arrived within a minute; Sanderson was found gravely injured, taken to Oktibbeha County Hospital and died roughly 30 minutes later. Authorities say three black male suspects fled the dorm in a blue Crown Victoria and remain at large. MSU has increased patrols, restricted residence-hall access, set up a call center, and issued campus alerts; officials describe the incident as isolated and say there is no known imminent threat.

The shooting came the same weekend as another student killing in Mississippi: 19-year-old Jackson State freshman Nolan Ryan Henderson III was shot and killed early Sunday at an off-campus apartment complex after attending a pool party. Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant and higher-education officials expressed condolences, offered state assistance with investigations, and reminded the public that campuses remain generally safe while counseling and support services are being provided. No arrests had been reported.

A 37-year-old man, Jedediah Ezekiel Fulton, was arrested March 16 in Sutherlin, Oregon, after reportedly becoming upset when workers at a McDonald’s refused to make his order of 30 double cheeseburgers. Police say Fulton destroyed a banner, attacked the restaurant’s golden arches, grabbed a person’s shirt, and prompted a witness—who feared for that person’s life—to draw a gun. He faces suspected charges including second-degree disorderly conduct, second-degree criminal trespass, second-degree criminal mischief and harassment. It was not immediately clear whether he has an attorney.

On Monday, May 11, 2015 at about 7:44 p.m., Antioch police responded to a reported burglary in progress on the 4900 block of Ridgeview Drive. The homeowner told officers she had been holding her baby when she saw a man enter through an unlocked door; she fled with the baby but accidentally left her 4‑year‑old daughter inside. Officers found the child at the top of the stairs; the child told her mother the intruder was hiding in her bedroom closet. Police searched the room and located 21‑year‑old transient Demaria Lopez in the closet. Lopez initially failed to comply and a brief struggle occurred, but he was taken into custody without injuries and booked at the Martinez Detention Facility on charges of burglary and resisting arrest. Detectives ask anyone with information to contact the Antioch Police.

President Obama made an unplanned, 18–19 minute on-camera statement from the White House briefing room after George Zimmerman’s acquittal in the killing of Trayvon Martin. He urged respect for the jury’s verdict and for peaceful protest, but gave his most extensive public remarks on race since 2008, speaking personally about how the case resonates in the African‑American community. Obama said, “Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago,” recounted everyday humiliations he and other black men experience (being followed in stores, hearing car doors click shut), and explained that those experiences shape how many African‑Americans interpret the shooting.

He balanced critique and hope: acknowledging racial disparities in the criminal justice system and the tendency to stereotype young black men, while noting progress across generations and calling for continued improvements. Obama urged individual “soul‑searching” about implicit bias and asked whether Americans are “wringing as much bias out of” themselves as possible. He proposed concrete steps—urging state and local review of law enforcement training, bans on racial profiling, and examination of laws like Florida’s “stand your ground” that could encourage deadly confrontations—and promoted long‑term efforts to support African‑American boys. He avoided attacking the trial or verdict directly and stressed that violent responses would dishonor Trayvon Martin and his family. The Martins said they were moved by his remarks; reactions from activists were mixed, with some praising the intervention and others calling it overdue.

La FDA propuso nuevas reglas para reducir los daños del bronceado en interiores, especialmente en menores. Puntos clave:

- Prohibición propuesta: se restringiría el uso de lámparas solares y camas de bronceado a personas de 18 años o más, para proteger a los menores (1,6 millones usan estos dispositivos anualmente).
- Consentimiento para adultos: quienes tengan 18+ deberán firmar, antes de la primera sesión y cada seis meses, un certificado que reconozca haber sido informado sobre los riesgos.
- Riesgos citados: el bronceado en interiores aumenta el riesgo de cáncer de piel (la exposición a camas de bronceado eleva en 59% la probabilidad de melanoma según la American Academy of Dermatology), además de quemaduras y daño ocular; la exposición acumulativa en jóvenes incrementa el riesgo futuro.
- Nuevos requisitos de seguridad para fabricantes y establecimientos: advertencias más visibles en los equipos; interruptor de apagado de emergencia (“botón de pánico”); mejora de la protección ocular limitando la luz que atraviesa las gafas; etiquetado claro de bombillas de repuesto; y prohibición de modificaciones peligrosas sin recertificación de la FDA.
- Alcance y aplicación: las reglas afectarían a fabricantes y operadores de aproximadamente 18,000–19,000 salones de bronceado y 15,000–20,000 otros establecimientos que ofrecen este servicio en EE. UU.
- Reacciones: organizaciones médicas (Academia Americana de Dermatología, American Cancer Society, Academia Americana de Pediatría) apoyan la medida; asociaciones de la industria la critican como innecesaria o excesiva.
- Procedimiento: las propuestas se publicaron para comentarios públicos por 90 días (plazo que cerró el 21 de marzo de 2016); incluyen orientación adicional para la industria.

En resumen: la FDA busca prohibir el bronceado en interiores para menores, reforzar el consentimiento informado de adultos y exigir mejoras de seguridad en equipos y locales para reducir casos de cáncer de piel, quemaduras y lesiones oculares.

PBS’s July 4 “A Capitol Fourth” broadcast drew heavy online criticism after producers admitted they had spliced in fireworks footage from past years into the live telecast. Viewers quickly noticed inconsistencies — the program showed bright, clear-sky fireworks while Washington, D.C., was foggy and overcast and the Capitol’s scaffolding was absent in some shots. After complaints on Twitter and Facebook, the show’s account and a spokesman said producers “showed a combination of the best fireworks from this year and previous years” because the overcast conditions made the live fireworks difficult to see and they wanted to “make the best television.” Many viewers objected that PBS did not disclose the pre-recorded footage up front and called the move misleading or “fake.” The piece also includes rehearsal comments from host Tom Bergeron about the weather and his attitude toward improvising during the live special. (The document appended an unrelated brief about a Texas teen seriously injured making a homemade fireworks device.)

The Metropolitan Police are assessing newly received information about the 1997 deaths of Princess Diana and Dodi Al Fayed. Scotland Yard said officers from its specialist crime and operations command are “scoping” the material to determine its relevance and credibility, but stressed this is not a re‑investigation. The force would not disclose the source; British press reports claim an Army source has passed allegations that the military was involved.

Diana and Fayed died when their hired Mercedes crashed into a pillar in Paris’s Pont de l’Alma tunnel on 31 August 1997 after leaving the Ritz Hotel, while pursued by paparazzi on motorbikes. Their driver, Henri Paul, was killed; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. A 2008 inquest at the Royal Courts of Justice found they were unlawfully killed, citing Paul’s drunken, high‑speed driving, the paparazzi pursuit and lack of seatbelts; the inquest followed earlier French and UK inquiries (including Operation Paget) that found no evidence of murder. Officials and former royal protection head Dai Davies have noted previous inquiries reached the same conclusion, while Mohamed Al Fayed said he had no comment but would be “interested in seeing the outcome” and trusted the Met to investigate any credible information.

In late December 2012 The Journal News (a Gannett paper serving Westchester, Rockland and Putnam counties) published an online, searchable Google map listing the full names and home addresses of thousands of licensed pistol-permit holders. Because New York law treats pistol-permit records as public, the newspaper obtained the data via FOIL requests; its reporter Dwight Worley’s FOIL language shows the paper sought not only names and addresses but also permit types and weapon details.

The map provoked intense controversy after the Newtown school shooting: critics argued it exposed private citizens to intimidation and danger and bullied lawful gun owners; supporters said it was lawful public-interest journalism. The paper later removed the map after state law changed to let permit holders request removal, with publisher Janet Hasson defending the initial decision as empowering public debate.

In retaliation, bloggers and readers crowd-sourced and published extensive personal information about Journal News staff—names, home addresses, phone numbers, photos and links to social media and real-estate listings—and built a counter-map of employees. That effort was actively updated and expanded, and included publisher Hasson’s contact details. The counter-campaign also compiled lists of Journal News advertisers and encouraged boycotts. The situation generated threats and security scares (e.g., a suspicious package), broad media coverage, and heated public debate over the ethics of publishing public records.

Key issues raised:
- Legality vs. ethics: the permit data were public records, but many argued publishing them in map form—especially so soon after Newtown—was irresponsible and intrusive.
- Reciprocity and escalation: opponents used the same public-record methods to expose journalists’ personal information as a protest/counterpunch.
- Transparency’s double edge: advocates of open data noted its civic benefits, while critics warned that public records can be weaponized for harassment or partisan ends.
- Process and accountability: FOIL correspondence shows the paper pursued extensive gun-record details; county clerks’ responses varied in speed and cooperation; subsequent changes in state law affected publication decisions.

The controversy sparked national and international attention, legal and ethical debate among journalists and open-government advocates, calls for boycotts and protests, and multiple media appearances and opinion pieces from both sides.

Researchers at Weill Cornell Medical College presented data suggesting a toxin made by certain strains of the common foodborne bacterium Clostridium perfringens may trigger multiple sclerosis (MS). The toxin, called epsilon and produced by C. perfringens types B and D, was shown in laboratory and mouse studies to increase blood–brain barrier permeability and to kill oligodendrocytes—the myelin-producing cells that are destroyed in MS lesions. The team also found epsilon toxin bound to other central nervous system cell types that may explain meningeal inflammation and cortical lesions seen in MS.

Prior work by the group identified a type B C. perfringens isolate in a 21‑year‑old MS patient, and screening of stored blood and spinal fluid showed MS patients were about ten times more likely than controls to have antibodies indicating past exposure to the epsilon toxin. In a small food survey, 13–13.5% of samples contained C. perfringens and roughly 2.7–3% carried the gene for the epsilon toxin.

Investigators and outside experts emphasize these findings are preliminary and do not prove causation, but they add a plausible environmental trigger to MS research. If confirmed, the association could point toward preventive or therapeutic strategies (for example vaccines, antitoxins or targeted eradication of toxin-producing strains). Further larger studies are needed to validate the link and clarify its role in MS.

Egypt has asked Cyprus to extradite Seif al‑Din (Seif Eddin) Mustafa, the Egyptian man who hijacked EgyptAir Flight MS181 on 29 March 2016. Mustafa — described by Cypriot officials as psychologically unstable — boarded the Alexandria–Cairo Airbus A320 with a fake explosive belt, forced the pilot to divert to Larnaca and demanded to see his ex‑wife, who lives in Cyprus. He held the aircraft for about six hours; nearly all 56 passengers, six crew and a security official were released unharmed during a negotiated standoff. In the end Mustafa surrendered on the tarmac and was immediately arrested; the “explosives” proved to be fake telephone‑case devices.

Cyprus remanded him in custody for eight days while Egypt has requested his extradition under a 1996 bilateral treaty. Possible charges include air piracy, kidnapping and threatening behaviour. Cypriot and Egyptian authorities have characterized the incident as not terrorism‑related but likely motivated by a personal/family dispute. Mustafa made incoherent demands at times, including asking for the release of female inmates in Egyptian prisons.

The incident renewed scrutiny of Egyptian airport security following the October 2015 Metrojet/ Sinai bombing. Egyptian media warned of potential damage to tourism and criticized security lapses despite official statements and CCTV shown by Egypt indicating Mustafa passed through two security checks and had his slim bag X‑rayed at Alexandria’s Borg El Arab airport. Crew members were widely praised for calm handling of the situation; one crew member slid out of a cockpit window during the event, and airline staff helped persuade Mustafa to free passengers.

The U.S. Census Bureau reported that Florida has become the nation’s third-most populous state, surpassing New York. As of the July 1, 2014 estimate, Florida’s population was about 19.9 million—up roughly 293,000 over the year, an average gain of about 803 people per day—while New York reached about 19.7 million, having grown by roughly 51,000. Nationally, the U.S. population rose 0.75% from July 1, 2013 to July 1, 2014 to about 318.9 million.

Population gains were widespread: 44 states and the District of Columbia grew. Six states lost residents (Illinois, West Virginia, Connecticut, New Mexico, Alaska and Vermont); Puerto Rico had the largest decline, down 1.3% (about 47,000). Growth was concentrated in the South and West, which together accounted for roughly 2 million of the nearly 2.4 million net new U.S. residents; the Midwest and Northeast gained about 300,000.

North Dakota led percentage growth at about 2.2%, driven by an energy boom. Other fast growers included Nevada, Texas, Colorado, Arizona, Utah and Idaho (all >1.3%). Texas added the most people in absolute terms (about 451,000). California (38.8 million) and Texas (27 million) remain the first- and second-largest states; Georgia surpassed 10 million for the first time.

A 19-year-old Dutchman forced his way into the headquarters of public broadcaster NOS in Hilversum on Jan. 29, 2015, demanding airtime and threatening bomb attacks if he was not allowed on air. Dressed in a black suit and tie and carrying what appeared to be a long pistol with a silencer, he forced a security guard to take him into an editorial studio but was led into an empty room. He paced and spoke on camera, at one point saying he and others were “hired by intelligence agencies” and claiming ties to a “hackers’ collective.” Police special units stormed the studio, the man dropped the weapon (later identified as fake), was arrested without resistance and taken into custody on suspicion of making threats, weapons possession and taking a hostage. No injuries occurred and searches for explosives found nothing. Authorities said he appeared to have acted alone; investigators were probing his motive and background. NOS canceled its main evening newscasts, evacuated staff and resumed broadcasting from The Hague after the building was declared safe.

A stolen pickup containing a 3-week-old infant was recovered after a passerby who mistaken a doll in the vehicle for an unresponsive baby called 911, Lumberton police said. Monday evening a woman left her three small children briefly while taking two inside her home; during that time someone stole her dark gray 2014 Ford F-150 with the infant secured in a rear car seat. Police broadcast an alert and the truck was abandoned about 10 minutes later in a grocery parking lot roughly three miles away. A man walking by noticed a window was down, saw what he thought was an unconscious child (later identified as a doll) and called authorities. Deputies found the baby unharmed and reunited the child with the mother. No arrests have been made; police are seeking two suspects and ask anyone with information to contact Detective Deana Locklear.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) at Los Angeles International Airport intercepted 67 live giant African snails in an air cargo shipment from Lagos, Nigeria. The two plastic packages weighed just over 35 pounds and were labeled as Achatina Fulica for human consumption and destined for San Dimas, California. CBP agriculture specialists quarantined the shipment on July 1 (notice received July 7 in one report) and sent samples to USDA specialists, who identified the mollusks as giant African snails (Archachatina marginata/related common names). 

Officials warned the snails are a highly invasive pest that can consume more than 500 plant species, damage buildings by eating stucco and paint, and carry parasites harmful to humans, including one linked to meningitis. This was the largest such seizure at LAX; the shipment was transferred to the USDA and the snails were ultimately destroyed by incineration. Authorities said the find highlights CBP’s role in preventing introduction of harmful foreign pests.

Tennessee state Senator Stacey Campfield drew criticism after posting a “joke” on his personal blog one week after the Boston Marathon pressure-cooker bombing. The post, titled “Here comes Feinstein again,” depicted a pressure cooker labeled with tongue-in-cheek “assault” features and mocked efforts by Sen. Dianne Feinstein to ban military-style assault weapons. When reporters questioned the timing and sensitivity of the post—coming days after the bombing that killed three people—Campfield replied, “People need to lighten up,” and insisted critics have a double standard for condemning gun rights advocacy after tragedies like Sandy Hook. He followed up on his blog criticizing liberals and gun-control advocates.

The incident came amid other controversial actions and statements by Campfield: he recently withdrew a bill tying student academic performance to family welfare after public backlash, threatened funding cuts to the University of Tennessee over a “Sex Week” event, and made inflammatory remarks about homosexuality and HIV education earlier in the year. The blog post prompted media calls and public complaints about its appropriateness.

Two dogs in Genesee County (Flint area) tested positive for lead toxicity, state veterinarian Dr. James Averill confirmed. The cases—one confirmed in October 2015 and one in January 2016—are the first canine lead-toxicity reports in Michigan in five years. Both animals (one a family pet, one a stray) are alive; officials have not released details on whether they drank Flint tap water, exact lead levels, ages, weights or symptoms, citing confidentiality and state law.

State officials say most canine lead tests in the area have been negative. There is no routine pet lead screening; testing is done when veterinarians suspect toxicity, and lab testing is provided free if a vet requests it. Veterinarians note lead poisoning can be chronic, produce broad, nonspecific signs (lethargy, behavioral change, digestive, neurologic or blood issues) and can be hard to distinguish from other illnesses. Pet owners should watch for any deviation from normal behavior and seek veterinary care if concerned.

To protect animals, residents are advised to treat pet water the same as their own: test tap water, use certified filters or bottled water, and avoid giving pets unfiltered Flint tap water (bathing is considered acceptable). If filtered or bottled water isn’t available, veterinarians suggested temporary alternatives like melted snow.

Researchers have produced the first data-driven global map and estimate of groundwater, distinguishing “modern” (recharged within decades) from much older stores. Using datasets from nearly a million watersheds and >40,000 models, the international team led by Tom Gleeson estimates total groundwater volume at ~23 million km3, of which only about 0.35 million km3 (less than 6%, possibly as little as 1% in the upper 2 km) is renewed within a human lifetime.

Key findings and implications
- Modern groundwater is concentrated in tropical and mountainous regions (Amazon Basin, Congo, Indonesia, along the western Americas and the Rockies); arid regions such as the Sahara have little modern groundwater.
- Modern groundwater is more connected to the active water cycle and can buffer climate extremes and droughts if managed, but is more vulnerable to contamination and climate change.
- Much deeper, older groundwater is often non-renewable on human timescales, can be saline or contain contaminants (arsenic, uranium), and is widely used for agriculture and industry.
- Knowing volumes of modern vs. old groundwater allows better estimates of how long supplies will last when combined with extraction and depletion rates; previous work identified global hotspots of groundwater stress (northern India/Pakistan, northern China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, parts of the US and Mexico).
- The authors plan further global-scale modelling to relate volumes to use and depletion to estimate time-to-depletion where resources are overexploited.

The study was published in Nature Geoscience and funded by several scientific bodies. It provides a quantitative foundation for groundwater management and policy in the face of rising demand and climate change.
