Ryder (Rick/Richard) Johnson, a 20–21-year-old Lafayette man, has been missing since Jan. 17 after finishing his shift at Eldora Mountain Resort near Nederland. His vehicle was found that night parked near Gross Reservoir/5800 Block of Flagstaff/Gross Dam Road in southwest Boulder County — more than 20 miles from Eldora — but searches of the surrounding area have produced no confirmed sightings or evidence of his whereabouts.

Boulder County investigators and multiple rescue teams carried out extensive searches (including drones, boats, cadaver dogs, horseback and searches of about 180 acres and eight miles of Nordic trails), but leads have largely been exhausted. The sheriff’s office says they cannot rule out any possibility, but their primary working theories are that Johnson either intentionally wandered into the mountains and harmed himself or voluntarily disappeared to start a new life; foul play has not been confirmed. Johnson was last seen wearing a red-and-black Eldora ski jacket and black pants; he is described as about 5'10", 155 lbs, with brown hair and brown eyes.

In June a severed left foot in a size-13 Rugged Outback boot was found at the base of Eldora; DNA testing by the Boulder County Coroner’s Office ruled out that the foot belonged to Johnson. Johnson’s father, with friends and family donations, has announced a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his son’s recovery or to criminal charges, payable at the family’s discretion. The reward offer runs through Jan. 17, 2017 (the one-year anniversary), and the family continues to pursue searches and appeals for information. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Boulder County Sheriff’s Office (303-441-4444) or Detective Mark Spurgeon at 303-441-3615.

Junot Díaz, the Pulitzer Prize–winning novelist, has publicly denied multiple recent accusations that he behaved inappropriately with women, including Zinzi Clemmons’s claim that he “forcibly kissed” her years earlier. In his first interview since the allegations emerged, Díaz said he was “distressed,” “confused” and “panicked,” insisted he had not been sexually inappropriate or abusive, and called one of his earlier statements about “consent and boundaries” poorly worded. He reiterated that the alleged stairwell kiss did not happen and pointed to a cordial follow-up email from Clemmons and a professor’s recollection that Clemmons appeared unshaken after the event.

The allegations—ranging from alleged unwanted kissing to verbal bullying and comments that left women upset—have divided the literary community. Some accusers (including Carmen Maria Machado, Monica Byrne, Alisa Rivera and others) have described encounters they found misogynistic, humiliating or demeaning; several say there are additional, unnamed women with similar stories. Díaz’s defenders stress his past support for women writers and call for due process, while critics argue that a spectrum of problematic behaviors should be addressed within the #MeToo conversation.

MIT and Boston Review each conducted reviews and decided to retain Díaz in his roles—MIT found no information warranting action after surveying students and records, and Boston Review’s review of public complaints and interviews led it to keep him as fiction editor—though the Pulitzer board’s inquiry remains ongoing. The debate around Díaz highlights tensions in how institutions and the broader public distinguish between different degrees of misconduct, how to weigh reputational consequences, and what counts as part of the #MeToo movement.

An Alabama truck driver, Keith Maddox, was arrested and charged with reckless endangerment after posting videos of himself threatening bicyclists while driving. In clips posted May 20–21, 2014, Maddox is seen revving his engine as he passes cyclists and saying things like “I ought to run him in the ditch,” and “I’m gonna hurt one of them one of these days.” Cycling groups spotted the videos online and alerted the Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office, which arrested Maddox and released him on $3,000 bond. Maddox later posted (and removed) a Facebook apology saying the videos were “in very bad taste,” that he would never intentionally hurt anyone, and asking people to “share the road.”

A 2016 analysis led by Toshihide Tsuda examined thyroid ultrasound screening data from Fukushima Prefecture after the March 2011 Daiichi nuclear accident and reports a markedly elevated rate of thyroid cancer among children and adolescents there. Using results from the mass screening program (roughly 298,000 examinees in the first round and continued screening into a second round), the study found prevalence and incidence rate ratios versus national rates and an internal prefecture reference area that in some comparisons reached 20–50 times higher than expected. The authors argue the excess is unlikely to be explained solely by increased detection from intensive screening.

The data come from the Fukushima Health Management Survey, a large, ongoing public-health program initiated after the disaster that includes thyroid ultrasound exams for residents who were 0–18 at the time of the accident, a basic survey estimating external doses, and other health and mental-health components. The paper notes that thyroid cancer is a known consequence of radioactive iodine exposure (as after Chernobyl), and while thyroid cancer is rarely fatal if treated, patients require lifelong medication.

External experts and agencies are divided. Critics emphasize major limitations of the study: it lacks individual-level radiation dose estimates, may conflate screen-detected lesions with clinically apparent disease, and comparisons to national clinical incidence rates can overstate differences because population screening uncovers many otherwise hidden cases. Review bodies such as WHO and UNSCEAR have predicted no discernible radiation-driven increase in cancer rates to date. Other scientists (including David Brenner) contend the elevated detection cannot be dismissed as a screening effect alone and call for further investigation. The paper’s conclusions carry policy implications for compensation, decontamination, and public-health planning amid ongoing evacuations and remediation.

Organisers and FIFA have decided not to ban vuvuzelas from South African World Cup stadiums despite widespread complaints about their deafening noise. The plastic horns—measured at around 127 decibels—have been compared to a swarm of bees or stampeding elephants, and players, coaches, broadcasters and TV viewers have said they disrupt concentration, commentary and team communication. High-profile players such as Cristiano Ronaldo and Patrice Evra voiced frustration, and some teams report sleep disturbance from early-morning blowing.

FIFA president Sepp Blatter and other officials defended the instrument as part of South African fan culture, with Blatter calling it “a different rhythm, a different sound.” Local organisers stressed the vuvuzela’s cultural significance and international popularity, saying many fans buy them as souvenirs. England players and the England Supporters’ Band offered mixed reactions—some enjoyed the atmosphere and even bought horns to take home.

Organising committee chief Danny Jordaan said the authorities will monitor use and could impose restrictions if necessary: vuvuzelas already are banned if thrown onto the pitch or used as weapons, and fans have been asked not to blow them during national anthems or stadium announcements. Jordaan expressed a preference for singing as a generator of stadium atmosphere but acknowledged the challenge of managing the vuvuzela’s presence. Broadcasters have logged complaints but also note the importance of reflecting the tournament’s live ambience.

Philadelphia police discovered a 36-year-old woman with special needs chained to a bed in the basement of a home on the 200 block of Linton Street in the Olney section after responding late Friday to a neighborhood dispute. Officers found the woman extremely thin, with sores and a limited vocabulary; they cut her free and she was taken to Albert Einstein Medical Center for evaluation. Neighbors and family members say the arrested resident, 46-year-old Regina Bennett, is the victim’s cousin and allegedly served as her caretaker; officers are still investigating the exact relationship and circumstances. Bennett was arrested at the scene for an initial dispute and has since been charged with a range of offenses, including unlawful restraint/false imprisonment, aggravated assault, terroristic threats, simple assault, public drunkenness and related counts. The case drew comparisons to other Philadelphia incidents in which disabled people were detained to exploit their Social Security benefits; police continue probing the situation.

A 29-year-old Crawford County man applying to be a Pennsylvania state trooper was arrested after he admitted during a polygraph pretest that he had sex with an underage girl in 2011. Joseph Adam White of Hartstown told the examiner he had consensual sex and other contact with the girl, who is now 19. Following an interview with the woman and corroboration of her account, state police charged White with four counts of unlawful sexual contact with a minor and 10 counts of corruption of minors. He was at the Meadville barracks for a cadet lie detector exam on Jan. 15; court records do not list an attorney for him.

Britain’s Duke and Duchess of Cambridge have released a third official photograph of their eight-month-old son, Prince George, ahead of the royal family’s April tour of New Zealand and Australia (7–25 April). Taken at Kensington Palace by photographer Jason Bell (who also shot George’s christening photos), the image shows William, Catherine and George looking through an open window—Catherine holding George on her knee while William holds the family dog, Lupo. George wears a pale blue jumper with his name; he is pictured watching the dog rather than the camera.

The tour will be the baby’s first overseas trip and Catherine’s first official visit to either country. The itinerary begins in Wellington, includes engagements in Christchurch, Dunedin and Auckland in New Zealand and visits to Canberra, Uluru, Sydney and Adelaide in Australia. Events include ceremonial welcomes (a Powhiri in Wellington), memorial and military commemorations tied to World War I and ANZAC Day (25 April), community visits, and light sporting activities such as informal yacht racing and “rippa” rugby. Kensington Palace said whether George will attend particular events will be decided closer to the tour. The Cambridges’ entourage will include George’s nanny and a hairdresser.

Historic England archaeologists have excavated a medieval holy well, St Anne’s Well, on private farmland in Rainhill near Liverpool. The site — identified from a 1983 photo and descriptions on the National Heritage List — had long been buried by ploughing and was on the Heritage at Risk Register since 2010. After a two-day dig by Oxford Archaeology North the team revealed a substantial sandstone-lined well roughly 2m x 2m with three steps down to a pool where medieval pilgrims bathed, believing the waters could wash away sins and cure ailments such as eye disease. 

Historic England stabilized and protected the feature by replacing fallen stones, installing wooden edging to prevent damage from machinery, and arranging a management agreement with the farmer; the well can now be removed from the at-risk register. Members of local societies visited the repaired site. Researchers date the foundation to the late medieval period when the cult of St Anne grew in England; local lore even attaches a dramatic 16th‑century curse story to the well, though that remains folkloric. Further analysis and formal publication of the excavation results are expected.

Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian ever with 22 medals (18 gold), will compete in his fifth Games in Rio at age 31 — a U.S. record for male swimmers. He qualified at U.S. trials to swim three individual events (200m butterfly, 200m individual medley, 100m butterfly) and could swim up to three relays. Phelps and teammate Ryan Lochte are notable older outliers in a sport dominated by youth; a solo gold by either in Rio would set a new mark for the oldest individual Olympic swimming champion.

Career highlights summarized:
- 2000 Sydney (age 15): Olympic debut in 200m butterfly, finished 5th — impressive for his age.
- 2004 Athens (19): Breakout performance — 6 golds and 2 bronzes. Set multiple Olympic records and won his first individual gold (400m IM).
- 2008 Beijing (23): Historic eight gold medals in one Games, with world records in seven events.
- 2012 London: Won six medals (four gold), became the most decorated Olympian (22 medals). Notable as first man to win the same individual event (200m IM) at three straight Olympics.

Phelps was also chosen by fellow U.S. athletes as Team USA flag bearer for the Rio Opening Ceremony — only the second U.S. swimmer to lead the delegation and the fifth swimmer to serve as flag bearer. He said the role reflects more than medals for him now: representing the country and his family. The Rio Games run Aug. 5–21, 2016.

A 27-year-old Bangladeshi immigrant, identified by police as Akayed Ullah, set off a crude pipe bomb strapped to his body in an underground passage linking the 42nd Street–Eighth Avenue and Seventh Avenue subway stations near Times Square in Manhattan at about 7:20 a.m. Monday. The device produced a large puff of smoke, wounded Ullah (burns and cuts to hands and abdomen) and caused minor injuries or symptoms — ringing ears and headaches — to three commuters who self-transported to hospitals. Commuters fled and the area was locked down while authorities searched for other devices.

Ullah told investigators he was inspired by Islamic State propaganda and upset with U.S. policy toward Muslim countries; a pro-IS media outlet later suggested a link to President Trump’s Jerusalem announcement. Federal and NYPD counterterrorism teams collected fragments of the bomb (which used a small battery and a string of Christmas lights) to study its construction. Authorities say Ullah acted alone; he was arrested, taken to Bellevue Hospital, and federal charges were expected.

The attack reignited debates over terrorism, public safety and immigration. President Trump and Attorney General Jeff Sessions linked the case to immigration policy, urging reforms; New York officials emphasized quick police response and the device’s amateur construction for preventing greater harm. Neighbors described Ullah as quiet and religious; local residents expressed fear about backlash against immigrant communities. Investigations continued, with officials asking witnesses to come forward and warning of increased security across the transit system.

Verizon is launching Share Everything, a family-style plan (available June 28) that pools data across all devices on an account and bundles unlimited voice and text with per-device access fees. For many families with multiple smartphones, tablets and uneven usage, the pooled model can be more efficient—letting heavy users draw from the household bucket while light users avoid wasted individual allowances. In a sample family of seven devices, Verizon’s shared plan cost about $10 less than the old plan but offered 1GB less data; adding overage charges makes the two effectively equal. 

However, the change is largely an administrative repackaging rather than a meaningful discount for most customers. Individuals and light-voice users typically face higher bills because Share Everything forces unlimited voice/text and levies sizable monthly access fees ($40 smartphone, $30 basic phone, $10 tablet, $20 for laptops/modems). Data pricing tiers run from $50 (1GB) to $100 (10GB). Existing customers can keep legacy plans unless they upgrade and accept a subsidized device (which may require moving to shared plans and losing grandfathered unlimited data). 

Bottom line: Shared plans benefit multi-device families who want unified data and unlimited voice/text, but they disadvantage many individual users and some moderate users who preferred smaller voice/text allowances or lower-cost, data-light options. The move also strengthens carrier “stickiness” by tying households to one provider.

North Dakota’s Republican-controlled Legislature has sent two restrictive anti-abortion bills to Gov. Jack Dalrymple after Senate passage, potentially creating some of the toughest state limits in the country if he signs them.

Key provisions
- HB1456 (“fetal heartbeat” bill): Requires physicians to determine whether a fetal heartbeat is detectable before performing an abortion. Performing an abortion after a detected heartbeat would be a Class C felony for the doctor (up to five years in prison and fines); patients would not be criminally charged. Heartbeats can be detected as early as about six weeks via transvaginal ultrasound (abdominal detection often occurs around 10–12 weeks). The bill includes exceptions to save the mother’s life or for severe medical emergencies but does not exempt rape or incest.
- HB1305: Makes it a Class A misdemeanor for a physician to knowingly perform an abortion sought because of the fetus’s sex or because of genetic abnormalities (e.g., Down syndrome). The bill was split and passed in parts before final passage.

Votes and reaction
- Both bills passed largely along party lines: HB1456 passed the Senate 26–17 (House 63–28) and HB1305 passed 28–15 in the Senate (House 64–27).
- Supporters framed the measures as protecting life and preventing discrimination or “eugenics.” Opponents called them an overreach that would govern women’s bodies, voiced practical concerns about medical practice (e.g., whether doctors would be required to use invasive ultrasounds), and warned of harms to patients and to recruiting physicians.
- National abortion-rights groups (ACLU, Planned Parenthood, Center for Reproductive Rights) condemned the bills and pledged legal challenges, arguing they conflict with Supreme Court precedent (Roe v. Wade), which protects abortion until fetal viability (generally ~22–24 weeks).
- If enacted, the six-week heartbeat ban would be among the earliest abortion restrictions in the U.S., stricter than recent 12-week bans (e.g., Arkansas). Experts and advocates expect immediate court challenges; critics say courts would likely find the measures unconstitutional.

Next steps
- Both bills now await Gov. Dalrymple’s decision; he had not indicated whether he would sign or veto them. Supporters say the measures are intended to prompt a legal challenge to Roe; opponents urge a veto to preserve reproductive choice. The state’s fiscal cushion and political makeup could support a prolonged legal fight.

Vanity Fair is moving ahead with a high-profile story on Gwyneth Paltrow despite the actress’ reported attempts to block the magazine. Editor‑in‑Chief Graydon Carter told The Times of London the piece “will run” and that the magazine has a strong writer assigned. The story follows reports that Paltrow emailed celebrity friends asking them not to speak to Vanity Fair and to avoid working with the magazine; Carter said that action “forced my hand” and made him more determined to publish. He defended Vanity Fair’s reporting as part of its job and noted that publicists and stars often react angrily. Carter also suggested Paltrow may be unprepared for a less protected celebrity culture in Los Angeles and criticized the transient fame of reality‑TV figures. The report comes amid longstanding coverage of Paltrow by Vanity Fair, which has featured her multiple times.

Here are the key takeaways from the collection of Sunday political interviews:

- Michael Bloomberg (independent, former Republican and Democrat) said President Obama would be a "credible, formidable" 2012 candidate and predicted a close race regardless of the Republican nominee. Bloomberg criticized anti-science positions in the GOP field but defended Rick Perry’s 2007 HPV vaccine mandate and Mitt Romney’s Massachusetts health-care plan as legitimate accomplishments. He praised New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie as a strong governor and dismissed President Obama’s use of Warren Buffett as a tax-theater example.

- Former Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels urged Republicans to give Texas Gov. Rick Perry time after uneven debate showings and praised Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) for his work on bipartisan deficit-reduction efforts.

- RNC Chair Reince Priebus mocked a perceived shift in the Obama campaign message away from “hope and change,” and in a joint interview with DNC Chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz he confronted Democratic talking points, citing a recent Republican special-election win as evidence against them.

- Sen. Mark Warner called the potential government shutdown over short-term spending measures “embarrassing,” blamed tea party-aligned House Republicans for hardline demands, and defended disaster-aid priorities. Sen. Lamar Alexander countered that Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid had manufactured the crisis and urged Senate approval of the House bill.

- Sen. Lindsey Graham warned that the U.S. must keep “all options on the table” with Pakistan after allegations its intelligence service aided terrorists, saying Pakistan needs to “choose wisely” and suggesting possible consequences, including military options.

- White House senior adviser David Plouffe said he does not expect major changes to President Obama’s senior staff or Cabinet before the 2012 campaign, urged passage of the American Jobs Act, and indicated the U.S. may continue reducing aid to Pakistan if it does not act against the Haqqani network and other anti-American militant activity.

U.S. job growth remained resilient in early 2016 despite global economic turmoil. February’s employment report showed a stronger-than-expected labor market: nonfarm payrolls rose by 242,000, beating forecasts and following upward revisions that added 30,000 jobs to January and December totals. The unemployment rate stayed at 4.9% as labor-force participation climbed to 62.9%, its highest in a year, with over half a million people entering the workforce.

Hiring gains were broad-based—construction, retail and health care led job creation and offset continuing losses in mining and oil-related industries and weak manufacturing hiring. Over the past 12 months the U.S. added about 2.7 million jobs. Wage growth has picked up modestly: average hourly earnings rose about 2.2–2.5% year-over-year depending on the measure, though February showed a 3-cent monthly decline in one report. Hours worked edged down to 34.4 per week, the lowest in two years.

Stronger hiring and rising incomes have supported consumer spending—auto sales, home purchases and restaurant receipts have all improved—creating a largely self-sustaining cycle of hiring and spending. Still, external headwinds remain: slower growth in China, low oil prices, a strong dollar and market volatility have pressured exports, energy-sector jobs, and some manufacturing employment.

The Federal Reserve is watching wage trends closely as it weighs further rate increases; investors largely viewed another hike in March as unlikely. Overall, the February data signaled continued U.S. labor-market strength amid global uncertainty.

An NBC employee was fired for posting a 1994 Today show clip — in which hosts Bryant Gumbel, Katie Couric and Elizabeth Vargas awkwardly try to define the Internet and complain about e‑mail addresses — to the web without authorization. NBC said the person violated company conduct standards by repeatedly copying and distributing various materials without permission; the network indicated the dismissal was for a pattern of unauthorized sharing, not just that single clip. The vintage segment circulated widely on Facebook, e‑mail and media sites, and Today later aired the footage with current host Matt Lauer joking that everyone felt the same confusion about the Internet at the time. Commentators noted that even redistributing old or already‑aired material can violate employers’ rules and raises broader issues about policing unauthorized uploads online.

Former Norwegian prime minister Kjell Magne Bondevik says he was held and questioned for about an hour at Washington Dulles Airport after customs agents saw a 2014 Iran entry stamp in his passport. Bondevik, who served two terms as prime minister (1997–2000, 2001–05) and now leads the Oslo Centre, was traveling from Europe to attend the National Prayer Breakfast. He says his diplomatic passport clearly identified him as a former prime minister and that he had traveled to Iran in 2014 to speak at a human-rights conference.

Bondevik was placed in a room with other travelers facing extra scrutiny, waited roughly 40 minutes and was then questioned for about 20 minutes about the Iran trip. He told ABC7 he understands security concerns but felt being a former head of government with a diplomatic passport should have sufficed. Dulles officials reportedly said the review related not to President Trump’s recent travel ban but to a 2015 law tightening Visa Waiver Program rules: travelers from VWP countries (including Norway) who have visited Iran, Iraq, Sudan, Syria, Libya, Somalia or Yemen since March 2011 generally must obtain a visa. DHS notes case-by-case exceptions exist, including for travel on behalf of international organizations; Bondevik says the U.S. embassy in Oslo had advised his passport and ESTA would be sufficient. U.S. Customs and Border Protection declined to discuss individual cases; the Norwegian embassy said the matter was resolved. The incident has prompted Bondevik to voice concern about the U.S.’s reputation and treatment of visitors under heightened entry controls.

A Pinellas County small-claims case ended with a judge ordering shared custody of a dog after neighbors each claimed ownership of a Labrador mix named Elario.

Background: In January 2016, 53-year-old Tina Marie Walker adopted an emaciated black Lab from the Pinellas County shelter for $5 and began bringing him to the apartment of her neighbor, 68-year-old Vietnam veteran David Somerville, who had been recovering from lung surgery and credits the dog with improving his health. For about two years Elario split time between their apartments and formed strong bonds with both people.

Dispute: The relationship deteriorated after Walker left Elario with Somerville during a vacation; later Somerville sought to have the dog’s microchip reprinted in his name, saying he was more financially stable and had paid vet bills when Elario was injured or sick. Walker says she adopted and cared for Elario and only offered to add Somerville’s name to the microchip. In December Somerville sued to be declared sole owner.

Ruling: Judge Lorraine Kelly found both had invested significant time with Elario and witnesses confirmed the dog’s affection for both. She ordered joint custody with a calendar specifying pickup times — likening the arrangement to divorced parents sharing a child. Walker has appealed, moved out of the apartment building to reduce friction, and continues to spend time with Elario at the dog park.

This document is a mixed collection of material: an opening note about Alexa Internet donating daily crawl data to the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine (added after an embargo), followed by an address and phone number for a Lexington, VA establishment, and then many user-submitted reviews and comments about a restaurant (clearly the Red Hen) dominated by anger over a political incident.

Key points:

- Technical note: Since 1996 Alexa has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive; those data are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.
- Business listing: 11 E Washington St, Lexington, VA 24450, (540) 464-4401.
- The bulk of the text is hostile online reviews and comments about the Red Hen. Themes include:
  - Strong political reactions: many posts reference the restaurant ejecting Sarah Huckabee Sanders (a Trump administration official), with commenters calling the owners “hypocrites,” “liberal,” and using abusive epithets; several accuse the restaurant of excluding conservatives and praise Chick-fil-A as an alternative.
  - Claims of review censorship: multiple writers allege Yelp repeatedly deletes their negative reviews or is biased/liberal.
  - Poor food and service complaints: numerous reports of overcooked or burnt food, cold/old or inedible dishes, rude servers, unsanitary conditions, and food poisoning/gastric distress.
  - Accusations of unsanitary operations and illicit activity: at least one claim mentions cockroaches, filthy bathrooms, employees selling drugs—presented as anecdote-level allegations without verification.
  - Extreme and sometimes profane language: several entries use insults, threats, or vivid hostile imagery (including a grotesque, likely satirical account of killing and eating a hen).
  - Calls to boycott and shut the restaurant down; some reviewers say they’ll never return.

Overall tone: overwhelmingly negative, politically charged, and often inflammatory; the content blends legitimate service/food complaints with politically motivated attacks, allegations of censorship, and some likely hyperbole or satire.

A grand jury in Cuyahoga County has returned a 977-count indictment against Ariel Castro, significantly expanding an earlier 329-count indictment to cover the entire period prosecutors allege he held three women captive in his Cleveland home. The new charges add 648 counts and span the full decade of the victims’ captivity. Castro is accused of abducting Michelle Knight (2002), Amanda Berry (2003) and Gina DeJesus (2004), repeatedly raping them, sometimes keeping them chained and seldom allowing them out of the house, and fathering Berry’s daughter. He faces 512 counts of kidnapping, 446 counts of rape, seven counts of gross sexual imposition, six counts of felonious assault, three counts of child endangerment, one count of possessing criminal tools, and two counts of aggravated murder tied to an alleged pregnancy termination. 

Prosecutor Timothy McGinty’s office did not include a death-penalty specification in this indictment; a capital review committee met to consider it but has not completed its evaluation, and prosecutors could seek the death penalty later. Defense attorneys said they were pleased the new indictment did not seek death and indicated they had presented mitigating material to the committee; they also suggested a plea could be possible if capital punishment is not pursued. Experts note legal and evidentiary obstacles to obtaining a death sentence, including proving aggravated murder tied to pregnancy termination and the victims’ willingness to testify.

The three women and Berry’s six-year-old daughter were freed on May 4 when Berry escaped and alerted neighbors. The case drew intense media attention; a victims’ fund has raised over $1 million. Castro, jailed in Cuyahoga County, was ruled competent to stand trial and is scheduled for arraignment July 17, with trial set to begin Aug. 5.

A 5,000-pound concrete memorial marking a reported 1969 UFO encounter in Sheffield, Massachusetts must be moved again because a recent land survey found it sits on a town right-of-way easement. The memorial, installed in 2015 and shifted about 30 feet after it was first found on town land, stands near the town’s historic covered bridge and includes a plaque bearing a gubernatorial citation, a bench and light posts. Town Administrator Rhonda LaBombard says town bylaws prohibit unauthorized displays on town property and the items must be removed by the owner or the town will do so in May; ownership of the monument is unclear.

Thom Reed, who was nine at the time of the Sept. 1, 1969 incident and is one of four family members who reported being enveloped by an amber glow and experiencing missing time, objects to the move and says he helped select the current site. Reed and others who witnessed the event — about 40 people from several nearby towns reported seeing the strange light — say the memorial is important to the community and are considering legal action to block its removal. The 1969 sighting has been recorded in the Great Barrington Historical Society archives and has been the subject of TV shows and documentaries.

The piece analyzes how shifting early Republican nominating dates could help—or hurt—Mitt Romney’s 2012 campaign and focuses on a standoff between New Hampshire and other early states.

Key points:
- Romney benefits from earlier voting because he leads the field and is a well-prepared, front-running candidate. Earlier contests limit rivals’ opportunities to build momentum and discourage late entrants.
- Romney’s campaign pushed Nevada to move its caucus up to Jan. 14 from Feb. 18 to speed the nominating process.
- New Hampshire Secretary of State Bill Gardner, protector of his state’s first-in-the-nation primary, threatened to move New Hampshire’s primary into December if other states (notably Nevada) do not give up dates that would allow New Hampshire to keep its legal requirement of being held a full week before any “similar election.”
- New Hampshire law requires its primary be on a Tuesday, before any other primary, and at least a week ahead of any similar contest; practical December options are Dec. 6 or Dec. 13. Those dates would isolate New Hampshire from the rest of the early calendar, creating a four-week gap before Iowa.
- A December New Hampshire could reduce the primary’s electoral relevance: any winner’s “bounce” might dissipate before January contests, and rivals could argue the compressed schedule disadvantaged them. The media might treat a December New Hampshire as a curiosity.
- If New Hampshire stayed in early January (e.g., Jan. 10) while Iowa and New Hampshire followed the traditional back-to-back pattern, Romney would have a buffer—losing Iowa wouldn’t be as damaging if he could rebound in New Hampshire. If New Hampshire instead voted in December, a poor Iowa showing could leave Romney with lasting negative momentum into Nevada and South Carolina.
- A simple fix exists: Nevada could move its caucus from Jan. 14 to Jan. 17, allowing New Hampshire to schedule Jan. 10 and preserve a January sequence similar to 2008. If Nevada agreed, Romney (who influenced Nevada’s earlier move) might benefit from encouraging that adjustment.
- Politico reporting shows Gardner publicly reiterated he would move the primary as far up as necessary to keep first-in-the-nation status, naming Dec. 6 and Dec. 13 as realistic options. His unilateral stance and refusal to negotiate have angered other early-state officials and the RNC, who worry a December primary would disrupt campaigning and the calendar.
- Nevada moved forward with a Jan. 14 date after failing to get firm coordination from Gardner; that decision eliminated Jan. 10 as an option for New Hampshire because of the seven-day buffer rule, intensifying the scheduling conflict.

Overall, the scheduling scramble could advantage Romney if early voting is compressed, but New Hampshire’s possible December move could also diminish its influence and complicate momentum dynamics—unless states like Nevada shift slightly to accommodate a January sequence.

In Other Words, a feminist community bookstore in Portland long used as the “Women and Women First” shop on IFC’s Portlandia, has ended its relationship with the show. The bookstore says production repeatedly mistreated staff, left the space damaged, forced neighboring businesses to close without warning, and refused to take accountability. The small flat fee paid per episode did not compensate for lost revenue or neighborhood impact; tourists mostly only take photos outside and do not provide financial or political support.

The collective criticized Portlandia for being politically harmful: its recurring “woman in a dress” gag is described as trans-antagonistic and trans-misogynist, contributing to ridicule of trans femmes amid real-world violence against them. The show is also overwhelmingly white despite filming in a historically Black neighborhood; producers once asked the bookstore to remove a Black Lives Matter sign, which the bookstore refused. In Other Words argues Portlandia has fueled gentrification and displacement by romanticizing the city for newcomers and real estate marketing.

The current board, staff and volunteers—many of whom were not involved in the original decision to allow filming—support discontinuing the partnership and back a volunteer’s placement of a “Fuck Portlandia” sign in the window. The statement asks for donations and volunteers to help the bookstore continue as a social-justice hub.

An alleged case of gross negligence in Chhattisgarh, India, left multiple women dead and many hospitalized after mass sterilization surgeries. On Nov. 8, a surgeon reportedly performed 83 tubectomies in about six hours using instruments that were not disinfected and exceeded official guidance limiting surgeons to 30 sterilizations per day. Of the 83 poor rural women (all under 32) who took part in the free government sterilization camp for a small payment (~600 rupees, ~$10), at least 10 died and dozens were hospitalized; reports at different times put deaths at eight initially and later at 10, with 69 reported ill in one account and 20–69 in others, and several remaining in critical condition. Officials cited infections causing septic shock, blood poisoning or hemorrhagic shock as likely causes; autopsies and a criminal investigation are under way. The surgeon, R.K. Gupta, and other officials have been suspended.

The incident has drawn national attention and condemnation. Chhattisgarh Chief Minister Raman Singh called it negligence; Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged a thorough probe. Human-rights and reproductive-health advocates blamed systemic issues: the one-day sterilization camp model, poor hygiene and accountability, and pressure from target-driven family-planning practices that persist despite official claims of a “target-free” policy. India has one of the world’s highest female sterilization rates (about 37% of married women in 2005–06), and millions of poor people have been offered small incentives to undergo sterilization. The tragedy has renewed calls to reassess mass sterilization camps and improve safety, oversight and voluntary contraceptive counseling.

The Episcopal Church’s General Convention in Salt Lake City voted overwhelmingly to permit same-sex religious marriages and to revise its marriage canon to gender-neutral language, making it the third major U.S. mainline Protestant body to formally offer such rites. The House of Bishops approved the new liturgy and canon changes earlier in the week; the House of Deputies then passed them by wide margins (liturgy about 184‑23; canon change about 173‑27). Beginning the first Sunday of Advent (Nov. 29), congregations may use a gender‑neutral rite called “The Witnessing and Blessing of a Lifelong Covenant,” and “trial” liturgies for same‑sex marriages where they are legal. Use of the rites is subject to diocesan bishops’ permission, and clergy may decline to officiate without penalty.

The votes follow the U.S. Supreme Court’s nationwide legalization of same‑sex marriage and decades of internal Episcopal debate that included earlier steps—recognizing LGBT members in 1976, adopting provisional blessing rites in 2012, and electing the first openly gay bishop in 2003. Supporters framed the change as pastoral inclusion and the result of long theological conversation; opponents warned it contradicts biblical teaching and could deepen schism. Archbishop of Canterbury Justin Welby expressed concern about the move’s impact on the wider Anglican Communion, though Episcopal leaders described the measures as accommodations balancing conscience and unity. The measures take effect Nov. 29, but practice will vary: some dioceses and clergy will allow same‑sex weddings, others will prohibit them.

This long document collects reporting and commentary about the persistent speculation that Idris Elba might succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond, reactions to that idea, and related Bond news.

Key points:

- Idris Elba: At a British Film Institute event Elba said the Bond rumors have “eaten themselves” and that any chance of him getting the role is gone. He confirmed he has never held talks with Bond producers and blamed Daniel Craig for starting the speculation after a compliment years earlier. Elba also discussed finishing Luther season four, potential spinoff plans, and his music projects — including a personal documentary, Mandela, My Dad and Me, and a tribute album made after his father’s death.

- Anthony Horowitz and Trigger Mortis: Horowitz, author of the new officially commissioned Bond novel Trigger Mortis, repeatedly praised Daniel Craig but said he would not cast Elba as Bond, calling Elba “a bit too rough” or “too street” (language widely criticized as racially coded). Horowitz suggested Adrian Lester instead. He later apologized for the remarks. The piece also summarizes Horowitz’s intentions for the book: to write in Fleming’s voice, restore a more straightforward, macho Bond, reintroduce Pussy Galore, and feature stronger female characters (including one, Jeopardy Lane, who outshines Bond). Horowitz criticizes aspects of recent Bond films (e.g., Skyfall), explains estate-imposed “ground rules,” and discusses other themes in the novel.

- Race and Bond: Commentary points out that while a black Bond remains controversial for some, there have been moves toward more inclusive representation: David Oyelowo was chosen to narrate the Trigger Mortis audiobook, making him — in voice — a new James Bond and prompting discussion about racism in reactions to nonwhite actors in traditionally white roles. An update notes Hugh Quarshie had earlier narrated Bond material. Oyelowo supports Elba as a prospective screen Bond and frames a black Bond as a cultural event.

- Extras: The document includes a long extract from Trigger Mortis and background material on Horowitz (his career, memoir-like anecdotes, and other projects), plus reactions and commentary threads responding to Horowitz’s comments.

Overall tone: The compilation contrasts Elba’s dismissal of the Bond rumors and his focus on other projects with controversy over who “should” play Bond, Horowitz’s contentious comments and subsequent apology, and evolving conversations about race, representation, and stewardship of the Bond legacy.

The document highlights major legal and social advances for women in the 2010s and contrasts global gender inequality using the U.N. Gender Inequality Index.

Key points:
- Women’s movements achieved major judicial victories in the decade, including strengthened abortion rights and legalization of same-sex marriage in some places.
- The Global Fund for Women marked International Women’s Day’s 100th anniversary by showcasing the top legal breakthroughs of the 2010s, and listed its Top 10 women’s movement wins for 2010. Notable 2010 developments included expanded labor protections for domestic workers worldwide and women’s pivotal roles in the uprisings that helped topple long-standing leaders in Tunisia and Egypt.
- Assessing “worst countries for women” is complex: metrics vary (humanitarian, education, health, cultural and economic factors), and quantitative indices can’t capture everyday lived experience. The U.N. Development Programme’s Gender Inequality Index (GII) is one useful measure, scoring countries from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality) across labor participation, empowerment (education and political representation), and reproductive health.
- According to the 2008 GII (the latest cited), the five worst-scoring countries were:
  - Yemen (0.853) — highest inequality, with documented violence and discrimination.
  - Democratic Republic of the Congo (0.814) — ongoing violence, rape, famine and disease despite the end of civil war.
  - Niger (0.807) — extremely high maternal mortality (1 in 7 women die in childbirth per a 2010 report).
  - Mali (0.799) — efforts to improve women’s legal standing met with protests.
  - Afghanistan (0.797) — concerns that women’s rights are not prioritized by local or international actors.
- The Netherlands had the best (lowest) score at 0.174. The United States scored 0.400, ranking below Croatia and Lithuania but ahead of Estonia.

Overall, the piece celebrates significant progress led by women’s movements while acknowledging persistent, severe inequalities reflected in global rankings.

Senate and House intelligence leaders and several lawmakers across parties criticized President Barack Obama’s pace and posture toward the rapidly growing Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL/ISIS) and other international threats, while some defended the administration’s caution.

Key points:
- Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said Obama is “very cautious” and possibly “too cautious,” and she agreed with a McCain-Graham op-ed calling for an immediate military plan to confront ISIL. Feinstein warned ISIL aims to seize Baghdad and threaten the U.S. embassy, but noted Pentagon and State Department planning is underway and praised the administration for involving Iraq’s new government so it can offer alternatives to Sunnis.
- Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, said Obama’s “don’t-do-stupid-stuff” approach is failing, arguing a tepid U.S. response to Russia, China and ISIL has worried allies and encouraged further aggression (e.g., Russian incursions, Chinese maritime pressure, Britain beefing up security).
- Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) urged sending “additional U.S. troops” in support roles (not direct combat), expanding airstrikes from Iraq into Syria, and providing more weapons to Kurdish fighters, calling ISIL a direct and possibly unprecedented threat to the U.S.
- Rep. Dutch Ruppersberger (D-Md.), top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, defended Obama’s remark that “we don’t have a strategy yet” for Syria, saying the administration is developing plans and must account for differences between Iraq (where the government has requested help) and Syria (with advanced air defenses and limited intelligence). He warned against rushing action for media pressure.
- Rep. Adam Kinzinger (R-Ill.), an Iraq War veteran, said the U.S. should have acted earlier against ISIL and criticized the president’s “no strategy” comment.

Overall, critics pressed for a more assertive, faster U.S. response—more planning, weapons, support and targeted military action—while some lawmakers cautioned that careful, appropriate planning is necessary given operational and intelligence constraints in Syria.

Vibrio vulnificus, a potentially deadly flesh-eating bacterium found in warm saltwater and on raw shellfish, has caused several serious, fast-moving infections that health officials are warning the public about. In Texas, Michelle O’Brien nearly lost her foot after stepping on an oyster while beachcombing; despite early antibiotics she required five days in the hospital and ICU and says the infection came on “unreal” fast. In Alabama, Lenny Buck, a diabetic cancer survivor, fell ill after eating raw oysters and has undergone multiple surgeries for an infected leg and faces months without walking. Florida health authorities have issued warnings after dozens of cases and multiple recent deaths linked to Vibrio vulnificus; officials advise people with open wounds or weakened immune systems to avoid warm saltwater, to wash off after swimming, and to avoid raw shellfish or thoroughly cook seafood. Infections can cause vomiting, diarrhea, fever, skin lesions and rapid deterioration; early treatment improves chances of keeping affected limbs.

Thousands of Spaniards, mainly young and calling themselves los indignados (the indignant), occupied central squares—most notably Puerta del Sol in Madrid—after a spontaneous sit-in protesting high unemployment, austerity cuts and political corruption. What began as a small group grew into organized encampments with tents, kitchens, legal and medical aid, and daily assemblies. Protesters rejected traditional parties, unions and media, demanding deeper democracy, electoral reform to break the two-party dominance, punishment of corrupt officials and measures to tackle youth unemployment (around 40–45% for young people; national unemployment about 21%).

The movement spread to dozens of cities, bringing some 60,000 people nationwide ahead of regional and municipal elections, and defied a legal ban on public rallies on the day before voting. Police largely did not forcibly disperse the crowds. Assemblies combined earnest policy debates and chaotic elements; volunteers processed proposals through committees but a single coherent platform had not yet emerged. Many participants compared their actions to recent uprisings in North Africa and the Arab Spring, saying they were inspired if not identical in stakes. The protests signaled broad public dissatisfaction and posed a political challenge as Spain faced deep economic hardship and likely losses for the ruling Socialists in upcoming polls.

Adam Mayes, 35, has been placed at the top of the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted list as the agency hunts him and two young girls he is suspected of abducting on April 27. Authorities say Mayes is armed and dangerous. He and his wife, Teresa Mayes, 31, have been charged with first-degree murder and especially aggravated kidnapping; Adam also faces a federal unlawful-flight-to-avoid-prosecution charge, giving the FBI jurisdiction.

According to affidavits and Teresa’s statements to police, Adam fatally shot JoAnn (Jo Ann) Bain and her 14-year-old daughter Adrienne in the Bain home in Whiteville, Tenn., to abduct the family’s two younger daughters, 12‑year‑old Alexandria and 8‑year‑old Kyliyah. Teresa says she witnessed the murders and drove with Adam, the two abducted girls and the bodies to the Mayes family home in Guntown, Miss., where the bodies were buried in the yard. The bodies were recovered this week from the Mayes’ backyard.

Adam was last seen on April 30 on grocery-store surveillance in Guntown. Police found a trailer he rented that contained personal items belonging to the abducted girls. Teresa Mayes and Adam’s mother, Mary Mayes, were arrested and charged—Teresa with especially aggravated kidnapping and Mary with conspiracy to commit especially aggravated kidnapping. Both women reportedly admitted assisting with transporting the children and bodies and witnessing Adam dig the graves; Teresa’s sister said Teresa knew about the killings but may have been too afraid to call police.

Investigators say the two younger girls are likely still with Adam and possibly in extreme danger; the FBI warns he may have altered his or the girls’ appearances. Authorities are offering about $71,000 in combined rewards (including $50,000 from the FBI/U.S. Marshals) for information leading to Mayes’ capture and the recovery of the children. No motive has been established publicly. An intense nationwide manhunt continues.

A Reuters/Ipsos national online tracking poll of 2,036 U.S. adults (1,336 likely voters) conducted the day after the first Clinton-Trump debate found a clear perception that Hillary Clinton won: 56% of adults said Clinton did better vs. 26% for Donald Trump. Among likely voters who watched the debate, Clinton led 44% to 39%. Thirty-four percent of likely voters said the debate improved views of Clinton, versus 19% for Trump; 31% said it improved Clinton’s chances for the White House, 16% said it helped Trump.

Despite perceived debate success, Clinton’s overall support among likely voters remained largely unchanged from recent weeks at 42% vs. Trump’s 38%, a lead consistent with the poll’s prior 4–6 point range. Reuters/Ipsos notes it can take days for a debate’s full effect to show. The daily tracking poll has a credibility interval of ±3 points for the full sample and likely voters (±4 for likely voters who watched the debate). Polling aggregators show Clinton’s lead has been narrowing to about 2 points across polls.

Ordonez et al. (2015) review the history, genetics, current spread, and management challenges of Panama disease of banana, caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc). Key points:

- Banana background: Edible bananas originated in the Indo-Malayan region from hybrids of Musa acuminata and M. balbisiana. Despite broad genetic diversity in wild and cultivated Musa, global production relies heavily on a few asexually propagated clones—most notably Cavendish dessert bananas—created and massively disseminated by tissue culture. That monoculture underpins extreme vulnerability to disease.

- Pathogen diversity and classification: Foc is part of the asexual F. oxysporum species complex and is historically categorized into races (1, 2, 4) and about 24 vegetative compatibility groups (VCGs). Molecular analyses (DArTseq and genome sequencing) reveal Foc is polyphyletic and divides into two major clades; pathogenicity to particular cultivars has arisen multiple times or via horizontal gene transfer. High-throughput genotyping is superior to older VCG methods for resolving population structure.

- Tropical Race 4 (TR4): The ongoing global threat to Cavendish bananas is caused by a single clonal lineage, TR4 (VCG01213). TR4 first devastated Cavendish in Taiwan and since the 1990s has spread through Southeast Asia, Australia, and into the Middle East, South Asia, and Africa (reported in Jordan, Lebanon, Pakistan, Mozambique, Oman, and more). Whole-genome and DArTseq comparisons of isolates from distant locations show extremely low SNP diversity (~0.01%), indicating dispersal of essentially one clone.

- Epidemiology and impacts: Foc is soil-borne, persistent, and has a long latent period; infected sites can remain unusable for banana cultivation for many years. Spread occurs via infected planting material, contaminated soil, tools, footwear, water, flooding, and inadequate sanitation. The combination of a clonal, highly virulent pathogen and a globally uniform susceptible host population explains the speed and severity of recent epidemics. Smallholder farmers and regional food supplies are especially at risk.

- Management recommendations: Because monoculture predisposes to catastrophic failure, exclusion and containment are primary short-term defenses: accurate, rapid molecular diagnostics for TR4 in plants, soil, and water, strict quarantine and sanitation, and surveillance. Understanding Foc epidemiology and developing effective removal and soil treatments to reduce inoculum are urgent. Long-term control requires deploying durable host resistance—exploiting resistance found in wild Musa accessions via breeding or genetic transformation—plus large investments in R&D and recognition of banana as a major staple crop. Somaclones of Cavendish offer only partial resistance and do not meet market needs.

- Policy implication: The finding that TR4 outbreaks worldwide are caused by the same pathogen clone underscores the need for coordinated international awareness, quarantine, and research efforts to prevent further spread and to develop resistant, commercially acceptable cultivars to protect both export industries and smallholder food security.

The study combines population genomics, phylogeography, and a synthesis of historical and management perspectives to argue that current global banana production is highly vulnerable and that immediate, coordinated action is required.

The National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) reported that the 1994 Honda Accord was the most-stolen vehicle in the U.S. for the fourth consecutive year. The NICB’s annual “Hot Wheels” list is compiled from law-enforcement theft reports submitted to the FBI’s National Crime Information Center (NCIC). The top 10 most-stolen vehicles for 2011 were:

- 1994 Honda Accord (1)
- 1998 Honda Civic (2)
- 2006 Ford full-size pickup (3)
- 1991 Toyota Camry (4)
- 2000 Dodge Caravan (5)
- 1994 Acura Integra (6)
- 1999 Chevrolet full-size pickup (7)
- 2004 Dodge full-size pickup (8)
- 2002 Ford Explorer (9)
- 1994 Nissan Sentra (10)

Key reasons cited: older models like the 1994 Accord lack modern security (immobilizers became common on Hondas after 1997), and the popularity and availability of these models make them attractive targets. NICB also highlighted rising thefts of later-model vehicles driven by criminals obtaining illegal replacement key codes and having new keys made, enabling rapid theft and resale or export.

Despite these trends, overall vehicle thefts continue to decline—FBI data showed a drop in 2011, with thefts at their lowest level since 1967. NICB recommends a “layered” approach to prevention: common-sense measures (lock and take keys), warning devices, immobilizers (kill switches, fuel cut-offs, smart keys), and tracking/telematics. NICB also offers VINCheck, a free vehicle-history tool, and urges reporting of theft or fraud tips.

Tonight (June 12) the Guadalupe‑Nipomo Dunes Center will hold a 1920s‑themed gala (6:30–9:30 p.m.; $25) to unveil a recently excavated plaster sphinx from Cecil B. DeMille’s 1923 silent epic The Ten Commandments and open a new permanent exhibit of film artifacts. Only 50 gala tickets remained at press time; a second, smaller “Brunch with the Sphinx” viewing ($10) is set for Saturday morning. The unveiling will feature 1920s music, themed food and drinks, archaeologists from the excavation, and an auction of the first giclée in Steve Thomas’ See America art‑deco poster series (a sphinx-by-the-sea image), with proceeds supporting Dunes Center exhibit renovations.

Background: DeMille built a massive Egyptian set in the Guadalupe‑Nipomo Dunes — including 21 sphinxes and towering pharaoh statues — for the film’s prologue. After filming, the set was abandoned and eventually buried by shifting sands. Archaeological work beginning in the 1990s and continuing with a $120,000 excavation project recovered fragments including a sphinx head in 2012 and, in 2014, a roughly 10.5‑foot section of a sphinx body nicknamed “Nora.” The plaster piece had broken into about 50 fragments; conservators dried and reassembled it (using reversible adhesives) so it could be displayed as an artifact rather than fully restored to like‑new condition. Other recovered items — tobacco tins, medicine bottles, photos, a burned piece of toast and evidence of graffiti and bullet holes — will also be on display when the exhibit opens to the public June 13.

The Dunes Center is seeking roughly $85,000 to fund a planned follow‑up excavation to recover the sphinx’s upper half. The center (1065 Guadalupe St., Guadalupe) is open Wednesday–Sunday, 10 a.m.–4 p.m. More info and tickets: dunescenter.org; the poster is available via Just Looking Gallery.

A comprehensive census of Earth’s biomass, published in PNAS, finds that plants overwhelmingly dominate life on the planet while humans comprise only a minuscule fraction by mass—yet have reshaped global biomass through agriculture and land use.

Key findings
- Total living biomass is about 550 gigatons of carbon (Gt C). Plants account for ~450 Gt C (~80–82% of total). Bacteria are ~70 Gt C (~13%), fungi ~12 Gt C (~2%), archaea ~7 Gt C, protists several Gt C, and animals only ~2 Gt C.
- Humans total ≈0.06 Gt C (≈0.01% of biomass). Despite low mass, humans have caused dramatic shifts: wild mammal biomass has fallen by about 83–85% since civilization, plant biomass is roughly half what it was 10,000 years ago, and livestock (cattle, pigs, etc.) plus humans now vastly outweigh wild mammals.
- Domesticated animals dominate many groups: farmed poultry make up ~70% of birds; livestock represent a majority of mammal biomass, with humans + livestock far exceeding wild mammals.
- Much biomass is terrestrial; marine biomass is smaller (~6 Gt C) and largely microbial. A substantial fraction (~15%) of global biomass lives in the deep subsurface, dominated by bacteria and archaea.
- Some common assumptions are revised: groups with many species (arthropods, nematodes) are not necessarily large by biomass; viruses collectively weigh more than humans; fungi outweigh all animals; fish exceed humans by an order of magnitude.

Methods and caveats
- The authors synthesized hundreds of studies, remote sensing data, genomic surveys and extrapolations to produce taxon-level estimates in gigatons of carbon, and report uncertainties (often large) especially for under-sampled environments like deep aquifers and deep ocean.
- Biomass is reported as carbon mass to avoid issues with water content; estimates can be converted to dry mass roughly by multiplying by two.
- The authors highlight gaps (e.g., deep subsurface sampling, many arthropod and protist groups) and provide open-source data and code for reproducibility.

Implications
- The census gives a quantitative baseline for the composition of the biosphere, informs carbon cycle and ecosystem models, and underscores humanity’s disproportionate impact despite small biomass. The results emphasize how dietary and land-use choices drive major changes in global biomass composition.

Pete Seeger (1919–2014) was a towering figure in American music and activism whose six-decade career blended song, social conscience and grassroots organizing. A prolific singer, banjoist and song-collector, he popularized or wrote enduring anthems—This Land Is Your Land, We Shall Overcome (which he adapted and helped make the civil-rights anthem), If I Had a Hammer, Turn! Turn! Turn!, and Where Have All the Flowers Gone—and taught generations to sing along.

Background and career
- Born in Manhattan to musically trained parents, Seeger dropped out of Harvard in 1938 to travel and learn songs. He worked at the Library of Congress collecting folk music and teamed early with Woody Guthrie and the Almanac Singers.
- He co-founded the Weavers (1949), whose cleaned-up folk/pop recordings yielded hits like Goodnight Irene but whose leftist politics led to blacklisting in the 1950s.
- After the blacklist he toured relentlessly—colleges, churches, camps—and recorded extensively for independent labels, helping spark the folk revival and mentoring younger artists (Bob Dylan, Joan Baez, Arlo Guthrie, Bruce Springsteen and many others).

Politics, blacklisting and controversy
- An outspoken activist, Seeger opposed McCarthyism, marched with Martin Luther King Jr., campaigned for labor, civil rights, peace, environmental causes and later supported Occupy Wall Street.
- He had been a member of the Communist Party in the 1940s (he later said he should have left sooner). In 1955 he refused to answer HUAC questions about his associations, was indicted for contempt of Congress, convicted in 1961 and had the conviction overturned on appeal in 1962. He and the Weavers were kept off much national television into the late 1960s.
- His antiwar song “Waist Deep in the Big Muddy” was initially censored on national TV. He once reportedly reacted angrily when Bob Dylan went electric at Newport—later explaining he could not hear the words over the volume.

Environmental work and legacy
- A lifelong Hudson River advocate, Seeger helped build and launch the sloop Clearwater in 1969; his Hudson River Sloop Clearwater organization successfully pressured cleanup efforts for PCBs decades later.
- He used his fame to raise money and awareness for causes and preserved traditional songs by teaching and recording them. He preferred to call himself a “river singer” rather than a folk star.
- Honors included multiple Grammys (including a lifetime-achievement Grammy), Kennedy Center and National Medal of Arts awards, induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (early influences), and widespread tributes from presidents, peers and younger musicians. He continued performing into his 90s and celebrated his 90th birthday at Madison Square Garden with high-profile colleagues.

Personal
- He lived for decades in Beacon, N.Y., with his wife Toshi (married nearly 70 years, died 2013). He is survived by children, grandchildren (including musician Tao Rodriguez-Seeger) and great-grandchildren.

Seeger combined scholarship, performance and organizing to make songs tools of community and change. He remained optimistically committed to music’s power to move people and “nudge history along.”

President Obama signed two executive actions on National Equal Pay Day aimed at narrowing the gender wage gap by increasing pay transparency among federal contractors. One order bars contractors from retaliating against employees who discuss their salaries; a presidential memorandum requires contractors to submit compensation data disaggregated by sex and race. The measures target “pay secrecy,” which the administration and advocates say hides disparities and hinders enforcement.

Obama framed the steps as part of restoring opportunity, lifting families out of poverty, and ensuring women have the same chances as men, while urging businesses and Congress to do more on childcare, college affordability and retirement savings. The actions apply only to federal contractors; advocates such as Fatima Goss Graves of the National Women’s Law Center praised them as an important step but stressed that broader congressional action (e.g., the Paycheck Fairness Act or Fair Paycheck Act) is needed to cover private-sector workers. That legislation has struggled in Congress despite evidence that transparency reduces pay gaps.

The administration cites the persistent gap—women earn about 77 cents on the dollar compared with men on average, with Black and Latina women faring worse—as unacceptable. Critics, including Republican spokespeople, called the moves political and warned of unintended workplace consequences. The White House acknowledged complexities—some of the gap reflects occupational choices and career patterns—while arguing that even conservative estimates show women earn 5–12% less than men for similar work and that more policy steps can help close the gap. The White House also faced scrutiny over its own internal pay figures but said it actively works to hire and promote women.

Paul McCartney sued Sony/ATV in U.S. federal court seeking a declaratory judgment that he will regain U.S. copyrights to many Beatles songs he co-wrote with John Lennon under the termination provisions of the 1976 Copyright Act. McCartney alleges he and Lennon assigned publishing rights for songs written 1962–1971 to various publishers, and that he began serving statutory termination notices starting in 2008; those terminations are set to take effect beginning Oct. 5, 2018 (and more broadly under the statute’s reversion timetable for pre‑1978 works). His complaint says Sony/ATV has refused to confirm the effectiveness of his terminations and appears to be reserving the right to contest them pending the outcome of a related U.K. case.

The suit was partly motivated by Sony/ATV’s successful defense in England of a challenge by Duran Duran, where an English court held certain contractual promises prevented that band from reclaiming rights—an outcome McCartney fears Sony may attempt to use against him. McCartney’s lawyers ask a U.S. court to affirm that U.S. termination rights supersede contractual provisions that would bar reversion. Communications attached to the filing show Sony/ATV executives, including chairman Martin Bandier, and counsel have been involved in negotiations; Sony/ATV publicly expressed disappointment at the suit, calling it “unnecessary and premature.”

The dispute was later resolved confidentially: parties reached a settlement and jointly asked the court to dismiss the action without prejudice, with the court retaining authority to enforce the settlement terms if disputes arise. Details of the agreement were not disclosed.

This piece critiques Mitt Romney’s 2012 tax and economic pitch, arguing his promises are mathematically and politically untenable and rest on wishful optimism rather than substance.

Key points:

- Romney repeatedly insists he will “keep the current progressivity” of the tax code and not cut taxes for high-income earners, while also proposing a 20% across-the-board rate cut. That plan would cost trillions and, as widely analyzed, skew heavily toward big benefits for the wealthy.
- The Tax Policy Center concluded Romney’s simultaneous promises—to cut rates, not raise middle-class taxes, preserve tax breaks for savings and investment, and remain revenue-neutral—are “not mathematically possible.” Because Romney won’t touch savings-investment breaks (e.g., capital gains), there isn’t enough remaining revenue to fund his cuts without adjustments elsewhere.
- Some conservative and academic studies (including work by Martin Feldstein and others Romney cites) create scenarios where the math can be made to work—but only under very optimistic, questionable assumptions and by redefining who counts as “middle class.” Feldstein’s framing treats households over $100,000 as not middle-class, and the feasible scenarios still require raising taxes on households in roughly the $100k–$250k range to finance big cuts for those above $250k.
- Romney has publicly embraced studies that support his plan, but when pressed he has shifted the definition of “middle income” to $200k–$250k and effectively admitted his promises can only be reconciled by taxing those he previously described as middle class—contradicting his repeated assurances.
- More broadly, Romney’s economic agenda is characterized as thin on specifics—recycling standard Republican themes (lower taxes on the wealthy, weaker regulation) and relying on the idea that his election would produce a confidence-driven surge in investment and growth without concrete policy action. The author calls this the “confidence fairy” argument.
- The essay argues there is little empirical support for the claim that merely electing Romney would spark a recovery. The post-crisis slump is explained chiefly by housing weakness and excess household debt, not just political uncertainty, and past reliance on confidence narratives (e.g., European austerity claims) produced poor outcomes.
- Romney’s own test—markets should favor his likely victory—has not borne out: markets rose even as his prospects dimmed, undermining the confidence-based thesis.
- Conclusion: Romney has leaned on optimistic rhetoric and selective studies to mask infeasible fiscal promises. That lack of substantive, realistic policy and dependence on rosy assumptions make him a poor bet to lead an economic recovery.
