The George Washington Bridge "Bridgegate" scandal centers on politically motivated lane closures in Fort Lee, New Jersey, in September 2013 that created severe traffic jams for four days and endangered public safety. Port Authority appointee David Wildstein acknowledged ordering the closures; he later pleaded guilty to conspiracy and testified that the shutdowns were intended as political retribution against Fort Lee Mayor Mark Sokolich for not endorsing Gov. Chris Christie’s reelection. Two Christie aides—Bridget Kelly (deputy chief of staff) and Bill Baroni (deputy executive director at the Port Authority)—were indicted on fraud, conspiracy and civil-rights counts; Wildstein cooperated as the government’s key witness. The federal trial of Baroni and Kelly ran in 2016, produced extensive testimony and documents, and resulted in convictions on all counts; both were later sentenced (Baroni to 24 months, Kelly to 18 months), with appeals filed. Wildstein received probation and community service.

Investigations: The lane closures prompted multiple probes—by the Port Authority inspector general, a bi‑partisan New Jersey legislative committee, the U.S. Attorney’s Office (which convened a grand jury), and federal and state inquiries. A taxpayer-funded internal review by Gibson Dunn (hired by Christie’s office) concluded Christie had no advance knowledge; that report was widely criticized as a whitewash and for limited access to key witnesses. Federal prosecutors pursued criminal charges against Baroni and Kelly and obtained Wildstein’s guilty plea; they did not indict Christie.

New development: During the 2016 federal trial testimony, Wildstein said Christie was informed about the closures on Sept. 11, 2013. Spurred by that testimony, Bergen County activist William (Bill) Brennan filed a citizen complaint in Fort Lee municipal court alleging second-degree official misconduct by Gov. Christie for knowing of the closures and failing to stop them. In late September/October 2016, Municipal Judge Roy McGeady found probable cause and issued a summons, sending the complaint to the Bergen County Prosecutor’s Office for possible indictment. Christie’s office vowed to appeal and characterized the complaint as meritless; the local prosecutor—an appointee of Christie—would likely recuse if charges were pursued. Ultimately, prosecutors later declined to charge Christie in connection with the matter.

Impact and aftermath: The scandal damaged Christie’s political standing and is cited as a factor in the collapse of his 2016 presidential ambitions. The episode exposed misuse of public resources for political ends, prompted scrutiny of Port Authority operations and ethics, and generated wide media coverage, legislative hearings, and public debate about accountability in the Christie administration.

Actor Michael Jace was arrested after allegedly shooting his wife, April Jace, multiple times at their Hyde Park, Los Angeles home Monday night; law enforcement sources told the Los Angeles Times that he confessed. April, a well-liked financial aid employee at Biola University, had just returned from picking up their two young sons from baseball practice; the boys, both under 10, were home and physically unharmed and are now staying with family.

Neighbors described the couple as affectionate and family-oriented, often seeing Jace with their children and dog. The shooting, heard by neighbors, left the community stunned. Police stated the motive is believed to be domestic violence.

The case renewed attention to earlier accusations of violence by Jace. In divorce filings from his first wife, Jennifer Bitterman, she alleged repeated physical abuse and recounted an incident in which Jace choked and hit her and slammed her against a wall while their infant son cried. Bitterman also said Jace once threatened to kill her over visitation disputes. Court records and a friend’s statements describe multiple violent episodes from the mid-1990s; however, Jace had no prior arrests reported in connection with domestic violence.

Reports note financial stress in the Jace household: Michael Jace filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy in 2011, listing substantial debts and later falling behind on payments. Neighbors observed the family had downgraded possessions in recent years. Investigations continue, including an autopsy on April Jace and police inquiries into the circumstances of the shooting.

Former Tesla process technician Martin Tripp has publicly alleged serious manufacturing and quality problems at Tesla’s Nevada Gigafactory, posting internal emails, photos and vehicle identification numbers he says show damaged battery cells were reworked and installed in vehicles, scrap and waste stored outdoors, and unsafe production shortcuts. Tripp, who was fired earlier this year and is the target of a Tesla lawsuit accusing him of hacking and leaking company data, filed a countersuit claiming Tesla smeared and intimidated him after he raised safety and waste concerns and that he submitted a whistleblower tip to the SEC.

Tripp tweeted the material on Wednesday but removed his account by Thursday; some tweets were temporarily suspended by Twitter for posting private information. Tesla denies his safety allegations, saying no punctured cells were used in Model 3 vehicles and that the VINs Tripp identified have safe batteries, and has called Tripp a disgruntled ex-employee with no personal knowledge of his claims.

Business Insider places Tripp’s situation alongside that of former Tesla engineer Cristina Balan, who says she was pushed out in 2014 after she and her interiors team raised repeated concerns about poor part quality, waste, and managerial obstruction. Her account — supported by emails, texts and arbitration records reviewed by Business Insider — describes a high-pressure culture where managers allegedly discouraged direct supplier contact and downplayed defects (one minor fix involved stuffing Styrofoam into a headliner gap). Balan pursued arbitration, which concluded Tesla misclassified and underpaid her but did not find discrimination or whistleblower protections, and she refused settlement offers that would have required silencing her.

Both cases portray an internal culture shift at Tesla, from scrappy engineering focus to a production-and-sales emphasis that critics say deprioritizes quality and discourages employees from speaking up. Tesla disputes these narratives; former employees and documents suggest staff who pressed quality concerns sometimes faced pressure, isolation, or departure. The controversy remains legally active and politically charged, with many of Tripp’s tweeted materials now removed or inaccessible.

Correction note: earlier misattribution of comments to Justice Scalia was fixed.

Summary:
The Supreme Court spent two days hearing high-profile cases on same-sex marriage, culminating Wednesday in nearly two hours of argument over the federal Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), which defines marriage for federal purposes as between a man and a woman and thus withholds federal benefits from legally married same-sex couples. The pivotal tone suggested a majority of justices may be prepared to strike down the contested section of DOMA. Justice Anthony Kennedy, whose views often decide such cases, emphasized states’ traditional authority to regulate marriage and warned DOMA risks conflicting with state decisions that recognize same-sex marriages. Liberals, led by Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Elena Kagan, pressed that DOMA inflicts tangible harms (taxes, Social Security, spousal leave) and may reflect animus against gays rather than a neutral aim of uniformity.

The Obama administration, having concluded DOMA is unconstitutional, declined to defend it but continued to enforce it until the Court rules; Chief Justice Roberts criticized that stance as lacking “the courage of his convictions.” Former SG Paul Clement, representing House Republicans defending DOMA, argued Congress acted legitimately to preserve a uniform, traditional definition of marriage. Solicitor General Donald Verrilli and others argued the law is discriminatory in effect and motivated by prejudice.

The case arises from Edith Windsor’s suit after New York recognized her 2007 marriage but DOMA denied her federal spousal estate-tax exemption when her wife died in 2009; Windsor sought a $363,000 refund. Lower courts ruled for Windsor. The Court also confronted procedural issues — notably whether House defenders (BLAG) have standing and whether the administration’s position allows the Court to reach the merits — with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Scalia sharply skeptical of the Court taking an unprecedented approach. Rulings in the DOMA and related Prop 8 cases are expected by June. Public opinion is shifting toward marriage equality, but the country remains divided across states; if the Court avoids a merits ruling on standing grounds, DOMA could remain intact in some jurisdictions and further litigation would likely follow.

Astronomers have used Hubble to image an unusual asteroid in the main belt, P/2013 P5, that displays six comet‑like dust tails. Discovered by Pan‑STARRS in August 2013 as a fuzzy object, P5 was imaged by Hubble on Sept. 10 and Sept. 23, which revealed multiple spoke‑like streamers whose appearance changed markedly over 13 days. The tails are not consistent with a single impact event; instead, modeling by Jessica Agarwal and colleagues indicates a series of discrete dust‑ejection events over several months (dates inferred include April, July, August and early September). 

The leading explanation is rotational disruption driven by the YORP effect: uneven solar heating and re‑radiation gradually spin up small asteroids, and P5 appears to be shedding surface material as centrifugal forces overwhelm its weak gravity. The nucleus is about 240 m (1,400 ft) across and has lost only ~100–1,000 tons of dust — a tiny fraction of its mass. Continued observations to see whether the dust is emitted in an equatorial plane would strongly support rotational breakup. Authors led by David Jewitt published the results in the Astrophysical Journal Letters; they suggest P/2013 P5 may be the first of many such rotating, disintegrating small bodies discovered in the asteroid belt.

Lindsay Lohan said she was racially profiled at London’s Heathrow Airport after being stopped while wearing a headscarf on her way back to New York. Speaking on Good Morning Britain, she recounted that an airport worker, upon seeing her passport, apologized and then asked her to remove the headscarf — an interaction that made her wonder how other women who aren’t comfortable removing theirs would feel. Lohan, who had been in Turkey meeting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said she wore the scarf there out of “personal respect.” She has been photographed with a Quran and says she finds solace studying the Muslim holy book and other religious texts.

Separately, Lohan teased on Instagram that she might sing as Ariel in a live-action Little Mermaid project, posting a side-by-side photo of herself and the animated character (initially captioned with director and soundtrack claims, later shortened). The post drew attention and some mockery online.

A Ladue High School mother sued after her junior son ("John Doe") was cut from the varsity soccer team and barred from returning to junior varsity. She alleges age and sex discrimination, claiming girls’ team rules differ and that her son is better than some who made varsity. The coach testified he kept some juniors off JV to give underclassmen development opportunities and said the seven juniors cut from varsity weren’t JV-level; he also said he gave the boy positive feedback to protect his self‑esteem. Coaches’ performance ratings introduced by the family’s lawyer were said to show the boy ranked above some varsity players. Testimony also revealed the district has no blanket rule banning juniors from JV; assignments depend on numbers trying out and roster spots and, per the coach, apply to both boys and girls. U.S. District Judge John Ross postponed a final decision and initially planned to rule Monday; he subsequently denied the family’s request for a temporary restraining order that would have allowed the student to play on the JV team.

Summary:

Greece faced a high-stakes referendum (July 5–6, 2015) that would determine whether citizens accepted creditors’ proposed bailout terms—decisions that could reshape Greece’s economy and affect the eurozone. The crisis grew from decades of chronic deficits, large debt revealed in 2009, and rising borrowing costs. Two major rescues (2010 and 2012) postponed a reckoning but imposed austerity that deepened recession, failed to restore sustainable growth, and left public anger and mass unemployment. The 2010 rescue notably did not include significant debt relief for Greece’s creditors, a choice later widely criticized.

The left-wing Syriza government under Alexis Tsipras, elected in January 2015, sought to roll back some cuts and tax hikes and to secure debt relief. Creditors—the European Commission, European Central Bank (ECB) and IMF (the “troika” or “institutions”)—insisted on continued austerity and structural reforms, citing concerns about precedent for other countries and mistrust of Greece’s commitment to implement reforms. Negotiations collapsed: Greece missed a €1.55bn IMF payment on June 29 (an official default on the IMF), the ECB limited emergency liquidity by refusing to accept more Greek-government-guaranteed collateral, and Greek banks were shut with tight withdrawal limits to prevent runs.

Tsipras called a referendum asking Greeks to reject or accept the creditors’ June 25 proposal. He campaigned for “No” as a stand against “blackmail” and to strengthen Greece’s negotiating hand; EU leaders warned a “No” could further weaken Greece’s position and risk eurozone exit. Polls were close and showed most Greeks wanted to stay in the euro, though the referendum question was complex and widely criticized as confusing.

Immediate consequences of a “No” were expected to include further economic contraction, collapse of tax revenues, potential wider default and use of government IOUs to pay pensions and wages (circulating as discounted quasi-money), and severe credit isolation. Reintroduction of the drachma would be illegal under EU treaties and likely catastrophic politically and economically, so it was seen as unlikely in the short term. The IMF insisted on repayment to preserve its lending credibility; the ECB would face losses but could survive a Greek default. Longer-term outcomes depended on post-referendum political decisions: a “Yes” might reopen talks and restore some support; a “No” would likely force a painful adjustment and possibly a change of government before any recovery—though eventually tourism and more competitive prices could help recovery.

The primer argued, controversially, that a Greek default in 2010 would have been preferable to the costly rescues that followed, which largely protected foreign banks and deferred the need for meaningful debt relief. The situation remained volatile and politically charged as Greeks prepared to vote.

A 103-year-old man and a 91-year-old woman married in Eastbourne, England, becoming the world’s oldest newlyweds with a combined age of 194 years (194 years, 281 days). George Kirby and Doreen Luckie, who have been together 27 years and living together since 1988, exchanged vows at the Langham Hotel before about 50 guests and a Guinness World Records representative. The bride wore a white dress with blue flowers; the groom, a former boxer now using a wheelchair after a recent fall, wore a suit and tie. They met later in life—George after a divorce and Doreen after being widowed—and were reportedly persuaded by elderly children to formalize their union. They became engaged on Valentine’s Day this year and have a large blended family: seven children, 15 grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren. George, born June 1912, is a former RAF physical training instructor and amateur boxer; Doreen, born September 1923, worked as a shorthand typist for the Director of Public Prosecutions. Both expressed happiness and no regrets about marrying later in life.

Former EastEnders actor Paul Nicholls, 38, was rescued on Thailand’s Koh Samui after spending three days trapped at the base of the Khun Si waterfall with a severely injured right leg. A local villager spotted the motorcycle he had rented, which led police to launch a search; rescue teams found him semi‑conscious, hypothermic and partly submerged in a rock pool, unable to climb out due to a smashed leg and a destroyed kneecap that Nicholls says will require full reconstruction. Rescuers applied a tourniquet and carried him up a steep path; he was treated at International Koh Samui Hospital before plans by the British Embassy to move him to a larger facility or repatriate him were reported. Hospital staff said he was seriously ill after contracting an infection during the ordeal; medical costs in Thailand were reported to be substantial. Nicholls, who made his EastEnders debut in 1996 and has appeared in shows including Ackley Bridge and Law & Order: UK and the film Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason, said he had a phone but lost it in the fall and could not reach help.

Two federal lawsuits filed by anti-drug group Safe Streets and three plaintiffs seek to shut down Colorado’s regulated recreational marijuana industry, arguing state legalization conflicts with federal law. The suits, filed Thursday, name Colorado officials (including Gov. John Hickenlooper and regulatory directors), numerous marijuana businesses and their service providers, and even a construction firm. Plaintiffs claim injury under federal racketeering statutes and ask courts to force the state to stop issuing licenses and close the industry, citing the Supremacy Clause because marijuana remains illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

Safe Streets is led by James Wootton; the individual plaintiffs say nearby marijuana operations have harmed their property and hotel business. The filings follow a separate interstate lawsuit by Nebraska and Oklahoma asking the U.S. Supreme Court to strike down Colorado’s laws as unconstitutional and harmful to neighboring states.

Colorado officials and marijuana reform advocates denounced the suits as misguided and unlikely to succeed. Supporters of legalization note Colorado voters approved Amendment 64 in 2012, retail sales began in 2014, and the industry has generated substantial economic activity and tax revenue used for schools. They also point to data showing no clear statewide harms—employment is up, Denver crime and highway fatalities are down, and teen use hasn’t spiked—though there have been isolated problems, including high-profile fatalities and some poisonings tied to potent products. Colorado’s attorney general said the state will defend its laws. Anti-legalization groups praised the litigation, while reform groups argue states have the right to regulate marijuana rather than leave it to criminals.

A public Twitter feud erupted between former Alaska governor Sarah Palin and rapper Azealia Banks after Banks reacted to a satirical Newslo article that falsely attributed racist comments about slavery to Palin. Believing the piece was real, Banks posted a series of now-deleted, graphic tweets suggesting Palin should be gang-raped — remarks that sparked widespread outrage. Banks later removed the tweets, posted a meandering Tumblr “apology” claiming she was joking and insisting her references were to consensual group sex (not rape), and added further insults about Palin’s family.

Palin publicly condemned Banks’ tweets, criticized the rapper’s past controversies, and announced plans to sue Banks “on behalf of all reasonable women,” calling the posts violent, defamatory and symptomatic of double standards that reward divisive behavior. Banks continued to taunt Palin afterward, so the dispute appeared unresolved. The article also notes Banks’ recent controversies and political stances (including support for Donald Trump) and mentions the deleted tweets were captured by media outlets before removal.

A Palestinian teenager, Muhammad (Mohammed) Abu Khdeir (16–17), was abducted near his home in Shuafat, East Jerusalem, early Wednesday and found burned to death in a forest outside the city hours later. Villagers and the boy’s family say surveillance footage shows two men forcing him into a vehicle as he was heading to dawn prayers during Ramadan. His father and other residents accused Jewish extremists of carrying out the killing in revenge for the discovery earlier that week of the bodies of three Israeli teens abducted in the West Bank.

The murder followed a night of violence by Jewish extremists in Jerusalem, who reportedly marched chanting “Death to the Arabs” and attacked Arab Israelis. After the body was found, clashes erupted around the Khdeir home between Palestinian youths and Israeli riot police, leaving dozens wounded; ambulances and heavy policing were present. The family said the body was badly burned and a post-mortem and DNA testing were needed to confirm identity; the father complained police delayed and pressured him.

Israeli leaders condemned the killing—Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called it “despicable” and ordered a fast investigation—and relatives of one of the murdered Israeli teens publicly decried the revenge killing if it was nationalistic. Palestinian leaders blamed Israel for creating the conditions that led to the murder and threatened international legal action; Hamas and Fatah tensions and mutual suspicions intensified, with some Palestinians skeptical of the official narrative around the earlier Israeli teens’ abduction.

Separately, Israeli forces struck targets in Gaza after rocket and mortar fire from militants, reinforcing border forces; tensions across Israel, the West Bank and Gaza rose, raising fears of broader escalation. International figures including U.S. and European officials strongly condemned the killing and expressed alarm at the potential for escalating communal violence.

This document is a compilation of policy positions and proposals from Donald J. Trump on immigration, taxes, and gun rights, presented as part of his "Make America Great Again" agenda. Key points:

Immigration
- Core principles: secure borders (including a southern border wall), enforce existing laws and the Constitution, and prioritize American jobs, wages and security.
- Mexico must pay for the wall; if not, the U.S. will take measures such as impounding remittances, raising fees on Mexican visas and border-crossing cards, and considering tariffs or aid cuts.
- Enforcement-focused measures: triple ICE staffing, nationwide mandatory e-Verify, end catch-and-release (detain until removal), mandatory return/deportation of criminal aliens, defund sanctuary cities, enhanced penalties for visa overstays, completion of visa-tracking, and cooperation between ICE and local gang task forces.
- End birthright citizenship.
- Economic focus: reduce legal admissions of low-wage workers to raise domestic wages and employment, require employers to hire U.S. workers first (including pausing new green cards until domestic hires are attempted), restrict J-1 program and redirect it toward American inner-city youth, tighten refugee/asylum admissions and redirect savings to care for American children, and bar welfare-dependent immigrants.
- H-1B and guest-worker reforms: raise prevailing wages for H-1Bs, require hiring Americans first, and oppose large expansions of H-1B numbers.

Tax Reform
- Individual taxes: collapse seven brackets into three (12%, 25%, 33%); raise standard deduction ($30,000 joint; $15,000 single); eliminate personal exemptions and head-of-household status; cap itemized deductions; retain capital gains structure; repeal AMT and the 3.8% net investment income tax.
- Childcare/eldercare: above-the-line deductions and Dependent Care Savings Accounts (DCSAs) with government matching for low-income families; EITC-based rebates for childcare for low earners.
- Death tax: repeal estate tax with a $10 million exemption and rules to prevent abuse.
- Business taxes: cut corporate rate to 15% for firms that retain profits, eliminate most corporate tax expenditures (keep R&D credit), corporate alternative minimum tax repeal, one-time 10% repatriation tax on offshore profits, and incentives/choices related to expensing capital for U.S. manufacturers.
- The tax plan claims to simplify the code, spur higher growth, increase revenue through growth and repatriation, and not add to deficits (though economic growth assumptions are disputed).

Second Amendment / Guns
- Absolute defense of the right to keep and bear arms; oppose gun and magazine bans.
- Prioritize prosecuting violent criminals and restoring tough federal enforcement programs (e.g., expand Project Exile-style prosecutions).
- Improve and fix the existing background-check system by ensuring states enter criminal and mental-health records; oppose expanding an imperfect system.
- Support national reciprocity for concealed-carry permits so permits are valid across all states.
- Address mass violence by improving the mental-health system and expanding treatment and preventative measures for those who are dangerous.
- Allow military personnel to carry firearms on bases and at recruiting centers.

Overall tone and emphasis: strong border/security enforcement, prioritizing American workers and stricter immigration control to raise wages and reduce crime, major tax cuts and simplification aimed at stimulating growth, and robust protection of gun rights with stepped-up criminal enforcement and mental-health reforms.

A New York Daily News article reports on a legal battle over 28-year-old Grace Sung Eun Lee, a Manhattan banker with an inoperable brain tumor who is paralyzed from the neck down and maintained on breathing and feeding tubes. Lee told reporters she wants life support removed; her court-appointed lawyer, David A. Smith, says she has clearly expressed a desire to die and faces no hope of recovery because her brain stem is irreparably damaged. After a Long Island judge initially authorized removal of the tubes, Lee’s devout Korean-born parents sought emergency relief and obtained a temporary appellate order keeping life support in place while a four-judge Appellate Division panel considers whether she is competent and whether her wishes should be honored.

The parents released a murky, soundless video they say shows Lee wants to remain on machines; the footage was recorded hours after she told the Daily News “I want to die,” and hospital spokesmen say it has not changed her care pending the court’s decision. The parents argue from their faith that deliberately ending life is suicide and a spiritual sin, and have asked to be appointed guardians; prosecutors and Lee’s attorney counter that her wishes to discontinue life-sustaining treatment are clear and that her parents are exerting pressure, telling her she’d be damned if she stops treatment. The appeals panel could rule imminently; separate proceedings on the father’s guardianship were still pending.

Sesame Workshop has expanded the storyline of Lily, a seven-year-old pink Muppet first introduced in 2011, to make her the first Sesame Street character portrayed as experiencing homelessness. As part of the Sesame Street in Communities initiative launched in December 2018, Lily’s family is shown doubling up with friends after losing their home. The project uses new online videos, storybooks, interactive activities and professional resources—free and bilingual—aimed at children ages 2–6, their caregivers, and service providers to help explain homelessness, reduce stigma, and teach coping strategies from a child’s perspective.

The materials (including short films like “Connect the Dots,” “Rainbow Kind of Day,” “Ribbons of Hope,” and “Home Is…”) encourage empathy, emotional vocabulary, routine-building, and caregiver–child engagement, and provide guidance for teachers, social workers and shelter staff. The initiative was developed with experts, pilot-tested with providers and families, and is part of Sesame Street in Communities’ broader aim to support vulnerable children through locally implemented programs and national partnerships. It responds to rising child homelessness in the U.S.—estimates range widely, but over 2.5 million children experience homelessness nationwide, with many under age six—and follows Sesame Workshop’s history of using Muppet characters (e.g., Julia, a character with autism; Kami, a Muppet with HIV in South Africa) to humanize complex social issues. The effort is supported by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and the Joan Ganz Cooney Fund for Vulnerable Children.

David Blankenhorn, founder of the Institute for American Values and once a leading, nonreligious opponent of same-sex marriage, has publicly shifted his position. In a New York Times essay and NPR interview he explained that although his longstanding concern remains that marriage’s core social purpose is to unite biological, social and legal parenthood for children, the public debate has become about equality rather than parenthood. He still believes same-sex couples cannot combine biological parenthood into a single bond the way opposite-sex couples can, and he stands by his prior arguments about marriage’s public purposes — but he no longer wants to denigrate or stigmatize gay relationships. Citing fairness, comity, and an emerging elite-and-young-adult consensus in favor of marriage equality, he says the time has come to accept gay marriage and to pursue conciliation instead of continued culture-war conflict.

Blankenhorn proposes a new strategy: build coalitions of gays and straights who want to strengthen marriage and family life. He suggests refocusing public discussion on shared pro-child and pro-marriage norms — e.g., encouraging marriage before childbearing, preferring marriage over cohabitation for couples who want lasting relationships, and debating whether children conceived by assisted reproduction should have rights to know their biological parents. He acknowledges uncertainty about whether this approach will succeed.

The commentary situates his shift in a broader social context: cultural change and family disruption are concentrated among groups that may not find mainstream conservative voices culturally credible. Diffusion of beneficial family practices depends on “wide bridges” across social networks; without those bridges, reforms that have taken hold among college-educated Americans haven’t spread to less-educated communities. That fragmentation helps explain why a message about strengthening marriage may not resonate where family instability is most severe. Critics from the religious right denounced Blankenhorn’s reversal, while others praised his integrity and willingness to seek common ground.

Suspected militants attacked the American University of Afghanistan (AUAF) in western Kabul on the evening of Aug. 24, 2016, using explosions and gunfire. The assault began at the main gate with a car bomb and subsequent blasts and shootings; witnesses reported attackers armed with guns and grenades. Students and staff barricaded classrooms, hid or fled (some jumping from second‑floor windows and injuring themselves), and dozens were trapped inside for hours while elite Afghan forces and special units surrounded the walled campus and carried out a clearing operation.

Casualty reports were initially inconsistent: hospital officials and multiple news outlets reported wounded students (reports cited 11–14 wounded), and Afghan police later said 12 people had been killed, including students, policemen and guards; authorities then said two attackers were killed when the clearance ended. No group immediately claimed responsibility. The assault came less than three weeks after two AUAF teachers (an American and an Australian) were abducted nearby and heightened concerns about Taliban and Islamic State attacks in Kabul. U.S. advisers embedded with Afghan forces assisted in the response; U.S. officials condemned the attack and expressed support for Afghanistan.

“Ketchup ’n’ Fries” (also sold as TomTato®) is a hand‑grafted specialty plant being offered to American gardeners for the 2015 season. Created by SuperNaturals Grafted Vegetables (the Mighty ‘Mato brand) and commercialized in the U.K. in 2014, the grafted TomTato fuses a cherry‑tomato scion onto potato rootstock so one plant yields cherry tomatoes above ground and white potatoes below. Production rights for North American starter plants are held by Plug Connection (San Diego County); Log House Plants and Territorial Seed Company (Cottage Grove, OR) are major distributors, and plants will be available through garden centers and mail‑order catalogs.

The TomTato is produced by grafting — not genetic engineering — a common horticultural technique that pairs a chosen scion (for fruit quality) with vigorous, disease‑resistant rootstock. Benefits promoted for grafted vegetables include greater vigor, improved water and nutrient uptake, extended harvests, higher yields, and increased resistance to diseases and environmental stresses. Territorial sells individual hardened‑off transplants (no minimums), ships within the contiguous U.S., and offers guarantees and shipping windows for spring delivery.

The plant drew wide media attention and public buzz as a novelty and space‑saving solution (it can be grown in a 10‑gallon container), though early reviews and customer comments are mixed—some praising the tomatoes, others saying they did not get potatoes. Grafting this combination requires skill, and commercial versions were developed after selecting compatible tomato and potato varieties to perform well together.

The piece opens by noting the long, mixed history between books and Hollywood—some of film’s greatest successes (The Godfather, Gone With The Wind, The Silence of the Lambs) came from books, while some notable flops did too. It raises the question of whether any books are truly "unfilmable," even though seemingly impossible works like Naked Lunch have been adapted. To explore this, the authors looked for books they believe Hollywood would avoid. They invite readers to name books they think could never work on screen or adaptations they hope never happen. The article then segues to casting news: Carey Mulligan has been chosen by Baz Luhrmann to play Daisy Buchanan in his adaptation of The Great Gatsby, beating out contenders such as Blake Lively, Natalie Portman, and Amanda Seyfried; Luhrmann informed Mulligan of the role at the CFDA awards.

Bristol Palin, whose memoir Not Afraid of Life: My Journey So Far was published in June last year to largely negative reviews and little lasting public interest, recently promoted the book at a Washington, D.C. signing with her mother Sarah Palin. To draw a crowd, Bristol and ghostwriter Nancy French posted a classified ad on Craigslist offering free autographed copies to the first 100 RSVP’d attendees for a Feb. 11 Books-A-Million event at Dupont Circle. The piece notes this move as evidence that Palin, who first rose to fame during her mother’s 2008 vice-presidential campaign and later appeared on Dancing with the Stars, has struggled to maintain the celebrity momentum she once had. The ad requested RSVPs with name, age and contact info and emphasized no phone inquiries or third-party recruiters.

The document collects farewell reflections from the principal cast and executive producer of the TV series Girls as the show ends, plus a brief note about classic YouTube videos.

- Lena Dunham (Hannah Horvath) describes the cast as a close-knit “family” and finds it emotional to say goodbye to their daily collaboration and the shared process of creating new stories for their characters.
- Allison Williams (Marnie Michaels) hopes viewers will feel compassion for Marnie, believes many can relate to her struggles, and praises the season for strong development of her character.
- Jemima Kirke (Jessa Johansson) will miss continuing to explore and evolve her role.
- Zosia Mamet (Shoshanna Shapiro) says she’ll miss the character’s presence in her life more than the act of playing her, noting Shoshanna has felt like a distinct entity after years in the role.
- Judd Apatow (executive producer) recalls a happy, calm atmosphere among the cast despite outside controversy and hopes the show demonstrated varying degrees of personal growth among its characters.

A final line briefly mentions “Best of YouTube,” pointing to some classic YouTube videos from earlier years.

A large, violent brawl broke out on May 14, 2016, at Khovanskoye cemetery on Moscow’s southwestern outskirts, involving between roughly 200 and 400 people armed with bats, shovels, metal bars, crowbars and, reportedly, firearms. Officials and multiple Russian outlets say the melee was a turf war over lucrative burial-service work and alleged extortion of cemetery workers. Participants were reported to include migrant laborers from Central Asia and groups from the North Caucasus.

Casualties and arrests
- Between two and three people were reported killed; several accounts say two victims were run over by a car driven by people trying to flee. One of the dead was reported to be a police officer in some early reports.  
- Dozens were wounded; hospitals received about 23–29 injured, with several in critical condition.  
- Police and National Guard units detained between about 50 and more than 100 people, seizing weapons and some defunct assault rifles. Three people in a car who were armed with pistols were arrested for questioning.

Other details
- Police fired warning shots to restore order; eyewitnesses reported up to 15 minutes of gunfire and bullet casings and broken windows at the scene.  
- Authorities said many participants were not cemetery employees and that some were in Russia illegally. Reports say the attack may have been planned, with attackers arriving in multiple cars and wearing bulletproof vests.  
- Moscow officials fired the cemetery director and said the private security firm responsible for the site would face action. Some burials were reportedly postponed and the area saw major traffic disruption.

Overall, Russian authorities characterize the incident as a violent dispute over control of burial services rather than a simple ethnic conflict, and investigations and detentions are ongoing.

In an interview with the Columbus Dispatch editorial board, Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney appeared to soften earlier statements on protections for people with pre-existing conditions while defending his plan to repeal the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare). Romney said policymakers should “deal with those people who are currently uninsured” and “help them have the opportunity to have insurance,” but suggested insurers should not be required to cover people who remained uninsured for years and then sought coverage after getting sick. He reiterated past comments that protections should apply to those who previously maintained continuous coverage, and repeated an argument he has made before: that lack of insurance does not mean people are left to die because federal law (EMTALA) requires hospitals to treat emergency patients and charity or government programs will cover care.

Romney’s remarks contrast with language on his campaign website—“Prevent discrimination against individuals with pre-existing conditions who maintain continuous coverage”—and with prior interviews (e.g., on Jay Leno) in which he explicitly limited protections to those who had been continuously insured. His Columbus comments prompted criticism from the Obama campaign, which cited studies estimating thousands of premature deaths annually tied to lack of coverage (estimates range widely: roughly 18,000 to 45,000 or more per year). Critics say emergency-room access does not substitute for preventive and ongoing care, and that many uninsured people delay care until too late. Supporters argue Romney would pursue state-based approaches and limited protections for those who maintained coverage.

Contextual data noted in reporting: about 49 million non-elderly Americans were uninsured in 2010, with over 70% uninsured for a year or more; research links lack of insurance with higher mortality and worse outcomes, while EMTALA requires emergency treatment regardless of ability to pay.
