In August 1978, 18-month-old Yohanna Cyr vanished from her mother Liliane Cyr’s small apartment in St-Laurent, Montreal after Liliane left her in the care of her then-boyfriend, Aaron Lewis (also called Aaron Lewis Guay). Liliane recalled giving a taxi driver the destination, kissing Yohanna goodbye and later being told conflicting stories by the boyfriend: first that Yohanna was with his mother, then that she had drowned and been buried. The taxi driver, the only immediate witness, died a month later. Liliane searched hospitals and morgues and reported the disappearance; evidence she handed police disappeared a decade later. Lewis was arrested and charged with abduction in 1978 but a judge found insufficient evidence to proceed—no body, crime scene or proof he’d been watching the child—and he was deported to the U.S. without further charges. The case went cold.

Over nearly four decades Liliane has kept the case alive, enduring false leads and heartache. In 2005 a U.S. woman who thought she might match was ruled out by DNA. In 2013 renewed attention included age-progressed photos released by the RCMP and a small memorial gathering on the 35th anniversary; Liliane held out hope that Yohanna might be alive or, if dead, that she could at last know the truth.

In 2016 a Facebook message revived new hope: a U.S. woman contacted Liliane asking about Yohanna’s identifying Y-shaped birthmark on an index finger and said she suspected she might be Yohanna after discovering a fake birth certificate and having vague childhood memories of air travel. Photos suggested a family resemblance and investigators arranged DNA testing between Canadian and U.S. authorities; results would take weeks to months. (A later update in Oct. 2016 confirmed the U.S. woman was not Liliane’s daughter.) The family continues to seek information; anyone with tips is asked to contact the Missing Children’s Network.

Two little-known Dallas-area attorneys, Thomas Bowers and Reggie London, announced Wednesday they have been retained by the family of 14-year-old Ahmed Mohamed to investigate and possibly pursue legal action over his arrest at school after a teacher reported his homemade digital clock as a suspected bomb. Bowers and London — who have handled a range of civil and criminal-defense matters — said they will seek a medical evaluation for Ahmed, review the city and school district’s actions, and explore legal options; they characterized public comments by officials as inappropriate and said they hope such remarks stop now that they represent the family.

Irving police say their follow-up investigation found no evidence Ahmed intended to create alarm, no charges will be filed, and the case is closed. The department also stated the clock has been available for pickup at police headquarters on weekdays since mid-September and notified a family representative. The family, citing "religious persecution," has pulled Ahmed and his siblings out of the Irving school district to homeschool and received widespread national attention and reactions, including support from public figures. The lawyers said they were recently contracted and do not yet know all case details or whether formal legal action will be filed.

On Christmas Day 2017, between 5:51 p.m. and 7:53 p.m., about 71,000 Holiday Cash Add‑A‑Play tickets in South Carolina were printed showing nine tree symbols and appeared to be $500 winners. The South Carolina Education Lottery (SCEL) shut the game down after two hours and, after a five‑month independent analysis by Gaming Laboratories International, concluded coding and quality‑assurance errors by its former computer vendor, Intralot, caused the erroneous tickets to be produced.

Under state law, tickets produced or issued in error cannot be paid as prizes. In May 2018 the SCEL Board voted to reimburse only the purchase price of the affected tickets (about $1 each) if mailed to the lottery by January 7, 2019, plus first‑class postage; players must submit original tickets. SCEL said paying the full prizes (roughly $30–35 million) would violate the statute; the board’s decision left the lottery out about $1.7 million in prizes that had already been cashed before the shutdown.

The incident prompted public anger and at least two lawsuits against the lottery and Intralot from players who say they were entitled to full winnings. SCEL attributed the problem to its former vendor’s coding errors and inadequate testing; Intralot acknowledged the error was identified and the game was quickly shut down.

Summary:

Since Paul Manafort reached a plea deal with special counsel Robert Mueller in mid-September, he has repeatedly visited Mueller’s Washington office—at least nine times in about four weeks—spending many hours in interviews as part of his cooperation agreement. Manafort’s talks reportedly have included questions about his contacts with Russians; what he has told prosecutors is not public. Other cooperating witnesses (Rick Gates, Michael Flynn, Michael Cohen) have likewise met extensively with Mueller’s team.

Despite Justice Department guidance to avoid public political acts before the midterms, Mueller’s investigation remained active through September and October: prosecutors have continued witness interviews, convened a grand jury most Fridays in D.C., and pursued sealed court actions. Chief Judge Beryl Howell has held sealed hearings and previously compelled testimony and contempt findings related to grand-jury matters. Roger Stone and several associates have also been the subject of recent contacts and subpoenas.

The President’s legal team has been negotiating with Mueller’s office over written responses to questions about potential collusion and obstruction (including Comey’s firing), and has not yet decided whether Trump will sit for an in-person interview. The White House lawyers have received some information from Manafort’s counsel but have no formal joint defense agreement. Many in Washington expect additional indictments and anticipate Mueller will produce a post-election report explaining prosecutorial decisions; whether that report will be public depends on DOJ officials.

Separately, Manafort appeared in a Virginia federal court for sentencing proceedings: Judge T.S. Ellis set sentencing for Feb. 8 on eight convictions (tax evasion and bank fraud) after a jury deadlocked on additional counts. Manafort, seen in a prison uniform and pushed in a wheelchair, sought expedited sentencing transfer due to health concerns. The sentencing in Virginia had been linked to delays sought by Mueller’s team to allow Manafort’s cooperation to proceed.

Kick-Ass 2 follows teen vigilantes Kick-Ass (Dave) and Hit-Girl (Mindy) after their attempt to live normal lives. Dave recruits with a new, self-made superhero movement led by ex-mobster-turned-born-again Colonel Stars and Stripes, while Mindy is forced to retire from crimefighting after being caught and must confront high-school life alone. When the supervillain Red Mist returns as the murderous Mother F%&*^r and targets the amateur heroes, Hit-Girl’s lethal skills become the last line of defense.

The film, adapted from Mark Millar’s comics, ups the violence and action from the original. Jim Carrey stars as Colonel Stars and Stripes in a vividly eccentric performance that Millar praises. Shortly before release, Carrey publicly withdrew his support, saying he could not in good conscience promote the movie’s level of violence in the wake of real-world mass shootings (notably Sandy Hook). Millar responded with a long defense of the film as fictional entertainment that addresses the consequences of violence and argued Carrey knew the script’s content well in advance. The dispute drew broader attention because Carrey has been outspoken on gun control and public violence; the movie remains set for release on Aug. 16.

EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt has broken months of silence about his frequent premium-class and noncommercial travel paid for by taxpayers, saying in interviews that security concerns and unpleasant encounters on flights have required him to fly first class or on military aircraft. He insisted he does not decide cabin class himself; his security detail, chief of staff and administration determine travel based on threat assessments. Pruitt cited unspecified “incidents” since his appointment and noted the politically charged environment around environmental issues.

Reports and public records have shown Pruitt’s travel has included multiple first-class commercial tickets (one D.C.–New York round trip cost $1,641), several noncommercial flights totaling more than $58,000, and a period in which travel bills topped $90,000. The EPA previously said Pruitt had a “blanket waiver” to fly first or business class; after POLITICO pointed out federal rules forbid blanket waivers, the agency revised its claim, saying waivers are submitted for each trip. Federal travel rules permit premium travel only when cheaper options are not “reasonably available” or for documented security reasons; past audits have found frequent violations by senior officials.

Pruitt is the first EPA head with a 24-hour protective detail and has authorized additional security measures at taxpayer expense (e.g., a $25,000 soundproof booth). His travel and weekend trips to Oklahoma are under review by the EPA inspector general, which expects to report this summer. Transparency around his travel authorizations has been limited, with some records withheld for security reasons and FOIA requests pending.

The controversy comes amid broader scrutiny of travel and expense practices across the Trump Cabinet (notably Tom Price and others). Supporters cite legitimate protective advantages of private cabins and accelerated boarding; critics and government ethics experts say routine premium travel without clear, documented, trip-by-trip justification appears inconsistent with federal rules and risks wasting taxpayer funds. Pruitt also used the New Hampshire trip to discuss Superfund cleanups and water contamination concerns, defending his agency’s approach and urging cooperation with industry.

Verizon’s agreement to buy Yahoo’s core internet business for $4.83 billion has put renewed focus on CEO Marissa Mayer’s future. Mayer said in a Tumblr post and a CNBC interview that she plans to stay to “see Yahoo into its next chapter,” but acknowledged she’s “open minded.” Analysts expect her to remain only through the transition and integration, after which Verizon could install new leadership—RBC’s Mark Mahaney suggested AOL chief Tim Armstrong might run the combined AOL-Yahoo unit.

Mayer’s tenure since arriving from Google in 2012 has been controversial and uneven. Early morale-boosting moves (free lunches, company phones) were offset by unpopular decisions such as banning remote work and scrutiny over her personal arrangements and maternity leaves, which fueled debate about parental leave and gendered media coverage. Strategic bets produced mixed results: the 2014 BrightRoll acquisition was praised, while the $1.1 billion Tumblr purchase and other content deals underperformed. Critics say she stabilized Yahoo but missed larger market trends, and some expect she’ll leave within a year.

If Mayer is pushed out after the sale she stands to receive a substantial payout—estimates range from roughly $59 million to $137 million depending on terms—with Equilar citing nearly $219 million earned through the end of last year. She has also publicly criticized “gender-charged” reporting about her.

Verizon will combine Yahoo with AOL (which it bought in 2015) to create a larger media and ad business aimed at competing with Google and Facebook. The sale excludes Yahoo’s cash, its stakes in Alibaba and Yahoo Japan (worth about $40 billion), convertible notes, certain minority investments and non-core patents. Yahoo will remain independent until shareholder and regulatory approvals are complete, and the transaction marks a significant retreat from Yahoo’s 1990s peak despite still-large user numbers. Critics question whether merging two weakened internet brands will produce a viable third competitor in digital advertising.

Sandy Hook Promise, a nonprofit founded by family members of victims of the 2012 Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, released a PSA as part of its “Know the Signs” campaign to mark the anniversary of the attack. The ad follows a boy named Evan who exchanges flirtatious messages scratched into a library desk and, unbeknownst to viewers focused on his story, a different male student in the background is showing multiple warning signs of preparing a school shooting (reading gun magazines, watching gun videos, being bullied, posting gun photos, making a menacing gesture at a teacher). On the final day of school, as Evan discovers his secret pen pal, the background student appears with a duffel and cocks an assault rifle; the screen then warns, “While you were watching Evan, another student was showing signs of planning a shooting. But no one noticed.” Sandy Hook Promise stresses that one sign alone doesn’t prove someone will become violent, but when several connected behaviors occur over time they signal risk and intervention can prevent violence. The organization aims to teach people to recognize at-risk behaviors and empower them to intervene—citing that large percentages of attackers had told someone of their plans before acting—and to protect children from gun violence.

Alipore Zoo in Kolkata is struggling to get its 10-year-old white tiger, Vishal, to mate. Despite repeated attempts over the past six months, Vishal has shown little or no sexual interest in neighbouring tigress Rupa (8). Keepers have tried de-worming, vitamins (A, D, E) and commercial libido enhancers, but none have worked. Veterinarians and specialists attribute his reluctance to shyness and inexperience from being bred and raised in captivity; he reportedly avoids Rupa’s advances rather than responding, though he is not hostile. Zoo staff note that prime mating age for male tigers is around 5–8 years and that fertility becomes difficult after age 10, so Vishal may be past his best. Breeding at the zoo is considered important to replenish aging big cats (the last tiger cub was born more than a decade ago), and officials are considering introducing Vishal to another, younger tigress, Rani, in hopes she might succeed where Rupa could not.

Attorney General Eric Holder visited Ferguson, Missouri, on Aug. 20, 2014, to meet community leaders, federal investigators and Michael Brown’s parents amid nearly two weeks of protests after the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Brown by a Ferguson police officer. Speaking at St. Louis Community College’s Florissant Valley campus, Holder acknowledged and validated local mistrust of police, drawing on his own experiences as a Black man who has been stopped and searched by officers. He said dialogue alone is insufficient and pledged concrete action, emphasizing that the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division and the FBI are conducting a “full, fair and independent” federal civil rights inquiry into Brown’s death and that the department has assigned experienced agents and prosecutors to the case.

Holder met privately with Brown’s parents, reassured officials and residents that the investigation will be impartial, and hoped his presence would help calm tensions. He also conferred with Missouri officials, including Gov. Jay Nixon and Capt. Ron Johnson of the Missouri Highway Patrol, who said Holder’s visit helped guarantee confidence in the probe. The trip underscored the Obama administration’s prioritization of civil rights enforcement in the matter. Meanwhile a grand jury began hearing evidence in nearby Clayton, protests continued in Ferguson with fewer arrests that night, and the Justice Department criticized selective public release of case materials while conducting an independent autopsy and sending federal agents to gather witnesses. Brown’s funeral was scheduled for the following Monday.

Starbucks Ireland accidentally invited its nearly 2,000 Irish Twitter followers to “show us what makes you proud to be British” during a diamond jubilee promotion, prompting swift backlash for the political/geographic gaffe. Followers criticized the error; one called for an apology before returning to stores. Starbucks Ireland apologized on Twitter and issued a formal statement saying the tweet had been intended only for its UK account and expressing regret to Irish customers and followers. The article notes the mistake follows a similar PR misstep by Nike months earlier, when a St. Patrick’s Day–themed shoe evoked the controversial “Black and Tans,” illustrating how global brands can offend when they misread Irish historical and cultural sensitivities. The piece also briefly reminds users that tweeting with location tags stores that data and can be switched off.

Nigerian authorities and international partners are intensifying efforts after Islamist militants from Boko Haram kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from a boarding school in Chibok on 14 April and launched a separate, large-scale attack on the border town of Gamboru Ngala in Borno state. The police have offered a 50 million naira (about $300,000) reward for credible information leading to the girls’ location and rescue, and the US, UK and China have dispatched small teams or offered intelligence, satellite and advisory assistance.

Witnesses, local officials and media report the Gamboru Ngala raid was brutal and prolonged: gunmen in military-style uniforms attacked a busy night market, burned shops and homes, used explosives against the police station, and killed scores—local sources put the death toll between 150 and as high as 300, with mass burials reported. Residents said militants used diversionary tactics that drew security forces away and enabled the assault. Boko Haram’s leader, Abubakar Shekau, publicly claimed responsibility for the Chibok abductions and threatened to “sell” the girls, most aged 16–18.

The abductions and the raid have provoked nationwide protests and global outrage, including high-profile statements from world leaders and activists and the viral #BringBackOurGirls campaign. Nigeria’s government has faced heavy criticism for its handling of the crisis and delays in public acknowledgment; officials say search operations, aerial reconnaissance and increased troop deployments are underway. The US will provide intelligence, investigations and hostage-negotiation expertise via a joint coordination cell in Abuja, while Britain will send a small expert team. Concerns remain about Boko Haram’s growing capability and the security of the porous borders in the northeast.

Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly challenged the US to present UN evidence that the Syrian government used chemical weapons in an attack near Damascus on 21 August, calling US claims a provocation and urging caution before military action. The US, citing intelligence it says shows 1,429 people (including hundreds of children) died in the attack, blamed the Assad government and said chemical-weapons personnel and rockets from government-held areas were linked to the incident. Washington released an unclassified summary of its evidence (satellite imagery, intercepted communications, videos and on-the-ground indicators) but the UN inspectors’ formal findings are pending.

UN weapons inspectors completed four days of on-site work in Syria and have returned to The Hague with samples (soil, swabs, biological material) for analysis by the OPCW; their mandate is to determine whether chemical weapons were used, not to assign blame, and results could take up to weeks. The UN warned against rushing to military responses and stressed a political solution is required.

President Barack Obama said he is considering a limited, non-ground-troops military response and announced he will seek congressional authorization for the use of force, sending legislation to Capitol Hill and scheduling debate when Congress reconvenes. The move aims to deter future chemical-weapons use; Obama argued failure to respond risks escalation and proliferation. Senior US officials say they retain authority to act even without congressional approval, though Obama opted to consult lawmakers.

Reactions are mixed: Russia and Syria denounced US claims and warned against unilateral strikes; Britain’s parliament recently voted against military involvement, surprising Putin; France remains more supportive though public opinion is largely opposed. Syrian officials deny responsibility and blame jihadists; Syrian state media and leaders dismissed US threats and said the army is prepared. Domestic US opinion is divided, with some lawmakers and allies backing consultation and others opposing action; protests against intervention occurred in the US. Military assets in the region (US destroyers, carriers, regional airbases, and French naval assets) are positioned and available if strikes are ordered.

Former NFL receiver Chad Johnson (aka Chad Ochocinco) was sentenced to 30 days in jail after a Broward County judge revoked a no-jail plea deal for a probation violation in his domestic violence case. Johnson had reached an agreement with prosecutors for counseling, community service and an extra three months of probation for failing to meet with his probation officer in three months. During the hearing, when Judge Kathleen McHugh asked if he was satisfied with his attorney, Johnson reached back and lightly slapped his lawyer’s backside. The courtroom laughed; the judge said she found the gesture disrespectful, declared she would not accept the plea deal, and ordered Johnson arrested. Johnson apologized, saying he meant no disrespect and that his life was “in shambles,” but the judge—citing prior behavior in her courtroom—was unmoved. Johnson had been on probation after pleading no contest to head-butting then-wife Evelyn Lozada last year; he has been undergoing domestic-violence counseling and remains unsigned by an NFL team.

A man armed with a gun barricaded himself inside a Connect Wireless store in The Marketplace shopping center in La Crescenta on Black Friday after allegedly robbing the Rite Aid pharmacy and stealing prescription drugs. Deputies were called around 4:00 p.m.; crisis negotiators and the Sheriff’s Special Enforcement Bureau (SWAT) responded, evacuated and sheltered nearby businesses and closed Foothill Boulevard for the investigation. After an approximately five- to six-hour standoff, tactical teams entered the store and found the man deceased, apparently from a self-inflicted wound. No shots were fired by deputies and no civilians or officers were injured. The barricaded store is a third-party Verizon retailer. Streets and stores were reopened after the scene was secured.

Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen’s first post-FOMC press conference spooked markets after she described the committee’s phrase “a considerable period” — used to signal how long rates would stay near zero after QE ends — as “on the order of around six months.” With the Fed’s tapering likely to finish in October or November, investors interpreted that remark to mean the first rate hike could arrive as early as April–May 2015, sooner than many had expected, and stocks fell while bond yields rose.

Yellen emphasized qualifiers — the Fed will base any move on a broad range of labor-market and inflation indicators and pledged to keep policy data-dependent — but her offhand specificity overrode those caveats in market reaction. Commentators and economists called the comment a communication error or “gaffe,” noting that the Fed intentionally uses vague guidance to preserve discretion and avoid prematurely moving markets. The episode highlights the difficulty of forward guidance during policy normalization and the sensitivity of markets to even minor signals from the Fed, though analysts also stressed that Yellen’s overall stance remains cautious and focused on achieving employment and inflation objectives.

Police departments and fire officials are warning people not to sleep with or charge phones under pillows or on beds because restricted ventilation can cause devices and batteries to overheat and potentially ignite. The NYPD’s 33rd Precinct tweeted the safety reminder, and the warning was reinforced by a 2015 Hamden, Connecticut, incident in which a teenager’s phone caught fire, scorching a bed and pillow overnight. Fire chiefs advise charging devices on hard, ventilated surfaces, not blocking laptop vents, checking and discarding frayed cords, and unplugging unused chargers. The guidance is precautionary—not signaling a surge in such fires—but officials urge people to keep chargers in well‑ventilated areas and follow basic electrical-safety practices.

Summary:

- The writer supports PETA’s work overall but criticizes them for overreaching in a recent incident involving a letter sent to the founder of the National Buffalo.

- Separately, the Internet Archive is running crawls to preserve web pages as they are created and the pages those new pages reference. The intent is to capture the live versions so that when original pages change or disappear, archived copies remain available. The Archive hopes these archived links will replace or accompany broken links, thereby reducing 404 errors across the web — part of its "No More 404" effort.

A novel coronavirus now called Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS‑CoV) has spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula and is considered a global threat by the World Health Organization (WHO). As of the reports summarized here, about 53 confirmed infections have been identified worldwide (earlier updates cited 44), roughly half of which have been fatal (around 30 deaths). Cases have been reported in multiple countries, including Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, France, the UK, Germany and, for the first time, Italy (three cases: a 45‑year‑old man recently returned from Jordan and two close contacts, a 42‑year‑old woman and a 2‑year‑old girl— all in stable condition). A patient in France also recently died after contracting the virus during travel.

MERS‑CoV is a coronavirus distinct from SARS but similar in that it attacks the respiratory tract. Symptoms start like a severe cold (fever, cough) and can progress to pneumonia, kidney failure and gastrointestinal problems such as diarrhea. Many confirmed cases have occurred in older men with underlying conditions, but the total number infected is uncertain because mild cases may go undetected.

Key concerns cited by WHO director‑general Margaret Chan: the pathogen’s unknown animal reservoir, unclear transmission routes, and limited understanding of how infections spread—factors that hinder prevention and control. The WHO urges international collaboration, rapid investigation (including joint missions to affected countries), and pooling of resources to study and contain the virus.

Donald Trump launched a broad, public attack on the news media after a New York Times piece and other reports portrayed turmoil inside his campaign. In a series of tweets he called the press “disgusting,” “dishonest” and “corrupt,” accused outlets—especially the NYT—of fabricating anonymous sources and mischaracterizing his words, and claimed that if the media covered him fairly he would be “beating Hillary by 20%.” He repeatedly complained that rallies aren’t reported properly (crowd size, enthusiasm, message) and suggested punitive steps such as revoking reporters’ credentials.

The media criticism came amid coverage of several campaign controversies that dominated news cycles (including his remarks about the Second Amendment and false claims that President Obama “founded” ISIS) and reporting on troubles in his campaign hierarchy—most notably New York Times reporting about Paul Manafort’s past Ukraine ties. Trump allies, including campaign chair Paul Manafort and surrogates, framed media focus as responsible for a difficult week; former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski drew attention by sharing the NYT Manafort story. Democrats countered with policy-focused pushes (Clinton’s voter registration drive targeting young undocumented immigrants and Joe Biden campaigning with Clinton), and Republicans defended Trump’s forthcoming national-security policy plans and messaging.

WikiLeaks says it has found a new way to accept donations despite a payment blockade imposed by Visa, MasterCard and other firms after WikiLeaks began publishing U.S. State Department cables in late 2010. The group plans to route donations through France’s Fund for the Defense of Net Neutrality, using France’s Carte Bleue debit-card system, although the precise transaction mechanics and whether Visa or MasterCard will allow it remain unclear. Founder Julian Assange, holed up in the Ecuadorian Embassy in London and fighting extradition to Sweden, challenged Visa to try to block the move and said lawyers are ready.

The payment cutoff has sharply reduced WikiLeaks’ finances: reserves fell from €800,000 in December 2010 to under €100,000 by June 2012, with spending of €246,600 versus donations of €32,800 in the first half of 2012. WikiLeaks is suing Visa, MasterCard and European partners over the blockade (it recently won a case in Iceland against processor Valitor). Critics, including U.N. officials and Reporters Without Borders, have warned the blockade risks corporate censorship and free-expression harms; U.S. officials had argued the cable releases endangered diplomats and sources.

Six newlywed women from Khesiya village in Kushinagar district, Uttar Pradesh — from both Hindu and Muslim families — have returned to their parents’ homes within weeks of marriage in protest because their husbands’ households lack toilets. The women, named in reports as Neelam, Kalawati, Shakina (Sakina), Niranjan, Gudiya and Sita (and alternately Nazrum Nisa), said they will not go back until proper toilets are built, citing difficulties, safety risks and the indignity of open defecation—especially during rain and when purdah restricts their movement.

Sulabh International founder Bindeshwar Pathak has pledged to build toilets free of charge for the six households and to honour the women for their stand. Pathak and others noted the episode as evidence of changing attitudes among women toward sanitation. The piece also recalls a similar case in Maharajganj where a bride, Priyanka Bharti, was honoured, became a Sulabh motivator and featured in a sanitation ad.

The report places the local incidents in context: nearly half of India’s population lacks toilets at home, a serious rural problem that disproportionately affects women through health, privacy and safety harms. Citing World Bank and UN findings, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent call to eliminate open defecation and build separate girls’ toilets in schools, the article frames the brides’ protest as part of a wider national push to improve sanitation.

San Francisco City Attorney Dennis Herrera is seeking to stop Monster Beverage Corp. from marketing its highly caffeinated energy drinks to minors, and Monster has sued in federal court to block his probe. Filed in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles, Monster’s complaint argues Herrera’s investigation would burden interstate commerce and violate commercial-speech and other constitutional rights, and accuses him of acting for publicity rather than on science.

Herrera opened his unfair-competition investigation in October over Monster’s marketing claims that its caffeine levels are “completely safe” and that consumers “can never get too much of a good thing.” Herrera’s office produced promotional material showing apparent outreach to children (including listings on a “Monster Army” site identifying an 11‑year‑old and a 6‑year‑old). Herrera also joined 18 medical experts in March urging the FDA to regulate caffeine in energy drinks, citing higher caffeine concentrations in energy drinks (often 100–300 mg per 8-oz serving and sold in larger cans) and evidence linking such levels to health risks for children, adolescents and young adults.

Monster responded that its drinks have less than half the caffeine of a Starbucks brewed coffee and noted children can buy large coffee drinks without restriction. Herrera’s office countered that Starbucks does not market sweet, highly caffeinated drinks to youth and maintained the scientific consensus that these energy drinks are unsafe for children. Herrera pledged to vigorously litigate to curb what he calls irresponsible marketing that violates California consumer-protection laws.

Windows 8’s Consumer Preview marks a bold, risky reimagining of Microsoft’s flagship OS that clearly signals a shift toward mobile and touch-first computing. The new Metro interface—borrowed from Windows Phone—uses bright, information-rich “live tiles,” full-screen apps, edge gestures, and a central Windows Store for curated apps. On tablets and touchscreens Metro is fast, elegant and in many ways superior to existing tablet OSs: app switching via edge swipes is fluid, the ability to show one wide and one skinny app side-by-side is useful, and live tiles surface data without opening apps.

But Windows 8 is also schizophrenic: it must support both Metro and the traditional Desktop. Desktop apps still run in the familiar windowed environment, yet Metro is the new default Start experience. That duality creates friction. On large non-touch monitors Metro’s full-screen, limited multitasking can feel wasteful and awkward for typical desktop workflows; many UI decisions (corner behaviors, edge interactions, scrolling inconsistencies, and imprecise tile rearranging) are unintuitive for mouse-and-keyboard users and conflict with long-established habits. The Consumer Preview still has bugs and rough edges—some performance hiccups, missing Store support, and incomplete app features (sharing/contracts exist but few apps support them yet).

Reviewers’ impressions: on a tablet with touch Metro is delightful and versatile (it even works well with stylus input), and with time users can adapt and become productive; with mouse and keyboard the experience is more disorienting and will likely provoke resistance from many longtime Windows users. Overall, Windows 8 contains many smart design choices that modernize Windows and make it promising as a competitor in tablets, but its radical changes and split interfaces are risky and will need polish and broader app support before general release.

Researchers led by Anna-Leena Orsama analyzed daily, self-recorded morning weights from 80 adults (ages 25–62, BMI 20.0–33.5) over 15–330 days (4,657 total measurements) to characterize week-to-week weight rhythms and how they relate to long-term weight change. Using semi‑parametric regression and mixed models, they found a clear weekly pattern: body weight tends to rise over the weekend (peaking on Sunday or Monday) and decline during the workweek (lowest typically Friday). Weight increases begin on Saturday and decreases begin on Tuesday.

When participants were grouped by net change over the monitoring period (loss >3%, gain >1%, or maintain between −3% and 1%), the weekday–weekend rhythm was strongest and most regular among those who lost or maintained weight. Paradoxically, weight losers showed the largest within-week fluctuations—higher on weekends, lower by Fridays—suggesting they compensated for weekend indulgences during weekdays. Weight gainers showed weaker, less consistent weekly rhythms. The authors interpret this as evidence that small, predictable weekend splurges paired with weekday compensation (a flexible restraint approach) may support long-term adherence and weight control better than strict, all-or-nothing dieting.

Limitations include small subgroup sizes (especially gainers: n=10; losers: n=18), reliance on self-reported weights, and retrospective pooling of different studies. Practical takeaways: expect normal, modest weekend weight increases; if you weigh yourself regularly, compare the same day/time each week; and occasional weekend indulgences are unlikely to derail long-term progress if balanced by weekday behavior.

A 23-year-old Pensacola woman, Ashley Taylor Wright, was arrested July 17 after allegedly shoplifting $261 worth of clothing from Dillard’s at the Santa Rosa Mall and using her three-month-old infant as a human shield to avoid arrest. According to the Okaloosa County Sheriff’s Office, Wright concealed two pairs of jeans and a shirt in a stroller, then got into a parked Nissan Pathfinder. When a deputy approached, she refused orders to exit, held the baby carrier between herself and the deputy and shouted, “You will have to shoot through the baby to get me!” She then reportedly threw the 14‑pound carrier with the infant inside at the deputy and ran; the baby was not injured when the carrier hit the ground. Wright fell, hit her head, and struggled with deputies—spraying them with her blood—before being taken into custody. At the hospital she admitted drinking “a few beers” and acknowledged the theft, claiming it was to buy school clothes for her children despite the stolen items being adult clothing. She was booked on felony child abuse, petty theft, and resisting an officer, held on $7,000 bond.

Researchers studying the wreck of the Swedish warship Mars—one of Northern Europe’s largest 16th-century warships—have revealed new finds from the vessel that exploded and sank in the Baltic Sea in 1564 during the Northern Seven Years’ War. Discovered in 2011 near Öland and lying 70 meters deep, the wreck has yielded skeletal remains (including a femur with trauma suggesting sharp-weapon injury), large guns, a hand grenade, helmets, swords, silver treasure found earlier, and a unique large grapnel (grappling hook) previously known only from illustrations.

Contemporary accounts and the wreck’s condition confirm the ship was heavily engaged with Danish and Lübeckian forces before a catastrophic gunpowder explosion destroyed its bow and sank it. Between 800 and 1,000 people—comparable to a medium-sized town’s population—were aboard; many died either in the blast or as the ship went down. Evidence also shows some 300–400 captured Dano-Lübeckian soldiers were aboard when it exploded.

Archaeologists note the wreck documents a tactical shift in Swedish naval practice toward longer-range artillery (cannons up to 4.8 m) while still involving intense close-quarters combat; anti-boarding nets and descriptions of hand-to-hand fighting corroborate written sources. The site offers an exceptionally well-preserved “snapshot” of the battle and period, although researchers have been restricted to filming with divers and ROVs and creating 3D models—no artifacts have been removed, both to preserve fragile materials and because recovery would be difficult and costly. The exploration was led by MARIS at Södertörn University with several diving and museum partners.

An off-duty FBI agent, Chase Bishop, 29, has been booked into a Denver jail and charged with one count of second-degree assault after a gun he dropped at a Denver bar discharged and struck a patron. Video of the June 2–3 incident at Mile High Spirits shows Bishop doing a backflip/back handspring, the firearm falling from his holster, and firing as he bent to retrieve it. The victim, identified as Tom Reddington (or Thomas Reddington), suffered a nonlethal gunshot wound to the leg and may pursue legal action against the FBI. Bishop, based in the FBI’s Washington Field Office, turned himself in and was released to an FBI supervisor after initial processing. Denver prosecutors said they filed the charge now because there is sufficient evidence, but additional charges could follow pending blood-alcohol test results. The FBI is conducting an internal investigation that could lead to disciplinary action, including termination, suspension, or reprimand.

In June–July 2017 the Internet Archive crawled the Luxembourg .lu domain on behalf of the National Library of Luxembourg; this document also includes a news feature captured in that crawl about a long-term homeless man in Detroit.

Key points from the Detroit report:
- A man who goes by "Honest Abe" (real name Abe Hagenston) panhandles near the I-75/8 Mile overpass in Detroit and accepts credit- and debit-card donations by using a Square card reader attached to his cellphone.
- Abe has been homeless in Detroit for about seven to ten years and sleeps under the 8 Mile overpass; he and other homeless people coordinate panhandling in shifts and have put up a website to solicit donations, hire out the homeless for odd jobs, and report fraudulent panhandlers.
- Abe says the card reader makes it easier for donors who lack cash; Square charges a small transaction fee and the reader is inexpensive.
- He cited needs such as new prescription eyeglasses and described the difficulty of rebuilding life without family or friends.
- The report was produced amid a volunteer street-by-street count of homeless people in Detroit and nationally. About 100 Occupy Philadelphia protesters remained on Dilworth Plaza at City Hall after a 5 p.m. Sunday deadline set by Mayor Michael Nutter passed, but no eviction occurred that night. Police and city officials declined to say when or whether they would remove the encampment; city spokesmen urged protesters to leave but emphasized they were not planning an immediate sweep. Chief Inspector Joseph Sullivan praised the largely nonviolent behavior of the demonstrators, while warning that new camps would require permits because the city must fence the plaza for ongoing renovations (SEPTA-tunnel work, new grass, café, stage and ice rink). Protesters — many homeless — fed each other, chanted, and slowly began taking down tents; by early evening about a third of roughly 300 tents had been removed. Occupiers and supporters criticized the city for not helping them find an alternate site and pleaded for a nonviolent response.

In Los Angeles, police repeatedly warned Occupy L.A. campers to clear the lawn at City Hall before a midnight deadline; officers closed nearby streets and declared an unlawful assembly early Monday but stopped short of a full clearing of the park. A pre-dawn confrontation briefly reopened rush-hour streets and led to four arrests for unlawful assembly after protesters briefly occupied an intersection and some debris was thrown at police. Hundreds to thousands of supporters had swelled the crowd overnight; commanders ultimately allowed the encampment to remain into daylight and said a complete eviction was unlikely that day. Occupy L.A. organizers later sought a federal injunction to block a forced dismantling, while city officials urged protesters to shift tactics and locations rather than hold the park. Both cities’ responses were noted for relative restraint compared with harsher clearances elsewhere.

The 70th Cannes Film Festival concluded with Ruben Östlund’s satire The Square winning the Palme d’Or. The film, about a museum installation called “The Square” and the chaos that follows, stars Claes Bang and Elisabeth Moss and earned praise from jury president Pedro Almodóvar for its wit and topicality.

Sofia Coppola made history as only the second woman to win Best Director (the first since 1961) for The Beguiled, her female-centered remake starring Nicole Kidman, Kirsten Dunst, Elle Fanning and Colin Farrell. Coppola was not present; Maren Ade accepted on her behalf. Kidman also received a special prize honoring Cannes’s 70th anniversary.

Other major awards:
- Grand Prix: 120 Beats Per Minute (Robin Campillo), a drama about ACT UP–Paris and the 1990s AIDS struggle.
- Jury Prize: Loveless (Andrey Zvyagintsev), about a couple whose child goes missing.
- Best Actor: Joaquin Phoenix for You Were Never Really Here.
- Best Actress: Diane Kruger for In the Fade, who dedicated her award to victims of terrorism.
- Best Screenplay (tie): Yorgos Lanthimos & Efthymis Filippou for The Killing of a Sacred Deer and Lynne Ramsay for You Were Never Really Here.
- Short Film Palme d’Or: A Gentle Night (Qiu Yang).
- Camera d’Or (best first film): Jeune Femme (Leonor Serraille).

The 19-film competition jury was led by Almodóvar and included members such as Will Smith, Jessica Chastain, and Park Chan-wook. The festival also saw controversy over Netflix entries (Okja, The Meyerowitz Stories); Almodóvar’s stance and industry protests contributed to Cannes deciding to bar streaming-only films from future competitions.

A federal criminal investigation has been opened into the July 19 sinking of a Ripley Entertainment “Ride the Ducks” vehicle (Stretch Duck 07) on Table Rock Lake near Branson, Missouri, which killed 17 of 31 people aboard. The U.S. Coast Guard referred the matter to the U.S. Attorney’s Office after concluding that the deaths “resulted from the misconduct, negligence, or inattention to the duties” of the vessel’s captain. Federal court filings identify the sunken boat’s captain, Kenneth Scott McKee, and the captain of a second duck boat on the lake that night, Barry King (Stretch Duck 54), as “targets” of the probe; Ripley Entertainment and several of its agents, employees or officers are also named as targets or subjects.

Separately, the National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the cause of the sinking and Missouri’s attorney general has opened a criminal inquiry examining possible violations of state law, while multiple civil lawsuits have been filed by survivors and relatives of the deceased. The Coast Guard’s preliminary findings noted that official operating limits for Stretch Duck 07 prohibited water operations when winds exceeded 35 mph or waves exceeded two feet; on July 19 warned storms produced winds up to 73 mph and waves over 3 feet. Video showed both duck boats struggling in the storm; Duck 54 reached shore, Duck 07 sank. Court filings request that federal investigators be allowed to question key witnesses before civil discovery proceeds, arguing civil actions could interfere with the criminal probe. Ripley says it is cooperating with federal, state and NTSB investigations. Federal law cited in the filings makes criminal penalties possible for vessel operators whose negligence or misconduct leads to loss of life.

A holiday potluck invitation sent accidentally to roughly 25,000 Utah state email addresses on Friday touched off a massive “reply-all” cascade. The erroneous invite—reportedly from the Department of Corrections—prompted thousands of responses within minutes: pleas and demands to stop replying to all, requests to be removed, jokes, and complaints that flooded employees’ inboxes and phones. State public information officers and Lt. Gov. Spencer Cox posted about the incident on Twitter; a state spokesperson shared screenshots showing dozens of quick-fire replies. The surge subsided by midmorning, and officials did not publicly identify the original sender or their department. The event echoed past large-scale reply-all fiascos and renewed reminders to use BCC or send large-group messages differently to avoid similar broadcast storms.
